**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, ENTIRE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, COMPARED WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND MOST CAREFULLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED BY DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE COMPLETION OF THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS PRODUCED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING THE INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ORNAMENTED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS WELL AS WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT TREATED; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH YET POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO COPIOUS GENERAL INDEXES: namely, one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each text of each book of Scripture, and in what places in their works. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one weighs the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the course of the work, the low price, and, above all, this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time assembled in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been issued in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The two hundred and sixty volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 800 francs.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

**INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF**

Continuation of the Registers. | Col. 9 |

**[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF INNOCENT III.]**

[Col. 0009]

**THE REGISTERS, OR LETTERS, OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF**

**BOOK SIX: THE SIXTH YEAR OF THE PONTIFICATE, A.D. 1203**

**I.** [Note: [Col. 0009C] Noted by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19. See also book V, letter 78.] **TO JOHN, PRIOR, AND THE BRETHREN OBSERVING THE REGULAR LIFE NEAR THE CAVE OF SAINT BENEDICT.** He grants them six pounds of currency from the annual rent of the castle of Porciano. (Lateran, 24 February.)

[Col. 0009A]

Among the burnt offerings of virtues, none is richer in marrow than that offered to the Most High from the fatness of charity. Considering this, when formerly, out of devotion, we visited the place of your solitude, which Saint Benedict consecrated at the beginning of his conversion, and found you there commendably serving the Lord according to his institution, we judged that apostolic assistance should be supplied to you, lest through a lack of temporal support the discipline of spiritual observance should grow slack. [Col. 0009B] We hope that this most blessed Benedict himself will commend the affection of our devotion, by his merits and prayers, to the most merciful Father and most just Judge.

Therefore, desiring to provide for your needs, we granted to you and your successors six pounds of current money, to be received annually from the Treasury of Saint Peter, until they should be usefully assigned to you in some fixed place; ordaining that, for this reason, what you had customarily received for your maintenance from the monastery of Subiaco should by no means be denied to you and your successors. Afterwards, when we had returned to the City, you sent certain of your brethren into our presence, humbly imploring us [Col. 0009C] to establish that grant permanently in some fixed place from which you might receive the aforesaid six pounds. Therefore, having taken the counsel and assent of our brethren, we grant to you and your successors the said six pounds, to be received every year from the annual rent of the castle of Porciano, [Col. 0010A] and confirm this grant by the present privilege.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our grant and ordinance, or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should do so, etc., down to “he shall incur.” Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, bishop-elect of Torres, on 24 February, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

**II.** [Note: [Col. 0009C] This letter is not found among the *Decretals*, but should be compared with two other letters of Innocent in the collection of *Decretals*, book IV, title 13, “On him who has known the kinswoman of his wife or betrothed,” addressed respectively in chapter 6 to the Archbishop of Magdeburg and in chapter 10 to the Archbishop of Esztergom. In those letters the same decree as in ours is issued, explained in exactly the same words.] **TO THE PRIOR OF OSENE.** On the salutary penance to be imposed upon a man who committed incest and adultery together. (Lateran, 24 February.)

[Col. 0010B]

In your letters you informed us that W., the bearer of the present letter, after contracting marriage with a certain woman, committed both incest and adultery with her sister; for three years he lay foul in this filth, and he begot two children by the aforesaid adulteress. Through this crime the matter became known to his neighbours. But the same W., appearing before our penitentiary, pleaded extreme poverty, asserting that he could not visit the province of Jerusalem. Since you are better able fully to ascertain his means, we have judged that he should be sent back to you, commanding by apostolic letters that you impose upon him such penance as you deem appropriate.

Moreover, because you asked how he should henceforth conduct himself [Col. 0010C] with his wife, we briefly answer your inquiry: [that [Note: [Col. 0010C] *Decretals*, cited place, chapter 10.] she should be most carefully admonished to abstain altogether from intercourse with him for the sake of public decency, and to remain continent until her husband has entered upon the way of all flesh. But if, perhaps, refusing to obey the admonition, she should be such a woman that there is reason to fear her fall, her husband may and indeed ought nevertheless, in the fear of God, to render her the marital debt, since affinity contracted after an unlawful marriage ought not to harm a woman who was not a participant in the wrongdoing.] Therefore, [by right [Note: [Col. 0011D] *Decretals*, cited place, chapter 6.] she ought not to be deprived of her right without fault on her part, although one of our predecessors [Note: [Col. 0011D] Namely Alexander; but that decretal was removed from the Gregorian compilation.] is said in a similar case to have drawn a distinction according as the adultery or the incest was public or secret, while others assert that a distinction should rather be drawn between a near and a remote degree.]

Given at the Lateran, 24 February, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

**III.** [Note: [Col. 0011D] Cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §67.] **TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT LUPUS OF TROYES** [Note: [Col. 0011D] The monastery of Saint Lupus of Troyes was then governed by Drogo, who is known from documents from about 1194 until 1206. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 588.] **AND HIS BRETHREN.** He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter and confirms their rights and privileges. (Lateran, 20 February.)

[Col. 0011B]

The fervour of religion and order which you maintain, and the fragrant reputation of your uprightness, induce us mercifully to assent to your just petitions and, God willing, to bring them to a useful effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; we receive the aforesaid church of Saint Lupus, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the safeguard of the present writing. First, indeed, we ordain that [Col. 0011C] the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of Saint Augustine shall there be observed inviolably for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named: the site itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the mills at the Bridge of Blessed Mary; and whatever you possess in that town from the gift of Charles the Bald, the illustrious king of the Franks, [Col. 0011D] both in persons and in lands; the vineyard beyond Saint Martin of Areis, called the Enclosure (*Clausum*); the vineyard called Haste, situated on the opposite side; the Treasury Vineyard; the vineyard called Laboras; the estate of Lusiniacum, with its parish, oven, mills, lands, meadows, and other possessions; the estate of Molins, with its church, tithes, land-rents, and other customary dues, together with jurisdiction, provision, and guardianship, which the beloved son, the noble Walter, Count of Brienne, bestowed upon your church as a perpetual alms, as is contained in his authenticated instruments, those of J . . ., his brother, of our venerable brother G . . . [Note: [Col. 0012D] Concerning him, see above.] bishop, and of J . . ., of good memory, Count of Troyes; [Col. 0012A] the parish of Lueriis, with the chapel of Fontibus, bestowed upon you by the said bishop out of charity; the land-rent and customary dues which you possess, both in persons and in lands, in that same estate; also the franchise of the mayoralty of that town, granted to your church by H . . ., Count of Troyes of illustrious memory, as is contained in his instrument; the revenues which you possess at Selerias, Arbrosellum, Curterangia, Tenelerias, Ruliacum, and Bairum, in persons, lands, and other customary dues; the church of Buceium, with [Col. 0012B] the chapel of Chart, and the church of Laneis, which M., Bishop of Troyes of pious memory, assigned to your church as an alms; the altar of Saint Vinebald; the land-rents and tithes which you possess in the Riveria of Arduceon, with the customary dues, rents, and serf-services of your people of that Riveria; the land-rents of Ouciacum and Marigniacum; the church of Marigniacum, as bounded from ancient times, with the alms which G., formerly lord of Triangulum, granted there to your church by pious generosity, as is contained in his authenticated instruments; possessions at Marigniacum granted to you by the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem; the churches of Lonsoldo and Ausona, with their tithes and other appurtenances; [Col. 0012C] the liberty of your house at Ausona and of all that belongs to you in that town, charitably granted to your church by G . . . ., formerly Count of Brienne; the grange of Bretoneria, with all its appurtenances, in waters, lands, meadows, and woodland; the freedom of the mayor and sub-mayor, and of the two matricularii, the granary-keeper and the cellarer, whom you have in the city of Troyes; the prebend of Saint Stephen of Troyes; the twenty shillings which you have in the church of Troyes on the four annual feasts; the houses and vineyards which Godfrey of Hesternai assigned to your church as a perpetual alms; the land-rent of Chamaio, with the freedom of its mayor and of his holding; the water assigned to you as an alms by Clarino of Chauderiacum; and what you hold by exchange from R., lord of Pogiacum, both at Troyes and at Molins, in persons or lands.

You may indeed receive into conversion clergy or laity who are free and fleeing the world, and retain them without any opposition. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave it without permission of his abbot. But one who departs, etc., down to “retain.” When a general interdict [Col. 0013A] has been imposed upon the land, you may, with closed doors and the excommunicated and interdicted excluded, etc., down to “celebrate.” We forbid any bishop or other prelate, without manifest and reasonable cause, to presume to excommunicate your members or subject your churches to an interdict.

Further, he who is to be placed over the church of Blessed Martin of Troyes shall by no means be chosen from elsewhere, but only from the church of Blessed Lupus of Troyes or that of Saint Martin, as has hitherto been observed and granted by our predecessors, provided that a person fit to govern as abbot can be found in one or the other. If he should, God forbid, fall away from the integrity of his state and the vigour of religion, he shall be restored to his former uprightness and religious life through the discipline and order of the church of Blessed Lupus. In order, moreover, that [Col. 0013B] the integrity of religious life may be preserved in the church of Blessed Lupus in times to come, we grant the abbot and his successors free authority, according to the order of their received profession, to correct the canons of that church and to judge them regularly, whether they belong to the head or the members of the aforesaid church, according to the character of their deserts; nor shall an appeal lodged in order to evade ecclesiastical discipline be any obstacle.

Moreover, we hold valid the liberties and immunities anciently granted to your church, its reasonable customs hitherto observed, and the privileges and indulgences granted you by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. Furthermore, we decree that burial in that place shall be free, etc., down to “shall hinder”; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are reserved. Therefore we decree, etc., down to “be beneficial,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore . . . . But to all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, bishop-elect of Torres, on 20 February, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

**IV.** [Note: [Col. 0013] See Raynaldus under the year 1203, §19, although he does not venture to assign this letter a separate number.] **TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF HUNGARY.** Since King Henry is about to go to the holy war, they are to ensure that the peoples render fidelity to his son Ladislaus. (Lateran, 25 February.)

[Col. 0013D]

Behold, our dearest son in Christ, H., the illustrious King of Hungary, having taken up the cross, proposes to follow Christ. He abandons a temporal kingdom that he may acquire an eternal one; he leaves his own possessions in order to drive Pharaoh out from the Lord’s inheritance and freely display the rod of that inheritance and its signs to those who declare that there is no prophet to know them further. Already he has raised his hand against their pride, so that those who hated Christ may no longer boast, but may rather learn that it is hard to kick against the goad [Col. 0014A] or for a human being to fight against God.

Therefore, in the absence of so great a prince, who journeys away from his kingdom in order to lead pilgrims into their homeland, let pontifical authority be so armed for the guardianship and defence of the kingdom that his realm cannot be transferred to enemies but is rather preserved for him. By apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood that, before the king himself undertakes the journey of pilgrimage, since, according to the Apostle’s teaching, honour is due from all to the king as supreme, you ensure that all persons, clerics and laymen alike, render the due oath of fidelity to Ladislaus, his son, whom the Lord through His grace has granted him as heir. After the departure of the aforesaid king, restrain by sentence of excommunication—setting aside every excuse and appeal—all who presume to act against the oath of fidelity which they have rendered. [Col. 0014B] You are likewise to ensure that due reverence is rendered, according to the king’s own disposition, to those whom he entrusts both with the care of his son—whom, the Lord consenting, we expect and desire to be heir and successor to his father in the kingdom—and with the administration of the realm. Should it happen, which may Christ avert, that the king himself pays the debt of human mortality during his pilgrimage, none of you shall withdraw from their direction until his beloved son reaches an age at which he can sit with power upon the throne of his kingdom and govern it happily.

[Col. 0014C] Given at the Lateran, 25 February, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

**V. TO THE BISHOP OF OURENSE.** He approves an agreement concluded between that bishop and the Archbishop of Compostela. (Lateran, 15 February.)

It belongs to us, by the office of administration laid upon us, to impose an end upon quarrels and disputes; therefore provision must be made lest controversies between persons possessing rank, which have been calmed by friendly settlement, be revived, and lest they again gird themselves for litigation concerning matters over which they have reached amicable agreement.

Now, when a dispute had arisen between you and our venerable brother . . . ., Archbishop of Compostela, [Col. 0014D] concerning the *votis* [so printed; perhaps “rights”] of the bishopric of Ourense, you finally endeavoured to make an amicable settlement concerning these matters, as we have clearly learned from your authenticated letters and those of the same archbishop. Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority that settlement, since it was prudently made without impropriety, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and hitherto observed; and we fortify it by the safeguard of the present writing. Let no one therefore . . . infringe this page of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 15 February.

**VI. TO THE SAME.** He confirms the judgment delivered by apostolic delegates concerning the dispute between the monastery of Cella Nova and the Bishop of Oviedo. (Lateran, 14 February.)

[Col. 0015A]

We have recently learned from letters of our venerable brother . . . ., Bishop of Astorga, and of our beloved sons, the abbots of Saint Isidore of León and . . . . of Carraceto, that, when we had entrusted to them for due determination the case pending between you on the one hand and our venerable brother . . . . ., Bishop of Oviedo, on the other, concerning the monastery of Cella Nova, they proceeded according to the apostolic mandate. They summoned the parties before them and, after fully hearing and considering the arguments advanced on both sides, [Col. 0015B] pronounced judgment for the church of Ourense, imposing perpetual silence upon the Bishop of Oviedo in this matter.

Moreover, our venerable brother . . . ., Bishop of Oviedo, voluntarily surrendered, by the common consent of his chapter, every right which belonged to his church, if it possessed any, in the said monastery or in any part of the bishopric of Ourense, as was contained in authenticated letters of the said judges and also in his own letters presented to us. By his letters he rendered the community of that monastery wholly free from his obedience and jurisdiction. Therefore, desiring that what has been prudently done by these judges should obtain its due force, we regard as valid and confirm by apostolic authority both that judgment—being just and neither suspended by a lawful appeal—and the lawful cession made by the Bishop of Oviedo [Col. 0015C] with the common consent of his chapter; and we fortify them by the safeguard of the present writing. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever . . . infringe this page of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

**VII. TO H., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE HUNGARIANS.** Those promoted to provostships immediately subject in spiritual matters to the Apostolic See are to appear before the Apostolic See within a year. (Lateran, 28 February.)

The royal magnificence recently asked us in its letters to decree that, because the royal provostships which are in Hungary belong immediately to you in temporal affairs and immediately to us [Col. 0015D] in spiritual affairs, a new provost should come to the Apostolic See within a year, either personally or through a suitable messenger bearing letters of royal assent, in order to display the favour of the person conferring the office.

Therefore, inclining to your requests, especially since they accord with canonical institutions, by the authority of the present letter we decree that all who are henceforth called to govern those provostships which immediately belong to us in spiritual matters shall appear before the Apostolic See within a year, personally or through suitable messengers bearing letters of royal assent, [Col. 0016A] in order to obtain the benefit of confirmation. Meanwhile they shall not minister in spiritual matters. If they neglect to come within the aforesaid term, they are to know that from then on they will be deprived of those provostships. Let no one therefore . . . infringe this page of our ordinance, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 28 February, in the sixth year.

**VIII.** [Note: [Col. 0015D] Raynaldus mentions this under the year 1203, §19.] **TO THE KING OF HUNGARY.** To the King of Hungary, who is about to take the cross, he promises that he will take care that scandals and disputes do not arise in the king’s absence. (Lateran, 28 February.)

Since among the most Christian kings and Catholic princes we embrace your person in the Lord with a special prerogative of affection, we willingly hear your prayers and requests in matters in which we are able to do so, [Col. 0016B] and gladly attend to what we know pleases your royal serenity.

It was proposed to us on behalf of your greatness that, since you have taken the cross for the aid of the Holy Land and have proposed to render to the Lord what you vowed, we should enjoin our venerable brethren, the Archbishops of Esztergom and Kalocsa, not to initiate in your absence, on account of their churches, any disputes by which dissensions and scandals might arise in the kingdom; and that we ourselves should not undertake, until your return, to hear or commission the cases already arisen. Although we desire to grant your petitions, as far as we can with God, both assent and favour, yet, since according to the Apostle we are debtors to the wise and the foolish, especially in matters of justice, [Col. 0016C] we answer your request as follows: we shall take such care to apply discretion and caution in these matters that, if any disputes arise among ecclesiastical persons of your kingdom, we shall proceed, God being the author, in such a way that the kingdom itself will have no cause to fear scandal on account of our proceedings. For we are prepared with ready will to provide whatever counsel and aid we can honourably offer for preserving it peacefully in fidelity to you.

Given at the Lateran, 28 February.

**IX. TO THE BISHOPS OF CHÂLON AND SENLIS, AND THE ABBOT OF TROIS-FONTAINES** [Note: [Col. 0015D] These have already been mentioned above.] **He entrusts to them the examination of the case concerning the election of Philip, Bishop of Beauvais, as Archbishop of Reims** [Note: [Col. 0015D] On the subject of this letter, consult Marlot and the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*; but the letter itself was wholly unknown to them.] **(Lateran, 25 February).**

[Col. 0016D]

Certain beloved sons—the dean [Note: [Col. 0016D] This man too has already been mentioned above.] and several other canons of Reims—having come to the Apostolic See, humbly presented to us letters from the suffragans of the church of Reims, the cathedral chapters, certain archbishops, abbots, and other religious men. In these letters they earnestly implored us mercifully to admit the postulation which they had made [Col. 0017A] for transferring our venerable brother Philip, Bishop of Beauvais, to the metropolitan see of Reims, because of the evident benefit and urgent need of that church. They showed, by the decree of postulation confirmed by the subscriptions of the canons, that two-thirds of the canons in number, three parts in dignity, and far more in rank, had agreed to consent to this postulation.

Our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious King of the Franks, sought the same thing out of great devotion, through his beloved son F. [Note: [Col. 0017D] Fulk I, concerning whom elsewhere as well.], Dean of Orléans, whom he had specially sent for this purpose to the Roman Church with his own letters and those of many nobles. Afterwards the beloved son T. [Note: [Col. 0017D] Thomas of Pertico, according to the cited authorities.], Archdeacon of Reims, arrived with certain canons of that church, maintaining that this postulation ought not to be accepted because it had been celebrated after lawful appeals had been lodged before us. When they had disputed for some time before us and our brethren concerning the legal force of the appeals, we, after hearing what had been advanced on both sides, declared in an interlocutory judgment that the office of postulation ought not to be impeded by the objection of that appeal, since the causes for which appeal had been made were shown false by the oaths produced.

But the same archdeacon subsequently raised certain objections both to the act and to the person, and wished to raise others. Since he could not then prove them before us, it became necessary to entrust the inquiry and decision of the matter. Therefore, commanding by apostolic letters, we enjoin your discretion diligently and effectively to induce the parties to peace. If, however, which God forbid, this cannot be achieved within eight days, then meet in a common place so that the right of each party may in every respect be preserved; hear what they consider should be proposed on each side; and, after prudent examination, unless the opposing side can sufficiently establish some canonical reason why this postulation ought not to be admitted, rely upon our authority, set aside every contradiction and appeal, approve the postulation, [Col. 0017D] transfer the aforesaid bishop to the metropolitan see of Reims, procure that due reverence and obedience be rendered to him, and restrain any opponents by ecclesiastical compulsion, setting appeal aside.

Otherwise, notwithstanding the aforesaid postulation, we wish that church to be provided with a suitable person according to canonical form. If either party, lawfully cited, does not appear, you shall nevertheless proceed according to the prescribed form, taking diligent care that the apostolic mandate is not prolonged beyond the coming feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul. If not all of you can or are willing to take part, [Col. 0018A] two of you shall nevertheless execute these instructions; provided that, if you do not agree upon one judgment, or the parties do not consent to your delivering a judgment, you shall remit the matter, adequately prepared, to the Apostolic See, fixing for the parties a suitable term within which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment. Should one of them perhaps fail to come, we shall nevertheless proceed as justice requires.

Given at the Lateran, 25 February, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

**X.** [Note: [Col. 0018D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1203, §67.] **TO ADELFONSO, BISHOP OF OURENSE, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY.** He is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. Privileges and possessions are confirmed. (Lateran, 25 February.)

[Col. 0018B]

Since we are debtors, by reason of the ministry we have undertaken, to ecclesiastical men—indeed, to all Christ’s faithful—we both wish and ought to assist our brothers and fellow bishops with proportionately greater readiness, insofar as they hold a more worthy place in the Church and more is accomplished for the salvation and advancement of clergy and people through their ministry. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously assent to your petitions; and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Popes Lucius and Urban, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Auriense, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: the very place in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the whole of Limium, otherwise called Palla Aurea; the churches of Penna Cornuria; the churches of Orzelon; the churches of Cusanc.; the castle of Buvalum, Caldelas, Intertisam, and the other churches which lie beneath the castle of Portello on this side of the river Tueha; Lumba, Baruncelo, Soutouerimni; the monastery of Cella Nova, adjudged to the Church of Auriense by judges delegated by us; the abbey on Mount Rama; the abbey of Saint Stephen on the bank of the Sili; the abbey of Saint Christina; the abbey of Saint Claudius; the abbey of Bouada; the monastery of Juncaria; the priory of Saint Martin of Grou; the priory of Juncaria; the priory of Saint Peter of Rocas; the priory of Saint Columba; the monastery of Ramirans; the monastery of Arnoia; the church of Villaruvin, with the whole village; the churches of Armentar. Jougues; the church of Masidi; the church of Eires; the monastery of Servaei, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Monte; the church of Saint James of Aleris; [Col. 0019A] the church of Saint Stephen in the same village; the church of Saint Marina of Frigidofonte; Rivus Calidus, with its appurtenances; Lovios; the estates of Saint Mary of Palo; Pereiram Malam, Parietes Rubeos, the monastery of Saint Mary of Palo, Goestei, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Nicholas of Portus Auriensis, with its estates; Canedo; Nugaria; Mauriscum; Nidum Aquilae; Padernum; the churches of Saint George and Saint Leocada, with their estates; the church of Saint Peter of Meschita, with its appurtenances; the entire estate of Cantor Avia; the castle of Araugis, with all its jurisdiction, just as King Ferdinand gave it to you and your successors as a perpetual alms; the other half of Rivus Calidus, as the same king granted it to the Church of Auriense; [Col. 0019B] all the old and new Cantum, and all other estates which that church is known justly to possess.

Moreover, wishing to provide for the preservation from loss of the church entrusted to you, by apostolic authority we forbid monks, regular canons, Hospitallers, Templars, brothers of the Militia of Blessed James, brothers of the Lord’s Sepulchre, or any other religious persons, without consulting you or your successors and despite your objection, to presume to claim churches within your bishopric or tithes, either by their own authority or through a lay grant. If they do so, their act shall have no validity, but such churches or tithes shall return without any contradiction to your power and disposition, unless they can protect themselves by lawful prescription or some other reasonable cause.

We further forbid them to admit to divine offices or to burial persons excommunicated or placed under interdict by you—saving the indulgence granted to certain religious persons to open churches once a year and celebrate divine services, excluding excommunicated persons, when the land is under a general interdict. If, however, any parishioners of your church choose to be buried among them, we command that canonical justice be preserved for the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, etc., up to “be to its advantage,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore … but to all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Blasius, elected Archbishop of Torres, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent [Col. 0019D] Pope III.

## XI. … BISHOP [Note: See above, book V, epistle 14, note], AND THE CHAPTER OF HILDESHEIM

He admonishes and commands them to receive the deacon Herman as a canon. (Lateran, sixth day before the Kalends of March.)

Since you have sometimes found us favorable and gracious, we believed that we should find you devout in granting our requests and humbly rendering us the obedience due; and that, when we ask, you would not await the compulsion of an apostolic command, so that you might rather be commended for obedience promptly rendered to us than reproved for rebellion and hardness.

[Col. 0020A] For we recall that we sent apostolic petitions to you on behalf of our beloved son Herman, deacon, asking that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you receive him as canon and brother; and afterwards we reinforced the request by entreaty and command. Yet it is known that neither command nor request prevailed with you, as the repeated efforts of the same deacon show. Therefore, lest we leave in any respect incomplete what we are known to have undertaken concerning that deacon for God and on account of God, we again carefully admonish and exhort your devotion; by these apostolic letters, commanding you that you delay no longer in receiving the said deacon, in view of divine mercy and at our request, as canon and brother, and in conferring upon him without any difficulty the prebend which C., bishop of Würzburg [Note: See also above, book V, epistle 99, note], of good memory, chancellor of the imperial court, held in your church, since it is said to be vacant.

Otherwise, know that we have instructed our beloved sons …, abbot of the Valley of Saint George …, provost of Saint Severus, and …, dean of Saint Mary at Erfurt, in the diocese of Mainz, that, if you fail to execute our mandate, they, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any objection or appeal, shall confer and assign that prebend to the same deacon if they find it vacant, or another presently vacant prebend; and shall compel you by ecclesiastical censure to receive him as canon and brother and assign him a place in chapter and a stall in choir.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth year.

[Col. 0020C] A letter concerning this matter was written to them.

## XII. TO MAXIMUS, CLERIC

He permits him to receive something from the revenues of the church of Saint Michael of Oliveto. (Lateran, fifth day before the Kalends of March.)

We recall that apostolic letters were sent to our beloved sons R. …, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter …, and the abbot and convent of Cassino, that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, they should confer upon you the church of Saint Michael of Oliveto. Yet the same convent, both by its own letters and through monks sent to our presence, steadfastly asserted that the aforesaid abbot, with the common counsel of the brothers, had irrevocably assigned that church for the use of the sick; they humbly requested that it not be withdrawn from their use, since without its revenues they could not provide necessities for the sick brothers. The abbot, however, informed us by his letters that, unwilling to incur our displeasure, he was prepared to obey our commands.

Therefore, lest what the Apostolic See determined to undertake in your behalf remain wholly unfinished, and lest what had been assigned for the needs of the sick by prudent deliberation and common counsel of the brethren be improvidently revoked, we have judged that paternal solicitude should make the following provision both for you and for that convent: that every year, [Col. 0021A] on the feast of Saint Michael in September, the aforesaid abbot and convent shall undertake to provide you with twelve ounces of gold from the revenues of that church, until they have provided for you in a greater or equivalent ecclesiastical benefice. As evidence of this provision, we have caused these present letters to be granted to you as testimony. Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our provision.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

## XIII. TO THE BISHOP OF MODENA

[Note: Ughellus identifies the bishop of Modena at that time as Aegidius, whom he states was elected in 1195. The same man was later transferred in 1206 to the metropolitan see of Ravenna. Paschalinus states that he was a Bolognese of the Garzoni family. *Italia sacra*, vol. II, col. 150. Innocent wrote to him frequently.]

He commands that the people of Cremona, because of the estates of Guastalla and Luciaria, concerning which they had brought suit against the monastery of Saint Sixtus at Cremona, be publicly denounced as excommunicate; that the city of Cremona be subjected to ecclesiastical interdict; and that contumacious priests be removed from offices and benefices. (Lateran, second day before the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0021B]

Your brotherhood is not unaware how proceedings have taken place in the case between the monastery of Saint Sixtus and the people of Cremona concerning the estates of Guastalla and Luciaria, which was delegated to you by the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, the people of Cremona persist in their contumacy, despising the sentences of excommunication pronounced against the podestà, consuls, and councillors, and of interdict against the city, we command and order your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, you publicly and solemnly [Col. 0021C] announce the aforesaid podestà, consuls, and councillors to be excommunicate until worthy satisfaction has been made; and that you order all neighboring persons strictly to avoid them, both in commerce and in other dealings. Under threat of anathema, forbid any city to appoint any of the aforesaid excommunicated persons as podestà, or to dare retain one already appointed; and announce that the city of Cremona is subject to interdict.

Further, because John, priest in the greater church …; likewise the provost of Saint Lucy …, the priests of Saint Apollinaris …, Saint Michael …, Saint Paul, and … Saint Saviour, after the sentence of interdict, publicly presumed to celebrate divine services in their churches, we will and command you under the same strictness that, if the matter is as stated, you do not delay, notwithstanding the obstacle of appeal, to suspend them, as well as the archpriest and … archdeacon of Cremona, who are said to have given authority to this rashness, [Col. 0021D] from every office and benefice; and compel them by ecclesiastical censure, while suspended, to come before us with your letters containing the course of events.

Moreover, lest the right of the aforesaid monastery perish through lack of witnesses, we will and command that you receive, all occasion, appeal, and excuse being set aside, the aged and infirm witnesses whom the beloved son … abbot of Saint Sixtus shall think fit to produce; that you do not delay to have their depositions put in writing by a public hand; and that, if out of favor, hatred, or fear they withdraw themselves, you compel them by ecclesiastical censure, appeal removed, to bear testimony to the truth.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of March.

## XIV. TO THE COUNTESS OF VERMANDOIS

He graciously requests from her, as one who held the right of patronage, one prebend that is presently vacant or first becomes vacant, acknowledging that this is a favor, although she may dispose of it by her own authority. (Lateran.)

Just as you believe and hope that your requests will find paternal favor with us, so we believe and hope, not without reason, that ours will find filial devotion with you. We therefore ask, carefully admonish, and exhort your nobility, commanding you by apostolic letters, that you cause a prebend, if one is presently vacant or first becomes vacant, to be reserved for our grant in the church of Saint Quentin, in which you are known to possess the right of patronage, so that it may be conferred upon a suitable person native to your territory.

Although by the fullness of power which the Lord granted us in blessed Peter we could do this ourselves, nevertheless, wishing to show deference to your nobility, we preferred to obtain by request from you what we intend rather than now carry it out by apostolic power. May you be willing to grant this first request of ours, so that we may not find refusal at the hands of your nobility.

Given at the Lateran.

A letter on this matter was written to the dean and chapter of Saint Quentin, in almost the same terms as above, up to the end: “Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you presume to receive no one as canon to a prebend which is presently vacant in your church, or first becomes vacant, unless it be the person to whom we judge fit to confer it.”

Given at the Lateran … in the sixth year.

## XV. TO THE BISHOP OF POLINIANO

[Note: Reported among the Decretals, book III, title 17, *On Purchase and Sale*, chapter 5. The words marked in italics are absent from editions of the Decretals.]

[Note: In the Gregorian collection this letter is addressed to the bishop of Palliensis; in the Innocentian collection, to Pallionensis; here, to the bishop of Polinianensis. In every case incorrectly, in our opinion. It should rather be read as Polymniacensis (of Polignano). For our letter must have been directed to the bishop of some city neighboring Trani. Yet Ughellus has nothing concerning bishops of Polymniacum around this time.]

He commands him to investigate whether a certain stipulation is contrary to the canons. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of March.)

[Col. 0022D]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, when R. …, a layman of Mar. [Note: “Bearer of these presents,” from M.], wished to receive a loan from …, a creditor in the diocese of Trani, the creditor received from him his houses and olive groves under the title of sale, so that he might not later be sued under the canon enacted against usurers. In fact, however, a usurious contract was being conducted. This is evident because, as the public instrument states, the creditor promised the debtor that, whenever between the seventh and ninth year he paid him sixty ounces of tareni—which scarcely amounted to half the just price—he would restore to him the houses and olive groves.

Therefore, because fraud and deceit ought to give protection to no one, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, notwithstanding the instrument of a condition drawn up in fraud of the canon promulgated against usurers, you compel the aforesaid M. …, by the penalty enacted against usurers in the Lateran Council and with appeal set aside, to restore the aforesaid houses and olive groves to the person to whom they ought to devolve by hereditary right, [Col. 0023B] since the debtor has entered upon the way of all flesh.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of March.

## XVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, PRELATES OF CHURCHES, AND ALL CLERGY ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SARDINIA

He grants that they are not to be compelled by letters of the Apostolic See to answer outside Sardinia, unless the letters expressly provide otherwise. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of March.)

Although the authority of law decrees that a person ought to be sued in his own province, this does not prejudice apostolic power, so as to prevent it from delegating disputes of subjects to whomsoever and wherever it wishes. Yet the Apostolic See so moderates its own authority that, considering more what is expedient than what is permitted, it conforms its power to public utility and delegates cases brought before it where they can be handled without burden to the parties.

Therefore, assenting to your petitions, by authority of these presents we grant you that you shall not be compelled by letters of the Apostolic See to answer outside Sardinia unless those letters make mention of this indulgence. Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our concession, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of March.

## XVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN SARDINIA

He orders them to denounce publicly as excommunicate the murderers of the bishop of Plavac and others, and not to allow them to remain in Sardinia. [Note: In this letter Innocent mentions a deputy of the prior of Camaldoli who was barbarously murdered in Sardinia; no further record of the matter survives. Tradition alone reports that around this time several monks of the Camaldolese and Vallombrosan congregations were slaughtered by Saracens invading or ravaging Sardinia. Mittarelli, *Annals of Camaldoli*, vol. IV, p. 192.] (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0023D]

Since impunity for crime produces an incentive to wrongdoing, negligence may be imputed to you because, as we have learned, heinous crime has so far taken root in Sardinia that it has become customary—while you often remain silent—for ecclesiastical men now to be slaughtered everywhere in those regions; nor does the wickedness of the presumptuous spare even those who exercise on earth the office of him who always spares and has mercy in heaven.

Indeed, in those regions N. …, bishop of Plavac, of good memory, … abbot of Sergo, and … deputy of the prior of Camaldoli were wickedly murdered. Yet, to our sorrow, you did nothing against their killers, as is said, like mute dogs unable to bark. Since we neither wish nor ought to overlook the offense of such audacity, we command and strictly order your brotherhood by apostolic letters to announce publicly every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, that those who presumed to do such things are excommunicate; and order everyone strictly to avoid them until they present themselves before the Apostolic See [Col. 0024B] to receive absolution.

Compel the noble judges of Sardinia by ecclesiastical censure to compel the murderers, with the authority entrusted to them, to make satisfaction according to canonical form. Do not allow such criminals, if they remove themselves from one jurisdiction to another, to remain in their jurisdiction until they have made adequate satisfaction. In whatever city, village, or town such murderers reside, forbid the celebration of divine offices for as long as they are present. Publicly announce as excommunicate, according to the prescribed form, those who have laid violent hands upon clerics. Proceed similarly henceforth if—may it not happen!—anything similar should occur.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

## XVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: He has been mentioned many times], AND HIS SUFFRAGANS

He signifies that he has received the Judge of Torres under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0024C]

The devotion of the noble man …, Judge of Torres, merits that, insofar as we can honorably do so, we should extend apostolic favor to him. Since, therefore, we have thought fit to receive under the protection of the Apostolic See him, his … son, and his land with all his goods, we carefully admonish and exhort your brotherhood and command you by apostolic letters to take care, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and ourselves, to uphold and defend that land and its people in their right and, insofar as the weight of your pastoral office permits, to protect them [Col. 0024D] from the assaults of the wicked. Restrain your parishioners by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, from attacking him and his land; nor allow him, insofar as lies in your power, to be unduly harassed by them.

Given at the Lateran, as above.

## XIX. TO THE ABBOT OF DOL; E., PAPAL SUBDEACON, PRIOR OF LEPROSO

[Note: The abbot of Dol has already been mentioned above.]

Despite the death of the bishop of Nevers, they are to cause a prebend in the church of Nevers to be assigned to P., nephew of the Archbishop of Torres, according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate concerning this matter sent to the said bishop of Nevers. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of May—rather, March.)

[Col. 0025A]

We recall that we wrote to N. …, bishop [Note: See book V, epistle 131], of good memory, and to our beloved sons, the chapter of Nevers, that they should procure the induction into possession of a vacant prebend, formerly reserved for our grant, of our beloved son P. …, nephew of our venerable brother …, Archbishop of Torres, on account of the death of B. … of Saint-Pourçain, who has entered upon the way of all flesh; and that you were assigned as executors in this matter.

[Note: It should be noted that Blasius—for it is he who is meant here, though his name is suppressed—who a little earlier, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March (see epistle X of this book), was still called “elect,” is now, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, called Archbishop of Torres. See the following note.]

Accordingly, we commanded the aforesaid canons that, notwithstanding that the aforesaid bishop of Nevers had meanwhile been taken from this life, they should not delay to execute the apostolic mandate. Therefore, we strictly command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the said canons neglect to fulfill our mandate, you do not delay, notwithstanding any objection or appeal, to proceed in the matter according to the tenor of the earlier mandate, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical discipline. If not both … one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May [Note: It seems altogether necessary to read “March,” since several epistles both before and after this one are expressly stated to have been issued in March], in the sixth year.

## XX. TO THE SAME

On a similar matter, in favor of L. in the church of Liniac. (Lateran, as above.)

[Col. 0025C]

Our beloved son G. [otherwise J.] of Pertico, dean of Blessed Martin of Tours, to whom the grant of prebends in the church of Liniac is said to belong, granted a certain vacant prebend there to our beloved son L., nephew of our venerable brother B. …, Archbishop of Torres, giving him letters on the matter sealed with his own seal. We therefore commanded by apostolic letters our beloved sons …, the provost and chapter of the same church, to hold valid and firm what the said dean prudently did in this regard; to receive L. himself, or Master P. of Vico in his name, as canon and brother; to pay to him in full the vacant prebend conferred by that dean; and not delay to assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter, notwithstanding that he ought first to be installed in the choir of Blessed Martin, since he cannot go there because of disturbances of war.

Therefore, we firmly command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if they neglect to do what we have commanded, you do not delay to execute the apostolic mandate in this matter, with the obstacle of appeal removed, restraining opponents, etc., as above.

Given as above.

## XXI. TO THE ABBOT AND BRETHREN OF SAINT MARY OUTSIDE THE GATE, AT FAENZA

[Note: Charters of this place identify Macchabaeus as abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary outside the Gate on 17 March 1202 (fascicle V). Soon afterwards, in October of the same year 1202, in the fifth indiction, Theodinus is found as abbot (*ibid.*); thereafter, in 1203 and also on 5 February 1204, in the sixth indiction, the same Theodinus appears continuously in instruments as party or witness. Yet on 5 December 1205, in the eighth indiction, Macchabaeus, as though restored to life, is again expressly named abbot. It is not for us to resolve such a difficulty. See *Monumenta Faventina*, col. 463.]

They are received under protection. Their privileges are confirmed. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of March.)

It is customary to assent, etc., up to “assent.” We receive your monastery [Col. 0026B], with all goods which it now reasonably possesses or may hereafter acquire by just means, God being favorable, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves.

In particular: the parish churches of Saint Reparata and Saint Andrew, with their customary portions of tithes, first-fruits, and offerings; the chapel of Saint Andrew at Lacuna; the churches of Saint Mary at Nocareto, Saint Mary at Casanico, Saint Martin at Fondo Rasonis, Saint Lawrence at Manzanico, Saint Michael at Bacagnano, Saint George, Saint Mary at Campora, Saint Mary of Casale, Saint Mary at Vezano, Saint Felicity at Mucello, Saint Blaise of Ravenna, Saint Mary at Runci, Saint Apollinaris, and Saint Mary at Andecimo, with all their possessions [Col. 0026C] and appurtenances; the estate of Ambroniaca, called Populanum; the estate on Mount Casalia, with their possessions and appurtenances; the court of Cuturn., with its appurtenances; namely, the villages of Adilian. and Nocareto, Rosan. Huminis, Mintignano, Mitian., Viulo, and Capezan., with all their possessions and appurtenances; namely, the castles of Varnellum and Andecimum, with their appurtenances; namely, the lands of Galiani of Casanola, Lacuna Viridis, Sidero, Albareto, Loreto, the Valley of Appiolis, and Vicelo, with all their appurtenances; and whatever right you possess in the estate of Vincareto.

Just as you possess all these things justly and peaceably, we confirm them by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to the same [Col. 0026D] monastery; and fortify them with the protection of this present writing. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and the same monastery the reasonable and ancient customs hitherto peaceably observed in your monastery, strictly [Col. 0027A] forbidding anyone to dare unduly harass you contrary to them. Further, by authority of these presents we grant you permission to appoint a suitable man as steward of your monastery, to manage its cases and, where necessary, take the oath concerning calumny. Therefore let absolutely no person … infringe this page of our protection, confirmation, prohibition, and concession, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the sixth year of the pontificate.

## XXII. TO THE SAME

He commands that goods of the monastery granted in emphyteusis return to the monastery according to the laws of emphyteusis. [Note: To what we have said in the note to the preceding letter, add, if you wish, that no mention of these letters of Innocent occurs in the documents collected by Mittarelli (in the cited place), although various letters of the same pontiff may there be read which are sought in vain in the Registers.] (Lateran, Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0027B]

You stated to us, son abbot, while present before us, that your church has granted many possessions in emphyteusis; and when one who has received them in this manner wishes, for the remedy of his sins, to relinquish them to that church so that at the end of the term they may return to the church, his nephews or relatives seize them and do not allow those possessions to return to the church for as long as anyone of that lineage survives.

Therefore, wishing by paternal solicitude to provide against injury to your church, by authority of these presents we forbid anyone, on the ground of that arrangement—which, as made contrary to canonical sanctions, we regard as void—to retain possessions of the said church; rather, they are freely to [Col. 0027C] return to that church as they belong to it. We decree that if those who have thus received any possessions from your church wish to leave them to the church or bequeath them by last will, they shall have free power to do so. Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our constitution and prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of March.

## XXIII. TO THE ABBOT [Note: The abbey of Saint Germanus of Auxerre was then governed by Radulfus, born in the district called Baseium in the diocese of Nevers. Elected in 1188, he presided with the highest praise until 1203; but afterwards, when dissensions arose between the abbot and monks through the bishop’s envy, he was afflicted by many troubles for four years. He went to Rome to plead his cause before the supreme pontiff, and on his return died at Piacenza, where he was buried on Christmas Day, 25 December 1208. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 384.] AND MONKS OF SAINT GERMANUS OF AUXERRE

He grants them permission, in a time of interdict, to bury deceased brethren with certain honors. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of April.)

The merits of your devotion deserve that we extend to you apostolic favor in matters in which we may honorably do so. [Col. 0027D] Therefore, assenting to your petitions, by authority of these presents we grant that, if any of you or your successors dies during an interdict, at his funeral, on the day of his burial, you may then ring a single bell, provided that there is neither a long interval nor prolonged ringing, [Col. 0028A] since this has been granted by the diocesan bishop to the monastery of Saint Julian in the city of Auxerre, and the cathedral church itself observes the same practice. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth year.

## XXIV. TO THE NOBLEMAN W., GRAND ŽUPAN (Meganippanus) OF SERBIA

[Note: Cited by Raynaldus, year 1203, §19.]

He admonishes him to return to the Catholic faith and to render obedience and reverence to the Archbishop of Kalocsa as the pope’s representative. (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of April.)

Christ Jesus, God and man, mediator between God and men (1 Tim. II), established the primacy of the Apostolic See in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Before his Passion he said to him: “You are Peter, [Col. 0028B] and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVI). And near his Passion he said to the same man: “Simon, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXII). And after his Passion, repeating the address three times, he commanded: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep” (John XXI).

He made no distinction between these sheep and those, so that whoever refuses to have blessed Peter as pastor may know himself wholly alien from Christ’s fold. Whoever despises his keys closes to himself the gate of the kingdom of heaven; nor can one escape Satan’s sieve who refuses to be confirmed in the Catholic faith through him.

We therefore, who, though unworthy, have succeeded blessed Peter in the office of apostolate, through which we have become debtors to wise and foolish alike, being concerned for your salvation, have determined to visit you through our venerable brother J. …, Archbishop of Kalocsa, a learned, prudent, and honorable man, to whom we have committed our office in this respect. Although bodily distant from us, you are near in mind: he is to strengthen you in orthodox faith and, receiving from you in our name spiritual obedience and bodily reverence, to lead you back to the apostolic fold, wherein, after Christ, the chief and first shepherd, blessed Peter is the subordinate and second shepherd.

We therefore carefully admonish and exhort your nobility, commanding you by apostolic letters, graciously to receive and honor the aforesaid archbishop in our stead, and humbly to strive to fulfill his salutary admonitions and commands. Thus, received in the ark, you may not undergo the flood, and we may effectively labor for your honor and advancement.

[Col. 0029A] Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh [Note: This is expressly read in the Conti copy. Some may believe that Raynaldus, in the cited place, read II, meaning “2.”] day before the Kalends of April.

A letter in the same terms was written to the archbishops, bishops, and barons established throughout Serbia.

## XXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF KALOCSA

[Note: See Raynaldus, in the same place.]

On the same matter. (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of April.)

“Mediator between God and men,” etc., in the same manner down to “debtors”:  being concerned for the salvation of the nobleman W. …, Meganippan of Serbia, and of the prelates of the Church, the nobles of the land, indeed of all those dwelling in Serbia, we have determined to visit them through you. Therefore, committing our office in this matter to your brotherhood by authority of these presents, since we have complete confidence in you, we command you by apostolic letters that, going personally into Serbia, you strengthen the said Meganippan, all the prelates, and all the nobles in the orthodox faith; receive from them a sworn assurance that they will henceforth faithfully take care to obey us and our successors and the holy Roman Apostolic See in spiritual matters; and, having received from them bodily reverence, declare them, supported by our authority, wholly absolved from the bond of obedience by which they seemed bound to the Patriarch of Constantinople, because, since he does not render us the obedience due, they are not bound to show him the reverence due to him.

Given at the Lateran, as above.

A letter on this matter was written to the illustrious King of Hungary.

XXVI. [Note: [Col. 0029D] This exists, but mutilated, among the Decretals, book V, title 35, *On the Common Purging*, chapter 2, where, through a manifest error, it is addressed to the prior of St Sergius. The passages printed there are here enclosed in brackets; the passages lacking there are distinguished by italics.] TO THE PRIOR [Note: [Col. 0030D] See letters 15 and 16 of book II.] OF ST GREGORY AT SPOLETO. He commands that goods taken from L. and his brothers on suspicion of theft be restored to them. (Lateran, as above.)

[Col. 0029C]

[You are to know that V. . . ., a layman, and his brothers have represented to us that, when a certain person accused them of theft, they were compelled, contrary to the custom of the land, to enter into a duel with him. In this duel, impeded by their other sins, they were defeated; and therefore, after an appeal had been lodged with us, the consuls of Spoleto despoiled them of their own goods. But theft has now been discovered in the possession of others, and it has been revealed, by the Lord's doing, that they themselves were innocent. We have therefore commanded the said consuls to restore to them everything taken away.] We therefore command your discretion by these apostolic letters that, if they neglect to fulfil our command, you shall summon the parties . . . and, setting appeal aside, cause . . . whatever is just to be done . . . through ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, as above.

XXVII. TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF TURRIS. He entrusts to him the matter that the judge of Turris, who died showing signs of penitence, should, once the truth is known, be absolved and given ecclesiastical burial.

[Col. 0030A]

On behalf of our beloved son, the nobleman . . ., judge of Turris, it was set before us that, when the Pisans had invaded a certain province of Turris, they then inflicted very many grave injuries upon the brother of that same judge of Turris. And when he afterwards wished to make an agreement with them, they, under the hope of peace and the pretext of a confederacy, presumed, in violation of their own oath, to invade the castle of Monte Cossiano; and, having taken all his goods, they led his wife [Col. 0030B] captive to Cagliari, where, as it pleased the Lord, she died. Furthermore, the nobleman . . . ., judge of Cagliari, into whose hands that castle had come, grievously harassed the said judge.

When afterwards our venerable brother, the Pisan archbishop [Note: [Col. 0030D] See book III, letter 9, note.], came to Sardinia in order to recall those in discord to concord, he ordered the castle itself from the judge of Cagliari and certain other pledges from the judge of Turris to be placed in his custody, with the consent of the parties. But before peace was concluded, that judge of Turris seized the aforesaid castle; and because he refused to restore it when the archbishop demanded it, the latter pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him.

Moreover, after a short interval, the same judge of Turris, being confined to a sickbed [Col. 0030C], summoned into his presence the late archbishop of Turris, your predecessor, and . . . . . the bishop of Sorres, in order to receive penance for his offences and obtain the benefit of absolution. But before he had obtained their desired presence, he entered upon the way of all flesh and was buried outside the church cemetery. Since, however, the foregoing does not stand established before us, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth concerning these matters. If it is established to you that signs of penitence preceded in him, then, since on that account he must be believed absolved before the Lord, so that the Church may conform to the divine judgment, grant the deceased the benefit of absolution, after his brother has rendered fitting satisfaction, with the penitential psalm, the customary prayer, [Col. 0030D] and sprinkling of blessed water. Thus you may grant him ecclesiastical burial. Take careful care to observe diligently the constitution which we formerly issued concerning this matter on the counsel of our brethren.

Given.

XXVIII. TO THE NOBLEMAN . . . . . JUDGE OF TURRIS. He is not to compel the laity and clergy of the province of Turris to pay the Pisans whatever they demand from them.

[Col. 0031A]

You are to know that it has come to our hearing that you formerly swore, at the Pisans’ request, that, if at any time one of them should present, concerning any debt, either sealed letters or a public instrument, you would cause satisfaction to be made to him within twenty days thereafter, according to what the instrument states and establishes. Therefore, fearing to act against such an oath, you compel not only laymen but also clerics, churches, and our venerable brethren and fellow bishops established in the province of Turris, without observing the order of law, to pay the Pisans whatever they may judge fit to demand from them [Col. 0031B], provided only that they produce either sealed letters or a public instrument concerning it. Thus it happens that many sums not owed, and certain debts, are paid twice or three times, with the most burdensome interest.

Since, therefore, no power whatsoever has accrued to you through such an oath, nor can the Pisans subject clerics or churches to your jurisdiction, so that they must be sued before you contrary to canon law, we earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility, and command you by apostolic letters, that henceforth you do not harass ecclesiastical persons on this pretext. Otherwise, while wishing to placate the Pisans, you will offend God and incur the displeasure of the Apostolic See, which could not endure this with equanimity.

Given.

XXIX. [Note: [Col. 0031D] This exists, but mutilated, in Raynaldus under the year 1203, §68. The portions found in his text are here enclosed in brackets.] TO THE NOBLEMEN . . . . . . JUDGES OF TURRIS, CAGLIARI, AND . . . ARBOREA [Note: [Col. 0031D] A certain instrument in Mittarelli, *Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, appendix, col. 240, chapter CXLIX, acknowledges Constantine as judge of Arborea in the year 1200.]. He commands them to ensure the execution of the commands of the archbishop of Turris.

[Col. 0031C]

[The more especially Sardinia is known to belong to the Roman Church, being subject to it both in spiritual and temporal matters, the more earnestly we will and ought to take precautions lest anything be attempted there by which its condition is disturbed and the Lord is gravely offended.] Certainly, since it has long been divided within itself, has suffered external enemies, and has had enemies of its own household within, and since it is now enough to remember its misfortunes, we are bound to employ vigilant diligence and diligent concern to remove what produces scandal and to plant what yields an increase of peace. [Col. 0031D] But because we cannot personally accomplish this, we have judged it appropriate to entrust the matter to our venerable brother . . . . . . . archbishop of Turris, whose integrity and prudence we have tested in many matters, relying upon his discretion.

[We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your nobility, and command you by apostolic letters, that, receiving him humbly out of reverence for the Apostolic [Col. 0032A] See and for us, and treating him honourably, you shall take care to trust and carry into effect what he will propose to you on our behalf concerning the judgeships of Gallura and Arborea, the noblewoman . . . . . . ., daughter of the late judge of Gallura, who is to be given in marriage when she reaches marriageable age, and other matters; for he knows our will fully in all these matters. Thus may we come more fully to know your devotion in this matter, and, through his diligence, may the longed-for peace come to the whole province.

Given.

XXX. [Note: [Col. 0032D] Cited by Raynaldus, year 1203, §68.] TO THE NOBLE JUDGES OF SARDINIA. That they are to render to the archbishop of Turris, in the pope’s name, an oath of fidelity.

[Col. 0032B]

Your nobility is not ignorant that Sardinia is also subject in temporal matters to the Apostolic See, for which reason your predecessors were accustomed to render fidelity to our predecessors. Therefore, lest we seem to neglect the right of the Roman Church—we who are accustomed to provide even for others in what is their right—we command and enjoin your nobility by apostolic letters that, into the hands of our venerable brother . . . . . . archbishop of Turris, in whose prudence and integrity we have full confidence and whom we have appointed for this purpose, you shall offer oaths of fidelity to us, our successors, and the Roman Church, under the form enclosed for you under our seal. [Col. 0032C] Fulfil the apostolic command in such a way that we may rightly be bound to have regard for your honour. Otherwise, we shall hold valid and cause to be inviolably observed whatever sentence he pronounces against the rebellious.

Given.

XXXI. [Note: [Col. 0032D] Cited by Raynaldus, year 1203, §68.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES; TO THE NOBLE JUDGES; AND TO OTHERS ESTABLISHED IN SARDINIA. That they are to pay the tribute due to the Roman Church. (Lateran.)

The fuller our confidence in the fervour of faith and constancy of devotion of our venerable brother . . . . . archbishop of Turris, [Col. 0032D] the more confidently we entrust to him the business of the Apostolic See for execution. We therefore command and enjoin all of you by apostolic letters that you take care to pay him, without any difficulty, the tribute which you owe to the Roman Church, so that we may rightly have cause to commend your devotion on that account. Otherwise, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

XXXII. [Note: [Col. 0033D] See the notes to letter C of book V. We carefully collated this thirty-second letter of the present sixth book, together with its copy, against the autograph preserved in the archives of the abbey of St Geneviève, which was diligently transcribed and most graciously communicated to us by M. Monges, learned member of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres. There is no discrepancy whatsoever.] TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS, THE ABBOT OF ST GENEVIÈVE, AND THEIR CHAPTERS. Confirmation of the agreement concluded between them. (Lateran, 26 March.)

[Col. 0033A]

Since a dispute had long been conducted between you concerning parochial right in the parish of Mont, concerning the chapel of St Geneviève situated in the city of Paris, and concerning the procurations which you, brother bishop, demanded in the parish churches of your diocese belonging to the aforesaid church of St Geneviève of Mont; and since, after various labours and manifold expenses borne by you on this account, it was settled by an amicable agreement through the mediation of good men, while the reverence due to the Apostolic See was preserved; [Col. 0033B] and since you then humbly requested that we deign to affix the hand of our confirmation to this agreement, necessary for you and your churches: we gave instructions by our letters to our beloved sons . . ., abbot of St Columba of Sens, and J., master of the schools at Orléans, that, if they found the agreement prudently made without impropriety, voluntarily accepted by both sides, and not prejudicial to the Apostolic See—to which the church of St Geneviève is known to belong directly, without an intermediary—they should confirm it in our stead by apostolic authority. They were then to report this to us by their letters, so that we too might confirm it when more fully informed by their report.

These men, proceeding lawfully in the business entrusted to them, as sons of obedience, carefully examined the terms of the agreement and the privileges of the church of St Geneviève. Finding that the agreement had been made and received on both sides as we had stated, they took care to confirm it by our authority, as we have seen more fully contained in their letters. Therefore, with equal desire and unanimous will, you humbly petitioned us that we might deign, from the benignity of the Apostolic See, to affix the hand of our confirmation to that agreement. We therefore, holding ratified and firm what was done by those delegates in accordance with the form of our mandate, confirm by apostolic authority the aforesaid agreement, as prudently made without impropriety and voluntarily accepted by you, [Col. 0033D] and as more fully contained in the authentic documents drawn up concerning it, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 26 March, in the sixth year.

XXXIII. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF JANI [Note: [Col. 0034D] So printed. Perhaps read *Fani*]. Concerning payment of tribute. (Lateran, 26 March.)

It is customary to grant assent, etc., by way of protection. As an indication, moreover, that you belong to the patrimony of St Peter and to our domain, you shall pay annually to our treasury, as tribute, two soldi of *affortiati* from each household. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 26 March.

XXXIV. TO THE DEAN OF BLESSED MARY OF THE MID MONASTERY [Note: [Col. 0034D] On the monastery of Méry at Bourges, see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 121.], AND THE ARCHDEACON OF BOURGES. He commands them to render justice to a certain cleric concerning a custom in the diocese of Bourges whereby no one may sell his patrimony except to one nearer to him in the line of kinship. (Lateran, 26 March.)

From the report of our beloved son, Master O. . . Mainel, canon of Blessed Mary of Salis at Bourges, we have learned [Col. 0034B] that, since a custom prevails in the diocese of Bourges that no one may sell his patrimony except to someone nearer to him in the line of kinship, if that person happens to have sufficient means to buy it, B. . . ., his late maternal uncle, presumed to sell a portion of his inheritance to P. . . ., a knight of the diocese of Bourges, to this cleric’s prejudice and injury; whereas he himself would have bought it at a fair price had he been consulted on the matter. Since the said cleric, wishing to rely not upon civil law but upon provincial custom, has asked us to render him justice, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties, etc., you cause whatever is just . . . to be firmly observed. Notwithstanding any letters, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 26 March, in the sixth year.

XXXV. TO THE ABBOT OF ST JULIAN AND THE MAJOR ARCHDEACON OF TOURS. He confirms by apostolic authority the sentence rendered by J., master of the schools at Orléans, delegated for this purpose by the pope, in the case concerning the election to the priory of Gracay. [Note: [Col. 0034D] See letter 37 of book V.]

[Col. 0034C]

When a dispute formerly arose between our beloved sons Master P. . . of Vico and A. . . Archenaud concerning the election or nomination to the priory of Gracay, and they were present at the Apostolic See, because the merits of the case could not be established before us, we judged it fitting, with the parties’ consent, to commit it under a specified form to our beloved son J. . . , master of the schools at Orléans. Having received our mandate, [Col. 0034D] he summoned the parties before him at Paris. After the matter submitted to him had been diligently examined and fully discussed, and after he had acquired fuller knowledge of every point through the solemn publication of witness depositions, the instruments of the parties, the decree of election fortified with the subscriptions of the canons, and other reasons; with both parties present and urgently requesting sentence; and after taking counsel with many teachers of law at Paris and other prudent men, he rejected, for certain reasons, the election or nomination of A. . . to the aforesaid church, and annulled whatever had proceeded in fact. He approved Master P.’s election by our authority and adjudged it canonical. He commanded the chapter of Blessed Austregisilus at Bourges, to which the aforesaid church belongs, to confirm Master P.’s election, which he had himself approved, notwithstanding the absence of the dean [Note: [Col. 0035C]

Concerning the deans of St Austregisilus of the Castle at Bourges at about this period, the following is found in the authors of *Gallia Christiana*:

“II. William, to whom Pope Alexander III granted a privilege in 1173 that bodies might be committed to ecclesiastical burial despite an interdict, is still found in certain charters in 1188, 1190, and 1199.”
