“III. Henry, dean of St Austregisilus, brother of Simon, cantor of Bourges, and uncle of Henry of Pouillac, recurs in various documents from 1208 to 1221. But he had already died in 1223, when his anniversary is found to have been celebrated.”

We considered it a duty here to pass over these facts, because in the notes [Col. 0035D] to letter 37 of book V, matters that should have been understood of the dean of St Austregisilus were, through inadvertence, understood of the dean of the cathedral church of Bourges.], who was staying at Bologna; otherwise, he himself would execute this by the authority of the apostolic rescript.

He also subjected the opponents to excommunication in accordance with the tenor of our letters. By our authority he charged our beloved son R. . . , archpriest of Bourges, and R. . . , archdeacon of Bourbon, to go to the aforesaid church of Blessed Austregisilus and effectively induce its chapter to obey the sentence rendered, reporting back to him the names of any opponents and rebels and the course of the case. Going there repeatedly, they found everyone except A. voluntarily and concordantly obeying the sentence rendered in favour of Master P.; they also found the canons of Gracay unanimous in this matter, and likewise those who had previously opposed him, as they faithfully reported in their letters.

But the said A., though repeatedly summoned and warned, obstinately opposes Master P. Therefore, since he had incurred the sentence of excommunication pronounced against rebels under the form of our rescript, he publicly announced him excommunicated and caused him to be announced by others as a person to be avoided by all. He sent the aforesaid master, confirmed as we had commanded, to the aforesaid church of Gracay, where he was received concordantly and unanimously, as the chapter informed us by open letters. [Col. 0036A]

Since the same delegate took care to make us more certain of the foregoing by his letters, and since we desire what he has so prudently done to obtain due firmness, we command you by apostolic letters to cause both the definitive sentence, as just, to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure by our authority, and the sentence of excommunication, as reasonably pronounced, to be observed until due satisfaction, appeal being set aside.

Given . . . . . in the sixth year.

XXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0035D] This letter exists, though very mutilated, in two places among the Decretals: first, book I, title 6, *On Election and the Authority of the Elect*, chapter 22; second, book II, title 27, *On Sentence and the Matter Adjudged*, chapter 19. What is found in either place is here enclosed in brackets.] TO . . . . . . . . . . . . THE BISHOP OF PRAENESTE [Note: [Col. 0035D] See the note to letter 8 of book V.], LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE; TO THE ABBOTS OF . . . . . . . . OF CAPEMBACH [Note: [Col. 0035D] Perhaps it should be read Cappenberg, an illustrious monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, founded on the site of the ancestral castle by Geoffrey, count of Cappenberg, in 1186. Bucelinus, *Germania Sacra*, part II, p. 159. At that time Hermann, a most noble son of the noble lineage of Count Lothair of Aren and Méren and Hildegund, presided over this monastery. After administering the prelacy for forty years with the remarkable favour and affection of all, he left it by dying in 1210. *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. I, col. 436.], AND . . . . . . . . OF SCELDE [Note: [Col. 0036C] Bucelinus says nothing concerning this abbey in *Germania Sacra*. But perhaps it should be read Scheida, also Sceida or Segor, a Premonstratensian abbey, daughter-house of Cappenberg, situated in Westphalia and the county of Mark in the diocese of Cologne. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 802. The *Annales Praemonstratenses* leave uncertain who was abbot of Scheida at that time. They record Hermann II in 1296, and then, in an undated year but at the beginning of the thirteenth century, Volmar, a man of singular prudence, learning, and practical competence. *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. II, col. 773.] SITUATED IN THE DIOCESES OF COLOGNE AND MÜNSTER. He commands them to arrange for a suitable person to be appointed to the provostship of the church of Cologne. (Lateran, 9 April.)

[Col. 0036B]

[Note: [Col. 0036C] See the Decretals, book II, place cited.] [In cases decided by the judgment of the supreme pontiff, both the order of law and the force of equity must be carefully observed, since in like cases others are bound to judge in the same way, unless perhaps he has judged that something should be established by dispensation, having regard to necessity and utility.]

Accordingly, when the major provostship of the church of Cologne had become vacant some time before [Note: [Col. 0036C] Probably through the death of Louis, who is recorded as major provost, together with Udo the dean, as a witness in the charter of the alliance concluded at Aachen on 4 July, the day of Otto IV’s coronation as king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, first indiction, between Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, and Windekind, abbot of Corvey in Saxony. After him, the authors of *Gallia Christiana* mention Theodoric of Heinsberg, who was made archbishop from being provost after Bruno IV in 1208. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 717.], and when the canons had met to deliberate over the appointment of a provost, their votes were divided into two parties. Some elected the provost of the Holy Apostles [Col. 0036C] [Note: [Col. 0036D] Named Theodoric, from the letters of Guy, cardinal-bishop of Palestrina, in which he appears as a witness for that cardinal in confirming the goods of the abbey of Pöhlde in 1202. Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 642, document 449.]; others, the provost of St George [Note: [Col. 0036D] Named Engelbert, from the same letters. See the note to letter 54 of book III and to letter 71 of book V.] to the said provostship.

Messengers were therefore sent to the Apostolic See, and, with the parties’ consent, a commission was obtained, under the following form, for our beloved sons A. . . of Laach [Col. 0037A] [Note: [Col. 0037C] Albert was then governing the abbey of Laach: “praised for distinguished wisdom, cultivation of virtues, devotion, and diligence, and appearing about 1199 in the letters of John, archbishop of Trier. Having governed for nineteen years, he put off mortality in 1219.” Thus far the authors of *Gallia Christiana* (vol. XIII, col. 606), who followed Bucelinus (*Germania Sacra*, part II, p. 203). Yet Hontheim published an instrument which he believes was issued before 1193 and in which Albert, abbot of Laach, is expressly recorded as a witness. *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 621, document 434.], J. . . . of Claustrum [Note: [Col. 0037D] It seems quite certain that the initial should be read not J. but H. For Hermann is found at that time as abbot of the monastery of Claustrum, or Himmerod. Born of noble blood, he was first a canon at Bonn, then became a monk of Claustrum, and was subsequently chosen to the office of prior. He later became abbot of the monastery of Heisterbach in 1188; then, before 1190, was recalled to Claustrum and served there as abbot. Only in 1215, zealous to extend religious life, he crossed the Rhine to become abbot for the establishment of St Mary’s. After eight years in that office, full of days and rich in merits, he gave up his spirit to his Creator. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 635. These facts are confirmed by instruments in Brower, *Annales Trevirenses*, vol. II, p. 110.], and J. . . . of the Valley of St Peter [Note: [Col. 0037D] Here too there appears to be an error in the initial [Col. 0038C] used for the name of the abbot of the monastery of the Valley of St Peter, or Heisterbach. It is certain that Gerard, or Gebard, formerly canon of St Mary ad Gradus, then a monk at Himmerod (or Claustrum), and finally, when Hermann, the first abbot of Heisterbach, was transferred to govern Claustrum, was appointed as his successor before 1190. In 1202 he laid the foundations of the monastery as it now stands; and in the seventh year of the work so begun, the thirteenth of his prelacy, on 15 February 1208, he departed to the Lord. Caesarius says much of him in book XII, chapter 5, of the *Dialogues*. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 792.] at Heisterbach [also: Heisterback], abbots: after hearing the matters advanced on either side, if the parties consented, they were to pronounce a definitive sentence; otherwise they were to remit the case, sufficiently instructed, to our hearing, fixing for the parties a suitable term within which they should come to the Apostolic See, in person or through suitable representatives, to receive sentence.

[Desiring faithfully to execute the apostolic mandate [Note: [Col. 0038D] Absent from the Decretals, book I.], they summoned the parties before them, received the witnesses produced on either side [Note: [Col. 0038D] Absent.], examined the consciences of the electors, and heard allegations from both sides. And because the provost of St George finally declared that he was unwilling to abide by their sentence, they sent to the Apostolic See, under their seals, the depositions of witnesses received on either side and the allegations of the other party [Note: [Col. 0038D] The Decretals read: “the record of the proceedings in the matter already mentioned and the allegations of the other party.”].] They fixed for the parties the approaching feast of St Michael as the term for coming to the Apostolic See; the provost of the Holy Apostles shortened it to the feast of St Servatius, alleging that so long a term was causing loss to the church.

[When the messengers of the provost of the Holy Apostles had come into our presence, the provost of St George neither came nor sent a suitable representative.] But our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0038D] Adolf I of Altena, son of Everard, count of Altena, and Margaret of Jülich. He was raised from provost of the major church to the see of Cologne in 1193 and is known to have held it until 1205. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 683.], . . . . . . archbishop of Cologne, excused his absence, asserting [Col. 0037C] that, while setting out to come to the Apostolic See, he had been captured and was detained by the nobleman W., count of Jülich.

But lest we appear to make any decision to his prejudice, through our beloved sons . . . . . provost of St Gereon [Note: [Col. 0038D] His name was Theodoric, not Arnold, as we had conjectured in the notes to letter 54 of book III. See Hontheim, place cited.], and B., his fellow canon, we ordered both parties to be cited peremptorily for the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. As we learned from their letters, they cited the provost of the Holy Apostles orally and the provost of St George by letters and messengers alike. On receiving the citation, the latter wrote that he would come to the Apostolic See. Yet, since he neither came nor sent a suitable representative either at the term or afterwards, though awaited even for eight weeks beyond the term, we held him contumacious and condemned him to the lawful expenses of the opposing party.

Having therefore considered the attestations and [carefully inspected the judicial proceedings, we found that authority supported the provost of the Holy Apostles, whereas the number of electors supported the provost of St George. The first had been elected by fourteen persons and canons, who surpassed the others in age, dignity, and rank [Col. 0038B] [Note: [Col. 0038D] The Decretals read: “in time”]; the second by twenty-four.]

The provost of St George was, however, charged with inadequate learning, deficiency of age, and being in minor orders. Since an archdeaconry was attached to that provostship, a dignity could not be conferred on him which would oblige him to be promoted to the diaconate within the period fixed by the canons. On behalf of the other man, it was put forward that he was a man commendable in age, learning, and character. Therefore his electors, moved by better zeal, declared that they had agreed upon him for that reason; and not only his own electors, but also some electors of the other party, asserted that he was the more prudent, especially in spiritual matters, although they testified that the other was more useful, particularly in temporal affairs because of his power. [Col. 0038C]

[But because the allegations submitted before those judges on behalf of the said provost of St George were not presented to us, we could not ourselves know what he had objected or what he had answered to the objections. Thus the remitted cause had not been sufficiently instructed before us. We therefore [Note: [Col. 0038D] This word is absent from the Decretals.] did not judge that we should proceed to a definitive sentence [Col. 0039A], but committed the decision of the case to our beloved sons . . . ., provost of St Gereon, etc. . . [Note: [Col. 0039D] Named Hermann. See Hontheim, place cited.], provost of St Severin of Cologne, etc. . . ., and the dean of Bonn [Note: [Col. 0039D] We have absolutely nothing at hand concerning this man.], commanding them by apostolic letters [Note: [Col. 0039D] The Decretals merely read: “we committed the matter to the judges, that . . .”] that, if it were either notorious or established by the acts already completed [Note: [Col. 0040D] The Decretals read: “the matters already stated.”] that the said provost of St George suffered, at the time of the election, from a defect in orders, learning, or age which, according to canonical sanctions, prevented his promotion to such office, they should impose silence upon him, appeal being set aside [Note: [Col. 0040D] Absent from the Decretals.], notwithstanding his bodily absence; adjudge the provostship to the provost of the Holy Apostles; place him in corporal possession; and cause him to enjoy peaceful possession. [Col. 0039B] [Note: [Col. 0040D] Absent from the Decretals.]

Otherwise, since not merely more electors, but almost two-thirds, had concurred in him, and since, once the impediments ceased, it should be presumed [Note: [Col. 0040D] The Decretals read: “it appears.”] that they had elected him with good zeal, they were to annul the election of the provost of the Holy Apostles, appeal being set aside [Note: [Col. 0040D] These words are absent from the Decretals.], confirm his election, and cause the aforesaid provostship to be assigned to him and obedience to be rendered to him henceforth as provost.] They were to restrain opponents, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. If all could not be present together for the execution of these matters, two of them were nevertheless to carry them out.

The delegates summoned the parties before them. Before them it was alleged on behalf of the aforesaid provost of St George that he was not bound to litigate before their tribunal, because one of them was closely related by blood to his opponent and another, his opponent’s fellow canon, was bound to him by excessive familiarity. Rejecting them as suspect, he appealed to our hearing, asserting that he would prove before us these recusations. But they paid no heed whatsoever to the appeal that had been lodged; they received additional witnesses concerning the defect of age and orders and, after their depositions had been published, pronounced definitive sentence against the aforesaid provost of St George, confirming the election of the other.

The same provost then came into our presence and obtained a delegation of the same case under a specified form. Under that commission, however, no proceedings at all took place. But after his return, when a grave disturbance had arisen among clergy and people on the feast of Pentecost because of this dispute, the parties were compelled once more to resort to the Apostolic See. The aforesaid provost of St George therefore appeared before us in person, while the provost of the Holy Apostles appeared through a suitable procurator. In our audience chamber we granted them a full and favourable hearing. [Col. 0040A]

The aforesaid provost of St George maintained that the sentence in question was either void or ought to be voided. He alleged that his appeal had been canonical because of the two aforesaid recusations, and that the delegates’ procedure was irregular for two principal reasons: namely, because the delegates had presumed, contrary to the form of law, to receive fresh witnesses concerning the defect of age and orders after the case had been entirely concluded before the first judges; and because this was contrary to the tenor of our commission, in which it had been expressly stated that they should proceed against him if the alleged defect was either notorious or proved by the acts already completed.

Therefore, since the fact that witnesses had been received concerning both alleged defects established that those defects were not notorious, and since attestations received in the prescribed manner could not legally prejudice him, he requested that, notwithstanding the aforesaid sentence, his election should be confirmed. Nothing canonical had been sufficiently shown against it; nor could the provost of the Holy Apostles object to him the aforesaid defects, since, when he had already received him approvingly as provost in another church among the senior clergy of Cologne (thus printed), this entire question had utterly ceased.

Moreover, the opposing party replied that the aforesaid recusations were not lawful, because one was false and the other frivolous: the delegate’s nephew had solemnly taken as wife the niece of the provost of the Holy Apostles, the man rejected as suspect on grounds of kinship, [Col. 0040C] and had begotten children by her. Although an objection of consanguinity had at some point been raised against their marriage, it had not yet been reconsidered by judgment of the Church. Nor did that close friendship render the other man suspect in law: namely, that he had been dean in a certain church in which the provost of the Holy Apostles had been a canon, and that the latter had sometimes been accustomed to call him, as a friend, to transact his affairs; for a judge ought not to be an enemy but a friend.

Further, whatever the character of such recusations, he nevertheless refused to prove them before arbitrators chosen jointly, as both canon and civil law alike prescribe. This provision was introduced not in favor of one who tries to evade judgment in pursuit of dilatory tactics, but rather against one who maliciously contrives to evade judgment; for human malice must not be indulged. The delegates received witnesses to prove the defect of age and of orders not as though either impediment were not notorious, but because they decided, for greater caution, to receive them in superabundance. Hence, since a judge does not form the conviction of his mind from only one kind of proof, [Col. 0040D] even if the delegates had received those witnesses with insufficient care, they nevertheless proceeded lawfully because of the evident notoriety of the matter—especially since no appeal had been made on these grounds.

Furthermore, their sentence was challenged on the ground that, when it had been objected before the first judges against the election of the aforesaid provost of the Holy Apostles that his election had been presumed contrary to the canonical sanctions—which expressly provide that one person is to be elected from another church only when, though this is scarcely credible, no suitable person can be found in that church—the said provost, who was not of the body of the cathedral church, in which many suitable persons were found, ought not to have been chosen to its provostship, to the prejudice of those persons, against the will of almost two-thirds, who did not wish to renounce their privilege. [Col. 0041A] This was especially so because, according to the canonical statutes, he could not leave the provostship to which he was attached without the authority of his own bishop and transfer himself to another.

But the contrary response was made: the electors of the provost of Saint George, because they had elected him below the required order and age, had incurred the penalty of the constitution promulgated at the Lateran council. By it, such presumptuous persons are decreed to be deprived, on that occasion, of the power of election for three years and suspended from receiving the revenues of their benefices. Therefore the power of electing was known to remain solely with the others, all of whom, by electing an outsider, could generally renounce their right—especially since they ought not to have elected any of the aforesaid presumptuous persons.

Yet [Col. 0041B] this reasoning might perhaps have had force if the aforesaid provost of Saint George had been elected first; but, on the contrary, it is presumed that the other had first been elected by the priors, who according to the order ought first to have made the nomination. Therefore, even if they were elected simultaneously, those men had not yet been deprived of the power to elect when these others presumed, to their prejudice, to elect an outsider. Nor was the following legally valid: that our commission had ordered without qualification that, if even one of the three defects stood in the way of either candidate, they should confirm the other. For this had been obtained from us by suppressing the truth, and we had not understood ourselves to have excluded lawful exceptions which could be raised [Col. 0041C] either against the person or against the act.

We therefore deliberated carefully with our brethren concerning these matters and the other matters which the parties took care to submit in our hearing. Besides the other reasons, we were rightly moved also because a grave scandal threatened from this dissension: many of the canons adhered irrevocably to one of the two elected men, and the metropolitan favored him with his whole effort; while the leading men supported the other without withdrawal, and the priors of Cologne gave him their full support. By apostolic authority we therefore decreed that the election of the one be annulled, especially because of the defect of age—how great it had been at the time of election was plainly shown by inspection of his body [Col. 0041D]—and because of the defect of orders, which he confessed that he had at the time of his election, since he was afterward ordained subdeacon. We likewise decreed that the election of the other be annulled, especially because of the opposition of many who wished a head to be set over them from the suitable members of their own body, and because of the opposition of the aforesaid archbishop, who did not consent to the privilege of his church being infringed.

Lest the church of Cologne be more seriously disturbed by a renewed dissension, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to admonish the chapter of that church diligently toward a canonical and harmonious election and to induce it effectively to make one. [Col. 0042A] If perhaps—God forbid!—this cannot be accomplished within a month, then, supported by our authority and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, you are to take care to place a suitable person over them as provost. As for opponents, etc. But if not all of you can or are willing to take part in carrying this out, let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 9 April.

### XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Bzovius cites this letter, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 101, §11.]

**To the Archbishop of Bourges** [Note: [Col. 0041D] Book V, letter 52, note.]; **and the Prior of Exoudun.** That he is to cause W., subdeacon of Gervais, who was deprived of a prebend in the church of Saintes, to be restored under penalty of excommunication. (Lateran, 15 January.)

When formerly the beloved son W. … Gervais, subdeacon, [Col. 0042C] had come to the Apostolic See and humbly requested restoration to the canonry of Saintes, of which he had been unjustly deprived, and when …, archdeacon of Aulnay, our subdeacon, opposed him in this matter on behalf of the church of Saintes, we granted as auditor our beloved son P., [Note: [Col. 0042D] Book III, letter 32, note.] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. After he had fully and faithfully reported to us the matters advanced on either side, it became known that the said man had been deprived of that canonry without observance of legal process, and had subsequently been restored by a judicial sentence of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of blessed memory, as he himself proved by displaying the latter’s letters on the matter.

By counsel of our brethren, we decreed that the sentence of our predecessor [Col. 0042D] concerning his restoration should be put into execution, while preserving, however, any lawful exceptions in other matters which the canons of the said church might think fit to raise and prove against him. We commanded the bishop, dean, and chapter of Saintes to receive the same subdeacon, fully restored as their canon, as a canon and brother; to treat him with brotherly charity; and, with all recourse to appeal removed, to assign him a stall in the choir and a place in chapter. We nevertheless commanded by our letters the venerable brother …, bishop [Note: [Col. 0042D] We deal with this man elsewhere.], and the beloved son …, dean of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0042D] This man also is discussed elsewhere.], [Col. 0043A] that, if they should refuse to fulfill this apostolic mandate, they were not to delay, after prior warning, in compelling them to do so by ecclesiastical censure.

When the aforesaid subdeacon had presented both our letters and those of the executors to the said … bishop, [Note: [Col. 0043D] Book V, letter 116, note.] dean, [Note: [Col. 0043D] Geoffrey I, dean of Saintes, is known from instruments dating from 1199 to 1207. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1088.] and chapter of Saintes, they scorned the apostolic mandate and the admonitions of the same executors. Under the pretext of a certain frivolous appeal—although appeal had been prohibited in the letters themselves—they refused to receive him. Therefore the aforesaid executors placed both their church and those persons who opposed the decree and did not expressly consent to it under ecclesiastical interdict, as was contained in the letters presented to us by them. Disregarding this sentence, [Col. 0043B] they nevertheless presume, in contempt of the Apostolic See and of us, to celebrate the divine offices.

Since limbs which do not feel the remedy of poultices must be cut off with iron, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to cause that interdict to be observed inviolate, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. But if, contrary to our expectation, they should refuse to observe it and should instead decide to resist contumaciously, you are to bind them with the bond of excommunication, all appeal and contradiction removed. Cause them to be publicly proclaimed excommunicate until they decide to admit the aforesaid subdeacon W., whom we have restored by judicial sentence, and until, coming into our presence [Col. 0043C] with testimony in your letters, they have made suitable satisfaction to us for their contempt and contumacy. No letters whose tenor is silent about these matters, etc., are to stand in the way. But if not both … you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 15 January, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

### XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0043D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §50.]

**To Master Prévostin, scholasticus of Mainz: the spirit of sounder counsel.** He exhorts and commands him to return to a better course and obey the Archbishop of Mainz; otherwise he will be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices. (Lateran, 10 April.)

Until now we had believed that wisdom reigned among the old [Col. 0043D] and prudence adorned the learned; but in you we now experience, to our sorrow, the contrary: you become foolish in old age, though you were wise in youth, and much learning leads you into folly. Have you not read that unwillingness to submit is the sin of divination, and unwillingness to obey the crime of idolatry? Have you not likewise read that obedience is preferred to sacrifices? Why then, abandoning the path of obedience, do you knowingly turn aside into the byways of disobedience [Col. 0044A] and prefer to kick against the goad rather than obey the ordinances of the Roman Church?

Do you not know that our venerable brother S., [Note: [Col. 0044D] See the note to letter 15 of Book V.] Archbishop of Mainz, received the pallium from the Roman Church? Did it escape you that it was publicly declared that you now, as we have learned, assert that the letters which we granted him are false, and thus at least silently, though rashly, defend those letters which counterfeiters procured in order to bear witness to falsehood? Or do you presume to reprove our judgment, judging us when you ought rather to be judged by us? Or have you perhaps forgotten what you have often not only read but also taught: that the servant stands or falls to his own master; that the Lord is he who judges us; and that it is akin to sacrilege to pass judgment upon the judgment of a prince? [Col. 0044B]

Although, by the power bestowed upon us from heaven, we are free from such accusations, we have nevertheless been ready, in apostolic humility, to render sufficient account concerning these matters. Though we could lawfully proceed more severely for your punishment, we desire to recall you to obedience. We therefore command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters that, returning to your senses, you promptly and humbly return to reverence for the aforesaid archbishop, and remain in it steadfastly and devoutly. Otherwise, know that we have commanded the same archbishop that, unless within a month after receiving these letters you fulfill what we command, he is thereafter, supported by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, to deprive you of all ecclesiastical [Col. 0044C] benefices and cause them to be assigned to suitable persons.

We rebuke you severely—and would that we may correct you effectively!—because we grieve that you have become a crooked bow, whereas the Apostolic See had thought otherwise of you.

Given at the Lateran, 10 April.

### XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0044D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §50.]

**To the canons and the whole clergy and people established in the diocese of Mainz: the spirit of sounder counsel.** He commands them to receive the Archbishop of Mainz. (Lateran, 9 April.)

That we withhold from you the address of our greeting and deny you the favor of the apostolic blessing, you should attribute not to our harshness but rather to the contumacy [Col. 0044D] of those who chose to incur a sentence of excommunication rather than obey apostolic commands. Indeed, we believe that all of you remember how, grieving over the discord in the church of Mainz, we committed its cause to our venerable brother G., [Note: [Col. 0044D] See the note to letter 8 of Book V.] Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See; how he, proceeding to execute our mandate, took care to confirm the election made of our venerable brother S., [Note: [Col. 0044D] Letter 14 of Book V, note.] Archbishop of Mainz; and how we, [Note: [Col. 0045D] [ [Col. 0045] This note appears at the foot of column 45, but its callout number (90*) has not been printed in the text.] Thus in the copy.] [Col. 0045A] finally ratifying what he had done, judged that the pallium should be granted to that archbishop.

You also remember how we commanded you to render due reverence and honor to that archbishop, entrusting execution of our mandate to other executors, who were to compel you to carry it out. But because you have not yet come to show reverence to the same archbishop, we admonish all of you and strictly command you by apostolic letters: admit him to the city and church of Mainz; render him the reverence due to him; assist him powerfully and manfully against those who harass him; and do not hinder him from freely exercising the administration of that church in spiritual as well as [Col. 0045B] temporal matters. Otherwise, in addition to the coercive measures which our executors have already exercised against some of you and will exercise in the future, you may rightly fear that the archiepiscopal see, because of your disobedience, will be transferred to some place where there are children of obedience.

Given at the Lateran, 9 April.

### XL

[Note: [Col. 0045D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §50.]

**To S.,** [Note: [Col. 0045D] Book V, letter 14, note.] **Archbishop of Mainz.** He permits him to declare void what the Bishop of Worms unlawfully did in the church of Mainz. (Lateran, as above.)

Since, according to lawful enactments, an accessory does not hold where the principal matter has not held, that which the Bishop of Worms [Col. 0045C] presumed to do in the church of Mainz, into which he rashly intruded himself, ought not to acquire force. His postulation was not accepted by us, and intrusion is hostile to the sacred canons. We therefore grant your brotherhood, by authority of these presents, permission to revoke as void—or rather to declare not to be valid—whatever the said bishop attempted in gifts, grants, or other matters, whether in the church of Mainz or in other churches of the same diocese, all obstacle of appeal removed. Let no one therefore, etc., infringe this grant, etc.

Given as above.

### XLI

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Raynaldus prints this letter in full, under the year 1203, §51.]

**To Siffred, Archbishop of Mainz.** He strongly admonishes him to apply himself diligently to his office. (Lateran, 9 April.)

[Col. 0045D]

You have undertaken the burden of the pastoral office in order that you may feed Christ’s sheep, to whose ministry you have been assigned, alike by word and example. When you have fed them with the bread of Sacred Scripture, you may truly be called a shepherd. Therefore we admonish [Col. 0046A] your brotherhood by apostolic letters to attend to your office and visit the diocese of Mainz, so that you may give milk to drink to the little ones and set solid food before those who are advanced.

And lest a little leaven corrupt the whole mass and a diseased sheep infect the entire flock, if you find any persons there instituted simoniacally, punish them canonically, with the obstacle of appeal removed. If, after their canonical deprivation, they must be stripped of their benefices, cause those benefices to be assigned to suitable persons. Moreover, correct canonically both subjects and prelates for their offenses, and labor utterly to refute the heresies that are springing up.

Given at the Lateran, 9 April.

### XLII

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Raynaldus cites it, under the year 1203, §37.]

**To the Landgrave of Thuringia.** He is received under protection. (Lateran, 11 April.)

[Col. 0046B]

The merits of your devotion deserve that, in matters in which we can honorably do so, we should bestow apostolic favor upon you. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, assenting to your prayers, we receive your person together with all your goods, etc., under the form of protection. By authority of these presents we grant you that no one may presume, without a manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce against you or your land a sentence of excommunication or interdict. A canonical warning is always to precede it, unless the offense is such as does not require judicial process.

We further grant that whenever you perceive yourself to be oppressed, you may freely appeal to the Apostolic See. If anyone, after an appeal lawfully lodged with us, should pronounce any sentence against you or your land, [Col. 0046C] we decree it null. We wish this our favor to retain the strength of full validity only so long as you remain obedient and devoted to us and to the Roman Church. Let no one therefore infringe this protection and grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 11 April.

### XLIII

**To the Abbot** [Note: [Col. 0045D] William II governed the abbey of Bec for thirteen years, two months, and two weeks, less one day; he died on 18 September 1211. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 231.] **and monks of Bec.** He confirms to them the church of Saint Albinus. (Lateran, 4 May.)

When what is asked of us is just and honorable, [Col. 0046D] both the vigor of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your just requests, we confirm to you—and through you to your church, by apostolic authority and under the protection of this present writing—the gift made to you by …, bishop of Évreux, of blessed memory. [Note: [Col. 0046D] The person in question is probably Guarin de Cierrey, who was elected Bishop of Évreux in 1193, during the detention in Germany of Richard, King of England, and died in 1201, according to the chronicle of Saint-Evroult. The authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 581, state that his name occurs in charters of the monastery of Bec in 1198.] Namely, he granted you, by pious [Col. 0047A] liberality, the church of Saint Albinus of Crovill[e], with its chapels and appurtenances. We confirm it as it was prudently made without impropriety and as is more fully set forth in his authenticated instrument. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 March, in the sixth year.

### XLIV

**To Henry, Provost of Saint Peter of Mainz, nephew of the nobleman …, Count of Linig.** He confirms to him the provostship of Saint Peter of Mainz. (Lateran, 11 May.)

“Customarily grants assent,” etc., as far as “assent.” We confirm to you by apostolic authority, etc., the grant of the provostship of the church of Saint Peter of Mainz, conferred upon you by our venerable brother …, [Note: [Col. 0047D] Book V, letter 8, note.] Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, with the assent of our venerable [Col. 0047B] brother S., [Note: [Col. 0047D] Ibid., letter 14, note.] Archbishop of Mainz, as it was canonically made. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 11 March.

### XLV

[Note: [Col. 0047D] Raynaldus published a fragment under the year 1203, §65; the passages found in his work are enclosed here in brackets.]

**To the podestàs, consuls, and councillors of Lombardy, present and future.** He threatens them with anathema and other canonical penalties if they harass clerics and churches with exactions and injuries. (Lateran, 16 April.)

Until now we have waited and hoped that the province of Lombardy, like a watered garden and a delightful vineyard, would bring forth acceptable fruits. But, to our sorrow, instead of the sweetness of grapes [Col. 0047C] it has offered the bitterness of wild grapes, and instead of the scent of roses it has emitted the stench of poppies.

For Pharaoh, king of Egypt, formerly subjected others to servitude, but preserved his priests and their possessions not merely in their former freedom; he also supplied them sustenance from the public treasury. Likewise Artaxerxes, king of Persia, forbade any tax, tribute, or provision levy to be imposed upon all priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, Nethinim, [Note: [Col. 0047D] That is, acolytes or persons in perpetual servitude. The Gibeonites were assigned to perpetual service by the decree mentioned in Joshua, chapter 9; and these Nethinim, when David appointed them, were to serve the Levites just as Levites served the priests. Cange, *Glossary*, vol. IV, col. 1147.] and ministers of the house of God.

But you, as we have frequently learned, to the disgrace and burden alike of churches and clerics, take up lawsuits as pretexts for lawsuits, in order to impose collections or tallages on them. You oppress them with shameful compulsory services; if perhaps they refuse to pay or undergo them, [Col. 0047D] you either ban them, exposing them to the attacks of evildoers, or forbid them the use both of common property and of common offices, or otherwise compel them violently to the aforesaid burdens, so that, driven by an almost unavoidable necessity, they make payment even unwillingly.

[Therefore, lest the priesthood be held today in a worse condition among the Christian people than it was formerly among Jews or Gentiles, we strictly command all of you, under attestation of the divine judgment, [Col. 0048A] to abstain from the aforesaid exactions and injuries and in no way compel clerics or churches to such burdens. Rather, receive humbly and with thanksgiving whatever assistance churches may decide to contribute, without any coercion, toward relieving common needs and necessities, whenever a bishop and clergy together perceive a need or advantage so great that lay resources are inadequate.

Otherwise, since the Lateran council also forbids the commission of such acts under pain of excommunication, and since it is certainly just that spiritual things be withheld from laymen who do not shrink from taking temporal goods away from clerics, any among you who hereafter presume to contravene our command are to know themselves bound by the chains of excommunication.] Nor [Col. 0048B] shall such contemners ever obtain the benefit of absolution without a special mandate of the Apostolic See, until they present themselves in person before the apostolic presence in order to make full satisfaction.

Moreover, we decree void and empty, never at any time to have force, the enactments and judgments promulgated by those excommunicated persons or at their command. Since fraud and deceit ought not to aid anyone, let none of you be deceived by the vain error of supposing that he may endure anathema during his term of office as though afterward he could not be compelled to render the debt of satisfaction. For we decree that both the person who refused to make satisfaction and his successor, unless he makes satisfaction within a month, are to remain bound by ecclesiastical coercion [Col. 0048C] until he has made suitable satisfaction to the church; for he who succeeds to the honor succeeds to the burden.

And so that a city which resists our command may feel our hand laid more heavily upon it, we shall order that its citizens, arriving at fairs with their merchandise, be detained until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at the Lateran, 16 April.

### XLVI

[Note: [Col. 0048D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §65.]

**To …, Archbishop of Milan** [Note: [Col. 0048D] Book III, letter 6, note.]; **the bishops, abbots, priors, provosts, and other prelates of churches established in Lombardy.** He complains that they did not oppose the consuls and other magistrates of Lombardy when these compelled clerics to pay burdens. (Lateran, as above.)

[Col. 0048D]

We have been pierced inwardly by grief of heart and troubled by heavy sorrow, because scarcely any among you have hitherto been found to set yourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord and, like the tower of David raised against Damascus, to resist manfully those who seek in every way to enslave the Church redeemed by Christ’s precious blood. Although the podestàs, consuls, and councillors of Lombardy have grievously burdened you, your churches, and your clerics [Col. 0049A] in many ways, we have nevertheless heard of none among you who resisted them in defense of his church. Like mute dogs unable to bark, you preferred that your churches be enslaved rather than undergo tribulations, straits, and pressures in defense of their freedom.

We therefore admonish, counsel, and exhort your discretion, strictly commanding you through apostolic letters and by virtue of obedience, that henceforth you set yourselves as a wall for the Church of God and do not allow yourselves, your churches, or your clerics to be burdened with the weight of exactions; for we are ready to grant you apostolic protection in your necessities. We have indeed strictly commanded our beloved sons, the podestàs, consuls, and councillors of Lombardy, present and [Col. 0049B] future, under attestation of the divine judgment, entirely to refrain from the aforesaid injuries and in no way impose the burdens of exactions upon clerics and churches. Otherwise, since the Lateran council also, etc., in nearly the same manner to the end.

Wherefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters to announce this sentence and take care that it is observed inviolate by all.

Given as above.

### XLVII

**To the Abbot of Abingdon** [Note: [Col. 0049D] Concerning the abbots of this monastery around the period with which we are occupied, the authors of *Monasticon Anglicanum* provide no information.], **the Prior of Henley, and Master M., canon of Bridlington, of the diocese of Bangor.** He confirms a sentence concerning the betrothal between the daughter of the Prince of the Isles and the Prince of North Wales. (Lateran, 19 April.)

[Col. 0049C]

Formerly the beloved son, the nobleman N., [Note: [Col. 0049D] The person denoted here by the initial N. is elsewhere, see the following note, indicated by the letter R.; but perhaps both are wrong. More correctly, as below in this very letter, L. A contemporary author, Gerald, himself Welsh, expressly names Llywelyn, Prince of North Wales, at this time: *On the Right and Status of the Church of St Davids*, part II, p. 554. Llywelyn, likewise, appears as founder of Aberconwy Abbey in Carmarthenshire in a charter given in 1198, the tenth year of his principate, 7 January: *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 918. Is he the same as Llywelyn, Prince of Gwynedd, to whom John, King of England, gave his daughter Anne in marriage and from whom he is said to have taken fortresses and towns in 1211, when he entered North Wales with a great army? *Annals of the Church of St Davids*, under 1211. See also *Annals of the Church of Worcester*, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, pp. 481–482.] Prince of North Wales, humbly asked us to grant him permission to take in marriage the daughter of the nobleman …, Prince of the Isles, whom he wrote that he had betrothed by earnest-money, etc. In nearly the same manner as in the Register of the second year, [Note: [Col. 0050D] Letter 233, addressed to the Bishop of Man—perhaps St Davids should be read—the Archdeacon of Bangor, and the Prior of the island of Glannaf; continuing through “may be able to unite [them in marriage].”] in the month of December, through “may be able to unite [them].”

When the parties had therefore appeared before the aforesaid judges, as they informed us in their letters, it was clearly established for them by witnesses that the girl, after completing eight years, had been betrothed by earnest-money to L., Prince of North Wales, with the consent both of herself and of her parents. But while he postponed taking her in marriage out of necessity, she was subsequently betrothed by her uncle without [Col. 0049D] his consent to another man. That man had never carnally known her and had entered upon the way of all flesh—that is, he had died. Therefore, after taking counsel with prudent men, the judges judicially granted authority, in the name of the Apostolic See, for the same girl to be betrothed to the aforesaid L., [Col. 0050A] Prince of North Wales, lest discord formerly arisen between them and now quieted should arise again, as they informed us in their letters.

We therefore hold their sentence ratified and firm, unless some other reasonable matter stands in the way, and command you by authority of these presents to cause it to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal removed. Let no letters obtained contrary to the truth, etc., stand in the way. But if not all … let two, etc.

### XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0050D] Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 99, §5, and Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §9, cite this letter.]

**To P.,** [Note: [Col. 0050D] He has already been mentioned frequently.] **cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, legate of the Apostolic See.** He replies on certain articles concerning which the latter had requested an answer. (Lateran, 21 April.)

[Col. 0050B]

Among the matters which you conveyed to us by your letters, you requested our answer on three articles concerning which you especially doubted: you feared that the Venetians, as fools, might refuse to obtain the benefit of absolution; that they might refuse to recognize you as legate of the Apostolic See; and that, as you had learned for certain, they intended to set out for Greece with the son of …, formerly emperor of Constantinople, whom they intend to take with them.

We therefore briefly answer your discretion on this matter and command you by apostolic letters: unless they receive absolution according to the form which we know that we expressed to you in other letters, promise firmly not to presume to take up arms against Christians, [Col. 0050C] and receive and treat you as legate of the Apostolic See, humbly and devoutly obeying you, you are to leave their army—lest you seem to consent to their wickedness—as an army rejected by the Lord and removed from his blessings, and direct your journey toward Jerusalem. But proceed confidently with the Franks if they choose to follow the treachery of the Venetians; and concerning the absolution of the barons, should they perhaps refuse to bind their successors or heirs, prudently do what God shall deign to inspire in you.

Given at the Lateran, 21 April.

### XLIX

**To the Prior and Brethren of the Church of the Holy Savior of Piller.** He receives them under protection, with an annual payment. (Lateran, 21 April.)

[Col. 0050D]

“Customarily grants assent,” etc., as far as “assent”; your churches and persons, etc., under the form of protection. As a token that this protection has been obtained from the Apostolic See, two pounds of wax, freely offered to us, shall be paid annually to us and our successors by that church. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 21 April.

In the same form to …, prior of the church of Saint James, etc., under the form of protection. “As a token,” etc. “Two pounds of wax,” etc.

### L

[Note: [Col. 0051D] Ughellus has already published this letter, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 469.]

**To the Bishop of Florence** [Note: [Col. 0051D] “Peter governed the Church of Florence from 1189 until 1205, in which year he died; and, apart from a few grants, nothing concerning him is found.” Thus far Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. III, col. 137. Yet there is a difficulty. In autograph acts drawn up in 1211, Peter, Bishop of Florence, is expressly named as still occupying the see. See Mittarelli, *Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, p. 180. And, more surprisingly, in a letter of Innocent, no longer extant, given in 1202 on 14 August from the monastery of Subiaco, the pope commanded John, Bishop of Florence, and the provost of that church to bring to a proper conclusion a dispute concerning tithes and certain other matters, brought against the Camaldolese hermitage by the Abbot of Vallombrosa. Ibid., p. 190.], **and the Abbot of Vallombrosa** [Note: [Col. 0052D] We have no ready information concerning the Abbot of Vallombrosa.]. **Concerning the transfer of the cathedral church of Arezzo within the walls of the same city.** (Lateran, 22 April.)

[Col. 0051B] On behalf of our venerable brother . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0052D] Amadeus was elected bishop of Arezzo in 1183, on the sixteenth day of January, in place of Gualandus, who, having been chosen bishop in the preceding year after the death of Heliottus, who died on 6 December 1181, had laid down the episcopal burden on 25 December 1182. He died shortly after the dispatch of these letters by Innocent, namely about the end of May; and on the fifth day before the Kalends of June Gregory was appointed in his place. MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, vol. IV, pp. 105 and 193.], bishop, and of our beloved sons, the provost of the canons, and the nobleman A . . . . ., podestà of the people of Arezzo, a petition has often been presented to us, and both by letters and by an envoy we have been entreated that, for the peace of the city and Church of Arezzo and for the common benefit, we grant them permission to transfer the cathedral church, together with the residence of the canons and all its rights and privileges, to a place within the walls of the city upon which they might mutually agree.

But, after careful deliberation with our brethren, we did not judge that such a petition should be granted under those terms. For if perhaps they should ask for another church, situated within the city, to be united with it as one cathedral church, it was first necessary to inform us which church should be joined to it [Col. 0051C], and whether that church belonged exclusively to the right of the Church of Arezzo or was subject to another, so that, without the consent of the one to whom it was subject, it might not be raised into a cathedral church. Moreover, the increase of privilege, liberty, right, and honour which the same church would acquire from such a union had to be set forth to us, so that, informed concerning all matters by their report, we might better determine what was more expedient.

Having received our answer on this matter, they humbly informed us that, in order to allay the discord and extinguish the long-standing hatred which had always disturbed both the Church of Arezzo and the city, by an equal vote and harmonious will they had chosen the church of Saint Peter Major, with all [Col. 0051D] its rights and appurtenances, both within and outside the city, to be united [Col. 0052A] to the cathedral church—on this condition: that the monastery of Saint Hora, which does not belong to the Church of Arezzo by any intervening title and to which that church is known to be subject, should receive, according to the judgment of worthy men, suitable compensation for all the services which it customarily receives from it annually. By devout supplication they requested that the Apostolic See’s kindness grant this church to them as a cathedral church; firmly promising that every reverence and honour which other cities render to their cathedral churches, both in festivals and in individual honours, should henceforth be rendered to the said Church by the clergy and people of the city of Arezzo, notwithstanding what has hitherto been observed up to this time because of the dissension which arose between the aforesaid city and Church.

Furthermore, the podestà, together with the entire council and commune of the city of Arezzo, of free and unanimous will, decreed that the aforesaid church should remain forever free and immune from all forced services and exactions; and he decreed that the rights and castles of the bishopric, and the honours and other possessions of the canonries of Arezzo, should everywhere be maintained and defended by the commune of that city.

Therefore, desiring to provide for concord in the city and for the Church’s benefit, especially since the said church of Saint Peter is subject to the diocesan law of Arezzo, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce the abbot and brethren of the said monastery [Col. 0052C], and, if necessary, to compel them by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, to grant favour and consent to the union of that church with the cathedral church, after suitable compensation concerning it has first been received according to the judgment of worthy men. By apostolic authority, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, you shall place the provost and canons of Arezzo in corporal possession, provided that at least four canons and two clerics remain in the former church, by whom it may be served sufficiently and suitably. Moreover, you shall provide the same church with the fullest security concerning the liberties, immunities, and other matters written above, so that it may never at any time be harassed concerning them.

[Col. 0052D] Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

LI [Note: [Col. 0053D] Raynaldus published part of this letter, under the year 1203, §46. The passages found in his work are enclosed here in brackets.]. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF CHRIST WHO SHALL EXAMINE THESE LETTERS. On the penance of those who killed C., bishop of Würzburg. (Lateran, fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 0053A]

It is more fitting to weep than to recount what an execrable deed and impious crime those committed who, in sacrilegious boldness, wickedly laid impious hands upon the Lord’s anointed, C. [Note: [Col. 0053D] See letter 155 of Book V.], bishop of Würzburg and chancellor of the imperial court, cruelly killing him. Yet, since divine mercy surpasses human wickedness, and human miseries cannot be measured against the mercies of the Lord, since the Lord does not will the death of the sinner but that he should be converted [Col. 0053B] and live—as one who is patient, most merciful, and abundant in goodness—we who, though unworthy, exercise His office on earth, knowing that there is greater joy among God’s angels over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance, could neither have nor ought to have denied access to pardon to such murderers when penitent, however grievously they had sinned; for we know that the Lord said through the prophet: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, I will remember none of his iniquities.”

[Bodo, therefore, Hen. Fuson, his vassal, knights, together with Henrod [otherwise Herold] and Conrad, his servants, having come into our presence and confessed that they had killed the aforesaid bishop [Col. 0053C], since they sorrowfully repented of their offences and humbly requested that penance be imposed upon them by us for so enormous a crime—because the gate of mercy is not to be closed to penitents—we committed them, on the counsel of our brethren, to the hearing of our beloved son II. [Note: [Col. 0054D] See Book III, letter 41, note.], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin. After hearing their confession, he caused them, at our command, to stand before us for several days amid a throng of people, stripped to their breeches, with ropes around their necks; and he imposed upon them such a penalty that henceforth they should never use arms except against Saracens or in defence of their lives; that they should wear neither vair nor grey fur, ermine, or coloured cloth; that they should not attend public spectacles; and that married men should not marry after [Col. 0053D] the death of their wives. They shall go, as soon as they can, to the province of Jerusalem, there to serve the Lord against the Saracens for four years. But Bodo, who was the principal offender, shall bring with him at his own expense three or two knights, or at least one.

Until these four execrable murderers undertake the journey to Jerusalem, they shall proceed as public penitents, barefoot and clad in woollen garments; they shall fast on bread and water on the second, fourth, and sixth weekdays, during the Ember Days, and on the vigils of saints; [Col. 0054A] they shall keep three Lents in the year, namely before the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord, and after Pentecost. Not only shall they eat no meat during these three solemn periods and on the day on which the aforesaid bishop was killed, but they shall never eat meat again. They shall chant the Lord’s Prayer one hundred times by day and night, and make fifty genuflections; they shall not presume to receive the body and blood of the Lord except at the last point of death.

Once they are overseas, they shall fast on the fourth and sixth weekdays, on saints’ vigils, and during the Ember Days, as stated above, with Lenten food; they shall eat meat only on Sunday and Thursday; and they shall always say the Lord’s Prayer and make the aforesaid number of genuflections. Whenever they can safely enter any city of Germany [Col. 0054B], they shall go naked, clothed only in breeches, with a rope around the neck and rods in hand, to its principal church, and receive discipline from the canons of that church. If they are asked why they do this, they shall say that they do it because of the perpetration of the aforesaid crime.

Whenever they can safely be in the city of Würzburg, at Easter, Pentecost, the Nativity of the Lord, and the feast of its principal church, namely Saint Paulinus, they shall leave the city; and nevertheless, naked, clothed only in breeches and carrying a rope around the neck and rods in hand, they shall attend the cathedral church at the celebration of the principal Mass. Prostrating themselves on the ground before the altar in the presence of the bishop and canons, they shall humbly request and receive discipline from [Col. 0054C] them. When they return from overseas, they shall come to the Apostolic See to receive counsel and command.]

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

LII [Note: [Col. 0054D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §69.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MESSINA [Note: [Col. 0054D] On him see Book V, letter 60, note.], A MEMBER OF THE ROYAL HOUSEHOLD. He praises him for expelling Markward from Sicily and restoring Messina to fidelity toward the Apostolic See and the king. (Lateran.)

From the letters of your brotherhood we have learned that, through your exertions, the son of pride has been driven from Sicily, and that the city of Messina persists in devotion toward us and fidelity to the king [Col. 0054D]; and, once tranquillity has been restored, the whole of Sicily will, with God’s help, shortly follow it in this purpose of devotion. Therefore, we render whatever thanksgivings we can to Him from whom every good proceeds, commending the diligence of your solicitude, which does not fail but rather advances amid adversities. Thus, by God’s grace, it has prevailed against that Philistine of uncircumcised lips, who was reproaching the ranks of the children of Israel.

Neither you nor others ought to doubt the constancy of the Apostolic See, which, founded upon the firm rock by Christ the rock [Col. 0055A], knows neither how to yield to winds nor be softened by rains, since it wholly avoids the mark of fickleness. Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your brotherhood, and command you by apostolic letters, that, persevering in devotion toward us and the Roman Church, you do not fail but rather advance; and, since you know it is written, “The end, not the struggle, crowns” [as written], persevere to the end, that you may deserve to receive a reward according to your labour. For we, God willing, shall attend to your honour and advancement in such a way that you will rejoice to have laboured for the honour of the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran.

LIII [Note: [Col. 0055D] Raynaldus, in the place cited.]. TO THE SAME. That he is to receive from all counts throughout Sicily, etc., and others, the oath of *balia* to be rendered to the pope. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0055B]

Having experienced the purity of your faith and the steadfastness of your devotion, we commit to you without any hesitation matters which we believe will promote the honour of the Apostolic See and our own, and the exaltation of the kingdom. Therefore we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to delay in demanding and receiving in our name, from all counts, barons, citizens, and others who have not yet rendered to us the oath of *balia*, that oath. As for opponents, etc.

[Col. 0055C] Given at the Lateran.

LIV [Note: [Col. 0055D] Raynaldus, ibid.]. TO THE NOBLE MEN, COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND OTHERS ESTABLISHED IN SICILY. That they are to take before the archbishop of Messina the oath called *balia*. (Lateran.)

Your whole body knows how greatly the Apostolic See has hitherto laboured for the defence and peace of the kingdom, for the exaltation of our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily. Therefore, since the Lord now seems for the most part to have assented to our prayers, we admonish and earnestly exhort you all, and command you by apostolic letters, that all who have not yet rendered to us the oath [Col. 0055D] of *balia* shall not delay to render it, in the hands of our venerable brother . . . . . ., archbishop of Messina, as an oath of royal fidelity. We have therefore commanded him not to omit demanding and receiving it. As for opponents, etc.

Given as above.

LV [Note: [Col. 0055D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §19.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM. He confirms to him the right of crowning the kings of Hungary and other rights. (Palestrina, third day before the Nones of May.)

[Col. 0056A]

To just petitioners, etc., as far as “assent.” The right which was expressly acknowledged to the metropolitan church of Esztergom by Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, by Béla, king of the Hungarians of illustrious memory, and by the Church of Kalocsa—namely, that the kings of Hungary must always be crowned by the archbishops of Esztergom—as is contained in their authentic documents, and which Clement and Celestine, our predecessors of happy memory, confirmed by their letters; likewise the right which you possess in conferring ecclesiastical sacraments upon the kings and queens of Hungary and their heirs; [Col. 0056B] and the ecclesiastical jurisdiction which you possess over the provosts who are officials of the royal household, and which the same predecessor of ours, Celestine, decreed that your church should possess; also the jurisdiction which you hold over the royal abbeys and provostships subject everywhere throughout Hungary to the Church of Esztergom; moreover, the tithes, first fruits, and incense due to the said Church from the royal treasury: just as all these matters are known by right or custom to belong to your church, we confirm them to you and your successors by apostolic authority, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Palestrina, on the third day before the Nones of May.

LVI [Note: [Col. 0055D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §19.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM. On royal provostships [Note: [Col. 0055D] See letter 7 of this sixth book.]. (Seventh day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0056C]

Since formerly our dearest son in Christ, H., the illustrious king of Hungary, informed us both through his envoys and by royal letters that certain royal abbeys and provostships belonged to him in temporal matters and to us in spiritual matters, with no intermediary, at his request we wrote to him in this form: “Royal magnificence,” etc., as far as the end of preceding letter 7.

But you, subsequently appearing before the Apostolic See, declared orally in our presence and that of our brethren that ecclesiastical jurisdiction over royal abbeys and provostships belonged to you and the Church of Esztergom. Therefore, desiring henceforth to provide against injury to you and that Church [Col. 0056D], we decree by the authority of these present letters that, on account of the letters which we first sent concerning royal provostships and abbeys subject everywhere throughout Hungary to the Church of Esztergom, no prejudice shall arise against you or your successors. Therefore let no one, etc. Seventh day before the Ides of May. [Note: [Col. 0055D] At the end of this letter, the Conti copy contains this note: “The term for appearing before the Apostolic See is extended for . . . . . the bishop of Passau, until the next feast of Saint Luke”; it is plainly evident that this belongs to an entirely different letter.]

LVII [Note: [Col. 0057C] Ughellus published this letter, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 56.]. TO ANDREW [Note: [Col. 0057C] Andrew had shortly before succeeded Raynald; chosen archbishop in 1200 from being archdeacon of Acerenza, he was confirmed by Innocent in 1201 by the privilege reported by Ughellus (place cited, col. 53). But in this year, 1203, owing to the urgent need and benefit of the Church of Acerenza, then almost desolate, Innocent established a cathedral at Matera and united it to the former cathedral of Acerenza together with use of the pallium. Under Pope Honorius III, Andrew was accused in 1217 of simony and collusion; when he neglected to present himself before the Apostolic See, he was deprived of office and benefice, then absolved through Honorius’s kindness and restored to his dignity. Under Gregory IX he returned to his vomit, and in 1231 Gregory again summoned him before the Apostolic See. But Andrew, with his conscience as witness, having refused to appear before apostolic delegates, was, willingly or unwillingly, deprived of the archiepiscopal dignity, and afterward ended his life miserably while Gregory still held the helm. UGHELLUS, place cited.], ARCHBISHOP OF ACERENZA, AND HIS SUCCESSORS TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. He establishes a cathedral at Matera and joins it to that of Acerenza [Note: [Col. 0058C] See Book II, letters 159 and 164.]. (Palestrina, Nones of May.)

[Col. 0057A]

“Our brethren and fellow bishops,” etc., as far as this point: because of clear benefit and urgent necessity, with the common counsel of our brethren, we have decided that a cathedral church be established at Matera in such a way that it is united to the former cathedral. Likewise, the use of the pallium, etc.

Given at Palestrina, through the hand of John, etc., on the Nones of May, in the sixth year.

LVIII [Note: [Col. 0058C] It is found, though mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book II, title 20, “On witnesses and testimonies,” chapter 33. The passages found there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are indicated.]. TO THE PRIOR OF SAINT FREDIANO OF LUCCA, AND MASTER B., CANON OF PISA. On rejecting the bishop-elect of Lucca [Note: [Col. 0058D] Letters 140 and 153 of Book V must certainly be compared.]. (Ferentino, second day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0057B]

[Having carefully heard both your letters and the depositions of the witnesses, we have clearly learned that nothing has been sufficiently demonstrated against our beloved son . . . ., bishop-elect of Lucca, except hearsay and public report alone, since concerning the other matters, even if some perhaps seem to have been proved, the witnesses are either alone or such that they could not lawfully establish them. But because witnesses were not received concerning the marriage which the same bishop-elect is said to have contracted with a widow, owing to the appeal lodged [Note: [Col. 0058D] The *Decretals* read: “the obstacle of an appeal.”], lest laymen or women be received against him in such a matter [Col. 0057C], as you informed us in your letters—although the envoys of the same bishop-elect tried to prove something else before us [Note: [Col. 0058D] The words distinguished in italic type are absent here and below.]—we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters, so that the objection of so great an irregularity may not remain unexamined: lawfully receive and prudently examine the witnesses, whether laymen or women, provided they are suitable, who are introduced within a month to prove this matter; and solemnly excommunicate anyone who presumes to impede them from bearing testimony to the truth.

Then [Note: [Col. 0058D] The *Decretals* read: “finally.”], once the testimonies have been published, if it should appear that such irregularity [Col. 0058A] has not been proved, prescribe for the same bishop-elect a canonical purgation concerning the matters included in the commission made to you and expressed in the testimonies which we remit to you under our seal [Note: [Col. 0058D] The *Decretals* read only: “concerning the objections.”], to be performed by seven canons of the principal church, or priors of the associated churches [Note: [Col. 0058D] This word is omitted by the *Decretals*.], of the city of Lucca—priests or deacons of good repute. Once this has been received, set him a suitable term within which he is to present himself before us for consecration.

But if either the impediment of irregularity is proved, or he does not perform the prescribed purgation within a month, then, strengthened by our authority and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, you shall wholly remove him from the prelacy of the Church of Lucca [Col. 0058B], and command the chapter on our behalf not to delay holding a canonical election of another. You shall also declare the archpriest of Lucca and G. Amfoss., sacristan, suspended from office and benefice until they deserve to obtain our indulgence, because they sent us letters against the aforesaid bishop-elect in the name of a far larger part of the chapter, whereas it is evident from the aforesaid testimonies that a far larger part of the chapter was unaware of such letters.]

Moreover, inquire diligently whether the often-mentioned bishop-elect, after an appeal had been lodged to us, presumed to open the letters directed to us, and faithfully inform us what you discover concerning this.

Given at Ferentino, on the second day before the Ides of May.

LIX [Note: [Col. 0058D] It survives entire among the *Decretals*, Book I, title 9, “On resignation,” chapter 9. Variant readings are given, although none is significant. Moreover, it must certainly be compared with Book V, letter 17; see that letter.]. TO . . . . . . ., ARCHBISHOP OF YORK. He confirms to the archbishop of Ragusa benefices in the bishopric of Carlisle.

[Col. 0058C]

At the urgent petition [Note: [Col. 0058D] The words distinguished in italic type, here and below, are omitted in the *Decretals*.] of our venerable brother . . ., archbishop of Ragusa, we judged that he should be released from the care and solicitude by which he was bound to the Church of Ragusa [Note: [Col. 0058D] See the notes to the letter cited above.], namely because he could not safely remain there, and, if he had access to it, danger of death threatened him. But lest the same archbishop suffer a deficiency in temporal means, to the discredit of our ministry, we earnestly admonish your brotherhood [Col. 0059A], and command you by apostolic letters, to preserve for his support [Note: [Col. 0059D] The *Decretals* add “the benefice.”] that which has been conferred upon him in the bishopric of Carlisle and the church of Maleborn [Note: [Col. 0059D] The *Decretals* read “Malebros.”], through the munificence and liberality of our dearest son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of England [Note: [Col. 0059D] The *Decretals* read “royal,” in place of “our dearest son in Christ, J., illustrious king of England.”], and through your grant. [Note: [Col. 0059D] Carlisle, formerly Lugubalia, is said by Matthew Paris and Matthew of Westminster to have been raised into an episcopal see by Henry I, king of England, in 1131. See also Roger of Howden under the year 1134.] For we have granted him, through the kindness of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0059D] In the *Decretals*, “to whom,” in place of “for we have granted him through the kindness of the Apostolic See.”], that in that bishopric he may exercise episcopal office without use of the pallium, while rendering reverence and obedience to you as metropolitan.

LX. TO W., A CLERIC. On an annual rent.

“It is customary to grant,” etc., as far as “assent.” The hospital [Col. 0059B] which you built at your own expense upon your own land for the reception of the poor, etc., under the form of protection. But, as a token that this protection has been received from the Apostolic See, one bezant freely offered, etc. Let no one, etc.

LXI. TO THE PRIOR OF SAINT FREDIANO OF LUCCA, AND MASTER B., CANON OF PISA. On the same matter as above, letter 58.

“Having heard both your letters and the depositions of the witnesses,” etc., as in the third preceding letter, as far as “expressed,” to be performed by seven bishops of Tuscany, or canons of the principal church, or priors of the associated churches of the city of Lucca, priests or deacons of good repute. Notwithstanding letters obtained by the opponents [Col. 0059C] in which no mention has been made of bishops. Once the purgation has been received, etc., as far as the end.

LXII [Note: [Col. 0059D] It is found almost entire in Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §62.]. TO THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0059D] This man has already been discussed above, Book V, letter 23, note.] AND CHAPTER OF WORCESTER. Decree concerning Saint Wulfstan’s enrolment among the saints. (Ferentino, second [otherwise seventh] day before the Ides of May.)

Since according to evangelical truth, etc., as far as the passage in the second book of the Registers [Note: [Col. 0059D] Thus in the Conti copy. Yet the letter to which we are referred here is sought in vain in Book II.]: among whom Wulfstan [Note: [Col. 0060D] Wulfstan, renowned for holiness, was elected bishop of Worcester from being prior of the church of Worcester on 29 August 1062; he died on 19 January 1095. Wharton published a brief account of the life of Saint Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, by Hemming, a monk of Worcester, in *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 541. William of Malmesbury composed a separate history of the life of the same prelate, which may be found in the same Wharton, ibid., part II, p. 241. See also Roger of Howden, frequently.], bishop of Worcester, while formerly living in the world excelled in great merits, and now living in heaven shines forth in many miracles, so that his holiness is demonstrated by sure evidences, etc., in the same manner as far as: “Indeed, when [Col. 0059D] the merits and miracles of so great a man [Col. 0060A] had reached our hearing, desiring to proceed with greater deliberation, since a judgment of this kind is divine rather than human, we commanded our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury, and the bishop of Ely, and our beloved sons, the abbots of Saint Edmund’s and Wiburn [Note: [Col. 0060D] Perhaps Woburn should be read. The reference seems to be to the abbot of Woburn Abbey in Bedfordshire, founded in 1145. See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 829.], that, coming together to the church of Worcester, they should prescribe a three-day fast for your entire body and for the people of the city, during which all of you should unanimously ask Him who is the way, the truth, and the life, that He reveal in this matter the way of truth unto life. Thereafter, they were to investigate the truth diligently, not only through testimonies, but through witnesses, public report, and authentic writing, concerning the virtue of his morals and the truth of the signs—that is, his deeds and miracles—and faithfully report it to us.

Accordingly, [Col. 0060B] when they had come to the church of Worcester, they proceeded according to the ecclesiastical command; and they arranged that you, brother bishop, should send us under their seals [Note: [Col. 0060D] Thus also in Raynaldus. It seems that “and” should be read.] a few among his many miracles, concerning which sworn witnesses had testified and to whose testimony the whole city gave acclaim, as well as an authentic account of his life written in the English language a hundred years before. You, later appearing in our presence, humbly requested that we enrol the aforesaid bishop among the catalogue of saints to be venerated.

It thus became evident to us from authentic writing and the depositions of witnesses that at his tomb the mute received speech, the leper cleansing, and persons afflicted with dropsy and paralysis received health; and that the Lord continually works very many miracles [Col. 0060C] when His own name and that of the aforesaid bishop are invoked.
