Therefore, having been rendered more certain concerning his merits and miracles by many great proofs, not only testimonies but also witnesses, and since, according to the Prophet, the Lord is to be praised in His saints, we have, with the counsel of our brethren, enrolled that blessed bishop and confessor Wulfstan in the catalogue of saints, and decreed that his memory be celebrated among the saints. Therefore, we admonish and exhort all of you in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters to observe humbly and devoutly what we have solemnly and carefully established, so that through his merits and prayers we and you may obtain pardon from the most merciful Judge [Col. 0060D]. We also issue the collect to be said in his commemoration [Col. 0061A], which we have caused to be written below on this page:

“Pour into us, O Lord, the spirit of Your love, that, through the intercession of blessed Wulfstan, Your confessor and bishop, we may deserve to taste Your sweetness in eternal blessedness. Through, etc.”

Given at Ferentino, on the second day before the Ides of May.

LXIII [Note: [Col. 0061D] Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1203, §61. See also Book V, letter 160.]. TO JOHN, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. He complains that he has not yet restored the archbishop of Dublin to favour; he threatens him with the penalty of an interdict. (Ferentino, twelfth day before the Kalends of June.)

We believe that the pitiable cry of our venerable brother, [Col. 0061B] the archbishop of Dublin, has now ascended to heaven; and would that, because we have shown such deference to your royal serenity, we have not offended our Creator. For, although before you were raised to the kingship you compelled that archbishop to go into exile from his church, and although repeatedly admonished by the Roman Church you have not troubled to receive him into your favour, once the Lord, looking down on you from on high, raised you to the throne of the kingdom, we believed that, with God in view, royal magnificence would provide for that archbishop and receive into favour him for whom divine providence had so magnificently provided. But our expectation has been disappointed; for neither for God’s sake nor at the entreaty of our prayers, which you have often received for that archbishop [Col. 0061C], have you taken care to restore royal favour to him. Nor have you allowed yourself to be moved by any prayers, because you have not willed it, to permit him to return to his church and restore to him the goods that were taken away.

Moreover, since he is old and decrepit, and you ought especially to have had pity on him because of his old age, you compel him, outside your whole kingdom, to beg for the necessities of life. If you carefully consider how greatly in all this you offend your Creator, who granted you such power on earth, you ought to fear lest He, who declares that He Himself is honoured and despised in His servants, should both in part avenge in the present the injuries inflicted upon His servants—so that affliction may at least give you understanding—and reserve another vengeance for Himself in the future.

And, in order to add a more grievous affliction [Col. 0061D] to one already afflicted, and further provoke your Creator, not content with having despoiled him of temporal goods, you stretched forth your hand to unlawful acts, commanding the justiciar of Ireland to cause the spiritual affairs of the Church of Dublin to be administered through our venerable brother, the archbishop of Cashel. This is clearly apparent from the copy of your letters which we send enclosed with these letters to your royal serenity.

Since, therefore, we can no longer pass over with closed eyes so great an oppression of the aforesaid archbishop, we ask, admonish, and exhort your royal mildness in the Lord, imposing this upon you for remission of sins: have due regard to God, benignly receive the aforesaid archbishop into your favour, and cause all that has been taken from him to be restored to him. Thus on this occasion you shall fulfil the apostolic command, so that the subsequent correction may expiate the offence of the past and make propitious and favourable to you the God whom you have grievously offended. Otherwise, however much we wish to show deference to your royal serenity, since we can no longer leave uncorrected the exile and oppression of that archbishop, if satisfaction has not been made to him within a month after receipt of these letters, you are to know that divine offices are forbidden [Col. 0062B] in whatever bishopric subject to your jurisdiction you may enter, for as long as you are present there. If even thus the royal heart cannot be softened, we shall, with the Lord’s help, provide otherwise for that archbishop, as we judge expedient.

Given at Ferentino, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June.

LXIV [Note: [Col. 0061D] See Raynaldus, in the same place.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND THE BISHOP OF ELY. On the same matter.

“It is written . . . . . .” If our command has not been fulfilled, let them firmly declare that the aforesaid sentence of interdict is to be observed by all.

LXV [Note: [Col. 0062D] See Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 101, §II.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS [Note: [Col. 0062D] He has already been discussed frequently.]. That he is to amend and correct what needs amendment in the churches subject to him. (Ferentino, twelfth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0062C]

The more strictly your brotherhood would be called to account by the Lord if He saw you neglecting the care of those whose solicitude has been entrusted to you, the more diligently you ought to labour, as is fitting, to correct the offences of your subjects. Know, indeed, that it has come to our hearing that many wicked acts are committed in the churches of your province which appear to require no small correction, and through which scandal comes not so much to the people as [Col. 0062D] no small harm to the churches themselves. Therefore, desiring that these matters be corrected through the diligence of your brotherhood, by the authority of these present letters we grant you permission to correct by our authority, in churches subject to you by diocesan law, both head and members, whatever you find in them needing correction, notwithstanding an appeal frivolously lodged in evasion of ecclesiastical discipline. Therefore let no person at all, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the sixth year.

LXVI [Note: [Col. 0063D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §51.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES [Note: [Col. 0063D] These persons have already been discussed above.], THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE [Note: [Col. 0063D] These persons have already been discussed above.], AND THE ABBOT OF FONTAINE-MORIGNY [Note: [Col. 0063D]

Concerning the abbots of Fontaine-Morigny at about this time, little is found in the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 199. One V. E., abbot, is found in certain charters of the years 1200 and 1202.

“VI. Abbot Guido, in the year 1205, obtains a distinguished privilege from Pope Innocent III.”]

. He commits to them the case of the people of La Charité suspected of the stain of heresy [Note: See Letter 36 of Book Five, and the notes there.]. (Ferentino, 12 Kalends of June [21 May].)

[Col. 0063A]

We have clearly learned from your letters and those of the same abbot how, and to what extent, the proceedings in the case of certain burgesses of La Charité, who had been accused of the crime of heresy, were committed under a specified form to you, brother archbishop, to the bishop of Nevers of good memory, . . ., and likewise to the beloved son, . . ., abbot of Cluny. We therefore, having carefully examined the tenor of those letters, have thought fit to send back to you—who have more fully investigated the truth of the matter—G. . . of Lorris, B. . . Marandi, and R. . . Caraille, who were sent to our presence on this account, together with the aforesaid letters containing the course of the case, which we return to you enclosed under our seal. By these apostolic letters we command and direct you that, after prior examination, you impose a fitting penance for their offences upon those whom you, brother archbishop, after their confessions, judged Catholic, as is expressly contained in the aforesaid letters. Do not permit them to be unduly harassed by anyone on account of this affair; rather defend them from the attacks of malicious persons. With regard to the rest, however, relying on apostolic authority, proceed as you know to be expedient for their salvation and for the establishment of the matter.

[Col. 0063C] Given at Ferentino, 12 Kalends of June [21 May], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

LXVII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT PAUL. He assigns and confirms Monte Porzio, in the Tusculan territory, to the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, on the Ostian Way.

Among the places set apart for divine worship, we wish and ought to venerate with especial devotion the basilica of Blessed Paul, in which you serve the Lord under the regular habit, in proportion as he whose honorable name it enjoys and whose special protection it rejoices in adorned more abundantly, both by life and teaching, the Church of God over which, though unworthy, we preside, and labored more than the other apostles in spreading the Christian faith. For he did not receive from man, but received from the Lord what he himself handed down to us; and his tongue became like the pen of a swiftly writing scribe, so that his sound went out into all the earth and he sowed everywhere the seed of the Lord’s words, as a sower of the word.

For although the prince of the apostles, the blessed apostle Peter, received the fullness of ecclesiastical power, Paul, nevertheless—called by the Lord a chosen vessel—received more abundant grace for preaching than the others, in order that he might bear His name before nations, kings, and the children of Israel, becoming Paul from Saul, and a preacher from a persecutor. Having received the apostolate among the Gentiles, he at length followed that same prince of the apostles, becoming both his companion in preaching and his colleague in suffering, so that together they might consecrate the Roman Church with their blood.

Therefore, that we may show by some effect, however slight, the devotion which we bear toward him, we propose to honor his basilica with a small gift, granting him at least a little from what is his own, since we can give nothing from our own resources. Yet we hope that he who looked upon Abel and his offerings, and accepted the two small coins of the poor widow, through Paul’s merits will look not at the size of the gift but rather at the devotion of the giver.

Moved by this consideration, we apostolically confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, Monte Porzio in the territory of Tusculum with its appurtenances, as it had been assigned to you by our grant, etc. Therefore let no one at all, etc.

LXVIII. TO THE KING OF THE FRANKS. [Note: Raynaldus cites this and the following two letters, Nos. 59 and 60, under the year 1203, §64.] That he should make peace with the king of England. (Ferentino, 7 Kalends of June [26 May].)

Since royal serenity does not fail to know that there ought to be no respect of persons with us, we believe that it will not take it ill if we discharge toward it the duty of our pastoral office, lest, besides offending the divine majesty—which we shall incur if we are negligent—our ministry should also come under reproach among men, should we omit anything arising from current events even in dealings with kings and princes, consulting their wishes rather than their welfare.

Indeed, the word of the Lord ought not to be bound in our mouth, but free, so that we may freely rebuke the disorderly and fulfill, whenever expedient, the Apostle’s saying—which we understand to have been spoken all the more particularly to us because we hold the greater, indeed the highest, place in the Church: having called the others to share in the burden of care, we alone have received the fullness of power. For the Apostle’s word is: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and teaching.” [Note: Thus in the Vatican copy and in Conti.] And the Lord speaks to us through the Prophet: “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up thy voice like a trumpet” [the printed text is corrupt: *quasi t. ex v. t.*]. Since, therefore, Jesus began both to do and to teach, leaving us an example, that we should follow in His footsteps [the printed text is corrupt: *ex v. se. v.*], it is fitting that we, who though unworthy exercise His office on earth, should walk as He walked, insofar as human frailty permits, and follow His footsteps; for we know that “Follow me” was said to Peter among all the apostles.

Your royal highness also knows that at the very beginning of the Lord’s Nativity an angel announced peace to people of good will, and that at the moment of His Passion the Lord bestowed peace upon His disciples as by hereditary right, when, as though making His final testament, He said to them: “My peace I give to you; peace I leave to you” [the printed text is corrupt: *pa. re. v.*]. And, that He might afterward as immortal confirm what He had said when about to die, after His resurrection He first used this greeting to His disciples: “Peace be with you”; and again I say, “Peace be with you.”

Therefore, lest we who, according to the Apostle, are heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ, should prove unworthy of the inheritance left us, and should show ourselves ungrateful for the grace which He has poured out upon us in more abundant measure, we are bound to proclaim peace, especially to the children of peace, so that our peace may rest upon them according to the Gospel’s word; since, according to the Prophet, we are bound to seek peace and pursue it.

We carry this out toward royal serenity with all the greater confidence because we know that you received more graciously our beloved son P. [Note: This man has already been mentioned several times.], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, formerly sent for a similar cause, and that in him you more fully approved our concern. For you know—as one who has read this daily in the book of experience—how great are the evils that, through sins demanding it, have arisen from the dissension between you and our dearest son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of England; evils which have come not only commonly upon your kingdoms, but generally upon the whole Christian people.

For behold: while you contend with one another, churches are destroyed, the rich are impoverished, the poor oppressed; and, while neither religion nor sex is spared, religious men who were accustomed to devote themselves to prayer are compelled to beg, and women who had vowed their virginity to the author of virginity are, to our sorrow, prostituted to the pleasure of robbers. The Saracens too now take courage against Christians; and those who, while you were reconciled and at peace with one another, feared exile, have recovered courage from your discord and have risen more strongly for the destruction of Christians. This is especially so because the princes of Gaul—concerning whom we lodge complaint before the divine majesty and your serenity—have departed from their good purpose, have turned their arms against Christians contrary to our prohibition, and have not even ceased so as to rise again, but, as has been reported to us, have proposed attempts worse than their former deeds.

Moreover, from such dissension follows both slaughter of bodies and destruction of souls; and we grieve all the more because the soul is more precious than the body, since, according to the testimony of Truth, it profits a person nothing to gain the whole world and suffer loss of his soul. Therefore, lest the blood of so many peoples be required at our hands; lest we appear guilty of so many deaths, if—God forbid—we keep silent in so great a necessity of the Christian people like dumb dogs unable to bark, and, as though our tongue clung to our throat, neglect to rebuke what must be rebuked: we have thought fit to send to your presence our beloved son, . . ., abbot of Casamari [Note: Concerning the abbot of Casamari, see frequently in the Registers of Innocent.], a religious, prudent, and faithful man, acceptable to us and our brethren by reason of his integrity. We have joined with him our beloved sons, . . ., abbots of Trois-Fontaines [Note: We have already dealt above with the abbot of Trois-Fontaines.] and of Duno [Note: Concerning this man we have nothing at hand.].

We ask your royal serenity, exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: at their admonition—or rather, truly, at ours—you shall either establish a firm peace with the aforesaid king or enter into suitable truces, so that meanwhile the question of a lasting peace to be restored between you, saving the justice of each party, may be discussed more freely and securely. Otherwise, however much we love both you and him in the Lord, we can by no means refrain from causing to be inviolably observed those things which our said messenger, according to the form given him by us, judges ought to be established.

We ask royal serenity to receive our said messenger graciously and, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, to take particular care to honor him.

Given at Ferentino, 7 Kalends of June [26 May], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

LXIX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. On the same matter.

[Col. 0066C]

“Since royal serenity,” etc., as far as “may rest.” “For you know,” etc., as far as “have risen.” “Moreover, from such dissension,” etc., to the end.

Given as above.

LXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF THE FRANKS. On the same matter.

“Since royal serenity,” etc., as far as “may rest.” “For you know,” etc., in nearly the same manner as far as “have risen.” “Moreover, from such dissension,” etc., in the same manner as far as “may be discussed.”

Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort all of you, and by apostolic letters command and strictly order you, that, faithfully and effectively assisting our same messenger, you diligently and advantageously press the aforesaid king of the Franks, so that he may humbly comply with your admonition. Otherwise, humbly receive and inviolably observe whatever the said messenger, according to the form given him by us, judges ought to be established; and do not presume, through any rashness, to act against it.

Nevertheless, we will and strictly command that you receive and treat our aforesaid messenger with kindly affection, and take care to honor him in such a manner that we may regard it as pleasing, and ought in return to respond graciously to you and your churches on that account; for we account devotion shown to our messengers as shown to us, and believe ourselves to be honored in them.

LXXI. TO WALTER, CHANCELLOR OF THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1202, §5; he cites it again and prints a fragment of it under the year 1203, §69. The few words printed there are enclosed here in brackets.] [Note: Concerning this man we have already dealt with him under Letter 39 of Book Five.] He receives him into favor, and accepts none of the four securities offered by him, except that he should confirm by deeds what he promised in words and what pertains to the right of the Roman Church. (Ferentino.)

Although you have grievously offended us in many matters, nevertheless, because we, though unworthy, bear on earth the office of Him who, even when angered, does not forget to show mercy, we caused you to be absolved from the bond of excommunication—would that you had then returned with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.

Now we have graciously received your letters, which you sent through James, your clerk, the bearer of the present letters [Note: “and others” appears to need to be added.], and have fully understood their tenor, carefully considering what those men took care to set before us by your command. They said that henceforth you desired humbly to show pure faith, sincere devotion, and complete obedience to us and to the most holy Roman Church. To secure this undertaking, they offered us on your behalf four securities: first, an oath to be given by you and your brothers, the noblemen M. and G., counts; second, a surety for whatever sum of money we should choose to assess, to be furnished, should you presume to undertake anything contrary to it, under the obligation of the noblemen P., count of Celano [Note: Thus perhaps it should be read, rather than “of Cologne.”], and R., count of Theate; third, the giving of hostages, namely two of your nephews, one through your brother and the other through your sister; fourth, the possession of one fortress which we might choose from two belonging in fact to the nobleman Walter, count of Brienne. They pledged that you would obey our commands in all things.

But because we seek voluntary devotion rather than compelled devotion, for the present we have not wished to accept such securities, desiring to test whether, without any compulsion, you will fulfill in deed what you promise in speech. [Note: Thus in the copy.]

We therefore admonish, advise, and exhort your discretion that henceforth you persevere firmly and steadfastly in obedience, fidelity, and devotion to the Apostolic See and to us, and do not waver in the services due to us.

[For from the advancement of many nobles and magnates of the realm, who have humbly obeyed us and the Church, and from the downfall of those who sought, in a spirit of pride, to kick against the goad, you may plainly learn the benefits and harms which have hitherto come, and may yet come, to you and yours from our favor and displeasure.]

For you know what great advancement those have obtained whom the sincerity of their faith commended to us, and how they have risen from the least to the greatest things. Nor are you ignorant of how great losses those have suffered whom faithlessness and arrogance stirred up, and how, falling from great things to the least, they have been reduced almost to nothing—both natives and foreigners alike. You have, alas, proved this by experience in your own person.

Since from the past you can consider the future, strive with all diligence to amend what you have imprudently done wrong, so that, wholly forgetting all things badly done and most wickedly said by you, we may with a good conscience and open countenance more graciously grant you our favor. You may indeed be secure of that favor if you take care to fulfill in word and deed the admonitions urged upon you by the present document. For, by God’s grace, our hands are generous and ample, so that, just as you have felt anger because your fault deserved it, so, because your satisfaction demands it, you may know kindness in favor.

Given at Ferentino.

LXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON. [Note: A fragment of this letter, enclosed here in brackets, appears in the *Decretals*, Book IV, title 43, “On one who has known the kinswoman of his wife or betrothed,” chapter 7. Another fragment of the same letter, likewise bracketed, is found in the *Decretals*, Book V, title 27, “On an excommunicated, deposed, or sometimes officiating cleric,” chapter 6. Finally, a third and last fragment is found there, title 8, “On schismatics and those ordained by them,” chapter 11.] [Note: See Letter 107 of Book Five, note.] He answers him, as he consults the Apostolic See on three points. (Ferentino, 12 Kalends of June [21 May].)

[Col. 0068C]

[To your brotherhood], consulting the Apostolic See on three points, to whose counsel all the faithful must resort in doubtful matters, we reply by the present letters.

On the first point, [we approve the sentence of divorce which you canonically pronounced against the man who afterward presumed to unite himself to the woman whose sister, after a betrothal had been contracted and while she was still seven years old, he is known to have violated through extraordinary lust.] [Note: The *Decretals* read: “we approve.”]

[You may also reasonably declare that priests and other clerics of your diocese] [Note: These words are not found in the *Decretals*.] [who, canonically bound by you with the bond of anathema for their excesses, have presumed or presume to celebrate the divine offices, are deprived of all ecclesiastical benefices.] [Note: In the *Decretals*: “you will be able,” and below “to deprive” instead of “to declare.”]

You may likewise without hesitation exclude from office the prior [whom you assert to have been ordained by a schismatic], unless he lawfully proves that a merciful dispensation was granted him by the person empowered to grant such a dispensation.

Given at Ferentino, 12 Kalends of June [21 May], in the sixth year.

LXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN. [Note: See Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 101, §11. See also Raynaldus under the year 1203, §61.] [Note: Concerning the archbishop of Rouen, see the note to Letter 31 of Book Five.] That, if the king of England does not receive the bishop of Sées into favor, he should place under interdict all Normandy within his jurisdiction. (Ferentino, 9 Kalends of June [24 May].)

Since in your youth you stood manfully for the defense of the Church’s liberty, now that, by the Lord’s permission, you have reached old age, you ought all the more vigorously to grant your protection to those who appear to labor for the same cause, because in this a service more pleasing to God is rendered.

Indeed, when our venerable brother, . . ., archbishop of Sens [Note: This man has already been mentioned frequently.], consecrated our venerable brother, . . . . . ., bishop of Sées, then bishop-elect [Note: See Letter 70 of Book Five, and the notes.], whom justice requiring it we judged should be confirmed in favor of ecclesiastical liberty, according to the command we gave him, this should neither burden nor trouble your brotherhood. It was not done to your prejudice, but for the defense of ecclesiastical liberty; and, in his consecration, the right of the Church of Rouen was reserved to it according to our command.

We therefore ask, admonish, advise, and exhort your brotherhood, and by apostolic letters command and direct you, that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, having put aside all resentment, you graciously receive the aforesaid bishop into your favor; and that you do not delay carefully to admonish and induce our dearest son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of the English, to receive him into his favor, to allow him peaceful possession of the bishopric of Sées, and to restore all that has been taken from both him and the canons of the Church of Sées.

Otherwise, however much we love royal excellence in the Lord and desire to show deference to its honor, because we cannot leave uncorrected what is presumed against the honor of ecclesiastical liberty, we will and strictly command your brotherhood by the authority of these present letters that, if the aforesaid king should perhaps fail within a month after receiving our letters to execute our command, you declare all Normandy which is under your jurisdiction subject to ecclesiastical interdict, and cause this to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical coercion until fitting satisfaction has been made, all appeal being set aside. We also direct by our letters the aforesaid archbishop of Sens not to omit carrying this out.

Given at Ferentino, 8 Kalends of June [25 May], in the sixth year.

LXXIV. TO THE BISHOPS OF ELY AND WORCESTER. [Note: This letter, together with several others no longer found today in the Registers of Innocent, may be read in the booklet *On the Right and Status of the Church of St Davids*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 54.] [Note: See Letter 54 of Book Five.] [Note: Ibid., Letter 23, note.] Having quashed the elections of two men to the bishopric of St Davids, he commands that the canons of St Davids be induced to celebrate a new canonical election. [Note: After the death, in 1199, approximately at the beginning of autumn, of Peter, bishop of St Davids, very serious difficulties arose concerning the election of a successor. Gerald, archdeacon of Brecon, appeared to have been elected by the better right and by the greater part of the chapter; whereas Walter, abbot of St Dogmaels, had been nominated by the archbishop of Canterbury. Gerald himself recounts the whole course of events in this case in his *History of His Own Deeds*, chapter 4 and following, and also in the work entitled *Seven Distinctions on the Right and Status of the Church of St Davids*.] (Ferentino, 7 Kalends of June [26 May].)

The case which had long been debated before judges delegated by us between the beloved sons, . . . . . . abbot of Saint Domuel [or Dogmaels] and G. . . ., archdeacon of Bretheno [or Brechene], each of whom claimed to have been elected bishop of St Davids, we at length carefully examined in consistory. Therefore, having heard and understood the depositions and allegations of the parties, by the common counsel of our brethren we quashed the election of each of them. [Note: For the text of the sentence itself, pronounced by the pope in consistory on the Tuesday after the close of Easter, see Gerald, *On the Right and Status of the Church of St Davids*, p. 584.]

But lest the Church of St Davids should be more gravely disturbed by renewed dissension, we command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters to admonish and induce the canons of St Davids canonically to celebrate within two months a unanimous election of a suitable person. If it is so conducted, let it be confirmed by their proper metropolitan. Otherwise, supported by our authority and setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, appoint for them a person as pastor, and have him consecrated bishop by that same metropolitan. Take particular care that the same archbishop receive from him no security by reason of which they may be unable to pursue the case concerning the status of the Church of St Davids. But if not both of you . . . let one of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 7 Kalends of June [26 May].

LXXV. TO GARCIA, BISHOP OF HUESCA, AND HIS SUCCESSORS TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. [Note: Compare the letter found among the *Decretals*, Book I, title 41, “On restoration to original condition,” chapter 5.] By apostolic authority and with their consent, he settles the controversy between him and Gombald, bishop of Lleida, concerning the rights of the Churches of Huesca and Lleida. (Ferentino, 6 Kalends of June [27 May].)

[Col. 0070D]

In order that lawsuits ended by amicable agreement may not again weary the parties with recurring contention, it is fitting that their settlement be strengthened by apostolic support, so that the greater the force which they have acquired from higher authority, the less opportunity may lie open to those wishing maliciously to attack them.

Indeed, when formerly the beloved son Master Ar., canon of Lleida, came to the Apostolic See, he set forth before us on behalf of the Church of Lleida that that church had been gravely injured by the sentence of Pope Eugene, our predecessor of happy memory, concerning the churches of Barbastro, Bielsa, Gesta[n], and Alquézar, with their appurtenances. He therefore requested that it be restored to a hearing, since it appeared to have been restored to one in the time of our predecessors.

For first Pope Anastasius of good memory, our predecessor, who immediately succeeded the same Eugene, and Alexander of pious memory, Anastasius’s successor, committed this cause at different times to Pope Celestine of happy memory, our predecessor—then cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin and legate of the Apostolic See. He would have brought it to its due conclusion had he not been challenged by the Church of Huesca, as is contained in his letters and as he himself repeatedly testified before us and our brethren in person.

Likewise, when he had been raised to the supreme pontificate, he committed the case to Gregory of good memory, cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo and legate of the Apostolic See, under the condition that, after examining the rescripts of the Church of Lleida and carefully hearing the parties’ reasons and allegations, he should, notwithstanding the aforesaid sentence or certain rescripts obtained from the Apostolic See, whether on occasion of that sentence or otherwise, to the prejudice of the right of the Church of Lleida, pronounce a definitive sentence—setting aside delay, contradiction, and appeal, on both the principal and incidental question—and, by putting it into execution, cause it to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside.

Under the same condition he also sent letters to our venerable brethren, the bishops of Tarazona, Osona, . . . and . . . Calahorra, who were to proceed according to the same form if the legate left the regions of Spain.

We therefore, having carefully deliberated with our brethren and other prudent men learned in both laws concerning such a petition, heard certain persons maintaining that, since our aforesaid predecessor Pope Celestine seemed to have granted the Church of Lleida the benefit of restoration against the aforesaid sentence—inasmuch as, notwithstanding that sentence, he directed that the cause be committed—we ought to admit that church’s petition. For by canonical statutes a sentence of the Apostolic See is not denied the possibility of being altered for the better, when something has been obtained by concealment or when, in view of times, ages, or grave necessities, it has decreed some arrangement by dispensation. And according to civil law, princes have allowed judgments thus rendered to be examined in their court through restoration to original condition.

But, wishing to provide for both the Church of Lleida and the Church of Huesca in their respective rights, since the merits of causes are disclosed by the parties’ assertions, we decreed that it must be determined in the presence of both parties whether restoration had been granted, or ought to be granted, against the aforesaid sentence. Accordingly, by repeated letters we directed you and our beloved sons, the chapter of Huesca [Note: See the *Decretals*, cited above.], that by the then forthcoming feast of Saint Luke you should take care to present yourselves before us, either in person or through a sufficient and suitable representative. There you were to show, if you could, that the said sentence ought not to be reconsidered; or, if justice perhaps required that it be reconsidered, you were to appear adequately prepared, either in person or through the same representative, so that canonical proceedings might be taken in the principal case.

You were to know for certain that, because we wished to put an end to the lawsuits, and because, owing to the great distance between places, recourse could not often be had to us in the foregoing question without great labor and expense, if you should contemptuously fail to fulfill what had been enjoined by the deadline which we had thought fit to assign you as peremptory, we would nevertheless take care to proceed in the matter according to law insofar as we could.

When therefore, after being awaited for a long time, you at last came personally into our presence, and our venerable brother Gob., bishop of Lleida, who had preceded you some time before, asserted that his church had been restored to a hearing and requested as a favor that it be restored if perhaps it had not been fully restored; while you, on the contrary, said that it had neither been granted a hearing against the sentence nor ought one henceforth to be granted: after the matter had been debated in our presence and various arguments introduced on both sides, by counsel of our brethren we judged that restoration to a hearing should be granted to the same bishop.

Thus, appearing in our presence, with the suit joined both as to possession and as to title, he set forth that, when the Saracens had formerly occupied the greater part of Spain, the then bishop of Lleida of good memory withdrew to the mountains and placed his episcopal see in a certain town called Roda.

The bishop who then presided over the Church of Huesca likewise went up into the mountains, took refuge in the town called Jaca, and established his see there. But at length, when Sancho, king of Aragon of illustrious memory, began to wage war upon the Saracens with a strong hand and outstretched arm, so that Christians now conceived certain hope of recovering that land, a controversy concerning boundaries arose between the bishops of Roda and Jaca. The bishop of Roda asserted that the River Alcanadre bounded their dioceses; the bishop of Jaca, on the contrary, maintained that it was the River Cinca.

When this controversy was brought before the king’s court, he, knowing the situation of the country, assigned fixed boundaries to the aforesaid dioceses with the consent of both parties, as the public instrument records. But after the king was struck by an arrow at the siege of Huesca and, as the Lord pleased, killed, his son Peter, king of Aragon of illustrious memory, freed Huesca from the hands of the Saracens, restored the pontifical dignity there, and, as far as lay in his power, transferred the see from Roda to Barbastro. Urban and Paschal of happy memory, our predecessors, confirmed this by apostolic authority.

The same king also caused the church to be dedicated by P. . . ., bishop of Barbastro; endowed and enriched it as a cathedral church; assigned it fixed boundaries; and granted immunities by royal liberality. Although the bishops of Barbastro possessed the Church of Barbastro peacefully for a long time, Geoffrey of good memory, sixth and last bishop of Barbastro, was violently expelled from Barbastro by the Church of Huesca.

After his successor had entered the way of all flesh, and the bishop of Huesca had appeared before the Apostolic See in the time of Eugene, our aforesaid predecessor, the bishop of Barbastro requested before G., cardinal of the holy Roman Church of good memory, appointed auditor for the parties, that his see, from which he had been violently expelled, should be restored to him. The bishop of Huesca, however, requested restoration of the churches of Bielsa and Gesta[n], of which he said he had been unjustly despoiled. Although each of them brought only a possessory action, the same bishop of Barbastro was nevertheless less than lawfully condemned both as to possession and as to ownership of the Church of Barbastro and of the churches of Bielsa and Gesta[n].

After Eugene aforesaid had entered the way of all flesh, he humbly petitioned Anastasius, Eugene’s successor, and obtained letters of commission to the aforesaid Celestine, our predecessor, then legate of the Apostolic See. Celestine proceeded as far as a definitive sentence, but, yielding to an appeal by the Church of Huesca, suspended the proceeding.

Again, in the same manner, the legate sent into Spain by Alexander, our aforesaid predecessor, and specially delegated in this case, proceeded in the matter.

[Col. 0073D]

Moreover, after he had been raised to the supreme pontificate, he committed this case to the aforesaid G., then cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo and legate of the Apostolic See, and to the aforesaid bishops of Tarazona, Osona, . . . etc. . . Calahorra, under the condition set out above. Although, after the cardinal had departed the limits of his legation, the bishops had proceeded in the presence of the parties as far as receiving witnesses, nevertheless, because an appeal was made to the Apostolic See on behalf of the Church of Huesca, those judges referred the cause to the Apostolic See.

Although your predecessor of good memory, . . ., and the aforesaid bishop of Lleida came into the presence of the same predecessor C., the case was not finally pursued. Instead, it remained in its existing state, and the parties were sent back to their own regions to aid the land, which the Saracens were then striving to invade.

Accordingly, on these matters the bishop of Lleida alleged that, since the aforesaid dioceses had been delimited with the consent of the parties, and that delimitation, with both the bishops and canons of the church of Huesca seeing and knowing it, had been observed for sixty years and more, those things which it had claimed by reason of this delimitation belonged to the church of Lleida. Even if that delimitation had perhaps from the beginning been invalid for some reason, nevertheless in the course of time, through the silence of the other party, it had acquired legal force, especially since it had been made with the consent of the parties and confirmed by the Roman Church. Moreover, even if such delimitation had held no force whatever, since the church of Lleida had for forty years [Col. 0074B] and more possessed in good faith and under a just title the goods which had fallen to it by the delimitation, it could defend itself by prescription alone, without support from other grounds. Nor does the opposing objection—that boundaries cannot be prescribed—avail, since the delimitation alleged by the party of the church of Huesca was null and could not be shown to have held force, even if it had been made; for such a delimitation had been attempted, apart from the consent of the parties, concerning things subject to the ownership of others, which it neither possessed at that time nor possessed afterwards.

Furthermore, since a public river was the boundary, the church of Lleida had not prescribed the river itself, but rather the things held within the boundaries, which canon law does not prohibit. Both delimitations could also stand together, since the delimitation introduced by your party, brother bishop, called the river Cinca the boundary, whereas that alleged by the church of Lleida called the river Alcanadre the boundary; and in fact the river Cinca bounded the diocese of Huesca for the greater part, and the Alcanadre for the lesser part. Likewise, even if the river Cinca divided the said dioceses as a boundary, and the delimitation which the church of Huesca said had preceded had at some time held force and had been confirmed by the Apostolic See, nevertheless the delimitation which had afterwards been made with the consent of the parties and observed for a very long time ought now to prevail. For in boundary disputes reliance is placed upon ancient evidences, unless it is proved by a change in successions or possessions that the boundaries were altered by arbitration.

Moreover, the sentence introduced against the church of Lleida by the aforesaid Eugenius [Col. 0074D] does no harm, since it was issued through negligence or error against matters already adjudicated, from which no appeal had been made. But the grant of Barbastro, made to the church of Lleida by royal liberality and confirmed by the Apostolic See, was to be observed inviolate, since it was also ratified by apostolic authority in the privileges of the other party.

Against this, however, you, brother bishop, maintained that Ramiro of illustrious memory, king of Aragon, together with his son Sancho, had earlier delimited the said dioceses—or rather had declared the delimitation made in ancient times—and this is contained in his privilege, to which the bishop of Roda and eight other bishops subscribed. Therefore Sancho himself could not subsequently and effectively act against his own deed, especially since the delimitation itself had been confirmed by Gregory and Urban of blessed memory, Roman pontiffs. Nor does the opposing objection avail, that Urban himself confirmed to the church of Huesca all that King Ramiro had granted it, excepting only those matters which Sancho, king of Aragon, together with his son P. . . ., altered from the constitution of his aforesaid father the king, with the consent of your predecessors. For he did not except these in favor of the church of Roda, but rather in favor of the chapel built in honor of our Lord Jesus of Nazareth, between which and the church of Huesca a dispute had long been litigated.

Nor were those places any less capable of being delimited, or of being shown to have been delimited, because they were held by enemies, since civil law lays down that things situated among enemies may be bequeathed because of the hope of postliminy. Likewise, it is no obstacle if the contrary contention is made that, although this delimitation had preceded, the other party had first obtained possession of Barbastro. For since it is the privilege of churches to acquire ownership even apart from possession, it is clear that the church of Huesca, just as it had been earlier in time, was likewise superior in right. In the same manner, the transaction objected to does no harm, since neither the bishop of Roda nor the bishop of Jaca strengthened it by his own subscription, nor was the consent of the clergy obtained, which was required in that matter no less than in an alienation.

Moreover, the privileges of Urban and Paschal, in which the episcopal see at Barbastro is read to have been confirmed, in no way stand in the way, since they are understood to have been annulled [Col. 0075C] together with the others which the aforesaid Eugenius annulled by his sentence, and since the aforesaid Alexander declares them to be false, although as regards their writing they are found intact in the Registers; this too may have resulted from negligence. The further point advanced by the opposing party—that it had been restored to a hearing—must be understood in this way: that it had been granted leave to show, if it could, that an unjust sentence had perhaps been issued. Therefore, if that party did not make use of such a concession, the sentence must remain in its force. Furthermore, although at the beginning only a possessory action had been brought, afterwards both possession and ownership were litigated, since privileges were produced on both sides by which not possession but ownership is established.

[Col. 0075D] The prescription objected to by the other side, however, was not proved and could not be proved; indeed, it could not even be effectively alleged, since the same party had asserted that ownership of those things which it claimed to have prescribed had come to it from another cause. It is clear, moreover, that no one prescribes his own thing unless it has first ceased to be his; nor should that party’s claim have been admitted under an alternative formulation, since a plaintiff ought to be certain of his right, although it is sometimes read that, because of the conduct and contumacy of the defendant, several actions may be brought alternatively.

Likewise, it could not be harmful if the opposing party objected that the case pending between King P. and S., bishop of Huesca, had been committed to Po., bishop of Barbastro, since it is not proved that the bishop of Huesca requested him as judge; and even if he had requested him, the wrongdoing of an individual ought not to be turned to the detriment of the Church. The depositions by which the church of Lleida appeared to establish that it had been violently expelled from Barbastro could not in law prevail, since they had been received without joinder of issue, as is established, they say, from the aforesaid letters of Pope Celestine, our predecessor. Nor ought the aforesaid depositions to have been opened, because, even if by them the church of Lleida had established what it alleged, possession ought nevertheless to have remained in its place, since ownership belonged to the church of Huesca by reason of the sentence. Therefore, before the aforesaid depositions were opened, the sentence should have been examined, because a person seeks fraudulently what he must immediately restore.

The party of the church of Huesca accordingly alleged on its own behalf: first, the delimitation of Ramiro and his son Sancho, kings of Aragon—not so much made by them as declared through them to have been made in ancient times; second, the privileges of the aforesaid Gregory and Urban, our predecessors, who not only confirmed that delimitation but decreed that it should thereafter be observed in that manner; third, the sentence of our said predecessor Eugenius, fortified by the subscriptions of cardinals, concerning which it would be rash—indeed sacrilegious—to presume that it had not been lawfully pronounced, since it is akin to sacrilege to pass judgment upon the enactments of princes. And although the church of Lleida [Col. 0076C] had been granted a hearing against that sentence, it had not been revoked, nor indeed ought it to have been revoked, since it was neither shown that anything had been obtained by concealment nor that Eugenius had considered a dispensation necessary in the matter because of the circumstances of places, times, or ages.

Fourth, the church of Huesca defended itself by prescription, since it had good faith by virtue of the sentence, fifty-eight years had elapsed since the date of that sentence, and no interruption was proved to the contrary: the other party had established absolutely nothing concerning the commission of the aforesaid Anastasius, and the commission of the repeatedly mentioned Alexander had been revoked. Celestine himself, our predecessor, as they say, also asserted in his letter of confirmation that no joinder of issue had occurred from the time when the sentence was issued. Moreover, the repeatedly mentioned Alexander granted it that it should not be compelled in any respect to answer concerning this matter, and imposed silence upon the church of Lleida; and Lucius and Clement, our predecessors of happy memory, confirmed Eugenius’s sentence. Finally, that party added that at the time of the delimitation it possessed the churches of Belsa and Gestan, and that the church of Alquézar had been given to it when it was liberated from the hands of the Saracens.

We therefore, having heard these and other matters advanced on either side, before the dispute thus deliberated upon was examined more fully, induced you and the aforesaid bishop of Lleida to make a settlement, and finally obtained from you—your wishes having been ascertained—that you would comply with our counsels. Having therefore carefully investigated your wishes, by prudent deliberation of counsel we decreed that the church of Barbastro, with its boundaries, as they had been assigned to Barbastro by the aforesaid King P., should remain to you and, through you, to the church of Huesca in perpetuity; confirming to the church of Lleida everything which it possessed between the rivers Cinca and Alcanadre. We ordered all the churches which you possessed between the aforesaid rivers, below Serra and Arbi, to be divided into two parts, together with the churches of Belsa and Gestan; and we commanded that one half be assigned to the church of Huesca and the other half to the church of Lleida. Moreover, with the consent of the same bishop of Lleida, we ordered the possessions held by his church at Jaca to be delivered to you and your church, for the good of peace, to possess in perpetuity.

> [Note: [Col. 0077D] Thus printed; but an error seems to be present.]

[Col. 0077B] Concerning those churches, however, the following settlement was reached between you: the churches of Presigneg, Torres, Peralta, Pertusa, Perdicaria, Monte Rubeo, Almerge, Castrum, and the church of Fornell, with all their boundaries, and all churches which are or shall hereafter be below them between the Cinca and Alcanadre, together with the churches of the valleys of Belsa and Gestan, shall pass by perpetual right to the church of Lleida, except for the churches of Berbegal, Lacunarota, Juverto, and Caxcorba, which, with every right and all their boundaries, shall be subject to the church of Huesca in perpetuity.

Likewise, the church of Alquézar, with all its churches and appurtenances, and all churches which are or shall be between the rivers Cinca and Alcanadre, above the boundaries of Pertusa, Perdicaria, Monte Rubeo, Almerge, and Fornell, [Col. 0077C] as far as the Pyrenean mountains, shall be subject to the same church of Huesca in perpetuity, except for the churches of Azlor, Alberola, Avosca, and Colungo, which, with every right and all their boundaries, shall be perpetually subject to the church of Lleida.

We therefore decree, establish, and enact that this settlement or division made by us with the consent of both parties shall obtain perpetual force, and that the church of Huesca shall never bring suit against that of Lleida, nor Lleida against Huesca. And lest this case may hereafter be renewed into the difficulty of contention, we declare by apostolic authority that all instruments or arguments which have hitherto been found, or may hereafter be found, for either party shall be utterly without force against these provisions.

Therefore let no one . . . infringe this our constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1203, and in the pontificate, etc.

Written in almost the same form to Gombald, bishop of Lleida.

## LXXVI. TO CARSIA, BISHOP OF HUESCA, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED, IN PERPETUITY

He receives him and his church under the protection of Blessed Peter, and the goods belonging to the church of Huesca are enumerated. (Ferentino, seventh day before the Kalends of June [26 May].)

[Col. 0078A]

“Established, though unworthy, on the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See,” etc., as far as “Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously grant your just petitions, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of Huesca, over which by God’s authorship you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.” First, indeed, establishing that the canonical order which according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, etc., shall be observed. Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., as far as “may remain.” Among these we have thought fit to specify by their own names the following:

[Col. 0078B] The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Lacunarota; the church of Berbegal; the church of Cazcorba; the church of Javerco, with all its appurtenances; the church of Alkasef; the church of Lacellis; the church of Poio, with all its appurtenances; the church of Archos; the church of Crescenzan; the church of Oz, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saltavo; the church of Costean; the church of Figarolis, with all its appurtenances; the church of Enat; the church of Coscollela; the church of Padul, with all its appurtenances; the church [Col. 0078C] of Solvas; the church of Aissa, with all the churches of Suprarbi and its appurtenances; the archdeaconry of Valle, with all its churches and appurtenances; the priory of Ravaga, with all its appurtenances; the church and villages of Pertinellis and Borres, with all their appurtenances; the church and village of Avos, and half the village of Japsa, with all their appurtenances; the priory of Liert; the church of Castello, with all its appurtenances; the priory of Sasave, with all churches and villages; the valley of Borau, with the other churches and villages subject to it and all its appurtenances; the priory of Saint Peter of Siresa, with all churches, villages, and other appurtenances; the archdeaconry of Aneo, with all churches and appurtenances; [Col. 0078D] the church of Maxons, with the village of Boliola and its other appurtenances; the archdeaconry of Sodorol, with all churches and appurtenances; the church and castle of Saint Felix, with all appurtenances; the priory of Lasieso, with all its appurtenances; the priory of Saint Mary of Latre, with the village of Stallo and its other appurtenances; the church of Saint Emeterius; the church and village of Marcellanico, with all their appurtenances; the village of Laios; the mills of Berdon belonging to the church of Maxons; the village of Aravos, with all its appurtenances; the village of Centenero; the village of Isus; the village of Idries, with all its appurtenances; [Col. 0079A] the village of Alborego; the village of Banarei; the village of Tabernas, with all its appurtenances; the church of Arascos; the church of Kinsano, with all its appurtenances; the church of Nisano, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Escanella, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Sessa, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Fananas, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Alkala; the castle of Zelun, with all its appurtenances; the church and estate of Pallarolo, with all its appurtenances; the priory of the Holy Masses (*Sanctorum Massarum*), with its tithes and appurtenances; the estates of Monzon and Abrisen, with all their appurtenances; the convent of nuns of the Holy Cross; the church of Peralta, with its appurtenances; and [Col. 0079B] all other churches, villages, and possessions belonging to the table of the canons of Huesca, with their liberties and immunities.

Moreover, we will that whatever shall have been canonically established by you in your diocese, with the common consent of your chapter or of its sounder counsel, shall remain ratified and firm. We prohibit any layman henceforth from being admitted as a canon of Huesca; if any such admission is subsequently made, we decree it null and void. We likewise establish that no secular cleric may presume to hold office in the same church, contrary to its approved custom, in a priory, archdeaconry, or any other dignity. No one shall possess church cemeteries or ecclesiastical benefices by hereditary right; and if anyone should attempt this, let him be restrained by canonical censure.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person at all to injure the aforesaid church, etc., as far as “to its advantage,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore in the future, etc., as far as “shall be subject thereto.” But may all . . . as far as “find.” Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], by the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church.

## LXXVII. TO . . . , BISHOP OF TORTOSA

He commands him to restore certain churches to the bishop of Huesca. (Ferentino, eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May].)

Pope Alexander, our predecessor of pious memory, formerly gave your predecessor instructions by his letters, as we have seen contained in those same letters, that he should not delay, within two months after receiving them, to restore to the bishop of Huesca and leave peacefully in his possession, all occasion and appeal ceasing, the churches of Alquézar adjudged to him by Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, our predecessor, which your same predecessor was holding by royal authority against justice. Yet he, being a deaf hearer of the apostolic mandate, did not take care to carry this out, as the complaint of our venerable brother Carsia, bishop of Huesca, who appeared in our presence, made known to us.

[Col. 0080A] Since, therefore, we are debtors to all in respect of their justice, and wish to preserve to each person his rights, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to defer restoring the said churches with their appurtenances to the aforesaid bishop within two months after receiving the present letters, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed; or else to appear in person before the apostolic presence by the coming feast of the Purification of blessed Mary, there to render concerning these matters what the order of law requires. We strictly forbid you, since you presently have possession of those churches, fraudulently to cease possessing them so that you may not be compelled to render him justice concerning them. Otherwise, since fraud ought to protect no one, know that you will be struck by the lawful penalty.

[Col. 0080B] Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May].

## LXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI

> [Note: [Col. 0079D] See letter 38, book III, note.]

He confirms by apostolic authority a sentence issued by the bishop of Bergamo in the case concerning the church of Sevitio. (Ferentino, tenth day before the Kalends of June [23 May].)

When the beloved sons V. and L. came to the Apostolic See and wished to litigate with one another concerning the church of Sevitio, of which L. asserted that he had been despoiled contrary to justice, we granted them as auditor our beloved son J., our subdeacon and chaplain. When they had appeared before him, the aforesaid V. . . ., procurator of our beloved son V. Rendevacca, [Col. 0080C] alleged that L., being publicly notorious, had a concubine in his house, as well as a tavern, and moreover practised usury. Our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Bergamo, the ordinary judge, summoned him through our beloved son . . . , archdeacon of the church of Bergamo, and certain others, to appear before him to make satisfaction concerning these matters. But he despised the mandate of the said bishop and utterly refused to come. The aforesaid bishop, having taken the counsel of the archdeacon and others, pronounced sentence against him; depriving him of the church of Saint Andrew, he assigned that same church to V. Rendevacca, as appears from the public instrument. The procurator of the aforesaid V. Rendevacca requested that sentence to be confirmed.

But L. alleged in opposition that, having been deprived of the same church with the order of law disregarded, he came to the Apostolic See and obtained letters directed to the beloved sons . . . , abbot of Saint Lawrence of Novara, and Master F. of Trino, canon of Saint Protasius, requiring that, if this were so, they should cause the said church to be restored to the complaining cleric, together with the fruits received from it, after V. and his procurator, or any other unlawful holder, had been removed. Although the said judges repeatedly summoned the aforesaid bishop, after many citations he at last procured to send a representative, who was not admitted because of pledges and certain other things sought from him by the judges, which he was unwilling to produce in any way. Finally, they set a peremptory term for the bishop, but he neither came nor took care to send any representative. Therefore the judges caused L.’s witnesses to be received; and when it had been lawfully proved by them that L. had had peaceful possession of the said church for ten years, they restored the church to him, removed V., and put L. in corporal possession of it.

L. obtained apostolic letters for judges to be delegated to confirm that sentence by apostolic authority insofar as it was just; and they took care to confirm it, as appears in their written act. Moreover, L. later obtained letters addressed to our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Bergamo, requiring him not to delay restoring the church to L. after removing V.; and the bishop fulfilled this by a sentence, though V. had neither been cited nor present.

But because the first sentence of the delegates is found to have been pronounced contrary to the order of law, since it ought not to have been issued against an absent and uncited person, without joinder of issue—especially because the benefit or detriment of that case concerned V. alone—and because apostolic letters are not proved to have been produced in court in the sentence of the said bishop of Bergamo, we have judged both sentences void. We command that you cause the sentence issued by the bishop of Bergamo for V. Rendevacca and against L., insofar as it is just, to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure under our authority. Thereafter, once they have been summoned, etc., to a canonical conclusion, etc. Witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding no letters except by consent of the parties, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June [23 May].

## LXXIX. TO . . . OF WENLOCK, AND TO . . . OF HENLEY, PRIORS, OF THE DIOCESES OF HEREFORD AND BANGOR

> [Note: [Col. 0081D] At Wenlock in Shropshire there was a very ancient community of nuns. There the most blessed Milburga, daughter of Merewalh, brother of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, and sister of St Mildred, lived and was buried. But after the coming of the Normans the place remained altogether deserted for some time. Later, about the twelfth century, Roger, count of Montgomery, gathered Cluniac monks there. *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 613. See also William of Malmesbury, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*, [Col. 0082D] book IV, p. 287, line 47.]

He commits to them the case pending between the bishop and the bishop-elect of Bangor. (Ferentino, fourth day before the Kalends of June [29 May].)

The case pending for a long time between our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Bangor,

> [Note: [Col. 0082D] His name was Robert. On the case pending between him and R., former subprior of the monastery of Aberconwy, see Giraldus Cambrensis, in the treatise *On the Right and Status of the Church of Menevia*, pp. 552, 555, and throughout.]

and the beloved [Col. 0081D] son R., former subprior of Aberconwy, and not yet brought to its due conclusion, we have decided, with the consent of both parties, to commit to you under a definite form, lest it remain undecided longer. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that one of you receive and examine diligently in England the witnesses of the bishop himself, and in Wales the remaining witnesses of the subprior, concerning absolutely all articles, both principal and incidental, appeal being set aside. Thus, if either party should perhaps be unable to be personally present, he shall pursue his right through a suitable procurator.

Cause the depositions, confessions, and allegations reduced to writing to be sent to us enclosed under your seals, setting the parties a suitable term within which they are to come, in person or through suitable representatives, into our presence to receive sentence, the Lord being its author. If either party, though lawfully summoned, should refuse to appear before you, nevertheless proceed in the matter according to our mandate. [Col. 0082B] Notwithstanding no letters except by consent of the parties, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June [29 May].

## LXXX. TO THE KING OF CASTILE

> [Note: [Col. 0082D] Raynaldus published a fragment in the year 1203, §63. What is found in his edition is here enclosed in brackets.]

That he should recall his daughter, incestually joined to the king of León, and obey apostolic commands. (Ferentino, Nones of June [5 June].)

The royal serenity is bound to render acts of thanksgiving to the Bestower of all good things, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them, distributing graces and dispensing gifts; for He has made your name great, like the name of the great ones who are on earth, and by His free bounty has granted you both power and prudence, so that, as each was aided by the other, prudence might not be barren through lack of the strength of power, nor power harmful through not being seasoned with the savor of prudence.

But since there is no wisdom or counsel against God, you ought to exercise your prudence in matters that belong to God and can laudably be done according to God, lest, if you act otherwise, the Lord make foolish the wisdom of this world and deprive you of the privilege bestowed, if, ungrateful for so many graces, you misuse His gifts against Him. Certainly, although we formerly took care to send into Spain our beloved son Brother Rainerius, a religious, prudent, and faithful man, to dissolve the bond of the incestuous union contracted between the king of León and your daughter, to the offense of the divine majesty, the scandal of the Church, and contempt of canonical ordinance, you evaded his censure with soothing words, as though you honored us—or rather God—with your lips while your heart was far from the fulfilment of our commands, indeed of the divine commands; and, casting your own fault upon another, you escaped the Church’s judgment.

[Col. 0083A] Yet, as we have learned by frequent report and as public rumor proclaims, you have so ensnared that king and so deceived his simplicity that he cannot, even if he wishes, separate your daughter from himself without great loss to his kingdom. For you have received in your daughter’s name many and the better fortresses of the kingdom of León, and have caused and do cause them to be guarded by your men; they are to remain to your daughter if she is abandoned by the king. Moreover, though we have declared the offspring born of this incestuous union illegitimate and never at any time to succeed to paternal goods under lawful enactments, you—at whom we marvel not a little—have craftily arranged that nearly the entire kingdom of León should swear fealty to that child.

For when you appoint counselors from your own land to the said king, and nearly all his fortresses are held [Col. 0083B] by your people, you have, as it were, put a bridle in his mouth; you lead him about at the discretion of your own will and dispose as though of his own kingdom no less than of his land. Since, therefore, we neither will nor ought any longer to dissemble so great a disgrace to the Apostolic See—indeed, to the universal Church—we admonish and earnestly exhort your royal serenity, and command under appeal to divine judgment, wholly to dissolve all bonds of this iniquity, which have bundles attached that drag souls down to the lowest hell; and to receive back—indeed, to recall—your daughter, so that, withdrawn from incestuous embraces, you may join her to anyone only in the Lord by a marital bond.

Otherwise, lest the souls of yourself, your daughter, and the king himself be required at our hands, we shall proceed against you and your land as we judge expedient; and a sharper vengeance than you believe will follow this admonition.

Given at Ferentino, on the Nones of June [5 June].

## LXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE

> [Note: [Col. 0083D] Bzovius cites it in *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 101, §11; Raynaldus also cites it, under the year 1203, §51.]

> [Note: [Col. 0083D] We have already discussed the archbishop of Narbonne above, book III, letter 24, note.]

That he should give up either the abbey or the archbishopric, since he cannot preside over both.

> [Note: [Col. 0083D] This letter must certainly be compared with the material concerning this prelate of Narbonne reported by the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 58.]

(Ferentino, third day before the Kalends of June [30 May].)

If you had noted more carefully what you read—that one deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power granted to him—you would not have abused the favor of the Apostolic See, nor would you through abuse lose what you could retain through proper use. Formerly, as we have learned, the Apostolic See granted you leave to ascend to pastoral dignity while nevertheless retaining the abbey of Monte Aragón over which you had previously presided. For the Roman Church believed that, by the honor which it conferred upon your brotherhood not without a great grace of dispensation, it would relieve the burdens both of the metropolitan church of Narbonne and of the abbey of Monte Aragón, provide for each without loss to the other, indeed assist each through the other, and detract from neither through the other. It hoped that you would so preside over and benefit both that you would in no way fail or harm either.

But, sorrowfully, we report that you preside over both in such a way that you benefit almost neither; and, while you follow the affections of flesh and blood, you seem, as it were, to persecute spiritual affection and pastoral duty.

> [Note: [Col. 0084D] Thus printed; apparently incorrectly.]

Behold: leaving the church of Narbonne, you reside in the said abbey; and while you love too fondly those whom the flesh has made dear to you, you are shown in some fashion to hate those whom charity ought to have made dearer to you. Certainly, if, forgetting your people and your father’s house, you had raised up seed for your dead brother in place of your fathers, sons would have been born to you who would more fittingly propagate the glory of your posterity. But because you either will not or cannot depart from your land and kindred, you have incurred the curse of the divine law by which all who leave no seed upon the earth are cursed. And while, when little ones ask for bread, you do not break it according to what pertains to pastoral office, you are shown to have killed those whom you did not feed.

[Col. 0084B] For ravenous wolves have now invaded the flock entrusted to you, raging the more fiercely against your fold because, like a dumb dog unable to bark, you neither frighten them off by barking nor lay down your life for your sheep after the example of the good shepherd; rather, you flee, leaving them to the bites of wolves. Behold: while you negligently perform God’s work, little foxes destroy the vineyard; they burn the Lord’s harvest with torches tied to their tails; and the enemy sows tares over the good seed that had been sown. For heretics, taking advantage of your absence—would that they avoided even your presence—now publicly set forth perverse doctrines in the province of Narbonne; and because they are resisted too little, a great multitude of the people follows them.

Therefore, lest the Lord require their blood from our hand if we negligently endure your negligence, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters either wholly to relinquish the abbey of Monte Aragón, so that provision may be made for it by a suitable person, reside in the church of Narbonne, and laudably discharge there the duty of pastoral office; or, if you prefer, to be content with the abbey and renounce metropolitan dignity. For we are unwilling any longer to endure so great a loss to the church of Narbonne—indeed rather to the Christian people—nor ought we in any way tolerate that the same Church should mourn the disgrace of widowhood while you live. Rather, unless you render her the marital duty owed, let her marry such a man as may console her in her distress and purge her of heretical depravity.

[Col. 0084D] Given at Ferentino, on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], in the sixth year.

## LXXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA

> [Note: [Col. 0084D] See Raynaldus under the year 1203, §67.]

He grants him leave to absolve lay judges who, through error, had punished clerics. (Ferentino, eighth day before the Ides of June [6 June].)

[The supplied source begins mid-letter.]

You are proved to be carrying out the office of a good shepherd when you strive to temper the rigor of ecclesiastical severity through the spirit of gentleness, so that you may recall and bring back to the bosom of Mother Church your sheep who, deceived by the appearance of righteousness, have been placed outside the folds; lest, if the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline is exercised against them, they fall into the abyss and, rather than receive saving medicine, come to despise it.

Indeed, through your letters you informed us that your city justices, having an associated multitude, zeal for justice, and believing that this was permitted them by their office, sometimes laid violent hands upon clerics entangled in crimes, punishing them with the penalty imposed on laymen—men whom the contaminating crime had made similar and equal to themselves. But when you announced to them that they had incurred the penalty of the promulgated canon, they in no way believed you, since they did not think that they had sinned by punishing those men, as evildoers, with lawful correction, as though justice itself dictated it. For this reason they can in no way be induced to come to the Apostolic See to receive absolution.

Therefore, since the contagion is widespread and you fear that they may commit something worse if the benefit of absolution is not granted them, you humbly asked us to have them absolved through you or one of your suffragans, so that justice might be tempered by mercy and discipline not be utterly weakened. We, therefore, considering that on earth we bear the place—although unworthily—of him who does not forget to show mercy, because the multitude is said to be involved in the matter, lest fire fall upon them and they fail to see the true sun, have judged it right, by the authority of this present document, in the kindness of the Apostolic See, to grant you permission to absolve them, once you have received from them a guarantee according to the form of the Church, relying on our authority. You shall take particular care that thereafter they cease from this and similar presumption, and that, according to your judgment, they send the expenses which they would have incurred in coming to the Apostolic See as aid for the Holy Land or for those resisting the Moabites in Spain.

Therefore, let no one … [lacuna: concerning our concession], etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Ides of June.

### LXXXIII [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 67.] TO THE SAME. Authority to absolve those weak through age or sex, and the sick, from the violent laying of hands upon clerics. (Ferentino, on the third day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 0085D]

You are pursuing the duty of the pastoral office when you strive to carry back the ailing sheep to the folds on your shoulders and endeavor, through the diligence of your solicitude, to uncover their weakness. Hence you humbly requested that we grant you permission, so that if it should happen that someone of your diocese, weakened by age or sex, or suffering from bodily illness, violently laid hands upon clerics, you might, by the clemency of our permission, grant such persons the benefit of absolution; and you asked that the same indulgence be granted you for those who laid hands upon them lightly.

We, therefore, trusting in the fullness of your discretion, grant you by the authority of this document the power to absolve such sacrilegious persons according to the form of the Church and to impose upon them whatever is to be imposed canonically, on condition that they make suitable satisfaction to those who suffered the injury and, according to your judgment, spend both the travel expenses and the recompense for the labor which they would have undertaken in coming to the Apostolic See on works of piety.

However, do not absolve those who have committed grave and enormous offenses and are able to undertake the journey to the Apostolic See in order to obtain absolution, on the pretext of the aforesaid indulgence, lest the sinew of ecclesiastical discipline—which can be bent by violence—be dissolved by insolence.

Given at Ferentino, on the third day before the Nones of June.

### LXXXIV [Note: The same, in the same place.] TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELLA. He confirms as firm the privilege granted by Pope Celestine to the church of Compostella concerning the prescription of certain vows which Spain had established for Saint James.
