(Ferentino, on the third day before the Nones of June.)

From the letters of Pope Celestine, of blessed memory, our predecessor, we have clearly learned that, in favor of your church and out of reverence for blessed James, he established that, since human law provides that prescription has no place in tributes and public obligations, and since those vows are like tributes—vows which Spain established to be paid annually to God and to the aforesaid apostle—the prescription which is alleged against you and your church concerning those vows has neither place nor force.

We, therefore, wishing, insofar as we can with God’s approval, to honor your fraternity, grant by this present document that, in those matters to which that constitution of Pope Celestine applies, you may freely make use of it.

Therefore, let no one … [lacuna: concerning our concession], etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the third day before the Nones of June.

### LXXXV [Note: Published by Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 59.] FROM INSEBURGIS, QUEEN OF FRANCE, TO THE POPE. She describes her most wretched condition and implores the pope’s assistance and authority.

To her spiritual father and lord, Innocent, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, the least of his daughters, Inseburges, queen of France in name only, prostrates herself at his feet with all humility.

In a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart I have very often endeavored to explain my miseries to your pious fatherhood, both through myself and through my people. Since my misfortune has been turned into the yoke of the Lord—which is not heavy but most grievous—and I bear it continually, I shall still, most holy Father, recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul. Remaining continually in that bitterness, I endure my beloved, made for me a bundle of myrrh, dwelling between my breasts, while I desire through you, the vicar of Christ, to obtain a remedy for my bitterness.

You, by God’s grace, are Peter’s successor, Paul’s colleague—he who did not fear to slay the Corinthian with the sword of the Spirit—an imitator of Phinehas, a mountain set upon the summit of the mountains, toward whom eyes must be raised, the protection of the oppressed, and the refuge of the wretched. Therefore I flee to you, most holy Father. Would that it had been granted me from above to embrace the feet of a compassionate Elisha, to water them with tears and wipe them with my hair, and thus expose the anguish of my soul more clearly by deeds than by little letters.

Rescue me, therefore, just Father, lest I be transfixed; free me from those who hate me and from the depths of the waters that persecute me without cause. My lord husband, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, persecutes me. He not only fails to regard me as a wife, but, desiring to weary my youth through the solitude of imprisonment, never ceases to provoke me through his agents with insults and accusations, to the indignation of my spirit. Through the forerunners of Antichrist—those who possess the appearance of piety but deny its power—he is in no way ashamed to provoke me to consent against the laws of marriage and the law of Christ.

Know, holy Father, that in my prison I have no consolation and suffer countless unbearable hardships. No one dares visit me there, unless some religious person comes to console me. I cannot hear a word of God from anyone’s mouth to refresh my soul, nor do I have access to any priest to make my confession. I can rarely hear Mass; the other Hours, never.

Moreover, no person or messenger from the land of my birth is permitted to come to me or speak with me, with letters or without letters. At times I am supplied with far too little food. Every day I consume the bread of tribulation and the drink of anguish. I can obtain neither anything medicinal, as the frailty of human nature requires, nor anyone who might advise me concerning the health of my body or do what would benefit me. I am not permitted to enter a bath. If I wish to have blood drawn, I cannot do so. For this reason I fear for my sight and fear that serious illnesses may come upon me. There is no adequate supply of clothing, nor is it of the sort that a queen ought to have.

To the accumulation of my misery is added the fact that those exceedingly base persons who, by royal will, live with me never offer me kind words. Instead, they afflict me with abusive and injurious speech. I have also heard and know that, although they feel compassion for me when they have withdrawn from me, they offer me no consolation because of it; rather, they continually compel me to remain sorrowful.

I am shut up in a certain house and cannot leave it. What more can I say? I could not recount my miseries one by one, because things are denied me that ought to be denied to no Christian woman, and things are done to me that ought to be done to no person, however lowly. I was unable to obtain the letters which Your Holiness sent me.

Through these and similar matters, which I cannot presently explain to Your Holiness, I have been so afflicted that I am weary of living, not knowing what I ought to do. My eyes are turned toward you, most holy Father, lest I perish.

Furthermore, I speak not bodily but spiritually: since I die every day, by your glory, in order to preserve inviolate the rights of marriage, how sweet, how welcome, how pleasant for me—the wretched, the desolate, rejected and cast out by all—would be the single bodily death by which I might flee so many dangers of death.

But since anguish surrounds me on every side—for if I act against God, death is mine, while if I do not act against him I shall not escape the hands of my persecutors—I ask consolation from you, who are the father of consolation. I make known to Your Holiness, as has already been indicated through myself and my clerics, and I ask and solemnly declare that, if compelled by threats and terrors, through feminine weakness I should propose anything against the rights of marriage, this must not prejudice the marriage named above. And do not in any way accept it, as an extorted confession [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. Rather, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, take care, kindly Father, to free me from this misery.

If it should happen that my lord Philip, illustrious king of the French, deceived by diabolical fraud, should again attempt to act against me concerning the aforesaid marriage, may Your Fatherhood arrange for me to be placed in such a location that, restored to my former freedom and to my first parents, I may freely declare my will in everything. And if, with an oath or sworn undertaking intervening, I have confessed what I have said under the pressure of fear, may you deign, through the favor of apostolic mercy, to free me from that obligation.

Act in such a way, holy Father, that you do not in any way withhold from me your consolation, your judgment, and the justice which you extend to all, so that at the final judgment you may receive a worthy reward from almighty God.

Farewell, holy Father.

### LXXXVI [Note: Cited, but not published, by Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 60.] TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRENCH. He writes to him in favor of Queen Inseburgis and sends the abbot of Casamari as legate. (Ferentino.)

Placed between God and man, while the clay honors the potter and the work fears its maker, while flesh again loves flesh and a father embraces his son too tenderly, we are almost uncertain what to do. We fear that, if we honor man against God, or even delay fulfilling our duty because of him, we may incur a grave offense against the divine majesty and his blood may be required from our hands. Yet if, when justice demands it, we burden such a man, we may distress more severely those without whom he cannot easily be distressed.

For if we do what pleases man because it displeases God, it is death for us; and we may perhaps not escape man’s offense if we choose to please God. Yet although it is more fitting for us to obey God than man, lest we seem to cast off his yoke of servitude and falsely call ourselves servants of the servants of God if we are not servants of Christ—for, according to the Apostle, if we pleased men we would not be servants of Christ—we have nevertheless judged that a middle course should be chosen. If it should be granted from above, we wish both to reconcile man to God and to make God favorable to man, so that we may please both alike.

We believe this will be obtained all the more easily because, although the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, the inner man, wholly submitted to the divine will, can more easily draw the outer man to itself, so that when both cling to God they may be one spirit with him.

Although she unwillingly and reluctantly reports these matters to the hearer, and her tongue avoids the ears of the king who slanders her, we believe that Your Royal Highness nevertheless knows how much is said against you concerning the conduct toward our dearest daughter in Christ, I., illustrious queen of the French—not only by outsiders but also by inhabitants of your kingdom and even by members of your household—and how much scandal the universal Church suffers from this. Everyone lays the blame upon us, asserting that by our patience toward her you have become still more hardened, and that our restoration of her—which they rather call abandonment—has not merely failed to benefit her but has harmed her.

For public rumor declares that she is worse today in the royal castle, after her restoration, than she would have been in the monastery after her abandonment. There, the nuns were her consolation, and with them she meditated on the law of the Lord by day and by night, walking with them in the law of the Lord in harmony. Here, however, the women assigned to serve her in whatever manner are a scandal to her: they continually exasperate her with curses in words and offend her by their deeds. Thus her soul is now almost weary of her life, since the queen is not only not served royally but is treated by some as a slave, in servile fashion.

Moreover, besides the fact that she is not provided with clothing or food as befits a queen, religious persons are forbidden to visit her and relieve her distress and pains through the consolation of the divine Scriptures. Since she finds no one to console her, she appears to have been handed over to a prison, and her tears are her bread day and night.

Indeed, even if neither fear of the Lord, nor reverence for the Apostolic See, your mother, nor nobility of birth, nor the holiness of the queen’s life were sufficient to induce you to have her treated royally, you ought at least, to escape the tongues of slanderers and preserve forever for yourself the good name which is valued above many riches, to provide for her royally and generously through honorable ministers. You should not assign to her service people who seem to hate her life and increase her misery with abusive words, adding affliction to one already afflicted, but people who would relieve her sorrow with the antidote of consolation.

To say nothing for the present of how much you offend the eyes of the divine majesty by this, how much you aggravate our reputation, scandalize the universal Church, and harm yourself, we have judged that at least this must be stated: if anything human should happen to the queen herself, everyone’s mouths would be opened against you, and it would be said that you had craftily plotted her death. You would thus be said to have killed a part of your own body, and you would thereafter be unable to turn to another marriage.

Therefore, to free both you and ourselves from the reproaches of those who reproach us and you—or rather, who reproach us on your behalf—we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Royal Serenity in the Lord to have that queen henceforth treated royally, as is fitting both for you and for her, so that by this you may make God favorable to you and merit the favor of men.

For when you have turned to the Lord, he will in turn turn favorably toward you. But surely, if you persist in offending her, you will rather offend yourself, and you may perhaps feel his hand in scourges, whereas until now you have felt it in gifts, since the Lord does not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous.

Would that you receive our admonitions—which proceed from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith—with devotion that is not feigned but true, and strive to fulfill them in such a way that you may thereby more fully merit divine grace.

In addition, grant free permission to our beloved son …, abbot of Casamari, our messenger, whom we have appointed to admonish you concerning this matter, to visit the queen herself with religious men, so that he may console her on our behalf.

[Col. 0090C] Ferentino, in the month of June.

### LXXXVII … TO THE PROVOST …, THE DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF MERSEBURG. He confirms the election of the archdeacon of Merseburg as bishop. (Praeneste, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.)

[Col. 0090D]

After the election which you had rashly made of our beloved son …, archdeacon of Merseburg, had been annulled—for, since he was of less legitimate birth, he ought not to have been elected by you, although he could have been postulated by us—we judged that a favor should be granted to you and him on this point: if you should again agree to postulate him from the Apostolic See, our venerable brother …, archbishop of Magdeburg, was to inquire carefully whether your agreement was canonical or extorted, and whether the archdeacon possessed both moral uprightness and adequate literary learning, and was to report this to us by letter.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] The matter of the archbishop of Magdeburg has already been discussed above.]

When, therefore, you had agreed to postulate him from the Apostolic See, the said archbishop received sworn testimony from both the canons and all the prelates of Merseburg, except the provost, who did not wish to swear that he would testify to the truth concerning these matters. He sent us their depositions enclosed in his letter, also indicating that the provost, although he had refused to swear, had nevertheless confessed before him that he had joined the others in agreeing upon that same archdeacon and still agreed upon him.

We, therefore, having examined and carefully considered the depositions of those who had sworn, learned from them that they had freely agreed upon the archdeacon in question, that the same archdeacon was upright in conduct and competently instructed in learning, and that he was especially useful in the present circumstances for governing the aforesaid church.

Accordingly, wishing to provide for the church of Merseburg because of its evident usefulness and pressing need, we have judged that a favor should be granted you by the kindness of the Apostolic See, mercifully admitting your postulation with the counsel of our brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] Concerning the bishop of Merseburg, whose election the pontiff confirms here, we have nothing at hand. Bucelinus gives a list of names, but without even the slightest chronological indication, German. sacr., part I, p. 42.]

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your discretion, and command you by apostolic letters, to show the said archdeacon, as your elected candidate, the reverence and honor due to him, humbly receiving his salutary admonitions and statutes and observing them inviolably.

We also will and command that you present the elected man to the aforesaid archbishop at the appointed times, to be ordained priest and consecrated bishop.

Given at Praeneste, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

### LXXXVIII [Note: [Col. 0091D] This privilege was published by Margarino, vol. I of the *Constitutiones Bullarii Casinensis*, no. 22. It was also cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 67, where a fragment is read which is enclosed here in brackets. The names of the places listed here often differ from Margarino’s edition; but, according to the practice of our office, we were obliged faithfully to reproduce the readings of the copy.] TO SAINT PAUL. The monastery of Saint Paul in the City is received under the protection of the Roman Church, and the goods belonging to it are enumerated. (Ferentino, on the Kalends of June.)

To the holy and deservedly blessed lord, the foremost preacher and eminent teacher, the apostle Paul, Innocent, an unworthy bishop and servant of the servants of God, offers the tribute of reverence with perpetual devotion.

When we seem to confer something upon you, most blessed Paul, vessel of election and preacher of grace, through the page of a privilege, we do not grant what is ours but rather confirm what is yours; for we confess that all the goods which we possess we have received through your merits from the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes. Therefore we consider them more yours than ours. Would that our possessions might be yours in such a way that yours might also be ours, so that we who have undertaken to carry out your office might also be received into the fellowship of attaining your company.

We therefore receive under the protection of blessed Peter, your fellow apostle, and under our own protection, and fortify by the privilege of this present document, the most sacred monastery in which your venerable body rests in honored remembrance, a monastery belonging by spiritual right to the jurisdiction and ownership of the Apostolic See. First, we establish that the monastic order, according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be observed … [and so forth, up to …].

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery at present [lacuna] may be able to acquire shall always remain secure and unimpaired for that monastery. Among these we have judged that the following should be expressed by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated; its borough, with the mill and other adjoining possessions; the offerings both of the high altar and of its confession and of the other altars; Saint Mennas, with the lands and vineyards on both sides of the Scilician Way as far as the bridge of Pisinnan; Centum Montes, with the vineyards and meadows beside the aforesaid monastery; Floran, with its appurtenances; the tower of John of Peter, with its appurtenances, which by the ancient name are called Draconi Mandram, together with the church and its other appurtenances; the church of Saint Proculus, with Gualdo, Lapigio, and Scizanello, and its other appurtenances;

Ardea, with its fortress and principal tower, its churches, and other appurtenances; Pattica, with its churches and appurtenances in the city of Ostia; the church of Saint Mary Mother of God of Salinae; seven Paria in the Old City, ten Paria situated at Albinea, and two Paria situated in the same territory, with Casamassancia and its serfs; the fortress of Decimum (*castrum Decimi*), with its churches, and the saltworks at Campo Maggiore and near Ostia; likewise the monastery of Saint Clement, with its village; the fortress of Fuscinanum, with its appurtenances; possessions in the city of Velletri, with the church of Saint Mary and its cells; the tower situated at Terrerevello of Lucembruca, with its appurtenances; possessions at Aricia, with vineyards, gardens, holdings, and mills;

At Albano, the cell of Saint Nicholas and the cell of Saint Mary the Younger, and the entire palace with its churches and appurtenances; Castellion, with its appurtenances; one-third of Lake Caprulacus, Villera, and Casanova, with their appurtenances; the fortress of Ose; the fortress of Longitia; Saint Julian; Saint Victoria of Cortorulum; half of Lake Boranus; Passaran and Mount Porculus, with everything belonging to the aforesaid fortresses; the church of Saint Lawrence beneath the Column and the church of Saint Mary in the Olive Grove, with all the churches of the fortresses written above, within and outside them; the house at Anagnia, with all the possessions granted to the aforesaid monastery there; one-sixth of Castellan of Duscignan.

[Col. 0092D]

In the city of Tibur, the church of Saint Agatha, two mills at Cornute, one at Vesta, and one at Forma by the Dark Gate, together with vineyards, olive groves, and other possessions; Mount Albanus, with all its holdings; the hill of Saint Christ; the fortress of Nomentum and Saint Primum, together with the other churches and the crypt of Maroha, with everything belonging to the fortresses or places written above; Saint Marcellinus and the hill of Caribna; Mount Fabalus and the fortress of Saint Paul, with everything belonging to the aforesaid fortresses; the monastery of Saint Mary of Mount Dominicus, with its churches and appurtenances;

In Marsia, the hermitage of Saint Mary of Mount Armentus, with its cells, holdings, and all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Gregory of Sublone, with its appurtenances; Saint Mary in Casis, with Girata—that is, Piscaria—in Lake Fucinus; Saint Leonard above Cantora, with its cells, villages, mills, and other appurtenances; at Anritemo, the hospital of Casas; in the Sabine territory, one-fourth of Castripozium; in the city of Interamna, the church of Saint Lawrence at the Pearl of Caesa; the hospital of the apostles James and Bartholomew in the city of Todi; the monastery of Saint Margaret, with its appurtenances;

At Stroncone, the church of Saint Antimus, with all the possessions which belonged to Guido of Saint Antimus; in the county of Narnia, half of the fortress of Saint Urban; at Ameria, the hospital of Saint James of Redden; the church of Saint Magnus at the Bridge, and the church of Saint Cataldus near the fortress of Torana, with their appurtenances; in the city of Civita Castellana, the lordships and possessions which belonged to Rainald Guideruld, with the churches of Saint Eutychius within and Saint John outside;

The church of Saint Stephen in its castle and borough near the city of Sutri, with all its appurtenances and revenues; the fortress of Santa Severa, with its church and appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Benedict of Nepi, situated at Pentorna, and the estate called Ulmetum, and the estate called Maian, situated in the territory of Nepi, and whatever it possesses from the Bridge of Nepi as far as Mount Rosulus, and the lake called Janula; the fortress of Vaccaritia, with the church of Saint Christina and its other churches and appurtenances; the fortress of Lepriniana, with its churches and appurtenances; Flaianum, with its appurtenances; the city of Colorum, with its churches and appurtenances; the city of Stertinian, with the church of Saint John and the lake with its appurtenances;

In the bishopric of Narnia, the church of Saint Nicholas of Mount Maselan; the fortress of Raian, with its appurtenances, and the New Fortress and the fortress of Tornellus; at Rome, the church of Saint Nicholas of Forma; the church of Saint Sergius in the Subura; fisheries in the river at the place called Marmorata; the lord’s landing-place, and the Posta, and other [fisheries] in the same river below Rome; rents and gardens; and everything which the same monastery is known to possess within and outside the city.

In addition, we confirm to the same monastery its liberties and immunities … [lacuna].

We further establish that the aforesaid monastery shall be subject to no one whatsoever in any matter except the Roman pontiff alone, and that no one there, other than him, shall exercise any jurisdiction or claim any authority.

By the authority of this present privilege we grant the abbot of that venerable place permission, for the honor and praise of the Most High, to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass in your holy honor with the mitre and ring, sandals, tunic, and dalmatic, and to bless the clergy and people present. This permission is granted in such a way that, if he was ordained priest by the hands of the Roman pontiff, he may celebrate at the high altar.

As for the consecration of altars and the ordination of monks who are to be advanced to sacred orders, the abbot and monks of the same monastery may receive these from whichever Catholic bishop they prefer, relying upon apostolic authority; and we command that they be provided without difficulty or corruption.

The same abbot, provided that he is a priest, may, by our indulgence, confer the minor orders upon his monks whenever necessary. We also grant him the power to bless the vestments required in the same monastery for use at the altar.

By this present decree we prohibit anyone whatsoever, without a special mandate of the Roman pontiff, from promulgating against the abbot and monks of the same monastery, wherever they may reside, a sentence of suspension or excommunication, or from summoning them to a synod. Nor may anyone do this against clerics, especially oblates, residing in those churches in which appointment, removal, and correction are recognized as belonging not to the bishops but to the abbot himself. If anyone should promulgate such sentences against them, we declare those sentences null and void.

When the abbot of the same place dies, no one is to be placed over it through any trickery or violence except one whom the brothers, by common agreement, or the greater part of the brothers of sounder judgment, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, choose from that congregation itself—provided that, upon examination by the Roman pontiff, a suitable person is found in it.

If, God forbid, no suitable person could be found in the same monastery, then the Roman pontiff shall appoint as abbot a suitable person from another congregation.

Moreover, following the footsteps of Pope Gregory, of blessed memory, our predecessor, we remit to the aforesaid monastery the obligation of wine, a boar, and a cow, which in ancient times it was accustomed to furnish to our predecessors, without prejudice to the free services and customary gifts which are owed annually to the Apostolic See on the feasts of the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord.

Let the abbot and the convent of the aforesaid monastery also be permitted to use the testimony of their brothers in their own cases, whether the matter concerns a civil or a criminal question, and so forth, up to … [the point at which it would] perish. Let them also lawfully receive into religious conversion clerics or free and legally independent laymen fleeing from the world, and retain them without any contradiction.

When a general interdict has been issued, let it be lawful for those same persons remaining there, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, to celebrate the divine offices in a subdued voice and without ringing the bells.

Furthermore, since the same monastery is a spiritual member of the Apostolic See and the proper seat of the Roman pontiff, we establish and decree that, just as a prescription of only a hundred years runs against the Roman Church, according to canonical constitutions and lawful sanctions, so too no prescription of a shorter period shall prejudice the aforesaid monastery.

We also decree that the burial of that place shall be free, so that [lacuna ending: “from whom the bodies of the dead have been taken”].

We decree, therefore, that no human being whatsoever may [lacuna: concerning] the aforesaid monastery … [lacuna ending: “beneficial”], without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the customary justice of the diocesan bishops in parish churches, except those in which the same monastery is known to have hitherto possessed full right.

If, therefore, in the future … [lacuna ending: “be subject”]; but let all … [lacuna ending: “find”]. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the first day of June, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1203, in the sixth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent III.

### LXXXIX [Note: [Col. 0095D] It appears in the booklet *On the Right and Status of the Church of Menevia*, p. 590. See letter 74 of this sixth book. It is also included, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book II, title 20, *On Witnesses and Testimonies*, chapter 34. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets.] … TO THE BISHOP OF DURHAM; THE DEAN, AND … THE PRIOR OF THE HOLY TRINITY OF YORK. That witnesses be heard in the case which was being litigated concerning the status of the church of Menevia. (Ferentino, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0095B]

[The supplied source ends here.]

[When formerly the beloved son [Note: [Col. 0095D] The words “beloved son,” “and now,” and “our venerable brother” are absent from the Decretals.] G., archdeacon of St Davids, had brought before us and our brothers a question against our venerable brother . . . archbishop of Canterbury concerning the status of the church of St Davids [Note: [Col. 0095D] The Decretals read “had set before,” omitting “before us and our brothers.”]:] we instructed that archbishop by our letters to appear before us on this matter, either personally or through a suitable representative, to make answer. But since [Col. 0095C] he neither came nor sent a suitable respondent for this purpose, wishing to provide for the church of St Davids with paternal concern, we deemed it appropriate to commit the case under a fixed form to our venerable brother . . . bishop of Ely, and to our beloved sons . . . dean of London and . . . archdeacon of Botingham [Note: [Col. 0096D] Giraldus, in the work already cited, p. 550, gives a fragment of the letters discussed here.], who have hitherto not proceeded in it according to our command. Therefore, lest the case remain undecided, by apostolic writ we command your discretion [that, unless the adverse party can lawfully bar the aforesaid archdeacon from bringing suit by an exception, after summoning the parties, if this can be done, or their representatives, to a suitable and safe place by your messengers and letters, and after the suit has been lawfully contested, you shall arrange to receive the witnesses whom [Col. 0095D] the archbishop considers should be produced in England, and those whom the archdeacon wishes to produce against him [Note: [Col. 0096D] The Decretals read “considers should be produced,” and below “or before you” in place of “against him.”] in Wales. But if the archbishop, though lawfully cited, should refuse to appear before you either personally or through a suitable representative, or even to contest the suit, nevertheless you shall admit [Note: [Col. 0096D] In the Decretals: “especially the witnesses.”] the elderly and infirm witnesses whom the archdeacon, personally or through [Col. 0096A] his representative, considers should be produced, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction [Note: [Col. 0096D] These words, and those below distinguished by italic type, are absent from the Decretals.] and appeal; and you shall ensure that their written depositions, sealed with your seals, are sent to the Apostolic See, assigning the parties a suitable peremptory term within which they are to present themselves before us, personally or through suitable respondents, to receive justice], etc. The witnesses, etc. Let no one, etc. But if you, etc., brother bishop, together with one of them.

Given at Ferentino, 14 days before the Kalends of July [18 June], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

XC. TO THE . . . BISHOP OF EXETER [Note: [Col. 0096D] It seems that “of Oxford” should be read.], AND TO THE ELECT OF . . . BURGOS. That they are to investigate charges against the bishop of Astorga. (Ferentino, 15 days before the Kalends of July [17 June].)

[Col. 0096B]

The beloved son D. . . ., canon of Astorga, coming to the Apostolic See, laid before us many enormous accusations against our venerable brother . . . bishop of Astorga, upon which he intends criminally to accuse him: namely, that while his predecessor was still living, had been violently expelled from his see, and stripped even of his bishopric, he rashly usurped his place through ambition; that he is tainted by the crime of perjury and the depravity of simony; that moreover he promoted two murderers, appointing one archdeacon and admitting the other, who was not legitimately born, to the office of deacon. Further, that he labours under public infamy for homicide: namely, that he caused Master [Col. 0096C] Michael, doctor of laws, to be killed through poison procured by evil contrivance. Since enormities of this kind ought not to be passed over by dissimulation, by apostolic writ we command your discretion that, after summoning the parties and hearing the allegations on both sides, you shall take care diligently to examine the case through to definitive judgment, and remit it to us adequately prepared, assigning the parties a suitable term within which they are to come to receive what justice shall dictate. Should they perhaps neglect to come at that time, we shall nevertheless proceed as far as we can in law.

Given at Ferentino, 15 days before the Kalends of July [17 June].

XCI. TO THE NOBLE MAN . . . COUNT DUNCAN. He confirms the prudent settlement made between him and the church of St Andrews. (Ferentino, 15 days before the Kalends of July [17 June].)

[Col. 0096D]

It is customary to grant, etc., as far as bestow. Now, whereas a controversy between you and the church of St Andrews concerning the right of patronage over certain churches and lands had [Col. 0097A] long been debated, at last, in the presence of our beloved son J., priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, legate of the Apostolic See, and of our dearest son in Christ W., illustrious king of Scotland, with the agreement of R., of blessed memory, then bishop of that same church, an amicable settlement was reached between you and that church. You asked that it be confirmed by apostolic rescript. Therefore, acceding to the requests of your nobility, we confirm by apostolic authority this settlement, as it was prudently made without impropriety, freely accepted by both parties, peacefully observed hitherto, and fully contained in the instruments drawn up on the matter, etc. Let no one therefore, etc. Given at Ferentino, 15 days before the Kalends of July [17 June].

XCII. TO THE BISHOP OF GERONA [Note: [Col. 0097D] It is found, though somewhat mutilated, among the Decretals, book IV, title 13, *On one who has carnally known the blood-relative of his wife or betrothed*, chapter 8.]. Concerning a man who had carnally known mother and daughter. (Ferentino, 13 days before the Kalends of July [19 June].)

[Col. 0097B]

[From the letters of your brotherhood we learned [Note: [Col. 0097D] In the Decretals: “that.”] that G., their bearer, showed us in an open confession that [Note: [Col. 0097D] These words are absent from the Decretals.] . . . he had often carnally known the mother of a certain girl whom, while she was under marriageable age, he had betrothed as his wife, and afterwards had intercourse with the girl when she was an adult.] You therefore humbly requested provision for the man’s soul, and asked whether the woman might marry a second husband during his lifetime, since this deed is held to be public and notorious. [We caused penance to be imposed upon the man for his sin, answering your consultation as follows: [Col. 0097C] if the matter stands thus, after they have been entirely separated from one another, the woman must not marry another man if, after learning of the offence of the man and her mother, she was not ashamed to have intercourse with him. The man also and the woman’s mother must never enter into other marriages, but are bound always to observe continence and bitterly lament the enormous offence which they incurred through so abominable a lust—especially if, in persons of this kind, there is no reason to fear a fall of the flesh.]

Given at Ferentino, 13 days before the Kalends of July [19 June].

XCIII. TO THE MONKS OF MONREALE, HOLDING THE CASTLES OF JATO AND CALATETRASI, AND THEIR ACCOMPLICES: WITHOUT GREETING. That they are to offer due satisfaction to their archbishop, whom they have gravely offended. (Ferentino, 15 days before the Kalends of July [17 June].)

[Col. 0097D]

You should know that our withholding from you the address of apostolic greeting proceeds from your own wickedness. For we have received a most serious complaint from our venerable brother, your archbishop [Note: [Col. 0098D] See above, letter 89 of book V, note.], that, having become rebels against him, you wickedly hold the aforesaid castles and the treasury of the church, waste them in luxurious living, and, lavishly supplying excommunicated persons and enemies to oppress that [Col. 0098A] archbishop, render him no assistance, or scarcely any. You swore allegiance first to the chancellor, secondly to his brother Markward of damned memory, and now thirdly to W. Capparone; and, contrary to the oath you gave, you did not shrink from wickedly disclosing a certain secret which ought carefully to have been concealed. From this, all the evils perpetrated at Palermo and throughout Sicily by that same Markward seem to have arisen. Moreover, after squandering the church’s treasury, you besieged the aforesaid archbishop for a month and more; and when you could achieve nothing by the siege, you did not hesitate, after paying money, to bring the aforesaid Capparone to besiege him. By giving his wife large silver cups and a dalmatic of *hulla* [Note: [Col. 0098D] Thus in the copy.], worth more than a thousand tari, you induced [Col. 0098B] him to seize, torture, and mutilate the archbishop’s men, and to make his friends and kinsmen go into exile. You also caused his messengers, travelling last year to the Apostolic See, to be seized at Messina and cruelly tortured. Further, greedily destroying the obediences of the church entrusted to you, you converted their revenues to your own property, contrary to the Rule of St Benedict, giving the archbishop nothing or very little, although those revenues amount to ten thousand tari yearly. In addition, with sacrilegious presumption you violated the tomb of G., archbishop of blessed memory, his predecessor; after removing from it the archiepiscopal vestments and leaving the tomb half-covered, you threatened to do like things to him. For [Col. 0098C] these and many other offences, and because you were altogether unwilling to obey our command, he pronounced a sentence of excommunication against you. Yet, damnably hardened in your wickedness, you have no fear whatsoever of your pastor’s censure. Therefore, since we neither wish nor ought any longer to endure such great crimes, by apostolic writ we command and strictly enjoin you to surrender the aforesaid castles together with the treasury to the said archbishop, all occasion, excuse, and delay ceasing, and humbly endeavour to offer him fitting satisfaction for all the offences mentioned, rendering him the obedience and reverence due to him as your father and pastor. But if [Col. 0098D] you decide to persist in your obstinacy and contumacy, holding valid and firm the sentence which he canonically pronounced against you, we shall, with the Lord as author, cause it to be inviolably observed. You may also fear that, because of your wickedness deserving it, you will be altogether excluded, and that the same archbishop, by authority of the Apostolic See, may establish either regular canons or secular clerics in that church.

Given at Ferentino, 15 days before the Kalends of July [17 June].

XCIV. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF CASTILE. He commends to him the abbot and convent of Triana. (Ferentino, 14 days before the Kalends of July [18 June].)

[Col. 0099A]

The greater the power which he through whom kings reign and princes rule has bestowed upon you among men, the more kindly and diligently ought you to cherish the churches and monasteries of your kingdom, in which the Lord is continually entreated for the living and the dead. Thus religious men, secure from worldly vexations through royal protection, may freely and willingly devote themselves to prayers for the salvation of you and of the people subject to you. Moved by this confidence, we earnestly commend to your royal highness our beloved son . . . abbot, and the convent of the church of Triana [Col. 0099B]; and by apostolic writ we ask, attentively exhort, and enjoin upon you for the remission of your sins that, out of regard for God and in reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you defend the aforesaid church—as a special daughter of the Roman Church—and likewise the aforesaid abbot and convent and their rights, from every unjust burden and undue molestation. Preserve them in their order and in the liberty granted them by the Apostolic See, as is known to be contained in the privilege granted to them, at your earnest request, by Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory. Yet we do not wish your royal excellence to consider burdensome our refusal to grant your request that the oft-mentioned church should be brought under the authority [Col. 0099C] of the monastery of St Facundus, since we could not lawfully do this.

Given at Ferentino, 14 days before the Kalends of July [18 June].

XCV. TO THE CHANTER, PENITENTIARY, WILLIAM ALBOINI, PAPAL SUBDEACON AND CANON, OF LIMOGES. That they are to cause A. Taines, subdeacon, to be received as canon and brother by the provost and chapter of St Junian, in accordance with the terms of the apostolic mandate already issued on this matter. (Ferentino, 14 days before the Kalends of July [18 June].)

The beloved son A. Taines, subdeacon, coming to the Apostolic See, informed us that, when we had formerly written to the beloved sons . . . provost and chapter [Col. 0099D] of St Junian that they should receive him as canon and brother, granting the beloved son . . . abbot of Uzerche [Note: [Col. 0099D] Peter V, abbot of Uzerche, is found in documents of 1202, indiction V; Raymond appears shortly afterwards, in 1205. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 596.] as their executor, to compel them by ecclesiastical coercion, all appeal and delay ceasing, to receive him unless they showed a sufficient and just cause why he should not be received by them, that abbot repeatedly appointed a day for the parties. At last, when certain canons of that church appeared before him for the body corporate, and the subdeacon himself was present, the following was objected against the subdeacon: that he had laid violent hands upon a cleric, and that the church lacked the means. But the subdeacon, because only hearsay witnesses had been produced to prove the laying on of violent hands, offered proof of his innocence. Although witnesses of the opposing party showed that the church lacked the means, he clearly proved in reply that, after they had received the apostolic mandate concerning his reception, four resident canons of that church, two non-resident canons, and one resident prebendary had also died [Note: [Col. 0099D] Thus in the copy.]. When these and other matters had been litigated before the same abbot, he eventually doubted [Col. 0100B] how to pronounce judgment and referred the case to the provision of the Apostolic See. We then appointed as auditor for the same subdeacon and for P., the priest who came on behalf of the adverse party, our beloved son B. [Note: [Col. 0099D] See letter 54 of book III, note.], priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna. In his presence much was alleged on either side, and afterwards reported to us by him. Since the letters of the said abbot stated that the death of the aforementioned canons had been clearly established to him, as set forth above, and since nothing had been proved against that subdeacon that would prevent him from being considered suitable to obtain an ecclesiastical benefice, we decreed that he should be admitted in the place of one of the deceased, lest he be defrauded of the provision in which the kindness of the Apostolic See had directed that assistance be given him. Therefore, [Col. 0100C] by apostolic writ we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, unless the said provost and chapter, upon your admonition, receive the subdeacon as canon and brother in accordance with our decree, you, supported by our authority, shall put him bodily into possession of that prebend and assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed. You shall restrain opponents . . .; nor shall the absence of the aforesaid provost impede you, since he is said to be staying at Paris, if the chapter seeks to invoke it in evasion of our mandate. Carry out the apostolic mandate in such a manner that the same subdeacon is not compelled on this account to labour further before the Apostolic See. But if not all . . . [Col. 0100D] two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 14 days before the Kalends of July [18 June], in the sixth year.

XCVI. TO THE BISHOP OF ELY [Note: [Col. 0100D] The bishop of Ely has been mentioned in book V, letter 54.], THE ABBOT OF TARRETON [Note: [Col. 0100D] We have nothing readily available concerning the abbots of Tarreton.], AND THE DEAN OF LINCOLN [Note: [Col. 0100D] See above.]. That clerics presented by the archbishop of York to churches belonging to the prior and canons of Hikerham are to be admitted. (Ferentino, 11 days before the Kalends of July [21 June].)

The beloved sons . . . prior and canons of Hikerham [Col. 0101A], in a petition sent to us, stated that our venerable brother, the archbishop of York, and his officials, contrary to the tenor of their privileges, scornfully refuse, at their own will and pleasure, to admit clerics whom they present to their churches. Therefore, unwilling that the churches of the said brethren should suffer loss on this account, by apostolic writ we command your discretion that, if the aforesaid archbishop and his officials maliciously delay admitting suitable persons canonically presented to them by those brethren to the care of their churches, you, supported by our authority, shall procure their admission upon the brethren’s canonical presentation, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal. This is to be done, however, in such a way that no prejudice may thereby arise hereafter to the successors [Col. 0101B] of that archbishop. But if not all, etc., you, brother bishop, together with one of them, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 11 days before the Kalends of July [21 June].

XCVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES [Note: [Col. 0101D] This letter is cited by Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 101, §11, and by Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §51. See letter 43 of book III, note.], AND TO THE BISHOP OF CAHORS [Note: [Col. 0101D] William III, bishop of Cahors, is mentioned in documents of 1199 and 1202. But the see of the church of Cahors was vacant in 1206. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 131.]. That they are to correct the chaplains and burgesses of the castle of Limoges. (Ferentino, 8 June.)

Formerly we gave instructions, first to you all, and secondly to you, brother archbishop, and your suffragans, that you should cause the sentences of interdict pronounced against the burgesses and the castle of Limoges, because of their many and enormous offences, and the sentences of suspension and excommunication pronounced against the [Col. 0101C] chaplains of that castle, because of their disobedience and contumacy, by our venerable brother the bishop of Limoges [Note: [Col. 0102D] See letter 68 of book V, note.], to be inviolably observed throughout the province of Bourges until fitting satisfaction was made, through ecclesiastical censure and with appeal removed, insofar as they had been reasonably imposed. In the second mandate we further directed that, if the said clerics and chaplains, after admonition, should refuse to offer their bishop due satisfaction within a month, you should compel them by the same censure, appeal ceasing, to come suspended before the Apostolic See with letters testifying from you. Although you have devoutly carried out the apostolic mandate to the extent that lay in your power, the said chaplains and [Col. 0101D] clerics, not returning to their senses but rather hardening their hearts with Pharaoh, have not merely remained in their stubbornness; becoming day by day more obstinate, so that their latter error is worse than the former, they openly preach in the churches of that castle things that savour of condemned heresy. Though excommunicated, they do not fear to celebrate divine offices. Moreover, as we have learned from the letters of the aforesaid bishop, the burgesses, after driving out the chaplains of the churches and the monks of St Martial [Col. 0102A], seized their goods; they punish with monetary penalties matrons and others who, fearing the sentence of excommunication, do not attend their services, and also those who on Easter Day refused to receive Christ’s body from their hands. Since new diseases must always be met by new remedies, and iron must be applied to a wound which does not accept the remedy of fomentation, lest the sound part be infected while the pestilential disease is already creeping in, by apostolic writ we command and enjoin your brotherhood that, if the aforesaid clerics and chaplains do not, within a month after receiving these letters, make satisfaction according to the tenor of our prior mandate upon your admonition, you, supported by our authority, shall deprive them of their benefices, appeal being removed. But if even thus affliction does not give them understanding, and if within another month they refuse to desist from their wickedness, then by apostolic authority you shall solemnly depose them from their offices, so that those who hear of it may be terrified at such disobedient and contumacious men, and that in those regions the spark of ecclesiastical correction, which now seems almost extinguished, may revive.

Given at Ferentino, 8 June, in the sixth year.

XCVIII. TO THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0102D] See letter 78 of book V, note.] AND WILLIAM ALBOINI, CANON OF LIMOGES. He commits to them for examination the case of the cleric Assalit, who is troubling the dean and chapter of St Aredius. (Ferentino, 12 days before the Kalends of July [20 June].)

[Col. 0102C] It has been reported to us on behalf of the dean and chapter of the church of St Aredius that, when our venerable brother O. [Note: [Col. 0102D] Letter 11 of book III, note.], bishop of Ostia, formerly legate of the Apostolic See in your regions, directed them to receive the cleric Assalit as canon and brother, they ultimately objected against that cleric that he had been born of a double adultery; and they refused therefore to receive him, especially because they are bound by oath to receive no such person as canon. The bishop himself, as we saw recorded in his letters, thought it proper to tolerate their conduct, provided that Hel., nephew of Hel., a brother of Grandmont, were received by them. Once he had been kindly received at the bishop’s request, the bishop provided for the said Assalit [Col. 0102D] in the church of St Front, a church far more eminent than the aforesaid one, lest the hope which Assalit had conceived from his request should be disappointed. Nevertheless, in order again to harass the aforesaid dean and chapter concerning his own reception, the same A. came to the Apostolic See and, suppressing the truth, obtained letters addressed to our venerable brother the archbishop of Bordeaux and to our beloved son . . . abbot of Aubeterre. When they learned of this, the dean and chapter appealed to the Apostolic See before they [Col. 0103A] were cited under those letters. The judges, disregarding the appeal, though the dean and chapter could not come to them, nor could the judges themselves go to the former because of the disturbances of war, ordered that they be avoided by all as excommunicated persons. Accordingly, Bernard, priest and representative of the aforesaid dean and chapter, and Master P. Aimeric Boiol, representative of the other party, appeared before us and requested that their arguments be heard. We appointed as auditor our beloved son L. [Note: [Col. 0103D] See letter 5 of book V, note.], priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross, who carefully reported to us what had been alleged before him. Unwilling, therefore, that anyone should be unjustly burdened, by apostolic writ we command and enjoin your discretion that, after diligently investigating the truth concerning [Col. 0103B] the foregoing, if it is established to you that provision had been made for the said Assalit in the aforesaid church of St Front by the aforesaid bishop after the objection against him mentioned above had been raised, and that the other man had been received in the church of St Aredius at the request of the same bishop, you shall cause Assalit himself to cease, by ecclesiastical coercion and with appeal removed, from troubling the aforesaid dean and chapter. Impose perpetual silence upon him in this matter and annul whatever you ascertain has been rashly attempted against them and their church on the occasion of the aforesaid letters. Otherwise, cause him to be received as canon and brother, provided that nothing in the canonical statutes stands in his way, restraining opponents, after prior admonition, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside.

Given at Ferentino, 12 days before the Kalends of July [20 June], in the sixth year.

XCIX. [Note: [Col. 0103D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §5; see also Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 99, §3.] LETTER OF THE CRUSADERS TO THE POPE. Concerning absolution for the affair of Zara.

To the most holy father and most dear lord I., by God’s grace supreme pontiff: B., count of Flanders and Hainaut; L., count of Blois and Clermont; H., count of St Paul; and their knights, with most ready willingness for every service, kisses of the feet.

Having learned your paternal command, and having received with due reverence, through the messenger of the venerable father P., priest-cardinal of the title of St Marcellus [Col. 0103D], legate of the Apostolic See, and through our own messengers, both your letters and his, we have carried them out in all things with ready devotion. Having taken or renewed the oath according to the form expressed in your letters, we have received the benefit of apostolic absolution; and, as you requested, we sent back to the said legate, according to his command, the letters whose tenor we have judged should also be made known to your Apostolic See through the bearer of the present letter. We trust in your apostolic mercy that your command, however stern it may outwardly sound in paternal severity, ought inwardly to contain nothing deceitful against us or our heirs in view of the obedience and most ready devotion of your sons. For the tenor of the said letters is as follows [Note: [Col. 0104D] This is printed in Raynaldus.]:

[B., count of Flanders and Hainaut; L., count of Blois and Clermont; H., count of St Paul; Odo of Chanliet; and W., his brother, to all whom these letters shall reach, greeting in the Lord. We wish it to be known that, concerning the fact that at Zara we have incurred, or fear that we have incurred, apostolic excommunication, we bind both ourselves and our successors to the Apostolic See, undertaking that at its command we shall see fitting satisfaction rendered.

Given at Zara, in the year of the Lord 1203, in the month of April.]

Indeed, we counts willingly and without contradiction appended our seals to these letters; but we understand that the seals of the following barons, namely Odo and W., his brother, were lacking, although they too acknowledged themselves to be barons, as we learned from those to whom your office of absolution had been delegated. Once absolution had been granted, they were enjoined, by virtue of the oath taken, immediately to issue the letters which you received. Concerning the action of the illustrious man and leader of our army, the marquis of Montferrat—namely, that, out of apostolic reverence and in order to fulfil your will regarding preservation of the fleet, he humbly prevented the display of your letters for a time, until your holiness by a renewed command should direct what was to be done in this emergency—we most humbly beseech your fatherhood not to take it amiss. For you may be entirely certain that, had the letters been shown to the . . . doge and the Venetians at that place and time, on that very day both the fleet would have been broken up and the army now dispersed. Indeed, through Master John of Noyon, our messenger, we learned that he had earnestly begged your fatherhood temporarily to overlook the excommunication of the Venetians because of the danger of dissolution of the army, but had not been heard, and that your command had imposed silence upon him on this point. Nevertheless, we preferred to seek your will by renewed consultation rather than, through the display of the said letters, cause the fleet to be divided, at the peril of our bodies and souls, the desolation of the Holy Land, and the mockery and insult of the enemies of the Cross—contrary even to your will, as we firmly believe and have learned through your messengers. But let the discretion of your fatherhood be wholly certain that whatever it commands concerning these letters, whatever may result from this, the said marquis, or whichever of us you enjoin, will do it without delay.

C. [Note: [Col. 0105D] This letter is read almost entire in Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §6. It was also cited by Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 99, §III.] LETTER OF THE MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT. He excuses his suppression of the pope’s letters.

[Col. 0105A]

[To the most holy father and lord I., by divine providence supreme pontiff: Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, with kisses of the feet and a willingness ready for every service.

After the barons of the army of the cross-bearers had received your fatherhood’s letters and, with every reverence and devotion, had taken or renewed the oath and obtained the benefit of apostolic absolution, I learned through the messenger of our venerable father P., priest-cardinal of the title of St Marcellus, legate of the Apostolic See, after consultation with the barons, that letters of excommunication concerning Zara had been issued by the Apostolic See through that messenger to the doge and the Venetians. [Col. 0105B] Considering, indeed holding it certain, that at that place and time your letters could by no means be shown without our army immediately being dispersed and the fleet broken up, and recalling your counsel that many things must be overlooked at the appropriate place and time if the Venetians should seek dissolution of the fleet, I decided, out of regard for divine love and also for reverence for the Apostolic See—from which the fleet had received both its messenger and subsequently its support—to suppress those letters for a time, until I should receive your mandate and counsel by a renewed command. I received them from your messenger’s hand with all humility, on bended knees and with a great spirit of compunction and devotion; I entrusted them for safekeeping for a time to the religious man . . . abbot of Lodi [Col. 0105C], awaiting thereby rather the merit of filial obedience than the offence of having necessarily incurred apostolic displeasure through an act of pious intention.

I also learned from the doge and from certain Venetians, my intimates, that concerning Zara they would immediately send their own messenger to your holiness. Whether he has yet reached the Apostolic See, we do not know; in expectation of this, I have until now delayed sending a messenger. Therefore, with every feeling of devotion and humility, I beseech your fatherhood that the suppression of your letters—accomplished by the service of my humility and in confidence in your discretion and mercy—may in no way disturb or unsettle the tranquillity of your peace, [Col. 0105D] particularly since both I and the barons of the army are prepared to carry out your command, whatever you may enjoin upon us by renewed command. For we trust that it will please your circumspection more that the fleet should remain intact through a small measure of forbearance than that it should suddenly perish through the display of your letters.]

Moreover, I excuse the simplicity of this messenger on the ground that, in that storm and amid so great a difficulty of passage, I had no readier means.

CI. [Note: [Col. 0106D] It is printed entire in the *Deeds of Innocent*, no. LXXXVIII. Bzovius cites it, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 99, §4. Raynaldus published it mutilated under the year 1203, §13.] TO THE MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT, B., COUNT OF FLANDERS, L., COUNT OF BLOIS, AND H., COUNT OF ST PAUL. That they are to cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land. (Ferentino, year VI.)

[Col. 0106A]

[Although you went forth from Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, in order to offer yourselves to the Lord as a sacrifice, we have grieved greatly, and do grieve, that Pharaoh pursues you in flight—or rather that you follow Pharaoh, who strives, under a certain appearance of necessity and veil of piety, to subject you to the old servitude beneath the yoke of sin.] We have grieved, as we said before, and we grieve both for ourselves and for you and for the whole Christian people. For ourselves: because, while we had sown in tears, [Col. 0106B] setting before you and others repeatedly, through our legates and letters, not without a certain bitterness of heart and no slight anxiety of body, the word of the Lord, and exhorting worshippers of the Christian name to avenge the injury done to Jesus Christ, we believed that we should reap in joy; suddenly the enemy has sown tares over our harvest, and has so corrupted the seed that the wheat seems to have degenerated into darnel. For you: because, although you had purged out the old leaven and were believed already entirely to have put off the old man with his deeds, a little leaven—and would that it were little—has once more corrupted the whole mass; and, because you did not preserve your garments white, you have as it were put on again the old clothing, withdrawing your hand from the plough and looking back with [Col. 0106C] Lot’s wife; so that, according to the Apostle, you no longer appeared fit for the kingdom of God.

[We have grieved and do grieve for the Christian people, because it is further humbled by that through which it was thought rather to be exalted. For when many who had preceded you to aid the Holy Land heard that you had not sailed there, they returned home, distrusting your impending passage; the Saracens, uncertain of your arrival and assured by those men’s departure, took courage against the Christians. We do not wish to recount how, as sins deserved, they prevailed over them, since it has been published almost everywhere. We rejoice, however, that, after receiving our letters and recognizing your erroneous transgression, you have devoutly and humbly carried out the apostolic command [Col. 0106D] and, having taken or acknowledged an oath, have received the benefit of absolution. You and your successors, the counts, sons, together with two French barons, have bound yourselves by open letters, to make satisfaction according to our command for having incurred at Zara the sentence of excommunication. Yet would that your repentance be genuine: that is, that you repent of what you have done in such a way as thereafter to beware of like acts. For he who still does what he repents of is not repentant but a deceiver; and the penitent who returns to sin is likened to a dog returning to its vomit. Moreover, a sin [Col. 0107A] committed once is lighter than one that, once committed, is afterwards repeated. Therefore let none of you rashly flatter himself that he may lawfully occupy or plunder the land of the Greeks, as though it were less subject to the Apostolic See, or because . . . . . . . . . the emperor of Constantinople, having deposed and even blinded his brother, usurped the empire. Certainly, however greatly that emperor and the men entrusted to his jurisdiction may offend in this or in other matters, it is nevertheless not yours to judge their crimes; nor did you take up the sign of the cross in order to avenge that injury, but rather the reproach of the Crucified One, to whose service you have especially devoted yourselves.]

We therefore admonish your nobility, earnestly exhort you, and, commanding you by apostolic letters, [Col. 0107B] order that you neither deceive yourselves nor allow yourselves to be deceived by others, so that, under an appearance of piety, you do those things—which God forbid!—that redound to the destruction of your souls. Rather, putting aside frivolous pretexts and feigned necessities alike, pass over to aid the Holy Land and avenge the injury to the Cross; there you will receive from the spoils of the enemy what, if you delay in the regions of Romania, you might perhaps have to extort from brethren. Otherwise, since we cannot and ought not to do so, we promise you no grace of remission whatsoever.

We wish you to retain in memory the tenor of our prohibition, by which, under threat of excommunication, we forbade you to attempt to invade or injure Christian lands, unless they themselves [Col. 0107C] wickedly impeded your journey or some other just and necessary cause perhaps arose, on account of which, with the advice of our legate intervening, you could act otherwise; and we admonish you not lightly to contravene it. Moreover, lest the fault of the doge and people of Venice redound to your punishment, we will and command that you cause to be delivered to them our letters which we have judged should be assigned to them and which are known still to be in your possession, lest they take an excuse for their sins.

Given at Fer . . . . . . in the sixth year.

## CII

> **Note:** [Col. 0107D] It is found, though mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book V, title 39, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*, chapter 39. What is there printed is enclosed here in brackets.
>
> It survives complete in the *Deeds of Innocent III*, §87, but with certain discrepancies, which we have also noted in the margin.
>
> Raynaldus gives a fragment of the same letter, [Col. 0108D] under the year 1203, §§7 and 8; here it is marked by a double stroke at the beginning of each line.

. TO THOSE SIGNED WITH THE CROSS. Advice which the pope sends them without a bull.

[If you truly] repent of what has been done and fully intend [Col. 0107D] to make satisfaction for the sin, we believe—indeed, we know—that the Lord has already been appeased toward you. Therefore, if

> **Note:** [Col. 0108D] In the *Deeds of Innocent III*: “truly” (*vero*).

the Venetians can be induced to make satisfaction and deserve to obtain the benefit of absolution, you may safely sail with them and fight the Lord’s battle. [But if

> **Note:** [Col. 0108D] The *Decretals* add: “the Venetians.”

they perhaps neither wish to make satisfaction

> **Note:** [Col. 0108D] The *Decretals* omit words distinguished here and below by italics.

nor to be absolved, since they are said rather not to grieve but to rejoice over what has been done, we permit you to sail with them as far as the land of the Saracens or the province of Jerusalem, [Col. 0108A] according as has been agreed, or may honourably be agreed, between you and them; communicating with them as little as you can, yet with sorrow and bitterness of heart and in hope of pardon. For since they have already received from you the greater part of the freight payment, and can neither be induced nor compelled to restore it, if things were otherwise you would seem to bear a loss from repentance and they a reward from obstinacy; whereas they remain bound to you for payment of this debt, and what is owed may be demanded and received from excommunicated persons. It is provided in law that, if anyone passes through the land of heretics or of any excommunicated persons, he may buy and receive necessities from them. Further, if the householder [Col. 0108B] of a household is bound by a sentence of excommunication, his household is excused from participation in it. Therefore, although the doge of Venice, as lord of the ships and like the householder of a household, remains under excommunication, you, as his household while you are aboard his ships, will not be touched by his excommunication; and you will be excusable before God if, being aboard excommunicated persons’ ships, you communicate with those excommunicated persons, in whom you cannot avoid communion, with sorrow of heart and hope of repentance.]

But when it happens that you disembark from the ships, whether in the land of the Saracens or in the province of Jerusalem, unless the Venetians have been induced or compelled to make satisfaction and receive the benefit of absolution [Col. 0108C] according to the form of the Church, do not in any way presume to fight the Lord’s battle with them. Otherwise, if they retain something of the anathema and you rise against the enemies of the Cross, you may not prevail over them, but may instead turn your backs, flee, and fall.

For in the book of Joshua it is written that, when Achan son of Carmi had taken from the accursed things of Jericho a very fine scarlet cloak, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels, the Lord was angry with Israel. Hence, when three thousand warriors went up against Ai, they immediately turned their backs and were struck down by the men of the city of Ai; thirty-six men fell, and their adversaries pursued them from the gate as far as Shebarim, and they fell headlong in flight. [Col. 0108D] Nor did the Lord first deliver the city of Ai into Israel’s hands until the people stoned Achan and consumed by fire all that was his.

Likewise in Chronicles, when Jehoshaphat king of Judah had entered into friendship with Ahaziah king of Israel, whose works had been exceedingly wicked, and they had made ships to go to Tarshish, Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah is recorded to have prophesied to Jehoshaphat and said: “Because you have made an alliance with Ahaziah, the Lord has struck your works; and the ships were shattered [Col. 0109A] and could not go to Tarshish” (2 Chronicles 20).

In the book of Maccabees it is written that, when Judas went up against Gorgias, governor of Idumaea, with three thousand foot soldiers and four hundred horsemen, it happened in the engagement that a few Jews fell.

> **Note:** [Col. 0109D] The word “Jews” is lacking in the *Deeds*.

When afterwards Judas wished to place the bodies of the slain in their ancestral tombs, he found beneath the tunics of the dead votive offerings of the idols that were at Jamnia, which the Law forbids Jews [to wear]. Thus it became manifest to all that those who had fallen had fallen for this reason.

Lest provisions fail you, we shall write to our most beloved son in Christ, the emperor of Constantinople, that, according as he himself promised us in his letters, [Col. 0109B] he shall cause provisions to be supplied to you.

> “But if perhaps these should be denied you, since you have vowed yourselves to the common service of the Crucified One—whose is the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it—it might certainly not seem unreasonable that, following the analogy of the emperor of the land, concerning whom civil law provides that if his army needs provisions it may take them from anywhere, you too may, in the fear of the Lord and with the intention of making satisfaction, take them only as necessity requires, without injury to persons.”

For in the book of Judges it is found that, when Gideon was urgently pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian, and first requested from the men of Succoth [Col. 0109C] and then from the inhabitants of Penuel loaves for the people who had come with him and were now almost exhausted, because they denied him what he had requested, he returned victorious, took the elders of the city of Succoth and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them crushed and bruised the men of Succoth. He also destroyed the tower of Penuel, killing the inhabitants of that city. For necessity, especially when a necessary work is being pressed forward, greatly

> **Note:** [Col. 0109D] The word “greatly” (*multum*) is absent from the *Deeds*.

excuses, and in many matters. When the Lord was passing through grainfields on the Sabbath, and his disciples plucked ears of grain and ate them, rubbing them in their hands, and some Pharisees cried out to the disciples, “Why do you do what is not lawful on Sabbaths?” (Luke 6), Jesus is recorded to have answered them: “Have you not even read what David did when he was hungry, he [Col. 0109D] and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God, took and ate the loaves of offering, and gave them to those who were with him, though it was not lawful for anyone but priests alone to eat them?” (ibid.). And he then added that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. But this undertaking too belongs to the Son of Man, and the battle which you intend to fight is the Lord’s battle.

We have introduced these examples from Holy Scripture not in order to authorize robbery, but to tolerate what could not be avoided from grave necessity without great loss. [Col. 0110A] But provide wisely and cautiously that, should the Venetians perhaps wish to find some pretexts for disbanding the army, you take care for the time being to overlook and endure much, until you have arrived at the appointed place, where, when opportunity is gained, you may repress their wickedness as is expedient.

## CIII

> **Note:** [Col. 0109D] It is found, though mutilated in some respects, among the *Decretals*, book III, title 3, *On Married Clerics*, [Col. 0110D] chapter 5.

TO THE BISHOP OF NORWICH.

> **Note:** [Col. 0110D] See above.

That he may deprive married clerics of benefices.

[Deceived by diverse frauds, they attempt to serve God and Mammon, although, according to evangelical truth, no one can serve two masters; for if he loves one, he will hate the other, or, despising one, he will support the other. [For we have received

> **Note:** [Col. 0110D] In the *Decretals*: “however” (*autem*).

that certain clerics of your [Col. 0110B] diocese, who have solemnly contracted marriage in the sight of the Church, strive to retain ecclesiastical benefices. In their manner of life, the lyre accords ill with the psaltery. Since a husband considers how he may please his wife, and therefore is less able to consider the things of God, being, as it were, divided into two and not having full power over himself to serve more fully him from whom he receives his stipend, we grant your brotherhood by the authority of these presents that, supported by our authority, you may deprive such clerics, without appeal, of the ecclesiastical benefices which they have obtained in your diocese—especially since the substance of ecclesiastical property is wont to be diminished through such men—unless perhaps you knowingly conferred ecclesiastical benefices on such persons; in that case, we decree that they are to be stripped of them, not by you but by a superior [Col. 0110C] authority]. Let no one therefore . . . [violate] our concession, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 12 Kalends of July [20 June].

## CIV

TO THE PLEBANUS AND THE BRETHREN OF THE PARISH CHURCH OF CALCINARIA. He adjudicates the case between them and the chaplain of Monteculo concerning their churches. (Ferentino, 12 Kalends of July [20 June].)

When formerly a dispute arose between your predecessor of good memory, son Plebanus, and Master R., chaplain of Monteculo, in the names of your respective churches, concerning the rendering of obedience which that predecessor of yours required from the same master and concerning certain other articles, we judged that case should be committed, [Col. 0110D] under a fixed form, to our beloved son . . . ., prior of Saint Fridianus at Lucca. When issue had therefore been joined, witnesses produced by either side received, and their depositions published, the parties eventually submitted the matter to that same prior as arbitrator, on the condition that whatever he should pronounce by arbitration concerning the foregoing they, both in their own persons and on behalf of their churches, should always hold valid and firmly observe, under whatever penalty should please that prior.

Under a penalty of one hundred pounds of Pisan currency, the same prior among other things arbitrated as follows: Master R., recognizing the aforesaid S. as his Plebanus, should render him obedience; and, since the Plebanus cultivated at his own expense those lands which the parish church of Calcinaria possesses in the territory of Monteculo, no one should be bound to pay tithes from them to the church of Monteculo. [Col. 0111A] He also established other matters to be observed, as is clearly evident from the written award itself.

However, the aforesaid master, believing that the award threatened a grave loss to his church, immediately opposed it and lodged an appeal to us. When the parties were therefore present before us, we appointed our beloved son B., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, as auditor.

> **Note:** [Col. 0111D] See letter 54 of book three, note.

Having more fully learned the grounds and allegations of both parties from the report of the same cardinal, we, weighing the equity of canonical moderation more highly than the subtlety of civil law, adjudged the aforesaid master, in the name of his church, liable for the costs prudently incurred from the time of his opposition to the award until the time of our pronouncement, in favour of the said predecessor of yours. Yet we graciously restored the aforesaid church of Monteculo to its position, so that, notwithstanding the earlier award, it might pursue its claim.

Accordingly, by letters we gave our beloved sons Master Robertinus, Rob. of Pipafracta, and E., our canons of Lucca (sic), instructions that, after summoning the parties before them and hearing the allegations of both sides, they should determine the mutual disputes without appeal, according to the depositions received and any others which they recognized [Col. 0111C] should by law be admitted, without canonical [procedure?—the text reads *sine canonico*].

When, by lawful citations, they had summoned the parties before them, you, son Plebanus—after that same S. had departed this life and you had been canonically substituted—following many and varied disputes of both parties, requested in the name of your church that the judges compel the aforesaid master, chaplain of the same church, to render you the obedience which the chaplains of the church of Monteculo had rendered to your predecessors, the Plebani. You added to your petition that the body of a certain woman, which to your prejudice that master had buried in the cemetery of his church, should be transferred to your church. Finally, you urgently requested [Col. 0111D] that, on Holy Saturday, the said chaplain come to the parish church to celebrate the solemn rites of holy baptism with the other chaplains of that parish church.

The chaplain, on the other hand, maintained that his church was bound in no respect to the aforesaid parish church; and therefore, because it was not subject to it, he asked to be absolved from its claim.
