But after the judges had litigated for a long time on both sides concerning all the questions and had become better informed, they pronounced a definitive judgment in favour of your parish church, by the counsel of prudent men. When, through Al., your prior sent to the Apostolic See, you sought its confirmation from us, the aforesaid chaplain came forward and objected; [Col. 0112A] but, considering his objection frivolous, we judged that sentence should be confirmed. We explain the article which we perceived contained in it—namely, that on Holy Saturday the chaplain of the church of Monteculo should go to the parish church of Calcinaria to celebrate the solemn rites of holy baptism—in this manner: that he should be present for the children being baptized. Let no one therefore . . . [violate] our confirmation, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 12 Kalends of July [20 June].

## CV

TO S. ROMANUS OF CARZOLA, OUR KINSMAN, RECTOR OF THE APOSTOLIC PATRIMONY IN TUSCIA. He entrusts to him the administration of the fortress and castle of Montefiascone. (Ferentino, 2 Kalends of July [30 June].)

[Col. 0112B]

Among all the fortresses and castles which the Roman Church holds, it not only intends but desires that the fortress and castle of Montefiascone be governed more prudently and guarded more diligently. Since, therefore, we have undoubted confidence in the purity of your fidelity and proven knowledge of the effectiveness of your discretion, we judge the custody and administration of that fortress and castle should be entrusted to you, for so long as it shall please us or our successors, as to our faithful man and vassal. By apostolic letters we command that, as you value divine favour and ours, you guard and administer that fortress and castle with every diligence and precaution, providing all things necessary, [Col. 0112C] so that you omit nothing required by circumstances.

For we command by apostolic letters our beloved son B., castellan of Montefiascone, to surrender to you the palace with all that is in it; and we direct all the servants to attend you reverently. We also advise the people that they answer to you as to their castellan.

Given at Ferentino, 2 Kalends of July [30 June].

## CVI

> **Note:** [Col. 0111D] It is found among the *Decretals*, book V, title 40, *On [Col. 0112D] the Meaning of Words*, chapter 19.

TO . . . . . . . . . THE ARCHDEACON, . . . . . . . . . THE PROVOST, AND THE CHAPTER OF PIACENZA. On the interpretation of clerics’ oath. (Ferentino, 6 Nones of July [2 July].)

[Since the clerics of Piacenza take an oath in [Col. 0112D] this form of words: “I, N., from this hour henceforth, shall be faithful and obedient to the holy church of Piacenza and to my lord the bishop of Piacenza,” you asked our advice by your letters whether “the church of Piacenza” should be understood to mean the clergy of the whole diocese or only the chapter of the cathedral church. We therefore answer your discretion in this present writing

> **Note:** [Col. 0112D] The *Decretals* read “thus” (*taliter*) in place of “to your discretion by this present page” (*pro discretioni vestrae praesenti pagina*).

that, by the designation “church of Piacenza” in the prescribed form of oath, the clergy of the whole diocese ought not to be understood; rather, the chapter of the cathedral church is understood. Nevertheless, he who takes such an oath is bound to the bishop as head.]

Given at Ferentino, 6 Nones of July [2 July].

## CVII

TO GUIDO, RECTOR, AND THE BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AT MAGUELONE. He confirms certain privileges. (Ferentino, Kalends of July [1 July].)

[Col. 0113A]

Since you are devoted to works of piety, possess a blessed cemetery, and have clerics professed in your community, it would be incongruous for you to lack an oratory. Accordingly, by the authority of these presents we grant you that, notwithstanding the agreement said to have been made between you and the church of Maguelone through G. of blessed memory,

> **Note:** [Col. 0113D] We have noted above certain matters concerning Gregory, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Angelus in Piscina. The year in which he died is assigned from this letter of Innocent.

cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Angelus, then legate of the Apostolic See, you may have within the precincts of your house an oratory in which [Col. 0113B] the divine office may be celebrated for you by your own clerics. You shall present to the diocesan bishop the priest whom you judge should be appointed to care for souls, and he shall entrust the care of souls to him.

We decree that, from all offerings which, on the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Hypapante [the Presentation of Christ], Ascension, the nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the feasts of Blessed Mary, the solemnities of the Apostles, the commemoration of All Saints, every Sunday, and the other principal feasts of the place, are brought by inhabitants of Montpellier to the altar of your oratory or as a gift to the priest while the divine offices are celebrated, you shall render without difficulty one fourth to the mother church or to the others to whom it belongs, except for utensils specifically offered for the use of the poor. But offerings on all the other [Col. 0113C] days, and generally all offerings made by other donors, you shall possess in full by our grant.

Furthermore, by this present writing we strictly prohibit you from presuming to receive anyone for burial in your cemetery unless he is your brother, a member of your household, or a pilgrim, who ought to have free burial everywhere. Admit no others to burial unless it be with the consent of the prelate from whose church the body of the deceased is taken; to that church we command that one fourth of the legacies be afterwards restored. Let no one therefore [violate] this concession and constitution, etc.

Given at Ferentino, Kalends of July [1 July].

## CVIII

> **Note:** [Col. 0113D] It is found almost complete among the *Decretals*, book III, title 24, *On Oaths*, chapter 24.

TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TARRAGONA. He adjudicates a matrimonial case. (Ferentino, 12 Kalends of July [20 June].)

[Col. 0113D]

[Your brotherhood asked our advice as to what you should do concerning this point

> **Note:** [Col. 0113D] This word is lacking in the *Decretals*, so that the phrase now reads “namely, what is to be done.”

—namely, [Col. 0114A] that R. of Belloloco and Agnes,

> **Note:** [Col. 0113D] In the *Decretals*, “B. and A.” The words printed below in italics are absent.

his wife, formerly swore to one another that they would never seek one another again. But he now urgently demands her back, whereas she on the contrary declares that she would sooner become a Saracen and lose her soul than return to him], though she would willingly dismiss the adulterer to whom she attached herself after leaving him, and would promise and swear chastity.

[We therefore reply to your brotherhood on this matter and command you by apostolic letters to admonish and induce both parties earnestly to observe continence. If they are willing to promise and keep it, allow both to live apart without the other. Otherwise, if the husband is unwilling to remain continent, compel the aforesaid wife

> **Note:** [Col. 0113D] In the *Decretals*, “her” (*illam*) in place of “the aforesaid wife” (*praedictam uxorem ipsius*).

to return to him and dwell with him as a wife with her husband, by sentence of excommunication and without appeal; for such an oath was rash, and adultery has been committed by both parties.] [Col. 0114B]

Given at Ferentino, 12 Kalends of July [20 June].

## CIX

> **Note:** [Col. 0113D] Fragments of this letter are found in the *Decretals*, [Col. 0114D] book V, title 33, *On the Privileges and Excesses of Privileged Persons*, chapter 14. Letters 327 and the last letter of book one, and letters 203 and 204 of book two, should be compared.

TO THE BISHOP OF COIMBRA. He decides the suit between him and the community of Santa Cruz. (Ferentino, 6 Kalends of July [26 June].)

[When formerly you had come to the Apostolic See and had remained there for a long time concerning the disputes

> **Note:** [Col. 0114D] The *Decretals* have only “on account of the disputes” and omit “beloved sons.” Below, they read “monastery” in place of “church.”

which you had against our beloved sons, . . . . . the prior and canons of the Church of the Holy Cross, and concerning which an appeal had been made to our hearing, because no representative appeared for the other party, we strictly commanded the same prior [Col. 0114C] and brethren by virtue of obedience to come to our presence, in person or through sufficient and suitable representatives, by the then forthcoming feast of All Saints, to receive a definitive sentence concerning all privileges and liberties which they claimed to possess from Roman pontiffs or from M., formerly bishop of Coimbra, and concerning the other disputes brought against them by the church of Coimbra].

> **Note:** [Col. 0114D] Thus the *Decretals* read: “we judged that a fixed term should be set, in which they should come or send [representatives].”

That the truth might more easily appear, we commanded the authentic originals with their seals to be presented to us by the same date and under the same compulsion. [Meanwhile, however, either party was permitted to plead and prove before our beloved sons . . . .

> **Note:** [Col. 0114D] The *Decretals* add “your.” Below, they read *Sarra* for *Seira* and omit the remainder distinguished here by italics.

abbot of Alcobaça, and . . . . abbot of Seira, and F. Menende, [Col. 0114D] monk of Alcobaça—to whom the case had earlier been delegated under a fixed form and before whom witnesses had been produced by both parties—whatever else they judged should be alleged and proved.]

We took care to assign them the aforesaid peremptory date, so that, if they should perhaps refuse to come or send representatives, we should nevertheless take care to proceed in the same matter as far as law allowed. We also gave those judges instructions that, if they proceeded by the will of the parties, they should receive any further witnesses whom the parties deemed should be produced concerning the privileges, liberties, and other articles; carry the proceedings through to a definitive sentence; and send all the acts under their seals to the Apostolic See.

When you afterwards came to the Apostolic See, two canons of Santa Cruz appeared, but they had neither letters of ratification nor had they been sent as procurators for this suit. We therefore deemed the party of Santa Cruz contumacious, as it was, since it had sent us not suitable representatives for the case but merely whatever sort of messengers [Col. 0115B] they were. We ordered the depositions received by the delegated judges to be opened, so that we might finally pronounce sentence if the merits of the case became clear to us.

But, wishing to restore to your favour the mind of our most beloved son in Christ, . . . . the illustrious king of Portugal, who had been moved against you on this account, you agreed with the aforesaid canons in this form: namely, that the same case, with the obstacle of appeal removed both as to the principal matter and the incident, should be committed for determination to our venerable brother . . . . bishop of Zamora and our beloved sons . . . . dean of Zamora and dean of Ourense. This was provided, however, that the party of Santa Cruz might, within forty days after receiving our letters, produce documents and witnesses concerning those articles on which you had produced your witnesses in its absence. [Col. 0115C] Otherwise, they might not challenge or object to the depositions received, on the ground that proceedings had taken place in this case before issue had been joined.

We therefore gave the said bishop and deans commands, requiring that, if the party of Santa Cruz wished to ratify what had been done by the said canons, they should receive that party’s witnesses and documents concerning the above-mentioned articles—provided that it chose to produce them within forty days after receipt of our letters—and, after your depositions had been published according to the aforesaid form, proceed in the case and determine it, appeal being set aside, without delay [*sine debito*, as printed]. But if they perhaps did not wish to ratify what had been done by [Col. 0115D] the aforesaid canons, since their contumacy would be understood not to have been purged but increased, the judges should proceed against them as contumacious persons; and, after carefully examining the received depositions, should decide the case without appeal and execute the sentence they rendered.

Since this case was to be conducted outside the kingdom of Portugal, they were first to assign the parties a suitable term under a peremptory edict, lest you be compelled to suffer prolonged hardship on account of the remoteness of places and distance of persons. If they could not cite the party of Santa Cruz through others, they were to compel its canons dwelling in the kingdom of León, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to present to it the letters of citation; and no letters obtained from the Apostolic See which prejudiced truth and justice, should any appear, were to stand in the way. [Col. 0116A] If not all of them could be present to carry this out, the bishop was nevertheless to carry it out with one of the others.

When the parties had been summoned to a fixed date and had appeared on that date, the aforesaid bishop and dean of Zamora, since the dean of Ourense could not be present, took care to ask the prior of Santa Cruz whether he ratified what had been done by his canons. The reply made on his behalf was that there was no place for the question, since he was prepared at once to prove that our rescript had been obtained through false representations in petitions. For when the dean of Coimbra had obtained against the monastery of Santa Cruz eleven letters of commission addressed to the aforesaid abbot of Seira and our beloved son P. Froildiz, monk of Alcobaça, although the party of the Church of Santa Cruz had first obtained the requested adjournments, yet because on the second occasion it could not obtain individual adjournments for each individual commission, it nevertheless appealed to our hearing, although appeal had been prohibited in our letters. At length that party and the dean of Coimbra took care to submit the dispute to the aforesaid king of Portugal, . . . . . of Costa, and . . . . . prior of Rimaran, and to the aforesaid judges, each side binding two sureties under a penalty; and thus the prior renounced the appeal with the assent of his men, the dean renouncing our letters.

Moreover, twelve canons on each side swore to bear witness to the truth concerning the whole matter. [Col. 0116C] The witnesses having therefore been received and their depositions reduced to writing, the king refused to be present, but committed his functions to the aforesaid priors of . . . . . de Costa and de Rimaranes, and proposed to the parties that they should pursue their right through the Roman Church or elsewhere, since a cause of this kind did not pertain to him. You, however, before the aforesaid bishop and dean of Zamora, alleged that neither the renunciation of the dean of Coimbra—who had been appointed procurator not to renounce but rather to act—nor the compromise was binding: both because arbiters ought not to be judges, because a compromise concerning ecclesiastical matters had been made with a layman, and because he had substituted others in his own place, although this had not at all been provided for in the compromise. [Col. 0116D]

But the party of Holy Cross alleged in reply that the compromise was binding, because it said that we had pronounced that proceedings could be had concerning its penalty. It added that you had ratified the dean’s renunciation and, suppressing this fact, had procured the aforesaid letters—which you could by no means have obtained had you more fully set out the truth to us on this point. Although that party produced four witnesses who stated simply and absolutely that you had ratified what had been done by the dean, the six witnesses whom you produced testified that you had expressed such ratification not simply but conditionally: namely, if the case should be concluded according to the completed attestations.

Moreover, John Caesar, canon of Holy [Col. 0117A] Cross, had been produced as a witness; and Michael Petri and others whom you produced testified on oath that we had caused the whole truth of this case to be investigated by the first delegated judges and everything reported to us, and that, having carefully examined all matters, we had thus pronounced that your claim was not obstructed by the objections raised. The same John and Michael Petri, when asked whether you had ratified the dean’s renunciation, said that they knew absolutely nothing about it. But Holy Cross objected against them that they had shown themselves contradictory, since they had first said that they had reported to us the entire truth of the matter, yet secondly had made no mention of the ratification, which was, as it were, the principal part of the case. You, however, said that the witness produced by Holy Cross [Col. 0117B] should properly be believed against that party.

The judges therefore, observing that appeal had been prohibited in our letters; that no condition existed under which you had said that you ratified what had been done by the dean; and that we, after examining the truth of the whole matter, had pronounced that your suit ought not to be impeded by the matters alleged by the canons of Holy Cross; and considering also that the party of Holy Cross had more fully discredited the aforesaid John, whom it itself had produced and who was instructing the judges concerning what had been done before us—they ruled, upon prudent advice, that the proceedings in the case delegated to them could not in law be impeded by the allegation of falsity raised.

Then, when they wished to proceed to the principal issue, [Col. 0117C] the prior of Holy Cross raised numerous grounds of recusal. Since the judges regarded them as frivolous and refused to admit them, the prior, abandoning every defense of his cause, contumaciously absented himself. We too later considered the aforesaid recusals invalid for the reason that the contumacy of Holy Cross was not diminished but increased.

[The judges—[Note: [Col. 0117D] The Decretals omit this word, as below in “the attestations . . . examined.”] believing that the case had been sufficiently argued, and having diligently examined the attestations and arguments of both parties—condemned the monastery of Holy Cross, on the prudent advice of wise men, to pay you the expenses which you had sworn that you had incurred over four years by reason of this litigation, amounting to fifty marks of gold. [Note: [Col. 0117D] The Decretals read “condemned.”] By their judgment they annulled the liberty which the aforesaid bishop of Coimbra had granted to the monastery of Holy Cross, to the enormous detriment of the church of Coimbra, [Note: [Col. 0118D] These words are absent from the Decretals.] after extorting the canons’ consent through the bishop’s herald and the king’s porter. Furthermore, because that same M. [Note: [Col. 0118D] The Decretals add “your predecessor” and omit the words below distinguished in italic type.] had been a regular canon and, after being promoted to the episcopate, had given to the said monastery two thousand marabotins which he had acquired, the judges condemned that monastery to restore them.

Moreover, they ruled that all tithes and churches which the monastery had received from the hand of the king or other lay or clerical persons without the consent of the bishop of Coimbra, [Col. 0118A] and which it had established by its own authority at Latren. or elsewhere, as contained in the attestations—namely, the chapel of Saint John built in the suburb of Coimbra; the churches of Taaveiro, Laurizal, Mira, Sorenes, Saint Facundus; the hermitage of Saint Martin of Agoada; the churches of Mortedi, Travancha, Saint Marina in Sena, Saint Romanus with both rights, Saint Sebastian, and all churches established in the castle of Leiria and its district—as well as the estates contained in the attestations, held under title of ownership, namely the estates of Lavaes with its church of Buarchos, Cassaira, Eimedi, Saint Verissimus, and Cabima, were to be restored, together with the fruits received in the intervening period, to the right of the church of Coimbra. This was because the party of Holy Cross had resisted the proofs made against it neither by prescription [limitation through long possession] [Col. 0118B] nor by defense. They ordered that the bodies of two dead persons who had died excommunicated be disinterred from the monastery’s cemetery and removed wholly from the monastery.

They also decreed that the portions of the parishes of Saint James and Saint Justa, divided by royal command without the Church’s authority and added to the chapel of Saint John, be restored to their original undivided state; that the chapel of Saint John, as regards parochial right, be subjected to the jurisdiction of the church of Coimbra; and that a portion of the goods of the deceased, according to the custom of the land, be restored to those churches [Col. 0118C] from which the deceased had received the ecclesiastical sacraments while living.

They further ruled that the vineyard once held in *praestimonium*—a benefice or tenure—from the church of Coimbra by Dominicus Rozocida, and granted by him to the monastery of Holy Cross, be restored to the right of the church of Coimbra; and that the church of Coimbra itself be restored to its right of procession, to which, as had been proved by witnesses, the canons of Holy Cross had customarily gone every Sunday. Likewise, they decreed that, for the houses at Porta Nova in which the church of Coimbra formerly had parochial right, the monastery of Holy Cross should compensate it in another suitable place with as much jurisdiction as the church of Coimbra had lost in the aforesaid houses.

But they caused the church [Col. 0118D] of Quiajos, which the aforesaid M., bishop of Coimbra, had granted to the monastery of Holy Cross with the consent of his canons, to be adjudged to that monastery. They decreed that the portion of the village of Pavea—which, although purchased in the name of the church of Coimbra with the money of M., formerly its prior, and later left to that church by testament, you nevertheless seized while the monastery possessed it—be restored to the monastery, saving the church of Coimbra’s right of ownership. They adjudged to the monastery, in full right, the remaining portion of that village, formerly granted to the monastery of Holy Cross by Pelagius F. [Col. 0119A] Furthermore, they ruled that three small holdings at Saint Joanninus be restored to the monastery, without prejudice to the question of the church of Coimbra’s ownership, and absolved the monastery from your claim for twelve measures of wheat.

Finally, when you and the other party had for this reason come to the Apostolic See, [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Decretals omit these words.] the procurator of the monastery of Holy Cross alleged that the judgment was not [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Decretals add “valid nor.”] binding. For, although the delegated judges did not admit sufficient grounds of recusal advanced in order to remove them, which the party wished to prove, nor permit them to be proved before arbitrators, the monastery’s party therefore considered that an appeal to the Apostolic See should be made; it was clear that the judges had proceeded after an appeal had been lawfully entered. [Note: [Col. 0119D] All this is absent from the Decretals. Below, “was” is printed instead of “had been.”] Even if the said judgment were otherwise binding, nevertheless, because [Col. 0119B] the monastery had been undefended, as the judges themselves stated in their letters, [Note: [Col. 0120D] The Decretals omit this.] and because the privileges of liberty had not been produced before them, it ought, lest an individual’s offense redound to the Church’s damage, to be admitted to produce its privileges. The procurator requested that this be granted through the customary benignity of the Apostolic See.

We, therefore, considering that these privileges served not only for the liberty of the monastery but also expressed our right and protected the justice of the Roman Church, admitted its party, by favor, to produce the privileges, lest injury to the monastery redound against us. In order that we might more fully understand the truth concerning the judges’ proceedings, we ordered all the records, as they had been conducted before them, to be produced to us by both sides.

[Col. 0119C] The monastery’s procurator therefore alleged that the aforesaid M., bishop of Coimbra, had granted to the monastery of Holy Cross, with its parishes, parishioners, and confraternities, full liberty from every episcopal right and exaction; that he had reduced his grant to writing; and that he had fortified it with the subscriptions of the canons of Coimbra, who had given their consent. Even if this grant might perhaps in itself have been invalid, it had nevertheless acquired perpetual force through the confirmation of Pope A., our predecessor of happy memory, who had confirmed it with such certain knowledge in his privilege that he not only set out its tenor but used its very words. Celestine subsequently imitated him in this respect and confirmed that grant as the former had confirmed it. [Col. 0119D]

But you replied that the said grant was not binding: first, because the bishop could not validly burden his church so enormously; secondly, because the canons’ consent had been obtained by the fraud of the bishop, who, in order more easily to induce them to consent, asserted that the monastery had always been free; and thirdly, because it had been extorted through his power and that of the king, since the king’s porter threatened the canons with confiscation of their goods [Col. 0120A] and the bishop’s herald with exile.

Moreover, the tenor of that grant could not fully be established, nor ought faith to be given to the written instrument presented by the monastery’s party. For, according to the testimony of certain witnesses, the page of that grant made by Michael had been erased in several lines, and each canon who had subscribed had done so in his own hand. Yet in the document produced to us, no erasure whatsoever appeared, while all the subscriptions were written in the same hand. Nor did it avail that Alexander, our aforesaid predecessor, had confirmed such a grant and had used its words, because even if he was aware of the words, he was [Col. 0120B] ignorant of the facts: he did not know that the canons’ consent had been extorted and that the page of the grant had been altered.

The other party replied, however, that even if neither such a grant nor its confirmation were binding, the monastery’s true and ancient liberty could nevertheless be established by its privileges. Pope Innocent, our predecessor of good memory, had received it into Saint Peter’s guardianship and protection; and, when stating its annual due, added: “as a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, let it pay two bezants each year to us and our successors.” Popes Lucius, Eugenius, and Adrian of happy memory expressed this in their privileges, although authentic copies of those of Lucius and Eugenius had not been presented to us.

[Col. 0120C] Against this, you, brother bishop, alleged that the said predecessors of ours had granted no liberty at all to the monastery; they had merely received it under protection, without mentioning liberty except where it is said: “as a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See.” Properly understood, this could not prejudice your church. For since the pronoun “this” there points to nothing visible but is recognized as making a reference in thought, and since its meaning would be wholly foreign unless shaped by what precedes, the pronoun seems to make, as it were, a relative reference and to call “liberty” the protection and confirmation mentioned in the preceding part. Some liberty is indeed conferred together with confirmation: namely, in accordance with the judgment of the aforesaid Alexander, no one may be sued, apart from the authority of the Apostolic See, regarding matters confirmed to them by that See. Thus what is read in the privilege can be understood as liberty of this kind.

That this ought to be the meaning appears from the privileges themselves. Innocent expressly preserves the reverence due to the diocesan bishop, while Lucius and Eugenius, after granting protection and expressly confirming certain [Col. 0121A] churches, preserve the diocesan bishop’s right.

The other party, however, argued in reply that if the aforesaid Innocent had wished to call protection “liberty” by an unusual term, he could have written “protection” where he wrote “liberty.” Nor is the argument concerning the demonstrative pronoun harmful, since in ancient times the Apostolic See received into special protection and its own guardianship only those churches which it regarded as special and its own. Thus, since both through the first chapter, in which the monastery is received under Saint Peter’s guardianship and protection, and through certain following provisions, liberty is known to have been granted to the monastery, the demonstrative pronoun indicates that liberty, understood more clearly than it is expressed. [Col. 0121B]

Far be it from anyone to believe that the Apostolic See wished to deceive the monastery by receiving an annual due from it in the name of liberty while granting it either no liberty or merely half-full liberty, as the opposing party alleged. Nor does it hinder, but rather helps, that the often-mentioned Innocent wished the reverence due to the diocesan bishop to remain intact: because, by expressly reserving such reverence to him, he is understood to have denied him everything else. He wished that reverence to be shown in this: as the Roman pontiffs who succeeded him, wishing to interpret what had been obscurely said, expressed in their privileges, the canons of Holy Cross were to receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars, and certain other matters specified in those privileges from the diocesan bishop, if he were Catholic, enjoyed the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and wished to provide them freely and without any improper exaction. [Col. 0121C]

Likewise, it does no harm that Lucius and Eugenius, having listed certain churches, said that the diocesan bishop’s right was preserved; for they did not mean this of the head, but of the members. Thus Adrian too reserved canonical justice to diocesan bishops, which cannot be understood of the head, since it is clear that none of the churches has more than one diocesan bishop. Alexander and his successors, in order wholly to remove any scruple of doubt on this point, mentioned only the authority of the Apostolic See. Furthermore, if so many and such great arguments did not suffice, prescription alone protected the church of Holy Cross. [Col. 0121D]

We therefore, having heard these and other matters and understood what had been alleged on either side, [distinguishing between the liberty granted to that church by the aforesaid bishop and the liberty which the Apostolic See had granted it long before the bishop’s time, as appears from the aforesaid privileges—[Note: [Col. 0121D] The Decretals omit these words and, below, the word “clearly.”]—because it was clearly established to us that in the bishop’s grant the canons’ consent had been extorted; that the page of the grant had erasures in several lines; [Note: [Col. 0122D] The Decretals read “erasures,” and below omit the word “rather.”] that the individual subscriptions had been entered in the hands of the individual subscribers; [Col. 0122A] but that the document produced to us displayed no erasure and was not varied by different hands and subscriptions, but was rather written from beginning to end in one and the same hand, we declare the liberty granted by that bishop void and invalid, confirming on this point the judgment of the delegated judges.

But because we clearly learned from the aforesaid privileges that our predecessors had granted the church of Holy Cross a privilege of liberty, and that it had remained in possession of that liberty for so long that, even if all else failed, it would have acquired it by prescription, we confirm by Apostolic authority the liberty granted by our predecessors, imposing silence upon you concerning it. In this, however, we in no way derogate from the judgment of the delegated judges, because [Col. 0122B] they had not taken cognizance of this liberty.]

After this, the procurator of the church of Holy Cross alleged before us that the duke of Portugal, of illustrious memory, . . . had granted to that church all churches already founded or thereafter to be founded in the castle of Leiria and its territory, together with all ecclesiastical rights; that a public instrument concerning this grant had been drawn up, which he called, in the customary language of the land, a *testamentum*; and that both the archbishop of Braga, metropolitan of the province, and the bishop of Coimbra had subscribed to this grant. The delegated judges, without examining the privileges of Holy Cross, had nevertheless pronounced no judgment against the church of Holy Cross concerning these churches, although the cause had not been specially delegated to them concerning them.

And although [Col. 0122C] the bishop of Coimbra subscribed to the aforesaid grant as diocesan, because Lisbon—the city to whose diocese these places are known to belong—was then held by the Saracens, yet after that city had later been restored to the Christians through the exertions of that duke, the bishop of Lisbon, as the true diocesan, confirmed the duke’s donation . . . by his own privilege. Pope Adrian, taking this carefully into account, confirmed by his privilege to the church of Holy Cross all the churches situated both in the castle of Leiria and in its territory, with all their appurtenances, as the duke’s charter and the aforesaid bishop’s confirmation contained.

But it was alleged on your behalf in reply that the duke’s grant [Col. 0122D] was not binding, since a layman had no power to confer ecclesiastical rights, especially spiritual ones. Nor did it avail that the archbishop of Braga and the bishop of Coimbra were said to have subscribed the duke’s charter, since the charter itself was not drawn up as a public instrument and their seals did not hang from it; therefore it deserved no faith whatever. Nor was it harmful that Pope Adrian had confirmed to the church of Holy Cross the aforesaid churches with their appurtenances, as contained in the duke’s charter and the confirmation of the bishop of Lisbon, since he had believed that the duke granted the right of patronage and temporal matters, and the bishop, [Col. 0123A] as diocesan, spiritual matters.

It is clear, moreover, from the other party’s admission and from the tenor of the aforesaid privileges of our predecessors Alexander and Celestine, that these churches belong to the diocese of Coimbra, because after listing them, together with certain others, their privileges add: “all of which are situated in the bishopric of Coimbra.” Therefore, since the other party relied on those privileges for itself and had also procured them, it neither ought nor could repudiate them on this point.

Furthermore, Adrian’s privilege had not conferred a new right on the monastery but confirmed a right already held; therefore the duke’s grant, previously invalid, had not acquired validity from that confirmation. In response, the other party replied [Col. 0123B] that the church of Holy Cross had possessed the said churches and the church of Saint John situated in the suburb of Coimbra for so long that it could defend itself by lawful prescription. From the time when Adrian confirmed those churches to it, and when it could possess them in good faith, until the commencement of the lawsuit, forty years and several months had elapsed.

It was therefore established to us, after careful examination of all matters and from the form of the judgment of the aforesaid judges, that the monastery of Holy Cross had acquired possession of the aforesaid churches in the time of the often-mentioned duke. For he had ordered all the churches which the monastery had received from the hand of the king to be restored to the right of the church of Coimbra, and receipt is known to pertain to possession. [Col. 0123C] It was also established by the form of your petition, in which you asked that they be restored to you, that the monastery still possessed the same churches. Likewise it was established that it had possessed them during the intervening period, and that forty years had elapsed by the time the suit began since Adrian, who had confirmed them to it.

Although the other party alleged before us that G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, of good memory, then legate of the Apostolic See, had imposed silence upon you regarding all these matters, and that it therefore appeared that the issue had been joined before him, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See above, epistle 107, note.] the truth was nevertheless fully disclosed to us by the depositions of witnesses: namely, that neither had the issue been joined nor judgment promulgated, because after examining the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, he had refused to hear you concerning these matters. Since, therefore, the monastery of Holy Cross had possessed the aforesaid churches long before forty years ago and also during the intervening period, and still possessed them, and since no interruption has been proved to the contrary, we adjudge to the monastery of Holy Cross, on the advice of our brethren, both the aforesaid churches of Leiria and the church of Saint John of Coimbra, imposing silence upon you regarding them. [Col. 0124A] In this too we do not derogate from the delegated judges, since Adrian’s privilege—by whose authority the canons of Holy Cross could believe themselves possessors in good faith—nor any other instruments had been produced before them.

As to the fifty marks of gold awarded as expenses and the two thousand gold pieces which the often-mentioned M., bishop of Coimbra, had granted to the church of Holy Cross, we have, with the parties’ consent, moderated the judges’ judgment as follows: of the fifty marks of gold, the monastery is bound to pay you twenty; and of the two thousand gold pieces, one thousand.

[Since we confirm the liberty granted to the monastery by our predecessors, we have decreed that the monastery is not bound by the possessory right, [Col. 0124B] which is contrary to liberty, without derogating from the delegated judges, before whom the privileges of liberty had not been produced.]

Moreover, regarding the decree of the same judges that, for the houses at Porta Nova in which the church of Coimbra had possessed parochial right, the monastery should compensate it in another suitable place with as much jurisdiction as it had lost in the said houses, we wholly correct the judgment which they rendered, deciding that the monastery is not bound to do so.

[In all other matters, we confirm by Apostolic authority the judgment rendered by the aforesaid judges both for the church of Coimbra and for the monastery of Holy Cross. [Note: [Col. 0123D] The Decretals omit the words distinguished in italic type.]] Etc. Therefore let no one infringe this determination and confirmation, etc. Should anyone do so, etc.

[Col. 0124C] Given at Ferentino, 26 June.

CX. [Note: [Col. 0123D] This occurs among the Decretals, book III, title 21, “On Pledges and Other Securities,” chapter 4.] TO CUALANDO, OUR SUBDEACON, AND B. VITALIS, CANONS OF PISA. He decides a dispute between private persons concerning certain lands. (Ferentino, 3 July.)

[We believe that you are endowed with such knowledge] that you clearly know what the law is regarding the matter about which you wished to consult us. Yet, because you requested instruction by our response, and lest the decision of the case be delayed while awaiting that response, we have thought it right to answer you by this letter.

[Indeed, in your letter to us [Note: [Col. 0124D] The Decretals omit the word “to us” and read “H. and B. . . . G.”] you informed us that, when we had committed to you the case pending between Henry and Bandus, sons of Guido [Note: [Col. 0124D] Addition: “on one side.”] of Cosa, and G., daughter of Tabert [Note: [Col. 0124D] The Decretals read “T. and her heirs, on the other side.”], and her heirs, concerning certain vineyards [Note: [Col. 0124D] The Decretals read “lands,” and below “three” for “four.”] pledged to the aforesaid persons for twenty-four pounds], we instructed you by our letters to compel G. and her heirs, by the penalty enacted against usurers at the Lateran Council, to restore the vineyards to those claiming restitution and likewise to restore whatever they had received from them beyond the principal. [Col. 0125A] In order to proceed in the said case according to our mandate, you caused the parties to be summoned.

When they appeared before you, it was alleged [on behalf of the said G. and her heirs before you [Note: [Col. 0125D] Omitted by the Decretals]] that the lands reclaimed by H. and B. were not pledged by them, but absolutely sold, as was more fully set out in the instrument drawn up concerning the transaction. But the said Henry, on his own behalf and that of his brother, firmly maintained that the lands had not been absolutely sold but pledged, because the sale had been made subject to this condition: if, from the time of the contract until the next two years, the purchase displeased the said T., G., Henry’s father, should within a further year pay twenty-six pounds, with the fruits received reckoned toward that sum, as he firmly asserted was contained in [Col. 0125B] the same instrument. [Note: [Col. 0125D] These words are absent from the Decretals.]

But because, as you indicated in the same letter, [Note: [Col. 0125D] Absent from the Decretals.] you doubted whether the sale was pure and absolute or whether the aforesaid agreement ought to be adjudged a pledge, you requested instruction by our letter. We answer your consultation as follows: whatever the parties’ intention may have been, the sale does not appear conditional from the form of the contract, but absolute, although it can be dissolved by a condition. Nevertheless, from two matters expressly included in the agreement—namely, that the fruits received were to be counted toward payment of the money, and that forty [Note: [Col. 0125D] The Decretals read sixty.] shillings were to be paid beyond the sum received—a strong presumption arises against the buyer, especially if he has been accustomed to practice usury [Col. 0125C] and commit the fraud of usury.

Given at Ferentino, 3 July.

CXI. TO J., [Note: [Col. 0126D] Innocent wrote to him frequently; see Epistle 5 of book V and Epistle 26 of book VI.] PRIOR, AND THE CLERGY OF SAINT GREGORY AT SPOLETO. He adjudicates the case pending between them and the brethren of a certain hospital.

When you, son prior, came into our presence, we committed for determination to our beloved son L., [Note: [Col. 0126D] From this letter of Innocent it is inferred that Leo, concerning whom see the note to Epistle V of book V, had exchanged the title of Saint Lucy in Septisolium for that of Holy Cross before 1205.] cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross, the case which you had against the brethren of the hospital situated beside your church. You alleged, when standing in our presence, that your predecessor R., wishing to devote himself to works of piety, because [Col. 0125D] it was not proper for him to receive the poor and the sick in the brethren’s dormitory, had specially assigned for hospitality a certain place within the cloister.

Having accordingly summoned Peter and Gir., laymen who, though of good conduct, had not received the religious habit and were not bound by a profession to any religious house or order, and when they offered themselves and their goods to the church of Blessed Gregory and promised obedience and [Col. 0126A] reverence to the said prior, he gave them religious garments and assigned them to the work of the hospital. The hospital, built at the expense of your church, that church possessed peacefully until the beginning of the lawsuit, ordering, correcting, and disposing of it at its own will. All who devoted themselves to the hospital’s service first offered themselves to your church, promised reverence and obedience to the prior for the time being, and were appointed and installed in each office by that prior of the hospital. Although the hospital had promised obedience and reverence to the aforesaid R. and his successors, [Note: [Col. 0126D] Thus in the apograph; but something is lacking.] it wholly denied these to you, son prior, and, without your permission, usurped for itself the office of prior.

Furthermore, since R., formerly [Col. 0126B] a brother of that hospital, had been offered to your church, your steward claimed the offerings which the hospital brethren had received at his tomb. He urgently sought that we should cause the work of the new chapel to be destroyed, which those brethren had erected over the burial-place of the same R., after an appeal had been made to us, against the liberties and immunities of your church and to your prejudice and burden. He also requested that the body of that offered person be restored to him.

Further, when an offered person of your church had built the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Ponte Manubiae and granted it to that church, as the public instrument records, and when the diocesan bishops had granted you their right in it and it had subsequently been confirmed to you by the Apostolic See, and when you had possessed it for a long time without litigation, your steward urgently sought its restoration, with the fruits received from it, and likewise the restoration of the lands situated at Salian., because the Hospitallers had violently expelled your clerics from it. [Col. 0126C]

But the procurator of that hospital, in the presence of certain brethren of the Cross-bearing Hospital of Bologna, alleged in reply that the aforesaid R., formerly prior of your church, with the consent of his canons, had freely granted to brother Cletus, and to Peter as well as all his ministers and officials, a certain holding in which they might build a hospital for the use of the poor and the advancement of the religion of the Cross-bearers. After it had been completed through their diligence, both they [Col. 0126D] and their successors possessed it peacefully in their own name for forty years, ordering and disposing of it according to their own will. But now you, son prior, were improperly raising a dispute against them by reason of the aforesaid R., formerly a brother of that hospital, whom some believe to be a saint, wishing to restore the hospital to the right of the church of Saint Gregory.

You also unjustly claimed the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Ponte Manubiae, [Col. 0127A] since its founder had been a brother of the hospital and, for greater security, had offered it to the hospital.

Moreover, he added that you were unjustly proceeding against them concerning the lands of Salian., since they belonged not to the church of Saint Gregory but rather to the hospital. Therefore, having learned through the same cardinal of these and the other matters proposed on either side, and having carefully heard the bishops’ authoritative reasons, the parties’ depositions, and allegations, we award the aforesaid hospital to you and, through you, to your church, on the condition that you impose no new exactions upon it, since its goods, according to the custom hitherto observed, ought to be applied to the uses of the poor. But we absolve the brothers of the hospital, by the counsel of our brethren, [Col. 0127B] from restoring the offerings which you demanded from them, since, even if the aforesaid R. had been your oblate, he was nevertheless a brother of the hospital.

But because it was clearly established from the witnesses’ depositions that, after an appeal had been lodged to us, work upon a new chapel had been constructed to the prejudice of your church, we decree by the authority of these presents that it is to be destroyed. We decree, however, that there is no place for restitution of the body: for, although your witnesses sufficiently showed that the body of the aforesaid R. had been buried in your cemetery, it was likewise proved on the other side that he was buried in the soil of the hospital; and since no translation of the body has been alleged or proved, it is clear that it still remains in its first burial-place. But we judge that the chapel of Saint Nicholas of [Col. 0127C] Ponte Manubiae belongs, without intermediary, to the house of that hospital, and through it to your church, since it was proved on the hospital’s side that Tantinus, formerly its brother, built it for the use of the Cross-bearers and the poor, and that the donation he made to the hospital preceded the donation he made to your church, as is shown by comparison of the public instruments drawn up concerning those donations; saving nevertheless the episcopal right which is known to belong to you therein by the donation of the diocesan bishops. We condemn the brothers of that hospital to restore to you and, through you, to the church of Saint Gregory, the lands of Salian. Therefore let no one … this determination, etc.

[Col. 0127D] Given at Ferentino, 8 July.

## CXII

[Note: [Col. 0127D] It survives, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book I, *On Election and the Authority of the Elect*, chapter 27.]

To the Prior of Saint Fridianus [Note: [Col. 0127D] See above.], and to C. and C., canons of Lucca. He adjudicates the case concerning the election of the prior of the church of Saint Peter at Lucca. (Ferentino, 8 July.)

Since we formerly thought fit to commit to you the case pending between the priest Bonus and Bruno, a canon of the church of Saint Peter at Lucca, concerning the fact that the aforesaid priest [Col. 0128A] Bonus was, as is said, elected prior by the greater part of the canons of that church, while the aforesaid Bruno and another opposed him; you, as we have learned from your letters, took care to summon the parties, so that according to our mandate you might bring the matter to a canonical conclusion.

When they had appeared before you, the said priest Bonus urgently requested that you should confirm by apostolic authority the election made of him. But the aforesaid Bruno replied to the contrary that he was unworthy to govern the priory, charging him with the crime of simony; he also alleged that his election had not been canonically celebrated and that, because he was not professed, he ought rightly to be rejected. Yet, since nothing concerning simony had been proved [Col. 0128B], nor anything shown against the manner of the election, you were greatly moved by the privilege of that church, which expressly provided that no one was to be installed there, by any craft of surreptitious procurement, unless the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, should judge him fit to be elected. Therefore, although many priors successively, one after another, had for many long periods been unprofessed in that church, nevertheless, because the aforesaid priest Bonus does not profess regular observance, you doubted—and rightly so—to proceed without consulting us against a privilege of the Apostolic See granted to the aforesaid church. [Note: [Col. 0127D] The Decretals omit “and therefore” and read “truly” instead.]

But because we must consider not only what has been done, but rather what ought to be done, [Col. 0128C] we answer your consultation as follows: since according to the divine law one must not plough with an ox and an ass together, nor may anyone wear a garment woven of wool and linen, you are to annul the aforesaid election, all obstacle of appeal removed, [Note: [Col. 0127D] The Decretals omit this.] and compel the aforesaid priest and the other unprofessed clerics either to profess and observe the Rule of Blessed Augustine established in that church, or to leave that church altogether. You are to restrain objectors, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. No letters concerning truth … should not all [be present], etc.; two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 8 July.

## CXIII

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Raynaldus published part of this letter, under the year 1203, §48. The passages found in his edition are here enclosed in brackets. Letters of book V, no. 155, and book VI, no. 51, should by all means be compared.]

To the Archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans. Against the murderers of the bishop of Würzburg, and concerning their punishment. (Ferentino, 3 July.)

[Col. 0128D]

Just as those who support the impious in their impieties exercise impiety under the appearance of piety, so those who temporarily punish their wickedness are proved pious toward the impious, lest it be punished more grievously in them eternally; in punishing them, they also repay them good for [Col. 0129A] evil and restrain others from like conduct. Indeed, Peter’s sword must be wielded also for the punishment of evildoers, lest, if rust consumes it, the corrupt part draw the sound part after it within the body of the Church; so that not only may the wicked become more wicked through the license of impunity, but matter for evil action may also be afforded to the otherwise upright, if others rejoice when they have done evil and glory in most wicked deeds.

For since the rapacity of wolves not only ranges through the Lord’s sheepfold and against the sheep, but now lays snares even for the shepherds of the sheep and guardians of the fold, thirsting for their blood and plotting against their souls, we should more truly be called hirelings than shepherds if we fled, abandoning our sheep and fellow shepherds, and beheld their slaughter from afar with dry eyes, without setting [Col. 0129B] ourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord against those advancing from the opposite side.

You know, we are certain, what bold audacity of rashness and what crime of monstrous cruelty those wicked men, sons of Belial, perpetrated in the murder of C. …, bishop of Würzburg of blessed memory and chancellor of the imperial court; for us, it is more fitting to mourn than to recount it. For it did not suffice those criminals that they had violently killed the Lord’s anointed; unless they also raged against him when dead, and, as though he lived in his members after having been killed, killed him again in them, dividing his lifeless body limb by limb into fragments. Would that some had possessed zeal for God according to knowledge, so that, after the example of the Levite, they might have sent the several pieces of the corpse, made by the aforesaid murderers, to the several regions of Germany, [Col. 0129C] and thus at least have stirred up the sons of the Church to avenge so great a crime.

[Moreover, although by earlier letters which we recall having sent you on this matter, we judged that spiritual proceedings should be taken against murderers of this kind and their supporters, nevertheless, so that they may also be punished temporally and that, just as their transgression is notorious, so the punishment of the crime committed may be remembered from generation to generation, we ordain by the authority of these presents that both the murderers themselves and their heirs shall be deprived forever of all fiefs and benefices of the church of Würzburg, which they especially offended, and also of those of other churches, since in that church they injured the universal Church; nor shall they ever obtain them at any time, unless perhaps some future [Col. 0129D] generation, by indulgence of the Apostolic See, deserves mercy.

We add also that, if they obtain any benefices or fiefs of churches wherever they may be, the whole diocese in which they presume to attempt this shall lie under interdict, so that no divine office or ecclesiastical sacrament shall be celebrated therein, except baptism of infants and penance for the dying; nor shall the bodies of the dead be committed to burial, until either they desist from their presumption or the inhabitants of that diocese oppose their attempts.

We further will that, when a bishop has newly been installed in the church of Würzburg, the laity shall not first swear him fealty nor the clergy promise him obedience, [Col. 0130A] until he has sworn that he will observe this. Moreover, since, when they killed the aforesaid bishop, certain persons cried out the name of Ravennesbure Castle—which, as is said, is built upon land of the church of Würzburg—as a battle-cry, as though sounding trumpets, thereby encouraging themselves to cut him down as to the glorious triumph of a contest, and since we ratify and approve the sentence which the nobles of that diocese pronounced concerning the demolition of that castle and of their other fortifications, houses, and possessions, we strictly command that it be executed. The nobles of that diocese, the ministerials of the church, and all the neighboring people are to be compelled by an interdict of the land to ensure that it is observed under the aforesaid penalty.

Moreover, since certain persons, immediately after the murder of the aforesaid bishop, [Col. 0130B] ran with arms to the aid of the murderers, in order to support them against the ministerials of the church and the nobles of the land, we command that they be subject to sentence of excommunication and that every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, they be publicly announced as excommunicated until they appear before the apostolic presence to make satisfaction.

We also will that those strongly suspected of having supplied counsel or assent for his death, whom the murdered man’s brother and kinsmen shall identify by their proper names, be compelled by sentences of excommunication and interdict to furnish canonical purgation. If they should fail therein, we command that they be declared excommunicated like the others aforesaid; and wherever they are [Col. 0130C] present, we forbid the celebration of divine offices in their presence.

Furthermore, since it is neither safe nor honorable that … son of Henry of Ravennesbure, brother of Boso, whose father and paternal uncle plotted the death of that bishop, should take part in the counsels of the church of Würzburg, we have commanded our venerable brother G. …, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, supported by our authority, not to delay, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, to provide for him by a suitable exchange in another church remote from Würzburg, assigning his prebend to others. Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your fraternity, and strictly command you through apostolic letters, that you frequently and solemnly publish the tenor of [Col. 0130D] our letters and cause what we have set forth to be fulfilled, compelling objectors by sentences of excommunication and interdict, appeal removed. No letters concerning truth shall stand in the way, should any appear that make no mention of these.

Given at Ferentino, 3 July.

## CXIV

[Note: [Col. 0129D] I have published fragments of this letter.]

To O., provost of Würzburg; the nobleman G., burgrave; and their kinsmen. On the same subject as the preceding letter. (Ferentino, 8 July.)

The universal Church grieves, and has grieved; and we have grieved with it and for it, and still grieve, that, as wickedness grows [Col. 0131A] beyond utterance, children tear open their mother, and generations of vipers thirst for their father’s blood. For behold: divine reverence set aside; not only clerical propriety neglected but even pontifical authority despised; laws spurned and canons made void; children arm themselves against their father, and sheep—or rather wolves lurking beneath sheepskins—plot against their own shepherd, setting snares to catch the innocent. Thus, we know, it occurred in the murder of C., bishop of Würzburg of blessed memory and chancellor of the imperial court.

[For certain sons of iniquity, observing that this bishop opposed their works and that his soul would not consent to them, devised how to destroy him.] Since enemies could not harm him, [Col. 0131B] and knowing that a familiar enemy harms more, they feigned friendship; then they rose against him when they were believed to have abandoned their former design of wickedness.

Although we mourn with you for his murder, and mourn also ourselves—chiefly because this crime becomes a precedent and impunity for crime supplies an incentive to wrongdoing—yet we have received consolation in this, and likewise console you: as we hope from divine mercy, in the very matter in which the Church militant was diminished by his death, the triumph of the Church triumphant has been increased. That bishop, with what was mortal in him having died and what could be corrupted having been corrupted, has put on immortality and [Col. 0131C] incorruption; he has exchanged temporal things for eternal, earthly things for heavenly, the road for the fatherland, and exile for an everlasting dwelling, where there shall be no more cry, mourning, or pain; these former things likewise passed away when he passed from the world to the Father.

[For, because he fought the good fight, completed the course, and kept the faith, there is laid up for him henceforth the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, shall render to him. And if through human weakness or diabolical suggestion he contracted any human dross, this washing of blood cleansed it from him, and the punishment which he endured in defending the liberty of his church expiated it.]

Therefore we admonish your whole community and earnestly exhort you to receive, in him who comforts us in every tribulation, the solace of consolation [Col. 0131D] in your tribulation; and to make it your care to comfort one another with these words. For one ought deservedly to rejoice for him whose joy shall hereafter not be changed into sorrow, and who will suffer no loss but increase. You will be able to learn from our letters how we have judged that proceedings should be taken to avenge the monstrous cruelty of such a crime.

Given at Ferentino, 8 July.

## CXV

[Note: [Col. 0131D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, §67.]

To the Prior and Convent of Bomin. [Note: [Col. 0131D] This concerns, we think at least, the Augustinian priory of Bodmyn in Cornwall. Nothing concerning this monastery is found in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 5, except one charter of King Henry III confirming to the canons of Bodmyn the manor of Nivetone—perhaps the same as the church here called Nivetunen.—[Col. 0132D] formerly granted to them.]

He receives them under protection and confirms their goods. (Ferentino, 8 July.)

[Col. 0132A]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., as far as “assent.” We receive under our protection your church and the persons serving the Lord there, with all that you now reasonably possess or … as far as “we receive”; ordaining that the canonical order which, according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, is established therein … as far as “shall be observed.”

Moreover: the parish church of Bomin., with the chapels of Lanhedroc, Saint Margaret of Biri, Saint Thomas, Saint Michael, and its other appurtenances; the church of Aldestowe, with the chapels [Col. 0132B] of Saint Cadoc and Saint Petroc of Trerofait, its harbor and harbor-toll, and its other appurtenances; the church of Helinton, with its appurtenances; the right which you possess in the church of Saint Marmura, its chapels and appurtenances; the church of Widiel, with its dependencies; the church of Saint Theta, with its appurtenances; the right which you possess in the church of Heglosseil, with its dependencies; the church of Holecumbe, with its appurtenances; the church of Niventunen., with its appurtenances; the town of Bomin., with Landa, the Wood of Bodan, and its appurtenances; Reiltun., with the Hondremannaria [Note: [Col. 0132D] *Hondremannaria* is thus expressly read in Counti’s copy. The word is unknown to both Spelman and Du Cange; perhaps it may mean “a manor of a hundred men,” since *hondredus*, *hundredum*, or *hondreda* is called among the English a *centena* or *centuria* (“hundred”). See Spelman, p. 302; see also Du Cange, vol. III, col. 1255.] of Pedresire, liberties, customs, and appurtenances; Aldestorwe, [Col. 0132C] with liberties and appurtenances; Lanweledic, with appurtenances; Rietterhe, with appurtenances; Widiel, with appurtenances; Bendere, with the fishery on the Alan. and other appurtenances; Pentir., with appurtenances; Tredernon, with appurtenances; Lanhidroc, with appurtenances; whatever you possess in Bodiniel; Fosnewit, with appurtenances; Holeinse, with dependencies; Niventon., with appurtenances. As you justly and peacefully possess these, we confirm them to you and, through you, to your church by apostolic authority, etc.

Concerning your newly cultivated lands, which you till with your own hands or at your own expense, or concerning gardens, etc., as far as “shall presume.” We likewise decree that the ancient liberties and immunities granted to your church, and its reasonable customs, etc., shall remain in force for all time. [Col. 0132D] Moreover, we prohibit anyone from pronouncing upon you or your church a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause, or from burdening you with new and unlawful exactions. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, etc., as far as “to celebrate.” You may also elect chaplains for your churches and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, [Col. 0133A] the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they must answer to him concerning spiritual matters but to you concerning temporal matters. Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, etc., as far as “to be elected.”

As a token of the protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors annually one bezant freely offered. Therefore we decree that no one at all … this grant and confirmation of our protection, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 8 July.

## CXVI

To the bishops of Palencia and … Zamora, and to P., archdeacon of Astorga, a Swabian. That they should inquire against the master of schools of the church of Astorga, suspected of forgery. (Ferentino, 11 July.)

[Col. 0133B]

Since Christ is truth and the devil did not stand in the truth, assuredly whoever hates truth and commits the vice of falsehood is proved to be, as a member of the devil, opposed to Christ. Hence this crime must be punished the more severely because by it one’s neighbor is more greatly injured and God himself more deeply despised. Therefore, since N., master of schools of the church of Astorga, is strongly suspected before us of falsehood on numerous presumptions, although nothing has been fully proved against him in our presence, yet, lest we seem to overlook so grave a vice, we judge that he—having been suspended by our delegates from performing his office—should be suspended from receiving his benefices also, [Col. 0133C] in detestation of so great a crime.

By apostolic letters we strictly command and enjoin your discretion publicly and solemnly to announce throughout Astorga and all the surrounding dioceses that, if anyone wishes to proceed against him upon the crime of falsehood, he shall appear before you and bring his allegation within three months from the time of the announcement. If that master of schools is convicted or confesses concerning this, or if the crime is notorious, you shall punish him according to the constitution we have issued against forgers. Otherwise, you shall assign him canonical purgation; should he fail therein, you shall proceed against him under that same constitution, appeal removed. [Col. 0133D] But if he canonically clears himself, you shall take care to restore him, by our authority, both to his office and to his benefices. No letters concerning truth, etc., shall stand in the way. Should not all [be present], two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 11 July.

## CXVII

To Vitello, our subdeacon and castellan of Lariano. That he should inquire concerning the appointment of two canons in the church of Saint Mary of Nemi. (Ferentino.)

[Col. 0134A]

Our beloved sons N. and J. complained to us that, although canons had been appointed in the church of Saint Mary of Nemi by our venerable brother J., bishop of Albano, [Note: [Col. 0133D] John, a Lombard by nationality, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement under Pope Clement III in 1188; bishop of Viterbo under Pope Celestine III in 1193; finally appointed bishop of Albano by Innocent in 1199. He died at Rome in 1210. Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1143.] … the prior and brothers of Saint Anastasius had unjustly expelled them from it. They therefore requested that we should have them restored there.

But the prior, appearing in our presence with another brother, produced a certain public instrument by which he sought to prove that the institution and removal of clerics in the aforementioned church [Col. 0134B] belonged not to the bishop of Albano but to the monastery of Saint Anastasius. Conversely, the aforesaid clerics alleged that, with the monks’ knowledge and without their opposition, they had been instituted in that church by command of the bishop aforesaid and had remained there peaceably for some time—something which the aforesaid prior and monk wholly denied.

Since a public instrument is presumed valid until the contrary is lawfully proved, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to receive and examine the witnesses whom either party chooses to produce concerning these matters, prudently inquiring into the circumstances; and faithfully to send us their written depositions, enclosed under your seal, fixing for the parties a suitable term within which they shall appear before us to receive judgment. [Col. 0134C] You, however, shall execute the apostolic mandate confidently and without respect of persons, compelling by ecclesiastical censure any witnesses named who withdraw through favor, fear, or hatred to bear testimony to the truth.

Ferentino.

## CXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, §67. We give only its subject-matter. We confess that we do not know why the text of this letter is not today found in our collection. Certainly, in the index of Counti’s copy, which we caused to be faithfully transcribed, it is said to occur on p. 459 of the manuscript.]

To J., minister of the house of the Holy Trinity of Cervi-Frigidi, and to his brethren. He receives them under the protection of Blessed Peter.

## CXIX

[Note: [Col. 0134D] It is read, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book IV, title 5, *On Conditions Attached to Betrothal or Other Contracts*, chapter 6.]

To the Bishop of Marsica. [Note: [Col. 0134D] Benedict, a Roman by birth, is thought to have lived after John VI, about the year of the Lord 1200. Perhaps during his tenure James, count and great justiciar of Apulia, is recorded as having confirmed, in 1208, the possessions of the church of Saint Thomas of Canterbury. Ughelli, in the series of bishops of Marsica, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VII, col. 708.]

He commits to him a matrimonial cause to be adjudicated. (Ferentino, 14 July.)

[Col. 0134D]

In your letters you informed us [Note: [Col. 0134D] The Decretals omit this, as below in the present passage.] that, when a certain woman named Pacifica [Note: [Col. 0134D] The Decretals read “P. and N.”] sought in your presence a certain man named Nicholas as her husband, asserting that there had been between them mutual present consent [Col. 0135A] and carnal intercourse, the man, though he did not deny the contract of betrothal and carnal intercourse, nevertheless asserted that he was not bound to take her as his wife because the betrothal had been contracted between them on this condition: namely, that his father and paternal uncle should consent to the betrothal. But, as soon as they learned of it, they opposed both the bridegroom and the bride; and the man sought to prove this by suitable witnesses.

But the woman replied that, although each had pledged faith under the condition stated, she had never been opposed by the man’s father or paternal uncle; and she said that before the time of opposition specified by the witnesses, and afterward, they had had carnal intercourse. She added further that, although they had contracted conditionally at first, [Col. 0135B] with the passage of time they freely consented to marriage without addition of the condition; and she asserted that she would prove this by witnesses.

Accordingly, after receiving the witnesses of each party, when you caused the woman’s depositions to be published in the presence of two examiners, the witnesses whose statements were being read immediately cried out that they had not said what was being read, and that what they had testified had not been written down. But one of the examiners then vigorously opposed them; and on this account the woman requested that the same witnesses, or others, be heard again on the same articles. Disturbed by this novelty, you fixed the following day for the parties. When they appeared before you, you ordered all the [Col. 0135C] examiners to be summoned, adjuring them under threat of anathema to say whether the depositions which the witnesses had opposed were genuine. They immediately produced other depositions. When the man’s advocate objected that the witnesses had opposed these just as they had the former ones, after many arguments the second depositions were accepted by the parties, and the man’s depositions were afterwards published.

Furthermore, the woman particularly insisted on the point that the man had carnally known her both before and after the renunciation of the betrothal, and had begotten a daughter by her; she sought to establish this by her own oath. Because you had received opinions concerning these matters that were not only diverse but contradictory, you had recourse to the instruction of the Apostolic See and humbly requested to be taught what should be decided [Col. 0135D] in such cases. But we, having inspected the depositions accepted by the parties which you sent us enclosed with your letters, answer your consultation as follows: since it is clearly established by the confession of both man and woman that carnal intercourse followed after the betrothal was contracted, there is a very strong presumption in favor of marriage, because the man appears to have withdrawn from the condition imposed. For even if it has somehow been proved by witnesses that, after the man’s father and paternal uncle opposed the betrothal, the man carnally knew that woman, [Col. 0136A] it has by no means been proved that his father and paternal uncle took care to oppose it before he knew her.

Given at Ferentino, 14 July.

## CXX

To R., cantor; R., prior of Monte-Leprosorum; and J. de Saggio, canon of Rouen. He revokes letters fraudulently obtained by R., priest of Colevill. (Ferentino, 12 July.)

From the tenor of the letters which you sent us through our beloved son Ph., bearer of these presents, we have clearly learned that R., priest of Colevill., and our beloved sons the priors of Prato …, Monte-Leprosorum, and Saint-Laud at Rouen, obtained apostolic letters concerning the dispute [Col. 0136B] pending between him and our beloved son, the abbot [Note: [Col. 0135D] William II, abbot of Le Bec, who died on 18 September 1211, held office, according to the *Chronographus*, for thirteen years, two months, and two weeks, less one day. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 231.] and convent of Le Bec, concerning the manor of Colevill. and other matters. Having summoned the opposing party, the said priest refused to litigate before them.

Afterward the same priest presented you with our letters concerning the same affair, in which no mention was made of the priors. When, with the parties summoned before you, you wished to proceed with hearing the case, the aforesaid abbot alleged before you that he was not bound by those letters to answer the said priest, since he had been summoned by other letters, which had not been revoked by authority of the former. But because you doubted on this matter, [Col. 0136C] you thought fit to consult the Apostolic See.

Therefore, observing the fraud of that priest in obtaining two commissions concerning the same affair, one of which made no mention of the other, and because fraud and deceit ought not to benefit him, we decree that he shall lose the benefit of both.

Given at Ferentino, 12 July, in the sixth year.

## CXXI

[Note: [Col. 0136D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §66.]

To the Chapter of Novara. He dissolves certain agreements contrary to the canons. (Ferentino, 21 July.)

Since C., our predecessor of pious memory, annulled—as justice required—a certain wicked arrangement which you had made for appointing canons to benefices not vacant: namely, an arrangement by which each of you had appointed his nephew, kinsman, [Col. 0136D] or friend in that church, now, as we have learned, using fraud and deceit against this annulment, you have proceeded to the same arrangement or plan. When a prebend happens to fall vacant, you elect one of those whose appointment has been annulled; he, or another on his behalf, is bound by agreements or stipulations to place the revenues of that prebend into the common fund and to receive from it no more than one of the other persons whose appointments were annulled. You have strengthened this by oath: you will in no way proceed to elect or appoint another [Col. 0137A] until every person whose appointment was annulled has obtained a full benefice. You even unlawfully substitute one for another, seek to nullify an apostolic statute, and try to possess God’s sanctuary as though by hereditary right.

Although, by that sentence of annulment, such annulled persons are not thereby rendered unworthy of obtaining ecclesiastical benefices, nevertheless fraud and deceit ought not to benefit anyone; and we, according to the prophet, must “loose the bonds of wickedness and the burdens that oppress” [the text reads *deprimentes*]. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin you wholly to rescind this collusion. Otherwise, we decree that all persons bound to this by any compact, oath, or any other bond shall be subject to sentence of excommunication unless, within [Col. 0137B] fifteen days after receiving these presents, they dissolve such a bond as hostile to the sacred canons.

Given at Ferentino, 21 July.

It is written to the archbishop of Milan and the bishop of Novara that they are to arrange for the foregoing to be published by apostolic authority.

Given as above.

## CXXII
