To R., bishop-elect of Lucca. He summons him to the Apostolic See to receive the rank of priesthood and the benefit of consecration. [Note: [Col. 0137] See letters, book V, nos. 140 and 153; book VI, nos. 58 and 112.] (Ferentino, 23 July.)

Dear sons, J., prior of Saint Fridianus of Lucca, and B. Fasolus, canon of Pisa, informed us by their letters that, after receiving the letters which we caused to be sent to them concerning your case, they waited for one month to see whether anyone might appear who would allege and prove anything concerning the marriage which you were said to have contracted with a widow. They solemnly excommunicated, and caused their excommunication to be announced in all the churches of the city of Lucca, anyone who should presume to prevent witnesses from bearing testimony to the truth.

But when nearly a month had elapsed, your adversaries suggested to them that Ingerannus, the podestà, R., councillor, and M., notary of the city of Lucca, had demanded and received from those who were to bear testimony against you an oath that they would propose nothing against you before them. The aforesaid prior and B., canon of Pisa, as they ought to have done, made this known to you. Thereupon the aforementioned podestà, councillor, and notary appeared before them and, touching the holy Gospels, swore that no one was bound by any obligation in this matter which prevented him from bearing testimony to the truth; that they themselves would neither compel nor allow anyone to be compelled, whether directly or through others; that they would not hinder anyone from proceeding to give testimony; and that, so far as lay in their power, they absolved all who might in any way be bound to them in this matter.

Since no one proceeded against you even then, the aforesaid delegates, absolving you from the accusation concerning marriage, commanded you by apostolic authority to undergo canonical purgation within the following month, in accordance with our mandate. Your adversaries, however, appealed to our hearing, seeking to prevent the delegates from admitting your purgation unless you employed at least two bishops as compurgators, since our letters had mentioned bishops. They likewise sought to prevent certain persons, whom they had heard would serve as your compurgators, from being admitted to the purgation, declaring that they were prepared to speak against them.

Although the delegates, repeatedly named above, did not think that such an appeal should be heeded, because the obstacle of appeal had been removed in our letters, and because it was already evident to them that your adversaries were unjustly persecuting you out of malice and hatred—while the said compurgators were of good repute, were tolerated by the Church in their ranks, churches, and honours, and the delegates had heard nothing unfavourable about them—a certain expression inserted in our letters moved them strongly. It was written, namely, that they should receive your purgation through seven men chosen from among the bishops of Tuscany, or the canons of the greater church, or the priors of the churches of the religious brethren in the city of Lucca, priests or deacons of good repute, notwithstanding letters which your adversaries had obtained in which no mention was made of bishops. From this they concluded that at least two bishops had to be employed in your purgation.

But, beloved sons, J., canon of Saint Martin, P. . . . priest and prior of Saint Reparata, and Master J., canon of Saint Mary Forisportam, swore in the delegates’ presence that the expression concerning the addition of bishops had been added by us at their own request, but on the understanding that, if you could have seven other compurgators among the canons and priors of the churches of the religious brethren, you were in no way obliged to employ bishops in your purgation, as they said they had heard from our own mouth. They added that this was why the conjunction “and” had been suppressed in that clause and “or” inserted instead.

Thereafter, when you came to the church of Saint Fridianus, the aforesaid prior being somewhat burdened by illness, and appeared before him and his co-delegate, in the presence of our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, of the greater part of the clergy and civic authority of Lucca, and many others, who cried out that they wished to clear your innocence by compurgation, you swore before the altar of Blessed Fridianus, touching the holy Gospels, that you had contracted no marriage either with a widow or with any other woman; that, to your knowledge, you had not carnally known another man’s wife; that you had not knowingly incurred perjury or excommunication, especially in the matters for which you had been accused. You also solemnly cleared yourself generally of all the charges that had been brought against you.

Moreover Tolomeus the cantor, J. the priest, Master Palmarius, and Opizo the deacon, together with the canons of Saint Martin, the priors of Saint Reparata, Saint Michael, and Saint Mary Forisportam, who hold the honour of priesthood, publicly swore that they believed you had sworn truthfully concerning all the matters which you had sworn you had not committed. Therefore, since no delay or difficulty ought to be introduced into proper arrangements, lest the Lord’s flock should long lack a pastor’s care, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to present yourself before us by the Ember Days now next approaching, in order to receive the degree of priesthood and the benefit of consecration.

Given at Ferentino, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August [23 July].

## CXXIII. To . . . the abbot of Saint Boscianus; and . . . of Cerreto, in the diocese of Lodi; and . . . priors of Saint Gabriel of Cremona

That they should inquire into the election of the abbot of Saint Peter of the Po. (Ferentino.)

[Col. 0139B]

By letters of our beloved sons, the chapter of the monastery of Saint Peter of the Po, . . . abbot of Saint Sigismund, . . . archdeacon, and . . . provost of Saint Lucy of Cremona—whom we appointed to receive the resignation of our beloved son Lanf., then abbot of that monastery—we have been informed that, after the said Lan., with our permission, resigned the government of the abbey, the brethren of that place assembled and unanimously elected our beloved son J., a monk, as their pastor. They humbly requested that his election be confirmed by apostolic authority.

But because we could not be fully assured of the suitability of the person, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if you find that this election has been canonically celebrated in the person of one who is suitable, you confirm it in our stead, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. But if not all of you can be present, let two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino.

## CXXIV. To the nobleman J., count of Tricarico

That he is to hold at the disposition of the Roman Church land which he recovers from the hands of German enemies. (Ferentino.)

Since we have hitherto found your nobility faithful and devoted, and hope to find it henceforth still more faithful and devoted, we grant by prudent dispensation that you may hold and preserve, at our disposition and in the service of royal fidelity, the land which you are able to free from the hands of enemies—namely Germans and their supporters. Until you have recovered the expenses which you show that you have usefully incurred beyond what was owed for its acquisition, you shall not be compelled to restore it within a suitable period when called upon to do so.

Let no one therefore infringe this our grant, etc.

Given at Ferentino.

## CXXV. To Master Gualfredus, clerk of Saint Maurice of Tardubiato

He receives him under protection. (Ferentino, fourth day before the Ides of July [12 July].)

[Col. 0140A]

“It is customary to grant assent,” etc., down to “we have received [it] under protection.” In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the church of Saint Maurice of Tardubiato, as you justly and peacefully possess it.

Let no one therefore infringe this our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Ides of July [12 July].

## CXXVI. To the abbot and convent of Villemagne

That no one be intruded into their monastery against their will. (Ferentino, eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August].)

[Note: Berengarius II is demonstrated from documents to have governed the monastery of Villemagne from 1173 until at least 1205. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 405.]

[Col. 0140B]

Know that it has come to our hearing that certain persons are attempting to thrust their relatives and friends into your monastery against your will, and do not fear not merely to induce but to compel you, by threats and terrors, to receive them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, wishing to provide for your monastery, by the authority of these presents we forbid anyone to intrude any persons into that monastery without the assent of yourselves or of the sounder majority of your counsel.

Let no one therefore infringe this prohibition, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August].

## CXXVII. To the same

He confirms to them temporal jurisdiction in Villemagne. (Ferentino, eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August].)

[Col. 0140C]

As has been reported to us, although you, son abbot, and your predecessors have customarily exercised temporal jurisdiction freely in Villemagne, which belongs directly to your monastery, punishing its inhabitants temporally for their offences, certain of them now, wishing to kick against the goad, are trying to evade your authority and flee to the protection of others in order to escape your power. Since we neither wish nor ought to permit that monastery to suffer an injury to its rights, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you freely exercise temporal jurisdiction over the inhabitants of the said Villemagne, in accordance with ancient and approved custom.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August].

## CXXVIII. To . . . the abbot of Subiaco

Concerning provision for the church of Scanzano. (Ferentino, second day before the Ides of August [12 August].)

[Note: See letter 82 of Book V.]

When our beloved son Nicholas, knight, formerly complained before us that our venerable brother, the bishop of Marsica, had instituted a priest, Bonus Homo, in the church of Scanzano at the presentation of certain patrons, without consulting, informing, or respecting him, though he was by no means the least among the patrons, we committed the case to our beloved son . . . provost of Saint Saviour of Paterno and Master John, canon of Celano. After summoning the parties and hearing their respective allegations, they found from the assertions of the parties that the said priest had indeed been instituted in contempt of the knight, a patron of that church. Yet, out of reverence for the bishop, they did not annul his institution, but decreed that each party’s right should remain unimpaired.

[Note: Above, letter 119 of this sixth book.]

We, therefore, having learned that the institution of that priest had been made by the bishop—who was not ignorant of Nicholas’s right—without consulting, informing, or respecting the said Nicholas, the patron, decreed that justice required it to be voided. By apostolic letters we command you that, lest the said church remain bereft of a rector, you order the aforesaid Nicholas and the other patrons, by our authority, to agree unanimously upon a suitable person and present him to the said bishop for institution in that church. If they refuse to agree on this, the said bishop may provide the church with a suitable person according to the canonical statutes.

Given at Ferentino, on the second day before the Ides of August [12 August].

## CXXIX. To S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes, legate of the Apostolic See

He exhorts him to undertake the patriarchate of Jerusalem, which he declined because of his integrity. (Ferentino, seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [16 August].)

[Note: Raynaldus, year 1203, §10, presents various fragments of this letter. The passages found in him are here, as usual, enclosed in brackets.

A fuller version, expressed in continuous sequence, may be read in the *Gesta*, §LXXXVIII. Yet there certain passages differ in two places, and some are entirely absent at the end. We present the complete text, in every respect finished, from copies of unquestioned reliability, Vatican and Conti. Material which is otherwise read in the *Gesta* or is absent there has been distinguished by a double stroke placed in the margin at the beginning of each line.]

[Note: He has already been mentioned frequently.]

[Col. 0141C]

In order to repair the fall of the human race, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, as the Apostle testifies, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He chose Jerusalem for his Passion, becoming obedient to God the Father unto death on the cross; he bore our sins in his body upon the tree, was reckoned among the wicked, and was crucified with thieves. Therefore, unless the useless servant wishes to be condemned for the fault of ingratitude, he will refuse neither yoke nor neck-yoke for the Lord, when the Lord gave himself up for the servant, condemned to a most shameful death.

[So that the Lord might remove from us every excuse and leave no room for excuses in the sin of negligence, he endured beforehand for the servant almost everything that a servant could suffer for the Lord. Who, then, would not leave all earthly things for him whom he knows descended from heavenly things to earthly? Who would not lay down his life for him who gave up his spirit upon the cross for him? Indeed, if we are to render him anything in return for all that he has bestowed on us, neither tribulation, nor distress, nor death, nor sword ought in any way to hold us back from tasting for his sake, should necessity demand and usefulness require it, the cup of suffering.]

For if we resolve to walk as he walked and follow his footsteps, we must not fear either the reproaches of revilers, the snares of a familiar enemy, or the power of a raging foe, so as to fail to walk in his ways and direct our feet in his paths; suffering with him for a time, that we may happily reign with him eternally when he reigns. For we know and hold certain, both from prophetic and evangelical reading, that his heart awaited reproach, while the tongue of those who cursed reproached him for being a carpenter’s son, a wine-drinker, and a friend of tax collectors. We know that he who ate his bread raised his heel against him. We know how he was sprinkled with spittle, struck with blows, crowned with thorns, patiently endured Pilate’s tyranny, and at last was crucified and pierced with a lance.

[Will you then deny yourself to your Maker by refusing to undertake the burden of the Church of Jerusalem, which he himself consecrated with his blood? If he has deigned in some fashion to choose you as his successor, will you not enter upon his inheritance and raise up seed for a deceased brother—he who perhaps through you arranged to propagate in the land of his pilgrimage and preaching the seed of the Gospel?]

Far be it from you to evade labours, pains, and fears, to flee poverty, anxieties, and necessities, lest you undertake the burden to which you are called by divine disposition. Far be it from you to avoid labouring for him who declares through the prophet that he laboured for you, saying in the psalm, “I laboured while enduring” (Jeremiah VI), and of whom the Evangelist testifies that about the sixth hour he sat by the well, weary from the journey. Far be it from you to avoid pains for him whom you do not doubt suffered pain for you, as he himself declares in the prophet: “O all you who pass by the way, consider and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lamentations I); and who testifies of himself in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Philippians II). Far be it from you to evade fears for him who is read to have said in the Psalm: “Fear and trembling came upon me” (Psalm LIV), and of whom the Gospel says that he began to be afraid and distressed. Far be it from you to flee poverty for him who became poor for you, as he declares in the Prophet: “I am poor and sorrowful” (Psalm LXVIII), and in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew VIII). Far be it from you to shun anxieties for him in whose person the Prophet speaks thus: “My spirit was distressed within me, and my heart was troubled within me” (Psalm CXLII); and who says of himself: “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke XII).

[Far be it from you to evade necessities for him who, to omit other things, brought himself for you into the necessity of hunger and thirst, as is read in the Prophet: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm LXVIII).] As the Evangelist testifies of him, after he had fasted forty days and forty nights he afterward hungered; and when he cried from the cross, “I thirst” (John XVII), the hand of his crucifiers offered him vinegar, or wine mixed with myrrh, or even wine mingled with gall.

If perhaps you are troubled because you are called to the prelacy of that Church whose possession you cannot presently enter, since it is now almost wholly held by enemies, turn the eyes of your mind to that time when James, the Lord’s brother, undertook the government of Jerusalem—not while it was favourable to him, but rather while it opposed him. For at that time those held power there who had crucified the Lord outside the city and later killed James himself near the Temple. And although John and Thaddaeus were brothers of the Lord according to the flesh, James is especially called his brother, as one who took the wife left by his deceased brother in order to raise up seed for him according to the Mosaic law. He is also not inappropriately called “supplanter,” since in a certain sense he supplanted the apostles: although he was not first among the others, he nevertheless seemed to seize from the rest the right of primogeniture when he undertook the government of the first-born Church, concerning which the Prophet testifies: “From Zion went forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” This is the city of the great King, of which many glorious things have been said; and this is added as though paramount: “Mother Zion shall say, ‘A man, even a man, was made in her; and the Most High himself founded her’” (Psalm LXXXVI).

Moreover, although a part of that Church, as we sorrowfully report, was captured and slaughtered by enemies in the destruction of the Holy Land, the part which escaped the hands of enemies—indeed the Church itself, renewed by a new offspring—asks for and awaits you as its pastor. Therefore do not make the place an excuse, when you have persons to govern; for the name of Church refers more to persons than to a place. Yet you should seek spiritually to be concerned for the place, striving with all your strength for its recovery and for the restoration of the land of the Lord’s Nativity.

For our beloved sons . . . prior, prior, and . . . canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, appearing before us, informed us humbly, both orally and by letters of their chapter, of the suffragans of the Church of Jerusalem, of our dearest son in Christ A., the illustrious king of Jerusalem, and of many others:

[Note: These differ from what is read in the *Gesta*, cited above.]

“After M., patriarch of Jerusalem of good memory, had entered upon the way of all flesh, they assembled together to deliberate jointly concerning the appointment of a pontiff over them. As they sought someone able prudently to govern so great a Church at this critical time, it came about, by the Lord’s action, that they unanimously placed their votes upon you, humbly begging us both to deign strictly to command you to assent to their wishes and to send you the pallium for the completion of the pontifical office. They further added that, unless we granted you to them as patriarch, the whole Eastern Church would fall into a dissolution of moral order and a weakening of religious life, and would stubbornly stray from knowledge of its mother, namely the Roman Church, to its own confusion.”

[Note: Monachus is meant here. Monachus, a native of the city of Florence, came to Jerusalem out of devotion. He was first made chancellor by the patriarch, then archbishop of Caesarea, from which Church he transferred to Jerusalem in 1194 and died in 1203. William of Tyre, book XXII, chapter 7, records that Baldwin IV sent this archbishop-elect of Caesarea to Antioch with Eraclius, patriarch of Jerusalem, and several other bishops, in an attempt to reconcile Prince Bohemond with his patriarch Aimery. Several letters of Innocent, Books I and II, concern him after his elevation to the patriarchate. Albericus also mentions him, *Chronicle*, year 1153, p. 324. See further Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. III, col. 487, and vol. IV, col. 1097. Those desiring more should consult Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1252.]

Although, on account of the evident usefulness to the Roman Church, whose great and honourable member we esteem you, it is burdensome and exceedingly painful to us and to our brethren to grant you at their request as pastor to the Church of Jerusalem—since you are very necessary to us, as a man noble, upright, eloquent, learned, prudent in temporal matters and circumspect in spiritual ones, especially because of the special affection of devotion which you are known to bear toward our person and the sweetness of familiar affection which we are shown to bear toward you—yet, yielding as it were to a kind of compulsion because of the pressing necessity not only of the Church of Jerusalem but of the entire Eastern province, we admonish and earnestly exhort your discretion. As remission of sins we enjoin, beseeching you through the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, that you consent to the divine call, comply with the wishes of all the aforesaid persons, and accept the election made of you.

[Note: What follows accords with what is read in the *Gesta*, cited above.]

Do this lest, if you act otherwise, you appear to resist the divine will, which is always fulfilled both by those who will and by those who will not. Consider prudently that, should a less suitable, or perhaps unworthy, person be set over that Church in accordance with certain persons’ wishes, this might not undeservedly be imputed to you because of your opposition. Do not decline this labour as though you could not succeed as you desire, because God rewards not so much success as labour. Hence the Apostle says: “Each shall receive his own reward according to his labour” (II Corinthians III); and another Scripture testifies: “God will render a reward for the labours of his saints.” Thus the Apostle prudently said: “I laboured more than all” (I Corinthians XV), and did not say, “I succeeded more than all,” though we hope that no small successes will spring from your labours.

[Note: From here to the end the *Gesta*, cited above, again differs.]

We therefore send, by the bearers of these letters, the pallium—the insignia of the fullness of the pontifical office—to our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, legate of the Apostolic See, for him to confer upon you according to the customary form, which we send him under our seal.

[Note: We have already discussed him above.]

You, however, are to have yourself consecrated bishop by our authority either by the suffragans or by any other Catholic bishops whatsoever. We do not wish you to labour in coming to us to obtain the gift of consecration, nor the Church of Jerusalem to incur the loss of such great expenses. Moreover, so that our goodwill toward you may appear not to diminish but rather to increase, we wish you nevertheless to carry out jointly with the said legate the office of legation entrusted to you. We wish to grant you thus to the Church of Jerusalem that we do not wish to take you away from the Roman Church.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [16 August], in the sixth year.

“It has been written to the cardinal that he should admonish and induce him to do this, adding that, if he cannot perhaps be induced by any means, you and he are to keep the pallium in your possession and arrange that the prior and canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre elect another person suitable for themselves and devoted to the Roman Church as their pastor. When the full course of the matter has at last been reported to us, you shall confer the pallium upon him according to the instructions which you have received from us.

Given as above.”

## CXXX. To S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes

He exhorts him patiently to bear the labours to be endured for the Holy Land. (Ferentino, fourth day before the Ides of August [10 August].)

[Note: Raynaldus, year 1203, §9, prints this letter, but not in full. Passages found in his version are here enclosed in brackets.]

If at any time in this great and wide sea, where creeping things beyond number and animals both small and great often frighten mariners, the mind of your discretion is shaken, fearing the onset of waves and the force of winds, we neither wonder nor are in any way disturbed. Every human being is afraid upon the sea; indeed even the chief of the apostles, to whom it had been granted by the Lord that he should walk upon the waves in coming to him, when he saw a strong wind arise, not only feared but was almost submerged, unless the divine right hand had raised him up.

For this world surges like the sea; it is not easy for anyone not to surge amid surging waters, or to remain unmoved in that which does not remain in one state. This is especially so since invisible enemies are not lacking, who both themselves invisibly and visibly through the visible enemies whom they send, strive not merely to frighten but to cast down those especially who set their hand to mighty things and, forgetting what is behind, continually stretch themselves toward what lies before.

Indeed, if you were of the world, the world might perhaps have loved what was its own, so that all worldly things would prosper for you and nothing you desired would fail you. But because you are not of the world to pursue worldly things, since you seek not what is yours but rather what is Jesus Christ’s, and do not seek your own glory but more truly that of the crucified cross, crying with the Apostle—if not outwardly with the voice, yet inwardly in the mind—“Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” the world hates you. Whom it could not win to itself by prosperity, it strives to trouble by adversity.

Therefore neither we nor you should wonder if, being especially devoted to the service of the cross and stationed in the land of the crucifiers, you are tormented in mind and body. The bearer of the cross cannot fail to be tormented while he shares in the weakness of his neighbours and grieves that the cause of the Crucified is neglected. Moses himself, who led the people out of Egypt and lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, endured the murmurings of his own people and suffered the plots of enemies. And an angel of Satan was assigned as a goad to the Apostle who gloried in the cross, lest the greatness of revelations exalt him.

But since each person will receive a reward according to his own labour, and the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which will be revealed in us, you ought neither to fail amid excessive labours nor to despair amid the burdens which you bear almost alone in those regions. Rather, take consolation in him who consoles us in all our tribulation, him whom you have read as saying: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI). Nor are you ignorant that no one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully.

If, therefore, you grieve that the house of the Lord has become a den of robbers, and that our inheritance—or rather that of Jesus Christ—has passed not only to strangers but even to enemies of the Catholic faith, in this you will be an imitator of him who says of himself in the Prophet: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm LXVIII), and whose own inheritance is glorious. If you are saddened because Saracens possess the land of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, defile the Temple, and as though with impunity shed the blood of the saints, you follow the footsteps of him who laments in the psalm: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a watchman’s hut in an orchard” (Psalm LXXVIII).

If you mourn because princes and others who had taken up the sign of the cross, like the sons of Ephraim drawing the bow and shooting arrows, have turned back in the day of battle and, departing from the purity of their former resolve, seem to neglect the remnants of the Holy Land, you will mourn with us and with him who reproaches them in the prophet: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isaiah I). You will show yourself the successor of him who says that the city of God has been abandoned in distress even by friends.

Let this grief, therefore, be material for joy to you, and let mourning be changed into gladness. Do not be grieved if not everything succeeds according to your desire, so long as you omit nothing within your power. Rejoice also if for a time you are wearied for him who, as the Apostle says, emptied himself for us, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man; if, in return for all that he has bestowed upon you, you drink even the cup which he himself drank, since he tasted for you the cup of suffering.

We, however, not only his unworthy vicars but also his useless servants, both sympathize with your sufferings and grieve with your sorrows. So far as we can, we strive to lighten your labours. We do not forget you or the remnants of the land of the Lord’s Nativity, although, owing to the distance of places and the infrequency of messengers, we cannot visit you as often as we wish by messengers or letters. Nor should you lose confidence because the army of the cross-bearers is said to have turned aside into Greece. For we are, as far as we can be, solicitous for aid to the Holy Land and strive with all our strength for its assistance. We also wish you to know that, although P., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, was unable to cross the sea with the Venetians, he nevertheless departed from our presence before your arrival, so that when we received the letters of your devotion he had entered the ship for the crossing.

How we have decided to proceed in the affair of the Church of Tyre will be clear to you from inspection of the letters which we are sending to you about this matter.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Ides of August [10 August], in the sixth year.

## CXXXI. To the elect of Tyre

He rebukes him because, scarcely elected to the archiepiscopal see, he did not avoid the fault of disobedience and presumption. (Ferentino, second day before the Ides of August [12 August].)

[Note: Nothing is found in the authors concerning the elect of Tyre to whom this letter is addressed. Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1316, recognizes Joricus—also Josius, Jorsius, or Josephus—as archbishop of Tyre from 1179 to 1190, but admits that he does not know who succeeded him or when.]

Since we believe that you have not only read but taught that everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted, you should have pursued humility in your exaltation, lest, if you acted otherwise, you should lament with the Prophet: “Though exalted, I have been humbled and confounded” (Psalm LXXXVII). At the first beginnings of your promotion and the commencement of so great a novelty, you were obliged to take more careful heed lest, once promoted, you assume the horns of exaltation and rashly grow proud against him who, after God, was the agent of your promotion and the confirmer of your election; lest, if you at once set your seat in the north, you change your condition into ruin with the apostate angel.

For we have received word that, when you sailed to the land of the Lord’s Nativity as a pilgrim and stranger, our beloved son S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes and legate of the Apostolic See, intervened as far as propriety permitted with our beloved sons, the canons of Tyre, that they might elect you as their pastor. When you had been elected by the canons and later confirmed by that legate, who also committed to you the administration of spiritual and temporal affairs, you were changed into another man, as is read of Saul. May you not follow his disobedience or suffer a like fall.

At once setting yourself against the legate, you presumed thereby to set yourself against us and the Apostolic See, whose authority he exercises. Ungrateful for the favour bestowed upon you, you did not avoid the fault of disobedience. Against the counsel of that cardinal, moreover, you afterward had yourself consecrated bishop, and on a solemn day celebrated solemnly in pontifical vestments. For this and certain other matters the legate pronounced upon you a sentence of suspension, until you should appear before him. Although he relaxed that sentence in part, you nevertheless persisted in your contumacy and delayed too long to appear in his presence.

Although the beginning of such grave lack of devotion can scarcely be believed likely to have good consequences, we nevertheless consider more the necessity of the province of Jerusalem. We have therefore decided to send the pallium—the insignia of the fullness of the pontifical office—to the aforesaid and beloved son P. . . ., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, legate of the Apostolic See, that they may dispose of it as they deem expedient: namely, that they confer it upon your devotion, according to the form which we transmit to them enclosed under our seal, if you are worthy to receive it.

May you show yourself such a man that you need not be dishonoured, but rather may deserve to be honoured.

Given at Ferentino, on the second day before the Ides of August [12 August].

## CXXXII. To the king of Jerusalem and Cyprus

He commends to him the Church of Tyre. (Ferentino, fourth day before the Ides of August [12 August].)

Although we know you to be a devout and faithful prince, we nevertheless more earnestly invite you to works of piety, so that you may rise with all the greater fervour to good works as you know that we have a greater concern for your salvation. Therefore we earnestly admonish and exhort your royal highness to hold the church of Tyre, which, through the exigency of sins, seems to weep over the misery of the land of Jerusalem and, while that land is captive, cannot be consoled, in more devoted commendation; and, relieving its present poverty, under which it labours, that you yourself may pay it tithes and its other due rights, and cause them to be paid by [Col. 0149A] your subjects. But because that church, by command of the Apostolic See, obeys the patriarch of Jerusalem, take care with diligent concern that, on the pretext of that subjection, that church suffer no injury contrary to justice in respect either of its rights or of its dignity.

Given at Ferentino, 12 August.

CXXXIII. TO S., CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SAINT PRAXEDES, AND P., CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SAINT MARCELLUS, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That they should protect the rights of the church of Tyre. (Ferentino, 7 August.)

That the church of Tyre, which, through the exigency of sins, has been overwhelmed by many calamities and losses, may through [Col. 0149B] you receive timely assistance in its rights, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, in every dispute which that church sees fit to lay before you concerning dioceses or other matters, you cause justice to be rendered to it through ecclesiastical censure, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. Witnesses, etc. No letters, etc. And if not both, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 7 August.

CXXXIV. TO C., BISHOP-ELECT OF THE ARCHBISHOPRIC OF TYRE.  
[Note: [Col. 0149C] See above, Letter 131.]  
He confirms tithes to him and to the church of Tyre. (Ferentino, 16 August.)

[Col. 0149C] It is customary to grant assent, etc.; by the authority of the present letters we decree that, if any possession of lands, vineyards, or other things, from which the churches of the province of Tyre have customarily received tithes, should come under the control of others, you, the church of Tyre, and your suffragans, shall suffer no loss in the customary tithes, provided that such is the custom of that province—that tithes are paid with regard not so much to persons as to estates—while the privileges and indulgences of the Roman pontiffs remain intact. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 16 August.

CXXXV. TO THE ABBESS AND NUNS OF SAINT MARY MAJOR AT JERUSALEM. Confirmation of possessions and of a certain chapel. (Ferentino, 14 August.)

[Col. 0150A]

Whenever a request is made to us, etc., in the form of protection. In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the chapel which, by the concession of our beloved son, S., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, legate of the Apostolic See, you have recently begun to build at Acre, in a house bestowed upon you, from pious regard, by our dearest daughter in Christ, the illustrious queen of Jerusalem, just as you possess it rightfully and peaceably, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

CXXXVI. TO THE READER OF THE HOSPITAL OF LA ROCHELLE (otherwise, LA ROCHELLO). He receives him under protection, with an annual payment of one gold obol. (Ferentino, 25 August.)

[Col. 0150B]

It is customary to grant assent, etc., up to “assent”: your person and that hospital of La Rochelle, which you are known to have newly built, together with all its possessions, etc., in the form of protection. Moreover, as a token that this protection has been obtained from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and to our successors every year one gold obol freely offered to us. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 25 August.

CXXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP  
[Note: [Col. 0149C]

“Luke, a Campanian by birth, a Cistercian monk, then abbot of Sambucina, succeeded Andrew immediately (of whom mention has already been made, Letter 106 of Book V). This man, outstanding in learning and distinguished for piety, assumed the monastic habit at the celebrated monastery of Casamari, of the same Cistercian family, near Veroli. Having at one time become prior there, he formed a close connection with Blessed Joachim, then abbot of Corazzo, because of the likeness of their character and the affinity of their studies. Greatly loved by Joachim, he was chosen as his secretary; he was taken into Calabria and remained long with him as a diligent assistant in his studies, until he was elected abbot of Sambucina, of his own order, in place of the deceased Simeon, in 1197.

His merit won renown among the supreme pontiffs, especially Innocent III. Of the many legations which he discharged, the more celebrated was that in Sicily and Calabria in 1199, together with Laurence, bishop of Syracuse, when they stirred up the peoples by preaching and proclaimed the cross against the enemies of the cross. Later, in 1202, Innocent entrusted Luke with a legation throughout Italy to continue the preaching. While he pursued it with the greatest ardour, Archbishop Andrew died about the end of 1203, or the beginning of the following year (indeed, at the beginning of 1203, as is evident from this letter of Innocent, dated 1 September 1203). Then Luke, a most celebrated preacher of the word of God, entered upon the archbishopric of Cosenza by election of the clergy and the grant of Innocent, to the rejoicing of all who knew the man well; and Luke’s recorded acts agree well with this calculation. For 1215 was the twelfth year of Luke’s pontificate, as is clear from a document inserted in a bull of Honorius III. Thus from 1203 Luke began worthily and laudably to exercise his pastoral office in the church of Cosenza, having shortly before not only been present, with the other monks of Sambucina, at the death of Blessed Joachim, but also, as he himself attests in the preface, written his life.

In 1206 Luke, at the request of Matthew, second abbot of Fiore, was appointed apostolic visitor of all the monasteries [Col. 0151C] of the Florensian order. He visited them all, and together with the same Matthew and the abbot of the Holy Spirit at Palermo established certain most salutary statutes to be observed thereafter; Innocent III subsequently confirmed these under the date: Lateran, 28 February, in the seventeenth year of his pontificate. Moreover, Luke governed the church entrusted to him with the highest love and the greatest justice. In March 1223, in the twenty-first year of his archiepiscopate, he gathered and compiled into one volume the documents, rights, and goods long sought for his church with the utmost labour and diligence. He called it the *plant* of all the churches of his diocese, or its register, destined to support his successors. The codex is preserved with due care in the more secure [Col. 0151D] archive of the church of Cosenza. Luke is last mentioned in a bull of Honorius III, 26 March 1224, in the seventh year of that pontificate. It is believed that he flew to heaven in that same year and was buried in the church at Sambucina, where he rests. Truly a most worthy prelate, illustrious for the exceptional holiness of his life, the most brilliant star of his Cistercian order and of the church of Cosenza, whom Mariofito, in his description of Calabria, lists among the blessed.”

Thus far UGHELLUS, *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 274 ff.]

AND TO THE CHAPTER OF COSENZA. That they should assign the place called Botrano to the abbot and convent of Fiore, in exchange for their monastery. (Ferentino, 1 September.)

[Col. 0150C]

Since, brother archbishop, wearing the religious habit under the discipline of monastic religion, you have borne the yoke of the Lord from your youth, and have been faithful in a few things so that you deserved to be set over many, in order that in the future you may be set over very many, you ought especially to aid the needs of those who, seated with Mary at the Lord’s feet, meditate continually on His law and choose the better part. Indeed, we have learned from the representations of our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of the monastery [Col. 0151A] of Fiore, that the monastery itself, situated in the mountains, is so exposed to the winds that, through the severity and constancy of the cold, winter has claimed for itself not merely spring and autumn but has extended its bounds into the summer months. The place is also open to attacks by evil men, and for this reason affords little peace to the brothers and is, first and foremost, hostile to their safety.  
[Note: [Col. 0151D] Thus in the transcript.]

Since, therefore, a certain place called Botrano, belonging to the church of Cosenza, is reported to be suitable for religious life, we earnestly admonish and exhort your devotion and command and enjoin you by apostolic letters that, after receiving from the said abbot and brothers an adequate exchange, according to your valuation, brother archbishop, you take care to assign to them the aforesaid [Col. 0151B] place with its appurtenances, granting it to them as freely as the exchange shall freely devolve upon you. Thus, just as the monastery of Fiore is subject directly to us, so the monastery which will arise at Botrano shall be subject to us without any intermediary. Otherwise, know that we have firmly commanded our beloved sons, the abbots of Holy Spirit and Corazzo, and Brother R. of Torciano, that, after prior admonition, they compel you to do this by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal excluded.

Given at Ferentino, 1 September.

CXXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT  
[Note: [Col. 0151D] This was Matthew, successor of Blessed Joachim, as is clear from the documents in Ughellus, *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 637.]  
AND CONVENT OF FIORE. He confirms their possessions. (Ferentino, 1 September.)

[Col. 0151C]

It is customary to grant assent, etc., up to “assent”: the churches of Saint [Col. 0152A] Peter and Saint Dominica, situated near the river Frigido, granted to you by our venerable brother, the bishop of Tropea, with the common consent of his chapter; likewise the possessions granted to you in pious liberality by the nobleman S. of Mamistra, as is contained in their authentic documents  
[Note: [Col. 0152D] The donation of Simon of Mamistra—mentioned in the preceding note—and also the grant of the bishop of Tropea, which the pope here confirms, are printed by Ughellus, in the place cited.]  
and as you possess them rightfully and peaceably, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your monastery, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Richard, bishop of Tropea of illustrious memory, elected in 1198, lived under Innocent III, from whom he obtained a privilege for himself and his successors in 1200. In the early years of this prelate, namely in the year of our salvation 1291 [probably an erroneous date], the monastery of Fonte Laureato was founded in this diocese of Tropea, with Richard’s consent, in the territory of the Frigido River, of the Florensian order, a daughter-house of the Cistercian order. Its founders were Simon of Mamistra and his wife Gattegrima, lords of the Frigido River, beside the church of Saint Dominica, where a monastery had long before been built but was at that time almost abandoned. To establish the house, the same Simon offered to Joachim—a man renowned for the gift of prophecy and learning, abbot of the monastery of Fiore, a Cistercian house from which the Florensian order sprang—a sufficiently extensive holding together with several other goods. For this purpose Simon drew up an instrument of donation and foundation, which survives in the archive of that monastery. UGHELLUS, *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 633. Richard entered upon the way of all flesh about the year 1215.]

Given at Ferentino, 1 September.

CXXXIX.  
[Note: [Col. 0152D] It survives, but mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book III, title 3, “On Married Clerics,” chapter 6. What is there printed is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied in the text.]  
TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ACERENZA  
[Note: [Col. 0152D] See Letter 57, note, of this sixth book.]  
On confirmation of the bishop of Anglona, even though his father had been in minor orders. (Ferentino, 5 September.)

[Col. 0152B] [When it had formerly come to our hearing that the canons of Anglona had elected our beloved son  
[Note: [Col. 0152D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*.]  
. . . cantor of Tricarico  
[Note: [Col. 0152D] UGHELLUS, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 122, mentions nothing else about this man besides this very letter of Innocent III.]  
as their shepherd,] we commanded you to examine carefully the election and the person, and, if you found the election canonical and the person suitable, to confirm that election by apostolic authority, proceeding as metropolitan in the other matters.

[Although you were satisfied concerning the canonical form of the election and the suitability of the person in other respects, you were nevertheless troubled and led to consult us  
[Note: [Col. 0152D] These words, and below the word *cantor*, are absent from the *Decretals*.]  
because the father of that cantor had been a Greek and, while in minor orders, had taken a wife according to the rite of the Greeks, and had begotten the cantor from his lawful wife while he was in priestly orders. We therefore, observing that the [Col. 0152C] Eastern Church has not accepted a vow of continence, so that  
[Note: [Col. 0152D] The *Decretals* read *quoniam* (“because”); below they read *contrahunt* for *contrahant* and *utuntur* for *utantur*, and omit the words “brother . . . letters.”]  
Easterners contract marriage in minor orders [Col. 0153A] and in higher orders make use of a marriage already contracted, command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, unless the custom of the region opposes it because Greeks of this kind live among Latins, and unless something else  
[Note: [Col. 0153D] The *Decretals* add *canonicum* (“canonical”); below they read *obsistat* for *obsistit* and omit the word *cantor*.]  
stands in the way, you proceed without hesitation to the confirmation and consecration of that cantor.

Given at Ferentino, 5 September.

CXL.  
[Note: [Col. 0153D] Raynaldus published fragments of this letter under the year 1203, §22. What appears in his work is enclosed here in brackets.]  
LETTER OF JOHN OF CASEMARI TO THE LORD POPE. He gives an account of his legation to the kingdom of Bosnia; informs him of the donation of Sibyl, wife of the late prefect of Constantinople; and proposes that new bishoprics be created and organized.

[After dealing with the business of those former Patarene heretics in Bosnia, as I wrote to Your Holiness some time ago, [Col. 0153B] I remained for several days in Hungary at the king’s pleasure. Meanwhile the envoys of that great man Kaloyan came to the king; with them, God guiding, I hope to go to him. The most Christian king made them swear upon the Gospels in church before the altar that they would bring me safely into his presence.] But I trust in the Lord that on the following day, which will be the feast of Blessed Barnabas, we shall begin our journey, accompanied by your prayers and followed by your blessing. Many persons, and the king himself, say that he is devoted to the Roman Church; and those now with me firmly assert and affirm it. Therefore I have received an assurance that, if he wishes to send envoys to Your Holiness, they will suffer no injury throughout the whole kingdom of Hungary or in the lands of his friends and relatives, either [Col. 0153C] going or returning.

[Moreover, Your Holiness should know that in the kingdom of Ban Kulin of Bosnia there is only one bishopric, and the bishop has now died. If it could be arranged that a Latin were placed there, and that three or four new bishoprics were also created there, ecclesiastical advantage would thereby increase considerably, since his kingdom extends for at least ten days’ journeys and more. Further, Your Holiness should know that a noblewoman, Sibyl, wife of the late prefect of Constantinople, in her last will left to the Roman Church a legacy from her dowry,] namely, as a certain priest whom I found in Hungary says, twenty thousand perpera. This seems true, because she herself told me with her own [Col. 0153D] mouth that she wished to bequeath her entire dowry to you and the Roman Church. I therefore thought it right to report this, so that, if it happens that a legate is sent there and sees it expedient, he may, supported by your authority, claim and vigorously demand it.

CXLI.  
[Note: [Col. 0154D] Raynaldus published the fragment under the year 1203, §23. What appears in his work is enclosed here in brackets.]  
Instrument by which the schismatic monks of Bosnia promise to observe the constitutions of the Roman Church. (At the Royal Island, 30 April.)

[In the name of the eternal God, Creator of all things and Redeemer of the human [Col. 0154A] race, in the year 1203 from His Incarnation, and the sixth year of the lord Pope Innocent III. We, the priors of those persons who until now have been called, in a distinctive manner, by the prerogative title “Christians” in the territory of Bosnia, appointed to act on behalf of all, promise for all those who belong above to our fellowship of brotherhood, in the presence of Lord J. . . . of Casamari, chaplain of the supreme pontiff and of the Roman Church, delegated to Bosnia for this purpose, and in the presence of our patron, Ban Kulin, lord of Bosnia, before God and His saints, to abide by the ordinances and commands of the holy Roman Church, both in our life and conduct, and to obey its authority and live by its institutions; binding ourselves on behalf of all who belong to our fellowship, and our places with all their possessions and goods, [Col. 0154B] if at any time hereafter we should follow heretical depravity. First, we renounce the schism by which we are said to be disgraced, and acknowledge the Roman Church, our mother, as the head of all ecclesiastical unity.]

And in all our places in which a community of brothers dwells, we shall have oratories, in which the brothers will publicly assemble together at night for Matins and by day for the chanting of the Hours. In all churches we shall have altars and crosses; and we shall read the books both of the New and of the Old Testament, as the Roman Church does. At each of our places we shall have priests, who must celebrate Masses according to the ecclesiastical order on Sundays and feast days, at least; hear confessions [Col. 0154C] and impose penances. We shall have cemeteries beside the oratories, in which the brothers may be buried, and visitors too, should they happen to die there. At least seven times a year we shall receive the Body of the Lord from the hand of a priest: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, her Nativity, and the commemoration of All Saints, celebrated on the Kalends of November.

We shall observe the fasts established by the Church and keep those things which our elders wisely prescribed. Women who belong to our religious community shall be separated from men, both in dormitories and in refectories; and no brother shall converse alone with a woman alone, so that no evil suspicion may arise. Nor shall we henceforth receive [Col. 0154D] any married man or woman, unless, by mutual consent and after promising continence, both are converted together. We shall celebrate the feasts of saints instituted by the holy Fathers, and shall henceforth knowingly receive no Manichaean or other heretic to dwell with us. And just as we are separated from other laypersons in life and conduct, so we shall also be distinguished by the dress of our clothing: these garments shall be closed, uncoloured, and measured down to the ankles. Henceforth we shall call ourselves not “Christians,” as hitherto, but “brothers,” [Col. 0155A] lest the distinctive title inflict an injury upon other Christians.

When the master has died, thereafter and forever the priors, with the counsel of God-fearing brothers, shall elect a superior, to be confirmed solely by the Roman pontiff. If the Roman Church wishes to add or remove anything else, we shall receive and observe it with devotion. That this may obtain permanent force, we confirm it by our subscriptions. Done in Bosnia, beside the river, at the place called Bolino Polje, 8 April. We, Dragite, Lubin, Brageta, Pribis, Luben, Rados, Bladosius, Ban Kulin, and Marinus, archdeacon of Ragusa, have subscribed.

Thereafter we, Lubin and Brageta, by the will of all our brothers in Bosnia and of Ban Kulin himself, journeying with the same Lord J., chaplain, [Col. 0155B] to H., the illustrious and most Christian king of Hungary, swore in the presence of that king, of the venerable . . . archbishop of Kalocsa, of the bishop of Pécs, and of many others, in the person of all, to keep these statutes and whatever else the Roman Church may wish to ordain concerning us and establish according to the Catholic faith.

Done at the Royal Island, 30 April.

CXLII.  
[Note: [Col. 0155D] Raynaldus published this letter under the year 1203, §20.]  
LETTER OF KALOYAN, EMPEROR OF THE BULGARIANS, TO THE POPE. He submits himself to the Roman Church.

Kaloyan, emperor of the Bulgarians, to the most holy lord, patriarch of the faith of Christians from East to [Col. 0155C] West, the Roman pope: I send you this letter, rejoicing if my messenger finds you well and happy, with all who are with you and all your relatives and friends. I am well through the power of the Lord and the Blessed Virgin, through the prayers of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and through your holy prayers.

I, Kaloyan, emperor of the Bulgarians, understand that you have from God the power of binding and loosing, just as Blessed Peter the Apostle had it, to whom the Lord said: “Whatever you bind on earth,” etc. (Matthew 16). Thus God has bestowed this grace upon you: therefore, whomsoever you bind is bound, and whomsoever you loose is loosed. I make known to Your Holiness that six years have passed since I sent to you once, twice, and three times; but my envoys could not [Col. 0155D] come to Your Holiness, set forth my word, and bring back your consolation to me.

The Lord inspired Your Holiness to send to me Dominic, archpriest of Brindisi, through whom I understood that you had not forgotten me, your servant. I honoured him as your own man and gave him letters [Col. 0156A] to carry to Your Holiness. Whether he brought them or did not bring them, God knows. When the Greeks learned this, the patriarch and the emperor sent to me: “Come to us; we shall crown you emperor and make a patriarch for you, because an empire could not stand without a patriarch.” But I did not wish it; rather I had recourse to Your Holiness, because I wish to be the servant of Saint Peter and of Your Holiness.

And let Your Holiness know that I have sent my archbishop to you with every provision, money, silken cloths, wax, silver, horses, and mules, that he may pay reverence to Your Holiness on behalf of me, your servant. And I beg, through the prayers of the blessed Apostle Peter and through your holy prayers, that you send cardinals, to whom Your Holiness may command that they crown me emperor and establish a patriarch in [Col. 0156B] my land, so that I may be your servant for the time of my life.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Thus far Raynaldus; in the place cited he adds: “The letters of Basil, archbishop of the Bulgarians, are appended (in the *Register*, after this letter). When, carrying them to the Apostolic See together with immense and most precious gifts, he had traversed a very long journey and reached Dyrrachium, he was prevented by the Greeks—who, stirred by envy, were trying to draw the Bulgarians away from union with the Roman Church—from crossing over into the West. At that time the tyrant Alexius still held the sceptre wrested from Isaac; for fear of him the archbishop could not carry out his legation, but sent most faithful envoys to Innocent.” These remarks should indeed be understood concerning the material presented here; but in Conti’s transcript they are read continuously and without distinction, as though they were a second part of Kaloyan’s own letter.]

Furthermore, let Your Holiness know that I, Archbishop Basil, was coming with this money to pay reverence to Your Holiness, and reached Dyrrachium. There I found the envoys of Count Walter, rejoicing with me and arranging to cross the sea together with me. But the Greek who was travelling with them did not allow me to cross with them, after consulting the duke of Dyrrachium, asserting that it would displease the emperor if I crossed. When they heard this, the archdeacon and the Latin clergy at Dyrrachium likewise advised me not to cross, saying that if I acted otherwise I would lose my property and my person. Therefore I sent to you good men, [Col. 0156C] faithful servants of the emperor, Sergius the constable and Constantine the priest, to whom the charge has been given of setting the truth before you. May the Lord inspire you to undertake this service properly.

CXLIII.  
[Note: [Col. 0156D] Raynaldus published part of this letter under the year 1203, §21. What appears in his work is enclosed here in brackets.]  
TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF ZAGORA. He replies to the preceding letter. (Ferentino, 10 September.)

Having received the letters which your fraternity sent us in the name of the nobleman Kaloyan, lord of the Bulgarians, through our beloved sons Constantine the priest and Sergius the constable, we received fuller joy, understanding from them that you both rightly hold the same view concerning the keys of the Church: that you acknowledge the primacy of the Roman Church, and in us [Col. 0156D] the power of binding and loosing and the teaching authority of ecclesiastical discipline.

For, understanding that the Lord said not only to us in Blessed Peter, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth,” etc. (Matthew 16), but also says to us in the prophet, “Behold, [Col. 0157A] today I have set you over nations and kingdoms, that you may pluck up and break down, destroy and overthrow, build and plant,” you ask us for both the royal diadem and the pre-eminent dignity of a patriarch, since the same nobleman wishes, by our authority, to have the crown placed upon himself and a patriarch established in his land through us.

Now, some time ago, in order that we might be better informed concerning his and his subjects’ devotion and the condition of the land—since we do not merely wish but also desire that, as he descends from a noble Roman stock, so he may follow the institutions of the Roman Church and receive from it the teaching of the Catholic faith and an increase in his honour—[we decided to send our beloved son Dominic, archpriest of Brindisi, into the presence of that nobleman.] When he had returned to the Apostolic See with [Col. 0157B] the letters of the same lord of the Bulgarians, as well as yours and those of Prince Bellota, and we had been better informed about these matters, we decided to send our beloved son J., our chaplain and legate of the Roman Church, to him.

[We granted him full authority to correct throughout that nobleman’s whole land, in spiritual matters, whatever he found needing correction, and to establish whatever ought to be established according to the Lord. Through him we also decided to send the pallium, the insignia of the fullness of the pontifical office, to one of the archbishops of his land, commanding him that, if there should perhaps be persons in that land to be promoted to orders or consecrated bishops, he should not delay in proceeding, through neighbouring Catholic bishops only, to the ordination of those to be ordained [Col. 0157C] and the consecration of those to be consecrated. We also commanded him to investigate carefully the truth concerning the crown granted by the Roman Church to the forebears of the aforesaid nobleman, and to discuss with the same man all matters which he recognized needed discussion, so that, once we have at last been informed of everything through him and the envoys of that nobleman, we may proceed in this matter more advisedly and deliberately.]

Recently, however, our same legate met envoys of the same nobleman who had been sent to our dearest son in Christ, H. . . . ., the illustrious king of Hungary; he stated that he would proceed to their lord with them without delay. Although you have therefore sent the aforesaid priest Constantine and Sergius the constable to our presence, nevertheless, because the aforementioned nobleman has particularly laid upon you the labour of coming to us and imposed on you the burden of his legation, we admonish your fraternity, earnestly exhort it, and command it by apostolic letters that, if it can possibly be done, leaving behind, if need be, your household and the multitude of your mounts, you present yourself before us. For we believe that you will inform us so fully concerning matters about which we wish to be informed that perhaps it will not be necessary for us to await the return of the aforesaid legate; indeed, we may send our own legate with you, through whom the desire and petition of the lord of the Bulgarians will be more fully [Col. 0158A] satisfied. Take care, therefore, to sail to Apulia, for from there we shall have you brought safely into our presence and sent back under safe-conduct to your regions, either elsewhere by sea or by land, so that you need not fear for your return.

Given at Ferentino, 10 September.

CXLIV.  
[Note: [Col. 0157D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, §21.]  
TO KALOYAN, LORD OF THE BULGARIANS. On the same subject. (Given as above.)

In almost the same terms, to the end. When, therefore, the archbishop himself has come to us, as we hope, we shall grant your petitions and his, insofar as we can do so with God and our honour, since we intend both to confirm you and the people committed to your jurisdiction in the Catholic faith [Col. 0158B] and to root them in devotion to the Apostolic See, and to honour your person as a special son of the Church. Furthermore, we earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility to endeavour to renew the bonds of peace with our beloved son, the nobleman Wlco, lest, through the occasion of discord, either your land or his suffer irreparable damage.

Given as above.

CXLV. TO THE JUDGE OF CAGLIARI. On the marriage of the daughter of the late judge of Gallura.  
[Note: [Col. 0158D] See Letter 29 of this sixth book.]  
(Ferentino, 15 September.)

[Col. 0158C] We regard it as pleasing and welcome that, as our venerable brother B., archbishop of Torres, informed us by his letters, you prudently removed your kinsman from the land of Gallura in order to remove the scandal that had arisen in Sardinia and restore concord. Therefore, lest the latter error prove worse than the former and Sardinia again be disturbed on account of the judgeship of Gallura, we earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility, and command you by apostolic letters, that you do not permit the noblewoman . . . ., daughter of the late judge of Gallura, to marry a suspect person, especially Isidore, brother of the nobleman . . . ., judge of Torres, who, as is said, is related to her in the nearest degree of consanguinity. Rather, as we commanded you and the other judges of [Col. 0158D] Sardinia by other letters, humbly comply in this matter with the statutes and admonitions of that archbishop, so that we may thereby understand the disposition of your devotion and be bound accordingly to give more particular attention to your honour.

Given at Ferentino, 15 September.

CXLVI. TO THE NOBLEMAN, THE JUDGE OF TORRES. On the same subject. (Given as above.)

Since, according to the testimony of truth, it profits a person nothing if he should gain the whole world and incur loss [Col. 0159A] of his soul, you ought not, for temporal advantage, neglect eternal goods or prefer the honour of a brother to the fear of the Lord; for unless you put your brother and everything you possess after Christ, you are not worthy of Him, as He Himself declares. We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility and command you by apostolic letters that, since our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman . . . . ., daughter of the late judge of Gallura, is related in the nearest degree of consanguinity to your brother, the nobleman Isidore, you do not permit her to be joined to him incestuously when she cannot be joined to him in marriage, or to be betrothed unlawfully when she cannot be betrothed lawfully. Rather, comply with the statutes and admonitions of our venerable brother B. . . ., archbishop of Torres, concerning giving her in marriage, [Col. 0159B] and, as we trust in your devotion, make effective efforts that she may be joined to a lawful husband according to his judgment. Execute the apostolic command in such a manner that we may thereby understand the disposition of your devotion and be bound to give particular attention to your honour.

Given as above.

CXLVII.  
[Note: [Col. 0159D]

Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, §68.

It is found, but mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book II, title 24, “On Oaths,” chapter 22. What is there printed is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also supplied.]

TO THE NOBLEMAN, THE JUDGE OF CAGLIARI. On the oath to be rendered.  
[Note: [Col. 0159D] See Letters 29, 30, and 31 of this sixth book.]  
(Ferentino, 15 September.)

[We believe you are endowed with such discernment that you understand for yourself that a burden is not lightened but increased when someone is rashly released from what another is bound to render. Indeed, our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Torres [Col. 0159C] [Note: The Decretals read “in the place of our venerable brother”; they omit what follows in italics, and read *mandate* for “in instructions”], informed us by his letters that, when he had required from you in our name an oath of fealty, as he had received instructions from us to do, you delayed to render it into his hands, asserting that you had rendered such an oath to our venerable brother . . . . . . the Archbishop of Pisa, saving the honor of the Apostolic See. Therefore, since you are bound to render fealty to us and to the Roman Church, as your own prudence also acknowledges: if you consider the oath already rendered contrary to that which you are bound to render to us, you must judge it unlawful; and, notwithstanding an unlawful oath, you shall render what is lawfully—indeed, what is owingly—required. Or, if by rendering the oath already rendered you are not acting contrarily, you shall render it without difficulty [Col. 0159D].] Therefore we admonish your nobility, earnestly exhort you, and by these apostolic letters [Col. 0160A] command and enjoin you that, setting aside every pretext and excuse, you render into the hands of that same archbishop an oath of fealty to us and to the Roman Church.

Given at Ferentino, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

CXLVIII. TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF TORRES. That he may proceed against the debtors of his church. (Ferentino, seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.)

Since a request is made of us, etc., as far as “assent”: by the authority of these presents we grant you leave, with respect to those who shall henceforth withhold, or have hitherto withheld, rents owed to your church from possessions granted to them under rent by the Church of Torres, to proceed according to the lawful sanctions concerning spoliation. Let no one therefore, etc.

[Col. 0160B] Given at Ferentino, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

CXLIX. [Note: [Col. 0159D]

Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 101, § 11, mentions this letter and also the following letters 150, 151, and 152.

Raynaldus published part of it under the year 1203, § 52; passages found in his work are enclosed here in brackets.]

TO THE COUNT OF AUXERRE, GREETINGS AND A MORE WHOLESOME SPIRIT OF COUNSEL. A threatening letter, that he should recall the Bishop of Auxerre, whom he had ordered into exile. [Note: [Col. 0160D] We have already discussed the Bishop of Auxerre above. The following, found in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 299, agrees with the subject of this letter: “Hugh of Noyers carried on grave and prolonged disputes with Peter of Courtenay, a man of ungovernable spirit and of ruinous greed against the sacred rights of churches. When Hugh had struck him with a dreadful anathema in 1203 for violating an interdict, he finally restored him to the Church, after public penance had been performed, at the persuasion of William, Archbishop of Bourges, his uncle; and he obtained from him that the Jews should be expelled from Auxerre, their synagogue having been converted into a church in 1204, to which Saints Nicholas and Reinobert gave their names.”] (Anagni . . .)

Since, forgetful of your own salvation, you conspire toward the destruction of your soul, you should not wonder if we deny you the address of greeting. For behold: exalted not by your merits but rather by divine benefits, you have forsaken Him who exalted you; you have endeavored to kick against the goad, returning evils for benefits; and, exercising upon the members the tyranny which you cannot exercise upon the head. Indeed, what do you make yourself, that you rage against the Church of God and, persecuting ecclesiastical liberty, [Col. 0160C] presume to vent your cruelty upon the anointed of the Lord, and compel our venerable brother . . . . the Bishop of Auxerre—a great member of God’s Church, a man endowed with learning, distinguished by uprightness, and worthy of reverence alike for his holy observance of religion and for the eminence of his episcopal dignity—to go into exile from his entire diocese?

He indeed, because truth cannot lie, shall be blessed if he suffers persecution for righteousness’ sake, and shall be crowned by the Lord if he has contended lawfully. But you, in accordance with your impenitent heart, store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s great judgment, when, while your conscience bears witness against you, you shall be bound hand and foot and cast into outer darkness; and there, tormented by avenging flames, [Col. 0160D] you shall vainly beg that the same bishop dip the tip of his finger in water and [Col. 0161A] cool your tongue. For then perhaps you will hear the Lord say: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me, and you grievously persecuted me in my ministry; and because you presumed irreverently to touch him, you touched the apple of my eye. But behold, the day of recompense and vengeance comes, when I shall render to you and to each according to merits, seated with the senators of my people.” What miserable excuse will you then offer? What plea will you bring forward on your own behalf, when your deeds themselves shall be manifest and the things you do in darkness, son of darkness, shall not have escaped the inaccessible light of Christ?

[Accordingly, you shall there be punished the more severely because, as though you could now presume everything with impunity, you hand down to posterity an example of greater destruction and bring disgrace upon the most renowned kingdom of France. For, while you persecute ecclesiastical [Col. 0161B] liberty—which the kings of France of illustrious memory were accustomed not merely to embrace but also to defend—you compel a bishop to go into exile precisely where bishops in exile had hitherto been accustomed to find a safe refuge and honorable reception. Why, wretch, do you cloak your guilt and rashly shift your crime onto our most beloved son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious King of France? For, as we have seen contained in your letters, you call this bishop a detractor from royal serenity, and intimate that you were moved against him as if in vengeance for a royal injury, whereas you were rather moved against him because he refused to spare your iniquities and excesses. But because you had utterly destroyed the Church of Saint Adrian, had presumed, in hatred of him and to the prejudice of ecclesiastical liberty, to put out the eyes of one of his vassals, and had committed depredations and robberies both against ecclesiastical goods and against others, he pronounced a sentence of excommunication against you and forbade ecclesiastical burial both to you and to your men.]

Yet you, though you ought to have understood for yourself that the words of one who corrects are better than the kisses of one who flatters, and to have cried with the Prophet, “Let the righteous man correct me in mercy,” [uncertain abbreviation in source: *o. a. p. n. in. c. m.*] [Note: Thus in the Vatican and Conti copies], became more obstinate because of his correction, and wished to turn his house into a cemetery, by causing the body of some man, perhaps three days dead and foul-smelling, to be buried in it to his reproach. Nor did it suffice for your folly [Col. 0161D] that you had compelled the same bishop to go into exile from his own see, unless you also forced him, fleeing anew, to leave the monastery of Pontigny, to which he had fled, and, after departing from the boundaries of the diocese of the Church of Auxerre, to withdraw into another diocese.

Desiring also to vent cruelty upon the persons of the Church of Auxerre, you pursued them through your retainers. Coming to the priory in which he had first taken refuge, they cleverly broke down its doors with axe and hatchet, searching everywhere in order that they might kill those whom they found and carry out your commands in their slaughter. Although you are known to have sinned gravely against God, the universal Church, and ourselves—but more gravely against yourself—[Col. 0162A] yet, because we are bound to recall those who stray to the path of uprightness, we admonish your nobility, earnestly exhort you, and by apostolic letters, under invocation of the divine judgment, command and enjoin you that, as you shamefully expelled that bishop, so you honorably recall him; and that, for all the losses and injuries hitherto inflicted upon him and his churches, you make satisfaction as fitting as it is devout, so that through him you may deserve to obtain the benefit of absolution.

Otherwise, know that by apostolic letters we strictly command our venerable brothers . . . . the Archbishop of Sens, . . . . the Bishop of Chartres, and . . . . the Bishop of Châlons, publicly to declare both you and all your principal counsellors and supporters excommunicated, unless you make satisfaction concerning [Col. 0162B] the aforesaid matters, on every Sunday and feast day; and to order all persons most strictly to avoid you. They are also to declare, by our authority, your whole land subject to a general interdict until fitting satisfaction has been made; and wherever outside your land you may go, so long as you are present there, they are to forbid the celebration of all divine offices and ecclesiastical sacraments, except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying. But if not even thus you desist from your presumption, we shall lay our hands upon you more heavily.

Given at Anagni . . . . in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CL. [Note: [Col. 0161D] See preceding letter 149.] TO THE KING OF FRANCE. That he should induce the Count of Auxerre to recall the Bishop of Auxerre, whom this count had caused to go into exile. (Anagni.)

[Col. 0162C]

May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the malicious tongue which endeavor, by poisonous whisperings, to infect the purity of the royal mind and to obscure, by their iniquities, the reputation not so much of the king as of the kingdom of France. [For that kingdom had deserved titles of everlasting praise because it preserved churches and ecclesiastical men in their immunities, defended ecclesiastical liberty, and not only did not rage against its own people but also gladly received from every quarter strangers who endured exile for righteousness’ sake. It treated them honorably, relieving their need from its own resources.
