The Apostolic See experienced this not only in its members but also in itself, when, in the time of its separation [Note: Thus in the copy; but these words are absent in Raynaldus.] and at a moment of necessity, it found refuge in the kingdom of France; there, devoutly received and honorably treated, it gained considerable relief from its distresses, indeed recovered strength, through which—though the Lord brought it about and turned righteousness into judgment—it rose stronger into its former happy condition, which had seemed to have fallen.]

Would that, therefore, if anything must be changed in that kingdom, it might be a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High; lest gold be turned [Col. 0163A] into dross and the finest color be altered, and lest the machinations of those who call good evil and evil good, and strive to make light darkness and darkness light, prevail over royal serenity, seeking to darken the light of your mind. Moreover, we give thanks to our God that, with your father L., King of France of illustrious memory, the talkativeness of such men was never able to prevail, so that his soul should enter into their counsel or his uprightness should turn to the right or left from the straight path. For he had not set his foot upon slippery ground, but had so established his steps in the fear of the Lord that he regarded his kingdom as service to Him and protected ecclesiastical liberty to the utmost of his power. Thus he obtained from God—not so much by prayers as by merits—that a son should be born to him already in old age; since he desired not so much an heir to the kingdom as a successor in character, longing that the Lord might set the fruit of his womb upon the throne of the kingdom of France, one who would keep the rules of the divine law and not overstep the bounds which his father had set in the worship of the divine Name and in reverence toward churches and ecclesiastical persons.

But now, what we report with sorrow, certain sons of iniquity—whose purpose is to trample the Lord’s commandments and hand down wicked traditions—strive by their perversities to corrupt royal purity, so that the prayer of the aforesaid king may prove vain and the son may not do what he saw his father do. They wish to induce it [the royal authority] to favor [Col. 0163C] a man against God, to foster those who do like things, either by consenting to their deeds or at least by tolerating the perverse in their iniquity through dissimulation. For we grieve, and report not without pain and sorrow, that, as truthful reports from certain persons have reached our ears—indeed, as the acts of certain persons themselves make plain—there are now, because sins demand it, being attempted in the kingdom of France things not merely unattempted in other kingdoms but unheard of.

Indeed, when our venerable brother . . . . the Bishop of Auxerre had pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon P. . . . the Count of Auxerre because he had utterly destroyed the Church of Saint Adrian, committed depredations and robberies both against the goods of churches and against private persons, and, in hatred of that bishop and [Col. 0163D] of ecclesiastical liberty, put out the eyes of one of his vassals; and when he had forbidden ecclesiastical burial, should they die, both to him and to his men: the count, in order to turn his house into a cemetery, buried in it a certain lifeless corpse. And although he had promised to make satisfaction to that bishop, pretending that he wished to be reconciled to ecclesiastical unity, and although, on the appointed day, both the bishop and the beloved sons . . . . the dean, . . . . the archdeacon, . . . . the cantor, the sacristan, and other persons of the Church of Auxerre had assembled for this purpose, he finally neglected to make satisfaction according to his promise. Thus, adding iniquity to iniquity and making his last error worse than the first, he had his retainers pursue the dean and the other persons as they returned home [Col. 0164A]. Although they, foreseeing his malice, had withdrawn from a certain priory in which they had first taken refuge and intended to spend the night, to another place, his retainers nevertheless, to fulfill their orders, broke down the priory’s doors with axe and hatchet, searching all its cellars and chambers.

Moreover, when the frequently mentioned bishop had fled from his presence to Pontigny because of his persecutions, the count himself—as we have seen stated in his letters—called him a seducer both against himself and against royal serenity and our venerable brother . . . . the Bishop of Beauvais. He ordered him expelled from that priory, uttering many threats by letters and more through messengers, since he did not fear to expose the monastery of Pontigny and its possessions [Col. 0164B] to robbers. Because of this, the bishop is compelled to go into exile from his entire diocese. We grieve further, and are disturbed, because, as we have learned, royal serenity, moved against him without cause [unless perhaps, treating a resentment as though it were a cause, it conceived hostility against him because he refused to declare excommunicated our beloved son J. of Périgueux, your cousin, whom he had not excommunicated, lest he bear witness to falsehood], confiscated his goods and occupied all his regalian rights.

Therefore, lest you incur further divine displeasure by this and bring disgrace upon the reputation of the kingdom of France, we admonish royal serenity and earnestly exhort you that, [Col. 0164C] setting aside absolutely every resentment, you do not hand down an example of destruction to your descendants but provide your subjects with a saving example: receive the aforesaid bishop into royal favor, and do not delay restoring to him both the regalian rights and everything which you are said to have confiscated. Furthermore, lest you incur the taint of hidden complicity if, though able, you refuse to oppose a manifest crime, restrain the aforesaid count completely from molesting him and persecuting his church, and compel him to render satisfaction, as fitting as it is devout, for the losses and injuries inflicted upon the aforesaid bishop and his church.

We, however, command our venerable brothers . . . . the Archbishop of Sens, . . . . the Bishop of Chartres, and . . . . the Bishop of Châlons, etc., as in the preceding no. CXLIX, as far as “our hands.” But wishing to show deference to your serenity, we do not for the present order any coercive measure to be exercised against you. With paternal gentleness we urge your serenity, as a Catholic prince, to correct these matters yourself in such a way that we are not compelled to apply the hand of correction against you or to burden royal serenity, which is dear to us. Otherwise, the more we defer to you now, the less we shall defer to you hereafter; and we shall choose rather to please God the King than a human king. Moreover, your highness ought not without reason to fear lest you seem to persecute him in favor of the heretics, against whom the same bishop acted manfully and contended lawfully.

Given at Anagni . . . . in the sixth year.

CLI. [Note: [Col. 0165D] See letter 149.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. [Note: [Col. 0165D] We have already spoken more than once concerning the Archbishop of Sens.] He sharply rebukes him because he had not proceeded against the Count of Auxerre, who had expelled the bishop. He orders proceedings. (Anagni.)

[Col. 0165A]

Until now we believed that, in your promotion, we had made useful provision not only for the Church of Sens but for the whole Gallican province, thinking that we had raised upon a lampstand a lamp formerly set under a bushel, and had appointed over the Lord’s flock not a hireling but a shepherd. But behold, what we report not without pain and sorrow: your lamp, as though already extinguished, now smokes and gives no light to those placed in the house, but rather allows them to wander in darkness, while, degenerating [Col. 0165B] from a shepherd into a hireling, you do not set yourself as a wall for the house of the Lord against those who attack from the other side; instead, seeing the wolf, you abandon the sheep and flee, comparable to a dumb dog unable to bark.

For we thought that in your mouth was the word of the Lord, living, active, and sharper than every two-edged sword; that without ceasing you would cry aloud and lift up your voice powerfully like a trumpet; that there would be no respect of persons in you, but that you would proclaim to the wicked his impiety and to criminals their own crimes, and would, for [Note: Thus in the copy.] . . . . meek persons, rebuke and correct the unruly. Yet, as the demonstration of your acts makes manifest, your tongue now clings to your throat, so that the word of the Lord is bound in your mouth; you do not know how to utter a good word [Col. 0165C] for executing vengeance upon the nations and rebukes among the peoples, nor do you dare rebuke before all one who sins. You have forgotten that the Apostle not only said, as you know, but also taught: “Rebuke, exhort, reprove in all patience and teaching”; and elsewhere he likewise insists sternly that rebuke must be administered.

Indeed, if zeal for the Lord’s house consumed you and the reproaches of those who reproach Him had fallen upon you, perfect charity would have cast fear out of you, and you would fearlessly have exercised upon the nobleman . . . . the Count of Auxerre—who destroys churches, plunders their possessions and goods, persecutes ecclesiastical liberty, and compels our venerable brother . . . . the Bishop of Auxerre, your suffragan, to go into exile—such vengeance that punishment for so great a crime would have reached our hearing before the complaint did. Yet because perhaps you have grown old with Eli, you caress rather than punish (thus the text) the vices of your subjects, whitewashing the wall of iniquity which they build when you ought rather to demolish it. For now Peter’s sword is consumed by rust in your possession, so that you cannot uproot, destroy, and overthrow the things which the Lord commands to be uprooted, destroyed, or overthrown in the Prophet: “Behold,” He says, “I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, and overthrow, to build and to plant.”

Therefore, lest, if we seem to tolerate such negligence in you calmly, so great a loss to the [Col. 0166A] Gallican Church be imputed to us, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood that, aroused from the sleep in which you have hitherto lain torpid, you be urgent in season and out of season, perform the work of an evangelist, and do not bring reproach upon our ministry; instead, laudably discharge your pastoral office, consecrating your hands in your brother and son by worthy punishment of the crime, so that a blessing may be given you. Together with our venerable brothers . . . . the Bishops of Chartres and Châlons, publicly declare the aforesaid count—who has been struck by that bishop with the sword of excommunication—excommunicated, along with all his principal counsellors and supporters, on every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted. Cause this declaration to be solemnly published throughout the entire province of Sens with the aforesaid solemnity, declaring by our authority his whole land subject to a general interdict until fitting satisfaction has been made. Wherever that count goes outside his land, for as long as he remains present there, forbid the celebration of divine offices and ecclesiastical sacraments, except baptism for infants and penances for the dying.

Also diligently admonish and induce our most beloved son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious King of France, to restore without diminution to that bishop the goods which he confiscated and the regalian rights which he took, and to receive him into the fullness of royal favor, lest, if he acts otherwise, [Col. 0166C] he seem to persecute him in favor of the heretics, against whom the same bishop has until now acted manfully and fought stoutly. Therefore execute the apostolic command in these matters in such a way that we are not compelled to lay the axe to the root of the unfruitful fig tree if it henceforth occupies the ground uselessly, to destroy the wicked husbandman miserably, and to lease the Church of Sens to another who does not bind in a napkin the talent entrusted to him but rather puts it out at interest, fearing not those who kill the body but Him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna.

Given at Anagni . . . . in the sixth year.

CLII. [Note: [Col. 0166D] See letter 149.] TO THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE. A consolatory and Catholic letter. (Anagni.)

[Col. 0166D]

Reflecting in bitterness upon our years and considering the evil of the present day, we can scarcely find a cause for so great sorrow as that which we conceived upon receiving your letters. For we grieve on your account, as for our venerable brother and one whom we bear in the inward parts of Jesus Christ, regarding your persecutions as our own; since the head cannot but suffer with so great a member, for with the Apostle it burns with scandalized brethren and is weak with those who are weak. We grieve also for the kingdom of France, concerning which, as the truth of the matter stood, its report went forth [Col. 0167A] into all the earth and its fame reached the ends of the world: that ecclesiastical liberty especially flourished there and the immunity of clerics was preserved. For in that realm the spiritual and material swords were bound together in so friendly a union that the material sword in no respect opposed the spiritual, but rather rendered to it—indeed, to God—welcome aid and necessary assistance; nor did it consider it unworthy that temporal power should defer to ecclesiastical dignity and serve its honors.

We grieve also for our most beloved son in Christ, Ph., the illustrious King of France, to whose power—or rather whose negligence—some persons attribute whatever wrongdoing is attempted by anyone in the kingdom. They count his dissimulation as favor, and say that he is not free [Col. 0167B] from the taint of hidden complicity when he ceases to oppose a manifest crime. For formerly his forebears of illustrious memory were accustomed devoutly to receive bishops in exile and not merely to treat them honorably, but to provide for them generously; but now it turns to his reproach that you are compelled to go into exile under his very eyes and to seek foreign assistance outside your Church and diocese. [Note: These words occur in Raynaldus at the place cited.]

[Yet while we sympathize with you, the reading of the Gospel comforts us with evangelical consolation, in which we know it is written: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.” For if the word of truth is true—indeed, because the word of truth is true—then, since you suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, blessedness will set a limit to such persecution [Col. 0167C]. Rejoice, therefore, that we too may rejoice with you, because you have been found worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus Christ. You discharge His ministry on earth in such a way that you may deserve to be received in heaven into the fellowship of Him whom you laudably serve in that ministry, He Himself declaring in the Gospel: “Father, I desire that where I am, there my minister also may be.” Glory with the Apostle in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, rejoicing if what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings is supplied in your body, because if you suffer with Him, you shall reign with Him. Knowing, therefore, that each shall receive a reward according to his labor, and that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us, rejoice because in a blessed exchange you will trade earthly things [Col. 0167D] for heavenly and receive everlasting things for temporal ones. Yet concerning the madness of the persecuting count we grieve in some measure inconsolably and mourn from the depths of our heart because, given over to a reprobate mind, he follows Pharaoh in obstinacy and Nero in persecuting the Church.

For since, lifted up in pride, he does not fear to kick against the goad, we fear that, when he has come into the depth of vices, he may despise them and not add amendment so as to rise again, but that the storm may sink him and the pit may press its mouth over him. Therefore we admonish your brotherhood, earnestly exhort you, and by apostolic letters [Col. 0168A] command you not to fail but rather to make progress, not to be moved from the steadfastness of your mind but instead to persevere therein, fearing not what man may do to you, since you have God as your helper. Stand as you have hitherto stood for the liberty of the Church, set yourself as a wall of defense for it, do not yield to those attacking from the other side, but advance against them manfully, prepared, if necessary, to lay down your life for the sheep.] [Note: Raynaldus ends here.]

We nevertheless believe that the Lord will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to endure, but will make a way of escape in the temptation. He will calm the king’s mind concerning you and your Church, so that, receiving you into the fullness of royal favor, he may restore to you not only the regalian rights and confiscated goods but may inflict worthy punishment upon [Col. 0168B] your persecutor unless he repents. Whatever the aforesaid king may do, the Apostolic See will not fail you; it regards your cause as its own and grieves that ecclesiastical liberty is being violated. We write to our venerable brothers . . . . the Archbishop of Sens, . . . . the Bishop of Chartres, and . . . . the Bishop of Châlons, and to the king as well as the count mentioned, as may be apparent to your inspection from the copies of letters enclosed and sent to you with these presents.

Given at Anagni . . . . in the sixth year.

CLIII. TO . . . . THE ABBOT OF ST PETER OF THE PO; . . . . THE PRIOR OF ST GABRIEL; AND . . . . THE PROVOST OF ST LUCY OF CREMONA. That they may accept the resignation of A., Abbot of St Thomas of Cremona. (Anagni, twelfth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 0168C]

On behalf of our beloved son A., Abbot of St Thomas of Cremona, humble petition has been made to us that, since he is so worn down by weakness and old age that he is deemed incapable of governing the abbey, we should deign to accept his resignation. Therefore, wishing to provide both for that abbot and for the church itself, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, going to that monastery, if it is immediately subject to us, as is said, and if the same abbot wishes to resign—not compelled by force or fear, but led by his own will—you shall, supported by our authority, procure the acceptance of his resignation, provided that this is advantageous to the abbey’s welfare. You shall direct the convent to endeavor to provide the same abbey, by canonical election, with a suitable person. And if not all . . . . two, etc.

[Col. 0168D] Given at Anagni, twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

CLIV. [Note: [Col. 0167D] This is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book IV, title 13, “Concerning one who has carnally known the female relative [Col. 0168D] of his wife or betrothed,” chapter 9. There it is said to have been addressed to the Archbishop of Magdeburg. Passages found there are enclosed here in brackets. Various readings are also given.] TO . . . . THE ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG. Concerning the penance to be imposed upon one who had carnally known his wife’s sister. (Anagni, seventh day before the Ides of October.)

[Conrad [Note: In the Decretal, “E.” in place of “the bearer . . . . declared”], a layman and bearer of these presents, coming to the Apostolic See, declared to us in humble confession [Col. 0169A] that, formerly, in the time of his childhood, upon the advice of friends, he had sworn that he would take a certain girl as wife as soon as he reached lawful age. The girl’s father, after this agreement had been mutually confirmed by the obligation of sureties, received him into his own house and brought him up together with the girl. But afterward [Note: The Decretal reads “then,” and below omits the passages distinguished by italics], having acquired intimacy with the entire household through long association, he carnally joined himself, by the prompting of the seducer of the human race, to the sister of the girl whose husband he had sworn to become. When the age arrived at which he could fulfill what he had sworn, his friends, unaware of his offense, pressed him to carry out the marriage. Conscious of what he had done, he told certain of them what he had committed with the girl’s sister. But since they did not at all [Col. 0169B] believe his words and sharply rebuked him, [he, overcome by their counsel [Note: The Decretal reads, “at last overcome by the insistence of his friends,” and below omits “lest . . . . wander”]], took as wife the woman whom he had sworn to marry; and, after the wedding had been celebrated, whenever opportunity presented itself, he knew both women carnally.

But although he was accused of this before you, he could not be convicted and would not confess his offense. Now, however, having returned to his heart and repenting of what he has done, he seeks counsel for his salvation, lest, like a horse and mule which have no understanding, he seem to wander into peril of his soul. Therefore, since the Apostle commands abstention not only from evil but also from every appearance of evil, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, after a suitable penance has been imposed upon the aforesaid man [Note: The Decretal reads “E.”] for so enormous an offense, [Col. 0169C] you give him counsel, healthfully admonishing and inducing him henceforth to abstain from both women.

Given at Anagni, seventh day before the Ides of October.

CLV. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1203, § 19.] TO THE KING OF HUNGARY. He exhorts him to assist his brother Duke Andrew in fulfilling his crusading vow. (Anagni, Nones of November.)

Our beloved son, the nobleman A., duke and your brother, has reported to our hearing that, when your father B., of illustrious memory, was prevented by death from personally fulfilling the vow which he had made, he entrusted its fulfillment to the same duke, so that when dead he might render to the Lord through his son what he himself had vowed while alive; and he caused the sign of the cross to be laid upon his shoulders. Although the duke intended to fulfill his father’s vow and carry out his command with filial devotion, yet because, through sins demanding it, a cause of dissension has arisen between your serenity and himself, he has not yet carried out his purpose, particularly since lack of funds has held him back. Although we know that your highness requires no small expenditure [Col. 0170A] to fulfill the paternal vow, nevertheless, at his urgent request, we admonish and earnestly exhort your magnificence that, unless perhaps he remains in the kingdom after you by prudent deliberation, you assist him suitably, according to your means and his need, with expenses for completing his pilgrimage vow. Extend the hand of royal liberality toward him in such a manner that he is thereby moved still more toward devotion to you and we may deservedly commend your liberality.

Given at Anagni, Nones of November.

CLVI. [Note: [Col. 0170D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 19.] TO THE NOBLEMAN, DUKE A. He confirms the agreement of peace concluded between him and his brother the king. (Anagni, Nones of November.)

[Col. 0170B]

Customarily, etc., as far as “assent.” We confirm by apostolic authority the agreement concluded between you and our most beloved son in Christ . . . . the illustrious King of Hungary, through the hands of our beloved son G. . . . . [Note: See letter 60 of book V, note.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, then legate of the Apostolic See, and afterward confirmed by him. Since it was prudently made without deceit, voluntarily accepted by both parties, peacefully observed until now, and is more fully contained in the letters of the same cardinal, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, Nones of November.

CLVII. [Note: [Col. 0170D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 19.] TO THE SAME PERSON. He receives him into his protection. (Anagni, Nones of November.)

[Col. 0170C]

Since, at the very beginning of your youth, both by your father’s command and by your own vow, you have dedicated the first fruits of your knighthood to Jesus Christ, you ought not to be excluded from that grace which the Apostolic See has granted to all who are signed with the cross. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, moved by your merits and inclined by your prayers, since, having made a vow of pilgrimage, you have resolved to set out in aid of the Holy Land, we receive your person, together with all the goods which you now lawfully possess, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; decreeing that, from the time when you begin your pilgrimage until certain knowledge is obtained of your return or [Col. 0170D] death, your land and all your goods shall remain secure under our special protection and that of all the prelates of God’s Church. We further will that, if meanwhile the Lord deigns to grant you a male heir, he shall succeed you in your duchy and, until he reaches lawful age, shall be especially fostered under the protection of the Apostolic See. Therefore let no one violate this protection and constitution, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the Nones of November.

CLVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF AUGSBURG. He grants them H., *vicedominus* of the church of Regensburg, as bishop. [Note: [Col. 0171D] See letter 99 of the fifth book, on the same subject.] (Anagni, 31 October.)

[Col. 0171A]

After the election which you had once made of our beloved son H., *vicedominus* of the church of Regensburg, had been annulled—as it ought by law to have been annulled, because he was not born of lawful marriage—although, according to the testimony of your letters, he was of approved and blameless reputation and was so advanced in learning, character, and age that, on account of the evident benefit and urgent necessity of your church, you had proceeded too hastily in the said election, fearing that delay might produce dissension, [Col. 0171B] and dissension bring injury upon the church: we dealt mercifully after judgment. Although you deserved both to be deprived of the power of election and to be suspended from ecclesiastical benefices for three years, nevertheless, lest that church should suffer grave harm through want of a ruler, we patiently permitted the person named—whom we had learned to be prudent and discerning—to administer both the church and the diocese of Augsburg, not as your elect, but as your fellow canon. And if you should again agree in requesting him from the Apostolic See, you were to take care humbly to present yourselves before our venerable brethren S., archbishop of Mainz, the bishop of Würzburg of blessed memory, and our beloved son the abbot of Salem.

[Col. 0171C]

We gave them instructions diligently to investigate whatever was to be investigated, both concerning the condition of the said church and concerning the merits and birth of the person named; and, faithfully committing everything to writing, to send it to our hearing within four months, together with some of your number who should hasten to us to receive a judgment of equity.

But after the aforesaid bishop of Würzburg had been killed by sons of perdition, and after the same abbot of Salem had entrusted his functions to the aforesaid archbishop because, being occupied with other matters, he could not attend to these, you sent to the presence of your metropolitan two of your fellow canons and our beloved son, the provost of St George of Augsburg. In the presence [Col. 0171D] of our venerable brother, the bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, he took care to examine the petition laid before him, as his letters sent to us stated.

Thus, as he informed us by those same letters, sufficient proof was furnished to him that the said *vicedominus* was fit for episcopal government, so far as man is permitted to know, unless the aforementioned impediment should prevent it. Yet, because he knew him to be a son of obedience and ready to obey the Church’s commands, he humbly requested that a dispensation be granted him, in view of the disturbance of the times, the desolation of the church, and the discernment of the person. [Col. 0172A] He added in the margin of his letter that at this time no one besides him could be appointed to govern the church of Augsburg without great loss and damage to it.

Our legate likewise instructed us concerning the course of the affair and, agreeing with the archbishop of Mainz, humbly urged us to grant a dispensation. You too humbly requested it by your letters and messengers; and the abbot of Salem, who had entrusted his functions to the archbishop of Mainz, sought the same with insistence.

Therefore we, observing that the archbishop of Mainz had not fully informed us concerning the impediment of birth, required and received, through our brethren, an oath from our beloved sons R., archdeacon, F., our subdeacon and your fellow canon, and Master L., who had come as messenger with them, that they would bear testimony to [Col. 0172B] the truth. Having sworn, they testified that, as they had heard from the elders of the churches of Regensburg and Augsburg, and as they themselves also believed to be true, the said *vicedominus* had been conceived in simple fornication, while his father was constituted in minor orders. They said that this was more fully evident from the fact that he was afterward ordained subdeacon. His mother, although she had been placed in a cloister to be maintained according to the custom of the country, and at last had assumed the monastic habit, had at that time neither married anyone nor made a vow of chastity.

Having therefore taken counsel with our brethren on these matters, on account of the urgent necessity and evident benefit of the church of Augsburg, and the discernment and [Col. 0172C] uprightness of the person named—concerning whom our aforesaid legate, the archbishop of Mainz, and many others thought it praiseworthy to bear testimony—we grant you a favour from the customary kindness of the Apostolic See. Dispensing with the said *vicedominus*, we grant him to you as shepherd, saving in all things the right both of the archbishop and of the church of Mainz. We therefore admonish your discretion and exhort you earnestly, and by these apostolic letters command you, that henceforth you render him the reverence and honour due to him as your shepherd, humbly receive his wholesome admonitions and commands, and inviolably observe them.

Given at Anagni, 31 October.

CLIX. [Note: [Col. 0172D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 69.] TO P., BISHOP ELECT OF PALERMO, [Note: [Col. 0172D] See letter 39 of the fifth book.] A MEMBER OF THE ROYAL HOUSEHOLD. He warmly commends him because, amid the tumults of the world and kingdom then raging, he had remained faithful to pope and king. (Anagni.)

[Col. 0172D]

If, as the evil of the day requires, the life of man is upon the earth such that he finds no rest in a troubled time; if, in the valley of tears and weeping, he drenches his bed with tears, nor does the pupil of his weeping eye remain silent: although we grieve with those who grieve and cannot but suffer with those who suffer, [Col. 0173A] yet we are neither greatly moved nor astonished. For the testimony of Truth cannot be untrue: it foretold wrath coming upon the whole world; it foretold not only that nation would rise against nation and that a man’s enemies would be those of his own household, but also that the powers of heaven would be shaken at the end of time. We now see this almost literally fulfilled in Sicily.

For behold: there not only does nation rise against nation, but brother is armed against brother, so that a familiar friend harms more grievously than an enemy. While there is no fidelity among the allies of the kingdom, the powers of heaven are shaken against one another: the greater prelates of the churches and the princes of the realm, who seemed to be pillars, waver; they do not stand in the day of the Lord, nor do they oppose those rising [Col. 0173B] from the other side. Rather, yielding—or indeed failing—they do not fear to take sides with those who strive to divide the royal tunic under the royal name, seeking not what belongs to the king but what belongs to themselves.

Since, therefore, a kingdom is divided against itself, it is no wonder if it is laid waste and house falls upon house, since its domestic dissension contributes more to its desolation than the attack of all the rest. Although almost all have turned aside and become altogether useless, and scarcely is there anyone who does good, not even one, yet we rejoice that the integrity of your faithfulness and the constancy of your devotion are proclaimed throughout all the kingdom of Sicily and publicly celebrated from sea to sea: that you have grown stronger under persecution and have not yielded to your persecutor.

For although the enemy has said: “I shall pursue [Col. 0173C] and overtake; I shall divide [Note: [Col. 0173D] Thus in the copy.] the spoils; I shall kill with the sword, and my hand shall rule”; although the wicked have plotted unjustly to kill the righteous man, nevertheless your faith burned against them all the more fiercely as their anger burned more fiercely against you. Thus you regarded their blows as arrows of children, and counted as nothing not only their tongues but also their hands.

For he who prayed that Peter’s faith should not fail raised Peter up lest he should be submerged in the waves of this sea; and still, unless he be of little faith, he will enable him to tread the swelling storms of the waves with dry and unharmed foot. If, then, those who hate you without cause mock you and repay evil for good; if it is said, “Where is your God?” do not heed the spells of enchanters, nor consent to their seductions, [Col. 0173D] who strive to bewitch your mind in order to make your glory void.

Let your glory be like that of the king’s daughters, inwardly adorned with golden fringes; let your conscience bear testimony for you before God; and we also, his unworthy vicars, who take account of your labours and sufferings, propose to respond to you according to your merits. Do not believe that we regret having made man, since you furnish us no cause for repentance; nor that we wish to turn backward and take away what we propose but defer. It is deferred rather in order that it may be bestowed more gloriously at an opportune time. For beside [Col. 0174A] the rivers of Babylon the instruments are hung up, and the Lord’s song is not to be sung in a strange—or, more truly, estranged—land.

We therefore admonish your brotherhood and exhort you earnestly, and by apostolic letters command you that, persevering in the strength of your accustomed fidelity, you may not fail but rather advance: so that crushed spices may give forth a stronger fragrance, gold may be tested better, and proved more truly in the furnace. We hope in him who does not forsake those who hope in him, that he who guards Israel will neither sleep nor slumber, nor leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous. Rather, he will comfort his servants, making a way of escape in temptation; and after tears and weeping you shall be clothed with joy and exultation.

But if, perhaps through the demands of sins, the enemy should become so strong [Col. 0174B] that you could neither resist him nor stand against him without danger, we do not deny that you may find a means of saving your life without injury to your fidelity and faith.

Given at Anagni.

CLX. [Note: [Col. 0173D] Raynaldus praises this letter and prints a small fragment, under the year 1203, § 50. The few passages printed by him are enclosed here near the end in brackets [Col. 0174D].] TO THE ABBOTS OF NEUBURG AND SALEM. [Note: [Col. 0174D] See letter 99 of the fifth book.] That they may deter the duke of Swabia from supporting Liupold, intruded into the see of Mainz. [Note: [Col. 0174D] See letter 14 of the fifth book.] (Anagni, 27 October.)

We have hitherto borne patiently the excess of unheard-of presumption which the nobleman Philip, duke of Swabia, has attempted in injury to the Apostolic See: in so far as lay in his power, transferring Liupold, formerly bishop of Worms, to the church of Mainz, and supporting him in his reckless [Col. 0174C] transgression even after his petition had been rejected by us in a just judgment. We believed that he would correct his error of himself, and would see to removing from it the idol of zeal which he had set up in the temple of God, like the abomination standing in the holy place. Nor should he claim for himself what none of the emperors or princes has hitherto attempted.

For he knows—or could and ought to know—that the Lord has granted to the Apostolic See alone the power of transferring bishops. Therefore he ought not to have put his sickle into our harvest and appropriated our office to himself. Although he has done this until now, we have nevertheless dissimulated and laboured in patience, lest we should appear to be moved against him by the heat of bitterness rather than zeal for righteousness. [Col. 0174D]

But the aforesaid Liupold, because he had presumed too greatly and did not desist from his presumption when admonished, first incurred sentence of excommunication and afterward sentence of deposition. Because, in his obstinacy, he does not observe that sentence, and the duke himself supports him in his obstinacy, according to the judgments of the holy Fathers he incurs both the brand and the guilt of error.

Still wishing to show deference to the duke, we have thought fit to admonish him through you, in case, guided by sounder counsel, he may desist from such presumption, cease to oppose himself to God and the Church, [Col. 0175A] and no longer irreverently assail the Apostolic See, which at least by reason of Christianity he ought humbly to revere.

We therefore admonish your discretion and exhort you earnestly; and, commanding by apostolic letters, we strictly enjoin upon you in virtue of holy obedience that you personally approach him, admonish him attentively on our behalf, and effectively induce him henceforth to give no aid or favour to the said Liupold. Instead, let him reject him as deposed and avoid him as excommunicated. Otherwise, [inform him that we shall take care, in fulfilment of our office, to lay our hand more heavily upon him and his land—perhaps more heavily than he expects—since we ought no longer to endure this in patience.] Whatever you find with him, notify us as soon as you can by letter and trustworthy messenger. And if not both … let the other, etc.

Given at Anagni, 27 October.

CLXI. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF LISMORE. That they receive M., abbot of St Benedict’s, elected bishop by them. (Anagni, Nones of November.)

Our beloved sons, the archdeacon and certain clerics of Lismore, coming to the Apostolic See with your letters, reported to us that after F., your former bishop, had resigned the government of the bishopric into the hands of our beloved son J., [Note: [Col. 0175D] See letter 83 of the fifth book.] priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill and then legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0175C] you assembled together and, having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, unanimously agreed upon our venerable brother M., now bishop but then abbot of St Benedict’s of the Cistercian Order, choosing him as your bishop. This was although your church together with its diocese was occupied by the bishop of Waterford.

Having been made certain, both by oaths and by documents, concerning the procedure of the canonical election and the fitness of the person elected by you, we confirmed his election. After conferring upon him the gift of consecration, we thought fit to send him back to your [Col. 0175D] church with the fullness of our favour. Therefore by apostolic letters we command and enjoin you humbly to receive him as bishop, as the father and shepherd of your souls; to render him the reverence and obedience due; and to observe his wholesome admonitions and … thus without contradiction. Otherwise, we would cause any sentence which he might reasonably pronounce against rebels and disobedient persons to be held ratified.

Given at Anagni, Nones of November.

CLXII. [Note: [Col. 0175D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 64.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CASHEL, AND THE BISHOPS OF DUBLIN AND FERNS. That they pronounce sentence of anathema against the bishop of Waterford. [Note: [Col. 0176D] See the preceding letter.] (Anagni, Nones of November.)

[Col. 0176A]

We have learned of a scandalous and utterly detestable affair against the bishop of Waterford: that, when our venerable brother, now bishop of Lismore but then bishop-elect, was preparing to travel to the Apostolic See, the bishop of Waterford presumed, by means of prepared ambushes, violently to seize and wickedly despoil him; and, laying hands upon him himself even to the shedding of blood, caused him, when placed in prison and bound in fetters, to be afflicted with harsh beatings. [Col. 0176B]

Since we can neither can nor ought to pass over under dissimulation the audacity of such great presumption—or rather the wickedness of so immense a rash act—and since these things are known to us and notorious to you, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin you, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any objection or appeal, to declare that the aforesaid bishop of Waterford and the others who laid rash hands upon that same bishop remain bound by the bond of excommunication until they make suitable satisfaction to the injured party … of your [lacuna], etc., as far as “of absolving.”

Likewise, compel the aforesaid bishop of Waterford by ecclesiastical censure to restore without difficulty to the aforesaid bishop of Lismore, for peaceful possession, the church and diocese of Lismore, which he is said violently to have invaded and occupied; and to make suitable satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted. This is notwithstanding that our beloved son J., priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill and then legate of the Apostolic See, had entrusted the diocese of Lismore to him, since his predecessor had violently invaded it and he himself had most presumptuously continued to occupy it through invasion. [Col. 0176C] If not all, etc. Let two, etc.

Given at Anagni, Nones of November.

CLXIII. [Note: [Col. 0176D]

Bzovius, *Annales*, vol. XIII, p. 99, § 6, mentions this letter and also the following letters 146, 165, 166, and 167.  

Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 55, prints various fragments of it. Passages printed by him are enclosed here in brackets. [Col. 0177D]]

TO THE KING OF THE FRANKS. A reply, because the king had said that in feudal law he was not bound by apostolic commands; with much else concerning peace with the king of England. (Anagni, 31 October.)

[Col. 0176D]

Holding from divine Scripture that “beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things,” we sent our beloved son, the abbot of Casamari, a religious and prudent man, into the regions of Gaul, that he might proclaim to you and to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious J., king of England—since you were at variance with one another—the good of peace; and might insist, in season and out of season, that he either restore a firm reconciliation between those in discord, or at least establish suitable truces, so that in the meantime, through us and other prudent men [Col. 0177A] intervening between you, the full bond of peace might arise between you.

We had confidence in this on the precedent that, when Richard, king of England of illustrious memory, was at war with you, we took care to send to your presence our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the title of St Marcellus, then cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See. You received him gladly on that occasion; and at his first exhortation, that you should make peace or a truce in his hands, you freely confirmed it by your own will. Although the aforesaid king was induced to this only with difficulty, being one who had been seriously injured before he returned from the pilgrimage of the Crucified One, nevertheless, obeying apostolic commands, he concluded with you a truce for five years.

[Col. 0177B]

Moreover, although that abbot had set forth our word in the hearing of your serenity and had publicly announced the cause of his coming, you were unwilling immediately to give him a final answer. Instead, you kept him waiting until the octave of the Assumption of blessed Mary last past, appointing that you would answer him after holding at Meudon … [Note: [Col. 0178D] Thus in the Vatican and Conti copies.] a council of archbishops, bishops, and your other magnates.

When the appointed day came, and both the prelates of the churches and the princes of your kingdom had been called and gathered together, after taking the counsel of some, you answered that by feudal right, and in regard to your man [i.e. vassal; Note: [Col. 0178D] Thus there, likewise.], you were not [Col. 0177C] bound to obey a command or judgment of the Apostolic See, and that an affair pending between kings did not concern us.

Having fully understood the tenor of this answer, we were greatly astonished and troubled that you seemed to have adopted counsel and composed a reply against the authority of the Apostolic See, as though you wished or were able to restrict its jurisdiction. It was expanded in spiritual matters not by man but by God—indeed, more truly, by God-Man—so greatly that it cannot be enlarged further, since fullness admits no addition.

[Would that you had considered more soundly and attended more carefully to the fact that the Apostolic See has hitherto striven to show itself not harmful to you, your forebears, or the kingdom of the Franks, but useful instead. Would that, in the day of good things, you had not forgotten evil things; and, since the outcome of wars is uncertain, had measured the instability of human prosperity not only by its present condition but also by that which may follow it in various ways and for various causes. You should have taken anxious care lest your answer might hereafter be alleged against you or your descendants. We do not say this as though we wished to usurp an undue power or impose anything that does not belong to the authority of our office. For what have we admonished? What have we urged? Anything dishonourable? Anything unjust? Certainly, if we remember rightly, that you should make peace or [Col. 0178A] truces, preserving the justice of both parties. [Col. 0177D]

Although we do not wish to enter into litigation with you about this cause, lest the royal reply obtain force through our silence, we are compelled briefly to answer it. We shall invent nothing against it as though it were our own, but rather bring forth powerful reasons from the treasury of the Holy Spirit.]

That we are bound by the office imposed upon us to proclaim peace, the Psalmist teaches us: “Seek peace,” he says, “and pursue it” (Psalm 33)—that is, pursue it until you find it. And the angels who announced to the shepherds the first tidings of the Lord’s Nativity expressed, in their song of new praise, at the birth of him whose office on earth we exercise, though unworthy, that peace of good will was proclaimed to humankind.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself [Col. 0178B] more expressly carried out in person, as he was about to drink the cup of the Passion, what he had done at his birth through the ministry of angels. For he says to his disciples: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14). And when risen, he first used these words to the apostles: “Peace be with you” (Luke 24); and again I say, “Peace be with you.” Likewise, when he instructed his disciples concerning the manner of preaching, he first commanded them to proclaim peace, saying to them: “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house’; and if a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him” (Luke 10).—“Whoever shall not receive you or hear your words, when you go out, shake the dust from your feet as a testimony [Col. 0178C] against it” (Mark 8). He commands them to go out, so that ecclesiastical communion may be denied to them; and he declares that the dust is to be shaken against those who do not receive words of peace—the dust which, when Moses scattered ashes from the furnace, became a plague of sores throughout all the land of Egypt.

How severe a sentence of censure those who do not receive their words are to suffer at the last judgment Truth itself subsequently shows, declaring not simply but with a certain affirmation: “Amen, I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrites on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matthew 10). By “city” he means its citizens, from whom he does not except kings themselves.

Furthermore, no person of sound mind doubts that it belongs to us to judge matters that concern the salvation or damnation of the soul. Is it not deserving of eternal damnation and destructive of eternal salvation to foster discord; to attack members of the household of faith; to destroy religious houses; to expose to the pleasure of plunderers the goods of religious men assigned to necessities and useful purposes; to oppress virgins consecrated to God; to force those who, forgetting what lies behind and continually stretching toward what lies before, had begun to serve the Lord, to turn back and again involve themselves in secular affairs; to afflict the poor, impoverish the powerful, shed human blood, [Col. 0179A] and profane churches?]

Certainly, if the word of the Lord were bound in our mouth concerning this, we should deservedly be called dumb dogs unable to bark; nor without reason would the blood of so many thousands of people be required from our hands. Does not the Lord indeed speak to us in the Prophet who was among the priests of Anathoth: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up, destroy, scatter, build, and plant” (Jeremiah 1)? Are we now not to pluck up the shoots of vices in order to plant the seedlings of virtues?

Again, when we see monasteries and other pious places entrusted in a special way to our protection not merely laid waste but almost entirely destroyed; when we understand that the sons of the Church, who, abandoning Martha’s office, had chosen to sit at the Lord’s feet with Mary, and “to be lowly in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” [source abbreviated *m. q. h. i. t. p.*; Note: [Col. 0179D] Thus in the copy.], are recalled from their pious purpose through the disturbances of war and the wickedness of combatants—if we refuse to rise against them and put ourselves forward as a wall for the house of the Lord, shall we not be called hirelings rather than shepherds? For, when we see wolves coming to scatter and slaughter the sheep, we flee by withdrawing protection, as though seeking milk and wool from them and caring nothing for their salvation. [Col. 0179B]

[Hear, finally, dearest son, a word not ours but rather of the Word which was in the beginning with God and which at last was made flesh and dwelt among us, declaring in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you two or [Col. 0179C] three witnesses, that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses. And if he does not hear them, tell the Church; and if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matthew 18).

Behold, the king of England, your brother, complains—not your brother by kinship of flesh, but by union of faith—that you sin against him and have stretched out, and continue to stretch out, your hands to his injury. At one time he rebuked you between you and himself alone, when by letters and by spoken word, not once only but frequently, he admonished you to desist from injuring him. He also brought forward not only two or three witnesses but many magnates, that they might restore the bonds of broken peace between you and him, and intervene with you that you should cease from wronging him. But because through this [Note: [Col. 0180D] Thus in the copy; in Raynaldus, “hitherto.”]] he achieved absolutely nothing with [Col. 0179D] your highness, he reported to the Church, according to the evangelical word, that you had sinned against him.

The Church, however, preferred to deal with you by fatherly affection rather than judicial power. Therefore, through the aforesaid abbot, she did not rebuke your serenity authoritatively but kindly admonished you to cease from injuring your brother and to agree with him either upon the bonds of true peace or upon suitable truces. What then remains henceforth, except that, if you do not hear the Church, as hitherto you have not heard it, she must regard you as a heathen and tax collector—something we say with grief—and, after the first and second correction, [Col. 0180A] avoid you? For if we must offend either you or God, we prefer to appease God by your offence rather than please a man by offence against the divine King.

But perhaps you will say that you do not sin against him; yet he will reply to the contrary that you do sin. What, then, shall we do at such a point of contradiction? Shall we, after truth has been more fully investigated and known, fail to proceed according to the Lord’s command? Shall we disregard the slaughter of bodies and the destruction of souls, fail to proclaim their wickedness to the wicked, and refrain from restraining violent persons from violence?]

Therefore, lest we seem to depart from the evangelical command, we admonish your royal serenity and exhort you in the Lord, giving wholesome counsel: do not consent to sinners who flatter you, [Col. 0180B] nor let the oil of the sinner make your head fat. Rather, lend a ready and kindly ear to our admonitions, which proceed from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. In accordance with the admonition of the aforesaid abbot—or rather ours, indeed God’s—either restore firm peace with the aforesaid king or enter into suitable truces.

For if perhaps you assert that you do not sin against the said king but rather exercise your right against him, while he complains that you grievously sin against him and exercise not right but wrong against him, then, lest in this matter of uncertainty we seem either to rush into a human judgment or to neglect a divine command, humbly permit the aforesaid abbot, together with our venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges, [Col. 0180C] to investigate the matter summarily. This is not by reason of the fief, judgment concerning which belongs to you, but on account of sin, the censure of which belongs to us beyond doubt. Thus, once the truth is known, if the complaint of the aforesaid king is supported by reason, you, who sin against your brother, shall be compelled by the Church’s censure, according to the evangelical word, to cease from injuring him. Otherwise the complaint shall be rejected as unjust, and the Church, if necessary, shall assist you in your justice.

But if the words of the Apostolic See, your mother, cannot soften you to this—she who still deals with you, and has hitherto dealt with you, gently—then you shall feel the severity of a father’s scourge, who has resolved henceforth not to spare the rod out of love for his son. [Col. 0180D] Whatever may result, since we do not fear man in opposition to God, nor, if necessary, avoid suffering persecution for righteousness’ sake or flee scandal to the prejudice of truth, we shall fulfil the duty of our office through the aforesaid abbot.

Given at Anagni, 31 October, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CLXIV. [Note: [Col. 0181D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 58.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. That he publish the sentence of excommunication against those who take up arms against the king of England, including against the king of France. (Anagni, 31 October.)

[Col. 0181A]

“Holding from divine Scripture,” etc., as in letter 163, down to “to the prejudice of truth,” we gave instructions to the same abbot that, unless the king himself, when admonished by him, does what we urge concerning the restoration of peace or establishment of truces, he shall publicly forbid on our behalf, under penalty of strict anathema, anyone to presume to take up arms against the aforesaid king of England, who humbly offers peace and truces, and against his land. Should anyone presume the contrary, let him know that he is bound by sentence of excommunication, and that his whole household is subjected to interdict, so that, apart from the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, no divine office may be celebrated for them nor ecclesiastical sacrament administered, nor may ecclesiastical burial be given to those who die. [Col. 0181B]

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood and strictly enjoin upon you in virtue of obedience that, after the said abbot has carried out this apostolic command, you solemnly publish his sentence—or rather, truly, ours—with bells rung and candles lighted, on every Sunday and feast day; and see that it is inviolably observed. Know that, should you act otherwise, we shall severely punish your disobedience.

[Col. 0181C]

Given at Anagni, 31 October, in the sixth year.

In the same manner, to the chapter of Rheims and the suffragans of the church of Rheims.

Likewise, to the archbishop of Bourges and his suffragans.

CLXV. [Note: [Col. 0181D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, § 57.] TO THE ABBOT OF CASAMARI. That he intervene for peace or truce between the kings; failing this, that he excommunicate. (Anagni, 31 October.)

We received the letter which your discretion sent us with becoming kindness, and we have carefully noted what you communicated in it. What we write to our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, and to our venerable brethren the archbishops of Sens and Bourges, and to our beloved sons, the chapter of Reims and the suffragans of the churches of Reims, Sens, and Bourges, may be seen from the open letters which we are directing to those prelates. We therefore admonish your discretion, earnestly exhort you, and by these apostolic letters command you that you continue to intervene with that king, both personally and through those prelates and other prudent men—not merely once, but repeatedly—that, according to the tenor of the letters which we address to him, he establish a firm peace with our dearest son in Christ, J., king of the English, or enter into suitable truces. But if, though repeatedly requested, he should perhaps be unable to be induced to this, publicly, under pain of strict anathema, etc., in nearly the same manner, down to “burial.” Therefore execute the apostolic mandate in this matter—as we trust in your discretion—in such a way that we may deservedly commend your diligence and obedience.

Given at Anagni, 2 Kalends of November [31 October], in the sixth year.

CLXVI. [Note: [Col. 0181D] The same, ibid.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES AND THE ABBOT OF CASEMARII. That they are to investigate the complaint of the kings. (Anagni, 2 Kalends of November.)

What we write to our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, you will learn more fully from the letters which we direct to those prelates. Moreover, son abbot, we have thought fit fully to explain in our sealed letters, which we send you on this subject, how you ought to proceed in the affair of the kings; therefore there is no need to repeat the same things so often. We therefore admonish your discretion and earnestly exhort you, and by apostolic writings command you under obedience that, since the aforesaid king of France has at least granted suitable truces for the purpose of determining in the meantime whether the complaint of the king of the English and his defence are just—not by reason of the fief, judgment concerning which belongs to him, but on account of sin, the censure of which unquestionably belongs to us—you shall, setting aside every favour and fear and without respect of persons, take steps to investigate this matter. If you find that his complaint is just, you, son abbot, shall proceed in accordance with the form of our letters, without appeal; otherwise, you shall prudently and patiently assist the king of France himself, should it be necessary, in obtaining his right.

Given as above.

CLXVII. [Note: [Col. 0182D] Raynaldus prints this letter, though mutilated, under the year 1203, §57. What is found in his text is here enclosed in brackets.] TO J., KING OF THE ENGLISH. The cause of the war begun against him by the king of France is explained, and the pope rebukes him because he ought to appear before that king, being his liege man. (Anagni, 2 Kalends of November.)

Let your royal conscience teach you what is due to your merits; it knows fully that in many things you have shown yourself ungrateful for our favour, that you have not repaid us according to what we have bestowed upon you, and that you have not taken care, as you ought, to honour the Roman Church according to the custom of your forefathers and predecessors. Yet, because we consider more what befits us than what you do, responding not to your merits but fulfilling the duty of the pastoral office, and believing that henceforth you will endeavour to show yourself still more obedient and devoted to us and to the Roman Church, we have proceeded, as far as we could honourably do so, in the affair pending between you and our dearest son in Christ, Ph., the illustrious king of France—indeed, more than some would have thought possible—as our beloved son, the abbot of Casemarii, our messenger, who knows the truth of this matter more fully, may inform your serenity.

But [we wish you to know that the king says that not he, but rather you, are guilty of the discord which has arisen, and affirms that you have supplied not merely the occasion but the cause of the dissension. For he recently informed us through his letters and messengers that, although you had inflicted no small losses and very many injuries upon the church of Saint Martin of Tours—which recognizes that whatever it possesses in temporal matters comes from him—and although your men had killed one of that church’s men, when you were repeatedly requested to make satisfaction, you successively sought and received three or four postponements. Although the king himself always sent his messengers on the appointed day, he was never able to obtain satisfaction from you; indeed, by such delays you kept his mind in suspense for more than a year.

Moreover, when you had, without cause and at your own mere will, taken from men belonging to his fief their castles and lands, he, as their superior, moved by the complaint of the despoiled, ordered you, not only once but often, to make satisfaction. Although you promised to do so, you did not; rather, you further burdened those already aggrieved. He endured this for more than a year, seeking and awaiting satisfaction. And when, after taking counsel with his barons and men, he fixed for you a definite term for appearing before him, so that he might do without delay whatever justice should dictate, you nevertheless neither went on the appointed day nor sent an advocate, though you were his liege man; instead, you wholly despised his command.

Thereafter he personally met with you and orally warned you concerning these matters, since he had no desire to wage war against you if you would conduct yourself toward him as your obligation required. But when you would not make satisfaction even then, although, upon the counsel of his barons and men, he had renounced fealty to you, he nevertheless, once war had begun, sent four of his knights to you, wishing through them to ascertain whether you would make amends for what you had committed against him. Otherwise, he wished you to know that from that time he would make a pact against you with your men wherever he could. But you hid yourself from those seeking you and took advantage of your absence, so that they could in no way see you. Your men, however, meeting the searchers, announced that they knew beforehand what the king himself had enjoined upon them and that they could not speak with you.

He further added that at that time he had entered into alliance with none of your men and had received homage from none of them; but afterwards he allied himself with certain of them and admits that he received homage from some, which he asserts must be imputed to your contumacy. Nevertheless, he is still prepared, if you request it, to give you the full measure of justice in his court, provided sufficient security is received that you will abide by the judgment of the court. We therefore admonish your royal serenity and exhort you in the Lord to devote yourself to the things that make for peace. Not only receive peace or truces if they should perhaps be offered to you, but do not be ashamed to offer them yourself. Take diligent care, moreover, lest, while you claim that the said king wrongs you, you yourself rather be found to wrong him and withhold from him the reverence and honour due to him. For, once the truth is known, just as we support you in your right, so we could not fail to support him in his justice.]

We earnestly commend to your serenity our beloved son S. of Fossanova, canon of York, your messenger, since he has employed diligent care with us in your affairs.

Given at Anagni, 2 Kalends of November [31 October], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CLXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0183D] See Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 100, §7. This letter is cited by Malingre (*Antiquities of Paris*, p. 452).] TO THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-VICTOR [Note: [Col. 0183D] At this time the abbey of Saint-Victor was governed by John I, commonly called “the German”; for he was born in the diocese of Trier, whence as a young man he came to Paris. There, after some time, he joined the Victorine community under Abbot Garin; and finally, after the death of Absalon—on whom see the note to Letter XLI of Book III—he was named abbot in 1203. He administered the Victorine house for twenty-six years. The Victorine Annals record his death in 1229, after he had shortly before voluntarily resigned office. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 675.] AND SAINTE-GENEVIÈVE [Note: [Col. 0184D] Book III, Letter XLV, note.] Reconciles a crusader, the count of Eu, who had cast off the cross so as not to go to the Holy Land. (Anagni, 2 Ides of November.)

[Col. 0184C]

When one who is besprinkled with the stain of spiritual leprosy is removed from the midst of the faithful and placed outside the camp, lest the Lord’s flock be defiled by his contagion, he is not cast out to everlasting shame but to a shame that brings glory [Note: [Col. 0184D] Thus in the copy.], so that the transgressor may return to his heart and present himself to the priest, to be restored by the priest’s judgment to the bosom of Mother Church. For Peter’s sword is not drawn for the destruction of the offender, but so that, with his right ear cut off, the servant may become Malchus: that is, that he may govern and direct himself in the path of God’s commandments.

Accordingly, although the nobleman . . . count of Eu, was delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh and separated from the fellowship of the faithful because he laid aside the sign of the cross which he had fastened to his shoulders before setting out to aid the Holy Land, nevertheless, because he has returned to his senses and offers to obey the commands of the Church, return to the camps of God ought not be barred to him. For he was excluded from them in order that, moved at least by shame, he might amend what he had done wrong. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after receiving from him sufficient security in accordance with the Church’s form concerning the matters for which he incurred the snare of excommunication, you grant him the benefit of absolution, enjoining upon him that he render to the Lord what he promised by fulfilling his vow of pilgrimage in aid of the Holy Land. But if he should perhaps excuse himself plausibly, let him not delay to communicate his excuses to us, under the testimony of your letters, so that he may execute without contradiction the command which has proceeded from us.

Given at Anagni, 2 Ides of November [12 November], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CLXIX. [Note: [Col. 0185D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §67.] TO THE . . . ARCHDEACON, THE . . . ARCHPRIEST, AND THE ENTIRE CHAPTER OF THE CHURCH OF GARGANO. Receives them under the protection of Saint Peter. (Anagni, 17 Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0185B] The administration of the governance entrusted to us compels us, and the office of piety admonishes us, to extend the gaze of our consideration over the whole body of the Church and to employ careful concern and diligence lest God’s holy churches be harassed by the undue vexations of certain persons. Thus, having been appointed by the providence of heavenly disposition to govern the universal Church, we may appear to labour with pastoral care for the condition of each individual church.

Your representatives formerly humbly petitioned us to provide, by apostolic protection, that you might not be wearied contrary to justice by anyone in matters concerning the dignities of your church—namely, the archdeaconry and archpriesthood—the customary and canonical nomination and presentation to them, and the other ancient and reasonable customs of your church. Therefore, wishing henceforth to provide for you in these matters with paternal concern, by the authority of the present letters we strictly forbid anyone to be permitted unduly to harass you or that church concerning the aforesaid dignities and the honourable customs hitherto observed. Therefore let no one . . . [violate] our prohibition, etc.

Given at Anagni, 17 Kalends of December [15 November].

CLXX. [Note: [Col. 0185D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, §64, but wrongly says that it was addressed to the bishop of Waterford, and gives an entirely different subject.] TO THE . . . BISHOP OF FANO [Note: [Col. 0185D]

This was Monaldus, concerning whom Ughellus writes as follows, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 710:

“XIV. Monaldus attended the Roman council under Alexander III in 1179. He witnessed the grant made in 1195 by Emperor Henry VI to Berard, archdeacon of Ascoli. He was present at the consecration of the church of Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana in 1197. The same M., bishop of Fano, is so named in a letter of Innocent III, dated 1204, 5 Kalends of March [25 February], to the prior of Saint Sophia at Fano.”

We shall shortly print that letter in Book VII, no. XXVII; but it concerns there the church of Saint Stephen, not Saint Sophia.]

Concerning his disobedience: that he desist from harassing the prior of Saint Stephen at Fano. (Anagni, Ides of November.)

[Col. 0185D] If you considered, as you ought, how greatly you are bound to the Roman Church and how you are subject to none through an intermediary beneath us, you would perhaps conduct yourself more moderately in your transgressions and would not presume to kick against us. We can restrain with bit and bridle the jaws of those who do not draw near to us, and, if necessary, heal rebels in Babylon [Note: [Col. 0186D] Thus in the copy.]. Yet our patience and the benignity of the Apostolic See lead you to impenitence; and the more mildly we deal with you, the more violently you rage against those who invoke our name. What we find more grievous is that, in order to nullify our jurisdiction, you set your seat upon the sides of the north, confirming what is weakened by our authority and shamelessly evading our judgment.

Now when formerly our beloved son, the . . . prior of Saint Stephen at Fano, came into our presence and asked us to renew a certain authentic document which Pope C., our predecessor of good memory, had granted to his church, you, wishing to hinder his purpose, informed us by your letters that the document had been obtained by fraud. Although we assigned you a fixed term within which you were to appear before us, either personally or by a sufficient procurator, and set forth and prove your claim, you declined to do so. Through a mere messenger you requested that examination of that document be delegated to judges in your own region. From certain indications we therefore judged you contumacious and condemned you to pay the moderate expenses which that prior had most recently incurred.

Although we commanded you to reimburse him those expenses, you not only despised this command, but presumed to reply to his messenger that you would have him bound to a pillar. You also extended your hands with still greater force to the detriment of the church over which he presides. Moreover, when formerly the same prior had waited a long time for you at the Apostolic See concerning a case pending between you and him, because we then wished to leave the city, he obtained from us a postponement for you. Although for this he ought to have found favour with you, when he presented our letters to you, you deprived him, without reasonable cause, of office and benefice. You commanded all clerics not to speak to him or his brethren, and afterwards caused them to be proclaimed interdicted and excommunicated. Furthermore, at a certain solemn feast you pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him and his brethren before all the people, thundering insulting words against them and threatening them with worse things than before.

Although we ought not to endure these things in the exercise of our power, nevertheless, wishing to show deference to you, we commanded you that, if the facts were as stated, you should publicly declare that sentence wholly null, commanding our beloved son [Note: [Col. 0186D] His name was Nicholas: “From the papers of Romualdus Blancus, of the city of Velletri, we learn that in the fifth year of his pontificate Innocent III granted a privilege of exemption and apostolic protection to the monastery of Avellana and to Nicholas, prior of that place, who had succeeded both Alberic, mentioned under the year 1197, and John, general superior, as prior of Avellana.” Mittarelli, *Annals of the Camaldolese*, vol. IV, p. 190b.] . . . prior of Fonte Avellana, to carry out our command in this matter if you neglected it. He faithfully executed it in default of you and, after learning the truth, declared that sentence null.

But you, persisting in your purpose against the prior, frequently and publicly proclaimed the prior himself excommunicated. Thus, when he returned from us and, having been invited to the funeral of a certain nobleman, wished to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, R. . . priest of Saint Andrew stripped the altar in the sight of clergy and people. You also refused, when one of his canons had gone the way of all flesh, to allow the bells to be rung according to the custom of churches; you prohibited all clerics from attending his funeral; nor did you permit the body of a certain woman, who had chosen burial for herself beside his church, to be buried in its cemetery.

Furthermore, through the parish priests you cause the sick to be forbidden to leave anything to the said church, because if they acted otherwise clerics would not come to their funerals. You prohibited the customary processions to that church. At the beginning of Lent, after publicly crying out before all the people that the prior himself was excommunicated, a leper, a perjurer, and a fornicator, you further presumed to add that he had spent one hundred pounds from his church’s goods at the Apostolic See and had not gained the value of five shillings. On another occasion, assaulting him in the street, you attempted to thrust into his eye the rule which you carried in your hand; but your hand missed, grazing his eyelids. In many other ways too, you have unjustly harassed him and his church.

Since, therefore, the office of apostolate imposed upon us requires us to deliver the poor from the powerful and to assist the needy who have no helper, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood to restore to the same prior his expenses according to the tenor of our sentence; to declare null the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, which our delegate asserted had no force; to make him suitable satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted upon him by you or your agents; and henceforth to desist from harassing him. You shall also exact due punishment from the aforesaid priest, who stripped the altar before the people. Otherwise, you are to present yourself before us by the coming feast of Epiphany to answer for these matters. Should you perhaps fail to execute our command, know that from that time you stand suspended from episcopal office.

Given at Anagni, on the Ides of November [13 November].

CLXXI. TO THE CHAPTER OF GENOA. He approves the translation of the bishop of Bobbio to the archbishopric of Genoa, dispenses him from the rule requiring a journey to the Apostolic See, and sends the pallium. [Note: [Col. 0187D]

Otto, an Alexandrian by birth, was bishop of the church of Bobbio in 1185. He was translated to the archiepiscopal see of Genoa in 1203. Ughellus, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1295.

A record of the same man occurs in the chapter *De arbitrio*; see the *Decretals*, Book I, title 43, “On Arbitrators,” chapter 19, letter to the archbishop of Pisa. Innocent further commissioned him to subject the Genoese to curses unless they restored the gifts sent to him by Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople, which they had taken; on this matter see Raynaldus under the year 1204. Innocent also wrote him various letters. Otto died in 1239, after governing the church of Genoa commendably for thirty-six years. The same work, col. 1221.]

(Anagni, 14 Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0188A]

He who is fairer in form than the children of men, from whose lips the fullness of grace is poured forth, who hates iniquity and loves righteousness, established the see of the Church—namely, his bride—in the prince of the apostles, so that from there virgins may be brought to the king after her, producing for him sons in place of fathers, who may be princes over the earth.

Now since the church of Genoa is a special daughter of the Apostolic See, the man called to govern it had customarily come in person to the Apostolic See, according to the hitherto approved custom, for the gift of confirmation, the benefit of consecration, and the gift of the pallium, so that, as from a parent’s house, the bridegroom might go out to the bride adorned with distinguished dowries.
