Therefore, following the laudable custom hitherto observed, we could have summoned our venerable brother into our presence so that, after his postulation had been examined as it ought to be, he might receive in person, in the customary manner, the benefit of translation and obtain the gift of the pallium while standing before us.

But since we have a special affection for the church and city of Genoa, and regard the person of its archbishop as acceptable in Christ, we have resolved to grant special favour to both. Moreover, lest you and the citizens of Genoa should incur harm in coming to the Apostolic See because of dangers on the roads and the hostility existing between the Romans and the Genoese, while we presently reside outside the city, we have relinquished something of our own claim in this matter in order to defer to your interests. Since, through diligent examination, we have found that all things have been duly done concerning the postulation which you humbly made to us of the person of that archbishop, we have thought fit, in the kindness of the Apostolic See, to approve it. Absolving him entirely from the church of Bobbio, we transfer him to the church of Genoa.

Furthermore, in order to show favour to the archbishop, your church, and the whole city, we send the pallium taken from the body of Saint Peter—the insignia of pontifical office—to our beloved son P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, through our beloved sons Master Angelo, brother of the Cistercian Order, and Tedisius and Oglerius, canons of Genoa, so that in our stead he may confer it upon that archbishop according to the form enclosed under our bull which we send him. We also associate with him for the assignment of the pallium our beloved son M., master of the schools of Genoa, archdeacon of Parma, our subdeacon. Although, at that archbishop’s request, you did not summon him when he was absent, nor was due consideration shown to him in this matter, we—who embrace him with the arms of special affection and desire his honour—have thought fit to honour him in these respects, so that through our favour what you omitted in one respect may be made good to him in another.

We therefore command your whole body by apostolic letters to render the said archbishop due reverence and obedience, obeying his salutary admonitions and statutes, so that his exercise of office may contribute to the salvation of you and of the others subject to him.

Given at Anagni, 14 Kalends of December [18 November].

CLXXII. [Note: [Col. 0189D] Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §67, cites this letter and the following Letter 173. We can give here only the subject of each, because the copy which we had caused to be transcribed from the Conti copy has, by some mischance unknown to us, slipped from our hands. Yet from our notes we know that these letters are found in the Vatican Archive manuscript, folio 89.] TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CARACETO. Confirms the union of that order with the Cistercian Order.

CLXXIII. TO THE SAME. Receives them under the protection of Saint Peter, and enumerates the goods belonging to them.

CLXXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF CHALON-SUR-SAÔNE [Note: [Col. 0189D] Note to Letter 16 of Book V.], THE ABBOT OF CLUNY [Note: [Col. 0190D] Hugh V, formerly abbot of Rading, became abbot of Cluny in 1199, with the consent of his predecessor, who was then at the point of death. He died in 1207. *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, cols. 1626 and 1663.], AND THE PRIOR OF SCILLO, OF THE CARTHUSIAN ORDER. Orders the visitation of the church and territory of Mâcon, which are filled with enormous vices. (Anagni, 10 Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0189C]

If those upon whom the Lord’s cords have fallen diligently considered the meaning of their name and the height of their dignity, they would strive with all their strength to show themselves distinguished before the Lord and to sleep among the allotted portions, that they themselves might become the wings of the silvered dove and the back parts of their body might shine like gold. But some of them—something we report only with grave sorrow—not only deny by their deeds that they are clerics; they do not even acknowledge that they are human beings. They have gone into the land of unlikeness and, being compared to senseless beasts, have become like them while they rot in their own dung.

For whereas they ought to set their face toward Jerusalem, they depart from the East and make for the plain—that is, the land of Shinar. Fleeing from Christ, whose name is East, they range through the plain of licence without obstacle or bridle; dwelling in the land of Shinar, devoted to gluttony (*gastrimargia*) and defiled by the stench of lust, so that fire and sulphur and the blast of storms may be the portion of their cup. In that land they make bricks instead of stones—that is, they practise carnal pleasures—in order to build for themselves a tower of confusion, which their pride may carry to heaven. For the heavenly nation [Note: [Col. 0190D] Thus in the Vatican and Conti copies.]—which began with an injury to the Creator himself and remains to the confusion of the creature—has so seized their hearts that they are not ashamed to commit publicly what laymen would be afraid to do. Thus the prophetic saying, “Be ashamed, Sidon,” says the sea [Note: [Col. 0190D] Thus in the copy.], seems fulfilled to their disgrace.

Indeed, like Sodom, they proclaim their sin and do not hide it; rather, they commit it with clamour, and their guilt is accompanied by licence. Because of them the name of the Lord is often blasphemed among the laity. For, as our venerable brother, the bishop of Mâcon [Note: [Col. 0190D] He has already been mentioned above, in the note to Letter 36 of Book V.], has shown us by his report, the church entrusted to him, to which the Lord had given blessing from the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, has through the wickedness of those dwelling in it so fallen in both respects that no soundness remains in it from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless, so that there is none there who does good—not even one.

Since, therefore, we have been established as watchmen over the house of the Lord and the general care of all the churches rests upon us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, proceeding together to that church, you diligently investigate its condition and take care to inform us by your letters what you find concerning these matters, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed to its correction as ought to be done. But if not all [can be present] . . . you, brother bishop, together with one of them, etc.

Given at Anagni, 10 Kalends of December [22 November], in the sixth year.

CLXXV. TO THE PROVOST OF SAINT STEPHEN OF BROLO. Entrusts to him the case pending between Al. de Daverio and G., a priest of Milan, concerning certain benefices. (Anagni, 7 Kalends of December.)

From letters of Pope C., our predecessor of good memory, which we have examined with our own eyes, we have clearly learned that the same predecessor ordered through our beloved son, the . . . canon of Milan, perpetual silence to be imposed upon Al. de Daverio, because he had produced forged letters in that pope’s name concerning a certain benefice which, by the authority of those letters, he sought to have conferred upon himself in the parish of Brivio. He also ordered Al. to be deprived, by apostolic authority and without obstacle of appeal, of every office and benefice.

But, as our beloved son G. . . priest, appearing in our presence, took care to inform us, the said A., concealing these facts, obtained from us letters to the archbishop of Milan [Note: [Col. 0190D] He has already been mentioned above.] and by their authority brought the priest before him in a suit concerning the aforesaid benefice. When the parties stood in his presence and the said priest asserted before him that he ought in no way to answer Al. concerning that benefice, because silence had been imposed upon Al. in this matter, and asked for a delay in order to prove it, the archbishop refused to grant him one. Therefore the aforesaid priest brought an appeal to the Apostolic See.

Since we neither can nor ought to tolerate the vice of falsehood, which must be detested by all, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to annul whatever was done by the authority of those letters, which had been obtained while the truth was concealed; to free the aforesaid priest from Al.’s suit; and not to permit him henceforth to be harassed by Al. concerning this matter.

Given at Anagni, 7 Kalends of December [25 November].

CLXXVI. TO THE . . . BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0191D] The series of bishops of Maurienne in the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 692, is incomplete. After Lambert, who died in 1198, it immediately records Aymar, formerly abbot of Saint Peter of Vienne, and states that he governed the church of Maurienne for fifteen years and died in 1245, after having been transferred to the archbishopric of Embrun as early as 1236.] AND MASTER ALBERT DE BOGES, CANON OF MAURIENNE; AND THE . . . PRIOR OF AQUA BELLA, IN THE DIOCESE OF MAURIENNE. That a prebend be granted by the chapter of Aosta to P., subdeacon. (Anagni, 7 Kalends of December.)

We are said to have written, at the petition of our beloved son P., subdeacon, to our beloved sons the chapter of Aosta, in the form by which we require those ordained to be provided for by their ordainers or presenters. Yet, as our venerable brother, the bishop of Aosta [Note: [Col. 0191D]

Concerning the bishops of Aosta around this time, Ughellus records only the following, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1337:

“XXII. Germanus, in 1189.

XXIII. Jacobus de Portia, bishop of this church in 1216. He was thereafter transferred to the church of Asti in 1219.”], and our beloved sons the priors of Saint Ursus and Saint Benignus, appointed auditors in this matter, informed us in their letters, neither in obedience to our command nor despite the frequency of their admonitions did they choose to provide, as we commanded, for that subdeacon—who had been found qualified to obtain an ecclesiastical benefice. Although at that time two prebends were vacant in their church, one of which could freely have been assigned to him, our beloved sons G. . . provost and A., archdeacon of Aosta, had also given him their assent and support in this matter, as we clearly gather from their letters.

Therefore, unwilling to leave incomplete what we know that we have mercifully begun concerning the said subdeacon, we command your discretion by apostolic letters under obedience that, after previous admonition, you compel the said chapter by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, either to confer and assign to him the prebend which is said now to be vacant in their church or, if none is vacant, to provide for him in a suitable ecclesiastical benefice according to our command. Restrain by a like penalty any persons who may think fit to oppose this. The witnesses, etc. Let none, etc. But if not all [can be present], etc. You, brother bishop, together with one of them, etc.

Given at Anagni, 7 Kalends of December [25 November].

[Col. 0192B] A letter has been written to the chapter on this matter.

CLXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0191D] This is found, though mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book I, title 20, “On Witnesses and Testimonies,” chapter 25, where it is said to be addressed to the prior of Bologna and J., rector of the church of Borell. What is found there is here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO THE . . . PRIOR OF BOELTUM, AND J., RECTOR OF THE CHURCH OF GOILLIS [otherwise, TOILLIS]. On admitting witnesses in a matrimonial case. (Anagni, 8 Kalends of December [24 November].)

[From the tenor of your letters we have learned that, since we had committed to you and to our beloved son . . . abbot [Note: [Col. 0192D] Perhaps one should read “abbot of Furness”; for the matter here seems to concern Furness Abbey, in Lancashire, founded in 1127. If this is accepted, it might then be believed that the abbot to whom the pope had entrusted this matrimonial case was Richard of Saint-Quentin. For the authors of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 704, recognize him as the thirteenth abbot of Furness, after the twelfth, Michael of Dalton, to whom Pope Celestine III wrote a privilege.] of Furness [Note: [Col. 0192D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are, below, the words “son . . . of E. and sister W. of A.”] the case pending between R., son of W. of Eston, knight, and M., a woman, sister of W. of Arches, to be brought to its due conclusion], the aforesaid abbot reasonably excusing himself on the ground that he could not take part in the hearing of the same case, you summoned the parties before you. When they had appeared in [Col. 0192C] your presence, the woman’s party alleged that the said knight [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Decretals add *prius* (“previously”) and omit the following words distinguished in italics.] had taken a bodily oath that he would take her as wife, and thereafter, having carnally known her, brought her into his house and had offspring by her. The aforesaid knight, however, wholly denied this, adding that, even if what she alleged were true, he could not lawfully have had her, because he had previously taken another woman, then living, as his wife. Accordingly, witnesses having been received from both sides and the depositions published, since it seemed to have been [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Decretals read *esse* (“to have been”); B. has *Belet* in place of M.; and they read *acceperit* in place of *accepit*.] proved by the witnesses of the said knight that before the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin he had solemnly taken M. Belet as his wife, while the witnesses of M., the woman of Arches [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Decretals omit these words and, below, read *praestiterit* (“had taken”) for *praestitit* (“took”).], declared that [Col. 0193A] in Easter week following the said feast he had sworn that he would take her, the aforesaid knight urgently sought to be absolved from her claim. But it was replied on behalf of the aforesaid woman that, at the time—and also before the time—when the witnesses of the said knight declared that he had contracted marriage with the other woman, he had always been staying in the province of York, whereas those witnesses said that this had occurred far outside the said province, specifying a time and place, a fact which she was prepared to prove by suitable witnesses. To this, however, the opposing side replied that, since the depositions had been solemnly published on both sides, there was now no place for the production of witnesses. Therefore, because you doubted whether, after publication of the depositions, witnesses ought to be admitted concerning that article, we answer your inquiry by the authority of these presents: witnesses for the woman are to be admitted to prove that article [Note: [Col. 0193D] The Decretals read: “the woman’s witnesses are to be admitted to prove that article.”].

CLXXVIII. TO MASTER PETER MUÑON, DEAN OF LEÓN. He receives him under protection. (Anagni, 12 Kalends of December [20 November].)

“It is customary to assent,” etc., down to “assent.” We receive your person, together with all that you presently possess, etc., in the manner of protection. And in particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the deanery of the church of León, with all its appurtenances, as you justly and peaceably possess it. Let no one therefore, etc.

[Col. 0193C] Given at Anagni, 12 Kalends of December [20 November].

CLXXIX. TO MASTER PETER MUÑON [Note: [Col. 0193D] Thus in the copy.], ARCHDEACON OF COMPOSTELA. He receives him under protection. (Anagni, Kalends of December [1 December].)

“It is customary,” etc., in the manner of protection. And in particular, we confirm by apostolic authority the archdeaconry of the church of Compostela, with all its appurtenances, as you justly and peaceably possess it. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of December [1 December].

CLXXX. [Note: [Col. 0193D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, § 67.] TO CELESTINE, ABBOT OF SAINT COLUMBA OF THE ISLAND OF HII [Note: [Col. 0193D] “To the abbot of Saint Columba of the island of Hii.” This probably concerns the monastery of Iona, whose founder was Saint Columba about the year 590. For the Venerable Bede relates that the island of Iona was given to Saint Columba by the Picts, who inhabited those regions of Britain—or rather [Col. 0194D] Scotland (book I, chapter 1). On the foundation of this monastery, see Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. I, p. 210.], AND TO HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter and enumerates the possessions belonging to them. (Anagni, 5 Ides of December [9 December].)

[Col. 0193D]

“To those choosing the religious life,” down to “we graciously assent”: we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of Saint Columba, in which you are devoted to divine service, etc., down to “we strengthen.” First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods, etc., down to “may remain unimpaired”; among these we have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the churches of Insegal, Mule, Colvansei, Cheldubsenaig, Chelcenneg, and Ile; the islands of Hii, Mule, Colvansei, Orvansei, Canei, and Calve; the lands of Magemburg, Mangecheles, Morimeam, and Gotensdal; the lands of Abberad, in Ile, of [Col. 0194B] Markarna, and of Camusnanesre. Concerning newly cleared land, etc., down to “may presume to extort.” Concerning burial, moreover, etc., down to “bodies are carried away.” Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, etc., down to “shall provide for the election.” As a token, moreover, of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors each year two Byzantine coins, freely offered. We decree therefore, etc., down to “shall be beneficial,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If anyone therefore, etc., down to “shall be subject.” But to all, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the 5th Ides of December [9 December], [Col. 0194C] in the seventh indiction, in the year 1203 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CLXXXI. [Note: [Col. 0194D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, § 64.] TO THE KING OF THE DANES. Concerning the release of Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig [Note: [Col. 0194D] See the notes of Bangert to Arnold of Lübeck, book VI, chapter 18.]. (Anagni, Nones of December [5 December].)

Would that that man—namely Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig—had not existed: he who, setting aside the gravity of the pontifical office, so that he might unite kingship to priesthood in himself and become a many-headed beast, rashly conspired against K., king of the Danes of illustrious memory, your brother, to whom he was bound by an oath of fealty; magnifying treachery against him whose bread he ate, and lifting up the horns of pride [Col. 0194D] in order to break the horn of the righteous man and abolish the memory of his name! Would that, since he had drawn back his hand from the plough and again involved himself in secular affairs, turning backward, he had been turned into a pillar of salt, so that, falling alone into the waters, he alone might lament his own disgrace and might neither put tears upon the cheeks of the Church nor stains upon the pontifical order [Col. 0195A]!

For it would have been more tolerable had he perished by his own sword, since he took up the material sword, and thus fallen into the pit he had prepared, than that he should have stained royal hands by his capture, darkened his reputation by reference to divine matters, or dug a pit for those who attend not so much to his guilt as to the punishment of his captivity, and who, following his example, take up the weapons of presumption against ecclesiastical liberty so that thereafter they may boldly and with impunity infringe the privilege of clerical immunity.

But the just Judge, the Lord our God, who repaid him according to his works and did not suffer his pride always to rise, but—because, forgetting his own condition, he had walked among great and marvelous things above himself—humbled and confounded him by divine judgment. And because he followed in his exaltation the footsteps of him who wished to set his seat on the sides of the north in order to be like the Most High, he fell lower after that example; and, placed in prison, he now recognizes, as we believe, his own iniquity [Col. 0195B].

Moreover, since the Lord strengthened the throne of the aforesaid king by Waldemar’s overthrow and deigned to establish his kingdom, we would wish that he had not received God’s grace in vain, nor proved ungrateful for so great a benefit, nor stretched out his hand against Him in injury and kept it stretched out to the end—he whose justice He had preserved and whose life He had mercifully rescued from death, delivering him from the hand of all who hated him. For he was bound to consider that a servant stands or falls before his own lord; and therefore he ought not to have judged another’s servant or raged against a bishop as though against a worthless slave, but ought to have shown deference to the Roman Church, left judgment to the Apostolic See, and kept his hands innocent.

Nor should he have doubted in any degree that the same bishop would evade the judgment of the Apostolic See or escape its discipline: from its mouth proceeds a two-edged sword, more piercing than every two-edged blade, flashing from sea to sea in a moment, for it flies over the sea as in the twinkling of an eye and passes beyond every mountain and hill, binding those whom it strikes not only on earth but in heaven. We do not say this as though we wished him to nurse serpents in his bosom or to offer an enemy a sword for his own throat; nor do we hold him guilty because, as is said, he seized in arms a man wickedly invading his kingdom. Rather, having removed from him the cause and opportunity of doing harm and rebelling, he should have humbly deferred to Him who declares that in His ministers He is touched not merely in Himself, but in the apple of His eye [Col. 0195D].

Certainly, however greatly that bishop may have offended, what sin had the Apostolic See committed, or what had the universal Church done, that the privilege of both should be injured in him? Had he gained liberty through his crime, so that because he had sinned he should be less subject to our jurisdiction? Was the universal Church to be punished for his sin, stripped of its privilege, rather than the soul that had sinned being punished? For neither father nor [Col. 0196A] mother should bear or lament the iniquity of a child, nor a child that of father or mother. Was there no balm in Gilead, and no physician there, who might pour oil and wine into the wounds of the children of the Church and apply iron to ulcers that did not respond to the remedies of fomentations?

Yet the king himself, although the Lord extended to him His right hand lest he perish and established his kingdom over all Denmark, doubted like one of little faith. And, fearing where there was no need to fear, he feared more the man whom he believed wished to kill the body than God, whom he knew able to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna. Thus, forgetting what he had read or heard in the Psalmist—“Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 104)—he not only irreverently touched the same bishop [Col. 0196B], but consigned him to strict custody, perhaps binding his feet with fetters and his hands with iron manacles—hands venerable at least by reason of their sacred anointing.

In this he gravely offended not only Him who declares that what is done to one of His least ones is done to Himself, but also greatly dishonored the whole Church, especially the Roman Church. He armed many tongues against her and gave occasion for sinners not only to build their structures upon her back, but even inwardly to rebuke her mercilessly because zeal for the house of the Lord did not consume her, because she did not set herself up as a wall against those advancing from the other side, but was like a dumb dog unable to bark, concealing the sins of her subjects.

Nor could this remain so hidden from the kings [Col. 0196C] of the earth that they would not adopt it as a kind of defense by which to protect their error, for excusing excuses in sins; and, in similar cases, allege the capture and detention of this bishop against the apostolic command. Thus H., the former emperor, who had sent our venerable brother . . . archbishop of Salerno into exile, when Pope C. of good memory, our predecessor, urgently petitioned him by messengers and letters for that archbishop’s release, did not hesitate to reply that the king of the Danes ought first and more urgently to have been pressed to restore the aforesaid bishop of Schleswig to his former liberty, since he had been seized earlier and was kept in chains, than to act for one whom the emperor himself was causing to remain [Col. 0196D] in Germany, though without chains or prison, lest he might be able to plot against the emperor’s life or kingdom.

We believe, however, that affliction has given the same bishop understanding, and that he has now been healed in Babylon in such a way that he will not hereafter add to his offences by rising again to those things through which he remembers descending into the pit of misery. Nor will he again stretch out his arms against the torrent or dare to kick against the goad. Therefore royal serenity need not fear that he will henceforth return to his vomit or set snares for your feet, by which he would know that he himself would rather perish—especially since the arm upon which he chiefly relied, and because of which the aforesaid king had particularly feared, has been broken by the death of Emperor H.; and in his place there has arisen one who, joined to you not only by friendship but also by kinship, will seek not the harm [Col. 0197A] but rather the increase of the kingdom of Denmark.

Therefore, let not your heart be hardened against that man, but rather softened; let it hear and heed our words, and reverently and devoutly defer to Him through whom kings reign and princes rule, and who can turn not only the hearts of fathers toward their sons and the dispositions of sons toward their parents, but also the affections of bishops toward kings, so that bishops may humbly defer to kings as to those who excel and to governors sent by them, and, if need be, lay down their lives for those whom they had previously opposed.

Since a human being never remains in the same state, and scarcely entertains the same thought by day as by night, but the surges of his mind are more wonderful and more frequent than the swelling of the sea, no one’s conversion [Col. 0197B] should be despaired of. For the affections brought by passing years are taken away by years that pass, and age, as it changes, alters dispositions. For sometimes a multitude of years teaches wisdom, and those who were foolish in youth become wise in old age. Otherwise the wicked would not be converted and cease to be wicked [Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus in the copy.], the bond of friendship would not be broken, and no hatred would arise.

Indeed, the enemy had stirred up matter for greater discord and a thorn of rancor between our dearest son in Christ, H., the illustrious king of Hungary, and the nobleman A., duke and brother of that king. Each had much to fear from the other, since after his father’s death the duke had risen against his brother and, having gathered many associates by conspiracy [Col. 0197C], had advanced so far against him that he invaded part of the kingdom and usurped for himself the royal diadem. Yet at last, through the mediation of the legate of the Apostolic See, full concord was restored between the disputants by the grace of God; so that those who previously attacked one another as enemies now treat one another with brotherly affection, and the duke himself remains faithful to the king.

We therefore send your serenity the form of the agreement concluded between them, although we wish to provide more fully for your security and that of the kingdom of Denmark. For, in addition to the assurances which the same bishop can give you in person or through others, we propose to hand over both him and all those who presume to attack you or your kingdom with him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh; so that whoever should presume to act against this [Col. 0197D] may incur the sentence established by canon. This shall be solemnly published once every year in all the cathedral churches of your kingdom, and we too shall renew it on the principal feasts.

Moreover, if necessary, all the magnates of the kingdom of Denmark shall be compelled by ecclesiastical coercion to give sworn security that they will never provide him aid or favor in this matter. To remove every suspicion altogether, the same bishop shall reside in Italy and shall never return to Denmark unless he obtains from you or your successors permission to return, with the consent of ourselves or our successors [Col. 0198A]. Yet, lest he be compelled, to the disgrace of the pontifical office, to beg, he shall appoint in his bishopric, according to your will, a vicar devoted to your serenity, who will provide him with revenues necessary for his maintenance and, insofar as possible, exercise his functions in his diocese.

We therefore admonish your serenity, exhort you earnestly in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: provide for your reputation and salvation, and by works of piety assist also in this respect the soul of your brother; seek the release of the same bishop, and do not delay in answering us concerning these matters, so that we may safeguard your security as honorably as we can. We wish you to know, however, that we cannot [Col. 0198B] bear his detention any longer with equanimity, since it redounds to an offence against the divine majesty, to the disgrace of the Apostolic See, and to the insult of the universal Church.

Given at Anagni, on the Nones of December [5 December].

CLXXXII. [Note: [Col. 0197D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1203, § 60. See also Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. [Col. 0198D] XIII, p. 101.] TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS. A sorrowful letter concerning his wife, whom he had abandoned. (Anagni, 5 Ides of December [9 December].)

Would that relentless labor conquered all things, and that a drop hollowed a stone not by force but by frequent falling, so that at least you might be overcome by our persistence and readily lend your ear to our admonitions! Certainly, if the Apostolic See had so often requested some great matter from you with repeated intercessions, you ought to have done it; how much more so because it has already written to you repeatedly that you should cause our dearest daughter in Christ, J., the illustrious queen of the Franks, your wife, to be treated with royal honor [Col. 0198C].

But behold, as we report with sorrow, you are said utterly to break the bruised reed and to crush the queen with a double crushing. For a twofold distress arises against her: besides being deprived of your presence, she is said also to suffer want of things needed for daily use. Thus she tempers her drink with weeping, and a stream of tears bathes her cheeks, because, placed amid straits, she does not find you, whom she sought, to comfort her; nor does she admit other comforters, being placed in solitude and banished in a royal castle as in a kind of prison [Col. 0198D].

For she had left brothers and sisters to cleave to you in marriage, so that you two might be one flesh and conjugal affection might unite the pair [Note: [Col. 0198D] Thus in the copy.] of persons. What then? If she is deprived of the marital due, so that your left hand is not under her head and your right hand, as she hoped, does not embrace her, shall she therefore be deprived of everything else also, and receive from you no compensation for all that she left behind? Surely it is the saying of Truth, whom you ought to imitate according to the measure of your ability, declaring in the Gospel: “Everyone who has left father, mother, brothers, and sisters for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold in this age and shall possess eternal life.”

But you repay the aforesaid queen far otherwise: since she left all things for you, you regard her, as is said, as abandoned and rejected; and, to the detriment of your reputation, you arrange that she should seem to have lost everything with you [Col. 0199A].

Moreover, even if nothing else moved you to compassion for her, at least this—that she was born of royal stock and married a king—ought to have led you not to add affliction to the afflicted, nor to deny royal honor in other things to her from whom you withhold the conjugal due. At least out of regard for Him who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished, you ought to treat her royally. And if even this did not effectively touch your mind, your heart should have been softened by our oft-repeated prayers, so that you would cause not only the queen herself, but any foreign and lowly woman, to be treated more honorably and more greatly honored.

But behold, as public report cries out, she has been left like a shelter in a cucumber field and like a solitary sparrow upon a building. She leads not a royal but a poor life, so that her soul is weary of life and she longs to be dissolved; she would rather be with Christ than be worn away in the castle of Étampes, as in a dungeon. There those who consume her do not sleep, and those assigned to her service—or rather to her misery—pierce her mind with the arrow of their tongue, while they offer her vinegar to drink [Col. 0199C], a stone for bread, and a scorpion for an egg. There not even the messengers of her brother, religious men, or the prelates of your kingdom have free access to her, nor can anyone comfort her in so great sorrow.

Would, therefore, that such miseries might thus die for her—[sic]—so that she herself not die in this misery, nor in dying bring him into ill repute before men, who would be said to have caused her death if she died at this time, since she would be believed not simply to have died, but to have been killed! We therefore admonish your royal serenity and earnestly exhort you in the Lord: provide for your reputation and salvation; do violence to yourself; and, since the wise person is stronger than the strong man and one who rules his own spirit than a conqueror of cities, conquer your own spirit. More than for your other victories, you should be commended for this victory; and, making virtue in some manner out of necessity, cause the queen herself to be treated with royal honor, as becomes both you and her.

Thus comply with our counsels and admonitions, so that you may avoid divine displeasure and escape the tongues of detractors; nor open their mouths against us, who attribute your hardness to our negligence, asserting that our patience brings you day by day more fully to impenitence [Col. 0199D]. For behold, we continually endure the reproaches of those who reproach us on your account. They say that, like dumb dogs unable to bark, we do not proclaim their impiety to the impious, and hence they declare that your blood is to be required from our hand by Him to whom, they say, we have preferred you. They add also that, because we wish too much to please you, we greatly displease God, who is not mocked; and that we depart from the paths of Him who says of Himself: “If I pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” (Galatians 1).

Let our counsel, therefore, please you, and do what we admonish, lest He who bears patiently and silently awaits your correction should, once angered, seize you and there be none to rescue you or withstand His wrath. Otherwise, we shall no longer be able to overlook her misery and endure with patience so great an injury to God and to the Apostolic See—indeed, to the universal Church—but, without respect of persons, we shall discharge the duty of our office [Col. 0200B], relying not on worldly power but on divine strength; for if the Lord is our helper, we shall not fear what man may do to us.

Given at Anagni, on the 5th Ides of December [9 December].

CLXXXIII. [Note: [Col. 0199D] It survives, but mutilated, among the Decretals, book V, title 39, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*, chapter 35, where it is said to be addressed to the bishop of London. What is read there [Col. 0200D] is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also supplied.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND. Concerning penalties to be inflicted upon clerics committing grave offences. (Anagni, 4 Ides of December [10 December].)

[“That you may provide for] your reputation and salvation, and so restrain the audacity of the wicked and protect the innocence of the good from them, you humbly consult us concerning matters touching the pastoral office, so that, secure in our answer, you may laudably discharge the duty of the care entrusted to you. [Indeed, your brotherhood has led us to be consulted [Col. 0200C] [Note: [Col. 0200D] In the Decretals: “you consulted us.”] whether clerics committing grave offences, who could not safely be assigned to monasteries to do penance because, since they do not repent of their crimes, they would seize an opportunity to escape, flee the cloister prison, and plunge more wickedly into their former crimes, may be consigned by you or their other prelates to strict custody;] and whether laymen, if they apprehend clerics in great crimes, incur the sentence established by canon, since they cannot either seize them or bring them before judges unless they lay violent hands upon them.

To the first question, therefore, [we answer that, since prelates ought to correct the offences of their subjects, and since it concerns the public authority that crimes not remain unpunished and that those who have been wicked not become more wicked through the boldness born of impunity [Col. 0200D], superiors not only may but ought to keep in strict custody those clerics who, after canonical conviction of a crime, are incorrigible and cannot be kept in monasteries, lest they readily fall into similar or worse offences. Laymen, however, may seize clerics without incurring a sentence of excommunication and bring them to judgment—even by force if necessary—provided they do this by command of the prelates to whose jurisdiction those clerics are subject and whose office it is to correct offenders. For the act is seen to be done not by the laymen themselves but by those under whose authority they act; provided, nevertheless, that [Col. 0201A] their violence extends no further than the clerics’ defense—or rather rebellion—requires.]

Given at Anagni, on the 4th Ides of December [10 December].

CLXXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS OF LOMBARDY. That they should protect and defend the Church of Pergamo [variant: Bergamo] against its harassers. (Anagni, 17 Kalends of January [16 December].)

The groan of the Church of Bergamo has risen to us, setting before us its misery and the afflictions it suffers all day long—not from enemies but from children, not from strangers but from its own and familiar enemies. For the children whom it had labored to raise and nourish, repaying evil for good and hatred for love [Col. 0201B], had not merely despised it, but, like a brood of vipers, conspired against their mother, thirsting for the blood of her at whose breast they had been accustomed to suckle.

For she had led them into her cellars; she had given drink and not food to the little ones; she had served solid food to those grown stronger, taking breads from the table of offering for their refreshment and setting before them the water of saving wisdom. But now fattened and now grown large, withdrawing from her, they raise their heel against their mother, kick against the goad, and give her whose bread they ate a stone for bread, a serpent for fish, and a scorpion for an egg.

Why then, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why do you despise in times of need and tribulation? Why do you not look upon the face of your Christ? Why has zeal for your house not consumed you [Col. 0201C], so that you rise like a mighty man overcome with wine and judge your cause, mindful of the reproaches you endure all day in your servants? For behold, your patience does not lead the people of Bergamo to repentance; rather, the more patiently you endure them, the more they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, more powerfully provoking your indignation against themselves.

But lest you forget us utterly, O Lord, and lest you turn your face away from us, remember your covenant and the Church that has been made, from mistress of the nations, a tributary. Spare not, O Lord, your rod; but you who rebuke and chastise those whom you love, chastise such presumptuous persons, lest their wickedness defile your flock. Therefore do not leave the rod of sinners any longer over the lot [Col. 0201D] of the righteous. Turn the wicked, that they may cease to be; and do not will the death of sinners, but that they may be converted and live—thus filling their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O Lord.

Certainly, as we have learned from the letters of many persons, the people of Bergamo, making no distinction whatever between sacred and profane, in order to enslave the Church of Bergamo and subject the free to servitude, received and read our letters which, as we remember, we had sent concerning the immunity of churches both to them and to the other Lombards. They assessed, at their own discretion, the possessions not only of all churches but of every religious place situated in the city or diocese of Bergamo [Col. 0202A], and exacted from them twelve denarii and from clerics fifteen [denarii] for every pound.

And when our venerable brother . . . bishop [Note: [Col. 0201D] This was Lanfranc, who had been appointed bishop of Bergamo—or, as it is read here, Pergamo—in 1186, having been a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict. He was a truly pious man of most approved character, whose administration of twenty-five years seemed to have overcome every hostility. He died in 1210, on 30 October: Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 669.], and our beloved sons, the canons and clerics of Bergamo, refused to submit their necks to so great a yoke, W. Lazar, the podestà, Albert Pazolus, judge, and other people of Bergamo appointed certain men of ill repute and evil character to collect the revenues of the churches, taking administration away from the bishop and clergy.

Moreover, so that the above-named church might become “a reproach of men and the scorn of the people,” and so that what had been a house of prayer might be turned into a dung-heap, they set up public latrines beside its walls in the cemetery, intending to purge their vessels and their bellies there—would that they were purging their entrails. Not thus do Saracens rage against churches and religious places: rather, they keep them reverently and devoutly and sometimes even venerate them, unwilling to pollute those houses which they know have been appointed for the invocation of the Lord’s name. But because familiarity breeds much contempt, and “a man’s enemies are those of his own household,” sons persecute the church which is revered even by foreigners—if indeed they should be called sons, who, having cast off filial affection, have put on a hostile spirit, cursing father and mother not so much in words as in deeds, so that they may die an everlasting death.

Although, therefore, by these acts they have deserved not only ecclesiastical but also divine vengeance, yet, that we may overcome evil with good and leave them no material from which to frame excuses for their sins, we will and, by the authority of these presents, strictly command that you, brother Archbishop of Milan [Note: See above.], personally go to that city; carefully admonish and induce the podestà, judges, councillors, and people; and, in the name of Almighty God and under adjuration by the divine judgment, enjoin them to restore without diminution whatever has thus been extorted from churches and ecclesiastical persons, wholly to desist from further exactions, and without delay to remove from the cemetery of the church of Pergamo the latrines, which ought rather to be hidden than exposed.

But if they cannot be softened by such admonitions, we strictly command your whole body, by virtue of obedience, that you place their city under sentence of interdict, so that, apart from the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying, no divine office may be celebrated there and no ecclesiastical sacrament administered. On every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lit, publicly declare excommunicated both the podestà and the consuls, councillors, and assessors, and specifically the aforesaid A., judge, Frederick Colion., L. de Mozo, P. Moizon, and C. de Roario, who, as is said, raged more harshly than the rest against the churches and clergy and were, as it were, the principal authors of this reckless counsel. Command that they be more strictly avoided by all the cities and citizens of Lombardy, in both dealings and every kind of contract, as excommunicates; and decree that anyone who presumes to communicate with them incurs a sentence of excommunication, which you shall subsequently publish solemnly.

Likewise declare that the aforesaid podestà, consuls, councillors, and assessors of Pergamo are so subject to excommunication that they cannot obtain the benefit of absolution unless, having made full satisfaction for the foregoing matters, they personally present themselves before the apostolic presence. Further, decree null and void, never to possess force at any time, the constitutions and judgments promulgated by those excommunicates or at their command. Decree also that those who succeed them in the administration of the aforesaid offices shall succeed to the sentence of excommunication, unless they make satisfaction within a month; for those substituted in honour succeed also to its burden.

And since the aforesaid podestà, consuls, and councillors grievously persecute ecclesiastical liberty, by the authority of these presents we decree that, unless they repent within a month, their sons, down to the third and fourth generation, shall henceforth in no way be admitted to ecclesiastical honours and benefices. And, that they may more fully feel in their hearts how grievously we bear so great an injury to God and to the universal Church, announce to them that, unless they repent within a month, we shall deprive their city of episcopal dignity and transfer its see elsewhere. If they cannot even thus be induced to make satisfaction within another month, then, lest they be able to aspire to recover the dignity lost, we shall divide the diocese of Pergamo among neighbouring bishoprics and command that this division be observed forever.

We further add that you, brothers Archbishop of Milan and Bishop of Vercelli [Note: See also above.], when requested by the same bishop of Pergamo, shall compel, by sentence of suspension and excommunication, all canons, clerics, and religious persons—both exempt and others—residing in the city and district of Pergamo, to leave that city and district and not return to them until satisfaction has been made, setting aside any obstacle of appeal. Since they will have gone into exile not so much for their own liberty as for that of the universal Church, provide suitably for them throughout all the churches of Lombardy, according to your prudent judgment, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure. Furthermore, compel the brethren both of Jerusalem and of the military Order of the Temple, with appeal set aside and notwithstanding their privileges and indulgences, inviolably to observe the sentence of interdict.

Given at Anagni, 17 Kalends of January [16 December].

## CLXXXV

[Note: Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1203, §67.]

TO THE BISHOPS, ABBOTS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES IN WHOSE PARISHES THE MONASTERY OF MONTE CASSINO IS KNOWN TO HAVE CHURCHES OR OTHER POSSESSIONS. He confirms the privilege by which the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Monte Cassino may pronounce sentence of excommunication upon invaders of the monastery’s property. (Anagni, 18 Kalends of January.)

The care of all churches entrusted to us, though our merits are insufficient, requires that we extend the attention of our consideration to protect them against the assaults of the wicked. But we especially wish to assist and benefit the monastery of Monte Cassino, which is subject to us without intermediary, lest the persons sitting there at the Lord’s feet with Mary, and meditating day and night upon the law of the Lord, be recalled from their religious purpose by the wrongful molestations of certain persons, and lest the better part which they have chosen be taken from them.

Therefore, since our beloved son R. [Note: He has already been mentioned frequently.], presbyter-cardinal of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter and abbot of Monte Cassino, has free authority, by our authority and that of our predecessors of happy memory, Popes Calixtus and Alexander, to pronounce sentence of excommunication against his wrongdoers if any, setting aside the fear of God, violently stretch forth their hands to plunder the goods of the monastery of Monte Cassino, and if the diocesan bishops of those wrongdoers, upon admonition by him or his brethren, refuse or maliciously delay to render him full justice concerning them: we command and enjoin you all by apostolic letters that, should any of your parishioners seize or violently invade possessions or goods of the said monastery, upon hearing a complaint concerning this from the abbot or brethren of Monte Cassino, you do not delay to administer strict justice against them, without any obstacle of contradiction or appeal.

Otherwise, firmly observe, all excuse and contradiction ceasing, the sentence of excommunication which the aforesaid abbot judges ought to be pronounced against them on this account, according to the tenor of his privileges granted by the Apostolic See to the Church of Monte Cassino. And you, brothers archbishops and bishops, shall cause it to be inviolably observed throughout your bishoprics until the same abbot and his brethren inform you that satisfaction has been made to them concerning the matters for which those persons had been bound by the bond of excommunication.

Given at Anagni, 18 Kalends of January [15 December].

## CLXXXVI

TO MASTER SYM., CLERIC OF OUR VENERABLE BROTHER G. [Note: He has already been mentioned frequently.], BISHOP OF PRAENESTE, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He confirms for him the scholastery of the church of Mainz. (Anagni, 2 Ides of December.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., down to “assent.” We confirm by apostolic authority the grant made to you, as canonically made, by our venerable brother S. [Note: The same person.], Archbishop of Mainz, of the scholastery of the church of Mainz, together with its prebend and other appurtenances, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, 2 Ides of December [12 December].

## CLXXXVII

TO THE ABBOT OF CORVEY.

[Note: “Hugoldus, the thirty-second abbot of the monastery of Corvey, held office for twenty-nine years, laying aside the burden of the body in 1229.” Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, vol. II, p. 165. The monastery here in question is Corvey in Germany.]

He confirms his privileges. (Anagni, 2 Ides of December.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., down to “assent.” By apostolic authority we confirm, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the liberties, immunities, and dignities granted to the monastery of Corvey by our predecessors and confirmed by their privileges, as well as the exemptions from secular exactions granted to it by secular princes. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, 2 Ides of December, in the sixth year.

## CLXXXVIII

[Note: Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1203, §67.]

TO THE SAME. He grants him permission to use a ring. (Anagni, 2 Ides of December.)

The Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside by the Lord’s authorship, having been raised to the fullness of ecclesiastical dignity, so pours the grace of paternal blessing into its sons that all receive from its fullness; and, just as it shares with them the burden of the care entrusted to itself, so it communicates to them also the honours and ornaments of the dignity it has received, endowing daughters in its sons and adorning sons in its daughters. Yet it shows itself more liberal toward, and more abundantly pours out its gifts upon, those who, not ungrateful for grace received, flee the vice of ingratitude and rise in acts of thanksgiving toward those who honour them, so that they may deserve grace to be given them in return for grace.

Since, therefore, you acknowledge the grace granted to you and your monastery by the Apostolic See, which bestowed upon your predecessors and their successors the use of the mitre, gloves, and sandals, and since we are moved both by your merits and by the prayers of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King O., elected Roman Emperor, in whose fidelity and devotion you persevere, we grant you by the authority of these presents that henceforth you may use a ring. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, 2 Ides of December, in the sixth year.

## CLXXXIX

TO THE BISHOP [Note: We have already discussed the bishop of Poitiers above.], THE DEAN [Note: The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1216, recognize William I as dean of Poitiers in 1198 and 1200; they next mention Philip immediately in 1211.], AND MASTER WILOT, CANON OF POITIERS. He commits to them the case concerning the election of the bishop of Angoulême [Note: This letter should be compared with the matters related by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1007.]. (Anagni, 4 Ides of December.)

Because, when the church of Angoulême was vacant, the votes of its electors were forced into varying directions among the persons of its canons, it had recourse to the Apostolic See. Thus it was set before us on one side that, after the bishop of Angoulême of good memory, . . . [Note: John I of Saint-Vallier, in French de Saint-Val, a man conspicuous for outstanding character and virtues, died in this very year, 1203, on 7 March, as is said in the annals of the monastery of La Couronne. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1006. See letter 133 of book V, note.], had entered the way of all flesh, the canons, repeatedly discussing the election of a bishop to be set over them, commonly named their beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Eparchius [Note: The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, from the chronicle of Bernard Itier and according to Dom Estiennot in the manuscript fragments of Aquitaine, state that Ranulfus was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Eparchius from 1171 until 1218, without mentioning this election of him to the bishopric of Angoulême. *Gallia Christiana*, ibid., col. 1034.], a man of praiseworthy life, learned and prudent in spiritual and temporal matters, without the solemnity of an election.

But, when his election had been delayed, they entrusted the power of election to four of their fellow canons, after receiving from them an oath that within a fixed time they would choose from the body of the church of Angoulême as shepherd the man whom they judged more useful; the canons likewise confirming by oath that without objection they would receive as elect the person whom those four should, before a fixed day, choose according to the form given them. Yet, because the time given them expired before the four electors had come together as one, they did not proceed to an election; rather, they mutually released one another from the compromise.

The canons therefore, meeting again, gave free authority to elect to their beloved son . . . archdeacon . . . precentor, and . . . archdeacon of Saintes, a canon of Angoulême; provided, however, that two could do nothing without the third, while the third could release the two if they could not agree together. Although the precentor declared himself ready to swear that he would nominate a person more useful for the bishopric, or accept one nominated by the others if they would swear that a person they nominated was more useful than his own nominee, neither of the others would accept this, nor could they agree upon anyone; for which reason they mutually released one another from the compromise.

Accordingly the archdeacon, who is the sole one in the church of Angoulême, . . . the treasurer, . . . the cantor, . . . the penitentiary, and the senior canons—indeed, the greater and sounder part of those accustomed to reside in the church—considering after due deliberation that almost all had previously agreed upon the aforesaid abbot of Saint-Eparchius, invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, elected him bishop, and, submitting themselves and their election to the protection of the Apostolic See, appealed to our hearing lest anyone attempt anything against them or their election. But after they had entered the church with the customary praises, certain persons who had been present at the election already completed yet had raised no objection whatsoever against the electors rashly nominated as bishop the dean of Bordeaux [Note: He was probably Gerald II de Malamorte; the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 856, mention him immediately after Stephen, of whom they say nothing after 1195.], a younger man, unlettered and insufficient for the government of a bishopric.

Therefore, because almost all the persons of that church and the resident canons had agreed upon the same abbot, all sought confirmation of the election of him which had been made first, and annulment of what had been done concerning the dean. On the other hand, however, it was alleged that when the canons of Angoulême had assembled together to discuss appointing themselves a shepherd, they confirmed by oath that no one would first break out into a nomination except after consultation with, and the assent of, each and every one; and binding themselves to this under the bond of excommunication, they obtained from their metropolitan, our venerable brother . . . Archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: He has already been mentioned frequently. See letter 96 of book V.], the promulgation of a sentence of excommunication against those who presumed to act otherwise.

And when afterward they had conferred the power to elect their bishop, the master of the schools, fearing that, if—as the copies read, “pro ubi”—the first electors had not agreed, the second might not be able to agree, and that something less than canonical might be done, appealed to our hearing so that no one might proceed to an election without common counsel and assent. But when the aforesaid three reported to the chapter that they had not agreed, the archdeacon and his followers, paying no heed at all to the appeal, immediately nominated the aforesaid abbot as bishop.

The others, more numerous and sounder in counsel, accordingly considered that those men had incurred the guilt of perjury and a sentence of excommunication, and that, both for this reason and because they had not thought fit to heed the appeal and had elected without consulting them, they had been deprived of the power of election. They held that the election had devolved upon themselves alone, since those men could no longer object an appeal against them, because they had acted contrary to it; for he who offends against the law invokes the law’s aid in vain. They unanimously agreed upon the aforesaid dean, a man suitable for governing a bishopric; his election was afterwards confirmed by the authority of the aforesaid archbishop, as appeared more clearly from his letters recited in our presence.

Since, therefore, the abbot of Saint-Eparchius had been nominated by only ten excommunicated and perjured men, after an appeal had been lodged with us and without consulting the others, whereas the dean had been elected by eleven men of sounder counsel, they sought confirmation of the dean’s election and a declaration that what had been done concerning the abbot was void. In reply, however, it was alleged that the abbot’s electors had incurred neither perjury nor excommunication, since the sentence of excommunication had been relaxed by the aforesaid archbishop, as they affirmed under oath; nor had the canons sworn, as had been alleged by the other side, that they would in no way proceed to an election without the counsel and assent of every single one and all, or without common counsel. This was expressed by our venerable brother, the bishop of Saintes [Note: See also there.], in letters which the opposing party used on its behalf.

Hence, since all the persons save only one, the senior canons, and nearly all those who maintained residence in the church had agreed upon the aforesaid abbot, the election had proceeded upon the common counsel of the canons, as the greater and sounder part. Although no procurator appeared for this party of electors, but only simple messengers who set forth what had been done—and thus the dean’s party urgently sought costs from them and their party—nevertheless, because the aforesaid abbot had sent a sufficient representative, we heard these matters and others alleged on either side, and formed our judgment from them.

It was established to us from the parties’ admissions that the same abbot had been elected by the smaller number after an appeal had been lawfully lodged with us. For, although twenty-one canons had assembled for the election, only ten had agreed upon him, without consulting the rest. We therefore judged his election void. But because the dean of Bordeaux, elected by the opposing party, is said to be insufficient for the execution of the episcopal office and is alleged to suffer deficiencies both in age and learning such that he ought not be promoted to the summit of so great a dignity, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings that, having God alone before your eyes, you meet together in a suitable and secure place for both parties; and, with the dean himself and the parties present before you, if they wish to appear when cited, carefully investigate the truth concerning the aforesaid impediments without respect of persons. If the parties agree, pronounce a definitive sentence.

Otherwise, take care to remit the case, sufficiently prepared, to us, fixing a suitable term for the parties to come to the Apostolic See to receive judgment. The aforesaid elect shall personally come there unless it is established that he is detained by some just impediment. If his election should perhaps be annulled in law, the parties, in the name of the whole body, shall be prepared either to celebrate a canonical election with our counsel or, if reason requires it, to receive from us a suitable person as shepherd. But if not all, etc. You, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Anagni, 4 Ides of December [10 December], in the sixth year.

## CXC

TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS [Note: He has already been mentioned frequently.]. He interprets the tenor of apostolic letters in certain cases. (Anagni, 15 Kalends of January.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to show itself generous to petitioners, but certain persons wickedly abuse its grace when they twist to malign purposes what it grants in kindness. For certain persons, wishing to act maliciously in our commissions, specify lesser and more insignificant persons by their proper names, but do not designate greater and more distinguished persons by special names; rather, they include them under a cloak of generality, in order to obtain such commissions from us more easily, in this form: “Such persons complain of this or that man, and of certain others to be specified by proper names, who are injurious and burdensome to them in such-and-such a matter and in certain other affairs.”

Therefore, wishing to prevent their malice, we decree that, when only lesser and more insignificant persons are designated in our commissions, greater and more distinguished persons are not to be understood as included under a general clause. Nor may an unbridled multitude be summoned to judgment on the pretext of such generality, nor may persons be heard concerning greater and weightier matters when they mention only lighter and lesser matters. But if someone has named greater persons, not because he wishes to litigate with them but so that he may descend to lesser persons, because fraud and deceit ought not to support him, he shall, as a lying sinner, lose the grants he has obtained.

Given at Anagni, 15 Kalends of January [18 December], in the sixth year.

## CXCI

[Note: Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1203, §70.]

TO THE ARCHBISHOP [Note: We are not in a position to determine with certainty who was the Archbishop of Brindisi to whom this letter is directed. Ughellus, *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 46, mentions Gerard in 1196. He then adduces Dominic, distinguished, as he says, by character and prudence in affairs, sent by Innocent in this very year, 1203, as legate of the Apostolic See to Bulgaria. But, with due respect to him, we say that he has erred remarkably. For the pope expressly calls Dominic not Archbishop but Archpriest of Brindisi. See letter 143 of this sixth book. Nor, even if it could be admitted that the archbishop had been legate to Bulgaria, could this letter concern the same man.], THE ABBOT OF SAINT ANDREW, AND THE PEOPLE OF BRINDISI. He sharply rebukes them for conspiring against the Count of Brienne and, after killing the castellan, treacherously occupying the castle. (Anagni.)

We are compelled to wonder and be moved no little that, although among all those established in Apulia you received as among the first our beloved son, the nobleman Walter, Count of Brienne, master justiciar of Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, and took care to honour him more highly, yet, led astray by whose counsel we do not know and deceived by what error, you turned backwards and raised your heel not so much against him as against us and the king; and, after killing the count’s castellan, not without the fault of treachery, you all rebelled together.

Certainly, when at the count’s arrival the enemies who had previously ranged through the kingdom with impunity—not merely seizing plunder but raging even against persons, extracting by tortures from them not only everything they possessed but also what they could not possess, and slaughtering whom they wished like cattle—were, by the Lord’s mighty right hand and through the count’s skill and prudence, with the authority of the Apostolic See added, marvellously crushed and scattered, he ought to have found with you such gratitude that you would not only have refrained from rebelling against him but would even have laid down your lives for him, since in a certain manner he had laid down his own life for you.

But to display more fully by deed the disposition you bore toward him and us: when he visited us as we lay upon a bed of sickness, you pretended that we were dead, conspired against him, and occupied the castle which he had held. Nor could the leopard put off its variegation or the tiger strip off its skin, since you, brother archbishop, practised, once vested with the pallium, the vice of infidelity which, under the appearance of great devotion, you had concealed until you received the pallium from us; you became an author of perjury and destruction, though you at least ought to have preserved fidelity to us.

But what we feared occurred; what we dreaded came to pass. Almost prodigiously it happened that you revealed, once pallium-clad, the infidelity you had concealed when without the pallium: for the pallium, intolerant of concealment, made you reveal yourself, and commanded you to do more quickly what you were doing. Yet, in order that you might spread a net before the eyes of birds, immediately after committing treachery you renewed, as we have heard, the oath of bailiwick sworn to us, as though we trusted rather your words than your deeds and were unable to distinguish actions from words, so as openly to recognize those who honour us with their lips while their heart is far from us. But perhaps this reasoning led you to it: your conscience reproached you, and you yourselves knew better that you had acted against the oath sworn to us; perhaps repenting of what you had done, you offered another oath to be kept in future.

Moreover, if the count himself had wronged you in anything, you ought not to have taken such vengeance by yourselves, but to have had recourse to us and demanded satisfaction and justice from him. For, however much we have loved him until now and still love him, you could nevertheless understand from us that we loved the king and kingdom more, and would not suffer him to attempt anything to the prejudice of the king and the harm of the kingdom.

But because even a just man falls seven times in a day and rises again, and a man cannot remain continually in the same state, we admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord, and command you by apostolic writings; and, under the obligation by which you are bound to us and the king, we strictly command that, returning to your senses and correcting by sounder counsel what you perhaps did rashly, you rise from your own fall. Having received security from the same count that, on account of this offense, he will neither injure the citizens nor oppress the city, return to his allegiance and surrender the castle into his hands.

Otherwise, you, brother archbishop, and you, son Abbot of Saint Andrew, shall present yourselves before us within a month after receiving these letters, to receive punishment or reward according to your deserts. If you delay or refuse to comply, know that from that time you are bound by the bond of excommunication. And you citizens, unless within the same term you execute the apostolic command, know that your city is under interdict and that all the principal counsellors and authors of this treachery are bound by the bond of excommunication. And that the material sword may be joined to the spiritual sword, we strictly command all counts, barons, and citizens established throughout Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, both on our behalf and the king’s, to give you no aid or favour, but to assist the same count against you manfully and powerfully. Choose, therefore, rather to obey and live than to persist in your contumacy and perish.

Given at Anagni.

In almost the same manner to the . . . Archbishop [Note: Ughellus’s series of the Archbishops of Otranto, *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 13, is far too incomplete: it mentions Jonathan in 1163 and 1179, then immediately Tancred de Anibaldis in 1219.] and people of Otranto, through: “against us and the king you raised your heel, and rashly rebelled,” etc.; in the same manner to the end, except that no mention is made there of the abbot.

In the same manner to the . . . bishop [Note: After Melchizedek, who attended and subscribed the Council of Nicaea, the acts and names of the bishops of Gallipoli are lacking for many centuries, down to 1325. Ughellus, *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 135.] and citizens of Gallipoli.

## CXCII

TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, AND NOBLEMEN, COUNTS, BARONS, AND CITIZENS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT APULIA AND TERRA DI LAVORO. On the same subject. (Anagni.)

Unless you neglected your own standing and reputation, you would yourselves, even if we said nothing, punish those traitorous sons who, through the vice of treachery innate in them, bring disgrace upon the whole people of Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro; thus you would purge the shame of the people and show yourselves faithful in the persecution of the faithless. [Col. 0212A] For behold, although the soul that sins deserves the sentence of death, and a son ought not to be punished for his father, nor a father for his son, yet, according to common practice, the crime of a few spreads among many, and many better persons are undeservedly defamed through a few low ones. Although we, who know the merits of individuals, distinguish people from people and city from city, and know how to separate the faithless from the faithful—lest we call good evil or evil good—and are more ready to spare offenders if they repent of their contumacy than to be angry with the good while they persevere, nevertheless those at a distance, who know only the name of the province and not the names of its cities, [Col. 0212B] assert that you committed what the people of Brindisi, Matera, Barletta, Otranto, and Gallipoli treacherously committed, imputing the crimes of a few cities to the entire province.

Some also, though they know the province, have seen its cities, and even know who sinned, nevertheless accuse the innocent of silence and turn forbearance into guilt against you, relying on that canonical saying: “To neglect, when one is able, to disturb the wicked is nothing other than to encourage them; nor is he free from the taint of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.” But if the count himself had in any respect offended against them, etc. In nearly the same manner down to: “to make an attempt,” since we do not believe that you are ignorant how much he has contributed to the whole kingdom. For at his arrival [Col. 0212C] the enemies, who previously ranged through the kingdom with impunity, etc. In nearly the same manner down to: “they were wonderfully crushed and scattered”; for which reason the aforesaid traitors ought to have been faithful to him, not faithless.

Therefore, that you may free not only yourselves but all inhabitants of the kingdom of Sicily from the reproach of this disgrace, we admonish and earnestly exhort your community; and by these apostolic letters, under the obligation by which you are bound to us and to the king, we strictly command that, unless the people of Barletta, Brindisi, Otranto, and Gallipoli execute within one month after receiving these present letters our command, which we are directing to them by our letters, you, brother archbishops and bishops, shall declare their lands subject to interdict [Col. 0212D] and their chief counsellors and instigators in this treason to be subject to sentence of excommunication. You shall cause both the sentence of interdict and that of excommunication to be solemnly published every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, in the cathedral churches and all other parish churches situated in your cities or dioceses, and you shall yourselves publish them personally.

But the archbishops of Brindisi and Otranto, etc., [Col. 0213A] and the bishop of Gallipoli—unless, just as they are said to have been causes of the treason, they also become authors of conversion, and either induce their citizens to carry out the apostolic command or personally present themselves before us within one month after receiving these letters, to receive punishment or reward according to their deserts—you shall solemnly announce as excommunicated in the same manner, and cause this to be announced in the places already mentioned.

And you, sons—counts, barons, and citizens—as you trust in our favor and as we hope in your devotion, give vigorous and powerful support, with strong hand and outstretched arm, against traitors and rebels of this sort, to the aforesaid count, who will specially prosecute in this matter our cause, the king’s cause, and his own; crushing the pride of the rebels [Col. 0213B] and binding their jaws with bit and bridle, so that they may return from the trackless way of faithlessness to the path of fidelity. Let none of you meanwhile presume to supply them with necessities, grant them assistance or favor; rather, so avenge upon them their offence and the injury done to yourselves that you show, by punishing the traitors, how greatly the vice of treachery displeases you. Against the people of Matera we shall proceed as we have commanded you by other letters.

Because we are prepared to render full justice, both concerning the count himself and concerning others against whom they may wish to bring a complaint, to the noblemen Count S. Gentilis, Robert de Butaro, Nicholas de Fontanellis and his brothers, Pandulf de Aquirio, and Tor., sons of Count S. Felix, we wish this to be announced to them through you. [Col. 0213C] We will and, under the same strict command, order you, brother archbishops and bishops, that unless they desist from their rebellion upon your admonition, cease troubling the kingdom through their seducers and assailants, and cease plotting against the count, you strike them with sentence of excommunication. Cause this sentence to be solemnly published every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, subjecting to the same sentence those who supply them with provisions or other necessities, by request, payment, or otherwise, or otherwise give them assistance and favor. And you, sons—barons and citizens—together with the count and also by yourselves, suppress their malice.

[Col. 0213D] Given at Anagni.

### CXCIII

[Note: A highly singular letter and exceedingly worthy of reading. Raynaldus published it, though mutilated in its larger and better part, under the year 1203, §71. We present it entire from a copy belonging to Conti and also from a collation of the manuscript of the Vatican Library, [Col. 0214D] which contains the *Formulary of Berardus of Naples*. Passages found in Raynaldus are here enclosed in brackets.]

**To J., former Archbishop of Lyon** [Note: See Letter 72 of Book V, note.] He replies to several questions with which the archbishop had approached the Apostolic See and sought its pronouncement. (Anagni, 11 Kalends of January [22 December].)

[That you willingly exercise yourself in the commandments of God by cultivating piety, and continually ponder his ways by meditating on the law of the Lord, is shown by the words of your letters [Col. 0214A] and attested still more strongly by the questions with which you approach the Apostolic See, so that it may open the door of truth to one who knocks and illuminate by its answer what seems obscure. You have accordingly consulted us by letter as to why the Psalmist assigned no psalm to the third day, although he assigned individual psalms to the other days in praise of the work of each.]

For on the first day of the week he assigns the twenty-third psalm; on the second, the forty-seventh; on the fourth, the ninety-third; on the fifth, the eightieth; on the day before the Sabbath, namely the sixth day of the week, the ninety-second; and on the Sabbath day, the ninety-first psalm.
