He wholly omits the third day, in which you believe some mystery lies hidden. The well is deep, and we are not sufficient of ourselves [Col. 0214B] to draw water from the fountains of the Savior; but we must ask him who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them, that he may deign to reveal to us, unworthy as we are, what he has hitherto hidden from the wise, as the Father so ordained.

[We believe, however, that since the third day is especially commendable above the others on account of the most holy mystery of the Trinity, the Psalmist—although he understood more than the aged, and his tongue was like the pen of a swiftly writing scribe—nevertheless wholly suppressed the praises of the third day, so as to indicate that ineffable, indeed most ineffable, mystery. He preferred to be entirely silent on the subject rather than stammer feebly. To signify this, moreover, the Apostle Paul, when he had been caught up into the third heaven, heard secret words which [Col. 0214C] it is not permitted for a human being to speak. By his silence concerning so great a mystery he exalted it more highly and commended it more strongly. Hence Daniel is commanded: “Seal the book and close the mysteries; many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12). For the book remained closed and the mysteries sealed until the Lion of the tribe of Judah opened the book and loosed its seals.

There is a threefold Trinity: of persons in God, of substances in Christ, and of species in the sacrament. In the first, there are three persons in one substance—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—because “there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.” In the second, there are three substances in one person: divinity, body, and soul; for as [Col. 0214D] a rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and human being are one Christ. In the third, there are three species in one sacrament: bread, wine, and water; for bread does not become body without blood, nor are wine and water changed into blood without body, since neither can exist without the other, but rather the whole exists in the whole and the whole in the whole. [Note: Read: “part.”] The third, then, is ineffable; the second more ineffable; the first most ineffable, so to speak. In comparison with this most ineffable Trinity, [Col. 0215A] the other trinities are diminished.]

Thus, though for a hidden yet certain reason, it was provided that, since there are three groups of three in the nine orders of angels in the daily Preface, with the middle member removed, six would nevertheless be named from the individual orders.

For Dionysius declares that there are three orders of angels, each comprising three ranks, in order that the likeness of the Trinity may be intimated as impressed upon them. There are three higher, three lower, and three middle ranks. The higher are named seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; the middle, dominions, principalities, and powers; the lower, virtues, angels, and archangels. Therefore cherubim are omitted from the higher ranks, principalities from the middle, and archangels from the lower, because in comparison with the eternal Trinity, whose majesty is especially [Col. 0215B] commended there, every other trinity is found diminished and imperfect. For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?

For there it is read: “Through whom the angels praise your majesty, the dominions adore it, the powers tremble, the heavens and the virtues of heaven, and the blessed Seraphim, in shared exultation, celebrate it”; the thrones, indeed, are denoted by the name “heavens.” Yet a certain trace of the uncreated Trinity shines forth in all creatures: in angel, human being, and world alike. For the angel is addressed through the prophet: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of God’s paradise” (Ezek. 28). Of humankind Scripture testifies: “God made man in his image and likeness” [Col. 0215C] (Gen. 1). Of the world the Apostle affirms that “the invisible things of God, understood through those things that have been made, are seen from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1).

Each of these trinities—whether spiritual in angels, bodily in the world, or both spiritual and bodily in human beings—displays a certain likeness of the divine Trinity, but does not attain the truth of that likeness. For God made two principal creatures, the angelic and the worldly; he created the first spiritual and the other bodily. He placed his likeness in the first, but impressed the divine image upon the other; in both, however, there shines as it were a mirror of the eternal Trinity. For in the angelic creature are power, knowledge, and will, which so mutually embrace one another [Col. 0215D] that each contains the others: the angel can know and will as well as be able; he knows how to will and to be able; he wills to be able and to know.

Likewise, in the supreme and indivisible Trinity, power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and will to the Holy Spirit. The three persons in the Godhead so cohere with one another that, as the Catholic faith holds, they are one God: for the Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son; the Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, he himself says in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14).

Likewise, in human or worldly creation there shines forth a certain image, as it were, of the supreme Trinity. The world is great, beautiful, and useful: by its greatness it indicates the Creator’s power; by its beauty, the wisdom that orders it; by its usefulness, the benevolence of the one who governs it. For, in the saying of the Wise Man, “from the greatness of the beauty and of the creature their Creator may be known and seen.” Between angelic and worldly creation, however, humankind was made as a mean: bodily with the world according to the flesh, whose image it bears in itself; spiritual with the angel according to the soul, whose likeness it represents. Hence, according to the philosopher, man is called a microcosm, and according to the Psalmist, made a little lower than the angels. Thus it is fittingly read in Genesis that God made man in his image and likeness.

Moreover, although the ancient faithful possessed some knowledge of the Trinity before the Law—whence Abraham is described as having seen three [Col. 0216B] and is read to have worshipped one—and under the Law a somewhat greater knowledge—whence Isaiah heard seraphim crying one to another, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6)—yet the mystery—which has not even been fully revealed to us, nor will be fully revealed to anyone in this present life—was then more firmly concealed from them, though not altogether completely. The Son revealed it on behalf of the Father when he said to his disciples: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; and if you ask anything in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14). And again: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you [Col. 0216C] from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15); and especially: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), along with many passages of this kind.

But the Son will reveal the mystery of the Trinity more fully in the future, when, as he himself promises in the Gospel, he manifests himself to his elect; when all shall be taught by God; when we shall see not through a mirror in an enigma but face to face, and shall know as we are known. To signify this, therefore: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I am God, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; and I did not make known to them my name Adonai” (Exod. 6). This name *Adonai* was not unheard by the first [Col. 0216D] Fathers; rather, the mystery of Trinity and unity in God had not been made known to them except perhaps faintly. That mystery is more explicitly denoted by the name which the Greeks call the Tetragrammaton, because it is represented by four letters: I. E. V. E., for which the Jews pronounce *Adonai*. Since they call that name ineffable, they do not dare utter it, but pronounce another in its place. For the name *Adonai* is written with six letters, but the other is represented by only four: I. E. V. E. Although the Lord had shown himself almighty to the Jewish people in many ways, he did not disclose this name to them until he revealed, in part, to Moses the mystery of the Trinity—Moses, who drove the flock into the inner desert and ascended Mount Horeb, the mountain of God, leading the flock.

For this name, I. E. V. E., [Col. 0217A] is of such power, as the most learned Hebrews assert, that if it is divided into three words, so that each is separately pronounced, each represents the fullness of its name; and the second is taken from the first, so that the third receives from the first and second whatever it has. This can be more fully shown, in order to express the mystery of Trinity and unity, in the figure set below.

[Col. 0217B] Therefore, because each division has something in common with the others and none is wholly foreign to the others, each person in the Godhead is shown consubstantial with every other. Because the second division takes its first vowel from the first, while the last receives its first from the second and borrows its second from the preceding one, it is more expressly indicated that the Son is begotten of the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Moreover, although each division by itself represents a single name, the several divisions nevertheless represent one complete name. Thus in the Trinity each person is called, and is, God; yet we worship not three gods [Col. 0217C] but one, neither confusing the persons nor dividing the substance.

Again, this name has three letters, but the middle one is doubled, because in God there are three persons, but the middle one—that is, the Son—has a double relational reference, since he is from another and another is from him. Therefore, because before the old [Note: Thus in the copies; read “new.”] Moses, our king and lawgiver, came in the flesh and became obedient to the Father unto death, the mystery of the Trinity was hidden, since the veil of the Temple had not yet been torn from top to bottom and the stone had not been rolled from the entrance of the tomb, it is not surprising that the Psalmist did not express what even in his own time had been only half fully indicated.

To suggest this as well, Pharaoh’s magicians are recorded to have failed at the third sign—or, more truly, at the sign of the third plague. For they performed three signs which Moses had performed: first, when they turned rods into serpents; second, when they changed water into blood; third, when they brought frogs upon the land of Egypt. But the first sign was not a plague; and they were unable to perform the sign of the third plague, to turn dust into gnats, saying to Pharaoh: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8).

For natural philosophers, guided by reason, attained knowledge of the Father and Son, whom they called *to agathon kai noun*—“the Good and Intellect” [Note: Thus in the copies; but it appears that [Col. 0218C] *T’ agathon et noyn* should be read: Greek τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ νοῦν. See Aristotle, *Eudemian Ethics*, Book I, chapter 8.]—but they did not at all attain knowledge of the third person, namely the Holy Spirit, who is called the finger of God. As Truth declares in the Gospel: [Col. 0218A] “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke 11). Hence another Evangelist says “in the Spirit” instead of “by the finger.” They named God’s finger, though they did not know it; and therefore they could not perform the sign of the third plague.

[Whoever, then, arrives at knowledge of the indivisible Trinity without preaching or reading has it revealed not by human reason but by divine inspiration, as to him who is reported to have said: “The first Monad begot the second Monad; the first and second reflect their own ardor back into themselves.” Hence, when Peter said, “You are the Christ, Son of the living God,” he deserved to hear: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood have not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

Finally, the seven primitive days signify seven principal [Col. 0218B] periods: those of the patriarchs, judges, kings, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins. We omit their assignment at present, lest we seem to be composing a book rather than writing a letter. Since the period of kings occurs in third place, David, from whom the period of kings began, entirely passed over the praises of the third day, assigning no psalm to it, lest praise become soiled in his own mouth if he happened to commend himself on the third day. He preferred to be praised in another’s rather than his own tongue.

Secondly, you asked: since certain prayers are directed jointly to the whole Trinity, some specifically to the Father, and some specifically to the Son, why none is individually addressed to the person of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0218C] although he is often invoked in the hymns, whether metrical or rhythmic, used by the Church.]

We reply, therefore, that a special collect is not directed to the Holy Spirit because sin against the Holy Spirit is that sin unto death of which the Apostle John declares: “There is sin unto death; concerning it I say that no one should pray,” since sin against the Holy Spirit is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come, according to the testimony of Truth. Power is appropriated to the Father as principle; wisdom to the Son as Word; kindness to the Holy Spirit as gift. Or power is attributed to the Father, lest he appear powerless like an old man; wisdom to the Son, lest he be thought foolish like a child; kindness to the Holy Spirit, lest he be believed malicious like one puffed up. Hence one who sins through frailty or weakness sins against the Father; one who offends through simplicity or ignorance sins against the Son; but one who blasphemes through malice or envy blasphemes against the Holy Spirit. Therefore sin against the Father and Son is said to be remissible, because frailty or simplicity offers a certain excuse. But sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible, because malice entails every possible accusation. Therefore, because nothing escapes the Father’s power and nothing lies hidden from the Son’s wisdom, it was fitting that supplication be made in the collects to the Father and the Son.

Yet, since according to the Apostle the kindness of the Holy [Col. 0219A] Spirit always intercedes for us with unutterable groanings, making us intercede with unutterable groanings, it was unnecessary, for a clearer distinction of appropriations among the divine persons, to compose a proper collect addressed to the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, prayer is frequently directed in hymns to the Holy Spirit just as to the Father and Son, because a hymn was principally devised not for supplication but for rejoicing, whereas a collect was especially instituted not for rejoicing but for supplication.

Thus, in the office of the Mass, the antiphon sung at the Introit signifies the desire of the ancients for Christ’s coming—not always through the meaning of the words, but through the jubilation of the melody. For just as the bishop’s entrance to the altar signifies the Redeemer’s coming [Col. 0219B] into the world, so the Mass Introit expresses the desire of those concerning whom the Lord said to the apostles: “Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 6). The Introit is therefore sung in the person of those through whom Christ entered the world, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “And when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: ‘Let all God’s angels worship him’” (Heb. 1).

Or [a special collect is not directed to the Holy Spirit because in the ancient primitive Church all collects were made to the Father alone, on account of the authority of the principle, which Christ in the Gospel wholly attributes to him, from whom the Son himself is born and the Holy Spirit proceeds: “He who believes,” he says, “in me does not believe [Col. 0219C] in me, but in him who sent me” (John 12). Again: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7), because “I have not spoken from myself; but the Father who sent me has himself given me commandment what I should say and what I should speak” (John 12). And again: “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself; rather, the Father abiding in me himself does the works” (John 14).

For the Father alone is unbegotten and unborn, because he alone is from no one, while all things are from him: the Son through generation, the Holy Spirit through procession, and the world through creation. This is still observed in the Prefaces, which are universally directed to the Father alone. But because certain heretics began to teach [Col. 0219D] that Christ is not true God but a mere human being, giving, among other causes of their error, this also: that collects were not made to the Son as they were to the Father, as though the Son were not God as the Father is—therefore, to refute this perversity of error, the Church prudently instituted that collects should be directed to the Son as well as to the Father, for a fuller expression of his divinity. They added the following form of conclusion: “Who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, livest and reignest, God, for ever and ever”; and they extended this same form of conclusion to the other collects, so that the same divinity of Father and Son might be shown in them as well.

But because there were also other heretics [Col. 0220A] who said, erroneously, that the Holy Spirit is not God, the Church subsequently instituted in hymns and litanies proper and special prayers to the Holy Spirit as to the Father and Son, while preserving the ancient and customary form in the collects. Other prayers directed to the Holy Spirit are also found, but they are not regarded as authoritative, nor does the Church use them in the night or day offices.]

Behold, out of charity we have communicated to your brotherhood what we think. We admonish you that, if our answer has been insufficient, you should attribute it to our imperfection and constant occupations. With Martha we are continually occupied, and so devoted to Leah’s weak eyes that we can seldom attain Rachel’s beauty.

[Col. 0220B] Given at Anagni, 11 Kalends of January [22 December].

### CXCIV

[Note: This letter is cited by Bzovius, *Annales*, vol. XIII, p. 114, §13. See also Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §61.]

**To the King of England.** That he should observe the agreement entered into with the wife of his late brother, the king, concerning her dower, since she was nearly reduced to begging. (Anagni, 2 Nones of January [4 January].)

The more fervently we love your person, the more deeply we are troubled whenever we hear about the royal serenity things that darken your reputation before men and stain your conscience before God. Among other matters which we report with sorrow, it has been made known to us that, after Richard, king of illustrious memory, your brother, had formerly entered upon the way of all flesh, our most dear daughter in Christ B., former queen of England and his widow, [Col. 0220C] obtained our letters concerning the dower and half of the movables to which she was entitled by law and custom. You made an amicable settlement with her concerning these matters, provided, however, that if you or your heirs did not inviolably observe it, the queen would remain free to return to claiming her dower and the other things. You subsequently obtained apostolic confirmation of this settlement, yet you did not choose to preserve it unimpaired, as royal greatness required; instead, you have repeatedly acted wrongfully and oppressively toward the aforesaid queen.

Therefore, when the revenues granted her by you in that settlement, from which she could support herself, were withheld, the said queen was compelled to leave [Col. 0220D] your land and, almost cast aside and impoverished, to beg from the noble lady B., countess of Troyes, her sister. In this you appear both gravely to have offended God and incurred disgrace among human beings, since you ought not to be an oppressor of widows but a comforter of those who mourn. Wherefore we earnestly request and admonish your serenity, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: out of regard for divine mercy and in response to our prayers, restore all that has been taken from the aforesaid queen, satisfying her in these matters in such a manner that you may appease the divine majesty, which you have gravely offended thereby, and deserve praise and glory before men.

Otherwise, since we are especially debtors to widows and orphans in securing their justice, and since we are providing rather for your salvation, we have commanded our beloved sons, the abbots of Casemary, of the greater monastery of Tours, and of Versun [Note: Read: “of Virzione,” for this appears to concern the monastery of Virzione, whose abbot at that time was William I. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 138, record William from 1185 until 1209, when he died on 3 Nones of January.], of the diocese of Bourges, [Col. 0221A] that, after prior admonition, they compel you by ecclesiastical coercion, without appeal, to restore all that has been taken and to render before them full justice concerning the dower, half of the movables, and the other losses and injuries inflicted.

Given at Anagni, 2 Nones of January, in the sixth year.

### CXCV

**To the Prior of Saint Mary the New of Monte Peloso.** That he present himself before the pope to hear the claims of the clergy and people. (Anagni, 3 Nones of January [3 January].)

[Col. 0221B]

As the beloved sons, the clergy and people of Monte Peloso, have taken care to inform us, they consider themselves not a little burdened by the sentence which Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, pronounced against them, because the merits of the case were not fully made known to them. They therefore humbly petitioned us to provide for them in this matter with paternal solicitude. Although nothing should rashly be undertaken against a sentence pronounced by our said predecessor, nevertheless we neither ought nor wish to refuse to hear their just complaint. By apostolic letters we command your discretion that within one month you present yourself before us, either personally or through a suitable representative, so that, in the presence of you or [Col. 0221C] your representative, they may set forth those grounds by which they intend to incline us to restore them a hearing. Once the truth has been ascertained, with God as author, we shall proceed as prudent counsel determines ought to be done.

Given at Anagni, 3 Nones of January.

### CXCVI

**To the Bishop of Pécs.** That he take more diligent care of his reputation. (Anagni, 7 Ides of January [7 January].)

Although we have often turned away our ears from that detestable accusation laid before us against you, which you utterly deny having been committed, and have often declined to order an inquiry into it—especially [Col. 0221D] because we could not in any way believe such things of your brotherhood, and do not believe them even now—yet, since this denunciation did not cease to importune our hearing, we could not at last refuse the duty of our office. For, according to the Apostle, we have become debtors to wise and foolish alike. Sparing you wherever we could consistently with our honor, we secretly ordered our venerable brother, the bishop of Győr (thus written), to investigate that charge [Col. 0222A] in order that your reputation might be cleared and the wicked perversity of your detractors put to shame.

Accordingly, since our venerable brothers C., bishop of Agria; B., bishop of Vác; H., bishop of Várad; K., bishop of Veszprém; and J., bishop of Istria, together with many other prelates of churches and the same bishop of Győr, have endeavored before us to excuse you in these matters and have amply commended your person for moral integrity and other qualities, we earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood to take care to erase the name of such a crime and to strive to conduct yourself in such a way that the earlier accusation may seem frivolous; that, cleansed of the stain of wicked detraction, the reputation of your name may rise more brightly in praise; and that those who pretended falsely to be truthful may appear liars.

[Col. 0222B] Given at Anagni, 3 Ides of January [11 January].

### CXCVII

**To the Abbot of Pratea** [Note: [Col. 0221D] At that time the abbey of Pratea was governed by Evrardus, concerning whom the authors of the new [Col. 0222D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 208, provide these few details:

> “VIII. Evrardus, in 1202, from a charter of William, archbishop of Bourges. In 1206 he found Odo, lord of Issoudun, a beneficent patron.”]

**To the Priors of Issoudun and Nohant, of the Diocese of Bourges.** That they ensure that W. de Securo is received as canon and brother by the bishop and dean of Clermont. (Anagni, Nones of January [5 January].)

Moved by the benevolence of the Apostolic See, which is accustomed to provide for those in need, we commanded the bishop [Note: He has already been mentioned above. See Letter 136 of Book V, note.] and chapter of Clermont that, upon the free resignation of its holder, they should without difficulty confer upon our beloved son W. de Securo—then a deacon, now a priest, concerning whose fitness [Col. 0222C] we have received the testimony of many—the prebend which our beloved son A., a canon of Paris, held in their church.

Furthermore, we commanded our venerable brother . . . archbishop [Note: [Col. 0222D] See letter 52 of Book V, note], and our beloved son . . . dean, of Bourges, that if the bishop and chapter should refuse to carry our mandate into effect, they themselves should not delay to execute our mandate in this matter, notwithstanding any objection or appeal, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure. But when the same bishop and chapter, repeatedly required by the archbishop and dean, as we have learned from their letters, neither wished, upon A.’s free resignation, to confer the prebend upon the same W., nor to appear in their presence, nor to show a reasonable cause against him, [Col. 0222D] they at length took care, by our authority, to invest that same priest with the prebend itself, enjoining the bishop and chapter to receive him as canon and brother and to treat him with fraternal charity.

Now, since the bishop and chapter resisted our mandate with excessive contumacy, as was unbecoming in them, the archbishop and dean, acting on the advice of prudent men, caused the church of Clermont and the other churches spiritually subject to the chapter to be placed under ecclesiastical interdict. Yet they afterward celebrated the divine offices in the principal church, disregarding the sentence of interdict. Therefore, since action must be taken against those who are disobedient to apostolic commands, by these apostolic letters we command and enjoin your discretion diligently to investigate the truth concerning the foregoing. If it is established that the aforesaid bishop and chapter rashly acted contrary to the sentence of interdict and celebrated in an interdicted church, suspend the bishop himself from pontifical office and the chapter from every office and benefice, and cause them to remain suspended until that bishop, in person or at least through a suitable representative, and the chapter, through four or three of their number in the name of the whole body, come into our presence [Col. 0223B] to make satisfaction to us for so grave an offence; and until they nevertheless receive the aforesaid priest as canon and brother and treat him with due charity. Witnesses, etc. No letters, etc. But if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the Nones of January, in the sixth year [Note: [Col. 0223D] See letter 37 of Book V, note].

## CXCVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

That he should induce the clergy to chastity. (Anagni, 16 Kalends of January [17 December].)

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, although you persecute the detestable vice of fornication and prescribe purity to the ministers of the altar, so that many, at [Col. 0223C] your exhortation and correction, have risen from the wallowing-place of mire and have resolved to serve the Lord in bodily chastity and purity of heart, nevertheless certain persons are still becoming foul in their foulness and returning to their vomit. Moreover, many canons of cathedral churches publicly keep concubines in their homes and show them, as it were, marital affection.

Wishing therefore, as far as lies in us, to apply a remedy to this disease, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin your fraternity that, if you find their bishops negligent in this matter, you compel both those canons and the other clerics established in your province to put away the concubines whom they publicly maintain—after prior warning—by suspension and, if necessary, deprivation of their benefices, appeal set aside. You are also to admonish and diligently induce the fathers, brothers, and kinsmen of such women to receive them, and even to compel them, insofar as you see fit.

Given at Anagni, 16 Kalends of January.

## CXCIX. TO THE SAME

On the penance to be imposed upon a cleric falsely accused. (Anagni, 16 Kalends of January [17 December].)

It was represented to us on your behalf that a certain cleric went over to the king’s enemies and revealed to them whatever he knew of royal secrets. Although he was often forbidden to return to the king, because he did not obey the prohibition but shamelessly presented himself before the eyes of the king’s household, he was seized and beaten by the king’s officers, as his wrongdoing demanded. Since you ask whether those who beat him incur the penalty of the promulgated canon, we reply that they have incurred it.

Moreover, since penance, in order to be meritorious, must be voluntary and not forced, we do not think that that cleric should be compelled against his will to do penance, when, falsely accused of a crime and convicted, he makes pecuniary satisfaction according to the custom of the land.

Given at Anagni, 16 Kalends of January.

## CC. TO THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 0224D] See letter 9 of this Book VI], AND CHAPTER OF REIMS

Upon rejecting the election of John, bishop of Beauvais, as archbishop of Reims, commands them to proceed without delay to another election. (Anagni, 4 Ides of January [10 January].)

[Col. 0224B]

After the death of W . . . , archbishop of Reims, of good memory, when you had appointed a day to discuss the appointment of a pastor and could not reach unanimous agreement, you, son Dean, and others, the greater in number and higher in dignity, agreed upon the postulation of our venerable brother John, bishop of Beauvais. But Theobald of Perche, the chief archdeacon, and certain others refused to consent to that postulation. Accordingly, when appeals had been made by both sides to the Apostolic See [Col. 0224C] and the matter had been litigated for some time first before us and afterward before delegated judges, the same case was at last remitted to us by them.

Therefore, after granting a full hearing to you and the other party, we carefully understood all that you wished to advance. Finally, having heard the reasons, testimonies, and admissions of both parties, since it was clearly established that, after an appeal lawfully lodged with us, proceedings toward the aforesaid postulation had been conducted irregularly through rash presumption arising from indiscreet zeal, we have, by the common counsel of our brethren and as justice required, judged that postulation to be rejected.

But lest your Church remain longer bereft of a pastor, by apostolic letters [Col. 0224D] we command your whole body that, within a month after receipt of our letters, you assemble together and, invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, canonically elect a suitable person as your pastor, and have him suitably consecrated as bishop by the suffragans of the Church of Reims as quickly as this can be done. The Most High will demand an account from you at the examination of strict judgment unless, setting aside human favour and worldly fear, you strive to set over that Church a person whom, according to your conscience, you judge suitable in spiritual and temporal matters.

But if perhaps you neglect to fulfil our command, know that we have ordered by our letters our venerable brother . . . bishop of Auxerre, and our beloved sons . . . abbot of Perseigne and Master R. of Courson, canon of Noyon, [Col. 0225A] that they, supported by our authority and setting aside every objection or appeal, with God before their eyes, appoint for you as bishop a suitable person equal to so great a burden and honour; cause him to be consecrated by the suffragans of the Church of Reims as stated above; and restrain any opponents or rebels, after warning, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

Given at Anagni, 4 Ides of January, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

Instructions have been written to them on this matter.

## CCI. TO THE NOBLEMAN, THE DUKE OF AUSTRIA

Confirmation of the judgment that he is not bound to contract the marriage promised by oath with the daughter of the duke of Bohemia, because the condition had not been fulfilled. (Anagni, 7 Ides of January [7 January].)

[Col. 0225B]

It was represented to us on your behalf that formerly, after betrothing . . . daughter of the nobleman . . . duke of Bohemia under a condition, you firmly promised, indeed also confirmed by oath, that you would take her as wife, provided that he should in no way separate her mother from himself. But when the duke himself had entirely separated her mother from himself, you refused to contract marriage with the daughter; and, after the duke himself had been released from the oath he had taken, [Col. 0225C] you likewise were released by him from the oath you had taken to him.

Subsequently, at your request, we committed an inquiry into these matters to our venerable brother . . . archbishop of Salzburg, to determine what he believed expedient. Having fully learned the truth, he declared that you were not bound to this union. Therefore, since that declaration was reasonably made after the truth had been investigated and ascertained, we will and command that it be held valid, and by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to act against it.

Given at Anagni, 7 Ides of January.

## CCII. TO THE ARCHDEACON OF VICENZA

Confirms him in the archdeaconry. (Anagni, 3 Nones of January [3 January].)

[Col. 0225D]

When a dispute that had arisen between you on the one side and our beloved sons . . . archpriest and canons of the church of Vicenza on the other concerning the archdeaconry of that church had formerly been committed by us to the bishop of Feltre, of good memory [Note: [Col. 0225D] See letter 39 of Book III, note], and that bishop, having understood the arguments of both parties, had by judgment adjudged the archdeaconry itself, together with the choir stall, to you, subjecting to excommunication those who should thereafter presume to molest you in this matter; and when afterward, with the representatives of both parties present before us, [Col. 0226A] the matter had been litigated for some time before our beloved son O . . . , our subdeacon and chaplain, whom we had appointed as their auditor; with the consent of those representatives, we committed the case to our beloved sons Master R. Tropen., dean, Viviano of Verona, and Walpert of Treviso, canons then residing at Bologna. We ordered them to proceed, after due consideration, according to the terms of the earlier commission, setting aside the obstacle of appeal, and provided that the said dean, with one of the others, should not fail to execute this if the third could not be present with them.

After proceedings in the case had been conducted by the dean and Viviano, who received witnesses on your behalf, and after both your representative and the representative of the canons had again appeared in our presence with the depositions and other instruments relevant to the case, [Col. 0226B] we granted them our beloved son B. [Note: [Col. 0226D] See letter 54 of Book III, note], cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, as auditor. Before him your representative asserted that, when the said judges wished to proceed with hearing the case in accordance with our mandate and the canons of Vicenza, summoned by them, refused to come to Bologna, alleging the dangers of the roads, the judges went to Vicenza, both to expose their malice and to learn the truth of the affair more effectively. When the canons maliciously objected that the case ought to be heard only at Bologna, where it had been committed, and absented themselves contumaciously, the judges, following the advice of prudent men learned [Col. 0226C] in law, proceeded in the case. Having fully understood your allegations and arguments and examined the instruments and the statements of witnesses produced on your behalf, they adjudged that you should be protected in possession of the archdeaconry in accordance with the judgment of the aforesaid bishop of Feltre, ordering by our authority, under penalty of excommunication, that no molestation be brought against you concerning possession of the archdeaconry, either within or outside the city of Vicenza.

The representative of the canons, however, replied that, because the aforesaid judges denied the canons time for deliberation, demanding pledges of fifty pounds from them, and because the canons could not obtain a copy of the apostolic rescript—which they urgently requested—in order to decide whether they wished to contest or abandon the dispute, they considered themselves thereby aggrieved and appealed to the Apostolic See. Rejecting the said Viviano as suspect, they were prepared immediately to prove that a blood relationship existed between him and you. But although the aforesaid Walpert admitted their appeal, the other two, disregarding it, nevertheless proceeded to render judgment, from which an appeal was again made on behalf of the canons.

When, therefore, the aforesaid cardinal had faithfully reported this to us, since the depositions clearly established that the archdeaconry [Col. 0227A] had continuously been assigned by the bishops of Vicenza to two archdeacons before you, without objection by the canons, and since the canons ought not to have rejected the aforesaid judge or requested a copy of the rescript—because the case had been delegated to those judges with the consent of the representatives of both parties, and the rescript had been obtained jointly from them—nor ought they to have requested time for deliberation, because the suit had been formally joined before the Apostolic See through the representatives of both sides: notwithstanding such frivolous objections, we have caused the aforesaid archdeaconry to be adjudged to you by definitive judgment. We impose perpetual silence upon the canons of Vicenza from any claim against you concerning that archdeaconry, including the stall assigned to the archdeacon and all its other appurtenances, [Col. 0227B] while reserving to them, however, the question of proprietary right concerning the collation of that archdeaconry, should they wish to litigate it against the bishop of Vicenza [Note: [Col. 0227D] See letter 126 of Book V, note], since a matter transacted between others ought not to create prejudice for others.

Given at Anagni, 3 Nones of January.

Letters have been written to our venerable brethren . . . of Verona, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0227D] See letter 39 of Book III, note], and . . . of Feltre [Note: [Col. 0227D] Ibid., note], and the bishop of Belluno [Note: [Col. 0227D] Ibid., note], that they are to ensure observance of the aforesaid judgment and cause F. peacefully to possess the archdeaconry itself, together with the choir stall assigned to the archdeacon and all its other appurtenances, through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

Given as above.

## CCIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF OSMA, BURGOS, AND ZAMORA

Commits to them the accusation brought against the bishop of Astorga. (Anagni, 2 Ides of January [12 January].)

[Col. 0227C]

Our beloved son D., canon of Astorga, appearing before the Apostolic See, alleged before us many grave charges against our venerable brother L., bishop of Astorga, concerning which he intended to accuse him criminally: namely, that while his predecessor was still alive, forcibly expelled from his see and also despoiled of the bishopric, he rashly usurped his place through ambition; that he was tainted by the crime of perjury and by the depravity of simony; and that he had moreover promoted two murderers, appointing one as archdeacon and another, born illegitimate, to the office of deacon. Further, that he was publicly notorious for homicide: namely, that he had caused Master Michael, doctor of laws, to be killed by arranging the crime of poisoning.

Conversely, our beloved sons F. John, archdeacon, and P., canon of Astorga, appearing for the bishop, replied that the aforesaid [Col. 0228A] D. had incurred perjury and had launched into accusing the bishop without any prior warning. They also alleged that he was a layman, undisciplined, a striker and brawler, lacking clerical respectability, a conspirator, and marked by the infamy of the sodomitical crime, asserting that he had been caught in this unspeakable vice and had likewise incurred homicide at Rome.

Because charges of this gravity ought not to pass unnoticed, with the consent of the aforesaid D. and the representatives of the said bishop we have committed the case to your examination. By apostolic letters we command you, after summoning the parties to a suitable place, to hear what they may choose to submit; and unless the aforesaid D. can be excluded from the accusation by a lawful exception, carefully examine the case, appeal set aside, as far as final judgment, [Col. 0228B] and transmit it to our presence adequately prepared, fixing for the parties a suitable term at which they may come to receive what justice shall decree. If one of them should perhaps neglect to come at that term, we shall nevertheless proceed as far as we can according to law. No letters are to obstruct this, apart from the consent of the parties . . . and if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, 2 Ides of January.

## CCIV. TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 0227D] John I, called of the Cell, then presided over the abbey of St Albans as its twenty-first abbot. He was appointed successor to Abbot Warin, who died in 1195 on 3 Kalends of May [29 April], and died in the year of the Lord 1214. “A man,” says Matthew Paris, “of exceptional piety, a lover of order and of the vigour of monastic discipline. In his youth a constant attendee at the Paris schools, he deserved to attain the company of the chosen masters; hence, when he had reached manhood, he might be considered a Priscian in grammar, an Ovid in metre, and a Galen in physics.” MATTHEW PARIS, *Lives of the Twenty-Three Abbots of St Albans*, Works, vol. I, p. 103], AND CONVENT OF ST ALBANS

That they should take possession of a certain church in order to pay the debts of its deceased holder, a crusader. (Anagni, 18 Kalends of February [15 January].)

[Col. 0228C]

We regard it as grave and vexatious that, on the basis of certain letters obtained from us while the truth was concealed, you granted to another, after his death, the church which Roger of St Edmund, of good memory, held from you. In so doing, you disregarded the mandate of the Apostolic See and the ordinance solemnly issued concerning certain debts to be paid from his benefices, under the indulgence of the Apostolic See granted to crusaders in England. Even if the same church had meanwhile been conferred on another, it ought rather to have been restored to the man whom, before the aforesaid Roger received it through royal favour, you had, as we have learned, canonically presented to it. For by your presentation alone he had acquired, according to the canons, a right in [Col. 0228D] that church, since the right of patronage is held more fully by clerics than by laymen.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your devotion, relying on our authority and setting aside every objection, appeal, and excuse, to take that same church into your own hands, removing from it every holder and faithfully collecting its revenues, [Col. 0229A] so that, at our command, they may be applied to payment of the money for which the aforesaid R., by our special indulgence in addition to the general indulgence granted to crusaders by our predecessors, obligated them for up to three years. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See may obstruct this, since this command proceeds from us with certain knowledge. Therefore, should executors have been obtained from us concerning the same church, we do not wish their acts of execution to have force, since, according to ecclesiastical and civil constitutions, a petitioner who lies ought to forfeit what he has obtained.

But if, through fear or favour—which we do not believe—you neglect to fulfil our command, this will undoubtedly redound upon your own head, since we grant you full power, appeal set aside, to restrain any opponents [Col. 0229B] who may exist.

Given at Anagni, 18 Kalends of February.

## CCV. TO MASTER MARTIN, CLERIC OF HOLY CROSS, COIMBRA

Receives him under protection. (Anagni, 9 Kalends of February [24 January].)

“Just requests,” etc., as far as “we grant”; we receive your person, with all, etc., under the form of protection. We particularly confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority the benefice which you hold from the church of Holy Cross of Coimbra, insofar as you possess it justly and peaceably, etc. “Let no one therefore,” etc.

Given at Anagni, 9 Kalends of February.

## CCVI. TO THE NOBLEMEN MANUEL, JAMES, ODO, CENSIUS, AND DEODATUS FRANGIPANI

Settles the disputes between them and the people of Terracina. (Anagni, 14 Kalends of February [19 January].)

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Raynaldus cites this letter and also reproduces the wording of the instrument by which the people of Terracina took the oath of fidelity to the pope, under the year 1204, §76.]

[Col. 0229C]

While you held Traversa through the Roman Church, the people of Terracina endeavoured to take it from you. When this came to our knowledge, we sent to them our beloved son P. Saxon, our subdeacon and chaplain, firmly forbidding them to presume in any way to demolish it; but they wholly refused to obey our mandate. Yet, dealing more gently with them, we sent to them our beloved son Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin, [Col. 0229D] admonishing and strictly enjoining them through him more prudently to remedy what they had rashly done. But, contemptuously disregarding our commands and the admonitions of the aforesaid cardinal, as was unbecoming in them, they took no care to do so.

Wishing to overcome evil with good, we ordered them by our letters at least to render you justice under our examination. When they refused, alleging certain frivolous excuses, we took note of their contumacy and bound the consuls of Terracina, their councillors, and their principal supporters with the bond of excommunication; and we withdrew fealty from [Col. 0230A] the entire people, commanding all our faithful established throughout Campania and the Maritime Province to provide you counsel and aid in making war upon the people of Terracina. Thereafter, when they had been attacked by you and our other faithful, and affliction had begun to give them understanding, they humbly rendered oaths of fidelity to us and to the Roman Church, firmly promising under oath that in our presence they would render you the fullness of justice.

When subsequently, at the term which we had fixed for you and them, you and the syndicus of Terracina, with certain leading men of the city, were present before us and our brethren, you urgently sought restoration of Traversa and suitable satisfaction for the losses inflicted and injuries done [Col. 0230B] to you.

The syndicus of Terracina, however, through his advocate replied to the contrary that you and your forebears had inflicted through Traversa many and great injuries and losses, grave and enormous burdens and affronts, upon the people of Terracina. It had therefore been lawful for them to occupy Traversa—the source of every evil—in order to avoid a danger which they could not otherwise escape. He sought restitution of the captives to them, after they had sworn to obey our command concerning the doing of justice.

Further, he alleged that, because your forebears had compelled them to abjure the oaths of fidelity by which they were bound to the Apostolic See, to which the lordship of Terracina specially belonged, [Col. 0230C] and to swear fidelity to you and them against all men, and because faith need not in any way be kept with those who do not keep faith with their lords, it had been lawful for them to cast off your dominion and return, with all possible speed, to the dominion of the Church, to which ownership was known to belong. The same syndicus added that, if they had perhaps incurred our indignation or offence by what they had done, they were prepared to make satisfaction to us according to our will and pleasure. He further asserted that, when they had repeatedly complained to our predecessors concerning your forebears and reported the burdens and injuries inflicted upon them, some of those predecessors had allowed them, if they could, to occupy Traversa in order to avert such dangers.

You, however, through your advocate denied all these allegations, asserting that, even if they had been proved, they could not in law prevent the benefit of restitution, adducing many arguments and laws on this point—especially since you had suffered greater injuries at their hands than they had suffered from you. After the dispute had been argued for some time before us by both parties, we, having heard and fully understood the arguments of each side, decreed in judgment, by counsel of our brethren, that Traversa should be restored to you with compensation [Col. 0231A] for damages, on the condition that, when they restore it, they assign it to be held for us until, having fully investigated the losses inflicted and injuries done on both sides, we settle these questions through justice and amicable concord, providing complete security and peace for each party. We further enjoin you to surrender their captives into our hands, while they are in no way to prevent you from exercising the customary rights which you are known to have received at Terracina until the time of the dispossession.

In order that this judgment, rendered after prudent deliberation, may be inviolably observed, we confirm it by apostolic authority, etc. “Let no one therefore,” etc.

Given at Anagni, 14 Kalends of February.

## TEXT OF THE INSTRUMENT

[Col. 0231B] By which the people of Terracina tender the oath of fidelity to the pope.

[In the name of Christ. Amen. We, the consuls and people of Terracina, from this hour forward shall be true faithful and liege men of Lord Pope Innocent and his successors and of the Roman Church. We shall not be, by word, deed, counsel, or consent, party to their losing life or limb or being taken by evil capture. We shall reveal to no one, to their harm, any counsel entrusted to us by them. If we should learn of any certain harm to them, we shall prevent it to the extent of our power. If perhaps we cannot prevent it ourselves, we shall report it, in person or through letters or our messengers, as quickly as we can to them or [Col. 0231C] to such a person as we believe will faithfully inform them.

We shall assist in retaining and defending the Roman papacy and the regalia of Saint Peter, which it holds both in the city and outside the city, and expressly Terracina with all its appurtenances; and in recovering, against all men, what it does not hold. Moreover, at their command we shall make war and peace against all men. We shall restore to the lord pope the fortress of Circeii and deliver it to whomever he commands. We shall also give the fortifications which we hold around the city, namely mountainous Peselum and Ferronum, to be held for the use and at the command of the lord pope; and we shall take them away neither by force nor fraud from those who hold them by his command. At his command we shall also render all regalian rights and revenues which the Roman Church has been accustomed and ought to have in that city and its appurtenances.

If the Frangipani press claims, we shall do them justice under the examination of the lord pope, provided that they likewise render us justice before him. All the foregoing we swear henceforth to observe in good faith and with right intention. So may God help us, and these holy Gospels of God.]

## CCVII. TO GONÇALO, PRIOR OF THE CHURCH OF HOLY CROSS, COIMBRA, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY

Receives them under the protection of St Peter and enumerates the possessions belonging to them. (Anagni, Ides of January [13 January].)

[Note: [Col. 0231D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §81.]

[Col. 0232A]

The care of the universal Church has been granted us by God, the provider of all good things, in order that we may cherish religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever gratefully rendered to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, etc., as far as “we grant”; following the example of Innocent II, Lucius, Eugenius, Adrian, Alexander, Urban, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs our predecessors of happy memory, we receive the aforesaid church—which is known to belong by right and ownership to blessed Peter—into the special protection of the Apostolic See, etc., as far as “we protect.” First, indeed, establishing, etc. Moreover, whatever, etc. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint John situated in the suburb of Coimbra, belonging to the aforesaid church of Holy Cross, as it is known to have been granted you by John, archbishop of Braga, and B., bishop of Coimbra, both of good memory, with the consent of A., duke of Portugal, of illustrious memory; all the churches of Lairen, both in its castle and in its territory, [Col. 0232C] with all that belongs to them, as is contained in the charter of the aforesaid duke and in the confirmation of Gilbert, bishop of Lisbon, of good memory; the church of Quiaios; also the houses which you bought to safeguard the bodies of kings, because of fear of the Saracens; and a part of Vila Franca, as all the aforementioned things were adjudged to you by our judgment against our venerable brother, the bishop of Coimbra; the hermitage of Arganil; the church of Alcuba in the diocese of Viseu, by grant of the bishop of Ciudad Rodrigo, with the consent of Ferdinand, king of León, of illustrious memory; in the city of Rodrigo, the church of Saint Michael and the church of Holy Cross of Cortes, and whatever you hold within the boundaries of that city; [Col. 0232D] likewise whatever the aforesaid duke granted you from his own right in the city of Coimbra, namely: Almonia with its revenues; the revenues of Eiras; and two vineyards there, free of every payment; a part of all the revenues of his mills in that city; one watermill at Matilas with four whole *canarii*; a share of all fish called *savales* [sic]; the vineyard which Fernando Petri gave you with the consent of that same duke; the village of Quiaios; the village of Laurizal; the village of Mosceti; the village of Talazeiro; whatever you possess along the coast; the village [Col. 0233A] of Saint Romanus; the village of Saint Marina; the village of Lagares; the village of Candaosa; whatever you possess in the district of Sena, and in Gaudela, Linares, Celorico, Covilhã, Ablantes, Scarnen., Alenquer, Lisbon, Sintra, Jorres, Jamugia, Alcanedi, and in the territories of all these places; whatever you possess in the diocese of Viseu; all the hereditary estates which A., king of Portugal, of illustrious memory, gave you in Alvorge, Germanelo, and Atcania; the valley called Alzazer, within its boundaries; likewise the island called Ozerroa; and whatever you possess in the district of Coimbra as far as the river called Dorium, and in the district of Braga.

Moreover, following the example of our aforesaid predecessors Eugenius and Lucius, we strictly forbid that from your labours, etc.

We further forbid that any of your brethren, etc. If any free and unencumbered person wishes to enter your church and there assume the regular habit, or if any clerical or secular person wishes, from pious regard, to confer upon you any of his goods, let no one dare prevent this. Moreover, following the example of our aforesaid predecessor Celestine, we more strictly prohibit any bishop from daring, in churches known to belong to you by right of foundation, to ordain anyone except upon your presentation; or from presuming, without manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce sentences of interdict or excommunication upon your churches or their persons, [Col. 0233C] or to burden them with new and undue exactions.

Following also in the footsteps of the aforesaid Adrian, we grant you permission freely to assign to your hospital the tithes of your produce that are contained within the bounds of your parish. But when a general interdict, etc. Chrism, however, etc. Upon your death, etc. Moreover, the burial place of that site, etc. Likewise, peace, etc. Moreover, freedom, etc. We therefore decree, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishops in the aforesaid churches. As a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay two bezants annually, as the right of the Roman Church, to us and our successors. If therefore anyone, etc. But to all, etc.

[Col. 0233D] Given at Anagni, by the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of January, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1203.

## CCVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF WELLS

That they should receive Master Roger Porretan as canon and brother. (Anagni, 18 Kalends of February [15 January].)

CCVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF WELLS. That they are to receive Master R. Porretanus as a canon and brother. (Anagni, 18 Kalends of February [15 January].)

Master R. Porretanus, subdeacon, our beloved son, appearing before us, humbly informed us that, although he had canonically obtained a prebend in your church, certain laymen were causing him serious annoyance concerning it. Our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Bath, [Note: [Col. 0233D] See letter 90 of book five, note.] having been petitioned by religious men to confer upon him another prebend which he might possess peacefully, granted him, upon the death of W. de Pleiz, a canon of Wells, that man’s prebend—namely, the church of Saint Decumanus with its appurtenances. After the resignation of the prebend which he had previously held, the bishop caused him to be solemnly invested with it before our venerable brother . . . , archbishop of Canterbury, and many others; he then assigned the resigned prebend to a clerk of that same archbishop who possessed other benefices.

After this had been done, the same R., lest anything be done to his prejudice, appealed to our jurisdiction concerning that prebend. Yet a certain clerk, named J., asserting that he possessed letters from the bishop of Bath concerning the second prebend to become vacant—letters which stated that the same archbishop was executor in this matter—lodged an appeal with us against the aforesaid R. W. de Wrotham, servant of our dearest son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of the English, who hitherto, it is said, had been accustomed to live as a layman, fled to the refuge of appeal in order to hinder R. He alleged that, after the aforesaid W. de Pleiz had obtained the said prebend, the bishop of Bath had agreed between them that W. de Pleiz, during his lifetime, should spend five marks yearly upon him from the revenues of the same prebend, and that, after his death, W. de Wrotham should have the whole prebend entirely.

But when the bishop, through . . . , vice-archdeacon of the place, had ordered the aforesaid R. to be put into corporeal possession of the same prebend, and a certain chapel belonging to the prebend had been assigned to him by that official, and both had gone together to the mother church so that it too might similarly be assigned to him, they found there, on behalf of the said W. de Wrotham, armed men. These men violently laid hands on them and shamefully expelled them from the parish. Consequently the bishop of Bath caused them to be publicly proclaimed excommunicate throughout his diocese, and placed under interdict the aforesaid church, which the same W. de Wrotham had occupied by intrusion. Subsequently, however, after a month had elapsed, that sentence was relaxed, to the grave prejudice of R.; and the bishop drew up anew an instrument for the aforesaid W. de Wrotham concerning the prebend itself.

Since, therefore, we have heard laudable testimony concerning the learning and morals of the aforesaid R., both from the bishop of Bath himself and from the archdeacon of the place, as well as from many other prelates, in their letters—for they also took care to write to us concerning the foregoing—and since it would be exceedingly unworthy that one thus circumvented by such fraud should be deprived of the benefit of provision, when he has no other benefice: by these apostolic writings we command and enjoin your discretion that you treat the aforesaid R. kindly as your brother and canon, and that, so far as lies in your power, you do not permit him to be hindered concerning that prebend or the rights belonging to it.

Given at Anagni, 18 Kalends of February [15 January].

CCIX. TO P., CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF ST MARCELLUS, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He rejoices that he arrived in Cyprus in aid of the Holy Land, and leaves to his judgment whether he ought to communicate with the excommunicated Venetians. (Anagni, 10 Kalends of February [23 January].)

That, by the Lord’s command, calm came upon the winds and sea while you were sailing; that he who raised up blessed Peter walking upon the waves lest he should sink led you, after crossing the sea, into the desired harbour; that in our stead you strengthened our brethren and fellow bishops in Cyprus; that, having corrected what among them required correction, you established those things which you knew to be expedient for the glory of the divine name, the advancement of the Christian faith, the honour of the Apostolic See, and their salvation; and that, after calming the war which had arisen at Acre between the Pisans and Genoese, you established a truce between them, not without anxious effort and immense labour—all this gives us joy, and we render thanks to him without whom neither the planter nor the waterer is anything; from whom comes every good gift and every perfect present; and who, even when our strength fails, does not forsake us, directs our steps, and makes our deeds acceptable to himself.

We likewise commend your devotion in the Lord, since, sparing neither person nor property, you strive commendably to discharge the office of legation imposed upon you, so that the peoples through whom you pass, seeing your good works, may glorify your Father who is in heaven and humbly reverence the Roman Church in you. We have graciously received the letters which your devotion sent us, as was fitting, and have carefully noted what you communicated through them concerning both the progress of the Christian army and the affair of the Empire of Constantinople, the condition of the province of Jerusalem, the messengers of the Christians sent to Saladin, and other matters.

But because you doubt whether, having been sent in aid of those who have taken the cross, should the army go to the regions of Jerusalem or should you reach it, you may communicate with the Venetians while they remain under excommunication—since you cannot avoid them without scandal, especially since even their envoys were recently scandalized because you would not communicate with them when they came to you—and because you devoutly seek our counsel on this matter, [we briefly reply that you should diligently warn and induce the Doge and the Venetians to repent of what they have done and to obtain the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church. But if they should perhaps decide to persist in their contumacy, we leave it to you, who, being present, can better discern the needs of the Eastern province, the circumstances of affairs, and the character of persons, to do without stain of sin that which you know to be more expedient. For the law also provides that, if anyone travels through the land of heretics or of any excommunicated persons, he may communicate with them in buying and receiving necessities; and, with respect to participation with an excommunicated head of household, the household is excused. Necessity, especially when one is engaged in a necessary task, excuses much and in many cases.]

For when the Lord, as we know you have read in the Gospel, passed through grainfields on the Sabbath, and his disciples plucked ears of grain and ate them, rubbing them in their hands, and certain Pharisees cried out against the disciples, “Why do you do what is not lawful on the Sabbaths?” (Luke 6), Jesus is recorded as replying to them: “Have you not even read what David did when he himself and those with him were hungry: how he entered the house of God, took the loaves of presentation, and gave them to those who were with him—loaves which none but priests were permitted to eat?” (ibid.). He then added: “And the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath” (ibid.); and this affair too is the affair of the Son of Man. Therefore, if urgent necessity requires you to communicate with the Venetians, whom you cannot avoid without grave scandal and great loss, be secure in our indulgence and have no fear whatever of incurring a stain of sin on that account.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your discretion, and by apostolic writings command you, to carry out the legation of Christ which you hold, and for which you have in some measure denied yourself, in such a way that you may obtain glory in the present and eternal reward in the future, and that we may be bound to attend ever more fully, day by day, to your honour.

Given at Anagni, 10 Kalends of February [23 January].

CCX. [Note: [Col. 0236D] A portion of this letter is printed by Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 97, § I. Raynaldus printed it entire under the year 1203, § 17.] LETTER OF ALEXIUS, EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He acknowledges the Roman pontiff as head of the universal Church and swears devotion. Given in the Imperial City, 8 Kalends of September [25 August].

To the most holy father and lord, I., by the grace of God supreme pontiff, ALEXIUS, faithful emperor in Christ, crowned by God, ruler of the Romans and ever augustus, devoted filial obedience with reverence.

What great things the Lord has done for me in these days according to his mercy I thought ought especially to be explained to your Blessedness, which is known to hold his place on earth, in whose hands are all powers and all rights of kingdoms. I am devoted to God and to your Holiness in thanksgiving, and I am bound, as is fitting, and shall remain bound for ever.

Your Holiness knows more fully that, parricide having been committed against a brother, the Empire was for a long time occupied and polluted, and that I myself escaped that detestable tyranny by a fortunate exile, during which it was divinely granted me to behold your apostolic person. Nor has that escaped your hearing: the blessed company of pilgrims, abhorring the cruelty of an unheard-of crime, undertook, with brotherly love—or rather paternal compassion—to relieve both my exile and a cause most just indeed but, among men, desperate.

And now the salvation both of myself and of my father has prospered in their hands by the Lord: the head of my illustrious father, raised from prison, has been shown adorned, as was fitting, with imperial insignia; and the diadem of empire has been restored with due solemnity to my head, after the flight by night of that detestable parricide, who had polluted the imperial insignia by the persistent usurpation of an unheard-of tyranny. He had indeed infected the Imperial City, which was yearning for us, with such poisonous speeches that he publicly asserted that Latins were coming to overthrow its ancient liberty, Latins who strove to restore the place and people to your apostolic authority; and he rendered me hateful even to friends, as the occasion and object for which Latin Christendom had begun so unexpected an undertaking.

I confess that this was the principal reason which inclined the minds of the pilgrims to our assistance: by a voluntary promise, under the sanctity of an oath, we have pledged in Christian devotion that, should divine mercy restore to us the empire due to us, we shall humbly acknowledge the ecclesiastical head of all Christendom—namely, the Roman pontiff, the Catholic successor of Peter, prince of the apostles—and shall induce the Eastern Church to do the same according to our ability. We understand plainly that great honour and benefit ought thereby to accrue to the Empire, and eternal glory to our name, if the seamless tunic of the Lord should recover its unity in our time and through our efforts.

As has been said, we promised this under oath to your pilgrims; and we most earnestly desire to offer it more fully to your fatherhood. By these letters we promise you and your successors canonically installed all the devotion which our predecessors, the Catholic emperors, are known to have rendered of old to your predecessors, the orthodox Fathers, the Roman pontiffs. We likewise promise that, should the Lord grant us a salutary opportunity, we shall incline the Eastern Church to the same end as prudently as we shall powerfully. In this matter we desire to rely upon the counsel of your prudence, having been induced to the foregoing above all by the salutary counsel and admonitions of the venerable Fathers N., bishop of Soissons; C., bishop of Halberstadt; S., bishop of Troyes; . . . , abbot of Lucedio; and Master John of Noyon.

Given in the Imperial City, 8 Kalends of September [25 August].

CCXI. [Note: [Col. 0237D] This letter is reported in the *Gesta Innocentii*, § 90, though not without some errors. Raynaldus gives the same letter in a more corrected form, under the year [Col. 0238D] 1203, § 14. We print it entire and cleansed of every defect from Vatican and Conti transcripts. Passages found in Raynaldus are here enclosed in brackets.] LETTERS OF THE CRUSADERS. The destruction of Zadar and the restoration to Emperor Alexius of an empire occupied by Isaac’s murderers; Alexius promises reverence to the Roman Church.

INNOCENT, etc. . . . . . . . . . . . . [Col. 0238A] . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . We set forth as briefly as possible the great things the Lord has done for us—or rather, not for us but the great glory he has given to his name in these days—observing first that, since we left the city of transgression (for thus we call Zadar, whose destruction we witnessed with grief indeed, though compelled by necessity), we remember nothing having been arranged among us for the common advantage of the army which divine providence did not alter for the better, claiming the whole work for itself and making our wisdom foolish.

Therefore we rightly reject from ourselves all glory for the glorious things accomplished among us, since we contributed little effort and no counsel to the work. Hence, if any among us wishes to boast, he must boast in the Lord, not in himself or another.

After the treaty of Zadar had been confirmed with Alexius, son of Isaac, formerly the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, we were in need of all provisions and resources. We seemed likely to bring a burden rather than any assistance to the Holy Land, as had other men among us who preceded us; nor did we believe that in such want we could reach the land of the Saracens. Yet, induced by plausible reports and arguments that the greater part of the Imperial City and the weight of the Empire longed for the arrival of the said Alexius, whom they would raise by unanimous election and with due solemnity by the imperial diadem, we reached the Imperial City prosperously and, contrary to the usual course of events, with favourable winds and sea obedient to the Lord, beyond all hope; and this in a short time.

Nor did we arrive unexpectedly. We found in the city as many as sixty thousand horsemen, besides infantry; and, crossing places most strongly defended—bridges, towers, and rivers—we besieged by land and sea, without loss to our own men, both the city and the tyrant who, after committing parricide against his brother, had polluted the imperial authority by long usurpation. Yet, contrary to everyone’s expectation, we found the minds of all the citizens hardened against us. They shut their city, fortified with walls and engines, against their lord no otherwise than if an unbelieving people had arrived, intending to pollute the holy places and inexorably uproot the Christian religion.

For the most cruel usurper of the Empire—despoiler and betrayer of his lord and brother the emperor, whom he had condemned without crime to perpetual imprisonment, and who would have done the same to his illustrious son Alexius had not his fortunate exile rescued him from the tyrant’s hands—had previously delivered before the people a detestable address. By poisonous speeches he infected both the powerful and the populace so thoroughly that he declared Latins were coming to overthrow their ancient liberty, to restore the place and people to the Roman pontiff, and to subject the Empire to Latin laws. This matter indeed so inflamed and armed everyone alike against us that all seemed to have conspired together against us and the exile.

[Therefore we repeatedly asked through our envoys—indeed through our exile himself and our barons—to be heard by the citizens; but we could explain neither the reason for our coming nor the nature of our request. Whenever, standing on land or sea before the wall, we offered speeches, we received missiles instead of words. Considering, therefore, that everything was happening contrary to our expectation, we were brought into such necessity that we had immediately either to perish or conquer, because an incredible scarcity of all provisions prevented us from prolonging the siege by any means for fifteen days. Thus, not in desperation but with a certain security divinely inspired, we began to long for battle, boldly exposing ourselves—very few of us [Note: [Col. 0239D] Raynaldus and the *Gesta*: “most ready.”]—to dangers, and winning incredible success in every encounter. Often drawn up also for battle in the open field, we drove an immeasurable multitude by shameful flight back into the city.]

Meanwhile, after engines of war had been prepared on land and sea, the city was forcibly entered on the eighth day of the siege; fire spread through it; and the emperor drew up battle lines in the field against us. But when we prepared to receive his advance, he marvelled at our steadfastness despite our small numbers, shamefully turned his reins, and withdrew into the burning city. That night he fled with a few men, leaving behind in the city his wife and young child. When this became known, the Greek nobles, without our knowledge, assembled in the palace; the solemn election—or rather, the declared restoration—of our exile was celebrated; and abundant lights in the palace proclaimed an unexpected joy.

At daybreak a great multitude of Greek nobles came out to the camp, joyfully sought their chosen ruler, declared liberty restored to the city, and showed the head of his father Isaac, formerly emperor, raised from prison, to his son returning to the imperial authority, with joy beyond measure. After the necessary arrangements had been made, the new emperor was led in solemn procession to the church of Saint Sophia, and the imperial diadem, together with plenitude of power, was restored to our exile without any opposition.

When these things had been accomplished, the emperor hastened to fulfil his promises and increased promises with deeds. He provides for all of us provisions useful for the service of the Lord for a year; proceeds to pay us two hundred thousand marks; maintains the Venetian fleet at his own expense for a year; and binds himself by oath that he will raise the royal standard with us and depart with us in the passage of March for the service of the Lord with as many thousands of armed men as he can. Under the same promise he undertakes to render to the Roman pontiff the reverence which his predecessors, the Catholic emperors, are known formerly to have rendered to the pontiffs his predecessors, and to incline the Eastern Church to the same end according to his ability. Throughout his life he will also honourably maintain, at his own expense, five hundred knights in the Holy Land for the service of the Redeemer.

CCXII. [Note: [Col. 0239D] Raynaldus has already published this letter entire, [Col. 0240D] under the year 1202, § 8.] FROM THE KING OF HUNGARY TO THE POPE. He informs him that Ban Kulin had firmly bound himself that, should he thereafter presume to defend heretics in his land, he would pay one thousand marks of silver, half to the Apostolic See and the other half to the king’s treasury. [Note: [Col. 0240D] See letter 110 of book five.]

Although all who are reckoned within the religion of the Christian faith are bound to venerate and love most highly the most holy Roman Church as a loving mother, we, whom that same Church cherishes and embraces spiritually among her devoted sons, desire above all others to promote, to the extent of our ability and with greater devotion, her honour and advantage.

Accordingly, when John, the humble and faithful chaplain of your Holiness, came into our presence, bringing with him two of the principal men among those who, it was reported, fostered the condemned sect of heretics in the land of Ban Kulin, we examined the articles of the orthodox faith. At John’s exhortation, those to whom he had been sent had already accepted these articles.
