We gave the same articles, contained under our seal, to the lord of that land—the son of the aforesaid Kulin—who was then with us, strictly ordering him to cause them, and any other ordinances which the Roman See might thereafter decide to send them in accordance with God, to be observed inviolate by all in his land.

Having accepted this according to our will, he subsequently bound himself in the hands of ourselves and J., archbishop of Kalocsa, that if he should thereafter knowingly presume to support or defend in his land the aforesaid persons, or any others, in heresy, he would pay one thousand marks of silver, half of which would fall to you and the other half to our treasury. Furthermore, the two principal men who came with your aforesaid chaplain John swore in our presence, both for themselves and for their brethren who had sent them, that they would firmly observe for ever the constitutions promulgated and delivered to them by your aforesaid faithful legate.

CCXIII. . . . TO THE PRIORESS OF THE MONASTERY OF CLARETIS AND HER SISTERS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE MONASTIC LIFE, FOR EVER. He receives them under protection. (Anagni, 7 Kalends of February [26 January].)

[Col. 0240D]

“To prudent virgins,” etc., as far as “we grant”; and the aforesaid monastery of Claretis, in which you are devoted to divine service, under blessed Peter, etc. First, indeed, establishing, etc., as far as “the rule and institution of the Cistercian brethren in that monastery,” etc. Furthermore, whatever possessions, etc., as far as “by their names”: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the lands of Boveria, with all their appurtenances, granted to you by our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman M., countess of Perche, foundress of that same place, as is more fully contained in the instrument of the countess herself. Indeed, “of your labours,” etc. Moreover, “free and unencumbered women,” etc. “Let no one, after having made,” etc. “Upon your death,” etc. “Blessings indeed,” etc. “Otherwise,” etc. “We therefore decree,” etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See, etc. “If anyone therefore,” etc. “But to all,” etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 7 Kalends of February [26 January], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1203 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

CCXIV. . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NIDAROS AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. The pope rejoices at the death of King Sverre, who had usurped the kingdom and banished many worthy men, and at the succession of his son, who recalled them. Finally, he sharply rebukes the archbishop for absolving persons whom he had no power to absolve. (Anagni, 9 Kalends of February [24 January].)

[Col. 0241B]

Our heart exulted in the Lord, and we rejoiced with exceeding great joy, rendering worthy thanks to almighty God, because after clouds he has brought clear weather and after the storm calm. We have learned, and rejoice to have learned, that, upon the death of Sverre, who had violently usurped the kingdom of Norway, through whom general confusion and disturbance threatened the whole land—so that, besides the countless slaughter of many others, several of the greater and better men had on that account been banished by him—the son of Sverre succeeds him in the kingdom but not in purpose. Having recalled to their own homes those who had been exiled on this account, he loves and honours churches and ecclesiastical persons, governing that land and people in the full tranquillity of peace.

Yet we have been moved by no small astonishment that you, brother archbishop, did not hesitate, in your own rashness, to absolve him and his accomplices from the sentence of excommunication by which they had been bound by our authority, usurping that which was not yours and in no way belonged to you. Like the ape which imitates human actions, you pretended to wish to do what you could not, and what by law you ought not, do. Thus not only have you manifestly fallen into error, but they too, who, though they remain bound all the more, falsely consider themselves absolved.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and enjoin your brotherhood publicly to announce that absolution void and ineffective; and thereafter, having received from them sworn security, to grant them, by our authority and according to the form of the Church, the benefit of absolution. Send several of them to our presence, both on their own behalf and on behalf of the others, with the testimony of your letters.

CCXV. . . . TO THE BISHOP OF LIÈGE. [Note: [Col. 0241D] Hugh II, son of Hugh, lord of Pierrepont and of Wasnadio, by Agatha Clementia of Rethel, daughter of Manasses, count of Rethel, and Beatrice of Namur, then wore the mitre of Liège. His brothers were Matthew, lord of Wasnadio, and Robert, lord of Pierrepont. Hugh became bishop in 1200 and sat for twenty-nine years. Though he was lax at first, he reformed his life; afterwards many praiseworthy good things were done by him in the bishopric, and he finally came to a commendable end. Alberic, *Chronicle*, under the year 1200.] That he compel the bishop of Utrecht to satisfy the creditors of his church, under penalty both of excommunication and deposition. (Anagni, 2 Kalends of February [31 January].)

Although concerning payment of the 1,250 marks which, in the time of the happy memory of Pope C., our predecessor, our beloved sons Parentius, Ja. de Tosto, J. Petrinius, and Bellushomo, citizens of Rome, Alexius of Winchester, and Garnellotus, merchants of Siena, and their associates had lent to the late . . . [Col. 0242B] bishop of Utrecht [Note: [Col. 0242D] If this concerns, as it seems, the bishops of Utrecht, he was Theodoric, count of Holland, brother of Baldwin—who himself had also been bishop—who died in 1199. Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, vol. I, part I, p. 60.] . . . , the bishop of Utrecht [Note: [Col. 0242D] Theodoric mentioned above was succeeded by Theodoric of Are, who died in 1210. The same source, ibid.] now presiding, we have repeatedly sent him our letters and determined to pronounce against him, unless he satisfied the creditors, a sentence suspending his office and benefice. At length, because he sent his own envoy to our presence, we granted, at his request, appropriate extensions for making payment. Nevertheless, forgetful of due obedience and devotion, he took no care to satisfy the creditors either at our command or at the admonition of our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, to whom we entrusted execution of this affair.

Indeed, as we have seen contained in that bishop’s letters, the creditors repeatedly granted extensions for payment. Yet though he promised to pay the specified money, the creditors derived no benefit from his promise. Therefore the same legate, compassionate toward the creditors’ labours and expenses, according to the tenor of our mandate announced that the bishop was subject to a sentence of excommunication, strictly ordering him to appear before us by the feast of the Lord’s Ascension which was then to come, but has now passed. He, however, turning a deaf ear to all these things, as we hear, neither regarded himself as excommunicate nor consented to come before us.

Since, therefore, the same bishop seems given over to a reprobate mind and, like one who has come to the depths of vices, now despises all things, by apostolic writings we firmly command and enjoin your brotherhood that, unless the aforesaid bishop within a year after receiving these letters makes satisfaction for the stated amount of money—so that during each four-month period of that year one third is paid at Ypres to the aforesaid creditors, with all interest entirely ceasing—and deserves to obtain from the aforesaid legate of ours the benefit of absolution from the bond of excommunication by which he is held, you shall cause his excommunication to be publicly announced throughout the whole province of Cologne every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted.

By our authority you shall order all clergy and laity of the diocese of Utrecht, under penalty of excommunication, to withdraw their services from that bishop and to render him no obedience, reverence, or honour due to a bishop. But if he should attempt to compel anyone of his diocese to render him service, then, unless after your admonition he sees to its correction within a month, or unless he makes satisfaction according to the form set out above, since a bad tree must be utterly rooted out and put to the uses of fire, you shall not delay, observing the order of law and removing the obstacle of contradiction and appeal, to pronounce against him by our authority a sentence of deposition, and you shall ensure that the Church of Utrecht is provided through canonical election with a suitable person.

Given at Anagni, 10 Kalends of February [23 January].

CCXVI. [Note: [Col. 0243D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1204, § 68.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP, DEAN, [Note: [Col. 0243D] The archbishop and dean of Bourges have already been discussed above.] AND ARCHDEACON OF BOURGES. He gives them authority to investigate the archbishop of Bordeaux, concerning whom the foulest reports were circulating. (Anagni, 5 Kalends of February [28 January].)

[Col. 0243C] We have frequently heard the land itself cry out against H., [Note: [Col. 0243D] We have already treated of Hélie I de Malemort, archbishop of Bordeaux, in the note to letter 96 of book five. What is said here of him does not accord with what is reported of him by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*.] archbishop of Bordeaux, and its furrows weep with it, because he exercises such perverse conduct toward his subjects that the unlearned and simple, whose souls he persecutes and afflicts, break forth into voices of complaint against his injustice; and, while the multitude of subjects laments, the whole neighbourhood comes with them to mourning, enduring as persecutor the man whom they ought to have as ruler.

It has been reported to our ears, and repeatedly affirmed by many, that, when Pope Clement, our predecessor of pious memory, formerly imposed upon him a canonical purgation because his entry was said to have been simoniacal, he presumed to exercise pastoral rule without having been purged. Moreover, after the death of R., king of England, when the people of that land withdrew to fortified places because of the king’s death, and no one, fearing for himself and his property, wished to go out to perform even their accustomed labours and agriculture, the same archbishop brought into that land Marchaderius and Ar. the Gascon, brigands, and others whom the enemy of humankind sent into the world to fulfil his iniquity. Summoning the people of his entire diocese, he said that he wished to establish peace under those accursed men.

Then, when peace had been feigned, and he had made the people secure about peace, and they had returned to their homes and, fearing no danger, had dispersed themselves and their property through houses and fields, the aforesaid brigands, after conferring with the archbishop, on the third day sent their raiders throughout the whole land. Plundering booty and seizing people, despoiling churches, and removing from the sanctuary of the Lord altar-cloths, priestly vestments, and books, they reduced the whole land to poverty and want, sharing the spoils with the archbishop himself. The same archbishop received them and their plunder in the castle of a certain nephew of his and there granted them refuge for a year and more. From there they went out even against the surrounding and distant population, utterly devastating the land and carrying off whatever they could find.

Even now he associates with persons of this sort; and, since they are excommunicated—as men who exercise against Christians a tyranny more cruel than that of those who do not know the Lord’s name—he openly communicates with them. To show that he consents to their wickedness, he has assigned them his own priest, who commits the bodies of the dead to ecclesiastical burial. If anyone reproves him concerning these matters, he asserts that he received authority from us, as though he made us serve his sins and imposed upon us labour in his iniquity. He is also said, with nefarious rashness, to have granted these laymen that, from any priest or cleric whom they happened to capture, they might take a redemption payment of ten solidi, thereby infringing ecclesiastical liberty and weakening the immunity which even faithless men have customarily preserved for all persons marked by the clerical character.

Moreover, as we have learned, against the beloved son [Note: [Col. 0244D] The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 942, record Arnald as abbot of Clariac from 1187 to 1190, and then, immediately, Peter from 1214 until at least 1228, from documents.] . . . . . abbot of Clariac, because he had proceeded, by authority of our delegation, in a dispute concerning the church of Moulins with our venerable brother . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0244D] The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* leave in doubt who was bishop of Agen at that time; ibid., col. 912.] bishop of Agen, he laid violent hands upon him; after first driving him from a certain house, he caused him to be seized by certain laymen and shamefully mistreated. Afterwards, breaking in with a band (`ruptis`, uncertain), they came to his monastery by his will and command, and utterly devastated both the monastery itself and the village, carrying off everything therefrom.

Furthermore, recently coming with armed men to the abbey of Saint Cybard, he brought horses, beasts, prostitutes, and other persons of ill repute into the cloister and other buildings; keeping them there for three days, he so despoiled the village and monastery that, after his departure, nothing was found there by which the monks and inhabitants of the place could be supported. Moreover, as we have learned, he committed a certain enormity that brings injury upon the divine sacrament: when he entered a church and heard the priest, in the solemn celebration of Mass, having proceeded as far as the hymn of divine glory which follows the preface, he presumed to remove the priest from the prayer which he had begun with the divine majesty, and caused the office to be begun anew.

We have also learned that he pronounced a divorce between certain persons lawfully joined in marriage; joined another man’s wife to someone else; and granted to a certain man, who had put away his own wife, the companionship of the woman subsequently brought in. For this reason he beat a certain priest in a full synod, having learned that he had been present at the marriage of those persons. He further commits other enormities, and seems to glory in them—things which we deem shameful to write, since, as is asserted, common report carries them to everyone’s ears and the chatter of entertainers spreads them abroad.

But since, if these things are true, we ought not to pass them over by dissimulation, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you to investigate the truth concerning these matters with the utmost diligence, all appeal set aside. Whatever he is shown to have committed through lawful proofs, common report, or notorious evidence, you are faithfully to inform us by your letters, so that, instructed by your inquiry, we may proceed more safely in this matter. Fix for him a suitable term within which he is to appear before us in person or through a suitable representative. But if not all of you, etc.; let two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year.

CCXVII. TO THE ABBOTS OF TENALIA [Note: [Col. 0245D] The series of abbots of Tenalia in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1122, is far too incomplete: it records no abbot of this monastery between William II in 1189 and Amelius or Amelinus in 1266.], AND OF MADIO [Note: [Col. 0245D] The same must be said of the chronological series of abbots of the monastery of Madion. Its learned authors confess that they know absolutely nothing of who founded it or when, and they name no abbot of this monastery before 1231. Id., [Col. 0246D] ibid., col. 1126.], AND TO THE CHANTER OF SAINTES. He entrusts to them the reform and ordering of the monastery of Albaterra. (Anagni, fifth day before the Kalends of February.)

Formerly J. de Cella, abbot of Albaterra [Note: [Col. 0246D] This abbot of Albaterra is wholly unknown to the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*. They recognize none between William in 1188 and Aimeric in 1229; ibid., col. 1488. The monastery of Albaterra, once founded by St. Maurus, is now the collegiate church dedicated to St. Saviour.], in the time of Pope C. of blessed memory, our predecessor, coming to the Apostolic See, obtained, as is said, permission to organize his church with suitable persons, with the counsel of . . . . . archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0246D] The archbishop of Bordeaux has already been discussed often.], his metropolitan. But certain canons of the church of Albaterra, considering that the revenues of the abbey could in no way then suffice for the canons resident there—as indeed they still cannot—appealed to the Apostolic See. They sent B. de Luco, their fellow canon, to the presence of our said predecessor in order to pursue the appeal that had been lodged. But when he entered upon the way of all flesh while at the Apostolic See, the said canons, because of the church’s most pressing poverty, were unable to pursue their appeal through another.

The abbot, however, having returned to his church, requested the aforesaid archbishop to come there. The archbishop compelled some of the canons, by threats and terrors, and others by accepting from them a sworn undertaking, to abide by his decision.

This having been done, the archbishop adjudged that the abbot himself should institute eight canons in that church, and should receive five hundred solidi from its goods for the expenses which, by coming to the Apostolic See, he had incurred to that church’s grave loss. On the occasion of this award, the archbishop and abbot presumed, against justice, to make canons in that church—against the will of its canons, who were unwilling—the following persons: P. Grossus, who, touching the holy Gospels, had voluntarily sworn that he would never hold or even seek a canonry of the church of Albaterra; W., P.’s brother; two little boys, namely William Rossinol, nephew of a certain cleric of the aforesaid archbishop, and W. de Verdellis, kinsman of that abbot; H. Cazor, a man nearly illiterate; P. Petit, through money which the abbot himself is said to have received; P. de Rossenac, who, bound by the bond of excommunication, had himself ordained priest and still, deceived by diabolical fraud, while excommunicated presumes to celebrate divine offices; and another man unknown to those canons. W., the brother of the same P., is said to have been notorious for the crime of theft.

Further, the same abbot extorted five hundred solidi, according to the tenor of that award, and three hundred solidi which he said he had expended in entertaining the archbishop while he stayed there, from the goods of that church, to the grave damage and loss of the canons. Moreover, despite their opposition and against their will, he presumed to apply to his own uses revenues that ought to be turned to the advantage of the church, and to inflict upon those canons many other injuries and burdens contrary to justice.

Furthermore, the aforesaid abbot is said to keep in that church, beside the pots of meat and to the scandal of the canons, H. de Burna, who, having resigned into the abbot’s hands his canonry of the church of Albaterra, and having sought and received leave from the people of the same castle, had made a vow to assume the monastic habit in the monastery of Blessed Mary of Faesia. The aforesaid archbishop also, for the reception of his clerk R. de Belundo, who is alleged to be nearly illiterate, saying that he had received executory letters from us on this subject, repeatedly refused, when asked, to provide a copy of them; and he does not cease to harass the said canons contrary to justice, pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against them and inflicting many burdens upon them.

Since we could not pass these matters over by dissimulation, we instructed our venerable brother the bishop, and our beloved sons L. and Richard, archdeacons of Périgueux, that, after summoning the beloved sons . . . . . abbots of Bornet [Note: [Col. 0247D] In 1201 Raymond I was abbot of Bornet, according to codex 2670 of the Colbert Library, fol. 169, col. 2, as Baluze attests.], Corona [Note: [Col. 0247D] See letter 96 of book five.], and Cancellata [Note: [Col. 0247D] Peter I Raimundi is found as abbot of Cancellata from 1199 until 1218, when he died—or rather abdicated. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1503.], and such other religious, God-fearing men as they knew ought to be called, they should go to that church. Having investigated the truth of the foregoing matters, both through the canons of that place and through others, they were to inform us by their letters of what they found, so that, instructed by their report, we might proceed more safely in the affair.

Accordingly, having received the apostolic command concerning these matters, they went to the place and summoned the said abbots and the other religious men whom they knew should be called. Since they could not obtain the presence of the abbots of Corona and Bornet, the abbot of Castris [Note: [Col. 0247D] This undoubtedly concerns the abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Castris, which belongs to the diocese of Périgueux [Col. 0248D]. See the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1504. After Stephen in 1179, they name Peter at an uncertain year, then R. in 1223, as abbots of this monastery.], . . . . . of Bornet, . . . . . priors of Seven Fountains, and many prudent men being present with them, they diligently sought, together with certain canons of the church of Albaterra, to ascertain the truth concerning the institution, the manner of instituting, and those instituted. They committed the depositions received to writing and took care to send them to us.

But although many clerics and laymen in the castle of Albaterra, when asked to bear testimony to the truth, were willing to come, they could not go out because the abbot’s messengers shut the gates of the castle. The abbot himself and H. de Burno also absented themselves at their own pleasure.

Therefore, having carefully examined the inquiry into the foregoing matters, and having clearly understood from it that the same abbot, after the beloved son Master B., canon of Albaterra, had appealed to us and set out on his journey, despoiled him of the church of Saint James, took wine from its vineyards, and afterwards did not permit them to be cultivated, with the result that they were left uncultivated, we decreed that the abbot should make full restitution of what had been taken and satisfaction for the injuries and losses inflicted upon him.

And since the aforesaid institution of those canons was fraudulently carried out, after an appeal to the Apostolic See had been lodged, with persons less suitable and unworthy, and since the church itself lacked resources for their reception, we will and command you by apostolic letters that, unless they raise and prove some reasonable objection against the witnesses received against them and against the proceedings of the inquiry, which we send to you enclosed under our bull, you, supported by our authority, shall wholly annul their ordination or institution, with no obstacle of contradiction or appeal.

Yet, wishing out of the kindness of the Apostolic See to provide for that church and for those persons, we grant that those who are suitable, provided the church has the means, shall be received anew into that church and treated with brotherly charity. Those who have rashly presumed to oppose these matters, after prior warning, you shall restrain by ecclesiastical coercion, all obstacle of appeal removed.

Further, if the aforesaid archbishop does not see fit to produce the apostolic letters which he claims to have received concerning the admission as canon in that church of the clerk R. de Belundo, or if their tenor is lawfully established, do not delay, by our authority and with no obstacle of contradiction or appeal, to absolve that church from the archbishop’s claim; and declare wholly void and without effect whatever he has done on that pretext.

Compel the aforesaid H. de Burno, who is said to have resigned the canonry of the church of Albaterra and made a vow to assume the monastic habit, by ecclesiastical coercion and without appeal, to enter without any delay the monastery which he vowed to enter, or another regular house, there to assume the religious habit. Notwithstanding any letters which may appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without mention of the tenor of these letters. But if not all of you, etc.; let two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCXVIII. TO THE SAME. That they compel the abbot of Albaterra to restore the church of Saint James to B., canon of Albaterra. (Anagni, fifth day before the Kalends of February.)

From the letters of our venerable brother . . . . . bishop [Note: [Col. 0248D] Raymond IV of Châteauneuf held the episcopal mitre of Périgueux from 1197 until 1208, when, by Innocent's command, he was deprived of episcopal rank because of his excesses. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1471.], and of our beloved sons L. and R., archdeacons of Périgueux, it has been reported to us that, upon the complaint of our beloved son Master B., canon of Albaterra, we had instructed them to compel . . . . . abbot of Albaterra [Note: [Col. 0248D] See the notes to the preceding letter.] by our authority to make restitution of the church of Saint James and of the other things of which the same master said he had been unjustly despoiled. They gave judgment for the said master, adjudging that church to be restored to him.

When the same abbot rashly presumed to oppose this judgment, those judges bound both the abbot and the priests celebrating in that church by the bond of excommunication. Yet, rashly violating this sentence, they presume to celebrate divine offices in that church, like beasts rotting in their own dung.

Therefore we strictly command your discretion by apostolic letters that you shall cause the aforesaid sentence of restitution—which by other letters we decreed should be made to the same master—and the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the priests, . . . . . abbot, and other opponents, since it was reasonably pronounced, to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside, until suitable satisfaction has been made. If, after the sentence of excommunication was pronounced against them, it is established that they have rashly celebrated divine offices, then, supported by our authority and with all obstacle of appeal removed, inflict the canonical penalty upon them. Witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. But if not all of you, etc.; let two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year.

CCXIX [Note: [Col. 0249D] It is found among the Decretals, book III, title 24, *On Oaths*, chapter 23. We give variant readings.]. TO THE BISHOP OF ALATRI [Note: [Col. 0249D] Leander, bishop of Alatri, was in office in 1200. He died about 1222. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 329.]. On annulling an oath unlawfully exacted for satisfaction of an injury. (Anagni, third day before the Nones of February.)

The vicar of Quintavalle [Note: [Col. 0249D] This word is absent from the Decretals, as below: “when formerly . . . Quintavalle.”] reported to us that formerly his daughters and Giborga and Venetia, daughters of John Berti, came to words and even blows. Desiring to make satisfaction to those women and their kinsfolk for the injury which his daughters had inflicted upon others [Note: [Col. 0249D] The Decretals add “women,” and below read: “that he would obey their command.”], Quintavalle, on the advice of his neighbors, swore an oath that he would obey their command concerning that injury.

After receiving this oath, they gave him, under the obligation of his oath, this command: whenever his sons, daughters, or wife should direct any insulting deed or word against those women, Quintavalle was to disinherit his sons and daughters [Note: [Col. 0249D] The Decretals read “he was to disinherit daughters and sons,” and omit the material distinguished below in italic type.] and put away his own wife. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate the truth of the foregoing diligently; and, if you find the matter to be so, since the oath was lawful but the command unlawful, enjoin the aforesaid daughters of John Berti to revoke that command. Otherwise declare, by our authority, that the aforesaid Quintavalle [Note: [Col. 0249D] The Decretals read “him.”] is not bound to observe that command.

Given at Anagni, the third day before the Nones of February.

CCXX. TO . . . . . BISHOP OF MARTURANO [Note: [Col. 0249D] Who the bishop of Marturano was at that time is unknown. Ughelli shows that Michael, fifth bishop of Marturano, attended the ecumenical Lateran council in 1179; then he names Philip, sixth bishop of that church, but only in 1220. *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 359.], TO . . . . . ABBOT OF CORATIO [Note: [Col. 0249D] It should perhaps be read *De Curatio*. In 1170 the Cistercian abbey of St. Mary of Curatio belonged to the church of Marturano; there Blessed Joachim had then been made abbot and enjoyed special favour with Michael, the excellent bishop of Marturano, from whom he obtained not so much a grant as assent to the privileges which Pope Alexander III had granted to the Cistercian order; see Ughelli, cited place. This abbey of Curatio lies on the banks of the river Crotalis in the diocese of Marturano, formerly a great monastery and already small in Ughelli's time, like the rest of Calabria groaning under the burden of commendams and commendatory abbots. That it was founded before 1060 by Roger of Marturano is established by letters of Pope Honorius II. Curatium was incorporated into the Cistercian order about 1162, according to Henriquez (*Annals of the Cistercian Order*, vol. II). The first Cistercian abbot of this house recorded is Columbus, succeeded by Joachim, who became the first abbot of Flora.], TO . . . . . ABBOT OF SAINT MARY OF AQUAFORMOSA, AND TO THE TREASURER OF MARTURANO. That they investigate the exchange of the church of Botrano between the abbot and convent of Floris and the archbishop and church of Cosenza. (Anagni, eighth day before the Ides of February.)

Upon representations formerly made by the beloved sons . . . . . abbot and brethren of the monastery of Floris [Note: [Col. 0250D] See letter 137 of this sixth book.], we learned that that monastery, situated in the mountains, is so exposed to the winds that, owing to the severity and constancy of the cold, winter has not only claimed spring and autumn for itself but has extended its bounds into the summer months. The place is also exposed to the incursions of hostile persons, which greatly disturbs the brothers’ peace and is exceedingly contrary to their safety.

Since a certain place called Botrano, belonging to the church of Cosenza, was reported to be suitable for religious life, the same abbot and brethren humbly petitioned us to provide for them in this matter with paternal care. Therefore, that the flower might pass into the cluster of grapes, assenting to their petitions for the benefit of their religious life, we instructed by our letters our venerable brother . . . . . archbishop, and our beloved sons the chapter of Cosenza [Note: [Col. 0250D] See the notes to the letter cited above.], to assign to the abbot and brethren the aforesaid place with its appurtenances, after receiving from them a suitable exchange, according to the assessment of the archbishop. They were to confer it upon them as freely as the exchange should come freely to themselves, so that, just as the monastery of Floris pertains directly to us, so the monastery to be erected at Botrano might likewise pertain directly to us.

We also commanded our beloved sons . . . . . abbot of the Holy Spirit, . . . . . abbot of Coratio, and brother R. de Fotian to compel them to this, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure without delay.

But, as we learned from the letters of the aforesaid archbishop and abbots, the archbishop, carrying our mandate into execution, assigned to the said abbot and brethren the church of Botrano with its holding and wood, reserving in perpetuity, for the use of his own table, the use of timber in a specified part of that wood marked by definite boundaries. From them he received the church of Bottul with its holding; another holding called Canale; the church of Saint Martin of Jore with its appurtenances, which his predecessor, with the chapter’s consent, had granted to the same brethren; and a holding in Great Sila, known by many names, as is more fully contained in the instruments drawn up concerning it.

To show us briefly the advantage of the exchange, he firmly asserted that, for the lands he gave, he received from them lands four times as many and better; for one mill, two mills with one fulling-mill; for the wood, a larger and better wood; and for the vineyards, better and more numerous vineyards. Only the distance of the holding in Sila impeded his judgment in assessing the exchange, since the disadvantage caused by its remoteness is compensated by the magnitude of the return.

But the aforesaid canons resisted and gave no assent to the said exchange. They asserted that such an exchange was neither adequate, expedient, nor useful for the church of Cosenza, which is, as it were, cut off in its arms and mutilated in its limbs, so that it appears deformed and is exposed to the mockery of all who see it. They further maintained that the place of Botrano is so useful, necessary, and near to the church of Cosenza that, in these times of hostilities, the church has no difficulty in transporting provisions, cutting timber, and obtaining other necessities. What the said abbot and monks offer them in exchange, however, is so far from the city that it can scarcely be reached in a day’s journey.

For they give part of the holding which they possess in Sila, granted to them by King Tancred of blessed memory, to the scandal of all the people of Cosenza, who, having their customs and usages in Sila, would by no means permit themselves to be deprived of their right. They assert that they do not abandon the place which they say they cannot inhabit because of cold and wars, but retain it for their own uses; and they intend to establish dwellings in the middle of the diocese of Cosenza and do not wish in any way to be separated from their former place.

Since, on this account, both the said abbot with some of his brethren and certain canons on behalf of the chapter came into our presence, we carefully heard what they wished to submit before us. Although we desire, out of regard for their religious life, to provide for the abbot and brethren with paternal care, we nevertheless neither wish nor ought to allow the church of Cosenza to be gravely harmed. We also observe that the archbishop himself, for the benefit of religion, could, even without a special mandate from us, by canonical permission itself grant a definite part of his possessions.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters to investigate the truth concerning the foregoing with diligence. If the compensation received by the aforesaid archbishop is adequate, or if adequate compensation is offered, then, after receiving it, cause the aforesaid exchange to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, all obstacle of appeal removed. Otherwise, since it ought not to have been made without adequate compensation, revoke it as void. But if not all of you, etc.; let three of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, the eighth day before the Ides of February.

CCXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP [Note: [Col. 0251D] William IV of Benevento then held the archiepiscopal mitre of Embrun. According to some, he had previously been bishop of Digne; a canon of Fréjus, he professed as a Carthusian at the Charterhouse of Mont-Rieu, where he was also prior; thence he was raised to the episcopate and was finally elected archbishop of Embrun in 1184. He lived until 1208. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, [Col. 0252D] col. 1075.], AND CANONS OF EMBRUN. That they receive Master P., papal scribe, as canon and brother. (Anagni, fourth day before the Nones of February.)

When we instructed you to receive our beloved son Master P., our scribe, as canon and brother, and, out of reverence for us and the Apostolic See, to confer upon his representative the prebend then vacant in the church of Embrun; and when you refused to fulfil our mandate, an apostolic mandate concerning this matter was issued to you, appointing as executors the beloved sons . . . . . abbot of Cluny, . . . . . abbot of Boscodunum [Note: [Col. 0252D] It seems it should be read “of Boscodunum.” The monastery of Boscodunum was then governed by W., known from 1201; in his time John of St. Paul, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, visited that monastery. He is still mentioned in 1205. Ibid., col. 1104.], and . . . . . provost of Ultiens. Through them we also ordered that anything done otherwise with respect to the prebend after receipt of our first mandate should be declared void.

But, appearing before the executors, you alleged that a fixed number of canons had been established in the church of Embrun by an indulgence of the Apostolic See. Since that number was full and our letters made no mention of such an establishment, you argued that you could not in any way be compelled to enlarge it. You earnestly requested them to report the truth to us by their letters, humbly promising that you would receive the same scribe as brother and canon if, notwithstanding that indulgence, we should order him to be received.

You also informed us by your letters that, since two of your fellow canons had no prebend in that church, one of them earnestly sought the vacant prebend; and you added that three among you had obtained prebends in that church through the Apostolic See. But because the scribe’s messenger alleged before us that that prebend had already been vacant so long that its grant had devolved upon us, and lest what had been begun concerning the said scribe should remain uncompleted, we commanded you that, if the prebend had been vacant for so long, you should assign it, together with a stall in choir and a place in chapter, to his messenger. We granted to the aforesaid executors authority to carry this out and to restrain any who might resist.

The aforesaid abbot of Boscodunum and . . . . . provost of Ultiens, however, informed us by their letters that, since their fellow executor could not be present, they went together to Embrun. There, when you repeated the aforesaid objections and proved sufficiently before them both the establishment of the number, its completion, and the authenticity of the indulgence, they found that a certain bishop, the nobleman R. de Bellojoco, and a certain regular canon had nevertheless been counted in that number. They also found, as they informed us in the same letters, that the said prebend had been vacant so long that its grant had devolved upon us.

When those executors would not deliberate upon the allegations made, you humbly asked them to report the full truth to us, since you were ready to receive the scribe as canon and brother if this proceeded from our will, notwithstanding the aforesaid objections, although you considered them reasonable.

Although, because that prebend—sought, as you informed us by your letters, by one of your canons who had not yet obtained a prebend—had devolved to our grant, and because the said persons are counted among the canons only as an excuse, and because after obtaining the indulgence you exceeded the number established by your church, we could have proceeded otherwise by law; nevertheless, because you submit yourselves to our commands and are ready to fulfil our good pleasure, thereby earning merit from us, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to admit the same scribe of ours, who may be of much benefit to you and your church, as your brother and canon. Without delay or excuse, assign to his messenger a stall in choir, a place in chapter, and the aforesaid prebend. We do not wish this to create any future prejudice against you concerning your indulgence.

But if even now you fail to fulfil what we write, know that we have strictly commanded the same executors by apostolic letters to carry out the apostolic mandate, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal and restraining any opponents or rebels by sentences of suspension from office and benefice and of excommunication. We would take it all the more grievously if you acted in any way against our mandate, because you would seem to have insulted not so much our said scribe as ourselves, if, after you have judged yourselves bound by our mandate once and again, you should now defer its execution.

The executors are written to in nearly the same manner, as far as “restraining.” Therefore fulfil the apostolic mandate in such a way that provision for the said scribe, which appears to have been delayed thus far not without your negligence, may not be further delayed, and that we may not henceforth be compelled to write again concerning this matter. But if not all of you, etc.; let two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COSENZA [Note: [Col. 0253D] See the notes to letter 137 of this sixth book.]. That he not alter the ancient customs of his church. (Anagni, the Nones of February.)

Different customs are observed in different churches, as your discretion does not fail to know; and the Roman Church neither rejects nor condemns them, unless they conflict with canonical ordinances. The beloved sons, the canons of Cosenza, have humbly reported to us that, since the church of Cosenza is one of the more ancient churches of the kingdom of Sicily, it has from ancient times possessed customs not at variance with the sacred canons concerning the celebration of divine offices, the appointment of vicars, and the services of clerics. Your predecessors, learned and prudent archbishops of Cosenza, did not wish in any way to alter these customs. Yet you, not adhering at all to your predecessors’ example, propose to alter many of your church’s ancient and approved customs.

Therefore we admonish, advise, and exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by apostolic letters to maintain and observe the reasonable and ancient customs of your church. Do not alter them yourself, nor, so far as lies in you, allow them to be altered by others.

Given at Anagni, on the Nones of February.

CCXXIII. TO THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 0254D] “XVI. Radulfus de Cierrey, known only by the initial R. in Register 31 of the treasury charters, was in 1201, with Bishop Luke, a witness to the composition made between John, abbot of St. Taurin, and Thomas de Loiis. He is found again in 1207, 1209, and 1219 in various cartularies. In this last year he becomes bishop.” *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 621.] AND CHAPTER OF ÉVREUX. He grants that anything obtained in apostolic letters against their rights shall be deemed void. (Anagni, eighth day before the Ides of February.)

As it belongs to our office to provide that what is reasonably established in the churches of God may obtain due firmness through apostolic favor, so it also befits us to provide that nothing obtained, with the truth concealed, against the reasonable statutes of churches may produce prejudice for those churches.

Therefore, following the example of Pope Lucius of happy memory, our predecessor, we enact by the authority of these presents that, if anything is obtained, without mention of those customs, against the ancient and reasonable customs of your church confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See, to the prejudice of your right, it shall lack force and have no validity—unless perhaps the Roman pontiff should see fit, in certain knowledge, to order otherwise. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, the eighth day before the Ides of February, in the sixth year.

CCXXIV. TO THE SAME. A similar privilege. (Anagni, eighth day before the Ides of February.)

Since it is the role of a good judge to settle disputes, not to increase them, we, as pertains to our office, prefer that questions arising among ecclesiastical persons be resolved without formal proof, rather than remain undecided for want of witnesses. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, acceding to your just requests, by the authority of these present letters we grant you that, whenever any dispute arises between you and your bishop concerning the customs of your church, [Col. 0255C] your procurator may produce three or four canons of that same church—men above every exception—to bear witness to the truth; and they shall be believed without hesitation as lawful witnesses. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CCXXV. TO THE ABBOT OF PERSENIA, H., ARCHDEACON, S. OF BAIRO, CANON OF CHARTRES. That they are to ensure the abolition of a bad custom in the diocese of Évreux concerning parish churches. (Anagni, 8 February.)

Just as we desire reasonable and honorable customs to obtain complete force, so also we wish and intend, insofar as belongs to our office, to uproot those things which are rashly and wrongly undertaken in the Church of God by anyone whatsoever. Indeed, from the report of our beloved sons, the dean [Note: [Col. 0255D] See Letter 223.] and chapter of Évreux, we learn that in the diocese of Évreux, during the past few years, a most evil custom has become established: namely, when a parish church happens to become vacant and is afterwards bestowed upon someone by canonical collation, our venerable brother, the bishop of Évreux [Note: [Col. 0255D] Luke, first a canon, then archdeacon; from archdeacon dean; from dean bishop in 1203 according to the Chronicle of Utica; and confirmed by the Apostolic See on 16 February. He governed until 30 January 1220. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 582.], receives in full the fruits and revenues of that church for the entire year after the institution of its incumbent. Thus it sometimes happens that, in order to obtain continuous and peaceful possession, the incumbents redeem from the said bishop the fruits of the churches for more than they can afford, [Col. 0256B] and seek their livelihood elsewhere as well. Moreover, the same bishop, it is said, does not shrink from selling the rural deaneries at farm.

Since, therefore, these practices undoubtedly savor of detestable perversity, and such a vice must be utterly driven from the house of the Lord, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to take care strictly to forbid the same bishop on our behalf to presume to attempt such things, compelling him thereto, if necessary, by canonical coercion, with appeal set aside. And if not all of you, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, 8 February, in the sixth year.

CCXXVI. TO THE ABBOTS OF ALNET [Note: [Col. 0255D]

Concerning the abbots of Alnet at about this time, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 443, state as follows:

“III. John I, the third abbot: while he was in office, the church was dedicated in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 29 April 1190. He was still in office in 1200 and 1201.

[Col. 0256D] “IV. Henry was in charge in 1209 and 1210. In 1211 he gave the chapter of Bayeux the right of patronage, tithes, and lands belonging to his monastery in the parish of Longvillers.”]

, OF ARDENNE [Note: [Col. 0256D] Robert II, abbot of Ardenne, governed the monastery with the highest praise for twenty-six years; and in 1206 he was judged by all worthy to ascend to the headship of the whole order. The later life of the elected man disappointed the hopes of his electors: indulging too freely in luxury, dissipation, and generosity, he was removed from office and dignity. *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. I, col. 190.], AND OF FONTENET [Note: [Col. 0256D]

The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 414, mention little concerning the abbots of Fontenet:

“VI. Robert II … formerly abbot of Fontenet, became abbot of Fontenelle in 1193. VII. Geoffrey II, formerly prior of Caen, became abbot of Fontenet. VIII. Alexander was in office in 1213, etc.”]

. He commands them to absolve the abbot and convent of Saint-Ouen of Rouen from promises of benefices made contrary to the decrees of the Lateran Council. (Anagni, 4 February.)

[Col. 0256C]

Just as we desire that the decrees of the sacred canons be observed inviolate by all, so we will that things rashly undertaken against them by anyone have no force, duly punishing with their severity the excess of those who, pursuing their own will or advantage, do not fear to weaken ecclesiastical vigor. For the report of our beloved sons, the abbot [Note: [Col. 0256D] Geoffrey, abbot of Saint-Ouen, appears in documents of February 1191. Innocent wrote to him in 1199. (See Book II, Letter 78.) He died in 1208. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 147.] and convent of Saint-Ouen of Rouen, has reached our hearing: on account [Col. 0257A] of promises formerly made by their predecessors and by themselves, contrary to the Lateran Council, concerning benefices not vacant and pensions to be paid in the interim, they are so burdened that, amid these matters and the other hardships of war, they cannot be sustained from the scanty revenues of the monastery unless swift aid is provided them by the Apostolic See.

Since, therefore, by the duty of the apostolate entrusted to us, we are bound to provide with paternal solicitude for the burdens of all churches, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, by our authority and with any obstacle of appeal removed, you absolve the aforesaid abbot and monks from promises of benefices and pensions made contrary to the decrees of the said council; and do not allow them to be troubled by anyone on this account. But those whom it is established before you made the promises themselves, do not delay to punish with the due penalty. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. And if not all of you, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, 4 February, in the sixth year.

CCXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF GENEVA [Note: [Col. 0257D] Nantelinus, or Namelmus, formerly prior of Vallon in the Carthusian Order, was bishop of Geneva in 1185. He sat for twenty years and seven months, dying on the Ides of February 1205. *Gallia Christiana vetus*, vol. II, fol. 595, no. 56.]. He annuls judgments rendered in the case between him and the abbot of Sixt. (Anagni, 7 February.)

When the beloved son, the abbot of Sixt, and Noradinus, your procurator and our subdeacon, had come into our presence concerning the disputes pending between you and the same abbot, we assigned to them our beloved [Col. 0257C] son Hugh [Note: [Col. 0258D] See Letter 41, note, of Book III.], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin, as auditor. Before him the said abbot alleged that, when the church of Samoëns had been granted to the monastery of Sixt by your predecessor Ar. of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0258D] Arducius de Faucigny; see *Gallia Christiana vetus*, ibid.], and it had long possessed it peacefully, you unjustly despoiled it of that church. Whereupon, after he had obtained letters from us to our venerable brother the bishop [Note: [Col. 0258D] See Letter 176, note, of this sixth book.] and our beloved sons the provost and archdeacon of Aosta, and after you had repeatedly been peremptorily summoned by them but neither came before them nor sent a suitable representative, they finally received witnesses and, having taken the advice of prudent men, awarded possession of the aforesaid church to the monastery of Sixt, in order to preserve the matter.

[Col. 0257D] He further alleged that, after he had obtained apostolic letters against you addressed to the same bishop and archdeacon and to the prior of Saint Ursus at Aosta, because, at the command of your metropolitan, you had refused to render him justice against W., count of Geneva [Note: [Col. 0258D] William, count of Geneva, son of Amadeus. See Spon, *Histoire de Genève*, vol. I, p. 48, note.], whose retainers, by that count’s order, had not feared violently to lay hands upon the abbot, taking from him two riding-horses, while you had not hesitated to associate with the count during his life and faithfully to perform the funeral rites due to him after his death: the aforesaid bishop and archdeacon, since the prior of Saint Ursus could not in any way be present, and since you, six times peremptorily summoned by them, had refused to appear in their presence either personally or through a messenger, forbade you entrance into church on that account.

Furthermore, the said abbot produced before us letters of the aforesaid bishop, provost, and archdeacon of Aosta, containing both judgments; upon these there hung only the seals of the bishop and archdeacon; and he produced certain other letters concerning the restoration of the church of Samoëns, upon which hung the seals of all three.

But, on the other hand, your procurator asserted that the judgment rendered against [Col. 0258B] you concerning the church of Samoëns ought to be declared void: first, because it had been pronounced after an appeal lawfully lodged with us, since that place was legally suspect to you because, owing to hostility, you could not safely approach it; second, because it was contrary to the customary order of law, in that witnesses had been received before joinder of issue and a judgment in the nature of a final determination pronounced; and third, because it had been rendered by only two judges, since the third had not affixed his seal to the instrument of judgment, though the judgment had been issued in his name, nor was it shown that he had been unwilling or unable to take part in the matter.

He likewise maintained that the judgment of interdict had no force, since it had been pronounced by only two judges and it was not established that the third had been unwilling or unable to participate; [Col. 0258C] especially since the instrument of judgment stated that the sentence of interdict had been rendered by the bishop, provost, and archdeacon of Aosta, whereas in that case not the provost of Aosta but the prior of Saint Ursus had been delegated with the others. Thus, because they refused to proceed with the person with whom they could proceed, they were unable to proceed with the person with whom they wished to proceed.

We therefore, through the careful report of the said cardinal and the production of those instruments, having carefully heard and more fully understood these and other matters, have decreed both judgments void and without effect.

Given at Anagni, 7 February.

CCXXVIII. TO MICHAEL THE SUBDEACON. By apostolic authority he confirms his possession of the benefice in the church of Castries granted him by the bishop of Maguelone. (Anagni, 7 February.)

[Col. 0258D]

“It is customary to assent,” etc., as far as “assenting.” The benefice which you obtained in the church of Castries, by apostolic command, through the bishop of Maguelone of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0258D] See Letter 34, note, of Book III.], [Col. 0259A] we confirm by our authority, etc., just as you possess it lawfully and peacefully. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, 7 February.

CCXXIX [Note: [Col. 0259D] Raynaldus prints this letter almost in full under the year 1204, §1. Passages appearing in his edition are enclosed here in brackets.]. TO ALEXIUS, EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. Reply letter [Note: [Col. 0259D] See Letter 210 of this sixth book.]. (Anagni.)

We have received with paternal affection the letter which Your Imperial Excellence sent us, and have carefully noted what it communicated. We rejoice in the Lord and render thanks to him who rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomsoever he wills, because in his mercy he has inspired you with the devout desire to seek ecclesiastical unity: that the member might return to the head and the daughter [Col. 0259B] to the mother; and that the Church of Constantinople, which for a long time had withheld from the Apostolic See the devotion due to it, might render it reverence, obedience, and honor—as, even while you were still an exile and stood in our presence, you declared that you desired with your whole heart.

Moreover, in order to demonstrate your desire more fully and induce the peoples subject to you thereto by example better than by words, once an exile and a second time raised on high, you confirmed by oath that you would render to us and to our successors every devotion which your predecessors, the Catholic emperors, are known of old to have rendered to our predecessors, the orthodox fathers, the Roman pontiffs. You also promised [Col. 0259C] that, when opportunity was granted, you would wisely and powerfully incline the Eastern Church to this end, as you intimated to us by imperial letters.

Certainly, if you match deeds to words and carry out in works what you promise verbally, you will make God propitious to you, since you will be shown to honor him in honoring the dignity of his spouse. Beyond this, he himself will establish your empire in peace, and the Apostolic See will endeavor effectively to strengthen it. For, since through the help of the Latins, after divine aid, you have been restored to the empire, you ought not without reason to honor the Roman Church, whose sons have stood by you in this way and which, after God, can especially provide you and the empire of Constantinople with necessary protection.

We say this not because we ambitiously seek dominion, but because we would dutifully [Col. 0259D] render service, following the example of him who came not to be served but to serve; nor in order to lord it over the clergy, but to become from the heart an example to the flock. For the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who wield authority among them are called benefactors; but among Christ’s disciples it is not so: rather, the greatest among them is the servant of all, and the leader is as one who ministers.

[We therefore warn and exhort Your Imperial Highness in the Lord to remain thus devoted to the Apostolic See and to perform what you have sworn, lest you appear to make void the things which have proceeded [Col. 0260A] from your lips; instead, show yourself true to your promise and faithful to your oath. For if your empire is strengthened in the fear of the Lord and reverence for the Apostolic See, it will not totter as it has hitherto tottered, but, founded upon the firmness of that rock from which the prince of the apostles was called Peter, and of which the Apostle says, “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), it shall endure with perpetual stability and shall fear neither the blowing of the winds, nor the rush of the streams, nor the onslaught of the rains. Otherwise, lest you be deceived by empty error, we wish you to know that not only will you be unable to subdue the rebellion of your enemies, but you will not stand before their face.

Given at Anagni,] … in the sixth year.

CCXXX [Note: [Col. 0260D] Raynaldus published part of this letter under the year 1204, §3. Passages appearing in his edition are enclosed here in brackets.]. TO THE NOBLE MEN B., MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT; B., COUNT OF FLANDERS; L., COUNT OF BLOIS; H., COUNT OF SAINT-POL; AND THE OTHER BARONS AND KNIGHTS SIGNED WITH THE CROSS: THE SPIRIT OF SOUND COUNSEL. Concerning the promise of the emperor of Constantinople, and that he ought to swear obedience and reverence to the Roman Church, and that the patriarch should receive the pallium from the body of Saint Peter. (Anagni, as above.)

[Col. 0260B]

Because we fear that you are again stained with the taint of excommunication—and would that you had not incurred an injury to the faith—we wish you, by way of greeting and blessing, the spirit of sounder counsel for your safeguard. For although, as we have learned from your letters, you have pressed [Col. 0260C] our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, and obtained from him that he should confirm by oath that he would render to us and to our canonically appointed successors every devotion, etc., as in the preceding letter, as far as “powerfully,” nevertheless some strongly presume that you did this rather to excuse yourselves, so as to veil your transgression thereby, than in order that the daughter might return to her mother, the member to its head, and the part to its body.

But because works bear witness to truth, the subsequent result will better show with what intention you acted: namely, if the emperor himself openly acknowledges in letters that he has taken such an oath, which letters he should send us to be preserved as testimony; if he causes the patriarch, through solemn envoys, to acknowledge the primacy and teaching authority of the Roman Church, to promise us reverence and obedience, and to request from the Apostolic See the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, without which he cannot lawfully exercise the patriarchal office.

But if perhaps at the beginning of his advancement he denies this beginning of devotion and refuses to fulfil what we write, neither will your eye appear single nor his intention pure. Rather, you will seem to have added [Col. 0261A] a second transgression to the first which you incurred at Zara, when you again turned against the destruction of Christians the arms which you were believed to have taken up against the enemies of the cross], unless perhaps, to lessen fault and punishment, you have endeavored, from the zeal you bear toward your mother, the Roman Church, to complete in the Church of the Greeks what you began, since they had been undevoted toward her. This, then, will be both a true sign of the devotion of that emperor and an evident proof of your singleness of purpose.

Furthermore, although we desire that through your effort and solicitude the Church of Constantinople return to devotion and reverence for the Apostolic See, nevertheless, because we incline more earnestly toward aid for the Holy Land, lest its relief, hitherto delayed, be delayed longer, we warn and exhort all of you in [Col. 0261B] the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters, that, reconciled to ecclesiastical unity, you expiate the stains of your sins by tears of repentance. Thus, cleansed from the stain of crimes, you may laudably wage the Lord’s war, in purity of heart and body, in accordance with your original intention. Therefore exert all your strength for the recovery of the Holy Land, since this will be for you especially meritorious before God and glorious among men. We, moreover, shall endeavor, God granting it, effectively to procure what we see to be expedient for that land itself.

Given at Anagni, as above.

CCXXXI [Note: [Col. 0261D] Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §4. See also Bzovius, *Annales*, vol. XIII, p. 101, §4.]. TO THE BISHOPS OF SOISSONS AND TROYES [Note: [Col. 0261D] We have already often discussed the bishops of Soissons and Troyes.]. On the same subject as the preceding letter. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0261C]

Confident of the sincerity of your minds and hopeful of the purity of your devotion, we hold for certain that you strive for the honor and advancement of the Apostolic See and seek its exaltation as your own. Hence we do not at all doubt that, among your devout desires, you ardently desire that the Church of the Greeks return to the Roman Church, the member to the head and the daughter to the mother; that there be one fold and one shepherd; and that there henceforth be no distinction between Latins and Greeks, but that they be united both in the Catholic faith and in ecclesiastical unity.

Yet, however much the crusaders assert that they have labored for this end, it appears to some [Col. 0261D] that they did what they did rather in their own excuse than from devotion to the Church, lest we should be moved against them on account of the second transgression as we were on account of the first. For if they had possessed a single eye and labored principally for ecclesiastical unity, they would have procured, as devoutly as effectively, that the emperor should send his envoys to us with open letters in which he acknowledged that he had sworn, as he is said to have sworn. They would also have caused the patriarch, by his envoys and letters, to recognize the teaching authority and primacy of the Apostolic See and, promising reverence and obedience both to us and to our successors, to ask of us for a pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, without which neither he nor anyone else can lawfully exercise the patriarchal office.

We therefore earnestly warn and exhort your brotherhood, and command you by apostolic letters, to labor effectively that what has hitherto been done imperfectly may be supplied. For unless this is done in your presence [Note: [Col. 0261D] Thus in the Vatican and Conti transcripts.] … the emperor’s oath or promise will not readily attain its due effect, and you will appear to have consented to the second transgression as well as the first.

Given at Anagni … in the sixth year.

CCXXXII [Note: [Col. 0262D] Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §4.]. TO THE SAME. That they should induce the crusaders to repentance. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0262B]

When formerly you, brother of Soissons, and our beloved son Master Jo… of Noyon [Note: [Col. 0262D] We have already discussed above the bishop of Soissons and J. of Noyon.], together with certain others on behalf of the crusaders, came to the Apostolic See, we believe you remember how severe we were in receiving you, and how grievously we took what the army had done at Zara. For, since they had presumed to act contrary to the prohibition of the Apostolic See, which had announced by its letters that all those who attempted to invade or harm the lands [Col. 0262C] of Christians were bound by the bond of excommunication and deprived of the indulgence which the Apostolic See had granted to crusaders—unless they themselves wickedly impeded the crusaders’ journey, or some other just or necessary cause perhaps arose on account of which, with the advice of the legate of the Apostolic See, they could act otherwise—they had incurred sentence of excommunication by the act itself.

We subsequently declared void the absolution which they believed they had received from us, since no one can at all relax a sentence of the Apostolic See without that see’s authority. Yet, wishing to assist them in this hour of necessity, we commanded our beloved son P…, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, either personally or through another prudent man, to grant them the benefit of absolution after receiving an oath-bound assurance from those [Col. 0262D] who had not yet sworn to abide by our commands, and after hearing the confession of those who had sworn: namely, that they acknowledged that they had so sworn.

Among other things which, under obligation of oath, we enjoined upon those absolved, we remember expressly stating this: that henceforth, wholly abstaining from similar acts, they should not dare invade or harm Christian lands except for the aforesaid causes and under the stated condition. Afterwards, when the counts and barons informed us by their letters [Col. 0263A] that, in accordance with our command, they had obtained the benefit of absolution, and that all of them and two barons had bound themselves and their successors by open letters to make satisfaction in accordance with our command concerning their incurring sentence of excommunication at Zara, we expressly noted in the letters which we sent them that none of them should rashly flatter himself that he might lawfully occupy or plunder Greek territory on the ground that it was less devoted to the Apostolic See, or because the emperor of Constantinople had usurped the empire after deposing and even blinding his brother. For it did not belong to them to judge their offenses, nor had they assumed the sign of the cross for this purpose. We also commanded them to retain in memory the aforesaid prohibition, made to them under threat of anathema.

Although, therefore, we would have desired that through their effort and solicitude the Church of Constantinople should return to devotion to the Roman Church, nonetheless, because we neither wish nor ought to deceive them, we fear that they have again incurred sentence of excommunication; and many hold that they are by no means free from the guilt of perjury, because they presumed to act contrary to what had been forbidden them under obligation of oath. Since, however, we bear pastoral concern for their salvation, we warn your brotherhood and command you by apostolic letters to press them with admonitions and exhortations, so that through our legates, or either of them, or another prudent man whom [Col. 0263C] both or either of them may judge fit to delegate for this purpose, they may take care devoutly to seek and receive the benefit of absolution in true contrition of heart. Thus reconciled to ecclesiastical unity and cleansed from the stain of crimes, let them proceed to the service of Jesus Christ, to whom otherwise, as we believe, they would not be pleasing.

You also, if by consenting to their deeds you incurred the stain of excommunication, should have yourselves absolved in the same manner. Yet although, so that truth may set them free, we have not wished to suppress the truth, you must diligently ensure that they do not reveal their shameful conduct to outsiders, and especially to Greeks, lest perhaps the spark of devotion which seems kindled in the emperor himself be extinguished, to their loss—not so much to ours as to their own.

[Col. 0263D] Given at Anagni … in the sixth year.

CCXXXIII. TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 0263D] Robert, abbot of Aumale in Normandy, is said to have held office in 1190 and 1204; he appears in documents in June 1198. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 276. But perhaps this concerns the abbey of Saint Martin of Aumale in England, concerning which certain matters are related in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. III, p. 152.] AND CONVENT OF AUMALE. Privilege.

“Upon the just requests,” etc., as far as “consent.” The churches of Plage and Flames, which, with the consent of the diocesan bishops and of the patrons of those same churches, you have converted to your own uses: just as you lawfully, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

CCXXXIV. TO THE CONVENT OF SAINT EUPHEMIA. That they should receive John, chaplain of PP., as abbot. (Anagni, 5 February.)

[Col. 0264A]

When the sons, after their father had entered upon the way of all flesh, did not soothe their mother’s grief as they should have done, but increased it by seeking to tear her tunic, they could not dwell together as brothers, because they were not of one heart and one soul. Rather, erecting diverse tents for themselves, insofar as lay in their power, and dividing the fold, they appointed diverse pastors for themselves, setting men after their own heart over their heads. They cared not if perhaps their mother’s love were divided between two, so that she might belong to two, provided each one received even some small portion of the mother’s inheritance and might choose, according to the decision of his own will, as a special father not one common to the convent but one belonging rather to himself and his party.

Thus, because you acted so, it came about that, while each of you sought not the things of Jesus Christ but rather his own things, and pursued not the common welfare of the mother but his own advantage, your mother, bereft of a pastor, long endured the reproach of widowhood. And because she was drawn into factions and compelled to serve various lovers, she was finally forced to send us her complaint, since a dispute arose among those nominated by you as to which of them was superior and ought rather to prevail.

Although, after very many commissions from us obtained under a fixed form, as you fully know, both nominations were annulled, [Col. 0264C] certain of you nevertheless presumed to elect as their abbot a man unsuitable to your way of life, as being of another profession: namely, our beloved son, the abbot of Cîteaux [Note: [Col. 0264D] See Letter 220, note, of this sixth book.].

Furthermore, although we know the abbot himself to be a religious and learned man, prudent in spiritual and temporal matters, nevertheless monks of the Cistercian Order, though they follow the Rule of blessed Benedict, have their own observances and differ from you in certain matters both in habit and rite. Knowing that one does not plow well with an ox and an ass, nor should a garment be worn that is woven of wool and linen, and in the saying of the pagan:

[Col. 0264D] Unequal bullocks do not draw the plow well together. (OVID)

we did not judge that such an election should be approved. But lest your church should remain vacant longer because of your dissension, and remain widowed to the further harm of her sons, we judged that a man from her own tribe and kindred should be provided for her—one who would show her a proportionately greater affection of love, take her necessities upon himself, and strengthen her weaknesses, because he was bound thereto all the more by a double reason.

We have therefore taken from the bosom of the Apostolic See our beloved son J., formerly our chaplain, a man distinguished for religious life [Col. 0265A] and commendable for learning, tried and approved by us in the monastery of Cava and in our chapel, and deservedly acceptable to our brethren because of his integrity. We have given him as husband to its daughter, namely your church, and placed him over you as father and abbot, hoping that through his industry and solicitude your monastery will, God granting it, receive increase in spiritual and temporal affairs.

We therefore warn all of you, exhort you more earnestly, and command and enjoin you by apostolic letters that you receive gladly as father and pastor the same abbot, who comes with the fullness of our favor to undertake the care of that monastery; that you treat him kindly [Col. 0265B] and accept his wholesome admonitions and statutes, observing them humbly and inviolably. Thus, when he has experienced filial affection and devotion in you, he will be bound to show you the grace of paternal love—not as one lording it over the clergy, but as one who becomes from the heart an example to the flock. Otherwise, we shall regard as valid any judgment which he regularly pronounces against the rebellious, and, with the Lord’s help, shall cause it to be inviolably observed.

Given at Anagni, 5 February.

A letter was written to the clergy and people subject to the jurisdiction of the monastery of Saint Euphemia, in nearly the same terms, as far as “treat him kindly”: henceforth give him the same heed and support as you have hitherto given his predecessor, assisting him in managing the affairs of the monastery. When it is required of you, do not delay to render him an oath of fidelity according to the custom of yourselves and your forefathers. If you have sworn anything contrary to the fidelity owed to that monastery, observe it in no way, as unlawful. Thus you shall fulfil the apostolic command in such a manner that the same abbot ought to love and cherish you as special sons of the church. Otherwise, etc., as above.

Given at Anagni, 7 February.

CCXXXV [Note: [Col. 0265D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1204, §74.]. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARAGON. He defers the legation to Spain to another time. (Anagni, 14 February.)

[Col. 0265D] The injury done to the divine law and zeal for the house of the Lord seem to have touched your royal heart, since you attend to their sighs and ardently seek the destruction of those who grievously persecute the children of Israel and would erase from the earth the memory of Christ’s name. For you consider that you have received the material sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, and therefore strive, lest you seem to have received it in vain, to wrest from their hands that land which the most Christian kings and Catholic princes of old acquired by the shedding of their own blood.

But because you judge yourself unequal to this unless you are supported by the aid of other kings, and unless you are of one heart and one soul, executing vengeance among the nations and punishments among the peoples who do not gather with us but seek to take away our place and nation—and because they do not think with you on this matter, but their mind is far otherwise, so that some of them appear to be fostering enemies of the cross to their own harm—you asked us to send our legate to Spain so that he might turn the hearts of those kings toward you and more firmly unite you with them. Thus your alliance would become like a fortified city, as brothers helped one another and a threefold cord was not easily broken.

But when you first communicated to us your intention in this matter some time ago, [Col. 0266B] considering that as the wickedness of the day grows, the love of many grows cold, since there is none who does good, no, not even one, and that the kings of Spain not only think differently but oppositely in certain matters, and that no peace of heart prevails among them, but rather the peace of the sinner, we then judged it right to advise you to stir up more vigorously at this time against Christians [Note: [Col. 0265D] Thus in the transcript.]. Now also we adhere all the more firmly to our purpose and to that former counsel, which we still judge salutary, because the hostile party seems strengthened further by the fact that, as we have learned, the king of Morocco has triumphed over the king of Majorca. The two kingdoms having been joined into one, the power and malice of that same king of Morocco have increased. For the aforesaid reason, therefore, we do not presently intend [Col. 0266C] to send a legate to Spain.

We therefore warn Your Royal Serenity and exhort you in the Lord that, having God before your eyes, you strive to dedicate your youth to him and serve him diligently, so that from the throne of a temporal kingdom you may attain the everlasting kingdom.

Given at Anagni, 14 February.

CCXXXVI [Note: [Col. 0265D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year [Col. 0266D] 1204, §57.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. He gives the reasons why he had previously written too harshly, and consoles him [Note: [Col. 0266D] For the subject, see Letters 149, 150, 151, and 152 of this sixth book.]. (Anagni, 14 February.)
