Although the letter which we sent to your brotherhood on behalf of our venerable brother, the bishop of Auxerre [lacuna], against the nobleman [lacuna], count of Auxerre, was severe and, as though sharper than any two-edged sword, pierced your mind—so that, upon receiving it, you were in some measure weary of your very life, since it contained much bitterness and no sweetness, having more aloes than honey, indeed wholly ignorant of honey, which the Mosaic law does not admit in sacrifice, and tasting only of salt, which is placed upon every sacrifice—nevertheless we do not regret having written thus. Rather, we rejoice that we made you sorrowful for a time: not merely because you were sorrowful, but because you were sorrowful unto repentance, or, what we desire no less, unto caution.

Although we thought it better to suppress the reasons why we wrote to you so harshly than to set forth any of them, nevertheless, lest you be swallowed up by excessive sorrow and, unwilling to be consoled, be utterly confounded if you seek but find none to console you, and be compelled to turn back and withdraw your hand from the plough, we now explain why we judged that you should be so sharply provoked.

Certainly, since the count is noble and powerful—indeed, reckoned among the more powerful and noble men of the kingdom of France—we wrote thus not to disgrace you but to provide for you, so that the severity which you might afterwards exercise against him by apostolic authority should be excused by the harshness of our letter, and that his kinsmen and friends, should you take action, might lay it to our charge rather than yours. Moreover, since very many prelates, as we report with sorrow, not only keep their hands, as is written, from bloodshed, but, as though their tongue had cleaved to their throats, have become like dumb dogs unable to bark, we wished through you and in you more vigorously to stir them up to “execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples,” to declare their impiety to the impious and their crimes to the wicked, to draw forth Peter’s sword, which rust had consumed among them, for the punishment of evildoers, [uncertain surviving fragments: “lau… vo… bo…”]. [Note: So in the Vatican and Conti transcripts.] We wished them also to carry out the work of God, not negligently but diligently, lest our ministry be blamed in them if henceforth they did not punish but indulged the faults of their subjects, and if there were among them respect of persons.

For, since it is known throughout the whole kingdom of France that we embrace you with a certain special affection among our brethren and fellow-bishops, and are especially zealous for your honour, by the aforesaid letter we rebuked the negligence of others, who would understand for themselves that, if we spare not you, neither would we spare them in a similar case. For how would one who does not spare the natural branches of the olive tree spare the adopted shoots of the wild olive?

Furthermore, since new maladies require new remedies, and since it has hitherto been unheard of that anyone should so harshly kick against the goad and so persecute ecclesiastical discipline that, because his diocesan bishop, on account of his offences, had laid his land under interdict and had forbidden ecclesiastical burial to those dying therein, he should turn the bishop’s chamber into a cemetery and bury in it the bodies of the dead: since we were ready, and wished you likewise to be ready, to avenge so great a presumption and to exercise ecclesiastical severity more severely against the presumptuous man, we harshly rebuked your previous negligence, lest you should neglect to fulfil our command. For the language of one who reproves has more force than that of one who merely admonishes, and moves the hearer more strongly to obedience, because words uttered by an adviser with a calm mind seem to have been spat from the very edge of his lips; [Note: So in the Vatican and Conti transcripts.] whereas one who reproves is believed, even in anger, to pour forth speech from the abundance of his heart.

Since, therefore, such evil beginnings had then to be vigorously opposed, lest you should act too leniently towards him, we judged you should not be mildly admonished but sharply rebuked. For although it is poetic, what is read in the Poet is nevertheless almost prophetic and moral:

> Resist beginnings; too late is the remedy prepared,  
> When evils have gathered strength through long delay.  
> —Ovid

Moreover, in view of the enormity of the crime committed, the same count ought, besides other penalties, to be enjoined to carry upon his own shoulders the corpse which he caused to be brought for burial in the bishop’s chamber, so that, as his offence is known, so too his penance might be marked, lest the ease of pardon give anyone an incentive to offend.

We therefore attentively admonish and exhort your brotherhood, and by these apostolic writings command you, that your countenance not fall and that you do not distrust our affection, in which you ought to have greater confidence precisely because we judged that you should be rebuked more severely. For you know it is written: “A father corrects the son whom he loves” (Prov. 3), etc.; “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. 13); for God too reproves and chastens those whom he loves. Know, therefore, that however harsh the words themselves may seem to you, such stern correction proceeded not from the bitterness of indignation but from zeal for righteousness.

We also will and command that, if you have conceived any resentment against the same bishop, you lay it aside. We bear witness to the truth that he did not request from us a letter in this form, but sent us only a tearful complaint concerning the count.

Besides, we cannot but wonder that certain persons have presumed not to explain but to distort a certain statement contained in the letter which we sent you, to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of France [lacuna], as though we regarded him as suspect in the matter of defending heretics—though we know that he rather attacks them. But since the Apostle commands abstinence not only from evil but from every appearance of evil, lest even enemies should find something in him to rebuke, we wished that, as he is free from guilt, so he should show himself free from ill repute; and that he should so provide for the bishop, exiled because of the count’s malice, that by recalling him he might appear to be persecuting the heretics who regarded the bishop’s exile as their own joy.

Therefore, go personally to the king; faithfully disclose to him the purity of our intention; and strive to recall him from that perverse interpretation, excusing the aforesaid bishop before him, since that statement was not inserted in the said letter at the bishop’s request.

Finally, although we send you the present letter for your consolation, lest perhaps excessive sorrow swallow up your mind, we nevertheless wish you to remember the former letters, so that you may set yourself as a wall for the house of the Lord against those coming up from the opposite side, in such a way that his zeal may seem to consume you.

Given at Anagni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

### CCXXXVII. TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF MOLÈSME

That they are not to borrow money without the assent of the abbot and convent.  
(Anagni, eleventh day before the Kalends of March.)

You are to know that it has come to our hearing that certain among you, apart from the assent of your abbot [Note: At that time Galcherus was head of the monastery of Molèsme; he held office from 1197 until 1209. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 736.] and convent, received a certain sum of money on loan, as a result of which your monastery and the obediences subject to it are oppressed by a heavy burden of debts.

Wherefore, by the authority of these presents, we strictly prohibit any monk or lay brother bound by the profession of your house, without the consent and permission of the abbot and of the greater part of your chapter, from standing surety for anyone or borrowing money from anyone beyond the amount fixed by the prudent determination of your chapter, unless this be for the manifest benefit of your house. If anyone should presume to do so, the convent shall in no way be bound to answer for it.

Given at Anagni, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March.

### CCXXXVIII. TO THE DEAN [Note: See letter 223 of this sixth book.] AND CHAPTER OF ÉVREUX

That no layman possessing a right of patronage in churches may exact tithes.  
(Anagni, seventh day before the Ides of February.)

It is fitting that we should have an effective concern for the advancement of churches, if we wish to carry out the duty incumbent upon our office and gladly extend apostolic assistance to those who strive to promote their growth.

Since, therefore, as we have learned, there are many laymen in the diocese of Évreux who possess rights of patronage in churches and, by an evil custom, retain tithes in many places as though by hereditary right, we, desiring with paternal benevolence to provide for your church, grant you by the authority of these presents that, if any of those laymen who hold rights of patronage in churches or tithes in the aforesaid manner cannot be induced to restore them to their churches and should perhaps wish to give them to the chapter of Évreux, you may, with the assent of your bishop [Note: See letter 225.], receive and peaceably possess them, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal.

Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the sixth year.

### CCXXXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE [Note: He has already been mentioned frequently.]

That he should rise up to root out heretical depravity.  
(Anagni, eleventh day before the Kalends of March.)

[Note: This letter is cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §57.]

Heretical perversity has built its house like a moth and made its shelter like that of a watchman, corrupting human minds with perverse persuasions and, by preaching error, taking from them the foundation of faith; so that, when wind rushes in from the wilderness, the corrupted house cannot stand, and the shelter which does not cling to its foundation is wholly blown away, and thus the corrupted descend alive into hell together with their corrupters.

Although, therefore, we have judged that the investigation and correction of those persons should be entrusted to you, to our venerable brother [lacuna], archbishop of Bourges, and to our beloved son [lacuna], abbot of Cluny, together with any others—those who, like the moth, have begun to build their place upon the priestly garment, and who are designated in the Gospel under the appearance of lepers, upon whose healthy colour a diseased whiteness is spread, since they mingle unsound things with sound and are varied by diversity of colour in their words—nevertheless, since you are their diocesan and are bound, as their proper physician, to know whence their infirmities arise and to what their symptoms tend, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writings that you yourself proceed with diligent concern to investigate this infirmity and cure it.

For if you do not expel the rottenness of a wound by opening it, sound flesh will by no means grow together in the place of the corruption; and if you do not uproot by the cutting of the ploughshare the thorns of the field whose cultivation is entrusted to you, the earth will not produce a crop from the seed it has received. For where he who has been appointed preacher is silent, neither rebuking what should be rebuked nor correcting what should be corrected, he seems to approve the fault—which, as it grows, is given to others as an example when the tongue of the shepherd does not cut it off.

Watch therefore, venerable brother in Christ, and guard your garments lest you walk naked, lest that moth of corruption spoil them and build there a place for decay, should heretics strip the people entrusted to you, as though untaught, of the covering of faith by their pestilent preaching, leaving them naked after taking away their clothing, so that the cold of perversity may destroy those whom the warmth of divine virtue had cherished.

Given at Anagni, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth year.

### CCXL. TO THE ELECT OF GRADO

[Note: Concerning the patriarch of Grado at about the time with which we are concerned, there is very little in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 1208.

“XXXIX. John Signale … to whom Pope Innocent III wrote various letters in the third year of his pontificate; in the year 1200 of the Lord’s Incarnation he died under the same Innocent.

“XL. Benedict Faliero, formerly primicerius of St Mark’s, was elected patriarch of Grado with the unanimous consent of the clergy. He received the pallium and blessing from Innocent after the year 1201, and died during the final years of that pope; he was a man endowed with nobility of birth and exceptional piety.”]

He rebukes him for delaying to receive consecration, and threatens him.  
(Anagni, tenth day before the Kalends of March.)

If we had sought to proceed against you according to the requirement of your deserts and with canonical strictness, the petition now made on your behalf would have found no place; for not only could you not be promoted to the episcopate, but you ought to have been deposed from the office of prelacy.

For you delayed so long after the confirmation of your election to receive the gift of consecration that, if you did so in ignorance, you ought wholly to be disregarded as ignorant; or neglected as negligent; or despised as contemptuous. For you did not take care to receive consecration within the canonical time, nor did you choose to seek it even long after the prescribed time—without mentioning the pallium.

But because darkness cannot be hidden before the light, though it can be obscured, the reason why you did this could not escape us; and the more you sought concealment, the more you came to public notice. Indeed, as we have clearly learned from your letters and those of others, infirmity and fatness—more of heart than body, more of mind than belly—have hitherto been able to hinder you, and indeed will be able to hinder you still more hereafter.

Let it therefore suffice you that you have hitherto been tolerated, and count it a great matter to remain standing when you deserved not to rise but to fall. Nevertheless, with God as our author, we shall determine what we see must be determined in this matter, preferring, for the sake of necessary caution, to leave you in suspense amid uncertainty rather than to suspend you from office.

Given at Anagni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March.

### CCXLI. TO THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-ÈVRE [Note: Garinus—also called Warinus or Warnerius—governed the monastery of Saint-Èvre from at least 1195 until 1227. He later became bishop of Toul. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 1079.] AND SAINT-LÉON [Note: Clement, abbot of Saint-Léon, is found in 1204, when the church of Manili was granted by Bishop Matthew. Ibid., col. 1105.]; AND TO MASTER R., ARCHDEACON OF TOUL

That a legate of the Apostolic See may confer benefices even without consulting the patrons.  
(Anagni, tenth day before the Kalends of March.)

Our beloved son R., canon of Metz, humbly informed us that, when our venerable brother [lacuna], bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, generously conferred upon him the church of Saint-Trond after its proper pastor had resigned it into the legate’s hands, our beloved son B., archdeacon of Metz, to whom the presentation to that church belonged, asserting that it could not be conferred by the legate without consulting him, unreasonably opposed the grant and presumed improperly to harass the said canon regarding the church.

Since a prelate has more right in granting than a patron has in presenting, and since a prelate suffers no prejudice if a church is granted by the legate of the Apostolic See without consultation with him, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, after prior warning, you compel the said archdeacon, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to desist from his improper harassment in this matter.

Notwithstanding any letters, etc. If all of you cannot do so, let two of you do it, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth year.

### CCXLII. TO THE BISHOP OF AGDE [Note: At that time the church of Agde was governed by Raymond II, descended from the illustrious and very ancient family of the lords of Montpellier. He held the episcopal staff from 1192 until 1213. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 679.]; AND TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-PONS [Note: Hermengaud, abbot of Saint-Pons, presided from 1181 until 1205, when he was raised to the bishopric of Béziers. Ibid., col. 232.]

He confirms by apostolic authority the sentence of suspension pronounced against the bishop of Béziers by P. of Castelnau and Ralph, monks of Fontfroide, legates of the Apostolic See.  
(Anagni, twelfth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Note: The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* cite but do not print this letter; ibid., col. 324.]

As has become known to us from the tenor of the letters of our beloved sons P. of Castelnau and Ralph, monks of Fontfroide: when, by our command, they were diligently and carefully labouring to root heretics out of the province of Narbonne, as discreet men possessing zeal for God and taking up arms and shield for the faith of the Christian name, the bishop of Béziers [lacuna] [Note: William IV of Roquessels, or Roquesel, formerly abbot of Saint-Aphrodisius and canon of Saint-Nazaire, was elected bishop of Béziers in 1199. He held office until 1205, when he is said to have been killed by the treachery of his servants. Ibid., col. 325.], though requested by them, refused to go with them to admonish concerning this matter the nobleman [lacuna], count of Toulouse.

Afterwards, when they asked him to join them in admonishing the consuls of the city of Béziers to abjure heresy and to defend the Church of God against heretics, he not only refused to comply with their admonitions but impeded the undertaking, making himself an enemy of Christ, although he was himself bound to do this by the duty of his office. And when, after summoning the clergy by our authority, they ordered him that, unless the said consuls had abjured their heresies by a fixed day, he should not delay to bind them with the bond of excommunication, although he promised to do so, he by no means carried it into effect.

For this reason the said P. and R. suspended him from administration and from episcopal office until he should present himself before us, strictly forbidding the clergy of Béziers, under pain of excommunication and by virtue of obedience, to obey him in anything in the meantime.

Although we have heard of very many enormities concerning him, which we neither can nor ought to pass over in dissimulation, since in rooting out the crime of heresy, through which the divine majesty is blasphemed, he has shown himself not only negligent but contumacious, we hold the aforesaid sentence of suspension to be ratified. We command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings that you declare him suspended from every office and benefice, and cause this to be publicly announced in all the churches of the diocese of Béziers, without appeal, until, while suspended, he comes into our presence with letters from the same monks. By our authority firmly enjoin all the clergy and people of the diocese of Béziers not to render him any obedience.

Moreover, lest the church of Béziers suffer loss, entrust its administration in the meantime, supported by our authority and without obstacle of appeal, to persons whom you know to be suitable for this; restraining opponents, appeal set aside, by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Anagni, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth year.

### CCXLIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE [Note: We have already dealt frequently with the archbishop of Narbonne.]

A lamentable letter that his entire province is filled with heretics.  
(Anagni, fourth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Note: This letter is cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §57.]

The wondrous architect, the power and wisdom of Christ God, built a house for himself by hewing out seven columns and setting himself as the chief stone in its foundation. Hope, together with prophetic utterance, raised its walls; evangelical teaching together with charity set upon it the roof of completion; and, establishing at its four corners the four cardinal virtues, he adorned it within besides with the varied ornament of virtues, so that “all the glory of the king’s daughter” might be “within.”

But he who did not stand in the truth from the beginning, unable patiently to endure the wondrous structure of this building, sent forth from himself a mighty wind from the wilderness, in order, if possible, to overthrow the foundation after shaking the four corners of the house. Yet, though the house is shaken in many ways, it cannot suffer total ruin, because it has been wondrously founded upon firm rock. Nevertheless, when battering-rams are brought round against it, he sometimes shakes certain stones out of the structure, while sons fight against their mother in a conflict more than civil, and tear the seamless tunic of Christ, which ought rather to have been allotted by lot to one person.

For the fly which is at the end of the river of Egypt and the bee which is in the land of Assyria have come, occupying the torrents of valleys and resting in the caverns of rocks and in every hollow. They can claim nothing over those who cling to the solid rock and are made firm by it; but the gathering of bulls rages among the cows of the peoples.

Yet those appointed to guard this house and established as shepherds of the Lord’s flock do not today come up against the enemy, to set themselves as a wall for the house of Israel, fighting for it with the beasts of the earth against such enemies. Scarcely anyone can now be found who, with Moses, places the sword upon his thigh to avenge the Redeemer’s injury against those who set up a molten calf to be worshipped; nor does Phinehas pierce with his dagger the Hebrew joined with the Midianite woman. Benaiah too does not descend on snowy days to strike the lion in the midst of the cistern; nor does Samson overthrow the Philistines with the jawbone of an ass. Ehud likewise does not draw his left-handed dagger against Eglon, king of Moab; nor do Simeon and Levi gird on swords to seek vengeance for the violation of their sister.

The shepherds, feeding themselves before all else, do not provide pasture for the Lord’s flock. They do not strive to strengthen what is weak, nor heal what is sick; they do not bind up what is broken, nor seek what has been lost. Instead, they keep their sword from blood and do the work of God negligently. A famine has arisen in the land, and little children ask for bread, but scarcely anyone is found to break it for them.

Thus, although your province has been infected with the stain of heretical perversity, not only do you fail, as we have heard, to strive to root out the tares sown over your field—though, following Naboth’s example, you ought rather to expose yourself to death than allow King Ahab to make your vineyard a vegetable garden—but you also deny your aid and support to our beloved sons Brother R. and Brother P. of Castelnau, monks of Fontfroide, who have been sent there by the Apostolic See to eradicate heretical perversities. You are unwilling to assist them in their necessities, although the mouth of the threshing ox ought not to be muzzled; and it is by no means fitting that you should deny aid to those who seek not their own interests but rather those of Jesus Christ, and who labour alike in word and doctrine. Even if they had not been sent by us, you ought, by the office laid upon you, to embrace them and receive them in the bowels of charity.

When they asked you to go with them to our beloved son, the nobleman [lacuna], count of Toulouse, so that by your persuasion as well as theirs he might be induced to swear that he would fight heretics in defence of ecclesiastical unity, you in no way chose to comply with them. You ought yourself to have asked rather than to have been asked. Nor would you even then grant them so much as one mounted escort for carrying out the work which they had begun, though afterwards, at their urgent and importunate insistence, you judged that one should be granted them.

Since, therefore, the tambourine ought not to be denied to those who give the psalm, nor should those who labour to sow spiritual things be forbidden to reap temporal things, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, whenever the said monks come to you, you receive them kindly and diligently provide honourably for them both in mounted escorts and in other necessities. Likewise, assist them against the heretics in such a manner that they may be able worthily to complete the work begun, and that you may no longer be reproved for negligence. Know that, if you act otherwise—which we do not believe—you may fear our indignation.

Given at Anagni, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

The same was written in nearly the same terms to bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established throughout the province of Narbonne.

It was written to [lacuna], abbot of Valmagne, and to Master Rodulf, canon of Narbonne, that, when requested by the said brethren, they should gird themselves for labour and go with them into the Lord’s harvest.

It was written to [lacuna], abbot of Cîteaux, that, if he knows any in his order to be suitable for the office of preaching, he should not delay, when requested by the said brethren, to send them in aid of those same brethren.

### CCXLIV. TO MASTER ROBERT

An exposition of the decretal letter *Licet Heli*.

[Note: It is found among the Decretals, book V, title 3, “On simony, and that nothing is to be demanded or promised for spiritual things,” chapter 32. For greater accuracy we indicate variant readings.]

By your letter you informed us that you are greatly [Note: The Decretals omit this word, and below read “without delay.”] doubtful concerning a certain decretal letter which, you assert, we issued concerning the admission of witnesses against simoniacal perversity. Know therefore without hesitation that we did not issue the letter which begins, “Although for the abolition” (*Quamvis ad abolendam*); rather, we acknowledge that we issued the other, which begins, “Although Eli” (*Licet Heli*) [Note: See letter 260 of the second book, which is also found among the Decretals, at the cited place, chapter 31.].

For understanding it, we believe distinctions must be made: whether the person against whom proceedings are brought for simoniacal perversity is simply denounced or criminally accused; [Note: The Decretals read *aut* (“or”); below they have *exstitit* in place of *consistit*, and *an* in place of *utrum*.] whether proceedings are conducted according to the strictness of law or according to the moderation of equity; whether he is a religious who has already renounced the world or a secular person who still remains in the world; and whether he is of a lower rank or of a more eminent dignity.

Further, whether he formerly enjoyed a clear reputation and good fame, or is gravely defamed and highly suspect; whether he can easily be punished or cannot be condemned without scandal. Moreover, whether the witnesses are respectable or criminal; and whether they have already amended their crime or still persist in it. Again, whether the crimes are the same or lesser, or equal or greater; and whether the witnesses are believed to have testified from zeal for justice or from a motive of malice. Finally, whether only the statements of witnesses are brought forward to expose simoniacal heresy, or whether other supporting evidence also assists. All these distinctions must be made in order to understand that letter, as a diligent investigator can perceive from its sequence. [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals; below they read *quidem* (“indeed”) for *namque* (“for”), and omit “against the aforesaid abbot.”]

For that abbot of Pomposa, who had long before renounced the world, was gravely defamed for simony, perjury, dissipation of goods, and incapacity. And when simony appeared to have been proved against the abbot in many ways through monks who had sworn to bear witness to the truth, he raised many exceptions against the witnesses—namely, conspiracies and mortal enmities, theft and adultery—in order to remove them from giving testimony.

But, lest the purity of innocence should be brought down in confusion or simoniacal perversity should escape unpunished, we admitted as needing proof only those exceptions which, if perhaps proved, would show that the witnesses had proceeded not from zeal for justice but from a motive of malice, such as conspiracies and mortal enmities. We judged the other exceptions raised, such as theft and adultery, to be rejected because of the enormity of simoniacal heresy, in comparison with which other crimes are reckoned almost as nothing. For although, if proved, they would somewhat weaken the witnesses’ credibility, they would not wholly destroy it when other supporting evidence assisted—especially when the witnesses had already amended their crime.

Thus we judged that such persons should be admitted against such a person in such a manner, not according to the strictness of law but according to the moderation of equity; for the proceedings were not criminal, so that he might be deposed from his order, but civil, so that, as unworthy and harmful, he might be removed from administration. Indeed, such prelates can be removed from administrations for lighter causes, especially by the supreme pontiff, who possesses authority not only to judge but also to make dispositions, [Note: These words are omitted by the Decretals.] as the approved custom of certain religious persons requires. Hence the aforesaid abbot, not awaiting sentence, withdrew, as though conscious of guilt.

### CCXLV. TO THE ABBOT OF CANCELLATA [Note: See letter 227 of this sixth book, note.]; TO MASTER B., CANON OF ALBATERRENSIS, IN THE DIOCESE OF PÉRIGUEUX; AND TO A. OF LA FAIA, CANON OF SAINT-FRONT OF PÉRIGUEUX

That they are to ensure that J. Morelli, clerk, named canon and brother in the church of Angoulême, enjoys his prebend.  
(Anagni, seventh day before the Ides of February.)

When we had sent our letters to our beloved sons [lacuna], abbot of Nantueil [Note: After Bernard, abbot of Nantueil in 1187, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1293, immediately mention William in 1215.], and [lacuna], abbot of Beania [Note: Nearly the same as in the preceding note. William, abbot of Beania, mentioned in 1188, is immediately followed by P., whose name is found in documents only in 1219. Ibid., col. 1119.], and [lacuna], cantor of Saintes, on behalf of our beloved son J. Morelli, clerk, concerning restoration of the prebend of Angoulême, of which he asserts that he was despoiled by the canons of that church, the same judges, as became known to us from the contents of their letters, took care to receive witnesses regarding the institution of the said J. and sent the attestations themselves, sealed with their seals, to our apostolic office.

When the same J. came before us with those documents, we appointed our beloved son Odo, subdeacon and our chaplain, as auditor between them and our beloved son El., canon of Angoulême. Since E. was unwilling to contest the suit on this matter, the attestations were opened in his presence; from them it was clearly established that the aforesaid J. had, by apostolic authority, been instituted a canon of the church of Angoulême and had been corporally invested, through a procurator, with the prebend of that church.

Wherefore, by apostolic writings, we command and enjoin your discretion that, if it is established to you that the same J. was unjustly despoiled of the aforesaid prebend or is contrary to justice not admitted to it, you cause it to be restored to him without appeal, restraining any opponents or rebels, appeal set aside, by ecclesiastical censure.

Furthermore, because the canons of Angoulême appealed on this matter to our hearing but did not pursue the appeal they had lodged, determine, without obstacle of appeal, what is canonical concerning the expenses to be restored to the said J.; and cause what you determine to be firmly observed by the same coercive means. If all of you cannot do this, nevertheless let two of you carry it out.

Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

# SEVENTH BOOK OF THE REGISTERS OR LETTERS OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

## Seventh year of the pontificate; A.D. 1204

### I. TO CALOJOHN, KING OF THE BULGARIANS AND VLACHS, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS

A privilege by which authority is granted to Leo, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross, legate of the Apostolic See, to anoint and crown him king.  
(Anagni, sixth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Note: This letter is reported in the *Deeds of Innocent III*, §73, but not without certain errors. Raynaldus published part of the same letter under the year 1204, §34. We print the complete and more correct text from the Conti transcript. Passages found in Raynaldus are here enclosed in brackets.]

To Kaloyan, illustrious king of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, and to his successors in perpetuity, succeeding him both in the kingdom and in devotion to the Apostolic See.

Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, to whom the Father gave all things into his hand, subjecting all beneath his feet, whose are the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it—indeed [Col. 0277C], before whom every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—has appointed the supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See and Roman Church, whom he established as his vicar in blessed Peter, over nations and kingdoms, granting him the power to uproot, destroy, overthrow, and scatter, and to build and to plant. He spoke to him in the prophet who was among the priests of Anathoth: “Behold, I have set thee over nations and kingdoms, that thou mayest uproot and destroy and overthrow and scatter, and build and plant” (Jer. 1).

To demonstrate this more expressly, not through another but through himself, when, for humankind, he assumed human flesh and extended his sandal over Idumaea, so that the foreigners might be subjected to him and that he might bring in his sheep which were not of this [Col. 0278B] fold, so that there might be one fold and one shepherd—in himself, who is God above all, blessed for ever—he laid the foundation of the universal Church, and conferred teaching authority and primacy upon Peter, prince of his apostles, saying to him: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and to thee I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18). There also he subsequently added: “Whatever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (ibid.).

Moreover, after his Passion, when about to ascend into heaven, he entrusted and commended his fold, that is, the Church, wholly to him, saying: “Feed [Col. 0278C] my sheep” (John 21), repeating the expression three times. By this he plainly showed that those sheep do not belong to his fold which obstinately deny that they have been committed and subjected to blessed Peter, and refuse to be instructed by his teaching and submit to his authority.

For the Church is that ark in which a few souls were saved when all the rest perished in the flood. Hence, just as all whom the ark did not receive perished in the flood, so all who are found outside the Church shall be condemned at the judgment. For the ark signifies the Church, the deluge the judgment, and Noah, ruler of the ark, Peter, shepherd of the Church. Noah is read to have walked with the Lord; Peter, however, is written to have come to the Lord upon the waves of the sea, which signifies this [Col. 0279A] world. In this it is also expressly indicated that not some particular Church alone, but the whole world and the universal Church, were committed to Peter. For as many waters are many peoples, so the great and broad sea signifies the whole world.

Therefore, when the others were called to share in the burden of pastoral care, the Lord received Peter into the fullness of power, when he said to him: “Thou shalt be called Cephas,” which is interpreted Peter (John 1), and “head,” thus showing Peter to be the head of the Church, so that, like the ointment which descended from Aaron’s head into his beard, he might diffuse it into the members, so that nothing might wholly be lost to him. For in the head resides the fullness of the senses, while some portion of them is communicated to the members.

Further, when [Col. 0279B] Peter asked whether, if his brother sinned against him, he should forgive him as many as seven times, the Lord is read to have answered: “I say not unto thee, until seven times, but until seventy times seven” (Matt. 18). Certainly, since all time is contained within the number of seven days, the number seven multiplied by itself here denotes all sins of all persons, since Peter alone can remit not merely every crime, but the crimes of all. For to him, and to no other, the Lord is found to have said: “Follow thou me” (Matt. 8); that is, imitate me in the office of the true shepherd and in the fullness of ecclesiastical power. For the Lord appointed him his vicar in office and successor in teaching, thus transferring to him the inheritance, into whose splendid portions [Note: Thus in the transcripts and in the *Gesta*.] his lot had fallen, so that through him and under him [Col. 0279C] he might, as it were, make others sharers [Note: Thus also in the Conti transcript.] in the inheritance bequeathed.

[Therefore, although unworthy, we act on earth in the place of him who rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomsoever he will, through whom kings reign and princes rule; and since we know that it was said to Peter and his successors, and to us in him: “I have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith fail not; and thou, when thou hast turned again, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22); and since by the Lord’s command we are bound to feed his sheep: desiring to provide with paternal care, in spiritual and temporal matters, for the peoples of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, who for a long time have been alienated from their mother’s breasts, and relying upon the authority of him through whom Samuel anointed David king, we establish thee [Col. 0279D] king over them. Through our beloved son Leo, [Note: We have already dealt with Cardinal Leo above, in note to letter 5 of Book V. Yet this first letter of the present, seventh book makes clear that Leo had been invested with the title of Santa Croce before 1204, not in 1205, as was there reported from Oldoin.] cardinal-priest of the title of Santa Croce and legate of the Apostolic See, a prudent and honourable man, especially acceptable to us among our brethren, we send thee the sceptre of the kingdom and the royal diadem, to be placed upon thee by him as though by our own hands. We receive from thee a sworn undertaking that thou wilt remain devoted and obedient to us, our successors, and the Roman Church, and that thou wilt preserve all lands and peoples subject to thy [Col. 0280A] authority in obedience and devotion to the Apostolic See.

Furthermore, at the petition of our venerable brother Blasius, bishop of Brandizuber, whom thou didst send to the Apostolic See, we grant thee free authority to strike public coinage in thy kingdom, bearing thine own image. We also grant to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Trnovo, the privilege of primacy throughout all lands under thy rule: he and his successors shall henceforth crown thy successors, having received from them the same oath, by authority of the Apostolic See; they shall hold the dignity of primate in thy land; the metropolitans established in the provinces both of Bulgaria and of Vlachia shall be subject to him; and, according to canonical form, they shall render the reverence and honour due to a primate.

Thus, dearest son, acknowledge the favour which the Apostolic See, thy mother, bestows upon thee; thus repay us for all that we grant thee; thus confirm thy kingdom in subjection and devotion to the Apostolic See, so that, being founded beneath blessed Peter upon the firmness of that rock of which the Apostle says, “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), it may fear neither the rains’ downpour, nor blasts of wind, nor assaults of rivers; and so that thou also, besides the aid of the Apostolic See which, according to thy devotion, thou shalt experience in the present, mayest pass from a temporal kingdom to an everlasting kingdom.

We therefore decree that absolutely no one shall … infringe this privilege of our enactment and confirmation, or, etc. But if anyone, etc.

[Col. 0280C] Given at Anagni, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1203, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

II. [Note: [Col. 0280D] This is read in the *Gesta of Innocent III*, §75, though not without some errors. Raynaldus gives the same almost entire, under the year 1204, §37. We give it complete in every respect from the Conti transcript. Passages found in Raynaldus are enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TRNOVO. He also establishes the archbishop of Trnovo as primate of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, and sends him such a privilege through the said legate. (At Anagni, as above.)

To the archbishop of Trnovo, primate of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, and to his successors canonically appointed, who shall succeed in devotion to the Apostolic See, in perpetuity.

The King of kings, etc., as far as “Samuel [Col. 0280D] anointed David king,” we have established as king over them our most dear son in Christ Kaloyan, hitherto their lord, through our beloved son, etc., as far as “shall preserve them in devotion to the Apostolic See.”

[We also establish thee primate in the kingdom of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, and by this present privilege grant to the Church of Trnovo the authority of primacy. We decree that thou and thy successors, who succeed thee in devotion to the Apostolic See, shall take precedence over the other [Col. 0281A] metropolitans of Bulgaria and Vlachia by reason of thy primacy, and that they shall render to thee and to them, according to canonical form, the reverence and honour due to a primate. We wish thy brotherhood to know that, in our view, these two names, “primate” and “patriarch,” mean almost exactly the same thing, since patriarchs and primates hold one and the same rank, although their names differ.

By this present privilege we grant thee, and through thee thy successors, free authority henceforth to anoint, bless, and crown the kings of the Bulgarians and Vlachs. Upon thy death, now primate of the aforesaid Church, no one is to be set over it through any trickery of usurpation, except one canonically elected to it according to approved custom. The person elected shall be solemnly consecrated bishop by the metropolitan [Col. 0281B] and the other suffragans of that Church who are able to be present. Once consecrated, he shall send his envoys to the Apostolic See to seek the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, the insignia, that is, of the fullness of the pontifical office. Upon receiving it, he shall take the oath to us, our successors, and the Roman Church which other primates and metropolitans customarily render to us, and which thou thyself didst render when receiving the pallium. We send its form, sealed with our bull, for perpetual remembrance, specifying therein that whenever they crown as king any successor of the aforesaid king, they are to receive from him the prescribed [Col. 0281C] oath.

Whenever one of the metropolitans who are subject to thee by right of primacy has entered upon the way of all flesh, thou shalt confirm the canonical election of a suitable person and consecrate the person elected as bishop. As for the pallium, thou shalt send thine envoys, together with the envoys of the Church over which thou presidest, to the Apostolic See, and we shall willingly and gladly transmit it through them to thee, to be solemnly conferred by thee upon the metropolitan bishop according to the form which thou shalt receive under our seal; provided, however, that, if our legate or envoy should be present, thou shalt perform this together with him.

We permit chrism and the oil of catechumens and of the sick to be made annually on the Lord’s Supper, according to the custom of the Roman Church, both in thy Church and in every Church of Vlachia [Note: The *Gesta*: “of Bulgaria as well as Vlachia.”], so that, [Col. 0282A] whenever necessary, those who are to be baptized may be baptized and those who are to be confirmed may be confirmed by their diocesan bishops; and so that neither the consecration of bishops nor the ordination of priests may be wholly impeded or unduly delayed because of any lack of these things. For although among you hitherto neither priests at their ordination nor bishops at their consecration have customarily received sacred anointing, we nevertheless will that henceforth, following not so much our rite as the divine command, by which the Law commands that bishops and priests be anointed, the hands of those to be ordained priests, and both the hands and heads of those to be consecrated bishops, be solemnly anointed.

Furthermore, we grant thy brotherhood permission to have the cross—the banner, that is, of the Lord’s Passion—borne before thee throughout Bulgaria and Vlachia [Col. 0282B].] We therefore decree, etc.

Given as above.

III. [Note: [Col. 0281D]

This letter has often been published. It is found, but mutilated, in the third collection of Decretals and thence in the Gregorian collection, as well as in the Innocentian collection, Book I, title 15, *On Sacred Anointing*, sole chapter.

It is found complete, though not without some errors, in the *Gesta of Innocent*, §76.

Raynaldus likewise gives the same almost complete and in a better text, under the year 1204, §39.

We give it complete in every respect on the authority of the Conti transcript. The passages found in editions of the Decretals are, as customary, enclosed here in brackets, and variant readings have also been appended. The passages reported by Raynaldus are distinguished by quotation marks placed at the beginning of each line. For greater [Col. 0282D] accuracy, we have also added the variant readings from various manuscripts which Baluze noted in the margin of his edition of the *Gesta*.]

TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF TRNOVO, PRIMATE OF THE BULGARIANS AND VLACHS. He informs him that he caused the bishop of Brandizuber to be anointed. He commands that henceforth both the primate and the metropolitan bishops and priests of that province receive anointing, etc. (Given as above.)

“[When our venerable brother, the bishop of Brandizuber, came to the Apostolic See, he made clear to us [Note: In the Decretals: “the bishop of Braga, who”; they read *sanctam* (“holy”) for *sacram* (“sacred”) and *acceperat* (“had received”) for *receperat* (“had received”), and below omit “came … John.”] that at his [Col. 0282C] consecration he had not received sacred anointing, because among you bishops have not customarily been anointed when consecrated. We therefore ordered that what was lacking in him should be supplied, causing his head and hands to be anointed with sacred chrism, in accordance with ecclesiastical custom, by our venerable brother John, bishop of Albano [Note: John, a Lombard by birth, was made cardinal-priest of the title of St Clement by Pope Clement III; then, by Celestine III, who was then residing at Viterbo, he was appointed bishop of Viterbo in 1193. Laudably governing his Church in deed and example, he received Pope Innocent III, successor of Celestine, at Viterbo in 1198. Having, with Innocent’s approval, resigned the Church of Viterbo, he was appointed bishop of Albano by that pope in 1199. He died at Rome in 1210. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1143.], assisted by two bishops.]”

For this is maintained by the Catholic Church not only by divine command, but also by the example of the apostles. In Exodus, indeed, the Lord is read to have commanded Moses to anoint Aaron and his sons, so that they might exercise the priesthood for him. And Anacletus, a Greek by birth, who was ordained priest by blessed Peter and afterwards succeeded Clement in the apostolic office, lays down [Note: Anacletus, letter 2.] that bishops should be anointed at their ordination [Col. 0283A], according to the custom of the apostles and Moses; for all sanctification consists in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power is mingled with sacred chrism.

Hence [we wish thee to know that there are two kinds of anointing: the outward, which is material and visible; and the inward, which is spiritual and invisible. By the outward, the body is visibly anointed; by the inward, the heart is invisibly anointed. Of the first the apostle James says: “Is any sick among you? (James 5.) Let him call the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith shall save the sick man.” Of the second the apostle John [Note: Third collection: James.] says: “The anointing which ye have received from him abideth in you, and ye have no need that anyone should teach you; but [Col. 0283B] as his anointing teacheth you concerning all things” (1 John 2).]

Visible and outward anointing is a sign of inward and invisible anointing; but invisible and inward anointing is not merely a sign but also a sacrament, because, if worthily received, it either brings about or undoubtedly increases that which it signifies. In order, therefore, to administer [Note: The Decretals read “to be administered,” and below omit “however.”] the outward and visible anointing, oil is blessed, called the oil of catechumens or of the sick, and chrism is prepared from oil and balsam, for a mystical reason. For by oil the brightness of conscience is signified, as is read: “The prudent virgins took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matt. 25); while by balsam the fragrance of reputation is expressed, whence it is said: “Like aromatic balsam I gave forth fragrance” (Ecclus. 24). This chrism, therefore, should anoint a bishop, not so much in body as in heart, so that inwardly he may possess brightness of conscience before God [Note: Royal manuscript: “before him.”], and outwardly the fragrance of reputation before his neighbour.

Of brightness of conscience the Apostle says: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). For all the glory of the king’s daughter is within. Of the fragrance of reputation the same Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place; to some a fragrance of life unto life, to others a fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2). A bishop must have good testimony both from those within and those without, so that curtain may draw curtain [Col. 0283D] and he who hears may say, “Come.”

With this ointment the head and hands of a bishop are consecrated. By the head the mind is understood, according to the saying: “Anoint thy head and wash thy face” (Matt. 6). By the hands works are signified, according to: “My hands dropped myrrh” (Song 5). Thus the hands are anointed with the oil of piety, so that the bishop may do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith. The head is anointed with the balsam of charity [Col. 0284A], so that the bishop may love God with all his heart, all his mind [Note: The Decretals add “his,” and below omit “is” and “holy.”], and all his soul, and his neighbour as himself. The head is anointed because of authority and dignity; the hands because of ministry and office. The head is anointed to show that he represents the person of him of whom the Prophet says: “Like ointment upon his head, which descended into the beard, Aaron’s beard” (Ps. 132). For the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God; and Christ says of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, wherefore he hath anointed me; he hath sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Luke 4).

The bishop’s hands are anointed to show that he receives authority to bless and consecrate. Hence, when the consecrator anoints them, he says: “Deign, O Lord, to consecrate and [Col. 0284B] sanctify these hands by this holy anointing and our blessing, that whatever they shall consecrate may be consecrated, and whatever they shall bless may be blessed, in the name of the Lord.”

But [Note: The Decretals read “whence”; below they read “also” for “and,” “road” for “way,” and “anoint Hazael king” and “anoint as king.”] in the Old Testament not only a priest but also a king and prophet was anointed, as the Lord commands Elijah in the Book of Kings: “Go and return by thy way through the wilderness to Damascus; and when thou hast arrived there, thou shalt anoint Hazael king over Syria, and thou shalt anoint Jehu son of Namsi king over Israel; and thou shalt anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, who is of Abel-meholah [Note: The Decretals: Abel.], prophet in thy stead” (3 Kings 19).

But after Jesus the Nazarene—whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles—was anointed [Col. 0284C] with oil [Note: The Decretals add “of piety.”] above his companions, and is, according to the Apostle, head of the Church which is his body, the anointing of the ruler was transferred from the head to the arm. Thus a ruler is henceforth not anointed [Note: Royal manuscript: “Rulers are henceforth not anointed.”] on the head, but upon the arm, shoulder, or upper arm, in which rule is suitably signified, as is read: “And rule was made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9). To signify this also, Samuel caused the shoulder to be set before Saul, to whom he had given the chief place among those invited. But sacramental anointing has been retained for the head of the pontiff, because in the pontifical office he represents the person of the head.

There is a difference [Note: Royal and Podian manuscripts read “refers.”] between the anointing of the pontiff and that of the ruler: the pontiff’s head is consecrated with chrism, whereas the ruler’s arm is anointed with oil, in order to show how great is the difference between the authority of a pontiff and the power of a ruler. Since Christ made us in his blood a kingdom and priests to our God, and for this reason the apostle Peter says, “Ye are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2), therefore in the New Testament not only priests and kings [Col. 0285A] are anointed, but all Christians as well: twice before baptism, namely with blessed oil, first upon the breast and then between the shoulders; and twice after baptism, namely with sacred chrism, first upon the crown of the head and then upon the forehead.

The candidate for baptism is anointed on the breast so that, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, he may cast off error and ignorance and receive right faith, because “the just man lives by faith” (Rom. 1). He is anointed between the shoulders [Note: These words are omitted by the Decretals.] so that, through the grace [Note: The Colbert and Angers manuscripts: “gift.”] of the Holy Spirit, he may shake off negligence and sluggishness and practise good works, because “faith without works is dead” (James 2), etc. [Note: The Decretals omit “and etc.” after “dead,” and add “through the work” before “of faith.”] Thus, through the sacrament of faith there may be purity of thought in the breast; through the exercise of works, strength for labours in the shoulders [Col. 0285B]; so that faith may work through love, according to the Apostle.

The baptized person is anointed upon the crown of the head so that he may be ready to give an account of the faith to everyone who asks [Note: The Decretals read “asks,” and below “which is the higher” for “which is the highest.”], because by the head the mind is understood, as is read: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head”; its higher part is reason and its lower part sensuality. Hence reason, which is the higher part of the mind, is fittingly understood by the crown, which is “the highest part of the head.” The baptized person is anointed upon the forehead so that he may freely confess what he believes, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth [Note: The Decretals read “indeed”; below they omit “confess” and “and confess him before my Father,” read “therefore” for “indeed,” and lower down “indeed” for “for.”] confession is made unto salvation,” mindful of what the Lord said: “Whoever shall confess me before men, him will I also confess before my Father” (Matt. 10).

“Before baptism, however, one is anointed with blessed oil, and [Col. 0285C] after baptism with sacred chrism, because chrism belongs to the Christian alone. For Christ is so called from chrism—or, rather, chrism is so called from Christ—not according to the form of the name, but according to the meaning of faith. Christians are called from Christ, as though the anointed were derived from the Anointed, so that all may run in the fragrance of his ointments [Note: The Decretals add “ointment”; below they read “or” [Col. 0286D] for “that is.”], whose name is poured-out oil.

By the chrismation of the forehead is signified the laying on of hands, which is also called confirmation, because through it the Holy Spirit is given for increase and strength. Therefore, although an ordinary priest—that is, a presbyter—may administer the other anointings, this one may be conferred only by the high priest, that is, the bishop, because it is read only of the apostles, whose vicars are bishops, that by laying on hands they gave the Holy Spirit, as the reading from the Acts of the Apostles makes clear: “When the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them; and when they had come, they prayed for them [Col. 0286A] that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8).

The coming of that Spirit is signified by the mystery of anointing, because the dove in which the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ at baptism, returning in the evening during the flood, brought back a branch of green olive. Foreknowing the sacrament of this, David the prophet proclaimed that the face should be made glad with oil. Moreover, according to ecclesiastical custom, [Note: In the Decretals: “is anointed”; below the word “and” is absent.] things are anointed when an altar is consecrated, when a church is dedicated, and when a chalice is blessed, not only by command of divine law but also by the example of blessed Sylvester, [Col. 0286B] who, when he consecrated an altar, anointed it all over with chrism. For the Lord commanded Moses to make anointing oil, with which he should anoint the tabernacle of testimony [Note: The Colbert and Angers manuscripts: “the door of the tabernacle.”], the ark of the covenant, and the table with its vessels.

Shouldest thou perhaps be in doubt concerning these anointings, when requested by thee we shall instruct thy brotherhood more fully. Yet [Note: The Decretals have “but,” omitting what precedes, and below “power” for “truth.”] the sacrament of anointing both accomplishes one thing and signifies another, in the New Testament as in the Old. Therefore, when the Church celebrates the sacrament of anointing, it does not Judaize, as some lie in saying, who know neither the Scriptures nor the truth of God.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort thy brotherhood, commanding thee by these apostolic letters, that at the command of our beloved [Col. 0286C] son Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of Santa Croce and legate of the Apostolic See, thou too receive [Note: Royal manuscript: “receive.”] sacred anointing, lest anything be lacking to thee for the fullness of the sacrament. Once thou hast been anointed with sacred chrism, thou shalt likewise anoint thy archbishops and bishops, and through them cause the hands of priests to be anointed with blessed oil, henceforth [in ordaining priests and consecrating bishops observing, and causing to be observed, [Note: The Decretals: “observe and cause to be observed.”] the custom which the Apostolic See observes], which, by the Lord’s ordering, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful.

We send thee through the aforesaid cardinal pontifical vestments: buskins and sandals, amice and alb, girdle and cincture, stole and maniple, tunic and dalmatic, gloves and ring, chasuble and mitre. We had previously sent the pallium through our beloved son John, our chaplain. And although [the Roman pontiff does not use a pastoral staff, both for a historical [Note: The Decretals: “history.”] and also for a mystical reason—which the same cardinal, [Col. 0287A] as he received it from us, will be able to explain [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals.]—] thou nevertheless mayest use it, after the manner of other pontiffs.

Given as above.

IV. [Note: [Col. 0287D] It is read in the *Gesta*, §70, and in Raynaldus under the year 1204, §28.] Instrument by which the king of Bulgaria and Vlachia subjects his empire to the Roman Church. (In the year 1204, seventh indiction.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Since it pleased our Lord Jesus Christ to make me lord and emperor of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, I investigated the writings and books of our ancestors and the laws of our predecessors, the emperors of blessed memory, to learn from whom they received the kingdom of the Bulgarians, the imperial establishment, [Col. 0287B] the crown upon their heads, and the patriarchal blessing. Having diligently examined them, we found in their writings that those emperors of blessed memory of the Bulgarians and Vlachs—Simeon, Peter, and Samuel, our predecessors—received the crown of their empire [Note: The Conti transcript and Royal manuscript read “for empire.”] and the patriarchal blessing from the most holy Roman Church of God, from the Apostolic See, and from Peter, prince of the apostles.

But my empire has desired to receive the blessing and the imperial strengthening of the crown upon the head of its empire, and the patriarchal blessing, from the Roman Church, from Peter, prince of the apostles of the Apostolic See, and from our most holy father, the universal pope Innocent III. And from whomever the patriarchal blessing and command [*sic*] shall be given and granted by the lord pope in Trnovo, the city [Col. 0287C] of my empire, for making and consecrating archbishops, metropolitans, bishops, and the remaining sacramental ecclesiastical observances, my empire grants that they shall have fullest authority throughout every possession and appurtenance of my empire [Note: The Conti transcript adds “therein.”].

For all churches throughout my empire and possessions, and my patriarch, metropolitan, bishops, archbishops, and all priests, shall be subject to the Roman Church and shall observe the law, custom, and observance [Note: The Conti transcript: “obedience.”] which the emperors of blessed memory of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, those ancient predecessors of ours, observed; and we likewise follow in their footsteps. To guarantee this, my empire affixes its chrysobull, declaring that my empire itself shall never depart from the Roman Church and Apostolic See, from Peter, prince of the apostles, nor shall the rulers of my empire be separated from it; but I shall be called the beloved son of the most holy and apostolic Roman See of Peter, prince of the apostles.

Henceforth, whatever lands of Christians or pagans my [Col. 0288A] empire acquires shall be under the power and command of that same most holy Roman Church and Apostolic See. And so that this present chrysobull of my empire may be held valid and firm, my empire gave itself into the hands of the most reverend man John, legate of the most holy Roman See and chaplain of the lord pope; and therein our pious empire, advanced by God, also subscribed, in the year 6712, seventh indiction.

V. [Note: [Col. 0287D] This letter may be read, though mutilated at the end, in the *Gesta*, §72. What is found there is enclosed here in brackets [Col. 0288D]. Raynaldus gives fragments of it under the year 1204, §32; we have distinguished them by a double quotation-mark placed at the beginning of each line.] Letter of Basil, archbishop of Trnovo.—He writes that, when he wished to proceed to the Apostolic See, his passage was impeded at Dyrrachium; afterwards, recalled by the emperor, he was invested with the pallium in September, on the feast of the Nativity.

> “To the Lord, most exalted and sharing the apostolic see, Father of all Christendom, and my lord, Pope Innocent III: Archbishop Basil, one of the least and humblest men of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, offers many bows and great prayers, together with [Col. 0288B] your perfect blessing. I pray the most merciful God and the most blessed Mother of God that this letter of mine may find Your Holiness well and rejoicing; and that which my soul has desired for eighteen years, behold, God and your holy prayer have today granted us: the blessing of the see of the blessed apostle Peter and of Your Holiness.  
>
> “May Your Holiness know how I conducted myself while seeking your blessing. In the month of July, on the fourth day, in the year 6711, indiction 6, my humility set out for our holy and most glorious Father, Innocent, pope of Rome, [Col. 0288C] and I remained thirty days at Dyrrachium by the sea. When I wished to board a ship to cross over, the Greeks detained me and did not allow me to pass.”  
>
> [Note: [Col. 0288D] Raynaldus ends here.]
>
> “Instead, they held me at Dyrrachium for eight days. Yet through my many prayers to God and to the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, and through your holy prayers, the Latins released me; for they had resolved to throw me into the sea, but the Lord and your holy prayer delivered me. Leaving the city, I returned to a village called Cavatochori, where I stayed fifteen days. From there I sent two of my good men to Rome to Your Holiness, [Col. 0288D] and whether they crossed over or not, God knows.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 0288D] Raynaldus resumes here.]
>
> “But letters came to me from my lord the emperor, Lord John, saying: ‘Return quickly, for a cardinal from the lord pope has arrived here.’ Having read the emperor’s letters and seeing that he summoned me, I returned and arrived at Drinovum”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0288D] The Trinovum transcript reads *Drinaum*; it seems that *Trinovum* should be read.]
>
> “in the month of September. There I found a holy, just, and upright man sent by [Col. 0289A] Your Holiness, named John the chaplain. He gave me all the letters from Your Holiness, and they were read to me. My soul therefore greatly rejoiced; stretching out my hands to heaven, I gave thanks to God, because the Lord had visited his people, and our blessed Father the pope was seeking the lost sheep, in order to bring it back into the holy fold.
>
> “And as was contained in the letters of Your Holiness, so Lord John the chaplain acted: according to the decree of your great holiness, he gave me your blessing and bestowed the pallium, for the fullness of the pontifical office, on the eighth day of September, the feast of the Nativity of our most holy Mother of God. Having received the pallium with great humility of devotion, [Col. 0289B] I rendered the obedience of fidelity, in the presence of the bishops who write to Your Holiness, our prince, and many others standing in the church.
>
> “Again, holy Father, I beg Your Holiness to make provision and complete the ecclesiastical order, and to instruct me how I ought to govern the flock entrusted to me”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0289D] The Trinovum transcript reads “committed to me.”]
>
> “by God and Your Holiness. We do not have holy chrism; indeed, we had received it from the Greeks, but henceforth they hate us as they hate you. Know, my lord, that all these matters rest with Your Holiness, which ought to make provision in all things. Teach us concerning holy chrism: how we ought to baptize the people, lest the people remain without holy chrism and sin result.
>
> “But in all things admonish us, your lost and perishing sons; and send me, good Father, pallia for the use of the two metropolitans of Priosthlava and Belebusdium, and whatever else Your Holiness knows to be needed for the full exercise of my pontifical office, let Your Holiness send it to me.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0289D] Raynaldus ends here.]

### Letters of Anastasius, Archbishop of Belesbuda, of the Archbishop of Prostlava, and of their suffragan bishops

[Note: [Col. 0289D] So in the transcript. Perhaps *Priosthlavae* should be read.]

Submitting the necks of their lordship beneath the yoke of his approval, they offer reverence, with bowed neck and bent knees, to the most holy Father and lord, the lord pope. First: Anastasius, sinner and humble metropolitan of the most holy church of Belesbuda; after him, Saccas, sinner and humble metropolitan of the great church of Prostlava; [Col. 0289D] Marinus, bishop—though unworthy—of the most holy church of the Mother of God at Skopia; Kiricus, humble bishop of the most holy bishopric of the most holy church of the blessed and most glorious great martyr Procopius at Niso; and Clemens, unworthy bishop and sinner of the most holy church of the Mother of God at Hydmens.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] “Abraham of Prisdian, sinner and humble bishop.”]

We humbly beg you, as our singular shepherd, [Col. 0290A] universal father, and lord, to deem it worthy to send the pallium for the fullness of the pontifical office, so that we in turn may never cease, all the days of our lives, to pray for your magnificence.

### VI. Letter of Kalojohn to Pope Innocent — On the same subject as the preceding letter

[Note: [Col. 0289D] See the *Deeds of Innocent*, § LXXI; Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 30; and the notes on the preceding letter.]

> “To the most holy and sovereign universal pope seated in the see of blessed Peter; to the lord and father of my kingdom, Innocent III, pope of the apostolic see and Roman Church, and master of the whole world.
>
> “I hope in God, the Saviour of all, that Your Holiness is well—indeed, very well—together with all those seated around the throne of Your Holiness, the cardinals [Col. 0290B] of the holy Roman Church. May Your Great Holiness know that I, your son and son of the Roman Church, emperor of all Bulgarians and Vlachs, together with all the princes of my empire, am very well through God and your holy prayer.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0290D] The Trinovum transcript omits “I.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0290D] The Trinovum transcript adds “holy.”]
>
> “My empire has often sent its messengers to Your Holiness, but they found no opportunity to cross over to Your Holiness.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0290D] Raynaldus ends here.]
>
> Indeed, they could not cross because those who were not at peace with my empire guarded the roads. Later, in the preceding month of June, my empire sent my archbishop of the whole Bulgarian land and of the universal holy and great church of Trinova, a great man of my empire, deservedly called primate, and archbishop [Col. 0290C] of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, named Basil. When he arrived at Dyrrachium, he was not permitted to cross to Your Holiness, so that Your Holiness might fulfill my empire’s desire, according to the custom of my predecessors, the emperors of Bulgarians and Vlachs—Simeon, Peter, Samuel, my ancestors—and all the other Bulgarian emperors.

[Note: [Col. 0290D] The *Deeds* omit the word “universal.”]

> “But, with God’s help and through the interceding prayers of Your Holiness, there came to me the present messenger of the apostolic throne, of the first see of the prince of the apostles, and of the holy and universal Roman Church: John, the chaplain. He brought me letters”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0290D] The Trinovum transcript reads “a pallium.”]
>
> “by command of Your Holiness and the apostolic see; he invested the said archbishop with the pallium, [Col. 0290D] made him primate of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, brought my empire letters of Your Holiness, and set forth everything Your Holiness had commanded him. My heart was filled with great joy, because God and Your Holiness granted me what my empire desired.
>
> “I pray and beseech Your Great Holiness
>
> [Note: [Col. 0290D] The Trinovum transcript reads “magnificence.”]
>
> to fulfill [Col. 0291A] my empire’s desire: send the pastoral staff for gathering the sheep, and the other things which a patriarch is accustomed to possess; make the present primate a patriarch in the holy and great church of Trinova, the chief city of all Bulgaria; and command that this church shall have a patriarch forever after the death of this patriarch. Since, because of the length of the road and the warfare of men, it would be burdensome to have recourse to the Roman Church upon the death of each”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0291D] The Trinovum transcript reads “any.”]
>
> “patriarch, let the Roman Church grant to the church of Trinova the right to elect and consecrate its own patriarch, so that through his absence that land may not remain without blessing, your consecration become incomplete, and sin redound [Col. 0291B] upon Your Holiness.
>
> “We now ask that chrism be made, by command of Your Holiness, in the holy and great church of Trinova city, for the baptism of Christians. Your Holiness should know that when those at Rome”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0291D] That is, the people of Constantinople.]
>
> “learn that we have received consecration from Your Holiness, they will not give me chrism.
>
> “I ask another thing of Your Holiness: send a cardinal to my empire—either the man who came to me, or another from the apostolic see—and let him give me the diadem and sceptre according to the blessing of the apostolic see and the prince of the apostles; send a privilege sealed with a golden bull, to be preserved forever as its exemplar in the church of Trinova. Let them give all these things to my empire and consecrate and crown my empire.
>
> “Let the present messenger of my empire, Blasius, bishop of Brandizuber, see all the things [Col. 0291C] which”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0291D] The *Deeds* omit “which.”]
>
> “must be sent to my empire by Your Holiness, so that he may report what you have written with your own hand. If Your Holiness fulfills all these things, I and the line of my empire, together with all Bulgarians and Vlachs, shall consider ourselves beloved sons of the orthodox holy Roman Church.
>
> “As for the frontier of Hungary, Bulgaria, and Vlachia, I leave it to the judgment of Your Holiness to direct this matter rightly and justly, so that the soul of Your Holiness may incur no sin: thus may my empire possess the rights of Bulgaria and Vlachia, just as the king of Hungary possesses the rights of Hungary; and may the killing of Christians cease against me and my empire.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0291D] So in the *Deeds*. But the Trinovum transcript and Raynaldus read “himself.”]
>
> “Your Holiness should know that five bishoprics of [Col. 0291D] Bulgaria belong to my empire; the king of Hungary has invaded and retains them, together with the rights of their churches, and those bishoprics have been destroyed. If this is just, let it be done. Whatever the present messenger of my empire, Blasius, bishop of Brandizuber, tells Your Holiness, accept as true, because he will speak on my behalf.
>
> “I have sent Your Holiness three double pieces of *examitum*,”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0291D] *Examitum*, alternatively *exametum*: a wholly silk cloth; in later Greek, ἐξάμιτος.]
>
> “a golden cup, [Col. 0292A] four pounds of hyperpyra, three silver bowls, and a silver gradual.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0292D] A gold coin of the Byzantine emperors, so called as though it were made of exceptionally brilliant, repeatedly refined gold. Cangius, vol. III, col. 1275.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0292D] A book containing the Gradualia or Graduals—that is, an antiphonary.]
>
> “Kalojohn, emperor of Bulgaria.”

### VII. To Anastasius, Archbishop of Belebusdium — He sends him the pallium

Since we are all one body in Christ, while individually we are members one of another, and since not all members are known to have the same function, but differ from one another not only in offices but also in form, such distinction—or rather difference—produces not deformity but rather beauty in the body; for even star differs from star in glory. It is fitting, therefore, that those who hold the higher place in the Church of God should receive greater honour and be adorned with special insignia of honour.

[Col. 0292B] Therefore, since we have judged that our venerable brother, . . . archbishop of Trinova, should be established as primate throughout all lands over which our dearest son in Christ, Kalojohn, illustrious king of Bulgarians and Vlachs, rules, granting the insignia of honour belonging to his office in accordance with the custom of the apostolic see; and since we wish also especially to honour you as an honourable member of the church of Trinova, metropolitan of the church of Belebusdium, and superior to its suffragans by metropolitan right: through our beloved son L., cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross and legate of the apostolic see, a man distinguished by upright conduct and the endowment of learning, whom among our other brethren we embrace with arms of special affection, [Col. 0292C] we send you the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter—the insignia, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office—to be conferred upon you according to the form of our bull, strengthened by its authority.

We therefore admonish and exhort your fraternity in the Lord, and command you by these apostolic letters, humbly and devoutly to receive it; and to use it, not for exaltation but rather for humility, within your church at the solemnities of Mass on those days which the same cardinal shall explain to you. Strive to show yourself such that the inward adornment of virtues may surpass the outward adornment of garments, and that the outward vesture may represent the inward disposition of the mind, not by an imaginary pretence alone but rather by a true expression.

### VIII. To the illustrious King of the Bulgarians and Vlachs — He informs him that he has instructed the legate to anoint him and confer the regalia

[Col. 0292D]
