Although, through the merits of the prince of the apostles, we are shepherds under him, the shepherd of the universal Church, who brought into one fold the other sheep which were not of his fold and entrusted them to Peter the shepherd to be fed—“Feed,” he said, “my sheep” (John 21)—and although our daily concern ought to be the continual care of all churches and the advancement of all peoples whom Mother Church, having purged away the old leaven, regenerated into new childhood and gathered into her bosom as a hen gathers her chicks: we consider ourselves under a more special obligation to the peoples of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, inasmuch as they not only formerly received the Catholic faith more devoutly through the apostolic see, but also descend from Roman blood. We are especially appointed for the advancement and ministry of the Romans, who, as our particular people, are subject to us in both spiritual and temporal matters without any intermediary.

Therefore, so that they may acknowledge the teaching authority of her from whom they know that they received spiritually what they believe and received carnally what they are, being descended in the flesh [Col. 0293B] from noble Romans, we—on whose behalf the Lord prayed, as successors of blessed Peter, that our faith might not fail and that, once converted, we might strengthen our brethren—wish to confirm them in the Catholic faith and strengthen them in devotion to the apostolic see.

So that the affection of fatherly love which we bear toward them may be made known to all, and the mother’s generosity toward her children may be commended, we wish to honour them in spiritual and temporal matters as special sons of the Roman Church. We therefore send from our side into Bulgaria and Vlachia our beloved son L., cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross and legate of the apostolic see, a man conspicuous for learning and endowed with uprightness, whom we embrace among our other brethren with arms of special affection, [Col. 0293C] so that by our authority and in our stead he may anoint you, grant you the royal sceptre, and place upon you the royal diadem.

Since through our beloved son J., our chaplain, we have caused the pallium to be sent to our venerable brother, . . . archbishop of Trinova, and have appointed him primate of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, we send through the same legate to the metropolitans whom that chaplain, when establishing the primate, newly subjected to him, the pallium—the insignia, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office—to be conferred upon them according to the form enclosed under our bull. We have likewise granted the legate full authority to correct what he finds in need of correction and establish what he judges should be established, commanding [Col. 0293D] him to instruct both clergy and people in matters pertaining to the advancement of the Christian faith and to make them more certain of our goodwill.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your royal serenity to receive this legate kindly as our own person—indeed, as ourselves and blessed Peter in him—and to treat him honourably. Receive and observe his salutary admonitions and statutes yourself, and cause them to be received and observed throughout all your land. Fulfil what we write in such a way that we may recognize in deed the devotion which [Col. 0294A] we believe you bear toward us and the Roman Church.

### IX. To the Archbishop of Trinova, Primate of All Bulgaria and Vlachia, and to the Other Archbishops, Bishops, Clergy, and People Established in Bulgaria and Vlachia — He sends him the pallium

“Although, because of this,” etc., down to “make them more certain.”

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort you all, and command you by these apostolic letters, to receive the legate himself, etc., down to “treat him honourably”; gladly receive and inviolably observe whatever he judges should be corrected or established among you. And although you have hitherto been like [Col. 0294B] wandering sheep, yet now that you have been converted to the bishop and shepherd of your souls, follow the teaching and pattern of him to whom the Lord entrusted the teaching authority and primacy of the whole Church.

Take care, moreover, not to be easily moved from the steadfastness of your minds; but persevere in your good purpose, humbly remaining devoted to the apostolic see, so that you may appear established upon the solidity of that rock upon which the Lord placed the foundation of the Church, granting the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that what Peter opened should stand open and what he shut should not stand open.

### X. The Form by Which the Pallium Is To Be Given to the Archbishops of Belebusdium and Trinova

[Note: [Col. 0293D] A fragment of this letter is found among the *Decretals*, book I, title 8, “On the Authority and Use of the Pallium,” chapter 4. The complete text is read in the *Deeds*, § LXXVII. What is printed in the *Decretals* is enclosed here in brackets.]

[Col. 0294C] “[For the honour of] almighty God, the blessed Virgin Mary, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, Pope Innocent, the Roman Church, and the church entrusted to you, we give you this pallium, taken from the body of blessed Peter—the insignia, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office. You are to use it at the solemnities of Mass within the churches subject to you on the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Stephen the Protomartyr; the Circumcision of the Lord; Epiphany; Hypapante; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter; Easter Monday; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the three feasts of Saint Mary; the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist; the solemnities of all the apostles; the commemoration of all saints; dedications of churches; [Col. 0294D] consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clergy; the principal feasts of your church; and the anniversary of your consecration.

“Certainly, the Roman pontiff alone always uses the pallium at Mass everywhere, because he has been assumed into the fullness of ecclesiastical power, which is symbolized by the pallium. Others, however, use it neither always nor everywhere, but on specified days in their own church, in which they have received ecclesiastical jurisdiction, because they are called to a share in the burden of care, not to the fullness of power.”

### XI. Form of the Oath Taken by the Archbishop of Trinova

[Note: [Col. 0295D] It appears in the *Deeds*, § LXXVII, and in Raynaldus under the year 1204, § 44.]

[Col. 0295A]

I, the archbishop of Trinova, primate of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, shall henceforth be faithful and obedient to blessed Peter, the holy Roman and apostolic see, my lord Pope Innocent, and his Catholic successors.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] The Trinovum transcript adds “pope.”]

I shall not, by act, counsel, or consent, cause them to lose life or limb, or to be captured or despoiled. I shall disclose to no one, to their detriment and knowingly, any counsel they entrust to me. If I learn of a certain danger to them, I shall endeavour to prevent it; and if I cannot prevent it, I shall take care to make it known to them as soon as I can.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] The Trinovum transcript reads: “I shall announce and make known.”]

To the utmost of my ability, saving my own order, I shall defend the Roman papacy, the honours, dignities, and rights of the apostolic [Col. 0295B] see against every living person. When summoned to a synod, I shall come unless prevented by a canonical impediment. Every four years, either personally or through my messenger, I shall visit the thresholds of the apostles, unless their permission excuses me. I shall devoutly receive and assist in his needs any legate of the apostolic see whom I know certainly to be a legate.

Whenever I consecrate any of my suffragans as bishop, I shall make him swear to render perpetual obedience and due honour to the Roman pontiff and the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] The Trinovum transcript adds “as bishop.”]

Moreover, when I crown anyone king of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, in accordance with the concession granted by the apostolic see to me and my successors, I shall receive from him a sworn assurance that he will remain devoted and obedient to whoever then presides over the apostolic [Col. 0295C] see, to that person’s successors, and to the Roman Church; and that he will preserve all lands and peoples subject to his rule in obedience and devotion to the apostolic see. I shall observe all these things in good faith. So help me God and these holy Gospels, now and hereafter. Amen.

### XII. To Kalojohn, illustrious King of Bulgarians and Vlachs — He sends him a banner

[Note: [Col. 0295D] It survives in the *Deeds*, § LXXIV. Raynaldus also gives it, though not complete, under the year 1204, § 36. What he prints is, as usual, enclosed here in brackets.]

So that you may glory with the Apostle in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, and henceforth ascribe your triumphs not to yourself but to him before whom every knee bows; so that you may experience his protection amid the changing outcomes of wars—he who teaches hands for battle and fingers for war, to whom the Lord granted the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing—we send to your royal serenity, in addition to the insignia of royal dignity, through our beloved son Leo, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross and legate of the apostolic see, a prudent and upright man, [a banner, to be used against those who honour the Crucified One with their lips but whose heart is far [Col. 0296A] from him. At the request of our venerable brother B.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] The *Deeds* omits this.]

, bishop of Brandizuber, we have judged it fitting to send it to you.

The banner bears the cross and keys, not without mystery; for the blessed apostle Peter both bore the cross for

[Note: [Col. 0296D] The *Deeds* reads “in.”]

Christ and received the keys from Christ. It represents the sign of the cross, on which Christ—as conqueror—reigns and rules, overcame the powers of the air, and, in which, taking prey, he swallowed the robber: dying Life conquered death and took Behemoth by the eyes as with a hook. It also represents the twofold key: one of discernment, the other of power. Thus, after distinguishing good from evil, light from darkness, holy from profane, you may wield the material sword committed to you for the punishment of evildoers and [Col. 0296B]

[Note: [Col. 0296D] The *Deeds* omits “in”; Raynaldus reads “and.”]

the praise of the good; and may take up arms and shield against those who have not set God as their helper], but who, trusting in their own fierceness and multitude, strive to kick against the goad.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your royal serenity, and command you by these apostolic letters, to use the same banner in humility of heart. Amid battle-lines, remember the Lord’s Passion, and acknowledge the teaching authority of him to whom the Lord himself said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18). For thus your enemies shall not only be unable to prevail against you, but, by the Lord’s gift, shall not stand before you.

### XIII. To Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and Other Prelates of Churches, and to All Clergy and Laity Established in the Kingdom of Hungary — He writes to them concerning the restoration of the Bulgarians and directs them to treat the legate well

[Note: [Col. 0296D] Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, § 45.]

[Col. 0296C]

The apostolic see desires to gather its children scattered throughout different parts of the world into one, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, so that it may know its sheep and be known by them, and there may be one fold and one shepherd, as the Lord himself says. It desires to recall to itself the Church of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, which, as though it did not know itself, had left the shepherd to whom Christ entrusted his sheep to be fed—“Feed,” he said, [Col. 0296D] “my sheep” (John 21)—had followed the tracks of flocks, and had departed like a wandering sheep from the fold. Thus, according to the prophetic word, it may be good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity; and there may be greater joy among God’s churches over that church when it returns to devotion to the apostolic see and is reconciled to ecclesiastical truth, than over the other ninety-nine which neither death nor sword has separated from reverence for the Roman Church.

Therefore, following the example of him who clothed the returning prodigal son in the first robe and gave him a ring, we wish to honour in spiritual and temporal matters the peoples of Bulgarians and Vlachs returning to devotion and reverence for the apostolic see. Through our beloved son L., cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross and legate of the apostolic see—a prudent and upright man, accepted among our other brethren with a certain prerogative of affection—we have ordered that they be visited, so that he may labour to confirm them in the Catholic faith and in devotion to the Roman Church.

But lest this cause scandal to the firstborn and arouse something like envy in those who are always with us, if we honour in this manner that church returning with the firstborn to its mother’s breast—killing [Col. 0297B] the fatted calf upon its return, while not giving him even a kid to eat with his friends—let him rather rejoice and feast together, because he ought to feast and rejoice: his brother who had been dead is now alive, and he who had been lost has been found.

We have granted the same legate full authority, in the provinces through which he passes, to hear and decide the cases brought before him; if he cannot decide them, to delegate them; and in their decision and delegation to reap away every scandal arising from them. Sowing the seed of peace, he should strive to bury controversies and become to all through whom he passes an aroma of life unto life.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort you all, and command you by these apostolic letters, gladly to receive and honourably treat the cardinal as legate of the apostolic [Col. 0297C] see. Both on his journey out and on his return, provide him generously with all necessities and safe-conduct, so that henceforth you may have him as your advocate before the apostolic see; and that it may hear you more readily, in proportion as he has been more greatly honoured by you for its sake.

### XIV. To Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, Other Prelates of Churches, and the Whole Clergy Established in the Province of Serbia — On the Same Subject

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, § 45.]

“The apostolic see desires,” etc., in almost the same manner, down to “has been found.” We have also judged that the duty of this legation should be imposed upon him in Serbia, [Col. 0297D] so that he may uproot, destroy, overthrow, and scatter; build and plant, according as he sees expedient for the advancement of the Catholic faith, the condition of the Church, and your correction and benefit.

We therefore admonish and exhort you all in the Lord, and command you by these apostolic letters, requiring obedience, to receive the legate himself as our own person—indeed, receiving us in him—and to treat him gladly and honourably. Receive his statutes and commands humbly and observe them inviolably; [Col. 0298A] otherwise, we shall hold valid the sentence which he pronounces against the rebellious, and, with the Lord as author, shall cause it to be inviolably observed.

### XV. To the Bishop of Ely and to . . . the Abbot of Saint Edmund

[Note: [Col. 0297D] The bishop of Ely and the abbot of St Edmund have already been discussed above.]

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Book V, letter 135.]

That they should ensure satisfaction to the Roman merchants concerning money owed them by Roger of St Edmund. (Anagni, 2 May.)

Although we commend in the Lord the devotion of one who is a diligent executor of our mandates, yet, since it is not our intention to command what is unjust, lest injuries arise from that whence rights arise, we are compelled to wonder and be troubled if anyone knowingly proceeds to execute mandates fraudulently obtained from us by surreption. For he ought not to be ignorant [Col. 0298B] that, according to our canonical and legal enactments, a false petitioner must wholly lose what he has obtained; for fraud or deceit ought not to avail anyone, and the laws assist not deceivers but the deceived.

Accordingly, our beloved sons James of Josto, S. Bobonis of Maximo, M. Guidonis Marronis, S. John Pantaleon, and his brother He., S. Capharellus, Nicholas Octavianus Deustegardet, and L. Pizulinus, Roman merchants, laid before us a serious complaint. They stated that Roger of St Edmund, of good memory, by virtue of the general licence which the Apostolic See granted to all who had taken the cross, and of another special licence which we granted to that same crusader, had pledged all his benefices to them until 3m [reading uncertain], for a specified sum of money which he received [Col. 0298C] from them when about to depart in aid of the Holy Land. After his death, we generally commanded that all benefices which he held at the time of death should be assigned to the said merchants, so that, from their revenues, they might receive the money lent, with interest suspended.

But our venerable brother, the bishop of Durham [Note: Book V, epistle 135], who had received the first and second apostolic mandate on behalf of those merchants, on the occasion of a mandate obtained for himself or for our beloved son, the abbot of St Albans [Note: Compare especially what we said in the note to Book VI, epistle 204], nephew of our venerable brother the bishop of St Albans [Note: See the note to epistle 3 of this seventh book], while suppressing the whole truth of the matters aforesaid, concerning a church which that same Roger had held from the monastery of that abbot [Note: Thus in the copy], to be conferred upon the bishop’s nephew [Col. 0298D], is said to have assigned that church to him. Through his procurator he has not merely taken possession of it, but also receives its revenues, to the prejudice of the merchants, who could have been more fully satisfied from the proceeds of that church. Thus the effect of the deed reveals the petitioner’s intention.

We recall also that the abbot himself had refused to do this in response to our first mandate, as he informed us by his letters: first, because before the aforesaid Roger had received that church through royal favour [Col. 0299A], the abbot had canonically presented a certain cleric to it when vacant, and by that presentation alone had acquired, according to the canons, a right in that church, since the right of patronage is held more fully by clerics than by laymen; and secondly, because that church, to which the care of souls is attached, especially as it is a large one, ought to have as its ruler not a hireling but a shepherd.

When the said cleric obtained apostolic letters for the restoration of his right, no mention of those letters was made in the first mandate. Although we mentioned them in the second mandate, since they were alleged to have been obtained through a defect of facility, we nevertheless ordered an inquiry to proceed, lest prejudice be caused to that cleric. Yet, as we have learned, he complains vehemently that serious prejudice has been done to him, whether by fraud employed or violence inflicted.

For just as we cannot judge doubtful matters until we are fully informed of them, so we ought not to doubt matters certain, but must freely determine concerning them. Therefore, by our letters we command the aforesaid bishop and abbot that, since justice requires that an act known to have been attempted on the occasion of a mandate obtained by surreption should lack all force of validity, the bishop shall without delay restore the said church into the hands of the abbot, and the abbot into his own hands, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. The procurator or vicar of the nephew of the said bishop of St Albans, or any other holder, is to be removed [Col. 0299C]; and they are faithfully to collect its revenues, so that at our command they may be applied toward payment of the aforementioned sum of money. They are likewise not to postpone recovering and receiving the fruits taken from it in the meantime; and the fruits which the bishop himself has received from it are to be delivered to the abbot for safe keeping. Any opponents are to be restrained by sentence of excommunication, appeal set aside.

Meanwhile they are to presume in no way to assign that church to anyone until they have received our will and pleasure concerning it. Thus they shall fulfil the apostolic mandate: they are to execute more diligently what proceeds from certain knowledge than what issued upon suppressed truth.

Wherefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if the above-named bishop and abbot neglect to carry out our mandate within twenty days, you shall by no means fail to execute it, all contradiction, appeal, and excuse ceasing [Col. 0299D–0300A]. This is notwithstanding letters which we remember having sent on another occasion to those same bishop and abbot concerning this very business, provided those letters reached them; and notwithstanding any other letters that may appear to have been obtained with the tenor of these letters suppressed.

We ourselves would, moreover, take care to punish their disobedience according to its deserts. For however much we may love the aforesaid bishop of St Albans as an honourable member of the Church, we fear more the God of heaven, who commands that there be no respect of persons among us, nor in our hand a double weight like a deceitful balance. But if not both, then one, etc.

Given at Anagni, the sixth day before the Nones of May.

XVI. [Note: Praised by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §81.] TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF THUREGAN. He receives them under protection upon payment of an annual census of one gold piece. (Lateran, the third day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0300B]

“It is customary to grant,” etc., down to “assenting persons”; and we strengthen, by way of protection, your hospital, which our beloved son, the nobleman … duke of Zähringen [Note: Thus in the copy], built for the remedy of his sins, together with all the goods which it presently possesses, etc., down to “we strengthen.” As a token of this protection obtained from us, you shall pay one gold piece each year to us and to our successors. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of May.

XVII. TO THE BISHOP OF OLORON [Note: Bernard I, surnamed de Sadarico, formerly abbot of St Peter of Générès, was promoted to the bishopric of Oloron shortly after 1170. His name occurs in instruments down to 1205. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 1269.], THE ABBOTS OF PLANA SILVA [Note: Very scanty information is given concerning the abbots of Plana Silva, whether in the *Annals of Prémontré*, vol. II, col. 571, or by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 892], AND ST SEVERUS [Note: There are two monasteries of St Severus, to whose abbots this letter could have been addressed.

At St Severus, at the head of Gascony, in the diocese of Adour, Arsius is counted as the fifteenth abbot about the year 1200. From the records of St Severus, he is the same man who died bishop of Lescar on the third day before the Nones of August, 1213. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 1177.

For St Severus of Rustan, in the diocese of Tarbes, the very incomplete succession of abbots gives no abbot for about this period. See ibid., col. 1244.]. That they assign a coadjutor to the archbishop of Auch, who suffers from epilepsy. [Note: Compare especially what we said in the note to Book V, epistle 96.] (Lateran, the third day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0300C]

It came to our hearing, through the report of our beloved son G. Donatus, canon of the church of Auch, that our venerable brother, the archbishop of Auch, while bound by the bond of excommunication, usurped the pallium; and from that time until now, unwilling to cast off from himself the yoke of excommunication, he has administered the ecclesiastical sacraments. Moreover, after thus receiving the pallium, he suffered from epilepsy and, through the crime of perjury, provoked against himself the indignation of the Most High.

But because full credence could not be given us concerning these matters, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion [Col. 0300D] that, after diligently investigating the truth, if you find that the archbishop suffers from that illness, you shall by our authority assign him a coadjutor in accordance with the canonical enactments; and, with the obstacle of appeal removed, make such other determinations as shall be canonical [Col. 0301A].

Furthermore, because the said canon, though he knew that the archbishop suffered from such an illness, made no protest whatever at the reception of the pallium, and indeed appears fraudulently to have suppressed the truth, we will and command that, if you establish that this is so, you shall canonically punish him, appeal removed. No letters, etc. But if not all, you, brother bishop, with one of them, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of March, in the seventh year.

XVIII. TO THE NOBLEMAN … DUKE OF THE VENETIANS: THE SPIRIT OF WISER COUNSEL. He exhorts the duke and the Venetians to come to their senses and do penance for the crime they committed against Zadar. (Anagni, the sixth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0301B]

Following in the footsteps of our predecessors, who honoured the city of Venice in many ways, we seek its honour and advancement. We have not shown ourselves difficult in petitions made to us on its behalf, but have taken care to promote them, so far as we could do so with God and with honour—as we ourselves know, and as we believe you remember.

Yet, the more we sought its advantage and increase, the more earnestly we desired that it should not provoke against itself the anger of him who exalts the humble and humbles the exalted. Your nobility knew, and the people of Venice also knew, how our dearest son in Christ [Col. 0301C], the illustrious King Emeric of Hungary, and the nobleman A., duke and his brother, had taken the sign of the cross and proposed to cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land; their departure has thus far been delayed by your obstruction.

Moreover, neither you nor the Venetians were unaware how, after the devastation of the Holy Land, the Apostolic See received under its protection all who came to aid its remnants, from the day they took the sign of the cross until their death or return, and commanded that both their households and their goods remain secure under ecclesiastical protection. You also know, we are sure, that although the king himself and his realm enjoyed apostolic protection because he had taken the cross, by authority of the constitution issued on this matter by our predecessors, nevertheless, since what is specially promised is commonly feared more than what is comprehended in a general undertaking, he specially requested and received, as a precaution, letters of our protection. We neither could nor ought to deny them to him, lest we seem to withhold from him what has been granted to all who have taken the cross.

We believe you also know how your envoys, who approached the Apostolic See together with the envoys of the crusaders, requested confirmation of the agreements concluded between you; and through them we ordered you and the Venetians not to injure the king’s lands in any respect. Further, so that the Lord’s journey might be undertaken in fear, and a little leaven might not corrupt the whole mass, by our letters—which we believe reached your hearing and that of the Venetians—we strictly forbade you [Col. 0302A] to attempt to invade or injure Christian lands, unless they themselves wickedly impeded your journey, or unless some other just and necessary cause arose on account of which, with the advice of the legate of the Apostolic See, you could act otherwise. Any who presumed contrary to this were to know themselves bound by the bond of excommunication and deprived of the indulgence which the Apostolic See granted to crusaders.

But you and your people, despising all these things and repelling our legate, first attacked the king himself, drew up your first battle-lines before Zadar, summoned an army of Franks to your assistance, and obtained from them their consent to join you and stain their hands with fraternal blood. You therefore seized and violently overthrew the city; you destroyed churches and dug up altars; and, to the offence of the divine Majesty and contempt of the Roman Church, committed a crime now almost wholly notorious throughout the whole world [Col. 0302B]. For you did not take the cross, nor ought you to have taken it, in the service of Jesus Christ in order to attack Christians, but rather to attack the Hagarenes, the faithless enemies of that cross.

We set these matters before you for your correction out of sincere charity, because a father corrects the son whom he loves, and God rebukes and chastens those whom he loves. We have received the letters of the emperor of Constantinople and yours, and have carefully taken note of what you signified in them. Yet, although we desire that, through your effort and diligence, the church of Constantinople should return to devotion to the Apostolic See, we aspire more earnestly to the aid of the Holy Land [Col. 0302C], lest its assistance, delayed until now, be delayed longer.

We therefore admonish your nobility and exhort you in the Lord, and by these apostolic letters command you, that you and the Venetians, reconciled to ecclesiastical unity, may expiate the stains of your sins with tears of penance. Thus, cleansed from the defilement of crimes, you may fight the Lord’s war in purity of heart and body. Do not presume upon your numbers or strength, or upon the prosperity that has thus far attended you. Rather, the more the Lord has granted you beyond your deserts, the more you should take care to humble yourselves in his eyes; and let his patience lead you to repentance. Having sought absolution in humility and received it with devotion, devote all your strength to the recovery of the Holy Land [Col. 0302D], for that will be especially meritorious before God and glorious among men. And we, with God’s help, shall endeavour effectively to procure whatever we see to be expedient for that land.

Given at Anagni, the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

XIX. TO THE PRIORESS AND NUNS OF RUESPERRA. He receives them under protection. (Anagni, the second day before the Nones of March.)

“It is customary to grant,” etc., down to “assent.” We strengthen, by way of protection, your persons with all your present goods, etc., down to “we strengthen,” strictly forbidding anyone to presume to exact from you anything from your newly cultivated lands [Col. 0303A], which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the feed of your animals. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, the second day before the Nones of March.

XX. [Note: Praised by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77.] TO THE BISHOP OF FIESOLE [Note: Raynerius was bishop of Fiesole from 1193. In 1218, accused of various crimes before Pope Honorius III by the abbots of St Galgano and St Michael, who had been appointed apostolic commissioners in the matter, he wasted away from grief of mind and died in the following year, 1219. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. III, col. 321.]. That he is not to obey the consuls of Florence, who had resolved to transfer the said bishopric to the city of Florence under an asserted right of patronage; he commands that this be rescinded. (Lateran, the third day before the Ides of March.)

We have received the tearful complaint of our beloved daughters in Christ, the nuns of St Peter of Florence, that the consuls of that city bound themselves by an unlawful oath to transfer the bishopric of Fiesole [Col. 0303B] to their own city, proposing to establish the episcopal see in that monastery. In their statutes they further provided that investigation of the right of patronage should be referred to their own judgment, ecclesiastical judgment being set aside.

We therefore commanded our beloved son, the prior of St Fridianus of Lucca, strictly on our behalf to forbid those consuls to attempt the transfer of the see of Fiesole, since—even if it were necessary for it to be done at a suitable place—this specially belonged not to them but to us. He was also to order them to rescind those statutes which they are said to have made concerning patronage rights to the prejudice of ecclesiastical law; and he was firmly to forbid you and your chapter to comply with those consuls in these matters.

But when that prior had warned the consuls and people of Florence to desist from this presumption, they paid no heed to his warning. Deferring neither to the divine Majesty, nor to the Apostolic See, nor to the female sex, they compelled the nuns to leave their monastery; and, after thrusting the nuns into a certain chapel, handed over that monastery itself to you [Col. 0303C].

Now, since you are bound by an oath of fidelity to us and to the Roman Church—which expressly contains the obligation that, saving your order, you shall defend the Roman papacy against every person to the extent of your ability, and, if you know of our harm, shall endeavour to prevent it—we are compelled to wonder at and be troubled by your discretion. For, although change of an episcopal see belongs by right solely to the Roman pontiff, as we know you understand and have taught others also, you do not defend the Roman papacy in this matter as you ought, but rather attack it; nor do you prevent our harm, but procure it, while, without our authority—indeed, against an express prohibition—you plot with the aforesaid consuls to transfer the see of Fiesole to the city of Florence, in the monastery mentioned.

In this too you gravely injure [Col. 0304A] ecclesiastical liberty, when you receive that monastery, in whatever manner, from a lay hand. You know that laymen, however religious, have not been granted authority to dispose of ecclesiastical property. Although your archdeacon came into our presence and seemed to offer many excuses for you, nevertheless one who ceases to oppose a manifest crime does not lack the taint of secret complicity.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood and strictly enjoin you in virtue of obedience that, upon receiving these letters, you shall go in person to the city of Florence. Whatever has been attempted, or shall subsequently be attempted, regarding the aforesaid monastery, you shall declare by our authority null and void. You shall diligently warn the consuls and people of Florence on our behalf that, once the said nuns have been restored to the monastery, they shall not delay for fifteen days to make satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted, and shall rescind the statutes which they are said to have established concerning the rights of patronage of churches against ecclesiastical liberty. Otherwise, bind those consuls, their counsellors, and their chief supporters by the bond of excommunication; and cause the sentence of excommunication imposed upon them to be solemnly published throughout your diocese on every Sunday and feast day, bells rung and candles lit, until fitting satisfaction is made [Col. 0304B].

If you neglect to fulfil this, suspended from pontifical office, you shall personally present yourself before us within a month, to make satisfaction to us for so great an offence [Col. 0304C], for, once placed before us, you will certainly learn whether your money—as you are said to have boasted—can redeem your guilt before us.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of March.

XXI. [Note: See Raynaldus, in the same place.] TO THE PRIOR OF ST FRIDIANUS OF LUCCA [Note: He has already been discussed often.]. On the same subject. (Lateran, the Ides of March.)

“The tearful [complaint],” etc., in nearly the same manner, down to “they handed [it] over.” Yet we grieve not so much for the nuns themselves as for the consuls mentioned, since it is no less [wrong] to commit an injury than to suffer one. More particularly, we grieve for the Apostolic See, whose special privilege they strive to violate, since alteration of an episcopal see belongs to it alone [Col. 0304D]; and for the universal Church, whose liberty they seek to impair, since laymen have been granted no power whatever to dispose of ecclesiastical property.

We therefore commanded that same bishop, strictly enjoining him in virtue of obedience, that, upon receiving our letters, etc., down to “offence.” Accordingly, by these apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, unless the aforesaid consuls and people of Florence take care to comply with your aforesaid warning [Col. 0305A; Note: Thus in the copy, but something is missing], you shall bind those consuls and their chief supporters by the bond of excommunication. Cause that sentence to be solemnly published in the surrounding cities, bells rung and candles lit; and by our authority strictly cause them to be forbidden to enter into any commercial dealings with the excommunicated persons, but rather to avoid them as excommunicated. Announce also on our behalf to the consuls themselves and to the entire people of Florence that, if they should determine to persist in their obstinacy, we shall cause their merchants, wherever they may go, to be seized and detained with all their merchandise. And since they wish to establish two bishops in their city, they will rightly have reason to fear lest we divide their single bishopric into two [Col. 0305B].

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of March.

XXII. TO THE ARCHPRIEST, AND TO G. AND R., MASTER CANONS OF LUCCA. In favour of Norad, subdeacon: that they not permit him to be harassed by an accusation of infamy. (Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

Our beloved son Norad, our subdeacon, informed us that, when a controversy had arisen concerning his inheritance between himself on the one side and his brothers S. and S., of the diocese of Pisa, on the other, B., their uncle, and R. and C., their kinsmen, bound them by an oath-bound guarantee that they would abide by their arbitration in this matter. Later, under the obligation of an oath of secrecy, they enjoined the same subdeacon [Col. 0305C] to lay aside clerical dress, marry without delay, and not claim any portion of his inheritance until he reached sixteen years of age. The aforesaid subdeacon refused, as indeed he ought, to obey their arbitration.

Since such a command was unlawful and inequitable, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion not to permit him on that account to be harassed by any vexation of infamy, for they are rather the guilty judges, who did not fear to issue such an arbitration. Notwithstanding the said oath or arbitration, and with appeal removed, cause him through ecclesiastical censure to be given the portion of his inheritance due to him [Col. 0305D]. No letters, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.

XXIII. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF CAMERINO. That they recover and preserve the possessions of the Roman Church in the castle of Camerino. (Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.)

Let it be known to you that it has come to our hearing that the possessions and rights which we have in the castle of Camerino [Col. 0306A] are badly administered and are being lost through carelessness and negligence. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command and enjoin your community that you take care to render account to our beloved son Bald., citizen of Ancona, for all the possessions and rights which we have in the castle or its dependencies.

For Bald. has sworn to us that he will in good faith recover, for the name and benefit of the Roman Church, the possessions and rights belonging to the Roman Church in the said castle, around it, and in its dependencies; and that whatever has already come, or shall hereafter come, into his hands in the said castle and its dependencies, however it may come to him, he will in good faith preserve for the name and benefit [Col. 0306B] of the Roman Church. He has promised under the same pledge of faith neither to diminish nor alienate them, nor consent to their alienation, but at our command, or that of our successors, to restore them all with every entirety and increase.

And we, lest the possessions or rights of that castle be alienated or diminished, decree every other contract null and void.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

XXIV. [Note: Praised by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §82.] TO THE BISHOP [Note: The church of Luni was governed by Gualter, or Walter, at least from 1198. Statutes for the good government of the town of Sarzana, made by him in 1200, survive. In the following year he granted the churches of St Andrew and St Basil, with their dependencies [Col. 0306D], to the chapter of Luni. By authority of Pope Innocent III, in 1204—as is stated in this very epistle 24 of Book VII—he transferred the ancient cathedral from the church of St Basil of Luni to St Andrew’s at Sarzana. In 1206 he reduced the number of canons to sixteen. In 1202—more probably 1203—on the sixth day before the Nones of March in the sixth year of his pontificate, Innocent confirmed to him all the rights and goods of the church of Luni, as well as the agreements and exchanges between him and the canons of Luni, by a diploma which may indeed be read in Ughelli, but is vainly sought in the registers. Gualter lived until 1212, when he died, a prelate worthy of everlasting memory. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 916.] AND CHAPTER OF LUNI. He confirms by apostolic authority the translation of the bishopric of Luni to Sarzana. (Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.)

By letters formerly presented to our apostolic office, we plainly learned [Col. 0306C] that the city of Luni, in which the cathedral see is known to be situated, so devours and consumes its inhabitants that few or none live there, and there is no people to protect and defend the rights and liberties of your church. After mature deliberation, you resolved—if the Apostolic See would grant this—to transfer the episcopal chair to another populous place, named Sarzana.

In the time of Pope Gregory, our predecessor of holy memory, the matter had, you stated, advanced so far that, when he was passing through those regions, he granted you by apostolic authority permission for this transfer, and gave you, sons who are canons, a blessed stone for building the church [Col. 0306D]. But because a few days later that same predecessor of ours entered upon the way of all flesh, you hesitated to proceed in the matter, believing that his mandate had expired with his death. Therefore, giving attentive consideration to the advantage and need of the clergy and people entrusted to the church of Luni, you sent to our presence our beloved son Ph., your canon [Col. 0307A], humbly and devoutly petitioning through him that we grant you permission to transfer the episcopal see to the aforesaid place.

Favouring your petition with the favour of the Apostolic See, and with the counsel of our brethren, we freely granted you authority to transfer the episcopal see by apostolic authority to the aforesaid place, no contradiction or appeal notwithstanding. When you had taken care to proceed in the matter according to our permission, you, brother bishop, came to the Apostolic See with certain of your canons and humbly petitioned that we might deem worthy of confirmation by apostolic protection what had been done by our authority concerning the said transfer.

Yielding therefore to your prayers and those of the canons, we confirm by apostolic authority the transfer, made to Sarzana by permission of the Apostolic See, of the episcopal see, etc. We decree therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

XXV. TO THE ABBOT OF ST STEPHEN AND MASTER LANFRANC, CANON OF BOLOGNA. Concerning the revocation of a judgment in a certain case not here explained. (Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

“To our beloved son, the cleric C.,” etc., down to “we command you to investigate the truth of the foregoing diligently; and, if you know that the said woman has been granted [the matter] by the aforesaid canons, notwithstanding the appeal which they assert they lodged on this matter before that abbot—since by subsequently consenting they appear wholly to have renounced the judgment—cause it to be granted without difficulty through ecclesiastical censure [Col. 0307C]. Otherwise, supported by our authority, you shall wholly invalidate the sentence of that abbot as regards this article, since in this respect it was expressly pronounced contrary to the tenor of what had been done. But in the other articles we command the judgment pronounced to be firmly observed. Witnesses, etc. No letters, etc.”

Given at the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

XXVI. N… [Note: The address is lacking.] That an inquiry be made concerning suspect privileges and indulgences. (Lateran, the third day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0307D]

Since matters which give rise to grave suspicion, and which might cause serious scandal if they were negligently left unexamined, must be diligently investigated, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood [Col. 0308A] that, after prior warning, you compel by ecclesiastical censure, appeal removed, the persons of your province who claim to hold privileges or indulgences from the Apostolic See and concerning whom suspicion is reasonably entertained, to produce them. If these are shown to be reasonably suspect, order them presented before us, or have the documents themselves kept by religious persons until, by a rescript concerning them, we have full knowledge of them.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Kalends of April.

XXVII. [Note: A fragment of this epistle is found among the Decretals, Book III, title 39, “On censuses, exactions, and procurations,” chapter 21. The words printed there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also given.] TO THE PRIOR OF ST STEPHEN OF FANO. By apostolic authority he settles the case between the prior and M., bishop of Fano, concerning the church of St Stephen. (Anagni, the fifth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0308B]

[When our venerable brother M., [Note: [Col. 0307D] See letter 180 of Book VI, note.] bishop of Fano [Note: [Col. 0308D] In the *Decretals*, “Favensis.”],] and you were present before us, and wished to litigate with one another concerning the dispute between you over the church of Saint Stephen of Fano, we granted you as hearers our beloved sons J., [Note: [Col. 0308D] He has already been mentioned often.] priest cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, and J., [Note: [Col. 0308D] John, count of Anagni, brother of Count James and Andrew, kinsman of Pope Innocent III; formerly a chaplain, he was appointed in 1200 cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin and chancellor of the holy Roman Church. He died in 1213.] cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. Before them you took care to state by allegation that, since the aforesaid church of Saint Stephen, through the malice of certain nuns who appeared to live there under the religious habit, had been brought almost to desolation, [Col. 0308C] C., bishop of Fano of good memory, by the authority of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of happy memory, removed them from the said church and established regular canons there. He decreed that the canonical order must be observed there in perpetuity, and entirely exempted it from every exaction, whether of himself, his successors, or the church of Fano, reserving to himself and his church one candle of three pounds’ weight, to be paid by it annually.

[Note: [Col. 0308D] The chronological succession of the bishops of Fano is very incomplete. Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 710) mentions no bishop of Fano in the time of Pope Eugenius III—that is, from 1145 to 1153.] And because the aforesaid bishop repeatedly burdened you concerning the aforesaid liberty, confirmed both by Pope Celestine of happy memory, our predecessor, and by ourselves, you sought the support of apostolic protection.

The said bishop, on the other hand, alleged that the privilege of his aforesaid predecessor caused neither him nor his church any prejudice, because, when that predecessor granted it to the said church, he had resigned the episcopate and received the regular habit in that church; and, repenting three days later, revoked that privilege. Furthermore, you and the canons of that church had not made use of that privilege, but, just as before the grant of the privilege, so afterward, had until the present time without any difficulty taken care to render all services of hospitality to every successor of that bishop, and especially to himself. He asserted that the confirmation by our aforesaid predecessor had been obtained by surreption and concealed until then; and therefore humbly requested that, if the church of Fano had perhaps suffered injury in any respect, restitution be made to it.

But you took care to answer these allegations as follows: that the privilege was valid in law, because when the bishop granted it he had neither resigned the episcopate nor received the regular habit; and that he had granted it with the consent of his canons, as is plainly evident from the instrument itself, in which the names of the canons of the church of Fano are subscribed, and which, as is expressly stated in it, was issued in the palace at Fano.

When the said cardinals had faithfully reported to us what they had heard, and after carefully examining the said instrument, we indeed learned that the aforesaid bishop remitted to the said church the *spallae* [Note: [Col. 0309D] *Spalla* is the same as *spadula*; in Italian *spalla*, in French *espaule*: a shoulder. In most ancient charters it is used for the shoulder, or a limb, of beasts, boars, or deer, which is customarily rendered to a lord for the right or privilege of hunting in the lord’s forests. Cange, vol. VI, col. 619.] which both he and his predecessors had been accustomed to receive from it, and decreed that he should impose no other service upon it, reserving for himself and his church an annual pension of a candle of three pounds’ weight.

Since provision for maintenance is attached to visitation—for no one ought to serve at his own expense, nor should the mouth of an ox be muzzled while it treads the grain—and since the bishop, by reason of the spiritual jurisdiction which he has over it, is bound to visit the aforesaid church for purposes of correction, and since that which had been imposed by common law from its very foundation is not to be understood as though it were something newly imposed, we have decreed, with the counsel of our brethren, that when the bishop goes to that church for correction, he shall receive from it moderate maintenance twice a year; but he may demand or even extort [Note: [Col. 0310D] The *Decretals* read: “or presume to extort.”] nothing else from that church beyond the pension and the aforesaid provisions for maintenance. [Note: [Col. 0310D] The *Decretals* read “therefore”; they omit below the words distinguished by italic type.]

We therefore decree that no one, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

XXVIII. TO R. OF GECLEWERDS, G. OF DRIBURG, AND MASTER T., RECTOR OF THE CHURCH OF LILLESCHAE. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Thus in the copy.] He entrusts to them for judgment the case between the abbot and monks of Melrose and the nobleman Alban. (Anagni, 6 March.)

[Col. 0309D]

Since the beloved sons, [lacuna] abbot and monks of Melrose, represented before us that the nobleman Alban, wishing forcibly to convert into forest certain lands which William, once his father, had assigned to their church of Machelin as alms, was improperly troubling them concerning those lands, we recall that we commanded you to compel A. by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to desist from improperly troubling them concerning those lands.

But, in order to carry out the apostolic mandate in this case, you proceeded carefully in the matter. With the parties present before you, you received witnesses on both sides; and, after long disputations and discussions concerning their testimonies and the instruments as well, you proceeded in the case as far as the rendering of judgment. Having remitted the sufficiently prepared case to our hearing, you assigned the parties the octave of Saint Andrew last past as their term.

Accordingly, when the party of the abbot and monks appeared on the appointed day, and the opposing party, though awaited for a long time, at last did not appear, we carefully deliberated with our brethren upon the instruments already mentioned, the depositions of the witnesses, and the allegations of both parties. Having carefully investigated and examined the truth, we plainly recognized that judgment in this case ought to be given for the said monastery.

Therefore, so that through your diligence an end may be imposed upon the case, we return to you under our bull, enclosed, the text of the instruments, the depositions of the witnesses, and the allegations, as we received them authenticated by the protection of your seals. By these apostolic letters we command and enjoin you that, strengthened by our authority, you proceed to pronounce judgment for that monastery, notwithstanding the contradiction or appeal of anyone; restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure and causing what you judge to be firmly observed by our authority.

For the tenor of the instrument plainly shows that this was the donor’s mind and intention: namely, that the clause concerning the Forest, placed at the end of the instrument, must in sound interpretation be referred not to the earlier donation—which was so free and unqualified that it was exempt from every secular exaction and custom—but to the later grant, in which a rent and a limitation are inserted. For in contracts an ample interpretation, in wills a fuller one, and in benefices the fullest interpretation must be applied.

But if not all, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the second Nones of March.

XXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0310D] It is found among the *Decretals*, Book I, title 29, “On the office and power of a delegated judge,” chapter 27. Variant readings are supplied.] [lacuna] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. He answers him concerning appeals. (Lateran, 27 March.)

[We answer your brotherhood as follows concerning the questions on which you wished to consult us: our constitution in no way derogates from the response of Pope Alexander of blessed memory, our predecessor, [Note: [Col. 0311D] The words “of blessed memory” and “our predecessor,” as below, are absent from the *Decretals*.] but explains it; indeed, more truly, it supplies in this constitution what had been omitted in the former.

[Note: [Col. 0311D] This constitution of Pope Alexander III, here under discussion, is found in Gregory’s collection of *Decretals*, Book I, same title, chapter 18, *Cum te consulente*.] For he replied that, if an appeal were lodged in a case entrusted to someone by apostolic delegation, from ecclesiastical persons—one or more—to whom the delegate, in order to spare the parties’ labour and expense, commits examination of the case and examination of the witnesses, while reserving judgment to himself, that delegate is not bound, on account of that appeal, to leave the case undecided.

We, however, decreed that although one to whom a case is entrusted, with appeal removed, cannot delegate it to others without the impediment of an appeal, nevertheless, if one delegated by us, or any judge whatever, appoints someone not so much as an investigator as an executor for a particular specified issue, no appeal may be made from him unless he exceeds the limits; provided that he is appointed or accepted with the consent of the parties. But if the delegate appointed by us considers it appropriate to commit to him either the beginning of the lawsuit or its conclusion—let alone the entire matter [Note: [Col. 0311D] The *Decretals* add “matter.”]—an appeal may lawfully be made from him as from a judge; both the suit ought to be joined before the judge, and the case determined by the judge.

Our intention, therefore, as may clearly be understood from the tenor of the foregoing constitution, was that judicial authority might be exercised more freely: a delegate appointed by us may lawfully delegate to another the beginning, end, and middle of the case entrusted to him, not only jointly but separately. This stands notwithstanding the statement that [Note: [Col. 0311D] The *Decretals* read “that,” and below omit “and.”] a judge ought personally to take cognizance at the beginning, middle, and end, since before pronouncing judgment he ought carefully to investigate everything done in court.

But when he entrusts to someone the whole case, or its beginning or its end, an appeal may lawfully be made from that person as from a judge. When, however, he entrusts only the middle stages to someone, an appeal cannot be made from him as from a hearer, unless he exceeds the limits of his mandate or is justly suspected. Therefore, lest he be subject to challenge, we prudently decree that he be appointed or accepted with the consent of the parties.

Further, if the delegate appointed by us transfers his entire jurisdiction to another, any appeal must be made not to him but to us. But if he reserves some part of the jurisdiction for himself, and the case was entrusted to him with appeal removed, an appeal may by law be made not to us but to him. Hence, if an appeal is perhaps made [Note: [Col. 0312D] The *Decretals* read “if perhaps an appeal were made”; and read *causae* for *quaeque*; below they omit “or.”] from the person to whom he entrusts any intermediate matters—whether he is called investigator or executor, or, better, hearer—because he either exceeds the limits of his mandate or is justly suspected, the delegate appointed by us may nonetheless, in accordance with the foregoing consultation, determine the case, so that the parties’ labour and expense may be spared.

Neither party may challenge the person whom our delegate appoints as hearer unless it shows before him a just ground of challenge. Therefore, if two persons are delegated by the prince and one commits his functions to the other, the latter can neither proceed, nor ought to proceed, with appeal removed, nor delegate the case to someone else, even though the commission issued to the two expressly provides that, with appeal removed, either may proceed without the other if both cannot be present together. For what he can do solely by the jurisdiction delegated to him by the prince, he cannot do with jurisdiction granted him by his co-delegate.

Hence, if an appeal must be made from him, although some have thought that it may also be made to the co-delegate, it nevertheless seems to us that appeal is to be made only to the original delegate, for the reason given above.

Accordingly, the appeal concerning which your brotherhood wrote to us—if, invoking our constitution, he appealed to our hearing because our delegate, while reserving final judgment to himself, committed the hearing of the case to certain persons who were neither appointed nor accepted with his consent—ought not to have prevented the hearers from proceeding, unless he showed against them a just ground of challenge or was prepared to show it before the delegated judge. [Col. 0312C] Even if they had been rightly challenged as suspect, the delegate appointed by us could nevertheless have judicially disposed of the case, once the evasion of appeal had been removed. But if the delegate refused to admit a just ground of challenge and compelled him to be heard before suspected persons, he could lawfully appeal to our hearing from such an injury; and whatever was undertaken after such an appeal must be judged void and of no effect.]

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April.

XXX. [Note: [Col. 0312D] Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §68.] TO THE DEAN AND CANONS OF HOLY CROSS AT STAMPIS. He receives them under protection. (Lateran, 27 March.)

[Col. 0312D]

Places devoted to divine worship, especially those which, after the blindness of Jewish unbelief, have received the light of grace under the name of Christian faith, ought to be fortified by apostolic protection and endowed with the gift of perpetual liberty. For it is clear that those who have chosen there to serve the Lord in freedom of spirit are no longer children of the slave woman but of the free woman.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of yours, which our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, with the consent of G., archbishop of Sens of good memory, decreed should be built in honour of the most victorious Cross in the synagogue from which he had expelled the Jews, together with all that it presently possesses, etc., as far as “may acquire,” after the example of Lucius and Urban, Roman pontiffs of blessed memory, our predecessors, etc., as far as “in common.”

We decree that the clerics who reside in the surrounding churches, just as they took nothing in that place while the Jews possessed it, shall henceforth impose upon the church established there no condition or burden prejudicial to its liberty. Otherwise the condition of the Church would become worse if that which was free while Jews inhabited it should become a slave under the observance of Christian piety.

Moreover, following the example of our said predecessors, we grant you by apostolic authority that you may have, without any contradiction, one mastership of schools in music and another in the other disciplines. We forbid anyone henceforth to presume to extort from you anything from your newly cultivated lands or from the fodder of your animals. We further prohibit any demand henceforth being made by laymen from your possessions.

In addition, by the authority of these presents we decree that no one shall pronounce a sentence of interdict against that Church, or of excommunication or suspension against its canons, without manifest and reasonable cause. But when a general interdict, etc., as far as “to celebrate.” We also grant you a cemetery in which the bodies of deceased brethren and members of your household may be buried. The liberties also, etc., as far as “we decree.” We therefore decree that absolutely no person, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh year.

XXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP [Note: [Col. 0313D] He has already been mentioned often.] AND DEAN [Note: [Col. 0313D] Richard I of Malpalud, dean of Rouen, was in office in 1200. He also occurs in the cartulary of the church of Rouen on the Nones of October and on the fourth Nones of February in 1206.] OF ROUEN. That they may, when requested, provide justice to the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem. (Lateran, 23 March.)

Since it would be exceedingly burdensome and costly for our beloved sons, the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem in Normandy, who live in remote regions, to approach the apostolic see for every complaint, and since they are frequently grievously wronged by many persons, clerics as well as laymen, [Note: [Col. 0313D] Thus in the copy, but incorrectly: “who live in remote regions.”] we have thought fit, at their request, to provide for them in this matter.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command and enjoin your discretion that, whenever you are requested by the said brethren, you restrain their wrongdoers living in the province of Rouen by ecclesiastical censure, with every avenue of appeal removed, so that they restore what they have taken from them and make adequate satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted; or that they submit to the decision of some persons who, with appeal removed, may proceed according to justice. etc. Notwithstanding no letters, etc. But if not both … you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh year.

XXXII. [lacuna] TO THE ABBOT OF CORONA; [Note: [Col. 0313D] See letter 96 of Book V, note, concerning Robert, who was in charge in 1200. But perhaps in this year, 1204, Adhemar was already in office; the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1046, mention him only in 1210.] [lacuna] TO THE ARCHDEACON OF SAINT-BRIEUC; AND [lacuna] TO THE SUBDEAN OF SAINT PETER, POITIERS. That, going to the monastery of Saint Hilary of the Cell, they may reform it. (Anagni, 1 March.)

The beloved son, the prior [Note: [Col. 0314D] The same authors acknowledge Seguin as prior of the Cell of Hilary in this year, 1204; nothing else is known of him. Ibid., col. 1336.] of Saint Hilary of the Cell at Poitiers, informed us by his letters that, although the Rule of blessed Augustine had been established in his church from former times, and the canonical order instituted there in accordance with that Rule had been confirmed by our predecessors, and although its brethren had assumed the regular habit under the profession of that Rule, they presume, contrary to the institution of their order, to retain private property for themselves. Leaving the cloister, they go out into the streets and, in the manner of secular persons, engage in trade, pursue litigation in other persons’ cases, and by the splendour and adornment of their clothing show themselves to be more secular than regular, offending God repeatedly in many other respects.

Moreover, since that church does not have suitable buildings, and even those which it used to have have almost collapsed, the said prior wishes to devote effort to their renewal and to reform of the order. Yet they not only refuse to consent to this being done, but even violently oppose its being done.

Since, therefore, things wrongly undertaken in churches must be corrected more sternly, we command you by apostolic letters that you go together to that church, keeping before your eyes Him who searches the secrets of hearts and the reins. With the counsel of the aforesaid prior, strengthened by our authority and with appeal set aside, correct in head and members whatever requires regular correction; enact whatever you see should be enacted for the increase of religion and the glory of the Lord’s name; and cause what you enact to be firmly observed by our authority through ecclesiastical censure. If necessary and if regular observance requires it, summon religious persons from other churches and establish them in that church. Should you find any opponents or rebels, restrain them from their presumption by ecclesiastical coercion, with appeal set aside, etc. Notwithstanding no letters, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of March, in the seventh year.

XXXIII. TO J., PRIOR, AND THE BRETHREN OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT STEPHEN OF FANO. [Note: [Col. 0315D] See letter 27 of this seventh book.] He receives them under protection. (Anagni, 20 March.)

Since you have chosen to be lowly in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners, and have professed the life of those who had one heart and one soul, we wish in paternal care to provide for your peace, lest, having chosen with Mary the better part, you be compelled through the disturbances of certain persons to be troubled with many things beyond what is fitting, like Martha.

Therefore, henceforth providing for your peace, by the authority of these presents we strictly forbid anyone, without manifest and reasonable cause, to presume to pronounce against you or your church a sentence of interdict, suspension, or excommunication; or, without your presentation or consent, son prior, to promote the canons of that church to orders; or to receive any of them into protection, thereby removing him from the enclosure of canonical discipline so that you may not exercise regular coercion against him when he offends.

Likewise, we strictly prohibit anyone from absolving, apart from due satisfaction, your persecutors and those of your church, or invaders of its goods, after they have been interdicted or excommunicated by us or by judges delegated from the apostolic see; or from vexing you by improper disturbance in the celebration of divine offices, the burial rites of the dead, and the other reasonable customs of your church. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

XXXIV. [lacuna] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY; THE BISHOP OF ELY; AND THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND. He confirms the judgment rendered in the case of the church of Filebi. (Lateran, 17 March.)

Your letters, brother archbishop, have informed us that, when John of Burgh, a cleric, was unjustly troubling Ernald Bil., a layman, over the presentation of Robert of Brom, a cleric, to the church of Filebi, in which Ernald held the right of patronage, Ernald obtained, through his messenger, apostolic letters concerning this matter addressed to our beloved son, the abbot of Sibeton, [Note: [Col. 0315D] The abbey of Sibeton, situated in Norfolk, was founded in 1150; but the authors of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 866, provide nothing concerning its abbots.] and his fellow judges. After carefully examining and establishing the merits of the case, they pronounced a final judgment against that cleric.

Later, after some time had passed, the aforesaid John began to attack those letters as forged, which, as he alleged, he had always regarded as suspect. He urgently requested that what had been done by their authority be revoked as void. For this reason, the said judges sent those letters to you by a trustworthy messenger—although they themselves had cancelled them by drawing lines of ink over them after the judgment had been pronounced—because you had received a special apostolic mandate to investigate such forgery.

When John asserted in your presence that the letters were forged, the opposing party produced in its defence a certain cleric, named W. of Brom, who stated that he had obtained the letters from us. Accordingly, after adequate security had been received from both parties concerning their allegations, you caused the letters, faithfully enclosed under the seals of the parties and your own, to be presented before us through our beloved son R., the bearer, P. of Maregni (thus written), chosen for this purpose with the unanimous consent of the parties. We found that the letters were genuine in script, thread, parchment, and seal.

We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having declared the letters genuine, you do not permit the aforesaid Ernald to be improperly molested by anyone concerning the judgment lawfully rendered by authority of those letters; rather, cause that judgment, being just, to be firmly observed with every impediment of appeal removed. Opponents, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.

XXXV. [Note: [Col. 0316D] Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §69.] [lacuna] TO THE BISHOP OF ELY; [Note: [Col. 0316D] The bishop of Ely and the abbot of Saint Edmund have already been mentioned often.] [lacuna] TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND; [Note: [Col. 0316D] The bishop of Ely and the abbot of Saint Edmund have already been mentioned often.] AND [lacuna] TO THE DEAN OF CISTERCIANS. That they investigate the privileges granted to the chapter of York. (Lateran, 1 April.)

Since every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, according to the Gospel saying, we fear the imminent desolation of the church of York through its long-standing division. There, to our sorrow, sons rise up against their father, and the father arms himself to the harm of his sons. For through the prevailing malice of many, charity has grown cold among them; and as the enemy sowed tares among them, concord has turned into discord, affection has perished, and hatred has reigned among them in place of affection.

Although the apostolic see has often laboured to remove the cause of dissension among them, yet because the disease had become inveterate and the scar hardened, it made no progress and did not heal them, because it delayed applying the iron to the root—or, as we believe is truer, because it did not know the cause of the ulcer, it did not cure it. Since it is the part of a good judge to diminish lawsuits rather than increase them, we intend fully to investigate the causes of discord and probe more deeply the paths of the disease, so that, once the root is uprooted, the tree may perish and wither altogether. For, though hitherto half-pruned in its branches, it has sprouted more strongly with more abundant growth, becoming more fruitful to its own harm.

It seems, indeed—and is true—that the privilege once granted by Pope C. of blessed memory, our predecessor, to the beloved sons, the dean [Note: [Col. 0317] We discussed the dean and archbishop of York above, Book V.] and canons of York, by which he confirmed for them their dignities, liberties, immunities, and proper customs, nourishes scandal and gives rise to disputes between them and our venerable brother, the archbishop of York. [Note: [Col. 0317] We discussed the dean and archbishop of York above, Book V.]

Now, although almost every chapter contains an inserted condition, so that all granted in that privilege appears to depend upon the ancient dignity of the church of York, the immunity of its chapter, and that church’s approved custom—as you will be able to learn more fully by inspecting the privilege—and although the archbishop calls all these things into doubt and raises a question concerning them, the dean and canons nevertheless, as that archbishop has informed us, behave as though the condition were established: they not only use but abuse the privilege. Distorting certain matters that might rightly have been understood, they raise the horns of pride against the archbishop, claim for themselves almost unrestricted liberty, and nearly wholly empty archiepiscopal jurisdiction of its force.

Therefore, lest wrongs arise from that from which rights arise, and lest the apostolic see, which preaches peace to others, be judged the promoter and author of discord on the occasion of such a privilege, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding the letters directed to you, brother bishop, and your fellow judges against the said archbishop concerning an investigation to be made, you summon the parties and investigate, with appeal removed, the dignities, immunities, and customs of the church of York and its canons, as well as archiepiscopal jurisdiction and right. Carefully receive the truth as to whether the aforesaid dean and chapter have abused the said privilege; receive such witnesses as the parties may choose to produce before you; examine everything diligently; and faithfully report to us by letter what you discover, so that, instructed by your report, we may better provide for the church of York. But set a term for the parties, etc. But if not all … two, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April.

XXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, COUNTS, BARONS, AND ALL CLERGY AND PEOPLE ESTABLISHED IN SICILY AND CALABRIA. He sends to them G., cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Adrian, legate of the apostolic see, and commends him to them. (Lateran, 1 April.)

[Col. 0317D]

Satan, having gone forth from the presence of the Lord, and having received power from Him, has hitherto sifted you like wheat—not only in all that you seemed to possess, but also in the persons of some among you; and, as one shakes out a bundle of straw, so he has shaken you, leaving nothing unshaken, but, by sending a wind from the desert region, has stirred up the elements both for your shaking and for your destruction. For although the Lord knows those who are His, since the secrets of hearts lie open before Him, He nevertheless wished to test—and did test—whether your faith would advance or fail in adversity, and whether you would withstand the blasts of the north wind, when, with the south wind blowing, you seemed to have flourished.

Would that affliction had given you understanding; would that in this sifting you had been purified, so that the testing of your faith might be far more precious than gold tried by fire, and so that, since in some among you gold and silver had rusted, now at least, with the rust consumed and the dross cleansed away, both might shine forth more brightly. Indeed, because life had not been a teacher foreign to you, so that you would need to seek examples elsewhere and afar off, the Lord wished you to experience in yourselves that every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and house falls upon house; and that things which grow through concord collapse through discord. For if you had been of one mind and had borne one another’s burdens, and if the envious man had not counted his brother’s misery as his own glory, but had thought his own affair at stake when the neighboring wall was burning, you would have kept your court in peace as armed strong men and would not have feared the attack of one stronger.

But because almost every one of you had made a separate party for himself, and you did not resist your enemies together, but rather fostered them individually, the head returned to the tail; and, the first becoming last and the last first, your enemies became the head. Your inheritances were transferred to strangers and your houses to foreigners; the low-born and abject trampled upon the necks of the noble and exalted; and even slaves assumed dominion over you. And because nothing is harsher than a humble man when he rises on high—since he rages against all men in order that they may think him powerful, and makes tyranny his power—many among you, blind and weak alike, and your giants, groan beneath the waters; and magnates, handed over to flames, scarcely even thus appeased the frenzy of those slaves, who stirred up against you the indignation and hatred of your superiors.

The vengeance of so great a chastisement—not human but divine—might have expiated in you the multitude of your sins, had not the vice of faithlessness increased in some beneath the scourge; and those who had descended into the depth of sins had become contemptuous, so that, hardened even to their own destruction, they preferred to cleave to enemies against their brothers rather than to their brothers against enemies. Therefore in all these things the anger of the Lord has not been turned away, but His hand is still stretched out, unless you return by another way and rise again through concord to the condition of your former prosperity, from which you fell through discord.
