For just as love is the fullness of the law, so hatred not only renders the law void, but assaults kings and kingdoms; and, no less than a mouse in a bag, fire in the bosom, or a serpent in the breast, it ill rewards its hosts, but rages more grievously against its own authors, when their sword enters their own heart and they perish in their own snare while falling into the pit which they prepared.

Although, because of the numerous offences and immoderate excesses of some among you, who glory when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds, we might overlook your ruin, nevertheless we neither will nor ought to fail the childhood of the innocent king, or to pass with closed eyes over so great a misery of the realm: lest the righteous be punished for the wicked, and the son be condemned for the father or the father for the son; rather, let the soul that has sinned—unless it adds repentance so as to rise again—die in its own iniquity. We have therefore judged fit to send to you our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, legate of the Apostolic See, a prudent and honorable man, whom among our other brethren we embrace with the arms of special affection, committing to him our authority in both spiritual and temporal matters,

> [Note: Col. 0319D. See Letter 140 of Book V, note.]

so that he may confirm in devotion to us and in fidelity to the king those who are faithful, recall those who stray, and lay heavy hands, both spiritually and temporally, upon those whom he cannot recall. We therefore admonish and exhort all of you in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command that, receiving this legate as our own person—indeed, receiving us in him—and treating him gladly and honorably, you humbly accept and inviolably observe whatever he determines among you in spiritual or temporal matters. Otherwise, whatever sentence he pronounces spiritually or temporally against rebels, we shall, with the Lord as author, cause to be firmly observed.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April.

### XXXVII. TO THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF SAINT JULIAN, THE HOSPITALLERS OF THE CROSS, AND THE OTHER CLERGY OF THE DIOCESE OF RIMINI

That they are to observe the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the bishop of Rimini against heretics.  
(Lateran, Nones of April.)

Since the sentence of a shepherd must be observed, and one who presumes to act against it deserves punishment, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters that those against whom our venerable brother, the bishop of Rimini, has promulgated sentences of excommunication or interdict on account of the crime of heresy, you admit in no way to divine offices, nor deliver the bodies of the dead to ecclesiastical burial, notwithstanding privileges granted to you in this matter; for, because of the enormity of this crime, which even civil laws prosecute with particular severity, we impose this upon you knowingly and deliberately.

> [Note: Col. 0319D. Bonaventura, otherwise Ventura, of the very ancient Trissina family among the Vicentines, was bishop of the church of Rimini. In 1194 he is called “elect” in the bull of canonization of Saint John Gualbert. In 1204, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, he obtained from Pope Innocent confirmation of all privileges formerly granted to his church. He founded the hospice of the Holy Spirit long ago and entered into an alliance with the Bolognese in 1216. He governed the church of Rimini until the year 1130. Having then become very aged, he resigned his office and took care that an excellent shepherd should be appointed for the widowed church. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, col. 425.]

For we have instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Populonia, that he shall cause the sentence which the same bishop has reasonably promulgated against you in this matter, with our permission, to be inviolably observed without appeal until due satisfaction has been made.

> [Note: Col. 0320D. This was Guelphus Belmontius de Belmontiis, son of Draco, a native of Rimini, according to Vecchiazzano. Because of his father’s virtue and the distinction of his family, he was elected bishop of Populonia by the clergy after the death of Lantfrand in 1203. He died about the year 1213. Rub., book VI.]

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April.

### XXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SIPONTO

Concerning a certain woman who, because her husband was impotent, took another man in addition to him; after the first man died, the second refused her although he had children by her: the pope directs that this cannot be permitted.  
(Lateran, Kalends of April.)

> [Note: Col. 0320D. His name was Hugh, and he held office until the year 1216, according to Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1124.]

As we have learned from the letters presented to us by you: a certain maiden of your diocese was joined in marriage to a certain man of frigid nature and was taken into his house. Because she could not remain continent, she fell in love with a young man; and, before she had publicly alleged before the Church the impotence of the husband whom she had married, she transferred herself to the said young man. He in fact betrothed her and knew her by carnal intercourse. When this came to your knowledge, you compelled the young man to leave her and to confirm by oath that, while the aforesaid husband lived and before she had been separated from him by judicial sentence, he would neither retain her nor touch her by carnal intercourse.

But when the first husband had received her back again, ashamed because of his impotence, he assumed the religious habit and after a few days discharged the debt of the flesh to all. The young man who, as stated above, had betrothed her, then received her again and took her into his own house, treating her with marital affection. Although he had offspring by her, he now seeks to leave her and take another woman as wife. You therefore asked to be instructed by our letters as to what should be done in this case.

Since there are many things which, although invalid at the beginning, nevertheless later become valid when other causes arise, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the facts are so, you compel the aforesaid young man, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to retain the said woman as his wife and treat her with marital affection.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April.

### XXXIX. TO VENTURA, BISHOP OF RIMINI, AND HIS CANONICALLY APPOINTED SUCCESSORS IN PERPETUITY

He receives him under protection and confirms the goods of his church.  
(Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of April.)

> [Note: Col. 0321D. Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §82.]

> [Note: Col. 0321D. See the notes to Letter 37 of this Seventh Book.]

By virtue of the office of apostolic ministry entrusted to us, etc., down to “saving in all things the right and reverence due to the Roman Church,” we grant to you and to the church of Rimini the gate of Saint Donatus, called Saint Andrew’s; the whole half of the Gallic Gate, called Saint Peter’s; the whole portico by which one goes to the sea, and the portico by which the bishops enter; the entire half of the shorebank of the sea, together with the half of its district which belongs to the shorebank, whether in respect of Jews or Christians; and also the seashore extending from the small stream as far as the river called Maricula.

For the aforesaid possessions, which are rights of the Holy Roman Church and which the aforesaid church of Rimini holds, you and your successors shall pay to us and our successors every year one pound of silver as rent. Moreover, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, and as they decreed, so we also decree henceforth that it shall remain forever that the church of Rimini shall be subject to no metropolitan except the Holy Roman Church alone, and that its bishop shall at all times be consecrated only by the Roman pontiff.

We also entrust to you and your successors, and confirm by the page of this present writing, the parish church of Saint Paternian, with its tithes and other appurtenances, together with the other possessions in the estate of Arginaria which likewise belong by right to Saint Peter, under an annual payment of twenty-four Luccan denarii to us and our successors.

Furthermore, the sentence, etc., to the end.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### XL. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CASA DEI

Concerning the restoration of the bishopric in the church of Montepiloso.  
(Lateran.)

> [Note: Col. 0322D. Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §77.]

We have received the grave and lamentable complaint of our beloved sons, the clergy and laity of Montepiloso: although their city is more populous than neighboring cities, and although it was formerly endowed with episcopal dignity, while an episcopal see was confirmed to it by the privileges of many of our predecessors and indeed even restored to it on several occasions, Pope C., our predecessor of happy memory, finally rendered judgment against them in this matter and stripped it of the see which it had previously possessed. This tends to disgrace and to the destruction of souls.

They assert that their church was grievously injured in this, because their party was undefended before that same predecessor of ours, since several and weightier arguments on its behalf had not been produced in court; and they therefore asked to be restored, by our grace, to a hearing. Having examined the rescripts of privileges granted in this matter by our predecessors to the church of Montepiloso, we found that Pope Coel., our predecessor of happy memory, had found a fitting arrangement by which provision was made for the honor and advantage both of the church of Saint Mary the New, which you possess at Montepiloso, and of the church of Saint Mary the Old. By his privilege he decreed that both should be designated by the dignity and name of one episcopal see, and that, by an election of monks and clergy together, one of the monks should be chosen for the episcopal office, presiding over both churches and exercising the office both of bishop and of abbot. Pope Innocent, our predecessor of blessed memory, subsequently confirmed this arrangement by his privilege.

But because the abbey was afterward changed into a priory, and it was unfitting that a bishop should be subject to any abbot, that arrangement could not suitably be observed. Although nothing should rashly be attempted against the sentence pronounced by the said predecessor of ours, nevertheless we neither could nor would fail to heed the just cry of the clergy and people of Montepiloso. We therefore instructed the beloved son, the prior of Saint Mary the New at Montepiloso, to present himself before us within one month, either in person or through a suitable representative, so that, in his or his representative’s presence, they might set forth the reasons by which they sought to incline us to restore them to a hearing.

He replied to us by his letters that, since the priory itself belonged to your monastery and he had been instituted there as prior by you and at your command, he did not dare answer concerning so weighty a matter. We therefore admonish your discretion, exhort you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters to send to our presence, within two months after receipt of this letter, a suitable man with whom we may discuss these matters more fully.

For regular observance has almost entirely perished in that priory, so that scarcely even traces of religious life are visible there; your monastery receives from it little or nothing; and so great a multitude of people suffers spiritual harm because of the lack of a shepherd. Since they are like wandering sheep, they rightly fear danger to their souls. We believe it expedient both for you and for them that someone from your order be appointed bishop of that place, and that, lest your monastery appear to be burdened in this, a suitable annual payment be established for you, or another fitting method be found by which wholesome provision may be made both for you and for them. But if you perhaps neglect to obey our command, we, considering more what is expedient for the salvation of souls than what is advantageous to your temporal interests, shall, God granting, determine in these matters what we judge must be determined.

Given at the Lateran.

### XLI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

That he restrain the podestà and consuls of Modena, who violate ecclesiastical liberty in the city of Modena.  
(Lateran, second day before the Ides of April.)

> [Note: Col. 0323D. Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §77.]

> [Note: Col. 0323D. See Letter 6 of Book V, note.]

If the Lord were to judge His own cause, lest He to whom the Father has given all judgment judge more heavily in the future those who, taking judgment and justice away from His presence, judge unjustly and reduce to the yoke of servitude the house of prayer once free, because the Son made it free, He would long ago have overthrown the province of Lombardy like Sodom and Gomorrah, so that at least in punishment it might recognize Him whom it refuses, as it ought, to honor in His gifts.

For iniquity proceeds from fatness, and God’s great goodness provokes the Lombards to contempt. Because He broke the yoke of their servitude and weakened the bow of the mighty—before which they had stood as a target exposed to an arrow—they, now enlarged and grown fat, have not merely departed from God but have turned their hands against Him and strive in every way to make His bride, namely the Church, into a slave. Behold how they acknowledge God’s benefits; behold how they repay the Lord for all that He has given them. Because He made the exacter cease from oppressing them, they themselves have become exacters against Him and strive to subject to tribute His free bride—the bride of Him who freed them from the hands of their enemies.

Geminian groans, and the church of Modena laments that it is being mutilated, while its children, subdued beneath the yoke of most wretched servitude, are wearied by public duties, exposed to the violence of laymen, burdened with exactions, and oppressed by forced labor and extra forced labor.

> [Note: Col. 0324D. This alludes to the name of Saint Geminian, who is especially venerated by the people of Modena.]

As our venerable brother, the bishop of Modena, informed us in his letters, the podestà of Modena, in order to crush both the church and the clergy with a double affliction and to add affliction to the afflicted, has imposed heavier burdens in addition to those by which his predecessors had sometimes burdened the church of Modena.

> [Note: Col. 0324D. See Letter 32 of Book III, note.]

For he not only compels clerics to submit to exactions and to labor at digging ditches, but, not content with the boundaries set by his fathers, he utterly destroys episcopal jurisdiction. Ignoring that a servant stands or falls before his own master, he compels clerics to answer in a secular court and to give testimony in lay causes. Moreover, in order to render void the rules of the divine law, and in offence against the divine majesty, wishing to abolish both the Old and New Testaments, he has forbidden tithes and first-fruits—which the Lord commanded to be brought into His storehouses and applied to the needs of the sons of Levi—to be paid to clerics and churches upon public proclamation; and he has forbidden other dues to be paid to them. He adds that he will render justice to no cleric against a layman unless clerics answer under his examination.

When our beloved son Guido de Manfr., our subdeacon and a canon of Modena, resisted him to his face and said that he would not submit to his judgment, the podestà immediately caused him to be seized and committed to custody. He did not release him until his friends promised, under a penalty of forty pounds, that they would cause him to give sworn security to obey his commands. He also subjects clerics to a public ban; forbids, under monetary penalty, bells to be rung for divine offices except at his discretion; and presumptuously usurps undue authority in the bishop’s castles, punishing their inhabitants according to his own will.

Since we neither ought nor wish to endure these things with equanimity, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you go personally to that city and carefully admonish and induce the podestà and consuls, as well as the councillors and the entire people, not to compel churches and ecclesiastical persons to submit to exactions or to serve in digging ditches and similar servile duties. Rather, they are to restore what has been violently extorted and refrain from extorting anything further.

If they cannot be softened by such admonitions, place their city under interdict, so that, except for the baptism of infants and the penance of the dying, no divine office shall be celebrated there and no ecclesiastical sacrament administered. Every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lit, publicly announce the excommunication of the podestà, consuls, councillors, and all the principal authors and supporters of that iniquity; and cause it to be announced throughout your whole province with like solemnity. Command that they be more strictly avoided as excommunicated persons by all the cities and citizens of Lombardy, both in meetings and in every sort of business transaction, so that anyone who presumes to associate with them incurs a sentence of excommunication, which you shall afterward publicly and solemnly proclaim.

Likewise declare that the aforesaid podestà, consuls, and councillors of Modena are subject to excommunication in such a way that they cannot obtain the benefit of absolution unless, to make full satisfaction for their acts, they personally present themselves before the Apostolic See. Decree moreover that the constitutions and sentences promulgated by these excommunicated persons, or at their command, are void and without effect, never to have force at any time. Decree also that those succeeding them in the administration of the aforesaid offices shall succeed to the sentence of excommunication unless they make satisfaction within a month, since one who succeeds to honor succeeds also to its burden.

And since the aforesaid podestà, consuls, and councillors grievously persecute ecclesiastical liberty, by authority of this letter decree that, unless they come to repentance within a month, their sons, even to the third and fourth generation, shall henceforth in no way be admitted to ecclesiastical honors or benefices. So that they may feel more fully in effect how grievously we take this injury to God and to the universal Church, announce to them that unless they repent within a month, we shall deprive their city of episcopal dignity and transfer their see to another place. If they cannot be induced to make satisfaction even within another month, then, so that they may never be able to aspire to recover the dignity removed from them, we shall divide the diocese of Modena among the neighboring bishoprics and command the division to be inviolably observed.

We add also that, when you are requested by the same bishop, you shall compel, by sentence of suspension and excommunication and without hindrance of appeal, the canons, clerics, and all ecclesiastical men, exempt and non-exempt alike, dwelling in the city of Modena and its district, to leave the city and district and not return until satisfaction has been made. Since they will have gone into exile not so much for their own liberty as for that of the universal Church, cause suitable provision to be made for them through the churches of your province according to the judgment of your discretion, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical coercion.

Furthermore, compel, without appeal and notwithstanding their privileges or indulgences, the brethren both of the Hospital of Jerusalem and of the military order of the Temple to observe the sentence of interdict inviolably.

It has been written to W. the royal crossbowman, justiciar of the city of Monte Sant’Angelo, that he is vigorously to oppose those who do not blush to alienate the royal revenues in that city, and by our authority faithfully receive and protect them for as long as it pleases us.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of April.

### XLII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT FRANCE

On the same subject as Letters 164, 165, and 166 of Book VI.  
(Lateran.)

> [Note: Col. 0325D. Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1203, §58.]

He who knows nothing imperfectly, the searcher of hearts and knower of secrets, knows that we love our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, with a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith; and that we earnestly seek his honor, advancement, and increase, reckoning the exaltation of the kingdom of France to be the elevation of the Apostolic See. For this kingdom has always remained blessed by God in devotion to that See and, as we believe, will never depart from that devotion. Although at times assaults may be made on one side or the other by evil angels, nevertheless we, who are not ignorant of Satan’s devices, shall endeavor to avoid his snares, believing that the same king will not permit himself to be deceived by their deceits.

Let no one therefore suppose that we wish to diminish or disturb his jurisdiction or power, since he ought not to impede or restrict our jurisdiction and power. Since we are not sufficient even for the full exercise of our own jurisdiction, why should we desire to usurp another’s? But since the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone; if he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you one or two more, that every word may stand upon the testimony of two or three witnesses. If he does not hear them, tell it to the Church; but if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” [Matthew 18]; and since the king of England, as he asserts, is prepared sufficiently to show that the king of France sins against him, and that he himself proceeded toward him in correction according to the evangelical rule, and finally, because he made no progress in any way, has told the Church: how can we, who by divine disposition have been called to govern the universal Church, obey the divine command without proceeding according to its form, unless perhaps he show before us or our delegate a sufficient reason to the contrary?

> [Note: Col. 0326D. Thus in the copy.]

For we do not intend to judge concerning the fief, judgment over which belongs to him, unless something has perhaps been taken away from their right by a special privilege or contrary custom; but we do intend to decide concerning sin, the censure of which belongs to us beyond doubt and which we can and ought to exercise upon anyone. The royal highness, therefore, should not regard it as an injury to himself if he submits to apostolic judgment in this matter, since the renowned emperor Valentinian is reported to have said to the suffragans of the church of Milan: “Take care to appoint to the episcopal see such a man that we also, who govern the empire, may sincerely submit our heads to him and, when as men we have sinned, necessarily receive his admonitions as remedies from a physician.”

Let us humbly pass over what the emperor Theodosius decreed and Charlemagne renewed, from whose lineage the king himself is known to descend: namely, that whoever has a lawsuit, whether he was plaintiff at the beginning of the suit or became such in the course of time, whether the case is being argued or sentence has already begun to be pronounced, if he chooses the judgment of the bishop of the most holy See, shall immediately and without any hesitation—even if the other party objects—be directed to the judgment of bishops together with the pleadings of the litigants. For we rely not upon human enactment but rather upon divine law, because our power is not from man but from God.

No one of sound mind is ignorant that it belongs to our office to correct any Christian whatsoever for any mortal sin and, if he scorns correction, to coerce him through ecclesiastical discipline. That we ought to correct and can do so is evident from both pages of the Testament. For the Lord cries through the prophet: “Cry aloud; do not cease; like a trumpet, raise [lacuna] your voi… [lacuna] and an… to the peo… [lacuna] their crimes” [Isaiah 58; the intervening text is defective in the copy]; and He adds there: “Unless you announce to the wicked man his wickedness, he shall die in the iniquity which he has committed, but I shall require his blood from your hand.” The Apostle likewise instructs us to correct the unruly, and elsewhere says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and doctrine” [2 Timothy 4].

> [Note: Col. 0327D. Thus in the copy.]

That we can and ought also to coerce is clear from what the Lord says to the prophet, who was one of the priests of Anathoth: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to root up and to destroy, to scatter, and to build and to plant” [Jeremiah 1]. It is clear that every mortal sin ought to be rooted up, destroyed, and scattered. Moreover, when the Lord handed the keys of the kingdom of heaven to blessed Peter, He said to him: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” [Matthew 16]. But no one doubts that everyone who sins mortally is bound before the Lord. Therefore, in order that Peter may imitate the divine judgment, he ought to bind on earth those known to be bound in heaven. Yet perhaps it will be said that kings must be dealt with differently from others.

But we know it is written in the divine law: “You shall judge the great as the small; there shall be no respect of persons with you.” Blessed James testifies that such respect of persons intervenes if you say to the man dressed in splendid clothing, “You sit here well,” but to the poor man, “You stand there,” or, “Sit beneath my footstool.” And although we can proceed in this manner with respect to every criminal sin, so as to recall the sinner from error to truth and from vice to virtue, we ought especially to do so when sin is committed against peace, which is the bond of charity. Christ particularly commands the apostles concerning it: “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house’; and if a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him” [Luke 10]. “But whoever does not receive you nor hear your words, go out from there and shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them” [Mark 6].

What is it for the apostles to go out from such persons, except to deny them apostolic communion? What is it to shake the dust from their feet, except to exercise ecclesiastical discipline? For this is that dust which, when Moses scattered ashes from the furnace, became a plague of sores over all the land of Egypt. How severe a sentence of discipline those who do not receive the messengers of peace or hear their words will suffer in the final judgment, Truth itself subsequently shows, declaring not simply but with a certain affirmation: “Amen I say to you, the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans will be more tolerable on the day of judgment than that city” [Matthew 10]. By “city” He means its citizens, from whom He did not except kings themselves.

Moreover, since, according to lawful enactments, what right anyone establishes in relation to another, the other may use against him; and since the wise man declares that one must obey the law which one has oneself made; and since the king of France himself used, in war against King R. of England, of illustrious memory—who, to speak with due respect for the king himself, was not of a worse condition than he—the aid and favor of our office: how will he fail to admit against himself on behalf of another what he admitted for himself against that king?

> [Note: Col. 0327D. Thus in the copy.]

Should there be with us weight and weight, measure and measure, both of which are abominable before God? Finally, since treaties of peace were made between the kings themselves and confirmed by oaths given on both sides, yet were not observed until the specified term, can we not take cognizance of the religious obligation of the oath—which unquestionably belongs to the judgment of the Church—so that the treaties of the broken peace may be restored?

Therefore, lest we seem by dissimulation to foster so great a discord, to overlook the destruction of religious places, and to neglect the slaughter of the Christian people, we have instructed our beloved son, the abbot of Casamari, that unless the king himself either restores a firm peace with the aforesaid king, enters into suitable truces, or at least humbly permits the same abbot and our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bourges, to determine summarily whether the complaint which the king of England brings against him before the Church is just, or whether the exemption which he has expressed against him in letters sent to us is lawful, he is not to fail to proceed according to the form given him by us.

We therefore command all of you by apostolic letters, and strictly enjoin you in virtue of obedience, that, after the same abbot has carried out the apostolic mandate in this matter, you humbly receive his sentence—or rather, more truly, ours—observe it yourselves, and cause others to observe it, assured that if you act otherwise, we shall punish your disobedience.

Given at the Lateran, … in the seventh year.

### XLIII. TO PETER DE MALIANO, RECTOR OF THE HOSPITAL OF PULCHICAVELLI

He receives them under protection with an annual payment.  
(Lateran, Nones of April.)

> [Note: Col. 0328D. Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204.]

“Just requests,” etc., down to “assent.” We receive under our protection your person and the aforesaid hospital, which you have built for the reception of the poor as a remedy for your sins, together with all the goods which it presently possesses, etc., down to “we protect.” As a token of this protection obtained from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors annually one pound of wax, freely offered.

> [§81. Col. 0329A.]

“Let absolutely no one,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April.

### XLIV. TO THE ABBOT OF CASAMARI

Commission for the investigation of the case between the kings of France and England.  
(Lateran.)

> [Note: Col. 0329D. Cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §66.]

We commend your fidelity and prudence in the Lord, and we accept your fidelity and prudence no less—indeed, all the more—because you execute the mandate prudently and faithfully advise what you recognize ought to be advised, fully setting before us the circumstances of the pending business. Although the position of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King Otto, has prospered sufficiently by God’s grace, it has not yet been strengthened and made firm to such an extent that we may presume upon his speedy victory. Therefore you shall press our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious King of the French, both personally and through others whose efforts you know to be effective for this purpose—not merely once, but frequently—that, in accordance with the tenor of our letters, he either establish a lasting peace with our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of the English, or enter into suitable truces, or at least humbly allow you and our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Bourges, to determine straightforwardly whether, as the King of the French himself alleges, the King of England is bound in this dispute between them to submit to the judgment of his court, or whether he can lawfully protect himself by an exception against this; and thereby whether the complaint which he brings before the Church against the other is just, or whether the other’s exception, which he sets forth before us against him, is lawful. If perhaps, when repeatedly requested, he is unwilling to do any of these things, take care to present the letters which we have directed to the prelates and which we are now also sending; and, if there is an appeal, comply with the appeal as a precaution, setting a deadline for its prosecution, since by the very fact that an appeal is made to our hearing, we shall be able to proceed more effectively, as the matter ought to be proceeded with. Nevertheless, notify the King of England of this, so that by the deadline you prescribe he may send us sufficiently instructed envoys to set forth his arguments before us. But if there has been no appeal, and you see that serious scandal will not result—which we entrust to your discretion to judge—proceed in accordance with the form given to you in the aforementioned affair. Moreover, whatever some may say, and however much they may belittle our statements, we nevertheless believe some of the arguments which we set forth in our letters to be plausible, and judge others to be valid; hence we have thought fit to explain some of them more expressly in other letters which we are now sending to the prelates.

Given at the Lateran, . . . in the seventh year.

XLV. [Note: [Col. 0329D] See BZOVIUS, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 113, §10.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE [Note: [Col. 0330D] Book III, letter 54, note.], . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER [Note: [Col. 0330D] Book V, letter 57, note.], AND . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS [Note: [Col. 0330D] Book III, letter 45, note.], AND TO THE CHAPTER OF RHEIMS AND THEIR SUFFRAGANS. That they are to cause the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the Bishop of Cambrai against the Count of Namur and others to be observed. (Lateran, 10 April.)

As wickedness issues forth as though from fatness, and presumptuous persons now publicly perpetrate the evils which they conceive in their hearts, while they endeavor by wicked presumptions to reduce to servitude the Church which the Lord liberated by His blood; and they do not fear to harass with grievous injuries and intolerable losses ecclesiastical persons, in whom that same Lord declares that He Himself is honored and despised. Now, indeed, sons rise at the devil’s instigation against their mother; and those who ought to have defended her against the attacks of others themselves tear open her entrails, violently seizing her goods and plundering them even by robbery, so that the mother may now rightly cry out against the sons whom she regenerated in the Lord: “I have nourished and brought up children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1), paying no heed to the Lord’s words: “Honor thy father and thy mother” (Exod. 20), and: “He who curses father or mother shall surely die” (Exod. 21).

Indeed, our venerable brother, the Bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0330D] Book V, letter 19, note.], tearfully informed us, and it has come to our hearing, that when the nobleman, the Count of Namur, had conceived an unjust resentment against that same bishop, on account of the house at Reumont—which had been built near the castle in the Cambrai district, contrary to the law and custom of the land, to the prejudice and loss of the Church of Cambrai, and which the aforesaid bishop later destroyed, although that house in no way belonged to the count’s jurisdiction—the same bishop, wishing to overcome evil with good, after many injuries had been inflicted upon him by that count, after the plundering of the town of Melin, and after the imprisonment of the bishop’s men, when the count had already remained for three nights in the bishop’s land with a great army, was willing to make suitable satisfaction to the count in accordance with the judgment of worthy men, or, if he preferred, to render him the fullness of justice. But the count wholly refused to accept the satisfaction and justice offered him. As we have seen recorded in testimonial letters which we received from many persons concerning this affair, he entered the land of the Church of Cambrai under arms with the noblemen, the Dukes of Louvain and Limbourg, the Counts of Aubroc and Los, and very many others whose proper names must be stated. He attacked the bishop’s castle, kinsmen, men, and friends by every means he could; and he and his supporters, devastating the land of the Church of Cambrai with hostile plundering, did not fear to consume a certain part of it by fire.

Although our venerable brother, the Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, after entreaties which he had addressed to the count, had taken care strictly to forbid him, by the authority which he exercised, to harass in any way the Church of Cambrai or the bishop himself, but to seek justice against him before the legate if he wished, the same count, disregarding the prayers and prohibition of our legate, entered the land of the aforesaid bishop with the noblemen mentioned above and others whom he had summoned in support of his wickedness. They seemed to have assembled as one, princes against the Lord and against His Christ; they are known to trust in their own strength and glory in the abundance of their riches, saying: “Our hand is exalted, and not God, who made all these things” (Deut. 32). There he did not fear to commit the wickedness which he had conceived in his mind.

But the bishop, seeing that the count and his supporters had been given over to a reprobate mind, so that they not only refused to amend their evil deeds but threatened to inflict worse upon him and his land, pronounced upon them a sentence of excommunication. Yet not even thus did they desist from their malice, but held the ecclesiastical sentence in contempt. Therefore, since we neither ought nor wish to endure such presumptions with equanimity, by the authority of these present letters we command and firmly enjoin your whole body that, publicly proclaiming throughout all your dioceses the same sentence of excommunication lawfully pronounced by the aforesaid bishop against his malefactors, you cause it to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, until suitable satisfaction has been made. This is not prevented if perhaps some of them are otherwise not subject to him by diocesan law, since by reason of the offence which they committed in his diocese he may take action against them.

But if their hardness cannot even thus be softened within a month, so that, returning to their senses, they make satisfaction to the same bishop for what they have committed, then subject their lands to ecclesiastical interdict. Wherever that count may be found—the chief perpetrator of the aforesaid wickedness—while he is present, forbid the celebration of divine offices, so that at least his face may thus be filled with shame and he may seek the name of the Lord, when affliction has given him understanding. But if, which we do not believe, you should be at all negligent or remiss in carrying out our mandate, we command by our letters our venerable brothers, the Bishops of Noyon and Senlis, that they carry out our mandate, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed; and when a complaint concerning you in these matters reaches us, we shall, with the Lord’s help, take care to punish your disobedience with due severity. No letters, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 10 April.

The same was written to them concerning this.

XLVI. TO MASTER THOMAS OF DISCE, CANON OF VUELLENSIS [Note: [Col. 0331] Thus in the Conti copy; perhaps *Wellensis* should be read.]. He confirms by apostolic authority a prebend conferred upon him by the Archbishop of York.

Since the Church of Vuellensis suffers want both in revenues and in the number of clergy, our venerable brother Geoffrey, Archbishop of York, in order to supply this deficiency and enlarge the worship of the divine name, with the consent of the chapter of the same church, established from a certain large prebend then vacant in that church two prebends to be conferred in perpetuity upon two clerics. One of these, namely the church of Muscham with its appurtenances, the same archbishop generously assigned to you; and you have requested that it be confirmed to you by the Apostolic See. Therefore, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm to you by apostolic authority that prebend, as you lawfully and peaceably possess it, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Let no one therefore, etc.

XLVII. TO THE BISHOP OF VARAD AND TO . . . THE ABBOT OF PETIS, IN THE DIOCESE OF VESZPRÉM. That they are to investigate whether a bishopric ought to be established in certain Greek churches of the kingdom of Hungary. (Lateran, 16 April.)

The illustrious King of Hungary, our dearest son in Christ, informed us that certain churches of Greek monks established in the kingdom of Hungary are being utterly ruined through the negligence of the diocesan bishops and through the Greeks themselves, who, as he asserts, are exceedingly undisciplined. He humbly and devoutly petitioned us that, by our authority, one bishopric might be made from them, immediately subject to us, or that Latin abbots or provosts might be appointed in them, through whose effort and diligence the condition of the same churches might be reformed for the better. Therefore, inclining to the petitions of the same king, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, going to the aforesaid churches, you investigate the truth more diligently: whether the same monasteries can be reformed in observance of religious life by the Greek monks themselves; whether, with the consent of the diocesan bishops, one bishopric can be made from them immediately subject to us; and that, faithfully setting down in writing what you discover concerning these matters, you send it to our presence under the testimony of your seals, so that, instructed by your inquiry, we may proceed more safely in this affair. Meanwhile, apply effective effort to their correction.

Given at the Lateran, 16 April.

XLVIII. [Note: [Col. 0333D] Cited in BZOVIUS, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 113, §10. See also Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §82.] TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-AUBERT [Note: [Col. 0333D] Hugh, abbot of St. Aubert, is found in May 1204 in a charter for Cantiprato, in *Notitiae Ecclesiae Belgii*, p. 517; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 155.], TO THE ARCHDEACON S., AND TO MASTER REN., CANON OF CAMBRAI. On the same subject as letter 45 of this book. (Lateran, 9 May.)

Since, because of sins, human wickedness is now great upon the earth, and presumptuous persons have no small boldness against churches and ecclesiastical men, endeavoring to overturn the rights and liberties of churches, their prelates are compelled, if they are to repel these attacks and defend ecclesiastical patrimony and rights, to undergo serious labors and expenses. They must expend in stipends not only that which ought to have been spent on the poor, but even borrow much else at interest; and while the wicked thus oppress them, the condition of the churches cannot increase.

Since, therefore, our venerable brother, the Bishop of Cambrai, has suffered many injuries and losses at the hands of the noble Count of Namur and other noblemen, his supporters; since his land has been almost wholly laid waste; and since, on account of the attack which he is said to have endured from his enemies, he is burdened by no small weight of debts: wishing, as is fitting, to relieve his need and provide for ecclesiastical advantage, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, with an injunction, that, after assessing the amount of his debts, you cause him, by our authority and as you see expedient, to assign from episcopal goods and revenues to his creditors, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, so that the bishop may not be forced to succumb through lack of resources, and the creditors who aided him in his necessities, and thereby deserved favor, may suffer no loss. Opponents, etc. No letters, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 April, in the seventh year.

XLIX. [Note: [Col. 0334D] Published in Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §55.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF BOHEMIA. Permission is granted that he may be called king in letters. (Lateran, 19 April.)

Although, before the time of your promotion, many men in Bohemia had been adorned with the royal diadem, they were nevertheless never able to obtain from our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, that they should call them kings in their letters. We also, both following the footsteps of our predecessors and carefully considering that you had caused yourself to be crowned by the nobleman Philip, Duke of Swabia—who, since he had not been lawfully crowned, could lawfully crown neither you nor anyone else—have hitherto not thought you should be called king.

But since, at the admonition of the Apostolic See and of ourselves, abandoning the Duke of Swabia, you have turned, following sounder counsel, to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King Otto, elected emperor of the Romans, and since he himself regards you as king, both in view of his prayers and because of your devotion we wish henceforth to regard and call you king. Therefore acknowledge the favor thus granted you, and take care so to avoid the vice of ingratitude that your devotion may deserve both that favor be granted you freely and that what has been freely granted be preserved perpetually. Take particular care to have yourself solemnly crowned by that same King Otto as soon as you can.

Given at the Lateran, 19 April.

L. TO THE ARCHPRIEST AND CLERGY OF THE PIEVE OF AREZZO. He settles disputes between them and the provost and canons of Arezzo. (Lateran, 19 April.)

When your beloved fellow canon, acting for your pieve, and the beloved son, the provost, together with certain canons of Arezzo, acting for the church of Saint Peter—which has recently been united by our authority to the cathedral church—had come to the Apostolic See, they litigated before us over various articles, in the presence of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Arezzo [Note: [Col. 0334D] See letter 50 of Book VI, note.].

Your procurator stated that, since the feast of Blessed Donatus the martyr had customarily been celebrated solemnly in your pieve, the provost and canons of Arezzo had recently celebrated it more solemnly at the church of Saint Peter, contrary to the custom hitherto observed and to the prejudice of your right. They did this not only to divert offerings which were customarily received by you abundantly at that feast, but also certain candles which some noblemen were bound annually to pay the same pieve as a rent; the procurator asked that these be restored to you. He added that many threats were directed against you, not so much by the provost and canons as by the podestà and citizens of Arezzo, concerning the chapter customarily held in your church at the beginning of the fast, the celebration of baptism, the litanies, and other dignities which your church had hitherto enjoyed without litigation. He therefore requested that the Apostolic See provide for your indemnity in these matters.

The provost, on the other hand, stated that, since the body of Blessed Donatus rests in the cathedral church, as appears from many privileges of Roman pontiffs, it would seem absurd if that church were deprived of such a solemnity, and if, while you celebrated his feast, the church of Saint Peter—which has been joined with the church of Saint Donatus into one cathedral church—were silent on the annual solemnity of its special patron. Moreover, he said that while the union of the said churches was being treated before the Apostolic See, we had commanded the citizens of Arezzo thereafter humbly to render to the church of Saint Peter all honors which other cities render to cathedral churches, notwithstanding that the contrary had hitherto been observed because of the city’s hostility. Devoutly obeying apostolic commands, they all and each cheerfully swore that they would do this. Therefore, since this feast is a special solemnity of the city, and chapters, baptism, and litanies are customarily celebrated in cathedral churches in other cities, they maintained that all these belonged to the church of Saint Peter by the authority of our mandate and by reason of the oath rendered by the citizens. They added that the aforesaid noblemen offered the candles concerning which your procurator had lodged a complaint before us not as a debt due under the name of rent, but gratuitously, from spontaneous devotion; and that even if they were paid as a debt, since the provost and canons had not taken them from you, you ought not to seek restitution from them, but pursue your right against the debtors.

Therefore, having heard these things and the other matters put forward on both sides, and wishing to provide for the peace of both parties, we decree by the authority of these present letters that, since the episcopal seat has not been transferred from the church of Blessed Donatus to the church of Saint Peter, but the church of Blessed Peter has been joined to that church—so that the former, though it has communicated its privileges to the latter, has not lost its ancient dignities—the feast of Blessed Donatus shall henceforth be solemnly celebrated by the bishop and canons in that original church which was founded in his memory. For just as it would be unfitting for the bishop and canons to celebrate the feast of Blessed Peter in the church of Blessed Donatus, so without doubt it would be absurd for them to celebrate the feast of Blessed Donatus in the church of Saint Peter. We ourselves observe this in similar cases, celebrating the feast of the Prince of the Apostles at his basilica and the feast of Blessed John at the Lateran church, although each church is a cathedral.

But because no injury is done to a saint—rather, honor is paid—when the faithful people venerate his merits in different places, we do not take from you the faculty of celebrating the feast of the same martyr in your church. We leave all persons free to visit on that day, for devotion’s sake, whichever of those churches they prefer, so that they are neither drawn away from one nor compelled to go to the other. We absolve the provost and canons from your claim concerning the candles and offerings; nevertheless, concerning such candles as are owed to you as rent, you may proceed against the debtors.

Concerning the chapter, we decree that the bishop shall celebrate it in your church very early in the morning at the beginning of the fast, so that, after it has been suitably celebrated, he may go with all the clergy to the church of Saint Peter to perform there the office of Ash Wednesday; for we too, on that day, celebrate the gathering at Saint Anastasia, and the station and solemnities of the Mass at Saint Sabina. Since it would seem altogether absurd if baptism were not performed in the cathedral church, we decree that baptism shall be solemnly celebrated in the church of Saint Peter; yet, in accordance with the custom hitherto observed, you shall baptize in your own church those parishioners of your pieve who are presented to you. For although we perform the office of baptizer in the Lateran church, nevertheless the sacrament of baptism is administered to those to be baptized in the titular churches of the city.

Moreover, since the procession of litanies has customarily ended at your church on the first and third days before the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, and on the second day at the church of Saint Peter, we, wishing to defer to the cathedral church, decree that the order be changed: namely, that on the first day the procession of litanies shall end at the church of Saint Peter, and on the following days at your church. So too among us such a procession is celebrated on the first day at the original church; and it is fitting that the Church of Arezzo imitate the custom of the Roman Church and follow the example of her, to whose jurisdiction it is subject without any intermediary. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 19 April.

LI. [Note: [Col. 0335] Cited in Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §53.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ [Note: [Col. 0335D] Book V, letters 14 and 15.]. Against the people of Mainz, and concerning the establishment of a metropolitan see in Bohemia. (Lateran, 20 April.)

The Church of Mainz has until now for the most part so opposed us in your affair, and has so stubbornly remained in its obstinacy, nor yet made any effort to rise again, that if we wished to answer it according to its deserts, we could not only wholly mutilate it of its members because it disdains to receive you as its head; but because it does not understand what a privilege of dignity and increase of honor it has obtained through the Apostolic See, we ought to reduce its head to a tail, make the first last and prefer the last to the first, in perpetual remembrance of its rebellion and for its everlasting reproach. Thus others might learn from its punishment that it is not safe to set one’s arms against a torrent or kick against the goad.

Yet because we sincerely love your person in the Lord with charity, we have thought fit, for your sake, still to show deference to that church. Nevertheless, the longer we defer its punishment, the more severely we shall punish it, unless it speedily expiates its fault; unless the brood of vipers which harbor their lurking places in it present themselves to be trampled beneath your feet; and unless, with the prodigal son, they cry before you: “Father, we are no longer worthy to be called your sons; make us as one of your hired servants, and admit us among them—we who have hitherto neither received you as our shepherd and bishop of our souls nor revered you.”

Indeed, our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king, and the people of Bohemia have petitioned us that, since because of the distance of places and the diversity of languages you are less able to exercise the metropolitan office among them, we—who are bound in Christ’s stead to provide for all the faithful with pastoral solicitude—should establish a metropolitan see in Bohemia. Since it is very extensive and populous, this would provide usefully not so much for their honor as for their salvation, both because of evident benefit and urgent necessity.

Although, because of the contumacy of the Church of Mainz, this petition ought rather to be expedited than deferred, lest we seem to act against you, we do not immediately admit it. Instead, we command inquiry into what must be investigated concerning it, so that, if evident benefit and urgent necessity should perhaps require this, we may provide for the Church of Mainz—provided it recovers from its error and humbly returns to the apostolic mandate—so that nothing may seem thereby to be taken from its honor, but rather added to it. We have therefore thought fit to notify your brotherhood of these matters, so that you may make your will known to us. Know that, if we decide we should proceed in this matter, we shall, God granting, take care to provide sufficiently for your honor.

Given at the Lateran, 20 April.

LII. [Note: [Col. 0337D] A fragment of this letter was published by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §53. What is found in his work is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF BOHEMIA. He defers his petition for the erection of a metropolitan see in Bohemia and orders him to obtain the consent of the Archbishop of Mainz. (Lateran, 21 April.)

Your noble devotion admonishes us, and the sincerity of your faith exhorts us, to admit your petitions more kindly in those matters in which we are able to do so with God and with honor. Since you have hitherto acquiesced in our counsels and henceforth submit yourself to apostolic commands, it is fitting that our affection answer your devotion, and that the Apostolic See honor you, since you endeavor effectively to advance its honor.

Indeed, through your envoys you petitioned us, and our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of Hungary, humbly interceded with us for you, that we should deem it fitting to establish a metropolitan see in Bohemia. The land is extensive and populous, and is separated from the Church of Mainz, to which it is subject by metropolitan right, both by distance of places and diversity of languages; thus, since through the Roman Empire it has deserved to obtain royal dignity, through the Roman Church it may deserve to obtain metropolitan dignity.

[Although we wish to honor both you and your land in every honorable way possible, the business is difficult and the petition contains a novelty. Therefore we do not wish you to wonder or be disturbed if we have not thought fit immediately to grant your prayers, since the matter needs great deliberation, so that what is decided may endure all the more firmly because it has been established with greater maturity. For there must first be shown to us both an urgent necessity and an evident benefit requiring this to be done; the means and willingness of the church in which the metropolitan seat is to be established; and whether dioceses can suitably be established in Bohemia to be subject to the metropolitan see that is to be established. Moreover, the Church of Mainz must be approached and admonished on this point, lest, if this is done otherwise, we seem to cast down our venerable brother G., Archbishop of Mainz, whom we raised up, should we thereby stir up against him greater hatred from his Church and scandal in the city.]

Therefore, so that we may be more fully informed of everything, we send to Bohemia our beloved son T., our subdeacon and chaplain—a learned, prudent, and discreet man, acceptable to us and our brethren by reason of his integrity—to investigate these matters and any others which he sees must be investigated, and fully report to us the truth concerning what bears upon this affair. You also may renew your petition, not only through your own letters and those of the people, but through your solemn envoys, bishops, and those of the Church for whom it is fitting to make such requests, so that we may proceed better in the matter as we see expedient. For we have a ready will to grant your petitions in these and other matters, insofar as we can do so with God.

You shall therefore cause that same subdeacon to be brought safely before the aforesaid Archbishop of Mainz, and our letters to be presented to the chapter of Mainz, lest, if anything is omitted from the matters which we entrusted to them for investigation, we be unable to proceed fully in the affair.

Given at the Lateran, 21 April.

LIII. [Note: [Col. 0338D] A fragment of this letter is given by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §54. What is found in his work is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE CANONS AND MINISTERIALES OF MAINZ: [WISHING THEM] A SPIRIT OF SOUND COUNSEL. Much concerning the rebellion committed by them against the Church and the archbishop. (Lateran, 21 April.)

They have humbly and devoutly petitioned us, etc., as in the letter sent to the archbishop, in nearly the same form, as far as “may be provided for”; namely, that as Bohemia has deserved through the Roman Empire to obtain royal dignity, so likewise it may deserve through the Roman Church to obtain metropolitan dignity.

Although many of the Church of Mainz—if they should indeed be called members of the Church, who, because of their sins, have been cut off from ecclesiastical unity—have deserved severe punishment for the excess of their rebellion and the vice of disobedience in which they stubbornly persist against the divine majesty, the Roman Church, and their own archbishop, we nevertheless, desiring their correction with fatherly affection and mindful that it is a special daughter and honorable member of the Apostolic See, have not thought fit immediately to admit such a petition. Rather, we have resolved first to investigate the matters requiring investigation, so that, if we should perhaps know that the petition ought to be admitted, we may provide in it for the Church of Mainz as we see expedient, provided that, recovering from its error, it does not make itself unworthy.

[Otherwise, you may deservedly impute it not to us but to yourselves if, in casting away the head, you perhaps lose a member.]

It will therefore be for you to show such deference to our honor that we also ought to show deference to yours, providing for you at a suitable time, lest perhaps after the time there may deservedly remain for you a place not for provision but for repentance.

Given at the Lateran, 21 April.

LIV. [Note: [Col. 0339D] Cited in Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §55.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF BOHEMIA. He confirms by apostolic authority the privileges granted him by emperors and recently confirmed by Otto. (Lateran, 15 April.)

The spiritual and material sword so lend each other the aid of mutual support, and reciprocally share their strength, that by reciprocal assistance they supply deficiencies and each completes what is lacking in the other. For it is fitting that they assist one another: among those who do not fear the spiritual sword, the material sword should assert its right by arms; and, when necessary, the spiritual sword should bestow the strength of its authority upon the temporal sword and give validity to matters that would be less valid without it.

Therefore, since our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King Otto, elected emperor of the Romans, has thought fit to confirm for you by his privilege the rights and privileges granted from ancient times by emperors to you and your predecessors, and has granted you liberties, lands, castles, and other things: so that the pontificate may add its support to the disposition of royal authority, we confirm by apostolic authority these grants, as being for the honor both of the Church and of the Empire, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 15 April.

LV. [Note: [Col. 0339D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §55.] TO . . . THE BISHOP OF PRAGUE, . . . THE BISHOP OF OLOMOUC, AND . . . THE ARCHDEACON OF BEHIN. That if anyone attempts to inflict injury upon the King of Bohemia, they are to restrain him by ecclesiastical censures. (Lateran, 21 April.)

Since our dearest son in Christ, P., the illustrious King of Bohemia, in accordance with our mandate, has placed himself at the aid of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King Otto, elected emperor of the Romans, and is prepared to suffer in his service, we neither wish nor ought to allow him to be oppressed by anyone, especially while he is engaged in Otto’s service. Therefore, so that provision may be made by apostolic authority for his protection from loss, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, if anyone should perhaps presume to devise anything to his prejudice, each of you shall restrain his lay parishioners by ecclesiastical censure and his clerics by withdrawal of benefices, by our authority and with all obstacle of appeal removed, from such presumption.

Given at the Lateran, etc., 21 April.

LVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM. Concerning the transfer of a certain provostship. (Lateran, 24 April.)

The illustrious King of Hungary, our dearest son in Christ, petitioned us that, because a provostship is situated in a certain castle of his, Posom, and because of people’s access to it he fears danger to himself from the castle, we should deem it fitting to grant him permission to build the provostship outside the fortification by our leave. Assenting to his petitions, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, concerning the transfer of that provostship, you establish by our authority what you know to be expedient for the necessity of the kingdom and the advantage of the Church, taking care that the body of the holy martyr resting in the said church is not deprived of due veneration.

Given at the Lateran, 24 April.

LVII. [Note: [Col. 0340D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §47.] TO THE SAME ARCHBISHOP. That he is to crown the son of the King of Hungary, since the king has proposed to go to the Holy Land. (Lateran, 24 April.)

He petitioned us, etc., as above down to “that,” because he had resolved to cross over in aid of the Holy Land, lest his kingdom should be left as though deprived of government, that we should deem it fitting to write to you that you should adorn with the royal diadem his most beloved son in Christ, . . . . his son. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your fraternity [Col. 0340C] that, when requested by the king himself, in accordance with his petition you shall not delay to crown his aforesaid son, although under age, receiving in person from the father himself, on behalf of his son, an oath concerning obedience to the Apostolic See and the liberty of the Hungarian Church, as his forebears rendered it with due humility and devotion.

Given as above.

LVIII. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE HUNGARIANS. He explains the mandate already issued concerning the provostships of the kingdom of Hungary. [Note: [Col. 0340D] See letters of Book V, no. 102, and Book VI, nos. 7 and 56.] (Lateran, 8 Kalends of May [24 April].)

Formerly, by his letters, your royal magnificence [Col. 0340D] petitioned us that, since the royal provostships which are in Hungary belong, in temporal matters, to you and, in spiritual matters, to us, without any intermediary, we should decree that a newly appointed provost should come to the Apostolic See within a year—either in person or through a suitable messenger bearing letters of royal assent—to obtain the grace of confirmation. Accordingly, moved by your prayers, we decreed that whoever henceforth might be called to govern those provostships which belong to us in spiritual matters without intermediary should come into the presence of the Apostolic See within a year, either in person or through [Col. 0341A] a suitable messenger bearing letters of royal assent, in order to obtain confirmation; provided that meanwhile they shall not exercise spiritual ministry. But if they should neglect to come within the stated term, they are to know that from that time they will be deprived of those provostships.

Thereafter J., of blessed memory, Archbishop of Esztergom, coming into our presence, stated orally before us and our brethren that ecclesiastical jurisdiction in the royal abbeys and provostships belonged to him and to the Church of Esztergom. He therefore asked that the aforesaid constitution, as one obtained by concealment, be revoked. Choosing a middle course, however, we have by prudent deliberation decreed that no prejudice shall arise for him or his successors, on account of the letters which we first sent concerning the provostships and [Col. 0341B] abbeys subject anywhere in Hungary to the Church of Esztergom. We therefore wish Your Royal Highness to know that neither by the second letters is any derogation made from either our right or the royal right, nor by the first from the justice due to the archbishop himself and the Church of Esztergom: for in the first instance provision was made concerning those institutions known to belong to us in spiritual matters without intermediary; in the second, a decree was issued concerning those alleged to be subject to the Church of Esztergom.

Given as above.

LIX. [Note: [Col. 0341D] See Raynaldus under the year 1204, §81, where he indicates this letter only by number.] TO HUGH, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT AUGUSTINE OF MONTEALTO, AND TO HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. He receives them under protection, and the property belonging to them is enumerated. (Lateran, 4 Kalends of May [28 April].)

[Col. 0341C]

“Whenever a request is made to us,” etc., down to: “assenting, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of Saint Augustine, in which you are devoted to daily divine service; and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander II, of pious memory, we apostolically confirm the transfer of that monastery from Monte Castello to Monte Gentile,” etc., down to: “we strengthen”; decreeing that whatever possessions, etc., down to “by their names”: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated [Col. 0341D], with all its appurtenances; its meadows, lands, vineyards, woods, rights of use, and pastures in woodland and plain, waters and mills, roads and paths, and all its other liberties and immunities; the churches of Saint Mary and Saint John situated at Montealto; the churches of Saint Nicholas, Saint Leonard, [Col. 0342A] Saint Peter of Poggio, Saint Paul-by-the-Sea, and Saint Manulian, with their cells; the entire forest of Anglo; the leper-house of Montealto; the church of Saint Nicholas of Ponteclo; the parish church of Valentano; the church of Saint Mary of Bulzia; and the churches of Saint Stephen of Piscia and Saint Peter of Cannino, with all their appurtenances; likewise the rights and customs which you possess at Montealto; the harbour of Morelli, the harbour on the river of Montealto, and the revenues which you receive from them.

Moreover, we prohibit that any of your brethren, etc. But should they depart, etc. Furthermore, it is permitted to you to receive from whomever you prefer, etc. Upon your death, moreover, etc. Furthermore, all liberties, etc., down to “we strengthen.” As a token of this privilege obtained from the Apostolic See, you shall pay us [Col. 0342B] one gold obol yearly. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in the aforesaid chapters, the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, 4 Kalends of May [28 April], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

LX. TO . . . THE BISHOP OF LINCOLN, AND . . . THE BISHOP OF WORCESTER. [Note: [Col. 0341D] We have already dealt above with the bishops of Lincoln and Worcester.] In favour of a certain canon: they are not to permit him to be troubled by the Archbishop of York. (Lateran, 5 Ides of May [11 May].)

[Col. 0342C]

Since formerly we had commanded our venerable brother . . . Archbishop of York that, to the messenger of the beloved son . . . nephew of our beloved son G. [Note: [Col. 0341D] Gregory, a Tuscan of Monte Carello, son of Lothair de Albertis, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint George at the Golden Veil, alternatively “in Velabro,” was appointed by Pope Clement III in 1190, in the third creation of cardinals. By command of Pope Innocent III, he served as legate in Tuscany and Umbria together with Peter, prefect of the City, in order to organize and govern those provinces. Innocent writes that he was a prudent and wise man, commended for the honourableness of his character and the nobility of his birth. He died under Innocent III, after the year of human salvation 1210. Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1146.] of Saint George at the Golden Veil, etc., down to “strictly commanding, we order that, after diligent inquiry into the truth of these matters, unless it shall be established that the aforesaid revenues ought, by approved custom, to have gone toward payment of the debts of the deceased canon, you shall cause them, together with the grain offered, to be restored by ecclesiastical censure to the messenger of the aforesaid cardinal; and you shall cause suitable satisfaction to be rendered to him for damages done both to the houses of the prebend and to other property. You shall also inquire into injuries inflicted upon the messengers of that [Col. 0342D] cardinal, and whether the archbishop, after the aforesaid sentence, celebrated the solemnities of Mass; and you shall report to us by your letters what you find on these points” [Note: [Col. 0342D] Thus in the copy, but something is missing.]; and, causing the messenger of the nephew of the same cardinal to enjoy peaceful possession of that prebend, you shall defend him from every molestation. For if anyone believes that he has a right in the oft-mentioned prebend, he may obtain his justice through us. You are to fulfil the apostolic mandate in such a way that we may deservedly commend your obedience. Witnesses, etc. But if not both, etc. No letters . . . without mention of these letters having been made, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Ides of May [11 May].

LXI. TO THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 0343D] We cannot determine with certainty who at that time was dean of the ducal chapel at Dijon. The authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 856, mention from documents Hugh I of Lippo down to 1195, and then immediately—but not before 1214—Robert I d’Ancenoys.] AND CHAPTER OF THE DUKE’S CHAPEL AT DIJON. They may not be excommunicated by anyone except in two cases. (Lateran, 6 Ides of May [10 May].)

Although the general care of all churches rests upon us, since we have been established as watchmen over [Col. 0343B] the house of the Lord, we are nevertheless bound to assist especially those which are special daughters of the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, your church is answerable to us without any intermediary, and since we wish to provide for you with paternal solicitude, we strictly forbid anyone, without authority from the Apostolic See, to dare pronounce sentences of excommunication or interdict against you or your church, except perhaps on account of another benefice or because of an offence committed elsewhere. Yet even in that case no one shall presume to pronounce such sentences against you without a manifest and reasonable cause. If anyone presumes to pronounce them otherwise, we decree them void in the first case and to be annulled in the second. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Ides of May [10 May].

LXII. TO . . . THE ARCHDEACON, . . . THE ARCHPRIEST, AND THE ENTIRE CHAPTER OF THE GARGANIC CHURCH. [Note: [Col. 0343D] See Book V, letter 43.] He confirms the ancient customs of their church. (Lateran, 6 Ides of May [10 May].)

[Col. 0343C]

“By the administration of the office entrusted to us we are compelled,” etc., down to “we may seem to strive.” For on your behalf a humble request was formerly made to us that, concerning the dignities of your church—namely the customary parish, feasts, archdeaconry, and archpriesthood—and canonical nomination and presentation, together with the other ancient and reasonable customs of your church, we should deem it fitting to provide the aid of apostolic protection, lest you might be unjustly harassed by anyone concerning these matters. Therefore, wishing henceforth to provide for you in these matters with paternal solicitude, by the authority of the present letters we strictly forbid anyone to be permitted improperly to trouble you or the church itself concerning the aforesaid dignities and the honourable customs [Col. 0344A] hitherto observed. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Ides of May [10 May].

LXIII. [Note: [Col. 0343D] Commended by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §70. See also *Gesta Innocentii*, §68.] TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF BEKEKEG. He receives them under protection. (Lateran, 12 Kalends of June [21 May].)

“Whenever a request is made to us,” etc., down to: “assenting, we receive under protection your persons and the hospital of Bekekeg, granted by its founders A. of Raze and his wife H. in pious liberality to the Hospital of the Teutons of Saint Mary in Jerusalem, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all that you presently possess,” etc., in the form of protection, down to “we strengthen.” As a token of this protection obtained from us, you shall pay yearly to us and our successors fifty-one denarii of Trisac coinage, freely offered. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of June [21 May].

LXIV. [Note: [Col. 0343D] See Raynaldus under the year 1204, §77.] TO . . . THE BISHOP OF MANTUA. [Note: [Col. 0343D] Henry was appointed to the see of Mantua in 1194. He presided until 1227, at least until 1220. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 933.] That he may receive, in the pope’s name, the lands of Countess Matilda situated in his diocese. (Lateran, 2 Ides of May [14 May].)

Having experienced your faith and devotion in many matters, by the authority of these presents we grant you leave to receive in our name the lands which belonged to Countess Matilda of blessed memory, situated in your diocese or adjoining your bishopric; to enter into possession [Col. 0344C] of them; and to receive their revenues, as you judge expedient.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of May [14 May].

LXV. TO . . . THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 0344D] See Book V, letter 96, note.] AND CONVENT OF SILVA MAJOR. He receives them under protection. (Lateran, 11 Kalends of June [22 May].)

“Just requests,” etc., down to “assent”: we receive under protection your persons and monastery, together with all goods which you presently possess, etc., down to “we strengthen.” Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of June [22 May].

LXVI. [Note: [Col. 0344D] It is found, but mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book III, title 31, “On Regulars and Those Entering Religion,” chapter 20, where it is said to be addressed to the abbot of Affligem and to Masters R. and G., canons of Utrecht. Material there printed is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO THE ABBOT OF AFFLIGEM, AND TO MASTERS R., PERSON OF THE CHURCH OF TENIS, AND GILBERT, CANON OF UTRECHT. That they investigate W., dean of Utrecht, who had passed from the regular life to the secular. (Lateran, Ides of May [15 May].)

[Col. 0344D]

[We have often been consulted by many whether one who [Col. 0345A] has entered a monastery by taking the novice’s habit [Note: [Col. 0345D] In the *Decretals*: “by receiving.”], if before making profession he wishes to leave during the period of probation, may lawfully do so without the stigma or penalty of apostasy, especially when, after the due correction of his conduct, he returns to the world. Although different persons have held different views on this question, we think a distinction must be made: whether he has resolved absolutely to change his manner of life, so that henceforth under the religious habit he may serve Almighty God; or whether he has conditionally resolved to test regular observance, so that only if [Note: [Col. 0345D] The *Decretal* adds: “within a year.”] it pleases him shall he profess the discipline of the order, but, if perchance it does not please him, he may return, with reformed conduct, to his former state. In the first case he must, in order to live religiously, transfer at least to a less strict rule. In the second he may return to the world, [Col. 0345B] though not in order to live a secular life. Therefore, so that his intention may be more fully known, at the beginning he should formally declare his purpose.]

Accordingly, after carefully weighing this distinction, diligently investigate regarding the beloved son W., dean of Utrecht, whatever you see ought to be investigated, and canonically determine whatever you know ought to be determined, causing, etc. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.
