Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of May [15 May].

LXVII. [Note: [Col. 0345D] Commended by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §70. See also *Gesta Innocentii*, §68.] TO . . . THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO, AND . . . THE BISHOPS OF BURGOS AND ZAMORA. He commands them to absolve B., daughter of the king of Castile, who had left the king of León and sought the benefit of absolution. (Lateran, 11 Kalends of June [22 May].)

[Col. 0345C]

Since we hold on earth, although unworthy, the place of him who does not desire the death of the sinner but that he should be converted and live, and who, even when angry, does not forget to show mercy, it is fitting for us to deal mercifully with those who humbly desire to return to the bosom of Mother Church and to render due satisfaction for their offences. Although the noblewoman B., daughter of our most beloved son in Christ . . . the illustrious king of Castile, grievously offended her Creator by presuming to join herself incestuously to the illustrious king of León, and for this deserved to be bound by the bond of excommunication, yet, since, as we have learned from your letters, brother Archbishop [Col. 0345D] and Bishop of Burgos, returning to her right mind, she has wholly withdrawn from him and promises to render due satisfaction for her offence, humbly requesting that the benefit of absolution [Col. 0346A] be granted her, we have judged that her petition should mercifully be granted.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your fraternity that, after receiving publicly and solemnly from her, in the form prescribed by the Church, sworn security that she will obey our commands, you shall take care, by our authority, to grant her the benefit of absolution. You shall impose upon her, under oath and without prejudice to other commands which we have judged should be given her, that she shall in no way return to the aforesaid king. But if not all . . . two, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of June [22 May].

LXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0345D] A fragment of this letter is found among the *Decretals*, Book I, title 28, “On Appeals, Recusations, and Referrals,” chapter 48. Material there printed is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO . . . THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0345D] Giles [alternatively Gilda], son of William de Breus, was elected bishop of Hereford in 1199 and consecrated in 1200. In 1208, when by papal order the general sentence of interdict was promulgated in England, he went into France, freely choosing exile, together with Eustace of Ely, William of London, and Mauger of Worcester, bishops. Afterward, having returned, in 1214 he blessed Hugh, prior of Tewkesbury, elected abbot of that house, in Worcester church, by command of W., bishop of Worcester. See Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, pp. 304, 479, 480, 482, and 654.], THE DEAN, AND . . . THE PRECENTOR OF HEREFORD. That they investigate the case of John, master of the hospital of York. (Lateran, 2 Ides of May [14 May].)

[Col. 0346B]

[The beloved son John, [Note: [Col. 0346D] The *Decretals* omit these words.] master of the hospital of York, informed us] that, when P., formerly rector of that hospital, had ended his last day, our venerable brother . . . Archbishop of York—because from ancient times the appointment of that hospital belonged to him and his predecessors, and because he was unwilling that it should suffer loss through the absence of a rector—appointed there the said John, a priest of that house, unanimously chosen as rector by his brethren, hoping that through him the house would prosper in both temporal and spiritual affairs.

As time passed, however, . . . [Col. 0346C] the dean and chapter of the Church of York, claiming that the appointment of that hospital belonged to them, sought to remove the master himself from his administrative office. On this matter they procured apostolic letters addressed to . . . the dean of Lincoln and his fellow judges, by whose authority they caused both the archbishop and the rector to be summoned to court. When the parties had appeared before those judges on the peremptory day assigned, the judges delegated their functions to others, reserving only the final judgment to themselves.

[Furthermore, the chapter of York appointed a certain person as plaintiff by authority of certain letters whose seal contained the seal of the chapter only for citations, although that chapter is known to possess another seal. [Note: [Col. 0346D] “A chapter possesses a seal, and the chapter’s seal is authentic—that is, it carries evidentiary authority without the subscription of witnesses. A chapter very often uses two seals, a greater and a lesser; but faith is not given in other matters to a seal established for certain acts, such as citations, as here.” Alteser, note on the cited place.] Yet although the opposing party alleged that, on the basis of those letters, the same plaintiff ought not to be admitted, and [Col. 0347A] further added that, by authority of certain letters obtained from us on this matter and addressed to our venerable brother . . . bishop of Ely and his fellow judges [Note: [Col. 0347D] The *Decretals* read “other judges” in place of “our venerable brother . . . bishop of Ely and his fellow judges”; and below, “summoned” for “was summoned,” etc.], it had been summoned earlier and therefore ought not to be summoned by later letters which made no mention of the earlier ones, the judges nevertheless refused to admit such exceptions. Therefore that same party [Note: [Col. 0347D] The *Decretals* read “on account of which” for “therefore that same party,” and below omit “to your discretion . . . by letters” and “and inquire . . . truth.”] lodged an appeal to us.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to investigate the truth of the foregoing diligently; and, if it becomes clear to you that appeal was made to our judgment for the aforesaid reasons or any one of them, after annulling whatever you find was attempted after the appeal lawfully lodged with us [Note: [Col. 0347D] The *Decretals* read: “you shall know that such an act has been done.”], summon the parties] into your [Col. 0347B] presence and diligently hear, with the appeal set aside, what they may choose to allege on either side. If the parties agree, proceed to a definitive sentence; otherwise, faithfully commit everything to writing and take care to send it to us, enclosed under your seals, setting the parties a suitable term within which they shall appear in our presence with the documents, there to receive judgment. Notwithstanding any letters whose tenor does not mention these letters, etc. But if not all . . . you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of May [14 May].

LXIX. TO THE SAME PERSONS. On the same subject as Letter 68. (Lateran, 13 Kalends of June [20 May].)

[Col. 0347C]

The beloved sons, the brethren and sisters of the hospital of York, informed us that, while a dispute was being conducted before the beloved son . . . dean of Lincoln and his fellow judges delegated by us, between our venerable brother the Archbishop of York and J., rector of the hospital, on the one side, and . . . the dean and chapter of York on the other, concerning the removal of that rector, they appealed to our hearing. They did so lest that same J., whom they had unanimously chosen as rector, should be removed to their prejudice and detriment, and lest anyone in secular dress should, against their will and protest, usurp administration of their house through the said dean and chapter, since appeal was not prohibited concerning matters not mentioned in our letters.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to inquire diligently into the truth of the foregoing. If you find that the matter stands thus, annul whatever you find was attempted after the appeal lawfully lodged with us; summon the parties into your presence; and diligently hear, with the appeal set aside, what they may choose to allege on either side. If the parties agree, pronounce a [Col. 0348A] definitive sentence; otherwise, faithfully commit all proceedings to writing and take care to send them to us enclosed under your seals, setting the parties a suitable term within which they shall appear in our presence with the documents, there to receive judgment. Notwithstanding any letters whose tenor does not mention these letters, etc. But if not all . . . you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of June [20 May].

LXX. TO THE PROVOST [Note: [Col. 0348D] In Conti’s copy “Prior” is read, but the context of the letter itself makes it clear that “Provost” must be read. On the provost of Saint Gereon, see Book V, letter 71, note.] AND CANONS OF SAINT GEREON AT COLOGNE. That they confirm for Ricc., the pope’s scribe, a prebend in accordance with the apostolic mandate. (Lateran, 5 Nones of May [3 May].)

[Col. 0348B]

Even if we had asked a weighty thing of you, we did not think that we would suffer a refusal. But, as we see, you have not avoided the vice of ingratitude, nor were you willing to make a virtue of necessity when you rejected the first of our requests, which we made to you for our beloved son Master Ricc., our scribe. Moreover, in order somehow to evade both our request and our command, you invoked an imperial privilege, to the disparagement of ecclesiastical authority. If that privilege were perhaps deferred to in this matter, others would thereafter take offence, and the execution of our mandate would be entirely impeded; thus the condition of rebels would be better than that of the devoted.

Certainly, when formerly we sent you apostolic letters on behalf of our same scribe, directing you freely to confer upon him, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, one of the three prebends vacant in your church [Col. 0348C], you let our command pass by deaf ears and took no care to fulfil it. You also wholly disregarded the requests and admonitions of our venerable brother G. [Note: [Col. 0348D] He has already been mentioned several times.] bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, to whom for this purpose we entrusted our authority and whom we ordered by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce you to do this. After diligently warning you, he made no progress at all. Finally, he learned that you wished, in evasion of our command, to proceed to an election—for you had frequently assembled for that purpose, though your votes had not yet converged upon one candidate. On our behalf he strictly forbade you to presume to make any election to the prebends whose presentation had devolved upon us, unless you received the master himself as canon and brother in whichever one of those three prebends you preferred. The same master also appealed to the Apostolic See, lest anything should be done to his prejudice and in contempt of our mandate.

But you, asserting that you possessed the right of election from the emperors and ought not on this account to be hindered or compelled by anyone, and denying that any right in your church accrued to us by reason of the long vacancy [Col. 0349A] of the prebends, disregarded our mandate, the legate’s prohibition, and that master’s appeal. You elected two boys to two of those prebends and a certain outsider to the third. After the repeated appeal of the same master, you, son Provost, bestowed upon them the gift of bread, and you, son Dean [Note: [Col. 0349D] Gerard, dean of Saint Gereon, is found in a document of 1202, in Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 643.], bestowed a choir stall and a place in chapter.

For this reason the aforesaid legate, finding your rebellion manifested in deed and taking grievously that he had been contemned in person, assembled together our venerable brother . . . Archbishop [Note: [Col. 0349D] Book III, letter 54, note 187.] and almost the entire clergy of Cologne, and by apostolic authority invested the same master with the prebend which had remained vacant longest in that church. Although many among the clergy were greatly displeased by what you had presumed, nevertheless II., your scholasticus, and Everard, your canon, always resisted obstinately and, with certain supporters, threatened him. Therefore, because the said master could not approach that church for fear of them, he specifically appealed to the Apostolic See against the said Scholasticus and Everard, who were especially the leaders of the rebels. He set the most recently past feast of Saint John the Baptist as the term of his appeal; they neither came on that date nor took care to send a representative on their behalf.

Wishing, therefore, still to test whether any spark of obedience remains in you, by apostolic letters we command and strictly order your entire body that, guided by sounder counsel, [Col. 0349C] you shall receive our same scribe as a canon and brother—at least on this occasion, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, and also in consideration of the man himself, who may be of great benefit to you and your church. You shall assign to him, or to his procurator in his name, the prebend conferred upon him by the aforesaid bishop under our authority, after removing from it every unlawful holder; you shall remove every obstacle of contradiction, excuse, and appeal; and you shall cause him peacefully to possess it. And you, Provost and Dean, shall confer upon him, according to the custom of your church, the gift of bread, a stall in choir, and a place in chapter.

Otherwise, because we do not wish to leave unfinished what we have begun concerning him, and cannot—and ought not—pass with closed eyes over matters rashly attempted in contempt of us, you are to know that by apostolic authority we have annulled the election made by you, after the prohibition of the aforesaid legate and the appeal lodged with us, to prebends that had been vacant beyond the period determined in the Lateran Council; and that you are suspended from conferring prebends, because he who abuses authority granted to him deserves to lose his privilege. Furthermore, lest ease of pardon produce an incentive to wrongdoing—for wounds which do not feel the remedy of poultices must be cut away with iron—we will and command that you, son Provost, together with the aforesaid Scholasticus and Everard, your fellow canons, appear in our presence by the approaching feast of Saint Luke, to make satisfaction for the contempt. If not even thus does affliction give you understanding, know that from then on you will be bound by the bond of excommunication as opponents and rebels, and that your church will be subjected to interdict.

[Col. 0350B] For we command by our letters the beloved sons . . . the provost of Saint Andrew [Note: [Col. 0349D] Theodoric, provost of Saint Andrew, is found in a document of 1202, in Hontheim, cited place.], . . . the provost of Bonn [Note: [Col. 0349D] See Book V, cited place.], and . . . the dean of Saints Apostles [Note: [Col. 0349D] Yvo, dean of Saints Apostles, is found in 1202 in Hontheim, cited place.], all of Cologne, that, should you fail to execute our mandate, they shall not delay to publish the sentences both of suspension and of excommunication and interdict, and, after bodily inducting the procurator of the aforesaid master into the choir stall and place in chapter, shall by the aforesaid coercive measures protect him in his induction, by our authority and with every impediment of appeal removed. We also command the priors of Cologne that, when our delegates decide that the sentences pronounced by us against you and your church are to be published, they too shall endeavour to observe them without opposition and shall cause them to be firmly observed by the clergy of Cologne under our authority.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Nones of May [3 May].

On this matter letters were written to . . . the provost of Saint Andrew, etc.; . . . the provost of Bonn; and the dean of Saints Apostles at Cologne.

Letters were also written to the priors of Cologne.

LXXI. TO . . . THE ABBOT OF WERDEN, IN THE DIOCESE OF COLOGNE, [Note: [Col. 0349D] Heribert II of Buren, abbot of the monastery of Werden—also called Werth, Werda, or Werdena—was present at Aachen in 1198, together with Theodoric, bishop of Utrecht, and Thiedmar of Minden, at the coronation of Otto, king of the Romans. In the following year the monastery of Saint Liudger at Helmstedt was destroyed by fire. On 15 January 1204, Innocent III granted Heribert a bull concerning the use of pontifical insignia, issued at Anagni in the sixth year of his pontificate; we do not, however, find it in the Registers. He is said to have died about 1230. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 729.] AND TO . . . THE PROVOST OF BONN, [Note: [Col. 0350D] Book V, letter 71, note.] ETC., AND . . . THE PROVOST OF SAINT CUNIBERT, [Note: [Col. 0350D] Theodoric, provost of Saint Cunibert, is found in a document of 1202, in Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 643.] AT COLOGNE. He entrusts to them the examination of the election of the bishop of Münster. (Lateran, 5 Kalends of June [28 May].)

From the letters of our venerable brother G. [Note: [Col. 0350D] He has already been mentioned several times.], … [Col. 0350D] bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, and of our beloved sons … provost, … dean, and, it is asserted, the greater part of the canons of the church of Münster, as well as certain abbots, we have received word [Col. 0351A] that, when the bishop of Münster of good memory [Note: [Col. 0351D] We do not venture to determine with certainty who was the bishop of Münster referred to here. BUCELLINUS, *Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 27, reports that Godelscalc the Saxon, of humble birth but distinguished by virtues—whom he places after Louis, count of Tecklenburg, known in 1190 and highly deserving of his church—died in 1200. Immediately afterwards the same author mentions Hermann, count of Katzenelnbogen, commonly called Ter, as Bucellinus says, on account of his remarkable benevolence toward all; he followed the emperor into Italy, was the first to obtain the title of prince and the power of the secular sword, and did not die, according to Bucellinus, before 1246. Yet in an instrument which HONTHEIMIUS reports as authentic and of unquestioned reliability, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 612, no. 435, Hermann, bishop of Münster, is expressly named and signs as early as 1182; and in another diploma in the same author, ibid., p. 657, no. 456, Theodoric, bishop of Münster, is found in 1220.] had happily completed the days of his life in the office of administration entrusted to him, the canons of that church assembled, at the appointed time, to elect a bishop to succeed him. One group nominated our beloved son, … provost of Bremen; another, the provost of Claholt. Hence an appeal was made on behalf of the provost of Bremen to the hearing of that same legate.

When, therefore, the parties had appeared before him, the electors of the aforesaid provost of Bremen presented their elect to him and took care to allege that the … provost, etc., … dean, together with the other prelates of their church, and a twofold greater and sounder part of the chapter of Münster, with the consent of the abbots throughout the bishopric, [Col. 0351B] had unanimously elected him in chapter as their pastor. They asserted that the provost of Bremen had been elected by the greater part of the chapter—indeed, by twice as many, or even many more—and by the prelates of the Church, namely the chief provost, dean, cantor, and custodian, while no prelate supported the other party; also by the senior members of the church, since all the electors on his side, except one, preceded all the electors of the other party in admission and stall; and likewise by the sounder part of the chapter, because he was elected upon the counsel of the abbots of the whole bishopric, who gave this counsel on your soul, and upon the judgment of their consciences, looking solely to the advantage of the church of Münster, while fasting in a suitable place, with good zeal in every respect and with every partiality arising from kinship [Col. 0351C] and familiarity removed.

They further alleged that the said provost of Claholt had not been elected by the prelates; rather, a few canons, joined to him by close familiarity and kinship, improperly nominated him after dinner in an unsuitable place, namely outside the city, after an appeal had been lodged with the aforesaid legate. The electors of the provost of Bremen therefore urgently requested that, after the election of the other party had been annulled, the legate should confirm their election by apostolic authority.

Moreover, our beloved sons, the envoys of that same provost of Bremen, firmly affirmed before us that the provost of Claholt had not been born of a lawful marriage, and that this was well known in his region.

Although the other party, when it first appeared before the legate, had alleged that an unlawful compromise had been made between ministeriales and canons; that the canons possessing the right of election had been disregarded; that even the consent of the advocate, and of certain other nobles and religious men, [Col. 0352A] had not been sought as it ought to have been; and that the ministeriales and citizens of Münster had caused the gates of their city to be shut [Note: [Col. 0352D] Thus in the copy.], and its towers to be garrisoned when the election was to take place, wherefore that party, together with certain nobles, had been compelled to move to another place and had there proceeded to an election—nevertheless, it advanced nothing in support of its election or its elect, but urgently requested a delay. The adverse party replied that a delay of eighteen weeks had already been granted to it, and therefore its request for the further delay it sought should be rejected, especially since the church of Münster faced grave danger from the vacancy of its pastoral office.

The aforesaid bishop, having heard what had been alleged before him, because [Col. 0352B] he could not settle the affair owing to difficult matters entrusted to him by us, and lest the parties be wearied by futile labor and expense, ordered them to appear before us on the Sunday called *Invocavit*, just past.

Therefore, although the envoys of the aforesaid provost of Bremen appeared before us with letters from the same legate, since no representative appeared for the other party and consequently full proof of the foregoing could not be made to us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having more fully investigated the truth, you confirm, with the obstacle of appeal removed, the election which you find to have been canonically made of a suitable person, rejecting all the rest entirely and restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure. But if both elections must be rejected, annul both, and cause provision to be made for that church within fifteen days through the canonical election of a suitable person. If perchance the canons of Münster neglect to hold the election within that same period, then, supported by our authority, appoint a suitable man as pastor of that church.

Thus, if it is established to you that the said provost of Claholt was illegitimately born, since it was decreed at the Lateran Council that no one be elected bishop unless he has completed his thirtieth year, has been born of lawful marriage, and is shown commendable in life and learning; and that clerics who elect anyone contrary to this rule are to know themselves deprived at that time of the power of election and suspended from ecclesiastical benefices for three years—then, before all else, declare that election not merely to be annulled but void, [Col. 0352D] and, with the obstacle of appeal removed, punish with the aforementioned penalty the clerics who presumed to elect him. Accordingly, if a new election must perhaps [Col. 0353A] be held, exclude those who proceeded to election contrary to the decree of the Lateran Council, and order the rest not to delay holding the election according to the prescribed form. But if not all … two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of June [28 May].

LXXII. … TO THE BISHOP OF ZAMORA. Concerning the case of a boy seeking promotion to sacred orders, although he was involved in the death of a man. (Lateran, 12 Kalends of June.)

You have informed us that, when a certain boy struck a dog, another boy, whose dog it was, struck in the face with his hand [Col. 0353B] the boy who had struck his dog. But when the latter seized a stick to strike back the one by whom he had himself been struck, and both held the stick, one at each end, the father of the boy who had struck the dog came upon them in order to punish his son. The boys fled, letting go of the stick they held between them; and when they had already moved some distance away from that place, the aforesaid father of one of them fell upon that stick in such a way that, by an unforeseen accident, it entered through one eye; his brain immediately came out, and he died.

Afterwards the boy who had struck the dog assumed the religious habit, and when he came forward to receive orders, the question of this deed arose through his own confession and that of many others. It caused you such doubt [Col. 0353C] that you sought our advice whether, this deed not standing in the way, he could be promoted to sacred orders. We therefore reply to your brotherhood that, from the foregoing, we do not believe that the boy was so culpable that his ordination ought by law to be impeded.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of June [21 May].

LXXIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF SAINT CECILIA. He confirms by apostolic authority the judgment rendered in their favor in the case between them and the archpriest of the church of Saint Lawrence at Pusciola. (Lateran, 6 Kalends of June.)

When formerly a dispute was pending between you and M., archpriest of the church [Col. 0353D] of Saint Lawrence at Pusciola, concerning the subjection which you claimed in that church, after hearing what was presented on both sides, we condemned the economus of that church in favor of your syndic [Note: [Col. 0353D] Thus in the Conti copy.] [Col. 0354A] in processions, scrutiny, and baptism, provided nevertheless that this should cause no prejudice to the Roman Church should it at any time undertake to pursue its right.

But in matters of appointment, removal, and chapter, we entirely absolved the economus of that church of Saint Lawrence from the claim of your syndic, imposing perpetual silence upon the syndic in this matter. Because the archpriest and clerics of that church sometimes did not obey the judgment rendered, lest they henceforth derive profit from their rebellion, we pronounce a sentence of suspension against the rebels, granting you by authority of these presents that, whenever they deny you the service due in scrutiny, baptism, and processions, you shall publish against them the sentence of suspension pronounced by us. Therefore let no one [Col. 0354B], etc. Let no one violate this page of our concession, etc. But if anyone does so, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of June [27 May].

LXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0353D] See book VI, epistle 240.] … TO THE ELECT OF GRADO. [Note: [Col. 0353D] UGHELLUS, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 1209, reports the following concerning the patriarch of Grado then holding office: “XL. Benedict Falier, formerly primicerius of Saint Mark’s, was elected patriarch of Grado with the consent of all the clergy, and received the pallium and blessing from Innocent after 1201; he died in the final years of the same pontiff. He was a man endowed with nobility of birth and exceptional piety.” Thus far Ughellus. He is correct in asserting that Benedict was raised from the primiceriusship of Saint Mark’s to the patriarchate of Grado, for Marin Sanudo expressly affirms this, *Lives of the Doges of Venice*, vol. XXII of *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, col. 528. He is also correct, if one wishes, in adding that Benedict received the pallium and blessing from Innocent only after 1201, for this is confirmed by Innocent’s letter. Whether he is likewise correct in suggesting that Benedict was raised to the patriarchate only after 1201, we do not know. Andrea Dandolo’s *Chronicle* appears to assign his election to the eighth year of the dogeship of Henry Dandolo, that is, to the year 1200 of the Lord’s Incarnation. See MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. XII, col. 319.] A threatening letter, because he had delayed seeking consecration and the pallium, and on account of the wrongdoing of the Venetians. (Lateran, Kalends of June.)

Although, apart from the fault of your negligence—for you delayed, contrary to canonical enactments, to seek the benefit of consecration and the ornament of the pallium—we could deservedly, on account also of the wrongdoing of the Venetians, which they have rashly committed against God, [Col. 0354C] the Roman Church, our dearest son in Christ … the illustrious king of Hungary, and indeed the whole Christian people, and which they do not yet cease to commit against Christians, not only defer your consecration but deprive you of hope of promotion, to say nothing of your personal merits; nevertheless, because we desire with paternal affection the correction of the Venetians, we have decided for the present to make no other disposition concerning you than that you remain in the condition which you have obtained alike through your election and confirmation, until we decide otherwise.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of June [1 June].

LXXV. [Note: [Col. 0355D] This letter is cited by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §57. Angelus Manrique published it in full, *Annales Cistercienses*, for the year 1204, chapter IV, §2, vol. III, p. 404, but not without errors and with certain omissions. For greater accuracy, we have noted all these in the margin.] … TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX [Note: [Col. 0355D] Book V, epistle 16, note.], AND TO P. AND R., MONKS OF FONTFROIDE, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That they are to investigate the archbishop of Narbonne, notorious for many vices and accusations. (Lateran, 5 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0355A]

“Because every head is sick and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no soundness in it,” as the prophetic voice testifies, it is no wonder that when the head is sick the members languish, and that the corruption of prelates is transmitted to their subjects. This is especially so when dumb dogs, unable to bark, return to their vomit or embrace what they ought to have vomited up, and shepherds, feeding themselves rather than their flocks, drive away neither by voice nor by staff the wolves raging in the Lord’s sheepfold. [Col. 0355B]

Indeed, if a priest sins, he causes the people to sin; and when the priest becomes like the people, once the shepherd has been struck both in mind and tongue, the little sheep are scattered and perish. Having no teacher in what is good, they turn aside to the doctrines of seducers and become the prey of those who lie in wait. For, as has been reported to us, … [Note: [Col. 0355D] See book VI, epistle 81, note.] the archbishop of Narbonne has been so remiss in the discharge of the pontifical office that he seems, not without reason, like a barren tree, to occupy the ground uselessly. He has held the church of Narbonne in occupation for thirteen years and has not even once visited either the province or diocese of Narbonne.

Accordingly, because there is no one to set himself as a wall for the house of the Lord against those coming up from the adversary, the negligence of that archbishop [Col. 0355C] has caused heretical depravity to spring up exceedingly in those regions. Heretics teach everywhere and publicly and deceive the unwary. They draw people after them all the more easily because, from the life of the archbishop himself and of other prelates of the Church, they derive a more pernicious argument against the Church and impute the crimes of some persons to the Church as a whole.

For that archbishop, as though he had not rightly observed what sort of man a bishop ought to show himself, neglecting the dignity of the pontifical office, has almost turned to idolatry, while he serves greed rather than doctrine. He presumes to teach that Simony is not a heresy—a view which he himself would not hold if he understood what the canons teach on this subject.

Moreover, since it was decreed in the Lateran Council that those who presume to hire or support Brabançons, Aragonese, Navarrese, Basques [Note: [Col. 0355D] Thus in the copy; Manrique has “Barellos.”], and Cotarelli are to be publicly announced as excommunicate in the churches on Sundays [Col. 0356A] and other solemn days, and are to be subject to the same sentence and penalty with them and not received into communion with the Church unless they renounce that most evil association and heresy: the archbishop himself does not merely fail to avoid such persons, but has installed Nicholas, leader of the Aragonese and ravager of the country, an almost continual destroyer of monasteries and churches—whom the archbishop’s predecessor of good memory … publicly declared excommunicate—as steward in his two castles, namely Capestang and Cruzy, where he has newly established a toll. In the archbishop’s presence, Nicholas did not fear to bring to one of those castles the booty which he had taken from a certain castle of Catholics.

And although, [Col. 0356B] [Note: [Col. 0355D] Manrique has: “Moreover, since…”] according to the Apostle’s word, a bishop ought to be hospitable, he offers no hospitality and gives no alms; though physically healthy, he often does not go to church for one or two weeks, and is consequently considered a heretic by some. Furthermore, although the churches of Capestang and Montell. have long been vacant, he retains them in his own hand contrary to canonical enactments. Before consecrating …, formerly bishop of Elne [Note: [Col. 0355D] He was probably Artaldus, whom we know to have borne the episcopal insignia of Elne from about 1198 to 1201. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 1050.], he extorted from him the church of Jessous, which he still holds in occupation [Note: [Col. 0356D] These words are absent in Manrique.].

Likewise, before conferring the gift of consecration upon …, formerly bishop of Maguelonne [Note: [Col. 0356D] Book III, epistle 24, note.], he demanded and received four hundred solidi, as the canons of Maguelonne were prepared to prove before our venerable brother … [Note: [Col. 0356D] Raymond of Peyreles, provost of Marseille, occurs in documents from 1180 to 1201; *Gallia Christiana*, old edition, vol. III, p. 675. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 431, recognize Raymond as bishop of Fréjus from at least 1203, but hold that he was raised to the episcopate from some religious order; how this can be reconciled with this letter of Innocent, we do not know.] then provost of Marseille, [Col. 0356C] now bishop of Fréjus.

Moreover, although there were formerly eighteen canons in the church of Narbonne, their number has now, through the negligence—or rather malice—of the aforementioned archbishop, been reduced by half. There are now only nine canons, three of whom, although they hold their dignities elsewhere, nevertheless presume to retain prebends there, to the detriment of the Church, which suffers an extreme lack of ministers.

The archbishop so shows himself negligent in spiritual affairs, though careful in temporal matters, that he not only does not forbid but permits Berengarius of Morian [Note: [Col. 0356D] Manrique has “Monan.”], although a canon regular—indeed, for two years now prelate of regular canons as their abbot—also to hold the archdeaconry and both the position and revenues of the vestry in the church of Narbonne, as well as four or five parish churches and the canonry of Béziers [Note: [Col. 0356D] Manrique has “the canonry of Béziers.”]. Likewise, [Col. 0357A] Master P. [Note: [Col. 0357D] The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 146, identify him from documents as Peter III, abbot of Saint-Paul of Narbonne from 1204 to 1221. The necrology cited by the same authors agrees: “In the year 1221, Master Peter, abbot of Saint Paul and archdeacon, died,” etc.] is abbot in the church of Saint Paul and holds the greater sacristy there, yet he holds the archdeaconry of Narbonne; and although by reason of his abbacy he ought to be a priest, he has not yet been ordained priest.

And though a full year has passed since Master B. …, formerly archdeacon of Narbonne, entered the way of all flesh, no archdeaconry formerly held by him has yet been bestowed. W. of Boian also holds a canonry at Narbonne, although he openly keeps a concubine by whom, with the people’s knowledge, he has begotten sons and daughters; and though he holds the archdeaconry of Béziers, he has not yet been promoted even to the subdiaconate [Note: [Col. 0357D] These words are absent in Manrique.].

The members derive such corruption from the infirmity of the head that many monks, [Col. 0357B] regular canons, and other religious men, having cast off the religious habit, openly keep concubines—some of whom they have taken from their husbands’ embraces—practise usury, devote themselves to dice and hunting, serve as advocates, assessors, and judges in secular cases for a fixed sum of money, assume the roles of entertainers, and usurp the office of physicians.

This example of destruction also passes down to laypeople. Many, while their own wives are alive, take adulteresses in addition, whom certain ecclesiastical persons are not ashamed to receive into processions, to the scandal of the people and the derision of heretics. Very many [Note: [Col. 0357D] Manrique has: “nor, what is worse…”] prelates do not fear to entrust their churches to supporters of heretics.

Therefore, because we neither wish nor ought to overlook such outrageous and enormous offenses, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters [Note: [Col. 0357D] These words are absent in Manrique.] that, when you come to the church of Narbonne, you investigate fully the truth concerning these matters and others requiring investigation. If the foregoing, or any of the aforesaid matters for which the archbishop ought deservedly to be deposed, is established to you, then lay the axe to the root of the unfruitful tree and, supported by our authority, depose him with the obstacle of appeal removed. Order those to whom the right of election belongs to elect, upon your advice, a suitable person as their pastor. If they should perhaps refuse to follow your advice within a month, then, keeping God before your [Col. 0357D] eyes, appoint to the church of Narbonne, notwithstanding their opposition or [Note: [Col. 0358D] These words are absent in Mansique.] appeal, such a person as may wholeheartedly become a model for the flock, instructing the lives of his subjects by word and example, and knowing not so much how to preside as how to be of service. But if not all … two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of June [28 May], in the seventh year.

LXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0358D]

Cited in BZOVIUS, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 121, §22. See also Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §57.

Published in full by Angelus Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, for the year 1204, chapter 2, §6, vol. III, p. 418; but, as we have already noted concerning the immediately preceding letter, not without certain errors and certain omissions.]

… TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX [Note: [Col. 0358D] See the notes to the preceding letter, no. 75.], AND TO THE MONKS OF FONTFROIDE, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That they are to proceed against heretics. (Lateran, 2 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0358A]

Although the little boat of our Fisherman is sometimes tossed by waves and shaken by blasts of wind when it suffers persecutions and afflictions from those outside, yet, confident in the protection of Him who raised Peter walking upon the waves lest he sink, and in the sure promise which says, “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16), it does not fear shipwreck outwardly; but inwardly it has greater fear of peril from false brethren.

For behold, the seamless garment of Christ, which the hands of those crucifying him spared, [Col. 0358B] is torn apart by those who crucify him anew in his members. Peter’s net is split not by the multitude but by the wickedness of the fish, while those who had been thought sheep turn into wolves and seize and scatter the sheep; those who went out from us because they were not of us persecute us all the more grievously because a familiar enemy does greater harm, and wolves are less avoided by sheep when clothed in sheep’s garments.

Behold, creeping things without number, which once, though they lay in wait for the heel in order to overthrow the rider along with the horse, nevertheless crept secretly and hid in the dust, now rise up openly and devise manifest snares. The little animals too, which, cherishing their dens, had been accustomed secretly to ravage the Lord’s vineyard, now openly burn God’s harvest with torches tied to their tails. And not like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding, but like a lion ready for prey, great beasts range about and seek whom they may devour, confident that the Jordan will flow into their mouths.

Behold, the grain which the evangelical householder sowed is choked by the growing tares which an enemy sowed over it; the caterpillar and locust consume what seemed to promise a hundredfold fruit; Dathan and Abiram shamelessly rise against Moses and Aaron; and sheep follow the tracks of other flocks, despising the one fold of the one shepherd and making separate tents for themselves. Although in this way the days of the Lord’s Passion seem in some measure to be renewed, as Herod and Pilate again unite in Christ’s death, Simon [Col. 0358D] nevertheless still sleeps, as though his eyes were heavy with sleep. He does not draw the sword against Malchus, but lets it remain idle in its sheath, while those whom he summoned to share his solicitude, that they might guard the people Israel, do not keep the watches of the night over their flock; they sleep and slumber instead, and keep their hands from blood, although in their sight [Col. 0359A] a man of Judah lies with a Midianite woman.

The shepherd also degenerates into a hireling when, feeding not the people but himself, he seeks milk and wool in the sheep. He neither confronts wolves invading the fold nor offers himself as a barrier or wall for the Lord’s house against those coming up from the adversary. But because the hireling has turned to flight when he could trouble the wicked and neglects to do so, he is convicted of favoring their iniquity. And when nearly all have turned aside and very many have become altogether useless, scarcely anyone remains who, with Moses, executes God’s cause by the sword among the people and pleads the people’s cause before God in prayers, or who, with Phinehas, appeases God with the blood of his neighbor and takes vengeance among the peoples.

Yet we rejoice, and render to the Giver of all good such thanksgivings as we can, because [Col. 0359B] in your Order many are found possessing zeal for God according to knowledge, powerful in deed and word, and ready to give an answer to everyone who asks concerning the faith and hope that are in us. We believe that charity is likewise strong in them, so that they would lay down their souls for their brethren if the necessity of the Church demanded it. They are so much the more fit to refute fabricators of perverse doctrines because an adversary can find less to reproach in them: they possess good testimony even from those outside, since in them the life of saints accords with sound doctrine. Their life no less gives life to doctrine, so that their word may indeed be living, effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, than doctrine forms their life, so that what is set forth in their words may be read in their conduct. [Col. 0359C]

Therefore, although you, sons R. and P., have undertaken to labor in response to our exhortation—to crush the head of creeping things, capture the little foxes, and restrain with bridle and bit the jaws of the raging wolf and roaring lion, lest they further tear Christ’s garment and rend the Church—and your labor has not been in vain, since the Lord has directed your steps, nevertheless, because the harvest is plentiful but the laborers few, we impose upon you, son Abbot, with the counsel of our brethren, the burden of this solicitude for the remission of your sins. By apostolic letters we command your discretion that all of you together proceed in the Lord’s name to uproot heretical depravity, so that you may bring wandering sheep back to Christ’s fold. If any perhaps persist in their obstinacy, refusing to hear the voice of that shepherd who succeeded blessed Peter in the pastoral office and refusing to return to ecclesiastical unity, publicly declare them delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh; declare their persons subject to exile and secular judgment, and their goods to confiscation.

Urge and enjoin more earnestly on our behalf both our dearest son in Christ, Ph., the illustrious king of France, and his son L., as well as [Col. 0360A] the counts, viscounts, and barons established in those regions, to confiscate their goods and banish their persons permanently, enjoining this upon them for the remission of all their sins. For we wish those who labor faithfully against heretics to enjoy the same indulgence that we grant to those who cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land.

So that you may exercise more effectively and freely the office of the legation imposed upon you—not so much by us as by God—we grant you full authority in the provinces of Aix, Arles, and Narbonne, and also in neighboring dioceses, if any are polluted by the stain of heretics, to destroy, scatter, and uproot what you know ought to be destroyed, scattered, and uprooted, and to build and plant what ought to be built and planted. Under threat of anathema, we forbid anyone to dare to extort anything for ecclesiastical sacraments [Col. 0360B] [Note: [Col. 0359D] See Bzovius and Raynaldus, cited above, letter 76.], intending canonically to punish those who presume to act contrary to your prohibition. If any incur the canon of an automatic sentence on account of violent laying on of hands, supported by our authority grant them the benefit of absolution, enjoining them to arm themselves against heretics.

If any difficulty should arise requiring the counsel of the Apostolic See, consult us about it by your letters. We desire and admonish you to proceed in such a way that your moderation, once known to all, may silence the ignorance of foolish men, and that nothing may appear in your words or acts which even a heretic could reproach. But if not all, etc. Two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Kalends of June [31 May], in the seventh year.

LXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0359D] See Bzovius and Raynaldus, cited above, letter 76.] It was written to the archbishops of … Aix, … Arles, and … Narbonne, and to their suffragans, and to abbots, priors, deans, archdeacons, and other prelates of churches established in their provinces—on the same subject as in the preceding letter.

Strictly commanding them in virtue of obedience that, giving powerful and effective assistance to the aforesaid … abbot and monks as legates of the Apostolic See, they humbly receive and take care inviolably to observe whatever those legates decide should be established among them, especially for the defense of the Catholic faith and the attack upon heretical depravity; and that they accept their correction without any contradiction. Otherwise, we shall regard as binding the sentence which they pronounce against rebels and, with the Lord as author, shall cause it to be inviolably observed.

LXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0359D]

See Raynaldus, cited above.

Angelus Manrique gives a fragment of the same letter in *Annales Cistercienses*, under the year 1204, chapter 4, § [Col. 0360D] 13, vol. III, p. 426; passages found there are enclosed here in brackets.]

… TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE [Note: [Col. 0360D] See book III, epistle 24, note; book VI, epistles 81 and 243; book VII, epistles 75, 76, and 77.]. He is deprived of the abbey of Montaragon, which had previously been entrusted to him, because of incompatibility. (Lateran, 4 Kalends of June.)

[Just as one found faithful in a few things deserved to be set [Col. 0361A] over many, so the servant who did not put out the talent entrusted to him with money-changers at interest, but tied it up in a napkin, was deprived of it by divine judgment. We say this of you: not considering when your lord will come and require from you a most strict accounting, you have tied up the talent entrusted to you so that it lies foul in a napkin; like a dumb dog unable to bark, you do not set yourself as a wall for the Lord’s house against those coming up from the adversary. But,] on account of the abbey of Montaragon, regarding which the Apostolic See formerly dispensed with you, you withhold the duty of the pastoral office alike from the church and province of Narbonne. While you seek to preside over both, as we say with grief, you benefit neither, since you can scarcely provide for one.

Long ago, wishing [Col. 0361B] to avert the disadvantages resulting from this, lest the Lord’s flock entrusted to you be exposed to wolves’ bites and heretical depravity spread further in the province of Narbonne, we ordered you [Note: [Col. 0361D] Book VI, epistle 81.] to abandon the abbey entirely and be content with the church of Narbonne, which you would be able to serve so much better as the care of the abbey drew you away less thereafter. Since you have not yet carried out the apostolic command, and carefully considering that one who abuses the power granted him deserves to lose his privilege, we ourselves deprive you of that abbey. We order the canons established there canonically to elect for themselves a suitable person as abbot. We also order our venerable brother … archbishop [Col. 0361C] of Tarragona that, unless they execute our command within a month, he himself appoint over them a suitable person who knows not so much how to preside over them as how to be of service to them.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of June [29 May], in the seventh year.

It was written to them on this matter.

LXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0361D]

This letter is cited by Bzovius, cited above.

Raynaldus supplies fragments of it under the year 1204, §64; passages found in his work are enclosed here in brackets [Col. 0362D].

Angelus Manrique published it in full, *Annales Cistercienses*, for the year 1204, chapter 2, §12, vol. III, p. 419.]

… TO THE KING OF FRANCE. That he is to assist the apostolic legates against heretics. (Lateran, 5 Kalends of June.)

[For the protection of His bride, that is, the universal Church, the Lord instituted pontifical and royal dignity: the one to nurture her children, the other to overcome her adversaries; the one to instruct the life of subjects by word and example, the other to restrain the jaws of the wicked with bit and bridle, lest they disturb the peace of the Church; the one to love enemies and even pray for persecutors, the other to wield the material sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, and to defend ecclesiastical tranquillity by arms. It is fitting, therefore, that spiritual authority and secular power, attending to the purpose of their institution, should come together as one for the Church’s defence, and that each should aid the other: so that those whom ecclesiastical discipline does not call back from evil, the secular arm may restrain; and that spiritual vengeance may follow those who, trusting in their own savagery, do not fear the material sword. Therefore, lest you seem to bear the sword without cause, you must take up arms and shield and rise powerfully to the aid of Him whose garment, as we report with grief, suffers a rent in the kingdom of France; whose vineyard is ravaged by the little foxes; and whose sheep are exposed to the assaults of wolves. [Col. 0362A]

[For ravening wolves in sheep’s clothing have entered that kingdom: they seize and scatter the sheep; and because they do not fear ecclesiastical discipline, being separated from the Church, they rage all the more freely in Christ’s sheepfold inasmuch as until now they have found no one to resist them temporally and to plead God’s cause against them with swords. We therefore admonish Your Royal Serenity, exhort you in the Lord, and, for the remission of sins, enjoin upon you that, either in person, if this can be done, or through our most beloved son in Christ, L., your son by birth, or another prudent man, you powerfully oppose their perversity; openly demonstrate how dearly you love ecclesiastical unity; and, by the power given you from heaven, compel both counts and barons to confiscate their goods and outlaw their persons. [Col. 0362A]

[Moreover, since one who ceases to oppose an open crime is not free from the taint of a secret partnership—so that an equal punishment may bind those who act and those who consent—if any counts, barons, or citizens refuse to expel them from their land, presume to receive them, or dare to support them, confiscate their goods and do not delay to annex their entire land to the royal domain.] [Col. 0362B]

Let Your Royal Highness likewise so assist our beloved sons, [lacuna] abbot of Cîteaux and P. and R., monks of Fontfroide, legates of the Apostolic See, whom we are sending specially for this purpose, that the material sword may be shown to supply the deficiency of the spiritual sword. And may you, besides the temporal glory which you will gain from so pious and praiseworthy a work, obtain that remission of sins which we grant to those who cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land. [Col. 0362C]

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

LXXX. [Note: [Col. 0362D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §81.] TO PETER OF PARIS, CHAPLAIN OVER LINCOLN BRIDGE. He receives him under the protection of Blessed Peter, with an annual payment of one bezant. (Lateran, Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0362D]

“Whenever a request is made to us,” etc., through “having inclined”: we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the chapel which W. of Paris, formerly your father, began to build, at his own expense, over the bridge of the city of Lincoln, which he himself constructed, in honour of Blessed Thomas the Martyr; and which you too propose to complete and to endow with possessions. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this present writing, the possessions which you or your aforesaid father have lawfully bestowed upon the same chapel, as it justly and peacefully possesses them. As a token of this protection received from the Apostolic See, the aforesaid chapel shall pay each year to us and to our successors one bezant, freely offered to us. Therefore let no one … violate this page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc. [Col. 0363A]

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of June.

LXXXI. [Note: [Col. 0363D] Cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §82.] TO THE CANONS OF COSENZA. That they should grant their consent to the exchange concerning the church of Botrano. [Note: [Col. 0364D] On the subject of this letter, see letter 220 of Book VI.] (Lateran, 4 June.)

[Col. 0363B]

Considering formerly that the planting of the new religious order, which Abbot Joachim of good memory—or rather God through his ministry—had planted and watered, mercifully granting it increase, was flourishing in flower; and lest the harshness of cold, which in those regions claims not only spring and autumn for itself but even assails the summer months, should freeze God’s flourishing vineyard, but rather that the flower might pass into a cluster and the cluster yield fruit of fragrance and worth, we commanded our venerable brother, your archbishop, to assign freely to our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of the monastery of Fiore, upon receiving suitable compensation, the place of Botrano, appropriate for religious life, belonging to the Church of Cosenza, with its appurtenances. Our beloved sons, the abbots of Holy Spirit and of Corazzo, and Brother R. of Tortiano, were appointed executors in this matter. [Col. 0363C]

That same archbishop, as a son of obedience, preferring humbly to obey rather than kick against the goad, received a fixed compensation—not merely equivalent, but four times better—and assigned the place of Botrano to the aforesaid brothers. But you withheld your consent from this exchange; for which reason those executors suspended you by apostolic authority from receiving your prebends. Afterwards, when some of you came to the Apostolic See on this account, with the said abbot present, they alleged the proximity of the place of Botrano, and the great advantage to your church arising from that proximity; the remoteness of the land exchanged, and the great disadvantage resulting therefrom; and the scandal of the citizens, who, because of the custom they had in Sila, would not patiently endure being deprived of it. [Col. 0363D]

But we, desiring to provide both for the brothers of Fiore and for your church—although the archbishop could, by canonical permission, have bestowed a certain part of his own possessions upon them in favour of religion—commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Martirano, and the aforesaid abbots of Corazzo and of Saint Mary of Formosa, and the treasurer of Martirano, diligently to investigate the truth of the foregoing. If the compensation which the archbishop had received was suitable, or if suitable compensation were offered, then, once it had been received, they were to cause the aforesaid exchange to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside. Otherwise, since under the terms of our mandate it ought by no means to have been made without adequate compensation, they were to annul it. If all could not be present for carrying this out, nevertheless three of them were to ensure its execution. Although one of these executors had entered upon the way of all flesh, the other two, the third dissenting, judged the compensation suitable. [Col. 0364A]

We are therefore greatly moved and astonished that our command, which ought to have been for you “an aroma of life unto life,” has become for you “an aroma of death unto death.” Neither the religious character of the aforesaid brothers nor the authority of the Apostolic See could move or soften you, so that, by consenting to works of piety, you might change your purpose for the better and, like members agreeing with the head, think one and the same thing with that archbishop. That neither zeal for God nor concern for the safety of the Church of Cosenza moves you to this is plainly apparent from the fact that, in respect of grants which the predecessors of the aforesaid archbishop are known to have made to their kinsmen, you not only gave your consent but strengthened them by your own subscriptions. [Col. 0364B]

But perhaps you fear lest, by the arrival of religious men, your irreligion be disclosed, and their uprightness, through the proximity of the places, more fully reveal your own dishonesty. Indeed, since you have received the same archbishop as your father and shepherd, entrusted to him the administration of the whole Church of Cosenza, and taken care to give us laudable testimony concerning him, we could approve what a man of sincere reputation and proven life had done concerning a small possession. Moreover, since two of our executors, one having entered upon the way of all flesh, judged the exchange itself worthy of approval, although the third dissented, yet because under canonical enactments the judgment of the majority prevails, we could in law approve what they had approved, and deal with you more severely, because you did not observe the sentence of suspension pronounced against you by the first executors. [Col. 0364C]

Yet, desiring to overcome evil with good, to confer a benefit even upon the unwilling, and to make you participants in the prayers of the brothers of Fiore when they have been transferred to Botrano, we admonish your whole body, earnestly exhort you, and by apostolic letters command you under obedience: give your consent to that exchange without any difficulty, and, becoming willing instead of unwilling, cheerfully lend your wills to so pious and praiseworthy a work. If you do this in accordance with our admonition and command, we shall accept your obedience, although late, and on that account shall more willingly see that you are heard in your own affairs and in those of your church. [Col. 0364D]

Otherwise, from the fullness of the power conferred upon us, we shall determine what we deem expedient; and you will rightly have cause to fear that you may incur our displeasure from that through which you could have deserved favour. Would that you choose rather to follow the way of obedience, so that you may be worthy of our goodwill and deserve to share in the prayers of the brothers of Fiore, rather than, persisting in contumacy, deserve rebuke for disobedience; and that what you could voluntarily have carried out may not be accomplished no less by apostolic authority! [Col. 0365A]

Given, etc., on 4 June.

LXXXII. TO THE CITIZENS OF COSENZA. On the same subject. (Lateran, 4 June.)

[Col. 0365B]

“Considering formerly,” etc., in nearly the same manner, through “they alleged.” Therefore, since we believe that it is to your advantage both spiritually and temporally that a monastery of religious men should arise in the diocese of Cosenza—for you may be aided in your needs by their prayers before God and their assistance before men—we admonish your whole body, earnestly exhort you, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: not only do not obstruct this work of piety, but rather expedite it; urge the canons of Cosenza to give their consent to the aforesaid exchange; and let them atone for their former hardness by subsequent obedience. [Col. 0365C]

If they cannot be softened to this, at least remove from them the ground on which they may, as hitherto, allege your opposition in their excuse and cast back upon you the cause of their contumacy. Let the prudence of your whole body not be unaware that, if in this matter you obey our admonition and command, we shall more willingly extend apostolic favour to you in your public and private affairs, insofar as uprightness permits, and shall take care to cherish and support your city.

Given at the Lateran, etc.

LXXXIII. [Note: [Col. 0365D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77.] TO THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF ASSISI. Concerning their oath to abide by the commands of the Apostolic See, and many other matters. (Lateran, 6 June.)

[Col. 0365D]

We regard as welcome and acceptable, and commend in the Lord, your devotion: as our beloved son L., [Note: [Col. 0365D] See the notes to letters 5 of Book V and 1 of Book VI.] cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross, [Col. 0366A] legate of the Apostolic See, informed us by his letters, you received him gladly and humbly and took care to treat him honourably. You also, son Podestà, together with fifty of the greatest and best men of the city, whom he named individually, swore to abide by apostolic commands concerning the matter for which your city had been placed under interdict. One man swore the same on behalf of the people, not merely with their consent but at their command. Afterwards, as the cardinal had enjoined upon you, you sent our beloved son Master Barnabas and the noble Master Michael into our presence to receive the apostolic command on your behalf.

Considering, then, that your city had been interdicted because you presumed to receive into office as podestà Gerard Giliberti, whom we had excommunicated, and that neither when admonished nor when repeatedly commanded by us did you remove him from the office of rector before the appointed time: in order that we may correct you with paternal affection in the matter in which you incurred our displeasure, as we directed the same envoys orally, so now we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters, under obligation of your oath, that henceforth you knowingly appoint no excommunicated person or enemy of the Church to the government of your city. [Col. 0366B]

And lest you fall into error through ignorance in this matter, whenever you freely elect anyone as rector, before receiving him or swearing to him, humbly request him through your envoys from the Apostolic See; and, unless he is excommunicated or an enemy of the Church, it will grant him to you without difficulty. But if you decide to elect as consuls some of your citizens who are our vassals and faithful and devoted to us, we do not wish you to apply to the Apostolic See on their behalf out of an obligation arising from the oath. Under the same strict requirement we command you to take care, within fifteen days, to notify us by your open letters that you have received this command. [Col. 0366C]

Given at the Lateran, on 6 June.

LXXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0365D] See Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 121, §22. See also Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §68.] TO [lacuna] OF EMBRUN [Note: [Col. 0365D] See the notes to letter 121 of Book VI.] AND OUR BELOVED SON, THE ABBOT OF BOSCAUDON. [Note: [Col. 0365D] See the notes to letter 121 of Book VI.] That they should diligently investigate the offences of the bishop of Vence. [Note: [Col. 0365D] This letter should be compared with letter 34 of Book II.] (Lateran, 8 June.)

[Col. 0366D]

You, brother Archbishop, had informed C., pope of good memory, our predecessor, by your letters of the offences and enormities of [lacuna] bishop of Vence. [Note: [Col. 0365D] This concerns Peter, surnamed Grimaldi, whom the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 1219, recognize as bishop of Vence from 1193 until 1202. That he continued to hold office beyond this is proved by the present letter of Innocent.] That predecessor accordingly took care to command you and our venerable brothers, the bishops of Digne [Note: [Col. 0366D] That is, B., Bertrand de Turrias, bishop of Digne, whom the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* recognize from 1192 and mention no later than 1196; indeed, they seem to assign his death to that same year, 1196. This letter of Innocent proves that Bertrand continued in life and in the episcopate at least until the present year, 1204.] and Senez [Col. 0367A] [Note: [Col. 0367D] The authors cited above, ibid., col. 1252, name Maurellius as bishop of Senez in 1189, then immediately William I in 1213, and say nothing of the others.], that, if his shameful manner of life were established to their satisfaction, they should suspend him from office and administration and send him to the Apostolic See with testimony in their letters, appointing procurators for that Church to make diligent provision concerning its offices and ecclesiastical goods.

Subsequently, however, you sent us your letters, reporting that you and the aforesaid bishops had found the said bishop of Vence stained by graver and worse offences than you had reported to the Apostolic See. You therefore ordered him, under suspension, to present himself before the Apostolic See; yet he neither came to the Roman Church nor ceased, on account of the suspension, to exercise episcopal functions. For this reason we strictly commanded you to declare publicly excommunicated the aforesaid bishop, who had scorned to observe the sentence of suspension pronounced against him, and to have him avoided more strictly by all until he should appear before us with testimony in your letters, to answer before us concerning these matters. [Col. 0367B]

Although you wrote back to us that there was no one who did not know his disobediences, rebellions, and monstrous offences, and that his error was daily found worse than the former, nevertheless, contrary to our command—at which we are greatly astonished and disturbed—you did not take care to proceed; but, as one disobedient and contemptuous of our strict command, you did not hesitate to pass over these matters by dissimulation, though you could and should have put them into effect without a special command from us. Therefore a lamentable complaint was again made in our hearing on behalf of our beloved sons, the provost [Note: [Col. 0367D] The incomplete series of provosts of the Church of Vence given by the authors often cited above (ibid., col. 1232) presents no provost of Vence before D., whom they place under the year 1239.] and canons of the Church of Vence: their church, through the bishop’s fault, has been brought almost to its foundations into utter destitution. Through him its buildings have been almost wholly ruined; divine offices are celebrated there no otherwise than in some parish church; and the same bishop openly abuses a certain widow at table and in his house, as is notorious. [Col. 0367C]

Although at your urging he abjured her, he is consequently said plainly to have incurred perjury. In addition, both in the exercise of his order and in other things he is so dissolute that the whole diocese, especially in spiritual matters, suffers grave harm from this. His ill repute, deserved by his manner of life, has spread not only through the province of Embrun but also through more distant regions, so that all regard him as a disgrace to episcopal dignity. Since, therefore, rotten teeth must be knocked out from the jaws of the Church, we command your discretion by apostolic letters and strictly enjoin you in virtue of obedience diligently to search out the truth concerning these matters and any others requiring investigation. If you find that he ought to be deposed, depose him by our authority, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, and grant the canons leave to elect a suitable person as bishop. No letters, etc. [Col. 0367D]

Given at the Lateran, on 8 June, in the seventh year.

LXXXV. TO [lacuna] PRIOR OF ESSEBI, AND MASTER H. OF GILLEVILLIS, CANON OF LINCOLN, AND MASTER A. OF WILNA, RECTOR OF THE CHURCH OF BARESWUH, IN THE DIOCESE OF LINCOLN. That proceedings should be taken in the case of Agnes, a woman whom her father and stepmother forced unwillingly into a monastery. (Lateran, 31 May.)

[Col. 0368B]

We have received your letters, stating that Agnes, a woman, caused it to be recited in our presence that her [lacuna] father and [lacuna] stepmother, of the diocese of Lincoln, in order to defraud her of her inheritance, forced her, wholly resisting and unwilling, into the monastery of Haverholme, and caused her to be kept there for a long time in chains. As soon as she was freed from the chains, she departed. We therefore judged it appropriate to commit this case to you. Before you, she proved all the aforesaid matters in law by trustworthy witnesses, beyond every exception. The canons and nuns of the order of Sempringham, into whose monastery she was said to have been forced, firmly asserted that she had devoutly received the religious habit, but always refused to affirm their bare assertion by oath. [Col. 0368C]

You therefore rightly doubted whether their bare assertion should be believed, and whether the truth should be elicited from the adversaries of the plaintiff, concerning whose wrong she had always brought her action. We, then, considering that their bare assertion is not to be believed against the sworn depositions of witnesses, command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, you proceed in the same case, all appeal set aside, according to the testimony received and after due consideration. No letters, etc. And if not all of you … two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 31 May.

LXXXVI. TO THE PRIOR AND MONKS OF SAINT ANDREW OF ARCE. [Note: [Col. 0368D] “Saint Andrew of Arce” should perhaps be read “of Ardes,” or “in Arde,” as it is written in the charter by which the abbot and convent of Saint Mary of Laon, of Le Mans, grant to Richard, archbishop of Armagh, the cell or priory of Saint Andrew *en le Arde*, in Ulster, belonging to them. *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 1019. See below, letter 88.] He receives them under protection and enumerates the goods belonging to them. (Lateran, 26 May.)

[Col. 0368D]

“It is customary to grant,” etc., through “consent.” We receive under our protection the monastery of Saint Andrew, in which you are devoted to divine service, with all that it at present justly [Col. 0369A] and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by lawful means, etc., through “we receive.” In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this present writing: the church of Yuchemackargi; the church of Archien; the church of Donanachti; the church of Saint Andrew of Duero; the church of Saint Nicholas in the fortress; the church of Kilkoikernau; the church of Kilbracti; the church of Saint Corcan; the church of Stakerole; and the church of Erderacheth; and all the churches and ecclesiastical benefices of the whole lordship of John de Courcy, from the water of Dalenard to the water of Carlingford, except the church of the castle of Maicone, assigned by the diocesan bishops to the monks’ own uses, as is contained in the authentic documents of those bishops, and as you justly and peacefully possess them. [Col. 0369B]

Therefore let no one … violate this page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 26 May.

LXXXVII. TO [lacuna] PRIOR AND MONKS OF FOLKESTONE. [Note: [Col. 0369C] The monastery of Folkestone, in Kent, was founded by Nigel de Muneville and his wife Emma, in the honour and love of God, Saint Mary, Saint Eanswythe, and the church of Blessed Mary of Laon of Le Mans, then governed by Abbot Ranulph; they wished it to be attached and given to that church in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095. See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 560. The same monastery, together with other alien priories, was suppressed by the Parliament of Leicester in the second year of King Henry V, A.D. 1414.] On a similar subject. (Lateran, 26 May.)

“It is customary to grant,” etc., through “consent.” We receive under our protection the monastery of Folkestone, in which you are devoted to divine service, with all that it at present justly and canonically possesses, etc., through “we receive.” In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, etc.: the church of Kanekinge; [Note: [Col. 0369D] These churches are named nowhere in the charter of foundation or in the charter of confirmation issued by William of Avranches, lord of Folkestone, one of the successors of Nigel de Muneville. See ibid.] the church of Aukeham; [Note: [Col. 0369D] These churches are named nowhere in the charter of foundation or in the charter of confirmation issued by William of Avranches, lord of Folkestone, one of the successors of Nigel de Muneville. See ibid.] half the tithes of Niweton; [Col. 0369C] [Note: [Col. 0369D] These churches are named nowhere in the charter of foundation or in the charter of confirmation issued by William of Avranches, lord of Folkestone, one of the successors of Nigel de Muneville. See ibid.] tithes of Teterlingham [otherwise Sterlingham], Waleton [otherwise Walton], Northewode, and Standene; and one third of the tithes of Fliete, as you justly and peacefully possess them. Therefore let no one … violate the page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 26 May.

LXXXVIII. TO [lacuna] PRIOR AND MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT ANDREW OF STOKES. [Note: [Col. 0369D] It should be read “of Stoke-Courcy.” The priory of Saint Andrew of Stoke-Courcy, in Devonshire, like the monastery of Folkestone mentioned above, formerly belonged to the abbey of Blessed Mary of Laon of Le Mans, [Col. 0370C] and together with the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0370D] was suppressed. See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 577.] On a similar subject. (Lateran, 11 June.)

[Col. 0370A]

“Upon the just requests,” etc., through “consent.” We receive under our protection your persons, with all the goods which at present, etc., through “we receive.” In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this present writing: the church of Wotene [perhaps Wyton]; the church of Lullinstoke [otherwise Lullingstoke]; the church of Hoilefort; and the church of Hichestoche, with all their appurtenances; two parts of the tithe of Corniton; the whole tithe of one sheepfold at Cumba; two parts of the tithe of Wileton; two parts of the tithe of Lullinstoke; the right which you possess in the chaplaincy of the castle of Stokes; in the territory of that castle, one hide of land; the land of Tinelande; one furlong of land; one acre of meadow; half a virgate at Brechei [otherwise Breche]; and the new mill. [Col. 0370B]

In Wales: the right of patronage of the church of Traigru [otherwise Tregru]. In Ireland, at Woltonia: all churches and ecclesiastical benefices of the whole lordship of John de Courcy, [Note: [Col. 0370D] The charter by which John de Courcy grants the benefices here mentioned to the church of Saint Andrew of Stokes is found in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 1019. But, remarkably, the authors of that work refer this instrument not as belonging to the church of Saint Andrew of Stokes in Devonshire, England, but as belonging to the church of Saint Andrew of Ardes (discussed above in letter 86), situated in Ireland.] from the water of Dalnart [otherwise Darnart] to the water of Kerlingfort [otherwise Carlingford], except the castle of Maincove; ten carucates of land in Arte [otherwise de l’Art], namely in the land of Maccollokan [otherwise Maccoloqua]; in Dalboing; in Hailo, namely, the town and church of Arderaschac, with their appurtenances, and ten carucates of land; and in Kinelmolan three carucates of land—as you justly and peacefully possess all these things. [Col. 0370C]

Therefore let absolutely no person … violate this page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 11 June.

LXXXIX. TO [lacuna] ABBOT OF SALEM. [Note: [Col. 0370D] Book V, letter 99, note.] Concerning the absolution of the bishop of Constance. (Lateran, 15 June.)

As has been reported to us, although a sentence of excommunication was pronounced against the bishop of Constance, [Note: [Col. 0370D] This letter must certainly be compared with what the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 915, report concerning Diethelm of Cleggoia, otherwise of Weissenburg and of Crenkingen. From documents they recognize this prelate, formerly abbot of Reichenau, as bishop of Constance from 1191 or 1192, and say that he governed the bishopric of Constance with great praise for fifteen years.] this did not come to the latter’s attention before the bishop of Bamberg, [Col. 0371A] [Note: [Col. 0371C] After Conrad, elected bishop of Bamberg in 1202 and dying the day immediately following his election, Eckbert, or Erimbert, brother of Stephen, king of the Hungarians, and son of Berthold, duke of Merania, governed that church laudably for thirty-two years.
