He waged war against Bernard, duke of Carinthia; while ravaging Bernard’s dominions, he was captured, but released under specified terms of peace. He died in 1235. Bucelinus, *Germania Sacra*, vol. I, part II, p. 24.] against whom it had been alleged at the Apostolic See that he had received the order of the diaconate from that excommunicated bishop, had returned home.

Since, however, he desires reconciliation to ecclesiastical unity and requests that the benefit of absolution be granted him, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after receiving from him a public sworn assurance that he will obey our commands concerning the matter for which he is bound by the bond of excommunication, you grant him, by our authority and according to the form of the Church, the benefit of absolution; and faithfully notify us within two months of your action, together with his open letters. [Col. 0371B]

Given at the Lateran, on 15 June.

XC. [Note: [Col. 0371D] It is found, though mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book III, title 8, “On the grant of a prebend and a church not vacant,” chapter 10. Passages read there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO [lacuna] BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0371D] He was Bernard, surnamed by Pancirolus and many others Circa, and by Ughellus Balbus. Formerly provost of Pavia, he was elected bishop of Faenza about 1192, then transferred to the see of Pavia about 1198 (see letter 324 of Book I), and died in the odour of sanctity in 1213. He was Bernard, chief and standard-bearer of the decretalists; see Mittarelli, *De litteratura Faventina*, col. 22. See also Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, part marked *, col. 31.] AND ARCHDEACON OF PAVIA. Concerning the conferment of certain prebends in the Church of Asti. (Lateran, 15 June.)

From the side of the Church of Asti it was reported to us that, when certain prebends in that church had been vacant for four years and more, our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0371D] The Decretals omit these words and what follows, “his canons,” etc.], the bishop of Asti [Note: [Col. 0372C] After the death, about 1198, of Nazarius II, Boniface, formerly a monk of Saint Benedict, became bishop of Asti. Having alienated several places and rights of his church to its grave prejudice, when the matter was referred to Pope Innocent III, he resigned the episcopate, willingly or unwillingly, in 1205 (or rather 1206), as is clear from letter 200 of Book VIII of Innocent himself, which we shall produce in its place. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 532.], carefully admonished his canons to provide for the church. When they would not heed his admonition, the bishop instituted certain persons in that church [Note: The Decretals there read “in the church itself” in place of “in that church,” and below “knowing” in place of “considering.”], believing that the Lateran Council permitted him to do so. But those instituted, considering that such an institution was not firm, [Col. 0371C] had recourse to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Milan [Note: [Col. 0372D] These words are absent from the Decretals; below, “who” is substituted for “whom,” and “took care to oppose such a proposal” for “that proposal.”] [Note: Book III, letter, note.], who ordained them as canons of the Church of Asti and put them in corporal possession of the prebends, with the consent of the chapter of that church. Only three were excepted; wishing to challenge that institution before us and prepared to defend the church’s side, we assigned them to our beloved son G. [Note: [Col. 0372D] Book V, letter 60, note.], priest-cardinal of the title of [Col. 0372A] Saint Vitalis, as auditor. Before him those three maintained that the institution ought to be quashed, because neither the bishop nor the aforesaid archbishop could, under the authorization of the Lateran Council, provide for the aforesaid church, since each had been negligent and dilatory in that provision beyond the time granted them by the canon. The other side, on the contrary, asserted that, although the bishop’s institution was invalid, the archbishop’s provision was valid in law, because the time granted him by the canon did not run except from the time when this had been declared to him; to prove this it advanced many arguments.

When both sides had set these matters forth, [they finally agreed in confessing that in the aforesaid church the prebends were not distinct [Col. 0372B], nor was the number of canons fixed. We therefore, having carefully heard these and the other matters advanced on either side [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals, as are those below from “since” through “fixed.”], clearly understood that the statute of the Lateran Council concerning benefices vacant for more than six months had no application whatever in this case. For, even if perhaps the Church of Asti suffered a shortage of canons, nevertheless no prebends in it were vacant, since in it there are neither distinct prebends nor a fixed number of canons [Note: The Decretals read “or,” and below “ought” in place of “ought to have.”]. Hence the institution made by the bishop and archbishop on the pretext of the aforesaid council lacked binding force. Yet because the whole chapter, excepting only three [Note: The Decretals omit this word, as also the words below distinguished by italic type. They read “may be available” for “are available.”], approves and desires the reception of the aforesaid persons, and because those three have neither raised nor shown anything reasonable against them, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after diligently ascertaining the truth, if the Church of Asti has sufficient resources, you shall cause the aforesaid clerics, according to the custom observed hitherto, to be regarded as canons, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal;] the opponents, etc. But if not both, etc. You, brother bishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of July [15 June].

XCI. . . . . To the abbot and convent of Casadei. He assigns them a peremptory term for answering concerning the affair of Montispeloso [Note: See letter 40 of Book VII.]. (Lateran, 15 Kalends of July [17 June].)

[Col. 0373A]

We regard it as serious and unworthy that, although we caused you to be summoned by a peremptory edict concerning the affair of Montispeloso, you were unwilling to come into our presence, merely setting forth certain excuses in your letters: that for the present you could not approach us because the harvests were before you and you feared inclement weather. You therefore humbly asked us to deign for the present to spare you from the summons issued.

We judge one of these excuses frivolous; the other [Col. 0373B] we have graciously deemed admissible. Therefore, unless you come meanwhile, after the heat of summer at least, do not delay to come into our presence without delay or any excuse on the coming feast of Saint Michael, which we assign you as a peremptory date; or send suitable representatives on your behalf. Otherwise know for certain that from that time onward we shall proceed in that business, since we are unwilling for it to be further prolonged, in your absence and without further summons to you.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of July [17 June].

XCII. . . . . To the archbishop [Note: Book VI, letter 171.] and the provost of Saint Mary of Albarium, Genoese. That they restrain S., mother-in-law of N. de Camilla, who is impeaching her son-in-law’s marriage. (Lateran, 17 Kalends of July [15 June].)

[Col. 0373C]

At the representation of N. de Camilla, a citizen of Genoa, it has been made known to our apostolic office that, when he, J., had lawfully taken a woman as his wife, S., the mother of that woman, undertook to challenge the marriage in order to extort money from him. Although wicked actions cannot accord with her judgment, she nevertheless wishes to have money, so that she may thereafter desist from accusing that marriage.

Since the malice of human beings is not to be indulged, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if what is alleged is true, you repel the aforesaid woman from accusing that marriage and [Col. 0373D] impose silence upon her in this matter. Witnesses, etc. But if not all, etc. You, brother archbishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of July [15 June].

XCIII. [Note: For the subject of this letter, see *Gesta Innocentii*, §68. See also Raynaldus, under the year [Col. 0374D] 1204, §70. Compare in addition letter 67 of this seventh book.] . . . . To the archbishops of Compostela and Toledo; . . . . to the bishops of Tarazona and Coimbra. That they induce the daughter of the king of Castile to restore to the king of León the towns which he had assigned to her, whether by title of dowry or as a marriage-gift. (Lateran, 12 Kalends of July [20 June].)

[Col. 0374A]

When it had formerly come to our hearing that . . . . the king of León, who had been separated from the daughter of our dearest son in Christ, . . . . the illustrious king of Portugal, whom he had incestuously married, had presumed to unite to himself the daughter of our dearest son in Christ, . . . . the illustrious king of Castile—his own niece—we sent our beloved son Brother Rainerius to Spain, that, in accordance with the prophetic word, he might “loose the bonds of wickedness” and “undo the burdens that oppress” [Note: Thus in the copy.].

Accordingly, when he entered Spain, he admonished the king of León once and again on our behalf to withdraw from so detestable [Col. 0374B] and abominable a union, dissolving every obligation that had been contracted to consummate that union. But since he achieved absolutely nothing with him, and since the king did not present himself before him on the appointed day and at the appointed place, even after waiting beyond the term, he proceeded according to the form of our mandate and pronounced sentences of excommunication against the king and of interdict against his kingdom. Against the king of Castile and his land he did not proceed in any way, because the latter submitted himself to the envoy’s commands and declared that he would receive back his daughter if she were returned to him.

Thereafter the king of Castile, through you, brother archbishop of Toledo, and our venerable brother . . . . bishop of Palencia, and the king of León, through our venerable [Col. 0374C] brother . . . . bishop of Zamora, humbly begged us to deign to dispense them concerning such a union. But when they had suffered refusal in this petition, you asked us at least to relax the sentence of interdict, since danger threatened the whole kingdom as a result.

We, wishing to test the spirits whether they were of God, and whether the expected benefit proposed by you would follow from this, relaxed the sentence of interdict—not wholly or perpetually, but only in one respect and temporarily, that is, for as long as it should be expedient and please us. Thus divine offices were to be celebrated in that kingdom, but the bodies of the dead were not to be committed to ecclesiastical burial, except clerics, to whom we granted by special favour [Col. 0374D] burial in an ecclesiastical cemetery, though the customary solemnity was to cease. But lest we seem to remit the punishment rather than to commute it, we bound the said king of León, the aforementioned daughter of the king of Castile, and all their principal counsellors and supporters by the bond of excommunication; and, wherever they might arrive—in any city, town, or castle—we forbade divine offices to be celebrated there in their presence.

Since certain castles which the king of León was said to have delivered to the daughter of the king of Castile [Col. 0375A] as dowry, or rather as a marriage-gift, on the condition that, if he should leave her for any reason, they should pass into her right, appeared very greatly to impede the dissolution of this union—and since those castles had been given not so much for a shameful cause as rather for no cause at all, since it was manifest that no marriage existed between them, and consequently neither dowry nor marriage-gift—we willed that those castles be restored, lest what ought rather to be turned against the daughter of the king of Castile as her punishment should redound to her advantage. We further decreed by apostolic authority that she should be constrained to this by a sentence of excommunication; and that any offspring then born, or thereafter to be born, of so incestuous, coupled, and condemned a union should be held altogether spurious and illegitimate, and under the lawful enactments should on no ground succeed to paternal property.

Moreover, the king of Castile—at which we are greatly astonished—cunningly procured an oath from the whole kingdom of León to the offspring conceived from so incestuous a union. Therefore we commanded him, under an appeal to divine judgment, entirely to dissolve the bonds of this iniquity; not only to receive back his daughter, but also to recall her from incestuous embraces and unite her in the bond of marriage, only in the Lord, to whomsoever he wished. Otherwise, we would take action against him and his land as we should judge expedient, and our admonition would be followed by a sharper vengeance than he supposed.

He, however, through his beloved son Master L., his envoy, sought by many means to excuse himself so as not to be compelled to restore the aforesaid castles, since they were held not by him but by his daughter. Although, therefore, that union has been dissolved—whence we ordered both the king of León and the daughter of the king of Castile to be absolved from the bond of excommunication, and his kingdom from the sentence of interdict, after sworn security had been given in the form of the Church that they would obey our commands—yet, so that everything which had wickedly been bound together because of that incestuous union may be completely dissolved, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, and strictly enjoin you by virtue of obedience, that, after the king of León has been absolved, you carefully admonish and induce the oft-mentioned daughter of the king of Castile, [Col. 0375D] commanding her on our behalf, under the obligation of the oath she has rendered, to restore to the king of León the castles given to her, whether as dowry, as a marriage-gift, or in whatever manner because of that union; or at least, if any matter remains disputed, to assign and deliver them into your hands, to be held until the matter is decided by arbitrators chosen jointly, or, if they will not or cannot agree upon arbitrators, by us through the means of justice.

If she refuses to obey our commands and your admonitions, then, setting aside every favour and fear and removing the obstacle of appeal, restore her to the sentence of excommunication. By the same sentence strike her father and mother, the king and queen of Castile, as well as all who presume to impede the fulfillment of the apostolic mandate in this matter; and wherever they may arrive, forbid divine offices to be celebrated in their presence. But if not all of you are willing or able to be present, . . . any three of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of July [20 June].

XCIV. [Note: See *Gesta Innocentii* and Raynaldus, in the place cited, on letter 93.] . . . . To the archbishop of Compostela; . . . . to the bishops of Zamora and Palencia. That they absolve the repentant king of León. (Lateran, 13 Kalends of July [19 June].)

[Col. 0376B]

Since, though unworthy, we hold on earth the place of Him who “does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live,” and who, even when angry, does not forget to have mercy, it is fitting for us to act mercifully toward those who humbly desire to return to the bosom of mother Church and to offer due satisfaction for their offences.

Although . . . . the illustrious king of León gravely offended his Creator by presuming through incest to cleave to the noblewoman . . . . daughter of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Castile, and for this deserved to be bound by the bond of excommunication, yet, because, as we have learned, having come to himself [Col. 0376C] he has wholly withdrawn from her and promises to offer due satisfaction for his offences, while humbly asking that the benefit of absolution be granted him, we have mercifully deemed his request worthy of acceptance.

Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after receiving publicly and solemnly from him, from his principal counsellors and supporters who incurred the same sentence with him on this account, and from those who communicated with him, sworn security in the form of the Church that they will obey our commands, you bestow upon them by our authority the benefit of absolution and relax the sentence of interdict pronounced against his kingdom. Impose upon him, under obligation of oath, while preserving our other commands which we may judge should be carried out by him, [Col. 0376D] that he must in no way return to the aforesaid noblewoman, nor receive her even if she wishes to return. But if not all of you are willing or able, etc. Any two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of July [19 June].

XCV. [Note: Cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77. See *Gesta Innocentii*, §144.] To Guido, master of the Hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia [Note: This letter should certainly be compared with what is found in *Histoire générale de Languedoc*, vol. III, p. 43 ff.], and to his brothers, present and future, who profess the regular life, in perpetuity. He unites the Hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia with that of the Holy Spirit at Montpellier, for the salvation of the Roman pontiff and cardinals; and grants many privileges. (Lateran, 14 Kalends of July [18 June].)

[Col. 0377A]

Among works of piety which, according to the Apostle, hold the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come, divine Scripture especially and frequently commends hospitality to us, since it embraces all those works for which the Lord declares that at the examination of the last judgment he will reward the good and punish the wicked. For it feeds the hungry, gives drink to the thirsty, receives strangers, clothes the naked, and not only visits the sick but, taking their infirmities upon itself, tends those who are ill; it assists those placed in prison, and, as it shares in the infirmity of the living, so it shares in the burial of the dead.

[Col. 0377B]

By hospitality some, having received angels as guests, pleased God: Abraham and Lot, devoted to hospitality, deserved to entertain angels, through whom Abraham, already old, received the promise of future offspring, while Lot was delivered from the burning of Sodom. Likewise the two disciples who constrained Jesus to accept their hospitality—whom they had not recognized in the exposition of Scripture—recognized him in the breaking of bread. Through hospitality the surplus of the rich, which perhaps if accumulated would be reserved for death, is distributed to relieve the poor for life. Through it earthly things are exchanged for heavenly and transitory things for eternal ones in a blessed commerce, while through the hands of the poor we lay up treasure in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys and where thieves neither break in nor steal; and we make for ourselves friends from the mammon [wealth] of iniquity, so that, when we fail, they may receive us into eternal dwellings.

[Col. 0377C]

Considering these things, not only for our own salvation but also for that of our predecessors, successors, and brothers—the cardinals of the Roman Church, bishops, priests, and deacons, both living and dead—we have built at Saint Mary in Saxia, a place altogether suitable for exercising the office of hospitality, a venerable hospital from the alms of the Roman Church. In it, by the Lord’s gift, the poor and sick are to be received and refreshed in future times, and other works of piety performed. We decree that the regular order established there by us according to God and the institution of the brothers of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

This is added, however: in the same church there shall always be at least four clerics professing the rule of that hospital. Offering special prayers for us, our predecessors, and our brothers, both living and dead, they shall freely administer all spiritual matters and, in these matters, be subject to the correction of no one except the Roman pontiff. Whenever expedient, after prior admonition, the brothers may make a charitable complaint to him for God’s sake, so that, once the truth is known, he may decide what he judges ought to be provided by his prudent counsel.

The clerics, content with the food and clothing which we order to be supplied to them according to the same rule, shall devote themselves to divine offices and attend [Col. 0378A] to ecclesiastical sacraments. They shall in no way concern themselves with the hospital’s other business, apart from the master’s permission, but shall leave all matters, without contradiction or complaint, to your disposition, son Master, and that of your successors, or of those appointed to this by you or them.

Furthermore, because hospitality flourishes greatly in the Hospital of the Holy Spirit in our days through God’s grace, we unite it to this hospital, and this hospital to it, by the counsel of our brothers: so that this hospital, being nearer to us, may more usefully give the other protection, since it can more easily seek our defence; and the other may more conveniently assist this one with ministers, since those dwelling there are more suited to the office of hospitality. Yet this union shall in no way withdraw the aforesaid Hospital of the Holy Spirit from the jurisdiction of the Church of Maguelone, provided only that the constitution which we decreed should be observed between that Church of Maguelone and the aforesaid Hospital of the Holy Spirit is retained.

[Col. 0378B]

We further decree that only one master shall preside over both hospitals. He shall visit each yearly, establish and correct whatever he sees should be established or corrected, and have free authority to transfer brothers wherever they may be, according as he judges most expedient. If perchance he enters upon the way of all flesh at Rome, or anywhere on this side of the mountains, the brothers of the Hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia shall promptly notify the brothers of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit of his death; and the latter shall send to Rome two or three of their brothers to celebrate a regular election with the brothers of the Hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia. But if he dies at Montpellier, or anywhere beyond the mountains, the brothers of the Holy Spirit shall report his death to the brothers of Saint Mary, who, as we have said, shall send two or three of their brothers to Montpellier for the regular celebration of an election.

Furthermore, since the Church of Saint Mary in Saxia and the hospital built there belong to us without intermediary—saving that, at our command, the clerics of that church owe attendance at the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles for the scrutiny, baptism, and litany—lest a person of unequal condition be preferred to it, and a servant who stands or falls to another master be placed over [Col. 0378D] the aforesaid hospital, which is subject only to our jurisdiction, we exempt you, son Master, and your successors from the authority of all prelates. Thus no one shall dare to pronounce against you or them a sentence of interdict or excommunication without a mandate of the Apostolic See; if it is pronounced otherwise, we decree that it has no force.

Although we unite the aforesaid hospitals, nevertheless, lest such a union create confusion—for although union is pleasing to God, distinction is nevertheless likewise acceptable to him—we establish by this present privilege that brothers appointed to collect alms for the poor of the Hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia shall confine themselves to Italy, Sicily, England, and Hungary. The brothers [Col. 0379A] of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit at Montpellier, however, may freely appoint collectors of alms in the other provinces. Each shall be content with its own bounds and shall not invade the other’s territories; alms collected for the Hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia shall not be transferred to the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, nor shall any alms bestowed upon the latter by the devotion of the faithful be conveyed to the former on any pretext.

If any of your brothers sent to collect alms arrive in any city, castle, or village, and that place happens to be under an interdict from divine offices, then, in reverence for almighty God and in joyful recognition of their arrival, once a year churches shall be opened and bells rung, so that in church an exhortation may be addressed to the people concerning the acquiring of alms.

[Col. 0379B]

We further decree that those who receive your confraternities or collections shall, without prejudice to the right of their lords, remain under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves and enjoy peace in the lands in which they are located. Likewise, we enact that anyone received into your confraternity, if the parish church of which he is a parishioner is under interdict from divine offices and he happens to die, shall not be denied ecclesiastical burial, unless he has been excommunicated or personally placed under interdict.

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from lands and vineyards which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense for the use of the sick and poor, nor from the increase of your animals or the produce of your gardens. You may also, in houses which you presently possess or may possess in future, have for your own use, that of your household, and that of the sick and poor dwelling there, an oratory and cemetery without hindrance from any opposition. But chrism . . . from the diocesan bishops, etc. Otherwise, you may choose whomever you prefer, etc. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may in your churches, etc., through “celebrate.” You may also receive free and absolved persons fleeing from the secular world, etc.

We further prohibit any of your brothers, after making profession in your houses, from departing without his master’s permission, unless for the sake of a stricter religious order; but one departing, etc., through “retain.” If any of your brothers, after making profession, are perhaps found to be disturbers of your religious life or useless, you, son Master, and your successors may, with the assent and counsel of the sounder part of the chapter, remove them, permit them to enter another order where they may be able to live according to God, and substitute others in their place. The latter shall be tested in your community for one year; [Col. 0380A] after that period, if their conduct warrants it and they are found useful for the hospital’s service, they shall make regular profession.

In addition, we strictly prohibit any ecclesiastical or secular person from demanding from you, son Master, from your successors, or from the brothers of the same hospitals, fealties, homages, oaths, or the other securities commonly exacted by laypersons. Finally, we confirm for you by apostolic authority the tithes which, by the counsel and assent of bishops, you may obtain from clerics or laypersons, and those which, with the consent of diocesan bishops and the clerics to whom they belong, you acquire. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to violate the aforesaid places . . . saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

Henceforth we beseech and adjure our successors in Christ Jesus, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, [Col. 0380B] that, as special patrons, they especially foster and defend your places, together with the persons and goods assigned to the work of hospitality. For although by the office of apostolic service they are bound to provide for other pious places, they ought nevertheless to bestow special care upon this hospital, which has been founded and endowed from the goods of the Roman Church and which, we believe, is to be enlarged in our days and those of our successors. If anyone therefore . . . but to all the same places, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 14 Kalends of July [18 June], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III [Col. 0380C].

XCVI. . . . . To the bishop [Note: Abrard II held the see of Uzès from 1203 to 1207. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 623. See also *Histoire générale de Languedoc*, vol. III, p. 121.] and the provost [Note: Bernard, provost of Uzès, is known from documents of 1203. But in 1205 Alberic, also called Albricius and elsewhere Alancus, occurs. [Col. 0380D] *Gallia Christiana*, cited place, col. 648.] of Uzès. He annuls letters of confirmation obtained concerning the administration of certain canons of Nîmes. (Lateran, 17 Kalends of July [15 June].)

At the representation of the beloved son . . . . provost of Nîmes [Note: He was probably Frotard, whom the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* mention in 1199, ibid., col. 466. His successor, William of Casulis, appears in documents only in 1233. Ibid.], it has come to our hearing that certain canons of the Church of Nîmes, accused of dilapidation or other crimes, are trying to obtain from us letters confirming their administrations while suppressing the fact of their religious status and profession. Since the Apostolic See is not accustomed personally to confirm anything for regular persons, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, supported by our authority, you declare void and without effect such confirmations as you know have been obtained in this manner by those canons, since they are regulars. But if not both . . . you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of July [15 June], in the seventh year.

XCVII. . . . . To the bishop [Note: Reginald I, surnamed Surdelle, then occupied the see of Laon. We know from documents that he governed this church from 1201 until 1210. *Gallia Christiana* [Col. 0382D], vol. IX, col. 536.] and chapter of Laon. That they admit to the sacerdotal prebend the person whom Hubald, subdeacon and canon of the Church of Laon, shall nominate when it falls vacant, by reason of the authority given him by the bishop. (Lateran, 10 Kalends of July [22 June].)

[Col. 0381A]

Our beloved son Hubald, our subdeacon and a canon of your church, appeared before us and humbly informed us that you, brother bishop, gave him authority to confer the sacerdotal prebend which should first fall vacant in your church. W., of good memory, [Note: Book III, letter 14.] archbishop of Reims and then legate of the Apostolic See, strictly commanded you, sons, chapter, by our authority, [Col. 0381B] as appears from his letters directed to you and read before us, that, when a sacerdotal prebend in your church became vacant, you should receive to it, without the intervention of any other person, the person to whom the aforesaid subdeacon wished to confer it, and should take care to invest that person in it without any difficulty.

The same subdeacon also asserted that, when he was about to approach the Apostolic See, he made a precautionary appeal, lest you, brother bishop, should perhaps meanwhile confer any sacerdotal prebend that might become vacant upon anyone, or lest you, sons, chapter, should receive anyone presented to it other than the person whom the aforesaid subdeacon should see fit to present.

Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, when it falls vacant, you admit without any opposition the person upon whom the said subdeacon shall canonically see fit to confer the sacerdotal prebend. We firmly prohibit you, brother bishop, from presuming meanwhile to confer any sacerdotal prebend upon anyone contrary to the terms of your concession. Otherwise, know that we have commanded our beloved sons . . . . the chancellor, and Helvin and Adam, canons of Paris, to compel you to do this by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, rendering void whatever they learn has been attempted contrary to the concession made to the aforesaid subdeacon concerning the sacerdotal prebend after his lawful appeal to us had been lodged.

Since concessions of this sort, if made into a precedent, could be used to evade the canonical enactment by which ecclesiastical benefices are forbidden to be granted or promised before they fall vacant, we do not wish that, on account of this mandate, which contains a personal favour, permission be given to those wishing to commit such an evasion.

Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of July [22 June], in the seventh year.

XCVIII. To the chapter of Vicenza. He confers the provostship of Vicenza by apostolic authority upon Nicholas, his subdeacon. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of July [24 June].)

[Col. 0382A]

We, being solicitous for the provision of each individual, ought to instil more abundantly the dew of apostolic blessing upon those in whom learning and uprightness are joined in a certain sweet union by a social bond. For such persons, who season uprightness with learning and adorn learning with uprightness, ought the more readily to be advanced to ecclesiastical benefices, inasmuch as, by the provision made for such men, the advantage is secured no less of the Churches in which they are received than of the men themselves.

Now, since the provostship of your church, as was lately reported to us, had been vacant so long that, according to the statutes of the Lateran Council, its bestowal had devolved upon us, wishing to confer upon you a special favour of our own, we had intended to admonish you by letter and, in admonishing you, to command that you should confer it, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for ourselves, upon our beloved son Nicholas, our subdeacon—whom, in view of the devotion which he is known to bear toward us and the Roman Church, we hold alike dear and acceptable—especially since, as had been reported to us, many of you consented to him; and that, every obstacle of contradiction removed, you should do so, thereby obtaining for yourselves a favour from us.

But when letters on this matter had been drawn up and publicly read in audience, … a cleric arrived and, on your behalf, the archdeacon’s sons, Al. de Bragantiis, Gabriel Pizo, Clari, and A., a priest, produced letters stating that we had commanded certain of your brethren to intend to set that same N. over them as provost, although no dignity or prebend in your church was vacant, except that of one simple canon, who had entered upon the way of all flesh in that year.

The said letters also stated that the provostship had been neither a dignity nor a personatus in the Church of Vicenza, but a certain simple administrative office, customarily conferred, at the canons’ discretion, sometimes upon clerics and sometimes upon laymen. Finally, since the office of such administration had formerly been entrusted to Master Guido, and because he prudently exercised the charge imposed upon him, he was not deprived of that office before he was deprived of life, nor did he cease from such administration before he died.

Moreover, when that same P. produced letters of procuration on behalf of certain of you, through our beloved son M. [Note: Book III, letter 45, note.], cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore—whom we granted him as auditor—we learned what he wished to submit and what the aforesaid letters contained.

Therefore, considering that our authority in conferring a favour is no less than yours, and granting to the same subdeacon the favour which you granted to the aforesaid master, we commit to him the office of administration which that master held in the Church of Vicenza, to be held by him so long as he lives and administers well. But if—God forbid!—he is found to be a wasteful steward and does not prudently discharge his office, then, upon your complaint and after the truth of the matter has been investigated and established, we shall see to his removal from that office according to the measure of his deserts.

We therefore admonish your discretion and earnestly exhort you, and by apostolic writings command and enjoin you, not to hinder him from laudably carrying out the office committed to him by us. Know that we have commanded our beloved sons Bono John of Saint Mary of Vercelli, and Tiso of Treviso, our subdeacons, and Dionysius, canon of Padua, to place him in corporal possession thereof and, once placed, to protect him by our authority, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, without regard to appeal.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of July. Letters were written to them concerning this.

XCIX. … TO THE BISHOP OF PASSAU.

[Note: Cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §75.]

[Note: Wolfker—otherwise Walter, otherwise Wolbert—a nobleman of Ellenbrechtschirchen, formerly provost of Celle and likewise a canon of Passau, was in 1191 elected bishop of Passau in the place of Dietpold, by the unanimous votes of all. He was, it is said, a man endowed with divine eloquence and exceedingly learned in sacred letters. In 1197 he departed for the East; on returning thence in 1198, he attached himself to the party of Philip of Swabia. In 1200 he was the principal author of peace between Emeric—otherwise Hemmerad—king of Hungary, and his brother Andrew. In 1202 he was summoned to Rome with other prelates who obstinately supported Philip. Wolfker obeyed the command, came to Rome, and cleared himself, at the same time promising that in the affair of the Empire, then at its height, he would comply with the pontiff’s will. Innocent himself testified to him that this promise would not prejudice the rights of the Empire, in letters given in this very year 1204, 11 Kalends of June; these may be read in the Register concerning the Affair of the Empire, letter 110.

So far concerning Wolfker, bishop of Passau; these particulars have been drawn from Hansiz, *Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 337 ff. A few points must be added concerning him after his election to the patriarchate of Aquileia.

Authentic letters of Innocent, of unquestionable authority, which we now produce, establish that Wolfker, having been called to the patriarchal see of Aquileia, could not have transferred there before this year, 1204. Accordingly, that document is shown to be erroneous in its chronological notices which Mittarellus published from the archive of Saint Matthias of Murano, *Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, Appendix, col. 256. In it Wolcherius, patriarch of Aquileia, gives a definitive judgment in a certain suit against the monastery of Saint Michael of Lemo in the year there said to be 1203, indiction VI, on the fourth day before the beginning of November. Plainly 1204 should be read.

Be that as it may, Wolfker, adorned with the patriarchal mitre, was very dear to Innocent and, after Innocent, to Pope Honorius III. As their legate *a latere*, he reconciled the Venetians and Paduans and attended the Lateran Council in 1215. He died about the year 1219. UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 71.]

He grants him authority, since he had been elected patriarch of Aquileia, to decide at his own discretion whether to transfer to that metropolitan see or remain in the see of Passau. (Lateran, 8 July.)

Since P., patriarch of Aquileia, of good memory, lately entered upon the way of all flesh, as it pleased the Lord, the canons of the Church of Aquileia, assembling together, with the assent of the nobles and ministeriales, unanimously agreed to request you from us. To obtain the assent of the Apostolic See to their request, they sent into our presence our venerable brother … bishop of Concordia, and our beloved sons S., master of the schools, and W., canons of Aquileia, together with certain vassals and ministeriales of the Church of Aquileia.

[Note: Wolderic, known in documents of about the period with which we are concerned. UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 332.]

Although your prudence and uprightness were known to us, yet, because your intention was not known, we could not—and ought not—immediately approve such a request without qualification, lest it result in a loss rather than an increase of your honour.

For, since you are bound to the Church of Passau, your bride, by the bond of spiritual marriage, you cannot marry another according to canonical sanctions unless you have first been released from the law and prior bond of the former. Hence, if we, as the Vicar of Him, were first to dissolve the spiritual marriage established by the Lord between you and the Church of Passau, before it were known to us whether you consented to the Church of Aquileia; and if, when this bond had been dissolved, you did not permit yourself to be transferred to the metropolitan church of Aquileia, you would thus accept the one only to lose the other, and what was believed to have been arranged for an increase of greater honour and burden would turn to the detriment of your honour.

Therefore, desiring to provide for the Church of Aquileia, which is a special daughter of the Apostolic See, without injury to the Church of Passau, and nevertheless to show due regard for your honour, we admonish and earnestly exhort your fraternity, and by apostolic writings command you, after carefully weighing the condition of each, if you believe that you can benefit the metropolitan Church of Aquileia without detriment to the Church of Passau, not to refuse consent to the request made concerning you within eight days after you have been asked.

Otherwise, if one cannot be aided without injury to the other, it is safer to aid neither than to injure one, as we know that you have read. And lest the Church of Aquileia be obliged to trouble the Apostolic See again by making a fresh request for you, we have commanded our venerable brother … archbishop of Salzburg and the bishop of Gurk that, if you decide to give your assent to such a request, they, supported by our authority, shall release from the bond by which it was joined to you the Church of Passau, and likewise, once you have been released from it, grant you leave to transfer to the Church of Aquileia.

[Note: It has already been mentioned often concerning him.]

[Note: Wernher was created in 1192 and died in 1212. BUCELIN, *Germania Sacra*, part I, p. 49.]

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of July.

Letters were written to them concerning this.

C. TO J., BISHOP OF FORCONA.

[Note: For the bishopric formerly called Forcona, now L’Aquila, consult UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 415. John, bishop of Forcona, to whom this letter and also the letter immediately to be presented, no. 112 of this seventh book, are addressed, was transferred to the Church of Palestrina in 1208. The same, ibid., col. 422.]

He confirms by apostolic authority a grant of the hamlet of Saint Gusano [otherwise Eusano], made by Roger, king of Sicily, to the bishop of Forcona. The instrument of donation is inserted. Lateran, 17 Kalends of July.

“It is customary to assent,” etc., down to “bestow.” Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority the donation of the hamlet of Saint Gusano, made by Rog., king of Sicily of illustrious memory, to Berard, bishop of Forcona of good memory, as is contained in the authentic instrument of that king; etc., down to “we fortify.”

[Note: This same Berard, in 1187, if Ughelli is to be believed, offered William the Good, king of Sicily, six knights and twelve serjeants for the service of the Holy Land, by reason of the fiefs which he held from that king. Ibid., col. 422.]

For the greater security of this matter, we have judged that the authentic instrument of the aforesaid king should be inserted word for word in this document of ours. Its tenor is as follows:

“In the name of the Lord God eternal and of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Roger, by the clemency of God, king of Sicily, of the duchy of Apulia, and of the principality of Capua. While we were residing in our palace at Terracina [otherwise Taranto], near Salerno, with our dearest son Rog., duke of Apulia, and the counts and magnates and other barons of our kingdom, Berard, venerable bishop of Forcona, coming before us, earnestly besought our clemency that we should permit him to build, within the territory of his bishopric, a castle called Collepaydonis. We, in accordance with our accustomed practice, assented to his request and granted what he sought.

“Moreover, we granted to the same bishop, out of our customary liberality and piety, the hamlet of Saint Gusano, concerning which a dispute between the aforesaid bishop and the bishop of Sinicium was heard before our presence and which, by judgment of the court, came to our regalian rights; believing that the said bishop would thereby be more faithful and obedient to our kingdom.

“For the remembrance and inviolable confirmation of this our gift and grant, we caused this present writing to be sealed with our seal and written by the hand of our notary Robert.

“Given in the city of Salerno, by the hand of Robert, our chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, in the month of November, indiction XI, and in the seventeenth year of the reign of Lord Rog., by God’s grace most glorious king of Sicily, of the duchy of Apulia, and of the principality of Capua. Happily. Amen, amen, amen.”

“Let no one therefore,” etc. “This document of our confirmation,” etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of July.

CI. … TO THE BISHOP OF AVIGNON … TO THE BISHOP OF TRICASTIN … AND TO THE BISHOP OF CAVAILLON.

[Note: The name of Rostagnus II de Margaritis, bishop of Avignon, first appears in documents from the year 1185. For safeguarding the liberty of the citizens of Avignon, he made many useful enactments and issued letters granting them numerous immunities in 1198. He is said in his epitaph to have died on 2 Kalends of July, 1209. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 815.]

[Note: Bertrand, who took his surname from the small town in the district of Tricastin called Petralata—Pierre-late in French—whether because he was native there or because its lordship belonged to his family, succeeded William I, surnamed Hugh, after 1193 and before 1198. He was still in office in 1205. Before his death he is reported to have abdicated, in order to withdraw and live for God and himself until his soul, released from the body, passed to heaven; this occurred about 1206. It is noted of him that in his letters he commonly styled himself supreme lord. Ibid., col. 713.]

[Note: The Church of Cavaillon or Cabellicum was then governed by Bertrand I. The records of Saint Andrew show that his surname was de Duroforti—Durefort in French—and that, before becoming bishop of Cavaillon about 1203, he had served there as sacristan. He held the see until 1222. Ibid., col. 946.]

He directs them to ensure strict observance of the sentence of interdict pronounced against the provost and canons of Sisteron in a dispute between them and the brothers of the Order of the Temple concerning a certain oratory. Lateran, 11 Kalends of July.

Since a dispute had long been conducted between our beloved sons, the brethren of the military Order of the Temple, on one side, and the provost and canons of Sisteron, on the other, concerning the construction of an oratory which the brethren proposed to build near the city of Sisteron, at length, both parties being present before us and their arguments having been more fully understood, we judged, by the common counsel of our brethren, that the following disposition should be made.

[Note: William II, provost of Sisteron, is mentioned in documents of the years 1174, 1202, and 1205, 12 Kalends of May. Ibid., col. 506.]

The provost and chapter of Sisteron, if they wished, were to receive from the Templars within two months sufficient security that no damage or prejudice whatsoever could arise to the mother church from that oratory; and, having done so, the brethren should have free authority, according to their privileges, to complete the aforesaid oratory. But should the said provost and canons refuse to accept that security, we granted the Templars apostolic authority to build an oratory, according to the tenor of their privileges, beyond the place where they had begun construction, wherever they preferred, provided it was upon their own ground, notwithstanding anyone’s opposition or appeal.

We also commanded you, brothers bishops of Avignon and Tricastin, earnestly to admonish the aforesaid provost and canons and to endeavour to induce them to accept, for themselves and the Church of Sisteron, the security offered by the Templars as stated above, and thereafter in no way to hinder construction of the oratory beyond that place, as has been set forth above; and, should they presume to act contrary to this, to restrain them by ecclesiastical censure.

But, as became known to us from the tenor of your letters, after you had diligently admonished the aforesaid provost and canons three times by your letters not in any way to hinder the brethren who wished to build an oratory upon their own ground, they utterly despised your admonitions, disgracefully threw away the letters sent by you, and did not fear to demolish by armed force the work on the oratory which had been begun. On that account you pronounced sentences of interdict against them as contumacious persons, and they utterly refused to observe them.

Therefore, lest they be able to rejoice with impunity in their rebellion, and so that those who will not return through devotion may at least be recalled to obedience by the punishment of ecclesiastical severity—if perhaps they are granted to return to their senses and affliction gives understanding—we command and strictly enjoin your fraternity by apostolic writings to ensure that the aforesaid sentence of interdict is firmly observed. Compel the said provost and canons, by sentence of excommunication and deprivation of their benefices, every occasion and obstacle of appeal removed, to render full satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted upon the brethren of the house of the military Order of the Temple, and henceforth utterly to cease troubling them over the construction of the oratory according to the form given by us.

Further, command and cause the aforesaid sentences to be publicly proclaimed in the churches of neighbouring dioceses every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, until, repenting of their error, they return with due humility to obedience to the Church. Likewise compel their accomplices and supporters, by ecclesiastical censure and without regard to appeal, to render the aforesaid brethren due satisfaction in this matter and utterly to desist from harassing them. And if not all of you … two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of July, in the seventh year.

CII. TO THE NOBLE MAN JOHN ODDONIS, OUR KINSMAN.

[Note: Cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77.]

He grants him lordship over Montorio and another castle named Caminaras, following the counsel of the city judges. (The judges’ counsel is inserted.) Lateran, 8 Kalends of July.

“To just petitioners,” etc., down to “fulfil.” We have received the counsel which the learned men of the city gave us concerning your affair; and, for greater caution, we insert it in these present letters:

“In the name of the Lord. Amen. We give you counsel, lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme and universal pope—we judges, namely Henry of Trastevere, Paul Consalinus, Oddo de Insula, Peter Malpilii, Andrew of Trastevere, and Andrew Bulgaminus; and assessors and advocates, Nicholas Tullius, John Bartholomaei, Oddo John Tiniosi, Bartholomew Peter Nicolai, and Nicholas John Bonifacii—that you invest John Oddonis, a Roman, with the whole castle called Montorio, inside and outside, together with all the possessions, appurtenances, and holdings of the said castles; and that you make and constitute this John the true possessor of the said castles, their possessions, and holdings; and that you and your successors for the time being defend him perpetually in the said possession and cause him to be stoutly defended.

“For it is clear to us that, upon the complaint of the said John Oddonis, you caused Abaiamonte of Montorio and O., his son, who presume violently to detain the said castles, namely Montorio and Caminatas [otherwise Caminaras], to be lawfully summoned several times, that they should render justice before you to the said John Oddonis concerning the said castles, possessions, appurtenances, and holdings. You granted those same Abaiamonte and O., his son, complete safe-conduct in going, returning, and litigating; yet they despised coming and obeying the law, and have always been contumacious and rebellious. Accordingly, you excommunicated Abaiamonte and Oddo, his son, and caused their excommunication to be published.

“Given over to a reprobate mind, they persisted obstinately for many years under the aforesaid anathema and excommunication, and do not cease even now to persist therein; they have always been contumacious and still are. We recognize that this ought to be done according to law and custom, and that you should cause this charter to be impressed with the seal of the Holy Roman Church.”

Given before Lord Hugh, by God’s grace cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustachius, in the seventh year of our pontificate [perhaps: of your pontificate], indiction VII, on the ninth day of June, written by the hand of Andrew, assessor and judge of Trastevere, by the common will and command of the aforesaid judges and advocates.

[Note: Book III, letter 15, note.]

We therefore, in accordance with the tenor of the foregoing counsel, caused you through our beloved sons, the noblemen Od. de Palumbaria and Rayner John de Paulo, to be placed in corporal possession of the aforesaid things; and, by a second decree, constituted you their true possessor. Let no one, therefore, infringe this document of our constitution and investiture, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of July.

CIII. TO THE NOBLEWOMAN … DAUGHTER OF THE LATE JUDGE OF GALLURA.

That, in contracting a marriage, she should follow the advice of the archbishop of Torres. (Lateran, 6 Nones of July.)

[Note: See Book VI, letters 29, 144, and following.]

We take it gratefully and acceptably that, following in the footsteps of your late … father, judge of Gallura, you persevere in devotion to the Church and desire to order your affairs in accordance with his provision and counsel. For he left both you and his land under the protection of the Apostolic See. But in contracting a marriage you commit yourself to our counsel; and therefore we the more earnestly seek your honour, because from this we receive a greater indication of your devotion and a more certain proof of your reverence.

We therefore admonish your nobility and exhort you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic writings to follow, in this matter, the counsels of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Torres, as we trust in your devotion and you hope in our favour.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Nones of July.

In almost the same terms, letters were written to the girl’s mother down to “we command,” as follows: that, awaiting our pleasure and command in this matter, she should not presume to unite her daughter to anyone, but should instead send our venerable brother, the bishop of Civita, into our presence, so that with him we may more fully determine what must be determined and carry out what has been determined.

CIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CAGLIARI, CONCERNING THE SAME MATTER. (Lateran, 6 Nones of July.)

We know that it has not escaped your fraternity how the late judge of Gallura, being at the point of death, left both his land and his daughter under the protection of the Apostolic See. Therefore, desiring to provide for that girl in accordance with her father’s intention, we propose to give her in marriage to a lawful husband through whom no discord may be stirred up in Sardinia but rather be quieted; one who can reasonably be suspected by none of the judges and who may therefore be better able to govern the judicature of Gallura in peace.

We therefore admonish your fraternity, exhort you in the Lord, and by apostolic writings command and strictly enjoin you: since you hold her castles, do not presume to assign them to anyone before we have provided the girl with a husband; rather, comply with the counsels and admonitions of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Torres. Otherwise, you shall present yourself before us to make satisfaction for so great a contempt. And, that our purpose may be more effectively completed, send in the meantime our venerable brother, the bishop of Civita, into our presence, so that with him we may more fully determine what must be determined and carry out what has been determined.

Given at the Lateran, as above.

CV. TO THE BISHOPS AND NOBLEMEN, FREE MEN RESIDING IN THE JUDICATURE OF GALLURA, CONCERNING THE SAME MATTER.

“It has not escaped your entire community,” etc., down to “in marriage.” We therefore admonish your entire community and earnestly exhort you, and command you by apostolic writings, that concerning this our command and pleasure, etc., as in the letter sent to the girl’s mother.

CVI. TO THE NOBLE MAN … JUDGE OF CAGLIARI, CONCERNING THE SAME MATTER. (Lateran, 5 Nones of July.)

That, in order to remove the scandal which had arisen in Sardinia and restore concord, you prudently removed from the judicature of Gallura the nobleman G., marquis, who wished to take as wife the noblewoman H., daughter of … the late judge of Gallura, and that at apostolic request and command you released … son of the late judge of Arborea, we regard as all the more grateful and acceptable because from this we receive a greater indication of your devotion and a more explicit proof of your sincerity.

We also commend in the Lord your prudence in having asked us by your letters not to give the aforesaid girl—whom her late father placed under our protection—as wife to a person who is suspect, but to one who would render us due service and on whose account Sardinia could not again be disturbed. Therefore, since we accept your counsel, which we judge salutary, we admonish and earnestly exhort your nobility, and command you by apostolic writings, not to permit that girl to be matrimonially united to anyone; for we intend shortly, God willing, to provide her with a suitable husband, one reasonably suspect neither to you nor to the noble man … judge of Torres.

Accordingly, carry out this apostolic command in such a manner that we ought on this account to give special attention to your honour and advantage.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Nones of July.

In almost the same terms, to the judge of Torres.

CVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TORRES.

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §79.]

Since the judge of Torres and his wife were related in the fourth and fifth degrees of consanguinity, while a grave scandal would otherwise arise from a divorce, he entrusts the case to the prelate’s discretion. (Lateran, 6 Nones of July.)

You informed us by your letters that the nobleman … judge of Torres and his wife … are mutually related in the fourth and fifth degrees of consanguinity; and that they have shown each other marital affection for so long that they have had a son, to whom the land has already sworn allegiance, and two daughters, one of whom has married a husband. Since that woman is the mother of the nobleman Hugh de Basso, judge of Arborea, such scandal is feared if a divorce is pronounced between them that it is believed to displease even themselves; for they have remained thus joined since the time of Pope A., our predecessor of happy memory.

Nevertheless, the judge asks that either he be permitted by us to remain with his wife, or, after a divorce has been pronounced, to contract another marriage. If this is done, he declares that he will dismiss the concubines whom, because he has long abstained from his wife, he keeps according to the depraved custom of the country, and whom in the meantime he testifies that he cannot dismiss.

Therefore, since you do not doubt the law but we have doubt concerning the scandal, we entrust the matter to your discretion, that, relying on our authority, you may do what appears to you more expedient.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Nones of July.

CVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SARDINIA.

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §79.]

He commands them to supply the archbishop of Torres, labouring for the Roman pontiff, with necessities for his maintenance. (Lateran, 5 Nones of July.)

Since no one is compelled to serve as a soldier at his own expense, we are greatly astonished and troubled that, when our venerable brother, the archbishop of Torres, travels to various parts of Sardinia on our business, you refuse him necessities with detestable greed, though you ought to show hospitality both to him and to others, especially since provisions cannot be found for sale in certain regions of Sardinia.

Therefore, since this redounds to the injury and contempt of the Apostolic See, we command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic writings, whenever the same archbishop goes forth to conduct our affairs and should happen to turn aside to you, to make reasonable provision for his expenses in such a manner that he may deservedly commend your devotion. Otherwise, know that we have commanded the same archbishop to compel you by a sentence of suspension to send suitable messengers to the Apostolic See to make satisfaction for so great a contempt.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Nones of July.

CIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA.

[Note: A fragment of this letter, enclosed here in brackets at the beginning, is printed by Raynaldus under the year 1204, §79. See Book VI, letters 17, 18, 27, 28, and following.]

[Note: See Book III, letter 9, note.]

That the marquis of Cagliari should swear fealty to the Roman Church, since Sardinia belongs by right and ownership to that Church. (Lateran, 5 Nones of July.)

[That the island of Sardinia belongs by right and ownership to the Apostolic See, and that its judges ought and are accustomed to render an oath of fealty to the Roman Church, has not escaped your fraternity.]

Accordingly, since you are bound to defend our rights, we cannot but wonder that you are said to have hindered the nobleman … marquis of Cagliari from swearing to us and to the Roman Church, on the ground that you had exacted and received an oath from him; although we have already commanded him twice that, notwithstanding the oath rendered to you, he should render us the oath of fealty due.

Therefore, since you ought not to usurp or otherwise disturb our rights, we command and enjoin your fraternity by apostolic writings to direct the same marquis by your letters, notwithstanding the oath which he rendered to you, to see that he swears fealty to us and to the Roman Church, as we have already commanded him twice. Take diligent care lest, if you act otherwise, wishing to maintain beyond what is due the fealty received from him, you improperly preserve the oath of fealty rendered to the Roman Church and thus deserve to lose your privilege by abusing the power granted to you.

Given as above.

CX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TORRES.

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §79.]

That he ought not to defer to the archbishop of Pisa except when the latter is in the province of Torres, although he possesses from the Apostolic See privileges of legation and primacy in Sardinia. (Lateran, 5 Nones of July.)

Although we do not wish to trouble our venerable brother, the archbishop of Pisa, and his Church concerning the privilege of legation and primacy granted to him by our predecessors and afterwards confirmed by us, nevertheless we neither wish nor ought to permit him to abuse the favour of the Apostolic See and turn to the burden of subjects what was granted him for their care and benefit.

Therefore, since at stated times he may exercise the office of legation in Sardinia by our authority, we command your fraternity by apostolic writings: when, at the times appointed, he visits that land according to the tenor of the privilege granted to the Church of Pisa, so long as he remains in that province, give heed to him as legate of the Apostolic See. But when he is absent, or comes at another time, you are not bound to answer him in any respect by authority of his legation. By authority of primacy, moreover, he has no greater power in the province of Torres than canonical sanctions grant to all primates.

Given as above.

CXI. TO THE PRELATES OF EXEMPT CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN SARDINIA.

[Note: Raynaldus prints this letter, though mutilated, under the year 1204, §80.]

He rebukes them because they resort to secular tribunals. (Lateran, 5 Nones of July.)

Since all things work together for good to those who love God, we infer from the fact that you do not love God that good things work in you toward evil, and that liberty degenerates into the worst slavery. For we have received word that, on the ground of the exemption with which the Apostolic See has endowed you, you endeavour to vindicate for yourselves and your churches a liberty which is true servitude, while you despise the ecclesiastical forum and even litigate ecclesiastical cases before a secular judge, asserting that you are subject to no judges except earthly ones.

[Since this insolence of liberty redounds to the prejudice of the Church, we command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic writings that, whenever a dispute arises among you, you are not to drag one another before a secular court contrary to canonical sanctions, nor litigate before the judges of the land or their officials, especially in ecclesiastical cases. Rather, pursue your claim against ecclesiastical persons through us, or through our legate when he is in Sardinia, or through arbitrators chosen by the fathers. Otherwise, since he who abuses a power granted to him deserves to lose his privilege, and since you do not know how to use liberty, we shall reduce you to perpetual servitude.]

Given as above.

CXII. [Note: [Col. 0393D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §79.] . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TURRITANO. He grants him authority to correct corrupt and disorderly clerics. (Lateran, 3 July.)

If you desire to root out thorns and briars from the Lord’s field, whose cultivation the Lord has entrusted to you, so that the seed which is the word of God may not fall among thorns but may bear fruit all the more abundantly as the ground into which it falls has been more deeply cleared and more diligently cultivated, you are laudably fulfilling your office. You show that you have marked—not merely superficially, but to the marrow—that which the Lord said to the prophet: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, that you may pluck up and destroy, and overthrow, and build, and plant” (Jer. 1).

We therefore rejoice that, with the wicked miserably destroyed, you wish to lease your vineyard to other husbandmen; and that, after removing from the church of Turritano the . . . . . archpriest and canons, who have no taste for anything canonical but rather are devoid of sense and entangle themselves in worldly allurements, you intend to plant there shoots of canonical religious life. Since, therefore, no delay or difficulty ought to be brought against proper arrangements, by the authority of these presents we grant your fraternity that, if this can be done without scandal, you may establish regular canons in that church, the impediment of appeal being removed, in accordance with the devout purpose of your mind; provided that you make suitable provision elsewhere for the aforementioned archpriest and canons, unless perhaps some of them wish to put on the habit of religion in the same church and thereafter live there under a rule.

But if scandal should arise from this, apply yourself diligently and prudently to correcting the archpriest and canons themselves, as is known to belong to your office; and, after prior warning, restrain by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside, those who set themselves against your correction.

Given as above.

CXIII. [Note: [Col. 0393D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §80.] TO THE NOBLEMAN . . . . . JUDGE OF TURRITANO. That he is not to interfere in clerics’ lawsuits or impede ecclesiastical liberty. (Lateran, 3 July.)

Since natural law forbids you to do to others what you do not wish done to yourself, you ought to take all the more diligent care not to attempt an injury against God when you are forbidden to commit an offense against a human being. Certainly, “weight and weight, measure and measure,” both are [Note: [Col. 0394D] Thus; something is missing.] an abomination before God; you must weigh this with careful reflection, lest you measure for the Lord otherwise than you wish men to measure [Col. 0394B] for you [Note: [Col. 0394D] Thus; something is missing.], and lest you usurp over His ministers that jurisdiction which you would not endure others to claim over your own ministers.

For although some clerics do not observe clerical propriety, but dishonor the insignia of clerical service by the shameful repute of a base life, their disgrace nevertheless does not, by divine authority, remove them from being subject to ecclesiastical judgment, which is God’s; and, as a servant stands or falls to his own master, so it is—as the continual example of those of your household and your servants plainly shows you, if we compare small matters with great. For if your servant commits an offense and is deservedly defamed for the crime committed, does your jurisdiction therefore pass to another, so that one who was your subject before his fault passes into another’s servitude after his offense, and you cannot punish or take action against him, however grievously he may offend you?

We grieve, moreover, that, attending to this less than was fitting, you have treated clerics called into the Lord’s portion, who are the Lord’s inheritance and for whom the Lord is their inheritance, as though you considered the Lord your equal. You not only judge them yourself, but have them judged by your subjects, and reduce them to such servitude that they are compelled, at a lay command, to give testimony in civil cases before a secular judge. And although canonical law does not admit trials by red-hot iron, cold water, and the like, wretched priests are compelled to bless and attend such proceedings; and, if they refuse to obey those compelling them, they are punished by the officials in whose [Col. 0394D] jurisdiction they live with a monetary penalty.

Furthermore, although churches, according to the custom of the land, possess their own serfs, they nevertheless cannot exercise the jurisdiction due over them, since in civil causes as well as others they are compelled to submit to secular judgment. Moreover—and this is worse—you judge not only ordinary priests, but also their superiors, and you strive to claim jurisdiction over the Lord’s anointed and, through them, over Christ the Lord.

Would that, dearest son, you considered carefully how terrible it is to fall into the hands of the living God, to store up [Col. 0395A] wrath for yourself on the day of wrath, and to provoke against yourself the indignation of the Most High! Would that you weighed with diligent reflection that it profits a man nothing if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul, nor can a man give an adequate exchange for his soul! Would that, in accordance with the saying of the wise man, you remembered your last things, so that, understanding that there is no redemption in hell, you would now, while you have time, do good to all, and especially honor churches and ecclesiastical men and uphold them in their proper liberty. Take careful care lest, if you despise the Church in the present, you seek its aid in vain in the future, and cannot obtain that any ordinary priest dip the tip of his finger in water and cool your tongue, if you now proudly [Col. 0395B] despise those in whom the Lord declares that He is honored and despised, and to whom He Himself says in the Gospel: “He who touches you touches me, and he who touches you touches the pupil of my eye!”

We therefore admonish your nobility and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: since every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, do not stretch out your rash hands against Him who bestowed earthly power upon you, nor usurp for yourself undue jurisdiction over His ministers and servants, lest you be stripped of what is yours while you covet what belongs to others. Know that one deserves to lose a privilege who abuses authority granted to him. Therefore strive to root out from your land this vice of presumption and abuse, and preserve ecclesiastical men [Col. 0395C] and churches in their liberty, leaving them to ecclesiastical judgment. Thus, when you honor God’s ministers on earth, you may deserve to be honored by Him in heaven and hear—not with the reprobate but with the righteous—these words: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25).

We have, moreover, commanded our venerable brethren . . . . . the archbishops of Turritano, . . . . Calari, and . . . . . Arborea, and their suffragans, ordering them that, unless you desist from the aforesaid acts at their admonition, they are to strike both you and the other judges of Sardinia who compel clerics to litigate in a secular court contrary to canonical enactments, or otherwise rashly violate clerical privilege, with sentence of excommunication, and to have the excommunicated publicly proclaimed [Col. 0395D].

Given as above.

CXIV. [Note: [Col. 0395D] Cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §56. See Letter 87 of Book Six.] TO THE BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM [Note: [Col. 0395D] See Book V, Letter 14, note.] AND THE PROVOST OF MAGDEBURG. Concerning the absolution of the elect of Merseburg. (Lateran, 1 July.)

From the letters of the . . . . elect of Merseburg [Note: [Col. 0395D] Concerning the bishops of Merseburg in the period with which we are now concerned, we find nothing certain in Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 42 [Col. 0396D].] we have learned that our venerable brother G. [Note: [Col. 0396D] Book V, Letter 8, note.], bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication because he could not obey his commands, after he had appealed to us. The same elect therefore humbly requested us mercifully to grant him the benefit of absolution, since he is prepared in every respect to obey our commands.

Accordingly, relying fully upon your discretion, we command you by apostolic letters that, after receiving from the elect a sworn assurance that he will obey our commands without condition, you grant him the benefit of absolution. Have the tenor of this oath put into letters, in which the elect himself is to acknowledge that he has taken such an oath into our hands; and do not delay in sending us those letters sealed with his seal.

But if the archbishop of Magdeburg [Col. 0396B] [Note: [Col. 0396D] See Book V, Letter 8, note.] has not returned to the unity of the Church within two months after receiving these presents, so as to deserve the benefit of absolution, then you, brother bishop, shall associate with yourself two bishops. After you have ordained the same elect priest, you shall, supported by our authority and with the impediment of appeal removed, confer upon him the office of consecration in accordance with the canonical enactments. Once he is consecrated, procure that he be strictly forbidden to render obedience or honor to that archbishop while the latter remains contumacious and rebellious toward us.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of July.

CXV. [Note: [Col. 0396D] See the notes to Letter 100 of this Seventh Book.] TO J., BISHOP OF FURCONENSE, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. He receives him under protection and enumerates the goods belonging to his church. (Lateran, 1 July.)

[Col. 0396C]

Established by divine mercy upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brothers and fellow bishops with more abundant charity and to fortify with apostolic patronage the churches entrusted to their governance. Therefore, etc., down to: following the example of Alexander, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of Furconense, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside; etc., down to: we strengthen it; decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same church, etc., down to: are to be expressed by name:

the greater church of Saint Martin, with the village called Civitas, one half of which belongs to that church, together with its people and possessions; the church of Saint Eusanus, with its chapel, people, and holdings; the castle of Collepaydonis, with its church and holdings; Podium, with its churches and holdings; the church of Saint Justa, with its chapel, people, and holdings; the church of Saint Justin, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Mary of Paganica, with its chapels, [Col. 0397A] people, and holdings; the church of Saint Euphemia, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Guasto, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Peter of Guasto, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Nicholas of Sagetica, with its possessions; the church of Saint Mary of Picentia, with its possessions; the church of Saint Martin of Picentia, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Angel of Besegne, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Peter of Limignan, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Nuntius, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Lucy, with its chapel, people, and holdings; the church of Saint Martin of Oruella, with its chapels, people, and holdings [Col. 0397B]; the church of Saint Scholastica, with its holdings; the church of Saint Mary of Unda, with its holdings; the church of Saint Candidus, with its chapels, people, and holdings; the church of Saint Mary in Planula, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Mary of Banne, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Martin, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Lawrence of Saxa, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Mary of Barano, with its people and holdings; the church of Saint Felix of Monte, with its holdings; the church of Saint Thomas of Troila, with its holdings; and the church of Saint Stephen of Roccha, with its chapels, people, and holdings.

Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you, as you reasonably possess them, the following [Col. 0397C] diocesan chapels subject to you by law [Note: [Col. 0397D] Thus in the copy.]: Bagnum, namely, with its villages, churches, and appurtenances; Castellian, Bagagnium, and Paganica, with their churches, villages, and appurtenances; Telettum, with its churches and appurtenances; Interveram, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Carmardam, with its churches and appurtenances;
