Podium and the village of Picentia, with their churches and appurtenances; Guastum, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Collebrengun., with its churches and appurtenances; Ragnum, with its churches and appurtenances; Pescumavire, with its churches and appurtenances; Sinicium, with Saint Demetrius, Saint [Col. 0397D] John, Saint Martin, and Saint Maurus, with their appurtenances; Stisia, with its churches and appurtenances; Bamili, with its churches and appurtenances; Rocca de Celici, with its churches and appurtenances; Rocca Atonesca, with its churches and appurtenances; Pere and Fossa, with their churches and appurtenances; the village of Unda, with its churches and appurtenances; Turris, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Gegnarum, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Rodium, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Pile, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances [Col. 0398A]; Saxa, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Podium of Saint Mary, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Luculum, with its churches, villages, and other appurtenances; Colementum, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; Tornamparte, with its churches, villages, and appurtenances; the town of Forula, with its two churches and appurtenances; Rocca of Saint Stephen, with its villages; Castellion de Ballo, with its churches and appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Colementis, with its chapels, people, and holdings; and the church of Saint Angel of Tupesclu, with its chapels, people, and holdings.

Furthermore, we decree that no cleric, of whatever order, etc., down to: shall be deemed void. But we prohibit that provosts or, etc., down to: shall be revoked. In addition, by this present decree we prohibit anyone within your diocese from presuming to build anew a church or any oratory without the assent of yourself or your successors, while the privileges of the Roman pontiffs remain unimpaired. Moreover, the liberties and immunities granted by our predecessors, etc., down to: we strengthen. We therefore decree . . . with the authority of the Apostolic See preserved in all things. If, therefore, anyone . . . But to all persons . . .

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of July, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

The following subscriptions were attached to the same diploma:

[Col. 0398C] I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere and of Callistus. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saints Martin and Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Cencius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, and of Pammachius. I, Benedict, cardinal priest of Saint Susanna. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint [Col. 0398D] George at the Golden Veil. I, Ugo, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace. I, John, cardinal of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

CXVI. [Note: [Col. 0397D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1204, §68. UGHELLUS published it in full, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 232; from him the Sammarthani had it reprinted in the older *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 520. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* had it reprinted [Col. 0398D] in vol. X, among the documents, col. 54, chapter LVII. We now present a more accurate text from the Vatican and Conti copies. Letters 9 and 200 of Book Six should certainly be compared.] TO THE CHAPTER OF REIMS. He raises many objections concerning the election of an archbishop, and provides Cardinal G., bishop of Palestrina, as archbishop, should that man consent. (Lateran, 6 July.)

Although it is neither blameworthy nor new that electors’ votes vary in elections of prelates, nevertheless through schisms of this sort—which sometimes arise more from impetuous frivolity than from good zeal—churches commonly suffer harm, as we see and lament has happened to your church.

Certainly, after your archbishop W. of good memory had paid the debt of all flesh, why could you not all assemble together as one? Instead, while some of you objected, others, by impetuous presumption and indiscreet zeal, named our venerable brother . . . bishop of Beauvais as archbishop after an appeal to us had been made; and the church of Reims suffered and burdened itself with heavy expenses.

But after the parties had appeared before us, and after the truth had been fully investigated and ascertained, we rejected, as justice required, the postulation made concerning the bishop of Beauvais. As an act of grace, we deemed that free election should be granted you, commanding you by apostolic letters that, within a month after receipt of our letters, you should meet together, invoke the grace of the Holy Spirit, canonically elect for yourselves a suitable person as shepherd, and have him consecrated bishop as promptly as opportunity permitted. We further added that the Lord would demand an account from you at the examination of strict judgment unless, setting aside human favor and worldly fear, you took care to place over yourselves a person whom, according to your conscience, you considered suitable in spiritual and temporal matters.

We also commanded our venerable brother . . . bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0399D] See note to the cited letter.], and our beloved sons . . . . [Col. 0399C] the abbot of Persenia [Note: [Col. 0399D] See note to the cited letter.] and Master R. of Corzon [Note: [Col. 0399D] See note to the cited letter.], canon of Noyon, that, if perhaps you neglected to carry out the apostolic command, they, supported by our authority, should, setting aside every contradiction and appeal and having God before their eyes, appoint for you as bishop a person suited to so great a burden and honor, and have him consecrated by the suffragans of the church of Reims.

But upon receiving our letters you met in the same place while remaining divided in mind, since you had not yet wiped from your heart’s eyes the cloud of former resentment. You named various persons for yourselves: some of you electing the . . . . provost [Note: [Col. 0399D] We cannot yet determine with certainty who was provost of Reims at that time. Baldwin II is said in documents to have held office from 1192 to 1206. Yet there survive in Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 988, letters of M., provost, B., dean, and the whole chapter of Reims, written in 1202, at least in 1203. From these one may infer that Milo of Nanteuil, son of Gaucher of Châtillon and Lady Helvide of Nantolii, also provost of Roset, whom we know to have succeeded Baldwin, had already held the provostship of Reims from 1202 or 1203 [Col. 0400D]. Milo became bishop of Beauvais in 1217. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 167.]; others the senior archdeacon [Col. 0399D] [Note: [Col. 0400D] Book VI, Letter 9, note.] as shepherd.

Therefore, since you preferred to appeal to the Apostolic See rather than attend the hearing and presence of the aforesaid executors, the concord of the discordant parties choosing our judgment, we granted a hearing to our beloved son J. [Note: [Col. 0400D] In Ughellus and the Sammarthani: T.] . . . . de Porta Carceris, [Col. 0400A] procurator for the party which had deemed the provost to be elected, and his associates; and to O., procurator for the opposing party, and his colleagues. We heard the parties’ allegations and admissions, received witnesses, made their depositions public, and carefully examined all matters.

It was thus alleged before us that the party which had named the provost had treated separately concerning the election, in the house of Hugh of Sparnac, their fellow canon—not only disregarding the opposing party, but even omitting some of those who later agreed with them in the election of the provost. They jointly decreed that, if they could not all agree upon the same person, they would receive as shepherd, pursuant to a compromise, the person whom [Col. 0400B] the dean [Note: [Col. 0400D] See Book V, Letter 149, note.] and the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0400D] In Ughellus and the Sammarthani: “predecessor.”] J. de Porta Carceris and Gervasius, the provost’s nephew—upon whom they jointly conferred this authority—should nominate for them as archbishop in this form.

It was further alleged that, when the . . . . vicedominus had elected the aforementioned archdeacon, appealing that no one should undertake anything to prejudice that election, the dean, as if carried away into fury, without holding any deliberation whatever concerning the provost in the chapter, and without prior common deliberation, suddenly seized the provost and said to his associates: “Let us take this man [Note: [Col. 0400D] In Ughellus and the Sammarthani: “not.”]”—or, in another reading, “Let us atone for this man [Note: [Col. 0400D] In Ughellus and the Sammarthani: *expiamus*]”—and, having thus seized him, while the dean did so, certain others enthroned him and sang the customary acclamations.

Whether, therefore, the dean named the provost pursuant to a deliberation held in Hugh’s house outside the chapter, or suddenly in chapter with no prior [Col. 0400C] deliberation, it is evident that he was named apart from the form of canonical election.

It was further objected that the provost was notorious for the vice of simony, that he had abused the chapter seal, that, as a herniated person [Note: [Col. 0400D] In Ughellus and the Sammarthani: “criminal.”], he suffered from the defect of rupture, and that he had been mutilated in the middle finger of his left hand. Yet the witnesses gave differing reports on this point: some testified that he lacked only the extreme joint of the finger, while others added that he did not possess its whole second joint.

When the canons were examined, they were found not to conflict on this point. For although some hold that certain persons physically impaired, especially those who have lost part of a finger by accident, are to be admitted to clerical office, others hold that those who have suffered losses of limbs are to be prohibited from sacred orders. These positions in no way conflict, since many may be promoted to minor orders who ought by no means effectively to aspire to higher ones. Greater sufficiency is required in those to be promoted to sacred orders than in those established in minor orders; just as greater perfection is required in a priest than in a deacon, in a bishop than in a priest, in an archbishop than in a bishop, in a primate than in an archbishop, and above all these in the supreme pontiff.

Thus four objections were raised against the act and four against the person. Against the act: unlawful compromise, contempt for the brethren, canonical appeal, and impetuous procedure. Against the person: the notoriety of simony, abuse of the seal, the defect of rupture, and mutilation of the finger.

Although nothing was shown or objected against the person of the archdeacon—indeed, he was commended in many respects by many persons—yet it was alleged against the act of his election that, after the dean had appealed to the Apostolic See that no one should proceed to hold an election without the consent of all, or of the greater and sounder part, the vicedominus and his followers, fewer in number, since scarcely a third part of the chapter followed him, lower in dignity, since none of the dignitaries of the church of Reims consented to the vicedominus, and inferior in rank, since none of the priests supported him, had named that archdeacon.

It was alleged also that they had proceeded from indiscreet zeal, since the other party had resolved to nominate for election both the dean of Reims and Chartres [Note: [Col. 0401D] Hugh II, dean of Chartres, is already so called in February 1203 and is still found in office on 17 April 1206. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1201.], a canon of the church of Reims, who had formerly favored the same archdeacon in the earlier affair, and very many prudent and honorable men to be requested of us; none of these did the archdeacon’s party wish to accept, since it aimed not at the Church’s advantage but rather at his promotion.

Furthermore, it was evident from both parties’ admissions that the archdeacon himself held the order of subdeacon. Canon law permits subdeacons, because they too minister at the altars, in a case of necessity and provided that they are of approved religious life and learning, to be elected bishops; but not without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff or metropolitan. Since the church of Reims has no metropolitan other than the Roman pontiff, and we had no knowledge of his election, it was clear that it had been undertaken [Col. 0401D] contrary to canonical form.

After various arguments concerning these and other matters had been made before us, and after we had carefully heard and fully understood the attestations, admissions, and allegations, we took care, with the common counsel of our brethren and as justice required, to reject both elections.

Yet, [Col. 0402A] because the duty of our office and the welfare of the church of Reims required us to provide it with a suitable person as shepherd—lest, if we restored to you once again the liberty of election, you should once again abuse the favor of the Apostolic See, divide the church of Reims, heap new troubles upon old, and add affliction to the afflicted—we turned the eyes of our consideration toward our venerable brother G. [Note: [Col. 0401D] Book V, Letter 8, note.], bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See: a prudent and honorable man, native of the kingdom of France, formerly the first abbot in the Cistercian Order, and, because the merits of his religious life required it, raised by us to the bishopric of Palestrina; a man indeed powerful before God and men in deed and word. We have provided him as ruler for you and for that church, provided only that his consent to this be obtained; for we do not wish to compel one unwilling, but to appoint one consenting.

We therefore admonish your entire body and exhort you in the Lord, and command and strictly enjoin you through apostolic letters that, if that bishop consents to our disposition, you receive him humbly as the shepherd and bishop of your souls, treat him honorably, and render him the obedience and reverence due to him. Know that we have firmly commanded our venerable brother . . . archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 0401D] See Book III, Letter 14, note.], and our beloved sons . . . abbots of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 0401D] See Book V, Letter 109, note.] and Saint Victor of Paris [Note: [Col. 0401D] See Book VI, Letter 168, note.], that, if any persons—which we do not believe—should set themselves against our act [Col. 0402C], they are to restrain them by ecclesiastical coercion, appeal being set aside.

We have likewise commanded them that, if perhaps that bishop does not permit himself to be transferred to the church of Reims, then, setting aside every favor and fear, having God alone before their eyes, and supported by our authority, they are to appoint for you as shepherd, appeal being set aside, a suitable person equal to so great an honor and burden, restraining opponents in the same way.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of July, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

CXVII. TO N. . . . . [Note: [Col. 0401D] The address is absent both from the Vatican copy and from the Conti copy.] He commits to him the case, between G. [Note: [Col. 0401D] Girard, Giraud, or Gerald of Cros [Col. 0402D] (otherwise Wlgrini), formerly archdeacon—see the petition submitted to the archbishop of Bourges in 1195 in BALUZE, *Proofs for the History of the House of Auvergne*, p. 72—who, as appears from this letter of Innocent, was dean of Clermont and was finally appointed successor to William, archbishop of Bourges, after the latter’s death in 1209. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 63.] of Cros, archdeacon of Clermont, on the one side, and the chapter of Clermont and Parent, papal subdeacon, on the other, concerning the deanery of the church of Clermont [Note: [Col. 0402D]

The following, concerning the subject of this letter, should be compared with what is read in *Gallia Christiana*, [Col. 0403D] ibid., col. 313, in its series of deans of Clermont:

“XIII. William I, archdeacon of Clermont, and Peter Parent, canon of Saint Genesius, contested the deanery of Clermont at the beginning of the thirteenth century. To settle this dispute, Pope Innocent III appointed as examiners and judges Hugh d’Anglars, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, and the abbot of Novem-Fontium, of the Premonstratensian Order.

XIV. Gerald, or Girard de Cros [otherwise Wlgrini], later archbishop of Bourges, about the year 1209.”]

. (Lateran, 12 July.)

[Col. 0402D]

Our beloved son G. [Col. 0403A] de Cros, archdeacon of Clermont, appearing before the Apostolic See, humbly requested us to have the sentence reasonably pronounced by our venerable brother . . . bishop of Limoges [Note: [Col. 0403D] Book V, Letter 68, note.] concerning the deanery of the church of Clermont—a sentence already partly put into execution—carried out in its entirety.

But when our beloved sons, the . . . abbot [Note: [Col. 0403D]

It is known that the chapter of Clermont had possessed three dignities—the provost, the abbot, and the dean—from the tenth century onward. Concerning the abbots around the time of Pope Innocent III, only the following few items are found in *Gallia Christiana*, cited place, col. 308:

“VIII. Bertrand de Murol, in 1203, in the cartulary of Saint Illidius.

IX. William d’Aubusson, in a charter of Bishop Robert, 1207.”]
, and G. Dalmas, canon of Clermont, procurators of the beloved sons, the chapter of Clermont, appeared in our presence and took care to set before us that this sentence had been pronounced contrary to justice and after an appeal to us had been lawfully lodged; and that therefore the same archdeacon ought in no respect to be heard upon his petition. The archdeacon, on the other hand, alleged that the said abbot and canon ought not to be received as procurators, since both they and those for whom they had come were bound by the bond of excommunication: for the aforesaid bishop had bound by excommunication all who should set themselves in opposition to the sentence pronounced by him for the aforesaid archdeacon. After litigation on this point for some time, we caused the aforesaid procurators to be absolved as a precaution.

Thereafter, when the same abbot and canon wished to proceed against him, the archdeacon still would not admit them as procurators, because they acted as procurators for persons who remained bound by excommunication and therefore could not bring an action at law on their behalf. And when the same archdeacon would neither admit them as procurators nor make any response whatever to their statements, our beloved son Parentius [Note: See above, note 316.], our subdeacon and a canon of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, opposed him on the other side, asserting that he had been canonically elected dean of the church of Clermont. Accordingly, the said archdeacon ought in no respect to be heard upon his petition, since the deanery belonged not to him but rather to Parentius. The aforesaid archdeacon replied that, until the sentence rendered in his favour had been carried into complete execution, the aforesaid P. ought not to be heard in order to impede the execution of the sentence. To this P. answered that the sentence rendered for the archdeacon by the aforesaid bishop created no prejudice against him, since a matter transacted between others does not prejudice others, but rather the lawful enactments [Note: Thus it is read, erroneously, in the Vatican copy.].

When they had disputed on these matters for some time, we issued an interlocutory ruling that the said P., if he could, should immediately establish the basis of his claim. At length, in order to establish his claim, he produced witnesses and documents. After argument had continued for some time on both sides concerning these, we pronounced by interlocutory judgment that the evidence shown established that Parentius had an interest in opposing the aforesaid archdeacon. Thus, proceedings having been lawfully joined between them both concerning the election and concerning the sentence, the archdeacon was asked before us whether he wished to admit in this trial the depositions previously submitted in the aforesaid interlocutory matter. After deliberation, he replied that he did, provided that he might object both to the persons of the witnesses and to their testimony.

On hearing this, the opposing party answered that it did not wish to use those depositions in this trial, since they had been received, without joinder of issue, not upon the principal matter but upon an incidental issue; accordingly, it wished, concerning the whole affair, to produce either those witnesses or others. The opposing party, however, replied that, since those witnesses had testified both concerning the sentence and concerning the election, and their depositions had been published in court, it was not lawful for that party, after it had learned what had been testified, to produce other witnesses upon the same articles—especially because in this very proceeding that party had used those depositions. We therefore, having heard what was alleged on either side, pronounced, justice requiring it, that witnesses should be received concerning the whole affair, whichever witnesses each party might bring forward.

Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, after receiving witnesses, examining the documents, and diligently hearing the confessions and allegations, you bring this cause, both as to the principal issue and as to the incidental one, to a canonical conclusion, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed; and that you cause what you decree to be firmly observed. And because matters transacted in a chapter cannot easily be proved except by the canons themselves, we will and command that, as a precaution, you absolve those same persons, so that, when called to give testimony, they may freely testify for either party. Witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding no letters, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth Ides of July, in the seventh year. [Note: It should be noted that two letters bearing on the argument treated here are found among the Decretals: one (said to be addressed to the abbots of Novofonte and Casa Dei), Book II, title 20, *On Witnesses and Depositions*, chapter 38; the other (addressed in the Gregorian collection to the bishops of Limoges and Cahors, but in the Innocentian collection to the bishops of Auxerre, Limoges, and Canterbury), Book II, title 28, *On Appeals, Recusations, and References*, chapter 45.]

### CXVIII. N . . . .

[Note: The address is lacking both in the Vatican copy and in the Conti copy.]

That they are to induce the prior and monks of Durham to render the bishop the obedience due to him. (Lateran, fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

The venerable brother, the bishop of Durham [Note: See letter 89 of Book VI.], having complained, be it known to you that it has come to our hearing that . . . the prior [Note: We have already observed that the prior of the church of Durham at that time was Bertram I; WARTH, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 788. Yet this letter of Innocent agrees ill with the history of the bishops of Durham. See Geoffrey of Goldingham, *History of Durham*, ch. 13 and following.], and the monks of Durham withhold from him their customary obedience and the reverence due to him; and, rashly disturbing and attempting many things against his rights, ancient liberties, and praiseworthy customs hitherto observed, and contrary to our prohibition made to them, they have proved injurious and grievous to him in these respects and in many others.

Therefore, desiring to assist our brethren and bishops in maintaining their rights—for we are debtors to all in justice—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior admonition, you compel the said prior and monks, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, humbly and devoutly to render the said bishop the reverence and obedience due and customary, and to make fitting satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted. You are to restore to its former condition whatever you ascertain that they have rashly attempted contrary to the rights of that bishop, the customary liberties and praiseworthy customs hitherto observed, and our prohibition. Notwithstanding no letters, etc. And if not all, etc. Let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.

### CXIX. ASSALITUS, CANON . . .

Dispensation for defect of birth. [Note: See letter 98 of Book VI.] (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of August.)

For this purpose God has established the fullness of ecclesiastical power in the apostolic see: that, after carefully considering the differing circumstances of persons and things, times and places, it may now exercise strictness, now prefer gentleness; at times execute justice, at times bestow favour, according as it sees fit to dispense differently in different cases. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, overcome by your bitter tears and moved by your devout supplications, since we have received on your behalf the commendable testimony of many religious men, and we ourselves know that you have made praiseworthy progress in literary learning, by the authority of these presents we grant to your devotion that, notwithstanding the defect of your birth, you may advance through the ecclesiastical orders as far as the priesthood, and may receive both prebends and dignities to which priestly orders are not attached; provided only that you lead an honourable life, lest you appear to imitate your father’s incontinence, so that, the more worthy of favour you make yourself, the greater favour you ought to obtain. Let no one therefore, etc. This page of our dispensation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the seventh year.

### CXX. N . . . . .

[Note: The address is lacking both in the Vatican copy and in the Conti copy; yet from the already cited letter of Book VI it is clear that this was addressed to the dean and chapter of the church of Saint Yrieix.]

On the same matter. (Lateran, seventh day before the Kalends of August.)

“For this purpose God,” etc., in nearly the same manner, as far as “obtain.” But since our venerable brother O. [Note: He has already been mentioned several times.], bishop of Ostia, formerly legate of the apostolic see in your regions, commanded you to receive the aforesaid Assalitus as canon and brother, and because you raised against him the objection that the defect of his birth stood in his way, and for this reason refused to receive him, the same A. came into our presence and obtained letters to the . . . archbishop of Bordeaux and the . . . abbot of Albareto, requiring that you be compelled to receive him. But you, having uttered an appeal to us, sent to our presence Bernard, a priest, on your behalf, and he sent for himself Master P. Haimeric Boiol. When they requested that their arguments be heard, we appointed as auditor our beloved son L., priest-cardinal of the title of Santa Croce [Note: See letters 5 of Book V, note; and 1 of Book VII, note.]. After he had heard what was put forward before him, we caused letters in a specified form to be sent to our venerable brother . . . bishop, and to our beloved son W. Alboini, our subdeacon and canon of Limoges. Seeing that an adverse decision threatened him from their examination, the same A. lodged an appeal to us.

Since, therefore, the objection which you advanced against him has been abolished by our dispensation, as is set forth above, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, out of reverence for Saint Peter and for us, you admit him as canon and brother, unless some other canonical impediment stands in the way, lest you appear to oppose apostolic benevolence, which admits him to receive ecclesiastical benefice. Otherwise, know that we have commanded our beloved sons . . . the cantor, Arnald de Montel, and Guido Guahan, canons of Limoges, to compel you to this by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside.

Given as above.

The same was written to them concerning this.

### CXXI. N . . . .

[Note: The address is missing in the Conti copy.]

Concerning the ordination by Greek bishops of priests, both Greek and Latin. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of August.)

It was set before us on your behalf that certain priests, both Greeks and Latins, have themselves ordained by Greek bishops without the laying on of hands, and receive all the orders at once outside the Ember seasons, contrary to canonical enactments. Since such presumption must be diligently rooted out, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, relying on our authority, you suspend, appeal being set aside, priests of this kind in your diocese from exercising orders so received—unless perhaps some of them were ordained in this way by Greek bishops with the permission of yourself or of your predecessor; in their case, supply what was omitted by those bishops. Nevertheless, take attentive care that you permit no further clerics of your diocese to be ordained by Greek bishops; and, if any have themselves ordained by them without your permission, suspend them perpetually from exercising orders so received.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

### CXXII. N. . . . . . . N. . . . . . .

[Note: The address is wanting.]

By apostolic authority he confirms the judgment whereby a tithe conferred by the bishop of Amiens upon G., a deacon, was adjudged to him against J. de Canduetre, of the diocese of Noyon, because J. had unjustly seized the same tithe; and he commands that they protect the said G. from all molestation and cause what has been taken from him to be restored. Lateran, sixth day before the Kalends of August.

The beloved son G., deacon, appearing in our presence, humbly informed us that a certain tithe, conferred upon him by the venerable brother . . . bishop of Amiens [Note: “When Theobald III (d’Heilly) died in the very year in which we are now engaged, 1204, his successor was appointed as Richard, born of the ancient family of the vice-lords of Gerberoy, son of the knight Eustace and Ermentrude. He had as brothers the knights Gervase and William. Brought up from youth in the church of Amiens, he had become dean from being a canon, and bishop from being dean. He held the see until 1210, when the see of Amiens is said in documents to have been vacant.” Thus far the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1180. Yet there is a difficulty. They assert that Theobald III died at the end of April in early 1204, and then say that Richard in 1205 had not yet been consecrated. But Innocent here expressly calls the prelate of Amiens “bishop,” not “elect,” as he would have said of a prelate not yet consecrated. It must therefore be said that Theobald died in 1204 according to the old style—that is, in fact in 1205 according to our mode of reckoning—and that this letter of Innocent, given in 1204, still concerns him.], in consideration of piety, had afterwards been unjustly seized by J. de Canduetre of the diocese of Noyon, who asserted that it belonged to him by hereditary right.

The said tithe had been adjudged to G. by definitive judgment of the beloved son . . . abbot of Longpont [Note: Galcherus de Ochies is found in documents as abbot of Longpont from at least 1201—for his predecessor Adam I is said to have died about 1198—until 1219, when he was raised to the headship of the Cistercian Order. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 476.] and W. Norman, canon of Soissons. And, because J. would not restore what he had taken or cease molesting G., a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against him. Finally, through the beloved sons, the dean [Note: From what we have said above, it may be inferred that the dean of Amiens at this time was Richard de Gerboredo (de Gerberoy) himself, who shortly afterwards became bishop. This agrees with what is read in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1218, where Richard, dean from 1191 until November 1204, is said to be found in documents either by his full name or designated by the initial R.] and . . . provost [Note: Concerning the provosts of Amiens, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* say nothing.] and . . . archdeacon of Amiens, both the definitive sentence and the sentence of excommunication had been confirmed by our authority and put into execution.

At last the aforesaid J., concealing the truth of these preceding facts, obtained from us letters to the venerable brother . . . bishop of Noyon and his fellow judges [Note: Book V, letter 41, note], by which he claims to have been absolved. For this reason the aforesaid G. came to the apostolic see a third time and remained for more than eight months, not without great expense; yet no qualified representative appeared for the other party. Therefore, holding the aforesaid definitive judgment to be valid, as it is just, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, since full proof of the foregoing has been made to us both by the letters of the delegates and by those of the aforesaid bishop of Amiens, you compel the oft-mentioned J., his father, and his supporters, by sentence of excommunication and without appeal, to cease their undue molestation of G. and to restore all that was taken in its entirety; and also compel those to whom it pertains to pay the aforesaid tithe, so that they may render it to G. without difficulty. You are to fulfil our mandate in such a way that the same G. is not compelled to come to us again for lack of justice. Notwithstanding no letters, etc. And if not all . . . let two of you nevertheless carry this out.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the seventh year.

### CXXIII. N. . . . . . . . . . .

[Note: The address is wanting.]

He assigns to Robert Vaisliaci, a deacon lacking every ecclesiastical benefice, the first prebend to become vacant in the church of Soissons. (Lateran, seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.)

Both the strictness of our office, by which we are debtors to all, moves us, and the condition of clerics, who have been assumed into the Lord’s portion and ought to live from the patrimony of Jesus Christ, strongly exhorts us to refresh them with the dew of apostolic provision—especially those whom uprightness of conduct forms and whom learning in letters renders commendable. Hence, for our beloved son Robert Vaisliaci, deacon, who possesses no ecclesiastical benefice, we have thought it right to request and admonish your discretion, commanding you by apostolic letters, that, out of reverence for Saint Peter and for us, you freely confer upon him without any difficulty a prebend in the church of Soissons, if one is vacant there. Otherwise, we command that the first to become vacant be reserved to our gift, to be conferred upon a suitable person.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, in the seventh year.

The same was written concerning this to the . . . provost [Note: Book III, letter 41, note], . . . dean [Note: Ibid., note], and chapter, in nearly the same manner as far as “to be conferred.” Therefore we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that you presume to receive no one as a canon to a prebend now vacant in your church, or to the first that becomes vacant, unless it be one to whom we shall think fit to confer it.

The same was written concerning this to the . . . dean [Note: See Book V, letter 149, note], succentor, and Bliard de Acreio, canons of Rheims, in nearly the same manner to the end, with this addition: Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you announce that our command is to be observed inviolably, fulfilling the apostolic mandate in such a way that your devotion may be proved by the effect of your action and that we may commend your obedience with worthy praises in the Lord.

### CXXIV. NN. . . . . . . . . . . .

[Note: The address is wanting.]

That they should procure the acceptance of Rog. de Bisatiis as governor by the citizens of Bisin., but without violence. (Lateran, Kalends of September.)

Our beloved son James, our kinsman and marshal, master justiciar of Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro, humbly petitioned us that, since the nobleman Rog. de Bisatiis has always been faithful and devoted to us, and a diligent executor of our commands—so that, at our command and the admonition of our beloved son, the nobleman G. . . . count of Brenne, who likewise petitioned us on his behalf, he relinquished to that marshal the city of Minerbien. which he held—we might in recompense grant him the city of Bisin., since such a grant could be made without burden or injury to anyone.

But because it is not, nor has it ever been, our will to alienate the king’s demesnes, as some are known to have done, who were rather squanderers, we do not wish the inhabitants of that city to be compelled to this by any violence. Rather, if it can be done by their own will, grant them, by our authority, the care of that city until the lawful age of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious F., king of Sicily; so that, when the said king reaches lawful age, he may dispose of that city according to the good pleasure of his will. Wherefore, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish and induce those citizens to this, and make effective efforts to ensure that they attend humbly and devotedly upon him as their governor.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of September.

### CXXV. N. . . . . . . . . .

[Note: The address is wanting, but from letter 124 it is clear that this was directed to the citizens of Bisin.]

On the same matter as in letter 124. (Lateran, Kalends of September.)

Since our beloved son, the nobleman R. de Bisatiis, has always been faithful and devoted to us and to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious F., king of Sicily, and has laboured praiseworthily in his service, we believe that your city may receive advancement under his government. Wherefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your whole community, commanding you by apostolic letters, that you attend humbly and devotedly upon him as your governor until the king reaches lawful age, so that through his skill your city may be governed better.

Given as above.

### CXXVI. H., KING OF HUNGARY

[Note: This letter is found inserted in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §78, but neither complete nor sufficiently corrected.

Raynaldus supplies a fragment of it under the year 1204, §45. Material found in the *Deeds* is enclosed here in brackets. Material found in Raynaldus is distinguished here by double quotation marks at the beginning of each line. Variant readings are also provided.]

He is deeply grieved that the king had wrongfully impeded, within the borders of Hungary, the passage of the cardinal legate to Bulgaria; he admonishes him to correct such an error, lest he be compelled to proceed against him. [Note: On the subject of this letter, see letters 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 of Book VII.]

Among other Catholic kings and Christian princes, dearest son, we take special glory in you, because you are faithful to God and devoted to us, so that you may deservedly glory in possessing the special grace and favour of the apostolic see, as very many proofs and examples on both sides demonstrate. For John, then our chaplain and now bishop of Forconium [Note: See letters 100 and 115 of this seventh book.], returning to the apostolic see, assured us confidently that, having been received by you with immense honour and devotion, he graciously obtained not only what he requested from your royal highness concerning the affair of Ban Kulin [Note: *Gesta*: “Culumbani.”], but also secured free passage and return through your kingdom into Bulgaria and Vlachia for himself and for other messengers and legates of the Roman Church.

You too, if we remember correctly, represented that it pleased your Serenity that the Grand Župan of Serbia should render to the apostolic see the reverence and obedience due and devoted, and should receive from us the royal crown, with your temporal right preserved. We remember therefore that we entrusted the execution of this matter to our venerable brother, the . . . archbishop of Kalocsa. Induced by these reasons, not so much general as particular, we judged that our beloved son Leo, priest-cardinal of the title of Santa Croce and legate of the apostolic see, should be sent through your kingdom to Bulgaria and Vlachia for the propagation of the Christian faith.

As he informed us by letter, he was honoured by your royal highness beyond even what he had expected. Indeed, as though you had laid aside royal gravity, you strove to do everything that you believed would please him. You first gladly gave an escort to the messengers whom he had brought to be sent into Bulgaria; and, after giving the kiss of peace, making with great joy a mutual promise of special friendship, and bestowing gifts, he obtained not only permission to cross, but you also ordered your messengers to convey him honourably into Bulgaria. You promised that you would send him your written instruction at the frontier, which he should retain more privately, and according to which he should labour faithfully for the restoration of peace.

Accordingly, advancing with your messengers as far as the boundary of the kingdom, he reached the fortress called Keve, where the Danube alone separates the kingdom of Hungary from the province of the Bulgarians. Many awaited him eagerly on the other side. But after one hour of the day, he unexpectedly received your messengers, who arrived in greatest haste and completely barred passage to him and to the . . . Bulgarian bishop. On the king’s behalf they proposed that he return to one of your estates, which he had already left three days’ journey behind, and that, staying there, he should notify the lord of the Bulgarians by messengers to come swiftly to a certain island situated on the frontier, so that he might first fully investigate the dispute between you and bring it to a proper conclusion; otherwise passage would not be open to him. [Note: The Pod. manuscript cited by Baluze reads otherwise.]

The cardinal replied, among other things, that he ought not to do this in such a manner: first, because if he received him as one returning to a mother’s bosom upon such terms, when the business concerned was spiritual no less than secular, the appearance of simoniacal depravity would seem to intervene; secondly, because he could not compel him to do anything until he was bound to the apostolic see by a special bond [Note: *Gesta*: “spiritual.”]. Therefore, since he would not turn back from the journey he had begun, an edict immediately went forth from the count of the fortress that whoever should dare sell anything to him or his party, or even to the aforesaid bishop, or offer any aid of humanity, would incur punishment in person and property. The cardinal and the aforesaid bishop were guarded by no fewer than three hundred attendants stationed around them, who pressed him so severely that they watched the door of his chamber—if indeed it deserves to be called a chamber—to say nothing of the base treatment inflicted upon him and his companions concerning the necessities of nature.

[Note: Raynaldus, cited passage.] “Alas, alas, dearest son! Where is royal [Note: *Gesta*: “the royal.”] clemency? Where is Christian religion? Where the special devotion which you profess to have toward us and the Roman Church? The finest colour has changed, and gold has been turned into dross. May God spare those who have seduced your mind by such wicked counsel, wishing to sow discord between kingdom and priesthood! Yet we firmly hope that either you have already corrected these errors yourself, or that, upon our admonition, you will amend them in such a way that the injury may turn into honour and the offence be converted into favour.” [Note: Thus far Raynaldus.]

Wherefore, trusting fully in your royal serenity, we earnestly request and admonish you, imposing this upon you for the remission of your sins: strive to remove the injury done to the aforesaid cardinal—or rather, done to us in him, indeed rather done to the Lord Jesus Christ in us—in such a way that we may be able in this matter to experience your devotion and may not be compelled on that account to do anything that could be burdensome to you. However burdensome it might be to us to burden you in any respect, we could not leave so perverse an example uncorrected; and we shall nevertheless carry out our purpose, which, with God as author, we have begun. [Note: *Gesta*: “with the Lord as author.”]

It was written to the suffragans of the church of Esztergom that they should earnestly admonish and induce the king himself to this, and should endeavour, all favour and fear set aside, to conduct themselves in this affair in such a manner that we may recognize in their actions the faith and devotion which they are bound to have toward their mother, the Roman Church.

This schedule was enclosed in the letters sent to the aforesaid king.

[Note: Raynaldus again.] “We write to you more mildly and graciously than the pressing matter would require, lest anyone perhaps inspecting our letters should think that the favour of the apostolic see had been withdrawn from you. That would in no way serve your advantage and honour, since many things have been done and are being done in your kingdom which, if brought to the file, would demand more severe correction: not only concerning your vow, the imprisonment of your brother, and the elections of prelates, but also concerning many other matters which, lest you be too greatly disturbed at present, we have thought should be suppressed.” [Note: Thus in the *Gesta* and in Raynaldus. In the Conti copy: “should be weighed.”] “Take care for yourself, therefore, lest you bring yourself into a difficulty from which you cannot escape.”

### CXXVII. L., PRIEST-CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF SANTA CROCE, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

[Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1204, §46.

It is read in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §78, but somewhat mutilated and also corrupted by certain errors. We present it complete and in all its particulars from a collation of the Conti copy and the Vatican manuscript.]

Reply to the complaints of the king of Hungary. (At Saint Peter’s, seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.)

To the letter which our dearest son in Christ, the . . . king of Hungary, sent us, we reply as follows.

[The letters of your royal highness which you sent to us through our beloved son, the nobleman E., knight, we have received graciously; and we have carefully noted what you communicated in them. To the first article, therefore, we reply that indeed your ancestors of pious memory, from the time when, through the diligence of the blessed Stephen, king, and by the prevenient grace of God, the kingdom of Hungary came to the unity of the Catholic faith, venerated the Apostolic See with great devotion. And all who descended from his stock succeeded them alike in the kingdom and in showing due reverence to the successors of blessed Peter, especially Bela your father, king of illustrious memory, who throughout his life strove to honor the Apostolic See; and you, succeeding him both in the kingdom and in devotion, have endeavored to do those things that would advance its advantage and honor.

Moreover, just as we acknowledge without doubt that these things are true, so you must without doubt acknowledge as true the things that must now be said. Although our predecessors strove to love and honor your ancestors, among other Catholic kings, with a certain special favor, endeavoring in every necessity to assist them according to God, the Apostolic See nevertheless took particular care, with all its strength, to promote your father of renowned memory. Thus, since for certain reasons—known, we believe, to you—he could not obtain the royal crown, our predecessor Pope Alexander, of happy memory, after many exhortations, commands, and admonitions to the archbishop of Esztergom that he should confer the royal diadem upon him, and since that archbishop could not in any way be induced to do so, finally strictly commanded the archbishop of Kalocsa to crown him king, without prejudice to the church of Esztergom. Thus, at the command of the Apostolic See, he obtained coronation.

How greatly the Apostolic See also took care to assist you at the beginning of your reign—which was certainly not lightly disturbed by the dissensions of many—the outcome of events itself demonstrates. At length, through its legate specially sent for this purpose, it brought you and your followers on one side, and your brother and his supporters on the other, back to peace. Though that peace was made and confirmed, would that it had been better observed!]

To the second article we reply as follows: you did indeed grant our envoys traveling to the land of Joannitius, lord of the Bulgarians, and his envoys wishing to travel to the Roman Church through your land, safe-conduct and free passage; and, at the request of our legate, you dismissed the army which you had assembled against him, after expenses had been spent to no purpose. For this we render abundant thanks to your serenity.

But concerning what you wrote—that the aforesaid Joannitius holds under occupation the land which your father . . . . gave as dowry to your sister, the empress of the Greeks; and that, having added to himself a great multitude of pagans, he cruelly devastated the land of Serbia, subject to your crown, so that, besides those slain through his tyranny, not a few Christians were carried away into pagan captivity—you should certainly know that whatever is known to have been attempted to your injury and loss is very grievous to us. This occurred, namely, at the time when, induced by our prayers, after the king of Bohemia had separated from Philip’s party and joined King Otto, you sent a strong army with the latter on behalf of the former against Philip. We shall devote diligent care and effective effort to ensuring that fitting satisfaction is made to you.

To the third article we reply thus: although you wrote that the aforesaid Joannitius is by right lord of no land, though for a time he occupies part of your kingdom and part of another, and although you wonder that, without consulting you, we proposed so suddenly to crown so manifest an enemy of yours king, the matter is nevertheless otherwise in some respect—speaking with due regard for your peace—because you do not fully know the truth on this point. For in ancient times many kings in Bulgaria were successively crowned by apostolic authority, such as Peter and Samuel and several others after them. Indeed, at the preaching of Pope Nicholas, our predecessor of holy memory—whose counsels the king of the Bulgarians very often sought—he deserved to be baptized after making a commitment together with his whole kingdom [the object of *commisso* is unstated in the supplied text]. But later, when the Greeks prevailed, the Bulgarians lost their royal dignity; indeed, they were compelled to serve under the heavy yoke of the emperor of Constantinople. At last, two brothers, Peter and Joannitius, descended from the lineage of the former kings, began not so much to occupy as to recover the land of their fathers, so that on one day they won a remarkable victory over great princes and countless peoples.

Therefore, we do not deny that they may perhaps have violently invaded some part of the land; but we firmly maintain that they recovered by paternal right the greater part of the land. Hence we intend to crown him king not over another’s land, but over his own, following the example of our predecessors. We desire both that he restore land unjustly held, and that land unjustly held be restored to him, since he has asked us to secure justice for both parties between you and him concerning the lands invaded.

Since, therefore, you granted to our envoys traveling to him and to his envoys traveling to us not merely free passage but also a safe escort, we ought not to have supposed that he was your most hostile enemy, although, through the diligence of our solicitude, once the occasion of enmity has been removed, you may be able to become friends from enemies. Nor did we proceed suddenly to bring this matter to completion: we repeatedly took care to send envoys to him with our letters for this purpose, that we might call the daughter back to her mother and bring the member back to the head, so that there might be one fold and one shepherd.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] So in both the Royal codex and the Pod. codex cited by Baluze; but in the *Gesta* it reads “but.”]

Yet in this case we might not without reason have considered also the following: when the nobleman Stephen, Grand Župan of Serbia [Note: [Col. 0415D] The *Gesta* reads: “Megajuppanus.”], humbly begged us through honorable envoys to send a legate into his land, to bring it back to obedience to the Roman Church and to confer a royal diadem upon him; and when, with the common counsel of our brethren, we had decreed that his petition should be granted, assigning this legation to our venerable brother J., bishop of Albano—then, having learned at length that this was exceedingly displeasing to your highness [Note: [Col. 0415D] So also in the *Gesta* and the Pod. codex cited by Baluze; “your serenity.”], we abandoned what we had begun, for your sake and not without some embarrassment to ourselves.

But after you had conquered Serbia, removed Stephen, and put Vulcan in his place, you informed us through your envoys [Note: [Col. 0416D] Omitted in the *Gesta*.] [Note: [Col. 0416D] So in the *Gesta*; in the Conti copy: “you sent.”] that you wished to bring that land back to obedience to the Roman Church and, while preserving your temporal right, would patiently permit the said Vulcan to receive a royal crown from the Apostolic See. Accordingly, on the counsel of your envoys, we judged the execution of this matter should be entrusted to our venerable brother . . . . archbishop of Kalocsa; but, although two years have now passed, we know that no progress has been made.

To the fourth article we reply as follows. Although you devoutly received and diligently honored our beloved son L., cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross, legate of the Apostolic See, so that after being graciously dismissed with the kiss of peace you caused him to be honorably escorted to the borders of the kingdom, with nothing then remaining except the crossing of the Danube from Hungary into Bulgaria, nevertheless, since, in the words of the poet:

> A guest is more shamefully expelled than not admitted.  
> (*Ovid, Tristia* 5.6.13)

we are not a little astonished and disturbed—indeed, more for your sake than for ours—that you immediately ordered him to be brought back. It would have been less unbecoming if you had not admitted him while traveling onward than that, once admitted, you should not allow him to proceed.

As for the reasons you set out in your letter for doing this, it would suffice to answer with Solomon’s saying: “The net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (*Proverbs* 1), unless we were obliged to answer what you humbly requested in your letters: that we should either wholly abandon the purpose of that coronation, or at least postpone it until the discord between you could be ended by judgment or arbitration, since you are prepared to abide by the judgment or arbitration of our legate.

We shall therefore give only a very few of the many reasons, lest an excessively explicit answer trouble you too greatly. Since the aforesaid cardinal made a long stay in your kingdom and was not only honorably received but magnificently honored both by you and by others, he could certainly not be a common mediator for restoring concord, or an impartial judge for resolving the dispute, unless he were received in the same manner in Joannitius’s land, so that every suspicion might be removed. Furthermore, he could not compel him to make peace or render justice before he had taken on the yoke of apostolic discipline and submitted himself to our instruction and command.

Moreover, since this legate proceeds to spread the sacrament of the Christian faith and to advance the honor of the Apostolic See, if you should perhaps impede him, you would certainly incur divine indignation and deserve our displeasure; you would make him still more your enemy, and achieve nothing, because we could fulfill the purpose of our will by another means. Consider carefully, moreover, how you would regard it if we wished to prevent your natural son from being crowned king; and understand that we regard it likewise if you attempt to prevent our spiritual son from being crowned king: that prodigal son who long ago, living luxuriously with prostitutes, squandered his substance, but who at last, returning to himself, returns to his father. The father runs to him, embraces [Note: [Col. 0416D] So in the *Gesta*; the Conti copy has “embraced.”] and kisses his returning son, and commands his servants to clothe him with the best robe, to put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet, and to kill the fattened calf, that they may eat and celebrate; for his son was dead and has come to life, was lost and has been found. How the father calmed the indignation of the elder son, the Gospel parable teaches you; and we wish you to imitate its teaching both in this matter and in others.

But if perhaps you fear that, after receiving the crown, he will become more arrogant through sudden exaltation, you ought to know [Note: [Col. 0416D] The *Gesta* reads: “you ought.”] for certain that he would gain less through contrived deceit than he would lose through feigned faith; and we say less to you, that you may understand more by yourself.

To the fifth article we reply that, although you wrote that nearly two years had now passed and that you had still been unable, through the Roman Church, to obtain justice for the irreparable damage done by those who, despising the sentence of the Apostolic See, destroyed Zadar while you provided nothing against the treachery of enemies under our safeguard; and that, if you permitted the aforesaid Joannitius to be crowned before the discord between you had been settled, justice could never afterward be rendered to you through the Roman Church—we do not wish you, dearest son, to be unaware that we took care to bind both the Venetian fleet and the French army with the bond of anathema because of the destruction of Zadar.

When the leading men of the French army sought the benefit of absolution, they could not be absolved until they had sworn to abide by [Note: [Col. 0417D] So in the *Gesta*; the Conti copy has “obey.”] our commands and had bound, by authentic and open letters, not only themselves but also their successors, that at our command they would endeavor to make satisfaction for that offense. But because the . . . . doge of Venice and his people have not yet sought the grace of absolution, we have already proceeded so far against them that we refused to consecrate their beloved son . . . . patriarch-elect; indeed, when he came personally to us, we sent him away, not without great shame and confusion.

We also informed you that at Zadar, which until now, together with its whole province, had been subject to the patriarch of Grado, you should cause a canonical election of a suitable person to be held, and send the elected person to us for consecration and the pallium, so that we might thus begin to punish Venetian pride. In like manner the aforesaid Joannitius would be punished if, after receiving the crown, he should refuse to obey the arbitration or judgment of our legate concerning the dispute between you, and his latter condition would become worse than the former, and his final error worse than the first.

But because, however greatly we may love the aforesaid Joannitius, we love you incomparably more, we have, as we believe, found a suitable means through which provision ought to be made for your honor and right, as you will be able to see clearly from the letters which we are now sending concerning this matter. Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish your royal serenity that, giving glory to God and honor to us, you do not hinder the propagation of the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0418D] The *Gesta* reads: “Christian.”] or the undertaking of the Apostolic See, whose counsel you will undoubtedly find fruitful.]

Thus far to the aforesaid king. For the rest, by apostolic letters we command your devotion, under strict injunction, to crown the aforesaid Joannitius king not over another’s land but over his own; and, having more fully ascertained the truth, to proceed, with justice as mediator, to settle the dispute between him and the aforesaid king of Hungary, causing what you decree to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding appeal.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

CXXVIII. . . . . . TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. Concerning the election of the abbot of Saint Giles in Hungary. (At Saint Peter’s, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.)

The beloved sons H. . . G. . . A. . . and D. . . , monks of Saint Giles in Hungary, having come to the Apostolic See, tearfully informed us that after the death of their abbot they elected another for themselves, according to the ancient and approved custom of their monastery [Col. 0418A], which until now has customarily had both Latin abbots and Latin monks. But you, dearest son—as they reported with devotion and reverence—were unwilling to grant them your royal consent, declaring that you would consent to no one other than a Hungarian.

Our venerable brother B. . . . , archbishop of Split, observing this, came into your serene presence and quickly obtained the monastery itself. If this is true, we are greatly astonished; for although he is a monk by profession and a Latin by nation, nevertheless, since he bears the office of a bishop, he ought not to usurp the ministry of an abbot, especially in another diocese and through lay power. Not long afterward, together with the servants of the said monastery, he gravely accused all the monks before your royal highness concerning the monastery’s treasure. But they, perceiving his intention, immediately, in his presence, delivered over the treasure of the church—whole and even increased—to a certain man of yours, whom he had brought with him, and to many other worthy men.

Yet the same archbishop, desiring to accomplish his will, seized an opportunity and violently attacked them with armed force. He personally scourged some of them; cast others into chains; deprived all of everything; and installed Hungarian monks according to his own will. He gave no heed to the appeal which the same monks made to the Apostolic See concerning so grave an oppression; the monks set its term at the Assumption of the Blessed Mary most recently past.

Since it is neither novel nor improper that communities of different nations in your kingdom should serve one lord under the regular habit, and since, although this is your one monastery of Latins, there are nevertheless many monasteries of Greeks there, we earnestly ask and admonish your royal serenity to restore to its due condition what you are said to have granted not so much of your own motion as at another’s counsel. Do not hinder, nor permit anyone to hinder, the aforesaid monks from choosing for themselves, by canonical election and according to the custom observed until now, a suitable person as abbot.

For we firmly command our venerable brother . . . . bishop of Várad, and our beloved sons . . . . abbot of Búcsa and . . . . provost of Esztergom, that, after diligently investigating the truth, if they find that the affair proceeded in this manner, then, unless the aforesaid archbishop of Split, at their admonition, takes care personally to correct his offense, they shall impose upon him a canonical penalty for so great a presumption. Having entirely excluded him from the aforementioned monastery, they shall cause it to be put in order according to the prescribed form, notwithstanding appeal; opponents, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

They were written to concerning this matter, with strict command that, setting aside every favor and fear, etc.

[Col. 0419A] It was written to B. . . . , archbishop of Split, in nearly the same terms, down to “setting the term.” Behold how you love and defend ecclesiastical liberty; how you promote and procure the honor of the Apostolic See; how you display and preserve episcopal moderation; how you pursue and zealously uphold the monastic rule! Certainly, unless you personally correct and amend the offenses described above, abstain from similar acts, and take heed, we shall punish you all the more severely because we love you more intimately, so that the punishment of one may be a warning to many, and the righteous may wash their hands in the blood of the sinner.

CXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0419D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §75. See also the *Gesta Innocentii*, §38.] . . . . . . . . . TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF SICILY. He sends G., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Adrian, to deal with the matters that must be dealt with in concert with the king and to establish peace. (Rome, fourth day before the Nones of October.)

[Col. 0419B]

The letters of your royal highness which you sent to us through our beloved son . . . . . abbot of Refesia, and Alb., provost, joined by our venerable brother Anselm [Note: [Col. 0419D] Book III, letter 49, note.], archbishop of Naples, and our beloved son Thomas of Gaeta, royal justiciar, we have received with paternal kindness. We have carefully noted what was communicated to us both by the envoys and by the letters, rejoicing in him who is the power and wisdom of God that day by day you advance, as in age so also in wisdom and virtue.

Since, therefore, we earnestly seek the honor and safety of your person and the tranquility and peace of your kingdom, we recently sent to your serene presence our beloved son G. [Note: [Col. 0420D] We have already dealt with him above.], cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian and legate of the Apostolic See, a prudent and honorable man, to transact and carry out in our stead those matters that ought to benefit both you and your kingdom. Accordingly, we refer to him what was offered and requested through the said envoys, expressing to him the good pleasure of our will: that, with appropriate concessions made on both sides, peace and security may be secured, lest the unhappy kingdom be destroyed by the continual disasters of wars.

Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish your royal serenity to comply with the counsels and admonitions of this cardinal. Know for certain that we, who have hitherto borne many and great labors for the defense of your person and land and have also incurred great and heavy expenses, will never fail you, but, effectually seeking your honor and advancement, will provide you with apostolic protection against the attacks of the wicked.

Given at Rome, etc., on the fourth day before the Nones of October.

CXXX. [Note: [Col. 0420D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §75.] TO THE NOBLEMAN W. CAPARONI, THE SPIRIT OF SOUND COUNSEL. On the same subject as in the preceding letter. (Rome, fourth day before the Nones of October.)

Since Markward and his supporters were bound by the bond of excommunication, and you assisted him to the extent of your power, you should not wonder that, before you deserve the grace of absolution, we deny you apostolic greeting and blessing. Nevertheless, we received with paternal kindness the envoys whom you sent to us with the royal letters, and carefully weighed what was offered and requested—rather than promised.

Moreover, if what was offered had corresponded not only fairly but even approximately to what was requested, we should certainly have granted the requests, since we earnestly seek the king’s welfare and the kingdom’s peace, and also wish to procure your honor and advancement, provided that the obstacle does not lie with you. Therefore, hoping that when you understand our good pleasure you will comply with our will without difficulty, we have judged that the matter of the peace under negotiation should be referred to our beloved son G. . . . . , cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian and legate of the Apostolic See, whom we have taken care to send to Sicily to the king’s presence.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we earnestly admonish and command your nobility to comply with the counsels and admonitions of the same cardinal, and to devote diligent care and effective effort, with that cardinal—to whom we have expressed our good pleasure—to the completion of the altogether necessary peace. Know for certain that our favor may prove greatly beneficial to you before God and before men, both now and hereafter. But if not, you may have grave reason to fear divine correction and admonition, and apostolic indignation.

Given as in the other [letter].

CXXXI. [Note: [Col. 0420D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §75.] TO L., THE ROYAL PROTONOTARY. On a similar subject. (Rome, fourth day before the Nones of October.)

Although Markward and his supporters were bound by the bond of excommunication, since we do not know whether you aided him, particularly in his evil, and since we have instead heard that you are faithful and devoted to us, we grant you the favor of our greeting and blessing. Yet if your conscience reproaches you concerning this, have yourself absolved through our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian and legate of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, that we may repay the gratitude due to your devotion not merely in word but in deed, we earnestly ask and admonish your discretion, commanding you by apostolic letters that, toward your mother, the Roman Church, advancing from good to better, you endeavor to do those things that contribute to her honor and advancement, and look to the peace and safety of the king and kingdom. Know for certain that we shall take care to return favor to you in exchange, so that you may deservedly glory in our favor.

Given as in the other [letter].

CXXXII. . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF LIMOGES [Note: [Col. 0421D] See the note to Letter 68 of Book Five.]. That they are to cause Master W. Brunater to be received as a canon in the church of Angoulême. (Rome, on the Nones of October.)

[Col. 0421A]

Our beloved son Master W. Brunater, for whose admission as a canon in the church of Angoulême we had written [Note: [Col. 0421D] See Letter 133 of Book Five.], came to the Apostolic See and informed us that, although our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Saintes [Note: [Col. 0421D] Book V, Letter 96, note.], and our beloved son G., our subdeacon and archdeacon of Aunis, whom we had appointed executors in the matter of the canonry of Angoulême, had long labored with the canons of that church to carry out the apostolic command concerning Master W.’s admission as a canon, those canons neither accepted their admonitions nor gave any reasonable reason why they should desist from executing our mandate. Supported by our authority, the executors therefore took care to invest the master with that canonry, binding opponents by a sentence of excommunication; but the canons refused to receive him. Therefore the same master made grave complaint to us.

On the other hand, the cleric Arnaud Chatet, sent by the said canons, alleged that the executors were excessively favorable to the aforesaid master and suspect to the church itself. He alleged also that you, who according to the apostolic mandate ought to have chosen impartial arbitrators through whom the suspected conduct of the executors themselves might be investigated, chose at your own pleasure men who held those executors in such reverence that they would rather declare them just than suspect in this affair and another.

The same Ar. . . further alleged that, since that church was bereft of a pastor, the chapter ought not to be compelled to receive the master, because while the church remained vacant it could not receive either him or anyone else; nor did the church’s resources suffice for receiving him. He therefore requested that the church be released from the master’s claim. But when the same Ar. . . was asked by us whether he wished to allege anything against the person [of the master], or whether anything had been alleged against him before the prelate-executors, he replied that he intended to allege nothing against him and knew of nothing having been alleged, except that the church’s resources could not support him.

Therefore, considering that the hand of a prince ought to be generous and liberal in conferring benefices, we ourselves took care to invest by our own hand the said master, for whose provision we had begun to make more generously, with a canonry of the church of Angoulême. And, to spare that church, whose resources were said at present to have been diminished because of the hazards of wars, we directed him to abstain from receiving its revenues until, in accordance with the customary course of the church, due and customary provision could be made from them for him as for the others.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your fraternity, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any obstacle of contradiction or appeal, to cause the same master to be graciously treated and received by those canons as their canon and brother, with full admission to all things pertaining to the honor of a canonry. Restrain opponents by sentence of suspension and excommunication, notwithstanding appeal, and cause the sentence you pronounce to be solemnly published throughout the diocese of Angoulême.

Concerning the resources of that church, diligently ascertain the truth; and, if you learn that they can suffice according to the observed custom, cause provision to be made for him from them, as for one of the others. Otherwise, if it is established that the resources are so inadequate that provision cannot be made according to the customary course of the church, then, after they have returned to a condition in which customary provision can be supplied to the individual ministers, compel the canons themselves, or those who may be there at the time, by ecclesiastical coercion notwithstanding appeal, to provide the said master with a canonical portion.

Given at Rome, etc., on the Nones of October, in the seventh year.

CXXXIII. [Note: [Col. 0421D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77.] TO THE NOBLEMAN RICHARD, OUR KINSMAN. He confirms to him various possessions. (At Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of October.)

From a public instrument written by the hand of Astaldus, notary of the holy Roman Church, we have learned plainly that Roland [Note: [Col. 0421D] Roland Bandinelli, son of Ranutius, a nobleman of Siena, was first an apostolic subdeacon, having been a cleric of the Church of Pisa; then, in the first creation of Eugene III, in the year 1185, he was made cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian; afterward, by the same pope, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church; finally he was elected Roman pontiff and called Alexander III. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1044.], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark and chancellor of the Roman Church, and Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Note: [Col. 0421D] Boso, an Englishman by birth, nephew and secretary of Pope Adrian IV [Col. 0422D], was formerly a monk of Saint Benedict at Saint Alban’s; he was made cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian and chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church by Adrian IV in the first creation, in the year 1155, and was afterward made cardinal priest and pastor of the title of Saint Pudentiana by Alexander III. He was greatly beloved by Adrian IV and, after that pope’s death, was the principal author of the election of Alexander III, whom he always followed, especially to Venice, and in all the negotiations for peace. He died about the year of our salvation 1181: a pious and learned man, rightly numbered by English writers among the principal theologians of his age. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1064.], chamberlain of our predecessor Pope Adrian of blessed memory, by his command and will granted, and by investiture delivered in fief, to Odo de Polo and his lawful heirs, and to the heirs of his heirs whom they should appoint by testament, in perpetuity, namely Polo Giustiniano, Anticoli, Rocca de Nibblis, Monte Magno, Guadannolo, Saracinesco, Rocca de Sorrecis, and Castel Nuovo, with all their appurtenances and revenues, on this condition: that he, his heirs, and the heirs of his heirs should forever render fealty to the aforesaid Roman pontiff and his successors, without any other fief; and that the same pontiff and his successors could not take the said fief from the aforesaid nobleman and his heirs, unless the nobleman himself or his heirs committed against him or his successors some act for which, by the judgment of their peers, who bore them no enmity, they ought to lose the aforesaid fief.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid Odo and Gregory his son had sworn fealty for the said fief to our predecessors then in office, and had possessed it through the Roman Church for more than forty years, at length, in our own time, the beloved son . . . abbot of the monastery of Cliviscauro, bringing the aforesaid Odo and Gregory his son before the senator of the City, impleaded them concerning the lands described above. They appealed to our presence and urgently asked us not to permit them to be summoned before another court concerning the fief which they held from the Roman Church, but rather to defend that fief for them.

We therefore withdrew them from the senatorial court; and, since we could not deny justice to the said monastery, we committed the cause between them to be heard in our court by Saxo of blessed memory, primicerius of the judges, Peter, advocate of John Adam, and also Marsicanus, our subdeacon. Before them, in the Lateran palace, the parties disputed for some time through their advocates.

Meanwhile the aforesaid Odo de Polo, while his father was alive and after his death, began negotiations with you concerning the marriage to be contracted between your son and his daughter; and, after many agreements had intervened, you came to terms with one another before our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0423D] He has already been mentioned several times.], through his mediation, at Saint Martina in his palace.
