When you had freed from the burden of debts the aforesaid land, which he and his forefathers had mortgaged for many debts, he and his brothers—who, while the land lay burdened with debt, could scarcely draw a scanty living from it—began anxiously to aspire to recover it.

When they presented their complaint against you before us, you repeatedly answered that you were ready, under examination by us, or by our brethren, or by judges, or even by arbitration of worthy men or persons chosen by common consent, to render them full justice; and we promised mercifully to supply them with the necessary expenses of the litigation. But, led by evil counsel, they began to invent many falsehoods not only against you but also against us, in order, as though under a pretext of piety, to stir up the outcry of the people. Thus they often went naked through the City, running with crosses to the churches. Though forbidden by us to attempt anything of this kind against us, they nevertheless refused to desist from their undertaking. Attempting worse deeds than before, on the Monday after Easter they stirred up a tumult and sedition among the people, so that, with blasphemous cries continually uttered, they disturbed the divine office in the very basilica of Saint Peter.

And when, as customary, we returned crowned through the City, we are ashamed to recount how many and how great were the plots and insults which we suffered, although these were manifest to almost everyone. Nor were they satisfied even with this; but, lest their latter error should be worse than the former, when the Roman people had been assembled before the senator on the Capitol by certain fraudulent devices, they presumed, so far as lay in their power, to grant to the senate and Roman people the aforesaid land—which belongs by right and ownership to the Apostolic See—by word, because they could not do so by deed, and in writing, because they could not do so by law.

But we immediately caused our right, after convoking the people, to be formally asserted through certain of our brethren; and, lest the Church’s right should be lost, we commanded you, acknowledging that you held the land through the Roman Church, to defend and fortify it. Yet they, with their accomplices, deceived the people by false fabrications against you and so incited it against you that, taking up arms for battle, they fiercely attacked your tower. At last, when you had scarcely escaped by flight, they captured it; and certain persons still occupy it under the name of the community, inflicting many losses and injuries both upon you and upon your helpers.

Although the sons of Gregory de Polo have gravely offended us and the Roman Church, we do not at all wish to prejudice their rights, since they have not yet been judged in our court. But desiring to provide for you with paternal concern, by the common counsel and assent of our brethren we grant and command that you shall hold and possess the aforesaid land until suitable satisfaction has been made to you for the damages which you show that you have incurred on this account and for the expenses which you show that you have made for the same reason, especially after we commanded you to defend and fortify that land for the use of the Roman Church. Nevertheless, every other right which you possess in the said land remains reserved to you, so that you may make war and peace concerning it at the command of the Roman pontiff, and he shall uphold and defend you, just as, according to good and approved custom, a lord ought to defend and support his vassal.

You, however, shall not presume to make any settlement concerning that land without his special permission; yet he shall grant it to you if urgent necessity or evident advantage requires it. Since we desire peace and concord between the Roman Church, the City, you, and the aforesaid nobles, if the necessity of making peace should require us to take the said land, or a part of it, into our own hands, you shall endeavor, upon receiving monetary satisfaction or a suitable exchange, to deliver it to us for this reason. Therefore let no one, etc. This page of our grant, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of October.

CXXXIV [Note: [Col. 0425D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 67. See also letter 44 of this seventh book.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT FRANCE. He declares them exempt from the sentence of interdict pronounced by the abbot of . . . Casemarium in the matter of peace between the kings of England and France. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of August.)

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, when our beloved son, the abbot of Casemarium, our messenger, had summoned you to a conference at Meaux and had produced letters sent to you by the Apostolic See for the restoration of peace between our dearest sons in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the French, and John, illustrious king of the English, you replied, after deliberation, that since the aforesaid king of England had not acted in accordance with the tenor of our letters, you had determined, because of the many perplexities and great calamities which you feared threatened the Gallican Church, to consult us. And, lest meanwhile the aforesaid abbot should proceed further, you appealed to our hearing, setting a fixed term for the appeal; to prosecute it, you pledged faith in the hand of the same abbot and bound yourselves by the kiss of peace, so that after that term anyone who failed to prosecute the appeal should be suspended from the pontifical office, in the presence of the envoys of your king, who likewise approved this arrangement with you.

Whether the aforesaid abbot required such a guarantee, or whether you offered it voluntarily, we do not know. Yet we commend his zeal, if he freely accepted what was offered, and your devotion, if you freely offered it. But because we and our predecessors have frequently experienced your fidelity and obedience, and in order to show the affection which we have not only toward you and the churches of France but also toward the king himself and the kingdom of the French, we do not wish you to remain bound by this obligation. Rather, prosecute the appeal entered, as you know to be expedient for kingdom and priesthood; for we so desire to preserve intact the rights of the priesthood that we also keep inviolate the rights of the kingdom.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of August, in the seventh year.

CXXXV [Note: [Col. 0425D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 75. See also the notes on letter 129 of this seventh book.]. TO G., CARDINAL DEACON OF SAINT ADRIAN, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. On the same subject as letter 129 of this seventh book. (At Saint Peter’s, fourth day before the Nones of October.)

We have received the messengers whom William Capparonis recently sent to our presence on the king’s behalf: namely, the abbot of Refesia and Albertinus the provost. At the royal command we caused our venerable brother Anselm, archbishop of Naples, and our beloved son Thomas, the royal justiciar of Gaeta, to be joined with them. With careful consideration we have weighed what they requested and offered, together with what they promised; all of which is contained in the enclosed schedule, along with the matters which we required.

But, wishing to defer to you, to whom we have entrusted our authority, we did not wish to give them a final answer; rather, we decreed that everything should be referred to you, commanding your discretion by apostolic letters that, having prudently considered the condition of Sicily, you should either complete, break off, or postpone the peace negotiations, as you judge expedient. We commit all this to your discretion, under this threefold alternative, because you can more fully perceive the circumstances of the cases, times, affairs, and persons.

Therefore, secure in the fullness of our favor, with God before your eyes, and considering us, yourself, the honor of the Apostolic See, the king’s welfare, and the peace of the kingdom, proceed diligently in all matters with the counsel of those whom you have found faithful and devoted. For your labor you will receive the first reward from God and the second from us. In addition, we write to all those to whom you suggested by your letters that we should write, commanding you by apostolic letters to seek to regulate the Roman and Messinese affair as the necessity of both requires.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Nones of October.

CXXXVI [Note: [Col. 0426D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 75. See also the notes on letter 129 of this seventh book.]. TO P., ELECT OF PALERMO [Note: [Col. 0426D] Book V, letter 29, note.]. He exhorts him to procure peace. (At Saint Peter’s, third day before the Nones of October.)

Since you have experienced our favor in many matters, you ought not to doubt that we love your person in the Lord; and, since steadfastness has been proven in us, you should not fear the vice of inconstancy. Yet discretion, the seasoning of virtues, compels us to adapt ourselves differently for the time being amid contrary events.

Therefore, secure in our favor, strive to do those things by which purity of faith and sincerity of devotion may shine forth in you ever more clearly. For we shall omit nothing, God being the author, so far as is granted to a human being, but shall proceed by the royal road, weighing the scales of equity, toward the faithful and devoted on one side and the unfaithful and undevoted on the other. Since the angel of Satan often transforms himself into an angel of light, do not readily believe every spirit until you have truly tested whether such a spirit is from God, lest, deceived by malignant error, you call good evil or evil good, make light darkness or darkness light.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of October.

CXXXVII. . . . TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. He congratulates him for having granted passage to the legate; he exhorts him to treat the legate kindly and honorably [Note: [Col. 0427D] On the subject of this letter, see letters 126 and following of this seventh book, with notes.]. (At Saint Peter’s.)

We regard it as welcome and pleasing, and we commend your serenity in the Lord, because, although at first, moved by certain considerations, you caused passage to be denied to our beloved son L., cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross and legate of the Apostolic See, so that he might not proceed to crown John, lord of the Bulgarians, until you had settled by judgment or agreement the dispute concerning territorial boundaries which is pending between you and him; nevertheless, afterward, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, adopting wiser counsel, you granted him full freedom to pass as he wished.

Indeed, as soon as that report reached our ears, we almost foresaw and foretold what we now see and rejoice to see fulfilled: namely, that, without receiving our letters and without waiting even for your messengers, you would yourself correct what might seem to have been attempted to the injury of the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, you have devoutly received and honorably treated the aforesaid cardinal, we earnestly ask and admonish your highness, in order that you may bring a good beginning to a better end, that, receiving him kindly and treating him honorably on his return, you shall have him safely conducted through your kingdom. Thus he, who holds a great place in the Church of God and is dear to us among our brethren, may be more firmly bound to your honor and advancement; and we, who count as rendered to our own person whatever honor is shown to him, may be obliged to commend your magnificence more warmly on this account.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXXXVIII. TO THE ARCHDEACON OF PAVIA. That he may proceed in the cause between William of Tabiaco and the abbot of Clavat., in the diocese of Milan, which had been committed to him. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of October.)

You should know that we have received word from our beloved son William of Tabiaco [Col. 0427D] that, when he and . . . the abbot of Clavat., in the diocese of Milan, were litigating before our venerable brother the archbishop of Milan [Note: [Col. 0427D] He has already been mentioned several times.], the ordinary judge, concerning a certain fief, that archbishop committed the cause to P. Menelotius, canon of Milan, for final determination. He pronounced a judgment against the said G . . . , from which the same G . . . appealed to our hearing.

Although his procurator, coming to the Apostolic See, obtained from you letters of commission making no mention of the aforesaid appeal, nevertheless, lest your jurisdiction might thereby be impeded, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, proceeding lawfully in the cause of appeal, you shall take care, with the appeal set aside, to confirm or annul that judgment as justice requires. Notwithstanding any letters opposed to the truth, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of October.

CXXXIX [Note: [Col. 0427D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 56.]. TO . . . THE ARCHBISHOP OF BREMEN [Note: [Col. 0427D] He was probably Gerard, count of Lippe, who, first bishop of Osnabrück, is said to have waged war against the Stedinger, enemies of the Christian name, in the time of Emperor Frederick; afterward he was transferred to the metropolitan see of Bremen—though in what year is uncertain—and is said to have presided there for thirty-nine years. BUCELIN, *Germania sacra*, vol. I, part I, pp. 32–33 [33].], HIS SUFFRAGANS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN THE PROVINCE OF BREMEN. That they should invite the faithful to take the cross against the barbarians of Livonia. (At Saint Peter’s, sixth day before the Ides of October.)

[Col. 0428B]

Although the words of those who proclaim peace and good things have gone out into all the earth, even to the ends of the world, so that the world may rightly be convicted concerning righteousness and sin, nevertheless Behemoth, sleeping beneath the shadow of the reed, who does not marvel when he drinks up a river but trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth, has made certain persons strangers to the light of truth and blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of Christ’s glory cannot shine upon them, nor can they know him who caused light to shine from darkness. They have been given over to a reprobate mind, so that the wrath of God may be revealed from heaven against their ungodliness and unrighteousness, because they hold down the truth in unrighteousness.

For although the light of God’s countenance has been marked upon them, so that they might perceive his invisible things through understanding, nevertheless, because when they knew the Lord they did not care to glorify him as God, they became like the cursed barren ground in Adam’s work, producing thorns and briars, though it ought to have borne fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. But the Lord, who took hold not of angels but of the seed of Abraham, that he might become a faithful high priest before God lest he utterly destroy what he had created, gave in the wilderness cedar, thorn, myrtle, and olive, in order to place the waterless land at the sources of waters.

Now although the people of Livonia had until these times been shrouded in the darkness of unbelief and had not come to knowledge of the truth, so that, like a wilderness, they bore no fruit of good work, the Lord recently sent into it the streams of holy preaching, that he might happily irrigate with waters flowing between the midst of the mountains that land to which, because of the harshness of its own dryness, the way had hitherto not been open to preachers. From these waters the beasts of the field now drink—those beasts which Peter, slaughtering them, ate by incorporating them into the Catholic faith.

In that land the Lord gave cedar: those, namely, who excel in virtues and are the good fragrance of Christ. He also placed thorn in it, so that through the office of holy preaching and the threat of judgment their minds may be pierced, as it were, by certain stings with the pain of compunction, causing tears—the blood, as it were, of the soul—to flow from their eyes. He likewise placed myrtle and olive: those, namely, who can console the desolate under oppression, lest they despair through excessive tribulation, and those who, devoting themselves to works of mercy, labor to assist the needy.

But because the Lord has rained upon that land in part and has hitherto left it in part without rain, our venerable brother Al., bishop of those same people, effectively laboring for their conversion, has sought to establish three religious orders: namely, Cistercians, monks, and regular canons, who, devoted alike to discipline and instruction, may fight with spiritual arms against the beasts of the earth; and faithful laymen, who, under the habit of the Templars, may vigorously and powerfully resist the barbarians attacking there the newly planted Christian faith. Thus he strives to recall to the knowledge of faith those who have gone astray.

But since the harvest is plentiful while the laborers are few, the same bishop humbly asked us to deem it fitting to send into his harvest, to proclaim Jesus Christ to the nations, priests and clerics of the neighboring regions who, having fastened the sign of the cross upon their shoulders, have vowed to go to Jerusalem; and likewise to permit laypeople, who cannot visit the land of Jerusalem because of lack of resources and bodily weakness, to proceed into Livonia against the barbarians, their vow being changed into another vow by our permission.

We therefore, extending favorable support to his prayers, judged that his requests should be granted, so that the word of God may run among them and the Christian religion be spread. Moreover, we add that when the said bishop has led preachers of the divine word to be sent to that people, in whatever city, castle, or village of the province of Bremen they enter, if the place lies under an interdict, the churches shall be opened once yearly upon their joyful arrival; and, with excommunicated persons and those expressly interdicted excluded, the divine offices shall be celebrated there, out of reverence for the Gospel which they have undertaken to preach among the nations. Thus, when the error of old has been abolished, they may be brought back from tracklessness to the way and from darkness to light; freed from bondage to corruption into the freedom of the glory of God’s children; and, beholding his glory with unveiled face, transformed into the same image.

Since he who sows and he who reaps shall not be without reward, and since we desire you to share in their reward, we command your whole body by apostolic letters that, offering them suitable assistance in evangelizing, you shall ensure that the concessions mercifully granted to them by us are announced and firmly observed throughout your parishes. Exhort also the people committed to you to assist them, so that those who go forth weeping, scattering their seed, may return with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

CXL. TO . . . THE ARCHBISHOP OF TORRES. That he shall arrange absolution for Ytochor de Thorum, who had killed an acolyte unknown to him. (At Saint Peter’s, third day before the Ides of October.)

Ytochor de Thorum informed us that, when the bishop of Empúries of blessed memory [Col. 0430B] had once expelled a certain acolyte from his household because of certain offenses and enormities which he had committed, that acolyte cast aside the clerical habit and went about in lay dress, with his hair uncut and without a tonsure.

Now . . . and . . . his father, who maintained grave enmity against the said Y., had almost entirely cut down a certain vineyard belonging to him, leaving only a small portion of it. Later, when the said acolyte was devastating the small remaining portion, which he had declared that he would destroy, the same Y., happening upon him by chance, killed the acolyte at the devil’s instigation. After he had performed the penance imposed upon him, and since you still assert that he remains bound in the snare of excommunication on that account, he humbly asked us, because he cannot come into our presence, to have him absolved.

We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, since, according to the foregoing, you could not discern in him, from his dress or tonsure, the order of cleric—unless other proofs should establish for you that you knew him to be a cleric—you shall neither avoid him as an excommunicated person nor cause others to avoid him. Otherwise, absolve him according to the form of the Church; and, imposing upon him what is customarily imposed in such cases, cause the expenses which he would have incurred in coming to the Apostolic See, his labor of travel being redeemed, to be expended in works of piety.

[Col. 0430D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Ides of October.

CXLI. TO THE SAME. That he is not bound to pay debts not proved to have been converted to the uses of the church. (At Saint Peter’s, second day before the Ides of October.)

It has been reported to our hearing by several persons that B., your predecessor of blessed memory, granted certain instruments to certain persons by which you are compelled to pay no small sum of money, and the Church of Torres has thereby suffered no small loss. Therefore, desiring, as we are bound to do, to safeguard the Church of Torres against loss [Col. 0431A], by the authority of these presents we grant that you are not bound, according to legal enactments, to pay those debts which are not proved to have been converted to the uses of the Church. Therefore let no one . . . of our grant, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

CXLII. TO POPO, ELECT OF PASSAU [Note: [Col. 0431D] After Wolfker had been transferred to the patriarchate of Aquileia—concerning whom see letter 99 of this seventh book—Popo, or Poppo, provost of Aquileia and, as Schritovinus writes, an abbot (though of which monastery is still unknown), was appointed in his place in this very year 1204, near the end of June. In the *Fasti Mellicenses* he is said to have died in the first year of his ordination. Some say that he sat one year and six months and died on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, not in 1206—which is inconsistent—but in 1205. HANSIZ, *Germania sacra*, vol. I, p. 350. See also BUCELIN, *Germania sacra*, vol. I, part I, p. 45.]. He confirms to him the parishes of Saint Agatha and Stadeloit assigned to the episcopal table. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of October.)

It was represented before us on your behalf that three of your predecessors, because of the ruin and poverty of the bishopric of Passau, generously granted to the episcopal table the parishes in Krhems [Note: [Col. 0432D] Thus it is read in the copy. Perhaps one should read: “In the districts of S. A. and of S.”], of Saint Agatha, and in Stadeloit [Note: [Col. 0432D] Thus it is read in the copy. Perhaps one should read: “In the districts of S. A. and of S.”]. They held and peacefully possessed them continuously for forty years. You therefore humbly asked us to deem it fitting to confirm those same parishes by apostolic authority both to you and to your Church.

We, therefore, inclining to your prayers, grant you by the authority of these presents that, saving the mandate of the Apostolic See, you may hold the aforesaid parishes as your predecessors are known to have hitherto peacefully possessed them. Therefore we decree, etc. This our grant, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of October.

CXLIII. TO THE SAME [Note: [Col. 0432D] See the notes on the preceding letter.]. He confirms to him the right of patronage of the Church of Saint Mary of Passau. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of October.)

[Col. 0431C]

When a request is made to us, etc., as far as: “assent”; by apostolic authority we confirm to you and to your Church the right of patronage of the Church of Saint Mary of Passau, where nuns reside, which Henry, formerly emperor of blessed memory, granted to Wolfker, your predecessor, and to the Church of Passau [Note: [Col. 0432D] The diploma is found in HANSIZ, *Germania sacra*, vol. I, p. 339. But there the emperor conveys—or rather restores—the Church of Saint Mary, which he calls an abbey, to Wolfker in exchange for the estate of Mending, in order that religious life might be reformed there. The diploma is said to have been given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1193, indiction XI, in the reign of Lord Henry VI, most invincible Roman emperor, in the twenty-third year of his reign and the second of his empire. Given at Speyer by the hand of Sigelo, protonotary of the imperial court . . . . . (thus), on holy Easter Day, the fifth day before the Kalends of April. In the year 1193 Easter fell on 28 March. See *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, vol. I, new ed., p. 24], for piety’s sake, with its appurtenances, as you justly and peacefully possess it, etc. We decree concerning our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

CXLIV. TO CHARLES, CANON OF AQUILEIA. He receives him under protection. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of October.)

[Col. 0431D]

To the just requests of petitioners, etc., as far as “assent”; your person [Col. 0432A], etc., as far as “we receive.” In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the prebend which you possess in the Church of Aquileia, as you justly and peacefully possess it, etc. Therefore let no one, etc. This page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

CXLV. TO HERLUIN, BISHOP OF LEIGHLIN, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. He receives him under protection. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of October.)

In the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, etc., as far as “to provide.” Therefore, etc., as far as “we assent”; and we protect the aforesaid Church of Leighlin, over which, by God’s authoring [Col. 0432B], etc., as far as “we fortify.” We decree that whatever possessions, etc., as far as “to be expressly named”: the city of Leighlin itself, in which the cathedral see is located, with its churches, possessions, native tenants, and all its other appurtenances; Clava Eidnec, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and its other appurtenances; Thechmochua, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and its other appurtenances; Thechmocdoch in Nuacongbail, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all its other appurtenances; Domnachescrach, Tulach, and Collabbain, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all their appurtenances; Strutar and Glondussen, with other churches, possessions, native tenants, and all their other appurtenances; Cetorlocth Slebre, with churches [Col. 0432C], possessions, native tenants, and all its other appurtenances; Glotach, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and its other appurtenances; Cluainerena and Achadarglaiss, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and their other appurtenances; Jurnaide, Lenidruim, and Urard, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all their other appurtenances; Techmolling, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all its other appurtenances; Midissel, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all its other appurtenances; Berrech, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all its other appurtenances; Athfadat, Cellasnad, Artingenoeda, and Iirecellend, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all their other appurtenances; [Col. 0432D] Dissurtrich and Balanna, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all their other appurtenances; Cellederggida and Radmor, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all their other appurtenances; Tilachfortchm [Col. 0433A] and Cluammormoedoc, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all their other appurtenances; Achadadall, with churches, possessions, native tenants, and all its other appurtenances; Druimcosinti, the church of Dathilec, and Celmecchatil, in the parish of Hubargaühuby; Leus, Hofclmeth, Fodereth, and Odron, with Thathmolig, possessions, native tenants, and all their other appurtenances. Therefore we decree, etc., as far as “to be of benefit,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the archbishop of Dublin. If any person therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of October, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CXLVI [Note: [Col. 0433D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 81.]. TO JOHN, PRIEST, RECTOR, AND THE BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF RIVO CENERARIO [otherwise RIVICENERATIO]. He receives them under protection subject to an annual payment. (At Saint Peter’s, third day before the Kalends of November.)

When a request is made to us, etc., as far as “inclining”; we receive under our protection and fortify by the patronage of the present document your persons and the hospital of Rivo Cenerario, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all that you presently possess by rightful title or may in future acquire by lawful means, etc., as far as “we receive.” As a token of this protection received, you shall pay annually to us and our successors three soldi of Luccan currency, freely offered. Therefore let no one [Col. 0433C], etc., infringe our protection, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLVII [Note: [Col. 0433D] Raynaldus gives a fragment of this letter under the year 1204, § 23. What is printed there [Col. 0434D] is here enclosed in brackets.]. TO . . . THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF GENOA. That they should compel the plunderers of gifts sent by Baldwin to restore the plunder. (At Saint Peter’s, second day before the Nones of November.)

Grievous and unworthy is the matter which we bear, and which we can no longer pass over by dissimulation: that very many Genoese, repaying us injury for honour, offence for favour, and wrongs for benefits, grievously persecute the most holy Roman Church, both in head and members, wickedly abusing our kindness; so that, because they have often found us easy and favourable in granting indulgence to them [Col. 0433D], they always prove ready and prompt to offend us. For recently, [when our dearest son in Christ, Baldwin, the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople, through our beloved son Brother Barrochius, formerly master in Lombardy of the houses of the Temple, sent us certain gifts as first-fruits of his devotion—namely, one carbuncle, bought, as he asserts, for a thousand marks of silver; one precious ring; five samites; and a most excellent cloth for the adornment of the altar—and through the same man was sending for the use of the Temple two icons, one containing three marks of gold and another ten marks of silver, with wood of the life-giving Cross and many precious stones; two golden crosses; and, among topazes, emeralds, and rubies, nearly two hundred [stones]; one crystal flask; two silver cups; one little casket gilded on top; two small chests; one silver flask; and, in addition, fifty marks of silver: Henry Belamuto and W. Portus, your citizens, with seven galleys in the harbour of Mothone, wickedly took from him all the aforesaid things. Although he protested vigorously on our behalf and on behalf of the aforesaid emperor, and carefully explained how great a loss the city of Genoa [Col. 0434A] might incur on this account, he made no progress whatever with them. At last, before their eyes, he separated and identified every item, showing what belonged to the house of the Temple and what to the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, injury to the Apostolic See and offence to the aforesaid emperor can bring you neither honour nor advantage, we admonish and earnestly exhort your devotion, commanding you by these apostolic letters effectively to compel your aforementioned citizens to restore the offerings,] and to cause them to be surrendered intact into the hands of our venerable brother, your … archbishop [Note: [Col. 0434D] Book VI, epistle 171.].

Otherwise, since to neglect to disturb the wicked is nothing other than to encourage them, and those who cease to oppose manifest wrongdoing are not free from the scruple of secret complicity [Col. 0434C], know that we have enjoined upon the same archbishop, under the obligation of fealty and by virtue of obedience, that, with every obstacle of appeal removed, he strike the aforesaid wrongdoers and their accomplices with the sword of excommunication, bells having been rung and candles lighted, and subject your city to a general interdict; so that, except for the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying, no divine office shall be celebrated there. And if satisfaction is not made even thus, we shall take care to lay our hands more heavily upon you; moreover, the aforesaid emperor will exact from you fitting vengeance for so great a presumption.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of November.

CXLVIII. [Note: [Col. 0434D] On the subject of this and the following letter, compare Book VI, epistles 137 and 120; Book VII, epistle 81. See also the notes on them.] TO MATTHEW AND THE BRETHREN OF THE MONASTERY OF ST MARY OF BOTRANO. He confirms by apostolic authority the exchange of the places of Fiore and Botrano made between them, on the one side, and the Archbishop and Chapter of Cosenza, on the other. (The instrument of exchange itself is inserted.) (At St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 0434D]

That the branch which the heavenly Father had planted might not so much flourish at Fiore as bear fruit at Botrano, and might yield a more abundant fruit of fragrance and honourableness [Col. 0435A], and that more might run after the fragrance of its sweetness if the South Wind more plentifully blew through the garden of spices, and the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts were not exposed to the blasts of the North Wind, we commanded our venerable brother Luke, archbishop, and our beloved sons, the Chapter of Cosenza [Note: [Col. 0435D] Book VI, epistle 137.], that, since at the place of Fiore the bitterness of the cold claimed not only spring and autumn for itself, but even encroached upon the summer months, and since the place of Botrano, belonging to the Church of Cosenza, was said to be suitable for religious life, they should take care, upon receiving from you an adequate exchange according to the valuation of the same archbishop, to assign to you the aforesaid place with its appurtenances, transferring it to you as freely as the exchange should pass freely to them; so that, as the monastery of Fiore belonged directly to us [Col. 0435B], so the monastery which should arise at Botrano should directly belong to us. We also firmly commanded the beloved sons … abbots of the Holy Spirit and of Coratio, and Brother Roger of Tarcian, that they should seek to compel them to this by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

And when the same archbishop had humbly carried out our command, insofar as lay in his power, but his canons opposed his will, the aforesaid executors, by apostolic authority, suspended those canons from receiving their prebends. Although certain of those canons, appearing before us with you, son Abbot, alleged the proximity of Botrano, the remoteness of the compensation, and the scandal to the citizens [Col. 0435C], nevertheless, wishing to make provision for you, since the archbishop could by canonical permission transfer to you, in favour of religion, a certain part of his possessions, we commanded our venerable brother … bishop of Martirano, and the aforesaid … abbot of Coratio, … abbot of Formosa, and … treasurer of Martirano [Note: [Col. 0435D] Book VI, epistle 220], diligently to investigate the truth concerning these matters; and, if the exchange received by the archbishop was adequate, or an adequate one were offered, then, upon its receipt, to cause this exchange to be inviolably observed; otherwise, since according to the tenor of our command it ought by no means to have been made without suitable compensation, to revoke it as void. Thus, if not all could be present for carrying these matters out, three of them should nevertheless fulfil them.

Although one of those executors had entered upon the way of all flesh, and the third dissented, the two nevertheless judged the compensation adequate. Therefore, because under the canonical sanctions the judgment of the majority prevails, although by right we could have approved what the aforesaid two had approved despite the dissent of the third, and could have punished the canons more severely because they had not observed the sentence rendered against themselves by the first executors, nevertheless, desiring to overcome evil with good, we commanded them [Note: [Col. 0436D] Book VI, epistle 81.] to consent to the said exchange without any difficulty.

Accordingly, as we have seen contained in their letters, by authority of our command and in view of the work of piety, and also considering the great advantage of the possession in Syla which you offered them with their common consent and will, they humbly executed what we commanded: they freely granted you the place of Botrano, bounded by specified boundaries, with the churches situated there; having received from you in exchange the possession in Syla, bounded by specified limits, the church of St Nicholas of Bottulo with all its holdings, the church of St Martin of Jove with its holdings, a certain mill situated on the river Cardon, and the holding called Canale. Therefore, that what has laudably been accomplished by our command may obtain greater firmness by our authority [Col. 0436B], we confirm the exchange itself by apostolic authority, as it is contained in the authentic instruments of the parties, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing.

Moreover, lest there be doubt in future concerning the form of that exchange, we have judged that the authentic instrument drawn up concerning it by the aforesaid Archbishop and Chapter of Cosenza should be subscribed word for word to this our confirmation. Its tenor is as follows:

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the eternal, omnipotent, and undivided Trinity. Amen.

The Apostolic See, which holds the chief dominion in the world, by the authority entrusted to it always gives its subjects salutary commands, which no one who proposes to walk the paths of justice ought stubbornly to oppose. For paternal mercy, which gathers without distinction the diverse orders of sons into its bosom [Col. 0436C], so provides at all times for all, that, temporal goods having been suitably disposed in an appropriate condition, the faithful may rejoice through them in acquiring eternal gifts. Hence it is that the lord pope, moved by the petitions of the venerable abbot and brethren of Fiore, sent us, the Archbishop and Chapter of Cosenza, letters of this kind. [Note: [Col. 0436D] See Book VI, epistle 157.]

“Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother … archbishop, and his beloved sons, the Chapter of Cosenza: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, brother Archbishop, you bore the yoke of the Lord from your youth in the regular habit under the discipline of monastic religion, and were faithful in a few things, so that you deserved to be set over many, in order that in the future you may be set over very many, you ought especially to aid the necessities of those who, sitting with Mary at the Lord’s feet, meditate continually upon His law, having chosen the better part.

Certainly, you should know that, from representations made by our beloved sons … the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Fiore, we have learned that that monastery, situated in the mountains, is so exposed to the winds that, because of the severity and constancy of the cold, winter has claimed not only spring and autumn for itself, but has extended its limits into the summer months. The place is also open to attacks by evil men; in this it is a considerable hindrance to the brethren’s peace [Col. 0437A], and in the former respect adverse to their safety. Since, therefore, a certain place called Botrano, belonging to the Church of Cosenza, is reported to be suitable for religious life, we admonish and earnestly exhort your devotion, and command and enjoin you by apostolic writings that, upon receiving from the same abbot and brethren an adequate exchange according to your valuation, brother Archbishop, you take care to assign to them the aforesaid place with its appurtenances, transferring it to them as freely as the exchange shall freely devolve upon you; so that, as the monastery of Fiore belongs directly to us, so the monastery which shall arise at Botrano may be subject to us directly.

Otherwise, know that we have firmly commanded our beloved sons … the abbots of the Holy Spirit and of Coratio, and Brother Roger of Turcian, that, after prior admonition, they compel you to this by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

Given at Ferentino, on the Kalends of September, in the sixth year of our pontificate.”

“Having therefore received these letters, when I, the aforesaid archbishop, after receiving an adequate exchange from the aforesaid brethren, had carried the apostolic command into execution, but our canons could not easily be induced to it because of the magnitude of the command itself, certain of them went to the Apostolic See, and the judgment concerning the exchange was entrusted by the lord pope to other executors. When they reported that the exchange was adequate [Col. 0437C], and the Supreme Pontiff again commanded by apostolic writings that it be done, considering both the piety and the force of the command, and considering the great benefit of the possession which the aforesaid abbot and brethren of Fiore had offered us in Syla, much better than they had previously shown, we at length took care, by common will and consent, humbly and faithfully to fulfil the apostolic command as we ought.

We therefore give to you, Lord Matthew, venerable abbot of Fiore, and to your brethren and successors for ever, the church of St Mary, the church of St Nicholas, and the church of St Angelo, situated in the holding of Botrano, with the holding itself, which is divided and bounded by these limits. It begins at the spring [Col. 0437D] of St John of Clauco, and rises on the eastern side by the public road as far as the fixed stones which divide the wood of Botrano from the wood of Crepisciti. From the south, a certain path goes through the middle of that wood and descends to the river Aiassa; it crosses that river by the boundary of St Vitalis and strikes the valley called Tornaricium; it ascends through that valley to the road of Pantanellis, and that road goes as far as the place called the Three Threshing-Floors. On the western side it descends through the little valley of Bubernet, which joins the valley of Ursata; and on the northern side it descends through that valley of Ursaia as far as the aforementioned river, as far as the valley called Clauc. It ascends through that valley as far as the lands called Abjuso [Col. 0438A], rises along the boundaries of those lands, and strikes the road leading to Casale Pulian. That road goes as far as the boundary of the land of Jac. of Pulian, and proceeds along that boundary as far as the dry little valley which descends to the valley of Clauc; it ascends through that valley as far as the aforesaid spring of St John of Clauco and closes at the first boundary.

We exchange and grant to you this holding, with woodland, vineyards, trees, waters, a mill, and everything which the Church of Cosenza has hitherto freely and peacefully held and possessed there as part of the demesne of the episcopal table. We nevertheless grant you and your successors the power to build a monastery there, as is contained in the aforesaid apostolic letters [Col. 0438B], and freely and peacefully to possess the place itself as the Church of Cosenza has hitherto possessed and held it; and to do in it and with it whatever shall please you and your successors. Only the use of cutting timber is reserved to our Church in the part of the wood bounded by these limits. It begins at the spring of St John of Clauco and descends through the valley of Clauc as far as the stream of Upper Serron; it ascends that stream to the road of Serra, and that road runs beside Serra eastward as far as the public road, then returns by that road and closes at the first boundary.

We reserve no right or power to ourselves or our church within the limits of this part; nor shall it be lawful for us or our successors to gather acorns there [Col. 0438C], or to build anything on the land itself, which we grant to you as we grant all the rest, or in any way to act to the detriment or scandal of your monastery. We shall be content solely with the use of timber, as stated; while the use of acorns and ownership of the soil are left to you for ever.

We grant you this entire holding in exchange, as described above, and shall at all times defend it, as is just, both for you and for your successors. We have received from you the church of St Nicholas of Bottulo, with its holding, vineyards, trees, fulling-mills, and mill located there; another mill situated on the river Cardon; and the holding called Canale, with the church of St Martin of Jove and its holding, which our predecessor Andrew of good memory had granted you with the common consent of the Chapter, under an annual rent of one pound of wax. After receiving that church, we have entirely remitted that rent to you. We have also received the holding in Syla, which is divided and bounded by these limits. It begins at the river called Loric, and from the south proceeds by the public road through Vallebona to the river Argentiol; it crosses by the same road to the stream called Cassand, and thence proceeds to Macla de Aren. On the eastern side it rises from the aforesaid Macla de Aren and extends through the wood to the Serra called St Angelo’s; it strikes the Oristas, which divide Mesocampum and Trag., and descends directly to the river [Col. 0439A] Garg. Within the district of that river, by the head of the Maclae, it crosses the river Garg and rises directly to the summit of the mountain; thence it descends straight to the river Net. From the north that river rises to the ford of the Castle of the Slavs; from the west the public road returns through Trigia, by Charlemagne’s stone and through the Serra of Grimald, as far as the aforesaid river Loric, and closes at the first boundary.

We receive from you this entire holding, with woods, waters, and everything contained within it, as the monastery of Fiore has hitherto held and possessed it by imperial gift. And that this exchange, made by command of the lord pope and by our unanimous will for the advantage of both Churches, may obtain inviolable force [Col. 0439B], we decree that all who, on behalf of our Church, at any time presume to hinder or invalidate it shall, unless they come to their senses after being admonished twice and thrice, be subject to the penalty of excommunication. We command this present privilege to be written by the hand of Albert, our scribe, secured by the impression of the seal of our Church, and by the subscriptions of ourselves and our brethren.

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1204; in the seventh year of Frederick, most glorious king of Sicily, duke of Apulia, and prince of Capua; in the month of July; in the seventh indiction; and in the first year of our pontificate.

I, Luke, by the grace of God Archbishop of Cosenza, have subscribed with my own hand. I, Jac., dean of Cosenza. [Col. 0439C] I, Peter, cantor of Cosenza. I, Michael, treasurer. I, Ruf., canon of Cosenza. I, Pag., canon of Cosenza. I, Bern., canon of Cosenza. I, Suardus, canon of Cosenza. I, Isaac, canon of Cosenza. I, Nic., canon of Cosenza. I, W., canon of Cosenza. I, Master Romoaldus, canon of Cosenza.”

Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of November.

CXLIX. [Note: [Col. 0439D] See the notes on the preceding letter, no. 148.] TO MATTHEW, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF ST MARY OF BOTRANO, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, FOR EVER. He receives them under protection and enumerates the goods belonging to them. (At St Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of November.)

[Col. 0439D]

Those who prefer to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners, and who, beneath the regular habit, humbly serve Him for whom to serve is to reign, rather than wander through secular enticements, ought to receive both apostolic protection and aid; so that they may meditate more freely upon the law of the Lord in proportion as our solicitude and authority have more beneficially provided for their needs.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclining to your former petitions [Col. 0440A], “That the branch which the heavenly Father,” etc., “might directly belong to us.” Since, therefore, the aforesaid archbishop and canons at length humbly received our command and carried it out unanimously, in order that we may more firmly strengthen by the favour of our protection what has laudably been accomplished by our authority, we receive the monastery of St Mary at Botrano into the right and ownership of blessed Peter, and under his and our protection, and fortify it by the privilege of this writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which, according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, is established in the same monastery, etc., shall be observed.

Moreover, the following possessions, etc., are to be expressed by name: the place of Botrano itself, with the churches of St Nicholas and St Angelo [Col. 0440B] and all its other appurtenances, as it has been assigned to you by the same archbishop and canons; the place of Fiore with its appurtenances; the place called Calosub. with its appurtenances; the place called Paraclomitus and another place called Semigari, with their appurtenances; the place called Eremita with its appurtenances; the place called Campus de Manna together with another place called Misdi, with all their appurtenances; the place called Gimellaria with all its appurtenances; the holdings of Garga; the holdings of Fragullis, Tassetan, and Caput Rosae, with all their appurtenances; arable lands, pastures, woods, waters, and everything enclosed by the following bounds: from the river called Lorica, proceeding westward by the public road [Col. 0440C] as far as Serraricum, descending by that road to the river Sabuti, ascending that river to its spring, and thence the boundary proceeds to the river Ampulini on the south; descending that river to the place where it joins the river Neto, ascending that river to the Serra which faces Gimellara and lies in the boundaries of the monastery of St Tripedius on the east; thence the boundary proceeds along the bounds of the monastery of Abbot Marcus as far as the road coming from Cherentea, and follows the portico—which road forms the northern boundary—as far as the place called Frassinetum. From there the boundary ascends by the river Neto, ascending that river [Col. 0440D] to the place facing Cristas, where it is called Three Heads; it goes directly to Cristas, which divide Mesocampum and Fragulum, proceeds to the Serra called St Michael’s, descends to the public road at the place called Macula de Arena, proceeds by that road of Vallebona, and closes at the first boundary; the holding of Fluca with all its holdings; the income from the saltworks of Neto, namely fifty gold bezants; the monastery of Abbot Marcus; the dependency of St Martin of Neto; whatever you possess in the holding of the river Frigidus; the houses which you possess in the city of Cosenza; also the house which you bought in the citadel of Cosenza; [Col. 0441A] the small houses situated around that house, bestowed upon you by W., the justiciar, out of piety; and the house which Brother John of Rublan offered to your monastery.

We establish and decree by this present act that your monastery shall be subject to no one except the Roman Church, whose right it is. Certainly, concerning the produce of your labours which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or the increase of your animals, none, etc., shall presume. You may also receive clerics or laymen, etc. We further prohibit, etc., anyone from leaving that place without the abbot’s permission. When the man departs, etc., to retain; strictly forbidding anyone to alienate lands, etc. If any donations, etc. We also prohibit any monk, etc., from acting contrary to its advantage. [Col. 0441B] But if anyone should perhaps presume to do so, etc., he shall answer, etc. Furthermore, it shall be lawful for you in your own causes, etc., not to perish. Moreover, by apostolic authority we prohibit any bishop, etc., from involving himself in any manner, whether by removing the one who shall be in office at the time or otherwise, without a mandate of the Roman Pontiff.

We further prohibit any archbishop, bishop, or other ruler of churches from daring to promulgate in your monastery a sentence of interdict, or against the brethren established there a sentence of suspension or excommunication. If this is done, we decree that such a sentence is null and void. Moreover, if against your hired servants, because you do not pay tithes, or for any reason concerning them, etc., we have judged it to be annulled. But when a general [Col. 0441C] interdict, etc. Chrism, however, etc., ordinations of clerics, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments, you may receive from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer who enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and who, supported by our authority, may provide you what is requested. Upon the death, etc., an abbot is to be chosen. The person elected, however, shall receive the blessing from the Roman Pontiff or from whomever he shall appoint. Likewise concerning peace, etc. Therefore we decree, etc., saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token that the same monastery belongs especially to the right of blessed Peter, you shall annually pay one gold coin to us and to our successors. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

[Col. 0441D] Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of November, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1204, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CL. [Note: [Col. 0441D]

The first part of this letter is found among the Decretals, Book III, title 46, *On the Observance of Fasts*, chapter 1.

The second part is also found there, but in a very mutilated form, among the Decretals, Book III, title 41, *On the Celebration of Mass, the Sacrament of the Eucharist, and Divine Offices*, chapter 5. What is found in both places is enclosed here in brackets. See also Raynaldus under the year 1204, §68.]

TO THE CLERICS OF ST PETER’S IN MAGDALONA. He replies that whenever a vigil falls on the Lord’s Day, the fast is to be observed on Saturday, and that the discipline of fasting is to be kept on the day before the feast of St Matthias. (At St Peter’s, on the Nones of November.)

[Col. 0442A]

[Note: [Col. 0441D] See the Decretals, Book III, title 46, chapter 1.] [It was asked of us on your behalf [Note: [Col. 0441D] These words are absent in the Decretals.] whether, if the Nativity of the Lord, the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, or the feast of any Apostle should fall on a Monday, the vigil ought to be fasted on the preceding Saturday, and whether a fast is to be prescribed on the vigil of the blessed Apostle Matthias. To this we have judged that a brief answer should be given: that both [Note: [Col. 0442D] In the Decretals this particle *and* is absent, as are below the word *aforesaid* and, after “feasts,” the addition “aforesaid.”] the vigil of the aforesaid feasts falling on Monday and that of blessed Matthias ought to be fasted on Saturday.] [Col. 0442B]

Moreover, you ask to be instructed by apostolic letters when the priest ought to take the ablution at Mass. To this we reply as follows [Note: [Col. 0442D] See ibid., title 41, chapter 5.]: [that the priest ought always to take the ablution with wine after he has consumed the entire sacrament of the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 0442D] The Decretals read “received.”], unless he is required to celebrate another Mass on the same day, lest, should he take the wine of the ablution, it hinder the other celebration.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of November.

CLI. TO THE … BISHOP OF TERMOLI [Note: [Col. 0442D] The interrupted and sparse succession of bishops of Termoli, in Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VIII, col. 530, mentions Aliforius about the year 1196, from the records of the monastery of Casanova in the diocese of Penne; then John, but not before 1265.], AND TO THE … ABBOT OF ST JOHN IN LAMIS. He entrusts to them the examination of the complaints of the people of Foggia against the Trojans and the Bishop of Troia. (At St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October.)

[Col. 0442C]

The beloved son …, archpriest of Foggia, has laid before us, on behalf alike of the clergy and the people of Foggia, a complaint: since Foggia has been established on the site where Arpi, once a populous and great city, stood—as is shown by the ancient buildings and the circuit of ditches—they regard it as no small burden that a person should be set over them who ought in no way to preside over them. For, after the destruction of that city, Siponto occupied part of its diocese and Lucera another part; and for some time they were therefore subject to the church of Lucera. Afterwards Troy, which had belonged to the diocese of Lucera, obtained from the Apostolic See the distinction of an episcopal see; and when the bishop of Lucera, after the destruction of his city, was lying concealed at Alesin., the bishop of Troy and the people committed to him occupied the church of Foggia, which was then established under the rule of no one. They utterly destroyed Foggia—which, like the city of Arpi, had belonged to the Chamber of the princes—in order that they might not be deprived of the lordship of that church: once under Robert Guiscard, a second time under Duke Raino, a third under Emperor Lothair, and a fourth under King Roger of illustrious memory. [Cols. 0442D–0443A]

Nevertheless, despite the opposition of the clergy and people of Foggia, that bishop was never able to obtain peaceful possession of episcopal rights there; nor does he possess the greater part of the diocese of Lucera which he had occupied. But whether that place belonged to the diocese of Lucera or to that of Arpi, the bishop of Lucera possesses it without dispute; consequently the bishop of Troy cannot reach Foggia except through the diocese of Lucera.

But when the storm in the kingdom had been calmed into tranquillity and Foggia, with the Lord’s help, had become populous, it obtained from the kings reigning successively privileges of liberty. Therefore, since the bishop and people of Troy could by no means obtain from the kings the subjection of Foggia to their jurisdiction, their fury was so inflamed that again and again they brought enemies of the kingdom against its destruction. For at the time when King W. of illustrious memory entered upon the way of all flesh, they gathered for Foggia’s ruin as many enemies of the kingdom as they could bring together, and, apart from the persons slain—so the text reads—they inflicted upon them losses amounting to twenty thousand ounces. Destroying churches situated outside Foggia, they did not fear to violate an altar which Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, had consecrated in honour of St John, carrying away the relics of the saints deposited therein. [Cols. 0443B–C]

Since the people of Foggia could in no way resist them, because Foggia, like the other cities of the kingdom, was then unfortified, they offered the bishop and chapter that they were ready to obey their commands, both in temporal matters—although this ought not legally to have been required—and in spiritual matters. Through their messengers they begged them that, if they perhaps would not spare the land, they would at least turn merciful eyes toward the churches; for they should know certainly that, if they would not cease from destroying churches, the people of Foggia would thereafter in no way answer to them in spiritual matters.

But the bishop and people together replied that they had resolved not merely to destroy the land, but to raze the churches themselves and carry the bells and the relics of the saints to Troy. They no longer wished to retain any temporal or spiritual right in Foggia, because they intended to render the place uninhabitable and reduce it to pasture or arable land. At length, however, when they had been driven off as it pleased the Lord and had returned shamefully to their own homes, the people of Foggia took care to set forth the course of events to King Tancred of illustrious memory. Confirming their privileges of liberty, he added that, so far as could be done by his grant, Foggia should henceforward use the title of city. [Cols. 0443C–0444A]

He wrote and petitioned Popes Clement and Celestine, our predecessors of blessed memory, that they might deign to grant the people a bishop. Favourably supporting their wishes, those popes gave them hope in their letters that they should be adorned with the episcopal mitre. But when Emperor Henry had acquired the kingdom, and the chancellor of the kingdom was the bishop of Troy, that bishop obtained Foggia from the emperor and caused the property of the people of Foggia to be granted by that same emperor to the people of Troy.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] We have already observed that Walter of Polena, chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily, was transferred from the church of Troy to that of Catania. See book V, epistle 39, note.]

He also obtained from him an order that the walls of Foggia should be demolished, so that they might at last afterwards destroy it altogether. When this came to the people’s hearing, they gave the aforesaid emperor eight thousand ounces of gold in order to free themselves from such servitude. He then granted them a privilege of liberty, retaining them in his own demesne, as his royal predecessors had done. [Cols. 0444A–B]

Yet at that time the clergy of Foggia were compelled by that emperor to answer to the bishop of Troy. When the bishop had confined them in custody, he extorted three hundred ounces of gold from them, appointing over them as his vicar the man whom the church of Troy now has as its pastor.

[Note: He was probably Gualbert, whom Ughellus, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, part marked with an asterisk, col. 237, records as bishop of Troy after Walter of Polena in 1195; Ughellus further states that his successor Philip received consecration in 1212, on 13 October.]

Being, as they assert, both ambitious and arrogant, this man removed benefices from the clergy of Foggia and sought to assign them to men of Troy. Moreover, utterly destroying the liberties and privileges of the aforesaid church, he inflicted upon them, first as vicar and afterwards as bishop, following in his predecessors’ footsteps, burdens whose extent will become clear from what follows. [Col. 0444B]

For although he ought to be a common father, he behaves like an enemy and foe. Since he cannot persecute them with arms, he uses stratagems against them, so that, under the pretext of the spiritual sword, he may oppress them. Without cause he pronounces against them sentences of interdict and excommunication; and, disregarding legal procedure, he sometimes summons clergy to Troy on the slightest, indeed on no, pretext. What they regard as most grievous is that, by making them dwell among their enemies, he restores neither office nor benefice to them unless at the entreaties of the people of Troy, whom necessity compels them to petition—so that they may appear to be deprived and restored through the Trojans.

Moreover, although, as the bishop himself asserts, their land is a distinguished member of his diocese, he takes no care to visit it at due and appointed times; indeed, he never goes there at all, so as to compel them to go to Troy and display himself before the Trojans not as their shepherd but as their enemy. Since more precious members deserve greater honour, it is manifestly gathered from the foregoing that he is neither father nor shepherd, since he grants them no honour but only heaps reproach and burden upon them. [Cols. 0444C–D]

Further, although the people of Foggia, in order to obtain justice from anyone, are not bound under the privileges granted them to leave Foggia except by our special command or that of the king; although the bishop himself ought to perform the correction of clergy and the confirmation of children in Foggia, and to hear matrimonial causes, as is contained in their privileges: he compels them to go to Troy, and hears matrimonial causes there, sparing neither their toil nor expense nor the dangers inflicted upon them by the robbers of the strongholds. And since Foggia is fifteen miles distant from Troy, children carried there by their mothers for confirmation often collapse in their mothers’ arms on the journey.

Furthermore, although, under the privileges granted them, he ought not to deprive clergy of Foggia of office or benefice without reasonable cause and judicial procedure, he pronounces against them now sentences of deposition, now of suspension and excommunication, disregarding legal procedure, at the mere discretion of his own will, and paying no regard whatever to law, custom, privilege, or a lawful appeal made by them to the Apostolic See. [Cols. 0445A–B]

He also presumes to appoint and depose the archpriest, the cantor, and the prebendaries without seeking the will of the chapter, although the election of that archpriest belongs to the chapter itself, while the appointment of the cantor and prebendaries is known, by privilege and approved custom, to belong to the archpriest. Moreover, from every church of Foggia he exacts two fourths of the tithes, although they are bound to answer him only for one fourth and for the cathedraticum; he is not ashamed to reap their temporal goods, although he makes no effort to sow spiritual goods among them.

He also disdains to observe, and insofar as he can renders void and infringes, the liberties and dignities of the church of Foggia established by a certain agreement concluded between them and confirmed by a public instrument. Although he ought not to permit any church to be built in their parish to their prejudice, he indiscriminately grants everyone permission to build churches for their ruin, so that they cannot receive the dues owed by their parishioners, who choose burial in religious houses. [Cols. 0445B–C]

To add affliction to the afflicted, he tries to take away from them certain plots of land belonging to the church of Foggia, as is shown by the authentic instrument of the aforesaid King Tancred, making his own will the rule. He also refuses to repay three hundred ounces which his predecessor extorted from those clergy, partly in the name of a loan and partly by imperial power, although that predecessor pledged his revenues to them as security, from which the bishop does not allow them to receive anything toward payment of this debt.

Indeed, he disdains to maintain at Foggia the legates of the Apostolic See out of revenues specifically assigned for this purpose, so that, contrary to their custom, the people are obliged to support those legates from their own property. To their still greater disgrace, when he happens to celebrate clerical ordinations, he summons the men of Foggia to orders only after all the clergy of his diocese. When he administers holy chrism to them, he does so mockingly, granting it first to hamlets and castles. [Cols. 0445D–0446A]

Consequently others cry out against them, throwing dung and grass upon their heads, sometimes the bedding of horses, and very often taking away the horses themselves. Yet, in order that the bishops who presided from time to time might complete the disgrace of the people of Foggia, they caused Foggia to be painted beside the door of their house, as though it had been entrusted to the church of Troy in both spiritual and temporal matters, writing above it: “The hamlet of Foggia granted to Troy.”

Furthermore, he neglects to dedicate their churches and consecrate their altars, nor does he allow them to be consecrated by other bishops. Although Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, had thought fit to grant them that, until the discord existing between the Trojans and themselves had been calmed by the restoration of peace, they might receive chrism, holy oil, and other ecclesiastical sacraments from whichever Catholic bishop enjoying the favour of the Apostolic See they preferred, this bishop nevertheless forbids everyone to administer the aforesaid sacraments to them. Consequently, on the Saturday before Easter many times they did not celebrate baptism, and infants died without the aforesaid sacrament and the anointing of chrism. [Cols. 0446A–B]

The said archpriest further added that, if we wished to have regard to the former state, they ought rather to be restored to Lucera, which at least originally held and possessed them. But if we should deign to look to the still more ancient and rightful state, restoring their land to its former condition, we should grant them the bishop whom the city of Arpi—upon whose site Foggia is built—is known once to have had. For since, because of the destruction of their land and the lack of population, they lost cathedral dignity and were joined to others because of their small number, we should in no way depart from the path of reason if, now that it has through God’s grace become populous, we took care to distinguish it with its former dignity.

But if we directed our attention to the injuries inflicted upon them by the church of Troy, we should wholly exempt them from its jurisdiction, since one who abuses the power granted him deserves to lose the privileges of his dignity. Therefore, in order that the scandal of so great a dissension may be quieted, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, with an injunction, personally to visit both Troy and Foggia and effectively to strive to restore peace between them. If they admit a peace negotiation, you are to reduce everything to writing and send it to the Apostolic See, so that the greater or more important part of the discord may be quieted by an amicable agreement, and the small portion of discord which remains may be removed at our discretion and authority. Otherwise, you are to investigate most diligently the truth concerning the foregoing matters and others which the parties may choose to set forth, and faithfully report to us in your letters what you discover, fixing for them a suitable term at which, with those letters, they are to present themselves before us.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on 28 September.

## CLII

[Note: [Col. 0447D] It is read in the *Gesta Innocentii*, §91, though not without certain errors. Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §6, provides a complete and more corrected text. It is therefore presented here enclosed in brackets and marked in the margin by a double stroke at the beginning of every line.

Arnold of Lübeck, *Chronicle of the Slavs*, book VI, chapter 20, recounts the same letter with some variation. We give it complete in every detail, carefully transcribed from the Conti copy and also from the Vallicellian manuscript.]

. . . . . . . . LETTER OF EMPEROR BALDWIN TO THE POPE. He informs him how the Byzantine Empire was seized by the Latins.

[Col. 0447A]

«To the most holy father in Christ and most dear lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: Baldwin, by the same grace Emperor of Constantinople and ever Augustus, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, his knight, offers kisses of the feet with an ever-devoted willingness of service.

[Note: Col. 0447D. Omitted in the *Gesta*.]

[Note: Col. 0448D. Omitted in the *Gesta*.]

Since Your Holiness, in the zeal of paternal solicitude and in special affection for our community united in one purpose, desires to know what is occurring around us, we have resolved to set it forth to you in sequence: how wondrously divine mercy has exercised its goodness toward us, and how it has given glory, not indeed to us, but to its own name—a glory to be admired throughout all ages. Ever greater marvels succeed its marvels concerning us, so that even unbelievers ought not doubt that the hand of the Lord accomplishes all these things. For nothing that occurred had been expected or provided for by us; rather, only when no human counsel seemed to remain did the Lord furnish us with new assistance.

Indeed, if we remember correctly, in letters sent to Your Paternity we carried the account of our progress and position as far as this: the populous city had been violently taken; the Tyrant had been driven out by a few men; Isaac’s son Alexius had been crowned; and our stay for the winter had been promised and arranged, so that any who seemed disposed to resist Alexius might be powerfully crushed.

[Note: Col. 0448D. In the *Gesta* and in Raynaldus: “might be secured.”]

We now undertake briefly to relate what afterwards befell us, having first observed that, just as the things which we inflicted upon the Greeks were not the works of men but of God, so the things which Greece repaid us with, in accordance with her habitual treachery, under the new emperor—a Greek in every respect—were not the works of men but of demons.

For we, lest the foreign barbarity opposed to our customs should furnish fuel for discord between ourselves and the Greeks, left the city and, at the emperor’s request, made camp opposite the city, with the harbor lying between.

[Note: Col. 0448D. The *Gesta* adds “in.”]

[Note: Col. 0448D. Thus in the *Gesta*; Raynaldus thinks “bridge” should be read.]

Then, unexpectedly—whether through inborn malice or because he had been led astray by Greek treachery—the emperor, upon whom we had conferred such great benefits, withdrew his heart from us. In every respect, together with the father-patriarch and the mass of nobles, he proved perjured and false to the promises made to us; he incurred as many perjuries as he had sworn oaths to us. Thus, when at last deprived of our support, he vainly planned battles against us and arranged for the burning of the vessel which had brought him and raised him to the crown; but, since God did not favor so cruel a desire, he was frustrated.

His party became worse in every respect; slaughter, fires, and plundering befell his own men. While battle threatened outside, he was hemmed in by fears within. The Greeks were preparing a rival emperor for him, taking the opportunity that he ought to have no recourse to our aid.

[Note: Col. 0448D. The Royal manuscript cited by Baluze reads *refugium*, “refuge.”]

Since his sole remaining hope of escape lay in us, he sent to our army a certain man bound to him by oath, named Marculfus, his blood-relative, in whom, because of benefits bestowed, he trusted above all others. This man promised us, under the emperor’s and his own oath, the Blachernae palace as a hostage until all that had been promised us should be restored. A noble marquis came to receive the palace; Alexius deceived the marquis and, scorning the hostages, did not shrink from his customary perjuries concerning those whom he had already delivered to us.

On the following night Marculfus, perjured both to his lord and to us, disclosed to the Greeks the secret plan for surrendering the palace to us and declared that, through this, their freedom would be taken from them forever, and that every means must be employed to bring this about unless Alexius were overthrown. As the deserved consequence of this treachery, a third emperor was raised in the city. He laid sacrilegious hands upon his lord, sleeping and unaware of the affair, confined him in a foul prison, and again imprisoned a certain Nicholas, a third emperor, who had recently usurped the imperial diadem at Hagia Sophia, after he had been delivered into his hands through the treachery of the Greeks who had created him.

[Note: Col. 0448D. So also in Raynaldus; the *Gesta* adds “and conducted him away.”]

After Isaac’s subsequent death—he who, as was said, had above all others turned his son’s mind away from us—and after the Greek clergy and people cried out that we should be removed from the land, the aforementioned traitor soon renewed war against us. The Greeks, thirsting for our blood, fortified the city with engines and defensive works such as no one had ever seen.

The wall, of remarkable thickness, built from small stones and mortar of ancient tenacity and strength, rose to a great height. Along the seaward side, where our assault was feared, it had very large towers, about fifty feet apart, more or less, from one another. Above the wall a wooden tower was erected, containing armed men on three or four levels. Between every two towers, moreover, either a stone-thrower or a mangonel was set up. Upon the towers were raised exceedingly high wooden structures of six levels; from their uppermost level, ladders, supports on either side, and battlements were extended against us, with the tops of the ladders only a little lower than an arrow could be shot upward from the ground.

[Note: Col. 0448D. Thus also in Raynaldus; the *Gesta* reads *assultus*.]

The wall itself was also surrounded by a lower wall, and by a double ditch, so that no engines could be applied to the walls beneath which sappers might conceal themselves.

[Note: Col. 0449D. Thus in the *Gesta* and Raynaldus; the Conti copy reads “lower.”]

Meanwhile the treacherous emperor attacked us by land and sea, but the Lord always protected us and frustrated his attempts.

[Note: Col. 0449D. Thus in the *Gesta* and Raynaldus; the Conti copy reads “and us.”]

For when our men, pursuant to our arrangements, went far out to procure provisions, as many as a thousand fighting men, the emperor met them with a large force; at the first encounter he was utterly routed. Not a few were killed or captured, while our men suffered no loss. Consulting his own safety by disgraceful flight, he threw away his shield, laid down his arms, and left to our men the imperial standard and a noble icon which he had caused to be carried before him. Our victors dedicated this icon to their Cistercian order.

He again attacked our fleet with fire.
