In the silence of the night, with a strong south wind blowing, he sent sixteen of his own ships, set ablaze, against ours—their sails spread high and gathered below at the prow. But by the Lord’s action, through the great labor of our men, we were kept unharmed; with iron grapnels fixed into the burning ships and chains holding fast, our men’s rowing drew them out into the open sea, and we were delivered by the Lord from the imminent danger of death.

[Note: Col. 0450D. Thus in the *Gesta*, Raynaldus, and the Conti copy; the Vallicellian manuscript reads “with [God’s] favor.”]

We therefore challenged him to a land battle. Having crossed the bridge and the stream which separated our army from the Greeks, we formed our ranks and stood for a long time before the gate of the royal city and of the imperial palace called Blachernae. In the name of the Lord, with the life-giving cross going before the hosts of Israel, we were ready to receive the Greeks in battle if they chose to come out. A certain nobleman who came forth for military exercise was killed by our infantry.

Thus we returned to camp. We were repeatedly challenged by land and sea, but, by the Lord’s gift, we always prevailed, and prevailed triumphantly. The treacherous usurper of the empire sent us envoys of feigned peace, requested and obtained a conference with the doge. When the high-minded doge had charged him that there could be no security of peace with one who had shut up his lord in prison, setting aside the sanctity of his oath and of faith and covenant—things which remain firmly binding even among utter unbelievers—and had robbed that lord of the empire, he faithfully advised him to restore his lord and humbly seek pardon. He further promised our prayers on his behalf and said that, if he wished, we ought to deal mercifully with that same lord, and would ascribe whatever he had maliciously done against us to his youth or to an error of judgment, if he returned to reason. But he offered vain words, for he had no reasonable reply.

He rejected so completely the obedience owed to the Roman Church and the aid for the Holy Land, which Alexius had established by oath and imperial written instrument, that he preferred to lose his life and see Greece overthrown rather than have the Eastern Church subjected to the Latin pontiffs.

On the following night he secretly strangled his lord in prison with a noose. Like Judas, he had eaten with him that very day; and with the iron club which he held in his hand he broke the dying man’s sides and ribs with unheard-of cruelty. He then pretended that a life which he had taken by the noose had been lost by accident; and, allowing an imperial burial, he concealed by the honor paid to the funeral a crime known to all.

[Note: Col. 0450D. Thus in the copies and in Raynaldus; the *Gesta* adds “similar.”]

Thus the whole winter passed for us. When ladders had been fitted to our ships and military instruments had been prepared, we and our possessions embarked. On 9 April—the Friday before the Passion of the Lord—we unanimously attacked the city by naval battle, for the honor of the holy Roman Church and aid to the Holy Land. On that day, though not with much shedding of our blood, we suffered such things that we became an object of reproach to our enemies. Their side was wholly superior that day, so that our military engines had to be dragged ashore and abandoned to the Greeks, and we were compelled to return, our undertaking unfinished, to the opposite bank, exhausted, as it seemed, uselessly that day.

Greatly troubled and terrified, but at last strengthened in the Lord, we took counsel and renewed the battle. On the fourth day, 12 April—the Monday after the Passion of the Lord—with the north wind blowing, we again came up to the walls, applying the ladders of the ships to the ladders of the towers, amid great labor by our men and very great resistance from the Greeks. But once they felt at close quarters the swords of our men, the issue of the battle did not long remain uncertain.

Two ships bound together, carrying our bishops of Soissons and Troyes, whose emblems were “Paradise” and “Pilgrim,” were the first to bring their ladders against the ladders of the towers. By a happy omen they brought the Pilgrims, contending for Paradise, against the enemy. The standards of the pontiffs were the first to take the walls; to the ministers of the heavenly mysteries the first victory was granted from heaven. Therefore, when our men rushed in, an innumerable multitude yielded, by the Lord’s command, to very few. As the Greeks abandoned the battlements, our men boldly opened the gates to the soldiers. When the emperor, armed and standing in tents not far from the walls, saw their entry, he immediately abandoned his tents and fled.

Our men occupied themselves in slaughter; the populous city was taken. Those of the Greeks who escaped our swords took refuge in the imperial palaces. After much Greek bloodshed, as evening was already approaching, our men gathered together again, laid aside their weapons in weariness, and intended to deliberate on the morrow concerning an assault on the palaces.

The emperor gathered his men and urged them to battle on the following day, claiming that he now held our men in his power, shut within the circuit of the walls. But, defeated, he secretly fled during the night. When this became known, the astonished Greek populace discussed appointing an emperor; and while, after daybreak, they proceeded to nominate a certain Constantine, our infantry sprang to arms without waiting for their elders’ deliberation. The Greeks fled; the strongest and most fortified palaces were abandoned; and the whole city was taken in a moment.

An innumerable multitude of horses was plundered; likewise gold and silver, silks, precious garments, gems, and every thing which human beings count among riches. Such incalculable abundance was found that the whole Latin world did not seem to possess so much. Those who had denied us very little left all things to us by divine judgment, so that we may safely say that no history ever recounts greater wonders amid the chances of war. The prophecy was manifestly fulfilled in us which says: “One of you shall pursue a hundred foreigners.” For, if we divide the victory among individuals, each of our men both besieged and conquered no fewer than a hundred.

[Note: Col. 0451D. In the *Gesta*: “because very greatly”; in Raynaldus: “just as very greatly.”]

Yet we do not claim the victory for ourselves, because the right hand of the Lord saved for itself, and the arm of his strength was revealed in us. This was done by the Lord alone, and it is, above all wonders, marvelous in our eyes.

[Note: Col. 0451D. Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript. The *Gesta* and Raynaldus read “and not”; the Conti copy reads “however.”]

Having carefully arranged what the outcome of events required to be arranged, we proceeded unanimously and devoutly to the election of an emperor. All ambition having been set aside, with six Venetian barons, we appointed as electors of our emperor under the Lord the venerable men—our bishops of … Soissons, Halberstadt, and Troyes; the lord of Bethlehem, elected bishop of Acre, who had been delegated to us from overseas by apostolic authority; and the abbot of Lucedio.

After prayer had fittingly been offered, the mercy of the Lord caused them unanimously and solemnly to elect our person, though this was far from our merits, while clergy and people alike acclaimed with divine praises. On the following Sunday—

[Note: Col. 0451D. The *Gesta* reads: “acclaiming. On the following Sunday.”]

—the Sunday on which *Jubilate* is sung, when the Apostle Peter commands that the king be honored and obeyed as one preeminent, and the Gospel announces that no one takes our joy from us, the aforementioned bishops, beloved of God and men, raised us, gloriously crowned, to the heights of empire. This was done with immense honor and rejoicing, while the Greeks also applauded according to their custom, in honor of God and the holy Roman Church and for the aid of the Holy Land, amid the acclaim of all and devout tears.

There were present inhabitants of the Holy Land, both ecclesiastical and military persons. Their joy and rejoicing surpassed all calculation; they declared that a service more pleasing to God had been rendered than if the Holy City had been restored to Christian worship, since the royal city—which for so long had stood in powerful opposition and resistance—now devoted itself to the holy Roman Church and the land of Jerusalem, to the perpetual confusion of the enemies of the cross.

[Note: Col. 0451D. Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript. The *Gesta* and Raynaldus read “and not”; the Conti copy reads “to each.”]

For this is the city which, according to the most filthy rite of the heathen, dared repeatedly to cement deadly friendships with unbelievers by drinking one another’s blood as a bond of brotherhood.

[Note: Col. 0452D. Thus in the Conti copy, the Vallicellian manuscript, the Royal manuscript, and Arnold of Lübeck cited by Baluze. The *Gesta* reads “heavenly.”]

It long nursed those same unbelievers at its most abundant breast and raised them up into the pride of the ages, furnishing them arms, ships, and provisions. What it has done, by contrast, to pilgrims is taught more adequately by examples throughout all the Latin nations than by words. This is the city which, in hatred of the apostolic see, could scarcely bear to hear the name of the Prince of the Apostles, and granted him not a single church among the Greeks—although he received from the Lord himself primacy over all churches.

[Note: Col. 0452D. Baluze observes that Arnold of Lübeck contains certain additional matter here.]

This is the city which had learned to honor Christ only in pictures and, among the abominable rites which it had devised for itself in contempt of Scriptural authority, often dared even to repeat the saving bath, thereby making it void. This is the city which did not consider any Latins worthy of the name of human beings, but called them dogs. The shedding of their blood was almost counted among meritorious acts; neither laymen nor monks, among whom—once priests were despised—the whole authority of binding and loosing was held, made satisfaction by any penitence.

[Note: Col. 0452D. Arnold reads “removed.” The Royal manuscript reads “taken up.” The Podian manuscript reads “utterly despised.”]

When their iniquities and these similar extravagances had been fulfilled—things which provoked the Lord himself to loathing—divine Justice struck them, through our ministry, with fitting vengeance. Having expelled men who hated God and loved themselves, it gave us a land abounding in every good thing: rich in grain, wine, and oil; fertile in abundant fruits; beautiful in woods, waters, and pastures; very spacious for habitation; and of a temperate climate such as no equal is contained in the world.

Yet our desires do not rest even in these things, nor shall we endure the royal banner to be taken from our shoulders until, after the land itself has been securely settled by our people, we may visit the regions beyond the sea and, God granting it, fulfill the purpose of our pilgrimage. For we hope in the Lord Jesus that he who began in us a good work for the praise and glory of his name will bring to completion, establish, and strengthen the perpetual overthrow of the enemies of the cross.

Therefore we more earnestly ask and beseech Your Paternity in the Lord to be leaders and guides of this glory, victory, and most desired hope, for which a great door has been opened to us. Attribute to your times and deeds the eternal honor which will undoubtedly befall you if, by salutary admonitions, Apostolic Holiness kindles those devoted to you—especially the inhabitants of the West, noble and ignoble, of every rank and sex—who are inflamed by the same desires, to seek true and immeasurable riches, both temporal and eternal. Let apostolic indulgence be offered to all who come, to serve faithfully us and our empire, whether for a time or permanently.

For, God granting, we suffice for all whom zeal for the Christian religion brings to us. We both wish and are able to enrich all alike with wealth and enlarge them with honors, according to their respective condition and the variety of their natural circumstances. In particular, beloved of God, may your paternal concern powerfully induce ecclesiastical men of every religious order or rite to kindle the people toward this same end by public preaching and persuasive words, to teach them by example, and themselves to hasten in companies to regions most delightful and fertile. There, no longer amid bloodshed but amid great freedom, peace, and abundance of every good, they will plant the Church—always preserving, as is fitting, the canonical permission of their own prelates.

No believer could doubt that it would concern the praise and glory of the Redeemer, the perpetual honor of Your Holiness, and the especial benefit of the universal Church if Your Paternity were to summon at Constantinople—a city honored by ancient councils—a general council, to be confirmed by the presence of your most blessed person; and if you were to unite New Rome to Old Rome by holy enactments of permanent force. We have learned that you have already invited rebellious Greece to a council, as though foretelling the times which you now behold; although, whether because of Greek rebellion or because of the concerns of the world and various occupations, you seem meanwhile to have delayed it.

Behold now the acceptable time, holy Father; behold now the day of salvation. The Lord seems in your times to have conceived thoughts of peace, who has placed your enemies beneath your feet as your footstool. Sound, we beseech you, the priestly trumpet in Zion, most loving Father. Call the assembly; gather the people; unite the elders and infants at the breast; sanctify for the Lord the acceptable day, the day for establishing unity and peace and for confirming the strength which we keep for the Lord.

For, however inadequate we may be in ourselves, we dare to hope in the Lord that the joy of the Lord is our strength for abolishing the scandal of the cross and subjecting on earth every opposing power that raises itself against the Lord and against his Christ. Remember, holy Father, those who have sat in your chair, whose souls rejoice in heaven and whose glorious memory lives on earth: John, Agapetus, Leo, and others who, for various reasons, are recorded to have personally visited the Church of Constantinople, as is contained in the apostolic archives. You will plainly find—if those who maintain that they have read this do not deceive us—that each of them came for causes far less weighty.

If, from ardent desire, we press ourselves upon you beyond what is fitting, forgive us, reverend Father, in your customary kindness; and look rather and more fully to our affection and to the supreme importance of the undertaking than to our words. Yet we must by no means be silent concerning the fact that our reverend bishops and abbots, and the venerable clergy of lower rank, conducted themselves among us so magnificently, fittingly, honorably, and prudently, and fought so steadfastly and triumphantly with weapons made powerful by God, that they ought deservedly to expect the crown of victory from the Lord. Their memory has deserved to remain forever blessed, and, lest anything be lacking to them in any favor, they should more visibly receive the fullness of apostolic favor and grace for services so well rendered.

We especially commend to Your Paternity, according to his merit and integrity, the illustrious man H. Dandal., Doge of the Venetians, dear to us and deservedly to be loved, together with our Venetian friends and companions, whom we have found faithful and industrious in every matter.»

CLIII

[Note: Col. 0453. Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §20, prints a fragment of this letter. Passages found in his text are enclosed here in brackets.]

**To Baldwin, illustrious Emperor of Constantinople.** Reply to the preceding letter. (At St. Peter’s, 7 November.)

[We have received with paternal kindness the letters of your imperial dignity, which your devotion sent us through our beloved son Barochius, brother of the military Order of the Temple. Having fully understood their contents, we rejoiced in the Lord and in the power of his strength, because he who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble has deigned to work magnificent miracles with you: for the praise and glory of his name; for the honor and advancement of the apostolic see; and for the benefit and exaltation of the Christian people—not to mention your own magnificence and valor. Yet among other things this is pleasing and welcome to us, and for it we commend your prudence: that you ascribe little or nothing to your own power, but everything to God and to us, so that humility may exalt him whom pride does not exalt.]

Therefore, hoping—indeed, holding it as certain—that you always desire, with a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, to revere the most holy Roman Church, mother and teacher of all the faithful, we wish to devote diligent care and effective effort to your honor and advancement. Accordingly, we receive both you and your lands and people under the chief protection of blessed Peter and our own special protection. We firmly command all archbishops and bishops, as well as other prelates of churches, kings, dukes, counts, all other princes, and all peoples, to maintain and defend your lands and people; neither to molest them themselves nor permit others to molest them. Archbishops and bishops are to restrain their molesters by ecclesiastical coercion, without appeal, and compel them to make complete satisfaction—both by excommunication of persons and by interdict upon lands—without any pretext for delay.

We likewise enjoin and command all crusaders, clerical and lay alike, who are with you in the Christian army, under hope of the remission and indulgence promised them by the Apostolic See, prudently and powerfully to assist you in defending and retaining the Empire of Constantinople. Through the aid furnished by this empire, the Holy Land may more easily be freed from the hands of the pagans. Meanwhile, we shall endeavor so to arrange assistance to be sent to you for both lands that you will prove the affection of our mind by the performance of the deed.

But, dearest son, you ought carefully to consider this: after the kingdom of the Greeks departed from obedience to the Apostolic See, it always declined from evil to worse, until, by God’s just judgment, it was transferred from the proud to the humble, from the disobedient to the devoted, and from schismatics to Catholics. Thus, by the power of obedience, it may rise again to good, having through the vice of disobedience fallen away into evil.

Wherefore we more earnestly admonish and exhort Your Highness, enjoining it upon you for the remission of your sins, to strive to preserve in obedience to the Apostolic See the Greek Church and the Empire of Constantinople, which divine grace has subjected to it at the See’s invocation. Through that obedience you will preserve the empire itself more securely. Take especial care that ecclesiastical goods, both immovable and movable, are diligently and faithfully guarded until they are beneficially ordered by the decision of our disposition, so that what is Caesar’s may be rendered to Caesar and what is God’s to God, without confusion.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, 7 November.

CLIV

[Note: Col. 0455D. Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §21, reports fragments of this letter. Passages found in his text are enclosed here in brackets.]

**To the bishops, abbots, and other clergy present in the army of crusaders at Constantinople.** He rejoices that the empire has been transferred from the Greeks to the Latins, and discusses the Greeks’ error concerning the faith. (At St. Peter’s, on the Ides of November.)

[Col. 0456A]

We read in Daniel the prophet that there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries; he himself changes times and transfers kingdoms. This we see, in our own times, fulfilled in the kingdom of the Greeks, and rejoice at it: for he who rules over the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomsoever he wills, has transferred the empire of Constantinople from the proud to the humble, from the disobedient to the devout, from schismatics to Catholics—that is, from Greeks to Latins. Surely this has been done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes. This is indeed a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, in which the right hand of the Lord has displayed power, so as to exalt the most holy Roman Church, [Col. 0456B] while he brings the daughter back to her mother, the part to the whole, and the member to the head. [Note: [Col. 0456D] Raynaldus, cited place.]

For the time seems to have come when, the golden calves having been destroyed, Israel may return to Judah and Samaria be converted to Jerusalem; so that, the court which, according to the Apocalypse of John, is outside the temple having been cast out, ascent may now be made to the Lord not in Dan and Bethel, but upon Mount Zion. Therefore, to him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect donation, although we render not such thanksgivings as we ought, yet such as we are able, and offer him the calves of our lips—him who in our times has given this glory to his holy and glorious name, which has been invoked over us. [Note: [Col. 0456D] Thus far Raynaldus.]

For now that which was once completed according to the letter is fulfilled according to the spirit. For we read that Mary Magdalene came early in the morning, while it was yet dark, to the tomb, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb, together with the other matters which follow in the Gospel reading. Now by Mary Magdalene is understood the Synagogue; by the tomb, the Old Testament is received; and by the stone of the tomb is signified the letter of the Law, which was inscribed on tablets of stone. Mary, therefore—that is, the Synagogue—came early, namely in the primitive age, while there was still darkness, that is, the time of blindness and ignorance before the Law had been given through Moses, concerning which the Apostle says: “I did not know concupiscence unless the Law said, Thou shalt not covet” [Col. 0456D] (Rom. VII). She came to the tomb—that is, she received the Old Testament, in which the mysteries of Scripture lay hidden, shut up like bodies in a tomb. And when at length the darkness was thinning and the true day was shining more fully—that light, namely, which enlightens every person coming into this world, at whose eclipse the rocks are recorded to have been rent and the tombs opened—she saw, in the first believers who were from the circumcision (for salvation is from the Jews), the stone removed from the door of the tomb: that is, the understanding of the letter separated from the Old Testament, [Col. 0457A] because through the teachers of evangelical truth she recognized that the Law ought to be understood not so much literally as spiritually. Thus one of them, the Apostle Paul, declares: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III); and, as he says elsewhere: “It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a bondwoman and one by a free woman; but he who was by the bondwoman was born according to the flesh, while he who was by the free woman was born through promise: which things are spoken allegorically” (Gal. IV). Again: “Not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are the seed of Abraham children, but ‘In Isaac shall thy seed be called’” (Rom. IX); and again: “Those who are children of the promise are not reckoned as the seed” (ibid.).

Mary Magdalene therefore ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple [Col. 0457B] whom Jesus loved, and said to them: “They have taken away my Lord, and we do not know where they have laid him” (John XX). As the Synagogue of the Jews is understood by Mary Magdalene, so the people of the Latins are understood by Peter, who was especially appointed for the Latins and received burial among them at Rome. But the people of the Greeks are understood by John, who was sent to the Greeks and finally rested in the Lord at Ephesus. Peter built one Church, namely the one head of all the Churches. Hence the Lord also said: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI). But John established several Churches in Asia, like many members of one head. Thus in the Apocalypse he speaks of seven churches and mentions each of them, so that, as [Col. 0457C] many members are governed under one head, so many particular churches may be governed under one universal Church.

Mary therefore came alike to Peter and John, because the Synagogue, through the first apostles who had believed from among her, preached the word of the Gospel both to Latins and Greeks. “For their sound went forth into all the earth”; and therefore Mary is said to have run, because the word of preaching ran swiftly. She came, I say, and said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him” (John XX); as if she said more plainly: The scribes and Pharisees, by killing the truth which is Christ, buried it in the Old Testament, so that, according to them, no mention of him might occur in it; and thus, according to [Col. 0457D] their exposition, it is unknown where Christ has been placed in the Old Testament.

Peter therefore went out, and the other disciple, and they came to the tomb. The two ran together, and the other disciple ran ahead more swiftly than Peter and came first to the tomb; and, having bent down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, yet did not enter. For at the preaching of that Church which had believed from the circumcision, the nations predestined to life heard—namely, Greeks and Latins—and strove eagerly toward an understanding of the Old Testament, so that through it they might recognize the truth of such great things as God had shown. Yet, although the people of the Greeks [Col. 0458A] had first received the Old Testament, first announced to them, and had bent themselves to understand it, and had understood the mysteries of Christ’s humanity before the Latin people—because more apostles reached them earlier, such as Paul, Barnabas, and John—nevertheless they did not enter the tomb, nor did they behold the napkin which was set apart, folded in one place. For the teachers of the Greeks have neither hitherto nor even now attained, except perhaps for a very few, to a full understanding of the Old Testament and the deep mysteries of the Godhead.

For by the linen cloths in which the body of Jesus was wrapped are signified the mysteries of Christ’s humanity; by the napkin which had been upon his head is understood the mystery of the Godhead. For, according to the Apostle: “The head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ [Col. 0458B] is God” (I Cor. XI).

[For we read in Isaiah that the two Cherubim, which are written to have six wings, covered their face with two wings and their feet with two wings, flying with two wings: because the mysteries of the Godhead, signified by the head or face, and those things which the Lord God did before the creation of the world and will do after the judgment, are hidden; but the intermediate things lie more open, and among these we too fly.]

Simon Peter, following him, therefore came and entered into the tomb, because the Latin people penetrated even to the inward and deeper mysteries of the Old Testament. Thus he saw the linen cloths lying, and the napkin which had been upon his head not lying with the linen cloths but folded separately in one place, [Col. 0458C] [Note: [Col. 0457D] Again, Raynaldus.] because he distinguished between the sacraments of humanity and Godhead: so that, as in God he does not distinguish the nature but distinguishes the persons, so in Christ he does not distinguish the person but distinguishes the natures. The Greek, therefore, although he believes there are three persons in the divinity and one substance in the Godhead, nevertheless does not believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as he proceeds from the Father. [Note: [Col. 0458D] Thus far Raynaldus.]

Hence John adds of himself, not as his own reproach but as a reproach to the Greeks: “For as yet he did not know the Scripture” (John XX). What else is signified by the fact that the Jewish people was chosen first for the worship of one God, while two peoples were received near the ends of the ages, except that in the Trinity there is one person who is sent by none, because he is from none, and two who are from one and are sent by one?

[Col. 0458D] But if the Jewish people, chosen in the Fathers, bears the type of him from whom all authority in heaven and on earth is named, whose type does the Latin people bear, to whom Christ’s vicar has been given, except that of the Son himself, who is reported to have met blessed Peter and to have said both to him and on his behalf: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again”? And because blessed John was given to the people of the Greeks, and from him began the religious life of perfect monks, that people fittingly bears the type of that Spirit who seeks and loves spiritual persons.

Moreover, if this be so, what is the reason that the Greeks have not yet accepted the possibility of believing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, except that they have indeed humbly received [Col. 0459A] teaching from the Jewish people, which bears the mystery of God the Father, but have hitherto disdained humbly to receive it from the Latin people, who in this respect bear the likeness of God the Son? Thus, just as the same Spirit is said to receive from the Son what he is to declare, so the Greek people, who once received teaching from the Hebrew people, may at last likewise receive it from the Latin people.

[Note: [Col. 0459D] Again, Raynaldus.] For the Father supremely loves the Son because the Father has bestowed upon the Son all that he has; and the Son supremely loves the Father because the Son has received from the Father all that he has. By the same reasoning the Father and the Holy Spirit supremely love one another, because the Father has given the Holy Spirit all that he has, and the Holy Spirit has received in full from the Father all that he has. Unless, therefore, such a relation existed between the Son and the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0459B] they would certainly not love one another supremely; and so the Son would love the Father more than the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit would love the Father more than the Son—which is unfitting, absurd, and altogether impossible. For since the three themselves are one and the same, with nothing variable or diverse in them, there is not in one more than in another to be loved, since equality admits no inequality. Therefore, in order that the three may supremely love one another, it is necessary that the Holy Spirit, just as he proceeds from the Father, should also proceed from the Son; so that, as the Father is from none and the other two are from him, so the Holy Spirit may be from the other two and none from him, and thereby there may be among all a relative distinction of persons, just as [Col. 0459C] there is among all a substantial identity of nature. [Note: [Col. 0460D] Thus far Raynaldus.]

Had the Greeks understood this mystery plainly, they would already have entered the tomb with the Latins, knowing that God is not a God of dissension but of peace. But because John did not yet know the Scripture, namely that Christ had to rise from the dead, it is not surprising if the Greeks still do not know that the letter is dead where the Spirit of Christ lives. Yet shortly, as we believe and hope, they shall know—indeed, they shall know—and a remnant of them shall be converted with all their heart. They shall come to Zion seeking the Lord and David their king; they shall worship at the altar erected at Rome as an everlasting sign; and from that time the hand of the Lord shall be with them.

At last, therefore, that which the Evangelist adds will be fulfilled—and perhaps is already beginning [Col. 0459D] to be fulfilled: “Then that other disciple who came first to the tomb entered also, and he saw and believed” (ibid.). Thus the first became last and the last first. For he shall see what Peter saw and believe what the Church of the Latins believes, so that henceforth they may walk together in the house of the Lord in harmony.

But Mary stood outside the tomb, weeping. While she wept, therefore, she bent down and looked into the tomb; and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain. For when the people of the Greeks enter, the Synagogue of the Jews stands outside, because it beholds the outer bark of the letter [Col. 0460A] and has not yet reached the inward marrow of truth. For the scroll which the hand sent to Ezekiel spread out was written within and without. Therefore she weeps as though hungry, because while she chews the outer bark, she is by no means nourished by the inward marrow; and, pursuing outward things, she does not grasp inward things.

When, therefore, at the end of the ages she sees herself deceived in her expectation, she shall bend herself from the hardness of her heart and, as though looking into the tomb, shall examine her Law more subtly. She shall see two angels seated in white, one at the head and one at the feet: that is, interpreters of both the New and Old Testaments speaking harmoniously and openly about Christ’s divinity and humanity. Nor will she ask them; rather, they will rebuke her, saying: [Col. 0460B] “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke XXIV). Accordingly, they call her a woman because she meditates not with a manly understanding but with a womanly sense; and so she says to them: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John XX).

She advances little by little toward an understanding of truth when she begins to understand that those who have taken Jesus—whose name is interpreted “Saviour” or “saving”—from the Old Testament have done so because the old Law brought no one to perfection, nor shall anyone be justified by its works. But she still does not know where they have placed him, because she does not yet fully believe the Gospel, in which Jesus is found. Yet at last, turned back toward the truth of the Gospel, she shall see Jesus standing, not lying down; but she will not yet know him to be Jesus, because she will already believe that he was the Messiah and [Col. 0460C] had come, and therefore calls him her Lord, but does not understand that he is God.

Then Jesus asks her: “Woman, why dost thou weep? Whom seekest thou?” (ibid.), because the grace of Christ will go before her. But she, thinking him the gardener, says to him: “Lord, if thou hast taken him away” (ibid.), etc. Mary is not mistaken in this judgment: for Jesus is the cultivator and keeper of that garden of which it is written in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song IV). At last Jesus will call her by name, when he turns the hearts of the fathers to the children, so that the remnant of Israel may be saved. When she answers, “Rabboni” (John XX), he adds: “Do not touch me; for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brethren and [Col. 0460D] say to them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (ibid.). As though he said: Although you believe me to be the Messiah promised by the Law and all the prophets, you nevertheless do not believe me equal to God the Father. Go, therefore, to my brethren—that is, by agreement to the preachers of evangelical truth—and tell them, that is, cry out and believe with them, that I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God: namely, that in divinity I am consubstantial with and equal to God the Father.

Behold, brothers and sons, you may now plainly gather that God at last fulfils through you in us the mystery described above, which he foreknew from eternity and prefigured in the Gospel. Understand that God works this mystery through your ministry not as though by chance, but by deep counsel, so that henceforth there may be one fold and one shepherd. For by a provident dispensation the Creator of times apportions all times, so that when the fullness of the Gentiles shall have entered the faith, then all Israel also may be saved.

We therefore admonish your whole body and exhort you earnestly, and by these apostolic writings command you, that, in order to kindle the devotion which the Christian army bears toward its mother, the Roman Church, you faithfully explain the foregoing matters to it; and that you endeavour to induce both our most dear son in Christ, B . . . . . . the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople, and the greater [Col. 0461B] and lesser persons established in that army, to strive to establish the kingdom of the Greeks in obedience to the Apostolic See, through which indeed its dominion may be retained by them, and without which it could by no means be retained.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of November.

CLV. [Note: [Col. 0461D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 56.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND. That he may collect the revenues of the Roman Church throughout the kingdoms of Denmark and Sweden. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of November.)

So that the devotion of your brotherhood, which we have recognized in many matters, may be more closely bound to us, we consider entrusting to you those things through which you can and ought to give greater satisfaction to us and to the Apostolic See. Therefore, fully trusting in your brotherhood, we earnestly request and admonish you, commanding you by these apostolic writings, to undertake this burden for us: faithfully to collect and preserve the due payment of Saint Peter throughout the kingdoms of Denmark and Sweden, and to send it to us through a trustworthy messenger, or to deliver it to those persons whom we shall direct you by our letters to appoint. And in order that you may accomplish this more fully and freely, we grant you full and free authority to restrain any opponents, should there be any, by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of November.

CLVI. [Note: [Col. 0461D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 56.] TO THE SAME. That he may absolve, under certain conditions, a steward who had cut off the nose and injured the tongue of a priest engaging disgracefully with his wife. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of November.)

[Col. 0461D]

It has been reported to us on your behalf that a certain priest, while he was accustomed to commit an abominable act with the wife of one of your stewards, was seized by the steward, who cut off his nose and injured his tongue, though he did not lose his speech. The priest therefore withdrew to the gate of the monks, so that he might save his soul among them. But [Col. 0462A] since the steward seeks absolution from you for this act, you have requested from us that you might absolve him. Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that, if the matter is so, you restore to communion that steward, who is avoided as though excommunicated, on condition that he send, in aid of the Holy Land or for the assistance of Christians labouring in those regions against the perfidy of the pagans, the expenses which he would have incurred on a journey to the Apostolic See concerning this matter; and that he also redeem the labour of the journey according to his means.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of November.

CLVII. [Note: [Col. 0462D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 56.] TO THE SAME. Authority to reform the churches of Lund and Uppsala. (At Saint Peter’s, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0462B]

The integrity of your brotherhood moves us to grant you more graciously those things which ought to be granted to ecclesiastical persons. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we grant your brotherhood authority, in our place, in the archbishoprics of Lund and Uppsala, to uproot and destroy, to lay waste and scatter abroad, to build and to plant, as you shall judge expedient for the honour of God, the exaltation of the Church, and the salvation of the people committed to you. In these matters and all others, therefore, show yourself such that the fame of your name, which spreads a sweet fragrance, may not wither amid the winter of temporal tribulations, [Col. 0462C] but may display in its deeds, through spring and summer, that which will render most abundant fruit in autumn to the husbandman entrusting his vineyard.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.

CLVIII. [Note: [Col. 0462D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 56.] TO THE SAME. He sends him a pallium to be delivered to the Archbishop of Uppsala in place of that destroyed by fire. (At Saint Peter’s, the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.)

You informed us by letter that our venerable brother . . . . Archbishop of Uppsala had lost by fire the pallium which he possessed; and you therefore humbly requested for him, by letters and messengers, that we might deign to send him another, since both he and his Church suffer great poverty and thus could not send a special messenger to the Apostolic See. Although it has been granted you by a privilege of the Apostolic See that, when the see of Uppsala is vacant and someone is appointed there, a pallium may be granted, upon the arrival at the Apostolic See of your messengers and those of the Church of Uppsala, to be conferred through you upon the appointed bishop, yet, because that see is not vacant and a new pallium is not required to be given to him, and because you sent your messengers only at his request and not he himself, we could by right have denied what was requested. Nevertheless, in order to grant favour to your supplication, to which, with the Lord’s help, we wish to accede as far as we can, [Col. 0463A] we have directed that the pallium itself be sent to you through your messengers, for you to deliver to that same archbishop, provided that this is not drawn into precedent hereafter.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.

CLIX. [Note: A fragment of this letter is found in the collection of Decretals, Book I, title 5, *On the Petitioning of Prelates*, chapter 5. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets [Col. 0464D]. Raynaldus also cites this letter, under the year 1204, § 47.] TO THE CHAPTER OF ESZTERGOM. He summons them to his presence, that they may hear judgment concerning the petition for the transfer of the Archbishop of Kalocsa to the archbishopric of Esztergom. (At Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Concerning the petition which you made] that our venerable brother J . . . Archbishop of Kalocsa be transferred to the metropolitan see of Esztergom, our venerable brothers, the suffragans of that metropolitan church—namely C., Bishop of Pécs; B . . ., Bishop of Vác; R . . ., Bishop of Veszprém; and J . . ., Bishop of Nitra—utterly object. By their letters they informed us that, after V . . ., your archbishop of happy memory, had entered upon the way of all flesh, without consulting them you held careful mutual counsel and sent certain of your fellow canons to the presence of our most dear son in Christ H., the illustrious King of Hungary, [Col. 0463B] expressly naming the person whom you wished to be set over you.

After no long delay, when the same bishops had assembled solemnly for the feast of blessed King Stephen and were discussing with unanimous deliberation the election for the Church of Esztergom, you were asked by those bishops whom you wished to be set over and appointed to that see. You answered that you dared elect no one unless he enjoyed the king’s full favour. You then took care to name the aforesaid Archbishop of Kalocsa, upon whom you had already long before agreed with the said king, adding that the suffragans had no right in the election of an archbishop. The suffragans replied that from the first establishment of Christianity in the kingdom of Hungary until those times, no one had been elected to the see of Esztergom except with the suffragans electing together with the canons, in accordance with canonical constitution and approved custom.

They also said that inquiry should first be made whether a useful and suitable person could be found from the body of that church, asserting that in it were many honourable, prudent, and learned men who might preside over that church more fittingly. They further informed us in the same letters that, since the aforesaid Archbishop of Kalocsa had, up to that time, asserted that the Church of Kalocsa was equal to the metropolitan Church of Esztergom and had inflicted upon it diverse and intolerable injuries both in word and deed, they greatly feared that, if he were transferred to that metropolitan see, mindful of his own confession and assertion, and, as if covered with shame, unwilling to seem contrary to himself, [Col. 0464A] he would undertake the promotion of the affairs of the Church of Esztergom less effectively and would not cease to oppress the bishops themselves, who had sometimes firmly resisted his words and acts as their duty required. Yet by canonical sanctions a judge suspected by certain persons ought not to be given to them.

But, beloved sons, . . . . . Abbot of Búkk and Master Peter, on behalf of the aforesaid king, and likewise . . . . . Provost of Pozsony and . . . . . Treasurer of your Church, on your behalf, alleged the contrary, firmly asserting that the matters put forward by those bishops were entirely false. They maintained that the bishops had been solemnly summoned through that same provost and others before the common discussion, and had come, and that their consent had repeatedly been requested as a favour. But since they refused to furnish you suitable counsel and assistance concerning provision for your church, you, wishing to provide for that church left desolate, assembled together after summoning the aforesaid bishops and, with them present, unanimously cast your votes upon the aforesaid Archbishop of Kalocsa, so as to petition us for him; humbly begging the bishops to request us by their letters on behalf of your petition. They wholly refused to do this.

When the aforementioned envoys asserted that urgent necessity and manifest advantage demanded the translation of that archbishop, it was advanced before us in the dispute that the said Archbishop of Kalocsa, to the grave prejudice of the Church of Esztergom, crowned the son of the said king as king despite your objections and despite your producing confirmations from the Apostolic See. Yet the coronation of the king of Hungary is known to belong not to the Church of Kalocsa but to your metropolitan see. Therefore, as an invader of another’s right and a contemner of an apostolic ordinance, he ought to have been severely punished; and it could plausibly be presumed that, since he would not bring a complaint against himself and his own act, he would leave undefended the right of your church in this matter, by which serious prejudice might arise to it. It was nevertheless replied in the contrary sense that the aforesaid coronation had been celebrated by the whole body without anyone’s opposition and without prejudice to anyone.

[Although, therefore, no right is acquired by anyone through such a petition, and we could consequently have rejected the aforesaid petition without prejudice to anyone, nevertheless, in order to provide for you by a special favour as far as we can with God’s help, we have determined as follows: if the aforesaid bishops persist in their objection and you insist upon obtaining the petition, since the foregoing matters have not been established to us, you are to appear before us by suitable procurators, sufficiently instructed in every respect, by the coming Septuagesima, [Note: [Col. 0464D] These words are absent from the Decretals.] so that, with both parties present, we may decree what is just.]

But if they decide to desist [Col. 0465A] from their objection and you wish to persist in obtaining the favour of the petition, nevertheless send suitable persons to our presence within the prescribed term, who are willing and able to give us assurance concerning such matters as may be necessary. But if, while the aforesaid bishops object, you consider that you have little confidence in your legal right, then, lest you incur labour and grief in vain alike, provide canonically for yourselves another suitable person as pastor.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of December.

Concerning this, a letter was written to the king, with this addition: We therefore admonish your highness not to hinder, nor permit the aforesaid bishops to be hindered, from freely pursuing before us [Col. 0465B] their justice.

Given as in the other letter.

CLX. [Note: Cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 81.] TO M . . . . . . PRIOR OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE OF VALLEFARES. He grants him a church built by Pope Alexander and left as the property of Saint Peter, subject to an annual payment of two pounds of wax. (At Saint Peter’s, the eighth day before the Kalends of December.)

As we have seen recorded in the authentic document of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, the nobleman P . . . de Lacopessel offered to the Roman Church the estate of Valle-Fares, in which the church of blessed Mary Magdalene, built by Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, was received into the right and property of Saint Peter. Therefore, adhering to the footsteps of those same predecessors, we receive the same church under our protection, etc., down to “we strengthen.” As a token, moreover, that the same church is of the right and property of Saint Peter, you shall pay to us and our successors two pounds of wax every year. Therefore let no one . . . of our protection, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

CLXI. TO . . . . . BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0465D] Peter, formerly a cathedral canon, rose to the see of Novara about the year 1196. He is said to have administered the Church of Novara for fourteen years, dying in 1210. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 968. See also Book III, letter 6.], AND TO THE CHAPTER OF NOVARA. He annuls the grant of a certain prebend made by the Archbishop of Milan. (At Saint Peter’s, the ninth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0465D]

In the letter of our venerable brother . . . Archbishop of Milan, [Note: [Col. 0465D] In the same place.] we have seen it contained that our beloved son M . . . Bruxuard, appearing before him, humbly requested that he would graciously deign to confer upon him a certain prebend which was legally vacant in the Church of Novara and whose grant had devolved upon that archbishop by the ordinance of the Lateran Council. Since many friends of that M . . ., clerics as well as laymen, pressed the said archbishop, agreeing in their assertion that this was so, he, wearied by their entreaties, granted the said M . . . the aforesaid prebend.

But our beloved son Master Guido, canon of Novara, later informed the aforementioned archbishop that a false representation had been made to him—namely, that the prebend was vacant—whereas at that time a dispute concerning the same prebend was pending before judges delegated by the Apostolic See between M . . ., nephew of the same master, and John Bruxuard, uncle of the aforesaid M . . . He therefore said that the grant was of no force, since it had been obtained by suppressing the truth. Advancing many further allegations concerning the matters aforesaid, he appealed to the Apostolic See, requesting that the archbishop report the course of the matter to us by his letters. Assenting to this request, the archbishop granted him what he requested and also notified the said delegates by his letters that he wished to prejudice no one, advising them to proceed in the said cause according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate. We therefore, considering that fraud and deceit ought to afford protection to no one, decree the grant of the aforesaid prebend made by that archbishop while the suit was pending to be void and of no effect.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the ninth day before the Kalends of December.

CLXII. W. [Note: [Col. 0465D] William III de Bonilis, formerly prior of Saint [Col. 0466D] Antony, was elected abbot of Montmajour. In this very year 1204, in the month of October, he proceeded to the Apostolic See together with Peter, King of Aragon, the Archbishop of Arles, and the provost, and received inauguration and blessing without dispute. He presided until the year 1233. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 608.] TO THE ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF MONTMAJOUR AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, FOR EVER. He receives them under protection, and the possessions belonging to them are enumerated. (At Saint Peter’s, the third day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0466C]

When we consider ourselves debtors to all the children of the Catholic Church by reason of the office of the apostolate laid upon us by God, it is nevertheless fitting that we devote ourselves with a more zealous concern of charity to those places and persons which are known to belong more especially to the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, to your requests, etc., down to: *we graciously assent*; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory—Urban, Paschal, Gelasius, Calixtus, Eugenius, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs—we confirm and protect the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 0466D] in which divine, etc., down to: *we protect*; decreeing that whatever possessions, whatever goods, etc., down to: *are to be specified by name*.

In the county of Arles: the monastery itself of Saint Peter of Montmajour, with its appurtenances; Castellet, with its whole territory; the church of Saint Isidore, situated within the walls of the city of Arles, with parish and cemetery; the church of Saint Mary of the Sea, [Col. 0467A] with all its appurtenances; the castle of Miramars and the churches of that castle, with all their appurtenances; the church and village of Saint Genesius, with their appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Martin of Lauria, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Lawrence, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Romanus, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint James of Moriers, with all its appurtenances; the church of Pellicana, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Serenus, with its appurtenances; and the church of Saint Peter of Mallan, with all its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Avignon: all rights and possessions which you hold in the castles of Tarascon and Bellicadre; all rights which you hold in the village and territory [Col. 0467B] of Laurada; the church of Saint Mary in the village of Saint Remigius, with half of that village and with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Genesius of Romanino; all rights which you hold in the village of Cabannis and its territory; the church of the Holy Sepulchre of Verqueriis, with its appurtenances, and the other things which you hold in that same village; all rights and possessions which you hold in the village of Saint Andeolus and its territory; all rights and possessions which you hold in the village of Moleges and its territory; the church of Saint Veranus, situated in the territory of Airaga, with all its appurtenances; all rights and possessions which you hold in the village and territory of Gravesons and in the village and territory of Lagoses.

In the diocese of Cavaillon: the church [Col. 0467C] of Saint Peter of Menomenas, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Cleu; all rights and possessions which you hold in the village and territory of Insulta, and all rights which you hold in the territory of Avellonegues.

In the diocese of Carpentras: the church of Saint Peter of Paternis; the church of Saint Maurice of Vennasca, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Lawrence of Marmoren, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Faith, with its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Anthony and half the castle of Bedonio, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint James of Valle-saltus, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael of Anesca, with its appurtenances; and the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Mary of Montiliis, with all their appurtenances [Col. 0467D].

In the diocese of Vaison: the church of Saint Mary of Forcas, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Andrew of Ramera, with its appurtenances; the church and village of Dolonn, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Andeolus of Cairan, with its appurtenances; and the church of Saint Peter of Revello, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Orange: the church of Saint Marcellus of Sirinnan, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Velloricha, with its appurtenances; all rights and possessions which you hold in the city of Orange.

In the county of Aix: the church of Saint Peter of Aleno, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael of Malamort, [Col. 0468A] with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Roccarossa; the church of Saint Mary of Plano, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen of Ronnas; the church of Saint John of Salletas; the church of Saint Peter of Mari; the church of Saint Mary of Chalican, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Honoratus of Rocca-fraudosa, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Julian of Agulla, with its appurtenances; the church of Vellaus; the church of Cabrer; and the church of Saint Peter of Pino, with all their appurtenances; whatever right you hold in the church of Oleras and one fourth of that same castle; the church of Saint Mary of Sesols; the church of Balcodenas; the church of Balles; and [Col. 0468B] the church of Saint Mary of Tous, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Julian situated in the territory of Joquas, with its appurtenances; the castle of Pertusio, with the whole adjacent village and with cultivated and uncultivated territory; all churches in that castle, with their appurtenances, together with all lordship over the whole castle in all things within and without, and the port of the Durance; the church of Saint Mary of Alneu and the church of Saint Lawrence of Robians, with all their appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary of Caroloco, with all its appurtenances; the churches of the castle of Rellan—Saint Peter, Saint Mary, and Saint Denis—with all their appurtenances; the church of the Holy Cross of Auribell; and the church of Saint Stephen of Crau, situated in [Col. 0468C] the territory of the castle of Saint Saturninus, with all its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Fréjus: the monastery of Correns, with all its appurtenances; in the castle of Villaepiscis, the church of Saint Michael with its parish; in the castle of Rocabruna, the parish; in the castle of Flachan, the churches with their parishes; whatever right you hold in the church of Saint Mary of Aurete; and the churches of Bersa, with all their appurtenances.

In the diocese of Riez: the monastery of Saint Peter of Stublon, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Vincent of Mesello; the church of Saint Peter of Riolas; the church of Saint Pontius of Castronovo, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Bruneto, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Vileta, [Col. 0468D] with its appurtenances; and the church of Saint Honoratus of Pallarols and the church of Saint Mary of Villanova, with all their appurtenances.

In the diocese of Senez: the castle called Noranta, with all its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Sisteron: the church of Saint Peter of Saumana, with its appurtenances, and the church of Saint Saviour of Valbaines, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Gap: the church of Saint Mary of Antonavas, with all its appurtenances, and the church of Saint Laugerius of Jaubia, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Vienne: the church of Saint Anthony of Mota, with its parish and all its other appurtenances; and the charitable house situated [Col. 0469A] in its parish and property, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Montanea; the church of Saint Marcellinus; the church of Saint John of Formental; the church of Saint Martin of Vunai; the church of Saint Peter of Monteluser; the church of Saint Mary of Quinceu; the church of Saint Desiderius of Castro; the church of Saint Cyprian; the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Baeu, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Lausonna; the church of Capreriis, with all its appurtenances; and the churches of Saint Evodius, Saint Bonitus, Saint Hilary, Saint Saviour, and Saint Mary of Lechis, with all their appurtenances.

In the diocese of Grenoble: the church of Saint Justus; the church of the castle of Rouo and lordship of that castle, [Col. 0469B] with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Romanus of Cranenco, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Stephen of Nacon, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Exarto; the church of Reneuvell; the church of Conniis; the church of Saint Justus and the church of Saint Mary; and Albaripa, with all its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Die: the monastery of Saint John of Roms; the church of Saint Martin of Coronel, with its appurtenances; and whatever right you hold in the church of Saint Mary of Auriolo.

In the diocese of Valence: the churches of Saint Peter of Mota, Saint Thomas, and Saint Mary of Jallans, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Maimanis; the church of Cerna; and the church of [Col. 0469C] Podio Rigaudo, with all their appurtenances.

In the county of Ventimiglia, beside the sea: the abbey of Blessed Appellen, with all its appurtenances.

Moreover, concerning your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or concerning the sustenance of your animals, let no one, etc., down to: *presume*. By this present decree we likewise forbid anyone, within your parishes, to presume to build a new church without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, while the privileges of the Roman pontiffs remain unimpaired. In parish churches, however, etc., down to: *who are suitable*, let him entrust the care of souls only upon your presentation, so that he must answer to the bishop concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters [Col. 0469D]. Likewise concerning burial, etc., down to: *obstruct*, while preserving the right of the mother church. But on your death, etc., down to: *the Rule of Saint Benedict*, they shall provide for the election of one who, after setting aside his profession, is to be ordained either by the Roman pontiff or by one to whom he has entrusted that authority. Nor may any bishop have authority, without the mandate of the Roman pontiff or his legate, to subject that monastery to excommunication or interdict [Col. 0470A]. We therefore decree, etc., down to: *advantageous*, while preserving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops in the aforesaid chapels. As a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors each year four solidi in the old currency of Mergurium. If therefore anyone, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## CLXIII. . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF PARMA

[Note: [Col. 0469D] Opizzo Sanvitalis, son of the knight Ugo, sprung from a very distinguished and ancient Italian house of the nobles of Parma, immediately succeeded Bernard—who died on 8 November 1194—to the episcopal see of the Church of Parma. Opizzo was a most eloquent man, highly learned in both laws, shrewd and prudent in affairs, and devout toward the worship of God and the saints. In 1207 he solemnly transferred the body of Saint Domninus to the town of Burhi, which thereafter took the name “town of Saint Domninus.” He enjoyed singular favour with Emperor Otto IV. He is frequently mentioned in the Register of Pope Honorius III. He died in 1224, on the second day before the Kalends of June, and was buried in the cathedral. UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, col. 220.]

By apostolic authority he confirms the settlement concluded between the abbot of Saint Sixtus and the commune of Cremona. (The instrument of the settlement itself is inserted.) (At Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of December.)

[Col. 0470B]

When the beloved son G., abbot of Saint Sixtus, lately came to the Apostolic See intending to lay before us a complaint against the people of Cremona—for the sake of whose monastery the city had been placed under interdict, and its podestàs, consuls, and councillors bound by the bond of excommunication—the beloved son John Bonus came on behalf of that city. At our admonition he took care to enter into an amicable settlement with the abbot. Therefore, afterward, at the request of both parties, we judged that the interdict to which that city had been subjected should be relaxed, [Col. 0470C] commanding your brotherhood by apostolic letters to announce that the interdict had been relaxed by us and, after receiving from the excommunicated persons sworn security that they would endeavour to obey our commands, to grant them the benefit of absolution. You shall require them, under the obligation of the oath they have sworn, inviolably to observe the aforesaid settlement, which nevertheless we wish to be observed without prejudice in all respects to the right of the Apostolic See.

The tenor of that settlement is as follows:

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. The abbot of the monastery of Saint Sixtus, through the mediation and with the authorizing support of the lord pope, by his own will and with the consent of Prior P., made the following agreement with John Bonus, envoy of Cremona: namely, concerning Guastalla and Luciaria, that the abbot, in his own name and that of his monastery, promised that neither he nor his monastery would bring any question or suit against the commune of Cremona concerning the aforesaid villages until the emperor should be crowned by the Roman pontiff, while preserving to himself and his church every right which it holds in the aforesaid estates and in all fruits of the past [Col. 0471A] period. Yet whatever has hitherto been done by the lord of Reggio—

[Note: [Col. 0471D] Peter was promoted to the see of Reggio—indeed, this seems the preferable reading—in 1187. He died in 1212. UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, col. 303.]

—or by the lord of Modena—

[Note: [Col. 0471D] Book III, epistle 32, note 430.]

—delegates of the lord pope, concerning the aforesaid complaint, shall not harm or prejudice the people of Cremona in their right or possession, except as regards interruption of time and preservation of the action. The depositions of the witnesses produced by the abbot before the bishop of Modena shall have only such force as they ought to have by law. For this delay and settlement the aforesaid abbot received one hundred and sixty imperial pounds from the people of Cremona; and before the supreme pontiff he acknowledged that he had received the aforesaid money, renouncing the exception of money not paid. Moreover, he received security and a guarantee for twenty imperial pounds [Col. 0471B], which he is to receive each year from the people of Cremona on the feast of Saint Michael until the aforesaid term.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of December.

## CLXIV.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §22.]

To the bishops and abbots established in the Christian army at Constantinople. That Latin priests are to be appointed in churches formerly held by Greeks, and that they are to arrange the election of a head. (At Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of December.)

Because it is no less a virtue to preserve what has been gained than to seek it, we believe it will contribute to your merit, to the enlargement of the empire of Constantinople, and to the honour of the universal Church, if you provide the churches abandoned by the Greeks [Col. 0471C] with Latin clergy, to be maintained in the worship of the divine name under the rule of the orthodox faith and in devotion to the Apostolic See. For it would be disgraceful—and deserving of vengeance at the examination of the last judgment—if you should depart from the territories of the Greeks in such a way that, with the churches left unprovided for, the kingdom remained, as it were, without a priesthood; and there should be no one to celebrate the divine offices according to their rite and duly administer the ecclesiastical sacraments to the Latin people who, God granting, were to remain there permanently.

We therefore admonish and exhort your discretion in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters: assemble together and, supported by our authority, take care to appoint Latin clergy in the churches of the city of Constantinople in which Latins have hitherto not been present. They are to render worthy service to God, preserve ecclesiastical goods, remain devoted to the Apostolic See, and provide their parishioners with divine offices and ecclesiastical sacraments. Since members cannot subsist without a head, however, lest those clergy should seem headless (*acephali*) [Col. 0472A] if they are without a superior, we will and command that all Latin clergy of every region and nation established at Constantinople be assembled. Together with them, you shall deliberate concerning the appointment over them of a suitable overseer: a man who fears God, mature in age, and venerable in learning. The person upon whom they canonically agree shall, by our authority, be appointed their head, to be confirmed by us or by our legates, whom we intend shortly to send to Constantinople, so that whatever is lacking may be supplied more fully by us or by them. You shall endeavour not merely to persuade, but—after admonition has been allowed—to compel by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, the person nominated for this burden to accept the charge imposed upon him by our authority [Col. 0472B]. Thus you shall carry out our mandate in such a way that you deserve commendation for diligence rather than rebuke for negligence. But if not all . . . three of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the seventh year.

## CLXV

[Note: [Col. 0471D]

Reported, but very mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book I, title 10, “On supplying the negligence of prelates,” chapter 4. The passages printed there are here, according to custom, enclosed in brackets; variant readings are also supplied.

Raynaldus gives a fragment of it under the year 1204, §66.]

. P. of Castronovo and Rodulphus, monks of Fontfroide, legates of the Apostolic See. He declares that, because provision for benefices has been omitted, it has devolved upon the pope. (At Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of December.)

We have received the letters of your discretion, in which you seek an apostolic response concerning matters that appear doubtful [Col. 0472C] to you: namely—

[Note: [Col. 0472D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*, as is below the word “to them.”]

—that, since in certain churches subject to your legation some benefices and dignities had been vacant for so long that both the prelates and the chapters, under the terms of the Lateran Council, were deprived of the right of appointment, after your arrival had become known to them they presumed to appoint less suitable persons to those benefices.

Accordingly, since you received advice from learned men that you should, by apostolic authority, annul such appointments—made by persons who had no interest in the matter and who through their own fault had deprived themselves of the right of appointment—you determined first to seek our counsel in this matter.

You further reported that a custom has arisen in certain churches whereby the biers on which the bodies of the dead are borne to churches pass to the use of the ministers of the church; and that, when the people’s charity grows cold and devotion ceases, scandal often arises between clergy and people on account of the biers. You also asked what you ought to do when many persons who have incurred the canon of a pronounced sentence, and who are not subject to you by reason of your legation, come to you for the benefit [Col. 0473A] of absolution, wishing to arm themselves against heretical perversity; and likewise when certain religious, because they have laid hands on secular clerics, are bound by excommunication, are unable to arm themselves against heretics, have no means of approaching the Apostolic See, and ask you for absolution.

[We therefore, replying briefly to your inquiry—

[Note: [Col. 0473D] The *Decretals*: “your discretion.”]

—command you by apostolic letters:

> [Note: [Col. 0473D] This is found in Raynaldus.]

> If you know that those benefices or dignities have been assigned to suitable persons, allow them to possess them peacefully by tolerance; otherwise, remove those persons altogether from them and, supported by our authority, [Col. 0473B] without delay appoint suitable persons, allowing no obstacle of contradiction or appeal.

> [Note: [Col. 0473D] This word is absent.]

> [Note: [Col. 0473D] These words are absent.]

> [Note: [Col. 0473D] Raynaldus ends here.]]

You shall restrain opponents by ecclesiastical censure. You shall also diligently admonish the clergy not to impose burdensome exactions or improper demands concerning the biers brought to their churches with the bodies of the dead. By diligent admonition, you shall induce the laity to observe in these matters the commendable custom hitherto observed out of the devotion of the faithful; if necessary, you shall compel them to do so by ecclesiastical coercion, appeal set aside.

Further, since the Apostolic See is accustomed, by a special grace, to entrust to its legates the absolution of those bound by the bond of excommunication for violent laying on of hands, we will and command that in such matters you proceed as you judge expedient for their salvation, unless their offence is grave and enormous—for example, if it has proceeded to mutilation of a limb or shedding of blood, or if violent hands have been laid upon a bishop or abbot—since offences of this kind and similar ones cannot pass without scandal [Col. 0474A].

Finally, concerning the matter on which you last sought our advice—namely, those who, under cover of their privileges, withdraw themselves from every correction by legates unless the legates have been sent specifically to them—since the notorious character of their conduct supplies the faithful with scandal and furnishes heretics with the strongest pretext for insulting you, we counsel and admonish you to attend more vigorously to the business entrusted to you, and not to seek in other matters persons who may impede the things committed to you, lest one impediment which creates unavoidable necessity be adopted through another which is tolerable [Col. 0474B].

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the seventh year.

## CLXVI

[Note: [Col. 0473D]

This occurs among the *Decretals*, book III, title 6, “On a sick or incapacitated cleric,” chapter 5. Variant readings are supplied; those distinguished by italic type are absent from the *Decretals*.

Raynaldus also cites this letter under the year 1204, §68; but the marginal indication of the number contains an error.]

. To the Archbishop of Arles.

[Note: [Col. 0473D]

At that time the archiepiscopal see of Arles was occupied by Michael de Moresio. We have already discussed him in the notes to letters 74 and 128 of book V, where we examined at length the date of his election as archbishop of Arles. Whether this election should be assigned to the year 1202 is uncertain; but it cannot be deferred beyond 1203, as is proved from documents cited by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* (vol. I, col. 565).

We know for certain that Michael held the see until 1217. Yet the chronological notes of Innocent’s letters give rise to various difficulties. We have already touched upon some; others we shall briefly indicate here, leaving their solution to others.

From letter 128 of book V—which contains no chronological indication of a particular year or day, but which we proved could not have been issued before the seventh day before the Ides of September 1202—it follows that the archbishop of Arles was then at the Apostolic See.

It is known from another source, as will appear from the document shortly to be printed in this seventh book, no. 229, that in 1204 the prelate of Arles was already present at Rome on the fourth day before the Ides of November, together with Peter, king of Aragon, whom he had followed to the Roman curia when the king came to receive the crown [Col. 0474C].

Finally, this letter 176 of the same seventh book, which we are now considering and which is expressly said to have been issued on the fourth day before the Nones of December in the seventh year of Innocent’s pontificate—that is, A.D. 1204—appears to have been directed to a bishop not residing at Rome but present in his own diocese.]

That he should appoint an associate and coadjutor for the bishop of Orange, who was suffering from a serious and incurable illness.

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

The following must certainly be compared with what is reported here by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* (vol. I, col. 775) concerning the bishops of Orange. They recognize Arnulph as the thirty-second bishop of Orange from the year 1182, on the evidence of documents. They then add:

> When this bishop suffered from leprosy, he received a coadjutor by order of Pope Innocent III and provided the occasion for this legal determination by the pontiff: “A bishop who cannot exercise the pastoral office because of an incurable illness must be given a coadjutor; suffering must not be added to one already afflicted, but rather his misery ought to be pitied.” This sick prelate withdrew to a rural place two leagues from Orange, in a suburban locality between Mont-Dragon and Mornasse, and there built a house in which to spend the remainder of his life; it was transformed into the hermitage of Saint Lupus. When illness compelled him to abstain from administering his church, we do not know. In 1184 he was present with William of Baux when the latter granted privileges to the canons of Orange; at that time he was probably healthy and had not yet withdrawn from human society. Innocent III did not ascend Saint Peter’s chair until 1198, shortly after which he decreed that a coadjutor should be assigned to him . . . .
