> “XXXIII. William Elias, whom Prevotius, following Ughelli, calls a Cistercian monk, became bishop in 1200 after having been Arnulph’s coadjutor . . . . He departed this life in 1221, as Albericus records, calling him an honourable and religious man.”]

(At Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Nones of December.)

[It was set forth before us on your behalf that, since our venerable brother . . . bishop of Orange—

[Note: [Col. 0474D] The *Decretals* read: “of Auragiensis.”]

—has suffered for almost [Col. 0475A] four years from a grave and incurable illness, so that he neither could nor can in any way exercise the pastoral office, the nobleman . . . of Baux, prince of that land, and the consuls and citizens of that city repeatedly ask you, since you are their metropolitan, to provide for both them and the Church of Orange. But because you can neither compel nor ought in any way compel the aforesaid bishop—

[Note: [Col. 0475D] The *Decretals* read: “him,” instead of “the aforesaid bishop.”]

—to resign, and because suffering must not be added to one already afflicted but rather his misery ought to be pitied, since that man has proved good and honourable and has beneficially governed the church committed to him—

[Note: [Col. 0475D] The *Decretals* read: “has governed.”]

—you judged that the Apostolic See should be consulted concerning what you ought to do in this matter. Therefore, wishing that suitable provision be made both for the aforesaid bishop and for his church—

[Note: [Col. 0475D] The *Decretals* read: “I shall provide.”]

—we answer and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters as follows: appoint for him a coadjutor, a prudent and honourable man, through whom suitable provision may be made both for the bishop and for the people committed to him [Col. 0475B].

[Note: [Col. 0475D] The *Decretals* read: “usefully,” omitting “committed to him.”]]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Nones of December, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXVII. TO ALL WHO SHALL EXAMINE THESE LETTERS

That abbesses in the City may not presume, without consulting the pope or his vicar, to sell, alienate, or grant in fief immovable property. (At Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of December.)

Because certain abbesses of the monasteries of the City, setting aside reverence for God and, as though forgetful of their own salvation [Col. 0475C], make alienations of possessions and other goods belonging to the monasteries over which they preside, to their very serious injury, we, wishing to provide for the preservation of those whose care specially concerns us, decree by this present constitution, with the common counsel of our brethren, that all abbesses of the City are suspended from the power of selling, pledging, granting in fief, leasing, or otherwise alienating immovable things. Thus every sale, pledge, grant in fief, lease, or alienation of immovable property made by them in any manner shall be deemed void by the law itself, unless the special permission of the Roman pontiff, or of his vicar for the time being, has intervened and has been entered in a public instrument. Let no one, therefore, etc., this page [Col. 0475D] of our constitution, etc., down to: *shall incur*.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXVIII.

[Note: [Col. 0475D]

Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1204, §69.

See also Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 448, col. 2, under the year 1205, chapter 4, §4.]

. . . . . To the Archbishop of Canterbury—

[Note: [Col. 0475D] He has already been discussed repeatedly.]

—the bishop of Ely—

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Book V, letter 54.]

—and the bishop of Worcester—

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Book V, letter 23, note.]

A commission concerning the restoration of the dower which the king of England must make to the wife of his deceased brother, formerly king. (At Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0476A]

If the judge who neither feared God nor respected man, moved by the persistence of the complaining widow, secured vengeance for her against her adversary, how much more ought we not turn our ears away from the cries of widows—we who, though unworthy, hold on earth the place of Him who renders judgment without respect of persons to all who suffer wrong, and who by the prophetic voice commands that the oppressed be aided and the widow defended? Although, as He who searches hearts and reins knows, we love J., the illustrious king of the English, as a most dear son, nevertheless we cannot yield to his greatness against justice, [Col. 0476B] since, setting aside favour and fear, we ought to deny it to no one, being debtors alike to the wise and the foolish in this matter by reason of the office of service we have undertaken. For we should believe that we offended the royal serenity more by sparing him in some degree in this matter than we bestowed a favour upon him, since we should appear to furnish him an occasion of hindering his own salvation, to which we are bound to exhort him by every means.

Therefore, since our most dear daughter in Christ, B., formerly the illustrious queen of the English, has caused our ears to be assailed by repeated complaints that the king himself was withholding at his own discretion her dower and certain other things belonging to her by right, we, showing due deference to the royal highness as far as we could in the Lord, caused him to be admonished by our letters to take care to satisfy the queen concerning [Col. 0476C] these matters, because in them he had offended the divine Majesty and appeared blameworthy in the sight of men. But he, proposing that A . . . of revered memory, his mother, was holding that dower—

[Note: Col. 0476D: Thus in the copy, but erroneously, it seems.]

—at last, after our admonitions and the prayers of many, entered into an amicable settlement with her concerning the aforesaid matters. Although he obtained apostolic authority to confirm it, he nevertheless did not take care inviolably to observe it, as the steadfastness of royal greatness required, but withdrew from her all the revenues which he had assigned in the said settlement. And when she again caused the dispute concerning these matters to be laid before us, desiring that they should be corrected through him himself, we asked and admonished him, enjoining it upon him for the remission of his sins, not to delay satisfying the complainant in such a way that he might appease the Most High whom he had offended, and thereby be able to merit glory and honour in the sight of men.

And, wishing rather to provide for his salvation, we nonetheless gave instructions to our beloved sons . . . the abbots of Casamari—

[Note: Col. 0476D: Concerning the abbot of Casamari, John, frequently mentioned in the Registers.]

—and of Marmoutier at Tours—

[Note: Col. 0476D: The abbots of Marmoutier are enumerated by the authors of the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 592, col. 1, letters A and B.]

—and . . . of Virson—

[Note: Col. 0476D–0477D: The monastery of Viryson—for it seems that the abbot of this monastery, otherwise called Dover, is intended here—was at that time governed by William I, known in documents as early as 1185. He died in 1109, on 3 January. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. II, col. 138.]

—that they should [Col. 0477A] endeavour, by ecclesiastical compulsion and without appeal, to compel him to render full justice concerning the dower, one half of the movable goods, and the losses and injuries inflicted upon the queen. Yet although the aforesaid abbot of Casamari orally admonished him to do this, he still did not take care to satisfy the said queen, as her repeated complaint to us indicates. At the very least, he ought to have been moved by the fact that . . . . . the former wife of his brother, who had been so great a man, is compelled, like a poor and despised woman, to beg from the noble lady B . . . countess of Champagne, her sister.

Moreover, since the mother of the same king has entered upon the way of all flesh, and at her death the dower which she held has devolved into the king’s hands, he will henceforth [Col. 0477B] be unable reasonably to excuse himself if he does not see fit to assign that dower to the oft-mentioned queen. Wherefore by our letters we ask and admonish the royal magnificence, and enjoin this upon him for the remission of his sins: that, for the sake of divine mercy and in consideration of our prayers, he not delay to assign the said queen her dower, making suitable satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted upon her and for the other claims which she declares herself to have against him.

Otherwise, because we are especially bound to widows and orphans in the matter of their justice, we strictly command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate diligently, without appeal, the truth concerning both the dower and the other claims [Col. 0477C] which the said queen may bring against the same king; and, proceeding to the rendering of a definitive judgment, you are not to delay sending us, under your seals, all the proceedings faithfully reduced to writing. You are to assign the parties a suitable term in which they may appear before us through competent representatives to receive judgment, restraining objectors nonetheless by ecclesiastical censure, with the obstacle of appeal removed. We also will and command that, because the procurator and messengers of the said queen cannot often have access to you owing to the dangers of sea and road, you assign to them and to the adverse party, by a single edict valid for all, without appeal, [Col. 0477D] a peremptory term, having regard to the length of the journey. The witnesses, moreover, etc. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. And if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year [of our pontificate].

CLXIX

[Note: Col. 0477D: This letter, almost in its entirety but divided into parts, is found among the Decretals in various places, as will be indicated separately in the following notes. What is read in the Decretals is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also given.]

. . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF ELY.

[Note: Col. 0477D: He has already been mentioned frequently.]

He answers his various consultations. (At Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0478A]

[Note: Col. 0477D: See the Decretals, book I, title 29, “On the office and authority of a delegated judge,” chapter 28.]

The diligence and solicitude of the pastoral office which you exercise in carrying out our commands, and the zeal of your uprightness, invite us, although we are hindered by the manifold occupations of our affairs, nevertheless to withdraw from them for the time in which we attend to and answer your consultations.

For the prudence of your brotherhood consulted us whether, if a delegate appointed by a prince wishes to delegate to another a case committed to him, he may compel a person unwilling to accept the delegation [Col. 0478B] to undertake it. To this, with the counsel of our brethren, we have thought fit to answer you as follows:

[Note: Col. 0478D: In the same place cited.]

[Since the jurisdiction to appoint a judge is granted by law to one to whom a case has been delegated by a prince, provided that he does not maliciously seek to unload himself, he may compel one who refuses, because that jurisdiction would seem to have no force if it possessed no power of compulsion. Yet the aforesaid delegate ought diligently to ensure that, if necessity requires him to delegate the affair to persons of higher rank, he shows proper deference both to their dignity and to their persons in applying compulsion.]

[Note: Col. 0478D: The Decretals read *delegata* (“delegated”) and *invicem* (“in turn”) in place of “judge”; below they omit the word “to be,” and read *delegatus tamen debet* (“the delegate nevertheless ought”) in place of *D. t. d. p.* [abbreviated in the source].]

You also subsequently asked whether a delegate, when he sees it expedient, may direct whomever he wishes [Col. 0478C] to summon the parties before him and to inflict a penalty upon them for contempt if they disdain to obey. To your brotherhood we briefly answer that:

[Note: Col. 0478D: In the same place cited.]

[Since he can entrust the entire matter to another, as is stated above, he may, after prior exercise of discretion, commit the office of citation to anyone whatever, and rightly punish a person guilty of contempt.]

[Note: Col. 0478D: The Decretals omit this word.]

[Note: Col. 0478D: *Ibid.*, book I, title 31, “On the office of an ordinary judge,” chapter 11.]

[Furthermore, you asked whether, if a case has been brought by appeal before an archbishop, he can delegate it, by right of his ordinary authority, to a subject of his suffragan, or punish that person if he refuses to accept the delegated case. To this we certainly answer that the archbishop cannot compel him against his will to accept such a delegation, since, except in certain specified matters, he has no authority over him, although his bishop is subject to that archbishop by metropolitan law.] [Col. 0478D]

[Note: Col. 0478D: The Decretals read “asked” instead of “requested”; shortly afterward they omit the word “certainly,” and below read “by” in place of “through.”]

[Note: Col. 0478D: *Ibid.*, book I, title 29, place and chapter cited.]

[Moreover, you asked to be instructed by the apostolic see whether, when an appeal has been made from a judgment rendered by authority of our letters, in which appeal is prohibited, [Col. 0479A] and, after the appeal, letters have issued to other judges—

[Note: Col. 0479D: The Decretal adds “from us.”]

—must execution of the judgment, entrusted to the former judges, be postponed at the command of the later judges, so that the former judges execute it neither themselves nor through others? We have thought fit to answer your inquiry as follows:

[Note: Col. 0479D: The Decretals have “we have thought fit to answer you thus,” and immediately omit the word “we.”]

Since we, with certain knowledge, commit the case of an appeal to other judges for examination, we appear to admit the appeal and to revoke the jurisdiction of the former judges, so that execution of the judgment may meanwhile be suspended until the merits of the appeal have been more fully examined.]

[Note: Col. 0479D: *Ibid.*, book I, title 3, “On rescripts,” chapter 14.]

[Moreover, you asked: when there is doubt concerning the revocation of letters, should the earlier judges or the later judges determine whether the first letters have been revoked by the second? To this we answer as follows:

[Note: Col. 0479D: The Decretal reads, “I answer you.”]

Unless the later judges decide to defer to the earlier ones, or conversely, both sets should investigate simultaneously; and if perhaps they cannot agree upon one judgment, even though there are more on one side than on the other, let this conflict be settled through arbitrators jointly chosen by the parties.

But since—

[Note: Col. 0479D: The Decretal reads “indeed,” and shortly afterward adds “to you” after “have.”]

—letters are frequently obtained from us in this form, namely: “We have thought fit to commit the case which such a person declares he has against such another and certain others concerning this matter and certain other matters,” you carefully asked whether, under such a delegation, a judge has authority, before the persons or things have been specified, over the persons or things to be specified. You added [Col. 0479C] whether, if before the persons or things have been expressly named, special letters concerning matters not specified in the prior commission but covered generally by it should issue from the apostolic see to other judges, making no mention of the prior commission, they ought to have the same force. We therefore answer these two questions as follows:

[Note: Col. 0479D: The Decretal reads “to you.”]

Since the general is undoubtedly derogated from by the special, jurisdiction conferred by general letters is wholly invalidated by special letters in respect of the matters specially stated, even though they make no mention of the earlier letters. Hence the first question is superfluous; although it may rightly be said that, until the jurisdiction is revoked, the delegate possesses it for specifying the articles of persons or things, yet before the persons or things are specified, the delegate cannot exercise such jurisdiction.] [Col. 0479D]

[Note: Col. 0479D: *Ibid.*, book I, title 29, place and chapter cited.]

[But because it often happens that execution of a judgment is entrusted to the Ordinary, you considered it necessary to consult the apostolic see whether, if the Ordinary [Col. 0480A] knows it to be unjust, he ought to put it into execution, or ought rather to suspend action. Therefore, considering that only execution and not examination is entrusted to him—

[Note: Col. 0479D: The Decretal reads “is entrusted,” and shortly afterward “we answer” in place of “we have thought fit to answer your inquiry as follows.”]

—we have thought fit to answer your inquiry as follows: since the Ordinary is bound to obey—

[Note: Col. 0480D: The Decretal adds “the delegate,” and shortly afterward reads *sciat* (“he knows”) in place of *sciant* (“they know”); below it reads “him” in place of “the judge,” and after “another” adds “Ordinary.”]

—even if he knows that judgment to be unjust, he is nevertheless bound to execute it, unless he can obtain from the judge that the latter absolve him from this burden.]

You also asked to be instructed—

[Note: Col. 0480D: *Ibid.*, book I, title 31, place and chapter cited.]

—whether anyone may, without a special mandate of the apostolic see, grant the benefit of absolution to a person who wishes to obey the law, where a delegate has bound that defendant by the bond of excommunication because of manifest contumacy, or restore possession within a year, after first receiving adequate security, to a claimant whom the delegate had put into possession of the things claimed for the purpose of preserving the property, when the delegate has died. To this we certainly say:

[Note: Col. 0480D: The Decretals omit “certainly,” as also the words hereafter distinguished in italic type.]

Since a delegate is, in this respect, superior to the Ordinary, a person excommunicated by such a delegate cannot obtain absolution from another without the mandate of the supreme pontiff, except at the point of death; unless perhaps the delegate is such a person as has another succeeding him in office and honour. Nor can he recover possession lost except through the supreme pontiff. Nevertheless, lest another become a true possessor after a year, he may, before the Ordinary—or, if he cannot have access to him, before public and reputable persons—offer and furnish security that he will obey the law, thereby, as it were, interrupting the annual prescription, so that after a year he may deserve to recover possession through the apostolic see.] [Col. 0480B–C]

[Note: Col. 0480D: *Ibid.*, book II, title 28, “On appeals, recusations, and references,” chapter 53.]

[You also carefully asked whether, when appeal is prohibited in a rescript as dilatory, only a dilatory appeal is thereby understood to be prohibited, so that appeal may be made from every grievance; or whether every appeal is understood to be excluded, except only in cases expressly provided by law. We therefore, considering that a case ought not be impeded by a dilatory appeal even if it had not been prohibited, briefly answer your diligence that every appeal is understood to be removed which is not expressly allowed by law. But if an appellant has been unjustly burdened, such a grievance [Col. 0480D] may be corrected by a superior.

But because it often happens that, through a lawful appeal, someone is temporarily exempted from the authority of his judge in respect of a particular article, the prudence of your brotherhood considered it necessary to consult us—

[Note: Col. 0480D: The Decretal reads “more strictly, you consulted us,” and shortly afterward reads “cleric” in place of “someone.”]

—whether, if a cleric bound by a sentence of excommunication, before its publication, has taken care to appeal from it as having been pronounced with insufficient reason, in a case in which appeal appears to have had force before judgment, the excommunicating judge may, because his jurisdiction appears to have been suspended through the appeal lodged, publish that same sentence at the time [Col. 0481A] and temporarily deprive the cleric of ecclesiastical benefices, since excommunication is not deprived of its effect by an appeal thus made. We have therefore thought fit to answer your inquiry as follows: since excommunication carries execution with it, and the excommunicated person is not further bound by publication, he may not improperly publish the excommunicated person—

[Note: Col. 0481D: The Decretal reads, more strictly, “you may,” and shortly afterward omits *nimirum* (“indeed”).]

—so that he may be avoided by others; and ecclesiastical revenues are rightly withdrawn from one to whom communion with the Church is denied.]

[Note: Col. 0481D: The Decretal reads *ipse* (“he”) and shortly afterward *eumdem* (“the same,” masculine) for *eamdem* (“the same,” feminine); below it reads *beneficiis clericum spoliare* (“to deprive the cleric of benefices”) and omits *cum in privetur* (“when he is deprived therein”); it reads *respondemus* (“we answer”) for *respondendum* (“to be answered”).]

[Col. 0481B] Since it often happens that lay patrons of churches present now one person and now another to vacant churches, you carefully asked to have it explained by the apostolic see—

[Note: Col. 0481D: *Ibid.*, book III, title 38, “On the right of patronage,” chapter 29.]

—whether a cleric presented to a church by a lay patron acquires any right in it through such presentation if his diocesan does not see fit to admit him; and, if he has perhaps appealed to the apostolic see, and after the appeal he lodged the same patron takes care to present another, and the bishop institutes the person presented second, whether that person ought rightly to be removed. We therefore, adhering out of reverence to the precedents of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory—

[Note: Col. 0481D: The Decretals omit *bonae memoriae* (“of happy memory”), as also the following *praedecessoris nostri* (“our predecessor”); below they read *inter praesentatos* (“among those presented”) for *in praesentatis* (“in cases of persons presented”), and *meliorem* (“better”) for *potiorem* (“preferable”).]

—who, distinguishing between persons presented by lay and clerical patrons, judged the condition of the possessor more preferable in cases of presentation by a layman, say that the institution of the person presented second by a lay patron has the strength of validity. Nevertheless, we decree that a bishop who maliciously refused to admit a suitable person presented shall be compelled to provide for him in a suitable benefice, so that he may be punished in the very matter in which he undoubtedly sinned.] [Col. 0481C]

[Note: Col. 0482D: *Ibid.*, book V, title 19, “On privileges and excesses of those possessing privileges,” chapter 19.]

[Furthermore, you asked whether religious men to whom the apostolic see has granted that, upon the death of the incumbents of churches, they may convert those churches to their own uses, may enter into possession of those churches on their own authority, or whether they should rather be put into possession by the diocesan. To this we certainly answer—

[Note: Col. 0482D: The Decretals omit *Interrogasti* (“you asked”), as also, below, *utique* (“certainly”).]

—that, unless perhaps this is expressly contained in the indulgence of the supreme pontiff, it is not lawful for them to enter into possession without consulting their [Col. 0482A] own bishop, because we do not believe that episcopal right is derogated from by such an indulgence.]

Furthermore, you carefully asked—

[Note: Col. 0482D: *Ibid.*, book III, title 10, “On things done by a prelate without the consent of the chapter,” chapter 9.]

—since parishes have been delimited by the authority of Dionysius, so that the revenues of each parish should accrue to the necessary uses of the Church and to the stipends of its ministers, whether a bishop may, without authority from the supreme pontiff or at least without the consent of his chapter, grant religious men the income of a parish church, reserving maintenance for the vicar; and, since the statutes of the Lateran Council prohibit the imposition upon churches of a new pension or the increase of an old one, you ask to be instructed whether a bishop may, with the patron’s consent, grant religious houses the entire church or [Col. 0482B] confer a new portion upon them. To this we briefly answer:

[Note: Col. 0482D: The Decretals omit *locis* (“places”); shortly afterward they read *quod* (“which/that”) for *quae* (“which”). The words below distinguished in italic type are lacking.]

Subject to the canonical constitution concerning the grant of a fiftieth portion to pious places, a bishop can do neither the first nor the second without permission from the Roman pontiff, without the consent of his chapter.]

[Note: Col. 0482D: *Ibid.*, book III, title 24, “On donations,” chapter 7.]

[Your prudence further considered it necessary to consult us whether, when a bishop, with the patron’s consent, grants a church to religious men and uses this simple form of words, “We grant you that church,” the church itself is thereby understood to have been granted for their use, or only the right of patronage. We have thought fit to answer your inquiry as follows: if the bishop confers the church upon them with the patron’s consent, the patron clearly appears to confer what is his, namely the right of patronage; and the bishop confers what he himself possesses temporally in it, so that, if he receives any share of the fruits of that church, that share is converted to their use. But if the bishop ought to receive no share from its revenues, we believe that all the revenues, apart from the cathedraticum, are to be converted to their use. Yet, for the bishop’s grant to be lawful, the consent of his chapter is required.] [Col. 0482C]

[Note: Col. 0482D: *Ibid.*, book III, title 30, “On tithes, first-fruits, and offerings,” chapter 28.]

[Furthermore, you asked to have it explained whether anyone may deduct necessary expenses from mills and fisheries before paying tithes from them, [Col. 0482D] as is allowed in trade. To this, without prejudice to a better opinion, we answer that although, in regard to things acquired or made with tithed money, when they are sold, we believe that expenses should be deducted and tithes paid from the remainder as from profit—for example, if a house, field, vineyard, oven, mill, flock, or any merchandise is sold—nevertheless we do not believe that expenses incurred for receiving fruits from things that yield fruits should be deducted, even if those things have been tithed. For, with the tithe preserved, the fruits become the property of those who incur the expenses. Nor do we believe that those fruits can be alienated except subject to the burden of tithes; nor do we believe that expenses for repairing loss in any things from which tithes are paid should be deducted from revenues to be tithed, because repaired things remain with their owner: as when some part of a herd dies, [Col. 0483B] a vineyard deteriorates, a portion of merchandise perishes, or an entire oven is destroyed.]

You also asked what evidences should be credited concerning decretal letters whose authority a judge may not unreasonably doubt, since many are found in the compilation of scholars and are alleged in cases, though they have not been established by a bull, nor were they promulgated through the metropolitan sees. Since it often happens that decretals of this kind are also produced before us, and we doubt whether they are authentic, we answer your brotherhood more kindly:

[Note: Col. 0483D: *Ibid.*, book II, title 22, “On the credibility of instruments,” chapter 8.]

[By the authority of these presents we have thought fit to decree that, when a decretal of which a judge may rightly doubt is alleged, if it is consonant with common law, he need not fear to judge according to it; but if [Col. 0483C] it is discordant with common law, he should not judge according to it, but consult his superior concerning it.]

[Note: Col. 0483D: *Ibid.*, book II, title 25, “On exceptions,” chapter 4.]

But since the conclusion of cases is sometimes maliciously prolonged through dilatory exceptions, we decree in answer to your inquiry that all dilatory exceptions must be put forward within a fixed time assigned by the judge; so that, if thereafter the parties wish to put forward any which they have not reserved by protest, they are not to be heard at all, unless perhaps some new matter has arisen, or the person wishing to raise it establishes by oath that it subsequently came to his knowledge.

[Note: Col. 0483D: The Decretal reads “them,” and below “are” in place of “have been.”]

[We further decree that the principal parties shall state the case not through advocates but personally—

[Note: Col. 0484D: *Ibid.*, book II, title 1, “On judgments,” chapter 14.]

—unless perhaps they are so lacking in judgment that their deficiency is, with the judge’s permission, supplied by others.] [Col. 0483D]

But since it often happens that, on the day which a judge delegated by us has assigned to the parties, the judge himself is summoned by a king or archbishop at the procurement of one party seeking to have the case postponed, we, wishing to oppose the malice of perverse persons, decree that, if it is established to the delegate that this was procured through the malice of either party, he shall punish that party with a fitting penalty. And, lest that party derive any profit from such fraud, he shall entrust the hearing of the case for that day to a person suspected by neither party, who shall proceed on that day without appeal, unless the parties themselves consent to postponement of the case. [Col. 0484A]

Moreover, you wished to consult us whether a person who was admitted to the order of deacon without the laying on of hands should be allowed to minister, and whether the sacrament of confirmation should be repeated for one who through error was anointed not with chrism but with oil. To this we have thought fit briefly to answer your brotherhood that in such matters nothing is to be repeated; rather, what was carelessly omitted must carefully be supplied.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends [Col. 0484B] of January.

CLXX. TO THE BISHOP OF LE PUY.

[Note: Col. 0484D: Bertrand I, otherwise Bernard, of Chalençon, succeeded Odilo of Mercœur in the see of Le Puy about the year 1202. He is known from documents down to 1213, in which year he is said to have died on 21 December. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 708.]

That he is to investigate the act of P., the cantor, involving a certain woman. (At Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.)

From the letters of your brotherhood we have learned that, when the Church of Le Puy was in need of priests, you wished to ordain as priest our beloved son P . . ., cantor of that church, a learned man distinguished in conduct. But he replied that he would not become a priest without our permission, because formerly a certain woman told him that he had once struck her on the back with his foot, causing her to miscarry. The cantor himself believed that he had once struck this woman, or another, on the back with his foot, but did not believe that she had ever miscarried. He also brought the woman to the penitentiary of Le Puy, in order that the fuller truth might be sought from her. After carefully asking what needed to be investigated on those matters, the latter could learn nothing certain from her, but believed that the woman was inventing such things in order to extort money from the cantor. For this reason you did not wish to proceed to his ordination until you had an apostolic response on the matter. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood diligently to investigate the truth of these matters; and, if the assertion of the said woman is not established as true, to take care to promote the cantor to the office of the priesthood, if he is otherwise found suitable, has not been defamed concerning this matter, and his conscience does not reproach him. [Col. 0484C]

[Col. 0484D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year [of our pontificate].

CLXXI

[Note: Col. 0484D–0485D: Raynaldus supplies a fragment of this letter, under the year 1204, §69. What is found in his work is enclosed here in brackets.

Another fragment of the same letter may be read in Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 448, col. 2, under the year 1205, chapter IV, §4.]

. TO THE KING OF THE ENGLISH. That he restore the archbishop of Dublin to favour and restore to him all that has been taken away, with a threat of interdict wherever he may remain. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of December.)

The complaint of our venerable brother, . . . archbishop of Dublin, not so much pitiable as deserving of pity, [Col. 0485A] has repeatedly struck our ears grievously, and does not yet cease to strike them, pressing home his cry with tearful and bitter groans. Thus we believe that the magnitude of his cry has ascended to the ears of the Lord of Hosts. Would that, if we have sinned, He may spare us for having spared so greatly a man who, while failing to defer to Him in His own concerns, has for so long afflicted His minister, and still does not spare him in his affliction!

[For your royal highness knows, and can sufficiently remember, how often we have thought fit to admonish you with gentle and flattering words on behalf of that archbishop—

[Note: Col. 0486D: See letters 160 of book five and 63 and 64 of book six.]

—and have caused others to admonish you, and how many and how great prayers we have offered you, that you should receive into your favour him whom you caused to live in exile outside the kingdom for seven years and, amid no small affliction and the shame of his pastoral office, to beg the support of others in unknown regions; and that you should cause all that had been taken from him to be restored. What force our admonitions and prayers had in this matter is plainly shown by the ensuing outcome, since we were not heard.]

Rather, we were shamefully disregarded; and, what is worse, the Creator was offended. He will not leave His offence unavenged, but will partly avenge in the present the wrong done to His servant and reserve another vengeance for Himself in the future. Certainly, lest we dwell too long upon our repeated letters which we have often taken care to send you on this matter, since, as we believe, you are fully aware of them—

[Note: Col. 0486D: This passage is found in Manrique.]

—recently, when our beloved son N . . ., abbot of Casamari, on our behalf [Col. 0485C] admonished you before many great men, and even rebuked you because you had not fulfilled our command in this matter, you firmly promised him that you would make everything right. But when the same archbishop, trusting in your promise, wished to return to his own country and stayed with you for some days, you put him off from day to day with empty words and would not perform what you had promised. Sad and disappointed in his hope, he was compelled to return to Paris.

[Note: Col. 0486D: Thus far Manrique.]

Instead of applying the oil of kindness to his wounds, you took care to apply the wine of harshness, so as wholly to break the bruised reed and force his old age to fail through poverty. For you extorted, it is said, one hundred pounds sterling from his procurators, which they had collected with great labour for payment of his debts; [Col. 0485D] and you also commanded the archbishop of Cashel to undertake the administration of the diocese of Dublin.

Therefore, that the royal highness, which has been so hard in heeding our prayers, may receive these paternal admonitions, however late, we ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity in the Lord, enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins: that, having due regard for the Lord Jesus Christ, who assumed the flesh of our mortality in order to make us His co-heirs in the Father’s glory; for the Roman Church, which He established in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and also for us, whom, if you recall rightly, you found favourable and kind in your affairs—you receive the aforesaid archbishop back into your favour with generous kindness and cause all that has been taken from him to be restored. Thus on this occasion you will fulfil, as we command by our pastoral office and admonish with the full affection of our heart, that which your correction, though late, may avail to expiate in respect of past offence. [Col. 0486A]

Otherwise, since henceforth we do not intend to spare you in this matter—for we fear that, by sparing you so much, we have incurred the Creator’s displeasure—you are to know that we have strictly commanded our venerable brethren . . . the archbishop of Canterbury and . . . the bishop of Ely, whom we have also severely reproved because they neglected our former command, that, if suitable satisfaction is not made by you to that archbishop within two months after receipt of these letters, they shall, by our authority and without the obstacle of appeal, pronounce an interdict over whatever bishopric subject to your jurisdiction you may enter, for as long as you remain there. [Col. 0486B] And if you cannot be induced even in this way, they shall lay the whole province of Dublin under interdict. Know for certain that, if you pass over such a command with a deaf ear and show yourself hard toward us where we ought to find you gracious, we shall not leave the cause of the Church—indeed, of God—so undefended that we do not make you learn what the hand of the vicar of Jesus Christ can accomplish. If we wished, under colour of still deferring to you, to postpone matters further, we should undoubtedly appear not to love but to hate you; for a father corrects the son whom he loves, and God rebukes and chastises those whom He loves. [Col. 0486C]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of December, in the seventh year [of our pontificate].

CLXXII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF NIGELLA.

He commands that they not delay at all in making whole the prebends of the canons Renelmus and Robert. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0486D] Renelmus, a beloved son and canon of your church, appearing before us, represented that he and Robert had been installed as canons in the same church by apostolic authority, with the benefit of half a prebend assigned to each. By authority both of our letters and of the Council of Tours, which forbids the division of benefices, they urgently requested that you make their prebends whole. You gave them your gracious assent, as your own letters also stated, and promised them that, as soon as the means became available, you would arrange without delay to make their prebends whole, without the intervention of another.

But Master W., without mentioning our letters—which Renelmus had obtained from us concerning the conferral upon him of a whole prebend, and Robert concerning the completion of his prebend—brought you our letters directing that you should generously provide for him in one of the prebends of your church. Moreover, when the said Renelmus came into our presence and humbly petitioned us, for himself and the aforesaid Robert, that we should not permit the completion of their prebends to be hindered in any way by those letters, the said master undertook to oppose him in this matter.

We therefore assigned to them as auditor our beloved son H., cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace. [Note: See Book V, Epistle 29, note.] Having heard the arguments advanced on both sides and taken counsel with prudent men, he considered that, by our command, silence should be imposed upon the said master concerning his objection to the completion of those prebends, since it was more consonant with reason that the prebends of those already long since installed as canons should be made whole than that one should be conferred upon a man who could not demand it by strict right of law.

Wherefore, by these apostolic writings, we command and strictly enjoin your whole body that, when the means become available, you do not delay in making whole their several prebends, which have been divided contrary to the statutes of the Council of Tours, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, in accordance with your promise. You shall take care more cautiously not to attempt, for the sake of completing their prebends, to divide other prebends, lest, while some prebend there always remains divided, the apostolic command can thus be impeded. Otherwise, we have commanded our beloved sons . . . . . . the abbot of Saint Aubert [Note: His name was Hugh. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 155.], and Masters P. of Saint-Symphorien and R. of Bekerel, canons of Cambrai, strictly to ensure, should you fail to carry out our command, that it be put into effect, without impediment of appeal; opponents . . . [shall not be assisted] by any letters contrary to truth, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of December, in the seventh year.

### CLXXIII. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN [Note: Book III, Epistle 6, note.] AND HIS SUFFRAGANS

That they are to cause the people of Piacenza to be avoided as excommunicated persons. (At Saint Peter’s, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0487D]

Although formerly the smoke of the wrongdoing of the citizens of Piacenza offended the eyes of apostolic watchfulness, and we were unable to suppress it by the rain of paternal admonition, but it rose more strongly on high, so as to infect regions both near and far, we are compelled to find another remedy: that one who will not admit the rain may fall beneath the storm, since perhaps he will cease to exhale vapour when he finds nowhere to breathe.

For you have heard well enough to what misery they have brought the bishop, [Note: Book V, Epistle 75, note.] clergy, and Church of Piacenza, and under what afflictions and sufferings they compel them to live rather than perish—a matter which we cannot state without bitterness of heart. Therefore, lest the vapour of their wrongdoing extend itself to neighbouring walls, by these apostolic writings we command you and, by virtue of obedience, strictly enjoin you that, wherever the aforesaid citizens may come within the province of Milan, you cause them to be rigorously avoided, as excommunicated persons, in conversation, lodging, and commercial dealings; and that their goods too be held wherever they may be found, [Col. 0488B] until by fitting satisfaction they deserve reconciliation with the Church. Thus carry out the apostolic command, lest you appear to be its contemners.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

### CLXXIV. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77.] TO THE ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT LOMBARDY

That they are to assist the exiled bishop of Piacenza from the annual payment due to the Apostolic See. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

Sharing the sufferings and pressures which our venerable brother . . . bishop of Piacenza is at present compelled by his citizens to endure outside the Church of Piacenza, we wish to provide for him from what is ours, since he cannot be maintained from his own resources. Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command and strictly enjoin you that, when requested by him, you shall take care to pay over the payment due from your churches to the Apostolic See, for as long as he is compelled to remain in exile outside his church; generously providing his messengers, whom he sends for this purpose, both with necessities and with safe-conduct.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.

In the same manner, to the abbots, etc., established throughout the province of Ravenna.

### CLXXV. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §77.] TO THE BISHOP OF PIACENZA [Note: See notes on the preceding letters.]

It grants that, while exiled from his church, he may retain both vacant prebends and those which are to fall vacant. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0488D]

Sharing your afflictions and pressures, which you are at present compelled by your citizens to endure outside the Church of Piacenza, by the authority of these present letters we grant you permission, while you are in exile, to retain for your support and that of the clerics of those churches both prebends now vacant in your bishopric and those which will fall vacant. Nevertheless, after this, those belonging to your gift shall be conferred by you, and the others by those bound to confer them, upon suitable persons. Therefore let no one . . . [violate] this our concession, etc. If anyone, etc.

Given as above.

### CLXXVI. TO THE NOBLEMAN COUNT GUIDO

It confirms by apostolic authority the judgment delivered in the cause between him and the elect and sisters of the monastery of Rosano. (At Saint Peter’s, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

Messengers sent into our presence by you and by . . . the elect and the sisters of the monastery of Rosano humbly requested that we should deign to grant them a hearing. We assigned as their auditor our beloved son Hu., cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace. [Col. 0489B] While litigation proceeded before him for some time on both sides, it was clearly established, both by instruments and by letters, that a definitive sentence had been promulgated in the case which was pending between you and the aforesaid elect, by our beloved sons J., prior of Saint Frediano, . . . . . . archpriest of Florence, and J. . . . canon of Pisa, to whom the matter had been committed with the consent of both parties.

Having been made certain, through the assertion of that cardinal, that the sentence had been promulgated, we confirm it by apostolic authority, as being just, etc., and strengthen it; saving to the other party the question of ownership, if it is established that the sentence itself was pronounced solely concerning possession. Therefore let no one, etc.

[Col. 0489C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### CLXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF AUSON [Note: It appears among the Decretals, Book V, title 33, “On the privileges and excesses of privileged persons,” chapter 18.]

That clerics or laypersons are not withdrawn from a bishop’s jurisdiction by letters of protection. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of December.)

[You asked us [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals; immediately below they read “and” instead of “or”; further on, “with his person expressly named” instead of “their persons,” and “is declared” instead of “are declared.”] whether clerics or laypersons who produce letters of protection—in which it is declared that, with all their goods, their persons are under apostolic protection, expressly named—are exempt from the jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop. We answer your inquiry in this way: [Note: The Decretal reads “we answer you” instead of “we answer your inquiry in this way”; and immediately afterwards omits “which we grant.”] by letters of this sort, which we sometimes grant personally to certain persons, they are in no way withdrawn [Col. 0490A] from the authority of their bishops.]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of December.

### CLXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF PADUA

[Note: Gerardus Pomedella, a nobleman of Padua, was advanced to the episcopal see of Padua in 1169, to the joy of the citizens of Padua, who had conceived great and exceptional hope of Gerard, though still a young man; nor did he in turn disappoint it. For by many salutary written laws he excellently organized his clergy, and, having made peace among citizens at discord, concluded a treaty destined to endure for a long time. He was at Venice in 1177, when a treaty of peace was concluded between Pope Alexander III and Emperor Frederick I; and he attended the Lateran Council in 1179. Gerard governed the Church of Padua outstandingly for forty-five years and, burdened with old age, resigned the bishopric in 1214; shortly afterwards he died. Rolandino, in Book I of his *Chronicle*, calls him a man mighty in deed and speech, prudent as well, and of holy memory. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 419.]

That he is to compel monks who have left the cloister to return to their cloisters. (At Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

It has come to our hearing, as our beloved son . . . the abbot of Columba of the Cistercian Order has stated, that certain monks of the same order, leaving the cloister without the requested permission of their abbots, have prepared secluded dwellings for themselves in the Venetian province, not under the pretext of a stricter religious life, but [Col. 0490B] in order to lead a more relaxed life. We therefore ordered our venerable brother . . . bishop of Castello [Note: We have already treated elsewhere of the bishop of Castello.] to compel them by ecclesiastical censure to return to the cloisters they had abandoned; but he neglected to carry out what we commanded. Wherefore, by apostolic writings we command you that, if the matter stands thus, after prior warning, you shall not fail to compel the aforesaid recluses, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to return to the cloisters they abandoned.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

### CLXXIX. TO ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS [Note: We have already often treated of Odo, bishop of Paris.]

It authorizes him to create twenty-two prebends from the eleven prebends of the church of Champeaux. [Note: Odo’s own letter concerning this reform is found in the *History of the Church of Paris*, vol. II, p. 228.] (At Saint Peter’s, the third day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0490C]

The care of the government entrusted to us urges us, in attending to the welfare of churches, to provide with paternal concern lest they be deprived of the due service of ministers. Since, therefore, in the church of Champeaux there are only twelve prebends, each of which exceeds in value nearly fifty pounds, and its canons, because it is a rural village, scarcely ever reside there, we grant your brotherhood, lest that church remain longer deprived of divine services, authority by these present letters, with the counsel of your chapter and if the matter stands thus, to make from those eleven twenty-two prebends [Note: Something is missing.], to be assigned in perpetuity to an equal number of canons, all appeal [Col. 0491A] set aside; the twelfth, belonging to the church of Saint Victor, being wholly reserved, as it is now canonically held; and the revenues of the prebends being reserved in full to those known now to possess them, unless they themselves perhaps consent that, during their lifetimes, half the revenues be conferred on others.

Further, lest because of the absence of canons the aforesaid church of Champeaux and the churches of Saint-Marcel, Saint-Germain of Auxerre, and Saint-Cloud, in which the conferral of prebends is known to belong to you, be deprived of the due celebration of divine offices, we have thought fit to grant your devotion authority, with the counsel and consent of the chapter of the Church of Paris and of the chapters of the said churches, all appeal ceasing, to establish that the canons shall make due residence in the same churches, as you may judge should prudently be ordained with those chapters, or with their greater and sounder part; the command of the Apostolic See being always reserved in all things. Therefore let no one . . . [violate] this page . . . of our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the third day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year.

### CLXXX. TO THE PRIOR [Note: Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 321, contains a succession of the priors of Lanthony, otherwise Lenton, said to have been drawn from a manuscript *History of the Priory of Lanthony* in the Cottonian Library. That chronological series is far too incomplete: after Geoffrey of Henelawe—who, following Roger’s death, received the priory of Lanthony as its seventh prior, and then became bishop of St Davids in 1203—it names Martin as eighth prior. But Wharton himself almost deprives this succession of credibility, adding that histories and monuments contain certain material concerning priors of Lanthony which cannot at all be reconciled with it.] AND THE MONKS OF LENTON, OTHERWISE LANTHONY

It receives them under protection and enumerates the properties belonging to them. [Note: A charter of King Edward II confirming the possessions of Lanthony Priory in Nottinghamshire appears in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 645. All the places enumerated here are there in fact listed, though with certain discrepancies in their names, which we have not thought worth recording.] (At Saint Peter’s, the seventh day before the Ides of January.)

To the just desires of petitioners, etc., down to “assent.” [Col. 0491C] The church of Falmarchsam, with the chapels of Papeha and Radewell and all their appurtenances; the churches of Maperthesal, Hecha, Rassenden, Hirencestr, Curtenhal, Herleston, Wichingestun, Fostun, and Bruchton, with all their appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Edmund at Bruchton.

From the gift of Richard de Daivill: two carucates of land at Abebi. From the gift of Richard Buissel: twelve bovates of land at Bruchton, and a certain part of his garden, fifteen acres of land, one and a half acres of meadow; within Lelund, three yardlands of land and three men granted to you by W. Poverell out of piety; [Col. 0492A] tithes in Blidesword, Neubothle, Duston, Ernesbi, Bareswrd, Cothis, Hoctun, and Piria; the tenth of the mill called Tuigrisl; tithes in Molentun, Desburch, Blaculuesle, Aversham, and in the territory of Empingeham, granted to your monastery in pious liberality by Robert, of blessed memory, bishop of Lincoln [Note: The Robert in question is Robert surnamed Bloet, as may be inferred from chronological synchronisms. Robert, bishop of Lincoln, together with Gerald, archbishop of York, appears as a witness for William Peverel in the foundation charter by which he bestowed properties upon the monks of Lenton; *Monasticon Anglicanum*, cited place. It is established that Gerald wore the archiepiscopal mitre of York at the same time when Robert called Bloet presided over the Church of Lincoln. See Gerald of Wales, *On the Lives of the Bishops of Lincoln*, chapter 21. See also various records in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I.], as is more fully contained in his authenticated document, and as you possess all those things justly and peacefully. We confirm them to you, and through you to the same monastery, by apostolic authority and strengthen them by the protection of this present writing. Therefore let no one, etc. If anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the seventh day before the Ides of January.

### CLXXXI. TO THE SAME PERSONS

On the same subject as in the preceding letter. (At Saint Peter’s, the seventh day before the Ides of January.)

[Col. 0492B]

It is accustomed to grant, etc., down to “assent.” The church of Saint Mary of Nottingham, and those of Saint Peter and Saint Nicholas in the same town, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Radford, Langar, Torluavestan, Lindebi, Barton, and Oscington, with all their appurtenances; whatever right you possess in the churches of Acdingburc and Cotgrave; the tithes which you possess in Chillewell, Watinho, Aspele, Suthon, Baseford, Jorph, Gunolveston, Stapelfort, Langelaia, Rudington, and Boneia, as you possess all these things justly and peacefully by grant of W., of blessed memory, archbishop of York [Note: William, a cleric, was elevated to the archbishopric of York by Stephen, king of England, in 1142, as is read in the anonymous history of the controversy between the sees of Canterbury and York concerning primacy, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 71—not in 1140, though Roger of Hoveden asserts this, *Annals*, first part, p. 485, lines 32 ff. But because of an unlawful election he was deposed in 1147. Restored to the archiepiscopal see in 1154 with the assent of Pope Anastasius, he was killed by poison in that same year, during the solemnities of Mass on the feast of Pentecost. See the *Chronicle of Holyrood, Edinburgh*, for the year 1154.], and as they are more fully contained in his letter. We confirm them to you and, through you, to your monastery by apostolic authority, etc. Therefore let no one, etc. If anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the seventh day before the Ides of January.

### CLXXXII. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §69.] TO THE BISHOP OF LONDON

[Note: His name was William de Sainte-Mère, as is gathered from the *Annals of the Church of Worcester* under the year 1208, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 480. When Richard Nigellus died on 10 September 1198, he was succeeded by William de Sainte-Mère, a Norman by birth, canon of St Paul’s and formerly secretary to King Richard I; he was consecrated on 22 June 1199. He was one of those who, in the pope’s name, placed the entire kingdom under ecclesiastical interdict and pronounced King John excommunicated. Besides punishing him for this with five years’ exile, John demolished and utterly destroyed in 1211 his castle at Stratford, which William I had bestowed upon the see of London. William voluntarily resigned the bishopric on 26 January at the beginning of the year. See Matthew Paris.]

It confirms the dignity of the Church of London. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of December.)

Since for a long course of time the Church of London, as the petition submitted to us stated, has hitherto enjoyed this prerogative of liberty: that the bishop then presiding there has customarily held the first place, as first in rank, among gatherings of fellow-provincial bishops, in sittings, processions, responses, and subscriptions—you humbly asked us to deign to confirm this dignity to that church. We, acceding to your just petitions, confirm to you, and through you to that church, by apostolic authority that dignity, as the church has hitherto possessed it by ancient, approved, and uncontested custom, etc. We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of December.

### CLXXXIII. TO THE ARCHPRIEST OF AUTUN, . . . THE PRIOR OF SAINT-SYMPHORIEN IN THE DIOCESE OF AUTUN, AND MASTER R. DE DENCEVOI, CANON OF DIJON IN THE DIOCESE OF LANGRES

They are commanded to cause a sentence, delivered in the cause pending between the abbot and monks of Clairvaux on one side and the monks of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon on the other, to be observed. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0493B]

From the letters of our beloved sons P. [Note: Peter II, abbot of the monastery of La Celle, occurs in records from 1191 until 1206. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 545.] . . . abbot of the monastery of La Celle, and D. [Note: Drogo, abbot of Saint-Loup, is known from at least 1196 until 1206. Ibid., col. 588.] . . . abbot of Saint-Loup of Troyes, we have learned that we had committed to them and to our venerable brother . . . bishop of Troyes [Note: See Book III, Epistle 11, note.] the settlement of the case pending between the abbot [Note: Book V, Epistle 109, note.] and monks of Clairvaux on [Col. 0493C] the one side, and . . . [Note: Nivard, formerly abbot of Saint-Seine, succeeded Peter III de Grancey as abbot of Saint-Bénigne in 1203; he himself resigned in 1206, or rather in 1205. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 684.] the abbot and monks of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, in the diocese of Langres, on the other, concerning the house of Moreins.

They duly summoned the parties, and, owing to the contumacy or failure to appear of the people of Dijon, placed the monks of Clairvaux in possession in order to preserve the subject matter of the suit. Later, they pronounced the noblewoman . . . lady of Suessifont, who had entered that house on behalf of the people of Dijon, subject to excommunication for as long as she presumed to remain in it.

Meanwhile, after the bishop had set out upon his pilgrimage, the people of Dijon, two years having now elapsed, came to those abbots, complaining that the monks of Clairvaux presumed to trouble them concerning [Col. 0493D] the aforesaid house. They asserted that they were prepared to prove that they had received the letters sent to them by the monks of Clairvaux concerning possession only at that time, though the letters had been made two years earlier. [Col. 0494A] The monks of Clairvaux, on the contrary, maintained that they could prove through suitable witnesses that the abbot of Dijon had received those letters in his own hands within two months after they had been made, and so had the prior of that house.

Although, whatever the truth of the matter might be, the people of Dijon offered sufficient security that they would submit to the law, the same abbots, because the bishop was absent—the case having been specially committed to him, so that he could proceed in it with either of them, whereas they could not do so without him—refused thereafter to involve themselves in the matter. Wherefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion to cause the aforesaid sentence, being just, to be inviolably observed; and, after diligently investigating the truth concerning the foregoing, if it is established to you that the aforesaid people of Dijon have been so contumacious that even within a year they have offered no security, to establish the monks of Clairvaux as possessors by apostolic authority, while reserving to their opponents lawful defence concerning the right of ownership. No letters contrary to truth, etc. And if not all [are able to act], two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s . . . . . in the seventh year.

### CLXXXIV. TO THE ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT VINCENT OF LE MANS

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.]

It receives the monastery of Saint Vincent of Le Mans under the protection of blessed Peter, and enumerates the goods belonging to that monastery. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifth day before the Ides of January.)

It is fitting that apostolic protection [Col. 0494C] should attend those choosing the religious life, etc., down to: “you have been devoted to service.” Following the example of Eugenius, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, we receive [the monastery] under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing; decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery, etc., down to “must be expressly named”:

the church of Contiliac; the church of Saint Lenogisilus, with the chapel of Saint John of the Lepers and the chapel of Saint Martin of Fossart; the church of Sagonia, with the chapel of Saint Karilefus; the church of Curgaa; the church of Noento; the church of Doscella; the church of Saint Cornelius of Balniolum; the church of Saint Peter of Tufeium; the chapel of Saint Hilary near Tufeium; [Col. 0494D] the church of Saint Peter of Soldaium; the church of Tricio; the church of Saint Vincent of Laboratorium; the church of Sarciac; the chapel of Saint Gervasius of Belin; and, in all these, synodal dues and *circadalia*; the church of Crucis Mons; the church of Maceriae; the church of Saint Peter of Laboratorium; and, in these three, half the synodal dues and *circadalia*.  

[Note: A term unknown to Du Cange as well as Carpenter, but used here for *circadae* or *circatae*. A *circada* or *circata* was a payment made to a bishop or archdeacon for visitation; it was so called from going around, because bishops and archdeacons visit their dioceses by travelling around them. Du Cange, vol. II, col. 628.

*Synodalia* likewise denotes the payment usually made to a bishop by clerics attending the annual synods which they were bound to attend. Ibid., vol. VI, cols. 934–935.]

The chapel of Saint Mary of the Abbey; the chapel of Saint Flocellus; the chapel of Campaniac; the church of Conerai, with two thirds of the altar offerings on five feasts and two thirds of the first-fruits of the whole year; the church of Cels; the church of Saint Mary of the lordly estate; the church of Saint Mary of Villana near Luceium; the chapel of Saint Peter of Valenceliis; the church of Toreium; the church of Flacium near the castle of Ligeris; the chapel of Saint Peter; the church of Saint Germanus; the church of Saint Mary of Noviomo; the church of Colungiac, with two thirds of the [Col. 0495B] altar offerings on five feasts and two thirds of the first-fruits of the whole year; the church of Pilimilium, with a third part of the tithe of Chenseles; half the tithe and first-fruits of Malmissestere; the church of Saint Maximus of Mosteriolum, with the chapel of Paleis; the church of Saint Victurius of Basogeriis, with the chapel of Saint Mary; the church of Altanoisia, with two thirds of the altar offerings on seven feasts and two thirds of the first-fruits of the whole year; the church of Nuiliac; the church of Ham, with two thirds of the altar offerings on six feasts and two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits of the whole year; the church of Meuldin; the church of Saint Patrick; the church of Saint Karilefus of Curia Dode; [Col. 0495C] the church of Saint Leonard; the church of Saint Mary of Ace; the church of Piace; the church of Juliac; the church of Saint Marcellus; the chapel of Saint Domnolus near Segrejum; the church of Saint Mary of Ceveneium; the chapel of Saint Audoenus of Ponte Baladonis, near the bridge of Baladonis; the lands, meadows, and fishing-water as far as the middle of the river, for the entire length of those lands and meadows, which Odo of Aleriis gave from his right to your church for one hundred shillings in Le Mans currency; and the tithe of the share belonging to the aforesaid Odo from the milling of the mill of Cuce, and the cemetery there; the church of Saint Martin of Dongolium, with the chapel of Magneniis; the church of Saint Mary of Mairoliis; [Col. 0495D] the church of Avenis; the church of Saint Martin of Bellifagium; the chapel of the Holy Trinity of Novemfontibus, with two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits from your land and livestock; the church of Sabla; the chapel of Saint Remigius near Tufeium, with two thirds of the offerings on five feasts and of the first-fruits of the whole year; the church of Saint Mary of Morciliac; the church of Reneium; [Col. 0496A] the church of Toreium on the Blane; the church of Saint Mary of Parvencheriis; the chapel of Saint George of the Castle; the chapel of Vizaio; the chapel of Grableio, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the prebend which you possess in the church of Saint Julian of Le Mans; the church of Saint Mary of Berthivini, and the church of the holy martyrs Vincent and Lawrence of Landa patria [Note: Thus in the copy.], with their appurtenances; the right which you have in the church of Gevre; the right which you have in the church of Monte Betonis; the right which you have in the church of Saint Rigomerus of Soliniac, in the church of Saint Julian of Tanet; a sixth part of the tithe in the church of Saint Martin of Soliniac near Baladon; a sixth part of the altar offerings on four feasts in the same parish; the tithe of Hugh of Curtahen, the tithe of Gautier of the Valley, and the tithe of Paganus of Soliniac, together with the tithe of Haimo near Mount Dublellus; the tithe of Musaldium in the parish of Saint Mary of Novavill; two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits from the land of Garinus Morant; two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits from the land of Fulk of Chaneveroliis; two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits from the land of Hervey of Saint Lenogisilus; two thirds of the tithe from the land of Paganus of Novavill; half the tithe and first-fruits from the land of William of Tusca; two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits from the land of William Faucillum; two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits from the land of Villana; all tithes and first-fruits from the land of Allandreis, which belongs to your monastery; the church of Saint Mary [Col. 0496C] of Monte Dublellus, with its appurtenances; in the church of Saint Sulpicius of Mosteriolum, two thirds of the tithe; in the parish of Saint Martin of Lamanai, two thirds of the tithe from the land of Reginald of Nuisement; in the parish of Buisseium, a sixth part of the tithe of the church and a certain vineyard beside the church chancel; in the same parish, two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits from the land of Roucheria; in the parish of Wlureium, a third part of the tithe from the land of Piro, and the tithe-collector [Note: Thus in the copy.]; in the parish of Dunel, a third part of the tithe from the fief of Dunel; in the same parish, from the land of Hubert Espechel called Landas, two thirds of the tithe and first-fruits; in the church of Madre, a ninth part of the tithe; in the church [Col. 0496D] of Quinta, a third part of the offerings on five feasts, and of the first-fruits of the whole year, and of the tithe, together with the right which you have in the cemetery and a certain open plot adjoining that church; in the church of Attanay, two thirds of the offerings on three feasts, and the first-fruits, and the cemetery freely, and Fredebert’s *oscha*.  

[Note: It is expressly read thus in the copy. But should it not be read *oschia*, or *olchia*, or *olcha*, or *olqua*, or *olca*? In French, *ousche* or *oche*; these terms denote a portion of arable land enclosed on every side by ditches or hedges. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. IV, cols. 1338–1339; there he recognizes *oscham* from the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Le Mans, fol. 68 verso.]

In the parish of Saint Anianus, two thirds of the tithe from the land of Paganus [Col. 0497A] of Tiron and from one part of the land of Albinus; the tithe on the pasturing of pigs in the forest of Paganus of Mount Dublellus, called Tiron.

Further, wishing to provide for your future need, we establish by apostolic authority that neither you nor your successors may ever give, sell, or in any manner alienate from your church the obedience of Campaniac or any other possessions of your church. We therefore decree that no one, etc., down to: “to be beneficial,” the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of diocesan bishops being preserved.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly [violating] this page of our constitution . . . . . should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrongdoing committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him lie subject to severe vengeance. But to all who preserve the rights of those same places, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata [Note: [Col. 0497D] John, formerly a subdeacon, notary, and priest of the papal chapel, was named cardinal deacon and vice-chancellor of the title of St Mary in Via Lata by Pope Innocent III in the fourth creation, in this same seventh year of Innocent’s pontificate, in March, according to Panvinio, or in December, according to Ciaconius. While King John of England was fiercely persecuting clerics, Innocent sent this same man as legate to England, to persuade the king to cease his wrongs against the clergy. Innocent wrote several letters [Col. 0498D] to this cardinal, who remained in England for two years. After completing his English legation, he served as legate in France together with Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus, to establish and secure peace between Philip, king of the Franks, and John, king of the English, and to persuade Philip to take back the wife whom he had unjustly dismissed. He died under the same Innocent; for Panvinio, when naming the cardinals who attended the election and chose Honorius as Roman pontiff, omits this John, and no further mention of him survives after 1210. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 24.], on the fifth Ides of January, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord [Col. 0497C] Pope Innocent III.

### CLXXXV [Note: [Col. 0498D] See Raynaldus under the year 1205, §68.]. TO HUGH, OF SAINT PETER OF CLUNY [Note: [Col. 0498D] See letter 174 of book six, note.].

He confirms the privileges enumerated below, together with their appurtenances. (At St Peter’s, on the Ides of January.)

The monastery of blessed Peter at Cluny, a mirror of monastic religion in modern times and an example in the regions of Gaul, was, from the very beginning of its foundation, offered to the Apostolic See as its own rightful possession. Accordingly, our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, endowed that place with the prerogative of singular affection and liberty, and fortified all that belongs to it by the enactments of their privileges. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just [Col. 0497D] petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter himself and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Cluny, which is specially [Col. 0498A] subject to the right of blessed Peter, and strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the brothers of Cluny, etc., down to: “be observed.”

Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., down to: “to be set forth by name”: the place itself in which your aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; in Burgundy, Karumlocum, Marciniacum, Paredum, Saint Marcellus of Chalon, Virgiacum, Troaldum, and all other priories, cells, possessions, and rights which you hold in the province of Lyons beyond the Saône; Nantuacum, Ginniacum, the monastery of the valleys of Polignac, [Col. 0498B] the monastery of Hautepierre; Vallisclausa beyond the Roman road, the monastery of Paterniacum; the islands and all priories, cells, possessions, and rights which you possess in that part of Burgundy or in Germany; in the province of Vienne, Saint Victor of Geneva, Condammum, Burgetum, Dominam [Note: [Col. 0498D] Thus in the copy.], Lavardum, and all the places and rights which you possess in that province of Vienne; in Provence, Saint Saturninus, Tornacum, Puy de Canagobia; outside Montpellier, Clunisetum and your other places situated in Provence; in Gascony, Carennacum, Mauriacum, Saint-Mont, and all your places which you possess in Gascony; furthermore, the monastery of Souvigny, Celsimen, Saint-Flour, Volta, Saint [Col. 0498C] Eutropius, Mogon, Agia, the monastery of La Charité, with all its appurtenances; Saint Stephen; Saint Saviour of Nevers, Saint Martin of the Fields; Longpont; Gaïa; Saint Margaret in Champagne, with the granges of Macricuria and Saint Petronilla and all their appurtenances; Crispiacum, Consiacum, Lehunum, with the priories of Saint Lawrence and Saint Nicholas, which . . . the prior of Lehunum has newly acquired for his monastery with their appurtenances; Saint Margaret in Codun, Mondidier, Abbeville, Saint-Loup, the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, Froewill, Renargias, and whatever you possess in the provinces of Bourges, Bordeaux, Sens, Reims, Trier, and Rouen; the monastery of Lowen, [Col. 0498D] Lenton, Mont-Aigu, Testord, Labdecumba, and the estates of Apeford and Tikesore, with all their appurtenances [Col. 0499A]; Saint Mary of Nájera, Saint Zoilus of Carrión, Villafranca, Saint Columba of Burgos, Cornelianum, the monastery of Pontida, the monastery of Saint Maiolus of Pavia, Saint Gabriel of Cremona, and the monastery of Saint Paul of Argon; the cell of Bertreis, the cell of Namarchia, and whatever you possess in England, Spain, Lombardy, and the diocese of Liège; in Tuscany, Saint Mary of Aquaviva near the crypts; in the city of Tuscania, Saint John of the Hill, Saint Peter of Alianum; in the bishopric of Tusculum, Saint Mary of Peselo; and in Sicily, the priory of Sacco, with all its appurtenances.

Moreover, you are henceforth to possess more peacefully, without any opposition from bishops or episcopal officials, the tithes of your labours—on account of which bishops have customarily troubled both you and other men of monastic religion—namely, of those lands which they call *dominicaturae* [demesnes], and which are cultivated at your expense by the dependants of your monastery and cells; for you distribute your goods to pilgrims, brothers, and the poor. You may also receive clerics and laypersons, free persons, etc. We further prohibit, etc. No one may presume to retain one who departs without the joint security of your letters. But if anyone should perhaps, etc., down to: “promulgate.” We also prohibit anyone from receiving a monk, etc., down to: “the benefit of your house.” But if he should presume to do this, etc., down to: “restore.” Furthermore, it shall be lawful for you, in your own causes, etc., down to: “perish.”

Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop [Col. 0499C] or any other person whatsoever to compel you to attend synods or assemblies, nor may anyone come to your houses, etc., down to: “of convening, or even of celebrating Mass,” unless invited by the abbot. We also decree that all churches, cemeteries, monks, clerics, and all laypersons dwelling within the boundaries extending from the stream of Salnai, from the church of Rufiaci, and from the cross of Lornant, likewise from the boundary of the mill of Tornasach, through the village called Varenna, together with the wood of Burserius, and from the boundary called Perois as far as the stream of Salnai, shall remain solely under the jurisdiction and protection of the Apostolic See. Nor are the priests or parishioners of the place of Cluny itself to be compelled to attend the synod or assembly of anyone except the Roman [Col. 0499D] pontiff, his legate, and the abbot of Cluny.
