Moreover, for the ordination of the abbot, monks, or clerics dwelling within the aforesaid boundaries; for the making of chrism; for the consecration of holy oil, churches, and altars; and for the blessing of cemeteries, let the monastery of Cluny summon whichever bishop it prefers, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See. No person whatsoever, except the Roman pontiff and a legate sent for this purpose, may excommunicate or place under interdict monks of Cluny wherever they reside; provided, however, that the obedience or reverence due to legates of the Apostolic See is in no way diminished by this.

We also grant to you, son abbot, and through you to the monastery [Col. 0500A] of Cluny, that in processions and the solemnities of Mass, both you and your successors may use the mitre, ring, gloves, sandals, and other pontifical insignia, and may impart the solemn blessing over the people, to the glory of the divine name and the honour of the monastery of Cluny.

We strictly forbid anyone to presume, without the knowledge of the Apostolic See, to which your monastery is specially subject, to alienate in any way its possessions, rights, or goods, or to violate its ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed. But if any donations, etc., down to: “we decree.”

Furthermore, by our authority you are freely entitled to redeem tithes and possessions pertaining to the right of your churches which are held by laymen; lawfully to free them from their hands; and to restore them to the churches to which they belong [Col. 0500B]. We likewise confirm for you, by apostolic authority, the striking of your own coinage, or money, as has hitherto been obtained.

Furthermore, we add that in all priories and cells now subject to your rule without their own abbot, no one may ever presume in future times to appoint an abbot. Rather, both those priories and cells, and all other things in whatever places which the church of Cluny possessed at the time of the Council of Clermont, celebrated by our predecessor Pope Urban of blessed memory, concerning which no dispute was then raised, are to be preserved forever to you, son abbot, and to your successors [Col. 0500C] in peace and quiet—except only those things whose condition has been altered by authority of the Apostolic See.

No bishop may impose upon you an undue burden in respect of your altars, churches, or tithes. Rather, as you have held some of these in part and some wholly by their permission, so you shall hold them in future times. Moreover, all your churches, wherever situated, and your chapels and cemeteries, shall be free and exempt from every exaction, except the customary procuration for the bishop and canonical jurisdiction over priests who have offended against the dignity of their order.

In parish churches which you possess, it shall be lawful for you or your brothers to choose priests [Col. 0500D] and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they are answerable to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. If, God forbid, the bishop refuses through perversity to commit this care to them, then, by the kindness of the Apostolic See, the priests shall receive permission to celebrate the offices, provided they are suitable. If diocesan bishops are unwilling freely to provide consecrations of churches or altars, receive them from any Catholic bishop enjoying the favour and communion of the Apostolic See.

Nor may the brothers of your cells situated anywhere suffer any suspension of divine offices on account of any interdict or excommunication. Rather, the monks themselves and their servants [Col. 0501A], and those who have dedicated themselves to monastic profession, shall celebrate the divine offices and perform the rites due for burial with the church doors closed, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells unrung, and voices lowered.

Moreover, we consider that the abbeys granted by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, to your predecessors should also be granted by us to you and your successors, so that through your diligence, with the Lord as author, the state of religion may be preserved in them: namely, the abbeys of Saint Martial of Limoges, the New Monastery of Poitiers, Saint John of Angély, the monastery of Lezac, Moissac, Figeac, Mauziac, Thiers, and Saint Germanus of Auxerre. Nevertheless, we decree that no abbot may under any circumstances be elected in them without the counsel of the abbot of Cluny [Col. 0501B].

Desiring also to provide henceforth with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority that, within the boundaries of the sacred ban distinguished by the aforesaid Pope Urban, or within the enclosures of your places or granges, any person of whatever condition or power may presume to commit invasion, plunder, robbery, or theft; set fire; shed blood; seize a person rashly; or commit homicide.

Furthermore, all liberties and immunities, etc., down to: “we strengthen.” Therefore we decree, etc., down to: “to be of benefit,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of diocesan bishops in churches [Col. 0501C] not exempt. If anyone therefore in future, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John [Note: [Col. 0501D] See the preceding letter, 184, note.], cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, on the Ides of January, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

### CLXXXVI [Note: [Col. 0501D] This letter is cited by Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 131, §X. Raynaldus also published it, but mutilated, under the year 1205, §57. The material appearing in his edition [Col. 0502D] is enclosed here in brackets.]. TO THE KING OF THE FRANKS.

That he should restrain the insolence of Jews residing in the kingdom and rise up against heretics. (At St Peter’s, 17 Kalends of February.)

[Note: [Col. 0502D] The following is in Raynaldus, cited place.] [Although it is not displeasing to the Lord, but rather acceptable to him, that the dispersion of the Jews should live and serve under Catholic Christian kings and princes, [Col. 0501D] whose remnant will at last be saved when “in those days Judah shall be saved and Israel shall dwell securely,” nevertheless those gravely offend the eyes of the divine majesty who prefer the children of the crucifiers—against whom the blood still cries in the ears of the Father—to the coheirs of the crucified Christ; and who prefer Jewish servitude to the freedom of those whom the Son has made free, as though the son of the handmaid could and ought to be heir together with the son of the free woman.

You should know that it has reached our hearing that, in the kingdom of the Franks, Jews have become so insolent that, under the guise of [Col. 0502A] the evil of usury, by which they extort not only interest but interest upon interest, they seize the goods of churches and the possessions of Christians. Thus that which the prophet laments in the person of the Jews seems fulfilled among the Christian people: “Our inheritance,” he says, “has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners” [Lamentations 5].

Furthermore, whereas the Lateran Council decreed that Jews are not to be allowed to keep Christian servants in their homes, whether under the pretext of rearing children, for service, or for any other cause, and that those who presume to live with them are to be excommunicated, they do not hesitate to keep Christian servants and wet nurses, with whom they sometimes commit abominations which it is more fitting for you to punish than for us to describe.

[Col. 0502B] Moreover, although that same council judged that the testimony of Christians against Jews should be admitted in common cases, since Jews use Jewish witnesses against Christians, and decreed that anyone preferring Jews to Christians in this matter should be struck with anathema, such deference is paid to them in the kingdom of the Franks that Christian witnesses are not believed against them, whereas they themselves are admitted to testify against Christians.

And if, on some occasion, those to whom Christians believe they have lent their money at interest produce Christian witnesses concerning payment made, more credit is given to the document which the imprudent debtor has left with them through negligence or carelessness than to the witnesses produced. Indeed, witnesses are not even received against them on this point [Col. 0502C]. They have become so insolent—to our shame in reporting it—that at Sens, beside a certain old church, they have built a new synagogue higher by no small degree than the church. There, unlike formerly, before they had been expelled from the kingdom, when they performed their offices in subdued voices, they now celebrate their rites loudly according to the Jewish custom and do not hesitate to impede the celebration of divine worship in that church. [Note: [Col. 0502D] Raynaldus ends here.]] 

Indeed, blaspheming the name of the Lord, they publicly insult Christians because they believe in a certain rustic whom the Jewish people hanged. We certainly do not doubt that he was hanged for us, since he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree; but we do not admit that he was rustic in morals or lineage. Indeed, they themselves could not deny that according to the flesh he descended from priestly and royal stock, and that his conduct was illustrious and honourable.

Also, on the day of Preparation, contrary to their former custom, Jews run and gather publicly through streets and squares and, according to their custom, mock Christians on every side as they adore the Crucified One on the cross, and strive by their taunts to recall them from the duty of adoration. The doors of Jews also stand open to thieves until midnight; nor, if something stolen is found among them, [Col. 0503A] can anyone obtain justice from them.

Thus Jews abuse royal patience; and, although they remain among Christians, they secretly kill their Christian hosts when opportunity is seized, as is said recently to have occurred when a certain poor scholar was found dead in their latrine. Therefore, lest through them the Lord’s name be blasphemed and Christian freedom become worse than Jewish servitude, we admonish and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: restrain the Jews from their presumption in these and similar matters, and strive to abolish such abuses from the kingdom of the Franks, so that you may seem to possess zeal for God according to knowledge. Since secular laws also punish more severely [Col. 0503B] those who blaspheme the Lord’s name, so punish such blasphemers that the punishment of some may be the fear of all, and that ease of pardon may not provide an incentive to wrongdoing.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Again Raynaldus, cited place, to the end.] [Furthermore, rise up powerfully to eliminate heretics from the kingdom of the Franks. Let not royal highness permit wolves hiding in its land under sheepskins in order to destroy the sheep, but show in persecuting them the fervour with which it pursues the Christian faith.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth Kalends of February, in the seventh year.]

### CLXXXVII. . . . . BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0503D] Concerning the bishop of Feltre, Torentinus de Curte, we have already dealt with him in the note to letter 39 of book three. From documents we know that Torentinus de Curte held office until 1205. His successor, Philip of Padua, is not known before 1209. See UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 344.] AND CANONS OF FELTRE.

He confirms their statute establishing ten canons in their church. (At St Peter’s, fifth Ides of January.)

[Col. 0503C]

It is customary to assent, etc., down to: “bestow.” On your behalf, indeed, humble petition was made to us that we should deem it worthy to confirm for you by apostolic authority the number of ten canons, which, when there had hitherto been eight canons in your church, you established there by prudent deliberation according to the resources of your church, especially since this appears greatly advantageous to that church itself. Therefore, assenting to your petitions, we confirm for you by apostolic authority that constitution, prudently made for the benefit of the church of Feltre, and strengthen it by the protection of the present [Col. 0503D] writing, unless the resources of the same church have increased to such an extent that this number ought deservedly to be enlarged, while the mandates of the Apostolic See are in every respect preserved. Therefore let no one, etc. If anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth Ides of January.

### CLXXXVIII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS.

He confirms their privileges. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0504A]

It is customary to assent, down to: “bestow.” Therefore, inclined by your just prayers, we deem valid the liberties and immunities granted to your church, and likewise its ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed both for you and your servants and for your possessions; and we decree that they shall remain inviolate in future times. Therefore let no one . . . violate this grant of ours, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

### CLXXXIX. . . . . TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARMENIA.

That he should make satisfaction for damages inflicted by him upon the brethren of the Order of the Temple. (At St Peter’s, fifteenth Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0504B]

In our presence, the beloved sons . . . the master and brethren of the Order of the Temple lodged a grave complaint that you had, without reasonable cause, burned certain of their villages, violently taken from them their beasts and grain, and, at your own discretion, inflicted damage upon them amounting to fifty thousand besants. Furthermore, after stripping some of their brethren of their own goods and afflicting them with beatings and blows, you consigned them to prison custody. You also inflicted grave injury and no small loss, both in persons and property, upon two of their castles—namely, the Rock of William and the Rock of Ruissol—which you had surrounded with hostile siege works.

[Col. 0504C] Wishing therefore in this matter to provide for the salvation of your soul and likewise for the honour and reputation of royal serenity, we ask and exhort your excellency in the Lord to make fitting satisfaction to the brethren for the aforementioned damages and injuries inflicted upon them; to withdraw both hand and intention from oppressing them; and, as far as lies in your power, not to allow them to be molested by others. Otherwise, know that we have instructed our venerable brothers, the bishops of . . . Biblos and . . . Valania, to summon the parties, hear the cause, decide it with justice as mediator and without appeal, and enforce inviolably by ecclesiastical censure what they decree.

[Col. 0504D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifteenth Kalends of February.

### CXC [Note: [Col. 0504D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.]. TO RICHARD [Note: [Col. 0504D] Richard I, formerly a monk and abbot of Compiègne, is known from documents from 1197 until 1212. Some maintain that he died on 21 September 1216 or 1217; but his successor Walter is mentioned in 1213. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 437.], ABBOT OF COMPIÈGNE.

He grants him the use of the mitre and ring. (At St Peter’s, fifteenth Kalends of February.)

It is customary for the Apostolic See to grant kindly favour to pious vows and to the honourable [Col. 0505A] desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son, graciously assenting to your prayers, we grant you personally, by the kindness of the Apostolic See, the use of the mitre and ring.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifteenth Kalends of February, in the seventh year.

### CXCI. TO THE PRIOR OF CAMALDOLI, AND . . . MASTER GUALANDUS, CANON OF PISA.

Concerning the transfer of the bishopric of Fiesole [Note: [Col. 0505D] See letters 20 and 21 of this book, and the notes there.]. (At St Peter’s, thirteenth Kalends of February.)

Since much labour has repeatedly been expended upon transferring the see of Fiesole to a more convenient location, we, desiring to attend to the peace and advantage both of the church of Fiesole and [Col. 0505B] of the city of Florence, command your discretion by apostolic letters to summon the bishop and chapter of Fiesole, the podestà, consuls, and councillors of Florence, and carefully deliberate with them. If, with the assent of the said bishop and chapter and the agreement of the aforesaid podestà, consuls, and councillors, you can find a suitable place in that diocese where the transfer of the see of Fiesole may advantageously be made, inform us by your letters, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed more effectively in this matter.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth Kalends of February.

### CXCII [Note: [Col. 0505D] It is found among the Decretals, book V, title 29, “Concerning a cleric promoted by skipping a grade,” chapter 1, where it is said to be addressed to the bishop of Bologna.]. TO . . . BISHOP OF OLOMOUC.

He writes in favour of P., who had been promoted to the order of priesthood while passing over the grade of deacon. (At St Peter’s, twelfth Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0505C]

Your letters, presented to us [Note: [Col. 0505D] These words, and shortly afterwards “good men received,” and “present letters,” are absent in the Decretals.], stated that, as you had learned from the report of certain good men, P., the priest and bearer of the present letters, had caused himself to be promoted to the grade [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Decretals read “order,” and shortly thereafter, omitting the words “and when . . . truth,” add also after “to you.” The word “humbly” is absent.] of priesthood while omitting the order of deacon. When you had carefully inquired of him concerning the truth of this, he humbly confessed to you in secret that he did not know for certain whether the matter stood so. But since good men, among whom he had lived, asserted this, he believed their assertion, because he himself [Note: [Col. 0506D] The Decretals omit “he himself,” and shortly thereafter the words “you . . . letters”; below, they read “which” for “and that.”], at the time [Col. 0505D] when he received the lower orders, had been under the age of discretion.

You therefore sent him to the Apostolic See and humbly petitioned us to deal mercifully with him. We, therefore, sympathizing with his misfortune, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to impose upon him a fitting [Col. 0506A] penance for such negligence. When he has completed it, since that is not understood to be repeated whose having been done is not known, procure that he be ordained deacon and then, by mercy, permit him to minister in the order of priest.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth Kalends of February.

### CXCIII. TO . . . BISHOP OF CHALON [Note: [Col. 0506D] See letter 16 of book five, note.], AND . . . ABBOT OF CLUNY [Note: [Col. 0506D] Book VI, letter 174, note.].

He commits to them the examination of the cause concerning the election of the abbot of Saint Martin of Troyes. (At St Peter’s, thirteenth Kalends of February.)

Formerly, when O . . . P . . . . and H . . . . had been sent to our presence for the beloved son P., chaplain of our venerable brother . . . archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 0506D] He has already been discussed frequently.], and [Col. 0506B] M., canon of Saint-Loup of Troyes—each of whom claims to have been canonically elected to govern the church of Saint Martin of Troyes—and requested that a hearing be afforded them, we appointed the beloved son M. [Note: [Col. 0506D] Book III, letter 54, note.], cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore, as auditor.

After he faithfully reported to us the matters presented before him, we directed you by our letters to investigate the truth concerning everything carefully. If you found either of the two elections canonically celebrated in the person of a suitable candidate, you were to confirm it, notwithstanding the evasion of appeal, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure with appeal set aside. Otherwise, after annulling both elections, you were to arrange for that church [Col. 0506C] to be provided with a suitable person through canonical election. Before all else, you were to provide that unless it was established to you that the aforesaid chaplain had been a canon of the church of Saint-Loup or of Saint Martin of Troyes when he was elected abbot, you should, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, entirely invalidate his election. Thus no prejudice might be created through it to the tenor of privileges of the Apostolic See, in which it is provided that, if either of those churches is vacant, an election may not be made from elsewhere, except from among their brethren, so long as a suitable person is found there.

Although such a privilege was granted to the church of Saint-Loup, for the reason that it derived from the monastery of Saint Martin, a like privilege could with equal reason have been granted to the church of Cantamerle [Col. 0506D] [Note: [Col. 0506D] Why the church of Cantamerle is mentioned here is not sufficiently understood, unless one may say that the person elected in question here—namely P., chaplain of the archbishop of Sens—was at the same time attached to the church of Cantamerle.], since it too was derived from the same monastery of Saint Martin. Therefore, observing equality in similar cases, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you confirm the aforesaid election, if it is otherwise found [Col. 0507A] canonical, notwithstanding the aforesaid privilege [Note: [Col. 0507D] It may be inferred from the succession of abbots of Saint Martin that P.’s election was confirmed by the judges here delegated by the pontiff. For documents prove that Peter I presided from at least 1207 until 1222. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 581.]. Yet we do not intend this mandate to derogate in future from that privilege, since from the aforesaid similarity we have drawn an argument not for declaring a right but for granting a favour.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth Kalends of February, in the seventh year.

### CXCIV. TO MASTER PETER, PRIEST OF SAINT COLUMBA.

That he must not allow the serfs of his parish to live with Jews. (At St Peter’s, thirteenth Kalends of February.)

It is unfitting that those whom the water of baptism has regenerated in Christ and adopted as children of the true light should live with those whom hardness of heart has blinded from knowledge of [Col. 0507B] the true light, lest they be darkened by the error of those whom true faith has brought into the light. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, who appears to possess zeal for God according to knowledge, we grant your devotion, by authority of the present letters, that, with every obstacle of opposition and appeal removed, you may restrain by sentence of excommunication, in accordance with the canonical enactments, Christian slaves who have presumed to live with Jews in your parish, so that those whom Judaism strives to reduce from the grace of liberty to the disgrace of servitude may be drawn back from such service.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth Kalends of February.

### CXCV. TO THE BISHOP OF CHARTRES [Note: [Col. 0507D] Book III, letter 14, note.].

That, if the trustees of deceased persons do not fulfil their wishes, he should fulfil them. (At St Peter’s, ninth Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0507C]

It is customary for the Apostolic See to grant kindly favour to pious vows and honourable desires of petitioners. Indeed, as we have learned from your report, very many men of your diocese, when certain persons at death entrust goods to them to be distributed for the remission of their sins, delay disbursing them for a year or more; moreover, very many trustees presume to appropriate bequests for their own use. Therefore, venerable brother, graciously assenting to your prayers, we grant you by the authority of these letters that if trustees of this kind, upon [Col. 0507D] your admonition, refuse to distribute the bequests to churches and clerics in accordance with the lawful wishes of the deceased, then you may, after due inquiry and with every evasion of opposition [Col. 0508A] and appeal removed, fulfil the pious wishes of the dying. Therefore let no one, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth Kalends of February, in the seventh year.

### CXCVI. TO . . . ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: [Col. 0507D] Book III, letter 9, note.].

He commits to him alone the adjudication of the case concerning the parish of Bujano. (At St Peter’s, seventh Kalends of February.)

The case known to be in dispute between the people of Massabuiano on one side and the people of Bujano [Note: [Col. 0507D] It appears that “Bujanenses” should be read, from letters of Pope Honorius III in MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, vol. IV, p. 279.] on the other, concerning the parish of that place, is said to have been entrusted by us to you and . . . the prior of Saint Alexander of Lucca. But because the other party says that it regards the aforesaid prior [Col. 0508B] as suspect, since he has been a supporter and advocate of the opposing party, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after a fuller investigation of the truth, that if you find the matter to be so, you shall remove the aforesaid prior and proceed alone in that cause, according to the form of the letters, without appeal and after due inquiry. The witnesses, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh Kalends of February.

### CXCVII [Note: [Col. 0507D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §59.]. TO THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 0507D]

Very little is found concerning the deans of Beauvais around the period with which we are concerned [Col. 0508D] among the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 770.

XIX. Waleran, or Galeran, from 1194 to 1204. Nevertheless, according to the Sammarthani, a certain Odo was in office in 1203. In 1202 Waleran issued statutes concerning the residence of canons.

“XX. John I, from 1205 to 1218. Nevertheless, Dionysius Simon, in the supplement to the *History of Beauvais*, p. 106, states that he died in 1217. Pope Innocent III wrote to him in 1213, chapter *Tua nos*, 34, *On Simony*.”]

AND CHAPTER OF BEAUVAIS.

That, so long as their bishop is willing to obey the law, they should not cease from divine worship against him. (At St Peter’s, tenth Kalends of February.)

When the force of ecclesiastical discipline was devised for punishing the disobedience of the contumacious, it ought to be moderated in such a way that, once contumacy has been removed, the penalty due to the contumacious is likewise set aside; lest, if good be called evil or evil good, impiety come to be practised under the appearance of piety. Indeed, our venerable brother . . . . . . your bishop [Note: [Col. 0508D] See letter 149 of book five, note.] has reported to us that, in contempt of him, you presume to undertake measures wholly contrary to reason: namely, that, so long as he is prepared to submit to the law, you suspend the offices of the Church against him—a measure introduced for the detestation of the contumacious. Therefore, lest the same bishop, whom we cherish with special affection, henceforth be unduly burdened by you in matters of this kind contrary to justice, by these apostolic letters we command your whole body, [Col. 0508D] enjoining you to take care to render him, as the father and shepherd of your souls, devoted obedience and due reverence; and, so long as he is willing to submit to the law, neither yourselves cease from divine offices against the bishop, nor cause others to cease, unless the cause be such as does not require judicial procedure. Otherwise, since we do not wish him to be burdened contrary to justice—he to whom we acknowledge ourselves indebted, each in his own right—we command that such an interdict is not to be observed.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh year.

CXCVIII [Note: [Col. 0509D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 59.]. TO . . . . . . THE BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS [Note: [Col. 0509D] Book V, letter 149, note.]. Commission to exact tithes, including those of wool, lambs, produce, and hay. (At Saint Peter’s, the ninth day before the Kalends of February.)

It was set forth before us on your behalf that [Col. 0509B] very many laymen of your diocese refuse to pay tithes of wool, lambs, produce, and hay to the churches and persons to whom they are due, alleging solely in their excuse that such tithes have hitherto not been demanded in the diocese of Beauvais, nor are they demanded in neighbouring dioceses. Since, therefore, such an exception—or rather, an excuse in sins—ought not to protect them from rendering those tithes, we grant you authority by these presents to compel them, through ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to pay without objection the aforesaid tithes to the churches and persons to whom they are due. Therefore let no one, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends [Col. 0509C] of February, in the seventh year.

CXCIX [Note: [Col. 0509D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 68.]. TO THE BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF SAINT JAMES OF COLLE BERTANNI. He receives them under protection, subject to an annual payment of one bezant. (At Saint Peter’s, the sixth day before the Kalends of February.)

It is customary to assent, etc., down to “assent.” We receive your persons and the hospital itself, with its appurtenances, under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and safeguard them by the protection of this present writing. Moreover, as a token of the protection obtained from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and to our successors annually one bezant freely offered. We decree therefore, etc.

[Col. 0509D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

CC [Note: [Col. 0509D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1204, § 25.]. TO THE BISHOP OF FERRARA [Note: [Col. 0509D] See letter 39 of book three, note.]. That he should go to Venice and investigate the consecration of the elected Patriarch of Grado. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifth day before the Kalends of February.)

Although the beloved son . . . the elected Patriarch of Grado [Note: [Col. 0510D] See letter 240 of book six, note.] was confirmed by our beloved son P. [Note: [Col. 0510D] He has already been mentioned frequently.], cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0510A] yet, because he neglected to request the office of consecration within the period fixed by the canons, we were able not merely to defer his consecration but even to refuse it altogether. We pass over the offences of the Venetians, who gravely offended the Roman Church in many ways: first, because they would not receive the aforesaid legate when he came to them as legate of the Apostolic See; and secondly, because they presumed to destroy Zara, contrary to our prohibition issued under threat of anathema.

But because we hold on earth, although unworthily, the place of him who, when angry, remembers mercy, and although we had been grievously offended, we nevertheless did not wish to confine mercy within anger, when he at length came into our presence [Col. 0510B] we deemed it right to arrange matters so that, while awaiting the correction of the Venetians, we might thereafter extend grace, provided that the same elect should remain in the status which he had attained by his election and confirmation alike. Since, therefore, our beloved son, the noble man . . . . . . Duke of Venice, has returned to obedience to the Church and, as he informed us in his letters, has obtained through . . . the messenger of the aforesaid legate the benefit of absolution, we command your brotherhood by these apostolic letters personally to go to Venice and, because certain unfavourable things are said concerning the person of that elect, to investigate the truth diligently. For, according to the Apostle, hands ought not hastily to be laid upon anyone. If you find nothing in him contrary to the canonical institutions, [Col. 0510C] then, lest the elect be compelled to make the journey to us again, summon the suffragans of the Church of Grado and confer upon him, in our stead, the office of consecration. But if any canonical objection is raised against him, hear what is alleged on either side and take care faithfully to report it to us.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

CCI [Note: [Col. 0510D] This letter is printed by Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 1.]. FROM EMPEROR BALDWIN TO THE POPE. He requests confirmation of the agreements concluded between himself and the Venetians.

[To the most holy Father and Lord, I., by God’s providence supreme pontiff, B., by the same grace most faithful in Christ, God-crowned Emperor of Constantinople, [Col. 0510D] ruler of the Romans and ever august, Count of Flanders and Hainaut: humble and devoted obedience with due submission.

We recall that we have more fully explained to your fatherhood, through our envoys and letters, the condition and progress of the Christian army and of ourselves. Now we have taken care to send you the agreements made before the conquest of the imperial city between ourselves and the pilgrims on the one hand, and . . . the Duke of Venice and the Venetians on the other, confirmed by the protection of our seal. We earnestly beseech your holiness, [Col. 0511A] as is our duty, to hold the said agreements valid and to confirm them by the protection of apostolic authority.

For we wish your holiness to know that we have maintained with the aforesaid duke and the Venetians a good and faithful partnership, and have found them most excellent and effective fellow-workers for the honour of God, of the holy Roman Church, and of our empire, as the deeds themselves demonstrate. We desire to retain them in the future also, since their association is useful and necessary both for the governance of our empire, for assistance to the Holy Land, and for preserving the unity of the Church; nor can our empire be suitably governed, to the honour of God and of your holy see, without their association and goodwill.]

CCII [Note: [Col. 0511D] This letter is printed by Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 2.]. FROM THE DUKE OF VENICE TO THE POPE. He excuses himself for the destruction of Zara and gives an account of the conquest of Constantinople; he then begs that the requests made through his envoys may be favourably heard.

[Col. 0511B]

[To the venerable Father and Lord in Christ, I., by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: H. Dandolo, Duke of Dalmatia and Croatia, your humble and devoted servant, offers service with every devotion.

I make known to your holiness that, when I had taken the cross in the service of Jesus Christ and of the holy Roman Church, and had set out from Venice for the crossing, the need imposed by the coming winter compelled me to winter at Zara with my fleet and that of the pilgrims [Col. 0511C]. Since that city had for a long time unjustly rebelled against me and the Venetians through treachery, in violation of the oaths given, I took vengeance upon the city and its citizens, as I considered just, according to the custom of enemies at war with one another.

But because, as was said, they were under your protection—which I did not therefore believe, because I do not think that you or your predecessors receive under protection those who take the cross merely in order to wear it, and not to complete the journey for which pilgrims customarily take the cross, but who acquire the possessions of others and hold them unjustly—it pleased your fatherhood to pronounce against me and the Venetians a sentence of excommunication. We bore this patiently and humbly, until, through Lord P., [Col. 0511D] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the holy Roman Church, having rendered suitable satisfaction, we deserved absolution, as may become more clearly known to your holiness from the arrangement made by your envoys and from the text of your letters.

Thereafter, through divine inspiration rather than human counsel, as we believe, we undertook a journey into Romania with Alexius, son of the former Emperor Isaac of Constantinople. Having received from him an assurance of obedience to the holy Roman Church, and having expelled [Col. 0512A] his uncle Alexius and captured the city of Constantinople, at great danger and labour we secured the same assurance first from his father Isaac, from his relatives, and from many other magnates of the city. But, when these proved false and deceitful in the said promise, we renounced them as enemies of the holy Roman Church and traitors to Christendom.

After father and son had been killed by Greek treachery, and other petty Greeks elevated, we endured the Greeks’ continual injuries and attacks: by sea, as they sent burning ships against us to burn our vessels, and waged prolonged wars; and by land, in many and various ways. Having taken counsel with all the clergy [Col. 0512B] and laity of the army, and after certain preliminary agreements had been made between ourselves and them—as your holiness will be able to learn more clearly from the wording of the copy of those agreements—we resolved to attack the city of Constantinople for the honour of God and the holy Roman Church and the aid of Christendom. By the aiding mercy of Christ, by your merit, and especially, beyond all others living, by our laborious effort, this was accomplished contrary to everyone’s expectation.

When the city had been taken and much slaughter of Greeks had occurred, Marcoflus, who was then emperor, fled from the city with his followers; and we fulfilled the written agreement and oath made between us. Let your holiness therefore know [Col. 0512C] that I, together with the Venetian people, have laboured in all that we have done for the honour of God, the holy Roman Church, and yourself; and we likewise intend to labour henceforward. Therefore I beg your holiness graciously to hear and bring into effect the requests made by my envoys—noble and prudent men, namely Leonardus Naugaiosus, my beloved nephew, and Andreas de Mulin—whom we send to the feet of your holiness.]

CCIII [Note: [Col. 0511D] A fragment of this letter may be read [Col. 0512D] in the Deeds of Innocent, § XCVI; but it belongs to the following letter, 204, where the same words, enclosed here in brackets, are repeated.]. TO THE BISHOPS AND ABBOTS, AND THE OTHER CLERGY RESIDING AT CONSTANTINOPLE. He rejoices that the Church of Constantinople has returned to obedience to the Apostolic See; declaring void the patriarchal election made by them, he himself elects the same man by apostolic authority. (At Saint Peter’s, the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0512D]

As Gospel Scripture teaches, we have learned that Jesus, entering one boat, which was Simon’s, asked him to put out a little from the land; and, sitting in the boat, he taught the crowds. As the sea signifies the world, so the boat signifies the Church and the net preaching. Simon’s boat, then, is Peter’s Church, which is blessed as one because the Catholic Church is one; Christ committed it to Peter’s governance, so that unity might exclude division.

Jesus entered [Col. 0513A] Simon’s boat in effect when he caused Peter’s Church to rise—a fact clearly apparent from the time of Constantine. From then on, he deigned to reign who had power to command, so that by prayers rather than commands he might more sweetly induce them to put out the boat a little from the land: that is, gradually to transfer the Church from earthly usage to heavenly, or rather from literal to spiritual teaching. And he taught the crowds sitting in the boat, because from then on he caused Peter to have a settled see, whether at the Lateran or at the Vatican; and he caused him to teach, because from then on teachers began to multiply in Peter’s Church—Leo, Gregory, Gelasius, Innocent, and many others after them.

For a time he ceased speaking when the word of preaching ceased in Peter’s Church, perhaps not so much because of the unworthiness of its prelates as because of the wickedness of its subjects, as the Lord says to the prophet: “I will cause your tongue to cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute and not like a man rebuking them, because they are a rebellious house; but when I speak to you, I will open your mouth” (Ezek. 3). Therefore, after he ceased speaking, he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch” (Luke 5). The boat is put out into the deep when the Church is raised to lofty doctrine or advanced to a better state. Whether in these days the boat has been put out into the deep, I prefer not to say, lest I seem to praise myself; but one thing I confidently affirm: I have let down the nets for a catch.

Simon, therefore, who, like an obedient servant, regarded his master’s requests [Col. 0513C] as commands, answered him: “Master, though we have laboured all night, we have caught nothing; yet at your word I will let down the net” (ibid.). Certainly, the night of adversity impeded us greatly, so that, although my predecessors laboured very much, they nevertheless caught almost utterly nothing. But when I let down the net at God’s word, my brethren and I enclosed an abundant multitude of fish: in Livonia, by converting pagans to the faith through preachers sent there; in Bulgaria and Wallachia, by restoring the divided to unity; and also in Armenia, by seeking out through legates sent to those peoples persons who had long been abandoned.

What, then, is meant by what follows, “their net was breaking” (ibid.), except that heretics strive to weaken apostolic preaching, so that some fish escape from the nets? Yet, although they have gained strength to some extent, they shall not prevail against it in the end. When they had enclosed an abundant multitude of fish, they signalled to their companions in the other boat to come and help them. The other boat was the Church of the Greeks, which made itself other when it presumed to estrange itself from the unity of the universal Church. We signalled to them when we warned them by our letters and envoys to come and help us—that is, to return and take up their share of the charge entrusted to us, as fellow-workers in its administration.

By God’s grace they have come, because, after in these days the Empire of Constantinople [Col. 0514A] was transferred from the Greeks to the Latins, the Church of Constantinople also returned to obedience to the Apostolic See, as a daughter to her mother and a member to its head, so that henceforth undivided fellowship may endure between us and them. Indeed, we acknowledge them as brethren, associates, and friends; for although we hold the office of pre-eminence over them, this pre-eminence does not introduce lordship but rather service, as the Lord says to the Apostles: “The rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors; but it shall not be so among you. Rather, he who is greater among you shall be servant of all, and he who goes before, as one who ministers” (Luke 22). Hence the blessed Apostle Peter says: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart examples to the flock” (1 Pet. 5).

Our companions, therefore, have come, and are still coming and will come, so that what follows may be fulfilled: “They filled both boats, so that they were almost sinking” (Luke 5). Certainly, both boats must be filled, for those who have withdrawn themselves from obedience to both the Roman See and the Church of Constantinople shall return to them; and then both will almost sink, because scandals must come. But God is faithful, and does not permit his faithful ones to be tempted beyond their strength.

When Simon Peter sees this, he falls at Jesus’ knees, saying: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.” For amazement surrounded him and all who were with him (ibid.). And I, seeing that these things now begin to be fulfilled, ought in humility and devotion [Col. 0514C] to approach the knees of the Saviour, that for so great a grace I may render him thanksgiving. I may also say that, being a sinful man, I am unworthy to enjoy his so glorious presence. For I am surrounded, together with all who are with me, by great amazement at the novelty of so great a miracle which has occurred in these days.

But lest I be confounded by excessive astonishment, I should diligently note what Jesus says to Simon: “Do not fear; from now on you will be catching men” (ibid.). It is as if he said: Trust certainly, because, after you have caught fish—that is, after you have brought back Christians—you shall thereafter catch men, that is, convert Jews and pagans. For fish, which live in water, signify Christians, who are reborn of water and the Spirit; whereas human beings, who live on land, signify Jews and pagans, who crave and cling to earthly things. But after all Christians have entirely returned to obedience to the Apostolic See, then the multitude of the nations will enter the faith, and thus all Israel will be saved.

Behold, then, our companions come to help us, because the Church of the Greeks returns to obedience to the Apostolic See, so that, aided by their assistance, it may free its two sisters, namely the Churches of Alexandria and Jerusalem, which are held captive under the yoke of the king of Egypt and unwillingly serve Pharaoh. Furthermore, although there are five patriarchates in the world—the Roman, Constantinopolitan, Alexandrian, Antiochene, and Jerusalemite—only three apostles are named here, namely Peter, James, and John, who are said to have been seized with like amazement. This is because three of those patriarchates have a special relation to Peter: he personally consecrated the Churches of Antioch and Rome; and the Church of Alexandria through his disciple Mark, whom he personally sent there. The Church of Constantinople has a special relation to John, who both preached to the Greeks in Asia and was buried among the Greeks at Ephesus. The Church of Jerusalem properly relates to James: either the son of Zebedee, who, first of the apostles to be killed, dedicated Jerusalem by his martyrdom; or the son of Alphaeus, whom the apostles ordained bishop of Jerusalem. Perhaps for this reason Jesus took these three apostles [Col. 0515B] apart onto a high mountain and was transfigured before them. Nor does it seem unreasonable that, although for the aforesaid reason the Roman pontiff possesses five patriarchal sees throughout the world, he is solemnly crowned at only three of them.

It is therefore clear from what has been said that our companions come to help us, because, when [Note: [Col. 0515D] See the Deeds of Innocent, § XCVI.] [the right hand of the Lord, glorified in power, transferred the Empire of Constantinople from the Greeks to the Latins, those who had been in the Latin army, wishing to provide the empire itself with a suitable person, unanimously elected as emperor one of the [Note: [Col. 0515D] The Deeds has “from.”] princes of Gaul. In order that the Venetians, who had shared in the labour, might likewise share in the honour, [Col. 0515C] it pleased the Latins collectively that a suitable man should be chosen from the clergy of Venice and placed over the Church of Constantinople as patriarch.

Accordingly, certain Venetian clerics had been assigned to the service of the Church of Holy Wisdom; and, lest they should appear headless, like an acephalous body, they met together to deliberate on appointing themselves a shepherd. They unanimously elected as patriarch our beloved son T. [Note: [Col. 0515D] Thomas.], our subdeacon, [Note: [Col. 0515D] Omitted in the Deeds.] and humbly sought confirmation of their election from us through their own envoys. The noble man . . . Duke of Venice likewise urgently made the same request through his solemn envoys.

The imperial highness also petitioned us in his letters to consider valid, and to strengthen by the protection of apostolic authority, the agreements concluded before the attack upon the imperial city between himself and the pilgrims on the one hand, and the duke himself and the Venetians on the other, and confirmed by the protection of his seal. He wished us to know, to use his own words, that he had maintained good and faithful association with the aforesaid duke and Venetians and had found them most excellent and effective fellow-workers for the honour of God, the holy Roman Church, and the Empire of Constantinople, as their deeds testified; and that he desired to retain them in the future, since their association was useful and necessary for governing the empire, [Col. 0516A] aiding the Holy Land, and preserving the unity of the Church, and since that empire could not suitably be governed for the honour of God and the Apostolic See without their association and goodwill. The noble men B., Marquis of Montferrat, L., Count of Blois, and . . . Count of Saint-Pol likewise informed us of the same in their letters, using the same words.

We caused the document containing those agreements, sealed with the seals of the emperor and of the marquis and counts, to be read before us; and we saw that it provided that the clergy of that party from which no emperor should be chosen might freely elect a patriarch. Although, when such an election was presented to us, we and our brethren had sufficient knowledge of the person elected because of the long time he had formerly spent at the Apostolic See—we knew him to be of noble birth, honourable in conduct, prudent in judgment, and adequately learned—we nevertheless examined the election according to custom. We found that it had been undertaken contrary to canonical form, not so much because many had opposed it and some had even appealed, although they subsequently withdrew both opposition and appeal, as because laymen, however religious, have no authority whatsoever to dispose of ecclesiastical affairs. Therefore, by the authority of any secular prince, a patriarch neither ought [Col. 0516C] nor could have been elected in the Church of Constantinople.

Nor had the Venetian clerics, who call themselves elected canons of the Church of Holy Wisdom, the right to elect in that church, since they had not been instituted there by us or by our legates or delegates. For this reason, with the common counsel of our brethren, we took care publicly in consistory to reject that election. Yet, because the fault of persons ought not to result in injury to churches, and because the same subdeacon had committed no fault—for he was absent and had been elected without being consulted—remembering the prayers of the aforesaid emperor, which seemed to indicate not only usefulness but necessity, wishing to provide for that church, whose ordering specially pertained [Col. 0516D] to us, and to extend favour to the Venetians in the hope that they might more vigorously devote themselves to the service of Christ’s cross, from the fullness of power conferred on us we elected and confirmed the same subdeacon, as a member of the Apostolic See, patriarch of that Church. [Note: [Col. 0515D] Thus far in the Deeds.]]

[Note: [Col. 0516D] What follows is thus read in the Deeds of Innocent, § XCVI.]

Therefore we admonish, advise, and exhort the imperial dignity that, when the patriarch comes to the city of Constantinople, you receive and honour him graciously, humbly revere him as bishop and shepherd of your soul, and uphold and defend him in his rights and in those of the church committed to him; thus honouring him in other respects, that you may deserve to be honoured by him whose minister he is.] 

Therefore we earnestly admonish your whole body and command you by apostolic letters to observe with ready devotion what we have established after prudent deliberation.

[Col. 0517A] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.

CCIV [Note: [Col. 0517D] This letter is found in the Deeds of Innocent, § XCVI. Raynaldus also cites it, under the year 1205, § 14.].

TO B., ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. On the confirmation of the Patriarch of Constantinople. (At Saint Peter’s, the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.)

“After the right hand of the Lord, glorified in power,” etc., as above, down to “we confirmed him patriarch of that church.” Therefore we admonish, advise, and exhort the imperial dignity that, when the patriarch comes to the city of Constantinople, you receive and honour him graciously, humbly revere him as bishop and shepherd of your soul, and uphold and defend him in his rights and in those of the Church entrusted to him; thus honouring him on [Col. 0517B] earth, that you may deserve to be honoured in heaven by him whose minister he is.

Given as in the other letter.

The same was written, in the same form, to the noble man, Duke of Venice.

CCV [Note: [Col. 0517D] It is found in the Deeds of Innocent, § XCII. It is also printed [Col. 0518D] by Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 4. Variant readings are given.]. Instrument of agreement between the counts of Flanders, etc., the Marquis of Montferrat, and the Venetians. (In March, indiction VII.)

[In the name of the Lord, amen. We, B., Marquis of Montferrat, and Baldwin, Count of Flanders and Hainaut [Note: [Col. 0518D] In the Deeds, “of Hainaut”; in Raynaldus, “of Hannonia.”], L., Count of Blois and Clermont, and II., Count of Saint-Pol, on our own part, with you, illustrious man, Lord II. [Col. 0517C] Dandolo, Duke of Venice, Dalmatia, and Croatia, and with your party, in order that unity and firm concord may exist between us and to avoid every occasion of scandal, with the cooperation of him who is our peace and has made both one, have judged the following order to be observed, both parties being bound by oath, to his praise and glory.

First, invoking the name of Christ, we must attack the city with all armed force; and, if through the aid of divine power we enter the city, we must remain and proceed under the command of those chosen to lead the army, and follow them according to what shall be ordained. All the [Note: [Col. 0518D] Raynaldus: “all.”] property found in the city by anyone must be brought and placed in common in the place appointed. From that [Col. 0517D] property, however, three parts must be paid to you and the Venetian people, toward the property which Alexius, formerly emperor, was bound to pay you and us. We must retain the fourth part until we are equal in that payment. If anything remains, we must divide it equally [Col. 0518A] between you and us until you have been satisfied [Note: [Col. 0518D] The Deeds: *apagati*. Raynaldus judges that *placati*, “appeased,” should be read.]. But if there is less, so that it cannot suffice to pay the aforesaid debt, then, from whatever source property is first acquired, we must observe the said arrangement from it; saving, however, provisions, which must be kept and divided equally between yours and ours, so that each party may be suitably maintained from them. Whatever remains must be divided among the other property according to the arrangement already named.

You also, and the Venetian people, shall freely and absolutely, without any controversy, have throughout the whole empire all the honours and possessions which you formerly customarily possessed, in both spiritual and temporal matters, and all rights or customs, whether written [Col. 0518B] [Note: [Col. 0518D] The Constantinopolitan copy: “in writings.”] or unwritten.

Six men must also be chosen on your side and six on ours. Bound by oath, they must choose in the army the person whom they believe best knows how to hold—and best can hold—and best knows how to govern the land and empire for the honour of God, the holy Roman Church, and the empire; and, if they are unanimous, we must have as emperor the person whom they unanimously elect. But if six agree on one side and six on the other, a lot must be cast, and we must have as emperor the person on whom the lot falls. If more agree on one side than on the other, we shall have as emperor the person for whom the larger party agrees. But if there are more than two parties, he upon whom the largest party agrees shall be emperor.

[Col. 0518C] That emperor shall have the entire fourth part of the acquired empire, the palace of Blachernae, and the Bucca Leonis. The remaining three parts shall be divided equally between us and you. It should also be known [Note: [Col. 0518D] The Deeds: “is.”] that the clergy belonging to that party from which no emperor is elected shall have the power to arrange the Church of Holy Wisdom and elect a patriarch, for the honour of God, the holy Roman Church, and the empire. The clergy of each party must arrange those churches which fall to its party. From the possessions of the churches, provision must be made for as many clergy and churches, and to such an extent, that they may live and be supported honourably. The remaining possessions of the churches must be divided and apportioned [Col. 0518D] according to the arrangement stated above.

Moreover, both we and you must swear that from the last day of the coming month of March we shall remain for a full year to uphold the empire and emperor, for the honour of God, the holy Roman Church, and [Col. 0519A] the empire. Thereafter, all who remain in the empire must be bound to that emperor by oath according to good and reasonable custom; and those who then remain in the empire, as aforesaid, must swear that they will maintain firm and stable the shares and partitions which have been made.

It must also be known that twelve men, or more, are to be chosen on behalf of each of our parties; bound by oath, they must distribute fiefs and honours among men and assign the services which those men must perform for the emperor, as seems good and suitable to them. Each person must freely and absolutely possess the fief assigned to him from heir to heir, in both the male and female line, and have full power to do with it whatever he wishes, saving nevertheless the right and service of the emperor and empire. The emperor must perform the remaining services which are to be performed, apart from those performed by the holders of fiefs and honours, according to the order laid upon him.

It is further established that no person of any people which is engaged in a common war against you and your successors or against the Venetian people shall be received into the empire until that war has been brought to peace. Each party is also bound in good faith to make every effort to obtain this from the Lord Pope: that, if anyone should attempt to act against this ordinance, he shall be bound by the bond of excommunication.

Moreover, the emperor must swear that he will hold firm and stable, irrevocably, the partitions and grants that have been made, according to the order set out above [Col. 0519C] [Note: [Col. 0519D] The Constantinopolitan copy: “the order stated above.”]. But if anything in all these matters is to be added or diminished, it shall lie within the power and discretion of you and your six counsellors, and of the lord marquis and his six counsellors. It must also be known that you, aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0519D] The Deeds and Raynaldus: “aforesaid.”] lord duke, are not obliged to swear to the emperor who is elected, or to the empire, to perform any services by reason of any grant, fief, or honour which ought to be assigned to you. Nevertheless, the person or persons whom you appoint in your place concerning what is assigned to you must be bound by oath to render every service to the emperor and empire [Col. 0519D] according to the whole arrangement declared above.

Given in the year of the Lord 1204, in the month of March, in the seventh indiction.]

CCVI [Note: [Col. 0519D] A portion of this letter may be read in the *Deeds of Innocent*, § XCVII. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets. Raynaldus provides fragments of the same letter under the year 1205, § 9. We have marked these by a double quotation mark placed in the margin at the beginning of each line [Col. 0520D].] TO THE NOBLE MAN . . . . . DOGE OF VENICE. He replies to his request that the agreements concluded between the French and Venetians be confirmed. (At St Peter’s, 29 January.)

[When your beloved sons, [Col. 0520A] L. and [Note: [Col. 0520D] Omitted in the *Deeds*.] A., noble citizens of Venice and your envoys, came to the Apostolic See, we received them kindly and carefully heard what they took care to set before us in our presence. Standing before us, therefore, they asserted that certain agreements had been harmoniously concluded between you and the Venetians on the one hand, and our dearest son in Christ, B., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, and the French on the other. They requested that, lest anyone presume to violate them, the Apostolic See should prohibit this under penalty of excommunication, so that whoever should thereafter act against them would be subject to sentence of excommunication.

But, after careful deliberation with our brethren concerning this first petition, we found three matters wholly contrary to the petition itself. For this chapter is expressly set out in the agreements themselves: that ecclesiastical possessions are to be divided between the Venetians and the French, with a portion reserved for the clergy from which they may be honorably maintained. Certainly, “ [Note: [Col. 0520D] This passage is found in Raynaldus.] since a violent hand has plundered the treasures of churches not without offence to the Creator, those who mutilated churches already stripped of their treasures by taking their possessions would incur a greater guilt; nor would it be fitting for the Apostolic See to defend in this way persons who thus offend ecclesiastical dignity. Moreover, since agreements of this kind were concluded for the honour of the Roman Church, and in almost every chapter it was stated that everything should accrue to its honour, we neither ought nor were able to confirm what, contrary to the oath jointly sworn by both parties, would derogate from the honour of the Apostolic See [Col. 0520C].” [Note: [Col. 0520D] Raynaldus ends here.]

Furthermore, since authority to add or remove provisions has been conferred upon you and six of your counsellors, and upon the noble man . . . marquis of Montferrat and six of his counsellors, how could we place our sentence at the discretion of laymen, so that those should incur a sentence of excommunication who did not observe lay enactments unknown to us and perhaps hostile to the sacred canons? And since our beloved son T., the elect of Constantinople, is soon to come to Constantinople, nothing concerning the possessions of the Church of Constantinople ought, before his arrival, to have been disposed of by laymen or confirmed by us, where this could redound to injury of his right and loss to his Church.] [Col. 0520D]

Secondly, the same envoys humbly requested us on your behalf that, since you are worn out by old age and broken by exertion, we would deem it fitting to absolve you from the vow of pilgrimage which you had undertaken, since nevertheless you are willing and able effectively to procure the sailing of an army of those signed with the cross for the aid of the Holy Land. “We therefore [Note: [Col. 0520D] Raynaldus again.], considering that the prudent probity, the keenness of vigorous intellect, and the mature soundness of counsel which you possess will in future be of great benefit to the Christian army—since the aforesaid emperor and the crusaders greatly extol your zeal and diligence, and men especially trust in your discernment—have not thought fit at present to grant such a petition. Otherwise someone might blame us if, on this occasion, the army prepared for the aid of the Holy Land were dissolved; or someone might reproach you because you had not taken up the cross in the service of the Crucified One, if, after avenging the injury done to you and yours, you did not avenge the affront to Jesus Christ, and, after defeating your own enemies, neglected to defeat the enemies of the faith.

But if, as we believe, the crusaders intend still to defer the plan of pilgrimage and to remain longer in the regions of Romania in order to consolidate the empire, we shall give further thought to your condition and to the need of the army, [Col. 0521B] and, God granting, shall decide what appears expedient.” [Note: [Col. 0521D] Raynaldus ends here.]

We therefore admonish your nobility, exhort you in the Lord, and command you through these apostolic letters: since until now you have served the world and have thereby attained no small glory, henceforth faithfully serve the Lord; give honour not to yourself but to his name; honour his ministers; and defend churches in their rights. Thus you may deserve to be defended and protected by him who leaves no good deed unrewarded and no evil unpunished. Know certainly that, so far as we can do so consistently with our honour, we shall effectively promote your honour.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 29 January [Col. 0521C].

CCVII. TO THE NOBLE MAN H., DOGE OF VENICE. He confirms his absolution. (At St Peter’s, 29 January.)

By your letters you informed us that, by the command of our beloved son P., cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, you and your people obtained the benefit of absolution. We therefore, giving credit to those letters, regard you and yours as absolved from the bond of excommunication; and, if the customary form of the Church was observed in your absolution, we hold it welcome and acceptable. Otherwise, we wish and command that what was lacking be supplied, lest in your person [Col. 0521D] we seem to have omitted anything which could hereafter be alleged to the prejudice of the Church. On this matter, however, we await more certain information from the reply of that cardinal.

CCVIII [Note: [Col. 0521] This letter is cited by Bzovius, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 106, § 4. See also Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 9.] TO B., ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He annuls the agreements insofar as they concern the division of ecclesiastical possessions. (At St Peter’s.)

How we judged it proper to proceed concerning the affair of our beloved son T., the elect of Constantinople, may become clearer to you from other letters which we sent to your imperial highness. But we have seen, from the written instrument of the agreements concluded between you and the pilgrims on the one hand, and the noble man H., the doge, and the Venetians on the other, and confirmed by oath—an instrument sealed with your seal and those of the noble men B., marquis of Montferrat, . . . count of Blois, and . . . count of St Paul, which we caused to be read before us—that certain agreements had been concluded which, if steadfastly observed, would gravely injure the Church of Constantinople and derogate from apostolic dignity. For the head cannot be without feeling the pain of the members, nor can the members fail to suffer with it when it suffers.

Therefore, desiring, as we are bound, to assist that Church, we have not thought fit to grant the petition which you procured to be presented to us for confirmation of those agreements. For they expressly contained [Col. 0522B] that ecclesiastical possessions must be divided between the French and the Venetians, with a portion reserved for the clergy from which they could be honourably supported. Since this could not be attempted without injury to the Creator, the oath sworn upon it plainly appears wholly unlawful and might rather be called perjury, unless, with the honour of the Apostolic See preserved, it had been rejected in that very oath.

Since, therefore, the honour of the Roman Church would not remain unimpaired if the Church of Constantinople, which is a special member of the Apostolic See, suffered loss through the mutilation of its possessions, we earnestly ask and admonish your serenity, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: in regard for him who raised you to the imperial dignity, hold his bride more earnestly commended to you; do not in any way proceed to divide her possessions, [Col. 0522C] and do not permit others to divide them. Thus, with that Church’s right preserved unharmed as is fitting, you may deserve from him, besides the heavenly reward, to be confirmed upon the imperial throne, whose bride you have taken care to honour. You ought to observe this all the more willingly because at your coronation you swore with greater devotion that you would uphold churches in their rights and defend them in their claims.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s.

In almost the same manner, to the noble man . . . doge of Venice, down to: we admonish you, and through apostolic letters strictly forbid you in the power of God to presume to proceed to the division of church possessions, or, so far as lies in your power, to permit it to be attempted by others. Otherwise, since we neither can nor ought to tolerate this patiently, we have firmly commanded the bishops and abbots in the Christian army at Constantinople to compel both you and all others who seek the division of ecclesiastical possessions, by ecclesiastical censure and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, to desist from such presumption; and, if it has been attempted, to cause it by the same coercive means to be restored to its former state [Col. 0523A].

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 8 February.

The same was written to the bishops and abbots concerning this matter.

Likewise to the noble men . . . marquis of Montferrat and all the counts of the Christian army.

CCIX [Note: [Col. 0523D] This letter was published by Angelus Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1205, chapter 11, § 10, vol. III, p. 445.] TO THE CHAPTER OF VIVIERS. Concerning the resignation made by their bishop and the holding of a new election. (At St Peter’s, 20 January.)

Moses, servant of the Lord, charged with the care and solicitude of the whole people of Israel, because he could not bear the labour alone, chose from all the people of Israel men who feared God and made them rulers of the people, and tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifties, and tens, so that, judging only easier cases, they might refer to Moses what was more serious and required punishment. In like manner, the vicar of Jesus Christ, having received in Peter the fullness of ecclesiastical power and having the solicitude of all churches laid upon him, summoned certain persons to share his solicitude, reserving to his own judgment matters difficult for himself, so that he might better attend to things pertaining to God.

Yet because it often happens that those appointed to govern and correct others grievously offend, furnish others with occasion for wrongdoing, and the cry of their iniquity rises to his ears, while he cannot himself descend and see, he sends his angels to uproot and destroy vices, and to build and plant virtues, obedient to the head as members are. We therefore, though unworthy, summoned by the Lord’s ordering to such a burden, desiring to perform the duty of our office, having learned that the province of Vienne and certain others are infected with the rough rust of long-standing corruption, judged that our beloved sons Brother R. and Brother P. of Castronovo, monks of Fontfroide and legates of the Apostolic See, should be sent to them, so that in our place they might correct what needed correction and establish what they knew should be ordered according to God.

They, as they informed us by their letters, coming to your church [Col. 0523D] in order, according to the tenor of our mandate, to correct what needed correction both in head and members, with appeal set aside, received a bodily oath from your former bishop . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0523D] Who was then bishop of Viviers is not sufficiently established. The incomplete succession of Viviers bishops given by the authors of the old *Gallia Christiana* (vol. III, p. 1182), based on documents, mentions Nicholas from 1177 to 1198. Colom., *On the Bishops of Viviers*, seems to acknowledge the same man down to 1202. The documents are silent from 1202 to 1206; nor is the name of Berno or Burno, whom the same authors of the old *Gallia Christiana* immediately place after Nicholas (loc. cit.), read before 1206. Yet the most learned author of the *History of Occitania* seems to think Nicholas is meant here (*History of Languedoc*, vol. II, p. 242).] from you and from the clergy of the city, that both you and they would tell the whole truth concerning the offences of that bishop and yourselves.

Then, when certain of your canons had alleged many grave charges against that bishop, and a considerable part of them was established both by his own confession and by the testimony of sworn witnesses, our venerable brother, the . . . . . archbishop of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0524D]

The authors of the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 802, report very little concerning the archbishops of Vienne around the period with which we are concerned.

LXVII. Aynard received a rescript confirming privileges of immunity from Emperor Henry in 1196, at Turin, 29 July, in the presence of Annon, archbishop of Tarentaise, and Angelo, archbishop of Taranto.

LXVIII. Humbert II, having professed religion in the Carthusian house of Cellion near Bourg, was raised to the summit of the pontificate; he is mentioned in the *History of the Antonines* under 1208 and in a diploma of Frederick under 1214.] came to your church and humbly asked the legates not to direct their purpose toward deposition, but rather toward the bishop’s resignation. Considering that this would better serve the welfare of the Church of Viviers, since the said bishop was powerful and noble, the whole bishopric might be endangered by his power and burdened by him with heavy expenses, and he might prolong the case at length, not without serious loss to ecclesiastical propriety, they judged the requests of the aforesaid bishop should be admitted. The bishop himself, assenting to their counsel, resigned his see, while the pontifical office was reserved to him.

After he resigned, when you wished to assemble in chapter to elect a pastor for yourselves, they took care, by apostolic authority, to forbid you to proceed with an election until our letters should make known that we had approved that bishop’s resignation. Like prudent and discerning men, they reserved grave matters to the judgment of the Apostolic See, since no bishop can resign either his place or office without the special permission of the Apostolic See. But because the absence of a pastor is known to threaten your church with no small danger, lest the tyrants of that land be able freely to rage against that church’s patrimony, they humbly asked us to deem it fitting to grant you a suitable man as pastor.

We therefore commend in the Lord their diligence and zeal for righteousness, ratify what they did concerning his resignation for the benefit of your church, and command your whole body by apostolic letters: having God alone before your eyes, with the counsel of our aforesaid legates, within eight days unanimously and canonically elect as bishop [Col. 0525A] a suitable man who both wishes and is able not so much to preside as to be of service. Otherwise, by these letters we command our same legates henceforth, appeal set aside, to appoint over you a suitable person as pastor. Opponents, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 20 January, in the seventh year.

CCX [Note: [Col. 0525D] This letter was published by Angelus Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1205, chapter 1, § 3, vol. III, p. 443; but his text abounds in some errors.] TO BROTHER P. OF CASTRONOVO, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. Concerning the patient and vigorous discharge of his legation. (At St Peter’s, 26 January.)

[The duty of charity, which does not seek its own interests, requires that one who embraces Rachel by ascending the mirror of contemplation should not, at a moment of need, refuse the embrace of Leah, though bleary-eyed, by undertaking the burdens of action. For although Rachel is beautiful, Leah is useful on account of the grace of children, bringing benefit and advancement both to herself and to others.

Although the repose of Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, is preferred to Martha’s service because that state is safer, being removed from worldly tumult, nevertheless the active life may be judged more useful, because, benefiting itself and others, it endures tribulations and pressures through which virtues gain increase. For, as the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, tested character; tested character, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5). And it often happens that, just as virtue is perfected in weakness and affliction gives understanding to the ear, so it grows lukewarm through tranquillity. For he ceases to be Abel whom Cain does not assail; and David, whom wars had not overcome, was overcome by leisure.

Therefore, since necessity has required us temporarily to call you away from the repose of contemplation which you had chosen, so that, sent into ministry, you may act as legate for us—or rather, for Christ—and entreat those to be reconciled to the Lord whose minds the angel of darkness has blinded and made alien to the thought of the true light, you ought not to refuse the labour, even though the people to whom you have been sent appears hard and incorrigible; for the Lord is able to raise children of Abraham from stones. Even if you have not yet advanced among that people according to your wish, you may nevertheless expect no lesser reward, because God rewards not success but labour, as Scripture attests: “God will render the reward of the labours of his saints,” promising a reward for labour, not for success. Hence the Apostle does not glory that he advanced more than all others, but that he laboured more than all others.

Since, therefore, we firmly hope in the Lord, whose office it is to grant increase, that he will give success to your labour, we admonish your devotion, exhort you in the Lord, and command you through apostolic letters to fulfil zealously the work of an evangelist [Col. 0526A] and the ministry committed to you: be urgent in season and out of season, rebuking, entreating, and reproving in all patience and teaching; firmly hope in the Lord Jesus Christ that he who gave you the desire to labour will also grant, lest your labour be reckoned useless, its effect and success.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 26 January.]

CCXI. TO THE ABBOT OF CLUNY [Note: [Col. 0525D] See letter 174 of Book Six, note.] He grants him authority to correct, according to God and the Rule of St Benedict, matters requiring correction in abbeys belonging to the monastery of Cluny. (At St Peter’s, 29 January.)
