The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant, etc., down to “inclined”; following the example of our predecessor Pope Celestine of happy memory, [Col. 0526B] we grant you by the authority of these presents free authority, with contradiction and appeal ceasing, in the abbeys belonging to the monastery of Cluny to correct whatever you see needs correction according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the statutes of the order, and there to establish what ought to be established. We also hold valid and firm any sentence which you judge should be canonically pronounced against the contumacious and rebellious, and, with God as author, shall cause it to be observed inviolably. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this page of our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 29 January, in the seventh year.

CCXII [Note: [Col. 0525D]

This letter is cited by Bzovius, *Annals*, [Col. 0526D] vol. XIII, § 10.

See also Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 57.

It was published in full by Angelus Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1205, chapter 8, § 5, vol. III, p. 443, though not free from some errors.] TO THE KING OF THE FRENCH. Concerning the extirpation of heretics. (At St Peter’s, 7 February.)

[Col. 0526C]

So that the people of Israel might not go up to Jerusalem to pray to the Lord, Jeroboam son of Nebat set up a golden calf at Bethel for worship, building a shrine and an altar on the high places, and compelling the aforesaid people to sin. When, in accordance with the invention of his heart, he had held a festival for the children of Israel and had gone up upon the altar to burn incense, at the word of the Lord a man of God came to him in order to call him back from such wickedness. But because, warned by the prophet, he would not correct what he had done, the Lord later raised up the spirit of Josiah, king of Judah, who utterly destroyed the altar Jeroboam had made [Col. 0526D] at Bethel and entirely cut down the grove he had planted.

Imitating Jeroboam’s footsteps, certain sons of Belial—though they are ravening wolves—have entered your kingdom in sheep’s clothing. In order that the people reborn in the font of baptism may put off Jesus Christ, whom they put on in baptism itself, and may no longer ascend to Jerusalem, they establish the calf at Bethel—that is, in those whom the Lord had inhabited—worshipping it through perverse teaching. As though an altar had been erected in pride upon the high places, [Col. 0527A] they sacrifice upon it Christ’s sheep, which they draw out of the sheepfold.

We therefore, compassionating them with paternal affection and wishing, as pertains to our office, to call them back from darkness to light, judged that our beloved sons, the abbot of Cîteaux [Note: [Col. 0527D] See letter 16 of Book Five, note.], P. and R., monks of Fontfroide and legates of the Apostolic See, should be sent to them with the word of the Lord, so that, pressing them in season and out of season, they might rebuke, entreat, and reprove them in all patience and teaching.

But, as the said legates informed us by their letters, they by no means receive sound doctrine. Instead, with itching ears they heap up teachers for themselves according to their desires and turn their hearing away from the truth; and they rage all the more freely in Christ’s sheepfold because they do not fear that their right ear will be cut off, since, standing outside the Lord’s sheepfold, they do not fear the sword which Peter himself wields. Since, therefore, those who rend the seamless garment of Jesus Christ are worse than Pilate’s soldiers, who did not presume to tear that tunic, and, like asps, stop their ears lest they wisely hear the voices of enchanters, it is fitting that the secular sword of power, borne by kings and princes for the punishment of evildoers, be drawn to avenge the Saviour’s injury; and that he who belongs to the Lord gird his sword upon his thigh, so that with Josiah he may hasten to overthrow the altar wickedly erected by Jeroboam and cut down the grove planted contrary to the Lord’s prohibition.

Therefore, so that you may not seem to bear without cause the sword which the Lord, from whom all power comes, entrusted to you, but may show that you sympathize with the suffering head, you ought, taking up arms and shield, to plead God’s cause by the sword against those who, with tails bound together like little foxes, have begun to burn the harvests in the kingdom of France while fighting as children against their mother. We therefore admonish your royal serenity, exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of your sins: if it can be done, rise powerfully against the aforesaid beasts, either in person, through our dearest son in Christ Louis, your son, or through another suitable man; as a Catholic son embrace with the arms of sincerity the king’s daughter standing at the bridegroom’s right hand, clothed round with variety [Col. 0527D]; and demonstrate this by deed, compelling counts and barons, by the power divinely entrusted to you, to confiscate their goods and proscribe their persons.

Since those whom a crime defiles it makes equal, and an error which is not resisted is approved, so that equal punishment may be inflicted upon perpetrators and those who consent, do not hesitate, if any counts, barons, or even citizens refuse to expel from their land such perverters of sound doctrine, or presume to receive or support them, to confiscate their goods and annex their entire land to the royal demesne [Col. 0528A]. Moreover, so that the failure of the spiritual sword may receive support from the material sword, let your royal highness powerfully furnish aid and favour to the aforesaid legates. Thus, besides the glory and honour you will obtain among men from so commendable a work, you may deserve to obtain the pardon of sins which we have judged should be granted to those going to assist the Holy Land.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 7 February, in the seventh year.

CCXIII. TO THE . . . . . BISHOP OF TOURNai [Note: [Col. 0527D] Goswin, archdeacon of Tournai, succeeded Stephen in 1203 and died [Col. 0528D] in 1218. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 216.] He exhorts him and grants him authority to restrain clerical offences. (At St Peter’s, 7 February.)

[Col. 0528B] A pastor’s care ought to be diligent, so that there may be no diseased sheep in the flock entrusted to him through which contagion threatens the whole flock; for, when blood touches blood and curtain draws curtain, evil often proceeds from evil, and virtue receives increase from virtue. We have learned that many clerics in your diocese are notorious for various offences: some pursue usury or disgraceful gain; some do not fear to commit adultery; some publicly keep concubines in their houses; and some commit many other acts contrary to clerical honour.

Therefore, lest you be judged a hireling by him whose flock has been entrusted to your care if that flock appears stained through your negligence when you are bound to cleanse it of stain, by the authority of these presents we command your brotherhood to show yourself such in correcting these offences that you may be proved prudent in your office. Moreover, so that you may carry out the apostolic command more fully, we grant you by the authority of these presents the power to restrain, by ecclesiastical censure, those who rashly set themselves against you in this matter. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe our concession, etc.

Given, etc., as in the other letter.

CCXIV. TO THE SAME [Note: [Col. 0528D] See the preceding letter, note.] Authority to perform church dedications on Sundays as well as on ordinary days. (At St Peter’s, 7 February.)

Your brotherhood requested to know from us whether it is lawful for you [Col. 0528D] to celebrate dedications of churches on Sundays as well as on ordinary days. We briefly reply that you are permitted in your diocese to perform dedications for churches on Sundays as well as on ordinary days.

Given, etc., as in the other letter.

CCXV. TO N. . . . . . . . . . (The address is lacking.) He commits the case pending between the Brothers of the Hospital of Jerusalem and the abbess of St Mary of Angers concerning an almshouse. (At St Peter’s, 8 February.)

The beloved sons, the Brothers of the Hospital [Col. 0529A] of Jerusalem, informed us that, after an appeal to us had been lodged, their beloved daughter in Christ, the . . . . . abbess of St Mary of Angers, caused them to be despoiled by secular force of an almshouse which they had acquired through the gift of R., king of England of good memory, and had peacefully possessed for some time; and that she unlawfully retained it under occupation. We therefore wrote in the following form to our beloved sons, the . . . . . chancellor, the . . . . . archdeacon, and the provost of Armeliac, of Chartres: if the matter stood thus, they were to cause that house, with the fruits received from it, to be restored by means of justice to the named brothers, every unlawful possessor being removed, through ecclesiastical censure and with the obstacle of appeal removed; and they were to restore to its former state whatever they found rashly undertaken after the appeal to us had been lawfully lodged.

But since we judged that the proceedings of the aforesaid judges should be annulled, because, after the appeal to us had been lawfully lodged, they proceeded without joinder of issue, we have committed that case to you by common consent of the parties. Through apostolic letters we command you, after summoning the parties and fully hearing and examining the arguments made on both sides, to bring the same case, appeal set aside, to its due conclusion, causing, etc. Witnesses, etc. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. And if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 8 February.

CCXVI. TO THE . . . . . BISHOP OF AVRANCHES [Note: [Col. 0529D] William III de Tollermen then presided over the Church of Avranches. His election, first annulled by Innocent in the second year of his pontificate, had subsequently been confirmed. He died in 1210. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 483.], AND THE ABBOTS OF . . . . . MONTMOREL [Note: [Col. 0529D] Tualdus, mentioned in 1200, succeeded Radulf, founder and abbot of the monastery of Montmorel, for seven years, according to the necrology recording his death on 27 August. The same work, ibid., col. 557.], AND LUCERNE [Note: [Col. 0529D] Ansgotus governed the monastery of Lucerne for forty-nine years, from 1157 until 1206, when, on the vigil of the Apostles Simon and Jude, he resigned of his own free will. See *Gallia Christiana*, ibid., col. 557.], IN THE DIOCESE OF AVRANCHES. He commits to them for examination the case pending between the prior and canons of St Barbara on one side, and W., chamberlain of Tankerville in the diocese of Rouen, on the other, concerning Mainerius of Montville. (At St Peter’s, 10 February.)

[Col. 0529C]

From the representation of our beloved sons, the . . . . prior [Note: [Col. 0529D]

Concerning the priors of St Barbara (in Auge), during the period in question, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, ibid., col. 859, provide only the following scant information.

IV. Walter had a dispute with Lisiard, bishop of Sées, and with the abbot of Troarn, concerning the abbey of Conches, about 1195. He died on 18 April.

V. William II, a hermit, is recorded in 1209 and 1210. He died on 29 January.] and canons of St Barbara, you are to know that, when a dispute concerning Mainerius of Montville was pending between them on one side and W., chamberlain of Tankerville in the diocese of Rouen, on the other, before a . . . ordinary judge, not our delegate [Col. 0530A], and the same chamberlain appealed from that judge to our hearing without setting any term for his appeal, the said ordinary, who seemed secretly to favour the chamberlain’s case because a certain cleric, his table-companion, had been advocate for the said chamberlain in that case, deceitfully and contrary to custom set this term for the appeal: that by the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary both parties should have returned from prosecuting the appeal.

Yet he could not impose a rule upon us requiring us to decide the matter within the stated term, since, according to lawful enactments, a suit expected to be brought before the prince’s consistory should remain untouched, without harm from delay, until he causes it to be introduced and determined by the great men in accordance with custom. Meanwhile, the envoy of the aforesaid chamberlain, arriving before their envoy and not even waiting for him until the lawful term, procured letters and departed.

Since fraud and deceit ought not to benefit anyone, through apostolic letters we command your discretion: if this is so, summon the parties, hear the arguments advanced on either side, and determine the case concerning these matters, appeal set aside, upon oath, causing what you decree to be firmly observed. Witnesses, etc. No letters, etc. And if not all . . . you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 10 February, in the seventh year.

CCXVII [Note: [Col. 0530D] It is found among the Decretals, Book II, title 30, “On useful or useless confirmation,” chapter 6. Various readings are given.] TO THE . . . . . ABBOT OF MOLÈSME [Note: [Col. 0530D] Gaucher, also Galcher, abbot of Molèsme, first ruled for five years from about 1188; deposed thereafter, he resigned in 1191 or 1192. Later made prior of St Quentin, he was finally appointed again after Odo and governed for twelve years and three months from about 1197, resigning in 1209. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 735. See also letter 237 of Book Six and its note.] Concerning letters of confirmation. (At St Peter’s, 9 February.)

[Col. 0530C]

[The petition presented to us on your behalf stated that several of your monks who preside over priories [Note: In the Decretals, “and other administrations” is added, and shortly afterwards the word “priories” is omitted.] assert that they have obtained from us letters of confirmation concerning possession of those priories for life. Under cover of these letters they alienate and consume the goods of those priories, asserting that they are in no respect subject to you in regard to those priories [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals, as are shortly afterwards the words “to your discretion.”]. Since we do not believe that such letters have issued from our chancery, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you punish as authors of forgery those who produce such letters [Col. 0531A], in which priories [Note: The Decretals add “or administrations,” and thereafter read “religious”; below, “of their religious order” for “of the prior or monk.”] are confirmed to them as monks. But if no mention is made in them of a priory or monastic status, you are to declare that they have no force, as having been fraudulently obtained by suppression of the truth.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of February.

CCXVIII. [Note: This letter is cited by Raynaldus under the year 1205, §68. It was published in full by Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercian Order*, under the year 1207, chapter 4, §3, vol. III, p. 478; he says it was sent to him from the Vatican Archives. But it is not easy to understand how it was assigned in his copy to the ninth year of Innocent’s pontificate, when the Registers expressly say that it was issued in the seventh year. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* also printed it, vol. IV, documentary no. 111, col. 197.] TO THE PRIOR [Note: For Guy, alternatively Viard, founder and first prior of Vallis-Caulium, who was still in office in 1213, see new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 742.] AND BRETHREN OF VALLIS-CAULIUM. He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter. (At Saint Peter’s, 10 February.)

“It is customary to grant,” etc., down to “bestow.” From the letters of our venerable brother G. [Note: See letter 116 of book VII.] elect of Reims, we have learned that, while he was passing through the diocese of Langres, he found that you at Vallis-Caulium [Col. 0531B] had undertaken a new institution of an order. Having carefully investigated its merits, he found in it nothing but what was religious and honourable. For he found, as those same letters stated, that among you one of the monks, whom you monk-brethren elect, is to be prior; that all of you—both monks and lay brothers, whose community is not to exceed twenty persons—are to take care to render to him reverence and obedience as to a spiritual father; that none of you is to possess private property; that every day Mass and the canonical hours are to be sung in the convent; that those who wish may also celebrate private Masses; that you are to hold chapter daily and perform the twelve readings at the appointed seasons; that you are to work together and eat together in the refectory, using neither meat nor [Col. 0531C] animal fat. The prior is to eat with you in the same refectory, content with the same food and clothing.

From the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection until the Exaltation of the Holy Cross you are to eat twice daily; during the remainder of the year you are to observe the abstinence of fasts, content on Fridays with bread, water, and one cooked dish. You are not to fast on the Nativity of the Lord, nor on a Friday in summer when a feast of twelve readings occurs. You are to live from revenues and preserve silence. Women are not to enter the inner enclosure, nor are you to go beyond the outer enclosure, except for the prior, unless an affair of the order requires it. Yet if the prior is occupied or ill, and urgent necessity or evident usefulness demands it, he may send whichever one he wishes. You are to wear hair-shirts next to the flesh, without compelling those unable to bear them; you are never to wear linen or hempen garments, but garments of coarse undyed wool and furs. All are to sleep in tunics, belts, and hose; and, in addition, you monk-brethren, wearing cowls, are nowhere and never to rest upon mattresses. Your novices are to remain on probation for a year; and you monk-brethren are to devote yourselves to reading, prayer, and contemplation from Matins until the hour for work and from Vespers until sunset, except those whom the prior’s judgment considers should be withdrawn for some definite and necessary reason [Col. 0532B].

Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under our protection the persons of yourselves and the place in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all that you now reasonably possess or may hereafter acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, etc., down to “we receive”; and we specifically confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of the present document, the order itself, established by provident deliberation with the assent of the diocesan bishop. Therefore let no one, etc. Let no one violate this page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the seventh year.

CCXIX. [Note: This letter is found, though very mutilated, among the Decretals, book III, title 21, “On Pledges and Other Securities,” chapter 5. What is there printed is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] … TO THE BISHOP OF AQUINO. [Note: 

Ughellus gives very little concerning the bishops of Aquino at about this time: *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 443.

“XIV. Gregory, a Florentine, monk of the Order of Vallombrosa, abbot of Saint John and close relative of Gualbert, was elected bishop by Pope Celestine III about the year of the Lord 1194. He governed the church of Aquino with great reputation for prudence; his death occurred on the second day of February.

“XV. Gregory succeeded Gregory while he was a monk and dean of Monte Cassino, in the reign of Innocent III, in 1206; and, as he himself says in a certain diploma dated at the Lateran on the Kalends of April, when he was confined to bed by a severe illness, he could not himself ordain the same Gregory of Cassino, as he had wished, but arranged for him to be consecrated on the seventh day of Holy Week, Easter Day itself, by the cardinal bishop of Ostia.”]

He decides a dispute between R. of San Giorgio and R., a woman of San Germano. (At Saint Peter’s, 12 February.)

[Col. 0532C]

[From the letters of your brotherhood we have learned that, when [Note: In the Decretals this is absent, as are shortly afterwards the words “of San Giorgio.” They read “A.” in place of “R.”; below they omit “of San Germano” and have “we have thought fit” for “we had thought fit.”] we had thought fit to commit to you the case pending between R. of San Giorgio and R., a woman of San Germano,] you had endeavoured for nearly two years to bring the same case to an end by agreement. Since the parties did not acquiesce, you summoned prudent men, examined the merits of the said case more diligently, and [Col. 0533A], on the advice of prudent men, thought fit to refer the matter to our presence, especially because it appeared to belong particularly to royal jurisdiction.

[For it was clearly proved [Note: Absent from the Decretals, as are below the words “R., count of Caserta, then.”] that, because of a crime committed by the husband of the said woman, when he had taken flight, both the husband’s aforesaid brother, namely R., and the woman herself were arrested—though less justly—by R., count of Caserta, then royal justiciar. By his order all the offender’s goods were sold off, and money was paid [Note: The Decretals omit this word, and below “By … aforesaid.”] to the merchant whom the husband of the said woman had wounded and stripped of his own possessions. The sale of those goods was carried out by the aforesaid R., but by order of the aforesaid justiciar; yet certain estates remained with that same [Col. 0533B] R., the woman’s brother-in-law [Note: The Decretals read *remanserant* (“had remained”) for *mulieris sororium* (“the woman’s brother-in-law”; probably an uncertain or corrupt reading); below they omit the words “firmly … that.”], which R. retained by order of the court, after money had been paid for them to the merchant, because, as he says, no other purchaser was available owing to the small size of the estates.

The woman’s side firmly alleged that, since a dowry takes precedence over all creditors and all the husband’s goods were pledged to the woman on account of her dowry, she ought not, being blameless in this matter, to lose her dowry. For this reason she urgently sought to have its value [Note: The Decretals read *dotis* (“of the dowry”), and shortly afterwards *restitui* (“restored”) for *conferri* (“assigned”).] assigned to her, or to be put, by virtue of the delegated office, into possession of the estates that had belonged to her husband], asserting that her husband’s guilt ought by no law to harm her. The husband’s side, however, replied to the contrary that he ought not in any way answer her concerning these matters, because nothing had been sold from the goods of the woman’s husband by his will or authority; rather, the treasury had caused them to be seized and ordered them sold, which he proved by witnesses’ testimony.

Now, since the woman’s side said that certain estates of her husband remained unsold and sought satisfaction for herself from them, you diligently inquired of both parties how much money had been paid to the merchant. From the confession of each party it became clear to you that immovable property had been alienated up to the value of twenty-four ounces of gold; but the aforesaid R. said that he had added eighteen ounces to those twenty-four and had thus made up for the merchant a total of forty-two ounces of gold. The said [Col. 0534A] R. also alleged that, since there were five sons of one father and all succeeded to the paternal goods, once the entire inheritance had been valued, the woman’s husband’s share of his paternal inheritance did not amount to more than twenty-four ounces of gold.

But because the case sent to us had not been sufficiently prepared, because it was not established for us whether the woman had given as dowry the ten pounds of *tarenes* [Note: A kind of Saracen coin used by Sicilians, as Alberic notes in his *Lexicon of Law*. Leo of Ostia also mentions it, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book II, chapter 74: “And, having been given a thousand *tarenes* by the abbot, he returned to Aversa to his father-in-law.” The same, book III, chapter 57: “Six hundred Byzantine coins and two thousand African *tarenes*.” The same, book IV, chapter 99: “He renewed for the monastery the privilege concerning remission of fifty [Col. 0534D] *tarenes*.” Innocent himself, book I, letter 257, confirms the statute of the Beneventans that judges are to receive as salary no more than a twentieth part of the suit, and that for subscribing wills or other contracts judges are not to receive from citizens more than two *tarenes*, nor notaries more than one.] which she claimed, or whether the same R. possessed anything from goods belonging to his brother, the husband of the said woman; and because we could not proceed with examination of the case, both because, as you say, allegations and proofs had been renounced before you and because suitable and adequate representatives had not appeared before us, we have thought fit to refer the same [Col. 0534B] case to your examination, commanding you by apostolic letters [“we command,” Note: The Decretals read *mandamus*.] that, if from what has been alleged and proved before you it is established that the woman gave her husband as dowry the amount she states and that the aforesaid R. possesses some goods of his brother, then, since women are owed much favour in recovering dowries and the law has also provided that a woman ought not be left without a dowry because of her husband’s wrongdoing, and since the husband’s goods, being tacitly pledged to the wife for her dowry, pass with their burden to any possessor, you are, all appeal set aside, to condemn the aforesaid R. to restore the dowry to that woman, to the extent that he is known to possess goods of his aforesaid [Col. 0534C] brother.]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of February.

CCXX. … TO THE BISHOP OF ELY [Note: These persons have already been discussed often.] … TO THE BISHOP OF NORWICH [Note: These persons have already been discussed often.], AND … TO THE BISHOP OF SAINT ASAPH [Note: Adam, bishop of St Asaph—of whom Gerald of Wales speaks in the tract *On His Own Deeds*, book I, chapter 6, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 471—died at Oxford in 1180. He appears to have been succeeded by a certain Reiner, who lived until 1220. Godwin, *On the Prelates of England*, p. 635.]. That they are to determine the matrimonial case pending between the daughter of the prince of the Isles and the prince of North Wales [Note: See letter 47 of book VI and our notes upon it.] (At Saint Peter’s, 17 February.)

When formerly the beloved son, the nobleman … prince of North Wales, had humbly requested us to permit him to marry the daughter of the nobleman … prince of the Isles, whom he asserted that he had betrothed, notwithstanding that she had been affianced within marriageable years to his … paternal uncle [Col. 0535A], although neither of them had taken her in marriage, we entrusted the determination of the case under a specified form to the bishop of Man of good memory and to the beloved sons … archdeacon and … prior of the Isle of Glannav [Note: See letter 233 of book II.]. When the parties appeared before the said judges, as they reported to us by their letters, it was clearly established by his witnesses that, after completing eight years, the said girl had been betrothed by L., prince of North Wales, with the consent both of herself and of her parents. But while necessity delayed him from taking her in marriage, L.’s paternal uncle afterwards betrothed her without the consent of L. himself and of his parents; and, without carnally knowing her, he entered upon the way of all flesh.

The said judges, therefore, after consulting prudent men, granted by apostolic authority to the said prince of North Wales that he might marry the same girl, lest discord formerly arisen and then stilled between him and the girl’s parents should arise again. Desiring their judgment to obtain due force unless some reasonable obstacle stood in the way, we instructed the beloved sons … abbot of Abingdon, … prior of Henley, and Master M., canon of Burlington in the diocese of Bangor [Note: See the letter of book VI, no. 47, already cited above.], to cause it to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside. Yet the said abbot and his fellow judges, because of the condition expressed in our letters, took pains, as we saw contained in their letters, carefully and diligently to investigate the truth concerning that marriage by receiving [Col. 0535C] witnesses.

Having held four productions of witnesses and reduced their depositions to writing, they took care, with the consent of both parties, to send us what they thought sufficient for deciding the case, so that the truth of the matter might become clear to us and provision might be made for the conscience of the aforesaid prince. He said that the earlier judges, especially the archdeacon and the prior, were ignorant of the law; that our letters had been obtained by a false suggestion; and that he did not believe he could be saved with the same girl, since she had been given as wife to his uncle and had repeatedly lain with him in one bed.

We therefore, after carefully examining the witnesses’ depositions, found by them proved [Col. 0535D] that L. had sworn that he would take the girl as his wife, but had neither taken her in marriage nor been proved by witnesses to have received a blessing with her or even to have been in the same land with her, since a middle sea divided their territories. We also saw contained in the judges’ records that sufficient testimony had proved before them that the girl was eight years old when L. had sworn that he would marry her. And because the girl’s father delayed taking his daughter to North Wales by the stipulated date, L., without any objection, married the sister of the nobleman … count of Chester about the end of that year; while his paternal uncle R. betrothed the girl [Col. 0536A] in question and, after a year, married her publicly in the face of the Church. From the beginning of May to the feast of Saint Vitus the martyr, whenever he wished, he lay with her in the same bed; and, after some time had elapsed, he returned to Wales.

Moreover, after the second year from the betrothal and the first from the wedding had passed, he returned to Man, peacefully cohabited with his wife, and took her with him by land and sea. But at last he left her in her parents’ care, returned to Wales, and there entered the way of all flesh. From the witnesses’ statements the aforesaid judges consequently inferred that R. had had the girl for three years and three months from the betrothal, but for two years, two months, and fifteen days [Col. 0536B] from the wedding.

There was, however, disagreement among the witnesses. Some inferred from the fact that the girl was then thin that she had not been carnally known, although she was of marriageable age and mature for the marriage-bed. Others said that they did not know whether she had been carnally known; others believed that she had not; and still others asserted that they had heard from R. himself that he had not carnally known her, though they added that they did not know whether he had afterwards been with her. Yet the said bishop of Man, as the writings of himself and his fellow judges appointed the second time showed, when his fellow judges were absent, learned under oath from the girl herself, her parents, nurse, and female attendants [Col. 0536C] that R. had not carnally known the girl.

After the uncle had entered the way of all flesh, L. asked the king of Man for his younger daughter in marriage, but could not obtain her because she had been joined to another. He subsequently married the oft-mentioned girl with the assent of the earlier judges. It is therefore established by the foregoing that between the said L. and the said girl—who was eight years old, though no expression of her consent is found—only a betrothal by words concerning the future had been celebrated before L.’s uncle contracted marriage with her. Thus L. had neither taken nor betrothed her, nor received a blessing with her; indeed, they had not even been together in the same land, because, as stated above, a middle sea divided their territories [Col. 0536D]. Hence it cannot be presumed that they attempted anything they could not consummate.

It is likewise established that the girl was betrothed to R. in her ninth year and taken in marriage by him in her tenth, and that she was frequently with him in one bed for more than two years. It is therefore plainly inferred that the first letters were obtained by false suggestion, since they state that neither man had taken her in marriage. Since they had been together in one bed for so long, the law presumes that they became one flesh; and because in her twelfth year, when in such a matter a girl possesses free and lawful [Col. 0537A] consent, she was voluntarily with him, it is clear that she lawfully consented to marriage with him and could not afterwards contract with his nephew. Therefore L. could not lawfully marry her; and, if after his uncle’s death he in fact joined her to himself, he must rightly be separated from her. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning those who should be summoned on this account, you determine the case according to the form set out above, disregarding appeal, causing, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March.

CCXXI. TO THE PRIOR [Note: William II, first prior of La Sesanne and then also of La Charité, is known from documents beginning in 1198. The name of his successor, Geoffrey, is not found before 1209. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, p. 407.] OF THE MONASTERY OF BLESSED MARY OF LA CHARITÉ, AND HIS BRETHREN. Confirmation of privileges and enumeration of all that belongs to them. (At Saint Peter’s, 16 February.)

[Col. 0537B]

Whenever something is sought from us with due devotion by our sons, whom for their religious life and honourableness we love with a special prerogative of charity, and which does not conflict with religion and honourableness, we ought to hasten all the more readily to grant what is requested, because it is more clearly fitting to the office entrusted to us. For, although unworthy, we bear the authority of the apostolic see; and thus we are obliged to provide for the welfare of all churches and to consider their peace with particular care, so that their rights may remain unimpaired and what has been done by our predecessors [Col. 0537C] may endure in firm and unshaken stability.

Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, after the example of our predecessors Urban, Paschal, Lucius, and Adrian of blessed memory, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the monastery of most blessed Mary, ever-virgin, of La Charité, in which by the Lord’s gift you serve, and strengthen it by the protection of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods, etc., down to “to be specified by name”:

In the bishopric of Auxerre: at Bonnay, the church of Saint Peter and Saint Aignan, with all its possessions and appurtenances; at Dommecy, those of Saint Mary and Saint Amator; at Balbigny, Saint Stephen’s; at Sept-Fonts, Saint Peter’s; at Conne, the church of Saint Aignan of Neuvy; at Poilly, Saint Peter’s; at Mézilles, Saint Julian’s; at Belou, Saint Martin’s; at Nargis, Saint Marcellus’s; at Varennes, Saint Martin’s; near Varennes, Saint Silvanus’s; at Dompierre, Saint Peter’s; at Moulins, Saint Martin’s; in the wood of Brittany, Saint Vincent’s; at Châteauneuf, Saint Symphorian’s; at Sully, Saint Symphorian’s near Sully; at Les Brévires, Saints Germanus and Aignan; at Magny, Saint Peter’s; [Col. 0538A] at Aunay, Saint Mary’s; at Cren, Saint Stephen’s; at Coulanges-sur-Yonne, Saint Mary’s church of Curcum; at Nannay, Saint Simeon’s; at Anlezy, Saint Saturninus’s; at Festigny, Saint Cyricus’s; the church of Vi-Saint-Étienne; at Menou, Saint Martin’s; at Celles, Saint Julian’s.

In the diocese of Nevers: the church of Saint Aignan at Albigny, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Sulpicius at La Chapelle-sur-Loire; at Parigny, Saint Victor’s of Nevers; at Biches, Jancourt, Saint-Sulpice, Beaumont, Roi, Patinges, Montigny, Sauvigny, Cercy, Coulanges, and above the castle of Cercy.

In the archbishopric of Bourges: the church of Monastel, with its borough and all its appurtenances; Sainte-Montagne; Argent, whose castle and other property lie in the monks’ land; at Parigny, the churches of Saint Celsus, with its borough and all appurtenances; Champ-Faraud; Saint-Florent; Civray; likewise, Brou; Valençay; Bardais; Zançay; Ulmes; Fontenay; the castle of Saint-Cyr; Blec; Neruda; Pera; Berry; the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Martin; at Montfaucon, Coola; in the diocese of Autun, in the suburb, the church of Saint Rozi; the churches of Rocta, Mont-Aubert, with the village of Brazi, Viverais, Saint-Honoré, and Larneneia.

In the diocese of Orléans: the churches in the suburb of Saint Lawrence, with all their appurtenances, and those of Brou. In the diocese of Chartres: the churches in the suburb of Saint Mary of Beaulieu, and at Morville, Saint John’s. In the diocese of Tours: the churches of Saint Michael, Saint Médard, and Ewra. In the diocese of Sens: the churches of Saint Mary of the Lion Gate, with all their appurtenances; Curtinay, Saint Peter’s, with its appurtenances; Dicy; Château-Renard; Saint Nicholas’s; the churches of Mont-Bouy, with all their appurtenances; Châtillon; Chavannes; Joigny, with all its appurtenances; Saint-Sidron, with all its appurtenances; Branches; Contention; Ladit; Château-Beliot; Venesy; La Croix, with all its appurtenances; Joigny-ville; Julliac; and the chapel of Fagi.

In the diocese of Troyes [Col. 0538D]: the churches of the Holy Sepulchre, with all their appurtenances; Saint-Just; and Sézanne, with all its appurtenances. In the diocese of Soissons: the churches of Bren, with all their appurtenances, and Villeries, with all their appurtenances. In the diocese of Châlons: the church of Mont-Maur. In the diocese of Meaux: the churches of Rodolio, with all their appurtenances; La Ferté; Ansculf; Calli; Chamini; Bussei; and of Belvédère and Saint Christopher in the suburb. In the diocese of Paris: the church of Saint Yonius, with all its appurtenances. In the diocese of Beauvais [Col. 0539A]: the church of Saint Christopher, with all its appurtenances. In the diocese of Rouen: the church of Longueville, with its appurtenances. In Venice: the church of Holy Cross, with its appurtenances. In Spain: the church of Saint Peter of Arratis, with its appurtenances. In England: in the diocese of Winchester, the church of the Holy Saviour of Bermondsey, with its appurtenances; in the diocese of Lincoln, the churches of Saint Andrew of Northampton, with their appurtenances, and the church of Daventry, with its appurtenances; in the diocese of Hereford, the church of Saint Milburga at Wenlock, with the whole town and its other appurtenances; in the archbishopric of York, the church of Pontefract, with its appurtenances. We likewise confirm to you by apostolic authority the other churches, chapels, and tithes of Laurent and Meua [Col. 0539B], and all the rest that you canonically possess.

Further, you may choose priests for your churches; if they are suitable, they are to receive the cure of souls from the bishops freely and without any improper exaction, rendering to the bishops due subjection in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. By the present decree we also strictly forbid any bishop to promulgate a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your place, namely La Charité, except by command of the apostolic see. Following the example of our predecessors Innocent and Adrian of blessed memory, Roman pontiffs, we grant you and your successors in perpetuity [Col. 0539C] that, in parishes belonging to your right, no order or religious community other than your own may in future be established.

Moreover, we forbid anyone, within parishes belonging to the right of your monastery, without the assent of your prior and chapter and saving the privileges of the apostolic see, to presume to build a church, chapel, or cemetery. You may also possess, for the support of yourselves and the poor, the tithes of your churches that are held by laymen, if reverence for your religious order can withdraw them from lay control in accordance with God’s will. As for consecrations of your altars or churches and ordinations of clerics, etc., down to “provide.” Otherwise, whichever person you prefer, etc., down to “render.” No bishop may, in respect of your altars, churches, or tithes [Col. 0539D], inflict upon you an undue burden or harassment; but, as you have canonically held certain things partly and others wholly by their permission, so you are to hold them in the future. Therefore we decree, etc., down to “beneficial,” saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical jurisdiction of diocesan bishops in the aforesaid chapels. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0540A], in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III, our lord.

CCXXII. [Note: This letter is printed in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §88. Raynaldus also cites it under the year 1205, §27.] … TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI [Note: See letter 38 of book III and its note.]. He advises and requests him to accept the patriarchate of Jerusalem. (At Saint Peter’s, 20 January.)

[“That you may repair the fall of the human race,” etc., as in the letter sent to S., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis and legate of the apostolic see, in the Register of the sixth year [Note: See letter 129 of book VI and the notes there.], in the same manner down to “you may labour.” For the beloved sons … prior and … canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, appearing before us, declared humbly to us both orally and by the letters which they brought [Col. 0540B] that, when our beloved son S., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis and legate of the apostolic see, could not be induced to consent to the election made of him for the church of Jerusalem, they assembled together and unanimously postulated you as patriarch. Their postulation received the assent of our dearest son in Christ, A., illustrious king of Jerusalem; and the archbishops and bishops consented, humbly requesting us by their letters not merely to induce but even to compel you to consent humbly to their postulation.

Likewise, the cardinals of Saint Praxedis and of Saint Marcellus, beloved sons and legates of the apostolic see, informed us by their letters that, whereas the suffragans [Col. 0540C] of the Church of Jerusalem claimed to have a voice in the election, while the prior and canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre denied this, it was finally arranged that, after two persons had been nominated, they should devoutly confer their powers and votes upon those two and elect from them as patriarch the person whom they judged more suitable. Similarly, the prelates of the province concordantly conferred upon those two whatever right they had in the election. They therefore, after deliberation, chose you rather from the two nominated persons and named you pastor of that Church.

Although you are very necessary to us in Lombardy, since we safely entrust our authority to you even in difficult affairs, yet, because of the pressing necessity not only of the Church of Jerusalem but of the whole Eastern province [Col. 0540D], etc., down to “that will result.” Therefore execute this apostolic command in such a fashion, for God and because of God, that we need not apply the hand of stricter severity. For although, according to canonical statutes, no one is compelled unwillingly to be promoted, nevertheless under lawful enactments some are drawn unwillingly to public offices. It concerns both the apostolic see and the universal Church—indeed, universally all and individually each of Christ crucified’s faithful—that a suitable person be set over that Church as pastor. You are being raised not so much to honour [Col. 0541A] as to a burden, since that Church today has more burden than honour.

Nor should you be troubled or make objection because the aforesaid cardinal of Saint Praxedis did not accept the postulation made of him by the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre. Perhaps, like Sarah for Tobias, that Church too was by divine judgment reserved for another husband; or perhaps this led him to refuse the burden, lest, while he was in those regions, he should seem to have procured his own promotion and thereby especially incur the stain of ambition—particularly because, as his office required, he had pressed opportunely and importunately for the removal of a certain perverse person improperly nominated to that Church, and, once that person had been removed, he would then have accepted a postulation made of himself.

[Col. 0541B] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March.

CCXXIII. TO P., CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SAINT MARCELLUS, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He reproves him because, together with S., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis, he left the Holy Land and went to Constantinople. Yet he commands that, since he was in that city, he arrange all matters there until the arrival of another legate, meanwhile not neglecting care for the affairs of Jerusalem. (At Saint Peter’s, 17 February.)

We have received from the report of many persons, and your messenger has informed us, that you and our beloved son, the priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes, [Col. 0541C] legate of the Apostolic See, have gone from the province of Jerusalem to Constantinople. We therefore distinguish whether you went to the army of the crusaders, over whom you received the office of legation, for the necessary assistance of the Holy Land, or crossed to the aforesaid regions in order to organize the churches of the Greeks. In the former case we do not disapprove of your journey; in the latter, however, speaking with due respect to you, we consider it rash—not so much we as our brethren—since you received from us no authority concerning these matters, unless perhaps some unforeseen emergency may excuse you. This is especially so because our dearest son in Christ, B., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, has begged us by letters and messengers to deem it fitting to send legates from our side [Col. 0541D] to those regions; and, with the counsel of our brethren, we have resolved to do so at an opportune time.

Yet, in order to make special provision, as an act of grace, for your honor, lest you be too greatly put to shame, and in order through your diligence to provide for the province of Constantinople, lest it long lack a governor, we grant you permission meanwhile to act in our stead in whatever you judge expedient for the glory of the divine name, the honor of the Apostolic See, and the salvation alike of clergy and people. You are, however, to take careful care that you do not [Col. 0542A] leave the province of Jerusalem, to which you were specially assigned, as though wholly deserted—especially since, when you arrived, it had a patriarch exercising pastoral care there, whereas at your departure it lacks a patriarch, so that no one has remained there to discharge pastoral office over it.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion diligently to ensure, together with the aforesaid legate, that until provision is otherwise made for that land, one of you shall beneficially provide for it. Do not hasten to return before you receive a special apostolic mandate on this matter.

Given as in the other letter.

CCXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0541D] A fragment of this letter is found among the Decretals, book V, title 39, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*, chapter 41. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets.

Raynaldus also cites it under the year 1205, §65.]

**TO ALL THE CHRISTIAN FAITHFUL ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT LOMBARDY.** He declares that persons excommunicated by the Apostolic See are not to be deemed absolved merely because the Pope sends them letters containing a salutation. (At Saint Peter’s, 9 Kalends of March [21 February].)

[Col. 0542B]

[If it should at any time happen that our letters containing a salutation are sent to persons subjected to excommunication by apostolic authority, the sentence of excommunication is not for that reason to be believed relaxed; for letters of this kind may be procured through ignorance, negligence, excessive occupation, or even surreptitiously.] Thus it is said recently to have happened in the case of the people of Piacenza. Since they are bound by the bond of excommunication because of the wrong which they committed against God and [Col. 0542C] His Church, they boast as though absolved by letters of this kind, which we are said to have sent them concerning the Templars, although we do not remember such letters. Even if they were produced after those persons had already been excommunicated, they may nevertheless have been obtained beforehand.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your whole community strictly to avoid them as excommunicates until they repent of their error, observing the same judgment in similar cases should they occur.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 9 Kalends of March [21 February].

CCXXV. [Note: [Col. 0542D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §65.] **TO . . . THE BISHOP OF PIACENZA** [Note: [Col. 0542D] Book V, letter 75, note.] **AND . . . THE BISHOP OF TORTONA** [Note: [Col. 0542D] Ibid., letter 73, note.]. Authority to absolve the people of Piacenza. (At Saint Peter’s, 9 Kalends of March [21 February].)

[Col. 0542D]

Since the bowels of mercy ought not to be closed against those seeking pardon, by our authority we grant you full power, so that if the people of Piacenza, who have grievously offended God and His Church, return to the command of the Church and take care to make satisfaction for their offences, you may grant them the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church—provided that, because of a few persons, the sinew of ecclesiastical discipline is not broken among the many.

Given as in the other letter.

CCXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0543C] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §§54 and 56.] **LETTER OF ANDREW, GOVERNOR OF HUNGARY.** On the translation of the archbishop of Kalocsa to the archbishopric of Esztergom.

To the reverend father in Christ, Innocent, by the grace of God supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman Church: A., by the same grace duke of Dalmatia and Croatia and governor of the whole kingdom of Hungary, greetings and filial reverence in all things.

Since, by the arrangement of our brother H., formerly king of Hungary, of pious memory, we have assumed the care of his son, King Ladislaus, while still of tender age, and the government of the kingdom, we are ready to preserve what has been well established and, so far as lies in us, happily to bring to completion what we know our brother laudably began. Hence, because the aforesaid brother of ours requested from the kindness of the Apostolic See that the archbishop of Kalocsa be transferred to the archbishopric of Esztergom [Note: [Col. 0543C] See letter 159 of this seventh book.], and because we fully recognize that this would benefit both churches, we earnestly ask your pious fatherhood, for God’s sake and in response to our prayers, without delay—if you have not already granted it—to grant that the archbishop of Kalocsa be transferred to the metropolitan see of Esztergom.

And since, after undertaking the helm of government, we know that this our first petition has been granted, may we be all the more devoted in every respect to the Roman Church, inasmuch as through this we shall more fully understand that your kindness embraces us with a certain special affection. But the fact that we send these present letters to you under our brother’s seal you should attribute to the novelty of our position, not to falsehood.

CCXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0543C] Fragments of this letter are found among the Decretals, book II, title 6, *That proceedings are not to advance to the reception of witnesses or to a definitive sentence before the suit is joined*, chapter 4. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] **TO . . . THE ABBOT OF COUR-DE-DIEU** [Note: [Col. 0543D] We cannot determine with certainty who at that time was abbot of the monastery of Cour-de-Dieu. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1584, record Hugh I from 1181 to 1189 on the evidence of documents, assigning his death to 21 October, though in an uncertain year, on the evidence of the necrology. They then state that Hervé’s name occurs in a document lacking chronological indications. Next they mention Hugh II, but not before 1209.] **AND . . . THE ABBOT OF L’AUMÔNE** [Note: [Col. 0543D]

“VIII. Ralph II obtained from Innocent III, on 24 February 1203, confirmation of a legacy of forty Angevin pounds made by Louis, count of Clermont, to L’Aumône for his mother Adelicia.

“IX. Hameric, or Aymeric, obtained a bull from Pope Innocent in 1205. We again find H. in November 1209. He witnessed a grant made to Étoile by John, count of Vendôme, in 1211. He was still governing in 1222.” *Gallia Christiana*, [Col. 0544C] vol. VIII, col. 1398.]

**ABBOTS, OF THE DIOCESES OF ORLÉANS AND CHARTRES, AND TO THE CHANTOR OF ORLÉANS.** He commits to them the case pending between W., viscount of Benaici [variant: Cenaici], and his wife Eustachia. (At Saint Peter’s, 13 Kalends of March [17 February].)

[Col. 0544A]

[Our beloved son, the nobleman W., viscount of Benaici [Note: [Col. 0544C] In the Decretals this word is absent; moreover, *Cenaici* should be read, according to the notes of Alteserra.], appearing before the Apostolic See, showed us in a humble complaint that, although he had lawfully taken the noblewoman Eustachia as his wife and had two daughters by her, this noblewoman at last, persuaded by the enemy of humankind, departed from him. Since he could not obtain justice in this matter from our venerable brother, the bishop of . . . Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0544C] Book V, letter 28.], his diocesan, we committed the case concerning their marriage, at the request of the messengers of the viscount and of the woman, to our beloved sons: . . . the abbot [Note: [Col. 0544C] Arnald II, abbot of Saint-Léger, is mentioned in documents from 1187 until [Col. 0544D] 1244. See *Bibliothèque Cluniacensis*.] of Saint-Léger; . . . the dean of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0544D] If this concerns the dean of the metropolitan church of Poitiers, dedicated to Saint Peter, he was either William I, mentioned in documents about 1200, or Philip, whose name occurs in charters from 1211 until 1222, when he became bishop. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1216.]; etc.; . . . the prior [Note: [Col. 0544D] Seguinus is called prior of the cell of Saint Hilary in 1204, in the incomplete series of priors of this monastery. Ibid., col. 1336.] of Saint Hilary of the Cell, all of Poitiers.

As they informed us by letter, since it had been clearly established for them that the aforesaid E. had of her own authority departed from her husband, by whom she had borne two daughters, they consulted prudent men and decreed that E. must return to her husband, while retaining full power, after her return, to accuse the marriage if she wished. When she refused to do so, they bound her by a sentence of excommunication and subjected her land and household to ecclesiastical interdict. Afterwards we commanded that this sentence, lawfully issued, be inviolably observed until suitable satisfaction was made.

At length, however, the same E., at the request of our venerable brother, the bishop of . . . Angers [Note: [Col. 0544D] See Book V, letter 28, note.], and of our beloved sons, the abbots of . . . La Grenetière [Note: [Col. 0544D] John I governed the monastery of La Grenetière in 1201; he is also mentioned in 1225 and 1246. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1430.] and . . . Bellefontaine [Note: [Col. 0544D] The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1385, mention no abbot of Bellefontaine in the period with which we are concerned.], obtained that the case be delegated, under the following form, to our venerable brother, the bishop of . . . [Note: [Col. 0544D] William, bishop of Cornouaille, is mentioned about 1203. *Historia Britannica*, vol. I, [Col. 0545D] p. 132. He died on 4 December 1219. Old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 351.], and to our beloved sons G., archdeacon of Cornouaille, and Master P. de Buter, canon of Angers.

They were to summon the parties before them—after rescinding whatever might be found rashly done to her prejudice after a lawful appeal to us had been lodged, notwithstanding the aforesaid commission—if it appeared to them that the same woman had been unable, because of wars, to come at the appointed place before the former judges, as the bishop and abbots had written us; and if she were willing to give the opposing party safe-conduct at the boundary of the dioceses of Poitiers and Angers and furnish the fullest security that she would keep them unharmed. Having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, they were to determine the case without appeal by due judgment and compel observance of what they decreed by ecclesiastical censure.

But, as we saw contained in their letters, after they had assigned dates to the parties at Vouvent and afterwards at Luçon, the same viscount excused himself by letters and procurator, asserting that he did not dare go to those places because his enemies held dominion there and he feared death. The opposing party and the barons present there replied that they had sent the viscount letters of safe-conduct through a messenger, together with letters of the viscount of Thouars, seneschal of Poitou. The viscount’s procurator answered that he did not dare go to a place suspicious to him merely on the strength of letters, but requested that a safe place be appointed for him and that his wife be restored. If the judges would not do so, he said that his lord was being burdened and therefore resorted to the remedy of appeal. Thereafter, although summoned, he would not answer before those judges, declaring them manifestly suspect, and renewed the appeal he had lodged.

The judges, believing the appeal not lawful and subsequently learning through witnesses that the sentence against the woman had been pronounced after the appeal, declared it wholly invalid. Finally, after a peremptory date had been set for the parties at Pouzauges, the dean of . . . Tours [Note: [Col. 0545D]

The following few facts concerning the deans of Tours are found in the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 789, col. 1: A. Theobald was present in 1202 at the settlement by Geoffrey, count of Perche, with the consent of Thomas his son and William, provost of Chartres, concerning the foundation of the collegiate church of the castle of Mauritania.

“John de Faye I, in 1206, was raised from dean to [Col. 0546D] bishop in 1208, as is written in the Chronicle of Tours.”]

, uncle of that viscount, offered to appear for him if a safe-conduct were granted him; nevertheless, by letters he alleged grounds of suspicion against the judges: namely, that the bishop was related to the nobleman G. of Thouars, count of Brittany, who involved himself excessively in the woman’s cause and held the bishop subject to his authority; that the archdeacon was a cleric and table-companion of that count; and that Master P. de Bucer was a native of the woman’s land.

Afterwards, when another peremptory date had been set for the parties, the judges received the testimony of the woman’s witnesses concerning consanguinity. At another date appointed at Malleon, they ordered the depositions to be published, while the viscount again excused himself by letter. Finally, when the parties had been assigned a date for receiving sentence, with messengers of the woman and the . . . archdeacon of Tours, brother of the viscount, present before them, the woman’s messengers demanded sentence, and the archdeacon requested a date for his brother. On prudent advice, the judges assigned the parties a date on which the case ought to proceed according to the order of law. But the woman’s messengers departed contumaciously and, on the next day, appealed to our hearing, saying that injury was being inflicted upon their lady because the judges had not been present at Malleon, where they had appointed the date for rendering sentence, and because they appointed a place outside the province, although they themselves belonged to the province of Tours.

When the judges deferred to the appeal, the woman’s messenger came to the Apostolic See and stated that the aforesaid judges had repeatedly summoned the viscount peremptorily to appear before them, at suitable places and with lawful intervals, in the case; yet the viscount, although the aforesaid woman appeared, neither chose to come nor sent a sufficient representative. They therefore received the woman’s witnesses, repeatedly citing the viscount by two peremptory edicts to appear before them and speak against the witnesses or their testimony. Since he neither came nor sent a sufficient messenger, they published the depositions and summoned the parties to hear sentence. The woman sought judgment in her favor while the viscount remained contumaciously absent. Although often requested to proceed, the judges refused; therefore the woman’s party, feeling injury to be imminent, appealed to our hearing.

Believing that the woman was laboring on behalf of the marriage, we ordered the judges, at the request of her messenger, to proceed lawfully in the same case according to the depositions received and determine it without delay, removing every obstacle of contradiction or appeal. We also commanded our beloved sons, the abbots of . . . La Grenetière, . . . Île-Calvet [Note: [Col. 0546D] The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1432, mention no abbot of the monastery of Île-Calvet in the period under consideration.], and . . . Alba Corona [Note: [Col. 0546D] The authors of the old *Gallia Christiana* say nothing concerning the abbots of Alba Corona, vol. IV, p. 17, col. 2.], that if the aforesaid judges proved negligent or remiss in executing our mandate, they should not delay in proceeding, according to the depositions received by those judges, to definitive sentence in the same business, removing the obstacle of appeal.

Moreover, the said viscount of Benaici, appearing in our presence, set forth a grave complaint against the said judges [Note: [Col. 0547D] The Decretals omit this word, as below they read “the said nobleman G. of T.”; shortly afterwards they read *since* for *as*.]: since the said bishop of Cornouaille was connected in the nearest degree of kinship with the nobleman G. of Thouars, count of Brittany, and his archdeacon was that count’s cleric and table-companion; since that count was the viscount’s principal adversary, presuming publicly to hold his wife and land; and since Master P. de Buter [Note: [Col. 0547D] The following words are absent in the Decretals, which read “the said count” for “and all exist under the district and power of that G.”; later they read *is evident* for *has become evident*, and add a conjunction after *them*.] was a native of his wife’s land, showed excessive favor to her, and all were under G.’s jurisdiction and power. The viscount could gain access to them only through that man’s jurisdiction. [Note: [Col. 0547D] The Decretals add: “to whom the case between himself and his wife had been committed”; shortly afterward they read *were willing* for [Col. 0548D] *wished*, *where* for *at which*, and *had* for *would have had*.] They never wished to assign him a place or date except in the land of his enemies, where he did not dare go without danger of death. Even if letters of safe-conduct had been sent to him, he ought not to entrust himself to his mortal enemies.

Further, although we had thought fit to prescribe them a definite procedure, after a lawful appeal had been lodged with us they abandoned the procedure we had prescribed. They investigated only the appeal, disregarding the order of law; although it had not been shown that the appeal was lawful, that nothing had rashly been done, or that they had inquired into the other points enjoined upon them, they unjustly declared void the sentence lawfully pronounced against the woman. Before the suit was joined, they presumed to receive witnesses concerning the principal issue [Col. 0547C] and, rejecting his lawful exceptions, omitted from their letters most of his allegations, especially those relevant to the case, while raising on behalf of the opposing party many matters that had not been alleged before them.

Moreover, the opposing party, which had procured delegation of the case to them by false representations, fraudulently sought to weaken the viscount’s right through untrustworthy witnesses. Under the pretext of a frivolous appeal, it secretly obtained letters from those same judges and from the aforesaid abbots of La Grenetière, Île-Calvet, and . . . Alba Corona concerning the issuance of sentence, while the viscount was on his way to the Apostolic See to pursue his appeal. Since the fraud of his adversaries ought not to aid them or create prejudice against him, and since it is clear that those judges, after a lawful appeal had been lodged with us, proceeded rashly in the case, contrary to the form of our mandate and as manifestly suspect persons, the viscount earnestly requested that we rescind whatever the judges or others had done to his prejudice after the lawful appeal; likewise revoke the letters obtained by falsehood while he was coming to us; compel his wife by sentence of excommunication and interdict upon the land to return to him; compel those holding her and the land, by the same coercion, to restore her and the land together with its revenues received; and cause these sentences to be published and firmly observed every Sunday and feast day throughout the provinces of Tours and Bordeaux, until full satisfaction had been made.

Since, therefore, in matrimonial causes we ought rather to be inclined to unite than to separate, lest a human being presume to separate what God has joined, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion [to do the following: since, as the viscount himself asserts [Note: [Col. 0548D] These words are absent in the Decretals, which shortly afterward read “when both parties have been summoned before you” for “when the parties have been summoned to your presence and, after inquiry into the truth of the foregoing, it is established for you”; and “from the aforesaid grounds” for “for reasonable grounds.”], you are nearer to the land of the aforesaid noblewoman than to his, the case can be determined more conveniently by you, and each party has safe access to you, summon the parties before you. Having carefully inquired into the truth concerning the foregoing, if you establish that, before the suit was lawfully joined or after an appeal reasonably lodged, witnesses concerning consanguinity against the marriage [Note: [Col. 0548D] The Decretals add “without fault of contumacy,” and shortly afterward omit “the appeal ceasing,” as well as the words “by ecclesiastical censure.”] were received, declare such depositions void and without effect. With the appeal ceasing, compel by ecclesiastical censure the aforesaid noblewoman to return to the husband [Note: [Col. 0548D] The Decretals add “her own” and shortly afterward omit “to execute the apostolic mandate . . .”] whom she rashly left, carrying out the apostolic mandate with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed; so that, after the husband has received complete restitution both of wife and land, you may hear the case concerning the marriage and determine it by a canonical judgment.]

Opponents, etc. Witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding no letters, etc. But if not all, etc. Two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 13 Kalends of March [17 February], in the seventh year.

CCXXVIII. **TO . . . THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF ANCONA.** That they should resist the intruder of Mainz.

Although Markward, of accursed memory—wealthy and powerful, cunning and bold—held dominion over the whole March, you and the other inhabitants of the March, recognizing his unbearable yoke, prudently and courageously shook it from your necks, not without many labors [Col. 0548D] and expenditures, and returned to the natural lordship of the Apostolic See. Of itself it can truly say: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light.”

We therefore wonder greatly and are moved that, although you have remained steadfast in our fidelity, you have nevertheless been negligent against the wickedness of those [Col. 0549A] who have come to overthrow your liberty—indeed, rather, to extinguish your life—in order to reduce you to a baser slavery, or rather to bring upon you a crueler death. Nor can you truly excuse your weakness because of their power, since in fact your power is sufficient to restrain their weakness, provided only that the rancor of envy among you should cease; that alone can hinder you. Nor should you be excessively alarmed by empty rumors, because, as you have often experienced, certain people, unable to harm by force, strive to prevail by fraud, inventing many things from a few, great things from small, and sometimes things from nothing. But their falsehood vanishes like smoke.

Further, since justice ought more strongly to encourage you in your defense—of which Sacred Scripture testifies that blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake—you should know that we have communicated a certain chapter from the testament of Emperor Henry to our beloved son C., [Note: [Col. 0549D] See letter 31 of the third book, note.] priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina and legate of the Apostolic See, for him faithfully to explain to you. Since there are two parties in the Empire, each desiring our favor, each is willing to leave the March peacefully to us, because neither party can obtain the imperial crown except through our favor.

Therefore, if you remain steadfast and strong in fidelity to us, we shall certainly take care to provide sufficiently for your liberty, whatever outcome the condition of the Empire may receive. Otherwise you may rightly fear that your latter state will become worse than your former and that the latter error will be worse than the former. Accordingly, we earnestly admonish your devotion and command you by apostolic letters to heed effectively, in our stead, the aforesaid cardinal, and to arm yourselves manfully for your defense against the intruder of Mainz. For, however much he may boast, if while you have the opportunity you strive to cast him down, he will not add strength to rise again; nor will another come after him when he sees that man frustrated in his purpose. Thus you will be able to enjoy the liberty you desire, carefully considering that it often happens by just judgment that those who will not act when they can cannot act when they wish.

Therefore let his threats not terrify you, nor his promises deceive you; for as lightning turns into rain, so his promises turn into deceits. It is wiser and better to accomplish your purpose now through lesser labors and fewer expenses than later, with much labor and great expenditure, to be unable to avoid your peril. For, as the writing testifies: “Delay has always harmed those who are prepared.”

Given, etc.

CCXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0549D]

This narrative, together with the documents inserted in it, is found in the *Gesta Innocentii*, §120.

It is printed in Raynaldus, under the year 1204, §71.

See also *Historia Occitana*, vol. III, p. 126.]

**The order of the coronation of Peter, king of Aragon.** (At Rome, 10 [variant: 11] November.)

[In the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III, in the month of November, Peter, king of Aragon, came to the Apostolic See in order to receive from the same lord pope the military belt and the royal diadem. He came by sea with five galleys and landed at the island between Porto and Ostia. He brought with him the archbishop of Arles [Note: [Col. 0549D] Concerning the archbishop of Arles, see above, letter 162 of this seventh book, note.], the provost of Maguelonne [Note: [Col. 0549D] He was Guy of Ventadour, son of Eble III [Col. 0550D] of Ventadour and Aleidis of Montpellier, brother of Eble IV, viscount of Ventadour, and of Eble, abbot of Figeac. Having been a canon of Maguelonne, he became provost and is mentioned in documents from 1190 until at least 1205. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 825.], the elect of Montmajour [Note: [Col. 0550D] See letter 162 of this seventh book, note.], and certain other noble and prudent clerics [Col. 0550B] who were with them.

He also brought magnates with him: his uncle Sancho, Hugh of Baux, Roscelin of Marseille, Arnald of F[?]otian, and many other noble and powerful men. The same lord pope sent nearly two hundred mounts and pack-animals for him and had him brought with full magnificence to Saint Peter’s, sending certain cardinals, the senator of the City, and many other nobles and magnates to meet him. He caused him to be honorably lodged at Saint Peter’s in the house of the canons.

On the third day, namely the feast of Saint Martin, the aforesaid lord pope, with cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons, the primicerius, the cantors, the senator, justiciars, judges, advocates, scribes, and many nobles and a great multitude of people, proceeded to the monastery of Saint Pancras the martyr near Trastevere. There he had the aforesaid king anointed by the hand of Peter, bishop of Porto. Afterwards he himself crowned him with his own hand, bestowing upon him all the royal insignia: namely the mantle and tunic, sceptre and orb, crown and mitre. He received from him a corporal oath, whose tenor is as follows:

“I, Peter, king of Aragon, profess and promise that I shall always be faithful and obedient to my lord Pope Innocent, to his Catholic successors, and to the Roman Church; and that I shall faithfully preserve my kingdom in its obedience, defending the Catholic faith and pursuing heretical depravity. I shall preserve the liberty and immunity of churches and defend their rights. In every land subject to my power I shall endeavor to preserve justice and peace. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.”

Then the aforesaid king, crowned with much proclamation of praise and acclamation of favor, returned beside the lord pope to the basilica of Saint Peter. Upon its altar he laid down the sceptre and diadem, and from the hand of the same lord pope [Col. 0551A] received the sword of knighthood. He offered his kingdom to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and made it tributary to him by the charter of a privilege which he delivered to the same lord pope upon that altar. Its tenor is as follows:

“Since I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the Roman pontiff, successor of blessed Peter, is the vicar of Him through whom kings reign and princes govern, who rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whom He wills: I, Peter, by the grace of God king of Aragon, count of Barcelona, and lord of Montpellier, desiring to be protected chiefly [Note: [Col. 0551D] So also in the *Gesta* and in Raynaldus. In the Vallicellian codex, marked B, no. XII, however, *principally*.] after God by the protection of blessed Peter and the Apostolic See, offer to you, most reverend father and lord, supreme pontiff Innocent, and through you to the most holy Roman Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0551D] Thus also in Raynaldus; in the *Gesta*, “the Church.”], my kingdom. Out of regard for divine love and for the salvation of my soul and of my forebears, I make it tributary in perpetuity to you and your successors, so that each year two hundred and fifty [Note: [Col. 0551D] In the *Gesta*: *Massenutinae*; in Raynaldus and also in the codex of Podio cited by Baluze, in the margin: *Massemutinae*. See note.] mussemutinae [Note: [Col. 0551D] Variant: *Masmodinae*; a Saracen coin, concerning which see Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. IV, col. 577.] shall be paid from the royal treasury to the Apostolic See, and I and my successors shall be specially bound to it in fidelity and obligation. I decree that this shall be observed by perpetual law, because I firmly hope and trust that you and your successors will defend me, my successors, and the aforesaid kingdom by apostolic authority, especially since, moved by great devotion in coming to the Apostolic See, you have deemed fit solemnly to crown me king with hands that are, as it were, those of blessed Peter.

“So that this royal grant may obtain inviolable force, I have caused it to be confirmed by the protection of my seal, with the counsel of the magnates of my court and in the presence of my venerable father, the archbishop of Arles, and of my uncle Sancho, Hugh of Baux, and Arnald of F[?]otian, my barons.”

Done at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1204, 10 November, in the eighth year of my reign.

After all this had been duly accomplished, the lord pope had him conducted through the City to the church of Saint Paul. Finding his galleys prepared there, he embarked, and, strengthened by the apostolic blessing, was granted a prosperous return to his own lands.]

CCXXX. [Note: [Col. 0551D]

This letter is printed in full in the *Gesta Innocentii*, §80, and is therefore presented here enclosed in brackets.

[Col. 0552D] Raynaldus prints fragments of it under the year 1205, §23. What is found in his text has here been marked in the margin by a double stroke at the beginning of each line.]

**LETTER OF KALOJOANNES, KING OF BULGARIA, TO THE POPE.** He announces the arrival of the legate, from whom he subsequently received the crown, and sends him certain gifts.

[Col. 0551D]

[Calojoannes, king of all Bulgaria and Vlachia, to the God-exalted, most holy, beloved in Christ, and most honourable father of my realm, Innocent III, most sacred pope of Rome and successor of Peter, prince of the apostles. The legate of the Apostolic See, Lord Leo, cardinal [Note: [Col. 0552D] See letters, book V, no. 5, note; book VII, no. 1, note.], delivered to my empire the letter of Your Holiness; and, learning also [Note: [Col. 0552D] In the *Gesta*, *addiscentesque* (“and learning,” plural).] of his health and safety, I glorified almighty God and His most holy Mother [Note: [Col. 0552D] “We glorified.”].
