Would that the letter of my empire may find Your Holiness living and dwelling in every joy and gladness; and my empire, through the grace of almighty God and the most blessed Mother of God, and through the intercessions of Your Holiness, is well and very prosperous, with every joy and exultation [Note: [Col. 0552D] Thus in Raynaldus.]. “Let this, moreover, be known to Your [Col. 0552B] Holiness, special father of my realm, lord pope [Note: [Col. 0552D] “Spiritual father of my realm, lord pope.”]: that Lord Leo, legate of the Apostolic See, came to my empire, bringing with him a crown; he blessed it and placed it upon the head of my empire; he put a sceptre and banner into my hands; and, by the command of Your Holiness, he blessed the most holy patriarch of my realm and of all Bulgaria. We glorified God and the most blessed Mother of God, and also the provident care of Your Holiness exceedingly [Note: [Col. 0552D] Raynaldus ends here.],” because, according to the petition of my empire, Your Holiness has fulfilled all its desire. And all Bulgaria and Vlachia, and every dependency of my empire, greatly glorified and magnified Your Holiness [Note: [Col. 0552D] Raynaldus again.]. [Col. 0552C] “I write to you also concerning Hungary [Note: [Col. 0552D] “the Hungarian,” in Raynaldus; *Hungaro* in the edition.], because my empire has no alliance of territories, nor any affair, with him, nor does it harm him; rather, he himself disparages and harms the territories of my empire. And Lord Leo, the cardinal, has seen this and will report to Your Holiness what is just or unjust on the part of my empire: whether I disparage the Hungarian, or whether he disparages my empire. Let Your Holiness write to him, therefore, that he should keep away from my kingdom, since my empire neither has any reason to disparage him nor to go against his lands. But if he should come against the lands of my empire, and God should help so that he is defeated, let not Your Holiness regard my empire as suspect, but let me remain free. I write also to Your Holiness concerning the Latins who [Col. 0552D] entered Constantinople: write to them that they should keep away from my empire, and, just as my empire does them no harm, let them not disparage us. If [Col. 0553A] perhaps they attempt something against my empire and disparage it, and some of them are killed, let not Your Holiness regard my empire as suspect, but let all remain free. I have sent to your great Holiness two boys: one is named Basil, the other Bethlehem; let them be given instruction by his command, that they may learn Latin letters in the schools, for here we have no grammarians able to translate for us the letters which you send. And after they have learned, let them be sent back to my empire.” [Note: [Col. 0553C] Raynaldus ends here.] I have now sent, as a token [Note: [Col. 0553C] “Token.”] of a small remembrance, two samite cloths, double *episima* [Note: [Col. 0553C] We have already discussed *examita* in the note to letter 6 of this seventh book. Here *episima* are so called from the Greek ἐπίσημος (“marked”); they are patterned with checks woven of gold or purple. Thus learned men interpret ἐπίσημον ἐσθῆτα (“a marked garment”) in Laertius, under Aristotle, book V, section I. Cang., *Glossarium*, vol. III, col. 111.]: one is red and the other white; and one camel. Whenever I send legates to Your Holiness, I shall always remember Your Holiness.

CCXXXI [Note: [Col. 0554C]

This letter is read in full in the *Gesta Innocentii*, §81. It is therefore presented here enclosed in brackets.

It is also cited by Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §23.]

. LETTER OF BASIL, PRIMATE OF THE BULGARIANS, TO THE POPE. He informs him that he was invested with sacred unction by the cardinal legate.

[Many obeisances and many wishes for health, from me, Basil, humble primate of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, to the father of all, lord and my father, the most magnificent and most holy pope, Innocent. We pray almighty God, the most holy Mother of God, and the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, that the writing of my humility may find you in health and safety; and by the magnificence of your lordship [Note: [Col. 0554C] In the *Gesta*, “our lord.”] I too live, by God’s grace, though enveloped in great sins. Let it therefore be known to [Col. 0553C] your great Holiness that Leo, cardinal [Col. 0554A] [Note: [Col. 0554C] See the note to the preceding letter, no. 230.], arrived safe and well, delegated by Your Holiness and the Apostolic See, and proceeded as far as our great city of Trinova on the fifteenth [Note: [Col. 0554C] “Fifteenth.”] day of October [Note: [Col. 0554C] So too in the Royal manuscript cited by Baluze; but in the *Gesta*, September.]. He brought the whole fullness of patriarchal dignity and all the vestments which had been delegated to me by your great Holiness; likewise he delivered the ring, the privilege, the letters, and the instructions. And by command of Your Holiness he anointed me with chrism, blessing me, and established me as patriarch in the month of November, on the seventh day, namely on the feast of the holy apostle James, the Lord’s brother. On that day I anointed two metropolitans and the remaining bishops, with great joy; the cardinal blessed two of the metropolitans and gave them the pallium and mitres, and [Col. 0554B] placed mitres upon the heads of the others. On the eighth day of the same month, namely on the feast of Saint Michael, he crowned and blessed Emperor Calojoannes, lord of all Bulgarians and Vlachs, placing the royal crown upon his head and putting the sceptre in his hands. He completed and carried out all these things according to the will of Your Holiness; and, after blessing us, he departed from us on the fifteenth day of November. Meanwhile, let Your great Holiness know that by command of the lord emperor I am sending you two boys: one is the son of the priest Constantine, the other of the king, so that by command of Your Holiness they may learn Latin letters. And whatever you are able to devise for the emperor’s honour, do it. May God preserve Your [Col. 0554C] Holiness for many long years.]

THE SEVENTH BOOK OF THE REGISTERS, OR LETTERS, OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF. THE EIGHTH YEAR OF HIS PONTIFICATE, A.D. 1205.

[Note: [Col. 0555B]

This letter is found in the *Gesta Innocentii*, §119, though not without certain errors and lacking chronological notes. It is cited by Raynaldus [Col. 0555C] under the year 1205, §35. It is also printed by Angelus Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, vol. III, p. 449, under the year 1205, chapter 4, no. 6.

We print it in full, following the Conti transcript; for greater accuracy we have also noted in the margin variant readings from the Vallicellan manuscript, marked B, no. XII. But we have deliberately omitted those found in Angelus Manrique, as being of less importance.]

. TO THE ABBOTS OF LUCEDIO AND MOUNT TABOR [Note: [Col. 0555C] Cardinal James of Vitry testifies, in his *Western History* (ch. 15), that the Cistercian order flourished on Mount Tabor in his own—that is, our present—time, in these exact words: “Monasteries of the Cistercian and Premonstratensian orders were also built in suitable places [namely, on that same mountain].”], AND TO THE NOBLE MEN COUNT BERTHOLD [Note: [Col. 0556B] So also in Manrique. In the *Gesta*, Bercoboc; in Raynaldus’s margin, Berroboc.] AND G. DE FORNIVALL [Note: [Col. 0556B] In the *Gesta*, Furnivale; in Raynaldus, [Col. 0556C] Furinvalt; in the Vallicellan manuscript, Firruallis; in Manrique, Foravalle.]. He entrusts to them for adjudication the dispute between the king of Armenia and the count of Tripoli concerning the principality of Antioch. (At St Peter’s, 5 March.)

[Col. 0555A]

Although mortal hatred always exists among those who are bound to love their neighbours as themselves and even to love their enemies for God’s sake, yet at this time discord among worshippers of the Christian name, especially those established in overseas regions, is harmful not only to themselves but also, and much more so, to the universal Church, since through it the undertaking for the Holy Land is [Col. 0555B] impeded. For the enemies of the Christian name—who now, because sins demand it, hold and defile the temple of God—have so diminished in men and strength the cities and castles which they boast of having wrested from Christian hands by the sword, that what they have lost would suffice for the remnant of our force, if only they advanced against the enemy with joined [Note: [Col. 0556C] In the Vallicellan manuscript, “married.”] hands, one mind, and equal desire, to avenge in some measure the wrong done to the Cross and free Christ’s inheritance from pagan hands. But they, paying less heed to this than they should, pursue their own injuries as though the injury done to the Crucified had been entirely neglected, [Col. 0556A] and, to the detriment of all Christendom, set private desires before the common good [Note: [Col. 0556C] “Will.”] [Note: [Col. 0556C] So too in the *Gesta*; but perhaps one should read “advantages.”]. Thus they prosecute one another with wrongful hatred and are so divided from one another that, because of their discord, the Gospel saying must be feared in no small degree for the Holy Land: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house” (Luke 11). For behold: on account of the discord which exists between our dearest son in Christ, L. [Note: [Col. 0556C] Leo.], illustrious king of Armenia, in the name of … his widowed sister and … orphaned nephew, on the one side, and the nobleman … count of Tripoli on the other, concerning the principality of Antioch, the advance of the Holy Land is almost completely hindered. While they fight one another, [Col. 0556B] they cannot attack the enemies of the Cross; others make common cause with either party [Note: [Col. 0556C] So too in the *Gesta*; in the Vallicellan manuscript, *praecationem* (“prayer/request”).], regard their dispute as their own cause, and the rest labour in vain to restore concord among the disputants. Long ago, wishing to oppose these evils, we entrusted this dispute for settlement to our beloved sons, S. [Note: [Col. 0556C] Soffredo.] of the title of St Praxedis [Note: [Col. 0556C] See book V, letter 6, note.], and P. [Note: [Col. 0556C] Peter.] of the title of St Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0556C] See book III, letter 20, note.], priests-cardinal and legates of the Apostolic See. But they [Note: [Col. 0556C] The Vallicellan manuscript adds “legate.”], although they spared neither labour nor expense in this matter—indeed, each separately and both together [Col. 0557A] [Note: [Col. 0557D] In the *Gesta*, “both persons and both”; in the Vallicellan manuscript, “with both persons and both.”] had laboured for a long time—nevertheless made no progress with the parties, since it had not been granted from above.

Recently the same king informed us by his letters [Note: [Col. 0557D] These letters do not survive in Innocent’s Registers, but are reported in the *Gesta*, §116. They are also found in a Vatican manuscript. Raynaldus prints them under the year 1205, §36.] that he had been unable to obtain justice through our legates, although he had repeatedly sought it and had always been ready to submit to the law. Accordingly, since he had at last humbly obeyed the commands of those legates, who had excommunicated him and placed his land under interdict for a far lesser matter, he asked that we not repel him as he knocked at the gate of the Apostolic See and sought justice, since we are debtors to all in justice. Therefore, considering that there must be no respect of persons with us and that we are bound to do justice between man and man, we command and order your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 0557B] to summon both parties and carefully admonish them either to come to agreement between themselves concerning that principality or to submit the matter to arbitrators, who must arbitrate within three months after your admonition. Otherwise, having thereafter summoned the parties, hear the allegations on both sides and settle the cause itself, any obstacle of appeal having been removed, if the parties consent. Otherwise, refer the cause to us with full documentation, appointing the parties a term within which they are to appear before us through suitable proctors to receive judgment. But, lest they undergo both litigation and war at once, compel the parties by apostolic authority to observe a truce in the meantime. [Col. 0557C] If either party proves contumacious, proceed against it as strictly as you can, spiritually and temporally, through yourselves and all Christians in those regions; prohibit our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious … king of Jerusalem, the Hospitallers, the Templars, and all Christians generally from giving aid or favour to the contumacious party. Rather, let them withdraw such support and assist manfully and powerfully the party ready to submit to the law. If not all … [act], let three of you, or at least two, one of whom is a layman and the other a cleric, execute this apostolic mandate. Nevertheless, we will and command that, if anyone is meanwhile appointed patriarch of Jerusalem, he shall participate with you in carrying these matters out.

[Col. 0557D] Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 5 March, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

II [Note: [Col. 0557D] See Raynaldus under the year 1205, §35. Angelus Manrique prints part of the same letter, [Col. 0558D] *Annales Cistercienses*, vol. III, p. 449, under the year 1205, chapter 4, no. 10. Text found in his edition is enclosed here in brackets.]. TO L., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARMENIA. On the same subject as the preceding letter. (At St Peter’s, 5 March. [Note: [Col. 0558D] This is found in Manrique.].)

[We regard it as welcome and acceptable that, recognizing the authority [Col. 0558A] of the Apostolic See, you humbly submit yourself to its judgment, and through it request that justice be done you in the name of … your widowed sister and … your orphaned nephew. Although we are debtors to each individual in justice, we nevertheless show you apostolic favour in this matter all the more readily because we continually find you more devoted toward us and the Roman Church, and your deeds bear witness to the truth that you are more firmly rooted in devotion to the Apostolic See. It would be superfluous to explain by letter how we formerly wrote about this matter to our beloved sons S., cardinal-priest of the title of St Praxedis [Note: [Col. 0558D] Book V, letter 6, note.], and P. [Note: [Col. 0558D] Book III, letter 20, note.], cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus, legates of the Apostolic See, and how they proceeded, since you yourself know this more fully and have informed us by their letters of the whole course [Col. 0558B] of events. But because, although much labour was reportedly expended by them, no progress was made in the case, desiring to satisfy your request, we command by precept our beloved sons, the abbots of Lucedio and … of Mount Tabor, and the noblemen Count Bertold and G. de Fornivall [Note: [Col. 0558D] In Manrique, “de Foravalle.”], to summon both parties and carefully admonish them either that you and the opposing party should reach agreement concerning that same principality, or that you should submit the matter to arbitrators, who must arbitrate within three months after their admonition. Otherwise, after summoning the parties, they are to hear the allegations on both sides and endeavour to settle the cause itself, any obstacle of appeal having been removed, if you and the opposing [Col. 0558C] party consent. Otherwise, they are to refer the matter to us with full documentation, appointing both you and the opposing party a term within which you are to appear before us through suitable proctors, to receive judgment. And, lest you undergo both litigation and war at once, they are to compel both you and the opposing party, by our authority, to observe a truce in the meantime. If either party proves contumacious, they are to proceed against it as strictly as they can, spiritually and temporally, through themselves and all Christians in those regions; they are to prohibit our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious … king of Jerusalem, the Hospitallers, Templars, and all Christians generally from giving aid or favour [Col. 0558D] to the contumacious party, but rather to withdraw support from it and manfully and powerfully assist the party ready to submit to the law. Therefore we admonish your royal serenity and exhort you in the Lord to advance from day to day in love for the Roman Church, and so establish your kingdom in devotion to it that we may deservedly be bound to attend to your progress and increase. Know that [Col. 0559A] the Roman Church will not fail you in your justice.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 5 March, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

III. TO THE ABBOTS OF … HETEWARDEN AND HEGEN, AND TO THE PROVOST OF GUSMAR, IN THE DIOCESES OF PADERBORN AND MAINZ. He entrusts to them the adjudication of the disputed election of the abbess of the Church of Heris. (At St Peter’s, 2 March.)

At the request of our beloved sons in Christ, R. … custodian of the Church of Heris, and V. … the cleric who had come against her, that a hearing be granted them, we appointed our beloved [Col. 0559B] son M. [Note: [Col. 0559D] See book III, letter 54, note.], cardinal-deacon of St Theodore, as auditor. In his presence the custodian alleged that, when the abbess of the church of Heris had died, the sisters and canons of that church, at the admonition of the bishop of Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0559D] “Bernard II of Osyde, called Dysede by others, eighteenth bishop of Paderborn, died in the year [Col. 0560D] 1202.” Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, vol. I, part II, p. 20.], their diocesan, who had come for the abbess’s burial, sat together to make an election and called Th., scholasticus of Paderborn, to examine their votes. But when they disagreed concerning one election, eight of the seventeen sisters then present, together with all fourteen canons of that church, elected the custodian herself, with the advocate, ministerials, and all the people giving their favour and assent. Seven of the sisters, on the other hand, nominated [Col. 0559C] the provost of that church as abbess.

Each side was then presented to the aforesaid bishop to obtain confirmation. The bishop carefully admonished the parties to seek peace and agree with each other upon the election, allowing them five days to deliberate upon this. On the sixth day, since they could not agree, the bishop ordered them to appear before the chapter of Paderborn after another five days, to give reasons for their respective elections. Accordingly, when the custodian and provostess, together with their electors, had appeared in the chapter of Paderborn, the provostess and her seven electors then presented first to the bishop G. …, a nun who had belonged to a certain black monastery [Col. 0559D] and had been confirmed and even blessed as abbess in another church, declaring that they had elected her. The other party was greatly astonished to hear that, without their knowledge or even consultation, they had altered what they had done. The custodian asked the chapter a second and a third time to grant her an advocate for presenting and defending her cause, but could not obtain one. Several advocates, however, were granted to the opposing party. Then the provostess openly confessed that she had wholly renounced her own election and, together with her seven electors, had unanimously consented to the nun G. When the aforesaid custodian heard this and realized that the bishop and many members of the chapter, being relatives of the same nun, wished to bend judgment toward her promotion, after argument had been made for some time regarding the right of the Church of Heris and the preservation of her own justice, she appealed to us, lest prejudice be done to her election. But the bishop, disregarding the appeal, pronounced judgment in favour of the aforesaid nun, his relative, and had her installed in possession of the abbey through his messengers.

The aforesaid cleric, procurator for the opposing party, alleged in reply that, since the aforesaid nun G. had been elected as abbess of Heris by the greater—that is, eleven—and sounder part of the chapter, namely the provostess, scholastic, dean, and certain other sisters, after two frivolous nominations had first been set aside by the aforesaid bishop, and had been confirmed by the bishop, the aforesaid custodian R. presumed to molest her in this matter, seeking to intrude herself into that church by lay power. Therefore the procurator requested on behalf of the nun that we should cause the confirmation made of her to be inviolably observed. He asserted that it ought not to prejudice her that she was a nun while the sisters of Heris wore the dress of canonesses, or that she had been confirmed and blessed as abbess elsewhere, since it was customary in that region for black nuns to be chosen for such abbeys, and sometimes [Col. 0560C] for a canoness to hold an abbey of black nuns. He further asserted that our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory had granted her permission to be chosen for another abbey.

The custodian replied, on the other hand, that the same nun neither ought nor could be chosen to rule their abbey, because she was not a sister of that church, but came from a black monastery and had been confirmed and blessed as abbess of a more distinguished church, from whose governance she was believed not to have been expelled without fault. Further, she was unable to produce the concession which she claimed to have from our predecessor. Thus it was urgently apparent that we ought to declare void what had been done concerning her, especially since the letters of the aforesaid bishop, which that procurator had in defence of his party, expressly stated that the bishop had proceeded to confirm that election after an appeal to us had been lodged. The appeal also appeared legitimate, since the kinship which the bishop admitted in his letters that he had with the same nun indicated a manifest ground for suspicion against him, apart from the fact that whenever she was aggrieved by her diocesan in any matter, she was permitted to appeal.

Having carefully heard from that cardinal these and the other matters proposed before him, we command your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 0561A] that, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, you declare void and without effect whatever has been done concerning the election of the aforesaid nun; and, after diligently investigating the truth concerning the election of the custodian herself, if you find that election canonical and her person suitable, confirm her by apostolic authority; restraining opponents, etc. If not all … two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 2 March, etc.

IV [Note: [Col. 0561C]

See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §62.

This letter is printed in full, though without chronological notes, in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, among the addenda, p. 980, where it is said to have been drawn from the *Chronicle of St Swithun of Winchester*, [Col. 0561D] p. 8.]

. . . . . TO THE PRIOR [Note: [Col. 0561D]

Concerning the priors of the Church of Winchester around the period with which we are concerned, nothing is found in the records relating to that church in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I. Only this is read in the *Annals of the Church of Winchester*, in the same author, ibid., p. 302:

“In the year 1187 … John, prior of the church of Winchester, a man of good simplicity, departed to the Lord; Robert son of Henry succeeded him.”]

AND MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF WINCHESTER, PRESENT AND FUTURE, IN PERPETUITY. He receives them under his protection and enumerates the properties belonging to them. (At St Peter’s, 3 March.)

[Col. 0561B]

[“Whenever we are petitioned by …,” etc., down to [Note: [Col. 0561D] The omitted material may be supplied from *Monasticon Anglicanum*, cited place.] “we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of Pope Lucius II, our predecessor of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Winchester, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions, whatever goods,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0561D] The same source.], down to “to be expressly named”: Chiltecumbe and all its tithe; Eston, Wordia [Note: [Col. 0561D] In *Monasticon Anglicanum*: Wasington, Aujutonia, Meones, Brekford, Henton, Halwarstokis, Havents, Crondola, Hodington, Waton, Hennenton, Chilbolton, Mitteshullengs; Melbrok, Eston, Stocton, Eneford, Asida, Wosnerichston, Westwod, Dludon, Harnie, Husseburig, Wentana, Chise.], Wensieston, Avinton, Lesser Meon, Brockenesford, Exton, [Col. 0561C] Enton, Helwarestoke, Haveunte, Crundel, Hodigaton, Wutron, Hennenton, Cilbodinton, Michelemareis, Nhutsilinges, Melebroc, Heton, Stocton, Enedeford, Patenga, Awelton, Fifhida, Ellendon, Hinnelton, Wuluricheston, Westiwud, Bludun, Hamma, Husseburn, Wittcherche; revenues in the city and suburb of Winchester; the fishery at Brenford; Clive; Brandesbiri; all the tithe of the demesnes of that church, for the works [Note: [Col. 0562C] In the *Monasticon*: “work.”] of the church and houses belonging to it; Portland; the lands, fiefs, and [Col. 0562A] military services belonging to that church; reasonable customs and liberties, both in buying and selling and in other matters, granted by royal charters; an annual pension [Note: [Col. 0562C] In the *Monasticon*: “annual pensions.”] of twenty pounds from the fair of St Giles; an annual pension of ten marks from the Hospital of the Holy Cross, for the church lights; the church of Drokeneford; the church of Crundel [Note: [Col. 0562C] In the *Monasticon*: Cromal.]; the church of Haveunte; the church of Wilhale [Note: [Col. 0562C] In the *Monasticon*: Winchale.]; the church of St Faith; the church of St Giles; the church of St James; and all Pentecost offerings [Note: [Col. 0562D] Omitted in the *Monasticon*.]; for the anniversary of Bishop H. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Henry of Blois, brother of King Stephen, succeeded William Giffard as bishop of Winchester from being abbot of Glastonbury, in 1129. He sat for forty-three years. See Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, pp. 282, 285, 299. See also the note to Innocent’s book V, letter 104.] of blessed memory, the chapels of Chittecumbe [Note: [Col. 0562D] In the *Monasticon*: “the chapel of Eddecunta.”], the church of Campton, and the church of the White [Note: [Col. 0562D] In the *Monasticon*: Abo.] Monastery; for the anniversary of King Henry II, the land of Cnoel; for the anniversary of Bishop Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0562D] Godfrey de Lucy, bishop of Winchester, died in 1204, on 11 September. *Annals of the Church of Winchester*, in Wharton, cited place, p. 305.] of blessed memory, the land of Childecnoel; for making books, the church of Elendon; for receiving religious guests, the church of Litleton. When the bishop of that see dies, no one is to be placed there by any craft of surreptitious dealing or violence; rather, you are permitted, without anyone’s objection, together with the archdeacons, by common counsel or the counsel of the sounder part, to elect a bishop in the fear of God and according to the ordinances of the sacred canons. Therefore we decree,” etc., down to [Note: [Col. 0562D] The omitted material may be supplied from *Monasticon Anglicanum*, cited place.] “advantageous, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore …,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0562D] The same source.] “But to all …”]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of [Col. 0562C] John, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, on 3 March, indiction 8, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

V [Note: [Col. 0562D] Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §61.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY [Note: [Col. 0562D] See book V, letters 54 and 104, notes.], AND TO THE BISHOPS OF ELY [Note: [Col. 0562D] See book V, letter 54, note.] AND LONDON [Note: [Col. 0562D] See book VII, letter 182, note.]. That the king of England should permit the monks of Winchester freely to proceed to the election of a bishop. (At St Peter’s, 9 March.)

If secular rulers carefully considered that Uzziah, king of Judah, [Col. 0563A] was struck with leprosy on his face because, clothed in the ephod, he presumed to burn incense, they would not presume to exercise any jurisdiction over ecclesiastical matters that do not concern them. But our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English, as has been reported to us, wishing unlawfully to usurp for himself what does not belong to him, does not permit our beloved sons, the convent and archdeacons of the church of Winchester, freely to proceed in that church concerning the election of a bishop [Note: [Col. 0563D] See the note to the preceding letter.]. Since it does not become royal eminence to dispose concerning the election of a bishop, which should freely be celebrated by those to whom it belongs, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters and precept carefully to admonish and effectively induce the king to permit the aforesaid monks and archdeacons free power to elect a bishop. Otherwise, compel those monks and archdeacons by ecclesiastical censure to provide canonically for the Church of Winchester with a pastor within forty days of receiving our letters, all obstacle of contradiction or appeal being removed; and restrain any disturbers by similar severity. If not all … two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 9 March.

VI. TO THE BISHOP OF ELY [Note: [Col. 0563D] He has already been mentioned often.], THE ABBOT OF ST EDMUND’S [Note: [Col. 0563D] See book V, letter 90, note.], AND THE DEAN OF CHICHESTER. That they grant the archbishop of York absolution from the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him for violently laying hands on clerics. (At St Peter’s, 26 February.)

[Col. 0563C]

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of York [Note: [Col. 0563D] See book V, letters 54, 56, 70, 129.], has shown us by his representation that, although we had committed to you for due settlement the case known to be pending between himself on the one side and the dean and chapter of York on the other concerning losses and injuries inflicted upon him by them [Note: [Col. 0563D] See book VII, letter 35, which is stated to be addressed to these same persons: the bishop of Ely, the abbot of St Edmund’s, and the dean of Chichester—for this is how it should be read, not “of Cîteaux,” as we there published it in error.], because the dean and chapter, in order to impede the progress of the case, repeatedly objected that he had violently [Col. 0563D] laid hands upon a certain priest and other clerics, you delayed proceeding in the case. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic [Col. 0564A] letters that, when the archbishop requests you to do so, after receiving from him sufficient security according to the form of the Church, you grant him, in our stead, the benefit of absolution; and, after diligently investigating the truth, inform us by your letters what you find concerning these matters.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 26 February, etc., in the eighth year.

VII. [Note: [Col. 0563D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §59.] … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN [Note: [Col. 0563D] See letter 31 of Book V, note.], AND … TO THE BISHOP OF AVRANCHES [Note: [Col. 0563D] See letter 226 of Book VII, note.] … TO THE BISHOP OF LISIEUX [Note: [Col. 0563D] See letter 70 of Book V, note.] … TO THE BISHOP OF COUTANCES [Note: [Col. 0563D] Vivian then presided over the Church of Coutances. He was consecrated in 1202 (according to the chronicle of Blancaelanda), held office until 1208, and died on 15 February. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 877.], AND … TO THE BISHOP OF SÉEZ [Note: [Col. 0564D] See letter 70 of Book V, note.]. Reply is made that, concerning the rendering of fealty which they are to make to the king of France, they should do what law and custom prescribe. (At St Peter’s, the Nones of March.)

From the letters which you sent to our presence, we have learned that, since our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, has now subjected the land of Normandy to his authority, and has received fealties both from the barons and from all laymen, he now persistently demands from you the fealty which the bishops of that region customarily render to the duke of Normandy. He asserts that, justice having gone before, he acquired Normandy by the judgment of his court, and that you are therefore bound to render him fealty. You accordingly requested to be informed by our letters what you ought to do in this matter. But since neither law nor custom is known to us in this case—for we do not know the cause, manner, and order, or the other circumstances—we cannot give you a definite answer on a doubtful matter, except that you, who can investigate the truth of the matter more fully, should prudently do what ought, according to God, to be done by law or custom.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of March, in the eighth year.

VIII. [Note: [Col. 0564D] This letter, though very mutilated and corrupt, is found among the *Decretals*, Book II, title 27, “On judgment and res judicata,” chapter 18. Schoefflinus published it entire, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, p. 312, document 372. There, however, it is addressed to the archbishop of Canterbury and the bishops of Ely and London.] … TO THE ABBOT OF BONGAR [Note: [Col. 0564D] This concerns the monastery of Pomarium or Pomerium, commonly Baumgarden or Baumgart, in French *Verger*, or St Bernard’s at Pomerium, now ruined. The incomplete series of abbots of this monastery in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 850, names no one in the period with which we are concerned except Maximian, abbot in 1195.] AND TO THE PROVOST OF ST ARBOGAST, IN THE DIOCESE OF STRASBOURG, AND TO THE CUSTODIAN OF ST THOMAS AT STRASBOURG. He adjudicates a case concerning the church of Westhusen. (At St Peter’s, the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0564D]

[Since Berthold, a knight, had once pledged to Peregrinus [Note: [Col. 0565C] In the *Decretals*, P.], a knight, his *curia* [Note: [Col. 0564D] A *curia* is a village or manor with a holding. [Col. 0565B] Abbot of Ursberg, on Lothar of Saxony: “Of this *curia* there are eleven hundred holdings, comprised in one *mallus*.” Its diminutive, *curtis*, has the same meaning in Flodoard, *Chronicle*, under the year 937: “A certain [Col. 0565C] priest of the *curtis* of Bononis—for so the village is called.” And Adam of Bremen, Book IV: “The archbishop therefore had fifty demesne courts, of which Walde, the largest, rendered one month’s service, whereas Ambergon, the smallest, rendered fourteen days.” Du Cange, however (*Glossary*, vol. II, col. 1252), explains it as: “a rural estate, possession, court, holding.”] or estate [Col. 0565A] in Westhusen, Berthold having died, Hartong [Note: [Col. 0565C] In the *Decretals*, A; shortly afterward they omit “of the diocese of Strasbourg” and “in Westhusen.”], his nephew and successor, of the diocese of Strasbourg, while the church of that place at Westhusen was vacant, claiming that the right of patronage had passed to him together with the estate, presented Bruno [Note: [Col. 0565C] In the *Decretals*, D; shortly afterward it omits the words “at the request … bishop.”]—a cleric of the same diocese—to the said church, at the request of C. of blessed memory, bishop of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0565C] Conrad II or III, born of the noble Alsatian baronial family of Hunnenberg, was elected bishop of Strasbourg in 1190. Since, in the imperial schism, he adhered to Otto, duke of Saxony, whereas the people of Strasbourg adhered to Philip, duke of Swabia (both having been elected kings of the Romans), he suffered much at the hands of the citizens, including imprisonment, and at last died amid those miseries in 1202.]; and the archdeacon of the same place, with the bishop’s consent and will [Note: [Col. 0565D] The *Decretals* omit this word.], to whom Hartong had presented Bruno for the said church, instituted him therein and caused him to be put in corporeal possession.

But the aforesaid Berthold [Note: [Col. 0565D] The *Decretals*, B; shortly afterward they omit the words “claiming … creditor,” and read “did not admit” in place of “refused … admit.”], lord of the estate, asserting that he had expressly retained the right of patronage when he pledged the estate to the creditor, presented T. …, a priest, to the aforesaid bishop [Col. 0565B]; but the bishop refused, at his own discretion, to admit him. When the aforesaid bishop had entered upon the way of all flesh, T. … brought a suit against the said Bruno [Note: [Col. 0565D] Omitted in the *Decretals*; shortly afterward D reads differently for “Bruno,” and again omits the words “before the deputy of the elect.”] concerning the said church before the deputy of the bishop-elect [Note: [Col. 0565D] Henry, a noble Swabian, descended from the illustrious family of the counts of Veringen, was a canon of the Church of Mainz before being raised to the bishopric of Strasbourg (George Christian, catalogue of the canons of that church, p. 405). He is also called custodian of the Church of Strasbourg in the *History of Alsace*. He was elected in 1202, although he was not consecrated until 1206 or even 1207 by the archbishop of Sens, at the pope’s command. The reason for postponing the consecration was the schism in the Church of Mainz; for he ought to have been confirmed and consecrated by the archbishop of Mainz. Indeed, Henry is styled merely bishop-elect of Strasbourg when he appears as a witness in 1204, on the day before the Ides of January, in a charter of Philip, king of the Romans, confirming many things to Adolf, archbishop of Cologne. A good and religious man and defender of the clergy, he died in 1223, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, and was buried in the chapel of St Andrew beside the cathedral, in which he had occupied the see for twenty-one years.]. From his examination an appeal was subsequently made to our venerable brother …, archbishop of Rheims, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, then bishop of Palestrina [Note: [Col. 0566C] Much has already been said of him. See letter 8 of Book V, note, and especially letter 121 of Book VII.], legate of the Apostolic See. He directed his beloved sons, … abbot of Neuburg [Note: [Col. 0566C] Peter I, abbot of Neuburg or Neoburg, occurs in instruments in 1201. In 1205 he obtained two charters from Emperor Philip, and one from Pope Innocent III, dated the third day before the Nones of May, indiction XI, pontifical year XI—that is, 1208. He still occurs in 1209, 1211, and 1212; and at last, on 7 October 1214, after eighteen years of rule, he departed this life. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 886.], and … dean of St Thomas at Strasbourg [Col. 0566A], to hear the allegations on both sides and, after receiving witnesses, to remit the case to him adequately instructed, assigning the parties a peremptory term by which they were to present themselves before him to receive judgment.

They received the witnesses and reduced their depositions to writing; under their seals they sent these to the aforesaid archbishop, having assigned the parties a peremptory term. When the aforesaid Bruno appeared at that term with his attestations, but T. … had not taken care to appear before him either in person or through a suitable representative [Note: [Col. 0566C] The *Decretals* read “had deposed”; the archbishop of Rheims, [Col. 0566D] legate of the Apostolic See, delegated the case to judges. When the attestations received from each side had subsequently been sent to him by the parties, and D. appeared with his attestations, T. took no care to appear either in person or through a suitable representative.], the archbishop, having diligently examined Bruno’s attestations, as we perceived them to be contained in his letters [Note: [Col. 0566D] The *Decretals*: “having examined the attestations of the aforesaid cleric”; shortly afterward, “by way of judgment” for “in rendering judgment.”], pronounced Bruno absolved from the claim of the aforesaid T. …, imposing silence upon T. concerning the said church.

Afterward, however, the aforesaid T., appearing before the same archbishop within a short time with his attestations, alleged a just cause for his absence. The archbishop therefore gave letters of mandate to the aforesaid bishop-elect of Strasbourg and to his beloved sons [Note: [Col. 0566D] The *Decretals* read “the same priest” in place of “the aforesaid T.”; shortly afterward they omit “with his attestations” and read “of Strasbourg” for “the aforesaid bishop-elect of Strasbourg.”], … abbots of Alta Silva and … Turceleburn [Note: [Col. 0566D] We have nothing at hand concerning the abbeys of Alta Silva and Turceleburn, as it is read here; or of Alta Silva and Tudebernen, according to the reading exhibited by the *Decretals*.], that, if the aforesaid man [Note: [Col. 0566D] The *Decretals* omit “beloved sons”; shortly afterward they read “of Alta Silva and Tudebern,” and below “gave their letters” for “gave letters of mandate.”] should establish before them a just cause for his absence, they should declare the preceding judgment to be of no validity and, after diligently examining the attestations of both parties [Note: [Col. 0566D] The *Decretals* omit “aforesaid” and shortly afterward add “he” after “cause.” The *Decretals* firmly omit the words “of both parties … examined,” as well as the following words, “finally, the judgment which he himself had rendered …”.], bring the case to its due conclusion; otherwise, they were to cause the judgment which he himself had rendered to be firmly observed.

But since the said bishop-elect, being occupied with other business, could not be present, he entrusted his authority to R. …, canon of Strasbourg; and the aforesaid abbots entrusted theirs to … the chief provost [Note: [Col. 0567D]

XI. Albert I, provost of Strasbourg in 1202, during whose time seven archdeacons were established in the Church of Strasbourg.

“XII. Arnold, 1209.” *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 823.]

and … the scholasticus of Strasbourg. Proceeding in the case, they received witnesses concerning the aforesaid issue; and, after their depositions had been reduced to writing, the aforesaid B. …, alleging that he was aggrieved by them [Note: [Col. 0567D] The *Decretals* read: “The bishop-elect and the aforesaid abbots, entrusting their offices to others, the subdelegates received witnesses concerning the aforesaid issue; by whom the said cleric …”], lodged an appeal to us.

When, therefore, both parties came before us with attestations sealed with the seals of the aforesaid judges [Note: [Col. 0567D] The *Decretals* omit “When, therefore … came”; they read “however” for “the aforesaid T.” and insert “priest” after “adequately.”], although the said T. had proved his just cause of absence less than adequately, yet, lest appearance prejudice truth, and wishing to proceed according to truth, since Christ [Col. 0567B] is truth, we granted them as auditor our beloved son R. …, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Dominica [Note: [Col. 0567D] The *Decretals* omit the words “wishing … Dominica,” and afterward omit “those things … had been”; below they read “all” for “fully and,” and shortly afterward lack the word “his.”] [Note: [Col. 0567D] “R., cardinal deacon of St Mary in Dominica,” or “R., cardinal deacon.” Thus it is explicitly read in Conti’s transcript and in the *Decretals*—incorrectly in both. We confess that we do not know what titular church “St Mary in Dominica” is. Perhaps *St Mary in Cosmedin* should be read. Yet at that time John, count of Anagni, of whom we have already spoken above, bore that title, and could not be designated by the initial R.]. When he had fully and faithfully reported to us the matters alleged before him, we diligently examined the attestations of both parties and the judgment of the aforesaid archbishop. We found that archbishop, from the tenor of his judgment, to have been misled: first, because it stated that Bruno’s attestations [Note: [Col. 0568D] The *Decretals* read “of the cleric,” and shortly afterward “A.” for “Hartong”; below, they omit “Bruno” and the words “on this point.”] had sufficiently proved that the aforesaid Hartong had been in possession of the right of patronage when he presented Bruno to the aforesaid church, whereas those attestations had shown nothing else on this point except that Peregrinus [Col. 0567C] and Hartong [Note: [Col. 0568D] The *Decretals* read “A. and P.” and omit what follows in italic type.] annually received ten solidi for a certain right which was customarily rendered from that church to its patrons, although the parish priest of that place always objected to paying them; secondly, because that judgment says that T. … wholly failed in proof, whereas it is manifest from his attestations that he had sufficiently proved his claim; and also because the archbishop had not received the case adequately instructed, having received the attestations of only one party, which contributed little to the case.

For these and other reasons understood [Note: [Col. 0568D] The *Decretals* read “therefore” for “these and other reasons understood.”], we judged that judgment should be annulled, adjudicating the aforesaid church to T. …, since the attestations [Col. 0568A] clearly established before us that he had been presented to the often-mentioned church by the true patron; and we impose perpetual silence upon his adversary concerning it.] Therefore, by apostolic writings, we strictly command your discretion that, supported by our authority, you cause our judgment to be inviolably observed, putting the aforesaid T. into corporeal possession of the same church and protecting him once installed. Opponents … notwithstanding no letters, etc. But if not all … any two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Ides of March.

IX. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Raynaldus supplies a fragment of this letter under the year 1205, §63. The words found in his text are enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE KING OF ARAGON. That he should desist from certain harassments of the Church of Elne. Many points are added by which it is recognized that he is bound to preserve fidelity to the Roman Church. (At St Peter’s, the fourth day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0568B]

Far be it from you, dearest son, that the story might be turned against you which reports that King Ahab demanded that Naboth the Israelite grant him the vineyard adjoining the royal house, so that he might make in it a vegetable garden; and when he could not obtain it, nevertheless took possession of it after killing its owner. For we have learned that, under the pretext that the canons proceeded to celebrate the election of a bishop of the Church of Elne without you [Note: [Col. 0568D] The succession of bishops of Elne around the period in question is uncertain. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 1050, give Berengar V in 1205. But in the year “4206” [probably 1206] William of Ortafano is found as bishop of that see; he died in 1209.], you have grievously harassed that church, violently occupying its castles and possessions [Col. 0568C] and plundering its land, until you received from it a ransom at the discretion of your own will.

Although we previously wrote to you on this matter, carefully entreated you, and even enjoined you, for the remission of sins, to restore without any obstacle of difficulty all that you had taken to the bishop and chapter of the same church, to usurp nothing further in that church to the peril of your salvation, and indeed to defend and foster it, together with the other churches situated in your kingdom, more generously: you, turning your royal face toward the wall against our commands, have been unwilling in any degree [Col. 0569A] to heed us in these matters. You are intent on appropriating that church to yourself as a vineyard adjoining your dwelling and reducing it to a garden which may yield you vegetables—that is, the continual services which you incessantly impose upon it. You have risen against it with greater zeal after an apostolic command intervened on its behalf, not considering that for several reasons you are bound to that church by fidelity, and displaying yourself as wholly undevoted in all things toward the church to which you ought to be devoted.

Even now you exact so many and such great exactions from it, and afflict it so severely, that you seem, as though its ruler had been stoned, to have seized the vineyard for yourself. Therefore, lest you thus covet another’s property—or rather, things to which you ought especially to furnish your protection—we earnestly admonish and exhort your royal serenity, [Col. 0569B] and by apostolic writings command you, enjoining this for the remission of sins, to desist from undue harassment of that church in these and other matters; not to impede the elections of its bishops, whoever they may be at the time, nor, so far as lies in your power, permit them to be impeded by others; and to restore all that you are known to have taken from it or caused to be taken, so that you may not appear thereby to hate the true owner of the vineyard, namely Jesus Christ, who introduced diverse laborers at diverse hours for its cultivation.

See, then, dearest son in Christ, what is expedient for your salvation and honor in this matter. For if you thus seize Naboth’s vineyard, that prophetic saying may deservedly [Col. 0569C] be turned against you: “You have killed, and moreover have taken possession,” if you reduce the vineyard of liberty to a garden of servitude. [But we, who do not wish your salvation to be impeded, but rather desire it more earnestly in Christ, enjoin our beloved sons, the abbot of Cîteaux [Note: [Col. 0569D] See letter 109 of Book V.], P. … of Castronovo, and R. …, monks of Fontfroide, legates of the Apostolic See, diligently to admonish and induce you on our behalf in these matters, and, if necessary, to compel you by such coercive means as they see expedient, any appeal being set aside.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the eighth year of the pontificate.

They were written to on this matter.

X. [Note: [Col. 0569D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §59.] TO G. [Note: [Col. 0569D] See letter 121 of Book VII.], ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. He commands him in a provincial council to compel archdeacons and deans to receive sacred orders. (At St Peter’s, the third day before the Nones of March.)

[Col. 0569D]

Since a burden is joined to honor, he who has received a benefice ought to perform its office. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, by the authority of these presents we grant you that, after you have solemnly enjoined your fellow bishops in a provincial council to compel both archdeacons and deans to receive the orders in which they are bound to serve the Lord, according to the decrees of the Lateran Council, if [Col. 0570A] they perhaps neglect within six months to fulfill this, you shall thereafter not fail to carry it out, the obstacle of appeal being removed. But if they refuse to be ordained, you may confer their benefices upon other persons, as is decreed in the same council. Therefore let no one … our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of March, in the eighth year of the pontificate.

XI. [Note: [Col. 0570D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §59.] TO THE SAME. That he should not permit any regular abbot to stand surety. (At St Peter’s, the Nones of March.)

We have learned that monasteries in both the diocese and province of Rheims have come to such impoverishment, because their persons and prelates [Col. 0570B] receive money on loan at interest and spend it where it is unlawful, that, their possessions being pledged and their servants dispersed, they cannot maintain themselves as they formerly did. Therefore, by apostolic writings, we strictly command your brotherhood to prohibit, under our authority, any abbot, prior, monk, or regular canon of your province from standing surety for anyone or receiving money on loan from anyone beyond the amount fixed by prudent provision for their chapters, except for a manifest benefit of their houses; and, if anything has been done, to declare that the communities are not bound to make payment.

And that our prohibition may have greater force, by the authority of these presents we grant you that you restrain, by ecclesiastical censure, those who presume to act contrary to it, notwithstanding any objection or appeal. Therefore let no one, etc. Let no one violate this page of our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of March, in the eighth year.

XII. [Note: [Col. 0570D] In the same place.] TO C. …, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. Authority to correct what requires correction in the monasteries of the province of Rheims. (At St Peter’s, the eighth day before the Ides of March.)

A ruler’s care ought to be such that, amid concern with outward affairs, he does not lessen his care for inward ones, nor abandon care of external affairs through concern for internal ones; and he should watch so diligently that, while conferring necessary benefit on others outwardly, he preserves inwardly the needful benefit for himself. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, that you may more fully fulfill in these matters what you ought, by the authority of these presents we grant you that, in the churches and monasteries of the province of Rheims, some of which suffer grave loss both within and without, in head and members, you may correct by apostolic authority whatever ought according to God to be corrected. By that same authority, you may, with the counsel of prudent men, change for the better the customs concerning the law and advantage of churches, if those to whom their correction immediately pertains are negligent in these matters; notwithstanding the interposition of any appeal against the observance of regular discipline. Thus serve the benefit of such churches that you advance regular discipline. But if anyone, etc. Therefore let no one, etc. Let no one violate this page of our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of March.

XIII. G. …, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. That he should observe the statutes of the Lateran Council concerning vacant churches and prebends. (At St Peter’s, the seventh day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0571B] The authority of the Lateran Council decreed that, when churches and prebends, or any offices, happen to become vacant in a church, they should not long remain in suspense, but within six months should be conferred upon persons able worthily to administer them. If the bishop, where their conferral belongs to him, delays to confer them, they shall be provided by the chapter. But if election belongs to the chapter and it neglects to do this within the prescribed term, the bishop shall carry it out with the counsel of religious men. If all perhaps neglect it, the metropolitan shall, according to God, dispose of them without their objection.

Since things specially granted are usually more effective than those generally conceded, we have judged it proper, by the authority of these presents, [Col. 0571C] to grant your brotherhood that you carry out, in both the diocese and the province of Rheims, without any objection or appeal, the decrees already enacted by the beloved council. Therefore let no one … violate this page of our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the eighth year.

XIV. G. …, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. That he may revoke alienations unlawfully made by his predecessors. (At St Peter’s, the eighth day before the Ides of March.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., down to “to confer.” Therefore, etc., down to “assenting,” by the authority [Col. 0571D] of these presents we grant you that you may lawfully revoke, notwithstanding any objection or appeal, whatever you find to have been unlawfully alienated by your predecessor W. of blessed memory from property belonging to the archiepiscopal mensa and from other things subject to the jurisdiction of the archbishop, whether held in fief or otherwise. Therefore let no one … violate this page of our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the eighth year.

XV. G. …, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. That he may revoke grants unlawfully made by his predecessors. (At St Peter’s, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0572A]

It belongs to a shepherd’s care to provide for his right in such a manner that it is not unjustly withheld from him by others, lest he be negligent where he ought to be diligent, since diligence brings increase and negligence loss. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, by the authority of these presents we grant you that it shall be lawful for you, without obstacle of objection or appeal, canonically to recall to your power and hand altars, tithes, revenues, jurisdictions, and other things which your predecessor W. of blessed memory withdrew from the disposal and authority of himself and his successors [Col. 0572B] by unlawfully granting them in perpetuity to churches and monasteries and to certain persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XVI. [Note: [Col. 0571D] This letter is found among the *Decretals*, Book II, title 24, “On Oaths,” chapter 20.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: [Col. 0571D] See letter 9 of Book III, note.]. Concerning a certain oath not to reclaim usury. (At St Peter’s, the Ides of March.)

[You should know that it has come to our hearing that J. Pellar [Note: [Col. 0571D] The *Decretals* omit the words distinguished by italic type down to “made his will.”] and his son G. had paid no small amount of usury to Peter [Col. 0572C] Soctan; and, having sworn an oath, they affirmed that neither personally nor through another would they reclaim the said usury or bring a suit concerning it before an ecclesiastical or secular judge. When that creditor, being at the point of death, made his will, he commanded his heirs to arrange for the restoration of such usury to all who could reasonably prove [Note: [Col. 0571D] The *Decretals* read “proved,” and shortly afterward “them” for [Col. 0572D] “the same persons.” Below they add “and” before “heirs” and have “neglect” for “neglect.”] that they had paid usury to him. Therefore, since the aforesaid J. and G. do not venture to reclaim the usury because of this oath, the heirs of the aforesaid P. neglect to satisfy them concerning it.

Therefore, by apostolic writings [Note: [Col. 0572D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*.], we command your brotherhood to cause, or yourself to cause, an announcement to be publicly made in church under pain of excommunication, that those who know the truth of this matter should come forward to give testimony. If by the statements of witnesses or other documents the foregoing is lawfully established before you, compel the heirs of the same P. [Note: [Col. 0572D] The *Decretals*: “of that man.”]—after prior admonition and by ecclesiastical censure, appeal removed—to restore all the usury which their father received from the aforesaid J. and G. [Note: [Col. 0572D] The words following are absent from the *Decretals*, which instead read “ecclesiastical censure” for “after prior admonition, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal removed.”].

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Ides of March.

XVII. TO THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0573D] John de la Mousche, the fifth of that name, governed the Church of Dol from 1199 to 1224. *Gallia Christiana vetus*, vol. II, p. 567.] AND TO HIS BELOVED SONS, … THE CHANTER AND … THE ARCHDEACON OF DOL. That they should grant W., a priest whose genitals had been amputated in addition to wounds inflicted upon him, permission to exercise the priestly office, and pronounce a sentence of excommunication against those committing such a crime. (At St Peter’s, the fifth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0573A]

Appearing before the Apostolic See, our beloved son W. …, priest, showed us in a grave complaint that, when long ago, during the days of the Lord’s Passion, he was passing through the village of Avortii and turned aside to the house of the knight Pelochin to quench the thirst incurred through the labor of the journey, the men of that knight [Col. 0573B]—who had long before quarreled with him over tithes and a certain debt—together with W. …, knight, his sons, and certain others of the diocese of Angers, in order to please the aforesaid Pelochin, rashly seized the priest, grievously wounded him, treated him most dishonorably while bound throughout the whole day, and finally, after cutting off his genitals, left him despoiled of all his possessions.

Therefore, showing mercy to the afflicted man, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that, if you know the matter to be so and no other canonical impediment stands in the way, you grant him by our authority permission to exercise the priestly office. But compel the said sacrilegious persons, so long, appeal removed, etc., down to “to absolve,” and nevertheless compel them to make due restitution of what was taken, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal [Col. 0573C] set aside. Witnesses … notwithstanding no letters, etc. But if not all … you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XVIII. … TO THE BISHOP OF ORVIETO [Note: [Col. 0573D] Matthew Alberic succeeded Richard in the bishopric of Orvieto in 1204. The name of his successor, John Castelli of Bologna, is not found before 1211. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, [Col. 0574D] special part, * col. 386.]. That in the matrimonial case between James, knight of Città della Pieve, and the woman M., he may proceed notwithstanding a certain decretal of Pope Alexander, whose meaning is here explained. (At St Peter’s, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.)

In your letters you informed us that, when we had committed to you for decision the matrimonial case between James, knight of Città della Pieve, and the woman M., brought before us by appeal [Col. 0573D], the knight, who impugned the marriage, proved that he and the same woman were related in the fourth and fifth degrees of consanguinity. But the woman sufficiently established through witnesses that she had cohabited matrimonially with the said knight for eighteen years or more, and had borne at least three sons by him. She accordingly maintained that, according to the decretal of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory [Col. 0574A], she ought not to be separated from him on such a ground.

Although both parties urgently sought judgment, you did not consent to their request, but humbly consulted us about it, because that decretal seemed contrary to the ancient canons. Therefore, having caused it to be read before us, we inferred from its tenor that the decretal applies to the case in which the suit has not yet been joined before a judge, since it says there: “If anyone has married a woman in the face of the Church and has cohabited with her for a long time, he ought not to be admitted to an accusation, unless other suitable persons, free from suspicion, appear who are willing and able lawfully to impugn the marriage; but even they ought not to be admitted if the man and woman have lived together for twenty or eighteen years without dispute.”

See: it says here that persons of this sort are not simply to be admitted to bring an accusation. Therefore, as we have stated, such a decretal applies when an accusation against the marriage has not yet been admitted. For then the Church, on account of the length of time, in a certain way dispenses by overlooking, and overlooks by dispensing. But where the party entitled to use the benefit of that decretal has neglected to do so, and after lawful joinder of issue the parties have produced their witnesses and, after publication of the depositions, renunciation has been made by both sides, so that nothing now remains except [Col. 0574C] the pronouncement of judgment, we do not see why the judge should not decide the case brought before him and examined according to the ancient canons—especially if both parties, or either one, insist that judgment be pronounced.

Given at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

XIX. [Note: [Col. 0574D] It is read in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §93, and is therefore enclosed here in brackets. Raynaldus supplies a fragment of the same letter under the year 1205, §16. The passages found in his text are marked by a double stroke placed in the margin at the beginning of each line.] TO THOMAS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. Concerning the consecration of the patriarch of Constantinople. (At St Peter’s, the third day before the Kalends of April.)

[Note: [Col. 0574D] This is found in Raynaldus.] “The prerogative of affection and grace which the Apostolic See showed to the Byzantine Church when it raised it to patriarchal rank plainly bears witness to the fullness of ecclesiastical power which not man but God—indeed, more truly, God made man—conferred in blessed Peter upon the Roman Church, and shows that the Roman pontiff is His vicar, he who makes the first last and the last first. For when that same Church, then called Byzantine and now Constantinopolitan, had neither name nor place among the apostolic patriarchal sees, the Apostolic See gave it a great name, like the name of the great ones who are on earth, and raised it, as it were, from the dust so high that it preferred it in the privilege of dignity to the Churches of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem alike, and exalted it above all others after itself; so that, although many daughters have amassed riches, this one alone, through the special favor of its mother, surpassed them all. Although that same Church at times turned aside from obedience to the Apostolic See, yet, because by God’s grace it has humbly returned to it, yielding to your prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves that Church over which, by God the Lord as author, you are known to preside, and we fortify it by the page of this present writing.” [Note: [Col. 0575D] Raynaldus ends here.]

Moreover, whatever possessions, goods, and estates that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs and of ecclesiastical or secular persons, of whatever condition or rank, shall remain unimpaired to you and your successors. We also confirm the liberties and immunities of that Church, and its reasonable and ancient customs which do not conflict with the ordinances of the Apostolic See; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time.

We also grant to your brotherhood the pallium, the insignia, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office, by the freedom of the Apostolic See, for use within the churches subject to your jurisdiction at solemn Masses on the days specified below: the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Stephen the Protomartyr; the Circumcision of the Lord; the Epiphany; Hypapante; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter; Easter Monday; the Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of blessed Mary; the Nativity of John the Baptist; the solemnities of all the Apostles; the commemoration of All Saints; dedications of churches; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clerics; the principal feasts of your churches; the anniversary day of your consecration; and the funerals both of the emperor and of other magnates and princes.

Further, as a sign of fuller favor, by the authority of these presents we permit you to grant your archbishops, your suffragans, the use of the pallium by authority of this concession, receiving from them, on your own behalf, what is canonical, and on behalf of ourselves and the Roman Church a promise of obedience. Moreover, we grant your brotherhood permission to have the cross, that is, the Lord’s banner, carried before you wherever you happen to travel, except in the city of Rome and in a place where the Roman pontiff is present; and in your processions we grant you the use of a horse-cloth (*nacti*). [Note: [Col. 0575D] Thus in the Conti copy. So also in the manuscript of the Vatican Library, from which we had copied the letters found in the Formulary of Berardus of Naples; but erroneously in both places. It should read *nacti*. For *nactum*, or *nactus*, is the covering with which the whole horse is draped; see Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. V, col. 1134.]

Nevertheless, by the present writing we decree that all clerics, of whatever nation or people, holding churches or ecclesiastical benefices in the city and diocese of Constantinople, shall render to you and to the Church of Constantinople due reverence and devoted honor, without prejudice in all things to the authority, reverence, and honor of the Apostolic See. Therefore let no one infringe this our concession and protection, etc. If anyone should do so, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XX. [Note: [Col. 0576D] It is read in the *Gesta*, §98, and is therefore enclosed here in brackets. Raynaldus also mentions it under the year 1205, §16.] TO THE SAME THOMAS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He grants power to absolve from censures for striking a cleric, and to anoint the emperor of Constantinople. (At St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0576B]

[As the Lord, through the merits of blessed Peter, pours out His gifts upon the Roman Church, so He has enlarged its privilege, so that, however generous it may be toward others, it need fear neither loss of honor nor diminution of power. For it takes nothing away from itself when it bestows even the greatest gifts upon some; neither does it lose what it confers nor withdraw what it gives. For it so dispenses burdens and honors to those whom it calls to share its solicitude that the care of all the churches concerns it no less, and the fullness of ecclesiastical power adorns it no less, than Peter’s privilege permits it to be diminished.

Since, therefore, you have personally journeyed to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0576D] So also in the *Gesta*; but the cited Royal manuscript, noted by Baluze in the margin, has “you have come.”], have received through the laying on of our hands the orders of deacon and priest, and have at last been consecrated bishop [Note: [Col. 0576D] The cited Royal manuscript adds “at that See.”], we desire to show you special favor and to honor you personally. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, yielding to your just requests, by the authority of these presents we permit you to absolve, by our authority and in our stead and according to the Church’s form, your subjects who have laid violent hands upon clerics and other religious men—unless perhaps the offense is so enormous that you reasonably judge that they should be sent to the Apostolic See. We also commit to your brotherhood the absolution of forgers, if perchance they have committed forgery in your seal or in those of your subjects.

And so that, like a bridegroom coming forth from his mother’s chamber to his bride, clothed in variety and adorned with the garment of our indulgences, you may personally anoint any kings who are to be anointed in the empire of Constantinople, provided that the anointing is requested from you and the imperial assent is given. Therefore let no one infringe this our concession, etc.]

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXI. [Note: [Col. 0577D] It is read in the *Gesta*, §98, in continuous sequence with the immediately preceding letter, no. 20, and without chronological notices; it is therefore enclosed here in brackets. Raynaldus also mentions it under the year 1205, §16.] TO THOMAS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He grants power to promote persons to orders and to appoint suitable men to office. (At St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0577A]

[Because favors are given from favor, the abundance of favors poured out upon you will show that you have found favor with us. Yielding therefore to your prayers, we specially permit your brotherhood, when necessary, on Sundays and the principal solemnities, to promote suitable persons to the subdiaconate; and, since in the Church of Constantinople either none or few have been canonically instituted, to admit suitable men to it, the obstacle of appeal being removed. Do not yield to flesh and blood except as is fitting, but weigh merits and attend to learning, since in every nation whoever does justice is acceptable to God.] Therefore let no one infringe this our indulgence, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXII. [Note: [Col. 0577D] It is read in the *Gesta*, §98, in continuous sequence with the two immediately preceding letters, nos. 21 and 20, with chronological notices omitted; it is therefore enclosed here in brackets. Raynaldus also mentions it under the year 1205, §16.] TO THOMAS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. That, with the advice of prudent men, he may decide as he thinks expedient concerning the goods of his Church, without recourse to the Apostolic See in these matters. (At St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April.)

Although the form of the oath which you made to us, according to general custom, upon receiving the pallium specifically states that you shall neither sell, give away, pledge, newly enfeoff, nor in any way alienate, without consulting the Roman pontiff, possessions belonging to the table of your bishopric; nevertheless, because you have humbly consulted us on these matters, alleging your recent establishment, the need of the Church of Constantinople, and the disturbance of the whole land, lest you be compelled to have recourse to us for every affair, we grant you by the authority of these presents [Note: [Col. 0578D] Thus also in the *Gesta* and in the above-mentioned Vatican Library manuscript; but the above-mentioned Vallicellian manuscript has “having first made known.”] permission, when necessary, to decide in such matters, with the advice of prudent men, what you judge expedient for that Church and for yourself. Therefore let no one infringe this our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXIII. [Note: [Col. 0578D] It is read in the *Gesta*, §98, in continuous sequence with the three immediately preceding letters, nos. 22, 21, and 20, with chronological notices omitted; it is therefore enclosed here in brackets. Raynaldus also mentions it under the year 1205, §16.] TO THOMAS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He determines what is to be done in elections of patriarchs of the Church of Constantinople. (At St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0577D]

[By the authority of these presents we forbid that, upon the death of you, now patriarch of the Church of Constantinople, or of any of your successors, anyone there be put forward through any crafty device or violence, unless he has been elected according to the canonical sanctions. When he has been consecrated according to ecclesiastical custom, he shall send his envoys to the Apostolic See to seek the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, the insignia, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office. Upon receiving it, he shall without any contradiction render to us and to our successors, according to the custom of the Apostolic See, the oath which you yourself rendered to us upon receiving the pallium.

In addition, we grant your brotherhood that your subjects may freely appeal to your hearing when necessary, except where the business has been committed by the Apostolic See; provided that you humbly and devoutly defer to appeals lodged to the Roman Church.] Therefore let no one infringe this our prohibition and concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXIV. TO THOMAS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He permits retention of benefices and the use of the services of clerics who travelled with him to those regions. (At St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April.)

Although the empire of Constantinople has by God’s grace been transferred from the Greeks to the Latins, yet because its condition is not yet so firmly established that it does not in some respect remain unsettled, we desire, as far as we honorably can, to provide for your need. Therefore, by the authority of these presents we grant your brotherhood that you may retain intact the benefices which you have hitherto held and receive in full the fruits accruing from them, until we are more fully informed of the condition both of the empire and of the Church of Constantinople and decide otherwise on this matter.

And because you need the fellowship and counsel of experienced clerics, who may be provident collaborators and prudent helpers to you, by this present page we permit that clerics who have travelled with you to the regions of Constantinople shall not lose their benefices, but their revenues shall be paid to them in full until the condition of that land becomes more fully known to us; provided, however, that through the number of clerics wishing to travel with you no church is excessively burdened. Therefore let no one infringe this our concession, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXV. [Note: [Col. 0578D] It is read in the *Gesta*, §98, in continuous sequence with Letters 23, 22, 21, and 20 [Col. 0579D], which see, with chronological notices omitted; it is therefore enclosed here in brackets. Raynaldus also mentions it under the year 1205, §16.] TO THOMAS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. That the rights of the Church of Constantinople shall not be impaired because the pope himself elected the patriarch. (At St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April.)

[Although we do injury to no one whatever when we exercise our own right, and nothing is lost to anyone when we exercise the fullness of ecclesiastical power entrusted to us, nevertheless we wish prudently to provide for the Church of Constantinople and to remove material for murmuring from those who have deceitful lips and a malicious tongue.
