Therefore, although necessity and advantage required that Church—since, after the empire of Constantinople had passed to the Latins, it had not been ordered, and its ordering thus belonged to no one but ourselves—to elect you patriarch of Constantinople, confirm you when elected, and finally confer upon you the gift of consecration; yet, because we do not wish to take from that Church the liberty of canonical election, in which we rather intend to sustain and foster it, we do not wish any prejudice to arise from our action, so that, whenever it happens to be vacant, it may be canonically provided for.]

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXVI. TO THE PATRIARCH OF GRADO [Note: [Col. 0579D] See Letters 240 of Book VI, with note, and 74 and 200 of Book VII.] AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. He informs them that he has decreed that clerics with the patriarch of Constantinople shall not lose their benefices. (At St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April.)

Since the Church of Constantinople is now, as it were, being reborn into a new infancy and, like a little child without nourishing breasts, is known to have great need of a mother’s care, we intend to nurse it at the breasts of our consolation and relieve its poverty from our riches. Since it needs prudent and experienced clerics, who may build up the lives of laymen by word and example, at the request of our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, we have granted that clerics travelling with him to the regions of Constantinople shall not lose their benefices, but that their revenues shall be paid them in full until the condition of that land becomes more fully known to us; provided, however, that no church is excessively burdened through the number of clerics wishing to travel with him.

We therefore carefully admonish and exhort your brotherhood, and command you through these apostolic letters, that you neither trouble in any way, contrary to the tenor of our concession, those clerics who wish to follow him, nor permit or cause them to be troubled by others; rather, if anyone presumes to trouble them, after prior warning you shall restrain that person’s presumption by ecclesiastical coercion, appeal set aside.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, III Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXVII. TO THE PRIOR [Note: [Col. 0579D] See Letter 132 of Book V.] AND CHAPTER OF ST. SYLVAIN OF LEPROSO. He receives them under the protection of blessed Peter and enumerates their appurtenances. (At St. Peter’s, VII Kalends of March.)

The authority of the Apostolic See, together with the duty of our pastoral office, induces and compels us to extend the gaze of our consideration to the condition of all churches, lest they suffer loss in the goods which ought to be preserved unimpaired for them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, following the example of Pope Callistus, our predecessor of happy memory, the Church of blessed Sylvain, glorious confessor, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we protect it by the patronage of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions, goods, and estates your church possesses through the grant of Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges, of good memory [Note: [Col. 0579D] Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges from 1096 to 1120.], or through the lawful donations of other faithful persons, or may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, etc., shall be preserved to it peaceably and unimpaired. Among these we have thought fit to name expressly: the churches of St. Peter and St. Mary of the Mills; the churches of St. Lawrence and St. Martin of Vico, on the Naum; the church of St. Anianus of Langiac; the church of St. Columba and the church of St. Falerius, with their appurtenances; likewise the ecclesiastical dignity which your Church is known to hold in the church of Blessed Mencildis at Paludes; and also that which Rad.…, lord of Dôle, bestowed upon your church out of pious regard, both in his men, in permanent hereditary holdings and their property, and in possessions and other things. Concerning burial, etc., down to “shall oppose,” saving nevertheless justice, etc., down to “are assumed.” We therefore decree that no one shall infringe this page of our protection, confirmation, and constitution, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, VII Kalends of March, in the eighth year.

XXVIII. … ABBOTS OF ST. JULIAN [Note: [Col. 0580D] The abbots of St. Julian, Geoffrey I in 1173 and 1182, then immediately afterward Reginald in 1207 and 1209, are mentioned in the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 546, col. 1. D.], AND OF TURPINIAC [Note: [Col. 0580D] The Sammarthani do not date the foundation of the monastery of Turpiniac earlier than 1208: old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 885, col. 2. A. That it must be dated earlier is demonstrated by this letter of Innocent.], AND MASTER BALD…, CANON OF ST. MARTIN OF TOURS. He commits to them the determination of Master Peter of Vico’s case concerning a prebend granted to him in the Church of Bourges. (At St. Peter’s, VIII Kalends of April.)

Master P…, subdeacon and our chaplain, whom we had assigned as auditor to Master P. of Vico, beloved son, reported to us that, although our venerable brother …, archbishop [Note: [Col. 0581D] See Letter 52 of Book V, with note.], and the beloved sons, the chapter of Bourges, had been directed by our letters—as the said master alleged before him—to receive him as brother and canon and treat him with fraternal charity, they used words designed to evade the apostolic mandate and promised to receive him, though in the end they did not wish to fulfill what they had promised.

Having come into our presence, he carried back mandatory letters to them, obtaining monitors directed to the beloved sons …, abbot of Domo Dei, … of Nigro Lacus [Note: [Col. 0581D] “… of Domo Dei … of Nigro Lacus.” This is expressly read in the Vatican and Conti copies; but we fear that it should be read “… abbot of Domo Dei of Nigro Lacus.” For the monastery of Domo Dei is one and the same as the monastery of Nigro Lacus, otherwise Nerlac, concerning which see the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 195. William, known from documents from 1178 to 1215, was then its superior; see new *Gallia Christiana*, ibid.], and … abbot of Fonte-Mauriniac [Note: [Col. 0582D] Guy, abbot of Font-Morigny, is known from 1205 until at least 1208; see Letter 66 of Book VI, with note.]. Since certain members of the chapter, as letters sent to us by the said monitors stated, were maliciously striving to resist the reception of that master [Note: [Col. 0582D] See Letters 132 and the notes there, and 142 of Book V; 19 and 35 of Book VI.], we directed letters to the beloved sons … abbot of Dôle [Note: [Col. 0582D] See Letter 72 of Book V, with note.] and Eug., our subdeacon, prior of Leproso. They provided that, if the majority of the chapter agreed upon him, they should confer upon him the vacant prebend and receive him as canon and brother.

For his reception, as those executors informed us by their letters, the reason was that the said master had rendered devoted service in that church from his childhood and had received there sacred orders up to the diaconate. Yet, after the executors had prohibited them on our behalf, the archbishop and chapter conferred the prebend then vacant in the Church of Bourges upon Master P. Petit at their own discretion, and the executors invalidated that grant. Master P. Petit and R…, procurator of the aforesaid Master P. of Vico, then came into our presence and, by common consent, obtained that the case be committed to our venerable brother the bishop of Nevers [Note: [Col. 0582D] See Letter 11 of Book V, with note.], and the beloved sons … abbot of Pratea [Note: [Col. 0582D] See Letter 197 of Book VI, with note.] and … prior of Fonte-Mauriniac.

The said abbot was not present, but excused his absence by letter. Witnesses having been received on both sides and their testimony published, when they were preparing to give judgment, … chancellor of Bourges, in the name of the said chapter, fled to the device of appeal. Master P., who pursued that appeal at no small labor and expense, no procurator appearing for the chapter’s side, humbly asked us to grant him the disputed prebend. He alleged that, as the majority of the chapter affirmed, he had served the Church of Bourges from childhood and received sacred orders there up to the diaconate; that we had commanded a prebend to be assigned to him absolutely and without any condition; and that before the aforesaid judges it had been shown and proved that the greater part of the chapter agreed upon him, as he sought to confirm and show by certain documents produced before the auditor.

Because the case had been delegated to judges by common consent of the parties, and proceedings had been carried through by them to publication of the witnesses while the suit was pending and the other party was absent, we did not think his request should be granted. Yet, lest he should appear to have labored in vain by coming to our presence, we command and direct you by apostolic letters to proceed in the case according to the tenor of the letters obtained by the bishop of Nevers, the abbot of Dôle, and their co-judges, upon the testimony and arguments received by them. We understand that those canons consented to his reception who requested us in their letters to cause him to be received.

Moreover, because the said chapter did not wish to pursue the appeal it had lodged before us, while the said master did pursue it, you shall condemn that chapter, according to the ordinances of the Lateran Council, to pay the master’s lawful expenses, the obstacle of appeal being removed. You shall annul, if anything [lacuna] has rashly [lacuna] been done to the prejudice of that master, taking care diligently that you execute the apostolic mandate in such a manner that, through failure of justice, the master is not compelled on this account to labor further before the Apostolic See. Notwithstanding no letters, etc. And if not all of you … two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, VIII Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

XXIX. TO THE NOBLE MAN MATTHEW OF ARGENT. He confirms the judgment rendered by G., cardinal deacon of the title of St. Mary in Portico, in the case between him and John of Zita concerning certain land and a mill. (At St. Peter’s, VII Kalends of April.)

In a complaint frequently and repeatedly made on behalf of A…, your niece, whose guardianship you exercised, you requested that John of Zita restore to you, with the fruits received from them, land and mills situated in Valle Rotunda, in the territory of St. Germain. You asserted that John had formerly lawfully sold and delivered them to Master Peter of Fondi, whose heir the niece was. John, however, argued in reply that the sale had been made as a cloak for usury. Since he could not otherwise obtain a loan from that master, they had agreed that whenever he wished to repay the purchaser the same sum of money, the purchaser was bound to resell to him. This, he said, subsequently became apparent: when the master received back the money which he had given, he resold to John what he had bought from him, as appeared from a public instrument which he showed before R., cardinal priest of the title of SS. Marcellinus and Peter and abbot of Monte Cassino, ordinary judge. [Note: [Col. 0583C] See Letter 108 of Book V.]

But because you said that instrument was suspect and the abbot appeared rather to incline toward your side, John appealed to the Apostolic See lest he be burdened by him. When you and the other party were before us, we assigned as auditor H., cardinal deacon of St. Eustachius. [Note: [Col. 0583C] See Letter 41 of Book III, with note.] John declared that he wished to produce witnesses fully to establish both the authenticity of the instrument and the entire course of the matter. You, however, said that you wished to use witnesses to defeat that exception, and thus obtained letters to the … archdeacon of Aquino for receiving the witnesses of both parties. Witnesses being produced by both sides and their testimony remitted to our hearing, we again assigned to the parties as auditor O., our subdeacon and chaplain.

When, by our command, he was sending to the same cardinal the documents received from each party, John maliciously removed your documents, either personally or through another, and presumed to retain them. During the absence of the said chaplain, therefore, the beloved son G., cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico, was assigned as auditor to your procurator and to John, to hear and duly determine the case. [Note: Gregory Galganus of St. Apostolo, cardinal deacon of the title of St. Mary in Portico, was created by Pope Clement III in his first creation of 1188. By that pope’s order he first served as legate in Cisalpine Gaul, where he issued several constitutions against heretics. Later, by order of Pope Celestine III, he served in Hungary and, according to Baronius, in Germany; under Pope Innocent III he again served in Cisalpine Gaul, to induce the people of Piacenza to make satisfaction for injuries done to Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. Shortly after the death of the Empress Constance, queen of Sicily, who had appointed Pope Innocent III guardian of her infant son Frederick II, he received from that pope a fourth legation to take charge of the whole kingdom, the protection of the orphan child, and the exercise in all things of the Apostolic See’s authority.

Ciaconius (see Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1139) writes that this Gregory was made by Innocent III cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia and died under Innocent. Oldoinus, conversely, contends that Ciaconius is mistaken. For, says Oldoinus, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico, in 1225, under Pope Honorius III, Innocent’s successor, confirmed Honorius’s letters issued to Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, as Ferdinand Ughelli states, having reproduced those letters in vol. II of the *Italia Sacra*. But, with deference to Oldoinus, he is greatly mistaken: the letters produced by Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, col. 365, belong to Pope Honorius II, not III, and were issued in 1125, not 1225.

Nothing therefore prevents the Gregory here in question from being the same as Gregory, cardinal priest of St. Anastasia, mentioned in diplomas of Innocent III issued in 1216, and whom Ciaconius—though calling him Theodulus rather than Galganus, and treating him as newly created and previously without any other title—reports to have been made cardinal priest of St. Anastasia after Roger’s death (see below, Letter 31 of this eighth book), in Innocent’s eighth creation, in 1212 or 1213, as Oldoinus himself acknowledges (*ibid.*, vol. II, col. 33). Yet, even if the identity is accepted, it remains false that our Gregory died under Innocent III: Gregory, cardinal priest of St. Anastasia—whether called Galganus and translated from cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico, or called Theodulus and first created cardinal priest of St. Anastasia—survived, as documents establish, until 1224.

[Col. 0584D] We nevertheless acknowledge that another difficulty remains. In the letters of Pope Honorius II recited by Ughelli at the cited place, the cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico is called Gregory. Yet around 1125, both before and after, the holder of that title was found not to be Gregory but Romanus. According to Ciaconius, without contradiction from Oldoinus, Romanus was created cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico by Pope Paschal II; in the schism of Anacletus he adhered to Innocent; and he subscribed to diplomas of Callistus II, Honorius II, and Innocent II for the Church of Genoa, the bishop of Fiesole, the archbishop of Pisa, and the bishop of Verona. He went with Innocent II to Siena and Pisa, and died under him after 1134. See Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 923.

We do not undertake to solve this knot; perhaps it is more than enough to have pointed it out, together with the errors of Ciaconius and Oldoinus, to the diligent reader.]

Before that auditor, your procurator demanded restoration of the documents which John had removed from you. John steadfastly denied this and, to remove suspicion, boldly offered an oath. After receiving this dispute and learning, both from the report of the already mentioned cardinal of St. Eustachius and from that of his chaplain and others, that all those documents had reached John, we ordered that unless he restored your documents to your procurator within a fixed period, he should be condemned in all things as convicted. Fearing this, he obtained a delay and restored not all, but some, of them. Although he seemed liable to condemnation for those not restored, yet because he appeared voluntarily to acknowledge their tenor, it was ordered that, notwithstanding this, the principal case should proceed.

Your side then alleged that, since the sale and delivery to the aforesaid master were established by a public instrument and by your testimony; since that master’s procurator had received, for the master’s heir, the fruits of the land in dispute; and since John had violently occupied that land and received its fruits, the aforesaid mills and land, with the fruits received from the time of the invasion and the penalty for invasion, ought to be adjudged to you. John argued in reply that he should be entirely absolved, since the resale had been sufficiently proved by his witnesses.

After diligently hearing these and other matters laid before him, the aforesaid cardinal condemned John by judgment to restore the mills and the aforesaid land, together with the fruits received from that land from the time of the invasion. Approving that judgment, we confirm it by apostolic authority and protect it by this present writing. Therefore let no one infringe this our confirmation, etc. If anyone should do so, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, VII Kalends of April.

XXX. TO THE BISHOP OF SPOLETO. [Note: [Col. 0585D] See Letter 5 of Book V, with note.] He annuls a judgment rendered against him in the case between him and the syndic of the Lateran Church concerning episcopal right in the Church of Scilian. (Given V Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0585B]

When our beloved son Ja . . ., your procurator, appearing before our beloved son J. [Note: See the note to letter 27 of book VII.], cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, whom we had appointed auditor for himself and the syndic of the Lateran Church, asserted that episcopal jurisdiction in the church of Saint Mary of Scilian belonged to you, because it is situated within the bounds of your diocese and is not shown to be exempt; and because those dwelling there had observed a sentence of interdict pronounced by your predecessors, who had also installed an abbot there and received lodgings and procurations there, as in other monasteries subject to them by diocesan law; and because the same procurator maintained that he could prove these things sufficiently by suitable witnesses. The opposing party, besides the prescription by which it strove most vigorously to defend itself, asserted in reply that, because of a certain ancient privilege, because of an instrument by which your predecessor had granted to the Lateran Church the right which he held in the often-mentioned church, and also because you had ratified what that same predecessor had done, the said church was in no respect bound to answer to you.

The cardinal, having duly and carefully considered these matters and the other arguments, allegations, and witness-depositions of both parties, reported them to us diligently. But we, observing that the Lateran Church did not produce publicly that ancient privilege by which it alleged that the church was exempt, that the instrument made by your predecessor was not confirmed by the subscriptions of clerics, and that prescription had not been sufficiently proved, annul the instrument of grant made by your predecessor; and we have judged that the syndic of the Lateran Church is to be condemned in favor of your procurator concerning episcopal jurisdiction over that church.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

### XXXI. To the Abbot of Saint Geneviève, to the Dean, and to the Chancellor of Paris

[Note: See the note to letter 44 of book III.] [Note: See the note to letter 36 of book V.] [Note: See the note to letter 98 of book V.]

He commits to them the case between the countess of Blois and the chapter of the Church of Chartres concerning the capture of a robber. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0586B]

Beloved sons, W. and Simon, clerics sent into our presence on behalf of our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman the countess of Blois, requested a hearing, that we might hear the injuries inflicted upon her and hers by the Church of Chartres. We appointed as auditor for them and for our beloved son S. of Bero, canon of Chartres, who appeared for that church, our beloved son R., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.

[Note: Roger, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, was appointed by Innocent III after Romanus, who had held the same title: according to Panvinio, in March 1205; or, if Ciaconius is believed, in December 1204. By Innocent’s command he discharged a legation in Sicily. He was considered a very learned man. Gregory, abbot of Monte Sacro—whose manuscript works were preserved, according to Ferdinand Ughelli in his additions to Ciaconius, in the library of the most reverend lord de Ruinis, but have now been brought to Spain through the efforts of the Duke of Complutum, formerly ambassador to the Apostolic See for the Catholic King—calls Roger, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, “Master” in the dedication of his works to Thomas, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Sabina, and describes him as a man outstanding in learning. Having confirmed Innocent’s letters sent on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May 1205 to Albert, bishop of Gubbio, and on the seventh day before the Ides of June 1209 to Michael, abbot of Saint Michael of Verruca in the diocese of Pisa, he died under that same Innocent. OLDOIN, in Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 19. See the note to letter 29 of this eighth book.]

Before him the countess’s envoys alleged that, when the countess’s provost of La Ferté had captured in the village of Nolio a robber who had committed theft, and justice had been done upon him, the robber was demanded from the countess’s bailiffs by the chapter of Chartres after justice had been done, because the chapter claimed that he had been captured in its territory. The bailiffs, on the contrary, maintained that he had been captured in territory in which the countess possessed the right of seizing robbers and other malefactors, because her husband, before he took up the sign of the cross, possessed that right, so as to have that jurisdiction in the place where the chapter asserted that he had been captured. They were prepared to prove this.

Yet, although they offered adequate security to obey the law in this matter, the canons of Chartres nevertheless caused the countess’s land to be placed under interdict through the . . . archdeacon of Dun, who, when later requested to absolve the land upon receiving sufficient security from them for obedience to the law, refused to receive it unless an amends were first paid.

Thereafter our venerable brother, the . . . bishop of Chartres, being requested concerning this matter and carefully admonished by letters of his metropolitan to absolve the countess’s land in the manner in which he could and ought to do by law, refused to do so, being forbidden by the said chapter.

[Note: See the note to letter 14 of book III.] [Note: At that time the Church of Chartres was subject by metropolitan right to the see of Sens. We have already discussed the archbishop of Sens in the note to letter 45 of book III.]

For the chapter said that its privilege contained the provision that no one might grant the benefit of absolution to persons excommunicated or expressly placed under interdict for the canons of Chartres, without suitable satisfaction. Seeing that they could not, as they ought, be absolved upon giving security, the countess’s envoys appealed to the hearing of the metropolitan, both placing the countess herself and her land and bailiffs under his protection, concerning this matter and the other cases pending between the countess and the chapter.

Meanwhile, the . . . dean of Châteaudun summoned the countess’s provost of Châteaudun to procure the restoration or delivery on security of the goods of a certain man which he had seized. Though he was ready to deliver them on security, the dean, having first examined certain letters which he had received on behalf of the chapter of Chartres, would not permit the provost to deliver the goods on security, but required their unconditional restoration. The provost refused to do this, lest the countess’s right should thereby be lost; he prohibited the dean from proceeding further, appealed to the metropolitan’s hearing, placing the countess’s land and bailiffs under that protection, and fixed a day for the appeal.

The following day the dean made the same demand of the castellan of Châteaudun as he had made of the provost. The castellan, giving a similar answer, appealed, promising with the provost to stand by the judgment of the Church in this matter. But the dean, asserting that he had received a mandate from the chapter, placed that castle under interdict in the evening.

The parties having therefore been cited by the metropolitan and appearing in his presence, the procurator of the said countess complained on her behalf that the chapter of Chartres, without citing or even requesting her in any matter, so burdened her that it frequently placed her land under interdict for any cause whatever, without making any request of her at all. He also complained that, though she or her bailiffs were cited in causes of the chapter to answer before the ordinary judge, they were now compelled to answer in the chapter itself; and that, although the castle of La Ferté had unjustly been placed under interdict, the chapter refused to accept from her the sufficient security for obedience to the law which she offered, though she was prepared to prove that she had exercised her right.

He further complained that Châteaudun had been placed under interdict after the appeal, and offered adequate proof that, in seizing the goods already mentioned, the countess had exercised her right—namely, the right of which her husband had been in possession at the time when he assumed the cross.

Moreover, when certain witnesses had been received in Paris by the metropolitan concerning this matter, and the countess’s procurator urgently requested that he absolve the land upon receiving sufficient security, the chapter’s procurator replied that neither the metropolitan nor anyone else could absolve the land, alleging the terms of the aforementioned privilege and wishing to produce witnesses on this point, as the countess had produced them. A further day was therefore assigned at Noliacum for the parties to produce witnesses and exhibit the privilege. On the appointed day, with the parties present, the metropolitan carefully examined the privilege and received witnesses on both sides. After they had been examined by the metropolitan’s official, another day was assigned to the parties. The countess’s procurator urgently requested publication of the depositions received and, beyond what was required, offered sufficient security for obedience to the law so that the sentence of interdict might be relaxed. But the chapter’s procurator alleged in opposition that, by reason of the said privilege, the land could not and ought not be absolved by him until amends had first been made to the chapter, interpreting the expression contained in the privilege, “suitable satisfaction,” as meaning an amends.

After prolonged litigation concerning this clause, the said metropolitan ruled that he would reserve this interpretation to apostolic examination, and assigned the parties a day concerning it. Nevertheless, he wished himself, or through his official, to inquire—because of the aforesaid appeal—whether those castles had justly or unjustly been placed under interdict.

The procurator of the aforesaid countess again urged that, once security had been received and the depositions published, the sentence of interdict should be relaxed. Simon and the chapter’s procurator requested time to produce further witnesses to prove the justice of what they had done. This was granted to them. At the day assigned to the parties, the countess’s procurator again urgently requested, as he had often done, the publication of the depositions and relaxation of the interdict upon receipt of security.

When the chapter’s procurator was asked whether he wished to establish by proof that what the chapter had done in this matter was just, he stated firmly before the officials of the aforesaid metropolitan that he wished neither to prove anything nor even to hear the opposing party’s depositions. Instead, he appealed against the absolution of the land, setting the octave of Saint Martin most recently past as the term for his appeal. The officials, however, judging that such an appeal was not to be allowed, received security up to one hundred marks for obedience to the law and absolved the said land.

The aforesaid Simon, since he did not have letters of procuratorship, appointed beloved sons the abbot of Saint John of Valette and Thomas, archdeacon of Dreux, as sureties, to be condemned in the penalty of one hundred marks if the chapter should refuse to ratify what he did. He then alleged in reply that, when the aforesaid castles had been placed under interdict for the chapter of Chartres, it had been argued before the metropolitan for that chapter that, by reason of the clause set forth above, he could not and ought not absolve the land placed under interdict for them, and that he would therefore reserve the interpretation of that clause to apostolic determination. But, wishing to determine whether the interdict had been pronounced justly or unjustly, he assigned the parties a day.

However, when the metropolitan was on the point of coming to the Apostolic See, Master J., his official, whom he had appointed auditor over matters brought before him, was challenged as suspect by the chapter’s procurator, because of manifest causes which he believed were not unknown to the metropolitan. But the metropolitan did not remove him entirely from the case; indeed, he joined to him the archdeacon of Autun. At that time there was no mention of adding another person, and the parties were present, as was the archdeacon, who by his silence gave consent. Subsequently, however, as the other party asserted, the metropolitan joined Geoffrey, a canon of Sens, in the archdeacon’s place if the archdeacon could not attend.

Accordingly, seeing the aforesaid Master—who had been challenged—and the said Geoffrey, whom he did not know had been joined in place of the archdeacon, sitting to hear the case, the chapter’s procurator asserted that in the archdeacon’s absence he was not bound to answer or make submissions, and objected to any proceeding without him, interposing an appeal to the Apostolic See. Since it was not lawfully established that Geoffrey had been substituted for the archdeacon, since through him the suspicion concerning Master J. had not been removed, and since it had not been canonically made clear that the archdeacon could not attend, they—namely Master J. and the said Geoffrey—disregarded the appeal and relaxed the sentence of interdict, accepting security, contrary to the terms of the privilege of the Church of Chartres and to the prejudice of the interpretation for which an appointed day was still pending. Simon therefore maintained that everything done by them in this matter should be annulled.

But the procurators of the said countess requested that it be made clear to them by apostolic interpretation what “suitable satisfaction” is, or how it should be understood, since the canons of Chartres use the occasion of this term to place the countess’s land under interdict whenever and however they please, and refuse to relax the sentence until an amends has been made. Moreover, even when the countess herself is present in the town which they wish to place under interdict, they do not summon or lawfully cite her. Rather, whenever they please, they call the provost or one of the bailiffs and say to him: “Either you shall do thus, or we shall subject the land to a sentence of interdict.” When the countess’s party submits that what they demand belongs to the countess’s jurisdiction, and offers to abide by the Church’s judgment, they nevertheless interdict the land. And whenever someone on the countess’s behalf is cited before the ordinary judge because of a complaint by the chapter, they do not permit him to answer unless in the chapter of Chartres. The procurators therefore requested justice for the countess regarding these burdens and others.

Having carefully heard these matters and the other things proposed before the cardinal, and since it was not established to us whether the appeal was lawful, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties and receiving witnesses on both sides—since neither side has yet renounced the production of witnesses—you take care to examine this case sufficiently and, the obstacle of appeal having been removed, bring it to a canonical conclusion.

If the chapter refuses to ratify Simon’s act, you shall, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, condemn the aforesaid sureties to the stated penalty and cause what you decree to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. You shall annul whatever has been improperly attempted against the countess by the chapter after her envoys set out to come to the Apostolic See.

In order to understand the clause of the said privilege, we think a distinction must be made: whether a sentence of interdict or excommunication has been pronounced against someone solely for contumacy, that is, because a cited person refused to stand to the law; or also for an offence, that is, because a person who had been ordered refused to make amends for a wrongdoing. In the first case, we think suitable satisfaction is made, so that such a sentence may be relaxed, if adequate security is given to stand to the law. In the second case, if the offence is manifest, we do not think suitable satisfaction is made so that the sentence may be relaxed unless adequate amends are first rendered. But if the offence is doubtful, we think it sufficient for relaxing the sentence if appropriate security is given to obey the order.

If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, nonetheless two of you shall carry it out.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of April.

### XXXII. To the Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Peter of Chalon and to His Brethren, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life, in Perpetuity

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.] [Note: Girard, abbot of Saint Peter of Chalon, is found in documents from 1202 until at least 1209. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 963.]

He receives them under protection and enumerates their possessions. (At Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April.)

“Religious life,” etc. “Therefore,” etc., as far as “we confirm.”

First, establishing that the monastic order which, according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, is observed in that place, etc. Further: whatever possessions, etc., as far as “to be expressed by name”; the site itself on which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the churches of Saint Andrew in the suburb and Saint George within the walls of Chalon; Saint Martin of Frames, of Verdun, of Seiz, and of Vosgeio; Saint Martin of Brixia, of Longovico, of Petra, of Branges, and of Joie; Saint Desiderius, of Montaral, and of Velergaudin; Saint Vincent at Brixia, Saint Germanus, Saint Stephen, Saint Gervasius of Cropellis, of Cules, and of Mont-Saint-Martin; of the monastery of Capasia, of Rose, of Moroges, of Gambles, of Marigny-Saint-Loci, of Usello, of Bassi, of Marciniaco; and the church of Nanto, with all their appurtenances and dependencies; and the burial of bishops, canons, nobles, and other citizens of the entire city of Chalon, as the monastery has hitherto held it freely and reasonably and as you now possess it justly and peacefully; the chapel of the castle of Branges; the chapel of Senciot and the chapel in the castle of Usello; two-thirds of the offerings on annual feast days in the chapel of Verdun, and the parochial rights which you possess there; one-thirtieth part of the tithes of Perreria, which is the grange of La Ferté; two-thirds of mortuary offerings in the parish of Saint Julian, and two-thirds of the offerings there on the feast of All Saints; the rent and other customary dues which you possess in the church of Lencheriis.

[Note: Thus in the Vatican copy.]

Indeed, concerning your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate q . . . for m . . . or . . . S . . ., or from the increase of a . . . u . . . none, etc. [Materially corrupt or lacunose as printed.]

You may also retain clerics or laymen, etc., as far as “without any opposition.” We further prohibit anyone from presuming, without a manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce against you, your monastery, or persons established there, a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict. Moreover, by apostolic authority we strictly forbid anyone to dare, within the bounds of your parish, to build a new chapel or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. On your death, etc., as far as “shall provide for the election.” Further, concerning liberties, etc., as far as “we decree.” Therefore we decree, etc., as far as “advantageous,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. “If anyone therefore,” etc. “But to all,” etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1205 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: Perhaps 1204.], in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### XXXIII. To the Bishop of Worcester, the Abbot of Chichester, and the Dean of York

[Note: See the note to letter 23 of book V.] [Note: See the note to letter 54 of book V.]

Concerning the assignment of the church of Wdehord to the nephew of the bishop of St Albans. (At Saint Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0591D]

Our beloved sons, the . . . prior and convent of Tinem, sent us a grave complaint: although the church of Wdehorn belongs to their presentation, our venerable brother the . . . bishop of Durham, after they had made protest and appealed to us, presumed to institute therein the beloved son . . ., nephew of our venerable brother J., bishop of St Albans, on the occasion of a certain mandate of ours. Because of concealed truth, that mandate deserved to be revoked with certain knowledge.

[Note: This concerns the monastery of Tynemouth, in Northumberland, a cell of Saint Albans. Several charters relating to this monastery are printed in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 33 ff.; but they contain nothing concerning the church in question.] [Note: See the notes to letters 57 and 135 of book V.] [Note: See the note to letter 3 of book VII.]

Although the aforesaid prior, compelled against his will by letters of his abbot, had presented him to the said bishop of Durham, the convent objecting, because of threatening letters sent to him by our venerable brother the bishop of Ely under our authority and addressed to our beloved son the . . . abbot of Saint Albans, the convent never wished to consent to that presentation, but rather objected to it.

[Note: See the note to letter 54 of book V.] [Note: See the note to letter 204 of book VI.]

They therefore humbly requested that we should deign irrevocably to annul what had thus been done. But our beloved son Wiscard, procurator of the aforesaid nephew of the bishop of St Albans, appearing before our beloved son the . . . cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace, whom we granted as auditor to him, alleged that, since he had already been violently dispossessed of the said church without observance of legal procedure, the aforesaid monks ought not to be heard to his prejudice on this petition before he obtained the benefit of restitution. But when he had obtained the favor of restitution, he was prepared to render them full justice.

[Note: See the note to letter 41 of book III.]

We therefore, wishing to show favor to one party and justice to the other, command by apostolic letters the said abbot of Saint Albans, who holds the aforesaid church by authority of our mandate, to assign that church to the nephew of the said bishop of St Albans, whom we have commended to him on our behalf, so that he may receive the revenues from the church commended to him and preserve and govern it without prejudice to the prior and convent of Tinem.

After he has obtained the church thus commended, you shall summon the parties and hear what may be advanced on either side both concerning possession and concerning title. Having God before your eyes, and removing every obstacle of objection and appeal, determine what is just, and cause what you determine to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure. If either party . . . witnesses, etc.; “no letters [shall prevail] against truth,” etc. If not all of you [can take part], you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

### XXXIV. To the Bishop of Ely, the Archdeacon of Cambridge, and the Prior of Barnoeta in the Diocese of Ely

[Note: This letter is found, but greatly mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book III, title 32, *On the Conversion of Married Persons*, chapter 17. Matters distinguished in italic type are absent from the *Decretals* or indicate variant readings.] [Note: See the note to letter 54 of book V.]

He commits to them a matrimonial case. (At Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of April.)

[Col. 0593A]

[Juliana [Note: In the *Decretals*, “J.”], a woman appearing in our presence, tearfully set before us that, although W., her husband, of the diocese of Ely, had lawfully joined her to himself in marriage, and had lived with her for nearly twenty years and begotten offspring by her, he eventually wished to assume the religious habit and humbly asked her to favor his so pious intention. Because of the many blows and burdens of other vexations which the said husband inflicted upon her, he asserted that he would put her away, and she consented to his wishes.

When the same man went to the house of Wardon [Note: Wardon Abbey, in Bedfordshire, founded in 1136. See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 784, col. 2, line 10.] [Note: In the *Decretals*, “Vader.”], of the Cistercian order, and assumed the religious habit there, the woman went to a house of nuns [Note: In the *Decretals*, “in a house,” in place of “she transferred herself to a house.”], where she remained without assuming any religious habit or making any vow of conversion; the nuns supplied her with the necessities of life for the work of her hands. But, after time had passed, the same man returned to the world and abandoned the religious habit. When the woman urgently asked him to take her back [Note: In the *Decretals*, “asked him”], he utterly refused to receive her and, besides the blows which he frequently inflicted on her, subjected her to many insults and grave injuries.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if these matters are so, and if the said woman is of such an age that there may reasonably be fear of her falling into fleshly sin, you shall, after prior warning and setting aside appeal, compel the said man by ecclesiastical censure to receive her and show her conjugal affection.] “No letters,” etc. If not all of you [can take part], you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of April.

### XXXV. To the Bishop of Dol, and the Abbots of Savigny and Ardennes

[Note: This letter is found, but mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book I, title 6, *On Election and the Authority of the Elect*, chapter 29. What is enclosed here in brackets appears there; variant readings are supplied.] [Note: See the note to letter 17 of this eighth book.] [Note: William of Douvres held the staff in the monastery of Savigny for twenty-one years, namely from 1187 until 1207, when he died—on the fourth day before the Ides of October according to the chronicle of Goffern, or on 10 April according to the Savignian chronicle. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. XI, col. 547.] [Note: Robert I, second abbot of the monastery of Ardennes, is known from documents from 1180 until 1206, when he was raised to the headship of the order. Ibid., col. 459.]

He commits to them the case concerning the election of the bishop of Bayeux. (At Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 0594B]

[Having heard and understood the merits of the case concerning two elections held in the church of Bayeux—one of Robert the archdeacon and the other of Master Robert—we find both to have been undertaken contrary to canonical form.]

[Note: At that time the Church of Bayeux was vacant through the death of Henry II, formerly dean of Salisbury, who became bishop of Bayeux and died in this very year, 1205, according to the chronicles of Saint Stephen of Caen.]

[Note: “One of Robert the archdeacon, and the other of Master Robert.” Thus it is expressly read in the Vatican and Conti copies, but we fear incorrectly in both. The authors of the above-mentioned new *Gallia Christiana* (*ibid.*, col. 336) state that three elections were held: first, of William, canon of Pezerollis; second, of Richard, later dean; third, of Robert, son of Drogo, canon of Bayeux. Our letter of Innocent proves that there were only two. Yet the man whom this letter first calls Robert the archdeacon, it shortly afterwards calls the same man W. the archdeacon; and it says not a word of Richard the dean as also elected.

After the election discussed here had been annulled—whether triple, as the authors of the *Gallia Christiana* wish, or only double, if we prefer the greater authority of Innocent’s letter—the often-mentioned authors state that Robert, elected again by a greater number of votes, was confirmed by the supreme pontiff and sent to the Church of Rouen to be ordained there. They affirm that this occurred on the fifth day before the Kalends of March 1205, that is, 1206. For the rest see *Gallia Christiana*, ibid.]

[Note: In the *Decretals*: “one [election] of W., archdeacon,” and shortly afterwards, “the other of M. R., subdeacon.”]

For, after the individual wishes of all had been investigated, . . . the dean [Note: The remarks of the above-mentioned authors concerning the dean of Bayeux are noteworthy (*ibid.*, col. 399); for this letter of Innocent does not fully accord with them.

“VII. Richard II, of Rohan or Rohon, perhaps Bohon, is styled chaplain and dean in chapter acts of 1205 and 1207. He had a dispute with the parish priest of Holy Mother Church concerning the tithes of that church; Innocent III appointed as arbitrators the abbot of Val-Richer and the archdeacon of Bayeux. They say that Richard, elected bishop in 1205 by a greater number of votes, resigned; and that he died in 1213.”]

with the smaller number had agreed upon Robert [Note: In the *Decretals*, “R. himself,” and shortly afterwards “the said W. archdeacon” in place of “W.” The *Decretals* add “a certain other man,” and shortly afterwards read *Algediis* for *Ablegiis*.], while the cantor with the larger number had agreed upon W. the archdeacon. The cantor alone named Master Robert of Ablegiis. An appeal was made to our hearing, lest the dean, who had the first voice in the election, should proceed to an election without the consent of the entire chapter, or of its greater and sounder part, in order that the gate of discord which already seemed open might be closed by the obstacle of appeal.

[Note: These words are absent from the *Decretals*, as are the word “election” and, immediately below, “at once.”]

But the dean, without obtaining the consent of the greater part of the chapter, but only of a far smaller part, suddenly broke forth into an election, appealing that no one should attempt anything against that election. Although he asserted that many others immediately afterward consented to the election made, what was invalid from the beginning could not be validated after the fact: for an election invalid by law itself could not become valid through subsequent consent while the appeal was pending.

[Note: The *Decretals* add *maxime* (“especially”); and below, they read “they presumed to elect the aforesaid subdeacon” in place of “they presumed not only to elect Master Robert . . .”]

When these men had returned home, the cantor and others who remained in the chapter, after that election had not yet been annulled and after an appeal had been lodged with us, abandoned the nomination of W. the archdeacon and again presumed, without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff or even of their own metropolitan, not only to elect Master Robert—though he was a subdeacon—but also, bells being rung, with a solemn procession and hymn-singing, to bring him into the church.

Having carefully heard these matters and the others proposed before us, and with the common counsel of our brethren, [we judge both elections to be annulled]. We command you by apostolic letters that, after the return of the dean, the archdeacon, Master Robert Balbus, and the other canons of the Church of Bayeux who have come into our presence, you shall assign the chapter a period of two months within which it may set a suitable person over itself as pastor by canonical election. Otherwise, thereafter, lest the Lord’s flock long lack a pastor’s care, you, supported by our authority and all appeal ceasing, shall provide them as bishop such a person as is suitable for so great a burden and honor. Opponents, etc. If not all of you [can take part], you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth year.

### XXXVI. To Duke Andrew, Governor of the Kingdom of Hungary

[Note: Raynaldus prints the greater part of this letter under the year 1205, §54.]

In reply to his letter, he commends to him King Ladislaus, a child, orphan, and his nephew. [Note: See letter 226 of book VII.] (On the seventh day before the Kalends of May.)

After the death of Henry, king of Hungary, your brother, of illustrious memory, we received [Col. 0595D] graciously and kindly the first letters of your devotion, which, being sealed with the seal of that king, you asked us to attribute to your inexperience rather than to falsehood. They expressly contained—as we use your own words—that, since by the disposition of the king himself, because of the tender age of his son King Ladislaus, you had undertaken the care of the boy and the governance of the realm, you have a ready will to preserve what has been well established and, insofar as lies in you, successfully bring to effect what you know was laudably begun by the same king.

Therefore, commending in the Lord the sincerity of your purpose, [Col. 0596A] we more earnestly commend to the diligence of your guardianship that same boy king—toward whom you are known to have sworn fealty, having made a promise concerning the administration of the kingdom and assumed his guardianship—so that true praises may accrue to your name when that king finds in his paternal uncle a kindly father and, in his protector, a gracious patron; and so that from the most high King, to whom kings coming from Sheba offered the boy gifts full of devotion, salvation and the crown of eternal recompense may come to you. Nor are you to admit against that king, your nephew, the evil suggestions of anyone; for you are bound to stand by him as a father in the place of his father. And since he is little and a child, you ought to cherish him all the more and to administer the affairs of the kingdom for him with greater diligence, in proportion as he will more gratefully acknowledge the benefits bestowed upon him when, by God’s agency, he reaches mature age and recognizes that he has not lost a father, but has exchanged one.

Given on 25 April.

XXXVII. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §55.] TO THE SAME PERSON. That he is to ensure the distribution of money which the deceased king had left to certain persons. (25 April.)

After the death, etc., as far as “bring to effect.” We have furthermore received a report from our dearest daughter in Christ, . . . queen of Hungary, that, when the aforesaid king, your brother, lay at the point of death, in the presence of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Kalocsa, and certain other princes of the kingdom, he made the following disposition concerning money which he had at the monastery of Pelle: two parts [Col. 0596C] thereof were to be received by the brothers of the houses of the Temple and the Hospital for the aid of the Holy Land, and the third was to be given to his son. Since, therefore, it becomes you to fulfil his last will, we earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility, commanding you by apostolic letters to have that money distributed in accordance with the disposition of the king himself.

Given on 25 April.

XXXVIII. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §55.] TO THE SAME PERSON. That he is to pay the revenues which he had promised to the king and to the king’s mother, the queen. (25 April.)

After the death, etc., as far as “bring to effect.” Moreover, since, after the death of your brother, you promised, as we have received, that you would give certain revenues to the same king and to our dearest daughter in Christ, . . . the queen, his mother, [Col. 0596D] we earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility, and command you by apostolic letters to cause them to be paid to him in full, so that in your dealings with them you may show yourself both father and patron, and that, on this account, the reward of eternal salvation may come to you and the favor of human praise increase, when he finds you merciful and kind where you are bound to be merciful and kind.

Given on 25 April.

XXXIX. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §55.] TO THE SAME PERSON AND TO ALL THE PRINCES ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM. He admonishes them to take such care of the boy king that they dare not alienate the royal possessions on any pretext. (25 April.)

[Col. 0597A]

After the death of Henry, king of Hungary, your brother, of illustrious memory, son Duke, the letters of your devotion, etc., as far as “bring to effect.” Therefore, in order that the rights of the kingdom may remain intact for the same king, we—who, by the office of the apostolate, are bound to protect an orphan, since, although unworthy, we act on earth in the stead of Him to whom it is said through the Prophet, “You will be a helper to the orphan”—entreat you in Christ Jesus, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and by the authority of these present letters, under attestation of the divine judgment, strictly forbid [Col. 0597B] that, while the same king is under age, the royal prerogatives be alienated to his detriment. Rather, devote diligent care and effective effort faithfully to preserving them.

Given on 25 April.

XL. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §55.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PROVOSTS, AND OTHER PRELATES; TO THE PRINCES, CLERGY, AND THE WHOLE PEOPLE OF THE KINGDOM OF HUNGARY. He commands them absolutely to keep faith with the king. (At St Peter’s, 25 April.)

After the death of Henry, king of Hungary, of illustrious memory, the letters of the devotion of his brother, our beloved son, the nobleman Duke Andrew, etc., as far as [Col. 0597C] “bring to effect.” Therefore, in order that you may preserve constancy of fidelity toward that king, who, after his father’s death, remains your lord and heir, we strictly forbid you by the authority of these present letters to give counsel or aid to anyone against his crown. On the contrary, resist utterly, defending the king’s honor, should anyone perhaps attempt to act against him.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on 25 April.

XLI. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §55.] TO THE . . . ARCHBISHOP OF KALOCSA AND THE . . . BISHOP OF VÁRAD. He charges them with restraining those who harass the household of King Ladislaus and of the queen. (Given 27 April.)

[Col. 0597D] Since honor is to be shown to a king as one who excels, according to the Apostle’s saying, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you restrain, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, those who have presumed improperly to harass, in possessions or revenues, the household or clerics of our dearest son in Christ, King Ladislaus, and of . . . the queen his mother, [Col. 0598A] without showing due respect to royal honor. For we wish that the household and clerics themselves should stand under our protection and that of the Apostolic See.

Given on 27 April.

XLII. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §55.] TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF KALOCSA. He commands them to remain faithful to the boy king. (25 April.)

That you may be steadfast in fidelity and preserve the integrity of your reputation uninjured, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0598B] that, in all matters concerning the protection of our dearest son in Christ Ladislaus, king of Hungary, and of . . . the queen his mother and of the kingdom, you faithfully support our venerable brother . . . the archbishop of Kalocsa, so that you may thereby obtain recompense from the Lord and thanks from us.

Given on 25 April.

XLIII. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.] TO M., ABBESS, AND THE SISTERS OF GANDERSHEIM. [Note: “A thoroughly royal convent of Benedictine virgins, situated in the duchy of Brunswick, founded in A.D. 842 by Liudolf, great duke of the Saxons, endowed by St Altfrid, bishop of Hildesheim, and thereafter wonderfully exalted in wealth and favor by the greatest emperors. Many princesses of imperial blood submitted themselves in this convent and chose to be lowly in the house of God, desiring admission with such eagerness that for many centuries access was open to none but the highest princes. Emperor Otto II consecrated there his two daughters, Sophia and Adelaide, following the memorable example of the founder’s own daughters; three women of Brunswick enclosed themselves there; and finally other princesses of Saxony so sought the gates of that holy convent that they despised the most ample principalities for the sake of the profession of that life. There, discipline flourished excellently with its original fervor, until, in the preceding century, everything fell headlong into ruin and sacred and profane were mingled, until the latter finally swallowed up the former.” BUCELIN, *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 17.] He renews and confirms the privileges granted them by Popes Agapetus II and John XIII; the popes’ diplomas are inserted. (At St Peter’s, 2 May.)

Since Christ is truth, we, who although unworthy hold His place on earth, ought to bear witness to truth; for He Himself is recorded as having said of Himself: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth” (John 18). Your representatives once humbly petitioned us that we should write to certain persons to inspect carefully the privileges granted to your church. Because they were worn away by age, and because they contained the liberty of your monastery, you feared to send them to our presence owing to the dangers of the roads. We, granting kindly assent to your petition, charged four bishops and as many abbots to go to your church, diligently inspect the privileges of your liberty, and faithfully send their written reports to us, fortified by the security of their seals. As we have learned from their letters, they obeyed our command, carefully examined the privileges of our predecessors of good memory, Agapetus and John, which were presented to them, faithfully transcribed their tenor, and sealed it with their seals to be laid before us. [Col. 0599A]

Moreover, our venerable brother G. [Note: See book VII, letter 116, note.], now archbishop of Rheims but then bishop of Palestrina, while exercising the office of legate in those regions, conferred the blessing upon you, daughter abbess, when you had then been elected; he reduced the tenor of those privileges to writing and decreed that it be presented to us, secured with his own seal. Therefore, giving due credence both to the legate and to the said investigators, since their reports agreed in every respect, and observing also that the monastery is recorded in the register of dues of our Camera, among the other free and exempt monasteries, [Col. 0599B] and that it is bound every year to render to us and to our successors two white stoles, woven with gold, of a weight of thirty bezants, we have thought fit to insert in this present document the privilege of the aforesaid John, lest the truth concerning this perish.

John [Note: John XIII, a Roman, son of Bishop John by a lawful marriage, bishop of Narni, was made pope under Emperor Otto the Great on 2 October 965. He sat for six years, eleven months, and five days. He died at Rome on 6 September 972 and was buried in the basilica of St Paul the Apostle outside the city on the Ostian Way. CIACON., vol. I, col. 725.], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gerberga, most beloved to us in Christ, illustrious in merits and nobility of blood, venerable abbess of the monastery of the blessed confessors Innocent and Anastasius, called Gandersheim, and to her successors for ever: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If we give assent to pious wishes and petitions, we believe that we please Almighty God. Therefore we wish all sons of the holy catholic Church, present and future, to know that, at the synod held at the body of St Peter, prince of the apostles, in the month of December and in the eleventh indiction, [Note:

“A passage most worthy of notice and altogether to be compared with what is read in the *Annals of Italy* of the most celebrated Muratori, vol. V, part II, under the year 907, p. 233. ‘Cardinal Baronius, and indeed no one else except Sigonius, has known of a council of very many Italian and transalpine bishops (the pope himself says that thirty-six were assembled), celebrated at the beginning of this year (967, though here there is a difficulty which we shall presently indicate) at Rome by Pope John XIII. A diploma of Otto the Great has preserved its memory for us, by which all its possessions and privileges are confirmed to the distinguished monastery of Subiaco. (See *Antiquitates Italicae medii aevi*, vol. V, col. 465.) There the emperor says that George, abbot of Subiaco, “came into the bosom of the basilica of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where we were present with Lord John XIII, pope, at the holy synod for the benefit of that same church and of the venerable places, while very many bishops from Roman territory, from Italy, and from the transalpine realm sat around with the archbishop of Ravenna, and also the prince of Capua was present, who was likewise marquis of Camerino and of the duchy of Spoleto. . . .” The Roman council mentioned above is also to be understood in Dandolo (see Andrea Dandolo, *Chronicle*, book VIII, chap. 14, part XVII, *Rerum Italicarum scriptores*, vol. XII, col. 209), when he writes that Pietro Candiano VI, doge of Venice, in the ninth year of his dogeship—that is, in the present year—sent John Contareno and John Venerio, deacon, as his ambassadors “to Pope John and Emperor Otto, being at Rome in the synod assembled there. . . .”’

So far the most distinguished annalist of Italy, with whom John XIII himself agrees most beautifully and exactly in this papal diploma, of undoubted authenticity, here presented, as regards the celebration of the Roman synod. Yet we doubt whether the chronological indications of this diploma can equally be reconciled with those of Otto’s diploma cited by the same author in the passage mentioned.

The Roman synod—which ecclesiastical writers pass over in such profound silence (see BARONIUS, [Col. 0600C] vol. X, under the years 966, 967, 968, pp. 778–79; PAGI, *Critica historico-chronologica*, vol. IV, pp. 14–21; HARDUIN, *Acta conciliorum*, vol. VI, part I, cols. 643–682)—is expressly affirmed by the pope himself at the beginning of this diploma to have taken place in December, in the eleventh indiction (XI); and he repeats the same chronological indication at its end. Moreover, lest we think that the copyist erred, the subscription of the scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church contains the same indication of month, December, and indiction, the eleventh. In the other subscription, that of the librarian of the Apostolic See, the same indication is repeated not only for the third time, but another is added: the sixth year of the reign of the elder Otto and the first of the younger. This year precisely coincides with the eleventh indiction and also with the year 967, according to the reckoning of chronologists (see *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 20) and of the annalist of Italy himself. Yet Otto’s diploma, printed in the *Antiquitates Italicae*, cited above, expressly bears these chronological indications: “Given on 11 January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 967, in the fifth year of the empire of the most pious lord Otto Caesar, in the tenth indiction. Done at Rome in the name of God, happily. Amen.”

To undertake the resolution of such a difficulty does not belong to the plan of our work. Indeed, perhaps we have lingered too long over these observations. But the matter seemed of some importance and not unworthy to detain a more attentive reader somewhat, especially because it concerned both a synod whose acts have either entirely perished or still lie wholly hidden and unpublished, and whose very celebration was unknown to almost all historians; and papal and imperial diplomas, of which the papal one, entirely beyond doubt in authenticity, now appears in print for the first time, whereas the imperial one is clearly convicted of error in its chronological indications by comparison with the other.”]

our beloved sons in God and spiritual sons, Otto the elder and Otto the younger, most serene August emperors, deigned humbly to petition our apostolic fatherhood, in the presence of thirty-six archbishops and bishops, namely Italians and Transalpine bishops, that we should fortify by the protection of our authority and receive perpetually under the guardianship and right of the holy Apostolic See the aforesaid monastery of Gandersheim, which is known to be under your rule, situated in the kingdom of Lower Saxony, [Col. 0600B] in honor of the aforesaid confessors of Christ, Innocent and Anastasius.

Rejoicing in their pious petitions, we have decreed with willing mind that this be done. By the authority with which we are endowed in the place of the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, we command that no secular person ever possess the aforesaid venerable monastery, nor that anyone usurp for himself anything from its tithes and possessions—not king, marquis, count, [Col. 0601A] bishop, nor any prince endowed with whatever power—except perhaps for the sake of protection and defense, and then only with your considered permission and that of the abbess who at the time is regular.

Be, then, abbess of that monastery to the praise of the almighty King; and do not cease, by prudent instruction, to urge the sisters subject to you to seek the joys of the heavenly country. Let those sisters always have the power and permission, after the death of an abbess, to appoint for themselves another mother from their own community in accordance with their Rule; and let them have the power, with equal purpose and consent, to elect whom they judge more worthy.

We confirm and strengthen to the holy monastery itself all movable and immovable goods and possessions which it now has and which, with God’s help, it ought thereafter to have by any lawful title of acquisition, so that from now until the end of the age it may freely hold and possess them, all human contradiction removed. But if anyone attempts to act against the protection of this our apostolic privilege and endeavours to overturn any of the things decreed by us, we, with the aid of the holy and undivided Trinity, the intercession of blessed Mary ever-virgin and of all the saints, and by the authority of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with the assent of the bishops of our province and of all the suffragan bishops of this our holy see, excommunicate that person; and, separating him from the thresholds of God’s holy Church and from the fellowship of all Christians, we pronounce him perpetually accursed.

Written by the hand of Stephen, scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 0601C] in the month and indiction stated above, the eleventh. + Fare well.

Given on 1 January, through the hand of Guy, bishop of the Church of Santa Silva Candida and librarian of the holy Apostolic See [Note:

“VIII. Ferdinand Ughelli in *Italia sacra*, and Marius Vipera in the chronology of the archbishops of Benevento, mention Tido [read: Guy] . . . bishop of Porto and Silva Candida, and librarian of the Holy Roman Church.”

Thus Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 730. Ughelli indeed reports another diploma of Pope John XIII, granted in favor of the Church of Benevento and Bishop Landulf, to which our Guy subscribed. This diploma may be read in his chronological series of the bishops of Benevento, *Italia sacra*, vol. VIII, col. 92, where he judged it proper to append it after having compared it most carefully with his own copy. At the end of the diploma one reads expressly: “Given on 26 May, through the hand of Guy—not Tido—bishop of the Church of Santa Silva Candida and librarian of the Apostolic See,” etc. The same Ughelli, in the chronological series of the bishops of Silva Candida (*ibid.*, vol. I, col. 108), mentions Wido, not Tido, around the year 963, from Liutprand of Cremona, book VI, chapter 6. See Liutprand of Cremona, book VI, chapter 6, vol. II, *Rerum Italicarum scriptores*, part I, p. 472, col. 2, letter D, where Wido, not Tido, is called bishop of Silva Candida.], in the third year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord John, supreme pontiff and thirteenth universal pope, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the Apostle; in the sixth year of the empire of the most serene lords, the elder and younger Ottos, the first year of the younger’s empire; in the eleventh month and indiction [Col. 0602A].

Since, however, the privilege of our aforesaid predecessor Pope Agapetus [Note: “Agapetus II—for the present matter concerns Agapetus II, not Agapetus I—the younger, a Roman, during the reign of Otto the Great, the Saxon Augustus, sat for nine years, six months, and ten days, having been created on 18 May 946 . . . Full of good works and deserving well of all, he died honorably at Rome on 27 December, at the beginning of the year of the Lord 956. His body was buried in the Lateran basilica.” CIAC., vol. I, col. 711.] appears to express more fully the liberty of that monastery, we have thought fit, for fuller knowledge of the truth, to append word for word to this document the chapter which is known to concern that liberty:

“Since Ademarus, venerable abbot [Note: Ademarus, or Hademarus, a German, abbot of Fulda, of the Order of St Benedict and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, flourished in this century. A man distinguished for piety and learning, and beloved of princes for that reason. Roger, in the *Life* of St Pantaleon, reports that he was sent to Rome to Pope Agapetus by St Bruno, bishop of Cologne, to obtain a pallium, and returned amid the great rejoicing of the people of Cologne, having obtained not only the pallium with a most ample privilege but having also brought back sacred relics from the very body of St Pantaleon the martyr. He is said to have been enrolled among the cardinals in the manuscript *Chronicle* of St Ulrich of Augsburg. Having returned to Germany, he died of the plague in A.D. 956. He was buried in the western choir of Fulda above the crypt of St Boniface. For more on him see Widukind, monk of Corvey, *The Deeds of Emperor Otto*; Sigebert, under the year 953; and Baronius, *Annals*, vol. X.], petitioned us that, through his intervention and entreaty, we should confirm to you by apostolic authority our monastery of Gandersheim, situated beside the river Echtern, in order that, established under the jurisdiction of the Church of Holy Mary, whom by God’s providence we serve, it may not be subjected to the jurisdictions of any other church: favoring these pious desires, we bring into effect by this our authority what is requested, [Col. 0602B] and therefore by our authority we forbid every priest of any church, other than the Apostolic See, to exercise any jurisdiction in the aforesaid monastery.

“By the authority of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we command that no king have leave to grant our monastery as a benefice to any persons, so that, indeed, in accordance with the firm privilege by which it stands subject to the Apostolic See, it may remain securely endowed and perpetually enjoy, without the contradiction of any person, the places and goods which it presently has or possesses, as well as those which divine mercy may in future times increase within the right of that monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful. Therefore we forbid [Col. 0602C] anyone to dare improperly to molest you or your monastery contrary to the tenor of its privileges. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, he shall incur the indignation of almighty God,” etc., as far as “shall incur.”

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on 2 May.

XLIV. TO THE ABBOTS OF PEGAVIA [Note: Pegavia, or rather Pegau, a monastery of distinguished name in Saxony, mentioned by Emperor Frederick III in his catalogue of imperial abbots who possessed the right of voting in imperial diets. BUCEL., *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 69. See book I, letters 317, 318.], CORVEY [Note: See book VI, letter 187, note.], AND . . . OF THE STONE OF ST MICHAEL [Note: “A distinguished monastery in Saxony of the Benedictine Order, of the sacred Cistercian family, so called from Campen, though for what reason we do not know. Its foundress was Beatrix, abbess of Quedlinburg. This abbey was, as they call it, a daughter-house of the monastery of Altenberg; a colony of monks was brought thence into it. There are extant letters of Innocent III and Honorius III to various abbots of the place, etc. For the abbot of the Stone of St Michael, in the diocese of Halberstadt, etc., consult the angel Manrique.” BUCELIN, *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 206.], IN THE DIOCESES OF MERSEBURG, PADERBORN, AND HALBERSTADT. He assigns them the task of investigating the subjection of the monastery of Gandersheim to the Church of Hildesheim. (At St Peter’s, 3 May.)

[Col. 0603A]

The beloved daughters in Christ, M., abbess, and the sisters of the church of Gandersheim, formerly petitioned us that we should write to certain persons to inspect carefully the privileges granted to that church. Because these were worn away by age and contained the liberties of the monastery itself, they feared to send them to our presence owing to the dangers of the roads. We, granting kindly assent to [Col. 0603B] their petition, charged four bishops and as many abbots to go to that church, diligently inspect its privileges of liberty, and faithfully send their reports to us, fortified by the security of their seals. As we learned from their letters, in obedience to our command they carefully examined the privileges of our predecessors of good memory, Agapetus and John, presented to them, faithfully transcribed their tenor, and sealed it with their seals for presentation before us.

Likewise, our venerable brother G. [Note: See the notes on the immediately preceding letter.], now archbishop of Rheims but then bishop of Palestrina, while exercising the office of legate in those regions, conferred the blessing on the same abbess when she had then been elected; he set down in writing the tenor of those privileges and decreed that it be presented before us, secured with his own seal. Since we gave due credence both to that legate and to the said investigators, because their reports agreed in every respect, and since we observed that the monastery itself is recorded in the register of dues of our Camera among the other free and exempt monasteries, we saw no reason why those privileges should not be renewed. Especially since [Col. 0604A] the same abbess and sisters had founded their claim both upon the tenor of those privileges and upon the testimony of our register of dues.

But because Cor . . . of the greater church, and J. of Holy Cross, canons of Hildesheim, appearing in our presence, asserted that the Church of Hildesheim had been in possession of the subjection of that monastery for a period of one hundred years and more, we did not think fit to renew those privileges, lest we seem to prejudice the Church of Hildesheim in its right. Although they were not procurators, they nevertheless petitioned devotedly on behalf of the Church of Hildesheim, to which they are bound, that its right be preserved; and they offered themselves to pay the abbess’s costs if their assertion could not be fully proved by the Church of Hildesheim.

Therefore, in order that we may preserve its right to both that monastery and that church—for in this matter we are debtors to all—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you jointly go to a suitable place and, by our authority, summon those who are to be summoned in this cause; investigate diligently the truth in all respects; proceed to the rendering of a definitive judgment; and send to the Apostolic See all proceedings faithfully written down under the attestation of your letters, appointing the parties a suitable term by which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment. We decree that the Church of Hildesheim, unless it sufficiently proves against the monastery of Gandersheim [Col. 0604C] the assertion of the aforesaid canons, or the aforesaid canons, should that Church perhaps refuse to ratify what they have done, shall be condemned to pay the lawful expenses of the same abbess, according to the constitution previously issued by us on such matters.

But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on 3 May.

XLV. TO THE . . . BISHOP OF ARRAS [Note:
