“Ralph (de Neuville), born at Vienne in Gaul, archdeacon of the Churches of Arras and Valenciennes, was appointed bishop in October [Col. 0604C] 1203 and governed until 1221, when he is recorded as having died on 26 March, before Easter. Locrius, in his *Chronicle*, p. 370, reports that he was consecrated at Rome by Pope Innocent III and admitted to the College of Cardinals under the title of St Sabina; Gazeus in the *History of the Church of Belgium*, the *Gallic-Flemish Annals*, Frizonius, and after him François du Chesne agree. Ciaconius makes no mention of his cardinalate.”

Thus far the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 329. Oldoinus indeed, in his notes to Ciaconius (vol. II, col. 39), lists Ralph among cardinals of uncertain creation. This letter of Innocent proves that Ralph, if he was ever admitted among the cardinals, had not been distinguished with that exalted title before 1205. Yet Oldoinus himself seems to have doubted his cardinalate greatly, for he gives him no place among the cardinals who attended the election of Pope Honorius III (*ibid.*, col. 43). Nevertheless, among the cardinals who died under the same Pope Honorius III, he names a certain Rodulf, a Gaul, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, who died in 1220.] . . . TO THE ABBOT OF ST BERTIN [Note: John III of Ypres, a monk of Lobbes, was elected abbot of St Bertin in 1187. He died in 1230. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 500.] IN THE DIOCESE OF THÉROUANNE; AND TO S. OF VALLIBUS, CANON OF LAON. He entrusts to them the examination of the cause concerning the election of the bishop of Amiens [Note: This letter must certainly be compared with the material found in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1180, and in the booklet entitled *Histoire des évêques d’Amiens*, by M. J. M. O. S., Paris, 1770, 12mo, p. 120. See book VII, letter 122, and the notes there.]. (2 May.)

[Col. 0605A]

Beloved sons, the . . . provost [Note: [Col. 0605D] Concerning the provosts of Amiens, there is nothing in the authors cited above.], the archdeacon, and certain other canons of Amiens, appearing before us, took care to set forth in our audience that, since their church was deprived of its pastor and the chapter of that church had assembled to deliberate upon appointing a bishop, they unanimously referred the matter to three persons. These, having sworn a bodily oath, were to ascertain the wishes of each individual and name as bishop-elect the man upon whom the sounder part of the chapter should agree; [Col. 0605B] and all were bound, setting appeal aside, to receive as their pastor the person whom those men should decree to be elected. They also granted those three the authority to determine which party was to be deemed the stronger.

Accordingly, when the arbitrators had sought the wishes of all the canons, they ordered the person whose duty it was to elect as father and pastor for them the dean [Note: [Col. 0605D] Richard of Gerberoy; see Letter 41 of Book III, note, and Letter 122 of Book VII.] of that church. [Note: [Col. 0606D] The authors of Gallia Christiana maintain, on the basis of a certain charter of Saint John, that this occurred before February of the present year, 1205.] But because the agreement had been secured by their taking an oath, some expressly consented to him; whereas the . . . chancellor . . . cantor of that church, and certain others, delayed giving their consent because the said dean was manifestly incapable of performing the episcopal office, since there could be no doubt about his state of health. They therefore urgently requested a postponement from their fellow canons [Col. 0605C] so that they might consult the Apostolic See whether, by reason of the oath taken, they were bound to receive as bishop that dean, so infirm and broken by old age, or whether they could lawfully dissent from him notwithstanding the binding force of the oath.

When they were in no way able to obtain from the others time for deliberation and consultation with a superior, some of them, fearing the disgrace lest it might at first sight be objected that they had incurred the stain of perjury, expressly consented to the aforesaid dean; while certain others held back, having not been asked. Moreover, when the opposing party sought confirmation of his election from our venerable brother . . . . . the Archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0606D] See Letter 116 of Book VII.], cardinal of the Holy Roman [Col. 0605D] Church and legate of the Apostolic See, they notified him that the said dean was incapable of discharging the pontifical office. Stating the grounds of his incapacity, they humbly asked the archbishop carefully to examine the dean’s person, being prepared to demonstrate his defect through suitable witnesses. John, canon of Saint-Firmin, appealed to the Apostolic See against confirmation of his election and promised that, where required, he would prove the man’s incapacity; a date being assigned for his appeal.

The aforesaid archbishop, however, assigned both them and the said dean a day at Paris, on which they were to appear before him and he would have the dean’s person carefully examined. But the archbishop did not come to the designated place on the appointed day. Instead, by his letters he instructed our venerable brother the Bishop of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0606D] See Letter 149 of Book V, note.], and our beloved sons Masters R. of Corthon [Note: [Col. 0606D] Thus in the Vatican copy.], and R. of Ableiges, [Col. 0606B] that, if they found the said dean suitable, they should confirm him by the archbishop’s authority, setting aside contradiction and appeal.

When these delegates were sitting in court and the commission of the aforesaid archbishop had been publicly read, the said provost, Andrew the priest and Master J., canon of Saint-Firmin of Amiens, and J. of Scalaphai, urgently requested that the letters in question be produced to them, so that they might consider whether those men could confirm the aforesaid election. But when the delegates refused to give them a copy of the letters, they, reserving their objection that the letters had not been shown, set forth before the aforesaid delegates that the dean’s election ought by no means to be confirmed. They alleged that the resignation of . . . . . the late Bishop of Amiens [Col. 0606C] [Note: [Col. 0606D] The Bishop of Amiens succeeded by Dean Richard of Gerberoy was Theobald III d’Heilly, of whom something has already been said in the note to Letter 41 of Book III. But attention should be given to what is said here about his voluntary resignation, concerning which the authors so often cited say nothing; they maintain that Theobald retained the mitre until the last day of his life.] was invalid, since it had been made without canonical form and apostolic authorization, because it had been accepted by persons who were not permitted to accept it.

They further alleged that the said dean was incapable of performing the pontifical office, since his hands shook so greatly that he could not perform the priestly office without scandal and danger; and that, though absent for a long time, he had received certain distributions made in the church of Amiens, which no one customarily received except when present or seriously burdened by illness. They further charged against him that letters presented in the chapter’s name, by which confirmation was sought, had been dispatched after securing the absence of those parties. [Col. 0606D] They were prepared, where required, to establish all this more fully.

These reasons having thus been alleged, both the said provost for himself and his associates, and the aforesaid Andrew and Master J., appealed to the Apostolic See. [Col. 0607A] Setting the term of their appeal on the Sunday on which *Invocavit me* is sung, they procured an apostolic prohibition addressed to the aforesaid delegates, forbidding them to presume to confirm the said election; they likewise appealed against the dean himself, that he should not accept the election.

Before us they also repeated concerning his weakness that, when the same dean had been accused by the chapter before W., of good memory, [Note: [Col. 0607D] See Letter 14 of Book III, note.] Archbishop of Reims, of not attending the canonical hours, he had sufficiently excused himself on the grounds of weakness and old age. They further added that four years had now elapsed since that dean had celebrated the solemnities of Mass in the cathedral church, whether privately or publicly; and that he had frequently suffered such a failure while celebrating Mass [Col. 0607B] that, in the very consecration of the Eucharist, he had to leave the altar. Moreover, his eyesight had become exceedingly weakened. They therefore asked that his election, made of a useless person, be wholly annulled, since he could not perform the priestly office.

On the other hand, our beloved son . . . . abbot of Saint-Josse [Note: [Col. 0607D] Florentius, who occurs in documents from at least 1203 until 1210. *Gallia Christiana*, ibid., col. 1293.], procurator for the dean, alleged that, when the see of Amiens was vacant and the chapter of that church had assembled together on the day fixed for election, they had, by common consent, referred the matter to three persons, as stated above. Having received from each an oath that he would in good faith declare his wishes concerning the appointment of a pastor, those three were to cause to be named as pastor a person from the body of the Church upon whom the sounder party agreed. [Col. 0607C] They were also, as the opposing party had alleged, empowered to determine which party was the stronger; for the parties were virtually in agreement in every respect about the form of the compromise. This document, as was said, had been sealed with the chapter’s seal by the common will of all, and was also produced before us.

Having examined the wishes of the individuals and deliberated carefully, the arbitrators announced to the chapter that the said dean was to be elected bishop. Although some had initially doubted, his election was afterward approved by all; and the chapter, through its messengers, presented it to the said archbishop for confirmation. But the archbishop delayed confirming it because at that time they presented him only letters of credence, which did not contain an account of the proceedings. [Col. 0607D] Later, however, when the same man and other distinguished messengers appeared before him at Reims on the appointed day with open letters of that chapter containing the entire course of the affair, and urgently sought confirmation of the election on behalf of the chapter, the aforesaid provost, M. the chancellor, Bodinus, J. of the Cross, and Walter of Bolencort—who had consented to that election and, when questioned by the archbishop, publicly confessed that they had consented and still consented—declared to him that, although the person [Col. 0608A] elected deserved commendation for his conduct and learning, he was nevertheless so burdened by old age and infirmity that he ought not at all to be appointed to the government of a bishopric, since he could not perform the priestly office.

Although the archbishop had no doubt whatsoever as to his prudence and uprightness, and although the manner of his election was clear to him both from the oral testimony of two arbitrators and others whose word rightly deserved credit, and from the letters of the third arbitrator and the chapter, yet, because it had been alleged before him that the man was incapable of exercising the pontifical office, and lest he appear to omit anything relevant or to proceed less cautiously than was proper in so important a matter, on the Saturday immediately following the most recent Epiphany [Note: [Col. 0608D] This date assigned to the parties should be noted. The authors mentioned maintain that the see of Amiens had already been vacant since April 1204.] [Col. 0608B] he assigned him a date at Paris, so that he might speak with him and carefully inspect his person.

But because the archbishop, occupied with certain other pressing affairs, could not be present there on the appointed day or then dispose of the matter, he entrusted his functions to the aforesaid judges, firmly ordering them to confirm the election of the said dean as speedily as possible by his authority, setting aside every contradiction and appeal—since contradiction and appeal had been excluded by the terms of the compromise—unless they found him so incapable that he ought by law to be rejected. If any opponents or rebels should arise after confirmation, they were to restrain them by ecclesiastical censure, setting appeal aside. [Col. 0608C] If all could not be present, the said bishop, with either one of the others, was nevertheless to execute these instructions.

As we have seen contained in the letters of the said bishop and masters, the aforesaid bishop, prevented both by his own affairs and by those of the archbishop, was unable to come to Paris on the appointed day to execute the archbishop’s mandate; but he arrived there the following day with his fellow judges. The said elect and messengers of the chapter were present before them seeking confirmation. The above-named provost and archdeacon, together with some of their fellow canons, who did not expressly oppose the election, declared that the dean’s election ought not to be confirmed: first because the resignation of . . . . . [Col. 0608D] the late Bishop of Amiens was invalid; secondly because the person elected was incapable; and thirdly because confirmation of such a matter could not be delegated to them. They urgently requested that the commission letters be shown to them and attempted by every means to prevent confirmation of the aforesaid election. The oft-mentioned provost, with two others who did not belong to the body of that Church, appealed to our audience that the aforesaid delegates should proceed no further.

But the chapter’s messengers alleged to the contrary before them that the said provost and archdeacon [Col. 0609A] with their associates had been present at and consented to the aforesaid resignation, and had approved, with the others, the compromise concerning the appointment of a pastor, having given a bodily oath. Furthermore, though at first they had raised an objection concerning the elected man’s incapacity and there had been some discussion of it, they afterward approved the election and, consenting to him, sent messengers with the others to the said archbishop to seek its confirmation.

Therefore they were not to be heard at all, since, alleging their own dishonorable conduct and reverting to what they had renounced, they appeared to contradict their own oaths and admissions. The aforesaid messengers also alleged that production of the instrument [Col. 0609B] should not be made to them, because the delegates had been assigned not the cognizance of the cause but only its execution. Nor was it their concern, even if there might be a just and reasonable ground for concern, to investigate at the instance of those against whom the objection of the oath, immediately established by the proofs offered, stood in the way—or at the instance of others not belonging to the body of that Church—whether he was incapable. That inquiry belonged solely to the metropolitan, to whom that office had been delegated.

Having taken counsel on all these matters with prudent men, the delegates were ready to give them a copy of the instrument and ordered them to appear before them the next day at the appointed hour, when they would hear and do what the order of reason required. But the aforesaid provost and archdeacon, [Col. 0609C] with their associates, appealed to the Apostolic See and contumaciously withdrew from their presence.

The aforesaid delegates met on the following day at the appointed hour and summoned before them our venerable brother . . . the Archbishop of Dublin [Note: [Col. 0609D] See Letter 160 of Book V.], our beloved sons . . . the cantor . . . the chancellor [Note: [Col. 0609D] See Letter 98 of Book V, note.], and a great many other masters of Paris. Having consulted with them, and being assured by direct observation that the said dean was competent for the priestly office—and that on that same day, in their presence and that of many others, he had celebrated divine service, as we have seen stated in the judges’ letters—they received suitable witnesses whom he had brought with him to Paris. These testified that, on one winter day after the Nativity [Col. 0609D] of the Lord and before the feast of Epiphany, he had travelled comfortably seven leagues or more, the same distance on the following day, and ten leagues or more on the third.

Since the delegates were thus fully satisfied concerning the inquiry imposed upon them and the other matters advanced by the chapter’s aforesaid messengers, they considered that no deference at all was due to the opponents’ contradiction and appeal, since these had been forbidden. Since delay seemed likely to bring danger upon them, they confirmed the aforesaid election by the authority of the said archbishop and decreed that any opponents and rebels who should hereafter appear were alike subject to sentence of excommunication.

The aforesaid procurator also produced before us letters of the chapter of Amiens, in which we saw it stated that, although the said dean had suffered from a grave illness in the preceding year, he had now been restored to his former health and could fully perform the office due from him. [Col. 0610A] He further produced letters sealed with the seals of many abbots, who humbly entreated us to deem ratified and valid the confirmation concerning him made by the aforesaid judges, since neither bodily strength was lacking in him nor the fervor of devotion and faith had grown weak.

We therefore, having carefully heard these and the other things which the parties wished to lay before us, with the common counsel of our brethren, have judged that the following provision should be made. By these apostolic writings we command your discretion that, because bodily weakness alone is alleged against the said [Col. 0610B] elect, whereas in other respects he is judged adequate, and because such weakness can best be perceived through direct personal inspection, you—to whom we entrust our authority in this matter, having great confidence in the prudence of your discretion—shall, once again and for greater caution, cause the said elect to appear personally before you. With God before your eyes, carefully examine in him every circumstance. Unless you find him burdened by such weakness that he cannot discharge the episcopal office, you shall firmly command his metropolitan, all appeal ceasing, not to delay consecrating him; opponents, etc.

But if he suffers from such weakness that he is deemed incapable of performing the pontifical office, you shall by our authority cause him to desist, [Col. 0610C] ordering the chapter of Amiens to elect unanimously, within fifteen days and with your counsel, a suitable person as their pastor. If perhaps they cannot agree within the prescribed period, or agree upon a person less suitable, then you shall thereafter, setting appeal aside, appoint for them as bishop a suitable person worthy of so great a burden and honor; opponents, etc. If not all of you can be present, you, brother bishop, shall nevertheless carry this out with either of the others.

Given on the sixth day before the Nones of May [2 May].

XLVI. TO THE . . . ARCHBISHOP OF COLOCZA. Concerning the restoration to devotion to the Apostolic See of a certain bishopric which is said here to lie in the land of the sons of Beloknese. [Note: [Col. 0610D] Thus it is read in the Conti copy.] (Fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].)

[Col. 0610D]

It has been made known to us by you that a certain bishopric is situated in the land of the sons of Beloknese. Since it is subject to no metropolitan, you intend to restore it to devotion to the Apostolic See and place it under the jurisdiction of the Church of Colocza, provided that we give you our consent in this matter. Accordingly, acceding to your desire insofar as we can with God, we grant you by the authority of these present letters that, if the foregoing is true, you may restore that bishopric to devotion to the Roman [Col. 0611A] Church and subject it to the authority of the Church of Colocza. But take careful care that that bishopric is not subject to the Church of Constantinople; for, since the Church of Constantinople has recently returned to unity with the Apostolic See, we do not wish it to be deprived of its right.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].

XLVII. TO THE . . . PRIOR AND CANONS OF SAINT PETER [Note: [Col. 0611D] Concerning “Turgarcan.” Thus it is read in the Conti copy; but undoubtedly it should be read “Thurgarton.” The matter here concerns the priory of Thurgarton, of the Order of Saint Augustine, in Nottinghamshire. We possess its foundation charter (*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 92, col. 1), issued by Ralph de Ayncourt. It lacks chronological indications, but, as its synchronisms show, it was given about the year 1145.] OF TURGARCAN [Note: [Col. 0611D] Read: Thurgarton.]. He adjudges to them the churches of Ttihebi [otherwise Tytheby] and Wetorp [otherwise Duthorpe]. (Second day before the Kalends of May [30 April].)

Formerly, before our venerable brother J., [Note: [Col. 0611D] See Letter 3 of Book VII, note.] Bishop of St Albans, who had been granted as auditor to Robert, procurator of [Col. 0611B] your church, and Master Columb, procurator of our venerable brother . . . Archbishop of York, [Note: [Col. 0611D] See Letter 54 of Book V.] concerning the complaint which they had against one another, your procurator set forth as follows. M. and R. [Note: [Col. 0611D] M. and R.: Matthew and Richard. They are expressly so named in the charter found in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, [Col. 0612D] ibid., col. 2.] of Vilers, knights, had out of piety conferred upon you the right which they held in the churches of Tithebi [Note: [Col. 0612D] Tithebi; in the charter cited above, Tytheby.] and Wectorp [Note: [Col. 0612D] It appears that it should be read, from the same charter, “Duthorpe.”]. With the consent of T., of blessed memory, then Archbishop of York, [Note: [Col. 0612D] Thurstan, who presided over the Church of York from 1114 to 1140. The charter of Ralph de Ayncourt cited above agrees; note 197. Goswin, *De praesulibus Angliae*, p. 668.] and later of R., of blessed memory, [Note: [Col. 0612D] Roger, who held the see from 1154 until 1181. Ibid., p. 673.] who succeeded that archbishop [Note: [Col. 0612D] Not immediately, indeed: between Thurstan and Roger, Henry Murdac and Saint William held the archiepiscopal staff.], having inspected both the knights’ charters and those of his predecessor, he granted you those churches with their appurtenances and confirmed them to you in perpetual alms.

Alexander, [Col. 0611C] pope of happy memory, our predecessor, granted you that in your churches, when they became vacant, you could appoint three or four of your fellow canons, one of whom you were to present to the diocesan bishop so that he might receive from him the care of souls. He was to answer to him for spiritual matters and to you for temporal matters. And although the aforesaid archbishop, following in his predecessor’s footsteps, had already granted and confirmed to you what he saw had been granted and confirmed by that predecessor, nevertheless, fearing that something might be attempted to your prejudice, you appealed from his burdens to the Apostolic See, committing those churches and all that you possessed to apostolic protection. Although you repeatedly renewed this appeal, the archbishop did not defer to it. He suspended you from the celebration of divine offices and afterward caused his clerics to announce on Maundy Thursday that you were excommunicated. He then assigned you a day on which [Col. 0611D] you were to produce your documents before him.

On that day, having presented your fellow canons to him so that one of them might receive from him the care of souls according to the terms of the aforesaid privilege, and having shown him your confirmations and privileges, he restored the rest to you but retained the privilege just mentioned, asserting that it was false. You therefore appealed to our audience. The archbishop nevertheless caused the goods of those churches to be violently plundered; imposing severe exactions upon you, he suspended at his will your chaplains who would not satisfy him in this matter and placed the churches under interdict.

But when G., your prior of blessed memory, was asked by the same archbishop whether your fellow canons were in the aforesaid churches by the archbishop’s authority or yours, he humbly replied that they had been instituted there by you under authority of the privilege of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0612B] The archbishop ordered him to pronounce sentence of excommunication against you. The prior replied that he would rather absolve than bind you, and would more readily resign the priory into the archbishop’s hands than bind you on this account in the bond of excommunication. Although the archbishop did not then receive the priory from him, shortly afterwards he suspended the prior, who was unwilling to resign, from the priory and ordered you not thereafter to regard him as prior. But, trusting in the appeal, you paid no heed at all to the sentences thus pronounced.

Master C., procurator of that archbishop, replied in opposition that you were bound by the bond of excommunication, first because you had rashly laid violent hands upon his clerics who resided in the aforesaid churches, and secondly because, without the assent of the diocesan bishop, you had occupied those churches. According to the custom of the English Church, confirmed by the Apostolic See, sentence of excommunication is pronounced against such persons in the synods and frequently every year. He further alleged that the privilege was legally suspect; and that, even if it were not suspect, it did not derogate from the general custom of the land, which it did not mention. For it is a practice of the English Church that, upon the death of incumbents, the custody of vacant churches devolves upon the diocesan [Col. 0612D] bishop.

The same procurator also added that you had despoiled that archbishop of the aforesaid churches, and therefore restitution was due to him. Further, [Col. 0613A] even if the aforesaid privilege were genuine, he maintained that it applied only to churches which belonged to you by both rights, not to those in which you had merely a right of patronage. Finally, he pleaded prescription of thirty years, asserting that the privilege applied to the aforesaid churches, since none of them was sufficient for so many incumbents. The privilege had not been taken away by the archbishop, but had been deposited as suspect with the sacristan Suellen, to be carried to us by a common messenger. It was subsequently offered to you twice. Nor was it true that the archbishop had exacted anything specifically from the said churches. Rather, when he sought assistance from his subjects because of expenses incurred in exile, and they offered him a fifth part of their income for one year, the revenues both of those present and absent were assessed. Moreover, through the archbishops’ confirmations no right had been acquired by your church; what the patrons had granted—namely, merely the right of patronage—had only been confirmed.

The procurator then offered to prove that the privilege had been produced by you to the archbishop and, with your consent, placed in sequestration for delivery to the common messenger, who would present it before us; and that it was subsequently offered to you twice, not secretly but before many persons. [Col. 0614A] He also offered to prove that the archbishop possessed the aforesaid churches, whereas you had violently occupied them after expelling his clerics and laying hands upon them; further, that after the archbishop’s promotion the said prior and you presented to him three clerics for the churches in question and that the archbishop instituted them therein; likewise, that after an excommunication not preceded by appeal, and after laying hands upon clerics, you presumed to celebrate divine offices; and that the same prior, after resigning the priory into the archbishop’s hands, had assumed its administration for himself despite the archbishop’s prohibition.

Since these matters had been advanced before the aforesaid auditor, but could not provide us with full certainty, we committed the cause to our venerable brother . . . . Bishop of Ely [Note: [Col. 0613B] See Letter 54 of Book V.], and to our beloved sons . . . . the Abbots of Leicester [Note: [Col. 0613B] This seems to concern the abbot of the monastery of the Meadows, near the borough of Leicester, of the Order of Saint Augustine, founded in the year of the Lord 1143. See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 308, col. 2.] and of Rievaulx [Note: [Col. 0613B]

The abbey of Rievaulx, of the Cistercian Order, in Yorkshire, was founded in 1147. A succession of its abbots is found in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. [Col. 0613C] 839, col. 2. From it one gathers that the abbot of Rievaulx in question here was Osmund, who, having been cellarer of Fountains, became abbot about 1184 and held office for thirty-nine years. “In whose [Osmund’s] time,” it is said in the aforementioned fragment on the succession of the abbots of Rievaulx, “King Richard remitted to the said house [of Rievaulx] 1,300 marks owed from Jewish moneylending, in which, a few years earlier, while Abbot Hugh of Wladdeworth, Osmund’s predecessor, was in office, it had been encumbered with great debts. In the seventh or eighth year of that King Richard, the said Abbot Osmund was made procurator of Cardinal Stephen for all his revenues in England, so that he, Reginald, who held the abbacy fifteen years, Richard, who held it sixteen years, and Walter, who held it fourteen years, received from the goods of the said cardinal, until Walter’s eleventh year, 400 marks annually at various terms. They provided suitably from that money both for dependents and for increasing all their lands, tenements, and rents; and for fifty-three years they were so enriched from the goods of the said cardinal that they were considered almost wealthy and in need of no temporal good.”

Thus far the author of this fragment, which we are greatly concerned should not appear to be of little importance. For the synchronisms agree poorly with one another. If, out of the fifty-three years during which Cardinal Stephen’s goods are here said to have been administered by the abbots of Rievaulx, eleven years are assigned to Walter, sixteen to Richard, and fifteen to Reginald, those goods must have been administered by Osmund for only eleven years. Yet the last eleven years of Osmund’s rule cannot in any way be counted from the seventh or eighth year of King Richard, the very year in which the author of our fragment wishes the administration of Cardinal Stephen’s goods to have begun under Osmund. By his own calculations, Osmund could not have assumed the government of Rievaulx before 1184, or at least not before 1180. But he held the abbatial staff for thirty-nine years. Therefore the eleventh year before the end of his rule—the year in which he began administering Cardinal Stephen’s goods—coincides with at least 1207, unless one prefers even 1211. But 1207 itself cannot be connected with the eighth year of King Richard, who died before the beginning of 1200.

What if, instead of the name Richard, we read the name of King John in our fragment? This certainly agrees better with the history. For it is most certainly established that Stephen Langton [otherwise de Langhtone]—the very famous Archbishop of Canterbury and likewise cardinal of the Holy Roman Church here in question—had already been made cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus by Innocent III many years earlier, that is, at least in 1207. Although Ciaconius and Panvinio maintain that he was raised to the cardinalitial rank no earlier than 1212 or 1213, and Oldoinus admits this (see Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 27), it is most certainly established that Innocent III had declared Stephen cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus many years earlier, that is, at least in 1207. Stephen already bore the cardinalitial title when he was elected Archbishop of Canterbury, and his election can be assigned only to 1207. It is therefore highly probable that about this time—namely around 1207 or 1208, which precisely coincides with the seventh or eighth year of King John, not King Richard—shortly after his elevation both to the cardinalitial rank [Col. 0614D] and to the archiepiscopal throne, Stephen entrusted the administration of his goods to the Abbot of Rievaulx.

Yet not even in this way does every difficulty disappear. Counting from 1207 or 1208 the fifty-three years during which Cardinal Stephen’s goods are said to have been administered by the abbots of Rievaulx, to such great advantage for the abbey’s affairs, we find that they held this administration until 1260 or 1261. But how this could have happened, when Stephen did not live beyond 1228, is not readily understood. We shall not attempt to solve this new difficulty. Let those skilled in the ecclesiastical affairs of England consider it. For us, given the nature of our undertaking, it is enough—and perhaps more than enough—to have pointed out these difficulties to more inquisitive readers, lest in publishing Innocent’s letters our diligence be thought excessively deficient.]
we deemed it proper to commit the matter to them, directing the same judges that, after summoning the parties, receiving back the indulgence thus withheld, and compelling its holder [Col. 0615A], by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to restore it, they should—unless the archbishop proved the objections raised, or any of them by which your purpose ought to be impeded, since by the nature of things it could scarcely be possible for them all to be proved—condemn that archbishop to moderate costs payable to the opposing party, as would be just, after restoring what had been taken; and should nevertheless hear what might be alleged on either side concerning the principal matter. Having examined the depositions which we sent them enclosed under our seal, they were, without appeal, to determine what was just and cause it to be firmly observed by our authority. Moreover, having received our mandate in this matter, the judges themselves, as we have learned from their letters, summoned the parties to appear before them [Col. 0615B]; and, having observed all judicial formalities as was fitting, and after the withheld indulgence had been restored, following publication of the depositions and the disputations held upon them, when allegations had been renounced on both sides—unless perhaps, in response to their questioning, either party thought something should be alleged—they considered the case difficult and declined to proceed to sentence; instead, with the consent of the parties, they referred it, fully prepared, to examination by the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, when the parties’ representatives were present before us, we appointed as auditor our beloved son M., cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore [Note: [Col. 0615D] See letter 54 of Book III, note.]. From his report we learned that four principal charges had been brought by you against the said archbishop: first, that after an appeal had been lodged with us, he had repeatedly suspended the aforesaid prior [Col. 0615C] and declared that you were subject to the bond of excommunication; second, that he had removed grain from the aforesaid churches; third, that he had compelled a certain one of your chaplains to make a payment for redemption; and fourth, that he had forced you on this account to incur great expenses.

On the other side it was answered to the contrary: that your appeal had no force, since, contrary to the prohibition issued under penalty of anathema in the general synod, according to the custom of the English Church, forbidding anyone to presume to appropriate vacant churches without the diocesan’s consent, you had appropriated the said churches after the death of their incumbents; whereby it was clear that you had incurred the sentence of excommunication [Col. 0615D]. Therefore, being bound by a general sentence, you could not protect yourselves by an appeal. As to his removal of the grain from those churches, he had exercised his right, since the custody of vacant churches in his diocese belongs to him according to an ancient custom observed hitherto. Nor had he compelled your chaplain to make a redemption payment, but had received from him what he believed that the chaplain had received from those churches. Nor had he driven you to incur expenses; rather, you yourselves had driven both him and yourselves to them.

Therefore, after diligent examination of the depositions and allegations [Col. 0616A], indulgences and grants, as well as privileges and confirmations, and since it has been fully established that many appeals were lawfully lodged, we decree that the sentences of suspension and excommunication pronounced by the said archbishop against the aforesaid prior and yourselves are invalid. By sentence we condemn that archbishop to restore everything which he took from those churches and extorted from the said chaplain, and also to reimburse the expenses which you are known to have incurred on this account. We adjudge to you the aforesaid churches with their appurtenances. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this page of our judgment, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given on 30 April.

XLVIII. [Note: [Col. 0615D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.] TO W., LORD OF GUIRCHIA. He receives him under the protection of Saint Peter, with an annual payment of one bezant. (9 May.)

[Col. 0616B]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious vows and to grant its benevolent favour to the honourable desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son and noble man, favourably assenting to your petitions, we receive your person, with all your goods, under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and strengthen that protection by the safeguard of this present writing. As a token of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall annually pay to us and our successors one bezant freely offered. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given . . . on 5 May, in the eighth year.

XLIX. [Note: [Col. 0615D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.] TO THE WOMAN ALFERADA. He receives under protection a church founded by her. (11 May.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent, etc., as far as “assenting.” The church which you founded in honour of Saint Mary in the town of Baroli, with all its goods, etc., as far as “we strengthen.” As a token of this protection obtained from us, you shall annually pay to us and our successors one gold halfpenny. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given 11 May.

L. [Note: [Col. 0616D] Raynaldus gives a fragment of this letter under the year 1205, §64. The words found in his text are enclosed here in brackets.] . . . . TO THE KING OF CASTILE. He rebukes him because Jews and Saracens are treated with honour. (5 May.)

[Col. 0616D]

We grieve and are deeply disturbed no less by the sin of those who commit such acts than by the harm suffered by those who endure them: namely, that the royal highness shows itself harsh and severe toward those to whom it ought to be kind and favourable, and vexes those whom it ought especially to cherish. We have learned that, although you had released all clerics of your realm from every exaction and levy, you afterwards changed your mind and impose levies and exactions upon them as you please. And when Jewish slaves, whether purchased or native-born, are converted to the faith, although the price to be paid for such persons is fixed by canon law, you cause the Jews themselves to retain from episcopal property as much as they affirm on oath that those slaves were worth.

Thus, recently, from our venerable brother, the bishop of Burgos, in the case of a certain Saracen woman, the slave-girl of a Jew, whom he declares was scarcely worth ten solidi, you ordered two hundred gold pieces to be received [Col. 0617A]. Further, although we considered it right to send you apostolic letters regarding the fact that you do not permit the Jews and Saracens of your realm to be compelled to pay tithes on their possessions, you not only refused to induce them to pay tithes, but even granted them a freer licence not to pay tithes and to acquire [Col. 0617B] more extensive possessions; so that, as the Synagogue grows, the Church may decline, and the handmaid may freely be preferred.

Moreover, when the same bishop had formerly appeared in our presence, you appropriated for yourself, together with all its appurtenances, the wealthiest church in his diocese, and granted it to a certain abbess of the Cistercian Order. Because the bishop had brought a dispute before the abbot of Cîteaux against that abbess concerning the same church, you compelled him to confirm that grant; and by threats and terrors you induced both him and his canons to grant that church and to make the abbess a canoness. You also occupied the church of Saint [Col. 0617C] Julian of Mena, which his predecessors had redeemed from you for a thousand marabotins, refusing to restore it to him. Nor are you willing to give the Church of Burgos tithes from the revenues which come to you from the diocese of Burgos, although your forebears customarily paid them. You also uphold in their error the abbot and clerics of Covarrubias, who are rebellious and disobedient toward that bishop, giving them assistance against him.

[Note: [Col. 0617D] These matters are found in Raynaldus.]

Therefore, dearest son in Christ, lest you appear to be suppressing ecclesiastical liberty and exalting the Synagogue and the Mosque, and lest you inflict upon the Church, Christ’s bride, or upon its ministers actions that may cloud the purity of your faith, we admonish and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord: correct all these things both in yourself [Col. 0617D] and, by the authority granted you, cause them to be corrected in others. Otherwise, however much we love your person in the Lord, because we neither wish nor ought to tolerate the oppression of churches entrusted to our care, we shall defer rather to God the King than to a human king. You should know that by our letters we have instructed our venerable brothers, the bishops of Huesca and Tarazona, and our beloved son, the dean of Tarazona, to compel you in such matters by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Given 5 May.

LI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF GNIEZNO. In response to his inquiry whether he could dispense in the case of a marriage contracted in ignorance within the sixth degree of consanguinity, he replies that it may be tolerated. (10 May.)

[Col. 0618A]

You show yourself to exercise the office of a provident shepherd when, in matters doubtful to you and capable of endangering souls, you seek the oracle of the Apostolic See, ready, as you state, to adhere to its counsels and obey its commands. Indeed, as has become known to our apostolic office from the letter of your brotherhood, one of your parishioners, after his wife had entered upon the way of all flesh, married another woman, who was related in the sixth [Col. 0618B] degree of consanguinity to his former wife, although he was wholly unaware of this. Later, when this came to the knowledge of both from the report of certain persons, although a child had been born and they had already remained together for three years, they humbly sought your counsel, and through you ours. We therefore reply to your brotherhood that, unless another impediment stands in the way, you may overlook the matter, so that they may by dispensation remain in the union thus contracted through ignorance.

Given 10 May.

LII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. [Note: [Col. 0618D] See letter 45 of Book III, note.] He is permitted to visit the province of Sens and correct what requires correction. (12 May.)

[Col. 0618C]

Because, as the age grows old, Mary grows sluggish in her contemplation, while Martha, inflamed in aid of her sister, is occupied with business, the continual occupations by which, in this evening of the world, we are more than usually harassed and more heavily burdened than hitherto, compel us to entrust our duties to those who, called to share our solicitude, do not bind in a napkin the talent entrusted to them, but rather put it out at interest; in whose mouth the word of the Lord is not bound, but who know rather how to pour forth a good word and bring forth from the treasure of their heart things both old and new.

Therefore, placing all the greater confidence in your learning and judgment because we have experienced them more intimately and frequently in many great matters [Col. 0618D], we have judged it expedient to provide for the entire province of Sens through you. By this present document we grant you leave, by authority not so much your own as ours, to exercise in that province the office of visitation, correcting what you find should be corrected and establishing what you see should be established. Since no one ought to be compelled to serve as a soldier at his own expense, nor should the mouth of the threshing ox be muzzled, receive moderate procurations. Assign to suitable persons those benefices which have remained vacant so long in churches of that province that, according to the decrees of the Lateran Council, their collation has devolved to us. Examine [Col. 0619A] causes brought to your hearing and decide them by a canonical determination.

Whenever an appeal is made from you, set a suitable term for the appellant, and unless the appeal lodged has been prosecuted by that date, thereafter proceed in the matter notwithstanding such appeal. By our authority, absolve according to the Church’s form those who have incurred, or shall incur, the sentence laid down by canon for sacrilegious laying of hands—unless perhaps their offence is so grave or enormous that you reasonably believe them to be persons who should be sent to the Apostolic See. We wish the sentence which you reasonably pronounce against the rebellious to be held valid, and command that it be inviolably observed.

[Col. 0619B] Given 12 May.

LIII. [Note: [Col. 0619D] This letter is printed complete, but inaccurately, in Ughellus, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 449; it is therefore given here in brackets.] TO THE BISHOP OF TORTONA [Note: [Col. 0619D] See letter 73 of Book V, note.] AND TO GOOD JOHN, OUR SUBDEACON, A CANON OF VERCELLI. He gives them authority to investigate the bishopric of Alessandria. (12 March.)

[We have seen it contained in letters of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, that he, wishing at the prayers of the consuls, clergy, and people of Alessandria to grant them benevolent favour, and at the instance and request of Galdinus of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0619D] Saint Galdinus, archbishop of Milan, born of the Sala family, devoted from childhood to the study of sacred letters, first archdeacon of the Church of Milan and chancellor of Albert Pirovani, archbishop of Milan, was made by Pope Alexander III priest-cardinal—of the title of Saint Sabina on the Aventine (according to Ciaconius and John of God), or of Saint Susanna at the Two Houses (according to Baronius)—in the second creation, in 1164 or 1165; afterwards he was appointed archbishop of Milan and legate of the Apostolic See in Cisalpine Gaul. For ten years he governed the Church of Milan with the highest praise; worn out by old age, after preaching from the pulpit against the heresy of the Cathars, he rendered his soul to God in the year of salvation 1177 or 1178, or, according to others, 1175. Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1087.], archbishop and legate of the Apostolic See, and of the consuls of Milan, also rulers of Lombardy and the March, after careful deliberation, conferred upon the Church of Alessandria [Col. 0619C] and the city itself, constructed in honour of Saint Peter, the distinction of episcopal rank. He granted them as bishop and pastor Arduinus of happy memory, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, assigning him a diocese nevertheless. But when that man had been elected, before he was consecrated bishop he entered upon the way of all flesh; another was substituted, who likewise did not receive consecration.

Then, at the advice of Algisius of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0620D] Algisius, as early as 1173, if Ughellus is to be believed (*ibid.*, col. 226), succeeded Galdinus. He governed the church entrusted to him excellently and, distinguished by merits, lived until 1183. Authors nevertheless disagree as to the year of his death.], successor to the aforesaid archbishop, so that scandal might be calmed and the hostility which many had conceived toward the said city might be allayed, our said predecessor ordered that the Churches of Alessandria and Acqui should be united, Alessandria being the first see and Acqui the second [Col. 0620A]. In his letters he commanded that same archbishop diligently to induce that same bishop [Note: [Col. 0620D] The Church of Acqui was then governed by Ubertus, who, having formerly followed the party of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, had received a sentence of excommunication from Pope Alexander III. But when reconciliation was later restored between Frederick and the pope, Ubertus also was restored to the unity of the Church. He attended the Lateran Council in 1179 and is also mentioned in 1189. UGHELLUS, *ibid.*, col. 467.] and, through him, his Church, to consent to this arrangement.

The archbishop, desirous of carrying out the apostolic mandate, was unable personally to go to Alessandria and therefore endeavoured to send there . . . the Modocian archpriest; but the elect of the city of Alessandria prevented him, and so the business could not then be completed through that agent. Therefore, lest what had been ordained for the good of peace should be delayed through the deceit of evil men, that archbishop summoned to Milan the aforesaid bishop and certain clerics of the said city, and united the said churches. He decreed that the bishop of Acqui should perform episcopal functions in the Church of Alessandria and be called bishop of Alessandria [Col. 0620B], while reserving to himself the right of the Church of Acqui; but this union did not obtain its intended effect.

Recently our beloved sons Anselm, priest, and the nobleman Rufinus, knight, appeared before us and, on behalf of both clergy and people of that city, humbly petitioned us that, since they wander everywhere like sheep without a shepherd, in peril to their souls, because they have no bishop of their own and wholly refuse to admit one from elsewhere, we might deign to provide them with a proper shepherd, lest they be obliged any longer to stray after the flocks of their fellows. We therefore, although we wish the rights prudently granted by the Apostolic See to the said city to remain firm and inviolate, nevertheless considering that, although two men were elected in the said city [Col. 0620C], neither was consecrated bishop; that the union subsequently established was not carried into effect; and that from the time of our aforesaid predecessor they have had neither bishop nor bishop-elect, have decided, after mature consideration and with the counsel of our brethren, to proceed in so great a matter. By apostolic letters we command your discretion that, having summoned those whom you consider should be summoned for this purpose, and having diligently investigated what you judge should be investigated concerning the matter, you shall, if it can be done without grave scandal and enormous prejudice to others, provide them, according to the first or the second arrangement, with a suitable person as pastor, without appeal. Otherwise, send to our presence everything which you discover in these matters [Col. 0621A], so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed in the matter as we deem expedient.

Given 11 March.

Instrument [Note: [Col. 0621D] Ughellus published this instrument, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 442. We have noted certain variant readings.] by which the people of Alessandria promise submission, reverence, and fidelity to Pope Alexander III, his successors, and the Roman Church.

(Year 1169, month of January.)

[In the name of the Lord, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1169, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of our lord Alexander III, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in January, in the third indiction: we, Rufinus Blancus and William of Bergamasce [Note: [Col. 0621D] In Ughellus: “Bergamonte.”], consuls [Col. 0621B] of the city of Alessandria, make known that, in the presence of the lords Bernard, bishop of Porto; Ubaldus, of the title of Holy Cross; John, of the title of Saints John and Paul; Ildebrand, of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles; John, of the title of Saint Anastasia; Albert, of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina; William, of the title of Saint Peter in Chains; Boscus [Note: [Col. 0621D] Ughellus: “Battius.”], of the title of Saint Pudentiana; Peter, of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso; John, of the title of Saint Mark; and Theodinus, of the title of Saint Vitalis, priest-cardinals; and of Hyacinth, of Saint Mary in Cosmedin; Cencius, of Saint Adrian; Manfred, of Saint George; Hugh [Note: [Col. 0621D] Ughellus: “Hyacinth.”], of Saint Eustachius; and Peter, of Saint Mary in Aquiro, deacon-cardinals; and of the subscribing witnesses who came at this request—namely Peter Sarracenus, seneschal; John, Marshal of God’s Handmaid; Peter, cupbearer; Albert and Albertinus, doorkeepers—on behalf of all the consuls and people of the aforesaid city, we offer by the rod to God, to Saint Peter, to you, our aforesaid lord Pope Alexander, to your Catholic successors, and to the Holy Roman Church in perpetuity, the land which is our own lawful property, lying within the aforesaid city, and which the people of that city bought in order to build a church there. By that same investiture we will that the said land shall at all times belong to the Roman Church by right of ownership [Note: [Col. 0622D] Ughellus: *preiario*].

Furthermore, by the common counsel of the consuls and command of the whole people, the houses of knights [Col. 0621D] and merchants, and of those whose means appear sufficient to maintain oxen [Note: [Col. 0622D] Ughellus: *bonos*, “good.”], shall pay each year, from each house, three denarii of the local currency on the feast of Saint Martin. All others shall pay one denarius from each house, within the octave of Saint Martin, to the person whom the Roman pontiff orders. The consuls who shall from time to time be appointed there shall swear fidelity to you and your successors, every pretext and objection set aside. We also, by command of the other consuls and the people of the city, have sworn fidelity to you and, placing our hands, although unworthy, within your most sacred hands, have performed homage to you. And when the people of the land swear collectively to the consuls, namely every three years as has been ordained, they shall likewise swear to the Roman pontiff.

Because I was present, I, Falco, notary and scribe of the sacred palace of Benevento, wrote this document. I, Peter Sarracenus, seneschal, witness; I, Guiscardus, witness; I, Peter, cupbearer, witness; I, Albert, doorkeeper, witness; I, Albertinus, doorkeeper, witness.]

LIV. TO ALL ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHERS SUBJECT BY DIOCESAN LAW TO THE CHURCH OF BURGOS. That they are not to refuse to attend the synod once a year. (5 May.)

[Col. 0622B]

The petition laid before us by our venerable brother, your bishop, stated that you have refused to assemble once yearly at his synod in the cathedral church, sheltering yourselves behind a prescription of long duration. Since such a pretext cannot and ought not to protect you in this matter, we strictly command you by apostolic letters to attend without any objection once each year the synod which the same bishop has decided to hold at the cathedral church, humbly and devoutly receiving his salutary admonitions and commands. Otherwise, we shall cause the sentence which the same bishop may reasonably pronounce against you on this account to be held valid [Col. 0622C].

Given 5 May.

LV. [Note: [Col. 0622D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §14.] TO THE EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He sends to the Greeks B. [Note: [Col. 0622D] See letter 54 of Book III, note.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, legate *a latere* of the Apostolic See, and commends him to the emperor. (15 May.)

When the other garments of the Lord Jesus Christ were divided, the seamless tunic fell by lot to one person, so that his Church, which he wears as a garment, might be one, and that in it one person, as in the sheep-pool, might be healed, while a multitude of the sick remained outside. “For the wicked walk round about” and cannot enter it and be healed, since a divided mind cannot obtain its petition, and “woe to one who enters the land by two ways!” Therefore, that his undefiled truth might be preserved, the Lord appointed for it one head and teacher, namely blessed Peter, so that he might bring it to completion “in one cubit” [Note: [Col. 0622D] Thus in the copy.] like Noah’s ark, outside which the creatures left behind were drowned in the flood. For Peter’s faith, lest it should fail in his Passion, he prayed especially, commanding him, once converted, to strengthen his brethren thereafter.

Yet the Church of the Greeks, declining from unity [Col. 0623A] until this present time and straying after the flocks of its fellows, withdrew itself from its teacher. Having become like Ephraim, like a deceived dove it called upon Egypt and hurried to the Assyrians; and, although by this time it ought to be a teacher, it seems again to need instruction in the rudiments of the first words of God, because it sinned against him who teaches all truth. Since the Father and the Son have the same goodness, the sin committed against him is presumed to have proceeded from malice, since it lacks every ground of excuse. Nor did it cast leaven out of the house, so that it sinned against him from whom it refused to confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds, failing to observe, as it should, that whoever dishonours the Son wrongs the Father, who is one with him.

Thus, like Ephraim, in its bitterness it provoked the Lord to anger [Col. 0623B] by departing from the teaching of him who deserved to be called Cephas, that is, “head”; it departed from Judah and set its throne in Samaria. Therefore his blood came upon it, its iniquity being brought to completion like that of the Amorite people. For the Lord called his sanctified and mighty ones, and they entered its gates; through them, after evil men had wickedly perished, he gave his vineyard to other cultivators, who would render him fruit in its seasons. The empire of the Greeks was transferred from the disobedient and superstitious to sons obedient and devout, who might offer upon the altar pleasing to the Lord the calves of their lips.

Since the empire has therefore been transferred, it is necessary that the rite of the priesthood should be transferred, so that Ephraim, returning to Judah, may feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth after the old leaven has been purged away. In order that the aforesaid Church may be more fully instructed in devotion and purity of faith according to the ordinances of the most holy Roman Church, which the Lord appointed mother and teacher of all churches, we—who bear the care of all churches, and to whom in blessed Peter the Lord commands that his sheep be fed—desire to visit it as a chief and special daughter. But continual occupations, by which we are more than usually burdened, do not permit us to come personally to that church. Although we have heard that our beloved sons S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis, and P., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus [Col. 0623D], legates of the Apostolic See, have arrived there from the regions of Jerusalem, nevertheless, because they had no special mandate for this purpose, we have judged it proper to send from our side to those regions our beloved son B., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, legate of the Apostolic See—a man indeed provident and discerning, learned and honourable, whom among our other brethren we embrace with arms of sincerity—that, according to the prophetic word, he may more effectively and powerfully uproot and destroy, build and plant, as he finds each matter to require by its character.

We wish the sentence which he canonically pronounces against the rebellious to be held valid, and command that it be inviolably observed. Therefore we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your imperial magnificence in the Lord to receive and honour him kindly as our own person—for in his person we regard ourselves as honoured—and to provide aid and favour to him, to whom we have given the special charge of diligently and prudently attending to your honour and advantage. Thus, through his industry and with your support, once the condition of that Church has been reformed, you may deserve to be established by him upon the throne, at whose right hand the queen stands, clothed in gold and arrayed [Col. 0624B] in variety; and we may be bound to offer your highness abundant thanksgivings for the honour shown to him.

Given 15 May.

LVI. [Note: [Col. 0623D] The copy of letters 56, 57, and 58, which we had arranged to have copied with the others at the end of the Conti transcript, slipped from our hands, by what accident we do not know. We can therefore give here only their summaries. Yet from our notes we know with certainty that these three letters are copied in the autograph of the Vatican archive, fols. 17 and 18. See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §14.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND ALL PRELATES ESTABLISHED IN THE EMPIRE OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He commands them kindly to receive and honourably treat the legate of the Apostolic See, and to observe his enactments.

LVII. TO THE MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT. That he should love and honour the Roman Church.

LVIII. LETTER OF THE MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT. Concerning his love and service toward the Roman Church, he sends an envoy to the pope and informs him of affairs conducted at Constantinople.

[Col. 0624C]

LIX. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CASA DEI. Concerning the establishment of a bishopric in the city of Montpellier. (Rome, 18 May.)

Two principal considerations move us to provide the city of Montpellier [Note: [Col. 0624D] See letters 195 of Book VI and 40 of Book VII.] with a bishop of its own: namely, the numerous multitude of people, who wander like a flock without a shepherd, to the peril of their souls; and the failing condition of your priory, which suffers irreparable loss both spiritual and temporal. In favour of your religious order, which at that time flourished greatly in that place [Col. 0624D], the Apostolic See granted you that episcopal dignity should accrue to the monastic order. But since, when the cause ceases, the effect ought to cease, especially where danger to souls is imminent, we have, with the counsel of our brethren, decided—not wishing to derogate from the enactments of our predecessors, but rather to make wiser provision for the salvation of souls—to restore episcopal dignity to that place.

Although for this purpose we have summoned you to our presence once and again [Col. 0625A], setting out in writing a definite arrangement by which we intend to provide for you, and although at last you sent two of your brethren to the Apostolic See, nevertheless, since they asserted that they had no mandate in the matter, we did not judge it prudent to proceed further in so important a business without greater precaution. Therefore, to remove every ground of excuse, we now summon you a third time peremptorily. By apostolic letters we command that, by the forthcoming feast of Saint Michael, you appear before us through suitable procurators who possess full authority in this matter. Otherwise, thereafter, even in your absence, we shall proceed, God favouring us, as divine prompting shall direct us.

[Col. 0625B] Given at Rome, 18 May.

LX. [Note: [Col. 0625D] In the Conti copy, according to which we arranged for this letter to be transcribed, the following marginal note is found: “chapter *Meminimus*, On Appeal.” By these words the annotator, whoever he may have been, seems to have intended to indicate that this letter is found among the Decretals; but we searched for it in vain, whether in the general Gregorian collection of Decretals or in the particular Innocentian collection.] TO THE BISHOP OF WORCESTER, THE ABBOT OF CIRENCESTER, AND THE DEAN OF YORK. On the same subject as letter 33 of Book VIII [Note: [Col. 0625D] See that letter and the notes appended there.] of this book. (16 May.)

We remember that we sent you apostolic letters in the following form: namely, that our beloved sons, the prior and convent of Tynemouth, submitted to us a grave complaint: although the church of Wodehorn belongs to their right of presentation, our venerable brother, the bishop of Durham, after they had lodged a protest and appealed to us, presumed to institute in that church the beloved son, nephew of our venerable brother J., bishop of Albano [Col. 0625C], on the occasion of a mandate of ours which, because the truth had been suppressed, deserved to be revoked by our certain knowledge. Although the aforesaid prior, compelled by threatening letters addressed, under our authority, by our venerable brother the bishop of Ely to the beloved son, the abbot of St Albans, presented him to the aforesaid bishop of Durham, against the opposition of the convent, and did so unwillingly through letters of that abbot, the convent never wished to give its consent to that presentation, but opposed it completely. They therefore humbly requested that we should deign irrevocably to annul what had thus been done.

But the beloved son Wiscard, procurator of the aforementioned nephew of the bishop of Albano, appearing before the beloved son H., cardinal-deacon of St Eustace, whom we granted to him as auditor [Col. 0625D], maintained that, since he had been despoiled by force of the said church without observance of legal procedure, the aforesaid monks ought not to be heard on such a petition, to his prejudice, before he had obtained the benefit of restitution; but that, once he had obtained the grace of restitution, he was prepared to give them the full measure of justice.

We therefore, wishing to extend favour to the one and justice to the other, command by apostolic letters the said abbot of St Albans, who holds the aforesaid church under the authority of our mandate, to deliver to the nephew of the oft-mentioned bishop of Albano, on our behalf, the church entrusted to him by us; so that he may receive the revenues from the church entrusted to him and preserve and govern it without prejudice to the prior and convent of Tynemouth. After he has obtained that church thus entrusted to him, you, having summoned the parties, are to hear what may be alleged on either side, both concerning possession and concerning title; and, keeping God before your eyes [Col. 0626B], removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, determine what is just, causing it to be carried out, etc. But if any party … let no letters stand in the way of truth, etc. And if not all … you, brother bishop, together with one of them, etc.

Since our judgment is common to all, we command you by apostolic letters that, unless both parties consent that the aforesaid matter be concluded by you according to the form prescribed, you shall proceed, appeals set aside, up to the rendering of a definitive sentence, and refer the cause, sufficiently prepared, to our examination, setting the parties a suitable term within which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment.

Given, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.

[Col. 0626C] It was written to the abbot of St Albans that he should deliver, on our behalf, to the nephew of the often-mentioned bishop of Albano, or to his procurator, the aforesaid church, which he holds under the authority of our mandate and which has been entrusted to him by us.

It was also written to the bishops of Ely and Durham that, if the abbot should neglect to deliver it to him, they themselves should deliver it to the same person.

## LXI

[Note: This letter is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, Book III, title 8, *On the Grant of a Prebend and of a Non-Vacant Church*, chapter 9. What is there found [Col. 0626D] is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are given.]

… BISHOP [Note: See Letter 14 of Book Five, note.] … DEAN, AND MASTER H., CANON OF HILDESHEIM. Concerning a prebend in the church of St Willehad at Bremen, to be assigned to the clerk Daniel. (Fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0626D] [We have received your letters, through which you took care to inform us [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals, which shortly afterward have only “D.” for “beloved son D.”], that, when we had written to you on behalf of our beloved son Daniel, clerk, that you should, by apostolic authority, take care to invest him with the prebend of the church [Note: The Decretals read “vacant,” and shortly afterward “Uniscard” for “Willehad.”] of Saint [Note: Thus it is correctly read in the Third Collection; wrongly, “St Unicard,” in the collection of Raymond. The church of St Willehad of Bremen is one of the two collegiate churches, called provostships, which Adalbert, archbishop of Bremen, founded at his own expense, so called because they had a provost in place of a bishop. Adam of Bremen, Book III, chapter 19: “Therefore, striving with great exertions of spirit and expense to make Bremen equal to other cities, he immediately made, from property which he himself had acquired, two provostships: one for St Willehad, where his body rests, or was translated; the other for St Stephen, whose servant he frequently declared himself to be.” Albert Krantz repeated this in nearly the same words, *Metropolis*, Book IV, chapter 32.] Willehad of Bremen [Col. 0627A], which he asserted had devolved to our grant under the statutes of the Lateran Council, if the canons to whom we had written concerning this should not take care to carry it out, Herbert the provost and certain canons of the same church, together with Daniel himself and Master B., a canon of that church, having appeared before you in your presence for this purpose, it was thus alleged in fact before you [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals, which below read “us” for “you”], that the same Herbert [Note: The Decretals have “H.” for “the said Herbert”; shortly afterward they omit the words “being a simple canon,” and below read “Uniscardi unius.”], provost, while formerly a simple canon of that church, was elected from that church to be a canon of the greater church; and afterwards, when the space of one year, or a year and a half, had elapsed, he was appointed provost in that church of St Willehad [Note: The Decretals: “Uniscard.”], nevertheless retaining the earlier prebend which he then held in that church [Col. 0627B].] The parties agreed with one another on this point, declaring that this was so.

It was also alleged on one side that the same provost, besides that prebend, held another prebend attached to the provostship; this the provost himself and his supporters denied to be a prebend. Furthermore, it was argued from law that, since the same provost had been called from the lesser church to the greater, the earlier prebend had begun to be vacant by law, according to the provisions of the canons. Then it was alleged on the clerk’s behalf that the original constitution of that church was that there should be thirteen persons in it, namely the provost with twelve brethren; this could in no way be observed unless that prebend were declared vacant.

But the provost alleged in reply that [Col. 0627C] it was almost [Note: The Decretals omit “almost,” and below read “and” instead of the added … “because.”] a general custom for one person to have several prebends in the same church. It was further added that the prebend was not vacant for another reason: when the archbishop of Bremen invested the provost himself with the provostship in full synod, he confirmed to him, with the consent of the canons, both the provostship [Note: The Decretals give this word here and omit it below.] and that prebend, binding with the bond of excommunication those who should disturb him concerning it. It was therefore objected to the aforesaid clerk that he had thereby incurred a sentence of excommunication. But he denied that any such confirmation had taken place; and even if it had occurred, he maintained that it was invalid in law, because no one could reasonably have confirmed to him a thing which could not lawfully be possessed. He also said that he had never been bound by a sentence of excommunication on this account, since he was pursuing the matter under the authority of a superior.

[But [Note: The Decretals omit “But,” and afterwards omit the words distinguished below in italics.], since it seemed doubtful to you whether, when someone is elected from one prebend to another [Col. 0628A], the former should immediately begin to be vacant, or should be adjudged to the latter by a judgment, or whether, because of the confirmation described above, that prebend ought to be called non-vacant, you wished to consult us before determining anything on the matter. Therefore, since, if the case is as stated, that prebend is known to be vacant in law, even if not in fact, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior admonition, you compel the said provost, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside, to resign that prebend without difficulty; and, when it has become vacant in fact, supported by our authority and removing the obstacle of appeal, take care to confer it upon the aforesaid clerk,] inducting him into its corporeal possession and defending him once inducted. [Col. 0628B] Those, however, who rashly presume to oppose this are to be restrained by ecclesiastical coercion. And if not all … you, brother bishop, with one of them, etc.

Given, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

## LXII

B., cardinal-priest of the title of St Susanna, legate of the Apostolic See. [Note: See Letter 55 of this Eighth Book and the notes there.] Permission is granted that, unless the patriarch of Constantinople appoint suitable men in the church of Constantinople, he himself may appoint learned and honourable men in that church, as he sees fit. (Thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

We entrust our office more confidently and fully to those whose integrity and learning we continually experience [Col. 0628C]. Therefore, since we have thought fit to commit to you, whose discretion we have tested in many matters, the full office of legation in the empire of Constantinople, we grant you by the authority of these presents free power, in order that you may discharge it better and more fully, to receive the resignations of bishops and to transfer, from wherever they may be, those who have been requested for other sees established within that empire. Likewise, we grant that you may absolve, according to the rule of the Church, those who have incurred the canon of automatic sentence for violent laying of hands.

Moreover, although we thought fit to grant to our venerable brother the patriarch of Constantinople [Note: See Letter 19 of this Eighth Book.] that he should appoint suitable men to the Church of Constantinople—that is, the patriarchal church [Col. 0628D]—in which at that time either none or few had been canonically appointed, adding that he should yield neither to flesh nor blood otherwise than was fitting, but should consider merits and weigh learning, because in every nation whoever does righteousness is acceptable to God [Col. 0629A], nevertheless, by the authority of these presents we grant you that, if that patriarch, after being admonished by you, should perhaps neglect or delay to proceed according to the form of the indulgence granted to him, you may appoint in that same church, which, just as it surpasses the other churches established in the empire of Constantinople in dignity, so ought to flourish among them in the quality rather than merely the number [Note: Thus in the copy.] of its persons, learned and honourable men of whatever nation, as you see fit. In this and in all the other matters written above, you shall proceed with the obstacle of appeal removed. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.

## LXIII

[Note: The copy of these two letters, 63 and 64, which we had caused to be transcribed together with the others from the copy of Conti, slipped from our hands—we do not know by what accident—and therefore we can give here only their summaries. Yet from our notes we know for certain that these letters are entered in the autograph of the Vatican Archive [Col. 0630D], folio 19. See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §§11 and 14.]

TO ALL THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE IN THE CHRISTIAN ARMY STATIONED AT CONSTANTINOPLE. He commands them to give aid and counsel to the emperor of Constantinople concerning the recovery of the Holy Land and the conquest of the barbarians.

[Col. 0629B]

## LXIV

[Note: The copy of these two letters, 63 and 64, which we had caused to be transcribed together with the others from the copy of Conti, slipped from our hands—we do not know by what accident—and therefore we can give here only their summaries. Yet from our notes we know for certain that these letters are entered in the autograph of the Vatican Archive [Col. 0630D], folio 19. See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §§11 and 14.]

TO THE PATRIARCH AND ALL THE CLERGY OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He decrees that all prelates of conventual churches situated at Constantinople shall, whenever the Church of Constantinople falls vacant, assemble in the church of St Sophia to deliberate concerning the election.

## LXV

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.]

… MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOUSE OF THE HOSPITAL OF ST RAINER. He receives their hospital into the right and ownership of St Peter. (Eighth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0629C]

It is customary to grant assent, etc. We have received, moreover, information from our beloved son G. [Note: See Letter 83 of Book Five, note.], cardinal-deacon of St Adrian and legate of the Apostolic See, in his letters to us, that, when you thought fit to offer in your name to him the place in which, afterwards, with his permission, you built a house of hospitality, in order that he might receive it into the right and ownership of St Peter, that cardinal received the place thus offered, granting you by our authority permission freely to build there a church and a cemetery, solely for the use of your brethren and household and of the poor who die there.
