We therefore, ratifying what was piously and prudently done in this matter by that legate, receive that same house into the right and ownership [Col. 0629D] of the Apostolic See and protect it by the safeguard of the present writing. Moreover, as a sign of this liberty obtained from the Apostolic See, you shall annually pay to us and to our successors one bezant, freely offered by you. Let no one, therefore, etc. If anyone, etc.

Given, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

## LXVI

[Note: See Letters 90 and 92 of Book Five, and the notes there.]

… Savaric, bishop of Bath and Glastonbury. He confirms the settlement of the Church of Glastonbury made by delegated judges. (The settlement is inserted.) (Sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0630A]

It is customary to grant assent, etc. Therefore, etc., as far as “consent,” we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen with the protection of the present writing, for you and your successors, the settlement of the Church of Glastonbury made by judges delegated by us, and the division of its possessions accepted both by you and by the monks, as is known to be contained in the instrument drawn up concerning it and as they were reasonably made. But lest doubt should arise hereafter concerning the aforesaid settlement and division [Col. 0630B], we have thought fit to insert in the present page the instrument itself word for word.

E., by the grace of God bishop of Ely; S., by the same grace abbot of St Edmund’s; and G., prior of Holy Trinity, Canterbury, to all Christ’s faithful to whom the present writing shall come, greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to come to the knowledge of all that we received a mandate of Pope Innocent III in these words: “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Ely, and to his beloved sons S., abbot of St Edmund’s, and … prior of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing. How the parties,” etc. (as in Letter 90 of Book Five—see it—through “year five”).

Having therefore received this mandate concerning the settlement of the Church of Glastonbury and the distribution of the possessions belonging to that church [Col. 0630C], to be made between the lord bishop of Bath and Glastonbury and the monks of the aforesaid church, so that a fourth part of all the possessions and revenues of that church should accrue to the use of the bishop, the parties, appearing before us, consented before us in law to the following form of peace or partition:

That the bishop shall have the island of Meare with all its appurtenances, saving the common fishing rights of bishop and convent in the water of Ferningem, and common hunting in the twelve hides of Glastonbury; that the bishop shall have the houses beside the chapel of Blessed Mary which belonged to the abbots, with their enclosure bounded by the wall which extends from the Larder to the northern corner of the aforesaid chapel; and that its gate shall be towards the market-place [Col. 0630D] of Glastonbury. The bishop shall have at Glastonbury, in the mills of Glastonbury, rights for brewing and baking, and for fuel and enclosure. The monks likewise shall have these at Meare when they happen to come there for lodging. All else in the island of Glastonbury and its twelve hides, and all their other manors, shall belong to the convent, with their ancient liberties and free customs.

Of the lands outside the island, the following named came to the bishop’s share: namely, Pukelech, Winescumb, Badebir, Eseber, Boceland, Lim, Blacford, Estbrent, Berges, and Pravemer. In order that the bishop might more fully yield to the wishes of the monks, and in remission of all preceding injuries and damages—concerning which the monks then reserved for examination before us a dispute, while retaining, nevertheless, complaints which they had against certain others at their own instance and petition—the bishop exchanged with them two manors, namely Estbrent and Berges, which had fallen to his share, for two other manors, namely Kinton and Cristemelford. He also granted, out of his own pure liberality, that all matters might be peacefully settled, that he might be received by them in full affection [Col. 0631B], and for the salvation of his own soul and of his predecessors and successors, and that his anniversary might be celebrated more devoutly every year, the manor of Lim, which from ancient times belonged to the monks’ kitchen, with its church and all its other appurtenances.

Concerning the knights also it was ordered as concerning the possessions: namely, that the bishop shall have a fourth part of the knights, namely those known to belong to the fiefs and lands of the fourth share assigned to him. The prior and convent, however, shall freely have those knights who belong to the three parts of lands and fiefs assigned to them, together with their homages, wardships, escheats, reliefs, and services, and with the marriage-gifts of maidens and widows, saving in all things the honour of the lord king and the services due to him, which [Col. 0631C] are to be performed through the hand of the bishop or his steward. They shall also have free disposal of all their servants and bailiffs, both in the house of Glastonbury and in all their lands.

All the offerings of the altars of the Church of Glastonbury shall belong to the fabric of that church. Concerning the churches belonging to the Church of Glastonbury, both parties ratified that the bishop should have the right of patronage in all the churches of the aforesaid manors which, as we have said, fall to him under this division. The bishop, however, graciously granted to them the pensions which they had been accustomed to receive in the same churches. The convent, in like manner, shall have the right of patronage in all its other churches, wherever situated.

Concerning the priories belonging to the Church of Glastonbury, it has been ordered that the priory of Ireland shall belong to the bishop’s administration, while the priories of Basselach and Lamecchia shall belong to the administration of the convent. The monks also promised in good faith to return all instruments which they had formerly obtained against the bishop, saving to themselves letters obtained concerning the settlement of the Church; and they promised that, on account of earlier complaints, injuries, or damages inflicted upon them by him, they would henceforth raise no suit, either personally or through others. The bishop likewise faithfully and firmly promised to observe the same concerning damages, complaints, and injuries inflicted upon him by them, and to surrender without difficulty whatever letters he may have obtained against them [Col. 0632A], saving to himself privileges and indulgences, apostolic confirmations and statutes, obtained concerning the Church of Glastonbury. He shall also in good faith restore the charters concerning the archdeaconry and the pensions of churches made to them by his predecessor, and shall confirm them to the prior and convent, as they had formerly been granted to the abbot and convent.

The prior shall be appointed by the bishop with the consent of the convent, or of its greater and sounder part; and likewise the sacristan, chamberlain, and cellarer. Thus neither the bishop without the convent nor the convent without the bishop may appoint any of these persons. Any appointment made otherwise shall be void and of no effect. By the same authority by which the aforesaid prior, sacristan, chamberlain, and cellarer are appointed, they shall be removed if, for reasonable cause, they are found less suitable [Col. 0632B]; so that, just as the consent of bishop and convent is required for their appointment, so it shall be required for their removal. The prior and convent shall have free power to appoint all other officials and servants of the monastery who receive their stipends from the monks’ portion.

There shall be in the same Church of Glastonbury one single common treasury, into which all the offerings and revenues of that church shall be paid. Four trustworthy monks, chosen by the prior and convent, shall hold this treasury in their custody as treasurers; and from it provision shall be made by them for all needs, both internal and external, of the three aforesaid officers and of the other servants. All of these shall render an account in due course of receipts and disbursements according to the direction of the prior and convent [Col. 0632C].

The seal of that church shall be kept under the custody of four keys. One shall remain with the prior; two shall be held by two trustworthy monks of the same monastery chosen by the convent; and the fourth shall always be held by a professed monk of the same monastery chosen by the bishop, who ought to be suspected by neither party, so that what must be sealed can be sealed without delay or difficulty. But no sealing shall ever take place except in chapter and in the brethren’s presence. The bishop shall have due and canonical coercive authority and jurisdiction over the prior and convent.

We confirm, by the authority which we exercise, this division of possessions accepted by the parties and the settlement established by us, saving in all things the authority and privilege of the Apostolic See [Col. 0632D].

We decree, therefore, etc., of our confirmation. But if anyone, etc.

Given, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

## LXVII

… bishop of Mâcon [Note: See Letter 36 of Book Five, note.], and … abbot of Balma, in the diocese of Besançon. That they are not to permit P., a monk and administrator of St Benignus of Dijon, under whose administration that church had been despoiled, to be raised to a prelacy. (At St Peter’s, tenth day before the Kalends of June.)

Since relapses are ordinarily more severe than illnesses previously cured, we must take diligent precautions [Col. 0633A] lest a disease which once stained Christ’s Church should, after it has been cured, flow back into its corruption. You should know that it has come to our hearing that, when P., a monk, formerly served as administrator in the Church of St Benignus of Dijon [Note: What is said here should certainly be compared with the accounts given by the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 684.], that church, which formerly had been enriched with wealth and adorned with regular discipline, suffered a most grievous injury in both respects, while he was squandering alike its property and its morals.

Now, however, having resigned the administration of that church, he is damnably aspiring to the honour of a prelacy [Note: Thus in the Vatican copy.], and does not cease to devote himself in many ways to his detestable ambition, by which, through recurrent evils, he may break into a prelacy in the same church. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after diligent inquiry into the truth of these matters [Col. 0633B], if it is established that the said P. despoiled the aforesaid church, you shall, every obstacle of appeal removed, impose perpetual silence on him concerning the prelacy of that church; and restrain by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, both him and his supporters if they should at any time presume to contrive anything concerning this. But if both are not able to carry this out … you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth year.

## LXVIII

[Note: This letter agrees with the fragment found in the Decretals, Book V, title 19, *On Usury*, chapter 14.]

TO THE ARCHDEACON AND THE ABBOT OF ST FAUSTINUS MAJOR AT BRESCIA. He writes on behalf of the nuns of St Peter of the Shore at Brescia, so that Vitalis Humazolus may not molest them concerning usury. (Fifth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0633C]

The beloved daughters in Christ, the nuns of the church of St Peter of the Shore in the city of Brescia, showed us in a petition sent to us that Vitalis Humazolus of Brescia urgently demands usury from them because one of their household, to whom they had entrusted a certain sum of money, exacted usury from the same usurer; and, just as this was done without their knowledge, so they received absolutely nothing of it. Therefore, since one who acts against the law invokes its aid in vain, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if it is established to you that the aforesaid Vitalis has at any time received usury, you shall, unless he gives adequate security for restoring it [Col. 0633D], impose silence upon him concerning this matter, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, so that he may desist from troubling those nuns; restraining him by ecclesiastical censure [Col. 0634A]. Let no letters stand in the way of truth, etc.

Given, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June.

## LXIX

[Note: This letter is printed in full in the *Gesta Innocentii*, §94, but only corrupted by certain errors. Raynaldus gives fragments of it under the year 1205, §10. What is printed by him is marked here by a double stroke in the margin at the beginning of each line. For greater exactness, we have noted variant readings found in the *Gesta* and also in the Vallicellian manuscript, marked B, no. 13 [Col. 0634D].]

… ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS [Note: See Letter 116 of Book Seven.], CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. That he should induce both clerics and laypeople to join the emperor of Constantinople in support of the Holy Land and in fighting the barbarians.

A man of Ramathaim had taken to himself two wives, namely Hannah and Peninnah. But she who had first been adorned with the glory of offspring, because she became proud when the other began to rejoice in the Lord through the fruitfulness of children, deserved to be weakened, as her own song makes clear [Col. 0634B]. For those things which are read as having occurred historically under the shadow of the Law, since, according to the Apostle, all happened to them in figure, come to pass spiritually in the people of God in the time of grace revealed [Note: Thus also in the Vallicellian manuscript. In the *Gesta*, “to be revealed.”], so that, when the veil is removed from the face of Moses, through the brightness of Gospel teaching the dark water in the clouds of the air may become clear, and the thing signified may plainly appear through its signifier [Note: Thus also in the Vallicellian codex. The words are absent from the *Gesta*.].

For the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, altogether one—not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person—calling to himself two peoples, namely the Greek people and the Latin, joined them to himself through the sacraments of faith. But one of them, namely the Greek people, which glories in the sevenfold number of Churches [Note: Thus also in the *Gesta*. In the Vallicellian codex, “the seventh.”], of which and of whose angels John makes mention in the Apocalypse, when it saw the cords of the Latin Churches being enlarged [Col. 0634C], as though driven by the spurs of envy, departed from unity [Note: Thus also in the *Gesta*; in the Vallicellian codex, and in the Royal codex cited by Baluze in the margin, “truth.”], failing to notice that, when the Bridegroom had first said in the Song of Songs: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number,” he immediately added: “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her. The daughters of Zion saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines also praised her” (Song 6). For many daughters have gathered riches; but this one has surpassed them all.

> [Note: This passage appears in Raynaldus.]

But after the Greek people, having broken the bond of peace, departed from unity, it also grew weak in respect of the faith, refusing to confess that the Holy Spirit—who is the bond of unity and equality—proceeds from the Son [Col. 0634D], as he proceeds from the Father. Therefore, because it refused to profess the truth concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit [Note: Thus also in the *Gesta*; the Vallicellian codex has “refused to confess.”], it deservedly incurred darkness of mind, since that same Spirit teaches all truth, as the Son declares in the Gospel [Col. 0635A]. For, deprived of spiritual understanding because it sinned against the Spirit, it did not cast the leaven out of the house so as to feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; but, retaining the old leaven, it eats the body of Christ, so far as lies in it, leavened [Note: Raynaldus ends here.].

But blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation. Desiring to console his Church, so that Ephraim may be converted to Judah and Samaria return to Jerusalem, he has wondrously deigned to raise a standard over that same people, as over a dark mountain; and those sanctified by the Lord entered its gates [Note: Thus also in the Vallicellian codex. In the *Gesta*, “by God.”], transferring the Greek Empire from the proud to the humble, from the superstitious to the religious, from schismatics to Catholics [Col. 0635B], and from the disobedient to the devout.

For when the Christian army had arrived there with Alexius, son [Note: Thus also in the Vallicellian codex; omitted in the *Gesta*.] of Isaac, and, Constantinople having been captured, that same Alexius had been crowned, the said army proposed to winter there. But it would take too long for this page to recount what the new emperor sought to render in return for the benefits conferred upon him by that army. Yet, to touch briefly upon much: their wickedness, like the iniquity of the Amorites, having been fulfilled, the right hand of the Lord wrought might and exalted the Christian army, striking them with deserved vengeance [Note: Thus also in the *Gesta*; the Vallicellian codex has “punishing.”], and granting to the said army their land, full of gold, silver, and gems, rich in wheat, wine, and oil, and abounding in stores of every good thing.

Therefore, after the Greeks had been expelled from Constantinople [Col. 0635C] and their land had likewise been subdued, by common and unanimous will they raised our most beloved son in Christ, B., Count of Flanders and Hainaut, to the government of the Empire. Thus what had been foretold concerning Cyrus seems fulfilled in him: “I will subdue nations before his face,” he says, “and turn the backs of kings; I will open doors before him, and gates shall not be shut. I will go before you and humble the glorious ones of the earth; I will break bronze gates and shatter iron bars; and I will give you hidden treasures and the secrets of mysteries” (Isa. 45).

> [Note: Raynaldus resumes here.]

This man, therefore, having been raised up, humbly entreated us to deign, by apostolic exhortations [Col. 0635D], to invite clerics devoted to the Apostolic See, as well as laypeople, noble and humble, of every condition and sex, to come to his Empire, where they would receive from him agreeable riches according to the rank and merits of their persons [Note: Thus also in the Vallicellian codex; omitted in the *Gesta*.]. Considering, therefore, that the change of this Empire is a change of the right hand of the Most High, and that it has been done by him who changes times and transfers kingdoms, since through it aid may more usefully be brought to the Holy Land—or rather, since through it that land is believed capable of being recovered [Col. 0636A] with ease—we admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, commanding you by these apostolic letters, effectively to induce both clerics and laypeople to approach the aforesaid emperor in order to obtain both spiritual and temporal riches. For, to use his own words, since he has enough for all whom zeal for the Christian religion has brought to him, he wishes and is able to increase each one in riches and advance each one in honours, according to their respective rank and variety of birth [Note: Raynaldus ends here.], so that, when the Empire of Constantinople has been strengthened and the Church there established in devotion to the Apostolic See, that same emperor may hasten, with strong hand and outstretched arm, to conquer the barbarian nations which, because sins demand it, hold occupied the land in which God our king before the ages deigned to work our salvation [Col. 0636B] [Note: Thus also in the *Gesta*; the Vallicellian codex has “to be restored.”]. We hope in the Lord Jesus Christ that he who has so wondrously begun to act through him will more wondrously complete the work begun, to the praise and glory of his name.

We grant to those who go to him and labour for the aid of the Holy Land the same indulgence of sins that the Apostolic See has granted to other crusaders.

Given at Rome, etc. … in the eighth year.

In the same form … to the Archbishop of Rouen and his suffragans.

In the same form … to the Archbishop of Bourges and his suffragans.

In the same form … to the Archbishop of Vienne and his suffragans [Col. 0636C].

In the same form … to the Archbishop of Sens and his suffragans.

In the same form … to the Archbishop of Bordeaux and his suffragans.

In the same form … to the Archbishop of Lyons and his suffragans.

In the same form … to the Archbishop of Tours and his suffragans.

## LXX

[Note: Raynaldus published part of this letter under the year 1205, §11. Passages found in his work are here enclosed in brackets.

A fragment of the same letter is given by Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercian Order*, vol. III, p. 449, under the year 1205, chapter 4, §11. These passages have here been marked in the margin by a double stroke at the beginning of each line.]

. TO ALL ARCHBISHOPS AND OTHERS IN FRANCE. He commands them to send from every Order men distinguished for morals and learning to the regions of Greece, in order to strengthen the Christian faith there. (At Rome, 8 Kalends of June [25 May].)

[Col. 0636D]

In many ways and by many means divine mercy rouses us, that we may awaken from the sleep of death to life and breathe again from the pit of misery into hope of eternal glory. We rejoice indeed, and with good reason the whole Church of the saints ought to rejoice, because the Dayspring from on high has visited us; so that a great part of the Eastern Church—namely almost the whole of Greece—which from times of greatest antiquity [Col. 0637A] had scorned to follow the footsteps of its mother, the Holy Roman Church, has in our time become obedient from being disobedient, and devout from being contemptuous.

> [Note: This passage appears in Angelus Manrique.]

The abundance of our joys is further increased because the most Christian man, our most beloved son in Christ, B., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, strives and applies all his strength to those things through which the Christian religion can and ought to be propagated; and he labours with ardent zeal and diligent concern so that the edifice, now constructed in large part, may not fall. Recently, spreading into branches of good works the devotion planted in his breast, he humbly begged us to arrange for religious and prudent men from the Cistercian Order, the Cluniac Order, the Regular Canons [Col. 0637B], and other religious orders [Note: Omitted in Manrique.], to be sent to the regions of Constantinople in order to establish the truth of the Catholic faith and strengthen it permanently; and that their prelates should provide them with what was necessary for reaching that place. He requested that missals, breviaries, and other books containing the ecclesiastical office according to the institutions of the Holy Roman Church should be sent to those regions, at least as exemplars.

> [Note: Angelus Manrique ends here; what follows is found in Raynaldus.]

Therefore, wishing to grant the same emperor’s requests the more generously because we have often experienced the greater sincerity of his faith in greater matters, we earnestly ask and exhort all of you, commanding you by these apostolic letters [Col. 0637C], to promote his pious desire insofar as you can. Take care to send to those regions, from every Order, men commendable for character and learning and fervent in religion, through whom that new plantation, trained in the discipline of the Lord, may yield fruit in its fitting season, and what has been wondrously begun among them may be more wondrously completed to the praise and glory of the Redeemer. Also take care to send to those regions, at least as exemplars, the aforesaid books, with which we know that you not merely abound but overflow, so that your abundance may supply their need, and the Eastern Church may not differ from the Western in divine praises, but, as there is one God and one faith, so East and West may praise and glorify him with one voice [Col. 0637D].

Given at Rome, etc., 8 Kalends of June [25 May], in the eighth year.

## LXXI

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §11. This letter [Col. 0638D] was unknown to the most diligent writer of the *History of the University of Paris*. See *Hist. Univ. Paris.*, vol. III, pp. 1–88.]

TO THE MASTERS AND SCHOLARS OF PARIS. That they should go to Greece to restore learning there, where it is known to have had its beginning.

“In many ways,” etc., down to “he humbly begged us to deign by apostolic letters to induce and admonish you that, going to Greece, you should endeavour there to restore the study of letters, which is known to have had its beginning there.”

[Col. 0638A] “Therefore, wishing,” etc., down to: “that, considering more carefully how great difficulties and burdens your forebears endured in order to imbue the first beginnings of their youth with literary disciplines, most of you may not be weary of going to a land full of silver, gold, and gems, rich in wheat, wine, and oil, and abounding in stores of every good thing, so that, to the honour and glory of him from whom comes every gift of knowledge, they may profit there both themselves and others, and may receive, besides temporal riches and honours, the rewards of eternal glory.”

Given … in the eighth year.

## LXXII. TO THE CHAPTER OF SOISSONS

It is written that, since the presence of the Bishop of Soissons is necessary in Greece for the recovery of the Holy Land, they should bear his absence humbly and devoutly.

[Col. 0638B]

We give thanks to the giver of every grace because, although he is great in great things, he works great things more gloriously in the least; humbling the proud of the earth, he grants grace and honour to those who fear him. How powerfully and wondrously he has deigned in our time to exalt his Church, bringing the Greek Church back to devotion to it by the power of his right hand, we believe to be sufficiently evident throughout the different regions of the world. Ascribing all that has been done to his glory, we ought to implore him with our whole and inmost affection that he may deign to preserve more gloriously what he has gloriously begun.

Therefore, considering [Col. 0638C] the manifold usefulness and benefit of this change, at the request of our most beloved son in Christ, B., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, we have thought fit, out of the kindness of the Apostolic See, to grant our venerable brother … your bishop [Note: See letter II of book III, note.], whose life and character are commended in many ways for good and by good men, whose presence in those regions has proved fruitful in much and in many respects and is hoped to be advantageous for the recovery of the Holy Land, a further period of three years. During this period he is to receive the revenues belonging to the episcopal table and to be able to fulfil the vow of his devotion to the honour and glory of Christ.

We therefore earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort all of you, commanding you by these apostolic letters [Col. 0638D], that, although his presence ought not without reason to be pleasing to you, you should nevertheless prefer the common advantage to private benefit and bear his absence humbly and devoutly. By God’s favour, when a suitable time has been granted, he will return to you, bringing spiritual mandrakes from the field of this world, which have already given forth a most sweet fragrance at our gates.

Given at Rome, etc. … in the eighth year.

In the same form … to the King of France, down to “may be able to fulfil.” We therefore earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort Your Serenity that, although his presence ought not without reason to be pleasing to you, you should nevertheless, preferring the common advantage to your private benefit, patiently and devoutly bear his absence, causing the episcopal revenues to be assigned to him in full. By God’s favour, when a suitable time has been received, he will return to you and bring spiritual [Col. 0639A] … etc.

Given, etc., in the eighth year.

## LXXIII. TO ALL ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER RELIGIOUS PERSONS TO WHOM THESE LETTERS MAY COME

That they should provide P., a monk sent by the Emperor of Constantinople to the Apostolic See, with provisions.

[Col. 0639B]

Although you are bound to render works of charity to all, it is especially fitting that you discharge this obligation toward those whom the same profession makes equal in purpose and ought also to make alike in sharing mutual affection. We have thought it right to bring to your knowledge that, when our beloved son P., the monk who bears these letters, was sent to the Apostolic See by our most beloved son in Christ, B., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, he was scarcely able to reach us after many attempts and labours over a period of eight months.

Since he states that he has been greatly distressed by the unforeseen toil of the journey and the burden of heavy expenses, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your devotion, commanding you by these apostolic letters [Col. 0639C], that, when he passes through your territory, you may be willing to provide him at least with provisions in such a way that, through the assistance of your charity, he may fulfil the commission laid upon him, and you may deservedly hope to receive grace for grace from the Lord.

Given, etc.

## LXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TUAM

[Note: See letter 163 of book VI.]

TO THE BISHOP OF MEATH

[Note: This is explicitly read in the transcript of Conti.]

AND TO … THE ABBOT OF KENAN

That, concerning the dispute between the canons of St Mary of Luivid and H. de Say, knight, they are to determine what is just. (6 Kalends of June [27 May].)

The beloved sons, the canons of St Mary of Luivid, have submitted a serious dispute to our hearing [Col. 0639D]. They state that, having acquired the land of Balinet-long-fortan by the gift of the late Okervail, king of Criel, and having possessed it peacefully for a long time both before and after the English came into those regions, H. de Say, a knight of the diocese of Armagh, unjustly occupied the same land by a grant from Hugh de Lacy. Although our beloved son J., priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill [Col. 0640A], then legate of the Apostolic See [Note: See letter 83 of book V, note.], forbade H. under threat of anathema to receive or hold that land, he nevertheless retains it and refuses to restore it.

He alleges a law introduced by the English: namely, that no gift made by any Irishman to a religious house is valid after the king of England grants the property given to any Englishman, even if, when the Irishman made that gift to the religious house, the donor is known to have held full possession of the property given and to have possessed it from ancient times. Since such a law contains neither natural justice nor the equity of written law, we command your discretion by these apostolic letters that, after carefully investigating the truth of these matters, disregarding the aforesaid law and setting appeal aside [Col. 0640B], you determine what is just, causing … No letters contrary to truth, etc. If not all of you, then two of you, etc.

Given, 6 Kalends of June [27 May].

## LXXV

[Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, §59. Marlottus published it in full, *History of the Church of Reims*, vol. II, p. 461. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* caused it to be reprinted, though mutilated at the beginning, vol. IX, col. 102. We give variant readings.]

TO GUY, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Note: See letter 116 of book VII.]

CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED, IN PERPETUITY.

Confirmation of his privileges, among which is especially reckoned the privilege that he alone may anoint and crown the kings of France. (At St Peter’s, on the Ides of May [15 May].)

The office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God, and consideration of ecclesiastical advantage, admonish and exhort us to love with more abundant charity our brother bishops, whom we know to excel in honourableness [Col. 0640C] and religion, and continually to show them greater honour and favour. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously grant your just requests, and, after the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of pious memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Reims, over which, by God’s providence, you are known to preside, etc., down to “we strengthen”; establishing that whatever possessions [Note: Marlottus: “of whatever kind.”], etc., down to “to be expressed by name”:

the bishoprics of Soissons, Laon, Cambrai, Beauvais, Châlons, Senlis, Noyon, Amiens, Arras, Tournai, and Thérouanne; within your own diocese [Col. 0640D], the monasteries of St Remigius, St Nicasius, St Dionysius, and St Peter within the city of Reims; and outside the city, the monasteries of Mouzon [Note: Marlottus: Mosomo; *Gallia Christiana*: Mosomico.], St Thierry, St Peter of Hautvillers, St Basolus, and St Mary of Igny—and, in all these monasteries, spiritual and patronage rights, with all their institution and ordering.

Furthermore, the monasteries of Épernay and Avenay [Note: Marlottus and *Gallia Christiana*: Avenayo.]; likewise, within the bishopric of Soissons [Col. 0641A], the right of patronage in the monastery of Orbais [Note: Marlottus, in the margin, “in the diocese of Soissons,” and in the text “of Tournai.”]; within the bishopric of Tournai, the right of patronage in the monastery of Cysoing [Note: Marlottus: de Cisoin; *Gallia Christiana*: de Cisuin.].

In the bishoprics of Noyon and Amiens, the jurisdiction hitherto exercised over the burgesses [Note: Thus also in Marlottus and *Gallia Christiana*.] of St Quentin and St Valery—namely, that those summoned shall come to the court of Reims; lordship over the city of Reims with all its appurtenances; the fief which the Count of Champagne is known to hold from your Church, for which, saving his fidelity to the king, he is bound to perform liege homage to you, namely Vitry, Vertus, Regi-Teste, Châtillon, Épernay, Rosières, Fismes, Braine, and the county of the castle in Porcien [Note: Omitted in *Gallia Christiana*.], with their castellanies; and the other possessions and castles which the same count holds in his own person [Col. 0641B], or which others hold from him.

Likewise, the fief of Bouillon [Note: Marlottus: Bouillon; *Gallia Christiana*: Buillon.], which the Bishop of Liège is known to hold from the archbishops of Reims, for which he is also bound personally to promise into the hand of the Archbishop of Reims that he will render him service and justice and faithfully maintain them [Note: *Gallia Christiana*: “servituurm.”]. For this fief the same bishop is also bound to procure that its eight barons perform homage to that archbishop; and, when summoned by the archbishop to make war upon his wrongdoers, he must provide aid and service by knights and armed men, as is known to be contained in authentic writings.

Likewise, the fief which the Count of Regi-Teste is known to hold from you—namely, the county of Osmonte—and the fief held from you by the Count of Grandpré, and the fief held from you by the Count of Soissons [Col. 0641C]; also the castle of Mouzon, Attigny, Britimville [Note: Marlottus: Betigni villa; *Gallia Christiana*: Betignivilla.], Septem-Salices, Cormicy, Curville, Chaumesy [Note: *Gallia Christiana*: Chammisiacum.], and Stonne [Note: *Gallia Christiana*: Stonne.], with their appurtenances.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we establish that no one except the Archbishop of Reims may anoint the King of France or [Note: *Gallia Christiana*: “etc.”] place the first crown upon him, as has hitherto been maintained. We command that appeals [Note: Marlottus: “appeals.”] made to you or to your court by any persons subject to your jurisdiction be brought with due devotion [Col. 0642A] [Note: Marlottus: “serve.”]; and we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors those special rights which your Church has hitherto possessed in such appeals, even during a vacancy of the see [Note: All this is omitted in *Gallia Christiana*.].

All these things, indeed, which your predecessors from ancient times, and you yourself until now, are known to have possessed, we have thought fit to confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors. We also bestow upon your brotherhood, by the generosity of the Apostolic See, the pallium—that is, the fullness of pontifical office. Remember that you are to use it within your church on those days on which you know your predecessors used it: namely, on the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Stephen the Protomartyr; the Circumcision of the Lord [Note: Omitted in *Gallia Christiana*.]; Epiphany; Hypapante (the Presentation); Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday [Col. 0642B] [Note: Omitted in Marlottus.]; Easter; the Monday after Easter; Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of St Mary; the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist; the solemnity of all the apostles [Note: Marlottus and *Gallia Christiana* add: “the Commemoration of All Saints.”]; dedications of churches; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clerics; the principal feasts of your church; and the anniversary day of your consecration.

We decree therefore, etc., down to “shall be advantageous,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of J., cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, on the Ides of May [15 May], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1205 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## LXXVI

[Note: It is found among the *Decretals*, book V, title 1, “On Accusations, Inquisitions, and Denunciations,” chapter 18.]

TO … THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES

[Note: See letter 142 of book VII, note.]

AND TO … THE ABBOT OF VALLEMAGNE

[Note: Concerning the abbots of Valmagne in the period with which we are dealing, the following should be added here, besides what we have already noted on letter 74 of book V, note, from *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 722:

“XI. H., abbot of Valmagne, is summoned by William, Bishop of Maguelone, to reconcile the disputing King Peter of Aragon and the citizens of Montpellier, 6 Kalends of November [27 October] 1206. Thus *Hist. Occitan.*, vol. III, documentary proofs, col. 204. Unless perhaps this first letter of the name was written incorrectly and H. read for P. For

“XII. Peter IV is known from documents from 1206 through 1211.”]

AND TO … THE ABBOT OF ST WILLIAM

[Note: Peter III Raimund, abbot of St William, is recorded in charters from 1204 through 1211. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 592.]

OF THE DIOCESES OF AGDE AND LODÈVE.

That they should remove the Bishop of Agde [Note: This letter must certainly be compared with what the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* say concerning Raymond II, Bishop of Agde, whom they state to have held the see from 1192 until 1213. Ibid., col. 679.] from the Church and elect another. (8 Kalends of June [25 May].)

[Col. 0642C]

When our beloved sons, the Abbot of Cîteaux [Note: See letter 16 of book V, note.] and P. and R., monks of Fontfroide [Note: These have already often been discussed.], legates of the Apostolic See, had come to the Church of Agde in order to exercise there the office of legation, many unfavourable reports concerning our venerable brother … Bishop of Agde had been conveyed to them by frequent outcry. They wished to investigate and see whether he had fulfilled the outcry by his deeds [Note: This passage is omitted in the *Decretals*.]. Therefore they bound both the bishop and the canons by the bond of an oath to tell them the truth concerning the condition of the Church. Having reduced their depositions to writing, when the bishop appealed, they sent them to our presence, appointing the bishop a suitable term within which he was to appear before us to receive the apostolic command.

The bishop came before us; after hearing his own confessions and the depositions of others, he tried in many ways to excuse himself, presenting his excuses to us in writing [Col. 0643B]. Therefore, after diligent consultation with our brethren, we judged that the aforesaid bishop should be suspended from administration of the Church of Agde, because we found him blameworthy in certain matters and his own confession made a prima facie case against him, rendering him legally suspect to us, since he had not yet proved his excuses—though he firmly promised that he would prove them.

But because it was not clear to us in what form [Note: The *Decretals*: “the bishop with the canons.”] he had taken the oath before the aforesaid legates—whether he had sworn to tell the full and unqualified truth concerning the state of the Church, or to answer truthfully to matters asked—we command your discretion by apostolic letters [Note: The *Decretals* omit these words down to “with the force of strict obedience.”] that you strictly command the same legates on our behalf, by virtue of obedience [Col. 0643C], faithfully to inform you under what form he swore. If, according to their answer, he swore under the second form, or if he sufficiently proves before you that he swore under that form, then, through the depositions of the witnesses whom he produced while present at the Apostolic See—depositions which we send to you enclosed under our bull—or through other witnesses, since those depositions have not yet been published and he has not seen fit to renounce the production of witnesses, because under that form he would be bound by the obligation of his oath only to answer questions asked, you are to take care diligently to hear the excuses which we send to you enclosed under our bull.

If he clearly proves them, then, since such excuses do not destroy those confessions but explain them—and the confessions are such that they can be interpreted either favourably or unfavourably and must therefore be judged according to the circumstances—you are to absolve him altogether, with appeal removed [Col. 0643D] [Note: The *Decretals* omit “and below, before us.”]. For, even if he has been found blameworthy in some matters, since he has nevertheless been punished through the labour and disgrace he has incurred on this account, such a slight fault ought to be lightly remitted to him.

But if he cannot sufficiently prove those excuses concerning waste, shipwreck, and simony, or if he swore under the first form—because under that form he ought neither to conceal truth nor mingle falsehood with it—then, notwithstanding those excuses which he newly advanced before us, since he made no mention whatever of them in his confessions, although he firmly asserted that he had set forth several of them before the aforesaid legates, who did not take care to write them down [Note: The *Decretals* omit this passage down to the words “with every obstacle removed”; below they read “take care to remove” for “remove altogether.”], and since he could not prove this, as one examined by them alone, you are, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed [Col. 0644B], to remove him altogether from the administration of the Church of Agde. In consultation with those legates, cause that Church to be provided with a suitable person through canonical election. Take especial care to have God before your eyes and to turn neither to the left nor to the right. If not all of you … then two of you, etc.

Given, 8 Kalends of June [25 May], in the eighth year.

## LXXVII

[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §53.]

TO … THE BISHOPS OF MINDEN

[Note: The Church of Minden was then presided over by St Dietmar, renowned for miracles. During his episcopate silver mines were discovered, from a share of which Dietmar was endowed by Emperor Henry VI. During his episcopate the monastery of Neudorf was founded by Simon, provost and uncle of St Dietmar. He died in 1206. Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 31.]

AND VERDEN

[Note: He was probably Rudolf, founder of Rodenburg Castle, who is said to have died in 1208. Ibid., p. 23.]

AND TO … THE ABBOT OF VERDEN.

That they should grant the Archbishop of Magdeburg the benefit of absolution, report and write back concerning certain other matters. (8 Kalends of June [25 May].)

[Col. 0644C]

If the Archbishop of Magdeburg … [Note: [Col. 0644D] See letter 8 of book five, note.] had more fully observed that obedience is preferred to sacrifices, and that disobedience is likened to idolatry, as the Lord says through the Prophet: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening than offering the fat of rams; for rebellion is as the sin of divination, and refusal to comply as the crime of idolatry” (1 Kings 15), he would not have gone so far as, after the Apostolic See had once remitted his fault to him out of sheer kindness, to contemn by his rashness the sentence of excommunication which our venerable brother G., now Archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0644D] See letter 116 of book seven.], Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, but then Bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, had pronounced against him in his presence; and, after that sentence had been published at our command by you, brother bishops, and by our venerable brother … Bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0644D] See letters 8 of book five, note.], to presume, against the keys of the Church, [Col. 0645A] whose force he ought by no means to have ignored, to celebrate the divine offices.

Although Master G. and Alberic, clerics sent by him into our presence, zealously endeavoured to excuse him before us, yet, since his excuse, from the very nature of the affair, turned rather into an accusation, we did not judge it admissible, but deemed it frivolous and empty. Moreover, since the archbishop himself, as we have learned, desires to return to the grace of the Apostolic See, which is accustomed to open the door of mercy to those who knock, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, having received from him sworn security that he will obey our commands concerning those matters for which we ordered him to be declared excommunicated, you grant him the benefit of absolution. And, lest his offence remain uncorrected and through impunity become an example to others, without prejudice to our other commands, impose upon him under oath the duty of disclosing to you the truth whether, after the sentence had been pronounced against him, and especially after it had been published, he celebrated the divine offices.

But grant a hearing, both to our beloved son R., canon of Magdeburg, who came into our presence not to persecute the same man as archbishop, but rather to obey God and the Apostolic See, and to others who may wish to make allegations against him. Having first given warning, compel, by ecclesiastical coercion and notwithstanding any appeal lodged, the persons and canons of the Church of Magdeburg to bear testimony to the truth concerning these matters and others that shall be alleged; and faithfully notify us by your letters what you discover, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed in this matter as ought to be done. Do not permit the aforesaid canon R., on this account, to be molested by the archbishop himself or by others; rather, defend him, and the others who may wish to make allegations against that man, by apostolic authority. If not all … two of you, etc.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth year.

LXXVIII. … ABBOTS OF PIGAVIA [Note: [Col. 0645D] See letter 44 of this eighth book, note.], AND OF SAINT GILES OF BRUNSWICK [Note: [Col. 0645D] Saint Giles of Brunswick, of the Order of Saint Benedict, was once a splendid monastery, founded in 1113 by Margravine Gertrude, widow of Count Henry of Northeim, when the body of Saint Auctor, received as a gift from Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne, had remained immovable at that place. Lothair, Duke of Saxony, who had married the daughter of the aforesaid Gertrude, completed the building and obtained its consecration in 1115 through Theodoric, legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0646D] and Reinhard, Bishop of Halberstadt. He also afterwards endowed it magnificently and fortified it with great privileges. Bugelin, *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 3.] IN THE DIOCESES OF HALBERSTADT AND MERSEBURG, AND … DEAN OF MERSEBURG. He commits to them the case of the cleric A., concerning a prebend in the Church of Merseburg formerly conferred upon him by the Archbishop of Reims, then legate of the Apostolic See. (Sixth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0645D]

When our beloved son A., cleric, and C. and R., canons of Magdeburg, had appeared in our presence, [Col. 0646A] we appointed as auditor our beloved son L. [Note: [Col. 0646D] See letters 5 of book five, note; and 1 of book seven, note.], cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross. Before him, the said A. caused it to be alleged that, since our venerable brother G., now Archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0646D] See letter 116 of book seven.], then Bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, had invested him with one of certain prebends that had stood vacant in the Church of Magdeburg for so long that, under the statutes of the Lateran Council, their grant had devolved upon us, entrusting execution of his mandate to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Merseburg [Note: [Col. 0646D] See letter 87 of book six, note.], should the chapter of Magdeburg refuse to carry out his order: because that same bishop was afterwards bound by the same legate under a sentence of excommunication, he could not proceed to execute the mandate.

[Col. 0646B] After obtaining absolution from us, that bishop once and again admonished the aforesaid chapter to fulfil the legate’s mandate, the execution of which he had received. And the same cleric, lest they make any disposition concerning those prebends while the mandate of the same legate was pending, appealed to the Apostolic See. Yet the said chapter, disregarding the appeal, assigned one of them to a certain cleric. Therefore the aforesaid cleric humbly petitioned us that we should deign by apostolic authority to confirm what had been established by that legate, after pious deliberation, for his provision.

On the other hand, the aforesaid canons alleged that at the time when the legate’s letters were presented to their chapter no prebend had been vacant in the Church of Magdeburg; for we had caused that prebend, which he now alleges to have then been vacant, to be assigned to a certain canon of Magdeburg who had not yet been emancipated. Another of those canons, namely R., alleged on his own behalf that, since the said A. had obtained letters from the said legate concerning the conferral upon him of a prebend in the Church of Magdeburg through a false representation, he himself, before any commencement of suit and even before the production of those letters, appealed to the Apostolic See against the same A., whom he charged with ambition, both in law and outside the law.

When the said cardinal had faithfully reported to us what had been alleged before him, and since we could not attain full certainty regarding the aforesaid matters, we command your discretion by these apostolic [Col. 0646D] letters that, if the said A. sufficiently proves that the prebend granted to him by the aforesaid legate had been vacant for so long that its grant had devolved upon us, you shall cause him by our authority to be received as canon and brother, and to enjoy peaceful possession of that prebend, unless it had previously been conferred upon another by our command. [Col. 0647A] Reducing opponents … to nought whatever, etc. But witnesses … by no letters contrary to truth, etc. If not all … two of you, etc.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth year.

LXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0647D]

The copy of this letter, which we had caused to be transcribed in accordance with the copy of Conti, slipped from our hands—we do not know by what mischance; therefore we can present here only its summary.

Moreover, it appears that it should be recovered from the letter printed, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book II, title 26, [Col. 0648D] *On Prescriptions*, chapter 28. See also Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 66.]

… ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: [Col. 0648D] See letter 9 of book three, note.]. That he absolve the judge of Carolita from the oath sworn to him, enjoining him not to delay in swearing fealty to the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0648D] See letter 109 of book seven.].

LXXX. J., ARCHPRIEST OF PERUGIA. He decrees that he is not bound by anything decreed in the Church of Perugia by a legate of the Apostolic See contrary to privileges granted by the Apostolic See. (Third day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 0647B] Appearing in our presence, you stated that, when our beloved son Master Roland, subdeacon and our chaplain, rector of Massa, legate of the Apostolic See, came to the Church of Perugia, he heard the confessions of you and your brethren concerning the revenues and expenses of that church; and, without receiving any oath concerning these matters and without observing judicial procedure, he pronounced a sentence, according to his own will, contrary to the privilege granted you. Although you asserted that other matters by which you were burdened were contained in that sentence, you nevertheless especially sought the correction of apostolic moderation on three points.

Indeed, the sentence contained the provision that a cloister prior should be appointed in the Church of Perugia, to instruct the brethren and train them in regular observances. [Col. 0647C] You, however, were forbidden to spend more than twenty solidi in a year. Moreover, these provisions and others contained in the aforesaid sentence were enjoined to be firmly observed under penalty of excommunication.

Since what the same rector decreed concerning the appointment of a prior seems contrary to our privilege, which provides that, of the eight canons who ought to be in that church, the senior shall discharge the office of archpriest, another that of ordinarius, and the next that of chamberlain—with no mention there of the office of prior—you asked us to deign to annul it by apostolic authority. You also requested a clearer interpretation from us of the ruling that it was not lawful for you to spend more than twenty solidi within one year, since our privilege specifies no fixed period of time [Col. 0647D] expressly including permission to expend the aforesaid sum. You further alleged that the sentence of excommunication seemed unjust to you, since the aforesaid rector ordered that his enactments be observed under that penalty; for it seems absurd that as often as anyone failed in their observance, so often he should incur the penalty of the sentence pronounced.

Therefore, wishing firmly to preserve what has been established by prudent deliberation in our privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever has been decreed by that legate contrary to the aforementioned privilege is not to be observed. We intend the provision that you may not spend more than twenty solidi without the consent of the chapter to be understood thus: namely, that without the consent of your chapter, or of its greater or sounder part, you may not spend at one time more than the stated sum, although we wish you to render an account in chapter concerning such expenditure, or even a smaller one. But we intend the penalty under which the said legate ordered his enactments to be observed to be not a penalty incurred automatically (*latae sententiae*), but one to be imposed (*ferendae sententiae*).

Given on the third day before the Nones of June.

LXXXI. … PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA [Note: [Col. 0648D] See letter 99 of book seven, note.]. He commands him to have inquiry made through the Bishop of Passau against the parish priest of Gonew., accused of the crime of apostasy. (Second day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 0648B]

We commend in the Lord your prudence in seeking the counsel of the Apostolic See in matters that trouble your mind with some doubt, because in this you show yourself to be a devoted son of him whose counsels you desire to follow and whose commands to obey. It has come to the hearing of our apostolate, as you reported, that, since the parish priest of Gonew. had often been accused of the crime of apostasy—because, in the church of Saint Mary in the diocese of Passau, after making a vow, he had assumed the monastic habit, and [Col. 0648C] later, changing both garment and mind, behaved as a secular cleric—your predecessor P. of good memory [Note: [Col. 0648D] See letter 26 of book three, note.], on the advice of prudent men, asked you, who then presided over the Church of Passau, diligently to investigate the truth concerning the aforesaid matters from the abbot and monks of that place.

After some time had passed, when you had commanded the said abbot and monks under virtue of obedience to disclose the full truth to you, they answered unanimously that the aforesaid parish priest had remained in that place under monastic vow and habit for five years. When you immediately added why they had been silent for so long, they replied that the parish priest had often come to them and had bestowed many goods on that church, so that his sin might not be made public by them.

Therefore, after the aforesaid Patriarch had entered upon the way of all flesh before these things had been communicated to him by you, and after you had been called by God to the see of Aquileia, you held a solemn chapter. In it, when the oft-mentioned parish priest had been accused of this same crime by his archpriest, although he laboured under public infamy, he utterly denied it. At last, after you had carefully set forth before the entire assembly the whole course of the affair, [Col. 0649A] the parish priest alleged that this accusation ought in no way to prejudice him because, since you sat in the place of judge, your testimony against him should not be admitted. Thus, on the advice of prudent men, you were unwilling to proceed against him until you had consulted us.

Therefore, unwilling that judicial procedure be omitted, or that the parish priest should escape ecclesiastical discipline by his evasions, we advise your brotherhood, commanding by apostolic letters that you cause the truth of this matter to be diligently investigated through our venerable brother … Bishop of Passau [Note: [Col. 0649D] He was probably Poppo, who had become Bishop of Passau in 1204, having been provost of Aquileia. See Hansiz, *Germania sacra*, vol. I, p. 350. Bucelin agrees, saying that Poppo did not die until 1206. Bucelin, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 45. See also letters 142 and 143 of book seven.], notifying that parish priest that, if he wishes, he should take care to be present at the inquiry. Once the truth has thus been investigated and ascertained by that bishop, determine what is canonical, and cause what you determine to be firmly observed, notwithstanding appeal. [Col. 0649B] But lest, because the same Bishop of Passau is not subject to you by metropolitan right, he should neglect to execute your command to make the inquiry, you may delegate this matter to him by the authority of the present letters.

Given on the second day before the Nones of June.

LXXXII. … ABBOTS OF HEISTERBACH [Note: [Col. 0649D] See letter 36 of book six, note.] AND RUMERSDORP [otherwise ROMERSDORFF] [Note: [Col. 0649D] Reiner, Abbot of Romersdorf, is mentioned in documents from 1202 to 1216. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 655.], AND … DEAN OF BONN [Note: [Col. 0650D] See letter 36 of book six, note.], IN THE DIOCESE OF COLOGNE. He commands them to inquire whether peace may be restored between two counts through a marriage between the parties, although they are related within a specified degree of affinity. (Second day before the Nones of June.)

From the letters of our beloved son … Provost of Bonn, you are to know that the enemy of the human race has kindled such a firebrand of hatred and envy between the late noblemen, Counts H. and E., and their brothers, and Count T. of Landesberg, and has so stubbornly incited them against one another, that, besides the slaughter of men resulting on both sides, according to the varying fortunes of war they plundered many possessions of churches, burned many villages, took spoils from widows and orphans, and committed against one another whatever yet more cruel thing could be done among enemies. The said count, moreover, once he had prevailed against them by force, devised crafty schemes against them; he seized them by ambush and, having consigned them to prison chains, afflicted [Col. 0649D] and oppressed them so outrageously that one of them, namely E., is said thereby to have suffered the loss of his life. This indeed kindled a greater firebrand of hatred among his heirs and those of his brother.

But a certain young man, the son of that brother, whom both men’s prompting and the youthful passions of his mind spur to avenge the wrongs done to his uncle and father, strives with all his might [Col. 0650A] to pursue the said count in hostile fashion according to ancestral custom; and unless the beginnings are checked, the conflict is judged likely to be grievous in its course and difficult in its end. Yet, since the said count has an only daughter, whom the aforesaid young man could marry were she not related to him by a line of consanguinity, the same provost humbly asked us to deign, by gracious dispensation, to permit a marriage to be contracted between them, since in this way an end is believed capable of being put to such great dangers.

Wherefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth of these matters; and, if you ascertain that peace can be restored by this marriage, an end put to such great evils, and the degree of consanguinity is dispensable, then, in order to avoid so great an evil, determine in this matter by our authority whatever you see to be expedient according to God.

Given on the second day before the Nones of June.

LXXXIII. [Note: [Col. 0650D]

Bzovius mentions this letter in *Annals*, vol. XIII, under the year 1205, § 17.

Raynaldus gives fragments of it under the same year, 1205, § 52. The passages printed by him are enclosed here in brackets.

Angelo Manrique published it entire in *Cistercian Annals*, vol. III, p. 450, under the year 1205, chapter 5, § 2.]

… PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA [Note: [Col. 0650D] See letter 99 of book seven, note.], AND … ABBOT OF NEUCASTLE [Note: [Col. 0650D] See letter 8 of book eight, note.]. He commands them to admonish the Duke of Swabia not to grant any assistance to the excommunicated Bishop of Worms. (At Saint Peter’s, second day before the Nones of June.)

If you are sons of the Church—indeed, because you are her sons—her zeal cannot but consume you, nor can you bear with equanimity the reproaches of those who reproach her and usurp her rights. For you are so deeply rooted [Col. 0650C] in fear of the divine name and reverence for ecclesiastical dignity that we do not in any way doubt that, if the cause of the Church, especially one so wholly ecclesiastical, is at stake, persecution or sword, things present or things to come, cannot separate you from the Church so as to prevent you, on the day of battle, from setting yourselves for the house of the Lord against those who come up from the opposite side, and raising yourselves against Damascus as a tower of strength.

For you cannot, and ought not, abandon in time of need her who regenerated you in Christ and called you to a share in her solicitude, raising you from the dust so that you may sit with the princes of the earth, to execute vengeance among the nations and chastisements among the peoples. You know that you must obey God rather than man, and that in his cause, in which he will be your co-worker and helper, you cannot fear what man may do to you. If the enemy should kindle the cauldron of persecution against you, and even stir up the elements to test or crush your courage, because the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which the Apostle foretells shall be revealed in us, [Col. 0651A] you ought to embrace persecution for righteousness’ sake, even if it were necessary to suffer martyrdom for the keys of the Church and the Catholic faith: for those to whom momentary death would become the beginning of everlasting life.

Certainly, we believe that you have learned from the Gospel reading that he who founded his Church upon himself, the rock, granted the keys of the kingdom of heaven to blessed Peter, saying to him: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). No one who does not ignore the privilege of Peter doubts that Luipold [Note: [Col. 0651D] See letter 14 of book five, note.], formerly Bishop of Worms, was justly bound by us. For, since he himself, having called the others to share in his solicitude, transmitted exclusively to his successors the fullness of power bestowed on him by the Lord, through which the translation of bishops pertains solely to the Roman pontiff, the same Luipold not only transferred himself to the Church of Mainz without our permission, through the favour of the nobleman Ph… Duke of Swabia—indeed, that duke rashly transferred him, so far as lay in his power—but also, when at last his petition had been rejected by just judgment because, after a lawful appeal to us had been lodged, he transferred himself without our permission to a see for which he had been sought in a disputed election, presumed to occupy it. Since, according to canonical sanctions, he had deserved to be deprived of both sees, he nevertheless, disregarding the favour granted him [Col. 0651C] by which we allowed him to retain the Church of Worms, held both, and still holds them, in occupation.

Since, therefore, he was admonished on this matter not merely once but frequently through our letters and delegates, and neither obeyed our commands nor acquiesced in our warnings, we considered his manifest contumacy. Having put away his heart of flesh, he had taken up a heart of stone and stopped his ears lest he understand how to act rightly or add to his conduct by rising from his presumption and making satisfaction for contempt. He therefore incurred first the sentence of excommunication and finally that of deposition, together with the censure deserved by his iniquity; and how he respects those censures is sufficiently manifest to all. [Note: [Col. 0651D] Thus far in Raynaldus.]

Moreover, although the same duke ought to have avoided one excommunicated and cast aside one deposed, he has, as though he held unsound views concerning the keys of the Church, cherished him even more from that time. Not only has he participated in the latter’s error as its first and principal promoter; as a further proof of favour, he entrusted him with the office of his legation into Italy and sent this enemy of the Church to attack the patrimony of blessed Peter. Behold how the same duke honours the Roman Church; behold how he reveres the keys of the Church, when, so far as lay in him, violating Peter’s privilege—something no prince, and not even any emperor, has hitherto attempted—he presumed to usurp for himself the translation of bishops, and publicly cherishes and seeks to increase with honours a man excommunicated and condemned by us, as though he did not believe the testimony of Truth, uttered by Christ himself when he bestowed the keys concerning their power.

For since, under the divine law, judgment concerning leprosy pertains only to priests, to whom it has been granted to distinguish leprosy from leprosy, he ought not to have touched a leper or arrogated the priestly office to himself, lest, with King Uzziah, he be struck with leprosy on the forehead and his fault become known to all. But if he were supporting a man conspicuous for religion, distinguished in letters, endowed with uprightness, and unjustly condemned, then, although it would not be his business to judge our judgment, he might perhaps appear excusable to some. But since he favours a pestilent man, whose crime is neither mitigated by learning, diminished by upright morals, concealed by religious profession, nor excused by an unjust punishment, his offence cannot in any way be excused.] [Note: [Col. 0651D] Raynaldus ends here.]

Furthermore, ignorance does not excuse him in this affair, for even if he perhaps does not know canon law, recent examples and events that have occurred in his sight in modern times could have made him cautious and instructed. For he knows—and it was proclaimed throughout all Germany—how our venerable brother … Archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0652D] See letter 4 of book three, note.], having been sought for the Church of Salzburg, transferred there without our permission; how his election was rejected; and how, recognizing and condemning his own error, he returned to the Church of Brixen. Although, on learning our command, he humbly and devoutly obeyed us, he could not obtain the favour of translation until, after the Church of Salzburg had again unanimously sought him, he personally came into our presence.

Nor could the aforesaid duke be unaware, since it was published in those regions, that C. of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0652D] See letter 99 of book five, note.], chancellor of the imperial court, had transferred from Hildesheim to the Church of Würzburg on the ground of an indulgence which he claimed to have obtained from C., Pope of happy memory, our predecessor—an indulgence by which he seemed in some degree excusable to certain persons. Yet, because, when warned, he did not correct his error, he was not only excommunicated but deprived of both the Church of Würzburg and that of Hildesheim; although at last, humbly and devoutly returning at our command, he deserved to obtain our grace.

We, however, although we thought it proper to wait a long time for that duke to correct his error of his own accord, eventually ordered you, son abbot, and our beloved son … Abbot of Salem [Note: [Col. 0652D] See letter 99 of book five, note.], to admonish him concerning this matter. Although the Abbot of Salem, when our letters had not, as we have learned, been presented to you, diligently admonished him, he could not [Col. 0653A] soften or bend his mind or recall him from favouring and associating with that condemned and excommunicated man. [Note: [Col. 0653D] Again Raynaldus.]

[Therefore, although, because the offence of the same duke is notorious and, once warned, he has refused to desist from such presumption, we could proceed more severely against him, nevertheless, still wishing to test whether at least now, as a Catholic man, or even as a Christian, he faithfully acknowledges in blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, the authority of the universal Church, and in us the keys of the kingdom of heaven, we command your discretion by apostolic letters and strictly enjoin you by virtue of obedience that, setting aside delay and excuse, you personally approach him; first privately, and then publicly, in the hearing of such ecclesiastical and secular princes as may be present, diligently and urgently admonish him not henceforth to grant any help or favour to the oft-mentioned excommunicate, but instead to cast him aside as deposed, avoid him as condemned, and ensure that the idol of zeal which he has raised in the temple of God, like an abomination standing in the holy place, be entirely removed from him.

Otherwise, publicly announce to him that, unless within three months after your admonition he humbly and devoutly complies with your warnings, we shall take care to lay our hands more heavily upon him and his land, perhaps more severely than he expects,] [Note: [Col. 0653D] Thus far Raynaldus.] since we can no longer bear this with equanimity. Indeed, for defending the justice of the Apostolic See, we should be ready, if necessity required it, not only to suffer persecution but to lay down our lives—although we need fear nothing of the kind.

Also diligently and faithfully make known the pure and complete truth of these matters to all the princes of the German kingdom, ecclesiastical as well as secular, so that, once they understand the merits of both sides, they may pass from the darkness of falsehood to the truth of light. If not both … you, brother Patriarch, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of June.

LXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0653D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 53.] TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS. That they place the Duke of Swabia under interdict unless he repents within the prescribed time. (At Saint Peter’s, second day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 0653D]

You know that we instructed you to admonish the nobleman Ph., Duke of Swabia, to desist entirely from favouring and defending Luipold, formerly Bishop of Worms and now excommunicated and deposed. Since, therefore, we neither wish nor ought to endure his contempt for the keys of the Church with impunity, and his contradiction—not in word, perhaps, but at least in deed, to his own ruin and that of others—of the word of truth whereby Peter is told, “Whatever you bind” (Matthew 16), etc., [Col. 0654A] we command your discretion by apostolic letters and strictly enjoin you by virtue of obedience that, unless perhaps, within one month after your admonition, recovering from such error or heresy, he withdraws his association and favour from Luipold, you shall announce by our authority in your churches that the whole land which he holds in his demesne is subject to interdict. Thus, apart from the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, no divine office shall be celebrated in it and no ecclesiastical sacrament administered.

In every place to which he comes, for as long as he remains present there, you shall forbid the celebration of divine offices. On every Sunday and feast day, moreover, cause this to be solemnly published through your churches, the neighbouring dioceses, and his land, adding that if he does not repent even then, we shall lay our hands still more heavily upon his person and the lands of all who favour him in this error. Carry out the apostolic command in such a way that the zeal of God’s house may appear to consume you. If not both … you, brother Patriarch, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of June.

LXXXV. [Note: [Col. 0653D]

A fragment of this letter is found among the Decretals, book V, title 7, *On Heretics*, chapter 11. Passages found there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are given.

[Col. 0654D] Raynaldus published a portion of it under the year 1205, § 66. The passages presented by him are here distinguished in the margin by a double stroke at the beginning of each line.]

TO THE ENTIRE PEOPLE OF VITERBO, THE SPIRIT OF SOUND COUNSEL. That they rise against certain Patarenes and furnish them neither help, counsel, nor favour.

[Col. 0654C]

[If the land should rise up against you [Note: [Col. 0654D] In the Decretals: “against us.”],] and the stars of heaven should reveal your iniquities and make your crimes known to the whole world, so that not only human beings but even the elements themselves should conspire for your destruction and ruin, and should wipe you from the face of the earth, sparing neither sex nor age, so that you might become an everlasting reproach to all nations, no vengeance sufficient or worthy could be exacted from you. For you neither fear God nor dread man; nor do you distinguish between profane and holy, but make light darkness and darkness light, and call evil good and good evil. You despise to cultivate a good reputation, which fattens the bones, and a good name, which is to be preferred above great riches; and [Col. 0654D] you care nothing for disgrace, since your brow is hardened and you have assumed the shameless brow of a harlot. For you have rotted in sins, like beasts in their dung, so that the smoke and stench of your corruption have now almost infected the surrounding regions and, as we believe, provoked the Lord himself to nausea. [Note: [Col. 0654D] These words occur in Raynaldus.] “Indeed, in sins you surpass all others, having become more faithless than the Jews and more cruel than the pagans. [Col. 0655A] The Jews indeed once fastened the Lord to the gibbet of the cross; but you, continually crucifying him in his members, tear him with reproaches and insults. And whereas they believe, albeit in the blindness of sin, that God the Father created all things visible and invisible, most of you believe that visible things were fashioned and created by Lucifer. The pagans raged in putting Christians’ bodies to death and slaughtering them; but you aim to kill the whole human being, secretly snatching the souls of the faithful away from Christ and destroying both the outward and inward person together. Yet neither these nor those knew Christ the Lord, and therefore they seem to have some excuse for their sins; but you, like the sons of Ephraim bending the bow, were marked with Christ’s character, [Col. 0655B] and still wish publicly to be counted by Christian profession; yet, withdrawing backward in heart and departing from the faith, you have become a perverse bow, ensnared by the traps of heretics and disfigured by their wicked teachings.” [Note: [Col. 0655D] Raynaldus ends here.]

Hence the prophetic word has truly been fulfilled in you: “The jackals bared their breasts and suckled their young” (Lamentations 4). For you have been made drunk, not with the wine of compunction, but with the gall of dragons, served to you by heretics in the golden cup of Babylon. Now the waters have overflowed and covered your heads—your sins sunk in the abyss of vices. Now the deep has swallowed you, and the infernal pit presses its mouth over you. For you have fallen into the pit of despair, since you scorn to rise from the depths. [Col. 0655C] Therefore we rightly fear lest the wrath of God come upon the children of unbelief; that he may now sharpen his sword like lightning and execute judgment upon you with his hand, nor in the day of wrath remember his mercy.
