[Note: [Col. 0655D] Raynaldus again.] “But we, having compassion upon your miseries, wish to avert your impending ruin and, if we can, to block the open road to your destruction, knocking upon God by prayers and following Abraham’s example: when the Lord wished to overthrow Sodom and Gomorrah, Abraham obtained through repeated intercessions that he would not destroy all for the sake of ten righteous persons. For we wish to discover whether any faithful persons remain among you who have not bent their knees before Baal, and who, following the example of the Ninevites, prostrate in sackcloth and ashes, may appease the Lord’s wrath and fury, so that many may be spared for the sake of a few and all may not perish together. Therefore, whoever belongs to God, let him join us, who wish to wield the sword of Phinehas, imitate Mosaic punishment, and, with Mattathias, punish those sacrificing to demons, so that, with the Lord’s help, the faithless and unworthy may be expelled from the temple and the leaven of heretical depravity may be wholesomely purged from the mass of the Lord’s dough. Therefore, by apostolic [Col. 0656A] letters we command and strictly enjoin you that, since certain of your fellow citizens, sons of Belial, out of hatred for Jesus Christ and contempt for the Apostolic See and for us, after our prohibition, have ventured to elect certain believers in the Patarenes as consuls, and have not feared to appoint as chamberlain even that arch-heresiarch, namely J. Tiniosi, son of perdition, who, because of his iniquities, has long since by our command been bound under the bond of excommunication and still persists in his contumacy, you shall rise vigorously against the elected persons and their electors, as well as their accomplices; resist them with courage and strength and assail them sharply; and strive to frustrate and crush their first attempts, lest they be able to take root firmly. [Col. 0656B] And so that, once the roots have been torn out, the stock may wholly wither and dry up,” [Note: [Col. 0655D] Raynaldus ends here.] under threat of anathema we more strictly forbid anyone to presume to swear to them as consuls or rectors, or in any other capacity. Those, however, who are bound to them by any oath, or who have presumed to swear to them after such an election, we deem absolved from that oath: for there ought to be no fellowship of Christ with Belial, or of light with darkness; nor is one faithful to an apostate who has rashly broken faith with the Creator in any way obliged to keep faith, as is provided in the canons.

Although many enactments and statutes against heretics have been issued by us and our predecessors, nevertheless, lest you have any excuse in your sins as though you had forgotten the commands of old, and because what is specially enjoined is usually more feared than what is generally commanded, [Note: [Col. 0655D] The Decretals add: “to you.”] we firmly forbid advocates and notaries to give, at any time, any aid, counsel, or favour to the aforementioned elected persons while they remain in their contumacy and error, or to believers in the Patarenes, [Note: [Col. 0656D] The Decretals read *haereticis* (“heretics”) for *praefatis . . . vero* (“the aforesaid . . . indeed”); shortly afterwards they read “or” for “and”; they omit the words “at any time,” and below omit some words, read “some” for “others,” and perhaps do not contain the word “any.”] their supporters, and defenders; nor are you to lend them your advocacy in any causes, affairs, or other litigants subject to their jurisdiction, nor to venture in any manner to draw up public instruments or make writings on their behalf. Should you perhaps presume to act otherwise, we decree that you shall be suspended from your office and perpetually subject to infamy.

Moreover, lest the [Col. 0656D] judges and notaries who agreed to join the aforesaid elected persons in this rash presumption should glory in their wickedness, since one deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power permitted to him, we judge them suspended from their office, decreeing null and void whatsoever has been done or established by them and by the said elected persons. We hold valid the sentences of excommunication and interdict reasonably pronounced by your bishop and clergy on account of such excesses against the rebels and the aforementioned elected persons, [Col. 0657A] and command that they be inviolably observed until due satisfaction has been made. Otherwise, if even thus your pride cannot be crushed and your folly restrained, then, the goats being separated from the sheep and the faithful from the unbelievers, we shall destroy the wicked wickedly, entrusting our vineyard to other cultivators who shall render its fruit in its seasons; and we shall take care to lay our hands upon you more severely, both temporally and spiritually, until you learn by experience what the right hand of the Apostolic See avails and can do, and until such filthiness is removed and iniquity extirpated from among you. You ought indeed to recall how great a danger you have incurred because you despised our counsel.

Given, etc.

LXXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0657C] This letter is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book I, title VI, *On Election and the Authority of the Elect*, chapter 24; and therefore it is here printed within brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO THE CLERGY OF SAINT AGATHA. They are restored to the receipt of a certain annual pension in the church of Saint Saviour, and a priest is condemned to pay the same pension. (2 June.)

[Col. 0657B]

[The complaint which the beloved son G., now cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, then cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, [Note: [Col. 0657D] See letter 60 of book V, note.] brought before Pope C., our predecessor of blessed memory, through the steward of your church, of which that cardinal is governor, [Note: [Col. 0657D] Because of their dignity, cardinals may, besides their own title, hold other churches under the designation of governance or commendam, and are called their governors or administrators.] against P. . . ., now [Note: [Col. 0657D] “Of Cornutis.” Thus in the copy; but from what follows it is clear that one should read “of Termini” or “of Thermae.”] priest, but then deacon, concerning the church of Saint Saviour called *de Cornutis*, [Note: [Col. 0657D] See letter 54 of book III, note.] he committed to us, while we held a lesser office, for hearing and examination. That steward therefore requested that the aforesaid [Col. 0657C] Peter be removed from the church of Saint Saviour, which he had presumed to occupy to the prejudice of your church and the injury of the said cardinal, since that church of Saint Saviour [Note: [Col. 0657D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are shortly afterwards the words “now, then … deacon, and now.”] belonged by full right to the church of Saint Agatha. He also requested that the pension of sixteen Pavia denarii, owed to the church of Saint Agatha for the church of Saint Saviour and its boundaries, [Note: [Col. 0657D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are shortly afterwards the words “now, then … deacon, and now.”] and newly withheld, be restored to it. But the said cleric P. [Note: [Col. 0657D] The Decretals read “of the church of Saint Saviour,” and below “that church,” in place of “the church of Saint Saviour called de Cornutis, before Pope C. of blessed memory, our predecessor.”] replied that he had inflicted no injury upon the cardinal, nor had he received the church of Saint Saviour to the prejudice of the church of Saint Agatha, [Note: [Col. 0657D] The Decretals read “Pope C., our predecessor,” and then omit the words [Col. 0658C] “and examine.” They read “the aforesaid” in place of “the same,” and “that the aforesaid Peter be removed” below.] since it belonged to that church by no right and owed it [Col. 0658A] no pension. Rather, he said, he had been canonically instituted, by election of the people—which by ancient custom belonged to the same people—by the cardinal of Saint Susanna, [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals omit this word, and later also omit it.] to whom the same church of Saint Saviour, as a chapel subject to his title, is subject in spiritual matters. [Note: [Col. 0658D] Thus in the Conti copy. But in the Decretals: “the same church of Thermae.”]]

When each party had repeatedly produced witnesses to prove its assertion, we received and diligently examined them. When their depositions had been published, we heard argument upon them; but before this controversy could reach its end, the aforesaid predecessor of ours paid the debt of the flesh. Thereafter both parties earnestly requested us to deign to decide the cause.

[We therefore, after diligently hearing and fully understanding the attestations, allegations, [Col. 0658B] and instruments [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals omit “and”; shortly afterwards they read “your” for “Saint Agatha,” and “the said church” for “the church of Saint Saviour.”] of both parties, and having taken counsel with our brethren, absolve the aforesaid priest from your steward’s claim concerning the election and institution made of him in the church of Saint Saviour; and upon these matters we deem silence to be imposed upon the aforesaid steward. For it has been clearly established to us through suitable witnesses [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals read “arguments” in place of “attestations, allegations, and instruments.” Shortly afterwards they read “the said P.” for “and fully understood, having taken counsel with our brethren.”] that, when the aforesaid cleric was elected [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals omit, as shortly afterwards, the word “clearly,” and below “to that church.”] to that church, the people were in quasi-possession of the right to present a cleric to it; and that the same church belongs by full right to the title of Saint Susanna in spiritual matters, without prejudice to the question of patronage between your church and the people [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals read “the said priest” for “the aforesaid cleric.”] of Saint Saviour. But because it was clearly proved through witnesses beyond every exception [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals add “of the frequently mentioned church of Saint …” and then omit the words “through … exception.”] that [Col. 0658C] a pension of sixteen denarii in Pavia currency had [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals read “shall have been,” and shortly afterwards “of Thermae” for “and boundaries.”] for a long time been paid annually to the clergy of your church for the church of Saint Saviour and its boundaries, but had lately been withheld, we [Note: [Col. 0658D] The Decretals read “you,” then omit the word “pension”; below they read “of Thermae” for “and boundaries,” then “we decree” for “we decreed,” and “we condemn” for “we condemned.”] decree that your church be restored to the same position of receiving this pension from the church of Saint Saviour and its boundaries, and we condemn the aforesaid priest to payment of the withheld pension, without prejudice to the question of ownership between the churches mentioned.]

Let no one therefore, etc., violate our definition, etc. But should anyone, etc.

Given, 2 June.

LXXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0659D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §53.] TO C. . . . ., ARCHDEACON MAJOR, MASTER R., PENITENTIARY OF SAINT VICTOR OF PARIS, AND MASTER R. OF CORZON, CANON OF NOYON RESIDING AT PARIS. He commands them to absolve the bishop of Toul from the bond of excommunication and to settle the case between the said bishop and the archdeacon of Toul. (7 June.)

[Col. 0659A]

The beloved son P., archdeacon of Toul, appearing before the Apostolic See, humbly requested that we open the eyes of our providential care over the church of Toul, which through the negligence and bad administration of . . . . . bishop of Toul [Note: [Col. 0659D] See letter 13 of book V, note.] had already fallen into grave decline and ruin; and that, as punishment for barrenness, we deign to lay the avenging [Col. 0659B] axe to the fruitless tree, lest fertile ground be turned into a salt waste through the injury and neglect of an evil cultivator. For when our venerable brother . . ., archbishop of Reims, [Note: [Col. 0659D] See letter 116 of book VII.] then legate of the Apostolic See, and the beloved son . . . . abbot of Saint Benedict of Metz [Note: [Col. 0659D] See letter 13 of book V, note.] diocese, had received apostolic letters against the aforesaid bishop, [Note: [Col. 0659D] Ibid.] and the said archdeacon wished to lodge a formal accusation against him, the archbishop, fearing for the safety of that archdeacon and his companions, sought to bring them to an agreement in this form: namely, that the bishop should personally swear in their presence that henceforth he would preserve inviolate the liberty of the churches and the rights of the clergy throughout the diocese, and would not presume to alienate or pledge the goods of the bishopric. He also ordered the priors and deans that, should the said bishop act contrary to his own oath, they should refuse him their customary obedience; and, under penalty of excommunication, he strictly forbade him to presume henceforth to alienate anything from the immovable property of the church of Toul without obtaining the consent of his chapter.

As time passed, while the bishop was present before the archbishop himself, the dean of Toul [Note: [Col. 0660D] Frederick of Brixei is mentioned as dean of Toul in 1200, and immediately afterwards Theoderic in 1216; in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 1062.] charged him, by way of denunciation, with the crime of dissipation, alleging that, in contempt of both the sanctity of his oath and the excommunication, he had presumed to alienate twenty-two villages belonging to the episcopal table; and that whereas the bishopric of Toul had revenues of one thousand pounds at the beginning of his promotion, it had been reduced by him to such exhaustion that its revenues could scarcely amount to thirty pounds in Toul currency. The bishop replied that the alienation of those properties had been carried out not through his own fault but that of his chapter. He added that he was content for an inquiry into the true condition of the bishopric to be conducted by worthy men of the same diocese. Accordingly, a fixed day was appointed for this by consent of both [Col. 0660A] parties. Although both the said archbishop and bishop, in the presence of many prelates as witnesses, had received the dean under their safe-conduct, the bishop’s brother and his servants nevertheless laid sacrilegious hands upon the dean, tied him by his feet beneath a packhorse’s belly, and brought him to the bishop. They refused to release him from harsh bonds until the bishop had been marked with excommunication on this account and his territory placed under interdict, unless he freed him within a fixed period.

When even this had proved ineffective, the dean was at last freed from his bonds after many efforts. A definite day was assigned to the parties, and, since the archbishop had already learned through the report of clergy and people that the church was in extremity, [Col. 0660B] he suspended the often-mentioned bishop—suspected of excessive dissipation—from the administration of temporal affairs and, gravely defamed for perjury, from the exercise of spiritual functions. Because the bishop scorned to observe this sentence of suspension, the archbishop afterwards bound him by the bond of excommunication.

When these matters had been set forth in our presence by Joffrey the archdeacon, W. and T., procurators of the aforesaid bishop, argued in our court in reply that the archbishop’s sentence was null for many reasons. Since judicial procedure is customarily observed in such matters, they asserted that it had not observed proper procedure: the suit had not been joined, as equity of law required; and, although the bishop had obtained a delay for deliberation until the octave of Saint Michael, an inquiry had nevertheless been made against him in the meantime without his knowing of it, whereas according to legal order the judge’s office ought to have remained inactive until the period requested had elapsed. Further, since a lawful appeal had been lodged by him in all matters, no proceeding against him could stand, since it was rendered void by the remedy of a lawful appeal. Moreover, when it was alleged against him that he had celebrated divine offices after excommunication, the procurators denied this altogether; and they maintained that the alienation of the aforesaid villages had occurred through the fault not of the bishop but of the chapter. Hence they thought that whatever had been done by the archbishop should be held by us null and void.

We [Col. 0660D] therefore, having diligently heard these and the other matters which the parties wished to set before us, and having found that the aforesaid legate had proceeded properly in all respects, command your discretion by apostolic letters to cause the aforesaid sentence of suspension to be firmly observed by our authority; to appoint a suitable procurator to administer meanwhile the affairs of that bishopric, while making suitable provision for the bishop’s just and moderate expenses until this cause can be heard; and [Note: [Col. 0661D] [[Col. 0661] This note appears at the foot of column 661, but callout number 366 has not been printed in the text.] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §55. See also letter 226 of book VII.] [Col. 0661A]—since we have learned that neither party renounced the production of witnesses—we send you the depositions received, sealed, nevertheless enjoining you to absolve the aforesaid bishop from the bond of excommunication according to the form of the Church. Receive the witnesses whom either party considers should be produced; once their testimony along with the earlier testimony has been published, carefully examine the cause and bring it, every impediment of contradiction and appeal removed, to a canonical conclusion. Thus, if it shall be lawfully established to you that the aforesaid goods of the church of Toul were alienated through the bishop’s fault, take care to remove him from that church. Otherwise, since the alienation is now established, although the bishop attributes the fault to others, yet because [Col. 0661B] he has been regarded as highly suspect and gravely defamed in this matter, prescribe canonical purgation for him. Take especial care that, if the said bishop has rashly presumed to celebrate divine offices after a sentence of excommunication was pronounced against him, then, because he has added contempt to contempt, weakening ecclesiastical discipline, you shall depose him from the pontifical office. If the witnesses who have been named withdraw through favour, hatred, or fear, compel them, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside, to bear testimony to the truth; no letters being an obstacle except by consent of the parties, etc. If not all of you … two of you, etc.

Given, etc., 7 June.

LXXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0661D] [[Col. 0661] This note is missing in Migne’s printed edition.]] TO ANDREW, LORD OF HUNGARY. He gives the reason why he does not comply with Andrew’s request concerning the archbishop of Kalocsa, proposed for translation to the archbishopric of Esztergom, and commands another to be elected. (24 June.)

[Col. 0661C]

He who searches hearts and knows secrets knows that we aspire with ardent desire to your honour and advancement, confidently hoping that you, adhering to the footsteps of your forebears, wish with ready devotion to venerate the most holy Roman Church, your mother. Although, therefore, in the first letters which you sent to our apostolic office after you ascended to the governance of the realm, sealed with a brotherly seal, you thought us to be entreated concerning the transfer of our venerable brother J., archbishop of Kalocsa, [Col. 0661D] to the metropolitan see of Esztergom, yet later, by other letters marked with your own seal, you humbly asked us to deign to admit the postulation concerning our venerable brother C., bishop of Pécs, called to that same metropolitan see. We deliberated carefully with our brethren concerning this matter; and, since we found that it had been rashly celebrated, after lawful appeals had been lodged to us, amid great discord not only among the suffragan bishops but even among the canons of the church of Esztergom, contrary to the form of our mandate and with regular procedure set aside, [Col. 0662A] justice required that we should not admit it. We grieve alike for you and for him that this postulation was not conducted in such a way that we could approve it according to God.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your serenity to regard in this matter not any harshness of our will but the censure of canonical sanction, which we wish—and are bound—to observe without respect of persons, since there must not be one weight and another weight in our hand, as on a deceitful balance. Know for certain that we are prepared effectively to grant the prayers which you consider proper to present to us according to God. But lest the church of Esztergom remain longer desolate, we command the chapter of Esztergom by our letters [Col. 0662B] not to delay, within a month after receiving our letters, in proceeding to provide itself with a suitable pastor through a canonical election or a unanimous postulation, after seeking the consent of the suffragans if this is required by ancient and approved custom. Otherwise, so that the Lord’s flock may not long lack a shepherd’s care, we shall proceed, according to the duty of our office and from the fullness of apostolic power, to provide that church with a suitable pastor; and in this we shall defer to your honour as far as we can consistently with our own honour.

Given, 24 June.

LXXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0661D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §68.] TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF THE HOLY TRINITY OF VERNOLIO. He receives them under protection, subject to an annual rent of one gold obol. (11 June.)

[Col. 0662C]

It is customary to grant assent, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclined by your just petitions, we receive under protection your persons and house, with all its goods, etc. In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to the same Hospital, by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the houses, lands, and other things which Herveus the Lesser bestowed upon that house; ten sous from the oven of George of Punt; ten sous annually on the anniversary of John of Saccenuill; the fief of Cochet; and the lands of Faudo—as you justly and peacefully possess them. As a sign [Col. 0662D] of the protection thus received from us, you shall annually pay to us and to our successors one gold obol freely offered. We decree therefore, etc., that no one violate our protection and confirmation, etc. But should anyone, etc.

Given . . ., 11 June, in the eighth year.

XC. [Note: [Col. 0661D] This letter was published by Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 313, diploma 373; and is therefore included here within brackets.] TO S., ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ. [Note: [Col. 0662D] See letter 14 of book V, note.] Concerning the consecration of the bishop of Strasbourg. (6 June.)

[It is often the case that delay draws danger to itself, [Col. 0663A] and that matters which could readily have been completed at the beginning, when suspended by prolonged delay, sometimes have grave and difficult outcomes. Fearing this no little, the beloved son H., bishop-elect of Strasbourg, [Note: [Col. 0663D] See letter 8 of book VIII, note.] came to our presence, not without much labour, reporting on his return that, after he had been canonically elected bishop of Strasbourg by the unanimous will of clergy and people, having taken counsel with his brethren and prudent men, he had sent special envoys to our venerable brother G., [Note: [Col. 0663D] See letter 116 of book VII.] archbishop of Reims, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and then bishop of Palestrina, exercising the office of legate in the German lands, and to you, to obtain confirmation of his election. Having freely [Col. 0663B] obtained it from us, he afterwards asked you humbly and reverently, through . . . . abbot of Sturzelb [Note: [Col. 0663D] Perhaps named Theoderic, whom the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, [Col. 0664D] col. 947, mention in 1200.] and others bearing letters from that legate, to grant him the benefit of consecration. You replied in your own letters that, after deliberation, you would assign him a suitable day and place to which both you and he could safely travel, and there would then consecrate him bishop.

After waiting long for your promise, the bishop-elect again sent his envoys to you. Although they were robbed on the journey, they nevertheless reached you on foot and diligently requested his consecration. At the insistence both of the bishop-elect and of his envoys, you assigned him a day at Andernach, on the Sunday called *Oculi mei*, in [Col. 0663C] the previous year, promising to confer upon him there the benefit of consecration. But when the bishop-elect was prepared to come to that place on the day appointed, he received letters from your fraternity in which you stated that you were hindered by weighty business and therefore could not come on the day assigned, nor fulfil his wish at the fixed time by conferring the gift of consecration.

As time passed, the bishop-elect saw that grave ruin threatened himself and his church: people of that region did not fear to lay hands on him, the provosts, abbots, and other clergy, taking encouragement for their perversity from the fact that the bishop-elect had not been invested with pastoral dignity. Therefore he sent an envoy to the Apostolic See, asking that, in this matter, provision be made through the kindness of the Apostolic See for himself and the church of Strasbourg, whose condition in both spiritual and temporal matters suffered continual harm. We granted him, from paternal kindness, letters to you ordering that, in a suitable and safe place, you should either consecrate him personally or have him consecrated by others.

Although you received our letters on this matter, and his consecration was sought from you with much urgency of prayer and devotion by the beloved son . . . . abbot of Bungart, [Note: [Col. 0664D] See letter 8 of book VIII, note.] whom the bishop-elect sent to you for this purpose with our letters, so that he might provide you a safe-conduct and stand at his consecration as one of the consecrators; and although the bishop-elect devoutly accepted your word in this matter, he very diligently requested through an envoy from the archbishop himself that the archbishop grant assent both to your request and to his own. But he could not obtain this from him in any way. The bishop-elect therefore informed you, through your clerk who was then present with him, and by letter, that the archbishop could not provide you the safe-conduct which you had requested, and that he himself was prepared to come to a safe place which you should designate for this purpose; but [Col. 0664B] he received no answer from you.

The bishop-elect therefore humbly asked us mercifully to grant him what he could not at present obtain from you, especially since many harms had resulted, and still result, to the church of Strasbourg and the clergy and people of the whole bishopric from the delay in his consecration. But wishing to defer to your fraternity, we did not judge that we should proceed to his consecration until we had been more certainly informed by your letters of the course of events and of your will. Therefore, by apostolic letters and with a peremptory command, we order your fraternity to inform us by letter of the plain and simple truth and also to set forth your will, so that, having understood all that concerns this matter, [Col. 0664C] we may proceed as we know expedient. Know for certain that, if we decide to proceed to his consecration, we shall take care to provide sufficiently for your honour and right.

Given, 6 June, in the eighth year.

XCI. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF MONTPELLIER. That they are not to impede construction of the oratory of the Holy Spirit; a threatening letter. [Note: [Col. 0664D] See letter 107 of book VI, note.] (3 June.)

We report not without grief, nor recount without shame, that certain persons given over to a reprobate mind, like the ungodly who, when they have come into the depth of vices, despise, are striving in many ways to obstruct the construction of the oratory of the brethren of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, contrary to our ordinance—indeed, rather, contrary to the divine command. They do not consider how impious and unjust it is wickedly to act against works of mercy, which, according to the Apostle, possess the promise of the life that now is and also of that which is to come. Since the audacity of so great a presumption ought to be crushed by ecclesiastical severity, we, in the name of God almighty—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, together with our own authority, excommunicate and anathematize [Col. 0665A] absolutely all persons, clerics or laymen, who by themselves or through others presume in any way to obstruct construction of that oratory. By apostolic authority we decree that, if anyone falls into the snare of this excommunication, he is to be absolved by no one, except when at the point of death, until he takes care to present himself before the Apostolic See, there to receive fitting penance for so great a crime.

We commend your devotion in the Lord, because, instructed by apostolic exhortations, you have hitherto stood firmly by the aforesaid brethren against such presumptuous persons, affording them timely aid. Unless they had been protected by your favour, the oratory already begun would not merely have been hindered but entirely destroyed. [Col. 0665B] Therefore, wishing you, as special sons, to persevere in this good purpose and always to rise from virtue to virtue, we earnestly admonish your charity and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: defend the said brethren from the attacks of malicious persons; extend to them a helping hand toward completing the oratory already begun; and do not allow its construction to be impeded by anyone. Thus, through these and other good works which, by the Lord’s inspiration, you perform, you may more abundantly obtain the rewards of eternal recompense and more fully deserve to obtain the favour of the Apostolic See.

Given, 3 June, in the eighth year.

XCII. [Note: [Col. 0665D] This letter is included in the *Gesta Innocentii*, § CXXII. Raynaldus also prints it in full, under the year 1206, § 34. Yet in both places it is said to have been issued in the ninth year of Innocent’s pontificate; and, remarkably, it is found repeated in the Register of the ninth year, no. 101, as will be seen in its place. Raynaldus, loc. cit., adds: “The day assigned to this diploma is not found in the *Gesta Innocentii*; but in the Register it is appended thus: ‘Given at Ferentino, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July.’” But the *Gesta* expressly reads: “Given at Ferentino, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year.”] TO P., KING OF ARAGON. He grants to him and to his successors that they may be crowned at Saragossa by the archbishop of Tarragona. (Sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0665C]

“Your Highness does not fail to know with how much glory and honour, rejoicing and acclamation, you received from our hand at Rome, in the monastery of Blessed Pancras, the royal diadem, after we caused you to be anointed king through our venerable brother P., bishop of Porto. [Note: [Col. 0665D] See letter 69 of the fifth book, note.] But in order that we might show more plainly, by the bestowal of a deed, the affection of love which we bear toward your person, we caused all the royal insignia—namely the mantle and tunic, sceptre and orb, crown and mitre—to be prepared for your use, no less precious than beautiful; and we freely gave them to you as a sign of special favour.

“But you, as a devout prince and Catholic king, offered your kingdom, upon the altar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to us and, through us, to the Apostolic See, with great devotion, by a charter of privilege; making it perpetually tributary to that See. You firmly promised that you would inviolably observe the oath of fidelity and obedience rendered to us at your coronation, and you desired that your successors should be bound to render and maintain it.

“We therefore, wishing that the favour shown you by us should pass to your successors, by the authority of these presents grant that, when they decide to be crowned and request a crown from the Apostolic See, they shall be solemnly crowned at Saragossa, by special mandate, through the archbishop of Tarragona, [Col. 0666B] after suitable security has been furnished concerning the matters aforesaid. [Note: [Col. 0665D] After these words the *Gesta* and Raynaldus add: “And since civil law has established that women are to be adorned with the honours of their husbands, by the authority of these presents we grant that they may be crowned by the hands of the same archbishop. Therefore let no one,” [Col. 0666D] etc. This addition is also found in another copy of this letter in the Register of the ninth year, no. 101.] Therefore let no one … our grant, etc. But if anyone, etc.

“Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.”

XCIII. [Note: [Col. 0666D] The copies of letters 93, 94, and 95, which we had caused to be transcribed together with the rest from the Conti copy, somehow fell from our hands; how, we do not know. We can therefore give only their summaries here. See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 63.] TO THE SAME. He promises that, if he obtains the island of Majorca, an episcopal see shall be established there.

XCIV. TO THE SAME. He grants him authority lawfully to possess whatever he may be able to acquire from the land of the heretics.

XCV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND PRELATES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE LAND OF ARAGON. He commands them to be ready with aid and counsel for the king in expelling the ungodly.

[Col. 0666C]

XCVI. [Note: [Col. 0666D] Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1205, § 63. Angelus Manrique printed it in full, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 457, under the year 1205, ch. 8, § 5.] TO THE BRETHREN OF CALATRAVA AND VELEZ. [Note: [Col. 0666D] On Velez: “I leave it to the reader to investigate the occasion or cause of this addition.” ANGELUS MANRIQUE, loc. cit.] He commands them to assist the king of Aragon against the Saracens. (Third day before the Nones of July.)

Our dearest son in Christ, P., the illustrious king of Aragon, represented before us that, since our dearest son in Christ, [lacuna], the illustrious king of Castile, has made a truce with the Saracens, you do not dare to wage war upon them from his kingdom. He asks that we should write to you, so that you may come into [Col. 0666D] his frontier region and there vigorously undertake to attack those same Saracens. We therefore admonish your discretion and command you by apostolic letters that, if this is so and you judge it expedient, you come into his frontier region to attack the aforesaid Saracens.

Given on the third day before the Nones of July.

XCVII. [Note: [Col. 0667D] This letter is mentioned by Bzovius, in the *Annals*, vol. XIII, under the year 1205, no. 10; and by Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 63. See also Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 448, under the year 1205, ch. 3, § 11; and, if desired, *History of Languedoc*, vol. III, p. 140.] TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX, [Note: [Col. 0667D] See letter 16 of the fifth book, note.] P. OF CASTELNAU, AND MASTER R., LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That they grant in fief to the king of Aragon the Castle of Scura—which is the property of blessed Peter—when recovered from the heretics by that king, for an annual rent at their discretion. (Sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

By apostolic letters we command your discretion [Col. 0667B] that, when, God permitting, our dearest son in Christ, P., the illustrious king of Aragon, has recovered the Castle of Scura from the heretics, you personally grant it to him in fief; provided, however, that he render to the Roman Church the fidelity due on its account, and that, in acknowledgment that ownership of the same castle belongs by right to blessed Peter, he establish a fixed rent, to be paid annually to us and our successors, and confirm and strengthen all this by letters patent.

Given … on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year.

XCVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF CENAD AND THE ABBOT OF STEKEDOR, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER. That they receive from the bishop of Pécs his purgation concerning an accusation of incest. (Thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0667C]

Our venerable brother C., bishop of Pécs, wishing to demonstrate his innocence, has humbly petitioned us that we deign to receive his purgation concerning that wicked stigma by which malicious invention has spitefully bespattered him concerning a certain abominable incest. Since no accuser appears against him, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you appoint him a suitable place and day, on which, together with two bishops and three abbots, you shall publicly receive from him canonical purgation; taking careful care that you execute the apostolic command faithfully and prudently.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

XCIX. TO S., BISHOP OF BATH AND GLASTONBURY. [Note: [Col. 0667D] See letter 90 of the fifth book, note.] A postponement of crossing the sea is granted. (Eleventh day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0668A]

Since you took up the sign of the cross in order to cross the sea for the aid of the Holy Land, and, having set out, came into our presence to obtain permission, we, having carefully considered the needs of your churches—since they are heavily burdened by debts—and considering also that you are not fit for fighting and lack personal resources sufficient to lead warriors with you, have thought fit, with the counsel of our brethren, to grant you a postponement. By the authority of these presents we enjoin upon you that, on returning to your churches, you should strive not so much to preside over them [Col. 0668B] as to benefit them, applying yourself more diligently to freeing them from the burden of debt under which they are held; and taking careful care not to be absent from those churches unless urgent necessity and manifest advantage require it.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July.

C. [Note: [Col. 0667D]

Angelus Manrique mentions this letter, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 457, col. 2, under the year 1205, ch. 8, § 7.

“Having been fortified by the privilege of Saint Julian, in this same year (1205) they became vassals of the Roman See. For Innocent transcribed verbatim and confirmed the privilege of Lucius, by which they were exempted from all diocesan jurisdiction; adding further provisions and enumerating the possessions of the order, which by this time were neither few nor insignificant, [Col. 0668D] but appending at the end the following clause: ‘AS A TOKEN,’ etc.” See below.

Part of the privilege of Pope Lucius III may be read in the same Manrique, ibid., p. 139, col. 2, under the year 1183, ch. 5, § 10.]

TO MASTER B. [Note: [Col. 0668D] He was probably Dom Benedict Suares, or Sugiz. See *History of the Monastic Order*, vol. VI, p. 55.] AND THE BRETHREN OF SAINT JULIAN OF PERARIO, [Note: [Col. 0668D] In Spanish, *del Pereyro*.] PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, FOR EVER. [Note: [Col. 0668D] On the foundation of the Order of Saint Julian of Perario, otherwise Alcántara, see Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. II, p. 279, col. 1, under the year 1136, ch. 2, § 2 and following.] He receives them under the protection of blessed Peter, subject to an annual rent of one marapetinus. (Sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

We have seen recorded in the Register of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, that, since your place, situated in the jaws of the Saracens, [Col. 0668C] had hitherto been subject to no bishop under diocesan law, he, at the request of the venerable brethren P., archbishop of Compostela, G., archbishop of Braga, G., bishop of Lamego, P., bishop of Ciudad Rodrigo, V., bishop of Salamanca, J., bishop of Viseu, and A., bishop of Orense, received into the right and property of blessed Peter and of the Roman Church your place, in which you are devoted to divine service, so that you might more freely and willingly apply yourselves to the defence of Christendom and other divine services. He strengthened it by his privilege, establishing that, apart from the Roman pontiff, no one should presume to subject that place to an interdict or pronounce a sentence of excommunication or suspension upon the brethren dwelling there.

We therefore, following in his footsteps, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the same place, which is known to belong to the right and property of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0668D] and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. By apostolic authority we establish that the monastic order instituted in the same place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, etc., shall be preserved. Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., down to “to be specified by name”: the place itself in which the house stands, with its church and all its appurtenances, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and mills; Radicata, with its appurtenances and all its boundaries; Villar de Torpino, with all its appurtenances and boundaries; Ferraria, with all its appurtenances and boundaries; Colmenar, with all its appurtenances and boundaries; Almendra Sica, with its fishery, pastures, appurtenances, and all its boundaries; the grange at Aldea de Ponte Sico, with vineyards, [Col. 0669B] fields, pastures, and all its appurtenances.

Further, concerning your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and concerning the fodder of your animals, etc., down to “shall presume.” It shall also be lawful for you to receive free clerics or laymen, etc. We further prohibit, etc., down to “to retain one who departs.” You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics or monks who are to be promoted to holy orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided that he enjoys communion with and the favour of the Apostolic See. Further, the burial-place of the same house, etc., down to “are received.” Moreover, we hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority the liberties and immunities prudently granted to you by legates, archbishops, bishops, kings, princes, and other persons, ecclesiastical [Col. 0669C] as well as secular. But when a death occurs, etc., down to “they shall provide for the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict in electing.” We decree therefore, etc., down to “beneficial,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 0669D] These passages occur in Manrique.]

But as a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one marapetinus each year to us and our successors. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1205, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III. [Note: [Col. 0669D] “Moreover, Pope Honorius III, Innocent’s successor, when confirming the same exemption to the place, appended the same clause. We may therefore reasonably infer that the fief was in fact paid for some years, although it afterward fell into disuse—as we see occurred in many other cases.” ANGELUS MANRIQUE, loc. cit.]

CI. [Note: [Col. 0670D] The copy of this letter which we had caused to be transcribed, together with the rest, from the Conti copy, somehow fell from our hands; how, we do not know. We can therefore give only its summary here. See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 27.] TO ALL ARCHBISHOPS AND PRELATES ESTABLISHED IN THE PROVINCE OF JERUSALEM. That they receive humbly and devoutly the legate of the Apostolic See sent to the kingdom of Jerusalem.

CII. [Note: [Col. 0670D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 27.] TO THE … PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. Authority to confer the benefit of absolution upon all those crossing the sea, however and by whomever they have been excommunicated. (Fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0670A]

Since you have attained the favour of the Apostolic See in greater matters, it is unfitting that lesser things should be denied you; rather, you should always receive from that source material for advancement from which you are known to have had the beginning of your promotion. Therefore, lest through lack of authority the progress which your mother, namely the most holy Roman Church, requires and expects from you in the overseas regions may be hindered, we personally grant you by the authority of these presents [Col. 0670B] that you may confer, according to the form of the Church, the benefit of absolution upon all whom zeal for the Christian faith has brought to those regions, or who reside there, however or by whomever they have been bound by sentence of excommunication; provided that you first receive from them suitable security concerning the matters for which they are held excommunicated, that they shall make fitting satisfaction.

Provided, however, that when they happen to cross to the regions on this side of the sea, they are bound to approach the Apostolic See with testimonial letters from you, there to receive our command in this matter. Care shall be taken that nothing may be obtained from you by cunning fraud to the prejudice of another; for we wish some to be aided in such a way that others are not harmed. Therefore let no one, etc.

[Col. 0670C] Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

CIII. [Note: [Col. 0670D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 27.] TO THE SAME. That clerics crossing the sea with him may receive the revenues of their prebends for three years. (Fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

If you are sent to remote regions so that, through the diligence of your proven worth, the people of the faithful may increase in merit and number, it is necessary that you obtain from the Apostolic See assistance by which the purpose of your honourable undertaking may be advanced to better effect. Since, therefore, you must have an honourable and suitable company of clerics, who ought to share alike in your labour and reward, we grant by the authority of these presents to all clerics who are to cross with you [Col. 0670D] that they may receive the income of their prebends for up to three years, or assign it in pledge to whomsoever they wish.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

CIV. [Note: [Col. 0671D] Fragments of this letter are found among the *Decretals*, book I, title 6, *On Election and the Authority of the Elect*, chapter 25. The passages read there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied. See letter V of this eighth book.] TO THE CONVENT OF WINCHESTER AND TO THE ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL THE CLERGY OF THE DIOCESE OF WINCHESTER. He confirms the election of the precentor of Lincoln as bishop of Winchester. [Note: [Col. 0671D] This concerns the election of Peter des Roches, archdeacon of Poitiers and precentor of Lincoln. See the *Annals of the Church of Winchester*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 305. Elected in 1205, he was consecrated at Rome on the Sunday immediately before the feast of Saint Michael, though only after liberal dispensations had been granted there, as Westminster records. A man endowed with great prudence, and of such influence with King Henry III that in those times no one was more prudent. He died in 1238, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, according to Matthew Paris. See also Goswin, *On the Prelates of England*, p. 217.] (Eleventh day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0671A]

[When the Church of Winchester was vacant of a pastor, the archdeacons [Note: [Col. 0672D] The *Decretals* read “the archdeacon,” and shortly afterward “but” in place of “for.”] with their supporters elected the dean of Salisbury, whereas the prior and his associates elected … the precentor of Lincoln as bishop.]

When the parties came into our presence on this account, since they differed not a little concerning the sequence of events, we caused witnesses to be received from both sides and their depositions to be published. Having carefully understood these, after sufficient arguments had been made by each side, we deliberated diligently with our brethren concerning the sentence to be given. We found that each election had been undertaken contrary to canonical form; and, to say nothing of the conspiracies, appeals, and excommunications, we found that the first had been made by disorderly presumption, the second by violent pressure. Therefore, proceeding by the royal road, we judged that justice required each election to be annulled by sentence.

After some days, however, the party which had elected the precentor of Lincoln came into our presence and produced an instrument under the seal of the chapter. It expressly stated that the convent of Winchester had entrusted its authority to the prior and certain [Col. 0671C] brethren concerning the election of a bishop to be celebrated in our presence, and had conferred upon them full and free power to elect a bishop for themselves. They therefore humbly petitioned us for permission to elect. We caused the instrument to be shown to the other party; and, when it had been approved by all, we asked whether these men wished to elect together with the others or rather without them. Having taken counsel, they replied that, saving the objections which they had against the others, they wished to celebrate a unanimous election with them.

[Although all had deliberated together concerning making an election, because they could not agree, they had recourse to us with the matter unfinished. And these, indeed, [Col. 0671D] [Note: [Col. 0672D] Here the *Decretals* add “who had elected the precentor,” and below read that those who elected the dean “were,” etc.] firmly asserted that the others were deprived of the power of election, chiefly because they had knowingly presumed to elect a man not legitimately born. Therefore, according to the statute of the Lateran Council, they had lost on this occasion the power to elect and were to be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices for three years; and they humbly petitioned us to make an interlocutory ruling on this matter. [Note: [Col. 0672D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*.] The others replied that, although the man whom they had elected had been less legitimately born, he had nevertheless deserved to be legitimated by grace of the Apostolic See, and they asserted that they would lawfully prove this.

We, therefore, considering that after the first election these men had admitted the others to celebrate the second, and that the decree of the aforesaid council ordains that such presumptuous persons are deprived of the power of election only once, judged that they should be admitted to elect, because the election which they wished to celebrate in our presence was not now the second but the third;] provided that [Col. 0672B] the procurator of the archdeacons should be present without prejudice to the monks.

When they had again assembled in one place to deliberate jointly concerning the election to be made, they nevertheless could not agree unanimously upon one vote, although both parties agreed in this: that unless an election were celebrated before us, irreparable harm threatened the Church of Winchester. But through the action of Him who made both one, they at last returned to unanimous agreement, electing the aforesaid precentor by equal consent as their bishop.

We, however, wishing to provide both for our honour and for ecclesiastical liberty, decreed that that election should not be confirmed until they had publicly sworn in our consistory that they were bound by no obligation and induced by no compulsion to celebrate such an election. When the oaths had thus been received, we examined both the election and the elect. By letters of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Tours, and of many others, it had been fully established to us and our brethren that his ordination was canonical and his birth legitimate. Moreover, our dearest son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of England—toward whom we willingly show, so far as honour permits, all possible deference—had given his assent, as became known to us from his letters patent. Since all other matters concurred regularly, and since no delay or difficulty should be introduced into rightful dispositions, lest the Lord’s flock lack a pastor’s care for long, we judged that the election itself should be confirmed, by common counsel of our brethren.

Accordingly, we command your whole body by apostolic letters that you render him, [Col. 0673A] as your pastor, due obedience and reverence, humbly and devoutly obeying his salutary admonitions and commands.

Given … on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year.

CV. TO THE … BISHOP OF VITERBO [Note: [Col. 0673D] See letter 93 of the fifth book, note.] AND THE … BISHOP OF ORVIETO. [Note: [Col. 0673D] See letter 18 of this eighth book, note.] That they exercise the authority granted them against the Patarenes, go to Viterbo, and remove the elected consuls from office. (Sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

Since ravening wolves who came in sheep’s clothing, brother bishop of Viterbo, have not only snatched away and cruelly occupied your pastures but have also stolen almost [Col. 0673B] all the sheep feeding there—slaughtering some of them to sate the insatiable gluttony of their voracity, exposing others as food to the birds of heaven, and leaving others half alive and torn by wolfish bites—it is incumbent upon you, by reason of the pastoral office you have undertaken, to keep the watches of the night. You must watch not only over what remains, that it may not perish or be stolen, but must diligently seek the lost sheep until you find them; when found, you must recall them to the folds and carry them upon your shoulders, confronting the wolves’ rapacity with strength and courage.

If they have assumed such audacity that they can be neither frightened nor driven away by the barking of dogs or by a staff, you must oppose yourself to them in person, not fearing to lay down your life for your sheep, in imitation of the true Shepherd. Otherwise, if you yield to the enemy or flee after leaving the sheep behind, you will deservedly be considered a hireling seeking milk and wool rather than a shepherd, and will be likened to the barren fig tree, against which the avenging axe threatens destruction.

But you, brother bishop of Orvieto, ought not to look on from afar with dry eyes at your brother’s distress. You are bound to suffer with your neighbour who suffers and to lay down your life for your brethren, as God himself laid down his life for us. Rise, therefore, to his assistance and hasten to their aid, bearing one another’s burdens, so that, joined by the bond of charity, there may be in you a true brotherhood which no conflict can violate.

Since, then, we have chosen you two for this ministry, that you may fight against the beasts of the desert which, like locusts, have filled the face of the earth, put on the armour of God, that you may stand securely against the snares and assaults of the enemy. Gird yourselves with the belt of righteousness, fortify yourselves with the shield of faith, take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Therefore we command your whole body, by apostolic letters and under strict injunction, that, coming in person to Viterbo, you strengthen the faithful there alike by the word of God and by teaching, induce and vigorously encourage them [Col. 0674A] to expel the Patarenes, and strictly command the people of Viterbo, under the obligation of fidelity by which they are bound to us and under penalty of excommunication, that they exert themselves and labour by every means to expel from the dominion which they have rashly usurped those excommunicated persons and believers in the Patarenes who, after our prohibition, were elected consuls by their fellow excommunicates and fellow believers, and J. Tiniosi, son of perdition, elected chamberlain. Let them proceed against these men and against the Patarenes and their believers, supporters, and defenders, in accordance with your command and as has been enjoined upon them by our other letters.

Otherwise, let them know that we have firmly commanded all our faithful established in the neighbouring cities and castles that, unless the said Viterbans take care to fulfil these things within fifteen days, they are thereafter to wage open war against them at your command. Publicly announce that those elected persons are excommunicated and deposed; declare them outlaws on our behalf, together with their accomplices and supporters.

Furthermore, because D. Delicate and J. Marchisan, judges, and M. Macarutii and R., notaries, refused to understand so as to do rightly, but rashly joined themselves to the aforesaid elected persons and, after we suspended them from office, did not turn from their evil way but stretched out their hands further to iniquity, publicly announce that they are permanently deposed from office and infamous, unless within fifteen [Col. 0674C] days they make suitable satisfaction at our command.

But since it is now fitting that you be sifted as wheat, take careful care that no fear may weaken or chill your faith, so that you may worthily and laudably execute the command imposed upon you. Since fear is not in charity, let perfect charity cast fear out from you, fearing only Him who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

CVI. [Note: [Col. 0673D]

Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1205, § 59. Angelus Manrique printed almost the whole of it, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 425, under the year 1204, ch. 4, § 10. The passages found there are enclosed here in brackets.

See also letter 78 of the seventh book and the annotations there.]

TO THE … ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE. He commands him to present himself before the Apostolic See and clear himself of the charges brought against him. (Sixth day before the Kalends of July.)

Since our legates were diligently investigating the truth concerning the matters reported to us against you, you, as we have learned, appealed to our hearing in order to evade canonical discipline. They, preferring to defer to the appeal rather than hasten to sentence, sent us under their seals the inquiry which had been faithfully conducted, so that a judgment of equity might proceed from our presence.

We waited and waited to see whether perhaps you would come in person, or at least send a suitable advocate to pursue the appeal you had lodged; but you took care to do neither. For although you sent a certain messenger to us, you sent him not to prosecute the appeal but to excuse your delay. Hence, had we wished to follow the strictness of the law, we could indeed have exercised canonical censure upon you according to the findings of the inquiry.

But, in order to remove from you every possible ground for complaint, we grant, of gratuitous kindness, that you present yourself personally before us by the coming Septuagesima, to defend yourself and receive a just sentence. If, because of the hindrance of illness, the infirmity of age, or some other just cause, you cannot come in person, after you have given us proof of the just impediment, we shall arrange to delegate the matter itself, under a specified form, to discreet men for examination and decision, before whom you may set forth your reasons, so that you do not undergo judgment undefended.]

We therefore admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters that, recognizing the favour granted you, you strive to watch more diligently than usual over the flock entrusted to you, and make yourself commendable both in life and teaching. Thus, when you have advanced by word and example, your subsequent diligence may seem to repair your preceding negligence.

[We also repeat more strictly the command which we remember having given you concerning relinquishing the abbey of Montaragón, lest, if you preside over both churches, you benefit neither.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year.

CVII. [Note: [Col. 0675D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 55.] TO DUKE ANDREW, GOVERNOR OF THE KINGDOM OF HUNGARY. He explains why he does not grant his requests concerning the bishopric of Bamberg.

So many and so great, so welcome and acceptable, have been the services rendered to the most holy Roman Church by your forebears and predecessors that we wish to show you—whom we believe to have succeeded them in devotion and fidelity—a special favour among the princes of the world, effectively applying ourselves to your honour and advancement. Thus you shall recognize by certain signs and evident proofs [Col. 0675D] how sincerely we love you.

Although we have not yet been able to grant your requests concerning our venerable brother, the bishop of Bamberg, because before the arrival of the solemn messengers whom we continually expect to be sent concerning the imperial affair, it is neither expedient for our honour nor fitting for the dignity of the Church to alter anything concerning his position, since we recognize that this specifically pertains to the imperial affair, nevertheless, when a suitable time is granted, if he endeavours to show himself worthy, we shall gladly admit your requests insofar as we can do so consistently with our honour.

We commend to you the bearer of these presents, your cleric, who, so far as lay in his power, has endeavoured prudently and diligently to conduct the business entrusted to him. We therefore admonish your nobility, earnestly exhorting and commanding you by apostolic letters, that you endeavour to show yourself so devoted to the most holy Roman Church, your mother, that we ought to apply ourselves ever more to your honour and advancement.

Given.

CVIII. [Note: [Col. 0675D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 53.] TO THE … PROVOST, … DEAN, AND CHAPTER OF THE CHURCH OF HALBERSTADT; TO THE PRELATES AND ALL THE CLERGY ESTABLISHED IN THE DIOCESE OF HALBERSTADT; AND TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF THE CHURCH OF HALBERSTADT. He informs them that the bishop of Halberstadt has been absolved from the bond of excommunication and commands them to render him due reverence and honour. (Sixth day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0676B]

When our venerable brother, your bishop, [Note: [Col. 0675D] On the death of Gardolf or Barthold in 1202, Conrad succeeded; he resigned in 1209 and spent the remainder of his life in the monastery of Sittichenbach. BUCELIN, *Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 21.] having fastened the sign of the cross upon his shoulders, visited the overseas regions in the service of Jesus Christ, he repeatedly excused himself concerning the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him by our venerable brother G., archbishop of Reims, [Note: [Col. 0676D] See letter 116 of the seventh book.] cardinal of the Roman Church and then bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See. Yet when he at length learned that we had ratified the excommunication, he obtained at Acre from our beloved sons, S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis, [Note: [Col. 0676D] These have already been mentioned often.] and P., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, [Note: [Col. 0676D] These have already been mentioned often.] [Col. 0676C] legates of the Apostolic See, the benefit of absolution, after bodily swearing that he would obey our commands.

When, on his return, he came to us, and we had heard his excuses diligently and kindly, we caused him to be absolved as a precaution. Since nothing was advanced in our presence against him, we send him back with our favour, released from the bond of excommunication.

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole body, commanding you by apostolic letters that, rendering him due reverence and honour, you take care to persevere with him in devotion to the holy Roman Church, your mother, so that our favour toward you and him may deservedly proceed [Col. 0676D] and increase.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

CIX. TO THE … PROVOST OF WÜRZBURG, THE … PROVOST OF HUSDORP, AND THE … DEAN OF SAINT MARY’S AT HERFORD, IN THE DIOCESE OF MAINZ. That they ensure that Master Martin enjoys peaceful possession of the prebend conferred upon him in the Church of Minden by the Apostolic See. (On the Ides of June.)

When the beloved son L., procurator of our venerable brother, the bishop of Meissen [Note: On the bishops of Meissen, Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 33, gives nothing beyond their names, without any chronological indication.], on the one side, and . . . , provost of Wurzen, Bercer, Ulrich, Master Nicholas, Master Albert, and Albert, procurator of certain canons of Meissen, on the other, had come to the Apostolic See, we granted them as auditor the beloved son L., cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross [Note: See letter 5 of Book Five, note.]. Before him, while the parties were disputing together, Master Martin, as a canon of the Church of Meissen, opposed the arbitration concerning which they were contending, asserting that it was wholly without force because it had been annulled by judges delegated from the Apostolic See; and because it approved a division of prebends which the Council of Tours condemns; and also because, although he had by no means submitted himself to those arbitrators, they had ruled to his prejudice that the scholastership ought to be taken from him. He therefore pressed more urgently that that arbitration should be declared entirely void.

To this the opposing party replied that Master Martin could not object to the aforesaid arbitration, because, since he was not a canon of Meissen, he ought not be admitted to matters to which canons alone, or others acting in their name, are admitted. For although we seemed to have conferred upon him a canonry of Meissen, yet, since he presumed to deceive us by alleging falsehood and concealing the truth, he must altogether forfeit what he had obtained. He concealed the truth, indeed, because, being sacrilegious and bound by a double sentence of excommunication, he took no care to disclose this to us. He alleged falsehood because, although he possessed the scholastership, from which he could be adequately maintained, he declared that he held no ecclesiastical benefice. Therefore, since the foregoing more clearly shows that he is not a canon, and since he does not appear to be the procurator of the canons, he is in no way to be heard against the arbitration.

And when these matters had been debated for a long time before the aforesaid cardinal, and he had faithfully reported to us what had been put forward by each side, we, considering that the allegations made against the aforesaid Martin were either frivolous or false, decreed that, in order that our favour toward him might attain its full effect without evasions, the prebend itself, being vacant, should be granted to him by apostolic authority; and with our own hand we took care to invest him with it. Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command your discretion that, supported by our authority, you cause the aforesaid master to enjoy full and peaceful possession of that prebend, notwithstanding opponents, etc. But if not all of you, let two of you, etc.

Given on the Ides of June.

CX. TO . . . , ARCHBISHOP [Note: See letter 45 of Book Three, note.], AND TO THE ABBOTS OF . . . SAINT REMIGIUS [Note: The abbot at that time of the former monastery of Saint Remigius at Sens was Fulco, known in documents from 1201 until 1212. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 122.] AND SAINT JOHN AT SENS [Note: William II is known to have governed the abbey of Saint John at Sens from 1203 until 1224. Ibid., col. 197.]. That they are to receive from H., deacon of Sens, the resignation of a certain benefice, notwithstanding that the diocesan bishop had promised that benefice after the said deacon’s death. (The fifth day before the Ides of June.)

[Col. 0678A]

On behalf of the beloved son H., deacon of Sens, it has been brought to our attention that, although he resigned his benefices because, broken by old age, he could no longer serve in them as he ought, he nevertheless retained a certain benefice in the church at Allemanches, in the diocese of Troyes. He would long ago have resigned it for conferment upon a suitable person, had not R., canon of Troyes, who abounds in many benefices, procured that it be promised to himself by the diocesan bishop after the former’s death, and even confirmed. [Note: See letter 11 of Book Three, note.]

The same deacon therefore humbly requested us to order that, upon his free resignation, that benefice be conferred upon a suitable person—excepting only him who, while the deacon was alive, received not merely a promise but even confirmation respecting that benefice. We therefore, assenting to the petition of that deacon, command your discretion by apostolic writings that, if the matter stands thus, you take care to assign the aforesaid benefice, upon his free resignation, to a suitable person, excluding, however, him who, as stated above, presumed not merely to seek but to receive a grant or promise of that benefice while its possessor was still alive, since in this he seems to desire the death of his neighbour, in whose place and benefice he believed that he would succeed. Witnesses . . . no letters contrary to the truth, etc. But if not all . . . you, brother archbishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June.

CXI. TO THE PROVOST . . . , THE DEAN, AND THE SCHOLASTER OF BOURGES, IN THE DIOCESE OF COLOGNE. [Note: Thus it is expressly read in the transcript.] That they are to admonish and induce E. de Hard., and also compel him through ecclesiastical censure, to receive G., his wife, notwithstanding the unlawful oath made by the spouses that henceforth neither should seek the other. (The second day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0678D]

G. . . . , a woman and bearer of the present letter, coming to the Apostolic See, showed us by a suppliant representation that, having contracted marriage in the face of the Church with E. de Hard., in the diocese of Cologne, and having lived with him for a considerable time, disagreement arose between them. Thus, at the prompting of the enemy of the human race, each of them swore bodily that henceforth neither would seek the other.

The man himself, however, assigned as a ground for divorce that he had formerly carnally known the woman’s maternal aunt before taking her as his wife. Yet, although a great many asserted this, proof of it was not made before the Church. When afterward each had entered upon a second marriage, and her second husband had gone the way of all flesh while her first husband was still alive, the said woman caused herself to be enclosed in a strict place in order to do penance. After she had spent six years there in devotion, she heard from certain prudent and religious persons that she could not thus be saved. She therefore came to the Apostolic See, humbly and devoutly requesting that we might grant her salutary counsel.

We therefore, considering that such an oath was unlawful, command your discretion by apostolic writings diligently to admonish and induce the aforesaid man—and, if necessary, compelling him by ecclesiastical coercion, without appeal—to receive the aforesaid woman, after excluding the woman whom he subsequently married. You are afterward to hear and duly decide, without appeal, any question that may arise. But if nothing sufficient is shown against the marriage, and the man, abandoning the secular world, should prefer to enter religious life, grant him permission to do so, so that she too may remain in her intended course as she desires. No letters contrary to the truth, etc. But if not all of you, etc.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of July.

CXII. [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §59.] TO . . . , ARCHBISHOP OF SENS [Note: See letter 45 of Book Three, note.], TO . . . , ABBOT OF SAINT MARIANUS [Note: Bernoaldus, alternatively Bernodalis, elected abbot of Saint Marianus in 1204 from being prior, presided for three years and nine months. *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. II, p. 229. See also *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 475.], AND TO MASTER R. DE CORZON. That they are to investigate and report to the Apostolic See concerning the accusation which O., duke of Burgundy, intended to bring regarding the marriage of one of his female relatives with the count of Nevers, as though they were related to one another in the fourth degree of consanguinity. (The third day before the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0679C]

The beloved son, the nobleman O., duke of Burgundy, [Note: Odo III, who began to govern the duchy of Burgundy in 1190; however, he was not styled duke until 1193, after the death of his father Hugh III. He died in 1218. *Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. II, p. 504.] informed us that grave scandal has arisen in the Gallican Church because the beloved son, the nobleman . . . , count of Nevers, has in fact, though he could not lawfully do so, contracted a marital union with his female relative, whom he touches in the fourth degree. [Note: The count of Nevers at that time was Hervé de Gien, who around 1200 married Mahilde, or Mahaut, daughter of Peter de Courtenay and countess of Nevers; he retained her until 1223, the year of his death. See *Historiae Antissiodorenses*, vol. II, p. 126 ff.; see also *Art de vérifier les dates*, cited above, p. 565. Those more expert in genealogy may determine how Hervé de Gien could have been said to be related to Mahilde in the fourth degree of consanguinity.]

The same duke, wishing to provide for the salvation of his soul, as prudent men have advised him and as has been imposed upon him for the remission of sins, is prepared to accuse so incestuous a marriage, since the woman herself is his blood relative. He humbly and devoutly requests that we may see fit to appoint judges for this matter. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that, if you judge such an accusation legally admissible, you hear the cause and, if the parties consent, bring it to a canonical conclusion without the obstacle of appeal. Otherwise, write down all the proceedings under the attestation of your letters and faithfully transmit them to us, setting the parties a suitable term within which they are to appear before us to receive justice. But if not all of you can carry this out . . . you, brother archbishop, with one of the others, shall nonetheless carry it out.

Given . . . on the third day before the Nones of June, in the eighth year.

CXIII. [Note: Raynaldus published this letter under the year 1205, §58. It is therefore printed here in brackets.] TO THE QUEEN OF FRANCE. He consoles her in her grief by letter and embassy. (At Saint Peter’s, the third day before the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0680B]

[He who knows all things, and is ignorant of nothing, knows that in the matter of your marriage we have done for you everything that a man could do; but, because sins demand it, we have made little progress. For the mind of our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks, cannot in any way be inclined to show you marital affection; nor can we inspire love in his heart, since God alone can do this, for the heart of the king is in His hand.

The king himself therefore believes, and many others likewise suppose, that he is perpetually hindered by sorcery. Hence he seeks separation from you not only on account of affinity, but also on account of sorcery. Although we do not wish to fail you—indeed, so far as we can with God, we always desire to support you—yet we cannot change God’s ordinance. Nor is it expedient that you and the king himself should remain longer in this wretched condition. We are therefore sending to you our beloved son, Master P., our chaplain, a prudent and faithful man, to offer you the consolation of our visit and carefully to ascertain your mind. Safely disclose to him your will, so that he may faithfully make it known to us; once it is known, we may be able to provide for you more suitably.]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of July.

CXIV. TO . . . , ARCHBISHOP OF ARMAGH [Note: Concerning the archbishop of Armagh, see the notes on letter 183 of Book Five.], THE BISHOP OF DOWN, AND . . . , ABBOT OF INCH, IN THE DIOCESE OF DOWN. That, if H. de Lacy has unjustly made war against John de Courcy, they are to cause him to restore what he has occupied. (The Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0681A]

As the statement submitted to us by the beloved son J. de Courcy [Note: Numerous charters of donations issued by John de Courcy around the year 1187 for the benefit of the monastery of Down are found in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 1020.] declared, he has recently experienced in his own person that the deceptive pleasantness of this life scarcely, if ever, remains in the same condition; and the more confidently a person clings to it, the more readily he falls with what is falling.

For while he enjoyed peaceful security and had placed considerable hope in certain members of his household and retainers, the nobleman H. de Lacy, entering his land with a large army on the advice of those whom he believed faithful, made war against him. When his own men failed in the encounter, although he himself with a few had for some time resisted so great a multitude, he was at length seized by his enemies and consigned to a prison cell.

Seeing that the danger of death threatened him, he escaped through the mediation of certain religious persons between them, but on these terms: that, renouncing the whole land of Ireland and every right of claim, he should surrender to the said H. de Lacy his fortifications, homages, and every authentic document regarding that land, whether obtained from the Apostolic See or from others; that, fastening the sign of the cross upon his shoulders, he should depart as a pilgrim for the land of Jerusalem; and that he should never return to Ireland.
