The said condition was made yet more burdensome because the aforesaid H. would not permit him to leave the country unless you, brother archbishop, and certain of your suffragans who were there with you in those regions, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against those who should violate the agreements made between them or in any way act contrary to them. The same H. immediately swore that, as soon as J. restored to him the fortifications, castles, and authentic writings, he would release him without delay, together with his two nephews whom he held captive in chains; that he would utterly disinherit no one to whom J. had granted a fief from his land; and that he would even freely allow him to take away with him his arms and chattels.

After H. had sworn such an oath, J. in turn swore that he would leave the whole land and all that he possessed in Ireland, adding another oath to the former: namely, that unless the aforesaid H. faithfully observed what he had sworn, J. would not be bound to him in any respect, but would, to the best of his power, procure his loss and damage.

But since the same H., despising the sanctity of his oath, still detains J.’s nephews and has not taken care to restore his arms and chattels, J. urgently requested absolution from the oath extorted from him through fear of death—especially since faith need not be kept with one who neglects to keep it with others.

Therefore, since by the Lord’s disposition we are placed in that position in which, according to the prophetic word, we ought “to loose the bonds of wickedness, undo the burdens that oppress, let the broken go free, and break every yoke,” we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, if it is established to you that the aforesaid H. unjustly made war against him, you diligently admonish and induce that H. to restore without delay to the complainant both his land and all other things occupied by such violence, wholly absolving J. from the oath sworn to H.

If H. should perhaps refuse to heed your admonitions, then, provided that the foregoing rests upon truth, compel him to this, subjecting his person to a sentence of excommunication and his land to a sentence of interdict, all objection and appeal being removed. The oath which J. says he last made does not bind him who made it, if it was made with the consent of both, while he to whom it was made neglects to keep what he promised. But if not all of you, let two of you, etc.

Given on the Kalends of July.

CXV. TO R., FORMER BISHOP OF TOULOUSE. [Note: Raimund de Rabastens, formerly archdeacon of Agen, was elected bishop of Toulouse about 1202. For his election and subsequently, in this year 1205, his deposition—or rather, as it should be termed from this letter of Innocent, his resignation—see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 21.

The following Decretal Letters should also be compared: Book I, title 6, “On Election and the Power of the Elect,” chapter 26, addressed to the abbot of Cîteaux and R. and P., monks of Fontfroide; and there, chapter 29, to the bishop of Comminges and the abbots of Grandselve and Belleperche; also the letter of John, bishop of Limoges, and the accompanying material in Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. III, new edition, p. 91.]

He grants that, although he has resigned administration of the Church of Toulouse, he may exercise episcopal functions, without prejudice to another. (The third day before the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0682C]

Since, at our counsel, you have resigned the administration of the Church of Toulouse, we, wishing to provide for your honour, grant you by the authority of the present letter that, on solemn feasts or when invited by ecclesiastical persons, you may exercise episcopal office without prejudice to another, provided that you conduct yourself in such a way that your life accords with your rank.

Moreover, lest you be compelled, to the disgrace of your order, to beg, we ordain that you receive annually thirty pounds of Toulouse currency from episcopal property for your support; provided that, diligently devoted to prayer, you apply yourself to works of piety, which, according to the Apostle, possess the promise of the life which now is and also of that which is to come. Therefore let no one . . . violate this grant and ordinance, etc. If anyone, etc.

Given on the third day before the Nones of July.

CXVI. [Note: This letter is found, though incomplete in some copies, among the Decretals, Book I, title 6, “On Election and the Power of the Elect,” chapter 26; it is therefore printed here in brackets. Variant readings are supplied.

The same letter is printed by Angelus Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, vol. III, p. 446, under the year 1205, chapter 3, §2. There it is worthwhile to consult his discussion of the election and deposition of Raymond, bishop of Toulouse.] TO . . . , ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX [Note: These persons have already been mentioned frequently.], AND TO R. AND P., MONKS OF FONTFROIDE, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That they are to remove Mascaron from the provostship of Toulouse. [Note: This letter should certainly be compared with the notes on the immediately preceding letter, no. 105, but especially with the material in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 77, where they expressly assert that Mascaron, provost of Toulouse, is still mentioned in documents as late as 1216.] (The second day before the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0683A]

[From the inquiry which you made at our command concerning the condition of the bishopric and bishop of Toulouse, we have clearly learned that Mascaro, the cellarer, [Note: Thus in the Vatican transcript; in the Decretals, “chancellor,” and shortly afterward only the initial “R.” is read for Raymond.] declared on oath that he knew for certain that Raymond, formerly bishop of Toulouse, [Note: See the immediately preceding letter, no. 115.] and Raymond’s friends had, before his election, held a meeting with certain expressly named canons and had solicited them by entreaties to elect him bishop. He further declared that he himself had both seen and heard the aforesaid bishop, while in the house of Saint Peter de Coquinis, [Note: These words are omitted in the Decretal text.] acknowledge in the presence of certain canons that he had sworn an oath in the house of Atto de Montibus to those canons who had opposed his first election. [Note: The Decretal text reads *jurasse* (“had sworn”) in place of “had taken an oath in the house of Atto de Montibus”; shortly afterward it reads *praestitum* (“rendered”) in place of *factum* (“done”).] He believed certainly that this oath was unlawful and had been made in order that Raymond might be elected by agreement; and that, after Raymond’s first election had been annulled, he himself held the episcopal residence in Raymond’s name, receiving certain revenues and proceeds which, with Raymond’s knowledge and consent, he expended on Raymond’s affairs.

Since therefore, by knowingly electing such a man bishop, as he confirmed by his oath, he has rendered himself unworthy of ecclesiastical benefices, we take it gravely and painfully that Mascaron is said to have been substituted as provost for the beloved son . . . , provost of Toulouse, [Note: His name was Sparagus. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* agree: in the passage cited they state that Sparagus, elected provost in 1201, is still found in 1204, was bishop of Comminges in the following year, was subsequently transferred to the church of Tarragona, and died on 16 March 1232, according to the necrology of Toulouse.] who had been elected bishop of Comminges. [Note: Compare the statements in the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 1096, concerning the uncertain year of death of Raimund Arnald, bishop of Comminges, to whom Sparagus, provost of Toulouse, was appointed successor.] [Note: The Decretal text reads “is said” instead of “is asserted.”]

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that, entirely removing the same Mascaron from the office of provost, you cause a suitable man to be appointed to that office. Notwithstanding opponents, etc. But if not all . . . let two of you, etc.]

Given . . . on the second day before the Nones of July, in the eighth year.

CXVII. TO BERTRAND, BISHOP OF AGEN, [Note: This letter should certainly be noted and compared with the statements of the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 912, concerning the uncertain year of death of Bertrand de Beceiras, first bishop of Agen. This letter of Innocent, supported by chronological indications of unquestionable authority, proves beyond all doubt that Bertrand lived at least until 1205. Accordingly, the notices of his death—whether in the Bordeaux necrology, “On the second day before the Nones of August died Bertrand, bishop of Agen, canon of this church,” or in the obituary of La Sauve-Majeure, “On the fourth day before the Nones of May”—must be understood as referring to the year 1206. William II, Peter, and John, whom some wished to place in the chronological succession of bishops of Agen around 1203, 1204, and 1205, must therefore be removed, since the monuments prove that Bertrand governed the Church of Agen continuously from at least 1187 until 1206.] AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. He receives him under the protection of blessed Peter and confirms privileges granted to him by the king of England. (At Rome, the second day before the Kalends of July.)

Both the order of reason demands it, and consideration of ecclesiastical advantage invites us, to love our brothers and fellow bishops with more abundant charity and to strengthen more generously, by the protection of the Apostolic See, the churches entrusted to their government, so that, in carrying out the office they have undertaken, they may always be more vigilant as they see themselves remaining more secure against the attacks of the wicked.

Therefore, etc., as far as “we grant,” and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Urban II, Paschal, Eugenius, Alexander, and Urban III, Roman pontiffs, we fortify under the protection of blessed Peter, etc., as far as “we fortify,” the church of Agen of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, over which, by God’s authorisation, you are known to preside. We ordain that the rule of canonical religious life, established by your predecessor Simon of good memory, through God’s grace, in that church and in the church of the blessed martyr Caprasius, and confirmed by apostolic authority by the aforesaid predecessor of ours, Urban II, be observed inviolably in those churches for all time; and that thereafter no one be made or ordained canon in them unless he has professed that he will live according to the canonical rule.

We also forbid by apostolic authority that a prior or any minister having the administration belonging to the community of brothers be appointed in those churches except one elected by the common consent of the bishop and the brothers living according to the canonical rule. We further decree that the churches, lands, and all things belonging to the community of brothers of both churches be administered by regular canons, according as the bishop shall make the better arrangement with them; and that those professed under the rule be provided for in all necessities.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church of Saint Stephen presently possesses, etc., as far as “may remain secure and unimpaired to you, your successors, and the religious brothers serving God in that church.” Among these, etc., as far as the following names: the church of Saint Colonius, with the chapel of Saint Stephen situated near the castle of Bugd., together with the borough and that part of the castle belonging to the parish of Agen; the church of Saint Mary of Courte; the church of Saint Saturninus of Monac, with all their appurtenances and with the chapel within the castle of Pennesitis; the hospital house, with its chapel and all appurtenances, namely that which was built near the city of Agen by the knight Jordan and given to that church; the church of Saint Peter of Condat with its appurtenances; the chapel of Fumet; the church of Saint Bartholomew of Pertica; the church of Saint Mary of Loires; the chapel of Saint Mary of Biron; the church of Saint Mary of Castelmoron; the church of Pujons and the church of Albaterra; the church of Saint Victoria of Clermont; the chapel of Saint Mary in the borough of the same castle; the church of Saint Hilary of Dombesca; and whatever right Simon and the other bishops of Agen are known hitherto to have held in the church of Saint Vincent of Furgat.

Further, after the example of those same predecessors of ours, we confirm the cemetery of the same church of Saint Stephen and the deanery, with all the goods which Unaldus, who had been viscount, is known to have left for the restoration of that see as he was making his way to the monastery. No one whatsoever may claim the deanery itself or goods belonging to it by hereditary right—God forbid.

We decree that the market customarily held before the aforesaid church of Saint Stephen shall continue to be held there in future and shall not be removed through anyone’s rivalry, saving the good customs of the church of Saint Caprasius; likewise, the fief of Marconis, with the churches called Francae; namely, that portion of the diocese of Agen which was canonically restored to the same Church at the Council of Bordeaux before the legates of the Apostolic See, Amatus, then bishop of Oloron, and Hugh, then bishop of Digne; the church of Saint Hilary of Agen; the church of Linarols, recovered from lay hands by Raymond, your predecessor; the church of Orzana, with its entire parish—that is, the fourth parts of tithes and the revenues called *Guazii* of the castle of Mont Caplis, both in grain and in money—as the aforesaid Simon, founder of the religious rule, acquired for the sustenance of the regular canons throughout the lands of the bishopric of Agen, and as he is known to have canonically possessed that church for sixty years and more until now; moreover, the comital rights and the mint; also the church of Canu, with its tithes, first-fruits, and lands; likewise the tithes of Sainte-Foy and Serinac, which, through your care and diligence, you possess free from lay hands and exempt from every exaction.

We strictly forbid any of your successors to alienate from the episcopal table or rashly divert to other uses the mill-dues of Agen, together with their *eminae* and revenues, which R., king of England of illustrious memory, while count of Poitou, generously granted you as alms and which you assigned permanently to the episcopal table.

We further forbid anyone, without suitable satisfaction, to presume to admit persons whom you have placed under interdict or excommunicated to ecclesiastical office or communion, except perhaps where danger of death is imminent, so that, if they cannot have access to your presence, one bound may have to be absolved by another according to the form of the Church after satisfaction has first been made.

In addition, we decree by the present enactment that the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to your church by kings, princes, and other persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, and its ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed, shall remain whole and unimpaired. We also confirm by apostolic authority the comital rights and mint, as they were granted, out of piety, to you and your successors by the aforesaid R., king of England, then count of Poitou. We likewise judge it right to confirm the burial of bishops of your church who may be in office from time to time, unless they choose in their last will to be buried elsewhere. On your death, etc., as far as “they shall provide for the election according to the fear of God and canonical institution.”

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may be permitted to injure the aforesaid Church, etc., as far as “for its benefit,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of J., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, on the second day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1205 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CXVIII. TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF TRANI, [Note: See letter 69 of Book Five, note.] LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He confirms a dispensation granted to Bartholomew, a deacon uncertain whether he had received the lower orders, and orders that the minor orders be conferred upon him as a precaution. (On the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0686D]

Bartholomew, a poor deacon and bearer of the present letter, appearing before us, humbly informed us that, when he was ordained deacon, he was so young that he does not know whether he had received the lower orders. But when he at length reached years of discretion, since his conscience troubled him about this, he disclosed his ignorance to you. You suspended him from office for half a year and afterward dispensed with him; and the same deacon humbly requested us to confirm that dispensation.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that, if this is so, you cause such dispensation to be firmly observed, through the mercy that triumphs over judgment, conferring the minor orders upon him as a precaution; for that is not said to be repeated which is unknown to have been done.

Given on the Nones of July.

CXIX. [Note: This letter is included in full in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §XCVI, and is therefore printed here in brackets.

Raynaldus reproduced the greater part of it under the year 1205, §30. Passages occurring in his text are here distinguished by a double stroke in the margin at the beginning of each line. We have also noted variant readings from the *Deeds*, from Raynaldus, and from manuscript codices, both French and Roman, even though they are of lesser importance, lest anything appear lacking in our diligence.]

LETTER OF LEO, KING OF THE ARMENIANS, TO THE POPE. He informs the pope that peace has been restored between himself and the Templars, together with certain other matters.

“To the most reverend Father in Christ and lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal [Col. 0687B] pope, L. [Note: In the *Gesta*, L.; in Raynaldus it is absent.] by the same grace and by the grace of the R. emperor [Note: That is, of the Roman Church, as is clear from the *Gesta*, § c. In Armenian, no doubt, it read “by the favor of Roman authority,” or something similar; for which the translator wrongly rendered “of the Empire.” In the *Gesta* and also in Raynaldus one reads “of the Roman Empire.”], king of Armenia [Note: In the *Gesta*, “of the Armenians”; in Raynaldus [Col. 0688D], “Armenian.”], devoted and obedient to his holiness, greetings, grateful service, and kisses of the feet.

Since it is evident that you, most renowned father and lord, most worthily bear, by the Lord’s gift, the care and primacy of the whole holy Church and of the Christian religion, it is certainly fitting that we should have recourse to your refuge as to the safest shelter, upon which, after God, our whole hope and confidence depend, and should seek help from your blessedness in our necessities. Therefore, most merciful Father and lord, fleeing to the feet of your holiness, with bended knees and every supplication, we complain, and do not cease to complain, concerning lord P. [Col. 0687C] [Note: The *Gesta* reads “Peter,” and below adds after “Tripolitan”: “who.”], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, your legate, suspect in our affairs—indeed, an open adversary.

For when he had come, as was thought, into the parts of our kingdom, both on account of the legation entrusted to him and in order to restore peace between our nephew and the count of Tripoli, who was usurping the principality of Antioch, contrary to justice and to our appeal made to an apostolic hearing [Note: The *Gesta* has “had usurped,” and immediately afterward adds “lord John.”], the lord Catholicos, our venerable father in Christ, together with certain of his suffragans and clergy, and we, with our faithful barons and many noble pilgrims standing by, received him with all the honor and reverence we could, out of reverence for you.

In the following days, we deliberated concerning the obedience of the Armenian Church [Col. 0687D] to the holy Roman Church, toward which [Col. 0688A] we had long labored, with divine grace assisting; and, at the time of your pontificate, through the merit of your achievements, we brought the Armenian Church [Note: The *Gesta*: “the Church of Armenia”; and shortly afterward it reads “Peter” for P.] to this with much effort—something which our predecessors had been unable to bring about through many preceding ages—as Cardinal P. himself became witness both of this and of the events. The lord Catholicos, with solemn ceremony, rendering obedience and reverence to the holy Roman Church and to you through the hands of that legate, according to the tenor and command of your letters, received with all humility and devotion, before the persons named above, the pallium sent by your blessedness. He promised that, in his rank, every five years, through his messengers, he would visit [Col. 0688B] the holy Roman Church, as mother and teacher of all churches, according to the apostolic capitularies; and that he would attend the transmarine councils, either in person or through his messengers. It was established by both sides that ecclesiastical councils ought not to be held in the transmarine regions in his absence or that of his messenger.

When these matters had been concluded, negotiations began for restoring peace between our nephew and the count of Tripoli. In those negotiations we presented to Cardinal P. the apostolic letters concerning the commission [Note: Raynaldus thinks that *lecta sunt*—“were read”—should be added here, but unnecessarily. Baluze, marginal note on the *Gesta*, p. 74, col. 2.], by which you had delegated to Lords S. [Note: The *Gesta* reads “Soffredus” here and below, just as it reads “Peter” for P.] of the title of Saint Praxedes and P. of the title of Saint Marcellus, priest-cardinals and legates, the task of duly bringing the case in question to its conclusion. We did so in confidence that, according to your command, the matter would be brought by him to the desired conclusion; Cardinal S., who was absent at Acre on business of Christendom, being a lover of equity and justice, as we found him throughout the whole case.

Having presented the apostolic letters, as stated, we entrusted our nephew’s case to him as exercising your authority; and from the beginning of the case we continually appealed to an apostolic hearing and committed the matter to his judgment, with the lord patriarch of Antioch, the Hospitallers, the Templars, and other religious men of Black Mountain [Note: “Concerning the abbeys of Black Mountain, see Odoric Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 38.” Baluze, marginal note on the *Gesta*, p. 74, col. 2. Yet in Raynaldus, at the place cited by Baluze, there is nothing concerning the abbeys of Black Mountain.] as witnesses [Note: The *Gesta*: “of Black Mountain.” Up to this point Raynaldus.].

But Cardinal P., the legate, in whom we hoped to have no suspicion at all—and truly none—entered into a private alliance with the count of Tripoli, the Templars, and the Antiochenes [Col. 0688D], fraudulently undermining [Col. 0689A] our party and supporting the opposing party to our ruin and loss, extending to them the hand of counsel and assistance. Accordingly, by the command of that legate, under whose hope [Note: Thus also in the royal manuscript cited by Baluze in the margin. In the *Gesta*, however, *specie*, “appearance.” Shortly afterward the *Gesta* reads “Antioch” for “Antiochene.”] we had been deceived, we came a second and a third time into the Antiochene territories to restore peace. The count of Tripoli, seeking evasions, never appeared on the appointed day in the case.

When the fraud of the alliance that had been made became known and understood, we regarded Legate P. as suspect—indeed, as an open adversary—and rightly appealed to an apostolic hearing, committing our nephew’s cause to your judgment and entrusting our person, kingdom, and peoples to the protection of God and of you, which we believed we possessed through a privilege granted by your blessedness.

It happened, therefore, on a certain night before Cardinal P.’s arrival, while with our whole army we were asserting our nephew’s inheritance and were harassing the Antiochene territories [Note: The *Gesta* omits this word; below it reads “of the Antiochenes” for “Antiochene,” and “Antioch” for “Antiochenes.”] because justice had failed, that, as it pleased the Lord, we entered within the walls of Antioch by force. Had we wished to extend the hand of our power to the shedding of Christian blood and the burning of that city, Antioch would have been taken. But, moved by piety and fear of God, and compassionating Christendom in its distress, we summoned the lord patriarch of Antioch to us and asked him to be mediator of the desired peace between us and the Antiochenes.

And while peace was being negotiated, behold: the Templars, whom we honored because of your prayers and commands, and to whom [Col. 0689C] we showed deference throughout the war, preserving their possessions and holdings—whom we hoped to have as friends rather than adversaries, as religious men—without any declaration of defiance [Note: The *Gesta*: “distrust.”] against us sharpened their teeth, fortified their towers, brought forth their weapons, shot at our army both within and outside the walls of Antioch, and prepared against us the banner [Note: Cangius considers that it should certainly be read *Baldanum*. *Glossary*, vol. I, col. 952.

Thus also in the royal manuscript cited by Baluze in the margin; the Podian and Fuxian manuscripts, cited by him, read *Baloanum*, whereas the *Gesta* reads *Baldanum*.—“*Baldanum*, a banner. Letter of Livon [read: Leon], king of Armenia, in the *Gesta Innocentii Papae III*, p. 127 (in our edition, p. 74): ‘Without a declaration of defiance against us they sharpened their teeth . . . they shot at our army inside and outside the walls of Antioch; they prepared the banner *Baldanum* against us.’ The royal manuscript has *balsamum*, the Fuxian *baloanum*. The very learned Stephen Baluze advised me to prefer the latter; hence perhaps *baldakinum* should be read.” Thus far Cangius.] *Balzanum*. What is more serious, setting aside their religious order, they shed Christian blood.

Thereafter [Note: This is explicitly read thus in the Conti transcript. We confess that we do not sufficiently understand what these words mean. The *Gesta* has, more correctly, “these.”], united with the count of Tripoli and the Antiochenes [Note: The *Gesta*: “the Antiochene.”], they allied themselves with the faithless sultan of Aleppo. By such machinations they deprived our nephew—an orphaned ward, entrusted to the protection of God and of you—of his acquired inheritance; and thus we received an unlooked-for wound from the enemy. Deeply grieved by this, we seized the possessions and holdings which the Templars held in our kingdom [Note: Thus also in the Vatican manuscript. The Vallicellian manuscript reads *sanxivimus*; the *Gesta*, *saisivimus*.], and expelled them from our land.

After this had happened, Lord Cardinal P., allied with the Templars and seeking to restore peace between us and them, urgently pressed us, first orally and afterward a second and third time through letters and messengers, to restore the things recently taken from the Templars. To this we answered: “For love of the Apostolic See, we are ready to restore to the Templars what was recently taken, provided that they promise in accordance with their order that henceforth they will not oppose, either within or outside the walls of Antioch, the justice and right [Col. 0690B] [Note: The *Gesta*: *recturae*, “right.”] of our nephew, but, as religious men, will remain safe and secure in their houses and possessions.”

Against this the Templars, sustained by the goad of arrogance, maintained that they would always defend the walls of Antioch [Note: The *Gesta* reads “of Antioch,” and shortly afterward “right” for *drictura*; below it omits the word “religious.”] against the justice and right of our nephew, setting aside the obligations of religion. Since no progress could be made toward concord between us and the Templars, Lord Cardinal P., in the absence of the lord Catholicos, our venerable father, held a council at Antioch [Note: The *Gesta*: “and the venerable patriarch of Antioch.”] concerning this same case. After our repeated appeal to an apostolic hearing, he promulgated a sentence of excommunication against our land, excepting the confessions of the sick, baptism, and burial of the dead. Concerning [Col. 0690C] this sentence he sent his letters [Note: The *Gesta*: “his letters together with the sentence.”] to the lord Catholicos of the Armenians, so that, abruptly, a judicial interdict might be promulgated throughout the whole Catholicate. Cardinal S., the legate, took no part in any of these matters [Note: These words are absent from the *Gesta*. Here Raynaldus resumes.].

[Note: “What follows has been added from the *Annals* of Odoric Raynaldus.” Baluze, note in the margin of the *Gesta*, p. 75, col. 1. We print the same on the authority of the Conti transcript.]

Accordingly, when the lord Catholicos and many suffragans of the Catholicate came together, after long consultation they were astonished at so great and sudden a harsh measure imposed upon the Armenian Church in the Catholicos’s absence. Recalling what had been established between Lord Cardinal P. [Note: Raynaldus reads “Peter”; here and below, and shortly afterward, he omits J.] and J., Catholicos of Armenia—namely, that the Catholicos had been absent from the council and that a sentence of interdict had been issued by the cardinal in [Col. 0691A] his diocese [Note: Thus also in Raynaldus. Baluze thinks it should be read “into his diocese.”] without his consent—our fathers decided that this sentence was not binding [Note: Raynaldus: “binding.”] and ought not to be observed [Note: Thus also in Raynaldus; but in his marginal notes he rightly says that “ought” should be added.], saying:

“We who hoped first to suck sweet and pleasant milk from the breasts of our mother now drink bitter and sour gall; we hoped to be watered with life-giving rain, not battered by hailstorms. For, as you well know, he who squeezes too hard draws blood.”

When this came to the knowledge of Lord Cardinal S. [Note: Raynaldus omits this here and below.], the legate, he took it badly; and, after consultation with his colleague Lord P., who had joined him, because we most insistently appealed to your hearing, they endeavored, on Cardinal S.’s counsel, to turn the storm into a breeze. Thus it came about that, by command of the lords cardinals, of the illustrious kings of Jerusalem [Note: Raynaldus omits this.] and Cyprus, and of all the noble pilgrims, in September we sent our messenger, the noble Constantius of Camarderio [Note: Raynaldus: “of Camardresio.”], our beloved kinsman, to Acre, for restoring peace between us and the Antiochenes and Templars. Through the wisdom and discernment of Lord Cardinal S., a lover of law and equity, peace was restored between us and the Templars, as you will be able to learn from his letters.

We, however, have never departed from the commands of the holy Roman Church, nor will we depart while life remains, although Lord Cardinal P. labors to exclude us from it. Therefore we, who by the grace of God and of you [Col. 0691C] have become your new plant during your pontificate, desiring to produce fragrant and pleasant fruits to the honor of God and the holy Roman Church, flee to the feet of your holiness. With bended knees we ask and beseech that you do not entrust our nephew’s cause to the judgment of Lord Cardinal P., the legate, whom we regard as suspect—indeed, as an open adversary [Note: Up to this point Raynaldus.]—and that henceforth he have no authority over us or the inhabitants of our land, of whatever condition they may be, by virtue of the legation entrusted to him.

And command the Templars by apostolic letters not to be adversaries in the Antiochene affair to the justice and right [Note: In the *Gesta*, *directurae*; in the Vallicellian manuscript, *astrictione*, “obligation.”] of our nephew, as neither the Hospitallers nor other [Col. 0691D] religious men are. Entrust our nephew’s case, about which we have repeatedly written to your lordship, not to suspect judges but to such persons as do not turn aside from the straight path, but, with the scales evenly balanced, after hearing both [Col. 0692A] parties and without respect of persons, render a just judgment. Thus may we find that the holy Roman Church has come for the building up, not the uprooting, of your new plant; and through the favor of your assistance may your plant rejoice that it has found pleasant outcomes at morning and evening.”

CXX. [Note: Part of this letter is printed in the *Gesta Innocentii*, § CXVII [Col. 0692D]. What is found there is here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are also supplied.] LETTER SENT BY THE CATHOLICOS OF THE ARMENIANS TO POPE INNOCENT III. On the same subject and on certain other matters.

“To the most reverend Father in Christ and lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope, John, by the same grace humble Catholicos of the Armenians, devoted and obedient to his holiness [Note: In the *Gesta*, “your holiness”; below it likewise reads “your” for “his.”], with due obedience and reverence, fullness of the joys [Col. 0692B] of salvation.

Through the ineffable providence of our Lord, from whom every good proceeds, the Armenian Church, recognizing the primacy and teaching office granted by God to the holy Roman Church, has become its most devoted daughter; and we, though unworthy, its [Note: The *Gesta* omits this.] minister [Note: The *Gesta*: “its ministers,” and shortly afterward reads “Lord Peter.”]. When Lord P., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, your legate, came under the legation entrusted to him into the regions of our Catholicate [Note: The *Gesta* adds here “where,” and below reads “embraces” for “glances.”], we went to meet him, out of reverence for you, with the clergy and flock entrusted to us by God. We received him with all the honor we could; and, sharing mutual glances and conversations, through his hands we rendered obedience and reverence to the holy Roman Church and to you, according to the tenor [Col. 0692C] of your letters.

Receiving with solemn ceremony and all humility the pallium sent by your blessedness, we promised that, in our rank, every five years through our messengers we would visit the holy Roman Church as mother and teacher of all churches, and would attend the transmarine councils. It was established by both sides that ecclesiastical councils ought not to be held in those same regions in our absence or that of our messenger. We received the institutions of the holy Roman Church in part; and in part, because our suffragans were dispersed far and wide and because this could not be done without a serious consultation of persons, we deferred them, proposing that, when our prelates, or the greater part of the prelates [Note: The *Gesta* reads “of them,” and shortly afterward “by assent” for “by consent.”

Raynaldus also cites this letter, under the year 1205, § 32.], had assembled at an appointed time, we would receive, by their consent and lest scandal arise in the Church, those of your institutions with which we agreed.”

Thereafter [Note: This is explicitly read in the Conti transcript. See the note on the immediately preceding Letter 119.]. Before the arrival of Lord Cardinal P., discord arose between our beloved L., illustrious king of Armenia, and the Templars, as you will be able to learn from his letters. We believed that the legate would sincerely devote himself to restoring that peace; but later we learned from reliable reports that he had allied himself with the Templars.

Since nothing could be achieved concerning the said peace, Cardinal P., exercising his authority in our absence, held a council at Antioch. Contrary to the provisions ordained by both sides at the reception of the pallium, he promulgated a sentence of excommunication throughout our whole diocese. He also sent us letters concerning that sentence. When we had them carefully read aloud, and understood that their tenor was steeped in every bitterness [Col. 0693B], we were grieved beyond belief—both because of the good hope and confidence which we had in your protection and because of the earlier examples which we trusted would be offered for our instruction.

Accordingly, after long consultation with our brethren, the archbishops, bishops, and other religious men present, we were greatly astonished at so severe a measure imposed upon the Armenian Church without our consent. Our brethren declared with one voice:

“We who believed that we should first suck sweet and pleasant milk from the breasts of our mother drink bitter gall and vinegar; we trusted that, by maternal kindness, we should advance from good to better by instruction in apostolic teaching and should be watered by life-giving rain, [Col. 0693C] not battered by hailstorms.”

And thus it seemed reasonable to our venerable chapter that the sentence issued in our diocese without our consent ought neither to be promulgated nor observed, until the matter had come to your knowledge through our letters and messengers, especially since the fraudulent alliance between the legate himself and the Templars had been discovered.

At last, through the wisdom and discernment of Lord S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes and legate of the Apostolic See, peace was restored at Acre in September between the beloved son, the most Christian king, and the Templars, as you will be able to learn from the royal letters.

In these matters we humbly beseech your reverend fatherhood not to grant the Templars the arm of presumptuous audacity [Col. 0693D] to the destruction of your new plant. By divine inspiration we have become your clergy, and we are bound with all our strength to watch and labor for your honor and that of the holy Roman Church, our fair mother. Therefore we counsel your reverend fatherhood to restrain the Templars’ arrogance for good, and to endeavor to sow peace, concord, and everlasting friendship between the illustrious king of Armenia, your beloved [Col. 0694A] son in Christ, and the Templars. For there is great cause to fear lest—God forbid!—if discord arises between them, the remnant of Christendom should incur some danger; and may you extend the hand of counsel and assistance to the imperiled ship before it sinks, so that through your care it may reach the harbor of salvation.

[Thus you will find us faithful and devoted executors in carrying out all your commands.]”

CXXI. [Note: This letter is found, though very mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book V, title 6, “On Jews, Saracens, and Their Servants,” chapter 3; it is therefore here enclosed in brackets, and variant readings are supplied.

Raynaldus also cites it under the year 1205, § 57.]

. . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS [Note: See Letter 45 of Book III, note.] AND . . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS [Note: See Letter 11 of Book III, note.]. That they should restrain Jewish insolence. (The Ides of July.)

[Col. 0694B] “[Although Christian piety receives and tolerates the cohabitation of the Jews, whom their own fault subjected to perpetual servitude, because they crucified the Lord whom their prophets foretold would come in the flesh for Israel’s redemption [Note: These words are omitted by the *Decretals*, as are shortly afterward the words distinguished in italics; below, for “should repay,” they read “repay.”], nevertheless, because of their unbelief, even the Saracens—who persecute the Catholic faith and do not believe in him whom the Jews crucified—cannot endure them, but rather expelled them from their territories, crying out vehemently against us because they are tolerated by us, who truly confess as our Redeemer him whom they condemned to the gibbet of the cross.

Yet they ought not to prove ungrateful to us by repaying Christians’ favor with insult and familiarity with contempt. Admitted, as it were, into our merciful intimacy, they render us the return [Col. 0694C] which, according to the common proverb, a mouse in a purse, a serpent in the bosom, and a fire in the lap are accustomed to render their hosts.

We have received reports that the Jews, whom the favor of princes has admitted into their lands, have become so insolent that they commit offenses insulting to the Christian faith which it is wicked not merely to speak, but even to think. For they employ Christian women as nurses for their children [Note: The *Decretals* add: “and which it is wicked not merely to speak, but even to think”; shortly afterward they insert “they cause” after “to pour out.”]; and when, on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, those women happen to receive the body and blood of Jesus Christ, they make them pour their milk into the latrine for three days before nursing the children. They also commit other detestable and unheard-of acts against the Catholic faith, on account of which the faithful must fear that they will incur divine wrath if they allow unpunished deeds that bring disgrace upon our faith.

Accordingly, we have requested our most dear son in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the French [Note: See Letter 186 of Book VII.]; we have also commanded the noblemen . . . duke of Burgundy and . . . countess of Troyes, to repress the Jews’ offenses in such a way that they may not presume to raise, against reverence for [Col. 0695A] the Christian faith, their neck submitted to the yoke of perpetual servitude. We strictly forbid [Note: The *Decretals* have “we therefore forbid” in place of “We have requested . . . forbidding,” and below omit the words which we have distinguished in italics.] them henceforth to have Christian nurses or servants [Note: Philip Augustus expelled the Jews from the territories of France because they were drawing the male and female servants whom they had in their homes away from the true religion to Jewish superstition. Rigord, *Life of Philip*. See also William the Breton, Book I of the *Philippid*.], lest the children of the free woman serve the children of the slave woman; but, as slaves rejected by the Lord, against whose death they wickedly conspired, let them at least recognize themselves through the effect of their deeds as servants of those whom Christ’s death made free, while making them slaves. For, since they have now begun to gnaw like a mouse and sting like a serpent, there is cause to fear that the fire received in the lap may consume it after gnawing it away.

Wherefore, by apostolic writings, we command your brotherhood, with an injunction, to take care diligently to admonish and effectively induce the said king and the others on our behalf, so that the perfidious Jews may by no means henceforth become insolent, but may always, in servile fear, display the shame of [Col. 0695B] their fault and reverence the honor of the Christian faith. But if the Jews do not dismiss their Christian nurses and servants, you, supported by our authority, shall strictly forbid all Christians under penalty of excommunication to dare to engage in any commerce with them.”

Given on the Ides of July.

CXXII. INSTRUMENT. By which William, marquis, son of Marquis Pelavicini, promises that he will obey the pope’s commands. (2 Kalends of April.)

In the name of the Lord. In the year 1205, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction, in the presence [Col. 0695C] of the undersigned witnesses, Lord William, marquis, son of Marquis Pelavicini, swore upon the holy Gospels of God that he would abide by the commands of the Roman Church and of the lord pope, specifically concerning the offense which he had committed against the Roman Church. Before Lord Egidius, bishop of Modena [Note: See Letter XXXII of Book III, note.], and before Lord Radulf, archdeacon of Reggio, to whom the bishop of Reggio [Note: Peter, promoted to the see of Reggio in 1187, died in 1212. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, col. 303.] had entrusted his authority—who had been delegated by the lord pope to receive him—they immediately absolved him after scourging him and admitting him into the church. Thereafter, by obligation of his oath, they commanded him henceforth neither to obstruct nor despoil a messenger of the Roman Curia, nor to lay violent hands upon any cleric, convert, or ecclesiastical person, except in self-defense or if he found someone shamefully cohabiting with his own wife.

Done prosperously beneath the portico of the house of the church of Saint James of Casa Dei. There were then called as witnesses Lord Guidottus, abbot of the monastery of Saint John of Parma; Lord Prosper, abbot of Reggio; Lord Radulf, his monk; Lord Albert, monk of Saint John; Lord Bernard, chaplain of the bishop of Reggio; Lord [Col. 0696A] Andrew of Casa Dei; Marcellus of Curviaco; Raymond Caput de Lupi; Gerard Armanellus and John Confalonerius, both of Piacenza; Gerard of Saint Mark; Hugh Punse Collus, servant of the abbot of Saint John; Odolinus; Nicholas; and many others who were called as witnesses to this act. I, Bernardus Laurentiorum, notary of the Sacred Palace, was present and, having been asked, wrote this charter.

CXXIII. INSTRUMENT. By which the same marquis, in order to obtain absolution, conveys the castle of Landasia to the bishop of Modena in absolute ownership, and receives investiture of it. (11 Kalends of April.)

In the name of the Lord. In the year 1205, [Col. 0696B] on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction, in the presence of the undersigned witnesses, Lord William, marquis, son of Marquis Pelavicini, gave and delivered in absolute ownership a certain castle called Landasia to Lord Egidius, bishop of Modena, and Lord Radulf, archdeacon of Reggio, to whom the bishop of Reggio had entrusted his authority regarding the granting of absolution from anathema to the said William, in the name of the Roman Church and of the lord pope. That is, Egidius, bishop of Modena, and Radulf, archdeacon of Reggio, acting in the place and name of the lord pope, immediately honorably invested the said William with the aforesaid castle as a fief.

There also the said William swore fealty to the Roman Church [Col. 0696C] and the lord pope against all persons, saving nevertheless the fealty owed to his former lords. Done prosperously beneath the portico of the house of the church of Saint James of Casa Dei. The witnesses called there were Lord Guidottus, abbot of the monastery of Saint John of Parma; Lord Prosper, abbot of Reggio; Lord Radulf, his monk; Lord Albert, monk of Saint John; Lord Bernard, chaplain of the bishop of Reggio; Lord Andrew of Casa Dei; Marcellus of Curviaco; Raymond Caput de Lupi; Gerard Armanellus and John Confalonerius, both of Piacenza; Gerard of Saint Mark; Hugh Punse Collus, servant of the abbot of Saint John; Odolinus; Nicholas; and many others called as witnesses to this act. I, Bernardus Laurentiorum, [Col. 0696D] notary of the Sacred Palace, was present and, having been asked, wrote this charter.

CXXIV. TO THE BISHOPS OF MODENA [Note: See notes to Letter 122 of this eighth book.] AND REGGIO. He orders that what they had done in absolving William Pelavicini be held valid [Note: See the immediately preceding Letter 123.]. (13 Kalends of August.)

Your brotherhood does not fail to know how seriously the nobleman William, son of Pelavicini, offended [Col. 0697A] not so much the Roman Church as the divine majesty, by despoiling our beloved son P. [Note: This man has already frequently been discussed.], now priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, then deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See, while he was returning from Poland to the presence of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory. For this has been publicly reported not only throughout Lombardy but also in other parts of the world.

Therefore, before that cardinal reached the Apostolic See, after our aforesaid predecessor had died and we had been installed in the office of the apostolate, we were greatly moved by so serious an offense. We took care to exercise the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline not only upon the perpetrator of so great a crime but also upon his accomplices, so that full satisfaction was made for all things taken, both to the cardinal himself and to his people.

But because we considered the injury greater than the loss, we did not deem William immediately fit to be absolved. Instead, we ordered him to be more strictly shunned by everyone as excommunicated, and his land to be placed under ecclesiastical interdict, until he made suitable satisfaction for the injuries inflicted. At last, pierced by divine inspiration, he humbly acknowledged his offense and, promising full satisfaction, implored the grace of absolution. Accordingly, following the example of him who wills not the death of the sinner but that he be converted and live, we commanded through you that he and his land be absolved according to the form of the Church.

You, brother bishop of Modena, in person, and you, brother [Col. 0697C] bishop of Reggio, through your archdeacon, received from the aforesaid nobleman an oath that he would in all things obey our commands. You absolved him according to the form of the Church concerning the aforesaid offense, imposing upon him by obligation of his oath that henceforth he should neither seize, despoil, nor hinder messengers of the Roman Church. Reverently receiving the command, he immediately gave and delivered into your hands, for the use and benefit of the Apostolic See and in absolute ownership, a certain castle of his called Landasia. In our name you granted it back to him as a fief, receiving from him an oath of fealty, as a vassal customarily gives to his lord.

Although you received no authority from us to grant that castle as a fief, nevertheless, because the service of the aforesaid nobleman and his heirs may be beneficial in many ways to us and to the Roman Church, we ratify what you did in good intention. By apostolic writings we command you to admonish the same nobleman that henceforth, through himself and his people, he should prudently and powerfully devote himself to the honor and advantage of the Apostolic See.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

CXXV. [Note: Raynaldus seems to cite this letter under the year 1205, § 12; but he in fact prints part of it there at §§ 28 and 29. What is printed there is here enclosed in brackets.] N . . . . (The address is lacking.) That they should induce Philip, king of France, to assist the Holy Land.

[Col. 0698A]

Amid the various—and would that they were not adverse—occupations which we endure beyond what is usual—indeed, more than usual—that matter afflicts and disturbs you the more which urges and invites us to aid the Holy Land. For although many have laboured for it in many ways, it has nevertheless now, through our sins, reached such a point of necessity that, unless aid is brought to it as speedily as possible, all hope will utterly perish, not only of recovering what has been lost, but even of defending what remains.  
[Note: What follows, as Raynaldus indicates in the place cited, is repeated in the immediately following letter.]

[For when the unexpected capture of the city of Constantinople was heard of, both the pilgrims who were in the province of Jerusalem and the natives dwelling there suddenly crossed over to the region of Constantinople; so that the province of Jerusalem itself was left almost entirely destitute of men and resources, indeed stripped also of wealth and labourers. And, what is considered more dangerous, since the Patriarch of Jerusalem has died, our legates have departed; and, with the death of the king’s son, who was to succeed to the kingdom, the king too has ended his days; nor is there anyone there who can preside or be of service, either spiritually or temporally. To increase yet further fear and grief, there is such discord, and such war is waged, between the Count of Tripoli and the King of Armenia, who contend over the principality of Antioch, that the small handful of men remaining in that land is as though wholly divided for battle. For the Templars support the count, and the Hospitallers favour the king. The people of Antioch follow the count’s party, and the patriarch pursues the king’s cause. The son of Saladin, who is sultan of Aleppo, seems to assist the man of Tripoli, but the lord of Denefin attacks him. Saphadin, however, who rules Damascus, Babylon, and Egypt, after hearing of Constantinople’s capture, grieved so deeply with all the Saracens that they would have preferred Jerusalem to be occupied by Christians rather than Constantinople by Latins. And, having immediately made a truce with all his enemies, he himself ranges far and wide in person to unite them all in alliance against the Christians. The king of the Vlachs and Bulgars, together with Cumans, Turks, and Greeks fighting against the Latins, by God’s permission prevailed, the greater men having been slain in battle. Consequently, when a multitude of crusaders wished to return home, our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the title of St Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See—over whom we grieve deeply—absolved them from their crusading vow in order to keep that multitude for the defence of the empire of Constantinople, granting full remission of sins to those who would remain there for a year. Therefore, since no assistance at all is presently expected to proceed to the province of Jerusalem, we greatly fear lest the Saracens be more boldly encouraged to occupy the remainder of the Holy Land; so that, once it is entirely occupied, Christians may lose the opportunity of crossing the sea, and the empire of Constantinople may thus be recovered by the Greeks—both objects which they ardently desire. Since, therefore, in so great an emergency we must by no means sleep, we certainly refuse neither anxiety of heart nor bodily labour, provided we can bring aid to the Holy Land. Accordingly, since the chief assistance in this matter is expected from our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious King of the Franks—whom God has for this purpose so magnified and exalted above all Christian princes that in this supreme necessity he should principally aid the King of kings—we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters, when you come into the presence of that king, faithfully to lay before him all that has been written above and diligently to induce him prudently and powerfully to devote himself to aiding the Holy Land; requesting on our behalf that he give us his counsel and support in this matter, and that you inform us as speedily as possible of what you discover.]

[Note: In Raynaldus the reading is *fraternitatem vestram* (“your fraternity”); shortly afterwards he has *monemus* (“we admonish”) for *mandamus* (“we command”), and his text ends here.]

CXXVI  
[Note: This letter is inserted, though mutilated, in the *Gesta Innocentii*, §95. Raynaldus gives fragments of it, from both the *Gesta* and the Vatican Register, under the year 1205, §§12–13. We publish it complete and with all its numbers intact, from the Conti transcript and also from another transcript copied, at our direction, from the already cited Vatican manuscript containing the formulary of Berardus of Naples. Passages found in the *Gesta* are here enclosed in brackets; those found in Raynaldus are distinguished by a double stroke placed in the margin at the beginning of each line.

For greater accuracy we have also noted in the margin variant readings, though of slighter importance, from the *Gesta*, Raynaldus, and the frequently cited Vallicellian manuscript.]

[Textual notes to CXXVI: The *Gesta* adds the name *Soffredus*. The text’s reading is *in multae necessitatis articulo* (“at a moment of great necessity”); the Podianus manuscript of the *Gesta*, cited by Baluzius, has *periculo* (“danger”), and below the *Gesta* reads *eidem* for *ejusdem*. Raynaldus’s excerpt ends after the kingdom’s deprivation of government. For “through your action,” the *Gesta* reads *horum* (“of these persons”), and below has *eam* for *terram illam* (“that land”). The Vallicellian manuscript reads *talia* (“such things”). The *Gesta* adds *illi* (“they”) after *cum enim* (“for when”), and Raynaldus resumes at “Behold indeed.” In “virgins, even consecrated to God,” Raynaldus also reads *etiam* (“even”), while the *Gesta* has *et* (“and”); for *garsionum* (“young men”), the Vallicellian manuscript has *garzonum* and Raynaldus *gartionum*. Raynaldus’s excerpt ends after “carrying off crosses and relics.” The Vallicellian manuscript has *devorabunt* (“will devour”) for *vorabunt* (“will swallow up”). Raynaldus resumes at “Therefore let not,” while the *Gesta Innocentii* ends after “more negligent.” Raynaldus’s excerpt also ends after the sentence concerning the proposed separate rebuke over the Venetian absolution.]

**TO PETER, PRIEST-CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF ST MARCELLUS, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE.** He reproves the legate for having abandoned the Holy Land, etc. (10 July.)

[Having long ago heard that you and our beloved son Soffredus, priest-cardinal of the title of St Praxedes and legate of the Apostolic See, had left the province of Jerusalem at a time of great necessity and sailed to Constantinople, we were not a little astonished and troubled, fearing the imminent danger to that land. And, “behold, what we feared has happened, and what we dreaded has now come to pass. For, besides the fact that, at that time, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, of blessed memory, had entered upon the way of all flesh, so that the Church of Jerusalem was vacant, and that, because of the war then being waged between our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of Armenia, and the Count of Tripoli over the principality of Antioch, there was a certain rivalry among Christians, subsequently, through the sudden death of A., King of Jerusalem of illustrious memory, and of his son, the kingdom of Jerusalem was left almost wholly deprived of all government.”]

And because you, who ought there to have awaited the greatest aid and to have stirred others to assist that land both by example and word, sailed thence to Greece at your own discretion, and not only pilgrims but also natives of the land, following in your footsteps, came to Constantinople, while our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Tyre, likewise followed you: that land, therefore, upon your departure, was left destitute of men and resources; and its latter condition, through your action, became worse than its former, since all its friends left it with you and there is no one among all its dear ones to console it. Thus its enemies seem to have become its head, should they choose to violate the treaty of truce—which some say expired with the death of the king and his son.

We are therefore greatly troubled within ourselves and are rightly moved against you because you reached this decision: that you should together abandon that land which the Lord consecrated by his presence and in which our King, before the ages, in these latter times wonderfully accomplished the mystery of our redemption. Although our venerable brother …, formerly Bishop of Vercelli, has been postulated as Patriarch of Jerusalem, and we, approving his postulation, have already determined to grant him the pallium, nevertheless, owing to his many occupations, perhaps he cannot cross the sea so quickly. You ought, therefore, to have considered the purpose of your legation and carefully reflected that we appointed you not to seize the empire of Constantinople, but to defend the remnants of the Holy Land and, should the Lord grant it, restore what had been lost; we sent you not to acquire temporal riches, but to merit eternal ones, since we and our brethren had made adequate provision for your expenses.

But when we recently heard, and learned from your letters, that you had absolved from their pilgrimage vow and the burden of the cross all crusaders who would stay in the defence of Constantinople from the preceding March until the next [date omitted in the supplied text], we could not but be moved against you. You neither ought nor could in any way have ventured upon such acts, whatever persons may have suggested them to you and however they may have led your mind astray. For they had especially and principally assumed the sign of the cross for this purpose, and had especially vowed this to the Lord their God: to cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land; and, later straying from that path, they have until now pursued excessive temporal advantages. Whether it was lawful for you thus to alter—indeed, rather to overturn—so solemn and pious a vow, we leave for you to judge.

“Behold, indeed, what we relate with sorrow and shame: where we had hitherto seemed to make progress, we fail and are distressed; where we chiefly believed we would be enlarged. For how will the Greek Church, however much it may be afflicted by afflictions and persecutions, return to ecclesiastical unity and devotion to the Apostolic See, when in the Latins it has seen nothing but an example of ruin and works of darkness, so that it now rightly abhors them more than dogs? Those who were thought to seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ, staining with Christian blood swords which they ought to have wielded against pagans, spared neither religion, age, nor sex; they committed incest, adultery, and fornication before the eyes of men, exposing both matrons and virgins, even those consecrated to God, to the filthiness of *garsiones* [young men]. Nor did it suffice them to drain the imperial riches and to tear apart the spoils of princes and lesser persons, unless they also stretched out their hands to the treasures of the churches and, more grievously still, to their very possessions—snatching silver tablets even from the altars and breaking them among themselves into pieces, violating sanctuaries, and carrying off crosses and relics.”

Moreover, since what has been undertaken among so many thousands of men cannot remain hidden, will not the Saracens—who were struck with excessive fear when Constantinople was captured—recover courage as soon as they learn that the crusaders are to return home after a year, and that divine vengeance now rages against them, beginning to scourge their iniquities? Will they not devour the few sheep whom you left, as it were, in a wilderness to the bites of wolves, unless the right hand of God alone withstands them? And with what face shall we henceforth be able to invite the peoples of the West to assist the Holy Land and defend the empire of Constantinople? Though not through their own fault, some may perhaps charge them, because of your act, with this: that the crusaders, abandoning the purpose of their pilgrimage, return home after being absolved; and that those who plundered the aforesaid empire, leaving it unfortified, turn their backs laden with spoils.

“Therefore let not the word of the Lord be bound in your mouth, nor be like a dumb dog unable to bark; but speak these things publicly and declare them before all, so that they may find you rebuking them for God and on account of God all the more sharply because they have hitherto found you more negligent.”

[Note: What follows, marked by a double stroke in the margin at the beginning of each line, Baluzio says was added from the Register, where Raynaldus writes that it survives, under the year 1205, §13, in his marginal note to *Gesta*, no. 95, p. 59, col. 2.]

But concerning the absolution of the Venetian people, wrongly undertaken contrary to the form of the Church, we do not rebuke you at present, since in other letters specially sent to you on this matter we have determined to rebuke you.

We have likewise decided for the present to refrain from discussing those things which you report you have done concerning the affair of the Patriarch of Antioch and the Abbot of St P., lest we seem to exaggerate every particular excessively. Moreover, since at the request of the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople we have determined to impose the burden of a legation in Greece upon our beloved son B., priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna and legate of the Apostolic See, who has already departed for Apulia, and since, as we have heard, the aforesaid Cardinal of St Praxedes has set out on his return journey, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters, in the exercise of your discretion, that, setting aside all else and allowing no excuse, you return to the Holy Land and there at least await the arrival of the aforesaid patriarch, meanwhile doing whatever may advance the needs of that land.

Given on 12 July.

CXXVII  
[Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, §55.]

**TO A., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY.** That he cause the goods taken from G., clerk of the Bishop of Porto, to be restored to him. (27 July.)

It is the duty of royal power to ensure that those going and returning through its land may travel safely, lest the kingdom seem to lack a ruler if subjects stretch out their hands to others’ property. We have received a complaint from our beloved son G., clerk of our venerable brother P., Bishop of Porto [Note: See Letter 69 of Book V, note.], that Georgius, brother Savin., Rodominus, and Gojan forcibly took from him, while he was returning from overseas:

- five *baldachins*;
- two *examita* [silks], one red and the other *jaline*;
- another *examitum* woven with gold;
- two cloaks;
- five *carpetas*;
- three small flasks of balm;
- three bags of aloeswood;
- fifty-three *buccararii*;
- fifty-two *cameloti*;
- gloves, purses, and pearls;
- *grammata*;
- Saracen cloths;
- one casket containing relics and a golden cross in which was wood of the Lord;
- twelve ivory vessels;
- two silver-bound Gospel-books containing relics;
- twenty-five rings, one of which had a large hyacinth;
- five hundred *mazamutini*;
- other cloths and books.

[Note: Concerning *examita*, see what has already been said above.]

[Note: For *hyanlium*, “of glassy colour,” Greek ὑάλινος.]

[Note: Perhaps *Carpettas* should be read. *Carpettae*, commonly *carpette*, says Hoffmann in his lexicon. Thus women’s tunics are still called at Venice; Capitolinus, in *Pertinax*, ch. 8, calls them the *chiridotae* of Dalmatian women. They are Greek καρπατοί, as others have noted, because they covered the καρπός, the wrist. See Octavius Ferrarius, *De re vestiaria*, book III, ch. 9.

It may also be understood otherwise. For the Academicians of the Crusca, *carpita* is “a cheap table covering, made of coarse woollen materials and pieces of different colours.” *Carpettus*, apparently in the same sense, occurs in Rymer, vol. II, p. 378, col. 1. There the furnishings are discussed of a collector of the Roman pontiff travelling in England.]

[Note: *Buccararios*: this reading is expressly found in the transcript. The word was unknown both to Du Cange and to Carpenter; perhaps it denotes some sort of garment or covering for the mouth.]

[Note: Might it rather be *camelaucos*? For *camelaucus*, *calamaucus*, *camelaucum*, or *calamaucum*—in later Greek καμελαύκιον—is a head-covering and a kind of cap made of camel hair, whence its name, as Cedrenus states, vol. I, p. 169: “There is also another construction of a woven cap, placed on the head instead of a felt cap. Among the Italians it is called *kamela*, from which come *camelaukia*.” There Jacobus Goar, in his later notes on Cedrenus, p. 31 at the end of vol. II, says: “Modern writers spell it καμηλαύκια and so call small caps made of camel hair, adhering only to the top of the head and falling toward the neck.”

Suidas, however, explains it otherwise (vol. II, p. 236, under Καμηλαύκιον): “Καμηλαύκιον: a Roman word. It might also be said in Greek to derive from καῦμα ἐλαύνειν.”

*Camelaucus*: a Latin word. Yet the term may be derived from the Greek καῦμα ἐλαύνειν, meaning “to drive away heat.”

*Camelaucus* is also the pope’s head-dress. Anastasius, in his life of Pope Constantine: “The Apostolic Pontiff, wearing a *camelaucus*, as he was accustomed to proceed in Rome, went out from the palace,” etc. Vignolius, in notes on the *Liber Pontificalis*, vol. II, p. 8, observes that the Vatican manuscript reads *caumelaugo*. Whoever wishes for more may consult Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. II, col. 73—though, as this little note of ours shows, one may say that something was lacking even to that most distinguished man’s diligence.]

[Note: On *mazamutini*, or *masmodini*, we have already dealt above.]

Since those same wrongdoers are said to dwell under your jurisdiction, we earnestly admonish and exhort Your Royal Serenity to compel them, by the authority entrusted to you, to restore intact the goods taken and make suitable satisfaction for the damages inflicted. Once restored, moreover, you are to order the goods to be kept with the diocesan bishop until, by a trustworthy messenger together with the aforesaid clerk, you have caused them to be brought to us.

Given on 27 July.

Written concerning this matter to [lacuna], Archbishop of Kalocsa.

Likewise [lacuna] to the Archbishop of Split.

Likewise [lacuna] to the Bishop of Pécs.

CXXVIII. **TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF ALBARENSIS.** He commands them to confirm the election of Andrew, provost of St Nicholas of Corneto, as abbot of St Augustine of Monte-Albo.

We have received a complaint on your behalf stating that the monks of St Augustine of Monte-Albo presumed, without your counsel and consent, son abbot, to elect as their abbot our beloved son Andrew, provost of St Nicholas of Corneto, contrary to the tenor of the privilege granted to you by the Apostolic See and to the custom hitherto approved. You therefore humbly and devoutly requested us to deign to annul this election and, by apostolic authority, to forbid any such attempt thereafter in that monastery; and to compel by ecclesiastical censure whoever might be elected at the time to render obedience to the Abbot of Albarensis. You maintained that both confirmation of the elect and correction of the monastery belonged to the Abbot of Albarensis under a grant of the Apostolic See.

But because the monks of the said St Augustine denied these assertions, we committed the examination of the case to the Bishop of Tuscanensis.  
[Note: Perhaps also the Bishop of Viterbo? For it is known that the bishopric of Tuscanensis was united with that of Viterbo in the time of Pope Celestine III. See Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, special part, p. *306. In the present year the united see of Tuscanensis and Viterbo was governed by Raynerius II, of whom we have already spoken above. See Letter 93 of Book V, note.]

After receiving witnesses from both sides, prudently hearing the allegations, and carefully inspecting the privileges, he remitted the case to our judgment with sufficient documentation. Having therefore examined closely the merits of the case, we have clearly learned that Innocent II, pope of blessed memory, entrusted the administration of the said monastery to the Abbot of Albarensis upon the condition that, saving the right of the Apostolic See, he should preserve religious observance in that monastery and attend to its spiritual and temporal advancement.

From the witnesses, moreover, we have found it manifestly proved that during forty years, with the consent of the Abbot of Albarensis, five abbots have been elected in that monastery; that they were confirmed by him; and that they promised him regular obedience, although the opposing party tried to prove that these practices had been usurped after objection and appeal. The opposing party also presented privileges by which it intended to establish that the election of the abbot belonged freely to the monks of St Augustine.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid monastery of St Augustine belongs to the right and ownership of Blessed Peter, and you can claim nothing in it except what has been entrusted to you therein by the Apostolic See, we judicially determine that the monks of the aforesaid monastery may canonically elect an abbot for themselves, after seeking the counsel of the Abbot of Albarensis. He may not reject a suitable candidate, but must canonically confirm the person elected; he is to correct in that monastery what he finds needs correction and establish what he sees ought to be established. Yet he may not presume to depose the abbot without a special mandate of the Roman pontiff. The person elected and confirmed shall in our stead promise him regular obedience, since the latter has there no authority save that committed to him by the Roman pontiff.

The election made of the above-named provost need not have been annulled, since, with the monks’ consent, he renounced the election made of him before they came into our presence. Therefore let no one, etc., contravene our determination.

Given.

CXXIX  
[Note: This letter is inserted in the *Gesta*, §107, though some material is lacking at the end. It is therefore here enclosed in brackets. Raynaldus likewise gives it, though mutilated, under the year 1205, §21. Passages found in his work are here marked by a double stroke in the margin at the beginning of each line.]

**TO KALOJOANNES, KING OF THE BULGARIANS AND VLACHS.** That he make peace with the Latins and release the Emperor of Constantinople, whom he holds captive.

[Out of the special favour by which we have glorified you among all Christian princes, we love you so greatly that we earnestly seek your advantage and honour, firmly hoping that you ought continually to advance in devotion to the most holy Roman Church, your mother, through whose merits you gained a glorious triumph over those who strove grievously to harass you.

“Since, therefore, you have received from us through a legate of the Apostolic See the royal diadem and military banner, so that your kingdom might be a special possession of Blessed Peter, we wish diligently to provide that, delivered from hostile attacks on every side, you may rejoice in tranquil peace. Know then, dearest son, that a great army is about to depart from the western regions for Greece, in addition to that which recently arrived. You must therefore take every precaution for yourself and your land, so that, while you can, you may make peace with the Latins; lest, should they perhaps strive to attack you from one side and the Hungarians from the other, you may not easily resist the efforts of both. Accordingly, we earnestly advise and counsel Your Serenity in good faith that, since you are said to hold Baldwin, Emperor of Constantinople, captive, you provide so as to make true and firm peace with the Latins through his release, so that they may altogether cease from attacking you and your land. For we command Henry, brother of that emperor, who commands the army of the Latins at Constantinople, by apostolic letters, to incline the Latins toward peace with you in exchange for the liberation of that emperor, and entirely to desist from molesting you. May God therefore inspire you to comply with our warnings and counsels, so that your kingdom, which you have most devoutly dedicated to Blessed Peter and the Roman Church, may be preserved unharmed from every disturbance—a goal to which we desire to devote diligent attention and effective effort.”]

“Written to [lacuna], Archbishop of Trnovo, Primate of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, that he diligently warn and induce him to do this.”

CXXX  
[Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §30.]

**TO ALL CHRIST’S FAITHFUL WHO WISH TO GO TO CONSTANTINOPLE IN AID OF THE HOLY LAND.** That they inform the pope of their plan. (16 August.)

Since it is confidently hoped that, through the retention of the empire of Constantinople—which the Latins have subjected to themselves by divine judgment—the province of Jerusalem will be freed from the hands of the pagans, whoever devoutly longs, out of reverence for Jesus Christ, for its liberation should also earnestly strive for the retention of that empire. Although, therefore, in general letters we recently enjoined upon all Christ’s faithful, for the remission of all sins, that they should go to Constantinople and labour for the assistance of the Holy Land, nevertheless, lest their labour be useless and vain because, upon their arrival, they cannot find passage or are compelled by a long wait to consume their necessary expenses, we command all of you by apostolic letters to appoint a fixed term by which you may suitably prepare for the journey, and to send suitable messengers ahead to us. Let them make us more certain of your intention, so that we may have a route, both short and safe, prepared for you through Apulia; and let your messengers go with our letters to Brindisi to hire shipping, so that, once everything has been duly arranged, you may cross without hindrance with our blessing.

Given on 16 August.

CXXXI  
[Note: This letter is found, though mutilated, in the *Gesta*, §105. Raynaldus provides fragments of it under the year 1205, §17 and following.

We publish the complete text in continuous sequence, with all its numbers intact, according to the Conti transcript. Passages found in the *Gesta* are here enclosed in brackets; passages in Raynaldus have been marked with a double stroke in the margin at the beginning of each line. For greater accuracy, we have also noted variant readings from the *Gesta*, Raynaldus, and the royal manuscript cited by Baluzio and the Vallicellian manuscript.]

**LETTERS OF HENRY, THE EMPEROR’S BROTHER.** He informs him that Emperor Baldwin was captured by the Bulgars and sends messengers. (At the Palace of Blachernae, in the year of the Lord 1205, 5 June.)

[To the most holy Father and lord INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, H. [Note: In the *Gesta*, “Henry.”], brother of the Emperor of Constantinople and governor of the empire, with due reverence, a humble and devout [Note: In the *Gesta* and in Raynaldus, “devout.”] kiss of the feet [Note: Ibid., “kisses.”].] Since my brother and lord the emperor has, through numerous letters [Col. 0706D] and messengers, made known quite clearly to your fatherhood the entire course of the Christian army and the sequence of the hardships of our pilgrimage, most recently down to this past March, I have judged it fitting to disclose to you, as Father and lord, our subsequent fortunes—very unlike the former ones, indeed, through our sins, most [Col. 0707A] wretched.

It happened, therefore, that the Greeks—who, from their inborn malice and habitual perfidy, always show themselves prone to treachery after every kind of assurance and safeguard—immediately after the departure of the messengers last sent to you, openly revealed, by rebelling against us, the treachery they had long conceived in their minds.
