When this became known, my brother and lord the emperor, opportunely accompanied by a rather small number—for we were for the most part dispersed among fortresses and border territories—set out from the imperial city against the center of the rebellion, namely Adrianople, a city of Greece most strongly fortified and adjoining the peoples of the Vlachs, with only mountains lying between, intending to exact vengeance.

For at that time [Col. 0707B] we were divided as follows: the Marquis of Montferrat was beyond Thessalonica with many men; I was on the other side of the Arm of Saint George at Andromiticum [Note: Thus both in the *Gesta* and in Raynaldus; in the royal manuscript cited by Baluze, in the margin, “Mandromiticum.”] with no small number; Payen of Orléans and P. of Bracel were toward Nicaea, on the same side of the Arm [Note: Absent in the *Gesta* and in Raynaldus.]; R. [Note: *Gesta* and Raynaldus: “E.”] of Tric was at Philippopolis with a larger force; and others were dispersed elsewhere among various places and fortresses.

Moreover, when Johannitsa, lord of the Vlachs, heard that the Latins, with so small a number of men, had besieged the aforesaid city—he whom the Greeks had also secretly summoned to their aid, so as to do us greater harm—that Vlach Johannitsa suddenly fell upon our men with an innumerable multitude of barbarians [Note: Thus also in Raynaldus; absent in the *Gesta*.], namely Vlachs, Cumans, and others. Our men went out against them with far too little foresight, [Col. 0707C] and, pressing forward farther than they should, were finally hemmed in on every side by the enemy’s ambushes. Alas! My lord the emperor, Count Louis, Stephen of Perche, and certain other barons and knights—something I cannot recount without shedding tears of blood—were overwhelmed by so great a multitude and intercepted by the enemy, though not without loss to them. [Note: Vallicellian manuscript: “slain.”]

We truly do not know who were captured and who were killed. Yet we have received from our most reliable scouts and from trustworthy report that my lord the emperor is alive and held captive; and, as they assert [Note: Thus also in Raynaldus; in the *Gesta*, “it is asserted.”], he is for the present treated honorably enough by Johannitsa himself, together with certain others whose names we still do not [Col. 0707D] expressly know.

Know, moreover, that from the day when we entered Greek territory until the day of that disastrous battle, whatever multitude encountered us and our men, although our force was sometimes extremely small, we nevertheless always withdrew in triumph and victory. [Col. 0708A] We believe that the incalculable loss which we then sorrowfully suffered and lament was occasioned by the rashness of our men, undertaken without counsel, and by the deserts of our sins.

Those, therefore, who escaped from the battle and evaded the hands of the enemy, after brief consultation with those who had remained to guard the tents, withdrew from the siege without further loss. As they made for the imperial city in such unexpectedly ruined circumstances, the Lord suddenly gave them so great a consolation that, as if in a moment, all who had been dispersed assembled, as though summoned by the Lord, at a certain city called Rodestoc [Note: In the *Gesta*, “Rodestock”; in Raynaldus, “Rodestec.”]. The marquis, however, remained safe and unharmed, by God’s grace, in his territories, prosperously [Note: In the *Gesta*, “faithfully.”] and victoriously; and R. [Note: In the *Gesta*, “R.”; in Raynaldus, “E.”] of Tric likewise remained so in [Col. 0708B] his region.

Having thus inspected our forces, we began thereafter to fortify those towns and castles which seemed capable of being held against the Greek rebellion; and in the meantime we proceeded as far as Constantinople. Although, then, a mournful misfortune has befallen us in the persons we have lost, we nonetheless hope in the Lord and confidently [Note: *Gesta*: “boldly.”] trust that, the Lord willing, we shall be able for a considerable time to withstand the snares and assaults of our enemies, and also to await assistance and aid from afar.

Yet behold: what we feared has happened, and that which public report proclaimed, and of which we were informed by the letters of that Vlach himself, containing his alliance [Col. 0708C] with the Turks and the other enemies of Christ’s cross; these letters, intercepted by us together with his messengers, we sent to your apostolic authority in both languages [Note: Raynaldus ends here.]. Although we have sustained a wound and disaster graver than we expected [Note: In the *Gesta*, “a wound and disaster are sustained.”], no one doubts that it belongs to you to undertake its remedy, as Father, patron and lord of our cause [Note: *Gesta*: “of all and of our cause.”], especially since we labor solely for the restoration of the Church’s unity and for the aid of the Holy Land; and one of these hitherto [Note: *Gesta*: “thus far.”] depends upon the other.

This is the common assertion of all Christians dwelling in the East, and especially of the venerable brothers of both the Order of the Temple and the Hospital, who are with us: the restoration of the former appears likely to bring about not only the liberation of the latter, but [Col. 0708D] also most openly to procure the complete overthrow of all pagans and enemies of Christ’s cross. Conversely, its disruption—which God [Note: *Gesta*: “which the Lord.”] avert!—would not only remove the hope of recovering the lost part of the Holy Land, but would undoubtedly also take away the hope of retaining that part which is at present devoted to Christian worship. [Col. 0709A]

Considering, therefore, as from the beginning, that our own insufficiency is unequal to the loftiness of so arduous a purpose, we flee to you with suppliant and devout purpose and mind, as to the supreme and principal—indeed the sole—refuge and foundation of our hope. You alone, above the sons of men, princes, and kings, however great their power, can bring us aid. Prostrate at the feet of your fatherhood in bowed humility, we implore you with all the urgency of prayer we can command and with tears: do not delay to show your customary affection of mercy toward your sons, placed in so narrow a strait and needing your counsel and help above all living persons.

We request this with the greater confidence from the gentleness of your [Col. 0709B] fatherhood because, beyond our solemn vow of pilgrimage, we devote our bodies and lives for the Roman Church. In this matter, beyond the common solicitude for all Christians which binds you, we know that both we are strictly bound to your fatherhood and you to us, as your soldiers and retainers in the pay of the Roman Church. [Note: Thus far the *Gesta*; the remainder is in Raynaldus.]

[“We therefore ask that legates, furnished with apostolic authority from your side, be sent into Italy, France, Germany, and other western regions, to bring, in aid and support of us, to those who shall come to us for the aforesaid reasons, the full plenary indulgence which has been granted by your apostolic see for a full year to those remaining in the service of the Crucified One in the land of Syria. [Col. 0709C]

But because the matters we wish to communicate to your fatherhood would take too long to set down in writing, I send to your fatherhood our faithful messengers: above all, our venerable father N., bishop of Soissons, who has labored as faithfully as steadfastly for the aid of the Holy Land and the cause of the Roman Church, and who still, as a faithful and prudent steward of the talent entrusted to him—as you yourselves see—does not cease to labor. His absence would be exceedingly harmful to us, were not the pressing necessity of the matter and the very difficulty of the undertaking to compel us to do without his presence for a time. I also send the noble men M. [Note: Absent in Raynaldus.] of Mailli and John Bliaut, asking and desiring that you be willing [Col. 0709D] to place firm and unquestioning trust in what they may set before your apostolic authority [Col. 0710A] concerning this affair; and that you provide your counsel and aid, as you shall judge expedient for the Church, for all Christendom, and for the liberation of my lord and brother, who everywhere conducted and called himself your devoted knight.”]

Given in the Palace of Blachernae [Note: Absent in Raynaldus.], in the year of the Lord 1205, on the Nones of June.

CXXXII [Note: Raynaldus prints this letter under the year 1205, §22.]. TO HENRY, BROTHER OF THE EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. That he should establish and confirm peace with the king of the Bulgarians.

[By apostolic letters we command your nobility diligently to attend to the liberation of your brother and establish a true and firm peace with our most dear son, Kalojohn, illustrious king of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, so that faithful and stable friendship may henceforth endure between Bulgarians and Latins. [Col. 0710B] We write briefly, because action is needed more than words. Friendship can indeed be greatly advantageous to both sides. Given, etc.]

CXXXIII [Note:

This letter is read in the *Gesta*, §XCIII; it is therefore printed here in brackets.

Raynaldus provides fragments of it under the year 1205, §7. Passages printed by him are distinguished here by a double marginal stroke at the beginning of each line; variant readings from different manuscripts, as in letter 131 of this eighth book, are also placed in the margin.]

. TO THE MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT. That he should defend and protect the conquered empire of Constantinople until the pope is better informed whether it was wrongfully acquired.

[That, amid diverse [Note: Absent in the *Gesta*.] and not merely manifold but pressing worldly cares and occupations, you are solicitous and zealous for the salvation of your soul, we commend your prudence and devotion in the Lord. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole [Col. 0710C] world but suffers loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul? A brother will not redeem; a man will redeem, he will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul; he will labor forever and live unto the end. [Note:

The passage is corrupt: the manuscripts do not supply the genuine reading.

[Col. 0710D] In the *Gesta* it reads thus: “Moreover, a man will not redeem, nor give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul. He will labor forever and live unto the end.” In the royal and Podian manuscripts cited by Baluze, in the margin, p. 56, col. 1: “A brother will not redeem; a man will redeem; he will not give,” etc. Thus also in the Vallicellian manuscript.

But in the manuscript of the Vatican Library, often cited already, containing the formulary of Berard of Naples: “A brother will not redeem a man; he will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul,” etc.]

For we have received your letters, presented to our apostolic authority through our beloved son S., [Note: In the *Gesta*, “Soffredus.”] priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. In them you took care to inform us that, with contrite heart and sincere spirit [Note: Thus also in the royal and Podian manuscripts cited by Baluze, in the margin.], in obedience to the command of apostolic admonition and prompted by the hope of a general indulgence, you solemnly made a vow of the cross and always intended to pursue it faithfully with an uncorrupted purpose. [Note: In the *Gesta*, “with an uncorrupted mind.”]

That you assumed the leadership of that young man who asserted that the empire of Constantinople was his by right [Col. 0710D] was the counsel [Col. 0711A] of our beloved son P., [Note: In the *Gesta*, “Peter.”] priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the apostolic see. It was not so much human counsel as pressing necessity, because after the destruction of the city of Zara [Note: Vallicellian manuscript: “of Jadera.”] the army had turned aside into Romania to obtain provisions.

But you and the other crusaders, making a virtue of necessity, chiefly intended to procure there an acceptable and devoted [Note: These words are absent in the *Gesta*.] service for the apostolic see, as well as the anticipated help for the Holy Land. You thought that this had been fully accomplished when, after the imperial city had been taken without bloodshed, its usurper driven out, and father and son restored there together to the height of imperial dignity, you caused them, without compulsion [Note: In the *Gesta*, “under compulsion.”], with their hands upon the Gospels, to render obedience to the most holy apostolic see. You sent us their imperial writing to make the faith more secure, so that they might fulfill in deed what they had promised in word.

And when you were preparing with all your strength to sail for Syria, the inborn malice of the Greeks, utterly violating oaths and agreements, wickedly obstructed your journey with fire [Note: Vallicellian manuscript: “a great fire.”], treachery, and poison—not once only, but often—and drew you, resisting and unwilling, into the occupation of the imperial city, to their own destruction. After that city was marvelously overcome by God’s power alone, whatever you subsequently did, in whatever manner or place, willingly or unwillingly, having consulted your clergy [Note: *Gesta*: “the clergy of our God.”], you always desired that through you the children of disobedience might return to due and devoted obedience to their mother, and that the Eastern Church, [Col. 0711C] as its principal member, might be united to its head. In order that this might be accomplished more fully and successfully, you have until now awaited, and still await with continual desire, the counsel of the apostolic see, without which undertaking and expenditure wholly perish.

But because, as you assert, you assumed the sign of the cross to erase the stains of your youth and remove whatever stain of apostasy human frailty had contracted in former times [Note: Thus also in the royal manuscript cited by Baluze; in the *Gesta*, “to extirpate.”], not in order to sin more gravely and freely under the cloak of religion and the banner of the cross [Note: The *Gesta* adds “and.”], referring every individual matter to the judgment of our examination and submitting yourself in all things and through all things to your mother’s [Col. 0711D] counsels and commands [Note: In the *Gesta*, “submitting yourself to our counsels”; in the Vallicellian manuscript, “you submit yourself to ours.”], so that, if we learn that the state of Romania and your stay there effectively benefit the apostolic see and the land of promise, and that through this you receive remission of sins, you do not refuse dangers and labors; otherwise, without regard for the possessions and honors which you enjoy in abundance, we should rather impose upon you that course by which you might more abundantly deserve [Note: Vallicellian manuscript: “appear.”] to avert the wrath of the supreme Judge.

Indeed, by what has been written above [Col. 0712A] you seem silently to have answered the objections that may thus be directed against the crusaders. For since you had vowed yourselves to the service of the Crucified One to free the Holy Land from the hands of pagans, and had been forbidden under threat of excommunication to attempt to invade or harm Christian lands—unless perhaps those Christians wickedly obstructed your journey, or some other just and necessary cause arose for you, on account of which, with the intervention of our legate’s counsel, you might act otherwise—[Note: These words occur in Raynaldus.] you seem rashly to have departed from the purity of your vow: having no jurisdiction or authority over the Greeks, you took up arms not against Saracens but against Christians; you aimed not at recovering [Col. 0712B] Jerusalem but at occupying Constantinople, preferring earthly riches to heavenly treasures.

And this is judged far more grave: [Note: What follows is repeated from letter 126 of this eighth book.] some spared neither religion, age, nor sex, but publicly committed fornications, adulteries, and incests [Note: In the *Gesta* and Raynaldus, “of all.”], exposing not only married women and widows but also matrons, virgins, and women consecrated to God to the filth of servants (*garsiones*). Nor was it enough to exhaust the imperial wealth or plunder the spoils of great and small alike; you stretched forth your hands to the treasures of churches, and, worse still, to their possessions. You carried off silver panels from altars; and, after violating sanctuaries, you took away icons, crosses, and relics. Thus the Greek Church, however much it may be afflicted by persecutions, scorns to return to obedience to the apostolic see, because in the Latins it has seen nothing but examples of perdition and works of darkness, and now rightly abhors them more than dogs. [Note: Thus far letter 126.]

You, however, alleged the counsel of the legate of the apostolic see against the claim that your authority was unjust and unlawful—or, rather, usurped—as though by it you had been permitted to set out with the aforesaid young man to restore to him the empire of Constantinople. You might also have alleged that, since want of provisions pressed upon you, without which you could not fulfill your vow of the cross, you were allowed, because of so necessary a cause, to hire out your services to one who appeared to be pursuing a just cause, especially since by this means you ultimately intended aid for the Holy Land and the advancement of the apostolic see.

And when they denied you the wage they had promised and owed, utterly violating oaths and agreements, and moreover often attacked you with arms, fire, treachery, and poison, you were, being pressed into a narrow strait, compelled [Note: Thus also in the *Gesta*; but in the royal and Podian manuscripts and in Raynaldus, “drawn.”] [Col. 0713A] to exact due vengeance upon schismatics and perjurers who unjustly denied what was due to you. For it seems to have been a divine judgment that those who, though long mercifully tolerated and often [Note: In the *Gesta* and Raynaldus, “so often.”] diligently admonished not only by others but also by us, refused to return to the Church’s unity or to provide any aid for the Holy Land, should lose their place and nation through those who sought both ends together; so that, after evil men were wickedly destroyed, the good land might be leased to good cultivators who render fruit in due season. [Note: Thus also in Raynaldus; in the *Gesta*, “in due seasons.”]

As is written in the prophet Daniel: “There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, changes times, and transfers kingdoms” (Dan. 2); “he rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomsoever he wills” (Dan. 4). The common [Col. 0713B] saying, moreover, holds that the rights of kingdoms have always been violent.

[“But since God’s judgments are sometimes so hidden that the Prophet calls them ‘a great deep’ (Ps. 35), so that even the Apostle is compelled to cry out: ‘O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?’ (Rom. 11)—we do not wish rashly to judge of so deep a judgment, especially before we have been more fully informed of the truth of the matter. For they may have been justly punished because of the sin they committed against God, while you nevertheless may have punished them unjustly because of the hatred you exercised toward your neighbors—if indeed those who disdain to draw near may be called neighbors. And perhaps, because of their just punishment, God gave you a just reward, as he is recorded to have said in the prophet: ‘Because you have served me in Tyre, I will give you Egypt’; whence he calls Assyria the rod of his wrath.

Leaving doubtful matters aside, we have judged it right to answer you this with certainty, beneficially counseling in one and the same matter both the Holy Land and the apostolic see, as well as your soul: in the fear of the Lord and hope of pardon, hold and defend the land acquired by divine judgment; acquire what is to be held and defended; govern the peoples subject to you in justice, preserve them in peace, and conform them to religion. Thus restore ecclesiastical goods [Col. 0713D] according to your own ability, repenting and making satisfaction for what has been committed [Note: Thus far Raynaldus],” since such an undertaking could scarcely have been carried out without guilt requiring expiation [Note: Vallicellian manuscript: “of expiation.”], for whoever touches pitch is defiled by it.

And firmly maintain the resolve of your vow: prudently and powerfully direct your efforts toward the aid of the Holy Land, to which you chiefly and spiritually dedicated yourself, since through this land that other land is hoped to be readily recoverable.

Furthermore, following the example of your fathers and brothers, who have always endeavored in every respect to reverence and venerate the most holy Roman Church with a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, you are faithful and devoted to us and the apostolic see. Therefore, from the fullness [Note: Absent in the *Gesta*.] of grace, we make you wholly secure, knowing with certainty that whenever opportunity offers, we desire to do such things as may redound magnificently to your honor and advancement.

Given, etc.]

CXXXIV [Note: Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1205, §8.]. TO M . . ., WIFE OF THE NOBLEMAN B., MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT, FORMER EMPRESS OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He congratulates her for having rejected Greek rites and embraced Latin ones.

We have received with paternal kindness the letter of your devotion, through which you took care to inform our apostolic authority that, although you were born of [Col. 0714B] orthodox and Latin parents, yet from your tender years, having been matrimonially joined to Isaac, formerly emperor of Constantinople, you conformed your customs and manner of life to Greek society. Growing old and reaching maturity in those practices, you wholly abandoned Latin rites through long disuse.

But when time passed and the imperial city was delivered into the hands of the Latins, after the death of the aforesaid emperor you voluntarily married the distinguished man B . . ., Marquis of Montferrat, according to Latin rites. Yet you shrank from returning to Latin customs, which you had so recently come to abhor, being too boldly an imitator of Greek practice.

Afterwards, however, softened by the persistent pious persuasions of the aforesaid marquis, your most dear husband, and frequently moved by the salutary admonitions and manifest reasoning of our beloved sons S . . ., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes and legate of the apostolic [Col. 0714C] see, and the abbots of Locedium—indeed, more by divine inspiration—having received with your husband the Latin blessing and the body of Christ consecrated according to Latin traditions, you consecrated yourself to Latin laws wholly in mind and body, in manner and bearing alike.

Accordingly, specially committing yourself and your children to the protection and custody of the most holy apostolic see, you humbly entreated us, in paternal gentleness attentive to your devotion, to preserve unimpaired, in due place and time, the right of yourself and your children.

We therefore, who sincerely love your lineage in the Lord with charity, welcome this change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, [Col. 0714D] and give him thanks because he has inspired in you so devout and pious an affection toward our person and the Roman Church. By apostolic letters we make known to your nobility that, so far as we can honorably do so, we shall effectively promote your honor and advancement. We earnestly admonish your devotion and impose this upon you for the remission of your sins: laudably persevere in the good which you have begun, and diligently induce others to it by word and example alike.

Given, etc.

CXXXV [Note: Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1205, §14.]. TO B., PRIEST-CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF SAINT SUSANNA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE [Note: See letter 55 of the eighth book.]. That he should confirm certain arrangements in the Church of Constantinople according to the agreements made.

[Col. 0715A]

Although the agreements concerning ecclesiastical affairs made between the French and Venetians are not binding by law, nevertheless, just as we proceeded in the election of the patriarch in order to preserve concord between them, so you should proceed in arranging the churches for the same reason, so that what was unlawfully established by their rashness may lawfully be done by our authority.

For among such agreements this is expressly contained: that clerics of each party ought to arrange those churches which fall to its party; and that certain [Col. 0715B] ecclesiastical benefices, by the common consent of the entire clergy, are to be assigned for safekeeping to certain clerics from beyond the mountains. By apostolic letters we command your discretion to grant, by our authority and with any obstacle of appeal removed, to those same clerics whatever you find assigned to the French party, if perhaps our venerable brother . . ., patriarch of Constantinople, after diligent admonition, does not judge that these ought to be granted to them. For it is not fitting that we deny the French in a lesser matter the favor we extend to the Venetians in a greater.

Given, etc.

CXXXVI. . . . . . TO THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE [Note: See letter 19 of the eighth book.]. That he should have Henry, a cleric, received as a canon of the Church of Saint Sophia. (7 Ids of September.)

[Col. 0715C]

Since, by God’s grace, you have been promoted to that church which, especially in these times, needs learned and honorable clerics, we earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood to receive, out of reverence for Saint Peter and ourselves and in view of his good character, our beloved son Master Henry, bearer of these letters, who is commended for his morals and learning, as a canon and brother of the Church of Saint Sophia, and to assign him there a prebendary benefice.

Given 7 Ids of September.

CXXXVII. TO FREDERICK, PROVOST OF CLARHOLTEN [Note: The distinguished provostship of Clarholt, of noble men, situated in the diocese of Osnabrück under the lordship of Rheda, was founded in 1133 by the illustrious Rudolf of Stenfordt, lord of the place. On the state of this [Col. 0716D] provostship, see *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. I, col. 513.]. Dispensation for illegitimacy of birth, permitting the reception of ecclesiastical dignities.

[Col. 0715D]

God established the fullness of ecclesiastical dignity in the apostolic see so that, after diligently considering the diverse circumstances of persons and affairs, times and places, it might sometimes exercise rigor and sometimes prefer gentleness, at times execute [Col. 0716A] justice and at times bestow grace, according as it sees that different cases require different treatment.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, at the most earnest request of our dearest son in Christ, the most illustrious King Otto, elected Roman emperor, and also of your kinsmen, who are exceedingly faithful and devoted to us and the Roman Church, and in view also of your religious life and uprightness—since you are a priest, a provost in the Premonstratensian Order, and, as is asserted, born of an unmarried man and unmarried woman—we grant you by special favor that, notwithstanding the defect of your birth, should you be nominated to ecclesiastical dignities, you may freely be postulated for them. Let no one therefore . . . this grant of ours, etc.

Given, etc.

CXXXVIII. . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ [Note: See letter 14, note, of the fifth book.]. That he should confer consecration upon the elect of Strasbourg [Note: See letter 8, note, of the eighth book.]; if he delays, the matter is entrusted to the Archbishop of Sens [Note: See letter 45, note, of the third book.]. (8 Ids of October.)

[Col. 0716B]

Your discretion does not fail to know how much deference we have judged due to you and your church in the case of our beloved son, . . . elect of Strasbourg [Note: See letter 90 of the eighth book and the notes there.], beyond the custom of the apostolic see, which is accustomed to confer the benefit of consecration upon the suffragans of any archbishops who come to it, though without prejudice to those archbishops.

For when the aforesaid elect came into our presence and requested the conferral upon him of consecration, which, as he said, he had been unable to obtain from you in any way, although he had repeatedly requested it, we did not judge that we should proceed to consecrate him, wishing to show deference to your brotherhood, until we had been more fully informed by your letters of your will and the course of events. We promised you by our letters that, even should we proceed to his consecration, we would take sufficient care for your honor and right.

Now, when we received the letters of your brotherhood requesting that he be sent back to you for consecration, we did not wish to consecrate him bishop, although for this very reason he most urgently implored us, alleging absolute necessity. Therefore, so that by your exercise of office provision may be made for that elect and for the Church of Strasbourg, which has long remained as though bereaved [Col. 0716D] of a pastor, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to proceed within a suitable period to some place safe both for you and him. Having summoned two of your suffragans, or other bishops who can safely be present—whom, if after admonition they refuse to attend, you shall compel by our authority under the testimony of these letters—you shall confer upon him the gift of consecration, or arrange for other bishops to confer it in your stead. After they have conferred the gift of consecration, they must not fail, either personally or through your messenger, to receive from him in your name the profession which he owes to you and to the Church of Mainz.

Otherwise, lest—God forbid!—through excessive delay in his consecration, serious harm be caused to the Church of Strasbourg and to the clergy and people of the whole bishopric, know that we have commanded our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Sens, by apostolic letters, after he has been assured of your failure, to summon two of his suffragans and, supported by our authority, without allowing any objection or appeal to prevail, [Col. 0717B] not delay in consecrating the same elect bishop. He is to receive from him in your name the profession customarily made by a suffragan of the Church of Mainz, enjoining him, as soon as he has the opportunity to come into your presence, not to delay in coming to you in person, so that he may acknowledge before you the due profession which he made before the Archbishop of Sens.

Given 8 Ids of October.

CXXXIX [Note:

This letter is found, though very mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book I, title 5, “On the Postulation of Prelates,” chapter 4. What is printed there is here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are supplied.

Raynaldus likewise mentions it under the year 1205, §56.]

. TO THE PROVOST AND CHAPTER OF STRIGONIUM. He appoints the Archbishop of Kalocsa as their archbishop [Note: On the subject of this letter, see letters 159 and 226 of the seventh book, and letter 88 of the eighth book.]. (At Rome, 2 Nones of October.)

When your venerable archbishop of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0717D] In the Decretals, “William.” Immediately afterward the words “and below,” etc., are omitted.] had entered upon the way of all flesh, you unanimously directed your votes to us in postulating our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Kalocsa; and having obtained the royal assent to this, the suffragans of the Church of Esztergom—namely, the bishops of Pécs, Vác, Veszprém, and Nitra [Note: [Col. 0718D] The Decretals add, “and certain others,” and below omit the words distinguished by us in italic type.]—took care to oppose your postulation. They asserted that, with contempt for those who possessed the right of electing together with you, that postulation had been attempted. Your messengers, however, alleged in reply that, concerning the appointment of a pontiff over you, the suffragans’ assent had repeatedly been requested as a matter of favor, but that they had denied you counsel and assistance.

Accordingly, when the messengers were present before us and the opposing party advanced certain other objections [Col. 0717D] against the course of your postulation—objections which we remember having set out more fully in earlier letters—we judged, because the allegations had not been established before us, that provision should be made as follows: if the suffragans persisted in their opposition and you wished to press your postulation, you were to come to the Apostolic See by the forthcoming Septuagesima [Col. 0718A], through suitable procurators sufficiently instructed in every respect, so that, with both parties present, we might determine what justice required. But if they ceased from opposition and you persisted in your proposal [Note: [Col. 0718D] Here the Decretals add “your.”], you were to send suitable persons to our presence within the aforesaid period, to make us more fully informed regarding whatever matters might be necessary. But if, while the bishops mentioned continued their opposition, you should come to despair of your right, then, lest you undergo labor and grief in vain, you were to provide yourselves canonically with another suitable person as pastor.

Moreover, since H., the illustrious king of Hungary of renowned memory, had meanwhile entered upon the way of all flesh, certain among you rashly withdrew from the postulation [Note: [Col. 0718D] The Decretals add “your.”] which you had presented to us [Col. 0718B] jointly, while others persisted in it and appealed to the Apostolic See. The former postulated the aforesaid bishop of Pécs as archbishop; none of the suffragans assented to their votes except the bishop of Nitra alone. And although our dearest son in Christ, A., the illustrious king of Hungary, then duke and governor of the kingdom of Hungary in the name of L., his nephew the king—whose guardianship and care of the realm his brother had entrusted to him—had sent to us the first fruits of his prayers in support of the postulation of the aforesaid Archbishop of Kalocsa, he nevertheless afterwards humbly petitioned us by letter for the transfer of the bishop of Pécs to the metropolitan see of Esztergom.

Therefore, after diligent deliberation with our brethren concerning that postulation [Col. 0718C], since we found that it had been rashly held, after legitimate appeals to us had been lodged [Note: [Col. 0718D] The Decretals read: “therefore, that postulation, which we found,” and below insert “also” after “Church.”], amid great discord not only among the suffragans but also among the canons of the Church of Esztergom, in contravention of the form of our mandate and with due procedure disregarded, we judged, justice requiring it, that it should not be admitted. Rather, we commanded you to proceed, within a month after receiving our letters, to provide yourselves with a suitable pastor by a canonical election or a unanimous postulation, after seeking the suffragans’ assent if, according to ancient and approved custom, it was required. Otherwise, from that point onward, lest the Lord’s flock be deprived longer of a pastor’s care, we ourselves [Col. 0718D], in accordance with the duty of our office and by the fullness of apostolic authority, would provide for the widowed Church.

Yet before our letters reached you, relying on the earlier mandate, you recalled to concord the suffragans present in the kingdom, apart from the aforesaid bishop of Pécs. Thus [Col. 0719A] the bishops of Vác, Veszprém, and Jánvi humbly asked us to transfer the Archbishop of Kalocsa, reserving their right for the future—a right which, because of the affliction and need of the Church of Esztergom, they were for the present setting aside. The aforesaid bishop of Nitra wrote that, if it did not please us to admit the postulation made for the bishop of Pécs, he humbly besought us, without prejudice to his right, concerning the postulation of another.

After this, when our mandate had been received, those who had agreed upon the Archbishop of Kalocsa [Note: [Col. 0719D] The Decretals have “of Kalocsa” in place of “as archbishop.”] refused, as was alleged before us, to withdraw from his postulation. Rather, renewing it after certain canons who had turned to the other party had returned to them, they sent to the Apostolic See, with letters from the aforesaid king and the suffragans [Col. 0719B], our beloved sons A., master of the schools; M., treasurer; A., archdeacon; and F. and N., canons of Esztergom, to seek the favor of a dispensation concerning their postulation.

But the others, who had postulated the bishop of Pécs, as was alleged before us on their behalf, assembled together and summoned the remaining canons to chapter, wishing within the period prescribed for them to proceed, according to the apostolic mandate, to a unanimous postulation or canonical election. When those others refused to assemble, they understood that the free power of electing remained with themselves alone, because the rest neglected to pursue their right. Therefore they again postulated the aforesaid bishop of Pécs [Col. 0719C], although the others had appealed to prevent this from being done.

When, therefore, the envoys of both parties arrived at the Apostolic See, those who had come for the bishop of Pécs maintained that their party had proceeded according to the apostolic mandate; and that the discord or opposition of those who, scorning to proceed according to the form of our mandate, after receiving it had neither canonically elected anyone nor unanimously postulated anyone, was no obstacle. Hence their postulation had to be regarded as unanimous, since the others, as despisers of the apostolic command, had deprived themselves of the right of electing and postulating by refusing not only to postulate or elect, but even to attend chapter.

To this it could be answered on the other side [Col. 0719D] that those who had postulated the Archbishop of Kalocsa had followed the form laid down for them by our letters. For, relying on the earlier postulation and according to the tenor of our former letters, they had made unanimous what had previously been discordant, when they recalled the suffragans to concord; [nor did the discord [Note: [Col. 0719D] The Decretals read “was an obstacle.”] of those who had postulated another harm them, since previously all of you together had agreed upon the postulation of the aforesaid archbishop, and had asked us, through common envoys, to confirm your assent, recorded in letters and strengthened by your own subscriptions [Col. 0720A]; and we had received your postulation for adjudication—if perhaps the suffragans persisted in opposition—or for approval, if they assented or believed it should be approved. For if, after a postulation has been strengthened by the subscriptions of those postulating and presented to the Roman pontiff for approval, the petitioners could withdraw from it, they would often deceive us, and our judgment would seem to depend upon their will.]

It could also be added that the other party had not observed the apostolic mandate, inasmuch as it had held neither a unanimous postulation nor a canonical election, since, when its position was stronger than before among not only the canons but even the suffragans, with the king himself favoring the adverse party, it had postulated the aforesaid bishop of Pécs [Col. 0720B].

Having therefore heard these and other matters advanced on either side, and having held diligent deliberation upon them with our brethren, [we understood [Note: [Col. 0719D] Here the Decretals add “therefore.”] that, although neither postulation was to be approved, nevertheless, according to the tenor of the later rescript, provision for the Church of Esztergom henceforth belonged to us. But because we did not have complete knowledge of the persons of that kingdom, and therefore could not, with a safe conscience, suitably provide that Church with another person native to the kingdom of Hungary—and since we were unwilling to set a foreigner over it—although it would have seemed more regular and proper for a suffragan to ascend to his own metropolitan see [Note: [Col. 0720D] The Decretals read “approach.”] than for an archbishop to be transferred from one metropolitan see [Col. 0720C] to another, we nevertheless chose the preferable course. We released that same archbishop, upon whom all those whose consent is required in the election or postulation of a pastor had agreed, though at different times, from the bond by which he was held to the Church of Kalocsa; we transfer him to the metropolitan see of Esztergom and grant him leave to proceed there, intending to send him the pallium in the name and for the use of that Church.]

We therefore earnestly admonish your discretion and command you by apostolic letters to render to that archbishop the reverence and obedience due to him, humbly receive and inviolably observe his salutary admonitions and commands, so that he may be bound to show you a fatherly affection if he finds in you filial [Col. 0720D] devotion, and so that we may deservedly commend your devotion.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of October.

CXL. [Note: [Col. 0720D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, §56.] TO THE CHAPTER OF KALOCSA. He declares that no damage to their rights follows from the archbishop’s transfer. (Rome, the second day before the Ides of October.)

Although necessity has led us to transfer your archbishop to the metropolitan see of Esztergom, we do not wish any prejudice to arise for your church, through such a transfer [Col. 0721A], in its right or dignity. We have therefore decreed that these present letters be granted you as testimony on this matter.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Ides of October.

CXLI. [Note: [Col. 0721D] This letter escaped the diligence of Alteserra and is not found in the Innocentian collection of Decretals published by him at Paris in 1661, folio. It is, however, inserted—though greatly mutilated—in the Gregorian collection of the same Decretals, issued at Paris in folio as early as 1585. See there, col. 1545, book IV, title 17, *Who Are Legitimate Children*, chapter 14, where it is said to be addressed to H. and R. (in the margin, alternatively H. and P.), canons of Benevento. The passages read there [Col. 0722D] are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO HENRY AND VITALIS OF COLLISVACON, CANONS OF BENEVENTO. They are to regard as legitimate a certain person whom the Apostolic See has declared legitimate, and in the pending case concerning his inheritance to proceed according to the tenor of apostolic letters. (Rome, on the Ides of October.)

[From the tenor of your letters, know that it has become known to us [Note: [Col. 0722D] In the Gregorian collection, “has become known”; and immediately afterward “R.” for “Robert,” here and below. That collection omits the portions distinguished by us in italic type.] that, when G . . ., a widow, sought before you—who were hearing the same cause by our delegation—the restoration to herself and to . . . . her ward-son, of the inheritance of Robert, her former husband, from Landulf of Granno [Col. 0721B] and his nephews, together with the fruits received from it, the opposing party endeavored to exclude her claim on the ground that Robert, the widow’s husband, had been born in adultery.] It alleged that the father of the said Robert, while his lawful wife was living, took another woman, named Marucia, in addition to her, and begot the aforesaid Robert, husband of that widow, by her.

The widow’s party, on the contrary, replied that because the aforesaid Marucia, not knowing that Robert’s father had another wife, contracted marriage with him in the face of the Church, the son whom she bore by him ought to be considered legitimate [Col. 0721C], since those not born of a woman knowingly committing adultery are not to be reckoned illegitimate. After the matter had been litigated for a long time before you, and the opinions of several learned men whose counsel you sought differed among themselves on this point, you judged the Apostolic See should be consulted.

We therefore, having understood these and the other matters which you reported to us by letter, and having held diligent deliberation with our brethren, [understanding that the father of the aforesaid Robert had married in the face of the Church the aforesaid Marucia, who was entirely ignorant that he had joined another woman to himself in marriage, and that, while she was considered his lawful wife, he had begotten the said Robert by her, incline rather to favor the offspring, considering the said Robert legitimate in this respect [Col. 0721D].] We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that you too regard him as legitimate and, in other matters, proceed according to the tenor of our letters, after due consideration of the case.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of October.

CXLII. [Note: [Col. 0722D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, §62.] TO P., BISHOP OF WINCHESTER [Note: [Col. 0722D] See letters 4, 5, and 104 of this eighth book.]. He is to correct what needs correction in monasteries and churches subject to him by diocesan law. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 0722A]

A ruler ought to take care diligently that he does not—God forbid—show himself negligent in matters entrusted to his administration, for cursed is the man who performs the work of God negligently. Therefore, that you may more carefully consider, in matters pertaining to your charge, how great is your obligation to correct in your diocese those things which call for the file of correction, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to correct, by apostolic authority, both head and members in the monasteries and other churches subject to you by diocesan law [Col. 0722B], wherever correction according to God is needed. By the counsel of prudent men, take care to alter for the better customs contrary to right and utility, should those immediately responsible for their correction perhaps prove negligent in this regard. Notwithstanding the objection of any appeal against the observance of regular discipline, serve ecclesiastical welfare in such a manner as to advance regular discipline.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLIII. TO THE SAME. He may reclaim property unlawfully alienated. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 0722C] “The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant,” etc., up to “granting”; by the authority of these presents we allow you to lawfully reclaim, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, those things which you find to have been unlawfully alienated by your predecessors from the appurtenances of the episcopal mensa or from other matters belonging to episcopal jurisdiction, whether held in fiefs or otherwise. Therefore let no one . . .

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLIV. TO THE SAME. He may compel archdeacons, deans, etc., to receive orders. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

Since a burden is attached to honor, one who has obtained a benefice ought to perform the office [Col. 0722D]. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if archdeacons, deans, and others of your diocese, after admonition by you, refuse within six months to be ordained to the orders in which they are bound to serve the Lord, you compel them—appeal set aside—to receive those orders in accordance with the decrees of the Lateran Council. Otherwise [Col. 0723A], you may, with appeal ceasing, confer their benefices upon other persons, as is commonly established in that same Council. Therefore let no one.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLV. TO THE SAME. He is to compel those who obtain personates to appoint vicars willing and able to serve personally. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

We have learned that in the diocese of Winchester there are certain persons who, having obtained personates of churches, place vicars in them; although these ought to serve in their own persons [Col. 0723B], they wholly withdraw themselves from the service to which they are bound, and nevertheless presume to receive the benefice of the vicarage, although they have sometimes obtained another sufficient ecclesiastical benefice. These vicars also appoint other vicars in their place; left scantily endowed in ecclesiastical benefice, first by the incumbents and then by the vicars, they are unable adequately to serve the churches themselves. Through such an arrangement, or rather through this wicked trafficking, the good of almsgiving and hospitality is extinguished, to the grave detriment of the prelate and ministers and the scandal of the laity.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce the incumbents of those churches either to compel their principal vicars to serve in them or to appoint others in them [Col. 0723C] who are willing and able to serve personally. If they perhaps refuse to do so, carry this out yourself, the impediment of appeal removed. Opponents, etc. Let no one, etc.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLVI. [Note: [Col. 0723D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §62.] TO THE SAME. He is to correct the offenses of clerics. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

In correcting the offenses of subjects, you must show yourself diligent, lest the blood of those whom you have negligently tolerated in sin, though able to restrain them, be required at your hand. We have learned, moreover, that certain clerics of the diocese of Winchester pursue usury or shameful gain; some are adulterers; some publicly keep concubines [Col. 0723D], or commit other acts contrary to the honor of the clerical order. Therefore we command your brotherhood, expressly by apostolic letters, to strive, supported by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, to restrain such delinquent clerics from their presumption by ecclesiastical coercion; to inflict canonical punishment upon those convicted or confessing in court, and also upon those whose offense is notorious, since manifest offenses require no proof. Take careful care not to be lukewarm in such correction; for where he who has been appointed preacher is silent, failing to rebuke what should be rebuked or correct [Col. 0724A] what should be corrected, he seems to have approved the fault, which, as it grows, is given to others as an example when the shepherd’s tongue does not cut it away.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLVII. TO THE SAME. He is to remove sons of priests. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

Know that it has reached our hearing that many sons of priests in the diocese of Winchester hold churches in which their fathers had most recently ministered, derogating from ecclesiastical dignity and canonical institutions. Therefore, that through the industry of your discretion provision may be made both for ecclesiastical dignity and for the observance of canonical institutions, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0724B] wholly to remove, supported by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, such incumbents as you know immediately succeeded their fathers in the governance of churches within your diocese. Endeavor to provide those churches with other suitable persons, upon presentation by those to whom the appointment belongs. If, however, through favor toward those whom they had presented there, or from malice or their own will, they should refuse, even after frequent admonition, to present suitable persons, then, relying on our authority, proceed according to God in providing for those churches. Opponents, etc.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLVIII. TO THE SAME. He is to prevent the alternation of benefices. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 0724C]

Know that it has been reported to our ears that several persons in the diocese of Winchester, while still retaining churches in their own right, fraudulently arrange with colleagues or laymen holding the right of patronage in those churches that their sons, nephews, foster-children, or any others are called incumbents in those churches and receive a pension of less than a pound of pepper, wax, or a single bezant, or some other small payment. Yet, by fraudulently alternating personates, the former secure for themselves by fraud the reservation of the entire income for as long as they live, and substitute others for themselves at death under the pretext of such a pension. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0724D], by the counsel of prudent men and supported by our authority, to strive to cut off such abuses. Opponents, etc. No letters, etc.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CXLIX. TO . . . , BISHOP OF LONDON [Note: [Col. 0723D] See letter 182 of the seventh book, note.], AND . . . , BISHOP OF WORCESTER [Note: [Col. 0724D] See letter 33 of the eighth book.], AND THE DEAN OF CHICHESTER [Note: [Col. 0724D] See letter 6 of the eighth book, note.]. They are to restore to its proper state what has been altered in the Church of Winchester. (Rome, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

Since our pastoral office requires us to provide diligently that ecclesiastical rights suffer no loss [Col. 0725A] or alteration for the worse, we command your discretion, expressly by apostolic letters, that if anything in the bishopric of Winchester has been introduced anew or changed after the death of G., bishop of Winchester of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0725D] See letter 4 of the eighth book, note.], to the prejudice of episcopal dignity, you are to restore it, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, to its proper state. Opponents—no one, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CL. [Note: [Col. 0725D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, §59.] TO . . . , ARCHBISHOP [Note: [Col. 0725D] See letter 43 of the third book, note.], AND . . . , DEAN [Note: [Col. 0725D] See letters 43 of the third book and 1[.....]2 of the fifth book, note.], AND . . . , ARCHDEACON OF BOURGES [Note: [Col. 0725D] See letter 34 of the fifth book.]. If the Archbishop of Bordeaux refuses to resign pastoral governance, they are to remove him and order the chapter to elect another suitable person as pastor. (Rome, the second day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 0725B]

The Apostolic See has waited and waited for a long time, in case that unfruitful fig tree, namely the Archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0726D] See letters 96, note, 146, and 150 . . . . . . of the fifth book. But this letter of Innocent agrees poorly with what the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* say concerning this prelate, as we have already observed in the note to letter 216 of the sixth book, on the same subject.], might perhaps produce its figs. Like a barren tree luxuriant in leaves and branches, it has hitherto held the mind of its expectant watcher suspended in hope of fruit. For when Pope Clement, our predecessor of pious memory, formerly heard of his barrenness—that, like a wild fig tree, he spread a harmful shade and useless branches over the earth, rendering almost wholly barren what had been accustomed to flourish in a full harvest—he then mercifully spared him, prescribing purification for him: the soil around it was to be dug more deeply with the mattock [Col. 0725C] of correction, and, with a border of dung placed about its root, it was to become fruitful, rising from the abomination of vices to the grace of honorable conduct.

Yet although that archbishop ought to have heeded the kindness shown him, so that, like a tree planted beside streams of water, he might yield in its season the fruit expected of him, after the deep digging and dung placed about the root, he has luxuriated still more in branches and leaves, producing none of the expected fruit; and he has made the ground, more widely occupied beneath the shade of his branches, even more barren. For he has rotted like a beast in its dung; and, like the man who, though placed in honor, did not understand, he has been compared with senseless beasts [Col. 0725D] and made like them. Thus the prophetic saying has been fulfilled in him: “As the people, so the priest” (Isa. XXIV), since one holding spiritual office has done the deeds of an untaught people—or rather has entangled himself in deeds which all who fear the examination of the last judgment shudder to contemplate.

But because we have often heard these things concerning him, and, like a fig tree producing no fruit, he has been waited for not only three but even more years [Col. 0726A], we commanded you to make a careful inquiry whether the matters which we had received concerning his wickedness from the reports of very many persons were true. You, according to what the exigency of the time allowed, caused a diligent inquiry to be made and faithfully reported to us what you found in him. Since, therefore, from that inquiry we have found that archbishop wholly useless and unworthy for pontifical office—one who is to no one a fragrance from life unto life, but to many a stench from death unto death—we command your discretion, expressly by apostolic letters, that unless the archbishop himself, at your admonition, sparing his own shame and considering ecclesiastical honor, should perhaps refuse within two months after receiving these letters to resign [Col. 0726B] the pastoral governance for whose exercise he has for so long been useless and unworthy, you are to cut him down from the ground which he has occupied to no purpose, like a barren tree with the axe laid to its root. Supported by our authority, and without impediment from any opposition or appeal, wholly remove him from the administration of the Church of Bordeaux, and command the chapter of Bordeaux to set another suitable person over itself as pastor by canonical election. If all of you cannot be present to carry this out, you, brother archbishop, shall nevertheless carry it out with one of the others.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of November, in the eighth year.

CLI. TO THE SAME. He is permitted to absolve his servants and clerics of his church from violent laying on of hands. (Rome, the second day before the Ides of November.)

[Col. 0726C]

Having regard to the circumstances of times and places, the rigor of justice ought sometimes to be tempered with gentleness, so that divine compunction may be softened by the mildness of oil and the sinner may not come to the depths and despise. Especially is this so when the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline cannot be exercised without detriment to churches. For, as was alleged before us on your behalf, the servants of your church violently lay hands upon clerics; and you could scarcely induce them, even at your own expense, to come to the Apostolic See to seek the benefit of absolution [Col. 0726D], while it would be detrimental to your church to be deprived in the meantime of their service. Moreover, clerics of your household often violently lay hands upon one another, at the prompting of the enemy of humankind, and you cannot determine who supplied the occasion for the offense. Therefore, since to lack their service is both burdensome and harmful to you, you humbly petitioned us to grant you free power to absolve your servants and clerics.

We therefore, fully trusting in your discretion, grant you by the authority of these presents that, after receiving from them the security prescribed by the Church, you may, supported by our authority, absolve them, provided their offense does not appear grave and enormous. Having imposed upon them what is customarily imposed in such cases, make them give suitable compensation for the labor of the journey [Col. 0727A]. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of November.

CLII. B. [Note: [Col. 0727D]

This probably concerns Berno, or Bruno, whom the authors of the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 1182, col. 2, mention in documents as bishop of Viviers from 1206 until at least 1214.

See also letter 209 of the seventh book and the notes there.] ARCHDEACON OF VIENNE, OUR SUBDEACON. Being elected bishop of Viviers, he is authorized to retain other ecclesiastical benefices besides the archdeaconry of Vienne. (On the Nones of November.)

[Col. 0727B] The kindness of the Apostolic See, carefully directing the eyes of its watchfulness toward its subjects, is accustomed fittingly to extend the aid of provision in order to relieve the need of those who prefer their own advantage to that of their neighbors. Since you have been elected to govern the Church of Viviers, which is said to suffer from poverty, lest the lack of temporal goods force you to succumb under the burden which the need of that church invites you to bear, we have judged it proper to grant you by the authority of these presents that you may freely retain for three years all the ecclesiastical revenues which you possess, except the archdeaconry of the Church of Vienne, and receive higher orders from your metropolitan. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given on the Nones of November, in the eighth year.

CLIII. [Note: [Col. 0727D] This letter is inserted in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §103; it is therefore printed here in brackets. Variant readings are supplied from the *Deeds* and from the frequently cited Vallicellian codex.] TO T., PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE [Note: [Col. 0727D] See above, letters 19 and following of this eighth book.]. He commands him not to delay consecrating the bishop-elect of Patras and investing him with the honor of the pallium. (Rome, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0727C]

[Among the four living creatures which, according to the Apocalypse of John, are described as existing in the midst of the throne and around it, although the eagle is placed after the others [Note: [Col. 0727D] So also in the *Gesta*; in the Vallicellian codex, “is placed before.”], it nevertheless surpasses the rest; for, since by such a throne is signified the Roman Church, which by customary usage is called the Apostolic See, and by the four living creatures—namely, the lion, the calf, the man, and the eagle—are understood the four patriarchal Churches, namely, those of Jerusalem, Antioch, Alexandria [Col. 0727D], and Constantinople, which are contained in the midst of the throne as daughters in their mother’s bosom, and are stationed around the throne as handmaids [Note: [Col. 0728D] So also in the *Gesta*; in the Vallicellian codex, “but particularly.”] in the service of their Lady [Note: [Col. 0728D] So also in the *Gesta*; in the Vallicellian codex, “the Lord making preparation.”]. Although the Church of Constantinople [Col. 0728A] is the latest among the others in time, it is nevertheless foremost among them in dignity; so that, just as Constantinople is called [Note: [Col. 0728D] So also in the Vallicellian codex; in the *Gesta*, “the city of Constantinople.”] New Rome, so the Church of Constantinople may be second after the Roman Church, preferred by the grace of its mother to its other sisters by the privilege of dignity, so that, according to evangelical truth, the last might become [Note: [Col. 0728D] In the *Gesta*, “may be,” and immediately afterwards “therefore” for “accordingly.”] first and the first last.

We therefore, who by the grace of the Redeemer have lately [Note: [Col. 0728D] Omitted in the *Gesta*; in the Vallicellian codex, “always.”] restored that Church of Constantinople to the obedience of the Apostolic See, as to the bosom of its mother, intend to preserve its privilege of dignity intact, lest injuries arise from it—rather, that rights may arise therefrom. And therefore, although our beloved son, the nobleman W. [Note: [Col. 0728D] In the Vallicellian codex, “our man William.”] of Champagne, prince of the whole province of Achaea, and the canons of Saint Andrew [Col. 0728B] of Patras, urgently and humbly petitioned us to deign to grant them our beloved son A., elected of Saint Andrew’s at Patras, who had come to the Apostolic See and whom those same canons had unanimously elected archbishop of that church; and, approving what had been done concerning his person, to send him back to them [Note: [Col. 0728D] In the Vallicellian codex, “and him.”] with full honor [Note: [Col. 0728D] Omitted in the *Gesta* and the Vallicellian codex.]; yet, wishing so to admit their petitions that we should not appear in any way to deprive others of their rights, by common counsel of our brethren we have not thought fit to approve what was done by those canons, as having been arranged less than canonically, since they themselves were instituted less than canonically.

But, having weighed both necessity and advantage, after we had been made more certain of the truth of the matter and of the state of the land through the oaths [Col. 0728C] of the associates of that same elect, by the power granted us by the Lord in blessed Peter we have appointed him pastor and rector of that church, granting him full administration both in spiritual and temporal matters [Note: [Col. 0728D] Omitted in the *Gesta* and the Vallicellian codex.], and moreover permitting, as a precaution, that he may, when necessary, have himself ordained priest by any Catholic bishop.

Although, by the fullness of power which, by the Lord’s disposition, we possess over all churches, we could have sent him back to that same Church invested with the gift of consecration and the honor of the pallium, yet, because we have so called you to a share in our solicitude that we have retained for ourselves the fullness of power, and do injury to no one when we use our own right, nevertheless wishing to show deference especially to you, to whom the Church of Patras is known to be subject, in the beginning of your tenure, we have thought fit to send him back to you. Thus, consecrated by you, or by another at your command [Col. 0729A], as archbishop and adorned with the honor of the pallium [Note: [Col. 0729C] In the *Gesta* and the Vallicellian codex, “having received the honor.”], he may acknowledge you as his chief father after the Roman pontiff. We give instructions in our letters to our beloved son B. [Note: [Col. 0729C] In the *Gesta* and the Vallicellian codex, “Benedict.”], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna [Note: [Col. 0729C] See letter 55 of Book VIII.], legate of the Apostolic See, that he shall cause what we have set forth concerning this man’s person to be carried out, any appeal being set aside. Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command your brotherhood not to delay investing him with the gift of consecration and the honor of the pallium, lest through your failure—God forbid!—he be compelled to have recourse to us.]

Given at Rome, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.

CLIV. . . . TO THE BISHOP OF ROCHESTER [Note: [Col. 0729C]

After the death in 1184 of Waleran, bishop of Rochester, Gilbert de Glanville was given as his successor. Formerly archdeacon of Lisieux, he was elected at Otford on 16 July 1185, ordained priest at Lambeth on 21 September, and consecrated at Canterbury by Archbishop Baldwin on the twenty-ninth of the same month. Four years later, when Baldwin set out on his journey [Col. 0729D] to the Holy Land, “the bishop of Rochester, from ancient times the archbishop’s vicar, undertook pastoral care both in the territory of Kent and in the churches of the archbishop’s manors.” Diceto, *Imagines Historiarum*, p. 615.

In 1195 he was appointed the king’s justiciar from October until the following May. Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 246, note (f), on Edmund of Hadenham, *Annals of the Church of Rochester*.

Great lawsuits and disputes arose between him and his monks. (For these, see Edmund of Hadenham in Wharton, cited place.) Death at last ended the long contest, as it ends all mortal things—namely, the death of the bishop, who died on 24 June 1214, according to Matthew Paris, likewise according to the *Florilegus* and the Canterbury Obituary. See also Goswin, *On the Prelates of England*, p. 528.]

AND . . . TO THE BISHOP OF LONDON [Note: [Col. 0729D] See letter 182 of Book VII, note.] AND . . . TO THE PRIOR OF SAINT ALBAN [Note: [Col. 0729D] The prior of the monastery of St Albans at that time was Raymond: “a man,” as Matthew Paris says (*Lives of the Twenty-Three Abbots of St Albans*, p. 103), [Col. 0730C] “of great judgment, prudence, and piety, to whom Abbot John (for whom see letter 212 of Book VI, note) entrusted the reins of external affairs to govern. . . . Through his industry and lawful acquisition there was made the great table which stands before the high altar of the Church of St Albans. . . . Distinguished and very useful books were written, especially the *Scholastic History with Allegories*, a most elegant book. . . . p. 115. Later William, the abbot, removed this man—than whom at that time no hooded monk of the Order of St Benedict was greater—so that he might reign alone and feel no obstacle or hear anyone’s contradiction. For he knew that, if he had subdued the greater man, the rest would be more silent through fear; and he sent him, unwilling and indeed disgraced, to the cell of Tynemouth, the monks’ customary [Col. 0730D] place of exile. . . . p. 116. And in his place he substituted Master Walter of Reims.” We conjecture that this occurred about the year 1216.] OF THE DIOCESE OF LONDON. He commits to them a case concerning the church of Faversham, pending between the abbot of St Augustine’s and the archdeacon of Canterbury. (Rome, eleventh day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0729B]

O. de Camera, parson [Note: [Col. 0730D] This was the name used in England for rectors of parish churches.] of the church of Faversham [Note: [Col. 0730D] In the Decretals, “of Fan.”; and shortly afterwards the words “beloved son” are omitted.], having entered upon the way of all flesh, our beloved son . . . the abbot of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury, entered into possession of that church—which he asserts belongs to him—first through certain monks and secondly in person; and he repeatedly raised to us the voice of appeal, lest anyone should presume unlawfully to molest him concerning possession of that church. And although he had for some time possessed the said church peacefully, certain laymen of the diocese of Canterbury, laying rash and violent hands upon [Note: [Col. 0730D] Omitted in the Decretals, as also shortly below: “them.”] the abbot and monks within that church, even to the shedding of blood [Col. 0730A], violently ejected them from possession of that [Note: [Col. 0730D] The Decretals add “church.”] church.

Therefore, having heard of the cruelty of the said laymen, and wishing with paternal concern to provide for the abbot and monks in respect of so great an injury inflicted upon them, we gave firm instructions to our venerable brother the bishop of Ely [Note: [Col. 0730D] See letter 90 of Book V.] and his fellow judges: if the facts were as stated, they were publicly to denounce the laymen and their accomplices and order all persons most strictly to avoid them until they had made suitable satisfaction for the injury suffered, and had presented themselves before the Apostolic See with testimonial letters of their own. By our authority, under threat of anathema, they were also most strictly to prohibit anyone, in cities, towns, villages, or other places to which [Col. 0730B] those men might come, from presuming in their presence to celebrate divine offices, except the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, or from exchanging anything with them under the pretext of any contract whatever.

Moreover, we added to the mandate that, after removing from the same church every unlawful holder there, notwithstanding anyone’s command and with the obstacle of appeal removed, they should restore and maintain the aforesaid abbot and monks in the state in which they had been before the violence was committed. Meanwhile, the dean of the place, by the introduction of the laymen who had violently expelled the monks, obtained possession of that church; afterwards our beloved son, the archdeacon of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0730D] Was this Henry de Sandford, whom we know certainly to have been raised in 1227 from the archdeaconry of Canterbury to the bishopric of Rochester? See the *Fragment on the Institution of the Archdeaconry of Canterbury*, from the Cottonian Library, Tiberius C. 9, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 150, where several matters are found which it will be worthwhile to compare with this letter of Innocent.], began to possess the same church and, converting its revenues to his own use, still, as is said, persists [Col. 0730C] in that possession.

Accordingly, when the procurator of the said abbot urgently sought before the aforesaid judges the restitution of the said Church [Col. 0731A], after removal from it of the aforesaid archdeacon who unlawfully detained it, so many exceptions were raised on both sides, so many delays granted, and so many evasive devices invented, that, after a very long period had elapsed from the time of the commission and the case had not received due progress, the aforesaid abbot and monks sought and obtained other letters from us. In these, reproving those same judges because they had yielded so far to vexatious appeals and frivolous exceptions that the case had still been unable to proceed before their tribunal—and consequently the abbot and monks had been compelled to endure not only serious injuries and heavy losses but also labors and expenses—we strictly commanded those judges, setting aside all favor and [Col. 0731B] fear, to remove every obstacle of contradiction and appeal; to compel the opposing party by ecclesiastical coercion immediately to join issue; and, within two months after joinder of issue, to receive and examine the witnesses whom either party might seek to produce, whether on the principal matter or on any incidental issue. If they could not attend in person, they were nevertheless to carry this out through others from whom no appeal could in any way be made. Once the testimony had been received, they were to appoint the parties a suitable term at which they should appear before us to receive judgment.

Having received this later mandate, the same judges expedited the business according to its tenor. When issue had been joined and witnesses admitted, they finally, after publication of the testimony, appointed a day for the parties to appear before us to receive judgment in the matter; and, as they had been commanded, they sent us the depositions, proceedings, and also other materials which seemed relevant to the case, enclosed under their seals [Col. 0731C].

At the appointed term our beloved son . . . monk, procurator of the abbot and monks of Saint Augustine’s, came to the Apostolic See and, by our command, waited almost three months for the procurator of the other party. At last, when both had appeared before us, the aforesaid monk alleged that, while the abbot and monks, as stated above, enjoyed peaceful possession of the Church of Faversham, they were violently ejected from it after an appeal lawfully and repeatedly lodged with us [Col. 0731D]. He therefore most urgently requested that, every unlawful holder having been removed from it, we should deign to restore them to possession of that church, together with the fruits both received and to be received, including those reckoned from the time of the ejection.

He also claimed expenses of forty marks and more, which the abbot and monks had been compelled to incur on account of certain exceptions frivolously raised by the archdeacon’s procurator and the appropriate delays required to prove them; yet the same archdeacon [Col. 0732A], or his procurator, afterwards did not prove those exceptions. For the aforesaid O. de Camera had possessed the said church in another’s name, since he paid the abbot and monks of Saint Augustine’s a fixed annual rent for it; and, since it had also been proved by several witnesses that, after O. the physician was removed from the scene and until O. de Camera was substituted, the abbot of Saint Augustine’s had had custody of the aforesaid Church, that possession continued after the death of the said O. de Camera, since the monks immediately took it into their possession after his death.

Furthermore, since that same abbot possessed the church, and had appealed both before the ejection and afterwards, nothing ought to have been changed while the appeal was pending. Nor, he said, was it an objection that the archdeacon is alleged to have acted in order to preserve his own right; for, since a question had already been raised on this point and the abbot’s side had denied that he possessed such jurisdiction, the matter became doubtful by reason of that denial. Therefore he could not be judge, since he had already become an adversary; and consequently, because he presumed to pronounce the law for himself in his own cause, he ought deservedly to suffer prejudice from his act, and the matter should be restored to its former state.

When these and many other matters had been alleged on behalf of the abbot and monks, [the procurator of the said archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Decretals omit this word, as below they also omit the words “nor . . . which.”] alleged in reply that the abbot and monks could seek this restitution neither on the ground of possession nor on that of ownership. For they had not possessed the aforesaid church by right of custody [Col. 0732C], which, when the parson of a church dies [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Decretals add “to the archdeacon”; shortly afterwards they omit “of Canterbury,” and below “of the province of Canterbury.”], is granted only to the archdeacon of Canterbury; and the archdeacons of Canterbury for the time being had always exercised this right, both by common law and by the general custom of the province of Canterbury, in that church as in every other church of the same diocese, as had been sufficiently proved. Such restitution therefore did not at all belong to the monks, nor did the archdeacon appear, in exercising his own right, to have done them an injury [Note: [Col. 0732D] The Decretals omit this passage; shortly afterwards, for “possessed,” they read “possessed that same [church]”; they do not have the word “its,” and read “paid” for “rendered.”].
