Furthermore, since the aforesaid O. de Camera possessed in the archdeacon’s name, inasmuch as he paid him annually one procuration and five shillings in the name of that church, when the same O. was removed from the scene, possession is known to have remained with the archdeacon for a year. That possession is not lost unless the archdeacon believed himself capable of being repelled, or unless, when he came, he was not admitted. Thus the monks’ possession ought rather to be called clandestine detention, since the archdeacon did not lose that possession and the monks therefore could not have it, because two persons cannot possess anything wholly and independently.

Accordingly, since the archdeacon could by his right enter into possession and eject the holders in fact, he could still more readily, when no one was present or offering any resistance, reserve his own right to himself, since the execution of a right is recognized to involve no injury. Moreover, the monks cannot in any way dislodge the archdeacon from possession [Col. 0733A], even if it were established that they had possessed it; for, since he did not in any way eject them from possession, and this was neither proved nor confessed in law, they have nothing to allege against an outside holder—especially since they themselves entered into possession by their own authority and, by injuring another, could not acquire any right for the monastery.

The appeal which the monks claim to have lodged was altogether void, since an appeal may be made only from a present, past, or future grievance. But the archdeacon had neither previously aggrieved them nor aggrieved them after the appeal, since he is known to have undertaken custody of a vacant church which he has the right—indeed, is bound by office—to guard. Finally, no deference at all was due to the monks’ appeal [Col. 0733B], because, even if that church belonged to them, they still ought not to have entered into its possession by their own authority, especially as they knew, or rather ought to have known, that custody of vacant churches belonged to the archdeacon, and that, if the same archdeacon had then been present, he would have refused it to them and would have held it for himself, as belonged to his office. Therefore, since their possession was clandestine, they could not be accounted true possessors, since no injury can be done regarding possession to a clandestine possessor.

Accordingly, when these and many other matters had been alleged on both sides before us, after examining the parties’ documents and depositions and carefully considering their allegations, by common counsel of our brethren [Note: [Col. 0733D] The Decretals read: “therefore, after the foregoing had been carefully examined, [we decree] the aforesaid”; shortly afterwards they read “to either party” for “of either [property],” and “we decree” for “we decreed”; they add “received” after “time,” and read “to be assigned” for “to be restored.”], saving the right of ownership of either party, we decreed that the abbot and monks [Col. 0733C] should be restored to the state in which they are known to have been at the time of the appeal lawfully lodged with us for plausible and probable reasons; and we likewise judged that the fruits of the intervening period should be restored to them.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretions that, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, you restore the aforesaid abbot and monks to the state in which they are known to have been at the time of the appeal, and cause all fruits of the intervening period likewise to be restored to them; restraining any opponents or rebels, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

[Col. 0733D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

CLV. . . . TO THE BISHOP OF ROCHESTER [Note: [Col. 0733D] See the note to the immediately preceding letter.], AND . . . TO THE BISHOP OF LONDON [Note: [Col. 0733D] Ibid., note.], AND . . . TO THE PRIOR OF SAINT ALBAN [Note: [Col. 0733D] Ibid., note.] OF THE DIOCESE OF LONDON. On the same matter as in the preceding letter, and ordering them to compel the archdeacon of Canterbury to restore a certain altar. (Rome, eighth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0734A]

When formerly we committed to you, brother bishop of London, and to our venerable brother . . . bishop of Ely [Note: [Col. 0733D] See letter 91 of Book V.], and to our beloved son . . . abbot of Saint Edmund’s [Note: [Col. 0734D] See letter 90 of Book V, note.], the case pending between, on the one hand, our beloved son . . . the abbot and monks of Saint Augustine’s and, on the other, . . . the archdeacon of Canterbury, concerning a certain altar which that archdeacon had caused to be demolished in the Church of Faversham, and other matters: because the parties had not consented to your proceeding to a definitive judgment, you sent the sufficiently prepared case to the Apostolic See [Col. 0734B], appointing the parties a fixed term at which they should appear before us.

When their procurators had therefore appeared before us, and we had carefully understood what they alleged, and had also examined the depositions and other documents which you took care to send us, desiring to deal more leniently, by common counsel of our brethren, with that archdeacon—who, in excuse of his act, alleged a mandate of the late . . . archbishop of Canterbury, examples from the Old Testament, and the general custom of the English Church—although the monks had celebrated at the altar which the archdeacon caused to be demolished after a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against them, yet because that sentence is known to have been preceded by a lawful appeal [Col. 0734C], we decreed that the same archdeacon should be condemned to make good the damages which the said Church of Faversham is known to have suffered in the demolition of the altar, the breaking of the chalice, and the burning of the cloths.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretions to compel the aforesaid archdeacon, if necessary, by ecclesiastical censure, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal having been removed, to make that restoration.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

CLVI. TO THE BISHOP OF FLORENCE [Note: [Col. 0734D]

At that time, if Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. III, col. 137, is to be believed, the Florentine see was held by John.

“XXXIII. John, a regular canon of Velletri, while serving as prior of St Fridianus at Lucca, was transferred to the Church of Florence after Peter’s death in 1205. He survived in that dignity for twenty-five years and died in 1230. . . . He was a prelate of the highest esteem and of singular prudence in conducting affairs; among his other distinguished achievements, he at last also brought it about that the clergy should be led back to the ancient and venerable manner of life.”

These and other matters are found in Ughelli. Yet there is a difficulty, which we touched upon above in letter 50 of Book VI; see what we noted there.]

. That he receive the canons’ witnesses in the case pending between the bishop and chapter of Volterra. (Rome, fifth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0734D]

We have learned from the letters of your brotherhood that, in the case pending between our venerable brother . . . [Col. 0735A] bishop [Note: [Col. 0735D] Ildebrandus de Pannochieschi, or, as others maintain, del Pannochia, succeeded Ugo as bishop of Volterra in 1184. Since he bore great spirit by reason of the nobility of his family, he soon seized the lordship of Volterra and was declared prince of the Holy Empire by Emperor Frederick in 1185. In most difficult times he exercised remarkable skill, seeming to obtain most easily from popes no less than emperors whatever he had determined upon in mind. Ildebrandus must have been of great name and great esteem among all, since in Etruria matters thought to concern either peace or war were almost settled at his discretion. From documents it is inferred that he lived until the year 1209 and survived only a little longer thereafter. UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, part I, col. 353.], on the one side, and the canons of Volterra, on the other, which case has been committed to you by the Apostolic See, the canons wish to produce as witnesses certain persons from among themselves, and this is opposed to them. On the other hand, you appear to doubt whether you may admit the canons as witnesses in the same case. Therefore, since only one of those canons has been appointed procurator in the case, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood not to omit receiving such witnesses as shall be produced for them from among the canons, proceeding in the case according to the tenor of our letters.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

CLVII. [Note: [Col. 0735D] Fragments of this letter were published by Angelus [Col. 0736C] Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, vol. III, p. 454, col. 1 ff., under the year 1205, chapter 7, §1 ff.; there he seems not to have known which monastery is concerned in this letter of Innocent. (See the following notes.) What is read there is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE BISHOP OF FERRARA [Note: [Col. 0736C] See letter 39 of Book III, note.], AND TO . . . THE ABBOT OF COLUMBA, AND TO . . . THE ARCHDEACON OF VERONA. That they establish a definite rule for the monastery of Castanasio. (Rome, seventh day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0735B]

When formerly we had instructed our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Proculus, to investigate more diligently the truth concerning the condition of the brothers and sisters of Castanasio—about whom certain unfavorable reports had reached us, while others, conversely, commended their manner of life—and to notify us by letter of what he found, he, a diligent executor of our command, went to the place with certain prudent men. Having remained there for two days, he investigated carefully, through the report of the neighborhood and through examination of the brothers and sisters, after receiving their oath, concerning matters which the nature of the affair required. Returning also to Bologna, he sought, under the sanctity of an oath, to elicit the truth from certain persons who had departed from that place and were said [Col. 0735C] by some to have “looked back”; and, having set down in writing the depositions of all, he sent them under his seal to the Apostolic See by his own messenger.

But our beloved son, Al., a priest, who had gathered the brothers and sisters at Castanasio, after the depositions of the witnesses had been received but not yet sent into our presence, approached the abbot and suggested [Col. 0736A] to him that a certain woman who had testified against him, in order to defame himself and the place, had confessed herself perjured. He therefore humbly requested that her confession be written down for us; and, since he was unable in any way to obtain this, he presented himself before us together with most of his brothers and sisters.

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] These words occur in Manrique.]

We therefore, having examined the depositions received by the abbot, questioned them ourselves, so that the truth might emerge more fully, and caused them to wait for some time at the Apostolic See. We heard, however, something hitherto unheard by us and not readily believable by any faithful person:

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] “In this same year, something hitherto unheard of—if we believe Innocent, the supreme pontiff—which had greatly disturbed him and exercised our own people, the Cistercians, to whose judgment it was at length referred. Namely, etc.” Angelus Manrique, cited place. See below.]

namely, that after brothers and sisters come to that place and humbly confess their own offenses with contrite heart, striving [Col. 0736B] to expiate them through works of penance, they are bodily seized and tormented by demons; they utter profane and blasphemous cries; for a time they become numb in matters of piety and interrupt divine worship; and they sometimes feel, as they say, a certain frightful sensation in their limbs, as though mice were running between flesh and skin, and behold certain dreadful, dark images.

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] Manrique omits these words.]

What we judge worse is that they do not grieve over such a scourge, but rather rejoice in it; and, considering those who are tormented to possess greater religious merit, they glory in such torments.

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] “Thus the same pontiff speaks of an event then recent and so astonishing that it could not lightly have disturbed him. Yet, although he does not define what he thinks of these matters, he nevertheless privately expresses it in the following words: ‘We know,’ etc.” Angelus Manrique, cited place. See below.]

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] Up to this point Manrique.]

They perhaps perversely understand the Apostle’s saying about himself: “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me. Because of this I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and [Col. 0736C] he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.’” And immediately he adds: “I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12).

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] Manrique again.]

We know from reading the divine page of Scripture—

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] In Manrique: “the divine Scripture.”]

—that our adversary, the devil, who “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour,” not only spreads his nets against those beginning to become accustomed to the Lord’s yoke, but sometimes [Col. 0737A] even lays his hand upon the strong, in order, if possible, to lead the elect into error, trusting that Jordan may flow into his mouth. Therefore Solomon warns us to beware his snares when he says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your heart for temptation” (Ecclus. 2).

> [Note: [Col. 0737C] Manrique reads: “See,” and below reads *for each* in place of *whence*.]

We know also that the children of Israel, having left Egypt, desired Egypt’s riches in the wilderness, in which they were most severely attacked by the Amalekites. We know that Job, a just and upright man, fearing God and withdrawing from evil, did not escape the devil’s temptations; and that Satan not only demanded the apostles in order to sift them, but also tempted Jesus Christ after his baptism and fast.

But we do not know, nor do we remember having read, that anyone, after true repentance and while devoted to works of piety, has been bodily tormented [Col. 0737B] in this way. We indeed read that many, previously possessed by demons, were freed by the Lord. We know that the Church has instituted a sure remedy against such torments: namely, exorcisms, the oil of the sick, and blessed water. Who, then, could believe that after bitter contrition of heart, true confession of the mouth, and fruitful satisfaction in deed—which chiefly consists in fasting and prayer—anyone would be bodily tormented by a demon? On the contrary, Truth declares in the Gospel that this kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.

Far be this from the Catholic faith! Far be it that the temple of God should be a dwelling-place of the devil, and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit a demon’s den! For there is no fellowship of light with darkness, [Col. 0737C] nor concord of Christ with Belial. We acknowledge, therefore, that holy men are sometimes outwardly assailed by demons, as Job was; but we deny that they are inwardly tormented as demoniacs. For the testimony of Truth is true; nor can he who did no sin, in whose mouth no deceit was found, be convicted of falsehood. He himself declares in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). How, then, would a demon dare to inhabit one in whom the Father and Son choose and make their dwelling?

We therefore consider this alleged matter a fabrication—unless perhaps such people are tormented precisely because they glory in such torments; or unless, because they lead an excessively austere life, having become mad they take a manic disorder for demonic [Col. 0738A] torment.

> [Note: [Col. 0737C–D] “These are Innocent’s words. Although they ought not to be regarded as infallible because they were spoken privately, it cannot be denied that they were spoken with the greatest gravity. He considered the matter of such weight that he immediately judged it worthy of personal investigation. Hence, immediately—indeed, at the beginning; see above—he says in the same letter: ‘We therefore,’ etc. Judgment in this most serious matter was expected from Innocent himself, who would define as pontiff what he had set forth initially as a teacher and pronounce a final sentence. But since the matter, argued and examined on both sides, did not admit an easy solution and a definition did not seem pressing, the judges decided to delegate the cause. Two men were selected from Italy, distinguished in piety and learning: namely, the bishop of Ferrara and the abbot of Columba. Innocent charged them that, etc.” Angelus Manrique, cited place.]

Wishing, however, to recall them to what is good, insofar as lies within us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters—

> [Note: [Col. 0737D] Manrique omits these words.]

—that, going to the place, you establish there a definite rule, approving what you see should be approved and correcting what you find should be corrected. Among other provisions, establish especially that sisters are not to live together with brothers, but are rather to reside separately; and that, in order that such torment may cease, special prayer is to be made to the Lord each day. We further command that it be established among [Col. 0738B] them that, if anyone henceforth is bodily tormented by a demon, or says that he is tormented, he is immediately to be removed from that place and placed elsewhere to do penance. If they are neither cured nor corrected even thus, notify us by your letters, so that we may divide such a community.

> [Note: [Col. 0737D–0738D] “Thus far Innocent, addressing in that case the abbot of Columba and his colleague. These matters, which it was not permissible for us,” says the author of the *Cistercian Annals* [Col. 0738C], “to pass over, I leave to the judgment of others whether they should be extended to similar cases.” Angelus Manrique, cited place.]

Moreover, on our behalf admonish our venerable brother, the bishop of Bologna . . .; and, if necessary, compel him by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to cease meanwhile from molesting them. But if not all . . . you, brother bishop, together with the other of them, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the seventh day before the Kalends of December [25 November].

## CLVIII. To the bishop of Basle

> [Note: [Col. 0738D] After Hugh II, in 1172, the authors of the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 354, col. 2, letter C, mention Lupold, or Lutold, or Lutolf, as bishop of Basle immediately after him, but only in the year 1207.
>
> Bucelinus, however, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 57, col. 1, reports that Leutold, lord of Rötteln, immediately succeeded Henry of Horneberg—called Homburg by some—who died during the expedition to the Holy Land in A.D. 1189, and that Leutold died in A.D. 1213.]

And to the abbot of Salem.

> [Note: [Col. 0738D] See letters of Book V, no. 99, note, and Book VII, no. 89.]

That, upon going to the monastery of Reichenau, they are to ensure the election of a suitable person as abbot.

> [Note: [Col. 0738D] This letter of Innocent must certainly be compared with what is said concerning Diethelm, bishop of Constance and at the same time abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, in the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, cols. 915 and 989, and in Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 10, col. 1. See also Book VII, letter 39.]

(5 December.)

[Col. 0738C]

Since the monastery of Reichenau, which belongs to the Roman pontiff without the intervention of any . . . bishop of Constance, was formerly entrusted for a fixed period to certain of our predecessors, it is now necessary, since that period has expired, that provision be made for that monastery through a suitable person. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command [Col. 0739A] and enjoin your discretion that, as you value the grace of God and ours, you both go together to that place and diligently admonish and induce the brothers of that monastery, after invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, to endeavor, together with you, to set over themselves as abbot such a man as knows how to benefit rather than to rule, and under whose governance the monastery itself may, with the Lord’s help, prosper both spiritually and temporally.

But if perhaps they wish to set over themselves as abbot either no one or a person insufficiently suitable, you are to endeavor, within a month after you have caused them to be admonished, to provide that monastery with a suitable person, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction or appeal and restraining any opponents by ecclesiastical [Col. 0739B] censure, without appeal.

Given on the Nones of December [5 December].

## CLIX. To C., cardinal priest, and the clergy of Saint Lawrence in Lucina

> [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Book III, letter 31, note.]

A certain settlement between them is confirmed. (Rome, the seventh day before the Ides of December [7 December].)

At your request for restoration of obedience concerning the chapter, scrutiny, and baptism—which, you asserted, had been withheld from you by the chaplains of Saint Mary of Posterula, Saint Blaise, and Saints Cosmas and Damian of Monte Granatorum—our beloved sons G., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis,

> [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Book V, letter 60, note.]

. . . rector of the church [Col. 0739C] of Saint Apollinaris, and its clergy, to whose temporal jurisdiction the said churches undoubtedly belong, undertook to oppose your claim in their defense. After the suit had therefore been joined, and testimony had been received and published on both sides, you at last came to an amicable agreement: namely, that restoration concerning scrutiny and baptism shall be made to you, saving the question of ownership, both concerning these matters and concerning the chapter, since the litigation has been in a possessory, not a proprietary, action only.

We therefore, holding the aforesaid settlement to be valid, as it was prudently made in our presence, confirm it by apostolic authority. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, the seventh day before the Ides of December [7 December].

## CLX. To the abbot and convent of Saint Peter de la Couture, in the diocese of Le Mans

All pensions granted or promised by R., former abbot, are annulled. (Rome, the second day before the Kalends of December [30 November].)

[Col. 0740A]

If, according to the Apostle’s command, one is bound to bear another’s burdens, we, who by the Lord’s disposition have undertaken the care of all and each, are bound to relieve the burdens of those known to have suffered grievous loss through the presumptuous audacity of a pastor. Therefore, since, as we have learned from the tenor of your letters, R.,

> [Note: [Col. 0739D] The incomplete series of abbots of this monastery given by the authors of the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 322, col. 1, letter D, identifies no abbot of Saint Peter de la Couture in the diocese of Le Mans who might be designated by the initial R. Between Andrew, mentioned as abbot in 1152, and Guy, in 1244, it lists the names of ten abbots, but without any chronological indication.]

formerly abbot of your monastery, who has been removed from administration of the abbey because his conduct so deserved, [Col. 0740B] gravely burdened your monastery with pensions which he granted to many persons, under the name of non-vacant benefices, contrary to the decrees of the Lateran Council, and promised non-vacant churches to many persons. Desiring to provide for you with paternal solicitude, we decree void and without effect such grants of pensions and promises of non-vacant benefices, attempted by the aforesaid R. contrary to the statutes of the said council. We strictly forbid anyone henceforth to presume to molest you on the ground of such grants and promises. Let no one, therefore, violate our prohibition, etc.

Given at Rome, the second day before the Kalends of December [30 November].

## CLXI. To the abbot of Saint Alban’s of the diocese of Lincoln, the abbot of Reading of the diocese of Salisbury, and the dean of Saint Paul’s, London

> [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §§61–62, although he does not cite this letter specifically.]

> [Note: [Col. 0739D] See Book VI, letter 214, note.]

> [Note: [Col. 0739D] This probably concerns the abbot of Reading Abbey, formerly a convent of nuns but given to Cluniac monks in the reign of King Henry I, in 1125. See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 417.
>
> The abbot of this monastery at the time was probably Elias, who had been blessed in 1200. See the *Annals of the Church of Worcester*, under the year 1200, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 479.]

That they are to hear witnesses concerning the case of the elected archbishop of Canterbury.

> [Note: [Col. 0740D] For the subject of this letter Matthew Paris must certainly be consulted, vol. I, p. 212, where he supplies another letter of Innocent, dated on the sixth day before the Ides of December in this very eighth year of his pontificate, which you will seek in vain in the Registers.
>
> See also the *Deeds of Innocent*, §131.]

(11 December.)

[Col. 0740C]

When our beloved sons Solomon, Gualter, Simon, Roger, and W., monks of the Church of Canterbury, had come to the Apostolic See and humbly requested confirmation of the election, made unanimously by them of the person of our beloved son . . ., subprior of the same church,

> [Note: [Col. 0740D] Matthew Paris, in the cited passage, calls him Reginald.]

as appeared more clearly from the decree of the brothers, our beloved son Master Peter of Englesham, acting on behalf of the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury, opposed their request, asserting that they had proceeded in that election in such a way [Col. 0740D] that it ought not merely to be denied confirmation but declared void. When the monks attempted to exclude him because he showed no mandate of procuration, he replied [Col. 0741A] that in the province of Lombardy, at the city of Parma, he had been stripped of both his letter of mandate and other belongings; but he was ready to furnish adequate security that the said suffragans would hold ratified and valid whatever he did in this case.

Although the monks endeavored to show that such security ought not to be admitted on this point, nevertheless, having weighed the advantage and necessity of the parties, and since there was plausible doubt about the mandate, we admitted the same master as an opponent of the election. First, however, we received from him security of one thousand marks; and, by our permission, our venerable brother . . ., bishop of Winchester, and Master John,

> [Note: [Col. 0741D] See Book VIII, letter 104, note.]

canon of Saint [Col. 0741B] Paul’s, London, bound themselves with him for the same penalty, so that the suffragans themselves would firmly observe whatever he did in this matter.

While the aforesaid monks pressed for confirmation of the said election, as one unanimously held by the entire convent of the Church of Canterbury, the said master appeared to attack it on several grounds: first, because after a lawful appeal had been made to us, it had not so much been held as presumptuously undertaken; second, because the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury had been disregarded in the election, since such an election cannot or ought not to be made without them—indeed, except together with them. He invoked common law and ancient custom, and alleged that the monks had agreed to a truce with the bishops for negotiations concerning the election until the feast [Col. 0741C] of Saint Andrew, which they had not feared to anticipate without consulting the bishops. He further requested restoration as if of possession, asserting that the said suffragans had been rashly dispossessed in this matter.

Although, on the other side, privileges of our predecessors and of ourselves, together with some other documents, were shown to you, and although many arguments in fact and law were adduced, we eagerly wished to end such a controversy, which cannot be prolonged further without grave loss to the parties. But because full confidence could not be placed in certain allegations advanced on either side, with the common counsel of our brothers we issued an interlocutory ruling [Col. 0741D] that the witnesses whom each party chooses to produce are to be sent to the Apostolic See by the coming Kalends of May [1 May], unless some of them are infirm or elderly, whose bodily weakness excuses them from such a burden. Concerning these, we ordered that they be examined by you in England and that their depositions, enclosed under your seals, be transmitted to us within the stated term.

Accordingly, by our letters we commanded the said suffragans to send to the Apostolic See within the stated term, setting aside excuse, appeal, and delay, all witnesses whom they choose to produce in this case, together with documents and arguments. They are to provide that, if the aforesaid infirmity prevents any persons from coming to us, they may, if they wish, produce them before you, so that their depositions may be presented to us within the same [Col. 0742B] term. They are also to inform us by their letters whether they wish to ratify what has been done in this case by the aforesaid master; and, if they do not wish to ratify it, to ensure that suitable procurators are sent to us within the stated term. These are to come, putting aside every evasion, so fully instructed that, so far as they are concerned, nothing may prevent this business from obtaining its due conclusion through us, with the Lord’s help.

Otherwise, since in the administration of justice there must be neither favoritism nor selection of persons, thereafter, giving heed not to honor but to God, we shall take care, with God’s help, to make such provision for the Church of Canterbury as law permits, so that it may henceforth enjoy the desired tranquility. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command [Col. 0742C] your discretion diligently to examine the witnesses whom either party chooses to produce before you and transmit their depositions, enclosed under your seals, to us within the aforesaid term. But the witnesses, etc.

Given at Saint Peter’s, the third day before the Ides of December [11 December].

## CLXII. To the bishop of Florence

> [Note: [Col. 0741D] This letter is found, but very mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book III, title 24, “On Donations,” chapter 5. What is found there is enclosed here in brackets. Passages set in italic type and not indicating variant readings are absent from the *Decretals*.]

> [Note: [Col. 0741D] See Book VIII, letter 156, and the note there.]

That he is to restore the fief to certain nobles who had stood by the Church during the schism. (Rome, the second day before the Ides of December [12 December].)

[You have endeavored to set before us in your letters that certain Florentines, noble and powerful men, [Col. 0742D] prompt in service and devoted, during the time of the schism sheltered in their house Julius, bishop of Florence, of good memory,

> [Note: [Col. 0741D]
>
> These matters must certainly be compared with what Ughellus says concerning the succession of Florentine bishops, *Italia sacra*, vol. III, col. 127.
>
> **XXIX.** Julius succeeded Ambrose in 1158. Borghini doubts whether this Julius is the same as that other Julius who, after this man, occupied the see after Zenobius [Col. 0742D]. But since the tenure of these two falls during the schism between Alexander and Victor the false pope, it must be said that there was only one Julius: first intruded through imperial favor, then, after reconciliation, restored to his seat after Zenobius, the true bishop, having been cleansed from excommunication. This occurred in 1174, the very year in which Zenobius died; Julius then lived until 1181, unless we prefer to affirm this very fact of Zenobius. For Louis Cavitellus, after recounting that schism in the *Annals of Cremona*, also narrates and enumerates the bishops deposed by Alexander, including a Florentine bishop whose name he does not disclose; and this consequently gives cause [Col. 0743C] to doubt concerning both.
>
> No other memory of Bishop Julius has been handed down to posterity except that, through Pope Alexander III’s mediation and with the chapter’s consent, he granted to the monastery of Saint Salvi the church and parish of Saint James, exempting it from several burdens. On account of this matter we have appended a historical document, which Pope Urban III afterward decreed to be ratified and confirmed by a diploma issued to Abbot Gilbert. (The diplomas follow; Ughellus continues.)
>
> **XXX.** Zenobius, bishop of Florence, is found in the year 1161. After his death or deposition Julius was again raised to the see, which he held until 1181, as we have shown above . . . Nothing else occurs in these disastrous times, overwhelmed by the calamities of schism massed on every side, beyond the almost bare name of our Bishop Zenobius.
>
> **XXXI.** Bernard was made bishop of Florence in 1182 and is believed to have lived until 1189.
>
> **XXXII.** Peter governed the Church of Florence from 1189 until 1205, in which very year he died; and nothing concerning him is found except certain grants. (See Book VI, letter 50, and the notes there.)
>
> [Col. 0744C] “**XXXIII.** John, etc.” (For him see Book VIII, letter 156.)]

against the assaults of the emperor and his supporters. When the turmoil of the schism had subsided, that bishop, by command of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, granted those same men four *modii* of land as a fief. After he had subsequently gone the way of all flesh, B., his successor of good memory, as is customary, invested the said nobles with the lawful fief.

> [Note: [Col. 0744C] The *Decretals* read “a certain” in place of “lawful.”]

But when they had had the land assigned to them measured, they found only two *modii*. They therefore urgently requested your predecessor to make their fief whole.

> [Note: [Col. 0744C] The *Decretals* read “that the fief be made whole” for “that he should make their fief whole.”]

Although he at one time promised that he would do this, he did not carry it into effect. They now continually and urgently request that you complete the said fief for them. But you, having some doubt—

> [Note: [Col. 0744C] The *Decretals* read “they requesting this, concerning which you doubt” in place of “they requested . . . you doubting.”]

because they are not in possession of it, lest you seem to make a new grant, although they have taken care to render you fealty and were invested with four *modii*, consulted the Apostolic See before deciding to grant their request. We therefore, considering that the Church ought not to employ fraud or deceit in its dealings, give your brotherhood this answer: you may safely restore the said fief in full to the same nobles,

> [Note: [Col. 0744D] The *Decretals* read “you will be able” for “you can . . . to the nobles.”]

since the land had been assigned to them under the designation of four *modii* and the said bishop had already promised to give four.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Ides of December [12 December].

## CLXIII. To the bishops of London and Ely, and the abbot of Saint Edmund’s, in the diocese of Norwich

> [Note: [Col. 0744D] This letter is found, but very mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book II, title 20, “On Witnesses and Testimonies,” chapter 32. What is found there is enclosed here in brackets.]

> [Note: [Col. 0744D] See Book VII, letter 182, note.]

> [Note: [Col. 0744D] See Book V, letter 54.]

> [Note: [Col. 0744D] See Book V, letter 90, note.]

That, in the case between the archdeacon of Canterbury on the one side and the abbot and monks of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury, on the other, concerning possession of the wardenship of the church of Midelton, they are to hear witnesses. (Rome, the second day before the Ides of December [12 December].)

[Col. 0743C]

[Present before us] was our beloved son [Col. 0744A] Master Walter, on behalf of our beloved son . . ., archdeacon of Canterbury,

> [Note: [Col. 0744D] See Book VIII, letter 154, note.]

by whom he had been sent as procurator for this purpose. He requested that possession of the wardenship of the church of Midelton,

> [Note: [Col. 0744D]
>
> Should one perhaps read *Miletune* instead? “For in the year 1046 Egelric Bigge gave to the Church of Canterbury Chert, Stouting, and Miletune.” See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 21, col. 2, line 45.
>
> Perhaps *Middletone* should certainly be read. Around the year 814, “Lyschild gave Middletone to Archbishop Wlfred and the monks of Christ Church, Canterbury; and afterward, namely in 822, Cenulph, king [Col. 0745C] of the Mercians, confirmed the same gift, free from every secular [Col. 0745D] burden and fiscal tax.” Ibid., p. 19, col. 2, line 55.]

which our beloved sons . . ., abbot and monks of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury, had unlawfully occupied, together with the revenues received in the intervening period, be restored to him—especially because, he asserted, both by common law and by the general custom of the English Church, the wardenship of vacant churches in the diocese of Canterbury belongs to the archdeacon; and because, when two incumbents had died in the church in question before the monks had most recently occupied that wardenship, the archdeacon of Canterbury had exercised this right in the same church. He said that this had been sufficiently proved before delegated judges by twenty-five witnesses, all beyond exception, whose depositions we heard read before us.

He further stated that, after the death of the last incumbent to die in that church, the same archdeacon had possession of the keys of the church, as four priests, one deacon, and one clerk most plainly testified. Therefore, since we decreed that the church of Faversham be restored to the aforesaid monks, the church in question ought by equal right to be restored to the archdeacon.

But our beloved son O., a monk of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury, asserted in response that the said church of Midelton belongs directly to his monastery and that it had hitherto possessed its wardenship without challenge, as had been clearly proved on its behalf by sixteen witnesses, likewise all beyond exception. Thus, in exercising their right, they did no injury to the said archdeacon. It had also been sufficiently shown through two monks that the monastery freely disposed of the church and its goods.

[Since, then, more witnesses have been produced on this side but fewer on that, and since it is evident that their testimonies not merely differ but are wholly opposed on certain points [Col. 0745A], and since one ought not to attend merely to the number but to the quality of the witnesses and to their depositions, in which the light of truth is more present, upon which the judge must firmly establish his mind, we command your discretion by apostolic letters—

> [Note: [Col. 0745D] Absent in the *Decretals*.]

—that, if the witnesses produced on both sides are of equal honesty and reputation, since it is established that the monks’ witnesses are fewer in number than the archdeacon’s witnesses—

> [Note: [Col. 0745D] The *Decretals* add “are,” then shortly afterward read “only” in place of the words “setting aside . . . for him,” and below omit passages distinguished in italic type.]

—you are to pronounce judgment for the archdeacon, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. But if the witnesses produced on the monks’ behalf are of such greater distinction that their authority ought deservedly to be preferred to the greater number of the others, then, notwithstanding contradiction and appeal alike, [Col. 0745B] absolve the said abbot and monks from the archdeacon’s claim.] But if not all . . . two, etc.

Given at Rome, the second day before the Ides of December [12 December].

## CLXIV. To the bishop and dean of Lincoln

> [Note: [Col. 0745D] We have already observed that the bishop of Lincoln at that time was William of Blois, who, from being a prebendary and precentor of Lincoln, was elected bishop of Lincoln in 1201, consecrated in 1203, and died on the vigil of the Ascension in 1206. See Godwin, *De praesulibus Angliae*, p. 288.]

> [Note: [Col. 0745D] See Book V, letter 147.]

That they may dispense, for three years, with G., son of Peter, justiciar of England, concerning his vow of pilgrimage. (Rome, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January [16 December].)

The beloved son, the nobleman Geoffrey Fitz Peter, justiciar of England [Note: On this man we have already spoken above; see letter 94 of book V, note. King John’s letters to the pope, in which he begs that Geoffrey Fitz Peter should not undertake pilgrimage before five years have elapsed, dated at Winchester, 24 November 1204, are found in Rymer, vol. I, p. 44.], informed us that, because of the war which, through sins demanding it, is being most perilously waged between our dearest sons Philip [Col. 0745C], illustrious king of the French, and John, illustrious king of the English, the same king of England and his magnates do not permit him to leave England, since in this crisis he is greatly needed by the whole realm; and the aforesaid king of France and his barons do not allow him to pass through their lands by any route. Thus he cannot fulfil the vow of pilgrimage which he took long ago when he received the cross, being now prevented by these circumstances. Added to this is that he has young heirs, who have exceedingly powerful enemies and who strive by every means in their power to disinherit them; indeed, they have already occupied a great part of the heirs’ inheritance, and what still remains to them they will easily be able to seize during their father’s absence. [Col. 0746A] Moreover, he has established, in his sons’ inheritance, a convent of nuns of the order of Sempringham [Note: This probably concerns the priory of Shouldham [Col. 0746D], in Norfolk, of the order of Sempringham (read *Sempringham*, otherwise called that of St Gilbert). The authors of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 820, col. 1, print its foundation charter, issued by Geoffrey Fitz Peter, earl of Essex, without chronological dates but while King Richard was still alive; there they discuss at length the life of St Gilbert and the institutions of his order.]; and under the law of the English province this foundation cannot stand if his sons are deprived of that inheritance. The same knight further promises to build a hospice for the reception of poor travellers in a highly suitable place. Therefore he has mercifully requested leave to defer, by our permission and for these reasons, the fulfilment of his vow, promising that meanwhile he will send sixty marks of lawful sterling every year in aid of the Holy Land.

For this same nobleman, whom, because of his proven prudence and courage, they know to be especially necessary to the whole realm at this critical moment, the aforesaid king of England, the archbishop of Canterbury of happy memory [Note: Hubert, whom we have already said above died this year, on 13 July.], and our venerable brother, the bishop of Ely [Note: See letter 54 of book V.], urgently petitioned us [Col. 0746B], setting forth in their letters the need both of the king and realm and of his children. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing rests upon truth, you grant by our authority to the aforesaid nobleman permission to remain, with our leave, for three years in the king’s service and for the protection of his children, unless in the meantime, after weighing the circumstances of affairs and times, we decide otherwise concerning him; provided that he faithfully performs what he promised concerning the building of a hospice for the benefit of the poor and the sending of money in aid of the Holy Land. We further command that the said money [Col. 0746C] be deposited in London in the house of the Temple.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXV. TO THE ABBOT OF VALLUMBROSA [Note: Was the abbot of Vallombrosa at this time that Benignus whose constitutions, made in the general chapter in 1223, were published, as is recorded by Lami, *Deliciae Eruditorum*, 1737, p. 239?], AND TO MASTER GUALANDO, OUR SUBDEACON, CANON OF PISA [Note: We have also seen letter 109 of book VI addressed to him.]. Concerning the transfer of the see of Fiesole to a suitable place. (Rome, seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.)

Since much labour has repeatedly been expended upon transferring the see of Fiesole to a more convenient place, we, wishing to promote the peace and advantage both of the church of Fiesole and of the city of Florence [Col. 0747A], command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning the bishop [Note: See letters 20, note, and 21 of book VII.] and chapter of Fiesole, and the podestà, consuls, and councillors of Florence, you hold diligent discussions with them. If, with the consent of the said bishop and chapter and with the peaceable agreement of the aforesaid podestà, consuls, and councillors, you find a suitable place in that diocese at which the translation of the see of Fiesole may advantageously be carried out, inform us by your letters, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed more effectively in this business.

Given at Rome, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXVI. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, § 61.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. That he should not allow the nuns of Holy Trinity at Caen to be summoned before lay judges. (At St Peter’s, tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0747B]

A complaint submitted to us by our beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess [Note: After Matilda II, who died in 1194, the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 433, list these abbesses of Holy Trinity:

XI. Isabella II of Yvetot, died 7 June.

XII. Adela de Tibouville, of the lords of La Rivière de Tibouville, died 28 December.

“XIII. Joanna II, to whom a grant was made under the initial letter of her name in September 1217, is found in the cartulary in July 1223.”], and convent of Holy Trinity at Caen, disclosed that, although they had possessed the manors of Osted and Felsted [Note: Also Hocstede and Felestede, as is read [Col. 0748D] in the charters of King Henry I and King Edward II, printed by the authors of the *Monasticon Anglicanum* in the appendix, vol. II, p. 958, cols. 1 and 2.] in free alms from the foundation of their monastery, the nobleman Earl Aubrey, of the diocese of Norwich, harasses them in many ways concerning those manors, claiming that they had been granted to his predecessors in perpetual emphyteusis and seeking to vindicate them for himself; yet he produces no instrument concerning that grant. Furthermore, he draws them into litigation on this matter before a secular judge, whose examination in ecclesiastical affairs they assert is dangerous and harmful [Col. 0747C]. Since, therefore, because of the weakness of their sex, we especially wish to support them in their right, we ask, admonish, counsel, and exhort Your Royal Serenity not to allow the said abbess and convent to be summoned by the aforesaid earl in a secular forum, since these are ecclesiastical matters which, as they assert, they have held in free alms from the monastery’s foundation.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXVII. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, § 68. See also the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1365, letter E; and col. 1372, letters A and B.] TO HAMELIN [Note: Abbot Hamelin governed the monastery of Holy Trinity at Vendôme from 1202 until 1222 or 1223. See *Gallia Christiana*, cited place.], ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF VENDÔME, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. He receives it under the protection of blessed Peter, with an annual payment of twelve shillings, and its possessions are enumerated. (At St Peter’s, tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0747D]

Although by the office of apostolic [Col. 0748A] service we are considered indebted to all churches, it is fitting that we provide more attentively for the advantage of those which undoubtedly belong in a special way to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Since, therefore, the monastery of Vendôme, over which, beloved son in the Lord, by God’s authority you are known to preside, is known to belong, by the offering of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, of illustrious memory, and Agnes, countess of Poitou, its founders [Note: In 1032. See *Gallia Christiana*, cited place, col. 1364, letter D.], to the right and lordship of the Holy Roman Church, we, assenting to your just petitions, receive the aforesaid monastery of Vendôme, following the example of our predecessors Alexander, Gregory, Urban, Calixtus, and Innocent of blessed memory, under the special care and principal protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it with the privilege of the apostolic see [Col. 0748B]. We decree that the monastic order established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall there be inviolably observed for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions [lacuna] which the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, the offering of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify these in their own names: the place itself on which the aforesaid monastery stands, with all its appurtenances; the church of St George on the island of Oléron, with a great part of the same island; [Col. 0748C] the church of St Mary of the Castle of Oléron; the church of St Nicholas of Oléron; the church of Blessed Mary of Surgères; the church of the Holy Sepulchre at Baugé; the parish church of St Clement of Créton, with all the churches contained within the bounds of that parish; the church of Alderic; the church of Crisitot; the church of Treet; the church of Puy-Revel; the church of St Saturninus, situated on the Loire; the church of Colombiers; the church of Mazé; the church of St Peter of Mont-Soleil; the churches of the Prison of St Nicholas, St Vincent, and St Mary; the church of St Mary of Castell; the church of St Mary of Cosmes; the church of [Col. 0748D] Majeure; the church of St Mary of Broc; the church of St Peter of Villerias; the church of St Hippolytus, the church of St Germanus of Arçay, and the church of St Medardus of Civiliac; the gift of Geoffrey of Vendôme and of Ricerdis, formerly countess, [Col. 0749A] his mother; the gift of Master Peter, archpriest, on the island of Oléron; a fourth part of the tithe of Ebriacopoolin; and the gift of Juhel of Meduan at Beaumont, with other possessions, meadows, vineyards, lands, woods, rights of use, and pastures in woodland and open country, waters and mills, roads and paths, and all their other liberties and immunities.

Although our predecessors granted to your predecessors the church of St Prisca, situated on the Aventine Hill, with all its appurtenances and also with cardinalitial dignity, as we have seen stated in their privileges, yet because, after some time, through their carelessness and neglect that church fell into ruin and desolation, certain of our predecessors [Col. 0749B] assigned it at various times to various cardinals whom they promoted to the title of that church. But we, wishing to show regard for your honour, grant from the customary kindness of the apostolic see that you and your successors shall nevertheless possess the dignity which your predecessors obtained by grant of that church. By apostolic authority we confirm to you in perpetuity the use of sandals, tunic and dalmatic, mitre and ring, as cardinal-priests use them.

We also restore, by special favour, the church of blessed Prisca itself to the monastery of Vendôme, subject to this provision: if we or our successors should perhaps promote cardinal-priests to its title, principally so that they may perform the customary office at the altar of the blessed Apostle Paul, as was established by the prudent decision of the holy fathers, then those to whom you commit for the time being the care and administration of that church shall render to those cardinals due, humble, and devout obedience; and the said cardinals shall receive a fourth part of the revenues of that church. You, however, shall exercise diligent care over that church, lest through your negligence it again be reduced to desolation; for he deserves to lose a privilege who misuses the power entrusted to him.

Moreover, the provision which we have seen contained in the privilege of the same monastery—namely, that a legate of the apostolic see should not dare on his own authority to make dispositions or corrections in that place, nor presume under colour of his legation to harass the ruler of that place or the brethren, but, if he discovers anything needing correction, may report it to the supreme pontiff—we have thought fit to qualify as follows: due honour shall be shown to the legate and the liberty of the monastery shall not be harmed. Thus, whenever a legate is to be sent to those regions, he shall bring a special mandate to the monastery of Vendôme, according to whose tenor he shall proceed in matters where he judges that action should be taken according to God.

The abbot of Vendôme shall not be compelled unwillingly to attend a council without a mandate from the Roman pontiff; nor shall anyone dare to lay under interdict churches subject to that monastery wherever situated, except for specific and manifest offences which the abbot of that place, after admonition by the bishops, has scorned to correct [Col. 0750A]. Nor shall anyone, without a special mandate of the Roman pontiff, subject to interdict the monastery of Vendôme itself or the church of St Saviour, situated beside the walls of Angers and belonging to that monastery, or subject persons serving God there to suspension or excommunication—even if the territories of Chartres or Angers should incur ecclesiastical censure for any offences.

If anyone wishes to sue it concerning any matter, it shall by no means be compelled to answer except before the Roman pontiff or a judge specially delegated by him, since, according to lawful and canonical sanctions, the plaintiff must follow the defendant’s forum. By this present decree we also establish that the counts of Anjou, Poitou, and Vendôme shall always be defenders and helpers of that monastery, to the honour of the apostolic see; none of them shall impose upon its property or persons any exaction or custom, nor presume to claim anything for himself in them other than protection alone, which they are permitted to provide for the honour of the apostolic see [Col. 0750B].

We further forbid anyone, without the knowledge and consent of the Roman pontiff, to whom the aforesaid monastery belongs in both spiritual and temporal matters, to presume to dispose of or alienate its goods, especially to its prejudice and detriment; and if this is attempted by damnable audacity, we decree it void. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and unbound, fleeing from the world, and retain them without any contradiction [Col. 0750C]. You may freely receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics to be advanced to holy orders from any bishop you prefer, provided he is Catholic and possesses the favour and communion of the apostolic see, without objection from the diocesan bishop, etc. We also decree that the burial place of that monastery shall be free, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of deceit or force, except the man whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall in the fear of God [lacuna] provide to be elected; yet not without the testimony of three abbots who happen to be the more religious in neighbouring places. Nevertheless, the proceedings of the election shall be set forth to the Roman pontiff by testimonial letters of the chapter, and confirmation shall be sought from him. The person elected shall be blessed by the bishop of Chartres, or by any bishop he prefers, provided only that he is Catholic and in communion with the apostolic see, and shall freely and willingly bestow on him the grace of blessing without exacting a profession or anything else. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, or retain those taken away [lacuna], saving [Col. 0751A] in all things the authority of the apostolic see and, in non-exempt churches, the canonical right of diocesan bishops. As a token of this liberty obtained from the apostolic see, you shall pay each year to us and our successors twelve shillings in the currency of your country. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin [Note: See letter 27, note, of book VII.], chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1204 [Note: Thus it is expressly read in Conti’s copy; but this is erroneous. It must unquestionably be read as 1205.], in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CLXVIII. [Note: This letter is found, but very mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book IV, title 1, “On Betrothals and Marriages,” chapter 24. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI [Note: Albert, transferred from the bishopric of Vercelli to the patriarchate of Jerusalem (of whom we have already spoken above; see letter 222 of book VII), was replaced in this very year, 1205, by Lothair Rosarius of Cremona. Lothair was afterwards transferred to the Church of Pisa, and in 1215 at last succeeded his predecessor Albert in the Church of Jerusalem [Col. 0752D]. He died in 1227.]. That he should dissolve the marriage between Opizo Lancavecla and Rufina, because the said Opizo was insane. (At St Peter’s, fifth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0751B]

[Our beloved son R., a knight of Alessandria [Note: These words are absent from the *Decretals*, as are shortly below “nobleman” and the words “Opizo Lancavecla Rufina.”], stated before us that he had joined his daughter Rufina [Note: The *Decretals* add: “to a certain person.”] in marriage to Opizo Lancavecla], not knowing that Opizo was insane. He therefore humbly requested us to deign to provide for both him and his daughter, [since [Note: The *Decretals* add “however,” and below read “suffers” for “would suffer.”] that woman cannot dwell with a husband who suffers from continual madness, and because of his mental derangement a lawful consent could not have intervened. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Note: These words are absent from the *Decretals*, as are the following words distinguished by italic type.] that, after fully investigating the truth, if [Col. 0751C] you find the matter to be so, you take care, all opportunity for appeal removed, to separate the aforesaid persons from one another].

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXIX. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM [Note: See letter 222 of book VII.]. Permission to visit the thresholds of the holy Apostles also through messengers. (At St Peter’s, fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

Moved by the special love which we bear toward you in the Lord, we yield to your prayers and, so far as we can with God, make provision for your welfare. Since, therefore, at fixed times you are bound to visit the thresholds of the Apostles, either personally or through a messenger, we declare to you by these present letters that we shall by no means impute it to negligence on your part if the messengers [Col. 0751D] whom you resolve to send cannot reach us at the appointed time because of an evident impediment; for the firm confidence which we have conceived regarding your brotherhood [Col. 0752A] permits us to suspect nothing untoward concerning your actions.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXX. TO THE SAME. That the four-year period of his legation shall be reckoned from the day on which the church entrusted to him receives him. (At St Peter’s, fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

Since your crossing of the sea has, by the will of Him whose office it is to direct the steps of men, been delayed beyond what you wished, and we cannot know when the will of heaven shall be that, as you set out for the Holy Land, He to whose service you have devoted yourself will open the ways of the sea to you, by the authority of these present letters we grant [Col. 0752B] that the four-year term within which you undertook the office of legate shall, God permitting, have its happy beginning when the church entrusted to you receives the arrival for which you have waited.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXI. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, § 27.] TO THE SAME. That he may use the pallium in any province whatsoever. (At St Peter’s, fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

Although the use of the pallium has been granted you at certain recurring times within your own church, yet, in consideration of your probity and from the special love which we bear toward you, we personally grant your brotherhood by the authority of these present letters that, wherever you may be, you may lawfully use the pallium for the glory of the divine name and the honour of the see of Jerusalem [Col. 0752C], provided, however, that this is done without scandal or prejudice to others.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXII. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, § 27.] TO THE SAME. That he may absolve from the bond of excommunication those wishing to cross with him. (At St Peter’s, third day before the Kalends of January.)

By the authority of these present letters we grant you free power to absolve any excommunicated persons who join your company with the desire to cross the sea with you in aid of the Holy Land, unless their offence is so grave and heinous that you reasonably believe they should be presented before the apostolic tribunal.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXIII. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, § 27.] TO THE SAME. He sends him money. (At St Peter’s, fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0753A]

Accompanying you with the affection of sincere charity in the labours of your journey, which you began in trust in Him for whose service you are setting out, we send to your brotherhood through the bearer of these present letters four hundred gold obols, from the blessing of blessed Peter, to be used for the necessities of your expenses, and twenty-four marks of silver found deposited with our almoner, to be assigned according to your judgment in aid of the Holy Land.

[Col. 0753B] Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXIV. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, § 47.] TO THE ELECT OF COLOGNE [Note: On Bruno IV of Sayn, who, from being provost of Bonn, was appointed in this year 1205 after Adolf had been deposed from the archiepiscopal see of Cologne, and died in 1208, see Raynaldus, cited place, and the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 685, letter C.]. That he may retain for two years the benefices which he had previously held. (At St Peter’s, fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

“It is customary to assent,” etc., down to “to grant.” For it was set before us on your behalf that the Church of Cologne, to whose governance you have been appointed, has suffered such severe losses and waste of property owing to the threatening storms of war that its resources do not suffice for your necessities. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, granting your just prayers, we permit your devotion by the authority of these present letters to retain in your own hand for two years all revenues and ecclesiastical [Col. 0753C] benefices which you held before you were appointed to the dignity of this burden, and to employ their proceeds for your own uses and those of the Church of Cologne, without anyone’s objection, provided that you ensure that the churches from which you receive the revenues are suitably served.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXV. [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1205, § 47.] TO THE SAME. That, if his suffragans neglect to consecrate him bishop, he may summon other bishops for this purpose. (Rome, tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0753D] By the authority of these present letters we grant your devotion that, if the suffragans of the Church of Cologne, when requested, either cannot or will not come to consecrate you, you may have yourself consecrated archbishop by any other bishops, provided that they are Catholic and possess the favour of the apostolic see. By the authority of these present letters you are granted permission [Col. 0754A] that, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, they may bestow upon you the gift of consecration. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXVI. TO THE SCABINS AND THE WHOLE PEOPLE OF COLOGNE. Their ancient liberties are confirmed. (Rome, tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

“It is customary to assent,” etc., down to “assent.” We hold ratified the ancient liberties and immunities and the reasonable customs lawfully granted to you and your city by emperors, princes, or others, and observed hitherto; by apostolic authority we confirm them and fortify them with the protection of this present writing [Col. 0754B]. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXVII. [Note: The copy of this letter which, together with the others, we had arranged to have transcribed from Conti’s copy, has slipped from our hands—we do not know by what accident. The fragment presented here is found in Raynaldus under the year 1205, § 47.] TO THE CHAPTER AND CLERGY OF COLOGNE. Confirmation of the elect of Cologne.

[lacuna] We therefore, having ascertained the truth of the matter, approve the deposition of that man (namely Adolf) and the election of this man (namely Bruno), and confirm both by apostolic authority in the power of the Holy Spirit. Under penalty of anathema we strictly forbid anyone to presume to oppose this confirmation [lacuna]. We command and admonish your whole community to avoid altogether the aforesaid deposed man as excommunicated, and to render due obedience to the above-named elect as your prelate. [Col. 0754C] We have therefore commanded the suffragans of the Church of Cologne that, when requested by him, they shall lay upon him the hands of consecration; and, so that nothing may be lacking to the fullness of the pontifical office, we send the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, in accordance with the customary grace of the apostolic see.

CLXXVIII. [Note: We must acknowledge the same concerning this letter as concerning the immediately preceding one. We give its subject from Raynaldus, under the year 1205, § 62.] TO ALL PRELATES THROUGHOUT ENGLAND. That they are to ensure that Peter’s Pence, which was indeed collected faithfully in England but did not reach the Roman pontiff in full because of the fraud of officials, is exacted each year and brought to him without any fraud.

CLXXIX. TO PETER, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER [Note: See letter 104, note, of book VIII.]. That he may not be excommunicated without consultation with the Roman pontiff. (Rome, fourth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0754D]

Since through our hands you were ordained priest and consecrated bishop, in order that we may show honour no less to your dignity than to our own—indeed, to yours more truly as though it were ours—we forbid by the authority of these present letters anyone to dare to pronounce upon you a sentence of suspension or excommunication without consulting the Roman pontiff. If anyone should perhaps—may it not happen!—pronounce such a sentence after becoming aware of this prohibition, without consulting him, we decree that it is not to be observed. Nor may anyone presume to pronounce sentence against your subjects contrary to canonical sanctions, especially where you are ready to render them full justice, since no one ought to put his sickle into another’s harvest, always saving in all things the mandate of the apostolic see. But you must carefully take heed not to turn the favour granted you into injury to another, or the privilege into abuse; for he deserves to lose a privilege who misuses the liberty granted him. Let no one [Col. 0755B] therefore violate this prohibition and constitution, etc.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

CLXXX. TO THE . . . ARCHBISHOP [Note: See letter LIII, note, of book V.], AND TO . . . B., CELLARER OF TOURS. He commits to them the case pending between J. . . . of Meduan and E. . . ., noblewoman. (Rome, third day before the Kalends of January.)

From the tenor of the letters of the nobleman G., count of Brittany [Note: This probably concerns Guy of Thouars; see Anselm, *Histoire généalogique*, vol. III, p. 55.], it has been made known to us that, although we had entrusted to you and to G., of happy memory, master of the schools of St Martin, for due conclusion the case known to be in dispute between the noblewoman E. and the nobleman J. of Meduan concerning her inheritance, that count commanded the same woman—for both she and the aforesaid J. belonged to his jurisdiction—to bring the case before him, promising her that in his court he would ensure that she received the fullness of justice. He also took care to inform you that a matter of this kind ought to be determined in his court. Yet you and the aforesaid woman, unwilling in any way to obey him, endeavour to proceed in the case and unreasonably deprive him of his jurisdiction [Col. 0756A]. He therefore humbly petitioned us to deign to remit the case to him, to whom it specially belongs.

We, therefore, considering that here we are debtors to widows for justice, yet ought not to inflict injury upon others, command your discretion by apostolic letters that, unless the case is such as is known to belong to an ecclesiastical judge, you shall take care to desist from it, provided she can obtain her justice through a secular judge; otherwise, notwithstanding his objection, you shall determine the case, after due consideration, according to the form set forth for you in other letters.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the eighth year.

CLXXXI. TO RAINER, TREASURER OF LIMASSOL [Note: Also called Nimotian. After Amathus, a city of the island of Cyprus, had been destroyed—also called Lemissus—the neighbouring city of Neapolis arose as the new Lemesos and was named differently by different writers: Limocium, Limiconium, Nemonicium, Nimocium, Nemosia, and finally Limisso, Lemissus, or Lemessus. In this city Gerard, archbishop of Nicosia, held a provincial council in 1298; its acts are printed in vol. XI of Labbe’s *Councils*, part II, col. 2417 E. In 1425 and 1557 it suffered immense damage from the Saracens.]. He confirms to him the treasurership of the church of Limassol. (At St Peter’s, on the Ides of December.)

[Col. 0756B]

“It is customary to assent,” etc., down to “assent.” We confirm by apostolic authority the treasurership of the church of Limassol, granted to you by A., archbishop of Nicosia, of happy memory [Note: Stephen Lusignan (*General History of the Kingdom of Cyprus*, ch. 19, fol. 85) writes that Alice, wife of Hugh I, king of Cyprus, while he was absent fighting the Turks, sent an envoy with letters to Innocent III and the Lateran synod, earnestly requesting that, just as in former times, after Salamis was destroyed, its archiepiscopal see had been transferred to the city of Famagusta, so it might also be transferred from there to Nicosia. This she obtained. Yet the mention, occurring more than once before 1215—as here—of an archbishop of Nicosia seems to indicate that this transfer was earlier, perhaps achieved at the very beginnings of the Cypriot kingdom, under Guy or under his brother and successor Amalric, Hugh’s father, although it must be admitted that the aforesaid transfer could have been confirmed at the Lateran synod.

We have no information readily available concerning the archbishop of Nicosia in question here. We shall see a letter addressed to the archbishop of Nicosia in book IX, no. 141, in which Pope Innocent III summons him to judgment so that it may be determined whether he ought to be subject to the patriarch of Constantinople or not. This man, however, was probably a Latin and the first archbishop of that rite on Cyprus; he died before the end of 1211, as Le Quien observes, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1201. For in that year Durandus, treasurer of the church of Nicosia, was elected archbishop by the chapter of the same church. But because a certain nobleman had written something against him to Pope Innocent III, which the elect himself protested was false, the pope entrusted the patriarch of Jerusalem to investigate the matter more carefully; if he found him innocent, he was to have him consecrated and invest him with the pallium which the pope was sending. See letter 134 of book XIV, dated 30 December 1211, in Baluze, vol. II, p. 570.], and confirmed by our beloved son S., cardinal-priest of the title of St Praxedes, then legate of the apostolic see in those regions, just as you possess it lawfully and peacefully, etc. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Ides of December.

CLXXXII. . . . TO THE CHANTER, SIGIBERT, AND M. OF SAINT-QUENTIN, CANONS OF NOYON. He commits to them the case pending between A., clerk of Noyon, and A. de Maisnil, knight. (Rome, 3 Kalends of January [30 December].)

[Col. 0756C]

The letters of our beloved sons H., dean [Note: [Col. 0756D]

Concerning the deans of Noyon about the period with which we are concerned, the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 1033, write as follows:

XV. Hugh de Coucy, elected from Vassor, is mentioned in 1183 [Col. 0757C], and still in the years 1187, 1192, 1201, and 1204.

“XVI. John de Buchy made an agreement in 1208 with Hugh, mayor of Thyecourt, according to the cartulary of Ourscamp; he was still presiding in 1219.”

That Hugh was still dean in 1206 is plainly established by this letter of ours of Pope Innocent III.] , S. de Montmédard, and D. de Cardoil, canons of Noyon, informed us [Col. 0757A] that, when A., a clerk, had obtained from us a delegation to these same persons of the suit which he had brought against A. de Maisnil, knight, they cited the said knight. The knight’s procurator appeared before them and, with the clerk’s consent, obtained that a day be granted to the said knight for reaching a settlement with the clerk, promising on the knight’s behalf safe passage to that clerk meanwhile, both going and returning.

But since they could by no means reach a settlement, a retainer of that knight, in sacrilegious boldness, killed the said clerk while he was coming into the presence of the said judges. The judges, presuming that such a crime had been committed by the knight’s command, because he had not appeared before them on the day appointed to him for litigation, [Col. 0757B] caused him, all his supporters, and those in communion with them, to be publicly proclaimed excommunicate throughout the neighboring dioceses.

After three months had elapsed from the sentence pronounced against him, however, he came into their presence, asserted that he was innocent of this crime, and complained also that a sentence of excommunication had been issued against him though he had neither confessed nor been convicted. He urgently requested that this sentence, as unlawful, be relaxed. Having received from him both surety and an oath as security, they relaxed that sentence, enjoining him either personally or through a messenger—since bodily infirmity kept him confined—to present their letters on this matter before us.

Therefore, by apostolic writings [Col. 0757C] we command your discretion to prescribe for him a purgation with the fifth hand of his peers: namely, that the crime was neither committed by him, nor ordered by him to be committed, nor assisted or favored by him in its commission. Once this has been made and received, release him as clear in this matter, since no accuser appears against him concerning it. But if not all . . . let two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, 3 Kalends of January [30 December], in the eighth year.

CLXXXIII. [Note: [Col. 0757D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, §38.] TO THE PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA [Note: [Col. 0757D] See letter 99 of book VII, note.]. That, during the absence of its pastor, he protect and defend the Church of Trent against the Count of Tyrol. (3 Ides of January [11 January].)

[Col. 0758A]

You represented before us that the Church of Trent is grievously oppressed by the Count of Tyrol and his accomplices during the absence of its pastor [Note: [Col. 0757D] His name was Frederick (or Frideric, according to Bucelin, *Germania Sacra*, part I, p. 48). Born of the noble and powerful Wanga family, he was promoted to the see of Trent in 1205, according to Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 514. By salutary written laws he compelled the people of Trent to obey ecclesiastical authority, and administered the church entrusted to him with admirable integrity. He adorned Trent with costly buildings. He received the regalian rights from Philip, King of the Romans, in 1207. He was the Emperor’s vicar in Italy and chancellor of Emperor Otto IV.
