He cultivated piety so nobly that he made a most devout journey through the holy places of the East; returning thence to his homeland, he was stricken by illness at Accaron, that is, Caesarea, and died there in 1217, on 6 November, and was buried there at St. Mary’s [Col. 0758C], where a lodging-house for the German nation had formerly stood open.]. You therefore humbly requested us to look favorably upon its affliction.

Accordingly, wishing in paternal kindness to provide for that church’s protection from loss, we command your fraternity by the authority of these presents to rescue it from the hands of its oppressors and to arrange to guard it [Col. 0758B] until the case pending between the bishop of that church and its canons has been duly concluded by our venerable brother . . . the bishop of Padua [Note: [Col. 0758C] Gerard Pomedella, of whom we have already spoken. He presided over the Church of Padua from 1169 until 1214. See letter 178 of book VII, note.], to whom we have thought fit to commit it. Do this in such a way that, in accordance with the petition of that bishop, you cause all the revenues of the church to be applied to payment of its debts; suppressing opponents, etc. Notwithstanding no letters, etc.

Given at Rome, 3 Ides of January [11 January].

CLXXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0758C] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, §38.] TO THE SAME [Note: [Col. 0758D] See letter XCIX of book VII, note.]. Authority to unite the bishoprics of Aemona and Justinopolis. (3 Ides of January [11 January].)

[Col. 0758C]

You represented before us that . . . the bishop of Aemona [Note: [Col. 0758D]

Probably Olderic, who, according to Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 222, settled a dispute in 1194 between Berthold, Margrave of Istria, and the bishop of Poreč.

After Olderic, the same Ughelli mentions Gerard, though not before 1227, from documents, *ibid.*

Mittarelli indeed (*Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, p. 235, under the year 1214) seems to recognize a certain Otto, bishop of Civitas (otherwise Civitas Nova, that is, Aemona), who subscribed as witness to the judgment issued by Volcher, Patriarch of Aquileia, on behalf of Folcher, bishop of Poreč, against the monastery of St. Michael of Lemno, in the year of the Lord 1214, indiction II, on Saturday, the fourth day of December. But in the document itself, *ibid.*, Appendix, col. 331, Otto is expressly called dean of Civitas, not bishop.] came into your presence and humbly confessed to you that he had obtained that bishopric by the perversity of simony, asking to be absolved from it. You, having imposed upon him an appropriate penance, sent him to a certain solitary place.

But because the said bishopric has revenues of no more than seven marks, [Col. 0759A] and any bishop of that place must live like a rustic, to the discredit of other prelates, you humbly asked us, once the bishop’s resignation had been received, to grant you permission to unite that bishopric with the bishopric of Justinopolis, which lies near it. Therefore, placing fuller confidence in your discretion, we grant you free authority to unite the said bishoprics by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0759D] From what is reported concerning the bishopric of Justinopolis in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 354 and following, it may be inferred either that this union was not made at all or that it lasted only briefly. He mentions Ardecar as bishop of Justinopolis in 1187, and Absalon in 1211.], as you judge expedient, lest the episcopal name be cheapened, since one man suffices to govern both.

Given 3 Ides of January [11 January].

CLXXXV. TO RICHARD, DEAN OF SALISBURY [Note: [Col. 0759D] This concerns Richard Poore, consecrated bishop of Chichester in 1215 [Col. 0760D], who moved to Salisbury in 1217 and later thence to Durham. Godwin, *De praesulibus Angliae*, p. 504.]. Dispensation for illegitimacy, enabling him to obtain benefices. (19 Kalends of February [14 January].)

[Col. 0759B]

He who bears general care for all must weigh with more attentive deliberation not only the person but also the cause for which, and from which, he intends to grant a dispensation, lest he perhaps dispense in such a way as to squander; indeed, lest he squander, he must dispense in such a way that truth is not overthrown on account of mercy, nor piety destroyed on account of justice. Rather, he must carefully attend to what the Psalmist testifies: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have embraced each other” (Psalm 84 [85]).

Although lawful sanctions vigorously pursue some persons born unlawfully, nevertheless canonical constitutions prescribe a caution [Col. 0759C] to be observed in such cases: those who imitate their father’s incontinence are to be rejected under the rigor of judgment, but those who through their own virtue reject in themselves another’s vice are to receive a dispensation by the grace of kindness. Therefore, taking account alike of your person, uprightness of conduct, fruitfulness of works, learning, and reputation for virtues—of which many eminent persons, both prelates of churches and other prudent and honorable men, bear commendable witness for you, and have most earnestly petitioned us on your behalf—we mercifully dispense with you concerning the defect of your birth, that we may obtain mercy from the Father of mercies.

By the authority of these presents we decree that henceforth this defect shall not impede you in spiritual [Col. 0759D] acts and ecclesiastical offices, not only in benefices and dignities already obtained but also in those to be obtained hereafter; provided that, forgetting what lies behind, you always press forward to what lies ahead, so that, with the spirit of ambition excluded, you may make yourself worthy of dignity and pleasing to grace. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our dispensation, etc.

Given 19 Kalends of February [14 January].

CLXXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0760D] See Raynaldus under the year 1206, §42.] TO THE ARCHPRIEST AND CANONS OF ST. PETER’S. He enjoins observance of statutes concerning the canons of St. Peter’s. (At St. Peter’s, 3 Ides of January [11 January].)

[Col. 0760A]

Those things which are decreed by command of the Apostolic See must be kept firm and inviolate, lest they be violated by anyone’s audacity. Therefore, that the ordinance which, at our suggestion, you made in our presence for the enlargement of the worship of the divine Name may be inviolably observed, we strengthen it by apostolic authority and the protection of this present writing, strictly ordering that both you and your successors observe it firmly.

It has indeed been decreed that, from the offerings arising from the fourth part of the ministries of blessed [Col. 0760B] Peter, which we have thought fit to grant you out of regard for piety, every canon who rises for Matins shall receive, through the hands of the obedientiaries appointed for this purpose, two denarii on each night; but for Mass and for Vespers, one denarius. If they are present but do not come to Sext, bread shall be withheld from them at dinner; and those who do not go to None shall be denied bread at supper. Terce is to be sung immediately after the Matins Mass.

If anyone lying in the dormitory does not rise for the Matins office once in a week because of some necessity, he is not at all subject to the aforesaid penalty; nevertheless, he should know that he will render an account to God for his negligence. Those under medical treatment for three days, those bled for two, and those who have been bathed for one, are deemed exempt from such penalty.

Those, however, who do not enter choir for Matins and Vespers, Sext and None, by the *Gloria* of the first psalm, and by the time when *Kyrie eleison* is sung at Mass, shall not receive the aforementioned denarii. Those entering, therefore, shall remain in the office and shall not leave before its end, unless perhaps they are compelled in the meantime to go out for a necessary reason; but they shall return as soon as they can. Nor shall they sit idle; rather, each according to his ability and knowledge shall diligently apply himself to chant and psalmody.

Whoever, in any manner, except when engaged in obediences by command of the chapter, has not attended the divine offices as expressed above shall lose the aforesaid denarii, lest the present [Col. 0760D] statute be evaded by various pretexts. If the aforesaid offerings are insufficient, what is lacking shall be supplied from the offerings of St. Peregrinus or from other sources.

At table, moreover, all, or the greater part, shall come together, recline together with modesty, and rise together from the table, attentive to the reading which is always to be read without interruption during dinner. [Note: [Col. 0760D] The passage is corrupt; but it is read thus in Vatican codex 7024.] All shall also jointly provide in common from [Col. 0761A] the proceeds of the *signa*, of valerian [*valerani*; reading uncertain], and of the ten pounds assigned from pensions.

Moreover, if any must go out on private business, they shall not depart without the leave of the archpriest or prior; and if anyone intends to go on foot outside the church, he shall not go alone without a companion. No one shall appear outside the precincts of the canonry without a cape or gown, unless perhaps he rides outside the city; and even then he shall proceed in decent dress. In the dormitory, after the candle has been lit, no one shall speak loudly, lest by shouting he disturb those sleeping. But if anyone presumes . . . let him be punished by deprivation of his benefice. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our confirmation and command, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, 3 Ides of January [11 January].

CLXXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0761C] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, §33.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES TO WHOM THESE LETTERS SHALL COME. That the election of the Dean of Salisbury is annulled because of a defect in the election, not because of a defect in his person. (Rome, 2 Kalends of January [31 December].)

[Col. 0761B]

Let it be known to you that it has come to our hearing that our beloved son, the Dean of Salisbury [Note: [Col. 0761C] See note to letter 185 of this eighth book.], is defamed by certain of his rivals, as though he were under suspicion of falsity in our eyes. We, on the contrary, regard him as a man of learning, prudence, and integrity, and of good repute, as we have learned from the letters of many eminent persons.

Therefore, that the mouth of those speaking iniquity may be stopped, [Col. 0761C] we bear witness to the truth: we judged that the election made of him should be annulled, not because of any suspicion of falsity or stain of any crime, but because of the irregular procedure. Nor have we pronounced against [Col. 0762A] him concerning falsity; indeed, we did not even mention it in our pronouncement.

Given at Rome, 2 Kalends of January [31 December].

CLXXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0761C]

Plessis published this letter in his *History of the Church of Meaux*, among the documents, vol. II, p. 94, no. CCXII; but there it is presented very mutilated and disfigured by many errors. The words found in his edition are enclosed here in brackets; the words distinguished in italic type, and those not indicating variant readings, are absent from Plessis.

[Col. 0761D] For the subject matter of this letter, the same Plessis should be consulted, *ibid.*, vol. I, book I, §§1–12, pp. 192, 201.]

TO G., DEAN OF SOISSONS [Note: [Col. 0761D] This letter of Innocent shows that Guy I de Chézy, or de Ripelongue—whom the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 387, recognize as Dean of Soissons only from 1207 to 1228—had already entered upon the deanery before the end of 1205. See letters 41 of book III, note; and 123 of book VII.] . . . TO THE CHANTER OF REIMS AND THE SUCCENTOR OF SENLIS. He commits to them the case concerning obedience, pending between the bishop of Meaux and the monastery of Rebais. (At St. Peter’s, on the Ides of January [13 January].)

When our beloved sons G., chaplain and procurator of our venerable brother the Bishop of Meaux [Note: [Col. 0761D] At that time Anselm wore the mitre of Meaux. According to the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 1618, he is said to have held the see from at least 1197 until 1207. See letter 130 of book V, note.], and Jac., monk and procurator of the monastery of Rebais, had come into our presence and we had granted them a gracious hearing in our presence, [Col. 0762B] [the same G., [Note: [Col. 0761D] Plessis omits “the same G.” and shortly afterward adds “of Resdoc” after “monastery.” Below, he reads Stephen for S.] procurator of the monastery, set forth] before us that, from the first foundation of the monastery, it had been exempt from the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Meaux and had looked to the Roman Church without any intermediary, as is contained in a privilege of Pope Innocent, our predecessor of happy memory, shown to us [Note: [Col. 0761D] Plessis prints that privilege, *History of Meaux*, vol. II, p. 27, document 46. It is said to have been given at Pisa, 2 Ides of January, indiction XII, in the year 1134.].

In the time of Brictius [Note: [Col. 0762C] Brictius, or Bricius, was governing the monastery of Rebais in 1145, according to the *History of the Miracles of St. Agile*. He was still in office in 1161, when Henry, Count of Champagne, in compensation for certain relics received from the monks of Rebais (see Plessis, *History of Meaux*, vol. II, p. 50, document 94), increased their holdings by several estates in 1164. With an exception, however, he bound himself and his monastery by oath to Stephen, Bishop of Meaux. He is said to occur in the records as late as 1173. According to the necrology, he died on 11 March. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1683.], abbot of that place, Stephen, Bishop of Meaux, of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0762D] Stephen, born at Paris, was brother of Walter (of Villebéon and of the chapel in Brie called Walter’s Chapel), chamberlain of Kings Louis VII and Philip II; uncle of Peter of Paris, Stephen bishop of Noyon, William bishop of Meaux, and Walter the younger, chamberlain. Through their mother Aveline they bore the family name Nemours. First a canon of Sens and Paris, then chanter of Meaux, he was made bishop and held the see from at least 1162, as is shown by what is related here. After the death of Peter de la Chastre, he was translated to the metropolitan see of Bourges in 1171. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1615.], in order to deprive that monastery of its liberty, began by himself and his agents to harass it in many ways.

And when for two or three years the monks of that place had endured very many burdens and vexations from that bishop, because at that time they did not have at hand the privilege that had fortuitously been lost, the abbot was compelled to make an agreement with him [Col. 0762C] in the following manner [Note: [Col. 0762D] What is said here must certainly be compared with what Plessis reports, *History of Meaux*, book III, §VI, vol. I, p. 197, and vol. II, p. 53, documents 6 and 8.]: namely, that he would render him obedience until he should produce the privilege of exemption or otherwise demonstrate his liberty, and that such obedience should not prejudice the monastery once the privilege had been found. [Col. 0763A]

Afterward, when that privilege had been found, the convent repeatedly urged Abbot Joscelin [Note: [Col. 0763D]

“Joscelin, according to a document of the monastery of Saint-Denis in France, was in office in 1188, and again appears in the records until the year 1200. He resigned in 1205, weary of the lawsuits which daily revived between his monastery and the Bishop of Meaux concerning jurisdiction.”

These statements are found in the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* (vol. IX, col. 1683), who drew the latter from this letter of ours of Pope Innocent III. For what follows in their work, see below, note.] to take pains to have the privilege renewed and restore the monastery to its former liberty, but he let these things pass by deaf ears.

When afterward Joscelin resigned [Note: [Col. 0763D] Plessis reads “the bishop.”] the governance of the abbey [Note: [Col. 0763D]

Plessis reads: “When afterward Bishop J. resigned the governance of the abbey.” This gave the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* (place cited) occasion to add to the statements reported above:

“At that time Joscelin became a bishop of an uncertain see, according to a bull of Pope Innocent III, which has these words: ‘When afterward Bishop J. . . .’—that is, Joscelin—‘resigned the governance of the abbey,’ etc.; unless the copyist there inadvertently wrote *episcopum* (‘bishop’) for *abbate* (‘abbot’). For in the necrology, where his death is recorded on 20 October, there is no mention of an episcopate.”

The genuine reading supplied by our copy, diligently transcribed from the Vatican and Conti copies, settles the controversy.], the convent of that place, having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, elected their beloved son G. as abbot by common consent [Note: [Col. 0764D] On the uncertainty of this abbot’s name, see Plessis and also the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, place cited.]. When they presented him to the aforementioned bishop to obtain the grace of blessing, he demanded that the elect promise him subjection and obedience.

But the elect showed him the privilege of the Apostolic See, by which he endeavored to establish that he was not bound to promise obedience to him, [Col. 0763B] asking him to grant the grace of blessing according to the tenor of the privilege. The aforesaid bishop replied that he cared nothing for that privilege and even refused to inspect it. The elect therefore appealed, on behalf of himself and the monastery, the clergy and people of Rebais, and all those belonging to the said monastery, to the Apostolic See, appointing the feast of St. Luke last past as the term of his appeal. The clergy and people of Rebais, together with Dudo, priest of St. John’s, afterward ratified that appeal and sent a procurator to our presence for this purpose.

The bishop’s procurator, on the other hand, alleged that the said monastery, situated in the diocese of Meaux, had from its foundation until the present been subject to the Church of Meaux, and that its abbots had rendered due and devoted obedience to the Bishop of Meaux. But in these days, after the resignation of J., then abbot of that place, the monks elected the said G. When he had duly presented himself to the Bishop of Meaux and sought from him the gift of blessing, the bishop appointed the vigil of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary as his term.

When the elect came on that day, the bishop summoned several abbots from neighboring dioceses and arranged to receive him honorably. Since it was Sunday, and after the solemn procession before Mass had been celebrated according to the custom of the land, [Col. 0764A] the bishop and elect [Note: [Col. 0764D] Plessis reads “the clergy.”], together with those abbots, approached the high altar clothed in sacred vestments. When the bishop began, according to the custom of the land, to conduct the examination customary at the blessings of abbots, and had questioned the elect concerning certain chapters, to which he answered, “I will,” as is contained in the rite, he asked him whether he wished to be obedient to him, to the Church of Meaux, and to his successors, according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers.

Before that question had scarcely been completed, the elect rose and, asserting that the bishop was oppressing him, appealed to the Apostolic See, setting the aforesaid term for the appeal. The bishop answered humbly and gently that he ought not [Col. 0764B] [Note: [Col. 0764D] Plessis reads “ought.”] to be disturbed at all, but should say in what respect the bishop oppressed him, since this was no place or time for disturbance; rather, he ought to invoke the Holy Spirit. The elect replied that he could not but be disturbed when obedience was demanded of him which he was in no way bound to render.

When the bishop replied that he sought from him nothing except what his predecessors had rendered to the bishop’s predecessors, [Note: [Col. 0764D] Plessis reads *impenderunt*; read *impenderant*, “had rendered.”] the elect replied that he did not wish to imitate his predecessors in folly, but would pursue the appeal he had lodged, because he was wholly exempt from the bishop’s jurisdiction. The bishop, asserting that he knew nothing of his exemption, prohibited him, under appeal to the Apostolic See, from having himself blessed by another. The elect then immediately departed with his followers, while the clergy and people were disturbed, [Col. 0764C] and the bishop [Note: [Col. 0764D] Plessis reads “bishop”; shortly afterward “celebrated” for “celebrating.”] duly celebrated the solemnities of Mass with the devotion fitting to it.

Therefore, having heard the arguments of both parties, and because the adverse party’s confession established that the bishop had possession of the obedience, we decreed, upon the counsel of our brethren, that he be restored to that possession [Note: [Col. 0764D] Plessis reads “we decree.”]. But because the privilege shown to us expresses full liberty, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, after the said bishop has been restored to possession of the obedience, unless within six months after his restoration he raises and proves some reasonable objection [Col. 0765A] contrary to the liberty of the privilege, you shall impose perpetual silence upon him concerning the subjection of that monastery, removing the impediment of appeal. You shall strictly prohibit him from henceforth daring to harass the monastery concerning the liberty of the privilege.

But if it be the will of the parties, remit the sufficiently prepared case to our presence, appointing them a suitable term at which they are to appear before us to receive judgment. Witnesses, etc. No letters shall stand in the way except with the consent of the parties, etc. But if not all . . . let two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the Ides of January [13 January], [Note: [Col. 0765D] Plessis adds “of our pontificate.”] in the eighth year.

CLXXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0765D] Various fragments of this letter are found in the *Decretals* in different places. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets; what we have distinguished in italic type is absent from the *Decretals* or indicates variant readings.] TO THE BISHOP OF BRESCIA [Note: [Col. 0765D] His name was John. He presided over the Church of Brescia from 1198 until 1212, in which year Pope Innocent III granted resignation to him in his advanced old age. See letter 140 of book XV; Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 741.]. He answers his various consultations. (Rome.)

[Col. 0765B]

[Note: [Col. 0765D] See *Decretals*, book IV, title 13, “Concerning one who has had intercourse with the blood-relative of his wife or betrothed,” chapter 10, where it is said to be addressed to the Archbishop of Esztergom.] [The devotion of your fraternity asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See whether a man who commits fornication with the sister of his lawful wife may afterward live with his wife and demand the marital debt and render it when demanded, or whether the marriage ought for this reason to be separated. We therefore briefly answer your inquiry: the wife is to be carefully admonished to refrain from intercourse with him because of public decency, and to remain continent until her husband has entered upon the way of all flesh. But should she perhaps refuse to obey the admonition and be such that [Col. 0765C] her fall is to be feared, her husband can and ought nevertheless, with the fear of God, to render her the marital debt; for an affinity arising after a marriage unlawfully contracted ought not harm her, since she is not a participant in the wrongdoing,] and therefore she ought not to be deprived of her right without fault. Although one of our predecessors is said to have distinguished in a similar case whether the adultery or incest was manifest or concealed, others maintain that a distinction should instead be made between a near and a remote degree.

[Note: [Col. 0765D] *Ibid.*, book II, title 6, “That proceedings are not to be taken for receiving witnesses or issuing final judgment before joinder of issue,” chapter 3.] You further asked whether, if someone cited by lawful peremptory summonses refuses to appear, the judge, before joinder of issue, ought to pronounce judgment against him so that, wearied by this, the man may at least present himself before the judge, intending to appeal. To this [we thought fit to answer your fraternity as follows: [Col. 0766A] if the defendant has deliberately kept himself absent in contempt of court, and the case is such that the plaintiff can be put in possession of the property claimed, he is to be placed in custody in that same case. But if the case is such that the plaintiff cannot be put into possession, then, in order that he may obey the law, the person who has contumaciously absented himself [Note: [Col. 0766D] The *Decretals* read *contumax* (“contumacious”) for “the person who has contumaciously absented himself.”] is to be compelled by ecclesiastical censure].

[Note: [Col. 0766D] *Ibid.*, book III, title 5, “Concerning prebends and dignities,” chapter 20.] Furthermore, you asked [whether, since it often happens that two clerics are elected to one prebend because of the excessive importunity of petitioners, such an election ought to be confirmed or rather annulled. Considering that if two held one prebend this would be contrary to the Council of Tours, which prohibits the division of prebends, and that if one of them obtained the prebend the other would remain in expectation contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, we answer your inquiry thus: under the strict rule of law, such an election should rather be quashed.]

[Note: [Col. 0766D] What follows appears to belong under title 19, “Concerning Usury,” of book V of the *Decretals*; yet it is sought in vain in the collections of the *Decretals*, both the special Innocentian and the general Gregorian collection.] Moreover, you asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See whether, if a debtor, of his own accord and without being pressed or even reminded, gives something from his own generosity to a creditor who lent him money without any agreement, that creditor ought to be compelled to return what he received as a gratuitous offering. To this we briefly answer that what the debtor has thus freely offered ought not to be reckoned usury, and the creditor is not to be compelled in any way to restore it.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] See *Decretals*, book I, title 38, “Concerning procurators,” chapter 5.] Your fraternity further asked us whether a husband can accuse his wife of adultery through a procurator, since both laws and canons appear to prohibit this. To this [we answer your fraternity as follows: if the husband accuses his wife of the crime of adultery before a secular judge in order that the legal penalty be imposed, then, because he must undertake the bond of inscription and bind himself to the penalty of retaliation, he must bring the accusation in person and personally appear, not act through a procurator.

But if the husband wishes to accuse his wife of adultery before an ecclesiastical judge in order to depart from cohabitation with her, then, even though he may perhaps have to make an inscription—that is, designate in writing the crime [Note: [Col. 0766D] The *Decretals* read *nomen* (“name”) for *crimen* (“crime”); below they read *consequatur* (“may attain”) for *consequeretur* (“would attain”), and *quamvis* (“although”) for *quam* (“than”).], place, time, and the other matters included in civil law—he ought not in any way bind himself to retaliation, lest perhaps, even if he failed in proof, [Col. 0766D] he attain the effect of his intention. If necessity requires it, he may be permitted to accuse through a procurator, [Col. 0767A] since such an accusation, although it concerns a crime, is nevertheless not criminal, but is as it were mixed between civil and criminal, though proceedings are safer in the presence of the principal persons.]

[Note: [Col. 0767D] See *Decretals*, book IV, title 1, “Concerning betrothals and marriages,” chapter 25.] [You also asked to be instructed whether marriage is contracted by words alone, and by what words, since some doubt whether a spiritual marriage is contracted by words alone. We therefore answer your inquiry thus: marriage is truly contracted by the lawful consent of a man and a woman; but, so far as the Church is concerned, words expressing present consent are necessary. For the deaf and mute may contract marriage by mutual consent without words, and children below the lawful age do not contract by words alone, since they are understood [Col. 0767B] not to consent at all.]

Given at Rome, etc.

CXC. [Note: [Col. 0767D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, §38.] TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE DIOCESE OF FERMO. That they render obedience to their bishop-elect.

Although pontifical authority and imperial power are distinct dignities, and the offices of kingdom and priesthood are separate, nevertheless, since the Roman pontiff acts on earth in the place of Him who is King of kings on earth and Lord of lords, a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, he possesses from the Lord Himself not only supreme power in spiritual matters, but also great power in temporal matters. Therefore, since the bishopric of Fermo pertains to him, both in spiritual and temporal affairs, without any intermediary, we, after receiving from our beloved son … bishop-elect of Fermo [Note: See Letter 28 of Book III, note.] a canonical purgation concerning matters alleged against him by certain persons, and after they had wholly desisted from prosecuting him, have taken care, by apostolic authority, to confirm his election—which we recognized as canonically celebrated concerning a suitable person—and afterwards to invest him, by the banner, with the regalian rights. Wherefore, by these apostolic letters, we command your prudence, strictly enjoining you to render him obedience and reverence, both due and devoted, in spiritual and temporal matters.

CXCI [Note: Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, §38.] TO … THE BISHOP-ELECT OF FERMO [Note: See Letter 28 of Book III, note.], AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. He grants immunities and privileges to him and his successors.

[Col. 0767D]

Although, by reason of the office of administration entrusted to us, we are bound to extend the favor of our grace to all churches, we nevertheless wish and ought to provide more especially for those which are known to belong to us by both laws, inasmuch as they are more fully subject to the Apostolic See. Therefore, although the Church of Fermo is fortified in spiritual matters by the privileges of the Apostolic See, wishing also to impart to that church the protection of the Roman Church in temporal matters, we strictly forbid, by apostolic authority, anyone other than the legate of the Roman Church to make exactions, hold a court, or hear causes, without a special mandate of the Apostolic See, in the city of Fermo or in the castles—namely Agello, Capite-Montis, and the others which the Church of Fermo now justly possesses or may lawfully acquire in the future—or in other property belonging to that same church. Rather, let all its goods remain whole and undisturbed, our right in all things being preserved. We further add that everything arising from judicial court, ban, market, public square, or ports outside the city, throughout the bishopric, or from other regalian rights, within or outside the city of Fermo, shall be paid to you and your successors without any diminution or contradiction, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to trouble the bishopric of Fermo, or seize or invade its goods, or in any way harass or burden its men. But whoever presumes to act against this or to violate this privilege in any respect shall pay, as a penalty, one hundred pounds of pure gold: one half to the sacred Lateran Palace and the remainder to you or to the successors who shall be in office at the time.

CXCII [Note: Raynaldus published this letter in full under the year 1206, §19; it is therefore printed here in brackets.] FROM THE KING OF THE DANES TO THE POPE. He sets forth various complaints against Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig, and asks him to ensure that Denmark is not disturbed by Waldemar.

[Col. 0768C]

[To the reverend father and lord in Christ, Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman See, … by the same grace king of the Danes and Slavs, duke of Jutland, lord of Nordalbingia, fullness of filial devotion with affection.

Although all adherents of the Christian faith, however widely scattered throughout the world, are bound to venerate and love the eminence of Your Holiness with the services of devotion—not servile but filial—yet those whom the special prerogative of your love and the manifest signs of clearer favor have honored ought to acknowledge themselves under still greater obligation, if they wish to respond in return as is fitting to the merits of your fatherhood. For although we are bound, by the general institutions of Christian profession and those common to all peoples, to obey and serve the good pleasure of Your Holiness, nevertheless, stirred by the more urgent incentives of your immense kindness and goodwill bestowed upon us, we acknowledge ourselves more firmly bound gladly to accomplish everything which we know will please your discretion. For, following in the footsteps not only of your predecessors, who always embraced our predecessors and their kingdom with the arms of sincere charity, you have made yourself heir to the love which they bore them; indeed, you have endeavored to enlarge it with still greater increase and to labor with paternal solicitude to accomplish our good pleasure and to promote alike our honor and that of the kingdom.

Having received the letters of your piety, in which you urged us with sincere affection and benevolence concerning the release of Bishop Waldemar, we received them graciously and kindly. Although, if we may speak without detracting from the fullness of your love, what was requested seemed to many difficult and altogether impossible, we judged nothing burdensome which you had decided could readily be done, whatever loss to ourselves or danger to our person or possessions might threaten. For such integrity and constancy of love has been shown us by your previous benefits that we are wholly certain that you watch over our advantage and advancement with such diligent concern that, in order to prevent all future losses and inconveniences which nearly the whole of our kingdom threatens and fears are impending upon us, you must apply such remedy and precaution that there can be no doubt concerning them. Therefore we recognize that we must obey, without hesitation and setting aside every deliberation, whatever your providence sees fit to command us, however arduous it may appear.

For unless, casting behind our backs all the offenses and wrongs in which the aforesaid bishop has sinned against us, and in no way turning our eyes back to them, we placed our hope and confidence in the Lord and in you, we, like almost all others, should regard as not merely difficult but impossible that which, through the fullness of your goodwill, we now especially judge easy. Indeed, although we reluctantly burden your providence, occupied with many matters, by a long account, we nevertheless judge that what has especially stirred him against us ought briefly to be disclosed to your love through a messenger, so that it may be more clearly shown that he has repaid us hatred for love and evil for good.

For when King Canute, our maternal uncle, had been innocently and undeservedly slain by his enemies, he begot this man, of whom we speak, by a certain woman concerning whom litigation is still pending as to whether he had her as a concubine. But because there was such uncertainty concerning this man’s birth—especially since, after the death of the man whose son he claims to be, and since he was born from an illegitimate marriage, it was left to our father’s judgment whether he wished to assert him to be the son of the aforesaid king or not—our father nevertheless, out of regard for divine recompense, interpreting the uncertainty in the sounder sense, graciously received him into the royal family and his own line, and adopted him not merely as a kinsman and blood-relative, but almost as his own son.

After our father had been removed from this world, when our brother King Canute of pious memory assumed the reins of the kingdom, he did not depart from his father’s pious deeds, but made himself successor and heir to that same love which our father had borne toward this man. He always showed him fuller goodwill and affection, increasing the great favor which he had received from our father. Among other things, while we were still of tender years, he granted him for a time the duchy which was due to us, and enriched him abundantly with innumerable benefits and honors. Yet that from which he believed he had earned fuller goodwill became the source from which he felt our brother’s indignation and hatred against himself and us most grievously and inexorably aroused.

For when, after the years of our childhood had passed, our duchy and our father’s inheritance were restored to us—of which he had, as stated above, been administrator for a time—he changed the reciprocal return of sincere affection, which he was bound to render both to our brother and to us, into unceasing rancor and hatred. This he afterwards disclosed by excessively evident indications; for, according to his own prognostic on the day of his consecration, “nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed, nor concealed that shall not be known.” Forgetful or ungrateful for all the benefits which he had received from our father and brother, to say nothing of those received from ourselves, he strove—though in vain, divine mercy assisting—to remove our aforesaid brother and us from the kingdom [Note: Omitted in Raynaldus.], and, having joined to himself the titles of king and bishop less decorously and justly than was proper, to form a battle-line against us. If, therefore, for brevity’s sake, all the other serious acts which he reported and committed against us are passed over and these alone recalled to mind, what good can be thought of one who did not fear to act maliciously even toward our death, so innocently and undeservedly, unless your goodwill toward us in all things and above all else be considered?

Since, therefore, we commit both ourselves and our interests entirely to your disposition, let your providence take care that, if we release him out of regard for your admonition, you arrange for him to be brought to you in such a manner that he cannot be seized by enemies on the road. For although we acknowledge that our own acts have in no way deserved this, Philip, duke of Swabia, nevertheless allies himself more with our enemies than with our friends; and it is not fitting to reveal to your magnificence the state of matters between us and the king of France. Therefore, if he should fall into the hands of our aforesaid adversary, they would, if they could, inflict troubles upon us and our kingdom through him. When he has arrived, as we have learned from your letters and our messengers, place him in some other place which you judge suitable. Since we cannot sufficiently increase, so as to secure sincere affection, the benefits previously bestowed upon him by our brother and ourselves, we fear that we can in no way earn his goodwill better now than before; and thus we desire his absence rather than his presence, since we fear that he cannot be joined to us in the constancy of sincere affection.

But if you can neither bring him safely to yourselves nor, as stated, provide him with accommodations in another place, permit him henceforth, with your goodwill, to be held so that he may not harm us. In doing this you will act all the more mercifully toward us, since, disregarding the counsel of almost all who are connected with us, we are unwilling in any way to depart from your counsel and good pleasure. We entrust the rest to be related by our messengers.]

CXCIII [Note: Raynaldus published this letter in full under the year 1206; it is therefore printed here in brackets.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF DENMARK. He exhorts him to clemency toward Waldemar, asks that he may be conducted under safe-conduct to the king of Hungary, and then promises to provide for the peace of his kingdom. (13 Kalends of February [20 January].)

[Col. 0771B]

[We give thanks to the Bestower of all graces, because He has amassed in your most serene breast such an abundance of virtues that there is in it what the whole world may draw from, nor is there lacking there what familiar affection may take up. Therefore, rejoicing in the special prerogative of your love, we pour forth prayers to you with so much the greater confidence as we possess, from the letters recently sent to our apostolic office by your highness, proofs of the purer devotion which you are known to bear toward us.

Thus, dearest son, it is fitting that by remembrance of the good things formerly bestowed abundantly upon you and your forefathers both by us and by our predecessors, you should stir yourself to greater things; nor should that destroyer of virtues, namely ingratitude—far be it!—find any place in you. Since it provokes evils and eradicates merits, wherever once it introduces itself, it scarcely withdraws without grave loss. For from the tenor of the letters mentioned we perceive that, although Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig, under the weight of his pontifical office, so that kingship might be joined with priesthood in himself, rashly conspired against Canute [Note: Omitted in Raynaldus.], king of the Danes of illustrious memory, your brother, to whom he was bound by an oath of fidelity, and although, shamelessly forgetting all the benefits which he had received abundantly from you and your ancestors, he committed many grave acts against royal honor, nevertheless you, as a merciful king and a Catholic prince—one who grieves whenever compelled to be severe—out of reverence for the supreme King and at the salutary admonition of the Apostolic See, however much that bishop offended you and your kingdom, and however grievous or even impossible this appeared to many, nevertheless, when we unceasingly exhorted and begged you concerning his release, judged that you should humbly comply swiftly, setting aside every deliberation. You considered nothing difficult which we thought fit to impose upon you, holding firm hope and confidence that we watch over your welfare and advancement with such diligent concern that, in order to avert all future losses and inconveniences which nearly the whole of your kingdom threatens and fears are impending upon you, we must provide such a remedy that henceforth you have no cause whatever to doubt concerning them.

Therefore, highly approving the purity of your royal devotion and wishing with diligent concern to provide both for your welfare and for the tranquility of your kingdom, with the common counsel of our brethren we have considered it fitting to send into your presence our beloved son Master P… , our clerk, a prudent and discerning man, acceptable to us and our brethren for his integrity and honor. We admonish and exhort your royal highness in the Lord that, in accordance with our prayers and exhortations, you cause the said bishop, absolved and free, to be delivered to him, and likewise provide him with a safe-conduct so that the bishop may be led, without injury from anyone, by the same man as far as our beloved son in Christ A… , the illustrious king of Hungary [Note: Omitted in Raynaldus.]. Thereafter, God assisting, we shall take care to arrange how he may safely come to us.

But because the said bishop could not complete so long a journey or remain with us for a long time without great expenses, which we do not believe him to possess, let the royal highness, by our command, grant him so much from the revenues of his bishopric that, upon coming to and residing at the Apostolic See, he may suitably and honorably maintain himself and his attendants. Further, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquility, we have instructed the said master, after assembling the magnates of your kingdom, ecclesiastical as well as secular, to pronounce by our authority a solemn excommunication—with candles extinguished and bells rung—against the person or persons who, on account of assistance or favor given to the aforesaid bishop, should presume to trouble you or your kingdom against the apostolic command. He is to receive from that bishop, before all, a corporeal oath that neither personally nor through another will he rashly attack you, your kingdom [Note: Omitted in Raynaldus.], or any persons of your realm on account of this matter, and that he will faithfully approach the Apostolic See, humbly to receive its command.

Regarding the matter upon which our beloved son … and the messengers repeatedly pressed us—namely, that we should, by the favor of an apostolic dispensation, appoint our beloved son … bishop-elect in place of the aforesaid bishop—let royal prudence know that we could not comply with such a petition, since the canonical decrees of the holy Fathers expressly prohibit anyone from usurping the place of a living man before that man has been removed by canonical censure. But when the bishop himself arrives in our presence, because then he may be understood to have been restored to his freedom, we shall, by the Lord’s authority, omit nothing in this affair that pertains to the necessary precaution. Finally, we admonish and also ask your highness to receive the said master with fitting dignity and treat him honorably, so that your magnificence may thereby deservedly be commended.]

Given on the 13th day before the Kalends of February [20 January].

CXCIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND. That he should visit the province of Lund and correct what needs correction. (15 Kalends of February [18 January].)

[Col. 0773B] “Because the world is growing old,” etc., as in the letter written above in the same book to … the archbishop of Sens [Note: See Letter 52 of this Book VIII.].

CXCV [Note: This letter is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, Book III, title 32, *On the Conversion of Married Persons*, chapter 14, where it is said to be addressed to the archbishop of Lyon. What is there printed is enclosed here in brackets; passages distinguished in italics are absent from the Decretals or refer the reader to variant readings.] TO THE SAME. He answers his consultation concerning a certain matrimonial case. (2 Ides of January [12 January].)

[It has been reported to us by you that a certain woman of your diocese assumed the veil of widowhood before two abbots, with solemn blessing, celebration of Mass, and litany duly accompanying it. Afterwards a certain nobleman, who was said six months earlier [Note: The Decretal reads *proposebat se prius* (“had previously declared himself”); below, it reads *ipsam* (“her”) for *eamdem* (“the same woman”).] to have betrothed that same woman through intermediaries by words in the present tense, with earnest-money also given,] upon hearing that the woman had assumed the veil, sent to her asking that the betrothal already made be followed by carnal union. But after the matter was brought before your hearing, you took care to forbid them to have sexual relations before the case had been examined. Later, when the woman herself stood in your presence, you asked whether she had consented to him and why she sought to be separated from him. [She confessed that she had consented to him, but said that she had heard he had been struck with leprosy and for this reason had abhorred his embraces.] But after sufficient proof had subsequently been made to you by suitable witnesses that, before the reception of the veil, mutual consent by words in the present tense had taken place between them, you considered it necessary to consult the Apostolic See whether the reception of the veil prevents marriage between them.

[We answer your brotherhood [Note: The Decretal reads “inquiry.”] as follows: although it may not unreasonably seem that, once marriage has been contracted by words in the present tense between lawful persons, it cannot in any case be dissolved while they live, so that, while the other lives, one party may pass to second vows—even if one of the faithful between whom there is a ratified marriage should become a heretic and refuse to remain with the other without insult to the Creator, unless perhaps otherwise occurred through divine revelation, which surpasses every law, as is read to have happened to certain saints—nevertheless, unwilling suddenly to depart in this respect from the footsteps of our predecessors, who, when consulted, replied that before marriage is consummated by carnal union, it is permitted [Note: The Decretal reads *licere* (“to be permitted”), and below has *per* (“through”) for *propter* (“on account of”).] for one spouse, even without consulting the other, to enter religion, so that the remaining spouse may thereafter lawfully marry another, we advise you to observe the same in the aforesaid case. This is so although the reason for which that woman was induced to receive the veil is false, since, even without any such reason, she could have done the same thing for the sake of religion.

Moreover, although the aforesaid woman seems, in receiving the veil, to have assumed the religious habit, nevertheless, if she wishes to remain in her own house, as though intending to preserve a purpose of chastity in the world, the marriage already contracted must be consummated, unless she has bound herself by a vow [Note: The Decretal has *matrimonium* (“marriage”) and immediately afterward *astrinxerit* (“has bound”) for *constrinxerit* (“has bound herself”).] to regular observance; in that case she may be compelled, after leaving the world, to carry out her religious purpose.]

Given on the 2nd Ides of January [12 January].

CXCVI. TO THE SAME. He confirms certain institutions established by him. (14 Kalends of February [19 January].)

Blessed be God, from whom all good things proceed, who has deigned to impart to you zeal as well as knowledge, so that, as a prudent and honorable man, you direct the gaze of your mind toward those things which adorn the holy Church and make her shine amid the darkness of the world. In our presence the tenor of certain institutions which you are known to have established for advancing the beauty of ecclesiastical propriety was recited. In them, according to the diversity of places and customs, you have established many measures, as is hoped, salutary for the inhabitants. Although you have humbly requested that we strengthen those institutions with the safeguard of apostolic confirmation, lest through such confirmation we should appear to establish a rule of common law, we have not thought fit, as a precaution, to confirm them specifically. Yet because from the prudence of the founder we presume the propriety of what has been instituted, we will and command that those provisions which you have established by prudent deliberation be caused by our authority to be observed inviolably in your province.

Given on the 14th day before the Kalends of February [19 January].

CXCVII. TO THE SAME. That he may ordain a bishop in a city which he has brought over to the worship of the faith. (Ides of January [13 January].)

[Col. 0775A]

Since, with just and pious thought for avenging the injury done to the Christian name, you have resolved, from a religious purpose of mind, to set out against the pagans, by the authority of these presents we grant you that, in a city which, after the foulness of the pagans has been removed, you shall be able, Christ helping, to bring over to the worship of the Christian faith, you may ordain a Catholic bishop. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given on the Ides of January [13 January].

CXCVIII. TO THE SAME. That an institution established by him concerning the condition of the monks of the black order should be observed. (15 Kalends of February [18 January].)

[Col. 0775B]

We receive with gratitude and approval, and pursue your brotherhood with due thanksgiving, because, like a prudent and honorable man, you extend the attention of your consideration with diligent solicitude toward those things by which sacred religion may be advanced in the house of the Lord. From the tenor of your letters we perceive that, while visiting the churches of the kingdom of Denmark in fulfillment of the office of supervision entrusted to you, you saw that the state of the monks of the black order was wavering in many places, especially because of differing customs of different regions, and you endeavored to bring the order back to uniformity.

But since, without a head, even the most firm discipline is dissolved and the integrity of the flock is scattered, at the request of the prelates of the same order you prudently granted them permission to elect, in a fixed place, a fixed ruler for themselves, who might provide for the welfare and salvation of the entire order and whom all the monks and abbots of the black order should universally obey. Therefore, when the whole general chapter of all the abbots of the monasteries of Lund had chosen a place for meeting and had set the abbot of that same monastery over them as their ruler, you confirmed, at their common request, what they had done in this matter, humbly and devoutly asking us to strengthen it by apostolic protection.

Although, both for the honor of the Church and because of your earnest prayers, which we know proceed from sincere intention, we wish what has prudently been done in this matter to be firmly observed, nevertheless, because in such institutions some new circumstances are customarily liable to arise which might counsel alteration, we will and command that the said institution be observed inviolably for four years. Within that period, unless something appears which counsels its alteration, it may thereafter safely be confirmed by apostolic authority.

Given on the 15th day before the Kalends of February [18 January].

CXCIX [Note: This letter is found among the Decretals, Book I, title 29, *On the Office and Power of a Delegate Judge*, chapter 25; there it is said to be addressed to the abbot of Bordesley (see following note) and the prior of the Holy Sepulchre. Passages distinguished in italics indicate variant readings or are absent from the Decretals.] TO … THE ABBOT OF BARDESLERA [Note: This appears to be written thus in Conti’s copy. But we fear that *de Bordesleja* should be read. For the matter seems to concern the abbot of Bordesley Abbey, of the Cistercian order, which was founded in Worcestershire by Matilda the Empress, daughter of King Henry, in 1138. See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 803.], AND TO … THE PRIOR OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE, AND TO … THE DEAN OF THE DIOCESE OF WORCESTER. That proceedings should occur in the case between R., rector of the church of St Aldate, on the one side, and Thomas, rector of the chapel of St John of Glovernia, on the other, unless the plaintiff has become a member of the judge’s household. (6 Kalends of February [27 January].)

[Col. 0776B]

[At the representation of our beloved son R., rector of the church of Saint Aldate [Note: The Decretal reads *Saldati*, and immediately afterward “our” for “of our apostolic office.”], it has come to the hearing of our Apostolic See that, whereas he had formerly obtained from us the delegation of the case concerning parochial right between himself and Thomas, rector of the chapel of Saint John of Glovernia, in the diocese of Worcester [Note: The Decretal has “T.” for “Thomas” … “diocese.”], to our venerable brother … bishop of Worcester [Note: The Decretal reads *Wigori.* See Letter 23 of Book V, note.] and his fellow judges, proceedings having afterwards taken place in that dispute, the bishop, after a lapse of time and before a definitive sentence was reached [Note: The Decretal has “before” for “until.”], admitted the said R. into his household. Without him the other two judges could not proceed in the case, as was directed in our letters [Note: The Decretal reads “the other fellow judges” for “the remaining two judges.”], and one of them [Note: The Decretal adds “fellow judges.”] was official of the aforesaid bishop; for this reason he could be regarded as suspect by the opposing party.

Therefore, since on this account both the bishop and the aforesaid official could rightly be challenged by the opposing party—as persons whom R. himself had requested as judges and whose household member he afterwards became—he asked that the decision of the case be committed to your discretion. Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, if this is so, unless after becoming his household member he has consented to litigate before him, you should not delay to proceed in the case according to the tenor of the earlier letters, after due inquiry and with the obstacle of appeal removed. Otherwise, restore the parties to examination before the former judges.] But if not both of you, etc.

Given on the 6th day before the Kalends of February [27 January].

CC [Note:

A fragment of this letter is found among the Decretals, Book V, title 1, *On Accusations, Inquisitions, and Denunciations*, chapter 17, where it is said to be addressed to the bishop of Vercelli and the abbot of Toleto. What is printed there is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are given.

Ughellus presents various fragments of the same letter in *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, cols. 532 and 1497. What is printed in his work is marked here by a double quotation-mark at the beginning of each line in the margin.]

TO … THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI [Note: See Letter 178 of Book VIII, note.], TO … THE ABBOT OF TILETO [Note: He was probably Gerard Sessius, from Reggio in Lombardy. First a canon of Parma, then a Cistercian monk, and then abbot of St Mary of Toleto in the diocese of Acqui, after the death in 1210 of Peter, bishop of Novara (of whom below), he himself was raised to the episcopal see of Novara. See UGHELLUS, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 969.], AND TO … PRIEST ALBERT OF MANTUA. How and in what manner they ought to proceed against the bishops of Novara and Ivrea. The resignation of the bishops of Asti and Verona is also discussed. (4 Kalends of February [29 January].)

[Col. 0777A]

“ [Note: See Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 532.] [[Note: These words are in Ughellus.] How and when] a prelate ought to proceed to inquire into and punish the offenses of subjects is plainly gathered from the authorities of the New and Old Testaments, from which canonical enactments on this matter afterwards proceeded. For it is read in the Gospel that the steward who had been accused before his lord as though he had dissipated his goods heard from him: ‘What is this that I hear concerning you? Render an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward’ (Luke 16). And in Genesis the Lord says: ‘I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry which has come to me’ (Genesis 18).

From these authorities it is manifestly proved that not only when a subject, but also when a prelate, commits an offense, if report and public rumor of his misconduct come to the ears of his superior—not from ill-wishers and slanderers, but from prudent and honorable persons, and not merely once but frequently, as the phrase “outcry” indicates and public report makes clear—the truth ought to be investigated more carefully before the elders of the Church. Thus, if the nature of the matter requires it, canonical severity may strike the offender’s fault; yet the same person should not be both accuser and judge, but, as though public report brought it forward or outcry denounced it, he should perform the duty of his office.

Although this must be diligently observed with respect to subjects, it must be observed still more diligently with respect to prelates, who are set up as a target for the arrow. Because they cannot please everyone, since by office they are bound not only to rebuke but also to reprimand [Note: Ughellus ends here.],” [Note: What follows is not found in UGHELLUS, at the place cited in the note.] and sometimes even to suspend, or at times to bind, they often incur the hatred of many and suffer plots against them. Therefore the holy Fathers wisely ordained that accusations against prelates should not easily be admitted, lest, when the columns are shaken, the building collapse—unless careful precaution is applied, by which the door is closed not only to false but also to malicious accusation.

Yet they wished so to provide for prelates that they would not be accused unjustly, while also taking care that they might not sin insolently. They found an appropriate remedy for each disease: namely, that a criminal accusation aiming at diminution of status—that is, at degradation—must not be admitted at all unless a lawful written accusation has first been filed. But when anyone has been publicly accused concerning his offenses, so that the outcry has risen to such a degree that it cannot longer be ignored without scandal or endured without danger, there should, without any scruple of doubt, be proceedings to investigate and punish his offenses, not from the fuel of hatred but from the motive of charity. Thus, if the offense is grave, although he is not deposed from his order, he is nevertheless wholly removed from administration. This accords with the Gospel sentence by which the steward is removed from stewardship because he cannot render a worthy account of his stewardship.

This procedure, [if, concerning our venerable brother … bishop of Novara [Note:

These matters must certainly be compared with what Ughellus relates, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 968 ff.

[Col. 0778C] “LVI. Peter, formerly a canon of the Cathedral, rose to the see of Novara; Pope Innocent III mentions his election in a letter to the bishop of Lodi, and likewise in another letter to the canons of Novara, summarized in chapter *Causa*, *On Judgment and Res Judicata*.”

(See, in Baluze, Letter 451 of Book I; and in the Decretals, Book II, title 27, *On Judgment and Res Judicata*, chapter 14.)

Ughellus continues, in the place cited:

“Later Peter went into exile from his own see in order to defend ecclesiastical jurisdiction, as Pope Innocent III records in his letters to the chapter of Novara, written in 1200 and extant in the Vatican Register, Book III, Letter 6.”

(See Letter 7 of Book III.)

Ughellus again, in the place cited:

“Peter subsequently assigned certain goods in trust to Jacob and other members of the Momo family, in 1202. He administered the Church of Novara for fourteen years and died in 1210.”]
the bishop, [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Decretals add “the procedure of the inquiry,” and shortly afterward omit the words “lest … loss.”] you have observed, we commend in the Lord your intention and discretion. But if on any occasion you have omitted the same procedure, lest a slight saving lead to a serious loss, we wish that this procedure should still be observed at a suitable time, lest injuries arise from the source from which rights arise. Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish your devotion, beseeching you in Christ Jesus, who is to come to judge the living and the dead [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Decretals contain only, in place of “and therefore … the dead”: “therefore we command,” and shortly afterward omit the word “perhaps.”], that, having recourse to the judgment of your conscience [Col. 0779A], if perhaps you have transgressed against the prescribed procedure as men, you should not be ashamed to correct your error—you who have been appointed to correct the errors of others—for before the most exacting [Note: [Col. 0779C] The Decretals read “strict judge … measure with which you measured,” and shortly afterward omit the little word “and,” as below the words distinguished in italic type.] judge, the measure with which you have measured will be measured back to you also. That is, you should find some fitting occasion through which, lest your authority be diminished, you may for the present suspend action as cautiously and prudently as possible, since what has been done disorderly cannot be dealt with orderly. But if you have observed the prescribed procedure, we will and command that, putting aside every favor and fear, having God alone before your eyes, and walking the royal road, you proceed in this matter without respect of persons, according to the form which we have thought fit to set out for you in other letters [Col. 0779B]; and do not fear any man against God, but rather fear God above every man.

Moreover, we wish the form of oath which you received from the clergy of Novara concerning the inquiry to be made in this matter to be observed in similar cases: namely, that the clergy swear that concerning those matters which they know or believe [Note: [Col. 0779C] The Decretals add “to exist.”] should be reformed in their church, both in head and members, excepting hidden crimes, they will state the unalloyed and complete truth to the investigators.]

“[Note: [Col. 0779C] See Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1497.] Concerning the bishop of Ivrea [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Bernard, a monk of Saint Benedict, attained this see (of Ivrea, alternatively Eporedia) by no honorable means in 1204; and shortly afterward, that is, in 1205 (that is, 1206), was deprived of his bishopric by the authority of Pope Innocent III. Innocent writes the following concerning him [Col. 0779D] in letter 4 of book VI (read letter 200 of book VIII) of his Register, addressed to the bishop of Vercelli, the abbot of Tileto, and Albert, priest of Mantua, directing them to compel him to resign: ‘Concerning the bishop of Ivrea,’ etc. …”], in reply to you, we command that you induce him effectively to resign the bishopric, since he is incompetent and useless; and, if he is unwilling to yield voluntarily, because his offences concerning dilapidation and simony have been proved [Col. 0779C], you are to depose him from administration of the church of Ivrea, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed. You are to ensure beneficially that the same church is provided with a suitable person, restraining any opponents by ecclesiastical censure.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] What follows, to the end, is also read in Ughelli, ibid., cols. 553 and 554.]

But we regard the resignation of the bishop of Asti [Note: [Col. 0779D]

Concerning him, Ughelli has the following, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 532:

“Boniface, formerly a monk of Saint Benedict, became bishop of Asti upon the death of Nazarius. In 1198 he sold Licinium and Saint Michael to William, marquis of Ceva; and in the following year he invested the commune of Asti with Masio, Rupa, Insula, a fourth part of the territory, and Azano. In 1202 he gave the church of Saint Andrew of Valfeneria to the canons of Saint Peter of Cuzano. But because he had alienated several other places and rights of his church, to its grave prejudice, when the matter had been reported to Innocent, he resigned the bishopric, whether willingly or unwillingly. When Innocent was informed of this, he wrote as follows from the Vatican Register to the bishop of Vercelli [Col. 0780C] and to the abbot of Tilieto of the Cistercian order: ‘How and when,’ etc.”

See the note at the beginning of this letter. Ughelli continues:

“After receiving these letters Gerard, abbot of Tillieto, one of the delegates, assigned to the monastery of Saints Philip and James of the Vallombrosan order near Asti—into which Boniface had withdrawn—a suitable portion from the episcopal revenues for his support: six Asti pounds, payable on the Kalends of August [Col. 0780D] for as long as he lived. During that time no successor was appointed to him; but Rebufus, a canon of the same church, was made administrator of the bishopric in 1206, when Valla of Casteletta in the territory of Asti, formerly provost of Saint Secundus of Asti, was elected bishop of Savona. His death is recorded in the cathedral necrology under the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

“Guidotto, or Guidetto, succeeded him after Boniface died among the monks. Of him we first have this: that in 1210, etc.”]

not merely as valid but also as pleasing. Yet you should know that we do not approve the provision which you determined to make for him from the goods of the monastery of Fruttuaria, should it please us: first, because, as we have learned, that monastery would suffer exceedingly grave harm from it; and second, because that bishop would destroy those goods, as he has already destroyed others, since he is a notorious dilapidator and a prodigal squanderer. Nevertheless, to avoid a scandal among his kinsmen, who are noble and powerful, we permit you to assign him annual payments—not excessive ones, but only those necessary—in different churches, without burdening those churches, so that, residing at some monastery, since he is a monk, he may expend them for the maintenance of an honorable life.

[Col. 0780B] [Note: [Col. 0780D] Thus far Ughelli, vol. IV, col. 1497. What follows, as we have already said in the preceding note, is found in the same author, ibid., cols. 553 and 554.]

Furthermore, let your devotion know that the bishop of Verona has often entreated us for permission to resign. [Note: [Col. 0780D] These matters must certainly be compared with what is reported by Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 765). On Adelard, bishop of Verona and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, see letter 39 of book III, note. It has been established from instruments issued in 1207, 1209, and 1211 that he did not in any way resign the bishopric.] Therefore, when you have come to visit the church of Verona, if you see it expedient, grant him by apostolic authority permission to resign, beneficially arranging for a suitable person to be set over that church as pastor.

We approve the constitutions which, for the correction of offences and reform of morals, we have learned that you have not so much made as renewed. We wish you to cause them to be laudably observed by the clergy, commanding the prelates in our name to ensure that full justice is rendered to laypersons who complain, notwithstanding frivolous appeals which the clergy frequently lodge to their prejudice [Col. 0780C], lest, through a failure of justice, clergy be drawn by laypersons before a secular court. We altogether forbid this to happen; and you must strive in every way that it shall not happen.

Moreover, we wish your vigilance against the deceits of heretics to be alert. We admonish and beseech you in the Lord to apply yourselves prudently and effectively to uprooting from the Lord’s field [Col. 0781A] the tares of heretical depravity.”

“Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.”

CC I [Note: [Col. 0781D] This letter is found among the Decretals, book III, title 41, *On the Celebration of Masses, the Sacrament of the Eucharist, and Divine Offices*, chapter 3.] … TO THE BISHOP OF WORCESTER [Note: [Col. 0781D] See letter 23 of book V, note.]. That, except on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, it is sufficient for a priest to celebrate one Mass. (Rome, seventh day before the Kalends of February.)

[You have asked us whether a priest may celebrate two Masses on the same day. To this we have thought fit to reply [Note: [Col. 0781D] The Decretals read “we reply” in place of “You have asked … reply.”] that, except on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, unless necessity counsels otherwise, it is sufficient for a priest to celebrate only one Mass once a day.]

[Col. 0781B] Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of February.

CC II [Note: [Col. 0781D]

This letter was published by Plessis, *History of the Church of Meaux*, vol. II, p. 96, document 215; it is therefore given here in brackets. Variant readings are supplied.

For the subject, see letter 137 of book V.]

… TO THE DEAN OF SAINT THOMAS OF CRISPEJAC [Note: [Col. 0781D] Peter, dean of Saint Thomas of Crispey, is recorded in instruments from the very year of its foundation, 1182, down at least to 1211. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 1482.], IN THE DIOCESE OF SENLIS, AND TO GERINDUS OF CRECH OF SOISSONS [Note: [Col. 0781D] In Plessis, “Germundus.”], AND MASTER GIR. [alternatively Gerard] OF SAINT DENIS OF NOYON, CANONS. He commits to them the case between the bishop of Meaux and the abbess of Jouarre. (Rome, fifth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Formerly, after a suit had been lawfully joined in our court between the procurators of our venerable brother … the bishop of Meaux [Note: [Col. 0781D] See letter 188 of book VIII, note.] and our beloved daughter in Christ … the abbess of Jouarre [Note: [Col. 0781D] See letter 130 of book V, note.], both concerning obedience, which the said bishop complained had been withdrawn from him by that abbess in the consecration of altars [Col. 0781C], dedication of churches, veiling of virgins, ordination of clergy, furnishing of procurations, and imposition of penances for more serious crimes, and in other matters which the bishop of Meaux had customarily exercised in the monastery and town of Jouarre; and concerning obstruction of jurisdiction, in respect of which the abbess complained that through that bishop grave injuries and losses had been inflicted on her and her monastery—we thought fit to commit examination of this matter to our beloved sons … the abbots of Longpont [Note: [Col. 0781D] Galcherus of Ochies, abbot of Longpont from at least 1201 until 1217, is known. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 475.] and … Saint-Just [Note: [Col. 0782D] Gervase, an Englishman by birth, educated in France, formerly prior of Saint-Just and seventh abbot there, to whom Philip, bishop of Beauvais, entrusted the governance and administration of the hospital of Saint-Just in 1203, appears in the charters of Selincourt in 1206. He was arbiter in 1207 between the bishop of Beauvais and the chapter. Thereafter he was abbot of Thenailles, of Prémontré, and bishop of Séez. He is entered in the necrology on 19 February. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 805. See also *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. I, col. 943.], and to Master G., archdeacon of Soissons. [Note: [Col. 0782D] Plessis publishes this commission, *History of the Church of Meaux*, vol. II, p. 95, document 213, from the cartulary of the Church of Meaux. There it is dated: Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of March, in the eighth year of the pontificate.] Having heard confessions, received witnesses, and understood the arguments, they sent the case, sufficiently prepared, together with transcripts of certain instruments, [Col. 0782A] to our examination, setting the parties a suitable term within which they were to appear before us to receive judgment.

Accordingly, when the parties had appeared in our presence, after we had been sufficiently informed concerning the merits of the case, by the counsel of our brethren we adjudged that obedience concerning the aforesaid matters should be restored to the bishop, the question of ownership being reserved. We excepted only those matters concerning which he alleged that obedience had been withdrawn from him among the clergy and people of the town of Jouarre. With respect to these we absolved the abbess from the bishop’s claim [Note: [Col. 0782D] In Plessis, “obstruction.”] as regards the possessory judgment. Nevertheless, we also absolved that bishop concerning the obstruction of jurisdiction, for which the abbess had sued him for restitution of damages.

Wherefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, causing the aforesaid sentence to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, after the said bishop has been restored, you hear whatever has been put before you concerning the right of ownership, and faithfully remit the case, when sufficiently examined, to our hearing, to be concluded by the judgment of our decision. But if the aforesaid bishop should refuse, within a month after the restoration made to him, to answer before you concerning the petitory action, you shall punish him for contumacy and restore the abbess to possession of liberty concerning the aforesaid matters. No letters shall stand in the way, except by consent of the parties, etc. [Note: [Col. 0782D] Plessis adds: “But the witnesses who have been named, etc. …”] But if not all … two of you, etc.

[Col. 0782C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the eighth year of our pontificate.]

CC III [Note: [Col. 0782D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, § 34.] … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO AND TO THE BISHOP OF ZAMORA. That they are to compel the kings of Castile and León to restore certain towns and possessions to the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem. (Fifth day before the Kalends of February.)

Let it be known to you that it has come to our hearing that, when, through the instigation of him who envies the works of peace, an uprising of war had arisen between our most beloved sons in Christ … the illustrious kings of Castile and León, and many hostile acts had been undertaken on both sides [Col. 0783A], our beloved sons … the prior and brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem established in Spain, trusting in Him who has made their borders peace, and nevertheless hoping in the kindness of those kings—who, although they waged war against one another, they did not suppose that the brethren’s poverty would be exposed to their attacks—did not fortify their castles and towns situated on the frontier of the two kingdoms as against enemies, but maintained them as for guests.

But the king of Castile, contrary to their trust, violently took from them two castles of that Hospital, namely Fraxin. and Paradinas, and three towns, namely Taurisella, Tarauca, and Porta, situated on the frontier of his kingdom. While doing this, he did not remember that, by invading the rights of his servants, it was exceedingly dangerous for him to become [Col. 0783B] an enemy of Christ while rising up against the face of the enemy.

Although you, brother archbishop, have by our command admonished that king to restore them, he has nevertheless not yet seen fit to comply; hence the aforesaid brethren complain that they have suffered most grievous loss. Since it is not conducive to the salvation of that king to hold such towns and castles against God, we have thought fit to admonish and exhort him by our letters not to delay restoring them, as he is bound to do, to those who claim them.
