Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your fraternity that, if the king himself—though we do not believe this—should perhaps neglect to fulfill what we command, you are to compel him to do so, as justice requires, after prior admonition, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal. However burdensome it may be to us to aggravate him in any respect [Col. 0783C], we must nevertheless defer more to God than to man. Take diligent care to fulfill the apostolic command in such a way that the aforesaid brethren suffer no loss through your failure and that we may deservedly commend your diligence; for we could not but take it ill if you showed yourselves lukewarm or remiss in carrying this out. But if not both … the other, etc.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

CC IV [Note: [Col. 0783D] Fragments of this letter are found among the Decretals, book V, title 33, *On Privileges and the Excesses of Those Privileged*, chapter 17. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets; what is not read in the Decretals is distinguished in italic type.] … TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 0783D] Roger Norreys succeeded Adam, formerly a Cluniac monk of La Charité and abbot of Evesham, who died on the day before the Ides of November 1191. Roger had formerly been a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury; without being requested or chosen by any community, he was raised to be abbot of Evesham by royal power as an intruder. This abbot cruelly oppressed the monks, withdrew from them much of their food and clothing, appropriated almost all their revenues and obediences to himself, and, because of his tyranny and disorderly acts, was deposed and made ex-abbot in the year of the Lord 1229 by the bishop of Tusculum, then the lord pope’s legate in England. *On the Abbots of Evesham*, from an old manuscript codex in the Deuvesian Library, in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 151, col. 2, end, no. 45.], AND THE BRETHREN OF THE MONASTERY OF EVESHAM. He decides the case between them and the bishop of Worcester concerning jurisdiction. (Fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0784A]

[From the mouth of him who sits upon the throne proceeds a two-edged sword, because from the mouth of the Roman pontiff, who presides over the apostolic see, there ought to proceed a most righteous sentence which spares no one contrary to justice but renders to each what is his own. Therefore, since a controversy had arisen between you and our venerable brother … the bishop of Worcester [Note: [Col. 0784D] See letter 23 of book V, note.] concerning the subjection and liberty of your monastery,] and we had committed it for examination to delegated judges [Col. 0784B], who sent the same case, sufficiently prepared, to our presence, setting the parties a fixed term at which they should appear before us with instruments and attestations in order to receive judgment, we granted the parties, who appeared before us through suitable procurators, a free and gracious hearing.

And indeed, [the procurator of your monastery alleged that the same monastery had been free and exempt from its very foundation, adducing in proof privileges of our predecessors—namely, two of Constantine, one of Innocent, and another of Alexander [Note: [Col. 0784D] The Decretals read “one.”]—as well as indulgences of Clement and Celestine; and he sought to demonstrate their continuous use from times long past through depositions of witnesses.]

[Col. 0784C] In the first privilege of Constantine it was expressly contained that Egwin, of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0784D] On Egwin, third bishop of the church of Worcester—who is said to have sat from 693 to 717; *Annals of the Church of Worcester*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 470—see Godwin, *On the Bishops of England*, p. 448.], bishop of Worcester, coming to the apostolic see, reverently related to our aforesaid predecessor a certain vision in which the Blessed Mary had appeared to him. [Note: [Col. 0784D] On this vision of Egwin, most foolishly invented by the monks in order to procure greater religious veneration for their founder and place, see Wharton’s discussion in his notes on the cited passage.] At that time the English kings Kenred and Offa, with whom the said bishop had visited the thresholds of the apostles, gave many benefactions from their possessions, by royal liberality, in the presence of the same predecessor of ours, at the place where the vision had been shown. He confirmed them by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0784D] The donation of Kenred, by the grace of God king of the Mercians, and Offa, by divine permission ruler of the East Angles, confirmed by Constantine, bishop of the Roman see, through the sign + of the holy cross, may be found in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 145, col. I, line 48.], so that a community of monks might be established in that place [Col. 0785A], according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, which then had little force in those regions, to the honor of the divine name.

Accordingly, the aforesaid pontiff commanded Brithwald [Note: [Col. 0785D] For almost two years after the death of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, who died on 19 September 690, the see was vacant; Brithwald, or Berechtwald, first a monk of Glastonbury and then abbot of Reculver, was then appointed to it. Bede says that he was a man learned in the knowledge of the Scriptures and thoroughly trained alike in ecclesiastical and monastic disciplines. No archbishop held the see of Canterbury for so long: he presided for thirty-eight years and six months. Godwin, *On the Bishops of England*, p. 43.], primate of the Britains, by apostolic letters [Note: [Col. 0785D] The authors of *Monasticon Anglicanum*, ibid., p. 144, col. 2, line 22, print this letter from an autograph written in Saxon script in the Arundel Library.] to establish, after convening a council, the divinely revealed fold, fortified by apostolic authority and endowed by royal liberality, for himself and his successors, with the said bishop Egwin present; especially enjoining upon him the care of souls of that church, so that, by the power entrusted to him, he should defend it against every assault of usurpers and incursion of tyrants. But if anything of an adverse character should be found arising there, it should rather be referred to the ears of that primate than that the holy place be unjustly corrupted by the covert judgment of anyone [Col. 0785B].

He also endowed that place with liberty, because the aforesaid kings had endowed it with liberty, and he forbade anyone of whatever rank from daring to corrupt or diminish what he himself had established by authority of the apostolic see.

[In the second privilege of the same Pope Constantine, we find it contained that he commanded the aforesaid primate by apostolic letters to protect and foster the churches of God established throughout Britain. Among them, he especially subjected to his authority the church which had only recently been established by the venerable man Egwin, bishop, through apostolic and royal authority, so that he should strive to preserve it forever free from every attack of adversaries. He decreed that the same place, under the sole rule (*monarchia*) of its own abbot [Col. 0785C], should be free from every tyrannical exaction and that no person of whatever rank should presume to inflict any burden there.

But, in accordance with canonical authority, the abbot is to be elected by the brethren either from that monastery itself or from the parish of the Wiccii; freely and canonically, without any exaction, he is to be blessed in that church by whichever bishop they prefer, provided that he is Catholic and has the favor of the apostolic see. In reverence for the venerable Egwin, who, having relinquished the episcopal see, became abbot in that monastery, he is to use a ring only in the celebration of Masses and is always to hold first place after the bishop of the Wiccii.]

From the provisions of these privileges, therefore, the procurator of your monastery sought to demonstrate that the monastery itself had, from its first foundation, been wholly exempt from all episcopal jurisdiction: first, because it is said to have been established by apostolic and royal authority alone, and thus is understood to belong, in spiritual matters, only to the apostolic see, and in temporal matters to the royal crown, since the supreme pontiff is not accustomed to command that a monastery be established by his authority [Col. 0785D] unless it is to be established on land granted to him; secondly, because he himself gave the place which the kings are said to have given by royal liberality, so that, just as they gave it liberty in temporal matters, he too may be understood to have given it liberty in spiritual matters, since temporal matters belonged to them and spiritual matters to him; further, because he especially entrusted the care of souls of that church to the primate of the Britains, to whose authority he is also said especially to have subjected it, so that if anything adverse arose there, it might be corrected by that primate’s diligence and prudence. Hence he seems to have entrusted the correction of that place to him alone, so that it belongs in no way to another.

Further, he decreed that the aforesaid place should remain under the sole rule of its own abbot [Col. 0786B]; and, since *monarchia* is interpreted “sole sovereignty,” it seems that the abbot of that place alone possesses principal authority there. That the words of those privileges ought to be understood in this sense seems to be declared more clearly by the subsequent privileges.

For the privilege of Innocent of happy memory contains that no bishop may presume to celebrate a synod or chapter, ordinations, or public Masses in the abbey itself or its chapels, unless invited by the abbot and brethren of that place; and when an abbot has been elected in the monastery, he is to be blessed in that church, without any exaction, by whichever bishop he may prefer, provided that the bishop is Catholic and has the favor of the apostolic see. Following Constantine’s footsteps, Innocent also decreed that the pastoral care of the entire household and church, and of the other places belonging to the same church, should rest only with the abbot of that place [Col. 0786C], and that their ordering should remain solely in his power, as has hitherto been observed.

The privilege of Pope Alexander appears to contain that the brethren of that place are to receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of clergy who are to be promoted to sacred orders from whichever bishop they prefer who has communion and favor with the apostolic see. It is decreed that the bishops of Worcester are not to exact anything unjustly from them, but are to remain content with only those things which it is agreed that their predecessors reasonably rendered to their predecessors [Col. 0786D]. At the end, moreover, is added: “Let the authority of the apostolic see be preserved”; and it is not said: “Let the canonical right of the diocesan bishop be preserved,” whereas, in monasteries not exempt, according to the approved custom of the Roman Church [Col. 0787A], canonical right is preserved to the diocesan bishop.

Moreover, the indulgences of Clement and Celestine of happy memory plainly indicate that the same monastery belongs to the jurisdiction of Saint Peter without any intermediary, since, after placing this in the preamble, they consequently add: “For this reason, therefore, we have thought fit to grant you the use of gloves and ring, dalmatic, tunic, sandals, and mitre.” Thus, by Innocent’s decree that pastoral care of the entire household and church remains only with the abbot, what Constantine had decreed is clarified: namely, that the same place should be free under the sole rule of its own abbot. Therefore, since pastoral care of the entire household and church must remain only with the abbot [Col. 0787B], it is clearly evident that the bishop ought not to exercise pastoral care there, especially since the abbot of that place ought to be blessed within his own church without any exaction. Therefore no profession or obedience ought to be required from him.

But because the abbot cannot personally exercise certain things pertaining to pastoral oversight, Alexander grants him, lest anything belonging to the fullness of liberty be lacking, freedom to receive the ecclesiastical sacraments from whichever bishop he prefers who has communion and favor with the apostolic see. And from the assertion that the same place belongs to the jurisdiction of Saint Peter alone, as is indicated in the indulgences of Clement and Celestine, it seems more clearly declared that Pope Constantine gave that place liberty, entrusting its protection to the primate of the Britains as his vicar or legate.

[Furthermore, the privilege of Constantine appears to contain something by which the same monastery seems to belong to the bishop’s jurisdiction: namely, that its abbot should always hold the first place after the bishop of the Wiccii [Note: [Col. 0787D] The Decretals read “of Worcester.”]. Since he cannot hold this place in a general or provincial council—for it would be incongruous for an abbot to sit first after that bishop above the other bishops—it follows that he is understood to hold this place in the episcopal synod. Therefore he is bound to attend the episcopal synod and consequently to receive and observe its statutes.

The privilege [Col. 0787D] of Pope Alexander, however, contains another point by which the diocesan bishop seems to have retained jurisdiction in that monastery, if not in all matters, at least in some. For it says that the bishops of Worcester are not to demand anything unjustly from the brethren of that place, but are to remain content [Col. 0788A] with only those things which their predecessors are known reasonably to have rendered to their predecessors. Hence it is clear that the abbots are bound to render certain dues to the bishops.

We therefore, having carefully heard and keenly understood these and other matters, and since prescription has been proved by witnesses by neither party, define by judicial sentence, with the common counsel of our brethren, that the monastery of Evesham is free in its head, as being wholly exempt from episcopal jurisdiction, and subject to the Roman pontiff and Roman Church alone, while its protection is reserved to the archbishop of Canterbury. But in its members—namely those which are not proved exempt—we decree that it is subject to the diocesan bishop. For this reason the abbot must attend his synod and hold the first place after the bishop of Worcester [Col. 0788B]. For these members also, as we have said, which are not exempt, the same abbot is bound to render to the bishop of Worcester the reverence, service, and honor with which the bishop of Worcester, when they have been fittingly rendered to him, ought to remain content.]

But because one who abuses a liberty granted to him deserves to lose his privilege, we will and command that, the freer you are from secular services, the more strictly you devote yourselves in all things to divine service. We therefore decree … of our decision, etc.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

CC V [Note: [Col. 0787D] Fragments of this letter are found among the Decretals, book II, title 26, *On Prescriptions*, chapter 15, where it is said to be directed only to the bishops of Ely and Rochester. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets; words distinguished in italic type are absent from the Decretals or indicate variant readings. See the notes to the immediately preceding letter, no. 204.] … TO THE BISHOPS OF ELY [Note: [Col. 0787D] See letter 54 of book V.] AND ROCHESTER [Note: [Col. 0787D] See letter 154 of book VIII, note.], and to Master B. of London. On the same subject as letter 204. (Third day before the Nones of February.)

[Col. 0788C]

[Having heard and understood the attestations, documents, and allegations in the case [Note: [Col. 0788D] In the *Decretals*, “the merits of the case.”] pending between our venerable brother . . . . . . . the Bishop of Worcester [Note: [Col. 0788D] See letter 23 of book V, note.], and our beloved son, the Abbot of Evesham [Note: [Col. 0788D] In the *Decretals*, “of Hevesham,” here and below.] [Note: [Col. 0788D] See letter 204 of book VIII, note.], concerning the churches established in the Vale of Evesham, which the bishop asserts belong to him by diocesan law, whereas the abbot maintains that they are entirely exempt from his jurisdiction,] we have clearly learned that those churches were not withdrawn from episcopal jurisdiction by the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, unless perhaps the Vale of Evesham is that place which Pope Constantine of blessed memory endowed with liberty, as is contained in his privilege, having been granted by the generosity of two kings, namely Kenred and [Col. 0788D] Offa. [Note: [Col. 0788D] Constantine does not in fact designate the place itself by a special name in the privilege already cited (see note to the immediately preceding letter), but uses only these words: “In the place of the vision shown, very many things from their benefactions, granted by royal generosity in our presence . . .”] [But the abbots of Evesham are shown by witnesses to have possessed them by full right for so long a time that they appear lawfully to have acquired a prescriptive right therein against episcopal jurisdiction,] unless perhaps the Church of Worcester had meanwhile been vacant for so long [Col. 0789A] that, after deducting the period of vacancy, the prescription has not been completed.

Although the case has been closed by both sides, yet, because each party alleges that it has omitted necessary proof, we, considering that each church has the status of a minor, and weighing equity, restore each against the other to prove the ground omitted, lest either suffer grave loss through such negligence. [Wherefore, by these apostolic letters, we command your discretion to inspect the privileges of the aforesaid kings [Note: [Col. 0789D] In the *Decretals*: “the privileges of King Kenred and King Offa,” and below “the aforesaid.”] which the abbot asserts that he possesses concerning the aforesaid liberty. If it is established from them that the Vale of Evesham is the place which our aforesaid predecessor [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Celestine,” read “Constantine.”] endowed with liberty, you shall absolve the Abbot of Evesham [Col. 0789B] from the Bishop of Worcester’s claim concerning the churches mentioned, adjudge those churches to be subject to the abbot in full right, and impose perpetual silence upon the bishop concerning them.

But if the abbot fails in this proof, hear the proofs concerning the period during which, within [Note: [Col. 0789D] In the *Decretals*, “during.”] forty years, the episcopal see was vacant; and if it is established that it was vacant for so long [Note: [Col. 0789D] The Worcester see is shown by the records of Warthon [Col. 0790D] and Godwin never to have been vacant for forty years.] that, after that period is deducted, the forty-year prescription has not been completed, adjudge episcopal right in those churches to the bishop and impose perpetual silence upon the abbot concerning that claim. But if the bishop does not prove such an exception, nevertheless, since he has proved an interruption concerning the Whitsun procession in the town and church of Morton, the reception and procuration of the archdeacon, [Col. 0789C] the payment of St Peter’s pence in the Vale of Evesham, cognizance of matrimonial causes, the suspension of the chaplain in the aforesaid town of Morton, and the interdict of the chapels in the aforesaid town of Evesham, you shall adjudge episcopal right to him in these matters—provided that, concerning such suspension and interdict, the interruption occurred within forty years—imposing silence upon him in the other matters, which the abbot is shown to have acquired by prescription.]

If perhaps they refuse to receive a definitive sentence from you, then, having received the aforesaid proofs, faithfully send them to us under your seals, setting the parties a suitable term within which they shall appear before us through suitable proctors to receive sentence. Witnesses . . . notwithstanding no letters except by consent of the parties, etc. But if not all . . . two of you shall carry this out, any obstacle of appeal having been removed.

Given, the third day before the Nones of February [3 February].

CCVI. TO THE SAME PERSONS. On the same subject as in Letters 204 and 205. (The seventh day before the Ides of February [7 February].)

By the authority of these presents we command you that, [Col. 0790A] if, in the case of our venerable brother . . . the Bishop of Worcester and our beloved son the Abbot of Evesham—which we have thought fit to commit to you under a specified form—a question of forgery should arise concerning the privileges of the two kings Kenred and Offa, which the same abbot is said to possess, you, supported by our authority, shall take cognizance of it, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, and bring it to its due conclusion; causing . . . notwithstanding no letters, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given, the seventh day before the Ides of February [7 February].

CCVII [Note: [Col. 0790D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, § 33.]. TO . . . THE BISHOP OF ROCHESTER [Note: [Col. 0790D] See letter 154 of book VIII, note.]. That he should persevere in governing and not seek resignation. (The Kalends of February [1 February].)

[Col. 0790B]

Having been brought, even unto old age and grey hairs, through the office of pastoral care, in your struggle you have learned how laborious is the warfare of human life upon earth. Although, with the Apostle, you can say, “I have fought the good fight” (2 Tim. IV), nevertheless, if the crown of righteousness is henceforth to be laid up for you, it befits you to complete the course of a finished work.

However greatly, weighed down by old age, you may count your toilsome nights; however much, like a weary stag, you may seek the shade of rest . . . however much, while panting among the steep places of the way, [Note: [Col. 0790D] Thus in the Vatican manuscript.] you may be drawn by love of your homeland; and however anxiously, like a hired labourer now discharged, you may await the end of your work: it is nevertheless fitting for you to perfect strength in weakness and to strengthen yourself more firmly in the Lord. Knowing that you have fixed your hand with [Col. 0790C] a stranger when you have taken upon your own soul the souls of the flock entrusted to you, you must not seek the haven of rest for yourself in such a way as to allow those sons who have hitherto sailed with you to be tossed upon this great and spacious sea, in fear of shipwreck, without the help of their oarsman. For you cannot so desire the beauty of fair Rachel as to be fittingly able to renounce the children whom she bore you.

Indeed, if you believe that the Davidic utterance calls down the Lord’s displeasure upon him whose days are made few and whose bishopric is received by another, you, being full of days, ought not to shrink from the pontifical office. For perhaps the Lord has caused the tally of your merits to increase along with the number of your years, so that what weak age may perhaps be less able to provide in word for instruction, venerable grey hair, full of merits, may supply by example. We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by apostolic letters diligently to consider that you are still necessary to God’s people; do not decline the labour of pastoral government. Casting your care upon the Lord, determine nothing concerning yourself contrary to the will of the Most High, who perhaps added days to your days because He had not yet foreseen a suitable bishop to be appointed in your place. Nor should you distrust your old age, which He who, when nature had failed, has power by miracle to make fruitful in the begetting of many—He who deigned to raise from the womb of old age and barrenness offspring which youth had refused—can render fruitful.

For since hitherto you have ministered beneficially in the Church entrusted to you, if, God forbid, another less useful person should be appointed upon your resignation, then even amid the very rest which you seek you would assuredly be much troubled, when, where you had exercised your ministry well, you saw, not without grief, the failure of a useless minister. Thus you would recognize that you had lost as much from the watchtower of contemplation as you saw withdrawn from the Church through you.

Given at the Kalends of February [1 February].

CCVIII [Note: [Col. 0791C] This letter should certainly be compared with the materials reported by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* in various places, especially vol. VII, [Col. 0791D] documents, col. 83 and following, documents 108 and 110.]. TO . . . THE PRIOR OF SAINT-VICTOR AT PARIS, . . . SIMON, SUCCENTOR OF SENLIS, AND MASTER S. DE LANGUET, A THEOLOGIAN RESIDING AT PARIS [Note: [Col. 0791D] Should it not be read: “EGIDIUS, PRIOR OF SAINT-VICTOR AT PARIS; SIMON, SUCCENTOR OF SENLIS; AND MASTER R. DE ORSON (or ROBERT DE CORÇON), CANON OF NOYON”? See the document cited by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 508.]. He commits to them the case pending between the Abbess of Footel and the Abbot of Saint-Denis in France. (The fourth day before the Nones of February [2 February].)

[Col. 0791B]

Our beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and sisters of Footel [Note: [Col. 0791D] The abbess at that time of the Abbey of Blessed Mary of Footel—also called de Nemore, or de Bolcodominarum—which adopted the name Malaenoae after acquiring an estate of that name, was probably Odelina I, or Edelina. She is known from charters from at least 1207 until at least 1218, and is greatly praised for her pious care for the sisters. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 587.], have made grave complaint to us that, although they had been put into possession of the priory of Argenteuil, concerning which there is litigation between them and the abbot [Note: [Col. 0791D] Henry I Troon, formerly a monk of Saint-Denis and prior of Argenteuil, is found as Abbot of Saint-Denis from June and July 1204 onward . . . In 1207 he made an agreement with Odo of Paris concerning the right to the church of the priory of Argenteuil, before arbitrators Geoffrey, Bishop of Senlis, Adam, Abbot of Charroux, and Ralph, Dean of Meaux, appointed by the Apostolic See [Col. 0792D] (see the note at the beginning of this letter). He died in 1221: *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 384.] and monks of Saint-Denis, in the diocese of Paris, under authority of our commission for preserving the subject matter of the suit, the monks violently expelled them from it. [Col. 0791C] Since the monks had not provided the lawful security for this, although we decreed that it should be provided, they requested that actual possession of that priory be granted to them, together with the fruits already received in the meantime.

But Master Thomas, proctor for the opposing party, said that the abbot himself had given the judges that security concerning the matter, with which they were satisfied. Therefore, since the nuns had not appealed, he earnestly requested that perpetual silence be imposed upon them concerning such a petition. Since the foregoing is not established to our satisfaction, we command that, the parties . . . what was [Col. 0792A] just . . . doing, etc. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given, etc., the fourth day before the Nones of February [2 February].

CCIX [Note: [Col. 0792D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, § 33.]. TO J., CARDINAL DEACON OF SANTA MARIA IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE [Note: [Col. 0792D]

See what has been noted on letter 184 of book VII, note; to which you may add, if you wish, what Matthew Paris says of this legate of the Apostolic See, vol. I, p. 214, line 33:

“During the same year (1206), John of Ferentino, legate of the Apostolic See, came to England and travelled through it, collecting a great sum of money; and at last, at Reading, on the morrow of St Luke the Evangelist, he held a council. When this had been done, after arranging his little bundles with great care and entrusting them prudently, he hastened as a traveller to the sea and, on reaching it, bade England farewell behind his back.”]

. He orders him to restrain the King of England from inflicting injuries upon the Dean of Salisbury and others. (The Kalends of February [1 February].)

When we had sent apostolic requests to our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of the English, asking him to show himself merciful and favourable toward our beloved son Master R., Dean of Salisbury [Note: [Col. 0792D] See letters 185, note, and 187 of book VIII.], and toward others, clerics and laymen alike, who had incurred his displeasure on account of the affair of the Church of Winchester; also to release any who were held in chains on that account, allow those suffering exile for this reason freely to return, and restore to them all things perhaps taken from them on this account—the same king, at whose conduct we are the more greatly astonished, did not heed the apostolic requests. Instead, after receiving our letters, he replied that he had not injured the dean or his clerics. As for the laymen, nothing at all concerned us; but if the man exiled from the kingdom wished to submit to the judgment of his court, that was agreeable to him.

We therefore thought fit to admonish and exhort him by our letters to remit entirely his displeasure toward that dean, who is most dear and acceptable to us because of the excellence of his merits, and toward his associates and also the laymen who had incurred royal indignation on account of the affair [Col. 0792C] of the Church of Winchester; and to be merciful to them, so that he might obtain mercy from the supreme Judge, who in His anger does not forget to show mercy. Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, should the king himself—something we do not believe—perhaps judge otherwise, you, because the duty laid upon us requires that we not allow the members of the Church to be treated without mercy, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, shall determine concerning the aforesaid dean, the Archdeacon [Col. 0793A] of Winchester, and the others, clerics as well as laymen, whatever you see fit to determine, restraining the king himself from molesting them, if necessary, by whatever coercive means you deem expedient.

Given at the Kalends of February [1 February].

CCX [Note: [Col. 0793D] See letter 208 of book VIII and the notes there.]. TO . . . THE PRIOR OF SAINT-VICTOR AT PARIS, SIMON, SUCCENTOR OF SENLIS, AND MASTER S. DE LANGUET, A THEOLOGIAN RESIDING AT PARIS. On the same subject as in Letter 850. (The Kalends of February [1 February].)

Our venerable brother G. [Note: [Col. 0793D] See letter 145 of book V, note.], Bishop of Senlis, and our beloved sons J., Abbot of Saint-Victor [Note: [Col. 0794D] See letter 168 of book VI, note.] at Paris, and F., Dean of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0794D] See letter 9 of book VI, note.], informed us in their letters that, [Col. 0793B] when the case pending between the abbot and monks of Saint-Denis on the one hand and the abbess and nuns of Footel on the other, concerning both ownership and possession of the priory of Argenteuil, had been committed to them by us, the nuns, having first entered suit on the question of ownership and produced witnesses in it, afterwards brought an action for possession while the proprietary action was suspended. Acting upon the advice of learned men, they declared by an interlocutory judgment that the nuns were lawfully entitled to do so.

Accordingly, when, in the possessory action sought by the nuns on the ground that those whom they succeeded had been violently expelled from the property, witnesses had been produced by each side, and the case had proceeded so far that publication should already have taken place, the aforesaid nuns requested that the depositions of witnesses be published in the possessory case only. But the monks objected, alleging that, as the case of ownership had been first begun, so it ought first to reach an end; or at least that the witnesses in both the proprietary and possessory proceedings should be published together. After hearing the parties’ respective submissions, they wished to issue an interlocutory ruling. Having taken the advice of wise men, the monks added that the nuns had renounced the production of witnesses in the proprietary action. Since the opposing party denied this and the matter was, as it were, disputed between the parties, they ruled that the attestations in the possessory proceeding should be published and that they would hear the monks’ proofs concerning the nuns’ renunciation. But from this interlocutory judgment [Col. 0793D] the monks appealed to our hearing.

The delegates then set another day for the parties to consider whether they ought to defer to such an appeal. Having summoned prudent persons, they did not repudiate their judgment, but, on their advice, allowed the monks’ party a hearing, in case they should allege some effective reason for reconsidering the aforesaid judgment. The monks ultimately maintained their earlier appeal firmly after presenting their allegations. Since assessors could scarcely be found at Paris who would not be said to be suspect, although the nuns’ party at last declared that it would in no way regard as suspect anyone whom the three judges jointly summoned, the delegates nevertheless, considering the difficulty of the business, thought it right to report these matters to us. They ordered the parties to appear before us with these letters on the feast of St Luke the Evangelist then next ensuing.

Although the aforesaid Abbot of Saint-Victor and Dean of Orléans had likewise appended their seals to the letters containing this account, the said Bishop of Senlis delayed affixing his seal because the monks of Saint-Denis complained that certain matters which should have been included had been omitted. Therefore, after recalling the parties, the delegates set the morrow of St Remigius as the day, the monks firmly asserting that the nuns had had three productions of witnesses in the ownership case [Col. 0794B] and that the case had already been closed as to these, so that they would not be heard further in producing witnesses concerning the ownership case; they offered lawful proofs on these points, but the opposing party denied all of them.

But since, on or about the octave of St Martin—which had been assigned as the term for their appearance before us—the abbess for her side and Master Thomas for the abbot and monks came before us, and we granted them a full hearing in our consistory, the same master added that the abbot and monks had often requested the delegated judges to allow them a fourth production of witnesses in the possessory action with legal solemnity. Because the delegates utterly denied this to them contrary to lawful enactments, the monks, believing themselves unjustly burdened, appealed immediately to our hearing after the interlocutory judgment ordering publication of the witnesses in the possessory case. He endeavoured to prove this by the testimony of certain special letters of the aforesaid Bishop of Senlis. Among many other matters, the bishop wrote that, in the addition made to the first letters when the parties were recalled, the monks asked for this clause to be inserted: namely, that there still remained to them, in the possessory proceeding, a fourth production of witnesses with the formalities of law observed. They offered necessary proofs of this, and the same master promised to prove his assertion by lawful [Col. 0794D] witnesses.

The abbess, however, relying on the report of the three delegates and certain of their letters which stated that they had assigned the third day after the Purification of Blessed Mary for publication of the witnesses produced by both parties concerning possession, maintained that what had been added by the master was altogether false. Therefore, after diligently hearing these and other submissions made by both parties, we, with the common counsel of our brethren, command your discretion by apostolic letters that you meet together at Paris. If lawful proofs establish before you that the abbot and [Col. 0795A] monks requested a fourth production of witnesses with the formalities of law in the possessory proceeding and appealed on that account within ten days after the interlocutory judgment, unless perhaps the judges denied the fourth production because they wished to restrain an unbridled multitude of witnesses, admit the aforesaid abbot and monks to a fourth production of witnesses with legal solemnity; should they fail in proof, condemn them in lawful costs.

And unless the proprietary action has already progressed so far that ownership can be fully ascertained, conclude the possessory action, to which the abbess and nuns first had recourse by benefit of law; thereafter proceed lawfully in the ownership case. Otherwise, bring both questions to an end together. Those whom it is established have laid violent hands upon the nuns or their chaplain, declare to be bound by excommunication until they make suitable satisfaction and come to the Apostolic See, with testimonial letters from you, to be absolved. If witnesses who have been named withdraw through favour, hatred, or fear, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal ceasing, to bear witness to the truth.

We therefore solemnly charge and beseech you in Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, to set aside carnal affection and worldly fear and proceed by the royal road, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left. Let frivolous exceptions and malicious pretexts be no impediment; with every appeal entirely set aside, judge justly what is just, since you must render an account to God for this at the strict judgment. Notwithstanding no letters obtained from the Apostolic See except by consent of the parties. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given . . . at the Kalends of February, in the eighth year [of the pontificate].

CCXI. TO OUR FAITHFUL VASSALS AND THE PEOPLE OF RADICOFANI. Authority to elect consuls.

The benevolence of the Apostolic See, which extends even to foreign nations, ought to overflow much more abundantly toward its own household and vassals, in proportion as their care and concern are more intimately joined to it. Since it desires rather to be loved than feared by its children, because servile fear—which charity casts out—does not please it, even though it is at times offended by its own people, it wishes, if they will turn back, rather to spare than avenge itself; and it chooses rather to correct offenders in a spirit of gentleness than strike them with the sword of vengeance. Thus, as by the mercy of its gentleness it calls and leads unbelievers and strangers to devotion to itself, so also it may establish and confirm its household and faithful people in their fidelity.

Although on this occasion you have offended us not lightly, and your act has provoked us to anger all the more because we had less expected to be offended by you, whom we embrace as special sons and devoted persons in the arms of sincere love, nevertheless, because you humbly came at our command, imploring mercy and furnishing oaths, hostages, and sureties for one thousand pounds concerning the matter of the consuls, we wish to deal more gently with you and to grant your requests more graciously, insofar as we can do so with honour. We have therefore thought fit to grant you, for as long as it shall please us, the election of consuls, without any prejudice thereby arising to us. By these apostolic letters we command and enjoin that you never presume to elect consuls without the knowledge and assent of us or our castellan; but, when you decide to hold such an election, seek the assent of us or our castellan. Before you deserve to obtain that assent, the consuls elected must not presume to exercise the office of consul; they shall swear faithfully to preserve our rights and customs. But if, God forbid, you presume to act contrary to our command, you shall incur alike the stain of perjury and the penalty of the suretyship.

CCXII. TO N., DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF LE MANS. He determines the case between them and the chapter of Saint-Pierre de la Cour concerning observance of an interdict imposed by the Bishop or Chapter of Le Mans. (The sixth day before the Nones of February [8 February].)

[Col. 0796C]

When a dispute arose between you on the one hand and the canons of Saint-Pierre de la Cour on the other because those canons did not observe a general interdict laid upon the city of Le Mans by our venerable brother . . . your bishop [Note: [Col. 0795D] See letter 53 of book V, note.] or by yourselves, each party sent its messenger to the Apostolic See so that the case might be brought to its due end. When the parties were represented before us by suitable proctors, we granted them a free and gracious hearing.

The proctor for your church alleged that, whenever the Church of Le Mans wished, in its proper place and time, to subject the city to interdict for the excesses of secular authority, the Church of Saint-Pierre de la Cour, like a member not joined to its head, had not failed—while the others ceased—to celebrate the divine offices with bells rung [Col. 0796D] and doors open. When our venerable brother Octavian, Bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0796D] See letter 11 of book III, note.], was then exercising the office of legate in those regions, they went into his presence and took care to set out their complaint on this point. After summoning the parties and diligently hearing and considering the reasons of each, he found that the party of the Church of Saint Peter could not show itself fortified by a privilege of the Apostolic See and was firmly persuaded that it acted from pride rather than reasonable cause. He therefore gave definitive judgment that, whenever an interdict was imposed in the city of Le Mans, that church must observe it; and he subjected to the bond of excommunication and to the penalty affecting order and benefice those who should resist his sentence.

Afterward, when the entire city of Le Mans was subjected to ecclesiastical interdict because of certain excesses of secular authority, and the canons of Saint Peter had been notified to cease celebration of the divine offices and to observe the interdict as the other churches of the city did, they increased the rashness of their audacity and performed their office with greater solemnity, not fearing to act against the legate’s sentence.

Their proctor, on the other hand, alleged that the Church of Saint Peter had been free and exempt from its foundation and had been founded and endowed from the goods of the forebears of our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of the English. He firmly asserted, believing this established his position, that the same king and his forebears conferred the deanery and prebends of that church without consulting the diocesan bishop. He further alleged that, by this custom, that church had hitherto enjoyed such liberty, which the same bishop of yours had often acknowledged: you could place under interdict the parish chaplain who celebrated outside the choir of the aforesaid church. He argued from this alleged custom that, even during a general interdict, it was lawful for them to celebrate the divine offices with bells rung and aloud, provided the interdicted and excommunicated were excluded.

Having heard the parties’ submissions, we determined, with the counsel of our brethren, to invalidate such a custom entirely, if it existed, because it would break the sinew of ecclesiastical discipline; it is to be judged not a custom but rather a corruption. We nevertheless grant the same Church of Saint Peter that, whenever a general interdict is in force in the city, by the graciousness of the Apostolic See it may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Therefore let no one . . . contravene our determination and concession . . . but if anyone, etc.

Given, the third day before the Nones of February [3 February], in the eighth year [of the pontificate].

CCXIII. TO THE CANONS OF SAINT-PIERRE DE LA COUR AT LE MANS. On the same subject. (The Kalends of February [1 February].)

[Col. 0797D]

When the case pending between you on the one hand and our beloved sons, the chapter of Saint Julian, on the other, concerning your failure to observe a general interdict imposed in the city by our venerable brother . . . the Bishop of Le Mans [Note: [Col. 0797D] See letter 53 of book V, note.] or by that chapter, had been argued before us, your proctor alleged from a certain custom that it had been lawful for you, even during a general interdict, to celebrate divine offices with bells rung and in a loud voice, provided the interdicted and excommunicated were excluded. Since that custom, if it existed, would break the sinew [Col. 0798A] of ecclesiastical discipline, we have determined, with the counsel of our brethren, to invalidate it entirely, since it is to be regarded not as a custom but rather as a corruption. Yet we grant to your church that, whenever a general interdict is imposed in the city, by the graciousness of the Apostolic See it shall be lawful for you to celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command and enjoin you to observe that sentence firmly. Otherwise, know that we have ordered our venerable brother . . . the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0797D] See letter 53 of book V, note.] and our beloved son . . . the Abbot of Marmoutier at Tours to cause the same sentence to be observed inviolably by ecclesiastical censure, all obstacle of appeal removed; opponents, etc.

Given . . . at the Kalends of February, in the eighth year [of the pontificate].

CCXIV [Note: [Col. 0798D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, § 26.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NIDAROS, AND HIS SUCCESSORS TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED, IN PERPETUITY. He confirms for him ancient privileges and concessions. (At Rome, on the Ides of February [13 February].)

Although to all alike the power of binding and loosing has been granted, and although one and the same command has come to all, to preach the Gospel to every creature, nevertheless a certain distinction of rank has been maintained among them; and one man alone undertook the care of the Lord’s sheep, which rested upon all, when the Lord said to him: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” [Col. 0798C] (John 21). He also obtained the title of primacy among all the apostles and received from the Lord a singular command concerning the strengthening of his brethren, so that succeeding posterity might understand from this that, although many might be ordained to govern the Church, yet one alone should hold the place and summit of the highest dignity, presiding over all both by the authority of government and by the honor of judgment.

Accordingly, a distinction of ranks has also been observed in the Church according to this pattern; and, just as in the human body different members are arranged according to the variety of their functions, so in the fabric of the Church different persons are established in different orders for the performance of different ministries. For some have been appointed for the ordering of individual churches, others for the ordering of individual cities and their affairs; and in each province others have been established whose judgment is held first among the brethren, and to whose examination the questions and cases of persons subject to them are referred. Above all, however, the Roman pontiff is known to hold the first place, like Noah in the Ark; by the privilege bestowed upon him from above in the prince of the apostles, he judges and orders the causes of all, and throughout the whole world he does not cease to strengthen the children of the Church in the firmness of the Christian faith, continually taking care to show himself such a one as may seem to hear the Lord’s voice saying: “And you, when once you have turned, [Col. 0799A] strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22).

This, indeed, after blessed Peter, those apostles and men who in the succession of time arose to bear the care of the apostolic see have diligently and unceasingly endeavored to fulfill: throughout the world, now in person, now through their legates, they have earnestly striven to correct what required correction and to establish what required establishment. Following in their footsteps, our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of happy memory, was solicitous, in accordance with the obligation of his office, to correct those things in the kingdom of Norway which seemed to demand correction, and to sow there the word of faith. What he could not accomplish in person, because the care of the universal Church prevented it, he committed for execution to his legate Nicholas, then bishop of Albano, who was afterwards raised to the Roman pontificate [Col. 0799B]. When he came to those regions, as he had received instructions from his master, he put out at interest the talent entrusted to him, and, like a faithful and prudent servant, endeavored to bring back its multiplied fruit.

Among the other things which he accomplished there for the praise of God’s name and the commendation of his ministry, he granted the pallium to John, your predecessor, as our aforesaid predecessor had commanded him; and, lest metropolitan care for the province of Norway should ever thereafter be lacking, he established the city of Nidaros, committed to his governance, as the perpetual metropolitan see of that province. He further decreed that the bishoprics of Oslo, Hamar, Bergen, Stavanger, the islands of Orkney, the Faroe Islands, the Hebrides, Iceland, and Greenland should be subject to it as to their metropolitan see for all time [Col. 0799C], and that their bishops should obey both him and his successors as their metropolitans.

Therefore, lest anyone should ever presume to assail the force of that constitution, we, adhering to the footsteps of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Eugenius, Alexander, and Clement, all of happy memory, confirm the same constitution by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the privilege of this writing. We decree that the city of Nidaros shall be regarded for all time as the metropolitan see of the aforesaid cities, and that their bishops shall obey both you and your successors as their metropolitan, and shall receive the grace of consecration from your hand [Col. 0799D]. Your successors, however, shall go only to the Roman pontiff to receive the gift of consecration, and shall always remain subject only to him and to the Roman Church.

Moreover, since the pallium—the fullness, that is, of pontifical authority—has been granted to you, your brotherhood may use it only within the church, at the sacred solemnities of Mass, throughout your whole province, and only on the days written below: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, the Resurrection, the Ascension, Pentecost, the feasts of the Blessed Mary, ever-Virgin Mother of God, the birthday feast of the blessed Peter and Paul, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist, the feast of blessed John the Evangelist, the commemoration [Col. 0800A] of All Saints, at consecrations of churches or bishops, blessings of altars, ordinations of priests, on the day of the consecration of your church, the feasts of the Holy Trinity and Saint Olaf, and the anniversary day of your consecration.

Let your brotherhood, therefore, having received the fullness of so great a dignity, strive to perform all things so resolutely that the adornments of your character may fittingly correspond to it. Let your life be an example to those subject to you, so that through it they may know what they ought to seek and what they are compelled to avoid. Be outstanding in discernment, pure in thought, unstained in action; restrained in silence and useful in speech. Let your care be to benefit persons rather than to rule them. In yourself you ought to consider not the power of your rank but the equality of your human condition. Take care lest [Col. 0800B] your life fail your teaching, and lest, conversely, teaching contradict your life. Remember that the government of souls is the art of arts. Above all, let it be your concern firmly to observe the decrees of the apostolic see and humbly to obey it as your mother and mistress.

Behold, dearest brother in Christ: among many other things, these are the requirements of the pallium, these are the requirements of the priesthood. You will easily be able to fulfill them all, with Christ’s help, if you possess charity and humility, the mistress of every virtue, and if you have inwardly what you show yourself to have outwardly. We decree, therefore, etc., to the end.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of February, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0800C] 1205, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCXV [Note: [Col. 0799D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1208, §26.]. TO THE SAME. Authority to absolve persons excommunicated for violently laying hands on clerics. (12 Kalends of March.)

It is customary to grant, etc., down to “inclined”; by the authority of these presents we grant you that, since men from your regions cannot come into our presence without great burden, because of the difficulty and danger of the journey, to be absolved for violently laying hands upon clerics, it shall be lawful for you personally, in our stead, first receiving from them the oath prescribed [Col. 0800D] by the form of the Church and after suitable satisfaction has been made to those injured, to absolve them from the bond of excommunication. This is provided that no mutilation or death followed from that assault, that no violent hand was laid upon a bishop or abbot, and that the act was not otherwise so heinous that they ought rightly to be sent to the apostolic see. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, 12 Kalends of March.

CCXVI [Note: [Col. 0800D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §26.]. TO THE SAME. That no one may consecrate bishops in his metropolitan province unless authorized by him. (3 Ides of February.)

It is customary to grant, etc., down to “granting”; by the authority of these presents [Col. 0801A] we forbid anyone to presume to consecrate as bishops, without the command of you or your successors, those who for the time being have been elected in churches subject to you by metropolitan law, unless perhaps [Col. 0802A] the Church of Nidaros is vacant of a pastor; and then we require the command and consent of the chapter of the same church.

Given, 3 Ides of February.

# BOOK NINE OF THE REGISTERS, OR LETTERS, OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

In the ninth year of his pontificate, A.D. 1206.

[Col. 0801]

I [Note: [Col. 0801C]

Fragments of this letter occur in the Decretals, Book I, title 9, *On Resignation*, chapter 10, where it is said to be addressed to the bishop of Arles.

Pithou supplied nearly all the lacunae from ancient Vatican manuscripts.

We present the complete text, complete in all its numbered portions [Col. 0801D], following the Conti transcript. Passages found in the Decretals are enclosed here in brackets; passages found in Pithou’s additions are marked by a double stroke in the margin at the beginning of each line. For greater accuracy, we have also noted variant readings from both the Decretals themselves and Pithou’s additions.]

TO THE BISHOP OF CALAHORRA [otherwise: TRALATANUS; otherwise: ARELATENSIS; otherwise: CLARETANUS]. That he should not seek resignation; and an account is given of the grounds on which a bishop is compelled to resign and relinquish his bishopric. (Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0801B]

[“Had we not believed that, when formerly] [Note: [Col. 0802C] What follows is absent from the Decretals. It is found in the additions, Pithou edition, vol. II, p. 32.] you entered the pastoral office for divine service, you had prepared your mind for temptation and had prudently foreseen that, in human frailty, the various agonies of distress which you knew you would suffer in that office could not be borne without great help from God, we should surely fear that you had afterwards neglected to dash your little ones against the rock, and allowed them to grow so strong within you [Col. 0801C] that you can now scarcely resist their urgings that you relinquish the ministry you undertook.

But since, as we believe, knowing that you would fight against spiritual wickedness, you put on, as the Apostle exhorted you, the armor of God by which you might stand against the snares of the tempter, and since, though inexperienced, you were not ignorant of the anxieties of pastoral care which perhaps now, through experience, you dread, we do not know why you so urgently wish uselessly to abandon the government you undertook [Col. 0802B], when you ought by no means to have avoided undertaking it usefully.” [Note: [Col. 0802C] Thus far Pithou in the additions, who reads *irritare* (“to provoke”) for *vitare* (“to avoid”).]

[ [Note: [Col. 0802D] What follows is in the Decretals.] “For if in such resignation you promise yourself the fruit of a holier [Note: [Col. 0802D] In the Decretals this is absent; they subsequently read “better” for “holier,” and “ought” for “ought to.”] life, you should know that you are not holier than the one sanctified in the womb; and therefore you ought not to abandon the ministry of preaching which you have now undertaken, since he who had previously [Note: [Col. 0802D] The Decretals omit “and”; they then read *susceperit* (“undertook”) for *receperit* (“received”).] refused to become a bearer finally received the word of God to preach.

But if perhaps you seek to descend from the summit of the pontifical office for the sake of humility, and, contrary to the decision of the heavenly will, strive to abandon the episcopate given to you by it [Note: [Col. 0802D] This is absent from the Decretals.], by that very fact you seem wrongly to raise the head of humility [Note: [Col. 0802D] The Decretals read *eligere*, “to choose.”], inasmuch as you show yourself excessively stubborn in your intention to resign. For then you will preserve true humility in yourself, when by it you flee a lofty position and yet through obedience do not leave it.

We wish you to consider, therefore, venerable brother in Christ [Note: [Col. 0802D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are what follows concerning the pastoral office and, below, “pastoral office,” together with the word “also.”], that these are the grounds on which a bishop may seek permission to relinquish the pastoral office: consciousness of a crime, bodily weakness, lack of knowledge, the wickedness of the people, and irregularity of person.

[Col. 0803A] But in all these matters discernment must be used and caution observed.

For on account of consciousness of a crime permission to resign the pastoral office may be sought—perhaps not on account of every crime, but only that through which the exercise of that office is impeded even after penance has been performed. For since the Lord declares that, at whatever hour a sinner turns, He will remember none of all his iniquities, and since Holy Scripture testifies that no one is without sin, it is clear that one ought not to resign the pastoral office because of consciousness of every kind of sin [Note: [Col. 0803D] This is absent from the Decretals and from Pithou.]. For if all whose conscience reproved them for any fault resigned, few, or perhaps none, would remain in that ministry. For we all offend in many things [Col. 0803B], and if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us—a truth which mercifully excuses the man who miserably accuses himself. [Note: [Col. 0803D] These are absent from the Decretals, but are found in Pithou’s additions.]

Bodily weakness [Note: [Col. 0803D] Otherwise, “physical,” with the addition “or another kind.”] is likewise a reason for which someone may seek release from the burden of pastoral care [Note: [Col. 0803D] This is absent from the Decretals.]. This weakness arises either from illness or old age; yet it is not every weakness, but only that which renders a person incapable of carrying out the pastoral office. For if the duty of service undertaken may be abandoned because of every bodily weakness, the Apostle would vainly declare that he glories in his infirmities; and one burdened with old age ought not wholly to excuse himself from care for pastoral government, since [Col. 0803C] at times the weakness of old age does not urge him more to yield than the maturity of character usually found in old persons urges him to remain in his office. For the Apostle says of himself in such circumstances: “When I am weak, then I am stronger” (2 Cor. 12) [Note: [Col. 0804D] One ancient manuscript adds: “and powerful.”]; because bodily weakness sometimes increases strength of heart.

A person may also often seek relinquishment of the pastoral office because of lack of knowledge, for knowledge is especially necessary for administering spiritual matters and expedient for the care of temporal matters. A prelate, who ought to govern in both respects the Church entrusted to him, wisely renounces its governance [Note: [Col. 0804D] The Decretals read *ei renuntiat*, “renounces it,” and then omit “because … exercise.”] if he does not know the knowledge by which he is to govern it. For since he must teach his subjects what [Col. 0803D] they ought to do and what they ought to avoid, he will not rightly teach them what he himself does not know how to flee, nor exercise what he does not know. “For you,” says the Lord, “have rejected knowledge, and I will reject you, that you may not serve me as priest” (Hosea 4). Yet although eminent knowledge is desirable in a pastor, adequate knowledge must nevertheless be tolerated in him [Col. 0804A], for according to the Apostle: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 7); and therefore perfection of charity can supply what is imperfect in knowledge.

Because of the wickedness [Note: [Col. 0804D] The Decretals read “however,” and then omit “and is … found.”] of the people, a prelate is sometimes compelled to withdraw from their government when the people are so stiff-necked and so stubborn in their rebellion that he can make no progress among them. Indeed, on account of their hardness, the more earnestly he strives to advance, the more he is permitted, by just judgment, to fail. Thus the Lord says to the prophet: “I will make your tongue cling to your palate, because the Lord is one who provokes bitterness” (Ezek. 5). The Apostles are also recorded as saying to the Jews: “Behold, we turn to the Gentiles, because you have made yourselves unworthy of the word of God” (Acts 13). A pastor must not, however [Col. 0804B], abandon his flock because of every fault, lest perhaps he be compared to the hireling who “sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees” (John 10). But by permission of his superior, he may at last not so much flee timidly as prudently withdraw when sheep turn into wolves and those who ought humbly to obey now resist irrevocably. Although such persons ought to be severely punished for their crime, they ought nevertheless for a time to be usefully endured, because “he draws blood who blows his nose too hard.”

To avoid grave scandal, when it cannot otherwise be quieted, it is permissible for a bishop to seek resignation, lest he seem to desire temporal honor more than eternal [Col. 0804C] salvation, mindful of the Apostle’s saying: “If food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat flesh, lest I cause my brother to stumble” (1 Cor. 8). [Note: [Col. 0804D] This is omitted by the Decretals.] But one scandal must be subtly distinguished from another, as the Lord himself distinguished them. When the apostles said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” (Matt. 15), he answered: “Let them alone; they are blind and leaders of the blind” (ibid.). But elsewhere he said: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths” (Matt. 18). For though scandals must come, woe nevertheless to the man through whom scandal comes! [Note: [Col. 0804D] This is absent from the Decretals.]

[Col. 0804D] Irregularity of person—if someone, for instance, is a bigamist or the husband of a widow [Note: [Col. 0804D] The Decretals read “or a widow,” and then omit “pontifical dignity.”]—is a reason for which someone may seek permission to resign the pontifical dignity, as the Apostle attests when he says: “A bishop must be the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3). Yet permission to resign should not be granted on account of every irregularity [Col. 0805A] of a person who has ministered lawfully [Note: [Col. 0805D] The Decretals read *ministravit*, “ministered,” and then *utpote* for *ut puta*.], as, for example, if he was not born of a lawful marriage. Although he ought not to have concealed such an irregularity, yet if both fault and cause are hidden, a dispensation may be made, no less usefully than mercifully, for one who has laudably fulfilled his office, after a fitting penance has been imposed. “I,” says the Lord, “am jealous, visiting the sins of the father upon the children to the third and fourth generation [Note: [Col. 0805D] The Decretals read “generation.”] of those who hate me” (Exod. 20), that is, of those who imitate against me their father’s hatred. Hence it is clear that the virtues proper to those who do not follow their fathers’ vices may avail them in such cases, with the moderation of discernment being applied so that a distinction is made between illegitimate children (*nothi*) and those born of prostitution (*manzeres*) [Note: [Col. 0805D] “Thus,” says the old interpreter, “he calls one born of a prostitute.” See Cardinal Paliotus, *Book on Illegitimate and Spurious Children*.] [Col. 0805B], natural children and spurious children.”]

[Note: [Col. 0805D] What follows is absent from the Decretals, but is found in Pithou’s additions.] “But since vices often falsely represent themselves as virtues to a mind insufficiently vigilant [Note: [Col. 0805D] These words are absent in Pithou.], you must carefully consider whether the purpose of resignation which you seem to bear so fervently in your breast [Note: [Col. 0806D] Pithou reads *gestas* and subsequently *affectu* (“by desire”) for *effectu* (“by effect”).] is worthy of God’s hatred or love. For if you sought to resign for any of the aforementioned reasons, we should grieve equally over both the cause and its effect. But lest, beneath the cloak of imprudent [Note: [Col. 0806D] Pithou reads *providae* (“prudent”) and subsequently “more detestable” for “detestable.” Below he reads *aut* for *videlicet*, “favor” for “honor,” “his” for “its,” *poterat* (“could”) for *potest* (“can”), and “in time of necessity” for “when a storm arises.”] compassion, a detestable impiety impel you to resign, we wish you to consider that there are other grounds for which one wrongly asks, and even more wrongly desires, to resign such an office.

For if someone wishes to abandon pastoral care through faintheartedness, perhaps to lay down labor [Col. 0805C] or escape persecution, or through vanity—far be it!—that he may devote himself more fully to leisure or indulge more freely in pleasures, he does not deserve release from it. Although by such vanity, as one who sins mortally, he makes himself unworthy of it, he must nevertheless endeavor, having cast off vanity, to make satisfaction for his sin.

We consider another reason for resignation wholly detestable: namely, if someone wishes to descend from pontifical dignity in order to gain human glory, as though he chose to be lowly in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners; or in order not to lose worldly honor, which he gained by hypocrisy—whether because his pretense is now beginning to be exposed, or because [Col. 0805D] his zeal is cooling for some reason and he does not wish it to appear that he has been bad or is becoming so. Therefore he wishes, under the pretext of religion, to conceal his perversity, as though, abandoning Martha, he embraced Mary, and, disdaining Leah’s bleary eyes, desired Rachel’s beauty.

Or what if he wishes to resign because, in a time of prosperity, when fortune smiled [Col. 0806A], he appeared to have ministered commendably because all things prospered for him; but when a time of adversity threatens, he fears that if adverse events should happen by any chance, they will be imputed to his negligence? Clearly, if he seeks resignation for this reason, he may be compared to an imprudent sailor who, while the sea lay calm, managed the ship’s helm without much labor, but when the storm rises abandons it and allows it to reach the depths.

We also utterly detest the reason for resignation if a bishop wishes perhaps to resign so that another may succeed him—whether for the sake of money, through carnal affection, or in order that, when one worse than himself succeeds, he may be exalted as the best. We reject and condemn as almost sacrilege the claim that a bishop cannot exercise the pontifical office without sin because of [Col. 0806B] worldly occupations and secular concerns, when the Church venerates many saints who administered spiritual and temporal affairs alike. Nevertheless, the left hand ought to be beneath the head and the right hand in the embrace.

But we also wish you to observe carefully lest, through [Note: [Col. 0806D] Pithou omits this word; subsequently he adds “his” after “arrows,” reads “more attentively” for “more carefully,” and below lacks the word “perhaps.”] this design of your own choosing, you become one of those of whom the Prophet says: “The children of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. 77). Rather, you ought to set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel against those coming up from the opposite side. For, according to the judgment of Truth, not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres [Col. 0806C], shall be saved. Take more careful heed lest you place a stain upon your glory, not only before men but also before God; for under this cloak you will be unable to hide yourself—not merely from God, who searches the reins and hearts, but not even from men, who infer such things from plausible indications. Consider prudently, too, that according to the saying of the Wise Man, the holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit and withdraws from thoughts that lack understanding.

But if you fear to incur a burden of difficulty in defending the liberty of the Church, you ought not therefore abandon the honor of the episcopate. Consider carefully whether perhaps you are being tried by the just judgment of him who is not the tempter of evils, so that it may be proved whether you are willing to make satisfaction in the matter in which [Col. 0806D] you perhaps sinned. He, however, who despises or neglects to make satisfaction for an offense stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath, when God will reveal the hidden things of darkness.

Behold, we have indeed placed a mirror before you, so that you may contemplate yourself in it and, having searched your conscience, recognize for what reason you importunately seek permission to resign. For we—God Most High knows it—do not know why you persist in your intention to resign. Neither bodily infirmity, nor length of years, nor lack of knowledge, nor wickedness of the people, nor irregularity of person renders you unfit; nor do you confess that you have consciousness of a grave crime [Col. 0807A].” [Note: [Col. 0807D] Thus far in Pithou’s additions.]

[Note: [Col. 0807D] Again in the Decretals.] “But if you desire resignation for other reasons, the petitioner is not [Note: [Col. 0807D] The Decretals add “to you.”] to be favored in this, since such a petition seems indiscreet. For—to pass over as most well known the fact that idleness and pleasure are weapons of the ancient enemy for taking wretched souls captive—you ought not, because of the hardships of labor or the assaults of persecution, abandon your bride, to whom you have joined yourself by the bond of faith. [Note: [Col. 0807D] The Decretals add: “having pledged your hand to a stranger, you,” etc. One ancient Vatican manuscript cited by Pithou in the margin reads: “having discharged your hand to a stranger, you,” etc.] You know that “blessed are those who suffer persecution [Col. 0807B] for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5), because, when they have been proved, they shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him.

But you will say: “The spirit breathes where it wills, and you do not know whence it comes or where it goes” (John 3); therefore no one can search out the ways of that Spirit. Those who are led by the Spirit of God are not under the law, because “where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3). Therefore, if permission to resign is not given you by man, you will nevertheless resign, because liberty to resign has been given you by God.

Certainly, you are foolish if this is your wisdom. For how can one be led by the Spirit of God who acts against the Spirit of God? If what we have set forth is true—indeed, because it is unquestionably true—then without doubt he acts against the Spirit of God who attempts any of these things [Col. 0807C] [Note: [Col. 0807D] The Decretals omit “these things.”] contrary to truth, because that Spirit is the Spirit of truth.

Moreover, if you say that perhaps there is another hidden reason for which the will to resign is divinely inspired in you, we answer you: How do you know that such an inspiration is heavenly? Do you not recall what that glorious pontiff said when he suddenly began to lose bodily strength? “Lord,” he said, “if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse labor; let your will be done.” He followed the example of the one who had said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1), but “to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.”

“[Note: [Col. 0807D] This is absent from the Decretals and is found in Pithou’s additions.] Since, therefore, we have distinguished for you various grounds concerning this [Col. 0807D] matter, and do not know for which of them [Note: [Col. 0807D] In Pithou, *sub* (“under”), and below he reads “the ground” for “them.”] you desire to resign, we have thought it right to leave you to yourself, so that, judging yourself at the tribunal of your own mind, you may see whether you can satisfy your desire to resign in such a way that you can withdraw without fault from care of the flock entrusted to you [Col. 0808A]. For if by resigning you desire to benefit yourself alone, you unquestionably diminish your own benefit by as much as you fail to bestow upon others what you could have bestowed; for you would acquire greater gain for your soul when you procured the salvation of many without your own salvation. It is of greater merit to gain many persons for God together with oneself than to seek one’s own salvation apart from those whose salvation is known to belong to one’s care.” [Note: [Col. 0808D] Thus far in Pithou’s additions.]

[ [Note: [Col. 0808D] Again in the Decretals.] “Indeed, even if you shine with however great an endowment of virtues, if you do not have charity in yourself, you are proved to have nothing [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Decretals read “with however great a flowering of virtues,” and subsequently “you prove yourself” for “you are proved.”]. Under what pretext of virtue, then, do you seek to lay aside the burden of pastoral care, which can scarcely be abandoned without loss of charity? [Note: [Col. 0808D] This is absent from the Decretals.] No charity can be greater than that a person [Col. 0808B] lays down his life for his friends” (John 15). Since it is fitting for you, because of this charity, to lay down your life for your subjects, you ought not, on any pretext, to excuse yourself from their government so long as you can benefit them—if not all, still many. For if you allege labor as your reason, the example of the Apostle will support you (1 Cor. 15), who urges you not to shrink from such labor, declaring that he labored more than the rest for the common salvation. For even if success does not always follow labor, labor itself is nevertheless meritorious before God, as it is written: “God will render the reward of the labors of his saints” (Wisdom 10).” [Note: [Col. 0808D] Thus far in the Decretals.]

“[Note: [Col. 0808D] Again in Pithou’s additions.] But suppose that until now you have labored greatly and fought the good fight, so that you can speak with the same [Col. 0808C] Apostle; still, in order that the crown of righteousness may henceforth be laid up for you, you ought to complete the course of a perfect work. However much you may count the nights of toil amid the pains of distress that accompany the pastoral office, and however much, like a weary stag, you may long for the shade of rest; however much, oppressed amid the roughnesses [Note: [Col. 0808D] Pithou reads “heat and hardships.”] of the road, you may be drawn by love of your homeland and, like a veteran hireling, anxiously await the end of your labor, it is nevertheless expedient for you to bring strength to perfection in weakness and crown your struggle with perseverance.

And since you have pledged your hand to a stranger when you took into your own soul the souls of the flock entrusted to you, you ought not [Col. 0808D] seek for yourself a haven of rest in such a way that you permit the children who have hitherto sailed with you to be tossed upon this great and wide sea, in fear of shipwreck, without a helmsman’s aid.” [Note: [Col. 0808D] Thus far Pithou’s additions.]

[ [Note: [Col. 0808D] Again in the Decretals.] “Nor should you think that Martha [Col. 0809A] chose the bad part because she was busy about many things, while Mary chose the best part, which shall not be taken from her (Luke 10). For though the latter is safer, the former is more fruitful; and though the latter is sweeter, the former is more useful, since Leah’s bleary eyes were preferred to Rachel’s beauty in the fruitfulness of offspring (Gen. 29). Yet you can be both contemplative and active at once, following the example of the lawgiver, who at one time ascended the mountain in order to behold there the glory of the Lord with greater freedom (Exod. 24), and at another descended into the camp in order more usefully to provide for the people’s needs.
