Therefore it is more readily permitted for a monk to rise to the episcopate than for a prelate to descend to monastic life.” [Note: [Col. 0809C] Thus far in the Decretals.]

[Col. 0809B] “ [Note: [Col. 0809C] In Pithou’s additions.] Therefore we admonish [Note: [Col. 0809D] In Pithou the words down to the conjunction “and” are absent.] your brotherhood and exhort you most earnestly, commanding through apostolic writings that, abhorring that utterance of David’s imprecation, and fearing lest it be applied to you by the effect of your deed—the utterance which prays that the days of the wicked man may be few and that another may receive his bishopric—” [ [Note: [Col. 0809D] Again in the Decretals.] “do not refuse the labor of pastoral government. Cast your care upon the Lord, and determine nothing concerning yourself against the will of the Most High. When he sees that you are necessary to his people, he may perhaps take it grievously if he is neglected by you; and [Note: [Col. 0809D] The Decretals omit the words down to “but perhaps.”] perhaps he would disdain to receive you at his feet with Mary, because you had disdained to minister to him as the busy Martha while he lodged with you.” [Note: [Col. 0809D] Thus far in the Decretals.]

[Col. 0809C] “ [Note: [Col. 0809D] Pithou’s additions.] This too ought to establish you more firmly in your purpose of ministering: since until now you have ministered commendably in the church entrusted to you, if—God forbid!—upon your resignation another less useful person were appointed to it, you would surely be not a little troubled in the very repose [Note: [Col. 0809D] Pithou reads “from that.”] which you seek. For where you had exercised your ministry well, you would see, not without sorrow, the failure of a useless minister; and it would come about that you would recognize yourself to have lost as much on the height of contemplation as you saw withdrawn through you, not without your shame, from the church over which you preside.” [Note: [Col. 0809D] Thus far Pithou’s additions.]

[ [Note: [Col. 0809D] What follows is in the Decretals.] “But since, both in person and through your messengers and [Col. 0810A] letters, you have already been excessively persistent with us [Note: [Col. 0809D] This is omitted by the Decretals.] in seeking permission to resign, behold, we have thought it right to leave the matter to you: once the grounds [Note: [Col. 0809D] The Decretals omit this word, as they do below the passages distinguished in italic type.] for which one ought or ought not to resign have been distinguished for you, if you persist in this intention for some useful and honorable reason, resign with our permission—although you should know that this is exceedingly grave and distressing to us. Otherwise, know that permission to resign is wholly forbidden you by apostolic authority. For though you have wings by which you endeavor to fly away into solitude, they are nevertheless so bound by the bonds of commandments that you do not have freedom of flight without our permission.” If finally your own will should impel you to flight, we wish and command that you have this letter read in the hearing of your chapter.

[Col. 0810B] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## II. [Note: [Col. 0809D] The copy of this letter, which we had caused to be transcribed along with the others from Conte’s copy, has slipped from our hands—we do not know by what accident; and therefore we can give here only its summary. See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §34.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF TOLEDO AND COMPOSTELA

He commands them to endeavour to settle the disputes which the kings of Castile and León were pursuing concerning certain towns.

## III. [Note: [Col. 0809D]

Various fragments of this letter are found in the Decretals: namely, book III, title 41, *On the Celebration of Masses, the Sacrament of the Eucharist, and Divine Offices*, chapter 4; and in the same book III, title 46, *On the Observance of Fasts*, chapter 11. Passages read in both places are here enclosed in brackets. For greater exactness, we have noted variant readings both from the Decretals and from the additions in Pithou.

Raynaldus gives a portion of the same letter under the year 1206, §35.]

. . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA

In reply to his inquiry, it is stated that the vigils of the apostles are fast-days, and other doubts are clarified. (At St Peter’s, 21 February.)

[Your counsel] “ [Note: [Col. 0810D] This is found among Pithou’s additions; he immediately omits *namely*, reads *some* for *many*, adds *of the Lord* after *Advent*, and below has *occur* for *celebrate*.] You asked us concerning certain points: namely, whether one ought to fast on all the vigils of the apostles, since many assert [Col. 0810C] that fasting is not required on all of them, but only on six; whether one should also fast during Advent, since people hold differing opinions on this matter—some, though fewer, saying that one ought then to fast, while more declare that they are not bound to do so; and, further, whether, if the feast of those whose vigils we fast falls on a Monday, the vigil should be kept on the preceding Saturday?” [Note: [Col. 0810D] Pithou’s additions end here.]

[ [Note: [Col. 0810D] In the Decretals and likewise in Raynaldus.] But we reply to you on this matter [Note: [Col. 0810D] The Decretals read, “to your inquiry,” then omit “among us all,” and add *are* after *vigils*.] as follows: among us all the apostles’ vigils are observed by fasting [Note: [Col. 0810D] The Decretals read “are to be observed”; then “apostles” for “saints,” “their” for “those,” “the vigils of saints” for “and the vigils of saints,” and “are to be fasted on the preceding Saturday” for “we fast them on the preceding Saturday”; they omit the words “we give you … counsel.”], except the vigils of Saints Philip and James and of blessed John the Evangelist. For the feast of the former falls [Col. 0811A] within the Paschal solemnity, and that of the latter within the Christmas season. Among us fasting is also observed in the Advent of the Lord; and we fast on the preceding Saturday the vigils of saints whose feasts must be celebrated on Monday. Concerning the feast of blessed Bartholomew the Apostle, as to whose observance some persons raise a doubt, we reply to your request for counsel that in this matter you should follow the custom of your own region.]

[Note: [Col. 0811D] See the Decretals, book III, title 41, chapter 4.] You asked whether, on weekdays when Mass happens to be celebrated in honour of the Holy Spirit, the Blessed Virgin, and the Holy Cross, the angelic hymn, the Creed, and the proper preface ought to be sung, “ [Note: [Col. 0811D] These words are absent from the Decretals, but are found among Pithou’s additions.] especially since in your regions Mass is solemnly celebrated in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary on [Col. 0811B] Saturdays?” [Note: [Col. 0811D] Again, in the Decretals at the cited place.] To this we reply [Note: [Col. 0811D] The Decretals read, “we reply to your inquiry as follows,” and then “is sung” for “should be sung,” “is chanted” for “should be chanted.”] that among us, on weekdays, when the solemnities of Mass are celebrated in honour of the Blessed Virgin, neither the angelic hymn nor the Creed is sung, although the proper Preface is chanted in the Mass, so that the difference between a commemoration and a solemnity may be evident. Therefore the *Te Deum laudamus* is more regularly omitted than sung at Matins. [Note: [Col. 0811D] The Decretals, book III, title 41, chapter 4, end here.]

[ [Note: [Col. 0811D] See the Decretals, book III, title 46, chapter 2.] Moreover, since you asked what penance should be imposed upon those who, in the days of Lent, at the time when such a famine raged that a great part of the people were perishing for want of food, were compelled to eat meat: we reply to you briefly [Note: [Col. 0811D] The Decretals omit this, and immediately add *such* after *in*.] that we do not believe that those whom pressing necessity alone [Col. 0811C] excused ought to be punished in this respect; nevertheless, pour out prayers to the Lord for them and with them, that this may not in any way be imputed to them, since it belongs to good minds to fear fault where none at all is found. [Note: [Col. 0811D] These words are absent from the Decretals but occur in the ancient compilation; immediately afterwards they read *fault* for *penalty*, and add *fault* after *where*.] Likewise, concerning those who eat meat on Saturday because of the weakness they feel in themselves, in accordance with the custom of other lands [Note: [Col. 0811D] The Decretals omit these words, as also shortly below “than … they feel”; and below they read *we reply* for *we give you such an answer*.]—something never customary in your regions—since this is resented by others and gives them an occasion for detraction, we give you this answer: cause the custom of your region to be observed in this matter, but in such a way that no danger results on that account to the weak and sick.]

[Note: [Col. 0812D] These matters are also found in Raynaldus.] Furthermore, you requested an apostolic answer [Note: [Col. 0812D] Absent.] concerning those who fall ill during Lent or [Col. 0811D] other solemn fasts and ask to be permitted to eat meat: some of them promise to give alms for this reason; others, because of the urgent necessity of illness, demand that you grant this to them as though it were their due. To this we have thought it proper to reply [Note: [Col. 0812D] “We reply,” instead of “some of them … to reply.”] that, since necessity is not subject to law, you can and ought, when urgent necessity requires, to accommodate the desire of the sick, so that a greater danger may be avoided in them.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0812D] In Raynaldus, the eleventh day before the Kalends of March.], in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## IV. [Note: [Col. 0812D] This letter is found among the Decretals, book V, title 39, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*, chapter 36. Raynaldus also cites it under the year 1206, §35.] . . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA

That the beating of clerics, as satisfaction for an injury inflicted upon others according to the custom of the country, is forbidden. (At St Peter’s, 23 February.)

[It sometimes happens in your regions, and is held to be a custom of the country, as your brotherhood [Col. 0812B] informed us [Note: [Col. 0812D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are, below, the words “or ten.”], that clerics, if they have offended someone and wish to satisfy the offended party, according to the custom of the country already observed among laypeople, voluntarily submit their bodies to thirty, or ten, or more or fewer blows of sticks. They often receive these not under compulsion but willingly, not only from the hands of other clerics but also of laypeople. You therefore humbly asked us whether persons giving such blows incur the sentence of the promulgated canon [Note: [Col. 0812D] These words are absent from the Decretals but occur among Pithou’s additions.]? But we reply to your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0812D] This is absent from the Decretals, as are the words below printed in italics.] as follows: such laying on of hands, although not violent, nevertheless appears injurious, since that canon was promulgated not so much in favour of an ordained cleric as in favour of the clerical order. Therefore we will and command that you prohibit this from henceforth [Col. 0812C] throughout the province of Braga. But if, after such prohibition, any cleric voluntarily submits himself to such a penalty, or any layperson inflicts such a penalty upon him, let both be excommunicated; provided that the cleric make suitable satisfaction to the injured person without injury to the clerical order, so that peace may reasonably be restored between them.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## V. [Note: [Col. 0812D] This letter is found among the Decretals, book III, [Col. 0813D] title 42, *On Baptism and Its Effect*, chapter 5, where it is said to have been directed to the bishop of Moros.] . . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NIDAROS

In reply to his inquiry, it is stated that there is no true baptism unless it is performed with water and by a priest. (At St Peter’s, the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0812D] [You requested that an apostolic reply [Col. 0813A] be given you [Note: [Col. 0813D] Absent from the Decretals, but found among Pithou’s additions.], not, as we believe, in order to add knowledge to yourself, but in order that through the oracle of our word you might better instruct the ignorance of your subjects: whether infants are to be regarded as Christians when, at the point of death, because of a shortage of water and the absence of a priest, the simplicity of some persons has anointed their head, breast, and between their shoulders with a sprinkling of saliva as baptism. [Note: [Col. 0813D] In the third compilation, “sprinkling.”] Since, therefore [Note: [Col. 0814D] There: “we reply that since.”], two things are always necessarily required in baptism, namely word and element, according to what the Truth says concerning the word: “Go into all the world [Note: [Col. 0814D] Added: “preach the Gospel to every creature, and”; Pithou notes in the margin that these words are lacking in all the ancient Vatican manuscripts.], baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XVIII); and says likewise concerning the element: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John III), you should not doubt that those in whom not only both of the aforesaid things, but one of them, has been omitted, do not possess true baptism.]

[Col. 0813B] Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Kalends of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## VI. . . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NIDAROS

That he should forbid his priests to bear arms and go about in lay dress. (At St Peter’s, the Kalends of March.)

You reported to us with no small bitterness of mind, and we learned what was reported with no lack of paternal compassion, that certain priests of your diocese, not fearing to blush for the Gospel of Christ, have cast aside the dress of the clerical habit as though it were shameful and at times take up the arms of secular warfare. In these they shed the blood of very many persons; giving themselves over to many enticements of life, they engage in worldly pursuits, [Col. 0813C] utterly forgetful of clerical moderation. You therefore asked to be instructed by us as to what you ought to do in such cases and whether those who kill them ought to be sent to the Apostolic See to be absolved.

Grieving, therefore, over the dissipation of such persons, we have thought it proper to reply to your brotherhood that, since a shepherd must take diligent care lest through his neglect the sheep stray, it is fitting for you both to warn priests of this sort, subject to the rule of your care, lest they lapse into such things, and diligently to call back those who have lapsed from their errors, as far as the Lord permits you. But if they perhaps prove themselves irreclaimable, since wounds which do not admit the healing of poultices must be cut away with iron, then, keeping God alone before your eyes, you must deprive them of ecclesiastical benefice and office. [Col. 0813D] But that those who kill such men can excuse themselves, on account of those men’s criminality, from coming to the Apostolic See for absolution, does not appear.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Kalends of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## VII. [Note: [Col. 0814D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] . . . . . . TO THE PODESTÀ AND COUNCIL OF FLORENCE

That they should avoid heretics and persevere in the faith. (At St Peter’s, 5 March.)

Certain violent and impious persons, who are commonly called heretics, having long ago entered your city [Col. 0814A] in order to attack truth through the error of a depraved doctrine, violently endeavour to twist to a perverse meaning the statements of Holy Scripture that contain right doctrines. Of them it may truly be said: “This is the portion of the impious man with God, and the inheritance of violent men which they shall receive from the Almighty. Though his children are multiplied, they shall be for the sword, and his descendants shall not be satisfied with bread.” For while they lead simple people astray in error, they acquire for themselves a share in impiety; and by the violence with which they pervert Holy Scripture, they prepare for themselves an inheritance, not above in the land of the living but below in hell. Their followers, who, because they consent to their error, are as it were begotten by their preaching, [Col. 0814B] shall be multiplied for the sword; having become their co-heirs, they shall descend to the infernal regions, where the sentence of the last judgment will devour their flesh as a sword.

And since, according to the prophet, the seed of the righteous does not lack bread, the descendants of those who are born from the preaching of erring children are not satisfied with bread. For, while seeking to find a foolish flavour in the pasture of the sacred word, they remain fasting from the knowledge of truth, and the propositions of doctrine which they labour to discover for seduction cannot serve for refreshment.

Since, therefore, such violent and impious persons have long assailed your souls and those of your people with depraved deceits, treacherously preferring low things so that the wickedness they teach might prevail, they have now, through God’s grace, for the greater part—as we have learned—fallen silent; their depravity is recognized by you [Col. 0814C] and their folly exposed. Who, then, being of sound mind, would involve himself in their filth, which, although it may at times please superficially, nevertheless grievously pierces the conscience in practice? Who would also suppose true the things uttered by such fools, who pervert the sayings of Holy Scripture and profane the writings taught by the holy doctors of the Church?

We therefore admonish and exhort your whole community in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters and strictly enjoining you: remain steadfast in the Catholic faith and in the unity of the Church; cautiously avoid the impiety of such people, lest their sharp sword pierce your minds by deceit. Rather, as Catholic men who acknowledge the Church as your mother, devote yourselves more earnestly to the teaching of Jesus Christ, her true spouse. Worthily observe the ordinance which you made against the aforesaid impious persons, so that their inheritance may not fall to you, since you have not been begotten through their depraved preaching; and so that your descendants, faithfully educated in the Catholic faith, may be satisfied from the bread which came down from heaven, whose fullness brings life everlasting.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## VIII. [Note: [Col. 0815D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF PRATO

They are commended for expelling heretics from their territory. (At St Peter’s, 4 March.)

[Col. 0815A]

In the same manner, as far as “they taught.” We therefore give thanks to the Creator and commend in the Lord the diligence of your discernment, because you have expelled such violent and impious persons from your territories, laudably establishing among yourselves that henceforth no one suspected of the faith shall hold public office in your land. We therefore admonish and exhort your devotion in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters and strictly enjoining you that you remain in the Catholic faith, etc., as above to the end.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Nones [Col. 0815B] of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## IX. . . . . . . TO THE DEAN OF ETTON AND . . . . . . THE PRIOR OF AQUA BELLA [Note: [Col. 0815D] See letter 186 of book VI.], OF THE DIOCESE OF MAURIENNE

That they should proceed in the case of Maurienne. (At St Peter’s, 3 March.)

The beloved son Umbert, cleric and procurator of our venerable brother, . . . . . . bishop of Maurienne [Note: [Col. 0815D] See the same place.], appearing in our presence, informed us that T. and R., clerics of the diocese of Maurienne, had obtained letters of commission against their lord before judges reasonably open to suspicion. One of these is a manifest adversary, since he is attempting to take from the bishop a portion of his episcopal jurisdiction; a dispute concerning this matter is still pending between them. Against [Col. 0815C] the other, he asserted that he would lawfully prove a just ground of suspicion.

We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the said bishop lawfully proves before arbitrators, to be chosen by both sides, a just ground of suspicion against the aforesaid judges, you shall proceed in the matter committed to those judges, according to the form directed to them, removing the obstacle of appeal and observing justice. Otherwise, refer the parties to the examination of those same judges.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## X. [Note: [Col. 0815D] This letter is read among the Decretals, book III, title 20, *On Fiefs*, chapter 1, where it is said to have been directed to the bishop of Maurienne.] . . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF MAURIENNE [Note: [Col. 0815D] See letter 176 of book VI.]

That he may retain a certain pledge. (At St Peter’s, the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0815D]

By the tenor of these present letters we declare to you that the pledge (*gageria*) [Note: [Col. 0815D] *Gageria*: a pledge, a thing pledged, sometimes placed in sequestration as complete security; French, *gage*. Cange, *Glossary*, vol. III, col. 779.] which you are known to have received at Argentinum from Nantelmus of Miolans [Note: [Col. 0815D] The Decretals: “from M.”] out of a fief of your church, with the consent of his brother Wiffred [Col. 0816A] [Note: [Col. 0815D] These words are absent from the Decretals.], may be freely retained by you without counting the revenues toward the principal. That is: so long as you receive those revenues without their being reckoned toward the principal, the same Nantelmus shall meanwhile be exempt from the service which he owes to you and to the church for that fief.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Kalends of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## XI. [Note: [Col. 0816D] This letter is found among the Decretals, book V, title 39, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*, chapter 37, where it is directed to the archbishop of Lund, or alternatively to the bishop of London.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

That he should send serfs who lay hands on clerics to the Servant of the servants for absolution, unless they acted in order to withdraw themselves from their lords’ service. (At St Peter’s, the Ides of January.)

[It has been reported to us that, when certain serfs of your [Col. 0816B] province [Note: [Col. 0816D] The Decretals omit the words from here to “your brotherhood … letters”; they add “the Lord’s voice” after “they,” and read “incur” for “have incurred.”] incur the sentence of the promulgated canon because of violent laying of hands upon a cleric, their lords allege that they do not wish to be deprived of their serfs. The serfs take no care to come to the Apostolic See for absolution and by such a pretext evade ecclesiastical discipline. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you compel them to come to the Apostolic See for absolution, since greater deference must be given to God than to man—unless they have done this fraudulently, in order to withdraw themselves from their lords’ service, or unless they themselves, through no fault of their own, have thereby incurred serious loss [Note: [Col. 0816D] The Decretals add: “For then.” Pithou notes in the margin that *for* is absent from the older manuscripts.]. In either case, by the indulgence of our permission, you may absolve them [Note: [Col. 0816D] The Decretals read “provision” and shortly afterward “another” for “a different,” and “be imposed” for “you impose.”], since they are very far from the Apostolic See; but, in recompense for the labour [Col. 0816C] they would have borne on the journey, impose upon them another satisfaction—provided their offence is not so serious and enormous that, in order to avoid scandal and remove a bad example, such serfs ought to come to the Servant of the servants of God for absolution.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Ides of January, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

## XII. . . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS [Note: [Col. 0816D] See letter 53 of book V.]

That he should give ecclesiastical burial to the body of a young woman who fell from a bridge, not voluntarily but accidentally, while fleeing to free herself from the hands of those pursuing her with dishonourable intent. (At St Peter’s, 4 March.)

[Col. 0816D] On behalf of the parents of Nivetha, a young woman now deceased, it has been reported to us that, at twilight, a nobleman, . . . lord of the island of Brucard in the diocese of Tours, lay in wait for that young woman, wishing to violate her; he had [Col. 0817A] repeatedly solicited her for fornication. When she encountered on a certain bridge the youths who were attempting to carry her off, she finally fell from the bridge into the river while fleeing their hands, and was accidentally drowned. After she had been drawn out of the river, the chaplains of that place doubted whether to give her body burial, and you too, being consulted, said that an apostolic reply should be sought on this point.

We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, since that young woman did not voluntarily throw herself from the bridge, but accidentally fell while fleeing the hands of those who were attempting to abduct her, as stated above, you shall cause her body to be given ecclesiastical burial. This is especially so because she is known to have fled for an honourable reason; and communion ought to be given [Col. 0817B] to her now dead, to whom it was given while living.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## XIII. [Note: [Col. 0817C] This letter is found among the Decretals, book IV, title 20, *On Donations between Husband and Wife, and on the Restoration of Dower after Divorce*, chapter 7.] . . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND O., ARCHDEACON, OF GENOA [Note: [Col. 0817D] See letter 123 of book V, note.]

That they should cause the dowry to be assigned to the husband to whom the wife’s body has been entrusted. (At St Peter’s, 8 March.)

[Through your letters you informed us [Note: [Col. 0817D] This word is absent in the Decretals.] that, after you had, by our authority, summoned Master Riccardus, a citizen of Genoa, to pay eight pounds of Genoese money to the poor man Hugh, bearer of the present letters [Note: [Col. 0817D] The Decretals read “R., concerning a certain sum of money, to H., a poor man”; then “which” for “which sums,” “H.” for “Hugh,” and “the said R.” for “Riccardus”; below they omit the words “namely,” “that,” and “our.”], which the same Hugh demanded from him as the dowry of his wife, Riccardus raised [Col. 0817C] an objection against him. Namely, he asserted that Hugh had repudiated his wife and had obtained our letters concerning the matter by concealing the truth [Note: [Col. 0817D] Pithou reads “obtained.”]; for when a dispute concerning the same dowry had previously been brought before the consuls of your city, they pronounced, according to the custom of the land [Note: [Col. 0817D] These words are absent.], that because Hugh [Note: [Col. 0817D] The Decretals: “H.”] seemed to be falling into poverty, the dowry should not be assigned to him unless he provided suitable security that it would not be lost.

Accordingly, after consulting prudent persons, you ordered Hugh to receive his wife and, according to the custom of the land, to give security for preserving [Note: [Col. 0817D] The Decretals read “to him, for paying,” and after “was deprived of the dowry” add “and you ordered him to receive his wife.”] the dowry; and until he could do so, the dowry was to be deposited, if he wished, in the treasury of the church of Genoa. Since he could not fulfil this, you caused these matters to be reported to us at his request [Note: [Col. 0817D] Absent from the Decretals, but found among Pithou’s additions.].

Therefore, since a small dowry can adequately be entrusted to him to whom the wife’s body has been entrusted, we command your discretion by apostolic letters [Note: [Col. 0817D] The Decretals add “to him,” and omit the words “your discretion … letters.”] to cause the dowry to be assigned to him, subject to such security as he can provide; or at least to have it entrusted to some merchant, so that from a share of the lawful profit the said husband may support the burdens of marriage. Thus, because the dowry is withheld, the wife may not be dismissed by her husband, or the husband who dismissed his wife may not incur the guilt of adultery.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## XIV. [Note: [Col. 0817D]

The copy of this letter, which we had caused to be transcribed from Conte’s copy, has slipped from our hands—we do not know by what accident; and therefore we can give here only its summary. See [Col. 0818C] Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §13.

“As the pontiff humbled the proud spirit of the raging Adolf, so he grants the benefit of absolution to Echembert, bishop of Bamberg, [Col. 0818D] who, having previously been bound by ecclesiastical censures and deprived of office because of his defection from Innocent, at last returned to a better course and sent his cleric to Rome to implore the mercy of the Apostolic See; and he encouraged him to keep faith” (letter 14).]

. TO THE BISHOP OF BAMBERG [Note: [Col. 0818D] Eckenbert, or Erimbert, brother of Stephen, king of the Hungarians, son of Berthold, duke of Moravia, governed the church of Bamberg commendably for thirty-two years, after Conrad, elected in 1202 and dead on the very day after his election. He waged war against Bernard, duke of Carinthia; after ravaging his territories, he was captured, but released under certain conditions of peace. He died in 1235. Bucelin, *Germania Sacra*, part I, p. 24.]

A time is set for him to come to receive absolution.

[Col. 0818B]

## XV. [Note: [Col. 0818D] This letter, or rather the form of the instrument, is found in Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §13.]

An instrument by which Echembert, bishop of Pabemberg [alternatively, Bamberg], attests under his own signature that he will keep the fidelity and obedience promised to the lord pope.

[I, Echembert, bishop of Pabemberg, wish it to be made known by this writing, authenticated by my seal, that by the oath of fidelity and obedience which I rendered bodily at my consecration, I acknowledge myself bound to obey the commands of the lord pope even in the matter of the Roman Empire. Therefore, under that oath, I pledge and promise [Col. 0818C] that, in the matter of the Roman Empire, I shall obey without fraud the commands of my lord Pope Innocent; and, when I have been summoned by him, I shall come into his presence, provided that a lawful impediment has ceased. Moreover, I have instructed my cleric Leopold, and have not revoked the instruction, to swear the foregoing on my soul.]

## XVI. [Note: [Col. 0818D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] . . . . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS [Note: [Col. 0818D] See letter 53 of book V, note.], . . . . . . MASTER, AND THE BROTHERS OF THE HOSPITAL OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN SAXIA

A property at Fonte Moron is attached to their hospital. (At St Peter’s, 8 March.)

It is customary to grant assent, etc., as far as “bestow.” At the petition [Col. 0819A] of our beloved son, the nobleman Roger of Palesti, we have received into the right and ownership of the Apostolic See the estate of Fonte Moron, which he acquired from his own property and freely offered to us. We have attached to your hospital the house built there, establishing by apostolic authority that this place shall henceforth belong directly to your house, which was built from the goods of blessed Peter. Therefore let no one infringe this page of our constitution, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## XVII. . . . . . . TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT COLUMBA OF SENS [Note: [Col. 0819D] Elias, formerly a monk of La Sauve-Majeure, abbot of St Columba, governed from 1196 until 1217, when he died on 23 September. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 150.]

He grants him authority to receive tithes from the cultivation of lands in his parishes. (At St Peter’s, 10 March.)

[Col. 0819B]

A request has been made to us on your behalf that, since, as you assert, you have been granted the right to receive in their entirety the tithes from the cultivation of your parishes, we should mercifully grant you authority, by our indulgence, to exact tithes from lands newly brought under cultivation within your parishes. Since, therefore, the greater grant has been made to you—namely, that you receive tithes from the cultivation of lands in your parishes—you may sufficiently exact them from newly cultivated lands also; for where the greater is granted to you, the lesser likewise appears to have been granted in this case.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## XVIII. [Note: [Col. 0819D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] . . . . . . TO THE PODESTÀ AND COUNCIL OF FAENZA [Note: [Col. 0820D] His name was Gherardinus Rolandini. From Tonduccio, or Cavina. See also the chronicle of Tolosano, chapter 128.]

That they should exclude the Poor of Lyons and the Patareni from their territory and city. (At St Peter’s, 10 March.)

Those who are later in time now deride the Church—their fathers he did not deign to place with the dogs of his flock—and the disciples of those masters who strove to pervert the sayings of Holy Scripture and devise new expressions in which they might mingle the deceits of error scoff at her. Since they could not be fathers of others in the Church by merit, at least the novelty of their error made them seem fathers. Going out from us because they were not of us, they left behind [Col. 0819D] followers who, later in time, rejoice in the novelty of perversity, which had for some time been buried and rejected.

While the dogs of the Lord’s flock give no bark, they themselves bark—not to repel the ambushes of the wolf, but rather to make the flock stray and scatter. Fabricating lies whereby they overturn the hearts of the simple, and offering the poison of error to the unlearned for their ruin, they have made their words softer than oil; yet they themselves are darts, since the flattering things they insinuate bring death to the soul.

We have learned [Col. 0820A] that the superstition of such perverse people has hitherto prevailed, and daily gains strength, in your city. They endeavour to turn the Lord’s flock from the way of truth and draw it into the trackless path of falsehood. Therefore, lest your discernment, which we believe founded in faith, be mocked or deceived by them, we earnestly admonish and exhort your devotion, strictly commanding you through apostolic letters, in the power of the Holy Spirit and under attestation of the divine judgment, utterly to exclude from your city such heretics called the Poor of Lyons, or Patareni, or other schismatics of whatever sect who may be named or identified in writing to you. Let them remain under perpetual ban; henceforth let them neither be admitted nor tolerated [Col. 0820B] in your city or anywhere throughout its district, unless they return at the command of the Church.

The goods of those who have no Catholic successors shall, according to lawful sanctions, be confiscated and publicly seized; and their houses shall be destroyed or assigned to the Church which they do not fear to persecute. Otherwise, since we zealously desire your salvation in the Lord and do not wish your church to be mocked, or you to be led into error by such depraved men, know that we have commanded our beloved sons, the abbots of . . . . . Saint Proculus and . . . . . Saint Stephen of Bologna, that, should you perhaps—which we do not believe—prove negligent, they compel you to this by ecclesiastical coercion, without appeal.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides [Col. 0820C] of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

## XIX. [Note: [Col. 0820D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] . . . . . . TO THE ABBOTS OF SAINT PROCULUS AND . . . . . SAINT STEPHEN OF BOLOGNA

That they should suppress by ecclesiastical coercion the heretics called the Poor. (At St Peter’s, 10 March.)

“Those who are younger in time now mock the Church,” etc., in the same manner as far as “draw it into the trackless path of falsehood.” Therefore, lest the beloved sons, the . . . . podestà [Note: [Col. 0820D] See the note to the immediately preceding letter.] and councillors of Faenza, whom we believe founded in faith, be mocked or deceived by them, we have earnestly admonished and exhorted them by apostolic letters, strictly commanding them, in the power of the Holy Spirit and under attestation of the divine [Col. 0820D] judgment, that they exclude such heretics, who are called, etc., as far as “which they do not fear.” Since, therefore, we zealously desire their salvation in the Lord and do not wish the church of Faenza to be mocked, etc., as far as “led into error,” we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you compel them thereto, etc., as far as “negligent,” by ecclesiastical coercion and without appeal.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year.

## XX. [Note: [Col. 0821D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §36.] . . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF FLORENCE [Note: [Col. 0821D] See letter 162 of book VIII and the notes there.]

That he should persuade and compel the commune of Pisa not to seize certain rights of the marquis of Massa which are held from the Church. (At St Peter’s, 14 March.)

[Col. 0821A]

If the commune of the city of Pisa would carefully consider how greatly and in how many important matters we and our predecessors have sought to honour that city; if it would weigh, on the balance of reason, the favour of the Apostolic See and what fruits of more generous advantage and increase of richer honour it may bring to it hereafter, then surely it would be bound to venerate the Roman Church as a kindly mother with manifold devotion, and to refrain altogether from injuring her. For filial sincerity is known by the brightness of deeds, [Col. 0821B] and purity of faith is proved by the fruits of devotion.

Now word has reached our apostolic hearing that the aforesaid commune—to our no small astonishment—is contriving to take from our beloved son, the nobleman W., Marquis of Massa and Judge of Cagliari, certain revenues and rights in Sardinia belonging to the Roman Church, which he possesses in that Church’s name. Certain Pisans, friends of that same marquis, bought those rights for him from men of the Cagliari association, who had been with him in the recovery of the land, a considerable sum of money already having been paid for this purpose. Moreover, by violently compelling the men of the aforesaid association to return that money and to allow the said friends to receive it, they cause an instrument of sale concerning those same revenues to be drawn up for themselves by the men of the association. They do not consider that those men have pledged faith to the marquis’s friends and that part of the money has been paid, so that the sale ought thereby to obtain full validity. In this action, indeed, danger threatens the commune itself, since it strives to violate pledged faith; and it also wrongs the Apostolic See, when it does not fear to stretch presumptuous hands toward its land.

Therefore, since we are unwilling—as indeed we ought not—to pass over so manifest a loss to the Church with our eyes closed, we strictly command your brotherhood, by apostolic authority, carefully to warn and induce the aforesaid commune not to delay, setting aside every pretext, to revoke that instrument of sale, since it was made to the detriment of the [Col. 0821D] Apostolic See, and to permit the foregoing matters to be restored to their former state; [Col. 0822A] or, if it relies on legal right, to pursue its claim before our tribunal, since a matter of this kind belongs to our examination. If necessary, restrain it by ecclesiastical coercion, all appeal removed. Thus carry out the apostolic command so that we may deservedly commend your diligence.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

XXI. [Note: [Col. 0821D]

A copy of this letter, which we had arranged to have transcribed with the others from Conte’s copy, slipped from our hands—we do not know by what mischance. We can therefore present here only its summary.—See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §36.

“Although Sardinia belonged to the right of the Roman Church, as we have often said, the archbishop of Pisa had extorted for himself and his Church from the Marquis of Massa, Judge of Cagliari, an oath of fealty which ought to have been rendered to the Apostolic See alone. And although Innocent had frequently pressed him to release the aforesaid marquis [Col. 0822D] from the obligation of the oath, he did not comply. In this very year he ordered the commands to be enforced by threatening letters: at least within a month, either the marquis himself or someone sent by him as his procurator was to appear before the Apostolic See.”]

. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: [Col. 0822D] See the note to letter 9 of book III.]. On the same subject.

XXII. [Note: [Col. 0822D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §26.] To A. [Note: [Col. 0822D]

Probably Albert, concerning whom Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 40:

“XIX. Albert, Count of Kirberg. During his tenure the cathedral church perished by fire. Having engaged Otto, who had been excommunicated, he was defeated and saved himself by flight.”]

PROVOST, ELECTED ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG. The election is confirmed, and he is appointed as shepherd. (At Saint Peter’s, fifth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0822B]

When our beloved sons, the provosts of . . . Saint Sebastian . . . Saint Mary, and . . . of Milden[?], C. and C., canons of the major church, Master G . . . of Saint Nicholas, L . . . canon of Saint Peter, and the nobleman G., castellan of Magdeburg, recently came to the Apostolic See and sought confirmation and the pallium for you, we and our brethren carefully heard and understood what they diligently laid before us, both orally and in writing. We learned certainly that your election was canonical; but that after your election you had rashly committed something for which, if we had wished to proceed [Col. 0822C] according to the strictness of law rather than according to the moderation of equity, we could have wholly rejected such a petition.

But because hitherto we have loved you with special affection, as your discretion does not fail to know, and because we wish still to test your devotion through the freely bestowed kindness which we bear toward you, lest we lose the benefit granted to you, we command you by apostolic letters to strive to show yourself to us, in the administration of the Church of Magdeburg, as a member conformed to its head. Thus, once you fully understand our purpose, you may deserve the fullness of our favour. Know certainly that we intend to do those things which ought to redound to your advantage and honour, provided only that [Col. 0822D] you humbly and devoutly strive to render to us the reverence and obedience due to us.

We, moreover, command by our letters our beloved sons, the chapter of Magdeburg, [Col. 0823A] mindful of the ancient devotion which the Church of Magdeburg is known to have shown to the Roman Church, its mother, as a special daughter not only in prosperity but also in adversity, to remain steadfast in that devotion and to induce you to observe it inviolably.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

XXIII. . . . TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT VICTOR AT PARIS [Note: [Col. 0823D] See the note to letter 168 of book VI.] . . . TO THE DEAN OF SOISSONS [Note: [Col. 0823D] See the note to letter 188 of book VIII.], AND MASTER R. OF CORZON, CANON OF NOYON. He commits to them the case concerning the election of the bishop of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0823D] The see of Troyes was vacant through the death of Garnier (de Traisnel), who died at Constantinople on 14 April 1205. See the note to letter 11 of book III.]. (At Saint Peter’s, fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0823B] When the procurators of our beloved sons . . . the dean [Note: [Col. 0823D] Milo I of La Chapelle, dean of Troyes, is known from documents from 1205 through 1210. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, col. 526.] . . . and the cantor of Troyes came recently to the Apostolic See concerning elections alleged to have been made of them [Note: [Col. 0824D] This letter of Innocent must be compared with the account given by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 504, concerning the election of Hervé, bishop of Troyes.], we considered that a hearing should be granted in our consistory.

On the dean’s behalf it was alleged that, when discussion had to be held in the church of Troyes concerning the appointment of a bishop, and the canons had therefore assembled repeatedly, after much discussion among them and examinations of their wishes, the greater and sounder part of the canons unanimously agreed upon the dean and elected him; and immediately appealed to the Apostolic See, as is contained in the decree of the electors.

On the cantor’s behalf, however, it was alleged in reply [Col. 0823C] that the chapter assembled on the appointed day to elect a bishop. Then Master Josbert lodged an appeal in this form: namely, that no election or nomination should occur unless it were canonical and unanimous. After this appeal all agreed upon our beloved son . . . the chancellor of Champagne; when he refused election, the chapter assembled again on another day appointed for the election. On that day, when the canons were gathered in chapter, mention was made of the cantor; many, with no one dissenting, said that he would be good in the governance of a bishopric, while no one discussed the dean.

Meanwhile the dean too appealed, that no nomination should take place unless the order which ought to be observed in such matters were observed, since the first right of nomination belonged to him. Then the cantor offered the dean many worthy men, both from that church and from others, that one of them might be elected bishop by them; but the dean would neither accept nor nominate any of them.

Now while these matters were being discussed, the aforesaid Master Josbert unexpectedly rose and impetuously nominated the dean himself as bishop. Hardly had he finished speaking when the . . . cellarer of Sens rose and said that the master was acting wrongly in nominating as bishop a person concerning whom there had been no discussion. [Col. 0824A] He immediately nominated as bishop of Troyes a suitable and prudent person concerning whom there had been discussion in the chapter, namely the cantor; and no one opposed his nomination.

After this, the cantor was led to the altar with the hymn customarily sung at elections. The canons who had led him to the altar afterwards returned with him to the chapter. Ten canons, in the dean’s presence, renewed their consent to the aforesaid cantor, all the others being present and not opposing the act; and they appealed to the Apostolic See lest anything be done against their election. After this they departed from the chapter.

Furthermore, on the cantor’s behalf it was objected against the dean that he was simoniacal, unlearned, excommunicated, and lame. [Col. 0824B] The dean’s party, however, did not wish to allege anything before us against the person of the cantor, but requested that this be reserved to it, so that, if necessary, it might allege matters against him. Yet in our consistory the party of the dean publicly admitted that the aforesaid appeals had been made as expressed above, and that scrutiny had been conducted with all except three, who, though summoned, refused to come to the scrutiny: namely, the brothers Atto and John, and the cantor—as the aforesaid decree submitted to us for the dean clearly shows.

Since therefore the foregoing has not been established before us and, according to the Apostle, hands should not be laid hastily upon anyone, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, within four months after receiving the present letter, to investigate most diligently and plainly, in judicial form, not only these matters but also all others concerning either the candidates or the elections. If the parties consent, proceed to judgment, in such manner that, unless it is sufficiently shown against the aforesaid dean that he is grievously lame, inadequately educated, or tainted with the stain of simony, you confirm his election, which is known to have been celebrated by the more numerous and more worthy party, provided that no other impediment from canonical statutes stands in the way. The objection of excommunication is not to stand in the way at all, since those who communicated with him cannot object excommunication against him, unless perhaps they prove that they later learned that he was then bound by the bond of excommunication.

But if any of the aforesaid things is proved against him, then, after annulling his election, hear in consequence the matters alleged for or against the cantor and, having God before your eyes, determine what is canonical. If both elections are lawfully annulled, prudently admonish the chapter of Troyes on our behalf and effectively induce it to set over itself as shepherd, by a common and unanimous canonical election, a suitable person equal to so great a burden and honour. [Col. 0825A] If the parties refuse to consent to judgment being pronounced by you, remit the matter, sufficiently prepared, to our examination, setting the parties an appropriate term within which they are to appear before us to receive judgment. If perhaps justice requires both elections to be annulled, those who come are to receive full authority from the chapter to set, according to our counsel, a suitable person as shepherd over the widowed Church; for we do not wish the Lord’s flock to lack a shepherd’s care any longer through disputes of this kind. If all of you cannot be present for carrying this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed.

[Col. 0825B] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XXIV. [Note: [Col. 0825D] This letter is found among the Decretals: in the old Collection, book II, title 15, *On Oaths*, chapter 13, p. 311; in the Gregorian and Innocentian collections, book II, title 24, *On Oaths*, chapter 26. Words distinguished in italic type are absent from the Decretals or indicate a variation of readings.] TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 0825D] He was probably Theodard, said to have succeeded Simon. Simon, however, having renounced the abbacy in 1200, was compelled merely to go elsewhere, as is demonstrated by Innocent’s letters, book I, 301, and book II, 38. Theodard’s successor, Hebert, is not known from documents until 1211. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XI, col. 639.], AND THE CHAPTER OF CHÂTILLON [otherwise, CONQUES]. In a necessary case even religious persons may lawfully swear. (At Saint Peter’s, twelfth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Although Christ commanded, according to evangelical truth, “Let your speech be: Yes, yes, and no, no” (Matt. V), that is, that affirmation or negation should proceed from the heart just as it proceeds from the mouth, nevertheless, because human wickedness has increased, a simple affirmation [Note: [Col. 0826D] The Decretals read “assertion,” and shortly thereafter add “from evil.”] or negation is scarcely believed. He therefore wisely added: “What is more than this is from evil”; [Col. 0825C] evil indeed not so much of guilt as of punishment, and not of those who give, but of those who exact, an oath. For such unbelief is more a punishment than a fault; hence he did not say “evil,” but “from evil.”

Although the Lord may seem to have forbidden oaths, nowhere did he forbid swearing by the Creator, but by a creature, lest through such an oath the honour due to the Creator be transferred to a creature. Therefore, after first saying in the Gospel, “I tell you not to swear at all,” he immediately added: “Neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne; nor by earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great king; nor by your head, because you cannot make one hair white [Col. 0825D] or black” (ibid.). Although one must not swear by a creature, nevertheless, if one does swear by a creature, the oath must be kept, provided what is sworn is lawful. [Note: [Col. 0826D] The Decretals add: “because, as Truth testifies, he who swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it”; and below they read “oath” for “to be sworn.”]

James likewise did not simply forbid an oath, but the will to swear, when [Col. 0826A] he says: “Before all things, my brethren, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath” (James V). For no spontaneous will should lead anyone to swear, because one who swears readily perjures himself readily; rather, pressing necessity should compel him. Then one may swear without fault, provided the oath has those three companions of which the prophet says: “And they shall swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’ in truth and judgment and righteousness; and the nations shall bless him and praise him.” [Note: [Col. 0826D] The Decretals read: “But what James adds, ‘Neither by heaven nor by earth nor by any other oath,’ forbids swearing by any creature whatever it may be.”]

Otherwise the Apostle would not have said: “Men swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is for them the end of every dispute for confirmation.” In this he plainly shows by whom one must swear when he says: “Men swear by one greater than themselves” (Heb. VI), that is, by [Col. 0826B] God; and why one swears: that an oath may be the end of every dispute. Likewise the angel whom John saw in the Apocalypse, “standing upon the sea and upon the land, lifted his hand to heaven and swore by him who lives for ever and ever” (Apoc. X).

Christ too is recorded in the Gospel as having said more than “Yes, yes, and no, no” (Matt. V), since he very often said: “Amen, I say to you” (ibid.). Explaining this according to Luke, after saying: “Amen, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country,” he next added: “Truly I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah” (Luke IV). The Apostle likewise swore when he said: “God is my witness” (Rom. I); and again: “I die daily, by your glory, [Col. 0826C] brethren” (I Cor. XV). The Greek manuscripts show most clearly that this is an oath.

For if swearing were evil in itself, surely the Lord would not have sworn, whereas in the Old Testament it is written: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent of it” (Ps. CIX); and again: “The Lord swore [Ps. CXXXI] truth to David.” [Note: [Col. 0826D] The Decretals add: “and will not disappoint him”; and shortly thereafter read, in place of “in the Testament, to render oaths to the Lord”: “Render to God his vows.”] Indeed, in the Old Testament he commanded that oaths be rendered to the Lord.

Some things are forbidden because they are evil in themselves, such as theft, adultery, and the like, which must in no way be done. Other things are forbidden for a reason, not because they are evil in themselves, but because, if they are done frequently and excessively, evils follow from them. Wine, for example, is not evil in itself, and yet [Col. 0826D] the Apostle forbids it, saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. V), because debauchery arises from frequent and immoderate drinking of wine. So too an oath is not evil in itself, since it is a confirmation of truth; yet it is [Col. 0827A] forbidden for a reason, because perjury often results from frequent and heedless swearing, as is written in Ecclesiasticus: “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall not depart from his house” (Ecclus. XXIII).

Accordingly, just as Paul, because of necessity, permitted [Note: [Col. 0827D] The Decretals read “permitted because of necessity.”] his disciple Timothy to use a little wine on account of his stomach and frequent infirmities (I Tim. V), so surely, when necessity requires it, one may safely swear concerning a true, lawful, and honourable matter, because when the cause ceases, its effect ceases. Therefore, although you ought to be perfect men, so as to avoid the bond of an oath insofar as you can, nevertheless, wishing with paternal concern to provide for the security of your monastery, lest through lack of witnesses it suffer injury to its rights, by the authority of him who says [Col. 0827B] in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone; and if he does not listen, take with you two or three witnesses, that every word may stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII), by the present [Note: [Col. 0827D] The Decretals: “to you.”] document we permit you and the lay brothers of your monastery, if other witnesses are lacking, to bear testimony to the truth in its cases.]

Therefore let no person at all be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, his apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XXV. . . . TO THE PRIOR [Note: [Col. 0827D] The prior of Glastonbury monastery at that time was Thomas. See Adam of Domerham, *On the Dispute between the Bishop of Bath and the Monks of Glastonbury*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 582. Compare also Innocent’s letters, book V, 90 and 92.] AND CONVENT OF GLASTONBURY. If their Church has not been adequately provided for, they are to pursue their right at the Curia. (At Saint Peter’s, second day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0827C]

He who searches hearts and knows secrets knows that, although Pope C. of good memory, our predecessor, raised your church to a cathedral see, uniting it with the Church of Bath so that one and the same bishop should govern both, and took care to confirm his constitution not only by a privilege but also by many other writings, nevertheless, because you alleged that this union was confusion and complained that it resulted in grave prejudice to the Church of Glastonbury—since through it [Col. 0827D] religious observance was dissolved, almsgiving defrauded, and hospitality destroyed—we, moved by your petitions, began diligently to seek, as was fitting, to restore the condition of your church.

Since it seemed improper that we should suddenly nullify in this respect the decree of our predecessor—for we wish to yield him, so far as we can before God, the same deference which we wish our successors to yield us, so far as they can before God—we retained the union, but otherwise made such arrangements as raised the state of your church to a better condition, however greatly this displeased Savaric [Note: [Col. 0828D] See the note to letter 90 of book V.], bishop of Bath, of good memory, who frequently laboured at the Apostolic See on this account. After various negotiations and much deliberation, what was ordained in this matter by prudent and honourable men under the authority of our mandate, we finally took care, at the petition of that bishop, after he was unable to obtain anything else from us, to strengthen by apostolic protection.

After the death of the aforesaid bishop of Bath, you came again into our presence and humbly requested that, because the time had arrived when the ruin of your church could be restored to its former state without scandal—since both the Church of Bath and that of Wells [Col. 0828B] jointly requested this, the king with the magnates of the realm asked it, and certain bishops with many abbots sought the same—we should completely dissolve the union and restore your monastery to its ancient state, to be governed under an abbot.

We, however, carefully observing that nothing ought to be altered in this matter while the episcopal see is vacant, since there is no one to defend the bishop’s right, especially lest we seem to have favoured the person more than the Church if we suddenly changed after his death what we had granted during his life, could not wholly grant your petition without injury to conscience and danger to reputation. Yet, so that according to the customary method—which you have found useful to yourselves and honourable to us—one may proceed gradually from the lower to the higher, we grant you by the authority of this letter that, once the Church of Bath has been provided with a bishop, if you wish to show that sufficient provision has still not been made for avoiding detriment or prejudice to your church, you shall be free to pursue your right before the Apostolic See. In the meantime, however, let the same monastery be freely governed under the care of the prior.

Therefore let no person at all be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him incur indignation, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year.

XXVI. To J. [Note: [Col. 0828D] See letter 184 of book VII.] CARDINAL-DEACON OF SAINT MARY IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That he should grant the prior and convent of Glastonbury leave to elect an abbot. (At Saint Peter’s, eighth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0828D]

By the authority of this letter we command your discretion that, once the Church of Bath has been provided with a bishop, if perhaps the man who is bishop wishes freely to consent—since both the convent of Bath and that of Wells have petitioned us concerning this by their [Col. 0829A] letters, that the Church of Glastonbury be restored to its former condition—you, supported by our authority, grant our beloved son . . . the prior and convent of Glastonbury leave canonically to elect an abbot for themselves [Note: [Col. 0829D] See the note to letter 90 of book V.]. [Note: [Col. 0829D] See Adam of Domerham, *On the Dispute between the Bishops of Bath and the Monks of Glastonbury*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 583, where it is said that the monks of Glastonbury did not obtain from Pope Honorius III the unrestricted faculty of electing an abbot until 1218.] If the aforesaid prior and monks consider that they must litigate against the lord bishop, set both parties an appropriate term within which they are to appear before us.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XXVII. . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES [Note: [Col. 0829D] See the note to letter 176 of book VII.]. That he should set offenders an appropriate time limit to prosecute appeals which they lodge solely in order to persist in their wickedness and to evade ecclesiastical discipline. (At Saint Peter’s, fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0829B]

On your behalf it was laid before us that, when you seek to recall your parishioners, who commit many offences, from their iniquities by restraining them with ecclesiastical censure—subjecting their persons to sentence of excommunication and a city, borough, or villages to ecclesiastical interdict according as the atrocity of the offence and the number or quality of the persons require—they, wishing to persist in their wickedness, break forth into an appeal in evasion of ecclesiastical discipline. Since the remedy of appeal was devised to aid the oppressed, not as an escape for the malicious, [Col. 0829C] and lest ecclesiastical discipline be wholly enfeebled by such insolence, we grant your brotherhood by the authority of this letter that you set those who appeal in this way an appropriate term for prosecuting the appeal lodged. If they have not prosecuted it within that time, unless perhaps they have been hindered by reasonable cause, thereafter exercise ecclesiastical justice upon them, notwithstanding the appeal made, as the order of reason requires; yet let severity be tempered with gentleness. We do not wish manifest crimes, which no evasion can conceal, to remain uncorrected under the pretext of appeal.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0830D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §8.] . . . TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM [Note: [Col. 0830D] See letter 222 of book VII.], LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That he should confirm the agreement between the king of Cyprus and Count H., then lord of the kingdom of Jerusalem. (At the Lateran, third day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0829D]

Since, by the disposition of heavenly counsel, you have received over the peoples [Col. 0830A] of the province of Jerusalem—who for their sins, not only their own but perhaps those of others, have received double punishment from the hand of the Lord—the authority of a twofold office, so that, set apart for God’s Gospel, you exercise the office of legate together with the honour of patriarchal dignity, it is clearly incumbent upon you diligently to procure by your devoted care those things which may be useful for maintaining the condition of that province.

Our ears have been informed by our beloved son, the nobleman G. de Montbéliard, constable of the kingdom of Jerusalem and guardian and bailli of the kingdom of our dearest son in Christ . . . the illustrious king of Cyprus, that formerly an agreement was prudently made between II., king of Cyprus of illustrious memory, and Count Henry, then lord of the kingdom of Jerusalem, concerning the reciprocal marriage of their sons and daughters and the county of Jaffa. Confirmed by an oath exchanged on both sides, this agreement was also reduced to a public instrument. Since both that king and the aforesaid bailli have humbly petitioned our apostolic office to command by apostolic authority that agreement to be observed, as advantageous not only to him but also to the whole province, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth concerning that agreement. If you find that it was prudently made and particularly that it concerns public as well as private advantage, cause it to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed; after prior admonition, restraining opponents by like coercion.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF ORLÉANS [Note: [Col. 0830D] At that time Hugh I of Garlande, who was raised to the bishopric in 1198 and in this very year 1206, in which we are now engaged, exchanged life for death, still wore the mitre of Orléans. His death is noted on the fourth day before the Nones of May in the necrology of Cour-Dieu. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VIII, col. 1457.]. That, after examining the truth, he should permit the subdeacon R. to exercise only the clerical office, because he struck a layman while repelling force by force. (At Saint Peter’s, ninth day before the Kalends of April.)

The beloved son R., subdeacon, appearing before us, showed by humble petition that a certain layman, suspected in connection with the death of one of [Col. 0830D] his uncles, came upon him with a drawn knife. Because, owing to the impediment of the canonical habit which he wore, he could not avoid the man’s fury, and perceived that he was in danger of death, he struck him while repelling force by force. Since the said layman, as a result of this blow, ended his final day after several days, the same subdeacon, moved to penitence, went to Jerusalem [Col. 0831A] in expiation of his sin; finally coming to the Apostolic See, he humbly petitioned us to permit him to minister in clerical office together with other clerics.

Therefore, inclining to his prayers out of that mercy which triumphs over judgment, we command your brotherhood by this letter that, if the truth supports the foregoing and it can be done without scandal, you permit him to exercise only the simple office of cleric among the other clerics.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XXX. [Note: [Col. 0831C] This letter is found among the Decretals, book I, title 37, *On Seeking Advocacy*, chapter 11.] . . . TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA. In answer to his consultation: the same judgment applies to regular canons as to monks regarding advocacy. (At Saint Peter’s, fourth day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0831B]

[It was laid before [Note: [Col. 0831C] In the Decretals the words “before us” are absent, as shortly afterward are the words “that they may roam about”; below, they read *is objected to them* for *is objected to the same persons*, and omit the words “according to canonical sanctions,” as shortly afterward they omit also the word “even.”] us on your behalf that certain regular canons, in order perhaps to display themselves as learned in law and to have occasion to wander outside the cloister, presume to exercise the office of advocate not only in ecclesiastical but also in secular causes. When it is objected to them that, according to canonical sanctions, they ought not to be undertakers or executors of secular or ecclesiastical business, unless perhaps the monastery’s advantage requires it and the abbot nevertheless commands it, they allege in excuse of their insolence [Note: [Col. 0831C] The Decretals: *insolertiam*. Pithou conjectured that *insolentiam* should be read [Col. 0831D].] that the chapter by which the aforesaid matters seem to be prohibited speaks plainly of monks, not of regular canons [Note: [Col. 0831D] Thus far in the Decretals; what follows is found in Pithou’s additions.].]

You therefore asked us whether such persons should be admitted to advocacy. To this we answer your discretion as follows: we believe that the same rule ought to be observed concerning regular canons as concerning monks in the matters mentioned above, although it is expressed specifically in the canon concerning monks.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year. [Note: [Col. 0831D] In Pithou the chronological notices are absent.]

XXXI. TO THE SAME. The sentence given in the case between the Templars and the Church of Compostela is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, fourth day before the Ides.)

[Col. 0832A]

When that which is just and honourable is requested of us, etc., down to “moved,” we confirm by apostolic authority, as just and not suspended by a lawful appeal, the definitive sentence lawfully pronounced by our venerable brethren M., bishop of Zamora, and G., bishop of Salamanca, judges delegated by the Apostolic See, in the case concerning the vows (*vota*) of Saint James, which was pending between the Church of Compostela on the one side, and the Templars, the Hospitallers, and the Brothers of the Order of Saint James on the other.

Let no one therefore . . . but if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year.

### XXXII. To the Bishops of Zamora and Salamanca

[Note: This letter is found among the *Decretals*, book III, title 39, “On censuses, exactions, and procurations,” chapter 18.] . . . . . . To the Bishops of Zamora and Salamanca. That, in paying the dues owed to the Church of Compostela, the ancient measure is to be observed in a specified manner. (At St. Peter’s, 10 Kalends of April [23 March].)

On behalf of our venerable brother . . . . . . the Archbishop of Compostela, it was set before us that, whereas those who continually pay the dues of blessed James have hitherto paid, and continue to pay, them according to the common measure of their land—that is, the measure by which they buy and sell—some persons who, from long past times, had ceased making these payments, are now, by your action and by authority of the Apostolic See, compelled to make payment of the same. They offer a certain very small and unknown measure, one not even assigned to ordinary uses, and endeavor to pay the aforesaid dues by that measure.

[Note: In the *Decretals* the words “our venerable brother” below are omitted; they read *qui* instead of *quia*, and omit the words “by you . . . compelled.”]

[Note: Col. 0831D.

See Vasaeus, p. 591; Platina, in Lucius III.

Ramiro, king of the Spaniards, after gaining victory over the Saracens through the aid of St. James—who, it is said, appeared in battle mounted on a white horse and carrying a banner in his hand—ordained by vow that a fixed annual payment should be rendered to blessed James and to the Church of Compostela. It was called *vota* (“vows” or “vow-dues”) because it had been established by a solemn royal vow. On this, see Roderic of Toledo, book IV, chapter 13: “Then they also paid vows and gifts to blessed James; and in some places they still pay them, not from sorrow or necessity, but out of voluntary devotion.”

And our Innocent himself, book II, letter 139, concerning the privileges of the Church of Compostela: “We also confirm to that Church the payment called *vota*, which the Catholic kings of the Spaniards generously decreed should be paid annually, for the welfare of the whole land, from every pair of oxen, from the river Pisuerga to the Western Sea, throughout the whole province of Lusitania, and also in Toledo and Transserra; and we absolutely forbid anyone ever, on any pretext, to withhold it from that Church.”

But, as the religion and zeal of the Spaniards grew cold, certain persons, having long ceased paying this payment—which is the subject of this chapter—offered an unjust and unknown measure by which to pay the due; whereas others, who had continued to pay it hitherto, paid it according to the common measure of the land, by which they were accustomed to buy and sell.]

[Note: What follows, distinguished in italic type, is absent from the *Decretals*, but is read in Pithou’s additions.]

They therefore asked us to make you certain on this point: whether those who offer an unknown measure for paying the prescribed dues are to be compelled to use the common measure of their land, in accordance with the practice continuously followed by those who have paid them.

[Note: In Pithou: “you asked” (*postulastis*).]

[Note: Col. 0833D: In Pithou, “to be paid” (*solvenda*) instead of “to pay” (*solvendum*).]

[Note: In Pithou, “aforesaid” (*praedicta*) instead of “prescribed” (*praescripta*).]

Since, therefore, it is not established by what measure their predecessors paid the prescribed dues, we think a distinction must be made: whether the inhabitants of that region who have continuously paid them render such dues by one and the same measure, or by various and different measures.

[Note: In the *Decretals*: “aforesaid” (*praedicta*).]

[Note: In the *Decretals*: “have paid” (*persolverint*) instead of “pay” (*persolvant*).]

For if all commonly use one and the same measure in paying the dues, the others too must be compelled to pay by that same measure.

[Note: In the *Decretals*: “in the first case” (*in primo enim casu*).]

But if the common payment is differentiated by various and different measures, and they wish to pay by the smaller measure, they certainly are not to be compelled to pay by the larger one; for, since dues of this kind were voluntary from the beginning, ecclesiastical men ought to exact them more leniently, lest they seem, like tax collectors, to be excessively eager for temporal profits.

[Note: The *Decretals* have only: “in the second case, those wishing to pay by the smaller measure are not to be compelled.”]

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, 10 Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

### XXXIII. To the Bishop of Ourense

[Note: Part of this letter was published by Raynaldus under the year 1206, §36. Passages printed by him are enclosed in brackets.] In reply to his inquiry: concerning the last wills of canons, the Lateran Council is to be observed; and answers are given concerning other doubts. (At St. Peter’s, Ides of March [15 March].)

It was set before us on your behalf that your canons wish to dispose as they please of houses built upon the ground of the Church, and of other goods acquired from the property of that Church, and to leave them by will to their kinsmen. You refuse to tolerate this patiently, maintaining that it is contrary not only to the statutes of the Lateran Council but also to ancient enactments. They assert that ancient canons have been derogated from by custom, and that the Lateran Council is not observed by other bishops. You therefore wished to consult us as to how you should proceed in these matters.

We therefore briefly answer your brotherhood that you are to cause the statutes of the Lateran Council to be firmly observed in these matters, with appeal set aside.

[Note: The following is found in Raynaldus.] You further asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See how, when bishops are summoned by their archbishop, or by another, for the consecration of bishops, and they present an elect to the metropolitan for consecration, saying, “Reverend Father, holy Mother Church asks that this elect be consecrated bishop,” and, when the archbishop asks whether they know him to be worthy, they answer that they know and likewise believe him to be worthy: since, in giving such an answer, in order not to offend a human being, you think that you have sometimes offended God, answering at times apart from, and at times contrary to, conscience, because the conduct of the elect is either insufficiently known to you or wholly unknown—how can you answer questions of this kind while preserving a good conscience?

[Note: In Raynaldus: *quinque* (“five”).]

To this we have thought it right to answer your brotherhood as follows.
