When we promote anyone to the diaconate or priesthood, the senior deacon who stands beside us says: “Holy Mother Catholic Church asks that this subdeacon or deacon be admitted to the burden of the diaconate or priesthood.” When we ask whether he knows him to be worthy, he answers that, insofar as human frailty permits knowledge, he knows and testifies that the man is worthy for the burden of such an office. Hence we do not believe that anyone sins in giving such an answer, provided that he does not speak against his conscience. For he does not simply assert that he knows him to be worthy, but says this insofar as human frailty permits knowledge; since one who does not know him to be unworthy ought to judge him worthy.

[Note: Raynaldus ends here.]

You may therefore safely use an answer of this kind, unless perhaps you have certain knowledge that the man to be consecrated is unworthy. But if you know him to be unworthy, you should take care to inform the metropolitan privately before the inquiry of this kind is undertaken, although, as we have said, we make such an inquiry not at the consecration of a bishop, but in the ordination of a deacon or priest.

You further asked to be informed what words the Roman pontiff uses at that place in the canon of the Mass where an inferior priest says, “together with our pope and our bishop,” since he then appears to pray for himself and to have no bishop above him. To your devotion we answer that there we say, “together with me, your unworthy servant,” where other priests use the aforesaid words.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the Ides of March, in the ninth year.

### XXXIV. To the Prior . . . and the Convent of Canterbury

[Note: See letter 161 of book VIII.] That they are to come for examination, to hear whether the provision of their archbishop was, as they maintain, bad. (At the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April [30 March].)

We cannot sufficiently express in words or set forth in letters the great amazement, indeed disturbance, into which we and our brethren have been led by what, on reliable report, we have learned was rashly perpetrated by you, as degenerate sons, in connection with the provision for the Church of Canterbury, your mother. She can now say of you: “I have nourished and brought up children, and they have despised me” (Isaiah 1), as though you were exposing her, like a prostitute, to diverse lovers.

Alas! Where is that decency of religious life, prudence of discernment, sincerity of truth, and constancy of virtue that used until now to be proclaimed abroad concerning you in such illustrious terms? The finest color has changed, and gold has been turned into dross. Indeed, we fear that under a garment of pretense you have hitherto concealed your depravity, which now, the veil torn away, has been shamefully laid bare.

Certainly, when formerly our beloved sons, your monks Solomon, Gual., Simon, Roger, and W., came to the Apostolic See and humbly sought confirmation of the election which, they maintained, you had unanimously celebrated in the person of our beloved son R., subprior of your Church—as was more clearly apparent from the decree of the brethren—the beloved son Master Peter of Anglesham opposed their petition as an adversary on behalf of the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury. He alleged that they had proceeded in that election in such a manner that it ought not merely to be denied confirmation but declared void.

When the aforesaid monks tried to exclude him because he did not at all show a mandate of procuration, he replied that in Lombardy, near the city of Parma, he had been robbed both of his letters of mandate and of other possessions; but he was prepared to give suitable security that whatever he did in this case would be ratified by the said suffragans. Although the same monks sought to show that security of this kind ought not to be admitted in this matter, nevertheless, having weighed the advantage and necessity of the parties, because there was probable doubt about his mandate, we admitted the same master to oppose the election. First, however, we received from him security in the amount of one thousand marks; our venerable brothers P., Bishop of Winchester, and Master John, canon of St. Paul’s, London, with our permission, bound themselves with him for that penalty on his behalf, so that the suffragans themselves would firmly observe whatever he did in this matter.

[Note: See letter 104 of book VIII, note.]

While the aforesaid monks pressed for confirmation of the election, represented as unanimously made by the entire convent of your Church, the said master strove to attack it in many ways: first, because, after an appeal had been lawfully lodged with us, it had been not so much celebrated as presumed upon; secondly, because the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury had been disregarded in the election, since such an election could not and ought not be held without them—indeed, unless it was held with them—he invoking both common law and ancient custom; and also because you had established a truce with the bishops, lasting until the feast of St. Andrew, for negotiating concerning the election, and yet had not feared to forestall it without consulting the bishops.

He further sought restoration to what he called quasi-possession, of which he claimed the aforesaid suffragans had been rashly dispossessed. Although, in reply, privileges of our predecessors and our own, along with several other documents, were shown to us, and many arguments, both factual and legal, were alleged, we earnestly wished to put an end to this dispute, which could not be prolonged longer without great loss to the parties. But because complete proof could not be produced before us of certain matters alleged on either side, by common counsel with our brethren we issued an interlocutory decision: the witnesses whom either party wished to produce were to be sent to the Apostolic See by the Kalends of May then next approaching, unless some of them happened to be ill or aged and bodily infirmity excused them from such a burden. Regarding these we ordered that they should be examined in England by the beloved sons . . . . . abbots of St. Alban’s, in the diocese of Lincoln, and . . . of Reading, in the diocese of Salisbury, and . . . . . dean of St. Paul’s, London; their depositions, sealed with the examiners’ seals, were to be sent to us within the said time.

Accordingly, we commanded the aforesaid suffragans by our letters to send to the Apostolic See, before the stated term and setting aside excuse, appeal, and delay, all witnesses whom they wished to produce in the case, together with their instruments and arguments, unless they were ill or aged. They were to provide that, if the aforesaid infirmity prevented any from coming to us, they should, if they wished, produce them before the said abbots and dean, so that their depositions might be presented to us within the same term. They were also to signify by letter whether they wished to ratify what had been done in the case by the aforesaid master. If they did not wish to ratify it, they were to ensure that suitable procurators were sent to us within the stated period, who, setting aside every evasion, should come so instructed that, so far as depended upon them, nothing might hinder this business from reaching its due conclusion through us, by the Lord’s authority. Otherwise, since in the administration of justice there ought to be no acceptance or choice of persons, we would thereafter, having regard not to man but to God, take such care, with the Lord’s help, to provide by law for your Church as lay within our power, that it might thereafter enjoy the desired peace.

But after the said monks and master had received letters from us on these matters and had departed from the Apostolic See to travel to England, the beloved sons G., E., H., T., R., and L., monks, and Master H., archdeacon of Richmond, unexpectedly came before us as envoys from you. They asserted that both you and the suffragans had renounced all appeals for the sake of peace and thereafter had freely and spontaneously agreed, unanimously and harmoniously, to petition the Apostolic See for our venerable brother . . . Bishop of Norwich. They showed this from letters both from yourselves and from the suffragans. They therefore humbly entreated us and our brethren, on account of the urgent necessity and evident advantage of the Church of Canterbury, to admit that postulation.

[Note: See letter 129 of book V, note.]

But the beloved son W., the monk who had remained with the aforesaid subprior, asserted that this postulation should be utterly rejected: first, because, after the matter of the election had come before our judgment, no one at all ought to make any disposition concerning it without awaiting our judgment, especially as we had already proceeded in the prescribed manner in that affair; secondly, because, according to canonical enactments, an outsider ought not to be chosen so long as a suitable member of the household could be found to govern the Church, and therefore he and others were entitled to resist if they saw anyone being imposed upon them from outside; thirdly, because in the letters which you sent to the aforesaid subprior and monks while they were at the Apostolic See, you plainly indicated that you had been induced to make such a postulation under pressure, fearing loss of property and danger to persons.

Although many replies were made to the contrary, with no less diligence than effect, we—who must not have “weight and weight,” like a deceitful balance—proceeding without respect of persons by the royal road and turning neither right nor left, by common counsel with our brethren judged that this postulation must be rejected, not because of the unworthiness of the person, but because of the unlawfulness of the procedure. We grieved greatly—as He knows who is ignorant of nothing—over the very numerous tribulations and distresses which, on account of this discord, have befallen the Church of Canterbury.

Once the postulation had been rejected, as stated, the beloved sons Master Honorius and T. . . . monk produced letters committing to them procuration on your behalf. They alleged that you had in no way elected the aforesaid subprior as archbishop. Rather, when you had heard for certain that our dearest son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of the English, and our venerable brethren, the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury, had sent envoys to the Apostolic See in order to obtain from us letters to you for the appointment of a certain person as archbishop, you adopted, by common deliberation, the following precaution. Of the three persons whom you had named among others—the prior, the subprior, and the precentor—one upon whom the larger number of brethren agreed was to be chosen and sent to the Apostolic See. If he should perceive that we were inclined to grant the requests of the aforesaid king and suffragans, he was to represent himself as elected. He was given letters drawn up in the form of a decree, which he was to use only in that contingency.

When a larger number of brethren had agreed upon the subprior, you sent him to the Apostolic See with the decree, made as though it concerned his election, and with certain brethren accompanying him. You commanded them, under authority of obedience and on pain of anathema, never to presume to use that decree unless perhaps the aforesaid contingency occurred. Yet he, blinded by the darkness of ambition and leading others with him astray by damnable perversity, represented himself as elected when he had never been elected. They promised to demonstrate this both through your letters and through witnesses above every exception.

The aforesaid monk, however, maintained that the same subprior had been elected by everyone unanimously and unconditionally, without any contradiction or condition. He sought in many ways to invalidate the procurators’ mandate, affirming that you, raising your own hands before the wood of the life-giving Cross and the crown of blessed martyr Thomas, had promised in chapter to choose as shepherd and father the man, from among the three persons previously named, on whom the greater and sounder part should agree.

After the matter had been disputed for some time, we issued an interlocutory ruling: reserving all lawful objections which the subprior’s party might wish to make against the procurators or witnesses, or even against the witnesses’ statements, witnesses were to be produced on either side. Witnesses were accordingly produced on both sides—five on one side and one on the other—and their depositions were written down. But since they were unwilling to be content with these witnesses alone, although we repeatedly pressed them toward an end of the litigation, we finally, by common counsel with our brethren, command and strictly order your discretion by apostolic letters that, by the next approaching Kalends of October, you, sons Abel, John of Hale, Eadmund, Joseph Gilbert the chamberlain, Roger of the Tomb, Carole, Honorius, Andrew of the Infirmary, Richard of Bendingham, together with six others who are to be named, present yourselves personally before us. After truth has been more fully investigated through you, we may, by God’s authority, impose a canonical conclusion upon this cause. You must receive full authority from the whole chapter, so that, should the subprior’s claim—which he says he pursues not for his own advancement but for the liberty of the Church of Canterbury—fail to prevail, you may canonically appoint a suitable person over yourselves as shepherd.

So that the truth may more fully be made clear to us, we give apostolic commands to our venerable brother . . . Bishop of Rochester and our beloved son . . . Abbot of St. Augustine’s, Canterbury: they are to go personally to the Church of Canterbury, investigate the whole truth from the remaining persons under the obligation of an oath, and report it to us in a faithful account.

[Note: See letter 154 of book VIII, note.]

And lest such a provision be delayed because of the absence of the king or suffragans, we write to the same king and suffragans that they too are not to delay sending suitable procurators for this purpose to our presence. Otherwise, since we neither wish nor ought any longer to allow the Church of Canterbury to lack a shepherd, to the loss of its goods and peril of souls, we shall, by God’s authority, proceed to provide for it, punishing the disobedient, rebellious, and contumacious in such a way that punishment itself will teach them how dangerous it has been to act maliciously in this affair.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

### XXXV. To the Suffragans of the Church of Canterbury

Concerning the same matter. (At the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April [30 March].)

How and to what extent we have proceeded in the business of the Church of Canterbury, your brotherhood may learn fully from the letters which we are sending to the prior and convent. Since, for the prosecution of the same matter, we summon certain Canterbury monks to appear personally before us, and wish, so far as we can with God’s help, to show due regard for your right and honor, we command you by apostolic letters to ensure that suitable procurators are sent to the Apostolic See within the term assigned to those monks, lest through the absence of procurators loss result either to you or to the Church of Canterbury. Otherwise, since we neither wish nor ought any longer to allow the Church of Canterbury to lack a shepherd, to the loss of its goods and peril of souls, we shall, by God’s authority, proceed to provide for it.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

### XXXVI. To . . . the King of the English

Concerning the same matter. (At the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April [30 March].)

How and to what extent we have proceeded in the business of the Church of Canterbury, royal prudence may learn fully from the letters which we send to the prior and convent. Since, for the prosecution of the same matter, we summon certain Canterbury monks to appear personally before us, and wish, so far as we can with God’s help, to show due regard for your right and honor, we inform you by these present letters that you should endeavor to send a suitable procurator to the Apostolic See within the term assigned to those monks, lest through the absence of a procurator loss result either to royal highness or to the Church of Canterbury.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

### XXXVII. To . . . the Bishop of Rochester and . . . the Abbot of St. Augustine’s, Canterbury

[Note: See letter 154 of book VIII, note.] Concerning the same matter. (At the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April [30 March].)

How and to what extent we have proceeded in the business of the Church of Canterbury, your discretion may learn fully from the letters that we send to . . . the prior and convent. Since, for the prosecution of the same business, we summon certain Canterbury monks to appear personally before us, so that the truth in these matters may be more fully made clear to us, we command you by apostolic letters that you go personally to the Church of Canterbury, investigate the whole truth from the remaining persons under the obligation of an oath, and ensure that you report it to us in a faithful account within the term assigned to them.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

### XXXVIII. To . . . the Scholastic of Hildesheim and . . . the Custodian and Scholastic of Minden

That they are to investigate, in a specified manner, the election of the abbess of Herford.

[Note: See letter 154 of book VIII, note.] (At the Lateran, Kalends of April [1 April].)

Dear daughter in Christ, R., custodian of the Church of Heris, having formerly approached the Apostolic See and asserted that she had been elected abbess, stated that, after the abbess of the Church of Heris had died, the sisters and canons of that church, at the exhortation of the diocesan bishop,

[Col. 0840B]

who had come for the deceased woman’s burial, sat together to hold an election . . . the scholasticus of Paderborn having been summoned to examine their votes. And whereas eight sisters [Note: [Col. 0840D] It seems that “ten” should be read.] of the seventeen who were then present disagreed in the election of one person, all the canons, who numbered fourteen, elected the custodian herself, with the advocate, ministeriales, and all the people giving her their favor and assent. On the other hand, seven of the sisters nominated . . . the provostess as abbess.

Therefore, both parties were presented to the bishop to obtain the grace of consecration. The bishop warned the parties to strive for peace and agree concerning the election, and granted them five days to deliberate on the matter. But on the sixth day, since they could not agree, the bishop ordered the parties to present themselves before the chapter of Paderborn after another five days, prepared to give account concerning these elections.

[Col. 0840C]

Accordingly, when the custodian and the provostess stood before the chapter of Paderborn with their electors, the provostess and her seven electresses then presented for the first time to the bishop the nun G., who came from a certain black-monastic monastery and had been confirmed and even blessed as abbess of a certain church, saying that they had elected her. At this the other party was greatly astonished, since, without their knowledge or even consultation, the former party had altered what they had done. The custodian therefore asked the chapter a second and third time to grant her an advocate, in order to state and defend her case; but she could not obtain one.

[Col. 0840D]

Several advocates, however, were granted to the opposing party. The provostess then openly confessed that she had entirely renounced her own election and had unanimously consented, with the seven electresses, to the said nun G. Upon hearing this, and learning that the bishop and many members of the chapter, being relatives of that nun, wished to bend judgment toward her promotion, the custodian, after arguments had for some time been made concerning the law of Heris and the preservation of her own rights, appealed to us, lest prejudice be suffered by her election. But the bishop, disregarding the appeal,

[Col. 0841A]

pronounced judgment in favor of the aforesaid nun, his relative, and caused her to be installed in possession of the abbey.

Volpert, a cleric who had come as procurator for the opposing party, stated that the aforesaid nun G. had been elected abbess of Heris by the greater and sounder part of the chapter—namely, eleven persons, including the provostess, scholastica, and dean, together with certain other sisters—after two frivolous nominations had first been annulled by the said bishop; and that she had been confirmed by the bishop himself with good zeal. He further stated that the aforesaid custodian, presumptuously harassing her on this account, wished to force herself into that church by lay power. The procurator therefore requested on the nun’s behalf that we cause the confirmation made in her favor to be firmly observed,

[Col. 0841B]

asserting that it ought not to harm her that she had been a black-monastic nun, whereas the other sisters of Heris wore canonical dress; nor that she had elsewhere been confirmed and blessed as an abbess. For, he said, it was customary in that region for black-monastic nuns to be chosen for abbeys of this kind, and it sometimes happened that a canoness held an abbey of black-monastic nuns. He further asserted that Pope C., of blessed memory, our predecessor, had granted her permission to be chosen for another abbey.

The custodian replied, on the contrary, that the same nun ought not, and could not, be chosen to govern their abbey, since she was not a sister of that church but had come from a certain black-monastic monastery; she had been confirmed and

[Col. 0841C]

blessed as abbess of a more distinguished church, from whose governance she was believed not to have been expelled without fault; and she was unable to produce the consecration which she said she possessed from our predecessor. The custodian therefore urgently requested that what had been done in the nun’s favor be declared void, especially since the letters of the said bishop, which the procurator possessed in defense of his party, expressly contained that the bishop had proceeded to confirm that election after an appeal to us had been entered. That appeal seemed lawful, since the kinship by which the bishop, in his own letters, was said to be related to the nun plainly created suspicion against him; besides which she was entitled to appeal whenever she was aggrieved in any respect by her diocesan bishop.

[Col. 0841D]

Having carefully heard these and other matters put forward both by the said procurator and by the custodian, we ordered the abbots of Heterward and . . . Hegens, and the provost of Gusmaria, that, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, they should declare null and void whatever had been done concerning the election of the said nun; and, after more carefully investigating the truth concerning the custodian’s election, if they found her election canonical and her person suitable, they should confirm her by Apostolic authority, restraining opponents through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

But when the custodian presented this mandate to the judges, they declared null and void, by our authority, what had been done concerning the aforesaid nun G.

[Col. 0842A]

And since she refused to relinquish the abbey, they subjected her to a sentence of excommunication and ordered that she be more strictly avoided. Yet she, together with her electresses, appealed by messenger concerning her election after several days. But the judges paid no heed whatever to the appeal, especially because her election had been annulled by our express mandate and appeal had been prohibited in our letters. Having summoned the convent of Heris, they wished to investigate the custodian’s election, as had been enjoined upon them. Finding her election canonical and her person suitable, and having taken the counsel of prudent men, they confirmed her election and took care, by definitive sentence and by our authority, to award the abbey of Heris to her.

[Col. 0842B]

Although the diocesan bishop appealed and forbade the convent of Heris to presume to obey her as abbess, they nevertheless installed her, with all gentleness, in corporal possession of the same abbey. From this she was violently expelled by the brother of the aforesaid nun and her supporters. In addition to the many evils perpetrated there by them, they compelled R. herself to confirm by oath that, until the feast of Saint Martin most recently past, she would not enter the Church of Heris or use even ordinary lodging or the stipend which she possessed there.

At length, since R. had long been afflicted by these and other matters, she considered it necessary to have recourse to our presence; the nun G. likewise came. When the aforesaid R.

[Col. 0842C]

had set forth the dispute and requested that the proceedings of the judges be confirmed, and that satisfaction be made to her for the damages and injuries inflicted, G. alleged in reply that, since she had been elected abbess of the Church of Heris by the greater and sounder part of the convent and her election had been confirmed by the diocesan bishop, the custodian obtained letters addressed to the abbot of Conradesburg and his fellow judges. When G., having been cited, came before them and showed that she had been despoiled on account of the custodian, she received from those judges a sentence that she was not at all bound to answer the custodian unless she were first restored. The custodian, however, uttering an appeal from that sentence to us, personally prosecuted her appeal.

[Col. 0842D]

And although G. sent a procurator solely in order that that sentence might be confirmed, her procurator, exceeding the bounds of his mandate, allowed the custodian to obtain what she wished against G.; and he brought letters to the above-mentioned judges, one of whom lay under a sentence of excommunication. This is contained in letters of our venerable brother, the . . . archbishop of Mainz, exhibited to us. With the other judge, while the third was absent, that judge proceeded irregularly in all matters. Although G. and the chapter of the Church of Heris appealed on grounds of a suspect forum and other grievances, the judges nevertheless proceeded and caused the same custodian to be installed in corporal possession through Albert, her familiar, who, as is stated in the same letters of the said archbishop,

[Col. 0843A]

was bound by the bond of excommunication, and through B., the parish priest.

To prove that the said procurator had received such a mandate, namely to prosecute the appeal that had been entered, she produced witnesses before an auditor assigned to her. But the reply was made that, even if those witnesses proved such a mandate, it did not thereby at all follow that he had not received another one. Therefore, since the presumption favors the sentence—that all things were duly done, especially matters pronounced by the supreme pontiff with such mature deliberation—it is plainly inferred that he received a general mandate concerning the principal business, as the custodian herself showed more fully in order to prove this through one witness.

Having therefore more carefully understood these and other matters advanced by both sides,

[Col. 0843B]

we have, justice requiring it, by sentence ordered the aforesaid nun G. removed from the administration of that abbey. By Apostolic letters we strictly command your discretion that, personally coming to that church, you commit the administration of the abbey to another suitable person, to whom there shall be made, for the use of that abbey, mutual resignation of the revenues withheld.

Meanwhile, you shall investigate the sentence of confirmation rendered by the delegated judges concerning the custodian’s election, in order that you may take care to confirm or invalidate it as the law requires. Thus, if it appears that the sentence must be invalidated because one of the delegated judges who delivered that sentence

[Col. 0843C]

was publicly bound by the bond of excommunication when it was rendered, as is attested by the metropolitan’s letters, or for another just cause, then, after annulling it, you shall again investigate the custodian’s election. Having heard and examined what is advanced both as to the facts and as to the person, if her election is found canonical, confirm it. Otherwise, after entirely invalidating it, grant the sisters free power of election; and confirm by Apostolic authority, with the obstacle of appeal removed, the election of the woman whom they judge should be regularly elected abbess. Cause suitable provision to be made for the aforesaid custodian from the goods of the church for her lawful expenses, compelling any opponents or rebels, appeal set aside, by ecclesiastical censure to desist from their rashness.

As for any witnesses who may be named, etc. Without any letters prejudicing truth and justice, etc. But if not all, etc. To these persons, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XXXIX. To P., Bishop of Porto. [Note: [Col. 0843D] See letter 69 of book five, note.] Authority to make a will is granted. (At Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Nones of April.)

Since, with prudent deliberation, you propose to make a testament disposing of your goods,

[Col. 0844A]

you have humbly requested us to deem it fitting to grant you permission in this matter. Therefore, favorably assenting to your salutary purpose, by the authority of these presents we grant you free power to dispose of your goods according to God.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of April, in the ninth year.

XL. To the . . . archdeacon, . . . chancellor [Note: [Col. 0843D] See letter 98 of book five.], and the . . . dean of Saint Germanus at Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0843D] Jobert, Josbert, or Jebert, dean of Saint Germanus at Auxerre, a Parisian, is known from instruments from 1204 through [Col. 0844D] 1207. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VII, col. 256.], of Paris. That they are to cause to be observed what had been definitively decided in the case between Walter of Picerel, for himself, and Hugh of Feversham, for the dean of Alveoli, concerning the church of Beavilla. (At Saint Peter’s, the ninth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0844B]

When our beloved sons Master Walter of Picerel, for himself, and Master Hugh of Feversham, for the . . . dean of Alveoli, were litigating with one another concerning the church of Beavilla, we granted our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, [Note: [Col. 0844D] See letter 29 of book eight, note.] as auditor to both parties. In his presence the same master alleged and showed that, when our venerable brother, the . . . bishop of Ostia, [Note: [Col. 0844D] See letter 11 of book three, note.] was exercising the office of legate in Gaul and had marked William of Montibus with clerical character, he ordered our beloved son the . . . archdeacon of Chartres to reserve for his disposal the first church which happened to become vacant in his archdeaconry,

[Col. 0844C]

forbidding him to confer it on anyone, since he intended to provide for the said William, who had no benefice, in that church.

Thereafter, when by the death of O., formerly dean of Alveoli, the church of Beavilla became vacant, the same archdeacon, contrary to the legate’s command, granted both it and the deanery to his brother G., who was known to possess another church in the same diocese. When this came to the knowledge of the aforesaid legate, he summoned them before him and, upon the advice of prudent men, annulled the archdeacon’s act and canonically granted the said church, then vacant, to the aforesaid William, as is contained in his authentic instrument. Subsequently both our venerable brother, the . . . bishop,

[Col. 0844D]

[Note: [Col. 0844D] See letter 14 of book three, note.] and the said archdeacon of Chartres, who was the patron of the church, gave their assent, as their letters attest. Thus the said William held that church for nearly four years and more, and the dean, who knew and saw this, did not bring him to suit at all.

But when a certain prebend in the church of Saint Maurice at Chartres, which by right belonged to Master G. himself, became vacant, the aforesaid bishop, in pious foresight—or provident piety—considering

[Col. 0845A]

that that prebend, to which no cure of souls was attached, suited the frequently named William better than the same church of Beavilla, which required a constant pastor, granted the church, when vacant, to the same master upon the presentation of the said archdeacon, no one objecting; and he assigned that prebend to the aforesaid cleric. Therefore the master humbly requested confirmation of that church in his favor, as one which, he said, he had canonically obtained without opposition and at the presentation of the true patron; and he requested that perpetual silence concerning it be imposed upon his adversary.

The procurator of the said dean denied this, adding that when, upon the death of C., formerly dean of Alveoli, the churches of Franconville and Beavilla had become vacant, the . . . archdeacon of Chartres, to whom their grant belonged,

[Col. 0845B]

conferred the church of Beavilla on his brother G. and, by order of the diocesan bishop, corporeally invested him in it, as is contained in the letters both of the bishop and of the archdeacon. After this, William of Montibus presented to that archdeacon letters of the aforementioned legate, containing that the legate had reserved to himself the grant of one church that should first become vacant in the archdeaconry of Chartres. By this William sought either that the archdeacon confer one of those churches upon him or reserve it for the legate’s grant. The archdeacon answered that he could fulfill neither request because he had already assigned both to others.

William then returned to the same legate and, falsely suggesting

[Col. 0845C]

that the church of Beavilla was vacant, obtained from him a de facto grant of that church and an order for his institution in it. When G. learned this, he appealed to the Apostolic See so that no one might disturb him in his possession. Coming personally to the Apostolic See, he obtained delegation of the case to judges. After G. had subsequently returned home, the aforesaid William, distrusting his legal position, renounced in the hand of the bishop of Chartres whatever right he had acquired through the same legate in the said church. This having been done, the aforementioned archdeacon presented Master G. of Picerel to the same bishop and caused him to be invested in the aforesaid church, to the prejudice of the absent G.

[Col. 0845D]

When G. learned this, he placed both himself and the church under the protection of the Apostolic See in defense of his right; and, refusing to allow himself to be ejected from possession, he appealed to our hearing. He requested that everything remain in the state in which it then stood. In particular, because the said archdeacon, by the command of the bishop of Chartres, wished to install the said master in corporal possession of the church in question, he appealed to the hearing of the metropolitan. Nonetheless, after that appeal, the archdeacon attempted to install the master in possession of the church.

[Col. 0846A]

Therefore, when, at G.’s complaint, the same case had been committed to our venerable brother the . . . archbishop of Sens, [Note: [Col. 0845D] See letter 45 of book three, note.] to the . . . subdean, and to the . . . cantor of Chartres, the aforesaid master, cited by them and appearing in their presence, refused to answer. Instead, immediately entering an appeal to the Apostolic See, he contumaciously withdrew from them. The judges nevertheless proceeded and received lawful witnesses against him, through whom it was clearly shown that, after an appeal had been entered to the court of Sens, the same master had been installed in corporal possession of that church, as was read in the letters of those judges. Thus the frequently named master, after his custodian had been expelled from that church, was lawfully despoiled of it; and it was finally entrusted to the care of another,

[Col. 0846B]

who celebrated there and received its revenues not under the authority of the said master, but in the name of the aforementioned dean.

Accordingly, since G. asserted that he had thus obtained the church, he requested that the judges be written to, so that they might protect him from the master’s improper molestation. The said master replied in opposition that it was wholly false that the dean had been invested with that church at the presentation of the true patron and by order of the bishop, especially because the bishop admitted in his letters that the dean had not at all been invested either with the cure of that church or with the church itself.

The opposing party alleged that the aforesaid William, fearing the dean’s return, had renounced his right into the hand of the bishop of Chartres. The master entirely maintained this to be false, since, after G.’s return, he had possessed the church for three years and more without litigation, with G.’s knowledge and in his sight.

[Col. 0846C]

The master did not deny that his adversary had appealed to the court of Sens, while the master himself appealed to the Apostolic See and prohibited the dean from presuming to molest him concerning his right. Yet the adversary nevertheless went to the metropolitan and caused the master to be cited. The master appeared before him on the appointed day but refused to contest the suit; renewing his appeal, he withdrew. Nevertheless the archbishop, as the adversary himself admitted, delegated the case to judges after the appeal.

[Col. 0846D]

The master therefore said that both his own allegations and the matters advanced by the opposing party established that he had been despoiled after an appeal had lawfully been entered to the Apostolic See. As to the adversary’s allegation that, after the dean had appealed to the archbishop of Sens, the master had been installed in possession of that church, the master answered that, if the dean had appealed to prevent the archdeacon from carrying out the execution entrusted to him, such an appeal was null, since there is no appeal from an executor where he does not attempt to exceed the limits of his mandate.

He further added that,

[Col. 0847A]

since the dean had no right in the church, it did not concern him to appeal. Even if he could in some respect have appealed, since the master defeated by objection of his appeal to the Apostolic See the appeal which the dean had made to the metropolitan, he ought not to have been despoiled in the meantime.

The dean’s procurator answered in opposition that, although the said legate had ordered that the first church to become vacant in the archdeaconry of Chartres be reserved for his grant, he could not lawfully do this in respect of the aforesaid church, because he lacked such authority. The presentation of a cleric to that church belonged to the archdeacon not as a cleric, but as though a layman, by reason of patronage and not by right of his archdeaconry. Therefore the archdeacon was not bound to observe the legate’s prohibition in this matter and could lawfully present another person to the church; and, since his presentation was made of a suitable person, it ought to be considered valid.

[Col. 0847B]

The aforesaid master insisted in reply that, even if it were true—which was entirely false—that the right of presenting a cleric to that church belonged to the archdeacon not by reason of archidiaconal office but by reason of temporal lordship, and that the legate’s prohibition had no force in this respect because he could not forbid a lay patron to act, nevertheless, for another reason, the archdeacon’s presentation of the said dean was null and void. For when he presented him, he had long before been suspended by our beloved son P., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, then cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, [Note: [Col. 0847D] See letter 20 of book three, note.] legate of the Apostolic See. That suspension lasted until after the return of the aforesaid bishop of Ostia, through whose intervention the archdeacon, appearing in our presence, deserved absolution from the bond of suspension, as is proved by that bishop’s letters.

The dean’s procurator replied that, even if the archdeacon were bound by a sentence of suspension, the grant of that church could nevertheless belong to him as a layman by right of patronage; he could not on that account be deprived of it either by the legate’s prohibition or by the suspension, especially since only his archidiaconal office

[Col. 0847D]

had been interdicted.

Having carefully understood these and other matters advanced before the same auditor and faithfully reported to us by him, we observe that, even if the aforesaid archdeacon had presented the said dean to that church as a layman, the dean was not admitted by the diocesan bishop, whereas another man, afterwards presented by the same archdeacon, was instituted by the diocesan bishop. Accordingly, under the ruling of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, not the first but the second acquired right in the same church. And if the said archdeacon presented the aforesaid dean as a cleric,

[Col. 0848A]

then, because he acted in this capacity as a cleric, he was subject to the legate’s jurisdiction. Consequently, after the same legate had decreed that the grant of that church was to be reserved to himself, the archdeacon could not present anyone to it as a cleric.

We therefore decreed that the presentation of the aforesaid dean to the frequently mentioned church was null; and, that presentation being entirely disregarded, we pronounced the grant of the same church made to Master Walter to have been canonical. We also annulled what had been attempted by judges delegated by the aforesaid archbishop of Sens after the lawful appeal to us had been entered, and adjudged the aforesaid church to the same master, to be possessed fully and peacefully with the fruits received in the meantime, imposing perpetual silence upon the aforesaid dean in this matter.

[Col. 0848B]

Wherefore, by Apostolic letters we command your discretion to cause what has been definitively decided by us to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical coercion, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed; restraining any opponents or rebels whom you find, appeal set aside, by like coercion. But if not all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year.

XLI. [Note: [Col. 0847D] This is wholly identical with letter 200 of book eight, [Col. 0848D] to which we refer the reader.] To the . . . bishop of Vercelli, the . . . abbot of Tiglieto, and Albert, priest of Mantua. How and when a prelate ought to proceed in punishing the excesses of subjects.

[Col. 0848C]

XLII. To the . . . bishop of Halberstadt. [Note: [Col. 0848D] See letter 108 of book eight, note.] In response to an inquiry: a monk moving a bell, whose fall killed a boy, may be promoted in his monastery to higher orders. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of April.)

From the letters of your fraternity we have learned that a certain monk, a youth of your diocese, while helping to lower a bell from the bell tower, moved it so that, when a piece of timber accidentally fell, it crushed and killed a little boy in the church beneath the bell tower. You therefore humbly asked us what should be done in this matter, requesting that a merciful dispensation be granted him.

[Col. 0848D]

Accordingly, by Apostolic letters we command your fraternity that, if the monk was performing a necessary and useful task, and when he was known to have moved the timber, he did so in a place through which he did not believe anyone would pass, be present, or customarily come, he may sufficiently be promoted, especially in the monastery, to higher orders.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of April, in the ninth year.

XLIII. [Note: [Col. 0849C] This letter is found, though mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book I, title 33, *On primacy and obedience*, chapter 7.] To the . . . bishop of Florence. [Note: [Col. 0849C] See letter 156 of book eight, note.] That subdeacons of the Roman Church who have acquired a benefice for which they owe him obedience are not exempted from that obedience. (At Saint Peter’s, the seventh day before the Ides of April.)

[Col. 0849A]

[By your letters [Note: [Col. 0849C] What follows, distinguished in italic type, is absent from the *Decretals*, but is read in Pithou’s additions.] you informed us that, when certain subdeacons of the Roman Church obtain prelacies in your diocese, for which they are bound to render you obedience, whenever justice requires you to exercise ecclesiastical discipline over them, they invoke the privilege of the subdiaconate and assert that they are not bound by it, as though by the office of such subdiaconate they were exempted from the obedience which they owe you on account of the benefice obtained.

[Col. 0849B]

You requested instruction by an oracle of the Apostolic See on whether such persons are withdrawn from the obedience owed to you because they have received from the Roman pontiff the order of the subdiaconal office. [Note: [Col. 0849C] In the *Decretals*, “quis per mox subdiaconatus” is read in place of “subd. off.” [the reading is materially uncertain]; below, the words distinguished in italic type are omitted.] To this we briefly reply: although it is fitting that you should show particular deference, insofar as is appropriate, among your other subjects, to those whom Apostolic benevolence has honored by the conferral of that order, they are by no means thereby released from the obedience otherwise owed to you.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the ninth year.

XLIV. To the . . . abbot [Note: [Col. 0849C] “XVIII. Rainaud II, abbot of Pultariæ, is called the brother of Peter de Raveriis in a charter of Ungiaci in 1203. He occurs in 1204 in an instrument of Alba-ripa; and in the registers of Clairvaux in 1199, 1206, and 1213, as well as in various charters of 1216 and 1220. The necrology mentions him on 28 October, and we conjecture that he is the Abbot R. [Col. 0849D] who as early as 1197 granted the brothers of Alba-ripa the tenure (*la tenure*) of Viard, son of Varin de Vaure.” *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 726.] and convent of Pultariæ. Their ancient privilege is renewed. (At Saint Peter’s, the sixth day before the Ides of April.)

[Col. 0850A]

Since Christ is truth, we, who, though unworthy, hold his place on earth, ought to bear witness to truth, since he is recorded to have said of himself: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth” (John 18).

For from the letters of our beloved sons O., [Note: [Col. 0849D] Oliver, abbot of Saint-Seine, occurs in instruments from at least 1205 through at least 1226. He was buried in the church of Saint-Seine beside the steps of the altar of Saint Andrew and Saint Theobald (from the monastic register, p. 63); his tomb, raised above the ground, was still standing in 1630. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 698.] of Saint-Seine; A., [Note: [Col. 0849D]

A. of Flavigny. The following material in *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, cols. 461–462, concerning G., or Gilibert, and Hervey, alternatively Arvey, abbots of the monastery of Flavigny, must certainly be compared here.

“XL. G., formerly a regular canon and then hospitaller of Virziliac, elected by only nine monks against twenty-two who had elected another, was nevertheless confirmed by Celestine III and, after being blessed by the bishop, was installed in possession. He in fact acted as abbot at least until the first year of Innocent III’s pontificate, in which that supreme pontiff approved the settlement entered into between him and the bishop of Autun, as is clear from letter 188, vol. I, p. 103. Furthermore, he appears to be the Gilibert later deposed by Innocent III because his deeds manifestly merited condemnation: letter 90, vol. II, p. 50, addressed to the bishops of Auxerre and Troyes and to the abbot of Saint-Bénigne.

“XLI. Hervey II, or Arvey, appointed Giles of Semur his procurator in 1214, to settle the dispute between Hervey himself and the abbot of Alba-ripa concerning the pastures of Champabain. In the same year, in February, he made an agreement with Duke Odo, according to the chest of gifts and donations in the Dijon chamber of accounts. He is also mentioned in a charter of Pontigny in 1212, and in the registers of Ungiaci in 1193, 1221, 1223, and 1228. Perhaps, indeed, he is the Hervey mentioned by the necrology of Saint-Bénigne on the Kalends of August. Indeed, he seems to be A., that is Arvey, kinsman of Rainaud, prior of Semur and monk of Flavigny, who was elected by twenty-two monks and nevertheless rejected by Celestine; he finally appealed to the judgment of Innocent III, in which he is shown to have prevailed, both from what has been said above and from the period during which he is known to have survived and acted as abbot.”] 
of Flavigny, and II. [Note: [Col. 0850D] “IX. Hugh I, abbot of Châtillon, is found in the records of Clairvaux in the years 1203 and 1211; in the charters of Val-des-Choues in 1216 and 1219; in a charter of Quincy in 1218; in the records of the abbeys of Mores and of Alba Ripa in 1219; and in a charter of Châtillon in January 1222. He died on 22 May.” *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 773.] of the abbots of Châtillon, and G., dean of Châtillon, we have received clear information that they found in your church a privilege of John, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, strengthened by the protection of a very ancient seal; and, having carefully examined it and caused it faithfully to be copied, they sent the copy, secured with their seals, to our presence, earnestly and humbly beseeching that we might deign, out of the customary benevolence of the Apostolic See, to renew it for your church. We therefore, giving favorable assent both to your prayers and to theirs, and observing that the monastery itself is recorded in the rent-roll book of our treasury among the other free and exempt monasteries, and that it is also bound to us and to our successors in one pound of silver annually, have judged that the transcript of the aforesaid privilege, which contains the freedom of your monastery, should be inserted word for word in this document, so that the truth concerning this matter may not perish, [Col. 0850C] and for fuller knowledge of the truth. [Col. 0851A] [Note: [Col. 0851C] This letter—or rather privilege—is not found among the already published letters of Pope John VIII. (See *Epistolae summorum pontificum*, vol. III.) It must, however, be compared with the other letters of the same pontiff concerning the monastery of Pultariis, ibid.; also with vol. IX of the writers of *Rerum Gallicarum et Francicarum*, p. 185, and elsewhere.]

“John, bishop [Note: [Col. 0851C] “John VIII, son of Gundo, a Roman, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, reigned under the emperors Louis II the Younger, Charles II the Bald, Louis III the Stammerer, and Charles III the Fat, Augusti, for ten years and eleven days; he was created and consecrated on 14 December in the year 872 (that is, by our manner of reckoning, 873, as will shortly appear from the chronological indications of this diploma). After Pope Adrian II died, the Romans, seeking his successor, agreed unanimously in heart and voice upon John; and, in the Roman manner, made a good bishop from a good deacon.” Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 659.], servant of the servants of God, to the venerable and religious abbot [Note: [Col. 0851D] “Saro, otherwise Hairo, appears to have been the first abbot of the monastery of Pultariis, as is gathered from the chronicle of St. Benignus, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 377. He himself was also for some time governor of that monastery under Bertilo, chorepiscopus and abbot. He lies in the abbey of Pultariis.” *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 724.], and to his successors forever, who, by divine prompting and divine providence, has been established in the monastery which was built from its foundations and endowed by you—namely Gerard, our most illustrious son and renowned count [Note: [Col. 0851D]

“Gerard of Roussillon, count of the province, lived in the times of Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and Charles the Bald, whose benefactions he boasts had enriched him [Col. 0852C] in his testament. (See *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 487.) He married Bertha, daughter of Pepin I, duke of Aquitaine, and niece of Louis the Pious. Together with his wife, not far from his castle of Roussillon, he founded before the year 868 a Benedictine monastery at Pultariis in honor of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul. Both spouses were buried there with their son Theodoric, who died in the cradle: Gerard on 4 March, according to the necrology of St. Mary and St. Lazarus of Avallon; [Col. 0852D] Bertha on 8 November (in 874), according to a fragment of the necrology of Pultariis; and Theodoric, lastly, on 5 October, according to an epitaph which survives entire, carved upon a marble tablet in the basilica of Pultariis.”

Thus far the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 724. But there is a difficulty, which we shall indicate shortly. See note (201).]

—and Bertha, our most noble daughter, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, beside the flowing river Seine, in territory looking toward the village which from ancient times they call Pultariis, in the district of Latica, within the borders of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0852D] This place is in the kingdom of Burgundy, in the diocese of Langres, in the district of Latica (in French, Laussois), on the Seine, about two leagues from Molesme and not far from Mussey, or Mussy, the castle of the bishops of Langres.]; and you made this holy Roman Church heir, together with all that belongs to the monastery by right, for the remedy and future recompense [Col. 0851B] of your souls, and by a charter of donation bestowed it upon the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0852D] See the testament of the aforesaid Gerard, cited above. Ancient documents of the same Gerard, subjecting the place and monastery of Pultariis to Pope Nicholas I and his successors, are found in *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, appendix, col. 132, ch. 8, from the chronicle of Vézelay, where it is worthwhile to read them in full.]

When, through divine clemency going before, the hearts of Catholics are kindled with such ardent desire for those things which are to be urged by the admonitions of pontiffs that they seek them of their own accord, they ought to be granted with so much the more eager and joyful a mind, since the very things which they desire ought to be sought even if they did not wish to perform them. Accordingly, in keeping with your petition, we grant, confirm, and establish by the decree of this present apostolic authority the following privileges for the monastery, founded by your religious devotion in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, in the parish of the city of Langres, in the aforesaid place and kingdom: that no king, no prelate, no person of any of the aforesaid ranks, nor anyone else, may under the pretext of any cause or occasion diminish or take away anything already given to that monastery by you, our most noble sons, or which may hereafter be bestowed from their own right by you or by any others; nor may anyone in any way apply such things to his own uses or grant them to others, under the pretense of pious causes as an excuse for his avarice. Rather, we will, and by apostolic authority command, that everything offered there or which may come to be offered, whether by you, by those who enter that place in the office of abbot or in religious life, or by those who offer their oblations there for the remedy of their souls, shall from the present time be possessed unimpaired and without disturbance, and shall in every respect benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

On this condition: that none of our successors in this holy see, in which by the Lord’s will [Col. 0852B] we serve, shall ever or anywhere permit any portion of those same goods to be granted as a benefice, exchanged, or granted or retained subject to a rent in times to come. Rather, our successors, receiving only the annual rent of one pound of silver specified in the testament of your conveyance, by which from that same monastery you made this holy mother Church your heir, shall diligently endeavor with pastoral care to extend the aid of pious fatherhood to that monastery and to the abbots and monks dwelling there under the Rule of the holy father Benedict, against all who assail them.

Likewise, we establish that, when the present abbot of the monastery dies, no other shall be appointed there through any contrivance of deceit, save one whom the consent [Col. 0852C] of the monks, according to the fear of God and the institution of the Rule of St. Benedict, has chosen, and whom the pontiff of this Apostolic See shall provide to be ordained, or shall consent to be ordained upon the monks’ recommendation.

We also add this provision, in order to exclude an occasion for avarice: no king, no priest, nor [Col. 0853A] any one of the faithful, either personally or through an agent, shall dare to demand tithes, or to receive anything in gold or in any other kind of gain or gift, on account of the ordination of the same abbot, or of clerics and priests, or on account of the provision of chrism, the consecration of the basilica, any benefit of spiritual or temporal service, or any causes whatsoever belonging to the same monastery. Nor shall that abbot presume to give anything for the sake of his ordination, lest under this pretext the things which the faithful piously offer to the place, or have already offered, should be consumed. Nor shall the bishop of the city in whose parish it lies celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of that monastery; nor shall he proclaim stations [Col. 0853B] in that abbey, lest the repose of God’s servants be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering; nor shall he presume to establish there provisions or lodging-dues.

Yet we decree—and indeed exhort—that, according to the capacity of the place and its resources, the reception and beneficence toward the faithful and religious, which the Apostle commands to be shown to all, shall be provided there not only freely. But let such moderation be maintained in the number of the community that neither a multitude may impose want nor a scarcity of inhabitants bring abandonment upon the place.

We decree that all these things contained in the text of this our precept and decree shall be observed forever by all who succeed you and retain under usufruct the same monastery constructed by you and [Col. 0853C] delivered to the holy Roman Church, or by those whose interest may be concerned. But if any priest, judge, or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, shall attempt to act against it, let him, struck by apostolic anathema, be deprived of the dignity of his power or honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; and, unless he has restored what he has wrongfully taken away, corrected what he has rashly undertaken, or mourned his unlawful deeds with fitting repentance, let him be cut off from the most sacred body of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to severe vengeance at the eternal judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, [Col. 0854A] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of George, notary, *regionarius*, and keeper of records of the holy Roman Church, in the month of September, in the twelfth indiction [Note: [Col. 0853D] The twelfth indiction during the reign of Pope John VIII coincides with the year 879. See *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new ed., vol. I, p. 18. See also Pagi, *Critica historico-chronologica*, vol. III, p. 723.] + Fare well +.

“Given on 19 September, through the hand of Walpert, most humble bishop of the holy Church of Porto [Note: [Col. 0853D] Walpert, bishop of Porto, succeeded Formosus after the latter’s deposition in 877, and is found subscribing in that same year. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 132. See also Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 666.], in the sixth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope [Note: [Col. 0853D]

*Sixth.* The annotator testifies that this is how he read it in the manuscript codex of the Vatican Archives, in the margin of Conti’s copy, from the authority of which copy we caused this letter to be transcribed. It seems, however, that *eighth* should be read. For 19 September, in the twelfth indiction of the pontificate of Pope John VIII, coincides with the eighth year of that pope’s pontificate, since nearly all chronologists unanimously assert that he was elected and consecrated in December of the fifth indiction. See Baronius, *Annales*, vol. X, [Col. 0854D] p. 488, under the year 872; Pagi, *Critica historico-chronologica*, vol. III, p. 699; Muratori, *Annali d’Italia*, vol. V, pt. I, p. 126.

It should further be noted that a certain difficulty arises from the chronological indications appended to this diploma, a difficulty we have already indicated above in note (196). From the records cited by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, it follows that Gerard of Roussillon—or at least Bertha, his wife—had already died by the year 874. Yet in our privilege, which is proved beyond all doubt from the repeated indication of the twelfth indiction to have been issued not before 878, or perhaps even 879, the pontiff speaks of Gerard and his wife Bertha as though they were still among the living; indeed, he seems to address the privilege to them. Let those more expert in chronology and genealogy consider how this difficulty may be resolved.]

, seated in the most sacred see of the blessed Apostle Peter, in the twelfth indiction +.”

Therefore, wishing that your monastery should enjoy its due [Col. 0854B] freedom, we strictly forbid anyone to presume unlawfully to trouble you or your monastery contrary to the tenor of the privilege written above. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the holy Roman Church, 8 April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1205 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

XLV. [Note: [Col. 0854C] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §8.] TO THE NOBLE MAN . . . , MARQUIS OF NAMUR, AND TO ALL CHRIST’S FAITHFUL WHO WISH TO SET OUT WITH HIM FOR CONSTANTINOPLE TO AID THE HOLY LAND. That they should go to Constantinople. (At St. Peter’s, 10 April.)

[Col. 0854C]

Since, through the retention of the empire of Constantinople—which the Latins, by divine judgment, have subjected to themselves—the province of Jerusalem is confidently hoped to be liberated from the hands of the pagans, whoever for reverence toward Jesus Christ piously longs for its liberation ought also effectually to strive for the retention of that empire. Although, therefore, we recently enjoined upon all Christ’s faithful by general letters, for remission of all sins, that, by going to Constantinople, they should labor [Col. 0855A] for the aid of the Holy Land, nevertheless, wishing to encourage you more effectively to this work of piety, since some of you may especially be hoped to be induced to set out for Constantinople on the ground that the vows which they have made concerning any pilgrimages other than a visit to the province of Jerusalem may be fulfilled through this journey of necessity, we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you, and enjoin this upon you in remission of such vows: do not delay in setting out for Constantinople for the aid of the Holy Land.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, 10 April, in the ninth year.

XLVI. TO . . . THE BISHOP OF BRIXEN [Note: [Col. 0855D]

Conrad succeeded Eberhard of Truchsen—concerning whom see letter 155 of book V—as archbishop of Salzburg, having been elected from the bishopric of Brixen in 1200. This Conrad, a nobleman of Rodeneck in Tyrol, bishop of Brixen, rededicated and consecrated the church of the monastery of Wilten in 1201.

Later, in 1204, he dedicated and consecrated the monastery of St. George’s Mount in the lower valley of the Inn; likewise a chapel in the town of Klausen, beneath Sabiona Castle, commonly called the Hospital, in the year 1208, by the founder of that chapel.

In 1214 Emperor Frederick II held an imperial diet at Augsburg, attended among many other princes by Conrad, bishop of Brixen; Frederick of Wangen, bishop of Trent; and the illustrious lord Albert, count of Tyrol. Both the aforesaid bishops also attended the diet held by Frederick II at Nuremberg in 1216. He died in 1217, according to the Annals of Passau and the aforesaid Catalogue. Wiguleus Hund, *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, vol. I, p. 446. See also Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, pt. I, p. 40.]

. . . AND TO THE BISHOP OF FREISING [Note: [Col. 0855D] Otto II. This Otto, a canon of Magdeburg, was elected in the year of the Lord 1184; a noble and generous man, descended, as is said, from the counts of Dießen: “There came the pure and noble Otto II, who gathers what had been scattered, a noble and generous man.” He had three brothers who were bishops: the first, Dietpold, of Passau; [Col. 0856C] the second, Henry, bishop of Würzburg; the third, Magnoald, of Passau; while he himself was the fourth, of Freising. Having thus attained episcopal dignity, he governed his Church vigorously, stood firm as a wall for the house of God, and, as a prudent and wise man, a pious shepherd kind to his sheep, presided for thirty-five years. He sat for thirty-five years. He died in the year of the Lord 1220 and was buried in the cathedral church, before the altar of St. Matthias. Wiguleus Hund, *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, vol. I, p. 162.], AND OF TRIESTE [Note: [Col. 0856D]

Concerning the bishops of Trieste at about the period with which we are dealing, Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, pt. I, p. 52, has these few remarks:

VII. Woscalus lived about the year of salvation 1192.

“VIII. Henry, bishop of Trieste, A.D. 1208.”]

. That they are to hear the case between the Churches of Salzburg and Gurk, and induce the parties to concord. (At St. Peter’s, 11 April.)

[Col. 0855B]

When the parties in the case pending between the Churches of Salzburg and Gurk appeared before us, it was alleged on behalf of the Church of Gurk that the freedom to elect its own bishop belongs to it both by common law and by ancient custom, and also by apostolic privilege. You were therefore asked to enable it to enjoy peaceful possession of that freedom, compelling the opposing party to cease its unlawful molestation on this point.

And since it was established by common law—that is, that a bishop is to be specially elected by those over whom he is chiefly to preside—privileges of the archbishops of Salzburg were produced to prove the ancient custom. From the time of Archbishop Geboard of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0856D]

Geboard, otherwise Gebehard, became archbishop of Salzburg in 1061 and held office until 1090.

In 1070 he obtained from Pope Alexander II leave to establish the bishopric of Gurk.

See Hansiz, *Germania sacra*, vol. II, p. 175 ff. See also the same, ibid., pp. 935–936.]

down to the next-to-last archbishop of that see, they had confirmed by their privileges the right of the Church of Gurk [Col. 0856A] to elect its own pastor. A privilege of Pope Lucius II of happy memory was also exhibited, by which it is granted to the Church of Gurk that, upon the death of its bishop, no one shall be set over it through any contrivance of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the council, according to God and the canonical sanctions, shall judge fit to elect.

Against this petition, however, the procurator of the Church of Salzburg raised the exception of a matter already adjudged, producing an authentic instrument of a judgment [Note: [Col. 0856D] This judgment may be read in Hansiz, *Germania sacra*, vol. II, p. 301.] which, by delegation of Pope Alexander III of blessed memory, the bishop of Freising and the abbot of Holy Cross are said to have pronounced in favor of the Church of Salzburg [Col. 0856B] against that of Gurk. Moreover, not in order to contest the suit but as if to reinforce the judgment, he produced a privilege of Pope Alexander II and a privilege of Emperor Henry, by which he sought to show that the right of electing the bishop of Gurk belongs to the archbishop of Salzburg, and that this had deserved confirmation by the charters of our predecessors Alexander and Lucius, and by ourselves also. [Note: [Col. 0856D] Concerning this confirmation by Innocent, see Hansiz, ibid., p. 312, where it is said to have been given at the Lateran, 3 February, in the third indiction, in 1200, the third year of Pope Innocent III’s pontificate. See also the same, ibid., p. 481, §9.] Since the aforesaid judgment had become res judicata and had been confirmed by both legates and prelates of the Apostolic See, nothing could now be attempted against it.

On the other hand, it was said that no proof whatever existed of the commission alleged to have been made to the aforesaid bishop and abbot. Neither the commission itself appeared, nor had it been proved by witnesses or otherwise in a lawful manner; therefore, the mere instrument secured with the seals of the aforesaid bishop and abbot could not prove that a judgment had been rendered. That instrument was not a judicial instrument, since it was clear that the aforesaid bishop and abbot were not ordinary judges in this [Col. 0856C] case, and it was not established that they were delegated judges or had been chosen by the parties. Certainly their testimony could in no way be believed to the prejudice of the Church of Gurk. Nor ought confirmation by the Roman pontiffs to be prejudicial, since they appeared to have confirmed such a judgment not after an examination, but conditionally; for an accessory cannot avail where the principal is lacking.

Further, a forged bull of Alexander III had been inserted in the privilege said to have been drawn up by Alexander II, as was apparent upon careful inspection, not only by comparison of the bulls but also from certain other manifest indications. And although it was said in favor of the judgment that, after twenty years, no action for forgery could be brought against it because under the lawful sanctions an accusation of forgery does not extend [Col. 0857B] beyond the twentieth year, it was nevertheless argued in reply that matters which are temporal as grounds of action are always perpetual as grounds of exception. Therefore, although an accusation of forgery had expired after the twentieth year, the exception of fraud still had place—especially since action could be brought under the constitution which we issued against the wickedness of forgers.

The privilege of Emperor Henry could create no obstacle for the Church of Gurk, because, under the canonical sanctions, no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical things is granted to laymen, however religious or great they may be. And since, according to lawful statutes, a judgment which contains neither condemnation nor absolution is void by law itself, it was alleged that such a judgment was void, since it contains neither absolution nor condemnation, as is clearly gathered from the tenor of the instrument. Even if it had been rendered, it would have been rendered contrary to the order of law, for since the archbishop of Salzburg was defendant in that proceeding, the plaintiff having failed to prove his case, he could indeed have been acquitted, but a right ought not to have been adjudged to him. Hence what has been done contrary to the laws deserves to be dissolved through the laws, especially when more was adjudged to the aforesaid archbishop than had been proved. For even if it had been proved that election of the bishop in question belonged to that archbishop—which was not proved—it was not proved that it belonged to him alone; therefore the entire right of election ought not to have been adjudged to him alone.

It was further alleged [Col. 0857D] that, even if the right of electing the bishop of Gurk belonged to the archbishop of Salzburg, he nevertheless ought not, according to the canonical sanctions, to elect an outsider so long as he found a suitable person in that Church; and that the canons of that same Church would have the right to resist if they saw anyone imposed upon them from elsewhere. It was also alleged on behalf of the Church of Gurk that, even if such a judgment had been rendered against it, it ought not now to harm it, since it had often thereafter exercised the freedom to elect, and since at Villach a settlement had intervened on this subject between the Churches of Salzburg and Gurk by their common and free will.

On behalf of the Church of Salzburg it was argued in reply that the aforesaid Geboard, [Col. 0858A] archbishop of Salzburg, with the consent and acquiescence of both the Apostolic See and the imperial majesty, created the bishopric of Gurk in a certain part of his diocese, establishing that the bishop of Gurk should be the perpetual vicar of the archbishop of Salzburg in both spiritual and temporal matters. Therefore, since the election of a vicar, just as of a *vicedominus* [deputy lord], belongs by law only to him whose vicar or *vicedominus* he becomes, the bishop of Gurk must certainly be elected by the archbishop of Salzburg by reason of patronage and vicariate.

There was no need to judge concerning Alexander II’s privilege, both because it had not been exhibited to us in judicial form and because it had been approved by Pope Lucius, who acknowledges that he examined and approved it. Hence, if by chance a forged bull had been appended to that privilege, it ought to be presumed that this forgery had been committed after the time of the aforesaid Lucius. Nor should it avail that the archbishops of Salzburg are said to have confirmed by their privileges the freedom of the Church of Gurk to elect its own bishop, both because the Church of Gurk did not use those privileges and because a judgment ought not in any respect be altered on the pretext of privileges discovered afterward.

Although the procurator of the Church of Gurk endeavored in many ways to refute the aforesaid arguments, because we believe it advantageous to both parties that this controversy should be settled by agreement, we have judged that a postponement should be granted in order to find an agreement, especially since the procurator of the archbishop of Salzburg [Col. 0858C] sought a postponement in order to prove the aforesaid judgment. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood to induce the parties to concord and suggest to them that they themselves find and accept a suitable form of settlement; or else that by the coming feast of St. Martin they appear before us, with full authority to bring and answer actions, make settlements and compromises, and receive judgment, so that the case itself may, with the Lord’s help, obtain a fitting end through us.

But lest anything necessary for the instruction of the case be lacking, we command you by apostolic letters prudently to receive and examine the witnesses whom either party considers should be produced concerning the commission, settlement, and exercise of the right of election, [Col. 0858D] and to take care to send us their depositions enclosed under your seals. The witnesses who have been named . . . notwithstanding any letters that may appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties. And if not all, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, 11 April, in the ninth year.

XLVII. TO . . . THE BISHOP OF TORTOSA. That he restore the churches of Alquézar to the bishop of Huesca. (At St. Peter’s, 13 April.)

We recall having sent you our letters in this form: that Pope Alexander, our predecessor of pious memory, formerly gave your predecessor instructions by his letters, as is plainly contained in them, that he should not delay to restore to the bishop of Huesca . . . the churches of Alquézar, adjudged to him by Pope Eugene, our predecessor of blessed memory, which your same predecessor was holding contrary to justice by royal authority; and, all occasion and appeal ceasing, should restore and leave them in peace within two months after receiving those letters. But he, being a deaf hearer of the apostolic mandate, did not take care to do this, as was made clear to us by the complaint of our venerable brother García, bishop of Huesca, then present before us.

We therefore, observing that we are debtors to all persons in respect of their justice and wishing [Col. 0859B] to preserve to each his own rights, commanded you, under precept, to take care to restore the said churches with their appurtenances to the aforesaid bishop within two months after receiving our letters, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed; or to appear before us by the then approaching feast of the Purification of the Blessed Mary, there to show him concerning these matters what the order of reason required. We strictly forbade you, since you then had possession of them, to surrender possession fraudulently, so that you might in no way be compelled to render him justice concerning them; otherwise, since fraud ought to protect no one, you were to know that you would be struck by the lawful penalty.

But you, as we have learned from the renewed complaint [Col. 0859C] of the same bishop, neither obeyed our command by restoring those churches to him, nor, although two years and more have elapsed since the term set for you, took care to appear before us in person or through a suitable representative, asserting that you hold the said churches by royal authority and will surrender them to that authority when necessary.
