Since, therefore, we neither can nor ought to deny justice to those who complain, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to postpone restoring the said churches with their appurtenances to that bishop within two months after receiving the present letters, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed; or else, before our venerable brothers . . ., archbishop of Tarragona, [Col. 0859D] and . . ., bishop of Tarazona, to whom we are sending our letters on this matter, to render him the full measure of justice. If, having been lawfully summoned by them, you do not take care to answer the aforesaid bishop before them concerning the aforesaid churches, we nevertheless command them to introduce the said bishop into possession of the aforesaid churches by our authority, removing from them every unlawful holder and every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, and not to fail to protect him once introduced into that possession; opponents, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, 13 April, in the ninth year.

[Col. 0860A] In almost the same form to . . ., archbishop of Tarragona, and . . ., bishop of Tarazona, concerning the same matter. Same date as above.

XLVIII. . . . THE ADDRESS IS MISSING. On the same matter. (Given 13 April.)

Although it befits your honor and salvation to honor the Church of God out of reverence for the Bridegroom, you ought nevertheless to assist one person in such a way that you do not injure another in his right; nor should you suppose that anything is lost to that person’s interests if things that have been alienated are restored. Indeed, you should know that it has come to our hearing, as our venerable brother the bishop of Huesca has reported, that when we instructed our venerable brother . . ., bishop of Tortosa, [Col. 0860B] to restore to the bishop himself the churches of Alquézar, adjudged to the Church of Huesca by Pope Eugene, our predecessor of blessed memory, or to appear before us in order to show him concerning these matters what the order of reason required, he, relying on your aid and favor, did not take care to do so.

Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish your serenity, enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins: do not support the aforesaid bishop of Tortosa to the prejudice of the Church of Huesca, and do not impede our venerable brothers . . ., archbishop of Tarragona, and . . ., bishop of Tarazona, to whom we have judged this affair should be entrusted, from carrying the apostolic mandate into effect. Rather, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, [Col. 0860C] give them your aid and favor in this matter, so that the aforesaid Church of Huesca may no longer be defrauded of its right and we may be able to commend royal devotion in the Lord.

Given 13 April, in the ninth year.

XLIX. [Note: [Col. 0859D] See Raynaldus under the year 1206, §34.] . . . THE ADDRESS IS MISSING. That he cause the sentence of interdict pronounced by the bishop of Huesca against the occupier of the church of Almudévar to be firmly observed. (At St. Peter’s, 13 April.)

It was laid before us on behalf of our venerable brother . . ., bishop of Huesca, that when our most dear son in Christ, L., the illustrious king of Aragon, sought to give the church of Almudévar, belonging to the table [endowment] of the canons of Huesca, to his brother, and the same bishop had taken care to oppose the royal will, the king’s brother came by force to the aforesaid church. But because the bishop had forestalled him and entered the said church, he, acting on the king’s behalf, forbade anyone to dare sell provisions to the bishop, so that the bishop would abandon that church, compelled by hunger and thirst. Moreover, after forcibly breaking the doors both of the church itself and of its houses, he dishonorably expelled those who were with the bishop.

The bishop, however, observing [Col. 0861A] that he could resist no longer, placed that church under interdict. But he, in order to add iniquity to iniquity, nevertheless caused divine offices to be celebrated in it. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to cause the sentence of that interdict, as it was reasonably pronounced, to be firmly observed, appeal being set aside, until suitable satisfaction has been made; and, unless the holders of that church take care to repent and cease from the celebration of divine offices, to strike them, as shall be just, with canonical punishment, appeal being removed.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, 13 April, in the ninth year.

L. [Note: This letter is found, but mutilated, among the Decretals, book II, title 1, *On Judgments*, chapter 16.] TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE KNIGHTHOOD OF THE TEMPLE ESTABLISHED IN ITALY. That the preceptors of the Knights Templar may litigate and defend matters concerning their houses; nor are they barred either by their religious profession or because their origin is unknown. (At St Peter’s, 10 April.)

[Col. 0861B]

[Since you have been appointed] to the service of Jesus Christ, who, being righteous, loves justice, and whose countenance beholds equity, we are bound by paternal solicitude to safeguard your interests, lest, because you devote yourselves to works of piety, you suffer injury in the pursuit of your rights. [We have plainly received [Note: In the Decretals this is absent.] word that certain judges in Italy, both secular and ecclesiastical [Note: These words are absent in the Decretals.], do not admit the preceptors whom you have in your houses to act in lawsuits for the prosecution of their rights, [Col. 0861C] as though it were not lawful for those who have resolved to adhere to peaceful pursuits to concern themselves with disputed business. In rejecting them, they allege that the lineage of those men is unknown to them: although, wherever they may have come from, called by divine grace, while they laudably perform the office of their order, knowledge of their nationality is demanded of them beyond all due measure. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, granting your petitions, we prohibit by the authority of these presents anyone [Note: The Decretals have only “therefore let no one,” and below omit the word *sub*, “under.”] from excluding the said preceptors, under such a pretext, from acting and answering in the prosecution of lawsuits.] Let no one therefore, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 10 April, in the ninth year.

LI. … The address is lacking. That he absolve the bishop of Toul from excommunication [Note: See letter 87 of book eight.]. (At St Peter’s, 18 April.)

[Col. 0861D]

When the beloved son Simon, archdeacon of Toul, [Col. 0862A] brother and procurator of … bishop of Toul, had come to the Apostolic See, he laid before us a serious matter: namely, that, when the same bishop had appointed the beloved son Master W., our subdeacon, as procurator in the controversy that had arisen between himself and the beloved son, the dean of Toul, who had attacked the bishop by way of denunciation concerning dissipation of property—and on account of this our venerable brother … archbishop of Reims, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, then bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, had pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him after an appeal to us had been lodged—he had intended to send that procurator to the Apostolic See. But because certain intervening affairs [Col. 0862B] had somewhat delayed his journey, the said bishop sent ahead the priests W. and T. with letters of procuration. Because he afterwards doubted their fidelity, however, he sought to revoke their mandate by his letters.

They, however, though they had received letters revoking their mandate, nevertheless proceeded in the matter. It may reasonably be presumed against them that they colluded with the adversaries, since they obtained an adverse judgment and the opposing party procured from us a delegation of the case, in a specified form, to the beloved sons J., archdeacon; P., penitentiary of St Victor of Paris; and Master R. of Corzon, canon of Noyon. When the same bishop, summoned by [Col. 0862C] them, had endeavoured to appear before them and refused to ratify what had been procured by false procurators, he asked them for a delay, in order to decide whether he should yield or persist in the case. But because the said judges wholly denied him this, he appealed to the Apostolic See and withdrew from their presence as an appellant.

The aforesaid judges, however, disregarding the appeal, nevertheless proceeded. They removed the same bishop from the Church of Toul by judgment; gave the chapter of Toul free authority to elect a bishop for itself; and pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after receiving sufficient security from the same bishop, you absolve him from the bond of excommunication according to the [Col. 0862D] form of the Church, setting aside the obstacle of appeal. You shall appoint for both him and the opposing party the octave of St Michael next coming as a peremptory term, so that they may present themselves before us in person or through suitable representatives; and, after the truth has been ascertained, with the Lord as author, we shall determine what we think should be determined concerning the question of the false procurator and any other matters that may perhaps [Col. 0863A] appear to require inquiry. But if not all, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 18 April, in the ninth year.

[Note: XXIII. Frederick II of Brixey, dean of Toul, nephew of the preceding Frederick I and of Bishop Peter, received administration of the diocese from his uncle, who was soon to set out on the journey to Jerusalem. He is mentioned in letters of Bishop Matthew in the year 1200.

“XXV. Theodoric, together with Theodoric, abbot of St Leo, was an arbiter in 1216 of the settlement made between Stephen, abbot of St-Maurueti, and Robert, abbot of Mairéval.” *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XIII, col. 1062.]

LII. … TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM [Note: See letter 222 of book seven.], LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, AND TO THE CANONS OF THE LORD’S SEPULCHRE. A date is fixed for their appearance before the Apostolic See concerning the archbishoprics of Tyre and Patras. (At St Peter’s, 20 April.)

When a controversy had formerly long been contested between the Churches of Antioch and Jerusalem concerning the archbishoprics of Tyre and Patras, and when we had fixed a peremptory term for your predecessor of good memory, brother [Col. 0863B] patriarch [Note: See letter 101 of book eight.], and for you, sons, canons [Note: See letter 505 of book one, in Baluze, vol. I, p. 290.], within which you were to present yourselves before us through sufficient and suitable representatives, an agreement was made between our venerable brother … patriarch of Antioch [Note: See the historical note following this letter.] and your predecessor, and you, sons, canons: the right of each Church being preserved, peace was to endure during their lifetimes; but when one of them had entered the way of all flesh, the survivor might freely bring his own action.

Since therefore, brother patriarch, your said predecessor has been removed from the midst, and the aforesaid patriarch wishes to seek judgment from us in these matters, although we love the Church of Jerusalem and wish to show you [Col. 0863C] favour in your present necessity, nevertheless we cannot and ought not fail the Church of Antioch in its right. We therefore command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, from the feast of blessed Luke next coming until three years thereafter—which term we assign to you as peremptory—you shall, sufficiently instructed, present yourselves before us through suitable representatives, to answer the Church of Antioch concerning the aforesaid archbishoprics. Otherwise, from that point we shall proceed in the matter as, with the Lord’s aid, we judge appropriate.

[Col. 0864A] Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 20 April, in the ninth year.

[Note: After Aimery, patriarch of Antioch, whom Onuphrius, Genebrardus, and others write to have died in 1187, the same writers, as well as Assemani in his *Arabic Catalogue*, maintain that Ralph II held the patriarchal see; the Bollandists agree, *Historical Chronology of the Patriarchs of Antioch*, July, vol. IV, p. 239, col. 1, no. 659A. Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1157, maintains that he did not remain in office beyond the year 1200. Peter, patriarch of Antioch, was in office in 1201, when, according to Sanuto (book III, part II, chapter 1), Raymond, count of Tripoli, entered the principality of Antioch: for he then bound himself to this patriarch by oath.

But in 1208, according to the same Sanuto (*ibid.*, chapter 3), the city of Antioch rebelled against the prince at the patriarch’s instigation, and Armenian soldiers expelled by the prince returned. The count, however, taking up arms and descending from the castle, overcame the commune and its auxiliaries, and did not hesitate to imprison the patriarch, [Col. 0864C] and there to kill him by harsh treatment. The cause of Raymond’s hatred of Patriarch Peter is found in the first letters of Innocent’s eighth book. Innocent took Peter’s imprisonment badly. See [Col. 0864D] letter 214 of book ten, in Baluze, vol. II, p. 130.

While Peter was alive, a Greek intruder was introduced, whom the pope caused to be deposed; this is gathered from letters 9 of book eleven and 11 of book sixteen (in Baluze, vol. II, pp. 142, col. 2, and 735, col. 2). Peter died in prison before 12 July 1208, as is clear from letter 11 of book eleven (*ibid.*, p. 190). The pope himself indicates that this patriarch was named Peter in letter 181 of book fifteen (*ibid.*, p. 685).]

LIII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH [Note: See the immediately preceding letter, no. 52, note 217.]. The offence incurred by not visiting the thresholds of the Apostles is remitted. (At St Peter’s, 22 April.)

It was formerly set forth before us on your behalf that, although you were bound every four years to visit in person, or through your own messenger, the thresholds of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, you omitted to do so when the time of visitation came, being occupied with many affairs—not from malice or contempt, but rather from forgetfulness brought about by the multitude of your occupations. [Col. 0864B] Therefore, when you asked pardon from us for this, we took care to notify you that we had, through the kindness of the Apostolic See, remitted the offence which you believed you had incurred thereby, since it had not occurred through contempt.

But your beloved sons B. and A., your messengers, appearing in our presence, stated that our pleasure on this matter had not reached you. They therefore earnestly requested that we should make you more fully certain of it. Accordingly, know by this notification that we have remitted, through the clemency of the Apostolic See, the offence which you feared you had incurred through such negligence. For the future, however, be so careful in this respect that you cannot appear contemptuous or negligent.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 22 [Col. 0864C] April, in the ninth year.

LIV. [Note: This letter is found, but not complete, among the Decretals, book III, title 43, *On a Priest Not Baptized*, chapter 3.] TO THE BISHOP OF FERRARA [Note: See letter 39 of book three, note.]. That J., promoted as far as the priesthood while unbaptized, after being baptized is to be promoted through the orders and to the priesthood. (At St Peter’s, 13 April.)

[The beloved son J., bearer of these letters, coming to the Apostolic See, showed us in a tearful statement [Note: In the Decretals: “set forth to us”; they then omit the words abbreviated “pers. o.” and do not have “with certainty”; they read *was* for *had been*.] that, having risen through the individual orders to the grade of priesthood, he finally learned with certainty [Col. 0865A] that he had not been baptized according to the form of the Gospel. We therefore had him duly baptized by our venerable brother N. [Note: Nicholas of the Romans, a Roman, chaplain to Pope Innocent III, was elected cardinal-bishop of Tusculum by that pope in 1205, in the fourth creation. He went to England as legate of the Apostolic See and worked to establish peace between the kingdom and the priesthood. In 1214 he lifted the sentence of interdict imposed six years earlier. Under Pope Honorius III he went again to England to promote the sacred war in the East. He also acted as legate in Prussia. He was closely associated with St Dominic. Honorius regularly called Nicholas an angel of peace and salvation, welcome to men and beloved by himself above others. He died under the same pope in 1219. Oldoin, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 22.] bishop of Tusculum [Note: The Decretals omit these words, and immediately afterwards read “for a longer time” in place of “before us … for some time.”].

When the matter of his orders had been discussed before us for some time, certain persons inclined to the opinion that, since baptism is the foundation of the sacraments, no other sacrament can be received before baptism has been received, because where there is no foundation nothing can be built upon it. But [Note: The Decretals add “all,” and after “But” insert: “on the other hand it might seem”; for], since someone becomes beyond doubt a member of Christ not only through the sacrament of faith but also through faith in the sacrament, and he who has Christ through faith, even though he does not have baptism, surely has the foundation beyond which no other can be laid, namely Christ [Col. 0865B] Jesus, it seems that, just as saving works, so also any ecclesiastical sacraments can be built thereupon. For it is not universally true, either of the new sacraments or of the old, that baptism is their foundation, since both the sacrament of marriage and even the sacrament of the Eucharist may be received by persons who are not baptized. Moreover, the sacrament of orders—not only episcopal, but priestly and also levitical—by its institution preceded baptism. From this it appears [Note: Perhaps: “from which it seems.” Pithou, however, has in the margin: “on account of which it might seem.”] that such orders can validly be conferred before baptism, especially upon those believed to have been baptized.]

[Note: What follows, distinguished in italic type, is absent from the Decretals and from Pithou.]

For what if someone who is believed to be baptized, but is not, has at least in fact been consecrated bishop? Must all whom he ordained be reordained? And since in the case of many bishops it is not known whether they have been reborn through the water of baptism—for neither do they themselves remember it, nor do others—will there then be doubt whether such persons were truly consecrated bishops? It is better to remain silent than to say what, and how many, consequences follow—not merely incongruous but absurd.

But since it is read that a council at Compiègne established [Note: The Decretals read “decreed,” and then omit the words “brother … writing.”] that, if anyone ordained priest discovers that he has not been baptized, he is to be baptized and ordained again, we, following the safer course in this doubtful case concerning the bearer of these letters, command your brotherhood by apostolic writings to procure his promotion through each order to the priesthood [Col. 0866A] and permit him to minister in the priesthood. For that is not understood to be repeated which is doubtful as to whether it was done; nor is there erroneous belief concerning a sacrament when it is excluded, not by contempt for religion, but by an exigency of necessity.

Certainly, in the case of someone born of Christian parents and faithfully kept among Christians, it is presumed so strongly that he was baptized that this presumption must be treated as certainty, unless perhaps the contrary be proved by the clearest evidence [Note: The Decretals: “were proved.”].

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 13 April, in the ninth year.

LV. TO … THE ARCHDEACON, N. … PENITENTIARY OF ST VICTOR OF PARIS, AND MASTER R. OF CORZON, CANON OF NOYON. That they are to proceed under a specified form to the absolution of the bishop of Toul [Note: This letter should be compared with book IX, letter 51.]. (At Rome, 14 February [Note: Perhaps one should read May.].)

[Col. 0866B]

When the bishop of Toul had formerly been denounced before us for certain excesses, we sent our letters, under an express form, to our venerable brother … archbishop of Reims [Note: See letter 116 of book seven.], then bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See in those parts, and to the beloved son … abbot of St Benedict [Note: This probably concerns the abbot of the monastery of St Benedict at Vaupré, French *Saint-Benoît-en-Woëvre*; concerning the abbots of this monastery the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 944, provide very little:

VI. Gennus, 1182, 1196.

VII. Bruno, died 4 December.

“VIII. Stephen, 1246, 1251.”], in the diocese of Metz. The legate indeed settled the matter between the parties; but because the complaint was renewed before him, he suspended the bishop from administration of temporal matters, and afterwards subjected him to excommunication because he did not observe the sentence of suspension. [Col. 0866C]

Moreover, when certain persons had come before us to accuse him and others to defend him, we carefully heard what the parties wished to put forward and learned that the said legate had proceeded lawfully against him. We therefore commanded your discretion to cause the aforesaid sentence of suspension to be firmly observed by our authority, appointing a suitable procurator to administer the affairs of the bishopric of Toul in the meantime, while suitably providing the bishop with just and moderate expenses until this case should be heard.

And since neither party had renounced the production of witnesses, we remitted to you the depositions [Col. 0867A] received, under seal, enjoining you nevertheless to absolve the aforesaid bishop from the bond of excommunication according to the form of the Church, and to receive the witnesses whom either party should choose to produce. We also gave you an express form for your future procedure, notwithstanding no letters obtained from the Apostolic See except by consent of the parties.

Now, desiring to provide not so much for the person as for the Church, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that you absolve the same bishop from the bond of excommunication according to the tenor of the earlier commission. If you have not yet proceeded to publication of the witnesses, set him a suitable time within which he shall restore to the Church’s ownership those things [Col. 0867B] which he has alienated or disposed of from the goods of the Church, as he has firmly promised us through the beloved son Simon, archdeacon of Toul, his brother and procurator. You shall also cause him, before our venerable brother … bishop of Chalon [Note: See letter 16 of book five, note.] and the beloved son … abbot of Moutiers [Note: “Guy I of Plamben, perhaps the same Guy who served as prior under Abbot Artaud. He is thought to be G., abbot of Moutiers, found in a charter of Hugh, duke of Burgundy, for La Ferté in 1187. Indeed, Guy received in 1190 the gift of the same Hugh when he was setting out for Jerusalem. He occurs with Nicholas, abbot of Miroir, in a charter of donation made to the monastery of Moutiers. In 1199 he obtained from Innocent III a privilege of protection; about this same time he is named in a charter of Molesme. In 1201 he and his sister Mathelia gave to their kinsman Guy, surnamed Garos, everything they possessed in the village of Plamben. He was still in office in 1205 and 1210, in which year he made an agreement with Bertrand of Saudun.” *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, cols. 1031.], at Langres, together with two bishops and three abbots, to make canonical purgation that, after the sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against him, he had in no way celebrated divine offices in contempt of ecclesiastical discipline; but perhaps believed himself protected by the pretext of an appeal which he asserts that he made.

After his purgation has been received in the prescribed manner, restore him without delay to spiritual matters, all contradiction and appeal ceasing; and take care to notify us by your letters what you have decided to do in this matter. But if you have proceeded so far that the witness depositions have been published, reduce everything to writing and faithfully transmit to us the entire process of the case. But if not all, etc.

[Col. 0868A] Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 14 February [Note: Since this letter is found in the Register after letters dated in April, it seems preferable to read 16 May.], in the ninth year.

LVI. [Note: This letter is found, but mutilated, among the Decretals, book III, title 13, *On Alienating, or Not Alienating, the Property of Churches*, chapter 11, where it is said to be directed to the bishop of Maurienne and the provost of Ulx.] TO … THE BISHOP OF MAURIENNE [Note: See letter 176 of book six, note.], THE PROVOST OF ULX [Note: Alternatively *Ultiensis*; alternatively *Ultrensis*; in the Decretals, *Ulconensis*.], AND … THE DEAN OF HELTON, IN THE DIOCESES OF TURIN AND MAURIENNE. That they shall relinquish the fief of Javen to the monastery of Susa [Note: *Clusin.* Thus in the Conti transcript. In the Decretals: *Tusien*; elsewhere *Secusien* and *Cussien*. In earlier editions: *Cussin*. It should certainly be read, with Pithou, *Secussien*. For this concerns the monastery of Susa, of the Order of St Benedict, in the diocese of Turin.]. (At the Lateran, 29 March.)

Let it be known to you [Note: The Decretals read “let it be known to thee,” then *Tusien* for *Clusin*; omit “beloved sons,” and read “a certain” for “which Javen”; they have only the initial B. for Bonevard; and omit the words “village” and “same.”] that it has come to our hearing that, when the monastery of Susa was burdened by a very great load of debts, its beloved sons, the abbot and convent, compelled by necessity, granted in fief to the layman Bonevard the village which is commonly called Javen, [Col. 0868B] on the condition that the same layman should pay eighty pounds, for which the same village had been pledged. He did not delay to carry this into effect.

[Note: The words printed in italics are absent from the Decretals, but are read in Pithou’s additions.]

But because the aforesaid monastery has, as they say, been enormously injured in this matter [Note: These words are absent.], since [Note: “In that.”] from the revenues of the aforesaid village [Note: “Aforementioned.”] the convent was accustomed to receive daily one dish, and on feasts of twelve lessons fish or an equivalent, they humbly petitioned us [Note: In the Decretals: “therefore.”] to cause the aforesaid fief to be restored for the monastery’s benefit—especially since the same layman received from its fruits in the first year more than the aforesaid sum, and afterwards took its [Col. 0868C] fruits for many years.

We therefore, wishing so to provide for the burdens of the aforesaid monastery that we do not appear to inflict injury upon others [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals.], command your discretion [Note: These words are absent, but occur in Pithou’s additions.] by apostolic letters [Note: In the Decretals: “therefore.”] that, after fuller inquiry into the truth [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals; they next read “said” for “aforesaid,” and below omit the words printed in italics.], if you find that the aforesaid monastery has suffered enormous loss on this account, you compel the aforesaid layman—after he has received from the abbot and convent the money known to have been spent by him for discharging the aforesaid fief or for the advantage [Col. 0869A] of the monastery—to leave the aforesaid fief to that monastery free and undisturbed. The fruits received hitherto must suffice him for his labour. Having first given warning, compel him by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal. Notwithstanding any letters contrary to the truth, etc. But if not all … thou, brother, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 29 March, in the ninth year.

LVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP [Note: See letter 45 of book three, note.] AND ARCHDEACON OF SENS. That they admonish the bishop and canons of Langres to assign to T., canon of Langres, the prebend which G., formerly bishop of Langres, had assigned him at the pope’s command. (At St Peter’s, 19 April.)

[Col. 0869B]

The beloved son T., canon of Langres, appearing in our presence, stated that, at the command of C., pope of good memory, our predecessor, G., formerly bishop of Langres [Note: See letter 141 of book five, note.], assigned him a certain prebend in the Church of Langres, and that the same had been confirmed to him by our aforesaid predecessor. Because the chapter of Langres scorned to admit him to that prebend, the beloved sons … abbots of Clairvaux [Note: The abbot of Clairvaux concerned here was then Guy, who presided from at least 1196 to 1214. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 803.] and Longuay [Note: Arnald, abbot of Longuay, is mentioned in documents from 1195 until at least 1212. *Ibid.*, col. 838.], by authority of our aforesaid predecessor, placed the chapter under ecclesiastical interdict when it would not in any way cease from opposition.

Later, when he had come into our presence, he obtained our letters directed to the beloved sons … abbot of Melun [Note: We cannot determine with certainty who was the abbot of Melun—elsewhere, Molesme—to whom the pope had committed this case. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 721.

X. William, 1180 and 1181 in charters of St Michael of Tonnerre.

XI. Goldwin, 1204.

“XII. Hugh II, 1208 and 1211, in charters of Tonnerre, and still in 1220 in an instrument of Molesme.”] and … abbot of Quincy [Note: The same must be said regarding the abbots of Quincy. From documents the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* recognize John I from 1196 through 1201 (*ibid.*, col. 831). Next they mention Oliver [Col. 0870C] from 1202 until at least 1215.]. But since he could not obtain his right through them, we, as he asserts, commanded our venerable brother … archbishop of Reims [Note: See letter 116 of book seven.], cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, then bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, to cause the aforesaid sentence of interdict, since it had been reasonably pronounced, to be firmly observed without appeal.

But when the same archbishop prolonged the business, and T., after many labours, almost despaired of advancing [Col. 0870A] the matter, being short of expenses, at the request and by the authority of the aforesaid archbishop an agreement was made between T. on one side and our venerable brother R. [Note: Robert II, surnamed of Châtillon, and, as the chronicle of Langres states, probably brother of Lambert of Châtillon-sur-Seine, knight, and uncle of Hugh, lord of Til-Châtel, was first treasurer and dean, then, after the death of Hilduin—see letter 141 of book five, note—bishop of the Church of Langres. He is mentioned in several charters in 1204. In 1208, having gone against the Albigensians with Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine, and a great force of armed nobles, he died soon afterwards. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 595.] the bishop, and the beloved sons, canons of Langres, on the other. The agreement provided that, after he had been received by that chapter, through the hand of the aforesaid archbishop, as canon and brother and had been granted a stall in choir and every participation in divine offices, he should not receive the fruits of any prebend of the same Church except at the place of the seventh vacancy.

Although we love the said archbishop with sincere charity in the Lord and wish to respect his honour, we neither wish nor ought to defer to him in matters known to have been accepted contrary to canonical sanctions. We have therefore judged void what he unlawfully did in this respect, while approving what was lawfully done. Since the admission of T. as canon and brother does not conflict with canonical enactments, whereas waiting for a vacant prebend undoubtedly conflicts with the Lateran Council, we reject what is unlawful and approve what is lawful. Because it seems unworthy that one admitted as a canon should be deprived of a prebend’s benefit, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, if what is asserted is true, to compel the said bishop and canons of Langres, after warning, by ecclesiastical censure and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, not to delay assigning him a prebend when the opportunity arises. Cause daily portions distributed in the aforesaid church to be assigned to him without any diminution; opponents, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 19 April, in the ninth year.

LVIII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CUPAR [Note: Cupar, a notable Scottish monastery, was founded by King Máel Coluim, whom the ancients surnamed “the Maiden.” Thomas Dempster writes in his *Apparatus*: “Cupar in Angus, of the Cistercian Order, was founded by St Máel Coluim IV, King, surnamed the Maiden, and dedicated to the Mother of God by that king in 1160.” Thus Dempster, giving an earlier year, though he immediately relates its beginnings to 1174 on the authority of Roger of Wendover. Hector Boece says of the same abbey: “By him—that is, Máel Coluim—the abbey of Cupar was founded, sacred to the blessed Virgin and endowed with very ample revenues. Religious men of the Cistercian Order lived there, renowned for great piety.” Elsewhere, listing monasteries of Scotland, he says: “There are, moreover, two others famous for religion and learning, Arbroath and Cupar: the latter of the Cistercian Order, the former of the greater monastery of Tours.” Monks were sent from Melrose; hence Cupar is also recorded among the daughters of that house in the line of Clairvaux. It belongs to the diocese of St Andrews, where I find it assessed at one hundred florins. Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. II, p. 406, under the year 1164, chapter 10, §3.] OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER. Certain goods given to them are confirmed. (At St Peter’s, 12 April.)

It is customary to grant assent, etc., as far as “assent.” The land of [Col. 0871A] Camberadon, which J., bishop of Dunkeld of good memory, granted you in free alms, and the land of Abrec, which he granted you at perpetual farm, with the consent of his chapter; and which our venerable brother R., his successor, afterwards confirmed. From the gift of our dearest son in Christ W., illustrious king of Scots, the lands of Calethin and Parthesin. From the gift of the late David Rufus, the land of Kincref and two tofts in the burgh of Forfar. Further, one stone of wax, which Robert of Graham granted to your monastery from his house in the city of St Andrews, to be received yearly with the assent of his heirs; and another which Geoffrey, son of Martin of Perth, granted to your monastery from motives of piety. As these things are said to be contained in their authentic instruments, and as you possess them justly [Col. 0871B] and peaceably, we confirm them to you by apostolic authority and strengthen them by the protection of this present writing. Let no one therefore, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 12 April, in the ninth year.

LIX. TO … THE BISHOPS OF LÜBECK [Note: *Lyubicensi.* Thus in the transcript. But it appears that *Lubecensi*, “of Lübeck,” should be read, for the matter seems to concern the bishopric of Lübeck. The Church of Lübeck was then governed by Theodoric, whom Bucelinus records as having become bishop of Lübeck from provost of Segeberg after Conrad’s death in 1183. The same author notes that Theodoric died only in 1211, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 53.], RATZEBURG [Note: *Racebergensi.* It seems preferable to read [Col. 0872C] *Ratzenburgensi*, “of Ratzeburg.” Bucelinus, *ibid.*, p. 54, gives a bare series of the names of bishops of Ratzeburg without any chronological note.], AND SCHWERIN [Note: *Querinensi.* Should one not read *Sverinensi*? [Col. 0872D] For this appears to concern the bishop of Schwerin. The see of Mecklenburg was transferred to Schwerin about 1170. Benno, a Cistercian monk, then wore the episcopal mitre; Alexander III confirmed him in 1177. Benno was succeeded by Brunward, also Brunard, who governed for forty-four years, if Bucelinus is to be trusted (*Germania sacra*, part I, p. 53), and who, according to the same author, died in 1237.]. That they shall impose a precautionary penance upon the priest during whose unwitting sitting an ill child died. (At St Peter’s, 2 May.)

Coming to the Apostolic See, H., a priest and bearer of the present letter, showed us in a tearful confession that, when he had entered the house of a certain niece of his in order to count out money which he was bound to pay her, he sat down, at that niece’s command, upon a pile of clothing placed beside a privy-seat, beneath which a sick little child had been put to sleep and entrusted to his father’s care; and no one had warned him about the child. But scarcely had he sat there when the child’s mother immediately came in, saying that the child was beneath the clothes; whereupon the priest, astonished, at once sprang up from the place where he was sitting. The child, however—whether suffocated by the weight of the garments, by the violence of illness, or crushed by the said sitting, though without any sign of crushing—was found dead. Yet because it is characteristic of good minds to acknowledge faults even where there are none, the same priest did not presume to perform his office until he had sought mercy from the Apostolic See. Therefore, having heard his confession and considered his contrition, although from the foregoing we did not ascertain that he had grievously sinned, we judged it fitting to grant him that, after a penance concerning these matters has been imposed upon him as a precaution, he may, if this is so and no other impediment arises, worthily perform the priestly office; and that henceforth, in humility of heart, he may devote himself more fully to works of mercy.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the ninth year.

LX. [Note: This letter is printed entire in Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §24; it is therefore presented here in brackets.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG [Note: See Book V, letter 29, note], THE ABBOT OF THE DIOCESE OF SALZBURG, AND THE DEAN OF GURK. He commits to them the case concerning the marriage of the King of Bohemia, up to the pronouncement of a definitive sentence; he orders them, once it has been sufficiently investigated, to refer it for his examination. [Note: For several years there had persisted the controversy over the divorce which Primislaus, King of Bohemia, had effected in 1199, repudiating Adela or Abda, daughter of Otto the Rich, Margrave of Meissen, and marrying in her place Constance of Hungary, daughter of Béla III.] (At Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.)

[On behalf of the beloved son, the nobleman . . . Margrave of Meissen, and his sister, it has been made known to our ears that, although our dearest son . . . the illustrious King of Bohemia had lawfully taken that same . . . as his wife, and had treated her as his lawful wife for eighteen years and more, having had sons and daughters by her, he at last, at the prompting of the enemy of the human race, separated her from his bed; and our venerable brother, the Bishop of Prague [Note: See Book V, letter 29], having taken the counsel of certain prelates in a certain monastery, at the petition and command of the king himself, although she was willing to come before them to set forth her reasons in their presence, while the same king’s soldiers twice or three times prevented her from entering, and although she had appealed to the Apostolic See, nevertheless did not fear to pronounce sentence between them. Finally, the king himself brought in another woman . . . namely, the sister of our dearest son in Christ . . . the King of Hungary.

When a complaint on this matter came before us, we judged it fitting to commit the case to our venerable brother the Bishop of Halberstadt [Note: See Book VIII, letter 108, note] and his co-judges; they subsequently sent the same case, once investigated, to our presence. When we had again committed this same case to you, brother . . . Archbishop of Salzburg, to the Archbishop of Magdeburg of good memory [Note: See Book V, letter 8, note], and to the beloved son . . . provost of Rome, they summoned the aforesaid king on account of this matter. But because that king, as is asserted, caused their messengers to be treated dishonourably, they proceeded no further with the case.

Meanwhile, however, the aforesaid king, corrected by the Lord, as is said, and with great adversity rising against him, returned to him and is reported to have said: “I deservedly suffer these things, because I dismissed my lawful wife without cause, and thereby dishonoured my sons and daughters.” And, thus recognizing his guilt, he summoned the leading men of his land, as well as the free men and ministeriales of the brother of that same wife of his, and swore—and caused his own men to swear—that he would expel the woman he had brought in and recall his lawful wife. This he subsequently did not fulfil, although he confirmed it by letters sealed with his own seal.

Therefore, although by the office of apostolic service we are debtors to all in justice, nevertheless desiring so to admit the just petitions of the aforesaid margrave and his sister that we do not injure the justice of the aforesaid King of Bohemia and the sister of the King of Hungary, we admonish and command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning before you at a suitable day and place the parties and those whom you judge should be summoned in this matter, you shall proceed according to justice, notwithstanding any obstacle of appeal, as far as the pronouncement of a definitive sentence; and, once the case has been sufficiently investigated, you shall refer it for our examination, setting the parties a suitable term within which they are to appear before us through fit procurators, to receive sentence, by the Lord’s authority. The witnesses, etc. No letters, etc. But if all, etc. You, brother archbishop, etc.]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the ninth year.

LXI. [Note: The copy of this letter, which we had caused to be transcribed with the others from the copy of Conti, somehow—by what mischance we do not know—slipped from our hands; we can therefore present only its summary here.] TO THE COUNT OF NEVERS AND HIS WIFE. They are granted that those who knew them to be joined in the fourth degree of consanguinity and did not speak up at the making of the marriage, if they later wish to accuse them, are not to be heard.

LXII. [Note:

This letter is printed entire among the Decretals, Book III, title 31, “On Religious and Those Passing to Religious Life,” chapter 18, where it is said to be addressed to the prior and convent of Dimoli; or, as Pithoeus notes in the margin, Dimelinensis; alternatively de Molend., Dubeolin., or Dunolien.

It should further be noted that this letter is wholly identical, with only appropriate changes of wording, to Book XI, letter 178, addressed to the Archbishops of Tarragona, Braga, and Compostela, in Baluze, vol. II, p. 227.]

. . . . . . TO THE PRIOR [Note: See Book V, letters 129 and 135, notes] AND CONVENT OF DUNELM. A religious may, out of zeal for a holier life, pass to a stricter religious order, having first sought the permission of his prelate, even if he has not obtained it; this holds even if the first monastery enjoys such a privilege that no one may pass from it to another, even a stricter, monastery. [Note: On the argument of this letter Pithoeus observes: “This is what it says; it is a notable and frequently cited case.”] (At Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of May.)

[Although certain monks and canons, and likewise Hospitallers and Templars, have received from the Apostolic See the privilege that, after anyone has made profession among them, he may not pass to another place against their will, even under the pretext of a stricter religious life, so that each may remain, according to the Apostle, in the calling in which he is known to have been called (1 Cor. 7); nevertheless, because “where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3), and those who are led by the Spirit of God are not under the law, because the law has not been laid down for the righteous man [Note: Pithoeus, in the margin: “imposed”], this concession seems to have been granted to them so that no one, through rashness or fickleness, to the loss and injury of his order, might fly over to another order under the pretext of greater strictness—as is clearly known to have been presumptuously done by many—not in order that permission to transfer should be denied one who thinks it right to seek it with humility and purity, so that [Note: The Decretal reads: “so that”] he may migrate not falsely but truly to the fruit of a better life.

Such a person, therefore, after seeking from his prelate permission to transfer, is released from the private law [Note: See the Decretals, Causa XIX, question II, canon 11] which prejudices public law, and may freely fulfil his resolve for a holier life, notwithstanding the unreasoned opposition of his paternal prelate; for he deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power granted him. Even the Roman pontiff, who possesses supreme authority in the Church, grants without difficulty permission to resign to archbishops and bishops who request it for just cause.

Accordingly, let all to whom such a privilege has been granted know that they are bound by law to grant permission to transfer to those who request it in this manner. For just as a subject ought to ask his prelate for permission to transfer with humility and purity, lest he seem to despise the good of obedience, so indeed [Note: Omitted in the Decretal] a prelate ought to grant his subject permission to transfer without difficulty or perversity, lest he seem to hinder a purpose inspired by God.

But if there is probable doubt whether someone wishes to transfer to a stricter or a laxer order, out of charity or out of rashness, the judgment of a superior is to be sought, lest perhaps an angel of Satan transform himself into an angel of light. This rule must always be inviolably observed: no bishop [Note: Omitted in the Decretal], without the permission of the Roman pontiff, may presume on any occasion whatever to abandon his bishopric. For just as a greater good is preferred to a lesser, so common utility is preferred to private utility; and in this case teaching is rightly preferred to silence, pastoral care to contemplation, and labour to rest. To signify this, the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, was not born according to the flesh from Rachel but from Leah; nor do we read that Mary received him into her house, but Martha. Therefore, as long as a bishop can both preside and be of service, he ought neither to ask nor obtain permission to resign.

Since, then, the beloved son [Note: These words are absent from the Decretal], R., your monk, has transferred to the brothers of the Cistercian order, not in order in any way to disparage your order [Note: The Decretal reads “might be disparaged,” and shortly thereafter omits “devotion . . . command”], but to live a stricter life among them, we command your devotion by apostolic letters that you are in no way to trouble him for what he is known to have done with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith; for charity is a proper fountain, in which a stranger has no share.]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the ninth year.

LXIII. [Note:

This letter is printed, though very mutilated, among the Decretals, Book II, title 11, “On the Competent Forum,” chapter 12, and title 26, “On Prescription,” chapter 17. Passages found there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.

Raynaldus likewise cites it under the year 1206, §36.

Compare letters 20 and 21 of this ninth book.]

. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: See Book III, letter 9, note]. That he release the Judge of Cagliari from his oath. (At Rome, on the second day before the Nones of May.)

[If, after careful] [Note: What follows, distinguished in italic type, is absent from the Decretals but is printed in Pithoeus, additions to Book II, title 26.] reflection, you had weighed what that ark of the tabernacle signifies, in which, by the Lord’s command, the rod together with the tablets and manna was placed, you would by no means have judged that we wrote to you harshly or severely. For in the breast of the Roman pontiff, who, by God’s authorisation, is known to preside over all prelates of churches, there ought to be both the rod of correction and the manna of sweetness, so that by one he may cherish the humble and devout, and by the other [Note: Pithoeus: “and by the other”] strike the rebellious and punish offenders. Hence wine and oil are applied to the wounds of him whom the Samaritan brought to the inn: so that, unless the wounds of sinners are soothed by the oil of admonition and exhortation, the wine of ecclesiastical severity may follow.

Although, therefore, because you despised our admonitions and commands, by which we frequently endeavoured to induce your brotherhood to release our beloved son W., Margrave of Massa, Judge of Cagliari, from the oath of fealty which you caused him to render to you and to the Church of Pisa, so that, notwithstanding that oath, he might swear fealty to us and to the Roman Church, we could perhaps have proceeded against you not only with harshness of words but by the enforcement of ecclesiastical discipline, [since the Judicate of Cagliari belongs to the right and property of blessed Peter, as does all Sardinia without any intermediary, and since nothing has been reasonably alleged on your side why you could lawfully receive for yourself or your church an oath of fealty from the aforesaid margrave] [Note: In the Decretals: “you could not lawfully,” and shortly after it omits “the aforesaid”], nevertheless we are greatly surprised and disturbed in this matter. We regard you as a prudent and discerning man; according to the duty of your episcopal office, the enactments of the holy Fathers ought not to be unknown to you; and you are known to have an abundance of learned jurists. [Note: See Decretals, Book II, title 11, “On the Competent Forum,” chapter 12.]

[You asserted that, until these times, you had held and still held it to be certain [Note: These words are absent in the Decretal, as are shortly afterwards “anyone”] that it is lawful for any cleric, at least in temporal matters, to renounce his right and appoint a lay judge for himself, especially where the adversary’s consent has been added; and thus you tacitly suggested that you had been reproved less reasonably because, by such an agreement, you answered that the oath entered into must be observed. You had forgotten that constitution which provides that the public law is in no way to be impaired by the agreement of private persons. For this law was expressly promulgated in the Councils of Milevis and Carthage [Note: Pithoeus, marginal note: “The words attributed here to the Council of Milevis are found in the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 13. The remainder is in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 9.”]: clerics are not to drag clerics, having abandoned their own bishop, before public courts; otherwise they are to lose their case and be held alien from communion. Bishops, deacons, and any clerics, in a criminal or civil matter, if, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, they wish to seek judgment in public courts, are to lose their office even if a judgment has been rendered for them; this is so in a criminal action. In a civil action, if they prefer to retain their office, they are to lose what they have won.

It is therefore manifest that they cannot make an agreement, not merely unwillingly but even willingly, to submit to secular judgments; for this is not a personal benefit which may be renounced, but a grant publicly and generally bestowed upon the entire ecclesiastical body, which cannot be derogated from by the agreement of private persons. Nor could an oath lawfully be kept which is framed by unlawful agreements contrary to canonical enactments.]

[Note: What follows is absent from the Decretals but is printed in Pithoeus, additions to title 26, chapter 17.] [On the other [Note: In Pithoeus: “on that”] point you answered as follows: that, from the time when you were raised to the office of bishop, you had received, on behalf of the Apostolic See, oaths of fealty from the Judges of Sardinia [Note: Absent in Pithoeus], knowing that Archbishop Villanus . . .]

[Note:

The statements made here about Villanus, Archbishop of Pisa, deserve special notice and should be compared with what Ferdinand Ughelli reports concerning the same prelate in *Italia sacra*, vol. III, cols. 459 ff.

Villanus, also called Villanius, a citizen and Archbishop of Pisa, succeeded Baldwin in 1145.

In 1146 Pope Eugene III confirmed anew, with repeated generosity, to this archbishop all the grants which Pope Innocent II had formerly conferred upon Baldwin. The document was given at Viterbo on the Kalends of June, in the year of the Incarnation, eighth indiction, through the hand of Robert, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.

In 1153 the canons of the metropolitan Church of Pisa received from Pope Anastasius IV apostolic confirmation not only of the prerogatives granted by his predecessors, but also of the very extensive donation by which Pope Eugene III, induced by the prayers of Villanus, Archbishop of Pisa—who enjoyed great favour and influence with Eugene III—had enriched them. The diploma was given at the Lateran through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of September, first indiction, in the year 1153 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the first year of the pontificate of Pope Anastasius IV.

In 1154 Raynald, Prince of Antioch, and his wife Constance, daughter of the younger Bohemond, granted to the Republic of Pisa, to Archbishop Villanus, and to his chief church, certain buildings in Laodicea and Antioch, in recognition of the outstanding services the Pisans had rendered them. . . . The document of Raynald, taken from the same archive:

“This was done through the hand of Geoffrey, our chancellor, in the year 1154 from the Incarnation of the Lord, second indiction. Witnesses to this matter are Garento of Soana, Galerius of Surda-valle, Gualfridus the Constable, Lord Leonard, Leo Duke of Majopolis, Marsaram of Margath, Arnald of Cafardam, Robert of Sarda-valle, Ugo of Volterra, Ilentasdus of Lenni, and Peter of Juvenale.

“The charter was given in the palace at Antioch on the tenth day of May.”

In almost the same words Pope Adrian IV confirmed to Leo, archpriest, and the other canons of the Church of Saint Mary of Pisa all their rights and privileges: “Given at Benevento, through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, fourth indiction, in the year 1156 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate.” The original diploma is preserved in the archive of the Pisan chapter, where two other documents of the same pontiff, addressed to the same Leo and other canons, are read; in them Villanus, Archbishop of Pisa, is expressly named.

Pope Adrian IV granted him these same things in 1157, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, fifth indiction: “Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.”

In 1157 Villanus obtained from Almeric, Count of Ascalon, brother of Baldwin II, King of Jerusalem, both certain rights in the city of Joppa and a broad tract of land, on which Pisan citizens might build houses and a church, if the Patriarch Leo so wished. . . . In this document also, taken from the same archive, the archbishop alone is named.

“Let it be known to all, present and future, that I, Almeric . . . give, grant, and confirm to you, Lord Villanus, venerable Archbishop of Pisa, together with its consuls and all Pisans in common, half of this right which belongs to me. . . .

“This was done in the year 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation, fifth indiction. Given at Ascalon through the hand of Rudolf, chancellor, on the fourth day before the Nones of June.”

In 1161 Lambertus Grassus and his fellow Pisan consuls, out of piety and to adorn and enlarge the metropolitan church called Saint Mary, granted to that church, in order to increase its magnificence and majesty, all the churches and rights which their ancestors had received from emperors in recompense for remarkable military service, and which the Pisans possessed at Constantinople. They did so not only to honour the merits of Archbishop Baldwin of pious memory, but also to comply with the wishes of Archbishop Villanus, who had urgently sought it from them. We supply the record of this great donation, taken from the Pisan archive:

“It is right that pious petitions . . . and because we, the aforesaid consuls, wish all these things to be observed forever, following also the will and written act of Lord Baldwin of pious memory, Archbishop of the Church of Pisa, and of Lord Villanus, now venerable prelate of that same church . . .”

“These acts were performed in the old chapter-house of the Pisan canonical church of Saint Mary, in the year 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, ninth indiction.”

It is clear that Archbishop Villanus was an excellent shepherd and deserved well of the Roman Church. For when the schism between Alexander III and the antipope Victor was raging, Villanus adhered with undaunted spirit to the true pontiff Alexander. For this reason, having been declared a public enemy by Aenobarbus, he withdrew into voluntary exile on the island of Gorgona. The Pisan people and clergy, who supported Aenobarbus, at his wish and demand intruded Benincasa de Benincasis, canon of Saint Mary Major at Pisa, into Villanus’s vacant see in 1167; and the pseudo-pope Victor installed him on Easter Day. Concerning this, the author of our Chronicle says:

“The Emperor Frederick sent Raynald the chancellor and the Archbishop of Cologne to Pisa. In the public assembly of the Pisans he determined to raise an army, in the coming summer, for Sicily, Apulia, Calabria, and against the Romans; and so the oath was sworn in that assembly by a certain chaplain of the lord emperor and by the consuls of Pisa. Furthermore, the aforesaid consuls there swore to hold Pope Paschal as Catholic and obey him as Catholic, and promised to make the Pisan clergy swear likewise. They made the same promise concerning Archbishop Villanus, who would in no way consent to obey him. Afterwards, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the Pisans, wishing to obey the commands of the aforesaid emperor and Pope Paschal, chose Benincasa, canon of Saint Mary Major of Pisa, as archbishop. That pope ordained him priest on Holy Saturday and, on Easter Monday, solemnly consecrated him archbishop with his cardinals.”

But after the Pisan people and clergy had come to their senses following Aenobarbus’s departure, they recalled their proper and true shepherd and drove the intruded Benincasa from the see. When Pope Alexander, who was then at Benevento, learned this, he wrote the following letter to the Pisan canons, urging them to persevere in what they had undertaken and to support the cause of Villanus, whom they had recalled; and, because the intruder Benincasa had finally been expelled, he praised them highly. Playing upon the man’s name, the pope branded him with the mocking name *Malincasa* (“Bad-house”). The following letters, although no year is appended to them, seemed most worthy to be transmitted to posterity and were extracted from the more sacred archive of the chapter:

“The letters of your devotion . . . etc. We ask and admonish your whole community that, as you have begun well, you work by every means for the expulsion of Malincasa and the recall of your venerable brother, your archbishop. . . . Furthermore, having learned from your letters that the aforesaid archbishop [lacuna] a chaplain . . . Given at Benevento, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.”

From many other letters written by Alexander to the Pisan canons, it may be inferred that the Church of Pisa was torn and divided into various factions; nevertheless, more adhered to Archbishop Villanus, supporter of Pope Alexander’s cause. Strong evidence is supplied by letters sent to the Pisan canons in which he censures and curses the obstinacy and crime of the canon B. . . . and other priests. While the rest of the chapter remained steadfastly faithful in its office, they had gone over to the party of the schismatic Victor and with utmost audacity strove to defend and advance it. Alexander commands them in very severe letters to withdraw from his association.

Indeed, Archbishop Villanus and the greater part of the canons of the metropolitan church supported Alexander with great courage. The close association they had formerly formed with Alexander, when he was a canon of that church, had readily moved them to do so. From that rank, by the favour of Eugene III, he had risen to the dignity of cardinal and finally to the supreme pontificate; accordingly, he showed that church singular benevolence and, whenever an opportunity presented itself, bestowed his patronage upon it and its canons.

Yet other letters of Alexander to the same Pisan canons are found in the more sacred archive, illustrating the exceptional affection with which he embraced them. Thus he expressed the particular joy he felt when they admitted as a canon his chaplain and notary whom he had commended to them. In those same letters he referred to Archbishop Villanus for decision the dispute between them and the abbot of Saint Savinus concerning the burial of the body of Count Tancred:

“Having received the letters of your devotion with our customary kindness and cheerfulness of heart, that the beloved son G. . . . [lacuna] henceforth, the case which is pending between you and the abbot and monks of Saint Savinus concerning the body of Count Tancred—because those monks set forth the event itself very differently from you—we commit to our venerable brother, your archbishop, to be decided in a specified form. . . . Given at Veroli, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.”

Villanus obtained the same from Pope Alexander III in 1169, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, second indiction: “Given at Genoa, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church.”

In 1170 Bohemond, son of Prince Raymond of Antioch, with the consent of his wife Urgolosa, granted to the holy church of Saint Mary, to Archbishop Villanus, and to the Pisan people a field at Laodicea upon which the Pisans might build houses; and he likewise generously renewed in their favour at Antioch the donation which Raymond, his father, had made, as we saw above, to Archbishop Villanus and the Pisan people. The record reads:

“Let it be known to all people, present and future, that I, Bohemond, son of Prince Raymond, by the grace of God Prince of Antioch, with the assent and will of my lady Urgolosa, my wife and most beloved princess, give and grant, and by perpetual right confirm, to the church of Saint Mary and to the Archbishop of the city of Pisa . . .”

“This privilege was given through the hand of Bernard, chancellor, in the seventh year of my principate and in the year 1170 from the Incarnation of the Lord.”

Nor did Villanus seem little blessed, or to have attained only a low summit of honour, since he saw two supreme pontiffs emerge from his church, refined by such great virtues and raised to the loftiest height of human dignity. These were Eugene III, vice-lord before he entrusted himself in the Cistercian family to Saint Bernard to be formed by monastic discipline; and Alexander III, a canon of the metropolitan church. Chrysostom Henriquez in his Cistercian *Menologium*, and the author who published commentaries on the life of Gelasius, without sufficient grounds attributed to Alexander the pursuit of monastic discipline and his reception in Gaul, at Clairvaux, of the religious habit from Saint Bernard’s hands. If this were true, it would never have been passed over in silence by Alan, Bishop of Auxerre, an author of that age who recorded Saint Bernard’s deeds, when he listed all the bishops and cardinals formed by Bernard. Thus, just as he adorns Eugene III with distinguished praises and mentions Cardinals Hugh, Henry, and Bernard, raised to that dignity by Eugene himself, he certainly would not have passed in silence Roland, a man celebrated by every praise, who later became Alexander III. Yet it is true that Alexander lived in the closest friendship with Saint Bernard and with Eugene, whose colleague he had been in the canonry and by whom he had been distinguished with the cardinalitial dignity.

Cardinal Baronius throws most brilliant light upon these matters by producing the words of a very ancient manuscript from the Vatican Library. In recounting the grades of honour which Alexander had passed through, he establishes that Alexander was a Pisan canon when he was summoned to the sacred purple. On this occasion I shall not omit that the same writer of Gelasius’s life, without any basis, invented the claim that this Villanus, Archbishop of Pisa, was made a cardinal by Lucius II and adorned with the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. He does indeed produce certain Pisan records, but whether they exist is unknown to everyone; and even those most expert in Pisan affairs do not know from what family Villanus derived his origin. Some nevertheless assert that the name Villani belonged to a most ancient and noble family which, while the republic stood, held the foremost offices and bore as its hereditary shield two towers painted red on a white field, with a third tower above them, likewise gleaming and bronze-coloured. I do not assert whether he sprang from that family.

This much is certain: he never attained cardinalitial rank. We find that he held the archbishopric of Pisa from 1146 to 1174, and in countless documents transmitted to us he is never styled cardinal, as is customary in the case of others. That title of dignity would certainly never have been omitted if the sacred purple had shone together with his archbishopric. The Roman pontiffs who wrote to Villanus never called him cardinal in their bulls, as may be seen in the bull of Anastasius IV addressed to Leo the archpriest and the Pisan canons.

To lend still greater clarity to this truth, in the very period in which Villanus lived we find Gerard, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, created by Eugene III. He succeeded another Villanus, cardinal of the same title, who had already been chosen by Lucius II and survived only a short time after Eugene, being acclaimed pope after him. Nor does Blessed Gregory contradict this in his registers when he relates that several cardinals of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill existed at the same time; for the offices of cardinalitial dignity had not then been marked off and distinguished by their own boundaries and titles as they were in Eugene’s time. Indeed, after that period we do not find the same title conferred simultaneously upon two persons.

It is enough to have touched briefly upon these matters in order to investigate the truth. In ancient and exceedingly difficult questions, where no light is supplied by monuments or writings, to pronounce a rash judgment, assign dignities to men which never adorned them, or derive their lineage from a family other than that which gave them birth, merely for the reputation of nobility or of hidden and recondite learning, is madness: it is to play the prophet and expose oneself to everyone’s ridicule.

Villanus died, a by no means ordinary example of changing fortune, after governing the church entrusted to him most prudently, in 1174, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, as the ancient calendar of Saint Zeno of Pisa records. It was to this very Villanus that Alexander III issued the letter concerning the agreement of married persons, chapter 3.]

…your predecessor, a man of great authority and integrity, who [Col. 0879A] for a long time was a cardinal in the Roman curia and knew more fully its customs and statutes, and that all your predecessors, who were men [Col. 0880A] of great authority, had likewise maintained and done this according to ancient custom, since nothing had hitherto been objected to you or to them by the Apostolic See.

> [Note: Col. 0879D] Pithoeus: “he himself also”; and below, Latin *tui* (“your”) in place of *tuos* (“your”).

> [Note: Col. 0880D] Pithoeus: “you [have maintained] the ancient custom.”

[Col. 0881A] [Decretals, ibid.]

> [Note: Col. 0881D] In the Decretals: “therefore, which.”

But having more fully considered these matters and others which our beloved son Master Bondinus, your messenger, wished to set forth, we did not understand that you or the Church of Pisa had any legal ground upon which you could reasonably excuse yourselves from carrying out our command. For you do not show an authorization from the Apostolic See by which you and your predecessors might require oaths of fealty from the aforesaid judges; nor are you protected by any prescription, since, according to your own admission, neither the Church of Pisa nor you were in quasi-possession of the right to exact such an oath. You acknowledge that this oath was received from those judges on behalf of the Apostolic See. It is therefore clear that the Roman Church has always been in quasi-possession, since the oath was exacted and rendered on its behalf through the agency of you and your predecessors; [Col. 0881B] and one is said also to possess in whose name possession is held.

> [Note: Col. 0881D] In the Decretals: “your” Church on this matter.

> [Note: Col. 0881D] These words are absent from the Decretals; moreover, they read “the Cagliaritans” for “the aforesaid [judges]”; below, they have “nor” for “not,” Latin *fueris* (“you were,” singular) for *fueritis* (“you were,” plural), and “by the Apostolic See” in place of “for the Apostolic See.”

> [Note: Col. 0881D] The Decretals omit “also,” as below “in whose name”; they read “was” for “is,” “because” for “nor,” and do not add “in” before “place.”

But if it is said that the oath was exacted in the name of you and your predecessors, and not in our name, it might be inferred that the oath sworn to preserve the right and honor of the Apostolic See was violated. Therefore that which was knowingly obtained contrary to such an oath could not lawfully be retained; nor, on that basis, could prescription have force, since good faith and a just title are required for prescription in ecclesiastical property. And even if prescription could have force, we do not believe that you cannot prove a centennial prescription—the only kind that runs against the Roman Church.

> [Note: Col. 0881D] The Decretals read “even if” and omit the word “you.”

> [Note: Col. 0882D] The remainder is absent from the Decretals and likewise from Pithoeus’s additions.

Yet because we propose, insofar as we can in the Lord, to show you deference, [Col. 0881C] and willingly intend to do what ought to redound to the advantage and honor of you and of the Church entrusted to you—hoping that, from what you stated in your letters, namely that you wished to defend the honors of the Apostolic See even to the shedding of blood, and that you intended to usurp nothing belonging to another’s right—we may believe this: you ought not on this occasion to pass over our command with deaf ears. Although we could compel you to do so by withdrawing the legation of Sardinia, on account of which we recognize that an injury has been done to us, [Col. 0882A] nevertheless by these apostolic letters we command and strictly order your brotherhood that, putting aside every proposed excuse, you absolve the aforesaid judge from the bond of fealty, so that, notwithstanding it, he may render us an oath of fealty.

Otherwise, unless you make a virtue of necessity—for it is the sin of idolatry to refuse obedience, and the crime of divination to refuse acquiescence—we shall compel you to do what we have commanded by exempting Sardinia from the office of your legation; and perhaps, though unwillingly, we shall see fit to lay our hands more heavily upon you. For he deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the authority granted to him.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second Nones of May, in the ninth year.

LXIV. … TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF STENDAL. Certain properties are confirmed. (Rome, second Nones of May.)

[Col. 0882B]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious requests, etc., as far as “assenting”: the churches of Stendal, Schinne, Elvebuie, and Rencherslache; the village of Garlippe with its appurtenances; two talents from plots of land and three talents in the merchants’ house of the same castle; five acres of land outside the ditch and as many beside Rencherslache; certain plots granted to you by the pious generosity of the faithful; the mill of Rokence; the villages of Rokence, Slantiz, and Bereche, with their appurtenances; four manses in Schadewachte; two in Nicwinkele, two in Bellinke, two in Elvebuie, [Col. 0882C] two in Ciple, and a half in Gerbrecktcflache; and three quarters in Reincherslache. As you possess these justly and peacefully, we confirm them by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your church, by the present writing, etc. Let no one therefore …; but if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second Nones of May, in the ninth year.

LXV. … TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI. That he is to receive, on behalf of the Roman Church, the offering made by the sister of the count of Montferrat from the castle of Montebello to the monastery of La Rocca, where she has established an annual payment of forty pounds. (Rome, seventh Ides of May.)

> [Note: Col. 0882D] Lothair Rosarius, a native of Cremona, was substituted by Pope Innocent III in 1205 for Albert, who had been elevated to the patriarchate of Jerusalem. He was afterwards transferred to the Church of Pisa; finally, in 1215, he succeeded his predecessor Albert in the Church of Jerusalem and attended the Lateran Council. He died in 1227.

[Col. 0883A]

A representation laid before us by our beloved daughter in Christ, the noble lady A… countess of Montferrat, made known that, when her brother, our beloved son B., the noble marquis of Montferrat, was preparing to depart for overseas lands, he conveyed to her the castle of Montebello for four thousand Pavia pounds which he was bound to repay her, as is said to appear from a public instrument.

Since the said woman has resolved to lead a religious life in the monastery of Saint Mary of La Rocca, she wishes to offer the aforesaid castle to that monastery, on this added condition: that the monastery shall receive its revenues, that the men of the said place shall render fealties to the Roman [Col. 0883B] pontiff, and that fifty Pavia pounds shall be offered yearly to us and our successors as a census-payment. But if her nephew, our beloved son W., the noble marquis, should wish to repay her the aforesaid sum of money, he shall have the castle itself; and the monastery, to which the aforesaid money will revert, shall offer us a suitable yearly census-payment.

Therefore, although the purpose of the said woman appears pious, we ought nevertheless to refrain from the scandal that could easily arise from it. Accordingly, we have thought fit to entrust this business to your brotherhood, in whom we have full confidence, commanding you by apostolic letters that, after the truth concerning these matters has been fully investigated, if these arrangements can be carried out without [Col. 0883C] grave scandal to the marquis, you receive the offering in our stead and determine such matters relating to it as you judge should be determined. Otherwise, take care to communicate to us in your letters the whole course of the affair, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed, with the Lord as author, as ought to be done.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh Ides of May, in the ninth year.

LXVI. … TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX, P. OF CASTELNAU, AND BROTHER R., LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. They are commanded not to molest the archbishop of Narbonne for the crimes of which he had been convicted, since he has already been granted time to perform penance. (Rome, seventh Ides of May.)

> [Note: Col. 0883D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §27.

> [Note: Col. 0883D] See letter 16 of Book Five, note.

> [Note: Col. 0883D] These persons have already been discussed often.

> [Note: Col. 0884D] Compare letters 81 and 243 of Book Six; 75, 76, 77, and 78 of Book Seven; and 106 of Book Eight.

[Col. 0883D]

Following the example of Him who makes His angels spirits and His ministers a burning fire, we sent our angels into the province of Narbonne, to burn up the thorns and briars which the accursed earth brings forth. Through our legates dispatched to that province, therefore, we went down to see whether our venerable brother …, archbishop of Narbonne, had fulfilled in deed the outcry that came to us. Through sworn men conducting a full inquiry, they faithfully sent us the depositions enclosed under their seals. By these, the same archbishop was marked as blameworthy especially in two respects: namely, avarice and negligence, [Col. 0884A] which two are numbered among the twelve abuses—when, that is, the bishop is negligent and the rich man avaricious—although each root is said to spread into many branches.

The same archbishop, appearing before us, offered many excuses regarding the accusations, yet asked mercy and promised amendment, so that he might atone for past deeds through future ones, recalling what the Apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” [1 John 1]; for “we all offend in many things.” We, therefore, considering that he has been greatly afflicted by the hardship and severity of a long journey, especially because of old age and bodily weakness, [Col. 0884B] and that through us he has been deprived of the abbey of Montearagón, which is said to have been worth more to him than the archbishopric of Narbonne, resolved to pour oil upon wine, so that he might find in us justice together with mercy—since the ark of the Tabernacle contained both manna and a rod—yet in such a way that the manna of sweetness might not make lax the man whom the rod of correction ought to render disciplined.
