Returning, therefore, to the Gospel parable of the fig tree planted in a vineyard: when the lord commanded the keeper of the vineyard to cut it down lest it occupy the ground uselessly, because, coming after three years, he had found no fruit on it, and the keeper answered the lord that he should leave it for a year, [Col. 0884C] until he dug around it and applied manure, and if it then bore fruit, well and good, but otherwise should cut it down thereafter—we have thought fit to grant the same archbishop a further period of time. We have dug around him by threatening and rebuking, and applied manure by warning and exhorting, so that we may test whether he bears the fruit he promised; and, if perhaps he bears no fruit, we may more justly lay the axe to the root of the unfruitful tree.

We therefore strictly command him that, pursuing not the gain of money but that of souls, he shall not engage in unlawful exactions or unjust dealings; rather, he shall devote himself diligently to hospitality and be generous and kind to pilgrims and the needy. Let him strive to visit the province, hold a council, [Col. 0884D] combat heresies, correct offences, and perform the other duties required by the pastoral office. For its useful execution we send him back with our grace and favor.

Wherefore, commanding you by apostolic letters, we direct your discretion to furnish him counsel and assistance in healthfully performing these things, so that, aided by your support, he may more effectively carry out the laudable resolve of his mind which he disclosed to us with many tears. Do not in any way molest the same archbishop without our knowledge. But if perhaps—though we do not believe it—he should presume to act contrary to his promise and [Col. 0885A] our command, faithfully report it to us, so that the judgment of equity may proceed from our countenance.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh Ides of May, in the ninth year.

LXVII. … TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT RUFUS AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO HAVE PROFESSED THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. They are received under the protection of Saint Peter. (Rome, second Nones of May.)

> [Note: Col. 0885D] This was Falco, whom the Sammarthani mention from documents in the year 1204, *Gallia Christiana vetus*, vol. IV, p. 803. They also say that Innocent wrote to him in the thirteenth year, letter 158.

Apostolic protection ought to be at hand for those choosing the regular life, lest an attack of anyone’s rashness turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 0885B] we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of Alexander, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and our own the church of Blessed Rufus, situated on the island called Esparveria, where you are dedicated to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that the canonical order, known to have been instituted in your church according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now possesses justly and canonically, or may in the future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, [Col. 0885C] the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these, we have thought fit to specify by their own names: the place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with the liberty and immunity of your churches, cemeteries, estates, lands, tithes, and other appurtenances of that church; the church of Saint Mary within the city of Lyon, with its cemetery, parish, tithes of vineyards, and its chapels—Saint Marcellus above the wall of that city, Saint Andrew of Courtiac, and Saint Marcellus; the church of Condrieu itself, with a sixteenth part of the port of the Rhône at Lyon; the church of Busca, with cemetery, parish, [Col. 0885D] its chapels, and tithes of Giren and Monloel; the church of Ordonnaz, with its seven churches, namely the church of Columneu, the church of Chimillin, the church of Corbillin with the chapel of Fouergiis, the church of Romaniaco, the church of Saint Symphorian, the church of Saint Martin of Vienne with its dependent churches, and the church of Saint Nicetius of the Mount of Cilizino and of Vernicello, with their appurtenances; the church of the hermits of Comba, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary on the island below Vienne, with the church of Vilosco and that of Losa and all their other appurtenances; the church of Saint Andrew of Costa, with the church of Flacceriis and [Col. 0886A] its appurtenances; the churches of Peludru, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Petrau, with its chapels and appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Ammoniaco, with the churches of Saint John, Saint Rusticus, Saint Michael, and Saint Dionysius, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint James in the city of Valence; the church of Saint Peter of Die, with the churches of Saint Peter of Valdrôme and Calanco; the church of Saint Mary of Chaellis, with its appurtenances; the church of Tauliniaco, with its chapel and appurtenances; the church of Argentio, with its appurtenances; the church of Voluento, with its appurtenances; the church of Medullione, with its subject churches of Podio, Verz, Rocha, and Villefranche, with their appurtenances; the church [Col. 0886B] of Sairrariis, with the chapels of Isone, Gaudeisart, and the Holy Sepulchre, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Andeolus, where his body also lies, with its churches and appurtenances—namely, the church of Saint Michael, the church of Saint Polycarp, the church of Chalo, and the church of Saint Julian, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Flactiano; and the church of Saint Nazarius, with vineyard, tithe-right, and appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Vallis-Longa; the church of Saint Mary of Albaniaco, with its appurtenances; the churches of Buorzita, Saint Mary, and Saint Stephen, and the church of Barbairaz, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Castelnuovo, with its appurtenances; [Col. 0886C] the church of Turre, with the churches of Saint Eulalia, Saint Victor, and Saint Peter of Ansuis, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Ventiis, with the church of Saint Cecilia and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Veredun, with its whole parish and other appurtenances; and the church of Saint Mary of Aquariis; the church of Saint Mary of Mandolio, with the church of Juano and their appurtenances; the church of Saint Saturninus of Armazanica, with the chapel of that castle and a third part of the tithes of the church of Teilliano; the church of Saint Martin of Cavairaco, with its chapels in the middle field of Canois, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint James of Melgorio, with its appurtenances; the church of Seta, with its appurtenances; the church [Col. 0886D] of Saint Peter of Castelnuovo, with its appurtenances; the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Felix, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Bisanduno, with its churches of Saint Vincent, New Saint Mary, Saint Martin of Capellada, Saras, Sacoaras, Babis, Saint Cornelius, Saint Silvester, Saint Quintin, and the church of Ribellis, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Saint Mary of Terracia, with the churches of Saint Peter, Saint Michael, Saint Fructuosus, Saint Julian, and Saint Eulalia, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Rufus outside the walls of the city of Lleida, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael [Col. 0887A] of Schalada, with the church of Saint Fructuosus situated in the same place; the church of Saint Martin of Ponte, with the church of Saint Mary situated in the same village; the church of Saint Felix with the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Cyprian of Villamors; the church of Scalada; the church of Villamorli; the church of Robolar; the church of Saint Peter of Cavafaia, with the church of Saint Maurice, Saint Hilary of Mollerone, and the chapel of Fossa; the church of Lotorderia; the church of Lilio; the church of Brolio; the church of Saint Sulpicius and of Taluc; the church of Saint Gennua, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Maurice of Cesai, with its appurtenances; the church of Mornaco, with its churches of Matis, Batia, Saint Stephen of Colione, [Col. 0887B] and Saint Peter of Caloveda, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael of Genoa outside the city walls, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Nicholas on Monte Colle, with its appurtenances; the church of Lovadisio, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen in Campania outside the walls of the city of Pavia, with its churches of Saint Mary in Campo and Saint Peter in Silva, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Pilia, with its chapels; the church of Saint Symphorian and Saint Reda, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Cuchis, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Belloloco, with chapel and other appurtenances; the church of [Col. 0887C] Marialdo, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Calonio, with the chapel of Saint James of Albarii and other appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Vallis-Clausa, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Bonæ Valles, with its appurtenances; the churches of Saint Andrew beyond Rocha and Saint Martin of Aviac, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of the Island near the castle of Chiren, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Maurice of Uzone, with the parish of Charnas and its other appurtenances; the churches of Ciulac and Nior, with their appurtenances.

Likewise, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your church the sale of the Island of Esparveria, situated below Valence, which Odo, bishop of Valence, of good memory, is known to have reasonably made to you and your church with the assent and [Col. 0887D] concurrence of his canons, as well as your other just acquisitions.

Moreover, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the feed of your animals. Nor may any bishop, without a hearing before the Roman pontiff or his legate, place you or your churches under interdict or excommunication, or burden you with judicial proceedings. All else, too, which was granted to you by our predecessors of happy memory, Urban and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, and [Col. 0888A] confirmed by privileges, we likewise grant and confirm by this present document.

We also decree that the burial-right of this place and of your churches known to possess cemeteries shall be free, following the example of Pope Paschal, our predecessor of pious memory; thus no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, without prejudice to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Further, you may receive into conversion clerics or laypersons fleeing from the world, provided they are free and absolved, and retain them without any objection.

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells [Col. 0888B] and in a subdued voice. Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving your cloister without permission of the abbot and the sounder part or the greater part of the chapter; and no one shall dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community providing security.

Therefore, we decree that no person whatsoever may impose undue and novel exactions upon your churches, take away possessions or goods, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations. Rather, may all remain whole and intact, to be wholly beneficial for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See [Col. 0888C] and, in the aforesaid churches, the canonical rights of the diocesan bishops according to the prescribed form.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly presumes rashly to contravene this charter of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 0888D] and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second Nones of May, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LXVIII. TO HELENA, LADY OF GALLURA. The pope’s cousin is sent to consummate marriage with her. (Rome, fifth Ides of May.)

> [Note: Col. 0887] See letters 103, 104, 105, and 106 of Book Seven.

You ought to render praise and thanks to the Most High because [Col. 0889A] you have found such favor in our eyes that we have given to you as bridegroom our beloved son T…, our cousin: a man distinguished in nobility, prudent in judgment, vigorous in courage, and adorned with good character. Having received, upon your soul, from our beloved son …, the bishop-elect of Galtellì, an oath concerning the consummation of the marriage compact, we send him to Sardinia with the number of persons proposed by that elect.

> [Note: Col. 0889D] Thus read in the copy.

He would, however, have come with more if necessity had required it and if this had proceeded upon the advice of the same elect, who knows the condition of the land fully. We have therefore firmly commanded him to love and defend you as his own person, and to treat your men justly and kindly, so that through his industry and strength, [Col. 0889B] with our protection and favor added, the hoped-for advantages may accrue both to you and to your land.

Wherefore, we most earnestly admonish your nobility and command you by apostolic letters that you receive our aforesaid cousin honorably and devotedly, solemnly and gladly consummate the marriage begun with him, and strive to please him in such a manner that you ought to be most sincerely loved and most dutifully honored by him. We also, who, though unworthy, hold Christ’s place on earth, may apply ourselves to your honor and advancement with a zeal proportionately greater as you are joined to us by a closer bond of affinity.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth Ides [Col. 0889C] of May, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

LXIX. … TO THE DEAN AND … SUBDEAN OF POITIERS, AND … DEAN OF ASIANUM IN THE DIOCESE OF POITIERS. He declares void the letters which C. Rufus had surreptitiously obtained concerning his claims against the chapter of Saintes. (Rome, seventh Ides of May.)

> [Note: Col. 0889D] See letter 146 of Book Five, note.

On behalf of our beloved sons, the chapter of the Church of Saintes, it was set before us that, when Master C. Rufus sought to harass them concerning a canonry in the same place, they appealed him to our presence and fixed a term at which the parties were to appear before us. But he, anticipating the term and not awaiting their messenger, who was detained on the journey by a serious illness, obtained from us, through a false allegation, two sets of letters addressed to our venerable brother, the bishop of Saintes, [Col. 0889D] for himself and certain others to be made canons there. He asserted in these letters that they had a fixed number of canons there. Our beloved son W., subdeacon and their procurator, stated that this was false, except insofar as Lucius, pope of good memory, our predecessor, [Col. 0890A] granted them that they should not be compelled to receive more than forty persons; they were, however, by no means forbidden to have fewer.

> [Note: Col. 0889D] See letter 96 of Book Five, note.

The same Master further alleged to us that several prebends were vacant there and distributed among themselves by the canons. The aforesaid procurator denied this, saying that on the death of any person they receive neither more nor less, just as the cloistered canons do not. The oft-mentioned Master further alleged that he held only a small ecclesiastical benefice; but, as the aforesaid subdeacon states, he possesses two churches, from whose revenues his vicars are honorably maintained and pay him an annual pension, and in another church receives one hundred solidi yearly.

For this reason the aforesaid procurator humbly begged us [Col. 0890B] to spare the said church, said to have been burdened by our command, since its revenues have been diminished to no small degree because wars are increasing there. Wherefore, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after the truth has been fully investigated, if it is established to you that the aforesaid Master suppressed such a truth that, had it been stated, he ought not to have obtained such letters, you shall declare by our authority, removing every obstacle of objection and appeal, that those letters have no force, since a lying petitioner ought to lose what he has obtained—especially if the resources of the same church are insufficient. Witnesses, etc. No letters contrary to truth, etc. But if not all, etc.

[Col. 0890C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh Ides of May, in the ninth year.

LXX. … TO THE BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT. In answer to his inquiry: the first marriage, notwithstanding a subsequent one, is in a certain manner binding and valid. (Rome, sixth Ides of May.)

> [Note: Col. 0889D] This letter is found, but mutilated, among the Decretals, Book IV, title 11, *On the Betrothal of Minors*, chapter 14, where it is said to be addressed to the bishop of Abbatensis. But Pithoeus notes in his marginal annotations that ancient editions also read “Aberstadem,” alternatively “Albertaden,” “Albeten,” “Abbataden,” and, in some copies, “Alberscaden” or “Alberstaten.”

> [Note: Col. 0890D] See letter 108 of Book Eight, note.

[Your letter presented to us contained that a certain nobleman [Col. 0889D] betrothed his daughter, about twelve years old, to a certain nobleman, who gave her an earnest-gift, with mutual consent having been added.]

> [Note: Col. 0889D] These words are absent from the Decretals, which next omit “to the man.”

> [Note: Col. 0889D] The following words, distinguished by italics, are absent from the Decretals but are read in Pithoeus’s additions.

But, after the wedding had been postponed for a while, … the girl’s father entered upon the way of all flesh. After he had departed from human affairs, … the aforesaid girl’s uncle married her to another man; [Col. 0890D] and he who had first betrothed her contracted marriage with her mother. Your predecessor, observing that he could not remain with the woman whose daughter he had lawfully betrothed, pronounced a sentence of divorce between them.

Afterwards, when the second husband, who had taken the aforesaid girl as wife, died, she married a third man while he who had first [Col. 0891A] betrothed her was alive. Both she and [Pithoeus’s additions: “her husband”] then humbly sought your counsel as to whether they might lawfully live together. After deliberation, you replied that, while the first bridegroom lived, she could not lawfully be united to another; but because your church requested that you consult the Apostolic See on this matter, you deferred further action and humbly asked us to write to you concerning it.

> [Note: Col. 0891D] Pithoeus omits this word.

> [Note: Col. 0891D] These words, as far as “certainly,” are absent; the Decretals read “the same” for “the first,” “whether” for “or whether,” and omit the words “to your brotherhood … thus.”

[But because, from the matters set out above, we could not know for certain the age of the girl when she was betrothed to the first man, since she is said to have been about twelve years old, or whether prudence then supplied the deficiency of age in her, we answer your brotherhood as follows: if at that time the girl was of marriageable age, and lawful present consent intervened between her and the first man, undoubtedly a lawful marriage was contracted between them, even though carnal intercourse did not follow. But if the girl [Col. 0891B] was not of marriageable age when the aforesaid man betrothed her, and prudence did not supply the deficiency of age in her, undoubtedly not marriage but betrothal was contracted between them, although the same girl had been given an earnest-gift by that man.]

> [Note: Col. 0891D] These passages are absent from the Decretals and likewise from Pithoeus.

Accordingly, if, according to the first alternative, she contracted marriage with him, she could not lawfully enter into a marital bond with another while he lived. But if, according to the second alternative, only betrothal was contracted, the marriage celebrated between her and the other man must be regarded as lawful, provided no other canonical impediment stands in the way.

[Col. 0891C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth Ides of May, in the ninth year.

LXXI. TO THE NOBLEMAN R., COUNT OF FONDI. He will approve the agreement which the count makes with the people of Terracina. (Ferentino, third Kalends of June.)

On behalf of our beloved sons, the noblemen James and Deodatus Frangipane, it was set before us that you promise to assist them effectively against the people of Terracina, so that you may compel those people of Terracina to obey our commands and those of the noblemen, provided they renounce in your favor the woodland which you granted to their fathers and paternal uncles, and grant, as compensation for expenses, the fishery of Vareis and two *sassones* established in the River Ligole.

Wherefore, know by this communication that we shall hold ratified the agreement which you make concerning these matters with the aforesaid noblemen, insofar as they are legally concerned and as regards their share.

Given at Ferentino, on the third Kalends of June, in the ninth year.

LXXII. … TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI. He is to declare void letters obtained concerning matters belonging to the secular forum. (Ferentino, second Kalends of June.)

> [Note: Col. 0891D] This letter is read among the Decretals, Book II, title 11, *On Competent Jurisdiction*, chapter 10.

> [Note: Col. 0892D] See letter 65 of Book Nine, note.

[Col. 0892A]

[Though from the office of service which we have undertaken] [Note: [Col. 0892D] What follows, distinguished by italic type, is absent from the Decretals, but is found in Pithou’s additions.] we are debtors to all in justice, yet it is fitting that we make provision for certain persons in their own right, lest we appear to do injury to others and—God forbid!—that matter for scandal be drawn from that which ought, by prudent consideration, to be allayed. From the representation of our beloved sons, the consuls and Commune of Vercelli, you should know that we have learned the following: although, in every dispute brought against them before the consuls of justice, they are willing, in accordance with approved custom, to render full justice to every complainant, certain persons, in order to nullify their jurisdiction and to burden them with labours and expenses concerning matters that do not belong to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, procure apostolic letters; and thus, besides weakening the jurisdiction of the consuls, they compel them to undergo manifold trouble. Desiring, therefore, to provide for their welfare in such a way that we do not permit the justice due to others to perish, by these apostolic writings we [command you that, whenever such [Note: [Col. 0892D] In the Decretals: “by laymen of Vercelli”; and shortly afterward they omit *eas* (“them”) and read *irritas* (“void”) in place of *inutiles* (“ineffectual”); they do not have the word *dicti* (“said”).] letters, especially concerning matters requiring a secular forum, happen to be obtained from the Apostolic See, you shall, our authority being invoked and any obstacle of appeal set aside, declare them ineffectual and void, provided that the said consuls and Commune render complete justice in a secular court to those who complain against them. Nevertheless, it shall be permitted to those [Note: [Col. 0892D] The Decretals read *Liceat* instead of *Licet*, and shortly afterward “under the same consuls” in place of “with them.”] who choose thus to litigate with them, if they feel themselves aggrieved in any respect, to appeal to your hearing, as has hitherto been observed, or to ours if they prefer—especially at this time, when, the Empire being vacant, those oppressed in their rights by their superiors cannot have recourse to a secular judge. But if the consuls of justice are rejected as deservedly suspect, the question of suspicion shall be dealt with before arbitrators chosen jointly; and, if the suspicion is proved to be just, recourse for justice shall be had to you or to us, as has been stated above.]

Given at Ferentino, 31 May, in the ninth year.

LXXIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF SAINT AREDIUS. That they are to confer the deanery of that church upon the clerk P. (Ferentino, 7 June.)

[Col. 0892D]

The office of the apostolate entrusted to us requires that, since we are bound to bear care and solicitude for all churches, we should provide suitable persons for those which suffer loss, both spiritual and temporal, through the lack of ministers; and likewise that provision should be made through churches for those enrolled in the ranks of the clergy who know and are able profitably to serve the churches from which they have obtained benefices. Thus we may, by reciprocal exchange, provide for churches in their persons and for persons in churches. You should know that it has come to our hearing that the deanery in your church has been vacant for so long that the right to grant it has, according to the decree of the Lateran Council, devolved upon us. Therefore, desiring with fatherly solicitude to provide for that church, we command and enjoin upon your whole body by apostolic writings that, if what is alleged is true, you receive our beloved son Master P., clerk of our venerable brother, the bishop of Tusculum [Note: [Col. 0893D] See letter 54 of Book Nine, note.], a man commendable for character and learning, as canon and brother, and liberally assign to him the aforesaid deanery, with its appurtenances and the full honour of the office. Thus the said bishop, who may be the more useful to you in proportion as he is known to hold a higher place in the Church of God, may be more strongly moved toward affection for you; and we may be able to commend your devotion in the Lord. Otherwise, we have by our letters commanded our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0893D] See letter 96 of Book Five, note.], that, as we enjoined him orally, having ascertained the truth he compel you by ecclesiastical censure to do this, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed.

[Col. 0893C] Given at Ferentino, 7 June, in the ninth year.

LXXIV. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. That, if his wife’s brother possesses adequate learning and age, at the king’s request he will confirm him as archbishop of Kalocsa. (Ferentino, 7 June.)

Before Him before whom it is not safe to lie, we confess that we love your person with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith; and that we strive effectively, so far as we can with God, for your honour and advancement. We wish you to know for certain that you will suffer no refusal from us in any matter in which we ought to grant the request of any other prince whatsoever. Yet we do not wish you to be ignorant of this also: by the office of apostolic service we are so bound to administer justice that, without the branding of conscience and peril to our reputation, we cannot turn either to the right or to the left. For a lamp set upon a lampstand cannot be hidden; and we keep ever before our eyes what Truth declares concerning us: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savour, wherewith shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer, save to be cast out and trodden under foot by men” (Matthew 5).

Although, therefore, you have offered us earnest prayers on behalf of the beloved son, the provost, brother of your wife, elected archbishop of Kalocsa, asking that we should confer upon him the gift of consecration and send him the pallium—him whom you trust will be useful and necessary to you and your realm in the archiepiscopal office—nevertheless, because the Apostle teaches that we should lay hands suddenly on no man, that is, before we have fuller certainty concerning him through canonical examination, and because we are uncertain of the said provost’s learning and age, indeed have probable doubts concerning them, we could not immediately carry out the royal petition in this respect. For under divine law both sufficient learning and lawful age are required in him. But since we desire, as far as honourably possible, to meet your wishes, we are now doing what we can: by our letters we command our venerable brother, the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0894D] See letter 29 of Book Five, note.], and the beloved son, the provost of Salzburg, diligently to inquire into his learning and age and faithfully report to us what they find. In this way, made more certain through their report, we may proceed more safely.

By these letters we notify your Serenity that, if learning not merely outstanding but at least adequate is found in him, and if age not merely complete but at least approaching completeness is found in him, we desire so greatly to satisfy—not so much your wish as your necessity—that, unless the defect in either respect is so serious that it ought not to be tolerated, we shall temper strictness and arrange a dispensation for him. Otherwise, the result may be attributed not to our harshness but to his own insufficiency, since, although we may sometimes bend the sinews of ecclesiastical discipline, we must never break them. Meanwhile, for the need of the Church of Kalocsa, we patiently permit him to administer both its spiritual and temporal affairs, provided that this is not drawn into precedent hereafter.

Given at Ferentino, 7 June, in the ninth year.

LXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM AND THE BISHOP OF EGER. That they are to dispense in the marriage contracted between the Palatine Count and his wife. (Ferentino, 7 June.)

Our apostolate has been informed on behalf of our beloved son, the nobleman, the Palatine Count of Hungary, that, having formerly united himself in marriage, before the face of the Church and with no one objecting, to a noblewoman related to him in the second kind and second degree of affinity, and being unaware that such a bond of affinity could impede marriage, he afterward, taking wiser counsel, judged that the mercy of the Apostolic See should be sought, lest he retain the aforesaid woman in his company to the detriment of his soul. He asks that, by authority of our dispensation, he may be able to retain the woman in question.

Furthermore, certain matters have been represented to us on account of which the benefit of a dispensation is usually more readily obtained: namely, that they have cohabited together for the course of many years now elapsed; that each has advanced in years; that they have received offspring from this union; that they could not be separated without the gravest scandal; and that no accuser appears against this marriage. But because these facts have not been established before us, we command your fraternity by apostolic writings that, if the truth supports the foregoing, you grant them by our authority the favour of dispensation and direct that henceforth they remain together freely and lawfully.

Given at Ferentino, 7 June, in the ninth year.

LXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0895D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §26.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES AND PRINCES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT HUNGARY. That they are to take an oath of fidelity to the offspring of the king of Hungary. (Ferentino, 7 June.)

[Col. 0895B]

Since father and son are, by a legal interpretation, deemed to be the same person, it follows with sufficient probability that those whom the father retains in the bosom of charity the son likewise ought to love and cherish. For our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Hungarians, has begun to order his realm with such watchful provision and strives to honour the princes of the realm with such demonstrations of affection, as you yourselves know more certainly because he has more frequently and generously bestowed the assistance of his bounty upon you and yours. From this it may reasonably be presumed that the offspring who, by the ordering of divine mercy, shall grow up from him ought, in strength of character and solicitude for government, to imitate its father’s foresight.

Therefore we admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic writings, that you shall without difficulty, at the command of the father, render an oath of fidelity to the offspring to be born to that king, which, by God’s aid, is hoped for soon. Otherwise, know that we have commanded our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Esztergom and the bishop of Várad, etc., to compel you, when necessary, to do this by appropriate coercion, with appeal set aside.

Given at Ferentino, 7 June, in the ninth year.

LXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES TO WHOM THESE LETTERS SHALL COME. That they are to absolve other Templars returning from the pathless waste to the way. (Ferentino, 3 June.)

[Col. 0895D]

Our beloved sons, the brothers of the Knights Templar, have informed us that, although certain persons bound by sentences of excommunication or interdict desire to return from the pathless waste to the way of truth and to be admitted into their fellowship, so that in their houses they may labour diligently in the service of God and exercise their knighthood against the enemies of Christ’s cross, the brothers nevertheless do not venture to receive them. Thus such offenders, like rotting beasts of burden, decay in their own dung. Therefore we command your whole body by apostolic writings that, when you are requested by those brothers, having received from such excommunicated persons security in accordance with the form of the Church and having imposed upon them what ought by law to be imposed, you grant them the benefit of absolution. You shall then permit them, free and absolved, fleeing the world, to pass over to the religious observance of the aforesaid brothers.

Given at Ferentino, 3 June, in the ninth year.

LXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0896D] See letter 75 of Book Five.] AND THE CLERGY OF PIACENZA. That the pope is prepared to receive an oath from the consuls of Piacenza concerning devotion to the Church. (Ferentino, 10 June.)

[Col. 0896B]

We have clearly learned from your letters that the consuls and councillors of Piacenza, acknowledging their own offence, desire humbly and devoutly to return to obedience to the command of the Apostolic See. We therefore rejoice in Him who wills not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live; and who “casts forth his ice like morsels of bread,” when He moves and draws those frozen by the malice of daily obstinacy to seek refuge in Mother Church.

But since the aforesaid consuls are bound by oath to Fulk Radin not to come to an agreement without him, while he neither wishes to give them leave nor to swear except on such terms that no command be made to him, or, if one is made, that he is in no way bound to observe it, you have earnestly asked us to receive his oath in this manner, so that a door of escape may be opened to them and the whole city may not fall into ruin because of one man alone. They also profess that they know an oath rendered apart from the form of the Church is not such that he could on that account obtain the benefit of absolution.

Although it is not our intention to enjoin upon anyone, especially under obligation of an oath, anything except what is just and honourable, we nevertheless do not wish to alter the form of oath which kings and princes customarily render to the Church in such a matter, lest this perhaps be drawn into precedent. And because we do not wish to deceive or be deceived, we do not wish to receive an evasive oath by which we or others might be circumvented. Moreover, since an oath ought not to be a bond of iniquity, nor may anyone be bound by it to what is unlawful, we answer you by this present notification that the aforesaid consuls may swear, even if he objects, without the stain or guilt of perjury, since he maliciously refuses to give them his consent in this matter; and we are prepared to receive them without him according to the customary form of the Church.

Given at Ferentino, 10 June, in the ninth year.

LXXIX. TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF TORRES. That he is to inquire whether H. and the daughter of the judge of Arborea are related in the fifth degree. (Ferentino, 9 June.)

[Col. 0897A]

You should know that we have learned from the letters of our beloved son, the nobleman W., marquis of Massa and judge of Cagliari, that, when he had arranged to unite one of his daughters in the bond of marriage with our beloved son, the nobleman Hugh de Basso, judge of Arborea, a common report arose in those parts that the said Hugh is related by a line of consanguinity to the daughter of the aforesaid judge. Therefore the said W., as a Catholic and God-fearing man, considered that recourse should be had to the apostolic oracle, in order that by our reply he might be more fully instructed how he ought to proceed in this matter with a safe conscience. He further adds that, if this marriage is brought to completion, great benefit and advantage will accrue to the Roman Church and to all Sardinia, especially since no small good of peace is hoped to result from it.

Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic writings that, summoning before you those whom it is proper to summon for this purpose, you diligently investigate the truth of the foregoing matters: in what degree of consanguinity the said persons are related; and whether so great a benefit is believed likely to result from this affair. You are to take care faithfully to notify us by your letters, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed more safely in this business as we judge expedient.

Given at Ferentino, 9 June, in the ninth year.

LXXX. TO J., CARDINAL DEACON OF SANTA MARIA IN VIA LATA [Note: [Col. 0897D] See letter 184 of Book Seven.], LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That he is to inquire into the condition of the priory of Bomin [Note: [Col. 0897D] See letter 115 of Book Six.]; alternatively, Bodmin. (Ferentino, 11 June.)

The prior and regular canons of the church of Saint Petroc of Bomin have humbly petitioned us that we should graciously convert their priory, which owes an annual census to the Roman Church, into an abbey by the benevolence of the Apostolic See. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, after diligently investigating the true condition of that priory, if you see that this can be done for the honour of God without prejudice to another’s right and that it is expedient for the church itself, you shall not fail, with appeal set aside, to raise that priory to an abbey.

Given at Ferentino, 11 June, in the ninth year.

LXXXI. TO ANGELA, FOUNDER, AND THE BROTHERS OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARY OF THE MOUNT OF GUARDIA. They are received under the protection of blessed Peter. (Ferentino, 10 June.)

[Col. 0898A]

Inclining to the just desires of petitioners, etc., as far as “inclining,” we receive the church itself, with all the goods which it now reasonably possesses or may hereafter, God favouring it, acquire by just means, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the safeguard of this present writing. Therefore let no person at all, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 10 June, in the ninth year.

LXXXII. [Note: [Col. 0897D]

This letter is printed entire in Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 451; therefore it is here presented in brackets.

Raynaldus also published it, but mutilated, under the year 1206, §39. What is printed by him is here indicated by a double stroke in the margin at the beginning of each line. See letter 53 of Book Eight and the notes there.] TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF ALESSANDRIA. On the union of the churches of Alessandria and Acqui. (Ferentino, 8 June.)

[Col. 0898B]

[Since the blessed apostle Peter received from Jesus Christ himself the fullness of ecclesiastical power, there can be no doubt that the bishop of the Apostolic See, who is the successor of blessed Peter, has full and free authority to dispose of ecclesiastical affairs. Truth herself says to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). From this prerogative of supreme power there proceeded the following: the pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0898D] This passage occurs in Raynaldus.], “considering the fervour of devotion and faith which the people of Alessandria showed him in a time of grave and great necessity, decreed by authority of the Apostolic See that, since the city of Alessandria is far larger and more populous than Acqui, the episcopal see should be transferred from the latter, whose diocese is adjacent, to the former.

“Accordingly, through honourable envoys, both clergy and laity, sent to our presence, you humbly petitioned us to cause to be put into execution what that same predecessor of ours had decreed after prudent deliberation, as we follow in his footsteps. But, wishing to proceed with due maturity in so great a matter, we first considered it necessary to inquire whether it could take effect without some grave scandal. Since it appeared that not only the city of Acqui but also that of Pavia, which had undertaken its defence, would be greatly scandalized by such a transfer, we granted a full hearing to the representatives of both parties, who had appeared before us. When they began to contend in many ways before us concerning this matter, we intervened to bring about concord, modifying the decree of our aforesaid predecessor in the following manner: we unite the churches of Alessandria and Acqui and establish by this present privilege that one and the same bishop shall be bishop of both, holding one and the same episcopal see in each.

“But lest union produce confusion, we have judged it salutary to decree the following specific distinctions between them. The bishop shall conduct the business and cases belonging to the church of Acqui with the counsel of the clergy of Acqui; and those belonging to the laity, with the counsel of the laity, within the city of Acqui or its diocese, in a place suitable and safe both for those laymen and for the bishop himself. Matters belonging to the church of Alessandria, however, he shall conduct with the assent of the chapter of Alessandria. He shall have a double seal: on one side bearing the image and inscription of the bishop of Acqui, and on the other those of the bishop of Alessandria. When he writes concerning affairs or persons of Acqui, he shall style himself only bishop of Acqui. But when he writes concerning other affairs or other persons, if he is in the diocese of Alessandria, he shall style himself only bishop of Alessandria; if in the diocese of Acqui, only bishop of Acqui, and conversely, so that, since their dignity is the same, neither may be diminished through the other.

“He shall prepare chrism one year at one church and the next year at the other; and he shall do likewise concerning baptism. He shall divide the greater solemnities equally between them, so that those which he celebrates in one year at one church he shall celebrate the next year at the other; but he shall celebrate special solemnities only where they belong specially. He shall hold ordinations for clerics belonging to the church of Acqui in the city of Acqui or its diocese, in a place, however, that is suitable and safe. He shall reside at each church or within its diocese for at least half the year, unless perhaps necessity, which knows no law, sometimes requires another course.

“The castles of the church of Acqui which the bishop holds shall be guarded by men loyal to and not suspected by the people of Acqui. And if—God forbid!—a disturbance should arise between the people of Alessandria and those of Acqui, the men of those castles shall not assist the Alessandrians against the people of Acqui, unless it is a special cause of the bishop. For we do not wish either of the churches or cities, because of this union, to have authority, power, jurisdiction, or lordship over the other, lest what has been provided for unity should at some time be turned to the contrary.

“When the bishop departs this life, the canons of the aforesaid churches shall meet at one of the two places upon which they can agree among themselves, or at any other place; and the election of whomever they unanimously, or the greater and sounder part of one, or the greater and sounder part of the other, elect as bishop shall be confirmed by the archbishop of Milan, provided that nothing in the canonical statutes stands against him. If they cannot agree according to this form, they shall either elect electors who will elect for them a bishop to be accepted by all as thus elected, or send suitable representatives to the Apostolic See, through whom they may receive as bishop whomever the Roman pontiff judges should be granted to them.

“Concerning the first arrival of a consecrated bishop at either of the aforesaid churches or cities, we decree that the turns shall alternate according to the succession of bishops: when one after his consecration has first been received at one place, the next shall thereafter first be received at the other, all envy being wholly removed. This is subject only to the condition that, in those things which he must perform alternately in both churches, he begins with Acqui. We forbid anyone henceforth to become a canon or office-holder in both of the aforesaid churches, lest confusion thereby arise. The privileges and other writings belonging to the church of Acqui shall be placed in the archive of that church.

“Although the representatives of both parties, present before us, have judged the foregoing arrangement acceptable, nevertheless, since he who abuses a power granted him deserves to lose the privilege, we decree that, if the people of Acqui should contemptuously violate this statute and, upon admonition by the Roman pontiff, fail to correct the excess of their presumption, the episcopal see shall be transferred from the city of Acqui to Alessandria, as our aforementioned predecessor decreed. But if the people of Alessandria violate the same statute and, upon admonition by the Roman pontiff, fail to make satisfaction for their offence, the bond of the aforesaid union shall be dissolved.” [Note: [Col. 0899D] Raynaldus ends here.]

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our constitution or rashly oppose it, with the authority of the Apostolic See always reserved in all things. Should any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly presume in the future to act rashly against this privilege, and, having been admonished a second or third time, fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let that person be subject, at the last judgment, to strict vengeance. But upon all who observe these provisions, may there rest the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 8 June, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1206 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LXXXIII. [Note: [Col. 0901D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1296, §40.] TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF ACQUI. On the same matter. (Ferentino, 8 June.)

Since the blessed apostle Peter received from Jesus Christ himself the fullness of ecclesiastical power, there can be no doubt that the bishop of the Apostolic See, who is the successor of blessed Peter, has full and free authority to dispose of ecclesiastical affairs, Truth herself saying to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16), etc., in the same manner as above to the end.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 8 June, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1206 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LXXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0901D] The copy of this letter which, together with the others, we had caused to be transcribed at the end of Conti’s copy, has slipped from our hands—we do not know by what accident. Therefore we can provide here only the summary. See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §33.] TO THE PRIOR OF ST ANDREW AND HIS BRETHREN. They are received under the protection of blessed Peter.

LXXXV. TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 0901D] The collegiate church of St Mary and St Perpetuus of Dinant appears to have been a monastery; for it is mentioned in the division of the abbeys and monasteries of Lothair’s kingdom, made in 870 between Charles and Louis, kings of the Franks. It subsequently became a secular abbey in the time of Richer, bishop of Liège, about 934. The chapter consists of twelve canons and an abbot; appointments to the canonries belong alternately to the abbot and the pope. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. III, col. 938.] AND THE CHAPTER OF THE CHURCH OF DINANT, DIOCESE OF LIÈGE. That they are to confer a benefice upon the clerk D. (Ferentino, 6 June.)

Although, according to the obligation of our office, it is fitting that we provide with fatherly solicitude for all enrolled under the title of clerical service, still we both wish and ought more readily to admit the petitions of those who, through the merits of their lives, deserve to be supported before us by the testimony of good men. Since our beloved son Master David, our chaplain, has freely resigned into our hands a portion of the prebend which he held in your church, we have judged that portion should be conferred, as an act of piety, upon our beloved son R., his nephew, a clerk commended by character and learning. We earnestly admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord, and command you by apostolic writings, that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you receive the said R. as canon and brother and freely confer upon him the aforesaid benefice. And because the Council of Tours forbids the division of prebends, you shall take care, as soon as opportunity offers, to make it whole for him. Otherwise, know that we have commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0902D] See letter 215 of Book Six, note.], not to delay in compelling you by ecclesiastical censure to do this, with the obstacle of appeal removed.

Given at Ferentino, 6 June, in the ninth year.

LXXXVI. TO THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0902D] See letter 182 of Book Seven, note.], THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 0902D] See letter 84 of Book Six.], AND THE CHANCELLOR OF LONDON. That they are not to permit E., a woman, to be harassed. (Ferentino, 13 June.)

It has been represented before us on behalf of E., a woman of Bendevilles, that, while she was under age, she was committed to the custody of nuns without making a regular profession or receiving the habit. Later she united herself in marriage to a man, by whom she has now had many children. Certain persons, disparaging that marriage, are accordingly endeavouring to tarnish her reputation. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, if the truth supports the foregoing, unless some other reasonable charge against that woman is made and proved, you are not to permit her or the offspring she has borne to be harassed in any way on this account. And if not all of you, etc., you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the Ides of June, in the ninth year.

LXXXVII. TO THE PRIOR [Note: [Col. 0902D]

“VII. Stephen, prior of St Pourçain, in the years 1190 and 1193; afterward elected abbot of Cluny.

VIII. Guiscard de Roanne, 1208, 1216, etc.; afterward elected abbot of Cluny.”

Thus far the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 373. In their incomplete series of priors of St Pourçain, the same authors mention Stephen as abbot of Cluny already from 1202, vol. IV, col. 970.

See letter 136 of Book Five.] AND THE CONVENT OF SAINT POURÇAIN, DIOCESE OF CLERMONT. That they are to delay no longer in conferring the church of Bajec. upon the clerk Durand. (Ferentino, 9 June.)

[Col. 0902C]

We recall that by our letters we commanded you to confer the church of Bajec., said to be vacant, with its appurtenances, upon Durand, clerk of our venerable brother, the bishop of Clermont [Note: [Col. 0902D] See letter 136 of Book Five, note.], out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves. But you have passed by with deaf ears both our command and the admonition of that bishop and of our beloved son, the archdeacon of Senlis, whom we appointed as his monitors, as we have clearly learned from the tenor of their letters. The said clerk therefore appealed to our hearing, lest you presume to make any disposition concerning that church in evasion of the apostolic command.

Accordingly, unwilling to leave incomplete what we judged should mercifully be begun for him, we command and enjoin you again by repeated writings that you freely confer the said church upon the said clerk, insofar as belongs to you. Otherwise, we have commanded our beloved sons—the abbot of Saint-Geniès [Note: [Col. 0903C] Pons, abbot of Saint-Geniès, is found in instruments from 1194 to 1215. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. II, col. 317.], the cantor of Clermont, and the prior of Montferrand, diocese of Clermont—that, unless some reasonable objection is made and proved before them why the apostolic command cannot or should not be fulfilled, they shall not fail to compel you by ecclesiastical censure to do this, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed; and they shall restore to its due state whatever they find unlawfully attempted after the appeal lawfully lodged with us.

Given at Ferentino, 9 June, in the ninth year.

LXXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0903C] This letter is found, but in a mutilated form, among the Decretals, Book III, title 28, *On Burials*, chapter 10 [Col. 0903D], where it is said to be addressed to the bishop of Clermont and the abbot of Mauriac. What is printed there is presented here in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO THE BISHOP OF CLERMONT [Note: [Col. 0903D] See letter 136 of Book Five, note.], THE ABBOT OF MAUZAC [Note: [Col. 0903D] Eustorgius, abbot of Mauzac, is attested as a witness in 1205 in an old charter for Lehunio. Next, and immediately thereafter, though not until 1212, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 353, mention Gerontius de Turre.], AND MASTER SIMON, ARCHPRIEST OF HERMENCO, DIOCESE OF CLERMONT. He commands them to ensure observance of what he definitively decided in the case between the prior of Montferrand and the representative of the Hospitallers, diocese of Clermont. (Ferentino, 12 June.)

[Col. 0903C] [When our beloved sons . . . , prior of the church of Montferrand, and B., procurator of the Hospitallers of the diocese of Clermont, appeared before us, we appointed our venerable brother, the Bishop of Sabina, as auditor, before whom the said prior alleged that the aforesaid Hospitallers admit his parishioners to the ecclesiastical sacraments and have received for ecclesiastical burial both excommunicated and interdicted persons, as well as certain others—namely William of Mazeries, William [Col. 0904A] Dretturer, John Bondiner, Durant of Lavor, and two boys, namely the son of William of Mazeries and the son of John of Ventador, who were under the lawful age—whereby that church suffered damage exceeding five thousand solidi. Therefore the same prior humbly petitioned that we should deign to forbid the Hospitallers to attempt such things henceforth to his prejudice, and compel them to repair the losses which he had thereby suffered.]

[Note: [Col. 0903D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as is shortly the initial B.]

[Note: [Col. 0903D] See the note to Letter 15 of Book III.]

[Note: [Col. 0903D] These words are absent from the Decretals.]

[Note: [Col. 0903D] In the Decretals: “they received for ecclesiastical burial certain of his parishioners, two of whom were under lawful age.”]

Conversely, the aforesaid procurator alleged that, both by privilege and by a special indulgence, the Hospitallers may lawfully receive for ecclesiastical burial all persons without distinction, except the excommunicated and interdicted, who have chosen burial among them; they may also lawfully accept legacies left by last will, provided only that the parish church from whose parish the bodies of the dead are taken receives the parish fourth, except in the case of horses and arms, which have been granted to them in aid of the Holy Land.

[Note: [Col. 0903D] Formerly there was no free choice of burial: one had to be buried where one had received the sacraments of the Church—that is, the sustenance of salvation—while alive (see *Decretum*, Part II, Cause XIII, Question VII, *Placuit*), because parishioners were regarded as servants of the Church. Later it became permissible to choose burial in another church or monastery, provided that a less religious place was not chosen. But today it makes no difference whether the place is less religious or not.]

[Note: [Col. 0904D] In the Decretals: *fideique commissa*, “bequests entrusted to faith.”]

[Note: [Col. 0904D]

It was an ancient religious custom that horses and arms should adorn the funeral procession, as at the funeral of Pallas in Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, v. 89:

> Then Aethon, the warrior horse, his trappings laid aside,  
> Goes weeping and wets his face with great drops.  
> Others bear the spear and helmet; for the rest Turnus,  
> The victor, possesses . . .

From such horses and arms—which, by military custom, were ornaments of funeral processions—the Hospitallers were religiously exempted from surrendering a fourth, in aid of the holy war; this Innocent, inspired by the Holy Spirit, had confirmed for them and for the Hospitallers. See Letter 507 of the book.]

They are not bound to deduct a fourth from these.

[Note: [Col. 0904D] What follows, distinguished here in italic type, is absent from the Decretals, but is found in Pithou’s additions.]

Therefore, when the same bishop had faithfully reported to us these matters and others proposed before him, and when we had heard and understood all the depositions and allegations, we judged, on the counsel of our brethren, that the following sentence should be pronounced: the aforesaid Hospitallers shall henceforth not receive the parishioners of the aforesaid church for ecclesiastical burial unless they have chosen burial among them; and then the parish church shall receive a fourth part of the offerings, beds, and other things which the deceased leaves in his final disposition for his soul, except horses and arms, while the Hospitallers shall retain the remainder—unless the deceased was induced by their deceit or fraud to make such a disposition. Nevertheless, we enjoin the Hospitallers to satisfy the aforesaid prior for a fourth part of the five thousand solidi, since it is established that they received those solidi from the prior’s parishioners and it has not been sufficiently shown that they were offered or entrusted to them.

[Note: [Col. 0904D] The Decretals omit this; and below read “his parishioners” for “the prior’s parishioners,” and “unless” for “nor unless.”]

[Col. 0905A] [Note: [Col. 0905D] The Decretals read *conversi* (“converted”); and shortly afterwards, “to the same persons.” Below, G., parishioner of the prior, for W. G.]

We further enjoin them that, unless they prove that William Gastasalt, who was killed in the fields, chose burial among them, they shall restore to the aforesaid prior everything which they received on his account; otherwise they shall be bound to restore only a fourth part. But concerning the son of William of Mazeries and the son of John of Ventador, who are known to have died under lawful age, we enjoin them to restore in full everything which they received on account of their burial.]

[Note: [Col. 0905D] The Decretals add “of him”; and below read “to them” in place of “for the place of the son of William of Mazeries and the son of John of Ventador.”]

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Minors incapable of puberty can neither make a will nor choose burial. Choice of burial is part of a testament. Formerly minors had no discretion concerning funerals; indeed, it was customary to carry them out at night by torchlight, without a funeral procession. See Servius on the following passage of Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, v. 142:

> According to ancient custom  
> They carried away the funeral torches.

“It is especially a Roman custom that minors should be carried out at night by torchlight, lest a household be made mournful by the funeral of immature offspring.”]

[Note: [Col. 0906D] These words are omitted by the Decretals.]

Accordingly, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion that you cause what has been judicially determined by us to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal and restraining opponents by like censure. But if not all of you can do so, you, brother bishop, together with one of the others, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 12 June, in the ninth year.

## LXXXIX. TO B., BISHOP OF PAVIA, AND TO HIS CANONICALLY APPOINTED SUCCESSORS

[Note: [Col. 0906D] See the note to Letter 90 of Book VII. See also Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, unnumbered page *, col. 32.]

The privileges and statutes of that church are confirmed. (Ferentino, 12 June.)

Both the very principle of justice and the kindness of the Apostolic See require that we should extend more abundantly and readily the hand of our protection and guardianship to places and persons especially devoted to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, and persisting in its devotion and obedience. Moved, therefore, by the obligation of this principle, we desire to preserve the honor and dignity of the Church of Pavia, as a proper and special daughter of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Bernard, whom we love with sincere charity in Christ, graciously assenting to your just petitions, and following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory—Callixtus, Innocent, Eugenius, and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs—we strengthen by the privilege of this present writing the aforesaid Church of Pavia, over which, by God’s authoring, you are known to preside. We likewise confirm, by the favor of our authority, every dignity granted to that church through the privileges or authentic writings of those same Roman pontiffs. In particular, we grant you the use of the pallium during the sacred solemnities of Mass; and we grant both you and your successors the right, in the procession of Palm Sunday and on the Monday after Easter, to ride a white horse covered with a *udone* [a cloth or covering], and likewise to have the cross borne before you while proceeding.

Moreover, confirming a provision for the greater dignity of the same Church of Pavia, we decree that, in the celebration of synodal assemblies, both you and your successors shall perpetually hold the first seat on the left side of the Roman pontiff. In monasteries or any chapels other than the mother church, we absolutely prohibit the performance of general baptism; and should any enactments contrary to the sacred canons happen to be found in them, they shall not prejudice our canonical ordinances. No one shall presume, without your knowledge, to summon to judgment clerics, religious women, or widows of your city, or to inflict force upon their possessions. Nor shall any person presume to remove from you either the care or authority over cemeteries situated within or around the city; nor shall any man, of whatever secular rank or power, under a pretext of hospitality or an occasion of patronage, dare to lodge in your episcopal residence or in the houses of your priests or clerics without the consent of yourself and your successors. Nor do we permit, against your will and without lawful cause, invasion or violence to be committed against movable or immovable property, or persons of whatever condition, belonging to your church.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being propitious, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the monastery of Saint Apollinaris, with its chapels and parishes; the monastery of Saint Peter called “of the Lepers,” with its chapels and parishes; the monastery of Saint Marinus, with its chapels and parishes; the monastery of Saint Gervasius, with its chapels and parishes; the monastery of Saints Paul and James of Vernanola; the Old Monastery and the monastery of the Senator, with their chapels and parishes; the monastery of Leani and the monastery of Saint Thomas, with their chapels and parishes; and the monastery of Saint Felix, with its chapels and parishes. The canonical governance of the said monasteries within the bounds of your diocese, and the examination, election, and consecration of the abbots and abbesses in them, shall always remain at your discretion. Further, we will that the priests of the aforesaid monasteries, as ecclesiastical necessity requires, shall come to your council without anyone’s rash opposition.

We also confirm to you the church of Saint Mary of Bethlehem; the hospital of Cropellis; the hospital of Saint Justina; the hospital of Tossicaria; the hospital of Galbera; the hospital of Guido Faber; the hospital of Tido; and the hospital of Pontiano. In the archdiocese of Milan: the monastery of Saint Donatus, founded by your predecessor at the place called Scoiola, with its chapels and parishes; and the monastery of Saint Mary of Charity, with its parish, chapels, and parishes. In the diocese of Lodi: the parish church of Pustino, with its chapels and parishes. In the diocese of Cremona: the parish church of Pagatiano, with its parish. In the diocese of Piacenza: the parish church of Fontan., with its chapels and parishes; and the parish church of Rivegozo, with its chapels and parishes. Between the dioceses of Asti, Acqui, and Alba: the parish church of Ponte, with its chapels and parishes. In the diocese of Vercelli: the parish church of Peningo, with its parish. Toward Alessandria: the parish church of Saint Syrus of Sala, with its chapels, parishes, and appurtenances; the parish church of Plovera, with its chapels, parishes, and appurtenances; the parish church of Bassegnan, with its chapels, parishes, and appurtenances; the parish church of Valenza, with its chapels, parishes, and appurtenances; the parish church of Astillian, with its chapels, parishes, and appurtenances; the parish church of the Holy Savior, with its chapels, parishes, and appurtenances; and the parish church of Petra, with its chapels and parishes.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, to be of every benefit for the use of you and of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved in all things. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this text of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and after a second or third warning does not amend the offense by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and know himself or herself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, etc., and subject to punishment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc., and may they attain at the end the fruits of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the holy Roman Church, 12 June, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## XC. TO THE CHAPTER OF COMO

That they are to receive B., the pope’s subdeacon, as a canon. (Ferentino, 14 June.)

[Col. 0908A]

Having long since become disobedient and rebellious toward us, you have shown yourselves—just as not the accomplishment of a thing but rather failure in its performance makes manifest—to be contemners of the commands of the Apostolic See and likewise perverters of ecclesiastical discipline. For although we formerly sent you our letters repeatedly, requiring you to receive our beloved son, B., our subdeacon, as your canon and brother, assigning him liberally a prebend in your church, you stopped up your ears like the deaf asp and utterly scorned to do this. And although for this reason you have long been bound by the bond of excommunication, your rebellion has still not been softened. How serious and grievous this is to us we would have shown otherwise, had not gentleness tempered rigor and mercy moderated the movement of our mind.

But because suitable provision has been made for the aforesaid subdeacon in the Church of Milan, we wholly release you from his claim. By our letters we command our venerable brother, your bishop, to relax by our authority, according to the form of the Church, the sentence of excommunication by which you have for so long been bound on this account. Nevertheless, by these apostolic letters we command your whole body that you presume not to make any disposition concerning the prebend which we had ordered to be assigned to the said cleric, until you receive our will and pleasure on this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0907D] William of Torre Mendritii, bishop of Como—also called Comense—succeeded Ardizzone (on whom see the note to Letter 154 of Book V) in 1204. At one time he incurred the displeasure of Emperor Otto IV (see Letter 31 of Book XV). For twenty years he administered the Church of Como vigorously and with a reputation for prudence; dying on 21 October 1226, he was buried at Saint Mary of Torello. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 291.]

Given at Ferentino, 14 June, in the ninth year.

## XCI. TO THE BISHOP OF PAMPLONA, P. OF CASTRO NOVO, AND BROTHER R., MONKS OF MONTFRIGID, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

[Note: [Col. 0908D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §34.

See also the most learned writer of the *History of Occitania*, vol. III, p. 145, to whom, however, this letter of Pope Innocent III was unknown.]

That they are to hear the matrimonial case between the king of Aragon and M., daughter of G. of Montpellier. (Ferentino, 17 June.)

Our dearest son in Christ, Peter, the illustrious king of Aragon, made known to us by a communication sent that, after he had in fact joined to himself by the bond of marriage our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman M., daughter of the late G. of Montpellier, it subsequently appeared that he had carnally known a woman related to that same noblewoman in a close degree of consanguinity. Moreover, the same M. has a husband still living, with whom she had previously contracted marriage, namely the nobleman . . . , count of Comminges. Therefore the king, as a Catholic man who fears God, having a conscience branded on this matter and fearing that danger to his soul might result, judged that he should hasten to have recourse to the judgment-seat of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if such an accuser appears whose accusation is admissible in law, you, having summoned the parties, hear the case; and, if the parties consent, bring it to a canonical conclusion after removing the impediment of appeal. Otherwise, write down all the proceedings and faithfully send them to us under the attestation of your letters, setting the parties a suitable term within which they are to appear before us through suitable procurators, to receive a just judgment, the Lord being its author. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 17 June, in the ninth year.

## XCII. TO THE CHAPTER OF ACQUI

[Note: [Col. 0909D] Letters 82 and 83 of this ninth book should be compared.]

All churches belonging to them are confirmed. (Ferentino, 16 June.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc. But since, after weighing utility and necessity, we have judged that the Churches of Acqui and Alessandria should be united, lest what has been beneficially provided concerning such a union should hereafter bring disadvantage to either church, we confirm to you, and through you to your church, by apostolic authority, all churches which the Church of Acqui has hitherto peaceably possessed in good faith and by just title; and [we confirm them] by the present writing . . . saving the reverence owed to the bishop of Acqui and Alessandria, as the nature of the union requires. Therefore let no person whatsoever, etc. If anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 16 June, in the ninth year.

## XCIII. LETTER OF THE ARCHPRIEST OF MILAN AND THE VISCOUNT

[Note: [Col. 0909D] This letter is printed in full in Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, p. 444; it is therefore presented here within brackets.

Raynaldus also presents it, but mutilated, under the year 1206, §41. Passages found in his version are marked here by a double marginal stroke at the beginning of each line.

Letters 82, 83, and 92 of this ninth book should be compared.]

How they carried out the commission entrusted to them concerning the making of peace between the cities of Alessandria and Acqui. (This is found in Raynaldus.)

“[To the most holy Father and lord, Innocent, supreme pontiff by God’s grace: W., archpriest of the Church of Milan, though unworthy, and Ariprand, called viscount, his humble and devoted subdeacon, offer in all things submission as devoted as it is due. Your Blessedness, most holy Father, was pleased to command us, your servants, personally to go to the city of Alessandria and prudently admonish and diligently induce its clergy and people to make peace and concord with the people of Acqui, and also to accept the union. But what we have done in these matters, and how greatly [Col. 0910A] we have labored, will be clearly shown by the parties themselves and by our letters sent through them to Your Majesty.

[Note: [Col. 0910D] In Ughelli: “so that.”]

Let Your Holiness hear the whole truth concerning what we did regarding the oaths of fidelity and the payment of tribute. We summoned the podestà, consuls, and councillors of Alessandria and showed them how they were bound and obligated to render tribute and oaths of fidelity to the Roman Church, and further how, as a sign of homage, they had placed themselves in the hands of Lord Alexander of blessed memory, from whom the city itself took its name. We also showed and read through to them the public instrument in which all these things were contained. Receiving and accepting our words no less eagerly than devoutly, they ordered the bell to be rung with all haste so that the multitude of the people might assemble. Knowing the reason for their summons, they ran as though at a welcome call; scarcely able, for joy and exultation, to await the proposal laid before them, they cried out, as with one voice, amid great gladness and the highest rejoicing: ‘Let it be, let it be the will of our lord!’ Thus in complete peace we received the homage and oaths of fidelity of the podestà, consuls, councillors, and all who had assembled in that place, and had a public instrument drawn up concerning it.

Then we appointed as our messengers certain honorable men called the city’s *monitores* (“inspectors”), whom we bound to us by oath, that they should make the rounds of every district, street, and square of the city; faithfully demand and receive from everyone the oaths of fidelity and tribute according to the tenor of the instrument; and show and deliver to us in a public written record everything which they did in these matters. All this was done well and solemnly.]

[Note: [Col. 0910D] Thus far Raynaldus.]

The total number of those who swore was five thousand eight hundred and sixty-six, as is contained in the instruments sent to your Paternity; and the total tribute was twenty-five Pavia pounds. We send all these things to your Paternity through John Torniellus, your subdeacon and canon of Novara, and certain of his companions, envoys of the people of Alessandria. Furthermore, let the immense discretion of Your Highness know that, from what we have plainly seen and learned, we believe and do not at all doubt that it will greatly enhance your glory and advantage, and that of the Church, if you devote attention to the honor and exaltation of the people of Alessandria.]”

## XCIV. TO P., PODESTÀ, AND THE PEOPLE OF ALESSANDRIA

[Note: [Col. 0911D] This letter is printed in full in Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 445; it is therefore presented here within brackets.

Raynaldus mentions the same letter under the year 1206, §40.]

On the same matter. (Ferentino, 21 June.)

[Col. 0911A]

[When our beloved son John Torniellus, our subdeacon, N., vicedominus of Acqui, and the noblemen R. Scacavel and P.
