Fantinus, your envoys, came to the Apostolic See, they presented the tribute due to us and the instrument in which were written all the particulars concerning those who had rendered us fidelity. They pressed diligently and earnestly for the advancement of your affairs and those of your city, so that they cannot in any way be reproached for negligence, but their diligence deserves commendation. And although the matter was not advanced wholly according to their wish, it nonetheless obtained an appropriate result, doubtless to your honor and advantage, as we recognized to be more expedient for removing occasion of scandal.

We therefore admonish your whole community and exhort you in the Lord, commanding you by these apostolic letters, to take care to persevere prudently in fidelity and devotion to the Apostolic See, as you have laudably begun; thus you may deserve to receive more fully the grace and favor of the Apostolic See, and we may deservedly devote effective effort to matters concerning your advantage and honor. As a token of special favor, moreover, we send you a banner bearing the insignia of blessed Peter, so that he may guard and defend you, as his special sons, against enemies of mind and body.

Given at Ferentino, 21 June, in the ninth year.]

## XCV. TO ALL THE CLERGY OF ALESSANDRIA

[Note: [Col. 0911D] This letter is printed in full in Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 453; it is therefore presented here within brackets.

Raynaldus mentions the same letter under the year 1206, §40.]

On the same matter. (Ferentino, 21 June.)

[Since we have judged that the Churches of Alessandria and Acqui should be united, so that both churches may have one shepherd, by the authority of these presents we command you that henceforth you heed our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Alessandria and Acqui, as the father and bishop of your souls, and render him the obedience and reverence that are due and devoted.

Given at Ferentino, 21 June, in the ninth year.

## XCVI. TO ADOLF, FORMER ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

[Note: [Col. 0912D] See the note to Letter 54 of Book III.]

That he should cease doing evil and return to the Church. (Ferentino, 23 June.)

Whenever we have sought, by warnings and counsels, prayers and commands, threats and terrors, to induce you not to become like a crooked bow and mock us without cause—you who by letters and envoys induced us to support the illustrious King Otto—you have not yet, we believe, forgotten, though your sins have required that you be given over to a reprobate mind, how we spared your salvation and reputation. But behold: by a just judgment you yourself first fell into the pit which you prepared for another; for when you wished to cast down the aforesaid king, you were yourself cast down first, because of notorious perjury, publicized treason, public excommunication, and manifest disobedience.

O, if you carefully considered what laypeople think of you, what clerics say of you, how you have debased your person, defiled your order, disgraced your office, made yourself contrary to yourself and rejected yourself, you would doubtless blush no less at the disgrace than you grieve at the loss! We indeed grieve with you—if only you grieve—not in order to exercise vengeance, but in order that you may perform penance; for you seek in vain to avenge yourself, whereas you could profitably repent. What benefit, after all, can killings, sacrileges, thefts, burnings, and the other crimes which you commit bring you? Do you think that through them you can merit pardon from the Lord, or even from us? Your latter deeds have become worse than the former, as, piling sin upon sin and weighed down by the burden of vices, you plunge yourself into the depths of hell.

Do not think that we utter these words from bitterness of heart. Although we hate your offense, we love your nature, still mindful of the former affection by which we loved you more warmly among our brethren and fellow bishops. But, God knows, we speak these words from compassion, for we groan and grieve when we hear that you are always going from evil to worse; for although you grievously harm others, you harm yourself more grievously, and you fail all the more in the very matter in which you are confident of making greater progress. Remember your last things, if perhaps you may come to your senses from so great an error, turning through humble penance to him from whom you turned away through stubborn disobedience; for this is the sole path left to you by which you can come to salvation.

For although you cannot return to the rank from which you deservedly fell, yet if you strive to humble yourself beneath God’s mighty hand, his right hand can still raise you up. But if, yielding to wicked counsels and persisting in unjust deeds, you provoke his anger more and more, you will beyond doubt not escape his hands, which will punish you severely in the present and more severely in the future. Therefore, brother, we admonish you with tears and exhort you in Christ Jesus, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, to comply with our salutary admonitions; through the remedy of penance, rise from death to life; and return to the breasts of Mother Church, which receives erring children with a merciful and loving disposition. For although you have brought the most holy Roman Church, your mother, into a grave difficulty from which it could in no way be freed through you, nevertheless he who is its founder and foundation commands the winds and the sea; and since he is our helper, we do not fear what man may do to us.

Given at Ferentino, 24 June, in the ninth year.

## XCVII. TO ALBERT, PROVOST ELECTED ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG

[Note: [Col. 0913D] See the note to Letter 62 of this ninth book.]

That he should treat the apostolic envoy graciously. (Ferentino, 23 June.)

The storm in the Empire, which drove you heedlessly to do that which could deservedly have impeded your promotion, necessarily delays us from proceeding yet to the confirmation of your affair. Although we were lawfully moved against you, your beloved son, Master G., your envoy, a man indeed prudent and faithful, has not ceased to calm our displeasure. Thus, when a suitable opportunity is found, we have proposed to bring the matter to completion, provided that you strive to conform yourself to us as a member to its head.

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish your devotion and command you by apostolic letters to receive graciously and treat honorably the same master, whom we sincerely love in the Lord for the sake of his worth. And, whenever necessity requires, send him back to our presence with all the greater security because he has found greater favor in our eyes. For he will explain to you more fully what he has received from us to be communicated confidentially.

Given at Ferentino, 23 June, in the ninth year.

## XCVIII. TO B., BISHOP OF PAVIA

[Note: [Col. 0913D] See the note to Letter 90 of Book VII.]

The monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Bartholomew is entrusted to his administration. (Ferentino, 19 June.)

The Apostolic See, which by the Lord’s disposition is the mother and teacher of all the faithful, is accustomed to weigh the merits of individuals on an even balance, so that it may render to each person what reason requires. We therefore, though unworthy, preside over this holy see by heavenly grace. Considering the faith and devotion which, following in the footsteps of your predecessors, you are known to have toward us and the Roman Church, and also observing the disorder and decline of certain monasteries, both of nuns and of monks, in the city of Pavia, which belong immediately to the Roman Church, we have resolved to provide both for you and for them, though in different respects: namely, to refer their burden to your honor, since in ecclesiastical matters honor is joined to burden, and burden to honor.

Since among such monasteries two chiefly need the office of a guardian—Saint Mary outside the gate of Pavia, a convent of nuns, and Saint Bartholomew in Strata, a monastery of monks—we have resolved, with the counsel of our brethren, to entrust them, with their chapels, parishes, and appurtenances, to your administration in spiritual and temporal matters. In them you shall act in our stead: correcting and amending, appointing and removing, establishing and decreeing whatever you know to be expedient for those monasteries spiritually and temporally. So that through you both the burden of honor and the honor of burden may pass to your successors, by the authority of these presents we grant that your successors also may succeed you in this burden and honor, provided that they strive to show themselves such in devotion to the Apostolic See and in the care of those monasteries that they do not deserve to lose the privilege if they abuse the authority granted to them. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate this text of our grant. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 19 June, in the ninth year.

## XCIX. TO THE BISHOP OF SABINA

[Note: [Col. 0913D] See the notes to Letters 15 of Book III and 14 of Book V. See also Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 185.]

He is restored to the same position of defending the Church’s rights as his predecessor held. (Ferentino, 27 June.)

Because, owing to the long absence of Conrad of good memory, Bishop of Sabina, when he exercised pastoral care in the Church of Mainz, and owing to the neglect of those to whom the care of the bishopric of Sabina was entrusted at various times, the rights of that bishopric have been neglected, you humbly asked us to provide for you in this matter with paternal solicitude. Therefore, assenting to your petitions, both through pastoral care and by special favor, and with the counsel of our brethren, we restore you, so far as concerns defending the rights of that bishopric, to the position which he held when that same Conrad received the episcopal office of the Church of Sabina. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate this text of our grant. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 27 June, in the ninth year.

## C. TO P., CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SAINT MARCELLUS, AND B., CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SAINT SUSANNA, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

[Note: [Col. 0913D]

This letter is found, though very mutilated, among the Decretals, Book III, title 7, *On Institutions*, chapter 5. What is found there is presented here within brackets; variant readings have been appended.

See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §2.]

[Note: [Col. 0914D] This man has already been discussed several times.]

[Note: [Col. 0914D] The same.]

That they should admonish the patriarch of Constantinople not to admit Venetians as canons of Saint Sophia, but others, provided they are worthy. (Ferentino, 21 June.)

[Col. 0914D]

[For the adornment] [Note: [Col. 0914D] The words here distinguished in italics are absent from the Decretals, but are found in Pithou’s additions.] and advantage both of the Church of Holy Wisdom [Col. 0915A] and of the other churches built in the city of Constantinople, it is known to be fitting that learned men, conspicuous for uprightness of character, coming from whatever parts of the world, should be appointed in them. But, as has been reported to us, our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0915D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are those below which we have distinguished by italic type.] . . . . . the patriarch of Constantinople, forgetful of what we suggested to him orally and afterwards directed in writing—if indeed our letters reached him—despising clerics of other nations, strives to place only Venetians in those churches, and especially in the Church of Holy Wisdom. He does not consider that in every nation whoever does justice is acceptable to God, nor that God’s sanctuary ought by right to be possessed as a hereditary estate. Therefore, by these apostolic [Col. 0915B] letters, we command your discretion that you should endeavor to admonish and induce that same patriarch [Note: [Col. 0915D] The Decretals read: “admonish,” instead of “admonish and induce that he should endeavor.”] not to delay appointing religious, upright, and learned men, from whatever origin they derive, in the aforesaid churches, and especially in the greater one. Put before him that, if he does not take care to comply with your admonitions, he will render himself unworthy that you should compel clerics of other nations to obey him—especially since they have, on this account, considered it necessary to appeal to our hearing—and [Note: [Col. 0915D] The Decretals read “otherwise” for “put before him that, if he does not take care …”; below they read “nor” for “especially … and.”] you will not be able to conceal from us that you have reported this to us, so that from this very fact we may judge whether it is true that he is said to have promised it to the Venetians.] But if any clerics have been appointed in the aforesaid churches by you, or by either one of you, setting aside appeal, cause them to enjoy peaceful possession, having those removed, as justice requires, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, and cause them to be restored to the same churches. But if not both . . . either one of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year.

CII. To P., the illustrious king of Aragon. That the kings of Aragon may be crowned by the archbishop of Tarragona.

“With how great glory,” etc. Entirely identical with Letter 92 of Book VIII; see it (p. 734), together with the annotations there.

CII. [Note: [Col. 0915D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §34.] To the same. That the goods of heretics whom he exterminates may be for his own use. (Ferentino, 9 June.)

[Col. 0915D]

Since, according to evangelical truth, the laborer is worthy of his wages, and elsewhere it is written that the mouth of an ox treading grain ought not to be muzzled, it is much more fitting that he should be fostered with the reward of due remuneration [Col. 0916A] who, zealously upholding the divine law, works effectively for the extermination of those little foxes which attempt to destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts—as though seeking by crafty devices to abolish observance of the Christian faith—especially since, once they have been wholly excluded, that same vineyard can bear fruit more abundantly through works of mercy. Prudently moved by this consideration, by the authority of these presents we have thought fit to grant you that you may freely retain for your own use all movable goods of heretics and their supporters which come into your hands while you endeavor, out of zeal for the orthodox faith, to exterminate them. You may also retain, without prejudice to another’s right, immovable goods which you can wrest from their hands for this reason. Let no one therefore . . . infringe this our concession, etc. But if anyone [Col. 0916B] shall do so, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the ninth day before the Ides of June, in the ninth year.

CIII. [Note: [Col. 0915D]

See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §34.

See also Letter 97 of Book VIII.]

To P. of Castelnau and R., monks of Fontfroide, legates of the Apostolic See. That they assign the castle of Scura [Note: [Col. 0915D] It should be noted that Raynaldus, in the cited place, seems to have read “of Siuna.”] to the king of Aragon for the extirpation of heretics. (Ferentino, 9 June.)

Our dearest son in Christ, P., the illustrious king of Aragon, has shown us by his representation that the castle of Scurra, known to belong to the Roman Church, is so situated and fortified in a place among heretics that those heretics can be restrained from it more conveniently than from any other place. Therefore that king, as a zealous defender [Col. 0916C] of the divine law, has humbly asked us that, when he undertakes war against the aforesaid heretics, the castle itself may be made available to him for carrying out his praiseworthy purpose. Accordingly, commending in the Lord the pious intention of that king, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, when the same king is equipped in those regions to defeat and extirpate the aforesaid heretics, you are to cause the castle to be assigned to him, if necessity requires it; provided nevertheless that by this means the castle itself is in no way withdrawn from the lordship of the Apostolic See. If both of you cannot be present to execute these matters, either one of you shall nevertheless execute them.

Given at Ferentino, on the ninth day before the Ides of June, in the ninth year [Col. 0916D] of our pontificate.

CIV. [Note: [Col. 0916D] This letter is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, Book IV, title 15, *On Frigidity, Sorcery, and the Inability to Have Intercourse*, chapter 6. The words distinguished by italic type are absent from the Decretals or indicate variant readings.] To . . . . . the bishop of Auxerre. [Note: [Col. 0916D]

This letter of Innocent should be compared with what the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* say concerning the death of Hugh (of Noyers):

“In 1206 he founded canons of the Trinitarian order and made many grants to the religious of Fontenay, while he was on a journey to Rome, undertaken concerning various affairs of his church, chiefly in order to deprive the abbot of Saint-Germain of the use of the episcopal insignia. But within ten days of his arrival in the city, struck by a fatal illness, he died at Saint Clement’s on 29 September 1206, in the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate; he was buried in the Lateran basilica on 6 December, with a most celebrated funeral attended by the supreme pontiff and the college of cardinals.” *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, col. 299.

See Letter 20 of Book III, where it is said, through a typographical error, that Hugh died in 1205.]

That he decide concerning a certain marriage of the woman O. (Ferentino, 3 July.)

[We have received the letter of your brotherhood, containing [Col. 0917A] that Odeardis [Note: [Col. 0917D] In the Decretals: “O.”] entered into marriage with a certain man, with whom she lived for many years but could not be carnally known by him. Although you had been informed concerning this by your . . . archpriest, nevertheless, desiring [Note: [Col. 0917D] In the Decretals: “But you, desiring.”] to have fuller certainty on the matter, you summoned before yourself certain prudent and respectable matrons of her parish, strictly charging them, under peril to their souls, wisely to inspect the woman and carefully inquire whether she was fit for male embraces. Finally, on their faith, they firmly asserted to you that this woman could never be a mother or a wife, since she lacked the natural instrument. Therefore you pronounced a divorce between her and that man, inducing the woman [Col. 0917B] to enter some religious order, where she would preserve perpetual continence; and you granted the man [Note: [Col. 0917D] In the Decretals: “and to the man.”] permission to take a wife in the name of the Lord, since he desired to become a father. But it happened later that the same woman found one who unlocked locks of this kind, abandoning the continence which she had promised; and she who had had another husband married William [Note: [Col. 0917D] The Decretals add “and,” and immediately read “G.” for “and she … William.”], the bearer of these presents. On their behalf you humbly begged us to deal mercifully with them. Although, therefore, you have only partly explained to us how the said woman promised to observe continence—whether by a simple word or by a solemn vow; whether she entered religion as she promised, or, contrary to her promise, [Note: [Col. 0918D] The Decretals add “her.” Pithou notes in the margin that it is absent from the ancient copy.] remained at home; and how she had those locks opened, whether by the skill [Col. 0917C] of a physician, by intercourse with a man, or by any other means—yet, carefully considering that the impediment was not permanent, because, apart from a divine miracle, it could be removed by human action without bodily danger, we know that the sentence of divorce was pronounced through an error, albeit a probable one. For it is clear from the subsequent event that she could be known by him with whose like she is joined; and therefore we declare that marriage existed between that woman and her first husband. Wherefore we judge that no marriage exists between her and the aforesaid William [Note: [Col. 0918D] The Decretals: “between her and the aforesaid G.”], and we command that they be separated from one another. If the aforesaid woman entered religion, as she is asserted to have promised, [Note: [Col. 0918D] The Decretals read, “as she asserts she promised.” Pithou notes in the margin that these words are absent from all Vatican manuscripts, but are read in other later ones and in the ancient Compilation. Immediately afterward the Decretals read “her” for “that woman.”] the first husband, who did not know [Col. 0917D] her, is to remain with the woman whom he subsequently married by authority of the Church. Otherwise, that same man, having dismissed her whom he subsequently married, must [Col. 0918A] return to this woman with whom he first contracted marriage, unless the woman herself has bound herself by a vow to observe continence—so that she is understood thereby to have fornicated with the aforesaid William—or unless she has joined herself adulterously to another man, so that the first husband may wish, on the ground of the fornication she committed, to avoid living with her. For if she promised only by a simple word to observe continence and afterwards, while this point was doubtful, married the said William in the sight of the Church [Note: [Col. 0918D] The Decretals: “G.” Below they read “these things” for “this,” and “her” for “that woman.”], it must not be presumed that she was fornicating with him; but henceforth she must by no means remain with him.

By this you will also know the solution of the question whether a woman so constricted that she cannot have carnal intercourse with anyone unless an incision is made, or some other [Col. 0918B] violence [Note: [Col. 0918D] Another reading, as Pithou notes in the margin: “similar means.”] is inflicted upon her—not merely slight violence, but perhaps so serious that danger of death is feared from it—ought to be declared fit to contract marriage. Likewise, if a woman is so constricted for the husband whom she married that she can never be deflowered by him, and, after being separated from him [Note: [Col. 0918D] The Decretals add “she has been,” and immediately afterward read “and afterward prepared”; below they read “him” for “that man.”] by judgment of the Church, marries another man for whom she is not constricted, and through frequent intercourse with the second becomes fit even for the first, whether she ought to return to him with whom she first entered into the marital covenant. Such cases, however, are not easy to judge, since the final judgment depends upon the future.] Therefore, in accordance with the distinctions set out above, cause what we have decreed to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

[Col. 0918C] Given at Ferentino, on the third day before the Nones of July, in the ninth year.

CV. To . . . . . the provost and chapter of Saint Peter of Ronais. That they receive the cleric Walter as a canon. (Ferentino, 12 June.)

Although unworthy, we are successors of him to whom the Lord commanded that he should feed His sheep; we are especially bound by paternal concern to assist in their necessities those whose learning and praiseworthy conduct we have come to know with greater certainty from the time which they are known to have spent at the Apostolic See. Therefore we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole body and, by these apostolic letters, command you [Col. 0918D] that, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, you generously receive as your brother and canon our beloved son Master Walter, a poor cleric who has conducted himself praiseworthily for a long time at the Apostolic See [Col. 0919A], so that, besides his service, which we regard as useful to you, you may also obtain a fuller measure of our favor if we are heard on his behalf.

Given at Ferentino, on the twelfth day before the Ides of June, in the ninth year.

CVI. [Note: [Col. 0919] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] To M., abbess of the monastery of Saints Innocent and Anastasius at Gandersheim [Note: [Col. 0919] See Letters 43 and 44 of Book VIII, and the notes there.], and to her sisters to be regularly appointed. They are received under protection. (Ferentino, 22 June.)

The Apostolic See [Col. 0919B] ought to grant protection to prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion, with lamps kindled, continually prepare themselves by works of holiness to go out and meet the Bridegroom, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or weaken—God forbid!—the strength of their sacred religious life. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, after the example of Agapitus and John, popes of Rome, our predecessors of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery at Gandersheim—which belongs to the Roman Church without any intermediary and is known to have been built upon the land and property of blessed Peter—where you are devoted to divine service, together with the clerics and all ministerials belonging to that monastery. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order hitherto observed there shall be observed inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s provision, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the place itself where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with the town, mint, toll, market, and all its appurtenances within the town; the church of Saint Mary, in which is the convent of nuns; the church of Saint Boniface at Brunesthosuse, where there are enclosed nuns [Col. 0919D] and a regular provost; the monastery of Clusa, where there are Black Monks, and the church of Saint George—all of which, near the town of Gandersheim, have been built upon the land and property of blessed Peter; the estate at Denghte, with its churches and all appurtenances; the estate of Hollenstod, with its appurtenances; the estate of Herreshusen, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Vanceleve, with parish, estate, and all its appurtenances; Ericae and Dennestede, with churches, estates, and all appurtenances; the estate at Gheneldohursen, with parish, churches, and all its appurtenances [Col. 0920A]; the castle of Bruchen, with churches, five hundred royal manses, forests, and every woodland resource; the castle of Dernebruch; the estate of Vochusen, with churches and appurtenances; Alnelincherot, with churches, mint, and all appurtenances; Crucht, Calchem, and Blithestroph, with churches, vineyards, and all their appurtenances; the church at Retineroth; the castle of Dalem, with churches and all appurtenances; the church at Kericherbech, the chapel at Schusen, and the tithes which you possess in the dioceses of Cologne, Halberstadt, and Hildesheim.

Furthermore, no one may presume to demand or extort from you tithes from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. Nor, after making profession there [Col. 0920B], may anyone lawfully depart from that place without the abbess’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life. No one may dare retain one who departs without letters of authorization from the community. Moreover, we wholly forbid the imposition of new and unlawful exactions by archbishops, bishops, deans, archdeacons, or any other ecclesiastical or secular persons. We command that chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, ordinations of your canons and chaplains who are to be promoted to holy orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments, be supplied to you without any improper charge by whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided that he enjoys communion and favor with the Apostolic See. We further forbid every priest of any church, apart from the Apostolic See, to exercise any jurisdiction in your monastery. For by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul we command that no king, margrave, count, or other secular person shall have leave to grant the monastery itself in benefice to any persons, so that, as it stands subject to the Apostolic See by the stability of this privilege, it may remain securely endowed; and that it may enjoy in perpetual security, free from contradiction by any person, the places and things which it now has or possesses, and which divine mercy may in future increase within the monastery’s right through gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful.

Upon the death of you, the present abbess of that place, or of any successor of yours [Col. 0920D], no one is to be placed over it through any contrivance of deception or violence, except one whom the sisters by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall provide to be elected from the community of that monastery itself, if a suitable person is found there, in the fear of God. We also confirm by apostolic authority, and by the present writing, etc., the liberties and immunities granted to your monastery by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and likewise the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person [Col. 0921A] may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in non-exempt churches, the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, etc., let him be subject to punishment: but to all who preserve the rights of that place, etc., unto the end.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint [Col. 0921B] Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twenty-second day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1206 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CVII. [Note: [Col. 0921D] This letter is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, Book II, title 20, *On Prescriptions*, chapter 14, where it is said to be directed to the abbots Hel. and Gu.] To . . . . . the abbots of Helwatheshusen and . . . . of Herwetheshusen [Note: [Col. 0921D] “To the abbots of Helwatheshusen and Herwetheshusen.” This seems the proper reading in Conti’s transcript. In the Decretals there are only “to the abbots Hel. and Gu.” Pithou notes that an old manuscript reads: “to the abbots of Helevartesnen and Hel. Wertesnen”; elsewhere also, “to the abbots Helien. and W.” We frankly confess our ignorance of which monasteries these are, to whose abbots this letter is directed; perhaps we may be forgiven, since the manuscripts agree neither on the names nor on their spelling.], and to . . . . . the dean of Paderborn. It is declared that, in a prescription of one hundred years against the Roman Church, the periods of schism are to be deducted. (Ferentino, 17 June.)

[Since by other letters] [Note: [Col. 0921D] The following words, here distinguished in italics, are absent from the Decretals but are found in Pithou’s additions.] we gave you instructions [Note: [Col. 0921D] In Pithou’s additions: “we have given.”] that, in the case known to be litigated between the church of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0921D] In Pithou: “Hildensem.”] on the one side, and the church of Gandersheim [Col. 0921C] [Note: [Col. 0921D] In Pithou: “Gand.”] and the Roman Church on the other, you should receive witnesses to prove prescription, we have thought fit by the present communication to declare to you that, after prescription is said to have begun against the aforesaid monastery and its liberty, the disruption of three schisms against the Roman Church intervened. Although it has been established by both legal and canonical definition that against the most holy Roman Church, which enjoys a special privilege, only prescription of one hundred years can take effect, we nevertheless do not wish the periods of intervening schisms, which according to the order of law impede the running of prescription, to be counted at all; rather, after careful consideration, they are to be deducted from the computation of time.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year.

CVIII. [Note: [Col. 0921D]

This letter is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, Book II, title 30, *On Useful or Useless Confirmation*, [Col. 0922D] chapter 4, where it is said to be directed to the dean of Paderborn.

It should be noted that it is almost the same as Letter 84 of Book XI.]

To the same. That they proceed in a specified manner concerning the adjudication of the subjection of the monastery of Gandersheim to the Church of Hildesheim. [Note: [Col. 0922D] See Letter 44 of Book VIII.] (Ferentino, 17 June.)

[When the beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and sisters of the church of Gandersheim [Note: [Col. 0922D] In the Decretals: “Garderen”; in Pithou’s margin: other readings, “Giudion,” “Gardenovens,” “Gerundus.”] desired to have their privileges renewed, they humbly petitioned us to write to certain persons who would carefully inspect the privileges of that [Col. 0922B] church, which [Note: [Col. 0922D] Absent from the Decretals. The Decretals add “distance, and.”] could not safely be sent to us because of the dangers of the roads, faithfully transcribe their tenor, and present them to us under their seals. But we, acceding to their petitions, [Note: [Col. 0922D] These words are absent from the Decretals.] charged four bishops and an equal number of abbots with carrying this out, [Note: [Col. 0922D] The Decretals read: “we thought fit to command that they inspect them carefully and, faithfully transcribing their tenor, send them to us under their seals.”] and they, [Note: [Col. 0922D] The following words, here distinguished in italics, are absent from the Decretals but are found in Pithou’s additions.] obeying the apostolic command, carefully inspected the privileges of Agapitus and John [Note: [Col. 0922D] Pithou adds: “pontiffs.”], our predecessors of happy memory, which had been presented to them, [Note: [Col. 0922D] “In their presence.”] and faithfully sent us their tenor under their seals. Our venerable brother G., archbishop of Reims, then bishop of Palestrina and exercising in those regions the office of legate, also caused the tenor of those privileges to be presented to us under [Col. 0922C] his own seal.

Giving due credence both to the legate [Note: [Col. 0922D] The Decretals add: “who caused them to be presented to us under his own seal”; immediately afterwards they add these words after “inquiry,” and read “Hildesheim … alleged” for “the canons … were alleging.”] and to the investigators, although we did not see why those privileges should not be renewed, nevertheless, because C., canon of the greater church, and J., canon of Holy Cross at Hildesheim, appearing before us, alleged that the Church of Hildesheim had been in possession of the subjection of that monastery for one hundred years and more, we did not then think fit to renew the privileges. But, in order to preserve justice both to the monastery and to that church, we gave instructions to the beloved sons . . . . . the abbot of Pigavien . . . [the abbot] of Corbejen, and . . . . . the abbot of Saint Michael of the Stone [Col. 0923A] [Note: [Col. 0923C] The Decretals read “therefore, to the judges,” for “but … abbots.”] that, coming together at a suitable place, [Note: [Col. 0923C] Absent from the Decretals, which immediately read “them” for “all.”] after summoning those to be summoned, they should carefully investigate the truth in all matters and, proceeding as far as final sentence, faithfully send all the proceedings, recorded under the testimony of their letters, to the Apostolic See, setting the parties a suitable term at which they should appear before us to receive judgment. They, desiring to carry out the apostolic mandate, summoned the parties before them; and when they wished to proceed in the case, the party of the Church of Hildesheim appealed to the Apostolic See on account of a certain interlocutory ruling which they had made. [Note: [Col. 0923C] The Decretals read “by whom only” for “and as far as … had made.”] For this reason those judges could not proceed in the case. [Note: [Col. 0923D] Absent from the Decretals, which immediately read “the parties appearing” again.]

Recently, when the parties had appeared before us [Col. 0923B], the aforesaid abbess urgently requested that we renew her church’s privileges, especially since before the delegated judges the party of the Church of Hildesheim had sought to show or prove nothing that would derogate in any respect from the monastery or its privileges. [Note: [Col. 0923D] These words are omitted by the Decretals, as is immediately afterward the word “urgently.”] On the other side, it was urgently requested that we should deign to entrust the case to prudent men, who would receive the witnesses whom they proposed to produce against the monastery’s privileges and to prove lawful prescription. For our part, carefully [Note: [Col. 0923D] The Decretals read “therefore,” and immediately “was prudently established” for “was established by provident deliberation.”] considering that civil law has wisely established that, when there is fear of losing witnesses, lest the truth be concealed and the ability to prove be removed by unforeseen events, sick witnesses and others concerning whom there is fear for some reason may be admitted to testify even before joinder of issue, we were moved by the analogy of the same equity to renew the aforesaid privileges, since they were apparently already worn away by excessive age and had been written not on parchment but on papyrus. We did not wish, however, that by such renewal the monastery should acquire a new right, but that its ancient right, if it possesses one, should be confirmed through the renewed privilege. [Note: [Col. 0923D] The Decretals read “but its ancient [right],” and afterwards “renewal of the privilege”; they have “aforesaid” for “ancient.”]

Since the aforesaid monastery is shown by the privileges of our predecessors to belong to the right and property of the Apostolic See, lest the right of the Roman Church remain undefended, we appointed the same abbess its procurator, so that, because against the possessions and rights of the Roman Church prescription runs only for one hundred years, she might prosecute on our behalf this matter and other matters which are to be prosecuted before you [Note: [Col. 0923D] The Decretals: “before you” (singular).] in court. Therefore, not wishing the status of the monastery to remain uncertain any longer, whereby the case might remain undecided further, by apostolic letters we command and direct your discretion [Note: [Col. 0923D] The Decretals omit “that”; immediately afterward, “and direct.”] that, choosing a safe and convenient place, within six months after receipt of the present letters, you receive [Note: [Col. 0923D] The Decretals read singular: “choosing … you receive.”] the witnesses whom the Church of Hildesheim considers ought to be produced to prove prescription [Col. 0924B], or whom the monastery of Gandersheim considers ought to be produced to show interruption. [Note: [Col. 0923D] Omitted by the Decretals.] And, if it proves lawful prescription as it claims, unless prescription has been proved [Note: [Col. 0923D] The Decretals read “interruption,” and below “the aforesaid bishop” for “the same [abbess],” corrupting “to corrupt,” “imposing” for “they imposing,” and “you pronounce” for “they pronounce.”] on the other side, adjudge the subjection of that monastery to it, since it is established that the monastery lies within its diocese, and annul the privilege which we caused to be renewed for the monastery. Otherwise, imposing perpetual silence upon it concerning this matter, pronounce that the monastery enjoys perpetual liberty, its privilege from us being delivered up.] But concerning the witnesses, etc. And if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year.

CIX. [Note: [Col. 0923D] Various fragments of this letter are found in the Decretals, Book II, title 7, *On the Oath against Calumny*, chapter 6; and title 20, *On Witnesses and Testimonies*, chapter 37.] To . . . . . the bishop of Piacenza. [Note: [Col. 0924C] See Letter 75 of Book V, note.] That in the case pending between the people of Ravenna and Faenza he receive a specified number of witnesses. (Ferentino, 22 June.)

[Col. 0924C]

[[Note: [Col. 0924C] See the Decretals, Book II, title 20, *On Witnesses and Testimonies*, chapter 37.] Since the case which is known to be litigated between our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0924C] Absent from the Decretals.] . . . the archbishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0924C] See Letter 6 of Book V, note.] and our beloved sons, the commune of Faenza, [Note: [Col. 0924C] The following words, here distinguished in italics, are absent from the Decretals but are found in Pithou’s additions.] concerning the village of Luci and Saint Polito, and the castle of Aureoli, and their district, honour, and jurisdiction, is being contested [Note: [Col. 0924D]

“In the year 1203, Albert, archbishop of Ravenna, brought suit against the people of Faenza concerning Luci and the village of Saint Polito.” Rubeus, Book VI, p. 369.

“In 1204, there was a proceeding in the lawsuit between Albert, archbishop of Ravenna, and the community of Faenza concerning the jurisdiction and lordship of Luci, Saint Polito, Aureoli, and other castles possessed by the people of Faenza, but claimed on the other hand by the archbishop. There survive two letters of Pope Innocent III to the bishop of Piacenza, entrusting the case to him; they are inserted in the Decretals under the chapter *Cum causam*, concerning witnesses and testimonies, and under the chapter *Licet causam*, concerning proofs. According to Tonducci, p. 235. But the lawsuit was not settled.

“In 1207, in the time of Pope Innocent, while the imperial throne was vacant, on the second day of December, in the tenth indiction, at Faenza in the church of Saint Peter, Orlandus, provost of the church of Faenza, and Martinus Auliverii submitted to the arbitration of the wise Lord Thebaldus the lawsuit between them, before Theophilus, notary of Faenza. From the Azzurini papers, bundle IV.

“In 1207 Aegidius, archbishop of Ravenna, received from Anastasius 700 Ravenna pounds to be spent on the case with the people of Faenza, namely concerning Lucum, Saint Polito, and Aureolum. From the archive of the archbishopric of Ravenna, chapter D, nos. 931, 942.” *Monumenta Faventina*, in Mittarelli, *Accessiones Faventinae*, col. 463 ff.]
, had been committed by us to different judges; but because [Note: [Col. 0925D] “We deemed it should be committed.”] it could not be brought to its due conclusion through some of them [Note: [Col. 0925D] “Nor could it have been.”] [thus far in the Decretals and in Pithou], we, wishing to put an end to the litigation, at last gave orders by our letters to our venerable brother …, bishop of Feretrano, and our beloved son …, abbot of Galeata: notwithstanding the commissions hitherto obtained, and with every ground and exception set aside, they were to assign the parties a period of three months, within which they should produce all witnesses whom they deemed should be produced in this case; and, after diligently examining them and faithfully putting their depositions into writing, they were, if the parties so wished, to settle the case by means of justice. Otherwise, sending the depositions, together with the instruments and other arguments, to our presence, they were to fix for the parties a suitable term at which they should appear before us to receive judgment.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid delegates had made no progress, [Note: [Col. 0925D] Decretals, book II, title 7, *On the oath against calumny*, chapter 6.] [we ordered the parties to appear before us concerning the case itself. Their procurators, having been constituted in our presence with instruments concerning ratification, disputed before us for some time concerning the joinder of issue, the reception of certain witnesses, and many exceptions. At length we caused the petition of the archbishop himself to be presented through his procurator, and the other party to answer it; and, after the interrogations and replies had been put in writing, and the suit had been fully joined before us, we caused the oath against calumny to be taken on both sides.] [Note: [Col. 0925D] These words are absent from the Decretals.]

[Col. 0925C]

[Note: [Col. 0925D] Ibid., title 20, *On witnesses and depositions*, chapter 37. The passages marked below in italic type are absent from the Decretals.]

But because it would be excessively burdensome to both parties to produce witnesses before us, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters, relying fully upon you, that within three months after receiving the present letters you receive, without appeal, the witnesses whom either party considers should be produced, both concerning the principal matter and concerning the persons of the witnesses; that you see that they are diligently examined; and that, prudently inquiring into every circumstance—namely causes, persons, place, time, hearing, sight, knowledge, belief, reputation, and certainty—you write down everything fully and carefully and faithfully transmit it to us under your seal. You shall direct the parties to come before us thus prepared, so that, once the depositions have been published and the instruments produced, after sufficient pleadings have been made, they may, God being the author, receive from us a just judgment. But the witnesses, etc.

If, moreover, the people of Faenza or others should presume to hinder those whom the said archbishop considers should be produced to bear testimony to the truth, then, after prior admonition, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to cease from such presumption.

Desiring, however, that the unbridled multitude of witnesses be restrained, we command that [Note: [Col. 0925D] The Decretals read: “We wish that on either side”—omitting what immediately follows, “our venerable brother,” and below reading *Pompon* for *Pomposiano*.] you permit the number of witnesses on either side not to exceed forty. Thus, if the people of Faenza wish the witness-depositions received by our venerable brother …, bishop of Ferrara, and by the abbot of Pomposa, to stand as valid, those witnesses shall be counted in the aforesaid number; otherwise, since those depositions are sealed, the same witnesses shall be produced again if necessary.

Given at Ferentino, 22 June, in the ninth year.

CX. [Note: [Col. 0925D] This letter is found among the Decretals, book II, title 23, *On presumptions*, chapter 14.] To W., bishop of Nevers, [Note: [Col. 0925D] See letter 11 of book V, note.] and to H., archdeacon of Bourges. He entrusts to them the case of W., a certain burgess of La Charité suspected of heresy. [Note: [Col. 0925D] On the subject of this letter, see letters 63 and 99 of book II; 36 of book V; and 66 and 239 of book VI.] (Ferentino, 1 June.)

[Col. 0926C]

[We have received your letters stating that, when the case pending [Note: [Col. 0926C] In the Decretals, “is pending,” omitting immediately thereafter “our beloved son …”] between our venerable brother …, [Note: [Col. 0926C] See letters 20 of book III and 104 of book IX.] bishop of Auxerre, and certain burgesses of La Charité [Note:

Robert, monk of St. Marianus of Auxerre, in the *Chronology* published at Troyes in 1608 by Nicolas Camusat, canon of Troyes, fol. 95: “In the year 1198 … at the village called La Charité, certain exceedingly wealthy men, notorious for the Poplicanian heresy, having absented themselves on the day when they had been summoned to clear themselves of this infamy, were cut off from the Church and delivered to the public authority.”

The same author, fols. 101–102: “In the year of the Lord 1206, Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, having gone to Rome, died there … He applied himself vigorously to persecuting the heretics called Bulgars; and through his insistence it came about that many were stripped of their property, others were banished, and others burned.”]

, whom that bishop charged with heresy, had been delegated by the Apostolic See to you [Note: [Col. 0926D] That is, to the bishop of Nevers; see the notes to Innocent’s letters cited above, note 444. The same monk Robert, at the same page: “At the city of Nevers also, the abbot of St. Martin and the dean of the greater church, accused of this most pestilential error, were brought before a council of bishops convened at Sens; there the abbot was deposed, the dean suspended, and they were then sent to the Apostolic See.”] and to our beloved son …, [Note: [Col. 0926D] The abbot of Callovium. In the Decretals, “abbot of Callon”; where Pithou remarks: “An old copy has *Colomnensi*; another, *Colonensi*; another, *Calonicensi*. Columna, of the Cistercian Order, diocese of Bourges.” We confess that a monastery of Columna in the diocese of Bourges is unknown to us. Certainly the name Columna is found nowhere, either in the particular list of monasteries, ancient and still existing, in the diocese of Bourges given by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, or in the general index of French abbeys in the Sammarthani, vol. IV. It must therefore unquestionably be read as we print it here, *Callovii*, the name of a monastery in the diocese of Bourges, in French Chalivoy. Armand I, abbot of this monastery after Bernard—whose name appears in charters before 1198—is found in documents from 1220 to 1233. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. II, col. 193.] abbot of Callovium [Note: [Col. 0927A] The Decretals read “Collonensi,” and immediately omit the words “at last … resolved.”], both parties at length, so that the protracted business might more easily be brought to conclusion, appointed you two as their arbitrators under a specified penalty, while nevertheless reserving the delegated authority to you.

But W., the bearer of these letters, one of those whom the aforesaid bishop charged, had publicly confessed his heresy at La Charité and had likewise acknowledged concerning a certain brother of his that he laboured with him under the same error.] [Note: [Col. 0927D] What follows, marked here in italic type, is absent from the Decretals but is found in Pithou’s additions.]

When he was questioned concerning his faith before our venerable brother …, archbishop of Bourges, and purification was imposed upon him through this same W., who was believed to be truly penitent and Catholic, [Note: [Col. 0928C] Pithou adds “then.”] W. himself, having sworn an oath, cleared his brother—whom he had publicly asserted to be [Note: [Col. 0928C] Omitted.] a heretic—[Col. 0927B] of the charge. [Note: [Col. 0928C] Pithou: “affirmed that he was Catholic,” and shortly after reads “the bishop had jurisdiction over him.”] Thus the aforesaid bishop maintained that he had made two contrary statements, and therefore regarded him as both perjurer and heretic.

On the other hand, W. himself maintained that, although he had publicly confessed something concerning himself, he had nevertheless confessed nothing concerning his brother. He could therefore properly have cleared him, especially since he had heard from two chaplains of Aubigny [Note: [Col. 0928D] Pithou’s marginal note: Aubigny, in French.]—who, he says, knew that man’s conscience [Note: [Col. 0928D] Pithou adds “he says.”]—that he could safely clear him as a Catholic. He later showed you their letters. But the bishop immediately convicted him before you, through himself, a priest, and another deacon, on the point that he had denied what concerned his brother; hence he called him a relapsed heretic.

You, therefore, observing these notable inconsistencies in the aforesaid W., sent him with your letters to our presence, having meanwhile sequestrated his goods until we should determine what ought to be decided concerning his person and property. You added that, although W., together with certain others, urged before you that you receive his purification, as you had received that of certain others, you declined to admit his oath because he seemed inconsistent with himself; nevertheless, you admitted a purification on his behalf by the eighth hand of worthy men. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Pithou: “by eight men.”]

Since the little foxes which strive to destroy the Lord’s vineyard must be caught with vigilant care—for foxes have holes and birds of heaven nests—[Note: [Col. 0928D] What follows, enclosed in brackets, is found in the Decretals.] we have, from the matters written above, a strong suspicion of heresy concerning the oft-mentioned W. [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Decretals read “the aforesaid G.” and shortly thereafter “we had” for “we have”; they omit what follows, “since … according to the faith.”]: both because he afterwards denied having said what he had said before, as he was convicted before you, and because either he first lied against his brother by asserting him to be a heretic, or later committed perjury against God by clearing him of heresy. Either course makes him highly suspect. Yet it appears more probable that, at the time when, as one truly penitent, he was returning from heresy to the faith, he would not have uttered so grave a lie, especially against a brother whom he had not everywhere asserted to be a legitimate [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Decretals read “most beloved.”] heretic unless he had been inflamed with zeal for the orthodox faith. It is therefore presumed that, when he later cleared him [Col. 0928B] of heresy, he shamefully committed perjury.

Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Decretals omit “that” and shortly thereafter “indeed”; below they read “receive” for “received,” “directing” for “direct,” and “truly” for “indeed.”] that, since we do not wish him to be condemned for so grave a crime upon suspicion alone, however vehement, you receive from him such and so great security, beyond the sworn assurance, that he ought to be restrained by fear of temporal punishment; impose upon him a fitting penance, by which it may appear whether he walks in darkness or in light, and whether he is truly penitent or falsely converted. If in this way you ascertain that he is truly Catholic, do not permit him to be unduly troubled; otherwise condemn him as a heretic.

Given at Ferentino, 1 June, in the ninth year.

CXI. To … bishop, [Note: [Col. 0928D] See letter 78 of book V, note.] Master Guido, archdeacon of Limoges, and … abbot of Bulle, [Note:

“Gerald, abbot of Bulle, in 1200; he is mentioned in the necrology on 24 October.

VI. Bargudus, or Bargaudus, is mentioned in the obituary on 9 March; he was alive about the year 1200.” *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. II, col. 632.]

in the diocese of Limoges. He entrusts to them the case pending between the abbot and convent of Mauzac on one side and the Templars of La Tourette on the other, concerning the tithes of the lands of Sancolt. (Ferentino, 1 July.)

[Col. 0928C]

When our beloved sons, Master Zacharias, …, procurators of the abbot [Note: [Col. 0929D] See letter 88 of book IX, note.] and convent of Mauzac on one side, and Brother Peter, procurator of the Templars of La Tourette, on the other, came into our presence, we appointed our beloved son J., our subdeacon and chaplain, as auditor. Before him the procurator of the abbot and monks alleged that, although they had long possessed in peace the tithes of the lands of Sancolt before those lands came under the power and lordship of the Templars, and although after the Templars acquired the said lands they had peacefully received the tithes of them for forty years and more, the Templars did not hesitate to withhold those tithes from them, inflicting other grievous injuries upon them. Although they had obtained our letters concerning these matters and at times submitted to arbitrators, they had thus far been unable to obtain their right through the obstructive malice of the Templars.

Conversely, the procurator of the Templars alleged that, protected by the privileges of Roman pontiffs not to be bound to pay tithes from lands which they cultivate with their own hands or at their own expense, they were nevertheless continually and improperly harassed by the aforesaid abbot and monks, who in other respects committed very many wrongs against them. Since we had committed to our venerable brothers …, archbishop of Bourges, [Note: [Col. 0929D] See letter 43 of book III, note.] and …, bishop of Clermont, [Note: [Col. 0929D] See letter 136 of book V, note.] the case pending between them and the aforesaid monks concerning these tithes, certain monks, while the question was being handled before them, gathered a multitude of armed men and violently entered the Templars’ lands. They carried away the crops as they pleased and burned the remainder with fire.

Having more fully understood these and other matters alleged before the said chaplain, and because full proof could not be made before us concerning them, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after fuller investigation of the truth, if the abbot and monks sufficiently show that they have received continuously, without litigation, the tithes from the aforesaid lands from the Templars for forty years, you compel the Templars, with appeal set aside, to pay them those tithes. For since they paid tithes for so long a period contrary to granted privileges, they are presumed tacitly to have renounced those privileges. If, however, the monks fail in proof, absolve the Templars from their claim, imposing perpetual silence upon the monks concerning this matter, without appeal. Hear also what either side wishes to allege concerning the remaining matters; and, with appeal set aside, cause what you determine to be just to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. But the witnesses, etc. And if not all, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 1 July, in the ninth year.

CXII. To Hugh, canon of St. Genoulf of Toul; W., canon of the church of Liverdun; and Lambert, canon of Linciennes in the diocese of Toul. He entrusts to them the case pending between G., a priest, on one side and the abbot of St. Leo of Toul on the other, concerning the spoliation of the benefice of Nais. (Ferentino, 9 July.)

The case pending between G., a priest, on one side, and the abbot of St. Leo of Toul [Note:

“VII. Clement, abbot of St. Leo of Toul, received the church of Manili from Bishop Matthew in 1204. He is recorded in the necrology on 2 April.

VIII. Hervinus occurs in a charter of Henry, count of Bar, in 1214; in the necrology he is called the eighth abbot.” *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XIII, col. 1107.

See letter 212 of book VI, note.]

and his canons on the other, concerning the spoliation of a certain benefice of the church of Nais with its appurtenances—which that priest alleged he had canonically obtained from the predecessor of the said abbot—we committed to your examination for settlement, beloved sons Hugh, canon of Toul, and W., canon of Liverdun. But although you had caused the same priest to be put in possession of the benefice, he complains that he was ejected from that possession without observance of legal procedure, by reason of certain forged letters which purported to be sent in our name to the abbots of the monastery of Moyen [Note: [Col. 0930D] Simon, abbot of the monastery of Moyen, occurs in instruments from 1193 until at least 1206. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XIII, col. 1404.] and Senones [Note: [Col. 0930D] Henry I, abbot of Senones, ruled for twenty years, from 1204 to 1225. Ibid., col. 1388.] and to the … prior of Belle-Lieu.

Since we consider those revocatory letters suspicious, because they state that the case had been brought to us by appeal from the hearing of judges who were hearing it by our delegation—whereas in our letters we rather deny than affirm that it had been brought by appeal from the hearing of judges who were not hearing the case by our delegation—we commit the matter to you for settlement. By apostolic letters we command your discretion to investigate diligently the truth both concerning the seal of those letters and concerning the letters themselves. If you find this to be so, or if the forgery otherwise becomes clear to you, punish those who used such letters with the penalty decreed against forgers; and, setting aside the obstacle of appeal, revoke as void whatever you learn was done less lawfully to the prejudice of the aforesaid priest. In the case itself proceed according to the tenor of the former letters, by means of justice. But witnesses: no letters, etc. And if not all … two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 9 July, in the ninth year.

CXIII. [Note: [Col. 0931C] Various fragments of this letter are found among the Decretals: first, book II, title 23, *On presumptions*, chapter 13; second, book V, title 34, *On canonical purgation*, chapter 12. Passages found in both places are here enclosed in brackets, and variant readings have also been supplied. The same letter, though mutilated, may be read in the Register of year XIII, no. 12, in Baluze, vol. II, p. 415, where it is said to have been copied from the Register of this ninth year.] To the bishop of Cenad and the … abbot of Cikedór. [Note: [Col. 0931D] In the Decretals it is addressed to the bishop of Genad and the abbot of Deciquorum. Pithou notes: “The old assessment of benefices mentions Chionadensis and Cenadiensis.” Elsewhere *de Ciquedor* or *de Ciquor* is read for *Deciquorum*. But in the Register of year VIII, no. 98, it is *de Stekedor*.] That they should protect and defend the bishop of Pécs, who had been falsely accused. [Note: [Col. 0931D] On the subject of this letter, see letters 196 of book VI; 159 and 225 of book VII; and 88, 98, 139, and 140 of book VIII.] (Ferentino, 7 July.)

[Col. 0931A]

[Note: [Col. 0931D] See the Decretals, book II, title 23, *On presumptions*, chapter 15.]

[Since in his youth our venerable brother O., bishop of Pécs, [Note: [Col. 0931D] The Decretals omit “that,” as well as shortly afterwards “by the Apostolic See”; below they read “the pallium” for “the adornment of the pallium,” and “came” for “had come.”] showed himself so mature, honourable, and prudent that, because of the sweet fragrance of his uprightness, he deserved to be adorned by the Roman Church with the ornament of the pallium, it is not lightly to be believed that, after reaching old age, he shamefully cast off the Lord’s yoke by embracing the stench and foulness [Note: [Col. 0931D] Omitted in the Decretals.] of lust. Such a stain, indeed, though sometimes contracted in youth, is more often expiated in old age.

Who, moreover, would readily believe that a man endowed with literary learning, forgetful of his own salvation, would turn himself to the disgrace of such a passion as to perpetrate abominable incest with his own niece, when even according to the opinions of the pagans the natural bond between such persons permits no suspicion of so foul a crime? Although King Emeric of illustrious memory [Note: [Col. 0931D] The Decretals read “king of Hungary” and below omit “at times,” “humbly,” and “urgently.”] had at times accused that bishop before us through messengers and letters of such a crime, humbly and urgently asking that we immediately [Note: [Col. 0932C] The Decretals read “as an example,” and shortly afterwards omit “from the Hungarian Church” and the words “since … manifest.”] remove so pernicious an evil from the Hungarian Church, yet, because his allegation seemed to proceed not from the root of charity but from the fuel of hatred—since he did not cease to persecute him as an enemy, as is manifest throughout the whole province—we did not wish to incline our ears to what were, as it were, malicious accusations. Rather, in order to test the spirits whether they were from God, we instructed the bishop of Győr, [Note: [Col. 0931C] “Whether the Spirit were from God,” bishop of Auria. Pithou’s marginal note observes that elsewhere it is read “of Genoa.”] of blessed memory, prudently and cautiously to inquire of his fellow bishops whether they believed the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0932D] Omitted in the Decretals.] bishop to be stained by such a disgrace. They subsequently wrote to us that they believed him a man of honourable conduct, commending his person in many ways.] [Note:

Thus far in the Decretals, book II, title 23, chapter 15.

What follows is found there in book V, title 34, *On canonical purgation*, chapter 12.]

[Col. 0932A]

[But because a father chastises the son whom he loves, we admonished the same bishop by our letters, directing him, for greater caution, [Note: [Col. 0932D] “We directed by our letters, for greater caution, the bishop of Quinquecclesiensis [as Pithou notes, another reading is ‘of Pécs’].”] to abstain from familiarity with her and to conduct himself before God and men [Note: [Col. 0932D] Absent from the Decretals, as are the passages marked below in italic type.] in such a manner that no sinister suspicion could be entertained concerning him. But an enemy, having surreptitiously obtained the reply to those letters, wickedly published it before the aforesaid king and the magnates of the realm, so that the bishop might thereby be further defamed, since he appeared to us unbelievable and suspect. Observing so great a wickedness of his rivals, although we were frequently urged against him, we could never be moved against him, knowing that a multitude easily follows its leader. [Note: [Col. 0932D] The Decretals read “the dictum of one man.”]

When, however, the same bishop was proposed for the metropolitan see of Esztergom, certain persons who opposed him in that election tried to rekindle the embers of that accusation in order more easily to obstruct his promotion. Accordingly, one of his procurators, appearing before us, on the advice of certain of his friends—who had a good zeal in this matter, but not according to knowledge—began insistently to request before us, in the presence of our brethren, that we order canonical purgation to be imposed upon the bishop, so that he might demonstrate his innocence.

We regarded this request as insufficiently prudent, indeed exceedingly imprudent, and often wished to withdraw that procurator from it, [Note: [Col. 0932D] What follows, marked here in italic type, is absent from the Decretals but is found in Pithou’s additions.] both because the oft-mentioned bishop did not seem to be defamed for that crime among good and serious persons—since his fellow bishops, [Note: [Col. 0932D] In Pithou: “bishops.”] questioned concerning it by apostolic mandate, had taken care to give us laudable testimony about him—and because the slander appeared to have proceeded from enemies and rivals, as stated above. Therefore, since his former life appeared praiseworthy [Note: [Col. 0932D] The same: “commendable.”] and such a deed seemed incredible, we did not believe that any purgation [Note: [Col. 0932D] Pithou adds “henceforth.”] ought to be imposed upon him.

Nevertheless, because the procurator persisted, we were compelled—not by legal necessity but by the petitioner’s importunity—to order that canonical purgation be imposed upon him through you, with two bishops and three [Note: [Col. 0933D] The passages marked below in italic type are absent from the Decretals.] abbots. Yet we declared to that procurator that the request was then imprudent for another reason: the suffragans of the Church of Esztergom would scarcely at that time clear the bishop, because they opposed him in the matter of his election; nor would the suffragans of the Church of Kalocsa then clear him, because a dispute concerning the metropolitan see of Esztergom was pending between him and the archbishop of Kalocsa. Since there were no other bishops in Hungary, it reasonably appeared that he could not clear himself at that critical point through the bishops of his kingdom. Consequently, some reasonably presume that this request was made as a fraud not so much for him as against him, especially as he himself had not ordered it to be requested.

From the letters of one of you, however, we learned that, when the other had gone with the king on an expedition into Ruthenia, the bishop came before him, bringing with him one of his fellow bishops who wished to clear him; and another fellow bishop wrote that, when he had been freed from the illness by which he was detained, he would come to clear the bishop. But he did not proceed to receive the purgation, both because his colleague was then absent and because one of the compurgators was ill. He wrote to us, if we remember correctly, that although the bishop could honourably clear himself, he had no need whatever of purgation, especially [Col. 0933C] since, when the cause ceased, the effect ceased.

For this reason we did not consider the mandate of purgation should be renewed, particularly because our dearest son in Christ, A., the illustrious king of the Hungarians, recently commended the bishop highly to us in his letters, asserting that such fabricated charges had been maliciously devised against him. But we most certainly declare that, if those bishops who, when the matter was raised, repeatedly commended his person to us as though excusing him, should refuse to clear him when requested by that bishop, they would make themselves highly suspect to us either of falsehood or of hatred, and could rightly fear the stirring of apostolic indignation—especially those who had promised to clear him. There is, however, no difficulty concerning the abbots.

Since, therefore, we love the same bishop with sincere charity in the Lord, as one whom we have hitherto known to remain an immovable pillar in the Church of God—and who could not fall without a grave and great ruin, perhaps greater for the Church than for his own person—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, although it may be fitting or expedient for the bishop still to endeavour to clear himself, and although it was not through his own fault that he did not clear himself when he took care to offer the purgation, not in order to ratify what had been procured by his messenger but lest he appear to despise the apostolic command: if you nevertheless see malicious plots being contrived against him, do not permit him to be crushed by unjust machinations. For from plausible indications we strongly presume that some are tormented by envy toward him, reckoning his downfall as their own advancement. When you deem it expedient, report to us the truth concerning every circumstance.

[Col. 0934B]

Given at Ferentino, 7 July, in the ninth year.

CXIV. To the bishop of Como. [Note: [Col. 0933D] Ardizzone II, bishop of Como—elsewhere “of Cumae”—died in 1204. His successor was William of Torre Mendrisio, who for twenty years governed the church of Como vigorously and with renowned prudence. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 291.] That he is to recover possessions unlawfully alienated. (Ferentino, 11 July.)

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, etc., until: “be brought into effect.” But since, as has been represented to our Apostolic See on your behalf, certain of your predecessors have presumed to alienate certain possessions and revenues of the church entrusted to you, to its grave loss, we grant you authority by these presents lawfully to restore to the right and ownership of that church whatever they have improperly alienated or sold. Let absolutely no one, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our grant, etc.; but if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at Ferentino, 11 July, in the ninth year.

CXV. [Note: [Col. 0933D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] To Odo, [Note: [Col. 0933D] Odo, formerly abbot of Marchiennes, had in this very year, 1206, according to the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 386, been appointed successor to Raymond, abbot of St. Vaast. Because the pontiff abhorred his avarice and pitied the ascetics of St. Vaast, he ordered that this man, unworthy of that rank, be removed. Odo died after twenty-two years of rule and sixty-four years of life, in the year of Christ 1228, on the feast-day of Pope St. Callixtus.] abbot of the monastery of St. Vaast of Arras, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity. The goods and statutes of the said monastery are confirmed. (Ferentino, 26 June.)

As it is fitting for successors to correct the unreasonable enactments of their predecessors by the moderation of ecclesiastical discipline, so likewise it befits them to confirm what has been well done. For it is plainly evident from the Acts of Pope Stephen, of revered memory, that when the religious and God-beloved Blessed Vindician, bishop of the people of Arras or Cambrai, and the monk Carloman, brother of Pippin, visited the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, they petitioned that same Roman pontiff [Note: A passage most worthy of notice. Innocent records that Vindician, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, visited the thresholds of the apostles in the time of Pope Stephen and obtained from that pontiff a privilege of confirmation; and he declares that this is plainly evident from the Acts of Pope Stephen. It is most certainly established from historical monuments that Vindician wore the episcopal mitre from at least the year 669 and did not live beyond 712; see the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 7. Yet from 669 to 712 no pope named Stephen can be found whom Vindician could have visited. See the note below.], that he might endow the monastery of the blessed confessor of Christ Vedast with an apostolic privilege.

For it had happened that Theodoric, king of the Franks, who, for the salvation of his own soul and of his royal predecessors, had bestowed many great gifts upon that same monastery of Blessed Vedast with royal generosity, summoned the aforesaid bishop Vindician, together with bishops and abbots, to a general assembly held at Compiègne in the royal palace, in order that whatever that king had bestowed upon Blessed Vedast by royal gift might be secured first by his episcopal privilege and then by apostolic privilege. Bishop Vindician himself, willingly acceding to the royal request, granted what was sought and confirmed it in writing before witnesses; furthermore, he separated from his city and bishopric the place called Noyon, which, as he acknowledges in his privilege, had hitherto belonged to and been subject to him, to be assigned to apostolic jurisdiction [Note: The instrument in question here is known, but its authenticity is very seriously doubted. See the observations in the new edition of diplomatic documents relating to French affairs, vol. I, p. 286, no. 112.].

Accordingly, on this occasion, approaching the clemency of our predecessor Pope Stephen, of apostolic memory [Note: We do indeed possess both a letter of Vindician to the supreme pontiff John V, in which the bishop asks him to deign to confirm the charter of his donation, and a confirmation by that supreme pontiff issued at the bishop’s request—two documents certainly of doubtful authority, which may be read in the place cited above. In both instruments the supreme pontiff to whom Vindician wrote is expressly named John. Should “John,” then, be read in place of “Stephen” in this letter of Innocent? Yet even so every difficulty would not wholly disappear, since in those instruments, whatever their authority, Vindician appears to write to the pontiff while absent, and the pontiff to send him the privilege of confirmation while he too is absent.], because his requests were just and reasonable, he readily obtained them.

Therefore we too, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors—the Roman pontiffs of happy memory Paschal, Innocent, Eugenius, Alexander, Celestine, and the aforesaid Stephen, who first received your monastery from the hand of Saint Vindician, bishop, into the right of Blessed Peter—we likewise receive under the protection and jurisdiction of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vedast of Arras, in which you are devoted to divine service. By apostolic authority we decree that henceforth bishops shall not presume to inflict any molestation upon the abbot or brothers of that monastery; rather, enjoying perpetual security and peace, both they and all that belongs to the same monastery shall remain unimpaired, without anyone’s burden or disturbance.

We also decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names:

namely, the church and village of Haspre, with the altars and appurtenances of that church: the altar of Moncelles, the altar of Alchim, the court of Mosterelles, the altar of Gisenniis, two sheaves of tithe together with the tithe of Fosses, the altar of Lovennes, the altar of Onelios and Donisel, the altar of Mulli, the altar of Haimoncanoit, the altar of Haumala, the tithe of Juverre, in Robertumcultura and Wattericultura;

and the toll from every transaction conducted in the city of Arras, together with the house-stays which each person shall render to you according to ancient custom;

at Anzin, two mills; at Dominicacurte, three mills with a fishpond; at Mellens, four mills with a fishpond; at Blangi, four mills with a fishpond; at Althiez, four mills with a fishpond; near Pabula, one mill with a fishpond; at Biarche, two mills with a fishpond; likewise three mills within the walls of the city of Arras, on the river Crinchon;

the church of Bercloens, with its altars, namely those of Douretin, Billi, Baluin, Provinz, Markelies, Merenies, and Serkingehem with Herberia; the church of Gorea with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Maurice; and three altars situated in the diocese of Thérouanne, namely Lengehem, Rombli, and Estrees, together with their other possessions.
