We also confirm these villages with their appurtenances: Montes in Papula, Amolinum, Murchin, Servin, Mares, Tilloit, Ransart, Burcurt, Moilens, Valles on the river Somme, Berni, Puteas Aguas, Angicurt, Pons, Campeiolas, Arven; half a vineyard in the suburb of the city of Arras; Cambac; the church of Vulfara in Batua with its appurtenances; half of Rikeburc; and the land situated beside the sea which William, advocate of Béthune, with the consent of Theodoric, count of Flanders, gave you in exchange for the remaining half of Rikeburc; and the court which you have recently built at Sentines beside the sea, with its appurtenances.

Moreover, we decree that all lands of your monastery which you cultivate at your own expense shall be free from *gavelum* [a due or rent], according to ancient and reasonable custom. Certainly, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the fodder of your animals. We also confirm to you by apostolic authority the tithes which you have peacefully possessed for the past forty years up to the present.

We decree that the two churches of Blessed Peter and Blessed Mary, situated within the castle, shall enjoy the same liberty as your monastery; and we likewise confirm to you the two chapels at Arras, namely those of Holy Cross and of Saint Mary in the Garden.

Moreover, we decree that the altars written below, belonging to your monastery and within the diocese of Arras, shall be free from every *personatus* [parochial benefice or right of presentation], in accordance with the constitution of our predecessor Pope Urban II and the peaceful agreement of Lambert, former bishop of Arras, and Allodius, formerly your abbot; and we confirm them to be possessed by you. The names of these altars are: Salli, Horbais, Leventies, Felchi, Vi, Contheam, Remi, Farbii, Hendecurt, Asscel, Hadas, Mons, Novavillis, Papule, Basilice, Bomiuler, Hamescas, Dangevillis, Guarlus, Fissan, Bairi, Fontanellis, Ateihas, Ballol, Gaurellis, Fuscarias, Bertricurt, Bigartii, Hamblen, Fraisne, Novevillule, Iser, Theulut, Mostaines, Imecurt, Bernevillis, and Illies.

In these and in the other parish churches which you possess, you may, in accordance with the decree of Pope Urban II of good memory, elect priests and present them to the bishops in whose parishes the churches are situated. If those bishops cannot canonically reject them, the priests shall receive from them the care of souls, provided that they answer to the bishops concerning parochial right, while rendering to you due subjection concerning temporal matters.

Furthermore, we establish, and by the present page of privilege prohibit, that no one who holds lands or any possessions from your monastery may, without your consent, grant them to other churches or religious places either during life or at death, or presume in any way to alienate them from your lordship.

We grant you, moreover, by apostolic authority, free power to receive in pledge fiefs, possessions, and tithes belonging to your monastery, lest they perish to that monastery through the fault of those who hold them. We also forbid any bishop of Arras to presume to enter your monastery or the castle of the monastery against the privileges granted you by the Apostolic See and against the will of the abbot.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any stratagem of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, determine should be elected. If the bishop of Arras, when requested, is willing to bless him freely and without any improper condition, and likewise without demanding or receiving any subjection or obedience, the elect shall receive from him the gift of blessing, provided that he is Catholic and has the favor of the Apostolic See. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, and he, supported by our authority, shall willingly confer blessing upon the elect without any rendering or reception of obedience, subjection, or reverence.

The abbot thus ordained shall conduct himself blamelessly according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and shall cause those subject to him to do likewise.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of diocesan bishops in the aforesaid parish churches.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, after a second or third warning, etc., let him be subject to vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that, etc., unto the end.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CXVI. . . . . . TO THE ABBOT AND CHAPTER OF SAINT VEDAST OF ARRAS. On the same matter. (Ferentino, sixth day before the Kalends of July.)

Although unworthy, we have been entrusted with the care and solicitude of all churches; and we ought especially to be concerned for those in which religion is better observed. Therefore, since many secular laymen press you, personally and through others, to obtain in your monastery a provision of food and drink such as one of yourselves is known to have, we, desiring diligently to remove this burden from the same monastery, following the example of our predecessor Pope Celestine of happy memory, forbid you by apostolic authority henceforth to presume to grant such provision, to the detriment of your church, to any layman except one suffering necessity, and then only for charity’s sake.

Likewise, we hold ratified and confirmed the ancient and reasonable liberties and customs granted to your church and hitherto observed; and we decree that they shall remain whole and inviolate forever. We also establish that no one shall dare to build a new church upon land belonging to your monastery without your consent and will. We further add that no one may place under interdict the chaplains who reside in your own churches and attend to their service, unless an evident and reasonable cause intervenes.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our prohibition and constitution, etc. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year.

CXVII. . . . . . TO THE PROVOST AND CHAPTER OF LENS. That they provide for Master P., clerk, with a benefice. (Ferentino, on the Ides of June.)

Piety, which has the promise both of the present life and of the life to come, strongly admonishes us and exhorts the pastoral office that we should provide for the necessities of life of those who have entered the Lord’s sheepfold through the mark of clerical service, especially those known to have commendably labored in literary studies.

Since, therefore, our beloved son Master P. has long labored, as he asserts, in the study of letters and has not obtained any ecclesiastical benefice, we have judged it right earnestly to request and admonish your whole body, commanding you by these apostolic letters that, for reverence toward Blessed Peter and ourselves, you provide him with a suitable benefice in your church, in which, as is said, no one has been received at our command. Thus he may not be compelled through lack of temporal resources to beg, to the reproach of our ministry; and by promptly carrying out the apostolic command as is fitting, you may more fully merit apostolic favor and grace.

Given at Ferentino, on the Ides of June, in the ninth year.

CXVIII. . . . . . TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW [Note: Lambert II, abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon, is known from instruments from at least 1202 until at least 1224. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 1117.], AND TO GOSBERT AND DROGO OF CORDOLIO, CANONS OF NOYON. That they ensure that S., clerk, enjoys peaceful possession of the church of Fraitoi. (Ferentino, third day before the Ides of July.)

From the letters of our beloved sons . . . . . dean [Note: Concerning the deans of Noyon in the times with which we are dealing, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* provide exceedingly little information, ibid., col. 1033.

“XV. Hugh of Coucy, elected, from Vassor, is mentioned in 1183 and still in the years 1187, 1192, 1201, and 1204.

XVI. John of Buchi made an agreement in 1208 with Hugh, mayor of Thyecourt, according to the cartulary of Ourscamp; he was still in office in 1219.”], and . . . cantor of Noyon, you are to know that we have received the following report.

On behalf of B., subdeacon, we had sent our letters to our venerable brother . . . bishop of Amiens, in the form by which we require ordainers or presenters to provide for those ordained, and monitors had been appointed for this purpose. When the same bishop was requested by them, he admonished . . . the prior and chapter of Mont-Desiderii, to whose presentation that clerk had been ordained, to provide him with some benefice. They promised to provide for the clerk in a benefice when one became vacant, and gave him letters on this matter fortified with the chapter’s seal.

But when the church of Fraitoi subsequently became vacant, those monitors invested the aforesaid clerk with it, commanding the prior and chapter, under threat of suspension, to arrange for that clerk to be received into that church. They entirely refused to do so. Therefore the clerk humbly petitioned us that we might deign to confirm by apostolic authority the act of those monitors.

Yet we, sympathizing with the labors and expenses of that clerk, do not in any way rely upon the act of those monitors, since they attempted to proceed less than lawfully; rather, out of the kindness of the Apostolic See, we wish that the church itself, which is represented as vacant, be assigned to him. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, placing him in possession of that vacant church, you cause him to enjoy peaceful possession of it, restraining any opponents or rebels by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. But if not all of you . . . let two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the third day before the Ides of July, in the ninth year.

CXIX [Note: This letter was published by Ángel Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, vol. III, p. 469, under the year 1106, chap. 6, § 2.

It may also be read in Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 30.]

. TO ALL ABBOTS ASSEMBLED IN THE GENERAL CISTERCIAN CHAPTER. That they pray for him. (Ferentino, fifth day before the Ides of July.)

After we were called by the Lord to the office of the Fisherman, we considered that the little ship entrusted to us had been set upon the sea, so that we might cast our net at the Lord’s word to catch fish. But this great and wide sea, stirred by the crash of a most savage storm, began to swell with so many and such great waves against that same little ship that not only has the work of fishing been somewhat hindered, but even the art of steering the vessel has nearly failed.

For the sea’s abysses roar; the hills of waters now diminish as the waves are driven, now swell again under the course of flooding. The entire surface of the deep rages and, impatient of calm, offers itself neither manageable for sailing nor fit for fishing. Moreover, when the hidden vents of the winds are opened, manifold winds emerge from the four quarters of the world, as though in a confederate company to shatter the little ship, and clash around it in mutual opposition.

The mast itself is compelled to sway, battered by the repeated blasts of storms; under the management of the ropes, threatening to break with their creaking, the canvas of the sails seems almost to be torn apart; and nearly every means of nautical control fails. Adding to this calamity, amid the vast expanse of the sea before us there dwell creeping things without number, and deadly beasts move among them. Unless they devour one another, they think it too little cruelty that they do not spare others’ lives.

Besides this, the snares of pirates do not sleep: they traverse the various paths of the sea, and those whom the sea, its monsters, and the fury of the winds ceaselessly assail, these men—more savage than all of them—harass by daily persecution; to say nothing of Charybdis and Scylla and the other perils of the sea.

Although we were surrounded by so many difficulties, we nevertheless took care to steer that little ship by every means we could. At times, casting the Fisherman’s net in this sea, we enclosed in it no small number of fish. When we thought to bring them to harbor, some of them broke the net and at once fell back into the belly of the deep; nor did they merely fall back themselves, but compelled others to fall back after them.

Finally, as we labored to repair the broken net and sought to cast out from the little ship the waters which had entered it and corrupted within it, and lest the imminent tempest, amid the confusion of sea and waves and shipwreck, might sink it, we must steady it in the name of God alone by the anchor of faith.

What these things are, most beloved sons, and under whose pen they are said to you, we believe does not escape your wisdom, if you direct the keenness of discerning reflection to investigate them closely. Therefore, since we stand amid so many and such great dangers and need assistance from your merits and prayers, we ask and beseech you through the mercies of our God that you extend to us, as we are tossed upon the height of the sea, the support of your charity. Supporting the Fisherman and the little ship with the oars of your prayers, entreat Him who commands sea and winds that, shining upon us through his infinite mercy with his countenance, he may calm the inward and outward storm, restrain the winds on every side, still the sea all around, and direct and preserve us with his holy right hand as we spread the sails of our voyage to the breath of the Holy Spirit.

May he send us his Spirit from the four winds of heaven, so that, with him as helmsman and guide, when at last the net is filled with fish, we may escape the rocks of treacherous monsters and carry the Lord’s merchandise through the raging dangers of storms to the safest harbors.

Secure, moreover, in the fullness of our favor, apply yourselves with greater fervor to extending the worship of holy religion. From the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts entrusted to your care—which by his grace already stretches out its branches from sea to sea—endeavor to uproot what is harmful and take care to plant what is useful, so that, bringing forth before God and men the fragrance of good repute and the fruit of devout conduct, you may deserve to ascend from virtue to virtue until you behold the God of gods in Zion.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the ninth year.

CXX. TO THE CELLARER, MASTER ASINUS, AND R., CANONS OF SPEYER. That, if the judgment rendered concerning a certain election by their fellow canons is just, they cause it to be observed. (Ferentino, second day before the Ides of July.)

When the custody of the church of Saint Peter at Strasbourg was vacant, four canons of that church unanimously elected our beloved son Master B. as custodian. . . . The provost, to whom the investiture is known to belong, refused to admit that election, and an appeal was made to our hearing.

But because the matter could not be fully established before us, we committed the cause to H., S., and C., your fellow canons, commanding them by our letters, after summoning the parties and restoring the due state of affairs by revoking whatever they found rashly attempted after the appeal lawfully made to us, to hear the allegations on both sides, determine what was canonical without appeal, and cause their decision to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure.

Accordingly, when the parties appeared before one of the judges—who, with their consent and without his fellow judges, was hearing the matter—and when the letters of our commission had been publicly read, Master H., who opposed the aforesaid B. as adversary, presented certain letters on behalf of the abbots of . . . Saint Gregory and . . . the Parisian monastery, and . . . the provost of Lutenbach [Note: “Of Saint Gregory and of the Parisian monastery, abbots.” Thus it is expressly read in the copy of Conti. We frankly confess that we do not know which monasteries are meant whose abbots the pope mentions here. Certainly, it seems impossible that monasteries of the diocese of Paris are in question. Perhaps the copyist Amanuensis made an error.]. By these letters the judges were commanded not to proceed at all in the matter, since they had received other letters from us that entirely revoked the authority of the former ones, as they might fully learn from the transcript that had been sent to them.

But since that rescript seemed to differ greatly from the style of our chancery and was suspect on several grounds, he demanded an authenticated original from Master H. The latter not only refused to provide it or a copy of it, but, contumaciously departing from his presence, afterward refused to return, though he had been solemnly summoned a third time. Finally, when a peremptory day had been assigned to the parties by two of the aforesaid judges at the command of the third, H. refused to appear before them.

His contumacy, therefore, having been counted as presence, and having received [Note: Thus; yet something seems to be missing.] from the aforesaid abbots and provost, when they were asked whether they had sent such letters to them, the reply that the entire matter was wholly unknown to them, the judges, after taking the advice of prudent men, annulled—as justice required—the election of Master H., which had not so much been celebrated as presumed. They confirmed Master B.’s election as canonical, conferring on him by apostolic authority possession of the custody and the care of souls pertaining to it, and appointing executors to cause him to enjoy peaceful possession.

Subsequently, when the aforesaid abbots and provost urgently summoned B. before them, he appeared at their summons. Having obtained a copy of the letters which his adversary said he had procured from us, he found that they were false in many respects. When he wished immediately to prove this, they not only denied him a hearing on the matter, but, after suspending him from the income of his prebend, proceeded against him in the principal case after an appeal had been made to us.

Thereupon, Master B. and C., procurator of Master H., having appeared in our presence, we appointed our beloved son G. [Note: G., that is, Gregory. After the death of Matthew—concerning whom see the note to letter 54 of book III—Gregory of Crescentio, a Roman nobleman, formerly a regular canon of the monastery of Rhenau or a canon of the Vatican Basilica, was appointed cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. Ciaconius asserts that this occurred in the very year now under discussion, 1206, in December, in Innocent’s fifth creation of cardinals; Oldoinus himself seems to agree. Yet this letter of Innocent proves that Gregory may already have borne the title of Saint Theodore from 1205, or at least before July 1206. On his deeds and the uncertain year of his death, see Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 26.], cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore, as auditor. After lengthy litigation before him, those letters which appeared to revoke the earlier ones were presented to us. We discovered them to be false not only in the bull, which had been extracted from other letters and inserted in them, but also in many other ways; and for fuller certainty we send them to you enclosed under our seal.

Therefore, unwilling to leave the audacity of such great rashness unpunished, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the judgment of your aforesaid fellow canons is just, you cause it to be observed inviolably through ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. Compel any opponents or rebels by like coercion to desist from their rashness. Whatever you learn has been done on the occasion of those letters by the said abbots and provost, or any of them, you shall declare null and void, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. Cause the fruits of the intervening period, as justice requires, to be restored to B. himself; and punish, in accordance with our constitution issued to suppress the malice of forgers, both those who used the aforesaid letters and those who falsely claimed to have procured them from us, without appeal. Thus you shall carry out the apostolic command in such a way that by the deed’s effect you may be shown to hate the vice of falsehood. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the second day before the Ides of July, in the ninth year.

CXXI. . . . . . TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF NEWCASTLE OF DRIENCOURT. Their goods are received under protection. (Ferentino, seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.)

It is customary to assent, etc., down to “granting assent,” we receive your hospital, together with your persons and all the goods which it now reasonably possesses or may hereafter acquire by lawful means, through the Lord’s favor, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves.

In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the church of Saint Nicholas of Menonvalt and the grange of the fief of Periers, with all their appurtenances, as you justly and peacefully possess them; and by the present writing, etc. Let no one therefore, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXII [Note: The copy of this letter, which we had taken care to have transcribed with the others according to the copy of Conti, disappeared from our hands, by what accident we do not know; therefore we can provide only the summary here.]. TO THE DEAN [Note: Adam, otherwise Andrew, of Courlandon, a nobleman born in a village of the county of Roucy adjoining the city of Fismes, is mentioned as dean of Laon from at least 1196 until 1223. Ingelram III, lord of Coucy, imprisoned him about 1215, whence great disturbances arose in the church of Laon. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 561. See also Le Long, *Histoire ecclésiastique et civile du diocèse de Laon*, p. 286.], AND CHAPTER OF LAON. Confirmation of the statutes of the Church of Laon.

CXXIII. . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF LAON [Note: See letter 97 of book VII, note.]. That he confer prebends upon Master Alberic in the Church of Laon. (Ferentino, ninth day before the Kalends of August.)

If you took care to admit into the churches entrusted to your governance men endowed with learning and distinguished by honorable conduct, you could merit, in addition to human praise, divine grace; for just as God is honored in such men, so their provision is rightly believed to be pleasing to him.

We have certainly learned from the testimony of many that our beloved son Master Alberic shines with such uprightness of conduct that his merits rightly demand that he be provided for in a more substantial ecclesiastical benefice. Since formerly you received apostolic letters and a command concerning our beloved son S., directing that you should provide for him in the Church of Laon with a prebendal benefice, you conferred upon that same master, in evasion of the apostolic command, the prebend which first happened to become vacant, assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. But when, as justice required, he was afterward deprived of that prebend, you thereafter took no care to provide for him in any respect, although, as we have learned, opportunity to do so presented itself many times.

Therefore, unwilling that the same master should be thus disappointed in his hope, and that what you did concerning him should be regarded as a mockery, we earnestly admonish and exhort your fraternity, commanding you by apostolic letters that you confer one prebend upon that master in the Church of Laon. Through one reported fit for this by his conduct and learning, both your own benefit and that of the same church may be advanced; and if we are heard on his behalf, we shall be bound to render your fraternity a fitting return of thanks. Take care most diligently that our prayers and command alike obtain their due effect, since we have judged them to be offered solely for God’s sake.

Given at Ferentino, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXIV. . . . . . TO THE DEAN [Note: See letter 122 of book IX, note.] AND CHAPTER OF LAON. That, if disputes arise between the chapter and bishop concerning the customs of the Church, they may produce the canons themselves as witnesses. (Ferentino, eleventh day before the Kalends of August.)

It is customary to assent, etc., down to “inclined to your petitions,” by the authority of these presents we grant you that, whenever a controversy concerning the customs of your church arises between you and your bishop or archbishop, you may produce as witnesses to prove them your brethren who are beyond every objection; and whatever is sufficiently shown through them shall be observed inviolably, provided that it is not contrary to canonical enactments. Let no one therefore . . . of our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF SARAGOSSA. That he abolish the enactment providing that no one can be received as a canon unless all the canons consent, or understand “all” to mean the greater part. (Ferentino, eleventh day before the Kalends of August.)

Through your letters you informed us that the canons of your church had bound themselves collectively by oath that no one should be received by them as a canon unless this proceeded from the common consent of the whole chapter. Hence it frequently happens that, under the pretext of such an oath, one of the canons, lodging an appeal to the Apostolic See, prevents the reception of a person whom the greater and sounder part of the chapter has judged fit to elect. Although, therefore, the aforesaid canons appear to have understood in such an oath that no one could be admitted as their fellow canon unless the wills of all alike consented to him, nevertheless, since this is recognized as indiscreet and presumptuous unless it is understood, according to canonical and lawful enactments, that what is done by the greater and sounder part of the whole is done by the whole, we, by the duty of the office entrusted to us, wishing to provide both for the welfare of the same church and for the salvation and good repute of those fellow canons, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to enjoin them collectively to absolve themselves, by our authority, from such an oath, so that, notwithstanding it, that which the greater and sounder part shall reasonably have determined may obtain its due force.

Given at Ferentino, the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXVI. TO WALTER, CLERIC, PROVOST OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARY, CALLED IN GREEK *Ypanimnitos* AND IN LATIN “MERCY,” [Note: [Col. 0945D] It is called in Greek YPANIMNITOS and in Latin MISERICORDIA. Thus it is expressly read in the Conti copy. Should one not rather read I PANYMNITOS, for the Greek Ἡ ΠΑΝΥΜΝΗΤΟΣ, or, as one word, YPERYMNITOS, [Col. 0946D] for the Greek ΥΠΗΡΥΜΝΗΤΟΣ? Yet it is not easy to understand how these Greek epithets, meaning “wholly praiseworthy” or “praiseworthy above all things,” correspond to the Latin *Misericordia* (“Mercy”).] OF B., ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. His provostship is confirmed. (Ferentino, tenth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0946B]

“To the just petitions,” etc., as far as “granting assent.” We confirm to you by apostolic authority the provostship of Saint Mary *Ypanimnitos*, just as you possess it rightfully and peacefully, and by the present writing, etc. “Let absolutely no one therefore,” etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

Given at Ferentino, the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXVII. TO LAMBERT, PRIEST, CHAPLAIN OF B., ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE, PROVOST OF SAINT MICHAEL OF CONSTANTINOPLE. A similar confirmation. (Ferentino, tenth day before the Kalends of August.)

“To the just petitions,” etc., as far as “granting assent.” We confirm to you by apostolic authority the provostship of the church of Saint Michael, just as you possess it rightfully and peacefully, and by the present writing, etc. “Let absolutely no one therefore,” etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

Given at Ferentino, the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXVIII. TO ABSALON, PRIEST. The provostship in the church of Blessed Mary of Scota near Constantinople is confirmed to him by apostolic authority, just as he possesses it rightfully and peacefully. (Ferentino, tenth day before the Kalends of August.)

“To the just petitions,” etc., as far as “to bring to completion under [God’s] pursuing favor.” Therefore, beloved [son], etc., as far as “inclined by your prayers,” we confirm to you by apostolic authority the provostship in the church of Blessed Mary of Scota near Constantinople, just as you possess it rightfully and peacefully, and by the present writing, etc. “Let absolutely no one therefore,” etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

Given at Ferentino, the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXIX. TO WALTER OF COURTRAI. His appointment is confirmed. (Ferentino, eighth day before the Kalends of August.)

“To the just petitions,” etc., as far as “to bring to completion under [God’s] pursuing favor.”

[Col. 0947A]

Since, therefore, our beloved son B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna and legate of the Apostolic See, appointed you a canon in the church of Saint Sophia at Constantinople, we, graciously granting assent to your petitions and holding that appointment valid, as it was made canonically, confirm it by apostolic authority and by the present writing, etc. “Let absolutely no one therefore,” etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] See letter 54 of Book III, note.]

Given at Ferentino, the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXX. [Note: [Col. 0947D] This letter is found in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §99, and is therefore here printed in brackets. Raynaldus gives part of it under the year 1206, §2. The passages found in his work are marked here by a double quotation mark placed in the margin at the beginning of each line.] TO THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He is not bound to observe the oath made by him with the Venetians, that he will receive no one as a canon of Saint Sophia unless he is Venetian. (Ferentino, eleventh day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0947B]

[God has established the bishop of the Apostolic See, who possesses the fullness of ecclesiastical power, over nations and kingdoms, so that, in accordance with the prophetic word, he may uproot and destroy, scatter and lay waste whatever he finds useless and harmful in the Lord’s field entrusted to his cultivation; as elsewhere the Lord commands him through the prophet: “Undo the bonds of impiety; loosen the bundles that weigh people down” (Isa. LVII). Therefore, considering that that oath, as altogether unlawful, is not to be kept—the oath which, while you were established at Venice, was forcibly extorted from you by the Venetians, as your report to us made clear—namely, that you would make no one a canon in the church of Saint Sophia unless he were Venetian by nationality, or had resided continuously at Venice for ten years; and that in good faith, by every means in your power, you would labor to ensure that there should always be a Venetian patriarch in the church of Saint Sophia, while preserving in all things the right, authority, reverence, and honor of the Apostolic See—although you added this condition in such a way that it was not set down in writing—we command you by the authority of this present letter, and strictly enjoin you by the power of the Holy Spirit, not in any way to observe that oath. For the sanctuary of God is not to be possessed by anyone by hereditary right; rather, “in every nation, he who does justice is acceptable to God.” Take diligent care that, after this command of the Apostolic See, you do not in any manner offend against the foregoing articles.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] In the *Deeds*: “violate [them] and again offend.”]

For if henceforth you appoint only Venetians as canons in the church of Saint Sophia, or devote any effort whatever to ensuring that there is always a Venetian patriarch in that church, appointing no one as a canon there [Note: [Col. 0948D] In the *Deeds*: “not there.”] unless he swears that he will never elect or receive a patriarch from anywhere except among the Venetians, you will thereafter be unable to offer any excuse on these matters. Nor are you to observe what you are said to have promised without an oath: that throughout Romania you will appoint no archbishop except a Venetian.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Thus far Raynaldus.]

[Col. 0948A]

Lest hereafter such things be presumed upon under the pretext of an oath-bound undertaking or the plea of any promise, or, if presumed upon, be observed, we annul obligations of this kind by apostolic authority, forbidding under threat of anathema anyone to presume to observe them. We command you carefully to announce this to the canons of Saint Sophia, not only those already appointed but also those to be appointed, so that they may avoid this wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] These matters again occur in Raynaldus.]

“Although you ought to have feared God more than human beings, so as not to swear something before men against God, nevertheless, if in that oath extorted by force and fear you employed the stated proviso—namely, that you swore while preserving in all things the right, authority, reverence, and honor of the Apostolic See—we, granting special favor to you as you humbly confess your fault, allow that such an oath can create no prejudice against you, provided that you faithfully carry out the command we have beneficially given you to preserve the right, authority, reverence, and honor of the Apostolic See, against whose statutes the matters sworn to run counter.”

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Thus far Raynaldus.]

[Col. 0948B]

Moreover, although the foregoing was communicated to us in secret by your envoys, know nevertheless for certain that some of those matters had previously been made known to us by reliable report.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The Vallicellian codex reads: “had been concluded.”]

“Let absolutely no person,” etc., “violate this page of our annulment, prohibition, constitution, command, and concession,” etc.

[Col. 0948C]

Given at Ferentino, the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year.

CXXXI. TO . . . . . . . The address is missing. Reprisals are granted against the goods of the hostile Piacentines. (Ferentino, seventh day before the Kalends of August.)

Unless the wicked association of the people of Piacenza, clinging mutually together like the limbs of the flesh of him who delights in evil deeds, and, like the scales of Leviathan—each joined to the next so that no breath passes between them—had gathered itself into a single mass of treachery against the servants of the Lord, it would perhaps, either crushed by the lash of the wakeful rod upon its crimes, or at least, now that the report of its wickedness has gone out into almost the whole earth, confounded by public shame, have dissolved the bonds of its impiety.

[Col. 0948D]

But since it has made for itself the forehead of a harlot, and has through its sin been permitted by the Lord so to harden its own heart that it neither feels the worm of its wounded conscience nor is ashamed before the nations—to whom, though previously known, it has become better known through the infamy of its crime—the saying of the Wise Man seems applicable to it: “If you pound a fool in a mortar with a pestle as though [preparing] barley-gruel, his folly will not be removed from him” (Prov. XXVII).

[Col. 0949A]

Although, therefore, we may complain of it with the prophet, saying, “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed” (Jer. LI), “we killed and destroyed this people, and they did not return from their ways,” nevertheless, wishing still to test whether perhaps they will not refuse to receive discipline before the Lord afflicts them with the blow of an enemy and we lay our hand more heavily upon them—so that those who have thus far been struck as though by a light scourge, failing to observe that lightning precedes hail and grace precedes shame, may not at last be smitten with an incurable wound—we have judged that milder measures should still be pursued toward them.

Accordingly, strictly commanding by apostolic letters in virtue of obedience, we direct your brotherhood to take care to retain, and cause others to retain, merchandise or any goods of Piacentine merchants which may come into the power of you or of your people, until the people of Piacenza render to the Church, their mother—whom they have gravely offended and do not cease to offend—due satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted; compelling any opponents or rebels who appear by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

[Col. 0949B]

Given at Ferentino, the seventh day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXXII. [Note: [Col. 0949D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §27.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, [Note: [Col. 0949D] See letter 116 of Book VII.] AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. He orders that the sentence of excommunication which the bishop of Cambrai pronounced against certain criminal citizens of Cambrai be observed. (Ferentino, third day before the Ides of July.)

[Col. 0949C]

As we reflect most earnestly upon the straits and miseries by which the whole body of the Church, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, is pitifully shaken and disturbed, we are afflicted with intense sorrow of heart—more grievously because we are especially bound to imitate the footsteps of him who, as he himself declares, was made weak with weak brethren and burned when others were scandalized.

Indeed, the children of this world, whom Truth itself declares to be more prudent than the children of light, now, not as little foxes but as savage lions, lay waste and devour the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts. Their foolish heart has been so darkened that neither fear of God nor filial reverence restrains them from persecuting his Church with hostile cruelty. Nor is it enough for their rage to seize secular things contrary to justice; rather, with damnable recklessness, they strive to break apart and destroy the very fabric of the spiritual building.

[Col. 0949D]

But, to pass over for the moment the rest—whose multitude in this great and spacious sea has grown so vast that, as there is no number of wicked deeds, so there is none of the wicked—the citizens of Cambrai, abusing the kindness with which our venerable brother, . . . bishop of the same city, had always governed them gently and treated them mildly, have insolently risen in contumacy. By a new kind of treachery, not compelled but of their own accord, shamelessly withdrawing from his obedience, they gave themselves into the hands of those persecuting him. And, so that nothing might be lacking to their iniquities, they attack with arms and fire the towns and other possessions of the Church of Cambrai which they were bound by the duty of fidelity to uphold and defend; having violently occupied them and completely despoiled the bishop, they presume to retain them as stubbornly as shamelessly.

[Col. 0950A]

When they had been excommunicated for these acts, so that they might thus turn from the death of the soul to life, they caused apostate priests—publicly detesting obedience to the Apostolic See—to celebrate in violated churches, out of the richness of heretical perversity and in contempt of God and of the universal Church.

[Col. 0950B]

Therefore, unwilling to overlook or neglect this transgression, but desiring to cut off their insolence with the sword of vengeance in such a way that, once terror has been passed on to posterity, this crime may not recur as a precedent, we strictly command your brotherhood by apostolic letters: you are to cause the sentence which the same bishop reasonably pronounced, or shall judge fit to pronounce, against the same citizens of Cambrai and other plunderers of his goods—namely, William the uncle, William the advocate of Aquen., Sibodorus, Nivolo the bailiff, Baldwin of Bray, Iterius the royal door-keeper, John Fish, Alelm Tuebouf, Ralph the Miller, and any others to be identified by their proper names—or against those who rashly associate with them and give them aid, counsel, or favor, to be inviolably observed throughout all your dioceses.

[Col. 0950C]

On every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, renew and proclaim the sentence in every church subject to you, announcing in particular that they are to be more strictly avoided at fairs. Cause also the publication of the persons and goods of those same citizens of Cambrai, reasonably made by the bishop under common law or special custom, to be announced together with the aforesaid sentence in the same manner. Carry out the apostolic command so that the rigor of the ecclesiastical sentence may not be weakened by your sloth or negligence, but that by your diligence and careful solicitude they may be compelled, unwilling though they be, to make sufficient restitution for damages and fitting satisfaction for injuries.

[Col. 0950D]

And since the said bishop or his messenger has no safe passage through the regions of Gaul, you, brother archbishop, shall have our letters presented to your suffragans by your messenger.

Given at Ferentino, the third day before the Ides of July, in the ninth year.

CXXXIII. TO CLEMENT, PROVOST OF SAINT STEPHEN OF CONSTANTINOPLE. His provostship is confirmed. (Ferentino, fifth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0951A]

“When what is just and honorable is requested of us,” etc., as far as “granting assent,” we confirm by apostolic authority the provostship of the church of Saint Stephen of Constantinople, just as you possess it rightfully and peacefully, and by the present writing, etc. “Let absolutely no one therefore,” etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

Given at Ferentino, the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXXIV. TO MASTER CLEMENT, CANON OF SAINT SOPHIA OF CONSTANTINOPLE. On a similar matter. (Ferentino, fifth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0951B]

“To the just petitions,” etc., as far as “to bring to completion under [God’s] effective favor.” Since, therefore, our beloved son P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, appointed you a canon in the church of Saint Sophia of Constantinople, we, graciously granting assent to your petitions and holding the appointment valid, as it was canonically made, confirm it by apostolic authority and by the present writing, etc. “Let absolutely no one therefore,” etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0951D] He has already been mentioned repeatedly.]

Given at Ferentino, the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BARI [Note: [Col. 0951D] Dauferius, after the death of Raynaldus, was named archbishop of Bari in 1188 and consecrated by Pope Clement III on 13 December. He held the archiepiscopal dignity for fourteen [indeed nineteen] years, two months, and fourteen days, and died on 27 February 1207. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 881.] AND THE BISHOP OF SALPI [Note: [Col. 0952D] This was probably Paganus, of whom there is a brief notice under the year 1207 in the incomplete series of bishops of Salpi in Ughelli, ibid., col. 1242.]. They are to hear and decide the case between the archbishops of Trani and Acerenza. (Ferentino, sixth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0951C]

Although we have such confidence in our venerable brother . . . archbishop of Trani, legate of the Apostolic See, that he will proceed with discretion and maturity in the office entrusted to him, nevertheless . . . the archbishop of Acerenza [Note: [Col. 0952D] See letter 57 of Book VI, note.] has long and repeatedly not ceased to complain about him, both personally and through others, asserting that, after an appeal to us had lawfully been lodged, he unjustly suspended him from pontifical office.

[Note: [Col. 0952D] See letter 118 of Book VIII.]

[Col. 0951D]

We, who by the duty of apostolic service are debtors to wise and foolish alike, wishing both to show deference to the former and to provide for the latter, commanded our venerable brother . . . bishop of Troia and our beloved son . . . abbot of Terra Maggiore by apostolic letters to summon those whom they knew should be summoned and to investigate the truth diligently. If it appeared to them that the same legate had pronounced a sentence of suspension against the aforesaid archbishop after an appeal to us had lawfully been lodged, they were to declare that sentence wholly without force; or, if he had perhaps otherwise suspended him unjustly, they were to relax the said sentence of suspension. They were nonetheless to investigate the accusations made to our apostolate against that archbishop, which the said legate would explain more fully to them; and, if they found him innocent, they were wholly to absolve him of the charges, but to punish him canonically if they found him guilty. If, however, it could not be proved that the aforesaid legate had proceeded wrongly against him, they were to cause the aforesaid sentence of suspension to be inviolably observed and, together with that legate, faithfully proceed in making the inquiry.

[Note: [Col. 0952D] See letter 101 of Book VII.]

[Col. 0952A]

They wrote back to us concerning this as follows. They had instructed the aforesaid archbishop of Trani by their letters that, if he wished to allege anything against the aforesaid archbishop of Acerenza, he should submit it before them personally or through a sufficient representative. He replied that he had nothing to allege against the said archbishop, but asserted that they seemed to him to have exceeded their authority in directing him to submit before their tribunal any allegations he might wish to make against that archbishop, since he maintained that he was their superior judge and that they ought to be subject to his jurisdiction, whereas he ought not to be subject to theirs.

When, at his insistence, he was finally supplied with a copy of our letters, the same legate, adhering to the clause contained in those letters that the aforesaid bishop and abbot were to proceed together with him in faithfully conducting the inquiry, maintained that they could proceed in no article without him, and thus claimed to be a third judge in every point. The said judges replied that he could not lawfully do this, because, as the matter concerned the archbishop of Acerenza’s complaint that he had been suspended by him after an appeal to the Apostolic See, he could not simultaneously be defendant and judge in his own case. But if the archbishop of Acerenza could not prove that proceedings against him had been wrongful, they would proceed together with him in conducting the inquiry.

[Col. 0952B]

Finally, after they had peremptorily summoned him and informed him that, if on the appointed day and in the appointed place he did not personally or through a procurator submit whatever allegations he wished against the named archbishop, they would proceed in the matter according to the apostolic mandate—because the same legate appeared to be faltering in his own case and to be putting forward uncertainties as certainties, thereby keeping their minds in suspense—when the appointed day came, they heard the allegations of the archbishop of Acerenza in the presence of several prudent men. They received sworn witnesses, carefully examined them, and reduced their testimony to writing.

[Col. 0952D]

From this it was plainly established that the aforesaid legate had pronounced a sentence of suspension against the same archbishop after a lawful appeal to the Apostolic See, and had moreover otherwise oppressed him contrary to justice. Therefore, upon the counsel of their assessors, they declared that sentence without force, wholly absolved the aforesaid archbishop from it, and caused an announcement to be made throughout the entire diocese of Acerenza that, should anyone wish to allege anything against him, they should arrange to submit it before their tribunal. Since no one appeared against him wishing to allege anything, the said archbishop cleared his innocence with many compurgators. Finding him innocent, the said judges judicially absolved him of the accusations.

[Col. 0953B]

After the sentence had been pronounced, however, the aforesaid legate sent them a messenger, who said nothing to them except that he burst out with an appeal and departed without leave. Conversely, the aforesaid archbishop of Trani informed us by his letters that on the third day of June the said bishop and abbot had summoned him by letter to appear before them at Foggia, without assigning him any date. He replied by his letters that, if he were assured of an apostolic mandate to that effect, he was prepared to obey in all things, earnestly asking that, once a copy of the mandate had been supplied, they should appoint a common and safe day and place to which he could safely come. In his letters he inserted this form of appeal: if they should perhaps wish to proceed in any matter before appointing a common and safe place and a suitable term, he appealed to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0953C]

Within eight days, finally, the said bishop of Troia—whom, as his letters stated, the abbot of Terra Maggiore had deputed to act in his place—wrote again to him, without assigning him either place or term, directing him to state by letter whether he wished to allege anything against the aforesaid archbishop of Acerenza or to renounce the proposed question. The legate replied that, although he otherwise had nothing against him, he nevertheless wished personally to take part in the case in order to defend the sentence which he asserted he had justly pronounced against him, with no appeal whatever having been lodged, and in order to carry out the inquiry into the charges against him according to the apostolic mandate.

But because he understood that the said bishop was hasty to absolve that archbishop, he immediately sent him a messenger with letters, humbly requesting that at least eight days’ time be granted him, in which he could send suitable procurators to him concerning the affair itself. He appealed, both through the messenger and by letter, in the form expressed above.

[Col. 0953D]

Although that bishop had promised that during those eight days he would not proceed in any way without the presence of the legate or his procurators, later, within that period, before his procurators could reach him, on the twelfth day of June, after appeals had so often been lodged, he granted that archbishop an absolution for sale, in the absence of the said legate or his procurators, having been corrupted by money, as many persons plausibly report.

[Col. 0954A]

On the day after the sentence of absolution had been promulgated, the procurators of the same legate arrived before him and, as an additional precaution, appealed to the Apostolic See from that sentence. Furthermore, since the archbishop of Acerenza, on the basis of that sentence, presumed to celebrate publicly and solemnly, the said legate considered the sentence void and strictly commanded him by apostolic authority not thereafter to dare to celebrate the divine offices or to involve himself in the administration of temporal affairs until a special apostolic command should be issued on the matter. By the same authority, throughout the whole parish territory of the church of Acerenza, he strictly prohibited bishops, abbots, and the entire clergy from paying him heed or obeying him in temporal or spiritual matters until they received a special command from us; thus opposing the order of the said bishop, who had written throughout the whole territory that they should answer to him in temporal as well as spiritual matters.

[Col. 0954B]

Having carefully heard what was written to us on both sides, we understand that the aforesaid archbishop of Trani proceeded wrongly in this: after an appeal to the Apostolic See had been lodged—which he preferred to pursue rather than withdraw—in a matter removed from his jurisdiction through its commission to others, he forbade the aforementioned archbishop by legatine authority to celebrate the divine offices or presume to involve himself in the administration of temporal affairs, and forbade any of his suffragans, abbots, or subject clerics to answer to him in temporal or spiritual matters. We therefore hold that this prohibition lacks legal force.

[Col. 0954C]

We have nevertheless found that the said bishop and abbot also proceeded wrongly, in that, after an appeal to us had reasonably been lodged—especially since the letters of commission did not preclude the obstacle of appeal—they did not hesitate to proceed to investigate matters which, under the form of the apostolic mandate, they ought not to investigate unless the legate himself had specified them to them; and they presumed to absolve the archbishop of Acerenza from the charges, as though after receiving a purgation, though nothing had been commanded to them concerning the imposition of a purgation. We therefore decree that both the absolution and the purgation are void and without effect.

[Col. 0954D]

But because the legate and the delegates disagree on other points, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to summon those who must be summoned and investigate the truth with the utmost diligence. If it appears to you that the aforesaid archbishop of Trani was summoned only twice without a peremptory edict; or that in those summonses no fixed day was assigned to him; or that he was unable to obtain a delay of eight days; or that the appeal lodged to us was not treated with due deference—you shall decree that the relaxation of the suspension lacks force, restoring the case to the position in which it stood when the aforesaid commission was issued by us.

[Col. 0955A]

Otherwise, cause the relaxation of the suspension to remain in full force. And lest the same affair, not without damage to property and danger to souls, be prolonged further, we will and command that, when the same archbishop, who is said to be held captive, has been restored to liberty, you—whose discretion we fully trust—proceed in the matter according to the form of the aforesaid commission, appeal set aside: either on the point of inquiry alone, if you find that the sentence of suspension should reasonably be relaxed, or throughout the whole case, if you invalidate the relaxation of the suspension. Take diligent care, with God before your eyes, neither to turn to the right nor to the left, and to observe the limits of the mandate in such a way that you may deservedly be commended rather than reproved.

[Col. 0955B]

Given at Ferentino, the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXXVI. TO BROTHER AUGUSTINE, REGULAR CANON OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARY OF NORTON. He is to retain the name imposed on him, not at baptism, but at profession. (Ferentino, third day before the Kalends of August.)

Since, before you professed the regular life, you were called Henry by the naming received at baptism, and afterwards, when you made your profession and were as it were changed into another man, your prior decreed that you should be called Augustine, you humbly petitioned our apostolate either to restore your first name to you or to confirm the later one, because you fear that after death you may not be aided by those suffrages which fraternal charity renders for you under one of the aforesaid names. To this we have judged it right to reply to your devotion that you may safely retain the name imposed upon you at the time of profession, just as we ourselves without hesitation retain the name that, by the Lord’s ordering, was changed for us when we assumed the office of apostolic service.

Given at Ferentino, the third day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CXXXVII. TO . . . BISHOP, [Note: [Col. 0955D] See letter 178 of Book VII.] . . . ARCHPRIEST, AND THE CHAPTER OF PADUA. They are to receive C., a cleric, as a canon. (Ferentino, second day before the Nones of August.)

It is neither unfitting nor absurd that we should be solicitous for the provision of those through whom we believe churches from which they obtain benefices can be usefully served. In so doing, we invite the minds of prelates to that to which they are bound by their office and ought not make themselves difficult, since, desiring to show deference to their honor, we ask them to do what we could accomplish ourselves, we in whom the fullness of ecclesiastical power resides, having called others to share in our solicitude.

[Col. 0956A]

Therefore, on behalf of our beloved son Master Boniface, commended for learning and morals, we have judged it right earnestly to request and exhort your whole body; commanding you by apostolic letters to admit him, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, as a brother and canon, and liberally assign him a prebendal benefice in your church. Thus you may appear, as is fitting, to have fulfilled our request and command with prompt execution; he may be more firmly bound to the service of your church; and we may commend your devotion in the Lord.

[Col. 0956B]

Given at Ferentino, the second day before the Nones of August, in the ninth year.

CXXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0955D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §8.] TO . . . ARCHBISHOP OF TYRE. [Note: [Col. 0955D] See letter 131 of Book VI, note.] He is to send to the curia his proofs concerning the church of Saint Mark at Tyre, which the Venetians complain has been seized. (Ferentino, third day before the Nones of August.)

We have received the complaint of our beloved son, the noble man . . . doge of the Venetians, stating that, after an appeal to us had reasonably been lodged, you have in many respects unjustly oppressed the church of Saint Mark, together with the other properties which the Venetians have at Tyre.

[Col. 0956C]

Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to correct and amend these things yourself in such a manner that no just ground for complaint against you remains to him. Otherwise, we command by our letters our venerable brother . . . patriarch of Jerusalem and our beloved son P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, legates of the Apostolic See, to restore to its due state whatever they find to have been attempted unjustly by you or another after an appeal to us was lawfully lodged, or otherwise unjustly; then to hear any dispute that may remain. If the parties agree, they are to endeavor, appeal set aside, to settle it by justice or agreement; otherwise, they are to remit the case, once prepared, to our examination, setting the parties a suitable term within which to present themselves before us to receive judgment.

[Col. 0956D]

If the Venetian party prefers to produce witnesses and documents before us, they are nevertheless, after joinder of issue, to receive your proofs, lest you be burdened with excessive costs and labors. While the suit is pending, you are to refrain from improperly molesting them.

Given at Ferentino, the third day before the Nones of August, in the ninth year.

CXXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0957D]

This letter is printed in full in the *Deeds of Innocent*, §104, and is therefore here presented in brackets. Raynaldus gives fragments of it under the year 1206, §37. The passages found in his work are marked by a double quotation mark placed in the margin at the beginning of each line.

We have also noted, for greater accuracy, variant readings from the *Deeds* and from the frequently cited Vallicellian manuscript codex.]

… TO THE NOBLE MAN … DOGE, AND TO THE PEOPLE OF VENICE. They are reproved for the invasion of Zara and exhorted to be devout. (Ferentino, on the Nones of August.)

[Col. 0957A]

“[ [Note: [Col. 0957D] This is found in Raynaldus.] We laudably discharge the office of apostolic service if, as the Apostle teaches, we rebuke, entreat, and admonish in all patience and doctrine [Note: [Col. 0957D] Raynaldus ends here.].” Since therefore a father corrects the son whom he loves, and God rebukes and chastises those whom he loves, we accordingly corrected with paternal affection your beloved sons, the noble men R. Permar [Note: [Col. 0957D] In the *Gesta*, Mar.] and P. Quir., your envoys who came to the Apostolic See—rather rebuking you in them—for the many and grave offenses which you have wickedly committed not only against God and the Roman [Col. 0957B] Church, but also against the Christian people, and yourselves [Note: [Col. 0957D] In the *Gesta*, “us”: correctly.], and your neighbors [Note: [Col. 0957D] In the *Gesta*, “our”: correctly.], especially in the destruction of the city of Zara. There you yourselves went astray and caused the army of the Lord to turn aside from right to left, attacking Christian peoples when you ought to have been attacking the faithless Saracens; you repelled the legate of the Apostolic See, disregarded the sentence of excommunication, and violated your crusading vow, to the injury of the Crucified One.

For, to pass over the many wicked deeds which you perpetrated at Constantinople by plundering the treasures of churches and seizing ecclesiastical possessions, wishing, as though by hereditary right, to possess the sanctuary of the Lord—and for this reason also [Col. 0957C] extorting unlawful agreements—tell us: when will you be able to repair [Note: [Col. 0958D] Vallicellian codex: “restore.”] so great an injury to the Holy Land? For you diverted an army of Christians so great, so noble, and so powerful, assembled and brought together with such great effort and toil and at such immense cost and expense—an army through which it was undoubtedly hoped that not only the province of Jerusalem would be recovered, but that a great part of the kingdom of Babylon would also be occupied. For if it was able to subjugate Constantinople and Greece to itself, how much more could it have taken Alexandria and Egypt, and thereby snatched the Holy Land from the hands of the pagans?

Certainly, although it is pleasing to us that Constantinople has returned to obedience to the most holy Roman Church, its mother, it would have been more pleasing to us [Col. 0957D] had Jerusalem been restored to the power of the [Col. 0958A] Christian people. Nor should you suppose that you have therefore committed no sin because one city or another was delivered to you and to them, more by divine judgment than by worldly power [Note: [Col. 0958D] Thus also in the Vallicellian codex; in the *Gesta*, *potestatu*.]; for the suffering of the one scourged often pleases God when the action of the scourger displeases him [Note: [Col. 0958D] Thus also in the Vallicellian codex; in the *Gesta*, “the scourger.”], as is plainly shown by the authorities of both the New and the Old Testament.

“ [Note: [Col. 0958D] Raynaldus again.] Therefore do not attribute it to our harshness, but ascribe it to your own offense, that we have not yet [Note: [Col. 0958D] In the *Gesta*, “not.”] thought fit to grant the requests which you presented to us through the aforesaid envoys concerning the sending of a pallium to …, abbot of Saint Felix, whom you call the elect of Zara [Note: [Col. 0958D] Of this man Ughellus, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 1461, says nothing beyond what is derived from this letter of Innocent. See letter 91 of book sixteen.]. For, since the Christian people have been excessively scandalized against you by the acts which you have committed against Zara, we did not wish to do anything [Col. 0958B] concerning Zara on your account through which [Note: [Col. 0958D] In the *Gesta*, “for which.”] the universal Church ought to be further scandalized against us [Note: [Col. 0958D] In the *Gesta* and in Raynaldus, “could be.”]. This would certainly occur if, at your request, by granting him the pallium, we appeared to have remitted so great an offense without any satisfaction; since, according to the saying of Solomon, a person should be punished in that in which he has sinned. Yet this delay is not so much a punishment as a precaution, by which we intend to provide both for ourselves and for you [Note: [Col. 0958D] Raynaldus ends here.].”

For although in this matter the people of Zara have not sinned, nevertheless, because metropolitan dignity was specially granted to them by the Apostolic See for the sake of your honor—namely, that your church might possess patriarchal dignity not merely in name but in full right, once the metropolitan see of Zara was made subject to it—we wish in this to mark your fault rather than inflict their punishment. For it is neither unprecedented nor absurd that subjects should sometimes be punished for their prelates, just as the people of Israel were punished without personal fault when David sinned in numbering them.

We therefore reply to you through your envoys and by our letters that you should humbly incline yourselves to offer and render satisfaction to God and to us, at least following the example of those who, although they sinned less, because they were led by you into committing this crime, nevertheless firmly bound themselves to make satisfaction to us. Thus, when, rather than excusing your offense, you have acknowledged it and implored both divine and our forgiveness and have offered appropriate [Col. 0958D] satisfaction, we—who desire your salvation before [Col. 0959A] God [Note: [Col. 0959D] In the *Gesta*, “hope for.”] and seek your honor before men—will take care to grant your requests in these matters and in others which you may deem worthy [Note: [Col. 0959D] In the *Gesta*, “more worthily.”] to request.

Meanwhile, patiently awaiting your correction, we suspend that censure which the judgment of nearly all declares ought to be exercised against you [Note: [Col. 0959D] Vallicellian codex: “extended.”], so that, when you have been converted by the Lord’s inspiration, we may not only remit punishment but also [Note: [Col. 0959D] Vallicellian codex: “but,” etc.] bestow favor. Nor should anyone excuse himself on the ground that he was not bodily present at these acts, if perhaps he also consented to them in heart; for those who do and those who approve are condemned by a like guilt [Note: [Col. 0959D] Vallicellian codex: “are condemned by a like punishment.”].

Therefore let our words please you, most beloved sons: harsh indeed in their outer bark, but sweet in their marrow. For, as he knows who [Col. 0959B] knows nothing imperfectly, they proceed from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. Thus, just as the blows of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy, let a father’s correction please you more than a sinner’s flattery. Do not then be ashamed to humble yourselves beneath the power of him who by a mere nod can humble the proud and exalt the humble, attributing the victory granted you not to your own strength but to divine power. Although perhaps by a hidden judgment, it was nonetheless a just one, through which God willed by you to scourge others. Know that nothing is more abominable to God than the monster of ingratitude and the prodigy of arrogance [Note: [Col. 0959D] Both words are lacking in the *Gesta* and the Vallicellian codex.], each of which proceeds from swelling of the heart.

Take care also to render us full obedience and reverence with devotion, [Col. 0959C] for the glory [Note: [Col. 0959D] In the *Gesta* and the Vallicellian codex, “grace.”] and honor of him whose place and office we hold, although unworthy and undeserving, so that he may protect and exalt you in the present life, and glorify and crown you in the life to come: he who is King of kings and Lord of lords, a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

Given at Ferentino, on the Nones of August, in the ninth year.

CXL [Note: [Col. 0959D]

Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1206, §6.

It is printed in full in the *Gesta*, §102; accordingly, we have here marked it with a double quotation-mark in the margin at the beginning of each line.

Different excerpts from it may be read in the *Decretals*: first, book I, title 22, *On Foreign Clerics*, chapter 11; second, ibid., title 33, *On Primacy and Obedience*, chapter 8; third, book III, title 4, *On Clerics Not Resident in a Church or Benefice*, chapter 10; fourth, ibid., book III, title 36, *On Religious Houses Being Subject to the Bishop*, chapter 5. Passages found in the *Decretals* are enclosed here in brackets [Col. 0960D].

For greater accuracy, we have noted variant readings from the *Gesta*, the *Decretals*, and the frequently cited Vallicellian manuscript codex.]

TO T., PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. Reply concerning certain articles affecting the condition of the Church of Constantinople. (Ferentino, the fourth day before the Nones of August.)

“[Among the four] [Note: [Col. 0960D] The passages which follow, distinguished here in italic type, are absent from the *Decretals*, but are found in Pithou’s additions to the *Decretals*, book I, title 33, *On Primacy and Obedience*, chapter 8.] living creatures described as being in the midst of the throne and in [Note: [Col. 0960D] In Pithou the word “in” is absent.] its circle, Ezekiel mentions the face of the eagle [Col. 0960A] as above the four of them [Note: [Col. 0960D] In Pithou: “Ezekiel [mentions] the face of the eagle above the four of them.”]. This is because, among the four patriarchal Churches—Antioch, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Constantinople—which are signified by the aforesaid creatures [Note: [Col. 0960D] In the *Gesta*, “are represented.”], and which the Apostolic See holds in its midst and embraces as special daughters [Note: [Col. 0960D] In the *Gesta*, “spiritual [daughters].”], standing around it like attendant handmaidens, the Church of Constantinople itself, after the Apostolic See, excels in the preeminence of dignity.

We aspire all the more willingly to its exaltation because, embracing it more closely as a more honorable member of the most holy Roman Church, we recognize that in these times it has greater need of its aid; and we are disposed more willingly to advance your petitions—you whom, by the Lord’s ordering, we know to preside over it—when propriety does not oppose them and no injury is caused to others. For no act of injustice ought to arise from us, from whom rights flow to others as from a fountain.

Although, therefore, so far as we can with God, we wish to show due regard for your honor and bring your requests to effect, [we nevertheless could not grant that petition in which you asked us to annul by apostolic authority the grants of churches and benefices made by our beloved son P. [Note: [Col. 0960D] This man has already been mentioned frequently.], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See. You alleged that he made these grants while you were present and wholly unconsulted; that he conferred an excessive number of churches; and that he granted them to be possessed in perpetuity without your consent [Col. 0960C] and that of the chapter of the greater Church.

For that same legate informed us by letter that, after he received letters from us appointing him to exercise the legation in the empire of Constantinople, he granted certain churches to certain churches and religious houses of the province of Jerusalem, to whose care those churches had been assigned, so that in this way some assistance might at least be given to the necessities of the Holy Land [Note: [Col. 0960D] In the *Gesta*, “on both sides.”]. He also assigned certain others to other religious houses whose envoys had gone there at the summons of our dearest son in Christ, B., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople; and, considering the benefit that might arise from their establishment, he took care to ordain canons [Note: [Col. 0961C] Vallicellian codex: “clerics.” Absent from the *Gesta*.] in certain churches.

But [Note: [Col. 0961C] In the *Gesta*, “therefore.”], because it appeared to him that after his departure you intended to alter the arrangements which he had made, in the presence of our beloved son B. [Note: [Col. 0961C] See letter 55 of book eight.], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna and legate of the Apostolic See, of many clergy, and also of yourself, he placed under the protection of the Apostolic See everything arranged by him, lest you alter any of it. He appealed to our hearing, fixing for the appeal a term extending from the imminent passage overseas until the completion of one year.

Since, therefore, the said legate set a reasonable term for the appeal which he made—he who, for so reasonable a cause, namely good obedience [Col. 0961B] and service to the Holy Land, could have extended it to two years [Note: [Col. 0961C] In the *Gesta*, “could have.”]—while the appeal was pending, according to canonical and legal enactments, as your fraternity does not fail to know, nothing concerning these matters should have been altered in his absence. This is especially so because the acts may be presumed regular until the contrary is proved, and because this could not be done without prejudice to those upon whom the said churches or benefices had been conferred by apostolic authority: they had neither been cited, nor, being absent, had they been absent through contumacy or convicted; rather, they were wholly undefended.

If we judge that any of these grants should be confirmed for anyone, know that this must be done in the common form: namely, insofar as they possess them justly and peaceably. Nor should you be surprised, as the same legate asserts, that he conferred the churches and benefices in question while you were present and unconsulted, since you yourself took care to make much greater appointments—the church of Saint Sophia, which is the head of the patriarchate, as well as archbishoprics and bishoprics—while he was present and entirely unconsulted, though he was exercising our office there [Col. 0962A].

Although, therefore, for the foregoing reasons we could not grant your petition in accordance with your desire, nevertheless, wishing to show regard for your honor as far as we can without compromising our own propriety, we grant to your fraternity that those who possess those churches or benefices shall render you the obedience due and devoted to you, unless perhaps any of these churches had, before the capture of the imperial city, been lawfully exempted from the patriarch’s jurisdiction.

[Note: [Col. 0961C] See the *Decretals*, book I, title 33, *On Primacy and Obedience*, chapter 8.] We also did not think fit to admit the following [petition, in which [Note: [Col. 0961C] In the *Decretals*, “against,” and shortly afterward “which you requested for those.”] you asked that those churches should be made subject to you which, before the capture of Constantinople, were not answerable to the patriarch of Constantinople, for two reasons. [Col. 0962B] The principle of law required [Note: [Col. 0961C] In the *Decretals*, “requires.”] that we should make no disposition concerning them to the prejudice of those to whom the churches themselves are subject [Note: [Col. 0961D] In the *Decretals*, “make.”], since they had neither been cited nor convicted nor were absent through contumacy.] Prudence also advised against doing this at the present time, lest the Pisans, Venetians, and many others who have churches of this kind at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0961D] Venetians, Pisans, and other Latins resident in Constantinople for trade had churches of this kind which did not obey the patriarch’s jurisdiction, because they followed the Latin rite. Indeed, after Constantinople was recovered from the Latins by the Greeks and the other Latins were expelled from the city, Venetians, Pisans, and Genoese remained; but because it was deemed unsafe to allow them to remain in the city, residence was granted to them by Palaeologus in the town of Pera, also called Galata, situated opposite Constantinople, with the customs duty on all merchandise remitted. Thus the Venetians and others had not only their own churches but also their own magistrates, sent there to preside over their countrymen; these were called the Venetian *bailo*, the Pisan consul, and the Genoese podestà, as Gregoras writes, book IV. Likewise, by treaty the Venetians held in perpetuity, in every city of the kingdom of Jerusalem, a church of their own, a square, and an oven free from every exaction. William of Tyre, book XII, chapter 25.] should at this time be provoked against the empire, when they ought rather to be attracted by conciliatory treatment until it is strengthened with unshakable solidity. But if at a suitable time you judge that your right against them should be pursued, we shall, by the Lord’s help, ensure that full justice is done to you concerning them.

[Col. 0962C] [Note: [Col. 0962C] See the *Decretals*, ibid.] Concerning the obedience which you likewise requested that we should cause to be rendered to you by the archbishop and bishops of the kingdom of Cyprus [Note: [Col. 0962C] In former times the patriarch of Antioch presided over the entire East, and thus over the island of Cyprus, which was counted as part of Syria. But little by little the Cypriot bishops withdrew from the authority of Antioch, aided by the unsettled conditions of the times and changes in imperial affairs; hence canon 8 of the Council of Ephesus declared them free and exempt from the authority of Antioch [Col. 0962D]. Yet in the time of Zeno, when the relics of Barnabas were discovered in Cyprus and brought to Constantinople, the Cypriot bishops on that occasion fell under the rule of Constantinople. Cedrenus, under Zeno: “From this occasion Cyprus thereafter became a metropolitan see, so that it was no longer subject to Antioch, but to Constantinople.” On that occasion Cyprus was made a metropolis, so that it would no longer be reckoned under Antioch but would be subject to Constantinople alone. Nicephorus wrongly assigns this to the time of Anastasius, book XVI, chapter 37.
