But again, when the Church of Constantinople withdrew from the Roman Church with the foul stain of schism, the Cypriot bishops easily reclaimed their former liberty; and this was the state of affairs at the time when Thomas Mauroceno obtained the see of Constantinople.], we judged that nearly the same reply should be made to you as to the preceding petition [Note: [Col. 0962D] Absent from the *Decretals*.]. For they too had been exempt before your promotion, when [Note: [Col. 0962D] In the *Gesta*, “since.”] the Church of Constantinople was disobedient and [Col. 0963A] rebellious; and, in their absence, we ought not to alter [Note: [Col. 0963D] Vallicellian codex: “ought not.”] anything concerning their status [Note: [Col. 0963D] Vallicellian codex: “be altered.”]. Nevertheless, we shall not deny you justice when you judge it should be requested.]

Furthermore, it was represented to us on your behalf that certain bishops of Romania, though warned, disdain to obey you, even while they continue to receive episcopal revenues. Some of them flee from their bishoprics so that they cannot be warned, abandoning their dioceses for six months or more. You therefore humbly asked us [Note: [Col. 0963D] In the *Gesta*, “you earnestly besought us.”] to advise you soundly in this matter and to write to your devotion how you ought to proceed concerning them and their dioceses.

Accordingly, considering that, because of the recent change of empire [Col. 0963B] and the occurrence of new circumstances, proceedings must be conducted with the greatest maturity, we reply to your fraternity as follows. Ensure that they are cited not once but repeatedly—that is, a first, second, and third time. If they refuse to appear [Note: [Col. 0963D] In the *Gesta*, “obey.”] and choose to persist in their contumacy [Note: [Col. 0963D] Vallicellian codex: “obstinacy.”], unless perhaps they choose to protect themselves with the shield of an appeal, which they must pursue within the legal time, compel them by sentences of suspension and excommunication to come to your obedience.

If even thus their hardness cannot be softened, let our beloved son B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna and legate of the Apostolic See, remove them from the administration of their bishoprics, and together with you provide for the churches over which they preside by appointing suitable persons [Col. 0963C]. But let him not pronounce a sentence of degradation against them, so that they may more easily [Note: [Col. 0963D] In the *Gesta*, “more confidently.”] be dealt with mercifully if this proves expedient.

In the churches of those who fraudulently absent themselves so that a citation cannot reach them, have an edict of triple citation publicly proclaimed. If they still do not take care to obey, or if they abandon their churches for more than six months, so that according to canonical enactments they ought deservedly to be deprived of them, proceed against them also as prescribed above. When the legate has returned home, we grant to you personally, for as long as it pleases us and our successors, that you may proceed in the prescribed manner against the aforesaid rebels [Col. 0963D] as a delegate of the Apostolic See.

Your fraternity further requested that, because in those regions there is an excessive number of bishoprics, and they are too impoverished, we should permit you to reduce them to a smaller number. We have decided that provision should be made thus: whenever necessity or advantage requires it, the aforesaid legate, for as long as he remains in those regions, with your counsel nevertheless being obtained [Col. 0964A], may carry this out. That is, he is not to unite bishoprics; rather, he is to entrust certain such churches, as he sees fit [Note: [Col. 0964D] In the *Gesta*, “if.”], to the person whom he ordains for one church, so that, if perhaps other arrangements concerning them are made because of the necessity of the time [Note: [Col. 0964D] Vallicellian codex: “of that [time].”], what has been done may more readily be altered. When the legate returns home, you too, if necessary, shall do the same by authority of the Apostolic See as our delegate.

You next asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See how you ought to arrange those bishoprics in which Greeks alone reside, as well as those in which Greeks and Latins are mixed together, and whom you ought to appoint over them. To this [Col. 0964B] we briefly reply to your fraternity that in those churches in which there are Greeks only, you ought to ordain Greek bishops, if you can find men who are devoted and faithful to us and to you and who are willing humbly and devoutly to receive consecration from you. In those, however, in which Greeks are mixed with Latins, appoint Latins and give them precedence over Greeks.

Moreover, you asked us to permit you, by our authorization, to invest persons appointed or to be appointed to ecclesiastical dignities with staffs, mitres, rings, and sandals, and to dispense those who have presumed to receive major orders after omitting the minor ones. Wishing to confer a special favor upon you personally [Col. 0964C], by the authority of these presents we grant that you may bestow the aforesaid insignia upon those to whom, according to the custom of the Apostolic See, they may honorably be granted. You may also, by our authority, dispense those whose learning and gravity of character commend them concerning the omission of the aforesaid minor orders, after first imposing suitable penance upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0964D] See the *Decretals*, book I, title 22, *On Foreign Clerics*, chapter 11.] Your fraternity also consulted us [whether clerics who come to you without letters from those who ordained them, and who offer to swear bodily [Note: [Col. 0964D] Absent from the *Decretals*.] that they have been constituted in some ecclesiastical order whatsoever, should be promoted by you to higher orders. We therefore [Note: [Col. 0964D] Absent from the *Decretals*.] reply to your inquiry that, unless their canonical ordination has been established to your satisfaction by suitable evidence, you must neither receive them in those orders [Col. 0964D] nor promote them to major orders, especially before their manner of life has been examined and approved.]

You also requested instruction from the Apostolic See concerning the rite of the sacrifices and other sacraments: whether you ought to allow [Note: [Col. 0964D] In the *Gesta*, “admit.”] the Greeks [Col. 0965A] to perform them according to their own rite or rather compel them to the Latin rite. To this we briefly reply to your fraternity that you should tolerate them in their own rite for as long as they cannot be brought back by you, until the Apostolic See, after more mature deliberation, judges that something else should be established concerning this matter [Note: [Col. 0965C] Vallicellian codex: “done.”].

[ [Note: [Col. 0965C] Absent from the *Decretals*.] Concerning clerics [Note: [Col. 0965C] See the *Decretals*, book III, title 4, *On Clerics Not Resident in a Church or Benefice*, chapter 10.] who in this new situation retain churches or benefices granted them without [Note: [Col. 0965C] In the *Decretals*, “without”; in the *Gesta*, “abandon.”] just and necessary cause, and especially without your consent, we have judged it proper to write [Note: [Col. 0965C] In the *Decretals*, “reply.”] this to you: after they have been awaited for an appropriate time, if they do not return to them, they may justly be deprived of them, provided they are not detained by a lawful impediment.]

[ [Note: [Col. 0965D] See the *Decretals*, book III, title 36, *On Religious Houses Being Subject to the Bishop*, chapter 5.] Concerning monasteries of Greeks to be converted into [Col. 0965B] secular canonries, we reply to your fraternity as follows [Note: [Col. 0965D] In the *Gesta*, “briefly.”]: for as long as [Note: [Col. 0965D] The *Decretals* add “the monasteries.”] they can remain organized under regular men [Note: [Col. 0965D] Absent from the *Decretals*.], whether Greeks or Latins, they are not to be transferred to secular clerics; but if regulars are lacking, secular clerics may be appointed in them because of that lack.]

“You further humbly requested us, since it is difficult for persons subject to your jurisdiction to travel to the Apostolic See for every individual dispute, to establish a limit concerning appeals. Since Pope Gregory, our predecessor of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0965D] In the *Gesta*, “of holy remembrance.”]—Gregory VIII, as in chapter 47, *On Appeals*, in the second collection of the *Decretals*—decreed that, if a dispute concerning small matters valued at [Col. 0965C] less than twenty marks is litigated in the courts of archbishops or bishops and one of the litigants thinks deceitfully to appeal, the bishops, disregarding that appeal, are to compel the parties to choose judges, free from suspicion, within the boundaries of their bishoprics, provided suitable persons can be found there, in whose presence the dispute may be settled.

Considering that it would be excessively costly [Col. 0966A] and burdensome for your subjects to approach the Apostolic See for every complaint amid the many dangers of sea and land, we grant you personally [Note: [Col. 0965D] In the *Gesta*, “by apostolic writings.”] that, in causes which should be heard in your court, if either party appeals to the Apostolic See and the matter in dispute does not exceed the aforementioned sum, you shall proceed according to justice notwithstanding the raising of the appeal; or you shall compel the parties to submit to arbitrators who, with the appeal set aside, may hear the cause and decide it finally. You shall do the same in lighter causes, especially between lesser persons, which, since they are purely spiritual, contain no civil question.

Compel Venetians resident in the imperial city, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside, to pay tithes to those persons and churches at Constantinople to whom they are legally due [Col. 0966B]. The custom observed by the inhabitants of Venice shall not stand in the way—namely, that they tithe only at death what they acquired in life—lest, under this pretext, the Church of Constantinople be defrauded of its right if perhaps persons who have lived at Constantinople for a long time return to Venice near the end of their lives. Yet in these and other matters proceed with discretion and maturity, avoiding precipitancy and undue readiness; for in such matters it is better to be blamed for some slowness than for excessive speed.”

Given at Ferentino, the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the [Col. 0966C] ninth year.

CXLI [Note: [Col. 0965D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §6.] … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NICOSIA [Note: [Col. 0965D]

See letter 181 of book eight and the notes there. It has seemed worthwhile to add certain further matters here.

In the year 1191 Richard, king of England, set out with a numerous fleet to wage holy war against the Saracens, who had again seized Palestine. When he landed in Cyprus, he was badly received by Isaac Comnenus, the Greek ruler of the island, who was allied by an unholy treaty with Saladin the Saracen. Richard quickly and easily brought him to order; after expelling him, [Col. 0966C] he established Guy of Lusignan as king of Cyprus. Nicosia, or Leucosia, formerly called Ledra, immediately became the capital of the kingdom, and a Latin-rite archbishop was established there.

Meanwhile, the Greek-rite archbishop, in accordance with ancient custom, had his seat at Famagusta. At that time only a small number of bishops were subject to him—no more than four in all: those of Leucosia, [Col. 0966D] Solia or Soloi, Carpasia, and Amathus or Nimosia. Disputes over jurisdiction immediately arose between the two archbishops. By command of Pope Celestine III, the Greek pontiff was ordered to submit to the Latin; Celestine’s successor Innocent III confirmed this in a second constitution, found in his Register, no. 22.

The Greeks took it ill that they should be subject to the authority of a Latin prelate. When the matter was referred to Pope Alexander IV, he decreed that, after the death of Germanus, who was then archbishop of the Greeks, no other Greek archbishop of that kind should thereafter be created; rather, the Latin bishop of Leucosia should exercise jurisdiction over the Greek-rite bishops. This was observed thereafter until 1570, when Cyprus was taken from the Venetian republic by Turkish arms. The Greek-rite Christians, with whom the island abounded, then established an archbishop of their own, wholly independent—like the former *autokephalos* (αὐτοκέφαλος, “self-headed,” independent)—and subject to no patriarch, whether Byzantine or Antiochene.]

… That he should present himself before the Apostolic See. (Ferentino, on the Nones of August.)

Since, according to the Apostle, we are debtors to the wise and the foolish, we ought to receive the just petitions of all persons, lest, contrary to the divine law, there be respect of persons with us [Col. 0967A]. Although it is not expedient in these days for either you or our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, to litigate against one another—as we have informed that patriarch by our letters—nevertheless, because he has strongly urged through his envoys that we should cause justice to be rendered to him concerning the obedience which he contends is owed him by you and your suffragans, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, from the next feast of Saint Michael until two years have elapsed, you shall present yourself before the Apostolic See, either personally or through a suitable representative.

This is conditional, however, upon this citation reaching you at least one year beforehand, so that within that year you may be adequately able to prepare to execute our command. Know for certain that, although we do not wish to fail the aforesaid [Col. 0967B] patriarch in his right, we also wish, as duty requires, to support you in your justice.

Given at Ferentino, on the Nones of August, in the ninth year.

CXLII. TO T., PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. The observance is commanded of the agreement made between him and the governor of the empire of Constantinople. (See the *Gesta Innocentii*, §101.)

[Our daily duty—the care, by the Lord’s ordering, incumbent upon us for all Churches—admonishes and induces us to add apostolic authority to those arrangements which are made by prudent deliberation for the benefit of Churches, lest through the evasions of evil men, who envy the advancement and peace of Churches, [Col. 0967C] such arrangements might be brought to their detriment.

Therefore, since an amicable agreement has been reached between you and the clergy entrusted to you on the one part, and our beloved son, the noble man Henry, governor of the empire of Constantinople, together with the barons, knights, and people, on the other, concerning compensation to be made to the churches from their possessions, we, considering the necessity of the time, command that this agreement be firmly observed, as it was prudently made without force or fraud and freely and voluntarily accepted by both sides with full knowledge, provided that no prejudice is caused to anyone concerning such possessions and revenues.

For fuller information, we have judged it proper to insert word for word in this document [Col. 0967D] the form of that agreement as contained in the instrument drawn up concerning it.]

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, in the year of the Lord 1206, in the month of March, in the ninth indiction, at Constantinople. This is the form of the agreement made between Lord Benedict, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, legate of the Apostolic See, and Lord Thomas Maurocenus, patriarch of the holy Church of Constantinople, on the one hand; and Lord Henry, the barons, knights, and people, on the other; concerning territories conquered and to be conquered within and outside the Empire of Romania. [Note: [Col. 0967D] The Royal Codex and the Podian Codex, cited by Baluze in the margin, read “Roman.”]

Lord Henry, by the counsel and consent of all the princes, barons, knights, and people, grants to the churches, and promises to grant them, in compensation for their possessions, as set forth below, outside the walls of the city of Constantinople, one fifteenth part of all possessions: cities, castles, hamlets, fields, vineyards, groves, woods, meadows, orchards, gardens, saltworks, land and sea passages, tolls on land and sea, fisheries in the sea and fresh water, and all possessions, even if they are not fully specified in the present document. The following are excepted: from the land which they hold beside the walls of the said city, from the Golden Gate to the Gate of Blachernae, between its wall and the sea, they shall in no way be bound to give one fifteenth part. Nor shall they give it from the mint-hamlets, for whose compensation Lord Henry and the aforesaid persons shall be bound, at the first conquest, to satisfy the churches from the fifteenth part according to the value of those hamlets. [Note: [Col. 0968D] The Royal Codex, in the same place, reads “casinorum, casalinorum” (“of houses/hamlets, of small hamlets”).]

They shall not give one fifteenth part from the commercial revenue which they receive within Constantinople or outside it in the name of the city. [Note: [Col. 0968D] Baluze, in the margin: perhaps *commercio*, “trade.”] If trade dues are paid in the city of Constantinople in the name of another city or place, or elsewhere, they shall give one fifteenth part to the Church. But if they make an arrangement, in return for an annual rent, with any city, castle, territory, or island which Lord Henry cannot subject to himself and the empire, they shall give one fifteenth part to the Church. If, however, he wishes to enfeoff, donate, or alienate it, he shall do so only after first preserving the Church’s fifteenth part.

The division of possessions between the Church and the aforesaid persons shall be made as follows: within eight days after the present document has been sealed with a bull, worthy men shall be chosen by both sides. Having sworn an oath, they shall in good faith divide the possession of each land and water into fifteen parts; and, if they cannot agree otherwise, they shall cast lots. Whatever falls by lot to the Church shall belong to the Church. These matters shall all be completed in good faith by the coming feast of Pentecost.

All enclosed religious houses, both within and outside the city, shall likewise be free to the Church and shall not be reckoned in the fifteenth part. If a dispute arises about the extent of the enclosed houses, each party shall choose a suitable man within eight days after the dispute begins; those two shall, on oath, choose a third; and whatever those three, or the majority of them, bound by oath, determine in good faith within twenty days shall remain settled. If, because of an urgent necessity of the land, ancient enclosed houses must be fortified as castles, they shall be so fortified with the consent of the lord patriarch or the diocesan bishop. If they cannot agree with those undertaking the fortification, the dispute concerning the enclosed houses shall be resolved as stated above.

They shall also pay forever the tithes of all Latins: namely, from grain, legumes, and all fruits of the land and vineyards which they cultivate or have cultivated at their own expense; and from the fruits of trees and gardens which the head of household in good faith puts to use for eating and small gifts. Tithes shall be paid from the increase of animals and quadrupeds, and from bees and wool. If in time the Church is able, by exhortation and admonition, to obtain tithes from Greeks, they shall offer no obstacle to this.

Moreover, all clerics and churches, their possessions, those dwelling on such possessions and in churches, religious persons both Greek and Latin, those dwelling with the aforesaid persons, the enclosed houses of churches, those inhabiting them, and those who take refuge in the Church, shall be free from all lay jurisdiction, according to the more liberal custom of France, while preserving in all things the authority of the Roman Church and likewise of the Church of Constantinople, and the honour and right of the lord patriarch, the emperor, and the empire, as well as all the foregoing articles.

From territories which, God willing, are conquered hereafter, the Church shall first receive one fifteenth part before anything is distributed to anyone. Lord Henry and his barons shall in good faith observe all these things and, so far as they are able, see that they are duly carried into effect. Let absolutely no one be permitted to infringe this page of agreement or compact, or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone, etc.

The lord patriarch, for himself and his successors, and the others, excepting the common share of the Venetians, promised firmly to observe this settlement.

Given at Constantinople, at Saint Sophia, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March]. Let no one therefore … infringe this page of our command, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the Nones of August [5 August], in the ninth year.

CXLIII. [Note: [Col. 0969D] A fragment of this letter is found among the Decretals, book III, title 39, *On Rents, Exactions, and Procurations*, chapter 19. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are appended.] TO R., BISHOP OF SARAGOSSA. The abbot of San Juan de la Peña is condemned to pay tithes and to provide procuration. (Ferentino, 4 August.)

[When formerly] [Note: [Col. 0969D] What follows, here distinguished in italic type, is read in Pithou’s additions.] you had sent to us your complaint that the beloved son … the abbot of Saint John of the Rock [San Juan de la Peña], [Note: [Col. 0970D] This is the name of a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Jaca, mentioned more than once by Jerónimo Blanca in his *Commentary on Aragonese Affairs*, and by Lucius Marineus in *On Spanish Affairs*, and by Innocent himself below, in the chapter *Petrus*, *On Homicide*.] was in various ways defrauding you of the fourth part of the tithes which you ought to receive in the churches of Luna and Tauste, we thought fit to commit the case to the beloved sons … the provost of Jaca and P. … archdeacon of Monte Aragón in the diocese of Tarazona. In their presence your party requested that the abbot should pay you, without deduction, a fourth part of all the tithes which you had customarily received in the aforesaid churches.

The response made on behalf of the abbot was that, since the aforesaid churches belong by full right to the monastery, you could claim no right in them. On your behalf it was asserted in reply that both the fourth part of the tithe and other episcopal rights belonged to you in several ways in the churches mentioned; for, since these churches are situated in your diocese, you are entitled by common law to demand in them both a fourth part of the tithe and the other episcopal dues.

You also alleged a settlement made between your church and the monastery of San Juan de la Peña through B., archbishop of Tarragona of blessed memory, and R., count of Barcelona, by which you acknowledged that both the *coena* [customary episcopal entertainment or procuration] and a fourth part of the tithe, together with other episcopal dues, belonged to you in those churches. To prove this you produced an authentic instrument, asserting that the settlement had been confirmed by the authority of our predecessor Pope Alexander III, of blessed memory, as is plainly contained in that authentic document.

Likewise you advanced another settlement made through G., bishop of Pamplona of blessed memory, and the beloved sons F. of Otiñén and D., monk of Saint John, by which, you asserted, the fourth part was due to you; and you produced a public instrument concerning it. To strengthen your claim still further, you alleged forty years’ prescription, maintaining that, even if you had no other means of defence, a right had accrued to you through the long period during which you had received the aforesaid fourth part of the tithe.

The response on behalf of the abbot was that the aforesaid churches belong by common law and full right to the monastery of San Juan de la Peña. Sanch[o], king of Aragon of illustrious memory, had obtained from the Apostolic See an indulgence allowing him, if any places in his kingdom should newly come to be populated or be liberated from the hands of the Saracens, freely to grant to whomever he wished the churches to be built in them. After he had subsequently introduced inhabitants into the castle of Luna, he granted to the monastery of San Juan de la Peña the churches of Luna and Tauste built there; and, to prove this, the abbot produced instruments drawn up for the aforesaid grants.

Peter, bishop of Pamplona of blessed memory, in whose diocese the aforesaid churches were said to be situated, also granted those churches to the said monastery together with the tithes and other episcopal rights, as is contained in that bishop’s authentic instrument. To prove that the churches were situated in the diocese of Pamplona, the aforesaid abbot introduced witnesses.

The same abbot further alleged that García, your predecessor of blessed memory, granted those churches to his monastery with every episcopal right, except the consecration of churches and certain other matters which are more fully contained in the authentic instrument drawn up on that occasion. For this reason the abbot replied that you could by law demand nothing in the aforesaid churches.

The monastery’s party further argued that both the first and second settlements proposed on your behalf should be rejected, because each settlement had been violently extorted through pressure and fear exerted by a secular prince. It endeavoured to demonstrate this through witness depositions. It also maintained that a confirmation obtained for so unlawful a settlement could afford you no benefit of defence, since a right is by no means acquired through confirmation, but a right already acquired is more securely preserved.

Against the forty-year prescription which you advanced, the monastery’s party answered that, even if such prescription had been proved, it was shown to have been repeatedly interrupted, because, owing to the frequent controversies arising concerning those churches within periods of forty years, two settlements are shown to have intervened. Furthermore, since, according to canonical enactments, the periods of one who makes an unlawful settlement or alienation must be deducted from prescription, it is evident that the forty-year prescription was by no means completed if the time during which the abbot who made the unlawful settlement subsequently lived is deducted.

To this your party firmly replied that the aforesaid indulgence alleged to have been granted to King Sancho had never been produced in court. Even if it had been produced, or its authenticity had been most certainly established, it could cause you no prejudice, since the abbot himself had confessed before us in court that the indulgence had been granted to the said king without prejudice to episcopal right; and he asserted that he had made this same admission before the delegated judges.

Your party also consistently maintained that the grant of the bishop of Pamplona could not prejudice you, because it had not been sufficiently demonstrated by witnesses that the aforesaid churches were situated in his diocese. In reply to the grant by your predecessor, it was said on your behalf that, since the abbot, questioned in court, had replied that the same predecessor had not had authority to confer those spiritual rights, it is unworthy that he should gain advantage from an instrument which he did not blush to challenge in court. This is especially so because the instrument had not at all been shown to be authentic, and above all because, after that grant is said to have been made, the monastery itself is known for many years to have rendered to your church the tithes and other episcopal dues for those churches.

Your party further argued that the abbot himself should not be heard at all concerning the alleged fear through which the aforesaid settlements are said to have been concluded. For even if it were established that fear had been employed when the settlement was made, since payment of both the tithes and the other episcopal dues afterward followed voluntarily and freely, that abbot cannot reasonably excuse himself on the pretext of coercion.

Having fully understood these and other matters which were put forward before the aforesaid judges and before us, [when full proof had been given us [Note: [Col. 0971D] In the Decretals: “because proof had been given us that the churches of Luna and Bes….” Pithou, margin, variant: “of Luna, of Tauste.”] that the aforesaid churches [Note: [Col. 0971D] The Decretals add: “of Saint John of Prilaten.”] are situated in your diocese, not only by other evidence but also by the express provision of the instruments of settlement, that the abbot [Note: [Col. 0971D] Pithou, margin, variants: Platen., Praelaten., Praematen.; it should unquestionably be read Pinnaten.], must answer to you both concerning the fourth part of the tithes, regarding which alone he asserted that violence had been committed, [Note: [Col. 0971D] Omitted in the Decretals.] and concerning the other episcopal dues, [Note: [Col. 0971D] The Decretals read “to you.”] regarding which he complained that no violence had been inflicted upon him], we, with the counsel of our brethren, condemn the abbot of San Juan de la Peña [Note: [Col. 0971D] The words “of San Juan de la Peña” are absent from the Decretals, as is immediately the word “of rights,” added below after “episcopal.”] to full payment of a fourth part of all tithes, with no deductions made, and to the furnishing of procurations and other episcopal dues in the aforesaid churches.

For although under the terms of the second settlement certain deductions ought to have been made, yet because the abbot himself in no way approved that settlement but made repeated efforts to challenge it, [Note: [Col. 0971D] A safer objection was not lacking, although it is here passed over in silence: namely, that this monastery, together with its churches and villages, was exempt from every yoke and payment owed to royal or episcopal authority, according to the letter of Sancho IV, king of Aragon, which Blanca transcribed: “Sancho the king, my grandfather, of worthy memory, among the other works of his good will, established in the monastery of Saint John the Baptist of the Rock a community of monks; and, that they might freely serve God, he gave them privileges of liberty. For by a privilege made according to the privileges of the monastery of Cluny, he exempted them, their successors, and the place, with all monasteries, villages, and allods belonging to his right, from every yoke or payment due to royal, episcopal, ecclesiastical, or secular authority, through royal authority, with the favour and assent of Manlius, bishop of Aragon, etc.” Understand the diocesan bishop of Jaca, who was called bishop of Aragon because Jaca was once the royal city of Aragon. But perhaps this was not raised by the abbot.] he ought not to obtain from it a benefit which he seemed tacitly to have renounced.

Furthermore, it was absurd for him to deny that that church was situated in your diocese, when the instrument of your predecessor showed that it had lawfully been granted to his monastery, [by which the episcopal right was plainly apparent.]

Given at Ferentino, on 4 August, in the ninth year.

CXLIV. … TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT PONTIANUS OF LUCCA. They are not bound to receive J., removed from the monastery because of an offence. (Ferentino, 2 August.)

By your letters you informed us that John, who was once regularly removed from your monastery because his offences required it, although we caused the sentence of perpetual removal pronounced against him to be confirmed by apostolic authority, nevertheless troubles you and your monastery on the pretext of our letters, which he obtains by concealing the truth.

Therefore, wishing to oppose his fraudulent stratagems and to provide for your peace with paternal concern, by the authority of these presents we grant you that no one whatsoever, by letters hitherto obtained from us or to be obtained in future without mention of these letters, may compel you to answer the said John concerning your monastery. Let him know that, having been lawfully expelled from it, his return is forever barred. Let no one therefore … But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on 2 August, in the ninth year.

CXLV. [Note: [Col. 0973B] A fragment of this letter is found among the Decretals, book I, title 28, *On the Office of a Vicar*, chapter 5.] … TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT EUGENIUS; … TO THE PLEBAN [parish-church priest] OF SAINT PETER IN PISSIDE; AND TO BONIFACE, CANON OF THE PLEBS OF MARCULFO, IN THE DIOCESES OF SIENA AND FLORENCE. They are to cause an excommunication sentence pronounced by the bishop of Volterra to be observed. (Ferentino, 9 August.)

[Col. 0973B]

[By his representation to us,] our venerable brother … the bishop of Volterra [Note: [Col. 0973B] See letter 156 of book VIII, note.] has made known that, when the clerics of the plebs of Petiole had sworn to elect a provost in accordance with the will of laymen, and, after an election thus held, had presented their chosen candidate to him, he not only refused to confirm the election but also bound with the bond of excommunication both the consuls and other laymen who had induced the aforesaid clerics to do this, and the clerics themselves, for these matters and others in which they had shown themselves disobedient to him.

He obtained our letters directed to our venerable brother … the archbishop of Pisa [Note: [Col. 0973C] See letter 9 of book III, note.] and … the bishop of Lucca [Note: [Col. 0973C] See letter 160 of book V, note.], requiring them to cause the sentence, as it had been reasonably pronounced, to be firmly observed without appeal until suitable satisfaction had been made. The opposing party, however, obtained letters from our venerable brother P., bishop of Porto, [Note: [Col. 0973C] See letter 69 of book V, note.] our vicar, addressed to the same bishop of Lucca and to the beloved son P., cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0973C] Master Pandulf Masca, a native of Pisa rather than Lucca, as Didacus de Franchis writes in his *Life of Saint John Gualbert*, was ordained subdeacon of the sacred apostolic palace by Pope Callixtus II, as he himself testifies in his life of that same Callixtus II in these words: “He performed many ordinations in the city of cardinals and bishops, and promoted Pandulf to the subdiaconate.” By Lucius III he was named cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Holy Twelve Apostles; and by command of Celestine III he exercised the office of legate at Genoa, to settle civil discord and procure peace with the Pisans. He was also sent by Innocent III as legate, with Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Eudoxia, into Tuscany, to annul the leagues of Etruscan cities which had been made without consulting the Apostolic See, particularly because the duchy of Tuscany belonged by right and lordship to the Roman Church.

Godwin, in his catalogue of the bishops of Norwich, and Matthew of Westminster state that Pandulf also exercised a legation in England, but they are mistaken: they confuse our Pandulf with another, who, after being legate of the Holy Roman Church, was later named bishop of Norwich. He was present at the elections of the Roman pontiffs Urban, Clement, Celestine, and this Innocent III, and attended the canonization of Saint John Gualbert, founder of the monks of Vallombrosa.

He wrote the lives of the supreme pontiffs from Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, to his own age—that is, down to Innocent III. Some portions of these he composed, and some he excerpted from Damasus, Anastasius, and Peter William. Constantine Cajetan, abbot of Saint Barontius, reports in his commentaries on the life of Gelasius II that this work of Pandulf, still unpublished and written by hand, survives in the Vatican Library under numbers 226 and 3762, and in the possession of Alexander Cherubini, who has deserved well of antiquity.

He also described in a substantial volume the glorious deeds of the Pisans, at home and abroad, in peace and war. Yet this work, although most diligently sought by many, still lies hidden in obscurity. Concerning Pandulf—whom the records especially of the Vatican Library honour with the distinguished title of master, and who was a close friend and inseparable travelling companion of Pope Gelasius II—William Eisengren, in his *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, under the year 1184, wrote this encomium: “Pandulf of Pisa, doctor of Sacred Scripture, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal priest of the Holy Twelve Apostles, a man most worthy of everyone’s admiration, master of expression and eloquent orator, most celebrated historian, and second to no theologian.”

Among other records, both ancient and recent, diplomas of Lucius III, Urban III, Clement III, and Innocent III mention the same Pandulf; Innocent’s Register does so even more frequently.

“As regards the year of Pandulf’s death, the fact that he died worn out by advanced age is shown especially by this: already ordained subdeacon by Callixtus II, as we have said, he was created cardinal priest by Pope Lucius III in the year of our salvation 1182. The diplomas of Innocent III also show it, for Pandulf himself subscribed them in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1201, when they were issued to the church of Saint Mary of Glarea at Verona. Since after that year no mention of him is found, one may readily believe that he laid aside mortality not long after that year.” OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1114.

This letter of Innocent proves that Pandulf lived at least until 9 August 1206.]

By occasion of those letters, they absolved the aforesaid laymen and clerics and pronounced a sentence against the aforesaid bishop of Volterra. Although he believed that sentence to be null for many reasons, he nevertheless appealed to our hearing out of an abundance of caution.

[Therefore, judging the vicar’s letters to have been obtained by surreption, because the jurisdiction of a vicar whom the Roman pontiff leaves in the city [Note: [Col. 0974D] In the Decretals, “left”; and below the words “to your discretion … letters” are omitted.] does not extend beyond it [Note: [Col. 0974D] There were three vicars of the praetorian prefect of Italy: the first, vicar of the City; the second, of Italy; the third, of Africa. The vicar of the City had jurisdiction within the city and to the fortieth milestone. Cassiodorus, book VI, letter 15, in the formula for the vicar of the City: “Within the fortieth milestone you preserve the laws of the most holy city.” Beyond the authority which the vicar possessed in the city, ten Italian provinces obeyed him: Campania, Tuscany, Umbria, and others listed in the *Notitia of the Western Empire*.

Innocent indicates in this letter that the dignity of vicar of the City was restored by the popes, and that, in addition to jurisdiction in the city, he had his own diocese in the district lying between the provinces of Capua and Pisa. This follows from the statement that the vicar of the City’s jurisdiction does not extend outside the city unless specially granted to him, especially when he resides in his own particular province. Gregory III, *Dialogues*, chapter 3, mentions John as holding the place of the prefects in the city: “John also, a distinguished man, holding in this city the place of the prefects, etc.” The dignity of prefect of the City was likewise restored by the popes. Innocent III himself testifies, book I, letter 23, that immediately after Innocent’s consecration the prefect of the City rendered him fealty and liege homage and received investiture of the prefecture from him by delivery of the mantle.] unless it has been specially granted to him, particularly since he resides in his own special province, namely between the provinces of Capua and Pisa—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, revoking as null whatever was done on the occasion of those letters, [Note: [Col. 0976D] The Decretals read “revoke.”]] you shall cause the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, as it was reasonably imposed, to be firmly observed without appeal until fitting satisfaction has been made. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. And if not all, etc., two, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on 9 August, in the ninth year.

CXLVI. … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TORRES. He is to absolve the church of Thergo from payment of rent if he finds it exempt. (Ferentino, 9 August.)

The beloved son R., cardinal priest of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino, [Note: [Col. 0976D] See letter 108 of book V, note.] humbly petitioned us that, since the monastery of Monte Cassino has possessed the church of Saint Mary of Thergo for one hundred years and more without litigation, never paying anything to the Roman Church in the name of rent for it, as all its prelates and subjects constantly affirm, we should deign to write to you that you should not exact rent from the said church.

Although rents and public records are, under human laws, stronger evidence than witnesses, yet, wishing to comply with the said abbot’s request, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to hear what he may think fit to advance in his defence. If he can lawfully establish that the said church is not bound to pay rent, you shall wholly absolve it from such payment. Otherwise, you shall compel it, without appeal, to pay that rent in accordance with the form communicated to you.

Given at Ferentino, on 8 August, in the ninth year.

CXLVII. [Note: [Col. 0976D] A copy of this letter, which we had arranged to have transcribed together with the others on the authority of Conti’s copy, slipped from our hands—we do not know by what accident. Therefore we can provide here only its summary. See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §36.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SARDINIA. That, according to her promise and oath, they are to compel the lady of Gallura to contract marriage with the pope’s cousin.

CXLVIII. TO THE PATRIARCH [Note: [Col. 0976D] See letter 19 of book VIII.] AND CHAPTER OF CONSTANTINOPLE. They are to receive C., a cleric, as a canon of the church of Saint Sophia. (Ferentino, 26 August.)

The beginning of the new planting which the Church of Constantinople has received through the event of an unforeseen novelty ought, with the zealous care of great solicitude, to receive increase and progress. Thus what has happily been begun through provident ordering may be extended and beneficially supported by the strength of stability. This may occur more easily if men distinguished by learning and uprightness are established in the Constantinopolitan churches; they must indeed be induced, not only by honourable exhortations but also by generous benefactions, to come to the city of Constantinople, so that, the greater the dangers to which they expose themselves, the more richly they may be honoured with the rewards of benefices.

Accordingly, since the beloved son P., [Note: [Col. 0976D] This man has already been mentioned several times.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, has instituted his beloved familiar Master C. as a canon in the church of Saint Sophia at Constantinople, we approve his institution as canonical. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, receiving that master—whom, because of his proven worth, we hold exceedingly dear and acceptable, and who can be very useful to you and your church both in his own person and through that cardinal—as a canon and brother of the same church, you shall without delay put him into corporal possession of it and, once he has been installed, defend him, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction or appeal.

We do not wish the same master to be hindered in any way because, in obedience to the commands of the said cardinal, he travelled with his letters to the Apostolic See. For as he has so far diligently served the cardinal, so, we believe, he will strive to serve you effectively and devotedly. We also wish that it shall not be an obstacle to that cleric that you, brother patriarch, are said to have established a fixed number of canons in the aforesaid church of Saint Sophia, since this ought not derogate from the institution made by the said cardinal.

Take care to fulfil our command in such a way that the oft-mentioned cleric is not compelled on this account to travel again to us. We could not bear that with equanimity, since passage from the eastern regions to the Apostolic See is difficult and impeded in many ways.

Given at Ferentino, on 26 August, in the ninth year.

CXLIX. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF FOSSANOVA. The agreement between them and the people of Piperno is confirmed. (Ferentino, 28 August.)

Since the Apostolic See received from the very author of peace and unity the prerogative of primacy, we who, though unworthily, preside over it are bound by the office of service laid upon us to uphold in its force those matters settled by agreement, so that they may not be brought back into the difficulty of renewed dispute. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., up to “consent”: we confirm by apostolic authority, and by the present document, etc., the agreement made between you on one side and the consuls and people of Piperno on the other, as prudently made without wrongdoing, freely accepted by both sides, and observed until now.

We have caused the tenor of this agreement, as contained in the public instrument, to be recorded in the present letters:

> “Since things done among people often ought to be committed to public writings, I, Robert of Sette, judge of the Holy Roman Church, by command of Lord Guido of Babuco, subdeacon of the lord pope, make these public and memorial letters concerning an agreement concluded between the consuls and people of Piperno on the one side and the monks of the monastery of Fossanova on the other, so that, if doubt should ever arise about it, the truth may be shown by their testimony.
>
> “The tenor of the agreement is as follows. The monks of Fossanova promised to excavate the banks of the river from Stortura to Pila, to the width which the people of Piperno had begun, and in depth down to the water, without fraud; and for forty *canne* below Pila, provided that the lords of Somnino offer no impediment within those forty *canne*.
>
> “Once the work has been completed, the monks shall in no way be bound by the agreement to repair it. In return, the consuls and people of Piperno, having sworn a corporal oath, promised to keep safe the monastery of Fossanova and its property, inside and outside, and to inflict no violence on its persons or goods. They shall establish a fixed fine against every person acting contrary to this; the consuls and other worthy men specially sworn for this purpose shall exact that fine and shall not restore it.
>
> “Furthermore, the consuls who are in office at any time shall swear to observe this without fraud or malicious contrivance. They shall be bound to observe this henceforth for ten years; and, if within that decade the people of Piperno renew their customary oath, they shall likewise renew it for the monastery of Fossanova. When the decade has elapsed, they shall observe and maintain the customary oath and renew it for the monastery of Fossanova, just as they maintain and observe it for the church of Saint Mary of Piperno and the remaining churches of Piperno—without prejudice to the rights both of the commune and of the particular persons of Piperno, and likewise of the monastery of Fossanova.”  

Let no one therefore … infringe our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on 28 August, in the ninth year.

CL. TO THE CLERGY OF BARCELONA. That the sacrament of faith is not to be denied to either a Saracen or a Jew who seeks it. (Ferentino, 26 August.)

[Col. 0978A]

A tempest having arisen upon this great and wide sea, and the human race being endangered upon it, the true Jonah, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, coming into its depths, allowed himself to be submerged by that tempest, in order to reconcile us to God in his blood, transform us into his image, and renew us through the laver of regeneration consecrated by that same blood. He excluded neither rank nor sex, but, without respect of persons, instituted that common sacrament through which persons of every race may be received into the adoption of the sons of God. For, raising up children of Abraham from stones, he gathers and brings them from East and West, saying to the North: “Give,” and to the South: “Do not withhold” (Isa. 43), so that those children whom Gentile heathenism yields to him, or adversity brings to the faith, being reborn in the font of baptism—whose [Col. 0978B] spices flow forth at the breath of the south wind—and likewise those upon whom prosperity smiles, may not be prevented from being baptized; but, whatever the occasion upon which they receive the sacrament of faith, may rejoice and be glad, because brothers who were dead have come to life, and those who were lost have been found.

Nor ought they to prefer temporal profit to the joys of the angels, who delight more over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance, lest, by craving earthly things, they make themselves unworthy of heavenly ones and lose what is everlasting for the sake of what is temporal. Certainly, you should know that it has come to our hearing that, when a general baptism is celebrated in your church, very many Saracens flock to it and urgently request baptism. Their masters, both Jews and Christians, fearing the loss of temporal advantage, presume to prevent them, demanding from the Church a price for those whom she regenerates to the Lord through baptism, violently taking pledges from you on their account, and moreover inflicting other burdens and losses.

Since, therefore, the Church ought to receive all who come to knowledge of the faith, having abandoned the error of their former state, and to open her bosom to those who knock; and since the south wind ought not prevent the children of the north from being baptized: by apostolic letters we command your entire community, strictly enjoining you to deny the sacrament of faith to no one who requests it. Rather, baptize Jews and Saracens alike who humbly seek it, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy [Col. 0978D] Spirit, to the glory of the Redeemer. Christians who presume to obstruct this, or to demand from the Church payment for persons reborn, you shall, after prior warning, compel by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal, to desist from such presumption. As for the Jews, unless through our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Aragon, they are recalled from this wickedness, withdraw from them the commerce of Christians by ecclesiastical coercion, setting aside appeal.

Given at Ferentino, seven days before the Kalends of September, in the ninth year.

CLI. TO THE BISHOP OF PENNE. [Note: [Col. 0979D] See letter 10 of book III, note.] That he is to compel the clerics of Saint Serotinus to permit the inhabitants of the castle of Loreto to receive chrism in the church of Saint Peter in that castle. (Ferentino, eight days before the Ides of September.)

[Col. 0979A]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, whereas there are two baptismal churches at the castle of Loreto, one of which—namely, Saint Peter’s—is situated within the castle, while the other—Saint Serotinus’s—is outside it, one sixth of the inhabitants of that castle, who are accustomed to receive baptism at the church of Saint Serotinus, cannot, without great difficulty, come to that church for baptism. On this account humble petition was made to us [Col. 0979B] that we might deign to grant that baptism alone be celebrated at the church of Saint Peter, where the inhabitants of the castle can assemble more conveniently.

Therefore, unwilling to bestow such a favor on that church as would inflict serious loss upon the other, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood, after the truth has been diligently investigated, carefully to admonish and induce the clerics of that church to permit the inhabitants of the castle—who had been accustomed to receive there the baptism of their little children—to come to Saint Peter’s church for baptism, provided that, if possible, they receive suitable compensation from the aforesaid church of Saint Peter. Otherwise, compel them to this by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

[Col. 0979C] Given at Ferentino, eight days before the Ides of September, in the ninth year.

CLII. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF PAMPLONA. That they are to receive the cleric H. as a canon. (Ferentino, thirteen days before the Kalends of September.)

If you bore due regard with devotion toward God and the most holy Roman Church, your mother, you would receive both our requests and commands more devoutly, and would take greater care to fulfill them—especially where we strive to induce you by command to do what, if there are any bowels of compassion in you, your own generosity and brotherly fellow-feeling ought to induce you to do.

In our presence, our beloved son Hel., a poor deacon, represented to us in humble petition that, although we had already written a second time on his behalf to G. . . ., bishop of Pamplona, of blessed memory, and to you, sons, the canons, that out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves you should take care to receive him as your brother and canon, you had contemptuously refused to do so. You had turned deaf ears alike to our command and to the admonitions of our beloved sons P. Eximin., archdeacon of Mensal., G. Arnold, and M. of Tudela, canons [Col. 0980A] of Pamplona, whom we had appointed as admonishers for that cleric, as was stated in letters presented to us by those very admonishers. Yet the same deacon asserts that he was promoted to holy orders by your said predecessor, brother bishop, and served humbly and devoutly in your church for some time.

Therefore, wishing to bring to effect what we judged should mercifully be begun for that deacon, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters that at least on this occasion you take care to fulfill the apostolic command in such a way that the same deacon may rejoice to have obtained what he seeks, and that the fault of past disobedience may be expiated by subsequent obedience. Otherwise, you ought rightly to fear [Col. 0980B] that, before we cause this to be fulfilled through another, we shall take such vengeance upon you that you will learn by experience how rash it was to oppose apostolic commands so often.

Given at Ferentino, thirteen days before the Kalends of September, in the ninth year.

CLIII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT VICTOR; TO THE ARCHDEACON; AND TO THE DEAN OF SAINT-GERMAIN OF AUXERRE, PARIS. [Note: [Col. 0979D] See letter 168 of book VI.] [Note: [Col. 0979D] Jobert, Josbert, or Jebert, dean of Saint-Germain of Auxerre at Paris, occurs in documents from 1204 through 1207. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 256.] He commits to them the case between G., a deacon, and F. of Canduerre, in the diocese of Noyon, concerning a certain tithe. [Note: [Col. 0980D] Compare letter 122 of book VII.] (Ferentino, seven days before the Ides of September.)

Our beloved son [Col. 0980C] G., a deacon, appearing in our presence, represented to us with tears that a certain tithe had been assigned to him by our venerable brother Th., formerly bishop of Amiens; [Note: [Col. 0980D] See letter 45 of book VIII.] that F. of Canduerre, in the diocese of Noyon, had later unjustly occupied it, asserting that it belonged to him by hereditary right; and that it had been adjudged to G. himself by definitive sentence of our beloved sons, the abbot of Longpont [Note: [Col. 0980D] See letter 122 of book VII, note.] and W. Norman, canon of Soissons. Since F. refused to restore what he had taken and to cease molesting him, a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against him. Finally, through our beloved sons, the dean, [Note: [Col. 0980D] See note there.] the provost, [Note: [Col. 0980D] Note there.] and the archdeacon of Amiens, by our authority both the definitive [Col. 0980D] and excommunication sentences had been confirmed and put into execution.

At length the aforesaid F., before our venerable brother, the bishop of Noyon, [Note: [Col. 0980D] See letter 41 of book V, note.] and his fellow judges, obtained our letters, concealing the truth concerning the foregoing matters. On this account the said G., returning to the Apostolic See, waited for eight months and more, but no competent representative appeared for the other side.

We, however, holding the aforesaid definitive sentence valid, as it was just, strictly ordered our beloved sons, the abbot of Saint-Aubert, [Note: [Col. 0981D] See letter 48 of book VII, note.] the dean [Note: [Col. 0981D] Adam, dean of Cambrai, is known in documents from at least 1192 through at least 1219. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 70.] and the cantor of Cambrai, because full proof concerning the foregoing had been made to us through letters both of the delegates and of the aforesaid bishop of Amiens, to compel by sentence of excommunication, appeal set aside, the aforesaid F., J. his father, and his supporters to cease their unjust molestation of G. and restore all that had been taken; and to compel those responsible for paying the said tithe to pay it to G. without difficulty. [Note: [Col. 0981D] From this letter of Innocent the address of letter 122 of book VII must be restored: it was directed to the abbot [Col. 0982D] of Saint-Aubert, the dean, and the cantor of Cambrai, as is established beyond all doubt by what is said here.]

When they had taken care to proceed diligently in executing our command and had strictly commanded the sentence against the frequently mentioned F. of Canduerre, J. his father, and [Col. 0981B] the others concerning whom they had received instructions to be observed, letters were subsequently presented to them on behalf of the beloved sons, the dean [Note: [Col. 0982D] See letter 118 of book IX, note.] and S. and S., canons of Noyon. These contained the text of a certain rescript represented as having been obtained from us, which appeared to revoke another rescript. When they requested the original of this rescript, so that by comparing them they might determine to whom jurisdiction belonged, that dean and his fellow judges did not supply a copy of the original, but ordered F. and J. publicly proclaimed absolved, summoning G. the deacon to their court.

The aforesaid abbot of Saint-Aubert and his fellow judges, considering that rescript manifestly suspect because it did not have the customary style and form, consulted men learned in law. Their deliberation advised that they could proceed as freely as if no letters had subsequently been obtained. Having communicated this advice to the aforesaid dean and S., the canons of Noyon, and instructed them not further to impede the execution of our command, they nevertheless publicly proclaimed absolved those whom the others declared bound by the bond of excommunication. As a result scandal and dissension arose together, and the deacon’s business could not be completed; hence he was compelled once more to come laboriously into our presence.

Since we strongly suspect of falsity the letters by which the said F. and J. his father attempted [Col. 0981D] to revoke the others, we strictly command your discretion by apostolic letters to suspend whatever has been done on their occasion, compelling them by ecclesiastical coercion, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, to produce the aforesaid letters before you. Having examined them most diligently, if you are able to discover their falsity, impose perpetual silence regarding the case itself upon those who used them to such great injury of the Apostolic See and harm to the aforesaid deacon.

But if you cannot discover their falsity yourselves, send those letters to us by a trustworthy messenger, under the attestation of your seals, assigning the parties a peremptory term within which, fully instructed concerning the entire case, they are to appear before us to receive a definitive sentence. If, however, they will neither produce those letters nor come into our presence, cause the sentences pronounced for the aforesaid cleric to be observed inviolably by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside and every obstacle of contradiction removed, notwithstanding any letters that may hereafter appear to have been obtained at the request [Col. 0982B] of the adverse party, or may hitherto have been obtained after the aforesaid letters which we strongly suspect of falsity. Declare by our authority that those are bound by the sentence of excommunication who presume in any way to proceed on the occasion of such letters. For we are unwilling that the Apostolic See should any longer be assailed by the conflict of contradictory letters by persons who, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, rashly attribute such inconsistency to us.

But if not all [are able to act], two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, seven days before the Ides of September, in the ninth year.

CLIV. TO THE ABBOT AND BRETHREN OF THE MONASTERY OF FOSSANOVA. The agreement made between them and the people of Piperno is confirmed. [Note: [Col. 0982D] See letter 149 of book IX.] (Ferentino, three days before the Nones of September.)

[Col. 0982C]

That long-standing dispute which was long conducted between you and the people of Piperno over various and diverse complaints has, as we perceive from the public instrument made concerning it, finally reached an amicable settlement, with the Lord’s assistance. Among other things included in that settlement, it was established that you are henceforth to hold in complete peace the possessions which you now hold in the territory of Piperno, so that the people of Piperno may never be permitted to raise against you any suit or dispute concerning them, or inflict burden or molestation upon you—especially concerning the lands of Drogulus, Salconetus, or Turricella, or territory belonging to Saint Mary, or the adjoining lands of its *praeseptum* [estate or land grant]. Rather, the boundaries, as they are contained and marked out in the *praeseptum*, are to remain in wholly peaceful and undisturbed possession: namely, from the Roman height beside the old building on the road of Murellus. Another boundary is called Petraefictae, on the same road beside the place of Rocella. The greater reed-bed (*Cannetum*) which marks the side of that same possession [Col. 0983A] is the one found beyond the wood; and the possession extending as far as that reed-bed, and thence as far as the boundaries contained in the ancient *praeseptum*, is to remain yours without any dispute.

We hold that settlement, in these matters and in the others, valid and firm, as it was made by the common consent of the parties and is contained in the public instrument. Confirming it by apostolic authority after the example of Lucius, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing.

Furthermore, out of the clemency of the Apostolic See we have judged that you should be granted this indulgence: whenever any person holds any possession in the territory of Piperno, whether from the wood of Cesis, which pertains to the right and property of blessed Peter and ourselves, or from any other [Col. 0983B] lands, if that person wishes justly to confer it upon your monastery by title of donation, sale, exchange, or legacy, that person shall have free power to confer the possession without any opposition, and you shall have free power to receive it; nor shall anyone presume to inflict molestation or burden upon you or that person on this account.

Therefore let no one infringe, etc., this grant and confirmation of ours. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Ferentino, three days before the Nones of September, in the ninth year.

CLV. TO THE BISHOP OF VEROLI. [Note: [Col. 0983D] See letter 148 of book V, note.] That he is to restrain the inhabitants of the castle of Frosinone who seize ecclesiastical property. (Ferentino, four days before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0983C]

When we renewed the lease which we made of the castle of Frosinone, we expressly declared, in the presence of those to whom the lease was made, that we wished them entirely to desist from their customary burdens and abuses toward clerics and churches. Since, therefore, they possess nothing in that castle beyond what has been conferred upon them by our grant, by the authority of the present letters we forbid them to lay hands upon ecclesiastical property and persons, to their prejudice and burden. And by this present page we grant your brotherhood authority, unless they repent after warning, to restrain them from their presumption by ecclesiastical censure.

Let no one infringe, etc., this page of our prohibition and grant. But if anyone, etc.

[Col. 0983D] Given at Ferentino, four days before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year.

CLVI. TO THE CANTOR, FULCO OF SAINT-REMI, AND MASTER ADAM, CANONS OF REIMS. That they are to ensure provision is made for the priest H. by the bishop of Arras. (Ferentino, two days before the Ides of September.)

[Col. 0984A]

H., a priest, informed us that he had formerly obtained letters of ours in the common form addressed to our venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, [Note: [Col. 0983D] See letter 45 of book VIII, note.] whose predecessor [Note: [Col. 0983D] See letter 25 of book III, note.] had ordained him subdeacon upon the presentation of the abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi, of blessed memory. [Note: [Col. 0983D]

He was Rainald, concerning whom and his successor Asso the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 427, state as follows:

“X. Rainald, about the year 1195, transferred in perpetuity, for payment received, to Baldwin, abbot of Hénin, the woods which he possessed near Wavrin. Likewise, in 1197, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, he sold to Simon of Anchin, for three hundred Parisian pounds, the right which he held in the grange of Dorlens, in the presence of Peter, bishop of Arras, and of witnesses Gregory, a former abbot, and Desiderius, prior. He died in this same year, according to Le Loir—not, as the Sammarthani have it, on 30 August 1199.”

[Col. 0984D] “XI. Asso, prior of Aubigny, three miles from the city of Arras, after eleven years of administration passed to a better life on 19 April 1208.”]

He subsequently obtained from us executory letters addressed to our beloved sons S. of [Col. 0984B] Vaux and R. Surdelt, canons, and J., dean of Saint Peter of Le Port at Laon. But because it was objected before them by the opposing party that, since the same man had caused himself to be ordained deacon and priest by our venerable brother, the bishop of Tivoli, [Note: [Col. 0984D]

Concerning the bishops of Tivoli about the period with which we are here concerned, Ughelli states as follows in *Italia sacra*, vol. I, special part, col. 217:

“Milo, bishop of that church, attended the Lateran Council under Alexander III in 1179. Mention is made of him in 1183 in the Register of Subiaco.

‘N. . . ., bishop of Tivoli, received letters from Innocent III, supreme pontiff, and replied that the first woman’s vow must be upheld, although he learned afterward that she had borne a son by another. He flourished about the year 1209.’”]

without the consent of his diocesan, the said bishop was not bound to provide for him, nor was he willing for him even to celebrate in his diocese, they refused to proceed in the matter. Consequently H. was again compelled to come laboriously to the Apostolic See, asking that, sparing his labors and expenses, we should mercifully cause provision to be made for him through the successor of his presenter, notwithstanding the aforesaid objection.

Since provision for poor clerics is in itself a work [Col. 0984C] of piety, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, the aforesaid exception being of no effect, if no other canonical impediment stands in the way, you do not delay, after prior warning, to compel by ecclesiastical coercion, removing the obstacle of appeal, the successor of the aforesaid abbot—since he is bound by the presentation to do this—to provide for him according to the form in which we wish provision to be made by ordainers, or by their presenters, or by the successors of the ordained persons.

But if not all, etc.

Given at Ferentino, two days before the Ides of September, in the ninth year.

CLVII. [Note: [Col. 0984D] A copy of this letter, which we had arranged to have transcribed with the others according to Conti’s copy, has slipped from our hands by some accident—we do not know how. Therefore we can present here only the summary. See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] TO THE KING OF SICILY. He rejoices at his good progress and exhorts him to persevere in virtue.

[Col. 0984D]

CLVIII. TO ARCHADIUS AND ALL THE PEOPLE OF GAETA, ANTECLA, PLATANA, JACI, CELSI, AND TO ALL GAETANS AND SARACENS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SICILY: MAY YOU UNDERSTAND AND LOVE THE TRUTH, WHICH IS GOD. He commends them for their fidelity and constancy toward the king of Italy. (Ferentino.)

[Col. 0985A]

We greatly rejoice and commend the sincerity of your faith, because, though you have hitherto been tested in many ways and by many means, nevertheless the grace of him who repels no one from his mercy has worked mercifully in you, so that you could not succumb to your trials. You have not in the least departed from the constancy of fidelity which you bear toward our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king [Col. 0985B] of Sicily, your lord.

Since, therefore, the time is near when that king, who by God’s grace advances daily in wisdom and age, will recognize the desires for his peace of those who have almost grown weary of awaiting it, and, knowing how to reject evil and choose good, will be able to reward each according to merit, we earnestly admonish and exhort your entire community. Consider that a good work is undertaken in vain if it is abandoned before its end, and that one runs swiftly to no purpose who fails before reaching the goal. Persist in the purity of your faith in such a way that you may crown with praiseworthy perseverance the straits and labors which you have hitherto endured for royal fidelity. Thus the aforesaid king, who will soon be able, in accordance with our counsel, worthily to reward the labors of his faithful [Col. 0985C] servants, may devote himself to rewarding your fidelity in proportion as he sees that it has been preserved for him through your goodness and our concern. For both through us and through himself we intend to answer your devotion with a fitting return of rewards.

Given at Ferentino, etc.

CLIX. [Note: [Col. 0985D]

This letter is found, though divided into two parts, among the Decretals:

1. Book I, title 21, “On bigamists to be ordained,” chapter 5.

2. Book III, title 42, “On baptism and its effect,” chapter 4. Variant readings are supplied.]

TO OUR VENERABLE BROTHER . . . THE BISHOP OF METZ. [Note: [Col. 0985D] See letter 34 of book III, note.] He replies concerning various questions and inquiries. (Ferentino, five days before the Kalends of September.)

[Note: [Col. 0985D] See the Decretals, book III, title 42, “On baptism and its effect,” chapter 4.]

[The duty [Note: [Col. 0985D] The passages that follow, distinguished in italic type, are absent from the Decretals, but are read in Pithoeus’s additions.] of the pontifical office you discharge when, concerning doubtful points of law, you ask to be instructed by a reply [Note: [Col. 0985D] In Pithoeus: “by a response.”] of the Apostolic See. Certainly, in your letters [Note: [Col. 0985D] Absent from the Decretals.] you informed us that a certain Jew, placed at the point of death, when he was among Jews alone, immersed himself in water, saying: “I baptize myself in the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0985D] The Decretals add: “Amen.”] Now [Note: [Col. 0985D] Again absent from the Decretals; read in Pithoeus’s additions.] you ask whether that Jew, if he perseveres [Note: [Col. 0985D] Pithoeus adds: “also.”] in devotion to the Christian faith, ought to be baptized.

We reply to your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0985D] Absent.] as follows. Since a distinction must exist between the baptizer and the baptized, [Note: [Col. 0986D] Thus in the Decretals; but the Barberini manuscript cited by Pithoeus in the margin has “distinction of persons.”] as is clearly gathered from the words of the Lord speaking to the apostles: [Note: [Col. 0986D] The Decretals add: “Go,” which Pithoeus observes is missing in certain old copies.] “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), the said Jew must without doubt be baptized by another, so that [Col. 0986B] it may be shown that one is baptized and another baptizes. To indicate this also, Christ himself chose to be baptized not by himself but by John.

Although, if such a person had died immediately, he would have flown straightway to the heavenly homeland [Note: [Col. 0986D] Thus also in the Decretals; elsewhere “would have flown together,” as Pithoeus observes.] because of faith in the sacrament, though not because of the sacrament of faith. For in baptism is celebrated that spiritual generation of which Truth says: “You must be born anew; for unless one has been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). Just as, therefore, [Note: [Col. 0986D] Thus also in the Decretals; elsewhere “also,” Pithoeus observes.] in carnal generation, by which [Note: [Col. 0986D] Thus in the Decretals; elsewhere “through which,” Pithoeus observes.] offspring is born of man and woman, one is the person who carnally begets and another is the person carnally begotten, so too [Note: [Col. 0986D] Absent from the Decretals.] in sacramental generation, by which offspring is reborn from water and Spirit, one must be the person who spiritually [Col. 0986C] generates and another the person spiritually generated. Certainly, when the body is baptized outwardly, or the heart inwardly, fatherhood and sonship must be found in both respects, by which baptizer and baptized are related to one another.]

[Note: [Col. 0986D] See the Decretals, book I, title 21, “On bigamists not to be ordained,” chapter 5.]

[[Note: [Col. 0986D] The passages that follow, distinguished in italic type, are absent from the Decretals, book I, title 21, “On bigamists not to be ordained,” but are read in Pithoeus’s additions.] The second article of your doubt asked whether a man who married a woman previously married to another man, but not carnally known by him, may be promoted to the priesthood. Although a man who takes in marriage a woman left by another [Note: [Col. 0986D] In Pithoeus: “left by another man.”] appears to have taken a widow as wife, whether she had been known by him or had remained unknown, because her husband was dead when [Col. 0987A] he took her; just as a man appears to be a bigamist when he has lawfully contracted marriage with two wives, whether he has known neither, or only one of them, [Note: [Col. 0987D] In Pithoeus: “whether one or neither.”] because he was husband of two wives—nevertheless, we judge that the following reply should be given to your brotherhood.

Since marriage consists of two things, namely consent of minds and mingling [Note: [Col. 0987D] Thus also in the Decretals; elsewhere “union,” Pithoeus observes.] of bodies, one of which signifies charity, which exists in the Spirit between God and the righteous soul—to which pertains the Apostle’s saying: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6)—while the other signifies conformity, which exists in the flesh between Christ and the holy [Note: [Col. 0987D] This word is absent from the Decretals.] Church—to which pertains the Evangelist’s testimony: “The Word was made flesh [Col. 0987B] and dwelt among us” (John 1)—it is clear that a marriage not consummated by the mingling of bodies does not serve to signify that marriage which was contracted between Christ and the Church through the mystery of the Incarnation.

Accordingly, Paul, explaining what the first-formed man had said, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2), immediately adds: “But I speak of a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. 5). Since, therefore, a bigamist or husband of a widow is forbidden to presume to be promoted to holy orders because of the defect in the sacramental sign, since neither she is the sole wife of one man nor he the one husband of one wife, it is clear that, where mingling of bodies is absent between such spouses, this sacramental sign is not absent. Thus a man who marries [Note: [Col. 0987D] In the Decretals: “took as wife.”] a woman married to another man but not at all carnally known by him ought not, because neither he nor she has divided his or her flesh among several persons, to be prevented on that account from promotion to the priesthood.]

Given at Ferentino, five days before the Kalends of September, in the ninth year.

CLX. [Note: [Col. 0987D] This letter is found, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book V, title 1, “On accusations, inquisitions, and denunciations,” chapter 14. What is read there is here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TARRAGONA, THE ABBOT OF SAINT MARY OF POBLET IN THE DIOCESE OF TARRAGONA, AND THE ARCHDEACON OF BARCELONA. That they are to proceed against the bishop of Vic [Note: [Col. 0987D] Elsewhere “of Vicenza,” but incorrectly. The matter here concerns the bishop of Vic. Vic is an episcopal city, a suffragan of the metropolitan see of Tarragona, formerly Ausona, according to Lucas of Tuy and others.] if ill repute has preceded. (Ferentino, on the Kalends of September.)

[Col. 0988A]

[Since it is fitting that a bishop,] according to the Apostle, should have a good testimony both from those who are within and from those who are without, and according to the divine law his garment ought to be woven of twice-dyed scarlet and twisted fine linen, if at any time an adverse report concerning some bishop rises to apostolic ears, we are bound by the solicitude of the pastoral office to descend and see whether he has carried that outcry into effect by deed. [Now, when our beloved sons G. Grossi and G. of Monte-Regale, canons of Vicenza, came to the Apostolic See [Note: In the Decretals: “G. and H., canons of Vincenza”; so Pithoeus in his notes. “Vicen.”: Vicenza.
