[Col. 0988D] Nassaeus 499; Albig. 51.], and laid before us many grave [Note: Omitted in the Decretals.] and enormous charges against our venerable brother . . . bishop of Vicenza [Note: In the Decretals: “of Vincenza.”], because we ought not to pass these over by dissimulation [Note: Thus also in the Decretals; Pithoeus notes that some read “pass by.”], we judged their investigation should be entrusted to you, brother archbishop and son archdeacon [Note: Omitted in the Decretals.], following the footsteps of Him who, when He had a steward and that man was accused before Him of having squandered His goods, called him to account [Note: Omitted in the Decretals.]. But the said bishop, before your summons had reached him [Note: Thus also in the Decretals; Pithoeus notes that some read “him.”], appearing before us, alleged in our presence [Note: Omitted in the Decretals.] that those who had reported those enormities concerning him to us [Note: “To us” is omitted in the Decretals; for “had reported,” Pithoeus notes also the reading “had submitted.”], led rather by the stamp of malice than by zeal for justice, had announced such matters to us [Note: The Decretals have “made known.”], though they are most manifestly his enemies [Note: The Decretals read: “although they themselves are his manifest enemies.”], associate with his enemies, and intend to produce their own kinsmen and accomplices to testify against him—persons who ought not to be admitted to make denunciation or give testimony for some reason, as transgressors of an oath they had sworn and as entangled in other crimes. Therefore, lest a serious loss be reached by an easy shortcut [Note: Omitted in the Decretals, but printed by Pithoeus in his additions.], by these apostolic letters [Note: Omitted in the Decretals.] we command your discretion that [Note: The Decretals read “that.”], unless you know that his reputation has been injured in respect of the charges made before us against him [Note: The Decretals read: “the aforesaid charges, his reputation.”], you are not to proceed precipitately to investigate them; [Col. 0989A] and, if an inquiry is to be made [Note: “And” is omitted in the Decretals.], you are to admit neither the aforesaid men nor any others known to be his enemies, either to prosecute the inquiry or to bear testimony against that bishop. Rather, through suitable men, diligently investigate the truth concerning those matters reported to us [Note: The Decretals read: “the matters which were done.”; in the Decretals, “more diligently.”]; and if nothing serious is proved against him, require him to make canonical purgation.]

But if anything serious appears to you to have been proved against him, report the inquiry faithfully conducted to our examination, so that a judgment of equity may proceed from our countenance. And if not all [are able to act], nevertheless two of you shall carry these things out, any obstacle of contradiction or appeal being removed.

Given at Ferentino, on the Kalends of September, in the ninth year.

CLXI [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §38.]. . . . . . TO THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF SPOLETO. That they must not presume to appoint judges to the prejudice of the pope. (Lateran, 12 Kalends before October.)

We regard it as serious and grievous that you, as we have learned from the truthful report of many, presume, in contempt of and prejudice to us, to appoint notaries and judges at the discretion of your own will, although no such authority belongs to you. Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your whole community, strictly commanding you by these apostolic letters [Col. 0989C], that you wholly desist from such presumption. For we could not endure it patiently, since we declare that sentences promulgated by judges of this kind, as pronounced by non-judges, and instruments drawn up by notaries of this kind, as executed by non-notaries, are without validity, because we recognize neither those as notaries nor these as judges.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends before October, in the ninth year.

CLXII. TO B., ARCHPRIEST OF THE PARISH OF BRETONORO. He is received under protection. (Lateran, 7 Kalends before October.)

[Col. 0989D] It is customary to grant assent, etc., down to “assent.” We receive your person, together with all the goods which you now rightfully possess or may in future, by lawful means and with the Lord’s aid, acquire, under the protection of blessed Peter and [Col. 0990A] ourselves. In particular, by apostolic authority, through you we confirm to your church the possessions and rights which your parish rightfully and peacefully possesses, and by the present writing, etc. Therefore let no one . . . our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Kalends before October, in the ninth year.

CLXIII. TO . . . THE PROVOST [Note: The very incomplete list of provosts of Constance in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 928, gives no provost of Constance around the period with which we are concerned.] . . . THE DEAN [Note: The same must be said of the deans of Constance.], AND THE CHAPTER OF CONSTANCE. The election of the bishop of Constance is confirmed, and the administration of the Church of Constance is granted to him. (Lateran, 2 Kalends before October.)

[Col. 0990B]

We have learned from the purport of your letters that, after D., your bishop of good memory, had recently been removed from your midst [Note: See Letters 79 of Book VII, 168 of Book VIII, and our annotations there; to these may be added, if desired, confirmation from this letter of Innocent of what is reported in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 915—namely, that Diethelm died in 1206, or alternatively 1205, on the day before the Ides of January, and not in 1209, as is reported in Brusch and Bucelinus.], you assembled together to deliberate upon appointing a bishop. Having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, you unanimously chose as your pastor your beloved son W. of Staufen, your fellow canon, who from his youth had conducted himself commendably among you [Note: Concerning him the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 915, give only the following:

“L. Werner, baron of Staufen in Breisgau, elected about the year 1206, died in 1210, a bishop of proven life; he was buried in the choir of his church.”].

But because, on account of fear of the prince, to whose attacks the Church of Constance is exposed, you did not dare to seek confirmation of that election from our venerable brother G., Archbishop of Mainz, and lest, through delay in confirmation, your church [Col. 0990C] might suffer harm in spiritual and temporal matters, you humbly petitioned us, in view of the evil of the times, to deign by apostolic authority to confirm the election and entrust to the said elect the administration of both spiritual and temporal affairs. Accordingly, attending to the need of the Church of Constance and desiring to provide for it with paternal solicitude, we have judged that the administration of both spiritual and temporal matters should be entrusted to W.; and in it let him strive to show himself such that, at a suitable time, he may deserve to obtain from his metropolitan the grace of confirmation and the gift of consecration.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Kalends before October, in the ninth year.

CLXIV. TO . . . THE ARCHDEACON OF PARIS AND MASTER R. OF CORZON, CANON OF NOYON. He entrusts to them the case concerning the election of the abbot of Saint-Martin of Troyes [Note: What the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 581, write concerning Lambert and Peter I, abbots of Saint-Martin of Troyes, should certainly be compared:

“V. Lambert promised obedience to Bishop Garnier. In 1200 he settled a dispute between the monasteries of Saint-Memmie and Cheminon. In the same year, in February, he received from Theobald, Count of Champagne, confirmation of the house of Saint-Abraham. In 1201 he made an agreement with the monks of Arremar; he subscribed in 1202 to a donation made to them. His death is recorded in the necrology of Saint-Loup on the seventh day before the Kalends of October.

“VI. Peter I was in office in 1207, according to a charter of Saint-Étienne. Having been accused of simony by certain canons, he was absolved from their prosecution by Innocent III in 1208, on the Kalends of September, in the eleventh year of his pontificate. In 1209 he made an agreement with Ripar; he is found in a charter of the bishop of Troyes in 1213, and in the year 1215, in April and May, when he received from Theobald, abbot of Cantumerle, a donation confirmed by Blanche, Countess of Champagne. Charters of the chapter of Saint-Pierre attest that he was still alive in 1220 and 1222. He died on 20 October. He lies in the Chapter.”].

(Lateran, 6 Nones before October.)

[Col. 0991A]

After the resignation of the beloved son . . . [Note: See the preceding note.] formerly abbot of Saint-Martin of Troyes, the votes of the canons of that church being divided in the election, certain of them chose their beloved son Manasses, canon of the church of Saint-Loup; while others transferred their votes to the beloved son P. [Note: Ibid.], chaplain of our venerable brother . . . Archbishop of Sens [Note: See Letter 45 of Book III, note.]. Therefore we entrusted the case to our venerable brother . . . Bishop of Chalon [Note: See Letter 16 of Book V, note.] and to our beloved son . . . Abbot of Cluny [Note: See Letter 36 of Book V, note.] for determination under this form: that, investigating the rights of each election and the merits of the electors, they should confirm by apostolic authority that election which they found to have been canonically celebrated for a suitable person. But if they found neither canonical, then, both elections being annulled, they should arrange for that church to be provided with a suitable person.

Having summoned the parties before them and solemnly investigated the cause, they received numerous witnesses both concerning the acts of the electors and against the persons. When they had proceeded to the publication of the witnesses, . . . . . the procurator of the said chaplain P. appealed to the Apostolic See. The judges, however, because one of them—namely, the Abbot of Cluny—was occupied by weightier business and could not attend the investigation of the case, followed the advice of prudent men and deferred to this appeal. They instructed the parties to hasten into our presence with the depositions received, to receive from us a definitive sentence on that case.

When the acts of the trial had therefore been received from both sides, certain of the aforesaid canons appointed as their procurator their fellow canon V., in the presence of the bishop mentioned above, as we have seen stated in that bishop’s letters. But while that V. was on his journey to the Apostolic See, the said Archbishop of Sens was meanwhile travelling through the diocese of Nevers on a visitation. Messengers of the aforesaid church approached him [Col. 0991D], informing him that all the canons, except a few who, though they did not oppose, nevertheless did not expressly consent, had cast their votes for P., his chaplain. They begged the archbishop to come to the place as swiftly as possible in order to provide for the church. At their insistence he came; and all who had previously refused to express their consent, except Vitalis alone, who was absent, returned to agreement with the others and voluntarily consented to the aforesaid chaplain, asking pardon for their former dissent. Thus it came about that, at the request of all, on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, in the greater church of Troyes, the same P. received the blessing from the metropolitan already mentioned. Afterwards he was solemnly brought into the church of Saint-Martin amid the rejoicing of all and the general gladness; and [Col. 0992B], installed in the chapter of that church by the beloved son . . . dean of Troyes [Note: See Letter 23 of Book IX, note.], as is customary, he publicly received the professions of each individual.

The said Vitalis, however, came into our presence, presented us with the judges’ proceedings, and earnestly requested that we deign to dispatch his case as quickly as possible. While he waited for some time, the procurator of the said chaplain P. arrived in the meantime. Once both stood in our presence, the said procurator humbly requested that we approve what had been done concerning the chaplain by the archbishop, and that we give no hearing whatsoever to the aforesaid V., as one excommunicated. He alleged that V. had beaten L., formerly abbot of Saint-Martin, until blood was shed; that he had also beaten John, priest of the same church, with blows so severe that all John’s companions despaired of his life; and that he had recently subjected a certain priest of that church, returning from the Apostolic See, to beatings so violent that his face appeared grievously injured and horrible. For these excesses and others, concerning which he had been summoned and warned by the said metropolitan but had refused either to make satisfaction or even to appear, he had been bound by a sentence of excommunication. To prove this, that procurator produced letters both of the said Archbishop of Sens and of the dean of Troyes.

In answer to this, on behalf of the said Vitalis, it was replied that he ought not in any way to be impeded by the objection of such an excommunication. For the canons themselves, not avoiding him up to that time, had in no way declined communion with him either in the offices or in the judicial proceedings [Col. 0993A]; indeed, when he had been appointed procurator in the presence of the said Bishop of Chalon, they admitted him without any objection. Nor had the archbishop informed the judges or his fellow bishops that he was subject to excommunication. Hence he maintained that he ought to be admitted in the trial like any other person, notwithstanding such an exception.

The procurator for the other side answered that, whenever V. attended divine services with his fellow canons, this altogether displeased them; but, though forbidden, he forced his way into the divine offices to their distress, as is plainly gathered from the letters of the aforesaid dean. Nor had they communicated with him in the trial, because, although he was among those who opposed the election of the aforesaid chaplain [Col. 0993B], it had not been established in the proceedings that V. had been a procurator or witness in that trial, or that the aforesaid canons had otherwise communicated with him. He added that it could not create a prejudice that V. had not been excluded as excommunicated when he was appointed procurator before the aforesaid bishop, because this occurred in their absence. He further added that, if the archbishop did not denounce him as subject to excommunication in that trial, this was because he did not know that V. was litigating in that trial; but, once he denounces him as excommunicated by letters bearing his seal, he must be avoided by all as excommunicated.

Therefore, since this was disputed before us, and since the letters of the ordinary judge—which must be accepted until the contrary is proved—made it clear to us that the aforesaid V. was excommunicated when he assumed the office of procurator, we judged that he should not be admitted as procurator. But because the cause of election had been brought before us by appeal, and the delegated judges had sent us the sealed depositions and proceedings, although the canons afterwards returned to agreement, nevertheless, since the merits of the person still had to be judged according to the evidence of the depositions, we rejected, as rashly undertaken, what had subsequently been done concerning the aforesaid chaplain, as justice required.

And because the aforesaid V. was not admitted as procurator because of the impediment of excommunication, while the procurator on the other side had not come sufficiently prepared concerning the cause and did not possess the judges’ records, it could not be determined in our presence. Therefore we have judged it proper to entrust the same cause to your examination, commanding you by these apostolic letters that, after summoning before you those who ought to be summoned on this account and publishing the depositions which we send you enclosed under our bull, if the matters alleged against the person [Col. 0994A] have been reasonably disproved and the said canons persist in the same consent, you shall ensure that all the canons render him due reverence and obedience as their abbot, notwithstanding any opposition of the aforesaid V. If you find that he is implicated in crimes so many and so great as has been reported to our ears by the statements of many, punish him in such a manner that his penalty may deter others from wrongdoing.

But if the allegations made concerning the person are not sufficiently disproved, impose perpetual silence upon him concerning that abbey, and arrange that the church be canonically provided with a suitable person; compelling any opponents or rebels who appear, by ecclesiastical censure and without regard to appeal, to desist from their rashness. No letters contrary to truth, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Nones before October, in the ninth year.

CLXV. TO THE DEAN [Note: See Letter 227 of Book VII, note.] AND CHAPTER OF SAINT-MARTIN OF TOURS. That they are to receive Master J. of Cangé as canon and brother. (Lateran, 3 Nones before October.)

Since we formerly directed our venerable brother . . . bishop [Note: See Letter 11 of Book III, note.] and our beloved son . . . dean of Paris [Note: See Letter 36 of Book V, note.] to receive by our authority the resignation of the prebend which our beloved son Master P. of Capua, canon of Sens, held in your church [Col. 0994C], and to reserve that prebend for our grant, and since we were made certain by letters of that bishop and dean that the same canon had freely resigned the prebend into their hands, we granted it to our beloved son Master John of Cangé, clerk of our beloved son Roger, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia [Note: See Letter 31 of Book VIII, note.], a native of your region, and took care to invest him with it by our own hands. Therefore we earnestly admonish and exhort your discretion, commanding you by these apostolic letters, that, receiving the same master as canon and brother, you delay not to place him in corporal possession of the aforesaid prebend and ensure, insofar as lies in your power, that he enjoys its peaceful possession [Col. 0994D]. Otherwise, we have commanded our beloved sons . . . dean [Note: See Letter 9 of Book VI, note.], . . . cantor [Note: See Letter 227 of Book VII, note.], and the master of schools of Orléans [Note: See Letter 37 of Book V, note.] to compel you to do so by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, restraining opponents by a like coercion.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones before October, in the ninth year.

CLXVI [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §38.]. TO ALL ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS OF LOMBARDY. That, if the citizens of Piacenza do not desist from oppressing the Church of Piacenza, they are to be deprived of their episcopal see. (Lateran, 7 Ides before October.)

[Col. 0995A]

Although up to now the iniquity of the citizens of Piacenza has gone forth “as from fatness,” and has not yet ceased to go forth, we have endeavoured with pastoral diligence to bind up what was broken among them and restore what had been cast away. But because it is not always within the physician’s power to restore the sick person, we are compelled to apply an old remedy for them, lest there be no turning away of their death, in whose wound, examined for nearly three years now, we have found no firmness. Thus we may fittingly complain of them with the prophet [Col. 0995B], saying: “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed” (Jer. 51), because, though we have diligently applied the work of healing to them, we have not yet been able to recall them to the grace of salvation. For, at the instigation of him who is the inciter of every evil, they have hardened in the iron-rust of their iniquities, so that, although much labour has been expended upon them, their excessive rust has nevertheless not come out; and therefore he who says seems to heighten their impieties: “The smelter has smelted in vain; their evils have not been consumed” (Jer. 6).

But because some wounds that cannot be healed by incision are customarily healed by fomentations of oil; because those whom the medicine of potent drugs could not cure have often been restored to their former health by a draught of lukewarm water; and because the hardness of diamond, which does not yield to the cutting of steel, softens when drenched in goat’s blood, desiring through our patience to call the aforesaid citizens back to repentance, we have hitherto judged it right to proceed more gently with them than perhaps their fault required. We did so lest, if iron had been applied to their still-raw wound, the wound itself should appear to have been brought to the pus in which it festered, not through its own corruption but through our harshness; and lest the Lord’s voice rebuke us, saying through the prophet: “You ruled over them with harshness and with power” (Ezek. 34).

But now, since their iniquities have increased, and in their multiplication blood seems to have touched blood, lest we incur the prophet’s sentence: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48), we are compelled, intending to strike their crimes, to summon you also to avenge them, among whom their public injuries rage, saying with the lawgiver: “Whoever is for the Lord, join me, and let each man put his sword upon his thigh” (Exod. 32), in order to punish the enemies of the Lord. Yet although the Lord’s wrath, kindled against them, kindles us also, and we surely pursue them with hatred because of their iniquities, we nonetheless grow cold with a great fire of compassion at this: [Col. 0995D] they have brought us by their deeds almost to the necessity that, even if we wish to spare them while unrepentant, we cannot, and impiety may appear to show compassion upon their impieties.

Therefore, lest, if we continue longer to endure their malice—as though unwilling to displease them—not only to their shame but also to the harm of the universal Church, we fail in the duty of our office, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “If I were still pleasing men, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1), knowing that we ought to obey God rather than men, however much they insult us, we have resolved to honour them no more than the Lord, fearing no curses of men. For what are we? To use the humble words of meek men: the murmur is not against us, but rather against the Lord, for whose name may we be found worthy to suffer reproach! Since nothing is more just [Col. 0996B] than that a person be punished in the very matter in which he sinned, and since the said citizens, by what they have committed against God and the Church—not only rashly invading episcopal rights, but also causing their bishop and clergy to go miserably into exile—have made themselves unworthy of an episcopal see, unwilling that they should enjoy longer the impunity of so great a crime, indeed desiring to restrain it by such punishment that their penalty may be an example to all whom their fault has scandalized, we have deliberated with our brothers and by common counsel decreed: unless the aforesaid citizens return to the command of the Church, within one month after receiving the apostolic letters which we send them for this purpose, in order to render due satisfaction concerning the matters for which they have incurred ecclesiastical censure, their city shall be deprived of episcopal dignity and its diocese divided among the neighbouring bishops. Suitable provision shall be made for both the bishop and the clergy of the city—if indeed it is still to be called a city after losing its dignity—and it shall thereby deserve to lose its temporal county as well.

Accordingly, we send to them our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Portico [Note: See Letter 29 of Book VIII, note.], legate of the Apostolic See, who by admonitions and exhortations may bring them, if it is granted from above, back to the path of truth. Otherwise, after summoning you together, he shall solemnly execute the aforesaid decree, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. Therefore you, energetic bishops of Christ’s warfare, attend and see that we fight the battle of the Lord for a public, not a private, cause. You ought to rise more vigorously to our aid in it because by it we intend to defend, not so much certain persons in particular as all persons in general. For in this venture almost the entire condition of the Church is at stake; in this battle its liberty is either cast down or raised up.

Do not suppose that, if the beginning of so great a plague is not extinguished where it arose, it will not spread to those who think themselves free. Unless indeed it is now repressed, it will seize many near and far, and, having now begun with these as though with Satan’s firstborn [Col. 0997A], it will creep like a cancer and gradually extend itself to others, unless provision is made against it. Certainly, if, when the neighbouring wall is burning, our own concern is said to be at stake, and if the universal Church’s being shaken in one particular part means nothing else than that, its outer rampart having been broken there, an entrance is made into it in order to capture it within, then it is recognized as most necessary that you all hasten there to defend it, where the battering ram of malice has been brought up to overthrow its fortification.

Behold, brothers, many watch and observe this contest. If they see our side succumb in it, they will immediately be ready to attempt a like outrage against you; and you will then be able to resist them all the more difficultly, the more slackly you resisted their forerunners. You know indeed that the princes of Ahasuerus unanimously advised that the queen’s contumacy be punished, lest an example of contempt for their wives arise; and that keepers of fields, lest their crops perish in an inundation, meet the onrush of the torrent at the boundaries of another’s land. Thus you ought to make others’ dangers your own—or rather, to meet your own dangers in those of others—so that, by prudently resisting the evils of your neighbours, you may protect yourselves as by a shield through their triumph.

Therefore we ask and earnestly exhort your brotherhood, strictly commanding you by these apostolic letters, that if “the lamp of the Lord, the breath of man, which searches the inward parts,” does not deign, at the diligent admonition of the aforesaid legate, to enlighten the hearts of those obstinate men [Col. 0997C], but rather permits them to be hardened, then, as men rejected by divine judgment for the greatness of their fault, you take care to assist the same legate, harmoniously and wisely, in executing the decree prescribed above, so that the severity of ecclesiastical discipline may not be weakened by anyone’s presumption. Be certain that, if any of you proves negligent or remiss in this matter, we shall take it no less ill than if he were one of those against whose wickedness we have decreed that such severity be exercised.

But if, God forbid, the aforesaid citizens remain hardened and execution of the prescribed decree proceeds, we will and command that our venerable brother . . . Bishop of Piacenza [Note: See Letter 75 of Book V, note.] be sent to our presence, there to receive, with God’s help, the grace of apostolic provision. Concerning provision for the clergy, moreover, arrange matters with the same legate so that those who stood in great constancy against those who oppressed them may be provided for sufficiently and honourably. Though they suffered hardships before men, their hope ought nevertheless to be immortal in the Church, in whose defence they remained steadfast and immovable.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides before October, in the ninth year.

[Col. 0998A] In the same manner, to the same persons throughout, down to “lose its temporal county.” Accordingly, we send to them our venerable brother . . . Bishop of Vercelli [Note: See Letter 178 of Book VIII, note.], our beloved son . . . Abbot of Tillicto [Note: See Letter 200 of Book VIII, note.], and the priest Albert of Mantua, etc., down to the end.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides before October.

CLXVII [Note: See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §38. See also the notes to the preceding letter.

This letter is cited by Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 467, under the year 1206, ch. 4, §8.]

. . . . . . TO THE PODESTÀ, CONSULS, AND PEOPLE OF PIACENZA: THE SPIRIT OF SOUND COUNSEL. On the same matter. (Lateran, on the Nones of October.)

We were pierced with inward grief of heart, and the sword of sorrow passed even to our very soul, because, although the city of Piacenza has customarily been [Col. 0998B] most devoted to the Apostolic See, its finest colour has now changed and its gold has been turned to dross. It has shown itself so ungrateful that no spark of devotion or gratitude appears to remain in it. For, wholly despising its admonitions and commands, deceived by the seductions of heretics, it strives to enslave its mother, the Church of Piacenza—an honourable member of that See—wishing to reduce her like a worthless slave under tribute; so that, corrupting the other cities by its example, it alone may incite all against the liberty of the universal Church, and may say with the prophet: “I have reared and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1). From the disgrace of such guilt neither the justice of public honour, nor the severity of ecclesiastical discipline, nor the religion of the Christian faith, nor fear of the dreadful judgment has hitherto been able to call you back.

Would that the example of pagan clemency might lead you, lest the Church in our time suffer from you a harsher persecution than it suffered from the tyrant renowned for his cruelty. For Pharaoh, king of Egypt, after reducing the rest to servitude, not only preserved his priests and their possessions in their former liberty, but also supplied them with maintenance from the public treasury. And Artaxerxes, king of Persia, forbade tribute, tax, and provisions to be imposed upon any priests, Levites, or ministers of the house of God. You ought therefore to fear God—or at least to blush before men—to exercise upon God’s servants the inhumanity of that tyranny [Col. 0998D] which those men, who did not yet possess knowledge of the truth, did not exercise upon them.

Alas! Who has bewitched you so miserably, O citizens, that he should enslave your mother, make you slaves, offer the others an example of perversity, and render you utterly ungrateful for Apostolic favour—the favour which freely delivered your city from the yoke of the Church of Ravenna and adopted it as a special daughter? Certainly, even if you could accomplish such a crime with impunity, you ought not to offer so perverse an example to others; for though the crime is grave, the example is graver.

But if you spurn the benefit of the favour shown you, and, degenerating from children into stepchildren, compel us, because of your ingratitude, to reproach you with the grace of the Apostolic See, which has hitherto filled you with many goods, saying in prophetic words: “They grew fat and thick, and the beloved kicked”—will favour remain with the ungrateful? Or will a mother be able any longer to retain as adopted children alien sons who have lied to her and repay her evil for good and hatred for love? Rather, should not those who abuse freedom be reduced to servile condition, so that they may at least recognize, by losing it, the favour which they did not recognize while possessing it? Thus may they grieve the more that they have lost that house because, when they later wished to have it, they could not; for, while they could preserve it, they utterly refused to do so. And so, at last, strangers will receive your honour and a cruel man your years, once strangers have been filled with your goods; and, seeing your labours in an alien house, you will groan at the end.

As Solomon says in the proverb, we shall laugh at your destruction and mock you when that which you feared comes upon you. Perhaps then, when you wish to return, we shall refuse to receive you, having long called you while you refused; and we shall say with the Wise Man: “I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was none who regarded it. You despised all my counsel and utterly neglected my reproofs” (Prov. 1).

Return therefore, transgressors, to your heart, and do not make yourselves wholly unworthy of your own [Col. 0999C] dignity. For, having already waited for three years to see whether the barren fig tree, nourished with manure, might produce fruit of itself, there plainly remains nothing but to lay the axe to the root, lest, with unfruitful branches spread abroad, it uselessly occupy the surrounding ground. Since nothing is more just than that a person be punished in that in which he has sinned, and since by what you have committed against God and the Church—not only rashly invading episcopal rights, but even causing your bishop and clergy to go miserably into exile—you have rendered yourselves unworthy of an episcopal see, we are unwilling that you should enjoy impunity for so great a crime any longer. Rather, we intend to restrain it by such correction that, for all to whom your fault has been a scandal, your punishment may be an example.

Having deliberated with our brethren, we have decreed by common counsel that, unless within one month after receiving this letter you return to obedience to the Church’s command and render due satisfaction concerning the matters for which you have incurred ecclesiastical censure, your city shall be deprived of episcopal dignity and its diocese divided among the neighbouring bishops. Suitable provision shall be made both for the bishop and for the clergy of the city—if it is still to be called a city after losing episcopal dignity—and thereby it will also deserve to lose its temporal county.

Behold, the bow is drawn; flee therefore from the arrow which is not accustomed to turn back, for repentance after ruin comes too late, as nearby [Col. 1000A] examples can teach you. Do not therefore be ashamed to recover your senses from error; for in this battle it is far more glorious to be conquered than to conquer. Just as one who conquers vice is conquered by virtue, so indeed one who makes virtue captive is made captive by vice. It is a greater virtue to conquer oneself than another, especially if cruelty is conquered by mercy, as Solomon testifies: “The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than the conqueror of cities” (Prov. 16).

We therefore send to you our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico and legate of the Apostolic See, that he may, by admonitions and exhortations, bring you back, if it is granted from above, to the path of truth. Otherwise, after summoning the bishops of Lombardy and removing every impediment of contradiction and appeal, they shall solemnly execute the aforesaid decree.

Furthermore, with paternal sweetness we admonish, entreat, and beseech you that you grant us this at least through free generosity, in hope not only of the eternal reward to be conferred upon you by the Lord, but also of a temporal reward to be granted by the Apostolic See. Know certainly that we proceeded to pronounce the aforesaid sentence not without much sadness and great grief, as persons necessarily compelled—if you permit yourselves to lead us into this necessity—to sever an honourable part from our body, that we may obey the command of him who orders that, if our eye causes us to stumble, we should pluck it out and cast it from us.

[Col. 1000C] Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of October, in the ninth year.

CLXVIII [Note: [Col. 0999] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §38. See also the notes to the next-to-last letter.] TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI, THE ABBOT OF TILIETO, AND ALBERT, PRIEST OF MANTUA. (Lateran, Nones of October.)

In the same manner . . . . . up to “we should pluck it out and cast it from us.” Therefore, by these Apostolic letters, we command your discretion, ordering that, setting aside your other occupations—since we now regard this as the chief among all the affairs of Lombardy—you proceed together to the city of Piacenza and prudently and effectively induce its citizens, whom, as he who is ignorant of nothing knows, we do not intend to burden contrary to justice, by whatever means you can, humbly and devoutly to obey the Apostolic commands [Col. 1000D], lest they incur the aforesaid punishment, both disgraceful and damaging. Otherwise, because wounds which do not feel the healing of poultices must be cut away by iron, after summoning the bishops of Lombardy, proceed to execute the aforesaid decree with such promptness and diligence that, through your care, it may obtain its due effect. Know that we have granted you full authority, with every impediment of contradiction and appeal removed, concerning all things necessary to carry out that matter. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of October, in the ninth year.

CLXIX [Note: [Col. 1001D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §38. See also the notes to the third-to-last letter.] TO THE CONSULS OF PIACENZA: THE SPIRIT OF WISER COUNSEL. Rejoices that, having returned to devotion, they have ceased their offences against the Church and obey the Apostolic commands. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1001A]

We rejoice in the Lord and in the power of his might because, as we have learned from the letters which you sent to the Roman merchants, you desire humbly and devoutly to return to obedience to the command of the Apostolic See. For we desire with paternal affection the welfare of your city, as of a special daughter, prudently employing the art of an experienced physician, who, if he cannot heal a wound with plasters or ointments, applies iron or fire—not to kill, but to heal. In doing this [Col. 1001B] he does not hate but loves the wounded man, who, although he suffers while enduring the harshness of the remedy, nevertheless rejoices after obtaining the effect of the medicine.

The excess of your presumption was serious indeed, because you were endeavouring to enslave your mother, the Church of Piacenza; but the example of that presumption was more serious, because one city would by its contagion have corrupted all the others. Therefore, before the aforesaid merchants came into our presence to intercede for you, we sent you medicinal letters, bitter indeed in their outer rind but sweetest in their marrow.

Do not then refuse to accept the saving medicine. As Catholic men, render due satisfaction to God and the Church, through which you will avoid not only punishment but also gain both temporal and eternal glory. Know that we have commanded our beloved son, the cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico and legate of the Apostolic See—or, if that legate should perhaps be unable to be present, the visitors of Lombardy—to proceed finally in this matter according to the form prescribed to them.

Given at the Lateran.

CLXX. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF ST VINCENT OF LISBON. A settlement made between them and the bishop and chapter of Lisbon is confirmed. (Lateran, 17 Kalends of November.)

“It is customary to grant,” etc., up to “to bestow.” Certainly, as [Col. 1001D] we have learned both from your representation and from the tenor of the letters of our beloved sons F., prior, and P., cantor of Alcobaça, our delegated judges: when a dispute had arisen before them between you on the one side and, on the other, our venerable brother . . . bishop and our beloved sons, the chapter of Lisbon, concerning the liberty of the monastery, certain churches, tithes, and certain other matters, the dispute was settled by an amicable composition with the consent [Col. 1002A] of the parties and by the authority of those judges. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., up to “consent”: we confirm by Apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of the present writing, that settlement, since it was prudently made without impropriety, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and hitherto peacefully observed. Let no one therefore, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of November, in the ninth year.

CLXXI [Note: [Col. 1001D] Fragments of this letter are found among the Decretals, Book 1, Title 6, *On election and the power of the person elected*, chapter 31. What is there read is here presented within brackets; variant readings are appended.] TO THE BISHOP OF FLORENCE [Note: [Col. 1001D] See letter 156 of Book Eight, note.] Concerning the appointment of certain canons in the Church of Volterra. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of November.)

[Col. 1002B]

The Church of Volterra [Note: [Col. 1001D] In the Decretals: “Since the Church of Volterra.”], having long been deprived of the due service of canons, our venerable brother, the . . . bishop of Volterra [Note: [Col. 1002D] Note in the same place.], wishing to restore the lack of ministers in that church, chose and installed certain canons in it. The resident canons [Note: [Col. 1002D] The Decretals omit “resident.”] refused to receive them, asserting that such an election had been undertaken to their prejudice [Note: [Col. 1002D] What follows, distinguished in italic type, is absent from the Decretals; it is, however, read in Pithou’s additions . . .]. When the bishop himself had sent us his complaint on this subject [Note: [Col. 1002D] In Pithou: “the same bishop.”], we entrusted the case to you for canonical settlement [Note: [Col. 1002D] See the same letter.].

When the parties appeared before you, that bishop asked you through his representative to prohibit our beloved sons Master Mitidus, Ildebrand, Placidus, Ptolemy, and Sofredus from the injury [Col. 1002C] which they were inflicting upon him concerning the election of canons of the Church of Volterra; and to allow him freely to exercise the right of election, without their opposing either him while electing or his wish to elect. The bishop asserted that the right of electing canons belonged to him in several ways.

He maintained that it belonged to him by common law, because, as the decrees of the sacred canons declare, a bishop has full disposition, provision, and jurisdiction in his church. For although one of his subjects may take precedence in office and honour, the bishop is nevertheless the provider and administrator in all things. He further maintained that, by an approved custom, the election of canons in that church belonged to him, as it did to the other prelates of the region, who were accustomed either by themselves or with associates to elect clerics. But even if it were uncertain what custom should be observed there in such matters, recourse ought to be had to the Apostolic See, since in other churches subject to a metropolitan, recourse is had in such doubts to the custom of the metropolitan see. Therefore, since at the Roman Church the supreme pontiff alone elects cardinals [Col. 1003A], the bishop maintained that the election of canons in his own church belonged to him alone.

He further alleged that, even if such an election had belonged to him by no law, authority to elect had devolved upon him because of the canons’ negligence. The sacred constitutions permit every bishop to make good, by pastoral diligence, the negligence of his clergy. It is also known to have been decreed in the Lateran Council that, when the grant of a dignity or benefice belongs to a chapter, if it delays conferring it for six months, the bishop shall carry it out.

On behalf of the chapter, however, the reply was made that by common law the election of canons belonged not to the bishop but to the chapter itself, in support of which they alleged certain canons. Yet, because different provisions of the canons had been promulgated on this point, it appeared that this diversity should rather be referred to the customs of different places: in some places the election of canons belongs to the bishop alone, elsewhere only to the chapter, and elsewhere to both together. Nor did the custom of the Apostolic See, introduced by the aforesaid bishop on his own behalf, appear able to harm the canons. Although the supreme pontiff alone elects cardinals, in his own cathedral church—the Lateran, that is, or the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles—the chapter is accustomed to elect fellow-canons for itself. Yet even in those churches, as in others, the Roman pontiff sometimes elects canons by plenitude of power.

To the bishop’s subsequent objection, namely that the right to elect had devolved upon him because of the chapter’s negligence, the chapter replied that the bishop could not claim the right of election for himself on account of such neglect unless a canonical admonition had first been given. In such a case no period is fixed by canon law which might stand in place of admonition or create a legal presumption that notice had been made—especially since, at his own discretion, he had refused to confirm persons elected and presented by the canons and the bishop. Since it is a rule of ordinary law that admonition must precede punishment, and since the bishop, omitting admonition under the pretext of negligence, had imposed a penalty, the same party maintained that what he had rashly undertaken ought rightly to be disapproved [Col. 1003D].

The chapter also added that the decree of the Lateran Council does not apply in churches where ecclesiastical benefices are not at all differentiated, but in those in which there is a fixed number of canons and distinct prebends. Furthermore, if the aforesaid canons were found negligent according to the tenor of the Council, the bishop, who had been negligent for a longer time, acquired no right thereby and deserved rather to be punished; for no one ought, by one and the same act, to merit both a penalty and a reward. Indeed, in this case the power of election had rightly devolved upon the superior, as is plainly inferred from the tenor of the Council; hence he ought not to put his sickle into another’s harvest.

When these and other matters had been proposed before you, and you nevertheless wished to deliberate before pronouncing judgment because you found the councils too divergent and almost every person whose advice you wished to use in this matter was held suspect by one party or the other for some reason, you remitted the prepared case to our presence, transmitting under your seal the testimony and allegations of both parties. Having carefully examined the testimony and arguments of both parties, with the counsel of our brethren we, by the authority of these present letters, command your brotherhood [that, on the first article of the bishop’s petition, in which he asked you to prohibit the aforesaid canons from the injury which they inflict upon him concerning the election of canons of the Church of Volterra, you do not delay to absolve the aforesaid canons from the bishop’s suit, setting appeal aside. For, as the rule of law says, a person who uses his own right is not understood to inflict injury, and it has been proved far better by witnesses that the aforesaid canons exercised this right before the bishop in question.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] In the Decretals this word, and below *appeal*, when postponed, is absent. The Decretals read “does not appear” in place of “is not understood,” and “approved” in place of “proved”; they also read “the aforesaid” in place of “the oft-mentioned.”]

In the second article of the aforesaid petition [Note: [Col. 1003D] The Decretals omit this; below they read “the same” for “the bishop in question” and “the aforesaid” for “the persons mentioned.”], in which the bishop in question asked that the said canons allow him [Col. 1004C] freely to use the right of election, you should absolve the canons mentioned, especially if it is notorious that the general custom in Tuscany is observed whereby, in cathedral churches, the chapter alone, without consulting the bishop, has authority to elect canons. But lest the same church remain any longer deprived of the service of ministers, command the canons mentioned on our behalf to elect within fifteen days suitable persons as canons, according to the resources of the church, at least three of whom are priests, and to present them to the bishop for confirmation. Otherwise, from that time forward, supported by our authority and with every impediment of contradiction and appeal removed, do not delay to carry this out.]

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of November, in the ninth year.

CLXXII [Note: [Col. 1003D]

Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, §8.

[Col. 1004D] It is printed complete by Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1498, but disfigured by a very great number of errors.]

TO P., BISHOP OF IVREA [Note: [Col. 1004D]

Ughelli, cited place.

“After Bernard, bishop of Ivrea—on whom see above the notes to letter 200 of Book Eight—had been deposed, Peter, a Piedmontese by nation, monk of the Cistercian Order and abbot of the celebrated monastery of La Ferté in the diocese of Chalon, a man mighty in deed [Col. 1005C] and word, was elected bishop by the chapter in the same year, 1205, and confirmed. When he had come to the church entrusted to him, after a few days, intent on repose and divine contemplation, he abandoned it without permission of the Roman pontiff, sought the desert, and hid himself in secluded places, still unconsecrated. When Innocent III learned this, he wrote him a most learned letter, in which, by the authority of the Fathers and sacred canons, he showed most fully that an elected bishop could not at any time be released and severed from the bond to his bride without the authority of the Roman pontiff, any more than if he had received consecration. The tenor of the letter is as follows, copied from the Vatican register, Book IX, p. 116, no. 117:

‘To the bishop-elect of Ivrea, etc. . . . We have received your letter containing, etc. . . .’”

(Note that Ughelli says Innocent’s letter is addressed to the bishop-elect, whereas here it is said to be addressed to the bishop. Ughelli continues:)

“Peter obeyed the command of the supreme pontiff and humbly bowed his neck; returning to his own bride, he was consecrated bishop and, like a most brilliant star, illuminated his church and province. By command of the same Innocent, together with Cato, bishop of Vercelli, Gerard, abbot of Tiliéto of his own Cistercian Order and later bishop of Novara and cardinal of Albano, he performed with distinction the office entrusted to him as Apostolic visitor of the Church of Albenga. Shortly thereafter, that is, in 1209, he was created patriarch of Antioch in the East, as is mentioned in Innocent’s letters. In 1214 he committed the monastery of St George of the Black Mountain, otherwise called Jubin, near Antioch, to the Order, summoning his Cistercian monks from the monastery of La Ferté. In the following year, unable to attend the Lateran Council, he sent his vicar, the bishop of Antibes, to it; Innocent excused him because he was urgently necessary to Christendom in the East. There at last, laden with merits, he died in 1217. Angelus Manrique mentions him in volume I of the *Annals of the Cistercians*, in the catalogue of the abbots of La Ferté, though he did not recognize him as abbot of that monastery.”]

That he should return to his church and not seek separation from it. (Lateran, 12 Kalends of November.)

We have received your letter stating that formerly [Col. 1005A] fear and trembling came upon you and darkness covered you, and that with the Prophet you said: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and rest?” (Ps. 54). Therefore, lest you appear before the Lord as a transgressor of this quasi-vow, behold, you have fled far away and dwell in solitude, awaiting him who saved you from faint-heartedness and tempest.

You would have remained in the bishopric of Ivrea out of reverence for the Apostolic command, had not certain matters which appeared to conflict with your salvation intervened: namely, the purpose, as expressed above, of entering the desert, which did not permit your mind to be at rest; and the fact that the Church of Ivrea holds certain possessions under title of pledge, the revenues of which did not seem just to you. It also possesses tolls and transit dues, from whose revenues you feared to be supported. Moreover, its possessions are bound in pledge and are burdened with debt to such an extent that you hoped to make little or no progress there in temporal matters. You therefore humbly begged us to permit you, with our blessing and favour, to remain in the solitude to which you had gone, so that you might be free in spirit to attend to the Lord and nevertheless bewail your sins.

Subsequently, however, we learned clearly from the letters both of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Milan [Note: [Col. 1006D] See letter 6 of Book Three.], and of the beloved sons of the chapter of Ivrea, that, having received the election by our command and had it confirmed by the said archbishop, and having left the abbey of La Ferté to which you had been called [Note: [Col. 1006D]

A passage especially worthy of notice, since it sheds light on what the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1023, report concerning Peter, abbot of La Ferté.

“X. Audo, or Odo, in 1203 received Bartholomew of Genest, knight, into the house; he is mentioned the following year in a charter of Gerard, abbot of St Peter of Chalon.

“XI. Peter II, in 1206 made an agreement with Josceran of Saula, perhaps of Saulx, before Robert, bishop of Chalon. He is omitted by the Sammarthani, who put in his place Gerard in the same year, 1206, and after him Hugh, who died in 1217, on 8 April, and was buried in the chapter-house. Indeed, an R., abbot of La Ferté, is read in 1208 in the same Sammarthani, vol. IV, col. 61; but this seems a typographical error, for which the letter P. or S. should be substituted. Yet neither is mentioned in the domestic records.”]

, you came to govern that church, and thus a spiritual marriage was contracted between you and it. Yet after a few days had passed, without the chapter’s knowledge, taking wings like a dove, you fled and flew away into solitude [Col. 1006A], although your wings are so bound by the bonds of commands that you have no freedom to fly without our permission.

You must not doubt that, since the spiritual bond is stronger than the carnal, almighty God has reserved the dissolution of the spiritual marriage between bishop and church to his own judgment alone, just as he has reserved the dissolution of the carnal marriage between man and woman to his own judgment alone, commanding that what God has joined no human being should separate. For spiritual marriage is dissolved not by human but rather by divine power, when, by translation, deposition, or even resignation, by authority of the Roman pontiff—who is acknowledged to be the vicar of Jesus Christ—a bishop is removed from his church. Therefore these three matters which we have set forth are reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, not so much by canonical constitution as by divine institution.

Accordingly, just as a consecrated bishop cannot abandon without the Roman pontiff’s permission the church entrusted to him, so you, elected and even confirmed, could not leave that church without our consent, to which you are bound matrimonially. There can be no doubt that, after canonical election and confirmation, a spiritual marriage has been contracted between those who elect and the person elected. Hence, since the bishop’s bond to a church is no greater than that of an elected person—especially one who has been confirmed—the same law, and no other, applies entirely to both. Thus, as the translation, resignation [Col. 1006C], or deposition of bishops is reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, so also is that of the elected, although what was decreed concerning bishops was not formerly stated expressly concerning the elected, because of the evident similarity—or rather identity—about which no careful observer can doubt, since like cases must be judged alike.

Since it is therefore clear from the foregoing that you are bound to a bride through election and confirmation, do not seek release, lest, perhaps seeking to live for yourself alone and laying aside pastoral care, you hide in the earth, like the slothful servant, the talent entrusted to you. He deserved his lord’s rebuke because he did not commit his lord’s money to the bankers, from whom, upon his return, he might have received it with interest. His talent was therefore taken away and, as an unprofitable servant, he was ordered by his lord to be cast into outer darkness; whereas he commanded those servants who returned talents doubled to enter into his joy, promising to set them over many things because they had been faithful over few.

Remain, then, in the calling in which you were called, and do not hide your Lord’s money. For, according to Solomon’s saying, “He who hides grain is cursed among the people” (Prov. 11), while blessedness is promised to those who sow beside all waters. Nor should you allege as a reason that we sent you to a poor church and a small diocese. For our intention was not merely to provide for that church through you, but rather for all Lombardy—indeed, for the universal Church—which you can instruct both by the example of your life and by the word of doctrine, since you are a man mighty in deed and word, “turning the mouth of the turtle-dove toward its armpits” [an uncertain proverbial expression].

Do not therefore neglect the grace to which you have been called, lest you appear to quench the Spirit. Rather, say with that glorious pontiff: “Lord, if I am necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labour.” For the debt of charity requires that one who embraces Rachel not refuse the embraces of Leah; for although Rachel is beautiful, Leah is useful because of the grace of her children, bringing advantage and progress to herself and others.

Although the repose of Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, is preferred to Martha’s busyness in many acts of service, do not therefore think that Martha chose the bad part because she laboured about many things, while Mary chose the best part, which shall not be taken from her. For although the former is safer, the latter is more fruitful; and although the former is sweeter, the latter is considered more useful. Though you may at once be both contemplative and active, following the example of the lawgiver, who now ascended the mountain to behold there the glory of God with greater freedom [Col. 1007D], and now descended into the camp to provide more usefully for the people’s needs, you ought not on that account to abandon the church with which you have already contracted marriage.

Nor should you do so because, as you assert, you do not hope to make progress there. The Lord can give increase to your planting and watering; and even if you do not in every respect advance according to your wish, you may nevertheless expect no lesser reward, because God rewards labour, not success. Scripture testifies: “The Lord will render a reward for labours” (Wis. 10), promising recompense to his servants for labour, not for achievement. Hence the Apostle does not boast that he succeeded more than all others, but that he laboured more than all.

Nor should you excuse yourself on account of the Church’s poverty, because Christian poverty is always rich. Consider what the Psalmist says: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread” (Ps. 36). Do you not recall God’s word in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘With what shall we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and the righteousness of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6).

You may—and indeed must—abstain from any unjust revenues [Col. 1008B] which your church has customarily received. It will be more glorious for you before God and men, knowing certainly that the left hand will be beneath your head if the right hand is in embrace.

We therefore admonish your devotion and exhort you in the Lord, strictly commanding by these Apostolic letters that you return to the aforesaid church, apply diligent care and concern to your bride and to the people entrusted to you, return to the Lord the talents entrusted to you doubled, and deserve to hear that joyful voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over few things, I shall set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25). Firmly hope in the Lord Jesus Christ that he who gives you the will to labour will also grant result and progress, so that your labour may not be held useless.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of November, in the ninth year.

CLXXIII [Note: [Col. 1007D]

A copy of this letter, which we had arranged to have transcribed with the others from the copy of Conti, slipped from our hands by some chance unknown to us; therefore we can present here only its summary [Col. 1008D]. See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §35.

Add, if you wish, the account in Angelus Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, p. 467, under the year 1206, ch. 4, §9.]

TO THE BISHOP OF ZAMORA, etc. Writes to them in favour of the monastery of Lorvão against the king of Portugal.

CLXXIV. TO THE PROVOST OF NOVARA. That he is not to permit the cleric A. to be harassed concerning his benefice on account of a wound inflicted by him upon a certain robber. (Lateran, 2 Kalends of November.)

[Col. 1008D] Appearing before us, the cleric A. represented humbly that, when a certain robber, banished by the consuls of Castignaga, attacked him and threw him to the ground grievously wounded, he, lying on the ground as if half-dead, struck the aforesaid robber in the leg. On account of that wound, the robber is said to have died, although he lived for a long time after the wound was inflicted and peace had been restored between them. Therefore, since he was said to have paid nature’s debt on account of the aforesaid wound, to our venerable brother, the bishop of Tusculum [Note: [Col. 1009C]

Nicolaus de Romanis, a Roman, Innocent III’s chaplain, was elected by him cardinal-bishop of Tusculum in the year of our salvation 1205, the seventh year of the pontificate, in March according to Panvinio, or in December according to Ciaconius, at Rome, in the fourth creation of cardinals. He went to England as legate of the Apostolic See; he visited it again under Pope Honorius III to promote the holy war in the East. He also acted as legate in Prussia under the same pope. He was bound by very close friendship to St. Dominic. This Nicholas—whom Honorius III was accustomed to call an angel of peace and salvation, pleasing to men and, beyond others, beloved by himself—subscribed to many letters of both Innocent and Honorius. He died in 1219. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 22.

[Col. 1009D] It should indeed be noted that the privilege granted by Innocent III to Albert, bishop of Gubbio, on 30 April 1205, and subscribed by Nicholas, appears to support Panvinio’s assertion that Nicholas was raised to the see of Tusculum in March 1205. See below, at letter 86 of this ninth book, note.]

He humbly confessed this, and accepted from the same man the penance imposed upon him, humbly beseeching us to dispense mercifully with him concerning the benefice which he had obtained in the church of Castignaga. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if the matter stands thus, you shall not allow him to be troubled by anyone concerning the aforesaid benefice on such an occasion, but shall cause him to possess it in due peace, any obstacle of appeal having been removed.

Given at the Lateran, 31 October, in the ninth year.

CLXXV. [Note: [Col. 1009D]

Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, § 42.

Angelo Manrique published it entire, though marred by certain errors, in *Annals of the Cistercian Order*, vol. III, p. 463, under the year 1206, chapter 3, § 1 ff. There he maintains that it concerns the abbot of Lankenheim, not of Lakene, as is read here and in Raynaldus.

At about this time, when the pagans of Livonia and Prussia were holding certain Cistercian brothers—whether of the monastery of Lankenheim is uncertain—who had been sent to preach, in chains and wearing them down under close confinement [Col. 1010C], so that not only were they themselves suffering but the fruit of the word which they would otherwise have sown was also impeded, the abbot of that monastery, a man fervent in zeal, went there, intending to bring the captive brothers—or sons—out of the prison-house [Col. 1009D: Thus in Manrique], and to set free the preaching which, above all, he lamented had been bound. When he found a great harvest in that province but few labourers, and discovered the tyrant of the land to be approachable and not excessively hardened, he freed the brothers and, as he was about to depart, was detained by a divinely shown vision of a whitening field, and commanded to prepare himself for the harvest. Yet, trusting neither himself nor his vision, he returned home. There, prepared in every respect to obey and bidding farewell to his monastery, he approached Innocent, to be consecrated to that work and ministry—but only if sent [Col. 1010D]. There survives a letter of Innocent, the supreme pontiff, issued this year to the archbishops and bishops of Poland. In it, while he sends forth to preach the Gospel a man fervent in zeal and charity, he appoints him apostle of that people; indeed, he grants him power to take with him Cistercian monks and others whom he may associate with himself in a share of this pastoral concern. Bzovius mentions the letters in some fashion, corrupting the name of the abbey and suppressing the religious order. We shall give them entire and corrected, according to our custom: “To the archbishops and bishops of Poland,” etc.

“Man, when he was in honour,” etc.]

. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT POLAND. That they are to give counsel and support to the abbot of Lakene as he preaches the faith. (Lateran, 26 October.)

[Col. 1009B]

Man, who [Note: [Col. 1010D] Manrique omits *who*, and shortly afterwards the words “were made”; below, he reads “wisdom” in place of “eternal.”], though he was in honour, could have perceived through the things that were made the invisible things of God, even His eternal power and divinity, so that he was without excuse, because he understood not at all; he was compared to senseless beasts, and, becoming foolish, his heart was darkened. He changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed beasts, and serpents; and he chose to serve the creature rather than the Creator [Col. 1009C].

But almighty God, lest he should perish utterly whom He had exalted above the other creatures by the eminence of his dignity [Col. 1010A], rising because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, set forth Jesus Christ as a propitiator through faith in His blood, to demonstrate His righteousness, for the remission of former sins, in the forbearance of God [Note: [Col. 1010D] Manrique omits this.], so that He might Himself be just and the justifier of the one who is of faith in Jesus Christ. Without this faith no one can be justified at all, since, as the prophet testifies: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Habakkuk 2).

Thus, after this way of going to the living and true God had been set forth, the prince of this world blinded the minds of certain unbelievers, lest the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should shine upon them. Still wrapped in the darkness of unbelief, they do not call upon the Lord, who is near to all who call upon Him in truth, because “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” [Col. 1010B]. But since, as the Apostle says: “How shall they call upon Him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe Him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10), God stirred up the spirit of His beloved son, . . . abbot of Lakene [Note: [Col. 1010D] Manrique: “of Lankehim”; below, he omits the words “requested to be sent.”], so that he requested to be sent by us to those pagans who dwell around your regions—by us who, though unworthy, hold on earth the place of Him who said to His disciples: “Ask the Lord of the harvest to send labourers into His harvest” (Matthew 9)—in order that he might gather among them some sheaves and gather for himself fruit unto eternal life.

For when he had gone to those parts to free certain brothers [Col. 1010C] whom the pagans themselves held bound in chains, and when the lord of that land had received him kindly [Col. 1011A] and released his brothers, showing him also the tomb of the blessed martyr Albert, he lifted up his eyes and saw that the region was white for harvest. Yet he did not dare put the sickle into it, because he had not received from us authority to preach. Therefore, coming to the Apostolic See, he humbly begged us to deem him worthy to be sent into the Lord’s harvest.

Accordingly, commending in the Lord his pious purpose, we have thought fit by the authority of these presents to grant him leave to preach the Gospel to them and, acting as an ambassador for Christ, as though God were exhorting through him, to entreat them for Christ to be reconciled to Him. But because the harvest indeed is great and one labourer does not suffice for its reaping, we grant him by apostolic authority that he may take with him brothers of the Cistercian Order and also others who wish to join him in this work of saving ministry, so that they may preach the Gospel with him, baptize those who receive the word of God, bury the dead, and celebrate Masses for the baptized in places which they judge suitable [Col. 1011B].

Moreover, the aforesaid abbot may hear the confessions of penitents and grant some remission of sins to those who, with a pure heart and good conscience [Note: [Col. 1011D] Manrique: “pure.”], take care to lend assistance to the aforesaid ministry. He may also entrust to suitable persons for administration possessions piously donated to ransom Christians from the hands of pagans [Col. 1011C]; under threat of anathema we forbid these possessions to be diminished or taken away [Note: [Col. 1011D] Manrique omits this.]. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you, commanding that, with devout regard for this pious undertaking, you give him suitable counsel and assistance.

Given at the Lateran, 26 October, in the ninth year.

CLXXVI. . . . . . TO THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 1011D] See letter 147 of book five.] AND CHAPTER OF LINCOLN. That they are to elect a worthy person as their bishop. (Lateran, 31 October.)

By your letters you informed us that, after your bishop of good memory . . . had departed this life [Note: [Col. 1012D] See letter 164 of book eight, note.], you were disturbed by the desolation of your church [Col. 1011D] and carefully deliberated concerning the appointment of a bishop. But after many deliberations and much counsel, which you could not establish among yourselves, you decided to have recourse to the Apostolic See, from which assistance and comfort are customarily afforded to the afflicted and desolate. You humbly informed us that Hugh, your bishop of pious memory, being a prudent and discerning man, sought everywhere with the utmost diligence men eminent in learning and integrity, in whom his spirit might rest, and placed them in the church of Lincoln as chosen pillars in the house of the Lord. In them he considered more the merits of life than the rights of birth, and more personal worth than regularity of origin.

Among them, some are found in your church who are commendable in life and learning and who, in view of the need of the time, would, in human judgment, not be unworthy of the episcopate, if they had been born of lawful marriage [Col. 1012A]. Having considered, therefore, the advantages and disadvantages of your church and of the whole diocese, you would prefer, according to canonical form, to elect as pastor someone from the bosom of that church rather than summon one from elsewhere, as though begging for him, or admit someone thrust upon you through the pressure of magnates. You would also rather have a man tried and known, who knows and wishes to benefit the Lord’s flock, than some untried person who might perhaps walk paths new and unknown to you.

You therefore humbly begged us, in paternal sympathy with your weakness, mercifully to grant that, if the votes of all of you, or of the greater and sounder part, should concur in such a person otherwise qualified, you might on this occasion elect him pastor despite the defect of birth. But because you did not take care to state the person with whom you desire a dispensation, or how great his defect of birth is, we answer your whole body as follows: so long as an ordinary election can lawfully be held of a person legitimately born, an extraordinary postulation of a person illegitimately born is not to be made, unless perhaps common consent sometimes requires it because of outstanding usefulness and urgent necessity—provided only that the person’s defect is not excessively grave and that both merit of life and talent in learning support him [Col. 1012C]. Therefore, if you decide that a postulation should be made, when it has been presented to us we shall proceed as we see expedient.

Given at the Lateran, 31 October, in the ninth year.

CLXXVII. . . . . . TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 1012D] See letters 99 of book five, note, and 89 of book seven.] AND CONVENT OF SALEM. That they may lend money to those who trouble them. (Lateran, 4 November.)

It was set before us on your behalf that, although it has been granted to you, as to the other brothers of the Cistercian Order [Col. 1012D], by the Apostolic See that no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, you have hitherto refrained from using the privilege granted you, in order that you might mitigate the malice of certain clerics and laymen. You therefore humbly asked us to grant you permission to receive as a pledge the tithes belonging to you . . . Accordingly, providing for your interests, we grant you by the authority of these presents that, in return for the retention of tithes that belong to you by right, you may lend money to your persecutors, so that [Col. 1013A] they may cease troubling you concerning those tithes, either permanently or for a time.

Given at the Lateran, 4 November, in the ninth year.

CLXXVIII. . . . . . TO THE BISHOP OF FERRARA [Note: [Col. 1013D] See letter 39 of book three, note.]. That he is to induce the clergy and people of Trent to obey the patriarch of Aquileia, to whom administration of the church of Trent was entrusted because of their scandal. [Note: [Col. 1013D] For the subject of this letter, see letter 183 of book eight and the annotations there, incorrectly made through an error which we shall correct in the following note.] (Lateran, 31 October.)

Our venerable brother . . . bishop of Trent [Note: [Col. 1013D]

This letter must certainly be compared with what Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 514, reports concerning Conrad II, bishop of Trent:

“LXXV. Conrad II was bishop of the Tridentines about the year of the Lord 1190. A man of outstanding ability and of special love for the church entrusted to him, he recovered for his church many alienated properties, with the highest praise for his prudence. Wearied by human cares, having obtained permission, he withdrew into the cloister at St. George in the Val d’Ana in 1205, where he died in holiness and piety.

[Col. 1014D] ‘LXXVI. Frederick, of the noble and powerful Wanga family, was promoted to this see in 1205,’ etc.”

The remaining matters reported by Ughellus concerning Frederick Wanga we supplied in a note to letter 183 of book eight—dated 11 January in the eighth year of the pontificate, that is, in this very year 1206 in which we are now engaged. There, trusting Ughellus, we thought that the letter concerned this prelate, since he had supposedly been raised to the see of Trent as early as 1205. But this letter of Innocent proves beyond all certainty that Frederick did not wear the mitre of Trent until after the end of 1206, and that letter 83 of book eight concerns Conrad, not Frederick.]

asked us to grant him permission to resign, alleging certain reasons why he did not consider himself fit thereafter to exercise the episcopal office: namely, that his parishioners [Col. 1013B], both personally and through others, afflicted him with intolerable injuries and vexations; that, both because of advancing age and because of the labours by which he had been repeatedly wearied, he was broken by excessive weakness; and that many homicides, perjuries, and arsons had wickedly been committed on both sides in consequence of the discord which he had had with his parishioners.

Inclining to his petitions, we ordered our venerable brother . . . bishop of Padua [Note: [Col. 1014D] See letter 178 of book seven, note.], acting in our place, to receive his resignation and enjoin the chapter of Trent to assemble, invoke the grace of the Holy Spirit, and canonically elect for themselves a suitable person as pastor. But when, owing to his resignation, a dispute subsequently arose between . . . the dean and chapter on the one side, and the said bishop of Trent on the other [Col. 1013C], the same dean, with certain of his companions, and the bishop came to the Apostolic See.

The dean, appearing in our presence, stated that, when the bishop had resolved to enter monastic life, he assembled his brethren and explained to them that he proposed to serve the Lord in monastic life at the church of St. George on the mountain; that he had sent his own messenger to us to seek permission to proceed; and that, when the canons saw our letters concerning the permission granted, they would be entirely released from the oath of fealty and duty of obedience by which they were bound to him. He earnestly advised them not to choose anyone from the body of the church as their pastor. As the chapter laboured with earnest dissuasion to recall the bishop from such a purpose [Col. 1013D], the bishop is said to have answered that the whole world could not recall him from it, even if he were to grant the entire chapter authority to appoint a bishop in his place. To prove these matters, which the aforesaid dean set before us, he produced a public instrument.

He further added that after this the bishop went to the aforesaid monastery and there, after making a vow and solemn profession, assumed the monastic habit [Col. 1014A].
