When the bishop’s messenger later returned with the letters of resignation, the bishop, hindered by flesh and blood and maliciously induced—or rather misled—by his relatives, who wished to drain the remaining goods of the church of Trent, withdrew from the purpose he had undertaken. Thus, by the bishop’s fraud, the letters of resignation were suppressed, although a copy of them had been shown to those persons.

The dean and chapter, observing that the bishop was withdrawing from his purpose to the peril of his salvation and the detriment of the church, as devoted sons wishing to avert the misfortunes of their mother, notified us. They set forth many losses and burdens which the church had subsequently endured through the bishop. For this reason we commanded the aforesaid bishop of Padua that, unless the bishop of Trent showed a just and necessary cause for changing his intention to resign, he should diligently admonish and induce him to resign and, if necessary [Col. 1014C], endeavour to compel him by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

When the bishop and chapter of Trent had been summoned by the authority of those letters and appeared before the bishop of Padua on the appointed day, the bishop of Trent raised certain exceptions in order to decline the jurisdiction. Since the bishop of Padua doubted concerning these, he judged that we should be consulted. We, judging those exceptions superfluous, ordered him not to delay proceeding in the matter according to the form of our mandate, those frivolous exceptions in no way notwithstanding.

The bishop, appointing as his procurator the archdeacon of Vicenza, departed for Philip, duke of Swabia [Col. 1014D]. Having personally sworn him an oath of fealty, he received the regalian rights from him, promising him one thousand marks, . . . two hundred to his wife, and one hundred to his household servants. He pledged to him the village of Bolzano, belonging to the aforesaid church, as security for this money; but the vassals of the church prevented the duke’s messengers from occupying the said village [Col. 1015A].

Now the bishop of Padua, without summoning the chapter—and not because it was absent through contumacy—without joinder of issue and passing over the proper order of law, received the witnesses produced on the bishop’s side. He did not take further action in the case, but set the octave of St. Michael as the date on which the parties should appear before us.

The aforesaid dean repeatedly challenged the witnesses introduced to prove the reasons for which the bishop of Trent had changed his intention. One of them was a crossbowman and archer [Col. 1015B]; another a gambler and cheat, as the same witnesses attest in the text of their testimony. A third was found to be perjured, because, having sworn to the dean to keep a confidence, he later disclosed to the bishop the counsel entrusted to him, as that witness himself asserted. Moreover, a manifest inconsistency was found among these witnesses. Some declared that, without any oath having intervened, they had promised by a simple word not to reveal the confidence to the dean; others declared that they had pledged this solemnly, giving assurance [Note: [Col. 1015D] Thus in the copy.] upon a certain little document and saying, “So may God help us,” believing that in this way they were taking an oath.

One of those witnesses also, named Ro . . ., was found stained with the disgrace of simoniacal depravity. He asserted that he had received a promise from the dean that, if he and his brother Bertold worked to prevent the bishop’s return to his bishopric and to make the dean bishop, that witness would receive from the dean one half of the office of castaldia of the treasury and a specified sum of money [Col. 1015C]. Since, therefore, those witnesses were shown to be so base, inconsistent, and criminal, and since they had been received contrary to legal order while the suit had not been joined, the dean asked that testimonies of this kind be deemed void, because that which is attempted contrary to law ought to lack the force of validity.

The dean further requested that, since the bishop had not proved, in accordance with the terms of our mandate, a just and necessary reason for changing his intention, we should deem him worthy to be compelled to resign [Col. 1015D]. This was especially so because the reasons for which he had sought permission to resign had not diminished, but had rather increased: the bishop’s parishioners now persecute him more harshly than before. Moreover, he ought at present to fear homicides, perjuries, and other dangers all the more, since the savagery of his persecutors has been inflamed against him beyond its usual measure. The impediment of old age also, which was one of the reasons for which the bishop wished to resign, has undoubtedly increased according to the ordinary course of nature. For just as youth, once it begins, continually declines, so old age, once it begins, continually increases.

The dean also alleged that, even if the aforesaid bishop were not to be compelled to resign because of the reasons stated, he ought not thereafter to be admitted to administration of the bishopric because of his manifest dissipation of its goods [Col. 1016A]. By the bishop’s own confession, it was clear that he had burdened his church with debts exceeding forty thousand pounds in Veronese currency.

The bishop, however, vigorously contesting the dean’s allegations, set before us the course and progress of events differently from the dean. He asserted that, having conceived the purpose of changing his manner of life for the reasons mentioned above, he had sent his own messenger to us to obtain permission to resign. But he later changed his intention for probable and honourable reasons [Col. 1016B], namely because he saw his bride profaned by wicked schemes and shameful promises. For, as the authority says: “A wise man changes his counsel as often as he reflects upon something more prudently.”

The bishop also maintained that what the dean had alleged could not prejudice him: namely, that he had told his canons that, when they saw our letters granting permission, they would be released from obedience to him. A bishop, bound matrimonially to his church and not possessing free power over himself in this respect, could not release the bond of obedience by which his subjects were bound to him.

The bishop further said that the instrument produced by the dean proved nothing, because the person said to have written the little document [Col. 1016C] at the time alleged did not hold the office of notary. He denied having made a vow to enter religion, having professed at the monastery of St. George, or having assumed the monastic habit, although he had gone to that monastery for rest, as one vexed by such frequent persecutions and unable to reside peacefully in his church. He demonstrated this by the statements of his witnesses, which expressly stated that he was at the said monastery at his own expense and in his customary dress.

The bishop further asserted that the letters in question had been suppressed not by his fraud or contrivance, but rather by the deceit of the people of Trent [Col. 1016D]. He attempted to prove this because a copy of those letters had been sent to him from Trent. The bishop openly conceded that he had appeared before Philip, duke of Swabia, in order that Philip might restrain through the secular arm those whom he could not control by paternal admonition and ecclesiastical discipline. And although he promised Philip one thousand marks, he promised nothing to others. Although he was willing for Philip’s messengers to retain the aforesaid village of the church as security until he paid the money on the appointed terms, it was not his intention that the right and ownership of the village should be lost to the church [Col. 1017A].

To the dean’s allegation that the bishop of Padua had received witnesses without joinder of issue and after passing over the proper legal order, the bishop replied that in that matter the formalities of judicial procedure did not have to be observed in every respect. The bishop of Padua had not been entrusted with contentious jurisdiction, but with a certain plenary jurisdiction. He had been commanded diligently to investigate the truth concerning the bishop’s change of intention, not to decide a dispute between parties. Thus, without joinder of issue and with other legal formalities omitted, witnesses could be received in this case.

The bishop also answered the objections later brought against the witnesses. Although one witness was said to be a crossbowman, it had not been shown that through such office or occupation he had shed blood in cases not permitted; therefore his testimony was not to be rejected as that of a homicide [Col. 1017B]. Although another witness said that he was accustomed to play at dice, like other gamblers, he was not for that reason to be judged infamous, since many honourable men often play at dice—especially because the witness’s deposition suggests that he then intended to speak in jest, not to confess anything against himself.

The bishop maintained that the witness who disclosed the counsel to the bishop should not be rejected from testimony as perjured. When he promised to keep it secret, he understood either that something honourable would be disclosed to him or something dishonourable. If he bound himself to conceal something honourable, he was not obliged to suppress a wicked matter and a simoniacal bargain. But if he believed that something dishonourable would be entrusted to him, which he bound himself by oath or promise to suppress, such an oath was unlawful and bound him to nothing. He could publish that counsel without fault, since it is written: “In evil promises, break faith; in a shameful vow, change your resolve” [Col. 1017C].

Nor should the inconsistency noted among some of the witnesses harm them. Some say that they simply promised not to disclose the confidence; others say that they solemnly promised it under oath. These can readily be reconciled: when the first say that they promised simply, this must be understood to mean that they said so because they did not swear upon relics or the Gospels, as is customary. When the others say that they swore solemnly, they say so because they swore upon a certain document. This answer is clearly gathered from the witnesses’ depositions [Col. 1017D]. The objection of simoniacal depravity against the witness Rodulf does not matter, because the truth can sufficiently appear through the depositions of the other witnesses.

Having rejected, therefore, the objections which the dean raised against the witnesses and their statements, the aforesaid bishop asked that we restore his church to him and allow him to enjoy peaceful possession of it, asserting [Col. 1018A] that it had been sufficiently shown that he had changed his intention to resign for just and lawful reasons. The bishop further added that, even if nothing had been proved by witnesses, reason nonetheless showed that he could change his intention. No person of sound mind would say that, by asking permission to resign, he became bound to resign. For if the chapter of a church informed us by letters that it wished to elect one of our household as pastor, but did not proceed further and in the meantime changed its mind, it could not in any way be compelled to receive him as bishop. Likewise, if someone promises a woman that he wishes to have her as wife, but changes his mind before contracting marriage with her, he cannot be compelled to take her as his wife [Col. 1018B].

Nor should the bishop be said to have been bound to resign by the letters obtained from us, since they reserved to him the choice whether he wished to resign, when it was commanded that the bishop of Padua should receive his resignation. Since, therefore, he did not bind himself to resign by those or any other means, he could withdraw from such a purpose whenever he wished.

The bishop also sought to demonstrate this by another argument. The clergy and people of Trent jointly recalled him. Hence it was apparent that there was no need to fear scandal or persecution, and that the bishop was not broken by such great old age that, persecution having ceased, he would be unequal to governing his church. He could therefore rightly withdraw from the intention of resigning [Col. 1018C], because, when the cause ceased, the effect ought to cease.

The bishop thus urgently requested that we deign to restore his church to him, since, upon returning to it, he was received by neither clerics nor laymen. It is shameful and improper that a father should be despoiled by his children, a shepherd by his sheep, a lord by his servants, and a prelate by his subjects. He maintained that the accusation of dissipation ought not to prevent his restoration. For it is an established point of law that a person despoiled is not compelled to answer anyone—especially his rivals and despoilers—before everything has been fully restored to him, because he does not have the privilege by which one already stripped may be stripped again. This was especially so because it was through the fault of those persons, who had raised a less than reasonable sedition against the bishop, that the church was burdened with so great a debt [Col. 1018D].

Indeed, when he came to govern that church and had lived there for some time in peace, he reduced debts exceeding thirty-three thousand pounds to the amount of seven thousand pounds.

The opposing answer was that the bishop could not request restoration, since no one had despoiled him: he had himself voluntarily abandoned his see. A more forceful answer was also made: because, by our mandate and with the bishop’s own consent, the care of that church in spiritual and temporal matters had been entrusted to our venerable brother . . . patriarch of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 1017D] See letter 99 of book seven, note.] until the dispute between the canons and the bishop should be settled, the bishop could not reasonably ask to be restored to that church [Col. 1019A]. Rather, if anyone hindered the patriarch from administering freely, either the patriarch himself could bring a complaint on the matter, or we ourselves, who considered it proper to entrust this care to him.

Having carefully understood these and the other matters set forth on both sides, we have decreed, with the counsel of our brethren, that the following procedure be observed: lest the insolence of subjects grow against their aforesaid prelates and they presume everywhere to despoil them, the aforesaid patriarch shall hold fully and freely the care and administration of the church of Trent in temporal and spiritual matters, according to the tenor of our mandate [Col. 1019B]. In the meantime he shall take care to provide suitably for the aforesaid bishop of Trent from the revenues of the church, and shall have whatever remains applied to payment of its debts. We have caused the judgment privately pronounced concerning the bishop’s resignation to be retained sealed under our bull, to be published at an appropriate time.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood to admonish and induce the clerics and laymen, both of the church and of the diocese of Trent; and, if necessary, to compel them by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to render full and devout obedience to the aforesaid patriarch.

Given at the Lateran, 31 October, in the ninth year [Col. 1019C].

CLXXIX. . . . . . TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE LEPERS OF VAISLIAC. All the goods which they hold are confirmed. (Lateran, 23 September.)

“To the just petitions,” etc., down to “inclining.” We receive your persons, with all the goods which you at present lawfully possess and may hereafter, by lawful means and with God’s help, acquire, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and we strengthen them by the safeguard of this present writing. We further decree that no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on gardens or on the fodder of your animals. “Therefore let no one . . . violate this page of our protection” [Col. 1019D], etc. “But if anyone,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, 23 September, in the ninth year.

CLXXX. . . . . . TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE KNIGHTS TEMPLAR BEYOND THE SEA. The donation of Satalia made to them by the Venetians is confirmed. (Lateran, 31 October.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., as far as “bestow.” Since therefore our most dear son in Christ, [Col. 1020A] B., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, . . . the doge of Venice, the barons, and the knights of the army of the Latins, have granted to you and your house Satalia, with all its appurtenances, as alms, to be possessed in perpetuity; and our beloved son P. [Note: [Col. 1019D] This man has already been mentioned several times.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, has confirmed that gift by virtue of the office of legation which he exercised: we, holding the same gift valid, as having been made with pious consideration and prudence, confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the protection of this present writing. Therefore let no one, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of November, in the ninth year.

CLXXXI. [Note: [Col. 1019D] Raynaldus prints part of this letter, under the year 1206, § 38. What is found in his text is enclosed here in brackets.] . . . . . . TO THE PODESTÀ, CONSULS, AND CITIZENS OF FERRARA. That they should return to devotion to the Church and make satisfaction to the abbot of Pomposa for the assault. (Lateran, 9 November.)

[Col. 1020B]

[Note: [Col. 1020D] This is found in Raynaldus.] [How much effort was made before Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, while he was at Verona, to transfer your city from the lordship of the Roman Church to another power, your prudence, as we believe, does not fail to know. He, however, recognizing that this was in no way advantageous either to himself or to you, wholly refused what was requested with much insistence, wishing to retain you forever under the lordship of the Apostolic See, which can truly say of itself: “My yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matthew 11), since it does not oppress its faithful as slaves but cherishes them as children; from them it does not extort undue services, but bestows gratuitous benefits. Yet you, as we have heard, and grieve, in contempt of it have without cause submitted your necks to an alien lordship, so that it may say of you with the Prophet: “Alien sons have lied to me; alien sons have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Psalm 17). [Note: [Col. 1020D] Thus far Raynaldus.]] Nor was this enough for your presumption: you also violently invaded, and wrongfully retain, a great part of Saint Masselacus [Note: [Col. 1020D] Thus in the copy.], which the Apostolic See entrusted to the monastery of Pomposa at an annual rent. You compelled its inhabitants and [Col. 1020D] cultivators, after they had sworn an oath to you, to promise that thereafter they would answer to you alone concerning that land; and you received from them the fruits and revenues due to the monastery. Moreover, to crown this greater wickedness, you made an armed and club-bearing attack upon the abbot of Pomposa, and shamefully assailed both him and the monks who were with him with many injuries.

Although we have been grievously offended by you both in these matters and in others, nevertheless, because we cannot lay aside paternal affection even toward offending sons, we earnestly ask and admonish your community, commanding you by apostolic letters that, returning to your senses, you take care to make satisfaction to us and to the Roman Church, and likewise to the aforesaid abbot and his monastery, in such a way as to show yourselves children of obedience. Thus we need not, after pouring in oil, pour in wine, but may rather run to embrace returning sons. Know that the oaths which you are said to have sworn against fidelity to the Church, being unlawful, are not to be kept, according to the saying: “In evil promises, break faith; in a shameful vow, alter the resolution.” Otherwise, lest, according to Solomon’s sentence, we seem to hate our children if we spare the rod, we shall take care to exercise canonical severity against you. May he therefore inspire you, who wills that no one should perish, [Col. 1021B] so to accept paternal counsel that you do not thereby incur the divine scourge.

Given at the Lateran, on 9 November, in the ninth year.

CLXXXII. TO THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 1021D] Lambert, also called Lambin, a native of Bourges and son of Roland, formerly chancellor of Rheims, was elected bishop of Thérouanne, or of the Morini, in 1191. He bore the episcopal mitre until 1207, when he paid nature’s debt on 21 May. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. X, col. 1551.] AND CHAPTER OF THÉROUANNE. That they are to receive Master Ph. as canon and brother. (Lateran, 4 November.)

If, solicitous for the provision of those whom learning commends to us, we sometimes send apostolic requests and commands on their behalf to the prelates of churches, we perform an act properly belonging to our office; nor ought we to find anyone difficult in this matter, especially since we are known to do it because of the [Col. 1021C] merits of the persons and out of regard for piety. Since therefore we formerly sent you our letters on behalf of our beloved son Master Ph., bearer of the present letter, directing that you receive as your canon and brother this man who has long laboured in the schools and has made commendable progress in them, assigning him a prebendal benefice: as we have clearly learned from the letters of our beloved son . . . dean of Paris [Note: [Col. 1021D] See letter 36 of book five, note.], and of Master R. of Courson, canon of Noyon, whom we appointed monitors for the same master, you have turned deaf ears alike to our command and to their admonitions. He has therefore been compelled to renew his labour by coming to us.

Accordingly, that you may swiftly redeem your earlier disobedience through subsequent obedience, we again command and strictly enjoin your community [Col. 1021D] to receive the said master as your canon and brother and assign him a prebendal benefice as willingly as generously. Otherwise, since we do not wish to leave incomplete what we mercifully judged should be begun in his case, by our letters we command our beloved son J., master of the schools, and Masters J. of Candelles and Ph., canons of Noyon, that, unless some reasonable objection is brought and proved by you why the apostolic command ought not or cannot be fulfilled, they are to compel you to do this by ecclesiastical coercion, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed.

Given at the Lateran, on 4 November, in the ninth year.

CLXXXIII. . . . . . No address is extant. [Note: [Col. 1021D] That this was addressed to J., master of the schools, and to Masters J. of Candelles and Ph., canons of Noyon, is demonstrated by the immediately preceding letter.] On the same matter. (Lateran, 4 November.)

In the same manner, To the Executors, as far as “renew his [Col. 1022B] labour.” Therefore we again command the same bishop and chapter, strictly enjoining them to receive the said master as their canon and brother and assign him a prebendal benefice as generously as willingly. Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, unless some reasonable objection is brought and proved by the aforesaid bishop and chapter why the apostolic mandate ought not or cannot be fulfilled, you compel them to do this by ecclesiastical coercion, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed. And if not all . . . two, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 4 November, in the ninth year.

CLXXXIV. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-AUBERT [Note: [Col. 1022D] See letters 48, note, and 172 of book seven.], . . . . . THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 1022D] Adam, dean of Cambrai, is named in charters from 1192 until 1219. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. III, col. 70.], AND MASTER R. OF BEKEREL, CANON [Note: [Col. 1022D] See letter 172 of book seven.] OF CAMBRAI. That they shall cause a prebend to be assigned to R. of Wassigny by the bishop and chapter of Soissons, in accordance with the tenor of apostolic letters issued on this matter. (Lateran, 20 October.)

[Col. 1022C]

Formerly, while our venerable brother . . . bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. 1022D] See letter 11 of book three, note.] was in the regions of Constantinople, we thought fit to request and admonish his officials by our letters, nevertheless commanding them that they confer upon our beloved son R., deacon of Wassigny, who held no ecclesiastical benefice, a prebend in the Church of Soissons, if one should be vacant there, for [Col. 1022D] reverence of Saint Peter and ourselves, without any difficulty. Otherwise, we commanded that the first prebend to become vacant be reserved for our grant, to be conferred upon a suitable person. We also gave commands to our beloved sons . . . provost [Note: [Col. 1022D] See letter 41 of book three, note.], . . . dean [Note: [Col. 1022D] See ibid., note.], and the chapter of Soissons [Note: [Col. 1022D] See at the end of letter 123 of book seven.], that they should presume to receive no one as canon to a prebend which was then vacant [Col. 1023A] in their church, or whenever one should first become vacant, except a person to whom we should arrange for that same prebend to be conferred.

But when subsequently a certain prebend became vacant in the said church, the aforesaid bishop, who had meanwhile returned from his journey abroad, in contempt of the apostolic command granted it, as a matter of fact though he could not do so by right, according to his own pleasure, to . . . his nephew. Thereafter, although the chapter of Soissons wrote to us against the aforesaid cleric that he was in no way supported by merits of fitness for obtaining such a benefice, and although the bishop’s said nephew in the course of time earnestly asked us to deign to confirm that prebend to him by apostolic authority, we nevertheless, judging it unworthy that an apostolic command should thus be evaded, were wholly unwilling to grant his petition in this respect.

Yet the aforesaid cleric, remaining for a long time at the Apostolic See, diligently waited to see whether perhaps someone might appear willing to object and prove something against his person on account of which an ecclesiastical benefice should by right be denied him. But finally, as no adversary appeared against him in this matter, he humbly petitioned us to deign mercifully to provide for him. Therefore, considering that, even if he had committed some slight fault, he seems to have expiated it through the great bitterness of heart which, amid the hardships of the poorest estate, he has endured to this point through waiting so long at the Apostolic See, [Col. 1023C] we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, without any delay after receipt of the present letter, you assign the aforesaid . . . bishop and chapter a period of three months. Unless within that period some canonical objection against the cleric himself is presented and proved before you, on account of which the grace of apostolic provision ought not to be carried out for him, from that point onward, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed, you shall compel the bishop—or those who act in his stead, should he happen to be absent—and the said chapter, by ecclesiastical censure, to receive the same Robert as canon and brother and confer and assign to him the aforesaid prebend, or provide him with an equivalent [Col. 1023D] or greater one. Cause them sufficiently to provide him with the necessities of food and clothing until provision has been made for him in one of the foregoing alternatives. Any opponents or rebels who hinder fulfilment of the apostolic command you shall restrain by like coercion, appeal set aside; and you shall fulfil our command in such a manner that your devotion may be demonstrated by the effect of the deed and we may commend your obedience with worthy praises in the Lord. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See shall stand in the way, if any appear, where the tenor of these present letters has been suppressed. And if not all of you [Col. 1024A] can take part in carrying this out, let two of you nevertheless execute it.

Given at the Lateran, on 20 October, in the ninth year.

CLXXXV. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Raynaldus cites this letter under the year 1206, § 42.] TO R. [Note: [Col. 1024D] This man has already been mentioned several times.], MONK OF MONTFROID, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That he is to appoint preachers against heretics arising in the province of Narbonne. (Lateran, 17 November.)

The course of an age hastening unceasingly toward its end has entangled the misery of the human condition in so many snares of errors and stained it with so many infections of perversity that many, despising the borders of Zion and ascending the heights of Samaria, plaster their own walls with the pitch of the doctrines [Col. 1024B] of heretical depravity. Under a certain appearance of humility, masking the exaltation of their mind—by whose swellings they are inwardly carried beyond measure—they do not fear to despise the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and, enclosing their fatness within themselves, they do not dread incurring that curse: “Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria, saying, ‘We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse’” (2 Chronicles 10). To them the Lord might deservedly threaten: “I shall send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but rather of hearing the word of God” (Amos 11).

But because he himself wills no one to perish, indeed runs to embrace returning sons, he still entrusts the work of sowing the heavenly seed to his faithful stewards. Yet although the word of God has thundered throughout [Col. 1024C] the whole earth, while the heavens declared his glory, and though the rain of evangelical truth is still poured forth through the bishops of places, who have been called by the Apostolic See to share its solicitude, nevertheless, as the eminent Doctor professes concerning the Church’s growing beginning: “There must be heresies, so that those who were approved might at present become manifest” (1 Corinthians 11). Very many are weighed down by the burden of sins, and their foolish heart is darkened, so that they do not bring back to rectitude the winding paths which they follow, nor cry out with the Prophet: “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, God of my salvation” (Psalm 50). Rather, like a rebellious house, transgressing the law of Christ, they rush into the bitterness of senseless doctrine, despising the pastures of heavenly speech and ensnaring the souls of the simple with hidden [Col. 1024D] traps.

Indeed, among others, as has been reported to our ears, such a multitude of unbelievers has grown in the province of Narbonne that, material sword being lacking, the spiritual sword is held in contempt; and the corruption of wild vines creeps among Catholic shoots, while no one sets himself as a wall for the house of the Lord in defence of those who have not yet sunk like lead in the sea of pestilence, and for raising up, if possible, those lying in the hiding places of blindness; nor does anyone dare to go up against the enemy. Although the report of the madness of such foolish figs has reached the ears of certain religious persons [Col. 1025A] and has moved their minds to lead forth against them the streams of their learning, and with fervour of spirit to divide the waters in the streets, yet, because without one who sends them they have not dared on their own authority to undertake the office of preaching—lest they receive a portion with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive—there is no one to plead the Lord’s cause before the erring people.

But since zeal for his house consumes us—he who, though we are unworthy, granted us a place upon a lofty watchtower—and since we wish to be weak with the weak and to apply paternal counsels by which medicine may be offered to wounds and even a festering sore may receive care, insofar as lies in us, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to impose, for remission [Col. 1025B] of sins, upon approved men whom you judge fit for this work, that they hasten to those heretics. Imitating the poverty of the poor Christ, in despised dress and with burning spirit they must not fear to approach the despised, and by the example of their conduct and the teaching of their speech, God granting it, recall them from error. Thus, unless frequent sin has worn down their brow into shamelessness and it can deservedly be said of them, “You have acquired the brow of a harlot and were unwilling to blush” (Jeremiah 3), they may rejoice that they have attained hope through that saying of the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased my Father in you” (Luke 12); and those religious men, attaining Solomon’s saying, namely, “He who reproves a man’s ways shall receive more favour than he who speaks pleasing things” [Col. 1025C] (Proverbs 24), may return with rejoicing, able to bring back sheaves from the seed they have scattered.

Given at the Lateran, on 17 November, in the ninth year.

CLXXXVI. TO THE PRIOR AND CHAPTER OF GUBBIO. The election which they made of a bishop of Gubbio having been annulled, they are commanded to make another. [Note: [Col. 1025C]

This letter must absolutely be compared with what is found in Ughellus (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 686).

“XL. Albert, elected bishop of Gubbio in 1200, was removed from this life in 1205; in his place the chapter postulated a certain Raynald, a canon. But since Pope Innocent III had not approved the election, he raised Villanus to the see. Letters concerning this matter by the same pontiff to the prior and chapter of Gubbio survive in the Vatican register, dated at Rome, 26 November, year IX, letter 185, fol. 122.”

And this letter is precisely the one which we print here. Ughellus continues:

To Albert and his successors the same Pope Innocent III granted the following privilege:

“Whenever that is requested of us, etc.”

The text of the privilege follows. But you will seek it in vain in the Registers. Ughellus does not say whence he drew it. Certainly, he did not have it from the Registers; indeed, his chronological notes contain an error. It is said to have been given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, [Col. 1026C] chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 30 April, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1205, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III. But the ninth year of Innocent’s pontificate in no way coincides with 1205. [Col. 1026D] Perhaps, however, the eighth year should be read.

Ughellus again:

“XLI. Albert having been removed from this mortal life, Raynald, a canon of the cathedral church, was elected bishop, but for certain reasons was not confirmed by Innocent III, as appears from his letter of the ninth year.

“XLII. B. Villanus, on account of his reputation for holiness, was elevated to the see of Gubbio in 1206, etc.”

These are the statements in Ughellus, supported seemingly by Mittarellus (*Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, pp. 204), from Sartius, *On the Bishops of Gubbio*, p. 130.]

. (Rome, 26 November.)

Our beloved son R., our subdeacon and chaplain, legate of the Apostolic See and rector of Massa, informed us by his letters that, after your bishop Alexander of happy memory [Note: [Col. 1026D] Alexander. Should Albert rather be read, from the preceding note? Certainly Ughellus acknowledges no Alexander in his series of bishops of Gubbio. We recall indeed that Mittarellus mentioned somewhere a certain Alexander, surnamed Sperellus, likewise bishop of Gubbio; but he does not place him in the period with which we are concerned.] had entered upon the way of all flesh, you, in accordance with the custom of your church, began to deliberate upon appointing a pastor with our beloved sons . . . the abbot of Saint Peter and . . . . . the prior of Saint Secundus. But when you, son Prior, who had been appointed elector together with the aforesaid abbot and prior, were unwilling to take part in the election, you appointed your fellow canon Muricus, with the consent of the co-electors and the whole chapter, as elector. And afterwards, when, after deliberation, power to pronounce the election had been given to the said Muricus by his co-electors, he elected R., a deacon and your fellow canon, as pastor before clergy and people. [Col. 1026B]

You then presented the election through certain of your canons to the aforesaid legate and urgently petitioned him to confirm it by the authority he exercised. But wishing to proceed maturely in this affair, he came in person to your church; after receiving a bodily oath from the electors themselves, he carefully examined the proceedings, and took care to send us their depositions reduced to writing under his seal. Having carefully examined these attestations, we understood plainly—although the abbot differs somewhat from the others—that, when the aforesaid abbot and priors wished to deliberate on the election, they first gave one another the kiss of peace, so that none should disclose without common consent what they discussed together [Col. 1026C] until all things had been made public. Afterwards the abbot of Saint Peter asked the prior of Saint Secundus who seemed to him the better person to elect as bishop. The said prior replied that, as it seemed to him, and as he believed he understood to please the greater part of the clergy, the prior of Saint Marian seemed to him the better person. To this the abbot replied nothing, but by his silence seemed to consent, although one of them says that he answered that this pleased him well. The prior of Saint Marian rejoiced on hearing this, but nevertheless made no reply.

Furthermore, the abbot said to the same prior: “There is some disagreement between you and Muricus; but if you were willing to commit the pronouncement to him, the election could be carried out plainly and without disturbance.” The prior replied that he was very willing to do this and asked the same man to undertake the pronouncement of the election in his place, but did not state whom he would elect. Thereafter the aforesaid Muricus entered the chapter with his co-electors and received from the prior and chapter authority to hold the prior’s place in pronouncing the election. Before they entered the chapter, the aforesaid Muricus asked the same co-electors what they would think if someone were to pronounce Raynald bishop [Col. 1027B] by electing him. The prior of Saint Secundus replied that it would please him if he possessed one thing lacking in him, namely knowledge of letters, which he did not have. The abbot replied that he would have given four hundred solidi in order that the same man might possess what he did not have.

Then, on coming to the pulpit, the said Muricus, after addressing the clergy and people, asked his co-electors whether they were pleased that he should pronounce. The prior of Saint Secundus replied and said that he was pleased with the person whom he had named, and the abbot replied that he was pleased. Muricus then elected the aforesaid Raynald and pronounced him pastor before the clergy and people. Once the pronouncement had been made, the prior of Saint Secundus said that he had not named the person whom Muricus elected. Then the prior of Saint Marian, by virtue of obedience, forbade the aforesaid Raynald to accept that election, and he did not then accept it. Afterwards certain persons threatened the aforesaid prior because he had forbidden Raynald to accept the election and had appealed to the Apostolic See. Frightened by them, the prior renounced the appeal on that same day, placed Raynald in the seat, and endeavoured, with all the brethren, to show him reverence.

Having therefore learned these things, after counsel with our brethren we judged the aforesaid election to be annulled. By apostolic letters we command your whole body that, within fifteen days after receipt of the present letter, utterly excluding on this occasion the aforesaid Muricus, who committed such fraud, [Col. 1027D] you provide yourselves by canonical election with a suitable person as pastor. Otherwise, from that point onward, send certain of your number, endowed with the authority of all, into our presence, prepared to receive as bishop the person whom we judge should be provided.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on 26 November, in the ninth year.

CLXXXVII. [Note: [Col. 1027D]

The copy of this letter which, together with the others, we had caused to be transcribed from the Conti copy, has slipped from our hands by some chance unknown to us; and therefore we can give here only its summary. See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 26.

“Having received the joyful news of the birth of a son, the pope, writing from Rome on 29 November [Col. 1028D] to the bishop of Bamberg, the queen’s brother, directed him to visit the king and congratulate him in the pope’s name.”]

. TO THE BISHOP OF BAMBERG. That he return to the king of Hungary and convey the joy felt by the pope at the birth of a son. (Rome, 29 November.)

[Col. 1028A]

CLXXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 1028D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 42. See also Mittarellus, *Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, pp. 199 and 203.] TO THE SCHOLARS RESIDING AT VICENZA. He commends them for the devotion they show in constructing a certain church. (At Saint Peter’s.)

You show that you have made no small progress in the learning for which you sought the service of the schools, because, placing your hope in the Lord’s promise that all things will be added to you if you first seek the kingdom of God, you have begun to build at your own expense the church of Saint Vitus, [Col. 1028B] in which not only you but also others may call upon the name of the Lord. Since therefore, as we have learned, you have subjected this church to the Camaldolese monastery, we commend your devotion in the Lord, and regard and hold this work of piety as acceptable. Nevertheless, we admonish and exhort your whole body that you endeavour so to advance in the devotion which you have conceived toward the said monastery that the Almighty, moved by these and the other good works which you perform, may open your hearts and enlighten your understandings, so that, possessing perfection in learning, you may attain full knowledge of that Wisdom which, though one, can do all things, and, abiding in itself, renews all things, and [Col. 1028C] passes through nations into holy souls. May that same Wisdom, reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly, teach you temperance and prudence, justice and courage—virtues than which nothing is more useful to human beings in life.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CLXXXIX. [Note: [Col. 1028D] Raynaldus published part of this letter, under the year 1206, § 7. What is found in his text is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE NOBLE MAN B., MARQUIS OF MONTFERRAT. The pope’s goodwill is offered to him. (At Saint Peter’s, 27 November.)

We kindly received at the Apostolic See your beloved son . . . . . chancellor and messenger, a man indeed prudent and faithful, and diligently heard what he set before us on your behalf. So far as we could with God and consistently with our honour, [Col. 1028D] we took care to promote these matters, as the result itself shows and as he can report to you orally. For, since by sure indications we have experienced the devotion which you bear toward us and the most holy Roman Church, a devotion which you contracted from your ancestors as though by hereditary right, we firmly resolve to give effective and careful attention to matters that may conduce to your advantage [Col. 1029A] and honour. You may therefore have recourse to us with confidence in matters in which you think it expedient, because, insofar as honour permits, we shall, God granting, take care to bring your requests to effect. [[Note: [Col. 1029D] This is found in Raynaldus.] Concerning those matters about which you have endeavoured to consult us by your letters, we have already taken care fully to reply to you by our own letters. But because perhaps those letters have not yet reached you, we have judged that a transcript of them, taken from our Registers, should be sent to your nobility by the aforesaid messenger, so that from them you may perceive what reply we have taken care to give you concerning these matters. Concerning the affair of your stepson and the Church of Thessalonica, you will be able to see, from the transcript of those letters which we have granted to your messenger, what we judged should be written to our beloved son B., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna [Note: [Col. 1029D] See letter 54 of book three, note.], legate of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1029B] [Note: [Col. 1029D] Thus far Raynaldus.]] Furthermore, we admonish and earnestly exhort your nobility to persevere firmly in devotion to the Apostolic See and to us, as you have commendably begun. Know that you will find us ready and prepared to promote your honour and advantage, insofar as we can with God and consistently with our honour.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on 27 November, in the ninth year.

CXC. [Note: [Col. 1029D] Raynaldus gives part of this letter, under the year 1206, § 7. What is found in his text is enclosed here [Col. 1030D] in brackets.] TO B., PRIEST-CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF SAINT SUSANNA [Note: [Col. 1030D] See letter 54 of book three, note.], LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. On the same matter. (At Saint Peter’s, 27 November.)

[Col. 1029C]

You yourself learned by sure indications at your reception how devoted and faithful our beloved son, the noble man B., marquis of Montferrat, is to us and the Apostolic See, and how he attends to the honour and exaltation of the most holy Roman Church. We therefore willingly attend to, and devote effective labour to, matters which ought to redound to his advantage and honour. Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command and enjoin your discretion diligently to hear and give favourable heed to, insofar as you can with God [Col. 1029D] and consistently with the honour of the Apostolic See, the things which the said nobleman may propose to you concerning the condition of the Church of Thessalonica and the son of the former Emperor Isaac, his stepson, so that he may find the devotion which he has hitherto borne to the most holy Roman Church fruitful to himself, and may burn more ardently in it, becoming more devoted from being devoted.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on 27 November, in the ninth year.

CXCI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: [Col. 1030D] See letter 9 of book three, note.]. That he should labour to negotiate peace among certain discordant citizens. (At Saint Peter’s, 27 November.)

[Col. 1030A]

When God, about to pass from this world to the Father, bequeathed to his own the inheritance of peace by testament, saying: “Peace I leave to you; my peace I give to you” (John 14), uttering these words as it were last, so that the word of peace might be planted more deeply in our hearts, we ought to devote effective labour in order that the bond of peace may be restored among those at discord. Since therefore no small discord has arisen between Vernacius and Leolus and certain opponents of theirs, we earnestly ask and admonish your brotherhood, [Col. 1030B] commanding you by apostolic letters that, insofar as you can with God and honour, you apply diligent solicitude to restoring peace among them, so that thereby you may please the author of peace and the evil born of discord may be removed from their midst.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on 27 November, in the ninth year.

CXCII. TO THE BISHOP OF SAMARIA. A grant concerning Mount-Saint is confirmed to him. (At Saint Peter’s, 27 November.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., as far as “assent.” We command that the grant concerning Mount-Saint, prudently made to you by our beloved son B., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna [Note: [Col. 1030D] See letter 54 of book three, note.], [Col. 1030C] legate of the Apostolic See, in view of the pressing necessity of the time and with the consent of our beloved son, the noble man B., marquis of Montferrat, lord of the land, be firmly observed, always saving the mandate of the Apostolic See. Therefore let no one [infringe] this page of our command, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on 27 November, in the ninth year.

CXCIII. TO THE CLERGY OF THE ISLAND OF NEGROPONT. They are received under protection. (At Saint Peter’s, 27 November.)

When a request is made of us, etc., as far as “inclined,” we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves your persons and the churches in which you are devoted to divine [Col. 1030D] service, together with all that you now rightfully possess or may in future, God being propitious, acquire by just means; and [under the safeguard] of the present writing, etc., strictly forbidding anyone to presume wrongfully to molest you or your churches. Therefore let no one . . . [infringe] our protection, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on 27 November, in the ninth year.

CXCIV. . . . TO THE ELECT OF ATHENS. [Note: [Col. 1031D] “After Athens had been captured by Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, Michael Choniates, the Greek prelate, withdrew, as Nicetas, his brother of the same surname, testifies in his last book. Accordingly Berard succeeded him. Concerning him and two other recently elected Latin bishops, Innocent III says in Epistle 34, Book X, dated 30 March 1207: ‘Although he had been confirmed by our venerable brother . . . the patriarch of Constantinople, he could nevertheless not be consecrated by him, because he had no fellow bishops. Hence it was necessary to send him (the bishop-elect of Veroia) . . . the elect of Athens, etc. . . and Thebes to Syria in order to receive the grace of consecration.’ Vol. II, Baluze edition of the Letters of Innocent III, p. 17, col. 1. Several letters of the same pope to the archbishop of Athens, from the years 1208, 1209, 1210, and 1212, occur in the same Baluze. In none of these, except [Col. 1032D] Epistle 256, Book XI, dated 13 February 1208, which is addressed to Berard, archbishop of Athens, is his name found. Yet we infer that this is the same Berard because they never indicate that the archbishop to whom they are addressed was later than Berard or newly appointed. Odoricus Raynaldus, in the *Annals*, under the year 1223, no. XIII, writes that Honorius III, Roman pontiff, entrusted to the archbishop of Athens (who is not named here) the task of absolving pirates returning to the Church, who were commonly called Capelleti. Nothing prevents us from supposing that this archbishop was still Berard, though we do not know either how many years he occupied the see or in what year he died.” LE QUIEN, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 839.] His establishment is confirmed. (At St Peter’s, 27 November.)

[Col. 1031A]

At the just petition of those who ask, etc., down to “consent,” we confirm by apostolic authority all the jurisdiction which the Greek archbishop reasonably possessed over the churches and clergy of the province of Athens, in matters not contrary to apostolic enactments; and by the present writing, etc. Therefore let no one, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the ninth year.

CXCV. [Note: [Col. 1032D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 42.] TO THE NOBLE MAN P., COUNT OF CELANO, MASTER JUSTICIAR OF APULIA AND THE LAND OF LABOUR: THE SPIRIT OF SOUND COUNSEL. He is reproved for his obstinacy against the Church and warned to return to her. (At St Peter’s, 6 December.)

[Col. 1031B]

We have received your letter, which you sent through our beloved son J., abbot of Avezan. We had believed that you had returned to your right mind, so that, at least after considering the special favour which we showed you on the occasion of your reconciliation—repeatedly making it known to you not only through our notary but also through letters afterwards sent to you with paternal gentleness—you would give honour to the Lord your God and would not think it shameful to humble yourself beneath His mighty hand. Yet, failing wholly to acknowledge the favour shown you, you have still not accepted the counsels of those seeking your salvation and honour. Indeed, in contempt of them, you have added a heavier guilt to guilt, since you show yourself so weak in faith that you hesitate to entrust yourself to apostolic faith, which always stands in truth; and it is wicked to believe that it would begin to deal falsely with you.

Alas! What has so miserably bewitched you, noble count? Whose cruel counsels, I ask, have so credulously led you astray that, as though the first degenerate from your illustrious lineage, you abandon the footsteps of your Catholic forefathers, some of whom are reported to have borne, for the honour of the Church, not merely losses of property but exile from their persons? Yet you—unless, as we certainly do not believe, this is a sign of avarice—set yourself against the Church’s honour for temporal and perishable things, which we do not indeed intend to seize from you, but rather to establish your right in them. You do not avoid permanently undermining your name’s reputation; and, failing to consider that it is hard for you to kick against the goad, you have entered upon this struggle with us—indeed, with God. Although you know that you must be overcome, you nevertheless refuse to dismiss one who wishes to release you. And, as if you deemed glorious the example of certain persons who, after persisting long under excommunication, were at last reconciled, you delight, expelled from the Church, to wander outside her.

But since you are certain of their reconciliation, already accomplished, how are you secure concerning your own future conversion? If you are unwilling to turn while you can, perhaps you will be unable to turn when you wish; for although [Col. 1032B] God mercifully recalled them, albeit late, He has not promised you tomorrow’s day, while you defer returning to Him. You ought to fear lest His day come like a thief in the night, and that you then begin too late to repent, when you were unwilling to turn to Him while you could.

Accordingly, your prudence would seem altogether foolish if, while we still hope so much from your discernment that—although a living dog is better than a dead lion—you will, raised from the abyss of death in which you are held, prove better than some who appear to live, you should wish to take a pernicious example from those who, separated from the Church for their offences, were not ashamed to remain long under excommunication. But let those answer you whom, according to Scripture, “the turning away of the little ones will slay, and the prosperity of fools will destroy” [Prov. 1:32]: those who, because the Lord does not immediately punish sinners for their crimes, have become corrupt and abominable in their desires and, according to the Prophet, have grown accustomed to say, “There is no God” [Ps. 13]. These, I say, would perhaps be found first worthy of divine vengeance, if human sins were punished as soon as they occur in order to instruct them in their faithlessness.

On what hope can you securely rely, that the Lord will wait for your conversion so long as you choose to abuse the forbearance of His grace? For if this were so, it would beyond doubt seem that a truce with death was obtained for iniquities—to say nothing of the more serious consideration. For if under the pretext of this damnable hope you defer your repentance, you must fear lest your sin become unforgivable, since you would appear to sin neither from incapacity [Col. 1033A] nor from ignorance, but from malice, according to the sentence of Truth, which says: “Whoever sins against the Son, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit, it shall be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come” [Matt. 12].

But, that the mouths of those who speak iniquity may be stopped and that you yourself may more openly recognize how faithfully and devoutly those who introduce the example of others for your destruction are counselling you, we wish you to consider the end to which that former tyrant, notorious for faithlessness, Markward came. When he had raised himself in pride against God by despising the keys of the Church, then, by God’s just judgment, his entrails were poured out and he wasted away in the destruction of a horrible death, even though his power had seemed rather to be exalted, so that it might have been said of him: “I saw the wicked exalted and lifted up like a cedar of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not” [Ps. 36].

Finally, consider our venerable brother G., chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily. We recount this not to his reproach but in proclaiming the Lord’s power: see how, in the conflict which he undertook against God, he found himself cast down. Yet, because he is said to have returned to his heart and to walk with us in purity, we intend what concerns him to his honour and advantage. Moreover, consider Duibuld himself, whose reconciliation perhaps scandalizes you above the rest: how at last, as is said, entangled in the cords of his sins—because perhaps he dealt deceitfully with us, and this was the punishment of his sin—that he, having been reconciled, did not persevere in goodness, because for a long time, though he could have been reconciled, he despised reconciliation.

Would that these words penetrate your heart and pierce your liver with the health-giving blade of fear, so that you may remember yourself, like them, to be a frail, unstable, corruptible, and mortal human being; one who can and ought to tremble at the instability of fortune and dread the uncertain moment of death. Strive to turn not only the dangers of those aforesaid but also of many others like them into examples for your conversion. Even if you escaped temporal punishment for such faithlessness, you would nevertheless not be able—God forbid!—to escape eternal punishment.

Since, therefore, neither from your letters nor from the report of the aforesaid notary or messenger have we been able to understand that, after the letters which we sent you in paternal kindness, you offered any further promise to do what shortly before you had intimated through your notary—except that you consented to the abbot of Monte Cassino, to whom you had previously not consented—although we could have proceeded more severely against you in many respects, had not paternal affection rendered us gracious toward you (an affection which often does not allow an offended father to take vengeance on an offending son), we have nevertheless not wished to proceed further, but still to wait mercifully for you as a son, whose salvation would be our joy and whose disgrace our sorrow.

Therefore, lest, if you continue longer to disregard our warnings and counsels, our prayers and commands, we be compelled to denounce your obstinacy with the Prophet, saying: “To whom shall I speak and whom shall I call to witness, that he may hear? Behold, his ears are uncircumcised and they cannot hear; behold, the word of the Lord has become a reproach to him, and he has not received it” [Jer. 6:10], we ask and earnestly admonish your nobility. From a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, we counsel you most earnestly to reject in this matter every counsel of others and to acquiesce in ours alone; according to the matters which our aforesaid notary suggested to you, do not delay to return at the Church’s command.

Otherwise, however much, as we understand from your letter, you say that you are burdened contrary to justice—something which we ourselves indeed acknowledge concerning you, namely, that we proceeded contrary to justice in these matters because, perhaps yielding to you more than was fitting, we acted short of justice and did not follow the rigour of strict justice—we shall be compelled to lay our hand upon you heavily, not only in accordance with what was suggested to you by the said notary but also in other and many ways. That hand is certainly not shortened; rather, by God’s grace it is extended, and unless you turn and do penance, it will bring upon you an immense weight of oppression, both spiritual and temporal.

Choose therefore, dear son—provided that you make yourself worthy to be called the son of us and of the Church, indeed of God—to accept such salutary warnings and counsels, placing full trust in our word: just as we seek your reconciliation solely for your honour and salvation, so, with the Lord’s help, we shall undoubtedly cause that reconciliation itself to result in your salvation and advantage. Nor should you suppose, or be led by empty hope, that you can ever incline us to anything else; for for no one born of woman, not even for our own brother if he were in the position in which you are, do we intend to abandon the rule of the Church. Behold, if you are prudent, provident, and discerning, here you can demonstrate your prudence, foresight, and every discernment, by accepting or rejecting the counsel of one who does not wish to deceive you and who wishes to preserve for you, in the words set before you, the whole truth.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the ninth year.

CXCVI. TO RADULPH, [Note: [Col. 1033D] See Letter 45 of Book VIII, note.] BISHOP OF ARRAS. He forbids anyone to pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him without consulting the Roman pontiff. (Rome, 19 December.)

[Col. 1034D]

Since you have been ordained priest by our hands and consecrated bishop, and since we ought to show deference no less to our honour than to yours—indeed, more truly to yours than to ours—we forbid by the authority of the present letters that anyone should dare to pronounce against you a sentence of suspension or excommunication without consulting the Roman pontiff. If anyone, which God forbid, after notice of this prohibition, should pronounce such a sentence without consulting him, we decree that it is not to be observed. Therefore take diligent care not to turn the favour shown you into injury to another, or the privilege into abuse; for one who abuses a power granted to him deserves to lose his privilege. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this page of our prohibition and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth year.

CXCVII. [Note: [Col. 1035D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 8.] TO THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS. [Note: [Col. 1035D] See Letter 11 of Book III, note.] That he should remit ecclesiastical censures upon those who had engaged in tournaments, lest the holy expedition be delayed. (Rome, 10 December.)

Through your letters you informed us that, since you believed that the tournaments held in your regions greatly impeded your purpose of pilgrimage, you had pronounced, by our authority, a sentence of excommunication upon the tournament participants. Consequently many knights are so disturbed that they neither take the cross nor are willing to contribute anything to the aid of the Holy Land. You therefore asked us to permit you temporarily to mitigate that sentence. Although it is not our intention to permit tournaments, which are known to be forbidden by sacred enactments, nevertheless, because what was provided for advantage appears to tend toward harm, we grant you by the authority of these presents that you may arrange for the sentence itself to be relaxed with regard to all or some, as you judge expedient.

As for the matter in which your fraternity asked us to have the noble man . . . count of Namur and the bailiffs of Flanders compelled by ecclesiastical censure to assign, from the revenues of the county, pay for knights and serjeants to be sent in aid of the empire, in accordance with a command formerly given by the emperor of Constantinople of illustrious memory: we reply thus to your fraternity, that the aforesaid nobles and bailiffs cannot in law be compelled to do what you ask by reason of the said command, because with the death of the commander that which he commanded has also expired, although his brother has been magnificently raised to his place.

Furthermore, as we have learned from the letters of the noble men Ph., marquis of Namur; . . . count of Looz; J. of Bruges; William of Saint-Omer; S., castellan of Ghent; G., castellan of Lille; A. of Oudenaarde; W. of Sothengien; E . . . P . . .; of Prat; S. of Aria; and certain others: the knightly tournament participants, prompted by fear of excommunication, have resolved by common counsel that every tournament knight possessing land worth one hundred pounds shall pay one mark, and every one possessing land of lesser value half a mark, yearly for three years, in aid of the Holy Land. For this reason the said nobles have entreated us to deign to attach our authority to their proposal. Therefore, by the authority of the present letters, we command you—without prejudice to the statute of the Lateran Council—to arrange or provide in this matter as you shall see fit according to God.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the ninth year.

CXCVIII. [Note: [Col. 1035D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 8.] TO THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS, [Note: [Col. 1035D] See Letter 11 of Book III, note.] G., PROVOST OF DOUAI, BROTHER OF EMPEROR HENRY OF CONSTANTINOPLE, AND THE CHANTER OF PARIS. If they travel by land, he promises them safe conduct as far as Brindisi. (Rome, 10 December.)

[Col. 1036B]

Appearing before us, your beloved sons Ubertus and W., your messengers, took care to inform us that, having come to Genoa at your command and laboured to find a ship for you and other pilgrims, they had observed many advantages for which it would be expedient for you to cross by way of Genoa. Since they have therefore sought our will in this matter, and you too have inquired by your letters into our good pleasure, we reply to you by the tenor of these presents: hire a ship at the city of Genoa and, in the Lord’s name, proceed from there, since you could scarcely find a more convenient or safer crossing.

But if you cannot proceed by Genoa and wish to come to the City, so that, after receiving from us the blessing due to your devotion, you may hasten to the port of Brindisi and there hire a ship as best you can, we shall, God granting, give you safe conduct as far as Brindisi. Nevertheless, we wish and command that you should strive to warn and induce all who have taken the cross to come with you to the same port and proceed together in your company, lest perhaps the Lord’s army and the sheep of His pasture be divided for any reason. For in this matter we are sending our warnings and commands to all those who have taken the cross.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the ninth year.

CXCIX. [Note: [Col. 1036D] Raynaldus gives part of this letter under the year 1206, § 8. The passages found in his edition are here enclosed in brackets.] TO COUNTS, BARONS, KNIGHTS, AND ALL WHO HAVE TAKEN THE CROSS. He urges them to bring aid to Emperor Henry. (Rome, 11 December.)

[Col. 1036D]

Appearing before us, the beloved sons Ubertus and W., messengers of yourselves and of our venerable brother . . . the bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. 1036D] See Letter 11 of Book III, note.], and of the beloved sons G., provost of Douai, brother of our dearest son in Christ . . . the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, [Col. 1037A] and . . . the chanter of Paris, took care to inform us, etc., as in Letter 198, down to “you have requested.” We gave command to the said . . . bishop, G., brother of the aforesaid emperor, and . . . chanter, that at the city of Genoa, etc., down to “we shall grant.”

[Accordingly, by the authority of these presents we strictly command your nobility that you strive to come with the said bishop to the same port, intending to cross together with him, lest—God forbid!—the Lord’s army be broken up for any reason, and that you heed the counsels of this bishop, who is labouring faithfully and devoutly in this matter. Furthermore, let it be made known to you by these present letters that, after the emperor of Constantinople of illustrious memory had ended his last day under hostile guard, our dearest son in Christ Henry, his brother, the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, was unanimously and harmoniously raised by the whole army of the Latins to the height of empire. Since then he has repeatedly triumphed both over . . . the Vlach and over other enemies of the empire; indeed, even before his elevation he had proved victorious against them. You ought therefore firmly to hope that, once the saving breeze has driven you to those regions, even those who inhabit the borders of the empire will tremble at your arrival, and you will easily subject foreign nations to the service of the Crucified One.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Ides of December, in the ninth year.]

CC. [Note: [Col. 1037D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 8.] TO THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS. [Note: [Col. 1037D] See Letter 11 of Book III, note.] He grants that he may accept the Church of Thessalonica while retaining the Church of Soissons. (Rome, 10 December.)

[Col. 1037C]

Our beloved son B., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna [Note: [Col. 1037D] See Letter 54 of Book III, note.], legate of the Apostolic See, informed us, and the letters of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious Henry, emperor of Constantinople, contained the same report: the canons of the Church of Thessalonica, at the urging of our beloved son, the noble man . . . marquis of Montferrat, who holds princely authority in that land, unanimously and harmoniously requested you as archbishop of Thessalonica, most urgently beseeching us [Col. 1037D] to deign to grant you leave to transfer to the governance of the Church of Thessalonica.

Therefore, considering the urgent necessity and the evident benefit which may accrue to the regions of Romania through your presence, we have judged their petition should be granted. By the authority of these present letters we command you that you make such provision and arrangement concerning yourself that, when you have arrived at the port for the purpose of crossing, if it happens that you are to receive passage through us, you may be fit and ready to obey our commands and counsels in this matter. But if you must turn toward such a port that the distance of places prevents you from presenting yourself before us, we strictly command you by these present letters that, when you have arrived in those regions, you reverently receive and observe in this matter the command of the aforesaid legate, knowing that by authority of the present rescript leave is given you to transfer to the aforesaid church.

Because we embrace your person in the arms of sincere affection, we have thought fit to grant you this as a special favour: although, in accepting the care of the Church of Thessalonica, we wish you to be its true and proper pastor, nevertheless [Col. 1038B] you may freely dispose concerning the Church of Soissons and remain its proper bishop as before, until the condition of the empire of Constantinople is secured.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the ninth year.

CCI. [Note: [Col. 1037D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, § 38.] TO THE PEOPLE OF SUTRI. That they are not to appoint a foreigner to govern their city without consulting the pope. (Rome.)

Having received in person through our messengers the oaths sworn by you, and a surety of two hundred pounds of Provençal money having been furnished—for which our beloved son, the nobleman San Ranieri di Stefano, has lawfully bound himself to us—we command you, under obligation of the oath rendered, never henceforth, without the leave and assent of the Roman pontiff or his vicar, to appoint a foreigner to the government of your city, without prejudice to any other commands which we may judge fit to give concerning this matter. By the authority of these presents, however, we relax the interdict to which, for this reason, we had subjected your city.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s.

CCII. TO THE PRIOR AND CANONS OF SAINT PATERNIANUS, IN THE DIOCESE OF FOLIGNO. The subjection of the church of Saint Christina is adjudged to them. (Rome, 5 December.)

A question having formerly arisen between your church and [Col. 1038D] the church of Saint Christina, because the church of Saint Christina was harmed in its parishioners and parochial rights when the noblemen P. of Saint Christina and M., B., and R. had exchanged certain houses and possessions with one another, the clerics of that church lodged a complaint against you before A., bishop of Foligno, of good memory, the ordinary judge in this matter. [Note: [Col. 1037D] Anselm, a nobleman of the Actia family of Foligno, was appointed bishop in 1155 after having been archdeacon of the cathedral in his native city . . . On account of his merits of life and the weight of his prudent judgment, Pope Alexander III placed him over the Church of Nocera in 1170, so that he might bring equal strength to both dioceses at once . . . At Foligno he splendidly founded and erected the church dedicated to St Thomas, and assigned to the Actia family the rights of patronage, as they are called. That family exercised those rights as long as it flourished at Foligno—that is, until 1592, when it became wholly extinct, though it left its distinguished name to another family’s descendants . . . Anselm of Actia was carried off by untimely death on 20 August 1201; and, as though no successor had dared to be appointed to so incomparable a man, memory has failed as to who occupied the government of the Church of Foligno from 1202 until 1210. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 748.]

[Col. 1039A]

Provoked by this circumstance, however, you brought a counter-complaint before the same bishop against the said clerics concerning the claimed subjection of the churches of Saint Christina, Saint Donatus, Saint Silvester, and Saint Lawrence, and their possessions. The bishop, having taken cognizance of both disputes, received witnesses in each case. Meanwhile, however, Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, directed the same bishop by his letters not to allow the church of Saint Christina to be in any way harassed in its right on the pretext of the aforesaid exchange. On the basis of those letters, the aforesaid bishop examined the dispute concerning parishioners and concluded it by a definitive judgment. But he did not proceed in the controversy concerning subjection; rather, he deposited with the clerics of your church, sealed with his own seal, the depositions of witnesses which he had received in that case.

As time passed, your party obtained from us the delegation of the case concerning the aforesaid church of Saint Christina and the chapels and possessions belonging to it to our beloved son Master R. of Spoleto. But afterwards, at the petition of the other party, we thought fit to associate with him our venerable brother . . . bishop of Nocera. [Note: [Col. 1039D] Hugh succeeded Anselm (on whom see the preceding note) in the see of Nocera, having been appointed to that burden about the year 1196. He died in 1218. The same author, ibid., col. 1119.] Later, with the assent of the messengers of both parties, we likewise associated with them our beloved son . . . plebanus [parish priest] of *Telonica* [reading perhaps erroneous], for the decision of that case. [Note: [Col. 1040D] Thus it is read in the transcript, but perhaps incorrectly.] When the said judges, proceeding more carefully in the case, had formally received the witnesses of both parties and were hastening toward the conclusion of the matter, [Col. 1039C] an appeal was made to our hearing on your behalf.

When, therefore, the procurators of both parties had come before us on this account, it was stated on your behalf before our beloved son T., subdeacon and chaplain, whom we appointed their auditor, that the church of Saint Christina, together with the three chapels named above and their possessions, belongs to your church by full right. For when Count Offredus of good memory founded your church, among the other things which he assigned to it he granted, of his own free will, the church of Saint Christina with the said chapels. To prove this, your procurator produced a public and authentic instrument.

To this the party of Saint Christina replied [Col. 1039D] that, since a layman has no power to dispose of ecclesiastical property, the aforesaid count, being a layman, could not confer those churches. It added that, since your church had not used that instrument before the delegated judges, it could not and ought not thereafter produce it for its advantage. On your behalf it was replied in opposition [Col. 1040A] that, since the consent of the diocesan bishop had been added to the said count’s gift, your church had acquired even more the patronage of the aforesaid churches; and that, since in that judgment neither party had closed its case by proofs or allegations, the instrument itself could properly be presented even under our examination.

It was further alleged on the same side that the nobleman Munaldus of Ranuzo, together with his sons B. and T., had for some time held by violent occupation the church of Saint Christina with the other chapels belonging to your church. Afterwards, when he had undertaken the purpose of pilgrimage, he freely resigned those churches and their appurtenances into the hand of B., bishop of Foligno, of good memory, [Note: [Col. 1040D] This probably concerns Benedict, who, having been a monk of Holy Cross of Avellana, of the Congregation of the Dove, of the Order of St Benedict, was appointed to the bishopric of Foligno before 1138 and died in 1155, after governing commendably for seventeen years. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 744.] on behalf of [Col. 1040B] your church, as is contained in a public instrument. This shows that your church can claim a right in those churches by reason of his resignation.

The other party replied that, since by the statutes of the canons a layman has no power to give away or alienate churches or their goods, the said nobleman could not, by resigning the church of Saint Christina with the other chapels into the hands of the aforesaid bishop, create any prejudice to those churches; especially since that same nobleman had formerly arranged, with the knowledge and consent of the diocesan bishop, that the church of Saint Christina should become a conventual church. Your party replied that those laymen could not so dispose of that church to the injury of your church, and that the diocesan bishop could not give consent to such a disposition, to the not inconsiderable detriment of your church.
