Furthermore, your party maintained that it is manifestly inferred that the church of Saint Christina belongs to your church by full right, because, as the depositions of witnesses establish, the prior of your church was accustomed to send his own priests and clerics to the church of Saint Christina. After divine services had been celebrated there, they brought to your church the offerings which they had received there. To this the party of Saint Christina replied that even if your church had possessed some right in the said churches, it was clear that every right had been removed by prescription of forty years, during which the same churches had enjoyed full liberty, since every right and every action is extinguished by forty-year prescription.

Your party replied that, if from the prescription are deducted the eighteen years during which the schism lasted, and the three earlier schismatics governed your church, it is evident [Col. 1041A] that the remaining years do not attain the required period of prescription. But to this the party of Saint Christina subsequently objected that, even if the periods of schism are deducted from the prescription, forty-year prescription is nonetheless established, since the witnesses clearly testify that for sixty years the church of Saint Christina had rendered no service to your church but had remained in full liberty.

On your behalf it was answered that this prescription cannot be harmful because it was interrupted by civil action. For, as the steward of Saint Christina publicly confessed in court, sixty years have now passed since litigation arose between it and your church over the subjection of the church of Saint Christina. It was further added [Col. 1041B] that the witnesses whom the church of Saint Christina produced on its behalf prove nothing whatever: in saying that the church of Saint Christina was not accustomed to render any service to your church, they assert a negative; and in the ordinary course of litigation no proof is required of the party denying a fact. This is especially so because the witnesses seek not to establish a fact but to argue a point of law, asserting that the church of Saint Christina was obliged to render service to no one except the bishop.

It was further argued on behalf of the church of Saint Christina that no credence should be given to those witnesses through whom your party seeks to prove that the church of Saint Christina belongs to it by full right, since your church is accustomed to obtain full provision in it. [Col. 1041C] For the depositions of witnesses written down by the bishop of Foligno and assigned to the clerics of your church must be entirely rejected, because they remained openly in their possession for a long time and could have been corrupted or altered by them. Nor, as that party said, should the attestations subsequently received by judges delegated by us be admitted to prove anything; because, after your party had learned the testimony of the witnesses previously produced, a second production by it ought, according to the dictates of lawful enactments, to be ineffective and useless.

Your party replied that, since the statements of those witnesses are furnished with the judge’s seal and no part of them has been impeached or corrupted, full credence should without doubt be given them, especially as the witnesses subsequently produced affirm that, when the aforesaid bishop of Foligno did not wish to proceed in the case concerning subjection, he committed the witnesses’ statements, secured under his seal, to the said clerics. Your party also maintained that the attestations received a second time should be approved, since the other party had freely consented to the production of witnesses. Furthermore, even if those attestations were not admissible to prove the earlier articles, they would nevertheless be valid to establish new heads of claim.

Having fully understood these and the other matters submitted before the aforesaid chaplain, we, with the counsel of our brethren, adjudge the subjection [Col. 1042A] of the church of Saint Christina to your church, decreeing that it shall be perpetually subject to it as its own chapel.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of December, in the ninth year.

CCIII. [Note: [Col. 1041D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §36.] … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO. That he is to impose a salutary penance upon the priest G., who, through simplicity, had sung a psalm in place of the canon of the Mass. (Rome, 17 Kalends of January [16 December].)

The beloved son G., a priest, appearing before us, showed us in a tearful confession that, since he considered himself unworthy to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, he had on one occasion clothed himself in priestly vestments and, without chalice or offering, sung the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” in place of the canon of the Mass, as though performing the office of the Mass. This is called in those regions a “dry Mass” (*Missa sicca*). Since, therefore, as he asserts, he did not do this with the intention of altering the form of the sacrament or of introducing heresy, but rather through simplicity than malice, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters to impose upon him a suitable penance for this; and, once it has been performed, provided that no other canonical impediment stands in the way, grant him, by the mercy which triumphs over judgment, permission to celebrate, so long as no scandal against him has arisen among the people on this account.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January [16 December], in the ninth year.

CCIV. [Note: [Col. 1042D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] TO THE PODESTÀ, CONSULS, AND COUNCIL OF FAENZA. That they are to expel the Poor of Lyons and other heretics from their territory. (Rome, 2 Ides of December [12 December].)

The multitude of pressing sorrows with which Holy Church is continually surrounded, like a woman in labour, compels her to cry aloud with the prophet and say: “My belly aches, my belly aches.” For, since until now every creature groans and labours in birth, according to the Apostle, the sacred womb of mother Church is disturbed by the pain of her own bowels. Though made fruitful with spiritual offspring, she is cruelly torn apart while the wickedness of those of whom it is prophetically proclaimed—“They have cut open the pregnant women of Gilead, to enlarge their border”—destroys their offspring. [Col. 1042D]

For the savage impiety of heretics, who change truth into falsehood and do not fear damnably to move the boundaries set by their fathers, wounds pregnant souls to death, in order that the fetus of faith which they had conceived through divine love may not attain the birth of a completed work. Thus mother Church, who can say with the prophet, “The children have come to birth, but she who gives birth has no strength,” and we ourselves, who are bound to care for her fruitfulness, are, as it were, cut through by the blade of divisive perfidy, while we are wounded in her very entrails by the sword of heretics who tear open her womb. [Col. 1043A]

Since, therefore, as we have learned, the beloved sons, the citizens of Florence, have issued, in prudent piety, a certain statute for the destruction of such faithless persons, intending thereby to eliminate from their city the filth of heretical depravity—which, creeping on little by little like a cancer, had corrupted many souls by its contagion in order to enlarge its borders—we, believing that through their example we emulate the better gifts, have judged it right to show you a safer way by which you may resist the heretical pestilence reported to have infected some persons in your city.

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole community, commanding by apostolic letters that, unanimously adopting the statute itself, devised for the benefit of Catholic truth and for the confounding destruction of heretics, you strive, in accordance with it and otherwise as may be inspired in you from above, to expel from your city the Humiliati, the Poor of Lyons, and any followers whatever of heretical depravity, in such a way as to prove that you possess zeal for the Christian religion. [Col. 1043B]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of December [12 December], in the ninth year.

CCV. [Note: [Col. 1043D]

Raynaldus mentions this letter under the year 1206, §33.

Matthew Paris, *Historia Anglorum*, vol. I, p. 214, reproduces another letter almost wholly similar, differing only by appropriately altered wording, addressed to the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury. See him.

See also letters 34, 35, 36, and 37 of this ninth book.]  

… TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF CANTERBURY. They are absolved from the claim of their suffragans concerning the right to elect an archbishop. (Rome, 13 Kalends of January [20 December].)

[Col. 1043C] Both canonical authority and approved custom provide that major causes of the Church are to be referred to the Apostolic See, so that, since it is the mother and teacher of all the faithful, what has been decided by its judgment may be inviolably observed by all.

Since, therefore, a controversy had arisen between you and our venerable brethren, the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury, concerning the right of electing the Archbishop of Canterbury, they asserting that both by common law and by ancient custom they ought to conduct the election of that archbishop together with you; while you, on the contrary, replied that, by common law, special privilege, and ancient custom alike, you ought to elect the Archbishop of Canterbury without them: after the suit had been lawfully contested before us on this matter through suitable procurators, we carefully heard what the parties took care to set forth in our presence.

Their party indeed endeavoured to invoke both decrees and precedents, producing certain witnesses and presenting testimonial letters, by which it sought to show that the suffragans had elected three metropolitans. Yet it was proved by depositions and letters that they had held elections of this kind, without you, both in another place and at another time. [Col. 1044A] The witnesses produced on your side, however, lawfully proved that, from times long past until the present, the prior and convent of the Church of Canterbury had held elections of archbishops in their chapter without the suffragans, and had obtained confirmation of those elections from the Apostolic See. Moreover, decrees and precedents were repeatedly cited in support of your right.

Although customs differing from the common rule are sometimes found, nevertheless, if recourse is had not only to the custom of neighbouring churches but also to that of neighbouring kingdoms, this general custom is undoubtedly found among them: elections of metropolitans are conducted by the clergy of the metropolitan see alone. Furthermore, by a privilege granted by us and our predecessors, it has been established that, upon the death of your archbishop, no one is to be placed over you by any stratagem of surreptitious procurement or by force, except one whom you by common counsel, or the greater and sounder part of you according to God and the enactments of the sacred canons, shall determine ought to be elected; you having now and in future times the free election of your bishop, strengthened by the favour and protection of apostolic protection. [Col. 1044B]

Therefore, having carefully heard and clearly understood these matters and others alleged before us, since it has been clearly established that the suffragans, by their own assertion also, ought not to elect without you, and hence that their election, with you excluded, was invalid; while your election, conducted likewise without them, deserved confirmation by the Apostolic See, since one or the other necessarily had to be confirmed: by the common counsel of our brethren, we wholly absolve you and your successors, by definitive sentence, from the claim and molestation of the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury concerning the right of electing an archbishop. We impose perpetual silence upon them concerning this matter, decreeing by apostolic authority that you and your successors shall henceforth freely elect an archbishop without them. Let no one, therefore, infringe this page of our definition and constitution, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc. [Col. 1044C]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December], in the ninth year.

CCVI. … TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. Concerning the same matter. (Rome.)

[Col. 1044D] Having examined the cause which was pending between the beloved sons, the prior and convent of the Church of Canterbury, and our venerable brethren, the suffragans of that same Church, concerning the right of electing the Archbishop of Canterbury; and the cause pending between the beloved son, the subprior and his supporters, and the aforesaid prior and his associates, as well as the same suffragans, concerning the election of the subprior himself: by the common counsel of our brethren, justice requiring it, we absolved the said prior and convent by definitive sentence from the claim of the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury concerning the right of electing the Archbishop of Canterbury.

We also decreed null and void the election of the said subprior. It had been established that, after many appeals reasonably lodged with the Apostolic See, and after certain conditions had been added which were later found not to exist, this election had been not so much conducted as presumptuously undertaken. [Col. 1045A]

Wishing, moreover, to provide for the bereaved Church, we directed those monks who had received from the whole chapter authority to elect a pastor at the Apostolic See, should the election of the aforesaid subprior be annulled, to set over themselves, by canonical election, a suitable person as pastor, having God alone before their eyes.

Although at first they disagreed—some naming our venerable brother, the Bishop of Norwich [Note: [Col. 1045D] See letter 129 of book five, note.], while others named the aforesaid subprior—they nevertheless finally, after much deliberation, unanimously agreed upon our beloved son Master Stephen Langton, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, a man eminent in life, reputation, learning, and teaching. [Note: [Col. 1045D] A passage most worthy of notice, since it provides us an occasion to correct the error of Ciaconius and of Oldoinus himself. Ciaconius and Oldoinus alike (vol. II, col. 31) assert that Stephen was elevated to the rank of cardinal only in the year 1212. But this letter of Innocent proves, beyond all certainty, that Stephen had already borne the title of Saint Chrysogonus at least from the year 1206. See also *Gesta Innocentii*, §CXXXI.] All the rest concurred in him; they chose him to be postulated from the Apostolic See, and earnestly pressed your envoys—the beloved sons, the abbot of Beaulieu, the nobleman T., viscount of Stafford, and A., knight—to grant on your behalf the royal assent in this matter. They refused to express it. [Col. 1045B–C]

We, however, judging his postulation canonical and prudent both in form and in person, decreed it to be approved. We likewise approved his reply when he was asked to give his assent to the postulation: among other things, he answered that, since he was not his own master, but was in every respect subject to our authority, he was obliged to fulfil what pleased our disposition.

Although in elections of prelates conducted at the Apostolic See the consent of a secular prince is not customarily awaited—since it must not be presumed that anything is done there to anyone’s prejudice, for in all that it deliberates with prudent maturity it is accustomed to guard the justice of every person, lest wrongs arise from the place from which rights arise—yet, desiring out of abundant favour to defer to your Serenity, we informed you by our letters that, since we had written to the aforesaid prior and convent, firmly enjoining them to grant to certain of their monks, who were to come into our presence, full authority to elect an archbishop if the said election of the subprior were annulled, your royal prudence also should send suitable procurators into our presence, lest anything through any defect be ordered to the prejudice of your right or dignity. [Col. 1045D–1046A]

Therefore, since you sent the aforesaid envoys—men certainly prudent and faithful—to the Apostolic See for this cause, as we believe, and assuredly for no other than that they might discharge the royal office in this cause; and since royal assent was requested from them, with all humility and devotion, concerning the aforesaid postulation, it plainly did not seem that it needed to be sought from you again, unless, at the repeated entreaty of those envoys, we should deign to show you favour upon favour, such as we do not recall ever having shown anyone in a similar case.

Since, therefore, in all your actions, and especially—indeed above all—concerning the aforesaid Church, because of reverence for that glorious martyr who wrote its special privilege, as it were, with his own blood, you ought to seek not what is yours but what is Jesus Christ’s, we earnestly beg and more earnestly exhort your Serenity to consider carefully that so great a Church—known to be a principal member of the Apostolic See and a singular jewel of your crown—has now for a long time remained, through the malice of certain persons, bereft of a pastor’s consolation. Graciously grant your consent to the aforesaid postulation, or rather declare that you have already granted it, lest you seem to oppose the disposition of heaven. After the mother’s prolonged tears, that disposition has prevented the schisms of divided sons by the harmonious election of a father, made certainly in the case of such a person that, powerful before God and men in deed and word, he shines with such a lamp of merits and surpasses others by such integrity of character that, unless the necessity of relieving the threatening ruin of the aforesaid Church compelled us to transfer so firm a pillar of the Apostolic See, the Apostolic See would surely have much cause to envy him. [Col. 1046B–C]

We therefore ask that royal gentleness assume a spirit of mildness and show itself in this matter so ready and benevolent that, in duly supporting with favour what has been provided from heaven in so salutary a matter, you may seem not merely to consent to something done by another, but rather, by adding your favour, to show that you yourself have done it.

For in approving this person we have not so attended solely to the advantage of the Church of Canterbury that your honour has not also been fully considered: he derives his origin from your land and from a stock faithful to you, and is believed, with God's help, to follow your will in every respect. Therefore, dearest son, see to it that you preserve here both your favour before God and your reputation among men. You appear to have enhanced both in many matters: the Lord has begun magnificently to exalt you in one, while in the other your name is proclaimed very great and celebrated among the peoples. Do not allow either to be offended in this act, upon which your glory is known in large measure to depend. [Col. 1046D–1047A]

Open your eyes, most serene prince, and see that perhaps it was not without the decree of the heavenly will that your God caused you, beyond the expectation of many, to prosper in temporal matters especially at the time when the aforesaid Church lamented the losses of her widowhood. By such benefits you should recognize that the heavenly King wished by such benefits to admonish you that you should refrain from occupying that Church, when He chose to find you occupied with secular triumphs.

Hence royal prudence ought diligently to provide that it repays God in the peace of the Church for what it does not doubt has been bestowed on it by Him in worldly prosperity; so that it may prosper more happily in its course already begun, in proportion as it more reverently gives Him, as it were a price for this, ecclesiastical liberty. Otherwise, if—God forbid—you do not, in fitting devotion and gratitude, repay grace for grace granted to you, not only may God, by human law, demand back that which He is believed to have given for a purpose when the purpose has not been attained, but He will also most strictly require an account for the ingratitude committed. [Col. 1047B]

Therefore, most beloved son, turn the eye of your mind toward these things; pierce yourself with the penetrating blade of the fear of God. Set before yourself the aforesaid martyr—indeed, set yourself in the seat of your heart before him—and see him entreating you and commending his Church to you. Tremble, be afraid, and judge yourself unworthy to refuse his prayers, offered as the recompense of his blood. You ought not to doubt that you reign especially through his patronage; by his martyrdom he made your kingdom, already sufficiently renowned, still more renowned.

Do you suppose that he will with impunity allow his house to be harassed by the assaults of wicked men, he who shed his blood for it? Do you suppose that he will withhold his aid from those who deserve well in it, he who endured the torment of death for love of it? Is it not believed that his blood cries out against its persecutors because, by the hidden judgment of God, some wicked person is for a time permitted to persecute it? Or can anyone, without danger to himself, reduce to servitude the liberty of that Church whose privilege the martyr himself wrote in his blood? Indeed, what profit will there be in his blood if what was purchased at its price is finally reduced to the disgrace of slavery? [Col. 1047C–D]

For God’s sake, therefore, gracious prince; for the martyr himself; and finally for love of us: attend to our prayers in serenity of mind. Hear us as we ask and earnestly beseech you—indeed, as we request a precious gift—that, by supporting the aforesaid postulation with royal favour, we together with you, and you together with us, may usefully assist the aforesaid Church, which has grievously declined in spiritual and temporal affairs through its widowhood. Take care to write back to us within three months after receiving these letters, so that the same elect, about to govern the said Church with the fullness of the episcopal office, may be able to present himself before the royal presence.

Otherwise, however much we embrace the royal magnificence with arms of sincere charity in the Lord, and however specially we may wish to defer to it in this matter so that it may defer to us, we shall proceed in the matter itself, God granting it, as canonical authority requires. Take careful care lest, led astray by anyone’s evil counsel, you bring yourself into a difficulty from which you may not easily be freed, or impede the course of your prosperity, which, by the Lord’s ordering, is directed toward greater things. If you consider prudently, you have been accorded more than your right requires; nor do we wish any prejudice ever to be generated against you from what has been done or is to be done. [Col. 1048A]

We also render abundant thanks to your Serenity because, as we and our brethren clearly discovered in examining the aforesaid affair, you inflicted no injury or violence upon the monks concerning the election. Rather, as a most gracious prince and most Christian king, you dealt with them in every kindness and gentleness. Therefore, in public consistory, with your envoys present, we condemned with sharp rebuke whatever had been suggested to us by a contrary report; and it is punishment enough that the effort of the opponents in the affair of that election has been altogether frustrated.

Accordingly, we earnestly ask and admonish royal kindness that, since your desire has been satisfied in this matter, you show them no indignation on that account, so that the fullness of your gentleness may appear at its beginning, middle, and end. [Col. 1048B]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, etc.

CCVII. … TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF CANTERBURY. On the same subject. (Rome, 12 Kalends of January [21 December].)

[Col. 1048C] Having examined the cause, etc., in almost the same manner, as far as “to fulfil what pleased our disposition.” Therefore, wishing in fatherly concern to secure peace for you and your Church, we earnestly ask and more earnestly exhort the aforesaid king by apostolic letters that, since in all his actions, and especially—indeed above all—concerning the aforesaid Church, because of reverence for that glorious martyr who wrote its special privilege, as it were, with his own blood, he ought to seek not what is his own but what is Jesus Christ’s; and since it has been provided that so great a Church, known to be a principal member of the Apostolic See, etc., almost as in the other letter down to “be generated.”

Therefore, hoping that, if you recognize the time of your visitation, turn to God with your whole heart, and have recourse to the familiar patronage of the aforesaid martyr, he, stirred by your pious cries, will hear you and show that his blood does not plead for you in vain, we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole community, commanding by apostolic letters that you at least learn discipline from this, lest at any time the Lord become angry: through your disputes, not only has the peace of your Church been grievously disturbed in many ways, but the almost universal Church has also been offended. Indeed, we had to withdraw ourselves from the general care of that Church in precisely the measure in which it became fitting to devote ourselves specifically to resolving your difficulties. [Col. 1048D–1049A]

Although, through the occasion of the lawsuit which arose between you and the aforesaid suffragans concerning the right of election, great liberty has been gained for you, lay aside every zeal of bitterness and rancour toward one another. Return to the concord of unity; think unanimously the same thing, not what is yours but what is Jesus Christ’s. And in this matter—which through Jesus Christ has been done by all of you concerning the aforesaid postulation, since it has been prudently conducted by those who possessed authority from all—confirming your wills in every respect, lift up your hearts to the Lord in humility. Let your petitions in every prayer and supplication be made known before Him through your advocate, the aforesaid glorious martyr. [Col. 1049B]

Placing your hope in the Most High alone—if He is with you, you will not fear what man may do to you—pray to Him without ceasing that, by His great mercy, He may enable us so to bring this matter to completion that honour may result to His holy name, common salvation to you, and perpetual peace to your Church. We confidently trust that we shall undoubtedly obtain this from Him if we are aided by the support of your prayers while you remain in charity and unity.

Therefore see that no one’s cunning deceives you and no diabolical or human temptation corrupts you. But, remaining steadfast in your purpose of unity, have full confidence that, Christ’s perfection supplying what is lacking in us, we shall bring through Him to a happy conclusion what we have begun with Him. [Col. 1049C]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December], in the ninth year.

CCVIII. [Note: [Col. 1049D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §42.] … TO THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-MÉEN [Note: [Col. 1049D] Of the abbots of Saint-Meven, nothing is found in the writers of *Gallia Christiana* in its older form, vol. IV, p. 639.] … TO THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-MÉEN AND MONTFORT [Note: [Col. 1049D] After Tuallus, who died in 1205, the above-cited writers mention as abbot of Montfort William I, born in the parish of Saint-Maugond, ibid., p. 661. They add that he was buried in 1215.], AND TO R., ARCHDEACON OF SAINT-MALO. That they are to proceed against schisms and erroneous opinions. (Rome, 12 Kalends of January [21 December].)

In order that, when the external war of tyrants has been calmed and the theologians and lovers of God are silent, the most bitter bitterness of the universal Church may appear in peace, there have arisen against her “theophants” and “theophones”—that is, heretics and false brethren. They persecute her all the more grievously because they are thought to be more intimate; they have the appearance of godliness but wholly deny its power, and are sometimes counted among her children. The persecution of those who fight against their mother and tear her garment is most bitter to her. [Col. 1049D]

When peace had been restored to her from external enemies, men without peace therefore came in time of peace: lovers of pleasures rather than of God, who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, led by various desires, always learning yet never attaining knowledge of the truth. For they are persons corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith; departing from it, they give heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons. Speaking falsehood in hypocrisy and having a seared conscience, they do not fear to condemn the sacraments of the Church, and they strive to destroy her beauty—she whom the sun’s heat once made beautiful by darkening her somewhat. [Col. 1050A]

These are indeed the black horse shown to John in the Apocalypse. The devil sits upon it and seeks to harm those possessing a two-pound measure of wheat and three two-pound measures of barley: namely, love of God and neighbour, faith in the eternal and undivided Trinity, and also the wine and oil which the Samaritan applied to the wounded man’s injuries—that is, austerity and gentleness—those whom Jesus Christ redeemed by one denarius with His own blood; he seeks to make them suffer shipwreck concerning the faith.

Now the beloved son R., priest of the church of Roton, has shown us in a tearful report that certain of his parishioners and others of the dioceses of Nantes and Saint-Malo, infected by the poison of this depravity, are attempting secretly to infect others. They put forward many things to the simple that oppose the Christian faith, so as to draw them with themselves into error and have the deceived as companions in Gehenna. [Col. 1050B]

Moreover, when their neighbours fall ill, they come to them under the appearance of visitation, get ahead of the priests, and urge them, while the priests are absent, to put their household affairs in order; and not to confess to those priests, because, they say, confession made to wicked priests does not profit for salvation. They say that priests burdened by the weight of sins cannot confer upon others a remedy for sins; and thus “the moon burns them by night.” They also condemn marriage and advance many other propositions wholly alien to the purity of Catholic faith, through which the hearts of many simple persons are perverted. Among them they bellow, like an assembly of bulls among cows, not considering that the relation between priest and sacrament is the same as that between physician and medicine. Therefore, just as the illness of a skilled physician does not impede the efficacy of medicine, so the guilt of a Catholic priest does not impede the power of the sacrament—although life ought to accord with doctrine, lest one rebuked in word be corrupted by example. [Col. 1050C]

Since, therefore, by the office imposed upon us we are bound to gather scandals out of the kingdom of God and, so far as we can, to fight such beasts, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, aflame with zeal for the Catholic faith like Phinehas, after prior warning, you compel through ecclesiastical censure, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, those whom it is established are guilty of this spiritual adultery to repent, having renounced such impiety. But if they cannot be recalled from their perversity even in this way, take care to proceed against them according to the constitution which we issued for the confounding of heretical depravity. If not all of you can be present for carrying these measures out, nevertheless let two of you carry them out. [Col. 1050D–1051A]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December], in the ninth year.

CCIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX [Note: [Col. 1051D] Was he William II of Gébenne? Certainly, the writers of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 820, from the chronicle of Saint Stephen of Limoges, state that Elias of Malmort—of whom we have already spoken so often—died in 1206. Yet the same writers state, ibid., that William did not begin his archiepiscopate until 1207.], AND TO THE ABBOT OF THE GREATER FOREST [*Silva Major*] [Note: [Col. 1051D] On the abbots of Silva Major, see the remarks appended to letter 96 of book five, note. The abbot to whom this 209th letter of book nine is addressed was undoubtedly Amalvinus, whom documents recognize as having become abbot from cellarer already by 22 May 1206. He died in 1221, on the fifth day before the Ides of March [11 March]: *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 871.], IN THE DIOCESE OF BORDEAUX. That they are to determine what is canonical against Hugh Brun, who had presumed to remove from the monastery of Obazine a virgin betrothed to God and to take her as his wife. (Rome, 13 Kalends of January [20 December].)

The beloved son, brother II. Lamara, knight, took care to explain to us that the nobleman Hugh Brun, of the diocese of Poitiers, had not feared violently to remove from the monastery of Obazine a virgin who, after receiving the veil and making a vow to the Lord to preserve perpetual chastity, had been betrothed to Him. He did this to no small injury of such a bridegroom, who does not subject His bride to corruption, while she dwelt there among virgins consecrated to God. He presumed to take her as wife through the hands of the bishop of Cahors, of good memory. [Note: [Col. 1052D] See letter 97 of book six, note.] [Col. 1051B]

Since it is damnable not only to marry but even to wish to marry for those who have vowed virginity, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, after diligently investigating the truth of the foregoing matters, and setting aside every favour and fear, you determine, appeal set aside, what is canonical; causing what has been determined to be firmly observed, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See that prejudice truth and justice. If both of you cannot be present, you, brother Archbishop, etc. [Col. 1051C]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December], in the ninth year.

CCX. … TO THE ABBOT OF EVESHAM [Note: [Col. 1052D] See letter 204 of book eight, note.], AND TO THE … PRIORS OF WICHILICUMB AND EVESHAM, IN THE DIOCESE OF WORCESTER. That, in the case concerning the patronage of the church of Filebi, they are not to proceed on the pretext of letters falsely obtained. [Note: [Col. 1052D] On the subject of this letter, see letter 34 of book seven.] (Rome, 3 Nones of January [3 January].)

It was reported to us by our beloved son E. Bil that, when he had presented R., a clerk, to the church of Filebi, in which he holds the right of patronage, to the diocesan bishop, J., a clerk of the diocese of Norwich, had presumed, without reasonable grounds, to impede his institution. We therefore entrusted the controversy to our beloved sons, the abbots of Sibeton and Langele, and the dean of Broc, of the diocese of Norwich, to be brought to a canonical conclusion. Two of them, since the third could not be present and had excused his absence, gave a definitive sentence for the aforesaid E., imposing silence upon the said J.

As we have seen contained in the letters of our venerable brother, the bishop of Ely [Note: [Col. 1052D] These persons have already been mentioned frequently.], and of our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Edmund [Note: [Col. 1052D] These persons have already been mentioned frequently.], after some time had elapsed, J. began before the archbishop of Canterbury of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 1052D] See letter 94 of Book V.] to accuse those letters of falsity, urgently demanding that what had been done on their authority should be annulled. For this reason, the said judges—although they themselves had cancelled the letters, after the sentence had been given, by drawing lines of ink across them—sent the letters by a trustworthy messenger to that archbishop, who had received a special commission to investigate such alleged falsity.

When the aforesaid J., in his presence, alleged that they were false, and the opposing party had procured W. de Brom, a clerk, to appear in its defence, who asserted that he had obtained the aforesaid letters from us, the archbishop, having received sufficient security from both parties concerning their allegations, caused the letters, carefully enclosed under his own seal and the seals of the parties, to be presented to us by Robert de Marigni, elected for this purpose by the unanimous will of the parties. Finding them wholly genuine in script, thread, parchment, and seal, we instructed the aforesaid archbishop and the said bishop and abbot to declare the letters genuine and not to allow the aforesaid E. to be improperly troubled by anyone concerning the sentence justly pronounced on the authority of those letters [Col. 1052C]; but rather to cause that sentence, since it is just, to be firmly observed, the obstacle of appeal being removed, restraining opponents, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Accordingly, when the parties appeared before them and the judges wished, in accordance with the form committed to them, to confirm the sentence, the aforesaid J. alleged before them that the sentence was invalid because it was contrary to the testimony of witnesses and had been promulgated after an appeal to us had been lodged, striving to invalidate it by many arguments. Since the aforesaid E. contradicted every objection, the judges, observing the due formalities, received the witnesses produced by both parties. After their depositions had subsequently been published [Col. 1052D], and after attestations of both parties had also been received under the seals of the aforesaid judges, and the arguments of both parties seen and understood, they fixed a day for the parties to appear before them to receive judgment.

When the appointed day came, the aforesaid bishop of Ely and abbot, having taken the counsel of prudent men—since the archbishop had meanwhile entered upon the way of all flesh—supported by our authority, confirmed the judgment of the former judges. Because the aforesaid J. had wholly failed in proving his allegations, they imposed silence upon him and condemned him to pay the opposing party ten marks as costs. But J., making no mention of any of the foregoing, procured from us letters directed to you concerning examination of the aforesaid judgment, suppressing the truth.

Now the aforesaid E., appearing in our presence, alleged against him that he was not bound in any way to answer under the authority of those letters, since they made no mention of the confirmation of the judgment [Col. 1053B], and since J. lay under sentence of excommunication. Yet, because you refused to admit his exceptions, he appealed to the Apostolic See. Therefore, since the aforesaid sentence was confirmed by our authority through the aforesaid bishop of Ely and abbot, as is contained in their authentic instrument, and since a deceitful petitioner ought to be deprived of what he has obtained, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you in no way proceed in this affair under authority of those letters which were obtained by suppressing the truth. Without appeal, revoke whatever you decreed, on occasion of them and after the appeal lawfully lodged with us, to the prejudice of the oft-mentioned E.

But if not all of you … let two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF FOSSANOVA. The sentence given for them concerning a certain possession against A. Saracenus is confirmed. (Rome, 9 January.)

“It is customary to assent,” etc., as far as “assent.” We confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, the sentence which our beloved son R. …, judge of Sezze, pronounced in the cause which was pending before him between you on the one side and Adinulfus Saracenus and certain others on the other concerning a certain possession, since it is just, was not suspended by a lawful appeal, and is contained in the public instrument drawn up concerning it [Col. 1053D]. We have caused the text of that instrument to be copied word for word into these present letters.

In the name of the Lord. Amen.

Since, as the reasoning of the law declares, the merits of cases are disclosed by the assertions of the parties—that is, by statement and response—and since it often and frequently happens, through either the nature of the case or human malice, that the plaintiff’s claim is not established by the defendant’s confession, or, if established, the defendant seeks to defeat it by force of an exception, which in turn is not established by the plaintiff’s confession; and thus, in order to establish judicial proof and disclose the merits of the case, witnesses are introduced on both sides and documents produced in court, so that the judge, examining and weighing everything, may condemn or acquit according as, in conformity with the merits of justice, which gives to each person his own right, he judges best and most expedient:

Therefore I, Robert of Sezze, ordinary judge of the Holy Roman Church, examiner of the cause pending between Adinulfus Saracenus—acting in his own name and, under power of attorney, also by mandate of Theobald Saracenus and Transmundus, his brothers, Cynthius, lord Bertraimus, Winfrid, Cocca, and Jordan, Countess Maria, Posseduta Saracena, Maria Donna, and Agnes, on the one side—and Landinus, steward of the venerable monastery of Fossanova, on the other, have taken care diligently to record the course and procedure of the matter, so that, once it is known how this cause may through justice, without respect of persons, be brought to its proper conclusion, this may be seen more clearly and, as it were, with eyewitness certainty.

The aforesaid Adinulfus, in his own name and in the names of the above-mentioned Theobald and Transmundus, his brothers, Cynthius, Winfrid, Cocca, Jordan, Countess Maria, Posseduta, Saracena, Maria Donna, and Agnes, demands from Landinus, steward of the venerable monastery of Fossanova, the whole tract of land enclosed by hollowed boundaries, in the place called Laurentii, as was shown to me, Robert the judge [Col. 1054C], together with the buildings situated there and fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees. He seeks restitution of possession to himself in accordance with law and the sacred constitutions.

To this demand Landinus gave the following response, both personally and through his advocate. He says that the monastery has no possession within the stated boundaries which belongs by right to them or to any other person, but only to the monastery [Note: [Col. 1053D] Thus in the Apograph; but something appears to be missing.]. He asserts that these possessions lie within the boundaries of those possessions which were donated long ago, in ancient times, by John Demetrius, vestararius of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 1053D] *Vestararius*: the same as *vestarius*, one who has charge of garments or of the treasury. At Ravenna a *vestararius*, to whom the keys of that city were entrusted, is mentioned in a fragment of a letter of Pope John VIII, in Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. I, p. 402, col. 2. Ecclesiastical *vestararii*, or those having charge of church wardrobes, occur in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VII, p. 610, and elsewhere. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. VI, col. 1510.], to Saint Mary of Fossanova; that they have been possessed as such by the monastery from that time onward in complete peace and quiet; and that this may be proved from the grants of the Roman pontiffs, from the time of Pope Innocent II of blessed memory, who gave and granted to the Cistercian Order the venerable monastery of Fossanova, called Saint Stephen’s, together with the church of Saint Mary of Fossanova and all their appurtenances [Col. 1054D], as well as from their privileges and grants and, he asserts, from living witnesses.

To prove and establish his claim and contention, the aforesaid Adinulfus introduced certain witnesses, whose statements I carefully reduced to writing in my own hand [Col. 1055A]. Conversely, Landinus, steward of the venerable monastery of Fossanova, in order to contradict what had been alleged and introduced by the aforesaid Adinulfus acting for himself and the persons named above, to weaken and defeat his claim, and to prove and strengthen his own exception, produces a public instrument in which John Demetri is recorded as having donated extensive and broad possessions, which are contained, as it were, at the very centre.

He also produces privileges and grants of the Roman pontiffs from the time of Pope Innocent II of holy memory down to the times of Pope Innocent III. All of these, among other things which they appear to have granted to the venerable monastery of Fossanova, make special mention of Saint Mary of Fossanova with all her appurtenances, defining certain boundaries therein, within which the aforesaid possessions in dispute plainly appear to be included [Col. 1055B].

He also presents a public instrument stating that Theobald of Stephen—by whose grant the aforesaid Adinulfus appears to demand and sue in his own name and in the names of those previously named—renounced to Lord Peter, the reverend abbot of the venerable monastery of Fossanova, every right of patronage which he might have had in the church of Saint Mary of Fossanova. He promised that neither he, nor his heirs, nor any person acting at their instigation would act against the decree of Pope Innocent, who subjected and placed under authority the church of Saint Mary of Fossanova [Col. 1055C], under a promised penalty of ten pounds of Pavia denarii should they do otherwise. In return, he received a specified measure of land for himself and his third son-in-law, situated in the place called “the wall of John Subtilis.”

He further produces another instrument stating that Transmundus, in Theobald’s name, renounced whatever right he possessed in one clearing at Laurentii to Lord Crescentius, abbot of the venerable monastery of Fossanova, situated within the precinct of Saint Mary of Fossanova. In addition, to establish fuller proof and elucidate the merits of the case, he introduces witnesses through whom it appears proved not merely by a presumption of thirty or forty years, but even by one of greater antiquity [Col. 1055D].

Therefore I, Robert of Sezze, ordinary judge of the Holy Roman Church, examiner of the present dispute, having seen, heard, diligently considered, and understood what was alleged and introduced on both sides, since it is not established by the testimony of the witnesses introduced by the plaintiff that possession of the lands demanded by them belongs to them, and since the instruments produced by Landinus and the witnesses brought forward by him clearly show that the lands belong by right to the monastery, absolve the aforesaid Landinus, steward of the venerable monastery of Fossanova, from the claim of the aforesaid Adinulfus Saracenus, made in his own name and in the names of Theobald and Transmundus, his brothers, Cynthius, Winfrid, Cocca, Jordan, Countess Maria, Posseduta Saracena, Maria Donna, and Agnes.

Given at Piperno, in the year of the Lord 1206, the tenth indiction, the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III, on the third day of November.

Therefore let no person at all … violate this page of our constitution [Col. 1056B], etc. But if anyone does so, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXII. TO THE BISHOP OF SPOLETO [Note: [Col. 1055D] See letter 5 of Book V, note.]. That he is not to harass the rectors of the parish church of Saint Fortunatus. (Rome, 11 January.)

[This complaint was sent to us by G. and A., rectors of the clergy of the parish church of Saint Fortunatus: though they had been condemned by an arbitration to pay you forty pounds, and a penalty of thirty pounds had been imposed upon them unless they paid you the aforesaid forty pounds within the appointed term, they had at last paid thirty-three pounds within that term. On the pretext of the seven pounds remaining, you obtained from us certain letters by suppressing the truth, through which [Note: [Col. 1055D] The *Decretals* read: “through certain of our letters obtained by suppressing the truth.” Pithou notes in the margin that the word *our* is absent from most ancient codices.] you secured their condemnation to pay you the aforesaid thirty pounds by our beloved son Paul, our subdeacon and delegated judge.

Since it does not become you so greatly to forget episcopal moderation that, panting after dishonourable gain, you should desire to enrich yourself at another’s loss, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, content with payment of the aforesaid seven pounds, you do not henceforth presume to harass the said rectors concerning the penalty of thirty pounds [Note: [Col. 1055D] The *Decretals* read: “do not henceforth harass.”], as was definitively determined through our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison [Note: [Col. 1055D] Gerardus Gallus, a Cistercian monk and ninth abbot of Pontigny, was enrolled by Innocent III among the cardinal deacons in his first creation of cardinals and was named cardinal deacon of the church of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. Claude Robert, in the *Gallia Christiana*, and Pierre Frizon, in *Gallia Purpurata*, with whom Aubery agrees, assert that Gerard, cardinal deacon, received from Innocent the church of Palestrina; but Ferdinand Ughelli, in his series of bishops of Palestrina, omits him. Indeed, though Ughelli sets out in order all who presided over that church in Innocent’s time, he is silent about this man, although he names another under Clement III. Our Gerard is recorded, in the same year as his appointment, together with Cardinal Hugolino, nephew of Pope Innocent, as examiner or judge in a serious controversy [Col. 1057C]. Nothing further is found written concerning him. He subscribed letters of Innocent issued to the Lateran Church in the year of our salvation 1199. He died in the year of our salvation 1210, while Innocent III was Roman pontiff.].

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXIII. TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 1057C]

His name was Peter:

“In the year 1207 Pope Innocent III commands Peter, abbot, and the monks of Saints Hippolytus and Lawrence of Faenza to exhume the body of a certain heretic named Otto, which had been granted ecclesiastical burial in their church, and to arrange that it be buried outside the holy place.” *Monumenta Faventina*, col. 465, B.]

AND THE MONKS OF SAINT HIPPOLYTUS OF FAENZA. That they are to have the body of a heretic disinterred. (Rome, 9 January.)

[Col. 1057A]

It was set before us on behalf of our venerable brother, the bishop of Faenza [Note: [Col. 1057C]

Historians and records disagree sharply among themselves about the bishop who then bore the mitre of Faenza. First let us hear Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, col. 522.

“XXIII. Theodoric lived in the year 1203.

XXIV. Hubald, bishop of Faenza, administered the church of Faenza for scarcely a full year before he was promoted to the archbishopric of Ravenna. After his translation, when John, a cathedral canon, by agreement of the chapter had elected Joachim—formerly bishop of Luni and then a regular canon of Saint Fridianus of Lucca—as bishop of Faenza, the pope, though earnestly petitioned, opposed that election, declaring on the authority of the Council of Constantinople that one who had exchanged episcopal dignity for the monastic state, that is, the state of penitence, could not be restored to the same dignity. Therefore he wrote to Ubald that he should examine the matter repeatedly, so that one worthy of so great a burden might be appointed.

XXV. Accordingly Rotland, after Ubald had recently been translated, was appointed as a worthy successor, being provost of the cathedral [Col. 1058C], in the year 1210. He died in 1219.”

Thus far Ughelli. If we accept his testimony, we must conclude that Ubald was raised to the see of Faenza only in 1208, or even 1209, and that Theodoric lived until 1208 or 1209. For Ubald, who is said to have immediately succeeded him, administered the church of Faenza for only one year, whereas Rotland was appointed in 1210 after Ubald’s recent translation. But wholly different documents of Faenza are available, col. 464, A, from Tonducci, p. 235:

“In 1205 Ubald became bishop in place of Theoderic, bishop of Frascone, who had succeeded Bishop Bernard (concerning whom see letter 90 of Book VII, note), after Bernard’s translation to the church of Pavia in 1198, according to Campi …

In 1207 Ubald, bishop of Faenza, is mentioned [Col. 1058D] in a charter of the archive of the archbishopric of Ravenna.

In 1208, a letter of Erri of Medicina to Hubald, bishop of Faenza, contains an inventory of the goods of the churches of Buita and Prata. It also mentions the church of Saint Blaise, which it says belongs to his own right and not to that of the monastery of Saint Adalbert at Pereo. From the archive of the archbishopric of Ravenna, case F. 2097, vol. IV; *Annales Camaldulenses*, appendix, col. 274.

In 1208 Pope Innocent III writes to Hubald, bishop of Faenza, elected archbishop of Ravenna, and approves his election on the Kalends of June. From the archive of the archbishopric of Ravenna, case M. 5611, and in Rubeus, p. 371.”

Thus, from these instruments of unquestionable authority, it is proved that Ubald governed the church of Faenza for three, or even four, years.]

It was represented to us that Otto, of damnable memory, whose end judged him to have savoured of heretical depravity while he lived, was buried in the cemetery of your church. Although the same bishop, on the counsel of our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico [Note: [Col. 1058D] See letter 29 of Book VIII, note.], legate of the Apostolic See, and of other prudent men, placed your church under interdict unless you promptly arranged for the deceased’s body to be disinterred, you have so far been unwilling to do either.

Since we not only execrate such opponents of the orthodox faith while they live, and restrain them, if we can, lest they destroy the Lord’s vineyard, but also condemn their memory after death—so that those whom a simulated Christian life, concealed under an outward covering, hid from view may be pursued by the diligent investigation of Catholics, at least for the terror of those suffering from a similar disease—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, lest there be any fellowship of the faithful with the sons of Belial, you put aside every delay and arrange to have his body disinterred, or observe the interdict imposed upon your monastery. Otherwise, know that we have instructed our beloved sons, the abbots of Saint Proculus and Saint Stephen of Bologna [Col. 1058A], not to delay in compelling you to do this by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure, without appeal and with justice as their guide.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP [Note: [Col. 1058D] See letter 22 of Book IX, note.], THE DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF MAGDEBURG. That they are to receive the emancipated O. as a canon. (Rome, 8 January.)

Our beloved son Otto, nephew of the nobleman … duke of Poland and our subdeacon, informed us that by custom no one in your church can obtain a stall in choir and a place in chapter before being emancipated [Col. 1058B]. Since we have thought fit to receive him as a subdeacon of the Roman Church, and it would be improper for him to be deprived of the aforesaid privileges as one not emancipated, we have thought fit, by authority of the Apostolic See, to emancipate him. Therefore we command all of you by apostolic letters that, regarding him as emancipated, you gladly assign these things to him.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXV. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF MAGDEBURG [Note: [Col. 1059D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §11.]. That they are to confer the provostship upon O., nephew of the duke of Poland. (Rome, 8 January.)

[Col. 1059A]

After the example of Him of whom the prophetic voice testifies that “the lines have fallen in pleasant places,” in the measure permitted by human frailty we take into the service of Him whose office on earth we bear, though unworthy, those whom we believe distinguished alike by learning and upright conduct, so that the queen, clothed in gold and arrayed in variety, may stand at the bridegroom’s right hand—the queen to whom sons are born in place of fathers, to be appointed princes.

Therefore, hoping that our beloved son Otto, nephew of the nobleman … duke of Poland, whose upright life and learning commend him [Col. 1059B], ought to advance from good to better and serve the Church of God usefully, we have thought fit to ordain him subdeacon. We hold firm confidence that the churches in which he obtains benefices can be provided for no less through his person than provision has been made for him in those churches.

But because a good thing seems half-full when left without an addition, wishing from the kindness of the Apostolic See to bestow grace upon grace upon him, we have thought fit earnestly to ask and admonish all of you, commanding you by apostolic letters to confer generously upon him the provostship of your church which your venerable brother, your archbishop [Col. 1059C] [Note: [Col. 1059D] See letter 22 of Book IX, note.], is known to have held before his promotion. Execute this apostolic command in such a way that he, who can be of no small benefit to your church, may be bound more firmly to the affection of every one of you, and that we, who sincerely love him in the Lord with charity, may be held bound to respond to you with correspondingly greater favour, insofar as we know that you have more liberally complied with our request.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF GNIEZNO [Note: [Col. 1060D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.]. That he is to absolve Duke Wladislaus. (Rome, 12 January.)

By authority of these present letters we grant you that, if the nobleman Duke Wladislaus, softened by fear of the Lord, should wish to amend his obstinacy, you are to absolve, according to the form of the Church, both him and his supporters, who have incurred the *latae sententiae* canonical penalty for violent laying of hands upon clerics and have finally been denounced by you; and you are to impose upon them what is customarily imposed in such cases.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXVII. TO THE NOBLEMAN … DUKE WLADISLAUS, A SPIRIT OF SOUNDER COUNSEL. He is rebuked for his obstinacy and commission of evils, and exhorted to come to his senses. (Rome, 4 January.)

[Col. 1060A]

[We ask you, son—would that of mercy and not of wrath!—what is this confidence in which you trust, or by what strength or counsel do you intend to rebel against the Most High? Since you have been cast out from His presence because your sins demand it, do you perhaps devise a counsel which you cannot establish, so that by withdrawing from Him you may find a place of refuge apart from Him? Surely, if you ascend to heaven, He is there; and if you descend even into hell, He is present there.

What thought has seized you, son of man [Col. 1060B], that, adding transgression to transgression, you do not fear wickedly to raise yourself against God, as though clay should plot against the potter and insult its maker because he did not make it? What perverse seduction, I say, has seduced you, duke, so that you have made yourself a cattle-thief, though you ought to have shown yourself the leader of others? Did the Lord make you duke in order that you might reduce ecclesiastical freedom to the disgrace of servitude? Did He give you the sword so that you might whet it against the entrails of your mother? Or did He subject peoples to you so that you might arm yourself with their strength for the destruction of His ministers?

Gather your senses and enter into yourself with them. Look more carefully at how great your power is; measure your strength, count your resources, and see whether by your own force you could so trample Christ’s Church, unless He Himself had raised you up by the abundance of those resources. Without them, even if perhaps you bore tyranny in your will, you would by no means possess such power. Perhaps you regard yourself as great; but in relation to the vain grandeurs of the world you ought not to regard yourself as greater than that most powerful king who, because he did not acknowledge the Lord above him, was by just judgment changed into a beastly form. Nor was Manasseh, king of Israel, inferior to you: because he ignored the Lord’s power, the Lord’s power subjected him to the extremity of captivity.

The memory of such great punishments is dreadful indeed. But since like fault ought to fear like vengeance, far more dreadful to you [Col. 1060D] ought to be the consideration of your own fault. As though you did not acknowledge the Most High as superior to you, in the oppression with which you are said to have afflicted the church of Gniezno, you appear to have set yourself against God and God against yourself. By making the punishment of sin worse than the sin itself, while you rashly despise the discipline which you underwent for your fault, you are made more guilty by punishment of the fault than perhaps you were by the fault punished: for although the former comes mortally through presumption, the latter comes more mortally through contempt.

Previously, indeed, report had already struck our ears of the detestable cruelty which you were said to exercise in many ways against the aforesaid church and ecclesiastical men. But at last, when our venerable brother, the archbishop of Gniezno, a man of outstanding holiness, came to the Apostolic See, although we learned much from him about the afflictions under which that Church groans, very many matters concerning its oppression were reported to us by religious and distinguished men of the surrounding province [Col. 1061A].

Among these, we deeply lament for you—if indeed you yourself also grieve—that, when the aforesaid archbishop declared that you had incurred the *latae sententiae* canonical penalty because of violent laying of hands upon clerics, in whom, as you ought, you are not said to reverence Jesus Christ, and had further exercised canonical censure upon you because you refused to restore the entire property of a certain deceased bishop which you had seized, you despised ecclesiastical discipline. You not only refused to offer due satisfaction for these matters, but also continue in many ways to increase the yoke of servitude upon him and his church [Col. 1061B].

Moreover, although by the general custom of the surrounding province the conferral of prebends belongs to the bishops of the respective places, you either attempt yourself to confer prebends of the church of Gniezno, or sometimes cause them, at your own will, to be conferred upon certain persons by pressure. You also cause the relics of the saints, the ornaments of that church, and every treasure of it, bestowed upon it by the devotion of your predecessors, or dukes, or other faithful persons, to be held in your own custody. You do not allow them to be administered by the said archbishop and chapter according to the custom of the churches of Poland [Col. 1061C], failing to consider that such matters are known to belong not only to ecclesiastical men under the New Law, but also that under the Old Law the Lord commanded the vessels and ornaments of the tabernacle to be kept by Levites.

Furthermore, disregarding the immunities of the Church, you placed a certain prisoner under guard in the aforesaid church, ordering the canons to keep watch over him and to provide him with necessities from their own resources. You sometimes afflict clerics in holy orders with prisons and tortures, to the dishonour of Jesus Christ. In these and other matters you persecute the aforesaid archbishop and the church committed to him so cruelly that, even if he should be silent in word, he confesses your oppressions by his exile [Col. 1061D].

Therefore, since we neither wish nor ought to conceal the affliction of the aforesaid church and your own peril which lies in it, we earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility. By the salvation both of your soul and body, and through Jesus Christ, in whose name every knee bends—of those in heaven, on earth, and even in hell—we strictly command you: humble yourself beneath His mighty hand; do not delay to return to obedience to the command of the Church concerning the matters for which you incurred ecclesiastical censure; neither hinder nor allow anyone to hinder the said archbishop from freely conferring the prebends and parsonages of the said church, as belongs to him by law [Col. 1062A]; and allow him personally to keep, and, as expedient, to cause the chapter to keep, the relics of the saints, the other ornaments of that church, and its treasure, as stated above.

Cease altogether from persecuting the archbishop, the Church, and ecclesiastical persons, and do them no injury in any respect. Rather, holding the aforesaid archbishop in full reverence and honour, reconcile yourself to him—and indeed to God in him—by humble satisfaction in the matters in which you are known to have provoked divine wrath. For we hope that, if you are converted and do penance, and seek to cleave to that archbishop as to your father with filial devotion, his merits will advance you in many things. We believe that God has so been pleased with him that he will not be thought lacking in prayers for the salvation of his subjects, since God has especially stirred up his spirit for the defence of ecclesiastical freedom [Col. 1062B].

Moreover, do not delay to restore, together with the fruits received from them, the estates or other benefices, whether ecclesiastical or patrimonial, of which you are alleged to have despoiled the said archbishop or those who stood beside him in defence of the Church. Likewise, by the power committed to you, compel your subjects to make full restitution of what has been taken from those persons by them. Also allow the monks of Molchina, whom you are said to have expelled, to return to their monastery and to remain there in due freedom.

Otherwise, however burdensome it may be to us to trouble you in any respect [Col. 1062C], because we must give greater deference to God than to man, we decree that the sentence which the aforesaid archbishop has pronounced, or may reasonably judge fit to pronounce, against you or against those who have received their benefices from your hand or have presumed to support you in persecuting him—whether for any of the foregoing matters, for all of them, or for each particular matter, whether you have hitherto committed acts against ecclesiastical liberty or, God forbid, may commit them in the future—shall obtain its due force. We command our venerable brothers, the bishops of Prague, Olomouc, and Meissen, and all the bishops of Poland, to cause it, whenever requested by him, to be inviolably observed by our authority until fitting satisfaction is made, just as it shall have been reasonably pronounced [Col. 1062D], solemnly renewing it every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXVIII. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF POLAND [Note: [Col. 1061D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.]. Concerning the same matter. (Rome, 10 January.)

For the report of detestable cruelty had indeed already struck our ears, which the nobleman … [Col. 1063A] Duke Władysław [inflicted] upon the Church of Gniezno, etc., in almost the same manner, to the end.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXIX. [Note: [Col. 1063D] Raynaldus published this letter under the year 1207, §15. It is therefore presented here enclosed in brackets.] To all the faithful of Christ established in Poland: that they should pay the due tribute to the Roman Church. (Rome, on the Nones of January.)

[If you kept in mind the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, who, for the sin of withholding part of the price received from their lands, were punished by dreadful vengeance and fell dead suddenly at the feet of the chief of the apostles, you would, as we believe, avoid deceit in paying the tribute which you owe to blessed Peter. For you should know that it has come to our hearing that, [Col. 1063B] although, according to the custom of the country, the currency in common use among you is renewed three times each year, and that which was formerly current subsequently becomes less valuable when another currency succeeds it, you defer payment of the tribute owed to that Apostle until the time when the currency with which you pay has become less valuable. Although the Almighty has no need of your goods, yet, because it is dangerous for you either to diminish by fraud what you owe Him or to withhold it through ingratitude, we admonish and exhort all of you and, by these apostolic letters, command you: pay that tribute, in the customary manner, without any taint of fraud. Otherwise, we decree that the sentence which our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, shall reasonably judge fit to pronounce against those who ungratefully withhold, [Col. 1063C] or rashly defraud, the said tribute, shall obtain its due force until fitting satisfaction has been made.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of January, in the ninth year.]

CCXX. [Note: [Col. 1064D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §15.] To all dukes established in Poland: that they should not impede payments of tithes. (Rome, 2 Nones of January.)

If the Lord had said to any one of you, “Your tithes and first-fruits are mine,” just as He declares them to be His, perhaps you could remit them to those indebted for them. But since giving away what belongs to another can in no way appear to be generosity, we cannot but wonder at your nobility: as we have learned, when you sometimes intend either to reward the services of those obedient to you or to procure the devotion of certain persons toward yourselves, you in fact absolve them from the payment of tithes, though you have no power to do so by right—perhaps thinking that you do God less injury because He endures this and does not openly repel your wrong. Therefore, lest the Lord at some time be angered with you and punish you in all that is yours, because you rashly lay hands upon His portion, we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you and, by apostolic letters, command that, [Col. 1064A] henceforth abandoning such rashness, you neither impede nor allow any impediment to be made to the full payment of tithes to their respective churches. Otherwise, the sentence which our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, shall reasonably judge fit to pronounce against you or those who withhold them shall remain in force until fitting satisfaction has been made, etc., as in another letter.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXI. To the chaplains of the Duke of … and of the other nobles of Poland: that they should pay cathedral dues. (Rome, 2 Nones of January.)

[Col. 1064B] Since service to secular lords does not entitle you to withhold from ecclesiastical prelates the reverence and honor due to them, by the authority of these presents we command and strictly enjoin you to take care to receive your archdeacons honorably when, while visiting the parish, they come to your places; to provide them with the procuration due to them; and to pay in full the cathedral dues owed to the archbishop or bishops. Otherwise, the sentence which our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, shall reasonably judge fit to pronounce against you on this account, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXII. [Note: [Col. 1064D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.] To all clerics holding ecclesiastical benefices in Poland: that they should support the Archbishop of Gniezno unanimously. (Rome, 2 Nones of January.)

[Col. 1064C]

Since every part which does not harmonize with its whole is shameful, by the authority of these presents we command and strictly enjoin you unanimously to support our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, who labors for your liberty and that of the Church. As most beloved sons, take care to cleave to him as to a loving father, so that, supported by the aid of you all, he may, with God’s help, effectively meet the injuries threatening the Church. For we have commanded him not to delay in compelling by suspension from office and withdrawal of benefice anyone among you [Col. 1064D] who rashly presumes to act otherwise.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXIII. [Note: [Col. 1064D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.] To all dukes established in Poland. (Rome, 2 Nones of January.)

Since, as we have learned, the insolence of certain persons in the regions of Poland is raging excessively against ecclesiastical liberty—appropriating to themselves the election of prelates and not allowing those clerics to whom it belongs [Col. 1065A] to celebrate such elections canonically—we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you, forbidding you by apostolic letters, under threat of anathema, to attempt to usurp for yourselves any undue authority in these elections. Rather, permit the elections to be held both canonically and freely by the canons or clerics to whom they belong, restraining, by the authority entrusted to you, all persons subject to your jurisdiction who rashly presume to act contrary to this apostolic prohibition.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXIV. To the chapter of the Church of Łęczyca: it confirms for them, as they possess it, a certain prebend. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of January.)

[Col. 1065B]

“Just requests …,” etc., down to “assent”: the prebend which the nobleman Martin established for your church from his revenues, and which our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, enlarged, with the consent of the chapter, by grants of tithes—we confirm to you and, through you, to your church by apostolic authority, as you possess it justly and peaceably, etc. “Therefore let no one …,” etc. “But if anyone …,” etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXV. To the same: similar, concerning the chantry. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of January.)

[Col. 1065C]

“It is customary to assent …,” etc., down to “assent”: the chantry, prudently established in your church by our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Gniezno, with the consent of his chapter and through the favor of Mesco, Duke of Gniezno, of distinguished memory, to you and, through you, to your church, etc., as in the other letter.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXVI. To the cantor of the Church of Gniezno: similar, concerning a chapel. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of January.)

[Col. 1065D] “When a request is made to us …,” etc., down to “assent”: the chapel which Duke Mesco of good memory granted in prudent piety to the chantry of the Church of Gniezno, whose office of honor you hold, together with the tithes granted to that chantry by our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno—we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to that church, as you possess it justly and peaceably, etc. “Therefore let no one …,” etc. “But if anyone …,” etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXVII. [Note: [Col. 1065D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.] To the Archbishop of Gniezno: he grants him authority to exercise canonical censure upon Duke Władysław and his supporters unless he repents. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Ides of January.)

[Col. 1066A]

Since your deeds speak for you, bearing witness that you possess a ready will in the law of the Lord, we have judged you worthy to receive special authority from us, so that, with His help, you may more fully defend ecclesiastical liberty—for the sake of which God is believed especially to have stirred up your spirit among the prelates around you. Therefore, having full confidence in your prudence, by the authority of these presents we grant you power that, unless the nobleman, [Col. 1066B] Duke Władysław, after paternal admonition from you, ceases from persecuting your church and freely permits you to exercise your pontifical office over it and its subjects, you may, after due consideration, exercise canonical censure against him, all his supporters, and also those who rashly presume to violate the immunities of your church, especially those secured by apostolic privilege. You may cause whatever sentence you pronounce in such cases, if necessary, to be inviolably observed by any bishops and prelates of the churches of Poland until fitting satisfaction has been made, compelling the contumacious by ecclesiastical coercion, appeal set aside. Furthermore, since certain prebends and personal benefices are said to have been granted, to the prejudice [Col. 1066C] of yourself or your predecessors, by the aforesaid duke and even by his father, contrary to the ordinances of the canons, we grant you by these letters authority lawfully to revoke their grant, as also any alienation of whatever goods made without the consent of your chapter to the loss of the aforesaid church, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal removed. “Therefore let no one …” our concession, etc. “But if anyone …,” etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 1066D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.] To all bishops established in Poland: that they should enforce the sentence passed against the Bishop of Poznań. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Ides of January.)

[Col. 1066D]

To the shame of the Bishop of Poznań, … it cannot fail to come to mind that one of the Twelve betrayed Christ, and that the Most High found perversity among His angels.
