For when the man of outstanding holiness, our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, had undertaken to oppose the children of this world for the liberty of the Church, he found in the named bishop—whom he had hoped would faithfully cleave to him among the children of light—a betrayer of Christ within his own Church. When at length the said archbishop, because of the bishop’s offenses, had reasonably pronounced a sentence [Col. 1067A] of interdict against him, and he, despising that sentence, had presumed to celebrate the divine offices in the presence of the principal persecutor of the Church, whom the archbishop had expressly excommunicated, he was therefore bound with the bond of excommunication. Although afterwards, through simulated repentance, as was proved by subsequent events, he was absolved, he nevertheless fell again into the same offense and was restored to the former sentence. We therefore, considering that the aforesaid bishop ought to be bound with a correspondingly stronger cord of ecclesiastical discipline, inasmuch as he has more damnably loosened in himself the reins of innocence which he ought to have moderated in others, command and strictly enjoin all of you to enforce that sentence, and also the sentence which the same archbishop reasonably pronounced upon the canons and other clerics [Col. 1067B] for a like offense with a like punishment, until fitting satisfaction has been made, etc., as above.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXIX. [Note: [Col. 1067D] Raynaldus prints this letter under the year 1207, §14.] To the Duke of Cracow: he is received under protection. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of January.)

“The most holy Roman Church …,” etc. [Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, considering the sincerity of devotion and faith which you are known to bear toward us and the Roman Church, we receive your person, together with the Duchy of Cracow and all your goods which you possess justly and peaceably, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and by the authority of these presents we more strictly forbid anyone to presume wrongfully to molest you concerning them. “Therefore let no one …” our protection and prohibition, etc. “But if anyone …,” etc. Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.]

CCXXX. [Note: [Col. 1067D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.] To the Archbishop of Gniezno: that he should restrain laymen despoiling clerics. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of January.)

Among the other burdens of distress which the Church of Christ is said to endure in the regions of Poland, many laymen do not fear, without observing due process of law, to despoil ecclesiastical persons of movable and immovable property belonging to them by right of patrimony. Since the insolence of laymen must therefore be resisted in their oppression of clerics, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to restrain such presumptuous persons from their rashness by ecclesiastical coercion, after prior warning and with the obstacle of appeal removed. Furthermore, although the people of the Gentiles walked in darkness, they nevertheless deemed their priests and Levites so worthy of honor that Pharaoh, king of Egypt, after reducing the rest to slavery, preserved them not only in their former liberty but also supplied them with food from public resources. [Col. 1068A] Prudently admonish and diligently induce the secular princes who harass clerics established in Poland with these and other exactions to desist from such presumption; and, if necessary, compel them by canonical censure.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXI. To the Bishop of Pomerania: that he should obey the Archbishop of Gniezno. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of January.)

Our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, appearing in our presence, has represented that you refuse to render him the obedience due to him. Since we neither will nor ought to permit [Col. 1068B] the dignity of that archbishop to be rashly diminished by anyone, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin your brotherhood not to delay in rendering him the obedience and reverence due.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXII. To all bishops established in Poland: that they should assist the said archbishop. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of January.)

Since none of you could deny his hired servant the remuneration due to him, it is surely fitting that you should give religious consideration to the recompense of our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, who has labored and still labors amid many anxieties and dangers, not only for your peace but also [Col. 1068C] for the common liberty of the Polish churches. We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort all of you and, by apostolic letters, command that, considering that in the exile which he underwent for the common liberty of your churches he was burdened with many expenses—which he is known to have borne [Note: [Col. 1068D] Perhaps: “endured.”] not out of the resources of his own church but out of patrimonial goods and loans—you should, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, take care to assist him in these matters in such a way that, in the contest which he has fought and is fighting, he may both wage the struggle with your support and triumph through your merits.

[Col. 1068D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXIII. To the chapter of the Church of Łęczyca: their possessions and goods are confirmed as they justly hold them. (At Saint Peter’s, 7 Ides of January.)

“It is customary to assent …,” etc., down to “assent”: the *sanctuarii* [Note: [Col. 1068D] *Sanctuarii*, that is, persons holding land from churches. See Cange, *Glossary*, vol. VI, col. 121.], with their villages, whom our venerable brother, … Archbishop of Gniezno, with the consent of Dukes Mesco and Conrad and of his canons, granted in provident piety to your church—[Col. 1069A] namely, these are their names: Ozris, with his son Botcheli; Sara; Dalevo; Pirvos; Vogien; Cropidlo; Rosnat Chotemir; Golei; Targosa; Nedelis; Vencec; and Pet. with his sons; Vogen; Borecli; Brubno; Zelivy; Zetlic; Zlella; Rac; Cantro with his son Rados; Sotlec, with his sons Nicholas and Peter; Martin, with his brother Nezul; Vilcost with his son Milostrig; Neratde with his son Gozeslaus; Clivis; Nezbil; Zirac; Dommac; and Cotebic, their nephews—we confirm to you and, through you, to the Church of Łęczyca by apostolic authority and by the protection of this present document, as you possess them justly and peaceably, etc. “Therefore let no one …,” etc. “But if anyone …,” etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXIV. [Note: [Col. 1069C] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.] To the Polish Archbishop: that benefices of his church may not be conferred by secular persons. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Ides of January.)

[Col. 1069B]

We have been called, by the Lord’s ordering, to the summit of the supreme pontificate so that, through the diligence of our care, what needs correction in the churches of God may be reformed for the better, and whatever is undertaken in them contrary to the statutes of the canons may be cut away by the pruning-hook of apostolic governance. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, in order that what is right may be more freely accomplished in the church committed to you, following the example of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, by the authority of these presents we strictly forbid ecclesiastical benefices henceforth to be conferred by secular power [Col. 1069C] in that church or in the other episcopal churches committed to your jurisdiction, since such conferment manifestly conflicts with sacred ordinances. “Therefore let no one …” our prohibition, etc. “But if anyone …,” etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXV. [Note: [Col. 1069C] Various fragments of this letter are found in the *Decretals*: first, book I, title 17, “On the Ordination, or Non-Ordination, of Priests’ Sons,” chapter 15; secondly, book III, title 1, “On the Life and Conduct of Clerics,” chapter 12. What is read in both places is here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are also placed in the margin. Raynaldus also cites this letter under the year 1207, [Col. 1069D] §13.] To the Archbishop of Gniezno and his suffragans: that they should not admit men publicly married to ecclesiastical dignities. (At Saint Peter’s, 6 Ides of January.)

[Col. 1070A]

[Since you ought to love the beauty of the house of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1069D] In the *Decretals*: “of God.”] and the place where His glory dwells, you must take diligent care that nothing be rashly presumed in the churches entrusted to you which may either extinguish in them the lamp of religion or seem to stain the purity of the ministers of the Lord. For you should know that it has come to our hearing that certain men established in your dioceses, publicly contracting marriage with women, do not blush to receive ecclesiastical [Col. 1070B] dignities; and that canons of some churches, whose loins ought, in accordance with the word of evangelical truth, to be girded and in whose hands the lamps of good works ought to burn, have rotted so deeply in the filth of lust that they do not even wish to conceal their shame and disgrace. Indeed, they draw with them to the ministry of the altar, to which they render themselves unworthy, their sons born from disgraceful generation, rendering those sons still more unworthy—as though their incontinence were not sufficiently known to the reproach of the clerical order unless the displayed, public testimony of their offspring, appearing and speaking against them, continually confirmed it.

And since in churches where such clerics have a place many enormities are committed, while a leavened family connection of fathers and sons, even grandsons and relatives by marriage, ministers there without order—because, clearly, carnal affection predominating, spiritual reverence has grown cold among them, so that through their mutual insolence no one for another’s sake refrains from doing whatever he wishes [Note: [Col. 1069D] See *Decretals*, book III, title 1, “On the Life and Conduct of Clerics,” chapter 12.]—there are sometimes theatrical games in these same churches [Note: [Col. 1069D] The *Decretals* read “in certain [churches]” and omit the three words “of the year and below,” which … follow.] [Note: [Col. 1069D] In those times theatrical games were customarily held in churches, and grotesque masked figures were introduced for mockery. Indeed, at certain festivals clerics performed the mockeries of their madness: that is, they proceeded through the church masked or disguised. This custom—or, rather, corruption—is condemned here, lest the Church’s dignity be defiled by such shamefulness. The same custom had long before crept into the Church of Constantinople: clerics played masked games in church on the feast of Christ’s Nativity and of the Lights, clothed as monks or soldiers, or in the form of various animals. Balsamon notes this custom on canon 57 of the Sixth Synod, [Col. 1070C] in Trullo:

“But certain clerics also, at certain feasts, transform themselves into various masks; and at one time, bearing swords, they enter the nave of the church in military dress; at another, they proceed as monks, or even as four-footed animals.”

But, indeed, clerics at certain festivals assume and represent various characters; sometimes, girded with swords and wearing military dress, they enter the middle of the church; at other times, they proceed as monks or as four-footed animals. Latin writers pursued the same stain of the Church in various councils; this is what is called playing *verola* or *cervola*. Synod of Auxerre, canon 1: “It is not permitted, on the Kalends of January, to make *verola* or *cervola*, or to observe diabolical New-Year gifts, or to play the bear.” Council of Nantes: “Let none of the priests permit shameful games to be performed before him, whether with a bear or with female tumblers.” Canon *Nullus*, distinction 44; canon *Nullus*, “On Consecration,” distinction 5. Clerics are also forbidden to perform indecent games with a bear or female tumblers—that is, tournaments, or equestrian games and jousts, popularly called *torneamenta*, from the barbarous Latin *tornare*, used by Augustine himself, book I *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 89: “They learned not only to turn sticks, but also to brandish iron and whirl slings.”

A disgrace of the same age was that, on the solemn days of Easter and Pentecost, one of the clerics’ prostitutes used to be created queen. Clothed in purple and crowned, she was seated on a lofty throne, and dances were conducted around her throughout the day, not without idolatry. Aegidius of Orval, *On the Deeds of Liège*, chapter 40: “For priests and the other ecclesiastical persons, together with the whole people, on the solemnities of Easter and Pentecost, when they ought to attend the holy church more devoutly than on other days and serve God, would create as queen one of the priests’ concubines, dressed in purple and glittering with a diadem, placed upon a more elevated throne and veiled with curtains. Standing before her, they sang all day in dances, with drums and other musical instruments; and, having become as it were idolaters, they worshipped her as an idol.”

By “grotesque masked figures,” says the Council of Nantes in the passages just cited, it means masks of demons. Burchard, book II, chapter 161, adds that these are called *talamas* in the vernacular—our “masques.” Clerics are not, however, forbidden to stage pious spectacles, such as Christ’s Nativity, the adoration of the Magi, Herod’s slaughter of the children, and Christ’s Passion [Col. 1072D], because these serve more to stir up devotion than pleasure, as the Gloss says here and as commentators generally follow it.]—and grotesque masked figures are introduced into them not only for the spectacle of amusements, but also, during the three yearly festivals immediately following Christmas, deacons, priests, and subdeacons in turn [Note: [Col. 1072D] The *Decretals* omit “and immediately after,” and read “presume” in place of “performing.”] perform the mockeries of their madness; by the shameful excesses of their gesticulations they make clerical dignity cheap before the people, whom at that time they ought rather to soothe by preaching the word of God. [Note: [Col. 1072D] The words distinguished here in italics are absent from the *Decretals*, but are found in Pithou’s additions.] Therefore, because the zeal of God’s house consumes us by reason of the office entrusted to us, and the reproaches of those reproaching Him are known to have fallen upon us, [by apostolic letters [Note: [Col. 1072D] Absent from the *Decretals*.] we command your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 1072D] Up to this point in the *Decretals*, book III, title 1, chapter 12.]] that, lest the Church’s honor be defiled by such shamefulness, you shall henceforth not admit publicly married men to ecclesiastical dignities, and shall remove from such dignities those already admitted, [Col. 1071B] which they cannot retain without a perverse example and grave scandal [Note: [Col. 1072D] Omitted in the *Decretals*.].

[Moreover, do not permit prebends in those churches to be conferred upon the sons [Note: [Col. 1072D] See *Decretals*, book I, title 17, chapter 15.] of canons whose fathers are canons there [Note: [Col. 1072D] Pithou notes in the margin that another reading is *quorum*, “whose,” rather than *quarum*, “of which.”], since it is improper that an illegitimate son should minister to an unchaste father in the service of the altar, upon which the only-begotten Son is sacrificed to the eternal Father for the salvation of humankind [Note: [Col. 1072D] Up to this point in the *Decretals*, book I, title 17, chapter 15.]. [Note: [Col. 1072D] Again, there in book III, title 1, chapter 12. Below, the *Decretals* omit *vero* (“indeed”) and immediately read *taliter* (“in such a manner”).] Take care, however, to extirpate from your churches the aforesaid custom—or rather corruption—of such entertainments in such a way] that you may prove yourselves zealous defenders of divine worship and of the sacred order.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXVI. [Note: [Col. 1072D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §12.] To the noblemen, dukes established in Poland: that they should desist from occupying the resources of vacant churches. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Ides of January.)

[Col. 1071C]

If you acknowledge that you possess whatever you have on earth from Him who dwells in heaven, you should certainly judge it unworthy that, through the power you received from Him, you inflict injury upon Him in His ministers. We have learned that, when any prelates of your province depart from this present world, you—who, as their chief sons, ought to console the churches bereft of them—add sorrow to their sorrow by seizing the resources of the deceased bishops, which ought instead to be preserved for their successors. Therefore, [Col. 1072A] although you ought always to show deference to churches, you ought especially to honor them in the time of their widowhood. We earnestly admonish and exhort all of you and, by Him who, hanging upon the cross for our iniquities, inscribed the privilege of liberty for His Church with the sprinkling of His own blood, we have judged that you should be earnestly entreated and requested: permit the churches established within your territories to enjoy their due liberty; do not pant after the movable and immovable resources of deceased pastors with any ardor of greed; but rather allow them, as is just, to be kept freely by the chapters of the places, to be surrendered to bishops canonically appointed. Otherwise, however much, etc., as in the other letters.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides [Col. 1072B] of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXVII. To the provost and chapter of Harlebeche: that they should receive the cleric P. as a canon. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Ides of January.)

Since you ought carefully to consider that you should not deny to others the grace which you have received from Christ’s Church, you ought not to show yourselves reluctant to extend the favor of your brotherhood to him whom the kindness of apostolic patronage recommends to you. Rather, you should admit him all the more generously into the grace of your fellowship, because consideration of your own condition—since you are bound to give freely what you have freely received—ought the more effectively to move you to this. The beloved son Master P. of Saint-Venant, appearing before us, humbly petitioned that we, who are bound to consider provision for poor clerics, might deign to open the eyes of mercy toward him and, after his long labors in liberal studies, in which he has long toiled, provide for him through paternal care a place of rest in your church. We therefore, considering that the same master—whose conduct and learning receive commendable testimony from many—ought rather to be invited than himself to ask to be joined to you in the ministry of your church, since, by the merits said to commend him, he may, God granting, prove fruitful for you in many ways, earnestly ask and exhort all of you, commanding by apostolic [Col. 1073A] letters that, receiving him as a brother and canon out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, you treat him with brotherly love. Thus fulfill the apostolic command in such a way that it may be pleasing to God and acceptable to us, and that the same master may consequently be bound to show himself all the more devoted to you and your church because through you, after the exertions of scholarly service, he rejoices to have found there more generously the grace of repose.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year.

CCXXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 1073D] Raynaldus prints this letter under the year 1207, §13; therefore it is here enclosed in brackets.] To the Archbishop of Gniezno: that he may cause the sign of the cross to be borne through his province. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Ides of January.)

[Col. 1073B] [Since you know that you ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, you piously desire that, with our approval, the saving banner of His cross may be permitted to be borne before your venerable person—you who are believed continually to bear in your body, for love of the divine name, His mortification. We therefore, considering that the insignia of heavenly armor ought by no means to be denied to you, who, supported by the help of One stronger, labor in unceasing combat to triumph by the weapons of righteousness against the strong man armed in the court of the world, grant you by the authority of these presents that you may cause the sign of the saving cross to be carried before you throughout your province, except when a legate of the Apostolic See is established in Poland, so that in this matter you may show him the deference due to one sent from our side. Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides [Col. 1073C] of January, in the ninth year.]

CCXXXIX. [Note: [Col. 1073D] A copy of this letter, which we had caused to be transcribed along with the others from the copy of Conti, has slipped from our hands—we do not know by what chance. We can therefore give here only its summary. See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §15.] To the same: that he should compel the canons of Saint Albert and Saint Peter to pay the tribute.

CCXL. To the prior and brethren of Kening: they are received under the protection of blessed Peter. (At Saint Peter’s, 17 Kalends of February.)

We duly discharge the office entrusted to us when we cherish religious men with the charity owed to them, graciously assent to their vows and desires, and grant them the assistance of the Apostolic See’s defense so that they are not harassed by wrongful troubles. Therefore, considering more attentively the ardor of your religious life and honorable conduct, [Col. 1073D] and the steadfastness of faith with which you cleave to blessed Peter and to us in unshaken constancy, [Col. 1074A] following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive your church, together with all that it lawfully possesses at present or may, by just means and God’s favor, acquire in the future, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it with the patronage of this present document. We decree that neither your bishop nor his officials may impose undue exactions upon you or your churches, or further burden you with unjust oppressions.

In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose clerics and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. Furthermore, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the churches of Salford, Ezendum, [Col. 1074B] Brailes, Wellesburn, Herburgbir, and Stanleia, assigned by the indulgence of the said predecessor of ours, with the common assent of all of you and by reasonable provision, for the refreshment of the poor and the reception of guests. No one may rashly remove those churches from the use and benefit of the poor and guests. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this charter of our protection, grant, and confirmation, etc. “But if anyone …,” etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCXLI. [Note: [Col. 1073D] A copy of this letter, which we had caused to be transcribed together with the others from Conti’s copy, has slipped from our hands by some accident unknown to us; and therefore we can here present only its summary. See Raynaldus under the year 1207, § 12. “Since the archbishop [of Gniezno], in defending the liberty of his Church, had incurred debt, the pope, at his request, granted that, should he die before it was entirely discharged, his successor should be bound by the obligation of paying the debt, so that anxiety about discharging it might not trouble the mind of that excellent bishop.”]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF GNIEZNO. If he should happen to die first, his successor is to be bound for his debts.

[Col. 1074C]

CCXLII. TO GARINUS [Note: [Col. 1074D] Garinus, or Warinus, or Warnerius, abbot of Saint Aper of Toul, is mentioned in charters from 1195 until 1227, when he founded the priory of Saint George. Having subsequently become bishop of Toul in 1228, he was soon afterwards seized with a desire to return to the monastery and asked the canons to ratify his resignation. Having obtained this, he died on 11 May 1230. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, cols. 1013 and 1079.] ABBOT, AND TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT APER AT TOUL, BOTH PRESENT AND FUTURE PROFESSORS OF THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. They are received under the protection of Saint Peter. (At Saint Peter’s, 3 Ides of January.)

A devout request ought to be fulfilled by a corresponding result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Aper, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree first that the monastic order which is known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting it, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the village of Saint Aper, with its own *ban* [seigneurial jurisdiction], vineyards, meadows, lands, woods, mills, dependants, and all its other appurtenances; vineyards situated at Baromont, Barian, and Valleris; whatever you possess at Bruriac and Saponariae; the village called Videliac., with its *ban* and appurtenances; Alannum, with church, *ban*, and appurtenances; Silvinicurt, with church, *ban*, and appurtenances; Stephen’s village, with church, *ban*, and appurtenances; the village of Molonis, with church, *ban*, and appurtenances; Sensuries, with church, *ban*, and appurtenances; the chapel of Buleneville; the tithes of Waldon’s court, belonging to the mother church of Sansures; Martiniac., with its church; whatever you possess at Domno-Bricium; the church of Hurmetum, with its appurtenances; whatever you possess at Adholenisville; the church of Saint German, with chapel and all appurtenances, and whatever allodial land you possess there; Vallerium, with its *ban* and appurtenances; whatever you possess at Pont, Fens, and Roseries; the church of Vallibus and whatever you possess there; half the *ban* of Astons and whatever you possess there; Magnonicurt, with church, *ban*, and all its appurtenances; the church of Blandenac, with chapel and whatever you possess there; the possessions which you have at Rogerenges, Mandria, Clusereia, and Artengys; whatever you have at Fontonisville, both in the church and among the other things you possess there; Columbarium, with church, *ban*, and all appurtenances; the chapel of Hosgerius; the chapel of Girminei and the other things you possess there; the chapel of Angisville and whatever you possess there; the chapel of Condrecort, with all appurtenances; the cell of Castineium, with all appurtenances; the cell of Beaniville, with all appurtenances; the cell of Landecort, with all appurtenances; the cell of Darrileium, with all appurtenances; and a third part of the tithes of Vitel, which you acquired from Gerard, provost of Dawileium; the tithes granted as alms to that cell by Geoffrey, lord of Dawileium, which he held at Frana and Franel; Gibert’s court, with mill and all appurtenances; half the field of Spinalis, with people, lands, woods, and meadows; the vineyards and revenues you possess at Lai; the vineyards and possessions you possess at Luceium; whatever you possess at Masnil; that which you possess in the mill of Longort, together with the portion which you bought from Malvisin; that which you possess from Wacon, and whatever right Erard, lord of Sorceium, had in that same village; the mill of Sauz and Aragia, which the same Erard possessed at Malvage and bestowed upon you as alms in compensation for many injuries, together with whatever you had previously possessed in the aforesaid village, with people, lands, woods, and meadows; the mill on the Moselle, given to you as alms by Roselina and her son T.; by the gift of Master Matthew, the mill in Stephen’s village; six solidi of annual revenue for the vineyard which you possess in the territory of Firkes; whatever you possess by the gift of Walter, knight of Vodium, at Anbleniville, in tithes, lands, woods, and meadows; whatever you have held from ancient times in the church of Saint Christopher; the land which Charles, a knight, gave in alms to your church at Molonisville, with the approval and consent of . . . . bishop of Toul and of Tirricus, lord of Novovillare; and the wood called Fosnor, by the gift of Walter, knight of Vodium.

When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Moreover, we forbid anyone within the bounds of your parish to presume to build a new chapel or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves, without prejudice to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs.

We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or perhaps expressly interdicted; saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that everything be preserved intact and serve in every way the benefit of those for whose governance and support it has been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, should presume rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his fault by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office, and let him be liable, etc., to vengeance. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc., unto the end.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of January, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1206 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CCXLIII. [Note: [Col. 1077C] This letter is printed in full by Raynaldus, under the year 1207, § 19; it is therefore presented here in brackets.]. TO THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE [Note: [Col. 1077D] See letter 19 of book eight, note.]. The sentence pronounced against Venetians who forcibly entered his church in order to seize an icon is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of January.)

[Col. 1077A]

[The tenor of your letters has informed us that the dearest son in Christ, H., illustrious emperor of Constantinople, caused to be bestowed upon you, for placement in the church of Saint Sophia, a certain icon in which the blessed evangelist Luke is said to have painted the image of the blessed Virgin with his own hands—an icon venerated by all Greece out of reverence for that Virgin—and certain relics that were in the chapel of the Great Palace. The Venetian podestà, coming before you with the Venetians, urgently demanded the icon from you, claiming that it had been promised to him by the aforesaid emperor.

But since you knew that they had no right whatever in it, you refused to accede to his request. When he persisted for a long time, you gave him this answer: that you neither gave nor granted it to him, adding ironically that he might take it if he could then find it in the church. For the church was closed, and the aforesaid icon was not in it, but was placed in the sacristy under a triple lock. Yet when he could by no means obtain from you the opening of the church, in whose sacristy the aforesaid icon was located, he had a certain man lowered by a rope into it from a wing of that church. Searching for the oft-mentioned icon through the church and not finding it, that man, by command of the aforesaid podestà, violently opened one of the great doors of the church.

Then the Venetians, violently entering the church, learned from a certain little Greek where the icon was, and began to break down the doors of the sacristy. When this came to your knowledge, filled with bitterness, you went to the wing of the church, and, looking down upon those committing sacrilege, forbade them in the name of almighty God, under threat of interdict and excommunication, to presume to complete what they had wickedly begun. But because they did not even then desist from committing sacrilege, you publicly and solemnly bound the aforesaid podestà, with all his counsellors and supporters, in the bond of anathema, with candles lighted.

Nevertheless, despising both the sentence of interdict and that of anathema, they broke down the doors of the sacristy and violently carried off the icon, placing it in the church called in Greek *Pantocrator*, “Ruler of All.” You then approached our beloved son B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, legate of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1077D] See letter 55 of book eight.], and made known to him the course of events. On the same day he confirmed the sentence pronounced by you and subjected to interdict all the churches situated in the territory of those sacrilegious persons. You therefore humbly requested us to strengthen both sentences by apostolic authority.

Although we by no means approve as superstitious the opinion held by certain Greeks—that the spirit of the blessed Virgin Mary rests in the aforesaid image, and that for this reason they perhaps venerate it more than is fitting—and although we condemn as unlawful the agreement made concerning the division of relics and other matters, nevertheless, lest the crime of sacrilege remain uncorrected, we confirm by apostolic authority both sentences, namely those of interdict and excommunication, as having been reasonably pronounced; and we command that, all appeal set aside, they be firmly observed until due satisfaction has been made. Therefore let no one . . . . infringe this page of our confirmation and command, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of January, in the ninth year.]

CCXLIV. TO THE . . . . ELECT, AND THE CHAPTER OF THE CHURCH OF METHONE. [Note: [Col. 1077D]

Methone, according to Michael Antonius Baudrand, *Geography*, vol. I, p. 652, col. 1, is a city of the Peloponnese on the southern coast of Messenia. It is now called Modon, according to Sophianus; by the Turks Mutune, according to Leunclavius; it is still a celebrated place and a trading centre in the province of Belvedere. It has a very strong fortress and a spacious, safe harbour. Under Turkish dominion from the time of Bayezid II, it lies fifteen miles west-southwest of Corone, 120 from Nauplia, seventy-two west of Cape Taenarum, and 120 south of the city of Patras. It is an episcopal see under the archbishop of Patras and has had several bishops of the Latin rite.

In 1210 there was a certain bishop of Motone, or Methone, to whom, together with certain other bishops, are addressed letters 24 and 74 of Innocent III, book XIII, for the year 1210, vol. II of the Paluzzi edition. While that bishop, with Innocent’s permission, was making a pilgrimage to Compostela out of devotion, to visit the relics of Saint James the Apostle, certain persons of the dioceses of Methone, Corone, and Amyclae occupied possessions of the Church of Methone. Innocent ordered their restoration in letter 44, book XV, to the archbishops of Athens and Thebes and to the dean of Thebes, given on the fifth Ides—that is, 11 May—in the fifteenth year, A.D. 1212. On the same day he ordered the bishop of Methone that canons not residing in his church should be punished by withholding their benefices. In the same year, 1212, Innocent, by letter 55, to John, bishop of Methone, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity, dated the thirteenth Kalends of May—that is, 19 April—received the Church of Methone and its goods under the protection of the Apostolic See. From that latter letter we learn that the name of this bishop of Methone began with the letters “Jo.” and was probably John. See LE QUIEN, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1031.]

They are received under protection. (At Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1078C]

Since, when petition is made to us, etc., unto “assent,” we receive your church, with all the goods which it now reasonably possesses or may hereafter acquire by lawful means, God granting, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. In particular, we confirm to you—and through you to the same Church—by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, certain revenues which the . . . . emperor of Constantinople had customarily received from the aforesaid church, and which the nobleman W. of Campania, now prince of Achaea, is said to have remitted in perpetuity to that Church with the consent of our beloved son B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna [Note: [Col. 1079D] See letter 55 of book eight.], legate of the Apostolic See, as you justly and peaceably possess them. Therefore let no one . . . . infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCXLV. TO THE SAME. Their statute concerning tithes is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1079B]

It is customary to grant, etc., unto “bestow.” Therefore, since our beloved son B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna [Note: [Col. 1079D] See letter 55 of book eight.], legate of the Apostolic See, as was set forth before us on your behalf, decreed that from the lands, people, vineyards, gardens, olive-groves, hamlets, tithes, possessions, and other revenues of your Church, you, elect son, should receive two parts, while you, canons, should receive three parts: granting favourable assent to your petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority that statute, as prudently made and voluntarily accepted by you, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. Therefore let no one . . . . infringe this page of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCXLVI. TO THE SAME. That they are to apply the revenues of a vacant prebend to common uses. (At Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of February.)

Inclined by the just desires of petitioners, etc., unto “petitions,” we grant you by these present letters that, whenever any prebend in your Church happens to be vacant, you may freely apply its revenues to common uses, provided that on this pretext the prebend shall not remain vacant beyond the lawful period. Therefore let no one . . . . infringe this page of our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCXLVII. TO THE . . . . CHAPLAIN OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT NICHOLAS OF METHONE OUTSIDE THE HARBOUR. A revenue of forty hyperpyra, assigned to him by the prince of Achaea, is confirmed by apostolic authority. (At Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of February.)

Inclined by the just desires of petitioners, etc., unto “assent,” we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, for your devotion, the revenue of forty hyperpyra which our beloved son, the nobleman Ur. of Campania, prince of Achaea, mercifully assigned to you upon the death of the nobleman Henry Rondeth, of good memory, as you justly and peaceably possess it. Therefore let no one . . . . infringe this page of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCXLVIII. [Note: [Col. 1079D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, § 6.]. TO THE BISHOP OF PAMPLONA, P. OF CASTRO NOVO [Note: [Col. 1079D] These persons have already been mentioned frequently.], AND BROTHER RAD., MONK OF FONTEFROIDE, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That they are to proceed, in accordance with the former mandate, in the case concerning the king’s marriage [Note: [Col. 1080D] For the subject of this letter, see letter 91 of the present ninth book and the notes there.]. (At Saint Peter’s, 5 Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1080B]

We recall having formerly written to you [Note: [Col. 1080D] See the same place.] that our dearest son in Christ, P., illustrious king of Aragon, had informed us in a communication sent to us that, although he had in fact joined in the bond of matrimony our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman M., daughter of the late G. of Montpellier, it had eventually come to light that he had carnally known a certain woman related to that noblewoman in a near degree of consanguinity. Moreover, that same woman had a husband still living, with whom she had previously contracted marriage, namely the nobleman . . . . count of Comminges. Therefore that king, as a Catholic and God-fearing man, his conscience being seared over this matter and fearing imminent peril to his soul, thought that he ought to have recourse as quickly as possible to the oracle of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we instructed you that, if there should appear an accuser in this matter whose accusation was legally admissible, you should summon the parties, hear the case, and, if the parties gave their consent, procure its canonical conclusion, all obstacle of appeal removed. Otherwise, having committed the entire proceedings to writing, you were faithfully to send them to us under the attestation of your letters, assigning the parties a suitable term within which they should appear before us through suitable proctors to receive, God authorizing, a just judgment.

But the same king has lately caused us to be informed that the same noblewoman is also joined to him by a line of consanguinity. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic writings that, going as soon as possible to a place suitable for the parties and keeping God before your eyes, you proceed, in accordance with the form of the former mandate and all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, both upon the two matters previously set forth and also upon the articles of consanguinity and any other matters which the same accuser may see fit to propose according to law. And if not all . . . . two of you, etc.

[Col. 1081A] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCXLIX. [Note: [Col. 1081D] Raynaldus prints this letter under the year 1207, § 5; it is therefore presented here in brackets.]. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF SICILY. He rejoices that he has been released from the custody of unworthy persons and exhorts him to act well. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Kalends of February.)

What great gladness was poured into the treasury of the apostolic heart when we learned through the letters of your serenity that the hand of the Lord had freed you from the unworthy custody of those who had taken from you the care which your pious mother had assigned to you—as though a she-wolf should say to a lamb, “I shall suckle your lamb better than you”—you may judge from this: while, as it pleased the Lord, you remained in that condition, the gaze of our concern constantly turned itself toward you amid the anguish of many anxieties. For you caused us to waste away in most intense sorrow, as though you never ceased saying to us, “Upon you was I cast from my mother’s womb”; and because of you, to whom, moved by pity, we imagined ourselves saying, “Lord, I suffer violence,” we could not respond with prompt assistance.

Nor should it be thought strange that your detention so grieved us and your liberation so delighted us. For apart from the reason of the *bailia* [guardianship], which we undertook to execute not so much by maternal appointment as by right of the kingdom, we cannot fail in your guardianship and defence, since we must not turn our ears away from the voice of the Prophet saying to us, “You will be the helper of the orphan”; and we are bound especially to uphold you, an orphan, in your right.

This is why, in defending your justice, we have often spent sleepless nights and turned luncheon into supper, so that either by reflecting alone or deliberating with others we might discover useful means of restoring peace to your inheritance. How often swarms of messengers going and returning encountered one another, carrying through diverse regions of the world letters working for your peace! How often did letters to be sent for the tranquillity of you and your kingdom weary the pens of notaries and dry up the ink of scribes! How often did multitudes coming from every part of the world complain that their own affairs were delayed because of the pressing occupations in which we were engaged for your advantage! What shall we say of the many and great expenses which we have endeavoured to incur for the diverse and various needs of your kingdom? We have not spared even brothers and kinsmen; and although their labour has been very great, there is cause for rejoicing because it has sometimes proved fruitful.

Now therefore, since in your liberation God has almost made us forget all that has gone before, like the woman of the Gospel, who after bearing a son remembers her anguish no more, nothing remains for us but to rejoice. For although something appears still to be lacking for the fullness of your peace, we nevertheless hope that, if you cast your care upon the Lord and yield to the prudent counsels of those who, after your custody by violent men, have received you into the service of their diligent care, he through whom kings reign and princes govern will establish your throne and give you strength and power by which you may resist your enemies and govern your people happily.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your royal serenity, and command by apostolic writings, that, lifting your heart to God, you seek daily through prayers to be strengthened by him in body and mind. Rejoicing that you have been placed in the faithful custody either of those whom your mother assigned to have care of you, or of those who succeeded in the place of such persons as had died, attend to their mature counsels and endeavour to be instructed in moral disciplines. For we apply unwearied concern to your tranquillity and peace, and watch to promote the increase of your royal serenity by spiritual and temporal assistance, hoping in the Lord that, as a devoted son, you will always acknowledge in heart and deed the diligence and goodwill of the Apostolic See, your mother.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCL. [Note: [Col. 1081D]

A copy of this letter 250, and likewise of the following letter 251, which we had caused to be transcribed together with the others from Conti’s copy, has slipped from our hands by some accident unknown to us. We can therefore present here only the summary.

Raynaldus, under the year 1207, § 6.

“Furthermore, in the letters in which he congratulates the king’s household upon the king’s liberation, he says that, shortly before receiving their messengers, envoys of the king of Aragon had arrived with letters reporting that his sister was to be given in marriage to Frederick. He had also learned this from their messengers, and strongly commends Frederick to them. He likewise performed this office of commendation on Frederick’s behalf before bishops, counts, nobles, and others [letter 251]. Finally, he says that he transmitted Frederick’s letters and his own to the king of Aragon through the latter’s envoys, and urged him to prepare with the greatest care everything necessary for conducting his sister to her royal bridegroom.”]

TO THE . . . . MEMBERS OF THE KING OF SICILY’S HOUSEHOLD. On the same matter.

CCLI. [Note: [Col. 1082D] See the note on the immediately preceding letter.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND PRELATES, AND TO THE COUNTS, THROUGHOUT THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. That they are to obey and support the king of Sicily.

CCLII. [Note: [Col. 1082D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, § 20.]. TO THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS [Note: [Col. 1082D] See letter 11 of book three, note.]. That he is to cause acts undertaken against the property of his church to be annulled. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1082D]

By the authority of the present letters, after “The just requests of petitioners, etc., unto ‘fulfil,’” we decree that, since you have travelled to the western regions for the assistance of the Holy Land and the strengthening of the empire of Constantinople, enduring many labours and expenses, you shall not suffer loss from that for which you ought rather to earn favour. Accordingly, if after your departure any prejudice has been undertaken against you or against the church of Saint George of Constantinople entrusted to you, concerning the Hospital or other property belonging to that church, it shall be annulled and restored to its due condition. Therefore let no one . . . . infringe this page of our constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCLIII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM [Note: [Col. 1083D] See letter 222 of book seven.], LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. The deadline for appearing before the Roman curia is extended. (At Saint Peter’s, 3 Nones of February.)

[Col. 1083B]

A humble request has been made to us on your behalf: since, in the case concerning the church of Tyre, which is pending between the Church of Jerusalem and the Church of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1083D] See letter 505 of book one—Baluzio, vol. I, p. 290.], we had fixed for you and our venerable brother, the . . . . patriarch of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1083D] See letter 53 of book nine.], a peremptory term of three years from the past feast of Saint Luke; and since, by our permission, you might extend that term as far as you could agree with the same patriarch, or at least until the octave of Epiphany following the said three-year period if the other party consented, because at the time fixed for you and that patriarch you cannot conveniently appear before us in person or through suitable representatives: we, taking account of the necessities presently pressing upon both Churches, graciously grant the request.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third Nones of February, in the ninth year.

CCLIV. [Note: [Col. 1083D] Fragments of this letter are found among the Decretals: first, book I, title 22, “On Travelling Clerics,” chapter 3; second, book V, title 9, “On Apostates and Those Repeating Baptism,” chapter 3. The portions read in both places are here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are supplied.]. TO THE SAME. A response to an inquiry concerning doubts requiring clarification. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Kalends of February.)

[The discretion of your brotherhood requested instruction from the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1083D] These words are absent from the Decretals, but are found in Pithou’s additions.] whether you ought to permit those clerics [Note: [Col. 1083D] The Decretals omit this word.] who come to the region of Jerusalem without letters of recommendation to celebrate the divine offices, [Note: [Col. 1084D] What follows, distinguished in italic type, is absent from the Decretals but is found in Pithou’s additions.] since very many of them, whose canonical ordination is not established, presume immediately upon arrival to celebrate without requesting permission?]

Others also, whom public report declares to be monks or regular canons, go about in secular dress and falsely represent themselves as secular clerics. Since it cannot be proved of them that they have professed the religious life, you requested an apostolic response whether they ought to be sent back across the sea, so that by letters of their bishops and of the abbots of the monasteries in which they are said to have assumed the regular habit, they may demonstrate that they are not monks or regular canons; or whether they ought instead to be tolerated in secular dress.

[But, commending your solicitude in the Lord, we answer your brotherhood on the first article [Note: [Col. 1084D] These words are absent from the Decretals but are found in Pithou’s additions.] that, unless you have lawful proof, either by letters or witnesses, of the canonical ordination of those who are entirely unknown, you ought not permit them [Note: [Col. 1084D] The Decretals add *in*; Pithou observes in the margin that this word is lacking in the ancient manuscripts.] to celebrate among your people. Yet if perhaps some of them should wish privately, out of devotion, to celebrate, you may tolerate it. [Note: [Col. 1084D] Thus far in the Decretals, book I, title 22.]]]

[[Note: [Col. 1084D] See the Decretals, book V, title 9, chapter 3.] On the second article, however, we have considered that your inquiry should receive this answer: clerics who are accused of the crime of apostasy, namely of having cast off the regular habit, are not to be tolerated in secular dress, but are to be compelled by ecclesiastical discipline until, if proof fails by which the accusation may be removed, they arrange to make canonical purgation. [Note: [Col. 1084D] Thus far in the Decretals, book V, title 9, chapter 3.]]

Furthermore, you asked whether, since the houses of the Temple and the Hospital and other religious places grant immunity to those who flee to them after committing crimes, and under this pretext of refuge murders and many other enormities are committed in those regions, persons fleeing to the aforesaid places because of their offences may, with the integrity of their limbs preserved, be confined in a public prison and perpetually maintained upon the bread of affliction and water of distress.

You also asked, subsequently, whether, when debtors who have mortgaged their houses demand that creditors occupying those houses should credit against the principal as much as the debtors would have received from others had they leased the same houses, and no small scandal arises from this, the creditors may, in order to avoid such scandal, be tolerated in not crediting against the principal what the debtors would have received from others as annual rent.

But since we know that you are sufficiently instructed in law and are by no means ignorant of what the law is in the aforesaid matters, we have not considered it necessary to answer your inquiry concerning them, lest perhaps our answer should too strongly oppose your intention.

[Col. 1085A] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCLV. TO THE . . . . BISHOP OF ELY [Note: [Col. 1085D] See letter 54 of book five, note.]. That he is to absolve the subdeacon P. from his vow. (At Saint Peter’s, 7 Ides of February.)

Approaching the Apostolic See, the beloved son Henry of Wiceton, subdeacon of the diocese of Lincoln, humbly represented to us that, although formerly—more out of affection and favor for King Richard of illustrious memory, his father, whose clerk he then was, when that king undertook a pilgrimage—than from any other devotion, he had taken up the sign of the cross, nevertheless, because of serious impediments which fortuitously arose, he has not hitherto [Col. 1085B] fulfilled the vow he made. Now, overtaken by old age, the sign of which his face, sprinkled with the white of gray hairs, declares, he has, as he asserts, become unable to travel. Therefore, because he feared that, if compelled in his incapacity to cross the sea to the province of Jerusalem, danger might ensue for him and no assistance might thereby reach the Holy Land, he humbly petitioned us mercifully to absolve him from the labor of pilgrimage—especially since he wishes, according to his means, to send suitable aid to the Holy Land within appropriate terms. He promises that, on the coming feast of Saint John the Baptist, he will assign twenty-five marks; then, on the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, twenty-five pounds; and afterward, on that same feast in the following year, [Col. 1085C] twenty-five pounds sterling for the aid of the Holy Land, in England, to whomever we shall wish.

We therefore, considering the aforesaid impediments and wishing to spare him the labors of old age, since perhaps he may serve his Creator and Lord more usefully in this way, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, supported by our authority, you absolve the aforesaid subdeacon from such a vow. First, however, you shall receive from him sufficient security that he will arrange to pay the aforesaid contribution for the Holy Land to the beloved son, brother . . . . . . , master of the house of the Temple in London, within the prescribed terms; and you shall enjoin upon him that henceforth he devote himself more diligently to works of piety.

[Col. 1085D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh Ides of February, in the ninth year.

CCLVI. TO THE BISHOP OF FLORENCE. [Note: [Col. 1085D] See letter 156 of book VIII.] That he should promote F., a deacon, to holy orders. (At Saint Peter’s, eighth Ides of February.)

The beloved son F., a deacon and your parishioner, appearing before us, humbly represented that, because his enemies alleged that he was the son of a priest, you were unwilling either to promote him to the order of priesthood or to permit him to be promoted by another, although neither that allegation nor any [Col. 1086A] other charge had been proved against him.

Therefore, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the deacon has publicly been tainted by such a reproach, and you cannot lawfully establish the truth of it, then, after receiving his canonical purgation, provided that no other canonical impediment stands in the way, you shall not delay, on that account, to promote him to the office of priest. For although it is not the reproach of a crime, it is nevertheless the reproach of a defect which prevents promotion to holy orders.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth Ides of February, in the ninth year.

CCLVII. TO THE CHAPTER OF VASTIN. Certain arrangements made in their church by the chapter are tolerated. (At Saint Peter’s, seventh Ides of February.)

[Col. 1086B]

Unless both those men who made the arrangement and those concerning whom the arrangement was made in your church in the matter of the priory had been prudent and honorable men, we should have regarded that arrangement as highly suspect because of the pernicious example it might set. Thus, after a prolonged dispute, the determination concerning one of the two elected men—that he should have the priory—appears to have been made according to justice under delegated jurisdiction. The determination concerning the other—that he should receive annually twenty pounds from the revenues of the priory—appears to have been prescribed as a matter of prudent provision under arbitral power, since the matter had been submitted to the delegates by compromise; and, while retaining the authority entrusted to them, they acknowledge that they made this arrangement for the good of peace and [Col. 1086C] utility.

Since, therefore, this arrangement has been accepted by all, and since the prior and chapter may lawfully provide such an allowance from their revenues for the aforesaid reasons—not by an agreement of the parties, certainly, but by order of the judges—we tolerate it subject to this limitation: the dignity of the priory shall not be burdened with the payment of forty pounds, but the person of the prior shall remain liable, lest some division of the priory’s revenues seem to have been made, so that, upon the prior’s death, his successor shall in no way be bound to pay the forty pounds.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh Ides of February, in the ninth year.

CCLVIII. [Note: [Col. 1085D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §3.] TO R., BISHOP, [Note: [Col. 1086D] See letter 93 of book V, note.] AND TO THE CLERGY OF VITERBO. That they should restore what J. lost in defense of the faith and which had been taken away by the Patarenes. (At Saint Peter’s, Nones of February.)

[Col. 1086D]

We have received the tearful complaint of the beloved son John Boni: whereas our venerable brother . . . , bishop, [Note: [Col. 1086D] See letter 18 of book VIII, note.] and the beloved son C., archdeacon of Orvieto, had firmly commanded you under our authority that, unless . . . . the magistrate of Viterbo caused to be restored to the aforesaid John, within a fixed period, the things which the Patarenes had taken from him [Col. 1087A] out of hatred for the Catholic faith, you should cease from every ecclesiastical office until he had received full satisfaction for the aforesaid matters; yet you, although he has received no satisfaction in any respect, disregarding their command with deaf ears, have not ceased to celebrate the divine offices.

Since, therefore, by the office imposed upon us we ought not to fail one who is known to have incurred such loss in defense of the Catholic faith, we firmly command your whole body by apostolic letters: either, as the aforesaid bishop and archdeacon commanded you under our authority, cease from celebrating the divine offices, or furnish from your own resources to the aforesaid J. suitable compensation for the aforesaid losses.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of February, [Col. 1087B] in the ninth year.

CCLIX. [Note: [Col. 1087D] Fragments of this letter are found among the Decretals, book I, title 38, *On Procurators*, chapter 4. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets. Words distinguished by italic type are absent from the Decretals or indicate variant readings.] TO . . . . . . , BISHOP OF CHALON-SUR-SAÔNE, [Note: [Col. 1087D] See letter 16 of book V, note.] AND . . . . . . , BISHOP OF CHÂLONS, [Note: [Col. 1087D] See letter 137 of book V, note.] AND TO . . . . . . , PRIOR OF CLAIRVAUX. He entrusts to them for decision the case of the bishop of Toul. (At Saint Peter’s, Kalends of February.)

[Our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Toul, [Note: [Col. 1087D] See letter 13 of book V, note.] appearing in our presence, complained tearfully that, whereas formerly, to conduct the case pending between himself and . . . , dean of Toul of good memory, [Note: [Col. 1087D] What we noted on letter 87 of book VIII must be compared in every respect.] concerning waste of ecclesiastical property, excommunication, perjury, and certain other [Note: [Col. 1087D] Add “crimes,” a word which Pithou testifies is absent in all the ancient codices, in the margin.] crimes, he had appointed the priests W. and J. [Note: [Col. 1087D] The Decretals: T. and G.] as procurators [Col. 1087C] and sent them to the Apostolic See. Having afterward become doubtful of their fidelity, he revoked within a short time the mandate which he had given them. But although they had received letters revoking the mandate, they nevertheless proceeded in the matter and, acting as procurators, entered into litigation with his adversary, namely Joffrid, archdeacon of Toul. Finally, to the beloved sons G., [Note: [Col. 1087D] The Decretals alone read “to the Parisian archdeacon.”] archdeacon of Paris, Master R. of Corzon, canon of Noyon, and R., penitentiary of Saint Victor, [Note: [Col. 1087D] The Decretals read “colleagues” in place of “Master . . . penitentiary.”] they obtained, to his prejudice, our letters [Note: [Col. 1088D] See the same letter, book VIII, 87.] [Note: [Col. 1088D] The Decretals read *impetrarunt*, “they obtained.” What follows, distinguished by italic type, is absent from the Decretals but is read in Pithou’s additions.]

Although their citation was not served upon that bishop, nevertheless, when he learned that the case between himself and the said dean and archdeacon had been entrusted to them, [Col. 1087D] he hastened into their presence. When the [Col. 1088A] bishop, after much effort, had obtained a copy of our rescript and carefully examined its tenor with prudent men, he was greatly astonished that the aforesaid priests had obtained such letters as procurators. [Note: [Col. 1088D] These words are absent in Pithou.] To prove that they were false procurators, he requested from those judges a delay; but they, [Note: [Col. 1088D] The Decretals read: “when he had requested, they.”] regarding the exception raised as useless and superfluous, refused to grant him time for its proof. Therefore the bishop had recourse to the benefit of appeal and withdrew from the presence of those judges, appealing from them.

But they, paying no heed to the appeal, proceeded in the matter, [Note: [Col. 1088D] Pithou reads, “but they nevertheless,” and shortly afterward “him” for “the bishop.”] and, without joinder of issue and setting aside the order of law, presumed to receive witnesses against the bishop and, [Col. 1088B] removing him from the Church of Toul by sentence,] contrary to the form of our mandate, granted to the chapter of Toul free power to elect a bishop for itself.

When the said bishop and P., archdeacon, had recently come before us on this account and had litigated for some time before us concerning the proceedings of the judges, the bishop produced thirteen witnesses: certain abbots and monks of the black and white orders, and certain secular clerics. After they had been carefully examined, it clearly appeared from their depositions that, when the aforesaid bishop requested time to prove the exception described above, the aforesaid judges denied it to him; and that, although the bishop on that account appealed to the Apostolic See, [Col. 1088C] they nevertheless proceeded in the case after the appeal had been lodged with us.

[Although we could scarcely have believed that the oft-mentioned judges, being learned, prudent, and honorable men, had proceeded in the manner described—especially since in the report which they sent to us they made no mention of such an exception having been raised—yet, because the aforesaid bishop, through religious and honorable men alike, concerning whom it is not credible that, forgetful of their salvation and despising the sanctity of an oath, they should have borne false witness, gave us full assurance concerning the matters alleged; and considering that an exception of false procuratorship may be raised not only before sentence but even after sentence, according to canonical and civil enactments, [Note: [Col. 1088D] Pithou omits these words, as also shortly afterward the words “by counsel of our brethren.”] since, when it is proved, the judgment [Col. 1089A] and the controversy are deemed null and of no force, we have, by counsel of our brethren, pronounced the proceedings of the aforesaid judges void, restoring the case to] the state in which it stood when it began to be heard before us.

Thus the same bishop, as G., archbishop of Reims of good memory, [Note: [Col. 1089C] In 1206, when Guy—on whom see letter 116 of book VII, note—archbishop of Reims, had set out for Flanders to perform the office of his legation, he died of dysentery at Ghent, says the true Chronicle, in the monastery of Saint Bavo, on the third day before the Kalends of August. [Col. 1089D] On his deathbed he absolved the chapter of Reims, which he had placed under interdict; and the metropolitan see summoned Theobald of Pierrepont, although the election was obstructed.] legate of the Apostolic See, had decreed, shall be suspended from the administration of temporalities as suspected of waste, and shall be forbidden to exercise spiritual functions as defamed for perjury. And lest, meanwhile, the Church of Toul be left bereft of an administrator’s office, we have appointed the beloved son, the abbot of Saint Urban, [Note: [Col. 1089D] Walter, abbot of Saint Urban in the diocese of Châlons, occurs in tables from 1199 to 1221; but there appear to have been two abbots of Saint Urban of this name. One is mentioned in the necrology of Dervaux on the third Ides of October, the other on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IX, col. 926.] as administrator in both spheres.

But since the said J., archdeacon, has accused the bishop before us of waste and perjury, [Col. 1089B] adding that after the sentence of suspension the bishop presumed to celebrate divine offices; and since, after lawful joinder of issue, the archdeacon has produced certain witnesses; nevertheless, because concerning these articles the truth could not be fully established for us, we have decided to entrust the case to your examination. Sending you enclosed under our seal the depositions received, we command you by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties to a suitable and safe place—or, if you cannot find a more suitable and safer place, at Langres—you receive the witnesses whom either party shall choose to produce. After the depositions have been solemnly published and the grounds and defenses both of the bishop and of the other party have been heard, bring the case, if it proceeds by the will of the parties, to a canonical conclusion without appeal. Thus, if it is lawfully established before you that the property of the Church of Toul was alienated through the bishop’s fault, take care to remove him from that church.

Otherwise, since the alienation is already established, even though the bishop casts the blame upon others, because he is nevertheless held under vehement suspicion and seriously defamed in this matter, prescribe for him a canonical purgation. [Col. 1090A] But if the parties do not consent to have the question decided by you, send the case, most fully prepared, to our presence, and set the parties a suitable term within which they shall appear before us to receive sentence.

Moreover, inquire diligently how heavily the aforesaid bishop found the bishopric of Toul burdened with debts, how much of that debt he has paid, whether he has improved the bishopric in any respects and to what extent, and whether he wishes and is able to restore the alienated property without any sale or diminution; so that, should a report perhaps have to be made to us concerning all these things, you may make us more fully informed by your letters. But if witnesses named by either party on the article of waste withdraw themselves [Col. 1090B] through favor, hatred, or fear, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, etc. Notwithstanding no letters obtained from the Apostolic See except by consent of the parties. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCLX. TO . . . . . . , BISHOP OF LANGRES, [Note: [Col. 1089D] Robert II, surnamed of Châtillon, and, as the Chronicle of Langres maintains, probably brother of Lambert of Châtillon-sur-Seine, knight, and uncle of Hugh, lord of Tilchâtel, was first treasurer and dean, then, after the death of Hilduin—on whom see letter 141 of book V, note—bishop of the Church of Langres. He is mentioned in several charters from 1264 to 1208, in which year, having set out against the Albigensians with Count Milo of Bar-sur-Seine and a great armed force of nobles, he departed this life shortly afterward. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 595.] AND . . . . . . , BISHOP OF CHÂLONS, [Note: [Col. 1090C] See letter 137 of book V, note.] AND TO . . . . . . , PRIOR OF CLAIRVAUX. He entrusts to them the case concerning the primicery of Toul. [Note: [Col. 1090C] Compare in every respect what is written by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 1061: “After the death of Stephen, primicery of Toul—whose name is read in documents from 1111 to 1126—the dignity of primicery was extinguished and united to the chapter by Bishop Riquin, who held office from 1107 to 1126, or 1127. Nevertheless, under the pontificate of Odo of Vadenomont, who held office from 1192 to 1197, Theodoric of Lorraine, son of Duke Matthew I, arranged to have himself promoted to that dignity. Simon, archdeacon of Toul, also obtained provisions from the Apostolic See after Theodoric’s death. Judges were appointed in this matter and gave judgment in Simon’s favor. But the supreme pontiff, to whom the chapter appealed, gave a very different judgment: he ordered that the dignity remain extinguished. From that time, therefore, the office of dean was the first dignity of the chapter.”] (At Saint Peter’s, Kalends of February.)

When the beloved sons Sy., archdeacon and procurator of the chapter of Toul, [Col. 1090C] came to the Apostolic See, we granted them as auditor our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Ostia. [Note: [Col. 1090C] Compare in every respect what is written by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 1061: “After the death of Stephen, primicery of Toul—whose name is read in documents from 1111 to 1126—the dignity of primicery was extinguished and united to the chapter by Bishop Riquin, who held office from 1107 to 1126, or 1127. Nevertheless, under the pontificate of Odo of Vadenomont, who held office from 1192 to 1197, Theodoric of Lorraine, son of Duke Matthew I, arranged to have himself promoted to that dignity. Simon, archdeacon of Toul, also obtained provisions from the Apostolic See after Theodoric’s death. Judges were appointed in this matter and gave judgment in Simon’s favor. But the supreme pontiff, to whom the chapter appealed, gave a very different judgment: he ordered that the dignity remain extinguished. From that time, therefore, the office of dean was the first dignity of the chapter.”]

In his presence the said archdeacon alleged that formerly the beloved son Master Wls, our subdeacon, and H. and F., canons of Toul, had informed us that the primicery and the scholasteria in the Church of Toul had been vacant for so long that the grant of those personates had devolved into our hands. We therefore commanded the beloved sons, the abbots of . . . Haute-Seille [Note: [Col. 1090D] See what was noted on letter 8 of book [Col. 1091D] VIII, note; and add, if desired, what is read in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 1373: “Henry I, abbot of Haute-Seille, in 1197 appears in a donation conferred upon the monastery of Bongart; likewise still in 1200, in a donation made to the monastery of Stultzerborn [Col. 1092D] by Conrad of Harburg. He is perhaps the same H. who is mentioned in 1225. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. XIII, col. 1373.”] and . . . Belles-Prés, [Col. 1091A] [Note: [Col. 1092D] Rudolph, in 1200 and 1210, when he obtained from Otto, abbot of the Black Monastery, a plot of land near Marsal . . . . Ibid., col. 1369.] and the dean of the monastery of . . . Colombe, to investigate the truth in this matter. If it appeared that those personates had been vacant for so long that, under the statutes of the Lateran Council, their grant had devolved to us, they were to institute in those personates, in our stead, suitable persons from the Church of Toul or elsewhere, and cause them to possess them peacefully.

The judges, executing the apostolic mandate, cited the parties before them. On the appointed day, when Master W. and F. appeared before them, John, a priest, presented himself in their presence with letters of the chapter of Toul, in which the chapter excused itself for being unable to come, without danger to property and persons, [Col. 1091B] to the place appointed by those judges because of . . . , duke of Lorraine, who had declared them his enemies. The priest wished to establish this fact by his own oath and requested that a place be designated to which the canons of Toul could safely come.

After Master W. and the priest had litigated over this for some time, the priest, when asked to take the oath which he had previously offered, finally refused, and, uttering an appeal, presented letters of the chapter in which he had been appointed procurator only for the purpose of appealing. The aforesaid judges, however, regarding the excuses offered by the priest and the appeal lodged as dilatory, took counsel with prudent men and received the witnesses [Col. 1091C] whom Master W. and F. wished to produce. They set another day at Saint-Èvre for the aforesaid chapter. Since the chapter did not care to appear in court even on that day, the judges solemnly published the depositions; and, since it appeared to them that the primicery in the Church of Toul had been vacant so long that its grant belonged to us, they conferred it in our stead upon the aforesaid archdeacon S. The archdeacon requested that this grant be confirmed by apostolic authority.

But G., the said procurator of the chapter, answered on the other side that this grant and the proceedings of the aforesaid judges ought rightly to be revoked, since they had proceeded after an appeal had been lawfully made to us on account of various [Col. 1091D] grievances. For at the first citation they summoned the chapter by a peremptory edict; and when thereafter the chapter sent its own messenger to appear before them, although that messenger diligently requested that a safe place be assigned to the parties, alleging that, because of dangers on the roads and deadly ambushes, the chapter could neither come to the appointed place nor send adequate representatives, the judges nevertheless disdained to admit such an excuse. Therefore the messenger, as he had been instructed, [Col. 1092A] had recourse to the protection of appeal.

Furthermore, the procurator added that the proceedings of those judges should be adjudged invalid because they had proceeded to pronounce sentence without joinder of issue. In reply, the archdeacon’s party asserted that no heed should have been paid to such an appeal, since it had been made not on legitimate grounds but solely for delay.
