For, although the chapter had been summoned by lawful citations, it sent a mere messenger rather than a suitable representative. Having alleged the chapter’s excuse and offered his own oath in support of it, he later refused, when required, to swear it. Since, therefore, the excuse offered by that messenger rightly appeared deceptive, [Col. 1092B] the appeal lodged upon it was rightly to be rejected—especially because the messenger presented letters of the chapter expressly stating that he had been sent only to appeal.

Nor, that party answered, could it harm their case that the judges proceeded without joinder of issue, since they had been entrusted not with cognizance of a lawsuit but solely with an inquiry into the truth; consequently, the formalities of judicial procedure were not required in that inquiry. To this the chapter’s party replied that, although the whole solemnity of law is not observed in certain inquiries, the order of law nevertheless ought to have been observed in an inquiry of this kind. For certain persons were peaceful possessors of the properties and revenues [Col. 1092C] formerly belonging to the primicery, and they neither ought nor could be despoiled of them without due legal process.

Furthermore, even if the said judges were able to proceed without cognizance of the case, they nevertheless chose rather to hear the case solemnly, summoning the canons of Toul before their tribunal as a party. The chapter’s party further alleged that the rescript obtained for the aforesaid judges had been procured through a false representation. For it was evident that, by the common consent and unanimous will of the canons of Toul, it had been established that the dignity of primicery should no longer exist in that church, the revenues and possessions of the primicery having been distributed among the canons; and that this establishment was afterward confirmed by our predecessor Pope Alexander of good memory. [Col. 1092D] Thus the primicery itself had not been vacant for a long time, as had been represented to us by a false allegation.

To this the archdeacon’s party answered that, since that dignity had been instituted there for the public and common honor of the Church of Toul, it could not be abolished in that church without the authority of the Apostolic See. Nor could a confirmation obtained for so unlawful an enactment make valid that which was invalid by law itself. Furthermore, after all these events, [Col. 1093A] the same canons collectively elected Archdeacon Terric as primicery, and he was afterward confirmed by apostolic authority. Consequently, they appear not only tacitly to have renounced the confirmation which they had obtained, but also to have revoked their own enactment.

But the chapter’s party replied that what was done concerning T. could not prejudice them, since he had usurped the office of primicery for himself not through a canonical election, but rather by intrusion.

We therefore, having more fully understood these and other matters which the parties took care to set forth before the aforesaid bishop, annul, by counsel of our brethren, what was done by the aforesaid judges as a disorderly presumption, and, with the assent of both parties, entrust the case to your examination. [Col. 1093B] Therefore, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth. If it is established before you that the canons of Toul jointly enacted that the office of primicery should no longer exist in the Church of Toul, and that this enactment was afterward confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See, cause it to remain in full force, unless the said canons afterward acted contrary to it by electing someone as primicery.

But if it cannot be established that such an enactment was made or confirmed by apostolic authority as stated; or if it is sufficiently shown that the canons, after that confirmation or before it, acted contrary to the aforesaid enactment, remit the case to our presence, faithfully reporting to us by your [Col. 1093C] letters what you find concerning these matters. Notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See except by consent of the parties. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

CCLXI. [Note: [Col. 1093D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §11.] TO THE CHAPTER AND THE ENTIRE CLERGY OF MAGDEBURG. The election of an archbishop is confirmed. [Note: [Col. 1094D] See letter 22 of book IX.] (At Saint Peter’s, sixth Ides of February.)

That daily urgency—the care, namely, of all the Churches—which surrounds the ministry of apostolic service especially moves us diligently to attend to their consolation and benignly to fulfill their just desires [Col. 1093D] with swift effect, when they are deprived of the comfort of pastors. Thus they may not suffer loss in spiritual and temporal things through lack of a pastor, nor may the Lord’s flock be abandoned to the bites of wolves if there is none to keep the watches of the night over it.

Accordingly, when our venerable brother Albert, your archbishop, then elect, [Note: [Col. 1094D] See the same place.] came before us, we wished, with paternal solicitude, to provide for the Church of Magdeburg as for a special daughter. For it has always shown devotion to its mother, the most holy Roman Church, not only in prosperity but also in adversity. Long ago, after carefully hearing and understanding what the beloved sons . . . provost of Saint Sebastian, . . . . . provost of Saint Mary, and . . . . provost of Mildensee, together with C. and C., canons of the greater church, Master Germand, canon of Saint Nicholas, and Litulf, canon of Saint Peter, all canons of Magdeburg, had diligently set before us both orally and in writing, we learned for certain that the election of Albert had been canonical. We therefore decided to confirm it by apostolic authority, supplying from the fullness of our power any defect which it might have had because certain persons participated in the celebration of that election who had fallen into the bond of simple excommunication solely by participation, as was alleged before us by Rudolph of Ranies and Burchard of Glinde, canons of Magdeburg.

And because nothing should bring delay or difficulty to rightful arrangements, [Col. 1094B] lest pastoral care be long lacking to the Lord’s flock, on the Saturday of the Ember Days before the Lord’s Nativity we ordained him priest with our own hands, and on the following day took care to consecrate him bishop. We shall send him back to you, already adorned with the pallium, with the fullness of our favor, hoping in the Lord who called him to His ministry that, through his diligent prudence and circumspect care, the Church of Magdeburg will receive welcome growth in spiritual and temporal things.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort you all, commanding you by apostolic letters, that henceforth, giving heed to him as to your father and archbishop, and rendering him the [Col. 1094C] reverence and obedience both due and devoted, you humbly receive his salutary admonitions and devoutly observe his commands. Thus, knowing your devotion, he may be bound more fervently to pursue, as a diligent shepherd, the things which will promote your advantage and salvation; and you may likewise deserve to receive a worthy reward from Him who prefers obedience to sacrifices.

But because, by our command, he is awaiting the arrival of those who, as we have learned, are to come before us concerning the state of the Empire, we will and command that, during his absence, you show him in all things the deference which you know should be shown [Col. 1094D] to one present. And, attempting nothing before his return concerning the ordering of your churches to his prejudice, wait graciously and humbly for his arrival.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth Ides of February, in the ninth year.

CCLXII. TO . . . . . . , PROVOST, AND THE CANONS OF SAINT MARY OF MAGDEBURG. The hospital of Saint Alexis is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, sixth Ides of February.)

To the just desires of petitioners, etc., as far as “assent”: we confirm by apostolic authority, following the example of Pope Alexander of blessed memory, our predecessor, in favor of your devotion, the hospital of Saint Alexis, situated beside the aforesaid church [Col. 1095A], with its appurtenances, as you justly and peacefully possess it; and we strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. We decree that it shall be lawful for no person at all . . . our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth Ides of February, in the ninth year.

CCLXIII. [Note: [Col. 1095D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1207, §11.] TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS. Privileges granted to them by the Roman pontiffs are confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, fifth Ides of February.)

To grant effective relief to just petitioners is required both by the force of equity and by the order of reason, especially when equity supports the petitioners’ wishes and utility accompanies them. On your behalf humble supplication has been made to us that we should deem worthy of apostolic confirmation for your church the liberties, immunities, reasonable customs, and other rights which have been granted to you by the privileges of certain Roman pontiffs. Pope Innocent, of happy memory, our predecessor, ordained that in your church the canonical order should be observed for all time according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institution of Norbert, of good memory, Archbishop of Magdeburg; and that the same church should enjoy such liberty that, burdened by no yoke of undue subjection, it should answer only to the Archbishop of Magdeburg. In letters sent to the said Archbishop N., he granted this in the following words:

“We decree that religious observance be preserved for all time in the Church of Blessed Mary at Magdeburg according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and your institution. We further decree that the same church remain in such liberty that it shall have regard to no one save you, dearest brother N., and your successors, the Archbishops of Magdeburg, and that it be burdened by no yoke of undue subjection; but, supported by the privilege of your liberty, it shall answer only to its own archbishop in every matter.”

Moreover, Pope Lucius, of pious memory, following in his footsteps, confirmed by his privilege the liberty granted to the same church in these words:

“We confirm by apostolic authority that liberty which was granted to you by our predecessor Innocent, of happy memory, so that you shall have regard to no one, concerning order or any other matter, save the Archbishop of Magdeburg and his successors.”

Furthermore, Pope Celestine, of good memory, decreed that the church itself should remain in the liberty which it is known to have possessed from the time of the aforesaid Archbishop N. until then, in these words:

“We ordain that the Church of Saint Mary at Magdeburg remain in that liberty in which it is known to have existed from the time of the late Archbishop N. up to the present.”

The same predecessor of ours also strictly forbade the abbot and brethren of Prémontré to burden your church with undue exactions, in this form:

“Therefore, unwilling to permit anyone rashly to act contrary to the grants of our predecessors, by the authority of these presents we more strictly prohibit you from demanding from the Church of Saint Mary at Magdeburg—which you ought reverently to embrace in mutual charity and sincerity—that obedience of subjection which, contrary to what is known to have been reasonably established from its first foundation by the most reverend man N., formerly Archbishop of Magdeburg, you have not rendered to it, nor have your predecessors rendered to it, from the beginning of your order down to these times; nor from the other churches of its diocese. Rather, more earnestly imitating those things which belong to peace and concord, avoid the spur of reciprocal contention, since from it come both the loss of souls and the dissolution of the unity of fraternal love and religious observance. Instead, by the ancient exhortation of visitation and the love of fraternal charity, visit one another in a spirit of gentleness, not in any swelling pride or arrogance, so that religious observance may continually flourish among you and the spur of discord may, with the help of heavenly grace, be removed from your midst.”

[Note: Col. 1095D. Thus it is read in the copy.]

Therefore, graciously assenting to your petitions, approving the grants made to you and your church by the aforesaid Roman pontiffs, we confirm them by apostolic authority and strengthen them with the protection of this present writing, just as we have seen them contained in their authentic instruments and as you now peacefully possess them. We more strictly prohibit anyone of the Premonstratensian order, or of any other order, from rashly molesting that church or yourselves contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation and prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth Ides of February, in the ninth year.

CCLXIV. … TO THE PROVOST [Note: Col. 1095D. See letter 96 of the seventh book, note.] … THE CHANTER [Note: Col. 1095D. See letter 149 of the fifth book.], AND THE MASTER OF THE SCHOOLS OF RHEIMS. That they compel the Bishop of Tournai to provide for the subdeacon J., according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate already issued concerning this matter. (At Saint Peter’s, the third Nones of January.)

[Col. 1096D]

At the petition of our beloved son J., subdeacon, concerning provision for him by the Bishop of Tournai, of good memory [Note: Col. 1096D. See letter 4 of the third book, note.], who had ordained him subdeacon, we recall that we sent apostolic letters according to the general form. And when our beloved sons A., Abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi, and P., Abbot of Mareuil, and D., Prior of Albinac, in the diocese of Arras—whom we had granted to the same subdeacon as monitors—had found him suitable, as the letters transmitted to us by them stated, and the same bishop had, by the Lord’s disposition, gone to his death, the aforesaid monitors of his, having recourse to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Tournai [Note: Col. 1098D. See letter 113 of the seventh book, note.], successor of the said bishop, carefully undertook to admonish him to make provision for the subdeacon according to the form of the apostolic mandate. But that bishop passed over their mandates and admonitions with deaf ears.

[Note: Col. 1096D. Asso, formerly Prior of Albinac, three miles from the city of Arras, became abbot of the monastery of Mont-Saint-Éloi; after eleven years of government, he passed to the better life on 19 April 1208. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. XIII, col. 428.]

[Note: Col. 1097D. Peter I, an Englishman by birth and canon of Arrouaise, formerly abbot of Dondelville and of Valenciennes, was head of the Church of Mareuil in November 1210, according to the cartulary of Strumi. After governing for fourteen years, he resigned his office in 1216—not, as Locrius wrongly has it, in 1221, as follows from what will be said and from what has already been said—and returned to the place of his profession. There, surviving a few years, old and full of days, he rested in peace. In 1203, the abbot of Mareuil was exempted from the jurisdiction of the aldermen by letters of Radulf, Bishop of Arras. Ibid., col. 444.]

[Note: Col. 1097D. His name was Desiderius. For Desiderius, formerly dean of Saint Peter’s at Lille and then Prior of Albinac, became Abbot of the monastery of Mont-Saint-Éloi after Asso, of whom above, note.]

Therefore, unwilling to leave unfulfilled what we began, for God and on account of God, concerning provision for poor clerics, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings that you carefully admonish and induce the said bishop to provide for the aforesaid subdeacon according to the tenor of our letters; otherwise, setting aside every contradiction and appeal, compel him to do this by such coercion as is appropriate. If all of you cannot be present to carry this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third Nones of January, in the ninth year.

CCLXV. TO THE BISHOP OF LANGRES [Note: Col. 1098D. See letter 260 of the ninth book, note.]. Reply concerning the privileges of the chapel of the Duke of Dijon. (At Saint Peter’s, the fourteenth Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1097C]

Since the chapel of the noble man, the Duke of Dijon, is said to enjoy a privilege of this kind: that no archbishop or bishop may dare to pronounce against the persons of the canons of the same chapel a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or even interdict [Note: Col. 1098D. See letter 61 of the seventh book.], the dean of Christendom and certain other canons of the aforesaid chapel, who hold parish churches from you, claim, on the pretext of the said privilege, to be exempt even in matters whose jurisdiction belongs to you, to such an extent that, however gravely they transgress an interdict, they refuse to submit to your correction and sentence. You therefore humbly requested instruction from us concerning how you ought to proceed against such rebels.

Accordingly, by the authority of these presents we command your brotherhood that, insofar as they are exempt by reason of the same chapel, you reverently defer to the apostolic privileges; but insofar as they are known to fall under your jurisdiction by reason of parish churches or otherwise, freely exercise the duty of your office against them.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

CCLXVI. TO THE BISHOP [Note: Col. 1098D. See letter 260 of the ninth book, note.], THE DEAN [Note: Col. 1098D. Evrard III, also called Ebrard, dean of Langres, is mentioned in instruments from at least 1204 through at least 1207. In a certain charter, Nicholas is found as dean in 1212. But in a charter of Bishop Hugh of 1221, our Ebrard is called former dean. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IV, col. 647.], AND THE CHAPTER OF LANGRES. That they receive Hugh of Faverney as canon and brother. (At Saint Peter’s, the twelfth Kalends of March.)

The literary learning and moral probity of our beloved son Master Hugh of Faverney, known to us through the testimony of many and made better known by the services frequently rendered to us on your behalf through him, seem to aggravate the fault of ingratitude which, by despising the apostolic mandate issued once and again to you concerning his provision, you are shown to have committed not only against us but also against him. Even without our mandate, in view merely of his worthiness, or at least in consideration of the services rendered, you should by no means have left him without any of your benefices; for he laments that he has hitherto obtained no benefice in the Church.

Since, therefore, from the time when we began to interpose our good offices with you on behalf of this master, we are unwilling to fail him, but rather to complete toward him the work of mercy begun, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings that, removing every impediment of delay and excuse, you admit him as brother and canon, liberally granting to the said master the fruits of the prebend of your former fellow canon H. … Motez. Since that man is exposed to particular circumstances of pilgrimage, and you have no certainty whether he is alive or dead, you receive those fruits in common; nevertheless his right is preserved if, by God’s grant, he should return, in its complete integrity. Thus, at least on this occasion, you shall fulfil the apostolic command in such a way that, by making a virtue of necessity, it will not be necessary for you to be compelled to this by another.

Otherwise, we have instructed by our letters, as a command, our beloved son … the Chancellor of Chartres, … the Treasurer of Saint Stephen’s at Troyes, and Master R. of Courson, canon of Noyon, residing at Paris, that if you fail to execute our mandate, they are not to delay, after removing every impediment of contradiction and appeal, in compelling you to this by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

CCLXVII. TO THE BISHOP [Note: Col. 1099D. See letter 78 of the fifth book, note.], THE ABBOT OF SAINT MARTIN [Note: Col. 1099D. Bernard I Girbertus, formerly cellarer of Solignac, was chosen Abbot of Saint Martin. He wisely governed this church for twelve years and died in 1214, on the sixteenth Kalends of April. He expressly prohibited any display of candles at his funeral and ordered that only one candle be lit on his bier. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. II, col. 584.], AND THE CHANTER OF LIMOGES. That they subject to excommunication the invaders of the goods of P., subdeacon and papal notary. (At Saint Peter’s, the twelfth Kalends of March.)

If the Abbot of Solignac [Note: Col. 1099D. Hugh I of Malmont or Maumont is recorded in public acts from 1195 to 1228, when he yielded office to Ademar. In 1214 he entered into a confraternity of prayers with Radulf, Abbot of Saint Éloi at Noyon. He was still living in 1232. Ibid., col. 571.] and the others who, as we have heard, at his instigation, rashly seized the property of the mother and brothers of Master P., our subdeacon and notary, of good memory, after his death, had carefully considered how dear and welcome the same notary had been to us and our brethren during his life on account of the praiseworthy service of his fidelity, and how deeply we grieved at his passing lest we seem to begrudge him those blessed companies to which he is believed to have attained at the most Christian end of his life, then surely, if not for the honor of public justice, at least out of reverence for us and the Apostolic See, they would have avoided adding affliction to the afflicted and increasing in us the pious grief for the deceased through the complaints of those dear to him.

Therefore, lest we appear to disregard the sorrows of those to whom the same notary left, after God, no refuge other than the Apostolic See—especially since in this matter the complaint of the living is almost the cause of the dead, whose soul seems to cry out to us against those who perhaps persecute him in his survivors—we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings that, removing every impediment of contradiction and appeal, by our authority you make public and solemn excommunication, by which you declare subject to a sentence of excommunication those who, after the death of the said master, unlawfully occupied, or caused to be occupied, the goods of his mother and brothers, or rashly inflicted injuries upon them, or caused injuries to be inflicted upon them, unless within fifteen days after they have been admonished by you they render full and due satisfaction concerning these matters.

Cause the same sentence to be observed inviolate by ecclesiastical censure until worthy satisfaction has been made, solemnly renewing it every Sunday and feast day throughout the entire diocese of Limoges, with bells rung and candles lit. And since we wish them to be preserved in their rights through your diligence, whenever the mother or brothers of the aforesaid master complain that they are being unlawfully molested in any matter by persons whose judgment is known to belong to the ecclesiastical forum, restrain those persons from their unlawful molestation by ecclesiastical censure under the authority of these presents. But in the case of those whose causes belong to the secular forum, have them restrained from the same unjust molestation by their own judges. If those judges should perhaps refuse to accomplish this after your admonition, then, setting aside the impediment of appeal, restrain such molesters from unlawfully molesting the aforesaid persons by similar censure; for the Apostolic See is bound to defend the justice of wretched persons, since it ought to be the final refuge of the oppressed. Execute the apostolic command in such a way that you cannot be reproved for negligence but may rather be commended for obedience.

Moreover, in order that fuller provision may be made for their justice, we will and command that this jurisdiction, which we confer on you by the authority of these presents, be extended, if necessary, even to your successors, who, preserving them in their rights, shall proceed against their molesters in the manner prescribed, setting aside appeal. The witnesses, however, etc. No letters shall be an obstacle, if any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without mention of these presents. And if not all … let two of you, etc. …

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

CCLXVIII. TO ALBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG [Note: Col. 1100D. See letter 22 of the ninth book, note.]. That he annul certain grants of benefices made contrary to law. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of February.)

It has come to our hearing, as you have reported, that your predecessor L. [Note: Col. 1100D. Ludolph, of rustic family but noble in learning, a promoter of ecclesiastical discipline, was elected in 1194. Bucelin, *Germania Sacra*, part I, p. 40, col. 1.], while bound by the bond of excommunication, presumed to assign a great many ecclesiastical benefices to certain clerics. They presume to retain these, although they acquired no right in them through such a grant; indeed, they rather incurred the snare of excommunication, since in receiving them they participated with him.

Therefore, considering that he could not then give, nor could they acquire any right in those benefices from his grant, by the authority of these presents we grant your brotherhood leave, after setting aside appeal, to decree by authority of the Apostolic See that the grants of those benefices are void and empty, and to assign the benefices themselves canonically to suitable persons. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of February, in the ninth year.

CCLXIX. TO THE SAME [Note: Col. 1101D. See letter 22 of the ninth book, note.]. Confirmation of the establishment of certain churches. (At Rome, the fourteenth Kalends of March.)

To the just requests, etc., as far as “to fulfil.” Since, therefore, your predecessor Lut. [Note: Col. 1101D. See the note to the immediately preceding letter.], at a time when he enjoyed the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, established by prudent deliberation the collegiate Church of Saint Peter at Magdeburg, with three *mansi* at Sedorp; ten pounds in Magdeburg currency in the village of Wortuna; one *mansus* at Walteresdorp; the tithe at Willebeke; twenty-one *mansi* at Pokeriz; twenty-five *mansi* in the village of Mentiz; the Church of Saint Michael in the suburb of Magdeburg, granted liberally to that church by himself; and three plots in the same city, granted by Henry, Provost of Angaria: we, yielding to your prayers, ratify the said establishment and the donation of those possessions, as reasonably and providently made, confirm them by apostolic authority, and strengthen them with the protection of this present writing. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

CCLXX. TO THE ABBOT OF SICHEN, IN THE DIOCESE OF HALBERSTADT, … THE SCHOLASTICUS OF SAINT SEBASTIAN, AND MASTER ARNOLD, PARISH PRIEST OF SAINT JOHN AT MAGDEBURG. That they investigate the misconduct of the provost of Hunoldesburg and report it. (At Saint Peter’s, the thirteenth Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1101C]

Set upon the watchtower of the Lord, when matters concerning ecclesiastical persons are reported to our ears by which our ministry is blasphemed, we must go down and see, following the example of him who called the dishonored steward to account and, upon discovering that he had squandered his goods, removed him from his stewardship.

Know, then, that it has come to our hearing that Albert, Provost of Hunoldesburg, and Rodulf of Ranis, canons of the Church of Magdeburg, are publicly defamed throughout the whole province of Magdeburg for certain crimes. Therefore, wishing, as the office of oversight requires, that the truth be more fully investigated, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings that, if this is so, setting aside appeal, you inquire into those offences and fully investigate the truth; laying aside favor, hatred, and fear, faithfully set down in writing what you discover and send it to us under your seals, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed in the Lord’s authorship as shall be appropriate in these matters. If not all of you, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

CCLXXI. TO THE BISHOP [Note: Col. 1101D. See letter 68 of the fifth book, note.] AND CHAPTER OF LIMOGES. That they receive R. de Turribus (“of the Towers”) as canon and brother. (At Saint Peter’s, the eleventh Kalends of March.)

We cannot easily determine whether, by rejecting the requests which we sent to you on behalf of our beloved son R. de Turribus (“of the Towers”), canon of Saint Yrieix, you have displayed envy against him or committed ingratitude toward us; for in the former case you seem to have avoided the fellowship of an upright man, and in the latter, by refusing to render to us our due in his person, you seem to have committed the sin of disobedience.

Indeed, when we commanded you that, out of reverence for Blessed Peter and for us, you should admit him as canon and brother, you neither gave our requests the devoted regard due to them nor considered the merit of the same cleric. Distinguished by nobility of blood and of virtues, he is worthy of your fellowship—unless perhaps you consider yourselves unworthy of his—since he is known both to be related by blood to our dearest daughter in Christ, J., the illustrious Queen of England, and to excel in upright conduct. Yet you were unwilling to fulfil our command, although you rendered his person commended, as our beloved sons, the Abbot of Petrosa [Note: Col. 1101D. The very incomplete series of abbots of this monastery in the authors of the *Nova Gallia*, vol. II, col. 1505, names no abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Petrosa in the period with which we are concerned.] and the Prior of Saint John of Cola, who had admonished you by our authority concerning his reception, reported to us in their letters.

Although, therefore, from the very fact that you made no exception against the person of the said cleric but rather commended him, we could more unavoidably compel you to receive him, we nevertheless wish through our gentleness to win your favor for him. Accordingly, by repeated writings we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, at least on this occasion, you admit the aforesaid cleric as brother and canon and take care to treat him with fraternal affection. Carefully ensure that, by making a virtue of necessity, you fulfil our command in such a way that it will not be necessary for you to be compelled by another to execute it.

Otherwise, we have instructed by our writings our venerable brother, the Bishop of Saintes [Note: Col. 1102D. See letter 96 of the fifth book, note.], and our beloved sons, the treasurer and Elias of Greece, canon of Angoulême, that unless you undertake to raise and prove a reasonable cause why you cannot or ought not to fulfil this, they are not to delay in compelling you to do so by ecclesiastical censure, after removing every impediment of contradiction and appeal.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eleventh Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

## The Tenth Book of the Letters, or Registers, of Innocent III, Roman Pontiff. The Tenth Year of the Pontificate, A.D. 1207.

### I. To the Abbot of Evesham.

He remits to him his excommunicated monk A., in order that he may dispense with him concerning certain matters. (At Saint Peter’s, the second Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1103A]

Our beloved son A., a monk, appearing before us, tearfully explained that, having formerly made regular profession at the monastery of Chichester, prompted by the enemy of the human race, he departed from that place without asking permission, taking with him a certain sum of money. Although for such offences he had been bound by a sentence of excommunication, nevertheless, coming to your monastery, he assumed there the monastic habit.

When he afterwards disclosed to you in secret confession what we have stated above, and you had made requests to the said Abbot of Chichester that he should grant A. the benefit of absolution, but he did not consent to your request, you admitted the same A. to monastic profession and had him ordained priest. Although, as time passed, discord arose between you and, on that account, you suspended A. from the exercise of the priestly office, yet, after concord had subsequently been restored between you, you sent the same A. with your letters to the Apostolic See so that he might obtain both absolution and dispensation.

By our command he obtained absolution from our beloved son I., Cardinal Priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. When he returned to you with the letters of the same cardinal, you, not forgetting the former discord, refused to receive him back; indeed, you compelled him to lay aside the monastic habit. Therefore, unwilling that the same A. should have, under pretext of this occasion, further cause for wandering, we have thought fit to send him back to your monastery. By apostolic writings we command and enjoin you to permit him there to serve the Lord in monastic habit, dispensing with him as you consider expedient.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second Kalends of March, in the tenth year.

### II. To the Abbot and Convent of Saint Vedast at Arras.

Confirmation to them of Pope Alexander’s privilege prohibiting the grant of certain prebends received by the canons of Saint Peter. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifth Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1104B]

The more religious men need greater seclusion and quiet in order to preserve their way of life, the more diligently every opportunity by which secular men may disturb their peace ought to be cut off. Therefore, since Pope Eugenius, of happy memory, our predecessor, prohibited by apostolic authority that you should grant to anyone, upon the death of any one of them, those prebends which you were accustomed to confer from your own table upon secular canons in the Church of Saint Peter; rather, they were to return without any contradiction to the use of the brethren of your church—provided, nevertheless, that on this account the aforesaid church should by no means lack the celebration of divine offices—and since Pope Alexander thought fit to confirm this: we, following in their footsteps, confirm the same by apostolic authority, decreeing that it be observed inviolate in future times. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our confirmation and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth Kalends of March, in the tenth year.

### III. To the Same.

A certain proceeding is annulled and certain grants are confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, the fourth Kalends of March.)

When the proceeding held by our beloved son … the Archdeacon and Walter the Scholasticus of Tournai, concerning the case which was pending between you and certain clerics of Arras over the prebends of the Church of Saint Peter, had long been debated before us on both sides, the said clerics requested that we should deem worthy of strengthening by apostolic protection the sentence pronounced by those judges. You, on the contrary, replied that the same sentence ought to be deemed void and empty, since it had wrongly been given contrary to the grant of Pope Eugenius, of happy memory, our predecessor, which was subsequently confirmed by Pope Alexander, our predecessor of good memory. The aforesaid judges had declared that they had many reasons to regard that grant as suspect, considering the circumstances of its seal, parchment, and handwriting.

Having carefully heard and fully understood these and other matters, because we have found that the aforesaid grant contains no indication of falsity and that the aforesaid judges wrongly proceeded against it in the same affair, we have thought fit to revoke their proceeding as void; and, approving the aforesaid grant, we have ordered it to be confirmed. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our determination, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth Kalends of March, in the tenth year.

### IV. To the Abbot of Saint Aubert, … the Chanter, and Master R. de Bekerel, Canon of Cambrai.

That they cause the subdeacon Hugh to be received to a vacant canonry and prebend of the Church of Bruges. (At Saint Peter’s.)

Our beloved sons … the Dean of Saint-Frambault, and Masters I., the Poet, and II. of Orléans, canons of Senlis, informed us by their letters that, when they had undertaken, by apostolic authority, to move and induce the provost, of good memory, and our beloved sons … the dean and chapter of Bruges—whom we had addressed in writing on behalf of our beloved son Hugh, subdeacon—to receive him in their church as canon and brother according to the tenor of our mandate, and for the said provost liberally to assign him a prebend, if one should be vacant there, they judged the apostolic mandate entirely void because no prebend was vacant in that church and our letters made no mention of one which would become vacant.

Nevertheless, the same provost added that, if the aforesaid subdeacon would submit himself in this matter to his will, he would provide for him in such a manner that Hugh could not justly complain of him. The chapter likewise promised that whenever their provost should confer upon him some prebend in their church, they would liberally assign him a stall in choir, a place in chapter, and the other things pertaining to them. Yet the same provost later took no care to execute the apostolic mandate.

Moreover, after the aforesaid provost had entered upon the way of all flesh, the said subdeacon, when the chapter had nominated a canon of the same church as provost, appealed to the Apostolic See lest that man’s prebend be conferred upon another. Therefore, unwilling to leave unfulfilled what we began mercifully concerning the said subdeacon, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings that, after prior admonition, you compel by ecclesiastical coercion, setting aside every impediment of contradiction and appeal, the aforesaid dean, chapter, and provost—if one has in the meantime been instituted—to receive him to a vacant prebend in their church as canon and brother, assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. Let the witnesses who are named, etc. If not all of you, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

### V. To the Nobleman B., Duke of Saxony.

He and his possessions are received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifth Nones of March.)

[Col. 1106C]

Since, according to canonical enactments, proceedings ought not to be taken against anyone unless he has confessed, been convicted, his offence is notorious, he appears contumacious, or he has been publicly defamed; and since we wish, as is fitting, to observe the order of law, by the authority of these presents we grant you that, if anything has been obtained from us against you contrary to the prescribed order, no prejudice shall be generated against you by it, as though it had been surreptitiously obtained. We receive your person, together with those things which you now reasonably possess or may in the future, by God’s favor, acquire through lawful means, under the protection of the Apostolic See, as a Catholic and devoted prince. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our concession and protection, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth Nones of March, in the tenth year.

### VI. To Sophia, Abbess of the Monastery of Quedlinburg, and Her Sisters, Both Present and Those to Be Regularly Appointed in Future, in Perpetuity.

The monastery itself is made immediately subject to the Roman Pontiff, and certain other matters are granted to them, the annual payment of one pound of silver always being reserved. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of March.)

To prudent virgins, who beneath the habit of religion [Col. 1107A] continually prepare themselves by works of holiness to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, apostolic protection ought to be afforded, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery of Quedlinburg, which belongs by right to blessed Peter, was founded by King Henry of illustrious memory, and was offered to the Roman Church under an annual payment of one pound of silver, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Agapetus, John, Silvester, Innocent, and Lucius.

First, indeed, establishing [Col. 1107B] that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall there be observed inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, with the Lord’s assistance, acquire by grant of popes, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We also renew and altogether forbid that the same monastery should ever be subjected to any person or church other than the Roman Church. Nor shall any king have leave to grant it as a benefice.

But when you, the present abbess of that place, [Col. 1107C] or any one succeeding you, die, no one shall be placed over it through any trickery of usurpation or violence, unless she be one whom the sisters by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, have determined should be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. And just as we have established that the aforesaid monastery shall be subject solely to the Roman pontiff, so likewise by the present decree we enact, concerning both clerical and lay persons and all other things generally belonging to the same place and assigned to your service, what is known to have been established by the enactment of those same predecessors of ours.

Likewise we decree that the cloister of Saint Mary on the Mount shall be ordered according to the Rule of blessed Benedict; [Col. 1107D] and that the cloister of Saint Quichbert at the aforesaid place of Quedlinburg, together with the cloister of Saint Nicholas at Winethusen, shall be ordered according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. Furthermore, we confirm to you and to the same your church everything belonging to the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, situated in the place called Saint Michael’s Rock, from the goods of Burchard the knight of good memory. Adding also that whoever decide to serve God there shall live in common and according to rule, without private property, and shall always remain, as hitherto, under the right and disposition of the monastery of Quedlinburg.

We establish by the present writing the same concerning the church of Saint John the Baptist situated at Quedlinburg and the hospice beside it for receiving the poor. [Col. 1108A] Nevertheless, a religious and wise priest shall be appointed there, who shall also take charge of the poor. Excepting excommunicated and interdicted persons, if anyone wishes to be buried there, he shall by no means be forbidden, the rights and reverence of the mother church being preserved.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, or take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the complete benefit of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted. The authority of the Apostolic See being reserved. Moreover, as a sign that the same monastery belongs by right to blessed Peter, you shall pay to us and our successors [Col. 1108B] annually one pound of silver as a payment.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not amend his offence by suitable satisfaction, etc., let him be subject to punishment. But let all who preserve the rights of the same place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which, etc., unto the end.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of March, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## VII. TO THE CHAPTER OF MAGDEBURG

They are forbidden to sell or lease certain of their rights and goods to persons other than canons. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of March.)

[Col. 1108C]

Our venerable brother Albert, your archbishop, humbly petitioned us to deem it fitting to forbid you by apostolic authority that any of you should presume to give, sell, or lease to other persons the courts or cloister-yards which ought to be sold or leased only to the canons of Magdeburg. We therefore, inclined by his prayers, forbid you by the authority of these presents to presume to give, sell, or lease the aforesaid courts or yards to anyone other than your fellow canons, provided that they offer a just [Col. 1108D] price for them.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the 2nd of the Nones of March, in the tenth year.

## VIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF HALBERSTADT AND MERSEBURG, AND TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT JOHN ON THE MOUNT AT MAGDEBURG

That they must not refuse to receive priests and other suitable men into that church as canons and brethren, notwithstanding a privilege formerly granted them. (At the Lateran, 8 Ides of March.)

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Magdeburg, informed us that, since our predecessors of good memory, Popes Benedict and John, [Col. 1109A] had seen fit to grant to the canons of Magdeburg serving at the high altar the use of sandals on certain feast days, as is contained in their privileges, many of the canons, on the pretext of that concession, assert that no one ought to be admitted to service at that altar unless he has been ordained wearing sandals. On this account they oppose the admission as brethren and canons of prudent and honourable priests who could usefully serve the same church.

Since, therefore, they ought not to draw material for malice from the favour bestowed upon them by the Apostolic See, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to have the said privilege presented to you; and, after carefully examining it, if it contains nothing else concerning sandals [Col. 1109B] except that ministers of the altar are to use them on certain days, you shall enjoin upon the chapter of Magdeburg by our authority that for this reason they must not refuse, when necessary, to receive suitable priests and other honourable men as brethren and canons. Otherwise their own archbishop could not celebrate at the same altar either, since he was not promoted by us to the priestly office wearing sandals; for we ordain no one priest with sandals, but consecrate as bishop one who uses sandals. And if not all of you, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the 8th of the Ides of March, in the tenth year.

## IX. TO MASTER GERVAND

The grant to him of a certain prebend at Magdeburg is confirmed. (At the Lateran, 6 Ides of March.)

[Col. 1109C]

Although we committed for canonical final determination to our venerable brothers, the bishop of Merseburg, the bishop of Brandenburg of good memory, and the bishop of Havelberg, the cause pending between our venerable brother Albert the archbishop and certain canons of Magdeburg concerning the grant of certain prebends made by that archbishop, one of which was assigned to you by him; nevertheless, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward our person and the Roman Church, [Col. 1109D] and also in view of your probity and learning, we have judged it fitting to provide as follows: if, at the time when that archbishop conferred the said prebend upon you, its grant belonged to him, what was done concerning you in respect of that prebend shall remain valid. But if its grant had then devolved upon us, we have decided to confer it upon you by special favour.

Since, therefore, we wish you to have it in either case, we confirm it to you by apostolic authority and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our provision and confirmation, or oppose it by rash daring, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the 6th of the Ides of March, in the tenth year.

## X. TO THE CHAPTER OF MAGDEBURG

Concerning the same matter, and on behalf of the same G., they are instructed to receive and admit him. (Given as in the other.)

[Col. 1110A]

Although the cause pending between our venerable brother Albert, your archbishop, and certain among you concerning the grant of certain prebends made by that archbishop, etc., [is treated] in the same manner down to “we confirm,” therefore by apostolic letters we command your whole body that, receiving the same master as a canon and brother according to the custom of your church, you shall treat him with brotherly charity.

[Col. 1110B] Given as in the other.

## XI. TO ALBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG

Concerning the same matter and on behalf of the same G. (Given as in the other.)

Although the cause pending between you and certain canons of Magdeburg, etc., [is treated] in the same manner down to “we confirm,” therefore by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that you shall endeavour to assign to him, by our authority and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, a stall in choir and a place in chapter.

Given as in the other.

## XII. TO THE BISHOP OF MERSEBURG AND THE ELECTS OF BRANDENBURG AND HAVELBERG

Concerning the same matter. (Given as in the other.)

[Col. 1110C]

Although the cause pending between our venerable brother Albert the archbishop and certain canons of Magdeburg, etc., [is treated] in the same manner down to “we confirm,” therefore by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, causing the said master to enjoy possession of that prebend by our authority, with the impediment of appeal removed, you shall restrain opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. And if not all of you, etc., [Col. 1110D] let two of you, etc.

Given as in the other.

## XIII. TO ULRIC, CLERIC

The custody of Saint Peter at Liège, conferred upon him, is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 6 Nones of March.)

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, etc., down to “be brought to effect.” Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, inclined by your just requests, we confirm to you by apostolic authority, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the custody of Saint Peter at Liège, which you assert that you acquired by the grant of our venerable brother H., bishop of Liège, just as you possess it lawfully and peaceably. [Col. 1111A] Let no one, therefore, infringe our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the 6th of the Nones of March, in the tenth year.

## XIV. TO LUKE, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF BURGUEIL

A definite manner of living and governing the monastery is given, on the report of certain persons to whom its correction had been committed. (At the Lateran, 7 Ides of March.)

Placed by the Lord, who disposes over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to destroy, and likewise to build and plant, we are bound to grant apostolic strength to those things which, among religious men, are prudently established in order [Col. 1111B] to remove matter of laxity and cultivate virtues, so that young women may run with unhindered foot in the fragrance of the Lord’s ointments, and may sit more freely at the Lord’s feet with Mary.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclined by your requests, we confirm by apostolic authority and fortify by the privilege of this present writing those things which the beloved sons, the abbots of Savigny and Clermont of the Cistercian Order, and P. of Butera, canon of Angers—to whom we saw fit to entrust the correction of your monastery—prudently established, with your consent, for the instruction of religious life and the benefit of your monastery. For fuller clarity, we insert those constitutions word for word into [Col. 1111C] this page of ours, as they are contained in their authenticated instrument.

> “For the good of peace and the love of religion, we establish that the abbot, who ought to benefit rather than rule, and to teach his disciples more by example than by word, shall always sleep in the dormitory, unless he is sick or has been bled, or some manifest necessity requires otherwise, or he has endured great labour. Neither the abbot nor any monk shall have a coverlet except one of lambskins, catskins, or foxskins, arranged with black or white cloth.
>
> “He shall eat more frequently in the refectory; and if he eats in his chamber, he shall eat with brethren, whether clerics or laymen. We forbid long vigils after Compline. No monk shall eat in the infirmary without leave of the abbot [Col. 1111D] or prior. No cleric or layman shall eat except in the guest-house, except servants, who may eat in their workshops, unless they are persons of high rank.
>
> “The abbot shall attend the divine offices frequently and sit in the cloister for the purpose of edification. He shall not give revenues or possessions, or anything that a monk can properly administer for the benefit of the Church, to his relatives or others. He shall not be lavish toward his relatives or others in expenditures or gifts. In all his business and in visiting obediences, he shall be content with five or six mounts, unless perhaps he has summoned some worthy men for counsel. He shall not demand gifts from priors in return for granting priories. He shall not remove anyone from priories or bailiwicks while he performs well, except for a cause of outstanding benefit; and this [Col. 1112A] he shall do with the counsel of the elders.
>
> “He shall not tolerate a destroyer, but shall remove and punish him according to rule, so that others may be afraid. He shall make orderly provision for all brothers in all necessities, moderately and honourably but not superfluously, and shall cause priors to make such provision. He shall not alienate from the places to which they are given revenues and possessions granted or acquired, whether formerly or in future, without the counsel of the chapter. He shall not grant a pension to anyone except by the special command of the lord pope. He shall not borrow more than twenty-five pounds of Angevin money without the seal and knowledge of the chapter. He shall not stand surety for anyone. He shall not pledge the treasury or possessions of the Church except with the counsel of the elders and after summoning the external priors residing within one day’s journey.
>
> “Nor [Col. 1112B] shall he make any ordinance except in the general chapter held on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. If lesser matters must be managed during the year, he shall employ the counsel of the elders and do what he judges best. The abbot shall keep no obedience or bailiwick in his own hands; but, as soon as he can, he shall appoint a suitable prior or bailiff, except for the guest-house and the chamberlainship, which he may retain if he wishes. Two offices or priories shall not be entrusted to one person so long as individual monks can administer them beneficially; nor shall he grant them for life or for a fixed term, nor give them to monks from outside.
>
> “He shall not entrust to [Col. 1112C] secular clerics or laymen, nor permit priors to entrust, any bailiwicks, whether head offices or dependent offices, which can be administered by monks to the honour and benefit of the Church. But what cannot be administered by monks shall be administered by suitable lay brothers (*condonati*). All priors, both those within and without the cloister, shall firmly maintain community in the monastery, dormitory, and refectory. Nor shall anyone take in the refectory anything except common food. The infirmary shall have its own revenues. The infirmarian and the fish-keeper of the abbey shall be elected by the chapter. The abbot shall appoint the prior of the abbey according to ancient custom.
>
> “We establish and command that the chapter seal shall be kept under three keys: the abbot shall have one; two persons elected and sworn in general chapter shall keep the other two. Nothing shall be sealed with it except by the consent [Col. 1112D] of the present chapter; and this same matter shall be recited in the following general chapter. Each year the abbot, or the prior of the abbey with some honourable and prudent monk at the abbot’s command, shall visit all obediences once; and, if he finds anything requiring correction, he shall correct it, and report to the abbot and general chapter what he has corrected or left to be corrected.
>
> “Every year in the general chapter the abbot, bailiffs, and priors alike shall render account of the condition and debt of their offices for the past and present year. Their condition and debts shall be reduced to writing and preserved with the chapter seal, to be recited in the chapter of the following year. Neither the abbot nor any prior shall sell or pledge any revenues except for the current year. If a fief or other revenue accrues in any way, [Col. 1113A] it shall not be given or sold to outsiders, but shall remain to the cellarer. Likewise, ornaments shall be restored to the sacristy and books to the library.
>
> “Monks shall not be condemned on the accusation of secular clerics or laymen unless the crime is notorious. No one shall be judged or condemned unless present, unless he is contumacious. All lay brothers shall be distinguished from secular persons in habit and tonsure. Boys shall not be received below the age of fifteen. After their fifteenth year they shall be kept under supervision for three years. No monk shall be clothed in linen shirts, but only in woollen garments; nor shall he use boots reaching above the knee.”

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, infringe this page of our confirmation or oppose it with rash boldness. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, [Col. 1113B] let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the 7th of the Ides of March, in the tenth year.

## XV. TO THE BISHOP AND THE DEAN OF PARIS

That they are to proceed against certain forgers, punishing them under the penalty enacted against forgers. (At the Lateran, 5 Ides of March.)

Your prudence consulted us whether a decretal of this sort, recently alleged in a case before you, had proceeded from the Apostolic See; and you wrote it to us word for word in the following form.

[Col. 1113C]

> “Whoever hopes that relief can be supplied by us in his doubts should approach us with ready confidence. We therefore rightly commend your discretion because you wish to put an end to vain and useless questions, which are very frequently debated in your court with great disputation over laws, thereby consulting the benefit of the Church and providing for that of your subjects.
>
> “From your inquiry into these questions we have learned that some persons, without a case having been commenced before their ordinary, or, after a case has been commenced, without making an appeal, approach the Apostolic See and obtain letters directed to judges of another province. But when the cited parties appear before those judges, they seek to decline their examination: sometimes by objecting against their adversaries that they did not first warn them and disregarded the authority of their ordinary; sometimes because they refuse to seek or undergo the judgment of a foreign judge.
>
> “Desiring to remove this doubt from your mind, we establish that if anyone, disregarding the authority of his judge, has approached us and obtained letters, those letters shall bring him absolutely no assistance unless he obtains them for his ordinary judge. For the sacred laws, to whose authority we must give effect, say that if anyone, spurning the judge of the province, approaches the emperor, he ought to receive no answer from him, lest we appear in this matter to overthrow the laws, whose protection and support belong above all to us.
>
> “Concerning those who obtain letters while litigation is pending, we judge that their impetration [Col. 1114A] ought not benefit them, since a privilege obtained concerning a matter in litigation has no force—especially since the sacred canons provide that sacred commands are not to be obtained during the course of litigation. But if anyone, while a suit is being examined, obtains a pragmatic sanction, we do not wish it to benefit him.
>
> “Concerning those who obtain letters directed to foreign judges, we enact, in accordance with the authority of the laws, that such letters must in no way take effect unless the litigants have a cause against the metropolitan or governor of the province; especially since judges of our time sometimes place love of the world before love of God, failing to observe that those who kill the body are not to be feared when men are striving for justice.
>
> “By ‘province’ we mean that which, according to the Council of Chalcedon, has a metropolitan and is divided by fixed boundaries, such as Aquitaine, Brittany, and Normandy; and the same judgment applies in similar cases.
>
> “You have further asked whether time for deliberation should be granted to one who obtained it before an ordinary judge when he appears as defendant before a delegated judge. To this we answer that, when a rescript is issued by us upon appeal, no delay may be granted, for the same reason that it is not customarily granted in our presence.
>
> “As to your question whether time should be granted to one who has received our rescript inserted in letters of citation, we say that he ought not to request it, according to the decretal of Pope Felix, which establishes that bishops must notify accused persons in writing what is alleged against them, so that they may come prepared to answer; especially since before the delegated judge he possesses a copy of our rescript and can carefully ascertain where anything has been added to or removed from the rescript.
>
> “Concerning your doubt that villages are sometimes transferred under the title of donation and sometimes under the title of sale, both to laymen and to religious persons, and that laymen claim for themselves the right of patronage from possession of them, whether the right of patronage is transferred to them together with the whole property: we give this answer, that religious persons may claim it in villages they have acquired.”

In response to this, we have considered it necessary to say to you that, although some matters in the foregoing decretal—or rather, concocted decretal—appear consonant with the law, by which its rash fabricator coloured his falsehoods, [Col. 1114D] nevertheless we utterly reject and condemn it as false. By apostolic letters we command your discretion that, after restoring to its proper state anything attempted on its pretext in favour of anyone using it, you shall punish the authors of it, if they can be found, or those whom you know knowingly to have used it, by the penalty enacted against forgers.

Given at the Lateran, on the 5th of the Ides of March, in the tenth year.

## XVI. TO ELIAS, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF RADINGIA, OF THE CLUNIAC ORDER

The monastery itself and their goods are received under protection, and their privileges are confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1115A]

The most holy Roman Church has customarily, by the office of its accustomed mercy, to love more earnestly its devoted and humble sons and, lest they be harassed by the troubles caused by wicked men, to cherish them as a pious mother with the defence of her protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Radingia, in which you are devoted to divine service, with all goods [Col. 1115B] which it now reasonably possesses or may in future, with the Lord’s aid, acquire by just means, and also the persons serving the Lord therein.

In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority and fortify by the privilege of this present writing the churches, chapels, lands, possessions, revenues, liberties, immunities, and all else which you have hitherto acquired by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, purchase, donation, offering of the faithful, or other just means, just as you possess all these things lawfully and peaceably. We strictly forbid anyone to presume rashly to harass you or [Col. 1115C] your monastery concerning the privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs. Let no one, therefore, infringe our protection, confirmation, and prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the 4th of the Kalends of March, in the tenth year.

## XVII. TO THE SAME

They are granted leave to recover goods alienated from the monastery. (Given as in the other.)

Since, through the negligence of those who have at different times presided over your monastery, and through the harmful silence of the convent, which has often not dared to oppose their acts, certain of its goods are said to have been alienated contrary to the privileges of that monastery, to its grave prejudice [Col. 1115D] and loss, desiring with paternal care to provide for its freedom from loss, we grant you by the authority of these presents that you may lawfully restore to that monastery what is known to have been alienated from it in this manner. Let no one, therefore, infringe our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other.

## XVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF RADINGIA

That, in the external administrations of the monastery, he may appoint and recall, without opposition, brethren of the profession who have been approved in religious life, as he sees fit. (At the Lateran, 6 Ides of March.)

To the just desires of petitioners, etc., down to “assent,” [Col. 1116A] we grant you by the authority of these presents that in the external administrations of your monastery you may, with the counsel of the chapter or of its greater or sounder part, appoint brethren of your profession who are proved in religious life, capable, and prudent, without anyone’s opposition, as you judge expedient for the same monastery; and, when usefulness requires or necessity presses, you may recall them, when it seems good to you, with like counsel of the brethren. Provided, however, that the goods, possessions, revenues, and income of the said monastery shall be administered only through the hands of brethren who shall render account, as is due, to you and your chapter concerning what is entrusted to them. Let no one, therefore, infringe our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the 6th of the Ides of March, in the tenth year.

## XIX. TO THE PROVOST, DEAN, PRIORS, AND OTHER CLERGY OF COLOGNE

Afflicted by adverse tribulations, they are comforted and urged to be stronger and unafraid. (At the Lateran, 3 Ides of March.)

[Col. 1116B]

Although the Church of Cologne induced us to act in its favour in the matter of the Empire, and not we it, and therefore we may reckon more to its account than it to ours concerning that affair; nevertheless, because we subsequently found it faithful and devoted, we have regarded it as so welcome and acceptable that it maintained constancy in its purpose, as though the subsequent events had proceeded not from its initiative but [Col. 1116C] rather from ours.

Would that that man had never been born who defiled your Church and city with the contagion of his shameful acts and led it by his most ruinous deeds into manifold difficulty! Truly a son of Belial: for he himself was slippery and crafty, two-faced and faithless, always deceiving by cunning art. He suggested deceitful beginnings to our friends, so that he might at last the more easily work malice against them, inasmuch as, trusting him as though in work of his own, a familiar enemy might more grievously harm them by imitating the cunning of him who often entices some persons to good in order to bring more grievous evil out of that very good.

But because, after that dragon was cast down, through whom [Col. 1116D] Satan demanded you to sift you like wheat, your faith did not fail at all: the adversary drove you, but did not overthrow you; and the battering-ram of temptations, brought against the wall of your constancy, could not penetrate it. Since, therefore, the Lord proves His chosen ones like gold in a furnace, you ought to bear calmly the furnace of the persecution now threatening, so that, if you are gold, you may finally emerge from it purer; lest, if the gold of your faith does not endure the test of smelting unto perfect proof, that by which it might have been made bright should instead darken it.

Especially since, before this furnace is heated sevenfold, the Lord has power to send His holy angel, who, descending into it with you, may shake from it the flame of fire that would consume its own ministers, and extinguish the furnace itself by the sprinkling of saving dew. [Col. 1117A] Therefore be comforted, most beloved sons, be comforted; and endure with a strong spirit the battle which the ancient enemy, grown old in evil days, has stirred up against you. Without doubt it will seem to you not a contest, but a game and the shadow of a contest, if you consider that most valiant combatant who, when he had lost all his riches at once and heard that his children had been slain—having had a single tomb beneath the ruin of a shaken house—remained unshaken as successive messengers of misfortune came with each separate blow. Even when he was still to be scourged so severely in his own body that, his flesh consumed, his very bone clung to his skin, he nevertheless did not cease to bless the Lord with the lips which alone had been left to him around his teeth.

Accordingly, since the faithful God will in no way [Col. 1117B] allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, it is fitting for you to strengthen your spirit and enlarge your mind, fulfilling that commendation concerning the wise man:

> If the shattered world should fall upon him,
*“Ruins will strike the fearless man.”* (HORACE, *Odes*, book III, ode 3.)

For although your tribulations may seem very numerous, the Lord will nevertheless deliver you from them all; and, beyond what he may be able to repay you in the present, you may hope from him for a far greater reward in the future on account of your patience. For the sufferings of this age are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which we believe will be revealed in you; in it, beyond doubt, an eternal reward will be rendered to you for the defence of justice among those who [Col. 1117C] suffer persecution for justice’s sake and, when they have been tested, will receive the crown of life which the Lord promised to those who love him.

We therefore admonish your devotion and earnestly exhort you, commanding by apostolic letters that, placed between hammer and anvil, you evade the pressure threatening you through patience. For although, like shipwrecked persons, you may seem to have found robbers on the shore, and, according to the words of the prophets, while fleeing from a bear you may fear to be bitten by a serpent when you stretch out your right hand against the wall, you ought nevertheless to remain undaunted before the two tails of smoking firebrands which have formed a plan against you. For God, who knows the deceiver and does not fail to know the person deceived, will bring foolish counsellors to a foolish end; and, being able to loose the belt of kings [Col. 1117D] and gird their loins with a rope, he will pour contempt upon those who trust in their own strength to rule, raise up those who had been oppressed, and, just as he led away an evil priest without glory, so, when he wills, he will overthrow a prince.

Therefore be patient; and, though you yourselves are wise, willingly bear with fools. For through the shield of patience you will be able to break the blows of impending adversities, and through the wall of endurance to overcome every missile of persecutions. You have indeed fought a good fight thus far. But since none is crowned except one who has competed lawfully, in order that henceforth the crown of justice may be laid up for you, you ought to complete the course of perfect work. For it profits nothing to have run in the racecourse if one ceases to run before the [Col. 1118A] prize is gained.

Consider, moreover, from how great a good that man of Kerioth fell, who did not stand firm in the good of perseverance; what Solomon lost, because he did not preserve steadfastness of mind; and into what fall Saul came, because he departed from his good purpose. And, that a more familiar example may strengthen you in perseverance, consider into what ruin the fault of his inconstancy cast down a former prince of yours. By attending to his ruin, make it a warning to yourselves against your own condemnation; for it is written: “The wise man corrects his own fault from another’s vice, learning through another’s peril to avoid his own.” Learn also a parable from that tree which, whether it falls toward the south or toward the north, will remain where it falls. For he who judges the ends of the earth will beyond doubt judge each person [Col. 1118B] where he finds him.

For the serenity of a day is praised in the evening, and the state of a good work is commended at its end, because it is no great good to begin, but to finish perfectly. Many undertake difficult things, but fail on the way. Many depart from Babylon, but die on the journey. Perseverance, indeed, rewards the runner and strengthens the combatant. This is the just man’s ankle-length tunic, extending to the extremity of the feet. This is the tail of the sacrifice, which is commanded to be offered together with the victim. This is the heel of good action, which the wise man guards against the serpent. This is what reduces difficult matters to ease.

Take care, therefore, to preserve it in such a manner that through it you may easily overcome those difficulties into [Col. 1118C] which the unstable and apostate man led you when he abandoned it. Firmly hope that, with the Lord’s help, we intend soon to bring you such aid in your trials that, after the manner of the woman in the Gospel who, once she has borne a son, remembers her anguish no more, when the help which we await from heaven has been revealed among you, prosperous events succeeding adversity, you will be able to forget every hardship and send your messengers back to their own homes as soon as a suitable opportunity offers.

Also observe firmly and fearlessly the virtue of obedience, which is preferred to sacrifices, not only toward us but also toward our venerable brother Bruno, your archbishop. If anyone should perhaps depart from it by apostasy, he would beyond doubt be punished as guilty of the crime of idolatry, to which, according to [Col. 1118D] the prophet, disobedience is compared.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of March, in the tenth year.

## XX. … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, ETC.; … TO THE ABBOT OF CHALOCEIO, ETC.; … TO THE ABBOT OF ORATORIO, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER, IN THE DIOCESE OF ANGERS

That they are to induce and compel Hilary, abbot of Bourgueil, to go to the monastery of Saint Jovin and perform there the fruitful penance imposed upon him. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

It was laid before us on behalf of our beloved sons … the abbot and convent of Bourgueil [Col. 1119A] that Hilary, formerly abbot of their monastery, roams through various provinces and does not shrink from the disgraces of his former manner of life. Through his supporters and accomplices and certain neighbouring abbots of the dioceses of Tours and Angers, who are said to encourage him in his wickedness, he urgently demands that houses and revenues of the monastery of Bourgueil be assigned to himself and his followers, so that, thus obtaining a place and a voice in the said monastery, he may disturb its tranquillity.

Because the aforesaid abbot and convent refuse to grant this to him, having fully experienced his malice, his kinsmen, accomplices, and supporters violently plunder the goods of the monastery in those dioceses and in the diocese of Poitiers. Under the pretext of certain false debts they inflict insults [Col. 1119B] and losses upon the monks, threatening many of them with mutilation of limbs and others with death. Consequently, very many of them do not dare to come forward to transact the monastery’s business, knowing that these men shrink from no crime. They have indeed broken out into such madness and audacity that by night they devastated a grange of the monastery by fire, and would have laid waste the monastery itself together with the adjoining borough in the same fire, had not a contrary wind, raised by divine mercy, driven back the flames.

Since, therefore, the same Hilary has by our judicial sentence, justice requiring it, been removed from the administration of that monastery, and we have ordered him to reside at the monastery of Saint Jovin of Marnes in order to perform penance, [Col. 1119C] we command your discretion by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining that you diligently admonish and effectively induce the said Hilary to remain within the cloister of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Jovin, to perform fruitful penance there in accordance with what we have judged fit to impose upon him, and not to wander outside that monastery.

Otherwise, without delay, compel him to do this by sentence of excommunication, any impediment of appeal being removed. After prior warning, strictly restrain his kinsmen, accomplices, and supporters from undue harassment of the aforesaid monastery and its monks and from the exaction of false debts, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal; and cause due satisfaction to be made to the same persons for the damages and injuries inflicted. But if not all [Col. 1119D] of you can act, you, brother archbishop, etc.
