Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

## XXI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF BOURGUEIL

They are commanded and granted permission to revoke grants and pensions unlawfully made by Hilary, formerly their abbot. (Given as in the other letter.)

It was laid before us on your behalf that Hilary, formerly abbot of your monastery, seeking his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, in order to acquire for himself the favour of secular persons and powerful men, granted many persons annual pensions to be received from your monastery, to the prejudice and burden of that monastery. [Col. 1120A] Some of them, moreover, relying on secular power, do not hesitate to extort these from you by violence. You therefore humbly petitioned us to provide mercifully in this matter for the preservation of your monastery’s rights.

Accordingly, inclined by your prayers, by the authority of these presents we grant you permission lawfully to revoke, without appeal, the grants of those pensions unlawfully made by the same Hilary. Therefore let no one … of our concession … etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXII. … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, AND … TO THE ABBOTS OF ORATORIO AND CHALOCEIO, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER, IN THE DIOCESE OF ANGERS

That they shall cause full justice to be rendered to those complaining of debts due by lawful contract in the time of Hilary, formerly abbot of Bourgueil. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1120B]

Since we have commanded you, brother archbishop, and our venerable brothers … the bishops of Poitiers and Angers, to have it proclaimed through your dioceses that, if any persons believe debts to be claimable from the monastery of Bourgueil from the time of Hilary, formerly its abbot, they are to present themselves before you: we command your discretion by apostolic letters to cause the abbot and convent of the said monastery to render full justice, with interest excluded, to every person complaining concerning debts. After prior warning and removal of any impediment of appeal, subject to sentence of excommunication those who should presume otherwise to harass that monastery over debts. But if not all of you can act, you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXIII. … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, AND … TO THE BISHOPS OF POITIERS AND ANGERS

That they are to proceed against those who burned a certain grange of Hilary, formerly abbot of Bourgueil. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of April.)

As it was laid before us on behalf of our beloved sons … the abbot and [Col. 1120D] convent of Bourgueil, certain sons of Belial, accomplices and supporters of Hilary, formerly abbot of that monastery, set fire to and burned one of its granges. They also continue unjustly to oppress the monastery itself, while nevertheless exacting false debts from it. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that each of you solemnly pronounce, in his own diocese, a sentence of excommunication, without appeal, against all who burned the aforesaid grange; who gave aid or favour toward its burning; who, on Hilary’s pretext, presumed to harass the said monastery; or who exacted false debts from it. Cause that sentence to be firmly observed until [Col. 1121A] fitting satisfaction has been made.

Further, have it proclaimed through your dioceses that any persons who believe that they have debts to claim from the same monastery from Hilary’s time are to present themselves before you, brother archbishop, and before our beloved sons … the abbots of Oratorio and Chaloceio, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Angers, in order to receive full justice in this matter.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

## XXIV. … TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF BOURGUEIL

That they are to discipline certain monks of the said monastery who are accomplices of Hilary, formerly abbot of that monastery, and call them back to obedience, and not allow them to disturb the monastery. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1121B]

Our beloved sons H. and G., monks of your house, have informed us that, although we judged that Hilary, formerly abbot of your monastery, should be removed by sentence from its administration, certain monks, his accomplices, residing in your monastery refuse to render you, son abbot, the obedience and reverence due to you. Seeking to disturb the peace and unity of the monastery, they do not hesitate, both personally and through others, to exact false debts.

Since peace and unity promote the growth of religious life, we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you, commanding by apostolic letters that you persist steadfastly in unity and peace, and that you regularly discipline by our authority those monks [Col. 1121C] who presume, in these or other matters, to disturb the said monastery.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

## XXV. … TO THE ABBOTS OF MARMOUTIER, SAINT JULIAN, AND SAINT FLORENT, IN THE DIOCESES OF TOURS AND ANGERS

That they are to compel Hilary, formerly abbot of Bourgueil, to return to the cloister assigned to him in order to do penance. (Lateran, fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

Since Hilary, formerly abbot of Bourgueil, has by our judicial sentence, justice requiring it, been removed from the [Col. 1121D] administration of that monastery, and we have ordered him to reside in the monastery of Saint Jovin of Marnes to perform penance, we command you by the authority of these presents that you in no way presume to receive him while he wanders outside the aforesaid cloister, either in the enclosures of your monasteries or at your tables, lest you appear to encourage him in his malice. Repel him, so that he may thus return to the cloister assigned to him for penance.

Otherwise, by our letters we command our venerable brothers … the archbishop of Tours and … the bishop of Angers, and our beloved son … the abbot of Oratorio of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Angers, to restrain you [Col. 1122A] from such presumption by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

## XXVI. … TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, … THE BISHOP OF ANGERS, AND … THE ABBOT OF ORATORIO, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER IN THE DIOCESE OF ANGERS

Concerning the same matter, as above. (Given as in the other letter.)

Since Hilary, formerly abbot of Bourgueil, etc., in the same manner down to “reside,” we command by our letters our beloved sons … the abbots of Marmoutier, Saint Julian, and Saint Florent, in the dioceses of Tours and Angers, [Col. 1122B] that they are not to receive the same man while wandering outside the aforesaid cloister, etc., in almost the same manner down to “return.” Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid abbots should presume to act otherwise—which we do not believe—you restrain them from such presumption by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. But if not all of you can act, two of you, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXVII. TO MATTHEW, PROVOST, AND THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF BLESSED LAWRENCE OF JOUY, BOTH PRESENT AND FUTURE, IN PERPETUITY

They are received under the protection of the Apostolic See, together with all their goods, liberties, immunities, and privileges. (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1122C]

A pious request ought to be fulfilled with an effective result, so that the sincerity of devotion may laudably increase and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Blessed Lawrence of Jouy, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or [Col. 1122D] princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, obtain through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; whatever you possess at Jouy; the church of Ova, with its dependencies, and whatever you possess in that town; the altars of Saint Quentin and Berveres, with their dependencies; whatever you possess at Manisd. and Semincurten; at Wasseium; at Moruncurten; at Charmes; at Sememonten; and at Doniors; and the right which you possess in the prebends of Saleio.

We also decree that the burial ground [Col. 1123A] of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. We ratify, moreover, the liberties and immunities granted to your church, together with the ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain inviolate in future times.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, for the complete benefit of the purposes for which they were granted—for the governance and support [Col. 1123B] of those concerned—saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct his offence by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself to stand guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But let all who preserve the rights of the same place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit [Col. 1123C] of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1206 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

## XXVIII. TO ELIAS, ABBOT OF RADING, AND HIS BRETHREN, BOTH PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY

They are received under protection, etc., as above, together with certain other alms granted in favour of religion. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1123D]

Although unworthy, we have been raised, by the disposing mercy of God, to the summit of the supreme pontificate in order that, with pastoral concern and care, we should labour for the condition of all the Churches and afford them the protection of the Apostolic See, so that God may be more abundantly venerated in them to the extent that they are more free from the assaults of the malicious.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary of Rading, of the Cluniac Order, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this document.

[Col. 1124A] First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order, known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, obtain by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names: Rading, Chelsea, and Leominster, with churches, chapels, cemeteries, tithes and offerings, woods, fields, pastures, meadows, waters, mills, fisheries, and all other dependencies [Col. 1124B] and appurtenances; Tachea with all its appurtenances, and the church of Weregrava; Witellhie with all its appurtenances; Wiccheburia with all its appurtenances; Bleiburia with all its appurtenances; the land which you possess in Henreda, with all its appurtenances; Estona, with the church of the same town and all its other appurtenances; Rockenton, with the church of the same town and all its other appurtenances; the churches of Stanton, Haneborhe, and Inglesfelt, with their appurtenances; Dudelesfande with all its appurtenances; the land which you possess in Hectun, with all its appurtenances; likewise, the lands which you possess in Lingeborche and Stretfelda, formerly Hugh de Mortuomari’s, and in Sebrichteswrde, with [Col. 1124C] all their appurtenances; the lands and rents which you possess in London and Berchamstede, with all their appurtenances; the land which you acquired within the holding of Hou, as the dowry of your church, with all its appurtenances; the priory of Mai with all its appurtenances; and Lindegros in Scotland, with all its appurtenances.

Furthermore, no one may presume to demand or in any way extort tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or of the sustenance of your animals. When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

By apostolic authority we also prohibit anyone [Col. 1124D] from presuming, without manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce sentences of excommunication or interdict against you or your monastery, or to burden you with new and undue exactions. We command that chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of your monks or clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, be supplied to you freely and without any improper demand by the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from presuming to build anew a church or oratory within the parishes of your churches without the assent of the diocesan bishop and the chapter of Rading, [Col. 1125A] saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. Wishing also to provide henceforth with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your houses or granges from committing robbery or theft, setting fire, shedding blood, rashly seizing or killing a person, or daring to use violence.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm, and strengthen with the privilege of this document, all the liberties and immunities granted to your monastery by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties, immunities, and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, and other faithful persons. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever [Col. 1125B] may rashly disturb the monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, for the complete benefit of the purposes for which they were granted—for the governance and support of those concerned—saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct the offence by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, and be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God, etc., down to “be subject to vengeance.” But let all who preserve the rights of the same [Col. 1125C] place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that etc., down to the end. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1207 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

## XXIX. TO THE NOBLEMAN M. DE ROMANIA

A decision concerning restoration of the right of patronage of the church of Saint Angelus of Casaperota. (Lateran, ninth day before the Kalends of April.)

Having examined the case pending between you and the knights of Campone concerning the church of Saint Angelus of Casaperota, heard the confessions and considered the depositions, [Col. 1125D] inspected the instruments, and investigated the allegations, we have clearly perceived that the arbitral award which T., vicedominus of Sabina, is said to have pronounced in that matter was rendered contrary to the form of law and of the submission to arbitration. Therefore, notwithstanding the confirmation of our predecessor Pope Celestine of happy memory, who had confirmed it as prudently made and accepted by both parties, we have decreed it null and void.

We have also found unsuitable and inept the action which you brought against the aforesaid knights concerning the right of patronage of that church. For, since you produced witnesses to prove that, when the aforesaid vicedominus received that church as though in sequestration, you possessed [Col. 1126A] the church, you could certainly neither bring an action for recovery of property nor seek its restitution. We therefore pronounced that your claim does not stand in this respect, absolving the aforementioned knights from it. Provided, however, that if you should wish to bring a suitable and proper action, they shall nevertheless be bound to answer you. Therefore let no one … of our determination, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

## XXX. TO THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF FAENZA

A postponement is granted concerning the dispute which they have with the Church of Ravenna.

When recently, on your behalf, our beloved sons M. and Ar. came to the Apostolic See concerning the case pending between you and the Church of Ravenna, the procurator eventually appointed by your syndic, who remained at home, objected to the testimony of witnesses for the opposing party by alleging falsehood. [Col. 1126B] But when we asked him whether he would swear that he was not raising this objection fraudulently in order to delay the proceedings, but believed that it could be proved through lawful witnesses; or at least that the syndic who had sworn the oath against vexatious litigation had instructed him to raise this question, he replied that he would swear neither.

Therefore, although, because after a peremptory summons no sufficient representative appeared before us, we might according to the strictness of the law have determined otherwise, nevertheless, at the request of your messengers, who humbly petitioned us in this matter, [Col. 1126C] we have thought fit to grant you a postponement until the first Easter. In the meantime, send into our presence either the syndic himself or another suitable representative who can lawfully raise the aforesaid exception or any other competent exception, lest the case be delayed any further. Otherwise, from that time onward, we decree, justice requiring it, that you are to be condemned in the expenses which the opposing party has incurred while waiting on this account; and in the case itself we shall proceed as far as the law permits us.

## XXXI. TO … THE BISHOP, H., ABBOT OF ABEBBRUHOT, TH., PRIOR, RALPH, ARCHDEACON, AND MASTER LAURENCE, OFFICIAL OF SAINT ANDREW’S

They are commissioned to settle certain disputes concerning certain tithes. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1126D]

When our beloved sons the abbot and canons of Cambuskenneth had, by authority of our letters, brought our beloved sons … the abbot and monks of Dunfermline, in the diocese of Saint Andrews, before our venerable brother … the bishop of Dublin and our beloved sons … the abbots of Cupar and Scone in the same diocese, concerning certain tithes belonging to their church of Egles, and concerning damages and injuries inflicted; and when the latter, by our delegation, had summoned the same abbot and canons before our beloved sons … the prior of Holyrood and … the dean of Tyninghame in the aforesaid diocese, together with you, son official, concerning the chapel of Dunipast and [Col. 1127A] the tithes belonging to it: after many allegations and disputes, both parties submitted themselves to you by arbitration, so that, proceeding in the matters according to the order of law, you should settle the controversies, both concerning possession and concerning ownership, without appeal, by judgment or agreement. They confirmed under bodily oath that whatever two of you together with you, brother bishop, should decide, if all of you could not agree jointly, they would hold ratified and firmly observe, and would not hinder the arbitral proceedings through deceit or malice.

Accordingly, having heard the submissions of both sides, received witnesses, and published their depositions, because you had doubts concerning four points, you sent the prepared case [Col. 1127B] to our presence, invoking the pronouncement of the Apostolic See upon those four doubtful matters.

The first question arose before you from this: when the canons had sued the monks concerning the aforesaid tithes, the monks wished to countersue the same canons concerning certain other tithes, although no submission to arbitration concerning them had been made to you. The monks’ party asserted that, according to lawful enactments, one who is sued before someone may countersue that same person before the same judge. You therefore requested that the Apostolic See explain whether there is room for a counterclaim before arbitrators.

The second doubt arose because, after publication of the witness testimony, the aforesaid canons wished to produce certain instruments supporting their claim; the monks’ party asserted that, just as witnesses could not be produced after publication of the testimony, so instruments could not be produced. You therefore carefully asked whether instruments may validly be produced after publication of witness testimony.

The difficulty of the third doubt arose because the aforesaid monks, raising an exception against the aforesaid canons, asserted that the controversy concerning the aforesaid tithes had been settled by agreement in the time of King David of illustrious memory. They produced in evidence an instrument concerning the agreement made, authenticated with the seal of the aforesaid king. You asked our response as to whether that instrument, the witnesses having been removed from consideration, [Col. 1127D] is by itself sufficient to prove the proposition, since arguments had been made on both sides.

The fourth doubt arose because, when proceedings concerning possession and ownership had been conducted before you, one party submitted that both questions ought to be ended by a single judgment, while the other party submitted that the arbitral award concerning possession ought first to be pronounced and that, after restitution had been made, the question of ownership ought subsequently to be decided. Since much had been argued on both sides, you asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See whether the questions of possession and ownership ought to be settled by one sentence or two; and, if by two, whether the sentence [Col. 1128A] pronounced concerning possession should be executed before that concerning ownership is delivered. [Note: [Col. 1127D] Chapter *Cum dilecti*, “On Arbitrators.”]

We therefore reply to your discretion concerning the first point as follows: although in a judicial proceeding a person sued before someone may countersue that person before the same judge, nevertheless he cannot countersue before arbitrators, because arbitrators cannot judge except concerning those matters alone which were submitted to them by arbitration. [Note: [Col. 1127D] Chapter *Cum dilectus*, “On the Credibility of Instruments.”]

To the second question we have thought fit to reply as follows: either party may produce instruments even after publication of witness testimony, up to the rendering of final judgment, provided that the case has not yet been closed.

Concerning the third point, we reply as follows: investigate the truth more carefully. If the approved custom of that country is that credence is given in such matters to instruments of that king, you may safely admit the aforesaid instrument, especially since the often-mentioned king was of such integrity that his instruments carry the highest authority in the Scottish regions. [Note: [Col. 1128D] Chapter *Cum dilecti*, “On the Case of Possession and Ownership.”]

To the fourth point we reply briefly: when proceedings concerning possession and ownership are undertaken together, both matters ought to be ended by one judgment. But although possession ought to be stated first in the pronouncement, ownership ought nevertheless to prevail in execution.

Although you saw fit to send the prepared case to our presence, since many matters were presented before us on both sides through advocates which did not appear to have been argued before you, because they are asserted to be notorious in those regions, [Col. 1128C] investigate them more fully and decide the case with due finality, any obstacle of contradiction or appeal being removed. Do not under any circumstances prolong the matter beyond two months. But if not all of you can act, you, brother bishop, together with two or three of the others, shall nevertheless carry this out.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

## XXXII. TO THE PRIORS AND BRETHREN OF KIRKHAM, GISEBURN, BREDLINGAM, NEWBURGH, AND OTHERS OF THE SAME ORDER ESTABLISHED IN THE DIOCESE OF YORK

Authority is committed to them to reform and correct the churches subject to them. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1128D] It is a saying of the Wise Man which is read: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent.” And again: “Where there is much counsel, there is safety” (Prov. 11). But the Lord himself testifies of himself in the Gospel: “Wherever two or three,” he says, “are gathered in my name, I too am in their midst” (Matt. 18). As he showed after the Resurrection, when, placing himself as a third among the disciples speaking of him on the road, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. Therefore, since as the wickedness of the age increases the charity of many grows cold, it is especially fitting for those who have professed the regular life to proceed, in cutting off vices and planting virtues, with so much the more deliberation and gravity [Col. 1129A] as both the decline of the aging world itself and the weakness of the human condition more strongly oppose this purpose.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your discretion, and by apostolic letters command you, sons who are priors, that all of you, if it can conveniently be done, or at least the greater part, meet together annually; and, deliberating concerning the reform of the order, correct by wholesome counsel what you see needs correction in your churches, and establish what ought to be established according to God, notwithstanding an appeal interposed in evasion of regular discipline. Thus, whenever necessary, two or three of you shall go together to the church in which correction appears necessary and laudably carry out the office of correction, since concerning [Col. 1129B] observance of the order you are not bound to answer to the prior of another regular church.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

### XXXIII. To the Bishops of Monopoli, Polignano, and Conversano

That they may confirm the election of Benedict, bishop of the island of Cephalonia, if he is suitable and the election has been canonically made. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of April.)

By their letters, our beloved sons, the nobleman Count Maio, the clergy, and the people of the island of Cephalonia, informed us that, when the episcopal see of that island was vacant, and they had carefully deliberated concerning appointing a Latin pastor over themselves, all, with unanimous will and [Col. 1129C] equal consent, elected as bishop the priest Benedict, whom they highly commended for discretion and integrity. They humbly begged us, since the metropolitan see is deprived of a pastor—to which they could not have recourse even if it were not vacant, since it is still disobedient and rebellious toward the Apostolic See—to deign to confirm that election by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, having caused the same priest to be brought before you, you diligently investigate the truth concerning his learning, life, birth, and the other matters which must be examined regarding his suitability; and, if you find him suitable, confirm the election by authority of the Apostolic See and consecrate him as bishop in our stead, receiving from him, for us and our successors, an oath of fealty and obedience. Faithfully report to us what you have done.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

### XXXIV. To the Bishop, the Dean, and the Archdeacon of Noyon

That they are to cause a judgment pronounced and confirmed for Guiburg, a poor widow, to be put into execution. (Lateran, ninth day before the Kalends of April.)

Guiburg, a poor widow, appearing before us, humbly begged us to strengthen by apostolic protection the definitive judgment which you rendered for her, by our authority, concerning her dower and other property against the abbess of Montmartre, in the diocese of Paris. [Col. 1130A] Therefore, wishing to provide for the simplicity of that widow, who has already laboured repeatedly by coming to the Apostolic See on this account, by apostolic letters we command and strictly order your discretion that, since it is just, you cause that judgment to be observed inviolably through ecclesiastical censure, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. This is notwithstanding any appeal which may perhaps appear to have been lodged before our court by the said abbess, since she has not pursued it.

But because the aforesaid woman, being simple and ignorant of law, did not know how to explain to us the merits of her case, lest, as on another occasion, the opposing party, maligning her simplicity, should now also accuse her of false petitions, and thus her labour be multiplied, we will and command that, if you perhaps find the matter to be otherwise than her simple account led us to understand, you investigate with the greatest care the truth concerning those matters which she alleged against the aforesaid abbess; and, having God alone before your eyes, set down what is just, appeal set aside. Cause what you decree to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure, so fulfilling the apostolic command that, because of your failure, she is not compelled again to bring her complaint before us. Witnesses, etc. No letters, etc. And if not all … you, brother, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

### XXXV. To the Clergy and People of Verissa

That they are to render obedience and reverence to Master Garin, elected archbishop of Varissa. (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1130C] Both the authority of the Apostolic See and the need of the Church of Constantinople induced us to arrange that Master Guarin, then elect and now your archbishop, when he came into our presence, should be ordained deacon and priest and consecrated bishop, granting him the pallium, namely the fullness of the pontifical office. For thus the Roman Pontiff has called others to share his burden of care while retaining for himself the fullness of power. Hence canonical authority teaches that those coming to him [Col. 1130D] from whatever place receive protection and consecration from him, since one who exercises his own right is not understood to inflict injury upon others.

Although he was confirmed by our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Constantinople, he could not be consecrated by him, because he has no fellow bishops; hence it was necessary for him to send the elect of Athens and Thebes into Syria in order to obtain the rite of consecration. Therefore, for these reasons, we send him back to you, ordained, consecrated, and invested with the pallium by us, together with the favour of our grace; and by apostolic letters command you to render him reverence and obedience, both due and devout.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

[Col. 1131A] In the same manner to the Patriarch of Constantinople. Given as in the other letter.

In the same manner to Henry, illustrious Emperor of Constantinople, our dearest son in Christ. Given as in the other letter.

### XXXVI. To G., Archbishop of Verissa

It is decreed that sentences of excommunication and suspension pronounced without reasonable cause are not binding, and that a sentence which is launched after an appeal is not to be observed as being void. (Given as in the other letters.)

Since through our hands you have been ordained deacon and priest and consecrated bishop, in order that we may show due regard both to our own honour and to yours, by authority of these presents [Col. 1131B] we forbid anyone to presume to pronounce against you a sentence of suspension or excommunication without manifest and reasonable cause; and canonical admonition must always first be given, unless perhaps the offence is such that the judicial order need not be observed. But if you perceive that you are being oppressed, you may freely appeal to the Apostolic See, so that you may avoid the burden threatening you. And if, after such an appeal, anyone presumes to launch against you a sentence of suspension or excommunication, we decree that it is not to be observed, as void and without effect. Therefore let no one … violate this our prohibition, concession, and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letters.

### XXXVII. To the Same

Permission is granted for him to retain the benefices which he held in that city before his promotion. (Given as above.)

[Col. 1131C] Since the Empire of Constantinople has not yet been so firmly established that its condition does not still largely fluctuate, we wish, with fatherly care, henceforth to safeguard your security, so that whatever may happen outside the city of Constantinople in future events, you may have within it a special refuge to which you may resort in necessity. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, favourably assenting to your petitions, we grant that you may retain in their complete integrity the benefices which you had canonically acquired in the aforesaid city before you were assumed to the [Col. 1131D] burden of pastoral office, until it shall seem expedient to us and our successors.

Given as above.

### XXXVIII. To All the Faithful of Christ Who Have Taken the Cross and Are Established in the Regions of Romania

They are urged to stand firm and strong in the service of our Creator against the faithless, terrible, and powerful pagans. (Given as above.)

Since, in response to the summons of apostolic exhortation, you have left your native homes and possessions, for reverence of the divine name, held in contempt, and have transferred yourselves to the eastern regions in order to devote yourselves more vigorously to the recovery of the Holy Land, human strength is ineffective for this purpose and can accomplish nothing by itself unless this is bestowed upon it from above. Therefore you must return with all your affections to the author of all things in a spirit of humility and with a contrite soul, humbly imploring him in prayer to direct your journey to its desired end and to prepare for you eternal fruit through your present labour.

And because we care for you diligently with fatherly affection, we ask, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord, enjoining this upon you also for the remission of your sins: since all things are placed in the divine will, remain steadfast and strong in the service of your Creator, casting all your hope upon him. [Col. 1132B] For, if you remain in his fear, he will by his power turn the paths of the enemies of Christ’s cross into darkness and slipperiness, and, besides eternal glory, will turn all things presently adverse to you into prosperity. For, as we firmly hope, an abundant multitude of crusaders will soon come to your aid; with them, by God’s help, you will be able effectively to labour to blow the faithlessness of the pagans away from the borders of Christendom.

Given as above.

### XXXIX. To A., Illustrious King of Hungary

A reply urging him not to take it ill that the election of the provost of Pabenburg, the brother of his wife, as Archbishop of Kalocsa cannot be confirmed, because he was deficient in age and otherwise unlearned. (Lateran, Nones of April.)

[Col. 1132C] As we remember having informed your royal prudence in earlier letters, we love you with such a prerogative of charity that we wish to deny you nothing which we would ever grant to any prince, since, so far as we can with God, we earnestly seek your honour and advancement. Although you have offered us earnest petitions on behalf of our beloved son, the provost of Pabenburg, brother of your consort, elected Archbishop of Kalocsa, asking us to grant him the benefit of confirmation and send the gift of the pallium, since you trusted that he would be useful and necessary to you and to your realm in the archiepiscopal office; yet, because the Apostle teaches that we should lay hands suddenly on no one—that is, before we have acquired fuller certainty concerning him by canonical examination—and because we were uncertain about the provost’s age and learning, we instructed our venerable brother, the Archbishop, and our beloved son, the Provost of Salzburg, to investigate these matters diligently and faithfully report their findings to us.

By apostolic letters we notified your serenity that if he were found to possess learning not merely outstanding but at least adequate, and age not merely complete but at least near to completion, we were so desirous of satisfying your will that, unless such a serious defect appeared in both matters that it ought in no way to be tolerated, we would mitigate strictness and dispense with him by favour. Otherwise, if your petition on his behalf did not obtain the desired result, this could be imputed not to our harshness but to his insufficiency.

But the aforesaid Archbishop of Salzburg recently informed our Apostolic See by letter that, having come to the borders of Hungary and assembled in his presence two suffragans of the Church of Kalocsa and other suitable men, he proceeded to examine the said provost in accordance with the form of our mandate. He declared that he found him reading a text fluently, interpreting its words competently in his own language, and also answering suitably concerning grammatical construction. A certain knight, the provost’s tutor, after taking a corporal oath, affirmed that he was unquestionably twenty-five years of age or older and that the stature of his body corresponded to that age.

[Col. 1133B] We therefore, after careful deliberation with our brethren concerning these matters, clearly judged him to be commended neither in canon law nor in divine learning, even slightly, and judged his age to be not merely incomplete but not even near completion. These two matters—lawful age and sufficient learning—are so necessary for an archbishop, who must be father of fathers and teacher of teachers, that, according to the statute of the Lateran Council, if clerics presume to elect anyone who suffers deficiency in one or both of them, not only as archbishop but even as bishop, then, besides such an election being void, they are deprived on that occasion of the power to elect and suspended for three years from the receipt of benefices.

Therefore we could not hold valid what is void by law itself. Yet, acting mercifully for your sake and out of favour toward you, we decided not to inflict upon the chapter of Kalocsa the penalty laid down in the aforesaid decree. We are not a little grieved that we could not satisfy the royal will in this matter, lest, if we perhaps inclined either to the right or to the left, there should be in our hand weight and weight, measure and measure, both of which are abominable before God.

For the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, who received the Spirit without measure from his very conception, delayed exercising the office of preaching until his thirtieth year, thereby clearly showing that before the thirtieth year no one ought to usurp for himself the office of preaching, which belongs especially to pastoral care. But from the words read, that Jesus “was beginning at about thirty years of age,” it is noted that, if one elected bishop is near that age, a dispensation may be granted to him when necessity or usefulness requires it, provided that life and learning support him, after the example of him who began both to do and to teach. For “whoever shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” Otherwise—if the contrary is done—it must be reckoned not a dispensation but a dissipation.

We therefore ask and admonish your royal highness not to be troubled because your desire could not be fulfilled in that which necessity did not permit to be done contrary to law. Rather, have the aforesaid provost instructed in theological and canonical learning, so that, when in the passage of time he has advanced in literary knowledge, we may together with you seek his honour and advancement. For without doubt it would benefit neither you nor him that he should assume the pastoral burden against God, lest perhaps, where you thought to make progress, you should deserve rather to fall short; and you would rightly judge us worthless when you understood that, for the sake of an earthly king, we had not feared to offend the heavenly King, who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April, in the tenth year.

### XL. To the Abbot and Convent of Cambuskenneth, Diocese of St Andrews

It is decreed that, by confirming a privilege for them at the petition of the abbot and convent of Dunfermline, the pope did not intend to confer a new right but to preserve one already conferred. (Lateran, Nones of April.)

[Col. 1134B] Although the privilege which, at the petition of our beloved sons the abbot and convent of Dunfermline, we caused to be renewed for them after the example of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, contains certain matters concerning which a dispute is known to have arisen between you and them, we nevertheless do not wish that any prejudice to your right may be generated by this renewal of the privilege. For we do not intend to confer a new right, but to preserve one already conferred, against which prescription could not yet have run from the time of our aforesaid predecessor.

[Col. 1134C] Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April, in the tenth year.

### XLI. To the Illustrious King of the Danes

Thanks are given for the liberation of the bishop of Schleswig; and, the cause of accusations laid against him being reserved, the king is urged to permit that bishop to enjoy the revenues of his bishopric through his administrator. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of April.)

Concerning what we write to our dearest son in Christ, Ph., illustrious King of the Franks, husband of our dearest daughter in Christ, your sister, Queen of the Franks, your envoys will be able faithfully to report it to you. But because you released our venerable brother, the Bishop of Schleswig, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, we pursue your royal magnificence with sincere acts [Col. 1134D] of thanksgiving.

Although the same bishop, appearing in our presence, endeavoured in many ways to show himself blameless concerning the charges made against him, while your envoys endeavoured in many ways to show him guilty, we nevertheless could not proceed fully in the examination of those matters. Taking into account both that provision must be made for your security against the suspicion which has arisen, and that it is wholly unfitting for the Church of Schleswig to remain without pastoral governance, we have resolved, proceeding by the royal road between right and left, that the said bishop shall remain with us until the affair reaches a peaceful conclusion by means of agreement or justice. Meanwhile, through our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Lund, [Col. 1135A] provision shall be made for a suitable administrator of the aforesaid church, who shall take care of it both in spiritual and temporal matters, rendering an account of its revenues. From those revenues the money borrowed for the bishop’s use shall be repaid, and during this period of necessity what he needs shall be suitably supplied to him.

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and exhort your royal serenity to permit that church to be freely administered through the same archbishop in accordance with the foregoing arrangement of apostolic provision, and that provision be made for the aforesaid bishop from its revenues. And lest the case remain in suspense longer than is expedient, take care to send some prudent and faithful men from there to the Apostolic See by the first coming feast of the Nativity of the Lord, entrusted with authority so that through them and with them, if it be granted from above, we may effectively negotiate a settlement in your stead concerning that affair. Otherwise, after hearing and understanding what you choose to allege against the same bishop through them, and what he takes care to answer in his defence, a judgment of equity shall proceed from our presence. Moreover, the said envoys—men indeed prudent and faithful—will be able to report to your serenity what they have heard from us concerning these and other matters.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the tenth year.

### XLII. To Philip, Illustrious King of the Franks

He is urged to treat I., his wife, with marital affection. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1135C] The duty of the pastoral office, by which, according to the Apostle, we are debtors both to the wise and to the foolish, exhorts us to induce your royal magnificence, in season and out of season, by salutary admonitions to those things which are just and honourable. Therefore, although we have often exhorted your gentleness fully to restore to your favour your dearest consort in Christ, Queen I., and although, through God’s grace, you have listened to apostolic admonitions, if not wholly, at least in part, yet because full conjugal favour has not been restored to her, we are compelled to press you more earnestly on this matter with endeavours of charity.

For although before people who do not know your hidden circumstances you may strive to excuse yourself for not showing the said queen conjugal affection, you cannot at all excuse yourself at least for not having royal honour shown to her. We therefore earnestly ask and more strongly exhort your serenity, adjuring you through Jesus Christ, who is the mediator of the lawful covenant, that, since according to the Apostle married persons ought not to defraud one another lest they fall into the snare of Satan, you should, if it can ever be done, take care to treat the said queen with marital favour. Revere the Holy Spirit of discipline, who flees deceit; for you must fear lest—God forbid—he withdraw himself from your thoughts if they persist without such understanding.

But if you have God, who is not mocked, as witness of your conscience that you cannot treat her with such favour, at least let royal shame cover you, so that you no longer permit an illustrious woman—the granddaughter of kings, sister of a king, wife of a king, daughter of a king—to be held contemptibly, as though captive, to the disgrace of so great a lineage and the injury of your reputation. Instead, cause royal honour to be bestowed upon her; lest, if you withdraw manifest things from her longer, you may be proved to defraud her of hidden things also, and, revealing inner things through outward ones, have not God alone as your judge but the world as well. Though you may at last appease the former by repentance, you will scarcely be able to restrain the latter’s murmur if it begins to make an outcry against you on this matter.

For though you have been victorious in many things, you have never conquered so well as when you conquer yourself, so that you are conquered not by vice but by virtue. For the magnificent King Solomon testifies that the wise man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities. We also write to our beloved son, the Abbot of Sarnai, a man, as we believe, prudent and honourable, that he may present and explain our letter to your royal prudence, lest perhaps even now, as formerly, it be explained to you less faithfully by another.

Given as in the other letter.

### XLIII. To the Bishops of Ely and Chichester

That they are to persuade the justiciars of the realm of England, even by ecclesiastical censure, not to obstruct the vows undertaken by crusading pilgrims. (Lateran, eighth day before the Ides of April.)

Our beloved son, the nobleman G., son of Peter, Justiciar of England, formerly informed us that because of the war then dangerously raging between our dearest sons in Christ, Ph., illustrious King of the Franks, and I., illustrious King of the English, the King of England and his magnates did not permit him to leave England, since in so great a disturbance he was greatly needed by the whole realm; and the aforesaid King of the Franks and his barons did not allow him to pass through their territories in any direction. Thus, hindered by these obstacles, he could not then fulfil the vow of pilgrimage which he had formerly made when taking the cross.

He added that he had young heirs with very powerful enemies, who strove by every means in their power to disinherit them. Since they had already occupied a great part of the children’s inheritance, they could easily obtain the remainder in their father’s absence. Furthermore, he stated that he had founded, upon his sons’ inheritance, a monastery of nuns of the order of Sempringham; this could not stand according to the law of the English realm if his sons were deprived of that inheritance. The same knight further promised to build a hospice in a highly suitable place to receive passing poor persons. He therefore mercifully asked that, for these reasons and with our permission, he might defer fulfilment of the vow, promising that meanwhile he would send annually sixty marks of lawful sterling money in support of the Holy Land.

The aforesaid King of England, the Archbishop of Canterbury of blessed memory, and you, brother Bishop of Ely, also urgently petitioned for that nobleman, whom, because of his proven prudence [Col. 1137A] and strength, you knew to be most necessary to the whole realm in such a crisis, setting out to us in your letters the needs both of the king and the realm and of his children. We therefore instructed our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son, the Dean of Lincoln, that, if the matters set forth above were true, they should grant by our authority to that nobleman permission to remain for three years, by our leave, in service of the king and for defence of his children—unless meanwhile, after weighing the circumstances of affairs and times, we should decide otherwise concerning him. He was, however, to take care faithfully to perform what he had promised about building the hospice for the poor and sending money in support of the Holy Land.

But, as has come to our knowledge, the same justiciar has hitherto not used the aforesaid letters, nor has he endeavoured to pay annually the promised money for support of the Holy Land. Moreover, because the pressure of the wars which had arisen between the said kings has, by the Lord’s disposition, been pacified, the same justiciar is not as useful to king or realm as before. Therefore, since, in addition to the causes already mentioned, several others are said to have ceased which appear to have induced us to grant the aforesaid indulgence, and since reason further requires that when the cause ceases, that which it compelled should likewise cease, by authority of these presents we command you, if this is so, to endeavour to admonish and effectively induce the aforesaid justiciar—compelling him, if necessary, through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside—not to postpone carrying out the vow which he is known to have made. And if not both, one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the tenth year.

### XLIV. To the Archbishop, the Subdean of St Martin, and Master Socrates, Canon of Tours

The matrimonial cause of I. of Alcia and M., his wife, is committed to them for final determination. (Given as in the other letter.)

From the letters of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Tréguier, we have clearly learned that, although we had committed to him and to our beloved sons, the cantor and archdeacon of Tréguier, for canonical final determination, the matrimonial cause pending between the nobleman I. of Alcia and M., his wife, of the diocese of Angers, [Col. 1137D] they, being far away and wholly unaware that it had first been delegated by us to B., your predecessor of blessed memory, brother Archbishop, and to you, sons Subdean and Master W. Socrates, were induced by the aforesaid nobleman, who sought a divorce, and proceeded in the case as far as the taking of testimony.

But that nobleman, without awaiting a definitive judgment and using, as is said, certain false instruments, took another woman [as wife]. The said bishop further asserted that the woman had been kept under the power of the aforesaid nobleman, and had been entirely without defence before him and his fellow judges. Yet, when asked by them in law whether she objected or not, she gave her assent to the reception and examination of the witnesses produced, though she does not know by what spirit she was led to do this. Nevertheless, afterward, secretly, because she did not dare do so publicly, she revealed to them that she was held by her husband as a captive; and, compelled by him through threats and beatings, she confirmed by an oath taken that she would in no way dare to object to what might be alleged against her for dissolving the marriage. Therefore they suspended proceedings in the aforesaid case.

Since fraud and deceit ought to afford protection to no one, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if the truth supports the foregoing, [Col. 1138B] notwithstanding the aforesaid letters, and according to the tenor of the earlier letters, you proceed in this case according to reason, without any occasion or excuse, every obstacle of appeal removed, restoring to its due state whatever you know has been attempted, by occasion of those letters, to the prejudice of the said woman.

Given as in the other letter.

### XLV. To the Bishop of St Andrews

Concerning the clarification of obedience and the exception of parish churches, and concerning burials and certain other matters belonging to the bishop. (Lateran, eighth day before the Ides of April.)

Your brotherhood asked to be instructed by an oracle of the Apostolic See whether the abbot of an exempt monastery is bound to render canonical obedience to the diocesan bishop by reason of parish churches belonging to that monastery which are not exempt from episcopal jurisdiction. To this we judge that the following answer should be given: since, according to canonical sanctions, priests ought to be instituted in churches of religious persons which do not belong to them in full right, priests who answer to the bishops concerning the care of the people, while rendering to the religious persons a proper account concerning temporal matters, obedience for such churches should be rendered to the bishop not by the abbot but by such priests.  
[Note: [Col. 1137] See the addition to chapter 31, book VI, *On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire*.]

You further asked whether religious persons to whom parish churches have been granted for their own use may, when the incumbents of those churches die, enter into possession of the same churches by their own authority, or whether they ought rather to be put into possession by the diocesan bishop. To this we certainly answer that, unless they have been specially granted the right to enter them themselves when they fall vacant, it is plainly not lawful for them to enter into possession of those churches without consulting their bishop.

And because certain religious persons holding parish churches refuse to provide procuration to a bishop visiting his parish, alleging only prescription in their defence, we do not wish your brotherhood to be unaware that, since prescription can claim no place for itself in such matters, as we have reasonably shown elsewhere, [Col. 1139A] they cannot protect themselves from rendering it by means of prescription.  
[Note: [Col. 1139D] Chapter *Cum non liceat*, *On Prescription*.]  
[Note: [Col. 1140D] Chapter *Cum plerumque*, *On Donations*.]

Moreover, since it often happens that bishops successively grant religious houses, out of revenues belonging to the bishops themselves, more than a fiftieth share, so that these revenues are sometimes diminished by as much as a third or a fourth, sometimes by more or less, your brotherhood consulted us whether their successors may in any way revoke what has thus been granted in excess of the fiftieth part.

We therefore answer your inquiry as follows. Although it is determined in the canon that, if any bishop wishes perhaps to establish a monastery in his diocese and enrich it from the goods of the church over which he presides, he must grant there no more than a fiftieth part; and, if he wishes to form a church under monastic rules or enlarge it for his own burial, no more than a hundredth part of the revenues of the church over which he presides: yet the same canon subsequently adds that this equitable moderation must be observed, namely, that he give suitable support to the one to whom he grants, and not inflict serious losses upon the one from whom he takes. This safeguard must be observed: he is to take only one of those two benefits, whichever he prefers.

It must always be observed that no bishop may grant, with grave detriment to his church, not only more, but not even as much as, or less than, these amounts, whether he wishes to do this at one time and in one act or repeatedly and successively, granting to the same or to different churches. Therefore, whatever is shown to have been granted to grave detriment, whether from possessions or revenues belonging to the episcopal mensa or to the cathedral church, may lawfully be revoked, whatever the portion, unless such an action is excluded by prescription or another lawful exception.

For although at first sight it is presumed that a grant of a fiftieth or a hundredth part does not inflict grave detriment, nevertheless, whether it occurs repeatedly or even once, it can sometimes be discovered from varying circumstances to be very damaging. This may be known more from demonstration of the fact itself than from the expression of any statute. Neither a fiftieth nor a hundredth part, whether once or successively, may be granted with grave loss. But if the bishop is so abundantly supplied that, without injury to his church, he can provide for the need of another church even with more than a fiftieth or hundredth part, then, although he ought not on his own authority to exceed the sum prescribed by the canon—which guards against those wishing to make grants imprudently—by authority of a superior, provision may be made from his abundance for another’s need even in a greater sum.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the tenth year.

### XLVI. To the Marquis of Malaspina

He is forbidden to presume, under pretext of toll, to receive in his territory anything beyond what he received before the statute of the Lateran Council. (Lateran, fourth day before the Ides of April.)

[Col. 1140A]

By the authority of these presents we prohibit anyone from presuming to harass you by ecclesiastical censure on account of the toll which, before the decree issued on this matter by the Lateran Council, was customarily collected in your territory—unless perhaps you abuse an ancient and approved toll. Therefore let no one … of our prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 10 April, in the tenth year.

XLVII. TO THE … ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. He is granted permission to receive and use the pallium. (Lateran, 16 April.)

[Col. 1140B]

Although it was established by an ancient and prudent decision that an archbishop-elect of the Church of Ravenna should come to the Roman Church to receive the office of consecration, or, if he does not require consecration, to receive the pallium, nevertheless, in consideration of the necessity of that church and of your devotion, we have judged that this ordinance should be moderated by providing as follows: that the pallium taken from the body of Blessed Peter—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—be delivered to your brotherhood by our beloved son R., our subdeacon, in the form set out in the letter which we send under our bull. But as soon as opportunity permits, you shall present yourself before the apostolic presence within a year, there personally and orally making the profession which you have now made under oath.

We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by these apostolic letters, to recognize the special grace granted to you—which we by no means wish drawn into precedent—and, in the calling in which the Lord has called you, to strive to show yourself such toward the church committed to you that, though it appears to have been grievously injured in both respects, it may rejoice through your provision to be restored both in temporal and spiritual matters.

Given at the Lateran, 16 April, in the tenth year.

XLVIII. TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF GRANDMONT. That they may pour forth prayers for the soul of M., Archbishop of Tours, so that he may be freed from the punishments which he may perhaps have deserved for his offences. (Lateran, 9 April.)

[Col. 1140D]

Although the sincere affection of fraternal charity, which never fails, ought to be extended to neighbours while they remain in the exile of this present pilgrimage, yet help should be given them from the fountain of that same love with more abundant benefits when, released from the bonds of the body, they have neither time nor place in which they can themselves work further. For this reason the holy Fathers have prescribed certain remedies by which provision may be made for the distress of the dead: namely alms, fasts, offerings, and prayers,

[Col. 1141A]

which are known especially to benefit those who, while living, deserved that these things could benefit them after death. For by many testimonies of Holy Scripture it is demonstrated that some obtain salvation of soul and body through the merits and prayers of others. “When he saw their faith,” it says, “the Lord said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you’;” and he immediately added: “Take up your bed and go to your house” (Matthew 9). Simon’s mother-in-law likewise, who was held by a severe fever, deserved to be freed through the prayers of those remaining in the house who asked on her behalf. Mary and Martha too obtained life for Lazarus by their tearful prayers. And, at the tears of the widow with the accompanying crowd pleading, the Lord raised her son.

Although every believer is bound to offer such suffrages, according to what is read in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not withhold kindness from the dead; for we shall all die” (Ecclus. 7), yet those are especially obliged to this who, freed from secular cares, can more readily mourn both their own sins and those of others. It is also fitting that fuller aid be given through these offices of mercy to those who placed the hope of their deliverance in persons still living in the body.

Now the late Archbishop of Tours, of happy memory, when he drew near to the gates of death and stood at the end of his life, caused certain letters to be written. After his death they were presented to us under his seal by our beloved son Master P. of Vico, in which he humbly begged us to admonish you by our letters that you should take care to pour out your prayers and supplications to the Lord on his behalf.

[Col. 1141C]

We therefore commend in this matter the pious desire of his devotion—he who, before the strict Judge, sought the help of the Church’s suffrages—and ask, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord that you pour out your hearts before the Lord for the said deceased and most devoutly entreat the Most High for his soul, so that through your intercessions he may be freed from the punishments which he may perhaps have deserved for his offences. Hold firmly to the hope that he who, out of faithful devotion, sought the protection of your supplications will receive through your prayers both benefit and aid.

Given at the Lateran, 9 April, in the tenth year.

XLIX. TO THE BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL CLERICS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ACHAIA. That they should diligently assist the Archbishop of Patras with charitable aid in paying his debts. (Lateran, 26 April.)

[Col. 1141D]

Although everyone ought to help a neighbour in a time of need, it is fitting to relieve more liberally the necessities of one to whose reverence we are known to be bound by a duty of subjection. Since, therefore, our venerable brother …, Archbishop of Patras, coming once and again to the Apostolic See on business concerning himself and his church, has sustained, besides many labours, serious losses and expenses, and since his present resources are insufficient for paying his debts,

[Col. 1142A]

we have thought fit to ask and admonish all of you, commanding you by these apostolic letters that you strive to assist the same archbishop with charitable aid, so that, freed through the support of your generosity from the obligations of his debts, he may be able more readily to labour for your benefit.

Given at the Lateran, 28 April, in the tenth year.

L. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PATRAS. That he shall not permit clerics of his province to receive ecclesiastical revenues if they disdain personally to serve in them, unless it is established to him that they were canonically promoted; and that he shall compel beneficed clerics to reside in their churches. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1142B]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that certain clerics do not hesitate to receive ecclesiastical revenues in churches of your province, although they neglect to reside in them and to serve personally. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we command you not to permit the said clerics, who disdain personally to serve in the churches in which they have been ordained, to receive ecclesiastical revenues, since there is at this time a great shortage of clerics there.

Given as in the other letter.

LI. TO THE SAME. That he shall not permit those who come into the regions of Achaia to celebrate [the liturgy]. (Lateran, 19 April.)

[Col. 1142C]

From the communication of your devotion we have learned that, when the Latins occupied the region of Achaia, certain Greek bishops, your suffragans, terrified by fear, fled from their own places and abandoned their churches. Some of them, though often admonished, nevertheless disdain to return to their sees; others cannot, because of the dangers of war, be admonished through reliable messengers. You therefore humbly begged us to give you salutary counsel on this matter and to write how you ought to proceed with respect to them and their dioceses.

We, considering that because of the novelty of the change in that land and the occurrence of new circumstances one must proceed with great deliberation, answer your devotion as follows: procure that they be cited not once but repeatedly—namely a first, second, and third time. If they refuse to appear and wish to persist in their contumacy, unless perhaps they consider themselves protected by the shield of an appeal, which they must pursue within the lawful time, compel them by sentences of suspension and excommunication to come to your obedience.

[Col. 1142D]

If their hardness cannot be softened even thus, let our beloved son B., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna and legate of the Apostolic See, remove them from the administration of their bishoprics and arrange that the churches over which they preside be provided with suitable persons. But he shall not pronounce against them a sentence of degradation, so that, if expedient, they may more easily be dealt with mercifully.

In the churches of those who absent themselves fraudulently and to whom a citation cannot reach, have the edict of a threefold citation publicly proclaimed. If they do not then take care to obey, or if they abandon their churches for more than six months, so that under the canonical sanctions they ought rightly to be deprived of them, proceed likewise against them as prescribed above.

You further requested instruction from the Apostolic See as to whether you ought to permit to celebrate [the liturgy] those clerics who come into the regions of Achaia without letters of recommendation. To this we answer you as follows: unless you have lawful certainty, either through letters or witnesses, of the canonical ordination of those entirely unknown to you, you ought not permit them to celebrate among your people. But if some of them perhaps wish privately to celebrate out of devotion,

[Col. 1143B]

you may tolerate it.

Given at the Lateran, 19 April, in the tenth year.

LII. TO THE BISHOP OF PASSAU. At the request of the Patriarch of Aquileia, while he presided over the Church of Passau, he is commissioned concerning a notable place where he may establish a cathedral church in the region of Vienna. (Lateran, 14 April.)

Both canonical authority teaches and natural reason suggests that, when necessity demands or utility persuades, one bishopric may be divided into several and several united into one, lest any lack a pastor’s care or anything be lacking to pastoral care. For we read that, when there were many lesser priests,

[Col. 1143C]

whom they commonly called *Chananaei*, and one high priest, whom they specifically named *Arabartus*, David, the outstanding prophet, understanding through the Holy Spirit that one would not suffice for all, established twenty-four high priests: sixteen from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar. Yet over all these he set one man, whom he appointed prince of the priests. To each in turn he allotted by lot the weeks of his service; the eighth of these fell to Abijah, from whose line Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, descended.

Accordingly, our beloved son, the nobleman …, Duke of Austria, made known to us, both by his own letters and through a special envoy, that the Bishopric of Passau is spread over parish boundaries so extensive that one person, however experienced, cannot exercise the pastoral office concerning each individual sheep within it without danger to many souls. Our venerable brother …, Patriarch of Aquileia, while presiding over the Church of Passau, is said to have foreseen this prudently and to have desired earnestly to petition our predecessor Pope C. of happy memory that, in a province—or rather provinces—so extensive, he should ordain another bishop besides himself. For, from experience, he knew that spiritual sacraments could not suitably be administered by one immediate pastor.

Among the other regions of the same bishopric, Austria is known to suffer the greatest deficiency. Indeed, it is said to be so far from the cathedral see

[Col. 1144A]

that fresh chrism scarcely reaches certain churches situated there within the days before the Lord’s Supper. The consecration of altars, the sacrament of confirmation, and likewise the ordination of clerics are sometimes postponed for a long time, and often permanently, unless perhaps they are occasionally supplied by visiting bishops. What is more serious, the plague of heretical depravity is said to have grown so strong there that ravening wolves everywhere break into the folds of the Lord’s sheep; because the staff of the shepherd, the more sheep it is directed toward, is correspondingly less able to watch over each one in particular, and their savage madness is not kept away from the sheep by the office of pastoral diligence.

Therefore the said nobleman, considering that a great harvest cannot conveniently be cared for by few labourers, and that its Lord must accordingly be asked to send labourers into it, humbly begged us—after weighing both necessity and advantage—to deign to establish in his province a special pastor over the Lord’s flock. That province, the farther it lies from your see, is known to need the more the comfort of another bishop. He designated a suitable place in which a cathedral church might fittingly be established: namely the city of Vienna, which, after Cologne, is said to be one of the better cities of the German kingdom, pleasant through its river and situation, and populous with citizens. An episcopal see is known formerly to have existed there, but, owing to an incursion of a foreign people which devastated both it and many surrounding provinces, it was transferred first to Lorch (*Lauriacum*)

[Col. 1144C]

and then to Passau.

Moreover, lest he appear to request or seek what would impose an enormous burden on you, when his intention is rather to lighten your burden, he requested that one third or one fourth of Austria be assigned within the boundaries of the proposed diocese. All villages and castles, with all possessions and other temporal goods, except only parochial right, in that portion are to be reserved to you and to the Church of Passau. The same duke, together with the people of Vienna, will in pious devotion endow this bishopric from his own goods, for the salvation of his soul and those of his parents, with revenues of one thousand marks. He will also assign revenues from which a body of thirty prebends may be established there, each of which shall receive annual income assessed at twenty marks.

We, therefore, considering that spiritual sheep should not be governed with less care than bodily ones, since the ruler of the former employs many guardians for them when he sees that they cannot, because of their multitude, be guarded by one person, consider that another pastor besides you ought to be appointed for the governance of the Lord’s flock, which has multiplied too greatly in your fold—if what is asserted is true—so that he may know his sheep and be known by his sheep, after the example of him who said: “I know my sheep, and mine know me” (John 10). Although, not only under canonical statutes but also under certain examples of our predecessors, the request of the said duke appears rightly to deserve assent, nevertheless, wishing

[Col. 1145A]

to show deference to your brotherhood, we have wished, by an additional grace, to inform you of the matter itself. For although it is not necessary to obtain your consent in this matter, it is nevertheless honourable to seek it.

We therefore earnestly admonish and more strongly exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by these apostolic letters, that, pursuing so salutary a proposal with benevolent favour and preferring spiritual gain to temporal profit, you devote, insofar as lies in you, both will and effective action to it, writing us as soon as possible what you think concerning every circumstance of this matter.

For we have instructed our venerable brother …, Archbishop of Salzburg, to exhort the said duke more earnestly to carry out this pious purpose, and, having more diligently investigated the truth of these matters,

[Col. 1145B]

to write it to us with suitable promptness, stating precisely in what region and in what extent of the said province the episcopal see and diocese of the future bishopric may most suitably be located and assigned. Thus, once we have been made more fully certain, we may proceed to complete this business as the Lord inspires.

Given at the Lateran, 14 April, in the tenth year.

LIII. TO THE … BISHOP, THE … PROVOST OF SAINT LUCIUS, AND THE … SCHOLASTICUS OF CHUR. They are commissioned to secure for H., a poor priest of the Church of Rapis, peaceful possession, as justice requires. (Lateran, 18 April.)

[Col. 1145C]

Our beloved son H., a poor priest, once appearing before us, humbly represented that VI and Ha., canons of Constance, were unjustly harassing him concerning the Church of Rapis, to which he had been canonically presented. The same priest therefore obtained apostolic letters concerning this matter addressed to the Abbot of Capella and his fellow judges. Although much had been put forward on both sides before them, they ultimately refused, out of fear of the opposing party, to proceed to the rendering of judgment, as they themselves informed us in their letters.

The priest therefore appealed to our hearing and set as the term of his appeal the feast of the blessed apostles Philip and James, then next past. We consequently instructed you that, if it were established that the said priest held no ecclesiastical benefice and had been canonically presented to the aforesaid church, you should, notwithstanding the institution of another man, who was said to hold other ecclesiastical benefices, cause him to be invested with it, removing the obstacle of appeal.

[Col. 1145D]
