But, as you, brother bishop, informed us by your letters: although it was established that the adversary of the same priest held other ecclesiastical benefices, since an objection was made that the said priest had obtained the letters of the aforesaid mandate through a false representation and suppression of the truth, and since that adversary appealed to the Apostolic See, you deferred proceeding to judgment.

Since, therefore, the said priest has again come before us concerning this matter and has long awaited his adversary, who has not in any way pursued the appeal which he lodged, we sympathize with his labours and expenses. By these apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, if it is established that the said priest acquired a right in that church through that presentation, then, notwithstanding the assertion that he obtained the aforesaid letters through a false representation and suppression of the truth—since an assertion of falsehood or suppression of truth cannot alter this form, as being consonant with the common law—you shall proceed in the matter according to their mandate, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal and restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure.

[Col. 1146B]

You shall carefully provide that, since the said adversary is reported, after the priest obtained letters from us a second time, to have occupied possession of that church, if it should occur that the priest is invested with it according to the form of our mandate, then, after removing both that adversary and any other unlawful possessor from it, you cause the said priest to enjoy its peaceful possession, pronouncing canonical censure against those who should rashly presume to oppose him. You shall likewise compel the aforesaid adversary, by the same censure and setting aside appeal, to make due restitution to the same priest of the fruits withheld from him.

Carry out the apostolic mandate in such a manner that the said poor man need not hereafter toil in coming to the Apostolic See because of your failure, and that you yourselves cannot be reproached for negligence. We remit to your discretion the depositions of the witnesses which you sent us concerning this business, so that you may proceed canonically in the case according both to what has been testified concerning the same matter and to what shall lawfully be testified. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. But if not all … you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 18 April, in the tenth year.

LIV. TO THE PODESTÀ AND CONSULS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, AND TO THE ENTIRE PEOPLE OF TREVISO. They are urged to submit to and trust their bishop in correcting the abominable and schismatic errors which they maintain against the faith; and the same bishop is to correct the offences of clerics. (Lateran, 21 April.)

[Col. 1146D]

The glory of your name would shine far and wide, were it not so greatly obscured by the smoke of heretical depravity; for, according to the Apostle, not only much leaven, but even a little, corrupts the whole mass. Why, then, illustrious citizens, do you allow the Catholic faith, through which you were reborn from water and the Spirit in baptism, to be corrupted by certain undisciplined and unlearned persons, deceivers and deceived? They neither understand the Holy Scriptures nor acknowledge divine power; beneath a sheep’s skin they conceal wolfish rapacity, in order to offer the unwary dragon’s gall in a golden cup.

Therefore purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened—not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves, especially of the impious Manichaeans, who call themselves Cathars or Patarenes. The Apostle Paul, in the Holy Spirit, foresaw and foretold that their madness was to be avoided, writing among other things to Timothy:

“Now the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage, and requiring abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by believers

[Col. 1147B]

and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Timothy 4).

See how expressly and plainly the Apostle Paul, vessel of election and teacher of the nations, set apart for the Gospel of God—which he neither received nor learned from man, but only through the revelation of Jesus Christ—condemns and rejects the mad doctrine of the faithless Manichaean. It is wholly alien not only from the truth of orthodox faith but also from the judgment of natural reason.

For he, with his followers, teaches that bodily foods were created not by God but by the devil, whom he calls the prince of darkness; and he says that all bodily and visible things were created by him. Paul, on the other hand, teaches that foods were created by God and therefore should be received by believers with thanksgiving. The former forbids marriage, condemning matrimony and asserting that it is no greater sin to violate one’s mother or daughter than a stranger or an unknown woman. The latter commends marriage, declaring it to be a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church, in accordance with the prophecy uttered by the first-formed man upon waking: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife; and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2; Ephesians 5). He therefore says that it is better to marry than to burn.

Why dwell upon such matters, when among all insanities this is the most insane, and among all errors this the most horrible? For it not only attacks evangelical truth but overturns philosophical doctrine, which teaches that there is one Creator of all things, visible and invisible. Flee, then—flee the condemnable and condemned, indeed harmful and condemning error, which brings in inner darkness in order to lead to outer darkness. Do not be darkened with those who confess that they themselves were created by the prince of darkness; rather, be enlightened with those who confess themselves created by the Father of lights, with whom there is no darkness.

We pledge on your behalf before Christ Jesus, who is to come to judge the living and the dead,

[Col. 1148A]

that the faith taught by the Apostolic See, over which we, though unworthy, preside, is true and right according to apostolic and prophetic teaching. On the last day of strict judgment we wish to answer to him for you concerning this before his tribunal. We summon you before that tribunal of the divine majesty, before which you will at last stand to receive according to your merits, that, rejecting and detesting the false doctrines of heretical depravity, you may embrace and follow the true teaching of the Apostolic See, founded with immovable firmness upon the solid rock. Remember what you formerly promised us by an oath placed in the hand of our venerable brother …, Bishop of Ferrara, when through his ministry we restored to you, in paternal mercy, the grace of communion which had long been withheld from you.

We therefore admonish and exhort your devotion in the Lord, commanding you by these apostolic letters to trust and submit in matters which display upright morals and savour of orthodox faith to our venerable brother …, your bishop, to whom we have commanded that he strictly correct the offences of clerics whose evil examples trouble you. Do not let your souls be scandalized because some live otherwise than they teach: for as the infirmity of a physician does not impede the power of medicine, so the iniquity of a priest does not nullify the efficacy of a sacrament. [Note: [Col. 1147D] See Baluze’s notes on Agobard, p. 66.]

Given at the Lateran, 21 April, in the tenth year.

LV. TO THE BISHOP OF BRIXEN, H., PROVOST OF AQUILEIA, AND S., SCHOLASTICUS OF AUGSBURG. They are commissioned to examine witnesses concerning the election of a pastor of the Church of Gurk, to which election the Church of Salzburg claimed a right. (Lateran, 19 March.)

[Col. 1148C]

The Church of Gurk complained to us that the Church of Salzburg was unlawfully troubling it concerning its freedom to elect a bishop—a freedom which the procurator of the Church of Gurk maintained belonged to it both by common law and by ancient custom and special privilege. When, on the other side, a certain judgment was alleged to have been issued on this matter in favour of the Church of Salzburg, he asserted that no judgment on the matter had been delivered.

[Col. 1148D]

But when certain letters of our venerable brother … bishop of Freising and of our beloved son … abbot of Holy Cross were produced before us, which appeared to contain the judgment said to have been delivered by them, he subsequently maintained that the aforesaid judges had been neither ordinary judges nor arbitrators jointly chosen by the parties, nor was it established that they had been delegated; consequently, what they had determined could have no binding force. He contended that the canons of Gurk had hitherto freely elected their own bishop, a practice which he declared himself able sufficiently to prove. And when it was answered against him that the said judges had authority, by delegation from Pope Alexander III of blessed memory, to settle the matter concerning the practice of election, we decided to entrust to our venerable brothers … bishop of Freising and … bishop of Trieste, together with you, brother bishop of Brixen, the reception of the witnesses whom either party might wish to produce.

[Col. 1149A]

When the parties had appeared in our presence and had submitted to us, sealed, their depositions upon those two articles, the procurator of the Church of Gurk protested in court that he did not believe a judgment had been rendered in this matter; but, if one had been rendered, it had been adjudged against that church through fear. We summoned him privately and inquired as to the nature of the fear. But since he described to us such fear as, if proved, would bring no assistance to his side, and admitted that he did not wish to prove any other, while requesting time to establish the fear which he had described, we advised the parties, aiming at an agreement, to await the arrival of our venerable brother … archbishop of Salzburg.

[Col. 1149B]

After he had been awaited for a long time, and meanwhile certain canons of Gurk had gone to their church, they returned bringing with them certain witnesses, through whom the procurator wished to prove another fear: namely, that the canons of Gurk had been compelled by the Count Palatine and the full brothers of the then archbishop to confess against themselves. Only then did he admit that the judgment had been rendered, alleging that, since civil law expressly provides that the praetor will never hold valid anything done by force or fear, a judgment issued by the aforesaid judges on account of fear ought not now to be held valid either. Nor, he maintained, did the exception of res judicata bar an action by reason of the passage of time, so as to prevent an action founded on fear from now being brought: for not only had the forty-year period—noted as an obstacle if it applies to a religious institution—not elapsed, but not even thirty years had passed since the judgment was pronounced. Indeed, by authority of a canon, the entire proceeding must be reopened in which a party, because it had confessed something against itself, suffered an adverse judgment, if it proves that it endured violence in making the confession. Likewise, no confession made under necessity is trustworthy, and it is most wicked to judge anyone on suspicion or an extorted confession.

[Col. 1149C]

Likewise, it is certain that, just as an exception is the exclusion of an action, so a replication is an aid to an action. Therefore, since matters which are limited to one year for bringing an action are said to be perpetual for raising an exception, and since a replication is, as it were, the exclusion of an exception, an action regains its force through the support of a replication whenever it would otherwise endure but for the exception. Accordingly, notwithstanding the exception of res judicata, he said that he could, as before the judgment, now also vindicate free election.

To the objection that the judges had directed their minds not to one kind of proof alone, but had delivered judgment against the Church of Gurk from confessions, witnesses, and certain documents, he answered that fear, involving bodily torture, had entered into the whole proceeding.

[Col. 1150A]

The other side sought to maintain, on several grounds, that his adversary should not be heard at all: first, because he had admitted that he did not wish to allege another fear; next, because although at first he had denied that a judgment had been rendered, he later admitted the contrary by fraud; and fraud and deceit ought to afford protection to no one. Therefore, as a penalty for his denial, the action ought to be refused him, as the law provides in a similar case. Further, because he had admitted that, after the said judgment, the canons of Gurk had rendered obedience to the archbishop of Salzburg in such matters, thereby confirming the judgment by their consent, civil law presuming from a subsequent voluntary consent that no compulsion had intervened in the delivery of the judgment.

[Col. 1150B]

It added that, after the people of Gurk had lodged a complaint concerning that judgment with Pope Lucius III of blessed memory, he confirmed it; and that the canons of Gurk had voluntarily obeyed the judgment for many years.

The adversary answered these arguments as follows: anyone may indeed repent of his answer, provided that the claimant suffers no disadvantage from that repentance. But since the Church of Salzburg, in raising an exception, occupies the position of claimant, and since nothing is thought lost to ecclesiastical interests if what belongs to another is restored, there may be room for repentance by one employing a replication in order to preserve his entire right. Moreover, the aforesaid procurator offered an oath that this fear had only recently come to his knowledge; hence he ought to be heard, by the analogous reasoning that, if someone was present at the time a marriage was contracted and then alleged nothing against it, but later wished to impeach it, and swore that he afterwards learned that the contracting parties were blood-relatives, he is heard as accuser.

[Col. 1150C]

Likewise, if a petitory action has been brought and witnesses have already been received concerning it, the claimant wishes to bring a possessory action, permission to return to it has been granted by our decretal. But because tolerable error exists where one is ignorant of another’s act, and by lawful enactments an error of fact harms no one while the case is not yet concluded, especially since the Church of Gurk is contending to avert loss and acquire—or rather preserve—its right, it ought not to suffer prejudice from such changes of position.

[Col. 1150D]

For sometimes the praetor does not reject one who changes his position, nor does he disdain the advice of one who changes his mind. The third and fourth objections were answered thus: the Church of Gurk’s confession of servitude ought not to create prejudice; for if by common law it ought to possess free judgment concerning the person to be set over it, and it has confessed servitude contrary to such freedom, then, with the aid of civil law—which holds that a free man is not made a slave by a confession of servitude—its free election must not be taken away. He added that, after the translation of the aforesaid archbishop to the Church of Mainz, the Church of Gurk, when it was able to make complaint, raised before our predecessor Pope Lucius III the issue of the violence; but that Pope, as in the privilege which Pope Alexander II of happy memory was said to have granted to the Church of Salzburg concerning the election, institution, and consecration of the bishop of Gurk, so also in the judgment, was deceived. Claiming that he had carefully examined the matter and found the privilege genuine—which we have plainly found to be false—he confirmed the judgment while the canons of Gurk were absent.

[Col. 1151A]

Having therefore understood these and other matters which the parties argued at length before us, we granted by interlocutory decision that the procurator of the Church of Gurk should have the opportunity to prove that fear, after swearing that he had learned of it only afterwards. He thus produced witnesses, whom we ordered our beloved sons L., cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross, and G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, to examine and whose depositions we ordered recorded.

[Col. 1151B]

Since, however, the procurator of the frequently mentioned archbishop wished to produce witnesses in his own country both on this matter and on the assertion that the people of Gurk had voluntarily obeyed the judgment, and that our predecessor Pope Lucius of blessed memory, after the matters alleged in court concerning both fear and other issues, had confirmed the aforesaid judgment by the document of the privilege, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to receive, around the feast of All Saints and in a secure place, without hindrance from any objection or appeal, the witnesses whom either party may wish to produce concerning the foregoing articles and concerning the settlement said to have been made after the time of the judgment, or against the persons of the witnesses. Faithfully transmit to us the written depositions, setting thereafter for the parties a suitable term within which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment—unless in the meantime they can reach an amicable agreement, which we believe advantageous to both parties. No letters shall obstruct this, if any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without the parties’ consent. If all cannot act, let two of you act, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

## LVI. TO THE CHAPTER OF PATRAS

That they are to receive the archbishop of Patras, elected by agreement, as their true archbishop. (Lateran, eighth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 1151D]

Since our beloved son, the nobleman William of Campania, prince of Achaea, and you together with him once earnestly and devoutly petitioned us that we should deem worthy to grant you as pastor our venerable brother … archbishop of Patras, then unanimously elected by you and coming to the Apostolic See, we investigated more carefully how the election had proceeded. What had been done by you, since it had been arranged less than lawfully and since you yourselves had been instituted less than canonically, we did not think fit to approve. But, after weighing both necessity and advantage, and after we had been made more certain of the truth of the affair and of the condition of the land through the oaths of the companions of the then-elect archbishop,

[Col. 1152A]

we appointed him, by our authority, pastor and ruler of your church, granting him full administration in both spiritual and temporal affairs. Although, by the fullness of authority which, through the Lord’s disposition, we possess over all churches, we could at that time have conferred upon him the office of consecration, nevertheless, because we wished in this respect to defer to our venerable brother … patriarch of Constantinople, to whom your church is said to be subject, we sent him to the said patriarch to receive from him the grace of consecration.

But the same archbishop, hindered by the dangers of the wars and disturbances prevailing in the regions of Romania, was unable to appear before that patriarch. Nor did he think it expedient, since the patriarch at that time could not consecrate him because he had no fellow bishops. The patriarch therefore sent the elect of Athens and Thebes, who had come into his presence, to Syria, there to receive consecration.

[Col. 1152B]

We, therefore, moved by paternal sympathy for him—who, by coming once and again to the Apostolic See, had endured, besides many labours, serious losses and expenses—conferred on him the gift of consecration. Adorning him with the honour of the pallium, that is, with the fullness of the pontifical office, and with the fullness of our favour, we sent him back to render to the aforesaid patriarch the obedience and reverence due and devoted. For, because he received consecration from us, we do not wish prejudice to be created for anyone, lest perhaps—God forbid—an occasion for injuries arise from that from which rights arise.

[Col. 1152C]

Nevertheless, if you wish to pursue your right concerning the condition of your church, we, who according to the Apostle are debtors to all in justice, will, with God as author, take care that justice is rendered to you. Therefore we command your entire community by apostolic letters to give heed to him as your archbishop, receiving his salutary admonitions and commands humbly and devoutly.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth year.

## LVII. TO … THE ARCHDEACON AND … THE PROVOST OF SETARA, OUR SUBDEACON, A CANON OF MILAN

That they are to hear and duly conclude the case between C., a scholar, and John, a cleric. (Lateran, fifth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 1152D]

Formerly we ordered … archdeacon of Milan of blessed memory to cause our beloved son C., a scholar, to be received by … priest of Saint Victor of the Forty Martyrs as a cleric and brother of that church. The priest alone performed service in that church, in which, as the scholar asserted, a cleric and a priest had formerly performed service; and the scholar maintained that the church’s resources had in no way diminished. But the aforesaid priest, maliciously evading the inquiry of the archdeacon,

[Col. 1153A]

sent the cleric John in his stead to our presence. We appointed our venerable brother B., archbishop of Trani, then legate of the Apostolic See and our subdeacon and chaplain, as hearer for him and the aforesaid C. Before him John asserted that the resources of the said church did not suffice for two clerics, adding that the aforesaid C. was unfit to hold a benefice of that church. Therefore, with their consent, we ordered our venerable brother … patriarch of Jerusalem, then bishop of Vercelli, that, if the aforesaid C. lawfully proved before him that the resources of the aforesaid church had not diminished but sufficed for two persons,

[Col. 1153B]

and that his own person was suitable, he should compel the aforesaid priest, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to receive him; restraining with like severity and without appeal any opponents or rebels who might perhaps appear. Otherwise, he was to impose perpetual silence upon the said scholar concerning this matter. He was also to compel, by canonical severity and without appeal, any witnesses named before him who withdrew through favour, hatred, or fear to bear testimony to the truth.

When the aforesaid scholar had repeatedly appeared before the said patriarch, then bishop of Vercelli, in order to prove that the church’s resources had not diminished but sufficed for two persons,

[Col. 1153C]

and the bishop had placed under interdict witnesses named by him, because, after admonition, they refused to bear testimony to the truth, our venerable brother … then archbishop of Milan lifted that interdict by his own authority. Consequently, the aforesaid C. could not obtain his right.

We therefore later commanded you, son Provost, that, after examining the depositions already received—which we wished you to have produced before you by ecclesiastical censure—you should conclude the case, according to those depositions and any others which the parties might lawfully wish to submit, in accordance with the tenor of the preceding letters, after removing every obstacle of objection and appeal; for the depositions already received had not yet been published.

Thereafter, when the parties had appeared before you on this matter,

[Col. 1153D]

and the said C., in order to prove that the church’s resources were sufficient, named certain patrons and parishioners of the church to bear testimony, and they, though repeatedly warned by you, refused to testify, excusing themselves on certain grounds, you bound them under sentence of excommunication unless, within fifteen days thereafter, they came to give testimony. But before the day set, they appealed to the Apostolic See; consequently no further proceedings took place in the case.

Wishing therefore that an end be put to the controversy, we have associated you, son Archdeacon, with the hearing of the same case.

[Col. 1154A]

By the authority of these presents we command you to grant the aforesaid laymen absolution as a precaution, and to conclude the case, without appeal and according to the tenor of the former letters, following the course of law. Thus the clause inserted in our rescript, namely, “if the person is suitable,” is not to impose on the scholar any obligation to prove himself suitable, since at first sight he is presumed suitable unless the contrary is shown. If witnesses named by either party—whether patrons or parishioners of the aforesaid church—withdraw through favour, hatred, or fear, compel them by ecclesiastical severity, without appeal, to bear testimony to the truth.

[Col. 1154B]

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth year.

## LVIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF ZAMORA, SEGOVIA, AND ÁVILA

That, if Master I., scholasticus of the Church of Palencia, proceeded maliciously against the bishop of Palencia by alleging crimes against him, he is to be suspended from office and benefice. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of May.)

When our beloved son I., master of the schools of the Church of Palencia, formerly came to the Apostolic See and reported to us various offences of his venerable brother … bishop of Palencia, we entrusted the examination of the alleged offences to our venerable brother … formerly bishop of León and now archbishop of Compostela, and to our beloved sons … abbot of Valbuena and … abbot of Mataplán, of the diocese of Palencia.

[Col. 1154C]

[Note: [Col. 1153D] Chapter *Cum dilectus*, “On Accusations.”]

After fully investigating the truth through witnesses, they faithfully sent us their inquiry together with the witnesses’ depositions concerning twofold simony, waste of property, the absolution of persons who had incurred the sentence laid down by canon, contempt for appeals made to us, holding a vacant dignity in his own hands beyond the period established at the Lateran Council, secretly removing a certain instrument in which the rights of the bishops are distinguished from the rights of the canons, and certain other matters.

When we had carefully examined the proceedings and the witnesses’ statements, and could not understand that anything of the aforesaid matters had been sufficiently proved,

[Col. 1154D]

we decreed, with the counsel of our brethren, that the bishop should be absolved from the accusations. By apostolic letters we command you to suspend the aforesaid master of the schools from office and benefice until he has canonically cleared his innocence—namely, by showing that he did not proceed to allege such crimes with an intent to malign—so that others, terrified by a like penalty, may not readily rush to defame their prelates. If all cannot act, let two of you act, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the tenth year.

## LIX. TO THE PRIORESS AND SISTERS OF SIXENA, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY

Privileges are granted to them, and their liberties and immunities confirmed. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 1155A]

To prudent virgins who, beneath the habit of religion, have lamps burning, etc., as far as “we graciously grant,” we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive your monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

[Col. 1155B]

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their own names: Sixena, where the aforesaid monastery is situated; Villanueva, Sena, Ontiñena, and Urgellet, with all their appurtenances.

No one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your own animals. You may receive into conversion free and released persons fleeing from the world and retain them without any objection.

[Col. 1155C]

Furthermore, we prohibit any of your sisters, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving it without her prioress’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life. No one may dare to retain a sister who departs without a letter of permission from the community. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may, with closed doors, etc., as far as “celebrate.”

Moreover, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from pronouncing a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your monastery without manifest and reasonable cause. Furthermore, we apostolically confirm the institutions reasonably made in that monastery, with the consent of our dearest daughter in Christ, S., illustrious queen of Aragon, by R., formerly bishop of Huesca, … master of the Hospital of Amposta, and other religious men.

[Col. 1155D]

When you, the present prioress of the place, or any of your successors die, no one may be set over it by any cunning of surreptitious procurement or by force, except the person whom the sisters by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of them, shall provide for election according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. If the sisters of the monastery should disagree over the election of a prioress, you shall summon to your monastery the master of the Hospital of Jerusalem at Amposta, whose habit you wear; through him, with the counsel of the diocesan bishop,

[Col. 1156A]

the discord arising among you shall be settled. We decree, moreover, that the Hospitallers may not expel the prioress or convent from that house, nor transfer or appoint any sister there. But if the prioress or any sister should commit an offence such that you cannot correct her, she shall be corrected in that monastery by the prior of Amposta and the diocesan bishop, according to the Rule of blessed Augustine which you observe. Nor may the same Hospitallers, with any rashness, act contrary to the provisions prudently laid down in the Rule of that monastery between you and them concerning election of the prioress.

While the church remains in its present condition, the number of thirty canonesses may not be reduced, but may be increased if its resources should grow enough to support more.

[Col. 1156B]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever, etc., as far as “beneficial in every respect.” Saving the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right of the diocesan bishop, and the due reverence owed to the master of the Hospital at Amposta. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall in future, etc., as far as “shall be subject to punishment.” But may all who preserve the rights of that place enjoy the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that, etc., as far as “unto the end.” Amen.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the ninth indiction, the year 1207 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## LX. TO THE CANONS OF SAINT MAURICE OF AUGSBURG, PRESENT AND FUTURE, TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED, IN PERPETUITY

Privileges and indulgences are granted, and liberties, etc., confirmed. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 1156C]

It is required by the force of equity and the order of reason that effect be given to just petitioners, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ will and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of pontiffs, etc., as far as “shall remain unimpaired,” shall remain secure and inviolate. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their own names:

[Col. 1156D]

The church at Baldeshusen, with its manorial court and all its appurtenances—namely pastures, meadows, woods, waters, and watercourses; the church at Mimmenushen, with its manorial court and all its rights; the village called Nanthereshusen; the village called Gerute; two estates in the village called Oberenhoven; an estate in the village called Niusazen; an estate

[Col. 1157A]

in the village called Gegingen; a manorial estate in the village called Warengereshoven; the church and manorial court in the village called Biberin, with one mill; the manorial estate in the village called Heinricheshoven; in the district of the city of Augsburg, fields, gardens, enclosed plots, and one mill; in the province called Franconia, the village called Chrowelshain; and the church and manorial court in the village called Goltpach, with a tavern.

Further, we decree that the chapel called Uffenburch, with the goods and revenues which it possesses there and in the village called Egevenburch and which are assigned to the use of the brethren, may not through anyone’s rashness be withdrawn from the brethren’s use without their consent.

[Col. 1157B]

We also decree that the burial-place of that location shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. The right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken is nevertheless preserved.

When the provost of your church then in office dies, no one may be set over it by any cunning of surreptitious procurement or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder majority of the brethren, shall provide for election according to the fear of God.

When your parochial churches are vacant, you may choose priests and present them to the bishop. If they are found suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they shall answer to the bishop for the care of the people, but to you for temporal affairs.

[Col. 1157C]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, etc., as far as “beneficial in every respect.” Saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall in future, etc., as far as “shall be subject to punishment.” But may all who preserve the rights of that place, etc., as far as “unto the end.” Amen.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the ninth indiction, the year 1207 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## LXI. TO THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE

Concerning the tithes of Jews, the revenues of scholars, and usurers. (Lateran, seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 1157D]

Your brotherhood’s discretion asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See how you ought to proceed against those Jews who, having bought villages, estates, and vineyards, refuse to render to churches and ecclesiastical persons the tithes due from them, since they cannot be compelled by ecclesiastical censure, which they disregard. We answer your inquiry as follows: the prince of the land must be diligently admonished to compel them, by the power entrusted to him, to make payment thereof.

[Col. 1158A]

If perhaps he does not take care to do this, Christians are to be forbidden, under pain of anathema, from having commercial dealings with them until they have made satisfaction concerning the foregoing.

[Note: [Col. 1157D] Chapter *Tuae fraternitatis*, “On Non-resident Clerics.”]

You further asked whether, when canons who have been granted permission, for the sake of study, to receive the revenues of their prebends during their absence obtain leave and go to villages or castles where there is no study or an insufficiently suitable opportunity for study, the revenues of their prebends ought to be assigned to such persons. To this we briefly answer that those who commit such fraud ought not to benefit from the aforesaid indulgence, since fraud and deceit ought to afford protection to no one.

Moreover, because there are very many usurers in your diocese,

[Col. 1158B]

concerning whom there is no doubt that they are manifest usurers, but no accuser appears against them because of fear of the princes and powerful men who protect them, nor have they been condemned by judgment, you thought it necessary to seek an oracle of the Apostolic See as to how you could proceed against them. We answer your brotherhood as follows: although no accuser appears against them, nevertheless, if by other proofs they are established to be manifest usurers, you may freely inflict upon them the penalty enacted against usurers by the Lateran Council.

[Note: [Col. 1158D] Chapter *Cum in dioecesi*, “On Usury.”]

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXII. TO THE DEAN MAJOR AND PRIOR OF COLOGNE

Concerning excommunicated and interdicted beneficed persons, etc. (Lateran, on the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 1158C]

You asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See which suffragan of the Church of Cologne ought to judge, while our venerable brother B., your archbishop, is held in chains, should the suffragans themselves be appealed to the Church of Cologne by their own clerics; and what should be done about vacant benefices known to belong to the presentation of the same archbishop. We briefly answer your inquiry: through the efforts of our legates, whom we are sending into Germany, we hope, God being the author, that the same archbishop will be restored to liberty; he will perform his office both in these matters and in others.

[Col. 1158D]

You also asked whether clerics who, while bound by the bond of excommunication, acquired ecclesiastical benefices may lawfully retain them after obtaining the benefit of absolution; and you likewise requested an explanation from the Apostolic See of the penalty by which abbots, abbesses, and other prelates of churches who knowingly conferred ecclesiastical benefices upon clerics subject to excommunication ought to be corrected.

[Note: [Col. 1158D] Chapter *Consequenter*, “On Excommunicated Clerics.”]

To this we have thought fit to answer as follows: since excommunicated persons must not be communicated with, ecclesiastical benefices cannot be conferred upon clerics bound by excommunication, nor may they lawfully retain them, unless perhaps a merciful dispensation has been granted to them, because they did not acquire them canonically.

[Col. 1159A]

Those who knowingly conferred those benefices upon such persons must be suspended from conferring benefices until they deserve to obtain pardon for this, so that they may be punished in the matter in which they presumed to offend.

You further asked how clerics and monks, and likewise nuns of conventual churches, ought to be punished when, after a sentence of interdict had been delivered, they had presumed hitherto, and even now did not fear, to celebrate divine offices in places subject to the interdict, although for this reason they were bound as by the bond of excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 1159] See Baluze’s notes on the councils of Narbonese Gaul, p. 18.]

We briefly answer that clerics who have presumed such things are to be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices; monks and nuns, however, are to be confined in stricter monasteries to perform penance.

[Col. 1159B]

You additionally requested that the oracle of the Apostolic See explain what should be done concerning those clerics who, when delegated judges had enjoined them—after granting them absolution—to present themselves before us, despised carrying this out; and concerning those who had sworn fealty and obedience to the aforesaid archbishop and afterwards, not fearing to violate that oath, did not observe the sentence of interdict. We answer this as follows: both classes are to be punished as perjurers with the canonical penalty.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of May, in the tenth year.

## LXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA

A matrimonial case is entrusted to him. (Lateran, seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 1159C]

The petition of the noblewoman B., submitted to us, stated that, although she had already reached the age of puberty, she had been joined in marriage to the Judge of Arborea by her father’s command rather than by her own free will. Although she bore him one child, neither the urging of friends nor the counsels of relatives could incline her to love him as a husband. While she thus remained with him unwillingly, she learned that, when he had taken her as wife, he already had another woman joined to him in marriage. The judge further asserted that he had known carnally a certain cousin of hers before contracting the marriage with her. Thus it came about that they separated from one another. How this was arranged she knew in no other way, except that she believed then, and believes now, that it was done reasonably and canonically. At length she returned to her paternal home and, remaining unmarried for about two years without any complaint, afterward publicly and solemnly married the nobleman Count Hugh in the presence of the Church. Having lived peaceably with him for fourteen years, she bore him two sons, whom she humbly requested might by apostolic authority be declared legitimate, because husband and wife had been joined in good faith in the presence of the Church and had lived together for a long time without any objection.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your fraternity that, after diligently investigating the truth, if it is established to you that the aforesaid judge, at the time when he contracted marriage with the aforesaid B., had another wife, or that he had previously known one of her blood-relatives carnally, or that her former husband had already died, you shall reconcile the aforesaid husband and wife to each other and cause them to treat one another with conjugal honor and marital affection; and you shall also have the children whom they thus received regarded as legitimate. But if none of the aforesaid three points is established to you, nevertheless, because the aforesaid woman solemnly married the aforesaid man in the presence of the Church and they remained joined in good faith as husband and wife for fourteen years without any objection, you shall cause their children likewise to be regarded as legitimate and called to their paternal rights.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXIV. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF PIACENZA

On preserving ecclesiastical liberty.  
(At the Lateran, … May.)

In the ark of the covenant, together with the tablets of the testament, were contained the rod and manna. For in the mind of a ruler there ought to be, together with knowledge of the divine law, the rod of correction and the manna of sweetness, so that severity may be tempered by gentleness, and gentleness by severity. Keeping this in view, having heard what our venerable brother …, bishop of Piacenza, and the clergy of Piacenza, as well as your beloved sons Ubert the viscount, John of Malamina, and Peter of Vilimercato, your prudent and faithful envoys, took care to set before us concerning the fulfillment of the mandate laid upon you—those seeking justice, these imploring mercy—we judged that the matter should be so moderated that mercy and justice might embrace one another in it, neither being abandoned by the other, but the matter itself being shaped by both virtues.

Therefore lift up your eyes straight ahead, and consider diligently to what end the necessary offense of your transgression has come. Although it is known to have been grave, perhaps it has nevertheless been brought about by divine counsel, so that both those near and those far away may be taught by it not to presume upon similar acts against ecclesiastical liberty, when they see you salutarily repent of your wrongdoing. For behold, many are watching the outcome of this affair. Just as the fault of your presumption became a scandal, so surely shall the discipline of your repentance become an example. Perhaps some would at one time have attempted a contest of similar strife; but since it happened that it was attempted by you, by yielding beneficially in it you will give warning to others, and will advance ecclesiastical liberty more usefully by such an exercise than perhaps you could have advanced it by remaining at rest. Accordingly, those who hear this will call your fault fortunate, if you strive, as you can, to turn it into a matter of general benefit for the Church.

You have been sufficiently discredited before the world by committing it. But the humble satisfaction offered for it will be far more able to bring honor to your name throughout the earth. See therefore how, from the offense you have committed, provided that you strive to expiate it by fitting satisfaction, you may magnify the proclamation of your praise and advance ecclesiastical welfare. For the Psalms of David, the Epistles of Paul, and the Gospel of Matthew are recited more often in the Church than the other Scriptures. The first was an adulterer and murderer, the second a blasphemer and persecutor, and the third a publican and tax-collector; yet they cleansed their guilt by satisfaction so that these things are recalled of them not for their disgrace but for their glory. The Church makes more frequent use of their writings so that sinners may be converted to repentance by their familiar example.

A like result will also befall you. For wherever your satisfaction is reported throughout the whole world, those who hear it will receive it with great praise for your name, deriving caution from your offense and discipline from your repentance. Therefore, because the righteousness of a righteous person shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins, and the wickedness of a wicked person shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from wickedness, we earnestly ask and more urgently exhort your whole community, imposing this upon you for the remission of your sins: weighing with fear the word of the Lord spoken through the prophet concerning a sinful nation:

> “If a nation repents of the evil which I have spoken against it, I too will repent of the evil which I intended to do to it. But if it does evil in my sight by not hearing my voice, I will repent of the good which I said I would do to it.”  
> (Jeremiah 18)

Strive to perform your repentance through prompt satisfaction, lest—God forbid—that which can be a cause of good should finally become for you an occasion of evil. For if, insofar as lies in you, you strive to bring this matter to its conclusion for the praise of the divine name, the honor of ecclesiastical liberty, and your own salvation, then, since godliness has the promise both of the life that now is and of that which is to come, besides the favor of worldly grace which you will thereby deserve, we promise you an eternal crown for such a work of piety.

We send enclosed under our seal the form of the aforesaid mandate to our venerable brothers …, bishop of Vercelli, and …, bishop of Ivrea, and to our beloved sons …, abbot of Tilleto, and the priest Albert of Mantua, visitors of Lombardy. We command them that all of them, or three, or at least two of them, shall proceed in carrying it out and, if necessary, shall cause it to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, … May, in the tenth year.

## LXV. TO OUR DEAREST SON IN CHRIST, KALOJOHN, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE BULGARIANS

That he should make and observe peace or a truce with the emperor of Constantinople and the Latins.  
(At the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of June.)

Since God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, as the Apostle James declares, you ought not to have attributed to your own strength the triumph granted you by the Lord, but rather to have imputed it to the sins of those who fell because of their deserts, trusting in their bow and confident that they would be saved by their own sword. Yet, claiming for yourself the triumph won over your enemies, you did not give, as you ought, glory to God, in whose hands are the hearts of kings.

This could be clearly perceived from the fact that, when we took care to send our envoy to you so that you might make peace or a truce with the Latins dwelling at Constantinople, not only were you unwilling to do so, but you also received and dismissed that envoy less honorably than royal dignity required. Out of reverence for the Apostolic See, you ought to have received him graciously and treated him honorably, considering that he had been sent to proclaim peace and preach salvation.

Although, then, through the aforesaid victory you were more exalted within yourself than was fitting, nevertheless, because we love you in the Lord with sincere charity as our dearest son in Christ, desiring salvation and peace for you, we graciously received our beloved son …, your envoy, and the letters that you sent us through him, and carefully noted what you communicated to us in them. Having understood, moreover, that you had long desired to send envoys to our presence, but that no route was open to them, since they did not dare pass through Hungary or through Durazzo because the Venetians held dominion there, we command by our letters our dearest son in Christ …, the illustrious king of Hungary, to permit your envoys whom you decide to send to the Apostolic See to pass freely and safely through his land. We likewise command our beloved son, the nobleman …, doge of the Venetians, to give those same envoys safe passage through Durazzo.

Concerning your firm assertion that you persevere in devotion to the Apostolic See and that, if need arose, you would expose your head for it, we commend your royal excellence in the Lord and return thanks to the Giver of all good things, who mercifully inspired this purpose in you. We therefore admonish and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord, commanding you by these apostolic letters to make and observe peace or a truce with our dearest son in Christ H., the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, and the other Latins dwelling in the empire of Romania. When we see it expedient, we shall take care to provide for sending our envoy to you, according as shall be inspired in us from above.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXVI. TO THE NOBLEWOMAN …, COUNTESS OF BLOIS

The terms of a certain privilege of the canons of Chartres are explained.  
(At the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Note: [Col. 1163D] Chapter *Cum olim*, “On the Meaning of Words.”]

When, on behalf of the canons of Chartres, a certain chapter was formerly alleged against you, said to be contained in the privilege of their church—namely, that no one may grant the benefit of absolution, without suitable satisfaction, to persons excommunicated or expressly placed under interdict for the sake of the canons of Chartres—and when the question was raised what constituted suitable satisfaction, we recall that, in order to understand that clause, we distinguished whether a sentence of interdict or excommunication had been promulgated against someone solely for contumacy, that is, because a person cited had refused to submit to law; or also for an offense, that is, because, when ordered, he had refused to make amends for wrongdoing.

[Note: [Col. 1164D] Chapter *Ex parte*, same title.]

In the first case, we held that suitable satisfaction was made, so that such a sentence might be relaxed, if sufficient security were supplied that the person would submit to law. In the second case, if the offense were manifest, we said that suitable satisfaction was by no means made, so that the sentence might be relaxed, unless sufficient amends had first been offered. If the offense were perhaps doubtful, we considered it sufficient for relaxing the sentence that suitable security be supplied for compliance with the command.

But because, while untying the strap, we are said to have tied the knot, in that the same canons, as you assert, maintained that the offense was manifest—not manifest to the judge, nor to another, but only manifest to themselves—a greater difficulty of interpretation arose from that word, namely *manifest*. Yielding to your humble requests, we write that we understand that offense to be manifest which has become known either through confession, lawful proof, or the evident nature of the matter, which can be concealed by no evasion.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND DEAN OF SENS

He writes in favor of the Count of Blois.  
(At Saint Peter’s, the fourth day before the Kalends of June.)

The Apostolic See, observing the evangelical truth that to those who seek first the kingdom of God other things are added secondarily, received all crusaders under its special protection. By provident deliberation it established that their goods should remain under its protection and that of all the prelates of God’s Church, intact and whole until their return or death should become certainly known.

Therefore, since L., Count of Blois and Clermont, of illustrious memory, having assumed the sign of the cross, devoted himself to the service of the Crucified One and ended his temporal life on the pilgrimage journey, desiring with fatherly solicitude more fully to provide for the noblewoman …, his widow, and for his ward, his procurators, and officials, and also to answer to the deceased count according to the devotion he showed, and to provide for the weakness of childhood and the frailty of womanhood—since it is difficult for recourse to be had to us in every individual case—we have judged fit to entrust our powers to you until his ward reaches the years of puberty.

By these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, since any oppressed person may appeal to the Apostolic See, whenever they judge an appeal necessary, you shall hear by our authority the causes in which appeal has been made against persons of that province. Once the obstacle of appeal has been removed, you shall decide them with due finality, declaring invalid those sentences which, after a lawful appeal has been made to us, have been promulgated against the countess, the procurators, and the land of the aforesaid count. Sentences issued otherwise, however, you shall relax according to the form of the Church, setting aside the appeal; and, having imposed what ought to be imposed according to law, you shall hear whatever matter is in dispute and, with the appeal removed, decide it with due finality, causing what you establish to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure.

But if perhaps the judgment of either of you is suspected by one party, compel the parties, appeal set aside, to choose arbitrators who shall execute the aforesaid matters, with the obstacle of appeal removed, as we have set forth; regardless of any letters procured from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice. But if not both … you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF COSORANO AND THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

They are entrusted with the case of the Archbishop of Narbonne, accused of certain crimes.  
(Given as in the other letter.)

Since we exercise on earth, although unworthy, the office of him to whom the heavenly Father gave all judgment, so that it might not be excessively strict through power nor overly lax through kindness, but moderated by wisdom through both mercy and justice, it is fitting that we judge subjects in such a way that our judgment is shaped by both virtues.

When formerly, through our legates sent into the province of Narbonne, we made inquiry whether the Archbishop of Narbonne had carried into effect the complaint which had reached us, those legates conducted a full investigation through sworn men and faithfully sent us their depositions enclosed under their seals. From these the archbishop was shown to be especially blameworthy in two matters: avarice and negligence. These two are numbered among the twelve abuses, namely, “a negligent bishop” and “a rich miser,” although each root is said to be spread into many branches.

The archbishop himself, coming into our presence, made many excuses concerning the charges brought against him. Yet he asked mercy and promised amendment, so that he might expiate the past by the future, recalling what the Apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”; for “we all offend in many things” (1 John 1). We therefore considered that he was exhausted by the labor of a great and arduous journey, especially in view of his old age and bodily weakness, and that through you he had been deprived of the abbey of Mont-Aragon, which, as was said, had meant more to him than the archbishopric of Narbonne. We resolved to pour oil upon wine, so that he might find in us mercy together with justice, since the ark of the tabernacle contained manna and the rod; but lest the manna of sweetness make lax the man whom the rod of correction ought to render disciplined.

Returning, therefore, to the Gospel parable of the fig tree planted in the vineyard: when its lord, finding no fruit on it after three years, commanded the keeper of the vineyard to cut it down lest it occupy the ground uselessly, the keeper answered his lord that he should leave it for one year, until he dug around it and put on manure; if it bore fruit, well and good, but otherwise he would cut it down thereafter. So we judged that a further period should be allowed to this archbishop. We had dug around him by threatening and rebuking, and had spread manure by warning and exhorting, in order to test whether he would produce the desired fruit; and if he should fail to bear fruit, we would more justly lay the axe to the root of the fruitless tree.

We therefore strictly commanded him, pursuing not gain of money but gain of souls, to devote himself in no way to illicit exactions and unjust dealings; rather, diligently practicing hospitality and mercy, he was henceforth to show himself generous and kindly toward pilgrims and the needy. Moreover, he was to endeavor to visit his province, hold a council, combat heresies, correct numerous offenses, and do the other things required by pastoral office.

But because, as we have learned, he not only has not corrected his past conduct, but has made his latter deeds worse than his former ones, wishing to proceed usefully against him in justice, though we are known to have proceeded fruitlessly in mercy, we command your discretion by these apostolic letters: after diligently investigating and ascertaining the truth, if you find him uncorrected in the matters set forth above, or guilty in similar or graver matters, you shall remove him altogether from the administration of the Church of Narbonne, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. With your counsel, cause a suitable person to be provided as bishop, one who both can and will benefit not only those subject to him but also his neighbors by word and example, and who will especially guard the Lord’s flock from ravening wolves that have emerged from the lurking places of heretical depravity against the sheepfolds of the Church. Any opponents or rebels you shall restrain by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

Given as in the other letter.

## LXIX. TO THE NOBLEMAN RAYMOND, COUNT OF TOULOUSE: THE SPIRIT OF SOUND COUNSEL

That he should cease persecuting the Church of God.  
(At Saint Peter’s, the fourth day before the Kalends of June.)

If we could break through the wall of your heart with the prophet, we would enter it and show you the most wicked abominations which you have committed within it. But because it appears to have hardened upon stone, it can indeed readily be struck by the blow of a saving word, but can scarcely be penetrated. Therefore, though we strive to rebuke you, we scarcely hope to correct you.

Alas! What pride has swollen your heart? What madness has seized you, pestilent man, so that you despise keeping peace with your neighbors and, departing from the divine laws, join yourself to the enemies of Catholic truth? Does it seem too little to you to trouble human beings, unless you also trouble God? For such great iniquities, is it not at least expedient to fear temporal punishments, if you think it a light matter to dwell amid everlasting burnings?

Consider, wretched man, and be afraid: while you lay snares for your neighbor and inflict the devastation of war, and while you wrong God and foster the plague of heresy, a double vengeance may also be inflamed against you for the twofold offense of your transgression. Woe to you, woe, if you do not fear to be crushed by a double destruction, according to the Prophet, and clothed, as it were, in a punitive double garment of shame. Surely, if your foolish heart were not altogether darkened, if God—whom you did not approve to retain in knowledge—had not given you over to a reprobate mind, you would consider this and, at least through fear of punishment, recall your mind from its wicked purpose.

Consider, therefore, senseless man, consider. Is not God, who is Lord of death and life, able suddenly to cut short your days, so that the one whom his patience did not bring to repentance may at last be delivered by wrath to eternal torments? And even if your present life is prolonged further, consider how many calamities may befall you. Your flesh is not bronze, nor are you of a different nature from those of whom some are suddenly seized by fevers, struck by leprosy, made paralytic, possessed by demons, and afflicted with incurable diseases—not to mention the other misfortunes which commonly befall a person who feels secure when none expects them. Although these sometimes happen to the just as a trial of patience, they nevertheless become the beginning of punishment for those of whom the righteous man says: “I saw those who work iniquity and sow sorrows and reap them, suddenly perishing at God’s blast” (Job 4).

Why, then, do you not reflect upon and fear these things—that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God, who is also able for this reason to change you into a beastly form, so that you may become like an irrational animal with the Babylonian king, abusing against God the reason given to you? But if perhaps the scourges of the present time do not recall your impenitent heart from iniquity, and you do not fear to store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, what excuse will you offer, what plea will you advance for yourself, when—unless through repentance you forestall the wrath of the final Judge—you will hear, with those appointed to everlasting fires, the fearful thunder of that sentence: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25).

Indeed, what do you make of yourself, that, while our dearest son in Christ …, the illustrious king of Aragon, and nearly all the great men of the surrounding region swear treaties of peace together at the exhortation of the legates of the Apostolic See, you alone reject them, placing your profit in the hostilities of war, as though you were a raven feeding on corpses? Are you not ashamed that you have broken very many oaths by which you promised to proscribe all heretics established in your dominion? For when, together with your Aragonese followers, you were ravaging the province of Arles with hostile devastation, you were asked by our venerable brother, the bishop of Orange, to spare monasteries and at least to cease from despoiling the lands during the holy season and the approaching feast days, you seized his right hand and swore by it that you would defer neither to the holy season nor to the Lord’s days, nor cease from harming pious places or ecclesiastical persons. This oath—or rather, this perjury—you observed more carefully than the others which you had made for an honorable cause.

Impious, cruel, and dreadful tyrant, were you not ashamed to descend so far into heretical depravity that, when rebuked for your defense of heretics, you answered that you would find such a heresiarch—namely, a certain bishop of the heretics—as would prove their faith better than that of the Catholics? Moreover, while you were besieging a certain castle, the brothers of the monastery of Candeli, who had come to ask you to spare their vineyards, received from you a reply that marked you as faithless: having shamefully driven them away, you caused their vineyards to be destroyed, while preserving unharmed those which the heretics possessed there.

We know that you have committed many other offenses against God. But in this especially we grieve for you, if indeed you yourself grieve: because you foster heretics, you are very strongly suspected of heresy. We ask you, therefore: what is this madness that has seized you, that you listen to frivolous opinions and support followers of such paths? Will you be wiser than all those who follow ecclesiastical unity? Or have all who kept Catholic truth been condemned, while those who held false vanities and insanities have been saved? Was it for this reason that many prudent and wealthy persons, though they possessed understanding of the Scriptures and abundance of worldly goods, forsook the world and withdrew to the wilderness with this faith? Was it for this reason that some fathers, defenders of the orthodox faith, shed their blood for it?

Surely you are foolish if you think thus. Either you will accept what he who was set apart for God’s Gospel says of such people: “In the last times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and teachings of demons, speaking in hypocrisy” (1 Timothy 4); or, by rejecting the minister of the Gospel, you are proved an adversary of the Gospel.

Since therefore, for this reason also, and because you keep the Aragonese familiarly with you and devastate the land with them; because you violated the days of Lent, feasts, and seasons which ought to have enjoyed the security of peace; because you refuse to render justice to your opponents, who offered themselves to justice and had sworn peace; because you entrust public offices to Jews in contempt of the Christian faith; because you have taken possessions and churches from the monastery of Saint William and other churches; because you have fortified churches as castles, from which you do not fear to wage war; because you have newly increased tolls; and because you have driven our venerable brother …, bishop of Carpentras, from his own see—the aforesaid legates promulgated sentences of excommunication against you and of interdict against your land. We ratify those sentences and command that, according to their disposition, they be observed inviolably until suitable satisfaction is made.

Although you are known to have sinned gravely against God and the universal Church, and more gravely against yourself, nevertheless, because we are bound to recall the erring to the path of right conduct, we admonish and earnestly exhort your nobility. By these apostolic letters, under the attestation of divine judgment, we command you to make such swift and fitting satisfaction concerning these matters that you may deserve to obtain the benefit of absolution. Otherwise, because we cannot leave unpunished so great an injury to the universal Church—indeed, to God—we shall cause the land which you are known to hold from the Roman Church to be taken from you. And if not even thus affliction gives you understanding, we shall command all the surrounding princes to rise against you as an enemy of Christ and persecutor of the Church, retaining for themselves whatever of your lands they can occupy, lest the stain of heretical depravity continue to infect them under your dominion. Nor in all these things will the Lord’s anger be turned away from you; but his hand, still stretched out, will press upon you and show that it will be difficult for you to flee from the face of his wrath, which you have grievously provoked.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXX. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF GRANDSELVE

That they should freely permit Hugh Vitalis to celebrate in the order of priesthood.

Our beloved son Hugh Vitalis, bearer of these letters, coming to the Apostolic See, disclosed to us in humble confession that, while he was in the order of acolyte, he took as wife in the face of the Church a certain girl named R. After they had lived together for some time and he had known her carnally, discord arose between him and the brothers of the said girl; and he left her of his own accord. Since he could by no means be induced to take her back, the matter having been diligently discussed before our venerable brother, the bishop of Rodez, between him and the girl’s friends, the said girl was joined to another man named Vitalis. The same bishop promoted the aforesaid Hugh to the order of priesthood and granted him a certain church.

But when Hugh’s conscience reproached him on this account, he took the religious habit by the counsel of certain religious of the Cistercian Order, and finally disclosed all the aforesaid matters to you, son abbot. When you had carefully admonished him to provide for the salvation of his soul in this matter, he acknowledged his own guilt and diligently urged the aforesaid girl to return to him, as she was bound to do, after leaving the adulterer. She wholly refused to do so. Therefore we command that, if this is so, since, after being admonished, she was unwilling to return to him and chose rather to remain with another, and since he could no longer reclaim her effectively, you shall freely permit the said Hugh to celebrate in the priestly order which he has received.

## LXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS AND THE BISHOP OF PARIS

Concerning the regalian rights of Auxerre.  
(At the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

The zeal for the house of God grievously afflicts and consumes us. By the Lord’s disposition we, though unworthy, have been appointed to its guardianship; yet it is afflicted by those who ought rather to foster it, and burdened by those through whom it ought to be defended against others. Sympathizing with them in paternal affection, we are no less consumed for their sake than for the house of the Lord which they afflict. Indeed, the more fervently we love our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, the more deeply are we distressed whenever reports of his actions reach us which cloud his reputation before men and stain his conscience before God; for he is said to rage against that Church in which, like a sparrow, he ought to build his nest, as in a cedar planted by the Lord upon Lebanon.

You should know that it has come to our attention that, when this king learned that Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, of good memory, had paid nature’s debt, he immediately caused his servants to seize the episcopal property which he calls the *regalia*. Ravaging it cruelly in the manner of robbers, they caused the forests of the Church to be cut down everywhere and put them all up for sale.

> [Note: Col. 1169. See the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, p. 483 ff.]

They also caused the fishponds to be demolished and completely drained of fish. Having seized the men of that Church, they compelled them by torture to pay a wretched ransom. Carrying off every animal, grain, wine, hay, timber, and even dressed stones which the bishop had prepared for building a chapel and other structures, they wickedly removed them. They stripped the episcopal residences of every article of furnishing, so that nothing was left in them except roof and walls; and they inflicted other losses and burdens upon the episcopal estate. Moreover, the same king wholly confiscated goods which the aforesaid bishop had, by a pious and provident disposition and in the presence of good witnesses, bequeathed to churches and to the poor in various places, as appears from his testament, confirmed by the seals of our venerable brother the bishop of Autun and of seven abbots, as well as by that bishop’s own seal. He assigned, at his own will, to his clerics two prebends which later fell vacant.

Yet, as the elders of that Church affirm, Louis, king of illustrious memory, his father, and his predecessors had until then neither conferred prebends while the episcopal see was vacant nor extended their hands to the *regalia*. Rather, the dean and archdeacon retained them in their hands and administered the said Church, reserving its proceeds and revenues for the future bishop.

But because the aforesaid King Philip, while still a boy, at the instigation of Giles of Tornelle—then his counsellor, who was working to have his brother elected bishop—seized the *regalia* (though he inflicted no injury upon the aforesaid Church in respect of them, and later freely resigned them at the chapter’s request; and, after Giles’s brother had been elected by one part of the chapter, he finally assigned the property seized to him as though to an elected bishop, and conferred certain vacant prebends upon his own clerics, whom that bishop, after confirmation of his election, tolerated—not by reason of the royal collation, but overcome by the king’s entreaties), the same king, when later setting out for Jerusalem, was admonished by the aforesaid bishop to make suitable satisfaction to his Church for these matters. He granted that bishop certain letters expressly providing that thereafter no one on the king’s behalf should dare lay hands upon the *regalia* until it had been fully determined between the king and the chapter who ought, during a vacancy of the see, to retain them in his hands.

But when letters of this sort had been presented and read aloud in the presence of the aforesaid king, he snatched them from the reader’s hand and afterward refused to surrender them. When our venerable brother, the bishop of Auxerre, amicably approached the aforesaid king both concerning compensation for the stated losses and concerning the letters retained, and humbly entreated him about them, the king in no way complied. Moreover, he claims to retain, to the prejudice of that Church, a castle held in fief from the Church of Auxerre, called Giem., whose lord owes homage and fealty to that Church; it had been delivered to him by the count of Nevers, who then held it.

Therefore, wishing with paternal concern to provide no less for his honor and salvation than for the aforesaid Church, we commanded our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Sens and the bishop of Nevers, effectively to admonish and induce the aforesaid king to make such satisfaction to the bishop and Church named above in all the foregoing matters that he may avoid the offense against the divine majesty which he is believed thereby to have incurred, and that his reputation among men, blemished by these acts, may be restored.

Although we love the aforesaid king as our dearest son in Christ and wish to show due regard for his honor, nevertheless we cannot, on any ground, defer to a man against God and the liberty of the Church, for which, if need be, we would fearlessly expose ourselves in accordance with the duty of our office. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, unless he complies with the admonitions of the aforesaid archbishop and bishop concerning the foregoing matters, you shall investigate them fully, ascertain the truth, determine what is just—removing every obstacle of appeal and opposition—and cause what you determine to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXXII. To the Bishop of Treviso and Albert, priest of Mantua. Concerning the election of the bishop of Trent.  
*(Lateran, 9 Kalends of June.)*

Long ago our venerable brother … bishop of Trent petitioned us to grant him permission to resign. He advanced certain reasons why he did not consider himself fit henceforth to exercise the pontifical office: namely, that his parishioners, personally and through others, were afflicting him with intolerable injuries and troubles; that, both because of advancing age and because of the labors by which he had been repeatedly exhausted, he was broken by extreme weakness; and that many homicides, perjuries, and arsons had wickedly been committed on both sides because of the discord which he had had with those same parishioners.

Yielding to his requests, we commanded our venerable brother … bishop of Padua, acting in our place, to receive his resignation and to direct the chapter of Trent canonically to elect for itself a suitable person as pastor. But afterward a controversy arose between the dean and chapter on one side and the said bishop of Trent on the other concerning that bishop’s resignation. The dean, with certain associates, and the bishop came before the Apostolic See.
