The dean therefore alleged before us that the said bishop, having resolved to enter monastic life, assembled his brethren and explained to them that he intended to serve the Lord in monastic life at the church of Saint George on the mountain, and that he had sent his own messenger to us to seek permission to resign. He added that, when those canons saw our letters on the matter, they would be entirely released from the oath of fealty and due obedience by which they were bound to him. To prove this, the dean produced a public instrument. He further alleged that after these events the bishop went to the aforesaid monastery; there, after taking a vow and making solemn profession, he assumed the monastic habit.

When, later, the bishop’s messenger returned with the letters of resignation, the bishop, hindered by flesh and blood, began to withdraw from the resolution he had adopted. The dean and chapter, observing that the bishop was revoking his purpose to the peril of his own salvation and to the detriment of the Church, as devoted sons wishing to avert losses to their mother, brought this to our attention, setting forth many harms and burdens which that Church had afterward suffered through the bishop. Therefore we commanded the aforesaid bishop of Padua that, unless the bishop of Trent showed a just and necessary reason why he had changed his intention to resign, he should diligently admonish and induce him to resign and, if necessary, endeavor to compel him through ecclesiastical censure, appeal removed.

When, by authority of those letters, the bishop and chapter of Trent had been cited and appeared before the bishop of Padua on the appointed day, the bishop of Trent raised certain exceptions in order to decline the jurisdiction. Since the bishop of Padua consulted us concerning them, judging those exceptions superfluous, we commanded him not to delay proceeding in the matter according to the form of our mandate, notwithstanding those frivolous exceptions.

The bishop of Padua, without citing the chapter and without its being absent through contumacy, received witnesses produced on the bishop of Trent’s behalf to prove the grounds on which he had changed his intention. The aforesaid dean challenged them in many ways. One of them was a crossbowman and archer; another a gambler and cheat, as the witnesses themselves attest in the course of their testimony. A third was proved perjured because, though he had sworn to the dean to keep confidence, he afterward disclosed to the bishop the counsel entrusted to him, as that witness himself testified. One of the witnesses, named R., was also found stained by the vice of simony. Manifest contradiction was likewise found among the witnesses.

The dean therefore requested that, since the bishop had not lawfully proved a just and necessary reason why he had changed his intention, we should compel him to resign; especially since the grounds for which he had sought permission to resign had not diminished, but had rather increased. The dean further alleged that, even if the bishop should not be compelled to resign for those reasons, nevertheless he ought not to be tolerated any longer because of his manifest wastefulness in administering the bishopric. He had burdened his Church with debts exceeding forty thousand pounds in Veronese currency, as appeared from his own confession.

The bishop, attacking the dean’s statements in many ways, recounted the facts and proceedings differently from the dean. He asserted that, although he had conceived the purpose of changing his life for the reasons noted above and had sent his own messenger to us to obtain permission to resign, he afterward changed his intention for a probable and honorable reason: namely, because he saw his bride [his Church] being profaned by wicked schemes and shameful promises. As to the dean’s objection that the bishop of Padua received witnesses before joinder of issue and without observing due legal process, the bishop answered that complete judicial formality was not required in this instance, since the bishop of Padua had been entrusted not with contentious jurisdiction but with a certain summary jurisdiction. Therefore, judicial formalities having been set aside, witnesses could be received in this case. He also excused by various answers the objections made concerning the witnesses and their statements, adding that, if his Church was burdened with debts, this was imputable not to him but rather to his subjects, who had stirred up an insufficiently reasonable rebellion against him.

Having heard and fully understood the arguments and allegations of both parties, we observed that, even if the bishop had lawfully and sufficiently proved by suitable witnesses the reason for which he asserts that he changed his intention, that reason could postpone, but not alter, his intention of resigning—especially since that reason wholly ceases now that we intend through our solicitude to provide for the Church of Trent. By counsel of our brethren, we therefore decree that the bishop shall resign without any delay, as he is known earnestly to have requested of us.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your discretion diligently to admonish the chapter of Trent that, within eight days after your admonition, they canonically elect for themselves, with your counsel, as pastor a suitable person free from every suspicion. If they should delay doing so, do not delay, by our authority and removing every obstacle of opposition and appeal, to carry this out. Opponents, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of June, in the tenth year.

## LXXIII. To the Bishop of Wacy. Reply to his inquiries.  
*(Viterbo, 5 Ides of June.)*

We respond all the more willingly to your inquiries because you venerate the Apostolic See with greater devotion. You have set forth that, concerning the tithes of the crusaders—who have been granted by the Apostolic See that they are not bound to pay tithes from newly cultivated land or from estates which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense—you suffer no small injury. You doubt whether, if estates or possessions from which you were accustomed to receive tithe-revenues are bestowed upon them as alms or acquired by them through a contract of purchase, you would seem to act against the privileges of the Apostolic See by exacting the customary tithes from those possessions when they are not cultivated by their own hands or at their own expense. You therefore requested to be certified on this point by an apostolic rescript.

> [Note: Col. 1173. Chapter “*Eo libentius*,” *On servitudes not ordained*.]

You added another question: whether children of those who are held by the Church in servile condition, being given by their parents to clerical service with the consent of their lords, so that they ought to serve God in the Church to which they belong, and thereby obtaining freedom, may afterward, leaving that Church, transfer themselves to another.

Wishing to satisfy your brotherhood on both points, we answer as follows. Since these crusaders, by the tenor of our privileges, are not bound to pay tithes from produce which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, if others cultivate their estates at their own expense, they are bound to pay tithes on the produce of others’ labor. In the other matter, we think a distinction must be made: whether they were manumitted and offered to the clerical order on the condition that, while they live, they owe service to the Church that manumitted them in divine worship; in that case permission to transfer to another Church must be denied them; or whether they were manumitted absolutely, and thus have freedom to go to another.

Given at Viterbo, 5 Ides of June, in the tenth year.

## LXXIV. To the Archbishop of Tours and his suffragans. Concerning tournaments and aid for the Holy Land.  
*(Viterbo, 7 Kalends of July.)*

Formerly our venerable brother … bishop of Soissons informed us by letter that, because he believed that tournaments held in his regions greatly impeded the purpose of pilgrimage, he had, by our authority, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against tournament participants. For this reason many knights were so disturbed that they would neither take the cross nor contribute any aid to the Holy Land. He therefore requested us to permit him temporarily to mitigate that sentence.

Although it was not our intention to permit tournaments, which are known to be forbidden by sacred ordinances, nevertheless, because what had been provided for benefit seemed likely to result in harm, we granted the bishop permission to relax the sentence as to all or some, as he should judge expedient. Proceeding in the matter with due deliberation, he received security in the form prescribed by the Church from all who had taken part in the jousts at Montisore and Laon, and relaxed the aforesaid sentence of excommunication. He caused notice to be given that both they and all who had communicated with them, whether in lodging or otherwise, were absolved, while the censure of the canon concerning such persons remained in full force.

Therefore the absolved knights, greatly rejoicing, unanimously and devoutly resolved that each should send a fixed sum of money in aid of the Holy Land. Approving what the bishop had prudently and usefully done, we command your whole body by these letters prudently to admonish and effectively induce the aforesaid knights, each in his own diocese, to pay what they promised with praiseworthy devotion to pay in aid of Christ’s inheritance. If necessary, compel them to do so through ecclesiastical coercion, causing the censure of the Lateran Council concerning such persons to retain its due force.

Given at Viterbo, 7 Kalends of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXV. To the Archbishop of Compostela. That he may reconcile the altar of Saint James.  
*(Viterbo, 12 Kalends of July.)*

> [Note: Col. 1175D. Chapter “*Proposuisti*,” *On the consecration of churches*.]

Appearing before us in person, you stated that pilgrims from diverse regions come to the church of Blessed James, and that, when some seek by disputes and quarrels to claim from others the nighttime guarding of the altar, homicides sometimes occur and wounds are sometimes inflicted. You therefore humbly requested that we might provide for that church by another means than the benefit of reconsecration.

Accordingly, while the church and altar remain standing, let it be known to your brotherhood by this present communication that it may be reconciled with water blessed with wine and ashes.

Given at Viterbo, 12 Kalends of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXVI. To the Same. Concerning procurations.  
*(Viterbo, 10 Kalends of July.)*

> [Note: Col. 1176D. Chapter “*Super eo*,” *On censuses*.]

Regarding the matter upon which your brotherhood wished to consult us—namely, because almost the whole province of Compostela has newly come under the jurisdiction of your Church, how it ought to show obedience and service to you when you visit the province or part of it, and how it ought to provide procurations—we think it right to answer you thus: it is bound to observe what is observed in neighboring provinces.

Given at Viterbo, 10 Kalends of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXVII. To the Abbot of Saint Aubert, and Master R. of Bekerel and R. Torel, canons of Cambrai. Concerning a cleric who had become a monk during illness.  
*(Viterbo, 6 Nones of July.)*

Appearing in our presence, our beloved son C., a cleric, informed us that, because of injuries which … provost of the church of Saint-Omer had formerly inflicted upon him concerning his benefice in that same church, he had appealed to the Apostolic See. While traveling to pursue his appeal before the Apostolic See, he was overtaken at Troyes by a grave illness. At length, in order to avoid a disturbance among the people, the cleric had himself carried to the monastery of Clairvaux. There, as his illness grew worse and he had fallen into a trance, the monks of that place clothed him in the habit of a novice. As soon as he recovered consciousness, he protested that he had never consented; laying aside the habit, he obtained permission from them to depart.

He therefore humbly requested that we would, by paternal solicitude, protect him in this matter against the cunning of his enemies. Yielding to his petition in paternal affection, we command you by this authority that, if this is so, you shall not allow the aforesaid cleric to be troubled by anyone on the pretext of this incident. If you find that his revenues, possessions, or other property have rashly been seized on that occasion, cause them to be restored to him in their full integrity through ecclesiastical censure, appeal removed. The witnesses who shall be named, etc. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. If not all of you, then two of you, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 6 Nones of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXVIII. To the archbishops and bishops established throughout Spain and Gascony. Concerning counterfeit badges of Blessed James.  
*(Viterbo, 13 Kalends of July.)*

The Apostolic See ought to oppose the presumption of the wicked and restrain their excesses with pastoral care. It has indeed come to the attention of our apostolate that certain persons established in Spain and Gascony do not hesitate, at the peril of their souls, to manufacture counterfeit badges of Blessed James, called shells. Wishing through the prudence of your discretion to restrain such presumption, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters strictly to forbid, under penalty of excommunication, all persons established throughout your provinces from presuming with any rashness to manufacture such counterfeit badges, to the peril of their souls.

Given at Viterbo, 13 Kalends of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXIX. To all archbishops established in Aquitaine. Concerning apostolic letters fraudulently obtained.  
*(Viterbo, 5 Kalends of July.)*

The wickedness of certain depraved persons, reported to us by our venerable brother the bishop of Saintes, could not fail to move us. Having discovered a novel fraudulent method of making profit, they bring grave vexatious suits, by means of our letters, against certain persons established in your dioceses. For, as it is said, some obtain from us letters of commission upon false complaints against persons whose persons they hate or whose wealth they covet; they turn legal rights into injuries, compelling their opponents, under pretext of justice, to suffer harassment by those letters until they have either wearied the persons at will through injustice or extorted a price for abandoning the litigation which they have stirred up.

One of them, for example, when unable to induce a certain married young woman to consent to his lust, demanded back gifts which he claimed to have sent her and caused her to be cited to court. Whether frightened by the fraud or prevented by her husband from approaching the judges, not only she but also one of her female relatives—who had refused to be a go-between for adultery—and certain others incurred a sentence of excommunication. In the meantime some of them died and were unable in any way to obtain ecclesiastical burial, although one of the judges extorted a fixed sum of money from a … priest who had received the aforesaid married woman, when she was at the point of death, to penance.

Moreover, he caused a certain cobbler to be cited before distant judges, and finally subjected to excommunication, over shoelace thread scarcely worth four denarii. Taking advantage also of the fact that a certain burgess’s servant had bolted the door against him when he wished to enter his lord’s house, after no small interval of time, when that servant wished to marry a woman, he objected that, for the injury done him, he had caused the man to be bound by the bond of excommunication. At last, after receiving ten solidi for lifting this obstacle, he himself absolved the man, saying that he had authority from the judges.

On another occasion, after causing nearly two hundred persons to be cited by a certain archpriest on various fabricated grounds of dispute, he afterward sued that archpriest before the same judges because he had negligently executed the apostolic mandate, and did not desist from harassing him until a ransom had been paid. Another likewise extorted fifteen solidi from a cobbler, charging that, in making his shoes, he had shortened their soles. The same man had hired a horse from another person and compelled him to pay a specified sum, because the horse accidentally fell into water beneath him and, by splashing, soaked his cloak.

Another received ten solidi from someone whom he had harassed over a bundle of cabbages. And—what is worthy of being recorded on wood (*recoli est in lignum*, an uncertain phrase)—another caused a young man to be cited before judges more than three days’ journey away because, when he went with him to public women, the young man had refused to wait for him. He complained that the young man’s absence had caused him loss of property, although this did not exceed one denarius; because he had been left alone, he had been compelled to pay for the shared reckoning.

Such acts, and similar ones, are committed by these persons all the more freely because certain judges are said more reprehensibly to share in them. They deliberately assign unsafe places for cited persons, and sometimes give the plaintiffs their own documents sealed with their seals, thereby conferring on them power to excommunicate and absolve such persons.

Since, if these things are true, we ought not to pass over them with closed eyes, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth; to decree void and without force such letters as are shown to have been obtained by these vexatious litigants for this fraud; to restore to due status whatever you discover has been wrongly undertaken through them; to compel such persons, appeal removed, to restore what they rashly extorted under this pretext; and otherwise to ensure that such punishment is inflicted upon them as may fittingly punish their wickedness and deter others from similar examples. Restrain any opponents or rebels whom you find through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

Given at Viterbo, 5 Kalends of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXX. To the Bishop of Troyes and A., Archdeacon of Paris. That they restore Abbot M. to the custody of the Church of Péronne.  
*(Viterbo, 12 Kalends of July.)*

> [Note: Col. 1177D. Chapter “*Cum ad nostram*,” *On institution*.]

When it had formerly come to our attention that, in the Church of Péronne, a certain dignity popularly called the “custody” had been vacant for two years and more, contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, we recall that we commanded our venerable brother the archbishop of Tours—then archdeacon of Paris—and our beloved son the dean of Saint-Quentin that, if the matter stood thus, since appointment to that dignity had devolved upon us, they should, supported by our authority, take it into their custody and report the truth to us by their letters, so that, once informed with certainty by those letters, we might confer that dignity upon a suitable person.

They peremptorily cited both the dean and chapter and Matthew, abbot of the Church of Péronne, who also acted as custodian of that Church. Since the said archbishop could not be present on the appointed day, he excused himself by letter. The aforesaid abbot’s procurator appeared before the dean and argued that our letters addressed to them were suspect for several reasons: because the archdeacon’s name stood before the dean’s in their salutation; because the docket customarily added to identify the person who had obtained the letters was written not on the back but in the margin; because the capital letter **S** in the word *salutem* had an excessively elongated trailing stroke; and because the opposing party, accuser, or even denouncer was not designated by name in those letters. He maintained that all this was contrary to the custom of the Apostolic See.

The same procurator also maintained that the matter had to proceed by judicial process, and urgently requested a postponement so that the abbot could attend the case in person, raising the obstacle of appeal should the requested postponement be denied. But the dean, treating these allegations as superfluous, wholly denied the postponement and took the aforesaid custody into his own care, appointing suitable overseers both for external and internal matters. In order to inform us more certainly of the truth of the case, he compelled the dean and certain canons of the Church of Péronne to give testimony concerning it, and sent their depositions, enclosed under his own seal, to our presence.

Reviewing the dean’s proceedings more carefully, we judged certain exceptions raised by the procurator of the aforesaid abbot to be frivolous and empty. Nevertheless, since according to lawful enactments, even when not judicial investigation but execution is entrusted, the truth of the petition must still be investigated—especially since the clause “if the matter stands thus” had been inserted in our letters—we considered void the proceeding of the dean, who took the custody into his care before investigating the truth.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion to restore the abbot to the aforesaid custody, since it is clear that he was deprived contrary to the form of the apostolic mandate. Thereafter you are to proceed according to the tenor of that mandate. Yet you must observe this: unless the said abbot shows a reasonable cause why he can hold both the custody and the abbacy in the same Church, you shall deprive him of it, take the aforesaid custody into your own care, removing the obstacle of appeal, and retain it until you execute the apostolic mandate concerning it.

We do not wish you to be ignorant that, after M. became abbot, he could not lawfully obtain the aforesaid custody. Since, by reason of the abbacy, the right of appointment both to the custody and to other dignities and prebends in the Church of Péronne belongs to him, he could by no means receive its custody from himself, since there must be a personal distinction between giver and recipient; nor could he receive it from another, since no other person possessed the right to confer it.

Given at Viterbo, 12 Kalends of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXXI. To the Bishop of Rochester. That he compel John, deprived of office and benefice, to live with his wife.  
*(Viterbo, 5 Kalends of July.)*

You informed us by letter that John, the bearer of these presents, publicly confessed before you in court that, after receiving the order of subdeacon, he had contracted marriage with a certain woman and afterward, concealing the truth of this matter, had caused himself to be ordained deacon. Although you subsequently established through suitable witnesses both the marriage contracted and the deacon’s order received after it, he was nevertheless unable to prove that he had become a subdeacon before contracting the marriage.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, if this is so, you shall deprive the aforesaid J. of office and benefice and compel him to cohabit with his wife.

Given at Viterbo, 5 Kalends of July, in the tenth year.

## LXXXII. To the Bishop of Angoulême. Concerning canons to be promoted to the priesthood.  
*(Given as in the other [letter].)*

It was set before us on your behalf that, although there were customarily several canons in the Church of Angoulême who celebrated the solemnities of Mass by weeks in the order of their turns, the only two priests presently there complain that they cannot bear this burden, which formerly six or seven could scarcely sustain. To remedy this deficiency, you admonished the canons in lower orders to have themselves ordained priests; yet none of them could be induced to do so.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood to admonish and induce the said canons either not to delay, if they are suitable, in being promoted to the office of priest for so necessary a purpose, or, together with you, as is fitting, to admit some as associates and brethren by whom ministry in that office may be rendered in the aforesaid church. Otherwise, you shall endeavor, by our authority and appeal removed, to supply their deficiency in the manner which may be useful in this matter. Notwithstanding any letters, etc.

Given as in the other [letter].

## LXXXIII. To the Bishop of Riez and the Abbot of Boscaud. Concerning the case of the Bishop of Nice.  
*(Given as above.)*
When formerly certain religious of the diocese of Nice submitted to us for inspection the tenor of certain letters, by which our venerable brother . . . bishop of Nice had proceeded against them concerning certain expenses, alleging that those letters were forged by him, we instructed our venerable brothers the bishops of Glandèves and Senez not to proceed in the matter on the occasion of those letters until, after examining them, we should proceed in the matter as expediency might require. [Col. 1180C] Meanwhile the same bishop of Nice, who until then had believed the aforesaid letters genuine, becoming suspicious of them, immediately approached our beloved son Brother Peter of Castelnau, legate of the Apostolic See. He explained that a . . . clerk, who had been familiar with him, had told him that he had obtained those letters from us, and that he himself, wholly unaware that they were forged, had used them; bewildered by this new report of so great a wickedness, he asked the legate what he should do. Therefore, hastening at once to the Apostolic See and presenting us with certain letters in which many religious men excused their own innocence, he voluntarily—though with shame—disclosed to us how confidently he had acted in the affair because he had proceeded simply.

Although, therefore, under the constitution issued against forgers, a grave [Col. 1180D] punishment seemed to threaten that bishop, nevertheless, since the same constitution provides that in such matters malice is punished more than negligence, and since we observe that, as he asserts, another’s fault, not his own, harms him in this case—although he was not as diligent concerning the said letters as he should have been in taking precautions—and since we note also that he does not appear to have been an abettor of the forgery, which, as soon as he first suspected it, he endeavoured to reveal to our legate, and finally, coming personally to us, voluntarily confessed before us: we have thought fit to remit him to you, suspended from the episcopal office, trusting in your discretion. By the authority of these presents we command you that, after you have received from him canonical purgation concerning this matter with [Col. 1181A] three bishops, you shall procure his restoration to that office; and that you shall punish, without regard to appeal, according to the aforesaid constitution, the person who is found to have procured the said letters. If not both of you, one of you, etc.

Given as above.

### LXXXIV. To the Bishop and Chapter of Elne. That the objection of one person shall not prevail against the public good. (Viterbo, 4 July.)

You are to know that it has come to our hearing that such a custom has grown up in your church: if you happen at any time to assemble for the transaction of its affairs, then, although a decision or some definite and common deliberation concerning any matter seems useful to all the canons, and indeed rests upon sounder counsel, nevertheless, if it displeases one person alone, unsupported by any reason and moved rather by his own will, it is said that the whole matter is nullified, however useful or honourable it may be and however unanimously it is approved by the others. Since this pernicious licence of mind, said to have been approved by custom, is wholly contrary to the sacred canons and ought to be restrained by apostolic governance, we command you by apostolic letters that henceforth you rely upon it in no way, but return to the observance of the common law.

Given at Viterbo, 4 July, in the tenth year.

### LXXXV. To the Bishops of Clermont and Nevers. They are entrusted with the case of the Bishop of Le Puy against his citizens. (Viterbo, 7 July.)

[Col. 1181C]

The beloved sons, the citizens of Le Puy, have informed us that, although our predecessor Pope Lucius of pious remembrance commanded, under penalty of deprivation from office, the bishop of Le Puy of good memory not to hinder the lawful marriages of widows, nor, contrary to canonical sanctions, to demand money for contracting such marriages or for the burial of the dead, or to allow it to be extorted or demanded from his subjects, our venerable brother . . . his successor has subsequently not only attempted such acts, but has also harassed the said [Col. 1181D] citizens in these and other respects, and does not fear rashly to launch against them, at his pleasure and without reasonable cause, sentences of excommunication and interdict.

We therefore commanded that bishop, under threat of canonical penalty, to restore, and cause to be restored, as he is bound to do, whatever has been extorted from those citizens contrary to justice by him or his clerics; and henceforth to refrain from such conduct in such a way that no just complaint against him need be repeated, for which we should deservedly have to lay a heavy hand upon him. He is also not to hinder, nor cause anyone to hinder, the said citizens or their messengers, so that they may safely and freely pursue their case in going and returning. [Col. 1182A] We command the aforesaid citizens by our letters that they render him reverence and obedience both due and devout, and that they diligently observe the commendable custom hitherto maintained through the pious devotion of their forefathers concerning the burials of their loved ones, lest perhaps, under the pretext of canonical purity, they appear to corrupt it through the leaven of heretical depravity. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after prior admonition, you cause our command to be observed inviolably by the aforesaid bishop and citizens, through ecclesiastical censure and without regard to appeal.

Given at Viterbo, 7 July, in the tenth year.

### LXXXVI. To the Podestà and Citizens of Florence. They are exhorted to peace and concord. (Viterbo, 11 July.)

[Col. 1182B]

If you carefully consider that a provident father often causes a servant to be chastised by a son, and often a son by a servant, for the offence of either, you will be unable not to mingle fear with the joy which you recently conceived at the victory over the Sienese. You do not know whether the Lord humbled them before you because of your justice, or because through your agency He wished to administer correction to them. In one respect it seems fearful that Assyria, the rod of the Lord’s anger, afflicted God’s people; although in the other respect confidence is drawn from the fact that David struck down the Philistine with a sling.

Although the Lord, strong and mighty, mighty in battle, who resists the proud [Col. 1182C] but gives grace to the humble, is believed to have stood by you in their conflict, you ought not to ascribe the glory of the victory received to your own strength, but rather attribute it to the sins of others. Do not exceed the proper measure in what you do, lest perhaps you seem like him concerning whom the Lord says through the prophet that He will command him against the people of His wrath, to take spoil and divide plunder, and to set that people underfoot like the mud of the streets. But he will not think so; rather, his heart will be bent on destruction and on the annihilation of not a few nations.

Since, therefore, the cause of so great a discord is known to result in enormous loss of property, grave bodily harm, and dreadful danger to souls; and since it pertains to us especially to call the discordant back [Col. 1182D] to peace, inasmuch as we inherit peace in a manner different from all others—we to whom Jesus Christ, mediator of God and men, whose office on earth we exercise, though unworthy, announced it not only at His birth through the angel saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2), but also bequeathed it as though by testament at His death, when He said, “I give you my peace; I leave you peace” (John 14), and finally, rising again, instructed His disciples to preach it when He said to them, “Peace be with you” (John 20)—we have resolved, with paternal solicitude, to bring you back to that peace, if it be granted from above.

Accordingly, we have taken care to send our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Portico, whom known [Col. 1183A] integrity and tested prudence make especially acceptable to us among our other brethren, in order to restore peace between you and the aforesaid Sienese and to secure the release of captives on both sides. We earnestly admonish and strongly exhort your whole community, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: preserve the humility which is believed to have exalted you, and proceed effectively in this affair according to his prudent exhortation. Take diligent care that, since the peace agreement which, at the exhortation of our messenger, you made before you had engaged in battle is in writing, it would appear wholly to tend toward pride and to depart from humility if you should strive to demand for peace beyond that agreement more than is due. [Col. 1183B] Thus the saying of Truth might not undeservedly be fulfilled in you: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted, and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled”; as Sacred Scripture testifies, “Before ruin the heart shall be exalted”—that is, after exaltation of heart follows ruin.

Indeed, it will be for you a title to everlasting glory if, giving honour to almighty God, you are content after victory, for His reverence and constrained not by necessity but by humility, with that measure which you approved before victory. We have commanded the aforesaid cardinal to pursue prudently and carefully the matters set forth above and, if he finds either party obstinate, to pronounce upon it ecclesiastical censure, without regard to appeal. [Col. 1183C] We also command all bishops established in Tuscany to cause any sentence which he may pronounce to be observed inviolably.

Given at Viterbo, 11 July, in the tenth year.

### LXXXVII. To the Prior and Convent of Kirkham. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Given as in another letter.)

You formerly complained to our Apostolic See that our venerable brother the Archbishop of York and certain other prelates of churches, contrary to privileges granted you by Roman pontiffs, did not fear unjustly to suspend you, your churches, and your clerics; that they inflicted many other injuries upon you concerning churches and ecclesiastical benefices [Col. 1183D]; and that they prohibited lay people from rendering to your churches what they were bound to render. We therefore instructed the beloved sons . . . the abbot of Thornton and his fellow judges to compel the said archbishop and others, through ecclesiastical censure and without regard to appeal, to desist from their undue harassment of you and to make suitable satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted.

As they informed us in their letters, they repeatedly cited those persons for this reason. But the same archbishop, peremptorily summoned by them for a whole year at suitable places and times, refused to appear before them either in person or through a suitable representative. [Col. 1184A] Indeed, through certain letters obtained from us addressed to our venerable brother the Bishop of Salisbury and his colleagues—letters in which no mention was made of our letters earlier in date and use—he repeatedly burdened you, for as many as eight days’ journeys, with severe labour and expense. Therefore your aforesaid judges, after taking prudent counsel, ordered the said archbishop, the Bishop of Salisbury, and his associates, by apostolic authority, to cease their unjust harassment of you. Since the archbishop would never desist, they suspended him from your obedience and from that of your clerics and churches on account of his manifest contumacy, until, wearied by this treatment, he should answer you in court.

[Col. 1184B] Finally, though repeatedly and peremptorily summoned by many edicts during a year, with suitable times and places assigned, he contumaciously refused to appear before them either personally or through a sufficient representative. The said judges accordingly condemned him to pay you the expenses lawfully incurred and proved through his unjust harassment, after a suitable assessment had first been made. Yet he nonetheless despised the authority of the Apostolic See and for a third and fourth year would not desist from harassing you. We therefore approve what was done by the aforesaid judges, and command you by the authority of these presents that, if this is so, until suitable satisfaction has been made for the matters aforesaid, you, your clerics, and your churches shall give the said archbishop absolutely no compliance in anything. If meanwhile he pronounces any [Col. 1184C] sentence against you or the said clerics or churches, you shall by no means observe it.

Given as in another letter.

### LXXXVIII. To the Abbot and Convent of Tulle. Concerning the number of mounts in visitations. (Viterbo, 11 Nones of July.)

[Note: [Col. 1183D] A similar letter appears in Book I, Letter 140.]

Since, to restrain the insolence of certain persons, the Lateran Council by prudent deliberation decreed that archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, and deans should not exceed a fixed number of mounts and persons in visitations of churches, and since, as we have heard, certain of the aforesaid persons do not observe this in [Col. 1184D] your churches, we have thought fit to provide for your convenience in this matter. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we grant to your devotion that if any of the aforesaid persons, when visiting churches, should presume to exceed, to your burden, the number of mounts and persons established at the said council and should demand procuration for them, you may freely refuse it by apostolic authority. If on that account he pronounces any sentence against your churches or clerics, we decree by apostolic authority that it is not to be observed. Let no one, therefore, [lacuna] of this our concession and decree, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 4 July, in the tenth year.

### LXXXIX. To the Bishops of Auxerre and Troyes, and the Abbot of Saint-Bénigne. They are entrusted with an inquiry against the Abbot and monks of Vézelay. (Viterbo, 19 July.)

[Col. 1185A]

Following the example of Him who, by the Lord’s command, dug through the wall and, entering, saw the most abominable acts which the house of Israel was committing in the temple, we descended through our angels to see whether the Abbot and monks of Vézelay had fulfilled in deed the outcry which came to us against them; so that, destroying evil men in an evil manner, we might let the good vineyard to good husbandmen. We also imitated Him who, when He had said to the steward who was accused of squandering his master’s goods, “What is this that I hear [Col. 1185B] concerning you? Give an account of your stewardship,” immediately added: “For you can no longer be steward” (Luke 16).

Accordingly, when the report of the inquiry which we had ordered our venerable brother the Archbishop of Sens and our beloved son Master Robert of Courson, canon of Noyon, to conduct concerning them had been laid before us, we learned that the following had been alleged against the said abbot. At the death of his predecessor, the monastery of Vézelay had remained free of all debt; thirty thousand solidi had come to this abbot, besides silver vessels weighing sixty marks; yet, having for the most part squandered all these badly, he had burdened the monastery with debts of 2,220 pounds. Although witnesses expressly proved this, [Col. 1185C] the abbot nevertheless admitted in his own confession that, besides vessels of sixty-one marks, twenty-eight thousand solidi from his predecessor’s treasury had come to him, while the monastery was now maintained on revenues of only 1,800 pounds.

It was also alleged against him that he was incontinent and had married off a son and a daughter from the goods of the church—children whom he seemed to have begotten after assuming the habit, since his own confession made clear that he entered the monastery at eight years of age. It was further said that he attended a wedding, dressed the girl in silk garments, and sat at the wedding feast; that he had entered through simony; and that, through simoniacal depravity, he had received certain persons as brethren and granted priories to others. [Col. 1185D] Certain witnesses, fully competent and beyond every exception, also proved that, against the ordinance of Octavian, bishop of Ostia of good memory, then legate of the Apostolic See, made under penalty of excommunication and subsequently confirmed by us, he had conferred a priory upon . . . his lay brother. In this he seemed to have transgressed in many ways: against ecclesiastical propriety, which does not permit laymen to preside over monks; against the authority of the Apostolic See, whose ordinances he had violated; and because flesh and blood had revealed this course to him.

Moreover, it was proved against him that he was excessively liberal, negligent, lax, and soft. This was clear not only from witness depositions; his deeds themselves also bore testimony to the truth, [Col. 1186A] since he had retained in offices and taken as advisers men whose incontinence was known, some of whom possessed private property contrary to the monastic order. Certain persons who had committed simony at his accession, on his behalf and with him, established this by their own oath, although each was isolated in his own testimony.

Since many enormous charges were brought against, and some established against, the prior, the almoner, the dean, the cellarer, the third prior of Flavigny, the priors of Fleys and of Sivry, and the chaplains both of the abbot and of the prior, we expelled them from that monastery and decreed that they should be distributed among other monasteries in which monastic discipline is more strictly observed. They are not to be placed several together in one monastery, but rather each is to be assigned individually to a separate monastery; nor are they henceforth [Col. 1186B] to be admitted to any office without authority of the Apostolic See.

Wishing also to provide for the security of the same monastery, we pronounced sentence of excommunication both against them and against the other monks of Vézelay who possess private property, unless they immediately resign it for the uses of the church. Although the abbot tried to excuse himself in certain matters, nevertheless, because his excuse in part turned rather into an accusation, being an excuse in sins, we proceeded against him not only under our office of provision but also by the rigour of law, removing him from the administration of the monastery and government of the abbacy.

Therefore, wishing to provide for the said monastery, we strictly command your discretion, in which we have full confidence, by apostolic [Col. 1186C] letters: go personally to it, and by our authority direct the convent within three days to set over itself as abbot, by regular election and in agreement with your counsel, a suitable person. Otherwise, from that point, whether from the body of the monastery itself or from elsewhere, you shall procure the appointment as its abbot of a prudent and honourable man, proved already in the past rather than merely to be proved in the future, through whom the house may advance in spiritual observances and receive increase in temporal goods. Cause due reverence and obedience to be rendered to him through ecclesiastical censure, without regard to appeal.

Thereafter, earnestly admonish and strongly induce both the removed abbot and the other persons named above, and also any brethren or lay brothers of the said monastery whom you find possessing private property, to resign it without diminution for the use of the monastery. Publicly announce as excommunicated those who do otherwise, and, if necessary, employ the secular arm to compel them. [Col. 1186D] You shall likewise distribute the aforesaid prior and others, as we have prudently decreed, among individual monasteries in which monastic discipline is more strictly observed, compelling objectors by our authority, if necessary, to receive them and causing them to apply themselves more strictly to regular observances.

Furthermore, that the aforesaid monastery may be more fully cleansed from every stain, we will and command that, once you have executed these measures [Col. 1187A] with prompt diligence, you again investigate most diligently its condition and that of its members. Having God alone before your eyes, correct what you see should be corrected according to Him, and establish what ought to be established, restraining any objectors or rebels, without regard to appeal, through ecclesiastical censure. Take care to hear and obey these first commands of ours in such a manner that in them, as the beginnings of your obedience, we may recognize how much the zeal of God’s house touches you, and what affection of devotion you have and will hereafter have toward us and the Roman Church. If not all of you, two of you, etc.

Meanwhile, until an abbot is installed, we have thought fit [Col. 1187B] to entrust the care and administration of that monastery to the beloved sons, the sacristan and the hospitaller, lest the monastery be scattered without governance. We send you under our seal, enclosed, the seal and two rings which we caused to be received from the aforesaid abbot, to be restored to the same monastery.

Given at Viterbo, 19 July, in the tenth year.

### XC. To the Same Persons. Concerning the deposition of Gilbert, Abbot of Flavigny. (Viterbo.)

Although nothing was alleged or proved against Gilbert, formerly abbot of Flavigny, in the inquiry made concerning the condition of the monastery of Vézelay—perhaps because he was not regarded as a monk of Vézelay—nevertheless, because his deeds of condemnation are manifest, we decree that he be excluded forever from the aforesaid monastery and placed in a stricter monastery to do penance for his offences. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters to cause what we have decreed with prudent reason to be put into execution through ecclesiastical coercion, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. We send the present letters sealed contrary to custom, so that we may enclose in them the seal, rings, and certain other letters. If not all of you, etc.

Given at Viterbo.

### XCI. To the Archdeacon and Chapter of Venafro. Certain rights and sentences rendered in their favour are confirmed. (At Montefiascone, 27 July.)

[Col. 1187D]

Formerly a dispute concerning certain dignities—namely the see, seal, chrism, and feast of Saint Nicander—arose between the churches of Venafro and Isernia in the presence of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory. It had previously been litigated for a long time, so that both churches and cities had already suffered grievous troubles and losses on its account. Wishing to put an end to the dispute, our predecessor gave instructions by his letters to his beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, then rector of Benevento, [Col. 1188A] to strive to restore peace and concord between the churches. If they could not be induced to this, he was to grant to both churches, by apostolic authority and removing every obstacle of appeal or contradiction by either of them and their bishop, the power to have their own bishop. The bishop then known to preside over both churches was to be free, within ten days, to choose whichever of them he wished as his see and retain it with its diocese; the other church could freely elect another bishop, who should both govern and benefit its diocese.

He also granted the cardinal apostolic authority to confirm, without regard to appeal, an election canonically held of a suitable person, while safeguarding in the future the right of the Church of Capua. [Col. 1188B] If the said bishop wished to choose neither, the cardinal was nevertheless to grant the church which wished to have another pastor the power to elect, directing it that, if the bishop should prefer the Church of Venafro, the city should provide such an addition from the common revenues to the episcopal income that he might be honourably supported thereby.

After very many delays and citations, the aforesaid cardinal, having taken the counsel of learned jurists, conferred upon you the power and authority to elect and have a bishop, and to hold this right perpetually by succession, so that both the city and church of Venafro should have a cathedral see forever, with the justice of the metropolitan Church of Capua in all things preserved. [Col. 1188C] The city of Venafro was to add enough from its common revenues to the episcopal income for the bishop of Venafro to be honourably maintained. Thereafter the Venafran clerics, having received from the aforesaid cardinal permission to elect canonically a suitable person as their pastor, unanimously elected our beloved son John of Abner. Our predecessor properly rejected his election because he had not yet been ordained in sacred orders.

But when you assembled again, and invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, you unanimously elected our venerable brother R., then archdeacon and now your bishop. When he came into the presence of our said [Col. 1188D] predecessor to obtain the favour of confirmation, the latter confirmed that election. He directed by his letters the archpriest and chapter of the Church of Isernia that, since both the churches of Venafro and Isernia had suffered considerable harm from the lack of a pastor, especially as the said churches had been deprived of a pastor for two years and more, and since under the decrees of the Lateran Council their ordering belonged to him, he granted the said R. to them as pastor with the counsel of his brethren, making no mention of the cardinal’s sentence. He ordered them to render R., as their elect and pastor of their souls, due obedience, and humbly to receive and observe [Col. 1189A] his salutary admonitions and commands.

Yet our same predecessor, wishing to remove from those churches material for complaint, directed the said elect in his letters that, when in the Church of Venafro, he should use a seal in which he was called only Bishop of Venafro; and, when in the Church of Isernia, he should observe the same rule. He was to make chrism one year in the Church of Isernia and another year in the Church of Venafro; which he likewise commanded to be firmly observed concerning the feast of Saint Nicander.

Now, when messengers of the Church of Isernia formerly came into our presence and humbly petitioned us to provide with paternal solicitude for their desolate church and end the dispute, we instructed our beloved sons R., elect of Capua, and [Col. 1189B] Master Ph., our notary and then rector of Benevento, to summon the parties, carefully examine the merits of the case, and, proceeding without regard to appeal until final judgment, refer the case to our hearing with adequate documentation, setting the parties a suitable term for appearing before us. But because the said elect could not attend the examination of the case, he committed his duties to the notary. Proceeding under our command, the notary took care to refer the duly documented case to our hearing, fixing for the parties the last-past feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin as the date on which they were to appear before us.

When the parties were therefore present before us [Col. 1189C], and we had fully heard the arguments of both, we clearly recognized that the mandate concerning a division had been obtained from our aforesaid predecessor through certain deceptions, and that he, afterwards recognizing this, attempted in some fashion to revoke it, although he did so while the other party was wholly unaware. With the counsel of our brethren, we decreed null and void everything undertaken on the occasion of that mandate concerning division.

Thereafter, so that bonds of peace might be restored between those churches, we made effective efforts, diligently warning the parties to seek an amicable settlement with one another. Through our mediation they came to the following agreement: for the sake of peace, you granted to the Church of Isernia that the castle of Fossa Caeca, which your church possessed, should be held by the Church of Isernia in perpetuity; and that the castle of Capriata, concerning which a dispute had likewise arisen, should remain forever with the Church of Venafro. The castle of Saint John, concerning which the dispute continued, was placed in sequestration in your hands until it could be fully determined to which diocese it belonged. Henceforth the Church of Venafro is to have its own separate bishop, content with the diocese which it is known to have possessed from ancient times; and the Church of Isernia, likewise content with its own diocese, is to elect a suitable person as pastor, capable both of governing and benefiting that church.

Therefore, lest the matters agreed and amicably settled in our presence [Col. 1190A] should relapse into the hazard of renewed dispute, we confirm by apostolic authority this settlement, prudently made without wrongdoing and voluntarily accepted by both parties, and strengthen it by the page of this present writing. We decree, therefore, [lacuna] of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Montefiascone, by the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 27 July, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1207 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### XCII. To R., Cardinal-Priest of the Title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, Abbot of Monte Cassino. Certain cases of usury are entrusted to him for hearing. (Viterbo, 24 July.)

[Col. 1190B]

From the complaint of our venerable brother . . . bishop of Venafro, you are to know that it has come to our hearing that, when the Church of Venafro was formerly placed in a grave extremity of need, the beloved son John of Abner, then elected to that church, pledged a certain piece of land to B. of Durazzo, a citizen of Venafro, for a fixed sum of money. In order that the creditor might not subsequently be proceeded against under the canon issued against usurers, he received that land from him under the title of sale, although in truth a usurious transaction was being carried out. This is evident because the creditor, as a public instrument records, promised the debtor that, whenever he [Col. 1190C] restored the aforesaid money, he would procure the land’s restoration to him.

Although the creditor has held it thus pledged for so long that he has already received from its fruits more than the principal, he nevertheless retains it, to the peril of his soul, alleging the instrument of sale and refusing to restore it. Since fraud and deceit ought not to protect anyone, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, notwithstanding the instrument of sale drawn up in fraud of the canon promulgated [Col. 1190D] against usurers, you compel the aforesaid citizen, without regard to appeal and through the penalty promulgated against usurers by the Lateran Council, to restore the land to the complainant, after accounting the fruits toward the principal and receiving whatever may be lacking from the principal. Witnesses, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 24 July, in the tenth year.

### XCIII. To the Dean and Chapter of Saint Anianus of Orléans. They are fortified by a privilege against letters of the Apostolic See. (Viterbo, 18 July.)

Since your church is a special daughter of the Apostolic See, desiring with paternal solicitude to protect its rights, we establish by the authority of these presents that no prejudice to the liberty of that church shall arise through apostolic letters obtained concerning any matters whatsoever touching you or your church [Col. 1191A] in any manner, addressed to . . . the Archbishop of Sens, . . . the Bishop of Orléans, or others established in their dioceses. We strictly prohibit any ecclesiastical person from pronouncing a sentence of excommunication or interdict against your churches, villages, or servants without manifest and reasonable cause. You shall also be free, should you perceive yourselves oppressed contrary to justice in these or other matters, to appeal to the Apostolic See. Let no one, therefore, [lacuna] of this our constitution and prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 18 July, in the tenth year.

### XCXIV. To the Abbots of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Saint-Geneviève, and the Prior of Saint-Geneviève of Paris. That they render full justice concerning wrongdoers against the Church of Saint Anianus. (Given as in another letter.)

[Col. 1191B]

Since the Church of Blessed Anianus of Orléans is a special daughter of the Apostolic See, we desire with paternal solicitude to safeguard its immunities; therefore, by the authority of these presents, we strictly command your discretion that, whenever you are requested by it concerning any of its wrongdoers situated in the province of Sens, you shall, without malicious delay, cause full justice to be rendered to it; restraining any opponents or rebels, if there be any, by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, and not relaxing any sentence which you judge must for this purpose be pronounced against anyone until fitting satisfaction has been made. If not all of you, two of you, etc. Moreover, in order that fuller provision may be made for the peace of the said Church, we will and command that, should anything human happen to you, this authority shall extend also to your successors; for it is fitting that we take special care for the peace of that Church which, belonging to the Roman pontiff through no intermediary, has no other protector after him.

Given as in the other letter.

XCV. TO W., DEAN OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT ANIANUS OF ORLÉANS, AND TO HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. Concerning the confirmation of privileges. (At Viterbo, 21 July.)

[Col. 1191D]

[Note: [Col. 1191D] Published by Hubert in the *Proofs* to the *History of Saint Anianus*, p. 121.] Although by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God we ought to exercise attentive care and solicitude for all churches, we must nevertheless be especially solicitous for those known to belong more particularly to the right and property of the holy Roman Church, which rely with greater devotion upon the protection of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1192A] and which ought likewise to be fortified by the aid of our authority lest they be harassed by the rash attacks of any persons upon their goods or even their dignities. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions; and, following the example of Alexander and Lucius, Roman pontiffs of blessed memory, our predecessors, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Saint Anianus, in which you are devoted to the divine service [Note: [Col. 1191D] The privileges of Alexander and Lucius are published in the same work, [Col. 1192D] pp. 116 ff.], and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s [Col. 1192B] favour acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to set out the following by their proper names:

namely, the estate of Sentiliacum with its church; the estate of Ruem with its church; the estate of Tilliacum with its church; the church of Chalo; and the estate of Artenay, exchanged to you by A., the illustrious queen of the Franks of blessed memory, for the estate of Chalo—an estate which you are to hold with the liberty and immunity in which L., formerly the illustrious king of the Franks of blessed memory, is known to have held it, as is contained in his authentic charter.

Also, one half of the revenues from small tithes, offerings, and all benefices of the living and the dead in the aforesaid church of Chalo, according to the grant formerly made to you by W., then archbishop of Sens [Col. 1192C] and subsequently archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Saint Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See, and entered in his authentic charter; on this condition, however, that if several parish churches should be built in the same estate, you shall have in all those established there the same right which you are known to have and possess in the aforesaid church.

The estate of Herbiliacum with its church and all its tithes and appurtenances. The church of Old Saint Anianus, called the Chapel, and the church of Saint Germanus within the city walls. Whatever you possess in the estate of Centolum, and the church of that estate. Whatever you possess in the estate of Fontenay, and the church of that estate, with its tithes and other revenues pertaining to your right. The water of the Loire from the wall of the old city [Col. 1192D] to Saint Lupus, and all the mills which you possess in that water, with their fisheries. Whatever you possess beyond the Loire and in Sicalonia [Note: [Col. 1192D] La Sologne.]. Whatever you possess in Gâtinais. The estate of Berziacum with all its appurtenances. Whatever you possess at Oscuras. Whatever you possess in the forest called Bolonia, and the estate of Casellis. Whatever pertains to the mayoralty of Jarria, and the estate of Seteis. Likewise, the mills which you have newly constructed in your estates, and that which you possess in the place called Domitiacum.

In the aforesaid parish churches—namely, those of Sentiliacum, Ruem, Tilliacum, [Col. 1193A] Fontenay, Centolum, Herbiliacum, and Chalo—which you hold, you shall elect priests and present them to the bishops. If they are suitable, the bishops shall commit the care of souls to them without payment, so that they may answer for the care of the people, but for temporal matters shall render you the obedience due and the customary subjection.

In the other two churches, namely those of Saint Anianus and Saint Germanus, and for service at the altar of the Crucified in the church of Blessed Anianus, it shall be lawful for you, freely and without anyone’s opposition or presentation, as heretofore so henceforth, to appoint priests. It shall likewise be lawful for you, whenever your parish churches are vacant, according to custom and the practice observed from ancient times until now, to appoint supply priests, who [Col. 1193B] shall serve Almighty God until you agree upon suitable persons to be instituted in them.

Moreover, we apostolically confirm the fairs granted to you and your church, for procuring lights for the two solemnities of Blessed Anianus, by L., the illustrious king of the Franks of blessed memory, and by John, formerly bishop of Orléans, and fortified by their charters, [Note: [Col. 1193D] The words enclosed by these notes were omitted in Hubert’s edition.] as is contained in their authentic documents. Nevertheless, by the present decree we establish that the two prebends formerly assigned to the office of the confraternity, together with a third which you subsequently added to it in provident piety, and the annual distributions of the canons—however the prebends may be altered—shall remain assigned to the office of the confraternity. [Col. 1193C] We further confirm by the protection of the Apostolic See the vineyards and all things conferred upon the aforesaid confraternity by you and through you upon that confraternity, according to what has been established by the common consent of the chapter and confirmed in writing; and we decree that this constitution shall remain valid and unshaken for future times.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of your canons or clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without money or any exaction. Otherwise you may have recourse to whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Furthermore, [Col. 1193D] we confirm by apostolic authority all liberties, immunities, and royal customs granted to you and your church by the kings of the Franks and fortified by their charters, and decree that they shall remain perpetually unimpaired. We also enact and establish by this present decree that no archbishop or any person may excommunicate the church entrusted to you, or you, or the clerics of your choir, nor place you under an interdict from divine offices, except the Roman pontiff or his legate, or by special mandate of the Apostolic See. No one may presume to demand visitation or procuration from your church except by authority of the Apostolic [Col. 1194A] See, since it is subject to it through no intermediary. We further prohibit any ecclesiastical person, or person of any order whatsoever, from imposing undue exactions upon your churches, chapels, or their priests.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, etc., down to “beneficial to it in every way.” Saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops in the aforesaid churches of Sentiliacum, Ruem, Tilliacum, Fontenay, Centolum, Chalo, and Herbiliacum. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, etc., down to “shall be subject to vengeance.” But to all who preserve the rights of that place, etc., to the end.

Given at Viterbo, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1194B] on 21 July, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1207 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

XCVI. TO THE BISHOP OF MEAUX. Concerning the subjection of the monastery of Rebbais. (At Viterbo, 15 June.)

When a dispute had long arisen between you and the monastery of Rebbais concerning that monastery’s subjection, the procurators of the parties came for this reason to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1194D] It exists in the cartulary of the Church of Meaux.—See below, letter 108.]. After they had litigated before us for some time, because it was established by the confession of the opposing party that you had possessed obedience [Col. 1194C] in that monastery, we decreed that you should be restored to that possession. But because a privilege of Pope Innocent, our predecessor of happy memory, produced to us on behalf of the monastery, expressed full liberty, we instructed our beloved sons Master G., dean of Soissons, … cantor of Reims, and … subcantor of Senlis, that, once you had been restored to possession of obedience, unless after your restoration you should within six months raise and prove some reasonable objection against the liberty of the privilege, they should arrange to impose perpetual silence upon you, with the obstacle of appeal removed, concerning the subjection of the aforesaid monastery. We strictly forbade you to venture further to harass that monastery concerning the liberty of its privilege. If it were the parties’ wish, however, they were to remit the case to our presence with adequate documentation and set them a suitable term within which they were to appear before us to receive judgment.

Accordingly, when the parties subsequently appeared before those judges, and you had a copy of the privilege, you wished to challenge it as forged, because, upon comparison of the bull of that privilege with other bulls, it appeared, as you alleged, smaller and unlike the others. You also alleged the authority of res judicata in order to nullify the force of the privilege, asserting that Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, had pronounced judgment against the monastery on this matter, as you showed by his letters. [Col. 1195A] You further sought to introduce the privileges of the said Alexander and of Pope Honorius, our predecessor of good memory, in which it is expressly found established that canonical obedience is to be rendered to the bishop of Meaux by the abbot of Rebbais.

The abbot of the aforesaid monastery, on the other hand, maintained that the monastery ought to enjoy complete liberty not only by authority of the aforesaid privilege, but for another reason as well: Saint Pharo, bishop of Meaux, had granted it a most generous privilege, as he openly declared was contained in that saint’s Life. The same abbot added that he had never, until that day, heard any mention of the aforesaid judgment which you had adduced on your side. [Col. 1195B] Yet, even if the judgment were genuine, it had nevertheless been silently departed from by a subsequent amicable settlement. For, as he said, the following settlement had been reached between B., abbot of Rebbais of blessed memory, and Stephen, bishop of Meaux: the abbot was to render him obedience on condition that, if the privilege of liberty which he did not have in hand were found, the abbot should enjoy liberty and should not be bound to render obedience to the bishop. The abbot asserted that he would prove that settlement and certain other matters which he had alleged.

When a day had accordingly been assigned at Paris, the dean and subcantor received the witnesses of the aforesaid abbot, [Col. 1195C] because the third judge could not be present; and, examining them at Rebbais, they received there certain other elderly and infirm witnesses. Finally, when your party had presented to the judges letters of certain cardinals and others in order to provide greater proof concerning Alexander’s judgment, the abbot’s party objected that, since our letters fixed a six-month period within which you had had the opportunity to prove what you wished, after that time had elapsed you could not submit documents or other proofs on your behalf. But, because the way to proof had not there been barred, it asked that an oath be received, which the chapter of Rebbais directed to be made at peril of their souls: namely, that they had never seen any judgment other than that [Col. 1195D] which you had produced.

Since the judges were unwilling to determine the dispute, they remitted the fully prepared case, with the procurators of the parties, to our presence. We subsequently appointed our beloved son John, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata, as auditor. When the parties had set forth these and other matters fully before him, and the same cardinal had faithfully reported to us what he had heard, we, having carefully examined the arguments of both parties and found yours the stronger, adjudged to you the subjection of the said monastery, so that you may exercise free authority there as diocesan bishop. This is, however, without prejudice to the Apostolic See, which may, at a lawful time, if it wishes, pursue its own right.

[Col. 1196A] Certainly, if the privilege of the aforesaid Innocent was presented to Alexander in the litigation and he gave judgment against it, he must be understood to have rejected it. But if it was not produced before him, the aforesaid judgment ought not to be reconsidered on the pretext of a privilege newly found.

Given at Viterbo, 15 June, in the tenth year.

There is also in the cartulary of the Church of Meaux a letter of Innocent to the bishop, dean, and chancellor of Paris for execution of the preceding judgment, copied word for word from that addressed to the bishop of Meaux, with the necessary changes. At the end of that letter the following is added:

Accordingly, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that you cause what has been judicially determined by us to be observed inviolably, appeal [Col. 1196B] removed, restraining any opponents or rebels, if there be any, by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. If not all of you can be present to carry this out, you, brother bishop, shall nevertheless carry it out with one of the others.

Given as in the other letter. This commission exists in part in the chapter *Suborta*, *On Judgments and Things Adjudged*.

XCVII. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT SAVIOUR AND SAINT ROTRUDE, SITUATED IN THE PARISH OF THÉROUANNE. Concerning the election of an abbot. (At Viterbo, 3 July.)

Since, by a privilege of Alexander, [Col. 1196C] pope of happy memory, our predecessor, which was presented to us and examined, your monastery has been granted that, upon the death of its abbot, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of fraud or violence except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall judge fit to elect according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, we strictly forbid by the authority of these presents that anyone presume rashly to attack or harass you concerning that grant. Rather, it shall be lawful for you and your successors, now and henceforth, whenever your church happens to be vacant of an abbot, to appoint by regular election a suitable person from among yourselves or elsewhere as your pastor, humbly [Col. 1196D] to be presented to the monastery of Karrofiensis, that he may receive confirmation from it and render it the reverence due.

Let no one therefore … our prohibition and grant, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 3 July, in the tenth year.

XCVIII. TO WIBERT, PRIEST. The institution made for him by the legate to a canonry and prebend of Saint Sophia is confirmed. (At Montefiascone, 29 July.)

To the just petitions, etc., down to “bring to completion.” Since, therefore, our beloved son B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna and legate of the Apostolic See, has appointed you a canon in the Church of Saint Sophia, we, yielding to your prayers, ratify and confirm by apostolic authority that appointment, as [Col. 1197A] canonically made, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

Let no one therefore … our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Montefiascone, 29 July, in the tenth year.

XCIX. TO THE SAME PERSON. A grant of the provostship of Saint Anastasia made for him by the legate is confirmed. (Given as in the other letter.)

When a request is made to us, etc., down to “be brought to effect.” Since, therefore, our beloved son P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, has granted you the provostship of the church of Saint Anastasia, [Col. 1197B] we, yielding to your prayers, ratify and confirm by apostolic authority that grant, as canonically made, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

Let no one therefore … our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

C. TO THE ARCHBISHOP, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, AND TO …, ARCHDEACON OF MILAN. That they should grant …, priest, permission to return to his church of Saint Michael at Vercelli. (At Montefiascone, 2 August.)

Our venerable brother …, bishop of Ypres, informed us by his letters that, formerly, before he had [Col. 1197C] been consecrated bishop of Ypres, when he had taken wings to fly into solitude, a certain priest, who then governed the Church of Saint Michael at Vercelli, desiring to live with him in the wilderness, came to him with letters from our venerable brother …, bishop of Vercelli, humbly and devoutly entreating that he might deign to receive him to live with him as a servant and attendant. Yielding to his petitions and moved by the prayers of the said bishop of Vercelli, he satisfied his desire in this matter.

It happened, however, that while the same priest was arranging to have a certain cloak made, others gathered in the same place advised him to make it a cowl, asserting that it would be more suitable for the service of the altar, [Col. 1197D] more convenient for writing, and also better adapted for labour and the other things which he needed to do. Yielding to their advice, he allowed a cowl to be made for him. When the same bishop wished to bless it according to custom, the said priest replied: “I do not wish to become a monk, nor do I receive the cowl as a cowl in name. I do not yet intend to bind myself by any vow, order, or profession. If you remain here, I shall be with you; otherwise I shall not remain in the wilderness.” [Col. 1198A]

A short time later, when the same bishop had returned by mandate of the Apostolic See to govern the Church of Ypres, the aforesaid priest followed him, declaring that he did not intend to return to the wilderness. He said: “Henceforth I am not bound to remain in the wilderness, because, when the cause ceases, the effect ought to cease. I came into the wilderness because of you. Since you are leaving, I shall remain no longer.” Though the bishop carefully sought to advise and persuade him either to remain in the solitude to which he had come or, if he preferred, to live familiarly with him, the priest, wavering greatly and uncertain, returned to the wilderness.

After he had remained there for some time, the neighbours of the aforesaid church, over which he had formerly presided and whom, as a provident pastor, he had nourished by word and example, with all their affection requested that their rector be restored to them. Thus, returning to the same city and staying there with the aforesaid bishop of Vercelli, he did not dare resume governance of the said church without special permission of the Apostolic See. Therefore, wishing to comply with the honourable wishes [Col. 1198B] of the neighbours, and desirous with paternal solicitude to provide for the welfare of that church—which is said to have greatly prospered under his rule both spiritually and temporally—we command you by apostolic writings that, if the foregoing is true, you grant the same priest by our authority permission to return to that church, so that through his diligence and upright conduct it may, by the Lord’s help, receive increase in temporal and spiritual things.

If not both of you … you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given at Montefiascone, 2 August, in the tenth year.

CI. TO THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF FLORENCE. They are urged to comply with the admonitions of the Apostolic See and its legate. (At Montefiascone, 4 August.)

[Col. 1198C]
