By the office of apostolic service, by which we are debtors to wise and foolish alike, and by the special favour which we bear toward your city, desiring with paternal solicitude to safeguard your interests in both spiritual and temporal matters, we have diligently endeavoured through our letters and those of our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Portico, to admonish your whole community: not to be exalted by victory, but rather, for God’s sake and in response to our admonitions, humbly and devoutly to return to the peace settlement which, before you had met in battle, you had concluded with the Sienese through our messenger.

But you, at the prompting of him who rules over the children of pride, whose constant concern is to obstruct the advance of peace, have hitherto passed over our admonitions and those of the said cardinal with a deaf ear, as we say with sorrow, having no due regard either for God or for us. You do not consider that Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and men, Man, in order to reconcile man to the Father—man who, by the devil’s prompting, had exalted himself against God into such pride that he had sought to usurp for himself the name of Deity, in accordance with the suggestion of the enemy of peace, “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3)—did not hesitate to be delivered into the hands of the guilty; and, upon the altar of the cross, catching before his eyes that apostate enemy of peace by means of the bait of his sacred body, [Col. 1199A] he shed his precious blood and offered himself to the Father as an unspotted sacrifice for the redemption of our souls.

Therefore turn back, dearest sons, turn back. Do not stop your ears against the voice of the cry of his vicar; give glory to God and humbly render your devotion to the Apostolic See. Otherwise—God forbid!—if you act thus and the said cardinal departs from you because you do not receive the word of peace, he may shake the dust of his feet over you in testimony; and what is subsequently written in the Gospel may follow: “It shall be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah than for that city” (Matt. 10).

Accordingly, by apostolic writings we strictly command your whole community, entreating you by the sprinkling [Col. 1199B] of the blood of Jesus Christ and by his coming, and imposing this upon you for the remission of your sins: humble yourselves beneath the mighty hand of the Lord, who resists the proud and bestows grace upon the humble; and comply altogether with our admonitions and counsels, as we have commanded you in other letters. For then you will know yourselves more truly victorious: when resisting carnal impulses, you yield in victory to God alone; for the wise man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than the conqueror of cities.

Given at Montefiascone, 4 August, in the tenth year.

CII. TO THE ABBESS AND CONVENT OF SAINT CIRIACUS AT GERONDOD. They are released from payment of an annual rent of one mark of silver. (At Montefiascone, 2 August.)

[Col. 1199C]

It has come to the knowledge of our apostolate that Otto, emperor of illustrious memory, confirmed by his privilege an annual rent of one mark of silver, payable by your monastery to the monastery of Saint Ciriacus at Rome. Furthermore, it has been established to us by letters of Emperor Frederick that this rent was paid by him to the said monastery for twenty years. But we, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide that your church may remain in its liberty, and with the consent of your representatives, have decided to add one mark to our own rent, completely releasing you from paying the said rent to the said monastery, because we shall ensure that the said monastery is satisfied.

[Col. 1199D] Given at Montefiascone, 2 August, in the tenth year.

CIII. TO R., ABBOT OF MONTE CASSINO. He states that he does not wish to answer his letters. (At Viterbo, 9 August.)

We have received your letters and have carefully noted what they contained. But we have not thought it proper to answer concerning the matters on which you wished to consult us, because that consultation contains a dispute of the Church of Monte Cassino, which is known to be under litigation between you and your men before a judicial tribunal. It could therefore more properly have been explained to us by the judges themselves.

Given at Viterbo, 9 August, in the tenth year.

CIV. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF VITERBO. That they must not allow the girl of Malfita to be harassed by anyone concerning her legitimacy. (At Montefiascone, 3 August.)

[Col. 1200A]

You should know that it has come to our attention that Thol., son of the late Girardus Manitutis, carnally knew a woman of Malfita and that, after a daughter had eventually been born of her, he subsequently married that woman. But because certain persons assert that the girl is illegitimate, the same T. humbly petitioned us to provide paternal protection for the girl in this matter. Since, according to canonical enactments, offspring first conceived in natural concubinage ought, by favour of a subsequent marriage, to be considered legitimate, [Col. 1200B] we command your whole community by apostolic writings that, if this is so, you shall not allow the aforesaid girl to be harassed by anyone concerning her legitimacy.

Given at Montefiascone, 3 August, in the tenth year.

CV. TO THE CONSULS OF VITERBO. (At Viterbo, 12 August.)

Since we have decreed that the property of the Paterines be confiscated, lest anyone seek fraudulently to retain it under the pretext of a deposit, we grant you by the authority of these presents that, wherever you find property of this kind, whether in Viterbo or its district, you may seize it and punish those who possess it, as may be expedient, by an arbitrary penalty. In order that you may carry this out more freely, we firmly forbid future consuls to presume rashly to harass you under pretext of this execution.

Let no one therefore … our grant and prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 12 August, in the tenth year.

CVI. TO ADELL., ABBESS OF SAINT MARY, MOTHER OF GOD AND EVER-VIRGIN, AND OF SAINT PETER, PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES, AND OF SAINT CIRIACUS, MARTYR, AT GERONDOD, AND TO HER SISTERS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. Their liberties and immunities are confirmed, and certain privileges are granted them. (At Viterbo, 9 August.)

Prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion, [Col. 1200D] with lamps kept burning, continually prepare themselves by works of holiness to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, ought to receive the Apostolic See’s protection, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery at Gerondod, which is known to have been built upon the estate of blessed Peter—an estate which G., margrave of good memory, offered with its entire ownership to the Roman Church out of piety—and in which you are devoted to divine service; this we do after the example of John and Leo, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, together with the ministering clerics [Col. 1201A] and all things belonging to that monastery.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that monastery according to God shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances [Col. 1201B]; the church at Forense, with its chapels; the monastery at Frose, with that village itself and two parishes situated in it; Greater and Lesser Aslevesen, with a chapel and two parishes; Egelen, with the abbess’s chapel and three other churches; Waledalen, with the abbess’s chapel and parish; Padeburnen, with two churches; Hetteborn, with a parish; the four villages called Polege, with a church; Nacterstede, with a church; Jezere, with a church; Strenze, with a church; Drogebulen, with a church; Bernezingerot and Ethelbelingerot, with a church; at Behem, Wellebeke, Genezendorop, Baleberge, Benendorp, Analaborc, and Hachebornen, twenty-five *mansi*; at Henrikestorp, twenty-seven *mansi*; at Plezege, seven *mansi*; at Alkendorp, twelve [Col. 1201C] *mansi*; in western Hegelen, thirty *mansi*; at Grovingen, thirty-three *mansi*; at Blekentorp, thirty-seven *mansi*, with a parish; at Ammendorp, three *mansi*; at Hergetstede and Werstherhusen, sixteen *mansi*; at Remestorp, seventeen and a half *mansi*, with a market and twenty holdings belonging to the market, with a church; at Wallenthorp, four *mansi*; at Mulendorp, six *mansi*; at Cumelez, ten *mansi*; at Nientorp, six *mansi*; at Asmerleve, twenty-two *mansi*, with a church; at Zorchewist, eight *mansi*; at Storniz, twenty-two *mansi*; at Drosege, thirteen *mansi*; at Chocstede, two *mansi*; at Sinselve, two *mansi*; at Wederstede, half a *mansus*; at Winnige, two *mansi*; [Col. 1201D] at Wicsedherothe, nine *mansi*; at Hachemerslephe, eighteen *mansi*; at Gaterslephe, three *mansi*; at Welpeslephe, three *mansi*; at Wedestorp, one *mansus*; at Daldorp, six *mansi*; at Remstede, one *mansus*; at Wipere, one *mansus*; at Avensleve, two *mansi*; at Rodolvesbure, two *mansi*; at Sulthen, two *mansi*; at Retmersleve, twenty *mansi*; at Menstede, two *mansi*; at Scolene, one *mansus*; at Burgewiz, two *mansi*; at Leveze, two *mansi*; at Lere, one *mansus*; at Thederzengeroth, one *mansus*; at Wendelmeresbroche, two *mansi*; at Mandorp, one *mansus*; at Cephen, two *mansi*; and at Abberoth, one *mansus*.

Moreover, no one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes of your newly cultivated land (*novalia*), which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens and shrubberies, [Col. 1202A] your fisheries, or the increase of your animals. In addition, we forbid archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches to impose new and unlawful exactions upon that church. Following in the footsteps of the aforesaid predecessors of ours, we forbid every priest of any church, except the Apostolic See, to exercise any jurisdiction in your monastery.

Furthermore, by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, we forbid any king, duke, margrave, count, or other secular person to have permission to give the monastery itself to any persons as a benefice, so that, as it stands subject to the Apostolic See with the security of privilege, it may remain endowed without disturbance [Col. 1202B] and may enjoy, with perpetual security and without objection by any person, its places and property—both those which it now holds or possesses and those which divine mercy may hereafter add to the rights of that monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful.

Upon the death of you, the present abbess of the same place, or of any woman who succeeds you, no one shall be placed over it through any stratagem of usurpation or violence, except one whom the sisters, by common consent—or the sounder part of their counsel—shall determine ought to be chosen, according to the fear of God and canonical decrees. We also hold valid the ancient liberties and immunities and reasonable customs granted to your monastery and hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. [Col. 1202C]

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid any public judge or anyone exercising judicial power to dare enter the places of the aforesaid monastery to hear lawsuits; to exact *freda* [judicial fines], tribute, or any imposts; to require lodgings or provisions to be supplied; to take sureties; to constrain the men of that church; to demand tolls or palfreys from its men; to summon those men, whether serfs or free, to a judicial assembly (*mallum*); or to exercise any authority—except the advocate whom the abbess of that place, with the common consent of her sisters, shall choose for this purpose. As a token of the liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors each year two and a half marks of pure silver. [Col. 1202D]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved entire, and shall in every way benefit those for whose governance and support they were granted. The authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of diocesan bishops in non-exempt churches being reserved. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, etc., let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, etc., unto the end. Amen.

Given at Viterbo, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, [Col. 1203A] chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of August, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CVII. TO THE ABBOT OF MALLEON. A. de Scobol is ordered to be compelled to return to his first wife. (Viterbo, fourteenth day before the Kalends of September.)

You represented before us that A. de Scobol had married . . . a woman and had lived with her for a long time, but had not carnally known her. Therefore W., bishop of Poitiers of good memory, having been fully satisfied concerning the man’s impotence by the confession both of the man himself and of the woman, pronounced a divorce between them. [Col. 1203B] But afterwards the aforesaid woman married another, and the said A. took another wife, whom he knew by carnal intercourse. You therefore asked that the Apostolic See explain whether the said man ought to return to the first woman or should rather remain with the second. We answer your inquiry as follows: since subsequent events show that the aforesaid bishop was deceived, the said A. must be compelled to return to the first woman.

Given at Viterbo, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year.

CVIII. TO THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF RESBACH. [Note: [Col. 1203D] See above, Letter 96.] Their privileges and all liberties and immunities are confirmed. (Viterbo, seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.)

[Col. 1203C]

Although your monastery seemed to enjoy the prerogative of full liberty through a privilege of Pope Innocent, our predecessor of happy memory, nevertheless, when afterwards a disputed question arose between the bishop of Meaux of good memory and that monastery concerning the latter’s subjection, Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, before whom the case had been brought, understood the merits of the case and adjudged episcopal right in your monastery to the bishop of Meaux. Afterwards, too, the subject matter of the same dispute having been raised before us, we caused the case to be diligently examined by our beloved sons, the dean of Soissons, H., cantor of Reims, and the subchanter [Col. 1203D] of Senlis. When they had sent the same case back to us with sufficient documentation, we, having understood the arguments of both sides, and recognizing the arguments of the bishop of Meaux to be stronger, took care to adjudge the subjection of your monastery to him, so that he may exercise free authority there as diocesan bishop. Yet this is without prejudice to the Apostolic See, so that it may, at the proper time, pursue its right if it wishes.

But since the possessions and other goods of the said monastery were confirmed to that monastery by Innocent’s privilege, we, following in the footsteps of that predecessor [Col. 1204A] of ours, apostolically confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery those things which you justly and peaceably possess, and strengthen them by the privilege of this present writing. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the borough of that monastery, called Resbach, with all its appurtenances, churches and tithes, male and female serfs, meadows and pastures, the water called Mucra and all fishing rights, islands and mills, fisheries, bridges and every crossing over that water, and all adjoining cultivated and uncultivated land; the village of Orlei and the village of Montbotr., with the churches, tithes, male and female serfs, meadows and pastures of those villages, and all land adjoining them, [Col. 1204B] cultivated and uncultivated; the village called Ultiacus and the village called Septemsortes, with the churches, tithes, male and female serfs, meadows and pastures of those villages, and their cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; half the port of Fai; the village called Brigein, with the mother church and the tithes belonging to it, male and female serfs, meadows and pastures, and other adjoining cultivated and uncultivated land; the village called Montinicus, with church and tithe, its adjoining meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands; the village called Capella upon the Mucra, the village called Curmajot on the same bank, the village called Malerei on the same bank, and the village called Veretum on the same bank, with the churches, tithes, male and female serfs, mills, fisheries, meadows, pastures, and all cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances of those villages; [Col. 1204C] the village called Campuscoellus, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and all cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; half the village called Saint Peter’s Wood, with its cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; the village called Meri, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, fisheries, and all its cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; the island called Belluslocus, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, fisheries, and all its cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; the village called Herbitia, with church, tithe, [Col. 1204D] male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and its adjoining cultivated and uncultivated land; the village called Agili Mansio, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and its adjoining cultivated and uncultivated land; the tithe of the village called Semonnia, with appurtenant land and male and female serfs; the land and tithe of the village called Saint-Lupus, with male and female serfs; the village called Luqueius on the bank of the river Materne, with male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and its cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; on the same bank, the property called Porterum, another called Vernolium, and a third called Capella, with male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and other appurtenances [Col. 1205A] cultivated and uncultivated; near the castle called Brejas, the village called Bruceium, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and other cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; at another Bruceium, the land-tax and rent, with male and female serfs; near the castle called Mons-mirellus, the village called Marcungia, with male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and other cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances.

We furthermore forbid the bishop of Meaux, on the pretext of the aforesaid judgment issued by us, to burden or harass you or your monastery unlawfully, because he who abuses a power permitted to him deserves to lose his privilege. Therefore let no person whatsoever violate this page of our confirmation and prohibition, or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1205B]

Given at Viterbo, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year.

CIX. TO ALL ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SAXONY. Concerning the privileges of the monastery at Gerondod. (Viterbo, eighth day before the Kalends of September.)

Since, by the duty of service entrusted to us, we are bound to provide every church with its due right, and since we have a proper regard for the church of Saint Cyriacus at Gerondod, [Col. 1205C] we have thought fit, with paternal solicitude, to make special provision for its tranquillity and peace. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, if our venerable brother . . ., bishop of Halberstadt, in whose diocese that church is situated, when requested by the beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and sisters of that church, refuses to administer chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, the ordination of clerics to be promoted to holy orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments—since that monastery belongs to the Roman Church without any intermediary—you shall provide these things to them freely and without any improper demand. Furthermore, we will and command that, whenever they bring you a complaint concerning their wrongdoers who are your parishioners, [Col. 1205D] you shall do them full justice against such persons, with all obstacle of appeal removed.

Given at Viterbo, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year.

CX. TO THE BISHOP OF ZARAGOZA. A declaration of what is meant by the term *novale*. (Viterbo, eleventh day before the Kalends of September.)

[Note: [Col. 1205] Chapter “Quid per novalis,” *On the Meaning of Words*. See Regino, book I, chapter 44.] Your brotherhood asked us what ought to be understood by the word *novale*. Some have said that a *novale* is land that has been ploughed up and lies fallow for a year; others maintain that it is land brought under cultivation from woodland after the trees have been uprooted. Both interpretations are derived from the civil laws. Yet we answer your inquiry as follows: we believe that the intention of our predecessors, when they granted to pious places an exemption concerning *novalia*, was that they understood a *novale* to be a field newly brought under cultivation, concerning which there is no memory that it had ever previously been cultivated. But we do not believe that the exemption was granted to them in respect of every such field, but only of one whose tithes a religious community can retain without grave loss to the parish church, since land is often uncultivated while the parish church receives large revenues from it by reason of tithes. [Col. 1206A]

[Col. 1206B] Given at Viterbo, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year.

CXI. TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX AND PETER OF CASTELNAU, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. To whom the lordship of the city of Marseille belongs. (Viterbo, twelfth day before the Kalends of September.)

As you have learned, the venerable brother, the archbishop of Arles, together with many bishops, reported to our hearing that, when the citizens of Marseille had entered into a league of peace with them, a grave complaint was made against them on behalf of our beloved son, the nobleman Hugh of Baux. B., formerly lord of Marseille, had entered upon the way of all flesh; and although the city of Marseille was known to belong by hereditary right to the noblewoman [Col. 1206C] B., his daughter, those citizens, having dragged Roncelin, the brother of the said deceased—an elected abbot, monk, and subdeacon—from the monastery in a popular tumult and torn his habit, set him up, with his consent and willingness, as their own lord and lord of the said city. This was not without great offence against the divine majesty and serious prejudice to the aforesaid noblewoman.

Accordingly, the said Hugh of Baux, who lawfully married the aforesaid noblewoman and had issue by her, together with his brother, the nobleman W. of Baux, prince of Orange, humbly petitioned the aforesaid bishops and us that, since they are faithful and devoted to the Church and strive vigorously and powerfully for the advancement of peace in accordance with our command, the Church might deign to assist Hugh in obtaining his wife’s inheritance. Since the Apostolic See ought to oppose the presumptions of evildoers and restrain their excesses through pastoral solicitude, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that you compel the said citizens—as justice requires, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed—by sentences of excommunication and interdict upon the city [Col. 1207A] and the land subject to its lordship, utterly to remove from his lordship the said Roncelin, an excommunicate, apostate, and perjurer, who occupies and holds it in contempt of God and to the reproach of the Christian faith, contrary to his own oath; and to restore the inheritance, as they are bound to do, to the aforesaid noblewoman. You shall take particular care that these sentences be observed inviolate in the monastery of Saint Victor, with appeal set aside.

Given at Viterbo, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year.

CXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COSENZA AND THE BISHOP OF MARTURANO. Concerning protection of the bishop of Mileto against Count Amfusus. (Viterbo, eighth day before the Kalends of September.)

Iniquity sitting upon a talent of lead has so miserably cast down certain persons burdened by the perversity of malice into the depths [Col. 1207B] of vice that, rejoicing when they have done evil and exulting in the worst deeds, they have through a habit of wrongdoing reached such contempt for grave transgression that, although by their manifold offences they not undeservedly provoke God’s wrath against themselves, yet, given over to a reprobate mind, they do not fear to stretch out their hands against churches and churchmen, presumptuously invading their goods and delivering them up to plunder and spoil.

We had indeed believed that affliction would have given understanding to the hearing, and that the sting of long tribulation would have taught the nobles of the kingdom of Sicily to walk in the path of justice. But, to our sorrow, some of them seem to have hardened amid the hammers of the scourges, since they abstain from unlawful acts all the less as the severity of persecution grows stronger. As our venerable brother P., bishop of Mileto, grievously complained before us, while the Church of Mileto was vacant, the noble Count Amfusus fraudulently seized its tower, in which the bells had customarily stood, and assigned it to his brother Count R. The latter, harassing both the bishop himself and his church with intolerable oppression, occupied the episcopal houses and also those of the canons and clerics of Mileto, retaining them for his own use and that of his followers less honorably than was fitting. [Col. 1207C]

Moreover, he seizes the bishop’s and the church’s wheat, wine, barley, and other goods, squanders and consumes them according to his own will, and does not cease to harass the men of the same church with unlawful forced services and various burdens. Furthermore, he often arrests the canons and clerics of Mileto without reasonable cause: he despoils some of their own goods and keeps others in prison custody for so long that he brings them to an almost intolerable ransom. The same Count R., having newly built a certain castle and being unable to induce the men of the Church to live there, devastated the hamlet of Karna, which belongs to that church, expelling those men from their own places. Count Amfusus likewise, when he occupied the aforesaid tower and church, violently took money, riding-horses, wheat, wine, barley, and several other things, for which he subsequently made no satisfaction at all. In these and many other ways the same counts [Col. 1208A] persecute and oppress the said bishop so severely that he has been forced to abandon his church.

Since we are unwilling, because we cannot, to pass over these and the other grievances which the bishop laid before us by dissimulation, we strictly command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, having made a full inquiry into the foregoing and learned the truth, you carefully admonish and effectively induce the aforesaid counts to restore without any difficulty to the bishop—as they are bound to do—the episcopal houses, those of the canons and clerics, the aforesaid tower, and the other things known to have been taken; to allow him peaceably to possess them; and to make him fitting satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted. Otherwise, by our authority, declare them bound by the chain of excommunication throughout all Calabria and Sicily, and subject all their land to ecclesiastical interdict. Cause both the sentence of excommunication and that of interdict, with all obstacle of appeal removed, to be observed inviolate until due satisfaction is made. [Col. 1208B] We further will and command that you endeavor to declare generally that, in whatever land those counts may meanwhile come, divine offices shall by no means be celebrated in their presence. If not both . . . one of you, etc.

Given at Viterbo, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year.

CXIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF LONDON, ELY, AND WORCESTER. Concerning the case of the archbishop of Canterbury against the king of England. (Given as in another letter.)

[Col. 1208C]

We call upon the testimony of Him who is the faithful witness in heaven: we have always loved our dearest son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of the English, with the most sincere charity. Indeed, the fullness of our favor toward him has so overflowed that very many princes have become not only less fervent in devotion to the most holy Roman Church, but some even undevoted. For whenever the crash of turmoil has threatened him or his kingdom, the Apostolic See, bearing tender compassion toward him, has powerfully aided him and relieved him, to the envy of many, from many distresses.

But, to our sorrow, he makes himself so ungrateful for our favor that we seem not to have drawn him by benefits, but rather provoked him by injuries. Opposing our dispositions—indeed, God’s—he does not fear, led by unsound counsel, to undertake things that may result in grave peril to himself. What those things are, we do not think need to be stated, since they are better known to you than to us. Yet although we regard that king’s devotion as very necessary to us, he can and ought to judge our favor toward him no less—indeed, perhaps far more—necessary to him, as he has already perceived more clearly if he remembers well. But, forgetful of all this, he strives not merely to impede but even to nullify our jurisdiction, although we have never sought to diminish his, but have always labored [Col. 1209A] to defend it.

He ought rather to consider that those princes who, by attacking ecclesiastical liberty, have attempted unlawfully to seize power over churches for themselves have almost utterly perished by divine judgment; while those who cherish Holy Church in her liberty and honor her as she deserves always prosper from good to better. Moreover, he does not consider to what end this persecution he has begun can lead; for if he prudently considered its end, he would undoubtedly desist from what he has begun. For, apart from offending God, unless he comes to his senses very soon, he will incur a grave loss, because it is hard for him to kick against the goad.

Far be it that, in so unjust a design, the English people—who are truly Christian and zealous for the orthodox faith—should follow an earthly king against the heavenly King, preferring temporal things to spiritual, since not only the clergy but also the laity possess such discernment and devotion that they know and wish to distinguish between what must be rendered to Caesar and what must be rendered to God. Since, therefore, we scarcely believe that a more useful provision can at this time be made alike for the king’s honor and salvation than that the Church of Canterbury should have a bishop distinguished in reputation, learning, and life, able by teaching and example to move him toward the things of God and, united to him in all the affection of his mind, provide him sound counsel concerning spiritual and temporal advantage; and since we know these qualities to be present in our venerable brother S., archbishop of Canterbury and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church—[Note: [Col. 1209D] See Matthew Paris under the years 1207 and 1208.]—although it was most painful to us [Col. 1209C] to separate him from our side, since he had hitherto almost jointly governed the universal Church with us, we nevertheless consecrated with our own hands this archbishop, canonically requested and elected by the convent of the Church of Canterbury. In accordance with the call made upon him, we appointed him over the metropolitan see of Canterbury in particular; and, having bestowed upon him the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, that is, the distinguished sign of the fullness of the pontifical office, we sent him to govern the church entrusted to him.

Therefore, although, to speak in the testimony of God, we love the king most sincerely and desire to show due regard for his honor, nevertheless, because it is fitting that we show greater regard to God than to men, and because there must be no respect of persons or partiality in the execution of justice, we carefully admonish and exhort your brotherhood, strictly commanding you by apostolic letters that, bearing diligently in mind the saying of the Wise Man, “Those who rebuke shall be praised, and blessing shall come upon them,” clothed with power from on high and taking up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, you approach the king together. Reverently exhort him as king in a spirit of liberty, and diligently persuade him as a son, so that, providing for the salvation of souls, peace for the peoples, honor for God, and [Col. 1210A] liberty for the Church, he may yield to sound counsels. Let him render due reverence and fitting honor to the aforesaid archbishop—whom we know to be faithful and devoted to him, whatever hostile slander may have been suggested against him—and recognize that this deed is from God rather than from man; let him consent with ready favor to the divine disposition, so that the archbishop, adhering to him in sincere devotion, may effectively perform his office toward the flock entrusted to him by the Lord.

Otherwise, setting aside all worldly fear and removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, pronounce throughout all England a general sentence of interdict, permitting no ecclesiastical office whatsoever to be celebrated there, except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying. You yourselves shall observe it fully and cause it to be observed inviolate by all through ecclesiastical censure. Know with certainty that, if any should perhaps—though we do not believe it—presume in a stubborn spirit to oppose this, we shall take care so to correct their presumption that, with terror transmitted to posterity, such insolence will not pass into precedent, but their correction will be able to terrify all. [Col. 1210B] If not even thus does affliction give the king understanding, since a father corrects the son whom he loves, and God rebukes and chastens those whom He loves, we shall take care to lay our hands more heavily upon him, so that, at last healed by a healing hand, he may rise to offer us thanks.

But let him despise as flatterers and expel as corrupters those who anoint his head with the oil of the sinner, encouraging him in evil. We too, who are not wholly ignorant of the corrupt practices of such persons, shall, with the Lord as author, take care to repay them according to their deserts. Therefore, take care to conduct yourselves in executing this command in such a way that you may be proved to fear God more than man; and do not be among those who are mute dogs, unable to bark. If not all . . . two of you, etc. [Col. 1210C]

Given as in another letter.

CXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF GENOA. A case of divorce on account of adultery is committed to him. (Viterbo, Kalends of September.)

[Note: [Col. 1210D] Chapter “Quemadmodum,” *On Oaths*.] Just as, if a man had sworn to a woman, when he contracted marriage with her, that he would always hold her as his lawful wife, he could not indeed dismiss her because of fornication she had committed previously; but he could dismiss her because of fornication committed afterwards, notwithstanding such an oath, since this condition must be understood in it: namely, that she should not sin against the law of marriage. So likewise, if someone swore that he would take a woman as wife, he certainly cannot allege against her fornication that preceded the oath; but he can allege subsequent fornication, so as not to take her in marriage. For this condition must be understood in that oath: namely, that she should not transgress against the rule of betrothal. [Col. 1211A]

Otherwise, if after such an oath she became a public prostitute, he would be bound to take her as his wife—which is wholly absurd. For if, after marriage has been contracted, a husband may lawfully dismiss his wife from cohabitation because of fornication, much more may a betrothed man lawfully refuse to admit his betrothed woman to cohabitation before the marriage is celebrated for the same reason. A guest is more disgracefully expelled than not admitted, notwithstanding the bond of an oath in either case; and because of the condition understood, that oath is such that the person who swore it may, without transgression, act in either way.

If, after such an oath, the woman were to become not only leprous but also paralytic, or lose her eyes or nose, or suffer anything more disfiguring, would the man be bound to take her as wife? Certainly, he could not dismiss her once married. [Note: [Col. 1211D] In the third collection: “once taken [in marriage].”] But would he not be bound to admit her if she had not been taken in marriage, even though what prevents contracting a marriage does not sometimes dissolve one already contracted?

But that oath is undoubtedly rash if a man swears to his wife that he will accuse her of no crime. For if the woman became an unbeliever and refused to live with her husband without insulting the Creator, or if she sought to draw him into the error of unbelief, the husband would unquestionably have to prosecute her before his judge, so that, unless she wholly came to her senses, he might altogether dismiss her according to canonical decrees. If he expressly swore that he would not prosecute her for adultery, should such an oath be observed, [Col. 1211C] when Scripture testifies that he is a protector of shamefulness who conceals his wife’s crime? And according to the rule of the Gospel, if, after a first and second correction, she refused to repent, the matter should be reported to the Church, so that she might thereafter be avoided as a heathen and a publican, and lest she be given free opportunity to sin through impunity.

But may not a husband forgive her when she sins against him, not only seven times but even seventy times seven, according to Gospel truth? In this case, therefore, it seems safer for the husband, because of the sacred obligation of the oath, to refrain from accusing his wife in order to procure a divorce, although he may report her so that she may perform penance. Having thus weighed the tenor of this response, proceed in the case concerning which you decided to consult us. [Col. 1211D]

Given at Viterbo, on the Kalends of September, in the tenth year.

CXV. TO THE CHAPTER OF THE CHURCH OF RAVENNA. That they should provide their archbishop with certain pontifical vestments. (Viterbo.)

To such necessity, as we have learned with sorrow, has your Church been reduced that, besides its other great and grave hardships, even its pontifical ornaments have been pledged, so that our venerable brother, your archbishop, has nothing with which he can fittingly celebrate the pontifical office. [Col. 1212A] Therefore, compassionating his need with paternal affection, we have ordered pontifical vestments to be made, in order that his want may be supplied from our abundance: namely, a tunic, dalmatic, and chasuble of the finest red samite, suitably adorned with embroidered bands and gold fringe. We grant both these and an amice, alb, stole, girdle, and maniple to the same archbishop and, through him, to the Church of Ravenna, under threat of anathema forbidding anyone to presume in any manner to alienate them; rather, by ordinance of the Apostolic See, they are always to remain in the right of the Church of Ravenna for the use of the archbishop who shall be in office at the time. Therefore let no one infringe this page of our donation, prohibition, and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

[Col. 1212B] Given at Viterbo.

CXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. Concerning the controversy between the Church of Ravenna and the commune of Faenza. (Viterbo, 1 September.)

[Note: [Col. 1212D] Chapter *Licet causam*, On proofs.] Although we have often committed to different judges the case which was pending between you and your Church on the one hand and our beloved sons, the commune of Faenza, on the other, concerning jurisdiction, honour, and district in the village of Lucius of Saint Peter and the castle of Ariolo, which were said by right to belong to your Church, nevertheless, since no useful progress was made in the matter by some of those judges, we finally instructed the parties [Col. 1212C] to present themselves before us concerning that case.

When their procurators, furnished with instruments of ratification, had subsequently appeared in our presence, and there had for some time been argument before us concerning certain objections, the steward [*iconomus*, perhaps *oeconomus*] of your Church finally set forth as follows: since complete jurisdiction, honour, and district, together with certain other matters pertaining to these, belong to the Church aforesaid in the said places, and since that Church had long possessed them in full and peaceful quasi-possession, the commune of Faenza was unjustly troubling it concerning the foregoing matters. It compelled the inhabitants of the said places to render it dues in levies, military service, riding expeditions, labour-services, bans and pleas, forced carriage-service and provisioning-service, and to establish residences for themselves in the city of Faenza. [Col. 1212D] The same steward therefore requested that we, by apostolic authority, restrain the people of Faenza from such unlawful disturbance and molestation.

In reply to this petition, the syndic of the commune of Faenza answered; and, after the questions and answers had been reduced to writing, we caused the oath against calumny to be sworn by both sides. But because it was highly burdensome for either party to produce witnesses before us, we commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Piacenza, that, within three months after receiving our letters, he should receive, without appeal, the witnesses whom either party chose to produce, both upon the principal matter and [Col. 1213A] against the persons of the witnesses. He was not to permit either side, after restraining the unbridled multitude of witnesses, to exceed in any respect the number of forty witnesses; he was prudently to examine them, diligently inquire into all circumstances, and faithfully transmit their depositions to us sealed under his seal. He was to enjoin the parties to come before us thus instructed, so that, after the depositions had been published and the instruments produced, they might obtain from us, with the Lord as author, a just sentence.

The said bishop received from each party witnesses according to the number fixed in our letters. Thereafter the procurators of both parties returned to our presence with the sealed depositions. [Col. 1213B] When the depositions had been solemnly published, the syndic of the people of Faenza declared that he wished to object to and prove certain matters against the persons of the witnesses produced by the other side. The steward of the Church maintained that this ought not to be allowed. After argument on both sides for some time, we finally decreed interlocutorily that he was in no way to be heard on this point, since he had neglected to produce such witnesses within the three-month period contained in our letters, within which alone either party could bring forward witnesses both against the persons of witnesses and upon the principal matter.

Thereupon the same syndic objected against the aforesaid witnesses that, having been corrupted, they had given false testimony, and requested leave to prove the charge of falsehood. Since such an objection may be raised, according to legal enactments, not only before but also after judgment, [Col. 1213C] although some believed that the Faentine party had advanced this objection from contrived malice in order to obstruct the course of the case, nevertheless, because we do not wish to depart from the path of law, we commanded by our letters our beloved sons Masters C. and G., residing at Bologna, to summon the parties and, within a month, receive and examine the witnesses whom the procurator of the people of Faenza chose to produce upon this objection. They were to inquire closely into every circumstance and faithfully reduce their depositions to writing. We then granted another month to the procurator of the aforesaid Church, within which, if he wished, he might produce witnesses before them to disprove those witnesses. [Col. 1213D] Having faithfully recorded their statements, they were to assign both parties a period of twenty days within which to appear before us with the said depositions, to receive judgment.

When the parties again appeared before us and these depositions had been published, we heard everything they wished to submit. Although the Faentine party produced many witnesses upon the principal matter to prove that the inhabitants of the aforesaid places had, from times long past, rendered them services in bans and pleas, ditches, levies, and riding expeditions, and in certain other matters pertaining to district, nevertheless scarcely six of these witnesses remained credible, since many others contradicted themselves in the course of their testimony [Col. 1214A] and certain others were isolated in their testimony. To disprove certain witnesses of your Church, moreover, though some witnesses were introduced by the Faentine party, most of them are rather themselves disqualified, because they contradict one another most plainly. Others, few in number, though not expressly disqualified, are nevertheless of such bad reputation and slight credit, as has been proved by the depositions produced, that no faith, or very little, should be placed in what they say.

The same Faentine witnesses are also rejected generally because they do not prove that which their syndic undertook to prove, namely, that the witnesses, having been corrupted, had spoken falsely. For, although they seem to say something about corruption, they say absolutely nothing about falsehood. By many witnesses of your Church, beyond every objection, it has been plainly proved [Col. 1214B] that your Church possessed the village of Lucius of Saint Peter and the castle of Ariolo for a very long time, with every honour, district, and jurisdiction, all the articles expressing jurisdiction, honour, and district being expressly named.

From the foregoing it therefore appears sufficiently clearly that your Church, through witnesses greater in number, with whom the light of truth more fully abides, and who in their testimony expressed matters more suitable to the case and nearer to the truth, has sufficiently shown that it possessed the aforesaid places with every jurisdiction, honour, and district during the last sixty years. It follows that, even if the commune of Faenza received certain [Col. 1214C] services in the aforesaid places during the last fifty years, as their witnesses seem to depose, they undoubtedly began to receive them without a just title; for two persons cannot simultaneously possess the same thing, in the same manner, as a whole. This is especially so since those of Faenza show no just title of possession and since, from privileges granted to your Church by emperors and Roman pontiffs, it is most clearly gathered that the Church’s possession in the aforesaid places was just.

Since, therefore, it is established that, from the time from which the Faentines attempt to prove that they possessed, they unjustly and without title rashly occupied certain things in the aforesaid places and in the course of time extorted them by violence—as is plainly proved by many witnesses of your Church—and since the steward [Col. 1214D] of that Church requested before us that the commune of Faenza be prohibited from disturbing or unsettling violence in the foregoing matters, we recognize that in this case there is no place for the interdict *Uti possidetis* such that we should say, “As you possess, so may you possess,” since the proofs of the Church are far stronger and it is therefore superior in the interdict. By counsel of our brethren, we condemn the commune of Faenza, imposing upon it perpetual silence, as regards the possessory judgment—on which alone proceedings have been had—concerning jurisdiction, honour, district, and all other matters generally pertaining thereto in the aforesaid places. We prohibit it from presuming, either by itself or through others, in any way to molest you, your Church, or the inhabitants of the aforesaid places concerning these matters. Therefore let no one infringe [Col. 1215A] this our determination, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 1 September, in the tenth year.

CXVII. TO THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF PISA. Answer to them concerning certain questions. (Viterbo, 10 September.)

When our beloved sons, the noblemen Gottifred the viscount, Opizus Cortevecele, and Ugo de Grotta, your envoys—prudent and faithful men—came to the Apostolic See, we received them with the fitting kindness; and we took care diligently to understand the matters which they prudently undertook to put before us on your behalf. We give thanks to the Most High that, following in the footsteps of your forefathers, you do not intend to depart from devotion to your most holy mother, the Roman Church. [Col. 1215B]

The satisfaction which these envoys offered us concerning both the affair of Sardinia and that of Sicily, although it was not altogether complete, we have nevertheless thought fit to accept for the present. We hope that, when our good pleasure has been more fully understood by them, you will wish to offer us fuller satisfaction, so that our favour towards you ought neither to be diminished nor disturbed. But because the matter of your archbishopric was then being dealt with before us, and because, according to the Apostle, we wished to abstain not only from evil but from every appearance of evil, we did not wish to receive from them any security regarding such satisfaction. They said that they were offering it not by your mandate but at their own discretion.

We communicate that satisfaction to you by our letters, so that, accepting the favour of our generosity, [Col. 1215C] you may take care to satisfy us more fully in proportion as you desire more earnestly to be heard by us. Take pains to explain to us your good pleasure in this matter within a month, so that we may be more certainly instructed how we ought to proceed towards you. The tenor of the satisfaction offered is as follows:

> “The noblemen Gottefred the viscount, Opizus Cortevecele, and Ugo de Grotta, envoys or messengers of the city of Pisa, promise the lord pope, under a penalty of five hundred pounds in Pisan money, that they will so prevail upon the podestà of Pisa that the said Pisan podestà shall command Lambert, a citizen of Pisa, by his messenger or letters to come to the Apostolic See, either personally or through a suitable representative. He shall submit himself without reservation to the commands of the lord pope concerning the fact that he received and holds the judicature of Gallura without the licence of the supreme pontiff, and took . . . the lady of Gallura as his wife; and concerning the damages, injuries, and expenses which Transmundus, kinsman of the lord pope, has suffered because of this affair. Or he shall render full justice concerning the foregoing before the lord pope himself.
>
> “If, after admonition, the said Lambert should refuse to do either of the foregoing within the period to be fixed, then the aforesaid podestà shall, without fraud, carry out the mandate of the lord pope out of all the goods which Lambert now has or shall hereafter have in the city of Pisa and its district. Moreover, they will so prevail upon the aforesaid podestà that the podestà shall give security on behalf of the commune of that city that they will not offend the king of Sicily. [Col. 1216A]
>
> “This promise shall be made to the lord pope by the said envoys upon these terms: after the aforesaid podestà, with the counsel of the city of Pisa, has acknowledged to the lord pope, by letters sealed with the seal of the commune or written by a public hand, that he ratifies the foregoing and lawfully binds himself and his successors to perform what the said envoys have promised to the supreme pontiff, the same envoys shall be wholly free and released from the said promise and from the prescribed penalty.”

Given at Viterbo, 10 September, in the tenth year.

CXVIII. TO THE ABBOTS OF DECIHAN AND MONTISGEROLD, AND THE PROVOST OF RHOTNAC, IN THE DIOCESE OF CAMBRAI. That they may grant a dispensation to G., a layman, and D., his wife, related in the fourth degree of consanguinity. (Viterbo, 18 March.)

[Col. 1216B]

Our beloved son G., a layman of Oudenaarde, informed us that he had married D., now his deceased wife, who was related to him . . . in the fourth degree of consanguinity. He lived peacefully with her for so long that he has already had five children by her. But because his conscience reproaches him concerning this, and certain persons are now maliciously attempting to trouble him concerning that marriage, he humbly petitioned us to deal mercifully with him, lest their children fall into poverty and contempt—which would indeed occur if a divorce should take place between them.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if this is so, after imposing suitable penance upon both the man and the woman concerning this matter, you are to grant a dispensation concerning the marriage and not permit them to be unlawfully troubled by anyone. But if not all of you . . . two of you, etc. [Col. 1216C]

Given at Viterbo, 18 August, in the tenth year.

CXIX. TO THE NOBLEWOMAN JULIANA, LADY OF PIRUCIS. Confirmation of what was granted her by the emperor of Constantinople. (Viterbo, 17 September.)

It is customary to assent, etc., as far as “assent.” At the request of the same emperor, we confirm for you by apostolic authority, and fortify with the privilege of this present writing, the village of Blaten, which our dearest son in Christ [Col. 1216D] Henry, the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, liberally granted you, as you justly and peacefully possess it. Therefore let no one infringe . . . this our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 17 September, in the tenth year.

CXX. TO HENRY, ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He is granted that he may not be excommunicated except for an enormous offence. (Viterbo, 12 September.)

Since, in governing the empire of Romania, the burden of grave and great care presses upon you, you ought rather to be assisted than burdened by ecclesiastical men, lest [Col. 1217A], oppressed by excessive difficulty, you succumb if you undertake beyond your strength both temporal and spiritual burdens. How much deference is due to kings, especially faithful and devout ones, the blessed Apostle Peter teaches in his Epistle, saying: “Be subject for God’s sake to every human creature, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good” (1 Peter 2).

Therefore, lest our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, be able henceforth to burden you improperly, as we have learned that you have hitherto burdened him improperly—thereby providing more for him than for you, since it is less evil to suffer injury than to commit it—we prohibit him by the authority of these presents from presuming to pronounce ecclesiastical censure upon your person or land without a manifest and reasonable cause. [Col. 1217B] He must always first issue canonical admonition, unless perhaps the offence were such as to require that judicial procedure not be observed.

If you perceive that you are being burdened, you may freely appeal to the Apostolic See in order to avoid the impending grievance. If, after such appeal, he presumes to hurl a sentence, we decree that it is not to be observed, as void and ineffectual, especially so long as you are prepared to obey the law before us, or before our legate or delegate, or even before an arbitrator chosen jointly. In such cases, moreover, time and place, necessity and usefulness, as well as the cause and the person, must be considered.

But you, dearest son, the more you need the aid of the divine majesty, the more constantly devote yourself to the service of divine mercy and reverence its bride, holy Church, more devoutly, so that by her prayers she may render you more abundantly commended to Him. Therefore let no one infringe . . . this our prohibition, concession, and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc. [Col. 1217C]

Given at Viterbo, 12 September, in the tenth year.

CXXI. TO THE MASTER OF THE HOUSES OF THE KNIGHTS TEMPLAR ON THIS SIDE OF THE SEA. Concerning observance of an interdict and honouring the apostolic legate. (Viterbo, 13 September.)

The grave complaints of our brethren and fellow bishops, repeatedly laid before apostolic ears concerning the grave offences of your brethren, cannot but trouble our mind, since these matters are undertaken to the scandal of us and of the universal [Col. 1217D] Church, to peril of their own souls, and to the detriment of your order. Having apostatized from the Lord and departed from the purity of their order, they are so unrestrained in their pride that, unafraid to cast a stain in the face of their mother, the Roman Church, which never ceases to foster the brethren of the Knights Templar by its benefactions, they dare publicly to preach that, by the indults of the Apostolic See, all churches of whatsoever city or town placed under interdict must, successively upon their welcome arrival, be opened and divine offices celebrated there, as they see fit now in one place, now in another. They do not consider that through such presumption the remedy of the medicinal penalty is despised and indeed [Col. 1218A] almost wholly rendered powerless.

And if they have churches in the aforesaid places when those places are subject to interdict, they are not ashamed solemnly to celebrate the divine offices daily in them, with bells rung and doors open, especially while the interdict lasts. Bearing the sign of the Lord’s cross upon their breast as if they were disciples of Jesus Christ, but taking no care to follow his teaching—for he forbids causing scandal to one of the little ones who believe in him, saying, “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18)—they despise not merely scandal to the little ones but also scandal to the universal Church. Burning with the heats of greed, they do not shrink from lies. For, employing doctrines of demons, they imprint the seal of the Crucified upon the breast of every [Col. 1218B] scoundrel, and go out to preach with them. Laden with the weight of sins, they no longer care, as it were, to add a long rope of sins to sins, asserting that whoever gives themselves to their fraternity by contributing two or three denarii annually cannot by law be deprived of ecclesiastical burial, even if under interdict.

Thus adulterers, manifest usurers, and other criminals placed under ecclesiastical interdict are buried in their cemeteries as though they were faithful Catholics, by reason of this insolence. Captivated by the devil, they do not cease to make captive the souls of the faithful, when they strive to give life to those whom they know to be dead. Alas! They no longer use the world moderately, like religious men, for God’s sake; instead, in order to satisfy [Col. 1218C] their pleasures, they use the appearance of religion solely for the world’s sake. And though they should have been to others “an aroma from life unto life,” they have become “an aroma from death unto death.”

Although for these and other abominations—which we refrain from setting out more fully, lest we be compelled to punish more severely—they deserved to be deprived of the apostolic privileges which they so grievously abuse, since one who abuses the power granted him deserves to lose his privilege, nevertheless, because we seek the advancement of your order, we earnestly admonish and exhort your prudence. By apostolic letters we command you, as a man of integrity and a zealous supporter of the Knights Templar, faithfully and wisely to explain to all your subjects the matters we have commanded you, so that, corrected by our exhortation and yours, they may be freed from such enormous [Col. 1218D] and pestilential foulness. Those whom regard for divine love and the authority of our admonition do not recall from evil, restrain by the severity of ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, if any evil befalls you in the future because of this, you will rightly be able to impute it not to us but to yourselves.

Moreover, command all of them to endeavour to honour our legates, who complain grievously concerning them.

Given at Viterbo, on the Ides of September, in the tenth year.

CXXII. TO JOHN, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. That he send a procurator to the Apostolic See. (Viterbo, 3 September.)

We have often recalled that by our letters we admonished you—whom, as he knows who searches hearts and reins, we love with sincere charity in the Lord—to provide for your salvation and honour by taking care to make satisfaction to our dearest daughter in Christ, B., formerly illustrious queen of the English, concerning her dower, half the movables of Richard, your brother of illustrious memory, and certain other matters which the said queen maintained were due to her. You were to satisfy her in such a way that no just ground of complaint against you remained to her and that you might appease the divine majesty, which you seemed grievously to have offended on this account. [Col. 1219A]

Since our prayers and admonitions did not in the least induce you to make satisfaction to her, as her repeatedly renewed complaint has shown, we entrusted the case for hearing to our venerable brethren, the bishops of Ely and Worcester, [Col. 1219B] and also at first to others on this side of the sea. But even so, because of the greatness of royal power, though seven years have now elapsed, she has not been able to obtain justice in these matters, since no one who would give her assistance dares to cross to England.

Therefore, since by the office of apostleship laid upon us we are specially bound in justice to widows and orphans, and since we do not wish to defer to a human being against God, who by the prophetic voice commands that the widow be defended, we command your royal majesty by apostolic letters to present yourself before us, through a suitable procurator, by the coming feast of the Epiphany of the Lord. In our presence you are to render to the aforesaid queen, or to her procurator, concerning the foregoing and any other matters which she may perhaps decide to allege against you, whatever the rule of reason shall prescribe. Otherwise, [Col. 1219C] since we cannot fail her in her right, lest perhaps she cry against us to heaven and the Lord hear her voice, we shall proceed in the matter, by divine clemency’s favour, as far as law permits. For by strict letters we command our aforesaid bishops not to delay assigning you the aforesaid peremptory term.

Given at Viterbo, 3 September, in the tenth year.

CXXIII. TO THE WOMAN ALTEROCCA AND HER SON MONTANELLO. Confirmation to them of a sentence rendered by a legate of the Apostolic See. (Viterbo, 12 September.)

[Note: [Col. 1219D] Chapter *Ranutius*, On judgments and matters adjudged.] Ranutius of Clera, who had two daughters, namely you, [Col. 1219D] Alterocca, and Ajecta, as well as a mother, Clera, and a wife named Adelasia, when at the point of death made a will. To you, Alterocca, his adult daughter, he left in the same will, beyond the dowry previously given, a certain house and garden. To Ajecta, who was under age, he left all his other goods, adding that you, Alterocca, and the child whom you carried in your womb—for you were then pregnant—were to succeed the said Ajecta if she died without children. The testator also instructed the guardians whom he had appointed for his under-age daughter Ajecta to marry her, together with all her goods.

After the testator’s death, these guardians, under Lombard law, gave Ajecta in marriage, together with all the goods [Col. 1220A] left to her by her father, to a certain Peter. After she had cohabited with him for four years and borne him a son, she finally died without children. Her surviving husband peacefully possessed her goods for some time. He then contracted marriage with another woman, had children by her, and died.

Thereafter a dispute arose between you on one side, and the children of the same Peter and their guardian Raynerius on the other, concerning the aforesaid goods of Ajecta. They began to litigate before Guezius, judge of Tuscany. Before him, you, Alterocca, daughter of the late Raynutius, claimed the goods of your former father as due to you by reason of fideicommissum or substitution. In opposition, the aforesaid Raynerius, guardian of the children of the said Peter, asserted that the annual prescription, prescription by possession for dowry, and the protracted silence of a long period barred you. [Col. 1220B]

The same guardian also alleged that, before all else, there had to be deducted from those goods one third for Clera, the mother of the aforesaid testator R.; one third for his wife Adelasia; and likewise one fourth, the Trebellianic fourth, in the name of Ajecta herself. After diligently considering the allegations and arguments of both sides, the said judge condemned the aforesaid Raynerius, in the name of the minors, to restore the goods formerly belonging to Raynutius. He first deducted the third of Clera, which she had given to Ajecta and her husband, and of which Raynutius does not appear to have thought at all in making the substitution; he also deducted the third of Adelasia, which she had [Col. 1220C] sold to the aforesaid Raynerius.

The same judge further ordered that those thirds be deducted from such property as could be subject to deduction under the custom of the city of Tuscany. He also ordered the deduction of the Trebellianic fourth, since any stranger burdened with restoration could have deducted it. But both parties appealed that sentence.

Subsequently our beloved son . . ., prefect of the City, who at that time heard appellate cases in the regions of Tuscany by authority of the Apostolic See, at Raynerius’s request summoned you to appear before him. He fixed for you the then approaching feast of Saint Andrew as a peremptory date upon which you were to appear before him to receive judgment. [Col. 1220D] Since you did not appear before him on the appointed date, Bartholomew, judge of Viterbo of good memory, by the prefect’s mandate pronounced judgment against you as contumacious parties, in the following manner. He declared Guezius’s judgment valid insofar as it acquitted Raynerius in the name of the minors; but insofar as it condemned him, he pronounced the judgment unjust and lawfully appealed. He added that, if you, Alterocca, had received less than your lawful share at your father’s death, he condemned Raynerius, in the name of the minors, to make up the deficiency, after taking account of the dowry and other paternal goods. An appeal was subsequently made from this judgment.

When, on this account, you and the other party came before us, [Col. 1221A] we granted to you and the adverse party our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, as auditor. Before him, when Raynerius’s party requested confirmation of the sentence of Judge Bartholomew, your party replied that although, as stated, the prefect had fixed the date on the feast of Saint Andrew, that date had nevertheless, at your request, been extended to the octave of the same Nativity, as was most plainly proved by your sole witness and another witness of the adverse party. For this reason you maintained that the judgment was void, as having been pronounced while the extension was pending. This was especially so because, before the appointed date, a citation had been made by our venerable brother, the bishop of Soana, to whom our letters concerning the same case had been obtained in the meantime, as seems proved by the witness depositions. [Col. 1221B]

After prolonged litigation between you and the other party before the aforesaid cardinal concerning these and other matters, he, having taken counsel of experts and by our mandate, pronounced the aforesaid sentence of Judge Bartholomew altogether void for the aforesaid reasons. As to Guezius’s judgment that the third of Clera and the third of Adelasia were to be deducted in full, the same cardinal pronounced it unjust and lawfully appealed. He determined that those thirds were to be deducted in such manner that the lawful share due to you, Alterocca, by natural law should remain intact for you in each of them; and he condemned the said Raynerius to restore that share.

But insofar as Guezius had held that [Col. 1221C] the Trebellianic fourth should be retained, he confirmed Guezius’s judgment: namely, that the fruits received from the goods from the time of joinder of issue are to be reckoned in that fourth. If they suffice for the fourth and its fruits, no other deduction is to be made on that account; otherwise, account is to be taken in proportion to the amount of fruits received. Since Ajecta’s father could not burden her in respect of her lawful share, he held that her lawful share—that is, the share due to the said Ajecta on intestacy—was also to be deducted and retained, but only from those things from which deduction was customarily made under the custom of the city of Tuscany. [Col. 1221D] Insofar as the same Guezius condemned Raynerius, in the name of his minors, to restore the remainder to you, he confirmed Guezius’s judgment.

Therefore, holding valid the sentence of the same cardinal, pronounced as justice required, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it with the privilege of this present writing. Therefore let no one infringe . . . this our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 12 September, in the tenth year.

CXXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF OTONIA. That a priest who lost a finger of his left hand may minister. (Viterbo, 18 September.)

[Note: [Col. 1221D] See Regino, book II, chapter 410.] O., a priest, appearing before us, humbly represented [Col. 1222A] that, while certain men were fighting one another in front of his house and he happened to leave that house, one of the combatants, though no fault on the priest’s part had preceded, rushed upon him and, at the devil’s instigation, cut off a finger of his left hand. He therefore humbly petitioned us to grant him permission to perform his office.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if this is so, you are to permit the priest freely to minister in his order, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed. For certain things sometimes prevent promotion but do not depose one already promoted.

Given at Viterbo, 18 September, in the tenth year.

CXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF VARIS, THE BISHOP OF SALIMBRIA, AND THE DEAN OF SAINT MARY OF BLACHERNAE AT CONSTANTINOPLE. That they institute R., a cleric, in the church of Kufan. (Viterbo, 17 September.)

[Col. 1222B]

Since provision for clerics contains in itself a work of piety, which has the promise of both the life that now is and that which is to come, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you confer, by apostolic authority and with all impediment of appeal removed, the church of the island of Kufan, which is said to be vacant, upon our beloved son R., cleric of our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious emperor of Constantinople, who holds no ecclesiastical benefice. Cause him to possess it peacefully, restraining by canonical censure any opponents or rebels [Col. 1222C] whom you find. But if not all of you . . . two of you, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 17 September, in the tenth year.

CXXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF MORAVIA. The case of the monastery of Melrose is committed to him. (Given, as in the other.)

It was once represented to us by the beloved son …, abbot, and the convent of Melrose of the Cistercian Order: that the nobleman P., count of Dunbar, of the diocese of St Andrews, had violently occupied part of a certain pasture which they had lawfully acquired, committing other injuries against them. We therefore committed the case, to be concluded under a specified form, to our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved sons …, archdeacon of St Andrews, and …, archdeacon of Lothian, in the diocese of St Andrews. [Col. 1222D] The count having, as we have learned, been repeatedly summoned by those judges at lawful intervals, and several peremptory summonses having subsequently been served upon him, yet failing to appear at the final peremptory summons although it had come to his knowledge, the said judges, deeming him absent through contumacy, and acting on the advice of prudent men, changed the penalty prescribed by law into another form. For they feared danger of death or mutilation, or at least the shedding of blood, if possession of the things claimed were conferred in order to preserve the subject matter of the suit. They therefore subjected the manors of that nobleman to ecclesiastical interdict, [Col. 1223A] excepting the baptism of infants and communion and penance for the sick.

Thereafter, when he came before the court and had given security to appear for judgment, without prejudice to the exemptions which might belong to him, the sentence of interdict having been relaxed, he raised, on the peremptory day assigned to the count for proposing all dilatory exceptions, an objection to the forum. He fortified it in three ways: namely, by reason of his person, because he was a layman; by reason of the thing, because it was a lay holding; and by the benefit of the common law, because the plaintiff ought to follow the forum of the defendant. When an answer was made on the other side to these arguments, the aforesaid judges, seeing that none of this had escaped our notice, since we had mentioned it in our letters, and that the general custom had hitherto been observed in those regions that a cleric could summon a layman before an ecclesiastical court, especially concerning things bestowed upon pious places in pure alms, ruled that such an exception was not to be admitted. [Col. 1223B]

But the count’s party, seeing its view disappointed, began to challenge the person of the said bishop. It alleged that, since he had called a certain church a chapel of another church in which the count possessed the right of patronage, and had appealed to the Apostolic See lest anyone should be instituted there to his prejudice, that same bishop had instituted in it, after an appeal to us had been lodged, a certain man presented by another. It further alleged that, because the count asserted that the penalty had been changed contrary to the form of law, even if he had been contumacious, and, after submitting an answer both in law and in fact, believing that they wished to proceed without admitting such exceptions, he appealed to our hearing. By that appeal he raised a certain dispossession by way of exception, in order to repel the other party from bringing suit. For proving it, first on one day, and then, after other dates had been fixed and accepted, for obtaining copies of the instruments mentioned in our letters and, if possible, disproving them, the monks appeared on both dates; but the count did not appear, nor did he send any representative for himself, and did not fear to disregard another peremptory summons. [Col. 1223C]

As time passed, a certain procurator of the aforesaid count laid before us a complaint concerning these matters and obtained apostolic letters addressed to our beloved sons the abbot of Holy Cross, the prior of the island of St Columba, and Master A., rector of the church of Cretton, in the dioceses of Dunkeld and St Andrews. [Col. 1223D] In these letters we ordered that, if the matters alleged to us by the said count rested upon a truthful account—namely, that although he had pleaded before the first judges that our letters had been obtained with the truth suppressed, and had also alleged that he could decline that bishop’s jurisdiction because in other cases he had oppressed him contrary to justice, and after an appeal had been lodged to us had presumed to inflict no slight injuries upon him, and had subjected his land to ecclesiastical interdict without any definite or reasonable cause, and that he was prepared [Col. 1224A] to prove these grounds and other manifest grounds by which he could rightly challenge the aforesaid bishop as suspect—nevertheless, the said bishop, refusing to admit proof of the allegations, had issued an interlocutory ruling that the count ought to answer before him in the matter; and an appeal to our hearing had been lodged on the count’s behalf from this ruling: then, restoring to its due state whatever they found to have been wrongly attempted against the count on the occasion of those letters, they were to hear the case, bring it to its proper conclusion without appeal, and cause what they decreed to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure.

R., a monk of the same monastery, opposing the hearing of our letters, caused his own account to be appended to those letters. But when, before the second judges, the matters reported to us had been somewhat debated in litigation, and those judges could not otherwise establish the facts concerning the allegations, they admitted and carefully examined witnesses concerning the earlier conduct of the case.
