After the depositions had been published, and leave had been given the parties to make objections to the witnesses’ statements and persons, and after objections had been raised by both sides against the statements and the witnesses, they referred the entire case to us. They fixed for the parties the Sunday on which is sung “As newborn babes,” on which day, sufficiently instructed either in person or through lawful procurators, they were to present themselves before us. [Col. 1224B]

The party of the said abbot and convent appeared before us at that term with the letters of the second judges, the depositions, and the mutual objections. We assigned to them as auditor our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico. The other party neither came nor sent anyone on its behalf, although it was waited for a long time. Therefore, wishing to spare the parties labour and expense, after seeing and more carefully understanding all the written materials, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you not to have regard to what was done by either the first or the second judges. Direct the parties that within fifteen days each is to appoint for you as colleague a suitable and honourable man, with whom, justice being observed and without appeal, you are to proceed in the case, notwithstanding the above-mentioned objection to the forum. If both or either refuse to appoint you a colleague, nevertheless carry out the apostolic mandate without either of them, or with only the other. [Col. 1224C–D] You shall do the same if both or either refuse to take part.

Given as in the other letter.

CXXVII. TO THE NOBLEMAN MAIO, COUNT OF THE ISLANDS OF CEPHALONIA AND ZACYNTHUS. Permission for him to choose a confessor. (Viterbo, 17 Kalends of October.)

Because, though unworthy, we hold on earth the place of Him who does not will the death of the sinner but rather that he be converted and live, who overlooks the sins of offenders after they have been corrected by penance, and bestows the gift of fuller grace upon those who repent and are converted in proportion as there is greater joy in God and His angels [Col. 1225A] over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who think themselves not to need the benefit of penance, we have rejoiced greatly and been delighted by what has come to our knowledge concerning your devotion.

For, as you have humbly informed our Apostolic See by your letters, although until now you have, as it were, led a piratical life and committed many acts to the peril of your salvation and the injury of the Creator, yet now, recognizing the condition of your frailty, you seek pardon for what you have done. And, so that, forgetting what lies behind, you may zealously and devoutly stretch forward to what lies before, you strive by the pursuit of a new manner of life to make amends for past offences, labouring with all your strength in the service of Jesus Christ and for the aid of the Holy Land. [Col. 1225B]

For this we give such thanks as we can to the Most High, who has so mercifully looked down upon you from on high that you grieve for past transgressions and strive to exercise yourself in meritorious works. We commend your purpose in the Lord all the more because you earnestly raise yourself toward what is more useful and offer both yourself and your land to the authority of the Apostolic See with the fervour of complete devotion. Therefore, that the vow of your desire may reach a happier conclusion, we have thought fit to entreat and admonish your nobility, commanding you by apostolic letters to reveal all your sins in humble confession to some discerning priest; and, receiving from him salutary penance, to strive, according to your ability, to perform the satisfaction which he judges should be imposed upon you. [Col. 1225C] For our part, assuring you of our favour, we fortify you with the shield of our blessing, hoping that, if you persevere in the undertaken purpose of devotion, besides the benefit of heavenly recompense which you will obtain, you will also receive no slight increase in temporal goods.

Given at Viterbo, 17 Kalends of October, in the tenth year.

CXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PATRAS. He writes that he is to bring the bishop of Cephalonia back to obedience to the Apostolic See. (Viterbo, 14 Kalends of October.)

Know that it has come to our hearing that on the island of Zacynthus, which belongs to the dominion of our beloved son, the nobleman Maio, count of Cephalonia, a certain Greek bishop is not only disobedient and rebellious toward the Apostolic See, scorning altogether to obey its ordinances, but also leads a dissolute life to the scandal of many. [Col. 1225D] Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you shall diligently admonish and induce the same bishop to strive to show complete obedience and reverence to the Apostolic See, reforming his life and conduct for the better, as the gravity of the pontifical office requires. But if he should perhaps scorn to comply with your admonitions, then, removing him altogether from the care of his church, cause that church to be canonically provided with a suitable person, without impediment from appeal, restraining opponents or rebels, after prior admonition, through ecclesiastical censure. [Col. 1226A]

Given at Viterbo, 14 Kalends of October, in the tenth year.

CXXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF PIACENZA. That he compel the monastery of Patramarina to restore certain goods. (Viterbo, 18 Kalends of October.)

It has been reported to our Apostolic See that, when a dispute had arisen between our beloved sons the cardinal, a citizen of Genoa, and J., son of the late Vassallus of Sinoria, concerning the goods of the cardinal’s mother and likewise of J.’s stepmother, it was meanwhile established that the mother of the aforesaid cardinal had offered herself and her goods to the monastery of St Michael of Petra Martina. [Col. 1226B] The same J. acquired the aforesaid goods, worth more than one hundred pounds, from the abbot of the said monastery under title of purchase for thirty Genoese pounds.

Since we are unwilling that that monastery should be so grievously harmed by the aforesaid alienation, we command you by apostolic letters diligently to admonish the abbot and monks of that place and not to delay effectively inducing them to pursue, in your presence, their claim to recover the aforesaid goods. Otherwise, since it is more equitable and more consonant with reason that the same cardinal rather than a stranger should obtain the aforesaid goods, which are known to have formerly belonged to his mother, we will and command that you firmly order the same abbot and monks on our behalf not to delay assigning, without appeal, to the aforesaid cardinal every right and action which they have for recovering the aforesaid goods. [Col. 1226C] This is to be done on the condition that the same cardinal keep the monastery indemnified and, for so great a benefit, become vassal and defender of that monastery, as he himself promised before us.

Given at Viterbo, 18 Kalends of October, in the tenth year.

CXXX. TO ALL OUR FAITHFUL SUBJECTS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE PATRIMONY OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER. How Paterines and their supporters are to be punished. (Viterbo, 9 Kalends of October.)

To eliminate entirely from the patrimony of blessed Peter [Col. 1226D] the filth of heretics, we establish as a law to be observed forever that whoever is found therein to be a heretic, and especially a Paterine, shall immediately be seized and handed over to the secular court to be punished according to lawful sanctions. All his goods shall be confiscated: one part of them shall be received by the person who seized him, another by the court which punished him, and the third assigned to the construction of the walls of the town where he was apprehended. The house in which the heretic was harboured shall be utterly destroyed, and no one shall presume to rebuild it; rather, it shall become a receptacle of filth, since it was a hiding-place of the faithless.

Moreover, believers in, defenders, and supporters of them shall be fined one fourth of their goods, to be assigned for public use. [Col. 1227A] If, even after being punished in this way, they again fall into a similar offence, they shall be wholly expelled from their places and shall never return to them except by mandate of the supreme pontiff, after due satisfaction has first been made. Proclamations or appeals by persons of this kind shall not be heard at all. No one shall be compelled to answer them in any case, but they themselves shall be compelled to answer others. Judges, advocates, and notaries shall render none of them their professional service; otherwise they shall be deprived of that office forever. Clerics shall not administer ecclesiastical sacraments to such pestilential persons, nor accept their alms or offerings; likewise the Hospitallers, Templars, and any religious. Otherwise they shall be deprived of their office and never restored to it without a special indult of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1227B]

Furthermore, whoever presumes to give ecclesiastical burial to such persons—namely, believers in, supporters, harbourers, and defenders of heretics—shall be struck with the sword of anathema until suitable satisfaction has been made. None of these persons shall be admitted to give testimony or be appointed to any public office or common council. Whoever elects such a person shall, as a supporter of heretics, be punished by the aforesaid penalty. This statute shall be entered in the civic register, and the podestàs, consuls, or rectors shall swear to it annually. It shall never be removed from that register, so that they may always swear that they will firmly observe this statute. Whoever scorns or neglects to observe it, having been removed from office, shall incur a penalty of one hundred pounds, payable [Col. 1227C] to whomever the supreme pontiff orders it assigned.

Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this page of our constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 9 Kalends of October, in the tenth year.

CXXXI. TO ALL CLERICS AND LAYMEN ESTABLISHED IN THE PATRIMONY OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER. That nothing be attempted contrary to laws and canons. (Given as in the other letter.)

Since by the duty of our office we are bound to provide with paternal solicitude both for clerics and for laymen, lest either suffer injury or commit injury, we utterly condemn and annul, by spiritual as well as temporal authority, unjust constitutions promulgated or to be promulgated by laymen contrary to laws and canons against churches or ecclesiastical persons. [Col. 1227D] Under the obligation of fealty and threat of anathema, we forbid them to presume wickedly to observe such constitutions. For we decree null and void whatever may have been attempted against churches or ecclesiastical persons on the occasion of those constitutions, notwithstanding any oath said to have been sworn for their observance, since, being unlawful, it ought not to be observed. We forbid judges and notaries to presume to exercise their office according to such condemned constitutions, if they wish to avoid the danger of losing their office.

Given as in the other letter.

CXXXII. TO ALL OUR FAITHFUL SUBJECTS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE PATRIMONY OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER. They are exhorted to peace and concord, and that no one offend another. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1228A]

Since the counts and barons, podestàs and consuls have sworn strictly to observe peace, justice, and security at our command, we command you all that, keeping true peace, you in no way offend one another: neither community against community, nor person against person, nor community against person; excepting robbers and brigands, and excepting those banished and publicly proscribed. Whenever you are required, render suitable aid to the rector of the apostolic patrimony for punishing them. [Col. 1228B]

If anyone is offended, he shall not immediately retaliate, but shall first admonish the offender to make amends. If disagreement arises concerning the amends, unless it can be settled otherwise, it shall be referred to the judgment of the rector of the apostolic patrimony. Otherwise, when publicly proscribed by him, the offender shall be attacked as a public enemy. When a dispute arises between any persons, it shall be settled by agreement or judgment; and judgment shall belong to the person whose jurisdiction it is, always preserving appeals lawfully made or yet to be made to us or to the rector of the apostolic patrimony. If anyone established within the patrimony of blessed Peter scorns to observe this arrangement, he shall be excluded by all persons according to the command of the rector of the apostolic patrimony. [Col. 1228C]

If anyone by his own authority has taken or caused to be taken plunder, or has stolen or caused theft, he and the person who knowingly bought it shall restore the plunder and the stolen property with a double penalty. Whoever bought stolen property or such plunder unknowingly shall restore it absolutely, with no compensation given or to be given to him; but the purchaser shall have his action against the seller. We enjoin all these things upon the counts and barons, podestàs and consuls, under the obligation of the oath they have sworn, to be observed: they are faithfully to observe them themselves and cause them to be observed by others within their jurisdictions. In all things the command of the Apostolic See is always reserved.

Given as in the other letter.

CXXXIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF NEVERS AND ORLÉANS, AND THE ABBOT OF COUR-DIEU OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER, IN THE DIOCESE OF ORLÉANS. Concerning Alberic, archbishop-elect of Reims. (Viterbo, 1 October.)

[Col. 1228D]

We believe that our venerable brothers, the bishops of Paris and Arras, and our beloved son the abbot of Clairmarais, possess such integrity that they proceeded with good zeal in arranging the Church of Reims, a matter which we thought fit to commit to them; especially since the man whom they set over that church is outstanding in life, learning, and reputation. For our part, God being witness, we aspire with the greatest desire that persons be raised to the office of prelacy in the Church of God who are not hirelings but shepherds, to teach the peoples entrusted to them alike by word and example. [Col. 1229A]

Now our beloved sons Theobald of Perche, archdeacon, and P. of Étampes, canon of the said church, among other matters which they reported to us by their letters against the proceedings of the aforesaid bishops and abbot, made this particular allegation against Master Alberic, named as archbishop of Reims: that he was irregular, indiscreet, and manumitted. Therefore, since an irregular person was unsuited to office, an indiscreet person to a burden, and a manumitted person to honour, they took care to forbid the bishops who had assembled for his consecration to presume to consecrate such a man bishop, since the said P. answered the bishops’ question by saying that he would prove this before them on that day. But the aforesaid bishop of Paris, who was striving in every way for that man’s promotion, while no one replied against Peter except the bishop himself acting as judge, summoned two priests, secretly received their testimony concerning infamy against Peter, who was absent and unaware, and thus Peter was not admitted to prove so grave an irregularity—namely, that Alberic had contracted conjugal intercourse with a widow. [Col. 1229B] Peter having thus been irregularly excluded, the bishop caused Alberic nevertheless to be consecrated bishop after an appeal to the Apostolic See had been lodged.

The aforesaid bishops and abbot, however, informed us by their letters that, proceeding in the matter according to the form of the apostolic mandate, they had set the aforesaid Alberic, archdeacon of Paris, a man of approved repute and pleasing to God and men in life, conduct, and learning, over the Church of Reims as shepherd, after he had given them assurance under testimony of divine judgment that he acted from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith. They caused the gift of consecration to be conferred upon him after summoning the suffragan bishops. The chapter of Reims and the suffragans who had been present at his consecration agreed with this assertion, as the letters sent to us by them declare. [Col. 1229C]

But because the aforementioned archdeacon and canon repeatedly urged us in letters to have the truth investigated, although it is troublesome to us to trouble the aforesaid church, we nevertheless do not wish to pass over with closed eyes so great a defect in a sacrament, since such an impediment cannot be tolerated. We therefore command your discernment by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you, after investigating and learning the truth, that if you find that the aforesaid Peter was repelled, in the manner described, from proving such an objection, notwithstanding the irregularity of what was done, you shall notify him and the aforesaid archdeacon that, if they wish and are able, both or either of them may duly prove, under your examination, the alleged irregularity. [Col. 1229D] If within two months they refuse or are unable to prove it, whether because they fail in canonical proof or because they are canonically excluded from proof, you shall immediately instruct our beloved son R., our subdeacon and familiar, through whom we send the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter—the insignia, that is, of the fullness of the pontifical office—that he is to deliver it to the aforesaid prelate of the Church of Reims according to the form given him. Although the latter is neither incredible nor suspect in our eyes, we approve it if, before receiving the pallium, he wishes to clear himself so as entirely to establish his reputation. [Col. 1230A]

But if, which God forbid, the alleged irregularity is sufficiently proved, you shall remove him entirely from the government of the Church of Reims and proceed concerning the provision of that church according to the form prescribed to the often-mentioned bishops and abbot. When, through your care, a suitable bishop has been appointed there, cause the aforesaid pallium to be delivered to him, so that he need not be compelled to labour further on this account. If, after the proofs have been received, anything doubtful or difficult appears which cannot be resolved by you, faithfully report the whole matter to us, fully making known the truth, so that instructed by your report, we may proceed, with the Lord as author, concerning both this man and those others as the law requires. But if not all can carry out these matters … two of you, etc., removing every obstacle of contradiction, appeal, and challenge, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 1 October, in the tenth year.

CXXXIV. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS. That the pallium be delivered to the same Alberic. (Given as in the other letter.)

Since without the pallium a metropolitan cannot exercise the fullness of the pontifical office, serious loss would threaten not only the Church but also the whole province of Reims if the conferral of the pallium upon its prelate were delayed too long. Therefore, lest Theobald of Perche, archdeacon, and Peter of Étampes, canon of the aforesaid church, through contrived malice procure an evasion or hiding-place so that the matter committed to you cannot take effect within the time specified in the other letters, we, wishing to oppose malicious devices, command your discernment by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you that, if the aforesaid archdeacon and canon cannot be found after diligent search, then, when the prescribed time has elapsed, you shall cause the pallium to be delivered to the aforesaid prelate. [Col. 1230C]

Nevertheless, for fuller caution, every canonical ground which may belong to them against him is reserved; for the exception alleged is such as not merely impedes one yet to be promoted, but deposes one already promoted, although he is in no way notorious, incredible, or suspect in this respect, being a man distinguished by manifold praise. [Col. 1230D]

Given as in the other letter.

CXXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF FERMO. Concerning clerics ordained by bishops other than their own. (Viterbo, 4 Nones of October.)

You represented before us that, when you had been banished from your church, you thought fit to forbid the clerics of your diocese, under penalty of excommunication, to have themselves promoted to sacred orders without definite titles. Yet, scorning your prohibition, they flocked in groups to other provinces and indiscriminately procured ordination for themselves from various bishops. [Col. 1231A] You therefore humbly asked us to instruct you by our letters concerning what should be done in such cases. We reply to your brotherhood as follows: those ordained and their ordainers, unless excused by probable ignorance, are to be suspended from office.

Given at Viterbo, 4 Nones of October, in the tenth year.

CXXXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF TERDONNE. Dispensation to contract marriage in the second and third degree, for the sake of peace. (Viterbo, 1 October.)

As we have learned from the tenor of your letters, grave scandal has arisen among certain citizens of Terdonne because one of them is said to have committed a homicide. But lest hatred proceed to action, the kinsmen of the slain seek to marry a certain niece of the killer to the killer’s nephew; and espousals in the present tense have already been contracted between them. [Col. 1231B] But because the prospective spouses are related in the third degree of affinity of the second kind, you were unwilling to permit the marriage to be contracted. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, since no small good may result from this, you shall permit them, by dispensation, to contract marriage with one another, if no other canonical impediment stands in the way.

Given at Viterbo, 1 October, in the tenth year.

CXXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, AND ALL OTHER CLERICS AND LAYMEN ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE KINGDOM OF HUNGARY. That they receive the legate of the Apostolic See honourably. (Viterbo, Nones of October.)

[Col. 1231C]

The Lord Jesus Christ, foundation and founder of the Church, after He had kindled the vessel of human frailty with the splendour of His divinity, in order to find the lost drachma and, as the merciful shepherd, to carry back on His own shoulders to the sheepfolds the wandering sheep which He had left among the ninety-nine, continually supplied daily remedies for the salvation of humankind. Indeed, if anyone not departing from the Catholic faith wishes to consider this carefully, then, just as He is the fullness of all grace, so His mercies abound in manifold ways amid the miseries of our condition, so that in all things His perfection supplies our imperfection. [Col. 1231D]

Among the other remedies which, by His wisdom, were provided for the Christian people, left as it were half-dead by the various wounds of sins, He established a suitable antidote in the firmness of the Apostolic See, making it the head and teacher of all Christendom. From it, as ointment on the head descends to the beard and even to the hem of the garment, may the bread of understanding and life go forth to the other churches with the teaching of faith and the water of saving wisdom.

But lest its shepherd and ruler, amid continuous and very weighty cares, should fail through the defect of human weakness if, exhausting himself in fruitless labour, he recalled every concern to himself alone, considering that one labourer is insufficient for the abundant harvest, he joins many labourers and fellow-workers in the word of the Lord to himself, and is obliged through them to carry out what he cannot personally perform alone. He is instructed by the example of Him who chose both the twelve apostles and the other seventy-two and sent them out two by two before His face to preach. [Col. 1232A]

Therefore, since the necessity of the kingdom of Hungary required that a legate be sent there from our side, we, directing our attention specially and effectively to the exaltation and advantage alike of king and kingdom, have thought fit to send to those regions one whom we sincerely love in the Lord among our brethren: namely, our beloved son G., cardinal-priest of the title of St Vitalis, a man noble by birth, endowed with learning, distinguished by upright conduct, discerning and prudent, and, by the merit of his qualities, exceedingly dear and acceptable to us and our brethren. We have granted him full power to uproot and destroy, build and plant whatever in that kingdom he recognizes must be uprooted and destroyed, built and planted. [Col. 1232B]

We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort you all in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters to receive the aforesaid cardinal humbly and devoutly as legate of the Apostolic See and as holding a great place in the Church of God—indeed, receiving our own person in him. Give ready attention to his salutary admonitions and commands, and receive and firmly observe, as children of devotion, whatever he judges should be established among you. For we have undoubted confidence in his prudent circumspection and circumspect prudence that, the Lord directing his steps, he will take such care to proceed by the royal road, without turning to right or left, that he may deservedly please God Himself, us also, and you alike. [Col. 1232C]

Therefore let every one of you strive to render him due reverence and devoted obedience, lest, which God forbid, anyone act otherwise and incur not only the displeasure of that cardinal—whose canonical censure, should he judge one must be promulgated against the contumacious or rebellious, we shall cause to be inviolably observed until worthy satisfaction has been made—but also our indignation; for, according to the Apostle, we are ready to punish every disobedience. [Col. 1232D]

Given at Viterbo, on the Nones of October, in the tenth year.

In the same form to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other clerics and laymen established throughout Dalmatia.

CXXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND ALL CLERICS AND LAYMEN ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT RUTHENIA. That they treat the legate of the Apostolic See honourably. (Given as in the other letter.)

Although hitherto you have been far removed from the breasts of your mother, like alien sons, nevertheless we, who, though unworthy, have been appointed by God to the pastoral office of giving knowledge to His people, cannot divest ourselves of paternal affection without striving, by sound exhortations and teachings, to conform you as members to your head, so that Ephraim may turn to Judah and Samaria return to Jerusalem. Would that you were willing to understand wisely and provide for the end, so that, all darkness driven from your minds, you might return from the trackless way to the path—you who long ago, wandering after the flocks of your companions, stubbornly withdrew yourselves from the teaching of him whom our Saviour appointed teacher and head of the universal Church, saying to him: “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1); and: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

When the Lord, by repeating the word three times, entrusted His sheep to him to be fed, He plainly made it understood that whoever, even in Peter’s successors, should disdain to have him as shepherd is estranged from the Lord’s flock. For He made no distinction between these sheep and those, but simply said: “Feed my sheep” (John 21), so that all without exception are understood to have been committed to him. Since, therefore, the Lord’s tunic is one and undivided, and the Bride of Christ has never suffered divorce, as the Bridegroom testifies in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, she is the only one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her; the daughters of Zion saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her” (Song of Songs 6), it is necessary that whoever withdraws from such unity should, submerged in the waters of the flood, receive a portion with the apostate angel.

But in order that its inviolate unity might be preserved, the Lord, as we have said, appointed over it one man—namely blessed Peter—as head and teacher; so that, like Noah’s ark, outside which animals left behind are drowned in the flood while the rest are saved within it, it might come to completion in one cubit. For Peter’s faith, lest it fail in his Passion, He prayed especially, commanding him, once converted, to strengthen his brethren. Since, therefore, the unity of the Church is proved by almost countless testimonies of Scripture—which it is neither fitting nor advantageous for you to ignore—it is not surprising that we, though unworthy successors of him whom the Lord commanded to feed His sheep, strive to bring wandering sheep back to the folds, so that, as there is one shepherd, there may be one fold; and that we labor with all our strength lest the body of the Church somehow become deformed if any part should be separated from it.

But, to say nothing for the moment of the rest: since the Greek empire and almost the whole Greek Church have returned to devotion to the Apostolic See and humbly receive its commands and obey its injunction, does it not seem discordant that a part should not accord with its whole, and that a singularity should differ from its universality? Moreover, who can doubt that, because of their rebellion and disobedience, they were given over to plundering and spoil, so that at least affliction might give them understanding and they might recognize in adversity Him whom they had not acknowledged in prosperity? Therefore, dearest brethren and sons, if we wish worthily to fulfill the pastoral office imposed upon us, we must, so far as human frailty permits, lead you toward those things by which you may avoid loss of temporal goods and the peril of eternal things.

Accordingly, we have thought fit to send to your regions our beloved son G., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis: a man noble by birth, endowed with learning, distinguished by upright character, discreet and provident, and, because of his merits, exceedingly dear and acceptable to us and to our brethren. He is to bring the daughter back to her mother and the member back to its head. Full power has been granted him to uproot and destroy, build and plant, whatever in your regions he shall find ought to be uprooted and destroyed, built and planted. We therefore admonish you, etc., as above, as far as “we obtain”; for, with the Lord directing his steps, he will take care to establish among you those things by which he may deservedly please God, ourselves, and you alike.

Given as in the other letter.

### CXXXIX. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF VITERBO

That the Church of Viterbo shall henceforth be a cathedral church.  
(Viterbo, 4 Ides of October [12 October].)

> [Note: Col. 1233D. See *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, part II, p. 306.]

From the privilege of C., pope of happy memory, our predecessor, we have learned clearly that, having regard to your faith and devotion, he, with the common counsel of his brethren, distinguished the town of Viterbo by the honorable name of a city and endowed it with the dignity of a pontifical see. By apostolic authority he decreed that the Church of Viterbo, together with the sees of Tuscania, Centumcellae, and Blera, should henceforth possess pontifical dignity.

We, however, having more certainly experienced your faith and devotion through our own bodily presence, and wishing to interpret more fully this principal benefit, confirm for the see of Viterbo, in relation to the dioceses of Centumcellae and Blera, that preeminence which the see of Tuscania is known hitherto to have exercised over them, to which see the Church of Viterbo is specially united—while the legal status of the said sees of Centumcellae and Blera remains unimpaired.

Therefore let no one … [Col. 1234D] violate this document of our interpretation and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Viterbo, 4 Ides of October, in the tenth year.

### CXL. TO THE CHAPTER OF UZÈS

The church of Balneolis is adjudged to Peter Mark.  
(Corneto, 8 Kalends of November [25 October].)

From the letters of our venerable brother the archbishop, and of our beloved sons the dean of Arles and the treasurer of Nîmes, we have learned that, when we had formerly committed to them the cause pending between our beloved son Master Peter Mark, our scribe, and yourselves concerning the church of Saint John of Balneolis [Col. 1235A], they summoned the parties before them. Having heard and fully understood the allegations of both parties, they received the witnesses produced. Since they did not wish to impose an end upon the case, they referred it to us sufficiently instructed, faithfully transmitting to us, under their seal, the depositions received.

We therefore, having heard the arguments of both parties and carefully inspected the aforesaid depositions, by the authority of these presents absolve you from Master Peter’s claim concerning the said church, imposing silence upon him in respect of it.

Given at Corneto, 8 Kalends of November, in the tenth year.

### CXLI. TO ALL COUNTS AND BARONS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE KINGDOM OF SICILY

That they should assist the king of Sicily.  
(Tuscania, 18 Kalends of November [15 October].)

[Col. 1235B]

Even if you did not fear either divine or royal displeasure, even if you did not fear either the guilt of disloyalty or the stigma of infamy, you ought at least to dread loss of possessions or danger to your bodies; so that, struck by this fear, you might take care to furnish due and necessary aid to our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious king of Sicily, who is placed in the extremity of necessity.

Certainly, while the violence of strangers held him captive, some sort of plausible excuse availed you. But now that he is guarded by the diligence of his own people, whom his pious mother appointed for him, no argument can excuse you from owing him fitting service [Col. 1235C]. Why do you not, heedless men, foresee that, if through attacks of enemies or the treachery of traitors he should either lose his life or be deprived of his kingdom, your latter condition will be worse than your former? For those who will undoubtedly invade the kingdom will spare neither persons nor property, confiscating everything together into one mass—as you have already experienced, would that you had not forgotten it. When unforeseen calamity has come upon you, repentance will indeed be late and useless. Therefore, while you still have time, provide for yourselves against the wrath to come.

Your king himself has laid before us, through his envoys and letters, a pitiable complaint, declaring that, although he has often commanded the counts, barons, and citizens of his kingdom to hasten to aid him in his many necessities, they, after the manner of the deaf asp stopping its ears completely lest it hear the enchanter’s voice, have deigned to help him in no respect. Each attends to his own concerns and has no regard for him out of loyalty or affection.

Therefore, since the spiritual and material swords ought mutually to assist one another, as is written, “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22), the king humbly begged us to compel by ecclesiastical censure those who do not fear earthly power to render him fitting aid. We, therefore, recognizing both his petition and his complaint to be wholly just, admonish and exhort your devotion in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command you [Col. 1236A] to take care to furnish the same king with prompt assistance—in provisions, arms, ships, persons, and other things variously necessary to him—if not to the extent that you ought, at least to the extent that you can. Thus, supported by your aid and that of his other faithful subjects, he may put an end to the disasters that threaten and govern his kingdom in tranquil prosperity.

Otherwise, since we have thought fit to issue both warning and threat beforehand, we shall discharge the obligation of our office against rebels and contumacious persons, perhaps laying upon them a burden of oppression and a sword of chastisement more grievous than they expect; for an acute disease requires an acute remedy. But we shall cause those who take care to obey us and assist the king to enjoy a welcome reward [Col. 1236B].

Given at Tuscania, 18 Kalends of November, in the tenth year.

### CXLII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF TUSCANIA

Concerning the privileges of the bishop of Tuscania.  
(Corneto, 4 Kalends of November [29 October].)

“Justice requires that the requests,” etc., as far as “inclined.” We have ordered the privilege granted by Leo IV, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, to Virobo, formerly bishop of Tuscania, to be entered word for word in this present document, lest it perish through being consumed by age. Its tenor is as follows:

> Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Virobo, bishop of Tuscania, and to his successors for ever.
>
> It accords with apostolic government to assist with kindly compassion those who flourish in pious religion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion, so that divine recompense may thereby be reckoned to us. Therefore, because your brotherhood has humbly asked us to confirm and strengthen for ever to you and your successors the bishopric of the Holy Church of Tuscania, together with its parish churches, churches, chapels, estates, hamlets, landed holdings, villages, lands, vineyards, courts, woods, and everything within the lordship of that bishopric, according to the rights of your predecessors: inclined to your prayers, by the text of this decree we confirm and strengthen to you the aforesaid bishopric of Tuscania with all that belongs to it.
>
> Namely: in the city itself called Tuscania, throughout and around the bishopric and throughout the whole city, the courts with houses and very many small holdings, as you retain them in your authority; likewise the church of Saint Quiricus, with the houses and cells around it; and outside that city, vineyards, lands, estates, hamlets, and mills, wherever they belong or may belong to the same church.
>
> We also confirm to you in that city the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, our Lady, which was formerly the head of the bishopric and has now become a parish church, with houses, cells, vineyards, meadows, woods, and the market extending to the gate of the same city, with everything belonging to it—namely houses, gardens, and all its appurtenances. Mount Saint Hermes, with houses and gardens; the church of Saint Michael the Archangel beside the river Mascla, with its estates and hamlets, lands, gardens, and woods, together with its *angarales* and tributaries; the church of Saint Christina, with woods, hamlets, meadows, and vineyards; the estate called Casanovula, with the little bridge and the stream of Saint Paul; the estate Ancaranula, or whatever other name it may bear, with all its appurtenances and adjacent lands, together with the two estates called Octiganum and Algorum, in all their entirety; likewise the estate called Attevile, with its appurtenances, extending far and wide as far as Gundimarius’s reed-bed.
>
> The church of Saint Christina in the Valley and the church of Saint Restituta, which are beside the river Marta, with all their appurtenances; indeed, the estate called Planum de Mola, with cultivated and uncultivated lands and all that belongs to it. On the river Mascla, six watermills; and on the river Marta, three, with all their appurtenances. On the estate called Fontana Guaralda, fifteen gardens. The mount called Vinea Montana, with its districts and appendages. Montascinum, Montemtremitum, Solonianum, and the valley of Ingonis, with vineyards, lands, and all their appurtenances, including the tenant farmers, tributaries, and *angarales* residing there.
>
> The estate of Petrella; the estate of Muratula; the valley of Corneto; the estate called Doliolum; the estate Marilian; the estate called Mola; the valley called de Nasso; and Mount Supponis, with lands, meadows, woods, vineyards, gardens, marshes, swamps, permanent buildings, ruins, adjoining and adjacent properties, and all their appurtenances. The valley of Vico, with vineyards and lands; the estate of Sarnanum, with the church of Saint Rufina; the estate of Malvanum; likewise Cava Scamerata and Cava Caprile, with all their appurtenances. The village called Peturanum, with the church of Saint Angel within it, its lands, incense-rents and tributaries residing there, and all its appurtenances.
>
> Likewise the parish church of Saint Martin above Sutri, with vineyards, lands, woods, tenant farmers and tributaries dwelling there, and all its appurtenances. The estate called Capecelo; the estate Fuscignanum; the estate Landenam; the estate Caiolum; Guido’s valley, extending far and wide to the bank; the estate Petella; and the estate called Cartafago, with vineyards, lands, and woods, as it extends to the river Marta, namely to Prando’s ford.
>
> We also confirm to you and your successors the parish church of Saint Andrew in Foro, the parish church of Saint Martin in Columnate, and the parish church of Saint Erasmus beside the seashore near Monte Alto, with their houses, cells or courts, estates and hamlets—by whatever names they may be called—the male and female servants living there and remaining in your service and jurisdiction, and all their appurtenances. Likewise the parish church of Saint Sebastian in Arenula, with the two estates, namely Storatianum and Fabritianum; the estate called Cavonis; the estate Ruginorula; the estate Carvaliolum; the estate Corgitellum; the estate Morazzanum; and also the estate of Formellae.
>
> All these, with their boundaries, limits, and landmarks, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, vineyards, houses, courts, tenant holdings, incense-rents, tributaries residing there, and all things adjacent or belonging to them. Within the maritime district, in the territory of Corneto, the estate called Poppe Lupuli on both sides, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, beside the river Marta, and all its appurtenances. Likewise the estate called Poppe Saint Mary’s, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, its districts and appendages, and all its appurtenances; Poppe near Waldimandia; the lands of Saint Stephen, with all their appurtenances; and the estate called Tureranzanula in its entirety.
>
> The parish church of Saint Mary situated at Tarquinia, with vineyards, lands, meadows, and all its appurtenances. At Ancarana, four estates: namely Monte Vulpium, Bultten, and Saccali, with their *poppes* on both sides of the river Marta and all their appurtenances. The estate called Fultona on both sides, with all its appurtenances.
>
> Furthermore, within the city called Orclae, we confirm to you and your bishopric the parish church of Saint Peter with the two churches of Saint John and Saint Angel; with courts and houses inside and outside the city, lands, vineyards, gardens, fields, meadows, woods, streams, mills, watercourses, and all that belongs to them. We also confirm the hamlet of Saint Peter and the church of Saint Sebastian, with their estates and hamlets and all their appurtenances; likewise the church of Saint Angel at Pietra Ficta, with vineyards, lands, and all its appurtenances.
>
> In like manner we grant and confirm to you, dearest brother Virobo, the holding called Campi, with the church of Saint Mary within it; the estate called Greater Cavi and the other called Lesser Cavi; with lands, vineyards, tenant holdings, compulsory laborers, tributaries, incense-rents, and every payment and rendering which they customarily paid to your predecessors, together with all its appurtenances.
>
> Moreover, on both sides, one half of the holding called Forum Cassii, with vineyards, lands, woods, estates, hamlets, courts, houses, male and female servants, and all its appurtenances. Likewise, on both sides, the holding called Mazzanum, with the parish church of Saint Stephen, vineyards, lands and households, and all its appurtenances; and three ounces from the other half of the aforesaid holding of Forum Cassii, with its male and female servants, hamlets, woods, houses, courts, and gardens; namely, of the following estates: Massa Lutia, Cisoranum, Attevile, Sippizzanum, Casale, Pastorinanum, Fraginanum, the valley of Petracius, the forks of the bishopric, Gemulo, Peculiare, Paparanum, Fornillum, Carnarum, Calianum, the plain of the wolf, the other plain, Moraldus’s crypt, Caiolum, Restrictum, Vilianellum of the monks, Menorella, Fonticela, the valley of Puzzu, and Mount Maurus, with all their adjacent properties and appurtenances and the male and female cultivators residing there.
>
> The court of Saint Lawrence called the *synodochium* [hostel], Cataassim with its estates and hamlets, vineyards, lands, male slaves, female slaves, tenant holdings, tributaries, and all its appurtenances. Within the castle called Viterbo, the parish church of Saint Lawrence with the church of Saint Michael the Archangel; with houses and courts within and outside that castle, estates, hamlets, lands, vineyards, gardens, watermills, streams, fields, meadows, woods, and all their appurtenances.
>
> Moreover, among the estates of the castle of Viterbo, the parish church of Saint Peter in the village of Palenzano, with its churches of Saints Julius and Valentine; the parish church of Saint Andrew in Campo, with the church of Saint Abundius; and the church of Saint Lucy at Solo Cotto. All of these with their estates and hamlets, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, houses, courts, and gardens; the male and female servants dwelling there; their tenant holdings, tributaries, incense-rents, compulsory laborers, and appurtenances; together with the following nineteen estates: Quinzanum, Cardoni, Polleianum, Latrinula, Maternum, the Folian valley, Antonianum, Lucianum, Silianum, Avenule, Messurianum, Cavoni, the court of Folianelli, Cava de Sonsa, the village of Renai, Occani, Pastrinianum, Stratilianum, and the village of Orazanum, with houses, courts, gardens, estates, hamlets, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, woods, adjoining and adjacent properties, all their appurtenances, tributaries, compulsory laborers, and incense-rents.
>
> The parish church of Saint Donatus, which is called [lacuna].

> [Note: Col. 1239D. This place was left blank in the original.]

> … with its estates and hamlets, namely Cortonula, Cardoni, Mount Averso, Recisa, Novelletta, and the Queen’s Valley, with all their appurtenances. The parish church of Saint Lawrence in Palmule, with the churches of Saint Lucy and Saint Euticius; with villages, estates, hamlets, houses, courts, gardens, olive-groves, and the estate called Alzanum and Tucinam; with lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, male and female servants dwelling there, and all their right and jurisdiction.
>
> Indeed, the court of Saint Saviour, which stands beside Lake Bolsena in the territory of Mantano, with lands, woods, vineyards, estates, hamlets, and the fishing rights of that lake: as much as the inhabitants of that court are able to fish, as your predecessors possessed it.
>
> Therefore we most certainly strengthen and in every way confirm to you, beloved and dear brother Bishop Virobo, and to the bishops succeeding you in your bishopric, the parish church of Saint Peter in the village of Pergulata beside the aforesaid lake, with all its churches, estates, and hamlets: namely the church of Saint Mary at Rumiliano, the church of Saint Agnes, the church of Saint Pancras at Nucerino, the church of Saint Andrew in Campo, and the church of Saint Mary where the body of the blessed martyr Flavian rests, with its hamlet and borough round about it; together with all their adjacent properties and appurtenances—namely houses, courts, gardens, lands, vineyards, estates, hamlets, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, chestnut groves, mountains, hills, districts, plains, incense-rents, tributaries, compulsory laborers, and all rights belonging to them.
>
> Likewise the following estates: the valley of the bishopric, Mount Flasconis on both sides, the valley of Saint Lucy, the valley of Orianus, Zuzzanum, and the Round Plain, with all their adjacent properties and appurtenances; moreover the lands and vineyards which appear to lie from the head of the aforesaid borough of Saint Mary as far as the road to Tuscania; and finally the village called Quarantianum on both sides, with churches, courts, houses, crypts, many households, and all its appurtenances.
>
> Within the lake called Bolsena, the island called Martana, with the monastery of Saint Stephen and all their appurtenances. The parish church of Saint Andrew beside the river Marta, with its churches of Saint Vitus, Saint John, and Saint Lawrence; with houses, courts, gardens, vineyards, estates, hamlets, mills, fisheries, reed-beds, and one half of that river in many places for supplying the mills with water, together with the male and female cultivators dwelling there and all its appurtenances. Likewise the following estates: Caiolum, Vallicellae, Silvabubla, the plain of Fontana, Mergone, Metata, Cazzanum, Metianum, the plain of Saint Vitus, Mount Saint Andrew, and Catillianum, with all their adjacent properties and appurtenances—lands, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, houses, courts, male slaves, female slaves, tenant holdings, and tributaries dwelling there.
>
> The holding called [lacuna].

> [Note: Col. 1239D. This place was left blank in the original.]

> … with the parish church of Saint John within it, which is above the river Marta, with vineyards, lands, estates, hamlets, compulsory laborers, incense-rents, and its appurtenances. The holding called the village of Marianus, with the parish church of Saint John, and the following estates: Rizzolanum, the meadow of Poppe Lupuli, Caium Flajanum, Finianum, Sclapplanum, Long Meadow, and Stonum, with houses, courts, lands, gardens, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, tenant holdings and tributaries, and all their appurtenances; together with the estate called Amitinum, with houses, courts, churches, dwellings, lands, vineyards, hamlets, all its appurtenances, and male and female servants dwelling there.
>
> The estate called Campo de Pinis, with the parish church of Saint [lacuna] beside the lake, with lands, vineyards, and its appurtenances.

> [Note: Col. 1240D. This place was left blank in the original.]

> The holding called Olenzana, with the churches of Saint Mary, Saint John, and Saint Felix, with their estates and hamlets and all their appurtenances; likewise the church of Saint Cassian, with the court of Saint Ambrose, situated at Feruleto, with their estates and hamlets, lands, fields, meadows, vineyards, gardens, woods, male and female cultivators dwelling there, and all that belongs to it. The estate called Septinianum with all its appurtenances. In the territory of Castrum, the two estates Amponianum and Astronianum, with their appurtenances. In the hall, the three estates Vicovalle, Paternum, and Tulizanum, with houses, courts, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, and all their appurtenances; likewise the parish church of Saint Lawrence called Intrintilianum, with estates, hamlets, and all its appurtenances. The holding called Soranum, with its estates and hamlets and all its integrity.
>
> We also confirm and strengthen to you, most beloved brother, your bishopric of Tuscania, with lands and all churches and monasteries which appear to lie within the boundaries hereafter set down, and which shall be built in future, whether in cities and castles or in the various towns, holdings, boroughs, and villages; together with jurisdiction over all churches and venerable places, priests and monks, so that through you they may be protected and, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, defended and ordered.
>
> Beginning from the boundaries of your bishopric: namely from the Great Sea, and thence by the river Mignone, as it extends straight to the crypt of Saint Pancras; and as it extends straight to the foot of Leuprand, which lies between the territories of Orclae and Blera; and straight onward to Cava Fardenga; thence to Butten, the aqueduct on the road of the blessed apostle Peter; thence to the summit of the mount called Folianum; and as the road passes over that mount to Civitellae; and comes to Staphile, which divides Orte from the county of Viterbo; and as it comes to the place of Plancula and passes between the territories of Viterbo and Bomarzo; and then proceeds as far as Pietra Ficta; thence comes to the Blood-Stream; proceeds to the stream called Arlinus at Mausileum; thence goes by the lake to Mausileum in the Campo Rosano; thence comes by the church of Saint Maximus; then comes to Saint Bartholomew, situated in Marsuano; then comes to Septinianum; thence to Musileum Caninum; and thence proceeds to Canestrasi; and as it enters Tamone, and that Tamone enters Armine, and thus runs into the sea.
>
> Within these boundaries lie the aforesaid parish churches, monasteries, cities, castles, inheritances, and various territories. Whatever else is enclosed within these boundaries that can in any way belong to your bishopric, from the present fifth indiction we confirm and strengthen to you and your successors for ever. By apostolic censure, under testimony of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no one—whatever dignity or power he may possess, nor any great or small person—shall ever presume in any way to take from your bishopric anything written above or to act against it.
>
> But if anyone, which we do not wish, should with wicked daring attempt to oppose or violate in any respect what we have decreed for the praise of God and the stability of your aforesaid bishopric, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and is to be burned in the punishment of eternal fire with the devil and his most cruel pomp, and with Judas, betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ. But whoever, with pious intent, shall observe and in all things keep this our apostolic constitution, which looks to the worship of God, may he receive in manifold measure the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.
>
> Written by the hand of Nicholas, notary, *regionarius*, and scriniary of our holy Roman Church, in the month of February, fifth indiction. Fare well.
>
> Given on 8 Kalends of March [22 February], through the hand of Leo, primicerius of the supreme Apostolic See, in the sixth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Pope Leo IV in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the aforesaid month and fifth indiction.

Given at Corneto, 4 Kalends of November, in the tenth year.

### CXLIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CAGLIARI

That he shall cause sentences issued against certain persons to be published.  
(Corneto, 6 Kalends of November [27 October].)

You are deservedly comparable to those of whom the prophet says: “They are dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56), since you not only neglect to correct, but even omit to correct, the grave and great excesses of your subjects. This is clearly shown by the fact that, with your eyes conniving, you allowed the incestuous union prohibited by us between the daughter of the marquis of Massa and Hugh de Basso to be contracted.

You may also deservedly be compared to those of whom Truth says: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests” (Luke 9), since you practice deceit under the appearance of respectability, as we have discovered you did in the affair of Gallura. We had thought indeed that your eye was single, containing no part of darkness. But, as we sorrowfully report, an angel of Satan transformed himself into an angel of light, and beneath a sheep’s skin lupine fury concealed itself.

Although you are forgetful and ungrateful for the affection and favor which we have endeavored to show you, nevertheless, still wishing to test whether some spark of devotion and obedience remains in you, by apostolic letters we strictly command you to admonish and induce carefully the aforesaid marquis and Hugh de Basso to dissolve completely the aforesaid incestuous union; solemnly to renew and declare the sentences of excommunication and interdict issued by our authority against the ladies and land of Gallura, and likewise against Lambert of Pisa; and to present yourself before the apostolic presence by the coming feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. Otherwise, know that from that time you are suspended from your pontifical office.

Given at Corneto, 6 Kalends of November, in the tenth year.

### CXLIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES, AND TO ALL CLERGY ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF ARAGON

Concerning the freedom of episcopal elections.  
(Corneto, 3 Kalends of November [30 October].)

[Col. 1243A]

> [Note: Col. 1243. See the addition to book VIII of *On the Harmony of Priesthood and Empire*, chapter 10.]

“It is customary to grant,” etc., as far as “bestow.” For in letters of our dearest son in Christ, Peter, illustrious king of Aragon, we have seen the following contained word for word:

> Peter, by the grace of God king of Aragon, count of Barcelona, and lord of Montpellier, to the venerable archbishop of Tarragona in Christ, and to all bishops, abbots, other prelates of churches, and their communities established in our kingdom and dominion: eternal greeting in the Lord.
>
> Rendering due reverence to the King of kings, through whom kings reign, and wishing to preserve unimpaired freedom for His bride, namely the holy Church, we relinquish, for love of God and of the holy Church and for the remedy of our soul and of the souls of our parents, the very bad custom hitherto observed by us, by which we did not allow the election of prelates to proceed without our counsel and assent. To you, all your successors, and your communities established in all our jurisdiction, we grant for ever, through ourselves and all our successors, free power of election, without any royal assent being required. We reserve only this to ourselves and our successors: that the person freely and canonically elected must be presented to ourselves and our successors as a sign of royal fidelity.

We therefore commend in the Lord this royal devotion, approve the king’s enactment in this matter, confirm it by apostolic authority, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Therefore let no one violate this document of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Corneto, 3 Kalends of November, in the tenth year.

### CXLV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT MARTIN OF THE MOUNT

Concerning the revocation of alienations of the monastery.  
(Given as in the other letter.)

To prevent a matter settled by judicial judgment from slipping back into the difficulty of renewed contention, a judicial determination ought to be set down in writing with an inked pen. Let it therefore be known by these present [Col. 1243D] letters that, having heard and understood all the attestations, instruments, and allegations presented before us in the case pending between your steward on the one side and Fortiguerra and Raynucius, son of Poli Guiddoti, citizens of Viterbo, on the other, concerning the dwelling-sites formerly belonging to Tornampart., and the lands of Risiare and Salicis, with the mill where a fulling-mill was established, we entirely quash the judgment unjustly rendered against the monastery by James and Matthew, judges of Viterbo; and we correct, in the following manner, the judgment insufficiently considered and promulgated against the aforesaid citizens by our venerable brother R., bishop of the city of Castellana, and P. Ismael, then abbot of Saint Andrew [Col. 1244A]: namely, since it is established that your monastery was cheated by more than half the just price in the sale of the aforesaid properties, the said citizens shall either restore the properties mentioned upon receiving back the price, or make up whatever amount shall lawfully be shown to have been lacking from the just price at the time of sale. Therefore let no one … our determination, etc. … But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

CXLVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND. Concerning a cleric promoted by skipping an order. (At Tuscania, 14 Kalends of November.)

By your letters you informed us that, in the time of your predecessor of blessed memory, a certain cleric, induced by the advice of a priest whom he had as a familiar associate [Col. 1244B] to hasten too quickly toward sacred orders, while he was an acolyte, presumptuously caused himself to be promoted to the diaconate, omitting the order of subdeacon. Afterwards, moved by repentance, he disclosed his offence to a certain priest, who enjoined him to serve the Lord in some monastery under the regular habit. After he had remained there for several years, he judged that a bishop should again be consulted about the aforesaid transgression; that bishop, imposing nothing upon him, reserved the matter of such an offence for your judgment. You afterwards enjoined upon him that he should not minister in the office of deacon until he had received the good pleasure of our will concerning what should be done in this matter [Col. 1244C]; and, placing him again in another monastery, you humbly begged us to deign to deal mercifully with him.

Therefore, having fuller confidence in your discretion, we command your fraternity by apostolic writings that, if his own merits otherwise recommend him, after causing him to receive the order of subdeacon which he omitted, you shall thereafter, by our authority and by way of dispensation, grant him permission to minister in the office of deacon.

Given at Tuscania, 14 Kalends of November, in the tenth year.

CXLVII. TO THE SAME. Concerning the election of the Archbishop of Uppsala. (At Corneto, 8 Kalends of November.)

Both through your letters and through those of our dearest son in Christ, S., the illustrious king of Sweden, and of our venerable brothers the suffragans [Col. 1244D], and our beloved sons the chapter of the Church of Uppsala and many others, we have learned that, after the archbishop of Uppsala of blessed memory entered upon the way of all flesh, that Church long remained deprived of a pastor’s office, both because of your absence on pilgrimage and because of the unruliness of the region. But now, through the inspiration of the grace of the Holy Spirit, clergy and people have come together with unanimous consent and petition in favor of a certain chaplain of the aforesaid king, a man named V., certainly learned, adorned with good conduct, and, as you believe, distinguished by virtues.

But because he was not begotten in lawful marriage, you, as a prudent and honorable man, described him in the same letters not as elected but rather as called [Col. 1245A] to the episcopal office. You humbly begged that, since, so far as human judgment can establish, the person seems sufficiently suitable and has been called by the election of the clergy, the consent of the king, and the petition of the people, we might mercifully dispense in his case. You declared that, unless it were advantageous to the Church in question, and unless you believed that king and people would especially thereby be brought to favor the Church and that its liberty would nevertheless be preserved, you would by no means offer prayers for him; for there is no church situated in any part of the world that is subject to so heavy a yoke of servitude because of the unruliness of its people.

When, however, we and our brethren carefully considered the matter, many uncertainties and doubts presented themselves: first, because we do not know how great a defect of birth the said V. suffers, since a manifold and discriminating consideration must be applied in this matter; secondly, because it is not established for us whether the province of Uppsala suffers such a lack of persons that no more suitable person can be found in it for assumption to the archiepiscopal office [Col. 1245B]. In addition, since in that province priests, according to a depraved custom, do not fear to marry women, if, as we have heard, you intend to root out that custom from it, it would at once be unbecoming and absurd for such a person to be assumed to so great an office; held up as an example, he could impede your purpose.

Therefore, considering that in such cases urgent necessity and evident usefulness merit the grace of dispensation, we command your integrity and discretion, in which we have full confidence, by apostolic writings, that, after diligently weighing the circumstances and keeping God before your eyes, you proceed concerning confirmation of his postulation and thereafter his consecration as you judge ought to be done for the glory of the divine name and the advancement of the Christian religion. Moreover, because of your devotion, the need of the Church of Uppsala, and the remoteness of the place, lest that Church be burdened with labors and expenses, we send you a pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—so that, if you judge that a dispensation should be granted, you may confer it upon him according to the form enclosed for you under our bull [Col. 1245D]. Otherwise, do not delay in sending it back to us.

Given at Corneto, 8 Kalends of November, in the tenth year.

CXLVIII. TO P., ARCHPRIEST, AND THE CANONS OF SAINT SIXTUS OF VITERBO. A certain agreement is confirmed. (At Sutri, 18 Kalends of December.)

When a dispute arose between you and our venerable brother Raynerius, bishop of Viterbo, concerning the fourth part of tithes and mortuaries, procurations, offerings, synod dues, and certain other episcopal rights which the same bishop claimed from your church as due to him, you finally reached, through our mediation and amicably, after publication of the witnesses [Col. 1246A] and production of the instruments, the following agreement: both you and your successors shall be obliged to render to the same bishop and his successors only the fourth part of tithes and mortuaries; from all other payments and services that church shall be wholly free and exempt, saving in all things the obedience and reverence which you owe to him as your bishop and to his successors in spiritual matters. But from whatever your donors may henceforth, while of sound mind, give you among the living, you shall not be compelled to grant any portion to the same bishop or his successors.

Therefore, approving the same agreement, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. Therefore let no one … [Col. 1246B] our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Sutri, 18 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

CXLIX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS. Indulgences granted to those fighting against the Albigensians. (At Saint Peter’s, 15 Kalends of December.)

The inveterate corruption of heretical depravity, which is continually growing in the regions of Toulouse, does not cease to produce monstrous offspring. By them, as the corruption of their own madness is transmitted to others, the detestable succession of the condemned immediately revives and sprouts anew. Glorying in the inventions of their own vanity, they despise the doctrines of the right faith; and the more they hear the truth preached to them, the more freely—while abyss calls to abyss and night announces knowledge to night—they suggest to others the fabricated falsehood of their lie, considering themselves singular in their false assertions [Col. 1246C].

These persons, indeed, having, according to the Apostle’s word, an appearance of godliness but utterly denying its power, under the image of religion—which they confess that they alone possess—entice many unwary people by the sweetness of their words and make them conform to their evils. In the Book of Wisdom that woman is designated who, prepared in a harlot’s adornment, cries: “I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread it with painted coverings” (Prov. VII). For heretics, by the texture of heavenly words and the painted ornament of eloquence, promise their hearers a healthful couch on which they may rest with hearts free from the tumult of vices; but they rather construct a place of perdition with the cords of sins. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “The inhabitants of Samaria have worshipped the cows of Beth-aven” (Hos. X). For heretics, who falsely claim to dwell in Samaria—that is, in the keeping of God’s commandments—while they do not understand but attack God’s law, nourish wanton sects of manifold novelty and error.

But when they suffer the deserved punishment of their wickedness, whether in the present or in the future, the people will mourn over them. For the Lord, according to the prophetic word, will strike both the summer house and the winter house, and the ivory houses shall perish: he will strike and scatter both those who, burning with the heat of lust, serve the pleasures of the flesh, and those who, in order to be considered religious by men [Col. 1247A], mortify their flesh by abstaining from certain vices, as well as those who fashion falsehoods in polished language in order to deceive the simple, causing their memory to perish with a crash.

Although we have often, by many means and through many persons, labored to correct this most wicked race of men living in your kingdom, who unite in one purpose for the overthrow of the Christian faith and to reduce to nothing the manifold forms of their deceit, yet, given over to a reprobate mind, they neither heed the reasons set before them, nor are frightened by threats, nor can be softened by entreaties. Therefore, since wounds which do not feel the remedy of poultices must be cut away with iron, and those who despise ecclesiastical correction must be restrained by the arm of secular power [Col. 1247B], we have judged it necessary to invoke your aid, dearest son, to avenge the injury done to Jesus Christ and to capture the little foxes that do not cease to ravage the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts among the simple. We earnestly admonish and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord, enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins: gird yourself manfully and powerfully to root out such degenerate shoots, which, having sent their roots deep down, produce wild grapes and not grapes; and also to remove so harmful a pollution. Thus may the purity of your faith, which you preserve in your mind as a Catholic prince, be declared in deed through vigorous actions, and may the followers of heretical perfidy, crushed by the strength of your power, be brought at least amid the afflictions of war to the knowledge of truth.

For the more graciously the Lord your God has stood by you amid the disturbances of your kingdom and granted you a glorious outcome, establishing your land in the quiet of peace, the more resolutely it is fitting that you oppose his enemies and those of his Church. So that you may attend to these things more securely, we meanwhile receive your land, your people, and their goods under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. If anyone—which we do not believe—should presume wickedly to harass you or yours, we would see to the redress, by canonical censure, of so great an injury as one inflicted principally upon the Apostolic See [Col. 1247C].

Moreover, we will that all the goods of those heretics be confiscated; and that the same remission of sins which we have judged should be granted to those laboring for the aid of the Holy Land shall avail both for you, whether you labor in person or furnish necessary assistance, and for the people of your realm who take up arms to defeat the faithless. We wish you and them to be mindful of that need, lest its assistance be impeded.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 15 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

In nearly the same form to all counts, barons, and knights, and to all Christ’s faithful established in the kingdom of France. Given on the same date.

In nearly the same form to the countesses of … Troyes and … Vermandois and … Blois. Given on the same date.

[Col. 1248A] In nearly the same form to the count of … Bar. Given on the same date.

In nearly the same form to the duke of Burgundy and the counts of … Nevers and … Dreux, and to the noble man G. of Dampierre. Given on the same date.

CL. TO W., BISHOP OF SAINT ANDREW’S. Concerning supplying for the negligence of patrons. (At Sutri, Ides of November.)

Your brotherhood represented in our presence, complaining that certain monks and other religious men hold certain parish churches in your diocese assigned to their own uses, and possess in some others, for which they receive an annual rent, the right of patronage. When these churches become vacant, they neglect to present to you, as they are bound by law to do, chaplains and other clerics to be instituted there [Col. 1248B]. You therefore humbly asked us to provide usefully for you in this matter.

Accordingly, by the authority of these present letters we grant your brotherhood that, if the aforesaid religious men, when churches known to belong to them in the aforesaid ways are vacant, maliciously refuse to present to you within the period prescribed by the canons chaplains or clerics, as they are bound by law to do, you shall have free power, supported by our authority and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, to provide those churches with suitable persons—provided nevertheless that no prejudice to them is thereby generated.

[Col. 1248C] Given at Sutri, Ides of November, in the tenth year.

CLI. TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS. The number of masters of theology at the University of Paris is fixed. (At Sutri, 18 Kalends of December.)

Just as we believe it expedient that in the city of Paris, to which there is a celebrated resort for the study of sacred Scripture, there should be an abundance of masters of theology to break bread for little ones asking for it and refresh hungry souls with the food of God’s word, so it is also fitting that their number be restrained, lest perhaps, because of a burdensome multitude, which has nothing honorable about it, their office either be cheapened or be performed with less order, since God has made all things in number, weight, and measure [Col. 1248D].

Therefore, prudently moved by this consideration, by the authority of the present letters we firmly forbid that the number of masters of theology at Paris exceed eight, unless perhaps great necessity or usefulness requires this. Therefore let no one … our prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Sutri, 18 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

CLII. TO THE SAME. Directions concerning how mandates to provide benefices are to be carried into execution. (Given as in the other letter.)

“It is customary to grant,” etc., as far as “to bestow.” Therefore, since we sometimes entrust to certain persons the examination of persons promoted by you or by your predecessors to sacred orders, for whom we order provision to be made in a suitable benefice [Col. 1249A], by the authority of these present letters we firmly forbid that such examination be conducted unless you or your representative is present, so that you may be permitted to set forth against those being examined whatever you reasonably judge should be alleged. No prejudice shall thereby arise against you from an examination attempted otherwise, unless perhaps, having been lawfully summoned, you neglect, in evasion of our mandate, to attend such examination in person or through a suitable representative. Therefore let no one … our prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

CLIII. TO THE SAME. That monks shall not live alone in monasteries. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1249B]

Since it was decreed in the Lateran Council that monks should not … we command your brotherhood, in whom we have assured confidence, by apostolic writings, that if you find any monk living alone in any church of your diocese subject to you by law, you shall compel him, after a prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal removed, either to return to his monastery or to have some honorable brother dwelling with him.

Given as in the other letter.

CLIV. TO THE SAME. That he should correct the monks and clerics of his diocese. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1249C]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that many grave offences are committed both by monks and other religious men and by secular clerics of your diocese; unless these are corrected by a superior’s file, they will furnish matter for graver transgressions. Although you have general jurisdiction, by reason of the office of bishop entrusted to you, to correct the excesses of your subjects, nevertheless, so that you may execute the duty of your care more freely by the authority of our mandate, we command your brotherhood, in whom we have firm confidence, by apostolic writings, that you correct, with every appeal removed, such matters as you see should be corrected among religious men as well as secular clerics subject to your jurisdiction [Col. 1249D], establishing for their reform whatever is regular and honorable.

Given as in the other letter.

CLV. TO THE SAME. He is given authority to reform the monasteries of his diocese. (At Saint Peter’s, 15 Kalends of December.)

Although the care of all churches rests upon us, we must nevertheless be particularly solicitous for the condition of monasteries, lest the observance of religion in them perhaps be dissolved—an observance which, by the Lord’s disposition, we desire in our times to plant and foster. Certainly, as has been reported to our apostolate, in monasteries [Col. 1250A] and other religious places subject to you by diocesan law, regular seriousness is neglected in food, clothing, conduct, and many other things; and many grave offences are committed there, tending not only to the loss of souls but also to the scandal of many. Moreover, the brethren of those places do not fear to retain private property contrary to the purpose of their profession.

Since these things, if true, ought not to be left uncorrected, we command your brotherhood, in whom we have assured confidence, by apostolic writings, that, after more fully investigating the truth about these and other matters, you correct, with every appeal removed, whatever you know should be corrected, establishing there whatever is regular and honorable.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 15 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

CLVI. TO THE SAME. Concerning the union of the monasteries of Vallis Profunda and Gyf. (At Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of December.)

[Col. 1250B]

You should know that it has come to our ears that the monastery of Deep Valley, situated in your diocese, is burdened by such a lack of temporal resources that its sisters cannot be supported from the goods of that monastery. Consequently, sometimes at the instigation of the enemy of the human race, they do not shrink from committing certain less lawful, indeed grave, acts in order to obtain necessities.
