Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, if this is so, supported by our authority and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, you shall take care to join and unite that monastery to the monastery of Gyf in your diocese, which labors under an equal necessity [Col. 1250C].

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

CLVII. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS. That he should promote J. to the order of subdeacon. (At Saint Peter’s, 9 Kalends of December.)

From the report of our beloved son J., a scholar, you should know that we have learned that formerly his mother, distressed by many hardships in his birth, vowed to the Lord that whatever child she bore she would assign to the Lord’s portion. Wishing afterwards to fulfill her promise, she caused the same J. to be instructed in letters and trained in the liberal arts. But J. himself, not differing from his mother’s will, after receiving the minor orders, urgently asked you to promote him to subdeacon. Yet, although he possesses a patrimony from which he can be suitably supported, and a certain kinsman of his was prepared to grant him one hundred solidi annually for his ordination, so that he could live honorably from the aforesaid resources, you refused to comply with the prayers offered [Col. 1250D].

We, however, considering his pious purpose, command your fraternity by apostolic writings that, if this is so and provided he is suitable, you do not delay to promote him to the order of subdeacon.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 9 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

CLVIII. TO THE CITIZENS AND THE WHOLE PEOPLE OF TORTOSA. He exhorts them to revere the Church of Tortosa. (At Saint Peter’s, 4 Kalends of December.)

[Col. 1251A]

It has come to our hearing, as our venerable brother G., bishop of Tortosa, has reported, that, because you refused fully to pay tithes and first-fruits, he formerly subjected you to a sentence of excommunication. In contempt of that excommunication, you presumed to bury almost one hundred bodies of the dead in the church cemetery. Afterwards, when judgment had been pronounced in favor of the same bishop through the course of justice concerning those tithes and first-fruits, you promised, under oath, that you would obey the mandate of the Church. But later absolved by the same bishop, you took care, as he had directed, to disinter the buried bodies, wishing thus to expiate your former contempt.

But as time went on, some of you turned back and, changing the devotion you had shown into hatred, to the destruction of your souls, at the prompting of the brothers of the Hospital of Amposta, presumed, after abandoning the cemetery of the aforesaid church, to choose burial among those brothers with a pledge of faith; thereby seeking to inflict injury upon that church [Col. 1251B]. Finally, some of them, returning to conscience and wishing to do penance for what had been done, confessed to the same bishop that this had been attempted by them to the harm of their Church; but others persist obstinately in their contrived malice.

Since it seems unworthy that the Church of Tortosa, your mother, which nourishes your souls with spiritual food, should find you not sons but stepchildren, we ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding such an oath, which you rashly swore out of hatred to the injury of the Church of Tortosa, you honor that Church according to the customary practice both in life and in death, and return to your former state.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 4 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

CLIX. TO ALL BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ENGLAND AND WALES. He exhorts them to defend ecclesiastical liberty. (At Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of December.)

[Col. 1251D]

[Note: [Col. 1251] See Matthew Paris, under the year 1208, and *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 132.] Although the virtue of obedience is great because of the goods that follow from it, the evils known to arise from its contrary, disobedience, seem in some measure to magnify it; for just as the comparison of a good thing makes an evil appear worse, so an evil compared with a good often adds some praise to that good.

For disobedience expelled the first-created man from paradise; Christ’s obedience finally came to his aid—Christ who, taking the form of a servant, became obedient for us unto death. Again, the earth, opening, swallowed alive the sons of Korah, who stubbornly resisted Moses’ commands [Col. 1252A]; and the sword of the Philistines slew the sons of the priest Eli, who, by despising their father’s warnings, neglected to correct their error. But to Abraham the Lord said: “By myself I have sworn, because you obeyed my voice and did not spare your only son, I will bless you and multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). Likewise the maiden Rebecca, when she humbly obeyed in watering the camels, deserved, upon receiving earrings and bracelets, to be joined in marriage to Isaac.

Moreover, the prophet’s speech to a rebellious people shows that one may earn merit by obeying or by not obeying: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you” [Col. 1252B] (Isa. I). Samuel too is recorded to have said to Saul: “Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, rather than that his voice should be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams; because resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. XV.22).

Therefore, lest you fall into the vice of disobedience, you must hold firmly to the virtue of obedience. You are bound to defend ecclesiastical liberty voluntarily, not merely because you have been compelled to do so by a special command, but by the obligation of your pastoral office; and to set yourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord against those coming up from the opposing side. Otherwise, if the word of the Lord in your mouth is bound and you cannot—or rather, will not—bark like mute dogs, you will appear to be among those of whom the Prophet says: “The children of Ephraim, drawing the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. LXXVII).

You must not in any way fear to fight for justice, because blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake; for when they have been tested, they shall receive the crown of life. If, therefore, any adversity threatens you because of it, you should rejoice rather than grieve, after the example of the Apostles, who, as Scripture testifies, “went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were accounted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V). For it is glorious not only for a bishop but for any Christian to be afflicted for a cause not shameful but commendable in the Lord, as the Apostle Peter testifies, saying: “Let no one suffer as a thief; but if, while doing good and blessing, you endure harassment, this is grace before God” [Col. 1252D] (1 Pet. IV).

Behold, a command to defend ecclesiastical liberty is laid upon you, that your obedience may become known; and perhaps persecution is imminent, that your patience may become known to your neighbors. Thus, whoever fears becoming a transgressor will at least render a fearful obedience; but whoever hopes for a reward from it will display a meritorious obedience. Then, if persecution comes, it will bring you testing, so that your courage may serve as an example to others; and it will indeed bring reward, so that each may gain a measure of recompense according to the measure of affliction [Col. 1253A].

Accordingly, if you pursue Christ’s cause from the heart, he will give you strength and courage, so that, preferring divine fear to human fear, you may revere the heavenly King more than the earthly one. Do not flatter him along with those who sew cushions under his elbow with a flattering hand; do not merely refuse to comply with him in that by which he endeavors vainly to empty the Church’s authority of effect, but also diligently endeavor at the proper time to draw him back from such a purpose. Do not doubt that for a time he will be displeased with you for the defense of justice; for, according to the Apostle, if you pleased everyone, you would not be servants of Christ. This work of piety will not bring you his hatred, but will advance you toward his love. For when he comes to himself and adopts sounder counsel, he will hold you dear for the purity of your counsel, but will hate those by whose wicked prompting he is now led astray; and thus, finally healed by a healing hand, he will recognize how contrary efforts have aggravated the sickness of his mind through the counsels of the malicious and healed it through the remedies of apostolic solicitude [Col. 1253B].

We too, who act toward him in place of physicians, will receive his thanks; and he will finally praise the effect of the medicine whose bitterness he had formerly dreaded. Recognizing that we loved him with the sincerest charity, he will confess that, when one who is loved is chastised, mercy is then exercised toward him. For love has its wounds, which are sweeter when they are inflicted more bitterly.

Since it has been brought to our hearing that some of you show yourselves lukewarm and lax in the affair of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church—in which is involved not only the liberty of Canterbury but also that of the whole English Church—we earnestly admonish and exhort you, commanding you strictly by apostolic letters that, laying aside every worldly fear, you take care to show yourselves such in this affair that by your constancy ecclesiastical liberty may be defended; and, as zeal for the house of the Lord makes you waste away, charity kindled through it may make you triumph over its persecutors. We hope that the Lord will impose a glorious end upon his cause [Col. 1253D], over which indeed all who persevere steadfastly will rejoice together.

For we, who would not shrink from fighting even to death for the justice of this cause, if it were expedient, shall see to the correction of the presumption of any persons who perhaps—which we do not believe—may presume in a contumacious spirit to oppose our commands, so that, when fear is transmitted to posterity, such insolence shall not pass into an example but their correction may terrify all.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 14 Kalends of December, in the tenth year.

CLX. TO ALL NOBLE MEN, THE MAGNATES ESTABLISHED IN ENGLAND. He commends to them the king of England, and urges them not to injure ecclesiastical liberty. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 1254A]

If you preserve the fidelity owed to our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English, know that this is pleasing both to God and to us. Yet you must adhere faithfully to an earthly king in such a way that you do not in any way offend the heavenly one. The sincerity of your loyalty should therefore be vigilant in recalling the same king, by faithful counsel, from the purpose which he seems to have conceived against God, by persecuting our venerable brother the archbishop of Canterbury and the church committed to him [Col. 1254B].

[Note: [Col. 1253D] See Matthew Paris under the years 1207 and 1208.] So far as lies in you, do not allow him to cast aside the counsel of piety and go into the counsel of the wicked, whose thoughts shall all perish in one day, while the counsel of the Lord—which they endeavor to nullify in vain—remains forever. Certainly, since according to evangelical truth you cannot serve two masters, it undoubtedly befits you, when the aforesaid king sets himself against God, not to support him in this at all. Preferring divine fear to human fear, do not flatter him with those who sew cushions under his elbow with a flattering hand; nor doubt that he may for a time be displeased with you for the cause of justice, since this work of piety will not bring you his hatred but will finally advance you toward his love. For, indeed, when [Col. 1254C] he comes to himself and adopts sounder counsel, he will hold you dear for the purity of your counsel, but will hate those, etc., as in the other letter, down to “inflicted more bitterly.”

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and more earnestly exhort your nobility, enjoining it upon you for the remission of sins by apostolic letters, that you press the same king with faithful persuasions and salutary counsels: that, by no means following the way of Rehoboam, he may not reject more mature counsels; that he may despise as flatterers and expel as corrupters those who, by making his head fat with the oil of the sinner, encourage him in evil; and that, recalling that Uzzah, because he stretched out his hand toward the ark—devoutly indeed, but unworthily—was struck by the Lord, he may not presume to lay hand upon ecclesiastical rights [Col. 1254D]. Otherwise, may he who permitted Belshazzar’s kingdom, by the judgment of the writing hand, “Mane, thecel, phares” (“numbered, weighed, divided”; Dan. V), to be unexpectedly seized by the Persians, be gravely angered with him on account of his Church, which he plans vainly to humble. Rather, let him consider God’s gifts: God, magnifying him by his kindness in the sight of kings, has through the favor of the Roman Church magnificently enlarged his name and power among the other princes of the world.

You therefore, whose fidelity and prudence the needs of king and kingdom ought effectively to experience, should meet the purpose of the aforesaid king faithfully and prudently in this crisis of evil, so that you do not suffer yourselves and his kingdom to be brought into that disturbance from which—God forbid!—it may not easily be delivered [Col. 1255A]. For we, who would not shrink from fighting even to death for the justice of this cause, should it perhaps be expedient, do not intend to withdraw the apostolic hand from the defense of ecclesiastical liberty. That hand indeed is not shortened; rather, through God’s grace it is so extended that it will be able to impose upon anyone against whom it is, by his deserts, brought to bear spiritually and temporally an immense weight of oppression.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CLXI. TO THE BISHOPS OF LONDON, ELY, AND WORCESTER. That they shall cause the sentence of interdict to be observed by all. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 1255B] Lest, under the pretext of liberty or of any privilege whatsoever, anyone refuse to observe the sentence of interdict which, for the business of the Church of Canterbury, we have ordered to be promulgated throughout all England, if necessary, through the prudent care of your solicitude, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhoods by repeated letters that, if in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic mandate you see that the said sentence must be promulgated, setting aside every recourse to objection, appeal, and excuse, you shall subject alike to that sentence all churches of seculars and regulars, of Hospitallers and Templars, and also of whatsoever religious persons. And, since in our earlier letters we made no mention of the churches established in Wales, we will and command that [Col. 1255C] by the authority of the present letters you proceed similarly against them, every impediment of objection and appeal being removed, since they too are subject to the metropolitan see of Canterbury.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CLXII. TO THE BISHOP AND ARCHDEACON OF ORVIETO. A certain case concerning Viterbo is committed to them. (At Saint Peter’s, 27 November.)

[Note: [Col. 1255D] See above, letter 145.] Since the case which was being disputed before us for some time between the steward of the monastery of Saint Martin of Monte Viterbo, on the one side, and F. and R., citizens of Viterbo, on the other, concerning the holdings formerly belonging to Tornampartis, the lands of Rasiare and Salicis, and the mill where a fulling-mill was made, had been brought before us, we, having understood the arguments of both parties and diligently examined the depositions, found that the monastery itself had been deceived in the sale of the aforesaid things by more than half their just price. We therefore decreed by judgment that the aforesaid citizens should either restore the properties mentioned upon receipt of the price, or make up whatever was lawfully shown to have been lacking from the just price at the time of sale. Therefore, since . . . the abbot and brethren of the same place intend to prove by witnesses [Col. 1256A] the value of the aforesaid properties at the time of the sale, we command you by the authority of these presents, within three months, excluding appeal, to receive the witnesses whom either party may see fit to produce, hear the case, and remit it to us with adequate documentary preparation; and you shall set the parties a suitable term within which they are to appear before us to receive judgment. But if the party of the monastery produces, in order to prove this point, the same witnesses whom it produced to prove another point, you shall nevertheless take care to receive them, because it is one thing to have proved the extent of the loss caused by deception, and another to prove the amount of the value.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 27 November, in the tenth year.

CLXIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF SENLIS AND ARRAS, AND THE ABBOT OF LAGNY. Concerning the election of the bishop of Meaux. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1256B]

Since the votes of the Church of Meaux divided into two parties, some electing the cantor of Meaux, while others petitioned for the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève as pastor, we, without hearing the matters alleged on either side, judged that justice required both the cantor’s election and the abbot’s postulation to be rejected—not on account of any defect or fault in either person, but because of the indiscreet and disorderly procedure attempted contrary to canonical constitutions. But lest the Church of Meaux remain any longer [Col. 1256C] deprived of a pastor’s consolation, we command you by apostolic letters, under injunction, to go to that Church; and, having summoned the canons, examine each person’s will. If either the whole chapter, or its greater and sounder part, agrees within eight days upon a suitable person, especially one from that church itself, you shall confirm his election, whether he is a subdeacon, deacon, or priest. Otherwise, strengthened by our authority, you shall appoint and grant them as prelate a learned, prudent, and honourable man, restraining any opponents by ecclesiastical censure. But if not all are present, two of you, every obstacle of appeal removed, etc.

[Col. 1256D] Given as in the other letter.

CLXIV. That a subdeacon may be elected bishop. [Note: [Col. 1255D] This letter, because it is general, has no title in the register, nor in the third collection. But because the decretal preceding it in the third collection is addressed to the bishop of Modena, Raymond likewise addressed this one to him. It was given [Col. 1256D] on the occasion of the election of the bishop of Meaux, as may be inferred from letter 163.]

[Note: [Col. 1256D] Chapter *A multis*, Extra, *On the Age and Qualifications of Those to Be Ordained*. See the addition to book VIII of *On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire*, chapter 13.] Many persons have repeatedly doubted whether a subdeacon can be elected bishop. For Pope Urban I decreed that no one should be elected bishop unless he be found to be in sacred orders and living religiously. “By sacred orders,” he says, “we mean the diaconate and the priesthood. For the primitive Church is recorded as having had these alone. But concerning subdeacons, because they too minister [Col. 1257A] at the altars, when necessity requires, we permit [their election], provided that they are of proven learning and religious character; but we do not permit this to be done without the licence of the Roman pontiff or metropolitan.”

These words indicate that Urban, referring to the condition of the primitive Church, in which the order of subdeacon was by no means called sacred, established that an election from among subdeacons could not be held except for a useful reason, and then only with the permission of the metropolitan or Roman pontiff. But since today the subdiaconate is counted among the sacred orders, as Pope Urban II stated in these words:

[Note: [Col. 1257D] Distinction 32, chapter 11, *Erubescant*.] “Let the impious be ashamed and understand that, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, those placed in sacred orders—the priesthood, diaconate, and subdiaconate—if they do not live chastely, are to be excluded from every dignity of those same [Col. 1257B] ranks.” And again:

[Note: [Col. 1257D] Same distinction, chapter 12, *Nemo*.] “Let no one be allowed to approach a sacred order unless he is either a virgin or of proven chastity, and has had, up to the subdiaconate, one wife who was a virgin. And, in the manner of a deacon and priest, a subdeacon must observe continence, as was decreed in the Sixth Synod: if any of those entering the clergy wishes to unite himself with a woman by marital right, he must do so before the order of subdeacon.” And since blessed Gregory is recorded to have established that bishops must not presume to make anyone a subdeacon unless he has promised to live chastely, we, wishing to remove matter for dispute on this point, decree that a subdeacon may freely be elected bishop, just as may a deacon or priest.

CLXV. TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS. Concerning appeals to the Apostolic See. (At Saint Peter’s, 12 December.)

[Col. 1257C]

[Note: [Col. 1258D] Chapter *Sollicitudinem*, *On Appeals*.] You prudently discharge the solicitude of your pastoral office when, concerning doubtful points of law, you seek instruction from the response of the Apostolic See. Indeed, as we have learned from your report, while two persons were litigating before their bishop, one of them appealed to the Apostolic See. The bishop, refusing to defer to the appeal made, treated the appellant as contumacious and bound him with the bond of excommunication. The latter sought justice against the bishop from his metropolitan, asserting [Col. 1257D] that, after an appeal to us had been lawfully lodged, the bishop had excommunicated him and caused him publicly to be announced as excommunicated. He requested restoration by the metropolitan to the condition in which he had been at the time of the appeal—namely, that he be declared absolved—and added that he did not renounce the appeal lodged, but wished to pursue it.

Your brotherhood therefore asked us whether the metropolitan may take cognizance of such a complaint; whether, if he finds that the man appealed lawfully, he ought to declare him absolved; and whether, should the bishop appeal before the archbishop to prevent the absolution of the man whom he had excommunicated, such an appeal must be deferred to.

[Col. 1258A] We therefore answer your inquiry as follows: just as the metropolitan has no power at all to take cognizance of an appeal lodged to us, so neither may he take cognizance of matters altered after that appeal, provided that those matters cannot be considered without considering the appeal at the same time, or without considering matters recognized as touching the cause of the appeal. In such a case, if the metropolitan should perhaps presume to take up the matter, the bishop could indeed have recourse to the benefit of appeal. For it belongs to the office of the person who is to take cognizance of the appeal prudently to correct what he finds to have been attempted against it.

But if it were perhaps notorious that the bishop’s command had been indiscreet or unjust, and that the subject was not bound to obey it, and if consequently it were evident to him that the subject had lawfully appealed, the archbishop may, by metropolitan authority, declare that the subject was unreasonably struck with the sword of anathema. But when the excommunicated man who had appealed, in the manner prescribed, brings an action against the bishop before the archbishop, so that he may take cognizance of the injury inflicted upon him by the bishop, the metropolitan himself may exercise jurisdiction to hear the case, since that man seems tacitly to renounce the prosecution of the appeal. But if by word or deed he declares that he wishes to pursue the appeal, as was stated above in the proposed case, he is not to be heard as seeking contradictory remedies and acting against himself.

[Col. 1258C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 12 December, in the tenth year.

CLXVI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT-BERTIN. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (At Saint Peter’s, 20 November.)

To the just requests, etc., as far as “assenting to the prayers.” We confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the grant which Baldwin, of blessed memory, count of Flanders, made to your monastery of Saint-Bertin concerning mills, insofar as it was made without prejudice to another’s right and is known to be contained in his charter. For fuller evidence of the matter, we have thought fit to insert that charter word for word into this page of ours.

> “I, Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, wish it to be known to present and future persons that, when, on the advice of certain persons, I proposed to build mills within the castle of Saint-Omer, near the monastery of Saint-Bertin—mills which, as had been represented to me, I thought I could make without anyone’s loss or injury—the abbot of Saint-Bertin came to me, showing me the privilege of Robert the Younger, count of Flanders. It contained the provision that no one except the church of Saint-Bertin might build mills between Arques, Bourbourg, and Lodic; and Pope Calixtus confirmed this by the privilege shown to me, strictly commanding, under threat of anathema, that no one presume to act against it.
>
> “Therefore, since for the salvation of my soul I had undertaken the journey to Jerusalem, and had it in my purpose and will to do justice to all rather than injury to anyone, I judge that the writing which the brethren of Clairmarais were said to have obtained from me concerning this matter must, by this present writing, be revoked, lest any injury may hereafter be inflicted thereby upon the church of Saint-Bertin. And I confirm anew, by the authority of these presents, the privilege of the aforesaid Robert, my predecessor, so that the brethren of the church of Saint-Bertin may always pray for me and my wife. Done in the year of the Lord 1202, 6 April.”

Let no one therefore . . . our confirmation, etc. But if anyone [Col. 1259B] should do so, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 20 November, in the tenth year.

CLXVII. TO THE ELECT OF THÉROUANNE, THE PROVOST OF WATTEN, AND THE DEAN OF SAINT-OMER, IN THE DIOCESE OF THÉROUANNE. The agreement made between the monasteries of Saint-Bertin and Clairmarais is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 13 December.)

On behalf of the beloved sons, the abbots and convents of Saint-Bertin and Clairmarais, a petition was made to our Apostolic See that we should deign to strengthen by apostolic protection a certain settlement made between them concerning a certain marsh and the complaints stated in the letters of arbitration, and secured by a specified penalty. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters to cause that settlement, as it was prudently made without wrongdoing and voluntarily accepted by both parties, to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside; restoring to its due condition whatever you find unlawfully attempted contrary to the terms of the aforesaid arbitration. Notwithstanding any letters prejudicial to truth, etc. But if not all are present . . . you, son elect, with one of them, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of December [13 December], in the tenth year.

CLXVIII. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF DURHAM. Privileges are granted to them. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1259D]

The most holy Roman Church, which shows herself favourable and gracious to all, customarily fortifies in a special manner with the shield of her protection, in matters not departing from the path of reason, those against whom the calumny of wicked men is known to rage. Therefore, since, as was represented to us on your behalf, the archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses you have possessions sometimes pronounce sentences of excommunication and interdict against you, your churches, and your people according to the arbitrary will of their own pleasure, we, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for your tranquillity, forbid by the authority of these presents [Col. 1260A] any archbishop or bishop to presume to pronounce sentences of excommunication or interdict against you or your churches without a manifest and reasonable cause. Let no one therefore . . . our prohibition, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

CLXIX. TO THE DEAN OF BEAUNE. He commits simony who bequeaths his goods to a church on condition that he obtain a prebend in it. (At Saint Peter’s, 3 December.)

Your discretion moved us to seek advice on whether, if someone offers certain goods of his own to a church, asking that during his lifetime he may be allowed to hold those goods in that church as a prebend, those goods ought to be received when so offered, [Col. 1260B] and whether that clerk may be admitted as a canon of the same church without the taint of simony.

[Note: [Col. 1259D] Chapter *Tua nos*, *On Simony*.] We therefore answer your devotion as follows. If a clerk gives or offers his goods subject to a condition or agreement that he may thereafter retain them as a prebend and be admitted as a canon, such an offering or reception cannot take place without the taint of simony, since, according to the canonical sanctions, every bargain and agreement must cease in such matters. But if he offers some of his goods simply and without any agreement or condition, humbly requesting that he be admitted as a canon and permitted to retain those goods during his life as a prebend, and the clerics of that church consent simply, such a reception may beyond doubt take place without any scruple of simoniacal wickedness.

Although [Col. 1260C] we have thought fit to answer thus, because it has been given to us to judge only manifest matters, nevertheless, if the person who makes such a donation is motivated by the intention of acquiring spiritual things by means of the temporal goods which he offers, and if the clerics who admit him as a brother would not have admitted him unless they were to receive temporal advantage, undoubtedly both he and they are judged guilty before the strict Judge, who searches hearts and knows secrets.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 December, in the tenth year.

CLXX. TO THE BISHOP AND DEAN OF SENLIS, AND THE ABBOT OF CHÂALIS IN THE DIOCESE OF SENLIS. Concerning the right of the abbot of Carroffe in the monastery of Andres. (At Saint Peter’s, 6 December.)

[Col. 1260D]

[Note: [Col. 1260D] See vol. IX of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, pp. 564, 567, 568, 575, and chapter *Cum dilectus*, *On Custom*.] Whereas, by a privilege of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, which was formerly presented to us and inspected, it has been granted to the beloved sons, the prior and convent of the monastery of Saint Saviour and Saint Rotrude at Andres, that, upon the death of the abbot of that monastery, no one may be set over it by any craft of deceit or by force, except the person whom the brethren, or their sounder counsel, judge according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict to be elected; and whereas, at the petition of the same prior and convent, we granted them letters concerning this matter and took care strictly to forbid [Col. 1261A] anyone rashly to assail or molest them concerning that grant: they and their successors are permitted now and henceforth, when the church is vacant of an abbot, to set over themselves by regular election a suitable person from their own body or elsewhere as pastor, to be humbly presented to the monastery of Carroffe, so that he may receive confirmation from it and render it the reverence due to it.

But recently a messenger of the Church of Carroffe came before us and stated that the place where the Church of Andres is founded, from the time when it first had monks, was granted in alms to the Church of Carroffe and long remained its priory. Yet at last, at the petition of the person who had made the alms-gift, it consented that it should become an abbey, be subject to it in full right, and always request and receive its abbot from the monastery mentioned. This institution was confirmed by several Roman pontiffs. But in the time of the aforesaid Alexander, our predecessor, no mention having been made of any of these matters, they obtained from him the said privilege in order that they might regularly set a suitable person over themselves as abbot; yet they have not hitherto used it.

Now, however, when their abbot had been transferred to another church [Note: [Col. 1261D] That is, to the Church of Ham.], they sought, deceitfully, to obtain from the Church of Carroffe permission to elect from among themselves only once and to present the elected man to that church; for this they offered no small sum of money both to the abbot and to the monks, as well as new revenues for the church. But when their petition was by no means admitted, and the bishop of Thérouanne, of good memory, had commanded them under penalty of excommunication to elect within a specified period, as they were accustomed, from the monastery of Carroffe, and the abbot had appealed to our hearing and set a term that they should change nothing concerning the election to be made from the ancient and approved custom, they, concealing all the aforesaid matters, obtained from us the aforesaid prohibition; and, before obtaining it, nevertheless made an election.

Furthermore, they granted to the noble count of Guînes [Note: [Col. 1261D] Guînes.], under whose lordship they are, letters of the chapter concerning this matter, that henceforth they might not elect without him. Thus they alienate the goods of the church through gifts and offerings, and undertake many acts [Col. 1261D] which can scarcely be revoked. Since, however, full proof of these matters could not be made to us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to summon before you those who should be summoned and diligently inquire into the truth of all the foregoing. If the parties consent, bring the case to a canonical conclusion, appeal being set aside. Otherwise, reduce to writing what you find and take care to send it to us enclosed under your seals, setting the parties a suitable term within which they are to appear before us to receive judgment. But witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding any letters [Col. 1262A] prejudicial to truth and justice, etc. But if not all are present . . . you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 6 December, in the tenth year.

CLXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. Concerning the authority of metropolitans and appeal. (At Saint Peter’s, 19 December.)

[Note: [Col. 1262D] Chapter *Licet*, *On the Office of the Ordinary Judge*.] Although, in correcting offences according to the canonical sanctions, recourse to appeal is excluded, and consequently our venerable brother the bishop of Paris received from us a mandate to inquire into and correct, appeal being removed, those matters which he finds require correction among monks and other religious men and also secular clerics subject to his jurisdiction, who are alleged to commit many grave acts tending [Col. 1262B] not only to the loss of souls but also to the scandal of many; and to establish for their reform whatever is regular and honourable: nevertheless, since it neither was nor ought to have been our intention to derogate from your jurisdiction by such a mandate, we have thought fit to declare by the authority of these presents that, if perhaps in investigations to be made by that bishop—not as a delegate, but as an ordinary—a case should arise in which an appeal to the metropolitan see is lawful, we do not wish the occasion of the aforesaid mandate to derogate in any way from your authority, so as to prevent an appeal being made to you as metropolitan.

You, however, must neither yourself impede nor allow others to impede the bishop from carrying out the duty of his office in correcting his subjects’ offences; and, if in a permitted case an appeal is made to you, proceed prudently and justly in the cause of the appeal.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 19 December, in the tenth year.

CLXXII. TO THE BISHOPS OF WORCESTER, ELY, AND HEREFORD. Concerning the affair of the archbishop of York and the bishop of Durham. (At Saint Peter’s, 18 December.)

We believe that the reading of the divine books is not so foreign to the hearing of royal majesty that it has not heard Luke recount that King Herod stretched out his hand to afflict [Col. 1262D] certain persons of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1262D] See book II, letter 87.] Would that the detestable memory of that king move our most dear son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English, so that what he ought to condemn in that man by religious judgment, he may correct in himself by maturer deliberation. For a cry has reached us, and has spread through many parts of the world, not without detriment to the royal reputation, that, led astray by wicked counsel, he did not fear to stretch out his hand against the Church. By grievously harassing our venerable brother, the archbishop of York, in many ways, he caused his movable and immovable goods to be plundered and seized; and through most impious officials he caused the most burdensome exactions to be extorted from his people, officials who seized the bodies of those resisting him and likewise confiscated their goods. Finally, although that archbishop and the bishop of Durham, with bended knees, supplicated him concerning this matter, forgetting royal gentleness, he despised their entreaty—indeed, the reverence owed to the Creator in their persons.

Since it is fitting that we, following His example, should rebuke on behalf of the meek of the earth Him who did not permit a man to harm His servants and rebuked kings on their account, we have thought fit earnestly to request and admonish the royal serenity to consider what is worthy of a king and cause full and due satisfaction to be rendered to the aforesaid archbishop, his people, and the Church—indeed, to God. Therefore we command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters [Col. 1263B] to present to the said king the letters which we are sending him on this matter, prudently admonish him to this effect, and effectively induce him to comply.

Otherwise, however much we love him in the bowels of Christ and desire to show deference to the royal honour, since we must not fail ecclesiastical liberty for the sake of human favour—a liberty which our Lord Jesus Christ purchased with His blood—we will and command that, unless at your admonition he fulfils what we have set forth, you subject the entire province of York to ecclesiastical interdict and cause it to be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction has been made, restraining opponents, appeal being set aside, by ecclesiastical censure. But if not all are present, etc., two of you, etc.

[Col. 1263C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 18 December, in the tenth year.

CLXXIII. TO I. DE LONGCHAMP, ARCHDEACON OF ROUEN. Agents are granted to him in his illness. (At Saint Peter’s, 12 December.)

Since, according to the Apostle, we ought to become weak with the weak, you, hoping to find in our compassion solace for your suffering, humbly informed us that, being sometimes afflicted with grave bodily weakness, you are accustomed to manage your affairs less advantageously; and that your relatives have on several occasions presumed, under the pretence of guardianship, to keep you in custody on account of such illness, so that they might more freely [Col. 1263D] appropriate your goods to themselves. Therefore, since certain of those relatives have attempted to alienate your revenues, although you now enjoy health, you nevertheless fear lest what has sometimes happened may happen again. You humbly requested that we deign to grant you as agents the beloved sons, the abbots of Gresten and Ardennes, and the prior of Saint Barbara.

We therefore, considering that we ought to assist weaker members with a more devoted care of compassion, appoint the aforesaid men as your agents, strictly forbidding by the authority of these presents anyone, without their consent, to dare to detain you or in any way prejudicially administer your goods or revenues. Let no one therefore . . . our prohibition, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

[Col. 1264A] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 12 December, in the tenth year.

CLXXIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CARROFFE. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (At Saint Peter’s, 12 December.)

It is customary to grant, etc., as far as “assent.” We confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery by apostolic authority, and strengthen with the protection of this present writing, the right which you are known to hold in the abbey of Ham; the church of Saint Christina of Beureria; the church of Saint Vedast of Eka; the chapel of Saint Peter; the right which you have in the tithe of the parishes of Beureria and Eka; the lands, houses, tithes, people, revenues, and other possessions which you hold in those parishes and at Gotnay, Vendin, Sevebenghe, Hersin, Hesdinol, Nod, Wandericurt, Werkin, Seins, Belgin, Bruay, Ruit, Pernes, Perti, [Col. 1264B] Tungri, Pinkeneham, Chokes, Rosbecque, Meternes, Enes, and Blessy; the church of Saint Leodegar of Aloannes; the chapel of Losinghem; the tithe of the livestock of the aforesaid villages of Aloannes and Losinghem; and the lands, meadows, revenues, people, and the whole jurisdiction of the aforesaid village of Aloannes—all of which lie in the dioceses of Arras and Thérouanne.

In the bishopric of Amiens: the village of Bouveresse, with its church, lands, wood, tithe, and every lordship; the right of the personate (*personatus*) of the church; and one third of the tithe of the entire parish of Formeries.

In the archbishopric of Reims: the demesne village, with its parish church, chapel, tithes, lands, vineyards, houses, people, revenues, and meadows; the church of Saint Euphrasia with the lands, tithes, and other rights [Col. 1264C] which you possess in that parish; the tithe of Corlandin; what you hold in the village of Besaines; and whatever lordship, jurisdiction, census-payment, and revenue you have in the aforesaid parishes and their appurtenances.

In the bishopric of Beauvais: the village of Fresnoy, with its church, tithe, lands, vineyards, people, revenues, and other appurtenances; the church, and one fourth of the entire village, parish, common jurisdiction, and lordship, together with all proceeds and forfeitures, of Audencourt; all the land of Renaud Bugin; half the arable lands; the whole tithe of all lands held from the lords of Audencourt; half the entire land-rent from the same holding; and one fourth [Col. 1264D] of the entire land, lordship, and jurisdiction of Bellencourt. As you justly and peacefully possess all these things, we confirm them to you and through you to your monastery by apostolic authority, and strengthen them with the protection of this present writing. Let no one therefore . . . our confirmation, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 12 December, in the tenth year.

CLXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF ST ANDREWS AND HIS SUCCESSORS, TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (At Saint Peter’s, 21 December.)

We have been raised, though by insufficient merits, by the providence of the heavenly dispensation to the governance of the universal Church, so that we should extend the gaze of our care over the entire body of the Church and afford apostolic assistance to our brethren and fellow bishops, both those near and those far away, lest through remoteness of place anyone lack the care or protection of the Apostolic See. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of St Andrews, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of bishops, the gifts of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

In Fife: Kilrymont, with the whole shire; Derveisin; Uhtredinunesin; the island of Loch Leven, with its appurtenances; Munemel; Terineth; Morcambus; Methkil; Kilecincath; Muccard; Pethgob, with the lands of the churches; Strathteihten; Rescolpin; Cas; Dulbrudet; Russin; Losse; and, near Perth, Lungportin.

In Marr and Buchan: Munemusch, Culsamuel, Elon, with the lands of their churches and all their appurtenances.

In Lothian: Listune, Egglesmanekin, [Col. 1265C] Keldeleth, Raththen, Lessuade, Wedale, Clerkintun, Thiningan with its appurtenances, and Brocchesmuthe.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors the possessions and revenues which are in Can and Cunevet, assigned to the bishop’s table, as you now justly and canonically possess them. Furthermore, by this present document we grant you permission lawfully to recover any possessions and goods of the church entrusted to you that have been unlawfully alienated or disposed of. You may also, when the priorate of St Andrews becomes vacant, install a prior there without any objection, as your predecessors and you yourself have hitherto done, and duly correct his faults whenever he is at fault.

We decree, therefore, that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved unimpaired and intact, to be wholly beneficial for the uses for which they were granted—the governance and support of those concerned—saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 21 December, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CLXXVI. TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRENCH. Concerning the cause of the divorce. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 1266B] We believe that it has proceeded from Him in whose hand the heart of the king lies, and who turns it wherever He wills, that, as you have taken care to inform us through our beloved son John, abbot of Saint Geneviève, a prudent and faithful man, and also by your letters, you intend to approach the queen, to try whether you can know her carnally—provided that no prejudice thereby arise to you or to your cause if perhaps you are unable to know her—setting forth two articles which it is not expedient now to explain, in which you assert that provision must be made for you.

Indeed, dearest son, if you wish to pursue the allegation of sorcery against the marriage, you must approach the queen in the fear of the Lord, and still carefully test in good faith, after first obtaining the aid of prayers, alms, and sacrifices, [Col. 1266C] whether you are able to have bodily intercourse with her, so that it may thereby be known whether that sorcery has been removed. For, desiring, insofar as we can with God’s help, to relieve you, we notify you by these present letters that, if perhaps you cannot have carnal intercourse with her, we do not wish any prejudice thereby to arise to you or to your cause; although in one of those two articles we can indeed make suitable provision for you as regards the law, while in the other you can better safeguard yourself as regards the facts. Therefore, if it is not permitted that you and the queen herself may become one flesh, and you wish to make trial concerning the impediment of sorcery, when we are asked we shall proceed to judgment; without such judgment you certainly cannot be released from this [Col. 1266D] bond.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CLXXVII. TO THE ELECT OF COLOGNE. His election is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 9 Kalends of January.)

Since, according to the canonical enactments, many things sometimes impede an election which ought not to impede a postulation, because in the former one proceeds according to the strictness of law, whereas in the latter the favor of grace is rather required, we did not judge that the election which our beloved sons, the canons of Cologne, had made of you should be confirmed, although they pressed us with many prayers for its confirmation, because justice required this on account of the defect of age under which you then still labored. [Col. 1267A]

But because they have recently humbly postulated you from us on account of the urgent necessity and evident benefit expected to arise from your promotion, we have judged that you, whose uprightness of character and adequate learning, as we believe, support you, should be granted to the Church of Cologne as pastor. We have given letters containing commands to the aforesaid canons, that, after our beloved son Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Vitalis and legate of the Apostolic See, has announced to them that what we have ordained is to be observed, they shall endeavor to obey you as their pastor, granted and confirmed by us, in both spiritual and temporal matters.

But lest it happen that our disposition be frustrated, we command your devotion by apostolic letters that, if perhaps by any chance what we command to be announced through the aforesaid legate cannot be announced, you shall nevertheless, by authority of the present letters, as one granted and confirmed by us, carry out the office of pastor in the province of Cologne. [Col. 1267B]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 9 Kalends of January, in the tenth year.

CLXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT HILARY, THE PARISH PRIEST OF SAINT PAUL IN THE DIOCESE OF CASTELLO, AND MASTER GALLO, CANON OF TREVISO. The execution of a certain sentence is committed to them. (At Saint Peter’s, 11 Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 1267D] Chapter *Ex litteris*, *On the Office of a Delegated Judge*.]

From the letters of our venerable brother, the patriarch of Grado, [Col. 1267C] we have learned that, when our beloved sons the primicerius of Grado and the parish priest of Saint Sophia at Venice—to whom we had delegated the case being pursued between the clerics of Saint Justina and the priest Albert, concerning the latter priest’s assertion that he was a cleric of that church—had ordered them that the patriarch himself should declare not bound by the bond of anathema the aforesaid clerics, who had been declared subject to a sentence of excommunication by the archpriest of Padua—before whom a rescript concerning the same affair had been obtained from us, in which, as is asserted, no mention was made of the earlier letters—unless they received the said priest as companion and brother; the patriarch himself, wishing in this matter to obey those same judges, [Col. 1267D] who acted by our authority—especially since our venerable brother, the bishop of Castello, when consulted on this matter, had not thought that they ought to be obeyed—communicated the command of the aforesaid judges by his letters to the clerics of Saint Mary Formosa. Those letters our beloved son, the archdeacon of Castello, parish priest of that same church, did not permit to be read publicly before the people.

And when, a few days later, at the monastery of Saint Nicholas, that same archdeacon had been kindly admonished on this matter by the patriarch, suddenly roused to anger, he assailed the patriarch with grave verbal insults in the presence of many people. Considering that the archdeacon [Col. 1268A] himself, by so great an excess of insults, had grievously offended not only him but also the Church of Grado—indeed, ourselves—the patriarch subjected both the archdeacon and the aforesaid church to ecclesiastical interdict. This was especially because, according to what is said, an ancient custom has obtained that letters sent through the patriarchate of Grado by the patriarchs of Grado are to be received without distinction by all.

Yet, at the entreaty of the clerics and parishioners of the aforesaid church, the patriarch relaxed the sentence of interdict so far as concerned the church itself, enjoining those clerics, under penalty of excommunication, not to presume to participate with the archdeacon in divine worship. When the said patriarch had gone with the aforesaid bishop to the monastery of Holy Cross for the celebration of a certain matter, [Col. 1268B] and the archdeacon wished to take part in the divine offices, the patriarch withdrew aside in order to avoid scandal. For this reason the archdeacon began to assail him with serious verbal insults.

The same archdeacon also, although he had abstained from divine offices for the period of one day, was thereafter not ashamed publicly to celebrate while under interdict. Moreover, the patriarch brought a serious complaint against the oft-mentioned bishop: although the bishop was bound to render obedience and reverence to him and to the Church of Grado, and although the patriarch had commanded him to regard the aforesaid archdeacon as under interdict and the clerics of Saint Mary as excommunicated, and to cause the sentences of excommunication and interdict pronounced by him to be inviolably observed throughout the diocese of Castello, that bishop, to the injury of the patriarch, permitted the archdeacon freely to minister in the Church of Castello. He commanded the clerics of his diocese, under penalty of breach of fealty, publicly to announce in their churches that neither the archdeacon nor the aforesaid clerics was subject to a sentence of interdict or excommunication. [Col. 1268C]

Accordingly, the patriarch humbly begged us to take care to punish such great injury and excess, attempted by both bishop and archdeacon not merely against himself but rather against the Apostolic See, in such a way that others might be deprived of an occasion to commit similar acts.

The said bishop, however, informed us by his letters that, when the patriarch had declared that the clerics [Col. 1268D] of Saint Justina were not bound by the bond of anathema—although the bishop himself had previously declared them excommunicated by command of the archpriest of Padua, a judge delegated by us, as is asserted—a dispute had arisen on this occasion between the patriarch and the archdeacon. In some agitation, the patriarch placed the archdeacon under interdict. The latter appealed; thereupon the patriarch pronounced a sentence of interdict upon the oft-mentioned church, and refused to receive the satisfaction offered by the archdeacon on that matter unless the archdeacon confirmed by an oath that he would obey the patriarch’s commands.

The bishop further added that he himself, fearing lest the patriarch should proceed [Col. 1269A] to something that would result in prejudice or injury to the bishop himself, his church, or his clerics, appealed to the Apostolic See, earnestly beseeching us to take care to restrain the patriarch from unjust molestation of himself, his church, and the clerics and churches of his diocese.

Therefore, after the matters set forth above and others had for some time been litigated before our beloved son John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, whom we had appointed auditor for the parties, and after he had faithfully reported to us what he had heard, since we could not determine whether the letters said to have been obtained for the archpriest of Padua—because they were not shown to us—had revoked the letters shown to have been obtained for the aforesaid primicerius and parish priest, [Col. 1269B] we have judged the case should be committed to your examination. By apostolic letters we command you, after fully investigating the truth of the foregoing, that unless it is established to you that the letters said to have been obtained secondly for the aforesaid archpriest made express mention of the earlier letters obtained for the oft-mentioned primicerius and parish priest, so that the first letters may appear to have been revoked by the second—since there is no doubt that the first judges possessed jurisdiction by authority of our letters, which jurisdiction they could afterwards entrust to the patriarch for execution of their sentence, and from which the patriarch himself also received coercive authority, for such delegated [Col. 1269C] jurisdiction would seem illusory if the subdelegate had no coercive power—you shall cause the sentence of interdict pronounced by that patriarch against the aforesaid archdeacon, because he impeded the execution by the aforesaid patriarch and did not permit his letters to be publicly read, to be inviolably observed, with any obstacle of appeal removed, until adequate satisfaction has been rendered to the patriarch for the injuries inflicted.

But if it is established that the first letters were lawfully revoked by the second, since it then appears that the first judges had no jurisdiction whatever, and consequently that the patriarch himself received neither jurisdiction nor coercive authority from them, you shall declare null and void the aforesaid sentence of interdict pronounced by the patriarch. [Col. 1269D] Nevertheless, after prior warning, you shall compel the aforesaid archdeacon by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, to render suitable satisfaction for the verbal insults which he presumed to inflict upon the patriarch. But witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding no letters except with consent of the parties, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 11 Kalends of January, in the tenth year.

CLXXIX. TO THE RECTOR AND BROTHERS OF THE HOSPITAL OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN SAXIA. Indulgences and privileges are granted to them. (At Saint Peter’s, 3 Nones of January.)

[Col. 1270A]

[Note: [Col. 1269D] See Spondanus, under the year 1198, §17. See the appendix to this book, and Book XI, letters 69 and 104.]

To commemorate the saving nuptials which, in the conversion of a sinner, are morally celebrated between the spirit of a human being and the grace of the Creator, from which affections and actions are generated as sons and daughters, on the first Sunday after the octave of the Epiphany, when the Gospel is read in which Jesus, with his disciples, was invited to a wedding at Cana of Galilee, where his Mother was, and turned water into wine, we have instituted a solemn station at your hospital. In it you are dedicated, by our institution, to divine [Col. 1270B] service, principally because six water-jars are reported to have been present at those nuptials according to the purification of the Jews.

Indeed, in this hospital, as in Cana of Galilee—that is, in a place where there is zeal to pass from vices to virtues—six water-jars have been placed: namely, the six instituted works of mercy. These are to feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, receive the stranger, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and go to the prisoner, for the purification of the Jews; that is, so that those who confess may be cleansed from vices through them. These six water-jars are filled up to the brim when those six works of mercy are carried out completely; and water becomes wine when, from the merit of almsgiving, the power [Col. 1270C] of charity is kindled.

But since Jesus with his disciples is read to have been invited to these nuptials at Cana of Galilee, where his mother was, we have accordingly and reasonably instituted that an image of Jesus Christ be reverently carried from the basilica of blessed Peter by its canons to the said hospital, where the memory of his most glorious Mother is celebrated, enclosed in a shrine specially made for this purpose from gold, silver, and precious stones, and desirably displayed to the faithful people who have devoutly assembled to celebrate these nuptials.

[Note: [Col. 1270D] Honorius III confirmed this in precisely these words; see Raynaldus, under the year 1223, §21.]

Moreover, in order that we, who by the Lord’s revelation have disclosed to others a venerable mystery, may by His inspiration also offer others an example to imitate, we grant, establish, and command that, for one thousand poor persons arriving from outside and three hundred [Col. 1270D] persons dwelling within, seventeen pounds of customary currency shall each year in perpetuity be supplied to you by the almoner of the supreme pontiff, so that each may receive three denarii: one for bread, another for wine, and the third for meat. And to each of the aforesaid canons who carries the prescribed image of the Savior in procession, twelve coins and a candle weighing one pound, to be carried lit, shall be supplied from the offerings at the confession of blessed Peter.

But because man does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God, the Roman pontiff with his cardinals ought to attend this station, [Col. 1271A] both to celebrate there the solemnities of Mass and to deliver an exhortatory sermon on this celebration; and lest the faithful people return hungry from these nuptials, besides material and doctrinal food he should also provide them spiritual food, granting remission of one year from the penances imposed upon them.

[Note: [Col. 1271D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 144.]

We therefore admonish and beseech our successors through Jesus Christ, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, to cause this institution—which, with Him as witness, proceeded from the fountain of piety—to be inviolably observed; forbidding, under attestation of the divine judgment, that any person at all may infringe this document of our grant, constitution, and command, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 Nones [Col. 1271B] of January, in the tenth year.

CLXXX. TO THE BISHOPS OF NEVERS AND ORLÉANS, AND THE ABBOT OF COURT OF GOD, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER, IN THE DIOCESE OF ORLÉANS. The penalty of an accuser if he fails in proof. (At Viterbo, 2 Nones of October.)

If customary rashness—which should rather be called corruption—were left entirely unpunished, free boldness for malicious evasion would be afforded to those wishing to act deceitfully. Therefore, so that the righteous man may wash his hands in the blood of the sinner, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, unless Peter of Stampes, canon of Reims, proves within two months after notification made to him by you that irregularity [Col. 1271C] which he has alleged against his bishop, you shall deprive him of his prebend in the Church of Reims for the excess of such great presumption, which he maliciously committed, and shall cause it to be conferred on a suitable person.

But Theobald of Pertico, archdeacon of Reims, who through that same Peter has shot an arrow from his own bow, you shall suspend from the power of election which he possesses not only in the Church of Reims but everywhere in the province of Reims, unless he has brought down the man he struck; so that they may recognize from the penalty how greatly they sinned in their offense.

Given at Viterbo, 11 Nones of October, in the tenth year.

CLXXXI. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF SENS. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (At Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of January.)

[Col. 1271D]

“It is customary to assent,” etc., as far as “assent.” Your ancient and reasonable customs, immunities, and liberties, as well as grants—especially those prudently made to you by Guy, archbishop of Sens, of blessed memory—as contained in his authentic document, which we have ordered to be copied below word for word, and which you possess justly and peaceably, we confirm to you by apostolic authority and strengthen with the protection of this document. The clause, namely, “If they do anything against their order, they are to be corrected by us only by means of penance,” having been explained, with the common consent of our venerable brother Peter, your archbishop, and of you, son Dean, the precentor, cellarer, and certain other canons of yours who were together with you in our presence, as meaning that the archbishop has jurisdiction over those priests in spiritual matters, while you have it in temporal matters. The tenor of the same authentic document is as follows:

GUIDO, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, to all whom the present letters shall reach, greeting in the Lord.

“Since things done in time must necessarily pass away with time, it remains that whatever we wish to preserve in memory, lest it perish through oblivion, should be committed to writing, so that by the same intermediary it may in times to come reach [Col. 1272A] the knowledge of posterity.

“Let it therefore be known to those present and future that good and holy Fathers of churches diligently watch over their children, and in order to sustain and nourish them abundantly bestow upon them the necessary benefits from motives of mercy and piety. Observing this not only in our own Church but also in other churches throughout the world, holy pontiffs, after conferring various benefits of their magnificence upon their children, have transmitted to posterity a pious memory of themselves.

“For this reason, we too have received with fatherly affection and gracious disposition the prayers of our most dear sons, the canons of the Church of Sens. The many churches which our predecessors of blessed memory gave at various times to that community, and which in our own time we have [Col. 1272C] granted to them, that they may have and peaceably possess them in perpetuity—we have judged that these churches should be specified by their proper names, and, with God as author, we grant and confirm them by the authority of our seal: namely, the church of Amorra, the church of Jolna, the church of Braio, the church of Moncellis, the church of Moisio, the church of Broisola, the church of Valonessa, the church of Compiniac with the chapel of Montiniac, the church of Eurio, the church of Ponte-Siriac with the church of Saint Giles of Nemore and its appurtenances, saving the right of Saint John of Sens; the church of Saint Albin with the chapel of Melers; the church of Curia Monunculi; the church of Sociac; the church of Saint [Col. 1272D] Martin; the church of Gumerio; the church of Saint Hilary within the city walls; the church of Saint Maurice between the two bridges; the church of Frateio with the chapel of Cantu galli; the church of Amiliac; the church of Daimonte; the churches of Brueria with the chapel of Saint Victor; the church of Borovilla; the churches of Roemvillari and Nangevilla; the church of Villerario; the church of Taloan with the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Villanova upon the Yonne; the church of Blessed Mary of that same Villanova; the church of Dimone; the church of Lorriac; the church of Allento; the church of Bosco Regis; the church of Chanquolla; the church of Castellariis with the chapel of Saint Getnina and the chapel of Escrevis; and the church [Col. 1273A] of Malleio Vicecomitis.

“We also grant the presentation of priests in the aforesaid churches to the chapter. Those priests shall pay to the same chapter, upon oath, half of their benefices, or whatever amount shall reasonably have been agreed among them; and they shall be altogether exempt from every exaction, levy, lodging obligation, circuits and synods, and every summons and jurisdiction both of archdeacons and archpriests.

“Moreover, if they do anything against their order, they are to be corrected by us only by means of penance. We also grant them, in all the aforesaid churches and those which may hereafter be conferred upon them, the right of provision whenever churches fall vacant. Furthermore, we grant them full power to administer and exercise justice upon [Col. 1273B] their lay wrongdoers, unless they are our own men, and upon their priests, insofar as pertains to them.

“It should further be noted that we granted and gave to the chapter the two aforesaid churches—the church of Allento and the church of Chanquolla—in the name of a certain prebend which we established in the Church of Sens, forbidding the revenues of the aforesaid churches to be spent for uses other than that prebend. We gave them the church of Bosco Regis. At our request, they associated with the minor distributions four canons, who must be priests, whom we established at the altar of Blessed Peter in the Church of Sens, so that two of them shall receive in the minor distributions made in choir as much as one of the greater canons receives. [Col. 1273C]

“We gave them the church of Castellariis; and they granted us that after our death they will distribute one hundred Parisian solidi each year on the day of our anniversary, so that two clerics who are not canons shall receive as much as one of the greater canons.

“Done publicly at Sens in chapter, in the presence of the persons of that church: Salon, dean; Hugh, archdeacon; Stephen, treasurer; Geoffrey, precentor and archdeacon of Vastenais; Haicio, cellarer and archdeacon of Provins; Simon, archdeacon of Melun; Hugh, archdeacon of Étampes; Jacquin, Roger, Walter, and Guido, priests and canons; Guido, Odo, Reynald, and Garnerius, deacons and canons; Ernaud, Geoffrey, [Col. 1273D] Reinaud, Anselm, Nicholas, Walter, Nicholas, Girard, Manasses, Bartholomew, and William, subdeacons and canons.

“Furthermore, together with the above-named churches, we likewise confirm to them the church of Varon. In testimony of this matter, we have caused the present document to be written and confirmed by the authority of our seal. Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1187. Given through the hand of Master Peter, our chancellor.”

Therefore let no one … infringe this document of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 2 Nones of January, in the tenth year.

CLXXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS. A case against the bishop of Périgueux is committed to him. (At Saint Peter’s, 7 Ides of January.)

[Col. 1274A]

Your promotion has been procured in the Church of God, by His own ordering, so that you may be a suitable co-worker of our order, especially in those matters that require wholesome correction within it. We believe that zeal for the house of the Lord consumes you so greatly in this regard that, wholly preferring divine love to worldly favor, you ought never to deviate from the path of rectitude in matters committed to your care.

For some time ago a grave outcry reached our ears concerning the bishop of Périgueux: besides many grave and enormous things publicly said of him, he was so negligent and useless in his pastoral office that he not only occupied the ground uselessly like an unfruitful fig tree, [Col. 1274B] but also, because of his deficiency, manifold danger threatened the flock committed to him. Perhaps perceiving this, he sought from us through his messenger leave to resign; but at last, when the flesh delayed the spirit, although permission to withdraw had been granted him, he took no care to withdraw.

And when, as his latter state became worse than the former, the outcry did not cease but grew more severe against him, we commanded our venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges and our beloved son the prior of Grandmont to induce him to resign; otherwise, appeal set aside, to compel him by ecclesiastical censure to present himself before the apostolic presence within three months after receiving our letters. As they informed us by their letters, after diligently admonishing him to do this and after he failed to comply with their admonition when the period of three months had elapsed, they finally struck him with a sentence of suspension. [Col. 1274C]

After some time, he informed them that he had set out to come to the Apostolic See, but that a quartan fever attacked him on the road so severely that he could not complete his intended journey without danger to his body. Thus, having received their leave, he returned to the Church of Périgueux. There, as is asserted, after the sentence of suspension had been imposed on him, he conferred many benefices and alienated not a few of its goods.

[Col. 1274D] Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to endeavor lawfully to revoke all grants or alienations of benefices or of any goods whatsoever of the Church which you find to have been made by that bishop while under suspension; restraining by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, those who rashly undertake to oppose you. And, after diligently investigating the truth, if it is established that he—indeed, to put it thus—asked leave from us to resign, lest he seem to look back with Lot’s wife and be changed into a pillar of salt, you shall compel him, appeal removed, to resign if, after warning, he should perhaps refuse to resign. [Col. 1275A]

But if this cannot be established to you, since his insufficiency and uselessness can be fully clear to you, you shall procure his removal from the administration of the Church of Périgueux, appeal set aside, and shall cause provision to be made for it by canonical election, with your counsel, through the appointment of a suitable person as bishop. Any opponents or rebels who hinder the fulfillment of the apostolic command, you shall restrain from their presumption by ecclesiastical severity, appeal set aside.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 7 Ides of January, in the tenth year.

CLXXXIII. TO THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW AT MILAN. An agreement is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 5 Ides of December.)

[Col. 1275B]

When our beloved sons D., syndic of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, and James, procurator of your church, appeared in our presence, we granted them our beloved son Benedict, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, as auditor. Before him the aforesaid procurator stated that, although secular clerics had occupied the said church of Saint Dionysius for a long period, Aribert, archbishop of Milan, of blessed memory, made that church into a monastery and established there an abbot and a complement of twelve monks, while nevertheless preserving every right for the four canons whom he found in that church at the time.

Although monks and [Col. 1275C] secular canons afterward ministered together in that place for a long time, those canons transferred themselves to your church, which they had founded upon an estate purchased from G., a physician. For many years they held in that church free election of brethren and free administration of property, rendering no services whatsoever to the aforesaid monastery.

But when afterward a disputed question arose between you on one side and the aforesaid abbot of Saint Dionysius concerning the election of canons of your church and certain other articles, Philip, archbishop of Milan, of blessed memory, pronounced a definitive sentence against you in the same case. You therefore appealed to the Apostolic See. When, by the will of both parties, the same case had been committed to G., formerly archdeacon of Parma, and afterward both your procurator and the abbot and syndic of the monastery had entered into a submission to him, that archdeacon settled the case by arbitration.

But because the successor of that abbot presumed to act against the aforesaid arbitration, you obtained our letters addressed to Master Guidotto, canon of the Decumani. When he had become acquainted with the merits of the case, he confirmed the aforesaid arbitration and, commanding the abbot of Saint Dionysius on our behalf not to presume to act against that arbitration, entirely annulled everything he found undertaken against it. [Col. 1276A] The same abbot, humbly approving that sentence, stated before the same master that he wished firmly to observe all the articles contained in that arbitration. That arbitration was subsequently also confirmed by the sentence of our beloved sons, the abbot of Saint Abundius and the archpriest of Grabadone, to whom the same case had been committed. The aforesaid procurator therefore requested that we would deign to confirm that sentence by apostolic authority and cause the aforesaid arbitration to be inviolably observed.

The aforesaid syndic, on the other hand, stated that, when the aforesaid Archbishop Aribert had established the aforesaid monastery of Saint Dionysius, he ordained that monastic observance should be maintained there; and O., his successor, later confirmed this. Arnold, formerly abbot of the same place, is likewise known to have ordained, when building your aforesaid church of Saint [Col. 1276B] Bartholomew upon the estate of that monastery, that the church should in all things be subject to the aforesaid monastery and that its administration and provision should wholly belong to that monastery.

Accordingly, when a certain abbot of that place had on his own authority ordained in your church a certain cleric named S., and that man had been sued by some canons of your church because he had been ordained without their concurrence, V., formerly archdeacon of Milan, who took cognizance of the case by delegation from A., then archbishop of Milan, absolved the said cleric S. from your suit.

When a question arose between the abbot of Saint Dionysius and yourselves concerning the election of canons of your church and certain [Col. 1276C] other articles, Philip, formerly archbishop of Milan, who took cognizance of that controversy, pronounced a sentence against you on all the articles proposed. But when a submission to the aforesaid archdeacon of Parma, to whom the same case had been committed, was afterward made less than lawfully, that archdeacon pronounced an unjust arbitration against the monastery.
