This was afterward rejected by our beloved sons the prior of Foncella and Baldwin, canon of Brivio, who took cognizance of the matter by authority of the Apostolic See, since the greater part of the monks of the aforesaid monastery, under oath in their presence, affirmed that the settlement made by the aforesaid arbitration had been made to the injury of the monastery, and that they had approved neither the settlement nor the arbitration. Therefore the said syndic requested that, once that arbitration had been rejected, we would deign to confirm the sentence of the said prior and his fellow judge.

[Col. 1276D] After the matters above and others had thus been litigated for some time before the aforesaid cardinal, and after he had faithfully reported to us what he heard, we, having understood the arguments of both sides and inspected the authentic documents which each party had seen fit to produce in proof on either side, because it was established to us that the aforesaid arbitration pronounced by the archdeacon of Parma, to whom the parties had submitted, had been jointly approved by both parties in the presence of the aforesaid Master Guidotto, approve that arbitration ourselves and [Col. 1277A] confirm it by apostolic authority, strengthening it with the protection of the present document. We establish that whatever may rashly be undertaken against its tenor shall lack all force of validity. Therefore let no one … infringe this document of our confirmation and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 5 Ides of December, in the tenth year.

CLXXXIV. TO THE CHAPTER OF SEGNI. The election of a bishop is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s.)

To our presence came the beloved sons, the archpriest and the … canons of Segni, who humbly petitioned us on your behalf to deign to confirm by apostolic authority the election of I., unanimously conducted by you. Having therefore caused that election to be examined more carefully according to the custom of the Roman Church, we discovered that neither had the death of your bishop of blessed memory … been notified to us, nor had permission to elect been sought from us, as ought to have been done; and also that, while that bishop was still alive, you rashly presumed, contrary to the canonical sanctions, to nominate certain persons to sound out everyone's wishes concerning the election of a future prelate, disregarding nevertheless certain of your canons then present at the Apostolic See. Moreover, lest any one of those men might be promoted in that church, you cunningly instructed the said examiners, [Col. 1277C] to whom you had entrusted the power of electing a bishop, to summon one of those then present to the governance of your church.

Accordingly, after diligent deliberation with our brethren, for the reasons stated above we judged that election null and void. Yet, because we cannot lay aside the paternal affection which we bear toward your church, even when offended, and because the person is deemed suitable and the unanimity of your consent is directed toward him, we have granted that same I. to you as pastor, not by virtue of your election but by our authority, commanding him to assume the care of your church and, God granting, to receive from us the office of consecration.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CLXXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF SENS. That they are to permit the dean to remain for three years studying at Paris. (At Saint Peter’s, 12 January.)

[Col. 1277D]

Although personal favour ought not easily to move us to grant something beyond what is commonly due, nevertheless, if a person’s merit requires it, we bestow upon him the grace of apostolic liberality the more readily as more evident indications make us more certain of the honourableness of his conduct and his learning. Thus, since our beloved son S., your dean, deservedly commended for learning and character, intends to reside at Paris for three years, in order during that period to benefit both others and himself by directing schools [Col. 1278A] in the faculty of theology; and since he has humbly petitioned us to grant him leave to reside there for so long a time, we have judged his prayers the more willingly to be admitted because his merits especially intercede for him with us, and because still greater advantages may thereby accrue to your church.

Therefore we have thought fit to request and admonish your whole body, commanding you by these apostolic letters that, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, you generously grant him permission to reside for the aforesaid period in the schools at Paris for this purpose, without meanwhile compelling him to receive priestly orders. Receive our command in such fashion that we may regard it as pleasing and acceptable.

[Col. 1278B] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 12 January, in the tenth year.

CLXXXVI. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM, APOSTOLIC LEGATE. Concerning provision of the archdeaconry of Antioch to a suitable person. (At Saint Peter’s, 9 January.)

To our beloved son John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, we assigned as auditor the beloved sons Master John and P., envoy of our venerable brother the patriarch of Antioch. Before him the said master alleged that, when formerly our beloved son Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, apostolic legate, had arrived in Syria, he learned that the archdeaconry in the Church of Antioch had been vacant for more than six months [Col. 1278C] and that, consequently, its right of grant had devolved to the Roman Church. By authority of his legation he granted that archdeaconry, with all its rights, to the same master; after making canonical investiture of it to him, he commanded the said patriarch to receive and treat him kindly.

The patriarch, asserting that he had granted the same archdeaconry to a nephew of his own, did not carry out what the legate had commanded, although the legate had later personally requested him to do so at Antaradus. But when reliable witnesses had established to the legate that his grant preceded the patriarch’s grant, and that the latter’s nephew was far below the age prescribed by canon for such offices, [Col. 1278D] the legate decreed that the patriarch’s grant to his nephew lacked force. He judicially confirmed what he had done in favour of the aforesaid master, and, appointing the prior of Bellimont and Master Milo as executors for this purpose, ordered that a stall in choir and a place in chapter be assigned to him, and that he be put into full possession of the houses, casalia, lands, and other things belonging to the archdeaconry.

Moreover, knowing that many prebends and dignities had similarly become vacant in the said church, he reserved them to his own right of grant. Of these he assigned one to Roger and another to Bartholomew, clerics, establishing them as canons in the aforesaid church. Since, on account of various acts of contumacy committed by that patriarch in the foregoing matters, the legate had pronounced certain sentences against him, at length [Col. 1279A] our venerable brethren the bishops of Tripoli and Antaradus came to the legate on behalf of the aforesaid patriarch with letters of ratification. They declared that the patriarch wished both the archdeaconry and the dignities and prebends conferred by himself or by the legate to remain subject to his own disposition, and that he should dispose of them and of other matters in the aforesaid Church according to his own will; this was expressly contained in the said letters.

Accordingly, the legate relaxed the aforesaid sentences and told the same bishops that henceforth the patriarch was to recognize the said master as archdeacon and the two men established by him as canons as canons of Antioch, rendering to the former all archidiaconal rights and to the latter all canonical rights. The bishops, accepting on the patriarch’s behalf that he would comply, exchanged the kiss of peace with Marinus, archdeacon of Nicosia, on behalf of the master and the aforesaid canons.

Furthermore, the above-mentioned legate had bound the canons of Antioch, because they had contumaciously resisted his ordinance, first by a sentence of suspension and afterward by a sentence of excommunication. Through the bishop of Valania and his colleagues, after receiving sworn security, he ordered them to be absolved, provided that, before they gave the oath, the following was stated to them, and that after their absolution they were commanded under oath [Col. 1279C] to observe inviolably what he had decreed concerning that archdeacon and the two aforesaid canons. If the said bishop and his colleagues exceeded this form, he wrote that he would deem their proceedings null and void.

The master therefore requested that we deign to confirm to him the aforesaid archdeaconry, cause him peacefully to enjoy possession of it, and order restored to him the fruits of it and of his possessions withheld since the time of his institution, together with reimbursement of expenses. He also requested that the aforesaid canons, who contrary to their oath refused to receive him, be punished. On behalf of the other of the two aforesaid canons—namely R., a priest, since the remaining one had died—he humbly petitioned us to confirm to him a canonry with one of the prebends then vacant for more than six months in the aforesaid Church and to cause him to possess it peacefully.

[Col. 1279D] In opposition, the patriarch’s envoy answered that, after W., formerly archdeacon of Antioch, and two of his fellow canons had perished at sea, so that no certainty whatever concerning them could be obtained until the next sea-crossing, the patriarch was unwilling hastily to dispose of the archdeaconry, but waited until he could be better informed about them. After the second crossing had passed—in which, he asserts, the legate arrived—when public report had made him certain of the danger to the aforesaid persons, he granted the archdeaconry to a nephew of his own. He intended immediately to send the nephew to our presence, so that, notwithstanding his defect of age, we might mercifully make provision concerning both the archdeaconry and himself.

Later the aforesaid legate informed him by letter that he had conferred that [Col. 1280A] archdeaconry upon the aforesaid master. The patriarch finally replied that he had already granted it to his nephew and asked the legate to suspend proceedings and permit the nephew, who had already set out on the journey, to come to the Apostolic See. But the legate did not admit his request. Rather, burdening the patriarch, chapter, and church harshly in the matter of the archdeaconry, he sent two envoys together with the aforesaid master to them. When they perceived that those men had come to their prejudice, they appealed to the Apostolic See, lest they proceed in any respect. But those envoys, disregarding the appeal, began in many ways to burden the chapter with suspensions and other measures.

The patriarch first by letters and special envoys, and later in person, not without great hardship, approached [Col. 1280B] the legate, devoutly begging him to desist from these acts, especially after the appeal, and to allow the case to come before us. Since he could obtain this in no way, he renewed the same appeal. When he departed from the legate’s presence, the legate suspended him from the power of imposing interdicts and excommunications, and caused a sentence of excommunication to be pronounced against the aforesaid chapter. He ordered that sentence to be renewed every Sunday with lighted candles. Pressing still harder upon them, he named two canons in their church without consulting them, despite their protest and against their will.

Since the prince and citizens of Antioch, who had already risen against the church, took from these acts done to the injury of the patriarch and chapter [Col. 1280C] an occasion to rage against them still more outrageously, so that the possessions of the Church were devastated and another man was elected patriarch by Syrians through the favour of that same prince, the patriarch saw grave danger threatening him. Antioch seemed likely thereby to be severed from communion with the whole Latin world. Perplexed between these two evils, the patriarch chose to incur the lesser in order to avoid the graver; thus, in the affair of the said master and the other two, he submitted himself to the cardinal’s will.

But afterwards, when the aforesaid master procured numerous insults and burdens against the patriarch and chapter, the patriarch received certain letters sent to him by the bishop of Tripoli. These stated that many men, under oath before that bishop, had testified that [Col. 1280D] the said master had been a monk of the monastery of the Holy Spirit at Palermo. Therefore, when the patriarch summoned him to answer in his presence concerning this apostasy and certain other excesses, he departed, confused within himself, appealing.

The patriarch ordered stalls to be assigned to the two aforesaid men and said that he would in no respect oppose them concerning the appointment made for them in the Church of Antioch by the cardinal. He therefore humbly requested us to look providently to the condition of his church concerning the aforesaid master, whom he asserts to be tainted by the stigma of apostasy, and concerning the aforesaid R., who, he asserts, is a notorious concubinary, unlearned, and base; and who is said to have made wooden engines before a certain fortress for the assault upon Christians.

[Col. 1281A] The same master, however, answered the accusation of apostasy as follows. Since he was physician to the abbey of the Holy Spirit at Palermo and was accustomed to go there in his illnesses—because his house stood near the sea and the river—he turned aside, as usual, to that abbey during one illness. One night, when he was suffering so severely from sickness that he did not perceive what was being done around him, a monk from his own country, left to attend him, despaired of his recovery and presumed his death. That monk clothed him in his own tunic, while he was wholly unaware of what was being done to him.

Thereafter, when the prior came to him and asked him not to be angry with the monastery over what had been done, he asked that the Rule be shown to him, so that by reading it he might learn more fully whether he could endure the strictness of the Cistercian Order. But after reading the Rule, he realized that he was unequal to the observance of so great a strictness. He removed the tunic—which, so far as he could remember, he had worn for ten days—and left the monastery in the clothing in which he had entered it.

[Col. 1281B] In answer to this, the patriarch’s envoy produced certain letters, sent to our Apostolic See in the name of the prior and convent of the aforesaid monastery. In them they testified that, as is well known to many people of Palermo, the same master had come to their monastery while detained by illness, had devoutly received the habit and worn it for several days, though he did not come to chapter; but, after recovering somewhat, he left the monastery [Col. 1281C] and thereafter followed his own will.

Having therefore heard these things and the other matters alleged on both sides, and having learned from the master’s own confession that he wore the novice’s habit in the aforesaid monastery for ten days, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters: unless he satisfactorily shows that he had declared to the prior that he wished to retain freedom to return to his former state if, during the period of probation, he should not wish to undergo the strictness of the Order, do not delay to impose perpetual silence upon him regarding that archdeaconry, since under the canonical sanctions he is bound at least to enter a less strict order.

But if he establishes to your satisfaction that he made such a declaration, then—since the cardinal’s sentence is to be presumed valid, by which the action taken concerning the patriarch’s nephew was set aside, especially since the patriarch himself informed us in his letters that his nephew suffered from a defect of age—restore the said master to the possession which he is known to have held. Then inquire carefully into the truth whether the conferral of the archdeaconry belongs to the patriarch alone, or jointly to the canons and to him.

[Col. 1281D] If it belongs jointly to both, and they neglected to confer it within six months after it became known that it was vacant, then, because from that point its right of grant had devolved to us, decree that what was done by the cardinal under our authority be inviolably observed; assign the archdeaconry to the said master before the aforesaid judges, and cause him to possess it, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure without appeal. Afterwards hear the patriarch or another person if he wishes to allege anything against him, and decide without canonical appeal.

We also will and command you to do the same if its right of grant belongs only to the patriarch and it is established that the canons consented to the patriarch’s grant or to that of the cardinal. Otherwise, since after six months had elapsed from the time when it became known to be vacant—and during those months the patriarch neglected to exercise his right—the conferral of the archdeaconry had, by common law, devolved not to us but to the chapter of Antioch, [Col. 1282A] if the chapter requests it, do not omit to impose perpetual silence upon the said master. This is notwithstanding that he produced certain letters of the aforesaid cardinal in which the cardinal acknowledges that he granted him the archdeaconry for multiple reasons. For in other letters of that cardinal, both preceding and following those letters, the cardinal assigns this ground for his grant: that the archdeaconry had been vacant for more than six months, and therefore its right of grant had devolved to the Roman Church.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 9 January, in the tenth year.

CLXXXVII. TO THE ARCHDEACON AND PRIOR OF SAINT STEPHEN OF THE BRIDGE, FLORENTINE DIOCESE. Executors appointed against the bishop of Lucca. (At Saint Peter’s, 5 January.)

To our presence came the beloved sons, … [Col. 1282C] monk of the monastery of Ficicolo, and …, procurators of the bishop of Lucca; and we assigned the beloved son Roger, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, as auditor. Before him, the procurator of the said monastery alleged that, when formerly we had committed to the abbot of Saint Mary and the prior of Saint Lawrence the case pending between the beloved sons, the abbot and convent of his monastery on the one side and the said bishop on the other, concerning the institution of a parish priest in the parish of Ficicolo, the bishop, cited by them, refused to appear before them. Subsequently he obtained from us certain letters concerning the same case addressed to the beloved sons, the provost of Saint Geminianus and the prior of Saint Reparata, making no mention of the earlier letters.

For this reason the aforesaid abbot refused to litigate before them, asserting that those letters had been procured by suppressing the truth, since they made no mention of the prior letters. But when the procurators of both parties came to our presence, they obtained the commitment of the same case to the beloved sons, the abbot of Sesto and the prior of Saint Fridianus. Yet one of them died before the suit began, and the aforesaid bishop drew the same abbot before a secular judge. The abbot’s party appeared before that judge and, alleging the commissions of the Apostolic See and the privileges of ecclesiastical liberty, appealed and prohibited the bishop from compelling him to litigate before a secular judge. But the bishop, disregarding the appeal, caused that abbot to be condemned by the judge whom he had himself chosen.

[Col. 1283A] Therefore, by our letters we instructed our venerable brother the bishop of Fiesole and our beloved son the abbot of Saint Mary at Florence to proceed in that cause, without appeal and after due inquiry, according to the tenor of the aforesaid commission; to determine what was canonical concerning the bishop’s having drawn the abbot to the aforesaid secular forum; and to cause their determination to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. But because the bishop, though peremptorily cited by those judges, refused to appear, they received the abbot’s witnesses and condemned the bishop to pay seventy pounds in expenses incurred by the abbot.

Since, however, we observed that those judges had proceeded in the matter without observing judicial order, we declared that proceeding void. By our letters we instructed the beloved son the archpriest and Master Hugh, canon of Florence, that, after summoning the parties and hearing the allegations on both sides, if it appeared to them that the aforesaid bishop had drawn the abbot before a secular court, they should suspend him from episcopal office, revoke whatever had been attempted by the secular judge against the abbot, and compel the bishop by ecclesiastical coercion to restore the books which he had caused to be taken from him by secular authority, together with the expenses and damages incurred on that account by the aforesaid abbot. Thereafter they were to hear the case and decide it justly, without appeal.

[Col. 1283C] Having received our mandate, the judges lawfully cited the bishop and assigned him an appropriate term. Before it arrived, he sent a certain messenger to them. The messenger presented letters containing frivolous objections and appealed, prohibiting them from proceeding in the matter. When the judges recognized that such an appeal was not to be admitted, they cited him again; but neither personally nor through a suitable representative did he appear before them on the appointed day.

Meanwhile, however, the judges received our command to proceed in the matter, according to the tenor of our earlier mandate and after due inquiry, setting aside the obstacle of appeal, notwithstanding the frivolous objections which the bishop was said maliciously to advance to the detriment of the aforesaid monastery. [Col. 1283D] They again peremptorily cited the bishop. But on the appointed day he appeared before them neither personally nor through a suitable representative. Rather, coming to our presence and alleging that the abbot had represented to us that he had drawn him before a secular court in a spiritual cause, he pressed insistently for us to revoke the letters sent to the judges. In the end, he obtained only this: we wrote to the bishop of Florence that, after fully investigating and learning the truth, if he found that the aforesaid bishop had drawn the same abbot before a secular forum concerning the institution of the parish or another spiritual cause, he should not delay to proceed against the bishop, without appeal, according to the form contained in the earlier letters.

The aforesaid judges, still unaware of this further commission, granted a delay of twenty-seven days at the request of a canon of Lucca who claimed to be the bishop’s messenger, in order to remove from him every ground for malicious objection. At length the bishop sent the parish priest of Capiano to them, and he showed them our letters sent to the said bishop. Then, when the point committed to that bishop had been disposed of in his presence and the judges wished to proceed in the case, the aforesaid parish priest came before them, though not sufficiently instructed to pursue the case. [Col. 1284B] Therefore, to expose his bad faith, they granted him a delay of six days. The aforesaid bishop then sent the parish priest, adequately instructed, to their presence on the appointed day.

When the parties appeared before them, the aforesaid abbot asserted that the bishop had drawn him before a secular court in a civil case, although it concerned the aforesaid parish, on the occasion of a certain arbitration rendered long before between bishop and abbot concerning that parish. On that account he had been condemned by the secular judge in fifty pounds and more. He therefore urgently requested that the bishop be punished according to the tenor of our mandate and compelled to restore the damages and expenses which he had caused him to incur.

The bishop’s representative submitted letters of the bishop which stated, among other things, that when questioned before us he had replied that he had drawn the aforesaid abbot before a secular forum concerning a civil right, and that he had not been rebuked by us for this. Thus he contended that he was not bound to answer the abbot on this point and that the judges ought not to proceed. He further asserted that our letters had been obtained by suppressing the true custom whereby, in the city of Lucca, clerics customarily sue one another before laymen called *treuguani* in civil cases. He also maintained that it had not been our intention that the bishop should be punished if he had drawn the abbot before a secular court only concerning a civil matter.

[Col. 1284D] The abbot’s party replied that such a custom was contrary to both canon and civil law, and that, after a reasonable appeal to us had been interposed—as appeared from public instruments and commissions obtained from us—the bishop had presumed to sue him in a secular forum. Since it was established by a public instrument before the aforesaid judges that the abbot had been drawn by the bishop before a secular court concerning a civil matter, and the abbot alleged that, even if the aforesaid custom affected other clerics, it could not affect him because he was exempt, as appeared from privileges of the Roman pontiffs, and since the judges were prepared lawfully to proceed in the aforesaid case, the bishop’s representative made certain frivolous objections, appealed to the Apostolic See, and departed at once without awaiting any reply.

Having carefully examined the tenor of both mandates and taken counsel with prudent men, the judges did not consider that they should defer in any way to such an appeal. Instead, they suspended the bishop, on account of his manifest and repeated contumacy, from celebrating Masses. In the name of Almighty God and of ourselves they commanded him henceforth not to presume to celebrate Mass until he appeared before them in person or through a suitable representative to render complete justice to the aforesaid abbot.

[Col. 1285B] Lest he profit from his fraud, they received from the abbot a bodily oath that he had itemized and carefully declared, according to their assessment, the expenses he had incurred and damages he had suffered on the bishop’s account, amounting to 250 pounds. They caused the abbot to be put in possession of all revenues held by the bishop in the castle, court, and district of Saint Mary on the Mount, and ordered the archpriest and chapter of Lucca to announce that the bishop was suspended from celebrating Masses. Although that archpriest announced the sentence of suspension to him, the bishop nevertheless publicly and solemnly celebrated on the feast of All Saints, disregarding that sentence. The aforesaid procurator therefore requested that we deign to confirm by apostolic authority the proceeding of the aforesaid judges.

[Col. 1285C] In opposition, the bishop’s procurator alleged that, since the matter had been committed to the bishop of Florence and the bishop had ultimately absolved him—because, as he had learned from the abbot’s confession, he had not even drawn him before a secular court in a spiritual cause—he had lawfully appealed from those who wished to compel him, after his absolution by the bishop of Florence, to litigate the matter again. He therefore requested that what the judges had done after the appeal to us had been interposed be deemed null and void.

Having fully learned, through the report of the aforesaid cardinal, these and the other matters alleged before him, we decreed the bishop’s appeal illegitimate and approved the proceeding of the aforesaid judges. We suspended from both priestly and episcopal office the bishop, who had presumed, after the suspension had been announced to him, to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. [Col. 1285D] Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters to publish the sentence issued by us and cause it to be firmly observed.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 5 January, in the tenth year.

CLXXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF REICHENAU, CONRAD, DEAN OF WILDE IN THE DIOCESE OF CONSTANCE, AND MASTER CONRAD, SCHOLASTICUS OF CHUR. Concerning a priest publicly accused of adultery and incest. (At Saint Peter’s, 10 January.)

[Col. 1286A]

[Note: [Col. 1285D] “Since the beloved sons,” *On canonical purgation.*] When, with our beloved sons H., priest, and G., procurator of O., clerics, present before us, we had appointed our beloved son T., subdeacon and our chaplain, as auditor, the said procurator alleged before him that the said priest had been publicly defamed on a charge of incest. The bishop of Constance, of happy memory, his ordinary judge, imposed canonical purgation upon him; and, since he was unable to clear himself, the bishop judicially deprived him, in a full [Col. 1286B] synod, of his churches, which he nevertheless retained for some time by force, having seized them.

And when afterward the same priest publicly kept in his house the abducted wife of one of his kinsmen, at the request of H., parish priest of Herisio [Note: [Col. 1285D] In the third collection, *Hemiso*; Codex Colbert, *Heviso*; [Col. 1286D] Andegavensis, *Haneso*.], and of certain other clerics of the diocese of Constance, we are said to have sent letters in the following form to our beloved sons, the deans of Scennis and Ustrou [Note: [Col. 1286D] Codex Colbert: *Wistrori*; Andegavensis: *Westori*.], of the same diocese: namely, that if the aforesaid priest could not clear himself before them of the crimes of adultery and incest, they should punish him with the penalty due. Proceeding in the matter according to the tenor of our mandate, when it had been established before them that the same priest, because he had failed in his purgation, had been condemned in synod by the aforesaid bishop, they deprived him by sentence, as contumacious, of the aforesaid churches; especially since it was plainly evident to them, as a notorious matter, that he was guilty of incest and adultery. They granted free authority to our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Gall, to whom the grant of those churches belonged, to confer the churches upon other persons; and he afterward assigned them to the aforesaid cleric.

But the same priest, coming to the Apostolic See and falsely asserting that he had been despoiled without observance of legal procedure, obtained our letters addressed to the abbot of the house of Saint Peter and his fellow judges, wholly suspect to the other party. They denied O. a copy of those letters and refused to admit his proof concerning the falsity of the letters; and, [Col. 1286D] disregarding legal procedure, after a lawful appeal had been made to us, pronounced a sentence of restoration in favor of the priest—a matter which O. proposed to prove at the appropriate place and time by lawful witnesses.

The said priest, on the other hand, replied that, although he had been defamed concerning the foregoing crimes by hostile rivals, and canonical purgation had on that account been imposed upon him by the chapter of Constance, nevertheless no one was willing to receive it, although he had been prepared to perform it within the term fixed for him. He added that the proceedings of the aforesaid judges ought rightly to be reviewed, since they had presumed to proceed against him without contestation of the suit and [Col. 1287A] after an appeal to us had been made.

Furthermore, the said priest complained that, when he had been violently despoiled of the aforesaid churches by O. and his aforementioned accomplices, he had first obtained letters of restoration from the aforesaid abbot of the house of Saint Peter and his fellow judges, and a second time from the bishop-elect of Constance; and through both he had deserved to obtain the benefit of restoration. Yet O. had not feared repeatedly to despoil him. Therefore, because O., together with his accomplices, remained obstinately contumacious while bound by a sentence of excommunication, we commanded the said bishop-elect and his fellow judges, supported by our authority, strictly to forbid divine offices from being celebrated in places where those excommunicated persons [Col. 1287B] were present, and, with any appeal set aside, to suspend them from divine offices until they had made adequate satisfaction to the oft-mentioned priest for the damages and injuries inflicted, or had presented themselves before us to answer for such great contempt of us.

But they fled to the refuge of appeal, celebrated divine services in defiance of the prohibition of those judges, and did not take care to send a representative to answer before us. Although the same priest, in order to remove every taint of infamy, caused the purgation imposed upon him by the same bishop-elect—not as delegate, but as ordinary—to be performed, his aforesaid rivals nevertheless do not cease to defame him. He therefore humbly begged us to free him from their accusations, to cause him [Col. 1287C] to enjoy peaceful possession of the aforesaid churches, and lawfully to punish those who, while excommunicated and under interdict, had presumed to celebrate divine offices.

To this the procurator added that the said purgation had been received by the bishop-elect while the other party was absent and wholly unaware, and he asserted that he would prove this as well. Having thus more fully understood these matters and others proposed before the aforesaid chaplain, although neither the letters said to have been obtained for the aforesaid deans of Scennis and Ustrou nor a transcript of them was shown before us, nevertheless, from the tenor of their report, which the said procurator produced, it was evident to us that—even if the letters themselves had been shown—the judges had proceeded without observance of legal procedure. Therefore, by apostolic authority we revoke both their proceedings and the grant of the churches made by the aforesaid abbot at their command, especially since the narrative of that report contains contradictions and inconsistencies.

For it is said that the crime of the same priest had been so public and notorious that there was wholly no room for denial, since the entire population of the neighborhood was witness. Yet it is there first stated that they fixed for the priest a peremptory term within which, if he could, he should canonically clear himself of the infamy of the aforesaid crimes. Plainly, if the crime was notorious, purgation ought not to have been imposed upon him; rather, a sentence of condemnation should have been pronounced against him.

We also approve the sentence of restoration [Col. 1288A] pronounced in favor of the same priest by various judges. By the authority of these presents we command you to put the same priest into physical possession of the aforesaid churches, removing every impediment of contradiction and appeal, and to defend him once installed. Any opponents are to be restrained by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside; and you are to ensure that the priest receives adequate satisfaction both for the fruits received in the meantime from the said churches and for the damages and injuries inflicted upon him.

Once full restoration has been made, if a lawful opponent appears who can and wishes lawfully to prove that the same priest was condemned by the aforesaid [Col. 1288B] bishop and despoiled of the oft-mentioned churches because he failed in purgation lawfully imposed upon him, you shall impose perpetual silence upon him concerning those churches, and cause canonical provision for them to be made by those to whom it belongs, with suitable persons. But if no lawful accuser appears, and you find that he is defamed among good and trustworthy persons concerning the aforesaid crimes, or either of them, impose canonical purgation upon him, notwithstanding that he is said to have cleared himself before the aforesaid bishop-elect; for, while a case was pending before delegates, the ordinary ought not to have imposed purgation upon one who was defamed. If he should fail in that purgation, remove him altogether from the churches in the manner stated above and cause canonical provision for them to be made. No letters are to stand in the way except the consent of the parties, etc. But if not all of you, etc.

[Col. 1288C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the tenth year.

## CLXXXIX. TO THE BISHOP, THE CHANTER, AND MASTER N., ARCHDEACON OF TROYES. Concerning the dispute between the dean and the bishop of Auxerre. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of January.)

[Note: [Col. 1287] See *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, p. 284.] When our beloved sons, the dean of the Church of Auxerre and Master B., procurator of our venerable brother the bishop of Auxerre, were present before us, the same master alleged before us that the said bishop had caused R., priest of the house of God at Mont-Atrit—in which house the bishop is known to possess full right of provision and disposition—to be held in chains, [Col. 1288D] because he refused to restore certain goods of that house which he had furtively taken away. For that reason he had also been bound by the bishop with a sentence of excommunication.

The aforesaid dean warned the bishop either to restore the priest or at least to deliver him into custody (*recredere*), firmly asserting that the priest belonged to his jurisdiction. The bishop, alleging many reasons why he was in no way bound to do this, wholly refused to restore or deliver him, declaring that he was prepared to render justice to the dean concerning this either in his own court, since the dean was his vassal, or before arbitrators jointly chosen, or before [Col. 1289A] the metropolitan. The dean rejected all this and began gravely to threaten that he would do something displeasing to the bishop.

Fearing therefore that the dean might attempt something to his prejudice, the bishop placed himself and his people, and the condition of his Church and city, under the protection of the metropolitan; he appealed to the hearing of the metropolitan see, appointing the recent feast of Saint Mary Magdalene as the term for the appeal. But shortly afterward, having summoned the canons of Auxerre, despite their objections the dean promulgated an interdict: while the bishop was present in the city, divine services were to cease in the Church of Auxerre.

Later, when the parties appeared on the appointed day before the official of the court of Sens, [Col. 1289B] the dean, alleging that he ought not to defer to the appeal made by the bishop because the aforesaid priest was still held in chains, appealed to us. The official, judging void the interdict promulgated by the dean after the bishop’s appeal to the metropolitan see, ordered the chapter of the Church of Auxerre not to observe that interdict in any way.

Afterward, while the bishop was present, the dean strictly forbade singing in the church; and, binding G., the bishop’s chaplain, with a sentence of excommunication because he sang there after an appeal to us had been made, he impeded the divine office in the church. Since, despite repeated warnings from the bishop, he did not cease disturbing the office, the bishop at length [Col. 1289C] struck him, as contumacious and incorrigible, with the sword of excommunication; afterward our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens publicly announced that he was to be avoided. The procurator therefore requested that we judge the aforesaid sentence of interdict void and cause the sentence of excommunication imposed by the bishop to be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction had been made.

The dean, however, alleged in reply that the bishop was causing R., a priest belonging to his jurisdiction, to be held in chains; that he had been severely reproached by both clerics and laypeople of the city as neglecting to defend a right belonging to him; and that, being bound by an oath given for the observance of the customs of the Church, he personally [Col. 1289D] warned the bishop to restore the priest to liberty, being prepared sufficiently to prove that the priest belonged to his jurisdiction. He had then caused the bishop to be warned by several others to return or deliver the priest to him, or at least place him in sequestration.

Since the bishop could not be persuaded to adopt any of these alternatives, the dean, having summoned the chapter and with its concurrence, placed this interdict in the church: while the bishop was present in the city, divine offices were to cease altogether in the church. Nevertheless, he suspended execution of the sentence until he could confer on this matter with the archbishop, who was shortly to come to the city, [Col. 1290A] through whom he hoped concord might be restored.

Moreover, although later, in the archbishop’s presence, he warned the bishop to accept one of the aforesaid methods for the priest’s release, he could make no progress with him. Indeed, the bishop appealed to the hearing of the metropolitan see, fixing the aforesaid term for his appeal. The dean therefore returned to the chapter and directed all the canons to observe the interdict as it had been imposed by him.

On the appointed day for the appeal, the dean appeared before the official of Sens with the bishop’s procurator. Fearing injury was about to be done him, he appealed to the Apostolic See, appointing Laetare Jerusalem Sunday as the term for his appeal, and placing himself, his position, and the Church of Auxerre under the protection of the Apostolic See. But when afterward, in the bishop’s presence, the dean had publicly announced G., a cleric of the same bishop, excommunicated because he had violently seized two clerics, and had ordered the clerics to observe the sentence of interdict pronounced by himself, the bishop pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the dean, notifying the oft-mentioned archbishop and the chapter of Sens that he was excommunicated. Consequently, on the advice of certain persons, the archbishop publicly announced that he was to be avoided, although certain canons of Sens, guided by sounder counsel, did not avoid communion with him.

From these matters and others alleged before us by both sides, we clearly understood that, although the bishop would wisely and usefully have provided against every ground of scandal if he had delivered [Note: [Col. 1289D] “To the dean.”] the aforesaid priest to the dean’s custody, nevertheless, since the bishop, as stated above, had set out different methods by which he was prepared to render complete justice to the dean concerning the seizure of the priest, and had appealed to the metropolitan see, the dean could not afterward pronounce a sentence of interdict.

Therefore, by counsel of our brethren, we decree that this sentence, promulgated by him after the lawful appeal, is void and without effect. Nor does it avail the dean that, as though changing his account, he alleged before us in excuse that he had pronounced the sentence before the bishop appealed, but had temporarily suspended its effect; for, once the appeal had meanwhile been made, he ought not to have proceeded to execute the sentence. We nevertheless judge rash the proceeding of the official who, after an appeal had been made to the Apostolic See, declared the sentence of interdict void and without effect and commanded that it not be observed at all, since, after an appeal to us, he ought not to have innovated anything.

Furthermore, although the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the bishop appeared at first sight to have been properly imposed—because, when the aforesaid official had ordered that the interdict not be observed in the church, and the dean, by forbidding celebration in the church, seemed to disturb the divine office—nevertheless, because after the dean’s appeal [Col. 1291A] to us, to which the official had considered it proper to defer by granting apostolic letters, not only the principal matter but also the ancillary matters had been referred to our examination, we decree that the sentence, having been pronounced after a lawful appeal to us, lacked force, and that the dean was not bound by it.

But although the archbishop, misled by the counsel of certain persons, after the appeal to us had been made—of which he had been informed by letters from his official—announced that the dean was to be avoided, we judge blameless the canons of Sens who, guided by sounder counsel, communicated with him, since they deferred to the appeal made to us rather than to the archbishop’s announcement.

Since we could not fully determine whether jurisdiction over the aforesaid priest belonged to the bishop [Col. 1291B] or to the dean, we have committed the cause to your examination. By apostolic letters we command you, after summoning those who are to be summoned, to hear whatever they may see fit to allege and, setting appeal aside, to bring the matter to a canonical conclusion, causing, etc. As for witnesses, etc. No letters are to stand in the way except the consent of the parties, etc. But if not all of you, two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the tenth year.

## CXC. TO THE NOBLEMAN, THE COUNT OF NEVERS. Against the Jews. (At Saint Peter’s, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1291C]

That Cain might be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, yet not be killed by anyone, the Lord placed upon him the sign of trembling of the head. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1291D] Perhaps: “because.”] the Jews, against whom the voice of the blood of Jesus Christ cries out, although they ought not to be killed, lest the Christian people forget the divine law, ought nevertheless to be scattered abroad over the earth as wanderers, so that their faces may be filled with shame and they may seek the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

For blasphemers of the Christian name ought not to be supported by Christian princes in oppressing the servants of the Lord, but rather constrained in the servitude which they deservedly rendered themselves worthy of when they laid sacrilegious hands upon him who had come to confer true freedom upon them, crying out that his blood be upon them and their children.

But, as has been reported to us, certain secular princes, having no regard for God—to whose eyes all things are naked and open—although it is disgraceful to exact His “usuries” (*usuras*), receive Jews into their towns and settlements in order to appoint them as their agents for exacting usury. They do not fear to afflict the churches of God and the poor of Christ. When Christians who have borrowed from Jews have paid them the principal and more, the officials and servants of those powerful men often seize pledges, and sometimes commit the same Christians to prison, compelling them to make the most burdensome payment [Col. 1292A] of usury. Thus widows and orphans are stripped of their inheritances, and churches are defrauded of tithes and other customary revenues, while Jews hold castles and villages by occupation and wholly refuse to render to the prelates of churches what is due by parochial right.

No small scandal is also produced in the Church of Christ through them. Since they shrink from eating, as unclean, the flesh of animals slaughtered by believers, they obtain through the favor of princes that butchers deliver animals to be slaughtered to them; having cut them up according to the Jewish rite, they take from them as much as they wish and leave the remainder to Christians. Jewish women do similar things with milk publicly sold for the nourishment of children.

They also presume upon another practice no less detestable to Christians: at vintage time a Jew treads grapes wearing linen stockings, and, after the purer wine has been drawn off according to Jewish rite, they retain from it whatever they please and leave the remainder—regarded by them as defiled—to Christian believers. From this wine the sacrament of Christ’s blood is sometimes made. Moreover, protected by the favor of powerful men, they admit no Christian witnesses against themselves, however good and beyond every exception they may be. [Note: [Col. 1291D] See the chronology of Robert of Auxerre, fol. 102.]

Certainly, our venerable brother the bishop of Auxerre, in order to remove such abomination from his diocese, after taking counsel with prudent men, prohibited these practices there under bond of anathema. In a solemn synod he enjoined the priests present [Col. 1292C] to forbid such things in their churches, under penalty of excommunication. Most believers, obediently complying, chose to abstain from the aforesaid abominations.

But certain nobles and powerful persons, and their agents, attending to the gifts of the Jews that pervert their hearts, presumed to frighten with threats and afflict with insults certain believers who, for the good of obedience and fear of the promulgated sentence, had resolved to refrain from such practices. They even seized some and compelled them to ransom themselves, refusing to release them except at the pleasure of the Jews. To prevent themselves from being restrained from these acts by a sentence of excommunication against their persons and an interdict upon their lands, they seek protection through the obstacle of an appeal made to the Apostolic See, in mockery of ecclesiastical discipline. [Note: [Col. 1292D] See book I, epistle 230, and book II, epistle 12.]

Moreover, if because of this a sentence of excommunication or interdict is at any time promulgated against Christians, the Jews glory because, on their account, ecclesiastical instruments are hung upon the willows of Babylon, while priests are nonetheless defrauded of their revenues. Yet you, as we have heard, although as a Catholic man and servant of Jesus Christ you ought, out of reverence for him, to oppose Jewish superstitions lest the enemies of the cross exalt themselves against the servants of the Crucified One, give them especial support and are their principal defender in the aforesaid abuses.

Would not your zeal be grievously aroused against one subject to you if he gave aid to your enemy? How much more, therefore, ought you to fear the divine offense in not being afraid to show favor to those who presumed to crucify the only-begotten Son of God and still do not cease from blasphemies? Wishing, therefore, to remove from the midst of the people the scandal arising from this and to abolish the excess of such presumption which you are said to have committed against Christ and his Church, we ask, admonish, and exhort your nobility in the Lord. By apostolic letters we command you to correct the aforesaid matters personally in such a way, refraining henceforth from like practices, that you may appear to possess zeal for the orthodox faith and that we may not be compelled [Col. 1293B] to lay our hands to their correction—for, according to the Apostle, we stand ready to punish every disobedience, since we have been established by the Lord to uproot what should be uprooted and to plant what should be planted.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

## CXCI. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS. He is absolved from the charges brought against him. (At Saint Peter’s, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.)

As you have learned from what you experienced, persecution does for a just man what the furnace does for gold or the flail for grain. For when Burchard, canon [Col. 1293C] of Poitiers, formerly reported many grave charges against you to us, we ultimately committed inquiry into them, upon his accusation, to our venerable brother the bishop of Nantes and our beloved son the cantor of Blessed Radegund at Poitiers. Proceeding in the matter according to our mandate, they received, both regarding the matters contained in our letters and others, witnesses whom he produced against you and witnesses whom you caused to be produced in your defense. They faithfully sent us the inquiry made under their seals.

We caused it to be diligently examined by our beloved sons, Guala, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, and John, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian; and both you and Burchard were granted the opportunity lawfully to argue concerning it. When each matter had been reported to us by the same cardinals, we found that absolutely nothing had been proved against you; indeed, the witnesses of the opposing party showed you innocent of some of the charges. Therefore, the wisdom of God having shown that he who had stained you was a liar, you have shone more brightly after this persecution, like gold passing through fire.

Accordingly, we, who by no means seek the ruin of our brothers and fellow bishops, but rather rejoice in their innocence, by the common counsel of our brethren absolve you from the charges—or, more truly, declare you absolved and vindicated by those very charges. Since, however, before Burchard suggested such matters to us, frequent complaint had already arisen against you concerning some [Col. 1294A] of them, we could indeed have imposed canonical purgation upon you according to canonical enactments. But because, when the case came to judgment, nothing at all was found against you, you appear also to have vindicated your former reputation. We have therefore judged moderation appropriate: if, according to the discipline which we have given you, you support your reputation by the praise of a more cautious life, we shall henceforth absolve you even from undergoing purgation; otherwise, we impose that same purgation upon you according to the canonical ordinances.

We also decree void and without effect the sentence of suspension which Elias, formerly archbishop of Bordeaux, pronounced against you because, though summoned by him, you did not attend the consecration of our venerable brother the bishop of Angoulême. For it has been established before us through suitable witnesses whom you produced on this matter at the Apostolic See that the sentence was pronounced after an appeal reasonably made to us; and we decree that you were not bound by such a sentence.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

## CXCII. TO MARGARET, ABBESS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY OF SAINT COLUMBA OF BLENDEKA, AND TO HER SISTERS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (At Saint Peter’s, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1294C]

For those choosing the religious life, apostolic protection ought to be present, etc., through “we grant”; and we receive the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary of Saint Columba of Blendeka, in which you are devoted to divine service, under blessed Peter’s and our protection, etc.

First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery at present justly and canonically possesses, etc., through “shall remain”; among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1294D] is situated, with all its appurtenances; the parsonage and altar of the church of Saint Columba of Blendeka, with its revenues, tithes, and other appurtenances; the chapel of Soieka belonging to the same parsonage, with tithes, revenues, and its other appurtenances; the altars of Witeca and Oudinghesela, with tithes and other appurtenances, which the same monastery possessed before it adopted the institutions of the Cistercian brethren; the holding at Sarto Riccarii, with its site and other appurtenances; two parts of the tithe of Streties near Mount Kaurel, and the tithe of flax of the same place, with its holding and other appurtenances; a third part of the tithe of Rinc; two sheaves of tithe from [Col. 1295A] Mortiers, of land both cultivated and uncultivated, with two landholdings; and two sheaves from Lefolie; also part of the tithe of Wivnegeval, with two sheaves from one field of land, both cultivated and uncultivated, and three landholdings.

Moreover, the donations, with possessions and other things, granted to you and your monastery by Desiderius, bishop of Thérouanne, of happy memory. [Note: [Col. 1295] His letters are published in vol. XI of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 330.] The tithes held by W. de Casteller and Henry of Lefolie in the parish of Altaribus, with their lands and appurtenances. Whatever you possess in the parishes of Altaribus, Bosinghere, and Curs in tithes, lands, and other property. The tithes of Curs which Peter and Gunfridus of Sarto Riccarii conferred upon you in alms. Part of the tithe of Kernemarese; the tithes of [Col. 1295B] Rech, Timbrona, and Lingiacho granted to you in alms. Two parts of the tithe of Lidringhere, with its lordship, lands, and other appurtenances. A third part of the tithe of Odinghetum, which Godfrey, a layman, granted in alms to your church. Also the mill and land adjacent to the precinct of Saint Columba, with twelve annual pence and its appurtenances. Land likewise adjacent to the same precinct, formerly belonging to the cleric Eustace and his co-sharers, with its appurtenances. The mill formerly belonging to Matthew, knight, with its appurtenances. Two measures (*raseriae*) of wheat, four capons, one landholding adjoining the mill of Bruai, and five annual shillings, conferred upon you by the castellan of Bergues; fifteen landholdings formerly belonging to Simon, knight of Roden.

The county-right of Witeka, and whatever you possess by gift of its castellan in cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, dwellings, waters, mills, and other things. The county-right which you possess in the parish of Blendeka, with its appurtenances, granted to your church by the gift of Philip, formerly count of Flanders. Thirty-two landholdings which you possess in the parish of the Church of Saint Omer. Twenty-five and a half landholdings, and a tenth part of one holding of woodland, which you possess at Reihout. Ten holdings of marshland charitably given to you by Count Reginald of Boulogne and his wife Ida. Also half the valley, with the whole right of lordship, [Col. 1295D] which Boidinus of Haveskerka gave you, with its appurtenances. Ten measures of Artois grain, which you possess in the mill of Witeka. A fourth part of the entire village of Wenningeval, except the wood called *le Fai*. The possessions you have in the parish of Altaribus, with tithes, lands, and other things conferred upon your monastery. One ploughland, and the lands that you possess in the parishes of Bosinghere, Sperleke, Guminelinghere, and Farkenberga. Forty-two holdings of woodland near Kercamp. The land you possess near Hassinghere. The revenues you possess in the parish of Artois. Seven quarters of oats which you possess by grant [Col. 1296A] of Hubert of Saint Omer. Whatever you possess in the parishes of Blendeka, Soieka, Werdrika, and Rakinghere in cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, dwellings, and other things. Whatever you possess in the borough of Saint Omer and outside it in lands, dwellings, meadows, marshes, waters, fishponds, and other things. Arable land adjacent to the precinct of Saint Michael. Arable lands and meadows in Werdrika. Whatever you possess in the parishes of Rakinghere and Soieka. Eight landholdings which Simon, priest of Hasebroc, granted you out of divine devotion. One *pisa* of butter, and the lands you possess in the parish of Brokerka. Five annual shillings at Rubroc. Thirty-six *hodi* of oats in the parish of Sudinghesela.

Certainly, from the produce of your labours, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, both from cultivated and uncultivated lands, etc. You may also receive free and absolved women fleeing from the world, etc. Furthermore, we forbid any of your sisters, after making profession in your monastery, to be permitted, etc. But one departing, etc. We strictly prohibit anyone from personally giving away or otherwise alienating lands or any benefice conferred upon your church without consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than has been stated, we decree them void.

For consecrations of altars or churches, holy oil, or any other ecclesiastical sacrament, no one may dare to extort anything from you under pretext [Col. 1296C] of custom or in any other way; rather, the diocesan bishop shall provide all these things to you freely. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer who possesses the favor and communion of the Apostolic See; supported by our authority, he shall provide you with what is requested.

Furthermore, when a general interdict of the land is in force, you may nevertheless celebrate divine offices in your monastery, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons. Wishing also to provide in future, with paternal concern, for your peace and tranquility, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your sites or granges, to commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, rashly seize or kill a person, or dare to employ violence.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority and fortify by the protection of the present writing all liberties and immunities granted to your order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons. We therefore decree that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery or take away its possessions, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop in the aforesaid chapel. [Col. 1297A] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc. But to all who preserve its rights for the same place, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CXCIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND THE ABBOT OF MARMOUTIER AT TOURS. The sentence pronounced for the abbess of Saint Mary of Angers is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1297B] Since the beloved sons, the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem, had formerly sent us their complaint that the beloved daughter in Christ, the abbess of Saint Mary of Angers, had caused them to be despoiled, by secular force, after an appeal had been lodged with us, of the charitable house which they had acquired by the gift of Richard, the illustrious king of England of blessed memory, and had possessed peacefully for some time; and that she was unjustly retaining the same house after occupying it: we committed the case to the chancellor, archdeacon, and provost of Armeliac in the diocese of Chartres. Subsequently annulling their proceedings, because they had proceeded after an appeal reasonably lodged with us and before the suit had been contested, we determined, with the common consent of the parties, to commit the same case to our beloved sons the abbot of Monastery-New, [Col. 1297C] the prior of Saint Radegund, and Master G., canon of Poitiers. Having diligently examined the case, they remitted it to us with adequate instruction.

Accordingly, the said abbess and the procurator of the Hospital being recently present before us on this matter, the procurator alleged that, through the depositions of witnesses produced before the aforesaid judges, many things had been proved which plainly demonstrated the violence inflicted upon them; for this reason he sought the remedy of restitution. Indeed, he asserted that it had been manifestly proved that the aforesaid abbess, having assembled a multitude of laymen, came to the said house, urgently demanding that the keys of that house be delivered to her. Although the brethren of the Hospital [Col. 1297D] dwelling there raised an appeal to us, so that nothing might be done to their injury, placing themselves under apostolic protection, the said abbess nevertheless brought with her to that house the provost of Angers. When he had firmly commanded them all to restore the keys of the house to the abbess, they immediately surrendered them in accordance with the command of one whom they greatly feared. But the abbess, having received the keys from them, assigned one portion of them to canons and another to her servants, ordering them not in any way to provide the brethren of the Hospital with food, nor to permit it to be provided by others. Having suffered grievously from hunger for three days, they were forced to depart from that place.

[Col. 1298A] Therefore, since, as the procurator asserted, fear had been instilled into those brethren through the multitude of men whom the abbess had brought with her; and since, after their appeal to us had been lodged, an injury appears to have been done to them, who were compelled, through pressure exerted by a secular lord, to restore the keys of that house and, through the withholding of food, to depart from that place: the aforesaid procurator sought their restoration to that house.

The abbess’s party, however, alleged as follows: S., seneschal of Henry, king of England of illustrious memory, had founded at his own expense the aforesaid house, with an oratory, upon land belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary; and subsequently, with the consent of the diocesan bishop, an order of regular canons following [Col. 1298B] the Rule of blessed Augustine had been established there. The regular canons to whom the house had been granted possessed it peacefully for a long time. Thereafter the aforesaid King Richard, while returning from the regions of Jerusalem and being held in custody, conferred that house upon the aforesaid Hospitallers. When they later came to it in order to take possession, the abbess and her sisters opposed them. Yet they, scorning both the sisters’ opposition and the appeal to us which had been lodged on this account, nevertheless entered the house and violently expelled the clerics ministering there.

When, in the course of time, the aforesaid king learned that the same Hospitallers were dissipating the goods of that house, which had been assigned to the use of the poor, he ordered that, the Hospitallers having been excluded, the canons who had been violently expelled from it should receive the full administration of the house. Those same canons continuously held it until the present time. Since, therefore, these facts appeared to establish that the Hospitallers had falsely alleged themselves to have been despoiled, restitution ought rightly, according to that party’s assertion, to be denied them.

To the objections raised by the aforesaid procurator, the abbess’s party replied as follows. Even if it had been proved that the abbess came to the house with a multitude of men, it was not at all shown either that she herself, or those who had come with her, inflicted any violence upon the brethren, or that the provost who came to the house used any [Col. 1298D] force or addressed the Hospitallers in threatening terms. Nor is anything found to have been attempted against the appeal lodged by them, although that abbess received from them the keys of the house which they surrendered. For although the abbess ordered that food should not be given to the Hospitaller brethren who wished to remain there on their own authority, they could not and ought not to have regarded this as an injury done to them, since the abbess was not bound, unless she wished, to provide those brethren with provisions.

Moreover, that party added that restitution of the said house was improperly sought against the abbess. Although the abbess claims certain rights in it for herself because she holds the right of patronage therein, [Col. 1299A] nevertheless it is possessed not by her but by the aforesaid canons. Therefore, since she does not possess it and has not ceased to possess it through fraud, a restitutory interdict could not properly be brought against her.

We therefore, having fully understood these matters and others which the parties took care to allege both before the aforesaid judges and before us, by the counsel of our brethren have decreed by judgment that the aforesaid abbess be absolved, as regards the possessory question—which alone is found to have been litigated—from the claim of the aforesaid procurator and the Hospitallers. Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that you cause what has been determined by our judgment to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside.

[Col. 1299B] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CXCIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE, THE BISHOP OF GENEVA, AND THE ABBOT OF CASSAN, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER, IN THE DIOCESE OF LYONS. Concerning the archbishop of Lyons, accused of various charges. (At Saint Peter’s, the ninth day before the Kalends of February.)

The outcry which has for some time arisen against the archbishop of Lyons has grown so great that we cannot further ignore it without danger. For, besides other serious matters frequently reported concerning him by many persons, it has recently been made known to us that he destroyed the monastery of Savigny, [Col. 1299C] devastated the monastery of Lérins by fire, invaded, contrary to his own oath, the castles of Mont-Trotier and Mont-Bloi, and drove all their inhabitants into exile. Moreover, he largely demolished Lyons, by fire and ruin alike, not only without keeping the peace he had promised but also without keeping the faith he had pledged. There more persons perished by the sword, and some by drowning, although its citizens had placed themselves and their property under apostolic protection and appealed to our hearing. Finally, scorning the appeal, the same archbishop did not blush to launch sentences of excommunication and interdict against them. He also continues to violate the public highway and impose new tolls upon merchants.

[Col. 1299D] Therefore, since, if these things are true, we ought not to pass over them with our eyes closed, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if a lawful accuser shall appear concerning these or other charges against him, you grant him opportunity for defence, hear what may be alleged against and for him, and, having God alone before your eyes and proceeding by the royal road, decide what is canonical, causing what you decide to be firmly observed by our authority. But if no accuser comes forward against him, since public report charges him before us with infamy in these matters, nevertheless investigate the truth with the greatest diligence, all obstacle of appeal removed; [Col. 1300A] faithfully set it down in writing and take care to send it to us under your seals. You shall appoint the archbishop a suitable term within which he is to appear before us in person or through a suitable representative, so that, with both him and those who proceed against him present before us and setting forth fully their arguments, should they wish to do so, we may, with God as author, render a just judgment.

If you find that the said sentences of excommunication and interdict were issued after an appeal lawfully lodged with us, declare by apostolic authority that they are null. Otherwise, after relaxing them according to the form of the Church, hear whatever question there may be and, with appeal set aside, decide it by due judgment, causing what you decree to be firmly observed by such coercion as is fitting. If not all of you, then two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CXCV. TO THE BISHOP, DEAN, AND CHAPTER OF AUXERRE. Concerning the regalian rights of Auxerre. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Note: [Col. 1299] See book XIII, letter 180; book XIV, letter 52; book XV, letters 39–40.] “To the just desires of petitioners,” etc., down to “to fulfil.” Since therefore our dearest son in Christ Philip, the illustrious king of the French, has, out of devotion to piety, granted in perpetuity to your Church whatever right he possessed in the regalian rights of your Church during a vacancy of the see, so that all revenues from those regalian rights and the prebends which might fall vacant in the meantime are to be reserved by you, [Col. 1300C] sons, dean and chapter, for the future bishop: we, graciously assenting to your prayers, confirm by apostolic authority this grant, made as it was from devotion to piety and more fully contained in the king’s own charter; and we strengthen it for you and, through you, for your Church, by the protection of the present writing. For greater clarity, we have caused the charter itself to be inserted word for word in this document of ours.

“In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Amen. Philip, by the grace of God king of the French. Let all present and future persons alike know that, out of devotion to piety and for the salvation of our soul and of the souls of our parents, we give and grant in perpetuity to the Church [Col. 1300D] of Auxerre whatever right we possessed in the regalian rights of Auxerre during a vacancy of the see. Thus, the dean and chapter of that Church shall keep the regalian rights during the vacancy, and all revenues arising therefrom, and any prebends which may happen to fall vacant in the meantime, for the benefit of the future bishop; saving our service of riding, military service, and summons, as the bishops of Auxerre have rendered them to us. And that this may obtain perpetual force, we confirm this present charter by the authority of our seal and by the character of our royal name inscribed below.

Done at Paris in the year of the Lord 1206, and in the twenty-seventh year of our reign. Present in our palace were those whose names and marks are set below. No seneschal. The mark of Guy, cupbearer. The mark of Matthew, chamberlain. The mark of Drogo, constable. Given, the chancellery being vacant, through the hand of Brother Guarin.” Therefore let no person at all … violate this our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CXCVI. TO THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE. Concerning the lectorship and schoolmastership of the Church of Auxerre. (At Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Note: [Col. 1301D] See *Gesta episcoporum Antissiodorensium*, p. 487.] It was set before us on your behalf that, since your archdeacon has the power to confer two offices in your Church, namely the lectorship and the schoolmastership, and since no one is found willing to receive them because they have no adequate revenues, he consents that their collation should pass to episcopal right, because you, having regard for the welfare of the Church, proposed to assign suitable revenues to the aforesaid offices. [Col. 1301B] But because you do not think this can have force without the authority of the Apostolic See, you humbly petitioned us to deign to grant the collation of the aforesaid offices to you and your successors.

Therefore, graciously assenting to your prayers, by the authority of these presents we permit you and your successors, if the consent of your archdeacon is obtained, freely to confer the aforesaid offices upon suitable persons, after you have taken care to assign to them adequate revenues. Therefore let no person at all [Col. 1301C] … violate this our grant, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CXCVII. TO MASTER P., DEAN OF BERTOIR. The division of the deaneries of Thouars and Bertoire is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, the sixth day before the Kalends of February.)

Since formerly the beloved son, the dean of Thouars, informed our apostolic office that his deanery had been divided contrary to the Lateran Council, and asserted that you held a part of it; and since we ordered the truth of this matter to be investigated by our beloved son the abbot of Ternay, the cantor, and Master C., native canon of Saintes, [Col. 1301D] and they remitted the case to us with adequate instruction: we committed it for hearing to our beloved sons Andrew, subdeacon, and Rainald, acolyte, our chaplains.

Before them the opposing party alleged that, while that deanery was vacant, our venerable brother John, formerly archbishop of Lyons and then bishop of Poitiers, without seeking the consent of the Apostolic See and with no utility requiring or necessity pressing, had not hesitated to make a division of it. By this, the Church of Thouars was more burdened in paying procurations, although one person could conveniently provide for both deaneries in each church, supplying the people in life and death and infants with the ecclesiastical sacraments through priests.

[Col. 1302A] On your behalf, however, it was alleged before us that the aforesaid deanery, like the others in the diocese of Poitiers, is known, when vacant, to lie within the power of the bishop of Poitiers, and that its grant pertains to him. The said bishop, having regard for utility and necessity, as he informed us by his letters, and considering its extent and recognizing how much danger would arise to the people and to the priests of the churches if it were entrusted, in the customary manner, to one person, after deliberation with his chapter—especially with … the archdeacon of that place and other prudent and discreet men—judged that it should be divided equally. He decreed that, after the deanery of Thouars had been reduced in part, the portion removed from it should be made subject to your deanery, established by that bishop at the castle of Bertoire.

[Col. 1302B] Wishing, therefore, to bring his prudent proposal to effect with due caution, he published it in a general synod. When that salutary arrangement, which brought salvation to many in many respects, had been commended by all sitting there and caused prejudice or injury to no one, he proceeded—without preference of persons or things—to carry out the division itself. He installed individual deans in the aforesaid castles, men prudent and honorable so far as human judgment could discern. Content with the portions thus assigned to them, they had no contention among themselves but complete concord until their deaths.

Moreover, the same bishop, who at that time was exercising the office of legate in the province of Bordeaux, [Col. 1302C] publicly confirmed this division, so solemnly enacted.
