Thus the matter remained until the present time without any objection, the act itself having been approved by his successors.

Furthermore, having understood these and other matters from the parties, the aforesaid auditors, by our command, sought the advice of experts in law. From their replies they understood that such a division ought to be confirmed: both because it had been made with the approval of the entire chapter and general synod, and especially of the archdeacon of the place, to whom jurisdiction over that deanery had particularly devolved by right; because there were so many churches under the former deanery that one person could not conveniently govern them; and because it had long continued peacefully, [Col. 1302D] as was proved by numerous witnesses and by the bishop’s own letters, he having confirmed it also by the authority of his apostolic legation. They faithfully reported all this to us.

We, therefore, adhering to the testimony of the aforesaid bishop, in whose life and faith we have full confidence, have determined to confirm by apostolic authority that division, which is known to have been made with regard to utility and necessity, absolving you in this matter from the claim of your adversary. Therefore let no person at all … violate this our confirmation and determination, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CXCVIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF DUNKELD AND BRECHIN, AND THE ABBOT OF KELCHOU, IN THE DIOCESE OF SAINT ANDREWS. Concerning confirmation of the election of the bishop of Aberdeen. (At Saint Peter’s, the fourth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1303A]

The beloved sons, the dean and archdeacon of Aberdeen, appearing before us with letters from their chapter, took care to explain that, when their Church was bereft of its own pastor, they unanimously elected as their bishop the beloved son Adam, a cleric, certainly a prudent and honorable man, not knowing that he had not been constituted in holy orders. In the meantime he was promoted to the order of subdeacon. Persisting in their former consent, they elected him again and requested that we deign to confirm his election [Col. 1303B] by apostolic authority.

Since the person of the elect is commended in many ways, and the prince of the land consents to him with much popular favor, as one from whom benefit to the Church is hoped in the administration of spiritual and temporal matters, we command your discretion by apostolic letters: examine both the election and the elect; and, if the said Adam has not intruded himself into the administration of episcopal affairs, nor caused himself to be promoted to the subdiaconate in order to obtain the bishopric, then, provided that no other canonical obstacle stands in the way, confirm by apostolic authority the election made of him, and cause the reverence and obedience due to him to be rendered. Restrain any opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal notwithstanding. No letters contrary to the truth, etc. If not all of you … then two of you, etc.

[Col. 1303C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CXCIX. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF SAINT MACLOU OF BAR-SUR-AUBE, IN THE DIOCESE OF LANGRES. Concerning a non-resident canon. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifth day before the Kalends of February.)

It was set before us on your behalf that your fellow canon R. departed for Hungary long ago, and, having resided there for twenty years and more, acquired abundant ecclesiastical revenues. Since you do not believe that he will henceforth return to your church, you requested instruction from the Apostolic See whether you, son dean, to whom the grant of prebends belongs, may assign his prebend to a suitable person capable of serving your church.

Therefore, tempering the rigor of the canons, we have determined to grant you this: appoint to his prebend a suitable person as vicar, [Col. 1304A] who shall receive its fruits and render due service to your church until the said canon, having been summoned, returns. If he refuses to return, or dies before he can be summoned, the same prebend shall be canonically conferred upon the person instituted as vicar, provided that by honorable conduct he has made himself worthy.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CC. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF NEVERS. Concerning revenues to be paid to a canon engaged in study. (At Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Kalends of February.)

Since, as you informed us by your letters, an ancient custom has hitherto been observed in your church and strengthened by a pledge of faith from every canon: namely, that boy-canons not constituted in holy orders receive the lesser distributions and are not deprived of half the greater revenues consisting in grain and money—you would readily have carried into effect our mandate, made so that you should pay without diminution, while he was at school, the revenues of his prebend to your beloved fellow canon P., nephew of our venerable brother the bishop of Torres, [Col. 1304B] had you not doubted that this would contravene the aforesaid custom. This is especially so because Master P. of Vico, procurator of the said boy, is said to have sworn upon his soul that he would observe that custom inviolate. You therefore requested an apostolic response as to what you should do, constrained as you are between these two considerations.

Although such matters ought not to be alleged against us, since in this arrangement it ought either to have been expressly stated or understood that the authority of the Apostolic See was always reserved—the See which, by the Lord’s disposition, holds plenitude of power over all churches and over ecclesiastical property as well as persons; otherwise that arrangement ought [Col. 1304C] to be rejected as rash—nevertheless, in order to remove every scruple of doubt, we are content with this: that you pay to the aforesaid P., especially while he is at school, from the common revenues only as much as he would receive from his prebend.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CCI. TO THE BISHOP OF GENEVA AND THE ABBOT OF BONNEVAL, IN THE DIOCESE OF VIENNE. Written in favor of Master Oliver. [Note: [Col. 1303] See whether he is the person whose letter we have in Bongars’s collection, p. 1185. Innocent III writes to him in book XVI, letter 29.] (At Saint Peter’s, the third day before the Kalends of February.)

Since virtue loves its counterpart and is known to disdain its opposite, if our venerable brother the bishop of Grenoble had more diligently observed the merit of virtue and grace in which the beloved son Master Oliver is known to excel, he would surely have loved in him that which ought to be present in himself as a bishop, and would not have compelled him to labor to come before us on account of that which virtue appears indeed to have conferred upon him, while vice removed it. Especially since, wishing to live temperately beyond poverty yet short of riches, he preferred, through his charity toward that bishop, to remain content with the necessary benefice which the latter had given him, rather than elsewhere abound more richly on account of his virtues—which could by no means endure that same lack of support.

[Col. 1304D] We are not unaware how that bishop, after receiving our letters granted to the said master concerning confirmation of the church of Aspernadi, formerly bestowed upon him by the bishop, burdened him in relation to that church. Sparing our own modesty, we do not wish to exaggerate what was done, lest we be compelled justly to do what is just. We therefore strictly commanded that bishop by our letters to resign without delay to the said master the said church, together with the revenues received from it, and, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, and in consideration of the master’s proven merits, to permit him to possess it peacefully.

[Col. 1305A] Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if the aforesaid bishop neglects to fulfil what we command, you compel him to do so with the appropriate coercion, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CCII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COSENZA. A letter of consolation. (At Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Kalends of February.)

We believe that you have read and learned by experience that the bird is born for flight and man for labor. For the life of man upon earth is warfare. Though this belongs to him by the condition of nature, it nevertheless also presses upon him through the command of Him who says: “Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus” (2 Tim. 2). For the Lord will render to his saints a reward not only for fruits, [Col. 1305C] but for labors. The Apostle was not without this, when he said: “I have labored more than all the rest” (1 Cor. 15), not saying, “I have borne more fruit than all the rest.”

Therefore, since the Lord has begun to show you how great are the things you must suffer for his name, and your enemy has beheld you entering into combat with him with terrible eyes, so that your wrestling is not only against flesh and blood but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, it is fitting that you put your hand to brave deeds and confidently await, through all the days in which you now serve as a soldier, until your change comes. Let it not happen—God forbid!—that when your tempters say to you, “Bow down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51), you bend from the state of your uprightness and begin to fall before them. Concerning them [Col. 1305D] you must say effectively: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail” (2 Sam. 22).

Accordingly, we attentively admonish and exhort your brotherhood in Him who is himself the strength of those who hope in him: in the struggle which the hammer of the whole earth has stirred against you through his ministers, do not fail, but advance; and resist with unconquered mind the principalities and powers of these darknesses. For God will not give the righteous man over to perpetual wavering, nor will he suffer you to be tempted beyond what you can endure. Therefore, if camps stand against you, do not fear. Rather, as it is written of the steadfast man, if the shattered world should collapse, [Col. 1306A] trust that you are to endure its ruins undaunted. Thus, when you have been found valiant in such warfare and have overcome the battle with the ancient serpent, he who gave you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions may grant you, as one who conquers, to eat from the tree of life which is in the paradise of your God, with those to whom he will say, “Come to me, you who have labored and are burdened” (Matt. 11), and may make you rejoice in everlasting rest for your transitory labors.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

CCIII. The case between the monastery of Fossanova and the commune of Piperno is decided. (At Saint Peter’s, the third day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1306B] In the name of the Lord. Amen. Since the case concerning the wood of Morgazani, pending between the monastery of Fossanova on one side and the commune of Piperno on the other, had been committed by the supreme pontiff for determination to Lord Hugolino, bishop of Ostia, he summoned the parties before him and received the monastery’s written petition, drawn up as follows:

“I, L., steward of the monastery of Fossa Nuova, on behalf of and in the place of the monastery, petition Your Holiness that, by virtue of your office and in accordance with the apostolic mandate, you forbid the people of Piperno to molest the said monastery concerning the forest of Morgazano, or to disturb our possession. Likewise, I petition that you cause satisfaction to be made for the losses and injuries inflicted upon the monastery.” To this petition the people of Piperno replied as follows. [Col. 1306C]

“I, B., procurator of the people of Piperno, state that the forest of Morgazano has always been in our possession—namely, that of our grandfathers, fathers, and ourselves; and I state that this forest was confirmed to us by the charters of Pope Honorius, Alexander, and Calixtus. Therefore, if the people of Piperno have done anything in it—cutting, grazing, or hunting—they have reasonably possessed it by their own right. Therefore I state that I am not liable for an injury or for any loss, if one has been inflicted.”

Accordingly, when the lord bishop of Ostia had for some time investigated this cause, he delegated his authority to the archpriest of Piperno and to the judge of Sezze. Having received the witnesses of both parties and carefully examined the instruments and arguments, they referred the cause to the lord pope [Col. 1306D] with sufficient instruction.

Although the lord pope repeatedly summoned the consuls and people of Piperno before him, they refused altogether to appear, either in person or through a competent representative. Yet, because the case required an inspection of the places and boundaries themselves, he entrusted to me, Peter of Sasso, by the grace of God cardinal priest and pastor of the title of Saint Pudentiana—who was then residing in those parts—the settlement of this controversy. By letters of mandate he directed me, by way of additional precaution, to summon the people of Piperno before me and, after carefully inspecting the places in question, the arguments, attestations, and instruments of both parties, enclosed under the seal of the lord [Col. 1307A] cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian and sent to me, not to delay in bringing the case to an end by the judgment of a definitive sentence.

I therefore, in accordance with the apostolic mandate, came to the locality, boundaries, and places over which the dispute arose, and there carefully inspected the arguments, attestations, and instruments of both parties. But because, owing to a scarcity of legal experts, I could not conveniently pronounce sentence there, nor could I bring them in any way to agreement, I fixed for both parties the octave of the Nativity as the date by which they were to present themselves before the supreme pontiff. When the lord abbot and certain monks of Fossa Nuova appeared on the appointed date, the people of Piperno refused by every means to come.

Thus, at the instance of the abbot and [Col. 1307B] monks, the lord pope again caused the lord Guido de Capite Porci and his associate, and the lord G. de Tocco, to be joined with me. Before them the abbot of Fossa Nuova alleged that he possessed the forest of Morgazano neither by force, nor secretly, nor by precarious grant; and he maintained that his claim was established by many witnesses. They stated that the monastery had given the land on which the forest of Morgazano now stands to tenants to cultivate; that it had received from them a share of the crops and certain services from that land; and that afterwards the monks of Fossa Nuova had raised a wood at Morgazano. They further stated that for thirty years up to the present year they had guarded and defended Morgazano as their own; likewise, that for forty years, and indeed fifty, the monastery had quietly and peacefully possessed that same forest. [Col. 1307C]

To defeat the monastery’s claim, the opposing party alleged that it was not the monastery but the people of Piperno who peacefully possessed the said forest. A certain rescript of Pope Calixtus of blessed memory, renewed by Pope Alexander, appeared to support this contention. It contained the statement that Crescentius of Sonnino had relinquished the land of Morgazano and Mortecto, and all other lands of the people of Piperno which the people of Piperno had possessed, as is expressly gathered from the rescript; and by these words they sought to prove possession.

Moreover, witnesses were produced to prove possession on the ground that the people of Piperno had entrusted the forest to the monks; and thus the monks possessed it, not for themselves, but for the people of Piperno. For he possesses in whose name possession is held. Likewise, men of Piperno had made use of the timber, pastures, grasses, and *mappalia* [probably cloths or coverings].

To all this the aforesaid monastery replied that the foregoing allegations did not prejudice it in any respect. First, it answered the rescript of Pope Calixtus thus: the dispute on account of which the rescript was issued was then being conducted not between the monastery and the people of Piperno, but between the people of Piperno and Crescentius of Sonnino. Therefore, a matter transacted between others can neither benefit nor harm others.

Likewise, even if that dispute had been litigated between the monastery and the people of Piperno, possession is not thereby proved. For the clause contained in the aforesaid rescript—“which they had possessed,” etc.—if the rescript is carefully examined, must be referred only to the matters immediately mentioned. [Col. 1308A]

The monastery answered the allegation of entrustment as follows: possession is not proved by it. For the witnesses do not prove that the community of Piperno entrusted the forest, but merely that certain people of Piperno did so. But even if this were proved, it could in no way prejudice the monastery, because, as the witnesses say, the entrustment was made to monks, not to the convent or corporate body of Fossa Nuova. Therefore, even if the monks had received such an entrustment, no prejudice to the monastery could arise through them, lest the Church be damaged by another’s rash fault.

Likewise, to their assertion that they had used the pastures, timber, and so forth, the monastery replied that possession is not proved by the use of timber, [Col. 1308B] and so forth; since not merely a person having a right of use, but even a usufructuary, could scarcely obtain under civil law that he naturally possessed. For the law does not say that he naturally possesses, but that he is deemed naturally to possess. But even if use produced possession, it is not proved that the community of Piperno used it, as was more fully alleged above concerning the entrustment; especially since other neighboring people use the same forest and cannot for that reason be said to possess it.

The monastery of Fossa Nuova also alleged on its own behalf that, as civil law provides, the claim should above all prevail which, at the time when the suit was joined, possessed neither by force, nor secretly, nor by precarious grant.

Having therefore heard and more fully understood these and other arguments, by the authority of the lord pope and with the counsel of the aforesaid legal experts [Col. 1308C] of the lord pope, we adjudge the said forest of Morgazano to the monastery of Fossa Nuova, to be peacefully possessed by it; and we definitively decree by sentence that the people of Piperno shall cease from every molestation concerning that forest, reserving the question of ownership without prejudice to either party.

For greater precaution we caused this sentence, written by the hand of B., our beloved chaplain, to be fortified with our seal. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, in the month of January, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

Therefore let absolutely no person … violate this our confirmation, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

## CCIV. To the Bishop of Auxerre. Against the usurers of the borough of La Charité.

[Note: [Col. 1307D] See above, letter 61.]  
(At Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January.)

[Col. 1308D]

You have informed us that certain burgesses of La Charité, although they reside there for nearly the entire year, or for the greater part of it, and conduct contracts of usury, nevertheless transfer themselves on the three annual feasts to villages of the king or of other princes outside your diocese. There they exercise parochial rights, so that, falsely claiming to be parishioners of another, they evade your jurisdiction and utterly refuse to submit to justice before you.

Since fraud and deceit ought to afford protection to no one, we grant you by the authority of these presents full power, if the matter stands thus, after prior warning, to compel the aforesaid usurers by ecclesiastical censure—despite the interposition of a frivolous appeal—to render to you, as their father and pastor, the reverence and obedience due, receiving your salutary admonitions and commands. [Col. 1309A]

Therefore let absolutely no person … violate this our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the tenth year.

## CCV. To Peter, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Martin of the Mount, and to His Brothers, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life in Perpetuity. Concerning the confirmation of privileges.

(At Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1309B]

Although [Note: [Col. 1309D] See *The Deeds of Innocent III*, ch. 126.] your monastery was poor from the beginning, yet in the course of time it fell into such poverty that scarcely three monks remained in it, its possessions having either been wholly alienated or seriously encumbered. Hence it was determined in the general Cistercian chapter that it ought to be separated from the Cistercian Order, since the Cistercian observance could not be maintained there.

But we, who intend to foster the religious life once planted, unwilling that religion should be entirely uprooted from that monastery, granted one thousand pounds for retaining its possessions. We commanded our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the abbey of Pontigny, which by God’s grace flourishes greatly in spiritual and temporal matters, [Col. 1309C] to adopt your church, by our grant, as a special daughter, and to send an abbot and convent there to reform it. They complied with willing affection and sent you, with certain lay brothers, to that monastery.

But because even thus the monastery could not support a suitable convent, we granted to you, and through you to your monastery in perpetuity, the church of Saint Saviour situated near Orvieto, with all its possessions and appurtenances. By the Lord’s help, we shall give you timely aid in your other needs when we learn that you are making laudable progress, as we desire and hope.

Therefore, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Eugene, Alexander, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, [Col. 1309D] we receive that monastery under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the protection of this present writing. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, etc.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, etc. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, [Col. 1310A] with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Erasmus at the gate of Salciccle; the church of Saint John of Petra; the church of Saint Peter; the church of Saint Vitus; the church of Saint Peregrine; the church of Saint Thomas; the church of Saint Lucy in the castle of Viterbo; the church of Saint Clement; the church of Saint John of the Valley; and the church of Leonard, with the hospital of Rescieti.

At Petrognano: the church of Saint Andrew, the church of Saint Mary, and the church of Saint Zeno, with their appurtenances; and the church of Saint Clement with its appurtenances. At Vetralla, the church of Saint Mary of Cajano. The houses which you possess within the castle of the aforesaid Petrognano; the lands, vineyards, gardens, and olive-groves which you possess in the territory of that castle. The lands which you possess near Saint Alexander, and [Col. 1310B] the church itself of Saint Alexander. The field of Larteso with the valley of Vignola; the vineyards, lands, woods, and chestnut groves which you possess around your monastery. The vineyards of Lugnano, with the olive-grove. The lands which you possess near Monte Monasterulo. In the castle of Saint Victor, the church of Saint Lucy with all its appurtenances. Likewise the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour situated near Orvieto, with all its possessions and appurtenances. The lands with trees and the houses which you possess near Casa Mala. The lands which you possess near the castle of Canapio. The forest which you possess in Valle Alta, and the fourth part of the castle of Salice with its appurtenances.

Certainly, concerning the produce of your labors, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, both from cultivated and uncultivated lands, etc. [Col. 1310C]

Likewise, it shall be lawful for you to receive clerics or laymen, free and absolved, fleeing from the world, etc. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, to be permitted, etc. But one who departs, etc.

If anyone should perhaps presume to retain him, etc. Also, following the model of the privilege of our aforesaid predecessor Lucius, which was presented to and examined by us, we forbid anyone within the parishes of your churches to presume to construct or build a new church or chapel to the detriment of the older churches—saving, however, the privileges of the Roman pontiffs.

We strictly prohibit anyone from personally giving, [Col. 1310D] or otherwise alienating, land or any benefice conferred upon your church without the consent of the entire chapter, etc. If any donations or alienations are made otherwise than has been stated, we decree them void.

Furthermore, we forbid any monk or lay brother bound by profession in your house, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, to stand surety for anyone or to borrow money from anyone beyond the amount established by the prudence of your chapter, unless this is for the manifest advantage of your house. If he should presume to do so, the convent shall not be bound in any way to answer for it.

Moreover, in your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, it shall be lawful for you to use the testimony of your brethren, etc. [Col. 1311A]

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop or other person whatsoever to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions; or to presume to come to your houses for the purpose of celebrating ordinations, hearing cases, or convening public assemblies; or to impede the regular election of your abbot, or to interfere in any way, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, in installing or removing whoever may at the time be abbot.

For consecrations of altars or churches, for holy oil, or for any other ecclesiastical sacrament, no one shall exact anything from you, etc. Otherwise, it shall be lawful for you to approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, one enjoying the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, etc. [Col. 1311B]

If the see of the diocesan bishop should happen to be vacant, you may freely and without objection receive ecclesiastical sacraments from neighboring bishops, provided that no prejudice thereby be caused in the future to your own bishops. Since you do not always have access to your own bishops, if any bishop in communion with the Roman See, as we have said, and of whom you have full knowledge, should happen to pass through your locality, you may, by authority of the Apostolic See, receive from him blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and the ordination of monks.

But if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict upon your monastery or persons established therein, or even upon your hired laborers because you do not pay tithes; or on account of anything granted you by apostolic benevolence; or upon your benefactors because in charity they have bestowed some benefits or services upon you, or assisted in laboring on those days on which you work while others rest, [Col. 1311C] we decree that sentence void, as pronounced against grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall any letters have force which are shown to have been obtained while suppressing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges.

Furthermore, when a general interdict of the land has been imposed, it shall nevertheless be lawful for you to celebrate the divine offices in your monastery, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons.

On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of surreption or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the judgment of the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. The person elected shall then approach the Roman pontiff for blessing.

Moreover, desiring with paternal concern to provide in the future for your peace and tranquility, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your places [Col. 1312A] or granges to commit robbery, etc.

Furthermore, all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, Roman pontiffs, together with liberties and exemptions from secular exactions granted by kings, princes, or other faithful persons, etc.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop in the aforesaid churches. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, etc., to the end.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1312B] on the Kalends of February, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## CCVI. To the Bishops of Auxerre and Troyes. Concerning an inquiry against certain heretics.

(At Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of January.)

[Note: [Col. 1311D] See above, Book II, letters 63 and 99; and Raynaldus, under the year 1233, §59.]

From the tenor of your letters, brother bishop of Auxerre, we have learned that although your predecessor of good memory, like a provident and discerning shepherd keeping the night watches over his flock, labored with diligent care and solicitude to eliminate heretical depravity from the borough called La Charité, yet that Babylon could not even now be wholly healed of this disease. Very many persons of both [Col. 1312C] sexes who had abjured every heresy before your aforesaid predecessor have, like dogs, returned to their vomit. It does not suffice them that they have delivered themselves to perdition; they also endeavor to draw others with them into destruction. Secretly they introduce into the people's *vaccas* [“cows”; reading uncertain] certain heresiarchs, whom [Note: [Col. 1312D] See the Council of Caraman, 1167, and Reiner, ch. 6 against the Waldensians.] they call “consolers,” in order that these may kill your sheep with the poison of pestilential teaching.

For Hervé of Lorriach, Hugh Rapterius, and certain others, as you have learned to be true, who in the time of your predecessor fled the aforesaid town because they were heretics, now under the pretext of trade visit suspect places with their kinsmen. Having remained there three or four months, when they return, as is said, [Col. 1312D] they bring back with them perverters of sound doctrine.

Thomas Morandus also, whom your predecessor had excommunicated because of confessed heresy, after obtaining from the archdeacon of Paris the benefit of absolution through certain letters of ours procured by concealment of the truth, has not sought to erase the infamy already incurred by the display of good works. Therefore, since you do not think that he, like an Ethiopian, has changed his skin, you requested that he be restored to the former sentence until it is established that he has made himself worthy of the benefit of absolution.

Furthermore, Geoffrey and W. of Monneto, Stephen Pasturelli, and …, widow of W. Senneverus, having been accused of heresy in the time [Col. 1313A] of your said predecessor, departed from the diocese of Auxerre. Now that they have returned, although you wish, as belongs to your office, to ascertain their faith, they seek an evasion for malice: though they have their residences in your diocese, they claim now to belong to the diocese of Nevers, now to that of Bourges.

You have therefore humbly requested that the sickle of the Apostolic See be applied to the aforesaid pestilent persons and to others suspected of heretical depravity, lest their shrubs overshadow the cedars of God.

Accordingly, as your predecessor, like a good husbandman, diligently and wisely applied himself to catching those little foxes which were attempting to lay waste the vineyard entrusted to him, so you ought carefully to watch over your flock, lest ravening wolves seize and scatter your sheep, knowing that as you have succeeded him in honor, so you have succeeded him in burden. [Col. 1313B]

We too, favorably assenting to your petitions, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, in which we have fuller confidence, to proceed by apostolic authority against the aforesaid beasts, as shall be divinely inspired in you, setting aside the impediment of appeal; rooting out the tares oversown in the Lord’s field and planting the purity of orthodox faith, while restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of January, in the tenth year.

## CCVII. To Gregory, Chaplain of the Church of Othcapella. That same church is adjudged to him.

(Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of February.)

[Col. 1313C]

When our beloved son Arnold, abbot of the monastery of Middelburg, sought to molest you concerning the church of Othcapella, which you canonically held, you interposed an appeal to the Apostolic See, came into our presence, and obtained apostolic letters concerning the same dispute addressed to our beloved sons, the provosts of the Greater Church, of Saint Mary, and of Saint Peter of Utrecht. Having diligently examined the matter and received witnesses produced by both sides, they referred the case to us with sufficient instruction.

When you and the procurator of the aforesaid abbot appeared in our presence, [Col. 1313D] we committed the hearing of the case to our beloved son Andrew, our subdeacon and chaplain. Before him you asserted that, when formerly you had been presented to that church by its parishioners, who held in it something like possession of the right of patronage, to Gilbert, the late abbot of the aforesaid monastery, and had been instituted without anyone’s opposition, the said abbot afterwards entered upon the way of all flesh. His successor then began to raise a dispute against you concerning the church in question. But, having been absolved by sentence from his claim by the bishop of Utrecht, you were, for greater precaution, bodily placed in possession of the aforesaid church by your same adversary.

You therefore petitioned us to impose silence upon your adversary concerning it, since you had lawfully acquired it from his predecessors. But when the aforesaid auditor faithfully reported to us these matters and the other matters which the parties wished to submit before him, and informed us of what had been proved on either side, we caused the aforesaid church to be adjudged to you, imposing perpetual silence upon your adversary concerning it. [Col. 1314A]

Therefore let absolutely no person … violate this our determination, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the tenth year.

## CCVIII. To Bishop T., the Archdeacon, and the Scholasticus of Tournai. That they inquire against the bishop of Utrecht.

(Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of February.)

[Col. 1314B]

Although the bishop of Utrecht, before our venerable brother the bishop of Ostia and our beloved son Leo, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross, legates of the Apostolic See, and many magnates, attempted in numerous ways to excuse himself by claiming that the sentence of excommunication by which we had bound him had not reached him, and that he had not entered into a conspiracy against the Apostolic See with certain clerics, yet, according to Solomon’s saying, the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.

But since he has humbly petitioned us to grant him the benefit of absolution—which ought in no way to be denied to one humbly requesting it—we strictly command your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 1314C] that, after receiving from him publicly a sworn security that he will obey without any condition or reservation the mandates of the Apostolic See, you procure to grant him the benefit of absolution.

Thereafter you shall carefully warn and effectively induce him to strive to make satisfaction, with interest ceasing, or to come to an agreement, with Parent. and P. de Cicc., citizens of Rome, Alex. and Accat., merchants of Siena, or their messengers, concerning the money which he owes them, as is contained in the authentic instruments. If necessary, compel him to this both by force of oath and by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside.

You shall also investigate most diligently, by the oaths of our beloved sons N., abbot of Saint Paul; Corr. de Staur. and N. de Ostbruoc, abbots; and R., provost of Saint Mary; W., provost of Saint Peter; Otc., provost of Saint Boniface; and others, whether knowledge of the excommunication pronounced against him came to that bishop, or whether public report attested that it had come to him; whether, after he learned that he was bound by the bond of excommunication, he nevertheless celebrated [divine offices]; or whether he conspired with any persons against the Apostolic See. Faithfully reduce to writing what you discover in these matters and transmit it under your seals to our presence. [Col. 1314D]

And if not all … you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the tenth year.

## CCIX. To the Illustrious Queen Maria. Against the bishop of Schleswig.

(Lateran.)

[Col. 1315A]

[Note: [Col. 1315D] See below, letter 215; Book XII, letter 63; Book XIII, letter 158; Book XV, letter 3; and Arnold of Lübeck, Book VII, chapters 12–13.]

The more ardently you cherish your husband’s advancement and honor, the more earnestly you ought always to induce him to do those things which ought to please God and us, entirely abstaining from those which would deservedly provoke divine and our own displeasure.

He himself, as a Catholic prince, very recently sent us certain letters full of devotion and not devoid of prudence, beseeching us to admit the postulation made by the chapter of Bremen concerning Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig, and to promote him to the metropolitan see of Bremen.

While we were deliberating on this, [Col. 1315B] a messenger of our beloved sons the provost, dean, and chapter of Hamburg arrived and presented us their letters. By these they informed our apostolate that, whereas formerly the church of Hamburg enjoyed metropolitan rank and Bremen episcopal dignity, the two churches had been united by authority of the Apostolic See; and that from that time to the present the canons of both churches had elected the archbishop of Bremen jointly.

Since, therefore, the provost, dean, and chapter of Bremen had recently postulated the aforementioned bishop as archbishop without consulting them at all, or certain religious men who ought to have been present at the election, they earnestly requested us to restore to its proper state what had been undertaken concerning that postulation to their prejudice.

Furthermore, after the same bishop had been released from prison by our command, [Note: [Col. 1315D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §§19, 22.] and after envoys of the illustrious king of the Danes had laid certain serious charges against him when he was finally present before us—charges concerning which he sought to show himself blameless—we commanded the king in our letters, with the knowledge and will of the aforesaid bishop, to send prudent and faithful men to the Apostolic See by the most recently past feast of the Nativity of the Lord. They were to be granted authority so that through and with them, if it were given from above, [Col. 1315D] we might negotiate a settlement concerning this matter.

Otherwise, after hearing and understanding what the king wished to allege against that bishop through them, and what the bishop might set forth in his own defense, a judgment of equity would proceed from our presence.

Subsequently, for this purpose, the beloved son [Note: [Col. 1315D] Peter, provost of Roskilde, below, Book XI, letter 10.] who was the king’s envoy, appeared before us while discussion was being held concerning the matter of the postulation. In his presence the aforesaid bishop petitioned us for the benefit of restitution, asserting [Col. 1316A] that the king had deprived him both of episcopal property and of patrimonial goods.

The said provost responded in opposition that he could not properly seek the assistance of restitution, since he had caused himself to be despoiled when, abandoning clerical dress, [Note: [Col. 1316D] See Arnold of Lübeck, Book VI, chapter 18.] he usurped for himself a royal title. Moreover, charging him with the crimes of lèse-majesté, apostasy, adultery, perjury, dissipation of property, and conspiracy, he maintained that not only ought the benefit of restitution to be denied him, but also that the postulation made concerning him ought altogether to be rejected—especially since he was irregular, having been begotten of a double adultery. His dispensation, moreover, had formerly been obtained from the Apostolic See by fraud, since it was concealed that he was illegitimate and stated that he was natural-born; and, imitating his father’s incontinence, he himself has sons born after receiving sacred orders. [Col. 1316B]

But we, attending to the things of peace, judged that his petition for full restitution both of the bishopric and of his patrimony should be admitted, in favor of ecclesiastical liberty. We granted him that, if he did not wish to entrust himself to the said king, he might receive corporal restitution through a suitable procurator, while he himself meanwhile remained wherever he preferred, in a place not reasonably suspect to the king.

When he answered that he wished to obtain the benefit of restitution through a suitable procurator, and had obtained deliberative time to decide where he would meanwhile remain, he proved ungrateful for the favor granted him and deceitfully and contumaciously fled from us without leave, [Note: [Col. 1316D] Arnold of Lübeck, Book VII, chapter 12.] doubtless in order, if he can, to carry out the malice he had already conceived. [Col. 1316C]

Therefore, in the name of Almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by the authority also of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and our own, we excommunicate and anathematize that same man, utterly rejecting the postulation made concerning him, of which he has made himself wholly unworthy.

Accordingly, we have judged that your serenity should be exhorted and requested. We faithfully and prudently advise and urge that you carefully admonish and induce your husband to give the aforesaid bishop no assistance or favor, but to avoid him as excommunicated; and not to permit scandal to arise in the Church of God through him or on his account. From this a serious scandal could also be generated against your husband, since we are unwilling to pass over in silence such daring wickedness in that bishop. [Col. 1316D]

Given at the Lateran.

## CCX. To the Bishop-elect of Würzburg. That he announce the bishop of Schleswig excommunicated.

[Note: [Col. 1316D] See the preceding letter.]

Our beloved sons, the provost, dean, and chapter of Bremen, informed us by their letters that, after their former archbishop had entered upon the way of all flesh, [Col. 1317A] they assembled together and, deliberating over the appointment of a shepherd, unanimously cast their votes for Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig. They humbly beseeched us to admit the postulation made concerning him.

Therefore, etc., in almost the same manner as above, as far as: “Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, appearing personally before the prince, you carefully warn and induce him in our behalf to grant the aforesaid bishop no assistance,” etc., as above, through “pass over in silence.”

We strictly enjoin your discretion to announce publicly that the aforesaid bishop is excommunicated and that his postulation has been utterly rejected. You are to fulfill the apostolic mandate in such a manner that we may deservedly commend [Col. 1317B] your devotion and discretion.

## CCXI. To the Abbots of Uterine Valley and Garniswika, of the Dioceses of Speyer and Metz. That they cause the sentence issued for the provost of Saint Paulinus of Strasbourg to be observed.

(Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of February.)

The case concerning the church of Walzelinhem, long since brought between the beloved sons A., provost of Saint Paulinus, and II., canon of Asela, in the diocese of Strasbourg, we committed for determination to the beloved son E., cantor of Metz, and his fellow judges. As they informed us by their letters, proceeding lawfully in the matter, they learned that the same provost had been canonically presented to the aforesaid church by the true patron, namely the abbot of Horembach; and they therefore took care judicially to approve his presentation. Since, however, the diocesan bishop and the archdeacon of the place, to whom institution belonged, maliciously opposed him, they themselves, by the authority vested in them, conferred upon him the cure of souls in that church.

But when the beloved son Frederick, procurator of the said provost, requested that the sentence of the aforesaid judges be confirmed by us in the presence of our beloved son John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, whom we had granted him as auditor, the said canon declared that the sentence ought to be deemed without force: first, because he had reasonably declined the jurisdiction of those by whom it had been rendered; and second, because, before they proceeded to sentence, he had lawfully appealed to our hearing. But after hearing these and the other matters proposed on either side, since we understood that nothing had been shown against that sentence sufficient to invalidate it, we deemed it right, justice requiring it, to approve it.

Therefore, by these apostolic writings, we command your discretion, under injunction, to cause that sentence to be inviolably observed by apostolic authority, restraining all opponents by ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding appeal.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of February, in the tenth year.

## CCXII. To Ubertus, Bishop of Bobbio

Concerning the subjection of the monastery of Saint Columbanus. (Lateran, 9 Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1318A]

[Note: [Col. 1317D] See vol. IV of *Italia sacra*, p. 1287 ff.]

In the time of our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of happy memory, when a dispute arose between O., bishop of Bobbio, of good memory, and the abbot and monks of Saint Columbanus concerning the subjection of that monastery and many other matters, that predecessor of ours, having diligently heard and more fully understood the arguments and allegations of both parties, and having taken counsel with his brethren, caused the monastery of Saint Columbanus, justice so persuading, to be adjudged to your said predecessor. He decreed that confirmation of the abbot, blessing, and regular correction of the monastery; the consecration of altars, churches, and basilicas; and the promotion of monks and clerics, both in head and members, belonged to that bishop and to his successors. He also ordered oil and candles to be paid to the same bishop and his successors, as had been established by his witnesses: namely, as much oil as would suffice honourably for his household during three Lents, and, for two parts of the year, one armful of candles each day.

In the course of time, when the abbot and monks of the aforesaid monastery stubbornly resisted the sentence rendered against them, our venerable brother the patriarch of Jerusalem—then bishop-elect of Bobbio—[Note: [Col. 1318D] See vol. IV of *Italia sacra*, p. 1295.] set forth before Pope Lucius, of happy memory, his case against them. At length, when the aforesaid sentence was found in the register of Pope Eugenius, Pope Lucius, with the common counsel of his brethren, condemned the abbot of Saint Columbanus, the monks, and their successors to obey that bishop-elect and his successors as their own bishops, confirming by apostolic authority the aforesaid sentence, as we have plainly seen contained in his authentic instrument.

Moreover, because the privileges granted to the church of Bobbio by Popes Anastasius and Adrian, of happy memory, had in part been maliciously erased, to the detriment of that church, Pope Lucius, wishing to provide for its security in the future, decreed that those privileges should never at any time be invalidated because of those erasures. All these matters were afterwards confirmed by apostolic authority by our predecessor Pope Urban, of pious memory, as is more fully contained in his privilege.

At the beginning of our pontificate it came to our hearing that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Columbanus belonged directly to the Roman Church, with no intermediary; and that, although a sentence had been pronounced against it, no prejudice ought thereby to have been created for the Apostolic See, since a matter transacted between others cannot prejudice another. We therefore instructed our venerable brother the archbishop of Genoa, then bishop of Bobbio, [Note: [Col. 1319D] See book II, letter 224.] that, if he possessed any documentary proof showing that the said monastery had been subjected to his bishopric by grant of the Apostolic See, he should not delay to send it to us by his own messenger on a fixed date.

When, for this reason, he came personally into our presence, he took care to set forth before us and our brethren his arguments and to show whatever documents he possessed concerning the matter. We, considering his devotion and also the poverty of the church of Bobbio—which, though endowed with pontifical dignity, is nevertheless represented as slight and scanty in revenues—then deemed it proper to desist from pursuing the case which we had raised concerning the aforesaid monastery. We ordered that the monastery should render him reverence and obedience according to the tenor of Pope Eugenius’s sentence; yet so that, by our desisting at that time from prosecuting the aforesaid matter through the favour granted to him, no prejudice could arise to the Apostolic See, preventing it, whenever it wished, from pursuing its claim.

Later C. and B., monks of the same monastery, came into our presence and humbly petitioned us on behalf of the abbot and convent. Since the said bishop, to whom we had decided personally to grant that favour, had been translated to the church of Genoa, and since you were oppressing them in many ways, they asked that we should see fit to pursue the right of the Apostolic See in this matter, since the aforementioned sentence ought in no respect to have created prejudice for the Apostolic See. This was especially so because he who pronounced that sentence was obliged, by the duty of his office and the necessity of law, to judge the case of which he had taken cognizance; and a matter adjudicated could not harm persons between whom judgment had not been rendered.

Therefore, since the Apostolic See is especially bound to preserve what it possesses and recover what has been seized, we instructed our venerable brother the bishop [Note: [Col. 1319D] Sicardus.] and the beloved son the abbot [Note: [Col. 1320D] John.] of All Saints, Cremona, that, if it appeared to them that you were unduly oppressing the monastery, they should appoint for the Apostolic See a suitable procurator in the matter. Having summoned the parties and heard the arguments put forward on each side, they were to proceed, notwithstanding appeal, as far as definitive sentence; then remit the adequately prepared case to our presence, assigning the parties a suitable term within which they should appear before us to receive sentence, God granting.

The said bishop and his colleague, as they informed us by their letters, [Note: [Col. 1320D] They are extant in vol. IV of *Italia sacra*, p. 126.] having more clearly learned that the said monastery was being unduly oppressed by you in many matters, wished to proceed in the case according to the tenor of our mandate. You, however, appealed to the Apostolic See in order to prevent their proceeding. Yet they disregarded the appeal and, proceeding in the matter, sent to our presence a certain monk together with privileges and other writings which seemed relevant to the case.

When on this account you were present at the Apostolic See, and urgently requested that the proceedings of the bishop of Cremona and his colleague—undertaken before joinder of issue and after an appeal lawfully entered to us—be declared wholly void and without effect, we, wishing to spare both parties labour and expense, and wishing by prudent care to prevent such a question from lapsing into the anxiety of renewed litigation, appointed the beloved son O., our acolyte and chaplain, procurator of the Roman Church. After issue had been formally joined before us and our brethren between that procurator and you, the procurator produced in court a certain privilege under the bull of Pope Formosus, of happy memory. It was so worn away by age that no mention of the monastery of Saint Columbanus, nor even a trace of it, appeared in it. Since he wished to found his claim upon that document, but that foundation was wholly nonexistent, everything built upon it appeared void and without effect.

Accordingly, having more fully understood the arguments and allegations of both parties, diligently inspected the privileges and sentences of our predecessors, and taken counsel with our brethren, we deemed that you and the church of Bobbio should be judicially absolved from the claim of the aforesaid procurator. Confirming by apostolic authority the sentence promulgated by Pope Eugenius in favour of the church of Bobbio against the monastery, we command and enact that the abbots and monks who may from time to time be in that monastery shall be subject to you and your successors by diocesan law, and shall answer to the bishop of Bobbio as their diocesan in temporal as well as spiritual matters.

And so that every ground of dispute may henceforth be removed, we impose perpetual silence concerning this question upon anyone wishing to oppose you. We decree that, if any documents should hereafter be found which appear to support the monastery and oppose the bishop, they shall be wholly without force and be considered useless. We decree, therefore, that no one shall … infringe this page of our determination, confirmation, and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of March, in the tenth year.

## CCXIII. To the Abbot and Monks of Saint Columbanus

Concerning the same case. (Lateran, 10 Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1320D]

Wishing to settle in such a manner the dispute long since raised between you and the bishop of Bobbio that neither party may thereafter be able to revive it, we appointed the beloved son O., our acolyte and chaplain, procurator of the Roman Church. After issue had been formally joined before us and our brethren between that procurator and our venerable brother the bishop of Bobbio, and after the arguments and allegations of both parties had been more fully understood, the privileges and sentences of our predecessors diligently inspected, and counsel taken with our brethren, we deemed that the bishop himself and the church of Bobbio should be judicially absolved from the claim of that procurator.

Confirming by apostolic authority the sentence promulgated by our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of happy memory, in favour of the church of Bobbio against your monastery, we command and enact that the abbot and monks who may from time to time be in your monastery shall be subject to him and his successors by diocesan law, and shall answer to the bishop of Bobbio as their diocesan in temporal as well as spiritual matters. And so that every ground of dispute may henceforth be removed, we impose perpetual silence concerning this question upon anyone wishing to oppose him, and decree that, if any documents should hereafter be found which appear to support your monastery and oppose the bishop or church of Bobbio, they shall be wholly without force and be considered useless.

Therefore, by these apostolic writings, we command your whole community, under injunction, humbly to accept and inviolably observe what has been judicially determined by us. Otherwise, any sentence which the said bishop may see fit canonically to pronounce against you on this account we shall hold ratified and, with the Lord’s aid, cause to be firmly observed.

Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of March, in the tenth year.

## CCXIV. To the Patriarch of Jerusalem, Legate of the Apostolic See

A case against the count of Tripoli is committed to him. (Lateran, Ides of February.)

[Col. 1321C]

That the heavenly indignation of Majesty, provoked by our sins, has exposed the Holy Land and the place of the tabernacle of His glory to the enemies of the Cross ought not to be wondered at. For there are committed there, by those who are Christians in name but not in deed, so many wicked crimes and criminal wickednesses, through the outrages of abuses and the abuses of outrages, that even those few remnants which seem to have remained there may, with the prophet, marvel at the many mercies of God by which they have not been consumed [Col. 1321D]—unless perhaps this itself proceeds no less from divine judgment than from mercy: namely, that the same place is perhaps inhabited more wickedly still by certain false believers than it is occupied by true unbelievers.

O wretched insolence and insolent wretchedness of those unhappy inhabitants! As though it were not enough that their souls are continually sought by enemies, they rage against themselves more cruelly than enemies do; and from domestic hostilities they add strength to the tyranny of foreigners. They pollute sanctified places; and, as Truth itself said of such persons, they betray one another, hate one another, and cause one another to stumble. As though before the eyes of Jesus hanging on the Cross, they perpetrate shameful acts; and where Truth mercifully sprang from the earth, there they act falsely and miserably. They suffer the neighbourhood of the Lord’s lodging to be polluted by the unclean, and themselves pollute it; nor, alas, are they ashamed through fear of so great an irreverence.

They do not fear lest, provoked by their injuries, the infant cry out from the nearby manger, and lest the Virgin mother, sitting near their filth, be ashamed. Although hostile wickedness grievously persecutes Christ by invading the portion of His inheritance, some of these persons, by persecuting His ministers, persecute Him more grievously. For, in order that a man’s household may become his enemies, they afflict the Church within worse than it is afflicted from without.

In particular, as we have learned from very many letters and the reports of many persons, the noble count of Tripoli [Note: [Col. 1321D] See below, book II, letters 9 and 110.] laid sacrilegious hands upon our venerable brother in Christ, the patriarch of Antioch, his lord—whose sworn man, co-godparent, and godson he is [Note: [Col. 1322D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1205, §37.]—and did not fear to hold him, or rather Christ in him, together with two of his nephews, in severe confinement.

Many matters have also been reported to our apostolic office concerning the dissensions which arose between the same count and the Templars, and our dearest son in Christ Leo, illustrious king of Armenia, both on his own account and on that of his nephew; and concerning other rivalries by which certain Christians in those regions provoke one another. Groaning over these things and saying, “Woe because of the scandals of the Holy Land” [Col. 1322C] (Matthew 18), we have not thought it necessary to report each of them to you in detail as we heard them. This is not because we do not wish to indulge the tears which their remembrance would draw forth, but because we do not think it expedient for us, strangers, to report rumours to you about matters more immediately present to you.

Therefore, we who have hitherto diligently laboured for the condition—or rather the calamity—of the Holy Land, but have not been able effectively to assist it, counselling its surviving remnant in many ways and by many means to grant one another peace and seeking aid for resistance to its enemies, although we greatly distrust our own merits, nevertheless still trust in God’s power. We judge that the safety of that land depends in no small part upon the foregoing matters. We have therefore decided to commit our authority to you in the matters which follow.

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by these apostolic writings: after carefully weighing every circumstance, devote yourself fully to the liberation of the aforesaid patriarch and his nephews; determine, supported by our authority, what you know to be expedient for the salvation and justice of each party and for the condition of the Holy Land concerning the satisfaction to be made both to the patriarch and to the Church—indeed, to God—the absolution of the aforesaid count, and the observance or relaxation of sentences already pronounced or yet to be pronounced for this sacrilege; and thereafter concerning the reciprocal justice to be rendered between the king and his nephew, the said count, and the Templars, and all other matters touching what has been set out above. Cause what you determine to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal; restraining by the same censure, any appeal ceasing, all opponents or rebels, if there are any.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of February, in the tenth year.

## CCXV. To the Lord Pope

Philip, king of the Romans, writes on behalf of the bishop of Schleswig.

To his most holy lord and reverend father in Christ, INNOCENT, supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman Church: PHILIP, by the grace of God ever august king of the Romans, greeting and the affection of filial love.

Since it may be fully evident to everyone that from that fountain in which resides the fullness of all spiritual and ecclesiastical law nothing can proceed or flow except what is holy and contains equity, one must always hope from it for that by which provision is made for everyone, while the integrity of its entire authority is preserved. Since, therefore, by divine ordinance the fullness of all ecclesiastical law resides in Your Holiness, Your prudence has full power, according to the necessity arising from the variety of different affairs, to temper the rigour of strict law and sometimes, where this is required, to preserve unalterably the severity of discipline according to the order of that same law.

Moreover, most holy Father, although we most firmly believe that the report has already reached your ears that Lord Hartwig, archbishop of the church of Bremen, having been called by God from this world, has now paid the debt of the flesh, nevertheless we have thought it right to notify you ourselves of the same. Upon the death of the said archbishop, lest the church of Bremen, deprived of its pastor, should remain thus widowed for long, the clergy of that church, together with all who ought to have taken part in the election of the future bishop, assembled for the election. Considering also the need of the said church, they unanimously transferred their votes to Lord Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig. [Note: [Col. 1323D] See above, letter 209.]

Since the transfer of bishops ought not to be made without the special permission of this Holy See, and since no bishop can pass from one church to another without your grant, we beseech Your Holiness with all the affection in our power: principally for God’s sake, and also, if the request of our majesty has any weight with you, grant to the aforesaid bishop of Schleswig that by your grace and concession he may pass to the church of Bremen, to which he has been postulated. Send him, confirmed and released by you in all matters belonging to Your Holiness, to the church of Bremen, mercifully tempering in his case the discipline of the aforesaid constitution.

Furthermore, we wish to commend to the discretion of your fatherhood that the said church of Bremen has for a long time lain pitiably under many burdens and miseries. Although it was once one of the nobler churches established within the Empire, it has suffered greatly in resources and honour for many reasons which need not now be enumerated. Yet especially through the negligence of the archbishop who has now died, and through his many personal deficiencies, the church of Bremen became greatly degraded under him; so much so that, even while he was still alive, it might justly have been called widowed.

May these considerations, therefore, move Your Holiness to provide paternally for the sufferings of the church of Bremen in this matter, by sending it Lord Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig, who is sought from Your Holiness. We further wish you to know that, in so far as concerns us and the right of the Empire, and in so far as lies in our power, we intend to employ pious and effective effort to ensure that the church of Bremen may be restored to its former condition, according to the dignity and honour which it was once accustomed to possess.

## CCXVI. To Hervey, Bishop of Troyes

The privileges granted to the church of Troyes by the king of France are confirmed. (Lateran, 7 Ides of February.)

It is customary to grant, etc. From the letters of your brotherhood we have learned clearly that, although a question arose between you and our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the French, over certain archdeaconries and prebends which that king had granted to certain clerics while your church was vacant, the king firmly maintaining that the granting of prebends belonged to him during the vacancy of that church, nevertheless the same king subsequently, recognizing your right and the liberty of your church, graciously granted that the archdeaconries, prebends, and other benefices which might fall vacant there while the church was deprived of a pastor should henceforth be reserved for the grant of the bishop subsequently appointed. He further decreed that you should dispose as you wished of the benefices which he had recently granted during the vacancy, freely admitting that he had possessed no right whatever in them.

Moreover, by royal authority the same king confirmed possessions and certain other matters for you and your successors, as we have more fully seen all these things set out in the privilege of the aforesaid king. We have thought it proper to insert its tenor word for word in these letters:

> “In the name of the Holy and Undivided Trinity. Amen. PHILIP, by the grace of God king of the French.
>
> Let all present and future persons know that our dearest late father Louis granted and confirmed in perpetuity to Matthew, then bishop of Troyes, and his successors the things appended below: namely, the village called Saint-Leu, with its appurtenances; all the right which that bishop held in the village called Avenz; all the right which he held in the village called Lanes; all the right which he held in the village called Angularia; and the island situated beside it in the river Aube; the village called Aquis, with its appurtenances, in the liberty granted to the bishop of Troyes by the lords of the village of Mauri. That is: whenever the church of Troyes should be vacant of its bishop, the lords of the village of Mauri or their officials shall take nothing from the goods of the bishop or of his men within the jurisdiction of that village; rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the use and disposition of the bishop who shall be appointed there.
>
> He granted also all the right which that bishop held in the village called Gumerium and in the village named Summus Fons, with the right and liberty which his predecessors had held in those places. Further, he granted to him and his church the liberty granted by Count Hugh, of good memory: namely, that those who, as servants of the same bishop, have obtained any public office shall, as long as they hold that office, be free and exempt from every jurisdiction and exaction of the counts of Troyes and their officials.
>
> Our aforesaid father, of good memory, further added that episcopal houses and courts, with everything contained in them, shall at the death of bishops enjoy the liberty which Count Henry is known to have granted and confirmed to him. He also granted one *modius* of grain, to be paid each year on the vigil of All Saints, which the same Count Henry gave him from the mills situated below the tower for the men dwelling at the courts of the island; and one *sextarius* of grain from the new mills near the church of Saint-Quentin, for the rent owed by Paganus of Tuso [Note: [Col. 1325D] In Camuzat: Tullo.].
>
> He granted also the oven in the bishop’s borough, with the full liberty which the aforesaid Count Henry granted and confirmed by his writing; likewise, one hundred solidi, to be paid each year by the same Count Henry to the matricularii of the church of Saint Peter from his Troyes toll; and the grange of the village of Cestin, with its appurtenances, which he had acquired and might acquire.
>
> Further, he granted the estate of Meriac, with houses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, rivers, waters and watercourses, meadows, pastures and woods, male and female serfs, as his predecessors had held them from our father himself and his predecessors. He granted also the holdings which the lords of Triagnel hold—namely, the castle of Venesiac—with the other properties which they hold from the church of Troyes; likewise the holdings which Guy of Domnipetra [Note: [Col. 1325D] Camuzat: Dampetra and Planceyo.] and Hugh of Planceo have until now held from the church of Troyes; likewise the holdings which … the viscount of Sens and the lord of Chasceney hold at the mill of Leu; the holding which Odo of Avelleio holds from the church of Troyes; and likewise the holding which the viscount of Saint-Florentin has from the church of Troyes, together with all other things which the church of Troyes is known to have held until now.
>
> We therefore confirm all the aforesaid things as they are contained in our father’s privilege. Furthermore, concerning the grant of prebends that fell vacant in the church of Blessed Peter of Troyes during the vacancy of that see: since we found no one who had seen that we had granted them, or that our father King Louis, of pious memory, had granted those which fell vacant during the vacancy; and since we also heard from the assertion of many persons that prebends, archdeaconries, and other benefices vacant at that time were reserved for the future bishop of Troyes to confer upon whom he wished, we grant to our beloved Hervey, bishop of Troyes, that he and his successors, bishops of Troyes, may confer them and possess the grant of them.
>
> We also grant to the same bishop that he may dispose as he wishes of the grants which we made in these matters, since we had no right whatever in such grants. In order that all the aforesaid matters may have perpetual force, we confirm the present charter by the authority of our seal and the royal monogram written below.
>
> Done at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207 [Note: [Col. 1326D] In Camuzat: the twenty-eighth year of our reign.], in the presence in our palace of those whose names and marks are appended below. No seneschal. The mark of Guy, butler. The mark of Matthew, chamberlain. [Col. 1326C] The mark of Drogo, constable. Given while the chancellery was vacant.”

We therefore commend in the Lord the king’s devotion in this matter, approve his grant, enactment, and confirmation, and confirm them by apostolic authority, strengthening them by the protection of this present writing. Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of February, in the tenth year.

## CCXVII. To the Same, Concerning the Same Matter

(At Saint Peter’s, 2 Kalends of February.)

For the just requests of petitioners, etc., up to “fulfil.” Since therefore our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the French, decreed that you should dispose as you wished of the benefices which he had recently granted while the see was vacant, freely admitting that he had possessed no right whatever in them, and since you afterwards assigned them to suitable persons, we, inclined by your prayers, confirm the same grant, as canonically made, by apostolic authority and by the present [writing], etc. Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 2 Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

## Stephen Baluze’s Notice Concerning the Following Letters

[Col. 1327]

What was done in the preceding books had also necessarily to be done in this one, because we found several letters of the tenth year which were not contained in the Register. There are, then, altogether five letters in this appendix. We obtained the first two from the history of Matthew Paris; the third from the cartulary of the monastery of Fossatus; the fourth from the twelfth volume of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*; and the last from the *History of Piacenza* by Pietro Maria Campi. We have additionally included a letter of the same Innocent III by which he confirms a prebend of the church of Chartres to the hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia. Although it was issued in the fourth year of his pontificate, it is included here because there was no more suitable place elsewhere. For letter 179 of this tenth book concerns the hospital of the Holy Spirit in Saxia. This letter was supplied to us by an old cartulary of the distinguished church of Chartres.

## CCXVIII. To John, King of England

He sends him gifts.

[Col. 1327A]

Among earthly riches, which the mortal eye covets and desires as though they were more precious, we believe that refined gold and precious stones hold first place. Although your royal excellence abounds in these and other riches, nevertheless, as a token of affection and favour, we send to your greatness four gold rings set with various precious stones. In them we wish you especially to understand the shape, number, material, and colour, so that you may consider the mystery rather than the gift.

For roundness signifies eternity, which lacks beginning and end. Thus royal discernment has in the shape something to seek: that it may pass from earthly things to heavenly, from temporal things advance to eternal. The number four, however, being a square number, signifies constancy of mind, which ought neither to be cast down in adversity nor lifted up in prosperity. You will fulfil this praiseworthily when it is ordered by the four principal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. Therefore understand justice in the first ring, to exercise in judgments; fortitude in the second, to display in adversity; prudence in the third, to observe in doubtful matters; and temperance in the fourth, not to abandon in prosperity.

By gold, moreover, wisdom is signified, because, just as gold excels all metals, so wisdom surpasses every gift, as the Prophet testifies: “The spirit of wisdom shall rest upon him” [Col. 1327C] (Isaiah 11), etc. Nothing, moreover, is more fitting for a king to possess. Hence that peaceful king Solomon asked of the Lord for wisdom alone, so that he might know how to govern prudently the people entrusted to him.

Further, the greenness of the emerald signifies faith; the clearness of the sapphire, hope; the redness of the garnet, charity; and the brightness of the topaz, good works, concerning which the Lord says: “Let your light shine” (Matthew 5). You therefore have in the emerald what you should believe; in the sapphire, what you should hope; in the garnet, what you should love; and in the topaz, what you should practise, so that you may ascend from virtue to virtue until you see the God of gods in Zion.

## CCXIX. To the Same

Concerning the affair of the archbishop of Canterbury. (Lateran …)

[Col. 1327D]

[Note: [Col. 1327D] See the deeds of Innocent III, ch. 131.] Although we [Col. 1328A] wrote to you humbly, carefully, and graciously concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury, exhorting and requesting you, you wrote back to us—as I may say without prejudice to your peace—almost threateningly and reproachfully, stubbornly and arrogantly. And whereas we have taken care to show you deference beyond what the law requires, you take no care to show us even the deference required by law, paying less attention than is fitting to the fact that, although your devotion is greatly necessary to us, ours is nevertheless by no means unserviceable to you. And although in such a case we have shown no prince so much honour as we have shown you, you seek to derogate from our honour to a degree which no prince has presumed to derogate in a similar case. You put forward certain frivolous pretexts by which you assert that you cannot give your consent to the election, made by the [Col. 1328B] Canterbury monks, of our beloved son Master Stephen, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus: namely, because he has associated with your enemies, and because his person is entirely unknown to you.

Moreover, according to Solomon’s proverb, “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of those that have wings,” since we understand that it should not be imputed to him as a fault, but rather reckoned to his glory, that, devoting himself for a long time at Paris to the liberal studies, he advanced so far that he deserved to be a doctor not only in the liberal arts but also in theological disciplines; and thus, since his life accorded with his learning, he was judged worthy to obtain a prebend at Paris.
