We therefore find it remarkable that a man of such renown, deriving his origin from your kingdom, could have been unknown to you even by reputation [Col. 1328C], especially since, after we promoted him to the cardinalate, you wrote to him three times that, although you had intended to summon him into the service of your household, you nevertheless rejoiced that he had been elevated to a higher office. But you ought rather to have considered that he was born in your land, of parents faithful and devoted to you, and that he had held a prebend in the Church of York, which is far greater and more eminent than that of Paris. Hence he is shown to love you and your kingdom with sincere affection, not only by reason of flesh and blood, but also on account of ecclesiastical benefice and office.

Your envoys, however, stated another reason to us why you had not consented to his election: namely, that he had never been requested by those who ought to have asked him of you [Col. 1328D]. They asserted that the letters in which we ordered you to send suitable procurators to us concerning this affair had never reached you, [Col. 1329A] and that the Canterbury monks, although they had appeared before you on other business, had sent neither letters nor envoys to request your consent. Therefore the same envoys urgently begged us, since it had pleased us to reserve to you this honour—that the Canterbury monks should seek royal assent—to grant a suitable delay, within which this might be done, because it had not been done, lest your right should suffer derogation. Finally, they advanced something against the person elected which, since it is manifestly false, they ought to have kept their mouths shut about—especially since, even if it were true, it could no longer impede his promotion.

Although the assent of princes is not customarily awaited concerning elections conducted at the Apostolic See [Col. 1329B], two monks were nevertheless specially appointed to come to you to request assent; they were detained at Ydivoria [Note: [Col. 1329D] Devoriam.], so that they could not carry out the commission imposed upon them. The aforesaid letters concerning the dispatch of procurators to our presence were also delivered to your envoys, that they might faithfully present them to you. We likewise, who possess plenitude of power over that same Church of Canterbury, deigned to request royal favour in this matter; and our courier, who presented you with apostolic letters, also offered to your royal highness the letters of the prior and monks, who, by mandate of the whole chapter of Canterbury, had conducted the election in question, requesting assent.

Accordingly [Col. 1329C], after all this, we did not see that royal consent needed to be sought anew. Rather, without turning to right or left, we determined to do what the canonical decrees of the holy Fathers prescribe: namely, that no delay or difficulty be brought to proper arrangements, lest pastoral care long be lacking to the Lord’s flock. Therefore let nothing be suggested to your discernment or royal prudence by anyone which might in any degree cause you to be withdrawn from the completion of this office. For, since the election has been conducted unanimously, canonically, and without force or fraud, in the person of a suitable man, we could not delay it without injury to reputation and peril to conscience.

Therefore, dearest son, whose honour we have taken care to respect beyond what the law requires, take care to respect our honour according to law [Col. 1329D], that you may deserve more abundantly the grace both of God and of ourselves. Otherwise, if you act differently, perhaps you may bring yourself into a difficulty from which you will not easily be able to extricate yourself, since in the end he must prevail to whom every knee bends, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal, whose office on earth we exercise, though unworthy. Therefore do not acquiesce in the counsels of those who always desire your disturbance, so that they may fish more successfully in troubled water; but entrust yourself to our good pleasure, which will certainly redound to your praise, glory, and honour. For it would not be safe for you, in this cause, to resist God and the Church, for which the blessed martyr and glorious pontiff Thomas recently shed [Col. 1330A] his blood—especially since your father and brother, kings of England of illustrious memory at that time, renounced that evil custom in the hands of the legates of the Apostolic See. But if you humbly comply with us, we shall take care to provide sufficiently for you and yours, so that no prejudice may thereby be generated against you.

Given at the Lateran . . . , in the tenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXX. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF FOSSAT. A certain grant is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 8 January.)

[Col. 1330B] The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant gracious favour to the honourable petitions of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclined by your just prayers, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the revenues which Isembard, abbot of blessed memory, with your consent, sons of the convent, granted at Longvilliers for the increase of the lights of the sacristy of your monastery, just as that same sacristy rightfully and peacefully possesses them. Let no one therefore at all, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth Ides of January, in the tenth year.

## CCXXI. TO THE BISHOP, ARCHDEACON, AND PROVOST OF ARRAS. On reducing the number of women in a house of canons. (At Saint Peter’s, 28 January.)

[Col. 1330C]

The beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Cison, have informed us that one of their houses, called Bel-Repaire, is so burdened, besides the canons and brethren, by a great multitude of women—whom they are compelled to receive at the requests and importunities of princes—that the resources of that house are wholly insufficient for their necessary maintenance. They have therefore humbly requested that they may henceforth receive no woman there, lest—God forbid—at the persuasion of the enemy of the human race, occasion for sin be afforded through them. Therefore [Col. 1330D] by apostolic writing we command your discretion, after diligent inquiry and ascertainment of the truth, to decree in this matter what you know to be expedient for the welfare of the Church and the salvation of those serving in it, notwithstanding opponents, etc. But if not all of you . . . you, brother bishop, shall nevertheless carry this out with one of the others.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth year.

## CCXXII. TO THE PROVOST AND CHAPTER OF PIACENZA. Commands made to the people of Piacenza are confirmed. (At Montefiascone, 28 July.)

[Col. 1331A]

Lest any doubt may hereafter arise concerning the command formerly made by us on your behalf to the people of Piacenza, we have thought it proper to transcribe it for you word for word:

> “To the consuls and citizens of Piacenza.
>
> “This is the command which we lay upon you under the obligation of the oath you have taken: henceforth, contrary to the tenor of the Lateran Council, you shall not burden the bishop or clergy of Piacenza with exactions or levies; and you shall restore all existing fruits which you have taken from them or caused to be taken. But concerning the other things taken away [Col. 1331B], we make this concession to you, provided that you are willing to receive this grace gratefully: that you presently pay them three thousand pounds, and that for the remainder, as you offer, you bind the communes to them, so that in their name you cause their revenues to be faithfully collected and assigned to them in full, until they have received full satisfaction.
>
> “But if you are unwilling to accept this arrangement, since sin is not remitted unless what has been taken is restored, and since there is no doubt that you can, if you will, find the money either by loan or otherwise, we command you under the same coercive authority to pay in full, within six months, the sum of money for the things taken, according to the valuation made. You shall also take care to restore the possessions which the Church [Col. 1331C] of Piacenza had to the condition in which they were at the time when violence was inflicted; nor shall you ever attempt anything against this command by force or fraud. Otherwise, besides the stigma and penalty of perjury, you shall be returned to the former sentence, and proceedings shall be taken against you according to the form of the later mandate directed to the visitors, whose contents were as follows:
>
> “We have been touched by inward sorrow of heart, and the sword of grief has passed even to the soul itself, because, although the city of Piacenza has customarily been greatly devoted to the Apostolic See, its excellent colour has now changed and its gold has been turned into dross. For it has shown itself so ungrateful that no spark of devotion or gratitude seems to remain in it. Having utterly despised its admonitions and commands, deceived by the deceits of heretics, it strives to enslave its mother, the Church of Piacenza, an honourable member of that See, wishing to reduce her, as though she were a worthless slave, under tribute; and, corrupting the other cities by its example, it incites them all together against the liberty of the universal Church. Thus we may say with the Prophet: ‘I have brought up and exalted children, but they have despised me’ (Isa. I).
>
> “If neither the justice of public decency, nor the severity of ecclesiastical discipline, nor the religion of the Christian faith, nor fear of the dreadful judgment has until now been able to recall you from the disgrace of such guilt, would that the example of pagan clemency might induce you not to make the Church suffer in our time a persecution more savage than that which she suffered from the tyrant of notorious [Col. 1332A] unbelief. For Pharaoh, king of Egypt, though he had reduced others to slavery, not only preserved his priests and their possessions in their former liberty, but even supplied them with maintenance from public funds. And Artaxerxes, king of Persia, forbade tribute, tax, and provisions to be imposed upon any priests, Levites, and ministers of the house of God. You ought therefore either to fear God or at least blush before men to exercise upon the servants of God that inhumanity of tyranny which those who did not yet possess knowledge of the truth did not exercise against them.
>
> “Alas! Who, O citizens, has bewitched you so miserably that he has made you slaves by enslaving your mother, has offered other cities an example of perversity, and has rendered you wholly ungrateful for apostolic favour? That favour freely liberated your city from the yoke of the Church of Ravenna and adopted it as a special daughter. Certainly, even if you could perpetrate such a crime with impunity, you ought not to offer so perverse an example to others; for although the crime is grave, the example is graver.
>
> “But if you spurn the benefit of the favour done to you, and, degenerating from sons into stepchildren, compel us because of your ingratitude to reproach you with the favour of the Apostolic See, which has hitherto filled you with many benefits, saying in the prophetic words: ‘They grew fat and became gross, and the beloved kicked’—will favour remain with the ungrateful? Or will a mother be able any longer to retain as sons by adoption alien children, who have lied to her and repay her [Col. 1332C] evil for good and hatred for love? Rather, those who abuse their freedom shall be reduced to servile condition, so that, if they did not recognize grace while possessing it, they may at least recognize it by losing it. At last they will grieve all the more that they have lost it because, when they seriously wish to possess it, they will be unable to do so, since they were wholly unwilling to preserve it while they could. And thus, when you have given your honour to strangers and your years to a cruel one, when strangers have been filled with your strength, and when you see your labours in a foreign house and groan at the end, we, according to Solomon’s proverb, shall laugh at your destruction; and perhaps, when what you feared comes upon you, should you wish to return, we shall refuse to receive you, whom we have long called and who refused us. With the Wise Man we shall say: ‘I called, and you refused. I stretched out my hand, and there was none who regarded it. You despised all my counsel and utterly neglected my rebukes’ (Prov. I).
>
> “Return, therefore, transgressors, to your heart, and do not render yourselves altogether unworthy of your own dignity. For, since we have waited for three years, if the barren fig tree, nourished with manure, has perhaps not produced fruit of itself, there plainly remains nothing but to lay the axe to its root, lest, spreading unfruitful branches, it uselessly occupy the surrounding ground. Since nothing is more just than that a person be punished in that wherein he has sinned, and since by what you have committed against God and the Church—rashly invading episcopal rights and even causing [Col. 1333A] your bishop and clergy to go miserably into exile—you have made yourselves unworthy of an episcopal see, we are unwilling that you should enjoy impunity for so great a crime any longer. Indeed, we have resolved with our brethren, and by this common counsel have decreed, to curb it by such chastisement that the punishment may be an example to all for whom your fault has been a scandal. Unless, therefore, within a month after receiving these letters, you return to obedience to the command of the Church, making the satisfaction due for the matters on account of which you have incurred ecclesiastical censure, your city shall be deprived of episcopal dignity and its diocese divided among neighbouring bishops. Suitable provision shall be made both for the bishop and the clergy of the city—if indeed it is still to be called a city after it has lost episcopal dignity, and thereby shall deserve to lose temporal countship as well.
>
> “Behold, the bow is drawn. Flee, therefore, from the arrow which is not accustomed to turn back, for repentance after ruin is too late, as neighbouring examples can teach you. Do not then be ashamed to recover from error, because in this conflict it is far more glorious to be conquered than to conquer: just as one who conquers vice is conquered by virtue, so indeed one who takes virtue captive is taken captive by vice. And it is a greater virtue to overcome oneself than another, especially if cruelty is conquered by mercy, as Solomon testifies: ‘The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than the conqueror of cities’ (Prov. XVI).
>
> “We therefore send to you our venerable brother the bishop of Vercelli, and our beloved sons the abbot of Tilleto and Albert, priest of Mantua [Col. 1333C], that by warnings and exhortations they may lead you, if it is granted from above, to the path of truth. Otherwise, after summoning the bishops of Lombardy and removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, they shall solemnly execute the decree set forth above. Moreover, with paternal affection we admonish, entreat, and ask you to grant us this at least by your free generosity, in hope not only of the eternal reward to be bestowed upon you by the Lord but also of a temporal reward to be granted by the Apostolic See. Know for certain that not without much sadness and great pain did we proceed to pronounce the aforesaid sentence, as those who are necessarily compelled—if you permit yourselves to be brought into this [Col. 1333D] necessity—to separate an honourable part from our body, that we may obey the command of him who orders that, if our eye causes us to stumble, we pluck it out and cast it from us.”
>
> Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of October, in the ninth year of our pontificate.”

Therefore, by apostolic writing, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, setting aside other occupations, since we now consider this the principal of all the affairs of Lombardy, you proceed together to the city of Piacenza and prudently and effectively induce its citizens—whom, as he who is ignorant of nothing knows, we do not intend to burden contrary to justice [Col. 1334A]—by whatever means you can, to obey the apostolic commands humbly and devoutly, lest they incur the aforesaid penalty, both disgraceful and damaging. Otherwise, since wounds which do not feel the remedy of poultices must be cut away with iron, summon the bishops of Lombardy and proceed to execute the aforesaid decree with such promptness and diligence that, through your care, it may attain its due effect. Know that we have granted you full authority, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed, concerning all matters necessary for the execution of this business. If all of you cannot be present to carry this out, let two of you nevertheless execute it.

Given at Montefiascone, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [Col. 1334B], in the tenth year.

## CCXXIII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF CHARTRES. On the prebend of the hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia. (At Anagni, 11 November.)

[Note: [Col. 1333D] See above, epistle 179.] In our presence, our venerable brother the bishop of Chartres, for the souls both of himself and of his predecessors and successors, with our consent, granted by pious liberality to the hospital of Saint Mary in Saxia a prebend in the Church of Chartres for the use of the sick and poor. In the name of that Hospital [Col. 1334C], we received his grant and took care to confirm it by apostolic authority, decreeing null and void anything which, concerning the prebend either now vacant or soon to become vacant, may be attempted contrary to this—which we do not believe.

But lest your church be deprived thereby of its customary service, desiring to provide with pastoral care, we will and by the authority of these presents grant that, according to the bishop’s arrangement, someone be appointed to serve that prebend. He shall receive in full one third of the revenues of the same prebend for the Church of Chartres, while the other two parts shall be paid in full each year to the aforesaid Hospital. Therefore, by apostolic writing, we command and enjoin your discretion that you hold acceptable and ratify, and inviolably observe, what was done by that bishop out of piety [Col. 1334D] and confirmed by us through apostolic authority; and that you take care to notify us of your consent by open letters. Otherwise, know that we have ordered the same bishop, our venerable brother the bishop of Orléans, and our beloved son the abbot of Vendôme, after prior warning, to compel you by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside.

Given at Anagni, on the third Ides of November, in the fourth year.

## CCXXIV. TO THE PRIOR OF THE PRIORY OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE OF SAMBLERIES AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 27 March.)

[Col. 1335A]

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, for this purpose: that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to foster religious orders pleasing to God. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of Innocent and Alexander, Roman pontiffs of blessed memory, our predecessors [Col. 1335B], we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the church of the Holy Sepulchre, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now rightfully and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God being gracious, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names:

The vill of the Holy Sepulchre, with its churches, all tithes, rights, and other appurtenances; annual prebends, as they have been granted to you by letters of the bishop and chapter of Troyes in the church of Saint Peter at Troyes; [Col. 1335C] the church of Mont-Suzanne; the chapel of Gued; the chapel of the Abbey; the mill of Gued; and everything you possess in the territory of that vill; one third of the offerings in the church of Bouilly—namely at Christmas, Easter, and the feast of Saint Lawrence—and the tithe in the fourth year; the house of Bouilly with its vineyards and appurtenances, and the vineyards of Laignes; the church of Viaspero; of Saint Victor of Bonavicina; the church of Albiniac, the tithe in the third year, and the small tithe.

The church of Mont-Hugon and the lands belonging to it, the small tithe, half of the greater tithe, the court-rent, and the hospice house with its appurtenances. In the church of Saint Leo, one third of the offerings at Christmas, Epiphany [Col. 1335D], the Purification of the Blessed Mary, Easter, Pentecost, the feast of Saint Leo, and All Saints; the offerings of those who receive bags; likewise burial dues, the court-rent, and half the greater and small tithes. The tithe of Redelor; the church of Belleville and the same vill with its appurtenances, the small tithe, and the tithe of all your cultivation. The church of Mergi, the small tithe of that same vill, the greater tithe in the third year, and everything you possess in the same vill. The church of Troyes with all tithes, one third in the mill of Mediavilla, the rent and jurisdiction of that mill, and everything you possess in that vill. In the Church of Human, two thirds of the offerings at Christmas, Easter [Col. 1336A], and All Saints, and the small tithe. The church of Villette and the court-rent, with all tithes. At the grange of Vulperia, from the hay-tithe, six sextaries of grain. The small tithe at Villerma, and half the greater tithe. At Sceleriis, one fourth of the greater and small tithe, and the court-rent. At Fontanis, one fourth of the entire tithe. The chapel of Galon and its jurisdiction, with all its tithes and appurtenances.

At Troyes, the site of the house of Saint Arrald, wholly free; and all the inheritance which that same Arrald gave, together with male and female serfs, to the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, free of all claims, all heirs excluded and without any reservation, as is lawfully contained in the instrument of Philip, bishop formerly of Troyes, of blessed memory. At Troyes, the house of Archdeacon Theobald and another [Col. 1336B] house which you possess in the market; the tithe of the revenues of the two fairs held at Troyes on the feast of Saint John and on the feast of Saint Remigius; the tithe of the wine of the enclosed estate of the count of Troyes; and four pounds in Troyes coin annually, given you by Hugh, count of Troyes. The vill of Fontanis and its jurisdiction with its appurtenances. The house of Drot with its appurtenances, and everything you possess at another Drot and at Villare. Everything you possess at Sosiac and Lintella, in cultivated or uncultivated lands, and at Sézanne; and the tithe of your vineyards at Bouilly and Laignes. Whatever you may lawfully acquire by gift or purchase from the holding of the count of Troyes, or from the holding of Geoffrey de Bullepot and his wife Alaïs. The safe-conduct of Fractaripa [Col. 1336C], and everything you possess in that same vill. The safe-conduct of Calciniac, Mergiac, Chauchiniac, Fontenis, and the Holy Sepulchre. Rights of use in all the woods of the count of Brienne, for all necessities, granted you by Bernard, count of Brienne. The pastures of Guy of Pedaniis at Expensarium, for all necessities, and the mills of Espiniac.

Furthermore, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. We therefore forbid anyone who holds lands or possessions from your monastery to confer them upon other churches or monasteries, whether in life or death, or to alienate them from it without your permission or consent [Col. 1336D]. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present them to the bishop; if they are found suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they are answerable to the bishop concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters. We also decree that the burial place of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, without prejudice to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person at all rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be kept unimpaired and entire [Col. 1337A], to be of benefit in every way to the uses for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment because of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 1337B] and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, John, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, John, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed.  
I, Guy, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Hugolinus, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed.  
I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed.  
I, Soffredus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed.  
[Col. 1337C] I, Cencius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed.  
I, Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross, have subscribed.  
I, Roger, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, “Pastoris,” cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, have subscribed.  
I, Stephen, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed.  
[Col. 1337D] I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.  
I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.  
I, Guala, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Theodore, have subscribed.  
I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1338A] 1207, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CCXXV. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF PEREIRO. On confirmation of possessions. (Lateran, 31 March.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant gracious favour to the honourable petitions of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting favourably to your just petitions, we confirm for you by apostolic authority the tithes, churches, and possessions which you have held quietly and peacefully for forty years and more. We strictly forbid anyone to presume unduly to trouble you concerning them. Let no one therefore . . . the prohibition, etc., down to “shall incur.”

[Col. 1338B] Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXVI. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF MONTPELLIER. He confirms a certain agreement. (Lateran, 13 April.)

Since we, though unworthy, hold on earth the place of him who detests discord, apostolic circumspection ought to provide lest, in matters known to have been done for the good of peace, any ground for dispute or tinder of discord should arise. Therefore, beloved sons, assenting favourably to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority the agreement reasonably concluded between you and our dearest son the king of Aragon, through our venerable brother the bishop of Maguelonne, concerning controversies, wars, and dissensions. Since it was made without wrongful dealing and freely accepted by both sides under oath, as is more fully contained in your authentic letters and those of the same king [Col. 1338C], let no person at all be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXVII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CLUNY. He confirms a certain donation. (Lateran, 16 May.)

[Col. 1338D]

We have received an authentic document of Pope Clement, our predecessor of blessed memory, in these words:

> It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect those wishes which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting favourably to your just petitions, we confirm for you, and through you for your monastery, by apostolic authority, and [Col. 1339A] fortify by the protection of this present writing, the chapel which you have canonically acquired in the city of Tuscania by the grant of our venerable brother John, bishop of Tuscania, just as you possess it rightfully and peacefully. We decree that no person at all may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

We therefore grant you by the authority of these presents that you may use that same authentic document freely and lawfully.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF CLUNY. On the correction of monks. (Lateran, 16 May.)

We have received presented to us an authentic document in the following form from Pope Alexander, our predecessor [Col. 1339B] of blessed memory:

> It has been reported to us that certain of your monks, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, sometimes contend to retain priories and obediences entrusted to them even when you refuse them; and [Col. 1340A], forgetful of their monastic profession, in order to avoid correction, they invoke an appeal contrary to our constitution. Since the remedy of appeal was not instituted in order that the monastic rule might be dissolved through it, by these present letters we grant you leave, every obstacle of appeal being removed, to correct your monks according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the customs of your monastery, and, when cause requires, to remove them from priories and other obediences, appeal notwithstanding.

We therefore, inclined by your prayers, grant your devotion by the authority of these presents that you may use the same authentic document freely and lawfully. Let no person at all be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 1340B] the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

# ELEVENTH BOOK OF THE REGISTERS OR LETTERS OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF. ELEVENTH YEAR OF THE PONTIFICATE, A.D. 1208.

## I. TO THE NOBLE MAN LEOPOLD, DUKE OF AUSTRIA. On aid for the Holy Land. (Lateran, 24 February.)

[Col. 1339C]

Experientially we have learned that you have not been a forgetful hearer of the words set forth in the Gospel for those who wish to go after the Lord. For, devoutly reflecting on what you should render to the Lord for all that He Himself has rendered to you, you purpose humbly to imitate Christ, who for you became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; and, for His love, leaving behind a dear wife, sweet offspring, a delightful homeland, beloved kindred, abundant riches, and worldly honors, you desire, as we have learned, by finally denying yourself together with carnal desires, to follow Him more freely [Col. 1339D], to take up your cross, and, with ardent longing, to hasten there where your salvation hung upon the cross, so that beneath the banner of the victorious cross you may set yourself against the attempts of the faithless, who seem already to have driven the Crucified One from part of the inheritance of the cross [Col. 1340C], and strive to drive Him out altogether.

Truly this purpose is devout and divinely inspired in you. For, in taking up the cross, you intend to render a return to Christ, who bore your infirmities upon it and carried your sorrows. Yet, although your devotion is sufficiently great, the exchange is very unequal. Apart from the difference of grace which appears in either case—since the Lord and Redeemer suffered for the redeemed servant, whereas the redeemed servant in turn suffers for the Lord and Redeemer—there is a great difference between the instrument of Christ’s cross and the sign of your cross. For although the glory of the cross is one, its punishment in you and in the Lord differs. You will take up a soft and pleasant cross; He underwent one harsh and hard. You will wear it upon the surface of your garment [Col. 1340D]; He bore it in the reality of His flesh. You will fasten it to yourself with threads of linen or silk; He was fixed to it with iron and hard nails.

Therefore, although, however greatly and severely you may resolve to expose yourself for the hope of eternal recompense, such sufferings are not worthy in comparison with the future glory which shall be revealed in you [Col. 1341A], nevertheless, considering the sincerity of your devotion and perceiving the most urgent need of the Holy Land, we commend your purpose in the Lord. We earnestly ask and exhort your nobility in the Lord Jesus Christ that, proceeding according to His good Spirit, which He is known to have poured into you, you may quickly and wisely gird yourself for the aid of that land in the service of God—though you do not know what the morrow may bring—and that, with His help, you may carry on God’s service in such a way as to apply yourself most zealously to defending the aforesaid land, which, as though placed in the extremity of need, is known greatly to require your aid and that of other faithful persons. Thus neither may God seem to have inspired this purpose in you [Col. 1341B] in vain, nor may you seem to have left behind in vain, for its sake, as it were all the glory of the world by which you are known to be distinguished; rather, in accordance with the disposition of such devotion, may the effect of full perfection follow in you.

In accordance with your request, we send you, through our beloved son Nicholas, prior of Saint John of the Carthusian Order, the sign of the life-giving cross to be imposed upon you; and we likewise dispatch the indulgence you requested, together with letters of protection.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year.

## II. To the Same. He is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Given as in the preceding.)

[Col. 1341C]

Because, mindful of the Lord’s Passion and of the effect of your redemption, you take up the banner of the saving cross and purpose to serve under it for the defense of the province of Jerusalem, in service of Him who gave Himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, a sweet-smelling savor, we commend your devotion in the Lord.

Therefore, in order that we may support you in this devout purpose, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, we decree that, from the time you have taken the cross, both your person and all your goods, together with your household, shall remain under the protection of the Apostolic See and of ourselves, as well as of the archbishops and other prelates of God’s Church in whose dioceses those goods are situated; and that, until certain knowledge is obtained [Col. 1341D] of your return or death, they shall remain whole and undisturbed. Therefore let no one at all … this constitution of ours, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the preceding.

## III. To the Abbot and Convent of Prémontré. Abbots are bound to manage the affairs of their congregations. (Lateran, fourth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Note: [Col. 1341D] Chapter *Edoceri*, “On rescripts.”]

By your letters you requested to be informed by us whether, under letters obtained for the abbots of your order without mention of their convents, the abbots themselves are bound to answer, when the convents complain against them, concerning cases which pertain to the convents [Col. 1342A]; and whether, even though appeal has been prohibited, they may protect themselves from having to answer by raising an appeal.

To this we have thought fit to reply that the said abbots cannot protect themselves by appeal from being bound lawfully to answer by authority of such letters, unless some other reasonable ground supports them; since abbots are bound by their office to manage the affairs of their congregations, unless perhaps the affairs of the abbot and of the convent were entirely distinct.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year.

## IV. To the Illustrious King of Aragon. That he send his sister to the King of Sicily as wife. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1342B]

[Note: [Col. 1342D] See Zurita under the year 1208.]

From the special affection with which we love your person and the kingdom of Aragon, we are moved not only to exhort your magnificence to those things which are useful to you and to it, but also to rebuke it if it does not employ the diligence which it ought concerning them; for we are to you a father in Him who corrects and chastises the son whom He loves.

Your royal serenity certainly does not fail to know how, concerning the consummation of the marriage between your sister and our dearest son in Christ Frederick, the illustrious king of Sicily—a matter which had long before been discussed by his mother—we have at times spoken with you in person, and often exhorted you through our letters [Col. 1342C]. But although you have recently sent two galleys to his assistance, for which we greatly commend your royal prudence in the Lord, nevertheless you have delayed longer than was proper and fitting the confirmation of that affair, accepted on the part of the aforesaid king with no small concern on our part, insofar as it depends on you.

Indeed, since you seemed formerly to have desired this not a little, you ought not to introduce delay; for, besides the fact that great advantage is impeded by such delay, the taunt could be made of you: “Behold the man who began and was not able to finish” (Luke 14). Moreover, that we may speak together with and for your honor: what sloth now holds you back? What sluggishness dissuades you from completing an enterprise so highly beneficial, that you defer a present opportunity to tomorrow and put off the progress of so fortunate a union until the future?

There is no reason, moreover, why your sister ought any longer to delay such magnificent nuptials. For her bridegroom is exalted, bearing the title of king from his mother’s womb. The nobility of his lineage does not falter; rather, standing firmly upon both feet, it advances, increasing the greatness of his blood, descending from generation to generation, through the majesty of his virtues. He is the son and grandson of emperors—of an emperor not only on his father’s side but also on that of his grandfather. He was born of an empress, who herself was queen of Sicily, sister once of a king [Col. 1343A], aunt of a king, daughter of a king, and moreover niece of him who, more gloriously a king in deed than in name, is reported on a single day to have triumphed magnificently in different parts of the world, by sea and by land, over two different and hostile emperors, Venetians, and other peoples.

Illustrious through the splendor of such birth, the bridegroom of your full sister, as is written concerning those equal to him—“Virtue came to the Caesars before its time”—passes with swift step through the gate of puberty into the years of discretion, and, anticipating his age by his virtues, wonderfully begins the first stages of a happily reigning life. Finally, his kingdom, rich and noble, is among the other kingdoms of the world their center and their harbor. From it and through it, benefits will be able to come to you all the greater because it is nearer to your kingdom by contiguity of sea [Col. 1343B], and because it is specially beloved by us with a particular prerogative, as belonging especially to blessed Peter.

Therefore, since our venerable brother, the bishop of Mazara—a man indeed prudent and faithful, and, all qualifications being weighed, suited to this affair—is being sent at the suggestion of your envoys and of yourself to bring over your aforesaid sister, we earnestly admonish and strongly exhort your royal highness not to delay sending her with fitting equipment and an honorable escort, so that she herself may proceed adorned as is appropriate for so great a bride, and so that her bridegroom may receive the aid of timely assistance. Do not in any way avoid the expenses which an undertaking of such advantage and honor demands, since, God prospering it as we trust, they may be restored to you tenfold.

[Col. 1343C] Given at the Lateran.

## V. (Lateran.)

In almost the same terms to the illustrious Queen of Aragon, to the end:

Wherefore we earnestly admonish and strongly exhort your serenity that you prudently and diligently induce the said king to do this, considering that, if you were to come in person with her, besides rejoicing with a mother’s affection at so happy an embrace of son-in-law and daughter, you could very beneficially govern both the king and the kingdom by your prudence.

Given at the Lateran.

## VI. To the Abbot and Convent of Saint John of Thérouanne. That they may have a mill. (Lateran, fifth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1343D]

By authority of the present letters we grant you permission, according to the rule of your order, to have a mill within your bounds, notwithstanding that the bishop and canons of Thérouanne, as is said, strive, for the sake of profit, to compel you to grind in their mills. Therefore let no one … this grant of ours, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year.

## VII. To the Nobleman Demetrius, Prince of Arbanon. The archdeacon of Durrës is commended to him. (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of March.)

Commending in the Lord the devotion and reverence which you are known to show toward the most holy [Col. 1344A] Roman Church, we give thanks to the Giver of all good things because He has mercifully inspired you and your people, dwelling among Greeks who hold less than Catholic views, with the true faith. You recognize that the Lord said to blessed Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16); and again, concerning His Passion: “Simon, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have once turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22); and again, after His resurrection, He said to the same man with threefold repetition [Col. 1344B]: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21).

Accordingly, in letters which we received with paternal kindness, you requested that we should deem worthy to send from our side a legate who might instruct you and your people in purity of faith. We therefore propose to send into those regions a legate who may feed, confirm, and correct what he finds needing correction. Meanwhile, we send our beloved son Nicholas, archdeacon of the Latins at Durrës, with instructions in our letters that he go to Arbanon and, together with our venerable brother Paul, bishop of Arbanon, instruct and confirm you and your people in those matters which he sees to be expedient, so that, when the legate arrives, he may find you already instructed in part.

We therefore admonish your nobility and exhort you in the Lord, commanding you through apostolic letters [Col. 1344C] that, receiving the aforesaid archdeacon honorably and treating him honorably, you devoutly accept and observe his salutary admonitions and commands. Thus an increase of eternal recompense may accrue to you thereby, and we may deservedly commend your devotion.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year.

## VIII. To All Clerics Established in the Abbey of Farfa in the Diocese of Sabina. On the liberty of the monastery of Farfa. (Lateran, fifth day before the Nones of March.)

When a dispute was pending between our venerable brother John, bishop of Sabina, and our beloved sons the abbot and convent of Farfa [Col. 1344D], the bishop sought episcopal jurisdiction both in the monastery of Farfa and in its churches situated in his diocese, excepting only six churches. In these, the said abbot and monks did not at all deny his episcopal jurisdiction. They, on the contrary, replied that their monastery, both in its head and in all its other members, was wholly exempt and subject to no one except the Apostolic See.

Having seen, heard, and understood the attestations, documents, and allegations produced by both sides, we, by counsel of our brethren, absolve them and their successors forever from the suit which the same bishop was bringing against them concerning the subjection of their monastery. We decree that the monastery itself is wholly free and exempt from the jurisdiction of anyone other than the Roman pontiff [Col. 1345A], and we have thought fit to impose perpetual silence upon that bishop concerning this matter.

But concerning their churches situated in the diocese of Sabina, excepting those six, justice requiring it, we have judicially determined that they are in no way bound to the bishop of Sabina in the payment of tithes, offerings, and mortuary dues, nor in the ordination of clerics and dedication of churches, because we have learned that by the privileges of our predecessors they are wholly exempt in these matters. Therefore, imposing silence upon him concerning these matters, we have decreed that they are to be absolved from his suit.

In all other matters, however, which are known to pertain to episcopal jurisdiction, we decree that those churches shall forever be subject to him and to his successors [Col. 1345B], and concerning these matters we judicially condemn the said abbot and monks in favor of the bishop. For greater precaution, this is expressly provided: they are to have in those churches free authority to elect priests and other clerics.

Wherefore, through apostolic letters, we command and enjoin upon all of you that you go without any difficulty to the place to which the said bishop summons you, there to hear and receive his command according to the tenor of the sentence promulgated. Otherwise, you shall firmly observe the sentence which he may reasonably pronounce against you on this account.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the eleventh year.

## IX. To the Patriarch of Jerusalem, Legate of the Apostolic See. That he not support the Greeks in their rebellion. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of March.)

[Col. 1345C]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, with the consent and will of the noble count of Tripoli and of certain citizens of Antioch, the Greek people and a portion of the Greek clergy, setting aside the fear of God, have presumed to intrude a Greek patriarch into the province of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 1345D] See Book X, Letter 214.]

Greek clerics, who had given oaths of fidelity to our venerable brother the patriarch of Antioch and had received dignities and benefices from his hand, rashly adhering to the intruded patriarch contrary to their own oath, refuse to observe the interdict of the aforesaid patriarch; and they admit to divine offices Latins subject to excommunication [Col. 1345D] and interdict.

Since we neither can nor ought to pass over with conniving eyes the audacity of so great a presumption, we command and enjoin upon your brotherhood through apostolic letters that, if the matter is as stated, you wholly depose the said intruder and cause him to be removed from the entire province. Restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, all hindrance of appeal being removed, you shall forbid, under pain of excommunication, the same count and also the mayor and consuls of Antioch rashly to presume to support the said intruder or the Greek clerics in such rebellion.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the eleventh year.

## X. To the Illustrious King of the Danes. On the election of the Archbishop of Bremen. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1346A]

If God, the Lord of knowledge, had infused into us the spirit of foreknowledge, we would more cautiously have guarded ourselves against the wicked and deceitful man—and you also [Note: [Col. 1345D] See Book X, Letter 209.]. Although perhaps he did not deserve to be delivered by apostolic aid from the pit of calamity into which he had fallen, yet, by the counsel of God who wisely disposes all things, he was rescued from it through our concern, so that, being at last ungrateful for the favor done him, he might be dealt with more freely for manifest crimes, since action could not easily be taken against him for doubtful matters.

Recently, when procurators of the churches of Bremen and Hamburg had been sent to our presence concerning the fact that Waldemar, a bishop, had been postulated as their archbishop by the chapter of Bremen without consulting the canons of Hamburg [Col. 1346B], our beloved son Peter, provost of Roskilde, a prudent and faithful man, arrived as envoy from your royal serenity.

[Note: [Col. 1346D] See Arnold of Lübeck, Book VII, chapter 12.]

When the bishop himself asserted in our presence that you had deprived him of both episcopal and patrimonial goods, for which he requested restoration from us, Peter prudently replied in opposition that he could not rightly seek the aid of restitution, since he had made himself despoiled by abandoning clerical dress and usurping for himself the title of king. Further, charging him with the crimes of lèse-majesté, apostasy, adultery, perjury, dissipation, and conspiracy [Col. 1346C], he maintained that not only should the benefit of restitution be denied him, but the postulation made concerning him should be wholly rejected. This was especially so because he is irregular, having been begotten through a double adultery; because his dispensation was formerly obtained from the Apostolic See by deceitful suppression, concealing that he was illegitimate while asserting that he was natural-born; and because, an imitator of his father’s incontinence, he has begotten children after receiving sacred orders.

Having therefore diligently heard these and other matters solemnly alleged in our audience, although we might perhaps have inclined our ears more favorably to the petitions made to us concerning the aforesaid postulation, had this been possible consistently with the honor of the Apostolic See, the salvation of our soul [Col. 1346D], the benefit of the Church of Bremen, and without prejudice to you and your kingdom—especially since we believed that by this means we would be freed from many disturbances—nevertheless, matters being as they were, we did not think the postulation should be admitted, by counsel of our brethren. The bishop’s petition, by which he sought to have his bishopric restored, seemed contrary to the postulation made concerning him for transfer to another church.

We decided to reply to the envoys from Bremen that, since the outcome of this affair remained pending and it was unknown whether it could soon be settled, they should take care to provide for their church. But, applying ourselves to what makes for peace [Col. 1347A], we determined, in favor of ecclesiastical liberty, to admit his petition for full restoration both of the bishopric and of his patrimony. We granted him that, should he perhaps not wish to entrust himself to your royal highness, he might receive corporal restoration through a suitable procurator, while he himself remained in whatever place he preferred, not deservedly suspect to you.

When he replied that he wished to obtain the benefit of restoration through a suitable procurator, and had obtained deliberative delay concerning the place in which he would meanwhile remain, he finally, ungrateful for the favor done him, fled from us fraudulently and contumaciously, without leave. Therefore, in the name of Almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and our own, we excommunicate [Col. 1347B] and anathematize him, wholly rejecting the postulation made concerning him, of which he has made himself altogether unworthy.

We ordered this sentence to be solemnly published through very many archbishops and bishops, as both we and your said envoy judged expedient.

[Note: [Col. 1347] That is, Philip, duke of Swabia, as is clear from Letter 215 of Book 10.]

We also caused the prince, in whose favor the same Waldemar perhaps vainly trusts, to be admonished and induced by authority of our letters not to give him any aid or favor, but to avoid him as excommunicated; and neither through him nor on his account to permit scandal to arise in God’s Church, by which no slight scandal could also be generated against himself. For we are unwilling to pass over in dissimulation the audacity of such wickedness in that bishop [Col. 1347C].

We have commanded the chapter of Bremen that, after gathering together those who are to be summoned to the election, and after the admonition delivered to them by our venerable brother the archbishop of Magdeburg—to whom we direct our letters on this matter—they shall within a month appoint for themselves, by canonical election, a suitable person as pastor. Otherwise, we command the archbishop himself, supported by our authority, to assign them henceforth, with the counsel of religious and prudent men, such a person as bishop as may be suited to so great a burden and honor, restraining by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, the rashness of any of clergy or people who, which we do not believe, may presume to oppose this or to favor the said Waldemar.

Moreover [Col. 1347D], pursuing with complete hatred the enormity of such wickedness, and wishing to provide more fully for royal peace, we have considered among ourselves and have finally held diligent deliberation with our brethren whether proceedings should be taken for the deposition of the same bishop. At length, after more mature counsel, we have decided to watch his heel and wait a little longer. Thus, if he perhaps attempts to contrive anything against you or even your kingdom—indeed, against us, or rather against himself—in either of these matters, though his efforts will be unable to prevail in any respect while resisted by divine help, our care, and your zeal, he will thereby render himself deserving not only of these penalties but of a greater one [Col. 1348A], and we may proceed against him more freely, as more justly, to his confusion.

We have also provided this precaution: lest, plunged into the abyss of despair, he act wickedly more freely and effectively at the outset. If he is frustrated in his first attempt, then, like a serpent whose head has been cut off, he will be unable thereafter to discharge the poison of his malice.

Wherefore we earnestly admonish and strongly exhort your royal magnificence that, rejoicing in divine justice, which appears in some way to have justified you against him, and pursuing with due gratitude what has hitherto been done, you await the outcome of future events with long-suffering patience; yet you must diligently meet the assaults of evil men by prudent effort. So that nothing may be lacking in precaution, meanwhile write to us your royal pleasure [Col. 1348B], so that, when we understand it more fully, we may proceed as ought to be done. For both in these matters and in others we effectively strive to advance, insofar as we can with God and with our honor, whatever may make for your peace and honor.

The aforesaid provost will be able to report our will to you more expressly on this matter. Indeed, he will be able to convey it to you with that prudence and fidelity with which he conveyed yours to us; for this reason we have not undeservedly thought fit to commend him to your highness.

Given at the Lateran.

## XI. To the Archbishop of Tours, and to the Bishops of Paris and Nevers. That debts or usury not be exacted from crusaders for two years. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1348C]

Among other measures reported to us as conducive to abolishing heretical depravity in the regions of Provence, this is especially said to be expedient: that debtors bound by borrowed money should be granted respite by their creditors, with interest meanwhile suspended, so long as they labor there for the cause of the faith; and that clerics wishing to labor for the same cause be permitted to pledge their revenues for two years.

Wherefore, through apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, supported by our authority, you decree and cause to be firmly observed in such a great necessity [Col. 1348D] of the Church whatever you know, according to God, to be expedient for its cause.

Given at the Lateran.

## XII. To Henry, Illustrious Emperor of Constantinople. That he not impede bequests made to churches. (Lateran, fourth day before the Ides of March.)

Since, as legal enactments teach, it has been established by Catholic emperors that anyone may freely bequeath his goods to churches and pious places, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity in the Lord that, if knights or others should wish to bequeath their possessions to churches, you in no way impede them or oppose yourself, but allow such possessions, at least with their burdens, to be freely and peacefully bequeathed to those churches [Col. 1349A].

But if someone who lies at the point of death should bequeath to churches possessions which formerly belonged to churches, since he appears not to leave what is his own but rather to restore what was taken, by authority of the present letters we strictly forbid you to presume to impede this through yourself or others. Otherwise, we command in our letters our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Varys and the bishop of Panidos, to restrain by ecclesiastical censure all opponents, every impediment of contradiction and appeal being removed.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the eleventh year.

## XIII. To the Archbishop of Varys and the Bishop of Panidos. Executory letter on the same matter. (Given as in the preceding.)

[Col. 1349B]

“Since it has been established by Catholic emperors,” etc., in almost the same terms to “impede.”

Wherefore, through apostolic letters, we command and enjoin upon your discretion that you restrain by ecclesiastical censure, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, any persons who, despising the prohibition of the Apostolic See, presume to impede this matter.

Given as in the preceding.

## XIV. To the Podestà and People of the Venetians Dwelling at Constantinople. On the same matter.

[Col. 1349C]

“Since it has been established by Catholic emperors,” etc., to “impede.” Otherwise, we command in our letters our beloved sons, the dean, cantor, and treasurer of Saint Sophia at Constantinople, to restrain all opponents, etc., as in the preceding.

In the same manner to the same persons.

## XV. To the Noblemen, the Barons Dwelling at Constantinople. On the same matter. (Given as above.)

“Since it has been established by Catholic emperors,” etc., as above to “impede.” Otherwise, we command in our letters our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Varys and the bishops of Salombreia and Kallipolis [Col. 1349D], to restrain all opponents, etc., as in the preceding.

In the same manner to the same persons, as above. “And if not all, two of you,” etc.

Given as above.

## XVI. To the Archbishop of Varys and the Bishop of Kallipolis. The case between the patriarch and the emperor of Constantinople is entrusted to them. (Given as in the preceding.)

Our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, informed us that Baldwin, of illustrious memory, emperor of Constantinople, retained for his own disposition thirty provostships within the city of Constantinople, in the better churches that had fallen to the share of the Franks [Col. 1350A], appointing provosts and deans in them; and that our dearest son in Christ Henry, succeeding him, presumes to dispose of those same offices at the peril of his soul.

He therefore humbly petitioned us to cause them to be left free and undisturbed for his disposition, especially since our beloved son Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, then legate of the Apostolic See, had adjudicated to him twenty-three of the thirty, while leaving seven neither adjudicated nor annulled, but to the discretion of our authority; and since, at the time of his appointment, we excepted no church, but rather entrusted to him the general care of the Church of Constantinople; nor had he committed any fault for which the church entrusted to him ought to be deprived of its right [Col. 1350B].

But because the aforesaid emperor requested that the conferral of those provostships be confirmed to him by the Apostolic See, declaring that he possesses no less right in them than many kings are known to have, by approved custom, in certain provostships of their kingdoms; and because the petitions of the two parties are mutually opposed, we command your brotherhood through apostolic letters to hear what is presented on both sides and, proceeding to the final judgment with every obstacle of appeal removed, remit the case, sufficiently instructed, to our presence. You are to appoint the parties a suitable term within which they may appear before us through suitable procurators to receive judgment.

[Col. 1350C] Given as in the preceding.

## XVII. To the Bishops of Kallipolis and Panidos, and to the Dean of Saint Sophia at Constantinople. The cause of the patriarchs of Constantinople and Grado is entrusted to them. (Given as in the preceding.)

From the complaint of our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, it has been made known to us that, although we granted him authority to compel, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal removed, Venetian inhabitants of the imperial city to pay tithes to the persons and churches to whom they are legally due—despite the Venetian custom of tithing their goods only at death [Col. 1350D]—the vicar of our venerable brother, the patriarch of Grado, compels by ecclesiastical coercion Venetian burgesses dwelling in the same city, whether they live in the five parishes of that patriarch of Grado, or transfer themselves to parishes subject to him, or to Pisan parishes, or indeed to parishes of those not subject to the patriarch of Constantinople, to pay tithes to himself.

Nor does he permit them to receive nuptial blessings anywhere except in churches of the patriarch of Grado, even though they do not live in the parishes of those churches; and he sometimes presumes on this account to pronounce against them a sentence of excommunication.

Since the foregoing has not been established before us, we command your discretion through apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties, you hear the case and bring it to a canonical conclusion, appeal being removed; causing, etc. And if not all, two of you, etc.

Given as in the preceding.

## XVIII. To the Archbishop of Varys and the Bishop of Panidos. That they cause the sentences of the Patriarch of Constantinople to be observed. (Given as in the preceding.)

Our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, informed us that prelates of churches not subject to him, residing in parishes subject to him, sometimes admit by name to divine offices persons excommunicated by him and subjected to interdict [Col. 1351B]; and by this the sinew of ecclesiastical discipline is dissolved.

We therefore commanded those prelates not at all to presume to admit to divine offices, or administer ecclesiastical sacraments to, parishioners of churches subject to the patriarch when they have been excommunicated by him or placed under interdict. Wherefore, through apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, if the prelates of the aforesaid churches henceforth presume to attempt this, you restrain them from such presumption by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside.

Given as in the preceding.

## XIX. To the Prelates of Churches Not Subject to the Patriarch, Dwelling at Constantinople. On the same matter. (Given as in the preceding.)

[Col. 1351C]

Our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, informed us that you, while sometimes residing in parishes subject to him, admit by name to divine offices persons excommunicated by him and subjected to interdict; and thereby the sinew of ecclesiastical discipline is dissolved.

Wherefore, by authority of the present letters, we command and enjoin upon you that you in no way presume to admit to divine offices, or administer ecclesiastical sacraments to, parishioners of churches subject to that patriarch when they have been excommunicated by him or subjected to interdict. [Col. 1351D] Otherwise, we command in our letters our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Varys and the bishop of Panidos, to restrain you from such presumption by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being removed.

Given as in the preceding.

## XX. To All the Clergy Dwelling in the Diocese of Constantinople, of Churches Not Exempt from Patriarchal Jurisdiction. On the Same Matter. (Lateran, the Nones of March.)

Divine ordinance seems to be resisted by one who resists authority, since every authority is from God, by whom all things are ordered. [Col. 1352A] Therefore no one ought to be ashamed humbly to obey a prelate set over him by God, whenever he commands something; for the Son of God, Jesus Christ, in order to become obedient to the Father, came into the depths of this sea and allowed himself to be overwhelmed by its storm, lest, if he should presume otherwise, he be transformed into the likeness of him who wished to set his throne in the north. Since, therefore, by the Lord’s ordering, our venerable brother the patriarch of Constantinople is set over you, we command and strictly enjoin your whole body by these apostolic letters that, humbly attending upon him as the father and bishop of your souls, you render him canonical obedience and honor, knowing that, if you presume to act otherwise, we shall not be able to pass it by with our eyes closed.

[Col. 1352B] Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of March, in the eleventh year.

## XXI. To the most dear son in Christ, the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople, and to the noble men . . . . nibus, Venetians, and all the people dwelling at Constantinople.

That they should give counsel and assistance to the patriarch of Constantinople. (Given as in the other letter.)

Since it is advantageous and honorable to you that the Greeks, clergy and laity alike, should return to obedience to the most holy Roman Church and to our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, and since [Col. 1352C] they have him as father and shepherd, we earnestly request and admonish all of you, commanding by these apostolic letters that you give counsel and aid in this matter to the aforesaid patriarch, firmly observing the sentence that he shall reasonably pronounce on account of this against the rebellious Greeks; so that your devotion may be manifest in affection, and the wandering little sheep may return to the shepherd.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXII. To the Prior of the Pisans.

He is forbidden to administer chrismation to children. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1352D] Our venerable brother the patriarch of Constantinople has brought to our hearing that, in his presence and that of other bishops, you presume to confirm children with the anointing of sacred chrism. Although you say that this was at some time granted to you by the Apostolic See, we nevertheless took care to forbid you to do it. Since, therefore, such confirmation of children is known to belong to bishops alone, by the authority of these presents we strictly forbid you henceforth in any way to presume to confirm children. Otherwise, we shall hold valid the sentence which the aforesaid patriarch reasonably pronounces against you on this account, and, with God as author, shall cause it to be firmly observed.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXIII. To the Patriarch of Constantinople.

Concerning the consecration of Greek bishops. (Lateran, VIII Ides of March.)

[Col. 1353A]

[Note: [Col. 1353D] See the chapter *Ex parte*, “On the times of ordination,” in the third collection.] It was set forth before us on your behalf that certain Greek bishops, returning to your obedience, have physically sworn to you an oath of fealty and promised obedience to us, but refuse to be anointed according to Latin custom. You therefore asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See what you ought to do concerning them. We reply to your inquiry as follows: if those who have already been consecrated cannot be induced to receive anointing, you may pass this over by toleration in this new circumstance. But do not under any circumstances consecrate those who are to be consecrated [Col. 1353B] unless they are willing to be consecrated in the Latin manner, since we ourselves consecrate Greeks only according to our custom.

Given at the Lateran, VIII Ides of March, in the eleventh year.

## XXIV. To the Bishop of Kallipolis, the Dean of Saint Sophia, and the Provost of the Holy Apostles at Constantinople.

Concerning tithes to be paid. (Given as in the other letter.)

Our venerable brother the patriarch of Constantinople showed us in his representation that the Pisans, Lombards, Longobards, Amalfitans, Danes, Englishmen, and certain other nations dwelling at Constantinople [Col. 1353C] in parishes subject to him refuse to pay tithes to him and to the churches from which they receive ecclesiastical sacraments. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, after prior admonition, you compel the said Pisans and others dwelling in parishes subject to that patriarch, by ecclesiastical censure without appeal, to pay tithes in their due entirety to him and to the churches from which they receive spiritual benefits. But if not all . . . you, brother bishop, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXV. To the Patriarch of Grado and His Suffragans.

Concerning the avoidance of excommunicated persons. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1353D]

Our venerable brother the patriarch of Constantinople informed us that, when he sometimes binds certain Venetians dwelling at Constantinople with the bond of excommunication because of their offenses, and sometimes because they are obstinate and rebellious toward him, and subjects some to interdict, they return to Venice and do not comport themselves as excommunicated or interdicted persons; nor do any take care to avoid them, but they are indiscriminately admitted to divine offices. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, when it has been made known to you by the patriarch’s letters, you strictly avoid as excommunicated those whom the same patriarch reasonably excommunicates or places under interdict, [Col. 1354A] cause them to be avoided by your subjects, and cause ecclesiastical sacraments to be denied to those under interdict.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXVI. To the Archbishops of Narbonne, Arles, Embrun, Aix, and Vienne, and Their Suffragans.

Concerning the murder of Peter of Castelnau. (Lateran.)

Lest we should incur the rebuke of him who, passing through the field of the sluggard and the vineyard of the foolish man, reproached them because nettles had filled it all, at the first, as it were, morning of our elevation, and afterward at the successive Gospel hours, we went forth to send laborers into the Lord’s vineyard entrusted to our cultivation. Observing long ago that the plantings of vices had grown too greatly in Provence, lest the spurious shoots put down deeper roots, we sent fitting men there to uproot what was useless from the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts and propagate what was useful, catching the little foxes that contrive to destroy that vineyard. But when they arrived, they found there, in the Apostle’s words, pestilential persons who would not endure sound teaching but instead amassed for themselves teachers of error according to their own desires. Since they judged the messengers of truth to be opposed to their deeds, they raged against them so fiercely that the prophetic complaint of the Savior plainly appears to have touched them: “Behold, I send you wise men and scribes, [Col. 1354C] and you will kill some of them,” etc. (Matt. XXIII).

Indeed, we have heard of a detestable deed, one to be brought into the common mourning of the universal Church: our brother Peter of Castelnau, of holy memory, monk and priest, a man illustrious among men distinguished for virtue by his life, learning, and reputation, had been sent by us with others into that province to preach peace and establish the faith. He had made laudable progress, and did not cease to make progress, in the ministry entrusted to him. [Note: [Col. 1354D] See the *History of the Albigensians*, chapter 8.] For he had fully learned in Christ’s school what he was to teach; holding fast the faithful word which accords with doctrine, he could exhort in sound doctrine and refute opponents, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asked, as a man Catholic in faith, learned in the law, and eloquent in speech. Yet the devil stirred up his minister against him, the count of Toulouse. Because of many and grave offenses which he had committed against the Church and against God, the count had often incurred ecclesiastical censure; and, as a two-faced and crafty man, slippery and inconstant, he had often been absolved through feigned repentance. At last, unable to contain the hatred he had conceived against Peter because the word of the Lord in Peter’s mouth was not bound from executing vengeance upon the nations and rebukes among the peoples, and all the more strongly so in proportion as the count himself deserved rebuke for greater crimes, he summoned both him [Col. 1355A] and his colleague, legates of the Apostolic See, to the town of Saint-Gilles, promising to render full satisfaction on every charge brought against him.

When they had assembled in the said town, the aforesaid count at one time promised, as though truthful and compliant, to do what had been salutarily urged upon him, and at another, as though deceitful and hard-hearted, utterly refused to carry it out. When they finally wished to leave that town, he publicly threatened them with death, saying that, whether they turned aside by land or by water, he would vigilantly watch their departure; and immediately, [Note: [Col. 1355D] In the *History of the Albigensians*, deeds matched words.] matching his words with deeds, he sent his accomplices to lay carefully planned ambushes. Since the madness of his rage could not be softened either by the prayers of the beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Gilles, or by the urgent entreaty of the consuls and burgesses, [Col. 1355B] they, against the count’s will and to his extreme displeasure, escorted the two men under the protection of an armed force near the bank of the Rhône. As night approached, they rested there, while certain retainers of the same count, wholly unknown to them, lodged with them—men who, as the outcome showed, were seeking their blood.

Accordingly, on the following morning, after Mass had been celebrated according to custom, as the innocent soldiers of Christ prepared to cross the river, one of the aforesaid satellites of Satan brandished his lance and wounded the aforementioned Peter from behind between the ribs. Peter, founded upon Christ the rock with immovable firmness, was unsuspecting of so great a treachery. Looking kindly upon his impious assailant [Col. 1355C] and following with blessed Stephen the example of Christ his master, he said to him: “May God forgive you, for I forgive you,” repeatedly uttering this word of such mercy and patience. Then, pierced in this manner, he forgot the bitterness of the wound inflicted upon him in hope of heavenly things; and, in the very moment of his precious death, never ceasing to arrange with the companions of his ministry matters advancing faith and peace, he finally, after many prayers, happily fell asleep in Christ.

Since he shed his blood for faith and peace—than which there is absolutely no more praiseworthy cause for martyrdom—he would surely already have shone forth, as we believe, through clear miracles, if the unbelief of those persons had not prevented it. Of people like them it is read in the Gospel that Jesus did not perform many mighty works there because of their unbelief. [Col. 1355D] For although tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, [Note: [Col. 1355D] Raynaldus substituted *miracles*. But the register and the *History of the Albigensians* read *tongues*, likewise the old [Col. 1356D] manuscript codex of the Colbert Library.
