Therefore one must read *signs*.] [Col. 1356A] nevertheless, when the Savior was brought before Herod—who, Luke testifies, was greatly delighted to see him because he hoped to see some sign performed by him—he disdained both to perform a sign and to answer his question, knowing that what delighted Herod in the working of signs was not the inducement to belief but the vanity of wonder.

Although that wicked and perverse generation is not worthy that a sign be given so quickly, as perhaps it seeks, concerning its martyr, we nevertheless believe that it was expedient for it that this one man should die for it, lest the whole perish; infected with the contagion of heretical depravity, may it be recalled from its error more effectively through the interceding blood of the slain man than he could have recalled it while living. This is the ancient artifice of Jesus Christ; this is the miraculous device of the Savior: when he is thought to be defeated in his own servants, then he conquers more powerfully in those same servants; and by the power by which he himself destroyed death by dying, he sometimes causes the conquerors of his defeated servants to be conquered by those servants. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but when it has died, it bears much fruit.

Therefore, hoping that from the death of this most fruitful grain much fruit will arise in Christ’s Church—since surely one is grievously blameworthy and blameworthily hard whose soul has not been pierced by his [Col. 1356B] sword—and never wholly despairing that so great a benefit ought to be present in his blood, so that God may grant the desired increase to the beginnings of his holy preaching in the aforesaid province, for which he went down into corruption, we earnestly admonish and more earnestly exhort your brotherhood. Through the Holy Spirit, in virtue of obedience, we strictly command you to cause the word of peace and faith sown by him to grow through the waters of your preaching; and, with untiring diligent zeal, to labor at conquering heretical depravity and confirming the Catholic faith, uprooting vices and sowing virtues.

Proclaim throughout all your dioceses as excommunicated and anathematized, by the authority of almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, by the authority also of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by our authority, the murderer of the aforesaid servant of God and all by whose aid or action, counsel or favor, he committed so great a crime; likewise his harborers and defenders. [Col. 1356C] Cause every place to which they, or any one of them, come to be subject to ecclesiastical interdict in their presence, on every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, until, coming to the Apostolic See, they deserve absolution through worthy satisfaction; solemnly renew this sentence.

To those who, inflamed by zeal for the orthodox faith, gird themselves manfully to avenge the righteous blood which does not cease to cry from the earth [Col. 1356D] to heaven, until the Lord, the God of vengeance, descends from heaven to earth to put to shame those overthrown and those who overthrow, promise with confidence that remission of their sins is granted by God and his vicar, so that such labor may suffice them as satisfaction by works for those offenses for which they have offered to the true God true contrition of heart and confession of mouth. For such pestilential persons now scheme not only to plunder what is ours, but to destroy us; and they sharpen their tongues not merely for killing souls, [Col. 1357A] but stretch out their hands also for destroying bodies, having become perverters of souls and murderers of bodies.

Although the aforesaid count has long since been struck by the sword-point of anathema for many and grave crimes, which it would take too long to recount one by one, nevertheless, because he is presumed on certain indications to be guilty of the death of the holy man—not only because he publicly threatened him with death and prepared ambushes against him, but also because, as is asserted, he received his murderer into close familiarity and rewarded him with great gifts, to say nothing of other presumptions more fully known to us—you shall also publicly declare him anathematized for this reason. And since, according to the canonical sanctions of the holy Fathers, faith need not be kept with one who does not keep faith with God, you shall declare by apostolic authority that all who are bound to the said count by an oath of fealty, association, or such alliance are meanwhile released from him. Since he is separated from the communion of the faithful, being one to be avoided rather than supported, you shall declare that it is lawful for every Catholic man, without prejudice to the right of the principal lord, not only to pursue his person but also to occupy and hold his land—especially with the aim that, through their vigorous care, it may be cleansed of the heresy by which it has hitherto been shamefully stained through his wickedness. For it is fitting that the hands of all should rise against one whose hand has been against all. If not even thus affliction gives him understanding, we shall take care to make our hands weigh more heavily upon him.

But whenever he promises to offer satisfaction, these signs of his repentance must unquestionably come first: that he entirely expel from all his power the adherents of heretical depravity and endeavor to reconcile himself to fraternal peace, since ecclesiastical censure was pronounced against him chiefly because he is known to have committed fault in both respects. Yet, if the Lord should wish to mark his iniquities, he could scarcely make adequate satisfaction, not only for himself but also for the multitude of others whom he has led into the snare of damnation.

Since, according to the saying of truth, those who kill the body are not to be feared, but he who can cast body and soul into Gehenna, we trust and hope in him who, in order to take from his faithful the fear [Col. 1357D] of death, died and rose again on the third day, that the death of the aforesaid man of God will instill not fear but love in our venerable brother the bishop of Comminges [Note: [Col. 1357D] See below, letter 32.] and the beloved son, the abbot of Cîteaux, legates of the Apostolic See, and in the other followers of the orthodox faith. Following the example of him who happily purchased eternal life by temporal death, may they not fear, if necessary, to lay down their souls for Christ in so glorious a struggle. Therefore we advise and admonish, impressing prayers by commands and commands by prayers, that, effectively attending to the salutary warnings and commands of those legates, you stand by them as valiant fellow-soldiers [Col. 1358A] in all matters which they may judge necessary to enjoin upon you in this cause, knowing that we command the sentence they pronounce, not only against rebels but also against the negligent, to be held valid and observed inviolate.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXVII. Concerning the same matter. (Lateran.)

In almost the same manner, to the archbishop of Lyons and his suffragans, as far as “impressing commands by prayers”; that you may provide counsel and timely aid for carrying forward so great a service of God, prudently and effectively explaining the foregoing to your subjects, clergy and laity alike, [Col. 1358B] exhorting them and enjoining it upon them for the remission of their sins, so that they too may render to the Lord worthy service in so holy an undertaking.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXVIII. To Philip, the Illustrious King of the Franks.

Concerning the same matter. (Lateran.)

If your royal serenity surveys all the princes of the world, it will find itself specially exalted above the rest by God, who in his grace, and on account of the merits which you and your forebears have achieved in his sight, has deigned in many ways to magnify your name, increasing grace for you in the present and preparing glory in the future—chiefly because, [Col. 1358C] confessing the one holy, Catholic, and apostolic Church, you have always hated and rejected the sects of heretical depravity.

Recently we heard of a cruel deed, one to be brought into the common mourning of the universal Church, etc., through to the end, as in the letter sent to the archbishop of Narbonne and the others. Come then, soldier of Christ; come, most Christian prince. Let the groaning of the holy universal Church move your most religious heart; let pious zeal inflame you to avenge so great an injury done to your God. Hear the voice of righteous blood crying to you, and take up the shield of protection for the Church against the tyrant and enemy of the faith, so that you who have hitherto fought commendably for the world may now fight more commendably for Christ, who [Col. 1358D] is grievously assailed by most wicked servants. Take the present time for doing justice, and do not turn your ears from the Church’s complaint as it says to you: “Arise, and judge my cause” (Ps. LXXIII).

Indeed, so great an offense by the perverse may be fortunate and necessary for you, because it has caused him who created you now to wish to use your service. Therefore, most beloved son, join to our sword the sword which you received from the Lord for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, so that together we may exact vengeance upon such criminal and inhuman malefactors. Consider the unity between kingdom and priesthood marked through Moses and Peter, the fathers, that is, of the two Testaments: one foretold a priestly kingdom, and the other called it a royal priesthood. To signify this, Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, according to the order of Melchizedek, priest and king, willed to be born from both stocks, priestly and royal. And the prince of the apostles is read to have answered, “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke XXII), that is, together; and then the Lord said, “It is enough” (ibid.), so that, as the material and spiritual swords assist one another, each may be aided through the other.

Since, therefore, after the killing of the aforesaid just man, the Church in those regions is said to sit in sorrow and mourning without a comforter, faith to have vanished, peace to have perished, and the heretical pest and hostile fury to have grown strong; and unless it is powerfully aided amid the newness of this storm, the ship of the Church there seems nearly [Col. 1359B] altogether to be shipwrecked, we earnestly admonish and urgently exhort the piety of your royal mildness. In this critical necessity, trusting in Christ’s power, we enjoin upon you and grant remission of sins, that you do not delay to meet so great evils. Consider that it belongs so much to royal office to advance the work of peace in its kingdom that Solomon, the wisest of kings, was called “peaceful” as a figure of the eternal King. Endeavor to make those peoples peaceful in him who is the God of peace and love, and, by whatever means God reveals to you, labor to abolish heretical unbelief, fighting its adherents with a strong hand and outstretched arm even more securely than Saracens, because they are worse than the latter.

Do not cease to press the aforementioned count—who, as though he had made a covenant with heresy, gives no thought to his own death—with the weight of royal pressure brought upon him, if perhaps affliction may give him understanding and, when his face has been filled with disgrace, he may begin to seek God’s name, so that he may make satisfaction to us and to the Church—indeed, to God. Drive him and his supporters from the camps of the Lord, and take away their lands. In those lands, once heretics have been banished, establish Catholic inhabitants, who, according to the discipline of your orthodox faith, may serve before God in holiness and justice under your happy rule.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXIX. To the Noble Men, Counts, Barons, and All Peoples Established throughout the Kingdom of France.

Concerning the same matter. (Lateran, VI Ides of March.)

[Col. 1359D]

We have heard of a cruel deed, one to be brought into the common mourning of the universal Church, etc., as in the letter sent to the king, as far as: [Note: [Col. 1359D] It appears in the *History of the Albigensians*, chapter 8.] Come then, soldiers of Christ; come, valiant recruits of Christian warfare. Let the groaning of the holy universal Church move you; let pious zeal inflame you to avenge so great an injury done to your God. Remember that your Creator had no need of you when he made you. Although he has no need [Col. 1360A] of your service, as though he might thereby be wearied in accomplishing what he wills, or as though his omnipotence might be diminished for lack of your service, he nevertheless gives you in this crisis an opportunity to serve him acceptably.

Since, therefore, after the killing, etc., as above, through: do not delay to meet so great evils; and: to make those peoples peaceful, etc., through: press him with the weight of pressure brought upon him; etc., through: once heretics have been banished, Catholic inhabitants may be substituted, who, according to the discipline of your orthodox faith, may serve before God in holiness and justice.

Given at the Lateran [ [Note: [Col. 1359D] These words have been added from the *History of the Albigensians*.] VI Ides of March, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.]

## XXX. To the Abbots of Persigne and Le Pin, of the Cistercian Order.

[Col. 1360B]

Concerning the making of a truce between the kings of France and England.

[Note: [Col. 1360D] See letters 31 and 33.] How necessary it is for God’s holy Church and for all the Christian people dwelling in the kingdoms of France and England that the two kings should have peace and concord with one another, we believe is not unknown either to their prudence or to yours. For, apart from the losses of property and dangers to persons arising from their mutual hostilities, the salvation of souls is gravely harmed, and in many places, especially in Provence, the heretical pest grows stronger as a result, since those wage war upon one another whose unity both ought and could more effectively abolish that same pest.

Since, then, after the murder of our brother Peter of Castelnau, of holy memory, the detestable and hostile fury in that same province [Col. 1360C] has begun to spread so widely that, after the power of divine might, it is believed capable of restraint only by their concord, by apostolic letters we command your discretion and strictly enjoin you in virtue of obedience to go personally to the said kings and prudently and effectively induce them, both by our authority and by your own earnestness, to conclude and firmly observe a truce with one another for at least two years. You are to fulfill our command in such a way that your diligence may be evident in its effect and that you may rejoice to have advanced the salvation of so many souls. But if not both, etc., one of you, etc.

## XXXI. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1360D]

In almost the same manner to the archbishop of Tours, through the end. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if by God’s reconciling the pact of this truce has been restored, you compel both parties to observe it, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal and disregarding every human favor.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXII. To the Abbot of Cîteaux, Legate of the Apostolic See.

Concerning the murder of Peter of Castelnau. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1361A]

[Note: [Col. 1361D] See above, letter 26 and following.] With paternal kindness we received the letters which your devotion sent us. Having understood from it that, setting yourself strenuously to God’s work, you are going to Provence to console the Church which, wounded by the unprecedented blow of a dreadful wound, laments with multiplied griefs the death of our brother Peter of Castelnau, of holy memory, we commend in the Lord your prudent constancy and constant prudence. For, since according to the saying of truth those who kill the body are not to be feared, but he who can cast body and soul into Gehenna, the death of the aforesaid man [Col. 1361B] of God has not only not instilled fear in you from carrying out divine service, but has inflamed love in you, so that, following the example of him who happily purchased eternal life with temporal death, you do not fear, if necessary, to lay down your soul for him in so glorious a struggle.

Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your devotion, commanding by apostolic letters that, as you proceed to that province together with our venerable brother the bishop of Comminges, namely your fellow legate, you endeavor prudently and steadfastly to advance the business of the universal Church as God may grant you the power. For at present we send you, according to your counsel, those letters which we believe necessary; and hereafter we shall provide timely aid, with the help of him who, in accordance with his promise, will not abandon his faithful until the consummation of the age, and who will not abandon either us or you, hoping in him, in so great a service of his.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXIII. To the Archbishop of Tours and the Bishops of Paris and Nevers.

That they should inflame the king and magnates against the heretics. (Lateran.)

[Note: [Col. 1362D] See letter 30.] We do not believe it unknown to your prudence how, after the murder of our brother Peter of Castelnau, of holy memory, which we mourn in common grief [Col. 1361D] with the children of the universal Church, the heretical pest has grown strong in the regions of Provence and the disturbance of peace there has increased. Since, therefore, holy mother Church is now known especially to need the protection of her sons there against those who tear her apart, we earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood, commanding by apostolic letters that, supported by our authority, you prudently and effectively induce both our most dear son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks, and all the nobles and magnates of his kingdom to establish peace in Christ and conquer the heretics in the aforesaid province. [Col. 1362A] Enjoin this upon them on our behalf for the remission of their sins, according to the form which you, brother bishop of Paris, obtained; likewise exhorting the prelates of churches to provide timely assistance for so holy and necessary a work. Fulfill the apostolic command in such a way that you show yourselves prompt zealots for the orthodox faith and that we may deservedly commend the diligence of your effort.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXIV. To the Consuls of the Society of Blessed Eusebius of Vercelli.

They are commended for their devotion toward the Roman Church. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1362B]

We received with special grace and favor our beloved son, the noble man Ambrose, your fellow citizen, when he came into our presence. Having clearly understood the contents both of what he set forth orally and of the letters presented to us through him, we have judged your prudence deserving of manifold commendation in the Lord, on account of the devotion which you show yourselves to bear toward us and the Roman Church, and likewise on account of the zeal of charity which you have for the general advancement of the brotherly community. Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your devotion, commanding by apostolic letters that, persevering in your good purpose, you conduct yourselves in such a way, for the honor of God, the benefit of the Church, the salvation of [Col. 1362C] your souls, and the common advancement of each one, that he who rewards every good thing, moved by your pious deeds, may increase grace for you in the present and glory in the future, and that we too, who intend, so far as we can with God and with our honor, to honor you, may be more strongly inflamed toward your affection and advancement.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXV. To the Archbishop of Verissa, the Bishop of Salembria, and the Provost of Saint Sophia at Constantinople.

Concerning the Hospital of Saint George. (Lateran, XVI Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1362D] The complaint submitted to us by the beloved sons, the provost and dean of Saint George at Constantinople, made known that the brothers of the Hospital of Jerusalem, the lord of Lamron, and certain other Constantinopolitans are injuring them concerning the Hospital of Saint George, certain revenues, and other movable and immovable property. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to summon the parties, hear the case, and bring it to its due conclusion without appeal; causing what you decree to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. But the witnesses who are named, etc. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

[Col. 1363A] Given at the Lateran, XVI Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

## XXXVI. To the Dean, Cantor, and Treasurer of Saint Sophia at Constantinople.

A certain case against the Templars is committed to them. (Given as in the other letter.)

We have thought fit to commit to you the case which the beloved son Master W., clerk, claims to have against the brethren of the Knights Templar at Constantinople concerning the church of Saint Yomenia. By apostolic letters we command that, summoning the parties and hearing the allegations on both sides, you determine without appeal what is canonical, causing it, etc. But the witnesses, etc. But if not all, [Col. 1363B] etc., two of you, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

## XXXVII. To the Deans of Saint Paul, Saint Michael of Bucca Leonis, and Saint Anastasia at Constantinople.

They are written to on behalf of Master W. Cocart. (Lateran, VI Kalends of April.)

The beloved son Master W. Cocart, priest, sent into our presence by the imperial magnificence and the entire body of clergy dwelling at Constantinople, humbly petitioned us that, if in the meantime he should be harassed by anyone concerning his church of the Holy Trinity and his other revenues, [Col. 1363C] we would deign to provide for his indemnity. Therefore, wishing to assist him in justice as we are bound to do, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if you find any persons established in the diocese of Constantinople to have meanwhile taken away or detained anything from his revenues, you compel them, after prior admonition, to restore it by ecclesiastical censure, as shall be just, without appeal. But the witnesses, etc. But if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, VI Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

## XXXVIII. To the Most Dear Son in Christ, the Illustrious Emperor of Constantinople.

Concerning the oath of fealty which prelates owe the emperor. (Lateran, VII Kalends of April.)

[Col. 1363D]

We embrace your imperial highness with such an affection of charity that we desire gladly to grant its requests insofar as we can do so with God and with due regard to our honour. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, inclined by your petitions, by the authority of these presents we grant to your Serenity that you may receive fealty for the royal fiefs which are known to be held from you, from the archbishops and bishops of your land and likewise from others established in the empire, from whom you can receive it without scandal; provided that [Col. 1364A] those fiefs are of such a kind as those for which fealty is customarily rendered to other secular princes. Let no one therefore … this our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

### XXXIX. TO THE SAME.

The churches of St Mary of Blachernae and St Michael of Bucca Leonis are exempted from ordinary jurisdiction.  
(Lateran, 11 March.)

With that affection of charity, etc., as in another letter. Indeed, through your messengers you petitioned us that we might receive under the special protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the churches of St Mary and St Michael, one of which is situated in the imperial palace called Blachernae, while the other is in that [Col. 1364B] called Bucca Leonis. [Note: [Col. 1363D] See below, letter 41.] You further asked that we might exempt them from the jurisdiction of every person other than the Roman pontiff. Accordingly, graciously assenting to your petitions, we receive the aforesaid churches under the special protection of the Apostolic See and ourselves, and fortify them by the safeguard of this present document. Moreover, understanding from certain writings presented to us among the petitions of our venerable brother the Patriarch of Constantinople by his procurators that he ought to endure this equably, we establish by the authority of these presents that the said churches shall be bound to answer in spiritual matters to no one other than the Apostolic See. Let no one therefore … this our [Col. 1364C] protection and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the eleventh year.

### XL. TO THE CHAPTER OF CRACOW.

He commends to them Vincent, their bishop.  
(Lateran, 28 March.)

When various letters sent to us by different parties of your chapter had formerly been read in our hearing, we learned both from them and from the assertions of those who supported each party that, after F., your bishop of good memory, had departed this life, when you began to deliberate concerning the election of a successor, some of you agreed to request from the Apostolic See our venerable brother G., Bishop of Płock, [Col. 1364D] hoping that, through his industry and religious character, many benefits would accrue to their church. Others unanimously elected the beloved son Master Vincent, provost of the Church of Sandomierz in the diocese of Cracow, a man indeed distinguished by manifold praise.

Having therefore carefully heard and considered what was proposed before us by each side concerning this disagreement, although each person was considered suitable, nevertheless, since—even if at the beginning a larger number appeared to have consented to the aforesaid request—many of them eventually consented to the election of the said provost should that request happen not to be admitted; and since ordinary law [Col. 1365A] more nearly requires that a suitable man from its own diocese be provided as pastor for a church than that a bishop already bound to another church be so provided, we did not judge the aforesaid request admissible. Thus, understanding that the said election of a suitable person had been canonically celebrated by the greater number, we took care, with the counsel of our brethren, to confirm it.

Wherefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion henceforth to render to the same elect, as to your pastor, obedience and reverence that are due and devout, answering to him in spiritual and temporal matters.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

### XLI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF VERRIA, THE BISHOP OF SALEMBRIA, AND THE ELECT OF NICOMEDIA.

Concerning the imperial churches of Constantinople.  
(Lateran, 10 March.)

[Col. 1365B]

Our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople, petitioned our apostolic office that we might order the churches situated in his empire which are called imperial churches, and which in Greek times had customarily answered only to emperors, to remain in this liberty: that they should be bound to answer the emperor concerning temporal matters, but us concerning spiritual matters. [Note: [Col. 1365D] See above, letter 39.] Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, having summoned those who ought to be summoned for this purpose, you carefully inquire into the truth. Of the aforesaid churches, cause those which you find either to have been free from [Col. 1365C] their foundation, or exempted by a privilege of the Apostolic See, or protected by lawful prescription, to remain in the prescribed liberty. Concerning the others which you find to be in a state of freedom, hear whatever may reasonably be proposed by anyone, and faithfully report the matter to us under your seals, setting the parties a suitable term within which they may appear before us together with them. If not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the eleventh year.

### XLII. TO THE ABBOT AND BRETHREN OF THE MONASTERY OF FOSSANOVA.

Concerning confirmation of privileges.  
(Lateran, 28 March.)

It is customary to grant, etc., up to “assent.” Following the example [Col. 1365D] of our predecessor Pope Lucius of blessed memory, we establish by the authority of these presents that throughout the territory of Piperno you shall have free and undisturbed rights of use in pastures and woodland, as you are known to have held them without challenge for forty years past. We also confirm to you and to your monastery those things which your monastery now lawfully possesses, or may in future acquire by lawful means, through the gifts of the faithful, exchange, or purchase from the people of Piperno, whether from their private property or from newly cleared land in the public woodland—which is known to belong by right and lordship to blessed Peter. We further [Col. 1366A] decree that whatever is hereafter justly granted to you from the aforesaid property, you may, as inhabitants of the said territory, receive freely both by right of residence and by concession of the Apostolic See, and hold without any contradiction.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we grant you leave to cultivate your wood at Loreto and to give it to others for cultivation, within the boundaries by which it is defined and distinguished in the authenticated document of your monastery. Let no one therefore … this our constitution, confirmation, and concession, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

### XLIII. TO THE ABBOT OF ST VICTOR, THE DEAN OF PARIS, AND MASTER ROBERT OF COURÇON, CANON OF NOYON, RESIDING AT PARIS.

Concerning the election of the Bishop of Thérouanne.  
(Lateran, 2 April.)

[Col. 1366B]

[Note: [Col. 1365] Chapter *Cum dilecti*, “On elections.” See below, letter 225.] When the beloved sons Henry, Archdeacon of Thérouanne, and Master H., canon of Arras, procurators of the elect of Thérouanne, together with Bernard, canon of Thérouanne, came to the Apostolic See, the procurators took care to state in our presence that the Church of Thérouanne, deprived of a bishop’s assistance, had deliberated concerning the appointment of a pastor. The canons of that church unanimously conferred upon the beloved sons Adam, priest, Goscelin, deacon, and Theobald, subdeacon, canons of Thérouanne, the authority to elect a bishop, promising under oath that they would receive as pastor [Col. 1366C] whomever those men should select as bishop from the body of that church.

Thereafter, having examined the wishes of each individual, these three elected as bishop John, archdeacon of the same church, a learned, prudent, and discerning man. When the chapter had jointly approved that election, they together requested their metropolitan to confirm it. He carefully examined both the election and the person elected, and diligently inquired into the truth concerning his age, about whose deficiency some had raised doubts. By his judgment, declaring that the elect suffered no defect of age, he solemnly confirmed the election made of him as canonically celebrated.

Afterwards, having received the royal temporalities from the king, at the petition of the same chapter he was ordained priest by our venerable brother, the Bishop of Arras, by mandate of the aforesaid metropolitan. For some time, with no one objecting, he held free and peaceful administration in both spiritual and temporal matters in the Church of Thérouanne. Therefore the said procurators humbly requested us to impose silence upon those who, after all these events, stirred by the goads of envy and rashly acting against their own deed, presume to raise a cause of discord against the elect; solemnly to approve the election, so harmoniously celebrated and confirmed; [Col. 1367A] and to cause the gift of consecration to be conferred upon him.

They presented us with letters on this matter not only from many abbots and chapters of the city and diocese of Thérouanne, but also from other priests. These bore testimony to all the foregoing and commended the elect to us in many ways for learning, discernment, and uprightness of conduct. Indeed, they also produced letters from the electors themselves, into which, as those electors asserted, the wording of the letters prepared in the chapter and sealed with the chapter’s seal concerning the authority granted to them in the form described above had been inserted word for word.

But the aforesaid B., who had come against the elect in question, asserted on the other hand that the power of election had been granted to the aforesaid three under an oath and in this form: that the chapter was bound to receive as pastor the man whom those three should elect from the body of that church after nomination by all or by the greater and sounder part. The electors, he said, had not observed the limits of the authority entrusted to them, but had presumed to elect the aforesaid archdeacon, whom only a few of the chapter had nominated. Consequently, the canons of Thérouanne, subsequently wondering how the aforesaid archdeacon had been elected when there were many worthier men in the church, began, while discussing the course of the election among themselves, almost all publicly to declare that they had in no way nominated the aforesaid archdeacon. Considering themselves deceived in this matter, they took care to disclose to our apostolic office through the same B.—to whom they entrusted their testimonial letters—what had been done in this respect. [Col. 1367C]

Before us he earnestly requested that the election be annulled and that we cause the church to be canonically provided with a suitable person. Almost all the canons of Thérouanne, he asserted, stood ready to confirm under oath that they had never nominated the aforesaid archdeacon as bishop. He further asserted that it could lawfully be shown that authority to elect had been granted to the aforesaid three in the form stated above: namely, that they should elect from the body of the church the one upon whom all, or the greater and sounder part, of the chapter agreed. B. also claimed that he would prove that the oft-mentioned elect suffered a deficiency of age.

We therefore, having carefully heard these and other matters proposed before us on either side, and considering that it would be a pernicious precedent if someone should rise to the summit of dignity through the cunning of deception, judged, with the counsel of our brethren, that the following provision should be made. The objectors must first swear that they are not maliciously raising this question against the aforesaid elect. Then the three named electors shall be bound by oath to tell the truth as to how many of the canons agreed upon the aforesaid archdeacon at the time of examination. If all three, or at least two, of them under oath say that the greater part of the canons agreed upon the archdeacon, you shall impose silence on the objectors, since their proof to the contrary would be insufficient, because they would be individual witnesses in their respective testimonies. [Col. 1368A]

But if their depositions establish that the aforesaid archdeacon was nominated by the smaller number, then carefully hear whatever each party may propose and prove concerning the form in which authority to elect is asserted to have been granted to the aforesaid three electors. If it is sufficiently shown that, according to the form given them, they were bound to elect from the body of the church the man upon whom all or the greater and sounder part of the chapter agreed, then wholly annul the election of the archdeacon and cause the Church of Thérouanne to be provided, by a canonical election, with a suitable person as bishop. Otherwise, holding valid what was done concerning him, restrain the objectors from assailing him by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. Deprive the aforesaid B. of his prebend in the Church of Thérouanne, since he bound himself to this penalty should he perhaps fail in proof. The objection concerning defect of age is no obstacle, since the same canon did not press that objection greatly, and the metropolitan has rendered judgment upon it; his sentence has passed into a matter adjudged, since it was not suspended by lawful appeal within ten years. If not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the eleventh year.

### XLIV. TO THE ABBESS AND CHAPTER OF ÉDERA.

Concerning confirmation of a fixed number of nuns.  
(Lateran, 1 April.)

[Col. 1368C]

At the just requests of petitioners, etc., up to “inclined”: confirming by apostolic authority the number of eighty nuns and lay sisters (*conversae*) which, because utility so advised and pressing necessity required, you prudently established in your monastery with the counsel and assent of our dearest son in Christ Philip, the illustrious King of the Franks, and of your diocesan, our venerable brother the Bishop of Paris, we command that this number be observed—unless, by the Lord’s gift, its resources should increase so greatly that the number of sisters also could be enlarged in proportion to that increase. Let no one therefore … this our confirmation, etc. But if [Col. 1368D] anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

### XLV. TO HUGH, CANON OF ST GEORGE OF FAYE.

His prebend at Faye is confirmed.  
(Lateran, 27 March.)

When the beloved sons B., canon of St Peter of Poitiers, and D., procurators of G. de Marnay, and you—answering and acting both for yourself and in the name of the beloved sons W., provost, and your other fellow canons—wished to litigate concerning the prebend of Faye, formerly held by R. de Poento, canon of that church, we appointed our beloved son Andrew, subdeacon and chaplain, as auditor.

In his presence you took care to state [Col. 1369A] that, by custom and long-standing usage strengthened by an oath, no more than twelve canons ought to be instituted in the Church of St George of Faye, nor may a promise or grant be made of any prebend that is not vacant. Further, no canon of Faye may simultaneously hold a prebend and one of the churches whose disposal belongs to the chapter; instead, when vacant, those churches are conferred by the chapter on other servants of the choir. If a chaplain of such a church is at any time admitted as a canon, he is compelled to resign either the chaplaincy or the canonry, since by custom they do not permit each other. Everyone who receives a chaplaincy also promises by a bodily sworn oath that he will serve personally in it.

When certain persons had been installed as precentor and canons in the said Church of Faye while the aforesaid B. was absent—although he was a canon there, he did not reside there—and he therefore brought the canons into litigation before the beloved sons the Abbot of St Jouin of Marnes, the Dean of Thouars in the diocese of Poitiers, and Master P. Barrilier, formerly canon of Blessed Radegund of Poitiers, judges delegated by the Apostolic See, the canons, preserving the customs of their church confirmed by oath, and the other party chose as arbitrators one of those judges, R. de Poento, O. de Maulay, and the knight R. Juret. Contrary both to the customs of the aforesaid church and to common law, those arbitrators imprudently granted to the aforesaid G. de Marnay, who held one of the aforesaid churches and did not take care to resign it, [Col. 1369C] the first annual income that should become vacant in that church, and likewise granted the second vacancy to the boy William de Grandchamp.

In the course of time, by authority of Octavian, Bishop of Ostia, of good memory, then performing the office of legate in those parts, the Bishop of Poitiers, our venerable brother, wholly annulled the grant to the aforesaid G. de Marnay. Yet G., suppressing mention of the aforesaid arbitration and annulment and concealing the truth in many particulars, procured from us letters sent to the priors of St Radegund, La Celle, and St Paul of Poitiers, directing them to compel the said canons by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, either to restore his prebend to him in full and satisfy him concerning what had been withheld, or to appear before them for the completion of justice. But G., whether by fraud or negligence, suppressed those letters and did not use them for almost three years.

Thereafter R., canon of Faye, entered upon the way of all flesh. The letters were then presented to the judges, and G., by authority of those letters, claimed that the now-vacant prebend should be conferred upon him. Although the canons, cited by the aforesaid judges, appeared before them on the appointed day and rejected them for lawful causes, alleging lawful exceptions against the letters—since they had been obtained from the Apostolic See by false suggestion and by concealing the truth in many matters—the judges nevertheless disregarded all this. After a lawful appeal to us had been made, [Col. 1370A] they pronounced sentence of excommunication against the canons and did not fear to assign to G. the prebend which had not been vacant when the rescript was obtained, exceeding in every respect the bounds of the apostolic mandate.

Since we had directed the beloved sons, the abbots of St Julian and Fontaines, and the subdean of St Martin of Tours, that if they found this sentence of excommunication to have been issued after a lawful appeal to us had been made, they should declare it entirely void; otherwise, after receiving from the canons sworn security concerning the matters for which they lay under sentences of excommunication, they should grant them the benefit of absolution, impose what law required to be imposed, hear and bring to a due conclusion any dispute that might arise: on the appointed day the parties appeared before the Abbot of Fontaines and the subdean of St Martin of Tours. Their third colleague excused himself by a certain messenger, saying that he could not attend to the business. In accordance with the tenor of our letters, the other two absolved the canons from the sentence by which they were said to be bound. But when the other party appealed and advanced various reasons why the canons ought not to be absolved, and litigation had continued for some time between the parties concerning revocation of the earlier letters while the Abbot of St Julian and the same subdean sat in judgment, those two, without their fellow judge—who, as he had notified them by letter, did not wish to be present at the hearing—sent us a written account, confirmed with their own seals and containing the proceedings of the whole case. [Col. 1370C]

You further endeavoured to assert on your own behalf that, after the death of the aforesaid R., you came to the Apostolic See and disclosed to our apostolic office that, by our mandate and that of the same Bishop of Ostia, then legate of the Apostolic See, you received annually in that church, where you had served from earliest youth, six sextaries of grain until you should obtain through its canons a suitable ecclesiastical benefice, whether in a prebend or elsewhere. Although the same prebend was vacant there, and almost all the canons of the said church wished to confer it upon you, you could not obtain it because a few opposed it.

We therefore directed by our letters the beloved sons A., chancellor, R., archpriest, and Master P. Parvus, canon of Bourges, that unless something were reasonably objected or shown by the smaller and inferior party which would prevent the consent of the greater and worthier part from prevailing, they should confer the prebend upon you by apostolic authority, without appeal, restraining objectors by ecclesiastical censure without appeal. The said judges, perceiving from certain letters of the chapter of Faye that the consent and wishes of all expressly concurred in your favour, ordered the chapter to make a virtue of necessity: freely to grant you the said prebend, to assign you a stall in choir and a place in chapter, and to summon before them, on a day appointed for this purpose, any persons who considered themselves bound to oppose your reception, there to hear the apostolic mandate. [Col. 1371A]

On the appointed day, you and your adversary G. de Marnay appeared before them. Almost all the canons requested the judges to fulfil your request effectively by their own apostolic authority. They also fully perceived from certain letters of the chapter sent to our apostolic office that the canons continued in their former agreement concerning you. Although, on behalf of the other party, certain letters were shown to the judges on another day appointed to the parties with a peremptory summons, whose contents testified that the aforesaid prebend had first been granted to G. de Marnay before you had set out to come to the Apostolic See, nevertheless the judges had found that the reception of G. made by the aforesaid Bishop of Poitiers, by mandate of the Bishop of Ostia, had been annulled. Since nothing reasonable was objected or alleged against you in fact, they took care by judicial sentence to invest you with the aforesaid prebend, issuing sentence of excommunication against any who might be rebellious. They committed execution of their sentence to the beloved son, the Abbot of Stella of the Cistercian Order, and did not consider themselves bound to defer to the appeal made by the other party; because executors cannot be appealed from unless they exceed the manner of execution, they declared that appeal null and void. [Col. 1371B]

But, having been received into the chapter in the full capacity of a canon, you came into our presence to answer your adversary concerning that appeal. Since he did not prosecute it within a year, and after the year had elapsed … [Col. 1371C] his nephew, having become procurator, remained at the Apostolic See but obtained nothing against you, you requested that the said subdeacon and our chaplain be appointed auditor for you. That procurator, having obtained certain letters without the auditor’s knowledge, fraudulently presumed, after you had opposed them, to have them issued under the seal; by subsequent letters we decreed that they lacked force.

On the other hand, it was alleged that, since we had sent letters in the form expressly stated above to the aforesaid priors, and those priors, having summoned the parties, learned both from the confession of the said precentor and canons and from certain public instruments that the aforesaid G. was receiving certain annual revenues [Col. 1371D] in the Church of Faye until he should obtain a full prebend, and that while the case was pending the prebend in dispute had fallen vacant, the precentor and the greater and sounder part of the chapter freely conferred it upon him before you came to us, with no one then objecting. When some later refused to admit him, the judges, after warning them, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against them. After that sentence had been issued, they appealed to us and obtained letters directed to the judges of Tours, who proceeded in this matter as you had narrated.

We, however, having been sufficiently instructed by the report of the aforesaid auditor concerning the matters proposed on either side, judged void the act of the judges of Poitiers because they had exceeded the limits of their mandate. We approved the proceedings of the judges of Tours, who had absolved the canons of Faye from the sentence of excommunication inflicted by the judges of Poitiers; and we held valid and firm the adjudication of the prebend made for you by the judges of Bourges. We therefore judged that both the chapter of the Church of Faye and you should be wholly absolved from the claim of the oft-mentioned G. de Marnay, imposing perpetual silence upon G. himself concerning these matters. Let no one therefore … this our determination, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

### XLVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON.

Reply to his questions.  
(Lateran, 22 March.)

[Col. 1372B]

[Note: [Col. 1371D] Chapter *Tuis quaestionibus*, “On prebends.”] We answer your questions as follows. You may promote to higher orders clerics in minor orders who possess patrimonial goods sufficient for their suitable maintenance, even if they have not yet obtained an ecclesiastical benefice, provided that no other canonical impediment stands in the way.

[Note: [Col. 1371D] Chapter same, “On witnesses.”] Monks may not produce as witnesses in their own cases their brethren or lay brothers (*conversi*) without administering an oath, unless perhaps the opposing party waives it. Nor may religious persons retain tithes from lands liable to tithes which they acquire by purchase or by other [Col. 1372C] lawful means, unless they have a privilege concerning this. Trial by boiling water is forbidden by canonical enactments, not only in matrimonial causes but also in other ecclesiastical causes.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

### XLVII. TO THE NOBLEMAN THEODORE LASKARIS.

He is urged to make peace with the Emperor of Constantinople.  
(Lateran, 17 March.)

In order to reduce the length of your letter to brevity, we have judged it necessary to confine it under certain heads. First, you rebuke the Latins dwelling at Constantinople on the charge of apostasy, [Col. 1372D] because, having assumed the sign of the Lord’s cross and pretended to hasten to the aid of the Holy Land against barbarian peoples, they turned back and turned their swords against their fellow Christians, attacking the city and empire of Constantinople. You charge them with treachery and sacrilege because, after capturing the imperial city, they spared not the most holy churches, killed Christians, deflowered virgins, and violated even married women. [Note: [Col. 1372D] See the *Deeds of Innocent III*, chapter 95, p. 59, col. 1.]

You also repeatedly declare them guilty of perjury because they have presumed several times to violate the truces they made with you. Abandoning the more excellent way taught by the Apostle, namely charity, they refuse to establish perpetual concord and friendship with you, but have again made a truce for a fixed term, although the Lord commands that charity be maintained not temporarily but perpetually. You therefore humbly petitioned us to make them enter into a perpetual peace treaty with you, since, under the Lord’s rule, love ought always to flourish among Christians; and to send a legate from our side to establish and arrange peace between you and them, so that neither you nor they may presume to cross the boundary appointed by God between you, namely the sea, but may be content with that boundary. You promise that, together with them, you will fight manfully against the Ishmaelites; otherwise, though unwillingly, [Col. 1373B] you will nevertheless make a pact with foreigners and pagans against them and will join the Vlachs, since you have sought peace and cannot find it.

We do not excuse the aforesaid Latins, whom we have repeatedly rebuked concerning their offences; but we have judged it fitting to set forth to you in this letter their excuses. They say that, after undertaking the leadership of that young man who acknowledged that the empire of Constantinople was owed to him by right, pressing necessity compelled them to turn aside into Romania to obtain provisions. Making a virtue of necessity, they intended principally to procure there both service pleasing to the Apostolic See and the hoped-for aid to the Holy Land. They thought that they had fully accomplished this when, having captured the imperial city without bloodshed, driven out the usurper of the empire, and restored there both father and son—Isaac and Alexius—to the height of imperial dignity, they caused them, without compulsion, to promise obedience to the most holy Apostolic See upon the Gospels. An imperial letter was sent to us for greater assurance of faith, so that they might fulfil in deed what they had promised by word.

When they were preparing with all their might to sail to Syria, the innate malice of those men, wholly violating oaths and agreements, wickedly impeded their journey by fire, treachery, and poison not once only but often, and drew them, resisting and unwilling, to the occupation of the imperial city, to their own ruin. [Note: [Col. 1373D] “Destruction” or “ruin.”] After that city had been marvellously conquered by God’s power alone, [Col. 1373D] whatever they thereafter did, willingly or unwillingly, in whatever manner or place, they always intended to bring the children of disobedience back to the obedience, both due and devout, of their mother, and through the empire of Romania to give aid to the Holy Land more opportunely and easily.

Although they are not wholly blameless, we nevertheless believe that the Greeks were punished through them by the just judgment of God, because they attempted to rend the seamless garment of Jesus Christ. For since God’s judgments are so hidden that they are called by the prophetic voice “a great deep,” it often happens by His hidden, though always most just, judgment that evil persons are punished through the agency of evil persons, [Col. 1374A] as the Lord himself says through the prophet: “Assyria is the rod of my anger, and the staff in their hand is my indignation” (Isaiah 10). Thus he said to Nebuchadnezzar: “Because you have served me at Tyre, I shall give you Egypt” (Ezekiel 29).

Justly, indeed, those perished in the Flood who would not remain with Noah in the ark; and those suffered the want of famine who refused to receive as their shepherd blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord entrusted the feeding of his sheep. They wandered after the flocks of their companions, repeatedly refusing, despite diligent admonition by our predecessors and by us, to return to unity. Nor did they ever choose to provide aid to the Holy Land, although they could have aided it more fully and effectively through both proximity of place and abundance of wealth. Therefore, not undeservedly, through men who directed themselves to both aims alike, they lost both land and people, so that, once evil men had been destroyed, the land itself might be leased to such cultivators as render its fruit in due season.

Moreover, because, as is read in the prophet Daniel, there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, changes times, transfers kingdoms, rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he wills, he has transferred the empire of Constantinople to those same men. We counsel your nobility to humble yourself in the presence of our dearest son in Christ, Henry, the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople, and to serve him, rendering due honour. Follow the example of Jeremiah, [Col. 1374C] who, as we read, counselled the people of Israel to serve King Nebuchadnezzar and live under him. For if the prophet advised that the faithful people should serve an unbelieving king, how much more ought you to be advised to serve the aforesaid emperor, to whom the Most High has given the empire, since he is a Catholic and faithful prince, so that, living under his empire, you may obtain the peace you desire.

As to your assertion that they lack charity because they have made a truce with you for a fixed term and refuse to make it perpetual, whereas love is not enclosed within a term, we briefly answer that charity can and ought to exist even without truces. Charity must be extended not only to friends but even to enemies, as the Lord says: “Love your enemies, [Col. 1374D] do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5). Certainly charity is not taken away by truces, but fostered by them, and an easier way is prepared toward its perfection.

You, therefore, consenting to the divine ordinance by which the same man has been raised to the empire, render him due service and honour. And endeavour, with all those who are with you, to show devotion and reverence to us, who, although unworthy, hold the place of blessed Peter; for through the legate whom we intend to send into those regions, we shall carefully admonish the emperor to deal with you in a spirit of gentleness. When you learn that that legate has arrived [Col. 1375A] in those regions, you shall send your messengers to him, so that he may take care to arrange between you and the aforesaid emperor those things which concern peace and salvation.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

### XLVIII. TO ALUF, CANON OF ST ANASTASIA.

His prebend is confirmed.  
(Lateran, 9 April.)

“As is customary, he assents,” etc., as far as “assent”: the prebend which you state that you have lawfully obtained in the church of Saint Anastasia, as you justly and peaceably possess it, we confirm to you by apostolic authority and by the present writing, etc. Therefore let no one, etc. But if anyone, [Col. 1375B] etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of April, in the eleventh year.

XLIX. TO THE DEAN OF SAINT MARY OF BLAKERNÆ, THE CHANTER OF THE FORTY SAINTS, AND MASTER G., CANON OF SAINT PAUL AT CONSTANTINOPLE. Written on behalf of the same Alufus. (Lateran, second Ides of April.)

Our beloved son Alufus, canon of Saint Anastasia at Constantinople, has laid before us a serious complaint: D., his fellow canon, and certain other men of Constantinople, setting aside the fear of God, rashly laid violent hands upon him. Since there is no doubt that those who lay such violent hands have incurred the penalty of the promulgated canon, [Col. 1375C] we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you shall keep the said offenders, etc., for so long. But if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Ides of April, in the eleventh year.

L. TO THE CHANTER OF THE FORTY SAINTS, MASTER G. OF SAINT PAUL, AND ARN., CANON OF SAINT MARY OF CINTURA AT CONSTANTINOPLE. On behalf of the same man. (Lateran, Ides of April.)

Coming to the apostolic see, our beloved son Alufus, canon of Saint Anastasia, showed us by his statement [Col. 1375D] that, although the dean of Saint Mary of Blakernæ and the canons of Saint Anastasia at Constantinople, on whose behalf he had laboured at the apostolic see, promised during his absence to provide him with the revenues of his prebend and other things belonging to him by right, they retain them and refuse to render them. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning, you compel the said dean and canons, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to provide him with those revenues and other things, as they are bound to do. But if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April, in the eleventh year.

LI. TO THE PROVOST AND CHAPTER OF BLAKERNÆ. On behalf of Arnulf, canon of Blakernæ. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1376A]

Appearing in our presence, our beloved son Arnulf, a canon of your church, humbly asked us to secure satisfaction for him: having come to the apostolic see, he laboured greatly to expedite your affairs and those of the entire clergy of Constantinople, and he seeks recompense for the revenues of that church received by you which he himself would have received had he been present in your church. Since, therefore, the same A. ought not to suffer loss from that through which he is known to have earned a reward, we have thought fit to request and admonish your whole body, commanding you by apostolic [Col. 1376B] letters to take care to make such provision for that canon from the revenues withheld from him while he was absent on common business, that he may thereby be held more bound to you and your church, and that we may deservedly commend your devotion on this account.

Given as in the other letter.

LII. TO OUR DEAREST SON IN CHRIST, HENRY, ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He is urged to restore property of the church of Saint Anastasia which has been taken away. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.)

It has come to our hearing, our beloved son Alufus, canon of the church of Saint Anastasia at Constantinople, reporting [Col. 1376C] that this church—which, before the capture of the city of Constantinople, held the foremost place after the greater church—is burdened by extreme poverty, its goods having been repeatedly alienated and consumed. Moreover, Baldwin, emperor of illustrious memory, your brother, whose successor you are, unjustly seized and retained the villages with their appurtenances, possessions, and other goods belonging to the said church; and you refuse, at peril to your soul, to restore what has been seized. But since the more prosperously your steps are directed by the Lord, the less burdensome you ought to be to churches, we earnestly request and admonish your Serenity that, if this is so, you restore these goods to that church out of reverence for the apostolic see and for us, and cease from unduly troubling it in this matter.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LIII. TO THE CHANTER OF BLAKERNÆ, THE PROVOST OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE, AND MASTER P., CANON OF SAINT PAUL AT CONSTANTINOPLE. The case of T., chaplain of Bucca Leonis, is committed to them. (Lateran, fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.)

You are to know that we have received the representation of T., chaplain of the church of Bucca Leonis, and certain other clergy of Constantinople, that H. of Arras and certain other clergy of Constantinople receive and divide at their own arbitrary will the revenues of certain properties known to have fallen to the share of those clergy, [Col. 1377A] wholly without consulting those who ought by right to be consulted on this matter; and, though repeatedly required, they refuse to render the share due to them. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning those who ought to be summoned and hearing what is put forward on both sides, you determine, without appeal, what is just, causing, etc. But witnesses, etc. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LIV. TO THE ELECT OF NICOMEDIA, THE PROVOST OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE, AND THE PRIOR OF THE PISANS AT CONSTANTINOPLE. A case concerning a certain mule is committed to them. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1377B]

The beloved sons A. and D., clerics residing at Constantinople, have made known to us in their complaint that the dean of Saint Sophia and certain other men of Constantinople unjustly retain a certain mule and other goods belonging to them and refuse to restore them, wronging them concerning grain and other things. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning those who ought to be summoned and hearing what is put forward on both sides, you determine, without appeal, what is just, causing, etc. But witnesses, etc. But if not all . . . two, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

LV. TO THE DEANS OF SAINT SOPHIA AND SAINT ANASTASIA, AND THE CHANTER OF BLAKERNÆ. The case of Arnulf, canon of Blakernæ, is committed to them. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1377C]

Our beloved sons Arnulf, canon of Blakernæ, and other clerics residing at Constantinople have complained to us that our venerable brother, the bishop of Salimbri, does not cease to inflict serious losses and injuries upon them concerning certain lands, vineyards, meadows, and other things. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties, you hear the case and, without appeal, bring it to its proper conclusion, causing, etc. But witnesses, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

LVI. TO OUR BELOVED SON, THE ELECT OF MEAUX. That he confer blessing upon A., abbess-elect of Iotrensis. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 1377D]

[Note: See the appendix to this book, Col. 1377D.] The nuns of the monastery of Iotrensis, our beloved daughters in Christ, showed us in their humble representation that the same convent has suffered no slight loss, both spiritual and temporal, because the blessing of its elect has been delayed. Desiring therefore to provide for it with paternal care, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, within fifteen days after you have been consecrated—without prejudice to the terms of the judgment formerly issued by us between [Col. 1378A] your predecessor of good memory and A., formerly abbess of Iotrensis, which has not yet been put into execution, and without prejudice to everything that belongs by right to either party—you shall not omit to confer the blessing upon that elect. Otherwise, know that we have instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Troyes, that thereafter, subject to all the foregoing, he is not to delay in blessing the same woman, by our authority and without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LVII. (Given as in the other letter.)

In the same terms to the bishop of Troyes, as far as “shall not omit.” Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the said elect [Col. 1378B] does not carry out our command within the aforesaid period, you thereafter, subject to all the foregoing, shall not delay in blessing that same elect by our authority and without appeal.

Given as in the other letter.

LVIII. TO THE DEAN AND CHANTER OF BLAKERNÆ, AND MASTER P. OF MONTIGNY, CANON OF SAINT PAUL AT CONSTANTINOPLE. A certain case of Constantinople is committed to them. (Lateran, seventeenth day before the Kalends of May.)

As our beloved son Ernulf, canon of Saint Mary of Cinctura at Constantinople, showed us by his complaint, the chanter of that church and certain other fellow canons of his rashly presumed violently to carry off its doors [Col. 1378C] and other goods, to the detriment of the said canon and church and to the scandal of many. But since the foregoing has not been established before us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning those who should be summoned for this purpose and hearing what is advanced on both sides, you determine, without appeal, what is just, causing, etc. But witnesses, etc. But if not all . . . two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LIX. TO THE CHANTER OF SAINT MARY OF BLAKERNÆ, MASTER G. OF SAINT PAUL, AND T., CANON OF SAINT GEORGE AT CONSTANTINOPLE. Concerning a similar case. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1378D]

The beloved sons, the dean and chapter of the church of Saint Mary of Cinctura, showed us through a complaint sent to us that Brino the crossbowman and certain other men of Constantinople are troublesome and injurious to them concerning a certain house of the aforesaid church granted to them as alms and concerning other things. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties and hearing what is advanced on both sides, you determine what is just, etc., causing, etc. But witnesses, etc. But if not all . . . two, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

X. TO THE DEANS OF SAINT ANASTASIA AND SAINT PAUL, AND MASTER G., CANON OF SAINT PAUL AT CONSTANTINOPLE. A certain case of the chapter of Blakernæ is committed to them. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1379A]

We have received the complaint of our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Blakernæ, stating that the brothers of the hospital [Note: Here a space was left blank in the original, Col. 1379D.] . . . . . of Bologna and certain others of the diocese of Constantinople wrong them concerning a certain mill, a certain sum of money, and other things. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties and hearing what is advanced on both sides, you determine [Col. 1379B] what is just, interest ceasing, etc., causing, etc. But witnesses, etc. But if not all . . . . . two, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

LXI. TO EUDES, PRIOR, AND THE CANONS OF THE ALMSHOUSE OF SAINT JOHN OF ANGERS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, eighteenth day before the Kalends of May.)

Although we are bound to extend paternal care to religious places, we ought nevertheless to hold especially dear those places in which works of hospitality and [Col. 1379C] other works of mercy are more zealously performed. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; and, following the example of Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid hospital-house of Saint John of Angers, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall there be observed inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same house now justly and canonically possesses, etc., as far as “shall remain unimpaired”; among them we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid house is situated, with all its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Stephen of the House of the Poor; the chapel of Saint James of Theson, with the bridge and all its appurtenances; the enclosure of Angers, with mills, fisheries, and all its appurtenances; the wood of Deserta with its appurtenances; your houses situated above the bridge of Angers and on both banks, together with the increase from the fairs; one half of the said bridge of Angers with its appurtenances; the jurisdiction and holdings which you possess in the king’s fief and in other demesne fiefs. The holdings which you possess at Verreries, Chesneia, in the fief of Sance, at Pyreio, Juncheries, [Col. 1380A] Jurleta, Morino, Corrourio, Telleia, in the fiefs of Fougere, Rameforti, Oliverii Andefrei, and Agnes of Chastellione. The rents which you possess at Chantoceio, Segreio, Salmurio, Castronovo, and what you possess at Agrifame, in the fief of Falconiers, and at Loicaneria. The estate called Fontanas Borrel, with all its appurtenances. The right of maintenance of your mill of the springs through the land of Boccardus of Marolium. The whole holding of Cuelcio, with its people and other appurtenances. A rent of thirty solidi at Syrenas. The estate of Rochetis, with its people and other appurtenances. The holdings which you possess in the fiefs of Foldonio and Brein. Your right to firewood at Valeia, your pannage at Mounes, and what you possess at Avalo and Floreio.

Furthermore, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. [Col. 1380B] We also decree that the bishop or his officials shall demand nothing from the aforesaid house except what is owed him by episcopal right; nor shall its ministers or brethren be subjected to excommunication or suspension by anyone without manifest and reasonable cause. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding those excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a low voice. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person rashly to disturb the aforesaid house [Col. 1380C] or take away its possessions, etc., saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc. But to all who preserve their rights to that place, etc., to the end. Amen.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1206 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LXII. TO THE BISHOP OF ARRAS. He is instructed how he ought to deal with usurers and with a priest who has relapsed into heresy. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 1380D] Since, according to canonical enactments, where there is a slaughter of many, something must be remitted from severity: with respect to the usurers, who are said to have increased so greatly in your city and diocese that, if the censure promulgated against such persons at the Lateran council were imposed upon all of them, the churches would have to be entirely closed because of their number, you may proceed with such caution that you do not involve everyone at once, but begin to exercise your office against some. Be instructed by the example of him against whom, when those receiving a denarius complained, he is reported to have said not to all but to one of them: “Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” etc. (Matthew 20.)

As for the priest, [Col. 1381A] cause him to remain in the custody assigned to him. As you assert, he was once a regular canon; then became a Cistercian monk; subsequently returned to the black order; and finally lapsed into the secular state. Because of the heresy which he publicly preached, your predecessor kept him for seven years in prison custody. At last, moved by compassion for him, you removed him from that custody, but afterwards placed him again in the same prison because he was sowing heresies as before.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LXIII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT CALIXTUS OF CISO. That they may take tithes and lands in pledge. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 1381B] Since, as you assert, certain laymen hold in fief certain tithes and lands of your monastery, we grant you by this present authority that you may take those lands and tithes in pledge and need not count against the principal what you receive from their fruits, provided that those men are not burdened in respect of the service which they are bound to render by reason of the fief.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LXIV. TO R. TROSELLI, CANON OF SAINT URSINUS OF BOURGES. A dispensation allowing him to retain a benefice although he was a judge in a duel.

[Col. 1381C] “It is customary to assent,” etc. Although you were elected prior by the greater and sounder part of the chapter of Saint Ursinus at Bourges, nevertheless the beloved son, the chanter of the church of Bourges, who had been elected by certain persons, objected against you in court that you had been one of the judges of a certain duel in which bloodshed had followed. He sufficiently proved this through two witnesses. We have therefore, with the counsel of our brethren, judged that election concerning you to be invalidated—not so much because of the stain of your fault as in order that a harmful example, which is known to have been created in your case regarding an election of this kind, may henceforth be avoided.

But since, according to the perverse custom of certain regions, judgments in such duels are customarily conducted not only by laymen and clerics in minor orders but also, as we have learned from the testimony of many, [Col. 1381D] by the higher prelates of churches; and since the aforesaid judgment of the duel was alleged against you not in the form of an accusation but merely by way of exception: yielding to your petitions, by the authority of this present writing we have thought fit to grant that, notwithstanding this entirely, you may be elected to any dignity, provided no other canonical impediment stands in the way—especially since no mutilation or killing followed from that duel.

Given.

LXV. TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRENCH. That he may build a house at Paris for the support of his officials. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1382A]

From the letters of your royal Serenity we have learned that, desiring mercifully to provide for your servants who have grown old in royal service, you intend to build at Paris, from your own goods and those of the servants themselves, a certain house in which the necessities of life may be supplied to them. You have humbly and devoutly asked us to deem worthy of receiving it into the right and property of blessed Peter, wholly exempting it from episcopal jurisdiction. Since it is more fitting that this house should be free from its foundation than that, after its foundation, it should be exempted from [Col. 1382B] episcopal due, we direct by our letters our venerable brother, the bishop, and our beloved son, the archdeacon of Noyon, to receive in our stead, as offered to blessed Peter, the site on which you intend to construct the house. Thus, upon land of the Roman Church, the house itself, with chapel and cemetery, may be freely built by our permission solely for the use of such servants; provided, however, that this does not diminish the rights either of the diocesan bishop or of neighbouring churches. For we intend to grant you this favour in such a way that we inflict no injury on them.

Given as in the other letter.

LXVI. TO THE CITIZENS OF SORA. Their reasonable customs are confirmed. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1382C]

As devoted sons returning to the breast of your mother, the most holy Roman Church, it is fitting that you should be nourished by her sweet milk; so that you who until now, under the stepmotherly hand of fortune, have borne the burden of unjust servitude may now, through assisting grace, find renewal of your accustomed freedom. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting favourably to your just petitions, we grant you with paternal benevolence and confirm by apostolic authority the reasonable liberties, good usages, and approved customs which you enjoyed from the time of the illustrious King Roger until the death of William, kings of Sicily, so that you may use them freely while preserving entire faithfulness toward us. Therefore let no one . . . [Col. 1382D] violate this page of our grant and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

In the same terms to the clerics, knights, and all the people of Rocca d’Arce.

Given at the Lateran.

In the same terms to all the people of Pesclo Solido.

Given at the Lateran.

LXVII. TO THE CONSULS AND ALL KNIGHTS AND PEOPLE, BOTH OF THE CITY AND OF THE BOROUGH OF ARLES, AND TO THE NOBLE MEN V. OF BAUX AND THE OTHER LORDS OF THE BOROUGH OF ARLES. That they render their customary services to the church of Arles. (Lateran, sixth day before the Nones of May.)

[Col. 1383A]

If you knew how sweet the yoke and light the burden of the Church are, surely you would not seek to withdraw yourselves from its free subjection and to give your free necks to the yoke of alien servitude.
