For we have learned, our venerable brother the archbishop of Arles reporting it, that although you were singularly bound to the church of Arles by loyalty and lordship, on account of an oath which you swore to the noble count of Provence, [Col. 1383B] you have gravely injured that church. You granted to him Salvaria, Vermellaria, and certain other places in the city of Arles, to its no slight detriment and burden; and you also bound yourselves to render him certain services which you cannot discharge without loss to the rights of that church, which is your principal lady. Since an oath was not devised as a bond of iniquity, we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole body, commanding you by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding such an oath—which, insofar as ecclesiastical liberty is injured by it, being unlawful, is not to be observed—you shall regard as void whatever has been undertaken in these matters to the detriment of the church of Arles; you shall render to the said archbishop [Col. 1383C] and his church their due and customary services; and you shall in no way presume unjustly to transfer to another the rights which it holds in you and in your city.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the eleventh year.

LXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. His privilege of not paying procurations to legates is confirmed. (Given on the same day.)

Although it has been granted by apostolic privilege that the province of Arles shall be subject to absolutely no legate except one sent from the side of the Roman pontiff, nevertheless, because we have necessarily dispatched legates to those regions to eliminate heretical depravity and quell hostile fury, and because we wish you prudently to assist and liberally provide for them, we provide for you by the authority of this present writing that no prejudice shall arise to you or your church from the services rendered to the said legates because of this necessity. [Col. 1383D]

Given on the same day.

LXIX. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT MICHAEL OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER. Concerning the hospital of the Holy Spirit in the diocese of Halberstadt. (Lateran, second day before the Kalends of May.)

Appearing in our presence, our beloved son, the noble Count of Blankenburg, showed us in a devout representation [Col. 1384A] that he fervently desires a hospital to be built beside your monastery from his own goods, in honour of the Holy Spirit and for the use of the sick and poor. He humbly offered us eighteen manses of excellent land at Elikestorp; likewise the tithe of the same place, which he is known to hold there from our venerable brother, the bishop of Halberstadt, if this can be done with that bishop’s consent or by an equivalent given in exchange; and one hundred marks of silver for construction of the hospital. He further requested that we cause the hospital to be built not in his name but in ours.

We therefore commend his pious purpose in the Lord and receive his gift into the right and power of the Roman Church and for the benefit of the Holy Spirit in Saxony [Note: See Book X, Letter 179, Col. 1383D.], to which two marks [Col. 1384B] of pure silver, as annual rent established by the said count, shall be paid each year. And so that the intention of the said count may achieve its proper result through your care, we have thought fit to entrust our authority in this matter to you, commanding your devotion by this present authority to strive to take corporal possession, in our name, of all the aforesaid things and to cause a hospital to be built in the aforesaid place solely for the use of the sick and poor. When it has been built and suitably ordered, take care faithfully to inform us of everything by your letters, so that, making such disposition concerning the place as we see fit, we may protect it by our privileges.

[Col. 1384C] Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS. A charge of adultery is committed to him. (Lateran, sixth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Note: Chapter *Intelleximus*, “On Adultery.”] We have learned both from the letters of our venerable brother, the bishop of Poitiers, and from what was presented by the parties before our beloved son Andrew, our subdeacon and chaplain, appointed auditor in this matter, that S., a layman, dismissed his wife Elizabeth from marital cohabitation without reasonable cause. Hearing that the same woman was committing fornication with a certain adulterer, their diocesan bishop bound both her and him by a sentence of excommunication. At length, after she abjured the man who was said to be her adulterer [Col. 1384D], she received absolution before the aforesaid bishop and asked that her husband be restored to her. But he objected against her an adultery of this kind, saying that she had borne offspring by it; and, asserting that she had not been driven out by him but had departed voluntarily, he maintained that he ought not to be restored to her. The said woman wholly denied this, and replied that he himself had committed fornication and had begotten offspring by fornication, so that he could not use such an exception against her. Since both parties were granted the opportunity to prove these matters, the aforesaid woman proved the adultery of the husband through certain witnesses; he claimed that those witnesses should be rejected as insufficiently qualified, [Col. 1385A] and finally appealed from this to our hearing.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you shall compel him to receive her unless both (i) it is established, either by the evidence of the fact or by the woman’s lawful confession, that she had committed adultery in this manner, and (ii) proof of the adultery said to have been committed by the husband has failed. But if the woman’s fornication is established in the aforesaid manner, then, unless the witnesses by whom the husband’s adultery was proved are lawfully rejected, since the right of marriage resides in both spouses and equal offences are removed by mutual compensation, you shall nevertheless compel him to receive her and treat her with marital affection. Otherwise, you shall not delay in imposing silence upon the aforesaid woman.

[Col. 1385B] Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year.

LXXI. TO THE CANONS OF THE ALTAR OF THE BLESSED APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL AT SENS. The grant to them of a certain church is confirmed. (Lateran, sixth day before the Nones of May.)

“It is customary to assent,” etc., as far as “to bestow.” Since, therefore, G. [William], archbishop of Sens of good memory, for the increase of divine worship assigned certain revenues in certain churches to the altar at whose service you are appointed, for the support of its ministers; and the chapter of Sens granted him that they should henceforth share in those distributions just as the canons serving the altar of blessed Stephen are known to do; and the same archbishop, in compensation for those distributions, gave to the said chapter the church of Bois-le-Roi to possess in perpetuity: yielding to your just prayers, we grant to you, and through you to the aforesaid altar, by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this present writing, the said revenues and the share which you have in the aforesaid distributions, as you justly and peaceably possess all these things and as is more fully contained in the letters of the same archbishop. Therefore let no one . . . violate this confirmation of ours, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the eleventh year.

LXXII. TO THE CHANTER AND CHAPTER OF BLESSED MARY OF MEUDON. Concerning the confirmation of privileges. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1385D]

“When a request is made to us,” etc., as far as “assent”: we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your church and the persons serving the Lord therein, with all goods, both ecclesiastical and temporal, which you now reasonably possess or may hereafter, by just means and with the Lord’s help, acquire. By apostolic authority we forbid the diocesan bishop, archdeacon, or anyone else to presume to extort from you an undue and unprecedented procuration, or to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or suspension against any of you without manifest and reasonable cause. Therefore let no one . . . [Col. 1386A] violate this protection and prohibition of ours, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

LXXIII. TO THE CONVENT OF CORBIE MONASTERY. Acts performed by the legates S. A. are ratified. (Lateran, fifth day before the Nones of May.)

[Note: Chapter *Cum venerabilis*, “On Custom.”] When our venerable brother the bishop of Ostia and our beloved son Leo, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross, were formerly exercising the office of legation in the regions of Germany, they found that the beloved son, the abbot of the monastery of Herford—which is known to belong immediately to the Roman Church—had, by his own rashness, transferred to Corbie monastery, likewise a special possession of the Roman Church, without either obtaining or requesting leave to depart or confirmation from us or even from those who at that time exercised our authority in those regions. When he arrived at Nordhausen to receive the regalia, those same persons being there [Note: Read *iisdem existentibus* (“with those same persons being there”); the error nevertheless occurs in the register and in the Corbie original, Cols. 1385D, 1386D.], he did not take care to approach them, so that his contempt might be more clearly apparent; rather, in every way he showed himself a despiser of their commands. Therefore the said legates gave firm instructions to our venerable brother, the bishop of Paderborn, to summon him before his presence; and, after all the foregoing had been carefully set out before him, not to delay in suspending him from every office and benefice until he presented himself before us or them to seek pardon for his contempt.

Moreover, when he sent his messenger to the presence of those same legates [Note: The authentic copy reads: “had sent,” *direxisset*.], [Col. 1386C] excusing himself through that messenger concerning all the foregoing, he alleged a general custom of that land: namely, that the supreme pontiff or his legates were in no way to be consulted for confirmation of an election, for obtaining a blessing, or even for permission to transfer from one monastery to another, since such a custom had hitherto been observed in those regions. The same legates, however, moved by the prayers of many ecclesiastical and secular princes who urgently interceded with them on his behalf, relaxed the aforesaid sentence. They ordered the bishop of Paderborn not to delay in enjoining the said abbot to send his messengers to the apostolic see by the Sunday on which is sung “Rejoice, Jerusalem” (*Laetare, Jerusalem*), last past; there he was to receive our command on this matter and on other matters through the same messengers. If he should perhaps neglect to do so, the bishop was not to delay thereafter in restoring him to the former sentence and causing it to be firmly observed.

Afterwards, when he had sent his messengers to the apostolic see, they, wishing in many ways to excuse him, alleged the aforesaid custom in his defence. Since, therefore, this ought rightly to be deemed not so much a custom as a corruption, being plainly hostile to the sacred canons, and since we do not wish it to be observed henceforth, we ordered the same legates to receive, in our stead, the manual obedience of the aforesaid messengers—namely Her., provost, and C., canon of the New Church—who, as was established before us by a public instrument, held full procuratorial authority from both the abbot and the convent of Corbie; this being done upon renunciation of the aforesaid custom. They carried out our command both in renouncing that custom and in rendering obedience, and took care to leave with us letters concerning this, sealed with their seals. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, holding valid what was done by the aforesaid messengers, you shall in no way observe this perverse custom hereafter.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the eleventh year.

LXXIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CORBIE. Certain privileges are granted to them. (Lateran, second day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 1387B]

The more devoted we have found the Church of Corbie to ourselves and to the Roman Church, the more especially are we moved to grant reasonable petitions concerning it. Therefore, since your monastery is exempt from the jurisdiction of every bishop except the supreme pontiff, by the authority of these presents we grant you leave to receive the ordinations of your monks and the consecrations of altars or churches established within the precincts of that monastery, as well as chrism and holy oil [Col. 1387C] and the other sacraments of the Church, from whichever Catholic bishop you may prefer who enjoys the favor of the Apostolic See. Let no one, therefore, … violate this our grant, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 30 April, in the eleventh year.

**LXXV. TO THE ABBOT OF CORBIE.** On the same matter. (Given as in the other.)

“The more devoted we have found the Church of Corbie,” etc., as in the other, down to “grant.” Wherefore, by the authority of these presents, we grant your devotion leave to compel by canonical discipline those officials of your monastery who unjustly withhold the brothers’ prebend to do what justice requires in this matter under your examination [Col. 1387D], as they ought; strictly forbidding them to presume, through the injustice of a secular judgment, to divert to their own use, with any rashness whatever, the stipends assigned to the monks. Let no one, therefore, … violate this our grant and prohibition, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other.

**LXXVI. TO THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** He is rebuked for many transgressions. (Lateran, 24 April.)

Against the most grievous plague recently arisen at Constantinople against the universal Church, we must exercise apostolic censure with greater severity in proportion as, through long establishment, it would corrupt more perniciously and, once rooted, grow more deeply. Thus, you are to know that we have proceeded with due caution in the matters set down below, not in derogation of your honor—which, so far as we can with God’s help, we desire to preserve unimpaired—but for the destruction of that plague, which we labor diligently to abolish. [Note: [Col. 1387D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapters 96 and 98.]

Now, when your election had formerly been presented to us, we carefully observed that it had been undertaken by persons who had no right to elect, since at that time none had been canonically installed as canons of Hagia Sophia. On the advice of our brethren, in a public consistory we publicly declared it to be annulled—indeed, more accurately, we declared that it had been void from the outset. Afterwards, wishing to provide for the Church of Constantinople from the bosom of the Apostolic See [Col. 1388B], when you were our subdeacon and had not sinned in the earlier election—for you had been elected unknowingly and in absence, if such a nomination can indeed be called an election—we elected you to that Church, whose provision then belonged exclusively to us. We caused you first to be ordained deacon and afterwards priest; and finally, when consecrated bishop through our ministry, to be adorned with the honor of the pallium.

Although, so ordained, consecrated, and invested with the pallium by us, you went to Constantinople carrying with you our letters concerning the entire course of the matter, by which all the clergy established at Constantinople were commanded to render you obedience both due and devout, the clerics of the party of pilgrims [Col. 1388C] nevertheless refused to do so. They firmly asserted that you had extorted all this from us by suppressing the truth. And when both you and our beloved son Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus and then legate of the Apostolic See, had admonished them to render you obedience, they appealed to the Apostolic See in order to avoid being compelled to do so in any way. Although the said cardinal deferred to their appeal, not so much because of canonical form as because this was the first appeal lodged in the Church of Constantinople, which had recently returned to devotion to the Roman Church, you did not defer to it. Rather, as they assert, you pronounced a sentence of excommunication against those clerics; and whereas the legate communicated with them as persons not bound after an appeal to which he had deferred, you avoided them even more strictly. [Col. 1388D]

Moreover, when our beloved son Benedict, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna and then legate of the Apostolic See, arrived at Constantinople to restore peace between you, a peace which he had been sent to proclaim, he intervened to secure concord. He worked so effectively with the parties that they jointly submitted the matter to him: you promised, under penalty in the cause, and they confirmed by oath, that whatever he should determine between you by agreement, arbitration, or judgment, you would observe inviolably. Therefore the cardinal, wishing after the manner of a good judge to diminish disputes rather than increase them, after deliberation commanded you to regard those clerics as installed in the churches in which they were; and he enjoined them to render you, as their patriarch, due reverence and obedience. The organization of Hagia Sophia, concerning which, as the clerics maintained, the matter had likewise been submitted to him, was temporarily deferred for a necessary reason. Yet concerning this he then commanded you, under penalty in the cause, humbly to receive and observe whatever he should subsequently determine. [Col. 1389A]

Although those clerics, as children of obedience, carried out the cardinal’s command without any delay, you forgot your promise. When the legate installed certain canons in the church of Hagia Sophia and strictly commanded you to receive without objection both them and those whom the aforesaid cardinal of Saint Marcellus had installed there, and to allow them peacefully to possess their prebends, you refused to do so. Consequently, since by the fault of disobedience you had brought detriment upon your cause, they withdrew obedience from you and appealed to the Apostolic See, fixing the past feast of the Nativity of the Lord as the term of their appeal; to that term you yourself subsequently appealed as well. [Col. 1389B]

When the representatives of both parties had therefore appeared before us and been granted a hearing in public consistory, the clerics alleged before us that, after their appeal, you had despoiled the church of Hagia Sophia of treasure amounting to one hundred thousand marks, and their churches of many goods. They urgently requested the restitution of all these things. Moreover, since the aforesaid cardinal of Saint Susanna was to be maintained from the common revenues, and 1,200 hyperpera had been paid for his maintenance through the hand of the emperor—who was jointly bound to the said clerics and to you—of which 300 belonged to you as your quarter-share, you received from the emperor and from others not only your own share in full, but also extorted another 300 hyperpera from their share. Thus they claimed 600 hyperpera from your representatives. [Col. 1389C]

They further alleged that you had been disobedient to the aforesaid cardinals and legates not only concerning the organization of Hagia Sophia, but rather to us ourselves; indeed, to such an extent that you had bound yourself by an oath for all time not to obey, or to be able to obey. [Note: [Col. 1389D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapters 92 and 97.]

Before the occupation of the imperial city, the Venetians and the Franks conspired to divide the spoils of the churches and ecclesiastical possessions. They also swore that, if the Franks held the empire, the Venetians would hold the patriarchate; and if the patriarchate should happen to go to the Franks, the empire would fall to the Venetians’ share. Accordingly, wishing henceforth to make provision for themselves so as to preserve the bond of this wickedness and possess the Lord’s sanctuary as an inheritance, the Venetians, when you were departing from our presence, demanded and received from you [Col. 1390A] an oath that you would admit as a canon of Hagia Sophia no one who was not Venetian by birth or who had not resided at Venice for ten years. [Note: [Col. 1390D] Ibid., chapter 99.] You were also to compel all canons, upon their reception, to swear that they would admit no one as a canon unless he took a similar oath, and that they would elect no patriarch except from among Venetians.

They also said that you had in good faith promised to devote careful attention and diligent effort, and to work effectively insofar as lay in your power, so that throughout all Romania no bishop or archbishop should be created unless he were Venetian. Although, as they said, this is known in the regions of Constantinople and exceedingly well known at Venice, and its disgraceful report had long since spread among us, they declared that they would prove it at a suitable time. If this is so, and you consider carefully how greatly you have sinned in this matter, you will plainly perceive it. For when, like a bridegroom coming forth from his mother’s chamber, you hastened to the embraces of that most worthy daughter, you ought not to have procured for her poisons of barrenness, but rather sought a remedy of fruitfulness. [Col. 1390B]

Indeed, in order that you might become the father of many nations, you had been commanded by the Father of fathers, both orally and by letters, to receive sons for your bride from every people and nation; and not to acquiesce merely in flesh and blood, but to do what his vicar had revealed to you—the one to whom, from every nation, whoever does justice is acceptable. This was, as it were, the first command of him who had made you patriarch; and because he wished to test your obedience in this, as in a first matter, it ought especially to have been observed. But you not only failed to keep the command; if the allegations are true, you swore an oath binding yourself to wickedness so that henceforth you could not keep it. [Col. 1390C]

Behold what fruits we gather from a new plant. Behold what an example, from your deed, is spread among kings and peoples—to the offense of the divine majesty, the injury of the Apostolic See, the detriment of ecclesiastical liberty, and the disgrace of the universal Church. Let the Romans therefore conspire, if we pass this over by dissimulation, that no one may be raised to the office of supreme pontiff or to the college of cardinals unless he is a Roman; and let them compel us to promise that throughout the whole world we shall appoint only Romans as patriarchs, metropolitans, and bishops. [Col. 1390D]

But perhaps you will say that you were drawn into this by force. Yet the violence was not so great that it ought to have overcome a steadfast man. Indeed, in such a case it was better to incur death than to consent to so great an evil by so great a man, to the scandal of the whole Church; better to lay down one’s life than to bind bundles that weigh down the entire Church.

On the other hand, your representatives alleged that you could not and ought not to have carried out the command of the said legate concerning the organization of Hagia Sophia, because the canons of that church had appealed to the Apostolic See concerning it, and because it could not have been accomplished without great scandal to the Venetians. Moreover, the legate had been commanded that, if you neglected or delayed the organization of the aforesaid church, he should proceed to organize it; and since you had already established there, according to your own resources, a suitable number of canons, he could not by the authority of our mandate install any persons in it. [Col. 1391A]

Concerning the treasury of Hagia Sophia, they said that you had drawn upon it for the common need of both Church and land; from it you had lent 3,000 marks to the emperor, 2,000 to the Venetians, and with 4,000 had purchased possessions for the use of the church, intending to do the same with the remainder when opportunity arose. Although your representatives entirely denied the allegation concerning the oath, we nevertheless heard from certain persons that, when the Venetians were pressing you vehemently to take it, had denied you passage, and were even preventing your departure from the city, while you could not avoid the demands of creditors to whom you were bound by an oath already taken, you swore only with the addition of this clause: “saving in all things the right, authority, reverence, and honor of the Apostolic See.” The Venetians, however, did not permit this clause to be inserted in the document drawn up concerning it. [Col. 1391B]

Therefore, because, as the Lord says to us through the prophet, we must “loose the bonds of wickedness” and “untie the bundles that weigh down,” we utterly annul all agreements, enactments, and conspiracies concerning ecclesiastical matters, made or to be made by the aforesaid laymen to the detriment of churches; and under threat of anathema we command that they not be observed.

Furthermore, by the authority of these presents we command you, and strictly enjoin you in virtue of obedience, that, if you freely acknowledge having taken such an oath, within two months after receiving these letters you shall convene both the clergy of Constantinople and such archbishops and bishops as you can have present; publicly renounce that oath; and likewise publicly swear that you will not observe it henceforth. You shall compel the canons of Hagia Sophia, who are said to have made such an oath, to renounce it and swear that they will not observe it in future, by suspension from office and benefice, without appeal. [Col. 1391C]

You shall also, by the same term, receive into the church of Hagia Sophia the canons canonically installed there by the aforesaid cardinals, and cause them peacefully to possess their canonries, restraining clerics and laymen who resist by ecclesiastical censure, relying both on our authority and your own and setting appeal aside. But if, in any of the aforesaid matters—which we do not believe—you are negligent or remiss, know that from that time you are suspended from office and benefice. We have strictly commanded our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Verissa, the bishop of Panias, and our beloved son, the cantor of Saint Paul at Constantinople, not to delay publishing your suspension and to carry out the apostolic command in the remaining matters. [Col. 1391D]

But if you deny having taken such an oath, since we cannot pass over in silence what has been alleged concerning it, we shall command the legate whom we intend shortly to send to Constantinople diligently to hear the arguments and proofs of both parties and without delay to remit the fully prepared case to us. If the said clerics fail in proof and you are unwilling to confess anything, since you are not slightly defamed in this matter, he shall impose canonical purgation upon you; and, whether you fail in that purgation or are able to clear yourself, he shall not omit faithfully to report these matters to us in his letters, so that, once instructed by his report in all respects, we may proceed as ought to be done. [Col. 1392A]

Concerning the 600 hyperpera, we commit the cause to our venerable brother, the Salimbrian bishop, and to our beloved son, the bishop-elect of Heraclea, and the cantor of Hagia Sophia, under this form: they are to compel you by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being barred and justice being observed, to repay the hyperpera which it is established that you either withheld from the maintenance of the cardinals or seized from the clerics’ share.

Moreover, although, because you had submitted the matter to the legate under penalty in your cause with those clerics and afterwards failed to observe his command, you appear by your disobedience to have caused them to withdraw obedience from you, since the question concerned obedience, we nevertheless, wishing to show you favor, have enjoined those clerics to render you due and devout obedience until the aforesaid term. They are thereafter to continue it if you are a son of obedience, but to withdraw it if you are disobedient and rebellious, as one suspended from office and benefice by authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1392B]

We absolve you from the claim of the clerics of Saint Anastasia concerning the marble columns which, it is said, you transferred from their church to the church of Hagia Sophia for the adornment of the altar. But concerning the allegation that you despoiled the church of Hagia Sophia of many thousands of marks, if the matter is so, correct by yourself what you have done in such a way that no ground for complaint concerning you remains. Take careful care henceforth not to lay hands upon such a treasury unless perhaps so great a necessity should press upon you that, with necessary supplies lacking from elsewhere, it would be necessary for you to take something from it—though only moderately. For we do not believe that your prudence is ignorant how detestable and condemnable is the crime of dissipation in prelates of churches. [Col. 1392C–D]

Given at the Lateran, 24 April, in the eleventh year.

**LXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF VERISSA, THE BISHOP OF PANIAS, AND THE CANTOR OF SAINT PAUL AT CONSTANTINOPLE.** On the same subject. (Given as in the other.)

When the representatives of our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, and of our beloved sons, the clerics of the party of pilgrims residing at Constantinople, had appeared in our presence and been granted a hearing in public consistory, the said clerics alleged before us that, before the occupation of the imperial city, the Venetians and the Franks had conspired to divide the spoils of the churches and ecclesiastical possessions. They also swore that, if the Franks held the empire, the Venetians would hold the patriarchate; and that, if the patriarchate should happen to go to the Franks, the empire would fall to the Venetians’ share. [Col. 1393A]

Accordingly, wishing henceforth to make provision for themselves so as to preserve the bond of this wickedness and possess the Lord’s sanctuary as an inheritance, the Venetians, when the patriarch was departing from our presence, demanded and received from him an oath that he would admit as a canon of Hagia Sophia no one who was not Venetian by birth or who had not resided at Venice for ten years; and that he would compel all canons, upon their reception, to swear that they would admit no one as a canon unless he took a similar oath, and that they would elect no patriarch except from among Venetians. [Col. 1393B]

They also said that he had in good faith promised to devote careful attention and diligent effort, and to work effectively insofar as lay in his power, so that throughout all Romania no bishop or archbishop should be created unless he were Venetian. Although, as they said, this was known in the regions of Constantinople, exceedingly well known at Venice, and had long since spread among us in disgraceful report, they declared that they would prove it at a suitable time.

Moreover, when our beloved son Benedict, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna and then legate of the Apostolic See, arrived at Constantinople in order to restore the peace between them which he had been sent to proclaim, he intervened to secure concord. He worked so effectively with the parties that they jointly submitted the matter to him: the said patriarch promised under penalty in the cause, and the others confirmed by oath, that they would inviolably observe whatever he should determine between them by agreement, arbitration, or judgment. [Col. 1393C]

Therefore, the cardinal, wishing after the manner of a good judge to diminish disputes rather than increase them, after deliberation commanded the patriarch to regard those clerics as installed in the churches in which they were, and enjoined them to render him, as their patriarch, due reverence and obedience. The organization of Hagia Sophia—concerning which, as the clerics asserted, the matter had likewise been submitted to him—was temporarily deferred for a necessary reason. Yet concerning it he then commanded the patriarch, under penalty in the cause, humbly to receive and observe whatever he should afterwards determine.

Although those clerics, as children of obedience, carried out the cardinal’s command without any delay, the patriarch forgot his promise. When the legate installed certain canons in the church of Hagia Sophia, and strictly commanded him to receive without objection both them and those whom our beloved son Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, had installed there, and to allow them peacefully to possess their prebends, he did not take care to do so. Therefore they withdrew obedience from him, since by the fault of disobedience he had brought detriment upon his cause, and appealed to the Apostolic See, fixing the past feast of the Nativity of the Lord as the term of their appeal; to this term the patriarch also subsequently appealed. [Col. 1393D–1394A]

On the other hand, the patriarch’s representatives alleged that the command of the said legate concerning the organization of Hagia Sophia could not and ought not to have been carried out, since the canons of that church had appealed to the Apostolic See concerning it, and since it could not be accomplished without great scandal to the Venetians. Further, the same legate had been commanded that, if the patriarch neglected or delayed organizing the aforesaid church, he should proceed to organize it; and, because the patriarch had already established in it, according to his own resources, a suitable number of canons, the legate could not install anyone in it by authority of our mandate. [Col. 1394B]

Although these representatives entirely denied the allegation concerning the oath, we nevertheless heard from certain persons that, when the Venetians were pressing the patriarch vehemently to take it, had denied him passage, and were preventing his departure from the city, while he could not avoid the demands of creditors to whom he was bound by an oath already taken, he swore only with the addition of this clause: “saving in all things the right, authority, reverence, and honor of the Apostolic See.” [Note: [Col. 1393D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 99, and book II, letters 119 and 166.] The Venetians, however, did not allow this clause to be inserted in the document drawn up concerning it. [Col. 1394C]

Therefore, because, as the Lord says to us through the prophet, we must “loose the bonds of wickedness” and “untie the bundles that weigh down,” we utterly annul all agreements, enactments, and conspiracies concerning ecclesiastical matters, made or to be made by the aforesaid laymen to the detriment of churches; and under threat of anathema we command that they not be observed.

Furthermore, strictly commanding the same patriarch in virtue of obedience, we order that, if he freely acknowledges having taken such an oath, within two months after receiving the letters he shall convene both the clergy of Constantinople and such archbishops and bishops as he can have present; publicly renounce that oath; and likewise publicly swear that he will not observe it henceforth. He shall compel the canons of Hagia Sophia, who are said to have taken such an oath, to renounce it and swear that they will not observe it henceforth, by suspension from office and benefice, without appeal. [Col. 1394D]

He shall also, by the same term, receive into the church of Hagia Sophia the canons canonically installed there by the aforesaid cardinals, and cause them peacefully to possess their canonries, restraining resistant clerics and laymen by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside, relying both on our authority and his own. If, however, in any of the aforesaid matters—which we do not believe—he is negligent or remiss, let him know that from that time he is suspended from office and benefice.

Wherefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if he fails to execute our mandate, you shall arrange for his suspension to be publicly proclaimed and for the apostolic command to be carried out in the remaining matters, coercing any opponents or rebels by ecclesiastical censure, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed. If not all, etc.; two, etc. [Col. 1395A]

Given as in the other.

**LXXVIII. TO THE SALIMBRIAN BISHOP, THE BISHOP-ELECT OF HERACLEA, AND THE CANTOR OF HAGIA SOPHIA AT CONSTANTINOPLE.** That the patriarch be compelled to repay the hyperpera. (Lateran, 17 April.)

Our beloved son W., provost of Holy Trinity, Drogo, cantor of the Forty Martyrs, and Arnulf, canon of Saint Mary of Zona, representatives of the clerics of the party of pilgrims residing at Constantinople, appeared in our presence and alleged that, since our beloved son Benedict, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna and then legate of the Apostolic See, was to be maintained from the common revenues, and 1,200 hyperpera had been expended for his maintenance through the hand of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious emperor of Constantinople—who was jointly bound to those clerics and to our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople—of which 300 belonged to the patriarch as his quarter-share, the said patriarch received from the emperor and from others not merely his own full share but presumed to extort another 300 hyperpera from their share. Thus the said clerics claimed 600 hyperpera from his representatives, concerning all of which the representatives said that they knew absolutely nothing. [Col. 1395B–C]

Wherefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to compel the said patriarch, by ecclesiastical censure and with the obstacle of appeal removed, justice being observed, to repay the hyperpera which it is established that he either withheld from the cardinal’s maintenance or seized from the clerics’ share. If not all, etc.; two, etc. [Col. 1395D]

Given at the Lateran, 17 April, in the eleventh year.

**LXXIX. TO THE CLERICS OF THE PARTY OF PILGRIMS RESIDING AT CONSTANTINOPLE.** On obedience to be rendered to the patriarch. (Lateran, 24 April.)

Although our venerable brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, because he submitted the matter with you, under penalty in the cause, to our beloved son Benedict, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna and then legate of the Apostolic See, and afterwards failed to observe his command, appears by his disobedience to have caused you to withdraw obedience from him, since the question concerned obedience, we nevertheless, wishing to show him favor, enjoin you by the authority of these presents to render him due and devout obedience for two months—a period which we have judged should be granted him to execute our command. Thereafter you are to continue it if he is a son of obedience, but to withdraw it if he is disobedient and rebellious, as one suspended from office and benefice by authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1396A]

Given at the Lateran, 24 April, in the eleventh year.

**LXXX. TO THE PODESTÀ, COUNCILLORS, AND PEOPLE OF PISA.** That they cease from every injury to the kingdom of Sicily. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[Col. 1396B] Neither can a mother forget the children of her womb, nor can even an offended father fail to love his children. Therefore, although in the affair of Sardinia and Sicily you have grievously offended us, yet, because we cannot divest ourselves of paternal affection toward you, and because your envoys—the beloved sons Count Tedicus, Hugh Sigerii, Bandinus, and Hugh Grotti, prudent and faithful men indeed—have promised us, so far as concerns you, satisfaction regarding the affair of Sardinia, as is contained in the public instrument drawn up thereon, and have likewise promised in the affair of the kingdom of Sicily that you will carry out our good pleasure, we highly approve your devotion. We assure you of our favor; and, as a sign of fuller favor, we renew the dignities, immunities, and liberties which the Pisan Church is known to have possessed in the time of the predecessors of your venerable brother Lothair, archbishop of Pisa. [Col. 1396C]

So that the same archbishop, who succeeded them in its governance, may use them more freely, we confirm by apostolic authority, for him and for that Church, all privileges, confirmations, and indulgences granted to that Church or to the predecessors of the said archbishop by our predecessors or by ourselves. We command him to absolve your fellow citizen L. from the bond of excommunication, on condition that his wife, mother-in-law, and their lands nevertheless remain under the sentence in which they now stand until satisfaction has been made to us by them.

We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your whole community to continue in devotion to the Apostolic See and to us in such a way that you may increase in us the desire to love and honor you more readily. Meanwhile, cease altogether from every injury to the kingdom of Sicily, and send to us suitable men who may give us adequate security concerning the indemnity of that kingdom, so that it may not henceforth be injured by you either collectively or individually; and let them render the satisfaction promised concerning Sardinia. For we shall render full justice if any of you has any claim against that kingdom. [Col. 1396D]

Given at the Lateran, 11 May, in the eleventh year.

**LXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA.** On confirmation of privileges. (Given as in the other.)

[Col. 1397A] The welcome services long rendered by the city and Church of Pisa to the Apostolic See have deserved that it should endeavor to adorn them with many and great privileges. Therefore we, who do not intend to diminish but rather to increase benefits to those devoted to that See, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, renew the dignities, immunities, and liberties which your Church is known to have possessed in the time of your predecessors. So that you, who succeeded them in its governance, may use them more freely, we confirm by apostolic authority, for you and for the Church itself in its own right, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, all privileges, confirmations, and indulgences granted to that Church or to your predecessors by our predecessors or by ourselves. Let no one, therefore, … violate this our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc. [Col. 1397B]

Given as in the other.

**LXXXII. TO THE PROVOST, DEAN, CANTOR, AND CHAPTER OF THE CATHEDRAL CHURCH, AND TO ALL THE CLERGY OF MAINZ.** That they humbly receive the commands of the Apostolic See. (Lateran, 15 May.)

We have learned from your letters that, although for a time you considered it right to communicate with excommunicated persons, it was not your own willing purpose but true and unfeigned necessity that induced you to do this. For such fury of hostility had arisen in your regions that, not to mention other things, you could in no way leave the walls of your city with your persons safe, nor send envoys to us to present your excuse. Although you could have advanced strong and sufficient arguments concerning your innocence, relying rather on our kindness than on disputation, you received the benefit of absolution, at the command of our venerable brother Hugolino, bishop of Ostia, and our beloved son Leo, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross, legates of the Apostolic See, from our beloved son the abbot of Eberbach. [Col. 1397C]

In accordance with their command, under the obligation of the oath which you had given, he firmly commanded you to send two of your number, such persons as we could deservedly trust, to the Apostolic See before the Sunday on which “Laetare, Jerusalem” is sung, in order to receive the apostolic command. When your envoys, our beloved son Frederick, scholasticus of Saint Victor, and Cunemannus, canon of the church of Saint Stephen, came to us on your behalf with these letters, they humbly begged us to deal mercifully with you. We therefore commit you to those legates and command you by apostolic letters that you humbly receive and observe the command which the same legates, or we through our letters, shall impose upon you. [Col. 1397D]

Given at the Lateran, 15 May, in the eleventh year.

**LXXXIII. TO OUR BELOVED SON JOHN, CARDINAL-DEACON OF SAINT MARY IN COSMEDIN, CHANCELLOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH.** Concerning a fulling-mill. (Given, etc.)

[Col. 1398A] Since at your own expense you have built a certain fulling-mill on the estate of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, belonging to the cardinal of that church, you humbly petitioned us to make this disposition concerning the said fulling-mill: after the debt of the Church has been paid from its revenues, one half of the income arising from it shall devolve upon the Church; of the remaining half, two shares shall be made, one of which shall belong to the cardinal who holds office at the time, and the other shall be administered for the hospital through the provision and counsel of that cardinal. [Col. 1398B]

We therefore, inclined by your petitions, establish and command that this be inviolably observed as set forth above. Let no one, therefore, … violate this our constitution and command, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given, etc.

**LXXXIV. TO THE ABBESS AND CONVENT OF SAINTS ANASTASIUS AND INNOCENT AT GANDERSHEIM.** On confirmation of the liberty of that monastery. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[Note: [Col. 1397] See chapter *Cum dilecta*, *On confirmation, “ut vel inutili”*.] Desiring formerly that the privileges of your monastery should be renewed, you humbly petitioned us to write to certain persons, who should carefully inspect the privileges of your church—which, because of the dangers of the roads, could not safely be sent to our presence [Col. 1398C]—and faithfully transcribe their tenor, authenticated under their own seals, to be presented before us. Accordingly, acceding to your petitions, we charged four bishops and an equal number of abbots to carry this out. Obeying our command, after the privileges of our predecessors of happy memory, Agapitus and John, had been presented to them and carefully examined, they faithfully sent us their tenor under their seals. Moreover, William of good memory, Archbishop of Rheims, then Bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, sent to our presence under his seal the tenor of those privileges.

And indeed, although faith ought not without reason to have been placed in both the legate and the aforesaid investigators in this matter, and although at that time nothing appeared for which those privileges ought not to be renewed, nevertheless, because C., canon of the Greater Church, and I., canon of Holy Cross at Hildesheim, appearing before us, alleged that the Church of Hildesheim had been in a kind of possession of the subjection of that monastery for a hundred years and more, we did not then judge the privileges themselves to be renewed. Rather, that we might preserve its right to both the monastery and the said Church, we commanded our beloved sons, the abbots of Pöhlde, Corvey, and St Michael’s on the Rock, to meet together at a suitable place; after summoning the parties, they were to investigate more diligently [Col. 1399A] the truth concerning all the foregoing matters, proceed in the business through to a definitive sentence, and send all the proceedings faithfully recorded to the Apostolic See under the attestation of their letters, setting the parties a suitable term within which they should appear before us to receive judgment.

Although they wished to execute our mandate and hastened to proceed in the cause after the parties had appeared before them, nevertheless, because of a certain interlocutory ruling which they delivered, the party of the Church of Hildesheim lodged an appeal before us; consequently, the aforesaid case could not proceed before them. Therefore, when the parties subsequently appeared before us on this account, you, daughter abbess, humbly requested that we ought to renew the aforesaid [Col. 1399B] privileges, especially since, in the presence of the aforesaid judges, the Church of Hildesheim had shown or proved nothing that derogated in any respect from the monastery or its privileges. On the other side, however, it was urgently requested that we should commit the same cause to discerning men, through whom witnesses might be received whom the Church of Hildesheim intended to produce against the monastery’s privileges, namely in order to prove a lawful prescription.

But, considering more carefully that civil law has established by prudent deliberation that, when there is fear concerning witnesses lest the truth be concealed and the means of proof be withdrawn by accidental events, sick witnesses and others concerning whom there is reasonable cause for apprehension may be admitted to give testimony even before joinder of issue, we, moved by the analogy of the same equity, judged that the aforesaid privileges—now as it were worn away by excessive age, since they had been written not on parchment but on papyrus—ought to be renewed. Yet this renewal was not to procure any new right for the said monastery, but to preserve more securely by the renewed privilege whatever ancient right it possessed.

Furthermore, because the said monastery was shown by the privileges of our predecessors to belong to the right and ownership of the Roman Church, lest the right of the Apostolic See perhaps remain undefended, we appointed you, daughter abbess, its procurator. Thus, since against the possessions and rights of the Roman Church prescription runs only after a hundred years, [Col. 1399D] [Note: [Col. 1399D] See chapter *Cum vobis*, *On prescriptions*.] you were to act before the abbots of Hermarhusen and Hersethusen and the dean of Palburn, to whom we then committed the cause, concerning this matter and the other matters which were to be pursued in court before them on our behalf.

And lest uncertainty about its status continue longer, or the aforesaid cause remain further undecided, we commanded the same judges to select a safe and convenient place and, within six months after receiving our letters, receive the witnesses whom the Church of Hildesheim might consider should be produced to prove prescription, or whom your party might consider should be produced even to show an interruption. [Col. 1400A] If the Church of Hildesheim proved a lawful prescription, unless interruption were proved on the other side, they were to adjudge to it the subjection of the monastery, since it was established that the latter lay within its diocese, and annul the privilege which we had caused to be renewed for that monastery. Otherwise, imposing perpetual silence upon that Church concerning this matter, they were to pronounce that your monastery enjoyed perpetual liberty, the privilege granted by us being delivered to it.

By other letters we also declared to the same judges that, after prescription was alleged to have begun against the aforesaid monastery and its liberty, three schisms against the Roman Church are known to have intervened. Therefore, although both legal and canonical determinations establish [Col. 1400B] that against the most holy Roman Church, which enjoys a special privilege, prescription can take effect only after one hundred [Note: [Col. 1399D] See Justinian, *Novels* 131, and chapters 13, 14, 15, *On prescription*.] years, we did not wish the periods of the intervening schisms—which, according to the order of law, impede the running of prescription—to be counted in any way, but, after careful consideration, to be deducted from the reckoning of time.

Before those judges, the party of the Church of Hildesheim requested that the authentic privileges of your monastery be produced in court and copies made available to it, so that, by inspecting them, it might argue whatever could reasonably be alleged against them. To this you, daughter abbess, replied that this was requested superfluously and that the opposing party ought not to be heard concerning it. For when you, the abbess, had formerly founded your claim upon those same privileges before us, the opposing party, raising absolutely no objection against them, alleged prescription alone in order to defeat your claim, having requested and obtained a postponement in order to prove it.

Against this the party of the Church of Hildesheim replied that the privileges ought at least rightly to be produced so that, should you perhaps receive an adverse judgment, then, together with the renewed privilege produced by you, the abbess, before those judges—which, according to our mandate, ought in the stated case to be annulled—the ancient privileges also might be torn up. And when before those judges, who had received the witnesses of each party and solemnly published their depositions, and were better informed concerning the merits of the cause [Col. 1400D] and deliberating upon the decision of the controversy, you and the opposing party did not cease disputing with one another over the production of the privileges, they referred the cause to us, sufficiently prepared with the attestations and allegations.

Accordingly, when the parties recently appeared before us on this account, although the allegations had been renounced and the case closed before the aforesaid judges, nevertheless, out of abundance of caution, we heard everything proposed by either side. And although the production of the privileges and certain other matters had been litigated before us for some time, because it was clearly established that we had formerly, with both parties present, carefully inspected and prudently examined those same privileges presented to us in court and approved them by judgment, we decreed that the petition of Master Hugh, canon and procurator of that Church, should be rejected.

But when we diligently investigated whether lawful prescription, namely prescription of one hundred years, had been proved, that procurator plainly confessed that it had been proved in no other way than by certain witnesses who gave hearsay testimony. He nevertheless added that hearsay testimony ought properly to be admitted in this case, since scarcely anyone could be found who retained memory of so long a time. We also clearly found that it would not suffice for the Church of Hildesheim to have proved prescription of a hundred years. For, since according to the order of law and the form of our mandate the periods of schism ought to be deducted from the computation, and since it is further established that schisms in the Roman Church endured at different times for almost sixty-four years within the limit of one hundred years, proof ought to have been made not merely of prescription for one hundred years, but also for one hundred and sixty-four years, in order that prescription of one hundred years might be understood to have been completed.

Therefore, deeming the aforesaid allegation—that hearsay testimony ought to be admitted in this case—frivolous, since in such a case law permits this not at all, especially because the inconvenient result would follow that two contradictory opposites could be proved, and since it was clearly established to us that your monastery, as stated above, belongs to the Roman [Col. 1401C] Church, and that the Church of Hildesheim had not proved the prescription of one hundred years which it alleged, by counsel of our brethren we absolve you, daughter abbess, in the name of the Roman Church, whose procurator you were, from the suit of the Church of Hildesheim. We decree that henceforth your monastery shall enjoy that liberty which is expressed in the privilege renewed by us.

Therefore let no one … violate this our determination and constitution, etc. But if anyone should do so, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the eleventh year.

LXXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS, ABBOTS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE. He commends to them Guala, cardinal and legate. (Anagni, fourth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 1401D]

The Lord seems to have bent his bow for the destruction of his people, as an enemy, and, as though a foe, to have strengthened his right hand, so that the blow of the enemy might strike the Holy Land. Its ruin is great as the sea, and none is found to heal it. For she has drunk the deep and broad cup of God’s wrath; filled with vehement bitterness, she has none among all her dear ones to offer her consolation. She cries to the Lord, but he does not hear; suffering violence, she cries aloud to him, but he does not save, because he has destroyed her and spared her not, making the enemy rejoice over her and exalting the horn of her foes. [Col. 1402A]

Who, then, would not appear ungrateful to Christ the Redeemer for his precious blood, if, seeing the place of his redemption shattered by so great a calamity, he does not suffer with it with his whole heart? Whose bowels, I say, harder than stone, are not broken by pity at so great a misery? In such an outrage against the Crucified, who ought not to be inflamed with such zeal that, to repel the injury done to him, he would not shrink, if need be, from exposing himself to a precious death there where Christ deigned for his sake to undergo an ignominious cross? For he sees places made holy by Christ’s birth defiled with pagan filth, and unbelieving blasphemers mockingly insulting before the eyes, as it were, of Jesus hanging upon the cross: “If you are the Son of God, come down now from the cross and save yourself” (Matt. 27)—you whom we crucify again in your own [places], and in your own [place], showing no reverence for the vicinity of the Lord’s lodging-place and not trembling lest, provoked by their injuries, the infant should cry from the nearby manger, and lest the virgin mother, sitting near the same people’s foul impurities, should be ashamed.

Struck, therefore, by the immensity of this grief and stirred by the enormity of so great an injury, we have hitherto applied ourselves in many ways and by many means, diligently indeed, though not effectively, to the liberation of Christ’s holy inheritance. We shall not cease to apply ourselves to it so far as the Most High supplies us with power. Since the duty of apostolic provision now requires us to send a legate from our side into the kingdom of France, we have especially entrusted to him, among the other matters to be handled by his ministry, the advancement of the business of the cross. [Col. 1402C]

Therefore, since that kingdom has always been, and is, among the other kingdoms of the world devoted and specially beloved by us and the Apostolic See, in order that we might show more clearly in the person of our legate the affection of sincere love which we bear toward it, we have judged that one should be sent there whom, among our other brethren, we love with special charity and embrace with familiar goodwill because of his merits: namely, our beloved lily, Guala, cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Portico, a man distinguished in life, reputation, and learning. We have granted him full authority to uproot and destroy, build and plant, whatever he recognizes in God’s Church ought to be uprooted and destroyed, built and planted.

Accordingly, by these apostolic letters we earnestly admonish and command the whole of you in the Lord: receive the aforesaid cardinal humbly and devoutly as legate of the Apostolic See, holding a great place in the Church of God—indeed, receiving our own person in him. Attend with willing minds to his salutary admonitions and commands, both concerning aid for the Eastern Church and concerning other matters which he shall judge should be arranged in our stead. As sons of devotion, receive and firmly observe his commands and statutes. For we have unquestioning confidence in his prudent circumspection and circumspect foresight: with the Lord directing his steps, he will take care to proceed along the royal road [Col. 1403A] and, as we have also commanded him orally, will not turn aside to the right or to the left.

Therefore, each and all of you must strive to offer him due reverence and devout obedience. For if—God forbid—anyone should act otherwise, besides offending the cardinal himself, whose sentence, should he judge one against the contumacious or rebellious to be pronounced as their deserts require, we would cause to be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction is made, that person would also incur our indignation; for, according to the Apostle, we are prepared to punish every disobedience.

Given at Anagni, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year.

LXXXVI. TO GUALA, CARDINAL-DEACON OF SANTA MARIA IN PORTICO, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. The matrimonial case of King Philip is committed to him. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1403B]

Having full confidence in your discretion, we have judged that the case pending between our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king, and our dearest daughter in Christ, Ingeburg, the illustrious queen of the Franks, concerning an impediment by a maleficium, from which the same king is alleged to suffer, should be entrusted to your experience. By these apostolic letters we command you, after full freedom has been provided for the queen, to examine the case diligently, setting aside appeal; and, if it proceeds from the parties’ will, to decide it by a canonical [Col. 1403C] conclusion. Otherwise, remit it to our examination sufficiently prepared, setting the parties a suitable term within which they may appear before us through suitable representatives to receive judgment.

Given as in the other letter.

LXXXVII. TO THE BISHOPS OF LONDON AND ROCHESTER, AND THE DEAN OF LINCOLN, CONCERNING THE OBSERVANCE OF THE INTERDICT UPON THE PROVINCE OF YORK. (Anagni, sixth day before the Kalends of June.)

Among the other distresses and afflictions to which the English Church is subject through sins that demand it, we have recently received the grave complaint of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of York: when our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of the English, had ordered a thirteenth part to be taken from the churches and alms of the province of York, the archbishop, foreseeing this, appealed to the Apostolic See in defense of ecclesiastical liberty, placing himself, his goods, and all the clergy of that province under the protection of the Apostolic See. Yet the king, not withdrawing from the purpose he had conceived, took, contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, a thirteenth part of their revenues not only from the archbishop’s domain and those holding from him, but also from religious houses and most of the clergy of the province of York. [Col. 1404A]

Moreover, when the same archbishop, unable to endure such evils, departed from England intending to come into our presence, the king stripped him and his people of temporal movable and immovable goods. [Note: [Col. 1403D] See above, book X, epistle 172.] He also, in many ways and according to his own will, obstructed the archbishop’s spiritual jurisdiction; he caused his possessions and woods to be alienated, to the grave prejudice of the Church of York; and in many other matters acted very injuriously and oppressively toward him and his people.

Since it is not fitting that we should pass over with closed eyes so great an injury to God and his Church, not so much because of the loss of temporal goods as because of the danger to souls, although we have caused apostolic letters concerning this matter to be sent to our venerable brethren, the bishops of Ely, Worcester, and Hereford, we nevertheless command you by way of strict precept, setting aside every worldly fear, to admonish and induce the said king as quickly as possible to provide for his salvation and honor. Within three months after he has been warned by you, he must restore everything taken away both to the archbishop himself and to the churches and others belonging to him, and make suitable satisfaction for the losses and injuries.

Otherwise, since we must give greater deference to God than to man, compel the aforesaid king to do this by an interdict upon the entire province of York, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. Do not permit any divine office to be celebrated there, except the baptism of infants [Col. 1404C] and the penances of the dying; and cause the interdict to be inviolably observed by our authority until fitting satisfaction has been made.

If the king himself should wish to bring any allegation against that archbishop, after full restitution has first been made, hear what is proposed on either side. If the question raised requires an ecclesiastical forum, take care to examine it diligently and, after it has been more fully prepared, remit it to our presence, setting the parties a suitable term within which they may appear before us through suitable representatives, by God’s gift to receive justice from us. But if the question is such that it pertains purely to the secular forum, let that archbishop endure that it be heard and decided before his own judge.

Moreover, provide diligently and, setting aside appeal, take care to prohibit more strictly under a similar penalty that, as long as the question raised continues, nothing be innovated to the prejudice of that archbishop or his people; rather, they are to have full and free liberty to return to and remain in England. If named witnesses withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal, to bear testimony to the truth. Apostolic letters obtained which prejudice truth and justice are to have no effect. If not all of you, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year.

LXXXVIII. TO THE DEANS OF THE GREATER CHURCH AND OF ST GEREON, AND THE PROVOST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES AT COLOGNE. A certain case of the Archbishop of Cologne is committed to them. (Lateran, third day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 1405A]

[Note: [Col. 1405D] See Raynaldus, under the year 1206, §11.] After Adolph, formerly Archbishop of Cologne, swore in the presence of our legates to obey our commands concerning the matters for which he had been marked by excommunication, he came absolved into our presence and laid before us a grave complaint: that our venerable brethren, the Archbishop of Mainz and the Bishop of Cambrai, together with our beloved son Master Henry, scholasticus of St Gereon, had unjustly proceeded to depose [Col. 1405B] him, both because they had exceeded the limits of our mandate and because they had not observed the order of law. He added that they had been manifestly suspect to him, and that the letters on whose basis they had proceeded had been obtained through the assertion of falsehood and suppression of truth. He therefore requested that we should deign to revoke their proceeding and restore him to the state in which he had been before such sentence was pronounced against him, offering to prove all the foregoing matters.

They, however, appearing in our presence and defending their proceeding in many ways, asserted that all this was wholly false. But our venerable brother Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne, against whom Adolph’s petition seemed to be directed, without contesting the suit or entering judgment, defeated his petition by alleging that Adolph had despoiled him of a certain town called Neuss, which he held by force. Since, according to canonical sanctions, one despoiled ought not to answer a despoiler in court, he said that Adolph should not be heard unless the aforesaid town were first restored to him.

Having heard these and other matters proposed before us, we, with the common counsel of our brethren, made the following provision. Since, with summer heat approaching, because of the unhealthiness of the air it was not safe for either party to prolong a stay in the city, and lest meanwhile the business of peace under negotiation concerning the Empire be disturbed on this account, we set the coming Advent as a peremptory term [Col. 1405D] for both parties. At that time they are to appear before us in person or through suitable procurators, so that, both concerning the despoilment and the other matters upon which they shall wish to pursue your cause, we may proceed, with God as author, as ought to be done.

The aforesaid Archbishop Bruno is meanwhile to exercise archiepiscopal jurisdiction in every respect, and all clergy and citizens, ministeriales, barons, nobles, and persons of whatever rank established in the province of Cologne are to answer to him in all matters in which they are known to be bound to an archbishop. We have not, however, provided that the said Adolph be meanwhile despoiled of those castles which he is known to have held before the captivity of the aforesaid archbishop. [Col. 1406A] We prohibit Adolph from presuming, personally or through another, to molest the aforesaid Archbishop Bruno, the churches, the city of Cologne, or the ministeriales of St Peter. He is also to leave in peace to the archbishop and his people all temporal goods which the latter possesses.

We revoke as void all acts which Adolph undertook in ecclesiastical benefices from the time of his excommunication. Nevertheless, as a precaution, we declare that, even if the aforesaid delegates had proceeded less lawfully in deposing him, we could do in orderly fashion what they had done irregularly. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion to cause what has thus been provided by us to be firmly observed by our authority without any opposition, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. If not all of you … let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of May, in the eleventh year.

LXXXIX. TO JOHN, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. Concerning the affair of Canterbury. (Anagni, sixth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Note: [Col. 1405D] See above, book X, epistle 219.] If you carefully consider that he who, being in the form of God, did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to God the Father unto death on the cross, you will surely deem it not injurious but rather glorious to humble yourself before his vicar. He is King of kings and Lord of lords, through whom kings reign and princes rule, and to serve whom is nothing other than to reign. This great example of your Redeemer ought indeed to incline a royal mind, so that, having begun to humble yourself before us out of reverence for God, you retain nothing that could impede the full merit of such humility. Do not let contrary inclinations take hold of you as you humble yourself beneath the most mighty hand of God; rather, like a prudent king ruling your mind, bend your whole freedom of choice toward this, considering the saying of Solomon, wisest of kings: “Better is the patient man than the strong man, and he who rules his mind than the conqueror of cities” (Prov. 16).

Enter, therefore, most beloved son, into your heart, and assail there the fortified city of enemies against you. Bring against it the battering-ram of divine fear, by whose saving impact you may break down the hostile camps established within yourself against you. Thus, removing the obstacles of the enemy’s engines, utterly conquer the fortress opposed to you; and finally, in this inward battle, yourself both vanquished and victor, drive out the tyrant entirely, and make peaceful the city of your mind. There, sitting and presiding as a king, bring the affection of the flesh under the dominion of reason in the affair of which we speak.

We rejoice in the Lord and in the power of his strength that in this manner you seem to have engaged in the saving struggle by contending with yourself. [Note: [Col. 1406D] See book XI, epistle 220.] And concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 1407A] in which perhaps we judged that more than was due had been yielded to your honor—not indeed that we might approve an unjust custom, but lest we seem in any way to derogate from your right—you have now for the greater part withdrawn from an unconsidered purpose and imprudent counsel. [Note: [Col. 1407D] See the following epistle and *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 132.] Through our beloved son, the Abbot of Beaulieu, by whom you wrote to our Apostolate that we should believe what he proposed on your behalf, you generously offered that, although in this affair you consider yourself gravely burdened in many respects, nevertheless, because of the devotion and reverence which you profess to have toward the Roman Church and our person, you are prepared to receive and treat our venerable brother Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, as Archbishop of Canterbury. You will provide such security both to him and to his people as shall seem suitable for this purpose, and promise full restitution of the goods taken away, to persons and churches alike.

You will also permit the monks of Canterbury to return to their church and remain in safety, although this seems exceedingly burdensome to you because you believe that, in this affair, they treacherously plotted against you. Moreover, through the same abbot you placed the regalia in our hands, that we might grant them according to our good pleasure. When he was asked why you did not yourself grant them but instead delivered them to us to be granted, he replied that your mind had not yet been able to be moved to show the archbishop familiar favor.

Having heard this, with counsel of our brethren we judged that the following course should be taken concerning the aforesaid regalia: we would receive them without prejudice to either ecclesiastical or royal right and command that they be given to the said archbishop, if perhaps you could not be induced to grant them to him yourself. He shall be bound to you for them as his predecessors were bound to your forebears. By our letters, we therefore command our venerable brethren, the bishops of London, Ely, and Worcester, that unless, when requested by them, you are willing yourself to grant the regalia to him, they shall, prudently providing that no deceit intervene against ecclesiastical liberty, receive the aforesaid regalia in the prescribed manner and grant them to the said archbishop in our stead. Once the matters expressed above have been duly carried out, they are to relax the sentence of interdict and cause the aforesaid archbishop, as is fitting, to proceed to the Church of Canterbury.

We also admonish and exhort him by our letters to place his chief hope in the Lord and strive to conduct himself toward you in such a way that, for the better advancement of the welfare of the Church committed to him, he may secure the favor of your familiarity and grace. For we hope in him in whose hand the king’s heart lies, and who will turn it wherever he wills, that, as he has now begun in part to direct your counsel in this affair, so he will pursue it to its final effect, so that you will not only bring no hindrance to the effective exercise of his pastoral charge, but will render aid. [Col. 1408A]

Although we greatly welcome your devotion in these matters, nevertheless, considering that it is honorable not so much for us as for you that the regalia be granted by yourself, we earnestly request and more strongly exhort your royal serenity—enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins—that you generously grant us this as a gift: namely, by personally bestowing the aforesaid regalia upon the said archbishop, receive from him the fidelity due to you, principally acquiescing in our counsels, which will without doubt benefit your majesty.

Now, therefore, secure in the kingly gentleness and not uncertain of the archbishop’s prudence, we confidently commend him and the Church of Canterbury to the highest God and, in him, to you. We hope and firmly hold that he will take care to conduct himself toward you in such a way that he will deservedly secure your favor and grace, and that in practical experience you will learn how faithfully and truly we have urged you on his behalf.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year.

XC. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. On the same matter. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Note: [Col. 1407D] See epistle 89 and *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 132.] Our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of the English, recently sent us letters through our beloved son, the Abbot of Beaulieu, asking that we should believe what the latter proposed on his behalf. The abbot proposed that, although the king considered himself gravely burdened in many respects in the affair of the Church of Canterbury, nevertheless, because of the devotion and reverence which he professes to have toward the Roman Church and our person, he is prepared to receive and treat you as Archbishop of Canterbury. He will provide such security both to you and to your people as shall seem suitable for this purpose, promising full restitution of the goods taken away to persons and churches alike. He will also permit the monks of Canterbury to return to their church and remain in safety, although this seems exceedingly burdensome to him because he believes that, in this affair, they treacherously plotted against him.

Moreover, through the same abbot he placed the regalia in our hand, that we might grant them according to our good pleasure. When asked why he did not grant them himself but instead delivered them to us to be granted, the abbot replied that the king’s mind had not yet been able to be moved to show you familiar favor. Having heard this, with counsel of our brethren we judged that the following course should be taken concerning the aforesaid regalia: we would receive them without prejudice to either ecclesiastical or royal right and command that they also be granted to you, so that you should be bound to him for them as your predecessors were bound to his forebears.

Accordingly, by our letters we command our venerable brethren, the bishops of London, Ely, and Worcester, prudently ensuring that no deceit intervene against ecclesiastical liberty, to receive the aforesaid regalia in the prescribed manner and grant them to you in our stead, [Col. 1409A] if perhaps the same king, to whom we write most earnestly on this matter, cannot be induced to grant them to you himself. Once the matters expressed above have been duly carried out, they are to relax the sentence of interdict and cause you, as is fitting, to proceed to the Church of Canterbury.
