Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by these apostolic letters to place your chief hope in the Lord and strive to conduct yourself toward the aforesaid king in such a way that, for the better advancement of the welfare of the Church committed to you, you may secure the favor of his familiarity and grace. For we hope in him in whose hand the king’s heart lies and who will turn it wherever he wills, that, as he has now begun in part to direct the king’s counsel in this affair, so he will pursue it to its final effect, so that the king will not only bring you no hindrance in the effective exercise of the pastoral charge you have undertaken, but will render aid. [Col. 1409B]

Given as in the other letter.

XCI. TO THE BISHOPS OF LONDON, ELY, AND WORCESTER. On the same matter. (Given as in the other letter.)

By the authority of these present letters we command your brotherhood diligently to observe in every respect the mandate which we now last give you by other letters concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury. When all matters contained therein have been duly carried out, if any question should perhaps arise concerning any point, after receiving from our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of the English, suitable security that he will obey our counsel and command concerning it, you are nevertheless to relax the sentence of interdict. [Col. 1409C]

Given as in the other letter.

XCII. TO NICHOLAS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF THE HOLY CROSS CALLED SAXOVIVO. Concerning the confirmation of privileges. (Anagni, third day before the Kalends of June.)

[Note: [Col. 1409D] See Book XIII, letter 207.] In the privilege of Pope Paschal II of blessed memory, we have ascertained that the following is contained word for word:

> “PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Albert, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Cross called Saxovivo, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity. We are instructed by divine commands and apostolic admonitions that we should watch with untiring effectiveness over the condition of all churches. Therefore we commit to your care and administration, and to that of your successors, the church of Saint Apollinaris beside the river Sambre. This church, it is remembered, was established by the judge Mevanius on land belonging to him in his own right and offered by him to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church; there too, having cast off secular concerns, he devoted himself to the monastic order. In that place, indeed, a relaxation of discipline had long since occurred. [Col. 1410A] Therefore, in order to reform monastic discipline, we commit to you and your successors the aforesaid church of blessed Apollinaris, and unite it in perpetuity to your monastery—which, by God’s grace, is said to flourish in discipline and religious observance—as a member to its head. We decree that everything belonging to the aforesaid church shall always remain under your administration, and that henceforth no person whatsoever may remove from the possession of your monastery either that church itself or any lands or goods belonging to it, wherever situated. Rather, it shall be preserved in perpetuity, just as the holy authority of our office establishes in the text of this present decree. But if anyone—which God forbid!—should presumptuously attempt to contravene this our decree, [Col. 1410B] let him incur the loss of his rank and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by due satisfaction. Moreover, for this church you shall pay annually to the Lateran palace a census of four denarii. Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.”

We therefore, following in the footsteps of our predecessor, renew by this present document the same constitution, so that his enactment may attain its due effect, decreeing that no person whatsoever . . . of our confirmation and renewal, etc. But if anyone, etc.

[Col. 1410C] Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year.

XCIII. TO THE NOBLE MEN THE RHINEGRAVE AND UBERT OF SUNNEMBURCH. The temporalities of the archbishopric of Mainz are committed to them. (Anagni, the third day before the Nones of June.)

The more sincerely we love in the Lord our venerable brother, the archbishop of Mainz, with charity, the more fitting it is that we should grant him fuller favour in preserving his rights. Therefore, since he, trusting in your loyalty and prudence, [Col. 1410D] has entrusted his affairs to you for administration, we earnestly advise and exhort your nobility to administer on his behalf and at his command all temporal rights belonging to the archbishop of Mainz, excepting only those which are known to pertain to royal rights, in such a way that you may be commended for faithful and prudent diligence. For we have sent our letters to the princes, counts, barons, ministeriales, and others established in the diocese of Mainz, among whom the same archbishop possesses such rights, directing them to answer you concerning those matters on his behalf, as they are bound to do.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Nones of June, in the eleventh year.

XCIV. TO THE ABBOTS, PROVOSTS, AND THE ENTIRE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF MAINZ. On the same matter. (Given as in the preceding letter.)

[Col. 1411A]

“The more sincerely we love in the Lord our venerable brother, the archbishop of Mainz,” etc., as far as “grant him fuller favour.” Therefore we advise and earnestly exhort your whole body, [Col. 1411B] commanding by apostolic letters that you answer, as you are bound to do, on behalf of those to whom he has entrusted the administration in his stead of the rights, both spiritual and temporal, belonging to the archbishop of Mainz, excepting only those now known to pertain to royal rights. Otherwise, we have instructed our venerable brother the archbishop of Trier, and our beloved [Col. 1411B] sons the abbot of Remestorf in the diocese of Trier and the archdeacon of Trier, to compel you to do this by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Given as in the preceding letter.

XCV. TO THE ABBOTS, PROVOSTS, AND THE ENTIRE CLERGY; THE COUNTS, BARONS, MINISTERIALES, AND OTHERS ESTABLISHED IN THE DIOCESE OF MAINZ. On the same matter. (Same date.)

“The more sincerely we love in the Lord our venerable brother, the archbishop of Mainz,” etc., as far as “grant him fuller favour.” Therefore we advise and earnestly exhort your whole body, [Col. 1411C] commanding by apostolic letters that you answer, as you are bound to do, on behalf of those to whom he has entrusted the administration of the rights, etc., as far as “concerning those matters.” Otherwise, to our venerable brother the archbishop of Trier, etc., as above to the end.

Same date.

XCVI. TO THE PROVOST, DEAN, AND CHAPTER OF SOISSONS. That they are to permit Robert of Vailly to enjoy a prebend at Soissons. (Lateran, eighth day before the Ides of May.)

Formerly, while the bishop of Soissons of good memory was in the regions of Constantinople, we considered it fitting, by our letters, to request and advise his officials, and nevertheless to command them under injunction, that they should confer without any difficulty, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, upon our beloved son Robert, deacon of Vailly, who possessed no ecclesiastical benefice, a prebend in the Church of Soissons, [Col. 1411D] if one were vacant there. Otherwise, we ordered that the first prebend to fall vacant be reserved for our grant, to be conferred upon a suitable person. We also commanded you not to presume to admit anyone as canon to a prebend then vacant in your church, or to one which should first happen to become vacant, unless it were one to whom we should provide for its conferral.

Subsequently, however, a certain prebend became vacant in that church. The aforesaid bishop, having meanwhile returned from his journey abroad, disregarded the apostolic command and granted it, according to his own will, to his nephew in fact, though he could not do so in law. Afterwards, although you wrote to us against the aforesaid cleric, [Col. 1412A] alleging that he was in no way assisted by merits of suitability for obtaining such a benefice, and although the bishop’s said nephew in the course of time urgently petitioned us to deign to confirm that prebend to him by apostolic authority, we nevertheless judged it unworthy that an apostolic command should be thus evaded and were wholly unwilling to grant his petition in this matter.

But the aforesaid cleric, remaining for a long time at the Apostolic See, diligently waited to see whether perhaps anyone would appear who wished to raise and prove against his person something on account of which he ought by law to be denied an ecclesiastical benefice. At length, however, since no adversary appeared against him in such a matter, he humbly petitioned us to deign mercifully to provide for him.

[Col. 1412B] Inclining therefore to his petitions, we gave strict commands to our beloved sons the abbot of Saint-Aubert, the dean, and Master R. of Bekerel, canon of Cambrai, that, without any delay after receiving our mandate, they should assign to the aforesaid bishop and to you a period of three months. Unless within that period some canonical ground should be shown and proved before them on account of which the favour of apostolic provision ought not to be carried out in his case, they were thereafter, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, not to delay compelling by ecclesiastical censure both that bishop—or whoever acted in his place, should he happen to be absent—and you, to receive the same R. as canon and brother and [Col. 1412C] confer upon him the aforesaid prebend, or provide for him without difficulty with one of equal or greater value. They were also to ensure that he was adequately supplied by them with the necessities of food and clothing until he had been provided for in one of the foregoing ways, restraining opponents and rebels by a like coercion, appeal being set aside.

Furthermore, as we have learned from their letters, the aforesaid executors summoned the parties before them. When our letters had been presented to you, you raised no objection against the person of the aforesaid R. within the period specified by our letters; for that reason they declared him wholly absolved from your challenge. But the treasurer of the same church, who was then acting in the place of the aforesaid bishop, [Col. 1412D] raised certain objections against his person and produced witnesses to confirm what he had alleged. Yet, after taking care to examine them diligently, they found nothing sufficient in their testimony by which he might appear unworthy of the favour of apostolic provision. Accordingly, publicly pronouncing this in a judgment, they firmly commanded the aforesaid treasurer by our authority to provide the same R. with a prebend at Soissons, or with one of equal or greater value, in accordance with the contents of our mandate.

Declaring himself ready to do this, the treasurer offered him before them a prebend in the Church of Roye. When the said cleric refused it, maintaining that it was neither equal in dignity nor in value to the prebend at Soissons, the treasurer added that another cleric was to be made a canon by our authority in the first prebend to become vacant [Col. 1413A] in the Church of Roye. But to both points the treasurer replied that he would lawfully prove that the prebend at Roye equalled the prebend of Soissons in value; and, if he failed in that proof, he would assign him a prebend of equal or greater value in the Church of Soissons or elsewhere. He also said that, if he accepted the prebend at Roye, he would make him enjoy peaceful possession of it.

When the same R. urgently requested that they arrange to write to us concerning his admission to the prebend at Soissons, they refused to do what he asked, because the treasurer firmly asserted that he was ready to execute our mandate. But disputes having arisen between them concerning the value of the prebends, the aforesaid R. requested that both he and the proceedings in his case be referred to the Apostolic See. Since this pleased the other party, they referred the case to our presence.

[Col. 1413B] The parties having therefore appeared before us and wishing to litigate against one another, we granted them as auditor our beloved son Guala, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. After they had litigated for some time in his presence, that cardinal faithfully reported to us what had been put before him. We therefore, observing that the said prebend, which we had ordered reserved for our grant, had been assigned to the said cleric in evasion of the apostolic mandate, annulled by apostolic authority whatever had been done concerning it and adjudged that prebend to the said deacon R. [Col. 1413C] We command you by apostolic letters to receive the same R. as canon and brother and permit him peacefully to possess that prebend. For we give firm instructions by our letters to our beloved sons the dean, the precentor, and Milo of Lagereio, canon of Rheims, to restrain opponents and rebels by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the eleventh year.

XCVII. On the same matter.

Written in almost the same form to the elect, as far as: commanding him strictly by our letters to receive the same R. as canon [Col. 1413D] and brother and permit him peacefully to possess that prebend. For we give firm instructions to our beloved sons the dean, the precentor, and Milo of Lagereio, canon of Rheims, etc., as in the preceding letter. Given.

XCVIII. On the same matter. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of May.)

Written in almost the same form to the same persons, as far as: commanding them strictly to receive the same R. as canon and brother and permit the same [Col. 1414A] R. peacefully to possess the prebend which we have ordered assigned to him by our beloved son, the elect of Soissons. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we firmly command your discretion to restrain any opponents and rebels by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. And if not all, etc. Two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the eleventh year.

XCIX. TO THE DEAN AND CANONS OF GURK. On the election of the bishop of Gurk. (Anagni, Nones of June.)

The most turbulent and highly complicated dispute concerning the election of a bishop to be made in your church, which had been litigated between you and the Church of Salzburg in the times of our predecessors [Col. 1414B] Alexander of good memory [Note: [Col. 1413D] See Aventinus, Book VII, near the beginning.] and Lucius, not without great expense and severe labour, has also arisen in our time. Your side firmly maintained that the freedom to elect your bishop belonged to you by common law, by ancient custom, and by special privilege. Therefore your procurator petitioned us to make you enjoy peaceful possession of that freedom, compelling the other side to desist from improperly troubling you in this matter.

When, from the other side, a certain judgment said to have been pronounced on this matter for the Church of Salzburg was objected, the same procurator maintained that no judgment at all had been delivered [Col. 1414C] on the matter. But after certain letters of the bishop of Freising of good memory and of the abbot of Holy Cross had been produced before us, which seemed to contain the judgment said to have been rendered by them, he subsequently argued that, since the said bishop and abbot were not ordinary judges, and since it was not evident that they had been arbitrators jointly chosen by the parties or judges delegated by the Apostolic See, what they had decreed could possess no binding force. He maintained that up to that time you had freely elected a bishop for yourselves, a practice which he declared himself sufficiently able to prove.

When the response was made to him from the opposing side that the aforesaid judges had authority to determine the case by delegation from our predecessor Pope Alexander III, we entrusted to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Brixen, Freising, and Trieste, the reception of witnesses whom either party wished to produce concerning the practice of election and that delegation.

Later, when the parties had appeared before us and offered us sealed witness-statements on those two articles, your procurator solemnly declared in court that he did not believe a judgment had been delivered on this matter; and that, if one had perhaps been delivered, judgment against your church had certainly been procured through fear. We called him aside and inquired into the nature of the fear. But since the fear which he described to us did not seem capable of being sufficiently proved so as to assist your side, and he admitted that he did not wish to prove another fear, while requesting a postponement in order to prove the fear he had described, we, intending reconciliation, advised both him and the procurator of the other side to await the arrival of our venerable brother the archbishop of Salzburg, who was then expected to come to the Apostolic See.

Since he did not come, though awaited for a considerable time, and since some of you had meanwhile returned to your church, they brought back with them certain witnesses through whom the aforesaid procurator sought to prove another fear: namely, that the canons of Gurk had been compelled to make admissions against themselves by the count palatine and the brothers of the then archbishop of Salzburg. [Col. 1415B] Only then did he admit that a judgment had been delivered. He argued that, since civil law expressly provides that the praetor is at no time to ratify what has been done through force or fear, neither should a judgment pronounced by the aforesaid judges under the influence of fear have been held valid at that time. He advanced certain other arguments to prove the same point.

The same procurator moreover tendered an oath that knowledge of such fear had newly come to him. [Note: [Col. 1415D] Chapter *A nobis*, “He who accuses a marriage may be heard” (*Qui matrimonium accusat, audiri potest*).] Therefore, he argued, he ought to be heard on the analogous ground that, if anyone was present at the time a marriage was contracted and then raised no objection to it, but later wishes to impugn it and swears that he afterwards learned that consanguinity existed between the contracting parties, that accuser is heard.

[Col. 1415C] Again, from such a change of position he argued that your church ought not to suffer harm, because the praetor sometimes admits a person who changes his position and does not reject one who has altered his purpose.

In response, the opposing party alleged that G., archbishop of Salzburg of good memory [Note: [Col. 1415D] Gebhard. See vol. I, *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, [Col. 1416D] p. 78.], with the knowledge and consent both of the Apostolic See and of the imperial majesty, created the bishopric of Gurk in a certain part of his diocese. [Note: [Col. 1416D] See *Deeds of Innocent III*, chapter 130.] He established that the bishop of Gurk should be the perpetual vicar of the archbishop of Salzburg both in spiritual and temporal matters. Hence, since the election of a vicar, as also of a *vicedominus*—a deputy or steward—belongs by law solely to the person whose vicar or *vicedominus* he becomes, he maintained that the bishop of Gurk ought to be elected by the archbishop of Salzburg by reason of patronage and vicariate.

[Col. 1415D] He added that the procurator ought not in any respect to be heard, for several reasons: first, because he had admitted that he did not wish to allege another fear; secondly, because, having initially denied that a judgment had been delivered, he afterwards fraudulently admitted the contrary; and thirdly, because he had admitted that you had rendered obedience to the archbishop of Salzburg in such matters after the said judgment. From these points it was presumed that you approved that judgment.

He further alleged that, after you had brought a complaint about that judgment before our predecessor Lucius III, [Col. 1416A] he confirmed the same judgment, and that you had voluntarily obeyed that judgment for many years. Refuting these arguments with various answers, your side added that, after the transfer of the aforesaid archbishop to the Church of Mainz, your church, when it was able to protest, laid before the aforesaid predecessor, Pope Lucius, the dispute concerning the violence. But he, deceived both by the privilege said to have been granted to the Church of Salzburg by Pope Alexander II of blessed memory concerning the election, institution, and consecration of the bishop of Gurk, and by the judgment itself, asserted that he had carefully examined the privilege and found it genuine—whereas we have plainly found it false or falsified—and confirmed the judgment against you in your absence.

[Col. 1416B] Having heard these and other matters which the parties variously alleged before us, we granted by interlocutory order that your procurator should have the opportunity to prove that fear, after taking an oath that he had learned of it only later. He accordingly produced witnesses, whom we ordered our beloved sons Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross, and Guala, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, to examine and whose depositions we ordered to be written down.

Moreover, because the procurator of the aforesaid archbishop intended to produce witnesses in your regions both on this point and on the claim that you had voluntarily obeyed the judgment, as well as on the claim that the said predecessor confirmed that judgment in the text of the aforesaid privilege after the fear and other matters alleged in court before the often-mentioned Pope Lucius, we commanded the aforesaid bishop of Brixen, the provost of Aquileia, and the scholasticus of Augsburg to receive witnesses whom either party might wish to produce on the foregoing articles, on the settlement said to have been made after the judgment, or against the persons of the witnesses to be produced. They were to transmit the written witness-statements to us in like manner and set both you and the opposing side a suitable date by which you should appear before us to receive judgment, unless in the meantime you could reach an amicable settlement, which we believed greatly advantageous to both parties.

[Col. 1416D] In accordance with the terms of our mandate, they received the witnesses produced by each side. Since they could not induce you to accept an amicable settlement, they sent your procurators and those of the opposing party to our presence, together with the witness-statements and authentic documents faithfully sealed under their own seals.

When they subsequently appeared before us, we published all the witness-statements, carefully examined both them and the authentic writings of each party, and attentively understood everything which the procurators saw fit to put forward. We then diligently urged the same parties toward an amicable settlement, to which, as is known, we had endeavoured from the beginning of the suit to lead both you and the other side.

[Col. 1417A] Complying with our admonitions, the provost of your church and Master G. produced your letters before us, from which it was evident that they had received from you authority not only to sue and answer but also to settle. Master Marcwald and R., procurators of the archbishop of Salzburg, although they did not produce letters of the archbishop proving that they had received authority to make a settlement, nevertheless publicly swore in consistory that they had received such authority from the aforesaid archbishop in accordance with the terms expressed to them by that archbishop and communicated to us by them; that, to their knowledge, the said archbishop had in no way revoked that authority; and that they would faithfully exert effective effort to ensure that the same archbishop observed the settlement to be made by us.

We therefore afterwards, having taken counsel with our brethren, and considering that it was in many ways advantageous both for you and for the opposing side that the controversy should be concluded by settlement rather than judgment, caused the following agreement to be made between you with the consent of the parties. When your bishop has died, the archbishop of Salzburg, summoned by you, shall come to the church of Gurk and shall name for you three persons: one from the body of that same church, whom in good faith he judges more useful both for governing the bishopric and for the office of vicariate, and two outsiders. You, separately, shall deliberate carefully concerning the persons named to you.

[Col. 1417C] Finally, when you and that archbishop are sitting in chapter, the person among those named by the archbishop who has first been elected bishop and vicar by the archbishop, and subsequently elected bishop by you, and upon whom all of you—or at least the greater part of you—have fully agreed, shall be chosen. After the election has been solemnly proclaimed publicly by the dean, provost, or any other canon of your church deputed for this purpose by the chapter, you shall take care to present the elect to the archbishop of Salzburg as your metropolitan, to receive from him the benefit of confirmation. That metropolitan shall gladly confer upon him, without any difficulty, both confirmation and consecration.

[Col. 1417D] But lest by the cunning of anyone’s machinations anything be attempted in this matter to the detriment of your church, by the authority of almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and also on the part of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of ourselves, we impose a sentence of excommunication, which the archbishop of Salzburg then in office shall incur if he ever presumes to name anyone from the body of your church unless he judges in good faith that person more useful for the governance of the bishopric and the office of vicariate.

The procurators jointly approving this settlement, humbly accepted it. At their request, we also confirm by apostolic authority this settlement, made by us in the prescribed [Col. 1418A] form and approved by the procurators themselves as stated above. We decree that neither judgment nor privilege nor any other instrument shall ever obstruct this settlement, and indeed that, in this respect, they shall be wholly invalid, so that the settlement itself may obtain the force of perpetual validity without any obstacle. Let no one therefore . . . of our settlement, confirmation, and constitution, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the Nones of June, in the eleventh year.

Written in the same form to the archbishop of Salzburg.

C. TO THE BISHOP OF AMIENS. On supplying for the negligence of patrons. (Anagni, Ides of June.)

[Col. 1418B]

The letters of your brotherhood submitted to us stated that, when certain persons who possess the right of patronage in certain churches of your diocese sometimes deserve to be bound by a sentence of excommunication issued under our authority, it happens that those churches remain vacant for a long time, since the patrons themselves, because of the impediment of excommunication, lack the power of presentation. You therefore asked us whether, after six months, in such a case you may lawfully assign those churches to suitable persons.

Accordingly, by this present communication we command your brotherhood effectively to admonish and induce those patrons to strive to make satisfaction for the matters on account of which they are known to be under excommunication, so that, having thus obtained the benefit of absolution, they may be able to present suitable persons to the aforesaid churches. But if they should scorn to obey your admonitions, then after six months from the time of vacancy, without appeal, assign the said churches to suitable persons, provided that no prejudice to those patrons is thereby created for the future.

Given at Anagni, on the Ides of June, in the eleventh year.

CI. TO THE SAME. A marriage ought not to be dissolved when both spouses are adulterers. (Given as in the preceding letter.)

[Col. 1418D] [Note: [Col. 1417D] Chapter *Tua fraternitas*, “On adulterers.”] Your brotherhood asked us whether, if someone denies the marital debt to his wife who has been discovered in adultery, and he himself afterwards openly commits adultery with another woman, the husband ought to be compelled—if the wife repents of what she has done and humbly seeks forgiveness—to receive her with marital affection. To this we reply that, since equal crimes are cancelled by mutual compensation, such a husband cannot decline married companionship on the ground of his wife’s fornication.

Given as in the preceding letter.

CII. TO THE BISHOPS OF NEVERS AND ORLÉANS, AND THE ABBOT OF COUR-DIEU OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER. That they are to deliver the pallium to the archbishop of Rheims. (Anagni, third day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 1419A]

Concerning our venerable brother Alberic, Archbishop of Reims, we see and rejoice that what we read and recall as foretold in the Psalm has been fulfilled: “The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to destroy him; but the Lord will not abandon him into his hands, nor condemn him when he is judged” (Psalm 36).

Now, when formerly our venerable brothers the Bishops of Paris and Arras, together with our beloved son the Abbot of Clairmarais, had, in accordance with the form of the mandate received from us, appointed that same Alberic—then Archdeacon of Paris, a man indeed distinguished in life, reputation, and learning—as pastor of the Church of Reims, Theobald of Pertico, archdeacon, and Peter of Étampes, canon of the said Church, rashly opposing them, among other things which they reported to us in their letters against the proceedings of those persons, specifically alleged against the aforesaid archbishop that he was irregular, indiscreet, and manumitted.

Accordingly, they had forbidden the bishops assembled for his consecration to consecrate such a man bishop, Peter himself promising that on the day appointed he would prove this before them. But the aforesaid Bishop of Paris, who was pursuing his promotion by every means, while no one answered Peter except that same judge alone, summoned two priests and secretly received their testimony concerning Peter’s ill repute, against Peter while absent and unaware. Thus Peter was not admitted to prove the irregularity—namely, that Alberic had entered into marital intercourse with a widow. Peter having thus been repelled from proof, the bishop nevertheless caused Alberic to be consecrated bishop after an appeal to the Apostolic See had been lodged.

We, unwilling to pass over such a defect in so great a sacrament with closed eyes—especially because the aforesaid archdeacon and canon repeatedly pressed the matter before us by letters—commanded you that, truth having been investigated and learned, if you found that the said Peter had been repelled in the prescribed manner from proving such an objection, you should, notwithstanding the disorderliness of what had been done, declare to Peter and the aforesaid archdeacon that, if they wished and were able, both together or either one of them should regularly prove under your examination the alleged irregularity. If they should not wish or be able to prove it within two months; or if they failed in canonical proof; or if they happened to be canonically excluded from proof, you were immediately to direct our beloved son Raynerius, our subdeacon and household officer, to deliver the pallium to the said archbishop according to the form given him. But if they sufficiently proved the alleged irregularity, you were to remove Alberic entirely from the government of the Church of Reims.

When, on the day appointed for this purpose, the parties had appeared before you, and after no slight disputes had arisen between them concerning the manner of proceeding, they eventually accepted our rescript and requested that the aforesaid case be handled according to its form. You then lawfully proceeded to an inquiry concerning the manner in which the said canon had been repelled. Having received witnesses produced on either side, published the depositions, and heard sufficient argument from the parties upon them, you perceived that the parties’ minds were inclined solely toward a judgment being given and a report made to our Apostolic See. Therefore, you took care to send us the case, fully prepared, with the witnesses’ depositions and the documentary evidence.

Having carefully examined the matter, we found that it had by no means been proved that Peter had been repelled in the prescribed manner from proving the irregularity. Rather, witnesses above every exception showed that, on the day when Alberic was nominated Archbishop of Reims, Theobald and Peter had objected against him insufficiency, and that on the following day Peter had objected both irregularity and insufficiency. On both occasions he promised to prove them immediately; but, although the delegates were willing to admit the proofs offered, he withdrew himself by every sort of evasion. The delegates, observing his trickery, publicly fixed a date, nearly three weeks later, for the consecration of the said archbishop.

Since Peter had in the meantime not approached them at all about this matter, he finally appeared before them on the Saturday preceding the Sunday upon which the archbishop was to be consecrated. Purporting, as it were, to preserve their proceedings against a fraud attempted, he urgently requested, while nevertheless lodging an appeal to us, that they should not proceed to the consecration but should receive proofs concerning the said irregularity, which he said he was prepared to offer at once. The judges, wishing to deliberate more maturely on the matter itself, ordered him to appear before them early the next morning. When he did so, he promised, as before, immediately to prove the irregularity alleged. But when the judges granted him, as he requested, the opportunity to prove it, he immediately changed his statement, asking that he be given time to find witnesses.

The aforesaid archdeacon was then asked whether he wished to produce witnesses concerning the irregularity. He answered that he did not wish at all to allege anything concerning irregularity. As for insufficiency, he produced no proofs and said that he would produce none. It is therefore clear that Theobald and Peter suppressed all these facts, and stated to us only concerning the alleged exclusion that Peter had disorderly been repelled, in the manner expressed above, from proving the objections. They proved absolutely nothing of this. The Apostolic rescript was therefore obtained by suppressing truth and asserting falsehood.

It has also been sufficiently shown that not merely two, but four priests were produced to prove Peter’s ill repute; that they were produced not by the Bishop of Paris but by Milo of Nantouillet; and that Peter was excluded not on this ground—that is, because of ill repute—but on another, namely because of his evasions, and not by the Bishop of Paris alone but also by his fellow judges. Even had they excluded him less canonically on that ground, he should not now be admitted to prove the irregularity, since he had promised to prove another ground for his exclusion and entirely failed in proving it.

Since, therefore, according to the form of our mandate—which both parties accepted and according to which they requested the case to proceed—it ought to have been proved that the aforesaid Bishop of Paris, who was pursuing Alberic’s promotion by every means, while no one answered Peter save that same judge alone, summoned two priests and secretly received their testimony concerning Peter’s ill repute, against Peter while absent and unaware; and that Peter was thus not admitted to prove the irregularity, namely that Alberic had entered into marital intercourse with a widow—so that, once this had been proved, Peter might then be admitted to prove the irregularity—yet, although the other matters prescribed had been proved, absolutely nothing has been shown concerning this point. Therefore, with the counsel of our brethren, we judicially absolve the said archbishop from the prosecution of the aforesaid archdeacon and canon.

This is especially so because the canon himself has wavered and changed his account repeatedly before us, and indeed stands manifestly convicted of calumny by his own confession: before us he confessed that he had only later learned the irregularity which he had alleged from the beginning, and thus had alleged against the oft-mentioned archbishop something which he did not know.

Lest his rash presumption and presumptuous rashness remain unpunished—he who presumed to set his mouth against heaven while his tongue passes over the earth, so that, according to what is written, “the righteous may wash his hands in the blood of the sinner”—we suspend the said Peter from every clerical office and benefice until he obtains pardon for his offense from you and from the same archbishop. We do not, however, mark him as infamous, since the proceedings to prove that ill repute are known to have been less than orderly; and even if it had been lawfully proved, it was not directly alleged against him, but was raised by way of exception.

Although we love the aforesaid archdeacon with sincere charity in the Lord, yet because a father rebukes the son whom he loves, and God reproves and chastens those whom He loves, we command your discretion by Apostolic letters to admonish him to seek humbly and devoutly, within one month, pardon from the archbishop himself for having shot an arrow from his own bow into him by another’s hand. Otherwise, forbid him throughout the entire province of Reims to raise an objection in elections of prelates until he has humbled himself to seek pardon.

Moreover, although the said archbishop is in no respect incredible or suspect to us, and although, as we have learned from the testimony of the king, of all the suffragans, of the abbots and chapters of the province of Reims, and of many others, his reputation has not been in the least injured by the objection of that irregularity, nevertheless, because he himself has offered a voluntary purgation in order to make his innocence clear, if he wishes to undergo it, you shall arrange to receive it, within one month, on a day publicly appointed for the purpose, with whatever number of bishops, abbots, or priests he may prefer. You shall personally come to the Church of Reims, where those opposing him may more conveniently be present, in order to receive the purgation.

You shall nevertheless direct our aforesaid subdeacon to assign to the said archbishop, according to the form expressed to him by us, the pallium taken from the body of Saint Peter, the insignia, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office. If not all of you, etc., then two of you shall nevertheless carry these things out, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed.

Given at Anagni, on the third Nones of June, in the eleventh year.

## CII (second letter). To the Bishops of Ely and London. Consolatory Letter.  
*(At Anagni, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June.)*

[Note: [Col. 1421D] See the Acts of Innocent III, chapter 132.]

Although we believe that through the letters which we recently sent to your brotherhood concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury by our beloved son the Abbot of Beaulieu and Master Simon, you have already learned what has been offered by the king and what has been commanded by us, nevertheless, for greater caution, we send you enclosed with the present letter a copy of those which we addressed to the king. We admonish and beseech you in the Lord that, just as you were prudent in binding, so you may be discerning in loosing; pouring in oil after wine with such moderation that the bruised and swollen wound may be perfectly healed.

But concerning the insult and injury which you endure for obedience and justice’s sake, we believe that you imitate the example of those who, as is written, went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were judged worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus. Keep ever before your eyes that obedience is better than sacrifices, and that to listen is greater than to offer the fat of rams; and that blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, because, when they have been proved, they shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love Him. You need, we believe, not consolation—which is known to be necessary for the sorrowful—but exhortation, which is wont to be fitting for combatants; although this very thought may suffice both for consolation and exhortation if you gather much from little, being rightly compared with those who were full of eyes within and without.

We therefore exhort you rather to perseverance. While the other virtues run in the racecourse, perseverance alone finally receives the prize; for the Lord declares that he who perseveres to the end shall be saved. Know that this sickness is not unto death, but that the Church of God may be glorified through it.

We answer your consultations as follows:

[Note: [Col. 1423D] See chapter 19, *De sententia excommunicationis*, in the Sixth Book.]

Since, because of the interdict, new chrism could not be consecrated on Maundy Thursday, old chrism must be used in the baptism of infants; and, if necessity requires, oil must be mixed into the chrism by the hand of a bishop or even of a priest, lest it fail. Although viaticum seems to belong to the penitence of the dying, if it cannot be had, we believe that in this case the saying applies: “Believe, and you have eaten.” For it is not the emergency of necessity but contempt for religion that excludes from the sacrament; and the necessity itself is hoped soon to cease.

[Note: [Col. 1423D] See below, letter 258.]

If, however, from the beginning religious men had been permitted, in accordance with the tenor of their privileges, to celebrate divine offices with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, the doors closed, bells not rung, and voices subdued, this would have been neither burdensome to us nor unfitting. By this means an appropriate remedy could be applied, both in this matter and in others—especially so that, through the offering of the saving Victim, the divine majesty might be appeased in this necessity.

Given at Anagni, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year.

## CIII. To the Bishop and Archdeacon of León. Concerning a priest whose genitals had been forcibly cut off.  
*(At Anagni, the eighth Ides of June.)*

Our beloved son G., a priest, appearing before us, stated that when he was formerly still a deacon, M., a knight of the diocese of León, concealing deceit and fraud under a show of generosity, invited him to a banquet. Because the deacon was falsely said to have carnally known a certain concubine of that knight, the knight, revealing the hostility which he bore in his breast, did not fear to cut off the deacon’s genitals.

When this came to the attention of the prince of the land, and the deacon was thought nearly dead, the prince, inflamed with zeal for vengeance, caused the knight and his concubine to be burned. Afterwards the aforesaid deacon recovered from the wound and, concealing this fact, procured his promotion to the priesthood. Coming to the Apostolic See, he humbly petitioned us to deal mercifully with him in this matter.

Therefore, by Apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if it is established to you that the aforesaid priest was wholly free from the charge of fornication imputed to him and wholly blameless in the vengeance carried out by the prince, you shall permit him to minister in the order which he has received and shall inflict upon him no injury on that account. You shall impose canonical purgation upon him if perhaps he has acquired ill repute concerning these matters.

Given at Anagni, on the eighth Ides of June, in the eleventh year.

## CIV. To the Brothers Serving the Lord in the Hospitals of the Holy Spirit at Rome and Montpellier. That the head of the Order of the Holy Spirit shall be in the city of Rome.  
*(At Anagni, the sixth Ides of June.)*

After the death at Rome of Guy, of happy memory, who was the first founder and rector of your hospitals, certain brothers of yours sent from Montpellier—

[Note: [Col. 1424D] See below, letter 169.]

—and others coming from the City for the appointment of a rector appeared in our presence. With their counsel and consent, since it seemed highly expedient, we decreed that the headship and mastership of your order should remain forever in the City, at the Hospital of the Holy Spirit in Saxia. The rector of that house shall preside over all brothers of your order, present and future; and all shall be bound to render him regular obedience and reverence.

When a rector is to be elected for the hospital at Montpellier, he shall be canonically elected with the counsel and assent of the rector of the hospital at Rome. Accordingly, in conformity with this constitution, we caused our beloved son Brother P. de Granier to be elected supreme rector of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit in Saxia, firmly commanding that, with his counsel and assent, a suitable rector be elected in the Hospital of the Holy Spirit at Montpellier.

Therefore, by Apostolic letters, we admonish all of you that what has been beneficially instituted by us be observed inviolably, now and always, by you and your successors; all other provisions expressed in the privilege granted by us to each hospital remaining in their full force. Let no one therefore … [violate] our constitution and command, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth Ides of June, in the eleventh year.

## CV. To the Archbishop of Ragusa and the Archdeacon of Trogir. A sentence pronounced against the Templars is annulled.  
*(At Anagni, the third Ides of June.)*

The brethren of the knighthood of the Temple in Croatia informed us that, although they had obtained our letters addressed to our venerable brother the Bishop of Knin against the Bishop of Nin, the same Bishop of Nin amicably settled with those brethren the matters disputed between them. Yet the aforesaid Bishop of Knin, taking occasion from our letters and moved by a grudge which he had conceived against the Bishop of Nin, bound that bishop in the bond of excommunication, without the brethren’s knowledge, being guided by the choice of his own will rather than by rational judgment.

Therefore, by Apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, having more fully investigated the truth, if you find the matter to be so, you shall declare the aforesaid excommunication null and void. Notwithstanding any letters, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the third Ides of June, in the eleventh year.

## CVI. To the Bishop of Ypres. That he consent to his translation to the Church of Thessalonica.  
*(At Saint-Germain, the fifth day before the Kalends of July.)*

Since the metropolitan church of Thessalonica, which in the kingdom of the Greeks is regarded as almost the chief see after that of Constantinople—

[Note: [Col. 1425D] He was afterwards made Patriarch of Antioch. See below, Book XII, letters 8, 38, 39.]

—is deprived of pastoral governance, and since we desire to provide for it with paternal care, we have judged your person, which we consider qualified by many gifts of virtue, to be appointed to its government, the consent—and indeed the desire—of the temporal ruler concurring.

Believing, therefore—indeed holding for certain—that, casting your thought upon the Lord, by whom the steps of a man are directed, you ought to reply: “Lord, if I am necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor,” we have thought fit to ask and admonish your brotherhood; by Apostolic letters, commanding and enjoining this upon you for the remission of sins, that, consenting to the divine calling, you reverently undertake this burden for God and apply the hand of irrigation to the new plantation. If it is cultivated by your labor, it is hoped to bring forth manifold fruit; and He who requires your ministry in this matter will grant the increase.

Having arranged whatever you know to be necessary for this purpose, present yourself before us, to receive from us appropriate counsel and assistance.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year.

## CVII. To the Chapter of Gerona. Concerning the election of a bishop.  
*(At Saint-Germain, the sixth Ides of July.)*

[Note: [Col. 1426D] Chapter *Dilectus*, *De concessione praebendae*.]

Our beloved son Master William, your fellow canon, formerly represented to our Apostolic See that, after your bishop of good memory had entered upon the way of all flesh, the greater and sounder part of you had agreed upon him and intended to elect him bishop. But because the noble Count of Cuntrone interfered, the election was not held.

Afterward, that count invested his own chaplain Madius with the bishopric and commanded you either to depart from his land or to elect Madius as pastor. When our venerable brother, then Archbishop-elect of Santa Severina, heard of this, he summoned the said William before him. Asserting that, because of your negligence, the authority of election had devolved upon himself, he induced William to consent to an election of himself. William obeyed his admonitions and was elected by that archbishop, with the concurrence and consent of his suffragans.

But when this became known to the aforesaid count, he summoned you before him and kept you in custody until you jointly elected the said Madius. Madius then appeared before our beloved son Gerard, Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Adrian and legate of the Apostolic See, and obtained confirmation from him.

The said William subsequently went to the same cardinal, appealed to our hearing lest he consecrate Madius, and finally, appearing before us, stated that Madius had betrayed a certain castle; that he had received investiture of the bishopric from a lay hand through the use of money; and that, even before obtaining confirmation, he had devastated many goods of the Church by wasteful dissipation.

Accordingly, we commanded our venerable brothers the Archbishop of Cosenza and the Bishops of Bisignano and Geneocastro to compel you and all others who might be named to tell the truth concerning all these matters. If they found that Madius’s election had been irregularly celebrated, they were to declare it null and void, compel him by due process to restore the Church’s property, and afterwards, having diligently investigated the truth concerning William’s election, determine what was just, without appeal.

As we have seen contained in their letters, after they summoned once, twice, and a third time peremptorily both the aforementioned Madius and you, as well as the abbots of the Church of Gerona, Madius, though awaited for four months, neither came to them nor allowed you or the abbots to come. Since, because of suspicion of dissipation, they suspended him from administration of episcopal goods, but he nevertheless presumed to administer, they pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him. He contemned that sentence obstinately and did not cease to celebrate.

Thus, since it had been established to them by sworn witnesses that Madius had received investiture of the bishopric from a lay hand, had incurred perjury, had repeatedly committed treason, homicides, and simony, that his election had been extorted, and that his consecration had been attempted not only after an appeal but also otherwise contrary to the canons, they finally, after taking prudent counsel, judicially annulled what had been done concerning him.

We, therefore, having carefully heard these and the other matters set forth to us concerning this case, and observing that the canon promulgated against the negligent by the Lateran Council is not ordinarily extended to archbishoprics or bishoprics but is restricted to other ecclesiastical dignities and lesser benefices—

[Note: [Col. 1426D] The Codex of Angers, and other manuscripts: “and lesser.”]

—annulled William’s election, because he had been elected by an archbishop and his suffragans, to whom the election did not belong; not on account of guilt in his person, but because justice required it.

We also judged that the said Madius must be wholly removed from the Church of Gerona. An inquiry conducted concerning him by the aforesaid delegates found him impeded by many crimes; he did not observe the sentence of suspension and excommunication pronounced against him, but administered while suspended and did not blush to celebrate while excommunicated, as was fully established by the judges’ report.

Unwilling, therefore, that the Lord’s flock should lack pastoral care any longer, we command your discretion by Apostolic letters that, within one month after receiving the present letter, you arrange for your church to be provided through canonical election with a suitable person as bishop. Otherwise, know that we have commanded the aforesaid archbishop and bishops that, thereafter supported by our authority, they shall appoint for you a suitable pastor, repressing opposition by ecclesiastical censure, appeal notwithstanding.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the sixth Ides of July, in the eleventh year.

A letter in almost the same form was written to Gregory, Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Theodore. It begins: “From the letters of good memory.” Thus the old Angers exemplar of the third collection of decretals instructs us.

## CVIII. To the Patriarch of Jerusalem, Legate of the Apostolic See. His legation is extended for four years.  
*(At Saint-Germain, the seventh Ides of July.)*

Since the end of the four-year period during which we entrusted to you the office of legate in the province of Jerusalem seems to be approaching, and since neither our favor toward you nor your devotion toward us has grown cold—indeed, the necessity of the Holy Land, for which this legation was granted to you, has not ceased—we have thought fit to entrust that legation to you for another four years.

We earnestly ask and admonish your brotherhood, and command you by Apostolic letters, that by the authority of the present letter you exercise commendably and prudently, for the fixed period, the ministry of the care entrusted to you.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the seventh Ides of July, in the eleventh year.

## CIX. To the Same Patriarch and to the Beloved Sons, the Masters of the Knighthood of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem. They are admonished to watch over the defense of the Holy Land.  
*(At Saint-Germain, the sixth Ides of July.)*

We shed tears as a torrent, day and night, over the misery of the Holy Land. We have neither ceased hitherto nor now cease to seek its assistance in every way and from every quarter that we can. At the urging of our diligence, a very great army of Christians is preparing in Germany with the noble Duke of Austria, and in France with the Count of Eu and other magnates, for its aid. In Germany a general collection for its support is being made, established with the unanimous consent of the princes and confirmed by the protection of our authority.

Because we believe that money is necessary to you for retaining that land, we command you by the authority of the present letter to receive the alms of the Cistercian Order, and the fortieth levy sent by our command by the venerable Bishop of Paris and deposited at the Temple; and to spend these, together with one thousand Provençal pounds—

[Note: [Col. 1427D] See below, Book XII, letter 28.]

—which we recently sent from the alms of Saint Peter for the aid of the Holy Land, as you know to be expedient for the need and advantage of the Holy Land.

We have with us certain other alms of the faithful, which we shall send you when an opportunity is found, intending without any interruption to devote diligent—and would that it may be effective—labor to the assistance of that land. We earnestly ask and exhort your discretion to apply yourselves prudently and steadfastly, through yourselves and the other helpers whom you have, to governing the remnants of Christ’s inheritance, not only within your own borders but also in Antioch and Tripoli, until, God leading the way, the Christian force now prepared and soon to be prepared comes to your assistance.

For this reason we ourselves are working without ceasing especially to restore peace, not only in the Empire but also in the kingdoms, wherever this may be granted from above, so that aid for the Holy Land may be supplied all the more abundantly as those whom the wrong done to the Crucified One concerns can work toward it more effectively once domestic conflicts have ceased.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the sixth Ides of July, in the eleventh year.

## CX. To the Patriarch of Jerusalem, Legate of the Apostolic See. Concerning the election of the Patriarch of Antioch.  
*(At Saint-Germain, the fourth Ides of July.)*

[Note: [Col. 1428D] See above, Book X, letter 214.]

As though the crimes of impiety and impieties of crime by which the province of Antioch had grievously provoked the Lord’s wrath had not sufficed, the Count of Tripoli added the act of laying his hand upon the Lord’s anointed: he committed to prison the Patriarch of Antioch, of pious memory, his father and lord, and there he finally died miserably.

O noble Antioch, city of perfect beauty and, as it were, joy of all the earth: how grievously you are seen to have been dishonored by so grave an outrage; how shamefully darkened by so shameful a crime! To what shall we compare you, or to whom can we liken your misery? For every calumny is in your midst. “As a cistern makes its water cold, so you have made your knighthood cold.” Moreover, you seem, by comparison with your apostasy, to have justified the souls of your sisters. Like an enemy the Lord has bent His bow and strengthened His right hand as an adversary. Unless you flee from the face of that bow by fruits worthy of repentance, the enemy’s stroke will strike and wound you with cruel chastisement. Your destruction shall be great like the sea; the Lord’s indignation shall go out over you like fire and burn, and you shall at last find no one who can quench it. You shall drink the deep and broad cup of God’s wrath.

Over all these matters, after that help which we hope for from heaven, to whose aid shall we turn but to yours, dearest and most beloved brother? Though you lament such a calamity with an affection equal to ours, perhaps you can nevertheless come to its aid with greater effect.

[Note: [Col. 1429D] See Book XII, letter 8.]

Therefore, because we believe that, owing to various circumstances, the Church of Antioch can be better assisted through your presence than we who are absent can arrange, we have thought fit fully to commit our authority in this matter to you. By Apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, after absolving any canons of that Church whom you find excommunicated, according to the Church’s form, you admonish and induce those to whom the election of the Patriarch of Antioch belongs to appoint for themselves, within a period to be fixed by you, a suitable person from that province or another, on this side of the sea or beyond it, as pastor by canonical election and with your counsel.

Otherwise, thereafter, having God alone before your eyes, appoint for them from whatever place a man suitable for so great a burden and honor. Cause due obedience and reverence to be rendered to him, and restrain any opponents or rebels by ecclesiastical censure, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed.

As for the dean of the said Church, who is said to have acted maliciously against it in many ways, although many maintain the contrary: truth having been investigated and learned concerning these matters, determine, without appeal, what you judge ought to be determined according to God and the welfare of that Church.

Cause the aforesaid count, who committed so great a sacrilege, to be strictly avoided as excommunicated, anathematized, and accursed until he deserves the benefit of absolution through fitting satisfaction—if indeed he is granted the ability duly to make satisfaction for so great a crime. Finally, lest we omit anything among contingencies, we confer upon you full power both concerning these things and concerning all matters touching this case, so that, in our stead, you may determine concerning everything and each individual matter, appeal notwithstanding, whatever you see to be expedient.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the fourth Ides of July, in the eleventh year.

## CXI. To Richard, Abbot, and the Convent of Saint Mary of Boulogne-sur-Mer, Present and Future Professors of the Regular Life, in Perpetuity. Concerning the confirmation of privileges.  
*(At Saint-Germain, the sixth Ides of July.)*
A pious request should be fulfilled by the effectual carrying-out of goodwill, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may undoubtedly [Col. 1430A] acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Honorius of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, at Boulogne-sur-Mer, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of the present document.

First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that church at present justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by grant of pontiffs, etc., shall remain unimpaired; [Col. 1430B] among which we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances: lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures and grazing-lands, woods, waters, mills, fisheries, churches, villages, houses, tenants, counties, households, advocacies, and all its movable and immovable property, cultivated and uncultivated. The whole parish of the city of Boulogne, together with its parochial rights and what is contained in the dependent properties. Within the walls of the same city, the Church of Saint John the Baptist. Outside the walls, the Church of Saint Martin, with its tithes and appurtenances. And in the same parish, the chapel of the lepers; the chapel of Saint Peter of Nienburc; the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Nienburc outside the walls; and the chapel of the Hospital of Saint Catherine within the walls, assigned [Col. 1430C] to your own use.

Within the walls of the same city: the two holdings of Carletus; the holding of Ardulf the baker; the holding of Peter de Rua; one holding of Eustace of Pernes; the holding of Allelm; the holding of William the chamberlain; the three holdings of Ingelram the dean; the small holdings; the holding of Lambert Siccus; the holding of Roger Lipard; the holding of Ermesendis; the holding of Bernard the cleric; the holding of Osto; the holding of Baldwin son of Azo; the holding of Baldwin Mundolf; the holding of Clarembald of Indreham; the holding of Godebert; the holding of Guarin of Felnes; the holding of Leivardis; the four holdings of Gozelin of Odra; the holding of Flameric; the holding of Otbert; the holding of Olric; the holding of Gumburgis; [Col. 1430D] the holding of Guarner; the holding of Frodo; the holding of Otbert the priest.

In the street called the Forum, the holding of Martin. By the postern, four holdings. In Nienburc, all the holdings on the sandy ground called Saint Mary’s. In Arkesten, the land of Radulf Bevarag; the holding of Elembert; the holding of Rayner; the holding of Eremberga; the holding of Alulf; the holding of Soimann; the holding of Soimer; the holding of Theobald; and the holding of Erkenfrid.

The altar-benefice of Hissingehen; the altar-benefice of Condeta; the altar-benefice of Badingetuna; the altar-benefice of Gestingehem, with its tithes; the altar-benefice of Curs; the altar-benefice of Belebrone; the altar-benefice of Alingetuna; the altar-benefice of Wirla, with its tithes and appurtenances; the altar-benefice of Hesding; that of [Col. 1431A] Nieles; that of Nameringehem; the chapel of Colesbere; the altar-benefice of Ingehem, with the whole tithe and two ploughlands in the same village; the chapel of Halkeca; and the estate of Avions, with its tithes and appurtenances; tenants and revenues in the castle of Lens; the tithe of Telingetum; the tithe of Guastina; the tithe of the chapel; the tithe of Godingetuna; the tithe of Aquingeham; and the tithe of Timbron.

From the tithe of Altafontaina, five *polkini* of oats. From the tithe of Issingehem, seven *polkini* of wheat, which Girard of Buxin formerly gave to your church; and the tithe of Huppen. In Licernes and Frenc, tenants and land. In Cormonte, tenants and land. In Camier, tenants and land with a share of the mill. In Dalnis, land; in Nieles, land; in Flemis [Col. 1431B], land; in Neufchâtel, lands and revenues; in Vacaria, land; in Froingehem, land and tenants; and land; in Letingehem, tenants and land; in Walbingehem and Tegata, lands; in Hermarenges and Isica, lands and a meadow; in Cahem and Helkeninges, lands and revenues; in Hockingehem and Issingehem, lands and revenues; in Badingetuna, land; in Tornes, land; in Makingehem and Celles, tenants and land; in Bellomonte, land and tenants; in Bovemberg, land and tenants; in Deningehem and Wicardenges, land and tenants; in Odra and Telingetuna, land and tenants; in Faingehem, land; in Ouringehem and Poteria, land and tenants; in Westrehoua, land and tenants; in Ostrehen, land and revenues; in Blokendale, land; in Stalis and Odressele, lands and tenants; in Squifein [Col. 1431C] and Hungrevelt, lands and revenues; in Tudingetuna, lands and revenues; in Wadingetuna, lands; in Hodingehem, lands and revenues; in Goningesele, land and revenues; in Seiles, land and revenues; in Lokingehem, land; in Raventun, lands and revenues; in Ambletue, revenues; in Basingehem, lands and revenues; in Ostova, revenues; in Wincela, revenues; in Pernes, revenues; in Yweslo, land; in Helingetuna, land; in Bukerdes, a share of the tithe; in Felnis, land; in Hardentuna, land; in Markisa, land and revenues; in Wisifra, land and revenues; in Holesfort, lands and revenues; in Hesdin, lands and revenues; in Hecolt, a meadow; in Wakingehem, eight *polkini* of wheat by the measure of Gisnes; in Pitesfelt, lands and revenues; in Fogenhove, lands and [Col. 1431D] revenues; in Manengeltem, lands and revenues; in Honingetuna, lands and revenues; in Wimulge, lands and revenues; in Lisingehem, lands and revenues; and in Ilumeris, land and woodland.

We also confirm by apostolic authority to you and your church the lands and holdings bestowed upon your church by Count Eustace; one half of one third of the tithe of Hissingehem; one sixth of the remainder of that same tithe; at Telingetuna, fourteen *polkini* of oats, two shillings, and two pence; at Fogenhove, four shillings and twelve pence which you hold from the Church of Anderne; and the dues (*subteriae*) which you possess from fishing boats.

We further decree that no one may presume to build a chapel in your parishes against your will, saving the privileges of the Roman [Col. 1432A] pontiffs. Nor shall any priest or cleric have leave, without your consent and free will, whether on his own initiative or through another’s compulsion, to remain in your churches or chapels or to assume any office there. As for your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and the produce from the nourishment of your animals, no one, etc. It shall also be lawful for you to receive clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing from the world, etc. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, it shall be lawful for you, with doors closed, etc. We also decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that provision may be made for the devotion and last will of those concerned, etc., while preserving the canonical right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one there, etc.

In the parish churches which you possess, it shall be lawful for you to elect priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they must answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. We also decree that no one may impose new and undue exactions upon your church, or pronounce against you, your church, or your clerics a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause. We ratify the ancient liberties and immunities and the reasonable customs granted to your church and hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid [Col. 1432C] church or to take away its possessions, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., let him be subject to punishment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, etc., unto the end. Amen.

Given at Saint-Germain, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF ATHENS. Confirmation of privileges. (At Saint-Germain, VI Ides of July.)

[Col. 1432D]

It is customary to grant assent, etc., as far as “consent”: we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and churches, together with all the goods which you now reasonably possess or may, with God’s help, acquire in future by just means; and, as you yourselves justly and peacefully possess them, we confirm them to you and, through you, to your churches by apostolic authority and strengthen them by the protection of the present document. Let no one, therefore, … [violate] our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the eleventh year.

CXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF ATHENS. That the Church of Athens be ordered according to the customs of the Church of Paris. (At Saint-Germain, II Ides of July.)

[Col. 1433A]

The most holy Roman Church, over which by the Lord’s ordering we preside, is accustomed to hear its subjects’ requests all the more effectively inasmuch as they seek its assistance more devoutly. Since, therefore, you have reverently requested us to deem it fitting to order your church according to the institutions of the Church of Paris, and to have its customs firmly observed in it, assigning to you the lawful portions of its possessions, revenues, and proceeds, while the definite number of canons established there by our beloved son Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, then legate of the Apostolic See, remains in force: readily acceding to your request, we grant to your whole body that, if it can be done without harm to that church and without just offence to the clergy, people, and prince of that land, you may freely order it according to the custom of the Church of Paris.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the second day before the Ides of July, in the eleventh year.

CXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF DIMIC. The bishopric of Calidonia is committed to him. (Given as in the other letter.)

We perceive that you render the due reverence to the Apostolic See because, apart from its counsel and command, you do not usurp undue jurisdiction; rather, in matters in which necessity compels you to seek it, you ask grace from that See. Now, appearing in our presence, you stated that, although you had been called to the governance of the Church of Dimic by a canonical election later confirmed by our venerable brother the Archbishop of Larissa, you could not be supported from its revenues. The nobleman A., constable of the Kingdom of Thessalonica and prince of that land, sympathizing with your poverty, wished to assign to you the neighbouring bishopric of Calidonia. You were wholly unwilling to accept that grant without our special permission, and requested our mercy in this matter.

Having taken counsel with our brethren, we have thought fit to grant you that, while possessing the bishopric of Dimic as your own, you may hold and have the bishopric of Calidonia in commendam, if this can be done without detriment to either church and without just offence to the clergy, people, and prince of that land, until something else shall be arranged by the Apostolic See or its legate; provided, however, that you administer its care beneficially.

Given as in the other letter.

CXV. TO THE ELECT OF CITRIUM. The bishopric of Platamon is committed to him. (Same date.)

Because you render reverence to the Apostolic See, etc., as in [Col. 1434A] the other letter, as far as “appearing in our presence”: although you had been called to the governance of the Church of Citrium by a canonical election later confirmed by our beloved son Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, then legate of the Apostolic See, you could not be supported from its revenues. The nobleman Roland Piscius, prince of that land, sympathizing with your poverty, wished to assign to you the bishopric of Platamon, adjacent to your own; concerning which grant, etc., as in the other letter, unto the end. Same date.

CXVI. TO THE NOBLE LORDS OF THEBES. That they pay tithes to the Church of Thebes. (Given as in the other letter.)

We have thought fit to ask and admonish your nobility, commanding you by these apostolic letters that, without presuming to exact *crustica* or anything contrary to justice from the Church of Thebes and the clerics of its archbishopric, you shall henceforth desist from undue exactions from them in such a manner that it may have no just cause for complaint against any of you. We nevertheless enjoin upon you that you shall pay to the said church the tithes which every Christian is bound by law to pay, since the Lord Himself commanded that tithes be brought into His storehouses; and that you cause them to be paid to it, as you are bound to do, by Greeks subject to you as well as by Latins.

Given as in the other letter.

CXVII. TO THE NOBLE LORDS OF NEGROPONT. Concerning the same matter.

[Col. 1434C]

To your nobility, etc., as in the other letter, as far as “commanding you that”: without presuming to exact from the Church of Avinon and the clerics of its bishopric, etc., unto the end.

Given.

CXVIII. TO THE NOBLE LORDS OF THERMOPYLAE AND THE LORDS OF THEBES. Concerning the same matter. (Given as above.)

To your nobility, etc., as in the other letters, as far as “commanding you that”: without presuming to exact tithes from the Church of Thermopylae and the clerics of its bishopric, etc., as in the other letters, unto the end.

[Col. 1434D] Given as above.

CXIX. TO THE NOBLE CONSTABLE OF THESSALONICA. That he restore dignities and possessions to the Church of Dimic. (Same date.)

To your nobility, etc., as far as “commanding you that” [Col. 1435A]: restoring, and causing to be restored, as is just, to the Church of Dimic the *papates* and ecclesiastical possessions withheld both by you and by those subject to your jurisdiction, together with the fruits received from them; do not presume to exact *crustica* or anything contrary to justice from that church, our venerable brother its bishop, and the clerics of the same bishopric. Instead, desist from undue exactions from it in such a way that they may have no just cause for complaint against you. We nevertheless enjoin upon you that you shall pay the tithes, etc., as above, unto the end.

Same date.

CXXI. TO THE NOBLEMAN O. DE ROCCA, DUKE OF ATHENS. Concerning the payment of tithes. (Same date.)

[Col. 1435B]

To your nobility, etc., as far as “commanding you that”: without presuming to exact from the Church of Athens and the clerics of its archbishopric, etc., as in the preceding letters.

Same date.

CXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LARISSA. Confirmation of privileges. (At Saint-Germain, VI Ides of July.)

It is customary to grant assent, etc., as far as “assent”: the possessions which your church formerly possessed and still justly and peacefully possesses, we confirm to you and, through you, to that church itself by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of the present document. Let no one, therefore, … [violate] our confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

[Col. 1435C] Given at Saint-Germain, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the eleventh year.

CXXIII. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF SAINT SAMSON AT CONSTANTINOPLE. Confirmation of privileges. (Given as in the other letter.)

When a request is made to us, etc., as far as “assent”: we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and the Hospital of Saint Samson, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all that you now reasonably possess or may, God being favourable, acquire in future by just means, and strengthen it by the protection of the present document. We also ratify the ordinances [Col. 1435D] which our beloved son Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna and then legate of the Apostolic See, is known to have made there; and, since they were reasonably made and are set forth more fully in his authenticated document, we command that they be firmly observed. Let no one, therefore, … [violate] our protection and command, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

CXXIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF FOSSANOVA. Concerning the dedication of an altar. (At the monastery of Cassino, XII Kalends of August.)

If the consecration of an altar [Col. 1436A] was held in honour in the Old Testament, how much more solemnly ought it now to be observed in the New, when the difference between that altar and this is no less than that between light and shadow. Upon that, indeed, fleshly and irrational victims were slaughtered; but upon this is always offered that one life-giving holocaust which was once sacrificed upon the altar of the Cross for the redemption of the human race—namely, the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, Himself both sacrifice and priest.
