He gave Himself as the price upon the Cross, that by dying He might redeem His faithful from death; and He gives Himself as food upon the altar, that by living He may nourish His faithful unto life, incorporating into Himself those who eat Him, so that through what He received from what is ours, and what we receive from what is His, Head and members may be inseparably united into one body. He Himself prayed that all might be one in Him, as He is in the Father and the Father in Him [Col. 1436B].

Since, therefore, the sacrament of the altar is great and arduous—indeed far greater than we can undertake—we had repeatedly been invited by you with much insistent supplication to consecrate in your monastery the new altar which you erected in the new basilica. We descended to that monastery—or rather, we ascended to Mount Bethel, where the sons of the prophets dwell, would that they were kindled with that fire from heaven which, according to the Lord’s command, must always burn upon the altar. With an honourable company of bishops and cardinals [Note: [Col. 1435] *Chronicle of Fossanova*, under the year 1208: “On Wednesday, when day broke, the Lord Pope dedicated the high altar of the new church.”], and with a great multitude of the faithful in attendance, we solemnly consecrated that most holy altar with our own hands on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. We [Col. 1436C] sought and awaited from Christ this reward: that, whenever the remembrance of His death is celebrated upon it in the saving mystery, He may remember us for good; and that, moved by the pious prayers of those who offer to Him upon that altar the rich holocaust for the salvation of living and dead, He may, through the power of His death, rescue us in the future from the death of Gehenna.

Therefore, that the venerable consecration of this altar may be celebrated more devoutly every year, we grant to all who devoutly assemble for the celebration of its consecration within fifteen days an indulgence of one year from the penances imposed upon them for their sins, trusting in the mercy of Him who is the remission of sins. Although your monastery belongs by a special right and property to the Apostolic See, yet because through this it has become, as it were, still more specially its right and property, we [Col. 1436D] receive it under the special care and chief protection of blessed Peter, together with all the things which it now possesses by just title or may acquire in future by just means. Thus, in accordance with the privileges of our predecessors and our own, it may always possess them without contradiction, enjoying everywhere all privileges and indulgences, general as well as special, obtained from the Apostolic See.

May the apostolic blessing attend all who preserve its rights, and may the divine majesty both justify them in the present and glorify them in the future. But let its disturbers, unless after warning they repent [Col. 1437A], recognize themselves as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity they have committed and deprived of the gift of apostolic blessing. Let them know that the relics of martyrs are laid up beneath the altar so that, there, vengeance for righteous blood may be sought against persecutors of that place, where righteous blood is commemorated as having been shed; as it is written: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony which they held; and they cried out, saying, ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?’” (Revelation 6). But may the consolation of the Holy Spirit be granted here and for ever to all who preserve their rights to that place. Amen.

Given at the monastery of Cassino, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, [Col. 1437B] in the eleventh year.

CXXV. TO RAYNALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CAPUA, AND HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. Confirmation of privileges. (At Saint-Germain, X Kalends of August.)

Since, by the office of the apostolate enjoined upon us by God, through which by the disposition of the heavenly judgment we stand over all Christ’s faithful, we ought to attend to the peace and tranquillity of each, we must especially be solicitous for the repose of those who are distinguished by pastoral dignity and elevated to the pontifical office. For unless we attend to their welfare, preserve their dignities and rights intact insofar as God permits us, and defend them by apostolic [Col. 1437C] authority against the attacks of wicked persons, they cannot be solicitous for the salvation of those committed to their governance by the Lord’s ordering.

For this reason, venerable brother Archbishop, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church over which, by God’s agency, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of the present document [Note: [Col. 1437D] See vol. VI of *Italia Sacra*, p. 400.]. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, etc., shall remain [unimpaired]; among which we have thought fit to specify in their proper names:

[Col. 1437D] The bishopric of Aquino; the bishopric of Venafro; the bishopric of Isernia; the bishopric of Teano; the bishopric of Sessa; the bishopric of Carinola; the bishopric of Calvi; the bishopric of Caiazzo; and the bishopric of Caserta.

In Capua: the abbey of Saint Mary Major; the Church of the Lord Saviour; the Church of Saint John at the Court; the Church of Saint Michael; the Church of Saint Mary of the Arch; the Church of the Holy Apostles; and the Church of Saint James in the Castle.

In the diocese of the Church of Teano: the Church of Saint Erasinus; the Church of Saint Mary; the Church of Saint Helena; and the Church of Saint Nicholas, which are [Col. 1438A] in the territory of Scarpati. At Bairan: the Church of Saint Elias and the Church of Saint Martin. At Fontana de Corrigiis: the Church of Saint Mary. In the diocese of the Church of Sessa: the Church of Saint Lucy in the place called Sorbelli. In the diocese of Carinola, at Rocca Montis Draconis: the Church of Saint Rufinus and the Church of Saint Mark. In the territory of Carinola: the Church of Saint Pancras.

In the diocese of the Church of Calvi: the Church of Saint Andrew at Cementa; the Church of Saint Germanus at Palera; the Church of Saint Tamarius of Monte; the Church of Saint Paul of Cormello; the Church of Saint Peter of Borleiano; the Church of Saint Simachus; the Church of Saint Erasmus of Moscardino; and the Church of All Saints in the place called Sanguinari. At Sclavos: the Church of Saint Michael; [Col. 1438B] the Church of Saint Peter; the Church of Saint Mary; the Church of Saint Nazarius; the Church of Saint Angelus of Jano; and the Church of Saint Mary. At Camillani: the Church of Saint Angelus; the Church of Saint Mary; and the Church of Saint Nicholas.

In the diocese of Caiazzo: the Church of Saint Angelus of Melanico and the Church of Saint Peter at Bagnatori. In the diocese of the Church of Caserta: the Church of Saint Vitus of Hercules; the Church of Saint Nazarius in the Buzarian field; the Church of Saint Peter at Boffoli; the Church of Saint Secundinus; and the Church of Saint Felix. In the territory of Mutilone: the Church of Saint Mary; the Church of Saint Felix; the Church of Saint Peter; and the Church of Saint Stephen.

Near the same diocese: the Church of Saint Euphemia; the Church of Saint John at Gajanum; [Col. 1438C] the Church of Saint Mary at Lupinum; the Church of Saint Felix; and the Church of Saint Priscus. At Casapuli: the Church of Saint Nicholas; the Church of Saint Lanctus Arpius; and the Church of Saint Peter of Sarsana. At Marzanesi: the Church of Saint Angelus and the Church of Saint Martin. At Campurcipi: the Church of Saint Caesarius; the Church of Saint Praecopius; and the Church of Saint Benera. At Airoli: the Church of Saint Juliana and the Church of Saint Nicholas at Ravulas.

In the territory of Castel a Mare: the Church of Saint Adiutor; the Church of Saint Marcellus; the Church of Saint Blaise; the Church of Saint Stephen; another Church of Saint Blaise; the Church of Saint John; the Church of Saint Nicholas; the Church of Saint [Col. 1438D] Catherine; and the Church of the Holy Cross.

At Cancelli: the Church of Saint Angelus; the Church of All Saints; the Church of Saint John; the Church of Saint Apollinaris of Patresano; the Church of Saint George; the Church of Saint John of the Tower; the Church of Saint Vitus; the Church of Saint Peter; the Church of Saint Nicholas; the Church of Saint Mark; the Church of Saint Castrensis; the Church of Saint Martin of Rosellis; the Church of Saint Flavian; the Church of Saint Barbara; the Church of Saint Juliana; and the Church of Saint Andrew.

At Arnona: the Church of Saint Mary; the Church of Saint Blaise; the Church of Saint Paul; and the Church of Saint Erasmus of Cazolis. At [Col. 1439A] Grazanesi: the Church of Saint John; the Church of Saint Mary; the Church of Saint Maximilian; and the Church of Saint Nicholas.

Moreover, the Jewish tithe (*Judecam decimam*), and an income of two hundred pounds of wax from the royal bailiwick; the proceeds of Castel a Mare; the fief of Pandulf Compalatius; and the bed of the river from the mill of Richard of Citro and Robert of Rocca as far as the bridge. Just as you possess all these things justly and peacefully, we confirm them to you and, through you, to your church by apostolic authority.

We have also thought fit to confirm by apostolic authority the definitive sentence lawfully promulgated by that same predecessor of ours concerning the case between your predecessor Alfanus of good memory and the abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Capua, concerning the subjection and liberty of that monastery [Col. 1439B], as is more fully contained in its authenticated text [Note: [Col. 1439D] It appears in the following letter.].

We also grant to your brotherhood, by the liberality of the Apostolic See, the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. You shall remember to use it within your church on those days on which you know your predecessors used it: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Stephen the Protomartyr; the Circumcision of the Lord; Epiphany; Hypapante; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter; Easter Monday; Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of Saint Mary; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the solemnity of All Apostles; the commemoration of All Saints; dedications of churches; [Col. 1439C] the principal feasts of your church; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clerics; and the anniversary day of your consecration.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church or take away its possessions, etc., as far as “in every way advantageous,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., let him be subject to punishment. But to all who preserve their rights to that place, etc., unto the end. Amen.

Given at Saint-Germain, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III [Col. 1439D].

CXXVI. TO RAYNALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CAPUA. The sentence issued by Alexander III is confirmed. (At Saint-Germain, XII Kalends of August.)

It is customary for the Apostolic See to grant assent, etc., as far as “moved thereto”: we confirm by apostolic authority the definitive sentence which our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory lawfully promulgated concerning the case between your predecessor of good memory and the abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Capua, concerning the subjection and liberty of that monastery, as is more fully contained in its authenticated text [Col. 1440A]. We have caused its tenor to be entered word for word in the present letters.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALFANUS, Archbishop of Capua: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“By the duty of our office and by our authority we are compelled to hear, with exact diligence and care, controversies brought before the judgment of the Apostolic See; and matters decided and suitably concluded there should fittingly be recorded in apostolic writings, lest they relapse into the uncertainty of renewed dispute. For divine providence established the most holy Roman Church as mother and teacher of all churches, so that it should unravel intricate and serious questions and, preserving the strictness of justice, determine by its judicial examination matters held in any doubt.

“Since you and our beloved daughter in Christ Mat[hilda], abbess of Saint Mary of Capua, had appeared in our presence concerning the dispute between you regarding the subjection which you claimed in that monastery and the freedom which the said abbess likewise asserted, the aforesaid abbess produced before us the privileges of princes and of three of our predecessors—namely, the Roman pontiffs Zachary, Leo, and Adrian. You, on the other hand, alleged that, since that monastery was founded within the boundaries of your diocese—indeed, beside the walls of your city—it ought by common law to belong to your church. On this point you declared yourself supported by the authority of many canons, which expressly show that monasteries and churches belong to the bishops in whose territory they are known to have been founded.

“You further alleged that, for the preceding sixty years, your church and those who had preceded you in the dignity of the archbishopric had possessed authority over that monastery: the blessing of abbesses and nuns, the celebration of public Masses, obedience and fealty, and the suspension of its clerics. You also produced four witnesses, three of whom, under oath, testified that, when the Church of Capua was vacant, Abbess Atta had been blessed by Robert, formerly bishop of Sessa, a suffragan bishop of that church; and that, when at the suggestion of the canons of the Church of Capua she was asked by that bishop to render obedience and fealty to that church, she swore obedience and fealty both to the church and to the archbishop when one should be appointed. You added further that, at your admonition and command, she received back a certain nun whom she had expelled, and provided for her in a certain cell of her monastery at Teano. Moreover, when the clerics of that monastery were required by you and your predecessor to render fealty, they rendered it to both of you.

“Now, although the matter had long been litigated on both sides, we placed no reliance whatever, as was proper, on the privileges of the princes as regards the grant of freedom and the monastery’s exemption, since neither they nor other laymen can grant such freedom to churches. We judged the privilege of Zachary suspect and unworthy of belief because of its style of composition, its corruption of grammar, and the simoniacal transaction which it contained—namely, that he had confirmed a church as having been sold, something which it is wicked to believe of so holy a man—and also because of the parchment, which appeared scarcely to be one hundred years old, whereas, as the chronicles record, four hundred years had elapsed since Zachary’s death. We likewise judged Leo’s privilege suspect and unworthy of belief because of its defective and corrupt grammar, since it is absurd to suppose that so learned and prudent a man had such ignorant scribes; and because of its seal, which plainly appeared wholly unlike and different from Leo’s seals produced before us, while those seals resembled one another in every respect.

“Moreover, the privilege of Pope Adrian, of happy memory, did not grant unrestricted freedom to the aforesaid monastery, but confirmed it under the condition under which it had held that freedom in ancient times. Furthermore, although the multitude of witnesses produced on the abbess’s side constantly affirmed that the aforesaid monastery had always been free and subject to none except the Roman Church and the prince of Capua, when asked whether they knew definite signs of subjection to the Roman Church, they declared that they did not know. They also testified that they had not seen the abbesses promise obedience or swear fealty to your predecessors. Nevertheless, they professed to have seen those abbesses blessed by your predecessors.

“Therefore, since we recognize, both from the matters alleged on your side and from the testimony of the other party, that your predecessors blessed the abbesses and nuns of the aforesaid monastery, celebrated public Masses there, received the obedience and fealty of the aforesaid Atta, and that the clerics of that monastery rendered them obedience and swore fealty; and since we also observe that the canons provide that every church must be subject to the bishop in whose bishopric it arises: by the common counsel of our brethren we absolve you from the claim of the said abbess concerning the freedom which she sought to assert against you, and we adjudge that monastery to you and to your church and decree that it shall remain perpetually subject to you.

“That this judgment of our determination may remain ratified and firm and be observed inviolate for all time, we strengthen it by apostolic authority and safeguard it by the protection of this present writing, decreeing that absolutely no person may infringe this page of our determination or in any way oppose it. But if anyone shall do so,” etc.

“Therefore let no one … [violate] this our confirmation,” etc. “But if anyone shall do so,” etc.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the eleventh year [of our pontificate].

## CXXVII. TO THE PRIOR AND CLERICS OF SAINTS JOHN AND PAUL AT TODI

The church of Saint Hilary is adjudged to them. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1442A]

When a dispute concerning the church of Saint Hilary at Todi was being litigated before our delegated judges—the venerable brother bishop of Todi and our beloved sons, the prior and I., canon of Saint Gregory at Spoleto—between you on one side and the beloved son, the abbot of Saint Peter of Monte in the diocese of Spoleto, on the other: it was alleged on your behalf, son prior, that by right one third of that church of Saint Hilary, both in possessions and offerings and also in its dependent chapels, belonged to your church. The abbot, on the contrary, alleged that the entire church of Saint Hilary, with its possessions and everything it possessed, belonged to him.

After witnesses had been produced, received, and examined on both sides concerning these matters, the same judges caused the witnesses’ attestations, sealed with their own seals, together with certain other authenticated documents, to be sent to us. They fixed a suitable term for the parties, at which they were to appear before us to receive judgment. When the parties had appeared in our presence, we granted them our beloved son A., subdeacon and chaplain, as auditor. After the attestations had been duly published before him, the matter was argued for some time; and he carefully reported to us what had been alleged before him.

Now, although your party, son prior, sought through its witnesses to prove that it possessed the right of patronage in the aforesaid church of Saint Hilary; that for forty years and more it had peacefully held one third of that church in offerings, mortuary dues, and other revenues; and that it belonged to your church to ordain clerics for the aforesaid district in the said church: we found sufficiently proved only that, for forty years and more, the church of Saints John and Paul had received one third of the offerings of the church of Saint Hilary, and had sometimes entrusted the collection of that portion to clerics instituted by the abbot of Monte and to clerics of Saints John and Paul.

Therefore, after carefully considering what had been alleged, we adjudged to the church of Saints John and Paul one third of the offerings in the church of Saint Hilary. By the authority of this letter we decree that it may entrust that portion for collection either to clerics instituted in that church by the abbot or to clerics of Saints John and Paul, as has been proved and has hitherto been customary; and with respect to all other matters we impose perpetual silence upon you.

“Therefore let no one … [violate] this our constitution,” etc. “But if anyone shall do so,” etc.

Given as in the other letter.

## CXXVIII. TO OUR NEPHEW STEPHEN

A prebend at Bayeux is adjudged to him. (At Saint-Germain, on the Nones of July.)

[Col. 1443A]

When our beloved sons P., your clerical messenger, and R., procurator of John, clerk of Vauré, had appeared in our presence, the messenger complained grievously that, although a prebend in the Church of Bayeux had been conferred upon you—a prebend which our venerable brother, the bishop of Bayeux, is known to have held before his promotion—you were unable to have free disposal of it or peacefully to possess the churches and other property belonging to it. This was because the said I. falsely asserted that he had been appointed perpetual vicar in that prebend and harassed you repeatedly under pretext of this claim. The messenger therefore requested that the aforesaid I. be restrained from harassing you.

The procurator, on the other side, alleged that I. had formerly been instituted perpetual vicar in the same prebend and was obliged to pay for it only an annual rent of thirty-four pounds in Tours currency. He humbly requested us to secure for the said I. free administration of that prebend and of the property belonging to it, as he had hitherto been accustomed to have, and not to permit him to be unduly harassed by anyone on this account.

In support of his claim and I.’s defence, he produced copies of certain letters, declaring that he wished to rely upon those alone, and saying that the originals were in I.’s possession. In one of these copies we saw it stated that the bishop of Coutances, of happy memory, at the presentation of H., formerly canon of Bayeux, had granted I. the church of Vauré with its appurtenances as a perpetual alms, on the condition that I. should pay the aforesaid H. twelve Angevin pounds annually.

Your party replied that, even if such copies were in no way to be credited, the copy itself did not prove I. to be vicar of the aforesaid prebend, but rather to have received a certain church in alms subject to an annual payment. Yet the liberality of this alms, granted to him by that bishop at H.’s presentation, could not be extended beyond H.’s lifetime to the prejudice of the canon to be substituted, especially since it was not alleged that the consent of the bishop and chapter of Bayeux, to whom the matter principally belonged, had been given.

In the copy of letters of our predecessor Pope Clement, of blessed memory, which the procurator produced, it was expressly contained that, at the request of I.—who had alleged that he had been instituted perpetual vicar in the aforesaid church and that the church’s rent had been increased far more than it had been at the time of the Lateran Council—our predecessor had commanded the bishop of Coutances to restore that rent, with appeal set aside, to the level at which it was proved to have stood at the time of the council. By authority of that mandate, the bishop caused the rent of the church, as having been increased, to be reduced by judgment to four Angevin pounds and ten shillings, as could plainly be inferred from the copy of his letters. Our predecessor is said to have confirmed that judgment, since it had reasonably been given. To prove this, the procurator produced a certain rescript.

Your party replied that since the aforesaid copy of the bishop of Coutances stated only that I. had received the church in alms, and not that he had been appointed vicar, it was clearly evident that the letters of our predecessor, in which I. alleged that he had been appointed perpetual vicar and that the church’s rent had been increased, had been obtained by a false representation. Therefore I. ought to derive no advantage either from those letters, or from the judgment of the bishop of Coutances, who had proceeded by their authority, or even from the subsequent apostolic confirmation. This was especially so because he appeared wholly to have renounced both the benefit of those letters and the judgment of the bishop when he afterwards took the same church at farm for a much higher annual rent, as is plainly gathered from the copy set down below.

For the procurator presented a copy of letters of the bishop, dean, and chapter of Bayeux, upon which he especially sought to base his defence. It expressly stated that Master R. of Ableiges—then a canon and now bishop of Bayeux—had, with their consent, granted his prebend of Varetum, with its appurtenances, including churches, people, the demesnes of the churches, and other property, to the said I., to be held perpetually at an annual farm-rent of thirty-four Angevin pounds. After his promotion, the same bishop renewed that grant; and it is known that the bishop of Coutances approved it, as seemed clearly proved by copies of their letters.

[Note: [Col. 1443D] See the chapter *Auditis*, “On Election.”]

Your party replied that the foregoing copy from the bishop and chapter of Bayeux proved I. not to be a vicar but rather a farmer or rent-payer. Since a farm of this sort could not by law or custom endure longer than the person granting it at farm had a right in the prebend, it was said to be clear that, after Master R. had been elevated to the bishopric, the farm necessarily ended. For although, when he granted the prebend at farm, he had granted it to be possessed perpetually, this must be understood to mean that the grant was to endure only so long as he retained some right in the prebend; thus the word “perpetually” must, according to sound interpretation, be referred to his own interest.

Nor could I. retain any right in the prebend by the consent of the bishop and chapter after the person who had granted it at farm had ceased to hold it. Since that consent had been attached to the act of the canon, I. could derive benefit from it no longer than the canon’s grant endured. This was especially true because the bishop and chapter could not have given their consent to so enormous a detriment to the canon who was to be substituted. Nor could I. hold the prebend permanently at an annual farm-rent of thirty-four pounds when it was alleged to be worth one hundred and twenty pounds yearly. Such an arrangement would bring not merely loss but disgrace upon the church: the canon would have to be content with a small payment for his prebend while I. abounded from its revenues. As to what kind of person I. is said to be in regular observance and manner of life, we pass over in silence.

Your party further alleged that the grant made by the bishop of Bayeux was void because it was made at a time when the matter did not belong to him at all. Consequently, the approval of the bishop of Coutances could cause you no prejudice.

Therefore, having fully understood these and the other matters which the aforesaid messenger and procurator took care to set forth, and having taken counsel with our brethren, we have judged the said I. to be condemned to restore the churches of Holy Trinity of Vauré, Saint Mary of Ver, and Saint Peter of Mainilhamant, together with their appurtenances and the other property belonging to the prebend of Vauré. We do so both in respect of the vicariate and in respect of the farm, which is now undoubtedly known to have ended. We impose perpetual silence upon him, decreeing that henceforth you may freely dispose, without anyone’s contradiction, both of those churches and of the other things belonging to your prebend.

“Therefore let no one … [violate] this our determination,” etc. “But if anyone shall do so,” etc.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the Nones of July, in the eleventh year [of our pontificate].

## CXXIX. TO OUR BELOVED SONS MAJOR AND WILLIAM, ARCHDEACONS, AND THE PRIOR OF SAINT VICTOR AT PARIS

Concerning the prebend of Saint Martin of Tours, adjudged to Master William. (At Sora, on the eighth day before the Ides of August.)

Moved some time ago by the commendable testimony rendered concerning the character and learning of our beloved son Master William, bearer of this letter, and yielding with paternal affection to his need, since he lacked an ecclesiastical benefice—which he was indeed worthy to receive—for the support of a poor life, we ordered the chapter of Blessed Martin at Tours to receive him as a canon and brother.

When the beloved son, the abbot of Vendôme, and his fellow-admonishers had earnestly urged them to do this, as they themselves reported to us by letter, the chapter delayed answering, first alleging the absence of its dean and treasurer. When these men finally gave their assent in writing to the reception of the master, the chapter ultimately replied that, although they knew him personally, since he had long lived honourably among them and could be useful to them as a discerning and prudent man, they were nevertheless bound by promise to receive certain others; and, since the resources of their church did not suffice, they could not conveniently then fulfil the apostolic command.

Yielding therefore to his repeated humble petitions, we commanded by our letters the beloved sons, the abbot of Saint Geneviève and his fellow-executors, that unless the aforesaid chapter should allege and prove a reasonable cause why this ought not or could not be done, they should compel it by ecclesiastical censure—removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal—to receive him as brother and canon and assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. This command was especially appropriate because the same master was commended to them for adequate moral character and learning.

As they informed us by their letters, they proceeded lawfully in the matter. Although part of the chapter alleged certain frivolous objections, and certain persons on behalf of that party vainly appealed to our hearing before one of the aforesaid executors, before the day assigned to the parties, nothing was ultimately shown against the aforesaid master that should impede the apostolic mandate. It was fully established, both by the parties’ admission and by the depositions of witnesses, that several canons of that church had died after its most recent organization and that no one had yet been substituted in their places. The executors therefore fixed a peremptory term for the parties to hear judgment.

Since the aforesaid chapter, repeatedly and peremptorily summoned, contumaciously withdrew itself, two of the executors—the third being lawfully excused—decreed by judgment that, notwithstanding the objections made by the chapter, the said master should be received as brother and canon of the aforesaid church and be assigned a stall in choir and a place in chapter. They firmly enjoined the chapter to carry this into effect. Because it contemptuously failed to do so, they first pronounced sentence of suspension upon it and afterwards, because it nevertheless celebrated after the suspension, sentence of excommunication. Thus at last certain members of that chapter came to their senses and received the aforesaid master according to the foregoing judgment, while others did not fear to persist in their contumacy.

Recently, when the same master appeared in our presence and sought confirmation of the proceedings of his executors, we ordered him and our beloved son A., canon of the aforesaid church, who had come to the Apostolic See as procurator for its affairs, to be heard by our beloved son Tullius, subdeacon and chaplain. In his presence, when that canon entirely refused to allege or do anything against the master, he finally received him, by our command, as brother and canon with the kiss of peace.

Since certain letters against the proceedings of the aforesaid executors are said to have been obtained from us by a messenger of the aforesaid church in the chapter’s name—although we are said to have repeatedly rejected his petition on this matter—by concealing the truth and expressly asserting falsehood, namely in this form: that, when a dispute concerning the master’s reception into their church was litigated between them on the one side and the aforesaid master on the other before the said abbot and his fellow judges, those judges had proceeded wrongly and, after an appeal lawfully lodged to us, had rendered an unjust judgment against them, wishing to put an end to the master’s labours and expenses: we command and strictly order your discretion by apostolic letters, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, that, if you find anything altered by such letters, you restore it to its proper state, and that you cause the said judgments—the definitive judgment, as being just, and the sentences of suspension and excommunication, as having reasonably been pronounced—to be observed inviolate by ecclesiastical censure until due satisfaction has been rendered.

You shall carefully ensure that through your failure the aforesaid master is not further compelled on this account to labour by coming to the Apostolic See; for by reason of this labour he has been severely exhausted, not only in property but also in person.

“Notwithstanding any letters contrary to the truth,” etc. “And if not all of you … let two of you,” etc.

Given at Sora, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXXX. TO THE COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND OTHER FAITHFUL OF THE KINGDOM RESIDING IN APULIA

Concerning assistance to be rendered to the king of Sicily.

[Note: [Col. 1447D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 40.]

Although we have often shown in many ways the affection of love and favour which we bear toward the king and kingdom of Sicily, we now demonstrate it more plainly and expressly in deed, since, pressed by urgent necessity, we have personally entered the kingdom, postponing in great part the other business of the world for this one purpose: namely, that we might restore peace and justice there.

Having therefore, by God’s grace, made a good beginning, we intend to make better progress, so that an excellent end may follow. Accordingly, we admonish and exhort your devotion in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters that, as you hold dear divine, apostolic, and royal favour, you receive gladly and observe effectively, after the example of the other counts, barons, and cities, the ordinance which we have made concerning aid and support for the king and the defence and peace of the kingdom. This ordinance is set forth in a capitulary document sealed with our bull. You shall humbly obey the Master Captains appointed by our command for its execution, lest, if—God forbid—anyone presume to resist, he incur the penalty established in the ordinance itself and we lay our hands heavily upon him both spiritually and temporally.

Since, because of the heat of summer, we cannot at present personally go down into Apulia, we commit the execution of these matters in our stead to our beloved son Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore and legate of the Apostolic See. We have joined to him our beloved son O., our acolyte, sent from our side.

## CXXXI. TO GREGORY, CARDINAL DEACON OF SAINT THEODORE, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, AND TO OUR ACOLYTE O.

Concerning the same matter.

Since, because of the heat of summer, we cannot at present go down into Apulia, we commit our authority to you, that you may lay before the counts, barons, and citizens residing throughout Apulia the ordinance which we have made concerning aid and support for the king and the defence and peace of the kingdom. Induce them, after the example of those who swore in our presence to observe that ordinance, likewise to swear that they will faithfully keep it. Appoint from among them two whom you judge most suitable as Master Captains.

Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to take care to execute this prudently and effectively.

In the name of the Lord. Amen. I, …, shall in good faith observe the ordinance made by Lord Pope Innocent concerning the support and assistance of the lord king and concerning the peace and defence of the kingdom; and, to the best of my ability, I shall cause others to observe it. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

## CXXXII

[Note: [Col. 1448D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 40.]

This is the ordinance which we make concerning the support and assistance of the king and concerning the peace and defence of the kingdom of Sicily. Namely: the noblemen P., count of Celano, and R., count of Fondi, shall be Master Captains, and all in Apulia shall obey them in these matters. Whoever receive this ordinance shall keep peace with one another. If anyone is offended by another, he shall not immediately retaliate against him; rather, he shall lodge his complaint before the aforesaid counts, who shall cause it to be redressed according to the law and custom of the kingdom. Whoever refuses to receive or observe this ordinance shall be regarded as a public enemy and attacked by the rest.

Two hundred knights shall be sent to support and assist the king until the Kalends of September, remaining in service at the expense of those by whom they are sent. They shall be apportioned at the discretion of assessors whom we shall appoint especially for this purpose, with due account taken of the services owed and the resources of the counts, barons, and cities. Provision shall also be made for provisions to be sent for their use.

The cities, counts, and barons shall, at the command of the aforesaid counts, assign at their own expense a fixed number of fighting men whenever war must for this reason be waged against anyone. In all matters we reserve to ourselves full power to add, diminish, alter, and explain, as we shall see expedient.

## CXXXIII. TO THE COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND OTHER FAITHFUL OF THE KINGDOM RESIDING FROM SALERNO TO CEPERANO, FROM SEA TO SEA

Concerning the same matter.

[Col. 1449A]

By authority of this letter we command and direct your whole community that you obey in every respect the noblemen P., count of Celano, and R., count of Fondi, whom we have appointed Master Captains concerning the support and assistance of the king and the peace and defence of the kingdom. Thus our ordinance may through them attain its due effect for the safety and tranquillity of the king and kingdom. You shall obey the statutes and commands of those counts without any contradiction, both regarding knights to be sent into Sicily to assist the king and regarding knights to be furnished against those who might presume to violate the peace of the kingdom, according to the assessment of those who, by our permission, shall distribute those knights at the command of the aforesaid counts.

We specially send the bearer of this letter, our beloved son W., our clerk, so that, after the example of those who swore in our presence to observe the ordinance, he may receive a like oath from the others.

## CXXXIV. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARAGON

Concerning the marriage of Frederick, king of Sicily. (At Sora, on the sixth day before the Ides of August.)

[Note: [Col. 1449D] See above, letter 4.]

We grant apostolic assent for our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious Frederick, king of Sicily, to take in marriage our dearest daughter in Christ, Constance, your sister, formerly queen of Hungary; and we approve what has been settled and granted concerning the two *dodaria*, that is, the marriage donations. As to the third matter, entrusted to our discretion, we direct your serenity as follows: we have judged that a middle course should be adopted. Thus, when all else has been fulfilled according to the tenor of the agreements, that which our providence shall decree in this regard shall be awaited for fulfilment, since it will certainly benefit the matter without a more explicit indication.

Accordingly, we faithfully exhort and carefully admonish your royal prudence that, without further delay, you proceed diligently to the completion of this business; for a far greater door than hitherto has been opened to you.

Given at Sora, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXXXV. TO THE NOBLE RECTORS, CONSULS, CASTELLANS, CITIZENS, AND OUR OTHER FAITHFUL RESIDING THROUGHOUT CAMPANIA

Concerning the currency to be accepted throughout Campania. (At Sora, on the Nones of August.)

Since many impediments arise from the scarcity of *denarii de Flore* and from their weighing, and wishing to provide for the common advantage in this matter, we command and direct your whole community by authority of this letter that henceforth you accept everywhere, in both major and minor transactions, our currency commonly called *de Senatu*, and cause it to be accepted throughout Campania. We strictly forbid anyone henceforth to weigh *denarii de Flore* or demand them for merchandise.

If anyone presumes to demand or weigh them, he shall pay forty solidi to our court as a penalty. Whoever owes census-denarii shall render sixteen *de Senatu* for twelve *de Flore*.

Given at Sora, on the Nones of August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXXXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF AVERSA

Command concerning the first prebend to become vacant. (At Saint-Germain, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 1450B]

Since at present no benefice was vacant in your church which you could confer upon our beloved son S., our acolyte, you promised him that you wished to assign to him the first benefice to become vacant in that church. When this came to our knowledge, we caused it to be proposed to you that you reserve for our grant the first prebendal benefice to become vacant in your church, to be conferred upon a suitable person. You freely accepted this.

Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you take care to reserve for our grant the first prebendal benefice which becomes vacant in your church.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXXXVII. TO THE ABBOT AND CLERICS OF SAINT MARY OF THE RIVER AT CECCANO

Concerning confirmation of privileges. (At Sora, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September.)

[Note: [Col. 1449] See vol. I of *Italia Sacra*, p. 725, and in the appendix, p. 483.]

“Yielding to the just requests of petitioners,” etc., “we receive under our protection,” etc., your persons and the church of Saint Mary of the River, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all the ecclesiastical and temporal goods which you at present rightfully possess, etc.

In particular, we confirm to you and, through you, to the same church by apostolic authority, and safeguard by the protection of this present writing, the churches of Saint Stephen and Saint Quiricus with all their holdings and appurtenances; the forest beside the church of Saint Stephen; [property] from the head of the bridge of Prato and of Gineis; mills; vineyards beside that church; another vineyard which you bought in the place called Marana; revenues, tithes, offerings, persons, gardens, and other possessions belonging to your church, just as you possess them lawfully and peacefully.

We also hold ratified the liberties, immunities, and exemptions from secular exactions granted with pious foresight by our beloved son, the nobleman John of Ceccano, to you and your church; and, as we have seen these contained in the original instrument of that nobleman, we decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. We have deemed it fitting to insert their tenor word for word in this document.

“In the name of the Lord. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1196, the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III, the fourteenth indiction, on 24 July. On this day I, John of Ceccano, in the presence of Lord Jordan, Cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, my most dear uncle, and of the venerable bishops Berard of Ferentino, Peter of Segni, John of Anagni, Taddeus of Alatri, Oddo of Veroli, and Thedelegarius of Terracina, and of many persons from all Campania and the Maritime region, both clerics and laymen, moved by divine love and for the redemption of my soul and of [Col. 1451B] my parents, past, present, and future, grant to the church of Saint Mary of the River, to Lord Landulf, beloved abbot of that church, and to its entire household, clerical and lay, present and future, full and perpetual liberty, renouncing the *data* [customary due], evil custom, and every exaction. And if anyone, for whatever crime committed, takes refuge in this church, neither I nor my successors, either personally or through my officials, shall inflict any violence or injury upon him while he is there—unless he has plotted my death, that of my heirs, betrayal of my castles, or the burning of those castles.

“I shall in no way interfere in the appointment or removal of clerics. But if a cleric or layman of the same church should at any time offend, the abbot together with the clerics in their chapter shall compel him to render justice, saving the right of patronage. Therefore, by the common counsel of Lord Cardinal Jordan and of all the bishops, and with the consent of Lord John of Ceccano, it is established that whoever acts contrary to this grant shall be bound by the bond of anathema and shall have a portion with Dathan and Abiram. For greater security, lest what has been done come into oblivion through the passage of time, we ordered the priest Benedict, our beloved notary, to write this, and caused the charter itself to be marked with the protection of our seal.”

Therefore let no one … our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc.

[Col. 1451D] Given at Sora, 19 August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF TROYES.

Written against the canons of Saint Martin of Troyes. (Sora, 16 August.)

Having carefully heard and perceptively understood the depositions of the witnesses received by our order in the case conducted between our beloved son P., the elect, on one side, and V., L., and A., canons of the church of Saint Martin of Troyes, on the other, we have, by the counsel of our brethren, judged that the same elect should be absolved from their accusation. By apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to require [Col. 1452A] the aforesaid elect, concerning the stain of simoniacal depravity alleged against him, canonically to clear himself with a third hand of his order; and, after he has cleared himself, to cause all the canons to render him the obedience and reverence due to him, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure without regard to appeal.

Divide from one another the aforesaid canons, who are known to have acted maliciously against that elect in many ways—as some of them freely confessed before us—and place them in other monasteries to do penance, assigning each to a separate house, so that the aforesaid church, grievously afflicted by their insolence, may recover its breath.

Given at Sora, 16 August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate. [Col. 1452B]

### CXXXIX. TO THE BROTHERS JOHN OF CARBONE AND BENEDICT.

Confirmation of an exchange made between them and the monastery of Monte Cassino. (Sora, 12 August.)

To the just desires of petitioners, etc., through “fulfil.” Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclined by your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this writing the reasonably made exchange between our beloved sons Roffrid, Cardinal-Priest of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, abbot, and the convent of Monte Cassino on one side, and yourselves on the other, concerning certain persons whom our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious king of Sicily, had granted to you, son John, and to your heirs in the castle of Plumbarola. In exchange for them, the aforesaid abbot and monks granted you a certain strip of land in the territory of that castle. This exchange was prudently made without wrongdoing, freely accepted by both parties, and is more fully contained in the instrument drawn up for it. For greater clarity, we have caused the instrument itself to be inserted word for word in this document.

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the year of his Incarnation 1208, the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Frederick, most glorious king, in July, on the eighteenth day of that month, in the eleventh indiction. We, Roffrid, by God’s grace cardinal and [Col. 1452D] abbot of Monte Cassino, declare that we received instructions from our aforesaid lord Frederick, by God’s grace most illustrious king, that we should assign to you, John of Carbone, son of Richard Benedict de Falco, the persons and revenues which the royal court had formerly held in our castle of Plumbarola, and which John of Ariano had formerly held by grant of that same court: namely, the holding of Deacon John Guinisi with his household; the holding of John Peter Guinisi; the holding of Leonard Guinisi; the holding of Roffrid John Boni; the holding of Richard John Sensi; the holding of Benedict de Taddeo; the holding of John de Litto; and the holding of Vigorita de Roffrido.

“But because it seemed burdensome to us to assign them to you, since we held the whole castle of Plumbarola in our demesne and it appeared that granting any of these persons to another would result in loss to [Col. 1453A] our monastery, you brought letters of request from our aforesaid lord king to our lord Pope Innocent, that the same lord pope might require us to fulfil that royal command. Therefore, by order of the aforesaid lord pope and lord king, with the consent of our brethren, and having with us Master Berengarius, judge and advocate of Monte Cassino, and with your consent, you aforesaid John, by reason of exchange we grant through this charter held by *libellus* tenure to you, the brothers John and Benedict, sons of the aforesaid Richard, our strip of land in the territory of the aforesaid castle of Plumbarola.

“It has these boundaries: on the first side, the public road; on the second, the land of the heirs of Guttefrid, the land of Peter de Ruben, the land of Peter de Juliano, and the land of the heirs of Donatus; on the third side, the public road; on the fourth, the land of Peter, son of the aforesaid Master Berengarius. Within these boundaries we grant you, John and Benedict, this strip of land, with everything situated there above and below, and with its right of entry and exit, by *libellus* tenure and by reason of exchange, to be under your authority and that of your heirs, to hold, possess, and do with it whatever you please for twenty-nine years. Each year, however, on the feast of Saint Benedict, you shall render to the monastery of Monte Cassino eight Amalfitan tari as rent.

“When the twenty-nine years have elapsed, we, or our successors, or the representatives of our monastery, must renew this *libellus* for you or your heirs for one ounce of gold. In this exchange we have received from you, the aforesaid John, all the persons and revenues granted to you by the aforesaid royal court; these we recognize to be far more useful to our monastery than the aforesaid strip of land which we have granted you. We therefore bind ourselves, our successors, and the representatives of our monastery to defend and warrant that strip of land to you and your heirs from this day until the aforesaid time against all persons and all parties.

“But if we do not defend it for you and fulfil all the aforesaid provisions, or if by any contrivance we attempt to invalidate this exchange or reject this charter in any respect, we bind ourselves, our successors, and the representatives of our monastery to pay to you and your heirs a penalty double the value of the aforesaid persons and revenues received from you, the aforesaid John; and furthermore this writing shall remain firm until the aforesaid time. Thus we, Roffrid, by God’s grace cardinal and abbot of Monte Cassino, with the consent of our brethren and having with us the aforesaid judge and advocate of Monte Cassino, have done what seemed suitable to us, and ordered you, Nicholas, our notary and public notary of the city of Saint Germanus, to write this charter. Done in the aforesaid monastery of Monte Cassino.

“I, the aforesaid Roffrid, by God’s grace cardinal and abbot of Monte Cassino. I, Brother Peter, Count of Monte Cassino, dean. I, Brother Vitalis, priest and monk. I, Brother Senioretus, priest and monk. I, Brother Peter, priest and monk. I, Brother Philip of Sora, priest and monk. I, Brother Lando of Monte Cassino, hospitaller. I, Brother John of Monte Cassino, vestry-keeper. I, Brother Maurus, priest and monk. I, Brother Roger, priest and monk. I, Brother Thomas, priest and monk. I, Brother Clement, priest and monk. I, Brother Girard, priest and monk. I, Brother John P., priest and monk. I, Brother Adenulf, deacon and monk. I, Brother Lando, deacon and monk. I, Brother Otto, deacon and monk. I, Brother John, [Col. 1454B] deacon and monk. I, Brother Alexander, deacon and monk. I, Brother Roffrid, deacon and monk. I, Brother Robert, deacon and monk. I, Brother John, deacon and monk. I, Brother Jeremiah, deacon and monk. I, Brother Philip, subdeacon and monk. I, Brother Simon, subdeacon and monk.”

Therefore let no one … our confirmation, etc. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, etc.

Given at Sora, 12 August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXL. TO THE MASTER OF THE KNIGHTS OF SAINT JAMES.

Reply to his inquiries. (Sora, 1 September.)

[Col. 1454C] On your behalf it was submitted before us that a certain knight, as he himself asserts, while confined by illness made profession only among the brothers of Grandmont, but did not receive the habit. When he had afterwards recovered his health and humbly requested it, the aforesaid brothers refused to grant it to him unless he brought with him the price of his inheritance; nor would they grant him leave to transfer to another religious order. The aforesaid knight then came to a certain house of the Knights of Saint James; there, having made profession, he received the regular habit, while the brethren of that house were wholly unaware of the preceding facts. You therefore asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See whether his bare assertion should be believed, so that he should depart from the aforesaid house, or whether he ought to remain in it, in which [Col. 1454D] he undoubtedly received the habit after making profession.

We answer your inquiry as follows: since the rule of the Order of Grandmont is far stricter than yours, no obstacle whatsoever should be placed in the way of one who especially wishes to return to it.

Moreover, your devotion asked us whether, since several brothers of the Knights of Saint James, having received leave from your predecessors—which, according to the institution of the order, ought not to be denied to those who ask—have chosen a stricter life outside the house entrusted to you, at that house’s expense, you may recall them to the community when this appears expedient to the same house, so that they may lead among the brethren the stricter life which they have chosen, as an example of better conduct. To this we briefly reply that, since no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God, none of such persons is to be brought back to the place which he prudently left for the kingdom of God, unless, because of pressing necessity or manifest advantage, a special exception is granted to someone by dispensation of the Apostolic See.

Given at Sora, 1 September, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXLI. TO THE BISHOPS OF LONDON, ELY, AND WORCESTER.

Concerning the case of the Church of Canterbury. (Sora, 22 August.)

[Note: [Col. 1455D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapters 131–132.] Far be it from us that we should deservedly be compared with those whom the Psalmist rebukes, saying: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Psalm 77 [78]); lest perhaps—may the supreme Shepherd avert it!—we also be compared to the hireling who, according to the Gospel parable, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. Rather, we are prepared to set ourselves as a wall before those coming up against the house of the Lord from the opposing side, and, if necessity should require it, to give our life for our sheep.

Although we desire that fullest peace be restored between kingdom and priesthood in England, wishing, so far as lies in us, to have peace with all people, nevertheless anyone labours in vain who attempts, either by another’s suggestions or by his own arguments, to persuade that on any occasion we wish to turn aside, to right [Col. 1455C] or left, against ecclesiastical liberty. For the cause of this conflict unquestionably tends to this end: that the Church of God, which lay enslaved, may arise liberated.

Therefore, by this communication we make your prudence fully aware that, turning your hearing altogether away from vain suggestions—which are indeed promptings sent through evil angels—you are faithfully to proceed according to the tenor and form of our mandates, setting aside every malicious interpretation. Namely, you are neither earlier nor otherwise to relax the sentence of interdict than after our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English, receives and treats our venerable brother Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, as Archbishop of Canterbury; after he has given such security, both to the archbishop and his men, as seems suitable in your prudent judgment; after he has made full restoration of what was taken away, both to that archbishop and to the monks of the Church of Canterbury, as well as to other churches and persons; after he has permitted those monks to return to their church and remain there in safety; and after he has conferred and assigned all the temporal rights (*regalia*) to the same archbishop, either personally or, if he prefers, through you acting in our stead. Thus the archbishop shall be bound to the king for these rights as his predecessors were bound to the king’s forefathers, prudent care being taken that no fraud arise from this, in any point, against [Col. 1456A] ecclesiastical liberty. When these things have been duly done, relax the sentence of interdict, causing the aforesaid archbishop, as is fitting, to proceed to the Church of Canterbury.

But if any question should arise concerning any of these matters such as may reasonably be doubted, then, after first receiving from the king suitable security that he will obey our counsel and mandate concerning it, nonetheless relax the sentence of interdict. If witnesses who have been named withdraw, through favour, hatred, or fear, from bearing testimony to the truth, compel them to do so by ecclesiastical censure without regard to appeal; so that, when the truth has been investigated and ascertained, whatever remains incomplete because of the question which has arisen concerning restoration of the property taken away, compensation for damages, and satisfaction for injuries, may be completed by apostolic counsel and command.

This is the tenor of our mandates according to their prudent and straightforward meaning. We clearly expressed it in our letters and carefully explained it to our beloved son, the abbot of Beaulieu, envoy of the aforesaid king. We therefore judge it not merely unworthy but impious if anyone, in sacrilegious boldness, says or believes that we expounded our intention to one in one way and to another in another way, deceitfully changing it; for the Apostolic See, by God’s grace, possesses both the prudence of the serpent and the simplicity of the dove.

Furthermore, know that it has been reported to us that, although all monks of the Cistercian order in England had begun jointly to observe the sentence of interdict, after a few days some began to celebrate services on their own authority, while others began to celebrate only much later by order of the [Note: [Col. 1456D] See below, letters 213, 258, 259.] Cistercian abbot; some still observe the interdict. Now, if, as we remember having answered you in other letters, religious men had from the outset been permitted, under the tenor of their privileges, to celebrate the divine offices with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, doors shut, bells not rung, and voices subdued, this would neither have troubled us nor been unfitting.

Nevertheless, if the sentence is weakened or the affair impaired because some have proceeded to celebrate, whatever the occasion—whether because of that clause granted them by the Apostolic See, namely that no letters obtained against the tenor of apostolic privileges, while concealing the name of the Cistercian order, shall have force; or because of the foregoing answer, which perhaps reached them through someone’s disclosure—you, supported by our authority, are confidently to determine what you judge expedient for the affair and cause what you determine to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, without regard to appeal.

Moreover, prudently admonish and effectively induce the aforesaid king to carry out without delay or any difficulty the things promised and offered on his behalf through the said abbot of Beaulieu, as set forth above. For without doubt it accords both with his advantage and his salvation that he be regarded by all as having more fully obtained the favour and grace of the Apostolic See. Nor could we refrain from making our hand heavy upon him if his heart should persist in being hardened, so that he did not care to make satisfaction to God and the Church.

Given at Sora, 22 August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXLII. TO THE BISHOP OF MEAUX AND THE ARCHDEACON OF PARIS.

That notorious and criminal persons are not to hold prebends in the Church of Chartres. (Sora, 15 September.)

[Col. 1457B] Our beloved sons P., provost, S. G., and H., together with certain other canons of Chartres, formerly reported and showed us that an ancient and approved custom has prevailed in the Church of Chartres, to the observance of which the bishop of the place is bound by oath: whenever a prebend is vacant, he chooses a suitable person for it and presents the person chosen to the dean, cantor, subdean, and succentor, to whom unquestionably belongs the right either to approve the person presented, if deserving, or to reject him. Once approved, the dean presents him in the chapter’s name to the bishop, so that the bishop may invest him with the prebend.

Now, when our venerable brother the Bishop of Chartres had recently chosen a certain chamberlain of his, namely R. de Salneriis, for a prebend in the aforesaid church and had presented him, in accordance with the aforesaid custom, to the dean, cantor, subdean, and succentor of that church, the dean, being certain that the man was stained with many public infamies—as one guilty of theft, sacrilege, usury, and of breaking testaments made by dying persons in their last wills, in order to divert legacies intended for pious purposes to his own and others’ uses—refused to receive him. He raised objections against him, appealed to the Apostolic See, and offered lawfully to prove that the said chamberlain laboured under public infamy on these counts. The aforesaid complainants requested an inquiry.

We therefore instructed our beloved sons, the abbot of Sarnaï, the prior of Saint Victor, and the dean of Saint Germanus of Auxerre at Paris, by our letters to investigate these matters carefully, ascertain the truth, decide what was canonical without regard to appeal, and cause what they decreed to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. As we have learned from their letters, proceeding in the case according to our command, they went to Chartres on the day appointed for the parties. After conducting the diligent inquiry required by the apostolic mandate, they found that the said chamberlain not only laboured under public infamy but was also implicated in the aforementioned crimes. Having returned to Paris and taken the counsel there of good and prudent men, [Col. 1458A] they imposed silence upon him concerning the prebend of the Church of Chartres which he sought; suspended him from every ecclesiastical office and benefice; and condemned him to restore the property of those whom he had wickedly despoiled by various thefts—namely, usury, the sale of marriages, and the breaking of testaments—retaining his ecclesiastical benefices in our hands.

Although the said chamberlain came into our presence and asked us to provide for him concerning the sentence of those judges, he was unable to obtain anything from us because the report of those judges had not yet reached us. But since both the letters of those judges and the attestations received by them, which they took care to send us sealed with their seals, have plainly established that the said chamberlain was implicated in the crimes set forth above, we approve what they did. By apostolic writings we strictly command your discretion that, notwithstanding other letters which he falsely claims to have obtained concerning the same business—since those letters have no bearing upon this case and were not obtained in the same matter, for the former direct proceedings concerning certain crimes by way of exception, whereas these direct an inquiry into crimes, as was plainly established by the careful argument held before us—you cause what the aforesaid judges have done to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure, without regard to appeal.

Moreover, so that others who hear of this may learn more cautiously to abstain from similar acts, firmly require the Bishop of Chartres on our behalf henceforth wholly to exclude persons of this sort from his familiar household. Since such things may be imputed to him, he should fear and dread that, having abused both divine and our patience, a graver punishment may be inflicted upon him.

Given at Sora, 15 September, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXLIII. TO THE BISHOP AND CLERGY OF NARNI.

That they are to observe the interdict pronounced upon the city. (Sora.)

[Note: [Col. 1457D] See *Gesta Innocentii III*, chapter 16.] Since the people of Narni have been so given over to a reprobate mind [Col. 1458D] that, having now fallen into the depths of vice, they show contempt, we, who by the office imposed upon us are bound to correct the errors of each, unable any longer to endure their insolence, subject their city to a most stringent interdict. Thus no divine office and absolutely no ecclesiastical sacrament is to be celebrated there, except only, at the point of death, penance for the dying and baptism for infants.

We utterly forbid burial, so that anyone who presumes to bury any of them in a Christian cemetery beside a church shall know himself bound by the bond of excommunication. We likewise forbid anyone to trade with them; and whoever, contrary to the apostolic prohibition, attempts in these matters to associate with them shall know that he is to be bound in the snare of excommunication, and otherwise punished by us temporally if he is subject to our temporal jurisdiction.

Therefore, lest you be defiled by their society, since he who touches pitch is defiled by it, by the authority of these presents we command your whole body and strictly enjoin upon you in virtue of obedience that you all leave the city of these evildoers and live in the surrounding places wherever you can do so more conveniently and honourably. Announce to them that, unless they repent of their contumacy, since they have rendered themselves and their city unworthy of episcopal dignity—if indeed it may be called a city when, by its sin, it will be deprived of the honour of being a city—we shall remove the episcopal see from them and divide its parish among neighbouring dioceses. Nevertheless, to you, brother bishop, whom we know to be obedient and devoted, we shall grant suitable compensation. Otherwise, God willing, we shall crush their stiff-neckedness spiritually and temporally to such an extent that, under the enormous weight of oppression brought upon them, they will recognize how grievous is the hand of the Church upon those who contemptuously reject God and the Church with hardened heart.

Accordingly, we command your devotion inviolably to observe the foregoing and to cause others to observe it, lest, if you do otherwise—which we do not believe—their guilt redound to your punishment. Announce that they have been declared outside our protection, [Col. 1459C] and enjoin all our faithful to assail them as persons outside our protection.

Given at Sora, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXLIV. TO THE ABBOTS OF VENDÔME, IN THE DIOCESE OF CHARTRES, AND OF SAINT JULIAN OF TOURS, AND TO THE PRIOR OF MARMOUTIER, TOURS.

Concerning the correction of the monastery of Bourgueil. (Sora, 20 September.)

We have examined, as included in the summonses, the tenor of letters said to have been presented to you on our behalf concerning the correction of the monastery of Bourgueil, which you sent to our beloved sons Luke, abbot, and the convent of that monastery. Yet, if you possessed the discernment proper to you, you could at least have believed that those letters did not proceed with our knowledge because you ought by no means to have considered us so inconstant and changeable that, after we had shortly before, and not without diligent concern, caused that monastery to be beneficially reformed through delegates appointed by us, we should recently have wished to overturn what had been well done and, under the pretext of a renewed correction, to trouble the restored discipline of monastic religion there.

Moreover, this ought to have shown you that the aforesaid letters did not issue with our knowledge: since the monastery is extremely well known to us, not only by its public name but also through its many affairs, which have frequently occupied us amid the pressing demands of our office, it is not plausible that we should have written of its monks as “of Burguol,” as those letters state, using the French idiom, whereas in Latin speech we are accustomed to call them “Burgulienses,” men of Bourgueil. In this, doubtless, it is detected that, if those letters proceeded in any manner from our chancery, it was fraudulently: an unfamiliar French name was used so that, by the accustomed Latin designation, the monastery itself might not become known to us.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we strictly command your discretion that, if you have not yet proceeded under those letters, you presume in no way to proceed under them; and that, if perhaps you have taken any action on their account, you wholly revoke it, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. Take diligent care that, after considering everything which you judge should be considered concerning those letters, if you are able yourselves to discover their falsity, you punish, without regard to appeal and according to the penalty enacted against forgers, both those who procured them and those who knowingly used them. But if you cannot discover their falsity yourselves, do not delay to send them to us enclosed in your letters. Take care to execute our mandate in such a way that it need not be fulfilled through another.

Otherwise, we have directed the abbots of Clermont, Chaloceio [uncertain reading], and Buxeria, of the Cistercian order in the dioceses of Le Mans and Angers, that if you fail to execute this mandate, they are not, after one month, to delay its execution without regard to appeal. If not all [are able to act], let two of you, etc. …

Given at Sora, 20 September, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXLV. TO LUKE, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF BOURGUEIL, AND TO HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY.

[Note: [Col. 1459D] See above, book X, letter 14.] Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Sora, 21 September.)

[Note: [Col. 1459D] See vol. IV of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 206.] Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest perhaps an attack of any rashness [Col. 1460D] either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions, and, after the example of Pope Silvester, our predecessor of happy memory [Note: [Col. 1460D] See ibid., p. 202.], receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter of Bourgueil, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the protection of this present writing. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which is recognized as having been instituted in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall remain there for all time, etc. Moreover, whatever possessions [Col. 1461A] etc. the same monastery now justly and reasonably possesses, etc., shall remain in perpetuity, among which are these, by their proper names, etc.:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its possessions and appurtenances. The estate of Bourgueil, with the church of Saint Germanus and the church of Saint Nicholas, and all revenues pertaining to that estate and churches. Likewise, the church of Chouzé on the river Loire, with its port and everything belonging to it. In the district of Tours, three fourth-parts from the benefice of the knight Carbon. Likewise, from the aforesaid knight, four fourth-parts of the estate of Souzay. Likewise, one half of the estate of Cassenias, with one half of the church of Saint Mary and all revenues pertaining to that half. Likewise, the church of Saint [Col. 1461B] Hilary, with one half of the estate of Vosalia and all its revenues. Likewise, certain purchases: that is, the village of Cruolio with what pertains to it. Likewise, the church of Saint Denis on the estate of Galnaica, and whatever pertains to that church or altar. Likewise, the villages called Boorias, Canavas, and Laliacum, and whatever belongs to them. Likewise, a church in honour of Saint Hilary, with the estate of Fusciacum and what pertains to it. Likewise, the church established in honour of Saint Mary at Bellomonte, with its tithes and revenues. Also vineyards, meadows, and houses, wherever situated around the castle of Fontenay, which Emma, Countess of Poitiers, of good memory [Note: [Col. 1461D] See vol. IV of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 201.], [Col. 1461C] founder of the same monastery, bestowed upon the monastery of Saint Peter of Bourgueil through pious generosity.

Likewise, the church in honour of Saint Stephen, with the whole village called Lotias. Likewise, the entire village of Cassania. Likewise, the church of Saint Christopher with the whole village and fair, together with the vicariate and toll in their entirety, free from the lordship of any person. Likewise, the village called Aldefred’s Brolium. Also the church of Oziacum with the whole village. Likewise, these villages: namely Podium Caninum, or the royal estate of Limoges; Podium Letardi of Donnavineda; the holding of Ledramnus and Aloda; and the village adjacent to the aforesaid Cassanum. The church in honour of Saint Martin, with the whole village called Villaris. Likewise, two villages, namely Drogiacum and Turtum. Likewise, four fourth-parts in the village of Odriniacum. In the district of Aunis [Col. 1461D], two churches, one in honour of Saint Peter and the other of Saint Nazarius, situated at Ingolinas above the seashore. Likewise, the prebend of Saint Martin from the royal abbey, as those who serve within receive it. Likewise, the prebend of Saint Martin of the town of Condat, with the churches, houses, and meadows belonging to it.

In the district of Évreux, the estate called Coldra and the village called Francavilla, with their churches and all their appurtenances, and one third of Longavilla on the river Seine. The priory of Saint Christopher of Châteaufort, with its parish churches and other appurtenances. The priory of Saint Saturninus of Cabrosia, with its parish [Col. 1462A] churches and other appurtenances. The priory of Saint Martin of Palatiolum; the priory of Saint Peter of Limos; the priory of Saint Mary of Plaisiacum; and the priory of Saint Andrew of Nielfa, with their parish churches and other appurtenances. Also the priories of Consannivilla, Espelteriolis, Bancort, Turtiniacum, Niolio, Saint Leodegarius, Saint Andrew of the castle of Mirebeau, Saint Porcarius within the city of Poitiers, Saint Hilary, Gorgeium of Raiatia, Faya, Saint Mary of Perusia, Saint Mary of Bellolocus in the city of Angoulême, Gratiacum, Trau, Coz, Someracum, Saint Melanius of the castle of Chinon, Saint Michael, Ingrandes, Darevalle, Essartis, Escol, Bremio, and the island [Col. 1462B] of Ulgerius, with their parish churches and other appurtenances. The parish church of Holy Cross at Tours; the parish church of Varennes; the parish church of Secundiacum; and the parish church of Oleta, with the revenues which you ought to receive from them. The estate of Plessiacum, the estate of Callonia, the estate of Millevrelo, the estate of Brollia, the estate of Roche-Monachus, and the estate of Buccellum, with its parish church and other appurtenances.

By the authority of these presents, we also forbid any bishop of whatsoever city to presume to hold a council in the same monastery without the consent and will of the abbot and monks of that place, as was established by our aforesaid predecessor with the consent of Raynald, then bishop of Angers [Col. 1462C]. Moreover, let the churches of your monastery, wherever they are situated, remain free from disturbance by any bishop, archdeacon, or other person, except for the synodal payment, or that which is commonly called *circada* or *parata*. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, etc., as far as “they shall provide for the election of one according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict.” When a general interdict of the land is in force, etc., as far as “celebrate.” Likewise concerning your peace and tranquillity, etc., as far as “presume to exercise.”

Moreover, by the authority of these presents we forbid anyone to presume to demand or extort from you tithes from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the feed of your animals. [Col. 1462D] It shall also be lawful for you to retain free clerics or laymen, etc., as far as “retain.” But chrism, holy oil, etc., as far as “render anything.” Otherwise it shall be lawful for you, etc., as far as “supply what is requested.” Furthermore, we entirely forbid new and unlawful exactions to be imposed by archbishops, bishops, or deans, or by any other ecclesiastical or secular persons.
