Likewise concerning burial, etc., as far as “bodies are carried away.” We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to disturb the aforesaid monastery, etc., as far as “profitable in every way for its uses,” while preserving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., [Col. 1463A] as far as “shall be subject to vengeance.” But may all who preserve the rights of that place, etc., as far as “find the rewards of eternal peace.”

Given at Sora, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [21 September], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

### CXLVI. TO THE RECTORS OF THE ROMAN FRATERNITY

A response to their inquiries. (Sora, tenth day before the Kalends of October [22 September].)

Concerning a man who, having followed military camps from his youth, took in marriage a woman who had successively been the concubine of two men, and who, after having children by her, assumed the religious habit after her eventual death: we judge that this answer should be given to you: as you ought not to be unaware, he must by no means be promoted to sacred orders. If perhaps he has been promoted, he must not be retained in the order thus received—especially if notice concerning such irregularity was given to him and to his ordainer, and, after it had been disregarded, he was ordained. Further, a person who passes from a stricter religious order to one less strict is not to be retained in the latter, unless perhaps a dispensation has been granted him, on account of weakness, illness, or another reasonable cause, by one who had power to dispense.

But we considered questions of this sort trifling—indeed, nonexistent—and such that there was no need to consult either the Fathers of the City or the Father of the World, since, being settled by canon law, they are plainly not found to contain any difficulty. [Col. 1463C] Yet you added a difficult question to easy ones, beginning with the smallest and reaching the greatest; indeed, when we carefully unfolded these questions, we felt your inquiry to have grown weightier, like an amphora emerging from the wheel which had been turning to fashion a little jar. [Note: [Col. 1463D] Chapter “*De homine*,” *De celebratione missarum*.]

For you asked us what should be thought of an unwary priest who, knowing himself to stand in mortal sin, doubts whether, because of awareness of his crime, he ought to celebrate the solemnities of Mass which he cannot omit owing to some necessity; and who, being gravely constrained by two alternatives, fears, while carrying out the divine ministry [Note: [Col. 1463D] In the third Collect, “mystery.”], to offend the people waiting for it, and shrinks from consecrating Christ’s body lest, by receiving it unworthily, he eat and [Col. 1463D] drink judgment upon himself. After completing the other observances, he pretends to celebrate Mass, suppresses the words by which Christ’s body is consecrated, and consumes only unconsecrated bread and wine, believing that by what he outwardly represents he satisfies the people, while by what he intends he ought not to provoke God.

Since false remedies, which are more serious than real dangers, must be rejected, although one who, owing to consciousness of his crime, considers himself unworthy ought reverently to abstain from such a sacrament—and therefore sins grievously if he irreverently presents himself for it—nevertheless he undoubtedly seems to offend who presumes fraudulently to simulate it in this way. [Col. 1464A] For the former, while avoiding guilt as he acts, falls into the hands of the merciful Lord alone; whereas the latter, while avoiding guilt by committing guilt, binds himself not only to God, whom he does not fear to mock, but also to the people whom he deceives.

Given at Sora, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October [22 September], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXLVII. TO THE RECTOR AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW IN SILICE AT LUCCA

The question concerning the election of the rector of that hospital is decided. (Sora, fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August].)

[Note: [Col. 1463D] Chapter “*Cum olim*,” *On arbitrators*.] When formerly a dispute arose between you and our beloved son [Col. 1464B] the prior of the church of Saint Bartholomew of Lucca concerning the election of a rector and brethren in your hospital, before the prior of Saint Fridianus and the primicerius of Saint Martin of Lucca, judges delegated by the Apostolic See; and when both parties, submitting the matter to those same judges, promised that they would abide by their arbitration; and when the judges judged that a definite award should be delivered: a doubt has arisen on both sides concerning the award delivered, which you requested to have declared by the Apostolic See.

We therefore carefully inspected the public instrument containing the award, and learned that, according to its terms, the prior of Saint Bartholomew of Lucca is bound to take counsel with the household of that hospital and discuss with it the finding of a rector; but whether the household agrees or disagrees with the prior, the same prior [Col. 1464C] must in either case elect the rector. Therefore, we declare that unless the prior has discussed the finding of a rector with the household of the hospital and sought its advice, he has no power to elect a rector; and if he elects a rector otherwise, his election must be held null and void.

But [Note: [Col. 1464D] In the third Collection, “*Unde*.” Yet the Vatican manuscripts have *Verum*, as here.] once he has taken counsel with the household and discussed the finding of a rector, the prior may freely elect a rector, provided only that he is suitable, whether the household agrees or disagrees with him concerning the choice of rector. But lest, when the household agrees upon a suitable person, the prior maliciously disagree with it, we strictly command, under the solemn invocation of divine judgment, that the prior not maliciously reject the suitable person upon whom the household has agreed, but elect him rector with its counsel and deliberation. [Col. 1464D] Thus, if he rashly proceeds contrary to this strict command, after this has been sufficiently demonstrated before his superior, both his election shall be annulled and he himself canonically punished.

Although, according to the terms of the award, brethren who are to be admitted to this hospital ought to be received through the hands of the aforesaid prior, promising him obedience, nevertheless, lest the prior maliciously refuse to receive brethren, so that, after those now present have died and no others have been substituted in their place, he may more freely arrange the hospital as he wishes, we command under the aforesaid strict sanction [Col. 1465A] that the prior not maliciously procure a deficiency of brethren, but, with the consent of the rector and household of the hospital, receive brethren without difficulty whenever necessity requires. If he disregards this order, after he has been convicted of such presumption, then, besides the canonical punishment which he deserves to have inflicted upon him, the rector and household shall on that occasion establish in the hospital such brethren as are necessary, without consulting him at all.

Given at Sora, on the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CXLVIII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF COLDRIZ, OF THE PREMONSTRATENSIAN ORDER

Confirmation of privileges. (Sora, seventh day before the Kalends of September [26 August].)

[Col. 1465B]

When what is just and honourable is sought from us, etc., as far as “effect.” Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, willingly concurring with your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and the place in which you are devoted to divine service, together with everything which you presently possess reasonably, or may hereafter, God willing, acquire by just means. In particular, we confirm to you and, through you, to your house by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the place of Neubon with Capella, the church of Acastre, a portion of the revenues of the church of Cuventona, the pasture of Destwissel, and the land and pasture of Chautim, as you justly and peacefully possess all these things. [Col. 1465C] Let no one, therefore, … infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, etc. But if anyone, etc., as far as “shall incur.”

Given at Sora, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September [26 August], etc., as in the other letter.

### CXLIX. TO THE CHAPTER OF TOURS

(Ferentino, fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October].)

Having carefully heard and clearly understood all that was proposed and alleged before us by the parties concerning the two elections held in your church, and since it has been plainly established to us thereby that the party which elected our beloved son [Note: [Col. 1465D] Robert de Vitré.] the cantor of Paris was far inferior both in authority and in number, and did not fear to elect him outside the chapter, without consulting many [Col. 1465D] of the brethren and in contempt of a lawful appeal, we have judged, as justice required, that the election made of him must be annulled.

But because the other party, which elected our beloved son [Note: [Col. 1465D] John de Faya.] your dean, was much greater both in authority and number, although it elected him after four appeals, yet because two of these were not lawful and therefore did not have to be respected, and nothing was attempted contrary to the remaining two; and since his person has been commended to us in many ways by the testimony of many, while absolutely nothing has been proved against him by the opposing party, we have, with the common counsel of our brethren, caused the election made of him to be confirmed by apostolic authority. [Col. 1466A] [Note: [Col. 1466D] See vol. I of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 774.] Therefore, by apostolic writing, we command your devotion that henceforth you take care to render him, as your shepherd, obedience and reverence both due and devoted.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CL. THE FOLLOWING LETTER LACKS AN ADDRESS IN THE OLD CODEX

Concerning the election of the abbess of Mantignano. (Sora.)

From our original letters, which we had sent to our beloved sons, the abbot of Plana de Septimo and the Camaldolese prior, concerning the election of the nuns of Saint Mary of Mantignano in the Florentine diocese, it has been plainly established to us [Col. 1466B] that the final clause of those letters was wickedly erased and that the same letters were presented to those judges in such form as we clearly learned from the letters of the same judges, in which their text was contained. On that occasion the said judges presumed to proceed.

Because this must not be passed over by us with our eyes closed, by apostolic writing we command your discretion to annul completely whatever was done on the occasion of those letters [“annul” is supplied by the editor], and, setting aside the obstacle of appeal, to punish as a forger whomever you know falsified the aforesaid letters. Moreover, because the liberty of that monastery is declared by a privilege of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, which we ourselves have inspected, we will and command [Col. 1466C] that unless our venerable brother the bishop of Florence shows and proves before you within two months why the said monastery may not enjoy that same liberty, you impose perpetual silence upon him concerning this matter. Afterwards examine the election of the nuns and the woman elected; and if you find that it was canonically celebrated in the person of one who is suitable, confirm her by our authority, setting aside the obstacle of appeal.

Given at Sora, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CLI. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF CARDICA

He is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Ferentino, third day before the Nones of October [5 October].)

[Col. 1466D] [Note: [Col. 1466D] See book XVI, letter 115.] To the just desires of petitioners, etc., as far as “fulfil.” Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, inclining to your petitions and those presented to our apostolate on this matter by our venerable brother the archbishop of Larissa, we forbid by the authority of these presents anyone rashly to presume to molest you concerning the benefice of Cardica and Valestino, which the same archbishop has granted you through provident generosity. Let no one at all … infringe this page of our prohibition, etc., as far as “oppose.” But if anyone presumes to attempt this, etc., as far as “shall incur.”

Given at Ferentino, on the third day before the Nones of October [5 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CLII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF PATRAS AND THEBES, AND THE BISHOP OF THERMOPYLAE

That they are to admonish the lady of Thessalonica concerning her duty. (Ferentino, fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October].)

[Col. 1467A]

The more sincerely in the Lord we love in Christ our beloved daughter, the noble woman, widow of the marquis of Montferrat, lady of Thessalonica, the more earnestly we judge that she should be admonished to strive to pass this brief span of corruptible life in purity of innocence, so that she may deserve to attain the joy of eternal blessedness. Therefore, although it is fitting that she be attentive to every work of piety, it especially befits her to have such religious devotion toward churches and ecclesiastical men [Col. 1467B] that she may reverence in them—indeed, him—the one who wishes to be honoured in his ministers and who cannot be offended in them without being himself offended.

You should know that it has come to our hearing that the aforesaid noblewoman, causing many troubles to our venerable brother the archbishop of Larissa and his suffragans, not only keeps to their prejudice abbots and abbeys, as well as priests of Larissa and Larimorond belonging to them, but even does not fear to lend her favour to Greek bishops against them, so that they may not obey us—something which, if true, we regard as grave and unworthy. Since, therefore, such conduct can neither be undertaken by the noblewoman without harm to her soul nor tolerated by us without injury [Col. 1467C] to ecclesiastical liberty, we have commanded the widow by our letters not to delay freely restoring the aforesaid abbots with their abbeys and the priests to the said archbishop and his suffragans, nor henceforth to attempt to molest them concerning these matters; and to desist in such a way from the wrong which she is said to have inflicted upon him concerning the aforesaid bishops—indeed, upon us—that we are not compelled to lay our hand upon the matter.

Otherwise, however much we may wish to defer to her, because one must not defer to a human being against God, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writing prudently to admonish the aforesaid noblewoman and procure that she carry out our command. Otherwise compel her to do so by ecclesiastical censure, as justice requires, setting aside appeal. [Col. 1467D] And if not all of you, etc.; two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

A letter was written to the same noblewoman on this matter.

### CLIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF LARISSA AND ATHENS, AND THE BISHOP OF SITHONIA

Concerning the tithes and first-fruits of the Church of Thebes. (Ferentino, sixth day before the Ides of October [10 October].)

The complaint laid before us by our venerable brother the archbishop of Thebes disclosed that the Hospitallers established in his province, by wicked insinuations, dissuade both the Theban lords and the people established everywhere from paying the tithes and [Col. 1468A] first-fruits owed to the Church of Thebes and to others, while they themselves endeavour to usurp them contrary to justice. Since the Church of Thebes has no more than nine hundred hyperpyra in revenues, the aforesaid Theban lords extort seven hundred of these annually as an exaction called *crostica*. Thus only two hundred hyperpyra remain for the aforesaid archbishop and his clergy to support themselves for the whole year.

Therefore, by apostolic writing we command your brotherhood prudently to admonish the said Hospitallers and Thebans to desist from their unjust burdening of the archbishop in these matters and effectively induce them to do so. Otherwise procure that they be compelled to do so by ecclesiastical censure, justice being observed and appeal set aside. [Col. 1468B] And if not all of you, etc.; two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixth day before the Ides of October [10 October], etc., as above.

### CLIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF ATHENS AND THEBES, AND THE BISHOP OF CASTORIA

A letter on behalf of the clergy of Larse. (Ferentino, fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October].)

Since our beloved son, the nobleman William of Larse, in the diocese of Larissa, cannot transgress the Gospel rule without harm to his soul—the rule which commands that what is Caesar’s be rendered to Caesar and what is God’s to God—we have commanded the said nobleman by our letters not henceforth to presume to molest the abbots and abbesses, priests, and ecclesiastical men of Larse, [Col. 1468C] as he is said to have done hitherto; but, content with the due payment which they are said to have rendered him, to permit them to remain in complete peace and freedom. Therefore, by apostolic writing we command your brotherhood that, if the aforesaid nobleman does not take care to carry out the apostolic command, you compel him to do so by ecclesiastical censure, as justice requires, appeal set aside. And if not all of you, etc.; two of you, etc.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

A letter was written to the same nobleman on this matter.

### CLV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LARISSA

That he is to observe the Latin rite in consecrations. (Ferentino, fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October].)

[Col. 1468D]

Concerning the consecrations of Greek bishops and the blessings of Greek abbots and nuns, on which you asked us for instruction, we judge that this answer should be given to your brotherhood: those whom you find consecrated or blessed, leave in their present state; but confer the office of consecration and blessing, according to the Latin rite, upon those who are to be consecrated or blessed, imposing upon nuns and monks a rule of life according to the approved rule which they have professed.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October], etc., as above.

### CLVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS, AND BELOVED SONS THE ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE

Crusaders are received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Ferentino, fifth day before the Ides of October [11 October].)

[Col. 1469A]

Since those who fight for the liberty of the Church ought to be supported by the Church’s protection, by apostolic authority we decree that our beloved sons who have taken, or are to take, the cross for Christ’s service against the heretics of Provence, from the time when they receive upon their breasts the sign of the life-giving cross in order to overcome those heretics in accordance with the direction of our legates, shall remain, together with their persons, lands, possessions, people, [Col. 1469B] and all their other goods, under the protection of the Apostolic See and ourselves. Until their return or death is known with certainty, all these things shall remain in their present state, free and undisturbed.

Therefore, by apostolic writing we command your discretion that, should anyone meanwhile attempt to disturb the aforesaid goods of those persons in your dioceses, when you are requested by their procurators, officials, or messengers, you restrain their wrongdoers or disturbers by canonical censure, appeal set aside.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Ides of October [11 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CLVII. TO ALL CLERICS WHO HAVE TAKEN, OR ARE TO TAKE, THE CROSS FOR CHRIST’S SERVICE AGAINST THE HERETICS OF PROVENCE

On the same matter. (Ferentino, eighth day before the Ides of October [8 October].)

[Col. 1469C]

Since, aflame with zeal for the orthodox faith, you have determined to set out to overcome heretical depravity, by the authority of these presents we grant you leave to pledge your revenues as security for two years in order to carry out this work of piety. Let no one at all be permitted to infringe this page of our concession, etc., as far as “oppose.” But if anyone presumes to attempt this, etc., as far as “shall incur.”

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Ides of October [8 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CLVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS, AND BELOVED SONS, OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE

On the same matter. (Ferentino, seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October].)

[Col. 1469D]

That the holy Church of God, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array, may go forth against its most cruel enemies to exterminate the followers of heretical depravity—a serpent which, like a cancer, has infected almost the whole of Provence—we have judged that the forces of Christian soldiery should be summoned from the surrounding regions. We have appointed as their leaders our venerable brothers, the bishops of Comminges and Riez, and our beloved son the abbot of Cîteaux, legates of the Apostolic See, so that, defending the honour of the Holy Trinity, they may triumph under the threefold rule of these masters. [Col. 1470A]

Accordingly, we have judged that your whole body should be exhorted and admonished, commanding you by apostolic writing to labour among your subjects by diligent preaching and exhortation, so that they may devote themselves and their resources to so holy a work—a service devoted to God and assistance needful to the Church. Let them know that remission of sins has been granted by God and his vicar to all who, inflamed with zeal for the orthodox faith, gird themselves for this work of piety, so that this holy labour may suffice them as satisfaction for those offences for which they have offered true contrition of heart and confession of mouth to the true God.

Since those who fight in defence of their brethren ought to be freed from the injuries of their brethren, [Col. 1470B] we will and command that, if any noble clerics or laymen proceeding against these pestilent persons are bound by oath to pay interest, then, when requested by them, you compel their creditors resident in your dioceses by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, to release them entirely from their oath and desist from any further exaction of interest. If any creditor compels them to pay interest, you shall similarly compel him, appeal set aside, to restore that interest after it has been paid. As diligently as you can, induce the creditors of such persons to extend the dates fixed [Col. 1470C] for payment of debts until those persons have devoted themselves to this work of piety, that the creditors may thereby share in the reward of those whose struggle they further by such assistance.

Furthermore, since it does not seem improper that those who undertake a public cause should be maintained at public expense, prudently admonish and effectively induce all clerics and laymen living in the lands of the noble duke of Burgundy and the counts of Nevers and Saint-Pol, as well as all others who have taken the cross for so glorious a struggle, to grant them a tenth portion of all their revenues of one year for carrying out this holy and costly undertaking, as our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens and his suffragans are known to have done. Appoint prudent and faithful men to collect this alms, and let them allocate what is collected as the aforesaid legates judge fit to direct. [Col. 1470D]

Given at Ferentino, on the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CLIX. TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS

That Jews are to remit interest for crusaders. (Ferentino, seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October].)

That the holy Church of God may go forth against its most cruel enemies, etc., as in the other letter, as far as: “Accordingly, we have judged that Your Royal Serenity should be exhorted and admonished,” enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins: when requested by the aforesaid legates, provide them with suitable counsel and assistance, inducing the peoples subject to you to endeavour to devote themselves and their resources to so holy a work, a service devoted to God and support necessary to the Church. Let them know that remission of sins, etc., as far as “have offered to the true God.”

Since temporal coercion may perhaps avail among those who do not admit spiritual persuasion in this matter, we beseech your royal gentleness in the Lord to induce, and by royal power compel, the Jews established under your dominion to remit entirely the interest owed by their debtors who are going forth for this service of God, and, if possible, suitably extend the periods fixed for repayment of the principal. Thus, besides [Col. 1471B] the other assistance which you will render to the Church in so holy an undertaking, the reward of eternal recompense may also increase for you from this.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CLX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LARISSA

He is granted leave to reside at Ferchika. (Ferentino, third day before the Ides of October [13 October].)

You petitioned us that, since because of the encircling enemy you cannot reside in your see without loss of property and fear for your own person, we might deign to grant you leave to reside at Ferchika, a place which is subject to you by diocesan law [Col. 1471C] and in which an archiepiscopal see is known formerly to have existed, especially since the constable of that place intends, if this is done, to enlarge the place with benefactions. Therefore, by apostolic writing we command your brotherhood, because of such necessity, to establish your residence in the aforesaid place, provided nevertheless that by this the archiepiscopal dignity is in no way taken away from the former place.

Given at Ferentino, on the third day before the Ides of October [13 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CLXI. TO MASTER AIMER, CANON OF SAINT ANDREW OF POITIERS

A response to his inquiries. (Ferentino, fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October].)

[Col. 1471D] Concerning letters which are obtained from us by some through malice and by others through ignorance, with truth concealed or falsehood alleged, we have understood that different persons hold different opinions: some asserting that such persons ought to be deprived altogether of every benefit of the letters, since a deceitful petitioner ought to forfeit what he has obtained; others saying that, although they ought to lose the form expressed in our letters, the delegated judge should nevertheless proceed in the matter according to the strictness of the law. We therefore believe that a distinction should be made between those who obtain letters from us through fraud or malice and those who obtain them through simplicity or ignorance: those who, in the former manner, state falsehood or suppress truth ought, as punishment for their perversity, to gain no benefit from the letters, [Col. 1472A] so that the delegate, once proof of this has been made to him, is in no way to take cognizance of the case.

Among the others, however, who obtain letters in the latter manner, we say that a distinction must be made according to what falsehood was alleged or what truth was suppressed. For if the falsehood stated or truth concealed is of such a kind that, even had that falsehood been withheld or that truth disclosed, we would nevertheless have issued letters, at least in the common form, the delegate, without following the form inserted in those letters, shall proceed in the case according to the order of law. But if, through the assertion of such falsehood or even the suppression of truth, letters have been obtained such that, had that falsehood been withheld or that truth disclosed, we would have issued no letters at all, the delegate is not to proceed in any respect, except perhaps so far as, having summoned the parties into his presence, he may inquire into the character of the petition; so that in either case the same consideration which would have moved the delegator may also move the delegate, and where the delegator would deny his letters, the delegate likewise shall in no way exercise the office of his jurisdiction.

Given at Ferentino, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXII. TO WILLIAM DOIARD, CANON OF THEBES. His prebend at Thebes is confirmed. (Ferentino, thirteenth day before the Kalends of November.)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., up to “bestow.” Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, favorably assenting to your petitions, we confirm for you by apostolic authority the prebend [Col. 1472C] which you have canonically obtained in the Church of Thebes, as you justly and peacefully possess it, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. Therefore let no one . . . our confirmation, etc. But if anyone should do this, etc., up to “shall know that he has incurred.”

Given at Ferentino, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXIII. TO WALTER, BISHOP OF CATANIA, CHANCELLOR OF THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. That he should show reverence and honor to the Archbishop of Monreale. (Ferentino, thirteenth day before the Kalends of November.)

We commend in the Lord your humility and the charity of our venerable brother [Col. 1472D] the Archbishop of Monreale, by which—seeking not what is his own but what belongs to Jesus Christ—his heart has not been lifted up because you do not refuse to humble yourself before him, offering him obedience and reverence, as we have learned through his letters, which are due to the Archbishop of Monreale by reason of the Church of Catania.

Since, therefore, you are bound up in close and necessary association with royal affairs and services, and for that reason it is necessary to guard against every suspicion concerning you, we have directed the same archbishop by our letters that, yielding to your and the king’s advantage and to our requests, he should defer, should necessity require, the matter of your rendering the oath owed to him. Wherefore we earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by apostolic letters [Col. 1473A] that, not being ungrateful for the favor he has shown you, you should hold him in that reverence and honor in which you would be bound to hold him after the oath had been rendered; and, if he wishes, for greater security, furnish him with your letters, in which you undertake and promise both that, at our command and at a suitable time, if necessary, you will render him the fidelity owed to him, and that in the meantime you will show him obedience and reverence as though you had rendered that fidelity. Take diligent care that, secure in the favor of our grace, you endeavor to conduct yourself toward us and the Roman Church in such a way that we, who proceed with you in truth because we now know that you also walk with us in truth, may be more fervently stirred to your honor and advancement—which we ardently desire—since in this respect we know that we are imitating the footsteps of Him who says: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1).

Given at Ferentino, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

A letter on this matter was written to the Archbishop of Monreale.

CLXIV. TO BARTHOLOMEW OF CEPERANO. A certain judgment rendered in his favor is confirmed. (Ferentino, tenth day before the Kalends of September.)

When the beloved son Orandinus of Pontecorvo, knight, had alleged before the beloved son James, our subdeacon and chaplain, whom we appointed auditor for you and him, [Col. 1473C] that you were his vassal, and that by reason of certain mills, houses, vineyards, and certain other possessions belonging to him, as he said, which you are known to hold at Ceperano, you were bound to serve him with one horse; and when you wholly denied the foregoing, after each party had sworn the oath against calumny for proving these assertions, the same Orandinus produced certain witnesses. After their testimony had subsequently been published, the aforesaid subdeacon faithfully reported to us both the witnesses’ statements and what had been alleged before him by either side. We instructed him to pronounce judgment with the counsel of the beloved son Pelagius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy at the Septa Solis.

Finding that the said Orandinus had not at all established [Col. 1473D] his claim—since, according to the legal sanctions, where the claimant does not prove his case, the defendant ought to prevail even if he has offered nothing—the subdeacon, at his petition and with the counsel of the same cardinal, judicially absolved you, imposing perpetual silence upon Orandinus concerning all the foregoing. We therefore ratify his judgment, confirm it by apostolic authority, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. Let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly contravene it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, etc., up to “shall incur.”

Given at Ferentino, the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. Whether fiefs may be alienated. (Ferentino, tenth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 1474A]

[Note: [Col. 1473D] Chapter *Ex parte*, “On Fiefs.”] On your behalf it has been represented to our apostolic office that you have often doubted whether, when it happens that your vassal dies and his fief reverts to you, you may grant his fief to another, since you are bound by oath not to enfeoff anew without consulting the Roman pontiff. Further, if it happens that your vassal alienates his fief, whether you may invest his son or kinsman, a participant in the same fief, with it. Another of your doubts also concerned whether, when you find a fief alienated which you cannot easily recover yourself, you may grant it as a fief to some [Col. 1474B] layman who will both recover it and acknowledge that he holds it as a fief from the Church.

Therefore, wishing to remove this scruple of doubt from your mind, we command you by this present communication that, whenever the aforesaid cases arise, in the first case you may freely grant the deceased man’s fief if you judge it expedient; in the second, you may invest the son or kinsman of the alienator; and in the third, you may lawfully grant the alienated fief to one through whom the Church may recover it.

Given at Ferentino, the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXVI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT VINCENT. Tithes are adjudged to them. (Ferentino, twelfth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 1474C]

When a controversy was pending between you and our venerable brother Ricc., Bishop of Trivento, before our beloved son Pelagius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy at the Septa Solis, to whom we committed your case for hearing, and the bishop alleged that the tithes of the possessions lying around the Dark Stream and toward the Sangro near your monastery, and cultivated by the inhabitants of the castles of Rivo Oscuro and Alfedena, belonged to him by right; and that chrism ought by no means to be administered by you in those castles, since they are situated in his diocese; while you, on the contrary, answered that, even if the aforesaid tithes did not belong to the same bishop by any other right, you were nevertheless secure through forty years’ prescription, which you undertook to prove: having heard and understood the arguments and testimony produced before the aforesaid cardinal by both parties and faithfully reported to us by him, justice requiring it, we absolve you from the bishop’s claim concerning the aforementioned tithes, imposing silence upon him concerning them; but we adjudge the administration of chrism in the aforesaid castles to the said bishop. Let no one . . . infringe this page of our determination, etc. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, etc., up to “shall incur.”

Given at Ferentino, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF LUCCA. The privileges of the monastery of Fichecchio are confirmed. (Ferentino, second day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 1475A]

[Note: [Col. 1475D] Chapter *Cum olim*, “On Prescription.”] Formerly, brother bishop, when you were litigating in our presence with the beloved sons, the abbot and monks of Saint Savior of Fichecchio, concerning the parish church of Salamazano and its adjacent chapels, and were claiming the appointment of clerics in them and other matters belonging to episcopal right, you relied principally, in establishing your claim, upon the common law. By its authority you maintained that all spiritual matters in the aforesaid places, situated in your diocese, belonged to you as diocesan bishop.

You also adduced an arbitral award issued concerning this matter by the late Bishop of Pistoia and by the archpriest and primicerius of Lucca, chosen by the parties, which had been approved jointly by both sides. It expressly provides that, after any convert has been elected by the abbot as parish priest in that parish, he is to be presented to the Bishop of Lucca to receive from him the grace of confirmation and, together with his priests, to promise him manual obedience in this form: that he shall go with his people to synod, chapter, and also the litanies at the church of Saint Martin; that he shall answer to the bishop for annual procuration and for a fourth of the tithes; that, whenever necessary, he shall furnish him assistance; and that he shall observe his sentence of interdict pronounced against the people of Fichecchio. And if the parish priest or his priests should perhaps offend the Church of Lucca in matters contained in the award, and the abbot, once and twice requested, should not cause the offence to be remedied within twenty days, the Bishop of Lucca might judge them for that fault as his own priests.

[Col. 1475C] To defeat your claim, however, the aforesaid abbot produced a privilege of our predecessor Pope Gregory VII, of happy memory, which appeared to have preceded the aforesaid award by a long time and by which both the monastery of Fichecchio and the said parish church and chapels seemed to have been granted liberty. For it states that our predecessor had granted the Church of Salamazano with the adjacent chapels to the said monastery, and established that no archbishop or bishop should dare molest the place itself, or the aforesaid parish church and chapels, or excommunicate or even judge priests appointed there by the abbot then in office; but that, remaining under the protection, immunity, and jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff, they should labor securely in the service of Almighty God.

The said abbot also relied on privileges of other Roman pontiffs—namely Urban, Paschal, Calixtus, Eugenius, Anastasius, Adrian, Alexander, and Lucius—obtained after the award was issued and appearing to grant him privileges of liberty. For in each of their privileges, among other things, the following is found: “We also decree that no bishop, archbishop, or any of their ministers may, without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff, excommunicate or place under interdict the place itself—that is, the monastery of Fichecchio—or its monks, or the neighboring churches of Salamazano with their chapels, or the priests appointed there by the abbot.”

[Col. 1476A] The said abbot further alleged that, even if the aforesaid matters belonged to you by common law, both he and his monastery were nevertheless protected by lawful prescription. Through his own witnesses and yours, produced by both sides before the beloved son, the prior of Saint Fridianus at Lucca, at our command, he said it had been proved that his monastery had enjoyed peaceful possession for forty years and more of all the foregoing matters. He further alleged that no prejudice to the monastery could arise from the aforesaid award, both because the greater and sounder part of the chapter of that place had by no means consented to the said submission to arbitration, and because the authority of the Roman See, to which the monastery and churches belonged, was not shown to have intervened.

To this, on your behalf, the response was that no credence should be given to Pope Gregory’s privilege, since it was manifestly suspect. For it was found to have been erased in that part of it upon which the force of the question depends, namely where mention is made of the chapels. You also maintained that the same abbot ought to derive no benefit from the other privileges, since they appeared to have been obtained by concealment, inasmuch as they make no mention of the aforesaid award approved by the parties, [Col. 1476C] which had passed into the authority of a matter adjudged.

You further added that you could not be defeated by the opposing party’s plea of prescription. For although certain witnesses testify that they remember forty years’ time, and add that they saw the monastery enjoying liberty in the aforesaid places concerning matters belonging to episcopal right, nevertheless the depositions of this kind do not establish continuous possession for forty years. For these two facts can quite readily coincide: that the witnesses remember forty years’ time and that they saw the monastery in possession of the aforesaid matters only from ten years ago onward.

The other party, considering this frivolous, replied that, although some witnesses used ambiguous language in this way, there were nevertheless many witnesses who plainly testified that they had seen the said monastery in continuous possession of all the aforesaid matters for forty years and more. Against this your party replied that, even if the forty-year prescription were established, the period of schism [Note: [Col. 1476D] See above, letter 84.] which had occurred in the Church of Lucca, as the witnesses had shown, ought properly to be deducted from the computation. The other party answered, on the contrary, that although proof had been given of the schism that had intervened, its duration had not at all been shown and it might have lasted only a short time; for that reason the plea of prescription could not effectively be impeded, especially since a prescription of forty-five years had been proved through several witnesses.

[Col. 1477A] Therefore, having carefully understood these and the other matters alleged before us by both sides, and because the aforesaid abbot sufficiently showed that his monastery was protected by lawful prescription concerning the appointment, removal, and regulation of the parish priest and clerics; baptism; penance for lesser sins; burial; the receipt of tithes; the celebration of divine offices both in the parish church and in the aforesaid chapels; and also excommunication, interdict, and absolution: with the counsel of our brethren, we have judged that the abbot himself should be absolved from your claim concerning the aforesaid articles, imposing perpetual silence upon you concerning them. But concerning all other matters known to belong to episcopal right, according to the tenor of the arbitral award, we judicially condemn the same abbot in respect of the aforesaid parish church and chapels. Let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our determination, etc. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, etc., up to “shall incur.”

Given at Ferentino, the second day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXVIII. TO THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF SAINT SAVIOR OF FICHECCHIO. On the same matter. (Ferentino.)

[Col. 1477C] When our venerable brother, the Bishop of Lucca, formerly litigated with you in our presence concerning the parish church of Salamazano and its adjacent chapels, claiming for himself the appointment of clerics in them and other matters belonging to episcopal right, he relied principally, to establish his claim, upon the common law, etc., in almost the same manner, up to: “But to defeat the bishop’s claim thus established, you, son abbot, etc.,” in almost the same manner as above, to the end.

Given at Ferentino, etc., as in the other letter.

CLXIX. TO GERARD, FOUNDER OF THE CHAPEL ESTABLISHED IN THE SUBURB OF VIENNA IN HONOR OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AND BLESSED ANTHONY. It is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Ferentino, eleventh day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 1477D]

The beloved son, the noble Duke of Austria, informed us by his letters that, having built, with his advice and consent, a chapel in the suburb of Vienna in honor of the Holy Spirit and Blessed Anthony, and having endowed it in pious love for the service of the poor with nineteen of your plots of land adjoining it there, you perceived the fragrance which, by God’s grace, proceeds from the religious order of our Hospital of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1477D] See the deeds of Innocent III, chapter 144.] in Saxia, and resolved to commit the chapel to it, on condition that it should render to it an annual payment of one mark of silver.

We therefore, yielding to your prayers and those of the same duke, receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the chapel itself, with all the ecclesiastical and temporal goods which it now reasonably possesses or may hereafter, with God’s gift, acquire by lawful means, and also the persons dwelling therein. We assign it, under the aforesaid annual payment, to the said Hospital of the Holy Spirit, commanding by the authority of this present writing that it shall, as hitherto, remain meanwhile under your governance until the master of the aforesaid hospital, visiting it in person or through his messenger, shall make provision for its welfare according to God and its Rule. Let no one, etc., up to “shall incur.”

Given at Ferentino, the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BENEVENTO. On the grant of a certain church. (Ferentino.)

[Col. 1478B]

Of happy memory, etc., up to “invest.” Moreover, although your letters sent to us contained that the church mentioned belonged to the grant of the Church of Benevento, and although it had been conferred upon the aforesaid cardinal by our predecessor Pope Alexander, of happy memory, yet because we have received from some persons that its grant belongs especially to the Roman pontiff, and have found the Roman Church in possession of it, we have judged that the same church should be conferred from our hand. We do not wish any prejudice to arise for the Church [Col. 1478C] of Benevento from such a grant, if you should wish or perhaps be able to show that it ought to belong to your grant.

Given at Ferentino.

CLXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF LARISSA AND THEBES. That they should inquire concerning the postulate to the Church of Thessalonica. (Ferentino, Kalends of November.)

[Note: [Col. 1478D] See book XIII, letter 13.] The beloved sons, the canons of Saint Sophia at Thessalonica, sent us their letters. In these, together with the beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman, widow of the Marquis of Montferrat, and also the beloved sons, the noble men Count of Blanderada, the Bailiff, and the other barons [Col. 1478D] of the kingdom of Thessalonica—who sent us writings on this same matter—they set forth the many needs and distresses of the Church and kingdom of Thessalonica. They humbly petitioned our apostolic office that we should deem fit to admit the postulation which the same canons, with the favor of the aforesaid persons, had made of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Verissa; for through his prudent foresight and circumspect prudence they singularly, as it were, hope that provision can be made for the needs not only of the Church but also of the kingdom.

Since we could not be fully assured concerning this postulation, and since such postulations, like elections, according to the custom of the Roman Church consonant with the canons, require regular examination—for more things must be considered in postulations than in elections—we command and enjoin your brotherhoods by apostolic letters that, having diligently inquired into and learned the truth, if you find that the postulation was canonically made by those who can and ought to make it, and that the aforesaid archbishop has not intruded himself into the administration of the Church of Thessalonica, as some had reported to us, you shall, because of the great necessity, admit that postulation in our stead. Having absolved him from the bond by which he was bound to the Church of Verissa, you shall enjoin him not to delay sending us the pallium which he received in the name of that Church of Verissa, [Col. 1479B] since, God willing, he is to receive another, as is fitting, in the name of the Church of Thessalonica.

But if you find either that the postulation was made less than canonically or that he has intruded himself into the administration, take care strictly to forbid him by our authority, after despising the modest rank of his former Church, to intrude himself in any way into the Church of Thessalonica as though it were more distinguished. Rather, remaining in the calling in which he was called, let him strive to govern the Church first entrusted to him. Let him consider that we show him great favor in this, especially if he is found to have thus crept into the aforesaid administration; for according to the canonical sanctions, if anyone, desiring ambitiously to be advanced beyond the measure of his right, leaves his former see and transfers himself to another without the consent of the Roman pontiff—to whom alone authority is reserved to grant translations of bishops—he ought both to lose the first, which he despised through pride, and to be rejected from the second, which he coveted through avarice. [Note: [Col. 1479D] Leo I, letter 84, and in Gratian, Causa 7, question 1, chapter 31, *Si quis episcopus*.]

Lest the aforesaid Church of Thessalonica remain any longer deprived of pastoral governance, admonish those to whom its election belongs to set a suitable person over it without delay as pastor through canonical election. But if, because of a lack of persons—which we believe afflicts not only that Church but the whole province—they cannot find a suitable person for its governance, inform us of this by your letters. If the aforesaid canons, with the favor of the aforesaid noblewoman and the others whom we named above, request it by letters sent to us, expressly setting forth their desire, then, God being the author, we shall take care to send them from our hand a worthy bishop, consecrated and adorned with the pallium, that eminent sign of the fullness of the pontifical office, who will know and be able, with the power of divine wisdom, to govern spiritually and temporally the Church entrusted to him.

Given at Ferentino, on the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXXII. TO THE BELOVED SON IN CHRIST PONTIUS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GILES, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS TO BE REGULARLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of November.)

[Col. 1480A]

Although the care and solicitude of all churches rests upon us, it is fitting that we provide with more attentive care for those places and persons which are known to adhere more especially to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church and to remain more devotedly in its fidelity and obedience. Moreover, the need laid upon us to keep diligent watch for the monastery of Saint Giles, over which, by God’s grace, you are known to preside, is all the greater because that place is known, from the beginning of its foundation, to belong especially to the right and lordship of that same prince of the apostles.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Pons, graciously assenting to your just requests, after the example of our predecessors of holy memory, Innocent, Eugenius, and Adrian IV, Roman pontiffs, by the present page of privilege we confirm every liberty and immunity granted to you and to your monastery by the privileges of our predecessors. We decree that no archbishop or bishop whatsoever may lay upon that monastery, or upon its abbot or the monks there serving the Lord, the hand of excommunication or interdict; but that, through the grace of almighty God, both you and the monastery with its town may always remain quiet and free from every episcopal exaction or burden. [Col. 1480B–C]

Moreover, we altogether forbid monks, priests, or clerics dwelling in your obediences to be seized, beaten, or compelled to ransom themselves by any laymen on account of their offences. Furthermore, we decree that whatever possessions or goods the said monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought it proper to specify these in their proper names:

namely, the abbeys of Saint Giles of Hungary and of Saint Eusebius of Provence; the churches of Saint Giles of Aceio; Saint Giles of Duno; Saint Giles of Supervia, with its town; Saint Eusebius of Lombardy; Saint Baudilius of Spain; Saint Eulalia of Barbasta; Revinas, with its town; Boccona, with its town; Saint Andrew of Lucapello; Saint Giles of Tolmone; Saint Giles of Creissaco; Saint Hippolytus of Melseo, with its town; Saint Lupus; Saint Mary of Fraixeneto; Saint John of Gardonenca, with its town; Holy Cross of Molazano; Saint Martin of Cerbario, with its chapel; Saint Stephen of Corconna; Saint Amantius, with its town; Saint Martin of Orianegnes; Saint Martin of Cinciano; Saint Andrew of Berniz, with its chapel; Saint Saturninus of Seura, with that town itself; the town of Bionz; Saint Cecilia of Stagello, with that town itself; Saint Felix of Aspirano, with that town itself; Saint Columba, with half the town; Saint Andrew of the field of Mariniano; Saint Mary of Saturanicis; Saint Giles of Missiniaco; Saint Stephen of Castlar, with its chapel; Saint Peter of Prevencheriis, with its town and its churches; Saint Andeolus of Robiaco, with chapel and town; Saint Victorinus; Saint Andrew; Saint Peter of Vannis, with that town itself; Saint Mary of Monte Alto, with the chapel of the town; Saint Baudilius of Somerio, with its chapel; Saint Servius beyond the Rhône, with its town; Saints Peter and Michael near the castle of Rossilianis; Saint Privatus, with its town; Saint Stephen of Menerba, with chapels and town; Saint Christopher of Vacheriis, with chapel and town; Saint John of Albenatis, with its town and the parish church of Saint Mary; Saint Mary of Redosc, with its town; Saint Columba of Capingo; Saint Giles of Padernis; Saint Maximus of Medenis; Saint Peter of Inter-montes, with that town itself; Saint Peter of Trincatallis; Saint John of Meiano; Saint Sebastian of Montepesato; Saint Peter of Launiaco; Saint Saviour of Caisanigis; Saint Eugenius of Orbesat, with its chapel; Saint Genesius of Mediogozez; Acione; Malbosc, with its chapel; Rocca; Camponaz; and Lardario, with their churches and all their appurtenances; the castle of Montfort; the castle of Lennatio; and five modii of land and four candles daily, which Berjac once left by testament to the monastery of Saint Giles.

[Note: [Col. 1480D] See book II of our *Miscellanea*, p. 183.]

Furthermore, we also confirm for you the agreements made and ratified by an authentic instrument between you and John, bishop of Nîmes, and Raymond, bishop of Uzès, concerning the fourth-parts of churches. [Col. 1481C–D]

By apostolic authority we forbid any abbot or monk to presume to alienate, dispose of, pledge, or grant in fief, rent, or benefice to any knight the treasure, honours, or possessions of the aforesaid monastery or of its dependent cells, whether now held or hereafter acquired by the Lord’s bounty—except, perhaps, for the ransoming of captives, for a common and exceptionally grave scarcity caused by famine, or for the purchase or redemption of property. If this should occur, it must be done by the common deliberation of the entire chapter, so that nothing may be undertaken through fraud or any clandestine contrivance, but only under the pressure of the aforesaid necessities.

Any abbot or monk who attempts this: if an abbot, let him be deprived of the administration of the abbey and struck by a sentence of excommunication; if a monk, let him be entirely excluded from the monastery and its honours and held under the same sentence of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction. [Col. 1482A]

We also forbid anyone within the town of Saint Giles, or around that town for the distance of one league, without the consent of the abbot and chapter, whether a Hospitaller, a Knight Templar, or any other person, to build a religious house, church, oratory, or fortification; to possess a cemetery; to celebrate divine offices for the people when the town itself has ceased to do so; to ring bells; to receive offerings from the people during the celebration of Mass; to baptize; or to receive your parishioners for divine offices. [Col. 1482A–B]

Upon the death of the abbot of your place, no one may be placed over it through any artifice of intrigue or violence, save the person whom the brethren of that monastery, by common assent or by the counsel of the sounder part, shall have judged, according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, to be elected. The person elected shall come to the Roman pontiff to receive blessing.

We further confirm by authority of the Apostolic See the renunciation made by Raymond, count of Toulouse, of noble memory. That count is known, at the council of Nîmes, to have surrendered into the hand of our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Urban, swearing an oath, to Abbot Odilo and his brethren, all the honours pertaining to blessed Giles, both in the valley of Flaviana and outside it—whatever he appeared to hold justly or unjustly—and all lawful and unlawful customs which his predecessors or he himself had possessed, for the honour of God and reverence for blessed Giles. He also subjected both himself and all his successors, insofar as it depended upon him, to damnation and a curse should they attempt to invalidate this gift, and procured from that predecessor of ours the pronouncement of a sentence of excommunication upon the matter in the council.

[Note: [Col. 1481D] See vol. X of the *Councils*, p. 610.]

Since Pope Adrian, our aforesaid predecessor, in response to the devotion of the said count, established by apostolic authority that none of his successors might, by any length of time, acquire a prescriptive right to anything left by the said Count Raymond to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Giles, in order to escape the curse and damnation established by that count, we confirm by apostolic authority what he prudently enacted. [Col. 1482B–D]

Moreover, for the greater veneration of blessed Giles, we decree that within the boundaries fixed by our predecessors no one whatsoever shall dare either to make a raid or assault upon the town of Giles itself, or to inflict a serious injury upon any person.

Therefore let no person at all rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole and intact, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishops in the aforesaid chapels. [Col. 1483A]

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance.

But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 1483A–B]

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 12 November, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CLXXIII. To the Archbishop of Lund

Concerning the election of the bishop of Schleswig. (Ferentino, 4 November.)

[Note: [Col. 1483D] See below, book XIII, letter 173.]

Since the devil had put it into the heart of Bishop Waldemar to set his foot in Judas’s track and fraudulently depart from our presence, plunging us into intense bitterness—we who, after he had been freed from a most harsh prison, had cherished him in the bosom of the Apostolic See with the sweetness of familiar favour, truly as a serpent in our bosom—we proceeded against him for his enormous and manifold offences, promulgating ecclesiastical censure not only against him but also against his supporters, as we recall having notified our venerable brother the archbishop of Magdeburg by our letters.

But he, given over to a reprobate mind, fulfilling Solomon’s proverb: “Even if you pound a fool like barley grits in a mortar, striking from above with a pestle, his folly will not be removed from him” (Prov. 27), refused to receive correction. Instead, adding iniquity to iniquity, he joined deceit and perjury to the offences he had committed by secretly fleeing from us: contempt for the keys and transgression of the canons, by wickedly intruding himself into the administration of the Church of Bremen. He did not know—or, if he knew, thought little of it—that according to canonical sanctions no bishop may transfer from one see to another without the special permission of the Roman pontiff, to whom alone authority is reserved to grant such translations. [Col. 1483C–D]

For this reason, even if all his other faults ceased, this fault alone would have rendered him unworthy not merely of the Church of Bremen but also of that of Schleswig. According to canonical ordinances, one who, abandoning his former chair without the Roman pontiff’s consent, presumes to transfer himself to another must both lose the first, which he despised through pride, and be rejected from the second, which he coveted through avarice.

[Note: [Col. 1484D] See above, letter 171.]

Since, therefore, we neither ought nor can endure any longer, amid so many monstrous abuses and abuses of monstrous kind, a man who is apostate and worthless, rebellious and contumacious, we have strictly commanded the said archbishop, his venerable brethren and the suffragans of the Church of Bremen, as well as the bishops of Osnabrück and Münster, firmly on our behalf to enjoin the aforesaid Waldemar—without excuse or delay—to set out within a month after their admonition for the Apostolic See, humbly to seek pardon for his offences. Otherwise, from that point, with every obstacle of objection and appeal removed, they are to ensure that he is declared, by our authority, deposed and degraded, deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice and office; and that all avoid him more strictly as one anathematized until worthy satisfaction is made, if indeed he is permitted to make worthy satisfaction for so many and such great perversities.

They are nevertheless to prohibit everyone from presuming to communicate with or assist him. If any should attempt the contrary, they are to ensure that laypersons of this kind are declared subject to excommunication and, if they hold a benefice from the Church of Bremen, deprived of it forever; and that clerics are declared deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice and office. If any city, castle, or community of persons whatsoever should presume, against this prohibition, to adhere to the said Waldemar, they are to place it under the strictest interdict, so that, apart from penance for the dying and the baptism of infants, no divine office or ecclesiastical sacrament may be celebrated there. If any cleric should dare to violate this, they are to depose him from every ecclesiastical benefice and office. If any have sworn him an oath concerning so unlawful a matter, they are to be declared entirely unbound from observing it. [Col. 1484A–C]

Since we have learned that an election in the aforesaid Church of Bremen was made amid discord, we have instructed the said archbishop and bishops, by apostolic authority, to require both those in favour of that election and those opposed to it, within a month after their admonition, either in person or through suitable representatives possessing the authority and power of the others, to set out for our presence. Thus, after a canonical examination, if the aforesaid election ought to be confirmed, they may obtain its confirmation; but if not, they are to provide their church, with our counsel, with a suitable person as pastor.

If, perhaps, those who oppose the aforesaid election do not take care to come to us within a month as stated, or should attempt to support the said Waldemar, they are to be declared thereafter to have no part in the business of the election. They are diligently to see that they execute promptly and effectively all these things which we enjoin upon them to be executed in the power of the Holy Spirit and under the obligation of obedience. We strictly command that, if any one of them, which we do not believe, fails to carry out the apostolic mandate, he shall send suitable representatives to our presence within another month, to make satisfaction for their contempt. If he should neglect this as well, we shall, God granting, punish his rebellion and contumacy by fitting chastisement.

We command them all to carry out this mandate with every obstacle of objection and appeal removed, not only jointly as a body but also individually, each acting separately. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your fraternity that, when this has been notified to you by them or by any of them, you shall ensure that the Church of Schleswig is provided with a pastor through canonical election, with every obstacle of objection and appeal removed. [Col. 1484D–1485B]

Given at Ferentino, 4 November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXXIV. To the Bishops of Västerås, Linköping, and Skara

That they are to restrain Eric, invader of the kingdom of Sweden. (Lateran, 13 November.)

You should know that it has reached our hearing how the predecessors of Eric, who violently intruded himself into the kingdom of Sweden, after procuring the death of King S. of Sweden, of illustrious memory, through one of that king’s chamberlains, afterwards killed his son, who had been raised to the throne by the unanimous will of the people. This son had placed no small trust in them, since, forgetting their crimes against his own kin, he had mercifully received them.

Finally, after the death of the father of the said Eric—who, after having caused the aforesaid kings to be killed in this fashion, had occupied the reins of government by violence—our dearest son in Christ, King S. of Sweden, illustrious, was assumed to the government of the kingdom. Being related in the nearest degree of kinship to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Danes, he had gone to him. Moved by merciful compassion toward the sons of the invader of his kingdom, whom he saw were grown up and destitute of every help, he adopted them as his sons, forgetting their injuries against him. He cherished them with such affection, delighting in their close companionship, that he could not bear their absence from his presence. [Col. 1485C–D]

But the enemy of humankind, envying so great a work of piety, sowed tares between them and the king through certain followers of his wickedness, and stirred them to plot the king’s death. At length, after three of them had been killed, their crime having been discovered, in the battle which they had raised against the king, the said Eric gathered a multitude after some time and violently entered the borders of the kingdom. Meeting the king with his forces and putting him to flight, he obtained the kingdom; whereupon the said king fled to the said king of Denmark, accompanied by our venerable brother the archbishop of Uppsala. [Col. 1485D–1486A]

Since these matters—both because of the destruction of churches and the oppression even of widows, and because the said king, being under the protection of the Roman Church and ourselves, is said to have been deprived of his kingdom contrary to justice—must not be overlooked by us with closed eyes, especially since he finds no one else to whom he may have recourse to obtain justice: by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood diligently to admonish and induce the said Eric to come to an agreement with the aforesaid king and to leave that kingdom peacefully to him, insofar as it belongs to him. Otherwise, with appeal removed, compel him to do so through ecclesiastical censure, as shall be just, taking special care that satisfaction is made to the aforesaid archbishop. If not all of you can act, then two of you, etc. [Col. 1486A–B]

Given at the Lateran, 13 November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXXV. To the Archbishop of Milan, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church; the Bishop of Ivrea; and the beloved son, the Abbot of Tiglieto

Against the city of Piacenza. (Lateran, 22 November.)

[Note: [Col. 1485D] See book X, letter 222.]

Among the manifold distresses and pressures by which Holy Mother Church is grievously afflicted and vexed in this evening of the world, what afflicts and vexes us more intensely is that those who, as sons, are filled at her breasts with consolation do not merely fail to help her in her distress, but add pain to her wounds. Despised by those whom she nourishes with maternal affection, she can scarcely now find among all her beloved any who pities her; rather, her friends have spurned her and become her enemies. We have recently and familiarly learned this, to our sorrow, in the bishop of Piacenza and his clergy.

For in former times, when the consuls and councillors of Piacenza, together with their fellow citizens, led astray by malicious deceptions and spurning also the admonitions and commands of the Apostolic See, sought to enslave their mother, the Church of Piacenza, and thus reduce themselves to slavery—for children follow their mother’s condition according to legal enactments—and did not fear God or blush before men to exercise the savagery of that tyranny, a tyranny which not even Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and Artaxerxes, king of Persia, exercised against the priests and Levites of their time, but instead they not only did not impose burdens on them but had provisions supplied from the public treasury: the aforesaid bishop and his clergy, choosing exile rather than to see their own evils and those of the saints, left the city, shook the dust from their feet in testimony, and were miserably scattered throughout the province. [Col. 1486C–1487A]

But the laymen hardened their faces against the rock and not only stretched out sacrilegious hands upon their movable goods, but through ministers of iniquity collected all ecclesiastical revenues and diverted the resources of the poor to unlawful uses. Therefore we pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the consuls, councillors, and other chief authors of this iniquity, and subjected the entire city to ecclesiastical interdict.

Compassionating their calamities and pressures with paternal affection, we caused suitable revenues from our own income to be assigned to the bishop and ensured that the bishop and clergy of Piacenza should be most honourably provided for by all the clergy of Lombardy. For many of them it was better in others’ houses than in their own, and they could regard exile almost as their native land.

When the said citizens persisted so long in their hardness that, after consultation with our brethren, we decreed that, unless within a month after receiving our letters they returned to obedience to the Church’s command and made due satisfaction concerning the matters for which they had incurred ecclesiastical censure, their city should be deprived of episcopal rank, its diocese divided among neighbouring bishops, and the goods of their merchants, wherever found, detained, they finally—whether vexation gave them understanding or the radiance of divine grace illumined their hearts—swore bodily into the hands of our delegates to obey us in all these matters. Thus they deserved absolution from the sentences of excommunication and interdict. [Col. 1487A–B]

They then sent the beloved sons, the noblemen Ub., viscount, and …, to the Apostolic See. Through them, in our presence, they gratefully and humbly offered to bind over to the bishop and certain clergy of Piacenza all the common property of the city, to be held until they should receive compensation from its revenues for what had been taken, since they lacked money with which to provide that compensation. But because the bishop and clergy did not accept this, we commanded the said consuls and citizens, under the obligation of the oath they had sworn, henceforth not to burden the bishop or clergy of Piacenza contrary to the tenor of the Lateran Council by exactions or levies, and to restore all fruits then remaining which they had taken from them or caused anyone else to take. [Col. 1487B–D]

Conceding to them concerning the other things taken, we commanded them to return three thousand pounds then, and for the remainder, as they had offered, to bind over the common property until full satisfaction had been made. But if they did not accept this arrangement, we commanded them under the same compulsion to pay in full, within six months, the monetary value of the goods taken, according to the valuation made, and to ensure that the possessions of the Church of Piacenza were restored to the state in which they had been at the time violence was inflicted. They were never to attempt anything contrary to this command, whether by force or deceit. Otherwise, besides the stigma and guilt of perjury, we decreed that they should be returned to the former sentence and that proceedings should be taken against them in the aforesaid form.

Accordingly, after restitution of nine thousand pounds, partly in money and partly in other movable goods, had been fully made by the citizens, the bishop with his clergy, on his own initiative—or perhaps at another’s persuasion—restored, or rather gave away, everything to his fellow citizens like a prodigal steward. He was excessively liberal to those who had been very insolent against him. In this, apart from other circumstances, he is clearly known to have gravely offended because, although he had received counsel from you, brother bishop of Ivrea, to consult the Apostolic See before making such restitution, he replied that he believed this was forbidden him by us. Thus, in grave contempt of the Apostolic See, in a case not permitted by the canons, he and his clergy alienated—or rather enormously squandered—the ecclesiastical treasure. He is rightly compared to the steward who, after squandering his master’s goods and being unable to render an account of them, was removed from his stewardship. [Col. 1488A–B]

He also grievously scandalized the entire province, left a pernicious example to posterity, and at once both lost his own labour and expense and caused others’ labour and expense to be lost. When this iniquity reached our ears through the report of many, wishing to know whether the bishop and his clergy had confirmed by action the report that had reached us, we commanded you, brother archbishop and bishop of Ivrea, and our venerable brother the bishop of Pavia, to inquire fully into the truth and take care faithfully to report it to us.

When you and the same bishop were assembled at Piacenza, you learned with the fullest certainty from the oath of the bishop and many others that no collusion whatsoever had occurred between the clergy and laymen, although the bishop, with his supporters, had restored or given away everything, as stated above. [Col. 1488B–C]

Although, therefore, by the strictness of law we could have deposed the aforesaid bishop forever from every ecclesiastical office, so that punishment might become an example to all whose fault had become a scandal, we nevertheless remembered the words which we expressed in our letters to the citizens of Piacenza, exhorting and beseeching them to give us freely and generously what was sought from them, in hope not only of an eternal reward to be conferred upon them by the Lord, but also of a temporal reward to be granted by the Apostolic See. Of this, as we have learned, they conceived no small hope and confidence.

We therefore judged that strictness should be tempered thus: the bishop and the other prelates of churches who were authors of this iniquity are suspended from every office of prelacy; and the benefices both of the bishop himself and of the other clerics who returned the money or pledges are to be divided into two equal parts. One part is to be retained for their support; the other is to be granted to those from whom they received aid during their exile, so that, since they proved generous toward their persecutors, they may be generous—even unwillingly—toward their benefactors.

We commanded Fredentius, canon of Saint Antoninus and chaplain of the aforesaid bishop, whom we learned had gravely offended in many ways in this matter in dealing with that bishop, to remain suspended from ecclesiastical office. [Col. 1488C–1489A]
