We believe that the aforesaid citizens, who are known—both by the oath which one man swore on behalf of the souls of the others, and by the sworn oaths of the bishop and other clerics who testified on this matter—to have employed no deceit or fraud, and indeed to have received neither promise nor hope that the money or pledges would be restored, are released from the restitution of the things taken which we had imposed upon them to make to the clerics and churches. The right remains reserved, if any belongs to the churches, to recover the treasure wrongfully alienated. Likewise reserved is our power, should the bishop and clergy not humbly bear the discipline imposed upon them according to their deserts, should the citizens perhaps deem the favour shown them insufficiently welcome, or should the scandal not cease, to stretch out the sinew of strictness which we have not loosened but bent. [Col. 1489A–B]

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion to ensure that the measures which we have established in prudent deliberation concerning these matters are inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure, with every obstacle of objection and appeal removed. If necessary, compel the bishop and clergy to assign, under oath, one half of their revenues to be distributed for the aforesaid cause according to your direction. Supported by our authority, you are to supply, with every obstacle of objection and appeal removed, their deficiency in the matters from which they are suspended. If not all of you can be present in carrying these things out, nevertheless two of you shall carry them out. [Col. 1489B–C]

Given at the Lateran, 22 November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXXVI. To the Bishop of Bayeux

Reply to his inquiries. (Lateran, 22 November.)

[Note: [Col. 1489D] Chapter *Cum in jure*, “On Elections.”]

Since you are learned in law and have an abundance of learned advisers, we cannot but wonder that you wished to consult us concerning certain points of law which are known to contain little or no uncertainty.

The first article of your inquiry stated that, when the dean of a certain church had died, the chapter of that place referred the matter, in the following form, to seven of its canons: whichever person, whether from among themselves or others of the body of that church, all together or the greater part of them should judge ought to be nominated, the same chapter should receive as dean. One of those seven was nominated as dean by three of them, while another, who was not among their number, was nominated as dean. Your brotherhood asked us which of them ought to be received by the chapter as dean.

[Note: [Col. 1489D] The Third Collection adds: “by three others”; likewise in the Colbertine and Angevin manuscript codices, [Col. 1490D].]

We reply that the person who is known to have been nominated by three of the seven should, according to the tenor of the reference, be received as dean, provided that he consents to the election made of him and no canonical impediment stands in the way.

[Note: [Col. 1490D] Chapter *Cum in jure*, “On the Office of a Delegated Judge.”]

Furthermore, you asked: when someone sends you a mandate in this form, “By the authority which I exercise, I enjoin you to declare that such a person lies under a sentence of excommunication,” and, while you hesitate concerning an apostolic mandate, no one provides you with proof thereof—are you bound to execute such a mandate? We give this response: unless you are certain that it is a mandate of the Apostolic See, you are not compelled to execute what is commanded. [Col. 1490A]

It also happened that, after someone had lawfully lodged an appeal to us, he was marked by excommunication; and concerning his absolution he obtained our letters through a messenger to certain judges. After the letters had been obtained but before they had been presented to the judges, he was bound by excommunication for another cause. You ask to be instructed by our response whether the same judges can take cognizance of the sentence of anathema pronounced the second time. We consider that your brotherhood should be answered that the jurisdiction of those judges ought not to extend to taking cognizance of that sentence, since at the time when our letters were obtained for them, that sentence had not yet been imposed, nor had it even been contemplated. [Col. 1490A–B]

Given at the Lateran, 22 November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXXVII. To the Bishop of Florence, the Abbot of Sassovivo, and the Prior of Camaldoli

The visitation of the monasteries of Tuscany is entrusted to them. (Lateran, 25 November.)

Since, by the office of apostolic service, in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, whose guardianship is known by the Lord’s disposition to have been entrusted to us, we are bound to uproot harmful things and plant useful ones, and cannot accomplish this everywhere in person, we sometimes call to this ministry of solicitude those whom we judge fit for it.

Since, therefore, among the other prelates of Tuscany we have fuller confidence in you, we have thought fit to entrust to you our functions concerning all monasteries situated both in Tuscany as far as Viterbo and Rieti, and also in the March.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that all of you together, or at least two of you, should visit these monasteries, whenever any one of you cannot be present, with a moderate number of companions and mounts; with appeal set aside, you are to correct what needs correction and establish in them what you judge conducive to salvation and honour. In carrying out the office of visitation, observe such maturity and moderation that those whom you visit may rejoice no less at your departure than at your arrival. [Col. 1490C–D]

Given at the Lateran, 25 November, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXXVIII. To the Archbishops of Tarragona, Braga, and Compostela

That brothers of Saint John of Jerusalem may not transfer to the Cistercians. (Lateran, 26 November.)

[Col. 1491A]

[Note: [Col. 1491D] Chapter *Licet*, On Religious.] Although certain monks and canons, as well as Hospitallers and Templars, have received an indult from the Apostolic See that, after anyone has made profession among them, he may not transfer to another house against their will, even under the pretext of a stricter religious life—so that, according to the Apostle, each may remain in the calling in which he is known to have been called—nevertheless, since where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty, and those led by the Spirit of God are not under the law, because the law was not [Col. 1491B] made for the righteous, this appears to have been granted them in order that no one, through rashness or fickleness, might fly from one order to another, to the detriment and ruin of his own order, under the pretext of a more religious life, as many are known frequently to have presumed to do; not, indeed, in order that permission to transfer should be denied to one who judges that he ought to request it with humility and purity, so that he may migrate, not feignedly but truly, to the fruit of a better life.

Therefore, after such a person has requested from his prelate permission to transfer, he is released from a private law which prejudices the public law, and may freely fulfill his purpose of a holier life, notwithstanding the obstinate and indiscreet opposition of a prelate, who deserves to lose his privilege when he abuses the power granted to him. For even the Roman [Col. 1491C] pontiff, who possesses supreme authority in the Church, without difficulty grants permission to resign to archbishops and bishops who request it for a just cause.

Accordingly, let all to whom such a privilege has been granted know that they are bound by law to grant permission to transfer to those who request it in this manner. For just as a subject ought to request permission to transfer from his prelate with humility and purity, lest he seem to despise the good of obedience, so surely the prelate ought, without difficulty and perversity, to grant the subject [Note: [Col. 1491D] In the third Collection is added: “in any case.” But this word [Col. 1492D] is not found in the Angers codex.] permission to transfer, lest he appear to impede a purpose divinely inspired.

But if there is probable doubt whether someone wishes to pass to a stricter or a more lax order from charity or [Col. 1491D] from rashness, the judgment of a superior must be sought, lest perhaps the angel of Satan transform himself into an angel of light. This rule must always be inviolably observed: no one may presume, on any occasion whatsoever, to abandon a bishopric without permission of the Roman pontiff. For as a greater good is preferred to a lesser, so the common good is preferred to a private good; and in this case teaching is rightly preferred to silence, pastoral care to contemplation, and labour to repose. To signify this, indeed, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, was not born according to the flesh of Rachel but of Leah; nor do we read that Mary received him [Col. 1492A] into her house, but Martha. Hence, so long as a bishop can both preside and be of use, he ought neither to request nor obtain permission to resign.

Now the beloved sons, the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem established in the regions of Spain, have shown us by a grave complaint that certain of their brethren, who have held administrative office and mastership in houses of the Hospital, and others of the same order, when they receive some command from their masters that displeases them or even seems harsh, transfer themselves to the Cistercian Order; and thus the houses of the Hospital are repeatedly stripped of their goods. Since we cannot pass by the grievance of these brethren with our eyes closed, we have commanded in our letters the beloved sons, all abbots of the Cistercian Order established in Spain, [Col. 1492B] that, carefully weighing what has been said, they should ensure that it is firmly observed, taking especial care not to do to the aforesaid brethren what they would not wish done to themselves.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your fraternity that, if the said abbots neglect to fulfill our command, you are not in any way to allow the said brethren to be molested contrary to the tenor of the foregoing. Rather, by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal, compel both the brethren who withdraw and those who may perhaps presume to receive them contrary to the aforesaid form to desist from such presumption. If not all of you, etc., let at least two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh year.

CLXXIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NEOPATRAS, THE BISHOP OF DAVALIA, AND THE ABBOT OF SAINT LUKE IN THE DIOCESE OF NEGROPONT. Written on behalf of Theodore, bishop of Negroponte. (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of December.)

[Col. 1492C]

Our venerable brother Theodore, bishop of Negroponte, has made known to us by his complaint that, although before our beloved son Benedict, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, then legate of the Apostolic See, he promised by an oath taken to render canonical obedience to the most holy Roman Church, and the same legate confirmed that bishopric to him by the authority he exercised, nevertheless the archbishop of Athens, his metropolitan, [Col. 1492D] taking occasion from the fact that he did not wish to be anointed according to Latin custom [Note: [Col. 1492D] See the deeds of Innocent III, chapter 75.], especially since the archbishop had no special apostolic mandate concerning this, presumed at his own will to depose him, disregarding the order of law; and, to his prejudice and injury, caused another to be elected bishop of that place.

Since the said bishop is prepared, as he asserts, to render canonical obedience both to us and to that archbishop, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, if this is so, you shall cause him to be restored, by means of justice and with every impediment of appeal removed, [Col. 1493A] to the aforesaid bishopric; nor shall you allow him to be unduly troubled concerning it, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure. If not all of you, etc., let two of you carry this out, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXXX. LETTER OF PHILIP, KING OF THE FRENCH, TO THE LORD POPE. On the case of divorce.

To the most holy Father and most dear lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman and universal Church, Philip, by the same grace [Col. 1493B] king of the French, greeting and reverence, both due and devout, in all things.

To your paternity, in which we have full confidence, we offer earnest prayers from the whole affection of our heart: grant to the venerable man, Lord Guala, your legate who is in our land, authority to dissolve our marriage, appeal being set aside, whether by reason of affinity, sorcery, entry into religion, or any other reasonable means by which marriages are customarily dissolved in your time and in the times of your predecessors; and, if it please you, make toward us the most lenient dispensation that you can. Concerning these matters and others, give unquestioning credence on our behalf to our faithful and familiar clerk Guy of Atheis, bearer of the present letters.

CLXXXI. TO HIS DEAREST SON IN CHRIST, PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRENCH. Reply to the preceding letter. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of December.)

[Col. 1493C]

On the matter of your marriage we have previously sent you rather lengthy letters, which for the most part contain the arguments of both parties, especially in order that, having examined them, you may deliberate with prudent men who have regard no less for justice than for persons, whether it is expedient for you to submit to judgment in this case—a judgment which ought certainly to be exercised without any respect of persons.

But we, who desire your salvation in respect to the soul and are zealous for your honour in respect to the body, advise and urge this upon your royal prudence in upright faith and sincere intention: that you not merely incline your mind, but compel it, as a strong and prudent king, who ought also to rule your own mind, [Col. 1493D] to render conjugal affection to our dearest daughter in Christ, Ingeburg, queen of the French, your wife. If you do this, we wish to be your sureties before God that, both in the present life and in the future, he will repay you a reward beyond your merits and beyond expectation.

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXXXII. TO THE SAME. On the same matter. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of December.)

[Col. 1494A]

[Note: [Col. 1493D] See below, book XV, letters 104, 105.] When our beloved son Guy, your messenger, came to the Apostolic See, he presented to us your royal letters, petitioning humbly on your behalf by word of mouth that, if our dearest daughter in Christ, Ingeburg, queen of the French, your wife, should voluntarily enter upon a religious vocation and publicly confess in a secure place, as our legate shall determine, and if you should swear that you have not carnally known her, you might be permitted to take another wife. For, as Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, replied [Note: [Col. 1493D] Chapter *Verum*, On the Conversion of Married Persons.], although in the Gospel the Lord said that a man may not dismiss [Col. 1494B] his wife except for the cause of fornication, this is nevertheless to be understood, according to the exposition of sacred Scripture, of those whose marriage has been consummated by bodily union, without which a marriage cannot be consummated. Therefore, if a woman has not been known by her husband, she may lawfully enter religion.

[Note: [Col. 1494D] Chapter *Ex publico*, under the same title.] Likewise it is elsewhere said that after lawful consent in the present tense it is permitted to either spouse to choose a monastery, even if the other resists, as certain saints were called from marriage, provided that carnal intercourse has not followed; and it seems lawful for the remaining spouse, if admonished and unwilling to preserve continence, to enter into a second marriage. For, since they were not made one flesh together, one may sufficiently pass to God [Col. 1494C] while the other remains in the world.

Since, therefore, he assigns this sole ground—that if a woman has not been made one flesh with her husband through carnal intercourse, she may migrate to religious life even against his will—without alleging any other circumstance, it is plainly apparent that, when the cause exists, the effect may follow. This is especially so because, just as union of the sexes signifies the union between the Word and human nature, since “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” so the consent of minds signifies charity between God and the righteous soul, since “he who cleaves to God is one spirit with him.” Therefore, just as the bond of union between the Word and human nature cannot be separated, so the marital bond between husband and wife, while they live, cannot be dissolved after they have been made one flesh through intercourse of the sexes. But just as the glue of charity between God and the soul is often dissolved, so the marital connection may be separated when there has been only consent of minds between spouses, because of what the Apostle says, expounding the word of the first-created man: “The two shall be one flesh. But I speak of this as a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. 5).

Moreover, since Truth itself, which is God, says, not through an apostle or prophet but in person in his Gospel: “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. 19); and: [Col. 1495A] “Let not a man dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication” (1 Cor. 7), we must not extend permission for a husband to depart from his wife, or a wife from her husband, for the sake of religion, except insofar as the examples of the saints and decrees of the Fathers make clear, lest human presumption seem to transgress the divine ordinance.

Certainly, we read that certain saints flew from marriage itself to the solitude of the desert and the poverty of pilgrimage. Perhaps moved by their example, certain of our predecessors said that parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man, but that she may choose a monastery for herself; and legal decrees judged that a betrothed woman, if she wished to convert, was to suffer no penalty.

[Note: [Col. 1495D] 27, question 2, chapters 27, 28.] Yet the examples of a few do not make a common law, especially when those few are believed to have acted by divine inspiration, since they are read to have been called from marriage. For, as the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3), and those led by the Spirit of God are not under the law. Some have wished the aforesaid decrees to be understood not of married persons but of betrothed persons, as their own words show, since they call her not a wife but a betrothed woman.

Nor can it be inferred from the aforesaid decrees or examples that, when either spouse—even if such persons are to be reckoned spouses—entered upon a religious vocation, the one left behind entered into marital union, except that Pope Alexander aforesaid is read [Note: [Col. 1495D] Chapter *Ex publico*, On the Conversion of Married Persons.] to have commanded a certain bishop concerning a certain woman that, if her husband had not carnally known her [Col. 1495C] and she wished to enter religion, he should receive from her sufficient security that she would either enter religion or endeavour to return to her husband within two months.

But whether your intention, dearest son, falls within these limits established by the examples of the saints or the decrees of the Fathers must be considered carefully, lest, if there should be error in this matter—which God forbid—great danger and grave scandal arise for us and for you. It is manifest that you approached the aforesaid queen, your wife, on several occasions in order to know her carnally, applying diligent effort to that end. Although you assert that you were unable to have carnal intercourse with her, perhaps in that intercourse you nevertheless did something unusual with her.

Now, although you suitably provide that her necessities of food and clothing be supplied, you nevertheless have her held in strict custody: she has with her none of her own, male or female; nor may she leave the palace in which she is detained; nor may anyone enter that palace to see her without your special command. While she was thus detained, you caused her to be urged in many ways by various persuaders, with many and great promises of gifts—not to mention threats held over her—that she should assume the religious habit and say that she had not been known by you, so that you might thus marry another wife. Yet she confessed before [Col. 1496A] our legates in court that you had carnally known her through sexual intercourse; and she has repeatedly informed us of the same, sending us three years ago, as testimony, certain open letters sealed with her seal, in which she most steadfastly declares that you carnally knew her. She adds that, if she should ever perhaps confess the contrary, we should never believe the contrary confession, because such a confession would be extorted from her either by fear of punishment or by the effort to escape—as Queen Theutberga is read to have written in a similar case against King Lothair to Pope Nicholas, our predecessor of holy memory.

But from the foregoing decrees or proposed examples it cannot be established that those who left their wives for the sake of religion had intercourse with them. [Col. 1496B] You, however, not only had intercourse with your aforesaid wife, but applied diligent effort to know her carnally. None of those men induced his wife to enter religion so that he himself might fly to another marriage. You, on the other hand, not only induced the aforesaid queen to do this, but also enticed her with many promises; indeed, you obtained from her an oath that she would do so, promising one thousand pounds of annual revenue. None of those men held his wife in confinement even for a short time. But you have now had the aforesaid queen held in strict custody for eight years. Indeed, whereas they are read to have passed from marriage, or others wished to pass before reaching marriage, she is urged to transfer after the sixteenth [Col. 1496C] year from the marriage contracted—would that she were not compelled!

No wife among those men demanded the marital debt. But the aforesaid queen frequently demanded it from you, and you refused to render it to her. No wife among those men said that she had been known by him. But the oft-mentioned queen steadfastly asserted, even in court, that you had carnally known her. Therefore, if she now confessed the contrary, her simple word should not be believed, since even concerning those who claim, because of frigidity, that they could not have intercourse with one another, the blessed Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1496D] See chapter *Laudabilem*, On Frigidity and Sorcery.] decreed that each of them, with the sacred relics touched by the seventh hand of kinsmen, should swear that they had never been joined by intercourse of the flesh and made one flesh. How much more, then, ought she to make a similar oath, who seems afflicted by excessive weariness—not to say seized by fear, led astray by counsels, or enticed by promises.

You see, therefore, dearest son, that in the case of the aforesaid queen you have proceeded much further than anyone proceeded, according to the examples proposed or the decrees set forth, who left his wife for the sake of religion, or whose wife left her husband for the same cause. Nor should you think that we say these things as though we wished to exercise excessive severity toward you, since by comparison with a similar case you can perceive that we have shown you great favour and kindness.

For in the time of our aforesaid predecessor Pope Nicholas, the said King [Col. 1497A] Lothair—by no means least but greatest among kings—rashly dismissed his wife Theutberga and brought in Waldrada, having the former held in strict confinement and treating the latter with royal honour. When Theutberga lodged her complaint before the aforesaid predecessor, she sent, among other things, a written appeal in which she made known not that she had yet confessed, but that she was being compelled to utter a false accusation against herself; adding that, if she were compelled further, it should be understood that she would say what the king wished, not through truth but through fear of death and a desire to escape, because she could not do otherwise.

From this you can and ought to perceive how much we have taken care to show deference to your majesty, both in words and in deeds. That predecessor called the introduced Waldrada Lothair’s concubine; but we have never called the woman introduced by you your concubine, but a noblewoman. He did not call the aforesaid Lothair simply king, but asked whether one could truly be called king who restrained no bodily appetite by wholesome government. But we have called you not merely king, but a most Catholic prince and a most Christian king. He deposed two archbishops, namely those of Cologne and Trier, because they had pronounced an unjust judgment in the marriage case. But we have not deposed even one archbishop—namely, the archbishop of Reims, your uncle—who promulgated a sentence of divorce, or rather a farcical tale. He struck King Lothair and [Col. 1497C] the introduced Waldrada with the sword of excommunication. But we, although we pronounced a sentence of interdict—not indeed upon your whole kingdom, but upon a certain part of it—have nevertheless not subjected either you or the introduced woman to excommunication; nor have we withdrawn divine offices or ecclesiastical sacraments from her or from you.

Although we have also very frequently admonished you to restore the aforesaid wife to her due freedom and have her treated with royal honour, we have not yet compelled you to this by apostolic power. Nor have we yet compelled you by ecclesiastical censure to render the marital debt that she has frequently demanded, although you have been carefully admonished many times. Do you suppose, magnificent king, that, although the aforesaid predecessor surpassed us in merit and [Col. 1497D] learning, we are his inferiors in office and power, so that we cannot act against you with the same zeal with which he is known to have acted, inflamed by zeal for justice, against so great a king; or that henceforth we may act less justly if we continue to defer exercising what perhaps until now we have delayed beyond what was just?

But so that you may know the affection of love and favour which we bear toward you, behold: moderating strictness, we command our beloved son Guala, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico and legate of the Apostolic See, that, as you requested by royal letters—to use your own words—he proceed, appeal being set aside, in the matter of marriage, whether the cause proposed before him be affinity, sorcery [Note: [Col. 1497D] See above, letter 180.], [Col. 1498A] religious profession, or any other reasonable ground by which marriages are customarily dissolved. Thus, although such shifting is suspect—at one time alleging affinity, at another sorcery, at another religion, or indiscriminately any other ground to dissolve the marriage—if you wish to have recourse to the question of affinity, he shall observe the form which we have prescribed to other legates concerning that point; but if you wish to pursue a charge of sorcery, he shall follow the form prescribed to him.

If the matter concerns religious profession, the same legate shall prudently attend to the foregoing and carefully consider the matters to be proposed. Finally, if he proceeds by the will of the parties, in any case he shall decide the cause by a canonical conclusion, [Col. 1498B] or remit it to our examination after it has been sufficiently instructed, assigning the parties a suitable term within which they are to appear before us through qualified representatives to receive, with God as author, a just sentence. In all things this shall always be observed: the aforesaid queen must be provided complete freedom, as the aforementioned predecessor Nicholas decreed in a similar case, saying:

“Whether judgment is to be held concerning the bond of marriage or concerning the accusation of adultery, no reason allows Theutberga to enter into contest with Lothair unless she is first restored for a time to her own control and freely joined with her kinsmen. Among these provisions, a place must also be provided where no violence of a crowd is feared, lest it be difficult [Col. 1498C] to produce witnesses or the other persons required in such disputes by both the holy canons and the venerable Roman laws.”

[Note: [Col. 1498D] 33, question 2, chapter *Sive*.] Behold, dearest son, we do not invent novel words from our own heart, but bring forward authoritative enactments from canon law, as prudent men will be able to explain to you more fully. Therefore we earnestly request and admonish your royal prudence carefully to consider what is lawful, what is fitting, and what is expedient to do in this affair; turning away your hearing from those who anoint your head with the oil of the sinner. For, to use divine words, “those who call you blessed deceive you.” Under the warning of divine judgment, for the remedy of your sins, we command you in the power of the Holy Spirit not to permit the aforesaid queen to be injured in any respect or compelled against her will to anything, but to cause her both to enjoy due freedom and to be treated with royal honour. Otherwise—though we do not believe you will act thus—you will deserve divine and apostolic indignation and, besides great offence, will incur severe punishment; and, by the merit of this sin, may your latter end not accord with its beginning and middle.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXXXIII. TO THE BELOVED SON GUALA, DEACON-CARDINAL OF SAINT MARY IN PORTICO, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. On the same matter. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1499A]

Concerning the marriage case we write to our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the French, as follows: “When our beloved son Guy, your messenger, came to the Apostolic See,” etc., as in the other letter to the end. Therefore, son legate, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that you proceed according to the prescribed form, after due consideration.

Given at the Lateran, etc.

CLXXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF MAINZ AND MAGDEBURG. On the marriage of the king of Bohemia. (Lateran, third day before the Ides of December.)

[Col. 1499B]

We formerly learned from letters sent to us by our venerable brother the bishop of Avelberg and our beloved son the abbot of Sichem that, when they had peremptorily summoned the illustrious King O. [Note: [Col. 1499] Ottokar. See above, book II, letter 188; also chapter *Constitutis*, On Witnesses.] of Bohemia, by authority both ours and that of our legates, concerning the marriage case pending between him and the noblewoman A., sister of the margrave of Meissen, and the woman’s party appeared before them, the same king contumaciously withdrew himself.

When it was alleged by the woman’s party that the said king had caused B., the priest whom the aforesaid judges had sent to him with letters of citation, to be seized [Col. 1499C] and committed to strict custody, and when the same judges had waited two days after the peremptory date in case perhaps someone should appear before them on behalf of the said king, they finally, on the third day, established through suitable witnesses that the letters of citation had reached him and recognized his manifest contumacy. They pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him.

Since the said king was reported to have challenged the aforesaid judges as suspect, we instructed our venerable brother the bishop of Ostia and our beloved son Leo, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross, who had then been charged with the office of legation in those regions for the affairs of the Empire and the Church, to receive sworn security from the king that he would obey the law, grant him the benefit of absolution, and inquire—if they could devote themselves to this—either personally or through suitable men, whether the aforesaid judges could reasonably be challenged by him. If they were reasonably challenged, they were to hear the case, or have it heard, appeal being set aside, so that, after proceedings had reached judgment, it should be remitted to us fully instructed, with a suitable term assigned to the parties within which they should appear before us through qualified procurators to receive, with God as author, a just sentence. Otherwise, the parties were to be remitted to the examination of the former judges.

But because those legates, owing to [Col. 1500A] that lamentable event which altered the state of affairs by the unexpected death of the prince, withdrew from the journey of legation which they had undertaken and could not attend to these matters, we command your fraternity by apostolic writings that, after the aforesaid king has been absolved according to the prescribed form, you yourselves diligently inquire whether the aforementioned judges can reasonably be challenged by him; and in all other respects ensure the execution of the apostolic command laid upon the aforesaid legates, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CLXXXV. TO ALL CHRIST’S FAITHFUL ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT LOMBARDY AND THE MARCH. On aid for the Holy Land. (Lateran, fourth day before the Ides of December.)

[Col. 1500B]

Would that the Lord granted both us effective speech and you and others perfect hearing, so that, at least through a parable, you might be induced to perform for an earthly king what we urge concerning service to the heavenly King. For when such a king had lost his own kingdom through the fault of his servants, he repeatedly sought their aid to recover it; and when they not only stubbornly refused to give him that aid, but even turned their hands against themselves in hostility, he finally recovered his kingdom by his own strength. Is there, then, any one of you so merciful—or so foolish—that, if he occupied the place of such a king, he would not, when the time came [Col. 1500C] to render justice, punish such servants as traitors to the king and faithless disloyal men by exile, burning, hanging, or perhaps some harsher penalty, so that, after the wicked had been wretchedly destroyed, he might install other faithful persons in their goods?  

But if an earthly king, who has power only over the body, would do this, how much more may the Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords—who bestowed on us both body and soul and is able to cast both into Gehenna—condemn his servants for the fault of ingratitude and, as it were, the crime of unfaithfulness, if, after he has been driven out of the land which he purchased at the price of his blood, through a fault assuredly not his own but theirs, they neglect to come to his aid in recovering it. Behold: driven from his inheritance [Col. 1500D] for our iniquities, he lives in exile. Behold: as though disinherited, he implores our help for his own relief; and there is no one either to comfort the exile or aid the suppliant. With arms outstretched upon the cross, he shows us, as it were, the renewed outrage of those who crucify him; and almost absolutely no one is moved by due devotion to avenge him. His side is pierced by a lance; his hands and feet are fastened with cruel nails; and scarcely anyone’s breast is pierced by compassion for such great cruelty, so that he may rise to Christ’s aid, repaying him with his own death—the death which Christ gave for him.  

For the hearts of all have been weighed down; and, though he is now almost breathing his last, crying with a loud voice [Col. 1501A], they cannot be aroused. Oh, how all have become without pity and altogether changed into cruel persons, when the Virgin Mother is driven from the poor lodging of the manger with her crying Child, and no one comes to her aid with the service of humanity due to her! Woe to the sinful nation; woe to the people full of sins! Truly your heart is hard, your brow bronze, and your neck an iron sinew. The Lord who made you, and bestowed upon you not only what you have but also what you are, is struck and spat upon, blasphemed and scourged; indeed, now that all the mockeries and punishments which he endured bodily are renewed spiritually, he is not merely led as far as the cross, but the cross itself is taken away from him. In this the rage of modern crucifiers surpasses the tyranny of the ancient ones: whereas they left him nothing upon the cross [Col. 1501B], these leave him not even the cross. Yet you ignore so great an indignity done to your Creator.  

Alas for ungrateful servants! Alas for undevoted retainers! When the Lord of heaven and earth implores their aid to recover his own patrimony, lost not through his faults but through theirs, they not only damnably refuse to give it him, but even turn arms against one another in hostility! Alas for sorrow! What madness is this, and what license, to stain domestic swords with blood through civil wars, while allowing perfidious and utterly savage nations to triumph over Christ’s patrimony? Has his hand become shortened and made small, so that he cannot redeem? Or does he lack strength to deliver? Could not he who, by his rebuke, makes [the sea] a wilderness, clothes [Col. 1501C] the heavens in darkness, and makes sackcloth their covering, save the portion of his inheritance by the single word of his mouth?  

For God is the everlasting Lord, who created the boundaries of the earth, who gives strength to the fallen and multiplies strength and power for those who have none. He will not fail or grow weary of rescuing the eastern province from the hands of the ungodly whenever and however he wills. Yet perhaps he foresaw that, in its occupation and detention, our sins should be punished in such a way that the punishment itself would become a greater fault for the impenitent, but would profit the penitent unto a crown: that from the same thing by which he increased the offenses of the obstinate, he might remit the guilt of those humbling themselves.  

For, knowing that all things work together for good to those who love him [Col. 1501D], he permitted the sign of the saving cross, upon which our salvation itself hung, and the land of his birth, which he consecrated with his own blood, to be seized by the enemies of the Christian faith—not that he might acquire knowledge through experience, since he has known and foreseen all things from eternity, but that he might make us more certain of our strength or weakness, and more fully reveal who are his: if perhaps anyone might be touched by this injury to him, if anyone might be inflamed by zeal for the divine law, and be stirred to avenge the outrage done to the cross.  

All men of riches were sleeping their sleep; they were sleeping and dozing amid their own wishes and pleasures, when suddenly there came from heaven a sound concerning the unexpected destruction of Christ’s inheritance—a sound that not only awakened sleepers but shook all the bounds of Christendom [Col. 1502A]. Since no one doubted God’s power, each might attribute the event to his own crimes and thus at least return to the Lord and repent of his offenses—those who had formerly said in their hearts, “There is no God” (Psalm XIII).  

Therefore, since the Lord perhaps wished in this to furnish us an occasion of salvation—indeed, to provide a cause of salvation—we earnestly admonish and exhort you in the Lord, and, for the remission of your sins, enjoin you: keeping before the eyes of your heart the exile of the Crucified One, let those who are able fight the Lord’s battle take up the cross and arms. Let those unable to fight send, at their own expense and according to their means, some warriors; and let no one excuse himself from this duty of aid without devoutly and willingly spending at least something small, even one imperial penny. For a cup of cold water sometimes suffices to purchase the kingdom of heaven; and the poor woman who cast two small coins into the treasury is praised as having offered more than the rest.  

Accordingly, dearest sons, while this common necessity presses, lay aside domestic quarrels, and devote to aiding the Holy Land the effort that you would otherwise expend in mutual wars or feuds. For, on account of our sins, it stands in such need—bereft of men and resources, laborers and wealth—as it is not known ever to have suffered from the beginning of its visitation [Col. 1502B]. So that you may undertake this most holy labor more confidently, already secure, as it were, of your reward: relying [Col. 1502C] on the mercy of almighty God and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by that power of binding and loosing which God, though we are unworthy, has bestowed upon us, we grant full pardon of their sins—sins for which they have performed repentance of heart and mouth—to all who undertake at their own expense the labor of this journey in their own persons; and in the reward of the righteous we promise them an increase of eternal salvation.  

We likewise grant full pardon of their sins to those who do not go there in their own persons but, at their own expense and according to their circumstances and means, send suitable men to remain there for at least one year; and to those who, although at another’s expense, fulfill in their own persons the labor of the pilgrimage they have undertaken [Col. 1502D]. We also wish all who suitably contribute from their goods to the relief of that land to share in this remission in proportion to the amount of their aid and the disposition of their devotion. From the time when they have taken the cross, we receive their persons and goods under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and we command that they likewise remain under the defense of the archbishops and all prelates of God’s Church, decreeing that their property shall remain whole and undisturbed until certain knowledge has been obtained of their death or return. Should anyone presume to act contrary to this, let him be restrained by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside.  

If any of those departing thither are bound by oath to creditors for the payment of interest, we likewise command that their creditors be compelled by the prelates of the churches, with the same strictness, to release them from the oath already made and desist from demanding interest [Col. 1503A]. If any creditor compels them to pay interest, we order that he himself be compelled, by a like penalty, to restore it. We also grant to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Cremona and Ypres, and to our beloved son the abbot of Tilieto, to whom we have specially entrusted authority to induce you to this work of piety, as well as to the other archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses you reside, that, concerning those who wish to assist the Holy Land from their goods, they may, upon advice of prudent men and after weighing the condition of persons and the amount of their resources, and considering also the disposition of their devotion, commute the work of imposed penance into the work of giving alms [Col. 1503B].  

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF THE CHURCHES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT LOMBARDY AND THE MARCH. On the same matter. (Given as in the other letter.)

“Would that the Lord granted both us effective speech,” etc., in almost the same manner to the end. Therefore we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you, commanding you by these apostolic letters to persevere among the peoples subject to you in diligent preaching and exhortation [Col. 1503C], so that, in accordance with our exhortation and that of the aforesaid bishops and abbot, they may aid the aforesaid Holy Land. In all other matters expressed above, carry out our constitution and command effectively, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. Further, cause the fortieth part of your ecclesiastical revenues and proceeds, and also those of the other clerics, together with the other alms of the faithful which we formerly ordered to be gathered for the aid of that land, if indeed they have been collected, to be assigned as soon as possible to the aforesaid bishops and abbot, to be transmitted for aid of that land according to their judgment. Otherwise, ensure that they are diligently collected and faithfully assigned to them [Col. 1503D].  

Given as in the other letter.

## CLXXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF YPRES AND THE ABBOT OF TILIETO, VISITORS OF LOMBARDY. On the removal of the bishop of Albenga. (Lateran, 12 December.)

From your letters we learn that, when you had gone with our venerable brother, the archbishop of Pisa, then bishop of Vercelli, to the Church of Albenga to carry out the office of visitation, the bishop of Albenga, among other matters brought forward against him, personally confessed to you this: that when a certain man in a town belonging to his jurisdiction was accused of theft, and he wholly denied it, offering to clear himself by the ordeal of hot iron and adding that he should be punished by hanging if he failed in it, the said bishop asked the judge what seemed proper to him in the matter. When the judge replied that it should be done as the thief himself had said, hot iron was brought in the bishop’s presence [Col. 1504A]. When that thief took it, he was burned. The judge, alarmed at this, consulted the aforesaid bishop as to what seemed proper to him; he replied that it would be evil if the thief should escape in this way. Although, in letters which the bishop himself has now sent us, he affirms that he used these words: “You have heard how great is the outcry of the people; all say that it is evil if he escapes unpunished.” Thus the bishop and judge left that town with the crowd; in their presence the aforesaid thief was hanged by the bishop’s authority. For this reason you sent the bishop, together with your letters, to the Apostolic See.  

But when he appeared in our presence, he put forward nothing whatsoever concerning these matters before us; nor did we see your letters, although he asserts that he presented them to us. Rather, as soon as the said archbishop came to the Apostolic See and fully informed us of the course of this affair, the bishop withdrew from our presence and, though sought, could not be found [Col. 1504B]. We carefully deliberated with our brethren on these matters; and because the bishop is known to have committed grave offenses not only in the ordeal of hot iron but also in the hanging of the thief—since he furnished not merely authority for these acts but also his bodily presence—we judge him unworthy of ministry at the altar.  

Since the episcopal office cannot be fulfilled without ministry at the altar, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to admonish him to resign his bishopric. Otherwise, removing him by apostolic authority from the Church of Albenga, with the obstacle of appeal removed, cause provision to be made for that church by a canonical election of a suitable person. Restrain opponents by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside [Col. 1504C].  

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate [Col. 1504D].

## CLXXXVIII. TO THE PRIOR OF OSEN AND THE SUPERIOR OF SAINT FREDESWIDE. Written on behalf of the abbot of Bello. (Lateran, 12 December.)

[Note: [Col. 1504D] Chapter *Ex tenore*, *On the granting of prebends*.]

From the tenor of your letters we have plainly understood that, when a dispute was known to be pending between I., a clerk, on the one side, and the abbot and convent of Bello on the other, concerning an income of ten or fifteen marks which he demanded from them—because they had promised to provide for him in that amount as soon as opportunity offered, yet had neglected to fulfill their promise—we committed the case to you. After the joinder of issue, the said clerk produced before you a certain charter of those monks, expressly stating that they had promised to assign him the first church subject to their patronage that should be worth ten or fifteen marks. He also proved through suitable witnesses that, after making this promise, although able to do so and despite having been admonished concerning it, they had refused to provide for him. Therefore he urgently requested that the abbot and monks be compelled to assign him an income of at least ten marks [Col. 1505A].  

The opposing reply was that they could not be sued on the basis of this promise, since it was made contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, as the charter produced seemed to prove; especially since our letters mentioned not a particular church but merely a promise. As some maintained that they could be sued on other grounds while others took the contrary view, and the matter was debated at length before you on both sides, you, doubting what the law was on this point, were unwilling to proceed further until you had received the expression of our will. You humbly requested that by our letters we should make you certain what was to be done in this matter [Col. 1505B].  

Therefore, considering that the aforesaid promise is not binding, since it was attempted contrary to the statutes of the aforesaid council, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to impose silence upon the said clerk in this matter and absolve the aforesaid abbot and monks from his claim [Col. 1505C].  

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CLXXXIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NEOPATRAS, THE BISHOP OF DAVALIA, AND OUR BELOVED SON, THE ELECT OF NAZARETH. On the obedience owed by bishops to their metropolitans. (Lateran, 8 December.)

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Larissa, has shown us in his complaint that our venerable brother, the bishop of Demetrias, a suffragan of the Church of Larissa, relying on lay power, refuses to render him due obedience and reverence [Col. 1505D]. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce the aforesaid bishop to render due obedience and honor to the aforesaid archbishop; if necessary, compel him to do this by suitable coercion, with appeal set aside. No letters prejudicial to truth and justice notwithstanding, etc. If not all of you, etc., let two of you, etc.  

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXC. TO THE ELECT OF NAZARETH. He is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Lateran, 9 December.)

[Col. 1506A]

“When what is just and honorable is requested of us,” etc., through “effect.” Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive the Church of Nazareth, with all that it now reasonably possesses, etc., under protection. We therefore decree that absolutely no person may infringe this document of our protection or, etc. Should anyone presume to attempt this, etc., through “shall incur.”  

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXCI. TO THE BISHOP OF DAVALIA. On the same subject. (Given as in the other letter.)

[Col. 1506B]

“When what is just and honorable is requested of us,” etc., through “effect.” Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, etc., through “assent,” we receive the Church of Davalia, with all that it now reasonably possesses, etc., under protection. We therefore decree . . . that no person may infringe this document of our protection, etc., through “shall incur.”  

Given as in the other letter throughout.

## CXCII. TO THE BISHOP AND ARCHDEACON OF CREMONA. On the election of the abbot of Cornu. (Lateran, 17 December.)

[Col. 1506C]

When our venerable brother, the bishop of Ypres, and our beloved son Albert, priest of Mantua, had gone to the monastery of Saint Stephen of Cornu for the work of visitation and correction, and had established there many regulations suited to regular observance, P., then abbot of that monastery, had been gravely accused of carnal lapse, the crime of simony, and many other offenses. When, in accordance with the duty of their office, they wished to investigate the truth concerning these matters, the abbot humbly requested that they proceed against him according to the form of law, since the matter was not notorious, neither public nor private report troubled him, nor did any accuser appear against him. When they refused to admit such petitions—or rather objections—as frivolous, the abbot appealed to the Apostolic See [Col. 1506D].  

But they did not admit this appeal, as being dilatory; and, having received sworn depositions from the prior and many monks of that monastery, they investigated the truth more fully concerning the foregoing matters. In the meantime, when the abbot had lodged before our audience a serious complaint against the aforesaid visitors, we instructed our venerable brother Hubert, archbishop of Milan and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, to inquire of the aforesaid bishop and priest what reason had induced them to make such an investigation. Unless they showed another reasonable cause, he was to prohibit them by apostolic authority from proceeding with the investigation, restoring the due status if they had undertaken anything prejudicial to the abbot after an appeal reasonably made to us; otherwise, they were to follow canonical procedure in that investigation [Col. 1507A].  

Since the course of their proceedings became fully known to us both through their letters and through the report of the aforesaid bishop, we judged that justice required the removal of the said abbot from that abbacy. We command your discretion by apostolic letters both to cause what we have established in this matter by prudent deliberation to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, and to enjoin upon the prior and brothers of that monastery by apostolic authority that they appoint a suitable person over themselves as abbot through canonical election. Compel the deposed man, by the same censure and with appeal set aside, to restore the monastery’s privileges and other things entrusted to his custody; restraining any opponents or rebels by like coercion [Col. 1507B].  

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXCIII. TO SICIBALD, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY OF ROSEVELDE, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 9 December.)

[Col. 1507C]

Whenever something is requested of us that is recognized as suited to religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford appropriate support to the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of the present writing, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary of Rosevelde, in which you are devoted to divine service, and which is known to belong to the right and property of the Roman Church, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Adrian and Alexander. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We have thought it appropriate to state these in their proper names [Col. 1507D]:  

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its appurtenances; the tithe of Lu, which Albero, archbishop of the Church of Hamburg of happy memory, with the consent of all the clergy and people, gave to your monastery in exchange; the tithe of Rosevelde, likewise given you in exchange for the wood called Frankenholt; the estate called Coningohof with all its appurtenances; Eliker’s office with all its appurtenances; the old office with its appurtenances; twelve holdings beside the Elbe with their appurtenances; in Slavia, the village called Lanchua; the possessions lying near Lu; the goods given to your church by Ermengard, marchioness of happy memory, at Tumarisco; namely, the estate of Crimpestede with all its appurtenances; the estate of Fragistede with its appurtenances; the whole land called Busin with its appurtenances; Odo’s office with its appurtenances; the office of Hermann and Wilbern with all its appurtenances; Sibern’s office with its appurtenances; and Hesing’s office with its appurtenances [Col. 1508A].  

“When there shall be a general interdict of the land,” etc., through “celebrate.” You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, etc., through “be willing to provide.” Otherwise, you may have recourse to whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by apostolic authority, shall grant what is requested. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, etc., through “they shall provide for one to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.” But if, God forbid, they should be unable to find in their own community one considered suitable for this governance, they may choose one from whatever place they prefer, provided he is of their order and profession.  

Furthermore, we prohibit any abbot of the monastery of Rosevelde from presuming to grant its goods in fief, sell them, or alienate them under any other title without the consent of the greater and sounder part of your chapter [Col. 1508C]. Moreover, as our aforesaid predecessors Adrian and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, are known to have decreed, we decree that no archbishop, bishop, or other ecclesiastical or secular person may arrange or order anything, or receive exactions or procurations, without the consent and will of the brethren serving God there; rather, the monastery shall be bound to obedience or service only to the Roman pontiff. We further enact that no one may ever presume to be advocate of your monastery except one whom the brothers have foreseen should be elected by common consent. “The burial place of the same locality,” etc., through “let no one oppose it,” while the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remains safeguarded. We therefore decree that it be lawful for no one whatever to injure the aforesaid monastery, etc., through “beneficial.” The authority of the Apostolic See being preserved.  

Moreover, as a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, in accordance with what Margrave Udo, together with his brother Rodulf and mother Odda, in whose patrimony that monastery is situated, is known to have established, you shall pay yearly to us and our successors one Byzantine coin. Should anyone therefore in the future, etc., through “shall be subject.” But may all who preserve to that place its rights, etc., through “find the rewards of eternal peace” [Col. 1508D].  

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III [Col. 1509A].

## CXCIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT VAAST OF ARRAS. On the liberty of that monastery. (Lateran, 17 December.)

It is evident from the privilege of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, granted by him to your monastery and renewed by us following its example, that the monastery belongs directly, without intermediary, to the Roman Church. Although the beloved son . . ., canon of Arras and messenger of our venerable brother the bishop of Arras, recently appearing in our presence, firmly asserted that under our predecessor Pope Urban of happy memory litigation had occurred on this matter between the predecessors of that bishop and of you, son abbot, nevertheless, because the privilege of liberty is evident and the bishop’s right has not been established, we have thought it necessary to prohibit that bishop by our letters from presuming, contrary to the tenor of the privilege, to molest you either in your persons or in matters belonging to the monastery [Col. 1509B]. If the bishop trusts in his right, however, let him pursue his claim by judicial procedure. Otherwise, we decree that any sentence—if it deserves the name of sentence—which that bishop may pronounce against you shall not be observed, as having been issued by one who is not your judge.  

[Col. 1509C] Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXCV. TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF ANDRES. That they may recover possessions pledged as security. (Lateran, 20 December.)

[Note: [Col. 1509D] See vol. IX of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 382.]

It was represented to us on your behalf that certain things belonging to the fief of your monastery have been pledged as security by their enfeoffed holders to powerful persons, not lawfully but merely in fact, and have thereby become alienated from the monastery as interest accumulates. You humbly requested that you might, with our permission, take in pledge lands, revenues, and other things belonging to your monastery in the manner aforesaid, so that they may not become wholly alienated [Col. 1509D], provided that the fruits received are not to be reckoned to you as interest. Wishing to safeguard the monastery from loss with paternal concern, we assent to your requests. Let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this document of our permission or rashly act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, etc., through the end.  

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXCVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF TARRAGONA. On the affair of Durand of Huesca and his companions. (Lateran, 18 December.)

[Col. 1510A]

[Note: [Col. 1509] See Book XII, letters 17, 66, and following; Book XIII, letters 77, 78.]

Following the example of him who is not the God of dissension but of peace, who wills all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth, we received with paternal kindness at the Apostolic See our beloved sons Durand of Huesca and his companions when they came to us; and we fully understood what they took care to set before us both on their own behalf and on behalf of their brethren. From what they said to us, after careful examination concerning the articles of faith and the sacraments of the Church, we learned that they hold the orthodox faith and uphold Catholic truth [Col. 1510B].  

Yet, for greater explicitness, after the Gospels had been placed before them and the written statement of their confession laid upon them, we received from them this oath: “I, Durand of Huesca,” he said, “before your consecrated hands, supreme pontiff, Lord Innocent, call God as witness upon my soul that I believe simply and truly exactly as this written statement contains in every respect; that I shall never believe the contrary; and that, so far as I am able, I shall oppose those who believe the contrary. Moreover, to you, as successor of the blessed apostle Peter, and to the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates in whose dioceses or parishes I shall reside, I shall render obedience and reverence, both what is due and what is devout.”  

The written confession was as follows.

[Col. 1510C] “Let it be known to all the faithful that I, Durand of Osca, and I. and E. and B., and all our brethren, believe in our hearts, understand by faith, confess with our mouths, and affirm in simple words that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons, one God; and that the whole Trinity is coessential, consubstantial, coeternal, and omnipotent, and each individual person in the Trinity fully God, as is contained in the *I Believe in God*, the *I Believe in One God*, and the *Whoever Wishes* [*Quicunque vult*].

We likewise believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the one God of whom we speak—is the creator, maker, governor, and disposer of all things bodily and spiritual, visible and invisible. We believe that the God who remains, as stated, in the Trinity is one and the same author of the Old and New Testaments [Col. 1510D], and that he created all things from nothing; and that John the Baptist, holy and righteous, was sent by him and filled with the Holy Spirit in his mother’s womb.

We believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that the incarnation of the divinity took place not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit, but in the Son alone: so that he who was, in his divinity, the Son of God the Father, true God from the Father, might be, in his humanity, the Son of man, true man from his mother, possessing true flesh from his mother’s womb [Col. 1511A] and a rational human soul; one person, one Son, one Christ, God and man in both natures together, one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, author and ruler of all things. Born of the Virgin Mary in a true birth of flesh, he ate and drank, slept, and, weary from his journey, rested; he suffered a true suffering in his flesh, died a true death in his body, and rose again in a true resurrection of his flesh and a true resumption of his soul to his body. After this, having eaten and drunk, he ascended into heaven, sits at the Father’s right hand, and will come in that same flesh to judge the living and the dead.

We believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths one Church—not that of heretics, but the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic Church—outside which we believe no one can be saved. Nor do we reject in any respect the sacraments [Col. 1511B] celebrated within it, though administered by a sinful priest, provided that the Church receives him; for, through the inestimable and invisible power of the Holy Spirit working with them, neither do we disparage ecclesiastical offices or blessings celebrated by him, but embrace them with a kindly disposition as though from one most just. For the wickedness of a bishop or priest does no harm either to the baptism of an infant, or to the consecration of the Eucharist, or to the other ecclesiastical offices celebrated for those subject to them.

We therefore approve infant baptism. If infants die after baptism before committing sins, we confess and believe that they are saved; and we believe that in baptism all sins are forgiven, both that original sin which has been contracted and those [Col. 1511C] voluntarily committed. We judge confirmation performed by a bishop—that is, the laying on of hands—to be holy and to be received with veneration.

The sacrifice—

[Note: [Col. 1511D] In Book XIII, epistle 78, it is written: “In the sacrifice of the Eucharist, those things which before consecration were [Col. 1512D] bread and wine, after consecration …”]

—that is, bread and wine, after consecration, to be the true body and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, we firmly and without doubt believe with pure heart and simply affirm in faithful words. In it we believe that nothing greater is accomplished by a good priest, nor anything less by a bad one; for it is effected not by the merit of the consecrator, but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. Hence we firmly believe and confess that, however upright, religious, holy, and wise any person may be, he cannot and ought not consecrate the Eucharist or perform the sacrifice of the altar unless he is a priest regularly ordained by a visible [Col. 1511D] and tangible bishop. For this office, we believe, three things are necessary: a definite person—the priest himself—appointed by a bishop, as stated above, specifically to this office; those solemn words set down by the holy Fathers in the canon; and the faithful intention of the speaker. Therefore we firmly believe and confess that whoever, without prior episcopal ordination as stated above, believes and maintains that he can perform the sacrifice of the Eucharist is a heretic, a participant and companion in the perdition of Korah and his accomplices, and must be separated from the whole holy Roman Church.

We believe that God grants pardon to sinners who truly repent, and we communicate with them most willingly. We venerate the anointing of the sick with consecrated oil. We do not deny that carnal marriages ought to be contracted according to the Apostle; but we altogether forbid marriages lawfully contracted to be dissolved. We believe and confess that a man may be saved together with his wife; nor do we condemn second or subsequent marriages. We do not at all condemn the eating of flesh. We do not condemn an oath; indeed, we believe with a pure heart that it is lawful to swear with truth, judgment, and justice.

[Note: [Col. 1512D] These words were added from Book XIII.] We affirm concerning secular authority that it may, without mortal sin, exercise judgment involving bloodshed, provided that it proceeds to inflict punishment not from hatred but in judgment, and not rashly but with deliberation.

We believe preaching [Col. 1512B] to be very necessary and praiseworthy; nevertheless, we believe that it is to be exercised by the authority or permission of the supreme pontiff, or with the permission of prelates. In every place where manifest heretics remain, renounce and blaspheme God and the faith of the holy Roman Church, we believe that by disputation and exhortation we ought, in every way according to God, to confound them and openly resist them, even unto death, by the word of the Lord, as enemies of Christ and the Church. We humbly approve and faithfully venerate ecclesiastical orders and everything decreed or sung in the holy Roman Church. We believe that the devil became evil not by his created condition but by his own choice. We believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths the resurrection not of another flesh but of this [Col. 1512C] flesh which we bear. We firmly believe and affirm that judgment will take place through Jesus Christ, and that each person will receive either punishments or rewards for what he has done in this flesh. We believe that alms, sacrifice, and the other benefits of the faithful can benefit the dead. We confess and believe that those remaining in the world, possessing their own property, giving alms and doing other things from their goods, and keeping the Lord’s commandments, may be saved. We believe that tithes, first-fruits, and offerings are to be paid to clerics by the Lord’s command.”

But because not only right faith but also good conduct is required for salvation—for just as without faith it is impossible to please God, so faith without works is dead [Col. 1512D]—we have thought fit to record in the present document also their proposed manner of life. Its tenor is as follows:

“To the honour of God and of his Catholic Church, and for the salvation of our souls, we have resolved to believe wholeheartedly and confess orally the Catholic faith, whole and inviolate in every respect and in all things, while remaining under the teaching and governance of the Roman pontiff. We have renounced the world and distributed to the poor what we possessed, as the Lord has advised; and we have determined to be poor, so that we take no thought for the morrow and will accept from no one gold, silver [Col. 1513A], or anything of that kind beyond daily food and clothing.

We have resolved to keep evangelical counsels as commandments, attending to prayer seven times according to the canonical hours, saying fifteen *Our Fathers*, besides the *I Believe in God*, *Have mercy on me, O God*, and other prayers. Since we are for the most part clerics and nearly all literate, we have determined to labour diligently in reading, exhortation, instruction, and disputation against every sect of error. Yet disputations are to be conducted by brethren more learned in the Catholic faith, approved and instructed in the law of the Lord, so that the adversaries of the Catholic and apostolic faith may be confounded. Through persons of greater integrity and more thoroughly instructed in the law of the Lord and in the judgments of the holy Fathers, we have decided that the word of the Lord is to be set forth [Col. 1513B] in our school to brethren and friends, with the due permission and reverence of prelates, through brethren suitable and trained in sacred Scripture, who are able by sound teaching to refute an erring people, draw them by every means to the faith, and bring them back into the bosom of the holy Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 1513D] In Book XIII one reads: “To be set forth to brethren and friends, with the knowledge and assent of prelates; so that neither attendance at churches [Col. 1514D] nor the preaching of clerics may for this reason be neglected.”]

Preserving virginity and continual chastity inviolate, we have resolved to observe two Lents and the fasts established every year according to the ecclesiastical rule. We have determined to wear a religious and modest habit, such as we are accustomed to wear, with shoes open at the top, arranged and varied with a special sign so that we may plainly and clearly be recognized as being, in body as in heart, now and forever separated from the Poor of Lyons [*Lugdunenses*], unless they are reconciled to Catholic unity [Col. 1513C]. We shall receive the ecclesiastical sacraments from bishops and priests in whose dioceses or parishes we reside, and shall render them the obedience and reverence due to them.

If any laypersons wish to remain in our counsel, we advise that, except for those suitable to exhort and dispute against heretics, the rest should remain in their homes, living religiously and orderly, administering their goods with justice and mercy, working with their hands, and paying the tithes, first-fruits, and offerings due to the Church.”

Therefore, having taken counsel with our brethren, we command you by these apostolic letters that, after receiving a like oath from the other brethren, you reconcile [Col. 1513D] them to ecclesiastical unity and declare them truly Catholic and orthodox in faith; that you and others preserve them, according to God, from every scandal and reproach; and that in testimonial letters and other assistance you mercifully help them for God’s sake.

Given at the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXCVII. TO DURAND OF OSCA AND HIS BRETHREN, WHO ARE CALLED THE POOR CATHOLICS, REMAINING IN THE CATHOLIC FAITH. On the same matter. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1514A]

Lest anyone henceforth unjustly calumniate your proposed manner of life, especially concerning those who have been reconciled to ecclesiastical unity according to the form which we have set forth in our other letters, we have thought fit to record and approve it under the safeguard of our authority in this present document. It is indeed as follows:

“To the honour of God and of his Catholic Church and to [Col. 1514B] the salvation of our souls,” etc., as in the other document, down to “paying.”

Given at the Lateran, etc., as in the other document.

## CXCVIII. TO DURAND OF OSCA AND HIS BRETHREN, REMAINING IN THE CATHOLIC FAITH. That they are not to be obliged to go to war against Christians. (Lateran, fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

You asked us to grant that those who, remaining in the world, resolve to remain in your counsel for the honour of God and the salvation of their souls should not be compelled to go to war against Christians or to render an oath concerning secular affairs, for example in seeking a commune [*pro petendo communi*]. [Col. 1514C] We grant the aforesaid so far as it can beneficially be observed without prejudice or scandal to others, especially with the permission of secular lords.

Given at the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CXCIX. TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF ANDRES MONASTERY. On chapels not to be built within the boundaries of the monastery. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 1514D] See vol. IX of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 581.]

When what is just and honourable is sought from us, etc., down to “be brought into effect.” Therefore, [Col. 1514D] beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your just requests, by the authority of the present letters we forbid anyone to presume to build oratories or hospices within the boundaries of your parishes against the will of yourselves and the diocesan bishop, without prejudice to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. Let no one, therefore, etc., down to “shall incur.”

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January [17 December], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CC. TO HENRY, PRIOR OF ANDRES MONASTERY, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. On confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 1515A]

[Note: [Col. 1515D] See vol. IX of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 578.]

Those choosing the religious life ought to enjoy apostolic protection, lest perhaps the assault of anyone’s rashness either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—impair the strength of their sacred religious life. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following the example of Pope Paschal II, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of the present document, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Saviour and Saint Rotrude the Virgin, in which you are devoted to divine service [Col. 1515B].

First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which, according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, exists in that monastery, etc., down to “be observed.” Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter obtain, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to name expressly the following:
