The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the altar of the village of Andres [Col. 1515C]; the chapel of Saint Mary within the town of Guînes; the altar of Bredenarde; the altar of Lullinghem; the altar of Ferques; and the altar of Ellinghem, with all their tithes and appurtenances; and everything granted to that monastery by Baldwin, count of Guînes, of good memory, with his wife Adela and his son Manasses, or by their barons: namely, all the pasture around the place of Andres itself; rights in water, marsh, and turf; the land of Hantinghem with its wood, villeins, and all revenues; in the village of Guînes, the pond and site of a mill; the land of Suavatas and its manor, with its villeins, water-rights, and one third of the tithe; the land of Campagnes and one third of the tithe; the land [Col. 1515D] and county of Bredenarde, with the manor situated there and the alms granted to you out of piety by the nobleman A., count of Guînes; the land, villeins, wood, pond, and mill granted from piety to your church by Garin of Fiennes and his mother; the altar in the village of Brocredes, with all its tithes and appurtenances; two portions of the revenues of the altar of Tardinghem; in the parish of Pithen, a manor with land and county-rights; on the hill called Mas, land and a manor with wood, pasture, and county-rights; in the parish of Spelleka, two parts [Col. 1516A] of the whole tithe;

[Note: [Col. 1515D] See vol. IX of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 498.]

in the village of Elcekam, the tithe acquired by Peter, your abbot of good memory; in the territory of Merch, the revenues which you have recently acquired from Walter Blond, Theodoric the clerk, and Herbert Folin, knight; in the town called Saint-Omer, land granted to you as alms; in the village of Craierwic, one mark charged upon the land of Baldwin, formerly your brother, assigned to you; in the village of Landertun, the tithe which you hold by the gift of the nobleman

[Note: [Col. 1515D] See ibid., pp. 488 ff., 534.]

Ingelram of Fiennes; in the village of Erudinghem, one third of the whole tithe; in the village of Buxin, the tithe formerly belonging to Daniel, and the land and revenues which you have recently acquired; likewise the duty on wines purchased for your use throughout the entire castle of Saint-Omer, granted to you by William [Col. 1516B], castellan of good memory, and also confirmed by his own document;

[Note: [Col. 1516D] See ibid., pp. 486, 527.]

in the villages of Iorni, Audenhem, Foxole, Landertim, Westehoc, and Antingherem, lands, associations, and tithes possessed by you from ancient times; the revenues and procurations which the Church of Wasto owes you yearly from a certain wood; two marks which the abbey of Belloloco is bound to pay you yearly from a certain manor; in the village of Hames, land, villeins, and revenues possessed by you from ancient times; in the village of Balinghen, by the grant of former nobles, one third of the entire village in lands, villeins, county-rights, pond, mill, pastures, and marshes, together with alms granted to you in that village by the noblemen Hugh and his brother Simon, Ralph Bailol and his associates; [Col. 1516C] in the village of Hochtinghem, all the householders you hold there, with revenues, county-rights, and marshes granted for your use by Baldwin, count of good memory and founder of your monastery; in the village of Ferques, lands with county-rights, villeins, and revenues possessed by you from ancient times; in the village of Odersele, revenues granted to you by Guy of Vlesoge, formerly your brother; also the tithe of the hill of Fiennes, the tithe of Dolo, the tithe of Dirlirgetun, and the right of appointing the chaplain to the oratory of that village; likewise vavasours enfeoffed by you and from ancient times bound both to plead on your behalf and to ride with you; and the market of your church with all its just and approved customs, [Col. 1516D] as you have hitherto justly and peaceably possessed them.

We further decree that burial in that place shall be entirely free, so that both the descendants of the aforesaid counts and all the barons called Peers of the castle may be buried there.

[Note: [Col. 1516D] The Chronicle of Andres adds: “according to their own wish and decision.”]

No one shall oppose the pious devotion and last wish of others who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; provided, nevertheless, that the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery or [Col. 1517A] remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, to benefit in every way the uses for whose governance and support they were granted. Without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop, and the due reverence owed to the monastery of Karroff. If anyone hereafter, etc., down to “shall be subject.” But may all, etc., down to “find the rewards of eternal peace.”

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CCI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF KARROFF. On confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 1517B]

The most holy Roman Church, by the office of its accustomed mercy, is wont to love more earnestly devoted and humble sons, and, like a loving mother, to foster them under the safeguard of her protection so that they may not be harassed by the molestations of wicked men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your prayers, we apostolically confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery the churches of Bovesrezia, Alnet, and Formerie, together with their rights and appurtenances, which you state that you have lawfully obtained, just as you hold them justly and peaceably; and we strengthen them by the protection of the present document. [Col. 1517C] Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to violate this document of our confirmation, etc., down to “shall incur.”

Given at the Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCII. TO THE BISHOP, ARCHDEACON, AND CHAPTER OF THÉROUANNE. That they are not to demand anything from the abbot of Andres for his blessing. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

We perform an act fitting to our office when we cherish religious men with due charity, graciously assent with apostolic favour to their vows and desires, and grant them the aid of the Apostolic See’s protection so that they may not be harassed by undue molestations. Therefore, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for the monastery of Andres, we forbid you by the authority of the present letters henceforth to presume to extort for the blessing of its abbot a palfrey, a meal, or a silk cope [Col. 1517D].

Given at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCIII. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF CHÂLONS. That they are to admit Walter to a prebend. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

When word had formerly reached us that Ferric of Dompierre, who held a prebend in your church [Col. 1518A], had transferred himself to lay knighthood by publicly contracting marriage with a certain woman in Apulia, and our venerable brother the archbishop of Benevento, whom we had instructed to investigate the truth of this matter, had replied in letters that the fact was notorious in those regions, we finally ordered Ferric by our letters to present himself before us within a month, in case he might perhaps show some reasonable ground in his defence.

But in reply by his own letters, together with testimonial letters from our venerable brother the bishop of Bivino, through whom we had ordered him to be admonished about this matter, he confessed that his father had committed him to the clerical militia when he was about eight years old, but, after his twelfth year had passed [Col. 1518B], he withdrew from it and devoted himself to secular arms. Finally, he entered Apulia with Walter, count of Brienne, of distinguished memory, and has remained there until now. Having pledged the revenues of the said prebend to certain creditors, he declared that he had held it against his conscience; and therefore, saying that the debt incurred upon that prebend had been wholly reduced, he resigned it into our hands.

Desiring to provide it to a suitable person, we have decided that it should be granted to our beloved son Master Walter, a prudent and honourable man originating from your region. By apostolic letters we command and direct your whole body that you arrange for him, through his procurator, to be placed in bodily possession of it and received as a brother and canon [Col. 1518C], assigning him also a stall in the choir and a place in the chapter; thus you shall fulfil the apostolic mandate in such a way that we may regard it favourably. Otherwise, we have instructed our beloved sons the dean, the cantor, and G. Pedilupi, canon of Reims, to compel you to do this by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

Letters have been written to them on this matter.

## CCIV. TO THE ABBOTS OF LONGPONT AND IGNY, AND TO THE PRIOR OF IGNY, IN THE DIOCESE OF SOISSONS. That the subdeacon R. is to return to his wife. (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 1518D]

From the letters of our beloved sons, the dean, cantor, and G., canon of Reims, we have clearly learned that Isabel, a woman, had obtained our letters addressed to them against R., her husband, of the diocese of Laon. R. did not care to provide her with necessities or render to her the marital debt. The letters directed that, if matters stood thus, they should compel R., by ecclesiastical censure and with any obstacle of appeal removed, to keep her as his wife and treat her with marital affection. They accordingly cited the parties lawfully.

When they appeared before them, the aforesaid woman sought to establish her claim, asserting that R. had lawfully contracted marriage with her and that he was unwilling to provide necessities [Col. 1519A] for her or render the conjugal debt. But R. entirely denied this. Witnesses were then produced and received; and, unwilling to pronounce judgment in the matter, the judges faithfully transmitted to us under their seals the witnesses’ depositions and the allegations submitted before them on both sides.

Having seen and understood the depositions of the witnesses produced, and since their statements have clearly established the marriage for us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to compel the said R.—notwithstanding that, after the marriage was contracted, he caused himself to be promoted to the subdiaconate—to receive his wife and treat her with marital affection, after a prior warning and by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. If not all of you, etc., two of you [Col. 1519B], etc.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Kalends of January [30 December], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCV. TO THE DEAN OF SALISBURY RESIDING AT PARIS, A., ARCHDEACON, AND MASTER P. PEVEREL, CANON OF PARIS. On the election of the abbot of Andres. (Lateran, third day before the Nones of January.)

[Note: [Col. 1519D] Chapter *Cum dilectus*, “On Custom.” See vol. IX of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 578.]

When our beloved sons William, monk of the Church of Andres, who acted as the elect of that church, and Geoffrey Daubins, monk and procurator of Karroff monastery, were litigating before us concerning the right of electing [Col. 1519C] an abbot in Andres monastery and concerning William’s election, William asked that his election, carried out unanimously by the brethren of Andres, be confirmed by apostolic authority. He asserted that the power freely to elect belonged exclusively to those brethren, both by common law and by a special privilege granted them by Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, and subsequently confirmed by us.

For by common law every community of monks ought to elect its own abbot; and Alexander’s privilege provides that, on the death of an abbot of Andres monastery, no one is to be set over it by any cunning of deception or force, save the person whom the brethren, or the more prudent part of them, judge should be elected according to God [Col. 1519D] and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

It is likewise known that we granted the aforesaid brethren permission that, when their church should become vacant of an abbot, they might appoint over themselves as pastor, by regular election, a suitable person from the body of that church or from elsewhere, to be presented to Karroff monastery, so that he might receive confirmation from it and render it the reverence due.

But Geoffrey, the procurator, alleged in reply that, at the request long ago of Count Baldwin, his wife, and his sons, patrons of the church of Andres [Col. 1520A], Gerard, bishop of Thérouanne, of good memory, had decreed that if, by divine gift, that place should flourish so greatly that a prior or abbot were established there, his election should depend upon the brethren of that place and the chapter of Karroff. Under colour of that statute, this practice had been observed from times long past: whenever Andres monastery was vacant, the brethren of Andres had elected for themselves as abbot, in the chapter of Karroff, someone from the body of Karroff monastery.

Therefore, he maintained, William’s election—undertaken less than canonically both contrary to the tenor of the statute and contrary to an approved custom, which is the best interpreter of laws—ought rightly to be annulled, and the aforesaid brethren should be ordered to proceed to the election of an abbot as they had hitherto done [Col. 1520B]. He added that neither the privilege of our aforesaid predecessor nor our own confirmation could prejudice Karroff monastery, since they had been obtained by concealment without any mention whatever of the said statute and approved custom.

G. further alleged that the election had to be annulled for another reason also: namely, because it had been performed by persons under interdict and while they were under interdict. For Lambert, bishop of Thérouanne, of good memory, had commanded the aforesaid brethren, as we have seen contained in his open letters, to go within eight days to Karroff Church, from whose body they were to elect an abbot, and there make the election as they ought. If they did not do so, they were to know [Col. 1520C] that they would be suspended from every office, benefice, and entry into churches. They had scorned the bishop’s command and failed to elect within the appointed time as they ought. Since, therefore, after the term elapsed they began to be bound by the sentence of suspension, the election they afterwards presumed to conduct ought to be held void.

The reply was made on the other side that the monks of Andres were by no means bound to elect in the aforesaid manner; consequently, they were not bound to obey the bishop, who had issued this peremptory command without examining the case. Thus the said sentence of interdict could not bind them, as it had been promulgated without sufficient reason—especially because, within the term fixed by the bishop, they had gone to Karroff monastery and requested permission [Col. 1520D] to elect from their own monastery, though they could not obtain it. The other party replied that, even if the said sentence had perhaps been less just, they were nonetheless bound humbly to obey it, since it had been promulgated by the diocesan bishop.

Having carefully understood these and the other matters submitted before us by both parties, because it was established for us that the election had been celebrated by persons under suspension and likewise during suspension, we annulled it, justice requiring, on the counsel of our brethren. Yet we have thought fit, by way of precaution, to relax the sentences of excommunication and suspension pronounced against William and the other monks [Col. 1521A] of Andres, and the sentences of interdict pronounced against their churches by our venerable brother the bishop of Silvanectes and his co-judges after an appeal to us had been lodged.

Moreover, since the aforesaid statute—namely, that the election of the abbot depends upon the brethren of that place and the chapter of Karroff—can reasonably be understood in such a way that it derogates neither from common law nor from apostolic privilege, namely, that election of the abbot belongs to the said brethren and confirmation to the chapter of Karroff, we command your devotion by the authority of the present letters that, after hearing the parties’ allegations, if Karroff monastery proves such a custom as prejudices common law in this matter [Col. 1521B], you are to decree that the election of the abbot of Andres shall henceforth be made according to that custom. But if no such custom is proved by which common law is prejudiced in this case, take care, with the obstacle of appeal removed, to adjudge to the monks of Andres the right of electing an abbot. Thus they may henceforth freely elect, either from the body of their own church or from elsewhere, by canonical election, a suitable person as abbot, to be presented to the chapter of Karroff so that, if the election is canonical, he may be confirmed by it.

But if the parties prefer that judgment be reserved to us, remit the case, fully prepared, to our examination, setting the parties a suitable term in which they shall appear before us, God willing to receive a judgment of equity. The witnesses [Col. 1521C] who have been named, etc., down to “give testimony.” No letters are to obstruct this, if any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without the parties’ consent. If not all of you, etc., two of you.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], in the eleventh year.

## CCVI. TO THE BISHOP OF VOLTERRA. A certain matrimonial case is entrusted to him. (Lateran, third day before the Ides of January.)

[Note: [Col. 1522D] Chapter *Ex parte*, “On the restitution of those despoiled.”] On behalf of the woman M. it was set before us that, while she was still below the age of puberty, a certain paternal uncle of hers had wished to unite her in marriage to the son of a citizen of Siena, who was not yet seven years old; and although she was taken into the house of that citizen, once she had reached marriageable age she did not wish to ratify what her said uncle had arranged in this matter, and sought from our venerable brother the bishop of Siena permission to marry another. When that bishop had summoned the parties, and the aforesaid M. appeared in court through a suitable procurator, seeking restoration of the possessions and other things given to her in her own right as dowry, while the other party sought restoration of that woman, asserting that she could not conduct the case through another but ought personally to take part in its handling, the aforesaid bishop, as he informed us by his letters, doubting what he could determine by law on these matters, suspended the proceedings.

Since, therefore, we do not believe there can be any doubt that the woman herself, although she is said to be a minor, may conduct the matrimonial case through a procurator, and that the other party is in no way entitled to have her restored, since it has been deprived of no advantage of right or possession—for by that transfer alone, which was preceded by neither betrothal nor lawful consent and was followed by neither, no binding tie was contracted between them—in order that an end may be put to the litigation, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, setting aside the aforesaid objections and summoning the parties, you hear what they may choose to allege on either side, and, with appeal removed, determine what shall be canonical; and cause what you determine to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. Notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCVII. LETTER OF HENRY, EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO THE LORD POPE. On the defeat of Voulla near Philippopolis. (At the expedition of Pamphylia, September.)

[Col. 1522C] To the most holy Father and lord INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme and universal pontiff: HENRY, by the same grace most faithful emperor in Christ, crowned by God, ruler of Romania, and ever Augustus, greeting and obedience in all things, as ready as it is due.

It was not chiefly the work of men but of almighty God, and especially of the merits and intercessions of most blessed Peter and of the Roman Church—not of our merits—that the empire of Romania should be subject to our power. For, although it was miraculously brought about that Constantinople was taken in honour of blessed Peter, yet more miraculously in these days, with most blessed Peter fighting for us, Christ has worked through us. By his aid, on the vigil of the feast of that same Peter called “in Chains,” we defeated at Philippopolis Voulla, the most wicked persecutor of God’s Church; and, after an immense slaughter of his men, we drove him from the field in flight. And, that you may rejoice with us in the Lord, we hold for our empire fifteen days’ journey of land taken from his dominion.

Our condition has improved and increases day by day. We attribute this not to ourselves, but rather to God, to you, and to the faith which subsists in the Roman Church. Let Your Holiness know that we are sound and safe; that we would most gladly hear news of you; and that, for the faith of the Church and of the most blessed Prince of the Apostles, whose office you hold, we do not fear to undergo martyrdom. Whatever we do and whatever we acquire is and shall be for his name and in him. We render you boundless thanks for the honour shown by you to our servant G., and for the matters concerning us which you have secured. We have received your letters gladly and devoutly.

We pray God in every way that he may establish you—whom he has raised as shepherd for his own honour and that of his Church—in his seat, sound and safe, to remain there long; and that he may preserve you for us, his servant. And you, whose prayers are most effective with God, pray for us, that he may grant saving aid to us who fight for him, and may give us long life and victory. We desire that the Roman Church should have us as executors of its commands, for we are not its lords but its ministers. Holy Father, may Your Holiness prosper by aiding us in our petitions, which will be sent to you on behalf of us and our land.

Until now your pious gentleness has benignly received our prayers and petitions; may that which was begun on a good foundation attain a peaceful result. For unless our land and the empire of all Romania are governed by your protection, there is no doubt that they will fall; but if we have your assistance, the adversity of wars will yield to us. For we can do nothing without you. See, therefore, that what you have well begun in the Lord you bring to completion in deed.

Given at our expedition of Pamphylia, in the month of September, in the twelfth indiction, the third year of our empire.

CCVIII. TO THE DEAREST SON IN CHRIST FREDERICK, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF SICILY. He is urged not to claim spiritual jurisdiction for himself. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of January.)

From the tenor of your letters it has been made known to us that, when the Church of Palermo was bereft of a pastor, the chapter of that Church repeatedly petitioned you to grant it leave to elect a pontiff. When at last you had given them your gracious assent, directing them, after invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, to agree upon a suitable person, the cantor, the succentor, and a certain other man withdrew from the rest, resisted your commands, forbade their fellow canons to proceed to a nomination, and appealed to the Apostolic See. Greatly angered by this, you intended sharply to avenge this injury upon them personally; but, out of reverence for us and for the clerical order, moderating your agitation, you imposed exile upon them alone, so that they might thereafter have no opportunity for malice in your kingdom. You took care to report this to us, lest we might be persuaded otherwise by those same men.

Having heard this, we were not a little astonished and were deeply moved against those who had presumed to urge such things upon you, dearest son, recognizing indeed that your advisers are wicked, who give you such counsel. Hence we naturally fear lest, induced by their persuasion—or rather led astray—you may wish to imitate the footsteps of cruel tyrants, who, because their iniquities demanded it, were cut off from the land of the living and are perhaps now more grievously tormented. Not content with your own lot, you have presumed to usurp ours by exercising jurisdiction over clerics. You ought to have been content with temporal matters, which indeed you hold from us, and not to extend your hands to spiritual matters, which belong to us.

Do you not know that when Uzzah rashly touched the ark of the covenant, he was struck by the Lord and perished; and that King Uzziah, when he wished to burn incense, was covered with the stain of leprosy? You ought, moreover, to have considered and feared lest perhaps, because of the sins of your predecessors, who had presumed to usurp certain spiritual powers, this tribulation came upon your kingdom, which has until now oppressed it and still presses and shakes it. You should likewise have humbled yourself before the Most High, so that, once appeased, he might turn the storm into a breeze and the crushing, disturbing shaking might cease.

Certainly, if you had observed these matters more carefully, and those which befell other kingdoms in which similar attempts were made, you would surely have feared to extend the hand of vengeance against clerics because they appealed to the Apostolic See; nor would you have banished them from the kingdom. Even if they had offended you most grievously, vengeance ought rather to have been reserved to us; for, according to the Apostle, “the servant stands or falls to his own master,” and it is not for you to judge another’s servant.

But perhaps you think yourself offended because a certain privilege granted—indeed, rather extorted from the beginning—for your predecessors contains a provision concerning appeals, as though the aforesaid clerics, by appealing, had acted contrary to it. [Note: [Col. 1523D] See Baronius, under the year 1097.] But if you had considered more carefully what was done concerning these matters in the time of the empress Constance of illustrious memory, then queen of Sicily and your mother, you would by no means have recalled this to mind.

For when she had sent to our presence our venerable brother the archbishop of Naples, and our beloved sons Ham., archdeacon of Catania, Master Thomas of Gaeta, justiciar, and Nicholas, judge of Vigliena, to have the said privilege renewed and granted and confirmed to her and to you in respect of the kingdom, and they had pressed us repeatedly on these matters, they could not obtain from us in any way that we should wish to renew that privilege, because of four chapters contained in it—namely, concerning councils, legations, appeals, and the elections of prelates. [Note: [Col. 1524D] See the letter of King William to Adrian IV, in Rocco Pirro.]

At last, two of them returned to the presence of your aforesaid mother, while the others remained at the Apostolic See, and explained to her our benevolent decision in these matters. Since she, as a religious person, endeavoured to acquiesce in it, they returned again to the Apostolic See and obtained from us renewal and confirmation of that privilege to her and to you in respect of the kingdom, with the three chapters concerning appeals, legations, and councils wholly removed from the privilege, and the fourth—concerning elections—modified. [Note: [Col. 1525D] See Book I, letters 410, 411, 412.] What, however, was arranged between us and your aforesaid mother concerning elections, the schedule enclosed with the present letter which we send you will be able to teach you more fully.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort Your Royal Serenity that, in consideration of God, you no longer attempt to claim jurisdiction for yourself in spiritual matters, lest on this account you provoke the divine Majesty against yourself and your kingdom. Rather, persevering steadfastly in devotion to the most holy Roman Church, your mother, show it due reverence and honour. Like a loving mother, it will provide with diligent care for your need and advantage in these and other matters. Recall the aforesaid clerics and permit them to dwell peacefully in your land and freely possess their benefices, wholly laying aside the resentment which you conceived against them because of the appeal which they lodged with us.

Know for certain that we shall cause the settlement concerning elections reached between us and your oft-mentioned mother, the empress, to be solemnly published throughout the whole kingdom, so that elections may thereafter be held in accordance with it. Let those who do not fear to bewitch you with perverse counsels beware lest they hereafter act maliciously in this matter, for they shall not escape divine and our vengeance. It is more tolerable that human vengeance should strike corruptors than that divine wrath, because of their iniquities, should rage against you and your kingdom if they remain uncorrected.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCIX. TO THE PRIOR OF SAINT THOMAS THE MARTYR AT ACRE AND OF SAINT GEORGE DE SISTO, AND HIS BRETHREN. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, fourth day before the Ides of January.)

When what is just and honourable is sought from us, etc., down to “effect.” Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gladly concurring in your petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the places in which you are devoted to divine service, and your persons together with all the goods which you now reasonably possess or may hereafter acquire by lawful means through the Lord’s favour. In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to your churches, by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this document, the churches of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, and Saint Nicholas of Campo Anglorum, the hospital of Saint Thomas, and the other possessions, as you justly and peacefully possess them.

Moreover, what Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, granted from the kindness of the Apostolic See to your predecessor, son Prior, and his successors—namely, the daily use of the ring, pastoral staff, and mitre on the chief festivals—we ratify, following in his footsteps. As a token of this protection and generosity received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay two *sarracenati* annually to us and our successors. We therefore decree that absolutely no person may infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, etc., down to “incur.”

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCX. TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF TINEMVAHE. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, third day before the Nones of January.)

It is fitting that we readily give our assent to the just desires of petitioners, and that we bring to effect the vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gladly concurring in your just petitions, we confirm to you, and through you to your Church, by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this document, the possessions bestowed upon you by the pious generosity of the faithful; likewise the liberties and other goods granted to your Church by King Richard of illustrious memory and by our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English, as you justly and peacefully possess them and as they are more fully contained in their authentic documents; also the churches and their revenues confirmed to that Church by the letters of the metropolitan and diocesan bishop; and likewise the liberties and immunities granted to the monastery of Saint Alban for its cells, since your house is a cell of that monastery. [Note: [Col. 1525D] See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 335.]

Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our confirmation, etc., down to “incur.”

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCXI. TO THE BISHOPS OF LONDON, ELY, AND WORCESTER. On the affair of Canterbury. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of January.)

[Note: [Col. 1526D] See the deeds of Innocent III, chapter 131.] Concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury, we write in the following terms to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the English:

“We have been touched inwardly with sorrow of heart and greatly troubled with grief, because, although on account of that prerogative of special affection by which the Apostolic See loved you above other princes we hoped that you would in return repay it with reverence and honour, you render hatred for affection. As though you had conspired against yourself, you spare not your own honour in order to derogate from ours; indeed, heedless of your own reputation and salvation, you rashly rise up to the prejudice of both against our ordinance and that of the Church—nay, of God. You do not consider that you strive in vain to annul it, since no one can turn aside the outstretched hand of the Most High, and no one can alter what has been decreed by him.

“Indeed, how much and in what manner we have deferred to your royal highness concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury cannot readily be erased from the memory of the universal Church, even if you, being ungrateful, perhaps do not remember it. Since goodness does not overcome malice, the Church marvels at our excessive patience toward you. Alas! Dearest son, what hardness has stopped your hearing, so that you have not received the salutary admonitions so often impressed upon you by us? What hardness has swallowed up your understanding, so that you have not observed the prudent counsels repeatedly suggested to you by us? You are now seen to be so hardened that you do not feel the wound whose injury increases without measure. You seem so bewitched that you admit neither the aid of medicine nor the work of the physician, so that we can almost complain of you with the Prophet, saying: ‘To whom shall we speak, and whom shall we admonish further? His ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear’ [Jeremiah 6].

“You are wearied by the word suggested to you for your salvation; you are disgusted by the good urged upon you for your honour. You neither pity the harm to your soul nor are ashamed to cleanse—[manuscript reading: *mandare*, ‘to command’]—your reputation, lest we say, your disgrace. Thus we pity you all the more over such hardness because you yourself, turned cruel toward yourself, have until now most miserably refused to have pity on yourself.

“Although the fatherly love from which we suggest these things to you may perhaps be hateful to you, nevertheless we perform toward you the office of a prudent and loving physician, who at times beneficially cuts and burns a sick man against his will when he resists unadvisedly. Therefore, if—God forbid!—we find your disease hardened, you will compel us to employ a more forceful remedy, as necessary care demands. Though perhaps you presently shrink from its severity, once health has been regained you will commend its effect and bless the skilled physician.

“But, that we may still apply the ointment of gentleness, lest, perhaps softened by it, you await harsher measures, we earnestly ask and admonish Your Royal Serenity, calling upon him who is to come to judge the living and the dead, that, taking sounder counsel, you withdraw from so great an error—at least by proceeding in this affair according to the tenor of the letters which the beloved son, the abbot of Beaulieu, formerly obtained from us in your name. For beyond your earlier fault, this may be imputed to you as a second fault if you appear to depart from what was sought with such insistence under the explicit testimony of your letters; in those letters, that is, you humbly petitioned us to give firm credence to whatever that abbot should say to us in your name concerning the affair.

“For this reason you ought, without any difficulty, to fulfil what was obtained through his efforts; especially since you appear finally to have accepted this when, after the matter had first been carefully heard and prudently examined by you, you caused our delegates to come to your presence afterwards, as though for the completion of the business. Therefore, dearest son, do not be obstinate and henceforth impose no difficulty upon this affair, lest—God forbid!—you bring yourself into a difficulty from which you cannot easily be delivered.

“Otherwise, however sincerely we love your person in the Lord, and however indignantly you may perhaps receive canonical discipline, nevertheless, since mercy is exercised toward one who is loved when he is chastised—for love has its wounds, which are sweeter when more bitterly inflicted—unless within three months after receiving or refusing the present letter you fulfil what we have set forth, from that time, on behalf of God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, whose authority, though unworthy, we possess, we decree you anathematized and cut off from the communion of the faithful. We give our venerable brethren the bishops of London, Ely, and Worcester firm commands not to delay, appeal set aside, in publishing that sentence. [Note: [Col. 1527D] See Matthew Paris, under the year 1208.] They shall cause it to be solemnly renewed every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, until suitable satisfaction has been made. We ourselves too shall solemnly publish it in our own voice, so that its penalty may become more certainly and forcefully known throughout the whole Church, which his offence is known to have injured generally. And with the assistance of the Most High we shall proceed against you in many ways, unless even then you hasten to correct your error.

“Behold, the bow is drawn. Flee, therefore, dearest son, from the arrow which is not accustomed to turn backward, lest, wounded by it, you become so grievously weakened that not only may you be unable to advance to better things, but may scarcely be able to return even to your former state; its wound indeed cannot be healed without an ugly scar.”

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and firmly enjoin your brotherhood that, if the said king does not fulfil the foregoing within the aforesaid time, you shall thereafter proceed in the affair itself according to the prescribed form, with every impediment of contradiction and appeal removed. And if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCXII. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF COVENTRY. On the election of the bishop of Coventry. (Lateran, on the Ides of January.)

Since fixed periods have been established beyond which churches ought not to remain vacant and deprived of pastors, our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of England, adding transgression to transgression, as we say with sorrow, causes the appointment of pastors to vacant churches in his realm to be deferred longer than is lawful. Thus perhaps he may opportunely appropriate their revenues to himself until persons pleasing to him are appointed, apparently hoping by multiplied offences to extort from us a greater favour. On the contrary, we are resolved to pursue injuries done to the Church of God so persistently against anyone, however dear to us, that no entreaty or rebellion shall turn us aside until he ceases from persecution or fails in it.

We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort that king by our letters not to impede, or allow his agents to impede, vacant churches, whether cathedral or regular, from freely and canonically electing suitable persons as their pastors. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command you all, under obedience, that you assemble together, invoke the grace of the Holy Spirit, and endeavour to set over yourselves as pastor through canonical election a suitable person equal to so great a burden and honour. Otherwise, with divine counsel and assistance, according to the obligation of our office, we shall take care to set over you as pastor one who can govern and benefit you; for no violence of injustice will make us abandon the pursuit of justice, and, by the Lord’s authority, we shall take care to punish your disobedience with fitting penalty.

[Col. 1529C] Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January, etc., as in the other letter.

In the same terms, written to the prior and convent of Durham.

In the same terms, to the dean and chapter of Chichester.

CCXIII. On the same subject.

In the same terms, to the chapter of Exeter: “Since fixed periods have been established,” etc., down to “turn us aside.” Since, therefore, however much we love the king himself in the Lord and wish to show regard for his honour, we ought not to offend the heavenly King for the sake of an earthly king, we earnestly admonish and exhort him by our letters, etc., as in the other letter, to the end.

In the same terms, to the dean and chapter of Lincoln, as in the preceding letter, to the end.

Given as in the other letter.

CCXIV. TO THE BISHOPS OF LONDON, ELY, AND WORCESTER. On permission to celebrate during the interdict. (Lateran.)

[Note: [Col. 1529D] See Matthew Paris, under the year 1209. See below, letters 258–259.] At the petition of our venerable brother Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, we entrust to your discretion that, notwithstanding the sentence of interdict which you pronounced, you grant to the conventual churches which have observed it patiently, humbly, and continuously from the beginning permission to celebrate divine offices once a week, in secret, for consecrating the Eucharist, so that the power of the most divine sacrament may obtain a saving end to this affair. And if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, etc., as above in the other letter.

CCXV. TO THE SAME. That one must not communicate with excommunicated persons. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of January.)

We regard it as grievous and unworthy that, although F. de Cantolu and R. de Cormeill have, as justice requires in the affair of the Church of Canterbury, been bound by the bond of excommunication, certain clerics and laypeople, both great and small, presume everywhere and knowingly to communicate with them. Therefore, unwilling that the sinew of ecclesiastical discipline be loosened through persons who make such presumptions, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate the truth of this matter diligently, appeal set aside, and faithfully report it to us in writing, so that, made more certain by your report, we may proceed by the Lord’s authority against such great insolence as ought to be done. Let the witnesses who shall have been named, etc., down to “bear testimony.” And if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCXVI. TO STEPHEN, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. On the same matter. (Given as above in the other letter.)

From the affection of fatherly kindness which we bear toward the salvation of all persons, wishing to give no one an occasion for becoming hardened but rather a reason for repentance, we grant your brotherhood by the authority of this letter that you may bestow the benefit of absolution upon F. de Cantalu and R. de Cormeill, who were excommunicated by name because they laid sacrilegious hands upon your Church, when they humbly seek it. If you judge it expedient, dispense with the labour which they would undergo in coming to the Apostolic See to seek absolution, especially if there is hope that peace may arise more effectively through their absolution.

Given as above in the other letter.

CCXVII. TO THE SAME. On permission to celebrate during the interdict. (Given as above.)

By the authority of this letter we grant your brotherhood that, notwithstanding the interdict pronounced for your Church, if for the peace of your Church you should usefully be summoned to the presence of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of England, you may permit divine offices to be celebrated in a subdued voice for yourself, for our venerable brethren the bishops of London, Ely, and Worcester, your fellow bishops, and for your household, in the places at which you stop in the course of your journey.

Given as above.

CCXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF WINCHESTER. That he fulfil what the above-named bishops shall enjoin upon him. (Lateran, on the Ides of January.)

By the authority of this letter we command your brotherhood and strictly enjoin you, by virtue of obedience and under the expectation of our favour, to take care to fulfil, setting aside every excuse, difficulty, and delay, whatever our venerable brethren the bishops of London, Ely, and Worcester—or any two of them—may think fit to enjoin upon you concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury. Otherwise, this would redound most gravely upon your own head.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCXIX. TO HERVÉ, BISHOP OF TROYES, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.)

Since your upright character, brother bishop, and devotion deserve that you should be heard by us in your petitions, we more willingly grant you what you judge should be requested according to God, inasmuch as you are known to have acquired a fuller measure of the favor of the Apostolic See. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just requests, and following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Troyes, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside,

[Col. 1531D]

and strengthen it by the privilege of the present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s assistance, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the church of Saint-Leon and the village itself, with their appurtenances and dependencies; the church of Aques and its village, with its appurtenances and dependencies; the tithe of Barberey; the tithe of the chapel of Saint Luke, both in grain and wine; the church of Calixtus;

[Col. 1532A]

the church of Villagruis; of Nigella; of Mont-Pothier; of Mont-Gevold; of Larbusia; of Ponts; of Nogent; the church of Saints Peter and Martin of Bocenay; the church of Avenay; of Marignac; of Chastres; the church of Saint-Savinien; of Saveries; of Sainte-Maure; of Corlavelley; of Verreries; of Lusigny; of Bouilly; of Villamour; the church of Saint-Medard; of Bretenay; of Fols; of Barbonne; of Esternay; of Champ-Guyon; of Bussières; of Cour-Givold; of Tombes; and of Saint-Just;

[Col. 1532B]

the church of Saint-Ferreol; of Arceis; the church of Trocy of Saint-Basle; the church of Saint-Ulf; of Salon; of Calderiacum; of Allebauderies; of Viaspere, with the chapel of Bonnevoisine; of Grandville; of Herbita; of Villeries; of Semonia, with the chapel of Champ-Grillon; of Ulmes; of Estraelles; of Bolegies; of Sommover; of Seven Fountains; of the monastery of Puellari; of Poenz; of Nucery; of Dienville; of Crespey; of Sublenis; of Pignei; of Hispania; of Loves; of Sumpsefi; of Saint-Susanna; of Pipere; and the church

[Col. 1532C]

of Guasconia; of Marcilliac; and of Summofonte.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we confirm to you and to your church the canonical churches belonging by right to the Church of Troyes, namely: the church of Saint Nicholas of Sézanne; the church of Saint Remigius of Pleiotro; the church of Saint Blicherius of Breccis; the church of Saint Flavius of Villamour; the church of Saint Nicholas of Pugey; the church of Saint Lawrence of Plancy; and likewise the church of Saint Stephen near the city of Troyes. The deans of that place must receive its pastoral care from your hands, with all obedience and subjection which those deans are bound to render to you and your successors, together with the performance of homage.

Furthermore, following the example of Pope Eugenius, our predecessor of good

[Col. 1532D]

memory, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to your church the abbey of Saint Lupus; the abbey of Saint Peter of Cella; the abbey of Saint Martin; the abbey of Saint Peter of Aremar; the abbey of Saint Peter of Nigella; the abbey commonly called Oia; the abbey of Saint Serenus of Cantumerula; the abbey of Saint Mary of Arripatorium; the abbey of Saint Mary of Bullencourt; the abbey of Saint Mary of Reclus; the abbey of Bellolocus; the abbey of Capella; the abbey of Bassofons; the abbey of Saint Mary situated in the suburb of Troyes; the abbey called the Paraclete; the tithe of Molcey; of Mariney; of Jardoury; of Summofonte; of Avantz; of Ville-Arduin; of Saint-Leon; of Martiley;

[Col. 1533A]

of Bretenay; of Saint Victor; of Claellis; of Novovicus; of Fontebetun; and of Bussières.

In addition, since Matthew, your predecessor of good memory, is said, on the advice of prudent and religious men, to have decreed that in the Church of Troyes there should be permanently resident at least seven canons who were priests and seven who were deacons, apart from the archdeacons; and that, upon their death, none should be substituted for them except priests or deacons, or others established in such orders, so that they might be admitted to those orders at the next Ember Days which occurred, having nevertheless made promise and profession that they would maintain residence in the aforesaid church: our predecessor Alexander, graciously and as was fitting assenting to the petitions of that bishop, held that constitution ratified and firm, and decreed that it should remain unimpaired for all time. He added that, if clerics of lower orders were substituted for them and, after admonition, did not receive those orders at the first Ember Days, it should be lawful for the said bishop and his successors to prohibit them from holding their places and receiving the fruits of their prebends; and that, if they did not then seek to receive those orders at the following Ember Days, they should be entirely removed and he should have free authority, by apostolic power, to substitute others.

Furthermore, with the knowledge and consent of that bishop, the same predecessor established that if any canons of the Church of Troyes were perhaps engaged in the service of that bishop

[Col. 1533B]

or his successors, or in the service of the same church; or, with the permission of the bishop and chapter just mentioned, were pursuing scholarly studies; or were detained by illness: they should nevertheless receive the full fruits of their prebends. Other canons, however, who did not serve the church continuously should receive only twenty shillings yearly.

Moreover, the same Alexander, our predecessor, added that, both under the aforesaid bishop and under his successors, whenever the said church lacked a dean, a priest who was a canon, or a deacon, should be appointed dean; and the deacon should be ordained priest at the first Ember Days which occurred. If, having been admonished, he should perhaps neglect to receive priestly orders at those Ember Days,

[Col. 1533C]

it would be lawful for the aforesaid bishop and his successors to prohibit him from exercising the authority and power of that office and from occupying his seat in choir and chapter. If he did not then receive priestly orders at the following Ember Days, he should be removed and another freely substituted in his place.

Therefore, following in the footsteps of the same our predecessor, and approving what he approved or established concerning the foregoing articles, we confirm the same by apostolic authority. Furthermore, following the example of our predecessor Alexander, we decree that neither you nor your successors may in any way alienate, without the authority of the Roman pontiff, the aforesaid parish churches which belong specially to the episcopal mensa

[Col. 1534A]

[the bishop’s endowment].

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire, to serve in every way the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should thereafter rashly presume to act against it, unless he correct his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself to stand guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated;

[Col. 1534B]

let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the reward of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1209 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## CCXX. To the Illustrious King of Hungary

Concerning the affair of the bishop of Bamberg and the archbishop of Kalocsa. (Lateran, XII Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1534C]

[Note: [Col. 1533] See below, book XII, letters 118 ff., and the register concerning the imperial affair, letter 182.]

Although the bishop of Bamberg has shown himself devoted to us in many ways, nevertheless, having due regard for royal honor and ecclesiastical propriety, we have thought fit to entrust his case to our legates under this form: if, concerning the death of Philip, duke of Swabia, of famous memory, a lawful accuser appears against him and he is proved guilty before them, they shall depose him from every ecclesiastical office and benefice, all hindrance of contradiction and appeal being removed. Otherwise, they shall impose canonical purgation upon him; if he should fail in that, they shall condemn him under the same censure; but if he lawfully clears himself, they shall declare him wholly innocent of the crime alleged. Before all else they shall take care that, if anything has been wrongly undertaken against him or his church, it be restored to its proper condition.

We grant, however, that if he prefers to prosecute his case before us, he may come to the Apostolic See and pursue it there in the fitting order. In either event, he is not to delay informing both us and the legates, so that it may be known without doubt where the case is to be heard.

Furthermore, we complain strongly to you yourself concerning your royal prudence: by your excessive insistence in the matter of the elect of Kalocsa,

[Col. 1535A]

you seem gravely to have misled us. Many criticize us—and indeed appear to have grounds for criticism—for having set over masters a master of masters who did not yet know how to be a pupil of pupils, since we permitted one to be promoted as a bishop of bishops who, it is asserted, lacks for the most part the learning appropriate to the episcopal office. So great is this lack that, abandoning the care of the church entrusted to him—a church which seems more grievously forsaken with a living shepherd than with a dead one—he has gone to Vienne and there occupies himself with elementary instruction. He has not guarded against making public, by disgraceful wandering abroad, the ignorance which he might at least to some extent have remedied by prudent study at home.

Accordingly, in letters commanding him, we directed that, laying aside every delay, he return at once to the Church of Kalocsa and, keeping some learned men familiarly with him, strive to advance in learning under their instruction. He must take diligent care to compensate for his defect of learning by such excellence of character and honorable conduct that, when one is balanced against the other, we may be able in some degree to tolerate him.

[Col. 1535B]

Otherwise, following the example of Him who says, “I repent that I made man” (Gen. 6), it will be necessary to think differently concerning him, so that what we built while deceived, we may finally, with the Lord’s favor, destroy while better advised. Therefore we earnestly admonish and exhort Your Royal Serenity to induce him to this so diligently that, if he acts otherwise, you may find that you have cast down rather than raised up the man whom you have taken such pains to elevate.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXI. To the Illustrious King of England

Concerning the affair of Canterbury. (Lateran, X Kalends of February.)

[Note: [Col. 1535D] See above, letter 210.]

In the manner of a compassionate father, who cannot hate a son who offends him even while offended, and is sometimes more troubled by his son’s evil than the son himself, we cannot harden ourselves against you though you are hardened. Rather, softened by fatherly compassion, we strive with every power and effort available to us to soften you, who are laboring so greatly to your own injury, and to recall you from your damnable and ruinous purpose. We should be deeply grieved if what we fear should happen to you;

[Col. 1535D]

but we should regard it as an even greater cause of sorrow that, though so often protected beforehand and warned, you had not been willing, when you could, to avoid it. For an accidental evil has some remedy for sorrow. But what a person incurs voluntarily brings upon him a harsher torment of regret.

You therefore, dearest son, take diligent care not knowingly and willingly to subject yourself to that danger from which we so earnestly desire to preserve you, and which would at length inflict upon you a punishment all the greater because you had more heedlessly rejected the warning shown you for avoiding it. We do not wish Your Royal Prudence to be unaware that much regarding the circumstances of the present affair comes to our knowledge which is concealed from you by the craft of those who do not wish to show you your wound: men who do not know how to pour in the wine of rebuke, but know how to apply the oil of flattery. Would that they do not cunningly contrive that you should remain always in distress, so that, placed in distress, you may always hold them dearer.

[Col. 1536A]

Therefore we, who both prudently perceive this and earnestly desire to cure it, pressing counsels upon warnings and warnings upon counsels, interweave threats with entreaties and entreaties with threats, after the fashion of a skilled physician varying the aids of medical art. Such a physician applies iron where fomentations are of no use, and remedies by a drink of lukewarm water illnesses which have not felt the violence of medicine. For even if you were hard as a diamond, the diligent application of so great an art ought surely to soften you, since the diamond, though it does not yield to iron, is softened by the pouring on of goat’s blood.

See also that you do not impede the course of your prosperity, for whoever wished to encourage you in this error could not have peace with us. Now therefore, as though applying almost our final remedies to you, we have no remedies remaining which we can apply beyond these. Between the conflicting inclinations of one who wishes to heal and one who refuses healing, so long as there was hope of such treatment, we preferred to heal you with gentle and mild means rather than with harsh and severe ones: for the former leave behind no suppuration, whereas the latter commonly leave an unsightly scar.

[Col. 1536B]

Lest, then, you bring us and yourself into a greater necessity: behold, we ask you familiarly; behold, we admonish you sweetly; behold, we counsel you fatherly; behold, we beseech you kindly. Under the sanction of divine judgment, and for the remission of your sins, we enjoin upon you that you do not delay any longer in making satisfaction to us and to the Church—or rather, to God—concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury. Grant us this at least as a gift, for that sincere affection with which we have both loved and love you among other princes. We certainly hoped, and do not yet despair, that, if we had asked greater things, you could not in any way have refused them.

[Note: [Col. 1536D] See above, letter 89, and book X, letter 219.]

Especially since, as we took care to inform you on another occasion, although more than was due to your right was accorded to it, we did not wish any prejudice ever to be generated against you from matters already done or still to be done. Choose therefore, dearest son, to yield to such sweet admonitions and saving counsels, and not to assent to the perversities of flatterers and the flatteries of perverse men. For, to use the divine saying: “Those who call you blessed are the very ones who deceive you” (Isa. 3).

[Col. 1536D]

Otherwise, we call heaven and earth to witness against you that, if you allow the apostolic hand to be made heavy upon you, this will result from your obstinacy, not from our severity. Until now we could scarcely restrain that hand; henceforth we shall never be able to restrain it. We beg you, inquire diligently of those who anoint your head with the oil of the sinner to what end you can come from this contest. Certainly they will not dare to answer otherwise than that you cannot conquer except by being conquered. Yet your victory will be more glorious when you have become victor over the conquered; for then, beyond doubt, you will conquer when you are conquered—not by a man, but by God, by whom it is glorious for a human being to be conquered, so that humanity may always give God glory and honor.

Therefore let no one deceive you by the vain suggestion that, unless you yield to us, we shall in any manner yield to you in this contest. We could more easily be killed than conquered.

[Col. 1537A]

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXII. To Girard, Treasurer of the Church of Thebes

He is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Sora, VI Kalends of September.)

When a request is made to us, etc., down to “effect.” Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, graciously concurring with your just requests,

[Col. 1537B]

we receive under protection your person, together with all your goods, both ecclesiastical and worldly, etc., down to “protection.” In particular, we confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this document, the treasurership of the Church of Thebes, as you justly and peacefully possess it. Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, etc., down to “incur.”

Given at Sora, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXIII. To John, Illustrious King of the English

That he restore the goods of Berengaria, Queen of the English. (Lateran, XII Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1537C]

How much we have hitherto deferred to Your Royal Highness in the affair of our dearest daughter in Christ, Berengaria, formerly illustrious queen of the English,

[Note: [Col. 1537D] See book XIII, letter 74.]

if you had observed it more carefully, perhaps you too would have taken care in this matter to defer to us—or rather to Him whose office, though unworthily, we bear, to whom rise the tears of widows falling from the cheek beneath the eye, and whom the Most High promises also to hear when they cry out to Him. At last, by wholesomely conquering yourself, you would have put into effect our prayers and admonitions on this matter, repeated to you more than eight times. Nor would you have compelled the aforesaid queen to be so often worn down by labor and expense, when, by reason of royal nobility and without our exhortation, you ought to have honored her and, to the extent of your power,

[Col. 1537D]

defended her against others—clearly considering that this would contribute to your honor and salvation.

Behold: for eight years and more, while continuing with prayers and admonitions to you on this matter, we have waited patiently to see whether, consulting for your salvation and honor, you might endeavor to give the same queen satisfaction concerning her dower, half of the movable goods of your brother King Richard of illustrious memory, and certain other matters which she asserts belong to her. This would have shown deference to God and to us, who perhaps in this matter have deferred to you more than was due. Yet even now we have been unable to prevail, as the result shows and as the complaint of the oft-mentioned queen, repeatedly pressed upon our ears, demonstrates: for you have not merely failed to take care to satisfy her,

[Col. 1538A]

but have even refused to render justice before those judges to whom we are known repeatedly to have entrusted the affair. You ought not only to have taken care that an action for injuries should not arise from you, but also to have restrained all subject to your dominion from injuring anyone, since you have received the sword to bear for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.

Certainly it would have benefited Your Royal Serenity no less than the queen herself—indeed, far more—to have complied with our admonitions and counsels. By these you could have appeased the divine majesty, which you seem grievously to have offended by the injury done to the aforesaid queen, and could also have earned praise in the sight of men. For, even if she had received satisfaction for the loss of temporal goods, you would have repaired for yourself the loss of innocence, which is undoubtedly greater.

Nevertheless, if perhaps you believe that you owe her nothing in any respect, you should at least have rendered her justice before us. We do not accept a person in judgment, but judge just judgment insofar as He deigns to inspire us—the One who gave all judgment to the Son. You should not have used the greatness of your power against her, knowing that mightier than you is He who performs mercy and judgment for all who suffer injury and rules in the kingdom of men.

[Col. 1538B]

But you, giving these matters no due attention, have hitherto been unwilling either to satisfy her or to submit with her to judgment concerning the aforesaid matters. For after eight years had elapsed, during which we deferred to Your Royal Serenity, and being unwilling longer to defer to a human being against God, who by prophetic utterance commands that the widow be defended, we commanded you to present yourself before us by a suitable representative no later than the Feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary last past. You were to render to the oft-mentioned queen, or to her representative, concerning the foregoing matters and any others which she might perhaps bring forward against you, whatever the order of reason required. You utterly scorned to do this, although the beloved son, the prior of Worcester, acting on the command of our venerable brother the bishop of Worcester, displayed our letters to you and assigned that term to Your Highness on our behalf as a peremptory deadline. This was reported to us by letters from our venerable brothers the bishop of Ely and the aforesaid bishop of Worcester, to whom we directed our letters on this matter.

[Col. 1538C]

The queen’s representative came to the Apostolic See for the stated term and waited for four months and more.

Since, therefore, we neither will nor ought further to defer to you, against our own salvation and yours, we earnestly admonish and exhort Your Royal Serenity, firmly enjoining you in the power of the Holy Spirit, that within six months after receipt of the present letter you either give the aforesaid queen fitting satisfaction concerning the matters stated, or, if possible, reach an amicable settlement with her; or present yourself before us through a sufficient and suitable representative, prepared to render to her or to her representative complete justice concerning those matters and any others she may bring forward against you.

Otherwise, from that time forward, we decree that the following shall be specially bound by an equal sentence, although all the things named are subject to a sentence of interdict on another ground: in Somersetshire, the manor of Ilchester and the manor of Mere, with their appurtenances; the whole of Rutland with its appurtenances; the manor of Ketton with the whole soke; Brudecrost and North[?]ham, with their appurtenances; in Berkshire, the manor of Lambourn with its appurtenances; in Wiltshire, Westbury, Wilton, and Malmesbury, with their appurtenances; in Sussex, the town of Arundel with its honor and appurtenances, and the city of Chichester with its appurtenances; in Oxfordshire, the town of Stanton with its appurtenances; in Northamptonshire, Rockingham with its appurtenances and the town of Northampton; in Devonshire,

[Col. 1539A]

the manor of Kenton and Leston with their appurtenances, and the manor of Alrichescote with the town of Sloncomb and Quenewke, with their appurtenances, and the city of Exeter; in Hampshire, the manor of Wlfintonia with its appurtenances; in Herefordshire, Berchamested with its whole honor and appurtenances; in Essex, the town of Waltham with its appurtenances; in London, the queen’s Eya; in Lincolnshire, Grahan with its appurtenances, and the town of Stamford with its appurtenances; and in Gloucestershire, the honor of Berkeley and its appurtenances, together with all other manors, towns, and castles known to belong to the dower of the aforesaid queen; likewise the royal demesnes, your manors situated in the aforesaid counties, from which the oft-mentioned queen ought to have wool.

[Col. 1539B]

The sentence of interdict shall in no wise be relaxed in any of all these places until you have made suitable satisfaction concerning this matter. We give strict commands, moreover, to our venerable brothers the bishops of Sées and Salisbury that, laying aside human favor and worldly fear, they publish that sentence and cause it, our authority being invoked and all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, to be firmly observed.

If not even thus your hardness can be softened, we shall take care to lay our hands more heavily upon you. Know that, however dearly we love you as a dearest son in Christ, yet because we do not believe that we should further defer to you to the detriment of your salvation, we shall omit no means whatsoever of fulfilling our office until, returning to your senses, you offer yourself to obey the Apostolic See in this matter.

[Col. 1539C]

[Col. 1539D]

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXIV. To the Bishops of Rochester and Salisbury

Concerning the same matter. (Lateran.)

If our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English,

[Col. 1540A]

had more carefully observed how much we have hitherto deferred to Your Royal Highness in the affair of our dearest daughter in Christ, Berengaria, formerly illustrious queen of the English, perhaps he too would have deferred to us—or rather to Him whose office, though unworthily, we bear—etc., in the same manner as in the other letter down to “observe.” Present to the aforesaid king our letters which we are directing to him for this purpose. Take care faithfully to notify us by your letters how you have proceeded in executing the apostolic command, fulfilling our command in such a way that you cannot be reproved for negligence but may rather be commended for obedience. And if both of you cannot carry these things out, etc., let one of you nevertheless carry them out.

Given at the Lateran, etc., as in the other letter.

## CCXXV. To the Provost and Chapter of Brioude

Concerning their exemption. (Lateran, V Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1540B]

[Note: [Col. 1539D] See below, book XVI, letters 72, 73.]

When the procurators of the beloved sons of your church and of the venerable brother, the bishop of Clermont, came to the Apostolic See and we granted them a gracious hearing, the procurator of that bishop stated before us that, since your church is situated in his diocese and therefore you ought to answer to him as your diocesan in spiritual matters, you utterly withdraw episcopal rights. In other churches of the same diocese which you assert belong to you, you do not allow him to exercise the jurisdiction due to him, withholding at your own pleasure the procuration which he and his predecessors at one time received from those churches.

[Col. 1540C]

But the procurator of your church asserted in reply that, since it is wholly exempt from the jurisdiction of everyone except the Roman pontiff, as is clearly evident from a privilege of Pope Calixtus, our predecessor of pious memory, you were not bound in any respect to answer to him, whether for the head or for the members that belong to you by full right.

The other party replied that the same privilege did not appear to have the form of a privilege, since it contained no word of exemption but only an inserted prohibition. They contended that it was not free from suspicion, because it did not exhibit the style of our chancery and did not appear strengthened by the subscriptions of cardinals; for this reason they argued that it ought to lack force and that it had conferred no liberty. Yet even if it possessed some force, although it in some way granted liberty to the head, it did not exempt the members from episcopal power, since it made no express mention of their liberty. Therefore they maintained that these ought to be subject to the said bishop by diocesan law, just as churches belonging to certain monasteries are subject to their bishops when those monasteries have no intermediate relation to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1540D]

To this your party replied that the liberty granted to your church through the aforesaid privilege ought not to be referred only to the head, but also extended to its members. For the provision contained in it—“You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer”—must refer to the lesser churches. Baptism is not celebrated in the greater church, and chrism and holy oil are chiefly necessary by reason of baptism; and for consecrations of altars and dependent churches, and likewise for the ordinations of clerics of both the members and the head, you have always been accustomed to summon neighboring bishops. Thus, if the lesser churches are exempt with respect to those matters which cannot be performed without the ministry of a bishop,

[Col. 1541A]

much more strongly must they be understood to enjoy liberty in other matters that can be carried out without episcopal office, since the one who granted greater things appears to have granted lesser ones.

The said procurator further added that, even if the foregoing were insufficient, your church, both in its head and in its members, had used such liberty for so long a time that it was fortified by lawful prescription against the aforesaid bishop. For in carrying out the aforesaid matters which, as stated above, cannot be performed except through a bishop, it had always summoned whatever bishops it wished. But it had always exercised by itself other functions: the appointment and removal of clerics; the coercion of both clerics and laypersons; and the determination of causes, both criminal and civil.

[Col. 1541B]

The sacristan and the weekly ministers of your church summon the priests and clerics of the dependent churches to synod twice a year, give them synodal commands, and correct in clerics and laypersons alike whatever they find requiring correction. Moreover, the lesser churches are so annexed to the greater that they form part of the body of its prebends and dignities. The greater church, in the town of Brioude, receives offerings and tithes, imposes penances, and receives the dead for burial. Although there are certain other churches there which wholly depend upon it, they exist because of the multitude of the people, as auxiliary churches.

Furthermore, when the bishop of Clermont places the land under ecclesiastical interdict, divine offices are celebrated in your church and its members; and in ecclesiastical offices they never imitate the custom of the Church of Clermont.

[Col. 1541C]

[Col. 1541D]

Therefore, having fully heard and carefully understood these matters and others proposed before us, because we perceived that the aforesaid privilege in two places contained the full liberty of your church, we have, on the counsel of our brethren, decreed that it is wholly free in respect of its head, so that it is never bound to answer to anyone in spiritual matters except the Roman pontiff. But we adjudged that its members are subject to the said bishop by diocesan law, except only in those matters concerning which you can prove that you are protected by lawful prescription.

But because one who abuses power granted to him deserves to lose his privilege, know that you shall be deprived of the liberty granted to you unless you take care to use it well. You must not seize the absence of a corrector as an opportunity to sin, but rather take from the favor of the giver an occasion for doing good; especially since this privilege has not been renewed by any of our predecessors.
