Let no one, therefore, infringe this page of our definition, etc., down to the end.

[Col. 1542A]

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXVI. To the Abbot of Saint Geneviève, the Archdeacon, and Master P. Peverel, Canon of Paris

Concerning the election of the bishop of Thérouanne. (Lateran, IV Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1542B]

[Note: [Col. 1541D] See above, letter 43.] We cannot but wonder at the prudence of our beloved sons the abbot of Saint-Victor, the dean, and Master Robert of Courson, canon of Paris: although, in the matter of the beloved son, the bishop-elect of Thérouanne, our letters had set before them a definite procedure, wholly consonant with reason, they exceeded it at their own discretion. For they had been instructed to bind by oath those three electors, to whom the canons of Thérouanne had entrusted the power of electing a bishop, to tell the truth concerning how many of the canons, at the time of the examination, had assembled in support of the aforesaid elect; and, if all three together, or at least two of them, swore that the greater part of the canons had agreed upon the same man, they were without delay to impose silence upon the objectors. But if their depositions established that the said elect had been nominated by fewer persons, then—and only then—they were carefully to hear whatever either party might put forward to prove the form under which the power of election had allegedly been granted to the aforesaid three electors. And if it were sufficiently shown that, under the form granted to them, they were bound to elect from the body of that church the person upon whom all, or the greater and sounder part, of the chapter agreed, they were entirely to quash his election. Otherwise, holding valid what had been done concerning him, they were to restrain the objectors, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, from challenging him.

Yet, as we have learned from their letters, they summoned those three electors before them. First two of them, and afterwards the third, appeared before them; and the judges diligently and carefully sought, under oath, to discover from them the truth concerning the number of canons of Thérouanne said to have nominated the aforesaid elect. But because they sometimes seemed to use the same premeditated language, while at other times they wavered and changed their account in many ways, so that the more faithfully they were examined the less credibility they inspired, the judges said in interlocutory fashion that they must proceed to another issue—wholly disregarding the form of our mandate. Therefore the party of the said elect, believing itself aggrieved, appealed to our hearing; and, on our behalf, the aforesaid judges were firmly forbidden to attempt any further proceedings in that matter. Nevertheless, paying no heed whatever to that appeal, they resolved to proceed in the case.

From the foregoing it is evident that in that commission we distinguished three questions: namely, whether it should become clear from the depositions of the three electors, or at least two of them, that more of the canons had agreed upon the aforesaid elect; whether fewer of them had agreed upon the same man; or whether neither proposition was proved by such testimony. In two of these questions—namely, the first and the last—they were to hold his election valid, imposing perpetual silence upon his objectors. In one only, namely the middle question, they were to quash his election, provided it were established that the power of election had been granted to the three electors under this form: that they should elect from the body of the Church of Thérouanne the person upon whom the greater and sounder part of the chapter agreed.

Moreover, as we have learned from the transcripts of the depositions sent to us both under the seal of our beloved son Guala, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in the Portico and legate of the Apostolic See, and under that of our venerable brother the bishop of Senlis, together with several others, the greater part of the canons of Thérouanne who were present at the time of the examination agreed upon the aforesaid elect. Therefore, whether the said delegates wished to give credence to the depositions of the witnesses or to withhold it, they certainly ought, according to the prescribed procedure, to have held his election valid. For, since it had not been proved that the smaller party had agreed upon him, it would have been pointless even to prove that, under the form granted to them, the three electors ought to have elected the person upon whom the greater part of the chapter agreed.

Accordingly, lest the aforesaid Church of Thérouanne be further burdened with labour and expense and suffer great loss both in spiritual and temporal matters, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties, you require the aforesaid judges, for greater security, to produce before you the original depositions of the witnesses. Compare the transcripts which we send you under our bull with the originals. If you find them to agree, then, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, decree null and void whatever you find to have been attempted against the aforesaid elect after his appeal to the Apostolic See had been lodged. Solemnly confirm what was done concerning him; impose perpetual silence upon his objectors; and notify his archbishop that he is not to delay consecrating him bishop. Deprive of his prebend in the Church of Thérouanne the person who voluntarily bound himself to this penalty should he perhaps fail in the proof.

But if the said delegates, within ten days after being requested, should refuse or be unable to produce the depositions, you shall nevertheless give credence to the rescripts—especially since, according to the tenor of the letters which they themselves sent us, the opposing party did not base its case upon their intention—and proceed in the case according to the prescribed procedure. You are to proceed in the same way if, contrary to what we do not believe, the originals differ in any respect from the rescripts, provided that they do not prove that the smaller party concurred in nominating the aforesaid elect. For according to lawful enactments, where the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant must be acquitted even if he has offered nothing in defence. If not all [can act], nevertheless let two of you carry this out.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXVII. To the Same. On the Same Matter.  
*(Lateran, 3 Kalends of February.)*

[Col. 1544B]

Lest pastoral provision be lacking for a long time to the Church of Thérouanne, we command you by apostolic letters that, if the adversaries of our beloved son the elect of Thérouanne cannot be found within thirty days in the province or neighbouring regions, you shall nonetheless proceed according to the procedure which we have thought fit to set out for you in our other letters, after a public edict of summons has been sent to their residence; since the case has already proceeded as far as the publication of the witnesses.

[Col. 1544C] Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXVIII. To the Bishop of Le Puy, and the Abbots of Saint Peter and of Sécurat at Le Puy. The Cause of the Canons of Brioude Is Entrusted to Them.  
*(Lateran, 5 Kalends of February.)*

Although by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us we are bound to assist all with fatherly concern, we especially owe apostolic protection to those who acknowledge no intermediary between themselves and the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, the beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Brioude—which is known to belong immediately to us—frequently suffer wrongs, losses, and robberies at the hands of many persons, and, having no diocesan bishop to whom they may have recourse whenever they are improperly burdened, we have judged it proper to provide for them at their petition.

Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that whenever you are requested by them, you shall cause the full measure of justice to be rendered to them by our authority, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, against their wrongdoers situated in the dioceses of Clermont, Le Puy, and Mende; compelling those wrongdoers, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal. If not all [can act], you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of February, as above.

## CCXXIX. To the Illustrious King of France. He Is Urged to Defeat the Provincial Heretics.  
*(Lateran, 3 Nones of February.)*

[Col. 1545A]

The religious faith and faithful religion which, transmitted in you from generation to generation from your most Christian forefathers, has made you the most Christian prince, move us confidently to entrust the business of God’s Church to your care when need requires. Since it has therefore been wisely determined that, for those who, inflamed with zeal for the orthodox faith, are preparing to overthrow the provincial heretics, one man should be appointed as commander, under whose sole counsel all may proceed unanimously, we earnestly ask and admonish Your Royal Serenity, laying this upon you for the remission of your sins, that, after summoning them, or some of them, as expediency requires, you do not delay to set over them by royal authority some valiant, prudent, and faithful man, who may lead those fighting the Lord’s battle beneath divine protection and your banner.

You will carry out this provision for the pious undertaking so prudently and gladly that, while you gird all men for the contest of holy warfare, you too may be shown, as it were by the hands of all, to wage the Lord’s war; and you may make yourself a participant in the reward of those whose contest you have thus shown yourself to assist. Above all and in all things, take diligent care that, in so great a service of God, they maintain that harmony of unity and unity of harmony, so that, through the cunning of Satan, who envies works of peace, no discord and no rivalry may arise among them. Proceed in this matter so energetically and cautiously, with your aid and counsel, that they may bring it to a happy and salutary conclusion; lest, if the contrary should occur—may God avert it—the cause of the Church should fail in the very matter in which it might have advanced, and the heretical pest, which might have been eradicated, should take root more deeply.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXX. To All the Faithful Who Will Fight in Christ’s Service against the Provincial Heretics. On the Same Subject.  
*(Given as above.)*

Blessed are you by the Lord who made heaven and earth, because, when the dragon was waging war and shaking God’s holy Church by the force of his engines of war, you took up arms and shield and rose to its aid. Therefore, since everyone who competes in a contest abstains from all things, so that he may complete the course of his struggle the better because the more freely, we earnestly ask and admonish all of you, enjoining it upon you by apostolic letters for the remission of your sins, that, as you undertake so arduous and so holy a service of God, setting aside everything that might hinder this holy struggle of yours, above all and in all things take care that you preserve that harmony of unity, etc., as above, to the end.

Come then, most mighty soldiers of Christ; come, most valiant recruits of Christian warfare. Oppose yourselves to the forerunners of Antichrist, and fight against the servants of the ancient serpent. Perhaps until now you have fought for transitory glory: fight now for everlasting glory. You have fought for the body: fight for the soul. You have fought for the world: fight for God. For we exhort you to so great a service of God not for any ordinary reward, but for the heavenly kingdom, which for this reason we most confidently promise.

Given as above.

## CCXXXI. To All the Faithful, Whether within or outside the Kingdom of France, Who Have Taken or Will Take the Cross for Christ’s Service against the Provincial Heretics. They Are Received under the Protection of the Apostolic See.  
*(Given as in the other letter.)*

[Col. 1546B]

Since, inflamed with zeal for the orthodox faith, you have resolved to set out to destroy heretical depravity, by apostolic authority we ordain that, from the moment when, in accordance with the ordinance of our legates, you have received upon your breasts the sign of the life-giving cross for the purpose of fighting the heretics, you shall remain, together with your persons, lands, possessions, men, and all your other goods, under the protection of the Apostolic See. Until certain knowledge is obtained of your return or death, all these things shall remain free and undisturbed in their present state. Let no one therefore … our constitution, etc., to the end.

Given as in the other letter.

## CCXXXII. To the Bishops of Riez and Conserans, and the Abbot of Cîteaux, Legates of the Apostolic See. On the Matter of the County of Melgueil.

[Col. 1546C]

Although the count of Toulouse long ago petitioned us through his messengers that we might deign to receive his oath of fealty concerning the county of Melgueil, which is of the right and property of Saint Peter, we did not think fit to grant his request, lest we should seem thereby in some manner to confirm that county to him. We took account also of what you, son abbot, suggested to us in your letters: namely, that if he should perhaps persist obstinately in the evil he had begun, he should then be deprived of it according to his deserts, and we should determine concerning it what would serve the cause of the Church.

But since we have been carefully asked how the faithful army of those who have taken the cross ought to proceed concerning that county, we have thought fit to advise you as follows: have recourse to the teaching of the Apostle, who says, “Being crafty, I took you by guile” (2 Corinthians 12), since such guile ought rather to be called prudence. After taking suitable counsel with the more prudent among the crusaders, endeavour to capture separately those who are divided from the Church’s unity—provided you see that by this means the same count will give less aid to the others, or will himself be less able to rage. Do not begin with him at once; rather, first evade him by the art of prudent dissimulation, and proceed to uproot the other heretics. Otherwise, if the scales of Leviathan join together and you attack all at once with one force, these followers of Antichrist will be harder to crush in proportion as they succeed more stubbornly in massing themselves together in a single bond of union.

Thus the others may more easily be overthrown because they are less strongly supported by him; and he himself, meanwhile, when he sees their destruction, may perhaps return to his senses. Or, if he persists in evil, action may at last be taken more easily against him when he is alone and deserted. We suggest these things to you as a precaution. But you, who will know the circumstances of affairs more fully because you are present, shall proceed in these matters in this way or another, as heaven reveals to you and to those whose counsel ought to be used. After prudent deliberation, proceed concerning the matter of the aforesaid count as you judge expedient for the honour of God and the benefit of the Church.

## CCXXXIII. To the Same. On the Matter of the Faith.

[Col. 1547B]

For the present we send you such letters concerning the crusaders and the destruction of the heretics as we know to be expedient. Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your discretion, commanding you by apostolic letters that, using them as need requires, you proceed prudently and steadfastly in each matter, cautiously and diligently providing above all and in all things that they preserve that harmony of unity, etc., as in the first letter.

## CCXXXIV. To the Same. That They Are to Absolve Guy, Count of Auvergne.  
*(Lateran.)*

[Col. 1547C]

[Note: [Col. 1547D] See above, Book I, letter 498.] Although the nobleman Guy, count of Auvergne, is known to have committed a grave offence in the capture of our venerable brother the bishop of Clermont, his own brother, yet, because pardon ought not to be refused to anyone who truly repents, we are moved by the prayers of that bishop, who petitioned our apostolate concerning this matter, and prompted by zeal for the Church’s advantage. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if you know this to be expedient for the Church—whose cause, it is said, may be greatly advanced by him against the heretics—you grant the aforesaid count the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church, and impose upon him what is customarily imposed in such cases.

Given at the Lateran, etc., as in the first letter.

## CCXXXV. To the Abbot of Cîteaux, Legate of the Apostolic See. He Is Rebuked for Improper Suspicions.  
*(Given as above.)*

Although we should have borne it patiently if our venerable brother the bishop of London and his co-executors had not, from the beginning, bound the monasteries of the Cistercian order so strictly under an interdict that they could not celebrate according to the apostolic privileges granted them, yet because they themselves, thinking that they were doing good, placed the monasteries under such an interdict, and those monasteries began humbly to observe it, they did not afterwards violate it without incurring the offence of grave presumption.

[Note: [Col. 1547] See above, letter 213, and below, letters 259 and 260.]

Furthermore, we commend you, but we cannot commend you in this: that, when consulted by those seeking advice, you replied that unless they were given a copy of our rescript, or unless it appeared that it had perhaps been obtained through the defect of surreption, they should protect themselves against the aforesaid executors by lodging an appeal. Even if, according to the strictness of the law, you might answer in this way by the cunning of such subtlety, you ought never to have suspected such distinguished and deserving pontiffs either of rashly arrogating to themselves an authority which we had not granted them, or of maliciously twisting an authority granted to them toward another purpose.

Especially since, measuring other minds by your own, it did not become you to fall into the scruple of such suspicion against men who, had they fallen into a like suspicion against you, you might perhaps have judged to possess an over-scrupulous conscience. Therefore, considering that it is neither useful nor honourable for us to arrange otherwise in this matter, especially with regard to this point, than the executors themselves have decided should be arranged, we declare that the rescript mentioned above proceeded from us with certain knowledge. We wish this to be firmly observed: whatever they, after weighing the circumstances of the case by prudent deliberation, have ordered to be observed.

[Col. 1548C] Given as above.

## CCXXXVI. To the Archbishop of Bordeaux. Concerning the Granting of a Prebend at Saintes to Fulch.  
*(Lateran, Nones of February.)*

Although it becomes us to be solicitous concerning provision for all clerics, we ought especially to take care for those whose upright conduct and distinction in learning commend them to us. Accordingly, since our beloved son, the nobleman Calo, lord of Pont, has through his letters thought fit to resign the prebend which he held in the Church of Saintes, and since our beloved son Master Fulch., a native of the diocese of Saintes, has been commended to us by many testimonies alike for his life and learning, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, after receiving from the same knight, for greater security, his resignation of the prebend, you shall confer and assign it by our authority upon the said master, setting aside the obstacle of appeal. Cause him to enjoy peaceful possession of the same prebend, restraining objectors by ecclesiastical censure without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXVII. To the Abbot of Saint-Aubert, the Dean, and Master R. of Bekerel, Canon of Cambrai. That They Are to Admit Aegidius to the Priesthood.  
*(Lateran, Nones of February.)*

[Col. 1549A]

When formerly we had written in the usual form on behalf of Aegid[ius], priest, to the abbot and convent of Saint-Michael, who were said to have presented him for the order of priesthood, our beloved sons the cantor of Saint-Quentin and his fellow admonishers, after his personal fitness had been established to their satisfaction, took care to receive witnesses concerning his presentation and sent us their depositions. Although, therefore, from those depositions read in our audience it did not appear altogether fully proved that the said priest had been presented by the aforesaid abbot, yet because in this matter a half-full proof ought to be aided by full mercy—for pious benefits do not always require rigid law—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you take care to admonish and induce the said abbot and convent to provide for the aforesaid priest according to the form of the former mandate; compelling them to do so, if necessary, by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. If not all [can act], let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXVIII. To the Archbishop of Athens. He Is Received under the Protection of the Apostolic See.  
*(Lateran, 10 Kalends of February.)*

[Col. 1549C]

[Note: [Col. 1549D] See below, letter 256.] When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the care of our office. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, favourably assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen by the patronage of this present writing, your person and the Church of Athens, which by God’s authorisation you are known to govern, together with all the ecclesiastical and temporal goods which you now reasonably possess or may in future, by just means and with the Lord’s assistance, acquire. Let no one therefore … our protection, etc., through “will incur.”

[Col. 1549D] Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXIX. To Hugh, Canon of Thebes. The Church of Kalenda Is Confirmed to Him.  
*(Lateran, 10 Kalends of February.)*

When what is requested of us, etc., [is] brought to effect. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, etc., as in the other letter through “we receive,” but we especially confirm to you by apostolic authority the church of Kalenda, as you justly and peaceably possess it, and strengthen [that grant] by the protection of this present writing. Let no one therefore … our protection and confirmation, etc., to the end.

Given as in the other letter.

## CCXL. To Robert of Suciaco, Canon of Athens. His Athenian Prebend Is Confirmed.  
*(Lateran, 10 Kalends of February.)*

[Col. 1550A]

When what is requested of us, etc., as in the other letter through “we receive,” but especially the prebend which you have canonically obtained in the Church of Athens, etc., as in the other letter to the end.

Given as above.

## CCXLI. To Master William, Canon of Thebes. On the Same Subject.  
*(Lateran, 10 Kalends of February.)*

When what is requested of us, etc., as in the other letter through “we receive,” but especially the church of Saint John of Araquio, as you justly and peaceably possess it, etc., to the end.

Given as in the first letter.

## CCXLII. To Hugh, Canon of Thebes. On the Same Subject.  
*(Lateran, 10 Kalends of February.)*

When what is requested of us, etc., as in the other letter through “we receive,” but especially the prebend which you have canonically obtained in the Church of Thebes, as you justly possess it, etc., as in the other letter to the end.

Given at the Lateran, etc., as above.

## CCXLIII. To Master Randulph, Dean of Davalia. The Deanery of the Church of Davalia Is Confirmed to Him.  
*(Lateran, 10 Kalends of February.)*

[Col. 1550C]

When what is requested of us, etc., through “effect.” Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, etc., through “we receive,” but we especially confirm to you by apostolic authority the deanery of the Church of Davalia, as you justly and peaceably possess it, and strengthen [that grant] by the protection of this present writing. Let no one therefore … our protection and confirmation, etc., to the end.

Given as above.

## CCXLIV. To the Archbishop of Larissa and the Beloved Sons, the Elects of Zitounion and Nazareth. They Are Written to on Behalf of the Archbishop of Athens.  
*(Lateran, 10 Kalends of February.)*

[Col. 1550D]

Know that it has come to our attention that our venerable brother, the archbishop of Athens, induced by fear, presumed to confer upon the nobleman Otto de la Roche, lord of Athens, who is married, a certain ecclesiastical office of the Church of Athens, commonly called the treasury, to that church’s serious injury. Therefore, wishing by fatherly concern to provide for the indemnity of the same church, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after diligently investigating the truth of the foregoing, you shall, setting aside the obstacle of appeal, restore to its proper state whatever you find to have been attempted in this matter by the said archbishop to the prejudice of that church. No letters [shall avail] against truth and justice, etc. If not all [can act], you, brother archbishop, with one of the others, etc.

[Col. 1551A] Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXLV. To the Noblemen Balmo, Constable of Thessalonica; Otto de la Roche, Lord of Athens; …, Marquis; …, Lord of Negroponte; T. de Ostremuncout; and the Other Princes of Romania. Concerning Tithes to Be Paid.  
*(Lateran, 9 Kalends of February.)*

The more sincerely we love your persons in the Lord with charity, the more deeply we are disturbed when reports reach us of your actions which cloud your reputation among men and stain your conscience before God. Since, therefore, as our venerable brothers the archbishop of Athens, the bishop of Thermopylae, and our beloved son the elect of Nazareth, appearing before us, have informed us on their own behalf and that of the other prelates of the churches of Romania, you hold churches and abbeys, ecclesiastical offices, and revenues in occupation, to the peril of your salvation, we earnestly ask and admonish your devotion, commanding you by apostolic letters that, freely resigning all the aforesaid things to the churches to which they are due, you pay them their tithes in full and cause your subjects—namely Greeks and Latins—to render obedience and reverence to their prelates.

Otherwise, we command by our letters our venerable brothers the archbishops of Thessalonica and Larissa, and the bishop of Davalia, that, after prior warning, they compel you to do so by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, through the administration of justice.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of February, in the eleventh year [of our pontificate].

They have been written to on this matter.

## CCXLVI. To the Archbishop of Athens. On the Residence of Canons.  
*(Lateran, as above.)*

You stated to us, when appearing in our presence, that certain canons of your church refuse personally to serve the Church of Athens as they are bound to do.

[Col. 1551D] Hence that church is greatly deprived of divine offices. Therefore, lest the said canons be able to derive profit from this and the said church be deprived of its due service, by the authority of these presents we grant you permission to compel them, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to maintain the due residence in that church.

Given at the Lateran, etc., as above.

## CCXLVII. To the Elect of Nazareth. On the Same Matter.  
*(Lateran, 8 Kalends of February.)*

[Col. 1552A]

You stated to us, when appearing in our presence, that certain canons of the Church of Nazareth refuse personally to serve that church as they are bound to do, etc., as in the other letter.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of February, in the eleventh year [of our pontificate].

## CCXLVIII. To the Bishop of Ely. Concerning the Precentor of the Church of London.  
*(Lateran, 2 Nones of February.)*

[Note: [Col. 1551D] Chapter *Cum olim*, On Custom.]

When formerly our venerable brother the bishop of London informed us that he proposed to establish a precentor in his church, assigning him a fixed revenue without injury to anyone, we, yielding to his requests, granted him leave to establish such a precentor, provided that no prejudice should be caused to anyone in assigning revenues to him. We further decreed that the precentor so established should possess in the Church of London, in sittings, processions, and other matters, the dignity which other precentors possess in other English churches.

Subsequently, however, it was reported to us that, although the same bishop had installed our beloved son B. as precentor in that church, he had not taken care, now two years having elapsed, to carry out what we had decreed concerning the aforesaid dignity. Therefore we commanded you not to delay in carrying this out, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, and restraining objectors by ecclesiastical censure.

More recently, however, our beloved sons the dean and certain other holders of ecclesiastical offices in that church sent us their complaint. They said that customs differ among English churches, and that some precentors possess a lesser dignity while others possess a greater; and that their dignities, being diverse or conflicting, cannot all be combined in one. The man newly installed as precentor in the Church of London, not content with what he can possess without injury to others, is trying, on the pretext of our letters, to arrogate to himself certain dignities of the said dean and other office-holders of the same church, to their prejudice.

Accordingly, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if you know that precentors possess differing dignities in English churches according to differing local customs, you shall cause the aforesaid precentor to hold in the Church of London, and to remain content with, that dignity which he can obtain without injury to others, while preserving the reasonable and approved customs of that church; and this without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Nones of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCXLIX. To Hubald, Bishop-Elect as Archbishop of Ravenna. That He Shall Cause a Bishop to Be Elected for the Church of Faenza.  
*(Lateran, 4 Ides of February.)*

[Col. 1553A]

[Note: [Col. 1553D] Chapter *Post translat.*, “On Resignation.” See below, letter 278.]

After your translation to the Church of Ravenna, when the beloved sons the provost, canons, abbots, and primicerius of Faenza, together with all the clergy of the city, as we have learned from their letters, had unanimously conferred upon the beloved son I., priest and canon of Faenza, free authority to elect, he, having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, chose the beloved son Joachim, canon of San Frediano of Lucca, formerly bishop of Sarzana, to be postulated as bishop of Faenza. Through his prudent diligence—he had first conducted himself commendably as a canon and afterwards as provost in the Church of Faenza—many benefits are expected to accrue to that church.

Moreover, after the beloved son, the prior of San Frediano, had been consulted on this matter and his consent obtained, the provost and the other persons named above humbly asked us to approve that same postulation. [Note: [Col. 1554D] See Book V, *De conc. sac. et imp.*, chapter 21, §12.]

But at first sight a chapter of the Council of Constantinople seemed to stand in the way of such a postulation, for it is recognized to have decreed that whoever descends from pontifical dignity to the monastic life and place of penitence shall by no means thereafter return to the episcopate. Hence the same postulation seemed wholly inadmissible in opposition to the said council, since it is one of the four principal councils which the Catholic Church venerates as it does the four Gospels.

There are, however, certain special cases in which, notwithstanding the aforesaid council, one who has chosen the monastic life may lawfully be again admitted to the episcopate. For if anyone, while the fury of persecution rages, or because bodily illness prevents him, is unable to make progress in pastoral government and, by authority of his superior, descends to the monastic life, he may, once the impediment of persecution or illness has ceased, return to episcopal dignity. Likewise, if anyone, because of a lack of learning, lest, like a blind man, he offer guidance to the blind, leaves a position of government by apostolic authority and withdraws into monastic leisure, and through the exercise of reading receives the pearl of knowledge, he may beyond doubt, when again called by the Lord, ascend the pastoral chair.

Again, if anyone, through the ambition of his relatives, though wholly without his knowledge, has obtained a bishopric and, upon discovering this, with his superior’s permission relinquishes that bishopric and chooses regular observance, then, although under the canonical sanctions he cannot afterwards return to the same bishopric, he may nevertheless lawfully be appointed to another. Although, therefore, in these and similar cases one who, having relinquished a bishopric, chooses monastic life may return to the pastoral office, nothing in such cases is understood to be undertaken against the aforesaid council. For it speaks of the case in which someone, abandoning the episcopate because of some crime, descends to monastic life for the sake of penitence.

Accordingly, some have said that the aforementioned chapter speaks in the case where a person, deposed from episcopal dignity for a crime of which he has been convicted or which he has confessed, is enclosed in a monastery to perform penance; or where someone, because of a grave crime for which he could not worthily perform penance while retaining the episcopate, obtains permission to resign and chooses monastic life. Others maintain that the aforesaid chapter should be understood thus: that he cannot return by his own right—that is, reclaim as due what he relinquished in that manner—although he may be elected, especially if he resigned only the place and not the order.

Since, therefore, we have been unable fully to determine for what reason the aforesaid Joachim formerly resigned his bishopric—for in our letters sent concerning this matter it is stated only that, having received letters concerning his resignation and commending in the Lord his purpose of preferring the salvation of his soul to temporal honor, we absolved him from the burden of pastoral care—although a certain canon of San Frediano has very recently informed us that Joachim sought permission to resign because it had come to his knowledge that certain of his relatives had given some things, albeit few, in order that he might be elected bishop: by the authority of these presents we command your brotherhood, after diligently investigating the truth concerning these matters, that, if it becomes clear to you that Joachim resigned the said bishopric for one of the aforesaid or similar reasons, you shall, by our authority and with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, provided that necessity and usefulness require it, grant him leave to assume the government of the Church of Faenza.

This is especially so if what the aforesaid provost and canons of Faenza, as well as the prior and chapter of San Frediano, have expressed to us in their letters is confirmed by the truth: namely, that Joachim resigned only the place and not the order or even the dignity. For then it would be most strongly presumed that he did not enter regular life because of a crime he had committed and in order to perform penance; particularly since, after his resignation, the Apostolic See would much less than before have permitted one entangled in such a crime to minister in pontifical order. Otherwise, since it would be far too harsh to admit such a postulation contrary to so solemn a council, you shall enjoin upon the aforesaid provost and canons that they elect another suitable person as their shepherd.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCL. TO THE ABBOT AND CANONS OF THE TEMPLE OF THE LORD

They are received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Lateran, 11 Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1555A]

The most holy Roman Church has customarily, from the duty of its accustomed piety, to love more devotedly its humble and faithful sons, and, lest they be harassed by the molestations of wicked men, to cherish them, like a loving mother, under the safeguard of its protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, considering the devotion which you are known to bear toward blessed Peter and ourselves, we receive your persons, with all the ecclesiastical and worldly goods which you now rightfully possess or may in future, by the Lord’s favor, acquire by just means, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves.

In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to your church, by apostolic authority and fortify by the protection of this document, the churches of Saint Nicholas of Varvar at Constantinople, the Holy Trinity at Athens, Saint Nicholas at Thebes, Saint Nicholas at Negroponte, and Saint Mary of Clusurio in the diocese of Thermopylae, with all their possessions and appurtenances; and also the Athenian prebend, as you possess them justly and peaceably.

Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, etc., down to “shall incur.”

Given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of February, in the eleventh year.

## CCLI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF MOLÈSME

Concerning the visitation of the monastery of Molèsme. (Lateran, 6 Ides of February.)

[Col. 1555C]

When it had formerly come to our hearing that the monastery of Molèsme had fallen grievously into decline in temporal and spiritual affairs, we instructed the beloved son, the abbot of Cîteaux, that, approaching it with the diligence with which he was accustomed annually to visit his daughters, he should correct what he found requiring regular correction, both in head and members, and establish what ought to be established.

Afterwards, however, several religious men informed us in their letters that, when the abbot himself visited the aforesaid monastery, it was found to remain in a good spiritual and temporal condition. And, as you, son abbot, had shown by clear reasoning, the debt of twenty-two thousand pounds, with which you had found it burdened when you assumed its administration, you had reduced through payments made, so that only fifteen hundred pounds remained to be paid. You had also restored to the monastery many great possessions that had been pledged at interest, apart from seventeen hundred pounds which, as was established through suitable witnesses, you had expended on repairing the monastery.

Accordingly, humble petition was made to us on behalf of that monastery that, since no benefit had accrued to it from the aforesaid visitation—which was said to have been procured by the enemies of the monastery—nor was any believed likely to accrue, but rather it had already been uselessly burdened with expenses on that account, especially because it was feared that under pretext of that visitation a right of perpetual correction might be usurped over it, we should deign to revoke the same.

Thus, as we had previously been saddened when the fall of that monastery was reported to us, so later we rejoiced at the report of its sound condition. Considering that the aforesaid abbot was departing by our command for the province of Narbonne, to discharge the office of the legation entrusted to him against heretics, and was therefore less able to attend to the affair of the said monastery, we instructed our venerable brother the bishop of Troyes and his colleagues that, since the same abbot had reported nothing of this to us, they should, notwithstanding letters obtained and addressed to him concerning the matter, investigate the truth of the foregoing more carefully and faithfully report the result of their inquiry to us, so that, being better informed by them, we might proceed in the matter as the Lord should inspire us.

They, proceeding diligently with their inquiry, took care to send the result to us. From it there appears to be shown that the said monastery has made much spiritual and temporal progress through the commendable care of your government. For, as several have asserted and none has contradicted, the abundant payment of debts formerly contracted, the diligent redemption of pledged possessions, the repair of the masonry, and the reform of moral discipline all declare that you, son abbot, have been well set over your house.

Highly commending in the Lord the prudence of your care in this regard, we earnestly admonish and exhort you to continue what follows upon what has gone before: do not fail in the good you have begun, but make progress. Like a ship ascending against the force of a stream, which is not permitted to remain in one place because it falls back to lower ground unless it strives upward, forgetting what lies behind, stretch yourself forward with the Apostle toward what lies ahead, and strive, with unceasing diligence, to bring the work you have begun to completion; lest—God forbid!—a relaxation coming upon you should render void the very work you have done.

Moreover, so that you may more effectively and freely advance the interests of the said monastery—which, through God’s grace and your diligence, is said to be in such a condition that it does not need the care of an external visitor—we absolve you by the authority of these presents from the aforesaid mandate of visitation. This is especially appropriate since he is occupied in the Church’s affairs against the heretics of the province through the office of legate imposed upon him and, even if it were expedient, would be less able to concern himself with these matters; and since, as you request, care must be taken lest under pretext of that visitation a right of perpetual correction be usurped in the monastery itself.

Therefore, son abbot, watch over it in such a way that no other watch need be applied there; lest, if you act otherwise, you compel us to think differently concerning it.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LARISSA, THE BISHOP OF DAVALIA, AND THE ELECT OF CITRUS

Concerning the residence of canons in a safe place. (Lateran, 8 Ides of February.)

[Col. 1557A]

The statement laid before us by our venerable brother the bishop and the beloved sons of the chapter of Thermopylae has disclosed that, after the city of Thermopylae had formerly been destroyed by the attacks of war, the bishop and canons then in office constructed, in a place called Bondonicia by the inhabitants, beside the sea, a certain oratory in which they might celebrate divine service. They assert that this place is so exposed to pirates and other evildoers that many of them come upon the canons when they wish to celebrate there; in fear of these men, the canons cast aside their vestments and other ecclesiastical ornaments, abandon God’s service, and flee, fearing danger to their persons. Indeed, a certain bishop, third in succession before the bishop now presiding, was cruelly slain by such evildoers in that very place.

They therefore humbly petitioned us, asking that, mercifully providing for the security of the Church and their own safety, we might deign to grant them leave to dwell in the abbey commonly called Communio, situated on land belonging to the Church of Thermopylae itself. Since, however, the foregoing has not been established for us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, after diligently investigating the truth of these matters, that, if necessity requires it, you grant them, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, leave to dwell in the said monastery without prejudice to the monks, until other provision is made for them, restraining opponents through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

Notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice. And if not all, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Ides of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLIII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT MAURUS OF ANGERS

The Church of Saint Peter of Culturis is adjudged to them. (Lateran, 3 Ides of February.)

When we had entrusted for decision to the beloved sons, the dean of Saint Peter and the priors of La Celle and Saint Radegund of Poitiers, the case concerning the right of patronage of the Church of Saint Peter of Culturis which was in dispute between you and the Church of Angers, they, having received the witnesses of both parties, examined the documents and other arguments, and proceeded according to the order of law up to a definitive sentence, sent the case to us fully prepared. They set a date upon which the parties were to present themselves before us with the attestations and other documents in order to receive judgment.

The parties having therefore appeared in our presence, we judged it appropriate to entrust the examination of the documents and the depositions of witnesses to the beloved sons John, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and Pelagius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy at the Septizonium. When they had diligently examined everything and faithfully reported to us, we adjudged the right of patronage of the Church of Saint Peter of Culturis to the monastery of Saint Maurus, imposing perpetual silence upon the Church of Angers concerning this matter.

Therefore let no one … infringe this page of our determination, etc., down to “shall incur.”

Given at the Lateran, 3 Ides of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLIV. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF LISIEUX

Concerning the treasury and prebend of Lisieux reserved by the pope. (Lateran, 2 Ides of February.)

Since we had some time ago reserved to our disposition, to be conferred upon a suitable person, both the treasurership and the prebend which John, our subdeacon of good memory, held in your church, we admonished and asked you, brother bishop, in our letters to grant us your willing assent in this matter and to write to us as quickly as possible concerning your intention, so that the collation of these benefices might be credited no less to your generosity than to our favor.

We indeed stated that we had retained their collation in our power in such a way that, until your reply had reached us and our final decision had returned to you, no one else might attempt anything concerning them; and we decreed that anything attempted in the meantime should be null and void.

But you replied in your letters that, when you had received certain knowledge of John’s death, on the tenth day before anything concerning our will in this matter had become known to you either by messenger or letter, you conferred the treasurership, by common consent, upon the beloved son Master William Arundel, whom you declare to be supported by manifold merit of character and learning. You divided the prebend into two portions and conferred them upon two suitable men, commendable in life and learning, so that more fully and sufficiently service might be performed in the two churches attached to the aforesaid prebend and, the burden being divided between them, the care of souls might be borne more easily and exercised more diligently.

You therefore humbly petitioned us that, if there had been error in such an arrangement, we should correct it; or, if it had been rightly made, that we should deign to confirm it under apostolic protection.

Although, if, after prior notice of our aforesaid decree had been received from any source whatever, either you had proceeded to confer or they to receive the aforesaid benefices, not only should what was so attempted be revoked as void, but both you and they ought also to be severely punished for contempt: nevertheless, if the matter stands as you have stated in your letters, you appear excusable from contempt. We therefore entrust to your discretion the task of determining whether, in view of the aforesaid decree, what was done can lawfully stand. If it can, those upon whom you conferred the benefices shall retain them securely, not only by our permission but also by our grant. But if what was done cannot stand in law, then, lest you offend both justice and conscience, restore matters to the condition set out in our decree and inform us of this as quickly as possible by your letters, so that we may make provision concerning them as the Lord inspires us.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLV. TO THE BISHOP OF ARRAS, AND THE ABBOTS OF THE DUNES AND URSICAMP, IN THE DIOCESES OF THÉROUANNE AND NOYON

Concerning the collation of prebends at Aire. (Lateran, 14 Kalends of March.)

[Note: [Col. 1559D] Chapter *Dilecto*, “On Witnesses.”]

The beloved son G., provost of Aire, has informed us that, when we entrusted to you, brother bishop, and son abbot of the Dunes, together with the beloved son the dean of Arras, the case being litigated between him and the noblewoman the countess of Flanders concerning the grant of six priestly prebends, that provost, before joinder of issue, alleged before you that the testimony of the dean himself was necessary to him in the said case, since he could establish his right only through that dean and one other witness. He therefore urgently requested that either you two should proceed in the case with the dean excluded, or that you should suspend proceedings until we ordered another to be substituted in his place.

You refused to admit his request in this respect; indeed, after the appeal which he made to us on this account and for other reasons, you suspended him from the grant of those prebends. Therefore, lest the justice due to the aforesaid provost fail through the absence of such a witness, we have decided to substitute you, son abbot of Ursicamp, in the place of the aforementioned dean. By apostolic letters we command that, if the truth supports the foregoing, after relaxing the aforesaid suspension of the provost, you proceed in the case in accordance with the tenor of the former mandate, reason guiding you.

And if not all, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 14 Kalends of March, in the eleventh year.

## CCLVI. TO BERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF ATHENS, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY

Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, Ides of February.)

[Col. 1559D]

[Note: [Col. 1560D] See above, letters 237, 243, 245.]

The renewal of grace does not permit the ancient glory of the city of Athens to grow old. For, as though it prefigured modern religion at its first foundation, it changed the worship which, divided into three parts, it had offered to three false deities into worship of the true and indivisible Trinity under three Persons. And, changing the pursuit of worldly knowledge into a longing for divine wisdom, it humbled the citadel of most famous Pallas into the seat of the most glorious Mother of the true God, having now attained knowledge of Him for whom it had formerly built an altar as the unknown God.

That city, indeed, illustrious in name and perfect in beauty, first instructed the world in philosophical art and later was instructed in apostolic faith. Since it both trained poets by letters and at last understood prophets through letters, it was called the mother of the arts and named the city of letters. If we wish to turn its meaning into an interpreted name, we may call it Kiriath-sepher, “City of Letters”; and because Othniel subjected it to Caleb’s rule, Caleb gave his daughter Achsah to him in marriage.

Therefore, venerable brother archbishop, since this distinguished city has been subjected to God, you have been joined to its church in spiritual marriage as to a bride, in order that you may preserve it in His obedience. Like Achsah, prompted as it were by you, we understand that she sighingly asks us to deign to water her dry places with the streams of apostolic blessing.

We therefore judge it fitting to send there, in writing, the gift of apostolic protection, from which we know that an abundance of literary learning flowed into almost the whole world. We graciously assent to your just requests and receive the Church of Athens, over which, by God’s favor, you are known to preside, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, fortifying it by the privilege of this document.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought it necessary to specify these by their own names:

The villages of Procovenico, Vertipos, Triclini, Platan, Felin, Curiomonaster, Cassas, Menidi, Ducheleos, Calixtes, Perseconar, Catraperseta, Clazazundas, Chandebride, Alianastasis, Pothamo, Pirgo, Hu, Marefon, Oargite, Largedo, Lalaconite, Vatia, Literne, and Mortar.

We likewise confirm to you and your successors the following bishoprics, subject from ancient times to your church by metropolitan right: the bishoprics of Negroponte, Thermopylae, Davalia, Abelon, Zorcon, Karystos, Koroneia, Andros, Megara, Skyros, and Kea.

In the bishopric of Karystos: the two villages of Lesboveries; Lepesin; Leperistere; Lamarogna; Locarimera; Lomoni; Lochichemi; Lopolistile; Cundegrat; Lapisto; the vineyards of Conizari; Muscarel; Catachephalar; and Agiafronesis.

Four hundred *palicae* and two hundred *papates* residing at Athens; one hundred *palicae* at Thebes; and one hundred at Negroponte. The mills of the church, gardens and baths, markets of Negroponte and Athens, and the streams by which the gardens are irrigated. The abbeys of Saint Sirianus, Saint Michael, Saint John, and Saint Nicholas. The monasteries of Blessed Nicholas of Catapersica, Blessed Nicholas of the Columns, and Saint Mary of Blachernae. The monasteries of the Cinoloitae, Saint Prothasius, the Holy Trinity, Saint George, Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, Saint Theodore, Saints Cosmas and Damian, Blessed Nicholas of Ducheleos, Blessed Nicholas of Menidi, Blessed Philip, Saint Luke, Saint George of the Island, the monastery of Koprea, and Saint Blaise.

We also grant to your brotherhood, through the generosity of the Apostolic See, the use of the pallium for the fullness of the pontifical office. Remember that you are to use it in your church at the solemnities of Mass on those days upon which you know your predecessors to have used it: namely, the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Stephen the Protomartyr; the Circumcision of the Lord; Epiphany; Hypapante [the Presentation of the Lord]; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter; Easter Monday; the Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of Saint Mary; the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist; the solemnity of all the Apostles; the commemoration of All Saints; dedications of churches; the principal feasts of your church; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clerics; and the anniversary day of your consecration.

Moreover, let no one possess by hereditary right the cemeteries of the churches of your diocese or ecclesiastical benefices. If anyone attempts this, let him be restrained by canonical censure. [Note: [Col. 1561D] Imitated from Urban II, 16, question 2, chapter 6, *Sane quia*.]

Furthermore, because certain monks seek to take away from bishops their right, by apostolic authority we prohibit monks in the diocese of Athens from holding priestly chaplaincies or usurping the benefice or office of chaplain without pontifical authority; whatever is recognized as belonging to the right of chaplaincy shall remain whole to priest-chaplains.

We further decree that no cleric of any order may, without the knowledge or consent of you or your successors, make liable to rent, or transfer into anyone’s power, churches belonging to the right of the archbishopric which are entrusted to him only during his lifetime; and if this is done, it shall be held void. Nor may monks, canons, or any other clerics dare to appoint or remove chaplains in churches belonging to your diocese without your authority, unless perhaps they are protected by a privilege of the Roman pontiffs or by ancient and reasonable custom.

Moreover, whatever has been canonically established in your diocese by you with the common consent of the chapter, or of the sounder counsel of its greater part, we will to remain ratified and firm. We prohibit priests or other chaplains of churches belonging to the right of your church from presuming, without your consent—while canonical institutions are nevertheless preserved—to alienate their possessions by disposing of, selling, pledging, or any other means. If this is done, it shall be held void.

By apostolic authority we further forbid anyone to admit persons whom you have interdicted or excommunicated to ecclesiastical office or communion without your knowledge and consent, or to presume to act contrary to your canonically pronounced and promulgated sentence. An exception applies if danger of death is imminent, so that, when they cannot have your presence, a person bound may need to be absolved by another, after satisfaction has first been made, according to the form of the Church.

In addition, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the privilege of this document, all the liberties and immunities, dignities, reasonable and approved customs of your church, and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you, your church, and its clerics by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the Church of Athens, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole and serve in every way the benefit of those for whose government and support they were granted. The authority, reverence, and command of the Apostolic See are always reserved in all things.

If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, rashly attempts to violate this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his fault by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance.

But upon all who preserve their rights to this same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of February, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CCLVII. TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS

Concerning a clerical forger. (Lateran, 14 Kalends of March.)

[Note: [Col. 1562D] Chapter *Novimus*, “On the Meaning of Words.”]

We know that it is expedient to explain more clearly the phrase contained both in the ancient canons and in our decree issued against forgers: namely, that a cleric degraded by an ecclesiastical judge is to be handed over to the secular court for punishment. [Note: [Col. 1562D] Chapter *Ad falsarios*, “On Forgers.”]

For certain of our predecessors, when consulted on this question, gave differing answers; and an opinion approved by many is that a cleric degraded because of this or another grave offense, not merely culpable but harmful, is, as one stripped of clerical privilege, consequently assigned to the secular forum when he has been expelled from the ecclesiastical forum. His degradation must indeed be performed in the presence of secular authority, and that authority must be notified when it is to be performed, so that it may receive the degraded cleric into its own jurisdiction; and this is what is meant by his being handed over to the secular court.

Nevertheless, the Church ought effectively to intercede for him, so that the court may moderate its sentence to spare him the danger of death. But concerning that wicked forger whom, at our command, you caused to be arrested, we judge this counsel should be given to you: confine him in perpetual prison to perform penance, sustaining him on the bread of affliction and the water of distress, so that he may lament the crimes he has committed and commit no more deeds requiring lamentation.

Given at the Lateran, 14 Kalends of March, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF AURIE

Concerning the right of patronage. (Lateran, 2 Ides of February.)

[Col. 1563B] [Note: [Col. 1563D] Chapter *Postulasti*, “On the Right of Patronage.”]

You have asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See whether, when rectors of parish churches sometimes present certain persons to be instituted to the titles of their churches, the election of such persons belongs to the rectors themselves or also to the patrons; and, if the assent of patrons is not required in such cases, whether the patrons’ right of election remains intact, so that when the churches themselves fall vacant, persons so instituted are not to be preferred to others.

To this we briefly reply to your brotherhood that no prejudice is created for the patrons by such institution, and they may present others to those churches when they fall vacant, unless the patrons’ consent has been given.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLIX. TO ALL BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ENGLAND

Commission against those who did not observe the interdict. (Lateran, 9 Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1563C]

[Note: [Col. 1563D] See Matthew Paris under the year 1209, and above, letters 102 and 214.]

When the monasteries of the Cistercian order established throughout England had begun strictly to observe the ecclesiastical interdict generally proclaimed by our authority in the affair of the Church of Canterbury, some of them afterwards, as we have learned, under pretext of an appeal which they are said to have made on the basis of their privileges, rashly violated it. They did so not only insofar as the grants of those privileges were concerned, but also presumed to celebrate more solemnly than usual, with bells ringing, chants resounding, doors open, and others invited to communion.

Although we can scarcely believe such presumptuous audacity of religious men, nevertheless, if what is alleged is true, the force of canonical discipline could thereby be weakened, not without grave injury to ecclesiastical liberty. We therefore command and strictly enjoin you all by apostolic letters to investigate the truth concerning this matter most diligently. You shall compel the abbots or priors of those monasteries which you find to have celebrated in this manner, being suspended, to appear before us through ecclesiastical censure, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, in order to make satisfaction for so great a contempt.

You shall likewise compel the monasteries themselves by the same censure to observe inviolably the aforesaid interdict, in accordance with the command of our venerable brother the bishop of London [Note: [Col. 1564D] See above, letters 141 and 214, and below, Book XII, letter 9.] and his co-executors, notwithstanding any privilege whatever; for no such privilege can stand against a command of apostolic authority, under which privileges of this kind are always granted with its authority reserved.

And if not all … each one of you shall nevertheless execute these things, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of March, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLX. TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

Concerning the same matter. (Lateran, 9 Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1564B]

[Note: [Col. 1564D] See the letter above.] We regard as grave and unworthy the fact that, although the monasteries of your order established throughout England [have violated] the ecclesiastical interdict, etc., as in the other letter down to “canonical discipline,” we have strictly commanded our venerable brethren, the bishops established throughout England, to investigate the truth of this matter with the utmost diligence; and to compel the abbots or priors of those monasteries which they find to have celebrated [divine offices] in this manner, being suspended, etc., down to “to come by ecclesiastical censure,” compelling the monasteries themselves by like censure to observe inviolably, according to the command of our venerable brother the Bishop of London and his co-executors, etc., as [Col. 1564C] in the other letter down to “are granted.”

But because we consider it all the more unworthy that this should be endured from the Cistercian Order, inasmuch as the Apostolic See and we have deserved so little from it that, in return for favour, it should repay us with injury and contempt instead of honour—wherefore, unless that zeal of most ardent charity which we bear towards you and the other religious of the same order tempered the reasonable emotion of our mind, we should have taken care to punish the perpetrators of such rashness with a more severe penalty—we earnestly admonish and exhort your discretion, commanding you by these apostolic letters that, grieving and lamenting that so great a contempt seems to have arisen at your instigation, since, as you yourself formerly informed us by your letters, and as we reproved you concerning this in our letters by familiar [Col. 1564D] argument, you suggested to those seeking advice both grounds for appeal and boldness to celebrate, you shall understand the command expressed above in such a way as to preserve the other members of your order from a like fault, lest a like or perhaps graver punishment than that now inflicted upon these persons should extend to them. For assuredly, if you should attempt otherwise—which we do not believe—we would punish head and members with due chastisement, according as this or those had sinned.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CCLXI. TO THE ELECT OF MEAUX, THE ABBOT OF SAINTE-GENEVIÈVE, AND WILLIAM, ARCHDEACON OF PARIS. On the election of the Bishop of Verdun. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1565A]

Our beloved son Master Herbert, canon of Verdun, appearing in our presence, stated that, after the Bishop of Verdun had formerly been killed in arms, the dean and chapter of the Church of Verdun, apparently taking advantage of the absence of outsiders and also of certain resident brethren who were away for study or other necessary reasons, set the eighth day after the burial of the slain bishop too hastily for electing a pastor. On that day the same master happened to be present, though he had not been summoned. When he entered the chapter with [Col. 1565B] the others, the dean, at the first word touching the election, said that he and the others had agreed upon the primicerius; and immediately, whispering secretly into the archdeacon’s ear, he repeated a similar statement, while certain persons added that what he had said was true.

When they immediately began to ask the primicerius himself to pay his predecessor’s debts, the aforementioned master, wondering whether they had proceeded so far, told the dean that the matter should not be rushed in this way, but that the election should be discussed with careful deliberation before any nomination; the chancellor replied that they had already discussed him beforehand. Therefore, disturbed by the novelty of the proceeding, the master rose and, approaching more closely, began by apostolic authority [Col. 1565C] to forbid anything to be done contrary to canonical form, declaring his intention to appeal and likewise to state the grounds of appeal.

But many, hearing that he had named apostolic authority, rose and surrounded him. Shouting improperly with one who was shouting, they interrupted the speaker’s words; and when he wished to resume his interrupted speech, the confused clamours prevented him from being heard amid their uproar. Finally, after violently quarrelling with him so that he should be silent, and forcibly pulling him by his surplice, they made him return to his own seat. At length, seeing that the primicerius rose and prostrated himself upon the pavement as though to give thanks for his election, he again cried out, immediately offering himself ready to show why the same primicerius ought not to be elected, appealing to us and appointing [Col. 1565D] the octave of All Saints then next to come as the term for prosecuting the appeal. Yet they overcame him, as before, with shouting, and nevertheless placed the primicerius himself in the episcopal chair.

When this came to the knowledge of four fellow canons studying at Paris, three of them joined the aforesaid master. Two of these, returning to the Church of Verdun, took care to object on their own behalf and that of the third. Having also received letters from that third fellow canon and from the aforesaid master, setting forth the events and forbidding, under objection of appeal, confirmation of such an elect, they went to the Archbishop of Trier. In his presence they diligently and faithfully endeavoured to impede confirmation of this election, but, at last [Col. 1566A] overcome by the entreaties of many, are said to have consented to it. Nevertheless, afterwards the often-mentioned master, appearing before the same archbishop with them and six others, jointly with them forbade him to proceed to confer consecration, appealing to our hearing on five articles—four concerning the facts and one concerning the person: first, that those absent had not lawfully been summoned to make the election; second, that due deliberation had not preceded the discussion of it; third, that a hearing with due tranquillity had been denied to the same master; fourth, that proceedings had been taken in the matter after a lawful appeal to us had been interposed; and fifth, that they said the same primicerius suffered from a deficiency of learning. They further asserted [Col. 1566B] that his election was suspect for many other reasons.

Although, on all these matters, the same master with his companions had alleged both arguments and canons, and repeatedly, by renewing the appeal, had forbidden both those presenting [the elect], those consecrating, and also the person to be consecrated to attempt to proceed to consecration, they nevertheless proceeded. Hence he and his companions humbly petitioned that, revoking as void what had thus unlawfully been done, we would deign also to punish with due penalty those through whom it had been attempted, and further order an inquiry into the truth concerning such other matters as they might think fit to propose.

On the other hand, our beloved son R., procurator of the adverse party, alleged that, since the dean and canons of Verdun [Col. 1566C] had been driven from their own city by its citizens for the liberty of the Church, and all their property had been consumed, after the death of the aforesaid bishop they finally assembled in a safe place. Considering not only civil seditions but also hostile wars, and wishing to provide beneficially for themselves in the appointment of a pastor amid both, they resolved to ask the citizens for a truce, so that they might be able to assemble in their chapter to elect a bishop. Since a short truce was granted to them, though with difficulty, they unanimously fixed a day for making the election. Before that day, having summoned all fellow canons who either ought to have been summoned or could conveniently have been summoned, they deliberated and carefully discussed, in choir and chapter, the person to be elected.

Accordingly, when on the appointed day all who had been summoned and wished to come had assembled [Col. 1566D] together, the dean—who in the meantime had used the greatest diligence in ascertaining the will and intention of each—by common assent and at the request of the whole chapter nominated and elected as pastor the aforesaid primicerius, a man of unblemished reputation, noble and eloquent, prudent in temporal affairs and adequately instructed in spiritual matters, in the fitting manner. All who were present consented, except only the aforesaid master, who was not among the resident members of the Church but was an outsider, and who showed no reasonable ground for his dissent.

When, according to custom, they presented his election to the aforementioned archbishop for confirmation, certain persons objected on the day of confirmation. But later, [Col. 1567A] consenting to him, they joined with the others in asking the same archbishop to confirm the aforesaid election and appoint a day for the conferral of consecration. Therefore, acting on the counsel of prudent men, the archbishop confirmed that election and appointed a day for consecration. On that day, finally, the oft-mentioned master and certain others who had previously consented to the election, together with two others who complained that they had not been summoned, attempted to prevent the consecration. They advanced certain arguments, carefully indeed but ineffectually; the archbishop at last considered these frivolous and, on the counsel of bishops, abbots, and jurists, consecrated the aforesaid elect as bishop, the master himself and his associates contumaciously withdrawing from his presence.

Accordingly, the said procurator humbly requested [Col. 1567B] that we would deign to hold valid what he endeavoured to establish had been done canonically with respect to the election and consecration of the aforesaid bishop—especially since, although he was not of outstanding learning, he asserted that the same man possessed adequate learning, and that the Church of Verdun had already advanced in many respects under his governance.

Since, therefore, the foregoing has not been made clear to us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having God alone before your eyes, and summoning those who must be summoned, you investigate the truth concerning these matters with the utmost diligence. Proceeding, with the impediment of appeal removed, up to the pronouncement of definitive sentence, you are to ensure that the cause, sufficiently investigated, is referred to us; appointing the parties a suitable term within which they shall [Col. 1567C] present themselves before us to receive judgment. If the said bishop prefers to come in person into our presence, you are in no way to proceed upon the article concerning learning alone, since by a present examination we can sufficiently ascertain it ourselves. Otherwise, after carefully examining him concerning it, transmit to our presence in like manner what you find. If witnesses who have been named withdraw through favour, hatred, or fear, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, to bear testimony to the truth. And if not all of you can carry these matters out, etc., nevertheless let two of you carry them out.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year of our pontificate [Col. 1567D].

CCLXII. TO CYNTHIUS, CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SAINT LAWRENCE IN LUCINA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. A reply to his inquiries.

[Note: [Col. 1567D] Chapter *Officii*, On elections.] You perform a praiseworthy act of your office when you seek instruction from us concerning matters about which you are uncertain. You informed us in your letter that a certain monastery, suitably endowed with possessions but situated in the midst of a depraved and perverse nation, lacked a pastor. When the monks were deliberating about the election of an abbot, they judged it necessary to elect some person whose power might enable them to be delivered from persecutors. [Col. 1568A] Since they could not find a suitable person of their own order, they turned their eyes toward a certain nobleman through whom they could be better defended. On the advice of certain jurists, they approached his father and humbly asked him to induce his son to receive the monastic habit, giving the father no assurance whatever concerning his son’s promotion. The father induced his son to do so: he was discreet, prudent, learned, and twenty-five years of age. He became a monk with, as he asserts, no hope of advancement being given him; but on the day on which he became a monk, he was elected abbot. His election was confirmed by our beloved son G. de Lab., our subdeacon and rector of Messana, legate of the Apostolic See, who was present at all the aforesaid events.

[Col. 1568B] Since the same man is prepared to clear himself of having been induced to this by no ambition, you ask to be instructed by our letters whether the said legate could confirm such an election or dispense so that what was done might stand; and whether, once the election has been duly annulled, he may again be elected abbot. We answer your inquiry as follows: although the circumstances which immediately followed show that such a man could not be elected abbot in such a manner—especially since, before he was a disciple, he wished to be a master—we decree that election null and void. But after he has been adequately trained in the Rule, if urgent necessity and the evident benefit of that monastery require it, then, once his exculpation has been received, he may be chosen as abbot, lest the monastery [Col. 1568C] be oppressed by the incursions of evil men.

[Note: [Col. 1567D] Chapter *Officii*, On testaments.] Secondly, you asked: when someone leaves his own share to a bishop in a will, and leaves many other things to monasteries, churches, or others, may the bishop claim from those things his lawful share? You add whether, when someone in his will fraudulently establishes a small mortuary offering and leaves more things for his soul, the bishop may nevertheless demand the share established by canon from the other things. We answer your inquiry as follows. If he bequeathed that share to the bishop on condition that he should be content with it alone, and the bishop accepted it, then, since by this he seems to have renounced the others, he cannot demand a share from the remainder.
