[Col. 1568D] But if he left it to him absolutely, the bishop may nevertheless claim from the remainder the share due to him. If it is established that he fraudulently made the mortuary offering small in order that the bishop might be deprived of his due share in the remainder, then, because fraud and deceit ought not to avail anyone, the bishop may demand from those things the share established by canon, saving the indulgences granted by Roman pontiffs to certain religious orders.

[Note: [Col. 1568D] Chapter *Requisisti*, On testaments. See below, book XII, letter 58.] You asked how things which a testator bequeaths for his soul in his last will are to be divided between bishop and churches. Certainly, as a general rule, it is true that the bishop ought to receive from them a third or a fourth share according to [Col. 1569A] differing customs. But one must carefully consider whether the testator bequeaths in this manner: “I leave this to the bishop”; or, “I leave this to the church”; or, “I leave this to the bishop and the church”; or, “I leave this to the bishop, and I leave that to the church.”

In the first case, one must distinguish whether the thing is left to the bishop by a stranger or by a relative. If by a stranger, it is generally true that it is presumed to have been left in consideration of the Church, not of the person. Therefore the cathedral church may claim its canonical share from it, just as the bishop is entitled to his share if something is left to the church itself. This is certainly true unless the testator expressly states that he wishes it to belong to the bishop alone and not to the Church. In that case [Col. 1569B] the testator’s disposition must be observed. It is otherwise, however, if he expressly states that he wishes it to belong to the Church alone and not to the bishop, [Note: [Col. 1569D] Angers manuscript: “left to the bishop.”] because the private disposition of a testator cannot alter the general constitution of the canon. Nor is this contrary to what is read in the canon [Note: [Col. 1569D] 12, question 3, chapter *Pontifices*], namely, that bishops to whom anything is left or donated by strangers either jointly with the Church or separately—because the donor is shown to offer it for the redemption of his soul, not for the priest’s advantage—shall reckon it not as their own property but as property left to the Church among the Church’s resources. For this is true when the testator leaves it separately to the bishop without expressing whether he wishes it to belong to the bishop alone and not to the Church.

But if [Col. 1569C] it is left to the bishop by a relative, it is presumed to be left in consideration not of the Church but of the person, unless perhaps the contrary is proved; and the Church can claim nothing from it during his lifetime. If, however, it is left to the bishop and the church, a canonical division of it must be made between them. But if this is left to the bishop and that to the Church, whether the things left are equal or unequal, they must be reduced to a canonical division between the bishop and the cathedral church, unless both wish to be content with the testator’s disposition. In favour of a last will, it is quite fitting that this be observed where neither fraud nor deceit intervenes and no one is excessively defrauded of the share due to him.

The case differs if something is bequeathed to the bishop and something to chapels, monasteries, [Col. 1569D] or other pious places. In that case, what is bequeathed to the bishop is his exclusive property as against the cathedral church, just as if it were bequeathed to anyone else; and he will nevertheless obtain a canonical share from what is bequeathed to those places. For there is not such close communion between the bishop and chapels, monasteries, or other pious places as there is between him and the cathedral church, [Col. 1570A] to which he is joined in a spiritual marriage. Therefore what the bishop acquires he acquires not for those places but for that church alone.

The following must, however, generally be observed concerning one who can own private property and does not hold a prelacy or administration of a church: if anything is specifically left to him, whether by a relative or even by a stranger, it is understood to be left not in consideration of the Church but of the person, unless evidence to the contrary appears. Consequently neither bishop nor Church can claim anything from it during his lifetime. This is understood to be true where fraud has in no way been procured; if fraud is discovered, it ought not to receive protection.

[Note: [Col. 1569D] Chapter 9, On penance.] You further reported that a certain woman had confessed in penance that, fearing lest her husband’s property [Col. 1570B] should devolve upon others, she had been induced by the advice of a certain sorceress to drink daily the juice of certain herbs, and thus her belly swelled. Pretending thereby to be pregnant, she finally substituted another’s child as her own. Fearing her husband, she does not wish to disclose the crime to him, and he believes the child without any doubt to be his own. Since you ask to be instructed by our letters whether penance should be imposed upon her while this fraud continues, we answer your inquiry as follows: just as penance is not to be denied to a woman who, without her husband’s knowledge, has conceived a child through adultery, even though she fears to confess it to her husband, so penance must not be denied to this woman either—especially if by “others” you mean persons not of the family, to whom [Col. 1570C] she fears that her husband’s property would devolve. But suitable satisfaction must be imposed upon her by a discreet priest.

And below: Finally, [Note: [Col. 1569D] Chapter 24, On judgments and excommunication.] you asked whether a person who, because of several offenses, has been bound by the bond of excommunication by several prelates having jurisdiction over him, and who wishes to make satisfaction to one of the prelates for only one offense, ought to be absolved by that prelate from the offense for which he wishes to make satisfaction; and, when he has not made satisfaction for the other offense, whether he may be declared absolved to the other [prelates]. Since, however, various scholars hold differing opinions on this matter, and since for the present we do not wish to prejudice any of them, we answer you only this concerning the point: an absolution fraudulently obtained does not benefit one who suppresses the truth, and one who knows the truth ought not to grant such an absolution.

[Note: [Col. 1569D] This letter is mutilated in the Register, where two chapters are missing; we have restored them from ancient collections of the decretals of this pope, namely the first and the third. For in the Register it begins thus: “*Officii*, etc. And below: Secondly, you asked.” [Col. 1570D] Then after the word “granted,” where the second chapter ends, one reads, “And below,” and immediately it is written: “You further reported that a certain woman.” We have removed those words, “And below,” and restored the missing chapters. There remains a fifth chapter, in whose place the Register has “And below”; but we have been unable to find it in books of Decretals.]

CCLXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND MASTER GERNAND, CANON OF MAGDEBURG. On the election of the Abbess of Heris.  

[Col. 1570D]

[Note: [Col. 1570D] Chapter *Cum dilecta*, On rescripts.] When the beloved daughter in Christ R., custodian of the church of Heris, and Volpert, clerk and procurator of G., a nun, had formerly come to the Apostolic See and had for some time litigated before us concerning elections held for the aforesaid custodian and nun, we, having carefully heard both what was put forward by that procurator and by the custodian, commanded the abbots of Helerward and Herg and the provost of Geismar, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any objection or appeal, to declare null and void whatever had been done concerning the election of the aforesaid nun. After diligently investigating the truth concerning the election of the custodian herself, if they found her election canonical and her person suitable, they were to confirm her by apostolic authority, restraining opponents through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside.

But when that custodian presented this mandate to the judges, they declared null and void what had been done concerning the aforesaid nun. Since she would not relinquish the abbey, the judges bound her with the bond of excommunication and ordered that she be avoided more strictly. Yet she, with her electors, appealed concerning her election through a messenger a few days later. The judges, however, in no way deferring to the appeal—especially since her election had been annulled by our express command and appeal had been prohibited in our letters—summoned the convent of Heris and proceeded to investigate the custodian’s election as they had been instructed. Finding her election canonical and her person suitable, and having taken counsel with prudent men, they confirmed her election and, by a definitive judgment, awarded her the abbey of Heris by our authority.

Although the diocesan bishop appealed and forbade the convent of Heris to presume to obey her as abbess, they nevertheless peacefully introduced her into bodily possession of the abbey. From this she was violently expelled by . . . the brother of the aforesaid nun and by her supporters. In addition to the other evils wickedly perpetrated there by them, they compelled the said R. to confirm by oath that, until the then next-coming feast of Saint Martin, she would neither enter the church of Heris nor use even an ordinary dwelling there or the stipend which she received there.

Since the said R. was gravely harassed concerning these and other matters, she deemed it necessary to have recourse to our presence; the aforesaid nun G. likewise came. When R. raised the question concerning these matters and sought confirmation of the proceedings of the aforesaid judges, together with satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted upon her, G. alleged in reply that, having been elected abbess of the church of Heris by the greater and sounder part of the convent, and her election having been confirmed by the diocesan bishop, the custodian had obtained letters addressed to the abbot of Conradesburch and his fellow judges. When G., summoned before them, appeared and showed that she had been despoiled through the agency of the custodian, she maintained that she was in no way bound to answer before those judges unless first restored; but the custodian, appealing from that judgment, personally pursued her appeal.

Moreover, since G. had sent a procurator only for the purpose of securing confirmation of that judgment, her procurator, exceeding the bounds of his mandate, allowed the custodian to obtain against her what she wished and brought back letters addressed to the aforesaid judges. One of these judges lay under a sentence of excommunication, as was contained in letters of our venerable brother the archbishop of Mainz presented to us. Together with another of them, in the absence of the third, he proceeded irregularly in all matters. Although both G. and the chapter of Heris had appealed because of various grievances, those judges nevertheless proceeded and had the custodian introduced into bodily possession through Albert, her household servant—who, as the same letters of the aforesaid archbishop proved, was bound by excommunication—and B., the parish priest.

To prove that the aforesaid procurator had received such a mandate, namely to arrange for pursuit of the appeal already lodged, she produced witnesses before the auditor assigned to her. But it was answered in reply that, even if those witnesses had proved such a mandate, this in no way showed that he had not received another; and therefore, since the presumption favored the judgment, especially as it had been pronounced by us after mature deliberation, it could plainly be understood that the aforesaid procurator had received a general mandate concerning the principal business. The custodian herself showed this more fully through the single witness whom she produced.

Having understood these and the other matters alleged on each side, we decided by judgment that the aforesaid nun G. must be removed from the administration of that abbey. By our letters we commanded the beloved sons, the scholasticus of Hildesheim and the custodian and scholasticus of Minden, to go personally to that church and arrange for the administration of the abbey to be entrusted to another suitable person, to whom the property withheld should be resigned on both sides for the use of the church. Meanwhile they were to consider the judgment of confirmation rendered by the delegated judges concerning the custodian’s election and, as justice required, either confirm or invalidate it.

Specifically, if, because one of the delegated judges who had rendered that judgment lay publicly under the bond of excommunication when it was rendered, as appeared from the metropolitan’s letters, or for some other reason the judgment had to be invalidated, they were, after setting it aside, to examine anew the custodian’s election. Having heard fully the matters alleged as fact and the person concerned, they were to confirm her if her election were found canonical. Otherwise, after entirely invalidating it, they were to grant the sisters free faculty of election and, appeal set aside, confirm the election of whomever they should canonically judge fit to elect as their abbess. They were also to provide for the aforesaid custodian’s lawful expenses from the goods of the church, and to compel all opponents or rebels, appeal removed, by ecclesiastical censure to desist from their rashness.

They were likewise to compel by the same coercive measures, appeal set aside, any witnesses who had been named and who withheld themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, to bear testimony to the truth. The judges summoned both the custodian and the convent of the church of Heris before them and allowed them a period of delay. While the delay was pending, however, the provostess of Heris, with her accomplices, presented our letters to the abbot of Reinvehusen, the provost of New Church, and the parish priest of Eschenshuseim. These letters commanded the same judges, appeal set aside, by ecclesiastical censure to compel the aforesaid custodian to restore through due process of law certain ornaments of that church, revenues of the custodianship belonging to the church’s use, revenues from Meinchsern which ought to supply the sisters’ necessities, and certain other things from their prebends, which she had maliciously taken away through certain robbers and retained at her own discretion.

When the custodian had been summoned under those letters and could not appear before the judges on the day fixed for her, they pronounced a sentence of excommunication against her, after an appeal had been lodged on behalf of that custodian by Lambert, a clerk. Although on the same day her procurator appeared before them and sought remission of the excommunication sentence as having been pronounced without sufficient reason, he was heard in no respect. He therefore ratified the appeal lodged by the aforesaid clerk Lambert and withdrew.

The judges, paying no heed whatever to the appeal, received witnesses produced by the provostess and her accomplices. After publishing their depositions in the custodian’s absence, they condemned her and her accomplices to restore one hundred and fifty marks and also condemned them for theft and sacrilege, subjecting them to a sentence of excommunication. Afterwards, when the procurator of that custodian appeared at the appointed time before the aforesaid scholasticus of Minden and his fellow judges to proceed in court for her, those judges asserted that, since the aforesaid custodian had been excommunicated by the judges just mentioned, as she herself could not sue, neither ought her procurator to be heard. They therefore barred him from proceeding by judgment.

The procurator replied that such a sentence of excommunication could not harm either him or the custodian, since it had been legally prevented by the obstacle of a lawful appeal which had preceded that sentence. When the judges considered this allegation frivolous and refused to consider the appeal, the aforesaid procurator appealed to the Apostolic See. But they refused to defer to that appeal and received the witnesses whom the other party wished to produce to prove that one of the delegated judges who had rendered the judgment for the custodian was then excommunicated when the judgment of confirmation in her favor was pronounced. They did so on the pretext that certain of those witnesses had come from distant regions. For this reason certain sisters of Heris appealed to the Apostolic See on their own behalf and on behalf of the aforesaid custodian.

Disregarding the appeal lodged, those judges removed the nun G. from administration of the church of Heris and entrusted it to the provostess of that church, who was to receive certain suitable persons as her assistants. The same judges, omitting the article concerning the resignation of the withheld property—which had been inserted first in the mandate of our letters—received witnesses concerning another article: namely, that a lawful appeal had formerly been lodged by the aforesaid abbot and his fellow judges, because they had refused to furnish the parties with a copy of our rescript. After later publishing the witnesses received concerning the foregoing articles, they entirely invalidated the judgment of confirmation rendered for the oft-mentioned custodian. They further investigated her election and annulled it as having been celebrated less than canonically, granting the sisters free power to elect.

The sisters assembled and unanimously elected the aforesaid nun G. The said judges confirmed her election and solemnly assigned to her possession of the abbey and the abbess’s seat, publicly declaring the aforesaid custodian and her female supporters excommunicated. Subsequently, those appointed by the aforesaid judges as auditors concerning the article noted above—namely, the resignation of the withheld property—received witnesses produced by the aforesaid provostess and her accomplices, and sent their depositions, enclosed under their own seals, to those same judges.

But when the custodian herself set out to come to the Apostolic See, the aforesaid judges refused to publish the witnesses’ statements, sending them enclosed under their seals to our presence. We therefore carefully considered these matters and the others which both the aforesaid custodian and I., a clerk who had come against her in the same business, wished recently to allege while present at the Apostolic See, together with the judicial acts presented to us by them. We plainly discovered that the aforesaid letters addressed to the abbot of Reineshusers and his fellow judges had been procured by deception, since they committed for determination, without our knowledge, the article concerning the resignation of withheld property. That article had been inserted in the earlier letters, of which no mention at all occurred in the later letters. We therefore judged that whatever was attempted on the occasion of those letters must be entirely annulled.

Furthermore, we found that the said scholasticus of Hildesheim and his fellow judges had proceeded without due care. Our letters had principally commanded them to go personally to the aforesaid church and entrust administration of the abbey to a suitable person, to whom the withheld property should be resigned on both sides for the use of that abbey. Yet, altering the form of the apostolic mandate, omitting that clause, and very irregularly examining the other articles, they acted contrary to the form of our rescript and to the order of law. We therefore decreed their proceedings null and void. By the authority of these present letters, in the power of the Holy Spirit, we strictly command and enjoin you to meet in a suitable and safe place, restore G., A., and certain other sisters of that church as justice requires, and, scrupulously observing the form of our mandate, proceed in the affair according to the tenor of the preceding letters, appeal set aside and reason leading the way. By your circumspect diligence, let a due end at last be imposed upon this affair, so long delayed. Since the church of Heris is known to have suffered grave losses because this cause has already been protracted for so long, we will and command that you, brother archbishop, endeavor to attend the hearing of the cause at your own expense.

CCLXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND THE ABBOTS OF THE GREATER MONASTERY AND OF SAINT JULIAN AT TOURS. The case concerning the subchantership of Poitiers is committed to them.

[Col. 1575B]

[Note: [Col. 1575D] Chapter *Inter dilectos*, On the excesses of prelates.] When a dispute had arisen between the beloved sons Bocard and Peter Coeth, canons of Poitiers, concerning the subchantership of the church of Poitiers, each firmly maintaining that he had canonically obtained that subchantership through the chanter of Poitiers, to whom its grant belonged, the aforesaid Bocard came to the Apostolic See on this account. Before our beloved son Guala, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in the Portico, whom we assigned as auditor to him and to the procurator of the aforesaid Peter, he affirmed that the subchantership had been canonically conferred upon him. He added that, even if the chanter had previously conferred it canonically upon the said Peter, that grant ought not to take effect because of the unworthiness of Peter’s person, since Peter was a public gambler and a manifest usurer.

Although, after many disputes, Bocard introduced certain witnesses to prove not only this but also the principal issue, because both he and the opposing party intended to produce several witnesses concerning the principal matter and the incidental questions, we committed the case for canonical determination to the beloved sons, the dean and chanter of Sainte-Radegonde of Poitiers and the dean of Thouars, transmitting to them under our seal the aforesaid witness-statements enclosed. When the parties subsequently appeared before them and Bocard sought to have his witnesses received, it was answered in opposition that he should not be heard at all, since he had been bound by a sentence of excommunication imposed by the beloved sons the archpriest, the master of the schools, and Master P. Parvus, canons of Bourges and our delegated judges, because he refused, at their command, to admit Hugh, a clerk, as canon of Faye.

[Note: [Col. 1576D] See above, Letter 45.]

When Bocard afterwards presented letters of those judges concerning his absolution, the opposing party began to charge them with falsity, because their final clause differed from the rest of the writing both in the color of the ink and in the form of the letters. It argued that B. should be entirely excluded from his claim as one accused of the crime of forgery. After many and varied disputes, the judges, with the parties’ consent, received witnesses both on the principal issue and on the incidental matters. But B. subsequently appealed to our hearing, and the judges sent the parties, together with the witness-statements and judicial acts authenticated under their own seals, to our presence.

The parties therefore recently appeared at the Apostolic See and litigated for some time before our beloved son Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, whom we assigned as their auditor. He faithfully reported to us what he had heard. After carefully examining the witness-statements of each party, we found it plainly proved that Peter was a public gambler and a manifest usurer, since he had publicly lent eleven pence for twelve in gambling. Although Peter alleged in mitigation of so presumptuous an offense that he had done this according to the custom of French clerics, under which almost all clerics frequently lend in this fashion and gamble, we—whose office obliges us to aim at rooting out such plagues, and who utterly condemn pleasure-seeking games through which, under a certain appearance of courtliness, men descend into the wickedness of dissipation—deemed this excuse frivolous. It is veiled by a perverse custom, which ought rather to be called a corruption; for an offense is more punishable in those through whom licence to commit wrong is arrogated in order to make excuses for faults.

Accordingly, what is known to have been done for Peter concerning the aforesaid subchantership we judged null and void because of his unworthiness and baseness, since, under lawful enactments, the gate of dignity ought not stand open to base and unworthy persons. Moreover, it was plainly proved against Bocard that the final clause had not been inserted in the letters of the aforesaid judges of Bourges with their knowledge, as is clearly stated in their depositions. Robert, a deacon introduced as witness to prove this, testified to the same effect and added that, when he was to seal those letters, he carefully inspected them and did not then find that clause attached.

The other party therefore alleged that, since B. had knowingly used letters thus falsified, he ought deservedly to be excluded altogether as a forger. But we observed that, even though it were most clearly established that the said clause had been attached to those letters without the knowledge of the aforesaid judges, no proof was made to us that B. had attached the clause, procured another to attach it, or knowingly used letters thus falsified. We therefore absolved him from this accusation of forgery, especially since, after this was alleged against him, he entirely ceased using those letters.

Further, the witnesses produced by Bocard on the principal issue sufficiently proved that the aforesaid subchantership had been granted to him on Thursday—or, to speak more expressly, on the Thursday after the feast of Saint Michael—two years previously. But his own confession showed that the feast itself had been celebrated on a Thursday in that year; consequently it was proved that the said grant had been made to Bocard on the eighth day after that feast.

On the other hand, six witnesses—the chanter, Oliver, W. Gerru, R. Agnellus, I. Marinus, and P. de Marcai—whom the aforesaid Peter introduced to prove that the grant made to him had come first, plainly proved that the aforesaid subchantership had been conferred upon him at an earlier time. Oliver, W., and I. expressly said that the grant was made to Peter on the second or third day after the said feast; the chanter said on the third or fourth day; and P. said within the week after that feast. But witnesses introduced by Bocard to challenge the aforesaid witnesses disqualified Oliver and William as manifest fornicators. The chanter was likewise convicted of perjury by many witnesses: although he swore that he had never granted the aforesaid subchantership to Bocard, many witnesses proved in reply that, in their presence, the chanter invested Bocard with it.

Moreover, R. Agnellus is found to have testified nothing concerning the principal matter, although Peter’s party, asserting that he had spoken ambiguously, tried to show that he had said on the principal matter the same thing as Oliver and William. Two witnesses remained, namely I. Marinus and P. de Marcai, who could not reasonably be disqualified. Bocard’s party alleged that P.’s testimony should not be believed because he had been Peter’s procurator. It attempted to establish this from the fact that Bocard’s witnesses said that I. had carried Peter’s letters, sought witnesses, and done certain similar things. But, since it was not established for us that he had been Peter’s procurator, we judged his testimony worthy of belief.

We also deemed frivolous the argument advanced by Bocard’s party: that because Peter de Marcai had said the grant was made to the aforesaid Peter within the week after the aforesaid feast, it followed that Peter’s grant could not have preceded Bocard’s grant made on the eighth day after the feast. For, since a week (*hebdomada* or *septimana*) extends no further than the seventh day, it is evident that a grant made within the week was certainly made earlier than one made afterwards on the eighth day. Therefore, since the depositions of at least two witnesses who were in no way disqualified plainly establish for us that Peter’s grant came first, although it deserved rejection because of Peter’s unworthiness, we decreed the grant made to Bocard null and void.

Since the chanter, to whom the grant of the said subchantership is said to belong, quite apart from his perjury, behaved so inconsistently in this affair that, as stated above, without the first grant having been set aside, he attempted to make a second, and since it is fitting that a person be punished in that matter in which he appears to have offended, we decided to punish his fickle inconsistency in this respect: on this occasion he shall have no power to grant the subchantership. By the authority of these present letters, we command you, supported by our authority and appeal set aside, to assign it to a suitable person, restraining opponents, etc.

CCLXV. TO THE BISHOPS OF PARIS AND TROYES, AND TO THE ABBOT OF SAINTE-GENEVIÈVE, PARIS. On the case of the monastery of Vézelay against the count of Auxerre. (At the Lateran.)

[Col. 1578B]

[Note: [Col. 1577D] Chapter *Cum olim*, On the office of a delegated judge.] When formerly the beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Vézelay, showed us by their complaint that the nobleman Peter, count of Auxerre, was attempting to construct a certain pond, mill, and house on their land, to their prejudice and injury, we committed this case to our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son the treasurer of Nevers. When the parties had appeared before them, as we learned from their letters, the suit concerning the church’s claims having been joined, witnesses having been received on both sides, and their statements published, and after the testimony had subsequently been argued between the parties, the count’s party at length alleged before them that they ought not to take cognizance of damages inflicted upon woods and other property, concerning which the witnesses seemed to be testifying, because our rescript made no mention of damages. It added that the things in dispute were held in fief from the noble duke of Burgundy, as that duke acknowledged in open letters, and therefore recourse concerning them should be had to the lord of the fief rather than to the said judges.

It was answered in reply that, although our letters did not expressly mention the damages inflicted, they mentioned them implicitly, since the term “injury” (*gravamen*) was included in them. The judges could therefore take cognizance of such damages, at least as accessories or appendages of the principal matter. Further, since the suit concerning every article on which the witnesses had testified had been formally joined, the judges were bound to take cognizance of and pronounce upon them. It was also asserted that the count ought not be heard concerning the exception of fief, since it had been raised far too late, namely after publication of the witness-statements.

The count’s party replied that, even if the suit concerning damages had been joined by his procurator, this could not prejudice him, because the procurator had not been appointed for that purpose, but only for the case set out in the letters of commission—namely, concerning the castle, pond, and mill. The other party answered that the count could no longer attack his procurator’s act, since he had not thought fit to revoke it until after publication of the witnesses. After consulting prudent persons concerning the allegations on both sides, the judges interlocutorily ruled that jurisdiction over damages inflicted by the count belonged to them. On hearing this, the count sought the benefit of appeal.

Although the judges summoned him and, because he appeared neither personally nor through a suitable representative, bound him with excommunication, they nevertheless sent the case with the witness-statements faithfully authenticated to our presence while he persisted in contumacy. When the procurators of both parties had accordingly appeared at the Apostolic See, the monastery’s procurator alleged before us that the village of Vetenedo was jointly held by the monasteries of Vézelay and Saint Germanus of Auxerre: that they had there the land-rent (*terragium*), grain-rent (*spanagium*), lodging-duty (*albergaria*), census-rents, thirds, *laudes*, sales dues, and rights of retention. The aforesaid count, who customarily received nothing other than two denarii annually from each peasant as a payment for custody or safe-conduct, was now unjustly usurping jurisdiction there. In a certain part of the village, after a prohibition made both to him and to the Hospitallers—who held that place in the monastery’s censiva and had received it from them by exchange—he was extorting five solidi from every villager, building a castle, pond, and mill to the monastery’s prejudice and injury, and causing grave damage to woods, stones, and other things.

The procurator therefore sought demolition of the aforesaid structures, as built after prohibition and formal notice, and that the aforesaid count be compelled to desist from harassing the monastery of Vézelay in this matter, making suitable compensation for the damages inflicted. The count’s procurator, however, alleged that murders and robberies were very frequently committed in the aforesaid place of Vetenedo, which was subject to his jurisdiction. Wishing to avert so many and such great dangers, the count had constructed a certain house for the security of travelers on ground received from the Hospitallers in exchange, where he had learned that a fortified house had formerly stood; and he had built there a pond and mill for the use of the guards of that house.

But the aforesaid abbot and convent, falsely saying that they were thereby aggrieved, procured letters to the aforesaid judges. When, in the judges’ presence, the count offered that, should they prove they had suffered any damages from those buildings, he would make good such damages not merely once but twice over, they utterly rejected both that offer and every other proposal of peace. When the judges had proceeded in the cause as far as publication of the witness-statements, it appeared from the published testimony that the witnesses had testified on many articles concerning which the suit had not been joined. The count’s party therefore alleged that the judges could not take cognizance of these. When the judges ruled that they could take cognizance of and pronounce upon damages inflicted, an appeal was made to our hearing.

Having heard these and the other matters which the procurators took care to put forward, and having carefully examined the witness-statements of each party, we understood that it was proved for the monastery that, in the aforesaid village, the land-rent, grain-rent, lodging-duties, census-rents, thirds, *laudes*, sales dues, and rights of retention belonged to the aforesaid monasteries; and that the aforesaid pond and lime-kiln (*calceria*) had been constructed partly on the property of the monastery of Vézelay and partly within its censiva and that of Saint Germanus. It was also proved that the Hospitallers, who paid the monasteries an annual rent for the aforesaid place, had been forbidden to transfer that place—that is, the censiva of the monasteries—to the count, and the count had been forbidden to receive that censiva.

For the count’s party it appeared proved that jurisdiction over the wood above the fortification belonged to him; that without injury to anyone the count could grant that wood for lodging the men of the village; that the count had jurisdiction in the village and customarily received two denarii from every house in the village for its protection; that the fortification itself stood on the meadows of the Hospitallers; that whoever holds something at rent may, subject to the rent, sell it to whom he wishes; and that there had formerly been in that village a fortified house enclosed with palisades and ditches.

Since jurisdiction concerning damages inflicted before the suit had been joined did not belong to the said judges, because our rescript made no mention of them, nor could jurisdiction be extended to them, since the procurator must be understood to have been appointed only for the matters expressly found in the letters of commission; and since, once the count learned from the published witness-statements that testimony had been given concerning those damages, he immediately objected, we pronounced that the said judges had ruled less than justly, and that the aforesaid count, who had on this account sought the benefit of appeal, had not been bound by the sentence of excommunication.

But since we learned from the confession of the count’s procurator that, after notice of new work had been given to him, he built the aforesaid fortification, pond, and mill, by the authority of these present letters we command and enjoin you prudently to admonish and effectively induce both parties to make an amicable settlement, which we believe necessary for each. If perhaps within a month after they have been diligently admonished by you they do not choose to comply with your counsels, then, by our authority and with every obstacle of objection and appeal removed, pronounce the judgment which we send you enclosed under our seal, and cause it to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure. If not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, in the twelfth year.

CCLXVI. How witnesses are to be received.

[Col. 1581A]

[Note: [Col. 1581D] Chapter *Quoniam*, “That a suit has not been contested.”] Since many frequently call into question whether witnesses may be received before a suit has been contested, we have thought it right to declare by the authority of these presents that the general rule is true: before contestation of the suit, one is not to proceed to the reception of witnesses, unless there is fear of the witnesses’ death or prolonged absence. In such cases, where proceedings are to be conducted according to civil law, lest the truth be concealed and the opportunity for proof be taken away by unforeseen events, the aged, the infirm, and other witnesses concerning whom there is fear for some reasonable cause are, without doubt, to be admitted even before contestation of the suit, whether the defendant is contumacious or absent without malice, so that he cannot be summoned.

But if the plaintiff does not summon his adversary within a year from the time when he can be summoned, or at least does not notify him of the reception of such witnesses, the depositions thus received shall have no force, lest he perhaps contrive this fraudulently, so that, with the passage of time, lawful exceptions for excluding the witnesses, or other objections, can no longer take effect. Moreover, special cases may arise in which something else should exceptionally be observed; for example, if a question is raised concerning someone’s election or a marital union. For then, lest through long delay the Church suffer injury in spiritual or temporal matters, or an occasion of fornication be afforded to a man or woman—especially where a degree of kinship forbidden by divine law is alleged—[Col. 1581C] in such cases witnesses ought rightly to be admitted, provided that the person against whom the action is to be brought has proved contumacious: either because, after receiving a peremptory summons, he scorns to come; or because he maliciously conceals himself; or because he prevents the summons from reaching him.

But if he is absent otherwise, and the matter concerns a spiritual marriage already contracted between a prelate and a church, especially where the election has been confirmed, we wish in this respect that to be observed which the sacred canons determine concerning waiting for such persons. But if the matter perhaps concerns contracting a spiritual marriage, the person elected as prelate is to be awaited for six months, unless, after weighing the circumstances of the business, he ought to be awaited for more or less time through the superior’s prudential judgment. If, however, a carnal marriage is at issue, either spouse is to be awaited until his or her death may plausibly be presumed. For, since the absent person is without fault—as, for instance, if perhaps held by captivity, illness, or some other just impediment, or even if, by his own but not malicious will, he stays in remote regions so that he cannot readily or soon be summoned—he ought not to suffer prejudice, since he may perhaps have lawful exceptions to defeat the contrary claim. Nor does the possibility of alleging sexual lapse prevent this, since in marriage many cases arise in which spouses are compelled to abstain without fault, though not without cause.

There are likewise other special cases, which we recall having distinguished elsewhere, in which witnesses may lawfully be produced without contestation of the suit, as when an inquiry into offences or the publication of witnesses’ testimony is imminent. In other cases, however, careful consideration must be given to whether a contumacious person is sued by a real or a personal action. If by a real action, the plaintiff is certainly to be put into possession of the thing claimed, so that, wearied by this, the defendant may come to answer. If he comes within a year, then, upon giving security to appear in court and making suitable satisfaction for expenses, he shall recover possession. But if he neglects to offer security within the year, after the year has elapsed the plaintiff shall be constituted true possessor, while a lawful defence concerning ownership alone remains reserved to the adverse party.

But if someone is sued concerning immovable property which he possesses in another’s name, he must immediately name the owner in court, within a fixed number of days to be set by the judge and communicated to that owner, so that the owner may either come himself or send a suitable representative to challenge the plaintiff’s claim. If, after the time granted, he is unwilling to fulfil what has been prescribed, then, as though the suit had been contested from the day on which the possessor was summoned to court, for interrupting prescription by long time, the judge shall summon the owner of the possession by lawful edicts; and, if he remains of the same mind, the judge, summarily examining the matter, shall without delay put the plaintiff into possession of the things, preserving to the absent party every allegation concerning the principal question. But if he is sued by a personal action, the plaintiff is either to be put in possession of his movable goods, or, if he has no movables, of his immovables, according to the amount of the declared debt; or an ecclesiastical sentence is to be pronounced against the contumacious person. The judge is, however, initially to be content with whichever of the two penalties is more feared, while nevertheless proceeding to the other if the obstinacy of the contumacious person deserves it. If he comes within a year, or even after a year, he shall be heard according to the distinction set out above in the other case.

## CCLXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF FERRARA. Reply to his inquiries.

[Col. 1582D] [Note: [Col. 1582D] Chapter *Responso*, “On Sentences and Excommunication.”] In your response you ask to be instructed whether, since the citizens of Ferrara are bound by sentences of excommunication and interdict, it is lawful for you to assemble men and women once a week or once a month at some church, preach God’s word to them, and lead them to amendment. To this we answer your fraternity as follows: you may do this without scruple of conscience whenever you see that it is expedient, provided that no divine office is celebrated for them contrary to the form of the interdict.

Furthermore, you asked whether, since the city of Ferrara is subject to interdict and excommunication, and therefore all ecclesiastical sacraments are forbidden there except baptism for infants and penance for the dying, it is lawful for you to sign baptized children upon their foreheads. To this we have thought fit to answer you that, just as children may be baptized, so those baptized may also be anointed by you upon their foreheads with sacred chrism for confirmation.

## CCLXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF ST ANDREWS, THE ABBOT OF BERBORC, T., PRIOR, R., ARCHDEACON, AND MASTER L., OFFICIAL OF ST ANDREWS.

Since the beloved sons, the abbot and canons of Cambuskenneth, had drawn the abbot and monks of Dunfermline, in the diocese of St Andrews, before our venerable brother the bishop of Dublin and the beloved sons the abbots of Cupar and Scone, of the diocese of St Andrews, by authority of our letters, in a case concerning certain [Col. 1583B] tithes belonging to their church of Egres, and damages and injuries inflicted; and since the latter had, by our delegation, sued the aforesaid abbot and canons before the beloved sons the prior of Holyrood and the dean of Tinihec in the same diocese, before you, son Official, concerning the chapel of Nipast and tithes belonging to it: both parties, etc., as above, Book X, letter 31.

## CCLXIX. Reply to someone’s consultation.

[Note: [Col. 1583D] Chapter *Inquisitioni*, “On Sentences of Excommunication.”] Briefly answering your inquiry, we think a distinction must be made whether one spouse knows with certainty of an impediment to marriage on account of which he or she cannot engage in sexual intercourse without mortal sin, although unable to prove it before the Church; or whether he or she does not know such an impediment with certainty, but believes it. In the first case, therefore, the person ought rather humbly to endure a sentence of excommunication than commit mortal sin through sexual intercourse.

In the second case, however, we distinguish whether such a conscience arises from a slight and rash belief, or from a probable and discerning one. Indeed, on the advice of his or her pastor, having rejected a conscience arising from slight and rash belief, the person may lawfully not only render but demand the marital debt. But when conscience troubles the mind because of a probable and discerning belief, though not an evident and manifest one, the person may indeed render the debt, but ought not to demand it, lest in either respect he or she commit an offence either against the law of marriage or against the judgment of conscience. Therefore proceed, according to the response aforesaid, upon the point concerning which you wished to consult us.

## CCLXX. TO THE BISHOPS OF FLORENCE AND FIESOLE, AND THE ARCHPRIEST OF PISTOIA. The Hospital of St Allucius is adjudged to the Hospitallers.

[Note: [Col. 1583D] Chapter *Inter dilectos*, “On Donations.” See also [Col. 1584D] chapter *Per tuas*, “On Arbitrators.”] When a dispute arose between the beloved sons, the Hospitallers of the Holy Sepulchre of Pisa of the Jerusalem Hospital, on the one side, and the brethren of the Hospital of St Allucius, on the other, and when the same Hospitallers had obtained a contrary judgment in possessory proceedings which they had brought once and again, though on different grounds, they finally had recourse to a proprietary action. Through their procurator, before the beloved son Andrew, our subdeacon and chaplain, whom we appointed auditor for them and for the procurator of the other party, they alleged that B., formerly rector, and the fathers and patrons of the same Hospital of St Allucius, after common deliberation had resolved to subject that hospital to the aforesaid Hospitallers, entrusted their authority in this matter to three procurators, jointly determining that they would accept whatever those procurators did concerning it.

Afterwards these procurators approached the aforesaid Hospitallers and agreed with them that persons should be sent to the hospital to receive, in their name, its assignment. Accordingly, they sent brother M. and B. there for this purpose; and in the chamber of the aforesaid rector, they received the donation and assignment of the said hospital from the aforesaid master, the aforesaid procurators, and the other brethren of that house.

And below: The procurator of the other party, on the contrary, answered that the aforesaid donation ought not without reason to be revoked, because it had been made by the aforesaid rector and a smaller number of brethren, without consulting many of the brethren, while they were nevertheless excommunicated and perjured; because it concerned a matter in litigation; and because it was made in fraud of the pleban of Pistoia, who had raised a question concerning the same hospital. He alleged that all this had been sufficiently proved by the depositions of the witnesses produced. The other party responded in many ways; and the matter was disputed on both sides for some time.

Therefore, having understood these and the other matters which the parties chose to set forth before the aforesaid chaplain, and having carefully examined their depositions, we observed that the brethren and patrons of St Allucius were alleging, on their own behalf—or rather against themselves—their own disgrace: namely, perjury, excommunication, and fraud, committed not against them but by them. Understanding that the donation made by them to the aforesaid Hospitallers had been pure and simple, and since the law aids not deceivers but the deceived, they could not lawfully defend themselves against their own act by the matters alleged above, especially since some of these had not been proved. With the counsel of our brethren, we therefore adjudged the aforesaid Hospital of St Allucius, with its appurtenances, to the Hospitallers of the Holy Sepulchre; provided that this judgment of our determination shall create no prejudice for the diocesan bishop and the pleban of Pistoia, since a matter done between certain persons ought not to create prejudice for others.

## CCLXXI. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS. Reply to his inquiries.

[Note: [Col. 1584D] Chapter *Licet undique*, “On the Office of a Delegate Judge.”] Although the abundant multiplicity of affairs flowing in upon us from every side does not cease to impel our mind toward various concerns, nevertheless your fraternity, whom we embrace with sincere charity in the Lord, has compelled us for a time to lay aside the care which we bore, by the debt of pastoral office, in carrying out other matters, and to resolve your doubt by an apostolic answer.

Since, therefore, you have asked us whether, if we delegate a case to three judges and insert in our letters this clause: “If not all of you can be present in carrying these matters out, nevertheless two of you shall carry them out,” and if one, after entrusting his authority to one of the others, is removed by death, while the third is rightly rejected as suspect, may the surviving colleague determine the matter in his own name and that of the deceased? We answer your inquiry as follows. If he did not begin, during the lifetime of his colleague, to exercise the jurisdiction conferred upon him by that colleague, then, since such a mandate expired with the death of the mandatory while the matter remained untouched, he does not alone possess the office of judging. But if before the other’s death he began to exercise the jurisdiction thus delegated, he may carry out both his own authority and that of the other.

## CCLXXII. TO THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE.

Since in your diocese, etc., as above, Book X, letter 71.

## CCLXXIII. TO LEO, PRIEST CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF HOLY CROSS. On appointing an abbot of St Quiricus.

[Note: [Col. 1585D] Chapter *Tuam in Domino*, “On Times of Ordination.”] Commending your diligence in the Lord, which you are known to employ in reforming the monastery of St Quiricus, we command your devotion by the authority of these presents that, if you cannot provide more suitably for that monastery with an appropriate person, you shall appoint as abbot the monk whom in your letters you commended for integrity and diligence, and through whom the condition of the place is believed capable of reform. You are to have absolutely no regard for the unlawful request made by certain laymen, but act solely by virtue of your own office of provision; provided that he does not proceed to sacred orders, since in an urgent necessity a man established even in minor orders may be appointed abbot; and provided that the aforesaid laymen are not related to the said monk by consanguinity or affinity, lest some unfavourable suspicion arise against him from their request.

## CCLXXIV. TO ALL DOCTORS OF SACRED SCRIPTURE, DECREES, AND LIBERAL ARTS RESIDING AT PARIS. Their statute is confirmed.

[Note: [Col. 1586D] Chapter *Ex litteris*, “On Oaths.”] From the letters of your devotion we have learned that certain present-day doctors of the liberal arts had departed from the footsteps of their elders, especially in three matters: indecorous dress; failure to observe order in lectures and disputations; and the almost wholly neglected pious practice of celebrating the funerals of deceased clerics. Desiring to provide for your honourable standing, you unanimously selected eight sworn members from among yourselves, so that, upon the advice of prudent men, they might in good faith establish what was expedient and honourable concerning these matters; and you bound yourselves collectively by oath henceforth to observe it. Only master G. was excepted: refusing to swear and fearing suretyship, he offered merely a guarantee by sureties on his own behalf.

Furthermore, as a precaution, you immediately determined upon pledged faith that if any master should decide to resist the others and, after a first, second, or third warning, should scorn to obey the community of masters within three days, he should thereafter be deprived of the benefit of their fellowship in the masters’ body. Some of you indeed confess that you understood this last provision without qualification; others, only if he did not make satisfaction; and still others, only unless he secured from us admission by the others.

When, after being required to do so, the aforesaid master G. did not obey the community within three days, he was thereafter regarded by you as excluded according to your agreement. When he afterwards offered to make worthy satisfaction, he submitted, under oath, to the decision of four of you, undertaking to hold their ruling acceptable and ratified for the sake of peace. Having taken counsel of wise men, they jointly promulgated their ruling, forbidding the said master, by virtue of his sworn oath, thereafter to resist the community of masters in lawful matters; and enjoining him to remain in the condition in which he then was until, personally or through his procurator, he should obtain from the Apostolic See the ability to be admitted by the other masters, with honour in all respects preserved.

You therefore humbly petitioned us that, by apostolic kindness, we should cause this master—a prudent and honourable man, who, like a son of obedience, humbly accepted and patiently observes what the aforesaid four enjoined upon him—to be restored to the fellowship of the masters. We, therefore, understanding from the foregoing that he had been commanded to remain in his then condition until he should be restored to the fellowship of the masters by command of the Apostolic See, and that he is prepared to make fitting satisfaction in the matters aforesaid—although it had been determined that any master who chose to resist the others and, after being warned first, second, or third, scorned within three days to obey the community of masters, should thereafter be deprived of the benefit of their fellowship in the masters’ body, and although for this reason he was deprived of their fellowship—yet because it was not determined that such deprivation should last forever, and because both canon law and our custom provide that one deprived of fellowship for contumacy obtains restoration when he has made fitting satisfaction, we command your university by the authority of these presents to admit the aforesaid master, who humbly endeavours to obey your statutes, into partnership in your fellowship of masters.

## CCLXXV. Apostolic letters are not valid after a year.

[Col. 1587A]

It frequently happens that persons who have obtained our letters against others concerning certain matters, having long delayed to use them, finally arrange to produce them when, by authority of other letters, they begin to be sued by the same persons against whom they first obtained letters. They say that the later letters are invalid because they make no mention of the earlier ones. Since human malice ought not to be indulged, we decree by the authority of these presents that if anyone obtaining our letters, within a year after having access to the judges, maliciously or negligently postpones using them, he may be sued by authority of later letters, even though these contain no mention of the earlier ones.

## CCLXXVI. TO THE ABBOTS OF ST MARY IN CAGIA AND OF THE SECRET VALLEY, AND TO M., CANON OF RHEIMS. An accusation against the abbot of St Denis of Rheims is committed to them.

[Note: [Col. 1587D] Chapter *Cum I. et A.*, “On a Judgment and a Matter Adjudged.”] When I. and A., canons of St Denis of Rheims, had some time ago come into our presence, on behalf of certain canons of the same church they disclosed to our apostolic office that their abbot was gravely accused on many counts of waste, perjury, simony, and certain other matters. After they had litigated for a time at the Apostolic See concerning these and other matters with the procurator of the abbot himself, we afterwards commanded our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons and the beloved sons, the dean of St Quentin in the diocese of Noyon and master Simon de Vallibus, canon of Laon, to go together to that church and, setting appeal aside, correct what needed correcting in both head and members and establish what they saw should be established.

And below: Accordingly, the judges, with the consent of the parties, restored the abbot himself to administration of spiritual matters and entrusted the care of temporal matters to certain prudent and faithful men. Thereafter, receiving the oaths of the abbot and canons, they examined some of them on the same day and fixed another day for examining the rest; this both parties gladly accepted. But on the day set, the abbot did not appear before them at all; his maternal uncle, the abbot of St James of Provins, presented himself with open letters of ratification on his behalf. Since he did not object, the judges proceeded with the examination. When they were prepared to pronounce sentence on the following day, the aforesaid procurator produced letters before them expressly stating that the appeal which he had lodged on the first day was renewed.

But the judges, observing that the same abbot had tacitly renounced the aforesaid appeal by taking an oath and submitting to their judgment—especially since the obstacle of appeal had been excluded by our letters, and irreparable ruin of that church was feared—after consulting prudent men removed the said abbot by sentence from the administration of that church. They deferred the correction of the members, which they could not then complete. From that sentence, as unjust, the aforesaid procurator appealed to our hearing, because the delegates had ruled that, for the aforesaid reasons, the appeal had been abandoned.

The aforesaid abbot and the procurator of the canons subsequently came to the Apostolic See on this account. Before our beloved son John, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, whom we assigned to them as auditor, the abbot alleged many matters through which he maintained that the sentence ought rightly to be rejected: first, because the letters under whose authority the judges had proceeded had been obtained by suppression of unity, since the canons through whom they were obtained had failed to mention that they were bound by a threefold sentence of excommunication imposed upon them by him because they were gamblers, frequently entered taverns, and were disobedient to him; secondly, because after the appeal to us was lodged, the judges proceeded in the inquiry without a charitable admonition first preceding the denunciation, without restoring him, and without contestation of the suit; and thirdly, because, after receiving the oaths of conspirators, the judges presumed to proceed against him to sentence when the depositions had neither been published before the parties nor shown to him.

And below: Since, however, full proof could not be made to us concerning the charge of conspiracy, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, after more fully investigating the truth, if it is established to you that those persons whose oaths the judges received were conspirators; that the abbot sought to prove this very point before them; and that the judges, following their statements alone, pronounced sentence when the same matters had not been proved through others, you shall, setting appeal aside, annul their proceedings and proceed in the matter according to the prescribed form contained in the earlier letters. But if it cannot be proved that they were conspirators, or if, although this is established, it nevertheless appears that they deposed nothing concerning the matters for which the same abbot was removed; or if they did depose something concerning them, but these matters were sufficiently shown through the statements of others, you shall, the obstacle of appeal removed, confirm the proceedings of those judges. For although conspirators ought not to have been admitted against the abbot, their oaths to speak the truth concerning the condition of that house could nevertheless be received, so that their statements might establish belief concerning other matters not affecting the abbot—especially as it had not then been proved that they were conspirators.

## CCLXXVII. TO THE CHAPTER OF MESSINA. He is granted permission to cohabit with the second wife whom he married while the first was alive.

[Col. 1589A]

[Note: [Col. 1589D] Chapter *Veniens*, “On One Who Has Married.”] G., a layman and bearer of these presents, appearing before us, humbly represented that he had formerly married a certain woman in the city of Limoges and cohabited with her for two years, but afterwards left her through levity of mind. Wandering through the world, he came to Messina, where he solemnly married M., a woman wholly unaware that G. had another wife; by her he is known to have had two sons. But when, in penance, he was ordered to return to his lawful wife, he returned to his native country and found that his wife had died. He returned to the city of Messina and cohabited with the aforesaid M. as though she were his lawful wife.

Now, while performing the penance imposed on him for his former offence, he humbly and devoutly requests from us permission to cohabit with M. Although the aforesaid G. could not marry the said M. while his lawful wife lived, yet, after his wife’s death, being freed from her bond, he could newly consent to marriage with the same M., provided that he did not pledge fidelity to an adulteress or plot his wife’s death. We command your discretion by apostolic writings that, if the truth supports the foregoing, you shall grant the same G. permission to cleave to the aforesaid M. with marital affection, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, and shall not permit him to be unduly troubled in this matter by anyone.

# APPENDIX TO BOOK ELEVEN

## CCLXXVIII. TO THE BELOVED SONS, THE BRETHREN OF THE MONASTERY OF ST PROSPER, SITUATED BENEATH THE CITY OF REGGIO, BOTH PRESENT AND FUTURE PROFESSORS OF THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 10 Kalends of February [23 January].)

[Col. 1589B]

Whenever what is asked of us is known to accord with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford suitable support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander and Celestine, the aforesaid monastery of St Prosper, which is known to belong to the Roman Church and in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of St Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions, etc., down to “shall remain,” among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its holdings and appurtenances and its cemetery. Nine *iugera* of land with the chapel of St Nazarius, which the abbot then in office received through a lawfully made exchange from a certain provost of the same church of St Prosper situated within the fortress of that city; and likewise all that land at Corticella or around the monastery itself which has been given to the said monastery by bishops, canons, or any of the faithful.

Further, twelve *mansi* at Fossule; four at Palude; four at Campagnola; three at Quingenta; one at Curtenova; one at Gurgo; one at Fossadunde; five at Bagnolo; and the chapel of St Mustiola with its appurtenances; one *mansus* at Old Crustulo; one in the village of Sbregato; one at Great Casale; and the chapel of St Silvester with the demesne of the same village of Great Casale; three *mansi* in the region and district of Reggio; the King’s Braida and all the land of the aforesaid monastery situated around that city; three *mansi* at Rodano; three at Marmirolo; one at Aliano; one at Bibiano; one at Piano; one at Mulazano; one at Planzo; one in the castle of Oleriani; and the estate of Nasseto with Lama Praularia and its field, and the stream of Nasseto, which are known to have been given by the most pious king Charles, by precept and according to designated boundaries, to the Church of Reggio; and the land which Roland, son of Heribert, gave.

At Mutilena, four *mansi* with a chapel and a certain part of the castle. At Albinea, four *mansi* and the chapel of St Mary at Pisignano, with the adjacent olive grove. At Vergnano, two *mansi*, and eight *mansi* which Ardicio, son of Atto, son of Gandulf, gave; and the chapel of St Dalmatius at Medule, which Count Ubert gave with seven *mansi*. The chapel of St Peter of Canarolo with all its appurtenances. At Spezano, one *mansus*; one at Floriano; one on Mount Baranzonis; a fourth part in the chapel of St Martin at Revere; and four shares in the aforesaid Revere, two in the church of St Mary, one in St Florentinus, and one in St Lawrence; two *mansi* at Pulianello; and whatever right it lawfully possesses, or ought by right to possess, within the kingdom of Italy.

Moreover, concerning your newly cultivated lands, etc., down to “shall presume.” It shall also be lawful for you to receive into your monastery for conversion clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing from the world, and to retain them without any contradiction. Furthermore, we forbid that any of your brethren, after making profession in that monastery, etc., down to “retain.” But when you, the abbot, die, etc., down to “to be elected.”

Also, out of reverence for blessed Prosper, confessor of the Lord, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander, we establish that the abbot and brethren of that monastery whom the abbot himself appoints, provided they exercise the priestly office, may publicly celebrate the solemnities of Mass upon the saint’s sacred relics for people who come from anywhere to visit the threshold of that most holy confessor, or for inhabitants of the land who come to that church, provided they are not excommunicated or under interdict. They may nourish them with the bread of God’s word; and, after solemn and public confession made by them, pronounce over them general remission and blessing, and grant them participation in your prayers and in the other good works continually done in your monastery, according to the merit of their devotion.

We further command that no bishop or metropolitan of that city, nor any great or small ecclesiastical or secular person, shall dare to disturb anything that we have set forth above, nor on any pretext publicly celebrate Masses there, perform any ordination, however slight, without the will of the abbot and brethren, pronounce excommunication against them, oppose any office, or presume to exercise any authority or jurisdiction against that venerable monastery, as has hitherto been maintained.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that location shall be free, etc., down to “the bodies of the dead shall be taken away.” Therefore we decree that no one, etc., down to “beneficial.” Saving the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token of the liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay one Byzantine coin annually to us and to our successors. If anyone therefore in the future, etc., down to “shall find.” Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the 10th Kalends of February [23 January], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CCLXXIX. TO THE CHAPTER OF BIVINENSIS. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 3 Nones of February [3 February].)

Since what is asked of us, etc., down to “effect.” Therefore, beloved sons, favourably assenting to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority, desiring that they possess perpetual validity through the clemency of the Apostolic See, the donations and grants of estates—namely, St Peter at Drugazzano, Bagno, Castelluccio, of the Slavs, the estate of Lord Leo, the estate of St Mary of Nebula, the estate of Sabuceto—and the other rights or liberties which Robert, formerly Count Palatine of Loretello, made to the Church of Bivino, and which are more fully and explicitly contained in his privilege shown to us. This was confirmed by the beloved son of the Church, the illustrious William I, king of Sicily, by his charter sealed with a golden bull for perpetual remembrance. We likewise confirm a certain estate and territory of St Peter of Matrice, given by the same count especially to the chapter of that church and contained in his special privilege, together with ancient customs and rights obtained by the same chapter at a time beyond memory, as was clearly apparent.

We have ordered the text of the privilege written below—which contains the donations made to the chapter, omitting the others that are strengthened by its royal confirmation—to be inserted word for word in this our present confirmation:

[Note: [Col. 1591D] *Italia sacra*, vol. VIII, p. 364.] “ROBERT, by God’s grace Count Palatine of Loretello, etc.”

Having first made the aforesaid confirmation, we strengthen all these things by the protection of this present writing, decreeing that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the said church and chapter or harass them with any vexations, but that all things shall remain intact, etc., down to “vengeance.” But let all who preserve the rights of the aforesaid Church and chapter, etc., down to “obtain.”

Given at the Lateran, through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the 3rd Nones of February [3 February], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CCLXXX. TO HUBALD, BISHOP OF FAENZA. He is transferred to the Church of Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 1592D] See above, letter 249.] The Church of Ravenna having been deprived of its pastor, its suffragans and the chapter of the same Church of Ravenna, meeting together concerning the replacement of a pontiff [lacuna] our venerable brethren John, bishop of Cervia, and Albert, bishop of Sarsina, and to our beloved sons John the priest and Donatus, canons and priests, Vobert and Martin, cantors of the same church, Bernard, abbot of Saint Apollinaris in Classe, Ambrose, abbot of Saint Apollinaris in Nuovo, and John the priest, together with Peter, the deacon, primicerius [primicerius of the deacons], the election or postulation of a pontiff [lacuna]; after diligent [lacuna], they postulated you as archbishop, humbly begging us to deign to assent to their postulation.

We therefore, not merely approving but also ratifying the postulation [itself, have thought fit to release you from the bond by which] you were held to the Church of Faenza; and by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood, upon proceeding to the Church of Ravenna, to apply yourself diligently to its government in a wholesome and prudent manner. For we give orders by our letters to the suffragans of that church, and to the clergy and people of Ravenna, that they [render] and show you, as their pastor, the reverence and honour due to you.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year.

## CCLXXXI. TO ROFFRID, CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SAINTS MARCELLINUS AND PETER, ABBOT, AND TO THE CONVENT OF CASSINO. Concerning the revocation of alienations.  
(At Saint-Germain, the eighth day before the Kalends of August.)

Although, by the office of apostolic service, through which we are generally debtors to the wise and the unwise, we are bound to exercise care and concern for all churches, yet it is fitting that we extend the attention of our provision more earnestly to your monastery, inasmuch as it belongs in a more special manner to the right and property of the Apostolic See, since it is known to have no pontiff above it except the Roman pontiff.

Now, when we had come to that monastery for the purpose of visitation and had diligently investigated its condition both internally and externally, we discovered that many things had been unlawfully alienated from the hospice, wardrobe, sacristy, infirmary, and cellarer’s office; and these aforesaid offices suffered manifold loss from this deprivation. Therefore, desiring with paternal solicitude to safeguard the unimpaired condition of the said monastery, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that you take care to restore in full to those offices everything known to have been unlawfully alienated from them, so that it may in every respect benefit the uses for which it was assigned. By apostolic authority we establish that neither you, son Abbot, nor any of your successors may presume to alienate, dispose of, or grant either the things which you shall thus restore or those which the aforesaid offices presently possess, the command of the Apostolic See being always reserved in all matters.

Moreover, lest this provision of ours should be hindered by anyone’s rashness, by the authority of these presents we grant you leave lawfully to recover for the monastery itself, with every obstacle of contradiction or appeal removed, both the things expressed above and also the *terratica* [land-rents], as well as other things known to have been unlawfully alienated or granted from your monastery to its detriment. You may also exact, in the name of the aforesaid churches, tithes from possessions belonging by parochial right to your churches, in which you possess full jurisdiction; and, since tithes are due to churches by the precept of both the Old and the New Law, you may compel those refusing payment to pay, by spiritual and temporal coercion if necessary, since you possess both jurisdictions in those places. You shall make a reasonable arrangement with the clerics serving the aforesaid churches concerning such tithes, as though they had hitherto received none of them.

Furthermore, if you, son Abbot, have yourself disposed of any property belonging to the prescribed offices which perhaps cannot readily be recovered without scandal or injustice, we will and command that, according to its valuation, you assign to their uses an equivalent amount from things belonging specifically to the abbot’s table, freely to be applied to those uses until the former things are recovered. We firmly enjoin you to devote yourselves more fully to hospitality and almsgiving, and to desist altogether from unjust and excessive exactions, so that Christ’s poor may rejoice in pious assistance and the men of the monastery may not be distressed by an unjust burden.

Moreover, graciously assenting to your petitions, we grant you for our lifetime the revenue of two pounds of silver which our venerable brother, the archbishop of Torres, exacted for the Apostolic See from the church of Saint Mary of Teugo. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our command, constitution, concession, and donation, or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Saint-Germain, the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXXII. TO OUR BELOVED SONS ROFFRID, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT BENEDICT OF CASSINO, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY.

We give abundant thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than lives, because he is glorious in his saints and wonderful, and in his ineffable goodness manifests his powers wherever he wills. For by the power of his condescension he established the most blessed father Benedict as the father of monks, ordaining that he should be the giver and practitioner of the monastic law, so that the monastery of Cassino, in which he lived most holily and died most gloriously, might deservedly surpass all monasteries throughout the West by the privilege of its dignity.

Therefore, since it is fitting that the Apostolic See should embrace in a special manner so renowned and solemn a monastery, following the example of Pope Clement, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive that monastery under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of the present document. First, indeed, we establish that the same monastery and all things belonging to it shall remain forever in full right, undisturbed and free from every yoke of mortals, under the jurisdiction and perpetual protection of the Holy Roman Church alone.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the concession of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:
