First, the monastery of the Lord the Saviour situated at the foot of Mount Cassino; the monastery of the holy Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, called Plumbarola; the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla; the cell of Saint Benedict at Capua with its cells and appurtenances; Saint Angel at Formia with its cells and appurtenances; Saint John of the Maidens; Saint Rufus; Saint Benedict of Pizzoli; Saint Angel at Odaldischi; Saint Agatha at Aversa; Saints Cecilia and Demetrius at Naples.

In the city of Benevento: the church of Saint Benedict at the Gate of Rufinus; Saint Nicholas in the New City; Saint Benedict in Pantana; Saint Nicholas in Petrapulecina; Saint George in Fenuclo; Saint John in Turlecuso; Saint Peter in Roflano; Saint Angel in Capraria; Saint Januarius near Benevento; Saint Martin in the same place; Saint Dionysius at the bridge; Saint Anastasius; Saint Mary in Canneto beside the River Trinium; Saints Benedict and Lawrence at Salerno; Saint Liberator in the March, with all its appurtenances; Saint Benedict in the Marsi; Saint Mary at Luco with its appurtenances; Saint Cosmas at Civitella; Saint Angel at Bareio with all its appurtenances; Saint Mary of the Handmaids of God in the city of Cosenza; Saint Peter of the Lake; Saint Peter of Avellana with its cells and appurtenances; Saints Erasmus, Benedict, Scholastica, and Martin at Gaeta; Saint Magnus at Fondi with its cells and appurtenances; Saints Agatha, Benedict, and Stephen at Terracina; Saint Peter in the Forest with its cells and appurtenances; Saint Elias in Ambrisia; Saint Paul in the Forest; Saints Mary and Vincent at Pontecorvo with their cells and appurtenances; Saint Benedict at Bagnarola; Saints Mary and Lucy at Rivo Matricio; Saints Nicholas and Peter at Castello; Saint John at Carrica; Saints Angel, Nicander, and Thomas at Troia; Saint Eustace at Pantasia; Saint Benedict at Alarino; Saint Benedict at Pettinari; Saint Paul at Campo Martino; Saint Mary at Casale Piano; Saint Illuminata in the castle of Limosano; Moreover, following in the footsteps of our fathers of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Urban, Calixtus, and the said Clement, we declare that the venerable monastery is to be preferred before the other monasteries throughout the West. [Note: [Col. 1597] See the Preface to Book II of our *Miscellanies*.] We decree that both you and your successors, in every assembly of bishops or princes, shall sit above all abbots; and that in judicial proceedings you shall pronounce before all others of your order the sentence of law.

By apostolic authority we also grant to you, son Abbot, and to your successors the use of *campagi* [pontifical sandals], gloves, tunic, dalmatic, and mitre, the pastoral staff, and the daily use of the ring. Moreover, in that venerable monastery itself and in its cells, we forbid any bishop or priest of any church, except the Roman pontiff, to presume to exercise any authority of excommunication, interdict, or summons to synod; so that, unless invited by the abbot or prior of the place, he may not dare to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there.

The brethren of the monastery itself and of its cells may, without anyone’s opposition, receive for conversion clerics of any order or laypersons from any bishopric who flee from the secular world and come free and absolved. Likewise they may, without prohibition from any secular or ecclesiastical authority, judge persons subject to their monasteries, both monks and nuns. The brethren established in cells within cities may also, whenever they wish, ring the bells for divine offices, open the church doors, and admit the people of God both into the monastery itself and into its cells to hear God’s word and confess their sins; and no bishop, except in the case of a general interdict of the whole city or parish, may forbid this.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, and the consecration of monks or clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. You shall administer baptism, the oil of the sick, and visitations in your towns or villages belonging to you in full right, through your own clerics.

We also grant to you, son Abbot, and to your successors the cell of Palladium as a hospice in perpetuity, so that you may appoint there whomever you wish from your community. If it should please the Roman pontiff to promote such a person to be abbot, nevertheless we decree that he shall remain wholly under your direction as a monk of your community. We likewise remit to your ship, if one should arrive, the payment which our officials customarily exact at Ostia or Porto from ships.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any artifice of fraud or force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the majority of brethren of sounder counsel, shall provide to be elected from your community—or from another, if a suitable person cannot be found there—according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected shall come to the Roman pontiff to be consecrated.

Furthermore, opposing the avarice and wickedness of persons both present and future, we forbid by apostolic authority all riots, called *laevae*, and all plunderings committed upon anyone’s death or election. We decree also that the burial-place of your house and your monasteries shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken always being preserved.

Moreover, since free burial has been granted to you by the Apostolic See both in head and members, adhering to the precedents of our predecessors Alexander, Innocent, and the said Clement, we have thought fit to grant to you and your brethren, present and future, that whenever you go out in procession for the bodies of the dead, you may, by our permission and according to the custom of the land, freely carry the cross, incense, and holy water, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal.

Following the example of our father and predecessor Clement, we also grant leave to you and your lawful successors that, if anyone violently takes away the possessions or goods of your monastery and its cells, and after you have three times invited the bishops of those persons they wholly refuse to do justice in the matter, you may, after warning the same robbers a second or third time, pronounce against them the canonical sentence of excommunication.

We confirm by apostolic authority to you and to the same monastery the things which your monastery is known to have possessed peaceably and in good faith for the past forty years, so that you may never at any time be hindered or in any way molested concerning them.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and inviolate, and shall in every way benefit the purposes for whose governance and support they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being reserved.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly and rashly attempt in future to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his presumption by due satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Saint-Germain, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 1600B] and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

[Col. 1599] It has seemed proper to publish here also the following letters, although they were not issued in the eleventh year, because they concern the case treated in letter 56 of this book. For the same reason, we have added the letters of Honorius II and III and the letter of Cardinal Romanus concerning the settlement between the bishop of Meaux and the abbess of Jouarre; after these there follow again several letters of Innocent III and Alexander III concerning the same subject.

## I. TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS AND THE ABBOT OF LAGNY. Against the Abbess of Jouarre.

[Col. 1599B]

[Note: [Col. 1599] See below, letter 8, to the bishop-elect of Châlons and the abbot of Trois-Fontaines.] At the complaint of our venerable brother the bishop of Meaux, it has been made known to us that Hugh, priest of Saint Peter of Jouarre, although he received the care of souls from the bishop’s predecessor and is bound to answer to him in this matter, nevertheless, when summoned by him to come into his presence, refused; and, upon hearing his command, immediately broke out into an appeal, which, although a year has now elapsed, he has not pursued either personally or through another.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters to compel the same priest, ecclesiastical censure being applied and appeal set aside, to render the bishop the satisfaction due in this matter and thereafter to obey his commands, as he is bound to do. If witnesses who are named withdraw themselves through favour, hatred, or fear, compel them, ecclesiastical coercion being applied and appeal set aside, to bear testimony to the truth; notwithstanding any letters which may appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See and which would prejudice truth and justice. If both of you cannot be present for the execution of these matters, you, brother Bishop, shall nevertheless carry them out.

Given at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

## III. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

As our venerable brother the bishop of Meaux, appearing in our presence, showed us by his complaint, the abbess of Jouarre refuses to render him the obedience due to him; and the clerics and people of the same village likewise refuse to obey him as their bishop. Therefore, lest their disobedience, if it remains uncorrected, furnish them an incentive to wrongdoing, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to compel, through ecclesiastical coercion, appeal being excluded and justice being observed, the aforesaid abbess, clerics, and laypeople to render the said bishop the satisfaction due to him in this matter, and thereafter to show him obedience and honour as their bishop, as they are bound to do.

But the witnesses, etc.

Given as in the other letter.

## III. TO OUR BELOVED SONS, THE ABBOTS OF LONGPONT IN THE DIOCESE OF SOISSONS AND OF SAINT-JUST IN THE DIOCESE OF BEAUVAIS, AND MASTER G., ARCHDEACON OF SOISSONS.  
(At Anagni, the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.)

In our presence, the beloved son, procurator of our venerable brother the bishop of Meaux, stated before us [Col. 1600D] that, since the monastery of Jouarre had, from the time of its foundation, been subject to the Church of Meaux—such that the bishop of Meaux had customarily exercised episcopal jurisdiction both in the blessing and receiving of the abbess’s obedience, in the consecration of altars and churches, the veiling of virgins, ordination of clerics, procurations, the imposition of penances for graver crimes, and other matters in that monastery itself and the town of Jouarre—the abbess now presiding over the monastery, denying him the obedience, reverence, and procurations due to him and rendered to his predecessors, had also withdrawn the priest, clerics, and laity of the town of Jouarre [Col. 1601A] from his obedience.

When, because of this, the same bishop had sent us his complaint, we entrusted the matter for decision to our venerable brother the bishop of Paris and our beloved son the abbot of Lagny. Before them, when he had sought the remedy of restitution concerning the abbess’s obedience and the jurisdiction which his predecessors had exercised in the monastery and town of Jouarre, the procurator of the monastery and of the people of the aforesaid town made many allegations against him. Since the judges deemed these frivolous, as indeed they were, that procurator appealed to our hearing. The judges, however, by no means deferring to this dilatory appeal—especially since, by our letters, the parties had been deprived of recourse to appeal—pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the abbess [Col. 1601B] and of interdict against both the clergy and people of the town of Jouarre, and subsequently ordered both sentences to be published in neighboring churches.

But neither did the abbess regard herself as excommunicated, nor did the clergy and people observe the sentence of interdict. Yet, since the judges began to summon them, certain neighboring persons, through messengers sent to the Apostolic See, obtained letters in a specified form addressed to our venerable brother the then bishop-elect of Châlons and our beloved son the abbot of Trois-Fontaines [Note: [Col. 1601D] See the chapter *Ex parte*, *On Privileges*, below, no. VIII.]. Although the monastery’s party had proved none of the exceptions which it had raised before us, they relaxed the aforesaid sentence, setting the parties a fixed date upon which they were to appear before us [Col. 1601C].

Accordingly, the bishop’s procurator requested, on behalf of the said bishop, that before all else the benefit of restitution be granted him, since he ought not to enter into the cause while despoiled; and that the abbess, clerics, and laypeople of the town of Jouarre be canonically punished because they had not observed the sentence pronounced against them.

The procurator of the other party, on the contrary, alleged that the monastery of Jouarre enjoys full liberty, and that the abbess possesses both spiritual and temporal jurisdiction in the town of Jouarre, as the privileges granted to the monastery of Jouarre by our predecessors more fully demonstrate. The aforesaid bishop, not ignorant of those privileges, had nevertheless seriously harassed the monastery and town of Jouarre by letters obtained against them and addressed to the aforesaid judges. When that party had appeared before them through its own procurator [Col. 1601D], it did not join issue but rather objected against them, alleging its liberty and the right of the Apostolic See. It added that, when our venerable brother the bishop of Ostia, then legate of the Apostolic See, had learned from those privileges of our right and of the monastery’s exemption, he blessed the abbess elected by the nuns and received from her, for us and the Roman Church, her profession and the customary oath.

But when the delegated judges and their assessors had denied the abbess and … the requested adjournment for producing the privileges of liberty, their procurator appealed to the Apostolic See, objecting against the delegated judges [Col. 1602A] that, since the aforesaid bishop of Paris had raised a similar question against our beloved son the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève [Note: [Col. 1602D] See Book V, Letter 100.], he was legally suspect to them, because it seemed scarcely credible that he would pronounce a different judgment from that which he would wish to be rendered in a similar case in his own favor. Furthermore, since he wished to issue an interlocutory ruling without his fellow judge, although the abbess’s party requested that the latter be awaited, and since by this he had incurred with them the taint of surreption and brought his colleague into suspicion—whom he asserted would do whatever he himself wished—and since they made no mention of the privileges of the Apostolic See, though the monastery defended its liberty by those privileges, it was not bound to answer the aforesaid letters.

Nevertheless, the judges, giving no heed either to the appeal to us which had been entered or to the objections raised [Col. 1602B], pronounced sentences of excommunication against the abbess and of interdict against the clergy and people.

Therefore, when the messengers of the Church of Jouarre appeared before us and showed us an apostolic privilege establishing that the monastery of Jouarre specially belonged to the Roman Church, and since no adequate representative appeared for the other party, although he had been awaited for a considerable time—even though a certain simple messenger of the aforesaid bishop of Paris and his fellow judge had presented letters to us—we considered that the privilege granted to the Church of Jouarre should be renewed. This renewal, however, was not to add any right to it beyond that acquired by the privileges of our predecessors; by it we intended not to grant it a new right [Col. 1602C], but rather to preserve its ancient right.

Since, however, we could not be fully satisfied concerning the aforesaid objections, we instructed the aforesaid bishop of Châlons and abbot of Trois-Fontaines that, if the party of the Church of Jouarre persisted before them in proving those or other objections concerning the said sentences, they should, after summoning the parties, hear what was alleged on either side. If it were established that those sentences had been pronounced after an appeal to us had been lawfully entered, they were to declare, without impediment from an appeal, that the sentences had no force. But if they had otherwise been pronounced less reasonably, they were to revoke them as justice required. Otherwise, since they had been issued solely on account of contumacy, they were to receive from the abbess and from the others from whom they saw fit to demand it [Col. 1602D] sworn security that, concerning these matters, they would submit to the law at the Apostolic See’s command; and thus they were to relax the said sentences. For greater caution, they were to do the same if the abbess, avoiding the turmoil of litigation, should refrain from proving her objections.

Moreover, since we did not wish others lightly to judge concerning the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, we instructed the same persons that, if the bishop of Meaux wished to test his own right, they should appoint the parties a suitable date upon which they should appear before us in person or through suitable procurators. Accordingly, since the abbess, avoiding the tumult of judicial proceedings, had not wished to prove the objections she had raised, the judges, proceeding in accordance with the apostolic mandate, relaxed the aforesaid sentences.

Since, therefore, for this reason we ordered the parties to be sent into our presence, because we did not wish the privileges of the Apostolic See to be judged by others, and since by privileges not possession but rather ownership is demonstrated, the monastery’s procurator asserted that he had come to litigate concerning ownership and was not bound to answer concerning the article of restitution [Col. 1603A]. Furthermore, after a certain market had been confirmed to the monastery of Jouarre by the Apostolic See, the same bishop had rashly despoiled it, when, under penalty of excommunication, he forbade anyone thereafter to frequent it as had been customary; thus he inflicted upon the Church of Jouarre no slight losses and damages. The same bishop also inflicted no slight losses and damages upon certain persons of the Church of Jouarre [Col. 1603B]. The same bishop exacted from certain persons of the Church of Jouarre [probably “men, whom”]—whom he had presumed, by his own rashness, to absolve—an oath, to the prejudice of the monastery, that during the interdict they would henceforth not return to Jouarre.

We, therefore, considering that, although we had not commanded but had in some manner forbidden others to judge concerning the privileges of our predecessors, wishing to reserve judgment concerning them to ourselves, nevertheless we had added that, if the aforesaid bishop perhaps wished to test his own right, a date should be appointed for the parties to appear before us; and that the expression “right” extends not only to ownership but also to possession, command your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 1603C] that, once issue has been joined before us both concerning the bishop’s despoiling and concerning obstruction of jurisdiction, you shall hear and receive what is alleged concerning the foregoing, excluding appeal; you shall publish and lawfully examine both documents and witnesses’ depositions; and, if the parties consent, you shall proceed to judgment.

Otherwise, take care to remit the sufficiently instructed cause to us, appointing the parties a suitable date upon which they are to appear before us, in person or through suitable representatives, to receive judgment. If witnesses who have been named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, compel them, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to bear testimony to the truth. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See shall obstruct this, except with the consent of the parties [Col. 1603D]. If not all of you can be present to carry this out, nevertheless two of you shall execute it.

Given at Anagni, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## IV. TO THE BELOVED SONS THE DEAN OF SAINT THOMAS OF CRISPIACUM, IN THE DIOCESE OF SENLIS, GERMUNDUS, CANON OF SOISSONS, AND MASTER GIRARD OF SAINT-DENIS, CANON OF NOYON

Formerly, when litigation had been lawfully joined in our court between the procurators of our venerable brother the bishop of Meaux and our beloved daughter in Christ the abbess of Jouarre, both concerning the obedience which the said bishop complained had been withdrawn from him by the abbess [Col. 1604A] in the consecration of altars, dedication of churches, veiling of virgins, ordination of clerics, provision of procurations, imposition of penances for graver crimes, and other matters which the bishop of Meaux had customarily exercised in the monastery and town of Jouarre, and concerning obstruction of jurisdiction, with respect to which the abbess complained that serious injuries and losses had been inflicted upon her and her monastery by the bishop, we considered that examination of this matter should be entrusted to our beloved sons the abbots of Longpont and Saint-Just and Master G., archdeacon of Soissons.

After hearing the admissions, receiving witnesses, and considering the allegations, they remitted the sufficiently instructed cause, with transcripts of certain instruments, to our examination, appointing the parties [Col. 1604B] a suitable date upon which they were to appear before us to receive judgment. Therefore, when the parties appeared before us, after we had been sufficiently informed concerning the merits of the cause, by counsel of our brethren we adjudged that obedience in the aforesaid matters should be restored to the bishop, without prejudice to the question of ownership. We excepted only those matters concerning which he asserted that obedience had been withdrawn from him by the clergy and people of the town of Jouarre; with respect to these we absolved the abbess, as regards the possessory action, from the bishop’s claim. We nevertheless absolved that bishop concerning obstruction of jurisdiction, for which the abbess had sued him for restitution of damages.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, causing the aforesaid judgment [Col. 1604C] to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, after the said bishop has been restored, you shall hear what is alleged before you concerning the right of ownership and shall faithfully remit the sufficiently examined cause to our hearing, to be concluded by the judgment of our decision. But if the aforesaid bishop should not wish, within a month after restitution has been made to him, to answer before you concerning the petitory action, then punish him for contumacy and restore the abbess to possession of liberty in the aforesaid matters. The witnesses who shall be named, etc. No letters, etc. If not all of you, etc., nevertheless two of you, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, shall carry this out [Col. 1604D].

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

## V. TO THE BELOVED SONS THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-JUST, IN THE DIOCESE OF BEAUVAIS, AND OF LONGPONT, AND G., ARCHDEACON OF SOISSONS

Our venerable brother the bishop of Meaux informed us that, whereas we had entrusted to you in a specified form the cause pending between him, on one side, and the abbess, clergy, and people of Jouarre in the diocese of Meaux, on the other, concerning obedience, procurations, and other matters which the bishop claimed belonged to him by diocesan right in the monastery of that place and in the town of Jouarre, [Col. 1605A] you had issued an interlocutory judgment that the said bishop could not proceed against the clergy and people by those letters.

Accordingly, the same bishop humbly petitioned that you be instructed by us to hear him both against the abbess and against the said clergy and people, and, after proper inquiry, to proceed in the aforesaid cause according to the tenor of our earlier mandate. Since our beloved son Master P., procurator of the clergy and people of Jouarre, opposed this on the other side, we gave them our beloved son A., subdeacon and chaplain, as auditor.

In his presence, the same master alleged that, although the bishop had obtained apostolic letters against the abbess, clergy, and people of Jouarre, without any mention whatsoever of the liberties or privileges [Col. 1605B] granted them by the Apostolic See—of which the bishop himself was not ignorant—he wished, on the authority of those letters, to proceed against them. On account of alleged contumacy he caused sentences of excommunication and interdict to be pronounced against them after an appeal to us had lawfully been entered. Subsequently, when our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons and our beloved son the abbot of Trois-Fontaines, by apostolic authority, relaxed those sentences, they appointed the parties a fixed date, by mandate of the Apostolic See, upon which they were to appear before us.

When the procurators of both parties had appeared before us on the appointed date, the bishop’s procurator, proceeding against the abbess, made no allegation at all against the clergy and [Col. 1605C] people. Therefore he ought not again to be admitted to revive against the clergy and people the question which he had once omitted.

Since, however, we could not be fully satisfied concerning the foregoing, by apostolic letters and with the common consent of the parties we command you that, after proper inquiry, you proceed according to the tenor of the commission entrusted to you against the abbess as well as the clergy and people of Jouarre.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of March, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

## VI. LETTER OF HONORIUS III CONCERNING THE SAME CONTROVERSY

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the archdeacon and cantor of Saint Peter’s and the treasurer of Saint Stephen’s at Troyes, greeting and [Col. 1605D] apostolic blessing.

On behalf of our venerable brother the bishop of Meaux, humble petition has been made to us that, since the abbess who now presides over the monastery of Jouarre was blessed by our special mandate, and since what we caused to be done in this matter ought not to prejudice him, we should cause full justice to be rendered to him concerning the right of blessing abbesses to be elected henceforth in the monastery of Jouarre.

Therefore, acceding to the petition of the same bishop, and unwilling that prejudice should be generated against him by the blessing conferred by our authority, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, with the consent of the procurators of both parties, that, after summoning the parties [Col. 1606A], you hear the cause and, excluding appeal, bring it to its due conclusion; causing what you decree to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. The witnesses, etc. If not all of you, etc., nevertheless two of you shall carry this out.

Given at Viterbo, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

## VII. SETTLEMENT MADE BETWEEN THE BISHOP OF MEAUX AND THE CHURCH OF JOUARRE

Romanus, by divine mercy cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, legate of the Apostolic See, to all who shall see the present document: greeting in the Lord and the affection of sincere love.

Let all of you know that, when a dispute had arisen between the venerable father Peter, bishop of Meaux, on one side, and the beloved in Christ abbess and convent, clergy and people of Jouarre, on the other, concerning the subjection of that monastery and of the same clergy and people, the bishop submitted the following written petition against them in law [Col. 1606B]:

> “The bishop of Meaux demands of the abbess and convent of Jouarre that they obey him as their bishop in conducting visitations, correcting offences, hearing civil, spiritual, and criminal causes whose cognizance belongs to the diocesan bishop as ecclesiastical judge, deciding those causes, and all matters pertaining to their cognizance and decision—namely, appearing upon citations, receiving the assignment of days, and other matters pertaining to cognizance and decision—and in observing his lawful commands and statutes; in holding processions for the bishop of Meaux when, after his consecration, he first comes to their church; and in all other matters belonging to episcopal right.

> “He also demands that the abbess promise him obedience in all the aforesaid matters, except those in whose possession the same bishop is and whose possession has been adjudged to him by authority of the lord pope: namely, the consecration of altars, dedication of churches, veiling of virgins, ordination of clerics, provision of procurations, and imposition of penances for graver crimes. He does not presently proceed concerning these, because he is in possession of them.

> “The same bishop also demands that they not prevent him henceforth from exercising in the clergy and people of Jouarre every jurisdiction which a diocesan bishop can exercise over his subjects. The bishop of Meaux demands of the clergy of Jouarre that they obey him as their bishop in conducting visitations, correcting offences, hearing civil and criminal causes whose cognizance belongs to the diocesan bishop as ecclesiastical judge, deciding those causes, and matters pertaining to their cognizance and decision—namely, appearing upon citations, receiving assignments of days, and the other matters pertaining to their cognizance and decision [Col. 1607A] and to their execution—and in observing his lawful commands and statutes and in all other matters belonging to episcopal right, excepting that in whose possession the same bishop is, namely their ordination.

> “The bishop of Meaux demands of the people of Jouarre that they obey him as their bishop in correcting all offences whose correction belongs to the diocesan bishop as ecclesiastical judge; in hearing civil, spiritual, and criminal causes whose cognizance belongs to the diocesan bishop as ecclesiastical judge; in deciding those causes and matters pertaining to their cognizance and decision, namely appearing upon citations [Col. 1607B], receiving the assignment of days, and other matters pertaining to cognizance and decision; that they observe sentences of excommunication and interdict pronounced against them by him; and that they obey him in all other matters belonging to episcopal right. Whatever the same bishop demands of the abbess and convent and the clergy and people of Jouarre, he demands without prejudice to his right to add, diminish, or alter.”

To these demands the procurator of the abbess and convent, clergy, and people of Jouarre answered as follows:

> “The abbess and convent say that the monastery of Jouarre is exempt and subject immediately to the lord pope in all things, and that ownership of all ecclesiastical jurisdiction in the monastery of Jouarre belongs immediately to the lord pope, without intermediary; and that the monastery has enjoyed this liberty from the most ancient time, as we shall prove, if necessary, by privileges, witnesses, and documents.

> “Therefore, the abbess and convent say that they are not bound to obey the bishop of Meaux in conducting visitations, or in anything connected with conducting visitation; in correcting offences; in hearing civil, spiritual, or criminal causes; or in deciding those causes. Nor are they bound to appear upon his citations, receive assignments of days, observe his commands or statutes, hold a procession for him when he first comes after his consecration to the church of Jouarre, or otherwise obey him in any matters pertaining to episcopal right. Likewise, the abbess is not bound to promise him obedience in the foregoing, or in any one of the foregoing, or in any thing in the world [Col. 1607D].

> “As to the bishop’s assertion that he is in possession regarding the imposition of penances for graver crimes, the abbess and convent deny that he is in possession. Regarding the other articles in whose possession the bishop says that he is, they say that he has no right of ownership in them. The abbess and convent also say that all ecclesiastical and secular jurisdiction over the clergy and people of Jouarre belongs to the abbess.

> “The clergy of Jouarre say that they are not bound to obey the bishop of Meaux in conducting visitations, correcting offences, hearing civil, spiritual [Col. 1608A], or criminal causes whose cognizance is said to belong to the diocesan bishop as ecclesiastical judge, deciding those causes, appearing on his citations, accepting assignments of days, observing his commands, or obeying him in any respect.

> “The people of Jouarre say that all ecclesiastical and secular jurisdiction over the people of Jouarre belongs to the abbess of Jouarre. Therefore they answer on their own behalf the same things that the clergy answer on theirs: that in no respect are they bound to obey the bishop of Meaux. The abbess and convent, clergy, and people of Jouarre make all these answers without prejudice to the privileges of the lord pope, the right of the Roman Church, and the right to add, diminish, correct, and alter.”

After litigation concerning these matters had continued for a long time before judges delegated by the Apostolic See [Col. 1608B], at last both parties, both concerning the matters over which the dispute had existed and all other matters which could in any way, by reason of ownership or possession, pertain to episcopal right under diocesan law, common law, or any other law whatsoever, submitted themselves to our judgment, decision, or ordinance under these forms:

> To all who shall inspect these present letters, Peter, by God’s grace bishop of Meaux, greeting in the Lord.
>
> Let all of you know that, whereas a question had arisen between us, on one side, and the abbess and convent, clergy and people of Jouarre, on the other, concerning the subjection of that monastery and the same clergy and people, in both petitory and possessory proceedings, we maintained that the monastery, together with the clergy and people, was subject to us by full right [Col. 1608C], and that every right of subjection belonged, under diocesan law, to us and our successors as diocesan bishops; and that we might freely receive procuration, conduct visitation and correction, and exercise all episcopal rights in that monastery, clergy, and people of Jouarre. The abbess and convent denied this and maintained that the monastery, clergy, and people of Jouarre belonged immediately, without intermediary, to the right and ownership of the Roman Church.
>
> Concerning the foregoing and all other matters which could pertain to episcopal right, with the consent of our dean, archdeacons, and chapter, we have submitted ourselves to the judgment, decision, or ordinance of the venerable [father] Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo [Col. 1608D], legate of the Apostolic See, consenting to him as legate and judge, and promising that we shall observe his judgment, decision, or ordinance forever and never at any time act contrary to it; renouncing all judges, commissions, proceedings, and acts which belonged or might belong to us in this cause.
>
> In testimony whereof, and for the greater confirmation of all the foregoing, we have caused these letters, drawn up for that purpose, to be confirmed by our seal.
>
> Done at Meaux in the year of the Lord 1225, in the month of October.

> To all who shall inspect these present letters, the dean, the archdeacons of Brie and Meaux, and the whole chapter of the Church of Meaux, greeting in the Lord.
>
> Let all of you know that we have inspected letters sealed with the seal of our venerable … [Col. 1609A], containing the following form: “PETER, by God’s grace bishop of Meaux,” etc., as set out above. Having carefully examined the tenor of the aforesaid letters, we approved and ratified the act of our said bishop in this matter, giving our assent to all the foregoing. In evidence thereof, we have caused our seals to be appended to these present letters.
>
> Done at Meaux in the year of the Lord 1225, in the month of October.

> To all who shall inspect these present letters, the abbess and convent, clergy and people of Jouarre, greeting in the Lord.
>
> Let all of you know that, whereas a question had arisen between us, on one side, and the venerable father Peter, bishop of Meaux, on the other, concerning our subjection in both petitory [Col. 1609B] and possessory proceedings, the same bishop maintained that the monastery of Jouarre and ourselves were subject to him by full right, and that every right of succession belonged to him and his successors as diocesan bishops under diocesan law; and that he could freely receive procuration, conduct visitation and correction, and exercise all episcopal rights in that monastery and over us. Denying this, we maintained that the said monastery of Jouarre belonged immediately, without intermediary, to the right and ownership of the Roman Church.
>
> Concerning the foregoing and all other matters which could pertain to episcopal right, we have submitted ourselves to the judgment, decision, or ordinance of the venerable father Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, legate of the Apostolic See, consenting to him as legate and judge [Col. 1609C], and promising that we shall observe his judgment, decision, or ordinance forever and never at any time act contrary to it; renouncing all judges, commissions, proceedings, and acts which belonged or might belong to us in this cause.
>
> In testimony whereof, and for the greater confirmation of all the foregoing, we, the abbess and convent, have caused these letters, drawn up for that purpose, to be confirmed by our seals. We, the clergy and people, having no seal of our own, wish full credit to be given to the seals of the abbess and convent.
>
> Done at Meaux in the year of the Lord 1225, in the month of October.

But we, after carefully hearing the arguments of both parties, examining the privileges of the monastery of Jouarre [Col. 1609D], and holding careful deliberation on the matter with prudent men, pronounce, decide, and ordain that the abbess and convent of the monastery of Jouarre shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, blessings of nuns, and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to orders from the said bishop of Meaux and his successors, and from no others, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to supply these things freely and without difficulty. Otherwise, they may freely approach whichever Catholic bishop they choose, who may lawfully provide what they request.

Whenever it happens that the bishop of Meaux is summoned by the abbess and convent to perform these acts [Col. 1610A], the said bishop shall be honorably provided for, since, according to the Apostle, no one is bound to serve as a soldier at his own expense. Furthermore, the abbess may freely be consecrated by whichever bishop she prefers, without profession or promise of any obedience.

In all other matters, we pronounce, decide, and ordain that the said monastery of Jouarre, together with the whole clergy and people of the town and parish of Jouarre subject to it, is wholly free and exempt from every episcopal right and jurisdiction and from every kind of subjection to the Church of Meaux. Thus, in the said monastery, clergy, and people, or in any persons of the monastery, town, and parish of Jouarre, the said bishop, Church of Meaux, or any other person of the Church of Meaux may not in any way claim either the procuration once adjudged to that bishop by the Apostolic See [Col. 1610B] or anything else whatsoever apart from the foregoing, saving the two modii which the bishop possesses in the grange of Trocy, belonging to the Church of Jouarre, and the wax due to the treasurer of Meaux.

We further ordain that the said abbess and convent shall annually pay to the said bishop and his successors in perpetuity, at Malleus before the Purification of Blessed Mary, eighteen modii of tithe grain by the measure of Meaux, two parts of winter grain (*hibernagium*), and a third part of oats. If the tithe of that town is insufficient for payment of the said grain, the remainder shall be paid within the said period at Trocy from the tithe which the Church of Jouarre possesses there. Thus, if the abbess and convent of Jouarre can lawfully obtain such grain [Col. 1610C] from any tithes [probably “from any tithe-holders”] of the diocese of Meaux, the bishop shall be bound to give his assent to the contract, and, accepting the grain thus acquired, shall be content with that alone, provided it is worth as much to him as it would be worth in the places noted above. In tithes which are held as a fief of the bishop, however, he shall not be bound to give his consent if he wishes to redeem them; in these the bishop shall have preference.

The parties have ratified and expressly consented to this ordinance. Wishing that knowledge of this ordinance should reach posterity and that it be inviolably observed in future times [Col. 1610D], we have caused this present document, drawn up for that purpose, to be confirmed by our seal.

Done at Meaux, in the year of the Lord 1225, in the month of November, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Honorius III.

Romanus, by divine mercy cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, legate of the Apostolic See, to all who shall inspect these present letters, greeting in the Lord. Let all of you know that we made, after prudent deliberation, a certain ordinance between the venerable father the bishop of Meaux and the abbess and convent, clergy and people of Jouarre. Having reduced it to writing and had it approved by the parties, we caused it to be confirmed by the protection of our seal. But before pronouncing it, we expressly retained to ourselves, by our authority and with the common consent of the parties, free power to declare and interpret anything found doubtful or obscure in the same ordinance [Col. 1611A].

Done at Paris in the year of the Lord 1225, on the second day before the Nones of November.

## VIII. LETTER OF INNOCENT III TO THE BISHOP-ELECT OF CHÂLONS AND THE ABBOT OF TROIS-FONTAINES, MENTIONED ABOVE IN LETTER 2, TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS AND THE ABBOT OF LAGNY
[Note: [Col. 1611D] Chapter *Ex parte*, On Privileges.] On behalf of the abbess and sisters of the Church of Jouarre it was reported to our hearing that our venerable brother, the bishop of Meaux [Note: [Col. 1612D] See above, col. 1601.], on the occasion of a certain commission obtained from us by our venerable brother the bishop of Paris and our beloved son the abbot of Lagny—in which no mention was made of their privileges—began seriously to harass them. [Col. 1611B] Those privileges declare that they, their church, clergy, and the people of Jouarre belong directly, without intermediary, to the Apostolic See; nor was he unaware of them. He demanded that they, together with the clergy and people of the town of Jouarre, who under the privileges of the Apostolic See enjoy a like liberty, render him obedience and complete subjection. And below: But when the judges and their assessors grievously oppressed them, they had recourse to the benefit of appeal. And below: Yet those judges, paying no heed whatever to the appeal and showing no compassion for the weakness of their sex, pronounced sentences of excommunication against the abbess [and convent], and of interdict against the clergy and people of the town of Jouarre. Indeed, when the representatives of the Church of Jouarre recounted before us the foregoing [Col. 1611C] and many other matters, by which, they said, they and their people had been burdened contrary to the liberty granted them, they showed us an apostolic privilege by which it was clear that the Church of Jouarre belonged in a special manner to the Roman Church. We, however, having detained them for a longer time because of the aforesaid appeal, since at last no suitable respondent appeared to defend the opposing party—although afterwards a certain mere messenger presented, concerning this matter, letters of the aforesaid bishop of Paris and abbot of Lagny—we deemed it proper to renew the privilege of the Apostolic See granted to the Church of Jouarre. Yet this is so that, through its renewal, no greater right may accrue to that church [Col. 1611D] than it obtained through the privileges of our predecessors; for by this we wish not to grant it something new, but to preserve its ancient right.

## IX. Letter of Honorius II concerning the subjection of the monasteries of Rebais and Jouarre

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BURCHARD, bishop of Meaux, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1612A] Established, by the Lord’s disposition, in the exalted watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought, by the duty laid upon us, to love our brother bishops and preserve for the churches entrusted to them by God their due right. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ Burchard, bishop of the Church of Meaux, the care of which has been entrusted to you by God, we beneficially decree that all persons, clerics as well as laypeople, dwelling in the towns of Rebais and Jouarre shall be subject to the Church of Meaux by parochial right, and that those things which belong to parochial right from them shall be preserved freely and unimpaired for you and your successors. We also decree that the abbot of Rebais and the abbess of Jouarre shall render canonical obedience to you and your successors. Their blessing likewise, just as it is shown to have been conferred hitherto by your predecessors, shall henceforth be conferred by you and your successors. The promotion of monks to ecclesiastical orders shall also be administered by the bishop of Meaux, provided that he is willing to confer them freely and without misconduct, and enjoys the favor of the Apostolic See. But should anyone—God forbid!—knowingly attempt to oppose this our decree, let him incur peril to his rank and office, unless he corrects his presumption through fitting satisfaction.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of May [15 April].

## X. Letter of Alexander III confirming the foregoing letters of Honorius II

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1612C] brother STEPHEN, bishop of Meaux, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

“Established in the exalted watchtower of the Apostolic See,” etc., as in that of Honorius, through “Therefore, dearest brother in Christ Stephen, bishop of the Church of Meaux, the care of which has been entrusted to you by God”: making beneficial provision, after the example of our father and predecessor Pope Honorius of holy memory, we decree that all persons, clerics as well as laypeople, dwelling in the towns of Rebais and Jouarre shall be subject to the Church of Meaux by parochial right, etc., as in that of Honorius, through: But should anyone presume to act against this document of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his rashness by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and rank, and become estranged from the most sacred [Col. 1612D] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon those who observe these things may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the supreme Judge, find the joys of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Tours in the year 1163.

## ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF.

SIXTH BOOK OF THE REGISTERS, OR LETTERS.—Sixth year of the pontificate, A.D. 1203.

I. — To John, prior, and the brethren living the regular life near the cave of Saint Benedict. — He grants them six pounds of the coinage from the annual rent of the castle of Porciano. (24 February.) 9

II. — To the prior of Osene. — Concerning the salutary penance to be imposed upon one who has committed both incest and adultery. (24 February.) 10

III. — To the abbot of Saint Lupus of Troyes and his brethren. — He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter and confirms their rights and privileges. (20 February.) 11

IV. — To the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Hungary. — Since King Henry is about to depart for the holy war, they are to ensure that the peoples render fidelity to Ladislaus, his son. (25 February.) 13

V. — To the bishop of Ourense. — He approves the agreement entered into between that bishop and the archbishop of Compostela. (15 February.) 14

VI. — To the same. — He confirms the judgment delivered by apostolic delegates in the dispute between the monastery of Cella Nova and the bishop of Oviedo. (14 February.) 15

VII. — To H., illustrious king of the Hungarians. — Those promoted to provostships which are immediately subject to the Apostolic See in spiritual matters are to come to the Apostolic See within a year. (19 February.) 15

VIII. — To the king of the Hungarians. — He promises, as the king of the Hungarians is to take the cross, that he will take care that no disturbances or disputes arise during his absence. (19 February.) 16

IX. — To the bishops of Chalon and Senlis, and the abbot of Trois-Fontaines. — He entrusts to them the examination of the election of Philip, bishop of Beauvais, as archbishop of Reims. (25 February.) 16

X. — To Adelfonso, bishop of Ourense, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity. — He is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. Privileges and possessions are confirmed. (25 February.) 18

XI. — To the bishop and chapter of Hildesheim. — He admonishes and commands them to receive Herman the deacon as a canon. (24 February.) 19

XII. — To Maximus, clerk. — He permits him to receive something from the revenues of the church of Saint Michael of Oliveto. (25 February.) 20

XIII. — To the bishop of Modena. — He commands that the people of Cremona, because of the estates of Guastalla and Luzzara concerning which they had brought suit against the monastery of Saint Sixtus of Cremona, be publicly declared excommunicate; that the city of Cremona be placed under ecclesiastical interdict; and that contumacious priests be removed from offices and benefices. (28 February.) 21

XIV. — To the countess of Vermandois. — He graciously requests from her, who possessed the right of patronage, one prebend upon its first vacancy, which he recognizes as granted by favour, although she may dispose of it by her own authority. 22

XV. — To the bishop of Polignano. — He commands him to inquire concerning a certain stipulation, whether it is contrary to the canons. (4 March.) 22

XVI. — To the archbishops, bishops, prelates of churches, and all clergy established throughout Sardinia. — He grants that they shall not be compelled, by letters of the Apostolic See, to answer outside Sardinia unless provision is otherwise made. (11 March.) 23

XVII. — To the archbishops and bishops established in Sardinia. — He orders them publicly to declare excommunicate the murderers of the bishop of Plavac and of others, and not to allow them to remain in Sardinia. (10 March.) 23

XVIII. — To the archbishop of Pisa and his suffragans. — He announces that he has received the judge of Torres under the protection of the Apostolic See. (10 March.) 24

XIX. — To the abbot of Dol; E., the pope’s subdeacon; and the prior of Leproso. — Although the bishop of Nevers has died, they are to cause a prebend in the church of Nevers to be assigned to P., nephew of the archbishop of Torres, according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate on this matter addressed to the said bishop of Nevers. (11 March.) 25

XX. — To the same. — On a similar matter, in favour of L. in the church of Liniac. 25

XXI. — To the abbot and brethren of Saint Mary outside the gate at Faenza. — They are received under protection; their privileges are confirmed. (11 March.) 26

XXII. — To the same. — He commands that the goods of the monastery which have been granted in emphyteusis revert to the monastery in accordance with the laws of emphyteusis. (1 March.) 27

XXIII. — To the abbot and monks of Saint Germanus of Auxerre. — He permits them, during an interdict, to bury deceased brethren with certain honours. (21 March.) 27

XXIV. — To the nobleman W. Meganippanus of Serbia. — He admonishes him to return to the Catholic faith and to show, in the pope’s stead, obedience and reverence to the archbishop of Kalocsa. (22 March.) 28

XXV. — To the archbishop of Kalocsa. — On the same matter. (22 March.) 29

XXVI. — To the prior of Saint Gregory of Spoleto. — He commands that what had been taken from L. and his brethren on suspicion of theft be restored to them. 29

XXVII. — To B., archbishop of Torres. — He entrusts to him the matter of absolving, after the truth has been ascertained, the judge of Torres, who died bearing signs of penitence, and committing him to ecclesiastical burial. 30

XXVIII. — To the nobleman …, judge of Torres. — He forbids him to compel laymen and ecclesiastics of the province of Torres to pay the Pisans whatever they may demand from them. 31

XXIX. — To the noblemen …, judge of Torres, [the judge] of Cagliari, and …, judge of Arborea. — He commands them to ensure the execution of whatever the archbishop of Torres shall order. 31

XXX. — To the noble judges of Sardinia. — They are to render an oath of fidelity, in the pope’s name, to the archbishop of Torres. 32

XXXI. — To the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches, to the noble judges, and to others established in Sardinia. — They are to pay the tribute due to the Roman Church. 32

XXXII. — To the bishop of Paris, the abbot of Saint Geneviève, and their chapters. — Confirmation of the agreement made between them. (27 March.) 33

XXXIII. — To the consuls and people of Genoa. — Concerning payment of tribute. (26 March.) 33

XXXIV. — To the dean of Blessed Mary of the Middle Monastery and the archdeacon of Bourges. — He commands them to do justice to a certain clerk concerning a custom in the diocese of Bourges: no one may sell his patrimony except to someone nearer to him in the line of kinship. (26 March.) 34

XXXV. — To the abbot of Saint Julian and the archdeacon Major of Tours. — By apostolic authority he confirms the sentence given by J., master of the schools of Orléans, papal delegate for this purpose, in the case concerning the election to the priory of Graciac. 34

XXXVI. — To the bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See; and to the abbots of Capembach and Scelde, situated in the dioceses of Cologne and Münster. — They are to see that a suitable man is appointed to the provostship of the Church of Cologne. (9 April.) 36

XXXVII. — To the archbishop of Bourges and the prior of Exoldun. — He is to cause W., subdeacon of Gervasius, deprived of a prebend in the church of Saintes, to be restored under penalty of excommunication. (15 January.) 42

XXXVIII. — To Master Praepositinus, scholastic of Mainz, the spirit of sounder counsel. — He exhorts and commands him to return to good conduct and obey the archbishop of Mainz; otherwise he will be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices. (10 April.) 43

XXXIX. — To the canons and all the clergy and people established in the diocese of Mainz, the spirit of sounder counsel. — He commands them to receive the archbishop of Mainz. (9 April.) 44

XL. — To S., archbishop of Mainz. — He permits him to declare void the acts which the bishop of Worms performed unlawfully in the Church of Mainz. 45

XLI. — To Siffrid, archbishop of Mainz. — He gravely admonishes him to apply himself diligently to his office. (9 April.) 45

XLII. — To the landgrave of Thuringia. — He is received under protection. (11 April.) 46

XLIII. — To the abbot and monks of Bec. — He confirms to them the church of Saint Albinus. (4 May.) 46

XLIV. — To Henry, provost of Saint Peter of Mainz, nephew of the nobleman …, count of Leiningen. — He confirms to him the provostship of Saint Peter of Mainz. (11 May.) 47

XLV. — To the podestàs, consuls, and councillors of Lombardy, present and future. — He threatens them with anathema and other canonical penalties if they harass clergy and churches by exactions and injuries. (16 April.) 47

XLVI. — To the archbishop of Milan; and to the bishops, abbots, priors, provosts, and other prelates of churches established in Lombardy. — He complains that they have not opposed the consuls and other magistrates of Lombardy when they compelled clergy to bear public burdens. 48

XLVII. — To the abbot of Abingdon, the prior of Henley, and Master M., canon of Burlington, in the diocese of Bangor. — He confirms the judgment concerning the betrothal between the daughter of the prince of the Isles and the prince of North Wales. (19 April.) 49

XLVIII. — To P., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, legate of the Apostolic See. — He replies concerning certain articles on which the latter had sought an answer. (21 April.) 50

XLIX. — To the prior and brethren of the church of Saint Saviour of Piller. — He receives them under protection, with an annual tribute. (21 April.) 50

L. — To the bishop of Florence and the abbot of Vallombrosa. — Concerning the transfer of the cathedral church of Arezzo within the walls of that city. (22 April.) 51

LI. — To all Christ’s faithful who shall inspect these letters. — Concerning the penance of those who killed C., bishop of Würzburg. (18 April.) 53

LII. — To the archbishop of Messina, royal familiar. — He praises him for expelling Markward from Sicily and restoring Messina to the fidelity of the Apostolic See and the crown. 54

LIII. — To the same. — He is to receive from all counts and others throughout Sicily the oath called that of the *baiulus* (regent), which is to be rendered to the pope. 55

LIV. — To the noble counts, barons, citizens, and others established in Sicily. — They are to render before the bishop of Messina the oath called that of the *baiulus*. 55

LV. — To the archbishop of Esztergom. — He confirms to him the right of crowning the kings of Hungary and other rights. (5 May.) 56

LVI. — To the archbishop of Esztergom. — Concerning royal provostships. (9 May.) 56

LVII. — To Andrew, archbishop of Acerenza, and his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity. — He raises the church at Matera to cathedral rank and joins it to Acerenza. (7 May.) 57

LVIII. — To the prior of Saint Fridianus of Lucca and Master B., canon of Pisa. — Concerning the rejection of the bishop-elect of Lucca. (14 May.) 57

LIX. — To the archbishop of York. — He confirms to the archbishop of Ragusa benefices in the bishopric of Carlisle. 58

LX. — To W., clerk. — Concerning annual tribute. 59

LXI. — To the prior of Saint Fridianus of Lucca and Master B., canon of Pisa. — On the same subject as above, Letter LVIII. 59

LXII. — To the bishop and chapter of Worcester. — Decree concerning Saint Wulstan, enrolled among the saints. (14 May.) 59

LXIII. — To John, illustrious king of England. — He complains that the king has not yet restored the archbishop of Dublin to favour, and threatens him with the penalty of interdict. (21 May.) 61

LXIV. — To the archbishop of Canterbury and the bishop of Ely. — On the same matter. 62

LXV. — To the archbishop of Sens. — He is to amend and correct in the churches subject to him whatever requires amendment. (21 May.) 62

LXVI. — To the archbishop of Bourges, the bishop of Auxerre, and the abbot of Fontaine-Morigny. — He entrusts to them the case of the people of La Charité, suspected of the stain of heresy. (21 May.) 63

LXVII. — To the abbot and convent of Saint Paul. — He assigns and confirms Monte Porzio, in the Tusculan district, to the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls on the Ostian Way. [Col. 1616] 63

LXVIII. — To the king of the Franks. — He is to make peace with the king of England. (26 May.) 64

LXIX. — To the illustrious king of England. — On the same affair. 66

LXX. — To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established in the kingdom of France. — On the same affair. 66

LXXI. — To Walter, chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily. — He receives him into favour; of the four securities offered by Walter he accepts none, except that Walter shall confirm by deeds what he promised in words, and shall do what serves the right of the Roman Church. 67

LXXII. — To the archbishop of Besançon. — He answers him, as he consults the Apostolic See concerning three articles. (21 May.) 68

LXXIII. — To the archbishop of Rouen. — If the king of England does not restore the bishop of Sées to favour, he is to place under interdict all Normandy within his jurisdiction. (24 May.) 69

LXXIV. — To the bishops of Ely and Worcester. — Having annulled the election of two men to the bishopric of St Davids, he commands them canonically to induce the people of St Davids to hold a new election. (26 May.) 70

LXXV. — To Garcia, bishop of Huesca, and his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity. — By apostolic authority, with their consent, he settles the controversy between him and Gombald, bishop of Lleida, concerning the rights of the Churches of Huesca and Lleida. (27 May.) 70

LXXVI. — To Garcia, bishop of Huesca, and his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity. — He receives him and his church under the protection of Saint Peter, and enumerates the possessions belonging to the Church of Huesca. (26 May.) 78

LXXVII. — To the bishop of Tortosa. — He commands him to restore certain churches to the bishop of Huesca. (25 May.) 79

LXXVIII. — To the bishop of Vercelli. — By apostolic authority he confirms the sentence given by the bishop of Bergamo in the case concerning the church of Sevitio. (23 May.) 80

LXXIX. — To the priors of Wenlock … and Henley, in the dioceses of Hereford and Bangor. — He entrusts to them the dispute between the bishop and bishop-elect of Bangor. (29 May.) 81

LXXX. — To the king of Castile. — He is to recall his daughter, incestuously joined to the king of León, and obey apostolic commands. (5 June.) 82

LXXXI. — To the archbishop of Narbonne. — He is to relinquish either the abbacy or the archbishopric, since he cannot preside over both. (30 May.) 83

LXXXII. — To the archbishop of Compostela. — He grants him authority to absolve lay judges who, through error, have fined clerics. (6 June.) 84

LXXXIII. — To the same. — Authority to absolve those weak through age or sex, and the infirm, for violently laying hands upon clerics. (3 June.) 85

LXXXIV. — To Peter, archbishop of Compostela. — He upholds the privilege granted by Pope Celestine to the Church of Compostela concerning the prescription of certain vows which Spain had established for Saint James. (5 June.) 86

LXXXV. — Ingeborg, queen of France, to the pope. — She sets forth her most miserable condition and implores the pope’s aid and authority. 86

LXXXVI. — To Philip, illustrious king of France. — He writes to him on behalf of Queen Ingeborg and sends the abbot of Casamari as legate. 88

LXXXVII. — To the provost …, dean, and chapter of Merseburg. — He confirms the election of the archdeacon of Merseburg as bishop. (3 May.) 90

LXXXVIII. — To Saint Paul. — The monastery of Saint Paul of Rome is received under the protection of the Roman Church, and the possessions belonging to it are enumerated. (1 June.) 91

LXXXIX. — To the bishop of Durham; the dean; and the … prior of Holy Trinity, York. — They are to hear witnesses in the case concerning the status of the church of St Davids. (18 June.) 95

XC. — To the bishop of Exeter and the bishop-elect of Burgos. — They are to investigate charges against the bishop of Astorga. (17 June.) 96

XCI. — To the nobleman …, earl of Duncan. — He confirms the agreement prudently made between him and the church of Saint Andrew. (17 June.) 96

XCII. — To the bishop of Girona. — Concerning one who had carnally known both mother and daughter. (19 June.) 97

XCIII. — To the monks of Monreale, who hold the castles of Iati and Calatabiano, and their accomplices. — They are to render worthy satisfaction to their archbishop, whom they had gravely offended. (17 June.) [Col. 1617] 97

XCIV. — To the illustrious king of Castile. — He commends to him the abbot and convent of Trianos. (18 June.) 99

XCV. — To the cantor; the penitentiary; and William Alboini, papal subdeacon and canon, of Limoges. — They are to cause A. Taines, subdeacon, to be received by the provost and chapter of Saint Junian as a canon and brother, according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate previously issued on this subject. (18 June.) 99

XCVI. — To the bishop of Ely, the abbot of Thorney, and the dean of Lincoln. — Clerks presented to their churches by the prior and canons of Hickerham are to be admitted by the archbishop of York. (21 June.) 100

XCVII. — To the archbishop of Bourges and the bishop of Cahors. — They are to correct the chaplains and burgesses of the castle of Limoges. (8 June.) 101

XCVIII. — To the bishop and William Alboini, canon of Limoges. — He entrusts to them the examination of the case of the clerk Assalit, who was troubling the dean and chapter of Saint Aredius. (20 June.) 102

XCIX. — Letters of the Crusaders to the pope. — Concerning absolution for the affair of Zara. 103

C. — Letter of the marquis of Montferrat. — He excuses the suppression of the pope’s letters. 105

CI. — To the marquis of Montferrat, B., count of Flanders, L., count of Blois, and H., count of Saint-Pol. — They are to cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land. (Year VI.) 106

CII. — To the Crusaders. — Counsel which the pope sends to them without a bull. 107

CIII. — To the bishop of Norwich. — He may deprive married clerics of benefices. (20 June.) 110

CIV. — To the plebanus and brethren of the parish church of Calcinaria. — He adjudicates the dispute between them and the chaplain of Monteculo concerning their churches. (20 June.) 110

CV. — To S. Roman. Carzoli, our kinsman, rector of the apostolic patrimony in Tuscany. — He entrusts to him the government of the fortification and castle of Montefiascone. (30 June.) 112

CVI. — To the … archdeacon, … provost, and chapter of Piacenza. — Concerning the interpretation of clerics’ oath. (2 July.) 112

CVII. — To Guido, rector, and the brethren of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit of Maguelone. — He confirms certain privileges. (1 July.) 113

CVIII. — To the archbishop of Tarragona. — He adjudicates a matrimonial case. (20 June.) 113

CIX. — To the bishop of Coimbra. — He settles the dispute between him and the convent of Holy Cross. (26 June.) 114

CX. — To Gualandus, our subdeacon, and B. Vitalis, canons of Pisa. — He settles a private dispute over certain lands. (3 July.) 124

CXI. — To J., prior, and the clerics of Saint Gregory of Spoleto. — He adjudicates the dispute between them and the brethren of a certain hospital. (8 July.) 125

CXII. — To the prior of Saint Fridianus, and C. and C., canons of Lucca. — He adjudicates the case concerning the election of the prior of the church of Saint Peter of Lucca. (8 July.) 127

CXIII. — To the archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans. — Against the murderers of the bishop of Würzburg, and concerning their punishment. (3 July.) 128

CXIV. — To O., provost of Würzburg; the nobleman G., burgrave; and their kinsmen. — On the same matter. (8 July.) 130

CXV. — To the prior and convent of Bomin. — He receives them under protection and confirms their possessions. (8 July.) 132

CXVI. — To the bishops of Palencia and … Zamora, and P. Suevus, archdeacon of Astorga. — They are to investigate the master of the schools of the church of Astorga, who is suspected of falsification. (11 July.) 133

CXVII. — To Vitellus, our subdeacon, castellan of Lariano. — They are to investigate the appointment of two canons in the church of Saint Mary of Nemi. 134

CXVIII. — To I., minister of the house of Holy Trinity of Cervi-Frigidi, and his brethren. — He receives them into the protection of Saint Peter. 134

CXIX. — To the bishop of Marsi. — He entrusts to him the adjudication of a matrimonial case. (14 July.) 134

CXX. — To R., cantor; R., prior of Monte-Leprosorum; and J. de Sagy, canon, of Rouen. — He revokes letters fraudulently obtained from R., priest of Colleville. (12 July.) 136

CXXI. — To the chapter of Novara. — He dissolves certain agreements contrary to the canons. (21 July.) 136

CXXII. — Concerning the bishop-elect of Lucca. — He summons him to the Apostolic See to receive the degree of priesthood and the benefit of consecration. (23 July.) 137

[Col. 1618]

CXXIII. — To the … abbot of Saint Boscian; … of Cerreto, in the diocese of Lodi; and the … priors of Saint Gabriel of Cremona. — They are to investigate the election of the abbot of Saint Peter of the Po. 139

CXXIV. — To the nobleman J., count of Tricarico. — He is to preserve, for disposition by the Roman Church, the land which he recovered from the hands of German enemies. 139

CXXV. — To Master Gualfredus, clerk of Saint Maurice of Tardubiato. — He receives him under protection. (12 July.) 140

CXXVI. — To the abbot and convent of Villamagna. — No one is to be forced upon their monastery against their will. (6 August.) 140

CXXVII. — To the same. — He confirms to them temporal jurisdiction in Villamagna. (6 August.) 140

CXXVIII. — To the … abbot of Subiaco. — Concerning the provision of the church of Scanzano. (12 August.) 140

CXXIX. — To S., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, legate of the Apostolic See. — He exhorts him to undertake the patriarchate of Jerusalem, which he had declined because of his integrity. (16 August.) 141

CXXX. — To S., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. — He exhorts him patiently to endure the labours to be borne for the Holy Land. (10 August.) 145

CXXXI. — To the bishop-elect of Tyre. — He rebukes him because, scarcely elected to the archiepiscopal see, he had not avoided the vice of disobedience and presumption. (12 August.) 147

CXXXII. — To the king of Jerusalem and Cyprus. — He commends to him the Church of Tyre. (12 August.) 148

CXXXIII. — To S., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and P., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, legates of the Apostolic See. — The rights of the Church of Tyre are to be upheld. (7 August.) 149

CXXXIV. — To C., bishop elected archbishop of Tyre. — He confirms tithes to him and to the Church of Tyre. (16 August.) 149

CXXXV. — To the abbess and nuns of Saint Mary Major of Jerusalem. — Confirmation of possessions and of a certain chapel. (14 August.) 150

CXXXVI. — To the rector of the Hospital of Rochelles. — He receives him under protection, with a rent of one gold obol. (25 August.) 150

CXXXVII. — To the archbishop and chapter of Cosenza. — They are to assign to the abbot and convent of Fiore the place called Botrano, in exchange for their monastery. (1 September.) 150

CXXXVIII. — To the abbot and convent of Fiore. — He confirms their possessions. (1 September.) 151

CXXXIX. — To the archbishop of Acerenza. — Concerning confirmation of the bishop of Anglona, although his father had been in minor orders. (5 September.) 152

CXL. — Letter of John of Casamari to Lord Pope D. — He gives an account of his legation into the kingdom of Bosnia, informs him of the donation of Sibyl, wife of Praetextatus of Constantinople, and proposes that he create and organize new bishoprics. 153

CXLI. — Instrument by which Bosnian schismatic monks promise to observe the constitutions of the Roman Church. (30 April.) 153

CXLII. — Letter of Kaloyan, emperor of the Bulgarians, to the pope. — He submits himself to the Roman Church. 155

CXLIII. — To B., archbishop of Zagora. — He replies to the preceding letter. (10 September.) 156

CXLIV. — To Kaloyan, lord of the Bulgarians. — On the same matter. 158

CXLV. — To the judge of Cagliari. — Concerning the marriage of the daughter of the late judge of Gallura. (15 September.) 158

CXLVI. — To the nobleman, judge of Torres. — On the same matter. 158

CXLVII. — To the nobleman, judge of Cagliari. — Concerning the oath to be rendered. (15 September.) 159

CXLVIII. — To B., archbishop of Torres. — That he may proceed against the debtors of his church. (15 September.) 160

CXLIX. — To the count of Auxerre, the spirit of sounder counsel. — A threatening letter requiring him to recall the bishop of Auxerre, whom he had ordered into exile. 160

CL. — To the king of France. — He is to induce the count of Auxerre to recall the bishop of Auxerre, whom this count had caused to be exiled. 162

CLI. — To the archbishop of Sens. — He sharply rebukes him because he had not proceeded against the count of Auxerre, who had expelled the bishop. He commands proceedings to be taken. 165

CLII. — To the bishop of Auxerre. — A consolatory and Catholic letter. 166

CLIII. — To the … abbot of Saint Peter of the Po; the … prior of Saint Gabriel; and the … provost of Saint Lucy of Cremona. — They may accept the resignation of A., abbot of Saint Thomas of Cremona. (21 October.) 168

CLIV. — To the … archbishop of Salzburg. — Concerning the penance to be imposed upon one who had carnally known his wife’s sister. (9 October.) [Col. 1619] 168

CLV. — To the king of Hungary. — He exhorts him to assist Duke Andrew, his brother, in fulfilling his crusading vow. (1 November.) 169

CLVI. — To the nobleman Duke A. — He confirms the agreement made between him and his brother the king. (1 November.) 170

CLVII. — To the same. — He admits him into his clientship. (1 November.) 170

CLVIII. — To the chapter of Augsburg. — He grants them H., *vicedominus* of the Church of Regensburg, as bishop. (31 October.) 171

CLIX. — To P., bishop, elected archbishop of Palermo, royal familiar. — He highly commends him because amid the tumults of the world and kingdom, then also raging, he had kept faith with pope and king. 172

CLX. — To the abbots of Neuburg and Salem. — They are to deter the duke of Swabia from supporting Leopold, intruded into the see of Mainz. (27 October.) 174

CLXI. — To the … dean and chapter of Lismore. — They are to receive M., abbot of Saint Benedict, elected bishop by them. (1 November.) 175

CLXII. — To the … archbishop of Armagh, and the … bishops of Dromore and Ferns. — They are to pronounce sentence of anathema against the bishop of Waterford. (1 November.) 176

CLXIII. — To the king of France. — A reply because the king had said that, under feudal law, he was not bound to obey apostolic commands; and much else concerning peace with the king of England. (31 October.) 176

CLXIV. — To the archbishop of Sens. — He is to publish the sentence of excommunication against those who take up arms against the king of England, including against the king of France. (31 October.) 181

CLXV. — To the abbot of Casamari. — He is to intervene for peace or a truce between the kings; if he cannot accomplish this, he is to excommunicate. (31 October.) 181

CLXVI. — To the archbishop of Bourges and the abbot of Casamari. — They are to investigate the kings’ complaint. (31 October.) 182

CLXVII. — To J., king of England. — The reason for the war begun against him by the king of France is set out, and the pope rebukes him because he ought to appear before that king, since he is his liege man. (31 October.) 182

CLXVIII. — To the abbots of Saint Victor and Saint Geneviève. — He restores to favour the crusader Count Augi, who had cast aside the cross in order not to go to the Holy Land. (12 November.) 184

CLXIX. — To the … archdeacon, … archpriest, and entire chapter of the Church of Gargano. — He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter. (15 November.) 185

CLXX. — To the … bishop of Fano. — Concerning his disobedience: he is to desist from troubling the prior of Saint Stephen of Fano. (13 November.) 185

CLXXI. — To the chapter of Genoa. — He approves the transfer of the bishop of Bobbio to the archbishopric of Genoa; dispenses him from the law requiring attendance at the Apostolic See; and sends the pallium. (18 November.) 188

CLXXII. — To the abbot and convent of Caraceto. — He confirms the union made between that order and the Cistercian Order. 189

CLXXIII. — To the same. — He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter, and their possessions are enumerated. 189

CLXXIV. — To the bishop of Chalon, the abbot of Cluny, and the prior of Scillo of the Carthusian Order. — They are commanded to visit the Church and territory of Mâcon, filled with enormous vices. (22 November.) 189

CLXXV. — To the provost of Saint Stephen of Brolio. — He entrusts to him the case between Al. de Daverio and G., a priest of Milan, concerning certain benefices. (25 November.) 190

CLXXVI. — To the … bishop and Master Albert de Boges, canon, of Maurienne, and the … prior of Acquabella in the diocese of Maurienne. — A prebend is to be granted by the chapter of Augsburg to P., subdeacon. (25 November.) 191

CLXXVII. — To the … prior of Boeltum and J., rector of the church of Goillis. — Concerning witnesses to be admitted in a matrimonial case. (24 November.) 192

CLXXVIII. — To Master Peter Munio, dean of León. — He receives him under protection. (20 November.) 193

CLXXIX. — To Master Peter Munio, archdeacon of Compostela. — He receives him under protection. (1 December.) 193

CLXXX. — To Celestine, abbot of Saint Columba of Hay Island, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in perpetuity. — He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter, and their possessions are enumerated. (9 December.) [Col. 1620] 193

CLXXXI. — To the king of the Danes. — Concerning the release of Valdemar, bishop of Schleswig. (5 December.) 194

CLXXXII. — To Philip, illustrious king of France. — A pitiable letter concerning his abandoned wife. (9 December.) 198
